title: ‘Freedom to succeed is also  freedom to fail’: In new epic poem Joseph Bottum explores the  facets of freedom, through a South Dakota lens
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Jeanne Bowman, who worked on children’s books like “Georgia Jipp: Blizzard Pilot” and “Bob Marshall: Defender of the Wilderness”has also  illustrated Joseph Bottum’s  4-part epic poem “This Far Country,” pictured. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
IMG_8742.JPG
Jeanne Bowman, who worked on children’s books like “Georgia Jipp: Blizzard Pilot” and “Bob Marshall: Defender of the Wilderness”has also  illustrated Joseph Bottum’s  4-part epic poem “This Far Country,” pictured. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

 IMG_8752.JPG
Rivers serve as both winding metaphors and characters in Joseph Bottum’s “This Far Country: South Dakota Lines on the 250th Anniversary of the Declaration of Independence.” Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — Joseph Bottum’s “This Far Country” started out as a complicated, even discombobulated project. It turned into a successful rumination on the unpredictable nature of freedom itself, and an exploration of the prairie’s place in the great American Experiment. 

The book has been selected for inclusion in the official US time capsule, which will be buried on July 4 in Philadelphia, Pa.

Bottum is a widely published author and public intellectual, with thousands of essays, reviews, poems, and short stories to his name. In “National Review,” Bottum has been called a “poetic voice” credited with “shaping the minds of a generation.” 

He lives in Montana, but has deep roots in South Dakota.

He was born in Vermillion to parents from South Dakota, whose parents — on both sides — put down stakes in the state.

“I have this relation to the state that is down in the blood,” Bottum said. “That is one of the lines in the last poem. You claim a place, grave by grave. You bury enough of your people in the land … this is how we civilize the land.”

That history made Bottum a natural fit for a semi-sesquicentennial project, commissioned by the state historian. The resulting book, “This Far Country,” comes with the subtitle “South Dakota Lines on the 250th Anniversary of the Declaration of Independence.” The subtitle is a nod to the historian’s tall order.  

“It was a fairly uncongenial project. There was just a lot that the commissioners wanted that was increasingly difficult. I felt at times like the architect who was commissioned to design a modernist house, and then the client says, ‘By the way, I’d like you to add ancient Greek columns to it,’” Bottum said. “There has just been too much jammed into this idea.”

Bottum said the epic poem, or series of poems, he was asked to write was supposed to offer both an appropriate celebration of the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, and a reflection of the South Dakota experience. His 4-part piece ultimately achieves that goal. 

In approaching the project, Bottum first dove into the stories of some of the state’s most colorful characters.

“South Dakota is the only state in the union whose state treasurer once walked off with the whole state treasury. It’s just a great story,” Bottum said.

But, in the end, those stories didn’t quite capture the spirit of the Declaration of Independence. Bottum then pivoted and focused on 4 symbols of both freedom and the prairie experience: rivers, meadowlarks, chokecherry jelly, and homesteads (“those gray wood buildings you see as you drive by. There’s never enough water, so they don’t rot, they just kind of crumble to dust.”).

“I’ve seen the fireworks. I’ve seen the searchlights splashing into the sky on the Fourth of July at Mount Rushmore,” Bottum said. “I’ve seen the cities with their little displays, but when I think of freedom, I think of the Meadowlark.”

Alongside the meadowlark, chokecherry jelly acts as a kind of hopeful metaphor. It’s a great image to evoke the thrift of early pioneers — putting away what the prairie had to offer to be savored down the road.

Not all of the 4 images are so hopeful. In his visit to a graying homestead, Bottum digs into the complicated nature of freedom.

“The most complex of these poems is the third one, which is looking at this abandoned homestead. It is looking at a brutal truth,” Bottum said. “You have to accept that the cost of freedom is freedom to fail. Freedom to be bad. Freedom to lose your soul. You can’t compel goodness if you have freedom.”

In Bottum’s framing, freedom to explore is part and parcel to South Dakota’s territorial origin story.

“In order to have a government that doesn’t sit on us, in order to have a society that doesn’t sit on us for our individuality, we have to accept that there are people who are going to use that individuality to do something that you or I would rather not see anybody do. That is the price we pay for freedom,” Bottum said.

There is something almost agoraphobic in Bottum’s characterization of freedom. With the yawning space the prairie provides, there is plenty of room to make mistakes.

“There was this sense of the prairie, in the third section, I describe it as us being in the gaps where nothing is left. We are not this positive presence; we are the negativity, the gap, in the prairie,” Bottum said.

Rivers run through the book, as a fourth metaphor for freedom. Rivers are unpredictable things, and Bottum describes America as “spilling” onto the prairie — as if the ideas, the principles of the burgeoning nation, burst forth from a failing dam.

“I don’t want to dictate how the poem is read. That is a fallacy. The author has no more privileged position than the reader, but there is that sense of an accident. They couldn’t have predicted what would have flown out. I could have said flow,” Bottum said. “I picked spill because I was thinking, the water goes where it will. … I imagine all of the thoughts of humankind piling up behind this dam. When the dam breaks, you don’t have an orderly flow; you have a spill.”

He describes the framers, the men who penned America’s founding documents, as “ceaseless” in their bookishness.

“Their ceaseless bookishness was not just scholarly interest. It was an existential need to find a way to free themselves from the oppressions of Great Britain,” Bottum said. “The episcopal bishop of Virginia has said, ‘It is almost as if God, in his providence, set a veil across the Atlantic so that the European powers would not discover the new world until they were ready to try this experiment.’ For some reason, they didn’t cross the Atlantic until there was this possibility of trying something new in the history of the world.”

Bottum said that South Dakota’s story is just one note in the nation’s history. That note is struck, and sings out in “This Far Country.”

“There is a note sounded there which fits in the chord of notes sounded by the Declaration. If it were the only note that would be something else, something dubious and questionable. The note of life in the west is not in dissonance. It is in concert with that great moment. There is this mystic chord that you and I can feel as South Dakotans,” Bottum said. “To be one note that sounds with the others, the founders thought of the revolution, of the great, strange, dangerous bet. They rolled the dice to see what would come of it.”

title: Deadwood purchases parcel of land, protects viewshed and historic landmark status
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: More than 21 acres of land above the Rodeo District, butting up against city-owned property near Mount Moriah, was purchased from a Florida-based investment group Monday by the city of Deadwood with the intention of protecting their historic landmark status and viewshed. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
1 Deadwood purchases land.jpg
More than 21 acres of land above the Rodeo District, butting up against city-owned property near Mount Moriah, was purchased from a Florida-based investment group Monday by the city of Deadwood with the intention of protecting their historic landmark status and viewshed. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

 2 Deadwood purchases land.jpg
Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

DEADWOOD — Continuing more than 2 decades of work to protect the city’s viewshed and historic landmark status, Deadwood city commissioners approved the purchase of 21.55 acres of land above the Rodeo District at their Monday meeting. 

The parcel of land, located adjacent to the newly created White Rocks Trail area, butting up against city-owned land near Mount Moriah and rising above the Rodeo District, was purchased from Rocky Waters 3 LP, an investment group in Florida. 

“It was purchased some time ago (by the investment firm) for development purposes and it came on the market,” said Kevin Kuchenbecker, director of planning and zoning and historic preservation. “Instead of having the hillside scarred and altering the viewshed and site and setting of the landmark district, we are acquiring that.”

Kuchenbecker said the acquisition gives the city the opportunity to continue developing new trails and outdoor recreation purposes. While the city has no current plans to develop trails in the area, the acquisition was accompanied by a $10,000 donation to build new or enhance existing trails. 

Kuchenbecker said the purchase of land to prohibit development in the area was a conscious move by the city, who wants to encourage more affordable developments for family and workforce in the area. 

“To develop those hillsides, the cost of site preparation and acquiring the land truly prohibits that affordable home building,” he said. “What would happen if (the city had not) acquired and protected the land, it could then be purchased by a developer with deep pockets, who could put a road up the hillside and then build a multi-million-dollar house overlooking the beautiful historic district.”

Over the last 20-plus years, Kuchenbecker said the city has made multiple purposes with the same intentions, including parcels of land around the presidential district and parts of the Fuller Brothers property above upper Main Street. 

“It’s what defines Deadwood,” he said. “Historically, we’re a town that’s built in the gulch with the natural hillsides and ponderosa pines being an important element of what people expect when they come here and what is historically accurate to the area.”

The 21.55 acres of land were purchased for the approved price of $350,000. The land will be purchased with the city’s reserve funds. A budget supplement to finalize the purchase is expected at the April 20 meeting.

title: Lead candidates agree on infrastructure priorities, differ on Handley Center funding
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: The 4 candidates for Lead City Commission addressed questions about major issues in the community, during a candidate forum on Tuesday. Pioneer photo composite by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
LeadCandidatesComp.psd
The 4 candidates for Lead City Commission addressed questions about major issues in the community, during a candidate forum on Tuesday. Pioneer photo composite by Wendy Pitlick 

LEAD — All 4 candidates for Lead City Commission support prioritizing city infrastructure, and only one candidate supports continuing funding for the Handley Recreation Center, according to answers given to some hot-button topics covered at a candidate forum Tuesday. 

 candidate forum 2.jpeg
Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

 Lead candidate forum.jpeg
Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

The Lead Area Chamber of Commerce organized the forum that was held at the Historic Homestake Opera House. Moderated by chamber president Levi Wilson, the event drew a large crowd of Lead citizens who listened to how commission candidates Dustin Schumacher, Valerie Meiners, Al Rohrer, and Jeremiah Fredericksen would handle key issues in the city. The 4 candidates are running for 2 seats, with 3-year terms each on the Lead City Commission. 

Schumacher started the forum off by introducing himself as a third and fourth-generation Lead resident, who has worked in public service his whole life. Schumacher has served for 22 years in law enforcement. 

“My sense of service is what drives me,” he said. “Lead is my hometown. It’s my family’s hometown for generations. I love it. I want to make informed, common sense decisions for the great people who live in my hometown.” 

Rohrer, the only incumbent on the ballot, cited the importance of experience in governing on the commission. Rohrer was appointed to his city commission seat in May when Mayor Dustin Heupel won the mayoral election and vacated his commission seat. 

“We have a very young commission,” Rohrer said. “Experience is no longer an option. It is now a necessity. Lead needs leadership that knows how to navigate the process and move projects forward, without spinning its wheels.”

Meiners said she is running for city commission so she can serve the citizens of the town she chooses to call home. Originally from Butte, Mont., Meiners said she has lived in Lead for 34 years, and she wants to work hard to make it as good as possible. 

Fredericksen, who is a fifth generation Lead resident, left for 17 years to join the Army and returned in 2010. He served with the Lead Police Department for 11 years, and he currently works at the Sanford Underground Research Facility. He said he plans to use his leadership experience from leading soldiers in combat, as well as his public service experience working for the city, to serve the citizens. 

All of the candidates said their top priorities for the city are fixing infrastructure such as streets, sewer and water lines. A city shop is also a necessity, they all said. Rohrer said the city has about $50 million in backlogged infrastructure issues it needs to address, and addressing those problems will take a multi-pronged approach that involves promoting business development to raise more sales taxes and expanding the city to grow a property tax base. The good news, he said, is that the city’s facility plan will be completed in May, and that’s the first step toward the city applying for grants and financing to pay for infrastructure. 

In addition to infrastructure, Meiners and Rohrer said they both want to focus on economic development, and promoting business in town in order to grow the city’s sales tax base. Specifically, Meiners said she wants to use available resources to encourage child care businesses, ancillary support services for the Sanford Lab, senior assisted living, and any businesses that will encourage shopping in Lead. 

“All of the goals in the comprehensive plan are dependent upon available funding, so the logical order of importance is to involve ways to increase revenue while supporting business in Lead,” she said. 

Rohrer said he wants to focus on revitalizing Main Street. Additionally, he said the city needs to focus on expanding to the southwest, to grow its property tax base. 

Related to economic development, Schumacher said he wants to encourage more development and new projects by promoting tax incentives for businesses and homes. He also wants to encourage building repair and renovations when possible, or replacing homes that aren’t repairable. 

Fredericksen said financial responsibility within the city’s ranks will be his number one priority. Additionally, he said the city needs to start saving for a city shop, and he wants to see more public transportation between Lead and Deadwood. 

Funding for the Handley Recreation Center was an issue commissioners were asked about, with three of the candidates reporting they do not support continued funding.

Meiners said she and several other citizens submitted 10 questions to the city, related to the city’s takeover of the Handley Center, and the condition of the recreation building. To date, she said, they have not received any response to those questions. She said citizens deserve to know the full condition of the building before the city takes it over, just like any purchaser would for a property acquisition deal. 

“I think just with that alone, we would be not so smart to move forward,” she said. “Anybody that buys a house gets full disclosure. It shouldn’t be any different when you’re going to invest our money into a business.” 

Fredericksen reminded the crowd of when citizens voted to defund the Handley Center in 2013. That election was close, with a 273-269 vote to suspend funding. Fredericksen also said the nonprofit board has not applied for federal grants. Therefore, he does not support continuing funding for the building. 

Rohrer, who has been involved with discussions about the city taking over the Handley Center, said there is a stalemate related to deed restrictions on the building. 

“There’s no deal to be had,” he said. “The city won’t agree to deed restrictions and the Handley board will not give it without them. Hope isn’t a fiscal strategy. Furthermore we have been giving them $125,000 a year and that’s barely enough for them to keep the lights on, let alone address any of the deferred maintenance to the tune of a half million dollars or more. I will not vote to grant another dime to the Handley Center because I’m not interested in subsidizing a decline.” 

Instead, Rohrer said he wants to put the $70,000 the city set aside to take over the Handley, “under your tires,” and use it to fix Lead’s streets. 

Schumacher, who uses the Handley Center regularly, said he doesn’t necessarily support the city taking over the building. However, he wants the city to continue funding it at least through this fiscal year, while city officials work with the Handley board to find solutions to the problem of funding recreation and fixing the building. 

“The comprehensive plan talked a lot about recreation,” he said. “They pointed out a lot of outdoor recreation opportunities. But Lead is dark and cold for a good portion of the year, and indoor recreation is just as important as outdoor recreation. The Handley Center is not just a gym. It’s children’s programs. It’s skate night. It’s Lead Live. It’s the Mile High Basketball Tournament. It’s part of our community. It benefits our children who are the future of our city. It benefits people like me who want to stay active. I regularly see elderly folks in there with their personal trainer, staying active and healthy later in life.” 

While Schumacher said he supports fiscal responsibility, there are some nonprofit organizations that should receive support from the city, because they make up the fabric of the Lead community. Some of those organizations, he said, include the Handley Center, the Lord’s Cupboard Food Pantry, and the Historic Homestake Opera House. 

“If those organizations aren’t assisted, we lose them,” he said. “With every organization we lose … we lose a little bit of our sense of community. Once a community program is gone, you will never get it back and subsequently, our community dies a little bit at a time.” 

However, Fredericksen said when it comes to funding nonprofit organizations, citizens should do that on a private basis. 

“The city needs to meet its needs before its wants,” he said. If citizens want to support organizations through time and money, they will.” 

Rohrer said he wants to see more accountability among organizations that receive city funding. He wants to consider funding on a case-by-case basis, and see what the taxpayers’ return on investment is. 

Meiners said she agrees with funding community organizations that help bridge a gap and provide services in the community, but they need to be held accountable with how they spend the funds. Additionally, she opposes funding organizations outside of Lead. 

“We have plenty to do here,” she said. 

Other questions at the forum related to candidates’ support for city employees, and whether they would reduce staffing levels. None of the candidates support reducing city staff, but Rohrer said the city already eliminated the city planner position when Robin Lucero was appointed as the Lead City Administrator. That saved the city $70,000, he said. 

Additionally, candidates agreed that the city offers a fair wage and benefits package for employees, when they were asked about whether employees should pay more for their health insurance. 

“Employees and citizens need to look at the overall compensation package,” Fredericksen said. “With the raises they’ve gotten these last 3 years, I do believe all of our employees are very well compensated with the overall package.” 

Schumacher agreed, saying public servants should have the benefits. 

“There should be benefits to committing your life to public service, he said. “None of these employees are getting paid $200,000 a year. We’re paying them a fair wage and we should be fair with their insurance.” 

Rohrer and Meiners both said the city employees’ benefit package could help with recruitment and retention. 

The Lead City Commission election will be held with the primary elections, on June 2. Early voting will start April 17, and registered voters can cast their ballots at the Lawrence County Auditor’s Office. The voter registration deadline is May 18.

title: Lead police chief  recommends policy changes  for employee retention
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Lead Police Chief Robert Williams recommended changes in the city’s residency and vacation policy to try and recruit and retain more employees. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
0409 Lead police(RGB).jpg
Lead Police Chief Robert Williams recommended changes in the city’s residency and vacation policy to try and recruit and retain more employees. Pioneer file photo 

 0409 Lead police Secret Santa(RGB).jpg
Pioneer file photo 

LEAD — Adjusting the city residency policy and changing the way employees qualify for vacation time could be changes the city can make to attract more staff, Lead Police Chief Robert Williams told the city commission Monday. 

On Feb. 16, a police needs committee, established by Mayor Dustin Heupel to discuss ways the city can recruit more police officer candidates, presented the city commission with a list of recommendations. Recommendations were varied, and included utilizing current civilian staff for non-criminal ordinance enforcement for the building inspection department, working with officer sharing programs with Deadwood, Lawrence County, and the South Dakota Highway Patrol, identifying multiple community events for the police to participate in and encouraging officers to engage with the community while in uniform, and developing a communication plan that includes social media and newsletters. 

After reviewing those recommendations, Williams told the commission there are only a few that the city doesn’t already do. Those two included adjusting its residency policy, and adjusting vacation time for new employees. Additionally, Williams recommended that the city’s policies be adjusted to include new recruits for all departments, not just the police department. 

The current residency policy requires city department heads to live within city limits, and employees to live within the Lead-Deadwood School District, which includes Rochford and Nemo, and in some places can extend to the Wyoming border. The committee recommended changing that policy to require department heads to live within city limits, but allow city employees to live within a 16-mile radius of city hall. That allows employees to live in parts of Spearfish, Whitewood, Sturgis, and the surrounding area. 

Valerie Meiners, who served on the police needs committee, said the committee considered the lack of adequate housing in the Lead-Deadwood area with its residency policy recommendation. Additionally, under the current policy she said employees could live up to 45 minutes outside of town, making it difficult for them to get to work during severe weather events. 

Former Lead police officer Jeremiah Fredericksen urged the city commission to allow police officers to live outside of the city limits, for the safety of their families. Many officers, he said, prefer to live outside of the communities they serve in order to avoid disgruntled citizens approaching them during their off times.

The second recommended incentive from the committee was modifying the vacation policy, to allow employees to have 40 hours of vacation time available on the first day of their employment. However, Williams said allowing employees to have vacation time before they complete a probationary period doesn’t work for the police department. 

Currently, the city’s paid vacation policy gives employees who have worked for one to 6 years 80 hours of vacation; employees with 7-12 years get 120 hours; those who have worked for 13-20 years get 160 hours; and employees who work for more than 20 years get 160 hours, plus one week of pay. 

Williams suggested changing that to allow employees who have been with the city for 1-4 years to receive 80 hours, and those who are employed for 5 years to receive the third week of vacation. Those who work for 10 years would get 4 weeks of vacation. Then on the 15th year, employees would receive 160 hours and one week of pay, and those who are with the city for more than 20 years would receive 160 hours of vacation with 2 weeks of pay. 

“Just because times have changed and it’s harder to hold employees longer, we would just cut that down a little bit so if you have 4 years and you have one more year until you get 3 weeks of vacation, you’re less apt to go apply for that job or you’re gonna start your vacation all over again,” Williams said. 

While some commissioners questioned whether it would also be possible to offer officers comp time instead of paying overtime, Williams said that doesn’t always work for a small department. 

“If we’re paying somebody out to take off time and a half, then on a smaller department I then have to pay somebody else to come in and work overtime and pay them time and a half,” he said. “If we’re full staff, it’s not that big of a deal because we have 2 on duty at one time and one guy can take over. But like right now in the last couple of years if we’re not fully staffed, one guy gets comp time, well, he gets paid time and a half in comp time and then I gotta pay somebody else overtime to come in and fill that spot.” 

The city commission did not take action on Williams’ recommendations for policy changes.

title: Gov. candidates clash over inmate rehabilitation as state builds new prisons
byline: By John Hult and Seth Tupper Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, left, and Gov. Larry Rhoden are two of the candidates for the Republican nomination for governor of South Dakota. They traded criticism recently over each other’s approach to preventing repeat crime. Photos by South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Gov. candidates clash over inmate rehabilitation as state builds new prisons
U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, left, and Gov. Larry Rhoden are two of the candidates for the Republican nomination for governor of South Dakota. They traded criticism recently over each other’s approach to preventing repeat crime. Photos by South Dakota Searchlight 

PIERRE — Two Republican candidates for governor of South Dakota spotlighted dueling plans Tuesday to prevent repeat crime.

As Gov. Larry Rhoden announced new efforts by his prison rehabilitation task force, U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson pledged to create his own task force while slamming the lack of progress on the issue during the recently concluded legislative session as “unacceptable.”

Their concern about recidivism is rooted partly in recent decisions by Rhoden, his predecessor Kristi Noem and the Legislature to build an $87 million women’s prison in Rapid City and a $650 million men’s prison in Sioux Falls.

As part of Rhoden’s efforts last year to win lawmaker support for the men’s prison, he created a Correctional Rehabilitation Task Force with a goal of rehabilitating inmates and preventing them from reoffending. Rhoden said at the time that “the next task” after deciding to build a prison “is to expand our rehabilitative programming.”

The task force continues to meet, but has yet to offer legislative proposals. Lawmakers rejected a bill last month that would have awarded $2.7 million to the state Department of Corrections to expand an existing rehabilitation program within the prison system, with some opponents arguing that the task force should finish its work and offer recommendations first. Lawmakers also said no to a bill that would have put $50,000 toward the study of juvenile corrections in other states. 

Rhoden’s office did support, and eventually sign, a bill that requires the Department of Corrections to make sure inmates are released with “suitable” clothing, and to transport them upon release to their home county, the county from which they were sentenced, or to a different location as close to their release site as the closer of the other two options.

Johnson criticized the lack of major legislative action during a roundtable discussion he organized Tuesday in Rapid City with officials from law enforcement, addiction counseling and other related fields.

“I just can’t believe that after we told everyone that we would have big new rehabilitation and treatment within the walls of the prison — that was a part of the deal of how we got the new prison — that the governor and some members of the Legislature walked away from it,” Johnson said.

Rhoden lobbed his own criticism Tuesday on the X social media platform, posting that “plans are fine, but when it comes to public safety, I have delivered RESULTS.”

Rhoden rolls out task force news

The rest of Tuesday’s news from Rhoden came through the state Department of Corrections, which announced a $160,000 contract extension that will allow the Council of State Governments Justice Center to continue providing consultation services to the Correctional Rehabilitation Task Force. The contract runs through March 31, 2027.

The council will perform a “comprehensive evaluation” of correctional programming and reentry, recommend changes, and will “help translate those recommendations into action,” according to a press release from the department. The consultant pulled together preliminary findings and presented them to the task force in December.

The department is also engaged in what Tuesday’s news release described as “an evaluation of parole” called the “Smarter Supervision Initiative.” That effort aims to help the state supervise parolees more effectively “and reduce violent reoffending across the state.”

Rhoden and Lt. Gov Tony Venhuizen, the rehabilitation task force’s leader, each wrote letters in support of an application for an $892,000 grant from the Bureau of Justice, which was submitted at the end of March. If awarded, the grant money would fund a three-year plan to address what Rhoden’s letter acknowledged to be a reoffense rate that’s higher than South Dakota’s neighbors.

Half of exiting inmates reoffend within three years, Rhoden wrote, which “tells us that our current approach to community supervision is not producing the outcomes we need.”

The state’s parole initiative, he wrote, represents “exactly the kind of data-driven, results-oriented investment in public safety South Dakotans deserve.”

Johnson offers competing plan, points to purported missteps

Rhoden and Johnson are each seeking the Republican Party’s nomination for governor in the June 2 primary election. The other candidates are Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden and state House Speaker Jon Hansen. On the Democratic side, one candidate has been certified for the ballot so far: Dan Ahlers, the executive director of the state Democratic Party and a former legislator.

Rhoden took over as governor following the resignation of Noem, who left in January 2025 for a Trump administration Cabinet post. 

Johnson is running for governor rather than seeking another term in the U.S. House. He released a “Safer South Dakota” plan Tuesday.

If elected, Johnson would convene a “Supervision and Release Task Force,” the congressman said, to be led by Minnehaha County State’s Attorney Daniel Haggar and former Pennington County Sheriff Kevin Thom. The group would explore ways to improve community supervision for parolees and people on probation. 

Haggar is a member of Rhoden’s task force. In Johnson’s public safety press release, Haggar is quoted saying the Johnson plan “is an important first step towards building safer neighborhoods.”

The Johnson group would also include other “representatives from law enforcement, the judicial branch, and the Board of Pardons and Paroles.”

Johnson supports clemency reform

Johnson’s task force would additionally discuss ways to “reform the clemency process” and “help ensure violent criminals are prevented from repeatedly harming the public.”

Under the South Dakota Constitution, only the governor can grant pardons or commutations. A pardon scrubs an old crime from a person’s record; a commutation shortens the sentence for a current inmate. Both forms of clemency typically begin with an application to the state parole board, which reviews it, holds a hearing on the matter and votes to recommend approval or denial for the governor.

Noem bypassed the board and granted commutations to 20 people over the course of two years, but she also signed commutations for people who’d been screened and recommended by the board. 

The two governors who served just prior to Noem’s first term, Dennis Daugaard and now-U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds, did not approve clemency applications without parole board review. Thus far, Rhoden hasn’t, either.

Johnson indicated Tuesday during an interview with South Dakota Searchlight that he was not aware of Noem’s granting of commutations without parole board reviews. But he said presidents of both major political parties have issued “highly problematic” pardons, adding that on the state and federal level, “we need to ask ourselves if we should have more than one person wield this power.”

“I would be supportive of a law that would mandate a role for the Board of Pardons and Paroles before the governor could issue that clemency,” Johnson said.

Drug distribution proposal

Johnson’s plan also proposes a change to state law on drug distribution, making possession of at least 3 grams of fentanyl or methamphetamine enough on its own to trigger what he called a “presumption of distribution.”

Asked how that position squares with concerns about filling up prisons, Johnson said “you can be tough on crime and smart on crime.”

“The reality is we should give no quarter for drug dealers,” he said. “They’re the ones that are killing our children. And through rehabilitation and treatment, we can get users healthy and we can help them live law-abiding lives.”

Under current law, prosecutors must prove a person sold or intended to sell drugs for that person to be convicted of felony drug dealing. People found guilty of dealing 4 or more grams of fentanyl are currently subject to stiffer penalties under state law than they’d be for selling other drugs.

Johnson also promised to push a law change that would require automatic parental notification from schools if a minor has an overdose or “drug-related emergency,” and to post drug overdose statistics “in real time.”

Rhoden: We’ve got results

A new approach to overdoses is necessary, Johnson said, because South Dakota’s rate of overdose deaths hasn’t dropped as quickly as it has in other states. Nationally, the U.S. had a nearly 20% reduction in overdose deaths over the past year, he said, while South Dakota’s overdose rate fell by a little under 12%. 

In response to a South Dakota Searchlight request for comment on Johnson’s plan, Rhoden spokesman Ian Fury pointed to the governor’s post on X.

The post says overdose deaths and “methamphetamine crimes” are down in the state since Rhoden took office, as are burglaries and murders. The new prison is “DONE,” the post says, and “Operation Prairie Thunder” — a branded series of city-by-city saturation patrols by state troopers — has been a “SUCCESS.” Fewer parolees have lost contact with their parole officers, the post says, and Rhoden added a new squad of state troopers to the Sioux Falls area.

Later Tuesday, Hansen said in a statement to South Dakota Searchlight that he stood “shoulder to shoulder” with state Attorney General Marty Jackley and law enforcement as the state “cracked down on crime,” including crimes of government corruption.

If elected, Hansen said, “we will deter crimes before they occur by spreading the message far and wide: there will be zero tolerance for crimes of violence and corruption — and any violations will be met with the strongest possible penalties.”

In a statement, Doeden said South Dakota is “on fire with a drug epidemic,” that drugs are “the driving force” for crime in the state, and that stiffer penalties for dealers and better options for addiction treatment are needed. He said Johnson and Rhoden “have been in political office for decades and have failed to bring forward anything meaningful to improve public safety.”

“It is not lost on the people of South Dakota that they only put forward plans when an election year rolls around,” Doeden said.

title: DOE pauses funding for larger dark matter experiment, encourages extension of LZ
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Markus Horn, senior research scientist at the Sanford Underground Research Facility, told members of the S.D. Science and Technology Authority recently that the U.S. Department of Energy has paused funding for a larger dark matter experiment, and instead is encouraging the LUX-ZEPLIN experiment in SURF to expand their search for dark matter. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
SURF tour Markus HOrn.JPG
Markus Horn, senior research scientist at the Sanford Underground Research Facility, told members of the S.D. Science and Technology Authority recently that the U.S. Department of Energy has paused funding for a larger dark matter experiment, and instead is encouraging the LUX-ZEPLIN experiment in SURF to expand their search for dark matter. Pioneer file photo 

 LZ experiment.jpg
Scientists at the Sanford Underground Research Facility say they are looking for ways to extend the LZ dark matter experiment, after the U.S. Department of Energy paused funding for the next generation experiment and encouraged continuing funding for LZ. Pioneer file photo 

LEAD — The U.S. Department of Energy has paused funding for a next-generation dark matter experiment, but it is encouraging the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment to continue past its planned decommissioning date. 

Markus Horn, senior research scientist with the Sanford Underground Research Facility, told members of the South Dakota Science and Technology Authority that original plans for the LZ dark matter experiment, located at the 4,850-foot level of SURF in the Davis Campus, were to wrap up data collections and begin decommissioning in early 2028. Plans are in the works for a larger, more sensitive experiment, called XLZD, that combines collaborations for 3 different dark matter experiments that use liquid xenon, including LZ. The experiment plans to use 60-80 tons of xenon to boost its sensitivity levels. By comparison, LZ, which has published multiple results that establish it as the most sensitive dark matter detector in the world, operates with 10 tons of liquid xenon. 

According to the XLZD website, a site has not yet been chosen for the next generation experiment, although SURF is one of the labs being considered. Other considerations include Boulby in the United Kingdom, LNGS in Gran Sasso, Italy, and SNOLab in Canada. 

“But the DOE has paused funding for XLZD for the next generation, pushing it out a couple of years,” Horn said. “But in the same breath, (the DOE) strongly encourages LZ to develop scenarios for what they call LZ2028+.” 

Horn said as a result, the collaboration has been working on different ways to extend the experiment, to increase its scientific reach to different types of potential dark matter candidates. Some ideas include “doping” the xenon with lighter elements like hydrogen, freezing and crystallizing the xenon, and improving calibrations to improve sensitivity of the experiment. 

The LZ dark matter detector is one of the major experiments in the Davis Campus section of the 4,850-foot level of SURF. Another major experiment, the MAJORANA neutrinoless double beta decay experiment, will conclude its decommissioning process later this year. However, he said a copper electroforming operation that supported MAJORANA will remain in place. The operation will support LEGEND 1000, another neutrinoless double beta decay experiment that will use 1,000 kilograms of germanium detectors, compared to the 44 kilograms of germanium MAJORANA used. The experiment is planned to set up in Gran Sasso, Italy, but Copper electroforming for the experiment will occur at SURF. SURF will also host research and development, and production capability projects for the experiment.

Clyde Ice memorabilia bound for display in new airport terminal 

SPEARFISH — Monday, the Spearfish City Council formally accepted the donation of a collection of memorabilia from area aviator Clyde Ice, including goggles, hats, books, newspaper clippings, posters, pictures, and aviation materials. Those items, donated by the Howard and Jane Ice Family Trust can now be displayed inside the new airport terminal at Clyde Ice Field. 

— Sierra Ferguson

Trail hub location approved in Spearfish 

SPEARFISH — Partnering with contractor and Magnolia Network star Jared “Cappie” Capp of Pangaea Designs, Spearfish Trails Coalition is planning the construction of a trails hub structure on city-owned property directly south of the city-owned parking lot located at the southeastern corner of Canyon Street and Winterville Drive. On Monday, the non-profit and International Mountain Biking Association (IMBA) affiliate received city council’s approval to use the location, moving the project forward. 

—Sierra Ferguson

City partners with SD Community Foundation to vet prospective grant recipients 

SPEARFISH — The city of Spearfish regularly awards between $70,000 and $100,000 in grants to area non-profits every year after they are vetted by the finance office. Now, the vetting process will be completed by the South Dakota Community Foundation. City council and the city’s grant making committee will still have the final say in grant awards, but the SD Community Foundation, for an annual fee of $500, will be in charge of ensuring each recipients eligibility to receive public money. 

— Sierra Ferguson

title: State providing $6 million to grow national security jobs, governor announces
byline: By Seth Tupper Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden, left, and his economic development commissioner, Bill Even, speak to the media on Wednesday, during the Black Hills Defense & Industry Symposium at The Box event center in Box Elder. Photo by Seth Tupper, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
State providing $6 million to grow national security jobs, governor announces
South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden, left, and his economic development commissioner, Bill Even, speak to the media on Wednesday, during the Black Hills Defense & Industry Symposium at The Box event center in Box Elder. Photo by Seth Tupper, South Dakota Searchlight 

BOX ELDER — South Dakota’s governor took the next step Wednesday in his effort to make national security the state’s “next big industry” by announcing the creation of the South Dakota Defense Institute.

Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden, who formerly served in the National Guard, identified national security as a primary economic development focus in his State of the State address three months ago. He made Wednesday’s announcement at the Black Hills Defense & Industry Symposium.

“The federal government is looking for partners who can deliver,” Rhoden said. “South Dakota is that partner.”

Rhoden will provide $6 million in grants from the governor-controlled Future Fund for economic development to launch the institute. The state gets money for the fund by charging a fee to employers. They pay the fee when they submit payroll taxes that support unemployment benefits.

Most of the grant money, $5 million, will go toward the establishment and operation of the institute for its first five years, including the hiring of three employees. The state will give $1 million to Elevate Rapid City, a local economic development group, to purchase a building in the city for the institute.

It’s unclear what type of entity the institute will be. Bill Even, the governor’s commissioner of economic development, said the institute’s employees won’t work for the state. He said the institute will operate as a “consortium” with industry, government and higher education partners, with the legal structure to be determined.

The mission of the institute, according to a news release, is to “serve as a central hub to coordinate industry, education and government partners” and “support businesses pursuing defense contracting opportunities.”

Even said there are “probably over 100” contractors and subcontractors doing defense work in South Dakota. Many are connected to Ellsworth Air Force Base near Rapid City on the west side of the state. On the other side of the state, in Sioux Falls, MMS Products won a $35 million contract last year to produce drone warheads.

Rhoden said he wants centralized support to bring more defense contracts to South Dakota companies.

“We’ve already got a number of businesses in South Dakota that have kind of happened at random,” Rhoden said. “We’re going to be a lot more coordinated and a lot more structured at providing people with the infrastructure and the ability and the communication to get together.”

Rhoden is in the midst of a campaign to keep his job. He was elevated from lieutenant governor when his predecessor, former Gov. Kristi Noem, resigned in January 2025 to lead the federal Department of Homeland Security.

Rhoden faces three opponents from his own party in the June 2 primary election: U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, businessman Toby Doeden and state House Speaker Jon Hansen.

title: ND to lead nation in federal ag tech research initiative
byline: By Jeff Beach North Dakota Monitor
description: CASSELTON, N.D. — North Dakota will lead the nation in a U.S. Department of Agriculture push to improve farm technology and research, federal officials announced Tuesday.
_full_text:
NorthDakotaMonitorLogo

CASSELTON, N.D. — North Dakota will lead the nation in a U.S. Department of Agriculture push to improve farm technology and research, federal officials announced Tuesday.

U.S. Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., said Grand Farm, a research campus west of Fargo, will be the national program manager for USDA’s National Proving Grounds Network for AgTech. Grand Farm will also be the first proving ground in the network, focusing on weed control. 

North Dakota launched Grand Farm seven years ago, integrating research capabilities from North Dakota State University at Fargo with industry partners such as tech giant Microsoft.

Hoeven said Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins, who visited Grand Farm last year, recognized that North Dakota provided a model for ag tech research and could be the manager for the rollout. 

“It’s a huge deal,” Hoeven said. “It’s Grand Farm going national.” 

Hoeven announced that $11 million will launch the proving grounds, a collaboration of Grand Farm, USDA’s Agricultural Research Service and NDSU. 

Scott Hutchins, USDA under secretary for research, education and economics, said the first year of research will be concentrated in North Dakota and Georgia. The University of Georgia announced a partnership with Grand Farm in 2024. 

He said after reviewing results from the first year, the department plans to accept proposals for research hubs in other states, eventually creating the national network. 

Hutchins said profitability is a top priority. He said there has been a boom in ag technology, but farmers need help sifting through it all. 

“Which one can provide the greatest return on investment?” he asked. 

Hoeven said focusing on profitability is a must during rough economic times. “Right now, if you’re growing a crop, in most cases, you’re not making money,” Hoeven said.  

The North Dakota Legislature invested $10 million in 2021 to help propel Grand Farm, which covers 590 acres near Casselton. Operating from tents and with portable bathrooms in its first years, the research site opened its first building in 2024. The Legislature invested an additional $7 million in 2025. 

“The National Proving Grounds is the next chapter,” said Brian Carroll, chief operating officer for Grand Farm. 

George Vellidis, of the University of Georgia’s Institute for Integrative Precision Agriculture, said Georgia is one year into operating its 250-acre research area similar to Grand Farm. 

He said the goal is to translate the research in the Upper Midwest to crops grown in the southeast. A robot that can be taught to recognize weeds in North Dakota will have to be taught a different set of weeds that grow in Georgia, for example. 

Grand Farm board member Kyle Courtney, who farms near Oakes, North Dakota, said the initiative will help field test practices “under a unified umbrella to help farmers make better decisions.”

title: A day after Iran-US ceasefire declared,  doubts linger amid continuing Gulf strikes
byline: By Ashley Murray States Newsroom
description: WASHINGTON — The United States and Iran both claimed victory Wednesday, a day after agreeing to a 2-week conditional ceasefire, though doubts loomed following continued strikes across the Gulf nations and an indication by Iran that it will continue to control the Strait of Hormuz, a major passage for one-fifth of the world’s oil and gas.
_full_text:
StatesNewsroomLogo

WASHINGTON — The United States and Iran both claimed victory Wednesday, a day after agreeing to a 2-week conditional ceasefire, though doubts loomed following continued strikes across the Gulf nations and an indication by Iran that it will continue to control the Strait of Hormuz, a major passage for one-fifth of the world’s oil and gas. 

Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth said during an early-morning briefing the U.S. achieved an “historic and overwhelming victory,” but also troops are “prepared to restart at a moment’s notice.”

“We’ll be hanging around. We’re not going anywhere. We’re going to make sure Iran complies with this ceasefire, and then ultimately comes to the table and makes a deal,” Hegseth said.

Oil prices dropped sharply after news of the ceasefire, with Brent crude, the international standard, sitting at $95 a barrel before noon Wednesday. That’s down from the previous day’s price of nearly $110 per barrel. 

U.S. stocks shot up Wednesday, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average, S&P 500 and Nasdaq Composite all on the rise.

U.S. and Iranian delegations were set to arrive in Islamabad Friday for negotiations, according to Pakistan’s Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, who in part brokered the pause in fighting.

White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt told reporters at an afternoon briefing that Vice President JD Vance, special envoy Steve Witkoff and the president’s son-in-law Jared Kushner will attend a first round of talks Saturday morning.

Nuclear material

President Donald Trump said early Wednesday morning that the U.S. “will work closely with Iran, which we have determined has gone through what will be a very productive Regime Change!”

“There will be no enrichment of Uranium, and the United States will, working with Iran, dig up and remove all of the deeply buried (B-2 Bombers) Nuclear ‘Dust,’” Trump wrote on his platform, Truth Social, referring to Iran’s buried enriched uranium following heavy U.S.-Israeli bombing in June.

When pressed at the briefing, Hegseth said of the nuclear material: “We’re watching it. We know what they have, and they will give it up, and we’ll get it, and we’ll take it if we have to. We can do it in any means necessary. So that’s something the president is going to solve for.”

Hegseth ended the press conference saying the Iranian public has been “oppressed by the previous regime, and they’ll have a new opportunity with this regime that remains to be seen,” adding that a civilian uprising was “not our objective.” 

“We wish them the best,” Hegseth said. 

Hegseth’s claim about a civilian uprising directly contradicted Trump’s message to the Iranian people on Feb. 28, when the U.S. and Israel began the bombing.

Iran’s new supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, is the son of the slain Ayatollah Ali Khamenei, who led the Islamic Republic from 1989 until U.S. and Israeli strikes assassinated him hours into the conflict. Experts point to Mojtaba Khamenei as being a conservative hardliner with close ties to the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps.

Reports across Iranian state media and Middle East regional news outlets Wednesday quoted the regime’s Supreme National Security Council as declaring an “historic and crushing defeat” over the U.S. and Israel.

Calls for invocation of 25th Amendment

Hegseth’s victory declaration came after Trump on Tuesday threatened Iran’s “whole civilization will die tonight” if the regime did not meet his self-imposed 8 p.m. Eastern deadline to open the Strait of Hormuz. 

The comments drew intense criticism, with some — from progressive Democrats to former Trump loyalists — calling for the president’s removal under the Constitution’s 25th Amendment.

Roughly 90 minutes before his deadline to order strikes on Iran’s power plants and bridges, the president agreed to stop the bombardment for two weeks, after receiving a 10-point plan from Iran that “is a workable basis on which to negotiate,” he wrote on his social media platform, Truth Social.

In a statement released early Wednesday morning Tehran time, Iran appeared to retain control of the narrow passage in and out of the Persian Gulf.

“For a period of two weeks, safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz will be possible via coordination with Iran’s Armed Forces and with due consideration of technical limitations,” the country’s foreign minister, Seyed Abbas Araghchi, said in a written statement posted on social media. 

Iranian drones and missiles

Strikes continued across the Gulf region, with Kuwait’s defense ministry reporting “an intense wave” of Iranian drones and missiles that damaged oil infrastructure, power stations and water desalination plants.

“Violations of ceasefire have been reported at (a) few places across the conflict zone which undermine the spirit of peace process. I earnestly and sincerely urge all parties to exercise restraint and respect the ceasefire for two weeks, as agreed upon, so that diplomacy can take a lead role towards peaceful settlement of the conflict,” Sharif warned on X just after 10 a.m. Eastern. 

The Pakistani prime minister tagged in the post Trump and numerous administration officials, as well as Iranian leaders.

Israel continued bombardment on southern Lebanon, launching widespread strikes across the region and in the capital city of Beirut Wednesday. By noon Eastern, which is evening in Lebanon, health authorities said 89 people were killed in the strikes and over 700 had been injured. An official with Doctors Without Borders reporting from a large public hospital in Beirut cited a higher death toll.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu claimed on social media early Wednesday that “The two-weeks ceasefire does not include Lebanon.”

title: Have any SD natives  been into space?
byline: By Michael Klinski South Dakota News Watch
description: Charles "Sam" Gemar
_full_text:
Charles “Sam” Gemar .jpg
Charles "Sam" Gemar 

 Official Portrait of Astronaut Michael E. Fossum
Charles “Sam” Gemar, top, and Michael Fossum, above,  were both born in South Dakota, became astronauts, and spent time in space.  

Has anyone from South Dakota been into space?

As a matter of fact, yes.

Two people who were born in South Dakota have spent some time in space and are among 800 astronauts. 

Charles “Sam” Gemar was the first person from the state to see space. Gemar was born in Yankton and grew up in Scotland, becoming an astronaut in 1986. He has spent 580 hours in space across three missions from 1990-94.

 “I always knew what I wanted to do,” Gemar said during a visit to Dakota State University in Madison in February. “I wanted to be an astronaut. I just never shared that because who’s going to believe that? You’re from South Dakota.”

Michael Fossum was born in Sioux Falls and grew up in McAllen, Texas. He was selected as an astronaut in 1998 and was on three space flights from 2006-2011, spending more than 194 days in space with 7 spacewalks.

title: Family demands justice, accountability  for Lakota woman allegedly killed by airman
byline: By Amelia Schafer ICT
description: A family member holds a sign for Sahela Sangrait, a Lakota woman who federal prosecutors say was killed on Ellsworth Air Force Base. Photo by Amelia Schafer, ICT
_full_text:
Family demands justice, accountability  for Lakota woman allegedly killed by airman
A family member holds a sign for Sahela Sangrait, a Lakota woman who federal prosecutors say was killed on Ellsworth Air Force Base. Photo by Amelia Schafer, ICT 

RAPID CITY — Sahela “Toka Win” Sangrait would have turned 23 on March 26. Instead, more than 50 people gathered on her birthday to demand justice and systemic change. 

Federal prosecutors have charged United States Airman Quinterius Chappelle with first-degree murder in connection to Sangrait’s homicide, which authorities say took place on Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota in August 2024. 

But those gathered say the crime could have been prevented.

Chappelle was court-martialed for aggravated assault following a February 2024 domestic incident not involving Sangrait, according to Jesse Fagerland, a sergeant with the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office. Fagerland testified during Chappelle’s November 2024 arraignment in the Sangrait case. The February 2024 incident was handled by Air Force authorities. 

Additionally, local Box Elder law enforcement officials responded to a report of domestic violence at Chappelle’s residence on the night of Sangrait’s death but did not contact anyone inside the residence, Fagerland testified. Because the 2024 assault case was handled internally by the Air Force, it’s unclear if Box Elder police were aware of Chappelle’s history. 

“This should not have happened to her, there were signs, there were things that could have prevented her from facing this tragedy,” said Lorna Cuny, Oglala Lakota and the executive director of the Medicine Wheel Ride, a group of motorcyclists who raise awareness for the Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women epidemic. 

Sangrait’s grandmother agreed.

“I don’t have a hard heart,” said Vonda High Hawk, Mnicoujou Lakota. “But this girl should have lived. I think they (the Air Force) should at some point be held accountable for the wrongful death (of Sangrait). There’s a chain of command … These senseless crimes need to be handled appropriately by their chain of command. There has to be some type of example made of that.”

Chappelle and Sangrait were in a romantic relationship, family members said.

“We want her story to get out,” said Hillary Dubray, Sangrait’s mother. “She was just (about to turn) 21, just getting her life started, but her life was cut short.”

Dubray, Mnicoujou Lakota, stood firmly, wearing a bright red hooded sweatshirt with her daughter’s face on it. Dubray gathered with family members, friends and community in chilly below-zero temperatures and drizzling rain on March 26 to demand justice for her daughter. 

“We want people to know she mattered,” said Sangrait’s other grandmother, Phyllis Bald Eagle, who is Mnicoujou Lakota and Mdewakanton Dakota.  

Community members are organizing a mid-April demonstration outside of the Ellsworth Air Force Base. Organizers from local MMIW advocacy groups, the Medicine Wheel Ride and the Red Ribbon Skirt Society said the demonstration will bring awareness to Sangrait’s murder as they await the accused’s trial in Rapid City. 

“It’s for justice,” said Frances Dupris, Sicangu Lakota/Northern Arapaho and an organizer with the Red Ribbon Skirt Society. Dupris spent 24 years as a United States airman before retiring. “The individuals that should be held accountable for Sahela’s murder are airmen … I was an airman, I retired, so this is not to say that all airmen are bad. But the people who do bad things need to be held accountable.” 

Nationwide, Indigenous women are reported missing at a disproportionately high rate. Further, homicide is one of the leading causes of death among American Indians and Alaska Natives, a significant proportion of which are the result of domestic violence. 

Sixty-one American Indian/Alaska Native people were reported missing in South Dakota as of March 26, compared to 95 total missing individuals, meaning roughly 65% of all missing people in the state are American Indian/Alaska Native. Natives make up only 11% of the statewide population. This percentage of missing Native people statewide has remained steady for over two years. 

Charges filed, trial pending

Two individuals are federally charged in connection with Sangrait’s murder: Chappelle and Drew Durand, both 25 and both residents of Box Elder where the Ellsworth Air Force Base is located. Chappelle is charged with first-degree murder and Durand with accessory after the fact and misprision of a felony. 

Sangrait’s remains were found by a hiker in a wooded area near Hill City on March 4, 2025. 

Police charged Chapelle days later with Sangrait’s murder. 

Due to the homicide having allegedly taken place on the Air Force base and the body being found on federal land, Chappelle and Durand are charged in federal court.

Authorities believe Chappelle killed Sangrait at his residence on the Ellsworth Air Force Base. Local law enforcement responded to a report of a domestic dispute at his residence on Aug. 10, 2024, but left without making contact with Chappelle or anyone inside the residence, according to police testimony at Chapelle’s March 28, 2025, arraignment. 

Due to Chappelle’s alleged assault history, his commanding officer required him to go to local law enforcement when he arrived at work on Aug. 12 with fingernail scratches across his face. Chappelle reported to Rapid City law enforcement officers that the scratches were the result of an Aug. 10 break-in at his residence. Chappelle declined to follow up with officers regarding an investigation, his federal judge noted in court at his March 2025 hearing. 

Crimes committed on an Air Force base are often prosecuted internally by the base’s court, meaning records of the incident are not available to the public or civilians. Due to this, no court records regarding Chappelle’s assault court martial are available to the public. Information regarding the incident was only made available to the public through law enforcement testimony at Chappelle’s arraignment. 

In February 2024, Chappelle was court-martialed for aggravated assault via strangulation. He was disciplined in November, two months after the alleged murder, Fagerland said. Chappelle also broke no-contact orders two separate times, according to Fagerland. 

Sahela’s story

Sangrait comes from a strong lineage of Lakota and Dakota warriors – a legacy that lived on through her, her family said. 

Her great-great-grandfather was Mdewakanton Dakota Chief Little Crow, also known as Ta-Oyate-Duta, who led the six-week 1862 Dakota Uprising in Minnesota. Little Crow is remembered as one of the Dakota 38+2, a group of Dakota men killed by the United States Government in retaliation for the uprising. 

Sangrait was also a descendant of Chief Dave Bald Eagle, a World War II veteran who parachuted into the D-Day invasion of Normandy. Bald Eagle was awarded a Silver Star and a Purple Heart for his service. Bald Eagle was also the grandson of Hunkpapa Lakota Chief White Bull, who was Sitting Bull’s nephew. White Bull fought in the Battle of Little Big Horn. 

“There’s a beautiful history this lady comes from,” High Hawk said. “She comes from a very strong lineage, and she will never be forgotten.” 

Sahela was given her Lakota name, Toka Win, which roughly translates to Different Cheyenne Woman, by her great-grandmother Clarenda Little Crow, who was Chief Little Crow’s Daughter.

“Everyone needs to know who she was and who she came from,” Bald Eagle said. 

High Hawk said it’s paramount to remember Sangrait’s ancestor’s battles and what they went through while fighting for justice for her. 

“These injustices and these atrocities go way back,” High Hawk said. “There needs to be more awareness, more events like what we just did. … We will continue to say her name.” 

Sahela grew up in the Black Hills area and moved to Rapid City at 18 years old, her mother said. In Rapid City she worked to fundraise for youth programming and was a vocal advocate for Indigenous youth.

“She was beautiful, just so pretty,” said Sangrait’s other grandmother Vonda High Hawk, who traveled over two hours from the Cheyenne River Reservation in South Dakota, to attend the vigil. “Regardless of the odds that were against her in this life she still radiated with beauty.” 

At such a young age, Sangrait hadn’t quite figured out what she was going to do yet as an adult, her family said. She was passionate about helping others and volunteered at Ateyapi, a local nonprofit youth program for Indigenous students in the Black Hills area. She also wanted to raise awareness for domestic violence victims, her mother said.

title: Sturgis VFW Auxiliary presents  250th anniversary flags to local entities
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Sturgis VFW Auxiliary presented flags to the city of Sturgis, Meade County Commission, Sturgis Chamber of Commerce, and the Sturgis VFW Club Tuesday at the Vets Club. Pictured from left are: Sean Henderson, veteran service officer, Nancy Worth, Jim Thompson, city of Sturgis, Sharon Vinson, Christina Koates, Doreen Creed and Gary Deering, Meade County commissioners, Travis Bartels, Veronica Grosek, Slater Tople, Mike Pauling, and Jessie Dufner, President of the chamber, board. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
Sturgis VFW Auxiliary presents  250th anniversary flags to local entities
The Sturgis VFW Auxiliary presented flags to the city of Sturgis, Meade County Commission, Sturgis Chamber of Commerce, and the Sturgis VFW Club Tuesday at the Vets Club. Pictured from left are: Sean Henderson, veteran service officer, Nancy Worth, Jim Thompson, city of Sturgis, Sharon Vinson, Christina Koates, Doreen Creed and Gary Deering, Meade County commissioners, Travis Bartels, Veronica Grosek, Slater Tople, Mike Pauling, and Jessie Dufner, President of the chamber, board. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

STURGIS — The Sturgis VFW Post 2730 and its auxiliary presented commemorative 250th anniversary flags to several local organizations Tuesday evening at the Sturgis Veterans Club.  

Flags were presented to Meade County, the city of Sturgis, the Sturgis Area Chamber of Commerce, and the Sturgis Veterans Club as part of a statewide effort to recognize the upcoming 250th anniversary of the United States.

Nancy Worth, past president of the Sturgis VFW Auxiliary, said the project was inspired by a challenge issued to auxiliaries across South Dakota.

“We have been challenged across the state to do something for the 250th anniversary of the United States,” Worth said. “So, what we’ve done is join forces with our local post and purchase four 250th anniversary flags.”  Each of the four flags will be displayed at a designated location in the community during the nation’s 250th anniversary celebration, particularly around the Fourth of July.

“One will be given to Meade County, one to the city of Sturgis, one to the Sturgis Chamber of Commerce, and one to the Sturgis Veterans Club, to be flown during the time frame of celebrating our 250th birthday,” Worth said.

Worth said the idea came after she discovered information about the commemorative flags online. 

“I saw the information online, and these flags are actually South Dakota-made, they came out of Sioux Falls,” she said. “I brought it up to our auxiliary, and they said yes, we’ll do it. The post went along with it, and we split the cost.”

During the presentation, Worth emphasized the auxiliary’s appreciation for the community partners receiving the flags.

Mike Pauling, commander of VFW Post 2730, said the event reflects the organization’s commitment to both honoring the nation’s history and supporting the local community.

“I’m here to show my support for the greater Sturgis community and this dedication to make South Dakota stronger,” Pauling said. “It’s also in remembrance of everything that has been sacrificed to get us where we are today in the land of freedom.”

title: Spearfish discusses next steps to address Main St., Colorado Blvd. chip seal failure
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — On Monday, Spearfish city staff fielded questions from the public and the city council about the Colorado Boulevard and Main Street Chip Seal failure.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — On Monday, Spearfish city staff fielded questions from the public and the city council about the Colorado Boulevard and Main Street Chip Seal failure.

On Sept. 2, 2025, the city awarded the project to Dakota Asphalt for $475,385.56. Simon Contractors of SD, Inc. and Bituminous Paving, Inc. also initially bid on the project. At the time, engineers estimated the total project cost at $519,385.56, including construction, consultant design, and construction administration. The budget for the chip seal project was $200,000, so the council voted to pass a supplement of $319,385.56.

The project got underway in the fall, and almost immediately, it became clear that the attempt to preserve the pavement through downtown and along Colorado Boulevard had failed, according to city staff at Monday’s meeting. 

“We have been and are still working on evaluating the cause of the failure,” Spearfish Public Works Director Adam McMahon said.

In recent weeks, community members and business owners have contacted city leaders with complaints about the state of the road and the dust and loose chips stirred up by the project.

“It is easily recognizable, whether it’s by a citizen, or an elected official, or business owner that the downtown project contractor did not meet any of the standards as intended,” said Spearfish Mayor John Senden. “The business owners with outdoor seating, this has caused additional work (for them), so we’re sorry indeed for any challenges that have been presented.”

On Monday, John Williams, who owns 2 businesses on Main Street, asked the council to treat the road repair as an infrastructure emergency.

“I would caution council as you are making a decision on this, time is of the essence. We are a tourism community,” said Spearfish resident Nathan Hoogshagen.

Councilman Larry Klarenbeek said it might be time to stop working on determining the reason for the chip seal failure and focus on a speedy repair.

“We really need a date or dates,” Klarenbeek said. “We don’t really need to determine cause. It seems to me we need to get it done.”

Councilwoman Ana Rath offered her agreement.

“We are evaluating our options,” McMahon said. “Some of the options that are being considered are: a refund of the project, a reapplication of the chip seal, a mill and overlay, a combination of a chip seal and mill and overlay, and concrete surfacing downtown.”

Try chip seal again

Dakota Asphalt representatives have acknowledged that the result of the chip seal project is unacceptable. They’ve also offered to re-perform the service they were hired to do, under warranty.

“They’re not any happier about it than anyone else. They are not trying to make the city accept this as it is,” said Spearfish Attorney David Knox. The current contract with Dakota Asphalt still stands. Until that agreement is dissolved, the city can’t bring in another contractor for the work under the document’s terms.

“Personally, I think that it is better to go ahead and proceed with the current contract,” Knox said. “I think we should give them the opportunity to perform like they are supposed to and then, at a minimum, give us additional time to decide longer term what we want to do.”

McMahon said the state offered to send support from the department of transportation to help the company calibrate its equipment, with the hope of increasing the likelihood of a successful round 2 result.

“One could build a case that says, ‘They didn’t do a very good job this time, and now we are going to ask them to do it again,’” said Councilman Dean Myers. Myers asked Knox to clarify if the city has a performance bond it could call in.

“I believe we do. If they fail or refuse to perform. At this point, though, they are offering to perform. They are offering to come in and make it right,” Knox said.

The city could negotiate to dissolve its contract with Dakota Asphalt and bring in another company to finish the job. That would require putting the project back out to bid, which could further delay the start of actual road work.

Even with Dakota Asphalt redoing the job, timing will remain an issue. Chip sealing requires ground temperatures to be high enough for the oil laid down by crews to bind with asphalt chips and “cure.” The job can’t be done in the winter. 

“We can’t, or shouldn’t start work until at least May 15, whether it is asphalt or chip seal. Those are the seasonal limitations for his work,” McMahon said. “Asphalt plants aren’t even open yet. They’re kind of forecasting that they’ll open late April or early May at this point.”

“If they are saying they are going to come back and fix it, let’s get it fixed. I don’t think we need to sit and wait for a cause, because they’ve already offered and said, ‘Now, we are going to fix it.’ Have a date,” Rath said.

Mill and overlay instead

Mill and overlay generally involves milling or grinding down the top of the road surface to lay down new asphalt. In answer to a question from Spearfish resident Doug Markworth, McMahon said the lifespan of chip seal is, “5-10 years versus 10-20 for asphalt.”

Mill and overlay on Main Street and Colorado Boulevard could be more expensive, and would also require either extensive contract renegotiations or the dissolution of the city’s contract with Dakota Asphalt. A mill and overlay project would need to go through the bid process.

Markworth said there is a citizen petition circulating to see at least a portion of the road surface asphalted with a mill and overlay rather than chip sealed a second time.

Apply a combination of chip seal, mill, and overlay

The petition asks that the city consider recovering funds from the fall 2025 chip seal project and applying them to a mill and overlay on the 500, 600, and 700 blocks of Main Street as a “long term solution.” The petition further asks that asphalt be applied to Colorado Boulevard “as feasible up to where infrastructure improvements are required.” 

“I know the combination of chip seal and overlay has been the heavily discussed option in the public, kind of the rough cost estimate for that would be in the $100,000-200,000 range,” McMahon said.

Hoogshagen asked in person if it might make the most sense to mill and overlay the downtown core and Main Street, then proceed with chip seal on Colorado Boulevard.

“Is there an opportunity to go in and perform some sort of adjustment to the contract and say, okay, we would like you to come and chip seal portions of Colorado further south, but then maybe have some sort of change to the contract to have them do mill and overlay on Main Street and that would still abide by the terms of the contract so that we are not going over that?” Hoogshagen asked.

Knox said that could be achieved through an amendment of contract of the change order process.

“There is a change order process, but both parties have to agree. I can’t guarantee or comment on whether the contractor would agree to that change. That would be one of the first steps in the process,” McMahon said. “There are limitations on change order, certain (dollar) amounts we can go up to on that to determine to what extent we can accomplish that.”

Explore concrete surfacing downtown

In a move that would require similar contractual renegotiations, McMahon noted the city had the option to try applying concrete downtown on the roadway. Little further discussion was had around that option at Monday’s meeting.

‘Time is of the essence’

“Our goal at this point is to make a determination sometime in April, with work starting in June,” McMahon said.

No matter what the council decides moving forward, timing in an issue. The work can’t start too early, or it might not be successful. Start too late, and roadwork runs up against peak tourist season and community events that help support Spearfish’s downtown businesses.

“(Mayor) John (Senden), I want to commend you for going and talking to all the businesses downtown. I want to thank you for that. If the decision is made to do something in June, please include downtown building and business owners in that before you pull the trigger on it,” Hoogshagen said. “That is when those folks make their money for the year.”

McMahon said Downtown Friday nights — a concert and festival on Main Street — poses a particular challenge.

“The city’s goal is to coordinate projects that impact events before they are scheduled so that other accommodations can be made,” McMahon said. Those kinds of accommodations are usually made at least a year in advance.

“You said we wouldn’t want to get a project started this year because of our downtown Friday night events,” said Councilwoman Jamie Hafner. “Is there not an option to move them?”

“Potentially,” McMahon replied. “There are a lot of factors to work out on that. Relocating can be challenging because of the power we need for the stage and other accommodations.”

Senden suggested that the event could be moved to 5th Street.
