title: Sturgis flags fly at half-staff to honor memory of former mayor
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Kevin Forrester. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Kevin Forrester mug.jpg
Kevin Forrester. Courtesy photo 

 Kevin-Forrester-Day-Proclamation.jpg
On Thursday, the city of Sturgis and Meade County declared June 10 as Kevin Forrester Day, to honor the former mayor before he died from pancreatic cancer. Forrester died Sunday. Courtesy photo 

STURGIS — Flags in Sturgis are flying at half-staff on all county and city properties, to honor former Mayor Kevin Forrester, following his passing. 

The city of Sturgis and Meade County both issued the orders to honor Forrester’s memory, after the former mayor and longtime county employee died from pancreatic cancer on Sunday. Flags will remain at half-staff through the day of Forrester’s memorial services, which have not yet been scheduled. 

“Kevin Forrester’s commitment, integrity, and contributions have left a lasting impact on colleagues, the organization, and the community,” according to the Meade County order. “His years of service reflect not only professional excellence, but also a deep sense of responsibility and pride in his work. He will be remembered with respect, gratitude, and honor.” 

Sturgis Mayor Pro Tempore Tony Dargatz said, “Forrester faithfully served the city of Sturgis with honor, integrity, and dedication, providing steadfast leadership and a deep commitment to the citizens of this community.” 

Sturgis City Administrator Aaron Jordan said Sturgis city employees were filled with sadness on Monday. 

“We’ve been preparing for this to occur, but it’s still kind of a kick in the stomach,” Jordan said. “Just in talking and listening to some of our staff this morning, you can tell there is sadness for a young life cut short and also for his family.” 

“He was such a vibrant person,” said Sturgis Communications Director Deb Holland. “He was larger than life and had such passion. To see that flame go out I’m just in disbelief. He was a great guy to work with.” 

Jordan said the city planned for a moment of silence at the regularly scheduled city council meeting, Monday. 

On Thursday the city and county issued a joint proclamation to honor Forrester before he passed. Dargatz and Meade County Commission Chairman Gary Deering read the proclamation on social media, declaring June 10 as Kevin Forrester Day. The designation coincides with the first Sturgis Music on Main event of the summer, and will be an opportunity for the community to come together, celebrate his legacy, and reflect on the impact he had on Sturgis and Meade County.

A lifelong Sturgis resident, Forrester served 28 years with Meade County as facility manager and IT director. He also briefly served as the Meade County auditor. He was appointed to Sturgis City Council (Ward 4) to fill the seat vacated by Steve Keszler in 2021 and became mayor of Sturgis following the resignation of Angela Wilkerson in October of 2024.

Throughout his career, he was known for his steady leadership, commitment to community, and a deep belief in the importance of public service.

As mayor, Forrester worked to strengthen the community through thoughtful decision-making and a focus on long-term growth, while preserving the character of Sturgis. Forrester’s lifelong friend, Jordan, served on the city council with him from 2021-2024, and accepted his call to serve as the city administrator when Forrester was appointed as mayor. Jordan said through his public service to the city of Sturgis, Forrester leaves behind a legacy of transparency, fiscal responsibility, and resiliency in city government. 

“As his administrator, it’s been just an honor to be able to serve with him,” Jordan said at a previous press conference that was held when Forrester formally resigned from his position, March 23. “We’ll continue emphasizing those legacies Kevin Forrester set in motion. Our hearts go out to his family.” 

Dargatz said Forrester transformed the city of Sturgis during a very difficult time of significant turnover for employees and elected officials. The city of Sturgis intends to carry on his work. 

“Kevin took the city when it was doom and gloom and he has turned it into a well-oiled machine,” Dargatz said. “He’s listened to the people and he has streamlined it. I’m proud to (have served) with him because of what he has done. He has some big shoes to fill.” 

Forrester’s service extended beyond city government through regional and federal advisory roles, where he advocated for responsible stewardship of the Black Hills and access to its natural resources. Through his business, K4 Trails, Forrester is also responsible for establishing multiple recreational trails in Sturgis and throughout the Northern Hills and Wyoming. 

“I would always catch him on the trails,” Jordan said. “That’s probably where I saw him the most.” 

Jordan said before Forrester died, he was surrounded with family, friends, and well wishes from the community. Jordan said Forrester was deeply moved by all of the people who reached out with messages of support during his battle with cancer. 

In his resignation letter to the city of Sturgis, Forrester emphasized his commitment to the community, and his confidence in Sturgis. 

“The strength of the city does not rest with one person,” Forrester wrote. “It rests with the team. I have been proud to serve alongside the amazing city of Sturgis staff and council.”

title: Sturgis man facing charges  for fatal accident
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — A Sturgis man who allegedly stole a pickup and lead police on a high speed chase up Lazelle Street, resulting in a fatal accident, has a series of felony convictions and at least 2 drug-related cases pending in Meade County.
_full_text:
STURGIS — A Sturgis man who allegedly stole a pickup and lead police on a high speed chase up Lazelle Street, resulting in a fatal accident, has a series of felony convictions and at least 2 drug-related cases pending in Meade County. 

Sturgis Police Chief Geody VanDewater said that charges from the crash are pending against Don Crisafulli, 50. 

Crisafulli allegedly stole a Ford F-250 pickup Tuesday, from a Sturgis residence. When officers attempted to make contact with him, he allegedly sped down Lazelle Street at more than 70 miles per hour, and crashed into the back of a Honda Accord, driven by Egon Lake, 26, of Whitewood. 

Lake sustained fatal injuries as a result of the crash. Crisafulli rolled the truck, and was initially listed in critical condition. But on Thursday police reported his condition is improving. 

Both Crisafulli and Lake had to be extricated from the vehicles.

VanDewater said the entire incident lasted about 39 seconds, from the time officers were advised the vehicle  was stolen to when the accident occurred. His officers, VanDewater said, were about 5-8 seconds behind Crisafulli, who was driving erratically and a high rate of speed even before officers arrived. 

“So, we weren’t up on this guy real close,” he said. “Our officers are doing due regard for safety, going through intersections and stuff and making sure to yield. Unfortunately, this guy didn’t have any due regard for safety, so he got a pretty good lead on us. There’s a lot of questions on to pursue or not to pursue, and that’s where we didn’t really have time to digest this before it was over. Unfortunately, whether we were actively pursuing or not, I don’t believe that would have changed the outcome.” 

VanDewater said his entire department has been affected by the incident, and the police department is working with officers involved to help them process what happened. 

“It’s a tragic event, and it’s unfortunate that an innocent person had to lose their life,” he said. “Our thoughts and prayers go out to (Lake) along with his family.” 

Crisafulli has a series of drug charges and convictions, as well as convictions related to the unauthorized use of a vehicle or vessel, petty theft, and more, that date back to 1998. Most recently, on Jan. 6 he was arrested in Meade County for impersonation to deceive a law enforcement officer, and sentenced to 30 days in jail after pleading guilty. He also has charges stemming from an October arrest for possession of methamphetamine, which have not yet been resolved. 

“We need to do a better job and start holding some of these criminals accountable and quit victifying them and villafying law enforcement,” VanDewater said. “This subject has a long history, and we need to make sure he’s held accountable for his actions.” 

VanDewater said the South Dakota Highway Patrol is investigating the crash, and authorities are still deciding about charges to file. There will be several upcoming criminal charges against Crisafulli, he said.

title: Virtually hitting the links
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: In Spearfish, golfers can play all year round in private, bookable simulator rooms at Golf 365. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
IMG_9355.JPG
In Spearfish, golfers can play all year round in private, bookable simulator rooms at Golf 365. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

 IMG_9372.JPG
Corey Miner is driving a golf ball on one of the links on the simulator. Pioneer photos by Sierra Ferguson  

SPEARFISH — Jaxson Miner was swinging a golf club when he was just 3 years old, accompanying his dad on the green. As life got more hectic, the one-day Black Hills State University football player pursued other sports, and his dad, Corey, stepped away from golf for a while. Jaxson forgot those early days on the fairway. 

Then, about a year ago, Corey took Jaxson to the golf course in Sundance, Wyo..

“This past summer, he took me out for the first time. Golf is a really mental sport. For my first time, I wasn’t really thinking much about it. I felt like I was doing really well. I wasn’t overthinking it. I was just swinging. I beat him my first time, too,” Jaxson recalled. “That was what set the fire in my gut, why I love golf so much.”

Jaxson is on track to graduate from BHSU in May. He’s been studying business, entrepreneurship, and marketing.

For Corey, golfing emerged as a great way to connect with his son.

“We had such a good time together when he was younger,” Corey said. “It is a good way to get hold of him for 4 hours.”

Corey has golfed for more than 25 years and has a deep love of the game. A love that’s dampened a little by the “merry-go-round” of skill building and skill loss that is perpetuated by the ebb and flow of golf season.

“I was frustrated in the winter, not being able to play golf,” Corey said. “The frustration of losing my swing in the winter and having to spend May and June getting it back. I would start to get good in August, September, and then it would start snowing again.”

He thought about getting a golf simulator for his home. Simulators have been around for a while, and they’re an easy way to keep engaged with the sport in the winter months.

The idea of owning a simulator and sharing it with the community came to Corey via a news article.

“I saw a news story about these indoor golf simulators,” Corey said. “The concept of having an unmanned facility open 24 hours a day, every day of the year that you can access with your phone, I thought that was a really great idea.”

Harnessing Jaxson’s education and Corey’s desire for 365 days of available golf time, the pair took a swing and launched Golf 365 in Spearfish.

Golf 365 opened in the brand new building facing Walmart at 3033 1st Ave. a month ago. If the doors aren’t open, it’s not because the simulators aren’t running. The doors are locked by design.

The Miners want to curate a private, custom golf-club experience — indoors. Customers purchase memberships and use an app to schedule tee times.

 IMG_9417.JPG
Jaxson, left, and Corey Miner are the father and son owners of Golf 365.  

Then, they can unlock the doors and settle into one of two simulator rooms.

“We tried to give it that upscale golf club feeling. We want it to be like your own private, cool little golf club. You can come in and practice golf whenever you want,” Corey said. “We wanted to make it a little nicer, calming, and peaceful, but you can also hook up to the Bluetooth, play music, and bring friends. It kind of fits every aspect.”

Each room comfortably fits about four people and boasts a 16-foot simulator screen. A local golf pro has already started utilizing the facility to teach lessons, Corey said.

The private nature of the rooms can take the pressure off practice, he added.

“It is a good place if you’re a beginner too, because you can just come in and no one is watching you. People aren’t trying to give you tips,” Corey said.

Memberships are available on Golf 365’s website, and prospective customers can book free demos to try out the system.

“You close that door if there is someone else in there blasting music, you can’t hear a thing. That is one of the things I like about this place. You don’t have to worry about anything. You have plenty of room, lefties and righties,” Jaxson said. The secludedness, other simulators, there’s a lot of noise going on, a lot of stuff. You can’t really focus. Here you really can. It is BYOB. Bring any food you want. It’s like your own space, it is your own time.”

title: Black Hills Pioneer at 150: The Pioneer
description: Pioneer file graphic
_full_text:
Black Hills Pioneer at 150 years
Pioneer file graphic 

The Black Hills Pioneer
The Black Hills Pioneer is the oldest continuously operating business in West River Dakota Territory; and 2026 marks our 150th year of telling the stories of the Black Hills. Over time our newspaper has absorbed the titles of numerous other publications, and we would like to share some of the more compelling stories from those early editions.
 Every Saturday we will be publishing stories from our archives, focusing heavily on the gold rush era of the 1800s, starting with our very first publication on June 8, 1876. These stories are re-printed exactly as they were first published, leaving in place the historic typos, grammar, style and terminology – politically correct or otherwise. It is our belief that history is sacrosanct and should never be edited to reflect the societal norms of the present.
 We hope you enjoy this historic journey. It is an honor and a privilege to be a trusted permanent record keeper of the Black Hills community; we look forward to the next 150 years of history in the making in the magnificent Black Hills.

~ January 1, 1891 • Deadwood Daily Pioneer-Times ~

The Pioneer.

Not Only in Name, But a Paper That Was In at the Beginning.

Something of the Labor and Cost of Publishing a Daily Newspaper.

Past and Present.

The PIONEER has been one of the permanent institutions of our city from the beginning. Its fortunes have been somewhat fluctuating, it has had divers and sundry homes, and has had its clouds and sunshine, but has always been here to stay; no unknown quantity in our formative influences, but a positive factor in all matters pertaining to our growth and development.

The first number was issued June 12th, 1876, Messrs. Merrick & Laughlin, editors, publishers and proprietors. Deadwood was then a wild, howling mining camp, composed of mostly saloons, gambling houses, restaurants, groceries, lodgings, etc. The nights were then more lively than the days, the streets were constantly thronged; people continuously going, all in quest of fortunes, either in the placers, or in the more uncertain channels of speculation or games of chance. The were no courts of justice, except such as the miners established, and no laws except those they enacted; no churches or school houses, no U. S. mails, and no certain connection with the outside world. In fact, it was a sort of primitive condition of affairs. With strange and novel conditions, the PIONEER made its first appearance, first finding a resting place on Main Street, and afterwards moving into quarters of its own on the alley near the locality of the present Scott building. Early in the spring of 1877, the experiment of a daily was entered upon, and with lively competition, and through many adversities, for more than thirteen years has contained the births and deaths, the failures and fortunes, the hopes and fears, the joys and sorrows, of our struggling, but constantly growing and thriving young city.

For several years it was published on Sherman Street, where, under the exclusive management of Mr. Merrick, it fought bravely to make that street a thoroughfare of trade and commerce equal to Main Street, but the fates were against it, and it finally gave up the contest.

In April 1885, it passed to the control of Willis H. Bonham, with whom were associated for a while, J. C. Moody and Chas. A. Maskrey. Later on the latter two were succeeded by that genial friend of all, and excellent newspaperman, Robert Dawson Kelly, now leading a pleasant and prosperous life at Fremont, Nebraska. A year later it passed into the hands of the PIONEER Publishing Company, with Hon. Edwin Van Cise, president; Hon. Eben W. Martin, secretary and W. H. Bonham, manager, and immediately entered upon a new life and career of prosperity. Today it is an 8-page paper, with the largest advertising patronage of any paper published in the state of South Dakota, and the largest circulation of any daily paper in the state, except it may be the Sioux Falls Press.

While the PIONEER has always been avowedly republican in politics, it has never been an “organ” nor the tool of any ring or clique, but has been independent and free from dictation. It has counted among its editors, reporters and contributors the best and brightest writers of the Hills, some of whom have gone to their long home, while others remain to help make the PIONEER in the future what it has been in the past, the leading paper.

Now looking out on the coming year, so full of hope and promise, with railroads, reduction works, smelters and kindred promoters of prosperity, we can assure our readers and patrons that no pains nor expense shall be spared to make the PIONEER better, if possible, a welcome visitant in every household, the fearless defender of what is right and best in politics and government, and in all ways the promoter of the welfare of society and the advancement of the best interests of Deadwood and the Hills. So, now and here, we make our bow and wish each and all a most “Happy New Year.”

Presses, Machinery and Type.

A description, in detail, of all the presses and machinery, their workings and uses would require several columns of descriptive matter and then it would be imperfectly understood by a majority of the readers. Most of the machines used in the PIONEER office are very intricate in mechanism, costly, and the best of the kind made. Perhaps the simplest are the tableting and proof presses—very primitive but from their simplicity cannot be improved upon for the uses to which they are designed. Next in simplicity is a paper cutter and the Old Washington Hand Press on which the paper was printed until after the first of September, 1879. The “forms,” or type from which the paper is printed, is placed on the “bed” of the press which is run out on the tracks, as shown in the engraving, by turning the small crank; the frisket—a light frame large enough to enclose the forms, and over which canvass is stretched, the bottom end fastened with hinges—is thrown back to beyond the perpendicular to an angle of forty-five degrees, the paper placed on it and deftly swung over onto the type, and the pressman turns the crank, slides the bed under the platen, pulls the big hand lever which presses the platen on the sheet of paper covering the type, lets go the lever, the heavy side springs raise the platen; the bed is then run out, the frisket or tympum raised and the printed sheet carefully removed and piled on a table. A boy inks the type and the same unvarying process is kept up for hours. Progress is slow and laborious. One man and a boy can only print about 150 sheets per hour. But this old press was superseded by a magnificent Cottrell and Babcock Air Spring Cylinder Press which is propelled, as all the presses in the office are, by a water motor. The cylinder press has a capacity of 2,000 sheets per hour and it only requires the services of a small boy to “feed” it.

In Platen or job presses the Gordon and Peerless are used, the best manufactured. For printing large sheets, or for making several impressions of the same kind at one time, the Gordon is used on account of its strength. For smaller work the Peerless is used on account of its greater speed.

title: Fire restrictions in effect April 17  for BHNF in Wyoming
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: CUSTER — Black Hills National Forest Supervisor Shawn Cochran has signed a Stage 1 fire prohibitions order for the Black Hills National Forest in Wyoming. The restrictions will be in effect through Dec. 15, unless rescinded sooner.
_full_text:
CUSTER — Black Hills National Forest Supervisor Shawn Cochran has signed a Stage 1 fire prohibitions order for the Black Hills National Forest in Wyoming. The restrictions will be in effect through Dec. 15, unless rescinded sooner.

Persistent, long-term drought conditions and unseasonably warm temperatures combined with the lack of moisture have dramatically increased the fire danger. Conditions are ripe for large fire potential, and people need to be extremely careful in the forest.

Stage 1 fire restrictions apply to campfires and smoking. Under Stage 1 restrictions, the following acts are prohibited: building, maintaining, attending, or using a fire or campfire (including fires fueled by charcoal or briquettes) outside of a permanent metal or concrete fire pit or grate that the forest service has installed and maintained at its developed recreation sites in the Wyoming Black Hills National Forest.

Other restrictions include, using an explosive; smoking, except in an enclosed vehicle or building, a developed recreation site, or while stopped in an area at least 3 feet in diameter that is barren or cleared of all flammable materials; and welding, or operating acetylene or other torch with open flame, except if in a cleared area of at least 10 feet in diameter and a chemical pressurized fire extinguisher (with a minimum 8 ounce capacity and rating of Class 2A) is kept with the operator.

Cochran issued the order to protect the forest and to provide for human safety as forest moisture levels drop and temperatures increase. The current fire restrictions will remain in place until fire managers determine that local conditions make it safe for the restrictions to be lifted.

title: ‘Absolute chaos’
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — County auditors and the state’s lead election official disagree about how to handle a delay of early and absentee voting for the June 2 primary election in South Dakota.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — County auditors and the state’s lead election official disagree about how to handle a delay of early and absentee voting for the June 2 primary election in South Dakota.

Codington County Auditor Brenda Hanten told local media on Wednesday that the county would begin early and absentee voting on time by using sample ballots as the county waits for official ballots, under the guidance of South Dakota Secretary of State Monae Johnson.

Hanten walked back those plans on Thursday, telling South Dakota Searchlight she hadn’t yet discussed the plan with her state’s attorney when she made those comments. Codington County will not use sample ballots and will wait until official ballots are mailed.

Ballot printing has been delayed due in part to a quirk of the calendar that created an unusually short window between the filing deadline for candidate petitions and the start of early voting. Earlier this year, lawmakers declined to heed warnings from county auditors and apply a fix for this year’s election, citing concerns about changing the laws governing a candidate petition process that was already underway.

A Thursday press release from the Secretary of State’s Office cited 2 state laws, one of which doesn’t mention sample ballots, that the office said support the option for county auditors to use sample ballots to accommodate absentee voting until they receive their official ballots.

Early voting is supposed to begin Friday, but county auditors alerted the public this week that it will be delayed. No one knows how long the delay will be, but they hope it will not last longer than April 24.

Split between county auditors and secretary of state

Hanten joined several other county auditors who told South Dakota Searchlight they are not following Johnson’s guidance. Auditors discussed the potential use of sample ballots earlier in the year when they were warning lawmakers about the expected delay in early voting. Auditors ultimately rejected the sample ballot option, Lincoln County Auditor Sheri Lund said, because South Dakota state law says sample ballots can be used “if the supply of official ballots has been completely exhausted.”

“We can’t run out of ballots if we haven’t even received them,” Lund said. She brought the issue to the Lincoln County state’s attorney, who agreed with her, she said.

Spokesman Tony Mangan with the state Attorney General’s Office told South Dakota Searchlight the office was not consulted about the sample ballot law before the Secretary of State’s Office issued its guidance on the matter.

Auditors wouldn’t be able to track sample ballots the same way as official ballots, said Harding County Auditor Kathy Glines, and auditors would risk a judge ruling the practice illegal and throwing out sample ballots used for voting.

“We are absolutely not going to use sample ballots to vote. That’s an integrity issue,” Glines said. 

“Which law do you want us to break?” Glines added. “The most important thing to us is to protect the ballot and protect the vote. If we start to use sample ballots, we lose that objective.”

Glines has been an auditor since 1991. She and 8 other auditors started to provide their own advice and guidance to auditors throughout the state in recent years.

“We work together so we’re on the same page and not just hoping someone shows up on our behalf,” Glines said.

The Secretary of State’s Office did not issue a press release to the public about the delay in early voting until Thursday — one day before early and absentee voting were supposed to start — and did not respond to several calls or emails beginning earlier in the week from South Dakota Searchlight, or immediately update the office’s website, leading to conflicting media reports about the status of early voting.

The Thursday press release from the Secretary of State’s Office listed a number of factors leading to the delay in early voting, such as a tight schedule, pending challenges to candidates’ nominating petitions, a more complicated process due to lawmakers’ introduction of federal-only ballots in the state, and the newly required combination of school and city elections with the June primary and November general elections.

Criticism of secretary of state, legislators

Johnson, a Republican, is up for reelection this year. 

Democratic challenger Terrence Davis said Johnson’s lack of communication and planning undermine confidence in elections and create unnecessary barriers for voters. He added that South Dakotans should still trust the election process even if they “don’t trust the administrator.”

“This is a lack of good statesmanship and lack of a good leader,” Davis said. “Uniformity and consistency breed trust.”

State Rep. Heather Baxter, R-Rapid City, is challenging Johnson for the Republican nomination.

“These timing issues are critical and I look forward to working with all stakeholders as secretary of state to ensure seamless processes in the future,” Baxter said.

Glines called the start to the election season “absolute chaos.” She said state lawmakers deserve blame for not passing a legal fix to avoid the time crunch.

“We knew it was going to be a perfect storm. I’m putting 100% of the blame on the Legislature for not listening to us on that,” Glines said, adding, “I hate to throw them under the bus, but you guys told us you didn’t care. So here we are.” 

To earn a place on the ballot, prospective statewide candidates from political parties had to gather the required number of petition signatures from registered voters and file them by the last Tuesday in March. Through a quirk of the calendar, there were 5 Tuesdays in March this year, and the last one fell on March 31. That left 17 days before the beginning of early voting for the review and certification of petitions and the printing of ballots.

Early and absentee voting is required by state law to begin no later than 46 days before the election, and ballots must be printed 48 days before.  

Lawmaker responds

Earlier this year, state lawmakers changed the legal deadline for the filing of nominating petitions to the third Tuesday in March, but declined to include an emergency clause in the legislation that would have made it effective immediately. The law therefore won’t take effect until July 1, after the June 2 primary.

Because petition circulation had begun in January and was still underway, some lawmakers were against changing the deadlines for prospective candidates who’d been operating under the assumption of a March 31 deadline. 

House Majority Leader Scott Odenbach, R-Spearfish, said some lawmakers viewed the emergency clause as an “incumbent protection measure” that would have disadvantaged challengers who needed more time to gather petition signatures. Absentee voting “goes on way too long” in South Dakota, Odenbach added, which contributed to his rejection of the emergency clause.

“Auditors and the secretary of state will have to find their way through this year and then the deadline issue should be resolved in future years,” Odenbach said. “I don’t think anybody will be disenfranchised because they only have 40 days to vote early rather than 45.”

Neither Glines nor other auditors could estimate when early voting would start. Pennington County Auditor Sabrina Green said the county’s ballots are being printed, and she’ll update her residents when voting can begin.

Glines’ biggest concern is equal opportunity for voters. She is worried some counties will have more early voting time than others because of differences in when ballots arrive.

“We want every voter to get the same kind of access, and we want every voter across the state to be equal,” Glines said. “The way this is panning out, one county might get 43 days of early voting while another gets 40 days. That hurts perception.”

But Glines said voters should not be concerned about the election as a whole. 

“The election is not in jeopardy. It’s going to go on. We’re going to pull it off,” Glines said. “We just need to get past this hurdle.”

title: Scores of Forest Service plans could be  upended after Boundary Waters mining vote
byline: By Alex Brown Stateline
description: WASHINGTON — Congress’ move to allow mining in a national forest near a wilderness area may have broad ramifications across the country.
_full_text:
StatelineLogo

WASHINGTON — Congress’ move to allow mining in a national forest near a wilderness area may have broad ramifications across the country.

The U.S. Senate voted Thursday to overturn a mining ban in Minnesota’s Superior National Forest, the headwaters of the Boundary Waters Canoe Area Wilderness.

By using an obscure tool known as the Congressional Review Act to open the national forest for mining, lawmakers have called into question the validity of every management plan issued by the U.S. Forest Service over the past several decades. That could result in legal chaos for thousands of permits covering logging, grazing, mining and outdoor recreation. 

Over the past year, Congress for the first time has used the Congressional Review Act to revoke management plans for regions managed by the Bureau of Land Management, seeking to allow more mining and drilling. Such plans had not previously been considered “rules” subject to lawmakers’ review. 

Under the act, federal agencies must submit new regulations to Congress before they can take effect. Because management plans, which function as high-level guidance documents, were never considered rules, federal agencies did not submit them to Congress for review. 

Using a new legal theory, Republicans in Congress have opened reviews and revoked several specific plans that limited resource extraction in Alaska, Montana, North Dakota and Wyoming. But those actions call into question whether more than 100 other such plans are legally in effect, since they are now considered rules that were not sent to Congress as the law requires.

Public lands experts say the new interpretation could create legal jeopardy across hundreds of millions of acres managed by the Bureau of Land Management, threatening any permit issued under a management plan drafted after the passage of the Congressional Review Act in 1996. 

Now, for the first time, Congress has used the review tool to overturn a management decision on Forest Service land. 

“There’s a huge playing field of actions that would be forbidden if none of these management plans are lawfully in place,” Robert Anderson, who served as solicitor for the Department of the Interior during the Biden administration, told Stateline earlier this year. “This could bring things to a screeching halt.”

Longtime outdoors writer Wes Siler, who has written extensively about the Boundary Waters review battle, said in a post Thursday that the vote will “destroy the Forest Service’s ability to conduct regular business for the foreseeable future.” If the agency’s management plans suddenly become invalid, he wrote, “not only could this grind industrial operations on (Forest Service) land to a halt as all of this winds its way through federal court, but it could also set (the Forest Service) the task of re-doing 30 years of work.”

On Thursday, the Senate voted 50-49 to revoke a Biden-era plan that banned mining on land in the Superior National Forest. The resolution will now go to President Donald Trump for his signature.

A Chilean mining company has proposed to mine for copper, nickel and cobalt along Birch Lake in Minnesota. The planned mine would sit at the headwaters of the wilderness area’s watershed. The Boundary Waters is the most popular wilderness in the country, and advocates say the water is so pristine that many visitors fill their bottles straight from the surface of its lakes.

Wilderness proponents say such mines have a long track record of pollution, and leaks from the proposed site would flow downstream and irreversibly contaminate the treasured Boundary Waters.

U.S. Rep. Pete Stauber, the Minnesota Republican who sponsored the review action, has said the mine would bring jobs to the region. Opponents have argued that the tourism economy centered on the Boundary Waters is a larger economic driver, and noted that the mine will be run by a foreign company that will likely export the copper to China. 

U.S. Sen. Tina Smith, a Minnesota Democrat, led the effort to uphold the mining ban on the Senate floor. Following the vote, she said that supporters of the Boundary Waters would likely mount a legal challenge, questioning the use of the Congressional Review Act to revoke a public land order from the Forest Service. 

“I question the legality of what Congress did,” Smith said, according to the Minnesota Reformer.  

Two Republican senators, Susan Collins of Maine and Thom Tillis of North Carolina, also voted against the measure. Tillus also questioned the use of the Congressional Review Act.

“It’s a precedent that I think our Republican colleagues are going to regret,” he told the Minneapolis Star Tribune. 

The Forest Service oversees nearly 200 million acres of land, managed for multiple uses, including timber harvests, grazing, outdoor recreation and wildlife habitat. Some legal experts fear the management plans governing those activities are now in legal jeopardy. 

“That right there is chaos,” Peter Van Tuyn, a longtime environmental lawyer and managing partner at Bessenyey & Van Tuyn LLC, told Stateline earlier this year. 

“Those (plans) go across the full spectrum of what land managers do: conservation and preservation, mining approvals, oil and gas drilling, resource exploitation, public access and recreation,” he added. “There’s a very real chance that a court could say that a resource management plan was never in effect and all the implementation actions under the umbrella of that plan are invalid.”

title: SURF completes DUNE steel beam test lift
byline: By Mike Ray Sanford Underground Research Facility
description: LEAD — A crew of technicians, riggers, hoist operators, and engineers at the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) have successfully completed the first test lift of one of the long steel beams that will be used to construct the far detector cryostats for the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE).
_full_text:
LEAD — A crew of technicians, riggers, hoist operators, and engineers at the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) have successfully completed the first test lift of one of the long steel beams that will be used to construct the far detector cryostats for the Deep Underground Neutrino Experiment (DUNE). 

The 43 foot-long beam weighed more than 15,890 pounds and was safely moved into the Ross Headframe on a set of rails, attached to the winch and rigging inside the specially constructed cage, and lifted into place. 

 “This project showcases the South Dakota Science and Technology Authority (SDSTA) team at SURF doing what they do best, safely and successfully completing a task necessary to support the next phase of DUNE,” said Wendy Straub, chief operating officer at SURF.  “This is the culmination of countless meetings with our partners at Fermilab involving planning, engineering, and hazard elimination, associated with transporting heavy unusual loads on the new skip conveyance. It was awesome to see all the teams come together and execute the test successfully.”   

The test lift of this massive beam took about 18 minutes. This is a process that will be repeated many times in the coming months. This beam is one of 2,100 structural components that will be transported underground by SURF in support of DUNE. 

“This test brings together extensive planning: the cryostat steel delivered by CERN, the utilization of new infrastructure such as the lifting adapter, the new skip conveyance as well as recent modifications to the Ross headframe, including raising the door and new rails,” said Jolie Macier, Fermilab’s far detector and cryogenics project manager for LBNF/DUNE-US. “Further, our teams worked together to execute this lift safely, efficiently and smartly, such that we can repeat such lifts hundreds of times to support the full range of DUNE installation activities.”

title: Lead-Deadwood  Middle School renovation nears the finish line
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: DEADWOOD — The renovation of the Lead-Deadwood Middle School is projected to be complete within the next month, bringing a year-long journey to a close and opening the chapter to new opportunities and improved safety in the district.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

DEADWOOD — The renovation of the Lead-Deadwood Middle School is projected to be complete within the next month, bringing a year-long journey to a close and opening the chapter to new opportunities and improved safety in the district. 

Superintendent Erik Person announced at the Tuesday school board meeting that the project is in the final stages of the $2.1 million renovation. The new administrative suite located on CC Curran Avenue is up and running and the construction of the career and technical education (CTE) classroom is nearing completion.

“The office is looking great,” said Person. “There are a few things that need to be fixed here and there with some door locks and some touch up things. We’re planning to make the transition on the traffic flow at the start of next school year, just because the timing is kind of odd right now.”

Separating bus traffic from pick up and drop off traffic was one of the main motivators behind the project, as well as providing the secretary with a clear line of sight of people approaching the entrance and creating new curriculum opportunities within the district. 

The new CTE classroom is expected to be completed next month, providing greater woodworking opportunities for the classroom and engineering tools.

“We’ll have a table saw, miter saw, scroll saw, router table, those kinds of basic woodworking tools,” said Person. “Then we’ve got a section that is kind of focused more on like a CNC (computer numerical control) tool, 3-D printer, and some more STEM (science, technology, engineering, and math) and engineering type stuff. So, kind of a multi-faceted area there.” 

School board members approved 2 new change orders for the project on Tuesday, bringing the total number of change orders to the project up to 12. New changes included bringing the galvanized ceiling of the CTE classroom higher to cover old windows that had been covered on the exterior of the building and changes to drainage for a shower. 

“Initially they were supposed to cut out the floor then the shower was going to be built into the floor,” said Bill Snow, director of maintenance and transportation. “They got to the point where they were ready to cut that out and they discovered that that shower sat above a tunnel, so there wasn’t enough room to cut it out. They put a shower pan in.”

Brick walls in the old administrative suite were found to be decrepit and will need to be replaced. 

“When they tore out the old planter box that used to sit outside (the principal’s) office, they found out that that brick under there was starting to fall apart,” said Bill Snow, director of maintenance and transportation. “It’s kind of a structural deal, so we’ll need to replace that brick.”

The district removed painting lines from SECO Construction, Inc.’s contracted scope of work, saving the district approximately $2,000.

The May 12 school board meeting is expected to take place in the middle school. School board members are expected to receive a tour of the completed facilities.

title: Nero named Distinguished  Faculty Award recipient at BHSU
byline: Pioneer Staff Reports
description: Dr. Jonathan Nero, professor of music and choral director at BHSU, was recognized with the 2026 Distinguished Faculty Award. Pictured from left are: Dr. Pam Carriveau, provost; Dr. Amy Fuqua, dean of the College of Liberal Arts; Dr. Jonathan Nero, professor of music; Dr. Rich Loose, associate provost; President Steve Elliott; Quintin Owens, chair of the School of Arts. BHSU photo by Ava Elliott
_full_text:
Nero named Distinguished  Faculty Award recipient at BHSU
Dr. Jonathan Nero, professor of music and choral director at BHSU, was recognized with the 2026 Distinguished Faculty Award. Pictured from left are: Dr. Pam Carriveau, provost; Dr. Amy Fuqua, dean of the College of Liberal Arts; Dr. Jonathan Nero, professor of music; Dr. Rich Loose, associate provost; President Steve Elliott; Quintin Owens, chair of the School of Arts. BHSU photo by Ava Elliott 

SPEARFISH — Black Hills State University recognized Dr. Jonathan Nero, professor of music and choral director, as the recipient of the 2026 Distinguished Faculty Award. Nero was honored for his excellence in teaching, service to the University, and active contributions to scholarship and creative endeavors. BHSU President Steve Elliott and Provost/Vice President for Academic Affairs Pam Carriveau presented the award to Nero Wednesday. 

Candidates for the Distinguished Faculty Award are nominated by BHSU faculty members and reviewed by the Distinguished Faculty Committee. The committee makes a recommendation to the Faculty Senate, which then recommends a final candidate to the provost.   

“Jon Nero exemplifies the values of Black Hills State University through his dedication to teaching excellence, community engagement, and student-centered leadership,” said BHSU faculty members in their nomination letter. “His tireless efforts, creative vision, and compassionate mentorship have had a lasting and positive impact on our students, alumni, and the broader community.”  

Nero joined Black Hills State University in 2007 as an assistant professor, was promoted to associate professor and granted tenure in 2013, and advanced to professor in 2018. He holds a Doctor of Musical Arts in Choral Conducting, along with a Master of Education and a Bachelor of Science in Vocal Music Education, from North Dakota State University.

At BHSU, Nero directs multiple choral ensembles, including Concert Choir, Chamber Singers, and the Northern Hills Chamber Choral. His ensembles have performed for American Choral Directors Association conferences and alongside the South Dakota Symphony Orchestra. 

One of Nero’s most celebrated contributions is his creation and continued leadership of the annual BHSU Madrigal Dinner, a fully immersive production blending choral performance, theater, and historical storytelling.  

Beyond the stage, Nero is deeply committed to outreach and music education. He regularly organizes clinics for hundreds of high school students across the region and has served as a clinician and guest conductor at events including the SDMEA Elementary Honor Choir and multiple state and regional music festivals. He has also served as artistic director of the Dakota Choral Union and Kantorei.

In the classroom, Nero is recognized for his commitment to student development across academic, musical, and personal dimensions. Colleagues note that he regularly supports students outside of his own courses and maintains a welcoming environment within the choral program. 

Nero also serves the University through committee work, including the Promotion and Tenure Committee and is the liaison between the Music Department and the Friends of Music to coordinate fundraising. Nero is a current member of the American Choral Directors Association, Music Educators National Conference, National Collegiate Choral Association, and Chorus America.

Knox came to Spearfish from Memphis, and brought more than 25 years if experience in corporate law to the job. He has served as city attorney since Oct. 16, 2026.

title: North Haines Ave. to  be closed for construction
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
North Haines Ave. to  be closed for construction
Courtesy photo 

RAPID CITY — North Haines Avenue will be closed to through-traffic when reconstruction of the road starts, Meade County Commissioners said Tuesday. 

Meade County Highway Superintendent Troy Eastman said the $3.1 million reconstruction project is scheduled to start on May 4. Eastman said once Western Construction and subcontractors start putting down base stabilization, they will need to keep traffic off of the road for at least 72 hours. Eastman said there will always be at least one lane open during construction for local traffic only. 

“In order to ensure the quality of the base we need to do whatever we can to keep cars off of it,” Eastman said. “It’s hard to stop people form (driving on it) without shutting it completely down. So I think that’s gonna have to happen at some point. I mean, people will still have access, the ones who live there, but we need to make sure that we avoid damaging the project.” 

Commissioner Rich Liggett said residents who don’t live in that immediate area, but who use Haines Avenue to access their property, need to start planning alternate routes. 

“People in the Golden Valley area need to drive around,” Liggett said. “I want to stress it is not open for traffic during that time. Anybody that lives to the north of the project needs to go around. Go down Erickson Ranch Road. Go down Elk Vale.” 

The project is located from a half mile south of Peterson Road to about a quarter mile north of Husker Place, and about 4 miles of the remaining Haines Avenue stretch in that area. 

Liggett said the road is scheduled to be shut down for about a month and a half, on May 5. 

In the meantime, commissioners urged motorists to observe the 35 mile an hour speed limit on Haines Avenue. On April 9, the Meade County Sheriff’s Office announced that deputies arrested a motorist who was traveling 102 miles per hour in the 35 miles per hour zone. Commissioner Doreen Creed said traveling at that speed is dangerous, no matter what the road conditions are.

title: A race to repair Main Street: Spearfish faces down summer event season  as negotiations continue
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Events like the Corvette and Camaro rallies, that bring show cars to Main Street in Spearfish, have citizens and community leaders concerned about the state of the road and the timeline for chip seal repairs. Pioneer file photos
_full_text:
Chip seal 1.JPG
Events like the Corvette and Camaro rallies, that bring show cars to Main Street in Spearfish, have citizens and community leaders concerned about the state of the road and the timeline for chip seal repairs. Pioneer file photos 

 Chip seal 2.JPG
Pioneer file photo 

SPEARFISH — Downtown Friday Nights kick off June 12. The Black Hills Camaro Rally is scheduled for June 17-20. The Black Hills Corvette Classic comes to Spearfish July 16-17. Each of the 3 events has one thing in common. They generally shut down Main Street — drawing crowds of pedestrians to the city center.

The condition of Main Street is a topic of concern, after a chip seal project this fall failed.

This week, the Spearfish City Council continued to discuss its options to improve the quality of the street’s surface and potentially address concerns about dust, debris, and pavement markings that citizens have brought to city leaders’ attention.

The contractor on the chip seal project, Dakota Asphalt, has acknowledged that their effort failed. They are working actively with the city’s public works department and attorney, and have offered to redo its chip seal operation on Colorado Boulevard from the mouth of Spearfish Canyon to Jackson Boulevard.

“The downtown area will need to be completed prior to June 12 when we start the Downtown Friday Nights events, and if they are not able to complete the remainder of the project at the same time, those other portions will need to be completed between the Camaro Rally and the Corvette Rally to minimize the impacts to those events,” Public Works Director Adam McMahon said.

The city never accepted the chip seal project, which started on Sept. 30. The city attorney, David Knox, and McMahon remain in negotiations with Dakota Asphalt.

“I would say I am in favor of chip seal. Obviously, the contractor is not happy with the product. We’ll trust that you have been working on great things with David on that,” Councilman Scott Hourigan said. “I, however, would be in favor of exploring the option of downtown Main Street mill and overlay (in the long term).”

McMahon said the city could allow Dakota Asphalt to chip seal again, evaluate the result, and explore mill and overlay in the future.

Mayor John Senden said chip seal could work as a long-term solution — citing a successful chip seal project on Evans Lane and another on Colorado Boulevard from Exit 14 to Exit 17.

“Mill and overlay, we certainly can do it, but we can budget it and do that part next year, but we might not need to if this turns into a success,” Senden said. “I emailed out to council a couple of things regarding the downtown project … I don’t know if any of you had an opportunity to, but if Evans Lane or Colorado (Boulevard), where Adam had indicated, if you had gone out and looked at that, we wouldn’t be having this discussion. It would be a chip and seal that would be acceptable for a period of time to buy us some additional life.”

Not everyone on the council was convinced that chip seal would be the best option.

“Full transparency, I am kind of concerned. How can we be assured that the quality will be different this time from the first time?” Councilman Larry Klarenbeek said. “The reason I ask that is that there are a lot of things involved in that, not just the application. We’ve heard issues with the businesses complaining about tracking in. That’s an issue. Then there are issues with folks and their vehicles. They are experiencing challenges with the finish, and how do you get that off of your vehicle? I would personally really like to see Main Street separated out of this, negotiated out of this, and that we would do a mill and overlay.”

Spearfish resident and business owner Doug Markworth raised concerns about the effect of chip seal on vehicle paint and finish. Loose chips and dust, often natural side effects of the chip seal process, might impede summer events too.

“My concern is, not only do we have the citizens’ vehicles that you guys mentioned, but our guests that we’ve invited with Corvettes and Camaros. If we do this, and we’ve got loose material kicking up, I know those are their babies,” Markworth said. “I would just say, there is a petition going on … the goal is to mill and overlay downtown and have a showpiece.”

To complete mill and overlay work, the project may need to go out to bid, extending its timeline. Then all of the work would need to be expedited, which McMahon said would almost certainly add expense.

“As far as mill and overlay, we are in the range of $500,000. There is also some other utility work that we would prefer to do, but that would be a longer-range project to get all of that scoped and planned,” McMahon said. He said that scoping, bidding, and finishing the project is “potentially doable.”

As a long-term option, McMahon also pitched paving the downtown core with concrete, rather than asphalt.

“It is something a lot more permanent. It results in a lot fewer future interruptions to business for shutting down those blocks or road maintenance, but it also comes at a lot higher cost,” McMahon said. “Over the life of the pavement, concrete is still more expensive.”

McMahon said, for three blocks of Main Street, concrete surfacing would likely cost more than $1 million.

Councilman Dean Myers asked McMahon if, given that mill and overlay might be difficult and pricey, the city might close Main Street all at once to redo the chip seal.

McMahon said that it is still subject to negotiation and may ultimately be up to the contractor.

“Typically, we avoid dictating means and methods, which is what we call that,” McMahon said. Contractors are obligated to reach the city’s goals under contract, but the city may be limited in its ability to dictate how those goals are achieved.

“We tell them what our end result goals are and they decide the best way to do that moving forward,” McMahon said.

Dust and debris mitigation measures, like adding sand to the chips or using water later in the process, were discussed by the council, but McMahon said those may or may not be employed by the contractor.

Discussions with Dakota Asphalt are ongoing, and the city council did not make any decision this week.

title: Tips sought on mountain goat death
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — On April 8, a dead mountain goat was found at the base of Bridal Veil Falls in Spearfish Canyon.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — On April 8, a dead mountain goat was found at the base of Bridal Veil Falls in Spearfish Canyon. 

That has prompted the South Dakota Game, Fish and Parks Department to seek tips from the public, not because it died, but rather that between the time that it was first reported to the GF&P and when staffers arrived, someone had removed the head and much of the neck of the animal.

Under South Dakota Codified Law 41-14-32, it is prohibited to unlawfully take, possess, sell, or transport birds, animals, or fish — including any parts of those animals. A mountain goat is classified as big game, making the crime a Class 1 misdemeanor.

Les Heiserman is a Spearfish photographer who frequently takes pictures of the mountain goats in the Canyon and who has become the unofficial go-to guy for information on the animals as even the GF&P uses his data collected in monitoring the herd. Heiserman said he talked to a GF&P biologist who said the billy, or male goat, likely either fell from the cliffs above, or was struck by a vehicle.

Heiserman did not personally see the animal, but has seen photos of it and believes it is a full-grown male. 

“It’s hard to know how old it was without the horns and teeth,” he said.

An examination of growth and wear helps biologists age the animals.

The goats, which can frequently be seen along the road, can just as often be spotted on the cliffs above — in places, well, only a mountain goat would go. Even the youngsters venture up the cliffs. The inside of the bottom of their hooves are soft allowing them to grip to the tiniest of nobs giving them traction. The outside of the hooves are hard.

Despite being nimble, the goats can and do fall from cliffs. Heiserman has seen them fall.

“But they always get up and recover,” he said. “They’re careful, but that goes with the territory.”

Mountain goats are not native to the Black Hills.

In 1924, Custer State Park officials obtained 6 mountain goats from Alberta, Canada, and placed them in a zoo at the park. The first night in the zoo, 2 goats escaped. By 1929, the rest of the goats had escaped. This was the beginning of the goat herd in the Hills.

Fast forward nearly a century. In 2013, a pregnant mountain goat ran away from her herd along the Needles Highway, where the majority of animals called home. She found shelter in the Spearfish Canyon. That spring, she gave birth to a billy, and sometime after that, she and her little billy had baby goats — together. The goats give birth in May and June.

That was the beginning of the current herd of mountain goats in the Spearfish Canyon.

Heiserman first noticed the nanny, a female mountain goat, in 2016 in the Canyon. He dubbed her “Granny Nanny.” Now, a decade later, the herd has expanded.

“They’ve really spread out,” Heiserman said. “They run the length of the Canyon from below Community Caves to above Savoy. They no longer are just seen within a mile of Bridal Veil Falls.”

Anyone with information about this incident is encouraged to contact the Turn In Poachers (TIPs) hotline at 1-888-OVERBAG (1-888-683-7224) or call local wildlife conservation officer at (605) 381-4704, or submit a secure online report.

Callers may remain completely anonymous. Individuals who provide information leading to a successful prosecution are eligible for a cash reward.

title: Quick picks: Kid Librarian
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Quick picks: Kid Librarian
Courtesy photo 

Every month, the Piedmont Valley Library nominates a ‘kid librarian’ from the community, to share the books they love to read with their peers. This week, our 6 picks come straight from April Kid Librarian Allison. Allison is 8, and loves to listen to audiobooks when she’s bored. Thanks for the recommendations, Allison! 

1. “Black Beauty” by Anna Sewell 

Genre: Classics

As a young horse, Black Beauty is well loved and happy. But when his owner is forced to sell him, his life changes drastically. He has many new owners — some of them cruel and some of them kind. All he needs is someone to love him again.

2. “The Fascinating Bug Book For Kids: 500 Startling Facts” by Krystal Monuque Toney 

Genre: Non-fiction, animals

Have you ever wondered how many bugs there are on Earth? Or which ones can fly the highest? “The Fascinating Bug Book for Kids” is packed with 500 incredible facts about insects, arachnids, crustaceans and other creepy crawlies for hours of exploration. Find full-color pictures that uncover life as a bug, alongside trivia about termite towers, beautiful butterflies, cool cocoons, and more. You’ll discover secrets of these amazing creatures,

3. “Sunset of the Sabertooth” by Mary Pope Osborne

Genre: Children’s fantasy

The Ice Age is very cool ... for two kids in bathing suits! Jack and Annie nearly freeze when the Magic Tree House whisks them back to the time of cave people and woolly mammoths. But nothing can stop them from having another wild adventure — not even a saber-toothed tiger. 

4. “Junie B. Jones Smells Something Fishy” by Barbara Park

Genre: Chapter book

Meet the world’s funniest kindergartner — Junie B. Jones! There’s going to be a pet day at school, only guess what? No dogs allowed! And that’s the only kind of pet Junie B. has! If Mother and Daddy won’t buy her a new pet, Junie B. will just have to find one on her own. Like maybe a jar of ants. Or a wiggly worm. Or — could it be — something even better?

5. “Ballet Backflip” by Meredith Costain 

Genre: Children’s fiction

Ella dreams of being the lead in the ballet recital, but she also wants to be taken seriously. She’s in Year 5 after all! When Mean Queen Peach takes up gymnastics, and executes an amazing backflip in the playground, the school is taken over by the new craze. Will Ella backflip on her love of ballet? Can she bear to go along with Peach and her traitorous BFF Zoe?

6. “Handbook to the Galar Region” 

Genre: Fiction

The new Galar Region Pokémon are here, and kids gotta catch ‘em all! The Handbook to the Galar Region has all the stats and facts kids need to know about the brand-new Pokémon from Sword and Shield, the new games for Nintendo Switch. Meet all the Pokémon of Galar, a brand-new region! Every amazing Pokémon featured in the new Sword & Shield video games is included in this comprehensive handbook.

title: American Legion Post 164 celebrates 107th birthday
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: SPEARFISH — The American Legion Post 164 celebrated its 107th birthday and annual awards dinner Saturday, honoring individuals and organizations whose service, leadership, and compassion reflect the Legion’s core values.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — The American Legion Post 164 celebrated its 107th birthday and annual awards dinner Saturday, honoring individuals and organizations whose service, leadership, and compassion reflect the Legion’s core values.

The evening highlighted excellence in education, community service, and veteran advocacy, while also recognizing outstanding members across the Legion Family. Several honorees will advance to Department (state) level competition.

Educator of the Year: Anton Peterson

Anton Peterson was recognized as Educator of the Year at both the Post and District levels.

A veteran of more than 20 years in the United States Air Force, Peterson now serves as a seventh-grade math teacher at Spearfish Middle School. He inspires students through hands-on learning, high expectations, and genuine care.

Beyond the classroom, he mentors students through Student Council, archery, and community-based projects, helping shape confident, engaged citizens. He will now advance to state-level competition.

Good Samaritan of the Year: Auxiliary Unit 164

The Spearfish American Legion Auxiliary Unit 164 was honored as Good Samaritan of the Year at both the Post and District levels.

The unit provides year-round service to veterans, families, and the community through outreach programs, youth support, and partnerships with local organizations.

In the past year, Unit 164 assisted 1,620 veterans, supported 2,048 children, contributed 1,651 volunteer hours, and donated more than $13,000 to community causes. They will now advance to the state level.

Legionnaire of the Year: John Herweh

John Herweh was named Legionnaire of the Year at both the Post and District levels.

A dedicated Legionnaire, Herweh consistently steps forward to volunteer and bring new ideas to the Post. Despite the demands of full-time work and raising a family, he remains actively engaged in supporting Legion programs.

He led the post’s inagural 2.2 Mile Walk for Heroes – Be the One, coordinating fundraising efforts and organizing a successful event that brought together more than 70 participants.

“Be the One” is the American Legion’s national initiative focused on preventing veteran suicide, encouraging individuals to reach out and support veterans in need.

Herweh will now advance to state-level competition.

Legion Family Members of the Year

The evening also recognized outstanding individuals across the Legion Family for their dedication and service:

Hope Herweh, Auxiliary Unit 164 Junior Member of the Year, for her compassion, positive spirit, and commitment to helping others.

Geney Holley, Auxiliary Unit Member of the Year, for her leadership as Unit Chaplain and her meaningful contributions across numerous programs and events.

Doug Henwood, Sons of the American Legion Squadron 164 Member of the Year, for his continued leadership and dedication to the Legion’s mission.

Buck DeWeese, American Legion Riders-Black Hills Chapter Rider of the Year, for his unwavering support of veterans, including funeral escorts, outreach, and community service.

The annual awards dinner serves as a powerful reminder of the strength and character found within the Spearfish community. Through their dedication to service, these individuals and organizations continue to make a lasting impact on veterans, families, and future generations.

As several honorees advance to state-level competition, they carry with them the pride and support of the entire community.

title: Windstorm, fire recovery efforts continue in Custer State Park
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: CUSTER — Recovery efforts continue in Custer State Park, after a December windstorm and a major fire in March caused significant damage.
_full_text:
CUSTER — Recovery efforts continue in Custer State Park, after a December windstorm and a major fire in March caused significant damage.   

Matt Snyder, regional park supervisor for the South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks, told members of the GF&P Commission recently that the park is still working with loggers to clear out debris from a major windstorm that hit the park, Dec. 18. The storm with 48 hours of wind gusts of 94 to 122 miles per hour, caused extensive damage throughout the park, and knocked all power out for about 6 days. The South Dakota Department of Transportation, Department of Corrections, and South Dakota Wildland Fire assisted with recovery efforts. Statewide, Snyder said park staff came from outside of Custer State Park, and from mid-January through February they averaged about 78 full time staff, who logged more than 10,000 hours cleaning up. 

Snyder said the staff hauled 1,400 tons of material to Sylvan and Center lakes, and to the State Game Lodge. The GF&P contracted with Baker Timber to grind the remains and to haul it away. 

Snyder said there are about 12 units in the park where timber crews could operate to clear brush and debris, but there are many areas that are inoperable because crews won’t be able to get equipment in for work. Of those 12 units, Snyder said the GF&P has sold 5 for timber sales — 4 near the Wildlife Loop Road and one behind the Coolidge store. So far, he said, crews have taken about 2,900 tons, with 139 loads of merchantable chips. Much of the timber is not useable though, Snyder said, and the park has had to bear the cost of that removal. 

On the southern side of Custer State Park, near Highway 87, Snyder said Morgan Logging has been clearing the area for firewood. To date, he said they have removed about 180 tons. 

Snyder said there are still about 7 logging units in the park that are not under contract, because loggers are hard to find. 

“A major change over the last 5 to 7 years with the closing of Neiman’s mill in Hill City, we’ve lost a lot of our loggers,” Snyder said. “We had loggers galore when we were in our pine beetle era. Now, it’s a lost business. They’re just not there anymore.” 

Part of the problem, he said, are that the logs from the wind storm are twisted and broken, making them unusable for planks. The only thing they can be used for, he said, is firewood or wood chips. 

“You have one contractor that does chipping in the Black Hills, and you got a few firewood vendors,” he said. “But there’s wood galore wherever you want to go.” 

To put it into perspective, Snyder said logging companies paid $1.50 to $2 per ton for salvageable logs after the Legion Lake fire in 2017. After the December windstorm, he said Baker is paying 25 cents a ton and Morgan is paying the GF&P 2 cents a ton for the logs. 

“It wasn’t about the money,” he said. “It was about trying to get this stuff off the landscape. So we’re going to continually work with them to see if they’ll continue to maybe look at taking some more areas off our hands and continually clean things out for us.” 

So far, Snyder said Custer State Park has spent about $186,000 in direct recovery efforts from that windstorm. Equipment and in-kind costs that were submitted to the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) are at nearly $700,000. Custer State Park Resort Company reported it had 82 facilities that sustained more than $510,000 in damage. 

Much of that damage has been repaired already, Snyder said. 

“We’re pretty much back in shape,” he said. “There are a couple of things we’re waiting on for a little better weather for shingling, but otherwise we’re going to be in good shape for the summer.” 

The Qury Fire, which started March 13, burned a total of 9,100 acres east of Custer, with about 1,200 acres burned in the park. No park structures were lost in the fire, and Snyder said geography and thinning activities helped the fire on Custer State Park lands stay close to the ground. At one point, he said the fire raged around Mount Coolidge, but because of the structure’s height and geography, winds blew the fire around it and over a 13-acre slope over U.S. Highway 87. 

“if the head of the fire would have come more south of Mount Coolidge, the winds would have drawn it over Highway 87 more and we would have seen more fire in the park,” he said. “We had done some thinning in years past, so that helped it stay on the ground. There are some places on forest service land and private areas, where the fire burned very intense.” 

Overall, Snyder reported there were about 319 personnel working the Qury Fire, with crews from the U.S. Forest Service, GF&P personnel, and volunteer fire departments from across the state and the nation. 

Despite the fire, Snyder said Custer State Park trails are open, and resort facilities are set to open May 1. 

“We are preparing just like a normal season,” he said. “I’d be lying if I didn’t say the staff are tired. But the staff in the park area are rebuilding. We’ve had to do stuff like this before. It’s just a matter of tying your shoe a little tighter, and out you go. Everybody just pitched in and did what they needed to do.”

title: Meade County passes burn ban changes
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Major changes to the Meade County burn ban ordinance mean the chairman of the county commission can declare an emergency ban, and fires are automatically prohibited during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

 

STURGIS — Major changes to the Meade County burn ban ordinance mean the chairman of the county commission can declare an emergency ban, and fires are automatically prohibited during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. 

On Tuesday, the Meade County Commission gave its first nod to the new ordinance, which states that no person shall set an open fire when the Grassland Fire Danger Index is at the high, very high, or extreme category. Changes to the ordinance give the chairman of the Meade County Commission the power to declare an emergency burn ban on open fires, that will remain effective until the next regularly scheduled county commission meeting. The ordinance requires the commission board chairman to notify the sheriff and Meade County dispatch about the emergency ban. 

The change comes after high winds and temperatures have raised concerns about severe fire danger in Meade County. This year there have been multiple small fires, and at least one large grass fire that burned 60 acres near Bear Butte State Park on Gravel Road. 

In previous years, the Meade County Commission has issued a resolution, banning open fires during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. However, with the new ordinance, the ban is set in place to automatically ban all fires in the county for 14 days before, and 7 days after the Rally.

title: Lawrence Co. Board of Equalization  delivers annual report, shows  housing market may be leveling out
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Lawrence County Board of Equalization delivered an annual report Tuesday, showing that the county continues to increase in overall growth and assessed value. The report hints that the discrepancy between assessed value and market value could be closing. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
BoardEqualization.jpg
The Lawrence County Board of Equalization delivered an annual report Tuesday, showing that the county continues to increase in overall growth and assessed value. The report hints that the discrepancy between assessed value and market value could be closing. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

DEADWOOD — The housing market could be leveling out after the upheaval lasting from 2021 to 2025 according to the Lawrence County Board of Equalization’s annual review, hinting that the gap between assessed value and market values of property could be closing.

According to the report, the preliminary sales ratio, determining the difference between assessed value and taxable value, continues to climb from 86.2% in 2025 to 86.96% this year. Brett Runge, director of equalization, said that the county has not received a factor from the state determining what value a property will be taxed at, but her office’s preliminary guess stands at 0.977. If the factor granted by the state is accurate to Runge’s office’s guess, she said a property with an assessed value of $100,000 would be taxed at a value of $97,700.

Runge said that the gap is closing, in part, because sales prices and market values are beginning to stabilize. 

“Last year, we were at 86.2% and it took a larger increase in assessment values to get to that percentage,” she said. “Our overall county value increased by 9.9%. This year, our overall county value increased only 5% to get a preliminary sales ration of 86.96%.”

Runge reported 625 “good sales” on all properties excluding agriculture last year, up from 573 in last year’s report. 

Runge said that a good sale, “requires that buyer and seller are informed and knowledgeable about the property, the property is offered on the open market for a reasonable amount of time, a willing buyer and a willing seller, and not sold under duress or with creative financing terms.”

“The state wants us and all counties to be at 100% of market value.  We perform a sales analysis of all the good sales in the county,” said Runge.  “We research the sales to make sure it is a good sale, see if we have missed anything about the property (if they finished a basement or remodeled the house) and call buyers or sellers to get more information.  We look at the sales to see if we need to raise or lower an entire area/neighborhood, so it is important that the sales are good sales, and the property information is correct.  Also, the State audits our sales and then calculates a factor from our median sales ratio (how close we are to market value).  The assessed value is multiplied by the state factor to come up with the taxable value. That state factor adjusts our full and true assessed values down or up to 85% of market value.  All counties in the state have an initial sales ratio calculated from their sales and the state gives them a factor to adjust their taxable values to 85% of market.  The taxable value is the amount that the mill levy is multiplied against to come up with the tax amount.”

Runge said that new legislation in 2025 changed the way her office was able to increase overall owner-occupied value last year and add value from building permit growth. Overall owner-occupied value in the county can only increase by 3% due to reappraisal. Growth is not included in that percentage. Runge reported that last year, owner occupied properties across the county increased by approximately 2.2% after reappraisal.

“When we go out to look at building permits, if an owner-occupied property, for example, has a deck put on, unless the value of that deck is 40% of the total value of the property, we can’t count it as growth. Which, before, we could have,” said Runge. “So, we’re going to have a lot less growth because of that. Decks, driveways, even maybe small additions or porches that won’t be 40% of the whole value so we won’t be able to count it.”

The overall assessment in the county increased by 5%, Runge said, increasing by $297,095,270 from 2024. Runge said that value has been larger in previous years, and attributes the lower number to the change in legislation.

After 4 tax increment financing (TIF) districts were dissolved between Spearfish and Deadwood in 2025, preliminary growth in the county jumped from $129,995,866 to $238,528,616. Runge said $130,089,798 of last year’s growth can be contributed to the dissolution of the TIF districts. 

“When they build houses or commercial buildings in these TIF districts, it doesn’t get added (to the preliminary growth) until that TIF district is dissolved,” said Runge. “So, the cities and the county doesn’t get any growth from that for years and then all of a sudden, boom, they dissolve, and they get it.”

Runge reported that the total number of parcels increased from 21,188 to 21,422 across the county and building permits continue to rise. She reported that between Aug. 1, 2024, to July 31, 2025, the county issued 919 building permits. That number is up 14 from the same period last year. 

“I was actually surprised there were that many compared to the year before,” said Runge. “I thought it might have slowed down a little bit, but we have so many houses being built out at Powder House and some of the new developments out by Whitewood and Spearfish. So, we’re still pretty strong as far as building permits.”

Runge said her office reappraised 1,118 parcels last year, most of which were located in the city of Lead and hadn’t been reappraised since approximately 2005. Last year, Runge and her team created a new 10-year cycle, planning to decrease the amount of time between reappraisals with new technology and more concentrated efforts.
