title: Prison reform group to hear public comment and plans for seminary program, drug treatment
byline: By John Hult Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: South Dakota’s Project Prison Reset group, which endorsed a $650 million prison in 2025, is pictured at a meeting in April of that year at the Military Heritage Alliance in Sioux Falls. Another group of officials called the Correctional Rehabilitation Task Force, formed following the new prison’s approval by lawmakers last fall, will meet today, at the same location to talk about reforms meant to address the state’s high level of repeat offenders. Photo by John Hult, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Prison reform group will hear public comment and plans for seminary program, drug treatment.jpg
South Dakota’s Project Prison Reset group, which endorsed a $650 million prison in 2025, is pictured at a meeting in April of that year at the Military Heritage Alliance in Sioux Falls. Another group of officials called the Correctional Rehabilitation Task Force, formed following the new prison’s approval by lawmakers last fall, will meet today, at the same location to talk about reforms meant to address the state’s high level of repeat offenders. Photo by John Hult, South Dakota Searchlight 

SIOUX FALLS — Members of a Correctional Rehabilitation Task Force plan to talk through South Dakota’s options for a prison seminary program, learn more about behavioral health at a soon-to-open Rapid City women’s prison and take comments from the public on Wednesday.

The third meeting of the task force will begin at 10:30 a.m. Central time at the Military Heritage Alliance in Sioux Falls, about an hour and a half after the planned groundbreaking for a $650 million men’s prison on a plot of undeveloped land a few miles to northeast. 

Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden formed the task force in the run-up to a special legislative session vote in September on the men’s prison, an outgrowth of a separate task force dubbed Project Prison Reset. The reset group was formed in the wake of the Legislature’s rejection in early 2025 of a more expensive plan to replace the oldest buildings on the South Dakota State Penitentiary campus in Sioux Falls, and Rhoden said the work of the rehabilitation task force would help guide discussions on how a new facility would address ongoing issues with repeat offenders, security and societal reentry within the Department of Corrections.

Around half of exiting inmates return to prison within three years of release — a higher average than neighboring states. 

The rehabilitation group is led by Lt. Gov. Tony Venhuizen, who also served as chairman of the prison construction task force.

The agenda for Wednesday’s meeting includes a presentation on the findings from a multi-month study of South Dakota’s existing prison programming, conducted by the Council of State Governments Justice Center. The nonprofit organization has a $160,000 contract with the state to offer technical support to the task force through March 2027. 

The meeting will also include a presentation from Northwestern College, a Christian university in Orange City, Iowa, on how it might operate a prison seminary program endorsed by the rehabilitation task force’s faith-based subcommittee and Rhoden. The program would train inmates to serve as degreed seminarians and faith leaders within the state’s prison system, using a curriculum developed in Louisiana in 1995 that’s since spread to several facilities across the U.S.

Corrections Secretary Nick Lamb told the task force in December he was initially skeptical of the program’s value until he saw it implemented in Illinois, where Lamb worked as a prison administrator for several years before stints in New Mexico and Iowa.

A leader of the department’s behavioral health system will also offer a rundown of programming at a new $87 million women’s prison that’s nearing completion in Rapid City. The new prison includes a building devoted to a mother-infant program, which lets qualifying inmate mothers live full-time with their babies under supervision. The program has shown promise since its implementation at the Pierre women’s prison in 2022, officials say.

Venhuizen, in a commentary published by The Dakota Scout, said the new women’s prison will also include a drug therapeutic treatment unit large enough to serve 96 inmates at the 288-bed facility. He also pointed to recent investments in security meant to stem the flow of illegal drugs into state prison facilities.

Just under half the women imprisoned in South Dakota are serving sentences for drug offenses, according to the state’s most recent Department of Corrections Annual Statistical Report, and eight inmates died from drug overdoses in 2025 in South Dakota prisons. 

The task force is scheduled to take comments from members of the public starting at 2:15 p.m. Wednesday. A tour of the penitentiary campus in Sioux Falls, open only to task force members, will follow the meeting’s adjournment at 3 p.m.

title: US military pushes for boost in 2027 spending  on drones and air defenses used in Iran war
description: U.S. Army Sgt. Kevin Tran, assigned to 173rd Airborne Brigade, sets up a one-way attack Hornet drone during a demonstration in the 7th Army Training Command’s Grafenwoehr Training Area, Germany, March 25, 2026. The demonstration provided leaders with insight into how AI-enabled one-way attack systems operate alongside Army fires formations. (U.S. Army photo by Spc. Thomas Dixon)
_full_text:
US military pushes for boost in 2027 spending  on drones and air defenses used in Iran war
U.S. Army Sgt. Kevin Tran, assigned to 173rd Airborne Brigade, sets up a one-way attack Hornet drone during a demonstration in the 7th Army Training Command’s Grafenwoehr Training Area, Germany, March 25, 2026. The demonstration provided leaders with insight into how AI-enabled one-way attack systems operate alongside Army fires formations. (U.S. Army photo by Spc. Thomas Dixon) 

WASHINGTON (AP) — U.S. military officials on Tuesday called for spending tens of billions of dollars in the next budget year on drones, air defense systems and fighter jets that have been a key part of fighting the Iran war.

As part of President Donald Trump’s push to boost defense spending to $1.5 trillion in the 2027 budget, the Pentagon wants to triple spending on drones and related technology to more than $74 billion and invest over $30 billion into more critical munitions, including missile interceptors, whose stockpiles have become critically low during the Iran war.

Military officials said the spending blueprint was developed before the conflict in the Middle East. They also did not discuss how much they will request in additional funds for the war, which would be on top of what the White House is seeking to boost defense spending in the next budget year.

“The overlap, you’ll see, is the request for munitions, which is something we always need,” Jules Hurst III, acting undersecretary of defense and the Pentagon’s comptroller, told reporters at a briefing. “We always need to increase our magazine depth. But outside of that, there aren’t any operational costs in here from Iran.”

Heavy investment in drone warfare

The missile interceptors whose numbers are under the most strain are the Patriot and the Terminal High Altitude Area Defense, or THAAD, air defense systems. The THAAD system is designed for defeating medium-range ballistic missiles, while the Patriot system is for taking down short-range ballistic missiles and crewed aircraft. However, they both also were used to shoot down cheap Iranian drones.

The $30 billion budget item also would aim to purchase long-range Precision Strike Missiles and Mid-Range Capability missile systems used by the U.S. Army.

The budget proposal would allocate nearly $54 billion for military drones and related technology, as well as $21 billion for weapons systems designed to take down enemy drones.

Drones and other unmanned vehicles have emerged as a key weapon in the wars in Ukraine and Iran, and top Pentagon officials say the U.S. must significantly increase its funding of both drones and counter-drone systems.

“Drone warfare is rapidly reshaping the modern battlefield,” Hurst said. “This budget is the largest investment in drone warfare and counter drone technology in U.S. history.”

As part of the 2027 budget, the Pentagon also intends to grow the military by 44,500 troops, or more than 2%, spend more than $2 billion on operations on the U.S.-Mexico border and make the largest shipbuilding request since 1962.

Dramatic increase in the Navy’s Tomahawk missiles

While officials said the budget was developed before operations began in Iran, it featured major jumps in many of the missiles that have been used in the conflict. One of the most dramatic increases was in the choice for the Navy to increase of its purchase of the Tomahawk cruise missile from 55 missiles last year to 785 in this year’s budget.

The long-range cruise missile was heavily used in Iran and led to concerns from experts that the military was using it much faster than it could replenish its stocks.

Vice Adm. Ben Reynolds, the Navy’s budget boss, wouldn’t say if he expected all 785 Tomahawk missiles to be delivered within the year. He acknowledged that weapons production capacity “is absolutely the challenge” and, in the case of the Tomahawk, he said the Navy expects Raytheon — the company that makes it — “to invest very heavily now to be able to ramp up production.”

The services also are addressing the difficulty in producing the advanced munitions favored by the military by slowly shifting toward more basic weapons.

Major Gen. Frank Verdugo, the Air Force’s budget chief, said the Air Force wants to invest $600 million to develop “affordable” munitions as part of an effort to move away from “small numbers of exquisite weapons toward a future where we can overwhelm an adversary with sheer volume.”

Trump-endorsed battleship is missing

The Navy said it would be buying 18 more warships using more than $65 billion — a 46% increase from the previous year.

However, the Trump-endorsed battleship that was announced to great fanfare last year is not in this year’s budget, according to the briefing. Instead, the Navy is planning to pay for the first battleship in next year’s budget.

The military’s spending proposal also lacked money for repairing U.S. bases in the Middle East, which Hurst said would be part of a future request.

“Part of it is we would assess what our posture should be in the Middle East,” Hurst told reporters. “We have to make sure we understand what we want to construct in the future. We might change how we build bases in the Middle East based on this conflict.”

title: Spearfish council votes on future  of Main Street, Colorado Boulevard
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Main Street, from Jackson Boulevard to Grant Street will not be chip sealed again, following a 5-1 vote Monday. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Chip Seal 1.JPG
Main Street, from Jackson Boulevard to Grant Street will not be chip sealed again, following a 5-1 vote Monday. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — Main Street from Jackson Boulevard to Grant Street, will not be re-chip sealed by Dakota Asphalt, following a 5-1 vote from the Spearfish City Council Monday night. 

The council voted to mill and overlay Main Street, laying down asphalt instead of oil and chips.

The stretch of Main Street and Colorado Boulevard from Grant Street to Old Highway 14A at Spearfish Canyon is still on track to be chip sealed again. 

Public Works Director Adam McMahon told the council that the mill and overlay project will need to go out bid and could cost about $150,000-$200,000.

Dakota Asphalt has been locked in negotiations with the city for a few weeks. They recognize that the chip seal project on Main Street and Colorado Boulevard that got underway last fall failed. The city has not accepted the results of their work, and the project is not closed. City leaders had discussed allowing the contractor to chip seal all of Main Street and Colorado Boulevard a second time, to make good on their obligation to deliver a finished product. McMahon said Dakota Asphalt had offered to chip-seal the 3 blocks of downtown Spearfish by the last week of May.

“From listening to my constituents, we want nothing to do with chip sealing Main Street,” Councilwoman Jamie Hafner told the Black Hills Pioneer. “In my opinion, mill and overlay is a must.”  

Councilman Dean Myers asked City Attorney David Knox, who was attending his final meeting in his capacity as city attorney before taking a job elsewhere, if there was any reason why the city could not pursue mill and overlay for Main Street instead.

Knox said no.

“I made the motion because it seemed like we’ve been talking about chip seal for quite a few months now,” Myers told the Pioneer. “It became apparent that people were unhappy, particularly unhappy about Main Street. We were hearing, ‘Don’t chip seal Main Street again.’”

Myers said the city has done a lot of work to ensure that Main Street “looks wonderful,” and that the chip seal was “tacky” and ineffective.

Now, the city will need to open up the bidding process for contractors who are interested in performing mill and overlay. Then, the council can select the lowest responsive and responsible bid and cement a project timeline.

“I’m frustrated that we didn’t have these conversations sooner, because now it is crunch time,” Hafner said. “I really hope that we can get the mill and overlay completed this year.”

During Monday’s meeting, Councilman Scott Hourigan asked if Dakota Asphalt might be able to expand the scope of the chip seal project, which was never closed, to mill and overlay Main Street instead.

McMahon explained that expanding the scope and the project cost so significantly would likely not be permitted by state law.

“As far as amending the contract and applying the change order laws would be difficult. That change order amount would be in excess of what is allowable by state law for change orders. That is the reason for the current approach of continuing the repair work we currently have and treating the mill and overlay as a separate project,” McMahon told the council.

He said fall completion for a mill and overlay project would be a “best-case scenario.”

“People who have a good understanding of these kinds of projects say that we could mill and overlay in the late summer or early fall. If temperatures stay above 40 degrees, this could be done. We just need to get the bid out,” Myers said.

Myers initially made a motion directing city staff to plan to repair Main Street from Jackson Boulevard to Grant Street with a mill and overlay, and repair Main Street/Colorado Boulevard from Grant Street to Spearfish Canyon with a new chip seal. Councilman Larry Klarenbeek seconded Myers’ motion.

Then, there was a discussion of amending the motion for clarification.

The amended motion clarified that repairs should take place “as soon as possible.” The amended motion also declared the road was not to be chip-sealed again from Jackson Boulevard to Grant Street downtown between now and the application of an asphalt mill and overlay.

As recorded in the city council minutes, that motion directed city staff to “leave Main Street from Jackson Boulevard to Grant Street as is and plan to repair that area with a mill and overlay project as soon as possible, and to repair Main Street and Colorado Boulevard from Grant Street to Spearfish Canyon Highway 14A with a new chip seal as soon as possible.” Councilman Larry Klarenbeek voted against amending the motion, and passing the motion as amended.

The amended motion passed. The council will need to approve contract amendments with Dakota Asphalt, bids with a new contractor, and potentially budget supplements in the coming weeks to see the Main Street and Colorado Boulevard repair through to completion.

LEAD — The 22nd annual LEGO Contest and STEAM Fair drew 76 entries from participants of all ages, and many smiles as children from throughout the Northern Hills showed off their creations.

“The competition is always fierce and judging is very hard,” said Karen Everett, executive director of the Lead-Deadwood Arts Center, which organizes the event. “The creativity of the participants is wonderful to see.”

“I believe the LEGO Contest and STEAM Fair is the perfect event to showcase the spirit of Lead and its history of technology and engineering, from the early days of the Homestake Mine to the cutting edge science and technology at the Sanford Lab today,” Everett said. Lead has truly become the STEAM capital of South Dakota, and if any community should host and sponsor a LEGO contest, it is Lead.”

title: Milbank goes out on a limb to  save ash trees from invasive beetle
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Ash trees make up more than 50% of Milbank’s public tree canopy, including parks and its cemetery. Photo courtesy of city of Milbank
_full_text:
Milbank goes out on a limb to  save ash trees from invasive beetle
Ash trees make up more than 50% of Milbank’s public tree canopy, including parks and its cemetery. Photo courtesy of city of Milbank 

MILBANK — It would cost up to $4 million to cut down Milbank’s ash trees, after state and city officials detected a beetle last summer that threatens to decimate the northeastern South Dakota city’s tree canopy.

It’ll cost roughly 60% of that price, or $2.4 million over 12 years, to reach herd immunity against the emerald ash borer — and the city of roughly 3,500 people will keep most of its trees, said city administrator Steve Pendergrass.

Herd immunity, a term commonly used in public health, happens when a large percentage of a population becomes immune to a disease, either through vaccination and treatment or previous infection, making it difficult for the disease to spread.

Ash trees comprise over 50% of Milbank’s public tree canopy — 1,657 trees throughout the city’s parks, cemeteries and public right-of-way. The emerald ash borer, an eastern Asian beetle first detected in the United States in 2002, burrows under ash tree bark and eats the tree from the inside out. A chemical injection, applied with a needle-like device after drilling a hole into the tree, kills adult insects, preventing another generation of larvae and protecting the tree.

Many communities across the country — including Sioux Falls, the first place emerald ash borers were found in South Dakota in 2018 — have opted to remove a majority or all of their public ash trees. Pendergrass hopes to avoid that.

“We’re dealing with tax dollars. We need to make sure we’re practicing due diligence while also taking care of public safety and while taking care of as many trees as possible,” Pendergrass said.

Milbank’s approach can serve as an example for other cities across the state, said John Ball, forestry specialist with South Dakota State University Extension. Ash trees typically comprise one-third of a public tree canopy in cities.

“Herd immunity could be a technique applicable in slowing the spread of the insect, controlling the damage it does, and providing long-term survival,” Ball said.

Instead of halving its tree canopy, Milbank is removing about a third of its public ash trees in the next decade — those already too infested, planted too closely together or too small to be worth saving. Officials plan to treat one-sixth of the remaining trees every year, leaving the remainder untreated until they cycle through and treat the remaining trees over the next 12 years.

“Ash trees are tough and can tolerate a low population of emerald ash borer,” Ball said. “The problem is when you end up with incredibly high populations with an epidemic, which is what kills the tree.”

Emerald ash borer is slowly making its way across the state. Watertown in Codington County, just west of Milbank’s Grant County, is the farthest west the insect has been detected in the state so far. Ball expects the insect will infest ash trees throughout South Dakota by 2035.

Ball said other mitigation efforts have helped slow the spread, including firewood quarantines in affected counties. 

The South Dakota Game, Fish and Parks Department has been removing ash trees from developed areas of state parks for over a decade. Dakota Dunes benefited from conducting an inventory of their ash trees before emerald ash borer was identified there. The city gradually replaced young or damaged ash trees with new trees before emerald ash borers arrived. The strategy helped the community deal with the infestation without significantly impacting the overall tree canopy.

“They were well along on their plan before we confirmed emerald ash borer there. They’re one of the best in terms of getting on it early,” Ball said.

The treatment effort in Milbank will begin this spring, after ash trees leaf out in May. Hired tree care companies will treat another random one-third of trees two years after the initial treatment. The cycle will continue for over a decade until the beetle population declines. Removals of damaged trees will continue through 2030.

The result will save a majority of the city’s canopy, Pendergrass said. It contrasts with Sioux Falls’ effort to fell every public ash tree in the city. The city has removed 17,000 public ash trees, and it plans to have residents remove or treat the remaining 45,000 trees on private property.

In Milbank, more than 950 ash trees are in boulevards throughout the city, which Pendergrass said homeowners will be responsible for treating. Boulevards — the strip of grass between a street and sidewalk — are technically city property but are cared for by property owners.

“If residents don’t do their part with treatment, all we did was buy ourselves time,” Pendergrass said. “Ideally it buys us our trees and herd immunity works, but if nothing else, it buys us time to remove and replant.”

Milbank will plant about 30 trees every year for the foreseeable future, Pendergrass said. It’ll cost about $20,000 this year.

The selection of the new trees must be diverse, Ball said. Because there will likely be a new threat.

“I don’t know what’s out there and coming. But if only 5% of a tree canopy is affected, that’s almost a yawn compared to 30% or 50%,” Ball said. “One of the things we all need to learn from the emerald ash borer, and that people failed to learn with Dutch elm disease that wiped out a large portion of elm trees in the ’70s, is that we want to plant diversity.”

title: Forest Service plan to close research stations stokes fear as wildfire season approaches
byline: By Alex Brown Stateline
description: WASHINGTON, D.C. — The U.S. Forest Service’s plan to close scores of research stations could threaten the nation’s wildfire readiness, many foresters fear, and erode decades of work to understand timber production, soil health, pests and diseases, watersheds and wildlife.
_full_text:
StatelineLogo

WASHINGTON, D.C. — The U.S. Forest Service’s plan to close scores of research stations could threaten the nation’s wildfire readiness, many foresters fear, and erode decades of work to understand timber production, soil health, pests and diseases, watersheds and wildlife.

Late last month, the Forest Service announced plans to close 57 of its 77 research stations, located across 31 states, merging them into a single organization in Fort Collins, Colo.

The agency described the move as a way to consolidate, not cut, the agency’s scientific work, and “unify research priorities.”

It’s unclear how many scientists will be affected by the transition, but it comes as part of a larger agency reorganization that is expected to move roughly 5,000 employees to new outposts. Forest Service leaders have framed the closures as a way to reduce the agency’s real estate footprint, citing a facilities budget Congress has shrunk, as opposed to curtailing its scientific work.

But many longtime foresters fear the closures will threaten vital research that has been the backbone of forest management for state agencies, timber companies and tribes. Many of the research stations slated for closure study fire behavior, forecast smoke dispersal and help inform evacuation decisions.

“The research arm of the Forest Service is one of the unsung heroes in forest management around the world,” said Mike Dombeck, who served as chief of the Forest Service under President Bill Clinton and remains a vocal conservation advocate. “It is the premier forest research entity in the world, on everything from invasive species to wildland fire risk, watershed protection, basic silviculture and harvest methods.”

The Forest Service’s revamp also will relocate the agency’s headquarters from Washington, D.C., to Salt Lake City and restructure its regional management system.

The Forest Service did not grant a Stateline interview request. The agency has not said how much money it expects to save by closing the research stations.

Many Western leaders are skeptical that the consolidated operation will be able to replicate the work of the existing research stations. State officials said they’ve been given few details about how the transition will play out and whether existing research will continue.

In Washington state, the Forest Service plans to close research stations in Seattle and Wenatchee, while maintaining a facility in Olympia.

“The station in Seattle does some of the most practical-based research that we use for fire and forest management,” said Washington State Forester George Geissler. “We don’t want to lose that work. They’ve said they’ll keep Olympia open, but we don’t know what that looks like. Are they making sure we don’t lose the ongoing research?”

Forestry veterans say it’s important for the agency to continue its scientific work across a wide variety of forests and climates.

“This is research that’s been going on for decades or even a century or more,” said Kevin Hood, executive director of Forest Service Employees for Environmental Ethics, a nonprofit that advocates for agency workers. “They’re able to see how climate change impacts are playing out in a dry ponderosa forest or a humid hardwood forest. There are research plots and experimental forests that have been diligently studied for decades. This could be a loss of a lot of knowledge.”

The Pacific Wildland Fire Sciences Laboratory, for instance, plays a crucial role in issuing wildfire smoke forecasts that are relied on throughout the Northwest. After a hot, dry winter, that work could be critical as a dangerous wildfire season approaches.

In Vermont, the Burlington research station slated for closure studied maple syrup production and the effects of acid rain on different tree species, according to VTDigger.

And in Mississippi, the Southern Institute of Forest Genetics, also on the chopping block, has guided tree improvement programs that improved growth and pest resistance in Southern timber forests.

Some conservation advocates are concerned that the research station closures are aimed at suppressing studies that might show the environmental harms of logging or mining. President Donald Trump has pledged to increase timber production on federal lands. He has moved to limit environmental reviews and protections for endangered species to speed up logging projects.

In an interview with the Deseret News, Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz said that the move was designed to ensure that the Forest Service’s research “will better align with the priorities of the administration” — minerals, recreation, fire management and “active management” of forests, which can include timber harvests and thinning projects. He said the research would support not just forests but also private landowners.

“It’s not streamlining, it’s dismantling,” said Chandra Rosenthal, Western lands and Rocky Mountain advocate with Public Employees for Environmental Responsibility, a group that defends whistleblowers in the federal service. “It’s going to really impact how the Forest Service makes decisions on the ground. The way the Trump administration is trying to make a lot of decisions is gut feelings.”

In a webpage set up to respond to news coverage of the move, the Forest Service said it is a “myth” that the station closures will eliminate scientific positions or cancel research programs. But many forestry veterans said that attrition is inevitable, as researchers are asked to move their families across the country to work under a new model with few details.

“There’s concern that we’re going to see a lot of really good individuals who cannot uproot their families that we’ll lose,” said Geissler, the Washington state forester. “It’s taken a long time to develop that kind of expertise. It’s scary.”

Foresters in both conservative and liberal states said they rely heavily on the research the Forest Service provides. Most were unwilling to comment extensively about the closures without seeing more details.

“That work is absolutely important, and I sure hope it continues,” said Wyoming State Forester Kelly Norris. “I don’t think research should stop. It may need to look a little different.”

Some leaders said there may be opportunities for states, through forestry agencies and universities, to pick up the slack and ensure research continues, even if the Forest Service is no longer playing a lead role.

“This is still a little bit of an unknown area, but we’ll have to make sure that if there’s a gap there, that we’re working with our universities and (state) research centers to make sure that is still being provided,” said Utah State Forester Jamie Barnes.

Nick Smith, public affairs director with the American Forest Resource Council, a timber industry group, expressed support for the agency’s effort to consolidate its work, saying he’d had “limited interaction” with the research stations.

While some of the Forest Service’s work is controversial, agency veterans say its research program is valued by loggers and tree-huggers alike.

“Nobody was asking for this,” said Robert Bonnie, who served as undersecretary of agriculture for natural resources and environment during the Obama administration. “There was no call to do anything like this.”

title: Lead firefighters name Rasmussen as  firefighter of the year, elect new leadership
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Lead Volunteer Fire Department President Preston Morrison and Fire Chief Nathan Allen presented Jeff Rasmussen with the Firefighter of the Year award Saturday. Members of the department selected Rasmussen for the 2025 honor.
_full_text:
LFD firefighter of the year.JPG
Lead Volunteer Fire Department President Preston Morrison and Fire Chief Nathan Allen presented Jeff Rasmussen with the Firefighter of the Year award Saturday. Members of the department selected Rasmussen for the 2025 honor.  

LEAD — Members of the Lead Volunteer Fire Department selected Jeff Rasmussen as their firefighter of the year, welcomed new firefighters, and elected new leadership during the annual fire banquet, Saturday. 

New officers on the fire department include President Preston Morrison, Vice President Hayden Lindsay, Secretary Jeff Rasmussen, and Treasurer Jena Sierks. 

Lead Fire Chief Nathan Allen reported that in 2025 the Lead Volunteer Fire Department responded to 279 calls for service. Of those, Allen said 87 were fire related calls, which doesn’t necessarily mean they were all fires, but that the skills of the fire department were needed for the response. There were 174 calls for emergency medical services (EMS). Overall, Allen reported there were 4 building fires last year, 10 motor vehicle accidents with injuries, 8 gas leaks, 15 fire alarms, 5 smoke scares, 3 hazmat calls, 2 wildland fire calls, and more. Tuesdays were the busiest days for calls at the fire department, Allen said, with 160 calls coming in between 7 a.m. to 4:59 p.m., and 119 calls for service coming in between 5 p.m. and 6:59 a.m. 

Members of the Lead Volunteer Fire Department contributed a total of 400 hours to respond to calls for service, and participated in about 90 training hours. 

Allen was also recognized for his one-year anniversary as the full time head of the department. In April 2025, the Lead Fire Protection District approved the full time chief position to be a full time presence at the fire hall, a move that has resulted in 20% faster response times. Allen has also helped with recruitment at the department, training, and taking care of a variety of administrative duties necessary. 

“Our response time has improved significantly, especially during the day, especially during medical emergencies,” said Capt. Taylor Ballert before the banquet. “In medical emergencies, every minute counts, so even a 10% increase in response time is a big deal.” 

 lead fire dept new officers.JPG
Newly elected president and vice president Preston Morrison and Hayden Lindsay smile from their table during the annual Lead Volunteer Fire Department banquet, Saturday. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

Longtime firefighter Rob Carr said under his leadership, and the leadership of other veteran firefighters Ballert, Joe Perdue, Ryan Gray, and more, training and response times have been better than ever. 

“The leadership that is in place at the fire department right now is as good as it’s been in many, many years,” Carr said. “They put in a lot of extra hours, a lot of extra time. I would like to congratulate Nathan on his first full year as being full time fire chief. It’s made a huge difference, especially in recruiting and some of the training that’s going on. Our training has really stepped up. Were not just sitting in classrooms, watching videos and stuff, which was the norm for the first several years I was on the department. The leadership at the department is top notch and they inspire confidence in the rest of us. They lead from the top down.”

title: Poll: Johnson widens lead in SD GOP governor race
byline: By Alexander Rifaat South Dakota News Watch
description: PIERRE — With 7 weeks until the June 2 primary, U.S. House Rep. Dusty Johnson is close to avoiding a runoff in the race to secure the GOP nomination for governor, according to a new poll sponsored by South Dakota News Watch and the Chiesman Center for Democracy at the University of South Dakota.
_full_text:
SDNewsWatchLogo

PIERRE — With 7 weeks until the June 2 primary, U.S. House Rep. Dusty Johnson is close to avoiding a runoff in the race to secure the GOP nomination for governor, according to a new poll sponsored by South Dakota News Watch and the Chiesman Center for Democracy at the University of South Dakota.

In the contests for U.S. House of Representatives and U.S. Senate, state Attorney General Marty Jackley and U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds have solid leads over their challengers.

The scientific survey of 500 registered Republicans, conducted April 7-11 by Mason-Dixon Polling and Strategy, found Johnson leading the four-way contest for governor with 34% of likely GOP primary voters supporting his candidacy.

The other 3 candidates are effectively tied for second due to the margin of error being plus-or-minus 4.5%. State House Speaker Jon Hansen, of Dell Rapids, has 18% support from GOP voters, and Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden and Gov. Larry Rhoden both have 17%. Roughly 14% of those surveyed were undecided.

If no candidate receives at least 35% of the vote on the June 2 ballot, a runoff between the top two finishers will take place July 28. The winner of the contest will meet Democrat Dan Ahlers in the Nov. 3 general election.

Rhoden’s support drops; Hansen surges

While Johnson, who grew up in Pierre and lives in Mitchell, saw a 6-point increase from the News Watch/Chiesman poll conducted last October, Rhoden’s support fell 10 points.

Julia Hellwege, director of the Chiesman Center and USD associate professor in political science, said Rhoden’s association with his predecessor, former Gov. Kristi Noem, could be behind the drop in poll numbers.

“He has aligned himself closely with Noem. They worked closely together, and he continues to champion her and stand by her,” she said. “There’s a potential that has been a side effect.”

Rhoden served as lieutenant governor under Noem and became governor in January 2025 when President Donald Trump made her secretary of the Department of Homeland Security. He fired her last month after severe criticism.

Hellwege pointed out the poll found that Johnson even leads in West River, a stronghold for Rhoden, who is from Union Center east of Sturgis.

She said one candidate more than any other has been the main beneficiary of the declining support for the sitting governor.

“Anyone shifting from Rhoden is more likely to shift towards Hansen,” Hellwege said, noting that Hansen is a state lawmaker, like Rhoden was, who plays up his conservative Christian credentials.

Hellwege said in comparing the new poll results with those from last year, a certain pattern can be seen. That includes the surge in support for Hansen and Johnson, a decline in support for Rhoden, a stable level of support for Doeden and a lower number of undecided voters.

“My interpretation is many Rhoden voters in the last poll shifted to Hansen voters and the undecideds went to Johnson,” Hellwege said.

SD governor: Johnson in driver’s seat

Hellwege highlighted the extent to which the math favors Johnson.

“Even if all the undecided voters go to one of those second-place candidates, plus if you factor in the margin of error, they still would barely reach where Johnson is sitting right now,” Hellwege said.

Brad Coker, founder of Mason-Dixon Polling and Strategy, ranked as one of the least-biased and most-factual pollsters, also believes Johnson is in a comfortable position.

“Johnson is moving into the clear front-runner status,” he said.

“People know him. People like him, and that’s probably why he’s ahead right now. Whether he can hold on to that will depend on what the other campaigns – particularly Hansen’s – are able to do in the coming weeks,” Coker told News Watch, pointing to the poll results that found Johnson has a 47% favorability rating, the highest of any of the candidates.

Coker said Hansen has the best chance to challenge Johnson not only because his candidacy has seen the biggest increase in support but also due to not many people knowing him – yet.

“Hansen’s name recognition is only 73%. He’s still got 27% of the voters who don’t know who he is, which I think gives him a much higher ceiling than Doeden and Rhoden,” Coker said. “That tells me Hansen is getting some traction.”

On the flip side, Doeden’s 35% unfavorable rating and high name recognition indicate his support has mostly peaked, Coker said.

“He has a higher negative rating than positive rating, which tells me he’s got a core group behind him, but his growth potential is far more limited, especially since he has 89% name recognition,” Coker said.

The poll was conducted after the four candidates met in the March 31 KELO-TV debate but before the April 13 SDPB and South Dakota News Watch forum.

U.S. House: Jackley has comfortable lead

Since Johnson ran for governor, that opened up South Dakota’s only seat in the U.S. House of Representatives.

In that contest, Jackley – who is from Sturgis and previously served as U.S. attorney for the District of South Dakota – has a comfortable lead toward securing the GOP nomination.

According to the poll, he has 68% support from South Dakota Republican voters surveyed, well ahead of challenger James Bialota Jr., who has 12%, with 20% of respondents undecided.

“This primary is definitely in Jackley’s favor, even if all the undecideds move to Bialota,” Hellwege said.

The winner will face Democrat Nicole “Nikki” Gronli in the November general election.

U.S. Senate: Incumbent Rounds ahead by large margin

Rounds – who’s from Pierre and was South Dakota’s governor from 2003 to 2011 – also enjoys a sizable lead over his challenger.

“The fact that McNeal, who is vastly outspent by Rounds, is able to get up to 18% is commendable. But at the same time, I don’t think there’s any expectation that Rounds will not be able to hold on to that seat,” Hellwege said.

The winner will take on Democrat Julian Beaudion in November.

title: Democrats fail to field candidates for a majority of SD legislative seats
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — Democrats are running for 46 of South Dakota’s 105 legislative seats — leaving 56% of seats without a Democratic candidate.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — Democrats are running for 46 of South Dakota’s 105 legislative seats — leaving 56% of seats without a Democratic candidate.

That doesn’t bode well for the party ahead of November, said Michael Card, professor emeritus of political science at the University of South Dakota.

“It doesn’t put them in a position to actually put forward their ideological policy preferences and have much of a success at getting those enacted,” Card said.

In the state Senate alone, Democrats have failed to field a candidate for 22 seats, which is nearly two-thirds of the chamber. In the House, Democrats have failed to field a candidate for 38 seats, which is 54% of the chamber.

There is only one Democratic legislative primary in the state: a state Senate race in District 26, which includes the Rosebud Reservation. 

There are no statewide Democratic primaries, after announced candidates for governor and U.S. House dropped out or failed to gather enough petition signatures to make the ballot, leaving one Democrat in each of those races.

Statewide candidates will have less name recognition than Republican candidates ahead of the general election, since they didn’t have primaries, Card said. In the Legislature, Card said Democrats “are guaranteeing they won’t get a majority.”

In contrast, Republicans have primary races for governor, U.S. House and U.S. Senate. Five legislative districts do not have Republican primaries, but do have Republican candidates. There is a Republican candidate running for every legislative seat, except for one House seat in District 27, which includes the Pine Ridge Reservation.

Card said there are several factors leading to poor candidate turnout among Democrats, including a self-fulfilling cycle of failure.

“A lack of winning makes fewer people willing to take a chance on running for office,” Card said. “Why run if I think I’m going to lose?”

Democrats haven’t held a statewide office since 2015, and they haven’t held a majority of either legislative chamber since 1994.

Joe Zweifel, deputy executive director of the South Dakota Democratic Party, said the organization worked “really, really hard” to convince Democrats to run for office.

“But you can’t force people to run for office,” said Zweifel, of Sioux Falls, who’s running for a legislative seat himself in District 12.

He’s heard the open seats called a “failure.” But he disagrees, choosing to focus on the Democrats who did step forward.

“We’re running quality, good candidates in those races,” Zweifel said.

The South Dakota Democratic Party hopes to build on legislative successes, such as a new law from Rep. Kadyn Wittman, D-Sioux Falls, that commits state funding to cover the family portion of reduced-price school meals.

“That specifically is a return on investment for our donors, and it shows that Democrats are doing good things for the people of South Dakota,” Zweifel said.

Wittman’s success helped inspire Democratic District 13 House of Representatives candidate Ali Rae Horsted, of Sioux Falls, to take a second run at the Legislature. Horsted ran unsuccessfully for the Senate against Sen. Sue Peterson in 2024, garnering 42% of the vote.

Horsted plans to build on that success and the name recognition she already has in the district. She hopes she’ll have “better odds” in this election, since there are two House seats for every district.

Horsted said it would better serve South Dakota if the state had a more balanced Legislature. While the latest Legislature was 92% Republican, 52% of voters in South Dakota are Republican. South Dakota has the lowest percentage of Democrats, 7.6%, in the Legislature nationwide.

“I think it’s important that people have options on the ballot,” Horsted said, “and people are able to vote for candidates that represent their values and their vision for the future of South Dakota.”

title: Lawrence Co. commissioners speak out at candidate forum
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Incumbent Timm Comer and newcomer Mike Davies, pictured right, spoke at the Lawrence County Commission candidate forum Saturday, where they discussed issues such as conditional use permits, property tax relief, and conflicts of interest. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
1 Lawrence County candidate forum.jpg
Incumbent Timm Comer and newcomer Mike Davies, pictured right, spoke at the Lawrence County Commission candidate forum Saturday, where they discussed issues such as conditional use permits, property tax relief, and conflicts of interest. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

SPEARFISH — Lawrence County residents gathered at the Heritage Center in Spearfish, Saturday, to hear from the five candidates for the 3 open, 4-year county commission terms.

Candidates answered questions gathered from constituents, including how to monitor conditional use permits, declarations of conflicts of interest, and property tax relief for owner occupied properties.

Incumbents Timm Comer, Brandon Flanagan, and Eric Jennings were present alongside challengers Mike Davies and Robert Haiwick to answer questions received from constituents. 

Monitoring conditional use permits

Candidates were asked how they think conditional use permits should be monitored in the county, who holds the responsibility for ensuring the conditions of the permits are being followed, and who is responsible for following up on complaints the county receives about the permits. 

Flanagan said the process starts with the public, who should file complaints when they see that conditions of the permits aren’t being met with the director of planning and zoning. 

“The planning and zoning director then does an investigation, they come to the county commission, and then the board does a review,” said Flanagan. “If the conditional use permit is found to be in violation, there’s a couple of options. They’re given a chance for remediation, and if they don’t fix the problem then we can revoke the conditional use permit. That’s exactly the process in a nutshell. I’ve been involved on both sides of that, so I’m probably the best one to have to ask that question.”

Haiwick said that he is not part of any commission and does not know the rules and regulations of conditional use permits. 

Jennings agreed with Flanagan’s response, who he said that he did an excellent job describing the process and he didn’t have anything more to add. 

Comer said that he also had nothing more to add to Flanagan’s response. 

Davies said that laws should be enforced by law enforcement, and conditional use permits should be enforced by the people who issue them. 

“We’re a problem-based commission right now,” said Davies. “Somebody reports a problem and that problem gets investigated. So, we’re reacting to things that come up, we’re not proactive on preventing things that could come up. So, my approach would be, why can’t we have some review of the 500 or so, I understand you can check that number that may not be right, conditional use permits that are out there. How do we know that all these conditional use permits are really complying with their conditions? I know people have come to me with complaints about conditional use permit grantees next to them and complain that there’s nobody to enforce it. Maybe it’s gone through that process, I don’t know, but I would say my instinct is we need some effort to make sure that the existing permits are continuing to operate within the rules that they were given at the beginning. It just doesn’t seem right to me that we have police out there enforcing the laws, but we have nobody essentially out there enforcing the conditional use permits unless there’s a problem that is brought to the attention of planning and zoning.”

 2 Lawrence County candidate forum.jpg
Pictured from left, incumbent Brandon Flanagan, challenger Robert Haiwick, and incumbent Eric Jennings spoke at the Lawrence County commission candidate forum Saturday. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

Jennings added that conditional use permits are annually reviewed. 

“We do an inspection there and make sure that the rules are being followed and there have been no complaints,” Jennings said.

Conflict of interest

Candidates were asked how they would identify a conflict of interest during their service as a county commissioner and if they would recuse themselves from voting if they thought a conflict of interest was present. 

Jennings said that a conflict of interest is clearly defined by state law.

“In the legal sense, a conflict of interest exists when, in this case a commissioner, has the opportunity to vote on an issue that he or she would financially benefit from. When that arises, the commissioner will declare a conflict of interest and recuse him or herself and sit in the gallery until the issue is decided,” Jennings said. “A perceived conflict of interest is a much harder target to hit. Everyone has their own definition of that. In a relatively small county like Lawrence County, if you select a commissioner who has lived here for a lengthy time and knows the county well, he or she may have a non-financial relationship with people bringing business before the county. Lawrence County Commission has stringently followed the legal definition of conflict of interest and will probably never be able to satisfy the perceived conflict of interest concerns. Me, personally, I operate I’m the sole proprietor of a ranch. I’ve not had any conflicts of interest arise in the county because I don’t have that many — my financial interests aren’t that spread out. I don’t think I can come up with an example that I can give you a conflict of interest and I’ve never had to do any business, selling the county anything or anything that I would have benefited from. 

Comer said that identifying conflicts of interest is an important part of every meeting. 

“We have the opportunity to declare if we think there is a conflict of interest and then others determine that based off of state law,” said Comer. “If I get into it where I’m going to matter an issue I didn’t think about, I would immediately declare I think there’s a conflict of interest and recuse myself if needed. I think that’s important. But again, small communities, you know a lot of people, you know a lot of businesses, and it’s a very different situations if we were in bigger communities where you didn’t know a lot of people. But growing up here, working in this area, running around this area, you get to learn and know a lot of people.”

Davies said that his experience working as an executive in the Department of Veterans Affairs, where he served as the head physician for the Fort Meade VA hospital in Sturgis, granted him exceptional experience in the dangers of ignoring conflicts of interest. 

“A conflict of interest occurs when there’s split loyalties,” said Davies. “When a person has loyalty to themselves and their job, their employer, and a loyalty to all of the people in the county, for example. In my past as an executive in the Department of Veteran’s Affairs, we were very careful, very careful about conflicts of interest. We could not have lunch with a vendor unless we paid for it ourselves. We could not take any gift from a vendor at all, and finally they said unless it’s less than $25. I have a former colleague, you can look it up, John Wyndham, who did violate that law, and now he’s facing somewhere between 20 and 25 years in prison for violation of conflict of interest laws on the federal level.”

Davies said that he thinks the county commission has been “loose” with their declarations of conflicts of interest. 

“I think if we’re working for an employer that owns more than 10% of the land in the county, or has privileges on those lands to mine, and we’re working for the people in the county? That’s kind of a built-in problem,” said Davies. “Yeah, there’s a legal definition, but conflict of interest is kind of like pornography. You know it when you see it. There’s a lot of people that, I think, push the edges of that around here. I’m a little concerned about this. In my own situation, I don’t think I have a conflict of interest. I’m retired from the VA, we live out in the country, I don’t do business with the county, I think I could represent you fairly. At the same time, if there was a conflict of interest that did come up, I know what it is, I would declare it and be honest about it.”

Comer spoke up and declared that he will be declaring conflicts of interest when issues regarding Dakota Gold come up with the board of county commissioners, something that he has discussed with his employer. 

Flanagan agreed with what had already been said about declaring conflicts of interest and gave an example of recusing himself at the April 14 board of appeals meeting. 

“We acted as the board of appeals for assessment valuation,” Flanagan said. “My landlord, at the restaurant, had 2 parking lots that I rent from him that came up. He was contesting their evaluation. I saw that immediately when it came up and I said, ‘Hey I need to recuse myself.’ I don’t have any direct financial involvement in that. The only thing I do is pay him rent, and they happened to be lots that are part of a parking arrangement that I have with that owner. But, just to make sure that there was any appearance, I recused myself and we went on with business.”

Haiwick said that as an owner of an automatic transmission repair facility, if the county brought one of the highway patrol vehicles to his shop to be repaired while he was a commissioner, he would ask them to take that vehicle to another shop. 

“I certainly do not want a conflict of interest within my business,” said Haiwick.

Property tax relief

Candidates were asked if they believe Senate Bill 96, which authorizes counties the option to relieve owner-occupied property taxes by imposing a half-percent sales tax. 

“I think it’s an opportunity that is out there, but we haven’t been presented with that yet because we can’t implement it until a certain time frame,” said Comer. “So yeah, I think we’ll be looking at that as the board of county commissioners and make a decision of what kind of impact that will have to the community and the people of Lawrence County. I, right now, would say it’s a positive impact and I would say if it turns out that it is a positive impact, yeah I would be in favor of implementing that. But I want to see the details of that first. I don’t go by hearsay, like to see facts, and I like to make my decisions based on facts. So, I’ll wait for that to make that decision when it comes before the board.”

Davies said that he thinks the opinions of the county residents are important when deciding whether or not to implement the tax. 

“We have to make decisions based on facts, I agree with that,” said Davies. “At the same time, in my travels here over the last couple of months, I’ve heard a lot of concern about property taxes from people. I had one gal who was almost in tears because she got her property tax bill, and she already had 2 jobs and a house she could afford and didn’t expect the rise in property taxes that she faced. It’s a painful thing for a lot of people in our county. We live in the same house, and we had, the valuation goes up, we didn’t do anything different, but all of a sudden we have greater and greater and greater expense.”

Davies said the 2 tax relief bills passed in the legislature this year are the only options that he’s aware of when reducing property taxes.

“My sense is, why wouldn’t we take advantage of this? My understanding is, with the half cent sales tax that the commission could put in, an average family would have to spend somewhere between $60,000 and $100,000 more to pay more in tax than they would in savings from the sales tax,” Davies said. “If we did the sales tax and used it for property sales tax reduction, we would have many of our visitors, by the way tourism is our number one source of economic activity here in Lawrence County, why not ask those visitors to bear some of that burden that would help our residents have an easier life?”

Flanagan said that he’s cautiously optimistic about tax relief options passed by the governor’s office and the legislature. 

“There’s some things that have yet to be seen,” said Flanagan. “There’s some processes that yet to be worked out. We, of course, work very closely with the treasurer’s office and the auditor and the state for guidance and suggestions on how to implement those things. And that’s really the thing, don’t jump headlong into something only to have to undo it because it’s a mess. I don’t think there’s anyone on the board currently or candidate wise that wouldn’t say whatever we can do to reduce property taxes, we need to try it. But I don’t want to make amess and then have to tear down the whole project to start over because it was either poorly implemented or incorrectly implemented or didn’t do what the intent was. With that being said, anybody that owns property in this county would really like to see some property tax relief.”

Haiwick said that he agrees with his opponents. 

“If we can implement the half cent on the sales tax to relieve a lot of the elderly and, of course, even the young people, that’s going to help them purchase a new home possibly if it lowers the taxes,” Haiwick said. “So, if it comes about and I get elected, I would be for it.”

Jennings said that he testified in favor of Senate Bill 96.

“I was in favor of the bill because it gave the individual counties the option of implementing a sales tax for owner occupied property tax relief instead of a one size fits all approach,” Jennings said. “Senate Bill 96 doesn’t become law until July 1, and the county cannot act until then. We are still learning about the mechanics of the bill and what the logistics of implementation would be. I’m also currently listening to as many citizens as I can about whether or not we should implement it. I have not chosen a position yet and I will not do so until I feel I have all the information in front of me. It’s important to remember that a sales tax represents a tax shift. It shifts to the visitors, but it also shifts to the people who do not own homes. We need to think about that aspect of it. The only true method for property tax relief is through the budget and being mindful of the budget and being fiscally responsible is the only way that we’re going to hold property taxes in check.” 

When to vote

Absentee voting is currently on hold while the state struggles to get ballots to auditors. Election day is June 2. To find your polling place and check your voter registration, visit the Secretary of State’s website at vip.sdos.gov.

title: Spearfish gets a new steakhouse,  inspired by the 100 year-old escape  of 6 cloven foot critters
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — The newest restaurant to take up residence in the Lown Mercantile Building at 701 N. 5th Street in Spearfish is open for business. Six Goats Tavern is a modern, American ranch-inspired steakhouse owned and operated by experienced restaurateurs Brad Prescott and Chris Panaia.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — The newest restaurant to take up residence in the Lown Mercantile Building at 701 N. 5th Street in Spearfish is open for business. Six Goats Tavern is a modern, American ranch-inspired steakhouse owned and operated by experienced restaurateurs Brad Prescott and Chris Panaia.

The pair is leaning into history as they launch the newest cuisine on offer in Spearfish’s culinary scene.

“We wanted to bring culinary craftsmanship and kind of a western heritage to an elevated hospitality experience,” Panaia said. “We wanted it to still be community-focused and comfortable. The duty within the community is to acknowledge its history. There was a steakhouse that was here. There is a bit of a revival essence to this.”

Panaia said the plan involved adding some of the menu items the community loved when Steerfish was up and running, alongside new dishes prepared in-house.

“The food is really steak-focused. We really do want to be a steakhouse. There is a lack of great steakhouses. I can name a few, but I think that we can bring something to the table that is a little bit different than what they’re doing here,” Prescott said. “At night, I like to say we are steak and potato focused, whereas during the day we are more ruffage. We are more focused on salads and soups, and quick service. We want to get people in and out and have a good quality meal.”

Prescott has mined the basement of the old mercantile, finding antique cast-iron fixtures to hold up new hard wood shelving inside the tavern and other unique display items for future use. The space, the two hope, will feel classy and cozy, with a spirit that harkens back to a particular moment in the region’s history — the escape of 6 mountain goats from Custer State Park zoo.

Some of those goats eventually made it to Spearfish Canyon, where they founded the local herd.

“100 years ago, during this time period that they escaped,” Panaia said. “We were like, ‘Hey, the great escape!’ It just kind of worked really well with our idea. We wanted to be something for the community first.”

Panaia envisions Six Goats as a community escape and gathering place. 

“Our success comes from people in the community saying this is our place,” Panaia said. “A place that we like to go to, where we seek community, connection, and gather. The tourists will be there, and if we could bring them in as well, with the history and all of that, that is great too.”

The other element of history Panaia and Prescott are leaning into is their own. The pair have worked together for decades, opening dozens of restaurants across the country. After Prescott relocated to the Northern Hills, they set their sights on expanding Spearfish’s culinary offerings with Six Goats Tavern. It won’t be their first steakhouse. Their first steakhouse, in Southern California, was the restaurant that brought Prescott and Panaia together.

“Our busiest days were Sunday and Monday, when all the hospitality industry wanted a night off, and they wanted to experience something comfortable and gathering. They would come to us,” Panaia said. “If we can replicate that into the local community here, it is a win-win.”

Panaia said that their first restaurant took off by word of mouth.

“I think we come from a place where that original steakhouse, we didn’t take reservations. If you didn’t know where we were, you would need to call your friend and ask,” Panaia said. “It was kind of an experience. (Customers) would come and realize that we delivered great food, a great environment, good music, and it was all the elements that brought it together.”

For weeks, a mountain goat silhouette has been up on the windows of the shuttered tavern as Prescott and Panaia prepared the restaurant for its soft opening. Building anticipation and opening with intention were part of the plan.

“I am in the 40s now, as far as the number of restaurants I have opened. You learn what to do and what not to do. You learn to make quick decisions operationally on things that aren’t working,” Prescott said. “Part of it is what we are talking about, the evolution of an opening.

You know, most places you open this day and it’s feast or famine. I don’t think that is the right way to do it. With us in full control of what we are doing and how we are doing it, it helps immensely.”

Prescott said the restaurant will ramp up slowly — starting with a limited menu and small staff before adding seasonal and limited time menu items and eventually expanding to serve brunch on the weekends.

“We hope to build our menu by input, and keep evolving,” Prescott said.

At one point, Prescott said he ran a handful of restaurants simultaneously — including 2 in Hawaii.

“The failures speak louder than the successes. You need to fail before you can succeed, and I’ve had both,” Prescott said. “I’ve had some huge successes and had several restaurants under my belt, and then in 2008, I lost all of those restaurants. You know, I like to say that I learned my operational savvy by being in Hawaii with 2 restaurants, and we were failing.”

Prescott said the most important lesson he has learned is that success in food service hinges on a restaurant’s culture.  

“The restaurant business is a love/hate, right? If you are hospitality-minded, and you like entertaining people, and you like community, and you like to have experiences. I grew up in an era where it wasn’t about technology. It was about customer experience. It was about showing up to places and having real, genuine relationships,” Panaia said. “When you are running restaurants, and you build a team, and you have culture, it is like having a family. If you do it right.”

The pair hope to make Six Goats a great place to work, and by extension a great place to dine. They’re aiming to cultivate a crop of regulars who come into the tavern to enjoy eventual favorites and to discover new flavors. Beef prices are high. Bringing people back over and over will require offering low-cost options alongside $100 steaks. Prescott and Panaia are OK with that.

“I think Six Goats will be shaped by the community,” Panaia said. “We are excited to see how we can connect in a community and bring back that customer service and hospitality community gathering. We want people to come in and know that they are here to have an experience and feel comfortable.”

title: Sturgis FFA celebrates state officer milestones as Cammack named president, Storm elected secretary
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: Jackson Cammack, left, was elected State FFA President and Ellie Storm was elected to serve at State FFA Secretary at the State Convention last week in Brookings.  Photo by Kendra Storm
_full_text:
1. FFA.jpeg
Jackson Cammack, left, was elected State FFA President and Ellie Storm was elected to serve at State FFA Secretary at the State Convention last week in Brookings.  Photo by Kendra Storm 

STURGIS — The Sturgis Future Farmers of America (FFA) chapter reached a milestone last week as 2 of its members were elected to top leadership roles during the South Dakota FFA State Convention in Brookings.  

Jackson Cammack was elected state FFA president, while Ellie Storm earned the position of state FFA secretary, marking a rare achievement for a single chapter to have 2 state officers in the same year.

Cammack called the experience both humbling and unforgettable.  

“Having two state officers from the same chapter is really unheard of,” Cammack said. “To be able to do it with someone that I’ve experienced my entire FFA career with is very special, and it means the world to me. It was an unbelievable experience, one I’ll never forget, and I hope I can serve the organization with pride.”

Cammack was selected from a competitive pool of 19 candidates, following an extensive interview process held two weeks prior at Dakota Wesleyan University. The final announcement came during an emotional moment on stage at the convention.  “To hear my name, it was just unbelievable,” he said. 

As state president, Cammack said his priorities include strengthening relationships across the organization, particularly with alumni and local communities.

“The alumni is where it really hits home,” he said. “It’s a great source of fundraising and connection to the community. I want to continue building those relationships and connecting with students, advisors and chapters across the state.”

Cammack also credited FFA with helping him grow personally. 

“As a freshman, I was very shy and not outgoing at all,” he said. “FFA has really grown my leadership skills and changed my mindset.”

Storm shared similar excitement about the opportunity and the impact of the state convention experience.  

 2.. FFA.jpeg
Jackson Cammack, elected State FFA President, stands with advisor Stran Holben, and Ellie Storm, elected as State FFA Secretary during the state convention last week in Brookings.  Photo by Kendra Storm 

“It’s an amazing time,” Storm said. “You see thousands of blue jackets and realize just how big and impactful FFA is across South Dakota. Every year you think it can’t get any better, and it still does.”

Storm’s journey in FFA is closely tied to her family. Her brother, Ben Storm, previously served as a state FFA Sentinel and played a key role in encouraging her involvement.

“He’s the one who got our family into FFA,” she said. “We’re first-generation FFA members, and he really pushed me to get involved and pursue leadership opportunities.”

As a state officer, Storm said she looks forward to building connections with members statewide and helping bridge relationships between districts.

“I really want to connect with members from all across the state and help people find their passion for FFA and agriculture,” she said. “There’s a place for everyone in FFA, no matter your background.”

Storm added that her time in Sturgis has been foundational to her success. “Sturgis is where the passion started,” she said. “I’ve had the opportunity to work with amazing teammates and advisors who have made a huge impact on my journey.”

Both Cammack and Storm encouraged younger students to get involved early, emphasizing the leadership and personal growth opportunities FFA provides.

“Get into an ag class and take advantage of every opportunity,” Cammack said. “I especially recommend doing the Creed as a freshman, it’s something I wish I would have done.”

Storm echoed that message. 

“FFA will help you become a better leader no matter what you want to do in the future,” she said. “Don’t count yourself out, there’s truly a place for everyone.”

Sturgis FFA advisor Stran Holben praised both students for their leadership and lasting impact on the chapter.  “They’ve been incredible members over the past three years,” Holben said. “Without them, our chapter would not be where it is today. They’ve been outstanding leaders and great ambassadors for FFA, from mentoring younger students to promoting the program throughout the community.”

With their elections, Cammack and Storm will spend the next year representing South Dakota FFA, traveling across the state and beyond while continuing to inspire the next generation of agricultural leaders.

title: What data can,  and can’t tell  us about crime
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: In 2025, Spearfish police officers responded to an average of 30 calls for service a day. They made an average of 5 traffic stops each day as well. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Crime stats 1.JPG
In 2025, Spearfish police officers responded to an average of 30 calls for service a day. They made an average of 5 traffic stops each day as well. Pioneer file photo 

SPEARFISH — In 2025, the Spearfish Police Department responded to 11,192 calls for service (an average of 30.6 a day) and conducted 2,018 traffic stops (an average of 5 a day). That means law enforcement officers interacted with citizens more than 13,210. Spearfish, for reference, has about 13,276 citizens. 

Spearfish police issued 1,043 citations, not including verbal or written warnings and not limited to traffic infractions last year. Officers made 319 arrests last year alone, not including incidents that resulted in requests for arrest warrants. 

While the numbers can give us some idea of what those officers did over the last year, they aren’t necessarily a good gauge of how “busy” uniformed cops are in the city. 

“One data point for ‘assault’ can be drastically different from another assault. The time invested for one case with the same data point, is never the same,” said Spearfish Police Chief Collin Smith. 

Data can offer a generalized picture of crime in a community, however. We can infer which types of crime might be most common, and get a feel for the relative safety of a community based on its statistics. 

 Crime Stats 2.JPG
Pioneer file photo 

Instances of crime 

For example, the most common calls at the Spearfish Public Safety Dispatch Center in 2025 were (in order of frequency): traffic stops, emergency medical (EMS calls, accidental 911 calls, calls involving animals, and welfare checks. 

In 2025, the Spearfish Police Department recorded 11 rapes and 18 aggravated assaults. There were no murders or robberies recorded last year in the city limits. 

Those numbers reflect a larger, statewide trend. Violent crime is down, overall. 

There were 64,261 criminal offenses reported in South Dakota last year — a 6. 03% decrease compared to 2024’s data. Homicides, rapes, burglaries juvenile arrests, and drug offenses all decreased in 2025 in South Dakota. At the state level, the most common type of crime is property related — crimes like burglary and arson. Drug crimes and violent crimes are the second and third most common categories, respectively. 

In Spearfish, there were 83 cases of burglary, 202 cases of theft or larceny, and 10 cases of motor vehicle theft reported last year. Spearfish saw 76 drug offenses, and 56 “drug equipment violations.” 

State statistics come with a warning label. 

“However, readers are cautioned that crime rates cited are reliable indications of crime only to the extent that population estimates are accurate, that victims report crimes … and data is submitted to the Division of Criminal Investigation’s Statistical Analysis Center by South Dakota law enforcement agencies,” according to the state’s annual crime data report.

Not all crimes are reported. Some crimes are left out of data, because juvenile suspects are involved, the document clarifies. 

Understanding arrests

Data can also give us an idea of who is being arrested in our communities. According to state data, men are most likely to be arrested for violent crimes (834 men were arrested, compared to 206 women for crimes including rape, murder, robbery, and aggravated assault). There were 750 men were arrested for aggravated assault compared to 200 women; 24 men were arrested for rape compared to 0 women. 

Women were also roughly half as likely to be arrested for property crimes (including burglary, larceny-theft, motor vehicle theft and arson), 50.7%. Half as many women were arrested for drug crimes in 2025 as men. The numbers don’t tell us why that is. 

They do indicate that age correlates to with likelihood to commit, and be arrested for, a criminal offense. 

According to state arrest data, people between the ages of 20 and 40 are most likely to be arrested for almost any crime. 

Out of 1,040 arrests for violent crimes in South Dakota, 317 were between the ages of 20 and 29 — more than any other age group. 293 people between the ages of 30 and 39 were arrested for violent crimes, compared to 160 aged 19 and under, 182 between 40 and 49, and 88 were aged 50+. 

The lion’s share of drug arrests involved suspects between the ages of 20 and 40 as well. 

28% of people arrested for drug or drug equipment violations were in their 20s, 26% were in their 30s, and 17% were in their 40s. That’s compared to just 11%, who were 50 or older, and 7% who were 17 or younger. 

While correlation is not causation, SD Attorney General Marty Jackley said, law enforcement is best armed with clear ad accurate data as they conduct efforts to make communities safer. 

“Accurate and timely crime data is essential to informed decision- making. For law enforcement agencies, reliable data helps identify emerging trends, evaluate strategies, and determine how best to deploy officers, training, and resources,” he said. “For policymakers and community leaders, it provides the foundation needed to craft effective laws, prevention efforts, and public safety initiatives. For the public, access to this information promotes transparency, accountability, and confidence in the criminal justice system.”
