title: Lab-grown meat could still be a long  way from widespread availability  when SD’s new ban expires
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: South Dakota’s new 5-year ban on cell-cultured protein targets a product whose path to mass market availability is operating on “generational-level timescales,” according to a scientist dedicated to the topic.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

South Dakota’s new 5-year ban on cell-cultured protein targets a product whose path to mass market availability is operating on “generational-level timescales,” according to a scientist dedicated to the topic.

Elliot Swartz works for the Good Food Institute, a Washington, D.C.-based nonprofit that describes itself as working to “advance alternative proteins.”

“There might be local retailers that have a few products on store shelves, but there won’t be a nationwide Walmart-, Costco-type of cultivated meat product within the next five years in the United States,” Swartz said. “Over the next five years, more and more products will be reviewed, and we will get an even more thorough understanding.”

Both the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the Food and Drug Administration began approving the sale of cell-cultured products in 2023. While a few products have been approved, there’s really only one product for sale now, Swartz said — cell-cultivated salmon — and it’s on the menu at four restaurants.

Rep. Tesa Schwans, R-Hartford, who supported a ban on cell-cultured protein, described the creation process as “a petri dish that’s full of hormones and sludge.” It’s actually more like “a beer brewery,” according to Swartz.

Cell-cultured protein, sometimes described as lab-grown meat, is produced by taking cells from an animal. The cells are grown in a controlled environment and fed nutrients until they become a large enough piece of tissue to be used as a food product.

It’s a relatively new science, according to Christina Bakker, a South Dakota State University Extension meat science specialist.

“Right now, most companies are kind of in that ramping up of the production phase. They’re trying to get it to a point where the product can be affordable,” Bakker said. “You’re not seeing it in your normal grocery stores or anything like that, so for the most part, it’s not widely available.”

SDSU does not do research on cell-cultured protein and does not collaborate with any companies that produce the product.

Moratorium signed after ban was vetoed

State Rep. Julie Auch, R-Lesterville, attempted during the recently concluded annual legislative session to add cell-cultured protein to South Dakota’s list of “adulterated foods,” which would have essentially banned the products permanently. She told fellow lawmakers that she introduced the bill with concern for the destruction of the livestock industry, which she said is being orchestrated by people claiming the industry is bad for the environment.

The bill made it to the governor’s desk, where it was vetoed.

Lawmakers shouldn’t ban a product because they don’t like it, Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden said. He instead signed into law a five-year prohibition on the sale, manufacture and distribution of cell-cultured protein.

“I think we need to tap the brakes on this product and have a little more research,” Rhoden told reporters in February.

The South Dakota Cattlemen’s Association does not support cell-cultured protein, but it testified against a permanent ban.

“Cell-cultivated products are no competition to real beef raised by real producers, and consumers do not need the government to tell them that,” the association’s president Craig Bieber told South Dakota Searchlight in an emailed statement.

The association also advocates at the national level for “an explicit prohibition on the use of any taxpayer dollars being used to purchase these products in schools, the military or in any nutrition program, and more transparency to address concerns rather than relying on a patchwork of state bans and moratoriums.” South Dakota lawmakers approved a law last year with prohibitions on the spending of taxpayer money to support lab-grown meat, with an exception for university research, and also approved a law requiring lab-grown meat to be clearly labeled.

The state’s Animal Industry Board, which oversees the state meat inspection program, spoke in favor of the labeling requirement.

“One of the foundations of meat inspection is truth and accuracy in labeling,” said Mendel Miller, the state veterinarian and executive secretary of the board. “When that customer picks up a package of meat, they know exactly what’s in the product.”

Motivations, concerns

Cell-cultivated producers don’t want to eliminate conventional meat production, according to Tamar Lieberman, a legislative specialist with the Good Food Institute. But she said the availability of cell-cultured protein could help in times of crises like avian flu or other livestock disease outbreaks.

“The way that meat is produced right now is very vulnerable to supply chain disruptions,” Lieberman said. “Having additional ways to feed people meat — if they choose it, of course — in times of disruption is going to be critical.”

Part of the drive for an alternative protein comes from the global rise in demand for meat products, Swartz said.

“We already know that there’s some negative externalities that come alongside meat production, in terms of the amount of land that’s used, water that’s used, and other resources that are impacted,” Swartz said. “This is a way for us to essentially help meet that growing demand for protein, while hopefully taking away some of those negative externalities that exist with the current system.”

Opponents of cell-cultured products alleged during South Dakota’s legislative session that the products contain carcinogens. Others raised concerns about an alleged lack of studies and transparency about the production process.

Bakker, the SDSU meat science specialist, said future research could unearth concerns, but “right now, what we see is that we’re not concerned, from a scientific side, about the safety.” The industry will rely on USDA and FDA standards that measure safety from chemical, physical or biological standpoints, Bakker said.

Time to learn

The five-year ban in South Dakota will give researchers more time to help answer questions for shoppers, Swartz said, though the products likely still won’t be readily available at mass market stores when the ban expires.

“This is really sort of generational-level timescales that we’re talking about here, rather than year over year, suddenly there’s going to be cultivated meat at Walmart,” Swartz said.

Miller also said the temporary ban could help answer some of the questions people might have about the production process or end product.

“It’s a good step to take until we learn a little bit more about the product itself,” Miller said. “It’s just a matter of the unknowns of what the product is, I guess, from our side of things.”

Miller said people should trust inspection systems, but he understands the concern.

“If there’s confidence in the system and confidence in the way products are approved, that says a lot right there, that it’s been approved,” he said. “However, it is kind of on the cutting edge of technology, so there probably are a lot of things that are unique to that product rather than past things that have been approved.”

The first products consumers will likely see in stores are crumbled products that replicate chicken nuggets or ground meat — something that is “texturally, a little bit easier to deal with,” said Amanda Blair, the assistant director of SDSU West River Research and Extension.

“I don’t know when we’re going to see a fully formed steak or pork chop made from these types of products” using the cell culture process, Blair said. Replicating a whole “muscle cut” like a steak or pork chop would be more difficult for bioprocessors, she said.

Seven other states have banned cell-cultured proteins. A federal appeals court recently upheld Florida’s ban on cell-culture proteins after one of the nation’s two approved cell-cultured chicken producers tried to overturn it. A lawsuit against Texas’ temporary ban is ongoing.

title: Confusion emerges over new SD voter ID requirements
byline: By Alexander Rifaat South Dakota News Watch
description: PIERRE — County auditors in South Dakota are, in certain cases, deciding how to implement new voter ID rules on their own due to uncertainty over guidelines issued by the state’s secretary of state, as early and absentee voting for the primary election is well underway.
_full_text:
SDNewsWatchLogo

PIERRE — County auditors in South Dakota are, in certain cases, deciding how to implement new voter ID rules on their own due to uncertainty over guidelines issued by the state’s secretary of state, as early and absentee voting for the primary election is well underway.

Senate Bill 175, passed in the 2026 legislative session, requires new voters to provide proof of citizenship as part of the registration process. The bill was enacted with an emergency clause, which allows the regulations to take effect for the upcoming primary ballot on June 2.

The secretary of state’s website outlines various documents first-time registrants can provide as a photocopy to show proof of citizenship, such as a passport or birth certificate. But confusion has emerged as to whether eligible South Dakota driver’s licenses, which identify a person’s citizenship status, can also be provided as a photocopy or have to be shown in person.

Since July of last year, as a result of Senate Bill 75 from the 2025 legislative session, driver’s licenses in South Dakota are now issued with an indication of a person’s U.S. citizenship status. The secretary of state’s website lists driver’s licenses as an acceptable form of proof but does not explicitly state whether they need to be physically shown at an auditor’s office or if a photocopy is sufficient.

Amy Scott-Stoltz, president of the League of Women Voters of South Dakota, a nonpartisan advocacy group, said that county auditors in charge of voter registration are having difficulty ensuring a uniform system across the state.

“They’re trying to follow the secretary of state’s guidelines, but the vagueness has led to certain issues,” Scott-Stoltz told News Watch. “Do they need to present this stuff in person? Can they accept it by mail? Different auditors interpret that differently.”

Hughes County Finance Officer Thomas Oliva, who acts as that county’s auditor, said his office is requiring new voters to show the physical driver’s license.

“The main reasoning behind that is because it’s the back of the license. There’s no other identifying information on the back we can tie back to that person, so we felt it’s in the best interest to see the physical card,” Oliva told News Watch.

Haakon County Auditor Stacy Pinney said she has not run into any issues yet with voter registration but also will require new applicants to physically show the driver’s license.

“I’m going to make it a policy in my office that I want to see the actual card. If I have to verify it, I want to see the real deal,” Pinney told News Watch.

Meanwhile, Harding County Auditor Kathy Glines said her office will accept a photocopy of the driver’s license.

“They would have to send a front and back,” Glines told News Watch.

“I hope they would call before sending it by mail,” she added, referring to the limited hours the office is open.

Need for clarity

In addition to questions over how to process new voter applications using driver’s licenses, Oliva said the secretary of state’s office has also created confusion in its communication with prospective voters who are missing the required citizenship documentation.

Oliva said voters who are deemed not to have provided proof of citizenship are sent a letter that indicates they are a “Federal Only” voter, which means, since the new voting law applies to South Dakota elections, they can only vote in statewide federal elections for U.S. President, U.S. Senate and the U.S. House of Representatives races.

“I do not necessarily agree with this approach and believe the individual should instead be notified and marked as incomplete or invalid until the required documentation is received,” Oliva said. “While the letter does inform the voter of their status, it does not provide a clear explanation as to why they were designated as such.”

Oliva highlighted the letter generated by the voter registration system only indicates a person is ineligible due to situations such as the use of a commercial mail receiving agency, mail forwarding service or post office box without sufficient residential description.

“While that explanation is accurate in those scenarios, it does not address the separate issue of missing citizenship documentation, which can also result in Federal Only status. This omission may lead to confusion for voters,” Oliva said.

In order to provide more clarity, Oliva created a letter addressed for those deemed to be a Federal Only voter based on a lack of proof of citizenship outlining their options.

In a copy of the letter provided to News Watch, Oliva’s office specifies the new voter was classified as Federal Only due to the lack of citizenship documentation and provides examples of eligible forms of documents they can submit to change their status.

As early and absentee voting for the primary election gets underway, Scott-Stoltz hopes officials in Pierre can provide more certainty on the registration process for new voters.

title: Opponents win temporary order  against drilling project near culturally  significant Black Hills site
byline: By Seth Tupper Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: RAPID CITY — Tribes and environmental groups scored at least a temporary victory this week in their multipronged effort to stop exploratory drilling in culturally significant areas of South Dakota’s Black Hills.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

RAPID CITY — Tribes and environmental groups scored at least a temporary victory this week in their multipronged effort to stop exploratory drilling in culturally significant areas of South Dakota’s Black Hills.

A federal judge in Rapid City granted a temporary restraining order Monday evening against exploratory drilling near the high mountain meadow known as Pe’ Sla, or Reynolds Prairie, in the central Black Hills. The ruling came after a hearing that drew an overflow crowd of people opposed to the project. 

Pe’ Sla is one of several Black Hills sites that corresponds with celestial features in traditional Lakota spirituality. Lakota people use the area, some of which is tribally owned, for prayer, ceremonies and cultural activities. 

The order requires Pete Lien & Sons to halt its project temporarily while the lawsuit against it continues. The company is exploring for graphite, which is used in electric vehicle batteries, lubricants, pencils and other products.

Two lawsuits are pending against the project, and the restraining order applies to both. The plaintiffs in one are nonprofits: the Black Hills Clean Water Alliance and an Indigenous rights group known as NDN Collective, both based in Rapid City, and Earthworks in Washington, D.C. Nine Native American tribes are the plaintiffs in the other lawsuit. The defendant in both cases is the U.S. Forest Service, which approved the drilling plan on federally managed land.

The company recently began drilling, according to the nonprofit plaintiffs’ brief in support of their motion for the temporary restraining order. Sacred religious ceremonies in the Pe’ Sla area began on Saturday, May 2, the motion stated, making the request for the temporary restraining order “especially urgent.”

“These industrial operations irreparably harm plaintiffs’ members’ use of the Pe’ Sla landscape,” they said in their brief.

Drilling is halted under the restraining order as the plaintiffs seek a longer-term order known as an injunction. Ultimately, the plaintiffs want to overturn the Forest Service’s approval of the project.

The federal agency said in a brief opposing the restraining order that the project is already “halfway complete,” and said the agency properly considered and approved the drilling plan.

Meanwhile, some of the plaintiffs and their supporters are engaged in another struggle against exploratory drilling for uranium in the southern Black Hills. That proposed project is near Craven Canyon, where the rock walls are carved with Native American petroglyphs believed to be thousands of years old.

The state’s Board of Minerals and Environment is scheduled to conduct a weeklong hearing beginning May 18 in Hot Springs on that project’s permit application.

title: TIF 10 approved amid  community concerns about ‘chasing a false goal’
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: This map shows the project location for the Pines in TIF 10. Map courtesy City of Spearfish
_full_text:
Project location TIF 10.png
This map shows the project location for the Pines in TIF 10. Map courtesy City of Spearfish 

 TIF 10 improvement plan.png
This is the improvements map for the city of Spearfish Tax Incremental District #10. Map courtesy City of Spearfish 

SPEARFISH — Despite concerns from citizens about the project’s affordability, the Spearfish City Council approved the formation of a new tax increment finance district, TIF 10, to support developing The Pines — a new 98-unit apartment complex south of Interstate 90 on St. Onge Road. 

Tax increment financing is a public financing system that uses future increases in property taxes to reimburse the costs of public improvements built within a designated TIF boundary. The value of all the properties inside the district is assessed or calculated, and the total amount of property tax generated by all those properties is noted — the base amount of property tax revenues. All property revenue above this base amount, for the life of the TIF, is captured by the TIF to refund the costs of the public improvements or project. This amount — the amount over the base — is called the “tax increment.” Over time, property values are presumed to increase in part due to infrastructure improvements brought about by the TIF project itself. When the TIF is retired, the total taxation values revert to the original taxing entities.

“The total amount of eligible cost that would be permissible under state statute is almost $3.9 million,” said Spearfish Community Development Director Peter Wysocki. “The applicant is seeking a little over $2 million as they are not including the entire cost of those improvements within the entire cul-de-sac, and are not including the cost for the land purchase.”

Councilwoman Jamie Hafner asked, before the council’s vote, if the developer HME Companies, would proceed with the project without TIF. Lane Warzecha, the vice president of development at HME Companies, said the company would only move forward with the multi-family housing project if the TIF was approved.

“A lot of cost items go into these types of developments. For us to make them economically feasible, we do look for economic assistance in order to develop them. This is not specific to Spearfish; we do this in other communities, as do many developers,” Warzecha said. “Without that, that funding mechanism would fall apart, the project would cease to exist.”

During a city council study session last week, Wysocki said the rationale behind establishing a TIF district for this project involves a general need for housing units —particularly housing units that meet the needs of the community’s “missing middle.” The missing middle can refer to members of the workforce who make enough to stay above the poverty line, but not enough to purchase or rent a home at market rate.

The housing units at The Pines will have rent restrictions, capped at 80% of Area Median Income — a number determined by the state. Area Median Income, as defined by the state, is more than $100,000.

The Pines anticipates rent rates for 23 studio units will be about $1,100 per month. The 33 one-bedroom units will rent at a rate of $1,300 or $1,400 for “one bed extra large units,” of which there are 6. The complex’s 30, 2-bedroom units will be set at $1,600, and 2-bedroom corner units (there will be 6) at $1,650.

“These are rents that are out of reach of many of our citizens. I think it is chasing a false goal to say, ‘We’re addressing affordable housing’ when the projects we are approving aren’t actually affordable for the citizens,” Spearfish resident Jeremy Smith told the city council. He asked that the TIF’s approval be tabled until the city thought through its own definition of affordability, as it related to applying tax increment financing. 

“I do have questions about the affordability piece that came up during the study session about the state AMI being $102,000. 80% of that is still over $80,000. So, when I do the math, and I am aware that there are lots of complicated equations, Spearfish’s AMI is $65,000 or almost $66,000. That is below the 80% AMI,” Smith said. “These rents are figured for an $80,000 average income. We’re not that, which means that in approving this, to me, it is saying that the renters from Spearfish who get this housing will still be cost burdened. It is not actually addressing the affordability piece.”

Smith said he understands the need to address workforce housing for the “missing middle,” but noted that the TIF might not be justifiable if the council views it as an affordable housing project.

Wysocki stressed that the TIF formation is allowed under the state program and the definition of an affordable housing TIF.

“We can become more restrictive, if we have a policy that a TIF can only be used for affordable housing projects that address local area median income levels. The way the state regulates rental rates is based on the state median income and then establishes a rental rate based on the affordability index, a cost-burdened index of 30% of gross income being spent on housing,” Wysocki said.

Shortly after Wysocki’s comments, Councilman Larry Klarenbeek moved to follow city staff’s recommendation and approve the formation of TIF 10. The motion passed, and the council approved the Pines project plan.

title: BHSU to host commencement  ceremony May 9
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: SPEARFISH — Black Hills State University will recognize more than 300 graduates during the 191st commencement ceremony, May 9.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — Black Hills State University will recognize more than 300 graduates during the 191st commencement ceremony, May 9.  

The ceremony begins at 10 a.m. at the Donald E. Young Sports and Fitness Center on the BHSU campus. The public is invited to attend and recognize the accomplishments of the graduating class. Degrees to be awarded include 26 master’s degrees, 241 bachelor’s degrees, and 38 associate’s degrees. David Hillard, branch director of RBC Wealth Management and financial advisor with the Hillard Williams Group, will be delivering the charge to the graduates.  

Regent Pam Roberts will offer greetings on behalf of the South Dakota Board of Regents. President Steve Elliott will present diplomas to the graduates with the assistance of April Meeker, registrar at BHSU. Vice President for University Advancement Steve Meeker will welcome graduates into the growing community of more than 19,000 university alumni. 

Music for the ceremony will be provided by the BHSU Wind Ensemble, which will perform the processional, a selection titled “Joy of Love and Life” by Tyler S. Grant, and the recessional. The National Anthem will be performed by Dr. Jonathan Nero, professor of music and choral director at BHSU.

“Commencement is an important day of celebration at Black Hills State University,” President Elliott said. “Our graduates have worked hard to reach this milestone, and we wish them success as they move forward into their careers and new opportunities. We are proud of their accomplishments and thankful for their dedication to BHSU.” 

The May 2026 commencement ceremony will be broadcast live at BHSU.edu/Commencement for those who are unable to attend. Also on this webpage, all are invited to submit words of congratulations to graduates. BHSU encourages attendees to share their commencement story on social media with the hashtag #BHSU2026 in social media posts.

title: Confusion emerges over  new SD voter ID requirements
byline: By Alexander Rifaat South Dakota News Watch
description: PIERRE — County auditors in South Dakota are, in certain cases, deciding how to implement new voter ID rules on their own due to uncertainty over guidelines issued by the state’s secretary of state, as early and absentee voting for the primary election is well underway.
_full_text:
SDNewsWatchLogo

PIERRE — County auditors in South Dakota are, in certain cases, deciding how to implement new voter ID rules on their own due to uncertainty over guidelines issued by the state’s secretary of state, as early and absentee voting for the primary election is well underway.

Senate Bill 175, passed in the 2026 legislative session, requires new voters to provide proof of citizenship as part of the registration process. The bill was enacted with an emergency clause, which allows the regulations to take effect for the upcoming primary ballot on June 2.

The secretary of state’s website outlines various documents first-time registrants can provide as a photocopy to show proof of citizenship, such as a passport or birth certificate. But confusion has emerged as to whether eligible South Dakota driver’s licenses, which identify a person’s citizenship status, can also be provided as a photocopy or have to be shown in person.

Since July of last year, as a result of Senate Bill 75 from the 2025 legislative session, driver’s licenses in South Dakota are now issued with an indication of a person’s U.S. citizenship status. The secretary of state’s website lists driver’s licenses as an acceptable form of proof but does not explicitly state whether they need to be physically shown at an auditor’s office or if a photocopy is sufficient.

Amy Scott-Stoltz, president of the League of Women Voters of South Dakota, a nonpartisan advocacy group, said that county auditors in charge of voter registration are having difficulty ensuring a uniform system across the state.

“They’re trying to follow the secretary of state’s guidelines, but the vagueness has led to certain issues,” Scott-Stoltz told News Watch. “Do they need to present this stuff in person? Can they accept it by mail? Different auditors interpret that differently.”

Hughes County Finance Officer Thomas Oliva, who acts as that county’s auditor, said his office is requiring new voters to show the physical driver’s license.

“The main reasoning behind that is because it’s the back of the license. There’s no other identifying information on the back we can tie back to that person, so we felt it’s in the best interest to see the physical card,” Oliva told News Watch.

Haakon County Auditor Stacy Pinney said she has not run into any issues yet with voter registration but also will require new applicants to physically show the driver’s license.

“I’m going to make it a policy in my office that I want to see the actual card. If I have to verify it, I want to see the real deal,” Pinney told News Watch.

Meanwhile, Harding County Auditor Kathy Glines said her office will accept a photocopy of the driver’s license.

“They would have to send a front and back,” Glines told News Watch.

“I hope they would call before sending it by mail,” she added, referring to the limited hours the office is open.

Need for clarity

In addition to questions over how to process new voter applications using driver’s licenses, Oliva said the secretary of state’s office has also created confusion in its communication with prospective voters who are missing the required citizenship documentation.

Oliva said voters who are deemed not to have provided proof of citizenship are sent a letter that indicates they are a “Federal Only” voter, which means, since the new voting law applies to South Dakota elections, they can only vote in statewide federal elections for U.S. President, U.S. Senate and the U.S. House of Representatives races.

“I do not necessarily agree with this approach and believe the individual should instead be notified and marked as incomplete or invalid until the required documentation is received,” Oliva said. “While the letter does inform the voter of their status, it does not provide a clear explanation as to why they were designated as such.”

Oliva highlighted the letter generated by the voter registration system only indicates a person is ineligible due to situations such as the use of a commercial mail receiving agency, mail forwarding service or post office box without sufficient residential description.

“While that explanation is accurate in those scenarios, it does not address the separate issue of missing citizenship documentation, which can also result in Federal Only status. This omission may lead to confusion for voters,” Oliva said.

In order to provide more clarity, Oliva created a letter addressed for those deemed to be a Federal Only voter based on a lack of proof of citizenship outlining their options.

In a copy of the letter provided to News Watch, Oliva’s office specifies the new voter was classified as Federal Only due to the lack of citizenship documentation and provides examples of eligible forms of documents they can submit to change their status.

As early and absentee voting for the primary election gets underway, Scott-Stoltz hopes officials in Pierre can provide more certainty on the registration process for new voters.

“We’re hoping for more clarification from the secretary’s office before the primary and are looking forward to working with the election board,” she said.

The secretary of state’s office didn’t respond to a request for comment by News Watch.

Ballots delivered; no extra documentation needed to vote

After early and absentee balloting in some counties were delayed in part due to the short time frame the secretary of state’s office had in validating eligible candidates, primary voting does appear to be back on track across the state.

News Watch reached out to all 66 county auditors, with 30 so far confirming they have received their absentee primary ballots.

Oliva said the challenges so far have been manageable and that a key focus for his team will be to also emphasize to voters who are already registered that they do not need to present new documents.

“We have received questions and concerns from individuals who believe they must bring additional documentation to the polls in order to vote. This is not the case, and it is important to correct these misconceptions and provide clear, factual information,” Oliva said.

Oliva said it’s unfortunate not every county is executing the new voting requirements the same but concedes “it’s entirely up to that auditor’s office.”

As for Glines, she said her county is doing the best it can to abide by the secretary of state’s guidelines.

“We are all feeling our way through it,” Glines said.

Jackley releases explanation on Amendment J

Concerns over the new registration rules come as state Attorney General Marty Jackley issued a draft explanation on an upcoming ballot measure tied to the U.S. citizenship requirement for voting in elections.

Amendment J, which will be on the ballot this November, would amend the South Dakota Constitution to add people who are not U.S. citizens to the list of individuals disqualified from voting.

Proponents of the measure argue it will provide greater clarity as to who can vote since, while non-U.S. citizens are already barred from voting in federal elections and registering to vote in South Dakota, there is no language in the state constitution that explicitly prohibits them from voting in state or local races.

Under state law, the attorney general is required to issue a draft explanation of the measure, which essentially acts as a preview of how the question will appear on the ballot.

The public has until end of day on May 8 to submit written comment on the attorney general’s explanation. A final draft is due to the secretary of state’s office on May 19 for approval. The finalized explanation will then accompany the ballot question in the fall.

title: Handley renovations costs nearly as much as new building estimate
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Handley Recreation Center includes a 24-hour access gym and walking track, along with a multi-purpose gym and office space. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Handley renovations costs nearly as much as new building estimate
The Handley Recreation Center includes a 24-hour access gym and walking track, along with a multi-purpose gym and office space. Pioneer file photo  

LEAD — Renovating the Handley Recreation Center building could cost nearly as much as building a new facility, according to recent construction estimates submitted to the Lead Community Center Foundation board. 

The Lead Community Center Foundation was formed in 2024 to raise money to build a new community center. The foundation worked with McGough Construction, which has a branch in Rapid City, to prepare an estimate for renovating the Handley Center; as well as an estimate from JLG Architects of Rapid City for building a new facility. 

Northern Hills Family Recreation Center board member Kevin Wagner serves as the director of business development for McGough Construction in Rapid City. However, he said he was not involved with an informal site visit at the Handley Center between construction managers, civil engineers from DGR Engineering in Rapid City, and JLG Architects. 

“My being on the board wouldn’t have had an impact on the results,” Wagner said. “The results of that report were not solely concluded by McGough. We had outside engineers that were there with us too, and architects that awere engaged that provided information in the conclusion of that report. In my specific position for McGough, I’m a business development director and don’t have construction knowledge.” 

Wagner stressed that the report was done as a “pro bono” service for the Handley Center, and none of the crews were under contract. The building examination was a high-level summary and investigation, but it did not include thorough engineering that could have involved ripping into walls to determine moisture levels. Crews from the 3 firms conducted the surface-level site inspection in January, which the Handley Center board uses as a resource to determine the condition of the building. 

The Handley Center board also uses an engineering report form Summit Structural Engineering, which the board commissioned in 2023. That report is also limited to visual observations of the facility, with no special tools or testing conducted. Conclusions from the report are that the overall structural integrity of the building is good to fair, with no major cracking on exterior walls, and structural steel beams are supporting the building as intended; exterior finish on the walls is deteriorating; and exterior site drainage is not appropriate. 

The McGough Construction estimate is for renovations to the existing facility, which it estimates at between $12.9 million to $15.6 million, depending on the cost of materials. It includes costs for earthwork, electrical updates, roofing, interior and exterior work, fire protection, heating, and more. 

Darla Auld, president of the Northern Hills Recreation Center board, which manages the Handley Center, said the reason for the high price is because the Handley Center was built into the side of a hill, which presents challenges for renovations because of a lack of extra space in between property lines. 

The report from JLG Architects addresses costs for building a new facility, and includes $500,000 for demolition costs, with a total construction cost of about $16.6 million. 

Members of the Lead Community Center Foundation said the reports are used to justify a $15 million request in federal appropriations, which the foundation board submitted with Sen. Mike Rounds’ office. 

Auld said recent reports about the facility’s leaking roof were false. The Handley Recreation Center replaced its heating system in 2025, she said. Since then, Auld said condensation that was leaking from the roof has been dried out, as the heaters have become more efficient. The roof, she said, is in good shape. However, Auld said the board is putting money away in savings to replace it in the future when it is needed. Additionally, Auld said the board is budgeting money to save to put a new heating unit in the multi-purpose room, where the all-purpose court is located. 

“We don’t have any necessary repairs to the roof,” Auld said. “We are budgeting for potential roofing issues. We were putting money away in case we had something happen. Right now it’s fine. It doesn’t leak, it’s just old.”

title: Heupel presents resolution for Handley Center takeover
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Mayor Dustin Heupel presented the Lead City Commission with a resolution that outlines terms for the city to take over management of the Handley Recreation Center. He asked commissioners to consider the resolution and take action on it at the next regularly scheduled meeting, May 18. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Handley weight room.tif
Mayor Dustin Heupel presented the Lead City Commission with a resolution that outlines terms for the city to take over management of the Handley Recreation Center. He asked commissioners to consider the resolution and take action on it at the next regularly scheduled meeting, May 18. Pioneer file photo 

LEAD — A proposed city resolution to take over the Handley Recreation Center includes deed restrictions, limiting the facility to recreation purposes for 2 years. 

After those 2 years have passed, Mayor Dustin Heupel said the Handley Center would become a city-owned asset that the city can manage as it deems appropriate. 

Heupel presented the resolution Monday for Lead city commissioners to consider, and asked for action to be taken on the issue at the next meeting, May 18. If the resolution is approved at that meeting, it will go to the Northern Hills Family Recreation Center board, the managing entity for the Handley Center, for consideration. Heupel said the Handley board has seen the resolution and doesn’t favor everything in it, particularly with regard to the limit of 2 years for deed restrictions. However, he said the timeline is a compromise to the restrictions the Handley board insisted on, as it will not tie future city commissions to the agreement. 

If the Lead City Commission approves the resolution, Heupel asked for a deadline of Aug. 1 for a decision from the Handley board. That aligns with the city’s budget discussions, which usually start in August and conclude in September. 

According to a funding model that the city approved in August 2025, the Handley Recreation Center is expected to run out of operating funds on May 31. The city’s budget includes $73,000 set aside in a recreation fund, which officials have told residents they would use to operate the facility if it takes over. Handley Center requests for the city to release those funds to be used for operations while negotiations are ongoing have been largely ignored. 

Darla Auld, president of the Northern Hills Family Recreation Center board, sent the commission a letter asking them to consider working with the board to create a “quasi-government entity,” which would provide greater financial oversight and partnership. She did not elaborate on that point. However, she said a proposal presented by former Commissioner Kayla Klein to take over the facility was not a real plan, but rather an outline, with many more decisions to make about the takeover process that have not been addressed.  

Heupel urged the commission to consider the resolution and approve it, to improve sustainability for citizen recreation and fitness programs, and to increase transparency for funds. He called the proposed deal a compromise that shows compassion for both sides of the issue. Currently, he said upkeep and maintenance of the building and its programs is primarily done with volunteers, and under the city’s ownership, city staff can handle cleaning and basic repairs to ensure a more reliable and safe service. 

He also said many other cities manage their recreation centers. 

“There is a reason why other communities do it, and that’s because they have the staff and they do have the manpower to provide the service at the end of the day,” he said. I personally don’t think I would throw a bunch of money into that building. I would love to see a new building. But in the meantime, we cannot just cut it. I have full faith in our city staff and Robin’s (Lucero, Lead city administrator) ability to raise money when she needs to.” 

 Handley renovations costs nearly as much as new building estimate
LEAD — Renovating the Handley Recreation Center building could cost nearly as much as building a new facility, according to recent construction estimates submitted to the Lead Community Center Foundation board.  

Heupel also said the city remains cognizant of infrastructure issues that need to be addressed. The 2026 budget included funding for a facilities study, which will make it possible for the city to obtain state and federal grants and loans to pay for some infrastructure repairs. 

Additionally, the city has started setting money aside to relocate the city shop, and in 2026 it allocated more money than ever before for street maintenance. 

On Monday, the commission appeared evenly divided about the issue. Commissioner Roger Thomas told Heupel he will not support any kind of deed restrictions on the deal, and Commission Al Rohrer has openly expressed his opposition to the takeover, or providing any further funding to the Handley Center. 

But Commissioners Rob Carr and Dory Hanson support moving forward with the resolution. Hanson, who was not present at Monday’s meeting, issued a written statement to be read at the commission meeting, in which she said taking over the facility will increase accountability and long term stability, allowing for clearer oversight and more consistent programming. 

Carr said the resolution is a way for the city to move forward with an issue that has been a major point of contention within city government for many years, even if the decision is referred to a citizen vote.

“From my standpoint I want people to understand we’re trying to make this work,” Carr said. “It’s not going to be necessarily smooth. It’s going to be really rocky and bumpy for the first few months. But I think we have to move forward somehow.” 

But the majority of residents who spoke at the meeting repeated the same objections they’ve been making for several years, citing the deteriorating building conditions, lack of transparency for how the Handley board uses $125,000 in city funds every year, and a general weariness of the discussion. 

“Commissioner Carr, the last thing the city needs is a rocky, bumpy anything,” resident Rose Burns said. 

Burns questioned the city’s ability to run the recreation center with a $73,000 budget, and she said too many questions have been left unanswered about how the city intends to operate the facility. 

Resident Valerie Meiners agreed, saying there are too many unanswered questions about the condition of the building and the finances involved with the takeover. 

“Recreation centers are a luxury that well-funded and maintained municipalities can afford,” she said. “Money does not grow on trees, even though the actions of the city would reflect a different understanding of this idea.” 

Shawn Sanders questioned the condition of the building, in light of a report Lead Building Inspector Dennis Schumacher wrote in December 2023, which states it is dilapidated beyond repair. The Lead Community Center Foundation used the report in 2024 to make its case to ask for $10 million from the state, to be used to build a new community center in Lead. According to the report, the building has drainage problems, doesn’t meet ADA standards, and has several other structural issues. 

“The community center is in dire need of reconstruction,” Sanders read from the report. “Years of deterioration left portions of the building unsafe and unstable or unusable.” 

Schumacher later walked back on his comments in that report, saying the building could be saved and is safe for use. 

Since that report was issued, the Lead Community Center Foundation solicited construction reports from McGough Construction and JLG Architects, to outline necessary work that needs to be done on the building. Both reports show repairs totaling between $12-$16 million, but state the building is structurally sound and usable. 

Heupel said there are many repairs that have been made on the building since that report was issued, including an ADA accessible ramp. He pointed to the construction report, which states the building is usable. 

“That’s why we would like to have it under the city’s control, so we can make it something that all of the community can be proud of,” he said. “The current state of the building is nothing that any of us can be proud of. That is what we’re trying to address. How do we address that and not lose a usable facility in the meantime?” 

Proponents to the city taking over the Handley Center have said it is a vital resource in the community. It’s primary importance is for the indoor space it provides for sports groups such as archery, hockey, softball and baseball to practice when the weather is not conducive to outdoor practices. A 24-hour access walking track and gym also provide wellness services for all ages in the community, they say. 

“I think it’s very difficult to put a monetary value on our idea that it is very important for our youth to have an area to go,” said resident Orion Nold. “The city providing that I think is an excellent idea. Some of the questions pertaining to transparency, I believe that is what the city is after so they can appease some of these questions. Currently, a private entity is not required to provide those to the general public. The city taking it over, that becomes something that will be much more transparent.” 

But resident Pam Berreth said she is tired of “emotional blackmail,” and being told she doesn’t support kids activities, because she doesn’t support what she called a bad business decision. Other residents have advocated for the city to put the recreation funding into street and infrastructure repair. Berreth said some streets are in such disrepair, that they are not even safe for kids to walk on. 

Heupel ended the discussion with a request to the commission to consider the resolution he presented, and come to the next regularly scheduled meeting, May 18, prepared to take action on the matter. Heupel said the city has examined the Handley Center’s financial reports, but is not at liberty to share them since they belong to a private nonprofit entity.

title: US Supreme Court decision on rulemaking won’t reopen Piper death penalty case, appeals court says
byline: By John Hult Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — A U.S. Supreme Court decision on bureaucratic overreach doesn’t give South Dakota’s lone death row inmate another chance to argue for a new trial or sentence, according to a ruling from the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals released on Monday.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — A U.S. Supreme Court decision on bureaucratic overreach doesn’t give South Dakota’s lone death row inmate another chance to argue for a new trial or sentence, according to a ruling from the 8th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals released on Monday.

Briley Piper, 46, was sentenced to death by a judge for the murder of Chester Allan Poage. Piper, Elijah Page and Darrell Hoadley tortured and killed Poage in 2000 near Spearfish. Page was executed in 2007; Hoadley remains in prison with a life sentence.

South Dakota has had as many as 5 people on death row since the punishment was reinstituted after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled it constitutional in 1976 in the case of Gregg vs. Georgia. Page was the first person executed in the state after that ruling, and 4 other men have been put to death since.

Piper successfully argued to have his death sentence from a judge reviewed by a Lawrence County jury, which again sentenced him to death in 2011.

Piper has since lost appeals at the state Supreme Court and in U.S. District Court. Last year, he again appealed to federal court to argue that his sentence ought to be thrown out.

He relied in part on the U.S. Supreme Court’s Loper Bright decision. That opinion gave judges greater authority to challenge bureaucratic regulatory decisions. The landmark decision upended a 4-decade precedent that courts should defer to federal agencies’ interpretation of laws such as the Clean Air Act or Clean Water Act.

Piper’s attorneys said Loper Bright also gave federal judges more leeway in reviewing state court decisions in death penalty cases. Federal law limits how deeply federal judges can delve into questions of constitutional rights in death row cases after state courts address them, but Piper’s lawyers — along with lawyers for a handful of other death row inmates around the U.S. — have argued that state courts are akin to bureaucratic rulemakers and that their rulings should be fully open to scrutiny.

U.S. District Judge Roberto Lange rejected that argument in Piper’s case in March 2025, a month after his lawyers raised it. Piper appealed to the 8th U.S. Circuit.

In its Monday ruling, the appeals court ruled against Piper’s Loper Bright claim. 

“Every court to address this claim disagrees” with the position argued by Piper’s attorneys, the ruling says, listing nine separate death penalty cases where similar arguments were made.

The 8th Circuit also rejected 5 other assertions from Piper, including that his 2001 guilty plea wasn’t voluntary and that his defense lawyers failed to consider the possibility that Piper suffers from fetal alcohol spectrum disorder — his lawyers did explore the issue, the appeals court found.

Piper could appeal the 8th Circuit’s decision to the U.S. Supreme Court. His attorneys did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley, whose office represents the state in Piper’s appeal, applauded the decision in a Monday statement.

“Briley Piper has never accepted responsibility for his actions and has consistently tried to shift blame onto others for his sentence,” Jackley wrote. “The 8th Circuit’s rejection of his appeal marks an important step toward final justice for Chester Poage and his family.”

title: Nourishing our neighbors
byline: Black Hills Pioneer By Sara Morgan
description: Wendy Pitlick, creator of Hope’s Kitchen, saw a need in her community when people were facing a cut to their food stamps in October during the government shutdown. Since then, she created a nonprofit soup kitchen, serving a hot meal to those in need every second and fourth Saturday. Photo courtesy of Mariana Pitlick
_full_text:
Nourishing our neighbors
Wendy Pitlick, creator of Hope’s Kitchen, saw a need in her community when people were facing a cut to their food stamps in October during the government shutdown. Since then, she created a nonprofit soup kitchen, serving a hot meal to those in need every second and fourth Saturday. Photo courtesy of Mariana Pitlick 

DEADWOOD — Hope’s Kitchen is set to open this weekend, filling a void in local relief programming by offering a free hot meal to those in need from 5-7 p.m. Saturday at the Trinity United Methodist Ministry Center in Lead.

Wendy Pitlick, creator, chef, fundraiser, and award-winning reporter for the Black Hills Pioneer, said the idea for a soup kitchen came to her in October 2025, when communities across the nation were facing hunger after their food stamps benefits were cut during the government shutdown. 

“There was this whole outcry about how we can help these people,” said Pitlick. “And for a lot of years I’ve been hearing reports that there were a lot of kids in the Lead-Deadwood school system and at the Boys and Girls Club, who only ate hot meals at the school and at the Boys and Girls Club. So, I’ve always had it in the back of my mind that I wanted to do something. I always said that if I ever won the lottery, I would start a pay-what-you-can café. Well, I didn’t win the lottery.”

That didn’t deter her, though. Pitlick said she took her inspiration from the Fork Real Community Café in Rapid City, a restaurant with a full breakfast and lunch menu offering meals at a pay-what-you-can price, and the Cornerstone Rescue Mission, a soup kitchen providing hot meals for the population that is unhoused in Rapid City.  After reaching out to both entities, she said they happily shared their business plans and planning materials, which gave Pitlick the foundation she needed to start building a plan for Hope’s Kitchen. She received her ServSafe certification, allowing her to manage a commercial kitchen, and began to look for a kitchen. 

“My first experience with (Pitlick) was when she came to the church to talk to our pastor, Jason Christensen, about her idea to have a soup kitchen kind of arrangement, especially for the kids in the area who often go with insufficient meals,” said James Wolff, co-chair of the Trinity United Methodist Church board of trustees and treasurer of the Hope’s Kitchen board of directors. “(Christensen) came to the board of trustees and asked us if we would entertain the idea of using our ministry center. We quickly jumped on board, thinking it was a great idea. And here was (Pitlick), who was full of energy and willing to take the lead and take on that responsibility of getting it off the ground.”

Pitlick said that while she began the paperwork of obtaining a 501(c)(3) status, labeling Hope’s Kitchen as nonprofit, tax-exempt charitable organization, the board at the church agreed to take her on as a fiscal partner in early February.

“Which was huge, because that allowed me to start applying for grants and things like that,” Pitlick said. “So, I went crazy with applying for grants and sponsorships and everything, because I knew I had my permission, I had everything in place. Well, about the time that the donations started coming in and the grants started coming in, I got my 501(c)(3) status on Feb. 25. That was 4 weeks from the time I applied to the time I received it. I was surprised by that, because my research shows that it can take between 6 and 18 months.”

Through March and April, Pitlick garnered support from the Lead-Deadwood communities, securing corporate and private sponsorships, including the Black Hills Pioneer, Lynn’s Dakotamart, Rasmussen Mechanical Services, and Feeding South Dakota. She’s gained volunteers from as far away as Rapid City, who are traveling to help serve Hope’s Kitchen’s first meal Saturday.

“I feel like this is a God thing,” said Wolff. “(Pitlick) came to us at a time when we had the capacity and the desire to utilize our facilities and give back to the community in a more concrete fashion. The people she’s gone to have been touched and willing to give, and it’s just falling together like it was intended to. It’s been amazing.”

The menu

Pitlick said that her mission is to create a hot meal consisting of an entrée, vegetable, a bread, and dessert, on meal days. However, she said that she cannot accept donations for Hope’s Kitchen during mealtimes. 

“The definition of a relief organization is that you can’t take money for food,” she said. “I’ve heard a lot of people ask me, ‘Well, can’t I eat and just donate?’ Well, no, you can’t. In order for me to qualify as a relief organization, and in order to utilize the services of Feeding South Dakota, I have to offer these meals completely for free.”

Pitlick said a donation jar will be set up during mealtimes, but all money collected there will go back towards the Christian Ministry Center to help pay for the use of the facility. 

Pitlick said that there won’t be anyone at the door, Saturday, asking for names or proof of income to come and eat. However, she said, she asks that people “self-police” to decide if they need the meal or if they should leave the opportunity for someone who could need it more. 

“You know whether you have food in your pantry or your fridge and if you need a service like this,” she said. “There are some people in Lead-Deadwood who don’t even have a cookstove that they can prepare a hot meal on. People know what their situation is, and if somebody who comes in for a meal who doesn’t need it, they could potentially be taking away a meal from somebody who does.”

Pitlick said that for the first run of Hope’s Kitchen, she’ll be preparing enough food for 100 people. She said that people who want to make sure that they get a meal should show up early, but doors won’t open until 5 p.m.

A meal worth remembering

Pitlick said that Hope’s Kitchen’s first meal will be a throwback to a time when she and her family were facing their own food shortage and financial woes. 

“More than 10 years ago, in 2010 I think it was, I quit working so that I could be a full-time mom. A month later, my husband lost his job,” Pitlick said. “So, I went to the Lord’s Cupboard in Lead, and they said, ‘Well, we need to see your last 2 pay stubs.’ Well, my husband made too much money with his last 2 pay stubs, but we didn’t have any money coming in. We didn’t have any groceries. So, Sharon (Narem) said, ‘OK. I can give you this pound of hamburger and then your choice of anything on the shelves.”

Pitlick said she found Spanish rice, beans, and enchilada sauce on the shelves. After spending $5 for tortillas, she went home and put together enough enchiladas to feed her family lunch and dinner for almost a week. 

“I stuffed it full of all that filling stuff,” she said. “We had a lot of leftovers, too. I made that pound of hamburger stretch just as far as I could.”

In remembrance of a time when her community gave what they could to support her and her family, Pitlick said Hope’s Kitchen’s first meal will be enchiladas, a tomato and lettuce salad, and a cookie tray.

“The enchiladas on Saturday will be chicken, because Lynn’s gave us an offer we couldn’t refuse on the price,” she said. “But that recipe is a direct result of that huge time of need for my family.”

Families in need

Pitlick and Wolff said that Hope’s Kitchen is looking for board members and volunteers with relevant experience who are willing to help. 

“I need people who have the skills and the knowledge to prepare meals in bulk like we are,” Pitlick said. “If they can find the time to, twice a month, help with this, because I know this is a lot to ask somebody, but if people have experience in this kind of thing, we need the help.”

Wolff said that if Hope’s Kitchen gets enough support and enough help, the mission could become larger, providing more meals more frequently. 

“If we can get other entities helping us, then all of a sudden it’s a burden the community is sharing and it’s not much of an effort for any one entity,” Wolff said. “It’s something that could really balloon and do beautiful things.”

To learn more about Hope’s Kitchen, check out its Facebook page. To inquire about donations, volunteering, or other questions, please email hopes.kitchen2026@gmail.com.

title: Aladdin Jr. live at  Sturgis Community Theater
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: STURGIS — The Black Hills Theatre Company hosts Aladdin Jr. for 3 performances starting Thursday.

STURGIS — The Black Hills Theatre Company hosts Aladdin Jr. for 3 performances starting Thursday.

The cast of 24 actors, ranging in ages from 8-18, began rehearsals in early March. 

The story follows Aladdin, a kind-hearted street thief living in the city of Agrabah. Though he struggles to survive, Aladdin dreams of a better life. One day, he meets Princess Jasmine, who has disguised herself to escape the palace and experience life beyond royal walls. The 2 form an instant connection.

Meanwhile, the villainous royal advisor Jafar is plotting to take control of the kingdom. He manipulates Aladdin into retrieving a magical lamp from the Cave of Wonders. Inside the lamp lives the hilarious and powerful Genie, who grants Aladdin 3 wishes.

With Genie’s help, Aladdin transforms himself into a prince in hopes of winning Jasmine’s heart. However, maintaining the disguise proves difficult, and Aladdin must ultimately learn that honesty and being true to himself matter more than appearances.

As Jafar seizes power using magic, Aladdin, Jasmine, and their friends must work together to stop him. Will Aladdin find a way to stop Jafar? 

The show features popular songs like “A Whole New World” and “Friend Like Me,” along with colorful costumes, comedic moments, and a message about self-worth, friendship, and integrity.

Performances are at 7 p.m. Thursday and Sunday with a 2 p.m. matinee Saturday. All performances are at the Sturgis Community Center Theater.

Admission is $7 and free for kids 12 and younger. Tickets can be purchased at the door.

byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Shared by the city of Spearfish, this image demonstrates where and when trees and shrubs need trimming. Image courtesy of Snohomish County Public Works Communication Team
_full_text:
Spearfish issues seasonal reminders on tree, shrub trimming and lawn maintenance
Shared by the city of Spearfish, this image demonstrates where and when trees and shrubs need trimming. Image courtesy of Snohomish County Public Works Communication Team 

SPEARFISH — Spring has arrived. That means flowers are in bloom and grass is springing up to new heights. That also means Spearfish residents will need to pull out their mowers, pruning shears, and gardening tools to ensure their properties comply with city code.

“It’s the time of year when we start cleaning up our properties from the winter and look forward to enjoying the summer months,” Code Enforcement Officer Jade Addison said. “It’s also the time of year we start hearing from residents concerned about nuisances in their neighborhoods, so we want to kindly remind homeowners to begin the maintenance of their property. Residents should be aware you may receive a door hanger or letter as an additional reminder.”

Grass and weeds taller than 10 inches, or any noxious weeds, are considered a nuisance, and property owners are reminded to keep their yards and any boulevards (the areas between the sidewalk and street) trimmed.

Some areas within 20 feet of the creek, with a slope steeper than 2 horizontal feet or 1 vertical foot, may be exempt from the 10-inch height limit, because their property is considered “highly erodible.”

As trees and shrubs bloom, the city is reminding residents to keep sidewalks clear of leaves and debris. Trees and shrubs should also be trimmed if they overlap onto the sidewalk or impede travel on the roadway.

“Once your trees, shrubs, and other vegetation are fully leafed out, take a walk on any sidewalk/street/alley adjacent to your property to check for anything on your property that needs to be maintained/trimmed/managed to allow free, safe, and full use of these spaces by the public,” a statement from the city reads. Trees should be trimmed to allow a minimum overhead sidewalk clearance of 10 feet. The city suggests trees be trimmed to allow a minimum overhead clearance of 14 feet above the street and alley. Property owners are also responsible for pruning tree branches and shrubs so that they do not obstruct the view of any street or alley intersection.

Bruch, Bradley, Bohn to run for Sturgis mayor Vasknetz, Keszler in race for city council seat
Courtesy graphic 

STURGIS — Richelle Bruch, Rod Bradley, and Tammy Bohn will run for mayor of Sturgis this year, and Brenda Vasknetz and Terry Keszler will run for Ward 1 City Council representative. 

The deadline for candidate petitions was at 5 p.m. Monday, and at the end of the day the city of Sturgis announced the 5 candidates. Additional candidates are possible only if a nominating petition was mailed by registered mail to the city finance office by 5 p.m. Monday, according to state law. 

The election is scheduled for Tuesday, June 2 with voting taking place in the lobby of the Sturgis Community Center theater and in the Meade Room at the community center. 

The mayoral seat became vacant following the resignation of Kevin Forrester. Mayor Pro Tempore Tony Dargatz is currently serving in the role until a new mayor is elected and sworn in. The Ward 1 City Council seat became vacant when Nick Jones resigned from the seat after accepting a work offer that will require him to move to Texas this summer. 

All registered Sturgis voters may vote in the mayoral election. Only registered voters residing in Ward 1 may vote in the Ward 1 City Council election.

Absentee voting will be available beginning May 18, at the City of Sturgis Finance Office during regular business hours, which are 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. Monday through Friday.

For more information about the upcoming election, contact the Sturgis Finance Office at (605) 347-4422.

title: Education board strips Common Core  math in favor of ‘simplified’ standards
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Members of the South Dakota Board of Education Standards meet Monday, at the DoubleTree convention center in Rapid City. From left are board members Linda Olsen and Tonia Warzecha, state Education Secretary Joe Graves, and board members Steven Perkins, Greg Von Wald, Phyllis Heineman and Rich Meyer. Photo by Seth Tupper, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Education board strips Common Core  math in favor of ‘simplified’ standards
Members of the South Dakota Board of Education Standards meet Monday, at the DoubleTree convention center in Rapid City. From left are board members Linda Olsen and Tonia Warzecha, state Education Secretary Joe Graves, and board members Steven Perkins, Greg Von Wald, Phyllis Heineman and Rich Meyer. Photo by Seth Tupper, South Dakota Searchlight 

RAPID CITY — The South Dakota Board of Education Standards unanimously approved revisions to the state’s math standards Monday in Rapid City, even as a math teacher flagged some problems state officials acknowledged they’ll have to fix.

The board, the state Department of Education and math educators throughout the state have gone back and forth over the last 6 months on the standards. The department accepted more than 50 changes to the original proposal over that timeframe.

Crystal McMachen, a middle school math teacher in Rapid City, told board members she worried the standards were oversimplified and rushed, leading to errors in the final product. She flagged three errors at the meeting, including duplicated standards, inconsistent wording and misalignment between grade levels.

“If I found these errors in an hour on a Saturday — and this was on a Saturday — I can’t believe these have been combed through,” McMachen said. “So, I’m really urging you not to adopt these standards. They are not ready, and South Dakota is better than this.”

South Dakota Department of Education Secretary Joe Graves told the board the current standards, which were copied from the national Common Core standards, are “unnecessarily complex” in some areas. The new standards don’t oversimplify the standards, he said.

“It simply changes the language so that it is heard and understood by more people,” Graves said.

A 20-person revision committee reviewed the original proposal after it was developed by a statewide advisory group last year. The proposal pulls from other states’ standards across the nation, and from the Archimedes standards, which were written by an assistant professor at Hillsdale College. The private Christian college in Michigan was also involved in South Dakota’s revised social studies standards, approved in 2023 and implemented this school year.

Sharon Vestal, a mathematics professor at South Dakota State University and president of the South Dakota Council of Teachers of Mathematics, attended every standards hearing held across the state for the new math standards. She said the standards fundamentally “prioritize procedures over concepts” and make mathematics “less precise” in the quest to make the standards easier for parents and elementary educators to understand.

“Mathematics is a language. It is universal, structured and exact,” Vestal said. “Like any language, it has vocabulary, grammar and syntax. When that structure is removed, meaning is lost.”

Earlier in the standards revision process, Graves told board members South Dakota students “lack significant progress” on math testing since the COVID-19 pandemic, which he attributed to the current standards. About 44% of students were proficient or above on the state test annually over the last five years, he said.

Math standards alone won’t raise test scores, said Shannon Malone, the department’s director of learning and instruction, while introducing the latest version of the standards.

“It’s clear that we also need all our educators to increase efforts and attention to mathematics,” Malone said. “Achievement requires excellent instruction in the classroom, parental support, professional development at all levels, solid instructional materials, school and district support.”

Malone added that a “more simplified set of standards and robust set of supports” could help South Dakota students “realize their true potential in math.”

The department accepted more than 80% of the actionable changes recommended by opponents throughout the process. 

Board President Steve Perkins acknowledged that the adopted standards would need minor corrections, but wanted to approve the standards so the state Department of Education would “move forward” with implementation.

Graves told the board that the department can bring back errors that “are not content changes” to be fixed at a later date. Addressing McMahon’s concerns about the misalignment would be a “substantive change,” Graves said.

“We can look at those and come back to you at a later time, but at this point we’d like to get the standards approved,” Graves said.

The exchange was evidence of a rushed process, Vestal told South Dakota Searchlight after the meeting.

“I suspect there are a lot of issues within the standards,” Vestal said. “I’m pretty sure there are more than the ones Crystal pointed out today. I want to make sure if we’re using these standards for multiple years that they’re done right.”

Vestal said the misalignment between concepts taught at different grade levels will “cause a lot of problems” within districts. As a university instructor, she plans to keep an eye on whether incoming students will be prepared for college-level courses.

“Mathematics is just too important to not do it right,” Vestal said.

title: Deadwood police respond to bomb threat, conclude threat to be false
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Deadwood police respond to bomb threat, conclude threat to be false
Courtesy photo 

DEADWOOD — At approximately 9:30 p.m., Sunday, Deadwood Police Department and Lawrence County Sheriff responded to a bomb threat at the Gold Dust Casino in Deadwood. The threat was quickly determined to be false. 

Cory Shafer, chief of Deadwood police, said that dispatch received a call from an individual identifying himself as “The Reaper,” who claimed to have planted explosive material in the vicinity of 688 Main St. The caller claimed to be armed with an AR-15 and was demanding $20,000 in cash.

Upon arrival, Shafer said that law enforcement immediately surveyed the area and conducted a thorough investigation of the premises and surrounding properties. Through the investigation and while maintaining communication with the caller, officers perceived several inconsistencies in their statements, ultimately leading law enforcement to conclude that the threat was a false report. 

During the investigation, Shafer said no explosive devices, weapons, or hazardous materials were found during the search. 

Shafer said the call is still under investigation by the Deadwood Police and Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office, who continue to search for the origin of the phone call. 

“Although this is an active and ongoing investigation, there remains no threat to the public, said Shafer.

The Pioneer will continue to report on the issue as more information becomes available.

title: Wrong way driver causes I-90 crash,  4 injured

description: SUMMERSET — Four people were injured when a driver entered Interstate 90 in the wrong direction Tuesday night near Summerset.
_full_text:
Wrong way driver causes I-90 crash,  4 injured

SUMMERSET — Four people were injured when a driver entered Interstate 90 in the wrong direction Tuesday night near Summerset.

The names of the people involved have not been released.

According to the South Dakota Highway Patrol, just before 9:30 p.m., a 22-year-old woman from Rapid City, allegedly began driving a 2007 Subaru Forester  westbound in the eastbound passing lane on Interstate 90 near Exit 48 when she collided head-on with an eastbound 2008 Honda Pilot. The Honda spun and flipped onto its roof. The Subaru then struck a 2008 Peterbilt head-on. 

The driver of the Subaru sustained serious, non-life-threatening injuries, as did the driver and 2 passengers in the Honda. The driver of the Peterbilt was not injured. Alcohol is considered to be a factor in the crash.

The interstate’s eastbound lanes were closed until shortly before 1 a.m.

The South Dakota Highway Patrol is investigating the crash.

title: Haivala awarded SD Drug Prosecutor  of the Year at DCI conference
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: Robert Haivala, assistant South Dakota attorney general, was recently recognized as South Dakota’s Drug Prosecutor of the Year at the annual Division of Criminal Investigation (DCI) conference in Deadwood. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
1. Haivala.JPG
Robert Haivala, assistant South Dakota attorney general, was recently recognized as South Dakota’s Drug Prosecutor of the Year at the annual Division of Criminal Investigation (DCI) conference in Deadwood. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

DEADWOOD — Robert Haivala, an assistant South Dakota attorney general based in Rapid City, was recognized as South Dakota’s Drug Prosecutor of the Year during an awards ceremony recently at the annual Division of Criminal Investigation (DCI) conference in Deadwood.  

A graduate of Spearfish High School (1979) and Black Hills State University (1982), Haivala currently lives in Sturgis and has built a reputation for his dedication to justice and his commitment to serving the community through his work in the courtroom.

Attorney General Marty Jackley praised Haivala’s efforts, noting both his professional excellence and personal character.  

“I have known Bob as far back as I can remember when our fathers taught together at Black Hills State,” Jackley said. “What makes him such an effective and strong prosecutor is how he treats and cares about people. He builds trust and relationships with victims, law enforcement, and witnesses. He is the type of leader deserving of the SD Drug Prosecutor of the Year, and that young prosecutors can look up to and learn from.”

Presenting the award, Jake Whittle of the DEA/DCI explained the thorough and impartial selection process.  

“We have a lot of really good nominations,” Whittle said. “To ensure fairness, the decision is made by an independent committee made up of law enforcement professionals from the east, central, and west districts. They review the nominations and determine the recipient.”

Whittle noted that Haivala stood out among a strong group of candidates. “This person was nominated numerous times,” he said. “He’s done an amazing job, and unfortunately, he’ll be leaving us very shortly. Bob Haivala is truly deserving of this recognition.”

One nomination read during the ceremony underscored Haivala’s impact on those he has worked alongside for years. 

“I first met Bob in 2010 and had no idea at the time the kind of professional relationship we would build,” the nomination stated. “Over the past 21 years, I’ve worked with law enforcement and attorneys at the local, county, state, and federal levels on cases ranging from simple traffic citations to complex drug conspiracies. Since moving to the Rapid City area in 2017, I’ve generated more than 500 cases, most handled by the South Dakota Attorney General’s Office.”  

In accepting the award, Haivala expressed humility and emphasized the teamwork required to combat drug-related crime. 

“I am very humbled by the fact I was given this award by these professionals who are protecting people of South Dakota from drugs and the drug dealers who profit from addiction,” Haivala said.  

He stressed the importance of collaboration across all levels of law enforcement and prosecution.  

“Prosecution of drug cartels requires total cooperation between federal, state, and local law agencies and prosecutors,” he said. “Drug dealers pay no attention to state borders or county lines. That means all jurisdictions need to cooperate when enforcing drug laws. That’s the way we do it in South Dakota.”

Haivala also highlighted the dedication of those working behind the scenes to build strong cases.  

“I’m most proud of the dogged pursuit our agents show when dismantling drug networks. They do it by the book,” he said. “I’m also proud of our support staff and attorneys. It takes a lot of work to bring a case to trial—much of it the public never sees. I will miss them as I go into retirement.”

Haivala’s recognition reflects not only his legal expertise but also his reputation for teamwork, dependability, and commitment to justice—qualities that have made a lasting impact on South Dakota’s law enforcement community.

STURGIS — The annual children’s production returned to the stage Friday, as members of the Scooper Thespian Society presented ‘Story Tails’ a lively, student-written performance for area youth under the direction of Hillary Hill. The 21-member cast brought 7 classic fairy tales to life, combining humor, creativity and storytelling in a production designed especially for elementary audiences across the Sturgis school district.

Hill said the show continues a long-standing tradition for the Sturgis High School drama program.  “We are performing ‘Story Tails,’ which incorporates 7 famous fairy tales,” Hill said. “This is a script that the drama students wrote together to perform for the elementary students of our district. It’s a long-running tradition for the high school drama club to present a children’s show for younger students.”

Elementary students from throughout the district attended performances, along with both middle school drama clubs, giving younger performers a chance to experience live theater and connect with the high school program.  The production not only showcased acting talent, but also highlighted the students’ work in writing, staging and collaboration, making it a theatrical experience.

Looking ahead, Hill said the program will continue to engage students this summer. A summer drama camp is scheduled for July 20–24 at the Sturgis Community Center Theatre and is open to students in grades 6–12.
