title: Elk wander to East River, and the state responds with unlimited hunting licenses
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Elk roam Wind Cave National Park in South Dakota. Photo courtesy of the National Park Service
_full_text:
Elk wander to East River, and the state responds with unlimited hunting licenses
Elk roam Wind Cave National Park in South Dakota. Photo courtesy of the National Park Service 

PIERRE — Elk hunters in South Dakota will have more opportunities in Custer State Park and east of the Missouri River after a legislative committee approved rule changes Tuesday.

The committee, made up of three state senators and three state representatives, voted 4-2 in favor of a rules package that includes an unlimited elk hunting season on the eastern side of the river and increases the maximum number of elk licenses in the park.

Sen. Liz Larson and Rep. Erik Muckey, Democrats from Sioux Falls, cast the 2 no votes.

East River elk hunting

More elk are starting to appear in the East River region, said Tom Kirschenmann, director of wildlife for the Department of Game, Fish and Parks. The elk, which typically are more at home in the Black Hills and other rugged terrain of western South Dakota, are unwelcome guests in East River farm fields.

“They can create a lot of damage, and it’s a very, very challenging management activity,” Kirschenmann said. He added that the agency has no intention of managing a permanent East River elk population.

The estimated population of elk in the Black Hills is about 8,000. There could be up to 2,000 on the western South Dakota plains, Kirschenmann said. East River populations are “nowhere near those numbers,” though he didn’t provide an estimate.

East River elk are usually found between Pierre and Chamberlain, particularly on the Crow Creek reservation, which will be excluded from the unlimited hunting unit. Kirschenmann said the agency is in conversation with the tribe’s wildlife department about its elk management strategy.

Larson doesn’t dispute that crops are being harmed, but she said it may be premature to declare open season on all East River elk.

“I don’t see enough evidence that we know how this would affect the elk populations,” she said. “I feel like this is a very new, new area that they’re going into.”

More Custer State Park elk licenses

The elk population in Custer State Park, in the Black Hills of western South Dakota, is above what the agency prefers to manage at the park, Kirschenmann said. Populations are usually kept between 500 and 600, but a recent estimate placed the number between 750 and 775.

That’s why the agency will increase the limit of antlerless elk hunting licenses for Custer State Park from 20 to 100. The agency will not offer all 100 licenses this year, Kirschenmann said. The number of licenses available will be decided based on the population and whether it’s anticipated to grow or shrink.

Hunters can expect 50 licenses to be available this year. Twenty-five will be available for 2 weeks in October and the remainder will be available for two weeks in December.

Splitting up licenses over those time periods will “minimize congestion of the hunters on each other,” Kirschenmann said.

Larson said she doesn’t see evidence supporting “that number” for the license cap “should be the one that’s pursued.”

title: Hearing held in Mitchell  baseball defamation lawsuit
byline: By Molly Wetsch South Dakota News Watch
description: MITCHELL — A judge heard arguments Tuesday for three motions in the civil lawsuit filed by a former Mitchell baseball player against 2 local news organizations and the American Legion Baseball league.
_full_text:
SDNewsWatchLogo

MITCHELL — A judge heard arguments Tuesday for three motions in the civil lawsuit filed by a former Mitchell baseball player against 2 local news organizations and the American Legion Baseball league.

Circuit Judge David Knoff said he will rule later on the motions, one of which could put an end to the case or send it to trial.

The case revolves around a sentence in a letter by a representative from the American Legion sent to members of the Mitchell Baseball Association.

Peyton Mandel, who is now 20, was a player for the Mitchell baseball team and one of 6 involved in a hazing incident that took place in 2023 at a Rapid City hotel room. The event, in which another player said the boys held him down and performed forcible digital anal penetration on him, was later characterized as a rape case. He pleaded guilty in 2024 to one count of accessory to a felony as part of a plea deal.

In November 2024, American Legion adjutant C.P. Van Delist sent a letter to members of the Mitchell Baseball Association saying that the organization had decided that Mitchell Baseball would be immediately barred from participating in the American Legion and provided a set of conditions that must be met in order for the association to be reestablished in the future.

In the letter, after naming the 6 former players involved in the case, Van Delist said, “All of these individuals are guilty of accessory to a felony, acknowledging by affirmation of their guilty pleas, that the felonies they were charged with, rape and aiding and abetting, did take place.”

In July 2025, Mandel filed a civil lawsuit saying that Van Delist made “false, malicious, and defamatory” statements about him. Nexstar Media Group, the owner of KELO-TV, and Forum Communications, owner of the Mitchell Republic, were also named in the lawsuit. Both organizations published stories containing Van Delist’s letter.

Case sees multiple First Amendment considerations

The lawsuit states that Van Delist’s statements and the subsequent news articles “falsely (represented) and (characterized) Plaintiff as an admitted rapist.” The lawsuit also says that Mandel was “denied reapplication for an employment or experiential opportunity in the medical field” as a result of news articles published by KELO and the Mitchell Republic.

Mandel’s lawyer, Tucker Volesky, said during the hearing that the contested sentence in the letter indicated Mandel was a rapist when that was not the charge that Mandel pled guilty to. Volesky said that because Mandel pleaded guilty to accessory to a felony, it was wrong to name him in the letter next to the statement of rape taking place.

The hearing spanned several First Amendment complexities, including what qualifies as “privileged” communication, whether Mandel can be considered a limited public figure in relation to the case and consideration about what constitutes the “truth” of the case.

Attorneys for the defendants said that even if Mandel’s record does not indicate rape, a rape still took place. One sentiment was that because Mandel pleaded guilty to accessory to a felony, he therefore acknowledged that the rape happened. Volesky said that Mandel should not be associated with rape and said that the intention of the lawsuit was to say that a rape did not happen.

Hearing ends without decisions

All 3 motions considered Tuesday afternoon were taken under advisement by Knoff. 

One was a motion for a judgment on pleadings filed by Volesky, which asked the judge to solely consider what Mandel affirmed by pleading guilty. Volesky also asked Knoff to consider the “narrow falsity issue” provided by the lawsuit and said that prior context was not relevant to the issue of whether Van Delist’s letter falsely accused Mandel of rape.

A motion to quash a subpoena was presented by Jessica LaMie, a South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation deputy attorney. That was in response to attorney Pete Heidepriem, on behalf of Nexstar, submitting a subpoena to the DCI requesting documents in the criminal investigation of the 2023 hazing case.

The final motion considered was a motion for summary judgment – which would have required the judge to rule on the case immediately without sending it to trial.

Attorney Sarah Collins, who represents Forum Communications and Mitchell Republic editor Luke Hagen, brought forward the motion. She said that there was no factual basis for the continuation of the case and that the plaintiff was “trying to prove malice when malice is not there.”

Volesky said in response that the articles written were single-sourced and failed to verify the facts in the court record, violating traditional journalistic ethics standards.

Knoff said during discussion of that third motion that he felt he was “being asked to close (his) eyes on the act that took place” by Volesky and was struggling to find a factual basis for the decision to consider the letter in a vacuum.

Knoff did not indicate when he would rule on the motions but said it would be as soon as he could. There is no specific limitation on how soon a judge must rule after taking a case under advisement, and it can range anywhere from a few days after a hearing to several months.

title: State changes intrastate CDL requirements to maintain federal highway funding
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: DEADWOOD — Approximately 28,000 South Dakota residents are facing new requirements to their Commercial Driver’s Licenses (CDL) after the passage of Senate Bill 10 in February, requiring them to pass a Department of Transportation (DOT) certified physical to maintain their license by July 1.
_full_text:
State changes intrastate CDL requirements to maintain federal highway funding

DEADWOOD — Approximately 28,000 South Dakota residents are facing new requirements to their Commercial Driver’s Licenses (CDL) after the passage of Senate Bill 10 in February, requiring them to pass a Department of Transportation (DOT) certified physical to maintain their license by July 1. 

Robert Perry, cabinet secretary of the Department of Public Safety, said that South Dakota has not required CDL drivers who do not drive outside of the state, called intrastate driving, to obtain a medical card for approximately 20 years, in spite of arguments from the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration (FMCSA regulation 49 CFR 391.11. 

“We made an argument for several years that, one, we didn’t have the legislative support for it. And 2, we argued that from our own research, there wasn’t a documented risk based on not having a medical card,” Perry Said. “However, most states implemented it before we did. So, essentially, they let it slide for a number of years.”

Perry said that FMCSA conducted an audit of South Dakota in 2025, wherein they concluded that the exemption made South Dakota’s Department of Public Safety non-compliant with federal standards and threatened to take away federal highway funding.

Sen. Randy Deibert, R-Spearfish, serves as a member of the senate transportation committee. He said that if South Dakota remained non-compliant, the state could lose 20% of federal highway funding in the first year, with that loss ramping up every year to eventually reach a 50% loss in funding. 

Senate Bill 10 was approved by the state legislature and signed by Gov. Larry Rhoden Feb. 17. From there, letters were sent out to every driver with a CDL, notifying them that they had until July 1 to come into compliance with the new regulation.

If drives fail to come into compliance by July 1, their CDL will be downgraded until they obtain the physical and medical card. Perry said he does not believe there is a penalty fee for not meeting the July 1 deadline.

“The rub, I think, is that this happened, and they don’t feel that they had enough notice,” said Deibert.

Perry said to come into compliance, drivers will need to schedule a physical exam with a DOT certified examiner, who will then be required to electronically transmit the medical card to the Department of Motor Vehicles (DMV) exam stations. He said a physical costs an average of $120. 

From there, the driver is required to obtain a new card from a exam station. The new card costs each driver $43.

“So, you’re looking at a cost of $160-200, which is less than a cost of an oil change in the truck,” said Perry. “It’s not cost prohibitive, but it’s not free.”

The short window of time for drivers to come into compliance means that exam stations across the state have had to extend their hours, including being open from 7 a.m. to noon on Saturday. 

“They can come in anytime, but we are specifically opening centers and paying people overtime on Saturdays to try and get these licenses turned over,” said Perry. “The thing that saves us is there’s a fee to get this license, and that generally covers our cost.”

Perry said that he doesn’t anticipate that all 28,000 people who hold a CDL in South Dakota will rush to come into compliance. 

“I know there are a number of people that this is affecting, and it’s somewhere really close to that 28,000, but it may be a little under or a little over,” said Perry. “Many of those people don’t need their CDL. They may be retired or no longer have a job requiring it and have just kept it because they didn’t need the medical exam to do so. I know I’ve gotten calls from a number of retired truck drivers who simply have it just in case they want to use it again. If they really think they may use it again, they’ll have to get the medical exam now.”

According to a letter sent out to CDL holders, exempt drivers include transportation performed by the federal or state government; transportation of human bodies or sick and injured persons; the operation of rescue vehicles;  commercial motor vehicles used primarily for the transportation of propane winter heating fuel or vehicles used to respond to pipeline emergencies; pipeline welding trucks; custom harvesting for farmlands or to transport farm machinery used for harvesting; beekeepers transporting bees; private motor carriers of passengers for non-business purposes; the occasional transportation of personal property by individuals not for compensation and not in pursuit of commercial enterprise; motor vehicles transporting between 9 and 15 passengers not for compensation; vehicles operated by a farmer but not a combination vehicle (power unit and towed unit) and is used to transport agricultural products, farm machinery, or farm supplies to and from a farm within 150 air-miles of the farm; and to transport migrant workers.

To find a certified medical provider, visit https://nationalregistry.fmcsa.dot.gov/home. 

To find an exam station, schedule an appointment, and view hours, visit www.sd.gov/dps.

SPEARFISH — In this issue, you will find the annual publication of financial summaries of insurance companies licensed to do business in South Dakota.

Insurance companies doing business in South Dakota are required by state law to publish these financial summaries each year. The summary lists the insurance company’s assets, liabilities, business in South Dakota for the year and the lines in which the company is authorized by the state of South Dakota to sell insurance.

“Public notices published in newspapers have an important role in keeping citizens informed and providing bonafide transparency. The publication of these insurance company financial summaries supports those principles and helps to inform South Dakotans about an important part of the financial industry in our state,” said South Dakota NewsMedia Association Executive Director David Bordewyk. “This is why public notices published in the local newspaper remain vital in our democracy.”

 For more information about any insurance company doing business in South Dakota, contact the state Division of Insurance in Pierre at (605) 773-3563.

 More than 8 out of 10 South Dakotans believe that publishing public notices in a local newspaper should be required. That is according to a statewide survey of 406 South Dakota adults commissioned by SDNA and conducted by Coda Ventures in 2024.

title: SD stays at No. 46 in teacher pay rankings
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — South Dakota ranks 46th in the nation in a new report on average teacher salaries, the same as last year.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — South Dakota ranks 46th in the nation in a new report on average teacher salaries, the same as last year.

The state’s standing is its highest since the National Education Association started ranking states in 1943, according to the South Dakota Education Association.

South Dakota’s average teacher salary during the 2024-25 school year increased to $58,486 — a 3.8% increase from $56,328 in last year’s report. The increase outpaced the 2024 inflation rate of about 2.9%. 

South Dakota lawmakers approved a 4% increase in education funding in 2024, 1.25% in 2025, and 1.4% this year. Education advocates warned the slight increase this year could cause teacher pay to fall behind inflation and drag South Dakota’s ranking down in next year’s report. 

South Dakota’s average teacher pay of $58,486 is lower than all its neighboring states:

North Dakota: $60,704.

Minnesota: $76,234.

Iowa: $65,312.

Nebraska: $63,326.

Wyoming: $65,668.

Montana: $59,305.

States that rank lower than South Dakota are West Virginia, Missouri, Louisiana, Florida and Mississippi (there are 51 spots in the rankings, due to the inclusion of Washington, D.C.). Mississippi’s average teacher salary of $54,975 is the nation’s lowest, according to the report, but is a 2.4% increase compared to the previous year’s salary.

California reports the highest average salary at $103,552 — a 2.4% increase from last year. Nevada teachers received the largest percent change in their salaries at 11.8%, increasing to 17th ($74,812) from 25th in the rankings.

South Dakota’s ranking for average starting salary fell to 27th in the nation — down from 25th. The state’s average teacher starting salary increased from $45,530 last year to $47,196.

title: Spearfish Destination Imagination  team gears up for global competition
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — A successful businesswoman falls into a mysterious coma. Her best friend and physician stands to inherit her fortune. A plot is unraveled.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — A successful businesswoman falls into a mysterious coma. Her best friend and physician stands to inherit her fortune. A plot is unraveled.

That’s not the plot of the next episode of your favorite soap opera. It is, instead, a skit that must be fully staged and performed in 8 minutes or less by 5 middle school students at an upcoming global competition in Kansas City.

Each year, teams of students in Destination Imagination (DI), formerly Odyssey of the Mind, from around the world receive a challenge prompt.

This year, the prompt had seventh graders like the 5 on the Spearfish team, researching neuroscience — specifically the science of memories.

Their skit takes place in a series of brief, clever flashbacks. The flashbacks must demonstrate that the team — The Spearfish Memory Menders — understands something true about how memories are stored and gathered for recall.

“With the skit, it all has to be scientifically backed up,” said Lydia Donovan, one of the members of the Spearfish team.

The students also had to design and construct a set, which must be assembled before their skit is performed. The skits’ staging and run time, together, must be no longer than 8 minutes total.

Every element — from research and writing, to set construction and performance — must be done without the assistance of an adult.

“We learn a lot of people skills, like how to work together,” said DI team member Brinley Keyes. “We also learn how to work in stressful situations and not panic.”

This year, Spearfish’s  team has qualified for a global competition.

“There are people from British Columbia, Cayman Islands, Guatemala, Toronto, Ontario, Pakistan, Quebec, Romania, Turkey, the UK, Ukraine, and Australia,” Aspen Limbo said. In the skit, she plays the doctor who discovers the cause of the main character’s illness. “It’s great to socialize with other team members.”

DI students take enamel pins with them to the competition, pins that they trade with other participants. It opens up conversations with other students their age from around the globe.

“This year, they did a fiddle set. There are 4 fiddles from places like the Black Hills, the Badlands, all the different places, and then a golden bow, a special one,” Donovan said. “Then every year in South Dakota, we do dream catchers, which are very popular at worlds.”

Keyes said the team has always worked hard to try to earn its place in the global competition. This year, getting there is pretty exciting.

“It’s so insane. There are people coming from all of these different places, and we’re just little old South Dakota,” Keyes said.

Every year, the team’s faculty sponsor Barb Baker applies for grant funding through the Spearfish Foundation for Public Education in order to fund the DI season.

However, in order for the team to go to Kansas City, they will need to raise additional funds.

“We have to cover travel, lodging, it’s just registration is $5,500,” Donovan said. “Our goal is $11,000.”

So far, the students have raised more than three quarters of that goal. They charged their peers for strips of duct tape, which were used to tape their principal, Don Lyon, to a wall at school. They partnered with local restaurants for one-night only fundraisers, they set up a GoFundMe, and now they’re running a raffle.

Donavan said while the team will certainly try their best to bring home a trophy from globals, they’re more excited about the experience and the chance to meet new people. Keyes added that the best thing about DI has been getting to know and working with the other girls on her team.

“It is just so fun to meet them every week and problem solve and make new stuff for our DI skit,” Keyes said.

title: Handley preschool not affected by rec center negotiations
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Judy Mackey welcomes a group of students into the Handley Center preschool. Mackey has operated the preschool for 19 years, and she is not concerned about the future of the program. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
Handley preschool not affected by rec center negotiations
Judy Mackey welcomes a group of students into the Handley Center preschool. Mackey has operated the preschool for 19 years, and she is not concerned about the future of the program. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

LEAD — The future of the Handley Center preschool will not be affected by any decisions about whether the city takes over the recreation center in Lead. 

“I do want to touch a little bit on the preschool,” said Mayor Dustin Heupel during the city commission meeting, Monday. “I know that’s a big concern for everybody. The Gnarly Pine said the preschool could go under their 501(c)(3) if the Handley does dissolve and go away or if the city takes it on.”  

Heupel’s comments came during a discussion about a resolution he presented to the city commission, which proposes the city will take over the Handley Recreation Center. Heupel asked the commission to consider the resolution and take action on it at the next regular meeting, scheduled for May 18. 

The Handley Center preschool operates as a sponsored program of the Northern Hills Family Recreation Center (Handley Center) nonprofit, and uses its 501(c)(3) status to obtain some operational funding. 

Nick Bennett, registered agent for the Gnarly Pine Foundation in Lead, told the Pioneer he does not have a formal agreement to take on the preschool, because the school already has a sponsoring entity in the Northern Hills Family Recreation Center nonprofit organization. 

“The Gnarly Pine would be willing to support the preschool both in structure (501(c)(3) and in implementation, if the need was to arise,” Bennett told the Pioneer. “It would align in our goals of supporting community and education.” 

Darla Auld, president of the Northern Hills Family Recreation Center board, said the board plans to continue sponsoring the preschool. The nonprofit status is separate from the building, and since the preschool operates in a different location — at Lead-Deadwood Middle School — the decision to continue operating the preschool is completely separate from the decision about whether to turn the recreation center building over to the city for management. 

“If for some reason we dissolve, which we’re not obligated to do in any way, we then would try and find something different,” Auld said. “The building is an asset of the nonprofit. It’s something that we own. So, since the preschool is at the middle school, we don’t necessarily need a building to keep that program running. But we certainly appreciate all people offering to help us.” 

Judy Mackey, who has overseen the preschool for 19 years, said she has no concerns about the future of the program. The preschool is funded with a mix of tuition dollars and grants, she said. With a large class expected to enroll next year, she said she hopes to stay at the middle school, where the facility and its safety practices are perfect for the operation. 

“I’m not really too worried about having a place to go,” she said. “We’re not a very expensive program to run. We’re pretty self sustaining.  

Dr. Erik Person, superintendent of the Lead-Deadwood School District, said there are no plans to move the preschool, and it is welcome to stay in its current location at the middle school.

title: Smoke but no damage at Homestake Opera House
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: LEAD — Firefighters reported a lot of smoke at the Historic Homestake Opera House, Tuesday afternoon, for an incident that was quickly cleared.
_full_text:
Smoke but no damage at Homestake Opera House

LEAD — Firefighters reported a lot of smoke at the Historic Homestake Opera House, Tuesday afternoon, for an incident that was quickly cleared. 

At about 2:30 p.m. Tuesday, the Lead Volunteer Fire Department responded to a call of a fire alarm at the opera house. Jay Jacobs, president of the Historic Homestake Opera House board, said a contractor was working on an electrical panel in the part of the building that houses the Lead-Deadwood Arts Center, and an issue occurred that caused the smoke. 

Historic Homestake Opera House Executive Director Todd Jones said there was no smoke damage. The electricity was shut off at the building Tuesday afternoon as a precaution. 

Jacobs said opera house officials were working with general contractor  Ainsworth-Benning’s master electrician Wednesday afternoon to determine exactly what happened, and assess the situation. He said there was no major damage to the opera house, and the incident was contained to a small area behind the Lead-Deadwood Arts Center desk. 

Play practice scheduled for Tuesday evening, for the upcoming production, “Love, Loss, and What I Wore,” was moved to a different location. The production is expected to open as expected on May 8. The Historic Homestake Opera House also still plans to host a watch party for the DUNE beam signing, scheduled for Thursday afternoon. 

The Historic Homestake Opera House is in the middle of a major renovation to move concessions to the arts center portion of the building, and open the space up for patrons to visit during shows.

title: SBHS Ceiling Tile Art Auction  raises $1,610 for students and supplies
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: The fifth annual SBHS Ceiling Tile Art Auction raised $1,610 for the support of the Japan trip, scholarships and art supplies.  From left:  Amora Jenson, Zoey Masiero, Hannah Johnson, Elise Henrichsen, Rachel Packman and Kimberly Somervold.  Photo by Kristina Coats
_full_text:
SBHS Ceiling Tile Art Auction  raises $1,610 for students and supplies
The fifth annual SBHS Ceiling Tile Art Auction raised $1,610 for the support of the Japan trip, scholarships and art supplies.  From left:  Amora Jenson, Zoey Masiero, Hannah Johnson, Elise Henrichsen, Rachel Packman and Kimberly Somervold.  Photo by Kristina Coats 

STURGIS — The fifth annual Sturgis Brown High School Ceiling Tile art project proved to be another success, raising $1,610 to support art supplies, student Japan trip balances, and scholarships. Eight student-created tiles were auctioned recently at the Sturgis Veterans Club, drawing strong community support for the Sturgis Brown High School art program.

Visual art teacher Kimberly Somervold praised the effort and dedication behind the project. 

“The students all worked so hard and diligently on the tiles,” Somervold said. “I am proud of all the work they completed. They take pride in what they create.”

This year’s tiles were the result of collaboration throughout the school year, with student artists investing time and creativity into each piece. Primary contributors included Elise Hendrichsen, Hannah Johnson, Rachel Packman, Miranda Jacobs, Alana Pritts, Kaelyn Schone, and Zoey Masiero.

The top-selling piece of the evening was the Vietnam-themed tile, designed and painted by Hannah Johnson with assistance from Elise Hendrichsen. The piece carried personal meaning and emotional significance for Johnson. 

“This year I was inspired to create a ceiling tile because I wanted to show respect to all the veterans that came before me,” Johnson said. “It was also my last year at the school, so I wanted to create something meaningful.”

Seeing her artwork displayed, and ultimately purchased, made the experience even more special. “I am so proud to have my ceiling tile displayed,” Johnson said. “I cried happy tears because my mom ended up getting my tile and dedicated it to my papa. I’m excited to have a piece of him live on.”

Johnson added that contributing to a meaningful cause made the project even more rewarding.  “It feels really great to know that I am doing something meaningful,” she said.

For Hendrichsen, the project provided an opportunity to honor others through art while also seeing the impact of community support.

“I was inspired to participate by creating art that people could dedicate to family members or themselves who fought for our freedom,” Hendrichsen said. “I feel very proud to have my art displayed. It reminds me that people are willing to support us and shows how much they love their friends and families.”

She added that the fundraising aspect brought an added sense of accomplishment.  

“It makes me feel good knowing that I worked for that money and that people are willing to spend that money on the art club’s artwork,” she said.

The annual ceiling tile project continues to blend creativity, community connection, and purpose, giving students a chance to showcase their talents while supporting meaningful opportunities within the school.

title: 6th graders help plant Liberty Tree in Lead
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: LEAD — There’s a Liberty Tree in Manuel Brothers Park.
_full_text:
LEAD — There’s a Liberty Tree in Manuel Brothers Park. 

On Wednesday, students from the Lead-Deadwood Middle School sixth-grade class joined the city of Lead parks department personnel, representatives from the U.S. Forest Service, and community residents to plant a hackberry tree, in recognition of Arbor Day. The tree is strategically planted near the Manuel Brothers Park shelter, because it is a common gathering spot for Lead residents and visitors. In that location, Lead City Administrator Robin Lucero said it will serve as Lead’s “Liberty Tree.” 

This year, in recognition of America’s 250th anniversary, the South Dakota State Historical Society’s America’s 250th movement, a network of partnerships across the state dedicated to marking the milestone anniversary in America, are encouraging communities to plant “Liberty Trees.” Liberty trees honor the original Boston elm tree that symbolized the colonial resistance of 1776. 

“The original Liberty Tree stood in Boston since 1646,” according to a statement from the National Arbor Day Foundation. “It served as a community gathering spot and focal point for political discourse. During the war for independence, the British loyalists chopped it down, but more in other towns from a variety of species soon appeared.” 

The Liberty Tree movement encourages communities to plant a tree in a prominent gathering place in the community. Lucero said the tree also commemorates Lead’s 150th anniversary. 

“Established in partnership with the Lead-Deadwood School District sixth grade class, the Class of 2032, and city of Lead officials, this tree represents the strength of community and the promise of future generations,” according to a prepared statement from the city. “May it grow as a living reminder of liberty, unity, and the enduring spirit of our nation.” 

Lucero said once the tree takes root, the city will place a plaque to mark its distinction. Additionally, Jerry Mertesdorf, parks and government buildings supervisor in Lead, said the city poured 2 concrete pads near the tree where picnic tables will be placed for the public to enjoy.

title: Sturgis band honors seniors, presents top awards at final concert
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — The Sturgis Brown High School band opened its final concert of the year Monday by recognizing 14 graduating seniors and presenting year-end awards, celebrating dedication, leadership, and musical achievement.
_full_text:
STURGIS — The Sturgis Brown High School band opened its final concert of the year Monday by recognizing 14 graduating seniors and presenting year-end awards, celebrating dedication, leadership, and musical achievement.

Seniors honored during the ceremony included: Kylina Homan (trumpet), Ethan Baker (baritone saxophone), Sophie McNaught (tenor saxophone), Brooklynn Baird (French horn), Graden Glodt (percussion), Kaitlyn Brown (tenor saxophone), Jocelyn Wolkenhauer (clarinet), Taylor Bestgen (tuba), Janessa Moelter (trumpet), Darrian Anderson (trumpet), Jade Mueller (alto saxophone), Riley Weishaar (trombone), Matthew Johnson (alto saxophone), and Kian Loftin (percussion).

Band director Emily Young praised the group for its long-term commitment to the program.

“This is a really dedicated group of kids,” Young said. “They chose band every year, every trimester, every semester, and made it a priority throughout their high school careers.”

Seven seniors were recognized for earning 4-year band letters: Wolkenhauer, Brown, Baker, Moelter, Baird, Weishaar, and Bestgen.

Three students, Baird, Bestgen, and Brown, also received White Letter honors, awarded to students who demonstrate excellence and commitment in both band and choir while maintaining strong academic performance.

The evening’s top honor, the John Philip Sousa Award, was presented to Taylor Bestgen. The award, given at the discretion of the band director, recognizes a single student each year for outstanding musicianship, leadership, dependability, and service to the band program.

“This award goes to the student who has truly done the most for the band over their four years,” Young said.

The recognition ceremony highlighted not only individual achievements but also the collective dedication of the senior class, closing out the year with a celebration of their contributions to the Sturgis Brown High School music program.

The band will perform next at the high school graduation on May 17.

title: Broken Boot Gold Mine receives emergency grants to ensure 2026 opening season
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: DEADWOOD — The Broken Boot Gold Mine, located between Deadwood and Central City, is in the middle of a 3-phase renovation project set to cost more than $150,000 total, with the goal of preserving one of the city’s most used educational resources.
_full_text:
DEADWOOD — The Broken Boot Gold Mine, located between Deadwood and Central City, is in the middle of a 3-phase renovation project set to cost more than $150,000 total, with the goal of preserving one of the city’s most used educational resources. 

Monday, the Broken Boot was awarded $8,160 in Deadwood Not-For-Profit Grant funding, the remainder of what was allotted to the mine per the grant’s guidelines within a 5-year period. The mine was also awarded $50,000 in emergency historic preservation funds to continue repairs in the exit of the mine and life safety issues, allowing the mine to open by May 23. 

 “This is for cribbing and repairs that, without this and the additional fund raising, the mine probably wouldn’t be open,” said Kevin Kuchenbecker, director of historic preservation and planning and zoning. 

Allen said the funding will pay only part of the required costs in what has been determined to be a 3-phase project to protect the longevity of the facility. 

“I have grant applications out to other entities, and I’m waiting on that, but due to the historic nature of it and it being such a cornerstone of Deadwood’s economy, tourism, family (entertainment), and education, I wanted to approach the historic preservation board,” said Allen. 

Allen said that the mine is open seasonally from Memorial Day to Labor Day. In those 3 months, Allen said approximately 21,000 tours go through the historic mine. The mine, a snapshot of mining done during in 1878 with only hand tools, candlelight, and dynamite, is used both for educational tours and as a popular tourist destination in the city. 

“It’s one of the most utilized tourist attractions in Deadwood for families,” said Allen. “We stay really busy, and that’s why it’s so important to keep it open long-term.”

Allen said that the area of the mine used for tours is inspected every fall and spring and every Sunday through the open season. Per those inspections, structurally supportive timbers in those areas are replaced as needed. 

“But this 3-phase project is on kind of a bigger scale,” said Allen. “We’ll go back into different parts of the mine and really reinforce and repair and remove some of the rock in the back of the mine.”

In the second phase of the project, the one currently underway, supports in the exit tunnel are being replaced and rock are being removed, requiring bolting, installation of mesh, and other supports. In the third phase, Allen said similar work will be done to secure the furthest tunnels of the mine. 

The work is being performed by Harrison Western, an underground mining contractor out of Colorado, under the guidance of RESPEC Engineering of Rapid City. 

“Harrison Western doesn’t do anything that’s not signed off by RESPEC as being structurally sound and safe,” said Allen. “We have been absolutely blessed with working with those guys, they are absolute pros at everything they do.”

Allen said that because of the mine’s nonprofit status, almost all money raised during the open season goes back towards annual repairs, maintenance, and payroll. 

“Every year is completely different, but I can tell you that all the money that we bring in goes completely towards operational costs and repair and maintenance,” Allen said. “Because, if you’ll notice, these costs of the phase 2 of the project are way more than the $58,000 that we were granted. We still have to be responsible and have some way to pay for some for these repairs and things that come up every single year.”

Allen said her fundraising efforts have been hobbled by the fact that the mine is an historic asset located in Deadwood when applying for grants from other South Dakota tourism entities.

“You get a lot of, well, you’re in Deadwood, which is a national historic landmark, they have historic preservation funds especially for this, they have an historic preservation board that offers grants,” she said. “So, you’re kind of lower on the list of priorities.”

Allen said the Broken Boot is constantly seeking corporate sponsorships and partnerships, with the ultimate goal of preserving the mine for future generations. 

“For one thing, it’s done the way it was in the late 1800s during the gold rush, so it’s preserved in time. You can go in there and it’s a completely different environment than any mine that you’re going to see past 1904,” she said. “It poses all kinds of different scenarios for people, education wise, training wise, and history wise. It really is a gem for the whole Black Hills, not just the Northern Hills.”

title: Spearfish School Board candidates
description: Voters in the Spearfish School District will head to the polls June 2. Two people are running for Spearfish School Board open position which is a 3-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.
_full_text:
Voters in the Spearfish School District will head to the polls June 2. Two people are running for Spearfish School Board open position which is a 3-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.

Alesha Limbo

Name and what you do for a living?

 1000065194.jpeg

My name is Alesha Limbo. I am a small business owner and entrepreneur. I also do life coaching, cohost The Purpose Effect podcast, help lead retreats, and assist with my husband’s local survey company.

What motivated you to run for this office?

I love our community. I grew up in Spearfish and have lived in the Black Hills most of my life. I am incredibly grateful for our school district, and I wanted to be a voice for parents, teachers, staff, students, and the community as a whole.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

I bring both education and lived experience to this role. I have a background in higher education and a master’s degree in counseling and student affairs. I have one child who graduated from Spearfish High School, four children currently in the district, and more than 13 nieces and nephews in Spearfish schools. I have also learned a great deal over the last three years serving on the school board, and it has truly been a privilege.

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

In addition to serving on the Spearfish School Board, I currently serve on the District Improvement Committee. I was also appointed by the governor to serve on the South Dakota Professional Teachers Practices and Standards Commission. Over the years, I have had the opportunity to serve in many different leadership roles, both publicly and in the community, and those experiences have shaped how I listen, lead, and work with others.

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I have regularly attended school board meetings, city council meetings, committee meetings, and other district-related meetings. Even before I ran for school board three years ago, I regularly attended school board meetings because I have always believed it is important to stay informed and involved.

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Yes, absolutely. Local newspapers are important because they help keep us informed, connected, and engaged in what is happening in our own community. They also play an important role in accountability and making sure local voices are heard.

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in the Spearfish School District?

One of the biggest issues we need to address is declining enrollment and how that impacts revenue and long-term planning. I am passionate about thinking outside the box and making sure we involve teachers, staff, parents, and the community in those conversations. We have many smart and creative people in this district, and I believe it is powerful when we bring those voices to the table.

How do you intend to solve these issues?

I believe part of my role on the school board is to be a voice for the community and help bring people together around solutions. That means asking good questions, listening well, planning ahead, and being willing to consider new ideas instead of simply doing things the way they have always been done. I want to continue supporting thoughtful, proactive decisions that are best for students and sustainable for the district.

What do you believe is working for the district, and how will you retain that progression?

There are a lot of great things happening in our district. I have really appreciated the unity among our principals and the way they work together to serve students and build strong school culture across the district. I also believe bringing the alternative school back under the district umbrella will create powerful opportunities. I am encouraged by the direction of the athletic department and the intentional work being done to build connection, culture, and growth. We have a lot to be proud of, and I want to help continue that momentum.

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

To me, transparency means being open, honest, accessible, and willing to have real conversations. It means building relationships and making sure people feel heard. Last December, I spent an entire day in each school building, sitting in classrooms, talking with teachers and staff, and seeing firsthand what is happening in our schools. My heart is truly to serve, and I want people to know they can reach out to me with questions, concerns, or ideas.

What else do you want people to know about you?

I care deeply about this community and this district. I want people to know they can talk to me, and I will do my best to help move things forward. I am passionate about helping our students grow and making sure we continue living out our mission of empowering all students to succeed in a changing world.

A study is underway for West Elementary School renovations. What are your priorities for the school?

I have the privilege of serving on the committee that meets with the architect twice a month regarding the West Elementary renovation study. My priorities are making sure we create a space that meets future needs, not just today’s needs, while also being financially responsible. There is always a wish list, but we need to be wise. That is why it is important to gather input, look closely at priorities, and make decisions that best serve students and staff long term.

After years of steady growth, the district enrollment has flattened out and even declined. What does the district need to do to balance rising costs and stagnant revenue?

I am grateful that our district has been proactive. We recognized early that enrollment and revenue were beginning to shift, and we have worked to make thoughtful adjustments along the way instead of letting bigger problems build up. I believe that is the smart way to handle it. At the same time, I think this is also an opportunity to be creative, intentional, and collaborative and to hear from teachers, staff, parents, and community members about how we move forward together.

What should be done to attract students in alternate education, ie homeschooled students, back to the district — at least part time?

I think we need to be willing to have real conversations about what families are looking for and where there may be opportunities to better serve students. One of the conversations I believe is worth having is whether a four-day school week is something we should seriously explore. I am not taking a position on it here, but I do think it is worth discussing. I also believe bringing the alternative school back into the district and into our CTE building creates another strong opportunity to better meet student needs.

With the newly passed property tax legislation, are you concerned the district will receive less revenue? How so?

Any time there are changes that could impact revenue, it is something we need to pay attention to. That is true not only with property tax legislation, but also with declining enrollment and the pressure that puts on school funding. My focus is on making sure we stay wise, proactive, and responsible with our spending so that we can continue serving students well no matter what challenges come our way.

Raeann Mettler

Name and what you do for a living? 

 BHP_photo - 1

My name is Raeann Mettler, and I am running for the Spearfish School Board. I work as a Research Specialist supporting tribal communities. I manage public health research projects and lead educational outreach programs. I am a proud alum of BHSU, where I earned a BS in Biology and an MS in Integrative Genomics. I completed my PhD research abroad at the University of Freiburg in Germany. This education enabled me to teach biology at several universities. As a small business owner, I lead local STEM camps and after-school programs. I also enjoy bringing programming to youth organizations and public libraries.

What motivated you to run for this office?

I am motivated by community support and the dedication of our educators. As a longtime resident and professional in Spearfish, I am committed to serving our schools by representing many voices and promoting community values. I prioritize fiscal responsibility and will advocate for teacher support to benefit our local children.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

With 10 years as a local educator and five as an educational business owner for preK–middle school, I emphasize enrichment, critical thinking, and teamwork. As a parent in the district, I care about educational quality and staff well-being. I have built partnerships with homeschooling families and supported the Spearfish Robotics Club by providing space when needed. I helped secure funding for students in underserved communities through grants such as the SD Biotech K–12 STEM Award and the Daniel Swets Robotics Materials Award, and I hope to continue this type of support for Spearfish School District educators.

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I have served on the Booth Society Board of Directors, including as Secretary and President. I support youth outreach as a STEM Ambassador for the South Dakota Afterschool Network and as a Science Communication Fellow at the SD Discovery Center’s Portal to the Public. I volunteer at Women in Science Conferences and Rock the Rez. I have completed leadership programs including Path2Impact, the Sutton Leadership Institute, and LEE. In 2025, I ran for the Spearfish City Council. Together, these experiences reflect my ongoing commitment to leadership and empowering others through STEM education and community engagement.

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I regularly participate in monthly research review board meetings and have attended several municipal meetings in Spearfish this past year, including City Council and School Board sessions. As a busy parent and professional who travels frequently for work, I value having online access to meeting minutes and public proceeding recordings. Reviewing these materials helps me stay up to date on issues impacting Spearfish residents, and I meet with constituents to discuss their feedback. Through these actions, I will strive to remain informed and responsive, ensuring that the concerns and needs of our community are represented at the Spearfish School Board.

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Local newspapers are essential for fostering community connection and informed citizenship. They cover local, regional, and national events and issues. Their reporting is often seen as more reliable than social media. Newspapers encourage civic participation and amplify diverse voices. The Black Hills Pioneer’s recognition as the “Official Newspaper of Spearfish” highlights its importance and legacy. According to the South Dakota Newspapers Association (www.sdna.com), nearly 90% of newspaper readers vote. We now invite all our readers: exercise your voice and vote again on June 2nd—your participation shapes our future!

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in the Spearfish School District?

The district’s main challenges are financial stability, attracting and retaining great teachers, and supporting students—especially those with learning challenges who need timely services. Investing in professional development, resources, and fair pay for teachers should be the district’s top focus.

How do you intend to solve these issues?

To solve these challenges, I will build informed consensus with diverse groups. The district must balance enrollment, staffing, finances, and trust. This means outreach for stable enrollment, competitive teacher pay, strengthened career and technical education, and better early support for students with learning needs. Clear communication, careful budgeting, and less politicized governance will foster lasting community trust.

What do you believe is working for the district, and how will you retain that progression?

Spearfish has strong teachers, solid academics, high graduation rates, and wide student opportunities. The CTE building enhances career readiness. Success depends on retaining quality teachers, sustaining rigor, and closing resource and experience gaps. I will focus on issues affecting educators and students to help fill these gaps.

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

Transparency at the school board level means making decisions open and clear to the community. These decisions should not be hidden or overly technical. Communication must be timely and use plain language when sharing agendas, budgets, and proposals. Open decision-making should follow both the letter and the spirit of open meetings laws. Explanations should be given after closed sessions when possible. Transparency also requires two-way engagement. This includes regular community forums, data collection, and open communication channels for families, staff, and taxpayers to provide input before decisions are made.

What else do you want people to know about you?

I studied abroad in Germany while doing my Doctoral research in songbird ecology. It was a wonderful time to challenge myself, connect with different cultures, and collaborate with researchers from around the world. I also learned how to travel Europe and Africa on a tight budget. Now, as a mom, the simple things bring me daily joy. My son and I love to be silly with drawing challenges, dance-offs, sing-a-longs, LEGO builds, and playing with the dogs. These life experiences have shaped my curiosity, adaptability, and joy in learning with and from others.

A study is underway for West Elementary School renovations. What are your priorities for the school?

A new, multi-purpose gym is an investment that would benefit students, staff, and the community for years to come. I regularly spend time sharing lunch with 1st graders in the West Elementary gym. During my visit with educators, I learned that the current gym is smaller than originally designed. Furthermore, the gym is unavailable for several hours each school day during lunch, reducing students’ opportunities for physical activity. By prioritizing input from all stakeholders and addressing current space limitations, we can create opportunities for physical education, extracurricular involvement, and community engagement, making either a renovation or a new gym addition a meaningful step forward.

After years of steady growth, the district enrollment has flattened out and even declined. What does the district need to do to balance rising costs and stagnant revenue?

Spearfish faces a common challenge: flat or declining enrollment and rising per-student costs. This reduces revenue while expenses grow. To balance budgets, districts often adjust staffing to match enrollment. They may consolidate or repurpose underused buildings, thereby slowing compensation growth. Reviewing and possibly reducing lower-priority or low-enrollment programs can also help. It is important to protect core instruction. Careful use of one-time funds and shared services can increase efficiency. Achieving long-term stability demands strategic planning, adaptability, and continuous community engagement.

What should be done to attract students in alternative education, i.e., homeschooled students, back to the district, at least part-time?

Spearfish School District could better engage homeschool and alternative education students by offering flexible, optional programming instead of requiring full-time enrollment. This could include showcasing part-time classes, high-quality coursework, dual credit, career certifications, and extracurriculars (e.g., arts, technology, athletics). A streamlined enrollment process and dedicated coordinator would improve access. With roughly 500 students receiving alternative instruction in Spearfish, there is a significant opportunity to re-engage families by providing value without full commitment. The proposed small alternative high school program for 30–40 students could serve as an effective starting point and baseline for future upward growth.

With the newly passed property tax legislation, are you concerned the district will receive less revenue? How so?

In the short term, state backfilling may prevent immediate revenue losses, but long-term concerns remain about funding stability, local control, and reliance on more volatile sales tax revenue. While the legislation aims to offset property tax reductions with potential sales tax increases, many voters oppose this shift due to concerns about consistency. Property taxes are generally viewed as a more stable and predictable funding source for schools, while sales taxes fluctuate with the economy. As a result, I am concerned the district may face increased uncertainty and less reliable funding over time, even if overall revenue initially appears unchanged.

title: Sturgis graduate Aiken selected as chancellor of the U. of Montana Western
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: DILLON, Mont. — Dr. Estee Aiken was recently selected as the next chancellor of the University of Montana Western.
_full_text:
DILLON, Mont. — Dr. Estee Aiken was recently selected as the next chancellor of the University of Montana Western. 

She begins her duties on May 21.  

Aiken graduated from Sturgis Brown High School in 1997 and her parents, Pat and Robin Baldwin are active members in the Sturgis community.  Aiken said that growing up in Sturgis lead her to want to raise her family in a small town, which is what attracted her to the University of Montana Western in the first place, as it is located in a rural community.  

“I can relate to many of our students’ experiences coming from small high schools where you knew everyone in your graduating class,” she said. “During my time at SBHS, I was able to benefit from strong relationships with teachers and peers, and I see our UMW students traveling similar paths from small high schools to a small college in order to be appreciated as individuals and feel like part of a community.”

Aiken is no stranger to the university, having advanced through various roles at the institution over the past 15 years. She joined the faculty at the university in 2011, earning the rank of tenured professor of education. She then moved into the position of dean of strategic initiatives, overseeing university accreditation, strategic planning, workforce efforts, and dual enrollment. Aiken is currently UMW’s interim provost and vice chancellor of academic afairs, where she works to advance UMW’s academic mission.

“Dr. Aiken’s broad and extensive experience as a teacher, administrator, and researcher as well as her demonstrated dedication to education at all levels, including teacher preparation, makes her an ideal fit to lead UM Western,” said Commissioner Clayton Christian. “Her stewardship will ensure that UMW sustains and grows its reputation as a high-quality university offering innovative programming and a unique student experience within the Montana University System.”

“It is my honor and privilege be the next chancellor for UMW. I value the experiences and relationships that have led me to this opportunity, and I look forward to what lies ahead,” said Aiken. “I’m fortunate to have called UM Western and Dillon my home for 15 years now, and I am thrilled at the possibilities as chancellor to invest further in this community, in this university, and especially in the students who are at its heart.”

_full_text:
SPEARFISH — The Arbor Day Foundation named Spearfish a 2025 Tree City USA in honor of its commitment to plant, grow, and maintain trees to benefit its community. Spearfish also received a growth award for demonstrating improved levels of tree care and community engagement. 

To earn the Tree City USA recognition, a city must uphold 4 core standards: maintaining a tree board or department, having a community tree ordinance, spending at least $2 per capita on urban forestry, and participating in an Arbor Day celebration.  

The Growth Award is an annual recognition to participating Tree City USA communities that demonstrate high levels of tree care and community engagement during the calendar year.

“The City of Spearfish Parks and Recreation Department is committed to ensuring the health of our urban forest and maintaining our Tree City USA certification, which we have held since 1984,” Spearfish Parks Maintenance and Forestry Superintendent Rex McDonald said. “We are honored to have received the Growth Award in 2024 and 2025, which recognized our efforts in implementing the Urban Wood Utilization Program (UWUP).”

Under the UWUP, the city makes wood debris (logs, wood chips, etc.) from tree removal operations available for public use free of charge. Tree removal operations, McDonald added, are often necessary to prevent Emerald Ash Borer infestation.    

“Because of the positive public feedback and participation that we’ve received with that program, we plan on continuing the UWUP in the fall/winter of 2026 and 2027 and into the future,” McDonald said.

To date, the city of Spearfish has been designated Tree City USA a total of 42 times. This year will mark the 8th year the city has received the Growth Award.

The Tree City USA program has recognized cities and towns that leverage urban forestry to enhance the livability and sustainability of their local area for over 50 years. 

“By recognizing the role of trees as a critical infrastructure, Spearfish is helping shape a healthier and more resilient future. We’re proud Spearfish is among the Arbor Day Foundation’s growing network of communities committed to creating positive impact through trees,” said Michelle Saulnier, vice president of programs at the Arbor Day Foundation. 

In cities and neighborhoods, trees are proven to help mitigate the urban heat island effect, reduce storm water runoff, improve air quality, and boost mental and physical health. When the right trees are planted in the right places, they can also reduce traffic noise, increase property values, and lower homeowners’ energy costs. 

Spearfish’s dedication to urban forestry has continued this spring. So far this year, the parks staff planted 93 trees of 18 different tree species throughout Spearfish’s parks system.

title: Letter carriers aim to ‘stamp out hunger’ Saturday
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — Plastic bags have started landing in mailboxes across the community.  That’s because, on the second Saturday of May, the United States Postal Service hosts “Stamp Out Hunger” — its annual food drive.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — Plastic bags have started landing in mailboxes across the community.  That’s because, on the second Saturday of May, the United States Postal Service hosts “Stamp Out Hunger” — its annual food drive.

Community members are invited to fill those plastic bags with non-perishable food donations and return them to their mailboxes on Saturday.

“We just pick everything up and deliver it right to the food pantry. It is always a big success. It is helpful that we get to put a bag in every box in the community,” said Tristany Swanson, a city mail carrier and the Spearfish event coordinator.

Together with the Boy Scouts of America, the mail carrier’s food drive is the largest philanthropic endeavor of its type in Spearfish. In 2024, the two groups’ combined effort 12,703 pounds of food into the Spearfish Community Food Pantry. In 2025, it brought in 17,863 pounds — 7,000 pounds came from the mail carrier’s food drive alone. 

Swanson said donors can give more than fits in the little white bags.

“It’s always hectic. Lots of, we still are delivering the mail and packages and stuff like that. It is very hectic picking it up. It is always very gratifying for us just to see how the community rallies together so that we can line the shelves at the food pantry,” Swanson said. “It is just very gratifying. It is a lot of work, but definitely worth it. It makes us happy.”

Swanson said the morning of the food drive, the carriers usually share a breakfast and hype each other up for the additional collections. That isn’t to say that if you forget to put your donations in the mailbox on Saturday, it’s too late to participate.

“Even if you missed that Saturday, we have food trickle out after that. We are usually picking up food for about a week,” Swanson said. “We usually pick up for about a week straight, sometimes 2, just depending.”

She added that if you have more canned goods to contribute than might fit in the provided plastic bag, that’s not a problem either.

“If it doesn’t fit in the box they can put it on the ground at the mailbox if it doesn’t fit in the box,” Swanson said. 

George Vansco,, the board president of the Spearfish Community Food Pantry told the Pioneer the pantry appreciates all canned good donations. However, canned fruit and canned ready meals (think Spaghetti-Os) are in high demand. 

Vansco said the pantry will be rallying volunteers from 11:30-3:30 p.m. Saturday to sort the incoming donations.

title: SD Supreme Court issues opinion in favor of Lawrence County
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: DEADWOOD — The South Dakota Supreme Court issued an opinion Thursday in favor of Lawrence County in which the county argued that Ordinance 24-05 was administrative in nature, granting power to the board of adjustment to grant conditional use permits and denying citizens the right to refer granted permits to a public vote.
_full_text:
DEADWOOD — The South Dakota Supreme Court issued an opinion Thursday in favor of Lawrence County in which the county argued that Ordinance 24-05 was administrative in nature, granting power to the board of adjustment to grant conditional use permits and denying citizens the right to refer granted permits to a public vote.

The ruling, in the case of Save Centennial Valley Association, Inc., versus Lawrence County Auditor Brenda McGruder and the county commissioners, all in their official capacities, affirms the 4th Circuit Court ruling by Judge Eric Strawn.

Save Centennial Valley attempted to refer ordinance 24-05 to a public vote, but McGruder denied the petition under the counsel of the county commission, who claimed that the ordinance was administrative and not legislative in nature. Administrative decisions, decisions made by government entities to bring them into compliance with laws made by a higher government power, are not subject to referendum.

The ordinance brings the county into compliance with South Dakota Codified Law, which states that the power to grant conditional use permits is held by the board of adjustment and not the county commission. The change denies citizens the option to refer decisions made by the board of adjustment to a public vote, requiring them instead to appeal those decisions in a circuit court.

Save Centennial Valley sought a writ of mandamus that would have forced the county to place Ordinance 24-05 to a public vote. The writ was denied in circuit court by Strawn. Save Centennial Valley then appealed Strawn’s decision to the Supreme Court, which heard arguments on the case March 19, ultimately ruling in favor of Lawrence County.

The Supreme Court’s opinion allows Lawrence County to uphold the ordinance and maintain conditional use permits granted since the passing of the ordinance in January, 2025. Most notably, the conditional use permit for the Larson gravel quarry on Homestake Road cannot be referred to a public vote.

title: Woodle Field turf project set to begin Monday; completion targeted  for fall
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS – Construction on the long-anticipated Woodle Field turf project is set to begin Monday, following an initial coordination meeting held Wednesday at the site between school officials and Mammoth Sports Construction.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

STURGIS – Construction on the long-anticipated Woodle Field turf project is set to begin Monday, following an initial coordination meeting held Wednesday at the site between school officials and Mammoth Sports Construction.

The meeting focused on the early phases of the project, including contractor mobilization, site setup and preparations for installing the new artificial turf surface.

Contractor John Moissan of Mammoth Sports Construction said the project is expected to take a couple of months, with substantial completion anticipated by Sept. 10.

“We’re planning to start (Monday), and it should be a couple of months and we’ll be done,” Moissan said.

Moissan noted that similar projects have been completed across South Dakota, including a comparable field in Garretson.

“We’ve done a lot of these throughout the state,” he said. “Whether it’s just a field or a track and field combination, it’s essentially the same process.”

One of the key benefits of the new turf will be improved field consistency and reduced maintenance compared to natural grass. The current playing surface at Woodle Field has developed uneven areas over time, something the turf installation will address.

“As you can see, the field now has dips and divots,” Moissan said. “Turf doesn’t require the same level of maintenance and care that a grass field does, and it provides a much more consistent playing surface.”

During construction, adjustments will be made for community access around the site. A portion of the existing parking lot will serve as a staging area, resulting in a minor detour for those using the nearby bike path.

School officials emphasized that the project represents a significant upgrade for student-athletes and the broader community, with the goal of having the facility ready for use during the fall sports season.

title: Meade School Board candidates
description: Voters in the Meade school district will head to the polls June 2 to vote on 2 vacant seats. Three people are running for 2 open position which is a 4-year term.
