We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.
_full_text:
Voters in the Meade school district will head to the polls June 2 to vote on 2 vacant seats. Three people are running for 2 open position which is a 4-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.

Brian Voight

 Meade School Board candidates
Brian Voight 

Name and what you do for a living?

I work fulltime for the South Dakota Army National Guard as the State Training Non-commisioned Officer. 

What motivated you to run for this office?

I believe public education is the foundation of what has made our communities, state, and country so financially and democratically successful. I want to ensure that children that enter any school in Meade County 46-1 have the best resources and education (teachers, curriculum, facilities, etc.) that we can provide. Students today are our leaders and workforce for tomorrow.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

I have spent the last three years on the Meade 46-1 school board and do believe that we are moving the school district in the correct direction. I have proven that I am willing to make difficult decisions to ensure our students are getting the education they need while ensuring the school district remains financially solvent.           

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I have spent the last twenty years with the South Dakota National Guard in various leadership roles to include manageing units of nearly 100 people and helping manage multi-million dollar budgets.

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

Currently being on the school board, I have attended nearly all of the regular, special, and committee meeting over the last three years.  

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

I do believe local newspapers are important. It is an easier and more reliable resource to access local news and government information.

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in the Meade School District?

The Meade 46-1 School District faces challenges with educational opportunities for the future workforce, declining enrollment, and rising fixed costs (insurance, utilities).

How do you intend to solve these issues?

The district needs more fully develop career pathways at a middle school and high school level. That means creating more career-technical education classes that will support our community’s future workforce.

The district needs to continue building the Homeschool connection program. The district needs to continue to offer the best educational opportunities in the I-90 corridor.

Managing our capital outlay budget to get to a point where we can self-insure our facilities would decrease liability insurance costs The South Dakota funding formula for education is broken and I believe our state legislature could do more to support public education.

What do you believe is working for the district, and how will you retain that progression?

The Meade 46-1 School District, over the last few years has seen more unity of vision in terms of how we treat staff, students, and other stakeholders in the district.  The school district needs to continue to provide educational opportunities for all of our students while building additional career pathways for our 7-12 students.

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

Transparency in government means that all conversations and decisions made on a particular topic are in a public meeting. Tranparency was one of the original reasons I got on the school board three years ago. I believe currently in the Meade 46-1 School District, that if a member of the public were to attend all committee and regular board meetings they would be as educated as I am as a board member to all governing decisions beside meetings that have to be held in executive session. There are certain decisions, when it comes to personnel and students, that can’t be held in public due to privacy and legal concerns.

What else do you want people to know about you?

I have two children currently in the Meade 46-1 School District and one that graduated from Sturgis Brown High School a year ago. Our school district has provided my children with the educational opportunities to be successful in school and after their K-12 education. I have a passion to ensure all the children in the district are provided with opportunities to be successful and competitive in post-secondary education

The district is in the process of reducing its budget to overcome a deficit. Is it making the right cuts, or should it shift its focus? How so?

Currently being on the school board and having to vote on reducing the budget I do believe the school district is making the most correct decisions to provide the most equitable educational opportunities to the students of the district.

The district has lost a significant number of students in recent years. How can the district bring new students in, and alternative education students back?

Total enrollment across the state has decreased outside of a few districts that include Douglas and the Sioux Falls area. The Meade 46-1 district needs to continue to develop relationships with alternative education students like we have with our Home School Connections program. We also need to continue to right size the district to ensure that our current students have the best educational opportunities available. 

Tammara Hannan

Name and what you do for a living?

My name is Tammara Phillips Hannan, and I’m a rancher. In the past, I’ve also worked in childcare and business management, which gave me valuable experience working with kids, families, and staff. Those experiences still shape how I look at education and community today.

What motivated you to run for this office?

Honestly, I care a lot about our schools and our community. I’ve seen where things are going well, but I’ve also seen where we can do better. At some point, it just felt important to step up and be part of making those improvements instead of just talking about them.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

I bring a practical, common-sense approach. I’ve worked with budgets, managed teams, and understand how decisions affect real people—kids, families, and staff. I also have experience finding and working with grants, which can be a big help when funding is tight.

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I haven’t held elected office, but I’ve had a lot of leadership experience through my work and community involvement. I’m used to making decisions, working with people, and advocating for what’s needed.

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I’ve attended multiple meetings over the past year and during my candidacy. It’s been important to me to really understand how things are currently working and where improvements can be made.

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Yes, I do. Local newspapers help keep people informed and connected. They play a big role in transparency and making sure communities know what’s going on.

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in the Meade School District?

We’re facing some real challenges—budget concerns, supporting and keeping good staff, and making sure all students across our large rural district have access to opportunities. Those are big priorities.

How do you intend to solve these issues?

It starts with listening. I want to hear from staff, families, and the community. From there, it’s about finding practical solutions—like bringing in additional funding through grants and partnerships, supporting our staff, and making sure resources are used wisely.

What do you believe is working for the district, and how will you retain that progression?

Our teachers and staff are doing an incredible job, and that’s something we need to continue to support. We also have strong programs and a community that cares. Keeping that momentum means backing what’s working and making sure those efforts continue.

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

To me, transparency means being open, honest, and easy to reach. People deserve to know what’s going on and why decisions are being made. I want to make sure communication is clear and consistent.

What else do you want people to know about you?

I’m someone who cares deeply about this community. I’ll show up, listen, and put in the work. I’m not afraid to ask questions or have tough conversations if it means doing what’s best for our students.

The district is in the process of reducing its budget to overcome a deficit. Is it making the right cuts, or should it shift its focus? How so?

Budget decisions are never easy. I think it’s important we’re careful about what we cut so we don’t negatively impact students or put too much strain on staff. At the same time, we should be looking for additional funding through grants and partnerships to help ease that pressure.

Derek Allen

title: Black Hills Pioneer at 150: 1894
description: Pioneer file graphic
_full_text:
Black Hills Pioneer at 150 years
Pioneer file graphic 

Black Hills Pioneer
The Black Hills Pioneer is the oldest continuously operating business in West River Dakota Territory; and 2026 marks our 150th year of telling the stories of the Black Hills. Over time our newspaper has absorbed the titles of numerous other publications, and we would like to share some of the more compelling stories from those early editions.
 Every Saturday we will be publishing stories from our archives, focusing heavily on the gold rush era of the 1800s, starting with our very first publication on June 8, 1876. These stories are re-printed exactly as they were first published, leaving in place the historic typos, grammar, style and terminology – politically correct or otherwise. It is our belief that history is sacrosanct and should never be edited to reflect the societal norms of the present.
 We hope you enjoy this historic journey. It is an honor and a privilege to be a trusted permanent record keeper of the Black Hills community; we look forward to the next 150 years of history in the making in the magnificent Black Hills.

 

~ February 21, 1894 • Queen City Mail ~

Couldn’t Bluff Buffalo Bill.

Fred May Tried it at Washington a Few Days Ago and Got It Where the Chicken Got the Ax.

A Washington special to the Omaha Bee of the 17th inst says: Col. William F. Cody, of Nebraska, who is here to secure permission from the secretary of the interior to take with his show this season a number of Indians from the northwest reservations, had a lively fistic encounter at Chamberlain’s last night. With George Beck of Wyoming and a number of other friends Col. Cody was entering a private dining room to take supper, when Fred May, the well known New York athlete and club man, who a dozen years or so ago fought a duel with James Gordon Bennett, approached the Nebraskan and gruffly demanded an apology for an alleged offence a decade since in New York. Col. Cody said that he was not aware that he ever had offended May, but that if he had he apologized, for he did not mean to wantonly offend any man. May was drinking and was somewhat under the influence of liquor. Then Col. Cody entered the dining room.

After support he and his friends were leaving Chamberlain’s, when May, accompanied by three or four companions, approached him and demanded further apology. May declared that the apology made was “no apology at all.”

“Yes,” said one of May’s companions, “make the d—d long-haired western ranger apologize,” and he applied an offensive epithet.

Up to this moment Col. Cody had been apologetical and good-natured, but now he struck out from the shoulder. May’s companion, a burly fellow, got Bill’s fist just under the left ear and went sprawling into the hat rack some distance away.

“Now you will apologize to me,” exclaimed May, approaching Col. Cody, and assuming a fistic attitude. “All right,” replied Buffalo Bill, and he let May have it in the neck.

No sooner had May “went to grass” than Bill’s first victim drew a revolver. Mr. Beck caught this and wrenched it from the stranger’s hand just as Bill hit the latter a right-hander in the eye and knocked him out. By this time May, who is a powerfully built man and a slugger from way back, was on his feet and coming at the Nebraskan. This was the climax. The Wild West showman hit May a blow on the chin, which actually knocked him ten feet under the table. This ended the fight. Neither assailant renewed the battle. Buffalo Bill had whipped two men, either of whom was his equal, if not his superior, in physical strength and size.

Col. Cody is much humiliated over the affair. He is not a quarrelsome man and after due apologies for fancied wrongs actually begged May and his friends not to make a row. The affair was kept a secret until today, and efforts have been made to have no publication made of it. Everybody says Cody was right. May and his friends are yet in bad blood, but the end has probably been reached.

~ April 11, 1894 • Queen City Mail ~

The Storm’s Victims

The Dead Body of a Young Man Found Near the Forked Lightning Horse Ranch.

Supposed To Be One of the Jolley Boys, Who Reside Near the Devil’s Tower.

The Body of George Dorsett, the Lost Mail Carrier. Not Yet Found.

 

The following extracts from a letter just received by J. P. Gammon from E. E. Height, foreman at the Forked Lightning horse ranch, seventy-five miles northwest from this city, are self-explanatory. The writer says:

On Friday, March 30, we found a boy frozen to death, hanging to the wire fence about thirty yards north of the big gate on east side of the big pasture. He is about seventeen or eighteen years old, and very thinly clad. He has on a pair of brown, striped pants on the outside, and pair of grey pants underneath, and a brown plaid coat. He had nothing in his pockets to identify him by. He had a pocketknife with about half of the big blade broken off. He had on a pair of heavy gaiter shoes that had just been half-soled; had no hat on. Tom Hill first saw him. It is hard to tell how long he has been there, as it has been impossible to travel down through there, but he evidently got lost in a blizzard. His hands were badly cut up by the wire by trying to follow the fence, and he still clung to the top wire with one hand, and was nearly snowed under. Some of the boys thought he resembled one of the Jolley boys. He was about the size of the one that went east with us, but his face was bloated and changed in color so I could not tell. The following were present and saw him before he was touched, and were also at the funeral: Tom Hill, Sam Bunker, George H. Whitney, Devere E. Carr, A. J. Groesbeck and wife, and myself.

Mr. Height says the storm which begun there on Monday evening, March 19, was the worst blizzard he ever saw. He thinks the losses of stock will be heavy, though he says he has not yet found any horses that perished by the storm.

It is learned from another source that one of the Jolley boys started from his home near the Devil’s Tower to cross the county to the Mitten ranch, and has not been heard from since, unless it turns out that he is the one found as above related.

George Dorsett.

A telephone dispatch was received here Sunday night stating that George Dorsett, the lost mail boy, was found near the head of Indian Creek, and the body returned to his home. The horse had made his way home before the finding of the boy. The place where he was found is nearly on a straight line from Minnesela to Short Pine Hills, the point he was endeavoring to make.

There is every reason now for the belief that the telephone message sent here last Saturday night from Belle Fourche, that the Dorsett boy had been found, was a base, cruel falsehood on part of somebody. After the visit here of Samuel Sandusky, an account of which was published Monday, Mr. Daggett called up the Belle Fourche operator and made diligent inquiry, but could not learn who brought the report to that place or who telephoned it here. Parties in from that neighborhood today have no knowledge of the finding of the boy, and do not think he has been found. The country where he was lost is cut up with deep washouts, now filled with snow. One gentleman from Hay Creek said: “If he has dropped into one of those washouts, he may not be found before May or June.”

*

Today Samuel Sandusky, who was one of the searching party that left David Dorsett’s ranch on Redwater last Wednesday morning, came into town for fresh supplies of provisions and horse feed. From him a reporter gathered much valuable information regarding the lost boy, and settling some disputed points in relation thereto.

David Dorsett and Samuel Sandusky started Wednesday morning, April 4, in search of the missing boy. On the way they were joined by others, making the total number fourteen. They proceeded to the Hash Knife ranch, where they learned that the boy left that place at 7 a.m. on Tuesday, April 3. From that point they tracked him to Beaver Dam creek, eighteen miles. From the creek he followed the old Hash Knife road to Dead Horse Creek. Here they found the cart and harness, which had been abandoned. The tracks indicated that he put the mail sack on the horse and started in a southeast direction, going with the wind, leading the horse. His tracks were found for a distance of about 600 yards, when all further traces were lost. The party made a thorough search along South Indian creek, Owl creek and Dead Horse creek. Sunday at 3 p.m. Mrs. Dorsett and Sandusky left the party and came to town for supplies. They had found no trace of the boy, except as about stated. Mr. Sandusky thinks, if the telephone report is correct, that there must have been another party of whom he knew nothing; that they were a little further up the creek that his party had been, but thinks the report is probably correct.

George Dorsett was between seventeen and eighteen years of age, a bright, intelligent boy, of good habit, and was the only support of a widowed mother. He was engaged in carrying the mail from Minnesela to Alzada, Mont., via Nashville and Camp Crook. He had been on the route for a considerable time and was perfectly familiar with the roads and the country generally. The location of the cart and harness when found seems to indicate that he had become confused and had lost his bearing in the storm, as he appeared to be going with the wind, when his right course was within a point or two of straight against the wind at the time he must have been there.

title: Hunger banquet to be held  at Lead opera house May 12
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: LEAD — Northern Hills Sources of Support (SOS) is excited to bring a hunger banquet to Lead in 2026 to increase awareness and support for hunger in the Northern Hills.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

LEAD — Northern Hills Sources of Support (SOS) is excited to bring a hunger banquet to Lead in 2026 to increase awareness and support for hunger in the Northern Hills. 

Participants in the hunger banquet will learn the reality of local hunger and poverty during the 2026 Lead Area Hunger Banquet at 5:30 p.m., May 12. The banquet will take place at the Historic Homestake Opera House theater in Lead. 

During the event, participants receive a ticket and are assigned to a class and served a meal coinciding with that class.  The event will highlight local stories and statistics to further the impact of the experience.

The event creates awareness about hunger and poverty issues in the Northern Black Hills, as well as generates exposure for SOS.  SOS is a non-profit organization located in Spearfish. Their mission is to create poverty-aware communities that build strong and supportive relationships with those in need.  SOS also coordinates with other non-profits in the area to help identify gaps and eliminate overlaps in services for those in need. 

“Our hunger banquet in Spearfish in January was a great success and we’re so excited to bring it to the Lead area, with hopes to also bring the event directly to other surrounding communities including Belle Fourche, Sturgis and Deadwood in 2026,” said Barb Donat, SOS outreach coordinator. “We received very positive feedback from past hunger banquets and it allowed us to spread the word about Northern Hills Sources Of Support and how we are helping to connect those in need to the resources they need.  This event truly opens people’s eyes to what hunger and poverty feel like.  It really hits home when you realize that these are local statistics and stories being shared at this event.  This is happening across the street or around the corner from you and across all of our Northern Hills communities.”

“Since the inception of SOS we’ve been building relationships with people in an effort to connect them to the resources they need and to advocate for them,” Donat said. “It’s crucial to build a relationship with the person so that they know they’re not alone in their situation. Feelings of alienation and despair are so common when you are struggling to make ends meet. Having a friend and supporter alongside you can make a world of difference and that is exactly what SOS provides. We’re so grateful that folks in the community have been so receptive and supportive of SOS and our mission and we look forward to another fantastic Hunger Banquet event!”

The Lead Area Hunger Banquet is limited to the first 100 people. The event is open to all ages but is recommended for those who are 10 and up. The RSVP deadline is May 7. To RSVP, visit  https://www.eventbrite.com/e/1987332799902?aff=oddtdtcreator 

There is no entry fee for the hunger banquet; however, cash or non-perishable food donations are appreciated. Cash donations will benefit Northern Hills Sources of Support.  Non-perishable food donations will benefit local food pantries in Lead.

title: Tribal law enforcement academy,  requested by SD, will be located in ND
byline: By John Hult Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: DEVIL’S LAKE, N.D. — Tribal police recruits in South Dakota will soon have an option for basic training through the Bureau of Indian Affairs that’s closer to home, but it won’t be as close as state officials had hoped.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

DEVIL’S LAKE, N.D. — Tribal police recruits in South Dakota will soon have an option for basic training through the Bureau of Indian Affairs that’s closer to home, but it won’t be as close as state officials had hoped.

Camp Grafton, a North Dakota National Guard base near Devils Lake, is currently the site of advanced law enforcement training for the BIA. It’s now set to host basic law enforcement training for BIA recruits, as well as for recruits from local tribal police departments, law enforcement communications and correctional agencies.

The news was tucked into a wider-reaching executive order from U.S. Interior Secretary and former North Dakota Gov. Doug Burgum to create an Indian Country Violent Crime Task Force. A news release announced the creation of the task force Tuesday, which was the National Day of Awareness for Missing and Murdered Indigenous People.

The task force “builds on the first Trump administration’s work to bring national attention and resources to the Missing and Murdered Indigenous People crisis,” the release says, and “expands that work with a broader focus on violent crime prevention, investigations and public safety across Indian Country.”

Among other things, the task force will focus on opioid trafficking, create a “Predatory Crimes Unit” to focus on child victims of exploitation and “refocus” efforts to solve missing persons and homicide cases.

Three of South Dakota’s nine tribes rely on the BIA for local law enforcement. Six others have their own tribal police departments. Misdemeanor-level crimes on tribal land are handled in tribal courts; felony crimes that occur there are prosecuted in federal court, and are often investigated by agents with the Federal Bureau of Investigation.

The task force, the release says, will “lead a coordinated effort with federal, tribal and state partners” to address public safety in tribal areas nationwide.

Earlier efforts from Burgum to bring BIA to Camp Grafton

Burgum advocated to bring BIA basic training to Camp Grafton while serving as North Dakota governor.

During a U.S. Senate Committee on Indian Affairs field hearing in 2019 in Bismarck, he said a Camp Grafton BIA academy would help recruit tribal officers across the region.

Tribal recruits nationwide, for local departments or the BIA, have traditionally attended basic training at a federal facility in Artesia, New Mexico.

He said tribal communities face the dual difficulties of high crime rates and a dearth of law enforcement, and that the distance between the training facility and their homes makes recruiting difficult.

“We believe that we can create a premier BIA tribal police officer training facility in North Dakota at Camp Grafton, in conjunction with the Lake Region Law Enforcement Academy in Devils Lake,” Burgum told the committee. “This is very close to Spirit Lake Nation, and not only could this help solve the problem in North Dakota, but for South Dakota, Wyoming, Montana, Minnesota, Wisconsin.”

The U.S. Indian Police Academy Advanced Training Center at Camp Grafton opened the following year. The facility offers higher-level training for officers who’ve already completed the 14-week basic law enforcement certification course in New Mexico.

The timeline on the “implementation of basic training” at Camp Grafton is unclear. Burgum’s Tuesday executive order directs the Office of the Assistant Secretary for Indian Affairs to “develop basic training curriculum” for police, corrections and communications courses at the site “beginning in the second quarter of fiscal year 2026.”

The second quarter of federal fiscal year 2026 began in January. 

No contact information beyond a general email address for the Interior Department is listed on the agency’s press release about Burgum’s order.

The Interior Department did not respond to an email from South Dakota Searchlight with questions about the start of the Camp Grafton basic training program, the number of recruits it could train, and other questions.

Calls to a spokesman for Camp Grafton were not immediately returned.

Basic training for the Great Plains

Like Burgum, South Dakota’s congressional delegation and its state-level leaders have also pushed for the establishment of a BIA training academy for the Great Plains for several years, but had hoped to see it in their state.

U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds and U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson have each argued for Pierre as an appropriate location, as the city already has a state-run law enforcement training academy.

South Dakota’s State Tribal Relations Committee twice endorsed a resolution urging the federal government to establish a BIA basic training academy in South Dakota. Lawmakers voted to support those resolutions.

While the executive order places the basic BIA training site in North Dakota, the discussion in South Dakota spurred state-level changes meant to ease the training burden for tribes in its borders

South Dakota’s basic law enforcement certification course for state and local officers is taught in Pierre, and the state recently began offering the course at a satellite site in Sioux Falls. 

The academy has always been open to tribal recruits. The availability of the Artesia program for tribal officers, however, has typically meant that local and state officers are given priority for the limited number of slots in each course.

Former Gov. Kristi Noem and Attorney General Marty Jackley partnered in April 2024 to open an additional basic training cohort that would prioritize tribal recruits. Tribal police need to complete additional coursework on Indian Country law that other state-certified officers do not, but state officials worked with their federal counterparts to include that information in an add-on unit during basic training.

The state began a second tribal-priority basic training class last year. 

By the time that second course had begun, 13 tribal officers had graduated and earned certification. At least 25 tribal recruits have completed the 13-week training since 2024, Jackley spokesman Tony Mangan said, including 12 in the second tribal-priority class last year.

Johnson, who’s running for governor in South Dakota, told South Dakota Searchlight in a statement that the choice of a North Dakota site isn’t ideal, but is welcome.

“Bringing tribal law enforcement training to North Dakota is certainly better than New Mexico, but I’d like to see more of South Dakota’s tribal law enforcement officers trained even closer to home at the state academy in Pierre,” Johnson said.

Rounds had no such qualification in his statement praising Burgum’s executive order.

“I’ve long called for a tribal law enforcement training curriculum closer to home that gives more South Dakotans the opportunity to serve,” Rounds said. “I’m grateful for Secretary Burgum’s leadership on this issue.”

title: The first credit union service organization  trust company in the state is chartered
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: RAPID CITY — Black Hills Federal Credit Union has expanded its service offerings to help members do more than bank. On April 13, it chartered Black Hills Trust Company LLC., a credit union service organization (CUSO) offering trust and estate services. It’s the first CUSO in the state.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

RAPID CITY — Black Hills Federal Credit Union has expanded its service offerings to help members do more than bank. On April 13, it chartered Black Hills Trust Company LLC., a credit union service organization (CUSO) offering trust and estate services. It’s the first CUSO in the state.

“We serve as trustee; personal representative; conservator for conservatorships, agency accounts, and custodial accounts,” said Alexa Stulken, the chief wealth and trust advisor at Black Hills Trust Company. “For Black Hills Federal Credit Union, they wanted to extend their services to their 116,000 members and growing.”

BH Trust was built to serve individuals and families at every stage of wealth, offering fiduciary support to anyone seeking trusted guidance. While Black Hills Federal Credit Union recognized the importance of offering dedicated fiduciary support to its members, Black Hills Trust Company was intentionally structured to serve all families, members, and nonmembers alike, who are navigating life’s most meaningful financial transitions.

Stulken, for her part, has more than a decade of experience in managing local bank trust divisions, and 26 years of experience total in the field.

“I was sought out, basically because they weren’t going to pursue this unless they had somebody experiences and somebody local in the community that could steward this from the ground up,” Stulken said. “It was a very rare opportunity and something you don’t usually see.”

Stulken said she hopes the trust company will be able to provide a “top-knotch” level of experience, integrity, and compassionate care to folks who intend to set up trusts or conservatorships at Black Hills Trust Company.

“(Black Hills Federal Credit Union) wanted to be able to offer that full one-stop-shop service through the credit union where you can get all of your retail accounts, your investment services, mortgage loans, personal loans, business loans, and then now through CUSOs like our insurance QUSO and our trust QUSO you can now have insurance services and also your trust services to plan for that long-term legacy and estate for your family,” Spulken said. “It makes it very convenient. It’s very community-focused. You know, our main thing was really to make it accessible and just really grounded in the community values that Black Hills Credit Union Stands for.”

The new trust company is headquartered in Rapid City, but is able to offer trust and estate management anywhere in the nation. 

All core fiduciary functions, including trust administration, legal oversight, audit readiness, and compliance, are carried out under South Dakota governance and within South Dakota’s statutory framework to ensure alignment with state law.

title: Making a mark on history
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: LEAD — At the same time that students of the Lead-Deadwood High School Class of 2030 graduate, scientists with the deep underground neutrino experiment (DUNE) collaboration hope to be taking some of their first data from the experiment — opening doors wide for research and discovery for the next generation.
_full_text:
LEAD — At the same time that students of the Lead-Deadwood High School Class of 2030 graduate, scientists with the deep underground neutrino experiment (DUNE) collaboration hope to be taking some of their first data from the experiment — opening doors wide for research and discovery for the next generation. 

That’s one of the reasons Dr. Wendy Walkins brought her eighth-grade social studies class to the Sanford Lab Homestake Visitor’s Center, Thursday. The students joined hundreds of community members for the chance to put their name on history, as the S.D. Science and Technology Authority, Sanford Underground Research Facility, Fermilab, CERN, and the U.S. Department of Energy, hosted a community beam signing event, to sign one of the steel beams that will be used to assemble the DUNE experiment.

“Our kids right now are the ones who are going to be making a difference in the future and having the opportunity for them to someday be down there and they’d be able to go back and find their name, we decided it would be a really neat opportunity for them,” Walkins said. 

Courtney Goddard’s 6-year-old son has a treasured collection of rocks brought up from underground at the former Homestake Gold Mine. He’s fascinated by science, and he persuaded his mother to take him to sign his name.

“I love science,” Goddard told the Black Hills Pioneer. “I have always been interested in it. But this is also important to my son. They need this in life. They need the good positivity from it to just continue research about it and be interested.” 

Some residents used the opportunity to pay homage to friends or teachers who had great influence on their lives. Matt Thalacker took advantage of the opportunity to honor his friend, Jason Rantapaa, who worked at SURF as a mechanical engineer, until his tragic death last month. 

“I’m going to put his name on in memory,” he said. 

Mark Thalacker used the opportunity to recognize Jack Williams, the teacher who got him interested in science, with the Lead High School Class of 1977. 

“This makes me remember my physics teacher at Lead High School,” he said. “He told us about the experiments at that time, where they were searching for neutrinos. That was 50 years ago. The changes that this has brought about are just amazing.” 

Former Homestake employee Marc Asmussen waited in line for more than 20 minutes to sign the beam, camera in hand and ready to fully document the occasion. 

“You went from nuggets to neutrinos, so you went from gold to studying all of these illusive particles, neutrinos, and everything that they mean,” he said. “I think it’s a good thing. We need to take care of science in our country for the young people. What the miners did for 125 years to make the Homestake Gold Mine happen, now it is up to the scientists to add upon that and do something with science.” 

The excitement among all ages was contagious, as the Northern Black Hills community joined dignitaries from around the nation and the world, to sign the red steel beam. Hundreds of people gathered at the Sanford Lab Homestake Visitor’s Center and the Historic Homestake Opera House, to listen to remarks from politicians and major influences in the scientific community, about DUNE — the largest science experiment ever attempted on United States soil, at the Sanford Underground Research Facility. 

Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., who as the 31st governor of South Dakota, is credited for the leadership and perseverance that made America’s Underground Laboratory a reality, said the educational opportunities and the chance for students to stay in South Dakota to do science and research, were a driving force for him. In early 2004, Rounds worked tirelessly to convince members of the S.D. Legislature to give the first $39 million to fund the effort to build the underground lab that will host DUNE. He said the lab and the science have always had bipartisan support. 

“They could see an opportunity for the future, for young people to have something they couldn’t get anywhere else — a chance to stay here and do research,” Rounds said. “This has been a team effort. It will continue to be a bipartisan effort to be able to look for new ways to make life for young people in the future better than what it is today. Science and research, healthcare, quantum physics, all go together. But it all starts with people having an idea and having a place to see whether their idea holds truth, not necessarily for this generation, but for generations to come.” 

U.S. Department of Energy Undersecretary for Science Dario Gil, told the crowd that DUNE is the largest construction project in the DOE Office of Science, and one of the most ambitious science experiments in the world. 

“The United Staes has a long history of investing in bold, scientific endeavors, like the space program and the creation of the Internet that have reshaped our nation and delivered benefits far beyond what anyone could have imagined,” he said. “More than 1,500 collaborators from around the globe have joined together to create a world-leading experiment that will allow scientists to observe how neutrinos change as they travel, capturing data that only DUNE can provide. It is the only experiment capable of making discovery level measurements of the ordering of neutrino masses. It will open the door to exploring new physics in domains previously out of reach, with the capacity to fundamentally re-shape our understanding of the laws of nature.” 

U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, R-S.D., told residents he wanted to set down his political hat, and address the crowd as a South Dakotan, to marvel at the science. 

“Ladies and gentlemen, we’re going to transform our understanding of matter,” he said. “It’s hard for politicians to understand that because, of course, these seeds, they are not harvested in the next fall. They are harvested years and sometimes decades later. The study of quantum mechanics used to be a purely abstract endeavor. Over time, what did it give us? Better semiconductors. Better lasers. Better MRI machines. Better LEDs. Modern computing. At the heart of the definition of exploration is the idea that you don’t really know where you’re going to end up. I’m not clever enough or prescient enough to understand how the world will be changed because of this effort, but I know the world will be changed because of this effort. The fact that we are going to transform our understanding of matter is pretty incredible.” 

The steel beam that so many people signed was provided by CERN laboratory in Switzerland, home of the famed Large Hadron Collider. CERN Director General Mark Thomson told the crowd that the European lab provided the steel for the cryostats, as well as the giant tanks that will hold liquid argon for the DUNE detectors. CERN also provided the prototypes, where scientists honed their plans to build DUNE. The major components represent the first time in 73 years that CERN has contributed to an experiment outside of its European boundaries.  

Thomson, who served as a leader and co-spokesperson for the DUNE collaboration from 2015-2018, helped draft some of the original construction plans for the experiment. On Thursday he went underground to see progress for the Long Baseline Neutrino Facility that will be the site of DUNE. 

“Seeing what we sketched out on paper at the time, turning into reality, was a very moving, very important moment for me,” he said. “I also remember sitting in a bar in Fermilab, thinking about whether this technology would actually work. We started talking about prototypes, and that’s where CERN came in.

“The reason CERN is here is because we believe in the science that is happening here,” he continued. 

 Jim Kerby, LBNF/DUNE-U.S. Project Director, gave a synopsis of the history marked by Thursday’s event. 

“The original Homestake Mine was the center of the community of Lead for over 100 years,” he said. “Neutrino research started in 1965, with Ray Davis. Then about 20 years ago it transitioned from a gold mine to America’s underground science laboratory. We look forward to the research this will bring, to the partnership this will bring, and the scientific excellence this will bring for decades.” 

For more information about DUNE at LBNF, visit https://lbnf-dune.fnal.gov/

Sierra Ferguson contributed to this report

title: SD Supreme Court rules in favor of Lawrence County
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: The South Dakota Supreme Court heard arguments on the Save Centennial Valley versus Lawrence County, et all, case March 19. Pictured from left to right, Justices Scott P. Myren, Mark E. Salter, Chief Justice Steven R. Jensen, Patricia J. Devaney, and Robert Gusinsky. Photo courtesy of South Dakota News Watch
_full_text:
SD Supreme Court rules in favor of Lawrence County
The South Dakota Supreme Court heard arguments on the Save Centennial Valley versus Lawrence County, et all, case March 19. Pictured from left to right, Justices Scott P. Myren, Mark E. Salter, Chief Justice Steven R. Jensen, Patricia J. Devaney, and Robert Gusinsky. Photo courtesy of South Dakota News Watch 

DEADWOOD — The South Dakota Supreme Court ruled in favor of Lawrence County in an opinion issued Thursday, allowing the county to uphold Ordinance 24-05 without having to put the ordinance to a public vote. 

Save Centennial Valley Association, Inc., filed a lawsuit against Lawrence County Auditor Brenda McGruder and the county commissioners, all acting in their official capacity, requesting a writ of mandamus that would have forced the county to put Ordinance 24-05 to a vote of the people. The ordinance transferred the authority to grant conditional use permits from the county commission to the board of adjustment and required that decisions made by the board of adjustment be appealed in circuit court, not put to a referendum and a public vote. The Lawrence County Board of Adjustment is currently made up of the county commissioners. The board has operated this way for approximately 15 years.

The petition went through several revisions and public hearings before commissioners voted to approve the ordinance Nov. 26, 2024. A petition to refer the ordinance to a public vote was submitted by Charles Brown, part of Save Centennial Valley, on Dec. 20 that year. After receiving counsel from Deputy State’s Attorney Bruce Outka and the county commissioners, McGruder denied the petition under the counsel that the move was administrative in action and not legislative in a letter drafted Jan. 2, 2025, after receiving counsel at the Dec. 31, 2024 county commission meeting. 

The difference between a legislative and administrative action meant that the ordinance was not subject to a referendum. 

According to South Dakota Codified Law (SDCL) 7-18A-15.1, an administrative action is, “one that merely puts into execution a plan already adopted by the governing body itself or by the Legislature.” The county argued that the ordinance was required in order to bring them into compliance with SDCL 11-2-53, passed in 2015, outlining the powers of a board of adjustment. 

Save Centennial Valley, in a lawsuit filed Jan. 13, 2025, countered that the ordinance was legislative. According to SDCL, “a legislative decision is one that enacts a permanent law or lays down a rule of conduct or course of policy for the guidance of citizens or their officers. Any matter of a permanent or general character is a legislative decision.” Save Centennial Valley argued that by transferring the power to grant conditional use permits to the board of adjustment and denying the petition to put the ordinance to a public vote, the county was wrongfully denying a public referendum both of the ordinance and any and all conditional use permits.

Strawn ruled in favor of Lawrence County April 16, 2025. Save Centennial Valley appealed the decision to the Supreme Court within the 30-day window required for an appeal. Arguments on the appeal were heard March 19, 2026. 

Supreme Court Chief Justice Steven Jensen wrote the official opinion, concurring with Strawn. In the opinion, Jensen asserts that the governing body issuing conditional use permits is irrelevant, because the appeal process is the same. Decisions must be appealed through a higher court, in this case a circuit court. Jensen cited Department of Game, Fish, & Parks versus Troy Twp., 2017, claiming that administrative decisions are “quasi-judicial if it ‘investigates, declares, and enforces liabilities as they stand on present or past facts and under laws supposed to already exist. … Perhaps as good a criterion as any for determining what is judicial is merely to compare the action on question with the ordinary businesses of courts: that which resembles what courts customarily do is judicial, and that which ahs no such resemblance is nonjudicial.”

Richard Williams, attorney at Gunderson, Palmer, Nelson, and Ashmore, LLP., in Rapid City, represented Lawrence County in the case. Williams said that the opinion explains that an administrative decision made by a governing body is subject to state statue, case law, and due process, the same as any court. 

“You look at the statutory process, for one, you look at what type of a decision it was, and then you look at the due process rights that need to be considered when you are regulating land use,” Williams said. “And so, for all those reasons, the (Supreme) Court said, ‘Look, this isn’t the type of decision that could be subject to a referendum and pointed out that there is the option for recourse. You could go to a circuit court and then appeal that decision to the Supreme Court. They’re not on a lock.”

Jensen wrote that previous decisions made by the Supreme Court, in which they ruled that some conditional use permits were referrable and others were not, while citing Kirschenman versus Hutchinson County Board of Commissioners as case law, “is not supportable.”

“The concern expressed in Kirschenman that a county has unfettered discretion to grant (conditional use permit) applications is inconsistent with the current requirements of state law and constitutional principles,” wrote Jensen. “Both state statutes and constitutional protections require zoning authorities to follow objective criteria and standards when deciding (conditional use permits).”

Jensen claimed that ordinance 24-05 was not legislative in nature because it, “did not create a change in the law or the criteria for considering (conditional use permits), nor does it impact any remedy provided by law.” Therefore, he concluded that Save Centennial Valley did not establish a clear legal right for the issuance of a writ of mandamus to force the county to place the ordinance to a referendum. 

Justices Mark E. Slater, Patricia J. Devaney, Scott P. Myren, and Robert Gusinsky all concurred, making the opinion unanimous. The opinion means that Lawrence County commissioners will continue to go through the statutory process of approving or denying conditional use permits as the board of adjustment and all permits approved since the ordinance became law in December are not referrable to a public vote. Most notably, the Larson gravel quarry on Homestake Road can continue to operate unchallenged. 

“The South Dakota Supreme Court and the legislature have been discussing conditional use permits for years, and I think this was a pretty good summary of where we are today with those statutes and judicial interpretations,” said Williams. “I think ultimately the Court sided with the county, stating that the county was simply following the rules and regulations already put into place by the state legislature.”

Commissioner Eric Jennings said the county commissioners are glad to have finality on the issue. 

“As county commissioners, we are bound to uphold the law. We take an oath at the start of our term to do that,” said Jennings. “We felt that we were following the law by changing the conditional use permit decisions to the board of adjustment instead of the county commissioners. Through legal counsel, we had an interpretation of the law, and we chose to pursue that path, and circuit court affirmed it and now the Supreme Court has affirmed our decision. We always felt that we were in the right doing so, and it’s nice to have this decision in public now.”

Matthew Lucklum, an attorney with Bangs, McCullen, Butler, Foye, and Simmons, LLP, who represented Save Centennial Valley, was not available for comment.

title: Spearfish issues call out for Art in  Public Places Advisory Board members
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: This mural, at the Spearfish city campground, was approved by the city council in the fall. At the time, the council discussed founding an art in public places committee to help allocate funds set aside for similar public art projects. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Spearfish issues call out for Art in  Public Places Advisory Board members
This mural, at the Spearfish city campground, was approved by the city council in the fall. At the time, the council discussed founding an art in public places committee to help allocate funds set aside for similar public art projects. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — On Monday, the Spearfish City Council voted to amend and streamline 2 existing ordinances on second reading, effectively forming an Art in Public Places Advisory Board. Now, applications are open for board members. 

The new, 7-member board is tasked with advising and assisting the city with selection, acquisition, display, maintenance, and removal of artwork in public places in the city. The board will also direct funds from the city’s art in public places funds. 

The art in public places fund was established roughly 20 years ago. Whenever building permits are issued, a 5% fee is levied and placed in the fund to support the creation and maintenance of public art. 

The fund was used for the Termesphere installation on Main Street, and last fall, a group of citizens approached the council about using some of the money to pay for a series of murals on restroom buildings and maintenance sheds in city parks and the city campground. 

Inspired by the public library’s summer reading program, themed “color our world” a grassroots effort launched to see a series of 5 murals painted throughout the city. 

Jeremy Smith, Trish Jenkins, and Black Hills State University art professor Desy Schoenwies, along with a cohort of community members and local artists prepared designs and a budget for the 2025 mural project. 

The council did not authorize the completion of all of the 5 proposed murals, which would have cost a total of $9,600 to install.  Instead, the council voted to move forward with just 2 of the public art pieces. 

In total, the city spent $1,800 from the art in public places fund on the 2 approved projects: a mural on the campground woodshop and a mural on the restroom building at Evans Park. 

The park board recommended allowing both of the murals. It did not issue recommendations on the other murals. However, park staff did prepare the sites for painting: cleaning and scraping the walls on the appointed buildings, and applying paint primer.

The Evans Park mural was completed by students in the BHSU ART-222 seminar class, so no artist stipend was needed, and some of the cost of paint and supplies for that mural were covered by the class. The trout-themed campground mural, designed by Zachary Cincotta, was paid for with art in public places funds. 

When those 2 murals were approved, the city council expressed concern about balancing public tastes, maintaining art in the face of possible vandalism, and directing funds without an advisory board. 

At the time, the council directed city staff to being drafting the ordinance amendment that passed this week. 

Under the ordinance, artwork is defined as sculptures, monuments, frescos, relief paintings, fountains, banners, mosaics, ceramics, weaving, carved art, and stained glass. Public art, as dictated by city code, must be on display for more than 2 weeks on or inside a city owned facility. The board will also have oversight over loaning city owned art for private display. 

Artwork will not “normally include landscaping, paving, or signs,” under the ordinance. 

Of its 7 members, one must be an active member of the planning commission and one must serve actively on the parks recreation and forestry board. The other 5 at-large members can be appointed with approval from the council by the mayor, but they must be residents of the city of Spearfish. Board members will not receive compensation for the role. 

Applications will be open on the city website soon.

title: Weapon reported earlier in week at Spearfish HS found off campus
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: SPEARFISH — A weapon that may have been brought onto the campus of Spearfish High School has been located off campus, and the individuals involved will not return to the building, school officials said Friday afternoon.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — A weapon that may have been brought onto the campus of Spearfish High School has been located off campus, and the individuals involved will not return to the building, school officials said Friday afternoon.

According to the Spearfish School District, earlier this week the high school administration received a report that a student may hav brought a firearm onto campus. School officials immediately launched an investigation in cooperation with the school resource officer and local law enforcement. 

While the initial inquiry and search found no weapon or intent to harm, they continued to follow leads, according to the report. Further investigation suggested hat the weapon may have been on school grounds at some point, and in response, school officials followed their safety procedures. A comprehensive K-9 search confirmed that no firearm was present. 

According to the report, following their investigation, law enforement officers  located and recovered the reported weapon at an off-campus location. The person or persons involved are no longer at school and will not be returning to Spearfish High School, district officials said.

The report assured the public that there is no threat to the school. To help assure their safety, additional law enforcement officers will provide a presence around the school through the end of the school year.

If you have additional questions, please contact the high school administration office.

WHITEWOOD — A juvenile was shot early Sunday morning at a party near Whitewood.

According to the Lawrence County Sheriff's Office, just after 12;30 a.m., Lawrence County dispatch received a call regarding a possible underage party at a residence north of Whitewood.

Upon their arrival, they discovered a juvenile with a gunshot wound.

The juvenile's name, gender, age, nor condition were not immediately released.

title: Girl shot at party near Whitewood
byline: Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Girl shot at party near Whitewood
Courtesy photo 

WHITEWOOD — A juvenile was shot early Sunday morning at a party near Whitewood.

According to the Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office, just after 12:30 a.m., Lawrence County dispatch received a call regarding a possible underage party at a residence north of Whitewood, on Whitewood Valley Road.

Upon their arrival, they contacted several people inside a shop building and discovered a juvenile with a gunshot wound.

The girl, suffering from a .22 caliber gunshot to the head, near her jaw, was conscious and alert. She was transported to a nearby hospital. 

During his investigation, Sgt. Detective Dustin Schumacher, with the Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office, learned that 2 men, including William Westberg, 22, of Whitewood, were in the building with 2 girls. Schumacher wrote in his report that Westberg was in a relationship with the victim, and he allegedly admitted to “joking” around with the revolver and shot the girl. He stated he had previously pointed the pistol, pulled the hammer back, and pulled the trigger on his friends, but said he didn’t know it was loaded and did not mean to shoot the girl.

Deputies learned that there were cameras in and outside of the shop; however, they were told by a relative of Westberg’s, that the internet inside the building was disconnected shortly after the incident. Westberg allegedly admitted he disconnected the cables because he was scared.

Upon obtaining and viewing the video, Schumacher wrote in his report that he saw 3 people sitting at a table. A hand holding a revolver raised up and pointed toward the girl. The pistol fired and the girl flinched. 

During his interview with Westberg, he allegedly admitted that the 2 girls brought beer to the shop and drank it while in the shop. Schumacher wrote that Westberg also admitted to using illegal narcotics and that he had smoked methamphetamine the night before. 

Westberg was arrested and charged with aggravated assault – bodily injury with indifference to human life, a Class 3 felony, reckless discharge of a firearm, social hosting, and possession of drug paraphernalia. The 3 latter charges are misdemeanors, but the aggravated assault charge is punishable by up to 15 years in prison and a $30,000 fine. 

He made his initial appearance in court Monday morning. Westberg pleaded not guilty and is being held on a $25,000 cash bond in the Lawrence County Jail.

Deputies declined to provide an update on the condition nor other information about the girl citing her age. However, numerous social media posts indicated that she was in the intensive care unit of a Denver, Colo., hospital.

This is not Westberg’s first serious incident with a firearm.

In July 2022, Westberg had gotten into an argument with his mom in Whitewood. A doorbell camera captured the incident. According to court reports, it shows that Westberg pushed his mom to the ground and then him exit a garage with an AR-15. He is seen aiming the rifle at his mom and then strike her in the head with the buttstock. He then appeared to throw the rifle into the grass near the driveway, walking to his pickup where he retrieved a shotgun. He was then filmed firing a round into the air.

He pleaded guilty to reckless discharge of a firearm and simple assault. Fourth Circuit Court Judge Chad Callahan sentenced Westberg to 180 days in jail with 135 days suspended. As part of the plea agreement, aggravated assault charges were dismissed.

According to court documents, Westberg has 2 additional cases he is facing. One is a driving under the influence charge filed in February, and the other is from January in which he was charged with possession of a loaded firearm while intoxicated.

Agencies assisting include the state Division of Criminal Investigation, Spearfish and Deadwood police departments, and the Spearfish Ambulance Service.

The investigation is ongoing.

title: 300+ graduate from BHSU
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: More than 300 students graduated from Black Hills State University Saturday. Pioneer photo by Mark Watson
_full_text:
Graduationn cover.JPG
More than 300 students graduated from Black Hills State University Saturday. Pioneer photo by Mark Watson 

SPEARFISH — More than 300 people graduated with degrees from Black Hills State University, Saturday.

Degrees awarded include 26 master’s degrees, 241 bachelor’s degrees, and 38 associate’s degrees.

Steve Elliott, president of BHSU, congratulated the graduates.

“Your day has arrived. Today you become a college graduate,” Elliott said. “Your degree will open doors to opportunities that you may not even be able to imagine today, and I’m so excited for you and your future. As hard as you’ve worked earning your degree, you did not get here alone, your family has been a great source of support to you throughout your college years. They are very proud of you, and many of them are here today to celebrate with you. I know as you walk across the stage today, they will be bursting with joy.”

 Jonathan Nero.JPG
Dr. Jonathan Nero, professor of music and choral director, was presented with the Distinguished Faculty Award, Saturday at the BHSU spring commencement ceremony. Pioneer photo by Mark Watson 

After recognizing the families of the students, Elliott continued. 

“There are 2 words commonly used to describe days like today,” he said “One is graduation, and the other one is commencement. I’m sure you’ve heard both. Graduation really signifies the end the finish line. It celebrates the fact that you’ve successfully completed this phase of your education, and it brings closure to this chapter of your life. Commencement, on the other hand, signifies the starting gate, the beginning of a new life. It’s a transition from the past into the future. Commencement really celebrates that the best part of your life is ahead of you. Both terms are most appropriate today, and both are very meaningful. I choose, however, to leave you with congratulations on your commencement, your new beginning. Your future is bright. You have ability, passion and commitment to make a difference. As yellow jackets, I know that wherever you go, you will carry your alma mater with you, and you will represent us well. So, congratulations graduates on commencement and all the bright and beautiful, beautiful possibilities that are waiting for you.”

Dr. Jonathan Nero, professor of music and choral director, was presented with the Distinguished Faculty Award.

Three students, Warren Feudner, Elise Patton, and Aden Scott, were then commissioned as second lieutenants into the Army by Maj. John Lundeen, assistant professor of military science.

The BHSU Commencement Wind Ensemble played “Joy of Love and Life.”

Then David Hillard, branch director of RBC Wealth Management and financial advisor with the Hillard Williams Group, delivered the charge to the graduates.

He congratulated the students.

“You’re undoubtedly a deeper thinker and hopefully a more well-rounded person. You will also reap financial rewards for the work that you put in. On average undergraduate degree holders will earn 60% more than those with a high school diploma. If you have a master’s or a doctorate degree, it’s more than that,” Hillard said. “Now, while there’s a strong link between education and income, it isn’t (exclusive). … So, if you want to be in that top economically performing board of graduates, you need to optimize the impact of your education, and therefore your very life itself. Your degree is simply a foundation upon which you build your career, and just like the building’s foundation, it isn’t the building itself. It is just the base. So just like the catalyst can accelerate a chemical reaction, I believe that there are some key behaviors that you can consider that will drive life outcomes in very significant and outsized ways. So, in all these three key behaviors, I encourage you to think big, dream big, but act small.”

He encouraged graduates to constantly pursue excellence. 

 Commissioning.JPG
Warren Feudner, left, Elise Patton, and Aden Scott, were commissioned as second lieutenants into the Army by Maj. John Lundeen, assistant professor of military science. Photo by Mark Watson 

 David Hillard.JPG
David Hillard, branch director of RBC Wealth Management and commencment speaker, gives inspiring speech to graduates. Pioneer photo by Mark Watson 

“Results produced by pursuing excellence versus settling for mediocrity are so incredibly worth it, and they will be readily apparent to everyone, including your bosses,” he said. “So in this pursuit, think big, but act small.”

Secondly, he encouraged students to act like an owner in everything they did.

“Treat everyone you engage just like a successful business owner would treat the most valued customers,” he said. “Regardless of your career path, treat your profession not as a job, but as an act of service to others. So, when you shift from simply performing the rudimentary actions that are required of your job.”

“Remember this, no company gets big instantly … so be patient,” Hillard continued. “Success, it’s the nearly inevitable long-term result of a series when we provide value and service one customer at a time. It’s not a social media campaign that gets it done, and it’s not a snazzy new web page. It’s a humble act of service that changes people’s hearts.”

Hillard closed with a challenge to graduates. 

“Don’t just tell the world what you believe. ... Show the world what you believe by your actions as you move into the next chapters of your life, remember to pursue excellence, act like an owner, and to serve others and on all these things,” he said. “When you’re dreaming big, remember to act small. So, Class of 2026, congratulations. May your future be filled with success, but more important significance.”

title: Tropical Smooth is the SD Veteran-Owned  Small Business of the Year
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Kelli Ewert is the owner of Tropical Smoothie Café. She’s also an Army veteran and the recipient of the South Dakota Small Business Administration Veteran Owned Small Business of the Year award. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Tropical Smooth is the SD Veteran-Owned  Small Business of the Year
Kelli Ewert is the owner of Tropical Smoothie Café. She’s also an Army veteran and the recipient of the South Dakota Small Business Administration Veteran Owned Small Business of the Year award. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — Kelly Ewert has made not one, but 2 careers out of caring for people.

She is a registered nurse and the owner of Tropical Smoothie Café in Spearfish.

“I was an Army nurse. I went through ROTC and grew up in Texas. I was stationed in Colorado and married into the Black Hills,” Ewert said. “I have been here since 2003, and then settled in Spearfish in 2008.”

Today, Ewert runs an IV business and works with the Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office to perform blood draws when needed.

As a nurse, care is a core principle. That same principle applies to her leadership of Tropical Smoothie Café, Ewert said.

As the owner of a small business, she’s leaned in to nurturing potential and providing a place for young people to step into the workforce.

Pull quote
I think I have employed half of the youth of Spearfish. It takes a village to get them all raised, and we love doing it. — Kellie Ewert
 Owner of Tropical Smoothie Café, Spearfish

“I think I have created and fostered a good environment for kids to have a first job and understand how the world works,” Ewert said. “I want them to like it here. I don’t just want warm bodies, I want them to like it and want  to be here. I think I kind of mother a lot of them, but they appreciate it.”

She employs high school students, college students, and a string of student athletes.

“I have kids who started at 14 years old, and now they’re coming back from college for the summer. I know so many of their parents. It has just been a big family here. I tell the kids all the time that this is an opportunity for them to learn leadership before they go off to school. Some of them aren’t sure they’re ready for leadership, but I see their potential,” Ewert said. “I think I have employed half of the youth of Spearfish. It takes a village to get them all raised, and we love doing it.”

Ewert also partners with Northern Hills Training Center to offer employment to adults with developmental disabilities.

“They have an opportunity to have a normal part of life, and it is good for the kids to see that there are other people in this world that want to work more and can’t,” Ewert said.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Ewert realized that many programs that rewarded children for meeting their reading goals had dissolved, so Tropical Smoothie started working with Spearfish teachers to provide free smoothies to young readers. At the café, Ewert occasionally takes on the role of tooth-fairy, too.

“We have a program for kids who lose their teeth. Anyone under 10 can come in and give us a smile, and say they lost a tooth, and they get a free smoothie,” Ewert said.

Ewert’s contributions as a small business owner earned her an accolade this year from the South Dakota Small Business Administration. Tropical Smoothie has been named South Dakota’s Veteran-Owned Small Business of the Year.

“It was really humbling to accept that award,” Ewert said. “One of the things I learned from the military was: you can’t be a good leader if you are not a good follower.”

Ewert takes pride in “rolling up her sleeves and slinging smoothies” right alongside her crew.

“I do the dishes. I come in in the morning and ask, ‘Where do you need me?’ I think working right alongside of them is the best example you can set. My nursing leadership in the military was really priceless,” Ewert said. “The business stuff you can learn as you go. The people you either have it, or you don’t.”

Ewert decided to add entrepreneur/restaurateur alongside titles like registered nurse, Army veteran, and mom of 2 in 2019, just a few months before the COVID-19 pandemic challenged restaurants across the country.

“I wanted something that my kids could be part of,” Ewert said. “It was difficult during COVID, but I went from nurse to restaurant (owner) which is a huge jump, but it broadened who I am and helped me learn a different side of life. Business ownership is a tough thing. I had to do a lot of learning on my own. The franchise wasn’t able to get here during COVID. I had to figure it out. I let the crew help me figure it out.”

Ewert hopes that, in being both a nurse and the leader of the crew at Tropical Smoothie, she can inspire her young employees to expand their own horizons. 

“It is good for the kids to see that you don’t have to just have one thing that you do. You can try different things, do internships, try all for those things,” Ewert said. 

She was nominated by the South Dakota CEO of the West Women’s Business Center for the Small Business Administration Veteran-Owned Small Business of the Year Award. She received the recognition on May 5.

“Without the community, any small business isn’t going to thrive. It has been really fun to grow the business with the community and have those relationships with the school district and the training center,” Ewert said.

title: Miller files federal lawsuit against city of Lead, building inspector
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: LEAD — A federal lawsuit against the city of Lead and Building Inspector Dennis Schumacher claims that the city improperly used condemnation procedures to try and force repairs for a retaining wall that supports public infrastructure.
_full_text:
LEAD — A federal lawsuit against the city of Lead and Building Inspector Dennis Schumacher claims that the city improperly used condemnation procedures to try and force repairs for a retaining wall that supports public infrastructure. 

 Failing retaining wall prompts late night evacuation notice  1.jpg
In June 2023, Lead Building Inspector Dennis Schumacher forced evacuation and condemned an apartment building, after a retaining wall began to slough off. On Friday, the owner of that apartment building filed a lawsuit in federal court, claiming the city used threat of condemnation to try and force repairs on the wall that holds up Washington Street. Pioneer file photo  

 Failing retaining wall prompts late night evacuation notice 2.jpg
A sign posted on the door of the Miller Apartments building in June 2023 warns that the structure is unsafe for human occupancy. Pioneer file photo 

Paul Miller, owner of the Miller Apartments on Grandview Avenue in Lead, filed the lawsuit Friday in U.S. District Court. The 20-page court document details events that started in May 2023, when a retaining wall behind one of the apartment buildings began to slough off. 

The retaining wall supports Washington Street in Lead. But city officials claim it is on Millers property, and according to city ordinance, property owners are responsible for retaining wall repairs. 

In the lawsuit, Miller alleges that Schumacher used the threat of condemnation of the apartment building to try and force him to fix the retaining wall. Miller also claims that Schumacher acted improperly when he issued the evacuation order, in June 2023. Schumacher subsequently posted a notice on the door, condemning the building until further notice. In September 2023, Schumacher lifted the condemnation and allowed residents to move back into the building, contingent upon the owner placing barricades around the retaining wall to protect the gas meters on the back of the building. The wall was not repaired before residents were allowed to return. 

In court filings, Miller claims the evacuation and subsequent condemnation was not related to structural issues with the apartment building, as required by section 116 of the International Building Code. That section states, “Structures or existing equipment that are or hereafter become unsafe, insanitary or deficient because of inadequate means of egress facilities, inadequate light and ventilation, or that constitute a fire hazard, or are otherwise dangerous to human life or the public welfare, or that involve illegal or improper occupancy or inadequate maintenance, shall be deemed an unsafe condition. Unsafe structures shall be taken down and removed or made safe, as the building official deems necessary and as provided for in this section.”

Schumacher told the Pioneer Monday morning that he did not know about the lawsuit, and he declined further comment. Messages left with Lead Mayor Dustin Heupel and City Administrator Robin Lucero, who was the city planner at the time of the incident, were not returned. 

In July 2023, the Pioneer reported Lead city ordinance states that it is the building inspector’s right and responsibility to condemn any walls that need repaired or replaced. In the same article, the Pioneer cited a separate ordinance that defines public nuisances as anything that is a danger to human health, but does not specifically address retaining walls. That ordinance gives the building inspector the right to abate a property that is a danger to human health. 

But Miller’s lawsuit alleges that the city erred when it did not consult an engineer before evacuating the building. The complaint also states that Miller’s engineer, Hermanson Egge Engineering, of Rapid City, confirmed the retaining wall supports Washington Street, that it had not been privately constructed by past or present property owners, and that it was not properly constructed or maintained. Court documents also allege that the city’s rationale about the retaining wall presenting an emergency threat to the building was not supported when the city did not close that section of Washington Street to thru traffic. 

In addition to discussing the Miller Apartments wall, Miller’s lawsuit mentions an instance when a retaining wall belonging to the Handley Recreation Center failed, in March 2024. The Handley Center wall supports Sunny Hill Road, and following its collapse, Lucero found a grant to help pay for the wall repairs and assisted the Handley Recreation Center board with the costs. 

“The contrast between the city’s handling of Miller Apartments and the Handley Center supports the inference that the city used condemnation against plaintiffs not as a neutral safety measure, but as leverage to force plaintiffs to accept responsibility for a public infrastructure problem,” court documents state. 

Miller’s lawsuit seeks a trial by jury for consequential damages for financial losses incurred when the building was evacuated and condemned, including lost rental income, business interruption, injury to marketability and insurability, and other costs, as well as compensatory damages. It also seeks a declaration that the responsibility for repairing and maintaining the wall belongs to the city of Lead. 

To date, the retaining wall near Miller Apartments has not been repaired and visibly remains in the same condition as it was when the building was originally condemned.
