title: Newell Scholl Board candidates
description: Voters in the Newell School District will head to the polls June 2 to vote on one vacant school board seat. Two people are running for one open position which is a 3-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.
_full_text:
Voters in the Newell School District will head to the polls June 2 to vote on one vacant school board seat. Two people are running for one open position which is a 3-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.

Kurt Hocking

Name and what you do for a living? 

 Kurt Hocking (MUG)
Kurt Hocking 

Kurt Hocking.  I retired from VA Black Hills.  Currently I work as an Emergency Medical Responder (EMR) with Butte County Ambulance - Newell

What motivated you to run for this office?

Make the school appealing again to students and families: Enrollment follows reputation. I want to help create a school environment where families are proud to choose—safe, welcoming, academically strong, and communitycentered.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

I am running to bring new ideas and a clear vision for the future: I am not running to maintain the status quo. I am running to help the district grow—academically, culturally, and operationally. That includes exploring innovative programs, strengthening communication, and supporting staff so they can do their best work.    

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I was elected to the Newell City Council as a Commissioner.  I also held a position on the VA Black Hills Employees Association.  I am a member of the Newell Festival of Trees Committee and the Newell Community Club. I am also the elected Maintenance Officer for the ambulance service. 

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I have attended 3 school board meetings in person and watched 6 on-line either live or the next day.  I have attended a couple of the Newell City Council meetings. I attended all 12 monthly meetings with the ambulance service.

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

In our area, I believe it is essential to have a local newspaper delivered to residents. Not everyone has consistent access to online news, and a printed paper ensures that all members of our community stay informed. A local newspaper strengthens communication, highlights local events, and preserves the stories that matter most to the people who live here. It helps keeps our community connected, engaged, and aware of the issues and activities that shape daily life 

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in the Newell school district?

Open communication, regaining trust, and working for the betterment of the entire district. 

How do you intend to solve these issues?

I will be accessible, transparent, and willing to have honest conversations about challenges and opportunities. Clear communication builds confidence and reduces misunderstandings.    Trust isn’t asked for; it’s earned. I will show up, follow through, and make decisions based on what’s best for students and the district. Every decision I make will be grounded in what strengthens the school, supports students, and builds longterm stability.

    

What do you believe is working for the district, and how will you retain that progression?

We have solid policies in place and community involvement that continues to grow. Many people in this area have a deep, genuine desire to keep the Newell School open, and that commitment shows in their actions.  I am seeing mentorship and support for new teachers, as well as volunteers stepping forward to help wherever they can.  Young families are becoming more engaged, bringing fresh energy and a shared determination to preserve and strengthen our school. This collective effort reflects a community that cares deeply about its students, its educators, and the future of the Newell School District. 

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

Open communication. I will be accessible, transparent, and willing to have honest conversations about challenges and opportunities. Clear communication builds confidence and reduces misunderstandings. I will be willing to listen and collaborate.  I recognize that good ideas come from many places. I will work respectfully with administrators, teachers, families, and fellow board members to find solutions that move the district forward.

What else do you want people to know about you?

I may be a Newell transplant, but after 20 years of living here, this community is truly my home. I own a home in the district, and I have two grandsons who attend Newell School, giving me a deep, personal investment in ensuring the school remains open and thriving for many years to come.  All five of my stepchildren are proud Newell School alumni, as is my spouse, and our family’s connection to this district run strong. Through my work as an active member of the ambulance service, I care deeply about the well-being of this community and its residents. My commitment to Newell is rooted in both family and service, and I am dedicated to supporting the future of our school and the strength of our community. 

Todd Youngberg

title: Creative Aging SD lends artists expertise to older generations across the state
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Eliza Blue, artist and writer in Bison, utilized the Creative Aging SD program to bring generations together in partner dancing lessons. Photo courtesy of Eliza Blue
_full_text:
1 Creative Aging SD lends artists expertise to older generations across the state.jpeg
Eliza Blue, artist and writer in Bison, utilized the Creative Aging SD program to bring generations together in partner dancing lessons. Photo courtesy of Eliza Blue 

SPEARFISH — The South Dakota Arts Council (SDAC) has announced the recipients of the “Creative Aging SD” program, including local artists from Bison and Spearfish, who will lead hands-on creative programs designed for older adults in communities throughout the state. 

These programs are designed to highlight creativity and provide sequential learning across multiple art forms, including storytelling, music, movement, writing, visual arts, traditional and folk arts, and shared community projects. They offer space for participants to learn something new, reflect on their experiences, and connect with others in meaningful ways. 

Eliza Blue, of Bison, has worked with members of her community to coordinate an intergenerational partner dancing curriculum, with live music, shared meals, and opportunities for people of all ages to build relationships in their shared rural setting. 

Anna Robins, of Spearfish, created a 10-week long curriculum, guiding residents of Edgewood Assisted Living Center through the decades of film, including trivia, storytelling, and memory-sparking discussions. 

Reviving Western culture and creating a ‘third space’

Blue, who has worked with SDAC on multiple projects, said that she’s recently been having discussions about reviving a ‘third space’ in communities. 

 2 Creative Aging SD lends artists expertise to older generations across the state.png
Anna Robins, local filmmaker, utilized the Creative Aging SD program to create a 10-week long curriculum, walking residents of Edgewood Assisted Living Center through decades of filmmaking and storytelling history. Photo courtesy of Anna Robins 

“The first space is your home, and the second space is the other place you have to go, like a job,” said Blue. “And the third space used to be church, or people would go to the bar or a bowling alley. There’d be other places that they would gather and that was their third place. Those have become harder to find, especially in rural communities.”

Another thing that Blue felt was slowly slipping away from rural communities was a deep, cultural love of partner dancing. 

“I would say it’s a huge part of western culture in general, but certainly in our town it’s something people really enjoy and love to do,” said Blue. “But over the last few years, it seems like there’s been less and less opportunities for it. So, now there are young people in our community who haven’t been exposed to it the way their parents and grandparents would have been.”

Blue said she was approached by Ari Albright, director of the Creative Aging SD program, who asked if she knew anyway that the program could be used in her community. Blue said she partnered with dance instructor Shauna Kopren and came up with a plan to get generations together, using the funds from Creative Aging, to solve the problem of the third space and the slow dissipation of dance culture in their communities. 

“The wonderful thing about living in such a small community is that, even though there aren’t a lot of options to gather and do something for fun, there are already strong intergenerational ties, just because so many families still live on the farm or the ranch (and) are in a multigenerational setting,” said Blue. “So, we saw this as an opportunity to actually get together and incorporate live music (and a shared meal) and get that dance culture going again.”

Blue said classes started in March, with Kopran teaching the basics of a two-step, leader and follower responsibilities, and building up to the waltz and jitterbug. 

“The jitterbug is, of course, everybody’s favorite, because everybody likes to be swung or to swing people around,” said Blue. “And then we just kind of set them loose to try it out.”

Eventually, Blue said the dance classes moved into Bison’s K-12 middle and high school music class, where older students shared their knowledge with the youngsters. One instructor, in particular, was a coveted dance partner. 

“It was really cute, because most of the older adults were women. So, when we went into the music class, several of them were grandmas of people in the music class,” Blue said. “There was one grandma in particular who is just a great dancer already and she’s just a really fun person, so all the kids wanted to be her partner. She came home and she’s like, ‘The kids were fighting over me.’ It was very fun.”

Finally, the lessons culminated in an intergenerational dance at the school’s cafeteria. Blue said that she hopes the lessons and dances have brought the culture back to the forefront of the community’s minds, and she hopes that dances continue to be a regular thing long after the funding from the grant runs out. 

“Anything with grants like this, it makes a huge, gigantic difference if you don’t have to do fundraising as part of making something happen,” she said. “I personally believe very strongly that artists deserve to be paid for their time. It’s tricky because most artists love what they do and would do it for free, but artists have bills just like everybody else. So, to be able to pay our instructor well and to be able to pay the people that are playing the music for us and to be able to pay for rental fees for facilities, it makes the undertaking much, much, much easier.”

History of film

Robins, who has worked in film for over a decade, said she was approached by Albright to bring her artform to the older generations of Spearfish early this year. Since then, she’s created a 10-week long curriculum, inviting senior citizens of Edgewood Assisted Living Center to spend one hour with her every week from the middle of May to the end of August, learning about film through the decades in South Dakota. 

“Famously, there’s been a couple of films that we know of in the Black Hills,” said Robins. “Dances with Wolves, National Treasure has some famous scenes, but there’s also some really old, interesting black and white films, some early experimentation with film technology, filming cowboys and herds and ranchers in the area.”

Robins said that she plans to show clips of films beginning in 1900 and moving through the decades every week. She plans to share her own knowledge of the films and the creative filming process with residents, while including trivia and asking residents to share their experiences with the film’s locations and time period.

“It’s fun, when we live in such a remote area and Hollywood feels so far away, we don’t always think about interesting stories or certain art forms happening in our communities. But they are, and they have been,” said Robins. “It’s fun to show residents of our area what’s being done in our area and what has been done in the area. Show them that we have this history here, too. It’s not just on the west coast and it’s not just in New York. The idea of sharing stories in this art form is not exclusive to certain areas or certain demographics. Anyone can share these stories.”

To create the curriculum, Robins said she went through archives of film in the public domain through each decade, combing out snapshots that would be relevant to her audience. 

“I’ve picked some clips that are from some pretty famous early films. If you were to study film, these are films that would be mentioned,” she said. “Certain people like Charlie Chaplin, including some of his really short films. We’re looking at public domain material and it’s easier for the early decades and a little harder in the later decades, but there are materials out there for teaching.”

Robins said she’s excited to launch the program and hopes that by discussing the films with the residents that they can offer context and first-hand information as they work through the decades. 

“I am trying to figure out other places to bring this program to, so it could be more available to the public in this area,” she said. “I’m really grateful to the SDAC and Albright for leading this program and making it available to artists. It’s really great to have programs that support artists doing what they love and bringing that to people in a way where people can just come and enjoy and learn something.”

title: Report details wide disparity between  Native American and white health in SD
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: The Indian Health Service office in Wagner. A new report says the health disparity between Native American and white South Dakotans is among the largest racial or ethnic health gaps in the nation. Photo by John Hult, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Report details wide disparity between  Native American and white health in SD
The Indian Health Service office in Wagner. A new report says the health disparity between Native American and white South Dakotans is among the largest racial or ethnic health gaps in the nation. Photo by John Hult, South Dakota Searchlight 

PIERRE — The health disparity between Native American and white South Dakotans is among the largest racial or ethnic health gaps in the nation, according to a new report from a foundation that advocates for equitable healthcare.

Native Americans in South Dakota die prematurely from avoidable causes at a rate of 1,089 deaths per 100,000 people, which is the highest rate of any racial or ethnic group in the nation, according to the 2026 State Health Disparities Report from the Commonwealth Fund.

That’s five times the rate of white South Dakotans. Preventable causes include infectious diseases, treatable conditions and accidents such as vehicle crashes and drug overdoses.

State data shows half of Native Americans in South Dakota die before age 58. The median age of death for white South Dakotans is 80.

Health disparities in SD are ‘completely addressable,’ organization leader says

The report analyzes 2023–2024 data on health care access, quality, use of services and outcomes across racial and ethnic groups in all 50 states and Washington D.C. South Dakota ranked last for Native American health among 21 states with sufficient Native American population data.

Even when income, insurance and access are similar, disparities persist, said Commonwealth Fund President Joseph Betancourt.

“As a primary care physician, I know what happens when care is out of reach: Conditions that are manageable become crises, and people have poor health outcomes and ultimately live shorter lives. This is unacceptable and completely addressable,” Betancourt said.

Native American health system performance in South Dakota ranked in the lowest percentile nationally. White South Dakotans experienced the best care in the state, scoring in the 79th percentile among all population groups nationally.

The report found states with stronger health systems also have smaller disparities and said targeted policy changes could help, including:

Funding housing, early childhood education and food access programs.

Ensuring affordable, accessible coverage.

Strengthening primary care in underserved communities.

Protecting preventative services.

Ensuring equitable use of digital health tools and artificial intelligence.

Tribal-managed Medicaid model and targeted programs could be ‘quite effective’

About 38% of Native Americans in South Dakota are uninsured — a key driver of disparities.

“Coverage is not the only thing that matters, but it is really the first thing that matters,” said Commonwealth Fund Senior Scholar Sara Collins, adding that states that expanded Medicaid have improved access. South Dakota voters approved expansion in 2022. Tribal members are exempt from federal Medicaid work requirements.

South Dakota officials, lawmakers and tribal leaders will launch an Indian Medicaid Managed Care Task Force later this year, which tribal officials hope will improve outcomes and efficiencies for tribal members.

In a managed care model, tribes could contract with the state of South Dakota to direct federal Medicaid dollars into a pool of funds for healthcare. An entity of the tribes’ choosing could negotiate costs with off-reservation providers and coordinate care — including preventative care or incentives for healthy habits — for tribal members who seek care on or off tribal land.

“Focused actions like that can really improve disparities we see across the country,” Collins said.

David Radley, senior scientist on the report, said efforts to address health outcomes and access among Native Americans in Oklahoma have “made a difference.” Tribal governments there have invested heavily in clinics, hospitals and medical education. 

Betancourt said progress in South Dakota will require high quality care and coverage to be “woven together.”

Radley added that health systems in rural states must be “built around rural places” to address coverage gaps and workforce shortages, including expanding telemedicine, improving licensing, and training more community health workers.

title: Big changes arrive July 1 for student borrowers,  including in loan repayments
byline: By Shauneen Miranda States Newsroom
description: WASHINGTON — The federal student loan system is set to see a dramatic overhaul beginning this summer, and critics warn it likely will make loans more expensive and difficult to obtain for borrowers — driving them to private lenders or altering their plans for higher education.
_full_text:
StatesnewsroomLogo

WASHINGTON — The federal student loan system is set to see a dramatic overhaul beginning this summer, and critics warn it likely will make loans more expensive and difficult to obtain for borrowers — driving them to private lenders or altering their plans for higher education.

Among the major changes are new loan limits for graduate and professional students, a restructured repayment system where new borrowers will have only two plans to choose from and the elimination of a key loan program for graduate and professional students that allowed for unlimited borrowing.

The provisions — most of which will take effect July 1 — stem from congressional Republicans’ mega tax and spending cut bill that President Donald Trump signed into law last year. 

The U.S. Department of Education finalized regulations, published May 1, that implement sweeping changes outlined in the GOP’s “big, beautiful” law. The department received more than 80,000 public comments before the rule was finalized. 

Under Secretary of Education Nicholas Kent said that “at a high level,” the reforms center on “lowering the cost of college, simplifying student loan repayment and restoring accountability to the federal student lending system,” during an April 30 call with reporters regarding the new regulations. 

The average federal student loan debt balance stands at $39,547, according to the Education Data Initiative.

As July 1 approaches, here’s a closer look at some of the biggest changes coming to the federal student loan system: 

Elimination of Grad PLUS 

The Grad PLUS program, which allowed for graduate and professional students to borrow up to the full cost of attendance, will soon be eliminated under the package and unavailable for new borrowers.

“If you are currently borrowing Grad PLUS loans, so you borrowed Grad PLUS loans before July 1, you will be allowed to continue using Grad PLUS until you finish your program, or until three years have expired, basically whichever is sooner,” said Preston Cooper, senior fellow in higher education policy at the American Enterprise Institute, a right-leaning think tank.

“Current students are grandfathered in — it will only be new graduate students, as of this fall, after July 1, who will be subject to the new loan limits,” Cooper said. 

New borrowing caps 

The package also sets forth new annual and aggregate loan limits for graduate and professional students, along with parents who take out federal student loans for dependent undergraduate students. 

Graduate student loans will be capped at $20,500 annually, with a $100,000 aggregate limit. 

Parent PLUS borrowers will have an annual cap of $20,000 and an aggregate cap of $65,000 per dependent. 

Professional student loans will have a $50,000 annual limit and an aggregate cap of $200,000. 

The programs that fall within the department’s “professional” category and are subject to that larger loan cap include: pharmacy, dentistry, veterinary medicine, chiropractic, law, medicine, optometry, osteopathic medicine, podiatry, theology and clinical psychology. 

The department clarified in a fact sheet on the finalized regulations that the “professional” student classifications “do not express a value judgment about the importance of any occupation or field” but instead serve a “loan-administration function.” 

The agency has received immense pushback from groups representing people in fields that do not fall under the department’s definition and will thus be subject to lower annual and lifetime borrowing caps. 

Incoming repayment options 

In another major shift, the regulations replace prior repayment options with two new plans — the Repayment Assistance Plan, or RAP, and the Tiered Standard plan — both of which will launch July 1.

RAP is an income-based repayment plan that “waives unpaid interest for borrowers who make on-time payments that do not fully cover accruing interest,” per the department’s fact sheet. 

Balances under the plan will also “decline with each on-time payment, as unpaid interest is fully waived and the Department then reduces principal by an amount equal to the borrower’s payment, up to $50,” per the agency. 

The Tiered Standard plan offers fixed monthly payments, ranging from a 10-year to 25-year period, depending on the outstanding principal balance of the borrower. 

‘A lot more expensive’

“The upshot is that loan repayment is going to get a lot more expensive for almost everyone, and for some people, it’s going to get significantly more expensive, and the transition is also going to be difficult for a lot of people to manage,” Michele Zampini, associate vice president for federal policy and advocacy at the Institute for College Access & Success, told States Newsroom.

Zampini, whose organization aims to advance affordability, accountability and equity in higher education, said she thinks “there will be a lot of students who will have to turn to the private loan market, who otherwise would have been able to cover their costs through the (Grad PLUS) program.”

Victoria Jackson, assistant director of higher education policy at the nonprofit policy and advocacy group EdTrust, said that with the new loan limits and “drastic cuts to aid availability” in the regulations, “you would really hope that it would come with other, more affordable and better forms of financial aid.” 

“And what they’ve done is just created this vacuum that right now can really only be filled with private loans, which are costlier and riskier for students, or students are just not going to go,” Jackson said.

Meanwhile, the Trump administration continues its efforts to eliminate the Department of Education, including through a series of interagency agreements that transfer several of its responsibilities to other departments. 

Under the most recent agreement, the Treasury Department will take over Education’s responsibility for collecting on defaulted federal student loan debt — the first step in a multiphase process toward Treasury taking on Education’s entire, roughly $1.7 trillion federal student loan portfolio.

Transition to new system

Zampini noted that, when it comes to the incoming student loan regulations, she does not have confidence in the Education Department’s “ability at this moment to successfully manage the transition without a lot of issues, as far as servicing and as far as account tracking and plan enrollment and things like that.” 

Jackson, of EdTrust, said that “by weakening the federal financial aid system, I think there’s a weakening of our higher education system and making it more difficult for low-income students, students of color and other marginalized students to access graduate education.”

She added that “people who complete those degrees tend to have more financial security in the future — they earn more over their lifetimes and, on markers of financial success and opportunity, do better.” 

“I think this is one prong of a plan of undermining our overall higher education system.”

title: Military panelists say lack of  ‘disqualifying’ evidence justifies  Wounded Knee Massacre medals
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Plastic flowers and American flags are placed atop graves at the Wounded Knee Memorial and cemetery June 30, 2024, on the Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota. Photo by Makenzie Huber, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Military panelists say lack of  ‘disqualifying’ evidence justifies  Wounded Knee Massacre medals
Plastic flowers and American flags are placed atop graves at the Wounded Knee Memorial and cemetery June 30, 2024, on the Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota. Photo by Makenzie Huber, South Dakota Searchlight 

Three military members of a panel that reviewed Medals of Honor awarded to soldiers who were at the 1890 Wounded Knee Massacre concluded there was no evidence of disqualifying conduct by the honorees, despite scholarly research to the contrary.

Those and other details are in a previously unreleased report from the panel obtained by South Dakota Searchlight. 

“While the actions of leadership were suspect, circumstances chaotic, and non-combatants tragically killed,” wrote the panel’s chairman, a retired Army lieutenant general, “three of the five panel members believe that individual soldiers distinguished themselves in action and found no disqualifying information.”

The massacre occurred on Dec. 29, 1890, near Wounded Knee Creek in southwestern South Dakota, where a large group of Lakota people camped while traveling to the Pine Ridge Agency. They were surrounded by hundreds of Army soldiers. A shot rang out while the soldiers were attempting to disarm the camp — some sources say it was the result of a struggle with an armed Lakota man — and the soldiers opened fire.

Fewer than 40 soldiers were killed (some by friendly fire, according to historians), while estimates of Lakota deaths ran from 200 to 300 or more, including men, women and children. After some of the bodies froze on the ground for several days, a military-led burial party placed them in a mass grave.

One hundred years later in 1990, Congress passed a resolution expressing “deep regret” for the massacre. But the medals awarded to soldiers have never been rescinded.

Panel’s views slow to emerge

The Department of Defense created a panel to review the medals during the Biden administration in 2024, but never announced or published the panel’s findings or recommendations. At the time, the department said about 20 soldiers had received a Medal of Honor for their actions during the massacre. Historians have said the records associated with some of the medals are incomplete or unclear.

President Donald Trump’s defense secretary, Pete Hegseth, announced in a September social media video that the medals will not be rescinded. He called the massacre a “battle” and said the soldiers “deserve those medals.” He cited the panel’s work as justification and held a copy of the panel’s report in the video, but the department did not immediately release the report.

The five-member panel included two retired Army veterans and one Army Medal of Honor recipient. Their names were redacted in most references in the report, but retired Lt. Gen. Thomas James’ name does appear in one portion of the document. 

The panel also included two Department of the Interior officials: Robert T. Anderson and Wizipan Little Elk Garriott, whose names are not redacted in the report. Garriott, a member of the Rosebud Sioux Tribe in South Dakota, told Searchlight he was not asked if his name should be redacted, “and we all operated under the assumption that our names wouldn’t be redacted.” Garriott left the department when the Biden administration ended.

‘The totality of the circumstances’

The report aligns with what Garriott previously told Searchlight shortly after Hegseth announced the medals will not be rescinded. Garriott said then that the panel’s majority military members focused narrowly on whether individual soldiers could be tied by evidence to specific misdeeds, rather than the broader question of whether any medals should be awarded for a massacre. 

Interior Department panelist Robert Anderson’s written assessment in the report argued that “actions do not occur in a context separate from the actions of the whole.” He wrote that the Army’s actions at Wounded Knee were not honorable and that awarding medals to any soldier who took part in the massacre was unmerited, regardless of any individual soldier’s role. 

Garriott wrote in the report that the massacre was “one of the most shameful moments in the nation’s history” and recommended rescinding the medals, apologizing to the Lakota nation and descendants, and creating another panel to work with Lakota people on healing. 

“People living under the banner of peace — infants, children, women, and elders — were killed indiscriminately,” he wrote. 

Garriott said this week in an interview with Searchlight that the panel was “not given nearly enough time” to complete a thorough review. The panel was created in July 2024 and was given a deadline in October of that year to file a report. 

“Only three of the five individuals took the time to go and do a thorough review of the site and to meet with descendants and survivors,” he said.

Garriott said that when the panel was created, “we were directed to look at the totality of the circumstances and the treaties,” but the review itself “did not.” 

Report findings

The report says 19 soldiers received the Medal of Honor. The panel’s retired military chairperson wrote in the report’s introduction that the review’s scope was limited to each “awardee’s individual actions during the specific engagement,” and that the panel answered two questions: whether each soldier distinguished himself, and whether each performed individual actions violating the “law of war.” The report says the panel was directed to conduct its review through the lens of standards, laws and regulations in effect when the medals were awarded.  

The three military panelists concluded that all 19 soldiers distinguished themselves in action and that none performed individual actions that violated the rules under the law of war. 

Anderson and Garriott concluded that none of the 19 soldiers distinguished themselves, and there was inadequate information to determine whether 18 of the 19 had committed individual law-of-war violations.

One of the military panelists wrote in the report that the panel had “discovered no evidence” that any of the 19 recipients were involved in the deliberate wounding or killing of noncombatants or other disqualifying conduct.

“I do not minimize the non-combatant loss of life,” the military panelist wrote. “This loss is a tragedy and rightfully outrages us. After years of service in combat zones, I know firsthand that there are often very bad actions (Law of War violations, loss of life, loss of non-combatant lives) and very positive actions (bravery, humanitarian action, acts of kindness and empathy) that occur on the same battlefield.” 

The same panelist wrote that an artificial intelligence-assisted review of more than 3,000 pages of documents “did not reveal any evidence of disqualifying behavior either.” 

Historical references to soldier conduct

A 2024 law review article by Dwight S. Mears was listed among the materials reviewed by the panel. Mears is an Army veteran with a doctorate in history.

In that article, Mears identified potential grounds for rescinding medals awarded to individual soldiers, including Paul H. Weinert and Harry L. Hawthorne, who were among the 19 ultimately reviewed by the panel.

“Weinert later attested that he continued firing his M1875 Hotchkiss mountain gun into the ravine full of commingled combatants and noncombatants even after being directed by an officer ‘to come back’ and that he ‘expected a court-martial’ for disobedience,’” Mears wrote. He added that Weinert “continued firing into the ravine until ‘everything was quiet at the other end of the line.’”

Similarly, Mears wrote that Hawthorne was an artilleryman and platoon leader at Wounded Knee who earned a Medal of Honor in part for the “effect with which he handled and served his (artillery) guns in action against hostile Sioux Indians.”

Mears wrote that Hawthorne took offense to an editorial criticizing the firing of the M1875 Hotchkiss mountain guns after resistance had ceased. 

“In his rebuttal,” Mears wrote of Hawthorne, “he admitted that the mountain guns continued firing at Natives” and the firing continued “well after ‘cease firing’ had sounded, but he claimed that this was necessary because ‘resistance had not ceased.’” 

Mears’ article did not argue that every Wounded Knee medal should automatically be rescinded. He warned against blanket revocation without review of individual conduct and wrote that some medals might survive a case-by-case review.

title: Company withdraws from controversial Black Hills exploratory drilling project
byline: By Seth Tupper Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Pe’ Sla, or Reynolds Prairie, is a high-elevation Black Hills meadow of sacred importance to Lakota people. A company that was conducting exploratory drilling in the area has withdrawn from the project. Photo by Seth Tupper, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Company withdraws from controversial Black Hills exploratory drilling project
Pe’ Sla, or Reynolds Prairie, is a high-elevation Black Hills meadow of sacred importance to Lakota people. A company that was conducting exploratory drilling in the area has withdrawn from the project. Photo by Seth Tupper, South Dakota Searchlight 

RAPID CITY — A company that’s being sued for exploratory drilling near a culturally significant site in South Dakota’s Black Hills is withdrawing from the project, according to a letter shared with project opponents.

The opponents include the Black Hills Clean Water Alliance, which posted a copy of the letter and a statement Friday on social media.

“This is a testament to the people, organizations, and tribal governments who showed unified action, determination, and courage in the face of what seemed to be overwhelming odds,” the alliance said.

The letter from Pete Lien & Sons to the U.S. Forest Service references the Rapid City-based company’s project near Pe’ Sla, also known as Reynolds Prairie, which is a high mountain meadow in the central Black Hills. 

Pe’ Sla is one of several Black Hills sites that corresponds with celestial features in traditional Lakota spirituality. Lakota people use the area, some of which is tribally owned, for prayer, ceremonies and cultural activities.  

After receiving approval from the Forest Service, Pete Lien & Sons has been drilling holes near Pe’ Sla in search of graphite, which is used in electric vehicle batteries, lubricants, pencils and other products.

Two lawsuits against the project filed by a coalition of nonprofits and 9 Native American tribes led to a hearing Monday in Rapid City, where a federal judge granted a temporary restraining order against the drilling. Meanwhile, opponents had formed a protest encampment at the project site.

In recently filed court documents, lawyers for the Forest Service said the project was already “halfway complete.” But the restraining order put the future of the project in doubt. The judge presiding over the lawsuits is scheduled to consider a longer-lasting injunction against the project later this month.

The company’s Thursday letter to the Forest Service asks for the project’s plan of operations and decision memo to be withdrawn. The letter says the company will conduct reclamation — restoration of the project area to a natural state — when it’s legally permitted by the judge who granted the restraining order. The company “does not intend” to file another plan of operations for exploratory drilling at the site, the letter says.

NDN Collective, a Rapid City-based nonprofit that advocates for Indigenous rights, is among the lawsuit plaintiffs. 

“From the land defenders who occupied two active drill pads for a week, to fighting in the courts through multiple lawsuits and a temporary restraining order, today’s win is multi-faceted and offers a blueprint for future land defense fights,” NDN said Friday in a press release.

Future fights include one scheduled for the week of May 18. The state Board of Minerals and Environment is scheduled to conduct a hearing in Hot Springs on a proposal to conduct exploratory drilling for uranium in the southern Black Hills. 

That project would be near Craven Canyon, where the rock walls are carved with Native American petroglyphs believed to be thousands of years old.

title: Belle Fourche residents flock  to open meeting to discuss possible chicken ordinance
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Belle Fourche is discussing the possibility of adding a chicken ordinance to its books. The ordinance would not prohibit, but rather formally allow, the keeping of backyard/urban flocks. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Chickens.jpg
Belle Fourche is discussing the possibility of adding a chicken ordinance to its books. The ordinance would not prohibit, but rather formally allow, the keeping of backyard/urban flocks. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

BELLE FOURCHE — The city of Belle Fourche may consider adopting an ordinance to formally allow residents to keep backyard flocks, with some possible caveats.

Those caveats are the reason members of the public flocked to city hall for a public works committee meeting on Monday, the first open discussion of a chicken ordinance in a public meeting.

“This is just a conversation, nothing is being finalized,” said Belle Fourche City Administrator Jason LaFayette.

LaFayette said city staff have been working on drafting an ordinance for more than a year. They’re now working on the sixth draft of that ordinance, and “substantial public input” will be needed before a version is ready to be reviewed by the city council, LaFayette said.

Why would Belle Fourche need a chicken ordinance?

Right now, Belle Fourche doesn’t prohibit chickens or roosters within city limits. It doesn’t expressly allow them either.

“The goal is not to take away anyone’s chickens. It’s not to limit the number of people’s chickens. It is not to create zoning regulations so that others can’t have chickens within the community,” LaFayette said. “The purpose of the draft is simply to establish guidance in an area where our current code book is largely silent.”

 Chickens 2.jpeg
As Belle Fourche city leaders draft an ordinance for city council’s consideration, they invited the public to provide input at a public works committee meeting Monday evening, pictured. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

Further, LaFayette said, city staff wanted to have an ordinance in writing that they could point to when citizens call with questions or complaints about urban flocks. The ordinance would also ask citizens with chickens to provide contact information to the code enforcement officer, so they can be contacted if their birds go missing or end up at large.

Still, some citizens spoke up on Monday with concerns about any regulation.

“I think this ordinance is a perfect example of government overreach,” Belle Fourche resident Ivy Zimmerstein said.

Alyssa Mehlhaff told the assembled committe that part of the appeal of Belle Fourche is its lack of restrictions when it comes to urban livestock.

“That is why we moved here and why we bought our house here. We were looking for houses in every other community and we bought a house here because we can have in our yard, we can have on our property, what we can take care of,” Melhaff said. “There were cheaper houses elsewhere, there were bigger houses elsewhere. I have 4 children that share a bedroom, but I love where I live.”

LaFayette said Belle Fourche doesn’t necessarily want to be more restrictive than it is right now, even if an ordinance is passed.

“Basically, we are just trying to get something in writing so that people who want to move here can see how unrestrictive Belle Fourche is,” LaFayette said.

That isn’t to say an ordinance would give residents carte blanche. As written in the fifth draft of the ordinance, which was provided to the public in the Monday meeting’s agenda packet, chickens would be allowed in back yards or side yards only — away from public areas and within designated property line setbacks.

One citizen said he felt that residents should only be required to provide written permission from neighbors to be formally allowed to keep chickens.

“I see your point. I don’t see how it is any different than a variance. The problem arises when John Doe, who has no problem, sells his property and Jane Doe moves in, and she does not like chickens,” said Belle Fourche City Councilman Vern Hintz. “We have to look into the future.”

“Chickens must be kept in an enclosure or fenced area at all times and must be secured in the coop during non-daylight hours,” the draft reads. Enclosures may be required to be “opaque” or equipped with a landscape screen and “predator proof.”

Why rule the roost, specifically?

Mehlhaff noted that her family keeps chickens, ducks, and sheep.

“Are my ducks allowed to be seen by my neighbors? Does this apply to all of them, or do they have different ordinances now? Where does that leave other animals, like my sheep, my dogs, or my cats?” Melhaff said. “To just focus on one animal is an interesting choice.”

Some of the screening regulations have already been removed in the sixth draft of the ordinance, LaFayette said. 

Still other rules might stand — including requirements that enclosures are kept “dry, neat, and clean.”

“(That) is rather ambiguous. I would like further explanation of what you mean by sanitary conditions. Is that daily cleaning or chicken boxes, I mean, are these things within reason?” Zimmerstein said. “ It is understandable that any animal needs access to fresh water, food, and adequate living conditions. You can give your chickens fresh water, and 5 minutes later, they may have tipped it over. Would we be fined for that?”

LaFayette said that the city is aiming to take a common sense approach to definitions and enforcement.

“This draft number 6, which you don’t have (completed), we got rid of the inspections. We are not going to come check your water. I understand all of that. Now, if your neighbors complain that you never feed your chickens, that would be the difference,” Lafayette said.

Cock-a-doodle-don’t?

It isn’t uncommon for cities that allow chickens to place a prohibition on roosters. Belle Fourche’s draft ordinance considers keeping roosters out of city limits.

“The most common issue is their wake-up call in the morning. Most cities don’t allow roosters. In fact, every ordinance that I have reviewed for a chicken ordinance doesn’t allow roosters,” LaFayette said.

Speaking at Monday’s meeting, residents said that roosters are necessary to protect hens and to fertilize eggs.

Melhaff pointed out that the city already has definitions of nuisance sounds and nuisance smells on the books.

“So this (proposed) ordinance addresses chickens. Presently, the ordinance addresses all animals, and it covers animals being a nuisance with both noise and smells,” Melhaff said. “I’m not sure why we have to specifically take a look at roosters. Presently, you can have them as long as they are not a nuisance. I’ve had them in the past until they get loud.”

Man arrested after trying to access Rapid City plane cockpit
Courtesy photo 

RAPID CITY — An Illinois man was arrested Saturday night after police say he attempted to gain entry into the cockpit of a flight inbound to Rapid City Regional Airport.

According to the Rapid City Police Department, around 9:15 p.m., police were advised of the incident. Upon their arrival at the airport, they made contact with airline staff at the gate. Police boarded the aircraft, and airline staff identified the suspect as Krish Mishra, 30, of Rosemont, Ill.

Airline staff told police Mishra had refused multiple requests to stay in his seat, even after the plane landed. He was escorted off the aircraft by police and placed under arrest for disorderly conduct before being transported to the Pennington County Jail. 

The report for the incident has been forwarded to the Department of Homeland Security for further investigation.

title: Niesent resigns from Spearfish School Board
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Ryan Niesent, right, the Spearfish School Board president, submitted his resignation Monday effective June 9. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Niesent Resigns.jpg
Ryan Niesent, right, the Spearfish School Board president, submitted his resignation Monday effective June 9. Pioneer file photo 

SPEARFISH — The Spearfish School Board president submitted his resignation Monday evening, effective June 9.

Ryan Niesent, who has served on the board since 2018, said he resigned following a promotion at his job, which will limit the time he has available to serve on the board.

“After careful consideration, I believe it is in the best interest of the district for me to step aside so that the position can be filled by someone able to fully dedicate the time and attention this important role demands, Niesent said in a prepared statement.

Niesent was promoted to chief operating officer of BankWest.

Niesent was first appointed to the board in 2018, filling a vacant seat. It was after years of the board discussing the creation of a career and technical education center that Niesent decided to join.

“I wanted the school to have a CTE center. It’s something that has been talked about a lot, you know, for years, but it just never happened,” he told the Pioneer. “And that was one of my big drivers, was to get on the board and see if I could help make that happen.”

The CTE center opened at the high school with the start of the 2024-2025 school year.

“I don’t even think we fully understand how important it is,” Niesent said of the facility. “You know, for years, we saw a decline in those types of careers, and so being able to reach out to kids who had interest, or even if they didn’t know they had interest, exposing them to those different fields, I think is going to be a really great benefit for not just our school district, but even for the surrounding communities. Hopefully some of those kids stick around here and go into those professions.”

The center houses classes for cooking, medical care, welding, wood working, automotive, computer sciences, and more.

Niesent was re-elected 3 times to the board.

The district is accepting applications for those interested in filling the seat. The application period will close June 3, with interviews being conducted June 8, the day of the regularly scheduled June meeting.

“It has been an honor to serve the Spearfish community in this capacity, Niesent said. “I am grateful for the opportunity to work alongside the dedicated board members and district leadership who are truly committed to student success.”

“I think the Spearfish School District does a great job for our kids,” he added. “I think you’ve got a lot of dedicated professionals who really care about the kids in our community and our future. And it was really nice to be part of that.”

title: Sturgis reports nearly $9.2M in cash accounts
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Sturgis Finance Officer Ann Bertolotto has been working to reconcile Sturgis city accounts from 2024 and 2025. Currently, she said the city has about $9 million across all of its financial accounts, with the majority of money in the city’s capital improvements coffers. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
Sturgis reports nearly $9.2M in cash accounts
Sturgis Finance Officer Ann Bertolotto has been working to reconcile Sturgis city accounts from 2024 and 2025. Currently, she said the city has about $9 million across all of its financial accounts, with the majority of money in the city’s capital improvements coffers. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

STURGIS — The city of Sturgis has seen an increase in cash balances over the last 3 years, and currently holds cash value across all accounts of nearly $9.2 million. 

Ann Bertolotto, Sturgis city finance officer told members of the city council that over the past 3 years, the city of Sturgis has seen a steady increase in its checking and savings accounts, for periods ending on April 30. In April 2023, she said those cash balances were $223,691 and in April 2024 they were at $683,381. By April 2025 those totals jumped to $4.8 million, and by April 2026 the total money in Sturgis checking and savings accounts was $7.6 million. 

Bertolotto said currently the total cash across all city accounts — including petty cash, ATM money, cash change, and more, is just under $9.2 million. 

The report was good news for a council that has struggled to build a budget for the last few years. In 2024, an audit by Ketel Thorstensen revealed that city financial accounts were not reconciled in 2023 and 2024. Since then Bertolotto and her staff have been working to update the city’s finances. It’s a project Bertolotto continues to work on, as she is still conducting audits for 2024. After that, she will move on to 2025 financials. Additionally, before the city starts budget talks in August or September, she plans to examine the city’s total debt, to give a complete picture of the city’s financial position. 

Facing economic uncertainty after Ketel Thorstensen’s discovery about the 2023 and 2024 accounts, the city of Sturgis 2025 budget of just more than $10 million cut $1.24 million in spending, including terminating 5 full time employees, 2 of which came from the city’s Rally and events department. The 2026 budget of $10.3 million removed 4 positions, and for the first time in many years it did not allocate funds to the Sturgis Ambulance Service. 

The Sturgis Ambulance Service operates as an enterprise fund in the budget, but in 2025 the city allocated $160,000 out of the general fund for the service. For 2026, former Mayor Kevin Forrester said he wanted to see the service be self-sufficient. 

Shortly after that, then-newly hired Sturgis Ambulance Service Director Aden Shillig contracted with a third-party billing firm to collect bills, significantly increasing ambulance income. Bertolotto told the Pioneer the changes in ambulance billing are part of the reason for the city’s change in financial position. 

On Bertolotto said the most notable growth in city cash accounts is in the capital improvements fund, which is supported with a dedicated .9% general sales tax allocation. In 2024, the city of Sturgis paused many capital improvements projects while it figured out its finances. In the meantime, she said those funds from sales tax have continued to accumulate. 

“The capital improvement, that looks good because we haven’t been spending it,” Bertolotto told the Pioneer. “But then we still put that money in every month from the sales tax. The increase in the city’s cash position is primarily the result of deliberate fiscal management actions implemented beginning in mid-2024. These actions include reductions in personnel related expenditures, deferral of capital improvement projects, and delaying or limiting other budgeted expenses.” 

Bertolotto said the city’s cash position gives her more confidence for talks about the 2027 budget, and it could mean the city can finish some projects it had started before capital improvement cuts were made.

title: Lead approves employee residency changes
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: LEAD — The Lead City Commission recently unanimously approved changes to its employee residency policy, but failed to approve changes to its vacation policy that were brought in an effort to boost recruiting efforts.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

LEAD — The Lead City Commission recently unanimously approved changes to its employee residency policy, but failed to approve changes to its vacation policy that were brought in an effort to boost recruiting efforts. 

The new residency policy requires city employees to live within 13 miles of Lead City Hall, which will allow city employees to live in parts of Spearfish, Sturgis, and Whitewood. The policy requires employees to perform their duties regardless of their residence location. It also requires city department heads to live within Lead city limits.

Previously, the policy required city employees to live within the boundaries of the Lead-Deadwood School District, which nearly touches the Wyoming border and stretches past Nemo, but prohibited employees from living in Spearfish, Sturgis, or Whitewood, because those communities are part of a different school district. By changing the policy, Lead city officials hope to recruit more employees who can take advantage of some housing opportunities in those communities. 

Commissioners also considered a vacation policy that would have allowed employees to accrue 80 hours of vacation for service that lasted 1-4 years; 120 hours for 5-9 years; 160 hours for 10-15 years; and 160 with one week of pay after 15-19 years of service. Employees who work for the city for 20 or more years would receive 160 hours of vacation plus 2 weeks of pay. 

The current policy allows employees to receive 80 hours of vacation for 1-6 years of service; 120 hours for 7-12 years, 160 hours for 13-20 years; and 160 hours plus one week of pay for employees who work for more than 20 years. 

The commission voted to take the vacation policy off the table for consideration. However, the issue died for lack of a motion to approve the changes. 

Commissioner Rob Carr recused himself from votes regarding the employee policies, as his wife, Lyubasha Carr, works for the Hearst Library.
