title: Lawrence County Commission candidates
description: Voters in Lawrence County will head to the polls June 2 to vote on vacant Lawrence County Commission seats. 5 people are running for 3 open positions which is a 4-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.
_full_text:
LawrenceCoCommissionComposite.jpg

Voters in Lawrence County will head to the polls June 2 to vote on vacant Lawrence County Commission seats. 5 people are running for 3 open positions which is a 4-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.

Timm Comer

 Comer, Tim.jpg
Tim Comer 

Name and what you do for a living?

Timm Comer, I joined Dakota Gold Corp in Lead as Environmental Director in May 2022.  I have over three decades of experience in environmental permitting, policy development, and compliance program implementation at operations with effective operation, reclamation, and closure focus.  My responsibilities include managing professional staff, developing and implementing new programs, including analyses of resource needs and estimating program costs.  I previously held environmental management positions with Sanford Underground Research Facility, Neiman Enterprises, Cloud Peak Energy Resources, AngloGold Ashanti, Meridian Gold and Wharf Resources. I hold BS degree in Mathematics from BHSU and graduated from Lead High School.

What motivated you to run for this office?

I’m a proud 6th-generation resident of Lawrence County, currently living in Spearfish with my wife. After growing up in Lead-Deadwood, I returned to be close to family and to give back to the community that shaped me. My time on the Planning & Zoning Board has given me valuable insights into local issues. As your County Commissioner, I promise to listen to your concerns and work towards solutions that benefit everyone in Lawrence County. I’m dedicated to problem-solving and fostering meaningful discussions.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

My background in mathematics shapes my analytical approach to addressing business challenges, particularly in estimating costs for existing and proposed programs. It’s crucial to assess not only the community impacts of new initiatives but also their implications for resources and funding. In Lawrence County, this involves determining whether new resources are required or if we will rely on existing ones, and whether funding will come from tax increases or cuts in other budgeted areas.  Let’s all not forget the 2026 Republican platform includes promoting economic growth, not recession; limited government, not growing it; and advocating for lower taxes, not higher.

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I was appointed to Planning & Zoning Board on January 3, 2023.  Appointed to the Board of County Commissions on February 20, 2026, that included appointments to Board of Adjustment, Board of Equalization, Forest Multiple Use Coalition Board, Butte/Lawrence Fair Board, Planning & Zoning Board (as alternate), Black Hills Council of Local Governments (as alternate), and Weed Board (as alternate).

Leadership positions in private sector are relevant. Leadership in that sector has value and can provide different perspectives.  I was one-of-two individuals asked to be first-time private sector participant in Advanced Leadership Training with the Regional Institute for Health and Environmental.

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I attended all four Board of County Commissioners meetings after my appointment on February 20, 2026, and participated in all ten Planning & Zoning Board meetings until my reappointment as alternate due to my new role.  I was appointed to the Planning & Zoning Board on January 3, 2023, where I attended all meetings (one virtually). After leaving the P&Z Board, I still review all available Meeting Minutes. I attended a couple Board of County Commissioners meetings in person before my appointment. I reviewed many of the Meeting Minutes from those meetings.

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Local newspapers are vital to society as they provide important information that impacts residents’ lives. They cover local government actions, community events, and human-interest stories, thereby fostering civic engagement and accountability. Furthermore, they contribute to the community’s identity by showcasing its unique culture. Personally, I review the headlines from the Black Hills Pioneer online almost daily, reading articles that enhance my understanding of the community, particularly the Opinion section.

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in Lawrence County?

(A) Understanding approved land uses by zoning types is essential for prospective land purchasers, as awareness of surrounding properties is crucial. Property owners have rights concerning the approved uses of their land, emphasizing the sentiment of “Good Fences Make Good Neighbors,” a concept articulated in Robert Frost’s poem “Mending Walls.” Additionally, it is vital to know the difference between factual information from misinformation circulating within communities. Those wishing to address potential issues must thoroughly understand them instead of relying on hearsay.

(B) County funding challenges faced today include the result of rising operational costs, and state-level policy changes that could impact local tax bases and funding allocations. 

How do you intend to solve these issues?

(A) Decisions in governance must be grounded in existing state laws and county ordinances, with consideration given to the perspectives of both opponents and supporters of the issue at hand. Adherence to legal requirements often dictates the outcomes. These constraints limit the range of possible decisions to those that comply with established legal frameworks.

(B) Promoting a variety of funding sources are key, including local taxes and state and federal grants. Key local revenues stem from building permit fees, service charges, highway fees, and other income like interest earnings. State revenues include general fund allocations, vehicle and license fees, as well as gaming revenue from Deadwood, which supports historical preservation.

What do you believe is working for the county, and how will you retain that progression?

Lawrence County offers a wonderful place for residents and visitors, makes for a great place to call home. With low cost of living and strong sense of community, the county boasts high homeownership rate, access to stunning outdoor recreational opportunities, and well-regarded education system. The area’s natural beauty, characterized by its creeks, lakes and the Black Hills, invites countless outdoor activities. That coupled with a community that reflects conservative principles, it’s no wonder Lawrence County is known for high quality of life and a desirable location to live and visit.  Decisions by actual conservative leaders are working, why change that?

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

Government transparency is essential for holding officials accountable, ensuring that citizens can access public records; spending decisions; and policy discussions. This openness is supported by several federal laws, including the Freedom of Information Act, which allows voters to access and engage with their government’s actions.  In alignment with this commitment to transparency, I have offered a personal handout about me and my professional resume to the residents of Lawrence County, reflecting my dedication to transparency and community involvement.  I am open about what value I bring to the residents of Lawrence County if elected, that others do not have.

What else do you want people to know about you?

I have heard concerns about water and air.  I am certified as Senior/Lead Auditor in Environmental Management Systems (EMS) through Quality Management International, Inc. EMS provides structured approaches for organizations to manage their environmental responsibilities, enhance performance, and minimize environmental impact. It emphasizes continuous improvement through proactive identification of all environmental risks, with a focus on transparency and accountability.  Implementation of EMS follows the Plan-Do-Check-Act cycle. I have developed/managed two certified EMSs at facilities and overseen the system at a third.  In my systems, I also account for both negative and positive activities, thereby enhancing the system’s overall effectiveness.

How best should the county regulate the drastic increase of OHV traffic?

Increasing popularity of OHVs, particularly UTVs, places significant pressure on environmental resources of the Black Hills.  Addressing this challenge may require multifaceted strategy, involving education, enforcement, financial measures, and long-term planning.  Considerations may include standardizing fees to manage costs, funding educational programs to promote responsible OHV usage, and establishing collaborative stewardship agreements with OHV organizations.  Strategy should aim to align local regulations with Forest Plan, facilitate stakeholder meetings for feedback, monitor environmental data, and conduct annual reviews of existing regulations to ensure effectiveness.  This approach may balance increase of use OHVs/UTVS with needed safeguards of environmental resources of the Black Hills.

Should sitting county commissioners also function as the board of adjustment, or should there be changes in the member make-up of the board of adjustment? Why or why not?

Yes. It is important that Board of Adjustment (BOA) represents those actually elected by and accountable to the public.  On 11/26/2024, an ordinance was enacted to align County Ordinance and South Dakota Laws 11-2-53 and 11-2-60.  It doesn’t create a “new Board”.  Amendments made to state statutes in 2015 empower BOA to approve or deny conditional use permits, with three options for appointing its members: the County Commissioners, the Planning & Zoning Board, or an independent Board.  Review confirms from 01/06/2015-01/13/2026, each year at first hearing of County Commissions, acting County Commissions have designated each elected County Commissioner as a member of BOA, because they are the sole elected officials serving the County.

Pine beetles are increasing in the forests of Lawrence County. How should the county address the issue so that they don’t grow to epidemic levels?

In 2014, Lawrence County began addressing a pine beetle outbreak in the Lawrence County portion of the Black Hills through forest management, timber sales, and collaboration.  A Memorandum of Understanding with the U.S. Forest Service was established to support comprehensive treatment across the forest, aimed at reducing mature tree density and lowering the risk of future outbreaks. Funding came from Lawrence County and other local entities, as well as staff from the Invasive Species Department.  To ensure ongoing success, active participation from private landowners is crucial, along with careful planning of cooperative agreements, funding, and staffing for future initiatives.

As more people are developing rural parts of Lawrence County, in areas such as Maitland Road, and in areas adjacent to paved access points, should the county allocate more funding to pave those roads?

Funding debate for paving rural roads in Lawrence County highlights the tension between infrastructure costs and residential development, particularly in expanding areas like Maitland Road. With the county managing about 322 miles of roads with only about 98 miles paved, the focus is on prioritizing areas identified in 2024 Master Transportation Plan. Improved roads can accelerate development, potentially outpacing capacity of essential rural services. If additional funds are approved, focus will likely be on “Collector Roads” that link significant residential areas to main highways, rather than on individual residential streets, which developers or homeowners’ associations are often expected to manage.

What should the county do to monitor rising levels of OHV vehicles and the subsequent damage to trails in the county?

To manage OHV activities in Lawrence County effectively, a comprehensive monitoring framework is necessary. This system should focus on data collection, enforcement visibility, and environmental monitoring to assess the impact of increasing OHV use and trail damage. Positioned within a prominent OHV region of the Black Hills, Lawrence County is confronted with resource and funding challenges due to extensive motorized roads and trails designated for OHV use in the nearby National Forest. As indicated, it is imperative to evaluate both the community impacts of proposed initiatives and their associated resource and funding implications to the County.  Funding option could be similar to non-resident hunting license for deer ($400) vs. residential ($50).

Mike Davies

 Davies, Mike.jpg
Mike Davies 

Name and what you do for a living?

My name is Dr. Mike Davies.  I am retired after working 36 years as an Internal Medicine Physician and Physician Executive for Veterans in the Department of Veterans Affairs.  Currently, my wife and I manage a small ranch in eastern Lawrence County.  I also work part time as a consultant for Federal Business through our Davies Consulting, LLC.

What motivated you to run for this office?

My motivation to run for office stemmed from learning about land use issues in Lawrence County, and the Piedmont limestone mining project.  The more I learned about Conditional Use Permits (CUPs) and how land use decisions are made within the Lawrence County commission, the more I became interested in contributing to future leadership.  Additionally, I believe there is a need to strongly advocate for competing issues in our county.  These include environmental concerns, water conservation, population growth, and the impact on our natural resources. 

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

I want our constituents to know my life experience includes living and raising a family here in rural Lawrence County for nearly 40 years.  We interacted with the county’s many services as citizens including roads, libraries, building permits, 4-H, and paying taxes.  My career experiences in the Department of Veterans Affairs locally as a physician and nationally as a physician leader taught me a lot about listening, communication and leadership skills. Over the years, I held 12 highly responsible leadership positions implementing change in the largest healthcare system in the US.  I believe many of these skills are applicable to the county commission.

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

While not elected to prior public office, I have extensive experience in leadership, successfully leading change in a large and very public organization. I have always been focused on how to better engage, listen and communicate with diverse public and private stakeholders to achieve positive outcomes. During retirement, I have enjoyed working as a medical volunteer for the Red Cross, Habitat for Humanity, and teaching for the Sanford School of Medicine. These experiences should equip me to help lead our county during this critical time in shaping our future. 

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I have attended several Lawrence and Meade County commission meetings, along with city council meetings in Spearfish, Sturgis, and Piedmont.  I also traveled to Pierre to attend legislative committee meetings on three bills during the last session.

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Yes, of course!  Local newspapers have always played an important role in our democracy locally and nationally.  Local newspapers reach thousands of people in our communities, contain important local news, and communicate information about many local events.  We read the paper closely and clip out articles of interest for future reference. We especially look for pictures of the grandchildren! 

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in Lawrence County?

First, restore trust in our elected officials.  From my conversations within the county, there is widespread frustration about the current county commissioners acting as the Board of Adjustment.  Under this governance structure, the Board of Adjustment has removed the right of our county constituents to petition their own local government decisions. By restoring trust between our commissioners and citizens, we can eliminate or better manage conflicts.  I also strongly advocate for lowering property taxes, protecting our air, water, and land, in addition to proactively managing our mining future.  We must remember that tourism is our number one economic driver, and we must protect the resources attractive to visitors.  

How do you intend to solve these issues?

The commission needs new leadership and a more citizen friendly environment. I would advocate for 1) an independent group to comprise the Board of Adjustment and 2) review or create clear strategic direction and goals. We need a robust community discussion about sustaining our natural resources, tourism and bolstering recreation.  The discussion should include support for mines and gravel pits.  We should review the budget with an eye toward improvement opportunities and consolidation of services where it makes sense.  

What do you believe is working for the county, and how will you retain that progression?

The Lawrence County web site is very useful and user friendly.  Our roads and bridges are great.  The new public safety facilities should serve citizens for many generations.  We seem to have productive and satisfied county employees.  Our fire departments have wonderful equipment and response times.  We can retain this positive progress by standardizing and documenting strong policies, procedures, job descriptions and training.  Our county budgets should support these successful operational practices, while continually looking for opportunities to improve them.  

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

Transparency means practicing openness, honesty, and accountability to make understandable information available to constituents.  Along with the county website, an important tool for transparency is the newspaper reporting. It seems to me the county commission should hold periodic public forums outside of meetings to communicate their thinking and hear ideas and concerns from our constituents. Additionally, if elected, I will continue to ask for your feedback, advice and ideas.  

What else do you want people to know about you?

I am honest and transparent.  My wife and I hope to spend our retirement years in Lawrence County.  We enjoy horseback riding and hiking on the numerous trails in Lawrence County.  You can also find me working in my shop on John Deere equipment or wood projects.  

How best should the county regulate the drastic increase of OHV traffic?

Over the years, many of us have known friends or neighbors killed or seriously hurt by Off-Highway Vehicles (OHV).  I also have seen first-hand the damage these vehicles can cause to the ground, serious subsequent erosion and the harassment of wildlife.  While I would need to learn more about Lawrence County’s specific issues and the county budget (if any) that supports damaged roads and property, I suspect we need to clearly designate legitimate OHV trails, safety rules, and establish meaningful enforcement.  

Should sitting county commissioners also function as the board of adjustment, or should there be changes in the member make-up of the board of adjustment? Why or why not?

No. Sitting commissioners should NOT function as the Board of Adjustment. Yes, there should be changes in the make-up of the Board of Adjustment members. I believe constituents have lost trust with the commission on this issue.  While it is legal for the commissioners to function as the Board of Adjustment, changing this form of governance would help in regaining the public’s trust with the commission.  

Pine beetles are increasing in the forests of Lawrence County. How should the county address the issue so that they don’t grow to epidemic levels?

As private landowners with forest land, we had to learn to identify infected trees and proactively manage them to prevent beetles from spreading.  Education helped us get started, and education would help any inexperienced landowner.  Long term management of forests includes periodic logging to keep trees healthy and resist beetle infestation.  Close monitoring of the specific areas where the beetle population is growing should include a response from private, county and federal landowners.  Speed to response is important.  I suspect a serious outbreak would require extra county and/or state resources.

As more people are developing rural parts of Lawrence County, in areas such as Maitland Road, and in areas adjacent to paved access points, should the county allocate more funding to pave those roads?

Personally, I think everyone loves a paved road.  Lawrence County has allowed many developments to spring up in rural areas where there are gravel roads.  The decision to pave a road is very costly.  Since the county contracts out the maintenance of paved roads, more contract dollars are necessary to maintain these roads in the future. Therefore, I would favor reviewing paving requests, traffic counts, financial impact, and expert recommendations in considering how to proceed.  

What should the county do to monitor rising levels of OHV vehicles and the subsequent damage to trails in the county?

Many visitors come here to enjoy Off-Highway Vehicle (OHV) trails. Best practices to manage trails include education, clear signage, enforcement, and trail maintenance. While I look forward to learning more about this issue, I do hear concerns about noise, traffic, and erosion from citizens.  The county also has trails that serve hikers, mountain bikers, horseback riders and cross-country skiers.  Many of these citizens volunteer numerous hours in trail maintenance and development.  That said, if elected, I am interested in helping to address these issues in the future.

Brandon Flanagan

 Flanagan, Brandon.jpg
Brandon Flanagan 

Name and what you do for a living? 

Brandon Flanagan

I own Flanagan’s Irish Pub in Spearfish.  I am also a current County Commissioner and I have a small music business.

What motivated you to run for this office?

I have been around the County Courthouse since I was a kid growing up in Lead when my mother was Auditor.  I was taught that service to community is an important part of living in that community.  I believe we live in a unique area and wish to continue preserving and fostering this by representing Lawrence County.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

I have been involved in County government for many years now.  I know the budget process and have seen our County grow and evolve over time.  I have experienced and worked through several issues over the years including COVID, pine beetle infestation and the building of the new Public Safety and Services Center, and I will continue to work on future problems if re-elected.

    

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I have been Chairman and Vice Chairman of the Lawrence County Commission several times.  I sat on the Planning and Zoning Board and was the P&Z Director for about 3 ½ years.  I have been on numerous boards over the years including, the Lawrence County Revolving Loan Fund Board, the Lawrence County Housing Board, Spearfish Economic Development Board, Teen Court, DC Booth Hatchery Board, Black Hills Council of Local Governments and several others.

    

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I have attended all County Commission meetings in the last year either in person or online, except possibly one, as well as attending the meetings for other boards I currently serve on.

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Local newspapers are an important source for information on local events.  i feel too often these days people are getting their “news” from social media rather than reputable, impartial news sources.  It is easy these days for someone with a computer or smartphone and an axe to grind to find a forum where opinions and speculation can be sold as factual information.  Our local newspaper takes the time to research more than just one person’s perspective on a topic.  Local newspapers care about the stories they tell and the people that read them because they are part of the community.

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in Lawrence County?

Lawrence County is a very diverse county.  We have Education, Healthcare, Tourism, Timber, Gaming  and numerous other “industries” employing thousands and serving tens of thousands more.  While the challenges change somewhat from year to year, the biggest and most consistent issues revolve around property taxes, budgeting for the various county offices and services, and growth and development, which can involve working on the relationships between the county/cities’ officials and staff.  We are all residents of Lawrence County.

How do you intend to solve these issues?

If there were simple ways to solve these problems they would no longer be problems.  We work diligently on the county budget every year to provide the best services to the taxpayer we can as cost effectively as we can.  We do not pave roads or hire employees unnecessarily.  Lawrence County Department Heads work diligently with the commissioners to try to get the citizens of the county the best bang for their buck. It is important to have an understanding of where we have been to find the path to where we want to be. 

What do you believe is working for the county, and how will you retain that progression?

Effective communication within the county departments and with the commission is essential. We all work together to help keep services effective and efficient.  This helps to save tax dollars in the long run.

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

Transparency in Government with respect to the County Commission means that you make decisions based on not only testimony of parties involved, but also the laws that govern those decisions.  We must disclose communications with people involved with proposals or the opponents of such, and possible conflicts of interest.  Decisions need to be made in open meetings for the public to see.

What else do you want people to know about you?

I have been actively involved in Lawrence County government on and off since 2002, which makes me the most experienced Candidate for Lawrence County Commissioner.  I was born and raised here - graduated from Lead High School and attended several semesters at Black Hills State.  I have been a small business owner and worked here in several industries over the last 30 plus years.  I am Lawrence County through and through and keep an open mind to ideas and suggestions on how to maintain the integrity and history of our county, and look at ways to improve and grow our county.

How best should the county regulate the drastic increase of OHV traffic?

“OHV” or Off Highway Vehicles are regulated by the Laws of South Dakota.  When OHVs, ATVs, or other motorized vehicles are used in Lawrence County they are subject to those laws that apply to any motorized vehicle.  The county is only allowed to regulate those vehicles on public roads and highways.  Drivers must be licensed and the vehicle must be licensed or be permitted.  

Should sitting county commissioners also function as the board of adjustment, or should there be changes in the member make-up of the board of adjustment? Why or why not?

I believe the Board of Adjustment could be any mix of elected and non-elected people.  I believe that there should be elected officials on the Board for accountability and certainly there could be members of the public as well.  State Law allows for the Board of Adjustment to be the County Commission, The Planning and Zoning Board, a separate Board altogether, or a combination of these.

Pine beetles are increasing in the forests of Lawrence County. How should the county address the issue so that they don’t grow to epidemic levels?

The County should continue to work with State and Forest Service Officials to monitor forest health and potential Pine Beetle increases.  We, along with the saw mills, should also continue to work with and educate the public on programs available for tree thinning and bug mitigation.

As more people are developing rural parts of Lawrence County, in areas such as Maitland Road, and in areas adjacent to paved access points, should the county allocate more funding to pave those roads?

Subdivisions are required to build and maintain their roads by HOA or preferably Road Districts.

Subdivisions in the National Forest are often serviced by Forest Service Roads, or roads that are sometimes a mix of jurisdictions. In those instances, it is important to know who the homeowners need to deal with.  In areas where development occurs off county roads, things like terrain and safety should be paramount, also the expense to improve such roads so they might meet design standards of an improved road.  

Paving a road is a huge expense.  Design requirements for safety can be cost prohibitive.  We try to use tax dollars in the most effective and efficient way, for the benefit of the entire County.

What should the county do to monitor rising levels of OHV vehicles and the subsequent damage to trails in the county?

At this point the County does not have anything to do with the OHV Trail System in Lawrence County and the Black Hills except where it has to utilize a county road to get from one trail to another. They are primarily on Private and Federal land. As stated earlier, the County can only enforce motor vehicle laws on county roads and highways.  

Robert Haiwick

 Haiwick, Robert.jpg
Robert Haiwick 

Name and what you do for a living? 

Robert D. Haiwick – Automatic transmission repair

What motivated you to run for this office?

I have a passion for the reservation of the beautiful Black Hills and the availability and quality of our water & air.  I will have a voice for all citizens in decisions that require a more balanced approach to the dynamic tension between responsible development and the careful stewardship of our Black Hills and our County.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

I am a fiscal conservative and, as I have run my successful small business for the last 30 years, I will give great attention to why, how and where we spend citizen tax dollars

In my business, I must listen carefully to my customers.  The citizens of this county are the customers of this commission and commission must listen to its customers much better than they have.  I will bring the transparency and ear to the people of the county.  

I will bring a new, fresh, unbiased and open perspective to the issues impacting the citizens and the county which is needed.      

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

While maybe this a fair question, it has little to do with how one can lead the County.  I have been a member of the Whitewood Rural Fire Protection District for over 12 years.  I have also been on the Lutheran Church Council board for 4 years.  

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I have attended at least twelve meetings.  We meet once a month for the Whitewood Fire Protection District.  

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

I have always believed that a fair and unbiased reporting through the newspaper is a critical tool to inform readers of the social, political, and important issues facing the community.  Newspapers are probably even more helpful in smaller communities like our county.  

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in Lawrence County?

Better balance of the competing desire for development and preservation of our uniquely beautiful Black Hills, its trails, rivers, valley and prairies along with the long view for quality of our precious and limited water and air all as envisioned in the County’s Comprehensive Plan.  

Better collaboration between the County and it’s cities and the National Forest Service.  

Fiscal conservative approach to our county budget, and property tax relief.  I have said before, whatever we can do to equitably reduce property taxes must pursued.  

How do you intend to solve these issues?    

Collaboration and intentional communication with all stakeholders in reaching solutions.    

Seeking the immense expertise that ow exists among our citizens, pulling them together from time to time for discussions and solutions.  The commission, regardless of who is on it, cannot hold all the answers which now seems to be the culture of the commission.  

Creativity and transparency must be among our primary tools in approaching all of our issues.  Rigidity and hiding behind state statues would not be my approach to solutions which each current commission member has said publicly.  

What do you believe is working for the county, and how will you retain that progression?

Responsible growth is working for the county.  I believe that we can retain progression with good leadership.  

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

In my opinion, we should have an open book policy.  

Invite citizens into conversations, be intentional and schedule open town hall meetings to engage in dialogue.  

Revise commission meeting agendas to allow for real time citizen input during the discussion on agenda items, not at the end on the way out the door as it is now.  

When I vote on an item, I will tell the community at the time of my vote WHY I am voting yes or no on an issue.  5-0 votes without any substantive discussion seems to be the order of the day at commission meetings.  

What else do you want people to know about you?

I am a hardworking, open-minded candidate an would be humbled by serving you as your County Commissioner.  

How best should the county regulate the drastic increase of OHV traffic?

I would expect the forest service has a stronger hand in regulating this traffic than the County.  But what I will tell you is that the County must be involved and partner with the Forest Service in addressing this issue.  I have witnessed the growth of this traffic.  In 2022, the Forest Service issued 30,000 permits for these types of vehicles.  The other issue is not just volume of this traffic, but the size and speed of the vehicles.   There is room for this recreational activity, but I believe it must have guidelines in order to preserve the beauty and stability of our Hills.  

Should sitting county commissioners also function as the board of adjustment, or should there be changes in the member make-up of the board of adjustment? Why or why not?

This is a very big issue.  The current commission adopted the BOA and put themselves on it right after the citizens, through an initiative petition, successfully overturned a gravel permit approved by the Commission.  To challenge BOA decisions, citizens must now sue the County in court.  Citizens are barred from using the constitutional right to petition their government to challenge land use conditional use permits.  

So now, we have 2 commissioners also sitting on the county zoning commission, who also sit on the BOA, which is the appeal body of decisions from that commission.  Not to mention, that immediate family members also sit on the zoning commission. 

Pine beetles are increasing in the forests of Lawrence County. How should the county address the issue so that they don’t grow to epidemic levels?

I would expect close collaboration with the Forest Service, which is likely the government entity to manage federal forests in the Hills.  I would expect that there are focus groups with stakeholders and experts who are knowledgeable about this issue.  Perhaps we would also involve our elected federal senators and representatives.  

As more people are developing rural parts of Lawrence County, in areas such as Maitland Road, and in areas adjacent to paved access points, should the county allocate more funding to pave those roads?

Yes

What should the county do to monitor rising levels of OHV vehicles and the subsequent damage to trails in the county?

The county should work closely with the Forest Service to monitor trail usage.

Eric Jennings

 Jennings, Eric.jpg
Eric Jennings 

Name and what you do for a living? 

I am Eric Jennings, after graduating from Spearfish High School and South Dakota State University and teaching Vocational Agriculture for two years at Lennox, SD, my wife Michelle and I returned to my family’s beef cattle ranch, which we have operated since 1989. We live northwest of Spearfish and have pasture and timber land near O’Neill Pass. 

What motivated you to run for this office?

 I have spent most of my life in Lawrence County and feel I know and understand the county very well. During my three years in office, I have learned a lot about being a commissioner and have developed many positive relationships that enable me to be a better commissioner. I also want to see through some projects and ideas that we have started and serve another 4 years to see them to fruition.  

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

As a commissioner, any decision made is not about what I want to do, but about what is best for the county and its citizens. Good decision-making for the county involves thorough research of the items that come before the commission and making objective decisions based on facts. It’s also recognizing the importance of being involved in the community and networking to find the best pathways to solutions for the challenges we face. With my leadership experience and business background, I feel I am qualified to continue in this position.

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I am currently President of the Spearfish Rural Fire Protection District, 1st vice president of the SD Association of County Commissioners, Vice-Chair of the Ag and Food Policy committee of the National Cattlemen’s Beef Association, Vice President of the Society of BH Pioneers, Treasurer of the Cedar Lodge #124 AF&AM, serve on the Board of Directors of the SD Historical Society Foundation, Past involvements are serving on the Board of Directors of SD Agricultural and Rural Leadership Foundation, Past President of SD Cattlemen’s Association, past President of Northern Hills Sources of Support, past president of the Spearfish Livestock Association

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

In the past year I have been present at all but one commission meeting.  I missed the first July meeting due to another position I hold.  The other commissioners and county staff accommodated me by moving the first budget discussion to the last June meeting instead of the traditional first July meeting so I could be involved in that process.  I also attended and presided over three Spearfish Rural Fire Protection District meetings.   

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Our founding fathers recognized the need for free press to report the action taken by our government and to provide transparency and hold our elected officials accountable in their decisions.  This is another example of the wisdom they had when our country was formed.  It continues to be important to have an unbiased source of information to keep the local citizens informed.     

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in Lawrence County?

Property tax

Land Use 

Public land management

How do you intend to solve these issues?

The only true method we have to address property tax is being mindful of the budget and spending tax dollars wisely.  SB96 would provide for some property tax relief, but it is only a tax shift from property tax to sales tax. 

Land use has been an issue in Lawrence County for years and we are fortunate to have a good zoning ordinance.  The comprehensive plan serves as a guide for future land use and is in need of being updated.  

Public land management is important because wildfire, invasive plants, and pests do not respect boundaries.  Continuing to develop a positive working relationship with the Forest Service will enable the county to be more involved in management decisions that affect us all.         

What do you believe is working for the county, and how will you retain that progression?

I continue to be impressed by the passion and dedication the employees of the Lawrence County exhibit every day.  Creating a good working environment, a competitive compensation package and continuing education avenues for them is important to retaining the staff. 

I feel that our protocols and processes for conducting county business are accessible and fair to the citizens.   

I feel that perhaps our greatest attributes are the natural resources we have in our county.  With proper oversight from the county and working with the other agencies involved, we can utilize and conserve our natural resources at the same time.   

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

I have been regularly attending commission meetings for four years now.  I can attest that decisions are made in an open forum and in accordance with the open meeting laws.  Lawrence County offers a virtual option to attend or view meetings live, and also provides a recording so viewers can watch as their schedules allow. I report on commission meetings on KDSJ radio. I also write a monthly article, which is published in the Black Hills Pioneer and on my website, that provides information on the decisions of the commission. My email address is listed on the LC website, and I attend community functions to be visible and accessible in our county. 

What else do you want people to know about you?

I don’t take leadership responsibilities lightly.  If re-elected I will continue to be fully committed to continuing to do the best job as County Commissioner that I can.  I was also elected to serve in leadership for the SD Association of County Commissioners.  Counties are greatly affected by the actions of the Legislature and this position allows me greater access to information and influence in the SD Legislature.   I am also the SD representative to the Public Lands Steering Committee for the National Association of Counties which enables me to be a more effective advocate for public land management. 

How best should the county regulate the drastic increase of OHV traffic?

OHV use is very popular in our county and brings in many visitors that support our businesses.   Regulating OHV use is far more complicated than it appears on the surface.  The County, State and Forest Service all need to be involved in addressing the use, safety concerns and subsequent resource damage.  The two biggest obstacles are funding and jurisdictional limitations.  The OHV trail sticker fund is a funding option for trail system enforcement; jurisdiction is more difficult to work through.  I feel that I have reached the right people to work through these issues and have been developing the relationships necessary to address OHV issue.    

Should sitting county commissioners also function as the board of adjustment, or should there be changes in the member make-up of the board of adjustment? Why or why not?

I believe the County Commissioners should continue to act as the BOA as they have done since 2015.  I believe this because the BOA has decision making authority and the impact that their decisions can carry should only be made by elected individuals.  Elected officials are accountable to all of the voting citizens, while appointed officials are only accountable to those who appointed them.  Although someone may not agree with the decisions made, it doesn’t mean the process is flawed. 

Pine beetles are increasing in the forests of Lawrence County. How should the county address the issue so that they don’t grow to epidemic levels?

Lawrence County has a great track record for addressing Mountain Pine Beetles in this county.  Mountain Pine Beetles not only affect the timber industry, but also recreation, cattle grazing allotments, wildlife habitat and wildfire risk.  The county is close to regaining Cooperative Agency status with the Forest Service which will provide an avenue for more sharing of information and give us the ability to be more involved in the management decisions within our county.  Proper forest management is the best method of limiting the spread of Mountain Pine Beetle and preventing an epidemic, being able to be more involved in the management process is our best method of preventing another epidemic.     

As more people are developing rural parts of Lawrence County, in areas such as Maitland Road, and in areas adjacent to paved access points, should the county allocate more funding to pave those roads?

I have not supported paving gravel roads in our county, and I have several reasons. First, our county highway department already has the equipment to maintain gravel roads, while paving and maintaining paved roads requires hiring outside companies. Paving a few roads in the county would not reduce the amount of equipment we have or significantly reduce the highway budget. Second, due to the slope, contour, and sharp corners many of our roads have, I worry that paving them could leave drivers to increase their speed, creating a safety issue. Third, I feel gravel roads contribute to the rural culture and character of our county.

What should the county do to monitor rising levels of OHV vehicles and the subsequent damage to trails in the county?

OHV use exploded to levels not anticipated by any of us the past six years.  Currently, due to federal regulations, the county is unable to issue citations for improper trail use to create safer conditions and limit resource damage.  Reaching an agreement with the Forest Service that would allow the county to patrol the trails and have the ability to issue citations is being explored right now.  Forest Service regulations are sometimes difficult to work through, but hopefully we can find a way to develop and fund county enforcement on the Forest Service trail system.  Fortunately, some local user groups have stepped up to help maintain and repair trail damage.

title: Group founded by candidate publishes ‘voter guide’ purporting to be from ‘watchdog organization’
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — Republican voters in South Dakota recently received text messages directing them to “the official Republican Voter Guide for the upcoming election,” with a link to a webpage that purports to be from “a policy watchdog organization” providing information about where each candidate for governor “stands on taxes, spending and South Dakota’s future.”
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — Republican voters in South Dakota recently received text messages directing them to “the official Republican Voter Guide for the upcoming election,” with a link to a webpage that purports to be from “a policy watchdog organization” providing information about where each candidate for governor “stands on taxes, spending and South Dakota’s future.” 

In reality, the text messages and the webpage are products of a political action committee founded and partially funded by one of the 4 candidates for the Republican nomination for governor: Toby Doeden, a businessman from Aberdeen.

The webpage, which provides negative information about Doeden’s 3 opponents and positive information about him, appears to be a product of “South Dakota Tax Watch.”

“South Dakota Tax Watch is a policy watchdog organization committed to sharing factual information about candidates’ voting history on taxes and spending,” the webpage says.

But South Dakota Tax Watch does not show up as a corporation, nonprofit, or political action committee in public listings maintained by South Dakota’s secretary of state.

A small disclaimer at the bottom of the South Dakota Tax Watch webpage identifies Dakota First Action as the page’s funder and approver. Dakota First Action is a political action committee that was formed in 2024 with Doeden as its chairman. Subsequent campaign finance reports showed the committee owed Doeden more than $200,000 for loans it received from him.

In July, 2 months after Doeden had announced his candidacy, the committee filed new paperwork listing Republican former state lawmaker Drew Dennert as chairman. 

The Dakota First Action website also features Doeden as its founder. 

South Dakota Searchlight asked Doeden for comment. He responded with a written statement.

“I have had ZERO association with DFA, or any other political organization since long before I made the decision to run for office,” Doeden wrote. “I am laser-focused on my campaign and my message. When I have something to say, I say it loud and proud from my own campaign. I don’t masquerade behind these PACs like my opponents.”

Dennert also provided a written statement on behalf of Dakota First Action.

“Obviously, lowering taxes for South Dakota residents is one of our top priorities,” he said, in part. “With such an important election taking place, it is important for voters to understand each of the candidates’ positions and history as it relates to taxes and spending.”

The other candidates for the Republican nomination for governor are Gov. Larry Rhoden, U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson and state House Speaker Jon Hansen. The primary election is June 2, and early voting is underway.

title: Tropical Smoothie is the SD Veteran-Owned  Small Business of the Year
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Kelli Ewert is the owner of Tropical Smoothie Café. She’s also an Army veteran and the recipient of the South Dakota Small Business Administration Veteran Owned Small Business of the Year award. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Tropical Smooth is the SD Veteran-Owned  Small Business of the Year
Kelli Ewert is the owner of Tropical Smoothie Café. She’s also an Army veteran and the recipient of the South Dakota Small Business Administration Veteran Owned Small Business of the Year award. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — Kelly Ewert has made not one, but 2 careers out of caring for people.

She is a registered nurse and the owner of Tropical Smoothie Café in Spearfish.

“I was an Army nurse. I went through ROTC and grew up in Texas. I was stationed in Colorado and married into the Black Hills,” Ewert said. “I have been here since 2003, and then settled in Spearfish in 2008.”

Today, Ewert runs an IV business and works with the Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office to perform blood draws when needed.

As a nurse, care is a core principle. That same principle applies to her leadership of Tropical Smoothie Café, Ewert said.

As the owner of a small business, she’s leaned in to nurturing potential and providing a place for young people to step into the workforce.

Pull quote
I think I have employed half of the youth of Spearfish. It takes a village to get them all raised, and we love doing it. — Kellie Ewert
 Owner of Tropical Smoothie Café, Spearfish

“I think I have created and fostered a good environment for kids to have a first job and understand how the world works,” Ewert said. “I want them to like it here. I don’t just want warm bodies, I want them to like it and want  to be here. I think I kind of mother a lot of them, but they appreciate it.”

She employs high school students, college students, and a string of student athletes.

“I have kids who started at 14 years old, and now they’re coming back from college for the summer. I know so many of their parents. It has just been a big family here. I tell the kids all the time that this is an opportunity for them to learn leadership before they go off to school. Some of them aren’t sure they’re ready for leadership, but I see their potential,” Ewert said. “I think I have employed half of the youth of Spearfish. It takes a village to get them all raised, and we love doing it.”

Ewert also partners with Northern Hills Training Center to offer employment to adults with developmental disabilities.

“They have an opportunity to have a normal part of life, and it is good for the kids to see that there are other people in this world that want to work more and can’t,” Ewert said.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, Ewert realized that many programs that rewarded children for meeting their reading goals had dissolved, so Tropical Smoothie started working with Spearfish teachers to provide free smoothies to young readers. At the café, Ewert occasionally takes on the role of tooth-fairy, too.

“We have a program for kids who lose their teeth. Anyone under 10 can come in and give us a smile, and say they lost a tooth, and they get a free smoothie,” Ewert said.

Ewert’s contributions as a small business owner earned her an accolade this year from the South Dakota Small Business Administration. Tropical Smoothie has been named South Dakota’s Veteran-Owned Small Business of the Year.

“It was really humbling to accept that award,” Ewert said. “One of the things I learned from the military was: you can’t be a good leader if you are not a good follower.”

Ewert takes pride in “rolling up her sleeves and slinging smoothies” right alongside her crew.

“I do the dishes. I come in in the morning and ask, ‘Where do you need me?’ I think working right alongside of them is the best example you can set. My nursing leadership in the military was really priceless,” Ewert said. “The business stuff you can learn as you go. The people you either have it, or you don’t.”

Ewert decided to add entrepreneur/restaurateur alongside titles like registered nurse, Army veteran, and mom of 2 in 2019, just a few months before the COVID-19 pandemic challenged restaurants across the country.

“I wanted something that my kids could be part of,” Ewert said. “It was difficult during COVID, but I went from nurse to restaurant (owner) which is a huge jump, but it broadened who I am and helped me learn a different side of life. Business ownership is a tough thing. I had to do a lot of learning on my own. The franchise wasn’t able to get here during COVID. I had to figure it out. I let the crew help me figure it out.”

Ewert hopes that, in being both a nurse and the leader of the crew at Tropical Smoothie, she can inspire her young employees to expand their own horizons. 

“It is good for the kids to see that you don’t have to just have one thing that you do. You can try different things, do internships, try all for those things,” Ewert said. 

She was nominated by the South Dakota CEO of the West Women’s Business Center for the Small Business Administration Veteran-Owned Small Business of the Year Award. She received the recognition on May 5.

“Without the community, any small business isn’t going to thrive. It has been really fun to grow the business with the community and have those relationships with the school district and the training center,” Ewert said.

title: New laws result in 1,500 federal-only voter registrations ahead of SD primary election
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — Chris Lee will drive hundreds of miles to vote in person.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — Chris Lee will drive hundreds of miles to vote in person.

The truck driver from Cleveland plans his route through South Dakota on Election Day. The Republican has been registered in South Dakota for nearly 10 years and has followed the campaigns for the June 2 primary election closely. He knows who he wants to vote for. 

But he’s not allowed to vote in state and local races this year. To his surprise, Lee is designated as a federal-only voter in South Dakota.

Since January, a person who lists only the address of a mail forwarding service or post office box without describing the location of their “habitation” must be categorized as a federal-only voter when the person “applies to register as a voter or vote by absentee ballot,” according to a new state law. Since March, a person who doesn’t provide proof of U.S. citizenship when registering to vote must also be designated as a federal-only voter. That means the person can only vote in federal contests such as presidential and congressional races — not other statewide, legislative, county, city or local races or ballot questions.

“I took it for granted that I was able to vote in all the elections,” Lee said.

South Dakota and Arizona are the two states that have implemented a federal-only voting system.

According to a South Dakota Searchlight analysis of voter registration data from all 66 South Dakota counties, there are over 1,500 federal-only voters in the state — a number that is likely increasing as more people register or request absentee ballots. More than 180 of those federal-only voters are due to a lack of U.S. citizenship documentation upon registration.

Some federal-only voters in South Dakota won’t have anything to vote on in June. Many of them are not Republicans, and the only federal races are Republican primaries, which are closed to non-Republican voters.

Of Minnehaha County’s 575 federal-only voters, 168 are non-politically affiliated, 148 are Democratic, 97 are independent and two are Libertarian. Of Pennington County’s 572 federal-only voters, 122 are Democratic, 106 are non-politically affiliated, 82 are independent, seven are Libertarian and three are listed as “other.”

Dispute over federal-voter law implementation 

Lee did not know he was a federal-only voter until South Dakota Searchlight informed him.

He registered to vote in 2016, when he was working for a company based in South Dakota. He currently lives in Cleveland with his wife, but he retains his South Dakota driver’s license, vehicle registration and voter registration in Minnehaha County.

“I like the state. I might retire there. That’s why I haven’t changed anything,” Lee said. “I stay up to date with the state.”

But Lee renewed his driver’s license and updated his voter registration simultaneously in January. He uses DakotaPost mail forwarding, and he likely received a card in the mail informing him that he’s been switched to a federal-only voter. If he did, he didn’t read it.

Voters can use the Voter Information Portal on the South Dakota Secretary of State’s website to check their registration status. But it does not tell Lee — or any federal-only voters — of their new status.

Lawrence County Auditor Brenda McGruder said her office changes voters’ statuses when they update their registration or request an absentee ballot. Her county had 184 federal-only voters as of April.

Amber Hobert, president of the mail forwarding service DakotaPost in Sioux Falls, said that’s not how she remembers the legislation described during the 2025 legislative session.

It was not supposed to be “applied retroactively” to current voters, even if they were updating their address or their political affiliation, Hobert said. She added that changing people to federal-only voters any time they interact with the election system — to update their registration or request an absentee ballot — leads to disenfranchisement.

“If you request an absentee ballot, you’re going to be treated differently than someone with the exact same address who manages to vote in person,” Hobert said.

Deputy Secretary of State Tom Deadrick told the legislative Rules Review Committee in September that the law was intended to apply to new registrations.

“For those who are already registered, nothing changes,” Deadrick said. He did not define whether a new registration includes updated voter registrations that come through the system.

Despite the dispute, state Rep. Tony Kayser, R-Sioux Falls, said he is pleased with how the law is being implemented. Kayser introduced the bill during the 2025 legislative session that changed how full-time RVers’ voter registration is handled.

“Keep the local elections local, for people who actually live here,” Kayser said, adding, “If you don’t qualify, then you should be updated to a federal-only ballot.”

RVer: ‘We ought to have a say’

Earnest Weaver lives in Virginia. As a member of the military, he moves frequently and chose South Dakota as his home base for vehicle registration, voter registration and mail forwarding.

Since he doesn’t live in the state, he planned to vote just for federal races even before learning he has a limited ticket. But he thinks that should be his choice, not a limitation imposed by law.

“My instinct is, if you are accounted for somewhere, then you should have the option to vote in any and all elections that take place there,” Weaver said. “I don’t do it as a personal choice — I would just vote in federal elections — but I think it should be a choice for anyone accounted for there.”

Janet Suffel, a fulltime RVer with her husband, misplaced her driver’s license in February and had to request a new one. She said she likely updated her voter registration information on the application, making her a federal-only voter.

If the couple came back to South Dakota to vote in person, her husband — who has not changed or updated his registration — could vote in federal, state and local races, but she could only vote in federal races.

Suffel and her husband, originally from Virginia, chose South Dakota for its lack of income tax and personal property taxes. The 64-year-old last visited three years ago but has paid fees and taxes in South Dakota when renewing her license and registration.

“I’m not driving on the roads, I’m not using any local services, I’m not using Medicaid, and I’m providing jobs for people at America’s Mailbox by using that service,” Suffel said, referencing the Box Elder-based mail forwarding company. “South Dakota is getting something for nothing.”

“I think, at the very least,” Suffel added, “we ought to have a say at the state level about who is going to decide on whether we can vote only in federal or state races.”

title: Comer appointed presiding judge of Fourth Circuit
byline: Pioneer Staff Reports
description: Michelle Comer, 4th Circuit judge
_full_text:
Comer appointed presiding judge of Fourth Circuit
Michelle Comer, 4th Circuit judge 

PIERRE — South Dakota Supreme Court Chief Justice Steven R. Jensen has appointed the Honorable Michelle K. Comer as presiding judge for the Fourth Judicial Circuit. 

Comer replaces the current Judge Michael W. Day, who is retiring effective June 8. 

Comer will begin her duties as presiding judge the following day.

South Dakota’s Unified Judicial System is divided into 7 judicial circuits. The Fourth Judicial Circuit is comprised of Butte, Corson, Dewey, Harding, Lawrence, Meade, Perkins and Ziebach counties. 

Comer graduated from Lead High School in 1986. She received a bachelor’s degree in psychology from Pepperdine University in Malibu, Calif., in 1990, and a juris doctor from the University of South Dakota School of Law, Vermillion, in 1994. 

Comer has served as a circuit court judge for the Fourth Judicial Circuit since 2015. Before her election as a circuit judge, she was a magistrate judge and drug court judge for the Fourth Judicial Circuit from 2006 to 2015. 

Prior to taking the bench, Judge Comer was sole practitioner/owner of Percy Law from 2004 to 2006, and a partner at the firm Fuller, Tellinghuisen, Gordon and Eckrich, where she worked from 1996 to 2004. Comer began her legal career as a law clerk for the Seventh Judicial Circuit in 1994 and deputy state’s attorney for Lawrence County in 1995.

“Judge Michelle Comer has demonstrated exceptional leadership, sound judgment and a deep commitment to serving the people of South Dakota throughout her judicial career,” said Jensen. “Her extensive experience as both a circuit and magistrate judge, along with her longstanding service to the Fourth Judicial Circuit, make her well qualified to serve as presiding judge. I am confident she will continue to lead the circuit with integrity, professionalism and dedication to the fair administration of justice.”

“Judge Michael Day has provided decades of distinguished service to the citizens of South Dakota and to the Unified Judicial System,” said Jensen. “As presiding judge, he has been a thoughtful leader and trusted colleague whose commitment to justice and public service has strengthened the Fourth Judicial Circuit. We are grateful for his many contributions and wish him the very best in his retirement.”

title: Fitzgerald resigns  as judge, makes  run for AG again
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: John Fitzgerald
_full_text:
Fitzgerald resigns  as judge, makes  run for AG again
John Fitzgerald 

SPEARFISH — Fourth Circuit Court Judge John Fitzgerald resigned Tuesday from his post.

This marks the fourth change in judge statuses in recent weeks within the Fourth Circuit Court.

Judge Michael W. Day announced his retirement effective June 8.

This prompted Gov. Larry Rhoden to appoint Judge Chad Callahan as a circuit judge.

Then South Dakota Supreme Court Chief Justice Steven R. Jensen appointed Michelle K. Comer as presiding judge for the Fourth Judicial Circuit, see related story on Page 2.

 The Fourth Judicial Circuit is comprised of Butte, Corson, Dewey, Harding, Lawrence, Meade, Perkins and Ziebach counties.

Fitzgerald told the Pioneer that he is stepping down so that he can run for South Dakota Attorney General.

“I think it is a very important job, and I am well qualified for it based on my experience as a state’s attorney and judge,” he said. “I have the skills, the experience, knowledge, and judgement necessary.”

Fitzgerald served 42 years as a state’s attorney in Butte and Lawrence counties, and he is believed to be the longest-serving state’s attorney in South Dakota history.

Fitzgerald said his experience in the courtroom is vast, having prosecuted cases ranging from misdemeanors to murder.

“Murder, rape, robbery, kidnapping, I’ve tried just about every case you can imagine over the past 42 years,” he said. 

Fitzgerald won the election for circuit court judge in November 2022. He was sworn in on Jan. 3, 2023

Due to age restrictions set in state law, Fitzgerald would have had to step down in January 2027. Judges cannot serve in the capacity at the age of 70. He added that he also could not serve as a judge while seeking office, hence Tuesday’s announcement.

Fitzgerald’s career in law began when he received a supervised license to practice law from the South Dakota Supreme Court, for an internship with the Pennington County Public Defender’s Office, during his last semester of law school at the University of South Dakota (USD).

Fitzgerald served as Butte County state’s attorney from January 1981 to March 1995. From there, he served as Lawrence County deputy state’s attorney from March 1990 to January 1995 and then took the head prosecutor’s position that year.

He ran for attorney general in 2018 against Jason Ravnsborng and state Sen. Lance Russell, a former Fall River County state’s attorney.

Ravnsborg won the election, which is done by delegates and not a vote of the public. He did not serve a full term. On Sept. 12, 2020, he struck and killed pedestrian Joe Boever on the outskirts of Highmore. He was impeached in June 2022, marking the first impeachment in state history.

Marty Jackley is the current attorney general, having served from 2009-2019, and again since January 2023. He announced his candidacy for Congress in September 2025.

“The Attorney General’s Office plays a critical role in protecting public safety,” Fitzgerald said. “I believe my judgment, courtroom experience, and knowledge as a lawyer have prepared me to lead the fight against crime in our state, especially violent crime.”

title: Defending your domain
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: The 2002 Grizzly Gulch fire, shown here, destroyed numerous homes in Lead. As residents prepare for what could be a summer with high fire danger, local and state fire authorities encourage homeowners to defend their property by taking precautions before fire season starts. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Defending your domain
The 2002 Grizzly Gulch fire, shown here, destroyed numerous homes in Lead. As residents prepare for what could be a summer with high fire danger, local and state fire authorities encourage homeowners to defend their property by taking precautions before fire season starts. Pioneer file photo 

DEADWOOD — With fire dangers remaining in high, very high, and extreme this spring, Logan Brown, fuels manager for South Dakota Wildland Fire, and Deadwood Volunteer Fire Chief Joel Ellis weigh in on how homeowners can protect themselves from losing property or endangering their neighbors.

Creating defensible space 

Brown said that the first step to reducing the risk of losing property to a wildland fire is understanding the concept of an ignition zone and defensible space.

“The home ignition zone is looking at the home itself and then the surrounding 100 feet and the characteristics of it,” Brown said. “That’s going to really influence how a fire reacts in that area when it’s burning towards the home.”

Brown said that there are 3 different ignition zones around a home: the immediate, surrounding 5 feet, the intermediate 5-30 feet, and the extended 30-100 feet surrounding a home or structure. 

In the immediate area, Brown said he recommends that property owners landscape using rock instead of mulch and choose ignition-resistant landscaping and plants. 

A list of ignition-resistant plants can be found at https://wfca.com/wildfire-articles/fire-resistant-plants/.

“There was a fire down in Hermosa last year where the fire burned right up against the house and then burned all the way around the house where it had rock, around 5-feet around the entire house,” said Brown. “So, we’ve seen that landscape design does work here in the Black Hills.”

Brown said it’s important to clean all brush, pine needles, and litter within the immediate ignition zone of a property and put fine-mesh screening on all vents on the house. 

“Outside of that, you’re looking at the intermediate zone,” he said. “That’s where we want to see trees trimmed up, hedges spaced out, and you want to keep that lawn mowed to less than 6-inches in length.”

Beyond the intermediate zone and into the extended zone, Brown said property owners should keep tree limbs trimmed to 6-10 feet above the ground and keep trees thinned out around the property. Removing the lower limbs of trees helps prevent ground fires from climbing into the canopy, creating a more intense blaze.

“If there is a fire burning towards the home or the structure, if it’s a crown fire moving along the crowns of the trees, it won’t be able to go from tree to tree (if you keep trees thinned out) and it should hopefully drop back down to a surface fire, meaning the lower grass is not going to have the flame length needed to put direct flame contact on the home.”

Brown said that 90% of structure loss from wildland fire is caused by embers, not from roaring flames. 

“In front of the fire front, there’s these embers that get blown in front,” he said. “Envision thousands of matches being lit and then thrown across your property. Then picture these embers, or these matches, landing where you’re seeing a pile of dead leaves that’s right up against your wood deck. Those are going to ignite those leaves, which will put direct flame contact on the deck and start the deck on fire, which can burn your home down.”

Brown said in recent years, South Dakota Wildland Fire has seen more structure loss as a result of home-to-home ignition. He said that’s why it’s important for entire communities to come together to make conscious decisions to protect themselves and each other from fire dangers. 

“There’s a lot of areas where, when you’re looking at 100 feet away from your house, you’re in your neighbor’s property,” said Brown. “That’s why it’s important to work with your neighbor and your community, because all it takes is one person that’s not maybe doing what they should be doing to protect their home and their neighbor’s home from wildfire, and that can create that weak link in the neighborhood.”

To create more ignition resistant neighborhoods and communities, Brown said communities should consider becoming Firewise certified. Through a process of assessment, 5-year planning, and community-driven efforts, neighborhoods can help protect each other from total devastation. 

To look into becoming Firewise certified, visit firewise.org. 

Local concerns

Ellis said that local residents should always follow their local fire department’s, city’s, and county’s social media pages, as well as subscribing to local emergency alert systems, like CodeRED. 

In addition to cleaning pine needles, dead grasses, and shrubs from the immediate zones of their homes, Ellis reminded homeowners to clean their gutters and roof regularly. 

“In the fall, leaves and pine needles will accumulate and go into those gutters, and those can be a big issue,” he said. 

Along with cleaning the tops of their homes, Ellis reminded homeowners to check beneath their decks as well. 

“People that have patios and decks, a lot of times debris can build up underneath them over the years,” he said. “It’s kind of out of sight, out of mind. People put lattice around them to make them look pretty on the outside and they kind of forget what’s on the inside.”

Ellis encouraged families to know of multiple evacuation routes, especially in neighborhoods with only one way in and out and keep a go-bag packed with important documents, medications, and spare clothes.

“Know where your fire roads are if you’re in a rural setting,” he said. “If you’re in an homeowners association, it’s pretty easy to find those. There are also Forest Service maps that show 2 tracks that can help you get out.”

Away from home, Ellis asked off-road vehicles, like side-by-sides, to stay on the designated trails. 

“There’s a lot of tall grasses around here and those things get hot,” he said. “It’s easy to start a fire with a side-by-side or by taking your vehicle off road. Stay on the trails.”

During red flag warnings, when weather conditions include high winds, low humidity, and dry vegetation, Ellis said he wouldn’t drive a side-by-side at all.

While working to clear fallen timber, Ellis encouraged chainsaw operators to have spark arrestors installed and be mindful of tall grasses and nearby metals while working. 

“When its hot, if you were working next to some metal while cutting a fallen tree, say a chain was nearby and for some reason your saw hit that metal, that could very easily cause a fire,” he said. “A spark arrestor is a fine mesh screen that stops any debris or embers from escaping.”

While driving, off roading, backpacking, or enjoying the views, Ellis warned cigarette smokers not to dump their lit cigarettes into the ditch. 

“It seems silly and it should go without saying,” he said. “But, with fire dangers and risks being what they are right now, no act of mitigation is too small.”
