title: Sturgis passes residential  camping ordinance
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: On May 4 the city of Sturgis passed a residential camping ordinance that allows residents to obtain a free permit for more than 3 camping units or 10 guests. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Sturgis passes residential  camping ordinance
On May 4 the city of Sturgis passed a residential camping ordinance that allows residents to obtain a free permit for more than 3 camping units or 10 guests. Pioneer file photo 

STURGIS — After months of public comment and revisions, the city of Sturgis passed what City Attorney Eric Davis has called the most liberal residential camping ordinance in the state. 

During the May 4 meeting, the Sturgis City Council put its final stamp of approval on the residential camping ordinance that distinguishes between non-Rally camping, by-right Rally camping, Rally camping by permit, and vacant-lot camping that is subject to transition and sunset provisions. 

The ordinance defines Rally camping as any residential camping that occurs 7 days before the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, and 3 days after. It allows property owners to have up to 3 camping units, with up to 10 guests, by right. More camping units and guests require property owners to obtain a free permit, which is available after the property owner submits a plan to the city building inspector or planner. 

During non-Rally periods, the ordinance allows property owners to have residential camping for up to 3 camping units, and up to 10 guests, for up to 6 days, twice a year. Property owners who need more than that must obtain a permit. 

The ordinance has been a hot topic at city council meetings since the council began revising it in January, as residents who have been renting out space on their property for as long as 40 years objected to regulations. However, Davis said the newly passed ordinance is significantly more liberal than the one it replaced. The former ordinance only allowed property owners to have one camping unit in their yard during the Rally, and while it required property owners  to obtain a permit for more units, it did not establish a permitting process. Under the former ordinance, the majority of all property owners who allowed residential camping were violating the law, Davis said. 

The new ordinance passed 6-1, with Councilman Mark Chaplin as the lone dissenting vote. Chaplin objected to the city allowing 7 days before the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally for Rally camping. 

“I think it’s too long,” he said. “I don’t think we need it that far ahead.”

But other council members and residents who spoke at the meeting said allowing Rally camping 7 days before the annual event officially kicks off makes good sense. Councilwoman Ruth Nichols and Councilman Jim Thompson said they both talked with residents who expressed that many people like to come to the Rally before the official start, in an attempt to beat the crowds. Additionally, businesswoman Tia Hartwell said vendors often come a week ahead of time to set up, and they often camp during that setup time. 

The new residential camping ordinance is scheduled to be printed in the Black Hills Pioneer on May 22, and if it is not referred to a vote it will become effective on June 18.

title: Meade County District 3 candidates
description: Voters in Meade County District 3 will head to the polls June 2 to vote on a vacant commission seat. Two people are running for 1 open position which is a 4-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.
_full_text:
Voters in Meade County District 3 will head to the polls June 2 to vote on a vacant commission seat. Two people are running for 1 open position which is a 4-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.

Michael Pauling

 Pauling, Michael.jpg
Michael Pauling 

Name and what you do for a living? 

My name is Michael Pauling and at present I am a Substitute School Teacher and a current member of the Meade County Planning Commission since January 2025. 

What motivated you to run for this office?

 I was asked by several members of the Piedmont Valley Community whom I hold in high regard to run for this Office partly on the fact the incumbent is not seeking reelection. I also believe I can make a significant contribution to the County Commission based on my past experiences and education in the public service sector. 

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

I do not think there is such a person as the best qualified candidate for Public Office. I believe that each Candidate brings strengths and weakness with them. My strengths are that I have decades of experience in working with individuals, Agencies and cooperative efforts to meet the needs of the people of Meade County as a whole. My weakness would be that I am still trying to figure out how best to secure the cooperation of the above. A work in progress that’s for sure always. 

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I have held several Leadership positions in various Veteran Service Organizations; I was once even a Girl Scout Brownie Leader- story for another time. I am an Army Retiree with a Tour in Afghanistan as well a Company Command while serving in the Army National Guard. Much of my leadership training comes from my military experience. Lead by example

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy? 

To date I have not missed a single County Planning Commission Meeting since my appointment. Add going to special meetings called as well as local Government Meetings all together about 20 meetings I have been in attendance. I take my obligations seriously. Public Service requires nothing less than participation and thorough preparation to engage the parties in meaningful productive discussions that lead to conclusions based on reality. 

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Well, I think the mining question in the Piedmont Valley area emphasized the importance of local newspapers to practically everybody I know. Not knowing what is going on in your own backyard can be just as shocking the headline grabbers of National News. We need local newspapers to hold local Government answerable to the people it serves. 

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in Meade County?

To Zone and enforce or to not Zone and not enforce sums it up to me. How to stretch our limited budget to meet the most needs of the people of Meade County while knowing that limited resources seem to collide with unlimited demand for services. We cannot make everybody happy all the time, but we do need to try to make life better for the people who put their trust and tax money in our hands. 

How do you intend to solve these issues?

Cooperative effort with the branches of the various Agencies of Government from Federal down to local municipalities. This Gordian knot cannot be solved by slicing it in half. We cannot just look at select angles of how to untie it either. Truth be told many Bureaucracies I have dealt with are great at insulating them selves for direct liability. As a County Commissioner I would be in the trenches with the people who voted for me as well as a steppingstone to the levels above County and in between.  I intend to solve these issues by not pretending that I can deliver “pie in the sky” answers that make great sound bites but have no real effect on change.     

What do you believe is working for the county, and how will you retain that progression?

I have got to know several people who work for the County Government. The individuals I have crossed paths are professional in my opinion and they take their responsibilities seriously. What also works for Meade County is that it is County full of Workers who just want to live their lives and continue their pursuit to happiness. I will retain that progress by not forgetting this County is for everyone who wants Liberty and Freedom. Yes, sacrifices may have to be made and if those sacrifices are not for another’s vanity, then progress will continue at a bearable cost. Let’s face it we cannot stop the train coming at us with the growth projections forecasted. We need pragmatic progress as a whole.

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

Half of all knowledge is knowing where to find it. I would encourage everyone to follow the agenda items on the Meade County Website. I will maintain regular communication with the local municipalities in District 3 so that there are no surprises coming at meeting time. Communication is a two-way street, and I expect to hear from the other parties what they are looking for. I would work for the people of District 3, not the other way around. While I do not expect everyone will always agree with what is being done, I do feel that they are owed reasoning behind the process. 

What else do you want people to know about you?

I owe no allegiance to any special interest group. I do not own a business, I do not own land that I seek to develop, I do not own an interest in a Contracting operation that relies on public projects. I am in short, a Citizen who sees a reality of life as it is. Politics is about perception and I know that belief is a powerful tool. I pay residential taxes and live in a Rural lifestyle. Freedom has a price and I will pay that price if I can live the way I wish like everyone else.

Do you support zoning in Meade County? Why or why not? 

I would support what my Constituents want. If there is a petition grass root type that comes up to the Commission, coupled with Proclamations from the local Municipalities supporting Zoning then I will do my best to make it happen. I do feel that SDCL 11-6-10 Joint Comprehensive Plan between the County and local Municipalities would be the efficient way to make it happen. However, to get to that point the County needs Zoning Ordinances first, which seems in many ways to be a large hurdle to get over. 

Meade County has over 1,100 miles of roads and has struggled with funding road maintenance. What ideas do you have for leveraging tax dollars for road maintenance and what roads should be top priority? 

This is an obviously huge issue and one that I have not fully investigated. I do know from my time with the US Army Corps of Engineers in Afghanistan that there is a lot more to it than putting down a layer of asphalt. The Meade County Master Transportation Plan of 2022 identifies both 5-year plan and long-range planning considerations. Short Range projects are identified on pages ES-5 and ES-6. The County spent money on getting these taskings identified and criticality of priority. With consultation from the County’s Subject Matter Experts, I would support what is in the plan. The bigger question is how to pay for it. That is an answer that if anyone truly had we would have found the money to meet all of requirements so we would have to prioritize the priorities it seems.  

In 2025 the Legislature passed a bill that allows counties to charge sales tax. Do you support instituting a sales tax in Meade County? Why or why not?

Unless we have a way of determining the projected revenue from such a plan, I will not support the sales tax initiative unless it can be conclusively proven to offset the projected loss of property tax collections in an equitable manner. Remember the “pie in the sky” promise? Rapid City and Pennington County will obviously most likely be able to break even on the offset but who in Meade County does not go shopping down that way if they can? What do we sell in Meade County to grab enough sales tax revenue to relieve property taxes as they are now? 

Philip Nelson

 Nelson, Philip.jpg
Phillip Nelson 

Name and what you do for a living? 

I am Philip Nelson and am running for Meade County Commissioner District 3.  I attended the University of Minnesota, College of Veterinary Medicine and graduated in 1972 with a Doctor of Veterinary Medicine degree.  I practiced in several states, working mainly with small animals but on occasion did some large animal work.  I am the father of seven children, fifteen grandchildren (soon to be sixteen), and 5 great-grandchildren.  My wife Sandra and I will have been married 38 years in June and have 3 children together.

What motivated you to run for this office?

In the back of my mind I had considered running for office in the past but it had never fit into the plan for our life until now.  I was circulating a petition to run for Delegate at Large to represent Meade County at the State Republican Convention in June.  I have listened too many who are frustrated with and complained about local government.  I checked and noted my District was open and only 1 person was in the race.  I believe citizens should have a choice in those that represent them.  I am in a good position in life now for me run.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

I believe in local control; and the best and most effective government is the one closest to the people.  I have been a serious student of our Constitution and history for many years.  I believe our rights come from our God not government.  Our Constitution was founded on the Bible and Christian principles and was created for a moral and religious people.   I believe governments’ purpose is to protect the people’s rights.  I believe in God, family and Country.  Our problems result from straying from those principles.

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I have never held an elected public office.  My wife and I have been heavily involved in campaigning and promoting strong conservative candidates for many years.  I am very active in my church and hold a position looking after over 300 men.  I have been very active in my professional associations and still sit on the Government Affairs Committee that oversees the effect of government on the profession.

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I have been to more than a half dozen meetings and attend several groups that discuss weekly and monthly what is happening in the Rapid City area as well as within the state or nation.  I feel I have a good sense as to what is happening around the area.  I am not afraid to ask questions and get the facts when I am concerned about something.

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

I do think it is important to have a way to communicate what is really going on locally and that needs to be done by stating the facts and let the reader make their own opinion.  

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in Meade County?

High Property Taxes and the concern over mining in Piedmont.  Property taxes will not ever be fixed in the legislature because they cannot seem to agree on anything that is why so many bills are proposed but never get enough votes to pass.  They play a shell game lowering some here and shifting responsibility for them to others.  My property tax is: Public Schools 56.7%, Meade County 30.4%, Ambulance, Fire, Library & secondary road 12.8%.  I cannot fix failing schools, I can work on the county.  The mining problem is a consequence of no zoning.

How do you intend to solve these issues?

I can work on lowering the county portion of property taxes by prioritizing money to be spent on legitimate county responsibilities and nothing else.  Live within the limits of tax revenue and allow the tax base to grow without continuing to spend every dollar so that property taxes go down and not up.  It’s a spending problem.  Sometimes you just have to say NO.  I make hard decisions.  No zoning made it easy to comply with limited regulation to allow mining.  This is not a reason to adopt zoning.  It doesn’t appear to be stoppable.  The quantity of limestone is limited so it should be over in a few years. 

What do you believe is working for the county, and how will you retain that progression?

I think the real question is if the majority of property owners are pleased with how the county is doing at preforming those functions that they cannot easily do for themselves.  This was the purpose for which people formed government.  Property owners are the ones who fund government.  

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

Transparency in government to me means everything is visible to the citizens, nothing hidden.  Minutes of all meeting should be easily available to everyone.  Citizens should know where I stand on issues and decisions should be made and not deferred.  It will be a priority to make information easily accessible.  I will always be available to talk to.  I will do my best to find answers.

What else do you want people to know about you?

I believe in God, family and country.  I believe in small government, individual freedom and self-determination.  I believe Private Property Rights are very important and government needs a very strong compelling interest before restricting them.  I believe good government was never meant to be charity.   Charity is an individual and personal choice.  I grew up poor and I got where I am in life by hard work and being financially responsible.  Today I am the result of my good choices.

Do you support zoning in Meade County? Why or why not? 

Zoning can be good and bad.  I was told it was put to a vote and defeated by a wide margin.  Zoning restricts property rights and since everyone in this county bought their property without zoning it is wrong to impose it now.  I think you need to respect your neighbor’s property rights also.  I am against zoning.  

 Meade County has over 1,100 miles of roads and has struggled with funding road maintenance. What ideas do you have for leveraging tax dollars for road maintenance and what roads should be top priority? 

Maintaining and managing the roads in the county is one of the legitimate responsibilities of the county.  The county has done a poor job here.  More tax dollars need to be spent on roads and they need more oversight.  I will do my best to fix this problem.  

In 2026 the Legislature passed a bill that allows counties to charge sales tax. Do you support instituting a sales tax in Meade County? Why or why not?

I am against a new sales tax for the citizens.  This is just a shell game and taking your money and then giving it back and convincing you they did you a favor and fixed the problem.  It’s a spending issue.  Control the spending.  The real issue here is that the public schools have failed to educate the children and have continued to lobby for more money to fix the problem.  Projected enrolments are going down and the distance between kids and schools is getting bigger.  Home schooling and private education is working according to test scores.  We need school choice and rethink public education.

title: Meade County District 1 candidates
description: Voters in Meade County District 1 will head to the polls June 2 to vote on a vacant commission seat. Four people are running for 1 open position which is a 4-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.
_full_text:
MeadeCountyCommissionDist1a.psd

Voters in Meade County District 1 will head to the polls June 2 to vote on a vacant commission seat. Four people are running for 1 open position which is a 4-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.

Steve Allender

 Allender, Steve.jpg
Steve Allender 

Name and what you do for a living? 

Steve Allender. I’ve been retired since July 2023. Prior to that I was Mayor of Rapid City for eight years. Before that I served 29 years with the Rapid City Police Department, the last seven years as police chief.

What motivated you to run for this office?

I have a strong interest in local government. I firmly believe local government is the most important because it is those officials who are closest to their constituents. When a person represents their friends and neighbors, listening to their thoughts and issues, it is virtually impossible to escape accountability. I have also been asked by many to run for either the legislature or county commission.  I choose the commission, because I can be more impactful. 

That, combined with my experience creates a good fit for the Meade County Commission

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

While serving in my previous capacities, in addition to a few boards of directors, I’ve developed a knack for getting things done. I understand that getting things done means balancing priorities and the limitations of government.  I am good at long-term projects, looking into the future, and communicating with constituents. I believe government should stay in its lane and out of people’s lives whenever possible. I do not have a personal agenda to chase.  I just want to do my part to make local government work for the people.

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

Mayor of Rapid City 2015-2023.

From 2005 to 2009 I was on the board of directors for the Mid States Organized Crime Information Center. I was chairman of that board from 2008 to 2009.

From 2008 to 2012 I was on the board of directors for Working Against Violence Inc.

From 2019 to 2022 I was on the Board of Directors for the South Dakota Municipal League. The last year of that service I was President of the board.

 I’ve been on the South Dakota Law Enforcement Standards and Training Commission since 2015.

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

Only one. Although I have watched commission meetings online. I have never thought it was important to attend meetings in preparation for holding an office. Partly because one of the lessons audience members can pick up from these meetings is the meeting culture, which is often more negative than positive. I feel much better about someone coming into office with a clean slate so to speak.  I have often discouraged those running for office to study meetings beforehand.

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Yes, I do.

Today, there are thousands of faceless media companies pummeling your senses with fantastical headlines, in an effort to compete with other media companies. Due to this, local news has become a standout as a reliable and credible news source. Local newspapers were there before the Internet, and after.

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in Meade County?

 As part of my campaign, I’ve been promoting a Meade County resident survey on my website steveallender.com/survey.  The responses are already shaping my priorities. One notable area is zoning as a local, common sense means of protection.

Certainly county roads are an issue. Public safety is very important. The legal relationship with the State of South Dakota is a concern. Counties are the most restricted form of local government, and the legislature holds the key.

Perhaps the most important priority at this time is proactively managing growth in a way that makes sense for the people who already live here. 

How do you intend to solve these issues?

First and foremost, a majority of commissioners must agree that these issues are important enough to solve. The first task at hand is working cooperatively to build a consensus while learning about and advocating for the needs of District 1.

I will work with legislators to address governing issues shared by South Dakota counties. I will use my experience and professional network to help develop proposals for zoning. I will assess challenges faced by the County Highway Department and the limitations of the county budget.  I will communicate and listen to the people and propose action based on this.

What do you believe is working for the county, and how will you retain that progression?

First and foremost, from a citizen’s perspective I believe county administration is working. It’s impressive that Meade County employs an Executive Director. The Register of Deeds, Treasurers Office, Equalization Office all appear to be working well. I believe that is a sign of competent staffing and is a credit to County Administration. 

An Important thing for an elected official to know, is when not to interfere when something is working.  I will offer support and give feedback where appropriate. I will listen to the needs of county departments and work with them to help them be successful. 

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

Transparency in government is important because the people paying the bill deserve to know what’s going on. The few exceptions to this are sensitive law-enforcement and personnel matters. Transparency is the one thing that will allow constituents to trust their government.

I have never refused a Media interview. I helped build the social media efforts in Rapid City starting in 2009.

If elected, I will produce a newsletter for county residents to hear about the important issues being handled by the commission.  I will also receive messages, comments, and criticisms from constituents in an effort to make informed decisions.

What else do you want people to know about you?

We bought property in Meade County in 2018, and moved here in 2023. We made a deliberate decision to live here and we love it! We chose Meade County for the people, the peace and the pace – and those are things worth protecting. 

I am not very complicated. What you see is what you get. I’m extremely open and forthcoming. I am honest. I like to have fun, even when doing the people’s work. 

I live with my wife in the Piedmont area, I have two adult children, two grandchildren growing up in Blackhawk, and another on the way.

Do you support zoning in Meade County? Why or why not? 

 I do support zoning, however, it is important to note zoning is not a one-size-fits-all treatment.

 Meade County residents value property rights. The latest issue with mining near Piedmont is a great example of how zoning regulations could have essentially made this a non-issue. 

Zoning regulations are not simply the government making up rules to force on the people. It is the people helping the government determine what is important for their communities. There can be different zoning regulations along the I-90 than there are in rural Meade County. Zoning should be local, practical and limited.

Meade County has over 1,100 miles of roads and has struggled with funding road maintenance. What ideas do you have for leveraging tax dollars for road maintenance and what roads should be top priority? 

Nearly 80% of all county funding is for mandatory functions dictated to us by the state.

There may be funding options within the budget but increasing that budget is directly related to property taxes and limited by state law.  

I know from experience that the highest priority road is the road you are living on. Government must manage and maintain these roads as assets, and that requires standards, schedules and skilled employees. It would be appropriate to investigate other funding,  maintenance schedules, technology or tools that may be on the horizon to help keep our roads in good working order.

In 2025 the Legislature passed a bill that allows counties to charge sales tax. Do you support instituting a sales tax in Meade County? Why or why not? 

First of all, I don’t like these two bills passed by the legislature. I think they are shortsighted and unfair to smaller counties. Having said that, I believe I would support implementing the tax. The fact is, it will provide some relief for property taxes. Hopefully, it will prompt Meade County residents to find a Meade County business to patronize, rather than traveling to neighboring counties for our needs.  The more we spend here locally, the better for our local economy, but also doing this will provide more property tax relief.

Terri Jo Bruch

 Bruch, Terri Jo.jpg
Terri Jo Bruch 

Name and what you do for a living?

My name is Terri Jo Bruch. I currently work at Sanford Lab in Lead as one of their emergency dispatchers. Before taking the job at the lab, I worked for Meade County Sheriff’s Office as a 911 emergency dispatcher for 10 years. I am also an EMT with Sturgis Ambulance.

What motivated you to run for this office?

I have been interested in the county commission since 2011. It was not until I ended my employment with Meade County that I could explore the option to run for the county commission. With my current employment I have the time to dedicate to the responsibility of being on the commission. Being a previous employee of Meade County, I saw things that need to be addressed. I have an open mind and understand the issues facing the county and its residents.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?  

I will give Meade County my dedications and I will always listen to what is needed and do my best to serve the citizens to the best of my ability.

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I am currently serving as treasure on the Meade County Rural Ambulance Board that was formed in 2020 by the citizens due to the need for ambulance service outside the city limits of Sturgis. 

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I have not been able to attend as many of the commission meetings as I would have liked to because of scheduling conflicts with my previous job. I have watched the meetings online.

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Local newspapers are vital to the public. They keep the public informed of the happenings. Not all people have access to the internet and having the option to pick up a paper or go online to read current news is important.

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in Meade County?

Conditions of the rural roads.

Figuring out ways the county can benefit from the tourism season. To earn money without increasing property taxes.

Employees.

The possibility of zoning. Zoning is going to be an issue that needs to be looked at. There are different types of zoning and if that is a route the commission decides to take, I am confident we can find common ground to benefit the citizens. 

How do you intend to solve these issues?

To address the issues the county is facing it is going to take teamwork, creative thinking, transparency, and accountability from the commission. As of now I know I do not have the answers to “fix” all the issues. If the commission can work together with the citizens, I feel we can solve many of the issues. 

What do you believe working for the county, and how will you retain that progression?

I think working together is the answer to keep the country moving forward.

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

I feel transparency is going to be key to helping the citizens understand choices made and the fiscal state of the county. Less closed-door meetings and more keeping everyone informed of what is going on with the county. The citizens elected the commission and need to know they can trust us to do what is best for the entirety of the county, not just the more populated areas. Meade County is huge and the commission has a responsibility to the whole county and all the citizens who live here. 

What else do you want people to know about you?

I am a very dedicated person and try my best in all situations. 

Do you support zoning in Meade County? Why or why not?

Zoning is going to be an issue that needs to be looked at. There are different types of zoning and if that is a route the commission decides to take, I am confident we can find common ground to benefit the citizens. 

Meade County has over 1,100 miles of roads and has struggled with funding road maintenance. What ideas do you have for leveraging tax dollars for road maintenance and what roads should be top priority? 

Roads are one of the biggest concerns of the county and is a priority. Safety of the citizens is also a priority and keeping the roads well maintained would help to keep them safe.

In 2025 the Legislature passed a bill that allows counties to charge sales tax. Do you support instituting a sales tax in Meade County? Why or why not?

Using all of the opportunities to keep taxes low is going to benefit the citizens, this is something that would need to be researched and discussed.

Tyler Woods

 Woods, Tyler.jpg
Tyler Wood 

Name and what you do for a living? 

My name is Tyler Woods and I run a registered cattle operation with my family. We have ties to the county clear back to the 1880s. 

What motivated you to run for this office?

 This county is at a big moment in time. We need leadership that can set a path forward that works for everyone. I have great ideas on how to fix the issues and experience enough to make them happen. 

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

I have spent much time as citizen in county commissioner meetings already testifying on issues at hand. I’ve spent time in Pierre doing same on issues that effects the citizens of this county. I’m not afraid to dig in and get to work! 

    

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

None

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I have attended several county commissioner meetings. Don’t have extract number of hand

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

I do believe they are important. Many people still rely on them to get local news and things happening in their local communities. 

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in Meade County?

Roads and the road structures within the county are number 1. Also the worry around data centers, wind/solar farms, and what is being done to protect private property rights are big as well. Not only are people being taxed hard but seems everyone wants to tell you what to do with your own property. 

How do you intend to solve these issues?

We need to make sure we have good leadership in place on every level first. We then need to look at grants and available funds to help fix roads. Need to put legislation on the books to protect property rights. We also need to address the building boom in the county so that everyone is paying share and getting same services county wide. 

        

What do you believe is working for the county, and how will you retain that progression?

I think there has been some forward-thinking ideas that have been brought up. Key is to build upon those ideas and keep moving the county to a better place. 

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

I think it is very important to be transparent. I don’t plan on hiding anything. Everything should be done in front of everyone so we are all on the same level. 

What else do you want people to know about you?

I’m a hard worker and very driven to do what I can to help this county and it’s citizens. We all deserve the same services and respect county wide and I attend to see that happens. 

Do you support zoning in Meade County? Why or why not? 

I do think it is something that needs to be looked at. It’s perceived as a bad thing, but maybe issues that face the county now is because we don’t have it. We can use it to help maintain roads and protect our property from outside sources that want to use our county for their own uses. We can do a simple zoning structure that works for everyone and doesn’t tell you how to use your own property. 

Meade County has over 1,100 miles of roads and has struggled with funding road maintenance. What ideas do you have for leveraging tax dollars for road maintenance and what roads should be top priority? 

There are grant opportunities out there. That is something that needs to be explored first and foremost. We also need to make sure these developers coming into the county are paying their share for the increase to the road structures they are bringing with them. Property taxes don’t make enough to fix the abuse the roads see. 

In 2025 the Legislature passed a bill that allows counties to charge sales tax. Do you support instituting a sales tax in Meade County? Why or why not?

I think it is something that could be very useful for the county. Now have to see how the parameters are set before committing to anything. If we were to do something, wee need to make sure the money made is set to go to road infrastructure, not just to the general fund. It’s a chance for the county to actually make money on things like the rally, vs just spend money on it. 

Glen Haines

SPEARFISH — In this issue, you will find the annual publication of financial summaries of insurance companies licensed to do business in South Dakota.

Insurance companies doing business in South Dakota are required by state law to publish these financial summaries each year. The summary lists the insurance company’s assets, liabilities, business in South Dakota for the year and the lines in which the company is authorized by the state of South Dakota to sell insurance.

“Public notices published in newspapers have an important role in keeping citizens informed and providing bonafide transparency. The publication of these insurance company financial summaries supports those principles and helps to inform South Dakotans about an important part of the financial industry in our state,” said South Dakota NewsMedia Association Executive Director David Bordewyk. “This is why public notices published in the local newspaper remain vital in our democracy.”

 For more information about any insurance company doing business in South Dakota, contact the state Division of Insurance in Pierre at (605) 773-3563.

 More than 8 out of 10 South Dakotans believe that publishing public notices in a local newspaper should be required. That is according to a statewide survey of 406 South Dakota adults commissioned by SDNA and conducted by Coda Ventures in 2024.

South Dakota NewsMedia Association, based in Brookings, represents the state’s newspapers and digital news outlets.

title: Sturgis Senior Walk gives Sturgis graduates  one last trip down memory lane
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: Sturgis Brown High School seniors who will graduate Sunday, participated in the annual Senior Walk through the elementary and middles schools in the district.  A group that stopped at the Sturgis Williams Middle School said the walk brought back a lot of memories. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
Sturgis Senior Walk gives Sturgis graduates  one last trip down memory lane
Sturgis Brown High School seniors who will graduate Sunday, participated in the annual Senior Walk through the elementary and middles schools in the district.  A group that stopped at the Sturgis Williams Middle School said the walk brought back a lot of memories. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

STURGIS — The annual Senior Walk brought back memories and plenty of smiles as Sturgis Brown High School seniors returned to the halls of their former elementary and middle schools ahead of graduation weekend. 

Two busloads of seniors traveled through the district, walking the hallways of the schools where many of their educational journeys first began. Younger students lined the halls with cheers, applause, and high-fives as the soon-to-be graduates made their way through the buildings, stopping to visit former teachers and staff members who helped shape their path. 

Principal Pete Wilson said the event gives seniors a chance to reflect on how far they have come.

“We’re giving the seniors an opportunity to go through their primary schools that they got to experience in elementary school,” Wilson said. “It’s been a long time since they’ve been in these buildings, and they really appreciate that.”

Sunday is graduation.

“We have just under 200 graduating, so it’s a good number,” Wilson said. “Not all of them participate in the (senior) walk, but graduation is Sunday at 2 p.m., and it will be a great time.”

For senior Ethan Graf, the walk through Sturgis Williams Middle School brought back memories of friendships and good times from earlier school years.

“It definitely brings back memories of me and my friends hanging out in middle school,” Graf said. “Just a lot of good times.”

Senior Jaxon Cano said returning to the school halls reminded him how quickly time passes.  

“I think it’s really good for us to come back to where we came from,” Cano said. “It’s just a great place to be.” 

Cano also hopes the younger students watching the seniors walk the halls realize how quickly their own school years will pass.

“I’m hoping the younger kids think back to when we walked through while they’re walking someday and realize it’s coming a lot faster than they think,” he said.

Brooklynn Baird said reconnecting with teachers and students made the event especially meaningful.

“It is really nice to see all of my teachers,” Baird said. “I also see a lot of the kids that I have coached, and my little brother is here, so seeing all of the kids is exciting.”

Baird said the event was also an opportunity to thank the teachers who supported her through the years.

“Being able to say thank you to the teachers that have helped me along the way means a lot,” she said.

Baird said she is excited for graduation and preparing for her next chapter in college.  

“I am ready and really excited for graduation on Sunday and then heading off to college in Iowa,” she said.

title: Governor awards $500,000 to program converting paraprofessionals to teachers
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — South Dakota’s governor awarded money from an economic development fund he controls to a teacher apprenticeship program, to continue reducing the teacher shortage across the state.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — South Dakota’s governor awarded money from an economic development fund he controls to a teacher apprenticeship program, to continue reducing the teacher shortage across the state.

Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden announced a $500,000 Future Fund award for the South Dakota Teacher Apprenticeship Pathway program on Monday. The funding will add 31 spots to the program’s upcoming cohort. The state recently closed applications for the original 40 spots.

The program, started in 2023, allows full-time paraprofessionals — sometimes called teacher’s aides — to pursue a teaching degree online through Dakota State University in elementary or special education, or through Northern State University in secondary education, at a steep discount while retaining their position. 

Rhoden’s announcement expands the upcoming cohort to 71 participants.

“Our teacher apprenticeship program is a proven model that supports our teachers and our communities by developing more certified teachers and keeping educators in our schools,” Rhoden said in a news release.

The state gets money for the Future Fund by charging a fee to employers. They pay the fee when they submit payroll taxes that support unemployment benefits. 

Rhoden, who is running to keep his job, recently committed $4 million from the fund to bring a gunsmithing program to Western Dakota Technical College and $6 million to establish a South Dakota Defense Institute in Rapid City.

The $500,000 teacher apprenticeship grant brought the unobligated balance of the Future Fund to $23.9 million, said a spokesperson for the Governor’s Office of Economic Development.

State law says only that the fund “must be used for purposes related to research and economic development for the state,” but that’s about to change. Lawmakers approved new restrictions earlier this year, in response to past uses of the fund by Rhoden’s predecessor, former Gov. Kristi Noem. Rhoden was elevated from lieutenant governor after Noem resigned in January 2025 to become secretary of the federal Department of Homeland Security.

Noem’s controversial uses of the Future Fund included a fireworks show at Mount Rushmore, the construction of a state-owned shooting range near Rapid City that legislators refused to fund, a rodeo in Sioux Falls where Noem carried the American flag into the arena on horseback, and a workforce recruitment advertising campaign that featured Noem as the star.

Rhoden signed the legislative Future Fund reforms into law in March, but they won’t take effect until July 1 — after the June 2 primary election pitting Rhoden against three opponents for the Republican nomination. 

The reforms add legal definitions for acceptable uses of the fund, mandate more reporting to legislators about awards, specify the information required of applicants, direct the Governor’s Office of Economic Development to formulate rules for the fund’s use, and require the office to make recommendations to the governor about potential awards.

The announcement of funding for the teacher apprenticeship program comes after nearly 50 people graduated from it last weekend. Since the launch of the program, it has produced 118 graduates.

State Secretary of Education Joseph Graves said he’s visited current students and graduates to “see the impact they are making in their classrooms.”

“I am incredibly grateful for Governor Rhoden’s commitment to strengthening the future of education and empower the next generation of teachers,” Graves said in a news release.

Statewide, 144 teaching positions were unfilled as of July last year, weeks before the school year started, according to the Associated School Boards of South Dakota. That’s the lowest number in recent years: There were 202 unfilled positions in July 2024, 256 in 2023, 225 in 2022 and 174 in 2021.

The Department of Education started the apprenticeship program, but it is currently funded through the state Department of Labor and Regulation with a combination of state and federal grants to reimburse universities for the discounted portion of tuition and other programming. 

School districts pay $1,000 a year per apprentice. Apprentices are responsible for up to $1,000 a year in tuition, books and state assessments.

title: SD tourism leader: High gas prices could hold  ‘silver lining’
byline: By Bart Pfankuch South Dakota News Watch
description: Fireworks are launched from Mount Rushmore on July 3, 2020, while President Donald Trump visited the monument. Fireworks are planed once again this summer. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
SD tourism leader: High gas prices could hold  ‘silver lining’
Fireworks are launched from Mount Rushmore on July 3, 2020, while President Donald Trump visited the monument. Fireworks are planed once again this summer. Pioneer file photo 

KEYSTONE — Members of the Foley family of Green Bay, Wisconsin, are the quintessential visitors that tourism officials and operators hope will push South Dakota to a successful 2026 tourism season.

The family of four drove 12 hours from home for a weeklong tour of the Black Hills of South Dakota in late April and refused to let high gas prices, inflation or a soft national economy delay or postpone their visit.

“It’s our family trip, so if we needed to pay a little more for gas, it’s no big deal,” said Ryan Foley, who had just finished a scenic helicopter flight in Keystone with wife Alexis and daughters Amelia and Mabel.

While it may seem counterintuitive, South Dakota tourism secretary Jim Hagen said the Rushmore State’s extensive travel industry could actually benefit from higher gas prices.

Hagen said South Dakota has outperformed other states in prior years when gas prices were high or rising.

Furthermore, recent national surveys show that 90% of Americans said they will travel this summer despite higher costs, and that many are considering driving to a destination rather than flying, Hagen said.

“The silver lining is that South Dakota is seen as a regional drive market and because we really are the ultimate road trip destination.”

The 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, also known as the country’s semiquincentennial, will be celebrated across the state this summer.

Rapid City, which promotes itself as the City of Presidents, will capitalize on the country’s 250th anniversary with the Real America Birthday Bash planned for downtown on July 1-4.

The Black Hills region as a whole hopes to benefit from the nation’s big birthday, including the fireworks show planned for Mount Rushmore on July 3. Gov. Larry Rhoden has invited President Trump, but no official announcement has been made.

“With the 250th and the fireworks, we’re hoping for a good season,” said Bria Dillavou, owner of Mackabee Boutique in Keystone.

Travel South Dakota said tourism generated 4.7% of the state’s overall economy and 16.5% of all state sales tax collections last year, a total of $406 million. The agency said that tourism supports more than 59,000 jobs and that without tourism, each South Dakota household would have paid $1,121 more in taxes in 2025.

Hagen said that last year, economic concerns caused trepidation among tourists, a sentiment not shown in traveler surveys this year.

“This year, I think people are like, ‘We’ve had it. Let’s get out, let’s go have fun, let’s travel, even if they’ll be looking for good value along the way,” he said.

While the Black Hills may benefit from the 250th and, as usual, from the 86th Sturgis Motorcycle Rally on Aug. 7-16, tourism operators elsewhere across the state are optimistic for a strong year.

Sioux Falls is increasingly seen as a strong regional tourism market for shoppers and “foodies” who enjoy varied cuisines, said Teri Schmidt, CEO of Experience Sioux Falls.

The city and the rest of eastern South Dakota are attractive for visitors who want a family-friendly place to attend a wide range of annual events, including the Rock the Country Music Festival in late June, and the Sioux Falls Airshow and Hot Summer Nites car show in July.

Hunting, fishing, camping and other outdoor activities remain major draws for other East River locales, including the Glacial Lakes area in the northeast and the Missouri River in the central and southeast parts of the state.

South Dakota had what could be considered a so-so year for tourism in 2025, with 15 million visitors spending an estimated $5.2 billion, a 1.1% increase in revenues over 2024.

Schmidt said she and other tourism officials are keeping a wary eye on the national economy, which has been soft.

“If gas goes to 5 bucks a gallon, we don’t know how people are going to respond and we could be looking at a much different situation.”

Michelle Thomson, CEO of the Black Hills & Badlands Tourism Association, said the high cost of living and rising fuel prices could drive more tourists to travel in the spring and fall shoulder seasons, when they anticipate lower prices.

“People are anticipating spending more, but they want to have those experiences and are willing to pay a little bit more for it,” Thomson said.

title: Summit describes new carbon pipeline  route as not including SD
byline: By Joshua Haiar and Seth Tupper Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: An anti-carbon pipeline sign stands along a road near Canton, South Dakota, in 2024. Photo by Makenzie Huber, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Summit describes new carbon pipeline  route as not including SD
An anti-carbon pipeline sign stands along a road near Canton, South Dakota, in 2024. Photo by Makenzie Huber, South Dakota Searchlight 

SIOUX FALLS — The Iowa company attempting to build a multi-billion-dollar pipeline to capture and bury carbon dioxide from ethanol plants described a new route Wednesday that does not include South Dakota.

The language came in a press release about Summit Carbon Solutions’ plan to adjust its route in Iowa.

“The project will travel west through Nebraska to advance a dedicated sequestration solution in Wyoming as the core of the system,” the press release said.

Sabrina Zenor, spokesperson for the company, declined to say where in Wyoming the sequestration site would be located as the company has not submitted permitting applications at this time.

Previously, the company planned to collect carbon dioxide from ethanol plants in Iowa, Nebraska, Minnesota, South Dakota and North Dakota, and transport it via pipeline for underground sequestration in North Dakota.

But the project met fierce resistance in South Dakota, where affected landowners led a property rights revolt that culminated last year in a law banning the use of eminent domain for carbon pipelines. Eminent domain is a legal process for large public-use projects to gain land access when landowners are unwilling to grant it.

A prominent opponent of the project, landowner Jared Bossly, of rural Aberdeen, said he suspects ethanol plants in South Dakota still want the pipeline, and Summit still wants to include South Dakota.

“You know it’s not the end,” Bossly said. 

A spokesperson for Summit issued a statement later Wednesday in response to questions from the North Dakota Monitor.

“North Dakota, South Dakota, and Minnesota remain important for our company,” the statement said. “While we are currently prioritizing a westward route through Nebraska to Wyoming, our permitted pipeline and sequestration assets in North Dakota, our South Dakota partners and easements, along with our Minnesota permit, provide valuable optionality for future phases. We remain committed to building systems that support economic growth and long-term U.S. energy production.”

The project was proposed to capitalize on federal tax credits incentivizing the prevention of heat-trapping emissions into the atmosphere. Summit has lately signaled that some of its carbon dioxide could be pumped into oil wells to force more oil to the surface, in a process known as enhanced oil recovery. Summit’s Wednesday press release said the company is “continuing to evaluate complementary CO2 utilization opportunities, including enhanced oil recovery where appropriate.”

The company’s proposed reroute in Iowa will result in fewer miles of land, and fewer landowners, being affected by the project, Summit indicated in a regulatory filing.

The North Dakota Monitor’s Jeff Beach, and Black Hills Pioneer staff contributed to this report.

title: Hiker recovering at home after  30-foot fall at Community Caves
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — After falling nearly 30 feet down the steep and rocky embankments of Community Caves Monday, Kelby Zeestraten is recovering at home and wants other hikers to hike smarter, wear appropriate shoes, and alert somebody of their location if they’re hiking alone.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — After falling nearly 30 feet down the steep and rocky embankments of Community Caves Monday, Kelby Zeestraten is recovering at home and wants other hikers to hike smarter, wear appropriate shoes, and alert somebody of their location if they’re hiking alone.

Friends Zeestraten and Brittany Wilkinson consider themselves to be very outdoorsy, spending their free time hiking around the Black Hills. On Monday afternoon, after spending their morning working in Wilkinson’s shop, Belle Flowers, the friends decided to hike to Community Caves in Spearfish Canyon, something neither friend had ever done before.  

 “It was nice out, so (Wilkinson) and me decided to go out for a hike that afternoon. We got up there and it was worse than we had expected. It was very steep and rocky,” Zeestraten said.

The trail, near mile marker 13 on Highway 14A through the Canyon, is notorious for its steep, approximately half mile climb over loose talus, fragmented rocks of different sizes. After parking at a nearby pull out, hikers crossed the highway to find a trail that leads to Spearfish Creek. After crossing the creek, hikers follow the path before coming to the steep climb. The climb up, while navigating loose rock, is commonly described as strenuous and treacherous during icy weather. Ropes have been placed in areas along the trail to help climbers reach the plateau, where a series of limestone caves overlook the Canyon. 

After reaching the first set of caves, Zeestraten said the pair turned around to head back to their vehicle. On the way down, Zeestraten said she misstepped and began to slide down the embankment. 

“I tried to pull myself back up, and as I pulled myself up, I caught momentum to go down,” she said. “I couldn’t stop myself, because it’s like a 45-degree angle, so it was just straight down. I got going too fast and I couldn’t stop, so I rolled.”

Zeestraten “barrel rolled” approximately 30 feet down the embankment before colliding with a boulder. 

“After I fell, I looked up to see where (Wilkinson) was at, and I looked down and saw the blood on my knee,” she said. “I couldn’t find my phone; it fell out of my hands. So, I looked up at (Wilkinson) and I was like, ‘I (messed) up.’”

Zeestraten said her friend’s next reaction was to call for help. Wilkinson’s phone didn’t have service, so she found Zeestraten’s found nearby. It had service but was at 9% battery. 

Zeestraten then took the most natural step — she called her mom. 

“(My mom) is a surgery technician in Spearfish, so I FaceTimed her. I didn’t know if I was going to have enough service, but I called her so (Wilkinson) could show her what (my leg) looked like, just to see how bad it was, because I wasn’t looking at it,” she said. “She was like, ‘I’ll call 911 and meet you at the hospital.’ She was definitely scared and a little sporadic, but she knew that I needed help, so she got in the car and met me there.”

Shortly afterwards, Zeestraten received a call from 911, who asked Wilkinson to try and get enough service that the dispatcher could get an exact location for first responders. Wilkinson stayed on the phone with dispatch until the phone died.

Wilkinson, who has past military experience, worked to keep Wilkinson calm while they waited for first responders to arrive. 

“We both have a dark sense of humor, so we were cracking jokes and laughing,” Zeestraten said. “I was worried I was going to pass out, so she talked to the 911 dispatch, which was good because there was no way I was going to be able to do that. She kept her calm and kept her cool, and that was definitely needed.”

Scott Deaver, chief of Spearfish Fire Department, said that dispatch received a call at 5:02 p.m. to respond to a fallen person in need of rescue near Community Caves. He said Spearfish Ambulance Service was the first to respond and called for assistance at 5:11 p.m. Deaver said 6 firefighters responded to the scene at 5:36 p.m. 

While waiting for Spearfish Volunteer Fire Department and Spearfish Ambulance Service to arrive, a father and daughter pair encountered the friends. Zeestraten said they went back down to the road to wait for first responders’ arrival, then hiked back up with 2 emergency medical technicians (EMTs) to help bring Zeestraten back down to the road.

“It felt like I was up there forever, I’m sure I wasn’t up there for as long as I felt like I was,” she said. “But 2 very nice EMTs came, and they sat with us for a while checked my vitals, got my leg stabilized.”

After Spearfish Volunteer Fire Department arrived, Zeestraten was placed into a basket and hiked back down to the road before she was transported to Spearfish Monument Health’s emergency room in Spearfish.

Zeestraten said she tore the skin of her knee open down to the bone, requiring 9 internal and 12 external stitches. Her legs are scraped up, her right arm is bruised, and she said she has scrapes and a bruise the size of her hand on her right side. She said she’s recovering well, taking only Tylenol and Ibuprofen for pain, and she’s grateful that her injuries weren’t any worse. 

“I’m so grateful to the EMTs, search and rescue, the (emergency room staff), and the father and daughter who was there to help,” she said. “It could have been so much worse.”

Deaver cautioned hikers to wear sturdy hiking boots with proper grip and ankle support when setting out on trails like Community Caves.

title: Dig in to summer reading
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: WHITEWOOD — Area libraries have a plan to keep kids’ reading skills from fossilizing over the summer months — this year’s theme is “Unearth a Story,” and it has a distinctly prehistoric flair. In Whitewood, library director Deb Terhune is preparing a dinosaur-themed reading log to encourage kids to dig up a story. Sign-ups open today.
_full_text:
WHITEWOOD — Area libraries have a plan to keep kids’ reading skills from fossilizing over the summer months — this year’s theme is “Unearth a Story,” and it has a distinctly prehistoric flair. In Whitewood, library director Deb Terhune is preparing a dinosaur-themed reading log to encourage kids to dig up a story. Sign-ups open today.

Young participants will receive reading logs, decorated with 20 dinosaurs, that they can color in as they finish books. Participants who turn in their logs can then receive a prize.

“I think summer reading is essential to keep kids reading during the summer, so that they don’t forget about their very essential (reading) skills. We also try to make reading fun,” Terhune said.

Throughout the summer, there will be activities at the library for kids to engage with, up until an end of summer party at the end of July.

“We will have water games outside, other activities outside, prizes, and snacks during that afternoon,” Terhune said.

Whitewood is not the only local library in the region getting ready to help patrons — of all ages — unearth a story.

“All ages can participate, we’ll have kids events going on, all ages events that we will have more details out on soon, we have some presentations for teens that will be fun. Everybody is encouraged to read. Read as a family, read as individuals,” said Grace Balloch Memorial Library Director Amber Wilde. “We are really excited. We don’t have everything finalized, but we are getting excited for sure.”

Spearfish plans to set up a fun dinosaur display in the library, starting their 8-week program in early June. Summer reading in Belle Fourche also starts in June and runs for 6-8 weeks.

“We’ll have a magician here at the start of the program, and then we’re going to have a presentation from the raptor center here at the end of the program as well,” said Deadwood library director Kennedy Penk. “We’ll have lots of activities getting people engaged, coming into the library, and reading.”

title: Quick picks: Summer Reading
description: Local libraries across the region are buried in preparations for this year’s summer reading programs. However, they aren’t quite as buried as the prehistoric critters whose fossils inspired the state-wide theme for this year’s effort to keep kids practicing their literary skills all summer long. The summer reading program theme across local libraries in 2026 is “Unearth a Story.” It’s all about dinosaurs and fossils.
_full_text:
Local libraries across the region are buried in preparations for this year’s summer reading programs. However, they aren’t quite as buried as the prehistoric critters whose fossils inspired the state-wide theme for this year’s effort to keep kids practicing their literary skills all summer long. The summer reading program theme across local libraries in 2026 is “Unearth a Story.” It’s all about dinosaurs and fossils.  

This week, we bring you 6 recommendations from the Whitewood Public Library — titles that might get you excited about reading this summer. 

1. “How do dinosaurs say goodnight?” by Jane Yolen

Genre: Picture books/children’s fiction

In a few simple lines of verse on each spread, fathers and mothers are ready to put their youngsters to bed. But in this book, the youngsters are a wide variety of dinosaurs. How do dinosaurs say good night?

2. “Super Hungry Dinosaur” by Martin Waddell

Genre: Picture book/children’s humor

Here’s a book that begs to be read aloud. From the very first “GRRRRRR!” and “ROAR!” of the “Super Hungry Dinosaur,” kids will be rooting for Hal to save his parents and his dog, Billy, from the huge beast. And Hal saves them in the most unusual way (hint: It involves spaghetti) in this delightful twist on the tantrum story from well-loved and bestselling author Martin Waddell and debut illustrator Leonie Lord.

3. “Who Would Win: Dinosaur Destruction” by Jerry Pallotta

Genre: Children’s non-fiction

Discover prehistoric animal battles in this exciting bind up featuring four action-packed “Who Would Win?” books! Which prehistoric creatures would win in a head-to-head battle? What if there was a dinosaur tournament? Which pterosaur will be the champion? Find out all this and more in this awesome bind-up of four books in the popular “Who Would Win?” series. The collection features a range of prehistoric battles to satisfy all kinds of dinosaur fans, including Triceratops vs. Spinosaurus, Tyrannosaurus Rex vs. Velociraptor, Ultimate Pterosaur Rumble, and Ultimate Dinosaur Rumble. Kids will learn about each animal’s anatomy, behavior, and more alongside photos, charts, illustrations, and amazing facts

4. “How Big Were Dinosaurs” by Lita Judge 

Genre: Picture book/non-fiction

Have you ever wondered what it would be like to take a Velociraptor for a walk, or try to brush a Tyrannosaur’s teeth? We think of dinosaurs as colossal giants, but how big were they really?

With kid-friendly text and seriously silly illustrations, this fact-filled book puts dinosaurs next to modern animals so that you can see exactly how they size up. And a huge fold-out chart compares the dinos to each other, from the tiniest Microraptor to Argentinosaurus, the largest animal to ever walk the land.

5. “Dinosaurs Love Underpants” by Ben Cort

Genre: Picture books/fiction

The mystery of dinosaur extinction is solved! Scientists have plenty of theories about why dinosaurs are extinct, but the UK’s bestselling author/illustrator team of Claire Freedman and Ben Cort knows the real The dinos were wiped out in an Underpants War! This wacky celebration of underpants is perfect for reading aloud, and the hilarious antics of T. rex and the gang are endlessly entertaining. Featuring fun, vibrant art and short, rhyming text, “Dinosaurs Love Underpants” is a prehistoric pleasure parents and kids will want to read again and again.

 

6. “Have You Seen My Invisible Dinosaur” by Helen Yoon

Genre: Picture book/fiction

Help! This little girl has lost her best friend. He’s a dinosaur (not the extinct kind). He’s enormous (bigger than a panda!). He was last seen before she gave him a bath and washed off all the mud (maybe that wasn’t a good idea?). She’s tried to lure him with snacks and put up Lost Dinosaur posters, but nothing has helped. If only it weren’t such a clear day — if only it were raining, or snowing, or the leaves were falling, or . . . something. Would it help if she drew a picture? With delicate visual sleights of hand and an underlying sweetness, author-illustrator Helen Yoon invites us to see through a child’s eyes.

title: The Mercy Sloane Chronicles:Chapter 3
description: Mercy Sloan Chronicles Installment #3
_full_text:
The Mercy Sloane Chronicles

Mercy Sloan Chronicles Installment #3

Mercy spent the first part of the silence glancing around Ardath’s house, which wasn’t much fancier than her own. Just like Mercy’s, it was one small room with a squat, round-legged potbelly stove in the corner; same bare walls, just more worn. The only decorations were hides stretched and hung on the walls, and the only object of comfort was a faded, threadbare quilt laid neatly at the foot of the narrow, iron bedstead. The mugs brimming with strong tea were cracked, and the one Ardath drank from was missing a handle. But beneath the shabbiness, the room hummed with efficiency.

Mercy waited, listening to the wind sighing around the corners of the small house. She pretended to take a sip of tea, but her throat was too tight to swallow, and when she set the cup back on the table, some tea sloshed out. Ardath reached over to wipe the spilled tea with her sleeve, and Mercy surprised them both by saying, “When he said he wanted to leave, I said I wanted to stay.” Ardath set down her mug, nodded calmly, and said, “Come with me.”

Behind Ardath’s house stood a simple, hand-hewn barn, built with care. Sturdy tree trunks sanded to softness served as the four anchored corners, and the planed wood of the walls was thick and square, so it looked almost as though the barn had grown there of its own accord. The doors were thrown open to let in the summer light and fresh wind. In the yard beside the barn, a few stout ponies grazed. As Ardath approached, they plodded toward her. 

“You’ll take her with you,” Ardath said, nodding to the first pony to reach them. The pony was red with a long, blond mane and tail, and Ardath patted the horse on the forehead with her scarred knuckles. “She’s old, but she knows this prairie better than any other man, beast, or child.” The pony knickered a little at Ardath’s touch. “I call her Red, but I’m not good with names. You call her what you want.” With that, she turned and walked into the barn.

Mercy hesitated, but the pony followed Ardath, so Mercy followed the pony. The trio passed through the wide door toward the eastern wall that was lined with well-used tack. Ardath pulled down a frayed rope halter from a row of hooks full of similarly worn halters and handed it to Mercy. 

“Do you know how to…” Ardath began, and for the first time in their whole, mostly silent, visit, Mercy felt she was supposed to speak.

“No,” Mercy said quickly. “I don’t know anything. ANYTHING.” She hadn’t meant to sound so desperate. “Anything,” she said again quietly, and then she knew she did mean to sound a little desperate; she was terrified the visit was coming to a close, and she wasn’t ready to go back to her empty homestead yet. But Ardath only nodded slowly and slung the halter over the mare’s ear and chin.

“You’ll have to go bareback until you get a saddle,” Ardath said with a squint that Mercy thought almost looked like a smile. “But it’s a good way to learn. You’re young enough to fall off and get back on.” Then she chuckled thoughtfully and winked.

 Eliza Blue TMC
Eliza Blue 

It was the laughter and the wink that changed everything. Mercy knew right then and there she didn’t ever need to tell Ardath about Granger or the long, awkward train ride or the strange night in the cabin where they’d lain like brother and sister even though it was meant to be their wedding night or even how she’d known as soon as she saw the front porch of that ridiculous house that he would go and she would not.

Ardath handed the horse’s lead to Mercy, then ducked into a grain bin in the corner of the barn. She pulled out a silky black-and-brown puppy from the shadowy corner. “He’ll come with too,” she said, handing the warm, wriggling body to Mercy. “He’s old enough to be weaned, and he’s from the last litter my dog, Howard, will sire.” Ardath said the second part with a sigh, and then she straightened up and winked one last time before adding in a tone completely different than any previous utterance: “I can promise you one thing, he’ll be as good-a company as any man, probably better.”

Did Mercy leave Ardath’s house and think with fear or pleasure: “That will be me in 50 years if I stay…” Well, you’d have to know Mercy’s every thought to answer that question, but when she saw the rickety porch come into view and realized she’d been thinking of the ride as the ride home, she figured that was as good an omen as any that she’d made the right choice.

title: McCook Lake refills amid debate about sufficiency of flood cleanup
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Birds stand atop a sandbar in McCook Lake on April 8. Photo by Joshua Haiar, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
McCook Lake refills amid debate about sufficiency of flood cleanup
Birds stand atop a sandbar in McCook Lake on April 8. Photo by Joshua Haiar, South Dakota Searchlight 

McCOOK LAKE — Nearly 2 years after a historic flood devastated the southeast South Dakota community of McCook Lake, local officials and community groups say the lake is moving closer to normal summer use. 

But people who use the lake are divided about whether it’s ready.

Renae Hansen, who lives in the McCook Lake community, submitted a petition asking the state to maintain a no-wake restriction on the lake until further cleanup is completed. Hansen said 468 residents and lake users signed the document in one week.

“The reality on the ground is it’s not good to go,” Hansen said.

The petition states that 11 acres of the 223-acre lake have been cleared of debris, evidenced by an Army Corps of Engineers survey conducted after the state’s cleanup work. Hansen said the state’s work has left submerged hazards and newly formed islands that could become dangerous to people unaware of what’s under the water.

Dirk Lohry, with the McCook Lake Association, said Hansen and others overstate the danger, and their views do not represent those of most lake residents and the immediate community.

“Most of those signatures are not people who live on McCook Lake or even use McCook Lake,” Lohry said. “I don’t think that having 500 signatures gives this particular position any more credibility.”

Lohry said the lake has been surveyed with sonar and by boat, and hazards have been marked with buoys. He said the low water levels exposed areas that could pose problems, allowing cleanup crews and volunteers to identify and remove debris.

“We’ve done a pretty good survey of everything,” Lohry said. “Anything that could be a problem has certainly been exposed.”

Meanwhile, a group of local entities including Hansen’s employer, the McCook Lake Izaak Walton League, issued a press release describing recovery efforts as “ongoing.” The other entities are North Sioux City, Union County, and the McCook Lake Association. 

The groups said more than 64 tons of debris and about 20,000 cubic yards of sediment have been removed through work involving South Dakota Game, Fish and Parks and Three Oaks Construction. Game, Fish and Parks used $1 million of state funds to contract with Three Oaks, of North Sioux City, after a competitive bidding process, according to the department. Work began on May 15 last year and concluded on the Aug. 1 deadline.  

Additional visible debris has been removed by the McCook Lake Association with help from Stockton Towing, and known debris will continue to be marked with buoys and removed as water levels rise, according to the press release. It also says that water quality testing showed conditions were within acceptable ranges for recreational use, and that fish sampling showed contaminant levels within safe consumption thresholds and consistent with pre-flood findings. 

Water has been pumped into the lake from the Missouri River since April 1, and the lake is expected to reach 7 feet of added depth soon. That will be the first time the lake has been full since the flood.

However, Hansen and some others fear that there won’t be enough depth between the hazards, like newly formed islands, and the surface.

“If you put 7 feet of water on top of one of these new islands, what happens if a 6-foot-tall person dives in?” she said. “You don’t think they’ll go 1 foot underwater?”

The June 2024 flood followed days of heavy rain and a record surge in the Big Sioux River. Authorities used a 1976 flood mitigation plan that diverted river water toward McCook Lake to protect North Sioux City and Dakota Dunes, hoping the lake would rise and spill over with minimal damage. Instead, the water slammed into dozens of McCook Lake homes, destroyed about 20 and carved deep gouges into the north shore. Some residents had to be rescued that night, but no one was killed. 

The South Dakota Department of Game, Fish and Parks lifted the lake’s no-wake restriction on April 1 this year after cleanup work concluded, meaning boats can now drive fast enough to cause a wake.  

Game, Fish and Parks did not respond to an interview request. Hansen said the department dismissed her concerns, arguing that swimming in any lake or river comes with risk.

“Not every other lake in South Dakota had a forced flood that took out the community,” Hansen said. “If South Dakota had a plan to divert the water to the lake, why did they not have a plan for recovery?”

Lohry said he cannot guarantee the lake is risk-free, but said that is true of any body of water.

“I’m confident that we’ve done a good enough survey on the entirety of the lake to where it’s certainly safe for boating,” he said.

Hansen said her concern is not only with residents who know the lake, but with Memorial Day and July Fourth visitors who may interpret the lifted wake restriction as a sign that the lake is back to normal.

“When they hear all that, why would they doubt what the authorities are saying?” Hansen said.

Lohry said there are plans to install additional signage that warns of safety risks.

The press release from the local groups says cleanup and testing will continue, and water levels are expected to drop again in the fall, creating more opportunities to plan for additional cleanup.
