title: TIFs, taxes, transparency, and tech take center stage at Butte Co. candidate forum
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Residents rose with questions for Butte County commission candidates during a forum in Belle Fourche. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Butte County Candidate Forum.JPG
Residents rose with questions for Butte County commission candidates during a forum in Belle Fourche. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

 Butte candidate forum.JPG
Candidates for Butte County Commission, auditor, and register of deeds gathered to answer questions from the public. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

BELLE FOURCHE — Transparency, taxes, and data centers loomed large at a Butte County candidate forum in Belle Fourche last week.

Candidates running for county commission in Districts 1 and 5, as well as the unopposed candidates for county auditor and register of deeds, were all present. Jason Kari, an incumbent running for commission in District 5, is unopposed. So is Annie Capp, the incumbent county auditor. Stephanie Lippincott is the sole candidate running for register of deeds.

Unopposed candidates do not appear on voters’ ballots.

“Any of the candidates that don’t have opposition are given that certificate of nomination following the election,” Capp explained.

Cory Tolley and Doug Larson are both running for the District 1 seat.

“I believe with my 30-some-odd years of being self-employed in construction-related fields, that I can help make the budget stretch a little further and start working on roads and some other things that need to be addressed without having to raise taxes,” Tolley said.

He told residents that he would like to see county commission meetings moved to the evenings, so that more residents can attend. Right now, the commission generally meets twice a month at 9:30 a.m. on Tuesdays.

“Once a quarter, we do have an evening meeting,” said Tom Brunner, the chair of the Butte County Republican Party and a sitting commissioner from District 2.

“I believe that the meetings need to be held, or at least part of the meetings need to be held in the evenings. Currently, the meetings are all held during the day, and it makes it very hard for people who are working, it makes it very hard for them to attend and voice their concerns,” Tolley said.

Larson said he believes one evening meeting a quarter is enough.

“I think that at least most of the commissioners that I know are open to phone calls and things that might get your interest,” Larson said. “If you have a really pressing issue, they can come and state their case.”

Tolley told members of the public assembled at the forum that he hopes to maintain a website where his constituents can express their concerns if elected.

“Voters need to be listened to longer than June 2. I would like to be able to, every time I go to a meeting, pull up and quickly refresh where my rankings are and where people feel they need help,” Tolley said. “I believe that is the level of transparency that needs to start coming to all government.”

Senate Bill 96 passed this legislative session, allowing counties to impose a “gross receipts tax not to exceed one-half percent” on taxable goods and services. Then, all proceeds from that tax can be deposited into a property tax reduction fund.

“For me, looking at it, it is going to cost everybody who shops in the county; it is going to cost them taxes. Everybody is going to be paying for it,” Larson said. “For me, it is more of a talking point at the legislature to try and make people happy rather than to actually cut taxes.  It’s just rearranging where taxes are coming from.”

Tolley said that he doesn’t support raising the sales tax in Butte County.

“I personally don’t support it. If we were able to break down the books and audit and start negotiating with contractors and where we are spending our money, then we could make the books budget out without raising taxes and without raising sales tax, which is going to hurt other people,” Tolley said.

Brunner said, as a commissioner, he’s not sure about the provision because it only provides relief to taxes on owner-occupied property.

“It is going to be some help to owner-occupied, but think about a young family that maybe doesn’t own a home that is renting, that spent a lot of money on groceries and other consumables for a young family, it is going to hurt them,” Burnner said. “They are going to feel the pain worse than anybody because it won’t affect rent. There are no tax cuts for commercial property, for rental property, it is all owner-occupied.”

Brunner said many of the people who would receive property tax relief if Butte County implements the new sales tax represent a reliable voting bloc.

“People who will benefit the most are elderly people who don’t spend a lot on food or consumables. They have a home that is paid for. They will get a nice cut,” Brunner said. “I think the legislature probably went after the votes when they did this.”

Tax increment financing also came up during the candidate forum.

Tax increment financing is a public financing system that uses future increases in property taxes to reimburse the costs of public improvements built within a designated TIF boundary. The value of all the properties inside the district is assessed or calculated, and the total amount of property tax generated by all those properties is noted — the base amount of property tax revenues. All property revenue above this base amount, for the life of the TIF, is captured by the TIF to refund the costs of the public improvements or project. This amount — the amount over the base — is called the “tax increment.” Over time, property values are presumed to increase in part due to infrastructure improvements brought about by the TIF project itself. When the TIF is retired, the total taxation values revert to the original taxing entities.

“I don’t think we should be giving out TIFs at all,” Tolley said. “Why are we giving away revenue? Why are we giving tax breaks to companies that want to come build multi-million dollar housing?”

Tolley said rather than offering TIFs as an incentive to developers, the county could explore a grant-system that favors local companies.

“I think that if we are going to put money into something, what about grants or opportunities for contractors to expand those projects, so that they hire our children and we stop exporting them, and spend the money locally,” Tolley said.

Larson also expressed distaste for TIFs.

“Big money people don’t need to have us give them the infrastructure and all the major expenses to come into our county,” Larson said. “It just doesn’t make sense.”

Belle Fourche City Councilman Clark Sowers attended the forum and asked the candidates to address data centers and explain why they would or wouldn’t support their construction in Butte County.

“I don’t believe that we have the power or the water or, honestly, the need to allow a data center into the county,” Tolley said. He said areas with more resources and infrastructure are welcome to give data centers a try, but Butte County would not be a good proving ground for that kind of development.

“I had a patient last week ask me about it, so I did some research on it,” Larson, who is a chiropractor, said. “Right now, it does not have a place in South Dakota or Butte County.”

The county commission may pass a resolution to ban data centers if Butte County voters decide that they should. A resolution will also appear on the June 2 ballot. If it passes, the county commission will have to pass an ordinance that keeps data centers out of the county.

title: Butte County commission candidates
description: Voters in Butte County will head to the polls June 2 to vote on vacant commission seat. Two people are running for 1 open position which is a 4-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.
_full_text:
Voters in Butte County will head to the polls June 2 to vote on vacant commission seat. Two people are running for 1 open position which is a 4-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.

Doug Larson

 Doug Larson
Doug Larson 

Name and what you do for a living? 

Doug Larson Doctor of Chiropractic

What motivated you to run for this office?

I have been in practice for 40 years. I have been interested in politics since a young age, I am nearing retirement age and I thought, now is the time to get involved. 

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

Over the years of my career, when an elected official would come to my office, I would have conversation about topics that were affecting city and county residents. Also, when a non-elected individual would come in, we could have short discussions about their concerns. All the while I would remain neutral. For 40 years I have heard both sides of the hot topics and now am ready to help solve what concerns our citizens. 

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I have been on the board for Christian Life Center for 12 years. I have been on the Belle Fourche School District Foundation Board for 19 years. I was a review Doctor for Chiropractic Associates of South Dakota for 10 years, reviewing doctors charges, looking for insurance over payment or illegal billing. 

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I am still full time at my chiropractic practice so getting to county commission meetings has been difficult. Once elected I will adjust my schedule to attend many meeting to get up to speed on issues before I take office in January. 

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Yes. We are in a rural area where the only local news that concerns us is with local news reporters. Rapid City news touches very little on things that concern Butte County. 

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in Butte County?

Most all of the residents I have talked to are concerned about property taxes. Then next topic is the county road conditions, followed by government waste. 

How do you intend to solve these issues?

Look at property evaluations and make sure all properties of equal utilization are evaluated equally across the board. Look at freezing home values for residents over 65 until properties are sold. I believe that our current commission is doing their best at containing spending waste, but having been on a board that reviewed my peers, I will look hard and be very diligent about how funds are spent. 

What do you believe is working for the county, and how will you retain that progression?

I believe that most of the county’s residents and government officials are on the same page as far as issues that need to be addressed. As an elected official I believe we need to lower the temperature when discussing topics so each side can be heard in a non-confrontational environment. 

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

Transparency in government means that every discussion or vote I make I should be able, to anyone who asks, explain to them why I voted the way I did and back it with facts. 

What else do you want people to know about you?

I am a family man with a wonderful, beautiful wife. We have 2 children. Dr. Jade Larson, a chiropractor as well, and his wife Rebecca, and Kelsi Kling, a registered nurse, and her husband Alex. We are blessed with 6 grandchildren. We are a caring family, not only for our own, but for our community as well. 

With new development planned for the county, how should the county ensure adequate infrastructure (especially water)?

When a permit request is issued, the development should show a final blueprint of the development as to how many properties will be sold. They should explain where the water will be coming from, whether a new well, which would need to be tested to ensure it could accommodate the plans. If and existing well, tests must be made to ensure it is not toing to cause and issue with previous users. I believe state government should be involved with these decisions as well. 

Housing prices and availability are putting a crunch on homeowners and the ability to purchase a home. What steps need to be taken to ensure residents are not taxed out of their homes?

Fair and equal assessments. Our assessor should be familiar with the area and assess according to the area. Butte County is very divers in my view. A cookie cutter app is not representative of our population. 

Cory Tolley

Name and what you do for a living? 

Cory Tolley – I am self employed with Mtn Man Metal Art & Mtn Man Hauling & Excavation 

What motivated you to run for this office? 

I am known for have great problem-solving skills and would like to apply them to several issues I see in the County. Roads being at the top of that list Followed closely by taxes. 

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position? 

I have been self-employed my entire life and work in the contractor fields. That experience can be used to better budget and make more cost effective solutions for the county’s needs. 

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held? I have never held any offices but have ran companies and crews my entire life. 

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I have not attended any meetings yet this year. I have, however reviewed all the minutes from the meetings. 

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not? 

I believe newspaper is a very important for news and keeping the community up to date. 

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in Butte County? 

Roads and taxes are a common topic not only in the meetings, but also from the people I have spoken with. 

How do you intend to solve these issues? 

I have set up a website www.Tolleyfordistrict1.com that allows the voters to register and tell me what they feel is in the most need. I want to hear from the people and address their concerns. I want them to have a voice with me as their commissioner and plan on keeping their concerns as my top priority. 

What do you believe is working for the county, and how will you retain that progression?

I think the counties growth is going well, and I will continue to support programs that lead to growth. 

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions? 

Feedback will be entered after each meeting to my Facebook page and to my website. I want feedback from my voters and also them to please come attend meetings I will be proposing the meets go to the evenings so more people can attend. 

What else do you want people to know about you? 

I am driven and dedicated to improving the roads and lowering property taxes. 

With new development planned for the county, how should the county ensure adequate infrastructure (especially water)? 

I believe the developers should be cost sharing these expenses. 

Housing prices and availability are putting a crunch on homeowners and the ability to purchase a home. What steps need to be taken to ensure residents are not taxed out of their homes? 

We need to be much more mindful of our expenses and our spending. Stop raising taxes and use our budget much more effectively.

title: Meet Spearfish’s 2 new orthopedic surgeons
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Rainbow welcome banners, made by the crew at the Monument Health Orthopedics and Sports Medicine Clinic in Spearfish, still hang over the desks of Dr. Jake Enos, pictured left, and Dr. Patrick Ensminger — both of whom are new-to-the-community orthopedic surgeons.
_full_text:
Meet Spearfish’s 2 new orthopedic surgeons
Rainbow welcome banners, made by the crew at the Monument Health Orthopedics and Sports Medicine Clinic in Spearfish, still hang over the desks of Dr. Jake Enos, pictured left, and Dr. Patrick Ensminger — both of whom are new-to-the-community orthopedic surgeons. 

SPEARFISH — Orthopedic surgeons are in the business of changing lives for the better — and Spearfish now has 2 more in practice. 

“I think, in medicine, our job is unique because, oftentimes, we can get fairly immediate gratification, even if that is within 6 months, someone who is totally debilitated, getting function back, that is really rewarding,” said Dr. Jake Enos. “I think in primary care, they see their reward in a lifetime of caring for someone. I think for us it is more immediate, returning people to function.”

Enos is one of 2 orthopedic surgeons who have recently joined the Monument Health team in Spearfish. Enos started working at the clinic on Colorado Boulevard on Sept. 1 — straight out of fellowship training at the University of Wisconsin.

In March, fellow orthopedic surgeon Patrick Ensminger also took a job at the clinic. Ensminger noted that a lot of doctors who chose to specialize in orthopedics are trained in engineering. They have to understand how things work — how they fit together and function.

“I think you have to be geared toward that mindset of structural integrity and all of that stuff. You’re fixing bones and joints and tendons,” said Ensminger.

He came to Spearfish from Louisiana, where he practiced for 3 years.

Enos and Ensminger were residents together in Kansas City, and were surprised to learn they had both taken jobs at Monument Health.

The orthopedic clinic in Spearfish drew both doctors for different reasons.  

“People genuinely like coming to work and working here. I think our patients feel that,” Enos said. “We’re a family, and I think when we take care of our patients, they are an extension of our family.”

Ensminger said Dr. Richard Little’s leadership is part of why he chose to move to Spearfish and work for Monument Health.

“It’s a great team, meeting Dr. Little, who has kind of built this up; he’s a great, great physician, great surgeon, great mentor,” Ensminger said.

“Meeting Dr. Little and his mentorship, the way that he captained the ship of this practice can’t be overstated. He just does a great job taking care of his patients, being a mentor to us, and just being an all around good guy, Enos added. “In taking my first job out of training, I knew that I wanted good mentorship and someone I could trust.”

Now, Enos and Ensminger are hoping to earn patient trust.

“I think that the message that I try to give my patients, and I try to make them feel that I treat my patients and the people that come to see me like my family members,” Enos said.

Ensminger said he enjoys taking patient questions and that all inquiries are important and valid. As a surgeon, he said, he wants his patients to always be able to make informed decisions.

“You have to remind yourself and remember that somebody, especially if you’re taking them to surgery, they are putting a lot of trust in you,” Ensminger said. “They deserve information. I try to give them information and let them make a decision.”

“I want the community to know, I think that is oftentimes a barrier to people seeking care as they think that they won’t be listened to or that they will be blown off, and that is just not the case,” Enos added. “I think what I would say for myself is that I am family-oriented. If you come into my clinic, I’ll be nice to you. I’ll listen to you, and I will take the time to get to know you and take your problem seriously. I think that is the most important thing.”

Answering detailed questions and building relationships takes time.

“Another benefit of Monument is that this isn’t a numbers game. I’m not in and out of the room where I don’t sit down, and the people barely see me,” Enos said. “I feel like we are afforded the opportunity to really develop a relationship with the patients and really, truly have conversations about what is bothering them and really do an in-depth physical examination to really get at the root of what’s bothering them. There are some practices where you just don’t have time to do that.”

Ensminger said it’s good that clinicians and surgeons aren’t pressured to “keep their numbers up.” That isn’t to say that Spearfish doesn’t have a relatively high demand for orthopedic care.

“We have younger folks who are really active in the outdoors, who are athletic. Then we also have an aging population, that is the retirement community, that has things like arthritis,” Enos said. “We like being able to take care of all of those folks.”

title: Free hunger banquet raises poverty awareness in Lead
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Participants in the NHSOS Hunger Banquet were assigned a class, with the lower class sharing beans and rice on the floor, while the upper class enjoyed table seating of a three-course meal. Pioneer photos by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
Free hunger banquet raises poverty awareness in Lead
Participants in the NHSOS Hunger Banquet were assigned a class, with the lower class sharing beans and rice on the floor, while the upper class enjoyed table seating of a three-course meal. Pioneer photos by Wendy Pitlick 

 Free hunger banquet raises poverty awareness in Lead

LEAD — The Northern Hills Sources of Support Hunger Banquet drew more than 50 people to the Historic Homestake Opera House, Tuesday. 

The event was intended to raise awareness about hunger and poverty issues in the Northern Black Hills. Participants were assigned a class, and were served a meal according to that class. Those who were in the upper class were given a full, three-course meal, but their food was taken away from them before they finished and visibly thrown into the garbage, to demonstrate food waste. The middle class was served half of a wrap and a bag of chips, and the lower class sat on the floor, where they shared beans and rice. 

The event also featured booths from area support organizations, such as the Society of St. Vincent DePaul, Clothe a Kid, Northern Hills Diversion, Hope’s Kitchen, the Lord’s Cupboard Food Pantry, and more. 

Northern Hills Sources of Support is a nonprofit organization based in Spearfish, with a mission to create poverty aware communities and to build strong and supportive relationships with those in need. The organization also coordinates with nonprofits in the area, to help eliminate overlaps and identify gaps in services. 

Northern Hills SOS plans to organize another hunger banquet in Belle Fourche this summer.

title: Sturgis tables  Rally sponsor decision  until June
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Last March the city of Sturgis voted to contract with a third party to handle Rally sponsorship contracts. But whether the city contracts with a local, national, or a nonprofit firm will not be decided until after the municipal election in June. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Sturgis tables  Rally sponsor decision  until June
Last March the city of Sturgis voted to contract with a third party to handle Rally sponsorship contracts. But whether the city contracts with a local, national, or a nonprofit firm will not be decided until after the municipal election in June. Pioneer file photo 

STURGIS — The city of Sturgis will wait until after the June election to make a decision about how to handle its Sturgis Motorcycle Rally sponsorship contracts. 

In March, the city council unanimously decided to outsource Rally sponsorship contracts. Under the approved plan, the city will have a publicly available contract with a third-party company that will handle all Rally sponsorship deals. The contract will include city assets made available to sponsors, deliverables, how much the city will pay the outside firm, and expected revenues from sponsorships. The outside firm will enter into confidential agreements with Rally sponsors. 

At issue is whether the city will contract with a national, local, or a nonprofit entity to handle Rally sponsorships. Each option has its own benefits and drawbacks, as outlined by City Attorney Eric Davis. For example, contracting with a national firm could cost more, but the firm could be able to leverage existing relationships with major corporations to sell more sponsorships. Davis urged the council to take its time making the decision that affects sponsorship revenue. 

In an average year, the city of Sturgis raises $800,000 to $1 million in Rally sponsorship revenue. That money goes into the general fund to be used for city operations. 

On May 4, the Sturgis City Council agreed to table the issue until its first meeting in June, after the newly elected mayor and city council ward 1 representative have been sworn in.  

While taking their time to make decisions about future Rally sponsorships, the Sturgis City Council assured the public that it has a plan to handle 2026 sponsorships for the Rally. The city will continue to execute and administer sponsorship contracts, but will stipulate the contracts must be public documents. However, information about sponsor-specific pricing, deliverables, and related business and operational information could be redacted from the public documents, to the extent that is allowed by state law. 

The idea to use a third-party agent came after city officials researched the possibility of opening up all Rally sponsorship agreements to the public, something former Mayor Kevin Forrester pledged to do when he was elected. However, City Administrator Aaron Jordan and Davis said as they began meeting with existing and previous Rally sponsors with the proposal for the new policy change, major Rally sponsors said they will not sign the public documents, which outline exactly how much sponsors are paying and what they are getting for their money. Davis said the more city officials met with sponsors, the more apparent it became that confidential sponsorship agreements are an industry standard. 

Councilwoman Ruth Nichols said the reason is because many of those corporations also sponsor other events throughout the country, and they don’t want those other events to know the details of their Sturgis contracts.

title: SD’s southern Black Hills mountain goats face an uncertain future
byline: By Nicole Schlabach Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Mountain goats run through the Needles Eye Tunnel, a popular place for visitors to see mountain goats in South Dakota’s Custer State Park. In recent years, tour guides have reported fewer sightings in the area. Photo by Nicole Schlabach, for South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
SD’s southern Black Hills mountain goats face an uncertain future
Mountain goats run through the Needles Eye Tunnel, a popular place for visitors to see mountain goats in South Dakota’s Custer State Park. In recent years, tour guides have reported fewer sightings in the area. Photo by Nicole Schlabach, for South Dakota Searchlight 

CUSTER STATE PARK — Daniel Milks, the founder and lead guide at My XO Adventures, has introduced many visitors in South Dakota’s Black Hills to mountain goats.

“It’s an eye-opener, and a jaw-dropper,” he said. “I’ve had adults just lose their minds when they see a mountain goat.”

Some wildlife photographers enjoy seeing the goats more than the bison on his tours. “They look like something out of a children’s storybook,” Milks said, “like little magical creatures from a fairytale land.”

He sometimes asks his clients what they loved best about a tour. “And if they saw the mountain goats,” he said, “I guarantee you it will be in their top 3.”

But mountain goats in the Southern Black Hills haven’t been doing so well in recent years. If the goats disappear from the area, it would be hard to estimate the impact on Milks and his business.

It probably wouldn’t affect the number of tours he books. But “would it affect the way we feel as guides going through the Hills? Yes, big time,” Milks said. “Would it decrease the experience of a guest in South Dakota, and leave less of a good impression? Absolutely.”

To keep track of the goats, South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks counts the animals observed by helicopter at the same rock outcroppings roughly every other year. This helps officials estimate their population size, while using other variables including radio collar data.

The department counted 29 goats in the southern Black Hills in 2024 — a continuation of a downward slide since a peak of 106 in 2016. The low numbers led to the cancellation of the mountain goat hunting season for 2026, the fourth year in a row.

“That is not good. That is definitely indicating we are in a big-time decline,” said Chad Lehman, senior wildlife biologist at the GF&P. “If they persist on that decline, that trajectory, my estimate would be that they would be gone in the core area by 2030.”

The core area extends over 150 square miles from Custer to Mount Rushmore and north of Keystone.

Meanwhile, an isolated population in Spearfish Canyon has been growing. Last year, there were up to 25 goats in the Canyon, as reported to the GF&P by Spearfish residents.

If the Spearfish population continues to do well, Lehman said, the GF&P could potentially reinvigorate the southern Black Hills population with younger goats from the canyon.

“At least we have a secondary population that is keeping us from going completely extinct in the Black Hills,” he said.

Yet the long-term outlook is uncertain for animals in a place they may not be built to thrive in.

Challenging environment in the southern Black Hills

In the 1920s, 6 goats from Alberta, Canada, escaped from a zoo in Custer State Park. Accustomed to mountainous regions, they headed straight for the area around Black Elk Peak. By the 1950s, the population had grown to more than 300, and by the late 1960s, hunting seasons were underway.

The rest of their history is defined by periods of decline and recovery. Based on these fluctuations, the GF&P has both moved goats from the Southern Hills to other western states and added goats from other states to the population.

The recent dip marks roughly the third time the population has declined.

There is no research on the recent numbers, but a 2006-2018 study led by the GF&P theorized that the goats’ survival was connected to the pine forest in the Southern Black Hills.

“It’s important to note that survival was heavily tied to the vegetation up there. If you have a lot of vegetation, it seemed like their survival rates declined,” Lehman said.

The forested Black Hills are different from many other mountain ranges where goats live, explained Greg Van Den Berg, the treasurer of the Rocky Mountain Goat Alliance, a conservation nonprofit.

Mountain goats thrive in exposed, alpine environments with grassy foraging areas where it’s easier to see predators approaching. When the goats sense danger, they quickly escape onto steep terrain.

The Black Hills have less visibility. 

“The elevation is not super high. We have a lot of cliffs, for example in the Black Elk Wilderness, but a lot of those trees are right up against that mountainous area,” Van Den Berg said.

Because mountain lions rely on stealth, they can use trees to stalk and attack. Mountain lion predation was the leading cause of death identified for radio-collared goats during the GF&P study.

Spearfish Canyon has more open areas leading to cliffs, Van Den Berg added, which might contribute to their growth in that area.

Although wildlife managers can’t change the geography of the Southern Hills to help mountain goats avoid predators, there are ways to create more open areas.

Natural and other ways to help the goats

The goats’ survival in the Southern Hills improved when a pine beetle epidemic, which peaked in 2012, killed many of the trees in their range.

“From about 2012 to 2018 we saw a huge resurgence in mountain goat survival,” Lehman said. “The beetle essentially came in and cleaned out a lot of the trees around those precipitous terrain spires.”

Over the last couple of years, pine beetle activity has increased a little bit. “It’s hard to say. If they do come back, that could potentially have a big impact on the goats,” Lehman said.

Forest and wildlife managers could also pursue human-made solutions.

The GF&P’s 2024-2028 Mountain Goat Management Plan says “prescribed burning and timber management in these landscapes can enhance mountain goat habitat.” The plan’s first objective is to “maintain, manage, and protect existing mountain goat habitat.”

But those habitat interventions haven’t begun. The next steps are dependent on collaborations with the U.S. Forest Service, which manages much of the land in the Black Hills.

“Hopefully we can continue to collaborate and work with our U.S. Forest Service partners in that area to try and provide more openings for them, especially around the granite outcroppings,” Lehman said.

South Dakota Searchlight did not receive a response to questions sent to the Forest Service.

Because of the difficult terrain, the habitat work could cost hundreds of thousands of dollars. The funding would likely need to come from multiple sources, including the Forest Service, the GF&P, and outside sources such as nonprofit organizations.

Adding mountain goats from other states is another option. But that is expensive, too, and those goats might face the same challenges upon arrival.

“I would not encourage us to bring goats in if we’re going to have a problem with our current landscape and vegetation,” Lehman said. “I would prefer to maybe do some habitat manipulations first.”

Even if everything else were in place, timber management is not permitted in a substantial portion of the goats’ habitat: the federally designated Black Elk Wilderness. In that area, “you’re relying on Mother Nature to either provide mountain pine beetles or wildfires,” Lehman said.

Look, but don’t approach

Les Heiserman regularly takes photos of the Spearfish Canyon goats, usually right from the road where he can see and listen to visitors’ reactions. “People will say, ‘I was just in Yellowstone, and I didn’t see this much wildlife. We’ll talk about this all the way home.’”

But visitors might like the goats a little too much. “People don’t want to keep their distance,” he said. “They think they’re animal lovers, and so they want to feed them banana chips, or trail mix, whatever they have in their car. They get the goats used to people, and that’s no good.”

In a rare incident, a mountain goat approached and fatally gored a hiker in Washington in 2010. Eleven years later, a mountain goat revealed the species’ strength by killing an attacking grizzly bear in Canada.

“They can’t look at humans as food sources because then they’ll start approaching people. They’re still wild animals with big horns,” Heiserman said, explaining that the goats get closer to the road and are easier to view in South Dakota than many other alpine places where they live.

Heiserman wants to see educational signage in Spearfish Canyon that explains how to behave around the goats.

“We’re lucky to have them here,” he said. “If people can leave them alone, hopefully they’ll stay here, there won’t be any problems, and they’ll continue to amaze us.”

Does it matter that the goats aren’t native?

People disagree about how important it is to invest in keeping the goats around.

“One person may think, well, they’re not native, so why are we managing for them?” Lehman said. “Another person who sees them as being on the landscape for more than 100 years as a naturalized species might consider them to be really important.”

His personal opinion is that the GF&P should continue to manage them. “We’ve had them here for over 100 years, the public really enjoys seeing them,” he said, adding “they’re an iconic species of the upper elevations of the Black Hills.”

Van Den Berg said the Rocky Mountain Goat Alliance doesn’t exclude non-native mountain goats from its conservation work. He is glad to hear support within the GF&P for that approach. “Most of the biologists I’ve talked to, they really feel strongly that they’ve been here. They don’t necessarily view them as an outsider.”

William Severud, a wildlife biologist and assistant professor at South Dakota State University, shared a different personal philosophy.  “For me, it seems like trying to manage as close to pre-European contact would be ideal,” he said, acknowledging that South Dakota won’t have populations of grizzly bears or wolves anytime soon, even though both are native to the state.

It would be interesting from a research standpoint, he said, to let the situation play out and see what happens. “But I understand they are popular, and there is interest in keeping them around.”

South Dakota isn’t the only state where mountain goats are facing challenges.

Different states, different approaches

Most native mountain goats are in the mountainous regions of Alaska and British Columbia. They were introduced to many western states in the 1900s for hunting and wildlife viewing. Since then, both native and non-native populations have experienced mixed success.

Brought to the state in the 1940s, Colorado now has more than 1,000 mountain goats, and more than 100 are hunted each year to manage the population.

Grand Teton National Park has culled almost all of its non-native goats to protect its native bighorn sheep from a bacterial disease they pass to each other. The disease is a risk in the Black Hills, but the populations rarely cross into each others’ territory, Lehman said.

After ecosystem damage and the fatal goring of a hiker in Washington, officials culled or translocated hundreds of non-native goats from Olympic National Park to the Cascade Range where they are a native species.

However, most goats brought to the Cascade Range did not survive long. A study found a link with climate changes, including a rapid spring snowmelt contributing to drier summer foraging conditions.

In Glacier National Park, a study found the native population has declined 45% since 2008, with scientists finding that climate variables, including decreased precipitation, correlated with the decline.

Van Den Berg wonders if climate changes might also affect the goats in the Black Hills. “I don’t have anything to back that up, but I would believe that not having that typical summer, fall, winter, spring maybe plays into it,” he said.

More broadly, he notices that habitat changes, whether due to recreation, development or weather shifts, are affecting goats across the United States. Because mountain goats are slow to breed, they are slow to recover from any threat.

The GF&P will count the goats in the southern Black Hills again in June. The data will inform revisions to the Mountain Goat Management Plan, which will be brought before the GF&P Commission for approval in 2028.

title: Special Olympics SD Summer Games underway
byline: By Brandon Woltkamp Black Hills Pioneer
description: Spearfish is hosting the Special Olympics South Dakota State Summer games this weekend on the Black Hills State University campus. Thursday’s opening ceremonies, including the lighting of the Special Olympics flame, officially began the 56th annual event. Events included track and field-style events along with soccer, swimming, volleyball, powerlifting, and a cornhole demonstration. Pioneer photo by Brandon Woltkamp.
_full_text:
Torch Lighting.jpg
Spearfish is hosting the Special Olympics South Dakota State Summer games this weekend on the Black Hills State University campus. Thursday’s opening ceremonies, including the lighting of the Special Olympics flame, officially began the 56th annual event. Events included track and field-style events along with soccer, swimming, volleyball, powerlifting, and a cornhole demonstration. Pioneer photo by Brandon Woltkamp. 

SPEARFISH — The 56th annual Special Olympics South Dakota Summer Games officially began Thursday evening as the cauldron was lit during opening ceremonites at the Donald E. Young Center.

More than 900 athletes from all over the state joined Thursday’s festivities, with over 10 teams participating in an overall joyful and cheerful atmosphere. 

 Special Olympics.jpg
The Spearfish Peaks team officially leads off the event as other teams are presented at Thursday’s opening ceremonies. Pioneer photo by Brandon Woltkamp 

Every team when announced was met with praise, cheers, and applause from the audience and their fellow competitors.

Mark Nore, the athletic director for Black Hills State University, inspired the athletes in a fiery speech describing the athletes’ vigor and bravery. Included with that were the athletes shouting ‘Yeah!’ at everything Nore chanted.

One of the individuals who were riled and had helped with the torch run was Kourtney Krebs of Spearfish Peaks.

Krebs said that this was the first time she lit the cauldron. “(It was) fantastic!” said Krebs.

Krebs has participated in the Special Olympics since she was 10. For over 20 years, she has dedicated her life to the event, competing in swimming, track, and weight lifting. 

Krebs said her activities for Friday will be a 500-meter freestyle swim. For Saturday, she will participate in the 3,000 and 1,500-meter runs. 

She will be participating in the nationwide Special Olympics to represent South Dakota later this year in Minneapolis, Minn.

title: News and Notes
description: Pioneer file graphic
_full_text:
News and Notes
Pioneer file graphic 

Fire department requests administrative help 

SPEARFISH — Spearfish Fire Chief Scott Deaver is asking the city council to authorize the creation of a new administrative position. Deaver said he, and the other paid fire fighters, need support to manage records, submit claims, and handle the business of the fire department. Previously, public safety shared administrative staff across the fire and police department. On Monday, the city council may consider creating the new position. 

—Sierra Ferguson

North Ave. speed limit up for discussion 

SPEARFISH — The Spearfish City Council is considering reducing the speed limit on North Avenue and Colorado Boulevard, just before Hillsview Road to 25 miles per hour. 

“Before you come to that crosswalk on Hillsview (Road) you’d be hitting a 25-mile an hour speed reduction sign. Then from the riverside You would be down to 25 miles per hour near Safeway and back up to 25 (miles per hour) past that Klym Coffee Hut,” Abbey Larson, Spearfish staff engineer.  

To implement the change the city will need to purchase new signs, and may consider dynamic speed signs — which would be purchased using funds from the police budget. 

— Sierra Ferguson

First change order in fire training tower project up for consideration

SPEARFISH — On Monday, the Spearfish City Council is scheduled to consider approving a change order for the fire training tower project in the amount of roughly $16,458. The original contract was $427,600. 

“The construction of the training center for the sawmill area that is going out in the sawmill area. They started excavation and pouring the foundation they ran into a lot of poor materials, funky soil, sawdust, trash, metal, debris. They required a lot of additional excavation,” Spearfish staff engineer Abbey Larson said. “About 131 additional cubic yards of excavation to get through all of that material to get down to a suitable base material and compact that to create a good foundation to pour the concrete foundation for the building on.”

— Sierra Ferguson

Therapy dog approved for Lead-Deadwood School District school resource officer

DEADWOOD — Members of the Lead-Deadwood school board agreed Tuesday to allow the school resource officer to bring a therapy dog into the school. Officer Brandon Webb said he intends to purchase a golden retriever puppy this summer, train the dog to become American Kennel Club Good Citizen Certified, and name the puppy Digs — short for Diggers, the school mascot. The dog will not be brought into the schools until it is trained.

— Sara Morgan

Lawrence Co. agrees to facilitate transfer of firetruck ownership

DEADWOOD — Lawrence County Commissioners agreed Tuesday to facilitate the transfer of ownership of a firetruck from Spearfish Fire Department to Nemo Fire Department. The county will work with both agencies to possibly move the truck from Spearfish to Nemo when the time comes.

 — Sara Morgan

title: Lawrence Co. Commissioners approve most malt
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: DEADWOOD — All but 3 applications for a malt liquor license were approved by Lawrence County commissioners Tuesday, with 2 being marked contingent upon paying property taxes and one continued.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

DEADWOOD — All but 3 applications for a malt liquor license were approved by Lawrence County commissioners Tuesday, with 2 being marked contingent upon paying property taxes and one continued. 

Approved licenses are as follows: DVC Cabin Investments, LLC., Barefoot Resort, Dark Horse Saloon, Steel Wheel, Alpine Outpost 385, Yesway store number 1192, Chateau at Rim Rock LLC., Bar 385 and Campground, Crow Beak Brewing Company, LLC., Custer Crossing Family Campground, Recreational Springs Resort, Elkhorn Ridge at Frawley Ranches, LLC., St. Onge Bar and Grill, Nemo Guest Ranch convenience store, Trailshead Lodge, Brandin’ Iron Restaurant and Ponderosa Bar, Spearfish KOA, Spearfish Canyon Lodge, The Merc Pizza and Pub, LLC., Tomahawk Lake Country Club Inc., Whitetail Creek Resort, LLC., and Mystic Hills Hideaway. 

Malt liquor licenses for The Crossing at Spearfish Canyon, formerly Cheyenne Crossing, and the Fish ‘N Fry Campground will be granted contingent upon the entities paying property taxes. Brenda McGruder, Lawrence County auditor, said the first half of the year’s property taxes are due April 30 and were still unpaid by both entities as of Tuesday morning. 

The license for the Boar’s Nest, a restaurant open seasonally near Lead, was continued until commissioners can be advised by the South Dakota Department of Transportation (DOT) and local law enforcement. The restaurant has ongoing complaints about excessive noise from neighbors, who complain about live music and a page system used to notify patrons that their food is ready. 

Bruce Outka, deputy state’s attorney, said DOT officials were at the restaurant Tuesday, where he assumed they were marking out places along the highway where patrons can and cannot park. The county receives complaints throughout the season of vehicles parking along the highway in the grass and right of way.

title: Main Street mill and overlay returns to Spearfish council agenda Monday
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: The pictured stretch of Colorado Boulevard could be chip sealed soon. On Monday, the city council is expected to consider at least one change order that would see the project completed by July 15. Main Street, from Jackson to Grant, will be milled and overlayed — that project is also up for discussion next week.
_full_text:
Colorado Boulevard.JPG
The pictured stretch of Colorado Boulevard could be chip sealed soon. On Monday, the city council is expected to consider at least one change order that would see the project completed by July 15. Main Street, from Jackson to Grant, will be milled and overlayed — that project is also up for discussion next week.  

 Colorado Blvd 2.JPG
Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — On Monday, DGR engineering is expected to bring a proposal before the Spearfish city council for the design and construction administration of the Main Street mill and overlay project.

Spearfish Public Works Director Adam McMahon said that DGR plans to work “quickly” to have plans prepared and the project ready to advertise for bid in 2 to 4 weeks. It is not yet clear how much that work will cost.

The project, by law, must be advertised for bids for 2 weeks.

“We’ll be in to late June or early July for potential bid opening, typically about a month,” McMahon said. “They may be able to start paving in August, maybe shortly after the Rally if things move really quickly for the contractor and it goes along with their schedule.”

Mayor John Senden said the project may start later than August.

“None of the downtown people want us to disturb Friday nights or the September harvest fest. It’s either going to be done late September or early October or next spring,” Senden said.

McMahon said, regardless of the winning bidder, the city plans to work time constraints into its contract to try and get the project done by the end of the year running from Jackson Boulevard to Spearfish Canyon Road. 

“Even starting this late on the design and bidding, they will still be able to have everything in place well in advance of when they could start work this fall,” McMahon said.  “I think it is realistic, but depending on who the low bidder is, it is going to be somewhat dependent on their schedule.”

Earlier this spring, the city council voted to mill and overlay Main Street from Jackson Boulevard to Grant Street. The rest of Colorado Boulevard will be chip-sealed. That decision was made to repair a failed chip seal that got underway last fall.

In September, Dakota Asphalt won the bid to chip-seal Main Street and Colorado Boulevard. After the project failed, citizens asked the council to consider asphalt, instead of a second chip seal, in the heart of downtown Spearfish.

Monday, the council is set to consider approving a change order that would allow Dakota Asphalt to begin re-chip sealing Colorado Boulevard from Grant Street to Spearfish Canyon. The no-cost change order would revise the completion date for the project to July 15 — allowing the contractor to finish work without incurring liquidated damages.

“July is the overall completion for the time extension. The reason why it is in July is they still have to have some time for the chip seal to cure out and do the pavement marking, but their intention, in the last updated schedule received from them, was still to have the chip seal completed late May, early June,” McMahon said.

McMahon said the public works department might also request a change order that would expand the scope of the chip seal reapplication so that a damaged stretch of pavement in front of Great Western Tire on Colorado Boulevard could be patched by Dakota Asphalt.

title: Spearfish mayor may receive $1,500 a week until a new city administrator is hired
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — Spearfish still doesn’t have a city administrator. On Monday, the city council plans to consider compensating the mayor for filling in.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

SPEARFISH — Spearfish still doesn’t have a city administrator. On Monday, the city council plans to consider compensating the mayor for filling in.  

The mayor could receive $1,500 per week, effective May 4, for taking on administrative responsibilities and additional hours in the absence of a city administrator. The previous city administrator parted ways with the city at the beginning of the year. The council approved a formal separation agreement with Bobby Falcon on Feb. 2. 

“This payment is temporary, and it just requests the sustained additional hours that Mayor Senden is putting in here at the city, just keeping the administrative functions going easily an additional 20-30 hours per week, includes the oversight of 10 direct reports, continuity among different departments, and just all of the administrative daily functions of the different departments that would normally be done by the city administrator,” Paula Gengler Spearfish human resources generalist said during Wednesday’s study session. 

Gengler said the human resources department used tools from the International City/County Management Association (ICMA) to research the cost of hiring a temporary or interim city administrator. 

“Looking through ICMA for a temporary or interim city administrator, we were looking at $12,000-13,000 every 2-week period for a person to come and fill that role while we are searching for a full-time city administrator,” Gengler said. “This (request) in comparison to that is a very fair ask for all of the work that he is currently doing for us on behalf of the city, employees and citizens.” Senden received similar payment for expanded duties following the November 2023 resignation of former city administrator Steve McFarland. At that time, the 

mayor received $26,613 for his mayoral duties alone. As mayor, he is expected to serve about 20 hours per week. Operating under the presumption of a 20-hour work week, that shakes out to about $25.59 an hour. The increase in pay Senden received after McFarland’s departure moved him up to $68.28 per hour with expanded duties. Until Falcon was hired, Senden earned about $3,754 every other week.

Spearfish community member Jeremy Smith asked how temporary the payments to Senden might be. 

“I have a question on the city administration role,” Smith said. “There is not anything about timeframe or duration. Is the position being advertised?”

Senden replied, “It is being advertised, it has been advertised for probably 20 days.”

He later told the Pioneer, “While seeking other options over the last few months it appears that as we start the new search there may be an extended time that we may be without that role filled.”

City Councilman Dean Myers asked if the council had discussed the matter prior to the study session on Wednesday. 

Senden said, “Yes. I didn’t have a chance to visit with you one-on-one about it, but there was some talk about it.”  

There is no mention of a council discussion of temporary compensation for Senden noted in the minutes of any public meeting since Feb. 2., nor has it been on any agenda. Sended said that is because he’s spoken to council members one-on-one. 

“After having discussed this situation with Council President (Pam) Jacobs and Council Vice President (Larry) Klarenbeek, some form of additional compensation for the additional time I must spend addressing all of the duties was reasonable in their opinion,” Senden said. “ I visited one on one with some of the other council members to advise them of this request and notify them it was being placed on the agenda for study session. This will give the council and public adequate notice of the agenda item and time to discuss the matter before voting on whether or not to provide the additional compensation.”

title: Sturgis to collaborate with GF&P on $50K Lions Park improvements
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: The city of Sturgis will collaborate with the S.D. Game, Fish, and Parks to improve shoreline fishing on the south, east, and west sides of Lions Club Pond. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
Sturgis to collaborate with GF&P on $50K Lions Park improvements
The city of Sturgis will collaborate with the S.D. Game, Fish, and Parks to improve shoreline fishing on the south, east, and west sides of Lions Club Pond. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

STURGIS — A more than $50,000 project to improve shoreline fishing access at Lions Park is a collaboration between the city of Sturgis, the S.D. Game, Fish, and Parks, and private citizens. 

On May 4, the Sturgis City Council approved a joint powers agreement with the GF&P that paves the way for construction that will enable shoreline fishing access on the west, south, and east side of the pond at Lions Park. The project includes building rock piers and related features, and will be completed by Todd Steffen, of Dakota Prairie Landscapes, LLC. 

City Administrator Aaron Jordan told the Sturgis City Council that the project is one former Mayor Kevin Forrester spearheaded, and felt very strongly about its completion before he passed away in April. Forrester was a staunch advocate for improving Sturgis trails and outdoor amenities. Currently, Jordan said fisherman use the north side of the pond, which is right next to the busy highway. The construction, he said, will significantly increase the safety and usage of the pond, which the GF&P stocks with fish. 

“This was just one of many projects Kevin Forrester had talked to me and Aaron about,” Public Works Director Rick Bush said. 

Bush added that the Lions Park pond improvements will be similar to the rock piers located at the entrance to Custer State Park. 

“We hope that by providing opportunities on the south side of the pond that will encourage them to keep away form that narrow strip along the road,” Bush said. 

Under the agreement, the city of Sturgis will oversee and manage the construction project, will maintain ownership of all the improvements, and is responsible for long term maintenance and free access for the pond. The GF&P will provide up to $15,000 for the project. 

In addition to the GF&P contribution, Jordan said an anonymous donor provided $10,000 for the project. The remaining $26,485 will be paid with money from the city’s capital improvements fund. 

 “This project represents a collaborative effort between state, local and private contributors to enhance a valued community amenity,” Jordan wrote in a staff report. “It also reflects the continuation of Mayor Forrester’s vision for expanding recreational opportunities and improving public spaces.” 

Jordan said he is confident the construction will be completed in plenty of time for the Lion’s Club Fishing Derby that is scheduled to be held June 5.

title: Black Hills Pioneer at 150: 1895
description: Pioneer file graphic
_full_text:
Black Hills Pioneer at 150 years
Pioneer file graphic 

Editor's Note
The Black Hills Pioneer is the oldest continuously operating business in West River Dakota Territory; and 2026 marks our 150th year of telling the stories of the Black Hills. Over time our newspaper has absorbed the titles of numerous other publications, and we would like to share some of the more compelling stories from those early editions.
 Every Saturday we will be publishing stories from our archives, focusing heavily on the gold rush era of the 1800s, starting with our very first publication on June 8, 1876. These stories are re-printed exactly as they were first published, leaving in place the historic typos, grammar, style and terminology – politically correct or otherwise. It is our belief that history is sacrosanct and should never be edited to reflect the societal norms of the present.
 We hope you enjoy this historic journey. It is an honor and a privilege to be a trusted permanent record keeper of the Black Hills community; we look forward to the next 150 years of history in the making in the magnificent Black Hills.

~ July 17, 1895 • Queen City Mail ~

Gave The Jurors Whiskey

Some very unpleasant disclosures were made in the Giles murder trial at Belle Fourche last week, in which it was shown that the jury, which tried Davidson and secured a life sentence for him, were supplied with whiskey by the bailiff while deliberating on the evidence in the case. Whether or not the whiskey in any manner affected the verdict, the MAIL does not know; but the knowledge of the fact brought before Judge Plowman was sufficient to cause that honorable gentleman to administer a severe rebuke to the bailiff and give the saloonkeepers a broad-gauge hint that henceforth any such action on their part would result in the wholesale closing up of those places. The taking of a human life unlawfully should not be condoned or in any way compromised; but at the same time the accused person should not have his case prejudiced by any such act which suspiciously implicates the jury in whose hands his life is placed. If Davidson is guilty of the crime charged, he has escaped his just deserts; but if there was a reasonable doubt of his guilt he should be given every opportunity to establish his innocence. The saloonkeeper admitted selling the liquor to the bailiff, that officer admits placing it where the jurors could find it, and the jurors admit drinking it. All this, however, may have had nothing to do with the verdict; but it looks bad, especially where the freedom of a human being was at stake.

~ October 9, 1895 • Queen City Mail ~

Calamity Jane Returns

“Calamity Jane,” well known by all old-timers in the Hills, and a character of world-wide reputation all over the west, arrived in Deadwood last Friday with the intention of remaining indefinitely. She is now Mrs. M. Burke, has two bright little girls, and has lately been living on a ranch near Ekalaka, Mont. That sort of a life didn’t suit her, however, hence her return to civilization. She had not been in Deadwood since 1877, and failed to recognize the town.

~ October 23, 1895 • The Deadwood Daily Pioneer ~

A Ride For Life.

Jack McCall’s Ride For Life and the Queer Verdict of a Deadwood Jury.

Judge Shannon of Canton, before whom Jack McCall was tried for the murder of Wild Bill, has a story of the murder, some parts of which are new. The Judge says that all the incidents of the case was brought out at the trial before a Deadwood Jury. The Judge says the prosecution made out a strong case of cold-blooded, deliberate murder. When it came to the defense, McCall, who was a man of some education and ability, addressed the jury himself. He struck the only chord that was likely to vibrate in his interest when he said he had known Wild Bill down in Texas that they were friends and that he had introduced him into his family. Wild Bill, he stated, had abused his friendship and betrayed his sister. For that crime he had visited vengeance on him. That began to put a new phrase on matters. While they condemned him for shooting a man without giving him a chance for his life, they regarded the killing as justifiable. The jury took the case and deliberated on it for some time and finally returned with one of the queerest verdicts that has ever been heard of by anyone. “They were not sure of his guilt, so they had decided to give him a chance for his life. They put him on a fast horse, filled his pockets with bread and cheese and gave him one minute’s start after which they would kill him if they could. They were all around with Winchester rifles and revolvers and were excellent horseman and excellent shots. When the word was given McCall started for his life. Before the minute was up he began throwing himself rapidly from one side to the other to divert the aim of his pursuers. At the end of the fateful minute the word was given and the pursuit and fusillade began. It seems almost incredible, but he escaped without injury. He ran into Wyoming and after about three weeks turned up in Cheyenne where he was arrested by a United States Marshal and turned over to a marshal in Dakota. On trial it was shown that the story of the seduction of his sister was a falsehood cunningly devised to save his neck. He murdered Wild Bill for the notoriety of having killed the famous scout, and thoroughly deserved the execution that followed his conviction. But the verdict of the lynch jury was unique and original in the history of criminal trails.”

~ October 23, 1895 • Queen City Mail ~

Monahan Case

No verdict in late years has created such profound surprise as that rendered last week in the Monahan case at Deadwood. That twelve intelligent men could arrive at such a verdict after listening to the evidence given in that trial is one of the things which no one had yet attempted to solve. That Monahan would be convicted and sentenced for at least ten or twelve years was the universal opinion among the best informed men in the country, but that he would go free was never for a moment considered probable. The facts in the case are yet fresh in the minds of our people, and it is not necessary to recapitulate them here. He has never denied the killing of Benson, but sought to establish an excuse for it on the grounds of self-defense. That this defense must have satisfied the jury is self-evident. The result of this trial is far from satisfactory to the people, and must necessarily encourage crime instead of discouraging it. Jay Hicks was hanged at Sturgis less than a year ago on the same charge, with less positive proof that he committed the crime. That he was guilty, every one believed, and that he got his just deserts no one denies. The MAIL does not criticize the jury in the Monahan case, because it is better to believe that they did what they considered to be right and justice; but it is extremely doubtful whether another body of twelve men could be found in Lawrence county who would have arrived at the same verdict. It is one of the evil results of our jury system; and until some change is brought about to remedy this evil, we must expect just such travesties on justice as has been witnessed in this trial.
