title: Lead city commission candidates
description: Voters in the city of Lead will head to the polls June 2 to vote on vacant city commission seats. Four people are running for 2 open positions for 3-year terms. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.
_full_text:
CityOfLeadCandidateComp.jpg

Voters in the city of Lead will head to the polls June 2 to vote on vacant city commission seats. Four people are running for 2 open positions for 3-year terms. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.

Jeremiah Fredericksen

 Fredericksen, Jeremiah.jpeg
Jeremiah Fredericksen 

Name and what you do for a living? 

I am Jeremiah J Fredericksen. I am currently working in security at the Sanford Underground Research Facility. 

What motivated you to run for this office?

I was a supervisor with the Lead Police Department. I served Lead for 11 years. I left due to the poor leadership of the City. Most of those “leaders” are now gone. There still is a lack of leadership and accountability.  I felt the commission took a shot at the departments without looking at themselves first. The commission must set the standard and lead the departments as they were elected and appointed to do.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

I spent 11 years inside the belly of the City. I’ve seen how the departments and the politicians try to “work” each other. They need to work with each other for progress and accountability to each other. The double standard and hypocrisy must end. Commissioners should not be allowed to tell Law Enforcement when and what laws or ordnances they are going to abide by. The City must maintain their sidewalks free of ice and snow just as is expected of our citizens.  Rules are to be even to all regardless of position or title. I will hold all sides to the same standard. 

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I served over a decade, active, Army. I was stationed in Germany, and Fort Campbell, Kentucky. I spent 6 years of that service overseas. I deployed to Kosovo, Afghanistan, and Iraq.  I have lead men oversees, in combat, and garrison. I was a Police Officer for over 11 years. I was the acting Police Chief on multiple occasions. I have proven my ability to lead men. I have managed mult-million dollar budgets before. I know what it is to hold oneself to a higher standard and make uncomfortable decisions for what is right rather than what is easy or popular.

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

During the past year I have attended the Commission meetings since deciding to run. Prior to that decision I watched the meeting on Facebook. 

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

I do believe local papers are important. They provide information of immediate local importance, and local matters. Local papers cover what the regional let alone national would not. What is important or relevant in Lead may not be in Rapid City, Pierre, or  Washington D.C.

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in the city of Lead?

There are several issues of importance in Lead. Budget, facilities, infrastructure, youth support, transportation, and supporting organizations for just a few. They all begin with budget control. Needs must come before wants. 

How do you intend to solve these issues?

I would like to see a focus on grants and budgeting for needs of the City before pet projects. In the end what grants can’t or won’t cover must be met in the budget. This is where needs before wants come in. Responsibility to meet the obligations to the residents comes before entertaining the residents. Maintaining parks and City assets rather than rebuilding and replacing. Beautification doesn’t always need to be new, paint and repair goes a long ways. We should maintain all City areas not just Main and Mill.

What do you believe is working for the city, and how will you retain that progression? 

The City departments try to accommodate our citizens, employees, and stakeholders extremely well. At times to a fault. I would like to continue that support to all. I am not afraid of telling hard truths when they need to be heard. The whole should not be punished for the failings of the few. The few that are the issue need to hear the hard truth. Whether it is employees abusing sick time, or complaining about compensation.  Whether it is citizens with complaints about ordnance enforcement or lack thereof. Performance matters, accountability matters.

What does transparency in government mean to you and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents?

I like roll call voting. The Commissioners being put on record individually for their decision. I vote for or against this, and this is why it is a good thing. .  I am not a fan of executive sessions. I feel that we are elected, appointed, and hired, by the public, to serve the public. We must all answer to the public. All employees of “The City” are representatives of the City. Complaints, disciplinary action, and accommodations should be recognized in the public. The good, the bad and the ugly. Stop sweeping the mess under the rug.

What else do you want people to know about you? 

I am a fifth generation local. I do not believe in the “good ole boy, or family” in system. During my 11 years of Policing Lead, I repeatedly proved that. I am a father of two amazing kids. Both kids are currently in college. I am married to an unbelievable lady, Dawn Allen, she continues to amaze me with her support and efforts for the community, and me. I am a combat veteran. I firmly believe in fulfilling the Oath of which one has sworn. A sworn oath is more than just words.

Do you support the city providing funding for the Handley Recreation Center? Why or why not? 

I had a membership with the Handley. The lack of maintenance of the facility at the time lead me elsewhere. I have been through the building during my time with Lead PD.  I do not have the current facts.  I am not in favor of continuing funding of the Handley Center. I do not believe neither the City nor the center have been up front with their intent or information. I do believe in supporting our youth.  As I did at the Boys and Girls club fund raiser. Honest  transparency by both sides could go a long way with this issue. 

Over this last year, the city has been discussing the possibility of taking over the Handley Recreation Center. Do you support the city taking over managing public recreation as a city department? Why or why not?

I am adamantly against the City taking over the Center. It will take more than one employee to operate, clean, and maintain the facility. That alone would cost the City more than we give now. If volunteers were the answer to keep costs down we wouldn’t be here now. City ownership will not save the City money. Again full disclosure from both sides is needed for the public. Even though I  criticize the commission for not making decisions I would like to see funding through to the next election where the voters could decide once and for all.

According to recent city bids, it costs about $65,000-$70,000 per quarter mile to tear up and lay a 3-inch overlay on Lead roads. What is your plan to raise money to pay for city infrastructure improvements? 

First is to get full knowledge of the budget, then get control over spending. Prioritize needs over wants. Save for projects rather than buy want to have items, let alone like to have items. Have the full-time staff seek out grants for needs rather than wants. Repair facilities, and equipment when possible, rather than replace. Bye quality used equipment when possible, rather than always new. We also need to promote development through incentives where feasible.

Should the city provide funding for nonprofits? Why or why not?

Last is nonprofit funding. The City should provide funding for these organizations as it is responsible, and then fiscally able. It must put needs before wants. The City must fulfil responsibilities before entertainment.

Valerie Meiners

 Meiners, Valerie.jpeg
Valerie Meiners 

Name and what you do for a living? 

My name is Valerie Meiners.  My main profession is as an independent Cosmetologist however I have irons in many fires.  

What motivated you to run for this office?

My philosophy is that if you have an issue with the way things are done, you should put your money where your mouth is and serve where you think you can make a difference. I see things on the federal, state and local levels that I think could be done better.  My efforts best serve my community, so this is where I am starting.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

I feel like any citizen of any community is qualified to serve their town.  It isn’t one person that changes things, it’s a consensus of ideas and abilities that changes dynamics.  I have a very diversified business background, multiple academic degrees and foremost an absolute passion to see Lead succeed in every way possible.  Those opportunities don’t just happen organically; they happen through effort and elbow grease.  I have a proven track record for making things happen on large and small scales.

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

Currently, I am a sitting member of the Lawrence County Public Defender’s Board as well as a founding member of the citizen’s action group Checks & Balances.  In my past I have sat on the Western South Dakota Community Action Agency as Chair and on  Executive board. Other boards include Lead Deadwood Arts Council.  Cub Scouts of America, and the Broken Boot Gold Mine. Projects I have accomplished include the Vaudeville Show  and an art project entitled,  “Deer, Dough and Van Gogh”.  I have also addressed ordinances and laws at the local and state level which I have felt were unfair or badly written.  

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

Over the past 19 months, I attended 39 Lead Commission meetings in person and every scheduled budget meeting last summer.   

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

I do believe in local newspapers as well as television and radio.  There is always a need for printed news especially for people who do not wish to engage in the internet of things.

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in the city of Lead?

The issues in Lead that are of the utmost importance to me include:

A failing infrastructure due to a lack of a clear path forward to fix pressing issues such as deteriorating streets, failing water systems and separation of sewer/ storm drain,

Inadequate transportation between Lead and Deadwood,

Business revitalization for economic development,

Lack of childcare facilities,

Low level of actual affordable housing as related to actual income of workers living in Lead and an aging population on fixed incomes,

How do you intend to solve these issues?

The way to fix these things is with a mixture of aggressive action such as utilization of state and federal grants as well as a well-informed city council with a firm grasp on business principles and budgeting.  Creating a stable infrastructure is paramount to a successful outcome.  

What do you believe is working for the city, and how will you retain that progression?

Lead has a heart of gold literally and figuratively.  We have the bare necessities to move Lead forward and have the rare opportunity to embrace rebranding through the idea of past, present and future. Gold, science and nature are our claims to fame and what we can build on. Our natural beauty and outdoor recreational activities are second to none in every season.  Our best asset is our citizens.  They are the heart and soul of Lead and they are the reason people love to come here and sometimes stay.

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

In the 1st Amendment of the Constitution of the United States, we have the right to petition the Government for redress of grievances.  In my mind, there is no redress necessary if all of the parties involved in governance are honest and forthright.  Transparency requires total honesty and public scrutiny especially when one is trusted to protect the community’s way of life, its assets and its security.   

What else do you want people to know about you?

What people should know about me is that I am passionate about what I decide to do.  I have worked diligently for Lead without a commission seat and I intend to continue working for our best future.  I am not afraid to tackle the difficult things.

Do you support the city providing funding for the Handley Recreation Center? Why or why not? 

The funding for the Handley Center would fall into the category of all of the other nonprofit organizations that ask for funding.  It would need to be considered on its merit and its past performance through petitioning the Commission.  

Over this last year, the city has been discussing the possibility of taking over the Handley Recreation Center. Do you support the city taking over managing public recreation as a city department? Why or why not? 

Funding the Handley Center under the current conditions of the building and the resolution put forth by their Board of Directors would not be a strategy I would support.  The Handley Center has the opportunity to operate without City funds through corporate sponsorships/partnerships, grant writing, membership drives and the like.  I think this issue is a very emotional one for some people but must be handled intellectually with fiscal responsibility first and foremost.  It boils down to common sense use of city funds.  

According to recent city bids, it costs about $65,000-$70,000 per quarter mile to tear up and lay a 3-inch overlay on Lead roads. What is your plan to raise money to pay for city infrastructure improvements? 

The condition of the streets is abysmal.  Without a Facilities plan any attempt beyond 500-1500 feet of street repairs is unattainable.  House Bill 1245 shows promise of funding though a one cent tax increase and must pass taxpayer scrutiny to be implemented.  This is a burden spread out in a way that is less intrusive to tax payers, preapproved by citizens and spreads the burden to tourists that are here to share our resources. Grant opportunities that require supplementation would be possible with this tax.

Should the city provide funding for nonprofits? Why or why not?

I believe to whatever extent the city is able to contribute to nonprofits is a goodwill gesture reinvesting citizen tax dollars in a positive manner.  I’d like to see is an application process that outlines what the organization offers, what funds are requested and how these funds are to be used to vet each opportunity on its merits.  In the following year, all previously funded organizations need to show that the monies received were used appropriately.

Allan Rohrer

 Al Rohrer.jpeg
Al Rohrer 

Name and what you do for a living?

Allan Rohrer. I currently serve as your Lead City Commissioner, and for my “day job,” I work at Jerry Greer’s Engineering in Deadwood, South Dakota.

What motivated you to run for this office?

My motivation comes from a deep love for the city of Lead. Having served as your incumbent, I’ve seen firsthand how much we can achieve when we work as a team. I want to ensure our town remains a place where families can thrive and businesses can grow. I’m running to keep our positive momentum going and to ensure our future is handled with common sense.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

I have the “on-the-job” experience that actually matters. I’ve already been through the city’s budget season and have seen exactly how the inner workings of our local government operate. I know where the “levers and buttons” are at City Hall, which means I don’t need a learning curve to get things done. I have a proven track record of showing up and making the hard decisions needed to keep the city running smoothly.

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I am your current sitting City Commissioner, and it has been an honor to serve in this role. One of the parts of this position I enjoy most is serving as the liaison between City Hall and the Chamber of Commerce. This role allows me to help bridge the gap between our local government and our business community, ensuring that we are all pulling in the same direction to help Lead prosper.

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I have attended all of the meetings. As your incumbent, showing up is my top priority. Beyond our local sessions, I’ve also traveled to Pierre for Municipal League trainings to make sure I’m bringing the best knowledge back to Lead. Simply put, I’ve spent enough time in the building that I know exactly where the coffee pot is. I am fully immersed in the daily business of our city.

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Absolutely. Local newspapers are the heartbeat of a small town. They keep us connected and hold government accountable. Without a local paper, the stories of our neighbors and the truth about our local government decisions would go untold. They are essential for a healthy, informed community.

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in the city of Lead?

The most important issues are maintaining our aging infrastructure—specifically our roads and the $50 million backlog of infrastructure work that needs to start taking front and center. This includes essential sewer separation work that must be addressed. We also need to focus on smart economic growth while preserving the “small-town feel” that makes Lead such a special place to live.

How do you intend to solve these issues?

I intend to solve these by sticking to our “teamwork” approach. For infrastructure, we must prioritize projects through smart budgeting and by being aggressive in seeking state and federal grants. For recreation, we need to bring everyone to the table to find a solution that provides the best service to our kids and seniors without overtaxing our residents.

What do you believe is working for the city, and how will you retain that progression?

The city’s sense of community and our recent “feel-good” momentum are working well. People are more engaged than they have been in years. To retain this, I will continue to be accessible to residents and keep our city government focused on positive, common-sense solutions rather than political bickering.

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

Transparency means that every citizen should know how and why a decision was made. I plan to continue being open about city business, explaining my votes clearly, and ensuring that our meetings and records remain easy for the public to access. No one should ever feel “out of the loop” regarding their own town’s business.

What else do you want people to know about you?

I want people to know that I am a neighbor first and a public servant second. Lead is my home, and I care deeply about its future. I value the trust you have placed in me and strive to be as accessible as possible. To see the work we’re doing first-hand and to stay involved in our community’s progress, I encourage everyone to follow my Facebook page (Commissioner Al). I am always here to listen and work for you.

Do you support the city providing funding for the Handley Recreation Center? Why or why not?

No. I do not support funding the Handley Center any further. Simply put, we must be responsible with our limited city resources and ensure that every tax dollar is being used in the most effective way possible for the entire community.

Over this last year, the city has been discussing the possibility of taking over the Handley Recreation Center. Do you support the city taking over managing public recreation as a city department? Why or why not?

Under the right circumstances, I could support this. However, there must be no deed restrictions. Deed restrictions are like a complicated lease, and the taxpayers deserve to own this property plain and simple. I am 100% behind the mayor on this; I’ve got his back and believe we can make a go of it. We are willing to give it two years to succeed, and I hope the community supports that effort.

According to recent city bids, it costs about $65,000-$70,000 per quarter mile to tear up and lay a 3-inch overlay on Lead roads. What is your plan to raise money to pay for city infrastructure improvements?

   We cannot simply keep raising taxes on our residents. My plan focuses on:

Aggressively pursuing state and federal grants for rural infrastructure to bring our tax dollars back home.

Carefully prioritizing our current budget to direct more existing revenue specifically toward road overlays.

Should the city provide funding for nonprofits? Why or why not?

I believe the city should support nonprofits that provide essential services the city cannot provide itself, such as food pantries or youth programs. These organizations do great work for our citizens. However, there must be more transparency and accountability when it comes to this funding. We need to ensure that every dollar is being used wisely and that taxpayers must see a clear benefit.

Dustin Schumacher

 Dustin Schumacher.jpg
Dustin Schumacher 

Name and what you do for a living? 

My name is Dustin Schumacher. My full-time profession is in law enforcement. I have been a Law Enforcement Officer for approximately twenty-two years. 

What motivated you to run for this office?

My dedication to public service and my love for my hometown community motivated me to run for the Lead City Commission. I am a “glass half full” kind of person. I think our city and community could use more positivity. I believe in Lead’s shared sense of community. I want to preserve and encourage that shared sense of community that I have always known Lead to possess. 

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?    

I have worked in public service my entire adult life. I have proudly served the City of Lead, City of Deadwood and Lawrence County in my professional and volunteer life. This service has given me invaluable experience in local government operations. I understand and respect the budget process, a commissioner’s roles and responsibilities, and I am dedicated to working on creative solutions to challenges. 

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I was a volunteer for the Lead Volunteer Fire Department for twenty three years. At the time that I moved on from the LVFD, I held the rank of Assistant Chief. I currently hold a Board Member position on the Lead Country Club Board of Directors. 

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I have attended all of the Lead City Commission meetings since deciding to run for Commissioner. I have watched many of the Lead City Commission meetings online throughout the last year. I believe that between the meetings I have observed, my connections within the community and my professional experiences; I am in tune with the issues within the community. 

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Of course, local journalism and newspapers are important. Local journalism is vital to impartially informing citizens of local news and events. I know that the Black Hills Pioneer is the official newspaper for most local governments in the Northern Hills, which is necessary to publish events and legal matters in accordance with South Dakota Codified Law. 

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in the city of Lead?

Some of the most important issues that need to be at the forefront for the City of Lead are expensive infrastructure issues. The city has streets that need to be repaired, sewer lines that need to be separated and replaced, water lines that need to be replaced, and a city shop that needs to be relocated and built. All of these items need to be addressed, while minimizing the financial burden to the city taxpayers. 

I also think that there are a lot of positive things happening in Lead. I think we can focus on positive progression, while finding effective solutions to the challenges. 

How do you intend to solve these issues?

The solution to these challenges will not happen overnight. I intend to find creative budget solutions, assist and encourage applying for grants, and renegotiating some long-term contracts. I intend to work with other commissioners, city employees, and citizens to find solutions. Solutions that have the least impact on City of Lead taxpayers. 

I may not have all the answers, but I believe my experience in public service, my community connections and humility to ask the right people the right questions, will assist in making the decisions for, and with the community.

What do you believe is working for the city, and how will you retain that progression?

I believe our open communication and determination are working for Lead. We have come a long way since Homestake closed. From closed businesses and empty houses, to tourism, recreation and community gatherings. I want to continue to encourage new business, new residents, and new ideas while holding onto those foundational values that make us Lead.  

We as citizens of Lead have been able to talk openly about the issues with different points of view. Everyone’s voice needs to be heard. I plan to be there to listen. 

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

Transparency in government is very important to me. All forms of United States government are the people’s government. It is the responsibility of all forms of government to be transparent. Without transparency and open discussion, the people lose their input and connection to the government.

Transparency is not difficult to maintain. Transparency is open communication.   

What else do you want people to know about you?

I am a lifelong Lead resident. I am a fifth-generation Lead resident on my father’s side, and a third-generation resident on my mother’s side. I was raised here. My wife and I built our family and life here. I have seen all the good Lead can do when community members come together. I possess those positive core values. 

    

Do you support the city providing funding for the Handley Recreation Center? Why or why not? 

 I support the city providing funding for the Handley Recreation Center. Most cities provide funding for community centers or recreation centers. It is not just a gym, but it is also a gym. The programs that are provided at the Handley Center are vital community programs. That money is an investment in the future of our community. If the Handley Center goes away, then all the programs that are maintained there will likely go away too. Once those programs are gone, they will not likely come back. Then there is less to draw people toward living in Lead. 

Over this last year, the city has been discussing the possibility of taking over the Handley Recreation Center. Do you support the city taking over managing public recreation as a city department? Why or why not? 

I think a viable solution needs to be implemented. As previously stated, I believe the Handley Recreation Center is necessary for our community. I think that if the city takes it over, the cost to taxpayers is going to be more significant. Right now, there are donors and volunteers to assist with cost savings for the Handley Center. I think the funding the city has been providing should continue, while a more permanent and viable solution to the future is determined. 

Indoor recreation and programs are vital to a community, especially one that is dark, cold, and snow packed several months of the year. 

According to recent city bids, it costs about $65,000-$70,000 per quarter mile to tear up and lay a 3-inch overlay on Lead roads. What is your plan to raise money to pay for city infrastructure improvements? 

 My plan is to find creative budgeting and acquiring grants. The solution to this problem can seem overwhelming. But with every overwhelming issue, we need to break it into smaller pieces. We have to set attainable goals and repair as many every year as we can afford, all while seeking new revenue streams, without adversely affecting the taxpayers. 

Should the city provide funding for nonprofits? Why or why not?

I believe that the city should responsibly provide funding for nonprofits. I do not think the city should give money to everyone that comes asking, but individually consider the benefit to the community. The city should assist with funding, or in-kind donations of nonprofit organizations that are an asset to our community values and maintain our shared sense of community.

title: Sturgis man injured in construction accident
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Rapid City LifeFlight transported a man who suffered serious injuries to his legs after a construction accident in Boulder Canyon, Thursday. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
Sturgis man injured in construction accident
Rapid City LifeFlight transported a man who suffered serious injuries to his legs after a construction accident in Boulder Canyon, Thursday. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick  

STURGIS — A Sturgis man suffered serious injuries Thursday as a result of a construction accident in Boulder Canyon. 

Tavis Little, chief deputy with the Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office, said the 58-year old Sturgis man was working at a construction site on Greenfield Lane when he was involved in an accident that caused major injury to his legs. Emergency responders received the call at 1:11 p.m. The man was transported by LifeFlight to Rapid City Monument Health Hospital. 

Agencies that responded to the incident included Lead-Deadwood Monument Health Ambulance Service, the Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office, Lawrence County Emergency Management, and Rapid City LifeFlight.

title: Governor candidate’s call for state gas tax holiday not endorsed  by opponents
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — Republican South Dakota governor candidate Jon Hansen wants to pause the state’s gas tax this summer and use an economic development fund to cover the cost, but none of his opponents endorsed the idea, and one called it a gimmick that could imperil the state’s federal highway funds.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — Republican South Dakota governor candidate Jon Hansen wants to pause the state’s gas tax this summer and use an economic development fund to cover the cost, but none of his opponents endorsed the idea, and one called it a gimmick that could imperil the state’s federal highway funds.

President Donald Trump has suggested temporarily suspending the federal gas tax as the national average cost per gallon increases — due largely to Trump’s war in Iran and its impact on crude oil shipments.

“President Donald Trump is calling for the suspension of the federal gas tax, and South Dakota should do the same thing,” Hansen said Tuesday in a press release.

Hansen, the speaker of the state House, said state lawmakers could consider suspending the state gas tax in a special legislative session. A special session can be called by the governor, or lawmakers can petition for it with two-thirds support from both the House and Senate.

South Dakotans pay 28 cents per gallon in state tax, whether they’re fueling up with gasoline or diesel. Federal tax is an additional 18.4 cents per gallon on gasoline and 24.4 cents on diesel.

South Dakota’s average gas price, $4.22, which includes taxes, is more than a dollar higher than it was a year ago, according to the AAA motor club. A pause on the state tax would lower the state’s current average price to $3.94 per gallon.

The pause could save taxpayers up to $50 million, Hansen estimated. He would use the state’s Future Fund, a pool of money under the governor’s exclusive control, to replace the revenue in the state budget. The state gets money for the Future Fund by charging a fee to employers. They pay the fee when they submit payroll taxes that support unemployment benefits.

In the press release, Hansen’s campaign said in reference to the Future Fund that the state “is currently sitting on more than $60 million in ready reserve dollars which can be used to completely fill any highway funding gap created as a result of the gas tax holiday.”

But after Gov. Larry Rhoden’s most recent Future Fund grant to a teacher apprenticeship program, which was announced Monday, the unobligated balance of the Future Fund fell to $23.9 million, according to a spokesperson for the Governor’s Office of Economic Development.

A spokesman for the Hansen campaign told South Dakota Searchlight that the Legislative Research Council “reports that the Future Fund has roughly $68 million in it,” without distinction between obligated and unobligated funds.

Given that employers pay into it routinely, “millions more will continue to pour into it,” said Hansen’s spokesman, Austin Goss. “Further, the state is reporting higher than expected revenues for the month of April, outpacing legislative estimates by $12.1 million. As he has throughout his political career, Jon Hansen has one obligation — to South Dakota families and workers. Any and all obligations outside of that are secondary.”

Republican candidates respond

Rhoden, who is campaigning to keep his job, has awarded more than $10 million from the Future Fund since the start of April.

He also signed a bill into law earlier this year that makes reforms to the Future Fund, including the addition of definitions for acceptable uses, requiring more reporting to legislators about awards, stipulating information required of applicants, directing the Governor’s Office of Economic Development to formulate rules governing the fund’s use, and requiring the office to make recommendations to the governor about potential awards.

Hansen voted in favor of that legislation in the House.

Ian Fury, a spokesman for the Rhoden campaign, told Searchlight that Hansen’s gas tax idea “is not ready for primetime,” pointing to the current balance of the Future Fund and the new law, which takes effect July 1. Fury said “this use of Future Funds would not be legal” under the new law.

The state could also lose out on federal highway funding if the tax holiday took effect and the state failed to pay its required percentage of matching funds for federal highway projects, Fury said.

“Maybe worst of all — doing this would cost South Dakota taxpayers $216 million in federal highway funding,” Fury said in a statement to Searchlight. “A governor should lead with thoughtful policy, not political gimmicks.”

U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, who’s led the race in all public polling, sent a statement to Searchlight.

“After voting for a new tax on just about everything South Dakotans buy, I understand why Jon Hansen is looking for a holiday from his record. I agree that gas is too expensive, and that’s why I’m working this week to get E15 across the finish line here in Congress. That will save South Dakotans millions of dollars at the pump.”

Earlier this year, Hansen voted in favor of a new law that gives counties the option to enact up to a 0.5% sales tax and use the revenue for homeowner property tax relief. He also voted in favor of a new law that will use the revenue from a 0.3-percentage-point increase in the statewide sales tax for homeowner property tax relief. Rhoden signed both bills into law.

Throughout the campaign, Johnson has criticized Hansen and Rhoden for raising sales taxes, but the two have defended the use of the higher sales taxes for homeowner property tax reduction. A third bill that Hansen opposed but Rhoden signed into law gives cities the option to implement an additional 1% temporary sales tax to pay for special projects, if approved by 60% of a city’s voters.

Johnson has been part of an effort to pass a bill that would authorize the sale of 15% ethanol-blended gasoline, known as E15, nationwide and year-round.

A spokesman for businessman Toby Doeden said the state “should be making cuts that directly benefit our residents.”

The summer is “peak visitor season,” when out-of-state tourists contribute the most to South Dakota’s economy, the spokesman said. “If Speaker Hansen cared to make a real substantive improvement for state residents, why didn’t he want to suspend the gas tax during harvest season so that our amazing farmers and ranchers would be able to save more on fuel as their operating costs increase?”

The Republican primary election for governor is June 2, and early voting is underway. The winner of the Republican primary will advance to the November general election to face Democratic candidate Dan Ahlers.

title: Data centers could be banned in Butte County, voters will decide in June
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Michelle Evans is an active member of the  Belle Fourche community and a business owner. She led the charge to place data centers on Butte County ballots this summer. She is pictured, making her case for a county-wide ban, during a recent candidate forum at Grap’s Burgers and Brews. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Butte ballot question.JPG
Michelle Evans is an active member of the  Belle Fourche community and a business owner. She led the charge to place data centers on Butte County ballots this summer. She is pictured, making her case for a county-wide ban, during a recent candidate forum at Grap’s Burgers and Brews. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

 Butte Ballot question 2.jpeg
Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

BELLE FOURCHE — Data centers are on the ballot in Butte County. If the majority of voters mark “yes” on June 2, the county commission will have to pass an ordinance prohibiting the construction of data centers in its jurisdiction.

Belle Fourche resident and business co-owner, Michelle Evans, spearheaded the effort to push back against future construction of data centers in Butte County.

“I am so grateful for the Constitution that allows us to petition our government, so that we can decide. That is the absolute number one reason why I did it. I got a fire in my belly, and I feel like we cannot let this happen,” Evans said.

Evans described her concerns about data centers and how they might reshape Butte County.

“How many of you have iCloud? How many of you have Dropbox? Anything that is on your phone goes into not the sky, but into a data center. It is a building full of servers, and they work all day and all night,” Evans said. “They create noise. They create pollution.”

Evans said data centers are a growing issue in rural areas.

“Large-scale data center projects are increasingly being proposed in counties with fewer zoning regulations, often in places where land is available, and development is less restrictive. Supporters of restrictions often point to concerns about long-term impacts, particularly related to water use, power demand, and how large developments may affect agriculture, infrastructure, and the physical health of citizens and rural communities,” Evans said. “On the other hand, some view data centers as potential economic opportunities, citing tax revenue, jobs, and growth. There are almost zero jobs, by the way, there are some jobs for a while, but then they go away.”

Butte County does not have zoning, which Brunner pointed out, is one typical way that data centers are proactively prevented in other communities. 

Petitioners gathered more than 500 signatures in order to add the resolution to the ballot, Evans said.

“This measure asks a straightforward question: Should Butte County create an ordinance to prohibit the construction of data centers? A ‘yes vote’ would require the county commissioners to draft that ordinance. A ‘no vote’ would be leaving things as they are today,” Evans said.

The language of the ordinance the commission would pass is not dictated by the ballot question.

Tom Brunner, the chair of the Butte County Republican Party, suggested that a 5-year moratorium might be more appropriate than a permanent ban.

“We don’t have enough power in Butte County, and water is always a problem,” Brunner said. “Sometimes you give up some freedoms, but with that regulation comes some protection. With that, the fine balance is why I appreciate the petition process.”

Jason Kari, who is running for Butte County Commission in District 5, said he believes property rights do sometimes come with a cost, but he maintained that he was not necessarily in favor of data centers.

“For me, when it comes to the property rights and stuff, freedom comes with consequences. There is no wall up to the sky that keeps everything from crossing that line. You want freedom, you’ve got to deal with some of the stuff that comes with it,” Kari said. “I definitely don’t want to see a data center here. We should do everything we can to prevent them from being here. Short of, I don’t want to take people’s property rights away, though.”

“With the amount of water and the infrastructure and everything that would have to go into it, right now it is not a place for South Dakota or Butte County,” said Doug Larson, who is running for county commission in District 1.

Cory Tolley, also a candidate for county commission in District 1, said that Butte County would likely not have the water or power necessary to welcome a data center.  

“I feel like if they want to put them next to large cities where they have larger infrastructure and they want to deal with the blowback from those power issues and not having enough water for their people, we will let places like California, Denver, they can take them jumps. It should stay out of our county,” Tolley said.

Evans said the ballot measure will help indicate what the public wants.                 

“At its core, this measure is about how our community wants to approach that balance between development and preservation, and how decisions of this scale should be handled moving forward,” Evans said.

NEWELL — Newell High School honored 7 graduates Saturday with the 2026 commencement ceremony. 

“If we wait until we are ready, we will be waiting the rest of our lives,” is the motto for the Class of 2026, but they were very ready for Saturday’s ceremony. 

The 2026 graduates included Valedictorian Sarah Kay Erk, Salutatorian Jessica Raisanen, Michael Alexander Lawson, Miya Lee Mailloux, Tayla Ann Neely, Rachel Irene Stranberg, and Rowdy Lane Wetz. 

The event was small, but meaningful, as a slide show detailing each graduate’s school career highlights was shown. Graduates also presented their loved ones with flowers, during a particularly meaningful part of the ceremony. 

Social studies teacher Wyatt VanderVorst delivered the class address, and discussed how much he enjoyed watching the graduates grow. Erk and Raisanen reflected on the good times they had with classmates during their valedictorian and salutatorian speeches. 

Following the presentation of diplomas, the graduates celebrated with confetti canons, and processed out of the gym to “Dancing in the Dark,” by Rihanna.

description: Voters in Whitewood will be heading to the polls June 2 to vote on vacant mayoral seat. Two people are running for the mayorial seat, which is a 3-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.
_full_text:
WhitewoodMayoral.jpg

Voters in Whitewood will be heading to the polls June 2 to vote on vacant mayoral seat. Two people are running for the mayorial seat, which is a 3-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.

Bruce White

 White, Bruce
Bruce White 

Name and what you do for a living? 

 Bruce E. White

Retired

(Owner) Blackies Barrel Shoppe  

What motivated you to run for this office?

 Concerns of what direction the City is going and the costs to thr citizensfor the services provided.

 What will happen if the property tax is reduced, where will the money come from.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

By the employment I have had and seeing the mistakes made bby others and having my own business and not having someone bail me out when over spending. 

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I served on the Whitewood City Council and served as the Council President

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

Since April 2024 to the present 43.

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Yes as long as the pros and cons are treated equal and not bias to ether side.

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in Whitewood?

 The sewer treatment plant, roads that was supposed to be built, and property that is in disarray.

How do you intend to solve these issues?

The mayor cannot solve any of the problems the city faces without the council and citizens coming to council meetings and expressing their concerns about the issues.

What do you believe is working for the city, and how will you retain that progression?

 Right noe it does not look like there is any progress thet will benefit the citizens of Whitewood.

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

That the citizens are who the Mayor, 6 members of the Council, and all the employees of the city for the citizen and not too forget that.

What else do you want people to know about you?

I am not looking for any recognition or advancement politically. I have been married going on 64 years to the same Lady.

Sara Fitzgerald

 Fitzgerald, Sara.jpg
Sara Fitzgerald 

Name and what you do for a living? 

My name is Sara Fitzgerald. I’m a graduate of BHSU and hold a Juris Doctorate from USD School of Law. I work for the Department of Veterans Affairs and serve as a Reserve Police Officer for the City of Belle Fourche. In addition, I am the Vice President of the Whitewood City Council.

I do not accept a salary for my role on the council, choosing instead to donate it back to the City of Whitewood. My career and public service are deeply rooted in a commitment to serving others and strengthening the safety and well-being of our community.

What motivated you to run for this office?

My motivation to run is a commitment to transparency, accountability, and doing things the right way. People deserve to know what’s happening in their city and trust that decisions are made openly and honestly.

While serving on the city council, I’ve worked to make meetings more accessible by ensuring they’re conducted properly and shared publicly. I don’t just show up, I ask questions, investigate the details, and ensure accountability. I understand how local government should operate, openly, and in accordance with the law. I’m committed to keeping residents informed, heard, and represented, and to moving our community forward with integrity.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

I genuinely care about Whitewood and have been actively involved in making our community better. I’ve worked to promote transparency and integrity in local government. I’ve also been fiscally responsible while serving on council, making thoughtful decisions with taxpayer dollars in mind.

I actively research and understand each agenda item to ensure every decision is made in the best interest of the city.

My legal background also gives me a strong understanding of the law and ensures we’re making sound, responsible decisions.  I want what’s best for this community, and I’ve shown that through my actions, not just my words.

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I’ve had the opportunity to serve in several leadership roles that have helped shape our community. I currently serve as Vice President of the Whitewood City Council, Secretary of the Whitewood Chamber of Commerce, and as a board member for the Whitewood Community Foundation.

Previously, I served on Whitewood’s Planning and Zoning Commission. I’ve also contributed to Lawrence County’s Teen Court Program and served as a consultant for Black Hills State University during the development of a diversion program for college students.

These roles have given me valuable experience in leadership, collaboration, and making decisions that benefit the community.

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I have attended every Whitewood City Council meeting over the past year. I also make it a priority to stay informed by attending, watching live, or reviewing recordings of County Commission meetings, neighboring city council meetings, and local school board meetings. 

Staying engaged across all levels of local government is important to me, as it helps me make informed decisions and better serve our community, while also staying cognizant of what’s happening across other local governing bodies.

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Yes, I absolutely believe local newspapers are important. They play a critical role in keeping communities informed about what’s happening right here at home, whether it be city council decisions, local events, or the issues that directly impact our daily lives.

Local journalism also creates transparency and accountability in government, which is essential for building trust with the public. Not everyone can attend meetings or dig through public records, so newspapers help bridge that gap and make information accessible to everyone.

At the end of the day, a strong local newspaper helps build a stronger, more connected community, and that’s something I fully support.

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in Whitewood?

Annexation is one of the most important issues facing Whitewood. Growth is necessary, but it must be done thoughtfully and responsibly to support long-term sustainability. 

Other key priorities include affordable housing and maintaining and improving our infrastructure. We need to ensure families and future residents have opportunities to live here while continuing to invest in the systems that support our community and maintain the quality of life our residents expect.

Whitewood’s wastewater treatment plant is a long-awaited project that must be advanced and kept on schedule.

How do you intend to solve these issues?

Regarding annexation, I will work to ensure the process is strategic and aligned with our long-term plans so that growth benefits both current residents and future development.    

As for infrastructure, long-term planning and responsible budgeting need to be prioritized to ensure we’re maintaining and improving our systems as we grow. Moving the wastewater treatment plant forward will be a priority by addressing delays and staying engaged in the process so the project stays on track.

My approach is to be involved, ask the right questions, and work collaboratively to make informed decisions that keep Whitewood moving forward.

What do you believe is working for the city, and how will you retain that progression? 

One of the biggest strengths of our city is our employees. We are fortunate to have loyal, hardworking individuals who take pride in their work. 

Whitewood has an almost entirely new city council that’s engaged, asks questions, stays involved, and is mindful of taxpayer dollars. To retain that progress, I will continue to encourage open communication, and ensure decisions are made responsibly, and in the best interest of our community.

Whitewood’s small-town charm is what makes it a community people are proud to call home, and it’s that same charm that creates strong potential for thoughtful growth and development opportunities. 

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

Transparency means being open, honest, and accountable to the people we serve. It’s about clearly communicating decisions, sharing information, and making sure residents understand not just what we’re doing, but why.  I’m committed to keeping the community informed through accessible meetings, clear communication, and consistent follow-through.

I’ve already taken steps to improve transparency by ensuring agenda packets are available online prior to the meetings and council meetings are recorded and shared on my Facebook page so residents can stay informed, even if they can’t attend in person.

Transparency builds trust, and trust is essential to strong leadership and a community that works for everyone.

What else do you want people to know about you?

Strong leadership means truly listening to the people you serve. It’s about being present, involved in the community, hearing concerns, asking questions, and making sure every voice has the opportunity to be heard. When you take the time to listen, you gain a better understanding of the needs, priorities, and challenges facing the community.

At the end of the day, this role is about service. I work for people, and that means decisions should reflect their best interests, not personal agendas. Listening builds trust, and trust is what allows a community to build a stronger future together.

title: Homeowners stuck in 6 years of sinkhole limbo
byline: By Bart Pfankuch South Dakota News Watch
description: This photo taken April 27, 2022, by Tonya Junker shows a sinkhole in the Hideaway Hills neighborhood near Rapid City. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Homeowners stuck in 6 years of sinkhole limbo
This photo taken April 27, 2022, by Tonya Junker shows a sinkhole in the Hideaway Hills neighborhood near Rapid City. Courtesy photo 

BLACK HAWK — Six years ago, a huge sinkhole opened in a residential neighborhood in this unincorporated town that serves largely as a bedroom community for Rapid City.

After all that time, the homeowners directly affected and those put at risk by the sinkhole have received no financial relief for their ongoing or potential losses. 

Meanwhile, the immediate area around the sinkhole in the northeast end of the Hideaway Hills subdivision – easily visible from nearby Interstate 90 – has an almost apocalyptic appearance.

Chain-link fences surround the roughly dozen properties where residents were forced to flee in April 2020, unable to return over fears of further collapse of the underground mine upon which their houses were built.

“I would think that an engineer or geologist who had access to that information (location of abandoned underground mines) could have seen this problem beforehand.” 

– Paul Santi, a sinkhole expert from Colorado, said.

Their homes and many of their belongings have since been left to rot, and their properties are virtually worthless. Tall grass and weeds have overgrown their yards and the road. A vehicle sits stalled in one driveway. Fences are collapsing.

Those families and about 150 other neighboring homeowners have pinned their hopes for help on a lawsuit against the state now pending before the South Dakota Supreme Court. They allege that the state, which previously owned and mined gypsum on the site, is responsible for monetary damages of more than $60 million.

“If the Supreme Court rules against us, we’re pretty much done,” said Carolyn Lorge, a retiree who lives with husband Mike on East Daisy Drive in Black Hawk, just two houses away from the condemnation area. “I mean, you can still move, you can still try to sell your home, but as for being compensated for your loss, you’re pretty much out of luck.”

As the Supreme Court considers the case, News Watch conducted interviews, reviewed documents and media accounts, and listened to the high court hearing to provide this update on the sinkhole saga that has simmered for six years without resolution. 

A sudden opening in the earth 

The origins of the sinkhole date back to the early 1900s when a company called Dakota Plaster dug underground mine shafts in search of gypsum, which slows the hardening of concrete.

When the state of South Dakota opened its own concrete plant in Rapid City in 1925, it began mining for gypsum, including on the future subdivision site. Lawyers for the state said mining was done only on the surface and that no underground mining was undertaken, though blasting did occur.

In the 1990s, the state ended mining operations, reclaimed it for grazing and sold it in 1994 to a private owner. That owner lived and ranched on the land before selling it to a developer who obtained permission from Meade County to build a subdivision in the early 2000s.

The presence of the mine was noted at several points during the land transactions, though homebuyers were not told, according to court documents. Terra Larson, a Pierre attorney representing the state in the Supreme Court case, said the developer disclosed the mine location to the home builder, “who fraudulently concealed it to all the people who would be living there.”

As early as 2008, Hideaway Hills homeowners began reporting shifting in the foundation of their homes, and in April 2020, the sinkhole opened in the northeast edge of the subdivision. No one was injured, though at least one neighbor was nearby when it happened.

Amateur spelunkers who explored the sinkhole said the main cavern is 85 feet deep, 650 feet long, and about 100 feet wide. They found construction debris and even an old car inside the cavern. Scientists found that the tunnel does not extend under I-90, but research by Montana Technical University found that two other tunnels exist under the subdivision with either high or medium risk of geological disturbances.

Seeking a high court ruling

In July 2024, a class-action lawsuit was filed against the state, arguing that the gypsum mining operation was not properly reclaimed when it sold the land. A circuit judge ruled in favor of the state in September 2024, and the homeowners appealed the case to the Supreme Court.

With representation by the national law firm of Fox Rothschild, the homeowners argued that the state improperly filled in areas where it had mined with overly soft materials that have worn away and led to the sinkhole. They argued that the state’s failure to properly close its mining operation is akin to an “inverse condemnation,” or a taking of their land similar to the use of eminent domain.

title: More than half the inmates Noem released early without parole board review have been re-charged
byline: By John Hult Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — Twelve of the 19 people granted early release from prison by former South Dakota Gov. Kristi Noem without a customary review by a state board have since been charged with new crimes.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — Twelve of the 19 people granted early release from prison by former South Dakota Gov. Kristi Noem without a customary review by a state board have since been charged with new crimes.

Nine of them have pleaded guilty to one or more of those charges.

During her time in office, Noem issued 27 total commutations. Those clemency orders, which can release a person from prison or shorten their sentence to make them eligible for parole, are typically reviewed by the state Board of Pardons and Paroles before a governor considers them.

But with 19 of the commutations she signed, Noem did something no governor had done in roughly 2 decades since former Gov. Bill Janklow: issue them to inmates who lacked an endorsement from the board.

Since then, the 12 people who have been accused of new crimes have largely faced drug charges. Seven of the charges were felonies.

Meanwhile, five of the eight people whose commutations from Noem were screened by the board have since been released. Of those five, one has been charged with a new crime.

Noem process

It’s unclear how the 19 people who got commutations without the board’s recommendation got their names in front of Noem. 

Each of those commutations came around Christmas in 2022 and 2023, and granted immediate freedom to all 19 recipients. The eight commutations issued after the board’s recommendation offered shorter sentences and a shot at early release, not immediate freedom.

Noem’s administration never responded to questions about her commutations. She left office in early 2025 for a post in the Trump administration.

Noem did not respond to inquiries for comment on this story. 

Her office issued a press release in 2022 about the seven commutations she’d issued on Christmas Eve. South Dakota Searchlight soon learned she’d gone around the board, that victims’ families were not notified, and that one person who was released early had been denied a recommendation by the board.

Three of the 7 people released that Christmas have since pleaded guilty to new charges: one for drug possession, another for misdemeanor domestic violence, and another for driving under the influence.

South Dakota Searchlight only counted charges for which a person can be jailed or imprisoned in its tally. Some of the people who’ve been released have picked up traffic citations. A fourth person on the list of early releases in 2022, for example, who’d been imprisoned for vehicular homicide and vehicular battery, was cited for exhibition driving. Another was cited twice for violating weight restrictions in a commercial vehicle.

On Christmas Eve of 2023, Noem issued 12 more instant-release commutations without the board’s recommendation, all to people imprisoned for ingestion of a controlled substance. About a year later, lawmakers would vote to reduce ingestion to a misdemeanor for first and second offenses. Gov. Larry Rhoden signed the bill into law.

Noem talked about the commutations in her State of the State address in January 2024, saying the people “qualified” for a commutation, and that “we will continue to evaluate these second-chance opportunities for those who can prove they deserve them.”

Nine of the 12 people released in 2023 have since been charged with new offenses. Six were charged with drug possession after release. Two others were charged with drug distribution. One of those two pleaded guilty to drug possession in 2024, was imprisoned and released again before her arrest for the distribution of hydrocodone. On April 2, she was sentenced to 10 years in prison, with five suspended, for that crime.

In total, 9 of the 12 people charged with new crimes after being granted no-review early release during Noem’s time in office have since pleaded guilty to new charges, and 2 have pending cases. One of them was charged with domestic violence, but the charge was dismissed.

Standard process

Governors in South Dakota have the exclusive state constitutional authority to issue commutations, and also pardons, which scrub an old conviction from a free person’s criminal record entirely. Noem issued 348 pardons.

The commutation process usually starts with an application to the Board of Pardons and Paroles, not the governor, a standard practice Noem pledged to follow with an executive order in 2019, but later strayed from.

Applicants to the board must first clear an initial two-person screening panel, then earn the recommendation of the full board. Both initial and full-board screenings include a review of the person’s record in and out of prison, an interview with the inmate, and interviews with the applicant’s supporters and opponents.

If five or more members of the nine-person board recommend a commutation, all the materials and a recording of the applicant’s full board hearing are sent to the governor’s office for review.

Five of the eight people who got reduced sentences from Noem after board recommendations have since been released from prison. 

One, Mark Milk, was charged with aggravated eluding of a law enforcement officer, a felony, in March after a short pursuit in central Sioux Falls. Milk remains in custody at the Minnehaha County Jail as he awaits trial.

A message to Milk’s attorney with the Minnehaha County Public Defender’s Office was not returned.

Milk pleaded guilty to manslaughter in 1994 for killing a man in the aftermath of a fight in Winner and was given a life sentence. Noem commuted his sentence in 2022 after a unanimous recommendation by the board.

High bar for board recommendations

One more person who got a board-reviewed commutation from Noem, John Proctor, will be released soon.

Proctor’s parole hearing in April offers a window into the level of personal growth and transformation the board tends to expect before recommending a commutation.  

On April 14, the board voted 6-2 to release Proctor, who killed a Meade County woman’s stepson in a 1973 murder-for-hire plot. Proctor was 19 at the time, newly married with a daughter on the way, and recruited for the $2,000 job from his home in Nevada. 

Acting on the board’s recommendation, Noem commuted Proctor’s sentence in July 2024.

Proctor is now 72, a born-again Christian with a theology degree he earned as a prisoner in Oregon, where he was moved in the 1980s to be closer to his family as he served his life sentence for the South Dakota killing. He works as a licensed supervising electrician and maintenance man at the prison’s workshops, and spends many of his evenings sitting with hospice patients to make sure, he told the board, that “they don’t die alone.”

Call for change from gubernatorial candidate

Gov. Larry Rhoden, who took over for Noem when she left South Dakota for a job in the Trump administration, has issued 90 pardons and two commutations.

U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, one of 3 candidates running against Rhoden in the June 2 Republican primary for governor, brought up commutations at a campaign event last month.

Johnson pledged to create a public safety task force if elected, and mentioned that the group would discuss ways to “reform the clemency process” and “help ensure violent criminals are prevented from repeatedly harming the public.”

Johnson, who later told South Dakota Searchlight he was unaware of Noem’s decision to release inmates without board approval, said the state ought to consider adjusting its laws to require a board review for all acts of executive clemency.

In a follow-up statement, Johnson clarified that such an adjustment would require a change to the South Dakota Constitution.

“At the federal level, I’ve seen pardon abuses from presidents of both parties,” Johnson said. “It’s convinced me that state pardons should require experts at the table, and I support a constitutional amendment making that the case.”

Rhoden hasn’t issued any pardons or commutations that weren’t first reviewed by the board. In a statement to Searchlight, he said “I expect that to continue to be the case,” but also said the state constitution “is not broken, and I do not support changing it.”

“I respect the review and recommendation of the members of the Board of Pardons and Paroles. They have experience and expertise in this area, but they are not elected or accountable to the people,” Rhoden said.

He called clemency “an important check and balance on the judicial branch to give a second chance,” and a responsibility he does not “take lightly.” 

Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden and Jon Hansen, speaker of the state House of Representatives, are also seeking the Republican nomination for governor. Neither responded to Searchlight questions about clemency.

title: Praise for simplicity, concern about brevity greet new format for SD water quality report
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: The Big Sioux River flows under a Highway 34 bridge near Egan in southeastern South Dakota. Photo by Makenzie Huber, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Praise for simplicity, concern about brevity greet new format for SD water quality report
The Big Sioux River flows under a Highway 34 bridge near Egan in southeastern South Dakota. Photo by Makenzie Huber, South Dakota Searchlight 

PIERRE — South Dakota’s environmental regulatory department has changed how it publicly presents its report on the quality of the state’s rivers, lakes and streams, leading to praise for the simplified presentation but concern about the reduced amount of information made available. 

Instead of publishing the 2026 Surface Water Quality Assessment as a 200-plus-page document, as it has in the past, the Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources is directing the public to a scrollable presentation on the department’s website. 

A separate, online Surface Water Quality Dashboard allows viewers to click waterways on a map for information.

The reports come out every two years. The 2024 report included detailed sections on monitoring, methodology, assessments, pollution control programs, pollution causes and more. 

That year, the state reported that 78% of assessed stream miles, as well as 68.5% of lake surface acres in the state, did not support one or more of their assigned “beneficial uses.” That refers to a practical purpose that a lake, river or stream is supposed to serve, such as swimming, fishing, boating or irrigation. If a waterbody is not meeting a beneficial use, it means the water is polluted beyond the standard set for that use.

The 2026 data show that 77% of assessed stream miles and 73% of lake acres are not supporting one or more of their beneficial uses. 

Mercury in water remains the primary cause of water bodies failing to support their beneficial uses. About 70% of the tested lake acres in the state have mercury levels exceeding their standards, which is about the same as in 2024. The toxic heavy metal ends up in fish worldwide, largely due to atmospheric deposition. Coal-fired power plants release mercury into the air before it settles into lakes and rivers.

Another major pollutant is E. coli, with 68% of river and stream miles testing at levels that are too high.

But unlike past reports, the new one does not include statements such as one from the 2024 report calling nonpoint-source pollution, such as E. coli, the state’s “most serious and pervasive threat” to water quality, or examples of causes such as livestock waste, and failing septic systems. Those kinds of explanatory passages do not appear at the same level of detail in the new format.

Paul Lorenzen, watershed protection administrator with the Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources, explained to lawmakers during the 2026 legislative session why the format change was occurring. He said the prior format made the percentage of unsupported beneficial uses sound “troubling” and got “quite a bit of attention,” without the public fully understanding the meaning.

“We’re really trying to limit the narrative and be heavy on pictures, graphs, tables, things like that,” Lorenzen told lawmakers.

Lorenzen said waters not supporting all their uses are not necessarily unsafe or unusable. He said that, often, only one parameter or sample fails, criteria can be conservative, and increases in the percentage of non-supporting uses over time can reflect more data or changed standards, rather than worsening quality.

Lorenzen said the new format is intended to make the report easier to understand and less dependent on a dense executive summary.

Travis Entenman is the executive director of Friends of the Big Sioux River. He said his organization is “excited that the report is in a more user-friendly system, more interactive and we have more access to the data.”

However, “We do feel like there is a lack of analysis of the causes, and the next steps beyond saying this is the water quality level,” Entenman said. “Now what?”

The streamlined public presentation arrives as concern about agriculture’s role in water pollution has grown. A legislative memo last year said E. coli from livestock was the primary reason some streams did not support recreational uses. 

In November, when that memo was shared, Senate President Pro Tempore Chris Karr, R-Sioux Falls, said the state could no longer “dance around” the possibility of stronger agricultural regulation if something was to be done about water pollution. Gov. Larry Rhoden then said he would set Karr straight. 

Karr then sponsored and Rhoden signed a bill into law during this year’s legislative session that put $10 million toward water quality improvement programs. It offers $8 million to incentivize an existing water quality initiative that helps landowners plant buffer strips that filter agricultural runoff, and $2 million to help improve local water, wastewater and stormwater systems.

title: Hold on to your hats, Broncs!: Belle Fourche graduates class of 2026 in bright, breezy Saturday ceremony
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: BELLE FOURCHE — Graduates the world over look forward to the moment when, having earned their academic accolades, they can send their caps sailing into the sky — marking the end of their achievement. In Belle Fourche, Saturday, the challenge for the 86-person graduating class at Lou Graslie Field was holding on to their caps prior to the big toss.
_full_text:
BELLE FOURCHE — Graduates the world over look forward to the moment when, having earned their academic accolades, they can send their caps sailing into the sky — marking the end of their achievement. In Belle Fourche, Saturday, the challenge for the 86-person graduating class at Lou Graslie Field was holding on to their caps prior to the big toss.

As this year’s class of Broncs looked toward the future and all that lay ahead, most were hanging on to their hats.

“Today we celebrate more than grades, awards, and diplomas; we also celebrate growth, determination, and the long path that brought us here,” said 2026 senior class president Andrew Pruitt, as he held on to his tassel in the breeze. He acknowledged that life, like high school, isn’t always perfect.

“Perfection is never the goal; what really matters is our learning, growth, and appreciation for the moments that make life truly wonderful. Today, we don’t celebrate perfect people. We celebrate the determination, hope, and capabilities that we have refined over the last 18 years,” Pruitt said. “We celebrate all of those qualities with optimism for the future, thinking that we are more than equipped for whatever may come our way.”

After the class president’s opening dedication and a formal welcome from Superintendent Orion Thompson, the choir performed, and honor graduates, National Honor Society members, and Regent Scholars were asked to rise for recognition. Out of the class of 86, 21 students were members of the National Honor Society. More than 30 graduated with honors, having maintained a cumulative grade point average of at least 3.25 throughout their high school career. Nearly a dozen graduated as regent scholars.

“I think a lot of people measure value off of the things that we achieve: getting good grades, receiving awards, that is something we should all be proud of, but they are only a small part of the people that we are,” Denali Larson, the 2026 salutatorian, said in her address. “I think that there is no single definition of success. Everyone here is going to make an impact, no matter what they do. Whether they are going to secondary school, working after high school, or joining the military, the impact that you make will be entirely up to you.”

Larson told her classmates that everyone makes an impression on the people that they meet.

“Every person that you meet, you will leave an impression with. Whether you provide them with kindness, strength, and love is entirely up to you,” Larson said. “There is nothing more important than lifting up those around you.”

In his address, Valedictorian Tegan Fredericksen said that he felt his personality was shaped by his high school classmates.

“I am thankful for each and every one of you. For all of the experiences I’ve had and all of the things that I have learned. It has really shocked me, just how much the people around you shape your own personality,” Fredericksen said. “Even people you’re not close friends with, small interactions, little conversations, and quick moments, can permanently change who you are as a person.”

Fredericksen encouraged his class to carry “3 Ts” with them into their futures.  

“Stay true to yourself, be tough, and finally be triumphant,” Fredericksen said.

He closed his remarks by expressing gratitude for his time in high school and all of the memories made along the way.

“A small part of us will always remain in this school,” Fredericksen said. “I am extremely thankful for each and every one of you, and I hope in these next few years you can reflect on all the great times you had and hold this small class of 2026 deep in your heart.”

When the time came to turn tassels and send those purple and black caps flying, the sound of Billy Joel’s “Vienna” rang out over the loudspeakers — and this year’s graduates embraced their families, one another, and the class quote from Dr. Suess, “Sometimes you will never know the value of a moment until it becomes a memory.”
