title: Ready to write their next chapter
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: LEAD — Friends, family and staff gathered at the Lead-Deadwood High School Sunday to celebrate the accomplishments of 46 graduates in a heart-warming ceremony.
_full_text:
LEAD — Friends, family and staff gathered at the Lead-Deadwood High School Sunday to celebrate the accomplishments of 46 graduates in a heart-warming ceremony. 

Superintendent Erik Person welcomed graduates and their friends and families, reminding students to be grateful to the people who have supported them throughout their journeys and to take pride in their accomplishments. 

“Over the past week or so, I’ve observed a lot of scurry in preparation for this day,” Person said. “Mr. Mike Embrock (high school principal) running around like his hair was on fire. (Staff) and even parents and family members getting ready for receptions and parties. A lot of hustles and a lot of things happening behind the scenes to make this day happen. The takeaway of that observation is 2 things I want to share with our graduates. First, always remember to express gratitude for the people outside the spotlight who make good things happen for you. Second, whatever your career path or life path might be, take pride in your work. People I just mentioned take pride in their work and it shows. And not only is there honor in that, but also, it’s just how things get done.”

Gracie Zopp, senior class president, took to the stage to address her class. Before giving her speech, though, she asked retiring teach Kim Loeffen to come to the front and lead the students in one last “speech-y wiggle.” Students raised their arms up high and had one last good shake. 

Zopp thanked the class for allowing her to lead them as class president. 

“I’m still not entirely sure how I got here,” she said. “I assume it was either my leadership skills or the fact that I answered one email on time.”

Zopp told the students that the day marked the cumulation of years of hard work, dedication, and courage. 

“Somehow, we survived early mornings, endless assignments, and teachers saying, ‘This will be on the test,’ like it was a personal threat,” she said. “Along the way, we picked up some very valuable lessons — like writing essays 5 minutes before the deadline, looking busy when teachers walked by, turning group projects into one person does everything and the rest just look.”

Zopp noted that the Class of 2026 was a memorable one for Lead-Deadwood High School. 

“The kind of class that may have accidentally made teachers cry, a few teachers question their career choices, and, rumor has it, contributed to a record number of retirements,” she said. “We definitely kept things interesting. If nothing else, we proved we were a challenging group to teach, but also one worth believing in. But beyond all the jokes, this journey was about more than the grades and exams. It was about growth.”

Zopp congratulated her class on their resilience and thanked friends and family for their support on their academic journey. 

“As we leave today, we carry with us not just memories, but support and belief of everyone who helped us get here,” she said. “As we step into the future, some of us have everything planned out, some of us are still figuring it out, and some of us are just hoping things will work out. And, honestly, that’s OK. Because if these past years have taught us anything, it’s that we are completely capable of more than we think. We handled the stress, chaos, and way too many alarms going off in the morning. The future doesn’t stand a chance.”

Rhonda Britzman, high school counselor, acknowledged the students who received scholarships and students who have been accepted into universities and trade schools. Collectively, the class received $89,450 in scholarships. 

After a performance of ‘Hallelujah’ by Leonard Cohen, performed by the Lead-Deadwood High School chorale, Embrock acknowledged the class Salutatorian Maeve Campbell and Valedictorian Mia Gifford. 

Gifford came to the podium for the commencement address. Gifford told the class that they were no longer subject to the whims and rules the school staff. 

“They’ve told us when to move, stop, eat, learn, and leave,” Gifford said. “Now, however, we begin to make those decisions for ourselves. We are able to learn a type of independency that one can only find in growing up. Now, no one can make us do anything. We are adults.”

Gifford congratulated her class on their years of hard work and dedication, their grades, awards, and accomplishments. She also congratulated them on the things that may have gone unseen, including their ability to withstand pressure, their resilience and ability to adapt, and their eventual growth. She asked her class to continue to grow and learn.

“To even begin this, we one must put themselves in a situation they may not want to be in,” Gifford said. “Maybe they have to stay up later or wake up earlier, or maybe they even have to crawl out of bed when the sheets try to pull them in closer, just to go to the gym. A good friend of mine once said, ‘Comfortability kills.’ I wish for everyone to know that if you never put yourself out there, if you never feel comfortable or unsure, then you’ll never truly grow. Everyone sitting here has more potential than they think they do, but staying in the same place, whether that be physical, emotional, or mental, will destroy from the inside out.”

Gifford reminisced on moments from the classes time at the Lead-Deadwood High School that made their time unique. 

“I mean, one time we got basically a week off of school because of that big snowstorm that was basically covering houses. And then, as soon as we were ready to come back, some kid decided to bring mercury to school,” she said. “And, maybe we got just a little more of a break.”

In December 2022, a mercury spill at the high school chemistry lab required a specialty hazardous material crew to clean the room. The material was also found in 7 homes of students.

“Or even that random study hall in 2023 when half of the school was crowding the fourth-floor hallway as Mr. and Mrs. Campbell gave their gender reveal for their youngest, Charlie. Mr. Campbell was already excited to teach little Charlie baseball,” Gifford said. “Or even that one homecoming week that was bring anything but a backpack day, and people brought things from lawn mowers to literal children.”

Gifford reminded her class that nobody is defined by a single moment in their life, and that their lives were just beginning. 

“What people will really notice is how you pursue your future, watching how you grow,” she said. “So, don’t let today just be a farewell. Let it also be a greeting to the things to come in the future. Growth does not stop when something ends — it starts again. So no, this is not the end of our story. It’s only proof that we’re ready to write our next chapter.”

The Lead-Deadwood High School senior choir gave a performance of ‘Sign of the Times’ by Harry Styles before Betty Campbell, high school math instructor, presented the class. 

Campbell spoke about how she met the class of 2026 in stages — some as sixth-graders looking for extra math tutoring, some as eighth-graders taking high school algebra, and some as rowdy freshman.

“Over the years, we’ve all grown, and we’ve all shared some memories together,” she said. “This includes some laughs, some jokes, some candy stealing, crayons all over my room, and tears, happy and sad,” Campbell said. “The things that I love the most over the years is that I got to watch you all grow as math students, but more importantly as individuals. You are not shy little sixth-graders or rotten freshmen anymore. You’ve grown into accomplished individuals.”

Campbell reminded students that as they start the next part of their lives, that they have the problem-solving skills and the resilience to be successful. 

“We’re all human. Everyone in this gym is going to make mistakes,” she said. “But it’s how you learn from your mistakes. You are going to struggle. But keep working through it. You can make it. Life is hard, but you’ve got it. There are different ways to solve a problem, and the best feeling in the world is when you succeed.”

title: Sturgis Brown graduates 199 seniors during commencement ceremony
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — The Sturgis Brown High School Class of 2026 celebrated a major milestone Sunday as 199 seniors crossed the stage during commencement ceremonies, receiving their diplomas before family, friends, faculty, and community members.
_full_text:
STURGIS — The Sturgis Brown High School Class of 2026 celebrated a major milestone Sunday as 199 seniors crossed the stage during commencement ceremonies, receiving their diplomas before family, friends, faculty, and community members.

The ceremony highlighted the accomplishments, memories, and future aspirations of the graduating class while recognizing the support of parents, teachers, mentors, and classmates who helped guide students through their high school journey.

The class flower was the white carnation, while the class song was “Good Riddance” by Green Day. The Senior Class President was Tori Williams. Diplomas were presented by Justin Jutting, president of the Meade School Board.

Wayne Wormstadt, superintendent of Meade School District, welcomed those attending the ceremony and encouraged graduates to remember the people who supported them throughout their school years.

“The one thing I ask you to do is say thank you,” Wormstadt said. “Take a moment to thank your parents, grandparents, teachers, counselors, office staff, employers, and everyone who helped you along the way. A simple thank you can build strong relationships and lift people up.”

Wormstadt congratulated the graduates for their hard work and reminded them that they will always remain part of the Scooper community.

Principal Pete Wilson praised the Class of 2026 for its perseverance and achievements.

“You worked hard, pushed through challenges, and made your mark,” Wilson said. “As you move forward, pursue your passions, stay true to your values, and never stop reaching for your dreams.”

Student speaker Madisyn Richter reflected on the graduates’ 4-year journey by comparing each school year to a class period in a final day of high school.

Richter described freshman year as exciting and intimidating, sophomore year as often overlooked, junior year as a time of growth and preparation, and senior year as a mixture of nostalgia and anticipation for the future.

“Today is our 1,052nd day together,” Richter said. “Thank you for the memories, the lessons, and the friendships. Class of 2026, we’ve made it — the final bell has rung. School is dismissed.”

Senior speaker Olivia Glover encouraged classmates to embrace the opportunities ahead while striving to make a positive impact on the world.

“We are no longer required to memorize the world as it was,” Glover said. “We are now tasked with imagining the world as it should be.”

Glover challenged graduates to pursue their goals with courage and purpose.

“True change in the world doesn’t start with grand gestures,” she said. “It starts with you. It starts with me. It starts with us.”

Elizabeth Markworth shared the class poem, reflecting on how quickly the four years passed and the importance of friendships and connections formed along the way.

“My parents told me these would be the quickest four years of my life,” Markworth read. “And now, standing here today, I finally believe them.”

As the graduates turned their tassels and celebrated with classmates and loved ones, the Class of 2026 closed one chapter and prepared to begin the next.

title: After a 4-2 vote, Mayor Senden will receive  compensation for interim administrative work
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Spearfish Mayor John Senden will now receive $1,500 per week in addition to his weekly mayoral wage of $560.40. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
John.JPG
Spearfish Mayor John Senden will now receive $1,500 per week in addition to his weekly mayoral wage of $560.40. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — Spearfish has not had a city administrator since Feb. 2. In the interim, Mayor John Senden has overseen the day-to-day operations of the city, and on Monday, the Spearfish City Council voted 4-2 to compensate him at a weekly, fixed rate of $1,500 in addition to his weekly mayoral wage of $560.40 for the additional hours and duties he has taken on. The compensation will be considered effective starting May 4. He will not receive compensation for hours worked in January, February, or March.

Spearfish Human Resources Jodi Mathis told the Spearfish City Council that Senden started picking up duties before the previous city administrator formally departed.

“Basically, in January, (he began) managing the day-to-day operations of the city of Spearfish. Several directors came to me requesting, or having concerns, that John wasn’t being compensated. He was easily putting in anywhere from 20-30 hours per week on top of his mayoral duties, so I visited with John,” Mathis said. 

Mathis said the city has paid mayors for interim work during city administrator vacancies, dating back to Mayor Dana Boke’s tenure. She added that, given Senden’s willingness to donate his time prior to May 4, she felt compensation was fair. 

 Dean.JPG
Spearfish City Councilman Dean Myers questions Mayor John Senden’s request for additional compensation at Monday’s city council meeting. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

“I had originally suggested the first step on the grade scale for the city administrator, which was $83.92 (per hour). He went back and looked at what he was paid the last time he took on these duties, and it was $68.28, so he came in the middle and requested the $75,” Mathis said. 

Spearfish City Councilwoman Jamie Hafner said she had heard concerns from constituents about that rate of compensation.

“I have had people reach out to me over the weekend and today, and they are adamant about this amount. Being paid $6,000 a month, plus the $2,000 a month for this mayor position. I realize those hours that you put in, John, but the message is that they want a more reasonable amount, and they are not happy,” Hafner said.

Councilman Dean Myers, a retired provost from Black Hills State University, also expressed concerns about the $1,500 weekly rate.

“I dealt with leadership and management for 40 years. When I look at some of the things that we are talking about here, management things. Leadership is hard. Leadership is what makes it difficult, but when I look at $1,500 a week to do some management kind of things, and coordinate some of the activities that go on, I just can’t get there on it,” Myers said.

Noting that his comments were strictly his own and had not been discussed with Senden or the rest of the council, Myers added “What I remember about some of this in the past, when we were talking about the departure of our previous administrator, I remember John making some comments about, ‘I don’t want to assume this role again.’ He was pretty adamant about that. I thought the council said at that time that we didn’t want you to do it again. We thought that we had qualified and competent directors and staff, and until we found a replacement for the city administrator, they had the skills to keep everything moving forward.”

Councilman Scott Hourigan made the motion to approve Senden’s compensation, effective May 4. Councilman Larry Klarenbeek seconded the motion.

 John 2.JPG
From the podium, Spearfish Mayor John Senden entered an exchange with Councilman Dean Myers about attempts made for the 2 to get in contact. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

“Dean, to your comment, when Bobby left town, you might say, we have 2 department heads that were strong department heads that are now gone,” Hourigan said. “Now we are down 3 qualified positions, so I strongly promote this. It is only for a temporary amount of time, so whether or not a person likes John’s leadership skills, he has done, in my opinion, a good job. My motion stands.”

Klarenbeek said he understood the apprehension around the price of compensation and adding more responsibilities for department heads.

“I explored the idea. Do we have strong department heads? Could we have an executive committee? But it is pretty hard to make decisions in a committee setting. When you look at it, it is kind of ideal that one executive is making a final decision,” Klarenbeek said.

On an annual basis, this is $78,000. When we did hire Bobby, we hired Bobby at my recollection of $168,000. This is in theory, a reduced amount.”

Senden told the Pioneer he discussed earning additional compensation one-on-one with members of the city council prior to a study session last week.  

“After having discussed this situation with Council President (Pam) Jacobs and Vice President Klarenbeek, some form of additional compensation for the additional time I must spend addressing all of the duties was reasonable in their opinion. I visited one-on-one with some of the other council members to advise them of this request and notify them it was being placed on the agenda for the study session,” Senden told the Pioneer. “This will give the council and public adequate notice of the agenda item and time to discuss the matter before voting on whether or not to provide the additional compensation.”

However, at the May 13 study session, when the topic was first discussed publicly, councilman Dean Myers said that he had not heard from the mayor about the compensation request prior to the study session.

“I was not happy, obviously, when we had our last city council meeting. When I saw that on the agenda, and I found out that I hadn’t been included in the conversation, anybody who knows me knows that I can tolerate a lot of things, but I can’t tolerate being ignored, and I felt like that was the case,” Myers said. “I’m going to go on record now and say that I am not going to approve this compensation.”

The mayor, who had stepped down from the dais for the discussion on Monday, approached the podium to respond.

“Dean, you happened to be unavailable the previous week. You were ill, and I respected that. Then, last Monday and Tuesday had full days, I tried to call you at 2 (p.m.) prior to the meeting,” Senden said. “Your wife said you were coming to the meeting, and I said, ‘Could you have Dean stop by?’ Since last Thursday, I have reached out to you via text, email, and left phone messages. I wanted to have a conversation with you prior to tonight. I made a significant effort.”

Myers said that he had attempted to reach the mayor earlier than last week to discuss different matters, but hadn’t received a reply. He said he was aware of Senden’s attempts to contact him after last week’s study session.

“The things that I wanted to talk about were way more important than that,” Myers said. “I’ll admit that I ignored you. This is something that is hot button with me, and obviously, I am not happy about it.”

Hafner and Myers were the 2 council members who voted against the motion to compensate Senden $1,500 per week to fill in until a city administrator is hired. The motion passed, with the majority of the council voting in favor of Hourigan’s motion. 

A job listing for the city administrator has been on the city’s website since April 27.

title: Bunches of BMWs in the Black Hills
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: DEADWOOD — Over the last week, drivers in Deadwood and the Black Hills may have noticed higher-than-average numbers of the Z series of BMW sports cars in the area.
_full_text:
DEADWOOD — Over the last week, drivers in Deadwood and the Black Hills may have noticed higher-than-average numbers of the Z series of BMW sports cars in the area. 

ZFEST, a gathering of owners passionate about the car, took place last week, bringing more than 100 people from across the country together to celebrate the German sports car. 

Jon Moorehead, vice-president of the Z-Series Car Club of America (ZSCCA), said that he bought a used, 2004 Z4 in 2015. Now, he said that car has 208,000 miles and he’s found some of his closest friends through the club. 

“This is like a reunion,” Moorehead said. “What brought us together was the car, but what keeps us coming back is the people, the friendships that we make, and the camaraderie that develops over time. It’s like a homecoming.”

The annual reunion moves across the country every year, moving from coast to coast and landing occasionally in the Midwest. In 2022, the event was held in Snowmass, Colo. Moorehead said fellow coordinator and ZSCCA President, Eric Peck, led a convoy of 30 cars through Deadwood on their way across the country from the East Coast.

“One of the places that they visited was Deadwood, and I think they stayed 3 days there,” Moorehead said. “People that were a part of this convoy loved it and all of them were like, ‘We should hold ZFEST here.’ And that’s how it all started.”

Moorehead said that Deadwood was chosen this year for its central location and its concentration of features that could be attractive to members. 

“With Mount Rushmore, Crazy Horse Memorial, Devil’s tower, these are all things that we felt possibly many people have not been to before, or if they have, it may have been many years before they were in that area. What we are finding, especially with our East and West Coast people, that this is a place they have all wanted to visit and haven’t done it before. This is giving them an opportunity to do that.”

The itinerary for ZFEST included drives, tours of local attractions, and banquets. Scheduled drives throughout the rally included the wildlife loop at Custer State Park, Needles Highway, Badlands National Park, and Iron Mountain Road, and visits to Crazy Horse Memorial, Minuteman Missile National Historic Site, Wall Drug, and the geographic center of the nation.

The main attraction, Moorehead said, is the Zedkana.

“It’s a driving skills event, but it also has humorous things that are involved,” he said. “There are 4 or 5 elements that people have to do after they pull into a parking place in the parking lot.”

This year, Zedkana was held in The Lodge at Deadwood parking lot. Participants donated $20 per run to shoot a gunslinger with a rubber band gun, rope a fake bull, try their luck at blackjack, and answer trivia questions about Mount Rushmore, before finishing the timed driving course. Prizes for the course include first, second, and third place, as well as slowest time and the most cones crushed on course. 

“It is so much fun,” Moorehead said. “We generally accumulate a large crowd that wants to watch.”

All proceeds raised by Zedkana go towards the Tire Rack Street Survival teen driving school. The course provides teen drivers with hands-on experiences meant to help them navigate real-world situations, like wet roads and unexpected car troubles.

“Generally, our club donates more money than any other group in the United States,” said Moorehead. 

The event, held at 2 p.m. Saturday, gathered more than 30 participants to the parking lot of The Lodge at Deadwood. Observers perched in lawn chairs to cheer on their friends and competitors. The event raised 

After ZFEST, Moorehead said he’s going to take the opportunity to travel to the eastern side of the state and visit the small town where he spent his summers with his grandparents. 

Next year, the event is scheduled to be held in Atlanta, Ga.

title: Lead rejects Handley resolution with 3-2 vote
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Residents of Lead and Spearfish gather regularly at the Handley Recreation Center to play pickleball. On Monday, the Lead City Commission rejected a resolution for the city to take over the Handley, but 2 of the 3 commissioners who voted against the measure said they support the city takeover. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Lead rejects Handley resolution with 3-2 vote
Residents of Lead and Spearfish gather regularly at the Handley Recreation Center to play pickleball. On Monday, the Lead City Commission rejected a resolution for the city to take over the Handley, but 2 of the 3 commissioners who voted against the measure said they support the city takeover. Courtesy photo  

LEAD — Deed restrictions on a resolution for the city to take over the Handley Recreation Center were the deal breaker, Monday, as the Lead City Commission rejected the proposal with a 3-2 vote. 

The resolution declared the city’s intent to accept ownership and assume management of the Handley Recreation Center. It committed the city to operating the facility for the purpose of providing indoor recreational opportunities and programming for the residents of Lead for at least 2 years. 

Commissioners Roger Thomas, Dory Hanson, and Al Rohrer all voted against the resolution, while Commissioner Rob Carr and Mayor Dustin Heupel supported it. 

Thomas, who has consistently said he would not support any deal that includes deed restrictions, told the Pioneer Tuesday that the city cannot afford the resolution. On Monday, Thomas specifically cited a provision in the resolution, which states the city will provide the personnel necessary to administer, operate, and support community and recreation programming.

“That could be the moon and beyond what we’re already providing. Now they’re going to say ‘well, you took it over and now you’re going to provide this, this, and this.’ If we can’t provide that, then what? We’re stuck with not doing what we said we were going to do,” Thomas said on Monday. “I’m not against funding or having recreation for these kids. We have a lot of recreation, We just don’t have indoor recreation for baseball, archery. We could do something with that. The Handley should be able to run it themselves with the same grants. If we can get them, they should be able to get them.” 

Before the city voted on the resolution, Hanson asked the commission to consider an amendment to the resolution, which would continue to fund the Handley Recreation Center for the rest of the year, with funds that the city set aside in its 2026 budget for recreation. However, Heupel said that money is for things the city would need to run recreation. The process for the Handley Center to get that money includes coming to the city with a specific dollar amount request, he said, which has not been done. Additionally, Heupel said the Handley Center board has cut back on services such as Lead Live and office hours. 

Rohrer told the Pioneer he believes the city would do well with the Handley Center, and he was surprised the resolution did not pass. However, he rejected Monday’s resolution because of deed restrictions and because of recent social media posts from the Handley Center, which appeared to try and influence the election. 

“I stuck to my principles and refused it based on the deed restrictions,” Rohrer said Tuesday morning. “I really do think that the city would have done well with it. I do think it would be a positive thing for the city to take over the Handley Center, and I think we would do a better job. I do think it’s worth saving. I don’t have a problem with the building. My problem is with the board and their social media practices.” 

Hanson told the Pioneer after the meeting that she supports the city taking over the Handley Center, but she wants to see a plan. 

“I believe a city takeover is ultimately in the best interest of both the city and the Handley Center,” she said. “However, responsible governance requires more than good intentions. Without a clear operational plan, a defined budget, and a realistic path forward, we cannot responsibly take on this commitment. My vote reflects the need to ensure that if the city moves forward, we do so with transparency, preparation, and a plan that sets both our taxpayers and the Handley center up for long-term success.” 

Heupel told the commission that the resolution was the first step toward the city’s plan for taking over recreation. He said in November 2025, former Commissioner Kayla Klein outlined a plan for funding the recreation center, which stated expenses for running the recreation center could be more than $300,000, but the city’s contribution would not exceed $125,000. The remainder of the funds, he said, would come from memberships, facility rental fees, grants, and other sources.  

Before the commission voted on the proposal, Heupel made it clear that he will always support giving $125,000 in city funds for recreation. 

“I have heard a lot of discussion about we need to fix the roads and that money can be spent better elsewhere,” he said. “No matter what happens with the way this resolution is voted on, or the Handley Center accepting it or not, it is my intention that the $125,000 will stay in the budget for recreation. For the past decade I have been a huge supporter of recreation in the community, and I will continue to be a huge supporter of recreation in the community. It is not my intent that money would ever go to road or infrastructure repairs. Those are bigger things that we can get grants to deal with. It’s been said that the Handley doesn’t know what our intent is. This is putting our intent out there, so they know what we can do. First it has to pass this commission, and if there are other hurdles, we will cross them at that time.” 

Before the vote, Carr told a room full of residents that he wanted to see the issue move forward. The 2-year deed restrictions are not substantial, he said, since 2 years can go by very quickly.  

“We have to try a different path because what we’ve got isn’t working,” Carr said. “Two years is going to fly by, and we’ll still be working through all the kinks in 2 years.”

Karen Everett, who serves on the Handley Recreation Center board, said the board would have likely supported the resolution if the commission passed it. The city could run it better than a volunteer board of directors, she said. 

“I don’t know how many directors we’ve had over the years,” Everett said. “We hire somebody and can’t afford to pay them a whole lot. They burn out and they quit. But if the city takes over, we can combine those duties.” 

Everett also pointed out that the city taking over daily operations at the recreation center could free up some of the board’s time to help raise money and help with programming. As an example, she said the Handley Center’s Mile High Basketball Tournament in March brought about 55 teams and 2,000 people in to Lead. The event raised about $18,000 for the Handley Center. 

“We are a working board,” she said. “We shovel snow. We haul pop to Lead Live. If the board doesn’t have to do the day-to-day stuff, this board can actually do what a board is supposed to do and help raise money. If we all work together I think we can write some big grants and make some really good things happen.” 

After the meeting, Carr told the Pioneer that the only way to save the project is if both sides can trust each other. 

“We needed to make an effort,” he said. “A resolution only states an intent to try something. It gives a direction. The commission as a whole seems to feel city management and ownership is the path forward, or at least worth trying. The implementation of deed restrictions will be what kills the deal evidently. The only thing that will save the project is if both sides will trust each other to do the right thing. This community was built on faith and trust. We need to get back to what made this community special.” 

Following the vote, Heupel told the Pioneer he was disappointed, and that he would have to double check with the city attorney to see if the issue can be revisited. 

“I thought there was great discussion, maybe solutions and even some positivity around it,” Heupel said. “But at the end I am disappointed in the way the votes came in.”

title: 2 Spearfish students expelled Monday
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — Two students from the Spearfish School District have been expelled for 12 months after they were alleged to have been involved in bringing a weapon to the Spearfish High School campus earlier this month.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

SPEARFISH — Two students from the Spearfish School District have been expelled for 12 months after they were alleged to have been involved in bringing a weapon to the Spearfish High School campus earlier this month.

The decision came Monday evening following executive sessions by the Spearfish School Board.

The board entered the first of 2 closed sessions shortly after 6 p.m., to discuss the expulsion, suspension, discipline, assignment of or the educational program of a student or the eligibility of a student to participate in interscholastic activities provided by the South Dakota High School Activities Association. The move is allowed as one of only several matters in which a board may exclude the public from proceedings.

An hour and a half later, the board returned to open session where it voted to expel the first student, only identified as Student 1, for 12 months.

A slightly shorter executive session proceeded for Student 2 who received the same expulsion timeframe.

On May 8, it was reported to parents of high school students, that a weapon was brought to school earlier in the week. 

Spearfish Police Chief Collin Smith told the Pioneer that the weapon was allegedly brought to the campus on May 5. School officials immediately launched an investigation in cooperation with the school resource officer and local law enforcement. 

While the initial inquiry and search found no weapon nor any intent to harm someone, they continued to follow leads, according to the report. Further investigation suggested that the weapon may have been on school grounds at some point, and in response, school officials followed their safety procedures. A comprehensive K-9 search, conducted by Cpl. Chris Woods, and the Spearfish police dog Davos, confirmed that no firearm was present. 

According to the report from the school district, during their investigation, law enforcement officers located and recovered the reported weapon at an off-campus location.

Smith previously told the Pioneer that one of the juveniles was in custody at the Pennington County juvenile services center. It was not immediately clear if that person is still in police custody.

Questions regarding what type of weapon was reported, the age and genders of the students, and others were not answered as the investigation continues. 

Answers to questions to the Spearfish School District were not returned. School officials are extremely limited in what they can report because the incident involved students.

title: Sturgis city council ward 1 candidates
description: Voters in Sturgis will head to the polls June 2 to vote on vacant ward 1 seat. Two people are running for one open position which is a 3-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.
_full_text:
SturgisCityCouncilComp.jpg

Voters in Sturgis will head to the polls June 2 to vote on vacant ward 1 seat. Two people are running for one open position which is a 3-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.

Terry Keszler

 Keszler, Terry.jpg
Terry Keszler 

Name and what you do for a living?

My name is Terry Keszler.  I am a candidate for the soon to be alderman vacancy in Ward 1.  I am retired from my profession as an anesthestist.  Most of my career was spent at the Fort Meade VA Medical Center.  It was my honor to care for America’s Veterans

What motivated you to run for this office?

My main motivation for running is that I care very much for the community of Sturgis.  I feel a strong attachment to this town and realize the City Council plays a significant role in shaping the place we all reside.  This also provides me an opportunity to serve this city.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

I am a past member of the Sturgis City Council.  I have also served on other committees and boards outside of local government.  All this offers me experience, insight, knowledge, and reflection.  I’m willing to listen to the residents and be their representative.  I have a strong desire to be part of a council committed to moving Sturgis forward.  My time on city council along with the different committees and boards are assets in filling this vacancy.

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I have spent 8 years on my church council.  The governing body for the church.  Responsibilities are managing property, approving the budget, and ensure effective operations. For 5 years I have been a member of the church endowment Committee.  This committee monitors investments and makes adjustment if warranted.  The committee also meets with the financial advisor as needed.  I›ve also served on the Supervisory Committee for Northern Hills Federal Credit Union.  This committee has broad powers.  The main duties are direct audits, verifying members accounts, and monitoring for any malfeasance.

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I usually view City Council meetings using the city website.  Over the last year I have attended three meetings in person.  Since my candidacy there has been one meeting and I attended in person.

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Yes, local newspapers are important.  They serve a role other options don’t.  They provide information that local citizens can use and need for knowledge.  Local newspapers supply data on things like school information, local governments, law enforcement, sporting events, current events, and public notices to name a few.   Local newspapers certainly assist in transparency for city councils.

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in the city of Sturgis?

Important issues before the city of Sturgis currently are outsourcing sponsorship for the rally, resignation notices from the city attorney and city administrator, continuing progress on the city’s financial situation, and continued transparency to the public.

How do you intend to solve these issues?

I alone cannot solve any of these issues, but as a city council member I will deal with issues through collaboration with other council members. I will educate myself on issues and be prepared before council meetings in order to stream line the process and respect the time of all involved.  Listening to the public and being transparent are always useful in council matters.  Obtaining input from appropriate city staff members is also invaluable in gaining insight into issues.  The benefits and costs should be weighed in as well. 

What do you believe is working for the city, and how will you retain that progression?

Three items come to mind immediately.  First, the current council is working very hard to listen to the public.  They are also trying to be transparent to increase trust.  Second, outsourcing the ambulance billing process has made it more self sufficient and has taken the burden off the tax payers.  Third, contracting with Kiefffer Sanitation for garbage service will eliminate maintenance, fuel cost, and replacement of garbage trucks for the city.  This will be a cost saving to the tax payers.  I support all this for our community.

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

Transparency is what develops public trust.  It means sharing information in as visible fashion as possible.  Being available to the public and using local news outlets assist in being transparent.  The desire is for people to feel informed.  I will answer emails, calls, texts, and questions as needed from the public.  My desire is to continue the transparency of the current council.

What else do you want people to know about you?

I was an active member during my term on the city council.  I served two years as Vice President.  I also have experience on Legal and Finance, Infrastructure Committee, Transportation Committee, Rally and Events Committee, and the Park Board. All is invaluable to the position I am now seeking.

The city finance officer recently reported a total cash value across all city accounts of nearly $9.2 million. She credited the cash position as a direct result of fiscal management actions implemented starting in 2024. How do you plan to watch over the city’s finances and what are your priorities for the budget? 

Requesting at least a quarterly report across all accounts would keep everyone informed about the current budget.  This would also aide in anticipating future situations and identify possible problems early.  Audits need to be up to date for stability.  As a council member fiscal responsibility is very important.  The desire is to operate as efficiently as possible and avoid waste.  Being transparent is necessary in financial matters.

The city of Sturgis recently voted to outsource its Rally sponsorship contract management. Should the city utilize a national firm, local company, nonprofit organization, or some other entity to solicit and manage Rally sponsorships? 

Currently the Rally sponsorship is vital to the city’s general fund.  All three choices have positives and possible negatives.  Not being on the council presently makes it difficult to make an educated choice.   Whatever decision the council makes must financially benefit the community and be a good partner with the community and sponsors.  Perspective sponsors need to feel comfortable with the possible future operator.  I think it would be prudent if the eventual operator could handle digital advertizing and licensing as well.  Sponsors want to feel they are getting value for their dollars.

Last year the city of Sturgis made severe cuts to its Rally and Events Department. Do you feel that department should be restored? Why or why not? 

No, I do not.  The department was cut for financial reasons.  Since then, the Chamber has taken over Music on Main and that seems appropriate.  Also many of the local events are things the city should not be sponsoring but rather promoting and supporting.  Now the city has voted to outsource the Rally sponsorship management.  The need for staff in that department seems unnecessary.  One staff member can probably handle event items and sponsorship questions.  This will be a cost savings for the community.

Brenda Vasknetz

 Vasknetz, Brenda.jpg
Brenda Vasknetz 

Name and what you do for a living? 

My name is Brenda Vasknetz.  I am currently the office manager at Baseline Surveying, Inc.  Prior to my employment with Baseline, I served the community as an employee for 27 years in several different capacities working for the City of Sturgis. Throughout those years, I gained a deep understanding of city operations, challenges, and opportunities. I served in the Water and Engineering Departments, as a Deputy Finance Officer, and later as Rally & Events Director, collaborating with departments across the board.  That hands-on experience gave me a broad and practical understanding of how Sturgis truly functions.

What motivated you to run for this office?

After stepping away from day-to-day city operations after resigning in 2015, I realized how much I missed being directly involved—serving the people, contributing to city events, and working with local businesses and organizations to make Sturgis a great place to live. After following the  City Council meetings and decisions over the past decade reminded me just how much I still want to serve and how much I can still contribute. 

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

My years of municipal service and relationships with past mayors, council members, department heads, and employees have given me the knowledge and perspective needed to advise the current council and residents on what has worked—and what hasn’t. As we move forward, I will focus on developing practical, fiscally responsible, and sustainable plans that protect the interests of future city leadership and the citizens.    

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

As Rally & Events Director through the 75th Anniversary, I lead and managed an amazing, dedicated staff orchestrating a beneficial service and revenue sources increasing income for the community. I participated in the Chamber’s Leadership Program, served on the Board of Directors with Black Hill’s Badlands Tourism Association, held a seat on Project Playground Committee, participated in Future Sturgis and led the Tourism Initiative; and collaborated with the Downtown BID, Downtown Beautification Committee, Sculpture Walk, and other nonprofits on fundraising and community events.

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I attend city council meetings, particularly when it is an agenda item that directly impacts residents’ quality of life or a non-budgeted expenditure request. Recently the ordinance modification to Residential Camping during the rally has been a topic of concern in our community. When I am not in attendance I do watch YouTube Live Stream.     

Do you subscribe to your community’s legal newspaper, the Black Hills Pioneer?

I do not. I receive daily news posts on social media from the Black Hills Pioneer. My grandma shares her subscription with me, so I can stay informed on Sturgis and area happenings.  

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

YES! I really enjoyed having a local paper highlighting the council meetings, school recognition, event happenings, the monthly Police Department Stats, and obituaries. It kept me informed about what was happening in the county, city and school district meetings, functions, and activities. They are a vital resource to keep the public informed. I ‘ve heard from residents who really miss having the local paper especially our Seniors who don’t always use the internet.  The Public Notice Section is essential to providing the public with knowledge of what decisions our government leaders act on. 

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in the city of Sturgis?

Getting back to the basics of running the city. Our streets have gone years without proper maintenance because other projects were prioritized over annual chip and seal maintenance.  Rebuilding reserve funds in our enterprise departments:  Water, Sanitation, Wastewater and Emergency Services to replace failing equipment and for future residential growth with developments requiring these essential services.  

How do you intend to solve these issues?

My years of experience with municipal budgets and understanding operations of city departments will provide guidance and support with the current administration and council to develop goals and plans to move towards fiscal responsibility and grow the city’s finances for the future.  I hope as we move forward, our focus remains on developing a practical and sustainable plan that safeguards the interest of future city leadership and the citizens of Sturgis.    

What do you believe is working for the city, and how will you retain that progression?

The dedicated employees that serve us.  Our organization is struggling—starting with employee morale and hiring. It should never take years to fill key positions. The city was once a desirable place to work. Employees deserve a council representative who understands what it is like to work there. I will support them and advocate for making Sturgis a great workplace again.

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

Reestablishing public committees will help rebuild involvement and trust in city decisions. Those committees should never have been eliminated because doing so pushed the community out of city decisions and input.  I am accessible, responsive, and care about this community and it’s future.  I plan to use social media platforms to inform the residents of upcoming meetings and actions taken by the city to better inform them.   The residents should be included in decisions and informed when our  tax dollars are being spent. 

What else do you want people to know about you?

I believe in accountability, fiscal responsibility, open government, trust, and integrity. I want our tax dollars spent carefully and wisely. I will represent your interests. I will listen. I will be accountable to you. It’s not about me—it’s about our community, the one I have been proud to serve for most of my life and the one I will continue to serve with dedication.

The city finance officer recently reported a total cash value across all city accounts of nearly $9.2 million. She credited the cash position as a direct result of fiscal management actions implemented starting in 2024. How do you plan to watch over the city’s finances and what are your priorities for the budget? 

I would implement a purchasing and bid policy that includes feedback from the residents and community stakeholders .  I want to involve the community and the council members once again in the budget planning and process.  Having public committees in place provided guidance to the department head on developing 5-10 year plans for projects and support from the members on the budget items when justifying these budget items.    

The city of Sturgis recently voted to outsource its Rally sponsorship contract management. Should the city utilize a national firm, local company, nonprofit organization, or some other entity to solicit and manage Rally sponsorships? 

Having experienced working with local and national sponsorship sales agents, outsourcing has worked well and benefited the City’s Sponsorship Program WHEN the agency understands:  our community, the city’s role in rally operations, the licensing program intended to provide benefits for community projects.  The rally department’s involvement with sponsorship fulfillment and contracts is important to ensure we can provide assets sold, that contracts developed are in our community’s best interest, and retain relationships developed with corporations. In 2016 we had twenty sponsors, today there are two.  We need to go back to what work ten years ago. 

Last year the city of Sturgis made severe cuts to its Rally and Events Department. Do you feel that department should be restored? Why or why not?

I know first-hand the potential and opportunities to generate financial and in-kind benefits for the community. It is sad that several things rally need to be rebuilt:  rally revenue streams dismantled, vendors relocating to other rally venues, relationships with long-term sponsors ended and frustrated local business owners who rely on tourism/rally to keep their doors open year-round. It is essential that we maintain a dedicated Rally Department with a focus on:  Educating rally-goers and vendors about the event and its history, providing clear information on all activities for the rally, promoting sponsors and supporting all local businesses to increase sales tax revenue.

title: Sturgis mayoral candidates
description: Voters in Sturgis will head to the polls June 2 to vote on vacant mayoral seat. Three people are running for this position which is a 3-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.
_full_text:
SturgisMayorComp.jpg

Voters in Sturgis will head to the polls June 2 to vote on vacant mayoral seat. Three people are running for this position which is a 3-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.

Rod Bradley

 Bradley, Rod.jpg
Rod Bradley 

Name and what you do for a living?

I am Rod Bradley, and I am a business owner in Sturgis.  My wife Cassie and I currently own and operate The Hotel Sturgis, Oasis Bar, Bradley Storage, and MB Enterprises, Inc.  We have also redeveloped a couple Sturgis properties into the Trailhead Subdivision and the 12th Street Apartments.

What motivated you to run for this office?

I am running for Mayor of Sturgis now because this is a really important time for our town.  Mayor Forrester was focused on providing better government and operations in our town, and the current city council and staff have worked hard to accomplish this.  I want to provide the strong and trusted leadership necessary to keep the progress going in order to get to where we want to be as a community.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

I believe my financial education and experience along with my business background and prior service as an elected official is well suited to serve as the Mayor of Sturgis.  I have a Master of Professional Accounting degree from the University of Nebraska Omaha and a Business degree with Accounting and Finance from Northern State University.  I have also passed the Certified Internal Auditor and Certified Public Accountant exams.  I bring a proven track record as an elected official, and I am a known leader in the community.  I have the skills and desire to lead Sturgis forward and make it a better place for all the residents.

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I was elected to serve a three-year term on the Sturgis City Council beginning in 2015.  I was also elected to serve a four-year term on the Meade County Commission beginning in 2019.  I successfully served both of those terms and have a proven track record as an elected official of leaving office in calmer political environments at the end of my terms.  I have also served on the board of the Sturgis Economic Development Corporation and Downtown Sturgis Foundation.

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I have made it a point to keep up with and follow local government since the end of my terms as an elected official.  I have read every city council agenda since running for city council in 2015, and I have read every county commission agenda since running for county commission in 2018.  I have also read every school board agenda for about the last five years.  I have attended a couple city council meetings in the last year.

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Local newspapers are an integral part of a community.  The work the Black Hills Pioneer does to keep the residents of Sturgis informed is invaluable.  They do such a good job of following and reporting on the issues being addressed by local government, the local news, the activities at our schools, and our youth sports.  It is important so support our local newspaper through subscriptions and advertisement.

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in the city of Sturgis?

Sturgis has a good city council that has worked hard to improve Sturgis.  They deserve to have all the information needed to make sound financial decisions for the residents of Sturgis.  Sturgis needs to have a solid financial plan and budgetary process so the city council knows the current financial position of the city.  A five-year financial plan is also needed to use as the framework to set the future direction of Sturgis.  Providing this information to the city council and residents of Sturgis will rebuild trust in the financial stability of our town.

How do you intend to solve these issues?

I plan to roll up my sleeves and put the necessary time into making sure all the information needed to make sound financial decisions is available to the city council and residents of Sturgis.  My financial background and desire to fix these issues will put improving this process on the fast track.

What do you believe is working for the city, and how will you retain that progression?

The current city council and staff have done a good job of moving our town through the divisive times we have experienced in the recent past.  They have operated open and honestly in the best interests of the residents of Sturgis.  I will work closely with the council and staff to continue the progress of having government and operations that serves the residents of Sturgis well.

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

Being open and honest is the best and only way to handle transparency in city government.  The residents of Sturgis deserve elected officials who take transparency seriously and whose actions reflect their commitment to discussing and providing the information needed to address the issues facing our town.  As Mayor, I am committed to leading Sturgis in an open and transparent manner that will enhance communication amongst the council and promote effective dialogue with the public.

What else do you want people to know about you?

I really care about Sturgis and want to help make it the place we want it to be.  I grew up here, and we are having our 40-year class reunion this summer.  Cassie and I are raising our kids here and are involved in the school system and multiple youth sports.  We have chosen to invest in Sturgis because we believe in what it can be for the families that choose to live here.  There is a lot of work remaining to be done, and I am willing to roll up my sleeves and put in the time to make that happen.

The city finance officer recently reported a total cash value across all city accounts of nearly $9.2 million. She credited the cash position as a direct result of fiscal management actions implemented starting in 2024. How do you plan to watch over the city’s finances and what are your priorities for the budget? 

This information is a good start at showing the significant progress this city council has made in the last couple years.  This city council has made tough decisions in order to balance the budget and eliminate deficit spending.  There is a lot more work to be done to identify and lay out the true financial position of Sturgis as well as put together a long-term financial plan.  I am determined to rebuild public trust in the financial stability of Sturgis and to make sure taxpayer money is spent well over the long haul.

The city of Sturgis recently voted to outsource its Rally sponsorship contract management. Should the city utilize a national firm, local company, nonprofit organization, or some other entity to solicit and manage Rally sponsorships? 

Rally sponsorship is an important piece of putting on the best rally possible for the people who come to the rally.  Sturgis has monetizable assets that provide a direct financial return to the citizens.  I believe the next steps for the city council are to put together and send out an all-encompassing Request for Proposal to anyone interested in partnering with Sturgis to manage rally sponsorships.  This will provide all the information needed for the council to determine who best to work with going forward.  This is an important decision, and I look forward to being a part of it.

Last year the city of Sturgis made severe cuts to its Rally and Events Department. Do you feel that department should be restored? Why or why not? 

I know the city council did not take those decisions lightly, and they were required to make hard decisions to balance the budget.  Last year, they really focused on the core city services and events required to put on the rally, and they were successful in hosting the best rally possible with reduced personnel and resources allocated to the rally.  I believe this is the approach that best optimizes the rally and allows city resources to be efficiently invested elsewhere in Sturgis.  This approach will need to be continually looked at and evaluated to result in the best outcomes possible.

Richelle Bruch

 Bruch, Richelle.jpg
Richelle Bruch 

Name and what you do for a living? 

Richelle Bruch. I am a wife, mother, grandmother, and lifelong Sturgis community advocate. Showing up for this community is not something I started when I decided to run for Mayor. It is something I have done every single day for years because Sturgis is everything to me. 

What motivated you to run for this office?

Sturgis has given me everything, my home, my family’s roots, my community. My motivation is simple. I want to make sure this city reaches every bit of its potential for every person who calls it home. I believe collaborative honest leadership that listens to all of us is how we get there and I am ready to provide that. 

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

Because I am already doing this work. I lead multiple organizations simultaneously, I attend every council and Planning and Zoning meeting, and I have been listening to this community for years. I understand its finances, its needs, and its people. Leadership is not something I am learning. It is something I have been practicing in this community every single day.  

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I currently serve as President of Sturgis Soccer Association, President of Golden K Kiwanis, Vice Chair of Planning and Zoning, Chair of Sturgis Outdoors, and Chamber Board Member with past service as President and Immediate Past President. I founded Challenge for Charity which returned $33,000 to local nonprofits. Every role has deepened my understanding of this community and strengthened my ability to lead it. 

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I have attended every City Council and Planning and Zoning meeting since January 2026. But showing up did not start with this campaign. I have been present in this community’s conversations long before any election was on the horizon because engaged leadership starts with showing up consistently. 

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Absolutely. Local newspapers are the primary source of information for community and government news. An informed community is a stronger community and local journalism makes that possible. Transparency in government starts with accessible information and local newspapers are a critical part of that equation. 

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in the city of Sturgis?

Financial diligence, employee retention, capital improvement projects, diversifying our economy, and ensuring the rally benefits the entire community. These issues do not exist in isolation. They are all connected. A stable budget funds improvements. A thriving economy retains employees. A united city government attracts investment. Solving one helps solve all of them. 

How do you intend to solve these issues?

By leading collaboratively and making smart responsible decisions at every level. That means empowering city staff, reviewing the Condrey Wage Study to ensure competitive salaries, and prioritizing capital improvement projects based on greatest community need. To diversify the economy I will work toward a unified city government that creates an environment where year round businesses choose Sturgis and every resident benefits.                       

What do you believe is working for the city, and how will you retain that progression?

The current council has made meaningful strides in communication, financial reconciliation, and genuinely listening to community members. That progress matters and deserves acknowledgment. As Mayor I will build on that foundation, maintaining financial accountability and adding the collaborative leadership that ensures every voice continues to be heard and every decision moves Sturgis forward. 

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

Transparency means honesty at its core. It means proactively sharing information with the community rather than waiting for residents to find out on their own. As Mayor I will maintain an open door policy, answer questions directly and honestly, and make sure communication flows to the community before decisions are finalized, not after. Every resident deserves that respect.  

What else do you want people to know about you?

My children and grandchildren are growing up in Sturgis right now. Every decision I make as Mayor I will make with their future in mind and with every other Sturgis family’s future in mind too. This is not a career move. This is a calling from someone who genuinely loves this place and the people in it. 

The city finance officer recently reported a total cash value across all city accounts of nearly $9.2 million. She credited the cash position as a direct result of fiscal management actions implemented starting in 2024. How do you plan to watch over the city’s finances and what are your priorities for the budget?

The $9.2 million reflects hard work through budget cuts and delayed capital improvements, progress that deserves acknowledgment. My priorities are maintaining a balanced budget, responsibly addressing capital improvement projects, and paying down city debt. I will work closely with the finance director, council, and staff to spend every dollar wisely while focusing on growing sales tax revenue by making Sturgis a place businesses and developers choose to invest in. 

The city of Sturgis recently voted to outsource its Rally sponsorship contract management. Should the city utilize a national firm, local company, nonprofit organization, or some other entity to solicit and manage Rally sponsorships?

A national firm is the right choice. The expertise, connections, and experience a national firm brings would maximize the value of our sponsorship contracts. With the rally being such a significant part of our financial foundation, securing the highest and best sponsorship outcome for all of Sturgis is non-negotiable. 

Last year the city of Sturgis made severe cuts to its Rally and Events Department. Do you feel that department should be restored? Why or why not?

Fully restoring the department to its previous form is not the right path forward. Instead I would explore creating a Community Director position that manages rally responsibilities alongside broader community initiatives year round. This serves the whole community more effectively and reflects the kind of collaborative forward thinking leadership Sturgis needs. 

Tammy Bohn

 Bohn, Tammy.jpg
Tammy Bohn 

Name and what you do for a living? 

My name is Tammy Bohn. My husband Justin and I own and operate Sturgis Guns in Sturgis. Being a small business owner has given me firsthand experience with the challenges and opportunities facing Sturgis and the people who live here.

What motivated you to run for this office? 

Listening to the frustrations of Sturgis residents and city employees over the last several years, motivated me to run. As a business owner, I heard concerns about the direction of the city and its financial condition, which led me to pay closer attention to city operations and leadership. On April 9, 2024, the citizens of Sturgis voted to return to a mayor-led government because the city-manager system was no longer working for our community. With the support of my husband Justin, I made the decision to run. I have the skill set and real-world experience to be an effective mayor and move Sturgis forward.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position? 

I have experience leading people, building businesses, managing employees, working with budgets, generating revenue, marketing, negotiating contracts, and making difficult decisions. Justin and I built businesses from the ground up, survived financial hardship, and rebuilt successfully. I understand the challenges of tourism, the motorcycle industry, and the Rally economy, because we live it every day with our business in Sturgis. Those experiences taught me how to lead under pressure, solve problems, build strong teams, adapt to change, and keep moving forward during difficult times. I have the experience, leadership skills, and work ethic necessary to effectively serve the citizens of Sturgis as Mayor.

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I have not held other elected public or nonprofit offices. That is best strength. My experience comes from the real world, not politics. I have spent my career building businesses, managing people, solving problems, and working directly with employees and the public. I am not interested in building a political resume or moving from one board or elected office to another. My focus is on doing the job of Mayor and doing it well for the citizens of Sturgis.

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy? 

I have attended several local government meetings over the last year and throughout my candidacy. I also believe staying informed today goes far beyond physically sitting in a meeting room. Many citizens watch meetings online, listen to recordings, read agendas and minutes, and research issues independently because work and family schedules do not always allow in-person attendance. What matters most is being informed, engaged, and willing to ask questions and find solutions, not simply counting meetings attended. As mayor, I will strive to make sure agendas and information are available to citizens and city employees well in advance and in whatever form works best for them.

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not? 

Yes, I believe local newspapers are important if they are committed to fair and unbiased journalism while covering all sides of an issue. Citizens deserve accurate information so they can make up their own minds. I also believe Sturgis would benefit from having its own dedicated local newspaper focused specifically on the issues, businesses, events, and people that directly impact Sturgis.

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in the city of Sturgis? 

Financial stability, communication and transparency from city government, long-term planning instead of reacting to crises, retaining quality city employees, understaffing in key departments, and strengthening the Sturgis Rally and tourism economy are major issues facing Sturgis. Vacant downtown and Rally properties hurting the city’s appearance and tax base, year-round economic development beyond Rally week, cooperation between the city, businesses, and citizens, restoring excitement and reputation around the Rally brand and the City of Sturgis, maintenance of streets and city facilities, and crime and public safety are all issues that deserve serious attention.

How do you intend to solve these issues? 

Back to the basics. Any CEO taking over an organization in trouble starts by honestly reviewing operations, identifying weaknesses, and building the right team. Review the city finances, spending, contracts, and accountability. Meet with city staff and council to identify problems and improve communication. Restart true citizen and business owner committee meetings. With the City Administrator, City Attorney, and Public Information Officer all publicly announcing they are leaving, review those positions for possible restructuring to better serve staff and the public. Focus on generating revenue, strengthening tourism and local business relationships, and rebuilding trust through transparency.

What do you believe is working for the city, and how will you retain that progression? 

What is working for the city is the dedication and experience of the city staff and employees who continued keeping the city running during financial challenges, staffing cuts, and leadership changes. They deserve a great deal of credit for that. The city cannot afford to lose experienced employees. Open communication, listening to staff and citizens, and creating a more stable working environment will be important moving forward.

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions? 

Transparency in government means citizens, council members, and city employees should have access to information before major decisions are made, not after. It means open communication, honest discussions, and making information easy to access and understand. I believe agendas, financial information, contracts, and major city discussions should be shared well in advance whenever possible. Transparency also means listening to questions and concerns instead of avoiding them. My goal is straightforward communication, fewer surprises, and making sure council, staff, and the public are informed enough to make good decisions.

What else do you want people to know about you? 

My faith in Jesus, hard work, personal responsibility, and treating people fairly are the values that guide my life. I am direct, straightforward, and dependable. Fourteen years ago, Justin and I moved to Sturgis and within two years we lost everything and had to start over. Rebuilding our lives and businesses taught me resilience, perseverance, and how t work through difficult situations instead of walking away. I also understand that none of us succeed alone, and I am grateful for the support of our family, friends, employees, and customers. As Mayor, I will be accessible, involved, and committed to helping improve and stabilize Sturgis.

The city finance officer recently reported a total cash value across all city accounts of nearly $9.2 million. She credited the cash position as a direct result of fiscal management actions implemented starting in 2024. How do you plan to watch over the city’s finances and what are your priorities for the budget? 

$9.2 million cash sounds positive, but it was premature to present those numbers as a financial success story before the 2024 and 2025 city audits are completed. My approach to city finances is simple: analyze the numbers, review spending and contracts, and make decisions based on facts, not assumptions. If the city does not have the money, it should not spend the money. We also need realistic maintenance plans and a stronger focus on growing revenue. My budget priorities are public safety and essential city services, retaining quality employees, maintaining infrastructure and equipment, and projects that make financial sense for the long-term stability of Sturgis.

The city of Sturgis recently voted to outsource its Rally sponsorship contract management. Should the city utilize a national firm, local company, nonprofit organization, or some other entity to solicit and manage Rally sponsorships? 

Prior to 2015, the city used a national firm alongside local Rally staff, and it worked well because it combined national contacts with local input and oversight. In 2015, the city had more than 20 sponsors. Today, there are two. I would like the council to revisit the outsourcing decision and look at this as more than a legal issue. Rally sponsorships are economic development, tourism, business relationships, and local control. A national firm may help open doors, but Sturgis needs local oversight and a structure that protects the cities and citizen’s long-term interests.

Last year the city of Sturgis made severe cuts to its Rally and Events Department. Do you feel that department should be restored? Why or why not? 

Yes, I believe the Rally and Events Department should be restored. The Sturgis Rally is one of the city’s largest economic drivers, tourism tools, and branding assets. Prior to 2015, the department was growing sponsorships, building additional events, and creating long-term opportunities for the city. Cutting an income-generating department while continuing outside marketing and sponsorship expenses does not make financial sense to me. The city should have evaluated performance, sponsorship growth, return on investment, and department structure before making severe cuts. The Rally is not just a 10-day event; it impacts tourism, local businesses, sponsorships, and the identity of Sturgis year-round.
