title: Deadwood steps back in time  to ‘save our tail’ again
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Deadwood invites the public to watch a reenactment of the 1980 FBI raid of the brothels in Deadwood and the ‘save our tail’ parade, pictured here, that happened shortly after to protest their closure.
_full_text:
Deadwood steps back in time  to ‘save our tail’ again
Deadwood invites the public to watch a reenactment of the 1980 FBI raid of the brothels in Deadwood and the ‘save our tail’ parade, pictured here, that happened shortly after to protest their closure.  

DEADWOOD — Deadwood History Inc., will be remembering their “working girl” history Friday, with a reenactment of the May 21, 1980, FBI raid on the city’s brothels, the city-wide protest of their closures, and a screening of ‘NITA: Hotbed in Deadwood.’

Rose Speirs, associate executive director and communications director of Deadwood History, Inc., said the fun will kick off with a reenactment of the raid at 1 p.m. at The Brothel Deadwood Museum at 610 Main St. She said observers can expect to see Deadwood Alive! actors dressed as FBI and state agents, pretending to arrest women from around town dressed in period costume and posing as prostitutes. 

Speirs said Chris Enss, author of ‘An Open Secret: The Story of Deadwood’s Most Notorious Bordellos’ will be present, posing as Deadwood’s infamous Madame Dora DuFran. DuFran ran several brothels in South Dakota, eventually marrying Joseph DuFran, who will be portrayed during the reenactments by Deadwood History Inc., Executive Director Jim Williams. 

The “agents” will lead the girls down the street near Mr. Wu’s, where the parade will begin. Speirs said at least 35 people are signed up to participate, all of which are encouraged to wear period costume ranging from 1876 to 1980. 

Speirs said several people will be attending the parade who were part of the 1980 event.

“Two women who were in photos that we have of the save our tail parade are coming back for it and are going to participate,” Speirs said. “That’s really fun, that we get people who were actually there and then those of us who read about it or heard about it afterwards, participating. We’re going to have a really good time with it.”

After the reenactments, a screening of ‘NITA: Hotbed in Deadwood’ will occur at the Eagle Bar at 2:30 p.m., with filmmaker Justin Koehler present to take questions afterwards.

“(Koehler) was here last year in May, so he’s coming back to show that film again. He did a brilliant job on it,” Speirs said. “Whatever (Koehler’s) subject matter is, he brings that person to life in a way that not every filmmaker can accomplish.”

At 4 p.m., the Johnny Lonesome Band will perform at The Eagle Bar and again later at The Nugget Saloon. 

Speirs said that the event will be kid friendly, shining a light on a part of Deadwood’s history with humor and education. 

“This is just to be fun and a little bit playful about what happened, because (the women) were a big deal with the economy in Deadwood,” she said. “It was a big economic engine for Deadwood. Losing that, losing that income, really affected the businesses in Deadwood. Those women were shopping and buying clothes and going to the flower shop and doing anything that any of us do. They’re people, just like us. It’s important that Deadwood acknowledges all of our history, the good and the bad, the vice and the virtue. All of it.”

Speirs noted that after the FBI raid and eventual closure of the brothels, “hunting season has never been the same again.”

“That was one of the busiest times in Deadwood,” she said. “You have to use humor when talking about this, because otherwise it could be really depressing. These women were mothers and daughters and sisters and cousins, they were all the same things that we are today.”

An unveiling of a bronze statue of DuFran was scheduled for Friday after the parade, but has been rescheduled because of delays with the artist, Edward Hlavka. City officials said they hope the statue will be completed by the fall.

title: Newell School Board candidates
description: Voters in the Newell School District will head to the polls June 2 to vote on one vacant school board seat. Two people are running for one open position which is a 3-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.
_full_text:
Voters in the Newell School District will head to the polls June 2 to vote on one vacant school board seat. Two people are running for one open position which is a 3-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.

Kurt Hocking

Name and what you do for a living? 

 Kurt Hocking (MUG)
Kurt Hocking 

Kurt Hocking.  I retired from VA Black Hills.  Currently I work as an Emergency Medical Responder (EMR) with Butte County Ambulance - Newell

What motivated you to run for this office?

Make the school appealing again to students and families: Enrollment follows reputation. I want to help create a school environment where families are proud to choose—safe, welcoming, academically strong, and communitycentered.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

I am running to bring new ideas and a clear vision for the future: I am not running to maintain the status quo. I am running to help the district grow—academically, culturally, and operationally. That includes exploring innovative programs, strengthening communication, and supporting staff so they can do their best work.    

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I was elected to the Newell City Council as a Commissioner.  I also held a position on the VA Black Hills Employees Association.  I am a member of the Newell Festival of Trees Committee and the Newell Community Club. I am also the elected Maintenance Officer for the ambulance service. 

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I have attended 3 school board meetings in person and watched 6 on-line either live or the next day.  I have attended a couple of the Newell City Council meetings. I attended all 12 monthly meetings with the ambulance service.

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

In our area, I believe it is essential to have a local newspaper delivered to residents. Not everyone has consistent access to online news, and a printed paper ensures that all members of our community stay informed. A local newspaper strengthens communication, highlights local events, and preserves the stories that matter most to the people who live here. It helps keeps our community connected, engaged, and aware of the issues and activities that shape daily life 

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in the Newell school district?

Open communication, regaining trust, and working for the betterment of the entire district. 

How do you intend to solve these issues?

I will be accessible, transparent, and willing to have honest conversations about challenges and opportunities. Clear communication builds confidence and reduces misunderstandings.    Trust isn’t asked for; it’s earned. I will show up, follow through, and make decisions based on what’s best for students and the district. Every decision I make will be grounded in what strengthens the school, supports students, and builds longterm stability.

    

What do you believe is working for the district, and how will you retain that progression?

We have solid policies in place and community involvement that continues to grow. Many people in this area have a deep, genuine desire to keep the Newell School open, and that commitment shows in their actions.  I am seeing mentorship and support for new teachers, as well as volunteers stepping forward to help wherever they can.  Young families are becoming more engaged, bringing fresh energy and a shared determination to preserve and strengthen our school. This collective effort reflects a community that cares deeply about its students, its educators, and the future of the Newell School District. 

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

Open communication. I will be accessible, transparent, and willing to have honest conversations about challenges and opportunities. Clear communication builds confidence and reduces misunderstandings. I will be willing to listen and collaborate.  I recognize that good ideas come from many places. I will work respectfully with administrators, teachers, families, and fellow board members to find solutions that move the district forward.

What else do you want people to know about you?

I may be a Newell transplant, but after 20 years of living here, this community is truly my home. I own a home in the district, and I have two grandsons who attend Newell School, giving me a deep, personal investment in ensuring the school remains open and thriving for many years to come.  All five of my stepchildren are proud Newell School alumni, as is my spouse, and our family’s connection to this district run strong. Through my work as an active member of the ambulance service, I care deeply about the well-being of this community and its residents. My commitment to Newell is rooted in both family and service, and I am dedicated to supporting the future of our school and the strength of our community. 

Todd Youngberg

title: International DUNE collaboration  brings hundreds of scientists to  Black Hills, public events planned
byline: Pioneer staff report
description: Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
dune collaboration.jpeg
Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

RAPID CITY — More than 250 physicists and researchers from around the world will gather in the Black Hills this week for the international DUNE conference hosted by South Dakota Mines.

The conference, taking place in Rapid City and Lead, will bring together the DUNE collaboration, an international effort involving more than 1,500 scientists from more than 220 institutions across 38 countries. Together, researchers are working to answer some of the biggest questions in physics and build a clearer understanding of how the universe works.

DUNE, supported by the U.S. Department of Energy and led by Fermilab, will allow physicist to study the elusive particles called neutrinos – tiny nearly-massless particles that are all around us. By studying them, scientists hope to understand why the universe is made of matter, and ultimately, why we are all here. 

Researchers will meet at The Monument this week before heading to Lead, May 22, for the final session. The DUNE collaboration’s internal scientific and technical meetings are closed to the public; however, there are public outreach events scheduled. 

On Saturday, some collaboration members will tour the DUNE caverns at the 4,850-foot level, where massive detector modules are being assembled. 

“This marks the first time many collaborators will see the scale and progress of the underground detector caverns in person,” said Juergen Reichenbacher, Ph.D., associate professor of physics at Mines, and organizer of the upcoming collaboration meeting. 

Several public events are planned throughout the week. Public outreach events scheduled in Lead include: 

Deep Talks: The Science and Technology of DUNE by Angela White, scheduled for 5-7 p.m. Thursday, at the Sanford Lab Homestake Visitor Center. White is a doctoral researcher working at the forefront of particle physics and DUNE. Currently, she serves as a light readout expert for the 2x2 Demonstrator, a prototype for DUNE’s near detector systems. 

A Lakota Hoop Dancing Presentation with Starr Chief Eagle and fellow performers, scheduled for 4-6 p.m. Friday, at the Historic Homestake Opera House.

title: Spearfish approves construction admin contract for Main Street mill and overlay
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Main Street will be milled and overlayed, instead of re-chip sealed moving forward. DGR Engineering now has the construction administration contract for the project. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
0521 Main Street(RGB).tif
Main Street will be milled and overlayed, instead of re-chip sealed moving forward. DGR Engineering now has the construction administration contract for the project. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — On April 20, the City Council passed a motion to repair Main Street from Jackson Boulevard to Grant Street with a mill and overlay, and repair Main Street /Colorado Boulevard from Grant Street to Spearfish Canyon Highway 14A with a re-applied chip seal after a fall 2025 chip seal project failed.

“The quality of the chip seal work was unacceptable and needs to be redone. The downtown section of this route has frequent events, including street dances and festivals, and chip seals are sometimes messy with loose chips and sticky tar. For these reasons, members of the public asked the council not to do another chip seal there,” an agenda item report from the Spearfish public works department said in explanation of the project.

The mill and overlay on Main Street is expected to cost between $125,000 to $200,000. On Monday, the city council voted unanimously to contract DGR Engineering for engineering services and construction administration of the project for no more than $31,500.

Dana Foreman is the project manager who will provide overall coordination and communication with city staff during the project.

“DGR’s approach emphasizes constructability, schedule, and budget control, and longterm pavement performance. Our goal is to deliver a project that meets the city’s objectives, minimizes disruption to the public, and results in a smooth, durable roadway surface that performs well for years to come,” Foreman wrote in DGR’s proposal.

DGR has performed similar services for a Main Street surfacing improvement project in Murdo, State Fair Midway asphalt improvements in Huron, an asphalt overlay on 41st Street in Sioux Falls, a Main Street overlay in Brandon, and citywide asphalt surface repair in Dell Rapids.

The remainder of Colorado Boulevard, from Grant Street to Highway 14 at Spearfish Canyon, will be chip-sealed again by Dakota Asphalt, the same company that performed the chip seal work last fall. The result of the 2025 project was never officially accepted by the council. Instead, on Monday, the governing body voted to extend the original project timeline, allowing Dakota Asphalt until July 15 to reapply chip seal on Colorado Boulevard.

McMahon said the contractor expects to complete the chip seal sometime between June 8 and June 18.

“As we get closer to that June 8 date, and get that finalized and are sure there are not going to be weather delays, we will send out a public service announcement on that to inform the public about the beginning of that project,” McMahon said.

The Black Hills Camaro Rally, in Spearfish, is scheduled for June 17-20.

“We are not doing the chip seal from Jackson to Grant, so it shouldn’t affect the downtown portion of that event. However, the procession of Camaros could be affected by that. title: Tension grows opponents at hearing on uranium drilling permit
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Signs are displayed on seats during a hearing about a uranium exploration permit application Tuesday, at the Mueller Civic Center in Hot Springs, South Dakota. Dozens of people gathered to oppose the permit. Photo by Meghan O’Brien, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Tension grows opponents at hearing on uranium drilling permit
Signs are displayed on seats during a hearing about a uranium exploration permit application Tuesday, at the Mueller Civic Center in Hot Springs, South Dakota. Dozens of people gathered to oppose the permit. Photo by Meghan O’Brien, South Dakota Searchlight 

HOT SPRINGS — Frustrations boiled over as a state regulatory board weighed whether to allow underground uranium exploration along the southern edge of the Black Hills on Tuesday.

Clean Nuclear Energy Corporation and its Canada-based parent company Nexus Uranium applied for a permit to drill near Craven Canyon, 7 miles north of Edgemont. The canyon is marked with Native American petroglyphs, and the Black Hills were formerly part of the Great Sioux Reservation.

On the second day of a hearing that’s scheduled to last all week, audience members raised questions about the validity of process decisions by the state Board of Minerals and Environment, including when portions of the meeting proceeded without being interpreted by a Lakota speaker. Lakota is spoken by tribes in the western part of the state.

“This is institutionalized racism, and you are promoting it,” Elizabeth Lone Eagle said, standing from her seat in the audience.

She said the board was “forbidding” the translator “from doing her job, because you want your white colonizer sanitized way of doing things.” The audience cheered, and the board did not respond.

Two Lakota interpreters entered into a contract to translate spoken testimony and began Tuesday. The state Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources had failed to provide an interpreter Monday, despite having agreed months earlier to appoint one.

As examination of witnesses began Tuesday, attendees held up their phones for photos, videos and audio recordings. Some livestreamed the hearing on social media. Law enforcement officers were posted at the doors, in seats and around the outside of the Mueller Civic Center, where the hearing is taking place.

The use of Lakota interpreters made for a methodical pace.

Clean Nuclear Energy’s legal counsel, Matthew Naasz, posed questions to Mike Blady, an executive for Nexus Uranium. Lakota interpreter Leola One Feather translated the questions for the audience. Then, when Blady responded, One Feather translated his response.

Board of Minerals and Environment Hearing Chair Bob Morris commented on the time-consuming nature of interpreting testimony into Lakota, which is something he said the board has no experience with.

“We are going through a process that is unprecedented,” he said during the hearing. 

Tensions rose when some exchanges went uninterpreted, and project opponents in the audience called out to allow One Feather to translate.

Lone Eagle and other opponents voiced complaints that the company’s permit application, which spans several pages, had not been translated into Lakota. Others said the lack of translation is a violation of human rights.

Morris said the state contracted for spoken interpretation services, not written translation services.

The state Board of Minerals and Environment can deny an application to explore for uranium for several reasons, including negative impacts on historical, archaeological or recreational aspects of an area, if those impacts outweigh the benefits of the exploration. The board can also deny the permit if it will negatively affect the productivity of aquifers.

The company said it plans to use 38 sites to drill holes — not 50 as previously indicated — as deep as 700 feet on state-owned land. Each hole would take about 2 weeks to drill.

“We always try and leave the project in a better state than we found it,” Blady said during the hearing. Some attendees chuckled at the statement.

Clean Nuclear Energy worked with the state and contractors to compile cultural, geological, wildlife and hydrogeological studies, Blady said. He said the project would bring better understanding of underground resources and could contribute to economic development.

Edgemont’s City Council and Chamber of Commerce passed resolutions in support of approving the permit.

Opponents are raising concerns about negative effects on the nearby canyon and petroglyphs, as well as potential pollution of local groundwater sources by drilling and possible future mining.

The company has additional drilling plans on federally owned land. That portion of the project is under review by the U.S. Forest Service, which estimates it will issue a decision next month.

The proposed drilling near Craven Canyon is separate from another nearby proposal to mine uranium in the Edgemont area that’s been pending since the early 2000s. That proposal, from Texas-based enCore Energy, has met staunch opposition from Native Americans and environmental activists, and has been in regulatory and legal limbo. Last year, the federal government’s Permitting Council selected enCore’s project for inclusion in FAST-41, a process intended to improve coordination among permitting agencies and hold them to deadlines.

Uranium is a metallic, radioactive element used as fuel in nuclear weapons and power plants. Interest in uranium exploration and mining has risen recently in response to nuclear energy’s potential to meet the growing electricity demands of data centers.

The hearing in Hot Springs comes on the heels of a victory for people fighting another drilling project in the Black Hills. Rapid City-based company Pete Lien & Sons recently withdrew from an exploratory graphite drilling project that was underway near Pe’ Sla, also known as Reynolds Prairie, a sacred ceremonial site for Lakota people in the central Black Hills. The withdrawal came after two lawsuits and the formation of a protest camp at the drilling site.

The hearing in Hot Springs is scheduled to continue through Friday.

title: Sturgis student arrested for bringing airsoft gun  to school
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — A Sturgis student was arrested Tuesday after he brought an airsoft gun to the Sturgis Brown High School campus.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

STURGIS — A Sturgis student was arrested Tuesday after he brought an airsoft gun to the Sturgis Brown High School campus.

In an email to parents and staff, Wayne Wormstadt, superintendent of the Meade School District, said fellow students reported the issue to school administration and the school resource officer. When the student arrived on campus, he was met by the school resource officer and administrators and placed under arrest without incident by the officer. 

Today a student was arrested for bringing a gun on to Sturgis Brown High School Campus. When the student came on campus, he was met by administration and SRO and was arrested by the Sturgis PD SRO. We are thankful to the students who reported this to the administration and SRO.

“We are grateful that students reported concerns they had heard, which allowed school administrators and the Sturgis Police Department to respond quickly and appropriately,” Wormstadt wrote in a follow-up email.

He declined to answer additional questions citing student privacy policies.

The district has a policy that follows state law. It prohibits dangerous weapons on campus, with a few narrow exceptions for educational or athletic purposes. It also prohibits “look-alike weapons,” which include airsoft guns.

“A student who has intentionally brought a firearm onto school property shall be expelled by the Board for a period of not less than twelve months. The Superintendent may modify this expulsion on a case by case basis,” according to district policy.

The incident follows the May 5 incident at Spearfish High School in which a student brought a firearm onto campus. That resulted in the expulsion of 2 students Monday for 12 months.

“The findings (of the Spearfish investigation and discipline hearing) resulted in a determination that there was a violation related to a firearm being present on our high school campus,” Kirk Easton, superintendent of the Spearfish School District wrote in a prepared statement to the Pioneer. “Although a weapon was not recovered on school grounds, evidence indicated it was transferred between the two students during the school day.” 

“This situation demonstrates that our established safety procedures are effective; without them, we may not have uncovered the evidence linking this weapon to our school environment,” he continued. “… Finally, we deeply appreciate the patience and support of our parents and community as we conducted a thorough and detailed investigation. We understand and respect the demand for information related to the safety of our schools. As a district, prioritizing safety of our students and staff remains the utmost priority. Doing so requires establishing a balance of appropriate information sharing, while thoroughly addressing every facet of the investigation process in collaboration law enforcement. We recognize this takes time, but it is necessary to ensure we provide accurate information that does not violate student rights, and does not impede potential criminal investigation or potential charges.”

title: Parole successes touted even as  criticism prompts changes from gov
byline: By John Hult Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — The South Dakota Department of Corrections’ parole division notched a series of wins in 2025, its leaders said recently, even as public scrutiny of people on parole reached a crescendo late last month loud enough to spark immediate changes from Gov. Larry Rhoden.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — The South Dakota Department of Corrections’ parole division notched a series of wins in 2025, its leaders said recently, even as public scrutiny of people on parole reached a crescendo late last month loud enough to spark immediate changes from Gov. Larry Rhoden.

Two top parole administrators delivered the message to the state Board of Pardons and Paroles. It was the board’s first full-group meeting since Rhoden announced plans to hire 5 new parole officers to do intensive supervision on high-risk inmates, requested faster decisions on parole violations and said the state would crack down on drug use and other misbehavior by people under state supervision.

The changes came a few days after a police officer in Sioux Falls was shot and injured, allegedly by a man on parole. The April 27 incident was the second time an officer was shot in Sioux Falls in the space of a year. The alleged shooter in a separate incident from April 2025 was on parole.

Earlier in April, Rhoden’s office issued a news release on what he branded a “Smarter Supervision Initiative,” which noted that the state had asked for an $890,000 Justice Department grant to improve data collection and parole officer training, and to “strengthen community partnerships.”

The state’s struggling to get a handle on its 50% recidivism rate, Rhoden wrote in a letter supporting the grant, referencing a term for people who return to prison within 3 years of release. 

Rhoden convened a Correctional Rehabilitation Task Force last year to address efforts to reform individuals inside the prison and address re-entry issues for people being released.

In response to repeated calls for parole reform from leaders in Sioux Falls and Rapid City, however, Rhoden, who is in the midst of a campaign to keep his job, has emphasized the public safety value of sending people back to prison.

“The stories I have heard about parolees receiving too many second chances are frustrating and wrong, so we have changed this process,” Rhoden wrote in an opinion column released on May 1. “I have directed the DOC to take a tougher stance on DUIs, drug use, simple assault, and weapons violations that are a danger to others.”

Extra work anticipated for board

Parole board Chairman Myron Rau said Wednesday that the group’s workload could grow considerably, because of “everything that’s happened recently in the Department of Corrections.”

Rhoden wants the parole board to process violations — which will now include more violations for drug use — more quickly, which Rau said could mean adding a day of work back onto the board’s monthly meeting schedule.

Rau leads a part-time, nine-person board with members appointed by the governor, attorney general and chief justice of the state Supreme Court. Parole officers supervise people and submit reports of parole violations, but members of the appointed board must sign off on those recommendations to send someone on parole back to prison.

The board holds in-person and virtual hearings during one week of each month, at which they hear requests for release from current inmates, as well as requests for clemency or early discharge from parole.

In recent years, the board added a one-day “special session” to the end of each month to make decisions on parole violations. During those sessions, two members consider the arguments of parolees who are accused of but deny violating the terms of their release. The two members also sign off on dozens of “paper violations” for people who admit to violating their parole terms.

The new system had worked so efficiently that the board meetings shrank from 4 days to 3, but Rau told the board they should be prepared to add that day back onto their calendars in the coming months.

Division leaders see improvement

Leaders from the Department of Corrections’ parole division regularly report to the board on issues of open positions and parolees contacted in the previous month, but they recently offered a series of year-end statistics from 2025. 

The division met or exceeded its goals, they said. Just 3% of the people on parole are now classified as “absconders,” said Brad Lewandowski, director of parole services, meaning they’ve lost contact with their parole officer on purpose.

“There’s no state in the country that’s done that,” Lewandowski said. “The average nationally is between 10 to 14% of your population as absconders. For our staff to get it there, they worked really, really hard.”

National averages for parole absconding are not readily available, as states have differing systems for defining the term and calculating rates. 

In response to follow-up questions about where Lewandowski pulled those national averages, corrections spokesman Michael Winder said the parole director found the figures prior to the meeting “when searching other states who have similar systems and the available information.”

The number of parolees ducking supervision now hovers at around 100 on any given day, Lewandowski said. Three years ago, when the state created an absconder apprehension unit, there were four times as many.

The state also has a status known as “attempt to locate,” which means parole officers have lost touch with a parolee but are unsure why. An attempt to locate sends notice to law enforcement statewide, signaling that any officer who makes contact with the parolee in question should hold them and reach out to their parole officer.

The man who allegedly shot the officer in Sioux Falls was not an absconder, but was on “attempt to locate” status. Per corrections policy, a person who remains out of contact with their parole officer can move into absconder status two weeks after the issuance of an attempt to locate bearing their name.

There are 47 people on “attempt to locate” status in South Dakota, corrections spokesman Michael Winder said in an email sent after the meeting. 

Kayla Stucky, associate director of parole field operations, pointed to a decrease in the number of people returning to prison on “technical parole violations,” a list of violations that includes absconding. 

“Our goal was to decrease it by 3%, and we actually decreased it by 25%, so that’s pretty exciting for us,” Stucky said.

Stucky also pointed to two classes for people on parole, a “newer program” called “Thinking for Change” and another called “Moving On.” Seventy-two people on parole completed the latter; 40 completed the former.

In the coming year, Stucky said, the division hopes to work on helping more people on parole find jobs. About one in five parolees is unemployed, she said. 

The division has assigned a staff member “to try and make sure our offenders are getting the right help that they need to get that employment,” Stucky said, and to find more businesses willing to hire people on parole.

Intensive supervision

The hiring of five new officers and the formation of an “enhanced compliance unit” was welcome and “probably needed,” Lewandowski said.

Unlike the typical parole officer, he said, the agents in the new unit will oversee 20 to 30 people, not 65 or more. 

Five veteran parole officers volunteered to become part of that unit, he said.

“We’ll find the toughest cases for them to supervise,” Lewandowski said, and the agents will keep up the intensive monitoring for “about four months” after an inmate is released. 

“They’ll be your aggravated assaults, your violent offenses, your high-risk sex offenders, and we’re going to throw in people that have been in prison for a long time,” Lewandowski said. “They generally need a little bit of supervision structure as they come out.”

Winder, the corrections spokesman, said the new positions will be funded with the existing corrections budget through the “internal reallocation of vacancies from other areas.”

title: District 28 senate candidates
description: Voters in District 28 will head to the polls June 2 to vote on vacant senate seat. Two people are running for 1 open positions which is a 4-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.
_full_text:
District 28 Senate Comp.jpg

Voters in District 28 will head to the polls June 2 to vote on vacant senate seat. Two people are running for 1 open positions which is a 4-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.

Ryan Maher

 Maher, Ryan.jpg
Ryan Maher 

Name and what you do for a living? 

Ryan Maher. I am an insurance agent for Insite Partners in Timber Lake. I also own a grocery store on Main Street in Isabel and operate a cattle business with my parents, sister, and brother.

What motivated you to run for this office?

I’m motivated by a desire to continue serving the people of District 28 and to be a strong voice for rural South Dakota. My background in agriculture, small business, and local government has shown me both the challenges and opportunities we face. I want to ensure our communities remain strong, our schools are supported, and our infrastructure keeps up with our needs. I believe in practical, common-sense solutions and working together to move our district forward.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

My years of prior service in the South Dakota Senate have prepared me for this role. I have served in various leadership positions, including Assistant Majority Leader, Majority Whip, and chairman of several Senate committees. I have a record of supporting tax relief and reducing government spending and waste. I have also been an effective advocate for Northwest South Dakota. I show up prepared, work hard, and am ready to fight for the people I represent.

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I have served on the Isabel School Board and the Northwest Area School Board. I have also served on the Isabel City Council for many years. In addition, I currently serve as chairman of the board for Moreau-Grand Electric Cooperative in Timber Lake.

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy? 

As Chairman of the board for the Isabel town council over the couple of past year, I have attended all council meetings. During the legislative session, I also followed the proceedings regularly by listening in during the afternoons when my schedule allowed.

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Yes, local newspapers are important, especially in rural areas of Western South Dakota. They help keep communities connected by sharing local news, events, and important updates. They also provide a valuable platform for businesses to advertise and for schools to highlight what students are accomplishing. Local papers play a key role in maintaining informed and engaged communities.

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in your district? 

The most important issues in our district are rural school funding, roads and infrastructure, and maintaining a strong business climate. We must ensure our schools have the resources they need despite declining enrollment, while continuing to invest in roads and infrastructure that keep our communities connected. It’s also critical to support existing businesses and promote opportunities for growth to keep our local economies viable and prosperous.

How do you intend to solve these issues?

Addressing rural school funding requires advocating for fair formulas that reflect declining enrollment and higher transportation costs. The current formula is over a decade old and needs review and updates to better serve rural districts. For roads and infrastructure, I will work with the state and counties to prioritize funding where it is most needed and ensure responsible use of tax dollars. I also support reducing unnecessary government regulations on Main Street businesses so they can grow and remain competitive.        

What do you believe is working for the district, and how will you retain that progression?

Our strong sense of community, local leadership, and agricultural foundation are working well for our district. Economic stability in areas like cattle ranching has helped maintain. I will continue supporting policies that strengthen these sectors, protect property rights, and encourage responsible development. Staying connected with constituents and listening to their needs will be key to maintaining that progress.

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

Transparency means open communication, honesty, and accountability. Constituents deserve to know how decisions are made and why. I plan to remain accessible through phone calls, community meetings, and regular updates. I will listen to concerns, explain my votes, and ensure people feel heard. Being present and responsive is the best way to maintain trust. My cell phone has been published and anyone is free to reach out any time. 

What else do you want people to know about you?

I am a hard-working individual who values honesty, accessibility, and common-sense leadership. I live, work, and employ people in this legislative district, so I understand the challenges our communities face. I ask voters to place their trust in me to be their voice in Pierre and to represent this very rural district with integrity and dedication. I have a proven record of showing up early, staying late, and doing the work necessary to deliver results.

The discussion of data centers coming to South Dakota has been on the rise. Do you support data centers coming to the state?  

Yes, I support data centers coming to South Dakota. From an electric cooperative perspective, we have been planning for this type of development in our service territory. We have made policy adjustments to ensure legacy members are protected from the costs associated with large-scale projects like data centers. When managed properly, data centers can provide economic benefits and help stabilize electric rates for our members.

Data centers use significant amounts of water and electricity as part of their operations. What legislation should be put in place to protect residents from the inevitable need for more electrical generation and water use? 

Not every data center is the same—each project should be evaluated on its own merits. While some use significant water, many now rely on closed-loop systems that recycle water and reduce overall usage. Recent legislation has been passed to help protect end consumers from bearing added costs. Moving forward, we should ensure policies continue to safeguard residents while allowing responsible development. Electric cooperative boards also play an important role in adopting policies that protect legacy members from increased rates tied to large-scale projects like data centers.

Tax Incremental Finance Districts (TIFs) are a widely used economic development tool. Do you support their use? Why or why not?

TIFs can be a useful tool when used responsibly to promote economic development and attract investment. However, they must be carefully managed to ensure they do not shift an unfair burden onto existing taxpayers. I support their use when there is clear benefit to the community and proper oversight in place. I think there should be a limit on how many can be active at one time.

Should the state provide greater oversight in mining gravel and sand, especially when it comes to dust? Why or why not?

Local control should remain a key part of the process, with the state providing guidelines that ensure fairness and consistency.

Would you support an increase in the BBB tax, often called the tourism tax, to help offset taxes paid by residents? Why or why not?

I would not support any tax increase. While tourism is important to South Dakota’s economy, we must consider the impact on businesses and consumers. In many cases, rural South Dakotans traveling to larger communities for goods and services end up bearing that cost.

As the federal government pulls back from funding programs widely used in the state, how or should the legislature backfill the lost revenue?

Backfilling federal funding should be approached carefully. The state must prioritize essential services while maintaining fiscal responsibility. This may involve reallocating existing resources, reducing unnecessary spending, and finding efficiencies before considering new revenue sources. Some programs may need to be scaled back or discontinued if they are not sustainable. The federal government has a history of funding programs short-term and leaving states responsible long-term, so we must be cautious about committing to ongoing obligations without stable funding.

Sam Marty

 Marty, Sam.jpg
Sam Marty 

Name and what you do for a living? 

 Sam Marty   I’m a rancher.

What motivated you to run for this office?

 Wanted to serve the people of District 28.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position? 

My years of seeing the upside and downside of things that have affected the people of South Dakota.

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held? 

I have served on the ambulance board for Harding County and served on my church board.

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy? 

Several

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not? 

I’m a strong supporter of newspapers ! Newspapers are a very important part of our society. 

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in your district? 

Our private property rights are under attack and I will always support those rights. Data centers are another issue that needs to be watched. And of course our ever increasing property taxes.  The education of our children is always at the forefront of all districts.

How do you intend to solve these issues?  

For property taxes and education the State needs to rework the funding formula. Private property rights just need to be guarded through good legislation.

                       

What do you believe is working for the district, and how will you retain that progression?  

Parent  involvement in this district seems to be pretty good. I like the really good  approach that Belle Fourche has with their votech program.

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?  

Everything is out for viewing by the public. I’ve always been very open about my decisions and don’t plan on changing that philosophy. 

What else do you want people to know about you?  

I’m a life long rancher of Butte, Harding and Perkins Counties. I am also a veteran of the Vietnam War(1968/1969) and was awarded The Purple Heart for wounds I received while serving in Vietnam.

The discussion of data centers coming to South Dakota has been on the rise. Do you support data centers coming to the state?  

Not as of now. There needs to be a lot of safeguards in place before I commit to Data Centers.

Data centers use significant amounts of water and electricity as part of their operations. What legislation should be put in place to protect residents from the inevitable need for more electrical generation and water use?  

We need very good legislation to protect the citizens from raising the electric rates and water usage. That can be done with good legislation.

Tax Incremental Finance Districts (TIFs) are a widely used economic development tool. Do you support their use? Why or why not?  

I support them for small projects but do not support them for big multi million dollar projects. 

Should the state provide greater oversight in mining gravel and sand, especially when it comes to dust? Why or why not?  

I think there is plenty of oversight already in place.

Would you support an increase in the BBB tax, often called the tourism tax, to help offset taxes paid by residents? Why or why not? 

I’m cautious about any tax increase-no matter how it’s  labeled-because too often it becomes permanent government growth instead of real relief. Before we talk about raising taxes, we should be cutting waste, controlling spending, and fixing the system that’s driving property taxes up in the first place. Relief should come first, not new revenue.

As the federal government pulls back from funding programs widely used in the state, how or should the legislature backfill the lost revenue? 

The legislature should not automatically backfill federal dollars with state tax increases-that’s how temporary federal programs turn into permanent burdens on our taxpayers. Every program needs to stand on its own merits. If it’s essential, core to the state’s responsibility, and delivering real results, then we evaluate how to fund it responsibly within our means. If it’s not, then it shouldn’t continue just because federal money once supported it. This is an opportunity to reset priorities, eliminate inefficiencies, and return decision-making closer to the people of South Dakota -not grow government by default.

title: Campaign finance deadline sheds  light on groups seeking to influence  SD governor race
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Clockwise from top left are campaign messages funded by the political action committees South Dakota Safety Action, Rushmore Principles, Defend US, and Dakota First Action. Illustration by Joshua Haiar, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Campaign finance deadline sheds  light on groups seeking to influence  SD governor race
Clockwise from top left are campaign messages funded by the political action committees South Dakota Safety Action, Rushmore Principles, Defend US, and Dakota First Action. Illustration by Joshua Haiar, South Dakota Searchlight 

PIERRE — The candidates themselves are not the only ones raising and spending money in South Dakota’s race for governor. Political action committees not officially associated with the candidates have spent over $1.3 million in recent months, and new campaign finance reports show where some of the money came from. 

The June 2 Republican primary includes Gov. Larry Rhoden, U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, state House Speaker Jon Hansen and Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden. The winner will advance to the November general election against presumptive Democratic nominee Dan Ahlers. 

Political action committees had to file their pre-election campaign finance reports Monday. Those reports show that the largest player among the independent committees active in the race for governor is Rushmore Principles, which is registered in South Dakota but run by Hadyn Smith of Mountain Brook, Ala. Smith has not responded to messages from South Dakota Searchlight.

The committee’s new report shows it received contributions from a federal committee, Republican Forward, totaling $1.4 million. Rushmore Principles reported about $1.3 million in spending, including about $1.2 million on digital media and direct mail opposing Rhoden. The anti-Rhoden messaging has criticized Rhoden’s approach to tax policy. Rushmore Principles also reported spending about $51,500 on direct mail opposing Hansen.

Republican Forward’s major contributions include large amounts from the Sioux Falls business community: $500,000 from POET ethanol, $300,000 from First Premier Bank Chairman and CEO Dana Dykhouse, $150,000 from MarketBeat founder and CEO Matthew Paulson, and $100,000 from Lloyd Companies. Among other donors, Republican Forward has also received $100,000 from Genesis Farms Cannabis Company, which has multiple medical marijuana outlets across the state. 

Republican Forward is a super PAC. Due to U.S. Supreme Court decisions, super PACs are legally allowed to raise and spend unlimited amounts as long as there’s no coordination with candidates. In South Dakota, political action committees can receive unlimited contributions from other political action committees.

A state-registered political action committee called South Dakota Safety Action has been active against Hansen. The committee is run by Tabor Shabot from a Sioux Falls address. It reported $20,000 in total contributions, all from Dan and Jan Joyce of Frankfort, Illinois. The committee spent about $18,000 on a “Jon Hansen Weak on Crime” mail and text message campaign, the committee’s report says.

Dakota First Action, a committee originally founded by Doeden, has promoted a “Republican Primary Voter Guide” through a website branded as South Dakota Tax Watch. The site describes South Dakota Tax Watch as a “policy watchdog,” but its disclaimer says it was paid for and approved by Dakota First Action. The guide criticizes Rhoden, Hansen and Johnson while presenting Doeden favorably.

Dakota First Action’s most recent state report showed little activity, with $6,600 raised and about $10,600 spent during the reporting period, leaving about $16,300 on hand.

A federally registered group, Virginia-based Defend US PAC, has been active against Johnson with messaging framing him as insufficiently conservative. The committee is on a federal reporting schedule, and its most recent report covered January through March, revealing little to no information about its more recent activity in South Dakota.

Defend US PAC’s contributions during the January to March period came from other political action committees or organizations, including $95,000 from the Affordable Energy Fund PAC, which in turn received its most recent contributions from other political action committees.

title: Speed limit changes approved for North Avenue, Colorado Boulevard
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Speed limit changes proposed for North Avenue and Colorado Boulevard have locations pictured. Courtesy maps
_full_text:
Speed limit changes approved for North Avenue, Colorado Boulevard
Speed limit changes proposed for North Avenue and Colorado Boulevard have locations pictured. Courtesy maps 

SPEARFISH — The Spearfish City Council voted unanimously Monday to reduce speed limits on North Avenue and Colorado Boulevard from 35 mph to 25 mph sooner than motorists are used to.

On North Avenue, the new 25 mph zone will extend from the entrance of Safeway to just north of Recreation Lane. On Colorado Boulevard, the speed limit will drop to 25 mph from 7th Avenue to the turn into the Great Western Tire parking lot.

Both speed limit changes were recommended in the city’s Safety Action Plan as low-cost measures that may significantly reduce the number of serious and fatal crashes in the city limits.

“Both of those areas were in our high injury network, and the increased speeds there do result in more severe crashes for motorists and pedestrians,” said Abbey Larson, a Spearfish staff engineer.

To implement the speed limit changes, the city plans to spend $13,836 on dynamic speed signs to help motorists adjust. That purchase is accounted for in the 2026 streets budget. As a result, the council did not need to approve the sign purchases. They did need to approve the speed reduction. 

The flashing speed signs will go in on North Avenue near Oriole Drive and north of the rec center, and on Colorado Boulevard near the west side of the Great Western Tire parking lot.

City Councilman Dean Myers asked if a fourth sign might be called for near Oriole as drivers travel from the direction of Main Street on Colorado Boulevard. There aren’t presently plans to have a fourth sign, but that could be considered in the future, Larson said.

“I think the reduction, which is near the curve of Colorado, is really important. There are a number of apartments there in that area specifically. That is a long walk across 4 lanes, and you are kind of blinded there, especially when you’re coming south,” said Spearfish Mayor John Senden.

SPEARFISH — In this issue, you will find the annual publication of financial summaries of insurance companies licensed to do business in South Dakota.

Insurance companies doing business in South Dakota are required by state law to publish these financial summaries each year. The summary lists the insurance company’s assets, liabilities, business in South Dakota for the year and the lines in which the company is authorized by the state of South Dakota to sell insurance.

“Public notices published in newspapers have an important role in keeping citizens informed and providing bonafide transparency.  For more information about any insurance company doing business in South Dakota, contact the state Division of Insurance in Pierre at (605) 773-3563.

 More than 8 out of 10 South Dakotans believe that publishing public notices in a local newspaper should be required. That is according to a statewide survey of 406 South Dakota adults commissioned by SDNA and conducted by Coda Ventures in 2024.

title: Hearing on proposed Black Hills uranium drilling opens with hours of opposition testimony
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Elizabeth Lone Eagle, far right, speaks to the South Dakota Board of Minerals and Environment at the first day of a hearing on an exploratory drilling permit Monday, at the Mueller Civic Center in Hot Springs. Photo by Meghan O’Brien, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Hearing on proposed Black Hills uranium drilling opens with hours of opposition testimony
Elizabeth Lone Eagle, far right, speaks to the South Dakota Board of Minerals and Environment at the first day of a hearing on an exploratory drilling permit Monday, at the Mueller Civic Center in Hot Springs. Photo by Meghan O’Brien, South Dakota Searchlight 

HOT SPRINGS — Persistent, drizzling rain didn’t keep dozens of people from rallying against a proposed uranium drilling project in the southern Black Hills on the first day of a weeklong hearing to decide on a permit application.

Law enforcement officers and vehicles flanked the parking lot and theater doors Monday at the Mueller Civic Center, where the hearing took place.

Opponents cited concerns about Craven Canyon, which is near the proposed drilling sites and is marked with ancient Native American petroglyphs. Opponents said they’re also concerned about the potential to contaminate underground water, and to negatively affect the state’s agriculture and tourism industries.

“A lot of the people in this room don’t live near Craven Canyon, but that doesn’t mean that you ditch the responsibility to protect it,” said project opponent Anissa Martin. She then referenced the Lakota name for the Black Hills. “So I ask you, where will we go when the He Sapa are uninhabitable, when we have no water in the Black Hills? And I ask you, what water will you drink?”

The hearing drew public testimony from not only residents of the Black Hills, but also from Wyoming, Minnesota and Pennsylvania. People who spoke Monday during the hour-long public comment period were all in opposition to the project.

The company proposing the drilling has maintained that it has gone through all the necessary steps in the permitting process, and the project will not harm the nearby canyon.

The state Board of Minerals and Environment can deny an application to explore for uranium for several reasons, including negative impacts on historical, archaeological or recreational aspects of an area, if those impacts outweigh the benefits of the exploration. The board can also deny the permit if it will negatively affect the productivity of aquifers.

In March 2024, Clean Nuclear Energy Corporation and its Canada-based parent company Nexus Uranium filed an application to drill exploratory holes in search of uranium near Craven Canyon, 7 miles north of Edgemont.

The company plans to use 50 sites to drill holes as deep as 700 feet on state-owned land, according to its application. Each hole will take approximately two weeks to drill.

The company has additional drilling plans on federally owned land. That portion of the project is under review by the U.S. Forest Service, which estimates it will issue a decision next month.

Besides taking public testimony, the state board dealt with several preliminary matters Monday.

The board’s hearing chairman, Bob Morris, declined to require the state’s commissioner of school and public lands to testify in person. That office manages the state land at the proposed project site.

Bruce Ellison, an attorney and project opponent, sought to require the commissioner’s in-person testimony. Ellison said he didn’t receive sufficient evidence from a records request about the commissioner as to “how he did his job.”

Morris said there is written material from the commissioner in the case file, and Morris doesn’t see “how it’s relevant” to question the commissioner.

The board also failed to produce a Lakota interpreter for the hearing, after agreeing to provide one. A staff member for the state Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources said potential interpreters had conflicts of interest or scheduling conflicts that prevented them from accepting the role.

The board decided to have a discussion Tuesday morning about whether to continue the hearing without an interpreter. The hearing is scheduled to continue through Friday.

The proposed drilling near Craven Canyon is separate from another proposal to mine uranium in the Edgemont area that’s been pending since the early 2000s. That proposal, from Texas-based enCore Energy, has met staunch opposition from Native Americans and environmental activists and has been in regulatory and legal limbo. Last year, the federal government’s Permitting Council selected enCore’s project for inclusion in FAST-41, a process intended to improve coordination among permitting agencies and hold them accountable to deadlines.

Uranium is a metallic, radioactive element used as fuel in nuclear weapons and nuclear power plants. Interest in uranium exploration and mining has risen recently, in response to nuclear energy’s potential to meet the growing electricity demands of data centers handling the computing needs of artificial intelligence.

The hearing in Hot Springs comes on the heels of a victory for opponents of another drilling project in the Black Hills. Rapid City-based company Pete Lien & Sons recently withdrew from an exploratory graphite drilling project that was underway near Pe’ Sla, also known as Reynolds Prairie, a sacred site for Lakota people in the central Black Hills. The withdrawal came after two lawsuits from opponents challenging the project and the formation of a protest camp at the drilling site.

byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Along the rec path between Jorgensen Park and Evans Park, the bank of Spearfish Creek has eroded significantly. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson

Spearfish Creek 1.JPG
Along the rec path between Jorgensen Park and Evans Park, the bank of Spearfish Creek has eroded significantly. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — Spearfish has hired Johner & Sons to armor a section of the creek bank between Jorgensen Park and Evans Park, where erosion is threatening the rec path. The $146,556 contract award marks the beginning of the first of 3 projects to fight erosion along Spearfish Creek. 

 Spearfish Creek 2.JPG
Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

“The budget for this is $850,000 for 3 combined projects: this one, some Yellowstone drainage improvements, and then also some underpass under Hillsview. The Hillsview portion has grown in scope, so that is going to be a future project to perform at a later time,” Spearfish Public Works Director told the city council Monday. All 3 projects will be paid for with dollars from the general fund.

“The engineer’s estimate on this project was $190,000. It came in well below the engineer’s estimates, so staff would recommend awarding this project,” McMahon said.

Now, Johner & Sons will need to remove the existing concrete sidewalk, salvage and replace topsoil, remove and reset the fence, install drainage fabric, pour a 6-inch non-reinforced concrete sidewalk, seeding/fertilization, mulch, install a water barrier, erosion and sediment control, and pedestrian traffic control.

“An important FYI for the community on this one, it will involve shutting down the rec path during this bank stabilization project, so there will be some interruptions to a very popular section of the rec path. We’ll be working closely with the contractor for notifications on that and the duration of that closure,” McMahon said.

The nearest street is Bridgewater Court, and the owner of a vacant lot has granted a temporary easement for access to the construction site. The trail will be closed during the project.

title: Sturgis Animal Shelter Fund to ensure donations stay with animals
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: A Sturgis Animal Shelter Fund, set up through the Black Hills Area Community Foundation, will provide a vehicle for donations to stay with the animal shelter, and could provide a way to save for large projects for the animals. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
Sturgis animal shelter 3.jpeg
A Sturgis Animal Shelter Fund, set up through the Black Hills Area Community Foundation, will provide a vehicle for donations to stay with the animal shelter, and could provide a way to save for large projects for the animals. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

STURGIS — A specific fund set aside for the Sturgis Animal Shelter will guarantee that donated funds will benefit its furry residents. 

On Monday the Sturgis City Council approved a proposal to establish the Sturgis Animal Shelter Fund through the Black Hills Area Community Foundation. City Administrator Aaron Jordan said the fund would provide a charitable giving mechanism for individuals and organizations that want to support the animal shelter. 

Currently, Jordan said donations to the shelter are passed through city accounts. Because of that, at the end of the year when the city’s audit is completed the unused funds are rolled over into the city’s general fund account, where it is not necessarily earmarked for the animal shelter. 

Under the Sturgis Animal Shelter Fund, all donations are reserved exclusively for use at the animal shelter, Jordan said. 

“This allows us to, over time, as people donate to the animal shelter we can build a larger set of funds for larger projects,” Jordan said, adding that demand at the current shelter has outgrown its available space. “We’re not in a position to do anything different at this point, but this may be an opportunity to allow us to consider a large infrastructure project on city property.” 

Under the agreement with the community foundation, advisors for the fund will be Sturgis Finance Officer Ann Bertolotto, Deputy Finance Director Robin Korth, and  Director of Public Safety Geody VanDewater. 

 Sturgis animal shelter 1.jpeg
Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

 Sturgis animal shelter 2.jpeg
Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

Sturgis resident Bonnie Alberts asked the council for assurance that establishing the fund would not affect normal budget allocations for the animal shelter. 

“What are the assurances that this money will certainly be used for tihngs the shelter needs, things the animals want, and that there is no way for that donated money to displace shelter services that the city is planning to pay for no matter how short we get,” Alberts asked. 

However, Jordan said the current city council cannot dictate to future councils how the city budget will be structured. Therefore, he said there are no assurances about the future of the animal shelter budget. However, he said the separate fund provides assurance that all donated funds are used for the animal shelter — a guarantee that is not currently in place.

title: Project opponent files federal lawsuit; uranium drilling permit hearing paused
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: A view of Craven Canyon in South Dakota’s southern Black Hills, where a company has proposed an exploratory drilling project. Photo by Meghan O’Brien, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Project opponent files federal lawsuit; uranium drilling permit hearing paused
A view of Craven Canyon in South Dakota’s southern Black Hills, where a company has proposed an exploratory drilling project. Photo by Meghan O’Brien, South Dakota Searchlight 

HOT SPRINGS — The status of a hearing on an exploratory uranium drilling permit was left uncertain Wednesday after a state board adjourned until further notice, following a private session to discuss legal matters.

The permit application is from Clean Nuclear Energy Corporation, which is seeking to drill dozens of holes up to 700 feet deep on state land. The proposed site is near the rim of Craven Canyon in the Southern Black Hills.

Dozens of people and some organizations have raised formal complaints about the project to the Board of Minerals and Environment, which will decide on the permit. Opponents have said the drilling could disturb ancient Native American petroglyphs on the canyon’s walls, disrupt Lakota ceremonies and potentially contaminate groundwater, among other concerns.

On Monday, the board started a hearing in Hot Springs on the permit application. The hearing was scheduled to continue through Friday.

On Wednesday, the third day of the hearing, project opponent Elizabeth Lone Eagle filed a federal lawsuit against the board, the state’s Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources, Clean Nuclear Energy, and state employees involved in evaluating the permit application, alleging violations of due process. Lone Eagle filed the lawsuit herself, without representation by an attorney.

Lone Eagle, along with 6 other people, including five described as Lakota first-language speakers, are listed as plaintiffs in the suit. The suit alleges “systematic, ongoing, and deliberate denial of meaningful participation to Lakota first-language speaking” project opponents.

Lakota is spoken by western South Dakota tribes, which once controlled the Black Hills as part of the Great Sioux Reservation. The board agreed prior to the hearing that the state Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources would provide a Lakota interpreter for the proceedings. The department failed to provide an interpreter on Monday, but provided interpreters Tuesday. At times on Tuesday, project opponents objected from seats in the audience when parts of the hearing proceeded without interpretation.

The lawsuit also alleges that a “significant multi-jurisdictional law enforcement presence” creates an “atmosphere of intimidation” at the hearing.

The board did not provide a date to resume the hearing, which was being held at the Mueller Civic Center in Hot Springs, a little more than 20 miles from the proposed drill site. Several project opponents who’d been attending the hearing told South Dakota Searchlight on Wednesday evening that they were going home to await a further announcement.

Neither the Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources nor Clean Nuclear Energy immediately responded to Searchlight’s requests for further information.

BHPioneerLogo

DEADWOOD — A bid for $1.8 million was awarded to Halme, Inc., May 12 at the Lawrence County Commission meeting, to replace 2 bridges on Nemo Road, located approximately 580 feet apart, with a completion date set for October 2027.

John Bey, highway superintendent, received 8 bids for the project and opened 7. The deadline to deliver the bids to the county auditor was 8:30 a.m. Tuesday. A bid from Woelber Excavating, LLC., of Belle Fourche, was received at 8:32 a.m. The bid was sent back to Woelber unopened. 

The engineers estimate for the 2 structures combined was $3,093,100.25, estimating $1,526,076.075 and $1,567,023.50 for each structure. Halme’s bid came in at $902,483.70 for the first structure and $935,214.55 for the second, for a total bid of $1,837,698.25.

Both structures are currently under load ratings and are set to be replaced with cast-in-place box culverts at the same time that a 3.63-mile stretch of Nemo Road, beginning near Old Ridge Road and proceeding northwest towards Hay Creek Lane, is paved. 

Bey said that he hopes work will be done before the 2027 completion date.

title: Lead Historic Preservation chair calls for penalties for demo permit violations
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: A garage structure at 515 Railroad Ave., was mostly demolished before city officials noticed and issued a stop work order until owners obtained a demolition permit. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
Lead demo permit.jpeg
A garage structure at 515 Railroad Ave., was mostly demolished before city officials noticed and issued a stop work order until owners obtained a demolition permit. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

LEAD — The city of Lead should consider putting some teeth into its demolition permit ordinances, instituting penalties for homeowners who do not follow the proper channels, Terry Smith, chairman of the Lead Historic Preservation Commission said Monday. 

Lead Building Inspector Dennis Schumacher told the city commission that recently a resident started demolishing a structure at 515 Railroad Ave., without obtaining a permit. Schumacher said when he discovered the work in progress without a permit, he issued a stop work order, while he checked with the county assessor to determine whether the structure is historic. 

While the demolished building is located within a historic district of Lead, it is not considered a contributing historic structure. Schumacher said a contributing structure is one that is listed on the South Dakota Register of Historic Places. 

The normal process for demolition in the city of Lead is for the Lead Planning and Zoning and Historic Preservation commissions to approve demolition permits. The Historic Preservation Commission checks to see if the building is considered a contributing structure, before issuing the permits.

But the old garage on Railroad Avenue was already mostly demolished before any city officials were able to make any determinations.  

“At the end of the day we do believe that anybody who comes into the city for demolition needs to get a request before it’s even started,” Smith said. “Just going out and doing the demolition without a permit, that’s a disservice to everybody else who’s come to us for a demolition request. So we think some type of penalty should be enacted.” 

Preston Morrison, whose grandfather owns the property on Railroad Avenue, hired a contractor to take the dilapidated building down due to safety concerns, said he thought the contractor obtained all the necessary permits for the work. The lack of a permit was not intentional and it was not the result of negligence, he said. Morrison added that he has since obtained a demolition permit, which he asked the city to approve, Monday. 

“We hired a contracting company, thinking that all permits would be taken care of through them, so it was a mistake that we didn’t verify that permits were required,” he said. “Not to pass the blame, but that was the point of hiring a contractor who is licensed and insured to take care of a project.”   

A representative from the contractor said they were unaware of the requirement for historic preservation approval. The company, F16 Services in Spearfish, is licensed and approved as a contractor to work in the city of Lead. 

The city of Lead’s demolition permit ordinance does not include penalties for not obtaining a permit. Therefore, Schumacher said there is little the city can do about the situation with the structure on Railroad Avenue. 

“If this ever happens again, we need to make sure there are some kind of repercussions,” Schumacher said. 

Following some further discussion, the Lead City Commission unanimously approved the demolition permit, and authorized the contractor to continue work to remove the structure.

title: Quick Picks: Bildungsroman
description: Graduation season is winding down in the Northern Hills. As grads across the region turn their tassels, then pack up their caps and gowns, their facing an exciting new chapter — an entre into adulthood.
_full_text:
Quick Picks: Bildungsroman

Graduation season is winding down in the Northern Hills. As grads across the region turn their tassels, then pack up their caps and gowns, their facing an exciting new chapter — an entre into adulthood. 

That’s why this week we’ve wrangled a list of some of our favorite coming of age stories. This genre, the bildungsroman, tends to follow a character on a psychological, physical, or emotional journey from childhood into adulthood. Pick one up, and enjoy the journey. 

1. “Educated” by Tara Westover 

Genre: Memoir 

Born to survivalists in the mountains of Idaho, Tara Westover was 17 the first time she set foot in a classroom. Her family was so isolated from mainstream society that there was no one to ensure the children received an education, and no one to intervene when one of Tara’s older brothers became violent. When another brother got himself into college, Tara decided to try a new kind of life. Her quest for knowledge transformed her, taking her over oceans and across continents, to Harvard and to Cambridge University. Only then would she wonder if she’d traveled too far, if there was still a way home.

2. “Demon Copperhead” by Barbara Kingslover 

Genre: Fiction 

Set in the mountains of southern Appalachia, this is the story of a boy born to a teenaged single mother in a single-wide trailer, with no assets beyond his dead father’s good looks and copper-colored hair, a caustic wit, and a fierce talent for survival. In a plot that never pauses for breath, relayed in his own unsparing voice, he braves the modern perils of foster care, child labor, derelict schools, athletic success, addiction, disastrous loves, and crushing losses. Through all of it, he reckons with his own invisibility in a popular culture where even the superheroes have abandoned rural people in favor of cities. “Demon Copperhead” speaks for a new generation of lost boys, and all those born into beautiful, cursed places they can’t imagine leaving behind.

3. “Where the Crawdads Sing” by Delia Ownes

Genre: Fiction

In “Where the Crawdads Sing,” Owens juxtaposes an exquisite ode to the natural world against a profound coming of age story and haunting mystery. Thought-provoking, wise, and deeply moving, Owens’s debut novel reminds us that we are forever shaped by the child within us, while also subject to the beautiful and violent secrets that nature keeps.

The story asks how isolation influences the behavior of a young woman, who like all of us, has the genetic propensity to belong to a group. The clues to the mystery are brushed into the lush habitat and natural histories of its wild creatures.

4. “Little Women” by Louisa May Alcott

Genre: Classics

Generations of readers young and old, male and female, have fallen in love with the March sisters of Louisa May Alcott’s most popular and enduring novel, Little Women. Here are talented tomboy and author-to-be Jo, tragically frail Beth, beautiful Meg, and romantic, spoiled Amy, united in their devotion to each other and their struggles to survive in New England during the Civil War.

5. “Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow” by Gabrielle Zevin

Genre: Fiction

On a bitter-cold day, in the December of his junior year at Harvard, Sam Masur exits a subway car and sees, amid the hordes of people waiting on the platform, Sadie Green. He calls her name. For a moment, she pretends she hasn’t heard him, but then, she turns, and a game begins: a legendary collaboration that will launch them to stardom. These friends, intimates since childhood, borrow money, beg favors, and, before even graduating college, they have created their first blockbuster, Ichigo. Overnight, the world is theirs. Not even 25 years old, Sam and Sadie are brilliant, successful, and rich, but these qualities won’t protect them from their own creative ambitions or the betrayals of their hearts.

6. “My Brilliant Friend” by Elena Ferrente 

Genre: Fiction

Beginning in the 1950s in a poor but vibrant neighborhood on the outskirts of Naples, Elena Ferrante’s 4-volume story spans almost 60 years, as its main characters, the fiery and unforgettable Lila and the bookish narrator, Elena, become women, wives, mothers, and leaders, all the while maintaining a complex and at times conflicted friendship. This first novel in the series follows Lila and Elena from their fateful meeting as 10-year-olds through their school years and adolescence.
