description: Voters in District 28B will head to the polls June 2 to vote on a vacant house seat. Two people are running for 1 open position which is a 2-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.
_full_text:
District28BComp.jpg

Voters in District 28B will head to the polls June 2 to vote on a vacant house seat. Two people are running for 1 open position which is a 2-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.

Lawrence (Larry) Schmaltz

 Schmaltz, Larry.jpg
Larry Schmaltz 

Name and what you do for a living? 

Lawrence (Larry) Schmaltz

Civil Engineer/Construction Management

What motivated you to run for this office?

It has been on my mind since I was honored to be selected to Boys State in high school. Recently it came to the surface since my service on City Council in Belle Fourche concluded and people across the state reaching out to ask if I would consider running. I enjoyed serving the citizens of Belle Fourche on city council and wanted to take my public service to the next level.  

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

I have been in business most of my adult life and have a wealth of experience running successful organizations. I have also been in a fiduciary position on the Foundation Board of Trustees at the South Dakota School of Mines, as well as several other nonprofit service organizations. Further, being on the Belle Fourche City Council and Planning and Zoning Commission, as well as the Economic Development Board has given me significant government experience. I want to tie these three experiences together to make South Dakota a better place for all to live and prosper. 

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

Belle Fourche City Council

Belle Fourche Planning and Zoning Commission

Belle Fourche Economic Development Board

Chairman, Real Estate Committee, South Dakota School of Mines Foundation

Board of Trustees, South Dakota School of Mines Foundation

Professional Advisory Board, South Dakota School of Mines Civil Engineering Department

Board of Trustees, Mount Marty College

Board Member, World Animal Care Foundation

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

More than ten. 

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Absolutely. Local newspapers are in many cases the sole source of local news for many people. The articles and reporting in local newspapers are about the people in the local area that make a difference. 

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in your district?

Property tax relief is on everyone’s mind. The state legislature did pass some property tax reform but the likely impact for our district will be minimal. 

The state must do everything it can to support our agriculture industry. 

I will support policies that encourage good quality job creation in the state while preserving South Dakota’s quality of life. 

I will also work with law enforcement to provide the tools to combat the growing concerns with cybercrime.

And, as fiduciary at the South Dakota School of Mines, I understand the importance of quality education in our state at both the primary and secondary level. 

How do you intend to solve these issues?

Work with the Governor’s property tax relief tax force to further implement ideas for additional tax reduction. 

Listen to the concerns of our agricultural community and work with them in making the state a partner and not a hinderance. 

Keep the state’s tax structure simple with no state income tax and no corporate tax, while simplifying the state’s regulatory environment.

Provide the tools that law enforcement needs to combat cybercrime and hold scammers accountable. 

Work with the South Dakota Education Association to promote fair and accountable standards for education.             

What do you believe is working for the district, and how will you retain that progression?

I believe that the best thing for our district and in fact for the state as a whole is the fact that South Dakota has no personal income tax and no corporate tax, except for the banking industry that is subject to a bank franchise tax. This is very appealing to the hard-working citizens and business owners in our state, and it brings prosperity to our local businesses as it allows them to invest more in their businesses and their employees. 

I will always vote to not allow additional new taxes to be placed on the citizens of South Dakota. 

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

Transparency means ensuring that the people I represent always know what I’m doing, why I’m doing it, and how it affects them. To me, it’s not just about sharing information—it’s about making that information understandable, accessible, and timely.

I plan to be transparent by:

Explaining my decisions publicly, including the data, community input, and values that shaped them.

Maintaining open communication channels, such as regular town halls, newsletters, and online updates.

Publishing voting records, budget rationales, and policy summaries in plain language so constituents don’t have to dig for answers.

Inviting feedback before major decisions, not after, so people feel heard rather than informed too late.

What else do you want people to know about you?

I have a passion for South Dakota and public service. I live in Belle Fourche because I choose to, not because I have to. My business and board experiences have taught me how decisions affect families, landowners, employers and employees. 

The discussion of data centers coming to South Dakota has been on the rise. Do you support data centers coming to the state?

This is not a yes or no question. There are so many factors that must be considered when answering this question. For instance, if a data center can prove that it will not cause a rate increase in the local electrical grid either by using available excess power from the power company or providing its own electrical source, such as LNG, clean coal, or modular nuclear reactor, and a cooling source that does not impact local water supplies or aquifers, then it becomes more of a local zoning issue and a property rights issue for the landowner. 

Data centers use significant amounts of water and electricity as part of their operations. What legislation should be put in place to protect residents from the inevitable need for more electrical generation and water use?

The 2026 Legislature addressed the concerns with data centers. 

SB 135— titled the “Data Center Bill of Rights for Citizens”— passed both chambers with strong bipartisan support and was signed by the governor,

The bill responds to concerns about the growth of data centers and their impacts on electricity costs, grid stability, and water resources.

Key Provisions included:

Data centers with peak demand of 10 MW or more must:

Operate under separate electric service terms.

Reimburse utilities for all costs attributable to their demand. 

This prevents residential ratepayers from subsidizing tech operators. 

The state cannot preempt local governments from regulating.

Tax Incremental Finance Districts (TIFs) are a widely used economic development tool. Do you support their use? Why or why not?

A TIF is only as good as the stakeholders make it. When a TIF is proposed it must first and foremost be for the long-term benefit of all of the stakeholders and communities that it impacts. Done properly, a TIF can be a win-win situation as it allows for a cost-effective way of augmenting the financing of a project that should bring long-term prosperity to a community and its citizens. TIFs should be used for developments that will bring good paying jobs to a community and/or affordable housing. By bringing these two benefits, a community prospers with more sales tax revenue and ultimately a broader base of property tax revenue.  

Should the state provide greater oversight in mining gravel and sand, especially when it comes to dust? Why or why not?

Mining operations are already heavily regulated at the federal level, and mining permits adopt the federal regulations by reference. For instance, dust control and suppression measures are required by the USEPA under the National Emissions Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants (NESHAP) 40 CFR 61. Additionally, the Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) regulates such things as dust minimization and suppression. Counties already have the ability to address mining projects with limitations and regulations regarding such things as dust suppression, noise limits and vibration monitoring and limitations. Pennington County has these limitations codified. 

Would you support an increase in the BBB tax, often called the tourism tax, to help offset taxes paid by residents? Why or why not?

Yes. This is a tax that does not impact South Dakota citizens but rather is paid by visitors to the state and at a low volumetric rate that has a very limited impact to the individual tourist but can benefit all property tax payers in South Dakota. 

As the federal government pulls back from funding programs widely used in the state, how or should the legislature backfill the lost revenue?

First, the state legislature, working with the governor, must always be diligent in assessing the state’s budget and expenditures. It must always be looking for ways to reduce unnecessary or wasteful spending. 

A state legislature has several levers it can pull when the federal government reduces funding for programs the state relies on. None of them are painless, but each comes with different political, economic, and administrative tradeoffs. 

Legislators can:

Shift money from lowerpriority programs to higherpriority ones

Tap unspent balances or program surpluses

Delay or scale back planned initiatives

Travis Ismay

 Travis Ismay(MUG).jpg
Travis Ismay 

Name and what you do for a living?

My name is Travis Ismay, I am a rancher with a welding business and a current legislator.

What motivated you to run for this office?

I’m running for reelection because while I was in Pierre, I saw various things that I believe we can remedy, that will make district 28’s citizens lives much better and more free.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

I believe with my experience as a legislator, my background in agriculture, being a small business owner and my love for my district and its people. I am the best qualified candidate for this position.

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit office have you held?

I am currently the chairman of the Concerned Citizens of South Dakota (CCOSD) a Christian conservative organization that promotes local conservative candidates to run for office and be community leaders across the State. I am also the chairman of the Butte County chapter of the Concern Citizens which we established in 2021.

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I’m not sure on the exact number, but I go to a lot of local government meetings, Cracker Barrel’s and meet and greets across my district. I don’t make it to every one, but I certainly try to make it to as many as I possibly can.

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Absolutely, I think they’re very important form of communication and information. I certainly miss seeing our local newspaper in my mailbox. I check it online from time to time, but there’s nothing like having physical media to read.

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in your district?

As far as what can be done at the state level, I truly believe that the expansion of state government over the past years is a major factor in the problems in local government. Local government is regulated to the point that they have no choice, but to raise their budgets every year. It is a use it or lose it system set up by the state. I believe that if people understood how and why their local taxes are collected by the county or the city they would pay a whole lot more attention to who they are electing in those positions.

How do you intend to solve these issues?

There are numerous ways that the state regulates the local municipalities. I started by going through the regulations set up by the state, I wrote bills that would incentivize reducing costs, thereby reducing budgets in-turn, reducing government which would reduce taxes and government overreach, even local and I will continue to do so.

What do you believe is working for the district, and how will you retain that progression?

I have to give the credit to our local elected officials for the things that are going right in my district. In the past few years, we have elected some amazing people to those positions. They are the ones that are the boots on the ground not state officials. A few things that I’ve noticed in the past few years is the growing attendance for local meetings such as, County commission meetings, school boards meetings, planning board meetings and the overall concern that I have seen from our citizens. It is a beautiful thing.

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

If we truly have a citizen government, everything has to be transparent that has to do with money land or regulation. All you have to do is ask me. I am an open book. My phone number is 605-490-6010 and is on the South Dakota legislature website.

What else do you want people to know about you?

I will continue to work for my constituents in all things that I can. I truly do adore my district and all of my constituents. The more I learn about state government the more I think we need less of it. I would be honored to continue to be your conservative voice for a conservative district.

The discussion of data centers coming to South Dakota has been on the rise. Do you support data centers coming to the state?

NO

Data centers use significant amounts of water and electricity as part of their operations. What legislation should be put in place to protect residents from the inevitable need for more electrical generation and water use?

We passed some significant legislation last session with SB 135 that will help with this problem. It should be a local matter if the people want a data center in their area it should be on a ballot and your local County or municipality should regulate accordingly.

Tax Incremental Finance Districts (TIFs) are a widely used economic development tool. Do you support their use? Why or why not?

No, I do not support them being widely used, and if a (TIF) is established in a county or municipality, it should be voted on by the people in the municipality or the county in each circumstance, with the proper information and knowledge of the repercussions to the county.

Should the state provide greater oversight in mining gravel and sand, especially when it comes to dust? Why or why not?

Yes, If the mining affects the adjacent property owners roads or the evaluation of their property. We should protect our citizens from circumstances out of their control.

Would you support an increase in the BBB tax, often called the tourism tax, to help offset taxes paid by residents? Why or why not?

No, it would not only elect tourists, it would affect the people in my district significantly.

As the federal government pulls back from funding programs widely used in the state, how or should the legislature backfill the lost revenue?

The state has certain essential requirements that they would be have to fund like Oahe Dam for instance. I believe that we should cut non-essential things from our budget as much as possible if the federal government decides to start pulling back significant amounts of our funding. We should only fund essential government responsibilities and shrink government as much as possible if these funding cuts happen in a substantial way.

title: Tom Lin, author of  “Babylon, South Dakota,”  is coming to Spearfish
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Henry’s Books to host critically acclaimed author for Q&A session May 28.
_full_text:
Tom Lin, author of  “Babylon, South Dakota,”  is coming to Spearfish
Henry’s Books to host critically acclaimed author for Q&A session May 28.  

SPEARFISH — What do we owe to each other? It’s just one of the ideas explored in Tom Lin’s newest novel, Babylon, South Dakota, which has been lauded as an ambitious epic about how choices reverberate across generations. On Thursday, Lin plans to be in Spearfish, at Henry’s Books, for a special event. 

“An Evening With Tom Lin,” hopes to offer local readers a unique opportunity for an intimate conversation with the highly-acclaimed author.

Lin, an assistant professor of English and Creative Writing at the University of Iowa, published his first novel in 2021 and was immediately recognized as a powerful new voice in the world of fiction. His debut, “The Thousand Crimes of Ming Tsu,” won the 2022 Carnegie Medal for Excellence and introduced Lin’s genre-defying style: a unique blend of historical Western fiction and magical realism featuring Chinese American protagonists. His newest work, “Babylon, South Dakota” follows in the same vein.

How do authors seamlessly blend historical fiction and magic? In Lin’s case, his “real magic” is intended “to trouble and defamiliarize — to slow down the experience of the present, and by doing so make room for anything, even magic, to arise.” 

“I think that this sense of a wild and uncertain future, full of total possibility, lies right at the heart of our Western imagination,” Lin said. 

Lin was born in China and immigrated to the United States when he was four. He is a graduate of Pamona College in southern California and also holds a doctorate in English from the University of California, Davis. His scholarly research investigates the role of science fiction and popular culture in the shaping of large technical systems.

This theme is very much alive in “Babylon, South Dakota,” a tantalizing saga about a Chinese American family trying to survive on their Dakota farm as a mysterious and morally dubious military secret shapes their lives. His protagonists, the Hsuis, move from China to the United States to take possession of a 160-acre homestead bequeathed to them by a distant relative. All they have are the possessions on their back, some hidden gold, and a pocketful of chrysanthemum seeds.  When representatives from the US Army Corps of Engineers buy an acre of the Hsiu’s farmland and begin building a missile silo, the inexplicable starts to occur and, in the years and generations that follow, increasingly impacted by the silo and its residue, the Hsius experience strange, wondrous, and tragic events on their farm.

title: SD revisits family benefit cuts  and hospital payment changes  after public backlash
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: SIOUX FALLS — The South Dakota Department of Social Services is taking a second look at 2 administrative rule changes the department originally proposed last year.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

SIOUX FALLS — The South Dakota Department of Social Services is taking a second look at 2 administrative rule changes the department originally proposed last year.

More than 100 South Dakotans spoke against proposed changes last year to reduce benefits for the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program and adjust payment methodologies for hospitals.

The new proposals back away from the most controversial elements of the original changes. Department officials held public hearings for both in Sioux Falls May 15.

Public comment remains open on the proposed changes until Monday, with comments accepted at Rules.SD.Gov. The legislative Rules Review Committee is scheduled to consider the changes at its June 9 meeting.

TANF change is partial restoration of earlier benefit reduction

TANF is a federal-state program used in South Dakota to provide assistance to families with children who need financial support because of the death of a parent, an absent parent, or the unemployment or physical or mental incapacity of a parent. Caregiver participants are required to work, search or train for a job.

Last year, the Legislature’s budget committee cut state TANF funding by 30%, authorizing the department to backfill the gap with leftover federal funds. Instead of fully replacing the state cut with those carryover funds, the department reduced benefits by 10% — saving the state about $1.5 million, department Secretary Matt Althoff said at the time. The cut reduced the average household benefit by $51 per month.

That decision set off a monthslong dispute between the department and Rep. Erik Muckey, D-Sioux Falls, a budget committee member, over whether the committee understood the department’s plan when it approved the cuts.

The South Dakota Legislature partially restored the cuts earlier this year. 

The Legislature’s approval pairs a $427,000 increase in state funding with another $427,000 in authority to spend carryover federal funds — together restoring half of last year’s cut through a 5% benefit increase.

The proposed rule changes adopt the 5% increase as well as a 1.4% inflationary increase for beneficiaries. That raises the average monthly TANF payment from $478.53 to $509.49 — or an increase of $30.96, according to a fiscal note.

The program distributed $15.3 million in benefits in fiscal year 2024, when the average monthly benefit per household was $518.06. Nearly 5,000 people in the state, most of them children, benefit from the program.

Three people spoke during public comment, including Cathy Brechtelsbauer, who organized a protest last year against the department’s cuts. She presented a “shoestring budget” for a parent with 2 children, totaling $1,420 per month. The estimate included rent at $650, utilities, phone and internet, transportation, clothing, and food not covered by other assistance programs.

The average TANF benefit still falls short of those needs, Brechtelsbauer said, adding that her estimates show why the state should “step up the payments.”

Medicaid changes attract support after previous concerns

Last year, the department proposed revising how it reimburses hospitals through Medicaid — the joint federal-state program that provides health coverage to low-income residents and people with disabilities.

Officials from LifeScape, the state’s primary caretaker for people with complex disabilities, and families who use its services testified last year about the risk the changes posed to the organization. Althoff pulled the proposals after the backlash.

On May 15, Althoff said hospitals “weren’t ready” for the original proposal. He called the new changes “a win for South Dakota taxpayers” because they modernize Medicaid reimbursement and help contain costs.

The changes heard should not negatively impact providers in the state, South Dakota Medicaid Director Heather Petermann added. They align hospital reimbursement methodologies more closely with industry standards and ensure more equitable reimbursement among providers, she said.

Petermann said the department “better explained” proposed rule changes to providers and adjusted proposed methodology for critical access hospitals. Critical access hospitals are small, rural hospitals that offer 24/7 emergency services.

“The intent is to make this better for hospitals,” Petermann said. “It had to be their buy-in and to make sure everyone was on the same page.”

The department received letters of support from LifeScape, Avera Health, Sanford Health, Monument Health and the South Dakota Association of Healthcare Organizations, Petermann said.

SDAHO President and CEO Tim Rave said the new methodology shifts money from out-of-state hospitals back into South Dakota facilities.

“While this does not bring our hospitals to a rate that covers what it costs to care for Medicaid patients in South Dakota, it does provide a much-needed boost to the rates as they are today, for which we are grateful,” Rave wrote in a letter to the department.

Critical access hospitals have not had a full review since the designation was established in 1997. Hospitals reimbursed below 100% of their allowable costs will be brought to 100% under the new rules. Hospitals already paid above that threshold will see no change. The changes carry an $8.6 million price tag, included in the state’s fiscal year 2027 budget.

“We want to thank the department for working with our members to come up with a solution that will keep hospital services open in rural South Dakota and not risk losing those services or hospital closures,” Rave added.

title: SD public university tuition rising  at least 2.4%, with some steeper hikes
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: South Dakota Board of Regents approved a tuition increase at state universities. Pioneer photo by Mark Watson
_full_text:
SD public university tuition rising  at least 2.4%, with some steeper hikes
South Dakota Board of Regents approved a tuition increase at state universities. Pioneer photo by Mark Watson 

PIERRE — The board overseeing South Dakota’s public university system increased in-person tuition by 2.4% systemwide at its Wednesday meeting in Custer, while approving a higher increase of 5% for South Dakota Mines.

Heather Forney, South Dakota Board of Regents vice president of finance and administration, told board members the increase is tied to staff and faculty salary increases. The Legislature approved a 1.4% raise for state employees during its 2026 session.

Forney said the tuition increase is also driven by “significant” increases in technology costs across the system, which rise annually around 4% to 7%.

Griffin Petersen, the student representative to the South Dakota Board of Regents, called the increases “pretty modest.”

“It ensures we continue to deliver a level of quality that prepares our students for the workforce and for their lives beyond school,” Petersen said.

Tuition at South Dakota Mines will rise 5% due to more experiential and “cost intensive” learning, Forney said. The Rapid City university specializes in science, technology, engineering and mathematics.

This is the second straight year the system has increased tuition, after three years of legislatively aided tuition freezes. The average annual tuition and mandatory fee cost for an in-state undergraduate student will increase from $9,651.50 to $9,914.90, an increase of $263.40.

In a regional survey of surrounding states during the 2025-26 school year presented to the board in April, South Dakota ranked fourth highest among seven states for undergraduate resident tuition and fees and third highest for graduate resident tuition and fees. For nonresidents, South Dakota ranked second lowest for both undergraduate and graduate tuition and fees.

Tuition will also beyond 2.4% for several programs: an 8% increase in Ph.D. programs at Dakota State University and 5% increases at the University of South Dakota’s law and medical schools. Forney said the medical school increase is tied to “significant costs we’ll be dealing with” as the school moves from Vermillion to Sioux Falls.

The board also approved a 2.2% increase in the mandatory general activity fee students pay systemwide, with exceptions at South Dakota State University and Black Hills State University where the fees will hold steady.

At South Dakota State University, a wellness center bond will be paid off, and the $1.83 per credit hour general activity fee previously covering that debt will be redirected toward career development, student organization funding and student union maintenance. Black Hills State University is in a similar position — a bond expiring there will free up $6.57 per credit hour, which the university will redirect to comparable student services. 

Dual credit tuition for South Dakota high school students taking college courses will increase 2.4%, raising the student cost per credit hour to $80.37. The state Department of Education covers the other half.

title: Belle Fourche woman launches statewide book drive for children in foster care
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Elizabeth Heggem, pictured, is organizing a statewide book drive for kids in foster care. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Belle Fourche woman launches statewide book drive for children in foster care
Elizabeth Heggem, pictured, is organizing a statewide book drive for kids in foster care. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — Elizabeth Heggem began selling books at fairs and community events around the Northern Hills as a PaperPie brand partner because she believes in the power of building literacy. She also recognizes that time spent with a book can be soothing.

“I have a 5-year-old and a 2-year-old. I just feel like the world is so busy anymore, it is just nice to sit down with my kids and a book,” Heggem said. “It takes us away from the busyness, the hustle and bustle of everything.”

For children in foster care, in particular, life can be especially tumultuous. Quiet time might be precious, and personal belongings aren’t always guaranteed.

That’s why Heggem launched a statewide book drive, in hopes of getting 4-6 age-appropriate children’s books into the hands of foster youth.

There are about 1,600 children in foster care in South Dakota, and fewer than 900 foster homes. As a result, children moving into foster care often have to travel long distances. In many cases, they can’t take much with them. 

“These children are traveling,” Heggem said. “It’s something to have that is theirs to keep.” Books, Heggem said, can offer hope, comfort, and even distraction as a child is heading into a new situation.

She set up an online fundraiser in partnership with PaperPie books and South Dakota Kids Belong to support kids through that transition process.

For every $35 donated, PaperPie is providing a matching grant to ensure one child receives $50 worth of books in a drawstring bag. Those books can move with them to their foster care placements, and they can keep them for as long as they like.

“$35 can help a kid get some books and feel like they belong. Their community is around them,” Heggem said. “They belong. They matter. Whether someone sponsors one child, shares the campaign online, or simply learns more about foster care, every action matters.”

Her goal is to raise enough money to purchase 540 book packs for kids across South Dakota.

“You don’t have to change the whole world to change a child’s world,” Heggem said. “I feel like a lot of people want to help, but they just don’t know how to help. Even though you may not be in the position to foster children, you can donate, and if you can’t donate, you can volunteer.”

To learn more about the South Dakota Kids belong book drive campaign, launched by Heggem, visit my.cheddarup.com/c/sdkb-book-drive.

title: The Mercy Sloane Chronicles: Chapter 4
byline: Eliza Blue
description: A work of serialized fiction, special to the Pioneer
_full_text:
The Mercy Sloane Chronicles

A work of serialized fiction, special to the Pioneer

“Decisions have a way of making themselves,” Mercy’s mother told her once when she was young. They’d been folding washing from the line in the gloaming of a late spring dusk, the light as soft and gentle as the warm evening air. “Money has a way of doing that too,” her mother added, almost as an afterthought. 

Mercy was immediately puzzled. If money made itself, how come they were always working so hard to earn it? Mercy’s father had died in a never-discussed accident when she was small—too small to remember him or to mourn his absence. Her mother, Mary, had taken in washing, cleaned houses, and sublet rooms in their home to make ends meet. Mercy knew how to scrub a floor before she was out of diapers, and though it wasn’t a bad life, it certainly wasn’t carefree, nor did it seem money was making itself. In fact, work to make money was all they seemed to do, except on Sundays, when Mary would wash both of their hair, then brush and wrap it in rags to set their curls for the week. After that, they’d dance in the kitchen to the music on their tiny, staticky radio, the stars sparkling through the open back door in the summer and through the little windows in winter. 

Eventually, Mary married one of their long-term tenants, an Italian man with a deeply lined face and bright, blue eyes named Augustine, who was so shy about his accent that Mercy wasn’t fully sure what his voice sounded like until well after she’d started calling him ‘Papa.’ For months he left Mercy and her mother tiny gifts on the breakfast table they set for their renters—a bird carved from a willow’s branch that sat in their palms as though in a nest, daisies collected from a rutted field a few blocks from their house, and finally, amazingly, a battered, but glowing golden ring he’d carried when he came across the ocean from Italy that fit her mother’s finger perfectly. 

Augustine was just as hardworking as Mercy and her mother, so after the marriage, things got a lot easier for Mercy. Mary and Augustine worked as much as ever, but Mary insisted that Mercy have the childhood she’d missed during the thin years. Mary especially wanted Mercy to have an education, and after many months of saving, sent her to a private Catholic high school in the nicest part of Iowa City for her senior year. There was enough money left after tuition was paid to purchase her first store-bought dresses, and Augustine surprised Mercy with a string of glass beads that somehow matched them all. With her new dresses, her rainbow necklace, a naturally dry sense of humor, and her talent for dancing, Mercy was surprised to find she had no shortage of friends and admirers, but one in particular stood out.

 Eliza Blue TMC
Eliza Blue 

Granger Sloan was rich and handsome, and they’d become a couple almost instantly, though they couldn’t have been more different. She appreciated the finer things in life, mostly because she’d lived so long without them. Granger wasn’t like that. He’d grown up wealthy and entitled, with a curmudgeonly demeanor to boot. Mercy scoffed and laughed as he bellyached, dragging him onto every dance floor they encountered. “You silly, spoiled boy,” she’d say, taking his hand. “How can you ever complain when you get to dance with me?” 

They had a long engagement. They’d both gone to college because Granger’s parents had insisted and even paid for Mercy to go, too, perhaps because they recognized his streak of laziness and her industrious nature, and knew he was unlikely to finish without her spurring him on. 

Mercy loved every minute of those four years—the parties and dances, but also books full of adventure and philosophy and discussions that lasted hours and more books and more dancing. Her life was suddenly a delicious, lavish banquet, when before there’d been mostly porridge, so she easily accepted all the things about Granger she didn’t like as part of the menu.

title: Dr. Trenton Ellis named RPI Research Fellow
description: Dr. Trenton Ellis
_full_text:
Dr. Trenton Ellis named RPI Research Fellow
Dr. Trenton Ellis 

SPEARFISH — Dr. Trenton Ellis, a sociologist and associate professor of human services at Black Hills State University, was named 2026 research fellow for the Rural Philanthropy Institute (RPI). RPI seeks to broaden the knowledge of philanthropy in rural America to create a stronger, more sustainable, and healthy nonprofit community by funding and supporting research fellows like Ellis.  

The role of research fellows is to study the aspects of rural nonprofits and philanthropy through diverse lenses and develop a robust research project that contributes valuable information that further nurtures RPI’s understanding of rural, nonprofit communities. 

Starting this spring, Ellis will lead a capacity-building effort and case study of the Spearfish Trails Coalition (STC) with his fellowship project: “Pedal-Powered Philanthropy: Data-Driven Capacity Building for Rural Trails Nonprofits.” 

“Nonprofit decisionmaking is part art and part science, partly because reliable, localized data can be difficult to access—especially for rural organizations. Newer rural nonprofits like the Spearfish Trails Coalition often lack the capacity, tools, or staff time to collect and analyze social data, even though they know that information may strengthen their planning, fundraising, and community engagement,” said Ellis. “This RPI Research Fellowship project will jumpstart STC’s socialdata infrastructure and expand the resources they have for understanding the community they serve. Any gains STC makes in this area ultimately translate into greater benefits for Spearfish as a whole.”

The STC is a trails nonprofit driven by its mission to create enriching trail experiences in the rural area of Spearfish through sustainable and thoughtful design.  

Combining his love for cycling and community-focused social research, Ellis’ project will include collecting information from a stakeholder survey, engaging BHSU students in research, and capacity-building in rural nonprofits in an effort to provide valuable insight to RPI that can be utilized by others who are working in rural nonprofits today. 

“There are also important advantages for BHSU,” Ellis added. “The fellowship brings external support for faculty research and creates new opportunities for students to engage in clientfacing survey design, data analysis, and community engagement—skills they can carry straight into their careers. And looking longterm, stronger trails mean stronger connections between BHSU, our Spearfish neighbors, and the surrounding land of our namesake—the Black Hills (Ȟe SápA in Lakota). I’m grateful that RPI saw the value in this project, and I›m excited to contribute to the work of STC and to the field of rural philanthropy.”

With the contributions of research projects like Ellis’, RPI can work towards achieving its mission of bringing together practitioners, academics, and interested people to develop data, share stories and experiences, and gain insights that offer a greater understanding of what’s required to have a healthy nonprofit community in rural areas.

BHSU media students earn recognition  across multiple competitions
The editorial team of the BHSU student-run magazine Ponder recently earned Silver ADDY Awards for Issues 3 and 4 at the American Advertising Federation’s District 8 ADDY Awards. (From left, back row) Noah Westergaard, Duncan Martin, Carly Smith, Tory Brown, Nathan Feller, Taylor SanFilippo, Sean Kilpatrick, Hayden Hill, Allie Schefers and Cole Marquez; (from left, front row) Maralee Rischling, Julia Wilson, Rae Hanzlik, Brooke Lammle, Zoe Stucke, Hunter Davis, Reyna Shirley-Brown, Caleb Minor, Brooklyn Berg and Alec Butterfield. SPEARFISH — Black Hills State University media students recently earned more than 20 awards across several competitions including the Northern Plains Collegiate Media Association’s Golden Leaf Awards, the American Advertising Federation (AAF) District 8 ADDY Awards, and the Region 6 Mark of Excellence Awards hosted by the Society of Professional Journalists. 

Golden Leaf Awards

BHSU student media received 12 awards at the Golden Leaf Awards, a contest that recognizes outstanding media work across the Midwest. This year, several students were able to take home awards across a variety of categories with 11 being awarded to Ponder Magazine and one to The Jacket Journal.  

“I think that winning Golden Leaf Awards is an outstanding representation of the strength of our student journalists,” said Allen Morris, assistant professor of multimedia journalism at BHSU. “It’s an indication that our students are capable reporters and story tellers that are dedicated to strong journalism.” 

Six students took first place with their entries. Nathan Feller won “Best Sports Feature,” Alec Butterfield won “Best Breaking News Story,” and Maralee Rischling won “Best Feature Story.” “Best Arts and Entertainment Story” was won by Hayden Hill, and Noah Westergaard won “Best Feature Photo.” Westergaard and Tory Brown won “Best Social Media Presence.” 

“The region is taking notice of the quality of these publications, even outside of academia, and other universities are starting to emulate the look and feel of our publications. That’s a huge deal for a small, but mighty university like BHSU,” said Morris.

Maralee Rischling: Best Feature Story

Hayden Hill: Best Arts and Entertainment Story

Noah Westergaard: Best Feature Photo

Noah Westergaard & Tory Brown: Best Social Media Presence  

Second Place Awards:

Hayden Hill: Best Arts and Entertainment Story

AAF District 8 ADDY Awards

title: BHSU names Nelsen as associate vice president of facilities services
description: SPEARFISH — Black Hills State University has announced the hiring of Kyle Nelsen as associate vice president of facilities services, bringing with him extensive experience in facilities operations, capital project management, and team leadership.
_full_text:
BHSU logo

SPEARFISH — Black Hills State University has announced the hiring of Kyle Nelsen as associate vice president of facilities services, bringing with him extensive experience in facilities operations, capital project management, and team leadership.

Nelsen joins BHSU from Wayne State College in Wayne, Neb., where he served as director of facility services since 2018. In that role, he oversaw more than 1.2 million square feet of campus facilities across 128 acres, managed a $4.2 million operating budget, and led a team of 60 employees. Nelsen has directed more than $120 million in capital improvement projects, including academic, residential, athletic, and infrastructure initiatives.

“Kyle brings a strong track record of leadership, collaboration, and strategic facilities planning that will support BHSU’s continued growth and student success,” said Kathy Johnson, vice president for finance and administration. “His experience and student-centered approach make him a great fit for our campus community.”

Nelsen’s professional background includes expertise in facilities management, preventative maintenance programs, and the implementation of systems to improve operational efficiency and extend the life of campus assets.

He succeeds Randy Culver, who retired from BHSU after 34 years of service to the university.

“It’s an honor to join Black Hills State University and serve in a role that supports the university’s mission and daily campus experience. I’m excited to work with the talented facility services team, build strong partnerships across campus, and contribute to the continued growth and success of BHSU,” said Nelsen.

Nelsen holds a bachelor’s degree from Wayne State College. 

He began his role at BHSU Monday

title: Excavation challenges bring  up cost of fire training center
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — The construction of Spearfish’s new fire training center is going to cost at least $16,458 more than originally planned.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — The construction of Spearfish’s new fire training center is going to cost at least $16,458 more than originally planned. 

On Monday, the city council unanimously approved a change order to cover the cost of additional excavation work that was required to pour a solid foundation for the tower facility. 

Zandra Construction was hired for $96,126 in October to grade the former McLaughlin Sawmill site, where the tower will be built. The council approved a change order for that project on Nov. 3, 2025 for $1,470.

The steel fire-training tower was purchased by the city from Fire Facilities Inc., for $413,182. The tower itself, which Spearfish Fire Chief Scott Deaver said is assembled a little bit like a massive erector set. The city hired American Contracting and Consulting LLC., to complete that assembly and erection for $427,600 in March. They will also install a 6-inch reinforced concrete apron around the new building.

Before the tower could be installed, American Contracting and Consulting had to complete site work and pour a foundation. When they started excavation, they found “large quantities” of sawdust and spongy soil as well as trash, metal, and debris on site. More than 131.20 cubic yards of soil and other “poor materials” had to be removed. Then, new soil had to be trucked in “compacted, engineered, and filled” to create a suitable base for the tower’s foundation. 

Once the training center is fully constructed, it should be a 30-foot, 3-story tower with 4 working deck levels. It features 2 burn rooms: 1 on the first floor and 1 on the second floor. The tower, on completion, should have removable partitions that can be used for active shooter and SWAT training by the police department. An outside course for fire trucks can also be used to train would-be snowplow and garbage truck drivers and to hold city “truck rodeos.”

All expenditures for the project will come out of the Spearfish Fire Department’s capital budget.

title: Spearfish applies for grant funds to  expand pedestrian infrastructure on North Avenue
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: This map shows where the city may install a sidewalk on North Avenue, if grant funding is awarded. Map courtesy city of Spearfish
_full_text:
Spearfish applies for grant funds to  expand pedestrian infrastructure on North Avenue
This map shows where the city may install a sidewalk on North Avenue, if grant funding is awarded. Map courtesy city of Spearfish 

SPEARFISH — After receiving authorization from the city council, Spearfish plans to apply for federal grant funding to improve the pedestrian crossing at Hillsview Road and install a sidewalk on North Avenue from Safeway to the edge of the Klym Coffee Hut parking lot.  

The project was recommended in the city’s safety action plan, which was adopted Feb. 17. The plan, which was funded in large part with federal Safe Streets for All grant funding, recommended projects to reduce or illuminate serious and deadly crashes within the city limits. The proposed projects, by virtue of their identification in the safety action plan, are also eligible for implementation funding through that same Safe Streets for All program.

To assemble the plan, consultants reviewed five years of crash data. They identified hot spots, which the plan refers to as a “high injury network.” North Avenue was part of that high-injury network, and consultants noticed a need for safer infrastructure for non-motorized transportation. They recommended improving sidewalk connectivity along North Avenue, and after gathering public input, city staff found that the project was popular enough to pursue.

“It’ll be a 6-foot sidewalk and other things that come along with it. There is a lot of storm drainage ditches there. There will be some grading and some stormwater infrastructure to be installed. We’ll also be installing curb and gutter along that whole length. Right now, there is no curb and gutter,” Larson said.

If awarded, a federal grant could cover 80% of the new sidewalk installation’s cost, with the city contributing the remaining 20%. The 20% can include “in-kind” funds —city staff could work on the project, and wages would count toward Spearfish’s total contribution.

The safety action plan estimates the price of extending the sidewalk from Safeway to the Klym Coffee Hut at $248,431. That number, Spearfish staff engineer Abbey Larson said, represents a massive underestimate.

“That basically is putting concrete on the ground to make a sidewalk. It did not account for grading, all the stormwater changes, and those signal improvements. Also, staff wanted to extend that sidewalk a bit further than what they were proposing.  We are working on coming up with a more accurate cost estimate, and I will include that with the grant application,” Larson said. “I would not be surprised if this was more like $1 million or $1.5 million.”

If the city does not receive grant funds for the project, Larson said the city has the option to budget for sidewalk connectivity on North Avenue in the future.

“I like this project. I think it is long overdue,” City Councilman Dean Myers said.

title: Sturgis residents shouldn’t notice change in garbage collection under Kieffer Sanitation
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: A city contract with Kieffer Sanitation includes an option for residents to pay for a curbside recycling service that will replace some recycling at the Exit 32 bins. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
Sturgis garbage 2.jpeg
A city contract with Kieffer Sanitation includes an option for residents to pay for a curbside recycling service that will replace some recycling at the Exit 32 bins. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

STURGIS — Sturgis residents and businesses should not notice a change when Kieffer Sanitation takes over garbage collection, June 1. 

After decades of providing municipal waste services in-house, the Sturgis City Council voted in March to negotiate a contract with Kieffer Sanitation. Public Works Director Rick Bush told the city that increased equipment and vehicle replacement costs, as well as employee retention, training, and wages, put a major strain on the city budget that could be alleviated with the third-party contract. 

The city of Sturgis has more than 3,000 customer service accounts for garbage collection, including 2,780 residential accounts and 352 commercial accounts.

Bush told the Sturgis City Council that the transition from handling garbage collection in-house, to contracting with an outside company, should be seamless. Rates will not increase in 2026, and any rate increases in subsequent years will be justified with raised gas prices, tipping fees, or other operational costs. A key component of the city’s agreement with Kieffer Sanitation, is that the city will remain the residents’ point of contact for the service. That means Sturgis residents will contact the city directly with any concerns or requests, and all billing will come from the city. The city will work directly with Kieffer Sanitation as a contractor for garbage collection, hauling, disposal, and recycling services. 

“A central feature of the proposed agreement is that the city is not transferring control of its municipal solid waste program,” Bush said. “The city retains municipal authority, policy control, customer billing, account administration, customer rates, delinquent account administration, route approval, service standards, and program rules.” 

The agreement states that Kieffer will take over municipal waste collection on June 1, with a 6-month transitional period focused on maintaining continuity for routes and procedures. 

“The agreement and transition structures are designed so customers should notice no difference in service,” Bush said. 

During the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, Bush said city crews will work with Kieffer for 3 years, before the outside company takes over garbage duties. The city will also provide 250 of its existing Rally-related garbage containers for use, and residents or businesses that require extra pickups should contact the city. 

“We’ve got 80-some years under our belt, so it’s pretty etched in to all of our employees,” Bush said of Rally garbage service. “Rally service is different from ordinary residential or commercial collection because of the volume, timing, location, and operational demands associated with the event. For that reason, the agreement treats Rally service separately.” 

Part of the contract for services includes providing a subscription for curbside recycling. Bush said instead of taking their recyclables to the bins at Interstate 90, Exit 32, residents will have the option to pay an extra fee for a recycling bin that will be placed on the curb for pickup. Residents will still have the ability to take their yard waste and cardboard to the Exit 32 bins.  

Bush said the curbside recycling program is an attempt at establishing tighter controls on resident recycling. Non-residents frequently use the free recycling bins that are only intended for Sturgis taxpayers, and that is resulting in increased operational costs. 

“The intent of what we’re putting together is for the residents of Sturgis,” he said. “We just can’t handle it for everybody. I wish we could. It’s just not sustainable when people do that. It’s not different than I wouldn’t take my garbage to Spearfish and dump it out. We’ve got to somehow try and address those things. I think we’re moving in the right direction. Exit 32 was a great idea and ait served us well. It worked. It’s quick. It’s where we need it to be. But that’s also the downside of it. It’s right off the Interstate. It’s quick and easy for anybody to go to and there are no controls over it.” 

In the long term, City Administrator Aaron Jordan said the Exit 32 recycling bins may be moved to the city rubble site, where there will be more oversight and controls to prevent nonresident dumping.

title: Sturgis proclaims ‘Poppy Day’ to honor fallen service members
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: Tony Dargatz, Sturgis Mayor Pro Tempore, signs a proclamation declaring May 22rd ‘Poppy Day’ with Ruth Mechling, a member of the Sturgis American Legion Auxiliary, also known as the Poppy Lady, along with other Auxiliary officers, on Monday at the Veterans Club in Sturgis.  Back from left:  Jean Eykamp, Joanne Jaeger, Carol Edwards, Kris Little, Bose Byars, and Jessica Kusser.  Front from left:  Ruth Mechling and Tony Dargatz.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
Sturgis proclaims ‘Poppy Day’ to honor fallen service members
Tony Dargatz, Sturgis Mayor Pro Tempore, signs a proclamation declaring May 22rd ‘Poppy Day’ with Ruth Mechling, a member of the Sturgis American Legion Auxiliary, also known as the Poppy Lady, along with other Auxiliary officers, on Monday at the Veterans Club in Sturgis.  Back from left:  Jean Eykamp, Joanne Jaeger, Carol Edwards, Kris Little, Bose Byars, and Jessica Kusser.  Front from left:  Ruth Mechling and Tony Dargatz.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

STURGIS — Sturgis Mayor Pro Tempore Tony Dargatz signed an official proclamation Monday declared Friday as “Poppy Day” during a gathering of the Sturgis American Legion Auxiliary at the Veterans Club.

The proclamation recognizes the red poppy as a symbol of the sacrifices made by military personnel in service to the United States. Each year, the American Legion Auxiliary distributes the memorial flower to honor those who served and to remind Americans of the cost of freedom.

Ruth Mechling, a member of the Sturgis American Legion Auxiliary known locally as the “Poppy Lady,” will distribute poppies through Saturday at Rockingtree, Runnings and Lynn’s Dakotamart.

“I started working at Fort Meade in the early ’50s, and I’ve been involved in some way with Poppy Day ever since,” said Mechling. “The poppy was first recognized in 1922 in honor of the blood that was shed. It’s important to recognize our fallen heroes and all veterans.”

Carol Edwards, President of Sturgis American Legion Auxiliary Unit 33, said the annual tradition serves as a reminder of the meaning behind Memorial Day.

“We honor the fallen with the poppy flower by distributing poppies every year,” Edwards said. “Many people confuse Memorial Day as a day to honor veterans. It is actually an opportunity for us to honor the fallen. Veterans Day is when we honor those who have served, and Armed Forces Day honors those currently serving.”

Dargatz said the proclamation is an important reminder for the Sturgis community to remember the sacrifices made by military members and their families.

“I think this is very important to the residents and the people of Sturgis,” Dargatz said. “Thank you to the Sturgis American Legion Auxiliary for doing this. It is a very good reminder of the past, present and future, and what we need to do for our Veterans.”

So while many people casually call them “poppy sales,” the deeper purpose is really a public act of remembrance tied to service and sacrifice, not simply fundraising.
