title: District 29 House candidates
description: Voters in District 29 will head to the polls June 2 to vote on a vacant House seat. Four people are running for 2 open positions which are a 2-year terms. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.
_full_text:
District29HouseComp.jpg

Voters in District 29 will head to the polls June 2 to vote on a vacant House seat. Four people are running for 2 open positions which are a 2-year terms. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.

Gary Cammack

 Cammack, Gary.jpg
Gary Cammack 

Name and what you do for a living?

My name is Gary Cammack.  I am a retired businessman, owned and operated Cammack Ranch Supply.  My family has a cattle ranch in central Meade County.

What motivated you to run for this office?

I have always supported policies and innovation that not only makes SD a better place to live, but also provides opportunities for this and the next generation.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

Common sense and experience.  I have been married to my wife Amy for 53 years, we have 4 grown boys that are all successful businessmen, and 10 grandchildren.  I owned and operated Stoneville Ranch Store, which later became Cammack Ranch Supply, for 50 years. I’ve spend a lifetime ranching.  I was a Meade County Commissioner for 2 years, spent 4 years in the House of Representatives and 2 of those years was Majority Whip, and spend 8 years in the Senate where I spent 2 years as President Pro Tempore and 2 years as Majority Leader.  

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

Meade County Commissioner, SD Senate, SD House of Representatives, President Midwest Council of State Governments, President of SD Retailers, Game Fish and Parks Advisory Panel, Dakota Resources, SD Trade, and Dakotas America.

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

Meade County Commission candidate forums

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Yes! Local newspapers are the only reliable coverage of local issues, day in and day out, no matter how large or small the issues are.

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in Meade County?

Schools:

1) Funding 

2) Maintaining optimum class size, not too big or too small 

3) Meeting demands of brick and mortar

Roads – maintaining and upgrading

Revenue – taxes

How do you intend to solve these issues?

Schools: These problems have been going on since statehood.  There may be some relief by sharing administrative duties and other services by adjacent school districts.  

Roads: Maximizing federal dollars in road projects

Revenue (Taxes): When it comes to lessening the individual tax burden there are three options:

Cut services

Shift the burden

Broaden the base

I have always been in favor of broadening the base by growing the economy in smart ways.

What do you believe is working for the county (Meade), and how will you retain that progression?

We have dedicated county public servants that have kept the county moving forward.  The continued economic activity has been helpful, but there is always room for improvement.

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

When I served in the past, I would have weekly radio broadcasts that would highlight the activity in the legislature for that week.  I have always attended cracker barrels to update the public. 

What else do you want people to know about you?

It is important that I help set the framework to provide opportunity and quality of life for our kids, grandkids, and the generations that follow.

Do you support zoning in Meade County? Why or why not?

I don’t believe countywide zoning is appropriate for Meade County because of its extremely diverse terrain of mountains and plains and its population both urban and rural. 

I do believe spot zoning has some potential, but will take a lot of study before it could be implemented. 

Meade County has over 1,100 miles of roads and has struggled with funding road maintenance.  What ideas do you have for leveraging tax dollars for road maintenance and what roads should be top priority?

The county should continue to pursue trading isolated state highway sections of Sturgis Road and other considerations for establishing New Underwood Road as a state highway.  This has been under consideration for years.  The success of this project would require a federal grand that has been applied for. 

In 2025 the Legislature passed a bill that allows counties to charge sales tax.  Do you support instituting a sales tax in Meade County? Why or why not?

I can’t give a definite answer without understanding the cost benefit as it relates to cost to residents compared to benefit in reduction in owner occupied residence property tax. 

Gary Deering

Name and what you do for a living? 

Gary Deering, along with my parents, my wife and I operate a family ranch that has been in my family since 1911. 

What motivated you to run for this office?

 I have been interested, and encouraged by others, to run for the legislature for quite a while now, I enjoy digging into policy, and love doing my part to help our communities. 

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

My roots run deep in Meade County, with of my great-grandparents homesteading throughout the county.  Meade County is the seventh largest county in the nation in number of cattle and calves; we are also home to a very rapid growing urban population.  Over the last twenty years I have worked diligently in the cattle and agricultural industries and the last three and a half on the county commission.  My experience of working in agriculture and on the county commission, provides me with the unique experience necessary to represent both urban and rural residents of Meade County, in the South Dakota House.

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

Chairman Meade County Commission

President South Dakota Stockgrowers

President South Dakota Beef Industry Council

Region 7 Vice President, and Executive Board of The Federation of State Beef Councils

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I attend countless local government meetings.  As important to my attendance, I have always made sure I make my position a priority, and I have very rarely missed a meeting, whether on the county commission or the agricultural boards I have served on.

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

I enjoy local newspapers, and I am a regular reader of The Black Hills Pioneer and Faith Independent.  There is not a better source to find information that goes on within our communities and region.  

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in your district?

Meade County is South Dakota’s second fastest growing county and among the largest counties by land mass within the country.  The rapid population expansion has brought up vulnerabilities within the county’s planning department, ordinances, and infrastructure, as well as put a strain on many homeowners when they pay their property taxes.  

How do you intend to solve these issues?

I have spent long hours working with Meade County’s Planning Director on common sense ordinances that work for Meade County.

Governments should live within their means and make every dollar that comes from the taxpayer’s count.  I have worked diligently to propose and pass fiscally conservative budgets.

        

What do you believe is working for the district, and how will you retain that progression?

This is such an exciting and important time for Meade County.  There are fewer places that have the natural beauty that Meade County and this region have.  With the growth and expansion this region is seeing, it is important to have effective leaders that understand planning, so we keep up with our infrastructure needs, and not harm the beauty of our natural resources that many visitors come to enjoy, as well as those of us that get the opportunity to view them year round.               

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

Transparency is the most important thing an elected official can offer their constituents.  There are many accomplishments and projects I am proud of, but the thing that I am the proudest of, is the fact that in everything I have done, I have remained, open, honest and transparent.  

What else do you want people to know about you?

I am a graduate of South Dakota State University with a degree in Range management and a minor in Economics.  My wife Jessica and I are proud of our three boys, Porter, Shea, and Dawson.  I feel honored to have been given the opportunity to work for the citizens of Meade County on the Conty Commission and I am extremely excited for this next chapter in my life.

The discussion of data centers coming to South Dakota has been on the rise. Do you support data centers coming to the state?

Local officials should decide whether a data center is a good fit for their community. Tax breaks should be limited or prohibited. Before approving a project, assess water and electricity use to determine whether local resources can handle the additional load now and in the future. Some areas can responsibly host more data centers and benefit from them; while many areas are not suitable. Local governments understand community needs and priorities best and should make many of these decisions rather than the state cramming it down their throats and selecting locations.

Data centers use significant amounts of water and electricity as part of their operations. What legislation should be put in place to protect residents from the inevitable need for more electrical generation and water use?

Water and electrical needs must be assessed and clearly understood for any project, whether a development, data center, or agricultural. Key questions to ask are: Is there enough supply now?  Will our current infrastructure meet future demand?  Will the project drive utility rates up for residents, negating any local benefit from the growth?

Tax Incremental Finance Districts (TIFs) are a widely used economic development tool. Do you support their use? Why or why not?

A well designed TIF can benefit a community, while poorly structured ones can, and have caused harm.  Each TIF should be evaluated individually vs. saying TIF’s are good or bad.  

I do think there are steps the legislature can take to help offset some of the negative effects that often occur with some TIF’s, such as allowing the government entity to enact, and limit, a clearer timeline.  Also allowing the flexibility, during the duration, of enabling local governments to recover inflationary growth.

Should the state provide greater oversight in mining gravel and sand, especially when it comes to dust? Why or why not?

Many of the situations and issues that we have with mining, especially in Meade County, is due to the lack of the ability for the local governments to have much, if any say in the creation, control, and rules mines must follow.  Dust is one place the state could help the local governments set up some parameters, and provide enforcement, to control dust, minimizing the harm to the citizens.

Would you support an increase in the BBB tax, often called the tourism tax, to help offset taxes paid by residents? Why or why not?

Any proposal to increase any tax needs to be carefully assessed.  There are often unintended consequences to increasing a tax. I am generally supportive to anything that will help our residents pay less in taxes, but all bills especially tax increases, need to be looked at on an individual basis. 

As the federal government pulls back from funding programs widely used in the state, how or should the legislature backfill the lost revenue?

Budgeting is something I have always taken great pride in, and have spent many hours working on Meade County’s budget, looking for ways to be more efficient, and fiscally conservative.  Government, just like a business needs to live within their means, so it will be important to prioritize what is important and find ways to fund them, which obviously means looking at things that are less important and making cuts if the money is not there. 

Terri Jorgenson

 Jorgenson, Terri.jpg
Terri Jorgenson 

Name and what you do for a living?

Terri Jorgenson.  I’m a retired Air Force Officer.  I’ve been married for 39 years and have two adult children and four grandchildren. I currently serve in the SD House of Representatives for District 29 on the Joint Appropriations Committee, House Appropriations Committee, and the House Military and Veteran Affairs Committee.   My website is terrijorgenson.com

What motivated you to run for this office?

My desire is to make a positive difference for all South Dakotans and to leave a better future for those who come after us.  This year has been personally challenging: cancer has hit my family and our community hard, taking my brother and former Sturgis Mayor Kevin Forrester far too soon. Whether I’m out in the community or putting up campaign signs, I hear similar stories of struggle and resilience from our neighbors.  These stories motivate me to establish a legacy focused on service, safeguarding our Constitutional rights, upholding West River values, preserving our Black Hills and supporting our people, who represent our most precious resource.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

I’m a proven legislator with a record of delivering results for South Dakota.  In my first session, I passed legislation to defend our infrastructure against drone attacks, protect the Second Amendment privacy of firearms owners, and establish critical safeguards for families against fertility fraud.  I also voted for major property tax relief.  My military leadership is an asset as the B-21 Raider makes its home at Ellsworth Air Force Base. As one of only nine veterans in the State Legislature, I ensure our policies for 60,000+ veterans are informed by actual service.  

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I have been deeply involved in Meade County Republican leadership for many years.  I currently serve as an elected Meade County Committee Woman and previously held the roles of Vice Chair of the Meade County Republicans and Vice President for the Meade County Republican Women.  Beyond my party leadership I have advocated for conservative values in Pierre as an unpaid lobbyist for a non-profit conservative women’s group and have served as a leader with an international women’s Bible study organization.

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I don’t track numbers, however, I have attended numerous in person and online county commission, school board and city meetings over the past two years. I find the information gained from these interactions to be very beneficial in my role as a State Representative.

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Local newspapers are the lifeblood of our community, keeping a steady pulse on the issues that matter most.  They provide a vital platform to celebrate local achievements – from the Sturgis Brown High School wrestling team’s third consecutive state title to the outstanding academic milestones of our students.  Beyond celebrations, local news provides the in-depth reporting we need on complex issues, such as the Black Hills (Piedmont) mining concerns and the critical work being done in our schools and local governments.

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in your district?

Important issues facing our district include homeowner property tax relief, land stewardship, and quality education.  My husband and I understand the strain of rising property taxes on a fixed income; my mission is to ensure no neighbor is taxed out of their home.  We must also protect our property values and the Black Hills through smart ming reforms.  I am committed to finding solutions for infrastructure challenges such as New Underwood Road, and maintaining our unwavering support for education, even as school enrollments evolve (due in part to declining birth rates).

How do you intend to solve these issues?

I’m going to keep pushing for mining laws that just make sense – the kind that protect the Black Hills we love while helping businesses thrive.  On the Appropriations Committee, my focus stays on balancing our state budget, fixing infrastructure such as roads, and lowering property taxes so that our neighbors aren’t taxed out of their homes.  We also need to keep a close eye on school budgets such as finding ways to lower insurance premiums and exploring efficiencies as enrollment numbers fluctuate.        

What do you believe is working for the district, and how will you retain that progression?

Community engagement is a positive driving force in our district.  I am inspired by the way neighbors have united through grassroots organizations such as Protect Piedmont’s Future to champion commonsense mining protections for the Black hills and to protect property rights. To sustain this momentum, I will continue to sponsor and support meaningful legislation that reflects our community’s shared goals to ensure safeguards for future generations.

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

Transparency means ensuring every constituent has a front-row seat to the decision-making process.  South Dakota Public Broadcasting provides an invaluable service by livestreaming and archiving all legislative committee hearings and floor sessions.  I encourage anyone wanting to understand the ‘nuts and bolts’ of state government to tune in or listen to the recordings.  To keep my district informed, I write a regular Substack at sdcapitoldiary.substack.com and maintain an active Facebook page.  I also prioritize face-to-face accountability by participating in legislative ‘Cracker Barrels’ hosted by the Sturgis Chamber of Commerce and community forums organized by the Meade County Republican Women. 

What else do you want people to know about you?

In 2025, I was honored to become the first woman legislator to receive the Attorney General’s ‘Top Gun’ Award.  Following that achievement, I remained a top three finalist in 2026.  Former District 29 legislator Dean Wink set a high bar by winning this prestigious award multiple times.  I am eager to return to the legislature to follow in his footsteps.  My goal is to once again secure the ‘Top Gun’ title and bring that winning distinction home to District 29.

The discussion of data centers coming to South Dakota has been on the rise. Do you support data centers coming to the state?

We already have several data centers in South Dakota – the largest one is in Sully County, and three large-scale projects are in the planning phase. I am concerned about our residents subsidizing them. That’s why I backed the Data Center Bill of Rights – a law that requires these companies to cover 100% of their energy costs and verify their water usage with local communities before they build.  I appreciate folks wanting the jobs and economic boost these projects bring, but we must have protections in place to protect our wallets and our state’s essential resources.

Data centers use significant amounts of water and electricity as part of their operations. What legislation should be put in place to protect residents from the inevitable need for more electrical generation and water use?

I voted for Senate Bill 135 (signed into law in 2026), also known as the Data Center Bill of Rights for Citizens, to establish necessary safeguards for South Dakotans.  This legislation ensures that large-scale date centers, those that have a peak demand of 10 megawatts or more, cover their own infrastructure and energy costs.  It also prevents them from straining our local water supplies and preserves the right of local communities to regulate these facilities.  By enacting these common-sense protections, we are proactive in avoiding the utility cost spikes and resource shortages that have plagued other states.

Tax Incremental Finance Districts (TIFs) are a widely used economic development tool. Do you support their use? Why or why not?

TIFs remain a powerful tool for job creation and economic growth, yet each one requires careful oversight to prevent a possible undue tax burden on residents.  The passage of Senate Bill 228 this session introduces essential guardrails such as mandatory independent fiscal reviews to ensure TIFS are used responsibly by cities and counties without stifling their ability to attract new businesses.

Should the state provide greater oversight in mining gravel and sand, especially when it comes to dust? Why or why not?

Absolutely! South Dakota’s current mining regulations often feel like the ‘Wild West’ leaving our natural resources and property owners vulnerable.  During this past session, I introduced two bills (HB 1287, HB 1288) aimed at implementing common-sense reforms and strengthening property rights.  While we didn’t secure the necessary votes this time, I remain committed to this fight.  I will stand in the gap to protect our property rights, our health and our beautiful Black Hills for today and beyond.

Would you support an increase in the BBB tax, often called the tourism tax, to help offset taxes paid by residents? Why or why not?

We must carefully re-evaluate our tourism tax.  The specific 1.5% state tourism tax is legally dedicated to promoting and marketing South Dakota as a travel destination.  While these funds have grown significantly over the last decade and successfully supported local businesses, I would consider shifting existing allocations rather than increasing the tax on residents and visitors.  This approach requires legislative changes but could provide the necessary relief for residents without further raising taxes.  However, my support depends on the legislative details and consideration of unintended consequences.

As the federal government pulls back from funding programs widely used in the state, how or should the legislature backfill the lost revenue?

It depends. We’ve seen significant government expansion fueled by COVID-19 relief funds.  As federal support has lapsed, we now face requests to replace that aid with state funding.  My stance is simple: if these initiatives weren’t essential before the pandemic, they shouldn’t be state funded now.  While some programs, like victim services, are critical, we cannot afford to sustain every federal cut.  It’s important to note that state Medicaid funding now exceeds state aid for education due to the voters approving an increase in eligibility through a Constitutional Amendment. Looking forward we must make cuts to live within our means and balance our budget.

Kathy Rice

 Rice, Kathy.jpg
Kathy Rice 

Name and what you do for a living?  

My name is Kathy Rice.

I have two small businesses. One is my husband’s dental practice; I’m the office manager and do all the hiring and firing, marketing, and liaison with all the employees. 

Second business is a vacation rental property. I make sure all handymen and cleaners are scheduled and guest are taken care of.

What motivated you to run for this office? 

“I ran because our district wasn’t being represented the way people vote. We need stronger conservative leadership—protecting our property rights, and lowering taxes. and I have more to do.

  

Why do you think you are best qualified for this positions?

I’m a mother of eight, a business owner, and a longtime advocate who’s fought for people on my own dime. I bring real experience—and I’ll go to work for you. I prove my steadfastness of being a strong conservative.

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held? 

“I’ve founded Citizens for Academic Transparency and a local twin club, and I’ve served in leadership roles with Eagle Forum and my church’s Relief Society.”

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy? 

I’ve attended all the meetings and committees meetings and never missed one. Plus, at least 30 other types of city council, Piedmont mine, and school board meetings

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not? 

I believe newspapers are vital for our communities to keep good information out there, so they are always informed about what’s happening in our country and local areas. 

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in your district? 

I still think property taxes, one of our biggest issues since it doubled in five years but also the Piedmont mine and how it’s going to affect their properties. We still need to help those people in Blackhawk area where their homes are over and abandoned mine.

How do you intend to solve these issues? 

We need to find new revenue source to fund our schools and take that part off our property taxes. we need to find some money for to pay back those people in Blackhawk. We need to get special zoning for Piedmont so we can protect their properties and their rights.

What do you believe is working for the district, and how will you retain that progression? 

I believe our representatives in district 29 as the freshman term ends are doing a great job. We are listening to the people and helping them with their issues. All the different scores card are coming back with great results. You need to vote us back to serve you.

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions? 

I’m transparency means not hiding anything always and open for any conversation about my vote.

What else do you want people to know about you? 

People should know I’m very determined. I don’t back down when something is right for the community. I’m committed to truth, justice, and serving the people, and I believe in the Constitution and the principles our country was founded on.”

The discussion of data centers coming to South Dakota has been on the rise. Do you support data centers coming to the state? 

I do support data centers coming into our state. We have a great weather for them. I don’t believe we should give any tax exemptions.

Data centers use significant amounts of water and electricity as part of their operations. What legislation should be put in place to protect residents from the inevitable need for more electrical generation and water use? 

I’ve been to many meetings about these data centers. I know they have a new water system. I believe they need to work on getting their own electricity.  We just passed a bill to protect the rights of the people from these data centers. 

Tax Incremental Finance Districts (TIFs) are a widely used economic development tool. Do you support their use? Why or why not? 

I do think they’re a good tool to use for communities as long as they’re not abusing them and doing more jobs than one TIF at a time.

Should the state provide greater oversight in mining gravel and sand, especially when it comes to dust? Why or why not? 

Dust is a problem for some of our elderly and younger people so if we could help them, keep the dust down with water or some other technology. that would make a good neighbor. They can mine further away from homes. That would be a good oversight our state could do.

Would you support an increase in the BBB tax, often called the tourism tax, to help offset taxes paid by residents? Why or why not? 

Our taxes right now aren’t too high so I will support a tourism tax if that helps our state keep our roads safer.

As the federal government pulls back from funding programs widely used in the state, how or should the legislature backfill the lost revenue? 

We should always try to get off the federal government Funded programs. we still have a lot of tax exemptions in our state that can help replace the revenue.

title: Black Hills Pioneer at 150: 1896
description: Pioneer file graphic
_full_text:
Black Hills Pioneer at 150 years
Pioneer file graphic 

Editor's Note
The Black Hills Pioneer is the oldest continuously operating business in West River Dakota Territory; and 2026 marks our 150th year of telling the stories of the Black Hills. Over time our newspaper has absorbed the titles of numerous other publications, and we would like to share some of the more compelling stories from those early editions.
 Every Saturday we will be publishing stories from our archives, focusing heavily on the gold rush era of the 1800s, starting with our very first publication on June 8, 1876. These stories are re-printed exactly as they were first published, leaving in place the historic typos, grammar, style and terminology – politically correct or otherwise. It is our belief that history is sacrosanct and should never be edited to reflect the societal norms of the present.
 We hope you enjoy this historic journey. It is an honor and a privilege to be a trusted permanent record keeper of the Black Hills community; we look forward to the next 150 years of history in the making in the magnificent Black Hills.

~ January 29, 1896 • Queen City Mail ~

A New Organization.

The meeting held at Deadwood last Thursday by representative business men from nearly every town in the Hills bids fair to result in the accomplishment of much good for this whole Black Hills country. It was called at the instance of the mayors of Hot Springs, Deadwood and Lead, every town being requested to send representatives. Nearly all of them complied with the invitation, Spearfish, Hermosa and Hill City being the exceptions. Mayor Evans of Hot Springs, who was chairman of the meeting, stated that the object of forming an alliance of all the towns and cities of the Hills is to unite in an effort to advertise the mineral and other resources and enlist capital in their development; for the erection of reduction works, opening up of mines, for providing irrigation facilities and increasing the growth of livestock, and for any and all other purposes that go for the increase and development of the country. It will therefore be seen that on all of these propositions Spearfish is directly interested and should be an active supporter of such a scheme. We know from experience that singlehanded we have been unable to accomplish much during the past few years— especially with certain influences working dead against every move inaugurated for our benefit. It would therefore seem probable that Spearfish has every thing to gain and nothing to lose by becoming identified with this association. We do know that our efforts to bring about the completion of the unfinished chlorination plant have proved unavailing. It is not to our interest, then, to become identified with an association which may be able to give us a lift in this direction?

The men who were in attendance at Deadwood meeting are prominent and influential in their respective localities, and it is fair to presume that unless Spearfish shows some interest in the association they will not put themselves to any inconvenience to assist us. It is an acknowledged fact that more interest is being taken in mining matters at present than at any time for years, and it is confidently asserted that the whole Hills country is entering on an era of great prosperity from a mining standpoint. Therefore the formulation of an association with mining development as its primary object is of more than passing interest.

The officers of the Black Hills Improvement association, as this new organization is to be called, are as follows: President, F. T. Evans, Hot Springs; Vice President, John R. Brennan, Rapid City; recording secretary, J. W. Jones, Lead; corresponding secretary, William Selbie, Deadwood; treasurer, D. A. McPherson, Deadwood. Local vice presidents were appointed for every town in the Hills, John Woizmuth being designated for Spearfish. We can do no less that to at least signify our willingness to get on the bandwagon and shout, whether it does any good or not.    

~ January 29, 1896 • Queen City Mail ~

Brief Local Mention

Mrs. W. D. Driskill entertained a party of young people at her home last Saturday evening in honor of her guest, Miss LaMontague.

Charley Zink sports a handsome meerschaum pipe, the same being a present from Jud Grant, who was in town last week on one of his periodical trips.

Nearly everyone is complaining from attacks of lagrippe. It is one of the most tenacious and disagreeable ailments with which human beings are afflicted.

It is understood that W. S. Cook, who went to Sturgis recently to engage in the saloon business, will remove to Lead City and go in with Gene Blackwell in the same line.

Mr. and Mrs. Jacob Bartels returned to Deadwood last week after a year’s absence in California. They will become interested in the management of the Keystone hotel.

The MAIL enters upon its eighth year with this issue. Seven years ago it made its appearance in Spearfish, and during its appearance in Spearfish, and during its brief existence has witnessed and recorded local history, which would fill several good-sized volumes. The town has made a great advancement during the past seven years, both in population and wealth, and with the apparent bright future for the whole Black Hills region it is fair to presume that Spearfish will receive its proportion of material wealth in the future.

Minneapolis papers last week contain an alleged picture of Calamity Jane, who is just now entertaining the twin cities with her thrilling adventures in the Wild West. She appears in the picture as dressed in a buckskin suit, a rifle in one hand, a knife between her teeth, and altogether looking like a veritable desperado. If she doesn’t get drunk and break up the whole show it will be a surprise to those who have witnessed her orgies in Deadwood and Hot Springs during the past few months.

Dr. G. L. Smith went over to Belle Fourche Monday on some legal business relating to the effort to release Burt Woodburn from the meshes of Arizona law. It will be remembered that Woodburn took some race horses to Arizona last summer, and was arrested on a charge of stealing one of the horses in his racing string. The animal in question was born and raised in Butte county, but it will cost no end of trouble and some time to prove that fact. There are any number of people here who can testify to the identity of the horse.

    

~ January 29, 1896 • Queen City Mail ~

Our City Schools.

Section two of grade eight will give rhetorical exercises on Friday of this week.

Miss Burris, one of the brightest teachers of they county, spent two days last week inspecting the schools.

January has brought an unusual number of visitors to school. Teachers and pupils are always glad to welcome them.

An examination is being given this week. The work of the present month has been the best since school begun.

Oscar Christiansen of grade eight was called home this week to assist his father in rebuilding their home which was recently destroyed by fire in Rockerville.

Earl Cathey, Eddie Driskill, Johnnie Walton, Jean Crawford and Frank Avery are five little ones in grade one who deserve special mention for splendid progress in writing.

Montana schools are soon to have a 850,000 apportionment divided among them. Wyoming schools will get $3 per capita. Both states have magnificent permanent school funds.

More children are now absent from school because of sickness than at any other time during the year. The prevailing disorders seem to be sore throats and bad colds. A few cases of sore eyes are reported.

Patriotism can not be cultivated too much in our public schools. We mean that patriotism which leads to the deliberate belief that our nation is the greatest and noblest on the earth—a belief drawn from a study of our country’s achievements, the heroes of its history and of its present commanding position.

In one afternoon the good people of Deadwood donated sixty volumes to their city school library, which leads us to remark that if any citizen of Spearfish has a book he has read and does not care to read again, he can win the gratitude of some 300 children by placing that book where it will do the most good—in the library of the city schools. Any standard book, poetry, history, fiction, philosophical and scientific works, magazines, etc., would be gratefully received.

News and Notes
Pioneer file graphic 

Miles of honor 

STURGIS — After running for more than 400 miles in combat boots and wrapped in an American flag, Mai Richards will wrap up her Miles of Honor journey in Sturgis, Monday. Adopted from Vietnam and raised in Spearfish, Richards said her mission is to honor and pay tribute to fallen soldiers on Memorial Day. During her trip, she has stopped at American Legion posts to connect with veterans and local communities. Richards’ journey will culminate with a special ceremony at Harley Davidson Rally Point in Sturgis, at 1:30 p.m., Monday. 

— Wendy Pitlick 

New Lead officers 

LEAD — The city of Lead recently welcomed a new police officer. Parker DeRouchey is a South Dakota certified patrol officer, whom Lead Police Chief Robert Williams said will start his duties in Lead immediately. The new hire comes on the heels of Officer Jerry Cunningham’s resignation, which the Lead City Commission accepted, Monday. 

— Wendy Pitlick 

Building permit breaks

LEAD — Anyone who has a home improvement or other construction projects is encouraged to get started in June, by applying for a building permit. That’s because in June the city of Lead will waive the first $2,500 in project value for its building permit fees. 

— Wendy Pitlick 

Sales tax receipts climbing

LEAD — Sales tax collections continue to grow in Sturgis, City Administrator Aaron Jordan said Monday. Jordan told the Sturgis City Council that for the first 4 months of the year, sales taxes are 7.5% higher than the same time in 2025, and 13% higher than in 2024. The first 3 months of the year, he said, have been the best months the city has seen in 3 years. The third-penny, or “bed and booze’ tax that is assessed on lodging, restaurant purchases, alcohol sales, and attractions, is about 5.7% higher than 2025, Jordan said. 

— Wendy Pitlick

title: Meade School Board approves preliminary budget publication
byline: By Brandon Woltkamp Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — The Meade School Board approved publication of the preliminary budget for the 2026-27 school year on May 11.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

STURGIS — The Meade School Board approved publication of the preliminary budget for the 2026-27 school year on May 11. 

It showed drastic changes to previous budgets due to decisions earlier this year to cut 13 positions, the Talented and Gifted Program district wide, the closure of the Atall Elementary School, and overall reductions to help in reducing the deficit.

Included in the budget is the projected drop of students in enrollment. 

The budget estimates approximately 2,875 students will attend for the 2026-27school year.

“Nationwide and statewide, we have fewer students, and we are all going to be struggling with that, regardless of districts and our neighbors,” said Meade School Superintendent Wayne Wormstadt.

The general fund budget for the 2026-27 year will be $24,662,285, a decrease in size by $683,023 from last year’s budget. 

State aid for the district increased to $13,234,916 for the 2027 year, an increase of more than $1.7 million from the previous year. 

Brett Burditt, business manager of the Meade School District, said that the state legislature’s focus on reduction of the owner-occupied property tax mill levy has caused an increase to state aid.

State aid will make up roughly the same amount of lost revenue from property tax to cover the budget. 

State aid money comes from sales tax collections and consumer spending. 

“If the state has a bad year on sales tax collections, it will have a big impact on possible revenue,” said Wormstadt.

Projected expenditures for the general fund include a reduction of instructional and support/administrative staff, increased operational costs such as contracted custodial service agreements, electrical utilities, and an increase in student transportation costs.

The saving grace for the general fund was a transfer of $450,000 from the capital outlay budget and the shifting of the property insurance premium of $505,000 to the capital outlay budget.

The capital outlay revenue has increased more than 10% from the previous year, going from $7,989,000 to $8,837,214 due to an increase in property tax revenue and reserves savings.

Expenditures for the capital outlay budget increased nearly $1.4 million from the 2025-2026 school year of $7,233,903 due to the transfer of $450,000 to the general fund, property insurance premium of $505,000, and increased costs in facility improvement such as roof replacements, HVAC upgrades and electrical system improvements in older facilities. 

The 2026-2027 school year is projected to see expenditures of $8,631,644. 

The general fund is used for personnel, operational, and other related support costs while the capital outlay fund is used for capital construction, facility improvements, technology, curriculum and debt service. The funds are limited in what can be transferred. For example, the turf project at Woodle Field is a facility improvement and is funded from the capital outlay fund.

Wormstadt said the capital outlay has been under-levied by around $400,000.

“One (reason) is reliance on the change in the form of sales

More discussions are expected to take place in the June 8 meeting on whether the Board should max out the capital outlay levy.

Special education services expenditures increased from $6,507,397 to $6,838,337.

Revenue for special education services increased from $6,535,689 to $6,877,499.

title: ‘Nine Little Indians’ tells story from SD’s ‘painful’ Native boarding schools
byline: By Molly Wetsch South Dakota News Watch
description: A documentary about nine sisters who attended a boarding school for Native American children in South Dakota and later underwent a lengthy legal battle with the Catholic Diocese of Sioux Falls will see a global premiere this month.
_full_text:
A documentary about nine sisters who attended a boarding school for Native American children in South Dakota and later underwent a lengthy legal battle with the Catholic Diocese of Sioux Falls will see a global premiere this month.

“Nine Little Indians” follows the Charbonneau sisters, who are members of the Turtle Mountain Band of Chippewa Indians. They attended St. Paul’s Indian Mission School, also known as Marty Indian School, in Marty, South Dakota. All nine sisters said they experienced abuse at the hands of priests and nuns at the school.

Native American children were sent to boarding schools as early as the mid-19th century. Many boarding schools were affiliated with religious groups, and many were directly funded or supported by the federal government through the Indian Civilization Fund Act. That legislation allowed for funding to religious groups that wanted to open schools for Native Americans in an effort to introduce tribes to the “arts of civilization.” At least 3,000 children died in Native American boarding schools in the United States between 1828 and 1970, according to an investigation by the Washington Post.

Shannon Kring, the film’s director, has worked with Indigenous communities across the world and directed the 2021 documentary “End of the Line: The Women of Standing Rock.” That film chronicles the yearslong fight of the Standing Rock Sioux and other Native American people against the Dakota Access Pipeline.

For “Nine Little Indians,” Kring worked with executive producers actor Leonardo DiCaprio and motivational speaker and author Tony Robbins.

Kring told News Watch that she wants the film to be a “healing tool” for all of those who were involved in the boarding school system, as well as their descendants, and acknowledged that it will likely bring up difficult feelings for many who have experiences at boarding schools, even outside of South Dakota.

Kring said that conversations throughout the film’s production and release rollout indicate a general unawareness of the country’s boarding school system. An important part of ensuring the film’s salience is hitting on the scale and scope of the system, she said.

Just 10 states in the country did not have any Native American boarding schools, and a study from the National Native American Boarding School Healing Coalition said that the United States had a total of 526 schools. 

The film will premiere at Lincoln Center in New York City in a sold-out showing on May 27. 

Darrell Red Cloud, a Lakota historian and the great-great grandson of Chief Red Cloud, will open the premiere with a prayer song. Kring told News Watch that the premiere will also include a recitation of the Lord’s Prayer.

Kring also plans showings in South Dakota this summer. She said that she hopes the documentary will resonate even with those who don’t have connections to the boarding school system. 

All of the nine tribes in South Dakota had boarding schools operating on their reservations at one point in time, and several existed outside of tribal lands.

The National Native American Boarding School Healing Coalition (NABS) is also doing its part to preserve the stories of those who attended Indian boarding schools throughout the United States. The organization, which was founded in 2012, is near the end of its two-year oral history project funded by the Department of the Interior.

That initiative has involved nearly 400 survivors of boarding schools across the United States sitting down with historians to share their experiences at the schools in video interviews, which will be stored in a permanent, public archive of survivor stories.

Charlee Brissette (Sault St. Marie Ojibwe), co-director of the oral history project, told News Watch that hearing real stories, like those told in “Nine Little Indians” and in the oral history project, can allow for a much more potent understanding of the system – especially considering survivors are still alive today.

“To be able to witness firsthand stories from survivors ... we’re able to see a face of somebody who’s been directly impacted. We’re able to hear exactly what they’ve gone through, and how that experience has impacted their life and shaped them as a person,” Brisette said.

Molly Wetsch is South Dakota News Watch’s Native and rural communities reporter. Wetsch was born and raised in South Dakota and is a descendant of the Cheyenne River Sioux Tribe. Her maternal grandfather attended Indian boarding schools in South Dakota: the Holy Rosary Mission School (now Mahpíya Luta) on the Pine Ridge Reservation and St. Joseph’s Indian School in Chamberlain.

title: Audition tonight  BFACT is casting a western penned by a father/son pair of playwrights
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Derek Olson is pictured left with his father and son. In addition to leading Belle Fourche Area Community Theater, Olson is a playwright. He wrote BFACT’s upcoming show with his father. Photo courtesy Derek Olson
_full_text:
BFCommunityTheatre.jpg
Derek Olson is pictured left with his father and son. In addition to leading Belle Fourche Area Community Theater, Olson is a playwright. He wrote BFACT’s upcoming show with his father. Photo courtesy Derek Olson 

BELLE FOURCHE — Auditions for Belle Fourche Area Community Theater (BFACT)’s summer show open tonight at 6:30 p.m. at the rec center theater. The show is a true Butte County original — its roots belong to a family tree. 

Before he was the executive director of BFACT, Derek Olson was a high school theater director. Before that, he was an aspiring screenwriter in college.

At the time, one important way that Olson kept in touch with his father was through a shared pursuit — writing and storytelling.

The pair penned a screenplay — a western called “Dry Creek” set in Belle Fourche’s neighboring ghost town of Minnesela, starring a fictional gunslinger called Tom Bragg.

“We actually got to the point where an executive from CBS looked at it. Unfortunately, it never went anywhere,” Olson said. “We had our brief brush with almost, but it was a story that stuck with us.”

Olson said theater and screenwriting were things he had become interested in in childhood. His father’s interest followed.

“My dad was always very much a person who loved to get involved with what my siblings and I were involved in. I really got involved in theater when I was younger, and writing became something that I was really interested in,” Olson said. “He always helped me with that, got excited, and we started writing together.”

The pair wrote several plays together over the years. Then, in 2010, when Olson was working with high school students in theater, they were inspired to revisit Dry Creek.

“It was this western comedy. As I got into directing theater and all of that, it was something that we always loved, but I knew that story wouldn’t translate the best to theater,” Olson said.

Undeterred, the pair used Tom Bragg’s story as a springboard to write “Minnesela.”

“It is about an orphan named Emma Williams from the big city whose favorite book is a book called “Dry Creek,” which is the adventures of a guy named Tom Bragg out in Minnesela,” Olson said. “She is so inspired by his stories that she runs away from the orphanage to go to Minnesela to meet Tom, the author of the book.”

Traveling cross-country in the wild west was never an easy feat. William’s character must pose as a man for her own safety, travel with a rowdy bunch of would-be bank robbers, and make her way to Minnesela with a nun from the orphanage in hot pursuit.

The story is zany, funny, and has all of the hallmarks of a western adventure — including shoot-outs and bar fights.

First performed by high school students in 2010, “Minnesela” has since been subject to some fine-tuning, Olson said. But two things remain true — it’s a labor of love for father and son, and it takes very little aim at historical accuracy.

“It is not based on any real history. I tell people it is fake history of a real place,” Olson said. “We definitely reference stuff from the area, but none of it is meant to be ‘this is a thing that happened.’ It is all made up.”

That being said, a western seemed like not only a good fit for Belle Fourche — Olson noted that the community requests western shows more than any other kind — it’s a great fit for Butte County in July. Performances will be later in the month than the Roundup, Olson said, but they’ll hopefully capture some of the spirit of the region and its history.

There are 24 named roles in “Minnesela”, of various sizes. That means there is plenty of room for a sizable cast. Olson said the show is adaptable. Actors can certainly play more than one character, but 24 roles offer ample opportunity for community participation. There are also a few slots for middle-school-aged actors to join the mostly adult cast.

Auditions begin tonight and continue on Wednesday from 6:30-8:30 p.m. at the Belle Fourche Rec Center. More information about auditioning and BFACT is available at bellefourcheact.com.

title: District 31 senate candidates
description: Voters in District 31 will head to the polls June 2 to vote on vacant senate seat. Two people are running for 1 open position which is a 2-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.
_full_text:
District31SenateComp.jpg

Voters in District 31 will head to the polls June 2 to vote on vacant senate seat. Two people are running for 1 open position which is a 2-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.

Randy Deibert

 Deibert, Randy.jpg
Randy Deibert 

Name and what you do for a living? 

Randy Deibert.  I am a Professional Land Surveyor licensed in multiple states.  My wife, Lori, and I own and operate Professional Mapping & Surveying, LLC, a local land surveying and mapping company.  My career began in 1979 and continues to this day.  I am pleased to have been instrumental in so many local projects benefiting cities in District 31 and surrounding municipalities.  

What motivated you to run for this office?

I was originally encouraged to run for office because I thought I could make a difference.  The past ten years in public service proves that I have accomplished that.  I want to ensure that everyone’s voice can be heard in the laws and policies that affect our community.  Serving the public in this capacity is the same motivation that drives me today, as I seek re-election to the Senate representing the people of District 31.

Why do you think you are best qualified

Serving as your elected South Dakota State Senator for District 31 has been my greatest honor and privilege.  I listen and seek information before making decisions, support the legislative process, and work alongside legislators for the common good of South Dakota citizens.  I have sponsored and co-sponsored bills signed into law by the Governor for the betterment of our society.  I am a Spearfish native, past Lawrence County Commissioner and lifelong Black Hills resident who cares deeply about the area and the people who live here.  As Senate Majority Whip, I am currently the only member of Senate Leadership representing the Mountain Time Zone, a reflection of the respect earned by my esteemed colleagues.    

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held? 

Elected as Lawrence County Commissioner I served over six years. Additionally, a few leadership positions include Chairman of Black Hills Council of Local Government, Chairman of Black Hills Association of County Commissioners and Officials, Executive Board of South Dakota Association of County Commissioners; South Dakota elected member of the Western Intestate Region of National Association of Counties; Vice President of the Kenadi Weis Foundation; member of the South Dakota Public Safety Communication Council. While in the South Dakota Legislature I am fortunate to be appointed as chairman of many committees, interim committees and summer studies.

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I have attended numerous governmental meetings in person during the last year. These include the several meetings of the following: Spearfish City Council, Spearfish Planning Commission, Lead City Council, Deadwood City Council, Deadwood Planning Commission, Lawrence County Commission, Lawrence County Planning and Zoning Commission, Butte County Commission, Butte County Planning Commission, Spearfish School Board, Lead-Deadwood School Board and Meade School Board.

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Yes, local newspapers are important. They remain a primary source of community news, events, and public information. Publications like the Black Hills Pioneer, along with weekly papers such as the Bison Courier and Lemmon Leader News, play a vital role in keeping residents informed and connected.

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in District 31?

Important issues in District 31 are protecting our quality of life and local values for generations of families. Another important issue is properly managing our natural resources and public lands. Public safety, quality education, promoting tourism, sustaining agriculture are also important issues. And lastly, creating a strong economy to promote good paying jobs, affordable living and controlled spending in support of lower taxes.

How do you intend to solve these issues?

Solutions include strong local planning to address population growth and managing the impacts of increased tourism. We must continue working with the United States Forest Service, the Bureau of Land Management, and the South Dakota Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources in collaboration with local governments to effectively manage our natural resources. These include water, timber, grazing, and mining. Proper management—through permitting and regulation, especially at the local level—is critical to preserving the sustainability of the Black Hills. A good senator actively gathers input through meetings with local leaders, and conversations with residents. This interaction identifies concerns as they develop and promote diverse informed solutions.

What do you believe is working for the district, and how will you retain that progression?

I believe strong local awareness of our unique area helps preserve the beauty of the Black Hills. Continued involvement from citizens and local governments is essential to maintaining the quality of life provided by our natural surroundings.

I also believe our public schools are delivering quality education. Increased parental involvement is key to the continued success of our students, teachers, and school districts. Encouraging engagement from busy, working parents supports better outcomes for our youth and strengthens our communities.

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions? 

Transparency means being open and accessible at multiple levels. I am always available to discuss ideas, legislation, concerns, and how I have voted with constituents in District 31 and across South Dakota. Clear communication is essential to transparency.

In local government, I consistently disclosed interactions with citizens, especially on-site visits related to agenda items. I also declared conflicts of interest and removed myself from the table during debate and action when appropriate. I encouraged public participation by inviting citizens to attend meetings or submit written input. I strive to ensure meetings are accessible and that citizens feel comfortable sharing their views.

What else do you want people to know about you?

My wife and I live in rural Lawrence County, west of Spearfish.  I am a Black Hills native who has enjoys the quality of life this region provides.  We have four children who attended Spearfish public schools and Black Hills State University.  We have ten grandchildren and are looking forward to the birth of our eleventh grandchild next month.  We continue to enjoy the stunning natural scenery, outdoor adventure and recreation, and local flavors our area offers.

The discussion of data centers coming to South Dakota has been on the rise. Do you support data centers coming to the state? 

I do not support data centers coming to the state without careful limitations and strict evaluation of their impacts. Each proposal must include a thorough analysis of facts, a comprehensive review, and a detailed financial pro forma. These decisions should be made at the local level with meaningful public engagement. We must fully understand the impacts of data centers, including differences in size, classification, and resource demands such as water and electricity, before any approval is considered.

Data centers use significant amounts of water and electricity as part of their operations. What legislation should be put in place to protect residents from the inevitable need for more electrical generation and water use?

During the 2026 Legislative Session, Senate Bill 135 was passed and will become law on July 1, 2026. This bill establishes processes related to electrical and water usage and represents a starting point for future legislation. As we continue to gather information on data centers, additional measures may be needed.

I support legislation that recognizes different classifications of data centers, including size, capacity, and electricity demand. Regardless, local control remains essential. One-size-fits-all legislation is rarely the best approach for local issues.

Tax Incremental Finance Districts (TIFs) are a widely used economic development tool. Do you support their use? Why or why not?

Historically, Tax Increment Financing (TIFs) have been a valuable economic development tool. Senate Bill 228 (2026) updates certain provisions related to TIFs. Each local government should evaluate TIF proposals based on a detailed analysis of facts, a comprehensive review, and a financial pro forma.

I do not support TIFs in which a city or local government acts as the developer or assumes loan or financial obligations. Taxpayers should not bear the risk if a TIF is unsuccessful.

Should the state provide greater oversight in mining gravel and sand, especially when it comes to dust? Why or why not?

A comprehensive review of the State’s current oversight responsibilities through the Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources (DANR) is the first step to understanding its role in regulating gravel and sand mining. It is also important to verify compliance with federal requirements.

We should first fully understand the existing state and federal framework before determining whether additional oversight is needed. Once that is clear, we can evaluate the appropriate role of state and local governments. Any changes should be based on facts and focused on protecting public safety.

Would you support an increase in the BBB tax, often called the tourism tax, to help offset taxes paid by residents? Why or why not?

I typically do not support new taxes or tax increases. I would need specific details on how any additional revenue would be used to provide meaningful equitable property tax relief or other direct benefits to residents before I could support an increase.

We recognize the importance of tourism in District 31. Any discussion of tax policy must balance not overburdening the tourism industry while also providing appropriate tax relief to local taxpayers.

As the federal government pulls back from funding programs widely used in the state, how or should the legislature backfill the lost revenue?

It is important to understand the impact of any significant reduction in federal funding to state agencies such as the South Dakota Department of Transportation and the South Dakota National Guard.

Federal transportation funding is often passed through to local governments for roads and bridges, and reductions would directly affect those projects. Likewise, reduced federal support for the National Guard would limit major equipment purchases and training, impacting readiness and response capability.

Given the scale of current federal funding, fully backfilling these losses at the state level would be extremely challenging and would likely require a combination of spending reductions and new revenue. 

John Teupel

 Teupel, John.jpg
John Teupel 

Name and what you do for a living? 

 John E. Teupel.  In my current position, I transport agricultural commodities to serve the needs of South Dakota farm families.  For the past decade, I have been employed in various aspects of the transportation industry.

What motivated you to run for this office?

 I am running because the citizens of District 31 deserve to have a conservative representing them in the State Senate.  I believe I am the best qualified candidate to serve the citizens of Lawrence County and South Dakota in the State Senate in these unprecedented times.  I have been asked by several prominent citizens and community leaders from District 31 to run for this office, and I believe the timing is right for me to step up to this challenge and to serve in this capacity.  

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

 I am a fifth-generation resident of Lawrence County.  I grew up in the Lead Deadwood area and have resided in the Spearfish area for the past thirty years.  I earned a bachelor’s degree in agriculture from South Dakota State University and a master’s degree in business from Black Hills State University.  For much of my adult life, I worked in various aspects of agriculture and as a self-employed entrepreneur in real estate sales, development, property management, and construction.  From 2001 and 2005, I served District 31 in the State House of Representatives.  I have the knowledge and experience to hit the ground running.

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

 As State Representative from District 31, I served on the House Taxation, Transportation, and State Affairs Committees.  From 2003 through 2004, I served as House Majority Whip.  In 2003, I was appointed as a Charter member to the Black Hills National Forest Citizen Advisory Board as the State Elected Official.  From 2006 through 2022, I served as a board member of the SD Historical Society Foundation, the non-profit partner to the State Historical Society.  From 2012 through 2018, I served as Chairman of that Board of Directors.

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

 Having served for several years as Chairman of the SD Historical Society Foundation, I regularly attended quarterly meetings of the State Historical Society Board of Trustees.  I have attended Lawrence County Commission, Spearfish City Council Meetings, Deadwood City Council Meetings, and the South Dakota Legislature in the past.  I have not recently attended any local government meetings.

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

 Local newspapers are vital to provide citizens with in-depth reporting on issues, happenings, and governmental actions of local concern that would not be communicated without a reporter.  It is crucial and vital that local newspapers remain neutral and unbiased in their reporting, stick to the facts and allow citizenry to debate the issues and decide for themselves what to believe about the issues.  I make it regular practice to keep myself abreast of the news through a variety of sources, including the local newspapers.

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in District 31?

 We are currently at an inflection point in growth and development of the Black Hills.  Spearfish has become the third fastest growing micropolitan area in the nation.  Development pressures are growing throughout Lawrence County, and with it, demands on groundwater resources.  High gold prices portend a renewed interest in mineral extraction in Lawrence County.  Controversies have erupted over mining aggregate and limestone to meet construction and development needs.  With persistent ongoing drought conditions proper timber management is critical to maintain our forests and to protect our citizens.  Residential home prices have doubled and with that, increased assessed valuations are pricing residents out of their homes.

How do you intend to solve these issues?

Community leaders must be willing to listen to the changing needs expressed by our citizens and respond accordingly.  We need statesmen who can provide innovative solutions to solve twenty-first century problems while staying true to the conservative principles of capitalism, personal freedom, low taxation, and limited government which have served us well as a state for generations.  Lawrence County is blessed with many attributes, not the least of which is its citizenry and community leaders.  I will work collaboratively to develop laws and policies to solve problems and capitalize on opportunities to the benefit of District 31.

What do you believe is working for the district, and how will you retain that progression?

 The Sanford Underground Research Facility has become a huge asset to District 31 and will continue to bring innovative employment opportunities to District 31.  Continued funding of research and development will be critical to maintain.  I have and will continue to support our timber industry and the management of our forest for sustained health, supporting its multiple uses.  We have many good things going on at Black Hills State University and continued support of this great institution is vital to our culture and economy.  With the expansion of Monument Health at the Spearfish Hospital and clinic, our health care system is better equipped to meet health care needs locally.

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

In our representative republican form of government, government belongs to the people.  I will do everything I can to be accessible to the citizens of District 31 via phone, email, social media, legislative cracker barrels, and informal coffee shop visits.  And when constituents come to Pierre during the legislative session, I will do everything I can to be available to visit with them and listen to their ideas and concerns.

What else do you want people to know about you?

 I am a straight shooter.  We may not always agree but you will always know where I stand on the issues of the day.  I will try to listen to all points of view and make decisions carefully and judiciously, based on what I believe is best for the citizens of District 31 and the State of South Dakota.  As a legislator, your word and your integrity are your only stock in trade.  I will keep my word to the citizens of District 31 and with my colleagues in Pierre.  I am Christian man who seeks to serve God in my daily life. 

The discussion of data centers coming to South Dakota has been on the rise. Do you support data centers coming to the state?

I am not opposed to building data centers in South Dakota as long as the advantages for our citizens outweigh the associated costs.  Proposals must include careful analysis and, if done properly, the tax revenue they produce could be used to provide property tax relief.  However, if their development results in increased cost for power generation and environmental harm, then the juice is not worth the squeeze.

Data centers use significant amounts of water and electricity as part of their operations. What legislation should be put in place to protect residents from the inevitable need for more electrical generation and water use?

 I think data centers should provide for their own power generation so as not to compete with consumers for electricity.  Their use of water needs to be carefully regulated, and water recycling should be required. SB135, also known as the “Data Center Bill of Rights for Citizens,” which passed this legislative session, was a step in the right direction. 

Tax Incremental Finance Districts (TIFs) are a widely used economic development tool. Do you support their use? Why or why not?

 The Spearfish Convention Center is an example of a properly executed TIF which provides benefit to the community.  However, I think TIF’s have been overused in some locales. I think TIF’s are an economic tool that should remain in the books to facilitate projects that provide broad based community benefits that otherwise would not occur. Some of the reforms during the recent legislative session are a step in the right direction to ensure projects benefit the community as a whole and not just special interests.

Should the state provide greater oversight in mining gravel and sand, especially when it comes to dust? Why or why not?

 I would need to review the existing laws and regulations regarding mining to see if the existing laws are being properly administered and verify if there is a need for more stringent regulation.  Where problems occur, those decisions are best made and administered locally, if the state provides a legal framework for local control.

Would you support an increase in the BBB tax, often called the tourism tax, to help offset taxes paid by residents? Why or why not?

 I support the BBB or tourism tax as it was originally designed to support tourism promotion.  I do not think it should be expanded as a source of general fund revenue.

As the federal government pulls back from funding programs widely used in the state, how or should the legislature backfill the lost revenue?

 I don’t know if the state can afford to backfill decreases in funding from federal programs.  An example of this is Medicaid expansion.  By adopting Medicaid expansion, the state has now locked itself into an ever-increasing expenditure competing with other items for available revenue.  We need to put taxpayers first and be willing to live within our means.

title: ‘A Night at the Derby’ raises $156,731 for hospice, breaking fundraising record
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: SPEARFISH —Monument Health Foundation broke its previous fundraising record at this year’s “Night at the Derby” event on April 25, raising $156,731 to support Northern Hills Hospice.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

SPEARFISH —Monument Health Foundation broke its previous fundraising record at this year’s “Night at the Derby” event on April 25, raising $156,731 to support Northern Hills Hospice.

Once again proceeds from this year’s event supported hospice care in the Northern Hills.

A fund-a-mission portion of the event supported the purchase of SoloProtect ID Touch technology: discreet, wearable devices that connect caregivers to 24/7 emergency support. Home health caregivers serve patients independently, often in private homes. This technology ensures support is always within reach if a caregiver feels vulnerable or in need of assistance, providing peace of mind without disrupting the compassionate, personal care our teams are known for. 

 “This year’s A Night at the Derby was an incredible example of our community coming together to support compassionate hospice care across the Northern Hills and Black Hills region,” said Hans Nelson, Monument Health Foundation director.

“We are deeply grateful to every donor, sponsor and volunteer whose generosity helps provide comfort, dignity and support for patients, families and caregivers every day,” Nelson said. 

 The event also honors those who have dedicated their lives to hospice programs throughout the Northern Hills and the greater Black Hills region. Each year, the Dignity Award honors a hospice caregiver who embodies the spirit of compassion, kindness and unwavering dedication — someone who makes a difference not just in the lives of patients and families but in the hearts of their team. Blake Benson received this year’s Dignity Award. 

 “Blake is the kind of nurse every person hopes to have during one of life’s most vulnerable moments. He is kind, caring, patient, and consistently positive. His empathy and compassion for patients and families are extraordinary, and it shows in the countless lives he has touched,” said Michelle Sieveke, Monument Health hospice director. “Blake goes above and beyond for his patients every single day. Many lovingly refer to him as an angel, and it’s easy to understand why. He brings comfort not only through his nursing care but also through his warm presence  —  and even through song. Blake is known for his beautiful voice, often singing to patients, offering a calming and peaceful presence during difficult moments.”

 Benson has been a nurse for nearly 18 years, with 15 of those years spent serving at Hospice House.

title: New pest control business  opens in Spearfish
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer
description: Rowdi Fellas Pest Control is now open in Spearfish. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
New pest control business  opens in Spearfish
Rowdi Fellas Pest Control is now open in Spearfish. Courtesy photo 

SPEARFISH — Rowdi Fellas Pest Control, a new pest control business, opened in Spearfish on Jan 1.

The business was founded and is owned by John and Jill Kolb, who also own a bat removal company called CP Bat Mitigation. Rowdi Van Zee, the son of Jill Kolb, and the business’ namesake, said that he is responsible for the business’ day-to-day operations, which include ant, spider, cockroach, rodent, and bedbug removal, among other services. 

“I was ready to go to a job with some more benefits,” Van Zee said. “I(‘ve) wanted to live out here my whole life, and we saw a hole in the market; we thought that there was room for another pest control business.”

He said that although many of his calls come from customers in Spearfish, the business takes him as far as Sundance, Wyo., and Rapid City. 

Van Zee said that he learned the ins-and-outs of pest control during ride-alongs with Ryan Anderson of Anderson Pest Control, a pest control business based in Sioux Falls. He and Jill Kolb passed an 8-hour exam so they could be properly certified.

“We love it here,” Jill Kolb said. “And what’s so great is that the community is very supportive of local (businesses)...We appreciate the community’s support and we look forward to growing with the community.”
