title: Army Corps grants final approval for Dakota Access Pipeline, 9 years after oil began flowing
byline: By Mary Steurer North Dakota Monitor
description: Lake Oahe just outside of Fort Yates on the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe Reservation is pictured on October 9, 2024. The Dakota Access Pipeline crosses underneath the reservoir just north of the reservation. Photo by Mary Steurer, North Dakota Monitor
_full_text:
Army Corps grants final approval for Dakota Access Pipeline, 9 years after oil began flowing.jpg
Lake Oahe just outside of Fort Yates on the Standing Rock Sioux Tribe Reservation is pictured on October 9, 2024. The Dakota Access Pipeline crosses underneath the reservoir just north of the reservation. Photo by Mary Steurer, North Dakota Monitor 

BISMARCK, N.D. — A federal agency officially granted the Dakota Access Pipeline a permit to cross under the Missouri River’s Lake Oahe reservoir, ending a six-year environmental review to determine whether the pipeline could continue operating.

The decision, issued by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers on Thursday, authorizes the pipeline crossing with additional conditions the agency says will make the pipeline safer. It follows the Army Corps’ December release of a 464-page report analyzing the environmental impacts of the pipeline crossing, which is in south-central North Dakota less than one mile upstream from the Standing Rock Reservation. The Army Corps was required by law to wait a minimum of 30 days before it could finalize its findings with the record of decision.

The Dakota Access Pipeline has been carrying crude oil from northwest North Dakota to southern Illinois since June 2017. The pipeline’s owner, Dakota Access, was required to seek the easement from the Army Corps, which manages Lake Oahe, to build the pipeline under the reservoir roughly 10 years ago.

The Army Corps initially granted the easement in 2017. 

The Standing Rock Sioux Tribe sued the agency in federal court, arguing the Army Corps approved the easement without completing the full environmental review required under federal law. The tribe claimed the easement was invalid and that the pipeline must be shut down.

A federal judge in 2020 sided with the tribe and vacated the easement. The judge ordered the Army Corps to conduct the environmental review before it could decide whether it was appropriate to re-authorize the permit.

The conditions added to the easement would mostly be the responsibility of Dakota Access to implement. The requirements are meant to prevent an oil spill and minimize the impacts of a spill, such as implementing new leak detection technology, monitoring groundwater and testing surface water. It would also require Dakota Access to provide an alternate water supply and to develop a food distribution plan for communities that rely on Lake Oahe for food in the event of an oil spill.

The Corps also said this option protects environmental resources and responds to comments raised by Tribal Nations.

The Corps also said this option protects environmental resources and responds to comments raised by Tribal Nations.

The Standing Rock Sioux Tribe in a Thursday evening statement said that the conditions added to the easement by the Corps decision do not assuage any of the tribe’s concerns related to the pipeline. 

“Today’s decision merely restates past conclusions and represents a pattern of minimizing and rejecting Tribal expertise in sustaining our lands, resources, and cultural properties,” the tribe said in the statement. The Standing Rock Sioux Tribe also said the Army Corps didn’t sufficiently engage with the tribe to develop an emergency plan to protect Lake Oahe, which the tribe relies  on for drinking water.

“The Tribe will evaluate all legal and political options to defend our Treaty rights, protect Mni Wiconi — Water of Life, and hold the Federal government and private corporations accountable to the highest standards of environmental stewardship and Tribal consultation,” Standing Rock Chair Steve Sitting Bear said in the statement.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum announced the development Thursday morning while presenting to the Williston Basin Petroleum Conference in Bismarck, drawing applause from the oil industry attendees.

Burgum, who became North Dakota governor in 2017 while Indigenous-led protests against the pipeline were ongoing, called the drawn-out environmental study “a cloud of uncertainty over the whole Bakken.”

“No more uncertainty,” Burgum said. “We’re all good.”

Adam Telle, assistant secretary of the Army for Civil Works, said in a statement that the Corps through the decision is “decisively putting years of delays to rest.”

“The U.S. Army Corps of Engineers are delivering the clear, consistent regulatory decisions required to provide certainty to the American economy and advance President Trump’s American energy dominance agenda, while protecting our natural resources,” he said in the statement.

When the federal judge pulled the easement in 2020, he initially also ordered the pipeline to be shut down. However, that part of his decision was reversed by an appellate court.

The Army Corps allowed the pipeline to continue operating while it was working on the environmental impact statement. The Standing Rock Sioux Tribe in late 2024 brought another federal lawsuit against the agency, arguing the pipeline could not continue carrying oil under Lake Oahe without the easement, among other claims. The judge concluded it was up to the Army Corps’ discretion whether to allow the pipeline to stay open while the environmental impact statement was pending. He noted the tribe could bring another legal challenge against the agency once the study was complete. Standing Rock appealed the dismissal.Vicki Granado, vice president of corporate communications for Dakota Access Pipeline developer Energy Transfer, said in a statement that the company is “pleased” with the Army Corps’ decision. 

“We want to thank the Corps for the tremendous amount of time and effort put in by so many to bring this matter to a thoughtful close,” Granado said in a statement.

Energy Transfer maintains the pipeline has always complied with regulations. The pipeline crosses at minimum 95 feet below the riverbed of Lake Oahe.

North Dakota Monitor Editor Amy Dalrymple contributed to this story.

title: CO2 scrubbing microbes discovered in underground laboratory
byline: By Mike Ray SURF Communications
description: Dr. Tanvi Govil, sampling for microbes on the 1,700-foot level of the ground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility. Photo by Stephen Kenny / SURF
_full_text:
Biology_Stephen Kenny_LR-12.jpg
Dr. Tanvi Govil, sampling for microbes on the 1,700-foot level of the ground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility. Photo by Stephen Kenny / SURF 

 Biology_Stephen Kenny_LR-17.jpg
Dr. Tanvi Govil and her team, sampling for microbes on the 1,700-foot level of the ground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility. Photo by Stephen Kenny / SURF 

LEAD — You might not know it, but the hot water and rocks deep within the Earth are teeming with undiscovered life. 

Dr. Tanvi Govil is one of the biologists studying this new frontier of microbial life that thrives in extreme places.

Govil and a multidisciplinary team of researchers discovered a set of microbes living 4,100-feet underground at SURF that eat carbon dioxide gas (CO2) and turn it into rock at an incredibly fast rate. The initial research showed a vast improvement in the efficiency to sequester carbon dioxide in storage underground — speeding up the process from years to a few weeks. 

Govil realized that instead of piping carbon dioxide  underground, this technology enables direct removal of greenhouse gas emissions on site. 

“The microbes we found at SURF help prove these biochemical reactions can be used to efficiently remove carbon from power-plant emissions. The discovery at SURF was the spark that started the whole thing,” said Govil, who is an assistant professor in the Karen M. Swindler Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering at South Dakota Mines.

Today, Govil is leading the effort to build a library of microbes from different parts of the world that have the right properties for carbon capture. Researchers are combining the best attributes from each microbe to engineer enzymes that can convert carbon dioxide from coal-fired power plant emissions into calcium carbonate — a mineral that can later be sold as a concrete additive or for other industrial purposes.

“The lab experiments we have done are based on some sample emissions provided by local industries. We took flue gases, and even leftover coal ash, to lab test and validate that this technology will be able to work in the larger-scale industrial environment,” Govil said. 

The idea involves taking a large tank of these carbon dioxide-capturing enzymes and bubbling emissions from a coal-fired power plant up through the enzyme solution. This process would remove the CO2 from the exhaust stream and convert it into a commercially viable biproduct.

Merle Symes is the CEO of Carb-N0, a company created by Govil and her team to speed this technology to market.

“There are heavy environmental pressures around the world to see this kind of climate solution put into place,” Symes said. “Many governments are very supportive of eliminating carbon emissions. We think we have a win-win solution.”

Scientists have known for a long time that microbes could be used to remove CO2 from emissions, but previous challenges included finding life forms that can survive the process. 

“Factory and power-plant flue gases are pretty nasty,” Symes noted. “There are high temperatures, high pressure, sometimes there’s high acidity. This research found out that these unique microbes, which evolved in extreme environments, actually thrive on these things.”

Govil and Symes recently won the South Dakota Governor’s Giant Vision Business Plan competition with their patent-pending technology. They are continuing to refine the process and create enzymes robust enough to be shipped anywhere they are needed. The next step, Govil says, is pilot-scale testing. Her team is planning to build an enzyme-based CO2 scrubber that can sit on a truck bed, then bring it to a facility and hook it up to a stream of emissions.

“One of these mobile units will be able to take almost one ton of CO2 per day. This will allow us to demonstrate the technology to different partners and industries, and validate the concept and business model,” Govil said.

The goal is to continue testing this year and launch enzyme production by 2027. “There’s some urgency in this, given the importance of what this technology could mean for humanity,” Symes said.

The carbon challenge is enormous—humanity currently emits more than 37 billion metric tons of CO2 per year. But Govil sees a path from the Black Hills of South Dakota to smokestacks around the world. The 2025 global market size for carbon capture and sequestration is valued at $4.51 billion. The market is projected to grow to $19.98 billion by 2034. If pilot testing goes as planned, Govil’s team aims to enter the marketplace by next year.

For a technology that started from samples taken 4,100 feet beneath the earth, inside a former gold mine turned laboratory in Lead, the timeline from discovery to market could be less than a decade.

title: American dipper strikes again  on the Elmore Road bridge
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: The replacement of a bridge on Elmore Road has been delayed again after an American dipper bird has returned to nest on the structure in spite of the county’s best efforts to encourage the bird to move on. Photo by Mark Watson
_full_text:
American dipper strikes again  on the Elmore Road bridge
The replacement of a bridge on Elmore Road has been delayed again after an American dipper bird has returned to nest on the structure in spite of the county’s best efforts to encourage the bird to move on. Photo by Mark Watson 

DEADWOOD — Work to replace a bridge on Elmore Road in Spearfish Canyon has been delayed again after an American dipper returned to nest on the existing structure despite the county’s best efforts to encourage the bird to move on. 

It was discovered that the bird was nesting in boxes placed on the bridge party last summer, when the bridge became eligible to go to bid. 

“We removed (the nests) at the end of last season,” said John Bey, Lawrence County highway superintendent. “It is unclear who put those nest boxes on there. We certainly did not do that, nor do we encourage anybody to do that for this very reason. In this case, it really is irrelevant because the bird went ahead without permission and went ahead and built its own nest.”

The American dipper is listed by South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks, as a state threatened species. The Black Hills marks the eastern limit of their home range. The bird is the only aquatic songbird of North America, and typically nests over streams. The bird’s nesting season typically lasts from May through July.

The bid for the Elmore Road bridge was awarded by Lawrence County Sept. 3, 2025, to Grangaard Construction for $950,750.37. The structure, crossing Spearfish Creek, is a 24-foot long, single-span steel beam bridge built in 1901, and is under a load restriction of single-unit weight of 8 tons and combination weight of 14 tons. To avoid disrupting Spearfish Creek, the structure is scheduled to be replaced with a single-span cement structure with abutments and steel piles. Construction on the structure was scheduled to start in May, but after it was discovered that the dipper had come home to nest again, construction has been put off until Aug. 1. 

“We can’t disturb the bird, so we’re going to do our best to get this project done in the time that we have,” said Bey. “At the preconstruction meeting, the contractor gave us a time frame of 8 to 12 weeks for construction.”

Bey said all easements and utility notifications have been completed for the project.

Funding for the replacement of the structure is part of a bundle grant from the federal highway department, provided to the county from the state of South Dakota. Bey said he believes the county will be responsible for part of 18% of the final cost of construction.

“Unlike other bridge grants or processes where we actually would pay up front and get reimbursed at the end, on this particular bridge we will just get a bill from the state and we will pay up our portion.”

title: 189 Spartans graduate in 99th Spearfish High School graduation ceremony
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: “We will never be in the same room, at the same time ever again, unless we have a crazy cool class reunion,” Senior Class Speaker Taylor Vitto said during Saturday’s Spearfish High School Graduation, marking the bittersweet tone of this year’s commencement. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
IMG_4332.JPG
“We will never be in the same room, at the same time ever again, unless we have a crazy cool class reunion,” Senior Class Speaker Taylor Vitto said during Saturday’s Spearfish High School Graduation, marking the bittersweet tone of this year’s commencement. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — On Saturday, 189 students crossed the stage at the 99th Spearfish High School graduation ceremony, turned their tassels, and entered the next chapter of their lives.

This year’s processional was led by junior class president Addison Keller, and junior class vice president Olivia Purcell led the 2026 seniors on their processional. Students took their labeled seats, picked up roses to present to the people who made the greatest impact on their high school careers, and turned their attention toward the stage.

Superintendent Kirk Easton delivered his final word of welcome to a graduating class as Spearfish Superintendent of Schools.

After a choral performance of “Hey Jude,” School Board Member Alesha Limbo delivered an address to the graduates. Limbo had 3 words of wisdom for the class of 2026: awareness, intention, and purpose.

Without awareness, Limbo said, people often drift in their adult lives.

“Awareness is where life begins. A lot of people don’t actually live awake. They live distracted, they live reactive, they live numb, and they live on autopilot. They follow the crowd. They chase what everyone else is chasing and their minds and their lives, but they never slow down long enough to ask, ‘What do I want to become?’” Limbo said. “If you’re not aware of it, you will drift. You will drift into habits you didn’t mean to build. You will drift into relationships that pull you away from who you really are. “

She encouraged students to pay attention to their lives and take action based on what they notice.

“Live with intention,” Limbo said. “You do not become a strong person by chance. You become a strong person by choice. You can choose honesty, discipline, humility, and courage. You choose who you surround yourself with.”

She noted that all adults make mistakes. As the class of 2026 leaves their high school careers and childhood behind, Limbo said, they should remember that they have purpose.

“Your value is deeper than your performance. You are not random,” Limbo said. “When you know that your life matters, you begin to dream bigger. You begin to stretch yourself , you begin to take risks, and you begin to push past the familiar.”

Liimbo told the graduates that growth is hard, but dreaming big is worth it.

Moments later, students delivered flowers to the people in their lives that encouraged them to dream big — exchanging often tearful hugs with teachers and loved ones in the audience.

Senior Class Speaker Taylor Vitto, who introduced herself good-naturedly as the student “most likely to talk your ear off,” kept the theme of gratitude going in her speech.

“As much as I would love to give you all amazing insight that I have on being a successful adult, I am barely an adult,” Vitto said. “I can still barely wear nice clothes without staining them. Therefore, I am going to stay away from that, and instead look at who and what brought us here to this moment.”

Vitto heartily thanked the family members, teachers, athletic clubs, extracurricular organizations, and peers that brought each student to the stage on Saturday.

“We continue to grow through every experience that is worth thanking yourself for. If you made it through COVID, no school for 3 years, and staying on campus for lunch as a freshman, there’s nothing you can’t accomplish,” Vitto said.

Candice Matsuda was recognized as the 2026 class valedictorian, and Mathilde Matsuda was salutatorian.

After diplomas were awarded, caps were tossed, and confetti shot from all angles, the graduates departed the Spartan gym with their families to celebrate the long weekend and their accomplishments.

byline: By Brandon Woltkamp Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Spearfish American Legion Post 164 organized a ceremony in remembrance of fallen soldiers in war, Monday, at the Rose Hill Cemetery and Spearfish Monument Memorial. Pioneer photos by Brandon Woltkamp
_full_text:
DSCF5226.JPG
The Spearfish American Legion Post 164 organized a ceremony in remembrance of fallen soldiers in war, Monday, at the Rose Hill Cemetery and Spearfish Monument Memorial. Pioneer photos by Brandon Woltkamp 

SPEARFISH — The Spearfish American Legion Post 164 organized a ceremony in remembrance of fallen soldiers in war, Monday, at the Rose Hill Cemetery and Spearfish Monument Memorial. 

Featured in the remembrance program were First Sergeant Bradley Limbo as guest speaker, Legion member Doug Henwood, and the Spearfish Boy Scouts Troop 17 to mast the flags and hang wreaths on crosses. 

Henwood said that his family and relatives have served in the armed forces for more than 80 years.

“We haven’t quit yet,” said Henwood. Henwood himself retired from the Air Force and is a disabled veteran, having been with American Legion Post 164 since 2012. 

“What we are here to do is honor those who have gone on. They gave the ultimate sacrifice,” said Henwood.

Memorial Day honors those who have fallen in the line of duty and pays respect to our fellow countrymen who sacrificed their lives in the name of freedom.

_full_text:
Voters in District 29  will head to the polls June 2 to vote on a vacant Senate seat. Two people are running for 1 open position which is a 2-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.

John Carley

 Carley John Sen-5570 RTJS.jpg
John Carley 

Name and what you do for a living? 

Senator John Carley – Businessman in tourism, hospitality, property management, IT

What motivated you to run for this office?

 Our district was in need of a true conservative legislator who actually voted with the US Constitution, South Dakota Constitution, Republican Platform and Conservative values.  I volunteered to step in and bring my business background, family background, church background, and involvement with the community to represent our citizens.  The people elected me to State Senate and I have appreciated serving the citizens of our district, and am running for re-election to continue helping our district and our state.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

The promises I made in originally running for Senator have been kept.  Honesty, integrity, transparency and strong principles help in serving in public office.  I have delivered votes that have protected our constitutional liberties [like 2nd amendment freedoms, stopping billion dollar corporations from data center tax credit abuse, and author of the Save South Dakota Act – making sure only citizens vote in our elections], Cut Taxes & Spending [largest property tax relief in SD history], Cherished Families [prevented woke by getting man-and-woman definitions into our state law, earned 100% pro life scores, and protected AG land from foreign ownership].

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

State Senate, Precinct Committeeman, Non-Profit Board of Directors positions, Trade Organizations Leadership positions.

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I attend dozens of city and county local government meetings, as well as the GOP County meetings.  I incorporate this into my service at the State Senate working closely with and listening to city and county officials.

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Yes, I believe local & newspapers are critical.  I also appreciate that newspapers are in written form, as writing always allows deeper thought, explanations, and organization of thought.  I hope newspapers can stay strong in our local community and hope we train our next generations to read them.

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in your district?

1)Constitutional Liberty, 2)Cut Taxes & Spending, 3)Cherish Families.  1-Our district is one of the most conservative in the state desiring our property rights, right to bear arms, citizens only voting, good schools and more. 2-Our citizens are asking for property tax relief, keeping taxes low, and not wasting or squandering taxpayer money.  3- Building up our next generation in values, knowledge, and opportunity is important by keeping out the woke-ideology, encouraging family farms and ranching, and keeping our community safe.

How do you intend to solve these issues?

In the legislature – DEFEND by voting NO on bills that will harm our citizens.  And SUPPORT by voting YES and winsomely working with other Senators to pass good laws and policies that improve the issues above.  Also, work with the Governor to help move these issues that preserve South Dakota.

What do you believe is working for the district, and how will you retain that progression?

True Conservative values – which I promised and which I kept now with great voting history.  Our district is one of the most conservative districts in the state which requires someone with experience and knowledge aligning with our US and SD Constitutions and sticking with the Republican Platform principles of limited Government, lower taxes, individual liberty property rights and more.  Working with other senators, county officials and city officials is important in making sure we are preserving and protecting.

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

I answer every email from constituents who email me. I call people back.  I tell people what my core priorities are in detail and even put them on my advertisements, not just one line slogans, or unknown ‘values’.  I think everything should be transparent in government as it’s taxpayers’ money being spent.  The people are the ‘kings’ of America and we that serve in government are their hired hands to get good work done.  I brought two bills this year in the legislature to make government more transparent.  Ironically, many legislators and government agencies testified against it.

What else do you want people to know about you?

I was the senator who authored and passed the “SAVE SOUTH DAKOTA ACT”, to make sure only citizens are voting in our elections with overwhelming support.  This hopefully encourages our US Senator Thune to pass the SAVE AMERICA ACT soon for the Federal government.

I am also a businessman, with skills in finance (so the state leadership has placed me on the appropriations-budget committee), and skills in people management and a varied degree of topics.  This works well in the legislature as we deal with a lot of different topics and my businesses in hospitality, tourism, amateur farming and ag, and technology all are helpful in the role.

The discussion of data centers coming to South Dakota has been on the rise. Do you support data centers coming to the state?

I support any business coming to the state except immoral businesses (like prostitution, pornography, etc).  I’m a free-market conservative and we are open for business and I love entrepreneurs who run businesses and provide jobs and honest economic growth.  Since datacenters are businesses too, I am fine with them as long as they have guardrails against excessive power usage that could disrupt residential or excessive water usage or noise that impacts our citizens.  Finally, I was one of the key senators that helped stop the tax-credit-state-giveaway of money to lure datacenters here.  To me, our citizens come first, and the ones unhappy about the halt of these data-center-tax credits were those in on the grift of taxpayer money.

Data centers use significant amounts of water and electricity as part of their operations. What legislation should be put in place to protect residents from the inevitable need for more electrical generation and water use?

I voted for Senate Bill 135 “protect residents from increased utility costs and utility shortages caused by data centers and clarify authority to regulate data centers” and it was signed by the governor. 

Tax Incremental Finance Districts (TIFs) are a widely used economic development tool. Do you support their use? Why or why not?

Many TIFs have been abused with extra discretionary spending and loopholes that hurt the citizens.  I supported Senate Bill 228 this year to close some of the overreach of TIFs.  I think we need to keep working on this to be a win-win for the citizens, companies, and the counties or cities that issue them.

Should the state provide greater oversight in mining gravel and sand, especially when it comes to dust? Why or why not?

I had a bill this year to make sure large mining or gravel operations would have to notify citizens in a two mile radius, city council, county commission and the media so people knew about it ahead of time and could speak up if they wanted to: Senate Bill 188 (revise public notice requirements for new sand, gravel, and construction aggregate mines).  Unfortunately, many East River senators didn’t see a benefit to them and several government agencies testified against the bill!  So, I will continue to encourage county and city officials to make sure they have oversight on these mines.

Would you support an increase in the BBB tax, often called the tourism tax, to help offset taxes paid by residents? Why or why not?

No, I am not for tax increases.  I voted against the 4.2% to 4.5% tax increases discussed in the legislature this past year.  Our 4.2% sales tax is the second lowest in the nation.  It is nice that tourists pay that same tax, and I did also support the concept if legislators forced it to go up to 4.5% that we’d give BACK those increased taxes to people in property tax relief.

As the federal government pulls back from funding programs widely used in the state, how or should the legislature backfill the lost revenue?

There are many federal Government programs that fund things that are not always a core role of government.  These federal Government dollars are ALSO South Dakotans’ money – it’s our federal taxes, so we must still be good stewards with it.  There are many organizations who had federal money that also have fundraising programs and those are already being scaled up, through which people can voluntarily contribute. In many cases, I would not say that a backfill is necessary.

William (Bill) Meirose

Name and what you do for a living? 

Dr William (Bill) Meirose Semi-retired and Pastor

What motivated you to run for this office?

To provide a commonsense voice in the legislature to represent the citizens of District 29

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

I am a lifetime resident of Meade County and have over 30 years of service to the community

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I am the past president of the Alliance of Churches in Sturgis

I am the past Executive Director of the South Dakota Joining Forces Initiative

How many local governmental meetings have you attended during the last year and during your candidacy?

I have attended many of the Sturgis City Council meetings, only missing one or two in the past months.

I attended 4 of the legislative sessions during the last session

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Yes, we need to have a variety of sources and viewpoints of the news in our communities

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in your district?

I believe that there are three issues:

School Funding

Property Taxes

Economic Development

How do you intend to solve these issues?

To start with open and honest discussions with all the principal parties to determine what possible actions are available and which of those options require legislative action.    

What do you believe is working for the district, and how will you retain that progression?

The desire of governmental institutions to have open communication with the constituents.  

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

This answers the above question also. Transparency is being available to discuss with the constituents the issues that they bring forward and to be available to discuss the reasons behind the decisions made.  

What else do you want people to know about you?

I have a lifetime history of showing up and doing the job.  I will show up for the people of District 29 and do the job for which I am elected.

The discussion of data centers coming to South Dakota has been on the rise. Do you support data centers coming to the state?

I support the data centers with reservations.  This needs to be a case by case decision.

Data centers use significant amounts of water and electricity as part of their operations. What legislation should be put in place to protect residents from the inevitable need for more electrical generation and water use?

Protection for the residents must be addressed in the permitting process. Each data center will bring their own unique issues.

Tax Incremental Finance Districts (TIFs) are a widely used economic development tool. Do you support their use? Why or why not?

I do support TIFs. I do believe that they need to be used in the manner intended.  Also, there is some language in the laws that needs to be clarified.

Should the state provide greater oversight in mining gravel and sand, especially when it comes to dust? Why or why not?

I believe that there needs to be some changes in the permitting process that allows for better notification to residents, a higher bond for reclamation of the area, and standards for dust control.  The use of county zoning would be very helpful in controlling where mines are allowed.

Would you support an increase in the BBB tax, often called the tourism tax, to help offset taxes paid by residents? Why or why not?

I would have to have more information on this issue before I would issue an opinion.

As the federal government pulls back from funding programs widely used in the state, how or should the legislature backfill the lost revenue?

These decisions would need to be made on an individual program basis.

title: Outdoor warning siren test scheduled in Spearfish
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: SPEARFISH — Spearfish has scheduled a test of its outdoor siren system at 2 p.m., Thursday.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

SPEARFISH — Spearfish has scheduled a test of its outdoor siren system at 2 p.m., Thursday. 

In advance of the siren test, the city will also be testing CivicReady, an electronic emergency alert notification system, by sending out a notification about the siren test minutes before tit begins. 

“We encourage everyone to sign up for this service,” Spearfish Police Chief Collin Smith said. 

He said the free service is used for significant and urgent events impacting the city of Spearfish. Alerts can be received via email, text, or voice call for emergency situations like severe weather, flooding, power outages, power outages, evacuations, and more. 

Users can sign up, edit their preferences or unsubscribe to CivicReady at any time by visiting “Sign up for Emergency Alerts” under “Popular Links” at www.spearfish.gov.

“Please spread the word so your family, friends, and neighbors are aware of the siren test on May 28, and please encourage them to sign up for CivicReady emergency alert notification system,” Smith said. “The more people we can reach during emergencies, the better prepared we are as a community.”

During the 2 p.m. test the sirens will modulate up and down in pitch. People do not need to take any action during the test.

The city currently has emergency sirens located strategically around the community to reach as many outside within hearing distance as possible. The sirens are meant to alert those who are outdoors to seek shelter; not everyone who is indoors will hear the sirens when they sound.

The outdoor warning sirens are activated for severe weather that may pose an immediate threat to life. 

Under ordinary circumstances, when the public hears the sirens, which emit one long tone that does not modulate up and down in pitch, people should take cover in the safest place available in their immediate vicinity as quickly as possible.

title: Spearfish student brings  airsoft gun to high school Friday
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — A Spearfish student was detained and questioned by law enforcement officers after they allegedly brought an airsoft gun to the school.
_full_text:
Spearfish student brings  airsoft gun to high school Friday

SPEARFISH — A Spearfish student was detained and questioned by law enforcement officers after they allegedly brought an airsoft gun to the school.

The incident took place Friday. School officials said the interaction took place in the school’s parking lot.

“During the investigation, officers observed an airsoft gun in the student’s vehicle. Law enforcement immediately removed both the student and the airsoft gun from campus. The student will not be returning to school,” Principal Joe Williams wrote in a message to parents.

“At no point was there a threat to students or staff. The situation was handled quickly and safely in coordination with law enforcement,” he added.

On May 5, a Spearfish student allegedly brought a firearm to the school and exchanged it with another student. Both have subsequently been expelled for a year. 

On May 19, a Sturgis Brown High School student allegedly brought an airsoft gun to the high school. He was met in the parking lot by the school’s resource officer and was arrested.

Both districts have a policy that follows state law. It prohibits dangerous weapons on campus, with a few narrow exceptions for educational or athletic purposes. It also prohibits “look-alike weapons,” which include airsoft guns.

title: Snowbirds allege  poll workers changed them to federal voters without instruction to prove residency
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: SIOUX FALLS — A couple who spend winters in Arizona and the rest of the year in South Dakota said they were given a federal-only ballot and denied a state-local ballot when they tried to vote in person last week at the Minnehaha County administration building.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

SIOUX FALLS — A couple who spend winters in Arizona and the rest of the year in South Dakota said they were given a federal-only ballot and denied a state-local ballot when they tried to vote in person last week at the Minnehaha County administration building.

Instead of retaining their Hartford home when they retired and started traveling south for the winter, Steve Nolte and Kelly Stewart sold their home 4 years ago, bought a recreational vehicle, and parked it year-round at a South Dakota lakeside resort. They use a mail-forwarding service in Sioux Falls, and they’re registered to vote in Minnehaha County.

Since January, state law requires that anyone who lists only a mail forwarding address or post office box — without describing where they actually live — be registered as a federal-only voter when they register or request an absentee ballot. That means the person can only vote in federal contests such as presidential and congressional races — not other statewide, legislative, county, city or local races or ballot questions. The law was motivated partly by some legislators’ opposition to full-time RVers voting in local and state races.

But poll workers didn’t instruct Nolte and Stewart to fill out a form with a description of their living situation before voting, they said later after learning what should have happened. They also cited a lack of communication about the law and how it would impact voters like them.

The 2 have been registered at their mail-forwarding address in Sioux Falls since 2023 and said they have not made any updates since.

“I felt like our voting rights were taken away from us,” Stewart said.

Stewart said she was shocked and frustrated she wasn’t allowed to vote in the Republican governor primary race or legislative primary races. Her ballot had two races on it: primary races for the U.S. Senate and U.S. House of Representatives.

Poll workers noticed the mail-forwarding address and told the couple they could only vote a federal ballot, then changed their voter status in the system without the couple’s permission, Nolte said. The couple said they voted before the voter registration deadline for the June 2 election, so they could have updated their voter registration if needed.

Minnehaha County Auditor Leah Anderson, whose office manages elections in the county, said the couple should have described their address on the envelope that in-person advance voters receive at the polling place and place their ballots in. Stewart and Nolte said they were not instructed to fill out any information on the envelope, until a poll worker told them to sign it before casting their ballot.

Anderson said she was “not immediately available” at the time to guide Stewart and Nolte through the process.

Nolte said the situation is evidence of a lack of “thorough training” regarding mail-forwarding voters and the new law.

The Secretary of State’s Office, which oversees elections at the state level, did not respond to questions from South Dakota Searchlight.

On Thursday, The Dakota Scout published an article in which Anderson and the secretary of state responded to concerns that auditors were incorrectly switching voters at mail-forwarding addresses to federal-only voters. Anderson told the Sioux Falls newspaper that her office is following the secretary of state’s guidance.

State Elections Director Christine Lehrkamp responded with a press release later that day saying “the Secretary of State’s office NEVER said we support the auditor in Minnehaha County and what she does concerning Federal-Only ballots.”

Lehrkamp added that absentee voters must submit an absentee ballot application and describe where they live in order to vote in state and local races. She did not describe how the law is applied to in-person advance voting.

Nolte and Stewart faced discrimination based on their address, said Amber Hobert, president of DakotaPost, which is the mail forwarding business where the couple are clients.

“There’s an idea that none of our customers come here and have a vested interest in South Dakota,” Hobert said. “We do have people who live here, but you’re treating an entire group of people based on what you believe to be, rather than actually giving people an opportunity to meet the requirements of the law.”

Stewart said she understands the purpose of the law.

“We do know people in the RV park down in Arizona that we call ‘fake South Dakota residents,’” Stewart said. “We would hope they wouldn’t vote here because they don’t spend time here. But we pay taxes on food and clothing and other things here.”

The RV park where Stewart and Nolte spend summers and early fall is in Lake County. They plan to register for the November general election using their rented space near Lake Madison as the description of their habitation, listing their private mailbox as their mailing address.

That guidance should have reached voters before they showed up at the polls, said state Rep. Erik Muckey, D-Sioux Falls. His district includes Nolte and Stewart, as well as all registered voters at DakotaPost.

At least 1,500 South Dakota residents have been reclassified as federal-only voters since January, many without realizing it. The Secretary of State’s Office’s online Voter Information Portal — where voters can check their registration status, find their polling place and download a sample ballot — does not show whether a voter is registered as federal-only. A voter can glean if they are federal-only if they attempt to view a sample ballot.

Muckey said the Secretary of State’s Office has not done enough to explain the options available to voters beyond posting the relevant laws on its website and adding the residency warning to election forms.

“Before the general election, the secretary of state has a responsibility when it comes to the rules around how to demonstrate residency, change their voting status and go back to being a local voter,” Muckey said. “How is this going to be communicated with the voting base?”

Muckey said the underlying law needs work, too.

“The only way to tackle this is to talk again about what defines residency and how we make sure people using P.O. boxes as registered voting addresses have a real ability to prove residency,” Muckey said. “If that’s not clear, we won’t have this problem just now but for many elections to come.”

title: Woman killed by bison in Custer State Park, weeks after another visitor was injured
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: A bull bison grazes in South Dakota’s Custer State Park in 2023. Photo by Seth Tupper, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Woman killed by bison in Custer State Park, weeks after another visitor was injured
A bull bison grazes in South Dakota’s Custer State Park in 2023. Photo by Seth Tupper, South Dakota Searchlight 

CUSTER STATE PARK — A 70-year-old Canadian woman died after being struck by a bison last week while hiking with her husband in South Dakota’s Custer State Park, after another park visitor was injured by a bison earlier this month. 

The couple were on the Grace Coolidge Trail and found themselves behind a group of about 5 bull bison, according to the Custer County Sheriff’s Office. The couple paused about 500 yards from the animals and waited for them to continue up the trail and out of sight. The couple then continued hiking, came around a corner and encountered the bulls at a distance of 50 yards.

The couple stopped again, and then continued trailing the bison as the animals moved away. A bull eventually broke from the group, charged the woman, hooked her and tossed her into the air. 

The woman died from her injuries.

Custer State Park is managed by the Department of Game, Fish and Parks. Spokesperson Nick Harrington said staff moved the bison from the area and are monitoring the animal’s behavior “to ensure public safety and prevent future incidents.” He said dry conditions have caused bison to spread throughout the park in search of grass, increasing the chance that visitors may encounter them on trails.

Harrington said park visitors should keep their distance from wildlife, make noise while hiking, use caution around corners and ridges, and keep pets on leashes.

“It’s important to remember that bison are wild animals and need to be treated as such,” Harrington said in a written statement. “Visitors are reminded to keep their distance from all wild animals and safely enjoy both the trails and wildlife within the park.”

On May 1, a 22-year-old hiker encountered a bison while hiking the Lost Trails by Center Lake, Harrington said in response to South Dakota Searchlight questions about prior incidents. The hiker was with a friend and their dog when they rounded a corner. 

“The hiker was struck by the buffalo on the back of her legs and was transported to a local hospital with non-life-threatening injuries,” Harrington said.

Harrington said the department is not aware of any other incidents involving bison within Custer State Park this year, and there had not been a fatal incident involving a bison in the park since 2001.

The 110-square-mile park in the Black Hills is home to a herd of about 1,400 bison, also known as buffalo. Bull bison can stand up to 7 feet tall at the shoulders, weigh 2,000 pounds and run up to 35 mph, according to the department.

title: Cano, Brengle honored by Meade School District
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: The annual Meade School staff recognition banquet was held on Thursday and Deb Cano, right, was selected as Teacher of the Year and Tina Brengle was named Support Staff of the Year.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
Cano, Brengle honored by Meade School District
The annual Meade School staff recognition banquet was held on Thursday and Deb Cano, right, was selected as Teacher of the Year and Tina Brengle was named Support Staff of the Year.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

STURGIS — The Meade School District recognized two outstanding staff members for their dedication and service to students, staff, and the community, naming Deb Cano as Teacher of the Year and Tina Brengle as Support Staff of the Year at the staff recognition banquet on Thursday.

Cano, a longtime educator in the district, was honored for her leadership, innovation in the classroom, mentorship of fellow teachers, and the positive relationships she builds with students and families.

“It means so much,” Cano said about receiving the award. “I have great colleagues, and there’s so many people that have helped me get to where I am today, and I’m so appreciative of everyone. I love working with the kids. They make every day unique, and there’s never a dull moment.”

Throughout the nomination process, colleagues, students, parents, and administrators praised Cano for her compassion, professionalism, and commitment to student success. Testimonials described her as approachable, caring, and dedicated to helping every student grow academically and personally.

Cano has served on the PASS Team, instructional council, and department leadership teams while also mentoring new teachers and supporting staff development initiatives. She helped lead Small Learning Communities for freshmen and has coached volleyball and coordinated community sports programs.

Supporters highlighted her ability to create a safe and encouraging classroom environment where students feel comfortable taking risks and building confidence. Her use of innovative instructional strategies, technology integration, and hands-on learning activities were also recognized as strengths that help meet the needs of diverse learners.

Cano earned a master’s degree in curriculum and instruction and continues to stay involved in curriculum review and professional development opportunities. She regularly incorporates educational technology platforms such as Infinite Campus, Planbook, Quizizz, and Pear Deck into her teaching.

Students and parents shared how Cano’s encouragement, patience, and belief in her students have made a lasting impact both inside and outside the classroom. Many described her as a role model who inspires resilience, critical thinking, and confidence.

Brengle, who serves as the technology and curriculum administrative assistant, was recognized for her outstanding technical expertise, leadership, and behind-the-scenes work that helps keep district operations running smoothly.

“I am truly honored to receive this,” Brengle said. “But I want to acknowledge that so many others are equally deserving of this recognition. This is a reflection of teamwork, support, and shared success. I am grateful to be part of a community where everyone’s contributions matter. Thank you.”

Nominations and letters of recommendation described Brengle as dependable, resourceful, proactive, and always willing to help staff and students. Colleagues praised her calm and solution-oriented approach to challenges and her ability to quickly learn and implement new systems and technologies.

Brengle played a key role in revising district procedures, including helping lead a district-wide overhaul of the K-4 report card system in Infinite Campus. Her work streamlined grading processes and saved teachers significant time each grading period.

She also resolved complex rostering issues for Homeschool Connection students, improving enrollment accuracy and daily operations across the district. In addition, Brengle manages curriculum access for more than 30 online platforms while overseeing technology inventory, repairs, and surplus management.

Fellow staff members noted that Brengle’s work often happens behind the scenes, but her contributions directly impact classroom success and district efficiency every day. Testimonials described her as hardworking, positive, flexible, and someone who creates a supportive work environment for everyone around her.

District officials said both Cano and Brengle exemplify the commitment, leadership, and dedication that make a lasting difference for students, staff, and the Meade community.

title: Development agreement approved for The Pines on St. Onge Rd. in Spearfish
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Community Development Director Peter Wysocki, pictured left, and Assistant Planning Director Jaymia Ecker are pictured answering citizen questions and presenting the development agreement for The Pines. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Development Agreement 1.JPG
Community Development Director Peter Wysocki, pictured left, and Assistant Planning Director Jaymia Ecker are pictured answering citizen questions and presenting the development agreement for The Pines. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — The Spearfish City Council unanimously approved a development agreement with BA Investments and SLH Holdings, the developers of The Pines at Elkhorn Ridge.  The Pines is not affiliated with Elkhorn Ridge Resort or RV Park, but it will be a neighboring multi-family development.

The developers plan to build a 98-unit apartment complex on the 28-acre parcel adjacent to Peaceful Pines senior living facility on St. Onge Road.

The city council approved the development plan for the project on March 2.

The development agreement, approved unanimously on March 18, establishes the developer’s responsibilities related to the construction and maintenance of public improvements, including utilities, roads, stormwater infrastructure, open space, and recreational path infrastructure.

“This agreement balances the responsibilities of both the developer and the city as it relates to the construction and maintenance of public improvements,” said Jaymia Ecker, the city’s assistant planning director. “At this point in time, the developer, of course, is responsible for installing that infrastructure, and then in the future you would see this come before council to dedicate that infrastructure, at which time it would become the city’s to own and maintain.”

In addition to installing utilities and roads, the developer will also construct a 1/3 mile stretch of rec path on the west side of St. Onge Road.

“That, along with the planned extension of the rec path from exit 14 to the intersection, will enable a continuous connection, non-motorized, from one end of town to the other, which is something we are pretty excited about,” Ecker said.

That 1/3 mile stretch of paved walking path has to be a minimum of 5 feet wide.

“Through negotiation of this development plan, the DRD, as well as the TIF, they did agree to install it at 8 feet. In order to bring that up to our standards for rec path at 10 feet, we are proposing a cost share in which the city would share in the cost of the difference, which comes out to just over $58,000. It breaks out to an 80/20 cost share with the city contributing 20% there,” Ecker said. “That was not included in the TIF plan.”

 Development Agreement 2.JPG
Spearfish citizen Jeremy Smith asks questions about the development agreement for The Pines in Spearfish. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

Before the city council voted to approve the agreement and cost share, Spearfish citizen Jeremy Smith asked about the rec path portion of the document.

“Part of my question on that cost share agreement on the rec path, because I am very excited about that,” Smith said. “A large portion of that rec path is happening in the area that the city council just approved a TIF for. TIF 10. That rec path infrastructure was part of that TIF agreement, is my understanding. It feels like a strange double-dipping as a citizen to get the TIF agreement, plus them coming in asking for a cost share to have us fund this infrastructure.”

Smith asked if the council might delay approval of the agreement.

“In that document, it is my understanding that the rec path requirement is for the 10-foot width. I think there are other places in the development agreement where the developers are meeting the new standards that haven’t been adopted, so I don’t know why they wouldn’t also meet the standards for the rec path or why the city might not table this development agreement until finalizing the design standards and then having the developer uphold our new or upcoming standards,” Smith said.

After the council approved the development agreement as written, Community Development Director Peter Wysocki took time to address Smith’s concern.

“It is our due process to review applications based on the standards that are adopted when the standards are submitted. We can’t purposely delay applications until new standards are adopted. That makes sense, right?” Wysocki said. “It creates a legal risk.”

Wysocki also noted recommended sizes for dedicated park space might appear in the Parks and Recreation Master Plan, but unless they are also adopted in code, the guidelines are just that. Guidelines.  

“The council did adopt the master plan, but we do not reference the parks and recreation master plan in our code,” Wysocki explained.

In the case of The Pines, the Spearfish Parks, Recreation, and Forestry Board did not recommend dedicating park space in the development.  

“We do have park space that is zoned in the exhibit that is associated with the multifamily that did go before both the planning commission and the parks, rec, and forestry advisory board. Ultimately, they did not recommend decimation of that park to the city because it doesn’t quite meet the standards in the park’s master plan as far as size and amenities go,” Ecker said. “Consistent with staff’s recommendation, the advisory board is not recommending that we take that on for ownership and maintenance, although there is a public access easement through that area, so we will have public access, but the city won’t be on the hook for maintaining that facility.”

title: Growing holes in mining museum display lot prompt closure while board considers options
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Black Hills Mining Museum board has fenced off its display lot on Main Street while it considers options to fix infrastructure problems. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
mining museum 1.jpeg
The Black Hills Mining Museum board has fenced off its display lot on Main Street while it considers options to fix infrastructure problems. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

 mining museum 2.jpeg
One of the solutions the Black Hills Mining Museum board is considering includes removing items that are being stored underneath the Main Street asphalt lot, then removing the asphalt from the top, and creating display space on the Julius Street side of the museum. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

LEAD — The Black Hills Mining Museum is in the process of assessing damage to a display lot next to the museum entrance, with an eye toward removing the lot entirely. 

Gordon Phillips, executive director of the museum said recently small holes in the former parking lot that holds some mine cars and other displays, have grown bigger and prompted the board to hire an engineering firm to assess the problem. Interstate Engineering examined the problem and delivered a report with several recommendations, including blocking the lot off to pedestrian traffic. The area will be blocked off for the summer, until the board finds a permanent solution to the problem, Phillips said. 

Phillips added that the problem is the parking lot asphalt that was laid on top of an original cement foundation. Asphalt is more porous, and cracks as water seeps through. But when the water reaches the cement it stops moving and causes deterioration. The lot was the site of the Hearst Mercantile store, that burned down in the 1940s. In its place, the Red Owl store was built on the same foundation. Those foundations are not holding up very well, and will need to be fixed, he said. 

But the cost of removing the top of the lot and rebuilding it could be prohibitive for the Black Hills Mining Museum board, that is preparing to re-start a capital campaign for a vision to build a new building at Gold Run Park. While Phillips said board members want to responsibly fix the deteriorating lot, pouring a lot of money into the project doesn’t align with the board’s long-range plan. 

“Basically, we’re not planning on being here long term,” he said. “Our plans are still to relocate. We need to do that for obvious reasons, this being one of them. So, I need an economical plan. We’re not trying to shore everything up forever. It’s just kind of to get us by for the two or three years or whatever it would take.” 

Phillips said engineers are still examining solutions and working on cost estimates for solutions to present to the board. The most likely solution, he said, will be to remove the asphalt lot at the Main Street entrance, and open up a lower lot on the Julius Street side of the museum. That lower lot, which is currently used for storage, would be cleared out and the museum will establish displays for the public in that area. Phillips said the board hopes to be able to do that by October this year. 

“First we will pull everything out and hopefully find a place to store it temporarily,” Phillips said of the items that are being stored underneath the asphalt lot, on the Julius Street side of the building. “Then we will take the things off the top, and then they’re gonna have to figure out how all this comes down. You can see it goes right up to the wall of our building, and it does the same thing  on the street side. So, when it all comes down, then we would be down here with some of our displays. So we will take it from not a very useful space, and try to turn it into a much more productive space while we’re here.” 

Until the board is able to address the problem, Phillips said the lot does not pose a safety risk. Though he declined to share the engineering report with the Pioneer, Phillips said there is no imminent risk of failure, and the measures to block the lot off to foot traffic are precautionary. 

“The board is basically waiting until they have full engineering estimates and everything, to decide what to do,” he said. “We haven’t approved any work or contract for how all that’s going to happen.” 

The damage to the lot is one of the many reasons the board is working toward building a new facility at Gold Run Park. The plan, which was unveiled in December 2021, was for a multi-million dollar ADA accessible building that included display space, a lobby, climate-controlled archive rooms, and a large parking lot that can accommodate busses. After more than 3 years of fundraising toward that goal, members of the former board cancelled the capital campaign and pledged to use dollars to improve the current facility. But during the Black Hills Mining Museum membership meeting in January, members voted to replace 7 of the 10 existing board members, with museum leaders who supported the new facility. In February the remaining 3 board members resigned. 

“We would be better served to be down at Gold Run Park location, because there we would have our own dedicated parking, we have more places for busses, RV trailers and stuff,” Phillips said. “Staying at this location doesn’t do anything to fulfill our business plan of getting those busses out. I’ve had people ask why can’t you just stay here, and the biggest reason is parking and we need to get more people through the door. Not being able to have necessary parking limits that. If you fix this, I can get cars, but I still can’t get the busses and that’s really important.” 

The capital campaign is still publicly suspended, but Phillips said one of the first acts of the new board was to formally reaffirm its dedication to the new building project. Now, Phillips said the museum board is working with Homestake officials to secure a deal to build in Gold Run Park. 

“Once that is done we’ll go back into active fundraising,” Phillips said.

title: Work on new MS track, field underway
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Four feet of substandard soil will be removed from the Spearfish Middle School track and field area. New fill will be brought in to prevent the new asphalt from cracking. Pioneer photo by Mark Watson
_full_text:
Work on new MS track, field underway 2.JPG
Four feet of substandard soil will be removed from the Spearfish Middle School track and field area. New fill will be brought in to prevent the new asphalt from cracking. Pioneer photo by Mark Watson 

 Work on new MS track, field underway.JPG
Construction crews got underway last week to replace the Spearfish Middle School track and field. Pioneer photo by Mark Watson 

SPEARFISH — Crews from Mammoth Sports Construction, LLC, have begun work on replacing the Spearfish Middle School track and field.

The existing track and field were constructed more than 30 years ago.

Built on sub-par soil, the asphalt that comprises the track, has cracked, and even a few potholes have appeared. The field also has drainage issues.

In January, the Spearfish School Board approved the replacement of the facility at a cost of $2,742,000 contract.

Kirk Easton, superintendent of the Spearfish School District, told board members in January, that he would try to attain at least 20 percent of the cost from donations or in-kind donations. That would be approximately $550,000, on Thursday he told the Pioneer that approximately $760,000 has been secured thus far.

The contract with Mammoth also allows for a deduction of $78,400 for the district to haul off and dispose of the “earthwork spoils” from the field, and another $52,320 deduction for the spoils of the track area. The contractor that is performing the hauling for the project will be taking the spoils to their location, he added.

The area consisting of the current track and field, will have 4 feet of soil excavated, to remove the substandard, clay-based dirt. School officials said that if this was not done, the new asphalt for the track would likely crack within months. New fill will be brought in, and the field will consist of artificial turf.

The warranty for the base of the drainage is a lifetime warranty, the turf as an 8-year warranty, and the track has a 5-year warranty.

The district had debated the topic for several months before approving the bid. The original cost was higher, but the district and Mammoth officials scaled back the design to reduce the cost.

Similar work is also underway in Sturgis at Woodle Field.

PiedmontMayoralComp.jpg

Voters in Piedmont will head to the polls June 2 to vote on a open mayoral seat. Two people are running for 1 open position which is a 5-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. We are publishing their responses verbatim although some answers may have been edited slightly for length without changing the context of their answer.

Aaron Clendenin

 Clendenin, Aaron.jpg
Aaron Clendenin 

Name and what you do for a living? 

Aaron Clendenin, Small Business Owner  

What motivated you to run for this office?

I’m running to help ensure Piedmont has a city government that is transparent, fair, and ethical; and that residents can trust.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

I’m a longtime Piedmont resident who genuinely cares about our people and our future. I want to bring steady, practical leadership that supports smart growth while protecting what makes our community special.

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I have not held an elected public office or a nonprofit leadership office previously.

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

I’ve attended more than a dozen local government meetings over the past year and during my candidacy. 

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

Yes. Local newspapers play an important role in keeping residents informed, increasing transparency, and helping people stay engaged in decisions that affect our community.

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in Piedmont?

Improving and maintaining infrastructure

Supporting business growth to increase sales revenue and create jobs

Planning for responsible community growth that benefits families and residents

How do you intend to solve these issues?

Hold regular public meetings to listen to residents, set priorities, and track progress.

Use responsible budgeting, long-term planning, and pursue available grants and outside funding.

Create incentives and a welcoming environment for business development and job creation.

Partner with families, schools, and community members to identify needs and invest in opportunities for youth and families.

What do you believe is working for Piedmont, and how will you retain that progression?

Piedmont’s biggest strength is its people. This is a community that cares deeply about where we live and takes pride in our town. To keep that momentum going, I’ll focus on investing in our youth, supporting and promoting our local businesses, and creating more opportunities for community involvement, so residents feel connected and heard. 

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

Transparency means residents can clearly see what decisions are made, why they’re made, how money is spent, and who is responsible—without having to dig for answers.

As mayor, I will communicate priorities and spending in plain language, ensure agendas are posted early, share regular updates, and stay accessible through office hours and community forums. I will explain decisions—even when people disagree—and report progress openly. My goal is simple: no surprises—just honest, open government that earns trust.

What else do you want people to know about you?

I’m a proud husband and father of two daughters, and family is at the center of why I care so much about Piedmont’s future. I love the natural beauty of the Black Hills—whether I’m hiking, fishing, hunting, or spending time outdoors with family and friends. 

Most importantly, I believe Piedmont is a community of honest, hardworking people who look out for one another. That’s the spirit I want to protect and build on through respectful leadership, open communication, and decisions that put families, safety, and long-term community growth first.

John Parks

 Parks, John(MUG).jpg
John L. (Jack) Parks 

Name and what you do for a living?     

John L. (Jack) Parks   Retired Blacksmith

What motivated you to run for this office?

Long time resident with interest in making a better community.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

Experience with 18 years as Vice President on this council and common sense to deal with the unknowns.

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

18 years as VP Piedmont city council, Past President of Dakota Artist Blacksmith Association, Past President of Piedmont Park Board

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

Approx. 50

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

The public needs to be fully informed but digital media is taking over.

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in Piedmont?

Piedmont needs a sewer system badly which when built will encourage business, then jobs will follow.

How do you intend to solve these issues?

Apply for grants and be frugal with taxpayers monies.

What do you believe is working for Piedmont, and how will you retain that progression?

The volunteerism in Piedmont is tremendous working to a common goal. Pointing out those common needs will focus these efforts.

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

Open meeting laws insure that transparency and I encourage people to participate in our discussions at the meetings.

What else do you want people to know about you?

Caring long time veteran resident, with some engineering experience along with blacksmithing which percolates down to knowing how things work.

Voters in Piedmont will head to the polls June 2 to vote on a open city commission seat. 2 people are running for 1 open position which is a 4-year term. The Black Hills Pioneer emailed questions to the candidates. Benjamin Neill

 Neill, Benjamin.jpg
Benjamin Neill 

Name and what you do for a living? 

My name is Benjamin Neill and I am a construction project manager.

What motivated you to run for this office?

I have always been motivated to run for an office position after watching my grandfather become mayor for Clark, SD when I was young.  After attending several city meetings and speaking with some locals to gauge interest I decided it was time to enter the race for a four year term for city council.

Why do you think you are best qualified for this position?

My younger age brings fresh perspective on the progression of community growth.  I have a deep knowledge of construction and deal with ordinances and state laws on a regular basis.  I am also a compassionate person who likes to work with people for the greater good of the community. 

With regards to leadership, what other elected public or nonprofit offices have you held?

I have not held an elected public or nonprofit office yet.  I have earned myself leadership positions at several jobs since 2012 and held a voluntary position in the Horton Inc. United Way Committee for several years while living in Britton, SD. 

How many local governmental meetings have you attended within the last year and during your candidacy?

My wife and I have attended nearly every city meeting and cracker barrel along with a few Meade County and one Summerset city meeting since November of 2025. 

Do you believe local newspapers are important? Why or why not?

I truly do believe local newspapers are important.  Even more so than social media.  Although social media can be a great tool for getting information out at lightning speed it can be horribly misused as a vehicle to misinform.  Newspapers can make mistakes from time to time but typically provide professional trusted in-depth coverage of global and local news.

What are the most important issues that need to be addressed in Piedmont?

I’m sure everyone is thinking the same thing while reading this question and that is the proposed gravel pit on the edge of our beautiful town being our number one issue.  While I do acknowledge this as being a huge issue I believe we have more on the horizon with Rapid City quickly expanding and putting pressure on our small town.  I believe Piedmont should be allowed to have its own growth but not at the expense of its small town safety and charm. 

How do you intend to solve these issues?

There wont be a magic pill to make any of the issues just go away.  It will take a proactive approach from here on out and not a reactive approach.  Proper consulting and ordinances would need to be in place.  I would listen to people in this community.  We have smart people here that have good ideas but are constantly shut down because they are not “lawyers.”  We have neighbors dealing with the same issues.  We need to be able to lean on each other. 

What do you believe is working for Piedmont, and how will you retain that progression?

Piedmont has made fantastic effort in infrastructure improvement with public water installation, road, and sidewalk installation.  Piedmont is also quick to address issues for people in the community.  I would love to be in this postition to continue to assist Piedmont in working towards its goals of improving the community’s living standards and providing safety for the residents.

What does transparency in government mean to you, and how do you plan to be transparent to your constituents with your decisions?

Transparancy in government is operating openly and honestly giving the citizens timely correct data that should be open to the public.  I am just like everyone else.  I don’t like negative surprises so I would do everything in my power to make sure people are not in the dark where transparancy should exist.   

What else do you want people to know about you?

When I am not working I enjoy spending time with my wife exploring the Black Hills, going to concerts, fishing, attending hockey games, and watching dirt track racing.  We also enjoy volunteering up in Keystone during the Haunting of Keystone.  In the short amount of time we have been here my wife and I have deeply fallen in love with Piedmont and its citizens and I hope to have the opportunity to serve this wonderful town.

Phil Aitken

title: Board of Regents ‘leaning in’ to AI while  planning to regulate its use at SD universities
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: CUSTER — South Dakota universities are “leaning in” to artificial intelligence, state Board of Regents President Jeff Partridge said at a Wednesday meeting in Custer.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

CUSTER — South Dakota universities are “leaning in” to artificial intelligence, state Board of Regents President Jeff Partridge said at a Wednesday meeting in Custer.

The system that oversees the state’s public universities plans to formulate regulations for AI use throughout 2026 and 2027, focusing on how the technology should be governed; how to teach students, faculty and staff to use it; and how to implement it into curriculum and research.

Board members said the plan will help prepare students to use AI ethically and effectively once they graduate.

“We want to lead in this area with our students,” Partridge said. “We’re excited for them to be career-ready, AI prepared and technology prepared.”

Starting this summer, the Board of Regents plans to implement a “systemwide strategy” to use AI, spokeswoman Shuree Mortenson said in an emailed statement.

The board’s information technology team will work with a committee to select “a systemwide technology solution to be implemented and utilized across the system,” according to the document presented on Wednesday. 

AI is already being used at the campus level within the system, Mortenson added. South Dakota State University launched an AI center this spring. President Barry Dunn said during a town hall last month that different approaches to AI use by universities could create educational disparities in the state.

The systemwide strategy isn’t about “taking over” the work that specific schools have done, Mortenson said, but rather “making it work together better over time.”

“As part of this plan, the system will look at where using shared tools or solutions would be a good idea, especially when there are advantages in terms of how much it costs, how secure it is, or how consistent it is,” Mortenson said.

The system plans to build the underlying infrastructure this summer — such as security, data management and design — and roll out tools to users in the fall. No final decisions have been made, Mortenson said.

The plan also calls for a pilot program this fall using “agentic AI” — technology that can act independently, such as with scheduling and processing forms — to reduce administrative workload.

Rules governing AI use across the system — covering data privacy, ethical guardrails and alignment with the university system’s mission — will be recommended to the board by its October meeting.

Each campus will use its existing teaching support center to train faculty on using AI in the classroom and handling students’ AI use in coursework. AI is expected to be integrated into curriculum by fall 2027, based on recommendations from the system’s academic affairs council at the Board’s December meeting.

Board members acknowledged hesitancy among faculty and students. No one spoke against the plan at the meeting, though Partridge acknowledged the use of AI “in some areas” makes board members “uncomfortable” as well.

“You just kind of want to do it right and you want to be very engaged, but at the same time we’re moving forward,” Partridge said.
