title: Flag etiquette program at West Elementary
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Flag etiquette program at West Elementary
Courtesy photo 

SPEARFISH — On May 18, the Spearfish Veterans Honor Guard and the Black Hills Chapter of the American Legion Riders #164, started the day with a meaningful flag etiquette program for 165 first graders. Students were reminded why it is so important to respect our American flag. 

Micheline Nelson, Riders secretary said, “respecting the flag stands for the freedoms, sacrifices, and values that built our nation over the past 250 years. As America celebrates its 250th birthday throughout 2026, it is an opportunity for us to help the next generation of young patriots to understand the importance of citizenship, service, unity, and gratitude.” 

Nelson explained the difference between Armed Forces Day, Veterans Day, and Memorial Day. 

“Memorial Day reminds us that freedom has never been free. Thousands of Americans gave their lives defending our country, our Constitution, and the liberties we enjoy every day,” she said. “Today, by learning how to show respect to our flag, you honor the memory of those who served, sacrificed, and died for our country will never be forgotten.” 

When students learned to stand respectfully during the National Anthem, the Pledge of Allegiance to the flag, and know how to handle the flag properly, or pause to honor veterans and fallen service members, they show respect to the many men and women who sacrificed everything so we could live in a free nation.

Respect for the flag also helps us show pride in our community and our country. It encourages all of us to appreciate the blessings we have while recognizing the responsibilities that come with being Americans. Those lessons become even more important as we celebrate America’s 250th birthday and reflect on the generations who will carry our nation forward through peace, war, hardship, and service. 

The Spearfish Veterans Honor Guard showed the students the proper folding and unfolding of the flag. Students and staff were united as when the honor guard unfolded a “piece of cloth” that became a symbol of our nation and freedom, the American Flag.

title: The wall and on the web New ways to honor SD Vietnam vets
byline: By Bart Pfankuch South Dakota News Watch
description: RAPID CITY — In 28 years of being Timothy Bjork’s best friend, travel buddy and devoted wife, Bonnie Bjork said there was one topic that her “Tim” was reluctant to talk about.
_full_text:
RAPID CITY — In 28 years of being Timothy Bjork’s best friend, travel buddy and devoted wife, Bonnie Bjork said there was one topic that her “Tim” was reluctant to talk about.

His 2 tours of duty in the Vietnam War.

Tim died in March 2025 at age 77 from multiple cancers tied to his military service. Bonnie said she can’t be 100% certain why he didn’t discuss the war.

But she knew him well and suspects it was because that while Tim was proud of his service and the important non-combat medical supply duties he performed, he was also somewhat bitter.

He was put off, Bonnie believes, because he was compelled to serve by the draft in an unpopular war that was horrific for both sides.

It bothered him that he was so disrespected by his fellow Americans that he had to change out of his Army uniform and into civilian clothes to avoid harassment at airports when he arrived home from war.

And – perhaps most of all – Tim came to realize that his service in Cam Ranh Bay and Phu Bai Combat Base exposed him to the carcinogenic defoliant Agent Orange, which would cast a constant shadow over his health and ultimately take his life.

“There was some anger in there, and he felt guilty about some of the things that we did to people over there,” Bonnie said.

And yet, Tim quietly supported his fellow veterans and support organizations. He spoke frequently with other sick soldiers he met at the VA hospital in Sturgis to soothe them, and he gave money to the Veterans of Foreign Wars and the Disabled American Veterans.

Decades after the war, Bonnie said Tim underwent a shift and began to open up more about the war and became more accepting of any appreciation he received for his service in Vietnam.

With that sentiment in mind, Bonnie said she believes Tim would welcome two posthumous forms of recognition he and other South Dakota veterans of Vietnam will receive in June.

From June 11-14, Tim and a few dozen other South Dakota veterans will be feted in Brookings when “The Wall that Heals” arrives to honor veterans killed in Vietnam and those who served there and have died since.

The healing wall is a three-quarter sized replica of the Vietnam Veterans Memorial wall that contains the names of fallen service members in Washington.

The traveling wall will be open to the public 24 hours a day from Thursday, June 11, through 2 p.m. Sunday, June 14, at the Fishback Soccer Complex, 1100 20th St. S. in Brookings.

Then, on June 20, Tim and two other late residents of South Dakota will be among 768 Vietnam veterans who will be formally inducted into the “In Memory” program run by the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Fund (VVMF) at a ceremony in Washington.

The names of the new honorees, including the three veterans from South Dakota, will be read aloud starting at 10 a.m. Eastern Time on June 20 in a ceremony on the East Knoll of the wall memorial. The ceremony will be shown live on the VVMF website.

Here are the 3, 2026 South Dakota In Memory honorees and links to their personal information pages on the memorial website:

• Timothy M. Bjork, of Rapid City. Born May 4, 1947, and died March 3, 2025. Worked for former South Dakota Department of Environment and Natural Resources and for South Dakota Parks and Wildlife Foundation. Due to exposure to Agent Orange in Vietnam, Bjork died of metastatic skin cancer.

• Theodore G. Knudsen, of Rosholt. Born Jan. 10, 1948, and died July 25, 2024. Served in Army in Vietnam, where he was awarded the Purple Heart, Bronze Star with “V” device, Air Medal, Army Commendation Medal, Combat Infantry Badge, and Parachutist Badge. Knudson worked as an administrator and coach in five school districts, including in Gregory, Wessington and Bowdle. He suffered post-traumatic stress disorder and exposure to Agent Orange in Vietnam and died of dementia.

• Gregory J. Overholt of Piedmont. Born March 21, 1948, and died July 17, 2025. Overholt served in the Army in Vietnam. He worked as a military recruiter and later retired as a corrections administrator at the Pennington County Sheriff’s Department. No cause of death was listed.Anyone interested in nominating a veteran for the In Memory program can visit https://www.vvmf.org/In-Memory-Program/ 

to learn the details.

title: Homestake Opera  House to host  ‘Raising the Light’ gala
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Pictures of the opera house chandelier as it appeared in the theater before the fire, and after the fire, are on display in the theater. The chandelier will be a focal point during the annual Historic Homestake Opera House gala, May 30. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
opera house gala1.jpeg
Pictures of the opera house chandelier as it appeared in the theater before the fire, and after the fire, are on display in the theater. The chandelier will be a focal point during the annual Historic Homestake Opera House gala, May 30. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

LEAD — “Raising the Light” will be the theme for the annual Historic Homestake Opera House gala. 

The event, scheduled for 5:30 p.m. May 30, will feature the original Tiffany glass chandelier on display in its current state, serving as a powerful symbol of the ongoing mission to restore the Opera House to its full Gilded Age prominence.

“We’re using the original chandelier as a focal point, to really highlight the love that’s being poured into this place,” said Todd Jones, executive director of the Historic Homestake Opera House. “If we focus on the light, if we pursue the light, as we do that we see things st art to get done and start to be completed and back to where they should be. So it’s really meant to be a symbol of what we’re up to.” 

Jones said the theme also reminds people of what the opera house means to the community. 

“We’re encouraging people to really consider what this place has meant to them,” he said. “It’s been kind of a light to the community and how it really needs to continue to be that. It needs to have the ability to shine as something that’s an economic generator for the community. It’s something that’s an anchor business for Lead. It needs to be shining its light and the way it shines its light is for the community to come in and engage it, to use their gifts here and to go to classes here and all those things that we love to do, to experience events and be on stage, and the whole gamut of that.”

During the event, Scotte Burns will serve as the keynote speaker. Burns, of Spearfish, spent a decade traveling the country conducting research. He will draw from his philosophical presentation, “The Ultimate Reality,” and share insights from his work “Journeys to Love,” his 6-year, 100,000 motorcycle exploration of human connection. 

Austin, Texas-based singer-songwriter Keith Hampton will also play selections from his album release party, which will also be held at the opera house, June 1.

In addition to performances in the theater, the gala will feature a full dinner in the atrium, and a silent auction of special items from the opera house. Some items will include antique chairs, old windows from the library, and old pictures.. 

“It’s all things that are coming out of the opera house,” Jones said. “We’ll have letters of authenticity with those too, so if people do purchase them they know this is actually where this came from.

All funds raised during the gala event will go to support operations and programming at the opera house.

title: Headed to The Show: McAdoo 1st Spearfish Sasquatch player to reach major leagues
byline: By Jason Gross Black Hills Pioneer
description: Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Charles McAdoo_6469.JPG
Pioneer file photo 

SPEARFISH — Former Spearfish Sasquatch baseball player Charles McAdoo is headed to The Show.

 0529 Charles McAdoo.jpeg
Courtesy photo 

He earned a promotion to the Major Leagues Wednesday, as he is now a member of the Toronto Blue Jays’ 40-man roster. He is the first member of the Sasquatch, the collegiate wood-bat team, to make it to the majors.

McAdoo is a native of Walnut Creek, Calif., and played for Spearfish during the 2021 Expedition League season. He earned team and league Most Valuable Player honors that season, hitting .372 with 8 home runs and 81 RBI.

“When you watched him play, practice and prepare, you just knew he was going places on the baseball field,” Spearfish Sasquatch owner/general manager Eric Schmidt said in a release as he described McAdoo during that 2021 campaign.

Schmidt said McAdoo was a leader in the dugout who helped with putting on the team’s youth camps and attended other community events.

The Pittsburgh Pirates drafted McAdoo in the 13th round of the 2023 draft. He played for single-A Bradenton in the Florida State League and hit .302 with 5 home runs and 24 RBI.

 SAS Charles McAdoo.JPG
Charles McAdoo played for the Spearfish Sasquatch during the 2021 campaign. Five years later, he has earned a callup to the major leagues for the Toronto Blue Jays. Pioneer file photos 

McAdoo started 2024 in the Pirates’ organization before joining the Toronto Blue Jays. He played for the Pirates’ minor-league teams in Altoona (double-A) and Greensboro (A-plus) before spending 37 games with the Blue Jays’ New Hampshire affiliate in the double-A Eastern League.

He batted .279 in a total of 124 games in 2024, including 17 home runs with 78 RBI and 21 stolen bases.

McAdoo stayed with New Hampshire in 2025 and played 121 games. He hit 16 home runs and drove in 45 runs while stealing 34 bases.

The 2026 season for McAdoo started with Buffalo in the triple-A International League. McAdoo played 49 games, hitting .250 with 8 home runs and 27 RBI prior to this week’s callup. He has also stolen 6 bases.

McAdoo is anticipated to be on the Blue Jays’ roster for this weekend’s series in Baltimore against the Orioles.

Schmidt enjoys talking with potential host families for each Sasquatch season. 

“I always say, ‘You never know, but you could host a future big leaguer. How cool would that be?;” Schmidt said in recalling his sales pitch. That has now become a reality.

“I couldn’t be more excited about Charles achieving what every player dreams of doing,” Schmidt said. He added this is a huge accomplishment for McAdoo and the Sasquatch organization.

title: NH Rec Association bike bash  fosters community on 2 wheels
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: LEAD — The decision to move the Schools Out Bike Bash from its planned location in Manuel Brothers Park to the Handley Center did not dampen spirits, but only seemed to add to the sense of community, as more than 100 kids and their parents celebrated 2 wheels.
_full_text:
LEAD — The decision to move the Schools Out Bike Bash from its planned location in Manuel Brothers Park to the Handley Center did not dampen spirits, but only seemed to add to the sense of community, as more than 100 kids and their parents celebrated 2 wheels. 

The second annual event organized by the Northern Hills Recreation Association drew a significant crowd of more than 100 kids and more than 50 adults for food, prizes, fun, and a chance to get their bicycles ready for summer riding. Professional bicycle mechanics from Strider Bikes, Black Hills Bicycles of Rapid City, Rushmore Bikes of Spearfish, and SRAM/Quarq of Spearfish provided free bicycle maintenance and repairs. The Northern Hills Recreation Center gave away 15 bicycles of various sizes, bike air pumps, bike locks, free food, and more. Several kids also applied to receive newly refurbished bicycles through the organization’s free bike program. Monument Health provided bike helmets for about 100 kids. 

“Because of the stormy weather, we were incredibly thankful to the Handley Center for welcoming us in,” board members from the Northern Hills Recreation Association said in a statement. “It was a great place to come together for an amazing evening. The goal of every kid in our community having a bike is now a little bit closer.”

title: Malt beverage license approved for Boar’s Nest, subject to reapproval in 2027
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: The malt beverage license for The Boar’s Nest, a restaurant located near Lead, was approved by Lawrence County Commissioners Tuesday. The license discussion was continued from the May 12 meeting after safety and noise concerns were brought to the commission. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
Malt beverage license approved for Boar’s Nest, subject to reapproval in 2027.jpg
The malt beverage license for The Boar’s Nest, a restaurant located near Lead, was approved by Lawrence County Commissioners Tuesday. The license discussion was continued from the May 12 meeting after safety and noise concerns were brought to the commission. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

DEADWOOD — The Boar’s Nest near Lead will be able to serve alcohol for another year after Lawrence County Commissioners approved the license Tuesday after a continued discussion about the safety, parking, and noise concerns raised by neighbors at the May 12 meeting. 

Commissioners chose to continue the approval or denial of the restaurant’s malt liquor license after having received multiple complaints from neighbors at the May 12 meeting. Complaints raised concerns about safety, including parking on the side of US Highway 14A, people walking in the highway to reach the restaurant, reports of burnouts, and noise complaints about an intercom system used to alert customers that their food is ready. 

Lawrence County Sheriff Brian Dean and Chief Deputy Tavis Little were present at the Tuesday meeting, presenting photographs of the establishment from 2023 and 2024 depicting motorcycles and vehicles parked on the side of the highway close to the guardrail.

“For the average citizen that travels that road regularly, it’s not alarming,” said Little. “Semis frequently come through that area with hot brakes where they can’t slow down very well. We also worry about campers that are coming down that hill that aren’t prepared for the grad of that hill. The congestion on that corner is certainly a public risk and a concern of public safety.”

Dean said that law enforcement has limited options when monitoring the parking along the highway. 

“With regards to state law, the parking is only illegal if any part of the car is on the road side of the white line,” Dean said. “So, it’s quite factual when I say that there’s nothing that we can do as far as law enforcement to remove those vehicles. I’ll also add that it presents a problem that we’re still trying to work through.”

Jim Schneider, owner of the Boar’s Nest, said that employees from the South Dakota Department of Transportation recently visited the area and painted lines on the road to try to encourage better parking habits. During the Sturgis Rally, Schneider said that he employs a shuttle driver to transport motorcyclists to and from a satellite parking location nearby.

“We’re trying to encourage people to go there, then we have lots of room for bike parking there,” Schneider said. “We have a van and a driver hired, trying to shuttle people back and forth. Last year was our first year doing that and it was used quite a bit. I’m hoping this year that it’ll take off even more if we try to put it out there as much as we can, that it’s there and please use it. We’re trying to do what we can to alleviate the problem.”

Commissioner Eric Jennings commented that beyond safety concerns of large trucks with trailers driving too fast on the road and potentially colliding with an illegally parked vehicle alongside the road, the commission is concerned about pedestrians crossing the busy highway.

“So are we,” said Schneider. “We don’t advertise to park on the road or walk on the road.”

 A video shown during the meeting, which Dean said was obtained through public domain, depicted multiple burnouts happening in the parking lot and on the highway.

Schneider said that the burnouts and congested parking have historically happened during Kool Deadwood Nites and Sturgis Rally. Otherwise, he said, the restaurant isn’t as busy during the 4 months that it’s open. 

Commissioner Timm Comer pointed out that the busy season accounts for a significant time the business is open. 

“You look at Rally and Kool Deadwood Nites, that’s probably a quarter of the time that you’re open,” Comer said. “That’s 25% of the time that you’re actually open that’s a noise issue or people out on the streets. I’ve been down there during the Rally and the motorcycle tires are definitely out past the white line. My concern is people coming around that corner. Somebody is going to get hit, it’s just a matter of time, because there is no path for people to walk other than out in the road.”

Dean said that monitoring behavior at the restaurant took “100%” of his workforce last summer. Dean said that not every available staff member was assigned to the Boar’s Nest, but that monitoring the behavior at the restaurant meant that it required a constant presence during an already busy time for local law enforcement.

“Quite literally it had to stop, and it had to stop in a profound way,” said Dean. “So, in order to get a high volume of focus on that particular area, that does not mean that we could just ignore every other call that we had, but in order to really get people there to be productive, it took everybody that we had.”

Little said that he has no reason to believe that the burnouts and congested parking were encouraged by Schneider. 

Bruce Outka, deputy state’s attorney, made commissioners aware that the approval or denial of a malt beverage license is subject to annual review for “ongoing consideration of appropriateness or suitable location.”

Commissioner Brandon Flanagan said that he believes that the continued problems reported to law enforcement and commissioners have been acknowledged by the owners and he believes that the owners are making efforts to mediate the issues. 

“I guess in my mind I’d like to give it a year and see how it goes,” Flanagan said. “If they can get things better under control, then good. And if they can’t, then we have next year and we’ll review it again. I’m sure they’re aware that there’s been a problem, because there’s law enforcement out there. But at least this way they’re on formal notice that we’re watching. There are some problems that need to be addressed, not just from the neighbors but also the public.”

The approval of the license was passed unanimously by commissioners.

Malt beverage licenses in Lawrence County run from June 30 to July 1 of the following year. The Boar’s Nest malt beverage license will be up for reapproval again next year in May.

title: Kids take ‘Center Stage’  in Belle Fourche
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: BELLE FOURCHE — There’s a new summer camp in town, and this one invites kids to take “Center Stage.”
_full_text:
BELLE FOURCHE — There’s a new summer camp in town, and this one invites kids to take “Center Stage.”

For years, the leaders of Belle Fourche Area Community Theater (BFACT) have wanted to expand their youth theater education offerings.

This summer, thanks to a partnership with the Belle Fourche Middle School Summer Jam program, the non-profit theater company is hosting its first Center Stage Theater Camp for upcoming fifth graders through ninth graders.

“Honestly, this year worked great because we were able to work with the Jam program, which is fantastic, because they have a lot of their own structure,” Olson said. “Working with them has been huge to get things going and set in motion.”

Olson said kids do not need to be enrolled in the Jam program to participate. They can register online on BFACT’s website. The program is also completely free for participants.

From noon till 3 p.m., June 9-12 and June 16-19, theater instructors have planned to present a packed curriculum.  

“They are going to learn a whole lot of stuff. We are going to teach them acting, improvisation, voice and character work, movement, stage, but we are also going to teach them behind-the-scenes stuff like set design, prop and costume design, evening lighting and sound, even some auditioning skills and things like that,” Olson said.

What sets this theater camp apart is its emphasis on skill building, which doesn’t hinge on preparation for a performance.

“A lot of camps are show-based. Like, sign up, come, be a part, and we are going to put a show together in a couple of weeks. We decided that what we want to do is more straight instruction,” Olson said.

At the end of the camp, students will still have the chance to show off their new skills. The camp will conclude with a showcase event on at 6 p.m. June 19.

title: Two stuck in Adam’s Museum  elevator, no injuries reported
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: DEADWOOD — Thanks to the quick work of the Deadwood Volunteer Fire Department, an incident involving 2 people and the elevator at the Adam’s Museum was resolved in less than 15 minutes with no injuries or hurt feelings.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

DEADWOOD — Thanks to the quick work of the Deadwood Volunteer Fire Department, an incident involving 2 people and the elevator at the Adam’s Museum was resolved in less than 15 minutes with no injuries or hurt feelings. 

Charles Fetter, assistant fire chief, said that the fire station received a call at approximately 2 p.m. Wednesday, requesting assistance to get 2 people out of the elevator at the Adam’s Museum. Fetter said after arriving on scene, he was able to use elevator keys to open the doors and let the trapped individuals out in “less than 5 minutes.”

Rose Speirs, communications director for Deadwood History, Inc., said that the elevator is back up and running again. 

“I know that happens on occasion at the Adam’s Museum, it’s an old building, but everything is fine now,” Speirs said. “Everything is working and operating correctly.”

Fetter said firefighters on the Deadwood Volunteer Fire Department are all trained on elevator rescue techniques, including how to open elevator doors, knowing where the emergency shut offs are, and understanding the different types of elevators that can be found in Deadwood. 

Fetter said that the city of Deadwood has more than 55 elevators. He said the best thing business owners can do to keep elevators safe is to have them annually inspected with routine maintenance performed. 

If you find yourself stuck in an elevator, Fetter said the best thing to do is keep calm and reach out for help using either the emergency button, the phone sometimes found inside elevators, or your personal cellphone to call for help. 

“You can Google the place you’re at and find the front desk number and explain where you’re at, what elevator you’re in, and what’s going on,” Fetter said. “That helps tremendously when we get called to an incident like this. That way we know exactly where they’re at, how many people are in there, and what the conditions are. Those are all key things to know, because time is of the essence.”

title: Introducing Belle Fourche’s new library director, Joshua Abraham
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Joshua Abraham is the new head librarian in Belle Fourche. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
New Librarian.JPG
Joshua Abraham is the new head librarian in Belle Fourche. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

BELLE FOURCHE — On May 8, Wanda Nelson retired as director of the Belle Fourche Public Library. Joshua Abraham is now in charge of stewarding the library and its beloved programs and collection into the future.

Abraham grew up in libraries.

“I always just feel that they are a safe and calming place to be. You can escape into whatever kind of world you want to escape into,” Abraham said.

Adulthood saw him pursuing a career in STEM education, teaching science in his home town in Minnesota. Fatherhood brought him to Belle Fourche — to be closer to family — and saw him working from home while raising his children.

Eventually, remote work started to wear on Abraham, who is an extrovert by nature. 

“There was an opening at the rec center for an operations manager, so I started there in September or the end of August. I was having a lot of fun there, great people working with great people over there,” Abraham said. “I learned through them that Wanda was thinking of retiring, the position might be opening up. Then my wife and I have always been very big fans of the library so we would come here fairly often.”

With encouragement from the librarians in Belle Fourche, Abraham “threw his hat into the ring” and took the library director position on April 27.

“I am really, really excited to be here. If you have ideas for books or book series or ideas for activities that we can do, I would love to hear them,” Abraham said. “Our public library is a service to the community, so I am making sure that we keep up our relationships with city hall and city council, and all of our missions are aligning in a way that allows us to move forward.”

He hopes to use some of his training as a science teacher to expand the library’s science, technology, engineering, art, and math (STEAM) programming.

“Whether we’re doing them on the front lawn or doing them here in the library themselves, connecting that a book or something. I think that could be a lot of fun,” Abraham said.

He’d also like to improve connections with the rec center and build stronger ties to the Tri-State Museum and Visitor’s Center.

Programmatically speaking, Abraham couldn’t have assumed leadership of the library at a busier time. Belle Fourche, along with most libraries around the region, has been busily preparing for its summer reading program — setting up fossil displays (the statewide program is dinosaur themed), and gearing up for a summer packed with activity.

“Wanda made sure that all of the wheels were in motion, that all of the things that needed to get ordered were ordered, and gave me the rundown of what is going on,” Abraham said.

Much like the summer reading program, the library’s story time puppet shows are poised to be preserved under Abraham’s leadership.

“We will not be getting rid of our story time puppet shows, which have been kind of a mainstay for 48 years. The building here has been doing that for 48 years,” Abraham said. “We might be making some small changes here and there to keep it fresh, keep it moving forward, and keep it relevant.”

Abraham has plans to get more young readers into the library in the near future as well.

“We’re trying to make it a little more welcoming for young adults. We are going to be shifting our young adult (YA) section over to this middle area and adding some soft seating there too, so that they can come in and be here,” Abraham said. “Trying to be inclusive, trying to be welcoming, and meeting the needs of the community.”

Abraham has a special pulse on the world of YA fiction. His daughter is currently reading Tracy Deonn’s “Legendborn” series.

“I am reading that so that she and I can talk about it,” Abraham said.

He’s also reading Matt Dinniman’s “Dungeon Crawler Carl” series and “Twelve Months” by Jim Butcher.

“(As a reader) I think my biggest non-fiction interest is military history, but other than that I find myself gravitating toward fiction,” Abraham said.

As a curator, he hopes to keep an eye out for what’s new in a wide range of genres and to build a catalogue that appeals to community tastes.

“It is always lovely to walk through the bookstore and see all of the books, but then you think, ‘I don’t have the funds, and I don’t have the space.’ It is fun to have the funds and the space,” Abraham said. “A big part of what I am wanting to do is let people know that this service exists. There is great literature in all respects being published on a regular basis, maybe more so now than in the past just because of the ease of getting things published. The idea that if you saw a book on the shelf and weren’t able to grab it, swing by the library. You might be surprised. We might have it.

title: Local author launches little free library, with a  hunger-fighting twist
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: RAPID CITY — Modeled after little free libraries, one little free food pantry in a Rapid City neighborhood has distributed an average of 500 items in need since it opened in October.
_full_text:
RAPID CITY — Modeled after little free libraries, one little free food pantry in a Rapid City neighborhood has distributed an average of 500 items in need since it opened in October.

Author and educator Whitnee Coy and her husband and fellow educator, Jesse, set up a cabinet in their yard last fall to help neighbors facing hard times in the community.

“As educators and parents, we see firsthand how many people are struggling right now,” Coy said. “This pantry was built on the belief that people deserve dignity, compassion, and access to basic necessities without judgment. People should not have to prove they are struggling in order to feed themselves or their families.”

Through a dignity-led model that is open 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, with no applications, income requirements, sign-ups, or barriers to access, the family-operated pantry has since distributed more than 18,000 food and household items.

The Coy family volunteers their own time, transportation, personal resources, and energy to keep the pantry stocked, cleaned, organized, and running smoothly for the community. At the same time, the pantry’s success depends heavily on a community-centered model of “take what you need, leave what you can.” Organizers say this approach has created a powerful cycle of mutual support and aid throughout the community. Some individuals and families donate items regularly and may never personally use the pantry. Others both donate and utilize the pantry at different points, depending on their circumstances. Many community members are simply grateful to know they can find what they need during difficult times without barriers, judgment, or complicated processes.

“This pantry works because the community believes in helping one another,” Coy said. “There are people who stock it after grocery trips, families who leave extra items when they are able, and neighbors who quietly take what they need to make it through the week. It has truly become a shared community effort built on dignity, trust, and care for one another.”

According to Feeding America’s Map the Meal Gap data, approximately 9,630 people in Pennington County experience food insecurity, with an estimated food insecurity rate of 8.9%. The annual food budget shortfall in the county is estimated at more than $6.6 million. Feeding South Dakota also reports that 1-in-8 individuals and 1-in-6 children in their service area face hunger.

The pantry was built to support families struggling to stretch groceries between paychecks, children grabbing food before or after school, college students in need of support, elders living on a fixed income, working families, mothers in need of formula and other baby essentials, and community members facing temporary unemployment or other unexpected circumstances, Coy said.

“There are days when kids stop by before school for breakfast items or snacks. We have helped families moving into housing with almost nothing, grandparents unexpectedly raising grandchildren, college students trying to stay enrolled while struggling with food and gas costs, and individuals going through cancer treatment who are trying to afford both medical bills and groceries,” Coy said.

Over the past year, the pantry has created “Meal Kits,” where all ingredients for a complete family recipe — along with the recipe itself — are packaged together to make meal preparation easier for families facing food insecurity. The pantry also hosted a community seed swap, allowing individuals and families to pick up free seeds to grow food and gardens during the summer months.

In celebration of Whitnee’s birthday, the pantry distributed 37 complete birthday cake kits that included cake mix, frosting, candles, and decorations so families could celebrate children and loved ones who may otherwise go without a birthday cake.

“These projects remind people that they matter,” Coy said. “Sometimes it’s not only about food — it’s about helping someone celebrate a birthday, stay warm during winter, plant a garden, or sit down together for a meal. Those moments of dignity, normalcy, and care are just as important.”

Coy is the author of  the children’s books “Elsie’s Adventures to Brainy Cove” and “Elsie’s Adventure to Harmony Hills” as well as a poetry collection titled “We Left Constellations in Each Other.”

title: The Mercy Sloane Chronicles: Chapter 5
byline: By Eliza Blue A work of serialized fiction, special to the Pioneer
description: When Granger came up with the plan to have their wedding the week after graduation and then travel immediately to western South Dakota to try their hands at homesteading, Mercy had agreed, reluctantly. “Think of it, Mercy. You and me, the open prairie, working side by side to make a living off the land,” he’d said, taking her hand to examine the sparkling engagement ring that did not look like anything a homesteader would wear. “I’ve always dreamed of being a farmer and leaving city life behind,” he’d remarked wistfully.
_full_text:
The Mercy Sloane Chronicles

When Granger came up with the plan to have their wedding the week after graduation and then travel immediately to western South Dakota to try their hands at homesteading, Mercy had agreed, reluctantly. “Think of it, Mercy. You and me, the open prairie, working side by side to make a living off the land,” he’d said, taking her hand to examine the sparkling engagement ring that did not look like anything a homesteader would wear. “I’ve always dreamed of being a farmer and leaving city life behind,” he’d remarked wistfully.

Mercy had cocked her head skeptically, but remained silent. Never mind that the last rush to open the west to homesteaders had been over for decades. Or that they were both city kids who didn’t know the first thing about homesteading or living off the land. Or that she’s really never seen Granger work at anything. He’d barely made it through college, even with her constant reminders to study. 

In the end, she’d agreed, however, because it did sound like an exciting adventure, and life so far had taught her to expect twists with happy endings. Even her mother’s tears and whispers the night before the wedding (“But Mercy, are you sure? Are you sure you love him?”) only gave her a moment’s pause, and when she’d walked down the aisle with Augustine carefully cupping her elbow, she had been sure. The West was the future, and the future was bright.

And now she was in South Dakota, as they’d planned, except she was alone, beneath the blazing western sun. Which is why she found herself thinking about her mother’s odd comment about decisions and money all those years ago, wondering what came next. Suddenly, she wasn’t a rich man’s wife in the midst of an ill-advised adventure, but a poor girl once again. She wanted to laugh at the latest twist her life had taken, mostly because she didn’t want to start crying for fear she wouldn’t be able to stop. 

Overhead, a red-tailed hawk circled, casting the only shadow for miles. Mercy shaded her face with her hand and tried to follow the hawk’s flight, but the sun was blinding. She looked away, eyes burning, and when she looked back, the hawk was gone.

 Eliza Blue TMC
Eliza Blue 

Mercy turned toward the house. Her new puppy leapt clumsily across the porch, chasing a grasshopper, while the pony grazed nearby on a picket line. Thank goodness the pony ate grass; there was plenty of that. She’d been feeding the dog and herself the dwindling rations of dried beef and tack they’d bought in Iowa, but they had maybe one or two days left. She still had the stout packages of beans and grains, but no kindling to light a fire, and she had a well, but not a single cup or pot to fill, only a dented bucket left by the last unfortunate owner of the house. 

And she was still sleeping on the floor, which was not getting more comfortable with time. She’d folded Granger’s blanket and set it in the corner for the puppy, but he kept creeping off it to curl up beside her. She’d never owned a dog and couldn’t understand what he was doing. “No, no!” she’d scold roughly, and carry him back to his bed, only to discover him folded in the crook of her knees the next time she woke. 

He followed her everywhere during the day as well. Something about this reminded her of Granger, and she could feel a familiar frustration rising in her chest, though she knew it wasn’t fair. The puppy was too young to be anything but completely dependent on her for food and comfort, whereas Granger’s helplessness was learned. 

Still, she’d tripped over the puppy more than once when she’d turned too quickly, or hadn’t noticed him trundling next to her through the tall grass, and every time she tripped, she thought of Granger and knew her mother was right about one thing — she’d never actually loved the man who was still technically her husband.

title: Quick Picks: Summer digs
description: Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Quick Picks: Summer digs
Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

With Memorial Day weekend in the rear view, it’s time for summer and summer reading. 

As you unearth plans for fun in the sun, libraries across the region are either gearing up for or have already launched their summer reading programs. The shared theme this year is dinosaur and excavation related, so here’s a round-up of thematically appropriate recommendations — straight from Whitewood Librarian Deb Terhune. 

1. “Diggersaurs” by Michael Whaite

 Genre: Picture book

What’s bigger than a digger? Bigger than a dinosaur? DIGGERSAURS are bigger — see them build and hear them roar. The DIGGERSAURS are busy building something — what could it be? Children will fall in love with these huge, colorful, lovable beasts as the wonderfully read-aloud rhyming story unfolds. And there are lots of funny details to spot along the way...

2. “Stalactite and Stalagmite” by Drew Beckmeyer

Genre: Picture book/Children’s non-fiction

Time flies for 2 charming little cave nubs, Stalactite and Stalagmite. Over millions of years, creatures and things pass in and out of their cave, everything from a trilobite, an ichthyostega, and a triceratops, to a ground sloth and a bat.

3. “The Diggers” by Margaret Wise Brown

Genre: Picture book 

Dig, dig, dig! A man and his shovel dig a tunnel under a river, into the country and through a mountain. Where will they dig to next?

4. “The Street Beneath My Feet” by Charlotte Guillain 

Genre: Picture book/Nonfiction

When you’re out walking around, whether on the city streets or a country trail, there’s always so much to see and hear. But do you ever stop and look down? Have you ever wondered what’s going on deep in the ground under your feet?

5. “Lady of the Lines” by Michaela MacColl

Genre: Biography

When scientist and explorer Maria Reiche visited Peru’s Nazca Lines in 1941, she was immediately captivated by the larger-than-life animal carvings. But what were they, and why were they there? This STEAM nonfiction picture book for young readers reveals the story behind one of the greatest indigenous artworks in the Americas, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

6. “Dig, Dig, Dinosaur” by Anjali Goswami 

Genre: Picture book/Nonfiction

Get ready to dig your way through this fun, informative, and dinosaur-themed board book!

3 young adventurers embark on “an expedition to a faraway land.” With the proper tools and an ambitious spirit, the adventurers dig for dinosaur bones, discovering and learning about various types of dinosaurs. Along the way, the adventurers strive to uncover dinosaurs bigger than the ones before, eventually revealing the biggest dinosaur at the end of the book. With the expertise of author Anjali Goswami, this book celebrates the expansive dinosaur population while encouraging young people to explore the world of paleontology.

 Former Sen. David Johnson, R-Rapid City, running for Senate District 33.
 Former Rep. Becky Drury, R-Rapid City, running for House District 34.
 Former Sen. Julie Frye-Mueller, R-Rapid City, running for Senate District 30.

PIERRE — A Republican rupture that shook the South Dakota Legislature 2 years ago is returning to the ballot Tuesday, this time with more money and organization on the side that lost control in 2024, plus a governor primary that’s expected to increase turnout.

Campaign finance reports reviewed by South Dakota Searchlight show a total of at least $2 million spent by 23 groups so far this year to influence legislative primary races. 

The result is a slate of Republican primaries that will test whether the 2024 intraparty revolt was a lasting or temporary shift. 

That year, 14 Republican legislators lost to challengers from their own party in the primary. Many of the ousted lawmakers had supported legislation that sought to regulate, rather than defeat, a proposal for a five-state carbon capture pipeline proposed by Iowa-based Summit Carbon Solutions that would have run through eastern South Dakota. 

Opponents of the legislation — expressing concern about the private property rights of landowners along the route — referred it to voters, who rejected it in the 2024 general election. Opponents also won enough legislative seats in 2024 to replace the Republican legislative leadership team and ultimately pass legislation banning eminent domain for carbon pipelines — a law that has so far kept the pipeline out of the state. Additionally, the pipeline opponents installed one of their own as the chairman of the state Republican Party.

The pipeline fight turned out to be the opening salvo in a broader struggle among South Dakota Republicans over economic development. Subsequent debates have centered on incentives and regulations for data centers, and state government’s role in aiding businesses.

Ten of the 14 Republican lawmakers who lost their seats two years ago are trying to rejoin the Legislature this year, aided by political action committee spending for them or against their opponents.

Dueling philosophies

Spearfish Republican Scott Odenbach, who became the state House majority leader in 2024 with support from newly elected lawmakers, called the spending against him and his allies in this year’s Republican legislative primaries “totally unprecedented.” 

“I think it’s a desperate attempt from the business class to take back what they lost in 2024,” Odenbach said. 

One of the people leading the spending on the other side is Rep. Taylor Rehfeldt, R-Sioux Falls. She voted for the pipeline regulations bill that was later placed on the ballot and defeated by voters. She won reelection in 2024 but was ousted by Republican colleagues from her position as assistant House majority leader.

“Rep. Odenbach has actively played in primaries himself since being elected, including through political organizations aligned with his own agenda, so his comments are a little amusing,” Rehfeldt wrote in a statement to Searchlight. 

Indicating that the fight is about more than just economic development, Rehfeldt criticized failed proposals from some Republican legislators that she described as extreme. One example is a bill that would have subjected librarians to criminal liability for failing to prevent children from obtaining materials deemed obscene.

“The reality is this effort is being driven by South Dakotans who are tired of dysfunction, political theater, and unserious legislating,” Rehfeldt said. “They are tired of watching energy get wasted on headlines and chaos while real issues affecting families, communities, healthcare, education, and public safety take a back seat.”

PAC ties to business leaders, governor race

One of the biggest spenders in this year’s primary is the South Dakota Republican Forward political action committee, chaired by Rehfeldt. 

So far this year, Rehfeldt’s PAC has reported spending $271,000 on ads, $216,000 on postage and $140,000 on printing to influence legislative races. 

Rehfeldt’s state-registered PAC received $675,000 from the federally registered Republican Forward PAC. Republican Forward is a super PAC. Due to U.S. Supreme Court decisions, super PACs are legally allowed to raise and spend unlimited amounts as long as there’s no coordination with candidates. In South Dakota, political action committees can receive unlimited contributions from other political action committees.

Republican Forward’s fundraising includes large amounts from the Sioux Falls business community: $500,000 from POET ethanol (which sought to capture carbon dioxide from its ethanol plants for the carbon capture pipeline, to capitalize on tax credits incentivizing the practice), $300,000 from First Premier Bank Chairman and CEO Dana Dykhouse, $150,000 from MarketBeat founder and CEO Matthew Paulson, and $100,000 from Lloyd Companies. Among other donors, Republican Forward has also received $100,000 from Genesis Farms Cannabis Company, which has multiple medical marijuana outlets across the state.

Dykhouse said he was motivated to get involved after seeing Republican legislators oppose state-funded economic development programs. He said that could result in “our children and grandchildren leaving the state because they didn’t have opportunities.” 

“That’s what we want to change,” Dykhouse said. “We don’t want our kids to have to leave to get jobs. We want them to stay here.”

The same federal super PAC has also funded spending by the state-registered Rushmore Principles PAC against Gov. Larry Rhoden and state House Speaker Jon Hansen in the race for the Republican nomination for governor. Rhoden signed a bill into law banning eminent domain for carbon pipelines, and Hansen has been a prominent opponent of the carbon pipeline and state economic development programs. 

The primary beneficiary of the spending against Rhoden and Hansen is another Republican candidate for governor, U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson. The other candidate in the four-way race is businessman Toby Doeden.

A committee that bears Johnson’s name, Dusty PAC, has also been active in legislative races. It has the same treasurer as Johnson’s candidate committee, and Dusty PAC is chaired by Jeff Erickson, longtime chairman of the South Dakota Board of Economic Development. The PAC has spent $232,000 this year to influence legislative races, in some cases supporting Republican lawmakers who lost their 2024 primaries. 

Nathan Sanderson was director of policy and operations in former Gov. Dennis Daugaard’s administration. Johnson served as Daugaard’s chief of staff. Daugaard has endorsed Johnson for governor.

Sanderson is now executive director of the South Dakota Retailers Association. The association’s PAC has spent $47,500 this year to influence legislative races. 

“I think that it’s very clear that a broad swath of South Dakota is interested in making state government boring again,” Sanderson said. “I don’t think that it’s any specific issue. It’s an approach to governance.”

Republican Sioux Falls Mayor Paul TenHaken expressed similar motivations for spending by his South Dakotans for Common Sense PAC. It reported raising $340,500 and spending $214,000 since the beginning of the year. That includes a $150,000 contribution from a federal PAC affiliated with NetChoice, a trade association that advocates for data centers.   

“I don’t, quite honestly, feel that the majority of the state even knows what it means to be a true Republican anymore. And so I think we have to just get rid of labels,” TenHaken said. “I just want people who are less loyal to a party and more loyal to our state and our future, our kids.”

Former lawmakers receiving support

Candidates receiving support from the Rehfeldt, Dusty, TenHaken or other similar PACs include Erin Tobin, of Winner, who lost her primary race in 2024 after supporting the carbon pipeline regulations bill. Tobin lost to Mykala Voita, of Bonesteel, whose efforts in the Legislature have included her successful sponsorship of a bill allowing concealed pistols on college campuses. Tobin is running against Voita on Tuesday. 

Another candidate receiving support is Katie Washnok, who ran a close but unsuccessful race two years ago against Sen. Carl Perry, who recently described himself as being in favor of “anybody but Dusty” for governor. Washnok and Perry are both from Aberdeen and are in a rematch Tuesday.

Other candidates with support from that same side of the Republican aisle include Sen. Glen Vilhauer, a certified public accountant from Watertown serving on the state budget committee. He faces a challenge from Rep. Josephine Garcia, of Watertown, who has backed failed legislation that would have banned lab-grown meat, required employers to use the federal E-Verify system to check whether employees are in the country legally, and required blood donors to disclose whether they’ve received a COVID-19 vaccine. 

Jean Hunhoff, who was the state’s longest-serving female lawmaker when she lost her primary in 2024, also has backing in her return bid. Hunhoff is in a rematch with the person who defeated her in 2024, Sen. Lauren Nelson of Yankton, who sponsored the bill that would have criminalized librarians and has unsuccessfully backed efforts to approve the use of state funds for private educational options. 

Current leader resists push from ‘business class’

Odenbach, who became House majority leader after the 2024 election, runs the state-registered Liberty Tree PAC. He uses it to support candidates on the “other side of the Republican divide” from those aligned with Republicans like Rehfeldt and Johnson. 

Odenbach said “the Sioux Falls business class” is afraid that “conservative principles and the free market might govern the state instead of crony capitalism and sweetheart deals.” 

Odenbach’s Liberty Tree PAC has spent $48,000 this year, including support for Voita in her race against Tobin; for Sen. Taffy Howard of Rapid City, who introduced several bills to restrict state economic development programs; and for Representatives Kathy Rice of Black Hawk and Terri Jorgenson of Piedmont, who in the 2024 primary beat out Gary Cammack, who was the House majority whip at the time.

Sen. Mark Lapka of Leola was elected in 2024 as a prominent opponent of the carbon pipeline. His Land & Legacy PAC gave $50,000 this year, including $5,000 to Voita, $5,000 to Howard, $10,000 to the Senate president pro tempore installed after the 2024 elections, Chris Karr, of Sioux Falls, and $10,000 to The People First, a PAC supporting Speaker Hansen’s campaign for governor. 

Rep. Phil Jensen of Rapid City and Sen. John Carley of Piedmont run the South Dakota Freedom Caucus PAC. The caucus says it advocates for liberty, limited government and conservative values. The PAC has spent $33,000 this year, including $3,500 each to Jensen and Carley’s campaigns, and donations to the campaigns of other members of the caucus, including Rice, Rep. Dylan Jordan of Clear Lake, and Garcia. 

Some spending to influence legislative races has focused on specific issues. One report filed by Forge the Future Project, based in Sioux Falls, shows $521,000 in spending on digital ads and mailers supporting 17 candidates. Forge the Future Project is not listed as a state or federal PAC, so information on its donors is not readily available. The group’s website says it advocates “for a favorable regulatory environment to bring valuable AI products to market in America” and “empowering parents to have oversight over their children’s online activities.”

News and Notes

Sandstone Hills remediation project on Spearfish City Council agenda Monday

SPEARFISH — In 2022, the city of Spearfish began a sewer upsize project in Sandstone Hills. Most of the sewer line installation and roadway repair was completed by the end of that year. Later, Sandstone Hills Road started to settle at its Colorado Boulevard entrance and further work began in the project area. On Monday, the city council is expected to discuss advertising and bid letting for a Sandstone Hills remediation project. “What we are remediating is the trench that settled as part of the sanitary sewer upsize,” Public Works Director Adam McMahon said. That trench is located at Sandstone Drive near the neighborhood’s main entrance. 

— Sierra Ferguson

Spearfish awaits details on change order for Colorado Blvd. chip seal project

SPEARFISH — On Wednesday, Spearfish Public Works Director Adam McMahon offered an update on the Colorado Boulevard Chip Seal project. As soon as Monday a change order, expanding the scope of the project to include an asphalt patch in front of Great Western Tire and curb and gutter work could come before the city council for approval. A contract amendment with Interstate Engineer with regard to the same chip seal project may also be presented at the upcoming meeting. 

— Sierra Ferguson

Spearfish likely to reject airport apron project bids 

SPEARFISH — Airport aprons are paved areas where aircraft can be parked, unloaded, refueled, boarded, or service. The city of Spearfish budgeted $6 million to install a new airport apron at Clyde Ice Field. The project went out to bid last week. 

“Bids were not what we were hoping to see. They were $2 million over the engineer’s estimate and more than $1.5 million over the budgeted amount for the project. We’re recommending you reject those bids,” Public Works Director Adam McMahon said. “We are working with the FAA and the state on the funding side of that to give us more time to break that project into phases and re-advertise just a smaller portion to get back into the budgeted amounts for the state.”

— Sierra Ferguson

title: The feds have embraced  medical marijuana. Now what?
byline: By Amanda Watford Stateline
description: WASHINGTON, D.C. — The U.S. Department of Justice’s recent decision to downgrade the drug classification for medical cannabis will help medical marijuana businesses. Companies will be able to claim some federal tax benefits. New research can start up at state universities.
_full_text:
StatelineLogo

WASHINGTON, D.C. — The U.S. Department of Justice’s recent decision to downgrade the drug classification for medical cannabis will help medical marijuana businesses. Companies will be able to claim some federal tax benefits. New research can start up at state universities.

But the broader divide between federal and state marijuana policy remains largely intact, leaving states to navigate a fragmented and still-evolving cannabis landscape with few clear answers about what comes next.

The unprecedented change in April reclassifying medical marijuana from Schedule I to Schedule III means the federal government is acknowledging an accepted healthcare use for cannabis. Recreational marijuana, however, remains a Schedule I drug under federal policy, even though 24 states and the District of Columbia allow recreational cannabis in various forms, from dried flower to vaping oils to processed gummy candies.

The U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration is set to hold its first hearing at the end of June on the possible de-scheduling of marijuana broadly, which would include recreational or adult-use cannabis.

Until then, some experts say little is expected to change for the more than half of states with medical or recreational marijuana programs.

“This change is sort of catching up to what states are already doing,” said Katharine Neill Harris, a drug policy fellow at Rice University’s Baker Institute for Public Policy. “In some ways the federal government is following the states on this issue.”

States have spent years building regulatory frameworks for medical and recreational marijuana programs — including licensing systems, tax structures, testing requirements and retail oversight.

Following the DEA’s announcement in April that it would reschedule medical cannabis, some state commissions acknowledged the decision but stressed that their laws have not changed and that they are awaiting further federal guidance.

In Nevada, for example, state cannabis officials released a statement noting that the rescheduling change allows medical cannabis licensees to register with the DEA, while also emphasizing that Nevada law still classifies non-medical marijuana as a Schedule I substance.

In mid-May, the California Department of Cannabis Control proposed emergency regulations that would allow businesses holding licenses for both medical and recreational marijuana to obtain separate licenses. The change could position cannabis businesses to take advantage of potential benefits tied to the rescheduling of medical marijuana.

Many of the day-to-day functions of state cannabis programs are expected to remain intact, according to experts.

“Right now, nothing would have to change for states because we don’t know what the federal regulations are going to look like for managing medical cannabis,” said Heather Trela, the director of operations and a fellow at the Rockefeller Institute of Government, a nonpartisan public policy think tank.

“Everyone’s kind of figuring it out right now, and we don’t have all the details, so it’s hard for states,” she said.

State cannabis regulators and officials in several states, including Oklahoma, Vermont and Washington, told Stateline they are waiting for guidance from the DEA and other federal agencies before determining whether businesses will be required to register with the DEA, qualify for federal tax relief or face new compliance requirements, and whether states may need to revise their own cannabis laws.

“None of us really can effectively advise our licensees, which is just incredibly frustrating, especially with a ticking clock,” said James Pepper, the chair of the Vermont Cannabis Control Board, which regulates the state’s medical and adult-use market.

In the coming months, other federal agencies may issue guidance on how rescheduling will affect existing rules, according to policy experts. The U.S. Department of Transportation said in December that drug testing and licensing standards will not change, and TSA rules still prohibit carrying marijuana on flights. Financial guidance from the IRS and the Treasury Department also are still pending.

‘Taxed like a normal business’

But some marijuana policy experts and industry leaders say the federal shift could bring major changes to cannabis business operations and scientific research.

Cannabis businesses have long been blocked from taking certain federal tax deductions because marijuana was classified as a Schedule I substance. Some industry leaders say moving medical cannabis to Schedule III could ease some of those constraints.

“Going forward, we can be treated and taxed like a normal business, which ultimately helps the bottom line and allows us to reinvest more meaningfully in the states where we operate,” said Lauren Niehaus, the executive director of government relations at Trulieve Cannabis Corp., one of the largest cannabis companies in the country. Trulieve, based in Florida, operates dispensaries in eight states.

The tax policy change is a central issue for cannabis operators across the board, from small businesses to large multistate companies, Niehaus said.

Ryan Hunter, the chief revenue officer of Spherex Labs, said rescheduling changes could shift investor and lender attitudes toward the cannabis industry, with some capital partners becoming more willing to invest.

But Hunter said the latest federal change also creates new uncertainty for companies operating in both medical and recreational markets, including Spherex Labs, which operates in Colorado.

“Our business is still very much in wait-and-see mode,” Hunter said. “There are a lot of positive gains here, but really more than anything, a lot more confusion.”

The federal government has effectively created different legal frameworks for the same substance, he added. Medical cannabis is now federally recognized, while recreational marijuana and its consumers remain in conflict with federal law.

The rescheduling change also carries federal registration requirements under the Controlled Substances Act, a law that would require medical cannabis businesses to register with the DEA, pay annual fees, and comply with detailed reporting, inventory and security rules that may overlap or conflict with existing state systems.

Spherex Labs has chosen not to register at this time, Hunter said, opting to wait for further federal guidance.

Earlier this month, the Oklahoma Bureau of Narcotics and Dangerous Drugs Control sent a letter to licensed medical cannabis businesses encouraging them to register with the DEA and warning of possible sanctions, including revocation of their state licenses, for failing to comply with federal requirements.

But the Oklahoma Medical Marijuana Authority, which oversees cannabis licensing and regulation in the state, told Stateline the letter came as a surprise and that it remains unclear whether federal officials actually intend to require DEA registration for medical operators.

Other states could adopt similar federal registration requirements, according to Trela, of the Rockefeller Institute of Government.

Cannabis research

Some researchers and experts say rescheduling marijuana could reduce longstanding barriers to studying its medical use, safety and long-term health effects.

Current research on marijuana’s effects falls short of what is needed to fully understand cannabis as a medical treatment, according to Chad Johnson, an assistant professor of pharmaceutical sciences at the University of Maryland School of Pharmacy. Johnson also is the director of the university’s medical cannabis graduate studies program.

“We really do need those randomized trials to really say that cannabis is effective for treating a particular condition,” Johnson said.

There are still major gaps in cannabis research, he said, including how it is formulated and delivered, such as whether methods beyond smoking, vaping or edibles may be more effective, and how to determine appropriate dosing for specific medical conditions.

Johnson added that rescheduling could allow academic institutions to study products already being sold in their respective states, making research more closely aligned with what consumers are actually using, rather than relying on cannabis sourced through federally authorized suppliers.

Some public health and addiction experts say the federal shift should not be interpreted as a signal that cannabis is risk-free, pointing to ongoing concerns about cannabis use disorders, dependency and effects on mental health.

“It’s going to reduce the public’s perception of risk of cannabis, and right now, I don’t think the public is aware of the high potency that cannabis has,” said Dr. Alta DeRoo, the chief medical officer of the Hazelden Betty Ford Foundation, one of the largest nonprofit treatment providers for addiction and mental health. DeRoo also is a board-certified addiction medicine physician and OB-GYN.

Some opponents of the change also argue it is driven as much by political and economic pressure from the cannabis industry as by evolving science.

“The issue is not research. The issue is money, tax breaks for an industry, and that’s really what the whole effort to relax marijuana laws is about,” said Kevin Sabet, a former drug policy adviser to three presidential administrations and the president and CEO of Smart Approaches to Marijuana, a nonprofit that opposes legalizing marijuana.

What’s next

New federal changes also could face court challenges or be reversed by a future administration, according to some cannabis policy experts.

Last week, the attorneys general of Indiana, Louisiana and Nebraska filed a petition for review in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, arguing that the Justice Department’s rescheduling order violates federal administrative law. Louisiana and Nebraska have medical-only cannabis programs, while Indiana does not have a cannabis program at all.

Smart Approaches to Marijuana and the National Drug and Alcohol Screening Association filed a similar lawsuit earlier this month, arguing that the administration exceeded its authority under the Controlled Substances Act.

At the same time, the White House’s latest National Drug Control Strategy document also raised concerns about high-potency marijuana and warned that international cartels and organized crime groups continue to exploit state cannabis legalization laws.

Aside from criminal justice implications, federal restrictions have limited cannabis businesses’ access to banking, investment and long-term planning, even as state markets have expanded into a multibillion-dollar industry.

Banks have largely avoided working with cannabis businesses because marijuana remains broadly illegal under federal law, which exposes financial institutions to potential regulatory penalties and compliance risks even in states where cannabis is legal.

Several bills have been introduced in Congress that would provide protections for banks offering services to cannabis businesses, but no legislation has been adopted.

title: Conservation groups, Forest Service add new public land near Yellowstone National Park
byline: By Darrell Ehrlick Daily Montanan
description: GARDINER, Mont. — A tract of land near Yellowstone National Park which had been identified as a potential gold mining site in 2023 has been added to the roster of public lands after The Conservation Fund, the United States Forest Service and the Greater Yellowstone Coalition came together to make the transaction happen, which including purchasing land as well as mineral rights.
_full_text:
DailyMontananLogo

GARDINER, Mont. — A tract of land near Yellowstone National Park which had been identified as a potential gold mining site in 2023 has been added to the roster of public lands after The Conservation Fund, the United States Forest Service and the Greater Yellowstone Coalition came together to make the transaction happen, which including purchasing land as well as mineral rights.

The 161-acre parcel was added to the Custer-Gallatin National Forest in two parcels, one acquired by the Greater Yellowstone Coalition, the other by The Conservation Fund. The deal also includes 208 acres of mineral rights to the Forest Service to ensure that the land which includes part of Palmer and Crevice Mountains will be shielded from gold mining forever.

The Greater Yellowstone Coalition had originally purchased the mineral rights, leases and claims on nearly 1,600 acres by the Crevice Mining Group, according to a joint press release put out by the two organizations. However, even after the purchase in 2023, the groups still had to work with the privately held land and mineral rights which could have reopened to mining.

The new public land will now be protected by the Yellowstone Gateway Protection Act, which passed Congress in 2019 and will protect the area from future mining.

“Protecting Yellowstone from the impacts of gold mining and securing new public land is a great outcome that benefits both iconic wildlife and local communities,” GYC Executive Director Scott Christensen said.

The groups note that the area provides habitat for grizzly bears, a migration corridor for elk, mule deer and bighorn sheep, and is one of the few designated places outside the boundaries of Yellowstone National Park where bison can freely roam.

“By securing land within this critical landscape on the edge of Yellowstone, we’re doing more than safeguarding a vital habitat,” said Gary Sullivan, Montana senior advisor at The Conservation Fund. “We’re honoring a way of life that defines Montana and ensuring future generations can experience the same wild, open spaces that make the place so special.”

The land is located near Gardiner, Mont.

The U.S. Forest Service was able to purchase the two parcels for about $2 million using the Land and Water Conservation Fund.

title: Visit Spearfish requests one-time  funds during leadership transition
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: After more than a decade driving tourism in the community, Mistie Caldwell, pictured, is stepping down from her role as executive director of Visit Spearfish to pursue new career opportunities. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Mistie 1.jpg
After more than a decade driving tourism in the community, Mistie Caldwell, pictured, is stepping down from her role as executive director of Visit Spearfish to pursue new career opportunities. Pioneer file photo 

SPEARFISH — Mistie Caldwell has been the executive director of Visit Spearfish since its inception 17 years ago. 

Visit Spearfish is a non-profit marketing agency that aims to attract tourist traffic to the Black Hills and the city. Under Caldwell’s leadership, the organization helped bring in nearly $1 million in hospitality tax revenue in 2024 alone. Her vision for preserving and sharing Spearfish’s unique “quality of place” with locals and visitors alike helped earn her accolades, including a “Best in Tourism” distinction from 605 Magazine in 2025.

“It’s been a roller coaster for sure,” Caldwell said. “It is a lovely job.”

Now, Caldwell plans to step down from her position, but before departing, she came before the Spearfish City Council to request budgeted grant funds from the 2026 Spearfish general fund budget for a series of one-time purchases that could help set up her successor for success.

“We are going to be transitioning to a new executive director after 17 and a half years, so we do have a one-time expense in here for a new laptop computer that will be needed versus limping along with my relic,” Caldwell told the city council. “Whether or not that person would like an HP or a Mac, we budgeted $1,200, which I feel can cover that.”

Visit Spearfish is funded by the city’s BBB (board, bed, booze) tax and a $2 per room fee that is collected by all nine of the city’s hotels with 36 or more rooms. Spearfish Canyon Lodge, which has a Lead address, also voluntarily contributes to Visit Spearfish’s work — bringing the total of participating hotels to 10. 

In the 2026 general fund budget for community grants, $50,000 was added as contingency funding available for Visit Spearfish.

Caldwell also asked for sufficient funds to buy a new office printer, but those pieces of equipment aren’t the only reason a dip into contingency funds might be warranted.

Visit Spearfish would like to update marketing materials by sprucing up its photo and video catalogue — a catalogue that is shared with the city for things like website updates. 

“We are requesting a on-time $25,000 expense to go toward acquisition of assets, including drone footage, videography, and photography,” Caldwell said. “You always have the opportunity to share those assets when you get to update the website for the city or the Booth Society, or the High Plains (Western) Heritage Center.”

All year, photographers and videographers will be capturing moments in the community — ensuring there are images of Spearfish in all seasons, and highlight reels that feature events like Downtown Friday nights. The last time Visit Spearfish took on a project of this scale was in 2018.

“This allows us to have professional people come in, USA-made drones, which have fewer limitations, to get quality things. They’ll deliver the final product, finished product, or edited product. We have access to all of that b-roll,” Caldwell said. “If you look at $25,000 over 8 years, it’s a pretty good investment, and it is not just Visit Spearfish; it is available to all of our partners, so request that $25,000.”

While they might be armed with new gear and digital assets, it’s not yet clear who will take over at Visit Spearfish when Caldwell leaves. However, she encouraged the council to award less than the $50,000 available in the budget so that the future executive director can come before the council and explain how and why they might need more grant funding if they decide those dollars are needed in the days and weeks ahead.

“I run a pretty lean, mean machine, but there may be new things that an executive director needs to be successful. I am not implying that it’s superficial in any way, but I feel like it is more transparent if they come and request it,” Caldwell said. “I won’t argue with $50,000, and we will use it for good, not evil, but I think it does put a transparency clause on it to allow that new director to come in and request the rest in reserves.”

The city council is scheduled to consider Visit Spearfish’s request during its regular meeting Monday.
