title: Answering the cal: Boxelder Job Corps  students face the flames
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Students from Boxelder Job Corps work to build a containment line around the Estes Creek Fire near Nemo on April 12. The C-15 Boxelder Crew were second on scene to the incident and assumed command. Pictured from left, Cory Red Owl, Angel Perez, Majhondra Jones, and Seqoiua Bautista-Ortega. Photo courtesy of Boxelder Job Corps
_full_text:
1 Boxelder Job Corps wildland firefighting.jpg
Students from Boxelder Job Corps work to build a containment line around the Estes Creek Fire near Nemo on April 12. The C-15 Boxelder Crew were second on scene to the incident and assumed command. Pictured from left, Cory Red Owl, Angel Perez, Majhondra Jones, and Seqoiua Bautista-Ortega. Photo courtesy of Boxelder Job Corps 

DEADWOOD — At Boxelder Job Corps outside of Nemo, a select group of students are working with the Forest Service-run program to seize opportunities in the trades and taking on the additional task of helping protect national forests through wildland firefighting program.

Derek Sukstorf, academic manager at Boxelder Job Corps, said that 23 students are currently enrolled in the program’s wildland firefighting program. The program is considered an extra responsibility on top of students’ academic programming and their time becoming certified in a trade. Being successful in the training while being in good standing with the Job Corps center allows students a unique opportunity to go on assignment around the country, helping crews with prescribed burns and active fires while making a wage. 

Students sent on assignment with the wildland firefighting crew make an average of $20.44-22.48 an hour. Most assignments last 18 days, with students working approximately 16-hour days. 

“The wildfire program is an amazing extension of our ability to provide workforce training,” said Sukstorf. “It gives the students an excellent opportunity to learn some skills, be trained as wildfire, have employability skills, and then they get to go out and use those skills on the job. They learn those really important soft skills — teamwork and communication, showing up on time, work ethic. They get great chances to put those skills in to practice along with all the things that they’ve learned at Job Corps, and then it’s also a great program to help them earn some transition money. So, as they leave the Job Corps program and graduate, they have some money in the bank to help get a car, get an apartment, leave here and be independent and start their time in the workforce.”

Adam VonEye, assistant fire management officer for the C-15 wildland fire crew, is part of the team that mentors and teaches students at Boxelder. He said that wildland fire at Boxelder is (an extra opportunity), not an option of trades students can learn at the school. However, he said students can choose fire-related trades, such as natural resource conservation and forestry, that coordinates with the teachings and mentoring of the wildland fire program. 

One student, Majhondra Jones, came to Boxelder from Chinle, Ariz., in April 2025, with a high school diploma. She’s currently completed 90% of the natural resource conservation and forestry program and has been part of the wildland firefighting crew. She said the 2 programs, “play hand in hand.”

“I get to learn more about fires than natural resources. I’m adamant and I have a desire to know more about the natural world,” Jones said. “I have a passion to be outside and not sit in an office. This is a way for me to maintain that balance.”

Seqoiua Bautista-Ortega came to Boxelder Job Corps from Sioux Falls in June 2025, with a high school diploma to pursue carpentry. He’s currently completed 91% of his training and was elected by his peers as student body president in February this year. Bautista-Ortega said that he chose to take on the wildland fire program to become a stronger, better person. 

“When you’re here at Boxelder, you’re here for opportunities,” said Bautista-Ortega. “Since you’re working hard for your trade, it balances out nicely. If I can stay responsible as a carpenter an also be a wildland firefighter, I know have 2 gigs. I now have 2 technical trades that keep me responsible and keep me on top of my game. That’s what I’m here for — I’m here to stay for a while and accomplish a lot of good goals.”

Pull quote
“The wildfire program is an amazing extension of our ability to provide workforce training.” — Derek Sukstorf, academic manager at Boxelder Job Corps

Before being able to respond to incidents across the country, students enrolled in the wildland firefighting program have to complete approximately 80 weeks of training on top of their regular academic work and trade, including daily physical training. That training culminates in an arduous work capacity test, where students are required to hike 3 miles with a 45-pound pack in less than 45 minutes. 

Jones said the hike was difficult for her. She said that she kept wanting to rest, but the other students also taking the test wouldn’t let her quit. 

“My companions who were also facing the process consistently gave me motivation,” Jones said “That’s what we want, is to see others succeed. That’s kind of what we’re all doing here. We’re all trying to succeed, and this teaches us that we can do that, we can do hard things.”

VonEye said that type of teamwork is vital to being part of the wildland firefighting team. 

“We don’t take students that don’t have any kind of qualities of teamwork,” said VonEye. “Some of these students, like (Bautista-Ortega) and (Jones), they are my best recruiters for new students. They talk to the new students and it’s not like they’re trying to recruit people to take their job, take their place, they’re just recruiting good team players. Every spring we grow a bigger crew just because of those people that have that experience and share that with the new students.”

 2 Boxelder Job Corps wildland firefighting kids.jpg
Boxelder Job Corps students and graduates Kevin Argueta-Ayala, Ryan Swartz, Nicholas Nichols, pictured from left, have worked to obtain their wildland fire certification on top of their trade and academic curriculum. Photo courtesy of Boxelder Job Corps 

Out on assignment

Sukstorf said that in 2026, the Boxelder wildland firefighting students have assisted with 8 wildland fires and worked on more than 12,00 acres of prescribed burns in the Ozark National Forest in Arkansas. 

Bautista-Ortega spent 21 days working 14-to-16-hour days in the Ozark National Forest assisting with prescribed burns. 

“It was hot, windy, and intense,” said Bautista-Ortega. “It was a lot of learning and a lot of supervision. The team leaders did a really good job training me. There were days where I didn’t think I could make it out alive, but I did it and it made me a stronger human overall.”

VonEye said that because of increased fire danger in the Black Hills, the crew has been called to local incidents including the Qury Fire in Custer State Park in March that burned close to 10,000 acres. Bautista-Ortega and Jones both spent 12 days performing everything from structure protection, constructing containment lines, and mop up.

“It was completely different from the Ozarks because it’s the Black Hills,” said Bautista-Ortega. “It felt almost mystical at times. It felt more safe. I knew we were going to make it out alive at the end of the day. It was friendly and nice (working with local agencies).”

Jones said that working with local agencies on the Qury Fire felt like a communal effort to save a shared home with people who cared about her success. 

“You can definitely feel the sort of father-like energy,” said Jones. “They want to teach you so that you are able to be competent enough without needing constant supervision.”

Bautista-Ortega said that working wildland fire incidents has made him more confident and able to make decisions on the fly. 

“Fire is an emotional roller coaster of events that are constantly happening every single second,” Bautista-Ortega said. “Every single second you’re thinking and moving. Sometimes you don’t know if you’re going to make it through. But you do, and when you’re done from fire you live your life that way. Now I’m handling everything much more smoothly because I’m ready for it.”

Jones said coming to Boxelder and working wildland fire has taught her that she’s capable of not only setting goals but reaching them. 

“I know that when I leave this place with the experience that I’ve gained so far, and especially during fire, I know that I’ll be able to accomplish the goals I set for myself no matter how strenuous it may be,” Jones said. 

Changed for the better

Sukstorf said that he can see a physical change happen in the students that come back from wildland firefighting assignments. 

“I watch these students go out every year and do these assignments, and the confidence that they come back with makes them different people,” Sukstorf said. “They’ve done something hard, and they come through it. Shoulders are back, heads held high, smiles on their faces, and they carry that with them for the entire time they’re here. It’s a great thing to see.”

Sukstorf said he’s incredibly grateful for the C-15 wildland firefighting crew and the mentorship and opportunities they offer the students at Boxelder Job Corps. 

“These students go out and do (physical training) every day with them, they coach them through it and they take them from wherever they’res tarting and they build the up to be ready to go out on those incidents and then they stand by them, side by side,” Sukstorf said. “They do an amazing job of building up our students. I can’t tell you how awesome it is and how special it is to have a crew that not only serves the forest, protects the structures around here, but also serves these students. It’s an amazing experience.”

title: Kusser named American Legion Auxiliary District 1 Member of the Year
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: Carol Edwards, president of American Legion Auxiliary Unit 33, stands with Jessica Kusser, the winner of the American Legion Auxiliary District 1 Member of the Year. The award was presented in Spearfish at the spring district meeting.  Edwards and Kusser displayed the certificate on Monday at the Sturgis Vets Club.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
1. Kusser.JPG
Carol Edwards, president of American Legion Auxiliary Unit 33, stands with Jessica Kusser, the winner of the American Legion Auxiliary District 1 Member of the Year. The award was presented in Spearfish at the spring district meeting.  Edwards and Kusser displayed the certificate on Monday at the Sturgis Vets Club.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

STURGIS — Jessica Kusser was recently honored as the American Legion Auxiliary District 1 Member of the Year for her outstanding service and dedication to Sturgis Unit 33 during the district spring meeting April 11 in Spearfish.

Kusser said the recognition was meaningful because of her passion for supporting veterans and military families across western South Dakota.

“It’s just nice to be recognized for what I do to support our veterans and their families in the Sturgis and Meade County area,” Kusser said.

District 1 includes communities stretching from Box Elder to Lemmon, Buffalo, McIntosh, Spearfish and Sturgis, most of northwestern South Dakota.

Kusser highlighted 2 projects that stood out during the past year. One was the creation of a “Hero Tree” at the Sturgis Veterans Club for veterans receiving care at the Fort Meade VA Medical Center.

“The idea was similar to an Angel Tree, but it was for the veterans out at Fort Meade,” Kusser said. “A friend helped gather wish lists from the veterans, and we were able to fulfill all of their wishes and deliver the gifts to make their Christmas special.”

Another project involved organizing a joint float for the Sturgis Parade of Lights that brought together local veterans’ organizations, including the VFW, American Legion and auxiliaries.

“The float was called ‘Camouflage and Christmas Lights,’ and it won the Heartstrings Award,” Kusser said. “I had seen the idea online and wanted to bring it to life in Sturgis. Being the child of 2 soldiers, it was something I felt needed to happen here in town.”

Carol Edwards, president of American Legion Auxiliary Unit 33, explained that units across South Dakota first select a local Member of the Year before nominees advance to the district level. South Dakota is divided into eight districts, with one winner selected from each district to compete for the state honor at the Department Convention June 20 in Aberdeen.

The statewide winner will receive a trip to the national convention in Louisville, Kentucky, later this summer.

“Jessica will be competing for that honor for the second time at the department level, and we hope she wins it this year,” Edwards said.

Edwards said Kusser’s lifelong connection to military service and veterans made her an easy choice for the nomination.

“Jessica was very worthy of this nomination at the unit level,” Edwards said. “She is the daughter of 2 Army veterans, so she understands what it’s like to have parents deployed. She has served veterans her whole life.”

Kusser currently serves as treasurer for Sturgis Unit 33 and is active in children and youth programs as well as veterans affairs initiatives.

“Veterans are very close and very dear to her heart,” Edwards said. “Not only did her parents serve, but several of her uncles also served. It was an easy nomination for me to make because she truly cares about helping veterans and their families.”

title: Tense hearing on uranium drilling tests new language-translation law before its effective date
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: HOT SPRINGS — A new state law requiring language translation services for some government proceedings — like a contentious recent hearing for a permit application to drill for uranium in the Black Hills — has had its first test drive, even though it doesn’t take effect until later this summer.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

HOT SPRINGS — A new state law requiring language translation services for some government proceedings — like a contentious recent hearing for a permit application to drill for uranium in the Black Hills — has had its first test drive, even though it doesn’t take effect until later this summer.

The law requires the decision-making office or board in an administrative contested case to hire an interpreter or translator when a witness or party needs it.

“Any proceeding that’s open to the public would receive or have those translation services available at no cost to the participants, so it would be covered by the state of South Dakota,” said Rep. Erik Muckey, D-Sioux Falls, the law’s sponsor.

The law was adopted in March, and it takes effect July 1.

Meanwhile, a decision on a permit application for a company to explore underground for uranium in the southern Black Hills near Edgemont has been pending since 2024.

Dozens of people have signed on as official project opponents, making the matter a contested case. Some have expressed concerns about potential water contamination they said could result from underground drilling, while others have said the proposed drilling site is too close to Craven Canyon — which is lined with ancient Native American petroglyphs and is used for prayer and ceremonies.

Some of those people speak Lakota, the language of tribes in western South Dakota. Elizabeth Lone Eagle, a project opponent, submitted a request for Lakota interpretation services last August and listed five interested parties in the case as Lakota first-language speakers.

Despite not being legally required to provide a translator since the new law hasn’t taken effect yet, Board Chairman Glenn Blumhardt referenced the new law during a March meeting, when the board was voting to overturn an earlier decision by Hearing Chairman Bob Morris, who had denied interpretation services.

“Is this bill currently in effect? The answer is no,” Blumhardt said. “The point is whether or not this is applicable at this time.”

The board voted to provide translation services as outlined in the law.

What the law says

Muckey introduced the legislation known as Helen’s Law, for Helen Red Feather, one of 5 Lakota first-language speakers who requested Lakota interpretation services.

“This isn’t just about this particular case and trying to tip the odds of this particular instance, but to make it a fair process for this case and virtually every case going forward,” Muckey said. “I’m just grateful that the department saw that need and was willing to change course to follow the spirit of a new law that was soundly supported.”

The state will pay for interpretation services needed during a proceeding. People involved in a contested case can pay for translation services for processes like discovery and document translation. If they’re successful in the case, they can recover those costs.

Oral interpretation slowed the pace of the uranium drilling permit hearing.

“But I don’t know that I was necessarily concerned about that when we were drafting the law,” Muckey said. “The concern was, are we leaving people out of the law? And the answer to that was yes. And so we had to find a way to correct that.”

Though the bill was inspired by Red Feather’s need for translation throughout the case’s proceedings, it’s not just for Lakota speakers, Muckey said.

“We’re also talking about folks who are hard of hearing. They might be blind, and they might need those types of interpretive or translation services, and you have a litany of other languages that are spoken in South Dakota,” he said. “We can’t turn people away from due process of law.”

State officials offered to pay $61.88 per hour for interpreters during the uranium drilling contested case hearing. The Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources said the rate would be split between the 2 interpreters who were hired, “so only one interpreter is being paid at a time.”

“I was insulted,” by the rate, said Alex White Plume, an Oglala Sioux tribal member, and one of the 2 interpreters hired.

“I did it anyway,” he said. “I did it because there was a need and it was important for the ones to hear exactly what it’s like in their own language so they can have a clearer understanding.”

Lakota has experienced a decline in speakers as an effect of colonization, and because of forced attendance at boarding schools that required Native American students to speak English in the 1800s and much of the next century. But White Plume said most of the people in his area still speak their own language.

“I grew up speaking Lakota, and English is my second language,” he said. “The vast majority of the members of my community will still speak Lakota, and it’s funny to hear somebody come speak white-man language amongst us, cause it sounds funny.”

Translating for Lakota speakers in the audience was an honor, White Plume said.

“That was really important for the Lakota speakers to really hear their language and get a clear understanding about what the legal jargon was that the lawyers were speaking,” he said.

Hearing started without interpretation

The uranium drilling permit hearing started May 18 in Hot Springs and was scheduled for 5 days. On the first day, state officials began the hearing without a Lakota interpreter, despite agreeing to provide one.

A state Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources staff member said potential interpreters had conflicts of interest or scheduling conflicts that prevented them from accepting the role.

After project opponents complained about the lack of an interpreter, the state entered into a contract with White Plume and Leola One Feather to interpret the second and following days of the hearing.

When some portions of the hearing’s second day proceeded without Lakota interpretation, project opponents objected.

“This is institutionalized racism, and you are promoting it,” Elizabeth Lone Eagle said, standing from her seat in the audience.

She said the board was “forbidding” the translator, One Feather, “from doing her job, because you want your white colonizer sanitized way of doing things.” The audience cheered, and the board did not respond.

On the third day, the hearing was adjourned indefinitely after Lone Eagle filed a federal lawsuit against the board, the state’s Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources, Clean Nuclear Energy and state employees involved in evaluating the permit application, alleging violations of due process. Lone Eagle filed the lawsuit herself, without representation by an attorney.

Lone Eagle, along with 6 other people, including 5 described as Lakota first-language speakers, are listed as plaintiffs. The suit alleges “systematic, ongoing, and deliberate denial of meaningful participation to Lakota first-language speaking” project opponents.

A spokesman for the Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources told South Dakota Searchlight “the Board has postponed the hearing pending resolution of the federal case. Because the Department is a party to the litigation, we are not able to comment on the lawsuit.”

Last week, a federal judge denied Lone Eagle’s request for a temporary restraining order that would have stopped the permit hearing’s proceedings, but the lawsuit remains active.

title: Meade School District honors retirees,  staff achievements, years of service at  annual recognition banquet
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: The staff that was recognized for 35 years of service, from left Roxanne Murphy (SES) and Becky Silvernail (Whitewood).  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
3.. awards.JPG
The staff that was recognized for 35 years of service, from left Roxanne Murphy (SES) and Becky Silvernail (Whitewood).  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

 4. awards.JPG
The Meade 46-1 School District honored 9 staff that will retire at the end of this school year at the Staff Retirement and Recognition Banquet on Thursday at the West Gym. Top from left: Theresa Hanzlik, Gary Nelson, and Janis Mathis Anderson.  Middle row:  Julie Meyer and Amy Richards.  Front from left:  Laura Sandness Coleen Keffeler, and Joan Wilson. Not pictured: Kim Cunningham Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

STURGIS — Nearly 500 staff members, friends and community members gathered May 21 for the annual staff retirement and recognition banquet, where they celebrated retirees, years of service milestones, special recognitions, Spirit of a Scooper awards, and the district’s teacher and support staff of the year.

The event opened with remarks from Superintendent Wayne Wormstadt, who thanked employees for their dedication to students and families throughout the district.

“Education is so much more than a test score,” Wormstadt said. “It is truly a dedication to making the world better. You give love to families and kids that need that desperately, and you support them beyond just education. You create great people for the future.”

The banquet also honored 9 retirees with a combined 237 years of service to the district:

Kim Cunningham — 32 years, Stagebarn Middle School

Theresa Hanzlik — 29 years, Central Meade County School

Coleen Keffeler — 36 years, Sturgis Brown High School

Janis Mathis-Anderson — 25 years, Sturgis Elementary School

Julie Meyer — 32 years, Sturgis Elementary School

Gary Nelson — 37 years, Stagebarn/Sturgis Williams Middle School

Amy Richards — 12 years, rural schools

Laura Sandness — 12 years, Social Services Department

Joan Wilson — 22 years, Piedmont Valley Elementary School

Staff members were also recognized for milestone years of service.

20 years of service: Dan Avery, Chris Koletzky, Chantal Ligtenberg, Shelley Loftus, David Olson, Kelly Remily and Jodie Taylor.

25 years of service: Janis Mathis-Anderson and Mike Roddis.

30 years of service: Kamette Keffeler.

35 years of service: Roxanne Murphy and Becky Silvernail.

Meade School Board President Justin Jutting presented the Spirit of a Scooper awards and reflected on the challenges and accomplishments of the school year.

“This year has not been easy for any of us,” Jutting said. “We faced difficult conversations, financial constraints, hard decisions and moments that tested us personally and professionally. Yet through it all, you showed up for your students, your coworkers, your families and your community.”

Jutting praised district employees for the lasting impact they make on students and the community every day. “You are not simply employees,” he said. “You are mentors, role models, protectors, encouragers and difference-makers.”

He encouraged staff members to take time over the summer to rest, recharge and reflect on the positive impressions they leave on students and colleagues.

“Take time to celebrate yourself, celebrate your accomplishments and celebrate what you do,” Jutting said. “Every one of you is important to our district.”

Jutting closed the ceremony with a humorous story about a misplaced speech draft that briefly hinted staff members might be dismissed early for the day, drawing laughter from the crowd. Despite the joke, he thanked employees for their continued commitment to the district and wished them a well-deserved summer break.

title: Spearfish citizen offers to donate trail improvements in Creekside Nature Area
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — Matt Polich is the owner of North Star Construction. He is also a dog lover. His French bulldog, Tucker, loved to go on walks in the Creekside Nature Area near Evans Park. Tucker recently passed away; Polich was looking for a way to honor his memory.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — Matt Polich is the owner of North Star Construction. He is also a dog lover. His French bulldog, Tucker, loved to go on walks in the Creekside Nature Area near Evans Park. Tucker recently passed away; Polich was looking for a way to honor his memory.

“We’re trying to find a way to kind of give back to other dog owners and other dogs, and make a nice improvement if we can,” Polich said.

Because of his expertise in sand and gravel, he offered to resurface a one-mile, 8-foot-wide stretch of trail using a road-base aggregate (think of the kind of rock surface hikers encounter on the Mickelson Trail).

Polich has offered to donate the materials, equipment, and labor necessary to improve the trail surface. It would not be paved. It would not be re-graded. It would be resurfaced at no cost to the city. Ordinarily, this kind of project would cost between $50,000 and $100,000 to complete.

“I don’t plan on doing much re-leveling in that area because of floodplain questions. I’m not really into changing the profile,” Polich said. “I’m not really intending on changing it, just improving the surfacing. When it's a nicely packed surface, it will be easier for my folks, for example, if they want to walk down to the dog park, it would be better for them, easier for them.”

The Spearfish Parks and Recreation Board recommended that Polich undertake the project in 2 phases if the council votes to move the trail enhancement project forward.

“That was kind of a concern some of the park members voiced was changing the aesthetic, just the feel in the nature area, to have a surfaced path taken away from that,” McDonald said.

The board recommended surfacing a half mile of trail on the west side of the nature area first, then, based on public feedback, the council could decide if they want the second half of the trail graveled as well.

Polich said he doesn’t have a preference. He’s happy to do the project in phases, or all at once, based on what the public wants and what the council decides.

“Whatever they want us to do, we would love to participate in, whether it is 100 feet at a time for however long, that is fine,” Polich said.

Councilman Scott Hourigan said he wouldn’t mind seeing the trail completed all at once.

“I think we should do the whole thing at once because that east side is in rough shape. With the cross country meets and stuff they do there, and with us doing the Creekside improvements, just down the street from here, I think this just adds to what we are trying to accomplish,” Hourigan said.

The clean roadbase aggregate would ideally improve the stability of the trail and improve the condition for runners. The area has been used in years past for high school cross-country meets, McDonald told the city council.

“We do host the middle school and high school cross country teams. Dalton Wademan, who is the athletic director at the high school, brought up the fact that there are teams that have dropped out of our cross-country meets. It is very uneven and not ideal for running<’ McDonald said. “It would change the look and feel a bit, but my personal opinion is that it would be an enhancement.”

Spearfish resident Joe Jorgensen said the improvement would be worth the change in the trail’s appearance.

“I attended the park and forestry meeting and listened to their discussion,” Jorgensen told the city council during its Wednesday study session. “I think we should do the whole thing, for the high school and the middle school kids who are over there running, and then for the old man who doesn’t want to twist his ankle.”

Spearfish Public Works Director Adam McMahon said the trail could help fill gaps in the existing system.

“Correct me if I am wrong, Rex. We don’t have a lot of compacted gravel paths available to our community. It is mostly the paved paths and the natural paths,” McMahon said to McDonald. “The compacted paths provide for a need that is not being met by those other two trail types, is that correct?”

“That is 100% correct. We don’t have anything like this,” McDonald said. “I refer to the Mickelson Trail, which I think most people are familiar with. Matt also did the Fort Meade Trail recently, which would be a similar type of trail in Sturgis on Fort Meade property that they have incorporated into their rec path. It is something that we don’t currently have in town, but it is something that is fairly common throughout the area.”

Spearfish City Councilwoman Jamie Hafner said she would be in favor of the donated project.

“Matt, I just want to say that this is an awesome idea. I love the area along the creek, and I am just grateful to have a citizen who is willing to make this enhancement on this path, so thank you,” Councilwoman Jamie Hafner said.

If the council votes to allow Polich’s donation, and the project is completed, a 16-inch by 16-inch plaque will be installed at the trailhead in memory of Tucker.

“We just really hope that other people can enjoy that little area as much as we have,” Polich said.

title: School’s out for Cpl. Stephen Schmeltzer
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Cpl. Stephen Schmeltzer is one of the first police corporals in Belle Fourche. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
SRO 1.JPG
Cpl. Stephen Schmeltzer is one of the first police corporals in Belle Fourche. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

BELLE FOURCHE — Last week, the Belle Fourche School Resource Officer Stephen Schmeltzer received a significant promotion. On May 18, he and Heath Hartner became the police department’s first two officers to earn the rank of corporal.

For Schmeltzer, stepping into the new rank and role is bittersweet. It means leaving a pretty treasured position behind.

For the past 4 years, Schmeltzer has been the Belle Fourche school resource officer (SRO).

“Starting out I really didn’t have any expectations other than I wanted to do my best for the kids. The whole reason why I wanted to be there was to help kids and make sure that they are OK and teach them the best way that I can, what I was taught in school,” Schmeltzer said.

Schmeltzer has understood the impact and value of school resource officers since his teenage years.

Once, as a middle school student, and once in high school, Schmeltzer interacted with the school resource officer in Sturgis.

“I did something kind of dumb and had to have a conversation with him. He listened to what I had to say, believed in what I had to say, and turned it into that teaching moment,” Schmeltzer said. “I thought that if I ever became a police officer, that is what I wanted to do. I wanted to help kids the same way he did for me. I got employed here (at the Belle Fourche Police Department) that was the one question I always had was, ‘Do you have an SRO program?’”

Four years ago, when the Belle Fourche School District applied for and secured funding for a school resource officer, Schmeltzer leapt at the opportunity.

 SRO.jpg
After promoting to corporal, Stephen Schmeltzer is leaving his school days behind. He has been the school resource officer in Belle Fourche for 4 years. He is pictured here on his first day of school as an SRO. Courtesy photo 

“More than anything, I wanted to do it to help the kids. Yes, make sure they are safe, but you can turn a kid that is having trouble into a great kid just by giving them the attention that they are needing,” Schmeltzer said.

But it took him a little while to learn that. In his first semester as an SRO, Schmeltzer said he felt a little out of place. He would rotate his time between all of the schools in the district, and kids weren’t always sure how to react to his presence.

“There is one little dude at the middle school,” Schmeltzer said. “When I first started, he was terrified of me. I don’t know why. By the end of the year, he was talking to me, and we were having fun. At the end of this year, he would do anything he could to get a jump scare out of me.”

That wasn’t the only student for whom Schmeltzer was able to flip the script.

“A couple of other kids, too, same boat. They’re knuckleheads, but I enjoyed seeing them every day and even getting to talk to some of them, sitting down to have conversations. They just ask to talk, 20 minutes go by, and they’re feeling better,” Schmeltzer said.

Schmeltzer said kids often need a listening ear most of all. Other times, as an SRO, he made memories not only by listening, but also by making a little noise.

“I was at South Park helping to serve lunch, which is something I like doing, because all of the kids can see me and I can interact with all the kids,” Schmeltzer recalled.

While serving lunch, there are long periods of standing and waiting. During one of those sessions, Schmeltzer started to tap on the Plexiglas at the serving station, absently at first. 

“I started kind of pounding on the sneeze guard to the beat of ‘We Will Rock You.” Within a couple of seconds, I had the whole lunchroom following along in perfect sync,” Schmeltzer said. “To me, it was just so cool to see 100 kids following along to that beat.”

Schmeltzer said the music teacher was impressed that he could maintain the attention of so many elementary schoolers all at once, guiding them to operate together. Another teacher, conducting tests next to the lunchroom, was less impressed.

Still, the memory remains a favorite of Schmeltzer’s. He also enjoyed chaperoning snowball dances and prom (although the middle school dances were his favorite, because of the infectious energy and fun that prevailed during those events). He had interactions with all kinds of students in numerous circumstances.

“For any future SROs, the word of advice that I can give is, go into everything with an open mind. You’re going to deal with the same kids on a repeated basis, but you can’t look at the kid and be like, well, so and so did that,” Schmeltzer said. “There will be a time when they come to you, and they really need help. A kid might be framed as being a ‘screw-up,’ quote-on-quote, but you can’t look at it like that. You can’t look at their past, you have to look at them as their current self.”

Moving forward, Schmeltzer will take on some command duties. He’ll be back on patrol and back working on investigations.

“That was something I found that I enjoyed as SRO,” Schmeltzer said. “I did fall under our detective here. Just to make his plate less heavy, I would take a lot of the investigations that would come onto his plate a little less heavy. I’ve enjoyed traffic stops, and responding to emergency calls and stuff, I’ve found I really enjoy investigation.”

Despite that, the new corporal said he is really going to miss the daily high fives and big smiles from the kids in Belle Fourche.

title: Lead Historic Preservation chair calls for penalties for demo permit violations
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: A garage structure at 515 Railroad Ave. was mostly demolished before city officials noticed and issued a stop work order until owners obtained a demolition permit. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
Lead Historic Preservation chair calls for penalties for demo permit violations
A garage structure at 515 Railroad Ave. was mostly demolished before city officials noticed and issued a stop work order until owners obtained a demolition permit. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

LEAD — The city of Lead should consider putting some teeth into its demolition permit ordinances, instituting penalties for homeowners who do not follow the proper channels, Terry Smith, chairman of the Lead Historic Preservation Commission said Monday. 

Lead Building Inspector Dennis Schumacher told the city commission that recently a resident started demolishing a structure at 515 Railroad Ave., without obtaining a permit. Schumacher said when he discovered the work in progress without a permit, he issued a stop work order, while he checked with the county assessor to determine whether the structure is historic. 

While the demolished building is located within a historic district of Lead, it is not considered a contributing historic structure. Schumacher said a contributing structure is one that is listed on the South Dakota Register of Historic Places. 

The normal process for demolition in the city of Lead is for the Lead Planning and Zoning and Historic Preservation commissions to approve demolition permits. The Historic Preservation Commission checks to see if the building is considered a contributing structure, before issuing the permits.

But the old garage on Railroad Avenue was already mostly demolished before any city officials were able to make any determinations.  

“At the end of the day we do believe that anybody who comes into the city for demolition needs to get a request before it’s even started,” Smith said. “Just going out and doing the demolition without a permit, that’s a disservice to everybody else who’s come to us for a demolition request. So we think some type of penalty should be enacted.” 

Preston Morrison, whose grandfather owns the property on Railroad Avenue, hired a contractor to take the dilapidated building down due to safety concerns, said he thought the contractor obtained all the necessary permits for the work. The lack of a permit was not intentional and it was not the result of negligence, he said. Morrison added that he has since obtained a demolition permit, which he asked the city to approve, Monday. 

“We hired a contracting company, thinking that all permits would be taken care of through them, so it was a mistake that we didn’t verify that permits were required,” he said. “Not to pass the blame, but that was the point of hiring a contractor who is licensed and insured to take care of a project.”   

A representative from the contractor said they were unaware of the requirement for historic preservation approval. The company, F16 Services in Spearfish, is licensed and approved as a contractor to work in the city of Lead. 

The city of Lead’s demolition permit ordinance does not include penalties for not obtaining a permit. Therefore, Schumacher said there is little the city can do about the situation with the structure on Railroad Avenue. 

“If this ever happens again, we need to make sure there are some kind of repercussions,” Schumacher said. 

Following some further discussion, the Lead City Commission unanimously approved the demolition permit, and authorized the contractor to continue work to remove the structure.

title: Spearfish poised to tap into state funding to tighten cybersecurity
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — In 2024, the South Dakota State Legislature passed Senate Bill 187, appropriating $7 million to the office of the attorney general to launch cybersecurity initiatives for municipalities and counties in the state.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

SPEARFISH — In 2024, the South Dakota State Legislature passed Senate Bill 187, appropriating $7 million to the office of the attorney general to launch cybersecurity initiatives for municipalities and counties in the state.

Spearfish plans to take advantage of some of those funds to participate in the SecureSD Cybersecurity program.

If the city council approves a memorandum of understanding on Monday, staff will partner with Dakota State University to test Spearfish’s cybersecurity.

“We’ve worked with Dakota State University multiple times in the past to do some testing on our cybersecurity networks for us to either make changes or improve our cybersecurity,” said City Finance Officer Michelle DeNeui. “There will be no cost for this agreement to work with Dakota State University, and they’ll be able to assist us in finding any cybersecurity lapse or any issues that we have within our cybersecurity program so that we can expand and enhance our cybersecurity.”

If the memorandum of understanding with Dakota State University is adopted, the city will be able to use state funding to purchase hardware, software, or services it may need to protect citizen information.

title: Coeur Wharf delivers  annual report: 11 years  of mining to come
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Coeur Wharf delivered an annual report to Lawrence County Commissioners, reporting 11 more years of sustainable mining to come. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
wharf.jpg
Coeur Wharf delivered an annual report to Lawrence County Commissioners, reporting 11 more years of sustainable mining to come. Pioneer file photo 

DEADWOOD — According to an annual report to the Lawrence County Commissioners Tuesday, Coeur Wharf has 11 years of continued mining ahead of them. 

Jasmine McCauley, environmental manager at Coeur Wharf, presented an annual and local impact report to commissioners, detailing progress made in the last year, plans for the future, and production numbers.  

McCauley said that according to a recent S-K 1300 technical report, the mine has 11 years of operations ahead of it. She said that it is unclear at this time whether the mine will have to expand outside of its current permitted boundaries to operate for another 11 years.  

McCauley said that active areas in the mind right now include the Copper Head waste dump and pit backfill area, the Boston Pit, and the Portland Ridgeline Pit.  

In 2025, McCauley reported 1,320.24 acres have been affected by the mine, and 74.06 acres of land were fully reclaimed. Another 19.79 acres were in interim reclamation stages by the end of 2025. This year, McCauley said another 60 acres are slated for reclamation.  

McCauley reported no changes with Golden Reward since last year.  

McCauley reported approximately 76 million gallons of groundwater were pumped by the mine for operations last year and approximately 136 million gallons of surface water was withdrawn.  

“A lot of that surface water is pulled so we can treat it,” said McCauley. “We did commission our new selenium treatment facility in the fall of last year, so that is included in that number. We were able to treat 126 million gallons and land applied, so we returned it (to the ground), and we returned 31 million (gallons) back into surface waters.” 

McCauley said work concurrent reclamation efforts continue while the mine is in operation, meaning that leach pads are active on site to treat ground water after it is used to extract ore from raw material.  

“Once the pad is complete, the leaching material is neutralized, denitrified, and then all of everything that goes through it has to meet the groundwater requirements, which is where our treatment comes in,” said McCauley. “Then we put that material back into a waste dump and we start the reclamation process with it.” 

According to the report, the unloading of pad one was completed in the first quarter of 2025. Pads 4 and 5 were neutralized and denitrified. The unloading of pad 4 began last year, and pad 5 was completed in the first quarter of this year. The neutralization, denitrification, and unloading of pad 3 is scheduled for this year, with pad 2 to follow and be completed by 2027. The cycle is scheduled to begin again with pad one in the fourth quarter of 2026.  

In 2025, McCauley reported that 4.2 million tons of ore was mined and nearly 15 million of overburden or waste rock was mined. Of those tons, the mine produced 97,327 ounces of gold and 135,722 ounces of silver.  

McCauley said that Coeur Wharf utilized drone spraying for weed control on a large section of acreage and seeded approximately 75 acres of reclaimed ground.  

“It’s actually coming up quite nicely, you can see it as you drive up,” said McCauley.  

McCauley said that reclamation efforts are expected to continue on the northern segment of Green and Bald Mountains and other areas throughout the mine.  

McCauley said that a fire to the crushing facility on site in November 2025 totaled the facility, necessitating contracts with 2 crushers to continue work on site.  Spent ore from the crushing operations will be placed in the American Eagle dump. 

Local impact review 

McCauley reported that Coeur Wharf employees an average of 266 employees. She said that number increases over the summer with the hire of summer help and student interns.  

A breakdown of the roles of employment lists more than 100 job in operations, 25 maintenance positions, 4 employees in exploration, 6 in environmental roles, 5 in crushing and processing, and more than 50 in professional positions. 

According to the local impact review, the mine has an annual payroll of more than $35 million The annual salary for full-time, hourly employees averages more than $80,000.  

“Our average is greater than the $56,000 that is published by the state of South Dakota, so it’s a really good opportunity for people,” McCauley said. 

McCauley said that over 90% of the employees reside within a one-hour radius of the mine site and have stayed with the company for an average of 7 years. 

Of the 266 employees, McCauley said that 52% are from and work in Lawrence County. A breakdown of the payroll lists 52% or $18 million to employees in Lawrence County, 20% or $7 million in Meade County, 15% or $5 million in Butte County, 10% or $3.5 million in Pennington County, and 1% or $353,051 in Wyoming.  

McCauley reported that Coeur Wharf tries to keep the majority of their spending local, reporting that the mine spent more than $36 million on purchase in South Dakota and paid more than $17 million in taxes. McCauley said the “lions share” of the taxes were paid towards the mining severance tax.  

In community investments, McCauley reported that more than $120,000 was spent on education, sports, and culture, $40,000 was spent on economic development and infrastructure, and $50,000 was spent on a sustainability fund as well as an additional $50,000 on health and well-being.  

“We are partnering with local schools and universities and a lot of local organizations,” said McCauley. “We do have very strong standings within the community, and we try to partner with school districts and all of the local non-profits to ensure that we are good partners.” 

McCauley spoke towards Coeur Wharf’s ongoing environmental responsibilities, including concurrent land reclamation and water management. 

“Water management is a fulltime gig,” said McCauley. “We do have our 4 water treatment plans that we run.” 

According to the report, Coeur Wharf owns and operates 76 groundwater wells and 18 surface water sampling sites that are tested several times per year.  

McCauley said that the mine aims to produce between 85,000 and 100,000 ounces of gold each year to continue long-term sustainability of the mine site. Those operations include moving approximately 40,000 tons of rock daily and crushing between 10,000 and 18,000 tons of rock daily.  

According to the report, gold mining’s economic and cultural significance means more than jewelry and investment. Gold is used in critical technologies, including electronics, smartphones, medical equipment, and aerospace and medical technologies.  

“Gold is essential,” said McCauley. “Tell your friends and tell your neighbors.”

title: Teen drowns at Belle Fourche Reservoir
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: BELLE FOURCHE — A teenage boy drowned Friday afternoon at the Belle Fourche Reservoir.
_full_text:
Teen drowns at Belle Fourche Reservoir

BELLE FOURCHE — A teenage boy drowned Friday afternoon at the Belle Fourche Reservoir.

According to the Butte County Sheriff’s Office, around 2:15 p.m. Friday, its dispatch center received a report of a swimmer in distress at the Tequila Beach swimming area.

When responders arrived, witnesses told them that the boy, 15, of Belle Fourche, was on a paddle board in rough water, lost hold of the paddle board in the wind, and went under the water. Butte County Sheriff Fred Lamphere told the Pioneer that the teen did not have a life jacket with him.

Bystanders attempted to locate the boy without success. His name is not being released at this time.

Boats were launched by members of the South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks department and Belle Fourche Fire Department. Immediate air and ground searches were conducted, and the paddle board was recovered within an hour. 

Assistance was requested from the Pennington County Search and Rescue Dive Team. They began searching where the boy was last seen. Around 7:50 p.m., the body of the teen was recovered.

Lamphere said this marks the second drowning at the reservoir in the past several years. 

In June 2023, Austin Jewett, 18, also drown at Rocky Point Recreation Swim Area while paddleboarding. The circumstances around his death were nearly identical to the recent tragedy — paddleboarding in rough water, no flotation device available, and he couldn’t hold onto the paddleboard.

Lamphere said the reservoir has hidden dangers. First the depth can drop off sharply deceiving swimmers. Its depth can drop from 3-4 feet to 8-10 within a step or 2. Secondly, winds can form rough waves quickly.

“I’ve been out there fishing with friends, and you’ll have a cloud that comes over the Black Hills and it will go from calm to 3–4-foot waves with whitecaps in a matter of minutes,” he said. 

Lamphere said Tequila Beach is somewhat protected from the southeast wind that had been blowing earlier in the day. The wind died down and the waters calmed before they increased quickly Friday.

State law requires personal flotation devices be available on all boats, to include paddleboards and innertubes.

“When the waves come up, it can be tough to survive with one on,” he said. “Without one, it’s almost not survivable.”

Additional agencies responding to the Friday incident were the Belle Fourche Ambulance Service, Nisland/Arpan, Butte, and Vale fire departments, and the South Dakota Highway Patrol.

title: High Plains Western Heritage Center  hires new director
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer
description: Juliet Main replaced Karla Scovell, the long-serving director of the High Plains Western Heritage Center. Courtesy photo.
_full_text:
High Plains Western Heritage Center  hires new director 
Juliet Main replaced Karla Scovell, the long-serving director of the High Plains Western Heritage Center. Courtesy photo.  

SPEARFISH — In January, the High Plains Western Heritage Center in Spearfish hired Juliet Main, a South Dakota native, to serve as its new executive director. 

Main graduated from Belle Fourche High School and attended the University of Wyoming on a rodeo scholarship. 

“The Western way of life is in my blood,” Main said. 

After graduating college, Main moved to Washington, D.C., where she worked for Wyoming Congresswoman Barbara Cubin, and later House Majority Leader Dick Armey. After leaving Capitol Hill, she worked in venue and event management. 

When Main returned to South Dakota, she became aware of the opening at the Heritage Center, though she said she had been attending events at the museum for 20 years. 

“I seized my responsibility to steward the mission and vision of the museum, but also (to) help drive it forward into this next season,” Main said. 

Main is the only full-time employee of the museum, but she is assisted by 35 volunteers and additional seasonal workers. 

“I’m just overwhelmed and very impressed by their (the volunteers’) dedication and investment at the museum,” Main said. “So many guests before they leave or get on the bus will say what a difference the volunteers made to their experience. They appreciated their South Dakota hospitality.”

Main said that during her tenure as director she hopes to make the Heritage museum, which preserves the history of South Dakota, North Dakota, Wyoming, Montana and Nebraska, the premier museum in the area, and the “don’t miss” museum. 

“Because to me that would be carrying on the legacy of our founders, Edgar Gardner and Harry Blair — their vision when they built this is that it would be here for the next generation,” Main said.

Main replaced Karla Scovell, who was the museum’s director for 10 years. 

“I know I have big shoes to fill, and I’m standing on the shoulders of Karla Scovell, the retiring director, and all those that have come before me. And I am humbled and honored for the opportunity to take the baton and move the baton into this next season. 

The High Plains Western Heritage Center is located at 825 Heritage Dr., in Spearfish.

title: Gaming continues  to profit in Deadwood

Gaming continues  to profit in Deadwood
Courtesy photo 

DEADWOOD — Gaming statistics in Deadwood continue to climb in Deadwood according to recent numbers released by the South Dakota Commission on Gaming. 

According to the recent report, the overall gaming handle in April is up 12.5% compared to the same month last year. Slot machines continue to be the leading driver of success in gaming, showing a 12.06% increase over last year, but table games saw a significant increase of 22.55%. Sports wagering saw the only decline, reporting a 6.06% decrease — the first drop in recorded stats in more than a year, said George Milos, director of the Deadwood Gaming Association. 

“The strong numbers for April are hopefully a sign of things to come,” said Milos. “Excellent weather, a strong slate of special events, and affordability for the customer all contributed to these results. As peak tourism season begins in May, we look forward to continuing to entertain our guests with everything Deadwood has to offer.”

Operators offered $2,298,809.18 in “free play” incentives in April, leading to taxable gross revenues of $13,037,260.60. 

Total taxes collected in April came to $1,173,353,45. That amount was distributed as follows: $130,372.61 to the state general fund; $417,192.34 to South Dakota Tourism; and $104,298.09 to Lawrence County.

title: Sturgis St. Francis of Assisi church to host new  Catholic high school
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — A new Catholic high school is coming to Sturgis.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

STURGIS — A new Catholic high school is coming to Sturgis. 

Jacques Daniel, one of 4 founders of Chesterton Academy of Blessed Alcuin of York, said plans are underway to start the new school at St. Francis of Assisi Catholic Church in Sturgis, which has dedicated classroom space. Organizers plan to start in the fall with classes for grades 9 and 10, but interested persons with students in 11th or 12th grade are encouraged to apply as well. 

The Diocese of Rapid City currently sponsors only one Catholic school system that includes an elementary and a high school in Rapid City. But Daniel said Chesterton Academy will be the first classical Catholic high school in the area. 

Named for the prolific author G.K. Chesterton, the school will be fully accredited through the National Council for Private School Accreditation, and is part of a national network of Chesterton Academy schools. The schools started in Edina, Minn., in 2008, and there are more than 100 schools in 30 states and at least 10 different countries, including Japan, Britain, Canada, Brazil, Nigeria, and Argentina. 

The 3 pillars of the school system include intellect, which focuses on the interrelationship of great ideas and teaching students how to think; character, which strives to help students grow in virtues of prudence, temperance, fortitude, and justice as the foundation of leadership; and spirituality, to teach students to know, love, and serve God. 

Founders of the Sturgis school include Daniel, Mario Rangel, Anthony Flores, and Matthew Remmich. Daniel said the school is the result of 20 years of talks about bringing a Catholic, classical education model school to the Diocese. A classical education model focuses on teaching the liberal arts through reading books and employing Socratic method discussions in the classroom, emphasizing grammar, logic, and rhetoric. The school will include a heavy curriculum in the liberal arts, with required classes in choir, music theory, theater, and art, as well as science, history, math, language arts, foreign language, theology, and philosophy. It will operate with a regular school day from 8 a.m. to 3:30 p.m., 5 days a week. 

“One of the beautiful things at Chesterton is when you look at the course catalog, there’s a very integrated approach. There is a way that the math is impacted by the history and the literature that you’re reading,” Daniel said. “It’s integrated as a grade level, which builds upon itself. It starts with the foundation of ancient civilization and goes into philosophy, then you progress through the incarnation, and then junior year is medieval times, and senior year is the modern world. It’s integrated and systematic, and they work together and it’s just this beautiful progression.” 

Daniel said the classical education model is one that is gaining popularity throughout the country in religious and secular institutions. One charter school in Texas, he said, has a waiting list of 6,000 students. The school is open for enrollment by students of all faiths, but Daniel said its focus will be Catholic — with daily Mass and Catholic teachers. 

One defining characteristic of the school will be the different “houses” students are sorted into, Daniel said, which is modeled after the Oxford Academy in Britain. Students will be sorted into four houses, named for the four pillars that hold up the chair of Peter in St. Peter’s Basilica — St. Augustine, St. Ambrose, St. Chrysostom, and St. Authanasius. 

“The idea of the house system is that the students are building community,” Daniel said. “They’re building friendship. They’re going to be doing things outside of class time together with their families. We’re building a community of people, not just shoving things in their brain.” 

For more information about Chesterton Academy visit https://chestertonalcuin.org/.

title: Sturgis Motorcycle Rally Grand Marshal fulfilling bucket list
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Two planes hijacked by Arab terrorists crash into the World Trade Center on September 11, 2001. The twin towers collapsed causing almost 3,000 deaths. NYC Firefighter Tim Duffy arrives downtown on his Harley after 1st tower collapse
_full_text:
Firefighter Tim Duffy arrives downtown after 1st tower collapse
Two planes hijacked by Arab terrorists crash into the World Trade Center on September 11, 2001. The twin towers collapsed causing almost 3,000 deaths. NYC Firefighter Tim Duffy arrives downtown on his Harley after 1st tower collapse 

 Grand Marshal Tim Duffy 2.jpg
Screenshot 

STURGIS — For Tim Duffy, motorcycles have never just been about the ride.

They’ve been about freedom, about clearing your head, about connection.

“Riding has meant freedom, independence, and stress relief,” Duffy says. “That’s what wind therapy is.”

This August, that lifelong connection to the road brings him to the Black Hills for the first time, as grand marshal of the 2026 Sturgis Motorcycle Rally.

Why Tim Duffy you may ask.

This year marks the 25th anniversary of 9/11, and on that Tuesday, Sept. 11, 2001, though off duty, Duffy put on his firefighter gear and rode his 2000 Harley-Davidson Super Glide Sport into lower Manhattan to help. He arrived at the World Trade Center just as the South Tower collapsed, burying him in debris.

He survived and went on to help rescue others throughout the day.

Photographer Allan Tannenbaum captured what would become a historic image of Duffy astride his motorcycle amid the debris-strewn streets of Manhattan. Duffy says that moment in history changed the course of his life.

Looking back on 9/11, Duffy describes the devastation as overwhelming. But even in that moment, his focus never shifted far from others.

“When everything went quiet it was time to go to work,” he said. 

That mindset, service before self, has stayed with him ever since.

More than two decades later, Duffy continues to live with purpose. He remains proud of his time as a New York City firefighter, calling it “the best job in the world,” and stays deeply connected to the people he served alongside.

What began in a moment of crisis has become a life defined by service, healing, and the freedom found on two wheels.

For Duffy, being named Grand Marshal of the 2026 Sturgis Motorcycle Rally is more than a personal honor, it is a chance to recognize the motorcycle brotherhood that has supported him throughout his journey. 

“I’m honored and humbled,” he says. “I feel like I represent a lot of people standing out in front of me. And it’ll be special for my family to see the motorcycle community and brotherhood that’s supported me over the years.”

Though he’s ridden across the country and attended rallies of all kinds, Sturgis has always held a special place in Duffy’s mind.

“This will be my first trip to Sturgis,” he says. “It’s been on my bucket list for a long time. I’ve been to all sorts of other rallies, but this is the mother of them all, and the one I’ve really wanted to get to.”

Like so many riders making their annual pilgrimage, Duffy is drawn not just by the roads but by the people.

“The best part of this (motorcycle) community is the generosity,” he says. “It’s one of the most giving groups of people I’ve ever come across.”

That sense of connection, of instant camaraderie between strangers, is something he knows well.

“The brotherhood is everything,” Duffy says. “I’ve seen it in different parts of my life, but the motorcycle community has its own kind of bond.”

Those ideas of freedom, brotherhood, and resilience, often used to describe the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, also happen to describe Duffy’s life.

“I feel like those three words are part of what defines me,” he said. “From my time in the Navy, to the New York City Fire Department, to the biker community, that brotherhood has always been there.”

And resilience, as he puts it simply, is something he carries with him every day.

“I’m still here,” he says.

When asked what his perfect ride during Rally week might look like, Duffy doesn’t hesitate.

“A long ride on a road less traveled,” he says, “with an old saloon somewhere along the way.”

It’s a vision that fits perfectly with the Black Hills, where winding highways, quiet byways, and unexpected stops define the experience as much as the destination.

And like many riders arriving in Sturgis for the first time, he’s ready to take it all in.

As Grand Marshal, Duffy will lead not just with presence, but with perspective, and his message to the hundreds of thousands who will roll into Sturgis this summer is simple and rooted in the culture that binds them.

“Enjoy the moment,” he says. “Respect the road. And enjoy being part of something bigger than yourself.”

Because to Duffy, that’s what the Rally is really about, not just the bikes, not just the miles, but the shared experience.

That perspective is shaped by a life of service, first in the United States Navy, and later as a firefighter with the FDNY, where standing shoulder to shoulder with others was part of everyday life.

“You take care of your own,” he says. “That’s just how it works.”

That philosophy continues today through his nonprofit, 1 Soldier 1 Dog 1 Team, which pairs veterans and first responders with shelter dogs to help address PTSD and mental health challenges.

“We’re saving two lives, the dog and the veteran,” Duffy says. “And showing people they’re not alone.”

Today Duffy finds hope in the next generation.

“What gives me hope is seeing young people who still believe in this country,” he says. “What it is, and what it should be.”

And now, that journey brings him to Sturgis, to the roar of engines, to the open road, to a community that understands, perhaps better than most, what freedom really feels like.

For Tim Duffy, it’s not just another ride.

It’s one he’s been looking forward to for a long time.

title: SD primary and local  election preview
byline: By South Dakota News Watch
description: Photo illustration by South Dakota News Watch
_full_text:
SD primary and local  election preview
Photo illustration by South Dakota News Watch 

PIERRE — For a non-presidential election year, 2026 has the makings of one of those political seasons that South Dakotans talk about years or even decades to come.

Advertising and communication in a contentious Republican race for governor has dominated airwaves, social media feeds and text notifications. But because of a law change that puts many local contests on Tuesday’s ballot, more than just the party faithful have something at stake in a lot of places across the state.   

Find out which district you live in through the South Dakota Secretary of State website and also see the list of candidates you can vote for as well as a sample ballot, though it may not include all local races.  

Early and absentee voting started last month, but if you’re early voting Monday or going to the polls Tuesday, here’s a summary of the key races along with links to South Dakota News Watch’s coverage.

South Dakota governor

Four Republicans are running to represent the party and meet Democratic candidate Dan Ahlers in the Nov. 3 general election nomination. Here are the Republican candidates with links to profiles by News Watch’s Alexander Rifaat:

Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden (R)  

State House Speaker Jon Hansen (R)  

U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson (R)  

Gov. Larry Rhoden (R)  

If Doeden, Hansen, Johnson or Rhoden doesn’t receive 35% of the vote in the  Republican primary, a runoff election between the two top vote-getters will be held eight weeks later, on July 28.

US Senate

U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds, one of two U.S. senators in Congress from South Dakota, is up for re-election this year.

Republican voters in Tuesday’s primary are choosing between him and challenger Justin McNeal. The winner will meet Democrat Julian Beaudion and Independent Brian Bengs in the Nov. 3 general election.

US House of Representatives

When Johnson opted to run for governor, it opened up South Dakota’s only seat in the U.S. House of Representatives.

Republican voters on Tuesday will choose between Attorney General Marty Jackley and James Bialota Jr., and the winner will meet Democrat Nicole Gronli in the Nov. 3 general election.

South Dakota Legislature

The South Dakota Legislature is comprised of 105 lawmakers from 35 legislative districts, each of which has one senator and two representatives.

Local races

A new South Dakota law about municipal election dates added a lot of races to ballots for many voters, but it also means many non-partisan voters have something to vote on Tuesday. 

That includes in Sioux Falls, where the city’s municipal elections used to be held in April. Voters will be choosing a new mayor, city council members and school board members Tuesday.

Elsewhere in the state, local ballots include positions like county commissioners, auditor, sheriff and the register of deeds.

title: Proposed Indigenous medical school aims  to boost Native physician numbers
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: RAPID CITY — As of 2024, 0.3% of practicing physicians in the nation were Native American.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

RAPID CITY — As of 2024, 0.3% of practicing physicians in the nation were Native American. 

A proposed Indigenous School of Medicine in Rapid City could help change that. 

The school would be the first of its kind in the nation, said Donald Warne, a physician, co-director for the Center for Indigenous Health at Johns Hopkins, and member of the Oglala Sioux Tribe. 

Warne envisions weaving traditions, ceremonies and cultures into the accredited school and its curriculum. Rather than cramming students full of information within four years, the school would prioritize wellbeing and competency — which would allow students to take longer to complete the program if needed, Warne said. 

The approach allows students to bring their full cultural selves into their medical training, he added. 

“There is still a sense we have to check our culture at the door to become a cookie-cutter doctor as opposed to maintaining who we are,” Warne said. “There are still students who feel they aren’t adequately represented or supported in medical school.”

The proposed Indigenous School of Medicine received a $1 million grant from the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation to conduct a feasibility study and business plan, along with a $100,000 NDN Collective capacity building grant. Warne hopes to start enrolling students in 2030. The location within Rapid City has not been finalized.

Tim Ridgway, dean of the University of South Dakota Sanford School of Medicine, said the state likely couldn’t sustain two public medical schools. But he said the Indigenous school would complement — not compete with — USD’s mission.

“How could I not be part of this?” Ridgway said. “It is, in essence, part of the mission of this school.”

The schools could collaborate on curriculum, share faculty, and work together to create residency programs tailored toward Indigenous students, Ridgway said.

The school’s presence in Rapid City could inspire young Native children to pursue medicine, Warne said, and help fill deep vacancies in rural and tribal health facilities with culturally adept physicians. South Dakota has one of the largest health disparities between Native Americans and white residents in the United States, according to a recent report from a foundation that advocates for equitable healthcare.

“Quality of care is improved when there is culture concordance between doctor and patient,” Warne said. “Quality of care and quality of communication are based on cultural competence.”

Kenzie Lindemann is a member of the Oglala Sioux Tribe and a medical school student at USD. Both her parents are physicians; her mother is a member of the Oglala Sioux Tribe and practices on the Cheyenne River Reservation. Lindemann participated in the InMED program — a pipeline initiative through USD and the University of North Dakota to support Native students pursuing medical careers.

Still, she’s drawn to the idea of a school where a Native American student wouldn’t constantly “have to explain yourself” — one surrounded by Indigenous peers, taught through the holistic, competency-based model Warne envisions.

During observed standardized clinical encounters, Lindemann sets aside Native American jewelry or a ribbon skirt. The patient — who determines her grade — is usually non-Native.

“I can’t really change the way I look — my skin or my face shape — but if I can take away some level of unknown biases the standardized patient might have about Native Americans, I’ll do that,” Lindemann said.

She sees the proposed school as a way to shift that dynamic.

“By slowly but surely increasing the number of Native American physicians, maybe people won’t see the stereotypes,” Lindemann said. “Maybe they’ll just see us as physicians in the community.”

title: Lawsuit challenges SD’s new ban  on abortion-pill advertising
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Mayday Health posted signs like this one at gas stations around South Dakota in December 2025 as part of a campaign to spread awareness about the availability of abortion pills. Courtesy of Mayday Health
_full_text:
Lawsuit challenges SD’s new ban  on abortion-pill advertising
Mayday Health posted signs like this one at gas stations around South Dakota in December 2025 as part of a campaign to spread awareness about the availability of abortion pills. Courtesy of Mayday Health 

PIERRE — South Dakota’s new law criminalizing the providing and advertising of abortion pills and other abortion-related items faces a lawsuit alleging the advertising prohibition is unconstitutional.

A New York-based nonprofit, Mayday Health, and a Democratic former South Dakota lawmaker, Nancy Turbak Berry, filed the lawsuit Friday in federal court against South Dakota’s Republican governor and attorney general.

The state’s Republican-dominated Legislature passed the bill in March, and Gov. Larry Rhoden signed it into law that same month. It’s scheduled to take effect July 1.

South Dakota already had a law that bans abortions except when necessary “to preserve the life of the pregnant female.” The new law says no person may knowingly dispense, distribute, sell or advertise an article or thing designed, adapted or intended to produce an abortion. The ban also covers any article, instrument, substance, drug, medicine or thing that is “advertised or described in a manner calculated to lead another to use or apply it for producing an abortion.”

Violations are felonies punishable by up to two years in prison and a $4,000 fine. The law also gives the state attorney general authority to recover civil penalties of $10,000 per violation.

The lawsuit alleges it’s unconstitutional to prohibit advertising that’s protected by the free speech guarantees in the First Amendment.

Turbak Berry previously led a group supporting a failed 2024 ballot question that would have restored abortion rights in the state. The lawsuit alleges her free speech is deterred by the new law. As an example, the lawsuit says the prohibition on advertising would prevent her from wearing a sweatshirt that features Mayday’s mission and web address.

“Unless this court grants relief, Turbak will be deterred from wearing the sweatshirt, and thereby deterred from engaging in lawsuit First Amendment-protected speech,” the lawsuit says.

Turbak Berry responded to South Dakota Searchlight with a written statement.

“Apparently, our state government isn’t satisfied with controlling women’s reproductive organs — they even want to control our eyes and ears,” Turbak Berry said. “They even want control over what women in South Dakota can see and hear. It’s outrageous.”

Gov. Rhoden responded to the lawsuit in a post on X, formerly Twitter.

“If Mayday Health and the abortion lobby want to sue us for defending unborn life, bring it on.”

State Attorney General Marty Jackley issued a written statement.

“The U.S. Supreme Court has made it clear that states have the right to protect life,” Jackley said. “As with Mayday’s previous unsuccessful lawsuit, I will defend innocent life.”

Mayday previously engaged in a legal battle with Jackley over advertisements Mayday placed at gas stations around the state saying “Pregnant? Don’t want to be?” and directing people to Mayday’s website, which includes information on obtaining abortion pills.

In dueling state and federal lawsuits, Jackley accused the nonprofit of violating South Dakota’s abortion ban. Mayday claimed its advertisements were protected under the First Amendment. The lawsuits ended with a settlement that included Mayday removing the ads.

In 2023, medication abortions accounted for 63% of abortions in the country, according to data from the Guttmacher Institute. The drugs mifepristone and misoprostol, commonly used in medication abortions, are also listed on the World Health Organizations’ list of essential medicines.

The U.S. Supreme Court decided earlier this month to preserve telehealth access to mifepristone until after the U.S. 5th Circuit Court of Appeals has ruled on the merits of the lawsuit Louisiana v. Food and Drug Administration. Louisiana, where state officials sued the FDA in October, is arguing that a rule allowing telehealth access to mifepristone undermines the state’s abortion ban.

EDITOR’S NOTE: South Dakota Searchlight has engaged attorney Jim Leach, who represents the plaintiffs in the lawsuit, in a past legal matter.
