title: Forest Service and SD sign agreement to work together on forest management
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — The U.S. Forest Service announced Friday that it has signed a 5-year agreement to work with the state of South Dakota to carry out projects on national forest and adjacent land, possibly including timber harvesting, prescribed burning, forest thinning, grazing, and habitat and watershed restoration.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — The U.S. Forest Service announced Friday that it has signed a 5-year agreement to work with the state of South Dakota to carry out projects on national forest and adjacent land, possibly including timber harvesting, prescribed burning, forest thinning, grazing, and habitat and watershed restoration.

Meanwhile, a former national forest employee said he suspects the agreement will allow the Forest Service to lean more on the state’s help to maintain logging levels.

The shared stewardship agreement is between the state Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources and the Forest Service. It follows similar agreements in other states and comes after President Donald Trump’s executive order last year calling for an “immediate expansion” of American timber production.

Following the initial 5-year term, the agreement may be extended in increments of three years. It does not authorize any project by itself. Specific projects involving money, services, property or other resources would require separate agreements and approvals.

Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz said in a press release the agreement is meant to align state and federal priorities, including work to reduce wildfire threats and address insect and disease outbreaks.

“With this agreement, we are aligning federal and state priorities to accelerate active management in high-risk areas,” Schultz said.

Gov. Larry Rhoden said in the press release that the agreement reinforces the state’s collaboration with the Forest Service to “reduce wildfire risk, improve rangeland health, and support the state’s forest products industry.”

Dave Mertz, a retired Black Hills National Forest natural resource officer, said in an interview with South Dakota Searchlight that he suspects the agreement’s purpose is to maintain or increase timber production by relying more on the state. The Trump administration fired thousands of Forest Service workers nationwide during Department of Government Efficiency cuts last year, although lawsuits resulted in rehirings. 

“I’m suspicious that the primary reason for it is to help the Forest Service get more trees cut,” Mertz said.

In recent years, a debate has raged about the quantity of trees large enough to serve as sawtimber in South Dakota’s Black Hills National Forest. Environmental and conservation groups have argued that decades of mountain pine beetle infestations and large wildfires have reduced the number of trees to a level that requires reduced logging for sustainability. Timber companies have argued that the forest can sustain a higher level of logging.

The Forest Service determines areas available for logging and sells the rights to cut trees. Timber sales in the Black Hills National Forest declined from 2021 to 2024 but increased last year. The roughly 8.4 million cubic feet of timber sold last year in the forest was still far lower than a peak of 25.3 million sold in 2008.

title: Belle Fourche School District offers  free meals to children in June, July
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Belle Fourche School District offers free breakfast and lunch to children during summer months. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
SchoolLunchMenu.tif
The Belle Fourche School District offers free breakfast and lunch to children during summer months. Courtesy photo 

BELLE FOURCHE — The Belle Fourche School District is offering children 0 to 18 years old free breakfast and lunch on weekdays from June 1 - July 10 at 1816 Valley Dr., in the South Park Elementary lunchroom. 

Breakfast is served from 7:45-8:30 a.m. Lunch is served from 11:30 a.m. to 12:35 p.m.

Ashley Nielsen, food services secretary for the Belle Fourche school district, said that the program usually feeds about 180 to 200 children per day.

Meals are available for those 18 and younger.

Nielsen said that most of the children who receive free meals are involved in Belle Fourche’s TRAK and JAM programs, which are free summer and afterschool programs for Belle students.

TRAK serves students through kindergarten and fourth grade. JAM serves students through the fifth and eighth grades. Participation in the TRAK and JAM programs is not required to receive food. 

“It (the program) just provides an activity for the students to do during the summer and keeps them busy, and provides free food,” said Nielsen. 

The free meal program is funded by the Department of Education.

title: Wyoming’s ‘Path of the Pronghorn’ is a signature away  from protections sought  for a quarter century
byline: By Mike Koshmrl WyoFile
description: Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Wyoming’s ‘Path of the Pronghorn’ is a signature away  from protections sought  for a quarter century
Pioneer file photo 

From afar, conservation biologist Joel Berger has tracked Wyoming’s long-lasting attempt to designate a migration corridor used by pronghorn that seasonally trek upwards of 150 miles from Interstate 80 all the way to Grand Teton National Park.

In the early 2000s, Berger, then a Jackson Hole resident, was among the loudest voices urging land and wildlife managers to take steps to ensure that pronghorn could continue moving across a fragmented landscape that was on the front end of the Pinedale Anticline and Jonah field natural gas boom.

In 2003, Berger authored a paper provocatively titled, “Is it acceptable to let a species go extinct in a national park?” That came at a time when then-Wyoming Gov. Dave Freudenthal was wary about protecting the southern reaches of the corridor — a hesitation shared by Sublette County elected officials and the Bureau of Land Management. Safeguards for the migrating pronghorn stalled except in the northern portion of the corridor, where in 2008 the U.S. Forest Service protected some 47,000 acres via a Bridger-Teton National Forest plan amendment.

Very slowly, times changed. A continued push to conserve the perilous passages animals encounter along a route dubbed the Path of the Pronghorn overcame inertia and skepticism.

This week, Berger was enthused to see Wyoming reach the penultimate step of a state-led process for protecting the route. A Gov. Mark Gordon-appointed working group completed its review of the migration corridor, agreeing to recommendations soon headed for the governor’s desk.

“Wyoming sometimes leads, and Wyoming sometimes lags way behind,” Berger told WyoFile. “It’s really nice to see Wyoming, after a quarter of a century, step up and formally declare how important migration corridors are.”

In Pinedale, where the 11-person stakeholder group convened Friday, audience members shared their appreciation for a process that’s almost done.

“I know it doesn’t feel like it — working through Google Docs in real time — but this is actually a historic moment,” Wyoming Outdoor Council staffer Meghan Riley told the working group. “This is the first time that the state has ever gone through the full designation process under the executive order. And it’s the very first time the state has ever tried to do this for pronghorn.”

“I hope you can all pat yourselves on the back,” she added, “and feel good about tackling this.”

Green River resident Bill Ames, a retired land surveyor who’s been a spokesman for the migration, was also effusive. He praised a plan that’s particularly permissive of development and “isn’t going to hurt” economically, yet still protects an “iconic species of Wyoming.”

“What an achievement,” Ames said. “I had no expectation that this would come out this way, this fast, with a very diverse group. Thank you.”

Division over designating the corridors used by the highly migratory Sublette Pronghorn Herd has been a through line of the protracted process. Over seven years ago, extractive industries, counties and agriculture-oriented groups coalesced to halt Game and Fish’s first attempt to protect the landscapes the herd migrates through. In the aftermath, Gordon introduced, via an executive order, a new migration policy that created the process with the working group.

The process culminates in a decision by Gordon or a future governor.

Sara DiRienzo, Gordon’s deputy policy advisor, explained to the working group that she’d be cleaning up the final set of draft recommendations that members fine-tuned on Friday and would give them one more chance to catch typos and make small changes. Then, she said, they’d get presented to the governor “for his review and decision.”

Some resistance to designating the migration corridor remained from industries and counties until the end.

At the onset of Friday’s meeting, working group member and Sublette County Commissioner Lynn Bernard clarified that his elected body still had reservations about designating the route.

“The position of the county (is) we’re thankful, but we’ll control our own county,” Bernard said.

Ultimately, however, none of the 11 working group members voted completely against the idea of designating the migration corridor.

One member, oil and gas industry representative Jasmine Allison, voted to let the designation go forward with “serious reservations.” Two others, agriculture industry representative Mike Henn and mining industry representative Craig Rood, voted to designate “with reservation.” The other eight members were fully on board.

The Wyoming Game and Fish Department has not yet formally announced what mule deer or pronghorn migration is next in the queue to go through the state’s designation process. There are dozens of known, mapped routes to choose from.

In 2019, the state agency started the process of designating the landscapes used by the Wyoming Range Mule Deer Herd, though those proposed protections remain in a state of limbo.

title: Answering the call: Boxelder Job Corps  students face the flames
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Students from Boxelder Job Corps work to build a containment line around the Estes Creek Fire near Nemo on April 12. The C-15 Boxelder Crew were second on scene to the incident and assumed command. Pictured from left, Cory Red Owl, Angel Perez, Majhondra Jones, and Seqoiua Bautista-Ortega. Photo courtesy of Boxelder Job Corps
_full_text:
1 Boxelder Job Corps wildland firefighting.jpg
Students from Boxelder Job Corps work to build a containment line around the Estes Creek Fire near Nemo on April 12. The C-15 Boxelder Crew were second on scene to the incident and assumed command. Pictured from left, Cory Red Owl, Angel Perez, Majhondra Jones, and Seqoiua Bautista-Ortega. Photo courtesy of Boxelder Job Corps 

DEADWOOD — At Boxelder Job Corps outside of Nemo, a select group of students are working with the Forest Service-run program to seize opportunities in the trades and taking on the additional task of helping protect national forests through wildland firefighting program.

Derek Sukstorf, academic manager at Boxelder Job Corps, said that 23 students are currently enrolled in the program’s wildland firefighting program. The program is considered an extra responsibility on top of students’ academic programming and their time becoming certified in a trade. Being successful in the training while being in good standing with the Job Corps center allows students a unique opportunity to go on assignment around the country, helping crews with prescribed burns and active fires while making a wage. 

Students sent on assignment with the wildland firefighting crew make an average of $20.44-22.48 an hour. Most assignments last 18 days, with students working approximately 16-hour days. 

“The wildfire program is an amazing extension of our ability to provide workforce training,” said Sukstorf. “It gives the students an excellent opportunity to learn some skills, be trained as wildfire, have employability skills, and then they get to go out and use those skills on the job. They learn those really important soft skills — teamwork and communication, showing up on time, work ethic. They get great chances to put those skills in to practice along with all the things that they’ve learned at Job Corps, and then it’s also a great program to help them earn some transition money. So, as they leave the Job Corps program and graduate, they have some money in the bank to help get a car, get an apartment, leave here and be independent and start their time in the workforce.”

Adam VonEye, assistant fire management officer for the C-15 wildland fire crew, is part of the team that mentors and teaches students at Boxelder. He said that wildland fire at Boxelder is (an extra opportunity), not an option of trades students can learn at the school. However, he said students can choose fire-related trades, such as natural resource conservation and forestry, that coordinates with the teachings and mentoring of the wildland fire program. 

One student, Majhondra Jones, came to Boxelder from Chinle, Ariz., in April 2025, with a high school diploma. She’s currently completed 90% of the natural resource conservation and forestry program and has been part of the wildland firefighting crew. She said the 2 programs, “play hand in hand.”

“I get to learn more about fires than natural resources. I’m adamant and I have a desire to know more about the natural world,” Jones said. “I have a passion to be outside and not sit in an office. This is a way for me to maintain that balance.”

Seqoiua Bautista-Ortega came to Boxelder Job Corps from Sioux Falls in June 2025, with a high school diploma to pursue carpentry. He’s currently completed 91% of his training and was elected by his peers as student body president in February this year. Bautista-Ortega said that he chose to take on the wildland fire program to become a stronger, better person. 

“When you’re here at Boxelder, you’re here for opportunities,” said Bautista-Ortega. “Since you’re working hard for your trade, it balances out nicely. If I can stay responsible as a carpenter an also be a wildland firefighter, I know have 2 gigs. I now have 2 technical trades that keep me responsible and keep me on top of my game. That’s what I’m here for — I’m here to stay for a while and accomplish a lot of good goals.”

Pull quote
“The wildfire program is an amazing extension of our ability to provide workforce training.” — Derek Sukstorf, academic manager at Boxelder Job Corps

Before being able to respond to incidents across the country, students enrolled in the wildland firefighting program have to complete approximately 80 weeks of training on top of their regular academic work and trade, including daily physical training. That training culminates in an arduous work capacity test, where students are required to hike 3 miles with a 45-pound pack in less than 45 minutes. 

Jones said the hike was difficult for her. She said that she kept wanting to rest, but the other students also taking the test wouldn’t let her quit. 

“My companions who were also facing the process consistently gave me motivation,” Jones said “That’s what we want, is to see others succeed. That’s kind of what we’re all doing here. We’re all trying to succeed, and this teaches us that we can do that, we can do hard things.”

VonEye said that type of teamwork is vital to being part of the wildland firefighting team. 

“We don’t take students that don’t have any kind of qualities of teamwork,” said VonEye. “Some of these students, like (Bautista-Ortega) and (Jones), they are my best recruiters for new students. They talk to the new students and it’s not like they’re trying to recruit people to take their job, take their place, they’re just recruiting good team players. Every spring we grow a bigger crew just because of those people that have that experience and share that with the new students.”

 2 Boxelder Job Corps wildland firefighting kids.jpg
Boxelder Job Corps students and graduates Kevin Argueta-Ayala, Ryan Swartz, Nicholas Nichols, pictured from left, have worked to obtain their wildland fire certification on top of their trade and academic curriculum. Photo courtesy of Boxelder Job Corps 

Out on assignment

Sukstorf said that in 2026, the Boxelder wildland firefighting students have assisted with 8 wildland fires and worked on more than 12,00 acres of prescribed burns in the Ozark National Forest in Arkansas. 

Bautista-Ortega spent 21 days working 14-to-16-hour days in the Ozark National Forest assisting with prescribed burns. 

“It was hot, windy, and intense,” said Bautista-Ortega. “It was a lot of learning and a lot of supervision. The team leaders did a really good job training me. There were days where I didn’t think I could make it out alive, but I did it and it made me a stronger human overall.”

VonEye said that because of increased fire danger in the Black Hills, the crew has been called to local incidents including the Qury Fire in Custer State Park in March that burned close to 10,000 acres. Bautista-Ortega and Jones both spent 12 days performing everything from structure protection, constructing containment lines, and mop up.

“It was completely different from the Ozarks because it’s the Black Hills,” said Bautista-Ortega. “It felt almost mystical at times. It felt more safe. I knew we were going to make it out alive at the end of the day. It was friendly and nice (working with local agencies).”

Jones said that working with local agencies on the Qury Fire felt like a communal effort to save a shared home with people who cared about her success. 

“You can definitely feel the sort of father-like energy,” said Jones. “They want to teach you so that you are able to be competent enough without needing constant supervision.”

Bautista-Ortega said that working wildland fire incidents has made him more confident and able to make decisions on the fly. 

“Fire is an emotional roller coaster of events that are constantly happening every single second,” Bautista-Ortega said. “Every single second you’re thinking and moving. Sometimes you don’t know if you’re going to make it through. But you do, and when you’re done from fire you live your life that way. Now I’m handling everything much more smoothly because I’m ready for it.”

Jones said coming to Boxelder and working wildland fire has taught her that she’s capable of not only setting goals but reaching them. 

“I know that when I leave this place with the experience that I’ve gained so far, and especially during fire, I know that I’ll be able to accomplish the goals I set for myself no matter how strenuous it may be,” Jones said. 

Changed for the better

Sukstorf said that he can see a physical change happen in the students that come back from wildland firefighting assignments. 

“I watch these students go out every year and do these assignments, and the confidence that they come back with makes them different people,” Sukstorf said. “They’ve done something hard, and they come through it. Shoulders are back, heads held high, smiles on their faces, and they carry that with them for the entire time they’re here. It’s a great thing to see.”

Sukstorf said he’s incredibly grateful for the C-15 wildland firefighting crew and the mentorship and opportunities they offer the students at Boxelder Job Corps. 

“These students go out and do (physical training) every day with them, they coach them through it and they take them from wherever they’res tarting and they build the up to be ready to go out on those incidents and then they stand by them, side by side,” Sukstorf said. “They do an amazing job of building up our students. I can’t tell you how awesome it is and how special it is to have a crew that not only serves the forest, protects the structures around here, but also serves these students. It’s an amazing experience.”

title: Lead-Deadwood High School graduation requirements set to change
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Graduation requirements could change for the classes of 2030 and 2031 at Lead-Deadwood High School. Pioneer file photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
Lead-Deadwood High School graduation requirements set to change
Graduation requirements could change for the classes of 2030 and 2031 at Lead-Deadwood High School. Pioneer file photo by Sara Morgan 

DEADWOOD — The required credits to graduate from the Lead-Deadwood High School are set to change for the classes of 2030 and 2031. 

Mike Embrock, principal of the school, proposed the changes to the district’s school board at the May 12 meeting with the first reading of an updated handbook. The changes are expected to have a second reading at the June 9 meeting.

“The big change with graduation requirements, starting with the class of 2030, which is this year’s eighth graders, as they come into high school, they still have to have 3 credits of social studies, but we’re requiring a full year of world history,” said Embrock. “Right now, you have a full year of American history, a semester of government, and the other one-and-a-half credits were your elective options in social studies. I worked pretty strongly with our high school social studies department and that’s what we came up with, was wanting them to have world history at the sophomore level.”

In other changes, the Class of 2031 will no longer be able to take algebra one in eighth grade and count the class as a high school credit. 

“When you have kids take algebra one in eighth grade and your graduation requirements just say you need 3 credits of math, we get some kids that will come through and stop taking math after their sophomore year. They do algebra one, probably geometry their freshman year, and algebra 2 their sophomore year. They can, not many of them do, but they could just be done taking math after their sophomore year.” 

Embrock said that he believes changing the handbook to require students take 3 math classes while in high school more closely aligns with the South Dakota minimum requirements for graduation. 

Embrock said the change in math requirements will begin with the Class of 2031 to avoid confusion with the graduating Class of 2030.

“If you took algebra one as an eighth grader and you only thought you needed 3 years of math and you wanted to stop after your 10th-grade year, now the goal post has been moved,” said Embrock. “I think we need to start with the cohort of 2031, so this year’s seventh graders are understanding as they come in, if you take algebra one, great, we want to challenge you. But that’s going to be a math credit you have, and it’ll count in your math credits as you come into high school, but you have to take 3 years of math while you’re in high school.”

title: Creekside nature area trail donation  tabled in the face of opposition
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Citizens spoke up Monday, most asking the city council to leave the Creekside Nature area, pictured, in its current condition. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Creekside Trail altJPG.JPG
Citizens spoke up Monday, most asking the city council to leave the Creekside Nature area, pictured, in its current condition. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson  

SPEARFISH — In the face of overwhelming opposition, the Spearfish City Council has tabled approval of a donated gravel-surface walking path in the Creekside Nature Area near Evans Park.

“Residents of Spearfish are passionate about our public open spaces and outdoor recreation for good reason. Those areas are some of our community’s greatest assets. They’re well used year-round, and they are a large part of what makes Spearfish a great place to call home,” said Spearfish Parks Superintendent Rex McDonald.

In May, a Spearfish resident and the owner of North Star Construction, Matt Polich, reached out to the city asking if he might be able to donate labor, materials, and equipment to surface a mile-long stretch of 8-foot-wide trail with roughly 4 inches of clean road-based aggregate in memory of his dog Tucker, who loved the Creekside Nature Area. Once completed, the trail would have a similar surface to the Mickelson Trail. 

“On completion of the surface trail, the city would remain responsible for the maintenance and upkeep of the trail, which would include mowing on either side of the trail and filling any areas of washout or erosion that occur over time,” McDonald said. “Because of the proposed materials and the expected finished product of the surface trail, we do not believe that these maintenance requirements would have a significant impact on our department’s operations in terms of labor or material costs.”

But it wasn’t concern about maintenance costs alone that led to more than 50 minutes of public comment at Monday’s city council meeting.

Nearly a dozen speakers came out to voice opinions on the proposed project — which would have been completed at no cost to the city, but could have altered the character of the nature area according to opponents. Opponents had a relatively simple message for the council: we want to walk on dirt and grass. 

Many speakers, including Leslie Kaitfors, described it as a “last remaining nature area” in the city limits.

Spearfish resident Bailey Sadowsky told the council she wanted to preserve the diversity of green space in Spearfish and felt it was important to have a space that felt wild located in a safe part of the city. Sadowsky also said she was concerned that the aggregate material might have qualities that could be detrimental to the environment, and hard on users’ pets. 

“The trail, even though it is not asphalt, it still does harm paws. It is sharp. It is gravel. I have done my research and gone out and looked at other spaces. Having a dog with sensitive paws, it is one of the reasons why I love the space. We can get out in the middle of town and still experience nature.” Sadowsky said.

Kelly Harnett, the founder of both Beautify Spearfish and Hobo’s Healing Heart, said she understood the desire to honor a “once in a lifetime dog,” but worried that a surfaced trail could interfere with pollinator habitat.

A senior citizen and wellness and aging advocate who has lived in the city for more than 20 years, Cheryl Jasper said she did not want to see the trail changed.

“The accessibility to senior citizens to have that hiking experience beyond the safe time for hiking alone or out in the woods is unspeakably important to me,” Jasper said. “We have to continually challenge our brain connections and our muscle connections. Uneven terrain is perfect for that. Solo hikers can hike here with some assurance that there would be responsive rescue if they ran into problems.”

Polich has said he did not intend to change the grade or alter the terrain beyond what might be required to offer a smooth and stable walking surface. He was also clear that the trail would not be paved.

Still, Spearfish Resident Jim Moravec told the city council a surfaced trail might be more appealing to eBikes and other trail users who could disrupt the feel of the green space. Kaitfors, who lives directly across from Evan’s Park, said she had already seen increased traffic in the neighborhood following improvements in Rocketship Park, and felt a trail change could result in yet another spike in use.

“When you compare what is there now to what has been proposed. It is clear the users of the area prefer it in its present state,” Moravec said. “I think at minimum council needs to pause and get more community input.

Opponents feared changing the surface of the trail in the nature area could have a number of impacts — including adding new trail users, interrupting riparian habitat, and changing the way that heat was retained in the area.

“There has been vocal opposition to the trail, citing concerns about keeping the area more natural and the detrimental health effects of walking and running on hard surfaces,” McDonald said. “There has been vocal support of surfacing the trail to correct the unevenness of the trail as it is currently and the muddy conditions that exist during and after a rain event. Two proponents of surfacing the trail were people who are involved in both the Spearfish High School and the Black Hills State University cross-country teams who feel the surfacing will be an enhancement to the trail system for their cross-country training events.”

On Monday, only 2 members of the public said they wanted to see the donation move forward — Luke Donovan and Joe Jorgensen.

Polich explained the intent behind the project.

“What am I trying to do here? What I am trying to do is participate in our community,” Polich said. “I have the ability to, what I think would be, improve that area, and I would like to. I would like to increase access for some people that may not be able to use that trail currently. For example, on one of my folks’ visits, I was going to take Tucker for a walk, and my mom wanted to go. My mom went; it was fantastic. I’m not sure she could go today. She’s in her mid 70s. She has bad knees. I would like to continue sharing those experiences with her and perhaps other people could benefit from some surfacing also.”

Then he added, given remarks made on social media prior to the meeting, that he believed the project should be tabled or scrapped altogether.

“Our intent is a good experience for our community. It’s positive. At this moment, with this uncertainty, I am not sure it’s positive. Whether we table it or we scrap it, I think those are the two options that are most appropriate today,” Polich said.

Spearfish resident Jeremy Smith asked if Polich might consider donating his resources to trail projects identified in the parks and recreation master plan instead.

“I helped a number of years ago with the parks and rec master plan, which has in its appendix a list of future trail connectivity and improvements,” Smith said. Smith suggested pursuing trail connectivity from Green Acres under the interstate to the cul-de-sac near the Atlas Building as an alternative.

“There is an off-leash dog park out there that could connect, kind of expanding that dog walking area and provide connectivity from the Green Acres, Mountain Shadows Subdivision through the Walmart side without the Exit 14 kind of challenge,” Smith said. “I don’t know if Matt would be interested in that potential change; I know he has a personal connection to the Creekside area, but if the item is tabled, I wonder if that could be explored.”

The Spearfish Parks and Recreation Advisory Board had recommended allowing Polich to surface the trail in sections, so that the community might see what the gravel path looked like and decide if they wanted the work to continue.

Councilman Scott Hourigan ultimately made the motion to table the donation discussion.

“There are certain things that I don’t agree with, like the bike paths on Lookout Mountain; I personally don’t love it, but a lot of people love it. I like that there are two sides to every story,” Hourigan said. “Matt, thank you for gifting this to us. Is there some more input and comments we should make? I know you came with a great heart. Thank you for your intent.”

Councilwoman Jamie Hafner said, based on constituent feedback, she would not vote in favor of allowing Polich to donate a freshly surfaced trail in the nature area at all.

“What a hot topic. I would just like to say that with all of the citizens that reached out to me, the majority wanted it left alone,” Hafner said.

Hafner and Councilman Dean Myers voted against tabling the topic, but the vote to move the discussion to the next city council meeting passed.

title: SDSU Extension provides free livestock water testing
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: BROOKINGS — South Dakota State University Extension is encouraging producers to take advantage of its free, on-site livestock water-testing services across the state.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

BROOKINGS — South Dakota State University Extension is encouraging producers to take advantage of its free, on-site livestock water-testing services across the state. 

Robin Salverson, SDSU Extension cow/calf field specialist, said water samples tested this spring have been across the board in quality, with several samples showing salt levels too high for safe livestock consumption.

South Dakota soils tend to be high in salt content, which can raise the salt levels in dugouts, creeks and streams. Salverson said the winter’s limited snowfall and continued drought conditions in much of the state have exacerbated those high salt levels. The state’s continuous high winds evaporate water at a faster-than-normal rate, causing the salt to concentrate even more. 

“If an area gets rain and the ponds fill with water, it does not mean the water is suitable for livestock consumption,” Salverson said. “Testing is the only way to know.”

SDSU Extension offers water testing services at all eight regional centers and at select county offices across the state. Samples must be collected in a clean plastic or glass container such as water bottles, pop bottles or jelly jars.

A quick test is conducted free of charge with an electro-conductivity (EC) meter to determine total salt levels in the water. After the results are reviewed, an SDSU Extension field or state specialist will discuss the results with the producers.  

Salverson said poor water quality can hurt livestock’s growth and reproduction, and severely contaminated water can cause illness or death. Even clear water can be of poor quality. She encourages producers to be proactive and test early to protect their livestock’s health. 

“Don’t use your animals as an indicator of water quality. Every pound gained can pay big dividends when the animals are sold,” Salverson said.

For more information, producers can contact Salverson at (605)374-4177.

title: Trump to withdraw $1.8B  ‘anti-weaponization’ fund, Thune says
byline: By Jennifer Shutt and Ariana Figueroa States Newsroom
description: WASHINGTON — U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Tuesday the Trump administration has rescinded its plan to use a nearly $1.8 billion fund to pay people who believe they were wrongly prosecuted by the Justice Department.
_full_text:
StatesnewsroomLogo

WASHINGTON — U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Tuesday the Trump administration has rescinded its plan to use a nearly $1.8 billion fund to pay people who believe they were wrongly prosecuted by the Justice Department. 

That decision, combined with testimony from acting Attorney General Todd Blanche to a House panel in the afternoon, could end the gridlock that has so far stalled floor debate on a roughly $70 billion package meant to fund immigration and deportation for the rest of President Donald Trump’s term. 

“I think his statements are going to be very definitive, very clear and create the certainty that I hope all of our members, and House members need as well, in order for us to proceed on the reconciliation bill,” Thune said, referring to Blanche. “But I’m not guaranteeing that happens yet.” 

Blanche previewed his testimony to the House panel during a phone call with Thune, who said he believes the fund is completely off the table. 

“The conversation I had with him was very definitive,” Thune, a South Dakota Republican, said. 

The DOJ posted on social media this week that it plans to abide by a temporary court ruling that blocked distribution of the funds, but Republican lawmakers said that wasn’t enough to end the impasse it created.

The Justice Department announced the creation of the fund last month as part of a legal settlement between Trump and the IRS over leaked copies of his returns during Trump’s first term. The settlement included provisions that precluded future IRS investigations into Trump and his family.

Senate Republicans weigh in

Thune said GOP senators had a “quite robust conversation” during a closed-door lunch about the DOJ fund and whether to move forward with their immigration and deportation package. 

North Dakota Sen. John Hoeven said after that meeting it’s up to GOP leaders to determine whether there are enough votes to move forward with the immigration package. 

“I think the next step is for our whip team to find out where everybody’s at based on the administration’s indication that they’re not going to move forward with the fund,” Hoeven said. 

Louisiana Sen. John Kennedy said there is a “chance” that Republicans could begin a marathon amendment voting session on the immigration bill as soon as Wednesday, if Blanche’s testimony alleviates concerns created by the DOJ fund. 

Montana Sen. Steve Daines, however, said he believes it’s “unlikely” that process begins this week. 

North Carolina Republican Sen. Thom Tillis said earlier in the day, before the lunch, that he wouldn’t accept taxpayer dollars going toward people who attacked the Capitol on Jan. 6. 

“To provide restitution to somebody who assaulted a police officer and pled guilty to it. I mean, man, I’ve seen some crazy stuff before, but that’s right up there with crazy,” he said. 

Utah Republican Sen. John Curtis said he needs to know “if it’s dead or nearly dead.” 

Oklahoma Republican Sen. James Lankford said he wants clarification from the White House about the settlement fund in light of the court’s ruling. 

He added that Republicans are waiting to see if “the court case set aside both the settlement fund and the audits.”

“We need clarification for what it is and isn’t, because the White House already said ‘we agree, we don’t like it, but we agree with the courts,’” Lankford said. “What does that mean?”

Amendment to ban fund

Democrats have also criticized Trump and those in his administration over the fund, vowing to block it in law. 

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., said during an afternoon press conference that promises from Trump and administration officials are “worthless.” 

“Trump sued his own government, had his own Justice Department settle the case and is now trying to use taxpayer dollars to pay off his MAGA allies, billionaire buddies and cop-beating insurrectionists,” Schumer said. 

“And let’s be clear, Trump has not killed this slush fund,” he added. “He has not revoked the special tax immunity he gave himself and his family. He has not ended the corruption. He hit a temporary roadblock. That’s it.”

Schumer said the first amendment he would offer during debate on Republicans’ immigration and deportation bill would “ban Trump’s slush fund permanently and revoke his family’s free rein to commit tax fraud forever.”

title: ‘Time is the enemy’
byline: By Jacob Orledge North Dakota Monitor
description: Oil pumpjacks operate in Williams County in September 2024. Photo by Kyle Martin, for the North Dakota Monitor
_full_text:
‘Time is the enemy’
Oil pumpjacks operate in Williams County in September 2024. Photo by Kyle Martin, for the North Dakota Monitor 

WILLISTON, N.D. — North Dakota elected officials are pushing to make rapid progress on the next generation of oil production technology before a change in federal administration, but oil and gas executives say there’s no guarantee of a quick breakthrough.

“We have a tremendous opportunity in the next two years, because we have an administration that understands this stuff. We have to get them to mobilize a little faster,” said Gov. Kelly Armstrong during a prominent oil conference in May. “Time is the enemy, but they understand this, and so we have gone from headwinds to tailwinds.”

But oil and gas executives say there are a lot of unknowns and success will depend on many factors.

“Future success is far from a given, it’s going to have to be earned,” said Danny Brown, CEO of Chord Energy. “But the reward is tremendous for this and for future generations.”

The technologies under development by the oil industry, collectively referred to as enhanced oil recovery, are billed as a way to double the amount of oil that can be extracted from the Bakken and expand the life of North Dakota’s oil fields by decades. 

The various techniques include injecting chemical surfactants to act like soap to scrape more oil off rock underground, as well as injecting gases, like natural gas, to restore the pressure of an oil reservoir.

The industry has yet to determine what method, or combination thereof, is the most efficient and cost-effective. 

“There’s not a silver bullet. We haven’t found one yet,” said Charlie Gorecki, CEO of the Energy and Environmental Research Center at the University of North Dakota, which is working closely with industry on the effort. 

There are questions as to whether the methods under development will prove to be profitable. 

“Economics are always going to rule the day,” said Pam Heatherington, general manager of ExxonMobil’s Americas division and CEO of Denbury, a subsidiary that focuses on CO2 transport and storage.

Carbon dioxide

Oil companies are working to test some of those methods with large-scale pilot projects in North Dakota, with financial backing from the state and federal governments. But there is still debate and speculation about what works best. 

That’s particularly true when it comes to repressurizing a reservoir. Oil and gas reservoirs begin with high pressure and decrease over time as more of the resources are pumped to the surface. Injecting a gas to refill that reservoir’s pressure can lead to improved production. 

The industry is searching for a gas that is low-cost, effective and available in large amounts. Companies have tested many possibilities, from propane and natural gas liquids to nitrogen, but carbon dioxide is often considered to be the most feasible option.

“I think CO2 is probably going to be the best long-term option for full scale up across the basin,” said Arvo Buck, director of new ventures at Chord Energy. “It’s going to take a tremendous amount of volume, and I just can’t say that enough.”

Carbon dioxide brings its own challenges. One is finding a supply. 

The best supply is from ethanol plants because it has a high purity, said Brad Musgrove, Williston Basin asset manager for Devon Energy. 

“But it’s limited supply and not necessarily available in the field,” Musgrove said.

Summit Carbon Solutions’ proposed CO2 pipeline to North Dakota would have collected CO2 from ethanol plants in five states, but that pipeline project has been rerouted to Wyoming. 

If a supply of carbon dioxide is available, the next challenge would be developing new CO2 pipelines to deliver it to oil wells.

“At scale, the need for CO2 is tremendous,” Brown said, adding that North Dakota doesn’t produce enough and will need to import more. 

If that new infrastructure is built, the industry will still have to prepare for the higher percentage of CO2 that will come back to the surface when a repressurized well begins producing oil again, Musgrove said. 

Chevron executive Birlie Bourgeois explained that carbon dioxide will mix with water underground and create carbonic acid. Oil wells were not designed to handle that, and virtually every piece of oil infrastructure would have to be retrofitted, he said. 

“That’s going to eat through pipe really quickly, so it is a huge capital burden if you’ve got to go retrofit every facility and every well to mitigate against that,” Bourgeois said. “We really need smart minds to help us come up with solutions there because if you could do that and not have to retrofit everything, like that’s a great solution.”

Dimmer switch, not a light switch

Government officials, led by Armstrong and U.S. Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., are leading the charge to make rapid progress in order to keep the oil, and the tax revenues that come with it, flowing in the state. 

“We’ve only tapped 15% of the Bakken and Three Forks. The other 85% is still trapped in the rock. If we can create the policy and the incentives, and you all can unlock even another 15% with EOR, that’s an entirely new boom,” Armstrong said to thousands of oil and gas executives and workers. 

Kyle Haustveit, a Tioga native recently confirmed as an undersecretary with the U.S. Department of Energy, said North Dakota is primed to lead the nation in finding a way to make that happen. 

Haustveit warned in an interview the deployment of the technology will not be as quick as some are hoping. It will be more of a “dimmer switch” rather than a light switch, and it could be five years before the industry begins to widely deploy enhanced oil recovery in unconventional shale oil fields like the Bakken. 

“The shale revolution was much more of a light switch, because we were energy dependent, importing oil prices skyrocketed, and the industry stepped up. But even that being more of a light switch still took multiple years to reach peak production,” he said. “It’s probably gonna be 10 or 15 years before we see a big incremental increase in U.S. oil production from unconventional EOR.”

The importance of finding a way to extract a greater percentage of the oil in shale formations extends beyond North Dakota. Vishal Gupta, president of EOR Ventures for Occidental Petroleum, said the growth of shale oil production in the United States is slowing down and will likely peak within five to eight years before entering a “fairly steep decline.” 

“Whereas the U.S. currently makes up about 15% of the global oil supply, this could be as low as 3% by the year 2040,” Gupta said. “We believe that it’s critically important for us to start investing in EOR now, so that we can offset this decline.”

While the bulk of the burden for avoiding that decline falls on the oil and gas industry, government policy will play a significant role as well. Lynn Helms, former state regulator and project manager for enhanced oil recovery efforts for the North Dakota Petroleum Council, said it’s crucial for North Dakota to ensure companies feel comfortable investing the necessary resources. 

“The enemy of capital deployment is uncertainty,” Helms said.

title: Sturgis & Meade County History Days to be held June 12-13
byline: By Pioneer Staff Black Hills Pioneer
description: The old Sturgis High School, later Erskine Building. Photo courtesy Deadwood History
_full_text:
Sturgis & Meade County History Days to be held June 12-13
The old Sturgis High School, later Erskine Building. Photo courtesy Deadwood History 

STURGIS— The 10th annual Sturgis & Meade County History Day will be held Friday, June 12, from 5-8 p.m. and Saturday June 13, from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. at the Sturgis Community Center. 

“The History of Schools in Sturgis and Meade County” is the theme of the event this year.

There has already been a lot of interest in the schools topic, with the Sturgis & Meade County Historical Society collecting 150 years of town and country school stories, and preparing exhibits and activities. 

Booths displaying a variety of historical artifacts, pictures and other information and memorabilia will be open both days in the Sturgis Community Center gymnasium. A round table discussion on “Memories of Education in Meade County” will take place at 6:30 p.m. Friday night. 

On Saturday, the first presentation will be at 10:30 a.m. by Betsey DeLouche about country schools past and present. At 11:30 a.m., Jim Holland and Mark Rambow will present a timeline of Sturgis schools in the Community Center Theater. Boxed lunches will be available. 

On Saturday afternoon, special tours of three surviving country schools will be held culminating in an ice cream social at the recently restored Pleasant Valley School. The first tour will be at 1 p.m. at Spring Creek School west of Bear Butte, followed by the Alkali School at the Threshing Bee Grounds at 2 p.m., ending with a tour of the Pleasant Valley School at 3 p.m. with an ice cream social.

For those who want to learn more about the Sturgis and Meade County Historical Society, a booth with information about the Society and membership will be available.

title: Front end loader  off-road slide a near miss  for Deadwood home
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: A front end loader fell off Railroad Avenue in Deadwood Monday and down an embankment towards a nearby residence. The loader was brought back onto the road without further incident. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Front end loader  off-road slide a near miss  for Deadwood home
A front end loader fell off Railroad Avenue in Deadwood Monday and down an embankment towards a nearby residence. The loader was brought back onto the road without further incident. Courtesy photo 

DEADWOOD — A front end loader operated by Underground Construction, working on a water line on Railroad Avenue in Deadwood, slipped off the road Monday evening. 

Deadwood Police Chief Cory Shafer said the incident occurred around 4 p.m. Monday. Due to wet conditions and a soft surface, the loader began to slip off the roadway and down an embankment towards a residence. The Deadwood Volunteer Fire Department evacuated the residence, “out of an abundance of caution,” and nearby utilities were shut off during the incident. 

Plains Towing was able to bring the loader back onto the road by 11 p.m. without further incident.

title: A quandary on Hwy 85 north of Spearfish
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Properties north of Spearfish along Highway 85 face challenges when it comes to development. Pioneer photo by Travis Potter
_full_text:
0604 Highway 85-Drone.tif
Properties north of Spearfish along Highway 85 face challenges when it comes to development. Pioneer photo by Travis Potter 

SPEARFISH — Landowners looking at future development opportunities on the north side of the city are in a bit of a bind. That’s why they’ve partnered with city staff to find a way to develop their parcels along Highway 85. 

The first piece of land city leaders have begun discussing is a 380-acre tract, known as the Prairie Addition, that runs along Highway 85 from Kerwin Lane to Kellem Lane. It was annexed by the city of Spearfish in 2008. The rest of the surrounding annex is zoned for agricultural use.

Just north of that is a second, 46-acre parcel, zoned highway service commercial. That tract, north of Kellem Lane, was annexed by the city in 2013.

When both parcels were annexed, it appeared that the city might see growth near its northern gateway. Over time, the focus of development moved to the east and the area around Exit 17. 

Before development of any kind can go up along this northern corridor, city ordinance requires the extension of city services — water, sewer, and urban roads — prior to any vertical construction. Achieving that kind of connectivity is cost-prohibitive under current economic conditions, Spearfish Community Development Director Peter Wysocki said during the city council’s study session last week. 

“Should we initiate our aggressive planning and financing mechanism for that infrastructure?” Wysocki said. “We could have a much more comprehensive discussion about our infrastructure needs, not just on Exit 17 on the Colorado Blvd. corridor. We also will be coming to a time where we also expand our sewer plan. The fact of the matter is it is not planned for near-term expansion.”

He said the city’s policy creates a choice between maintaining strict urban-level infrastructure, or allowing some level of development with rural level infrastructure — as landowners request it.

However, in both annexed areas, landowners are hoping to establish both flexibility and certainty, as they look at future uses for their parcels, Wysocki said. He approached the city council with a staff recommendation to keep the parcels within the city limits, but allow development to “rural infrastructure standards.”

“The city’s position has remained that the expectation was to develop the property to an urban level type of development, meaning higher density, higher intensity uses that would necessitate urban level infrastructure,” Wysocki said. “Urban level infrastructure, just so we are on the same page, is connection to city water and sewer systems and have urban level type streets — so paved roads, curb and gutter.”

That would mean development could use septic systems, or alternatives to city water connectivity.

The city could make policy changes to allow limited development, under specific conditions, and restrict development to low-density residential or low-impact non-residential land uses using development agreements. That method, Wysocki said, could support incremental development, provide flexibility to landowners, potentially boost sales or property tax revenue, and preserve the city’s influence on its north side. 

There is a risk, if the council pursues this option, that development could end up being a bit more piecemeal. Well and septic systems may be difficult to transition out later, if higher density growth ever takes off.

For Rick Furnish, an owner of Spring Creek Ranch along Highway 85 north of town, allowing more rural development is a desirable option.

“Our goal is just to subdivide this into 40- or 50-acre tracts. For us to comply with code, we have to provide city water, paved roads, and curb and gutter,” Furnish said. “For 40-acre lots that doesn’t work. This option really makes sense. It works for us. We would like to sell some bigger tracts. If in the future those folks want to subdivide and come back, and they’re going to need more services, then that could be addressed. Putting in curb and gutter for a 40-acre tract is really not feasible.”

 A quandary on Hwy 85 north of Spearfish
This map roughly outlines the location of 2 parcels north of town that were each annexed by the city of Spearfish more than a decade ago. With urging from landowners, the city is now considering policy changes that might allow for development in the area. Courtesy map 

The council has the option of pursuing de-annexation of the parcels — an avenue Wysocki said the property owners do not seem eager to explore.

“Should we de-annex? It sounds simple. We basically de-obligate the city of any expectations; however, there are challenges with that. De-annexation would need to be coordinated consecutive and contiguous. You can’t just leapfrog de-annexations,” Wysocki said. “It is my understanding that the property owners would like to remain within the city limits and come to a reasonable solution on how we move forward. Unless we start to de-annex the land from the very north and go sequentially to the south, de-annexation may not be possible or a feasible option.”

Wyosocki said the city may want to maintain contiguous control along the Highway 85 corridor.

“There is no doubt that Highway 85 north is the northern gateway to the city of Spearfish. With that, I feel that the city should have the ability to influence development, development pattern, land uses to basically protect the gateway, the aesthetics, the type of development we want near our city,” Wysocki said. 

The city could also elect to maintain the status quo and require strict compliance to the standing annexation agreements. Wysocki said that option will likely keep development in the area stagnate until funding urban infrastructure is feasible.

“One (option) is to maintain the status quo, and set an expectation that there is urban-level development in that area and for the landowners to come up with a solution, collaborate together, to provide for a large urban-type development, and confirm that they can finance all of those improvements,” Wysocki said.

Wysocki noted that it is possible to engineer lift stations, install booster pumps, establish distribution lines, and create capacity for water storage — all of that takes money, and could even impact the city’s fee rates across the community.

“That is a very high-level comprehensive discussion,” Wysocki noted.

Another landowner, Alan Crago, in the annexation area zoned highway commercial, said he has had parties interested in developing north of the city — one for more than 2 years.

“I have had a number of people want to do something there, but due to the current quandary of the stipulations, we just kind of held off and hoped for things to change,” Crago said. “We are hoping things have changed now.”

The city council has not formally considered any action based on Wysocki’s presentation. The conversation last week helped place the topic on the council’s radar for future action.

“I’d just like to say I have been in this process trying to find a solution for many months. I think I started last September. I just wanted to tell you I appreciate Peter so much. He and his staff have worked hard to say, ‘Let’s look for a yes that helps both parties,’” Furnish told the city council.

title: Sturgis Summer Music Camp to present  ‘Go Fish’ performance
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: Eighteen youth are spending the week at Summer Music Camp learning and preparing to perform ‘Go Fish’ on Friday in the Sturgis Park. The camp started Monday and continues through the week.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
Sturgis Summer Music Camp to present  ‘Go Fish’ performance
Eighteen youth are spending the week at Summer Music Camp learning and preparing to perform ‘Go Fish’ on Friday in the Sturgis Park. The camp started Monday and continues through the week.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts  

STURGIS — Young performers have been spending the week singing, dancing and rehearsing as part of the Sturgis Summer Music Camp, which concludes with a public performance of Go Fish at 5:30 p.m. Friday in Sturgis City Park.

The camp, led by Sturgis Williams Middle School music teacher Hillary Hill, is being held at the Sturgis Armory and is open to elementary students. 

Hill said the camp provides students with an opportunity to develop their musical and theatrical skills while building confidence and friendships.

“We have a music camp for grades one through 6, and this is an event sponsored by the Sturgis Area Arts Council,” Hill said. “We also received grants from the Sturgis Chamber and are working with Golden K Kiwanis as well.”

Throughout the week, campers spend four hours each day preparing for the production.

“We work on the songs, choreography and speaking parts,” Hill said. “We do some small-group work to help students memorize lines, and we also make time for fun games so the kids can get to know each other.”

Hill is assisted by several volunteers and student leaders, including new Sturgis Williams Middle School band director Sarah Rather and Sturgis Brown High School Drama Club members Abby Smith and Will Bruce.

The camp is one of 2 summer theater opportunities Hill is organizing this year. A second camp for students in grades 6 through 12 will be held July 20-24 and will feature a production of Into the Woods Jr.

“This week we’re doing Go Fish with the younger group,” Hill said. “The older students will perform Into the Woods Jr. later this summer.”

The public is invited to attend Friday’s performance, which will take place on the concrete stage located behind the playground in Sturgis City Park.

Admission to the performance is free, and community members are encouraged to come out and support the young performers as they showcase the skills they have developed during the week-long camp.

title: Man injured in crash with Sturgis police car
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: A Sturgis police car was involved in a crash Tuesday shortly after noon.
_full_text:
Man injured in crash with Sturgis police car
A Sturgis police car was involved in a crash Tuesday shortly after noon.  

STURGIS — A Belle Fourche man received serious, non-life-threatening injuries Tuesday shortly after noon in a 2-vehicle crash involving a Sturgis police car.

According to the South Dakota Highway Patrol, at 12:34 p.m. the 90-year-old man was traveling eastbound on Lazelle Street when he allegedly turned in front of the approaching 2022 Dodge Charger police vehicle with emergency lights activated. The officer was unable to avoid a collision with the Escalade. The Escalade spun and came to rest on the sidewalk. The police vehicle continued into a concrete barrier at 6th Street. 

The driver of the Escalade sustained serious, non-life-threatening injuries. The officer was not injured.

The South Dakota Highway Patrol is investigating the crash.

title: Rounds fends off  GOP primary challenger
byline: Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds, R-South Dakota, speaks at the Dakotafest agricultural trade show in Mitchell, South Dakota, on Aug. 20, 2025.
_full_text:
Rounds fends off  GOP primary challenger
U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds, R-South Dakota, speaks at the Dakotafest agricultural trade show in Mitchell, South Dakota, on Aug. 20, 2025.  

PIERRE —Tuesday night election returns showed U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., won his party’s nomination to seek reelection.

The 71-year-old Rounds, of Fort Pierre, is finishing his second 6-year term in the Senate after previously serving eight years as governor.

His opponent, Rapid City businessman Justin McNeal, did not mount a prominent campaign.

Rounds won with 76% of the votes while McNeal earned 24%.

All of the votes came from registered Republicans, whose primaries are closed to independents and voters from other parties. 

Rounds faces 2 opponents in the Nov. 3 general election: Julian Beaudion, a businessman and former Highway Patrol trooper from Sioux Falls who was unopposed for the Democratic nomination, and Brian Bengs, an Air Force veteran and former college professor who switched to independent after running unsuccessfully 4 years ago as the Democratic nominee against Republican U.S. Sen. John Thune.

title: Belle to celebrate the summer with River Fest, Hometown Thursday
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer
description: BELLE FOURCHE — Belle Fourche will mark the summer with a variety of events, including weekly Hometown Thursdays and River Fest.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

BELLE FOURCHE — Belle Fourche will mark the summer with a variety of events, including weekly Hometown Thursdays and River Fest. 

Hometown Thursdays, which feature a variety of food and musical acts, take place weekly from 6-9 p.m. today to Aug. 6, behind the Tri-State Museum, located at 415 5th Ave.

Stereo Trip will play today. Tyler Bills will perform on June 11. Camp Comfort will perform on June 18. Dakota Country will perform on June 25. Williams & Wright Experience will perform on July 2. Jessica Loobey will play on July 9. Brandon Jones will perform on July 16. The Wilt Brothers will perform on July 23. Tim Zach Band will perform on July 30. The final Hometown Thursdays happen on Aug. 6 and will feature J.J. Kent performing with Aces & 8’s. 

June will also feature Belle’s River Fest this weekend.

Friday, will feature the 5K River Run. Registration begins at 6:15 p.m. at the Belle Fourche Rec Center. The race begins at 7 p.m. at Rail Park.

On Sunday, there will be food and merchandise vendors behind the Tri-State Museum, a plastic duck race at 1 p.m., and a beer garden from 10 a.m.-2 p.m. at Hitching Post Tap House. 

A corn hole tournament, a disc golf tournament, and Battle of the Bones BBQ Contest are listed on the River Fest webpage, but Michaela Horn, executive director of the Belle Fourche Chamber of Commerce, said they would not happen.

title: Doeden, Rhoden advance to runoff in GOP governor primary, Johnson falls to third
byline: By Seth Tupper Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: From left, businessman Toby Doeden, Gov. Larry Rhoden and U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson speak at their respective watch parties on Tuesday night. Photos by South Dakota Searchlight’s Joshua Haiar, Meghan O’Brien and Makenzie Huber
_full_text:
Doeden, Rhoden advance to runoff in GOP governor primary, Johnson falls to third
From left, businessman Toby Doeden, Gov. Larry Rhoden and U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson speak at their respective watch parties on Tuesday night. Photos by South Dakota Searchlight’s Joshua Haiar, Meghan O’Brien and Makenzie Huber 

 PIERRE — Political newcomer Toby Doeden finished first Tuesday in South Dakota’s Republican governor primary but failed to reach 35%, setting up a runoff with Gov. Larry Rhoden while U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson — who led in several early polls — fell to third and out of the running.

Doeden topped the field with 31% of the votes, followed by Rhoden, 25%, Johnson, 23%, and state House Speaker Jon Hansen, 21%. 

State law requires a top-2 runoff eight weeks later, which falls on July 28, if nobody reaches 35% in a primary with 3 or more candidates for governor.

Doeden, a vehicle dealership owner from Aberdeen who’s been involved in other businesses and rental properties, said “the career politicians told me what we collectively have done across this state was impossible.”

“They said no outsider in South Dakota can break through three career, 20-year politicians,” Doeden said. “Well, guess what? You and I, we are doing it.”

Rhoden spoke of the challenge ahead.

“I kind of feel like that proverbial groundhog who came up and saw my shadow, and now there’s going to be eight more weeks of campaigning,” Rhoden said. “But that’s the price we’re going to have to pay. We are going to hit the ground running next week.”

Johnson had expressed confidence late Tuesday evening that he would make up ground and qualify for the runoff as the final returns came in, but that didn’t happen.

“This is still a great state,” said Johnson, of Mitchell. “We are still falling behind in some key areas. We still need to go build a better South Dakota, and I’m not turning away from that obligation just because I’m not the governor.”

Johnson’s loss means he’ll be out of a job in January when his current term in the U.S. House ends. He opted to run for governor rather than seek another House term.

Prior to Tuesday, no governor primary race had gone to a runoff since the passage of the runoff law in 1985. In previous instances when a candidate failed to receive 35% in a crowded field, the nominee was decided by delegates at a state party convention.

The candidate who ultimately wins the Republican nomination for governor will advance to the Nov. 3 general election to face Dan Ahlers, who was uncontested for the Democratic nomination.

Noem’s resignation ignites race

Former Gov. Kristi Noem opened the door for a Republican primary race when she resigned in January 2025 to accept a job in President Donald Trump’s administration.

Noem’s departure elevated Rhoden from lieutenant governor to serve the remainder of Noem’s second term, which ends in January. During his time as governor, Rhoden has worked with legislators to sign several major bills into law.

Those include laws capturing revenue from sales tax increases to reduce homeowner property taxes, a law banning the use of a legal procedure known as eminent domain to gain land access for carbon capture pipelines, and a law funding construction of a $650 million replacement for the oldest parts of the state’s 145-year-old penitentiary.

Rhoden, a lifelong rancher and welder from rural Union Center, built his campaign on his legislative achievements.

“Good policy makes good politics,” he said while launching his campaign in November.

At Rhoden’s watch party Tuesday night in Rapid City, Jim Hunt, of Faith, who has known Rhoden since high school, said his support for the governor is grounded in character.

“If it’s something that he doesn’t believe in, he’ll tell you why, because he’s honest and his integrity is number one,” Hunt said.

But Rhoden’s status as governor couldn’t prevent Johnson from entering the race last June as the presumptive frontrunner. Johnson had the highest profile due to his four terms in the U.S. House, his previous service on the state Public Utilities Commission, and his 20-plus years of involvement in statewide politics.

That long resume was an important factor for 55-year-old Republican voter Dan Harrell.

“I’m looking for experience, and so for me, the one who’s going to have the most experience for our state is going to be Dusty,” Harrell said in an interview with South Dakota Searchlight at a Sioux Falls polling place. “Just because he’s been representing us for longer than the other ones have.”

Johnson also began with more than $6 million in campaign funds he’d built up over prior election cycles.

“Ladies and gentlemen, President Trump talks about this as the golden age of America,” Johnson said in a campaign announcement speech last year. “South Dakota needs an energy and optimism to meet that moment.”

The Trump effect

Johnson’s opponents cited several examples from his congressional career to label him as insufficiently supportive of the Republican president.

Johnson was one of 13 House Republicans who voted with Democrats when they blocked Trump’s declaration of an emergency on the southern U.S. border in 2019. Johnson said at the time that he supported funding for border wall construction. But he opposed expanding presidential power at the expense of Congress, which he said would result from allowing the president to pay for the wall with money budgeted for other purposes.

Johnson also voted for the certification of the 2020 presidential election and the creation of an independent, bipartisan commission to investigate the rioters who attempted to stop the certification. The effort to create that commission failed, and Johnson voted against creating the Democratic-led House Select Committee that ultimately conducted the investigation. But he supported Rep. Liz Cheney when other Republicans stripped her of a House leadership position in retaliation for service on the committee.

Rhoden’s campaign published a website referencing some of those votes and describing them as indicative of “the real Dusty Johnson” — someone who’s “not with Trump.” A political action committee affiliated with Doeden sent a text message to Republican voters saying “if you hate President Trump and all that he stands for, Dusty Johnson is the candidate for you.”

Doeden, who spent at least $4 million of his own money in the race, tried to position himself as the most pro-Trump candidate. He often mentioned Trump in his initial advertisements — although not as much in the waning weeks of the campaign, as Trump’s national approval rating fell below 40%.

Candidate platforms

Doeden also ran on a promise to phase out property taxes, although opponents criticized Doeden’s plan as vague. He said the state would have enough money to eliminate property taxes after he reduces state spending, grows the economy and eliminates waste, inefficiencies and redundancies in state government.

Johnson largely ignored the critiques of his own record. His campaign was a mix of promises to strengthen schools, the economy and public safety, and criticism of tax laws approved by Rhoden and Hansen.

Rhoden signed 3 bills into law during this year’s legislative session that allow for higher sales taxes. Two of them devote the extra revenue — from a scheduled statewide sales tax increase in one instance, and a new, optional county sales tax in the other — toward reducing homeowner property taxes. Hansen supported those bills but not the third one, which creates an optional sales tax that cities can impose temporarily to pay for special projects.

Ads from Johnson and political action committees supporting him criticized Hansen and Rhoden for the sales tax increases, without mentioning the homeowner property tax reductions.

Hansen, of Dell Rapids, ran on a platform of “faith, family and freedom,” seeking to capitalize on his standing as co-chair of the anti-abortion Life Defense Fund, which led the successful fight against an abortion-rights ballot question two years ago. Another major facet of Hansen’s campaign was his criticism of the state’s approach to economic development, calling the use of state funds to give tax breaks and other incentives to large companies “a breeding ground of corruption.”

Total spending by all four campaigns in the race surpassed $10 million, according to campaign finance reports filed two weeks before the election, plus more than $1 million spent by political action committees. Final figures won’t be known until the next reporting deadline in October.

South Dakota Searchlight’s Joshua Haiar, Makenzie Huber and Meghan O’Brien contributed to this report.

title: AG Marty Jackley wins bid for  Republican US House nomination
byline: Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley speaks during a press conference on Dec. 19, 2025, in Sioux Falls.
_full_text:
AG Marty Jackley wins bid for  Republican US House nomination
South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley speaks during a press conference on Dec. 19, 2025, in Sioux Falls.  

PIERRE — South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley emerged victorious in the race for the Republican Party’s U.S. House nomination.

His opponent, James Bialota, of Piedmont, did not mount a prominent campaign.

Jackley earned 79% of the votes while Bialota gained 21%. 

All the votes came from registered Republicans, whose primaries are closed to independents and voters from other parties.

The 55-year-old Jackley, of Pierre, began his career in public service as U.S. attorney for South Dakota from 2006 to 2009. He was the state’s attorney general from 2009 to 2019, ran unsuccessfully against Kristi Noem for the Republican nomination for governor in 2018, and won election as attorney general again in 2022.

Jackley entered the race for the state’s only seat in the U.S. House last year after Republican U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson announced his campaign for governor.

In the Nov. 3 general election, Jackley will face Nikki Gronli, a former state director of rural development for the U.S. Department of Agriculture. Gronli was unopposed for the Democratic nomination.

Jackley’s U.S. House candidacy creates an opening for attorney general that will be filled in the general election. Party nominees for that office are not chosen by voters, but rather by delegates to state party conventions later this month.

title: Shriner’s Circus makes its 90th return to Deadwood
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Shriner’s Circus will make its 90th return to the Days of ’76 Rodeo Grounds Saturday at 2 p.m. and 7 p.m. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Shriner’s Circus makes its 90th return to Deadwood
The Shriner’s Circus will make its 90th return to the Days of ’76 Rodeo Grounds Saturday at 2 p.m. and 7 p.m. Pioneer file photo 

DEADWOOD — Circus goers aged 0-99 are set for a treat in Deadwood Saturday with the 90th return of the Shriner’s Circus to the Days of ’76 Rodeo Grounds. 

Kip Wagner, Deadwood circus chairman for the Naja Shriners, said that circus goers can anticipate much of the same acts they’ve seen in year’s past. For the children, Wagner’s target audience, he said it’s exciting every time. 

“The circus is kind of a tradition,” said Wagner. “When you realize our audience is little kids, I’ve seen lots of elephants and trapeze acts, but they haven’t. So, in essence, it’s always new for the little kids. And you got to have cotton candy, right?”

The show will go on twice on Saturday, at 2 p.m. and 7 p.m. Adult tickets are $10, and children’s tickets have been sponsored by local businesses. 

“Nobody likes to go around and raise money, but we’ll walk into a business, and they’ll look at us and say, ‘Yep, I got tickets when I was a kid,’” said Wagner. “They reach into their back pocket because they want to do this, they want kids to have the same experiences they did.”

Wagner said the circus is all about having fun, but the event is a fundraiser for their mission to help families obtain quality medical care for their children regardless of their ability to pay. He said the Shriners built their first children’s hospital in Shreveport, La., in 1920, followed by a second facility in the Twin Cities in Minn. Since then, they’ve sponsored critical medical advances in children’s healthcare. Shriner’s own the patent for artificial skin, a revolutionary treatment for burn victims, that they have given away for free. 

“At the end of the day, we have 23 hospitals across North America. Now we’re into Mexico and South America. We’ve got medical treatment centers in Canada, Hawaii, we’re getting to be worldwide,” said Wagner. “We’ve treated kids with debilitating injuries from the wars in Eastern Europe. We’ve been doing it for so long we forget to tell people what we’re doing.”
