title: Bradley elected as Sturgis mayor, Keszler takes Ward 1 council seat
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Businessman Rod Bradley will serve as the next mayor of Sturgis.
_full_text:
STURGIS — Businessman Rod Bradley will serve as the next mayor of Sturgis.

Unofficial results show that Bradley received 984, or nearly 58% of the votes cast for mayor in Tuesday’s special election. Candidates Richelle Bruch received 366 votes, or 21%, and Tammy Bohn received 360 votes, or 21%. Overall, there were 1,710 votes cast, or 32% of the 5,339 registered voters in Sturgis.

“You always have a good feeling when you win and when it’s a strong statement, you have an even better feeling,” Bradley said. “I feel like there’s a job to be done and now it’s time to get to work.”

Bradley said his first order of business will be to connect with council members and staff, to start building relationships in order to serve the citizens.

“We’re going to be in the trenches together and serving the council well, so you have to have those roles and relationships defined,” he said. “I don’t think any of the targets are secret. They’re well vetted and actually discussed well in public. We’ve got to figure out the sponsorship program and how the council wants that to look going forward. The Rally’s gonna be here before we know it. I feel like the council and the staff ran a good Rally last year, and I’m sure there’s planning already in place, but I’ve got to get up to speed on that. Before you know it, if not already, we’re in budget season. We really need to make sure we have all the information that’s needed to truly have a good budget process. Those are the targets.”

Sturgis voters in Ward 1 also selected Terry Keszler to represent them on the city council. Keszler defeated challenger Brenda Vasknetz, receiving 57% of the votes at 163. Vasknetz received 43% of the votes, at 121. A total of 284 votes were cast in the Ward 1 race. There are a total of 1,242 registered voters in Ward 1, which means there was a 23% turnout.

“I am very thankful for the support I received in my ward,” Keszler said. “There are some important things before this council. The main reason I ran, quite honestly, is I care very much about this community. I really don’t have a specific agenda, but my goal is to have this community move forward. We’ve got things before us that are really important, that need to be dealt with.”

The special election was held to fill vacancies created when former Mayor Kevin Forrester resigned in March due to health concerns, and Ward 1 Councilman Nick Jones resigned after accepting a work position in Texas. Forrester was diagnosed with pancreatic cancer in October 2025, and he passed away on April 5. In his resignation letter, Forrester named Bradley as his choice for a mayoral appointment, if the council decided to appoint a replacement. However, after much deliberation the Sturgis City Council opted to hold the special election and let the voters choose their next mayor.

Forrester was elected mayor in April 2025, and his term was scheduled to expire in 2028. Therefore, Bradley will serve for approximately 2 years, until 2028. Jones’ term was scheduled to expire in 2027, and Keszler will serve until then.

title: Schumacher, Meiners take Lead City Commission seats
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: LEAD — Dustin Schumacher and Valerie Meiners will be Lead’s newest representatives, for 3-year terms on the city commission
_full_text:
LEAD — Dustin Schumacher and Valerie Meiners will be Lead’s newest representatives, for 3-year terms on the city commission

It was a close race on Tuesday, as Lead residents cast their votes for up to 2 city commission candidates. Schumacher received 33% of the of the votes with 375; Meiners received 27% with 307; Jeremiah Fredericksen received 24% of the votes with 273; and incumbent Al Rohrer received 16% with 179 votes. Overall, 1,134 votes were cast in the election.

Schumacher and Meiners both pointed to building the 2027 budget as some of their major priorities, but each candidate had different ideas about where the money should go. The Lead City Commission is expected to start formal budget hearings in August.

“I am just truly humbled and excited to get to work,” Schumacher said. “We’ve got to get the budget figured out to where we can prioritize some infrastructure and community needs. We’re going to stick to community-oriented projects along with infrastructure. That’s what I’d like to do. Community oriented means bringing the community together for things like recreation and events, and bringing us back as one large community together.”

Schumacher, who was the only candidate who openly supported funding for Lead’s Handley Recreation Center, made it clear that the center is important for citizens of all ages.

“I think the community center and recreation as a whole is so necessary to the health and well-being of our community,” he said.

Meiners said she intends to focus on city infrastructure during her term on the commission. Fixing Lead’s streets, she said, needs to be a long-term priority with a plan. She also said she intends to listen to the people of Lead, and work to represent their interests.

“I thank the voters big time,” she said. “I will do whatever I can to make things happen the way they want them to happen.”

Meiners said she was pleasantly surprised at the number of votes that were cast.

“I’m really excited about the number of voters that came out,” she said. “There was 1,134 votes and that’s pretty impressive numbers. They must have wanted to see some difference.”

Lawrence County Auditor Brenda McGruder said there were a total of 648 ballots cast, including absentee ballots, in Lead. By comparison, there are 1,894 registered voters who reside in Lead city limits, which means voter turnout was at 34%. The turnout is higher than it’s been for the past 2 municipal elections, with a 25% turnout in 2022 and a 12% turnout in 2024.

“It is a 100% win for Butte County. Everyone got to vote. Even if they voted against it, they still had the opportunity to make their voice heard,” Evans said.

The measure will require the county commission to pass an ordinance prohibiting the construction of data centers in Butte County.

title: Unearthing forgotten stories
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: Lisa Wible, Sam Bambas, and Dr. Tony Krus, using a ¼ inch screen with a large magnet to catch any artifacts that maybe in the soil that was excavated on Tuesday near Fort Meade.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
1. dig.JPG
Lisa Wible, Sam Bambas, and Dr. Tony Krus, using a ¼ inch screen with a large magnet to catch any artifacts that maybe in the soil that was excavated on Tuesday near Fort Meade.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

FORT MEADE — For the fifth consecutive year, archaeologists and students from the University of South Dakota are digging into the past at Fort Meade’s historic Soapsuds Row, uncovering clues about the women and families whose contributions to military life have often been overlooked.

The 2026 excavation marks the fifth year of USD’s Archaeology Field School at the site, where students are working alongside faculty and researchers to investigate the former home and laundry facilities of the Army laundresses who supported Fort Meade’s cavalry troops.

Leading the project is Dr. Tony Krus, a professor in the anthropology department at University of South Dakota, who said this year’s primary objective is to better understand a feature discovered beneath a structure believed to have been associated with the laundresses.

“The main goal this year is to understand the fill below the potential structure that has been the focus of our excavations,” Krus said. “We want to determine whether this was a storage space beneath the building or if it was created during the demolition of the structure. The preliminary evidence suggests it may have been a storage area, but we’re excited to map it more completely and better understand how it was used.”

 3. dig.JPG
Dr. Tony Krus at the historic archeological dig site with his students on Tuesday commonly known as ‘Soap Suds Row’.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

Researchers are also tracing the footprint of the structure in hopes of learning more about its layout and function.  While historical records provide some information about Fort Meade’s laundresses, archaeology offers a rare glimpse into their daily lives.  

 4. dig.JPG
Twelve students from USD working on the dig site on the Bear Butte Creek Historic Preserve on Tuesday near Fort Meade. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

“What we’ve learned are the small, personal stories revealed through the artifacts,” Krus said. “It’s one thing to read about the laundresses in a history book or museum display, but it’s another to find objects that were part of their everyday lives.”

Among the discoveries made during previous excavations are fragments of cosmetic bottles, including what researchers believe may have been face bleach and a coconut-based hair product.

“These items help humanize the women who lived and worked here,” Krus said. “They remind us that these were real people with families, routines and personal lives.”

Excavations have also uncovered children’s toys, offering evidence of family life and the childcare responsibilities often carried by the laundresses.

The team hopes this year’s work will provide additional insight into what happened when the laundresses eventually left Fort Meade and whether belongings were intentionally stored or abandoned within the structure.

Training the next generation of archaeologists

The field school serves a dual purpose: advancing research while providing hands-on training for future archaeologists.

Aaron Mayer, archaeologist-in-residence at USD and a volunteer on the project for the past four years, said the experience is invaluable for students entering the profession.

“This field school helps train the next generation of archaeologists,” Mayer said. “Many experienced professionals in the region are retiring, so there is a need to prepare students with strong archaeological methods and field experience.”

Several students who have participated in the field school have gone on to graduate programs across the country, while others have found employment with public agencies and private archaeological firms in the Black Hills region.

Krus noted that approximately 34 USD students will have participated in the Fort Meade field school over the past 3 years.

“Several have gone on to prestigious graduate programs with full funding, and others have been hired as archaeologists in the Black Hills after graduation,” Krus said. “It’s rewarding to see students take what they’ve learned here and turn it into successful careers.”

Students gain hands-on experience

For many students, the Fort Meade field school provides an opportunity to gain practical experience while helping uncover a unique chapter of South Dakota history.

Grayson Baumberger, a USD anthropology major with an archaeology minor who recently completed his sophomore year, has spent much of the spring assisting with surveys and excavation preparation. Baumberger, a Lead native, said he and fellow student Natalie Wagner began conducting surveys across the Fort Meade property in mid-May before shifting their focus to excavation work.  

“We’ve been working on getting the backfill dug down so the students here can start working,” Baumberger said.

His long-term goal is to pursue a career in archaeology, though he is still considering which educational path to follow after earning his bachelor’s degree.

“We have people working for cultural resource management companies with bachelor’s degrees, and others who continue on to earn master’s degrees or doctorates,” Baumberger said. “I definitely want to get some more work experience before I decide what direction I’ll take.”

Natalie Wagner, a senior anthropology student at USD and incoming President of the University’s Anthropology Club, first participated in the Fort Meade field school in 2024 and was eager to return.

“I really like the area,” said Wagner, who is from Chatham, Ill. “I’ve never been in a landscape that’s as pretty as this, and it’s really interesting learning about these women who we don’t have in history books, but now we get to learn about their lives through what they left behind.”  

In addition to assisting with surveys, Wagner has been helping guide students participating in the excavation.

After graduating from USD, Wagner plans to pursue graduate studies in bioarcheology, a field that focuses on the study of human remains and skeletal evidence to better understand past populations.

Expanding research beyond Soap Suds Row

In addition to excavating at the laundress site, researchers are conducting broader surveys across the Black Hills Bear Butte Creek Historic Preserve.

Mayer said the team has surveyed roughly 200 acres, documenting numerous features associated with military training activities during World War I and World War II.

“We’ve identified a variety of depressions and features connected to military training exercises,” Mayer said. “We’ve also located previously undocumented artifacts, including intact ammunition and military-related items.”

Among the discoveries were a .38-caliber cartridge dating to the early 1900s and a label from a World War II-era shaving kit, providing additional evidence of military activity throughout the area.

“These finds help us understand how Fort Meade evolved over time and the many ways the land was used beyond the cavalry era,” Mayer said.

Preserving a forgotten chapter of history

For Krus, one of the most important aspects of the project is bringing attention to people whose stories are largely absent from traditional military histories.

“One of the goals of historical archaeology is to uncover the histories of people who are not well represented in written records,” Krus said. “Many of the laundresses were likely illiterate, which means they didn’t leave behind diaries or journals that historians can study.”

As a result, archaeology becomes one of the few ways to reconstruct their lives.  

“By excavating sites like Soapsuds Row, we’re able to glimpse a forgotten part of history,” Krus said. “These women played an important role in supporting military operations, but their stories are often left out of the historical narrative.”

“If people drive by and see us working, we ask that they stay outside the fenced area, but we’re always happy to talk if they wave us down,” Krus said. “The best way to learn about this history is to visit the Fort Meade Museum and see the Soap Suds Row exhibit. That’s available during the summer, while we’re only here for a short time each summer.”

“Artifacts recovered from the site have already helped shape exhibits at the Fort Meade Museum, and researchers hope future discoveries will continue to enhance public understanding of the laundresses and their families.”

Dr. Krus said one of the most significant discoveries from the past several years has been a collection of metal fragments that were eventually identified as parts of a laundry wringer.

“I think the artifact that’s most intriguing to me is actually about 10 artifacts that fit together to form a laundry wringer,” Krus said. “That’s pretty good evidence that this was indeed where the laundresses were living. While we have historical records and maps that indicate this was probably Soap Suds Row, the laundry wringer provided some of the strongest physical evidence we’ve uncovered.”  Researchers have also recovered numerous artifacts that can be dated to the 1890s and early 1900s, helping establish a timeline for activity at the site and providing additional insight into daily life at Fort Meade during that era.

As excavation continues over the next week and a half, each artifact recovered from the soil adds another piece to the story of the women, children and families who lived and worked along Soap Suds Row more than a century ago, ensuring their contributions to Fort Meade’s history are no longer forgotten while helping train the next generation of archaeologists who will preserve those stories for years to come.

title: Mill and overlay projects in Deadwood
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Summertime mill and overlay projects in Deadwood are set to include Washington Street and the Miller Street parking lot near the Deadwood Recreation and Aquatic Center. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
Mill and overlay projects in Deadwood
Summertime mill and overlay projects in Deadwood are set to include Washington Street and the Miller Street parking lot near the Deadwood Recreation and Aquatic Center. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

DEADWOOD — The arrival of warmer weather brings with it annual street and parking lot repairs in the city of Deadwood.

Projects this year are set to include Washington Street and the Miller Street parking lot. Johner Paving, of Spearfish, was awarded both contracts. Lornie Stalder, director of public works, said the city has not received a start date from Johner on either project, but both will be completed before the end of October.

Washington Street

Stalder said Washington Street and sections of Adams and Taylor streets are set to receive a 2-inch mill and overlay. The project usually takes 3 days from start to finish, he said, and the city asks that residents and visitors refrain from parking on the street during the entirety of the project. 

The project is part of the city’s annual initiative to repair a street in bad condition.

“We basically do a drive though of the entire town and try to determine which street is in the worst condition,” said Stalder. “We’ve been working in the presidential district for the last 3 years.”

The project is expected to cost approximately $60,000.

“Our streets budget is roughly around $1.6 million, and we set aside of $100,000 of that towards mill and overlay,” said Stalder. “I’d love to be to a point where we can drive around town and for it to be a tough decision to determine which roads are a priority, but we’re currently not there. I’d like to say in the next 5 years we’ll be to a point where all of our streets will be in better condition.”

Miller Street parking lot

Justin Lux, director of parking and transportation, said the parking lot near the Deadwood  Recreation and Aquatic Center on Miller Street has been selected for the department’s annual mill and overlay project. 

“We identified Miller Street as one of our most used parking lots. A lot of visitors see that as kind of their first stop in Deadwood,” said Lux. “It’s in very poor condition. We plan on leaving the parking lot layout and design as it is for now. In the next 5-10 years we might look at completely revamping (the design) of that parking lot, but for now it’ll stay the way it is.”

Lux said that he anticipates the project will take 2 weeks to complete once work begins. He said that his biggest concern with scheduling the project is working around major Deadwood events while ensuring an October finish date.

“As long as it’s not going on during the Sturgis Rally, or during Kool Deadwood Nites, I don’t see it being an issue,” Lux said. 

During construction Lux said that the parking lot will be completely closed. Patrons who use the parking lot to use the rec center will be accommodated. Plans for accommodation have not been declared yet. 

Lux said that the project was identified in the city’s capital improvement plan, but is being paid for by the parking and transportation enterprise fund, utilizing revenues made from paid parking.

title: Purple Park  renovations taking shape
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Crews work on laying down parts for the new playground equipment that will be installed at the Purple Park this summer. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
purple park.JPG
Crews work on laying down parts for the new playground equipment that will be installed at the Purple Park this summer. Courtesy photo 

LEAD — Crews are working to install playground equipment at the Purple Park, with plans to complete work this summer. 

Playground equipment arrived at the site on McClellan Street May 19, and crews from Dakota Playground, of North Dakota, will be working for the next few weeks to install it. The area is officially named Par Course Park, but was known as the “Purple Park” due to the purple play apparatus. It had fallen into disrepair, and the Lead-Deadwood Kiwanis Club adopted the park renovation as a legacy project, to mark its 100th anniversary. 

As a nod to the park’s nickname, the large tower for the slides and climbing apparatus is purple. 

The Lead-Deadwood Kiwanis Club raised nearly $300,000 in grants, donations, and in-kind work for the project. The playground equipment is largely paid with a $135,000 Land and Water Conservation Grant from the South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks Department and the National Park Service.  The city of Lead provided in-kind labor to tear down old equipment and help prepare the land for the new structures. 

On Monday, the city commission also approved spending $15,000 from the city’s third-penny sales tax, also known as the bed and booze fund. The money will be used to install historical lighting that was taken from Lead’s business district when Main Street was reconstructed in 2015. Commissioners and city officials said the lighting will improve safety at the park and for the walking path that is heavily used. 

Shelley Dragoo, who has been spearheading the Kiwanis Club’s efforts to renovate the park, said new equipment will include a tower with 2 or 3 slides and a climbing apparatus, a 2-bay zip line, 2 spinners, swings, and a merry go round. Dragoo said everything at the park will be accessible for all abilities, including the slide tower. An ADA accessible walkway will also provide access down to and around the park equipment. 

While Dragoo said original plans were to open the park in August, it is possible that it could be ready for the public by July 4 this year.

title: Lower turnout, shifting loyalties may drive results in GOP primary runoff for SD governor
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — The dust from Tuesday’s primary election has barely settled, but 2 of South Dakota’s governor hopefuls are back in a full sprint toward a July 28 special election — the first runoff in state history for a party’s gubernatorial nomination.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — The dust from Tuesday’s primary election has barely settled, but 2 of South Dakota’s governor hopefuls are back in a full sprint toward a July 28 special election — the first runoff in state history for a party’s gubernatorial nomination.

Advanced voting for the Republican runoff begins June 12, and ballots must be printed listing current Gov. Larry Rhoden and political newcomer Toby Doeden by June 10. Voter registration is open through July 13.

Political experts are still digesting Tuesday’s results and weighing factors that could shape the runoff — chiefly the potential for lower turnout and which of the finalists will draw support from backers of the two eliminated candidates.

Doeden, a vehicle dealership and rental property owner from Aberdeen, led primary results with 31% of the votes, according to unofficial election results on the Secretary of State’s website. He was followed by Rhoden at 25%.

U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson and state House of Representatives Speaker Jon Hansen earned 23% and 21%, respectively. South Dakota’s Republican primary is closed to independents and voters registered with other parties.

Doeden’s lead was unsurprising for Julia Hellwege, the director of the Chiesman Center for Democracy and a University of South Dakota associate professor in political science.

The Chiesman Center and South Dakota News Watch polled voters several times ahead of the primary, as did KELO-TV and Emerson College. While Johnson took an early lead, Hellwege said, voter preferences gradually shifted toward Doeden amid a “fairly anti-government sentiment” among likely South Dakota voters.

Michael Card, professor emeritus of political science at USD, said he believed it would “be Dusty all the way” until the final days leading up to the election. By then, Card said it was easier to predict Johnson’s “fall from grace with voters” and their displeasure with negative advertisements attributed to his campaign.

Political analyst Drey Samuelson worked for South Dakota’s last 2 Democratic federal officeholders, former U.S. Sens. Tom Daschle and Tim Johnson. 

Samuelson said he was also shocked that Johnson didn’t make the runoff, calling the congressman “the victim of the anti-incumbent spirit sweeping the country.”

Rhoden likely edged past Johnson by running on his gubernatorial record, Hellwege said, while Johnson struggled to shed the image of a “D.C. outsider” after serving in the U.S. House of Representatives for nearly eight years.

Primaries also tend to draw more partisan voters than moderate ones, Hellwege said.

A political action committee affiliated with Doeden sent a text message to Republican voters saying, “if you hate President Trump and all that he stands for, Dusty Johnson is the candidate for you.” Trump’s support in the Republican Party remains strong even as his approval ratings have fallen more broadly in recent months. Johnson voted to certify the results of the 2020 election, which Trump lost, and supported the creation of an independent, bipartisan commission to investigate the rioters who attempted to stop the certification of that election.

“Doeden voters were always going to be the motivated voters, and those were always going to be the ones to turn out,” Hellwege said.

Turnout, whims of Johnson and Hansen voters a factor

About 43% of registered Republican voters cast their ballots Tuesday. That’s comparable to 42% in the 2018 gubernatorial primary and 43% in 2022.

Turnout for July’s special election will be lower, Hellwege predicted, which could skew results toward more partisan voters since they’re more motivated to participate than moderates.

“Motivation attrition is going to be greater. Special elections always have lower turnout,” she said.

Doeden finished with the most votes, but nearly 70% of Republican voters chose another candidate. 

Doeden’s statements about wanting to “put an end to Dusty’s career” are likely to have largely alienated that base, Card said. If Johnson’s voters return for the runoff, they’ll likely shift toward Rhoden, Hellwege agreed. 

“All of those Johnson voters now have a choice: Are they going to turn out? I think it’s going to be a question for those voters of whether they’re sufficiently motivated by not wanting Doeden to win,” Hellwege said.

Hansen voters could “move either way,” Hellwege said.

It’ll come down to whether or not they are driven out to vote, Card said, and it’s going to be “easier for Rhoden than Doeden” to ultimately secure enough votes to win over the majority of voters in the runoff.

Neither Hansen nor Johnson responded to Searchlight’s request for comment. Neither had endorsed Rhoden or Doeden as of Wednesday afternoon.

Influence of money, direction of messaging

Beyond voter shifts, Hellwege said Johnson’s and Hansen’s campaigns could influence the race by directing money toward their preferred candidate.

“That question is whether the Dusty camp is going to move their money toward Rhoden or if they’re going to save their money for the next race or future potential candidacy,” Hellwege said.

Johnson had $931,000 on hand two weeks before the election, according to his pre-primary campaign disclosure. Doeden had less than $220,000, having loaned his campaign $4 million. Rhoden ended the pre-primary reporting period with $169,616 but reported raising significant additional funds after the deadline.

“We outperformed the other three candidates very dramatically in the closing weeks of the last campaign,” Rhoden said. “So I think that we’ll be in fine shape to be able to present our message and move forward through this interim campaign.”

Rhoden said the one-on-one format lets him focus on his vision and offer a “clear contrast” between him and Doeden.

Doeden did not respond to a request for comment. In a speech to attendees at his Tuesday night watch party, he said the success broke institutional expectations.

“They said no outsider in South Dakota can break through three career, 20-year politicians,” Doeden said. “Well, guess what? You and I, we are doing it.”

Tuesday marked the first time a primary for a South Dakota party’s nomination for governor has gone to a runoff since a law requiring one was passed in 1985. Previously, when no candidate reached 35% in a crowded field, party delegates chose the nominee at a state convention.

The candidate who ultimately wins the Republican nomination for governor will advance to the Nov. 3 general election to face Dan Ahlers, who was uncontested for the Democratic nomination.

title: Funds ‘misused’ from Spearfish Rams football organization
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: SPEARFISH — Money belonging to the Spearfish Rams’ organization in the Black Hills Youth Football League was recently discovered to have been “misused and no longer available.”
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

SPEARFISH — Money belonging to the Spearfish Rams’ organization in the Black Hills Youth Football League was recently discovered to have been “misused and no longer available.”

The board of directors shared the news on its Facebook page Tuesday. It asks anyone who has donated or sponsored funds to the Rams between Dec. 1, 2025, and now to contact the program right away, as those funds were never received.

The commissioner has also been terminated

“This discovery has been devastating to everyone involved, especially because this organization exists for one reason, our kids,” according to a post on social media by the Rams’ board of directors.

“We understand the anger, disappointment, and frustration many of you might feel. As leaders and volunteers within this organization, we take this situation very seriously, and we sincerely apologize to every family, sponsor, supporter, and community member who placed their trust in us. 

The post indicates that the situation was allegedly caused by the actions of one individual, and that the board recognizes that the organization should have had stronger financial oversight. 

“We are actively working to address those failures immediately by implementing additional accountability measures, reviewing all financial records, and cooperating fully with the local police department,” according to the Post

Former commissioner Lyndsay Schreiber was asked and agreed to step back in as interim commissioner to help the organization through this transition as a new commissioner for the 2026 football season is being sought.

“Right now, our biggest priority is making sure the kids in this program do not lose the opportunity to play, grow, and be part of the team they love,” according to the post. “Unfortunately, the financial impact of this situation has placed our organization in a very difficult position. We will not be able to offer any discount codes or player/cheerleader scholarships this season. We are also putting our pride aside and asking our community for support as we work to rebuild and keep this program alive for our athletes.” 

Inquiries for more information left with the Rams’ board were directed to Schreiber. Messages seeking comment from her were not returned.

A phone call and email to the Spearfish Police Department for comment were not returned. 

This marked the second time that the Spearfish Rams has had money taken from the organization. 

In 2018, Nicholas Edward Hoffman pleaded guilty to one count of grand theft by embezzlement from Spearfish Youth Wrestling Club. As part of a plea agreement, 2 other identical charges were dropped. Those charges were for embezzlement from the Queen City Futbol Club and Spearfish Rams Football. In addition of jail time, Hoffman was ordered to pay restitution of $14,549.33 total to the 3 clubs.

“Hoffman admitted that between and during 2015 through 2018, he had taken money that belonged to the wrestling club and used it for personal expenses,” said then Lawrence County State’s Attorney John Fitzgerald. Hoffman had been the treasurer of the club.

He was the former commission of the Spearfish Rams Football from 2016-2018. It was 2017-2018 in which the Rams had money stolen.

And, Hoffman was vice president of the Queen City Futbol Club and the thefts involved the years 2015-18.

title: SDSU and local nonprofit bring native plant expo to Spearfish for fourth year
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — Beautify Spearfish and South Dakota State University (SDSU) will bring a native plant sale and Educational Program to The Snapper’s Club in Spearfish at 416 S. Canyon St from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. Saturday.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

SPEARFISH — Beautify Spearfish and South Dakota State University (SDSU) will bring a native plant sale and Educational Program to The Snapper’s Club in Spearfish at 416 S. Canyon St from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m. Saturday.

The event will feature a variety of speakers, as well as vendors selling plants native to South Dakota. This year will mark the fourth year of the program. 

The event will feature a variety of speakers. Robin Buterbaugh will deliver a talk called Native Plants for Birds at 10:15 a.m. Stacy Goodman will deliver a talk called Why The Dark Matters to You at 11:15 a.m. Allison Boehm will deliver a talk titled Plugs v.s. Seeds at 12:15 p.m. Lora Perkins will deliver a speech titled Seed Storage at 1:15 p.m. Finally, Alex Kovary will deliver a speech titled Seed Sources at 2:15 p.m.

The first 28 people to attend each speech will receive a $25 voucher that can be spent at the vendors.

Kelly Harnett, founder of Beautify Spearfish, is responsible for creating the event in collaboration with SDSU. 

“I contacted them 4 years ago and said, ‘hey, if I put something together, would you guys come out and sell your plants?’” Harnett, who holds degrees in ecology and related fields, said. “And they said ‘yes.’”

Harnett said the goal of the plant sale is to educate residents about the importance of native plants and native pollinators, which she says are declining at very high rates. 

“Habitat fragmentation and habitat loss are the biggest impacts on our native pollinators,” she said. “Most native pollinators are gonna fly just hundreds of yards … versus the honeybee which can go miles.”

Harnett said that she first became interested in native ecology in 2020, when she used federal stimulus funds to remove her lawn and replace it with native plants. From there, she founded the nonprofit Beautify Spearfish, and advocates for wildlife causes.

“I just felt I had a voice I could use to teach people,” she said.

Harnett said that her goal is for every Spearfish resident to have a native pollinator habitat, and for real estate developers to plant native plants rather than non-native plants. 

Lora Perkins, a professor at SDSU, heads the university’s presence at the event. 

“It (the event) is one of our most successful events,” Perkins said. “We have a big table of extension materials that we give away and then we have the plants.”

She said that she and her team chooses the plants that go on sale during the event in the winter based on what seeds are locally available, which seeds do well in landscaping, and which provide the most value in terms of pollination.

Perkins also brings a group of graduate and undergraduate students to the sale each year.

“I think it is a terrific way for grad students to realize the impact of their work and learn the importance of outreach … and (learn) how to talk to the general public about native plants and their research.”

title: Man convicted in Jones Park Assault behind bars for attempted strangulation after escaping from custody
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Man convicted in Jones Park Assault behind bars for attempted strangulation after escaping from custody
Courtesy photo 

DEADWOOD — Ashton Lee Tusing, the Spearfish man convicted of aggravated assault after he attacked a then 15-year-old boy in Belle Fourche’s Jones Park in April 2024, is behind bars in Lawrence County again — charged with 2 counts domestic abuse aggravated assault. 

He faces one count of strangulation, a Class 3 felony, and one count of domestic abuse aggravated assault with a deadly weapon, also a Class 3 felony. The second count requires “physical menace with a deadly weapon, to put another in fear of imminent serious bodily harm.” Both counts are linked to a March 3 incident involving his girlfriend at the time. 

Since the Jones Park assault in 2014, Tusing has been charged with more than 9 different crimes, including the recent domestic violence charges, assaulting law enforcement officers, intentional damage to a patrol car, resisting arrest, false impersonation, and misdemeanor drug offenses in connection with an incident on I-90 last summer. He also faces multiple charges for failures to appear in court, and on May 14, he was indicted for possession of a stolen Toyota Rav 4 and a stolen 2011 Kia Sorento. 

In November, Tusing allegedly escaped from a court mandated substance abuse treatment program, with the help of 20-year-old Alexcia Boyd, of Spearfish. 

Boyd was also charged in the Jones Park assault after she allegedly helped to lure the victim to the park on April 18, 2024, for what Tusing described as a “set up” according to his testimony during his sentencing. She was nearly 18 at the time. 

Now, Boyd faces one count of concealing an escaped prisoner, a class 5 felony punishable with up to 5 years in prison a $10,000 fine or both, and conspiracy to commit second-degree escape. She appeared in court for a status hearing on the matter Tuesday morning. 

According to the probable cause statement for Boyd’s March 5 arrest, Tusing had been arrested on “several felony warrants” and placed in the care of a “rehab facility.” According to the probable cause statement for Boyd’s arrest, a friend of hers voluntarily told police that she had “assisted getting Ashton out of the facility” on Nov. 30.  

In the course of the investigation, police seized a cellphone from Boyd. Based on evidence found on the device, police allege Boyd and Tusing’s mother, Jacqueline Tusing, conspired to conceal Tusing from law enforcement after his escape — discussing plans to purchase hair dye, install surveillance cameras, and move Tusing frequently to avoid detection. 

Jacqueline Tusing is also charged with one count of concealing an escaped prisoner, a Class 5 felony.

According to court documents, Tusing and Boyd were allegedly on the run after November. 

“Since Ashton’s escape from the facility, there has been numerous photographs uploaded to his Snapchat and Facebook depicting Alexcia and him together,” the probable cause statement reads. 

Court documents indicate that Tusing may’ve stolen a vehicle in April, while alluding capture. 

Tusing faces 2 counts of criminal entry into a motor vehicle and one count of petty theft in the second degree connected to an April 28 theft of a Toyota Rav 4. Police reports also indicate Tusing was a suspect in the case of an attempted vehicle break-in, also on April 28. Police responded after the owner of a Ford Bronco observed that someone had attempted to drive away in his vehicle; because of after-market modifications made to the vehicle the theft was unsuccessful. 

On May 14, Tusing was indicted not only for the theft of the Toyota, but also for possession of a stolen Kia he allegedly had in his possession on Nov. 22, 2025. 

Following information from a witness, police say they arrested Boyd at an apartment on Colorado Boulevard on March 5. Police had also attempted to locate Tusing at the time, but only Boyd was apprehended. Boyd is scheduled to appear in court for a status hearing on July 14. 

A warrant for Tusing’s arrest in the domestic violence case was served on May 20 and returned on May 1. Tusing is scheduled for arraignment in that case on June 18. On the same day, he’ll also have a status hearing for charges connected to a July 2025 incident on I-90.

At the time, Tusing had multiple active warrants. A deputy stopped to assist the occupants of a car with a flat tire at mile marker 25.  Tusing allegedly provided a false name and a struggle ensued. He allegedly struck a Whitewood police officer in the head and a South Dakota Highway Patrol trooper in the leg. The deputies, along with a passing motorist, were able to place Tusing into handcuffs. He bonded out following that arrest. 

Back in 2024, when Tusing pleaded guilty to aggravated assault in the Jones Park attack he was sentenced of 8 years at the South Dakota State Penitentiary. That sentence was suspended, with Tusing able to serve 4 years of supervised probation, as long as he complied with a list of conditions that include: receiving treatment for substance abuse, finishing high school or a GED program, having no immediate contact with the victim or his family, maintaining gainful employment, sobriety and “exhibiting no threatening or violent behavior.” The charges against Boyd in connection with that incident were either dropped or transferred to the juvenile justice system.

title: Male shot, killed in RC
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Male shot, killed in RC
Courtesy photo 

RAPID CITY — A male was shot and killed early Thursday morning in Rapid City.

According to the Rapid City Police Department, around 12:30 a.m., Thursday, police were dispatched to a residence at 3350 Palm Dr., for a report of a shooting that had just occurred. 

On their arrival, police located a man in the parking lot who was allegedly determined to be the shooter. He was detained and identified as 21-year-old Christopher Tromp of Rapid City. Other officers entered the apartment and located the male shooting victim, obviously deceased. 

Tromp was transported to the public safety building to be interviewed by detectives. Following the interview, Tromp was placed under arrest for first-degree manslaughter. 

The name of the victim is being withheld until notification of next-of-kin can be accomplished. The investigation into the shooting remains active and ongoing.

title: Quick picks: Summer road trips
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Quick Picks: Summer road trips
Courtesy photo 

Maybe you’ve recently picked up a copy of Matthew Davis’ “Biography of a Mountain” and you’re bound for Mount Rushmore. Perhaps, you’re in possession of one of the “Black Hills History Tours” guides by local historian David Wolff. Both books provide excellent gateways into the world of the summer road trip. To further expand your horizons, we asked Olyn Smith at the Whitewood Library for recommendations to fuel your road trips — alongside snacks and gasoline that is. 

1. “101 Road Tales”

Genre: Motorcycle guide

Popular motojournalist Clement Salvadori has been sharing his stories from the road with the readers of Rider magazine since 1988.  Now, 101 of those engaging Road Tales have been brought together in one book, cleverly illustrated by his long-time friend Gary Brown.

2. “Hiking the Black Hills Country” by Jane Gildart

Genre: Guide

Hiking the Black Hills Country includes detailed descriptions and maps of 55 trails, from Devils Tower National Monument and Mount Rushmore National Memorial to Custer State Park, Wind Cave, and Badlands National Park.

3. “Into the Wild” by Jon Krakauer

Genre: Nonfiction/biography 

In April 1992 a young man from a well-to-do family hitchhiked to Alaska and walked alone into the wilderness north of Mt. McKinley. He had given $25,000 in savings to charity, abandoned his car and most of his possessions, burned all the cash in his wallet, and invented a new life for himself. Four months later, his decomposed body was found by a moose hunter. How Christopher Johnson McCandless came to die is the unforgettable story of “Into the Wild.”

4. “American Ramble: A Walk of Memory and Renewal” by Neil King Jr. 

Genre: Nonfiction/Travel 

Neil King Jr.’s desire to walk from Washington, D.C., to New York City began on a whim and became an obsession. By the spring of 2021, events had intervened that gave his desire greater urgency. His neighborhood still reeled from the January 6 insurrection. COVID-19 lock-downs and a rancorous election had deepened America’s divides. King himself bore the imprints of a long battle with cancer.

5. “The Road of Dreams: A Two-Year Bicycling and Hiking Adventure Around the World” by Bruce Junek

Genre: Nonfiction/Travel 

Follow the unforgettable exploits of Black Hills Locals and seasoned travelers Bruce Junek and Tass Thacker on their 26-month around-the-world bicycle trip. They crossed 4 continents through sweltering temperatures and winter snowstorms punctuated by 42 flats. This deeply personal travel book is also the story of an inner journey with a compelling message: Recognize what you value most in life, and pursue it!

6. “Guide to Climbing” by Tony Lourens

Genre: Nonfiction/Guide

Essential skills and techniques and equipment needed for each discipline. Emergency procedures and ways to prevent repetitive strain injuries. The book features a 3-month training program for competitions or multi-day challenges.

title: The Mercy Sloane Chronicles: Chapter 6
byline: By Eliza Blue A work of serialized fiction, special to the Pioneer
description: When she was down to her last twist of dried beef, Mercy knew she couldn’t wait any longer to walk to town.  She tried to wash some of her clothes in the old bucket she’d found behind the house, but with all the rust, she feared she’d done more harm than good. She’d laid her few flimsy garments across the broken stems of prairie grass and then stood watching to make sure they didn’t blow away, as there was nothing for 100 miles to stop their flight if the wind decided to take them.
_full_text:
The Mercy Sloane Chronicles

When she was down to her last twist of dried beef, Mercy knew she couldn’t wait any longer to walk to town.  She tried to wash some of her clothes in the old bucket she’d found behind the house, but with all the rust, she feared she’d done more harm than good. She’d laid her few flimsy garments across the broken stems of prairie grass and then stood watching to make sure they didn’t blow away, as there was nothing for 100 miles to stop their flight if the wind decided to take them. 

Looking down at her sunburnt arms, then back at her worse-for-the-wear laundry, she said aloud, “I guess I don’t mind looking a little desperate if it gets me a job.” She was glad she didn’t own a mirror.

She wasn’t completely destitute, though. Sewn into the seam of her second-best dress, there was the 20-dollar bill Augustine had slipped into her hand after the wedding, and a few more dollars she’d saved from working at a dress shop during college. She’d planned to use the money to set up “housekeeping”—to buy the womanly odds and ends she’d assumed Granger wouldn’t care about or understand and that she didn’t really want to explain. 

“My money will be your money,” he’d told her early in their engagement, with an oily, magnanimous smile that made her clench her jaw. 

“Our money will be our money,” she replied, returning his oily smile, even as she’d already begun tucking away whatever small change she could.

Looking out across the flouncy skirts and blouses in the grass, she finally knew what her mother meant about decisions making themselves.  She hadn’t expected to be 22 years old and living alone on the western prairie, but here she was. 

She still wasn’t sure about the money part, though, because one thing was certain: the time in her life when money came easy was over for now.

***

“A job? Well….” said Arlo Hanson, keeper of Antelope’s lone shop, as he adjusted his glasses and gazed over the thin frames at the dusty young woman who’d just walked in. “I don’t know….” He glanced around the store awkwardly. Mercy followed his gaze. The rickety shelves held dry goods, canned goods, home goods, and most of what you’d need to get a broke car or tractor up and running. 

Mercy hadn’t expected much, but she had to admit, this was still less than she’d anticipated. There were no customers in the store, and the dust on much of the inventory indicated that it was a fairly regular occurrence. It was clear he didn’t need help at all. 

 Eliza Blue TMC
Eliza Blue 

Antelope was created to be a railroad town, built when the railroad barons had been trying to entice new customers west. The plan had been to settle the country and line their pockets by shipping in goods. Of course, the barons had been told by the surveyors that the land west of 20 wasn’t going to be profitable in the same way that homesteading east of the Missouri River had been. Even seasoned farmers couldn’t make a living from the drought-prone hillsides of the shortgrass prairie. But they’d planned the railroad routes anyway, built the towns, and promised to build more. 

The railroad never arrived. Neither did the abundant crops. Now, decades into navigating the boom and bust cycle of drought that characterized the western plains, there weren’t many homesteaders left, and most who remained remained because they had nowhere else to go. 

Arlo was the exception. He ran sheep, ran the store, and kept score for the town baseball league in his free time. They were as close to comfortable as anyone in Antelope ever got because he’d come to Antelope with some family money when the land had first opened to homesteading. He didn’t like to dwell on that fact, but the fact of it remained–he’d worked hard, but he hadn’t gotten what he had by hard work alone.

Maybe he was thinking of that early head start and that’s why he couldn’t say “no” outright to the dusty girl in front of him, or maybe it was just easier to defer to his wife, but after another furtive glance at Mercy, his only reply was: “I better go ask Marla,” and he scurried out the shop’s back door to the little house that stood behind the alley.

title: Review: “Something We Said: Richard Pryor, A Notorious Word, and Me” by Elizabeth Stordeur
byline: By Terri Schlichenmeyer Special to the Pioneer
description: Sticks and stones may break my bones.
_full_text:
Sticks and stones may break my bones.

 Something We Said.jpg
“Something We Said” is part memoir, part exploration of the impact of language. Courtesy image 

You know the rest of that childhood rhyme, and you know it’s not true: words have meaning, and they can cut like a knife. And although sticks and stones and words are weapons, as in the new memoir, “Something We Said” by Elizabeth Stordeur Pryor, they can also hold people together.

The college lecture was supposed to have been about the 1850 Fugitive Slave Act.

It was supposed to have been a lively discourse and discussion but without intention, it quickly veered sideways. When a white student quoted a movie line featuring the “n-word,” the room went quiet and Professor Pryor panicked.

She’d grown up hearing that word, and seeing it, and she’d experienced the painful feelings attached to it. She knew who wrote that movie line. It was her father, Richard Pryor.

 Something We Said author CREDIT Isabella Dellolio Photography.jpg
Elizabeth Stordeur Pryor is the author of “Something We Said: Richard Pryor, A Notorious Word, and Me.” Photo courtesy Isabella Dellolio Photography 

In her first few years, Pryor spent most of her time in a white world, hearing her mother’s tales of her larger-than-life father, and trying to grasp meaning in her father’s albums, peppered as they were with a word that was off-limits to her. 

When she was six, she met her father for the first time. She began to visit him regularly. 

It was fun at her Dad’s house; though he was sometimes moody, he taught her to fish and play dominoes. She became close with her siblings, fearful of her great-grandmother, and confused about a word that her father’s uncles threw around like a beach ball. It was a forbidden word at her mother’s house, but her father used it. Differently. Often. 

The word hurt. She knew first-hand that it did.

“The word became a degrading slur that shackled all Black people together into a single, inescapable tribe,” she says.

So why was it okay if certain people said it?

Knowing that, in the years since Richard Pryor’s accident and his death from multiple sclerosis, he’s become somewhat of a legend is a very satisfying thing, isn’t it? So is reading about him, especially from the viewpoint of one of his seven children. But his is not the only story you get inside “Something We Said.”

Wrapped around the life of Richard Pryor is the life of a word that straddles a line between danger and provocation, a word that Pryor refuses to say or even print. As she tells readers about her father and her loving-but-difficult relationship with him, she warily circles that word, as if it might bite. You may cringe, but she weighs it carefully, helping readers see it as a chameleon before always bringing us back to her father, his work, and his life before and after her.

It’s a push-pull balance that holds readers fast, and keeps them there. It’s perfect for fans of this genre, or Richard Pryor, or of language – and it’s going to make you think. If you want a good memoir this week, one that may send you to your old album collection, “Something We Said” is rock-solid.

title: A timeline of the Black Hills Pioneer
description: Winter 1875 — W.A. Laughlin and A.W. Merrick purchase a printing press in Denver and have it delivered to Custer. By the time the press arrived, gold prospectors were starting to move out of Custer to go north, to Deadwood.
_full_text:
Winter 1875 — W.A. Laughlin and A.W. Merrick purchase a printing press in Denver and have it delivered to Custer. By the time the press arrived, gold prospectors were starting to move out of Custer to go north, to Deadwood. 

June 8, 1876 — The Black Hills Weekly Pioneer is the first established newspaper in the Black Hills, in Deadwood, using funds from Capt. C.V. Gardner. Due to failing health, W.A. Laughlin sold his interest in the paper to Gardner, who accompanied Merrick to Deadwood. 

Aug. 17, 1876 — The Cheyenne Leader reports that the Deadwood paper was published “with all the drawbacks incident to a frontier publisher’s life, the paper is spicy, prompt in the publication of news, and chuck full of business.”

Aug. 29, 1876 — Black Hills Weekly Pioneer hires its first reporter — Dick Hughes. Annie Tallent wrote that Huges was “practically the first newspaper reporter in the Black Hills.” 20-year-old Hughes took the job at the Pioneer to sustain his prospecting ventures. There are indications that Hughes wrote the story about Wild Bill Hickok’s death, though news articles of the time did not include a byline. 

Sept. 16, 1876 — The Pioneer reports that a provisional government had been established in Deadwood, with 1,082 affirmative and 57 dissenting votes. The Pioneer reported the value of buildings on Main Street was about $1 million ($30.2 million in today’s currency.) The federal government did not legalize occupation of the Black Hills until Feb. 3 the following year. 

Oct. 14, 1876 — Gardner sells his interest in the Pioneer to A.W. Merrick, who was the sole owner until 1878. For the next 20 years, the paper would have 15 different owners.

Dec. 2, 1876 — The Pioneer reports about the arrival of the telegraph in Deadwood. Prior to this, national news was often weeks, or months old, as it was re-printed from other newspapers that were brought into town. Deadwood residents celebrated the telegraph with a large bonfire and a grand ball at the Grand Central Hotel. 

Feb. 3, 1877 — An editorial complains about the high cost of producing the news in Deadwood, with telegraph charges nearly $75 a month “(the equivalent of $1,849 in today’s currency) and states that it needs increased support from the public. 

April 7, 1877 — Deadwood Daily Times publishes first edition as first daily newspaper in the Black Hills and the second daily in Dakota Territory.

Summer 1877 — W.A. Laughlin dies. 

June 2, 1877 — The last issue of the Black Hills Weekly Pioneer is published. 

June 17, 1877 — Volume Number One of the Black Hills Pioneer, as a daily newspaper, is published. (note: one source says May 15, 1877 is the date the Pioneer became a daily)

June 26, 1877 — The Black Hills Pioneer carries a brief notice that “Mark Twain was in the office yesterday.” 

1877 — Black Hills Daily Times starts in Deadwood, operated by Porter Warner. It merged with the Deadwood Pioneer in 1897 to become the Deadwood Pioneer Times.

Sept. 26, 1879 — Fire destroys 300 buildings in the original city of Deadwood, including the offices of the Black Hills Pioneer and the Deadwood Times. Presses, type, file copies, and early editions of Deadwood’s newspapers, including the Pioneer, from 1876-1879 lost in the fire, but enough issues were salvaged from various sources to produce a record from that historical time period. The Deadwood Times and the Black Hills Pioneer resumed printing shortly afterward, using borrowed equipment from Fort Meade.

1885 — After running the hand press for the Black Hills Pioneer, Willis H. Bonham stepped in to help relieve the Pioneer’s debts when he invested $190 into the paper. He became the publisher with the investment, and in 1897 he also bought the Daily Times. The May 13, 1897 edition read, “The individuality of the two separate paper sends and what good (if anything) they contain will be concentrated in the Daily Pioneer-Times, which in consolidated form will make its bow tomorrow morning.”

Jan. 30, 1889 — The Queen City Mail starts in Spearfish, founded by the Warren family. It was published from 1889 to 1984 as a weekly newspaper, according to the Library of Congress.

Aug. 15, 1894 — Lead Daily Call first appears. The paper was located across from the Miners and Merchants bank on the south side of Main St., west of Gold Street. The original printing press was previously stored in a shack across the street from the First National Bank building before it was purchased from A.W. Merrick. John W. Jones was the publisher and James B. Welch was an editor.

Jan. 1, 1915 — John A. Stanley purchases the Lead Daily Call, and would serve as the publisher and owner for the next 30 years. 

1929 — The Warren family sells the Queen City Mail to Art and Hazel Nisselius. 

1937 — Mike and Evelyn Heinbaugh assume ownership of the Queen City Mail. 

October 1945 — Fay Seaton, along with his sons Fred and Richard, purchase the Lead Daily Call. 

October 1945 — Printing plants for the Lead Daily Call and Deadwood Pioneer Times are combined under one roof, under a limited partnership known as Lead Publications. 

1946 — In July, the Seaton family purchases the Deadwood Pioneer-Times from Roy A. and Carl H. Sundstrom.

1974 — Allen and Alice Hermann purchase the Queen City Mail. 

November 1974 — Lead Daily Call and Deadwood Pioneer Times merge. 

1983 — Don Seaton oversees the start-up of the Queen City Star, a daily newspaper in Spearfish. 

1985 — The Seaton family purchases the weekly Queen City Mail in Spearfish from William C. Sniffin, Bill Kunerth, and other investors. They then merge the Spearfish Daily Star and Queen City Mail. The purchase also includes the Weekly Prospector shopper. 

1993 — The Lead Daily Call, Deadwood Pioneer Times, and the Queen City Mail merge into one daily publication — the Black Hills Pioneer. 

1996 — The printing plant is moved from Lead to Spearfish. 

1999 — Seaton Publishing Company purchases the Nation’s Center News weekly paper in Buffalo from Wally and Linda Stephens.

March 2010 — Letitia Lister is named the first female publisher of the Black Hills Pioneer. 

June 2026  — The Black Hills Pioneer celebrates it’s 150th anniversary of delivering the news to the residents of the Northern Black Hills.

title: Celebrating 150 years
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: A.W. Merrick, Publish of the first newspaper in Deadwood, SD.
_full_text:
A._W._Merrick,_publisher_of_the_first_newspaper_in_Deadwood,_South_Dakota.jpg
A.W. Merrick, Publish of the first newspaper in Deadwood, SD.  

DEADWOOD — Not all the Pioneers of Deadwood came searching for gold. 

Some worked knee deep in what was described as a slimy green, rainy swamp, as the rain pelted a humble hand press, and type was set in a half-finished cabin with a poor pole roof. The first edition of the Black Hills Pioneer was issued on Thursday, June 8, 1876, under some of the most difficult circumstances imaginable. But W.A. Laughlin and A.W. Merrick were just as focused and committed to bringing the news to the Black Hills, as the gold prospectors who toiled through the earth to find their riches. In fact, the Colorado newspapermen set up their presses in Deadwood before even giving a thought to their own shelter of a house. For them, delivering the news to the pioneers of Dakota Territory and the American people back east, was the richest mission of the land. Their fierce commitment to accurate and complete reporting would launch a legacy of dedication to informing the public, with publishers, editors, and reporters matching Laughlin and Merrick’s fervent and relentless pursuit of truth, documented with the permanence of paper and ink, for the next 150 years. 

“We issue today only a half sheet,” Merrick wrote on June 8, 1876, in the first edition of the Black Hills Pioneer. “Our regular issue will be just double the size of the present copy. But owing to the fact that we are working almost out of doors, with the elements apparently conspiring against us, it is impossible to fill the bill as we anticipated. Our material has been in Deadwood less than a week. Our house is not up. It has rained two days during the time, and we think everyone who knows anything about the mechanical work of a printing office will appreciate our condition and bear for the present with the very best it is possible to do. Everybody wants a paper. We proposed to give you one, and a good one, too … To all who see this paper, we wish to say that it is published under many difficulties and that it is not what we intend to make it. It is an enterprise that has not a parallel in the United States, and still we hope to overcome all the untoward circumstances that surround us. Our material to print this paper was transported in the depth of winter, almost 400 miles, and brought through and into a hostile Indian country, and in the first settlements made we have set up our presses and set the type of this number of our paper. 

“We came here not to try the gulches or leads for gold, but to give to those who have this work in hand the very latest news,” Merrick continued in his first editorial. “We shall say only what we know to be true and our readers, wherever they may be, may rest assured that nothing will be given the tinge of romance. We have come to stay and we shall devote our entire time to the paper and hope to make it acceptable to those who wish to learn what there is in the country.” 

 Black Hills Pioneer Deadwood Dakota Territory circa 1877.jpg
Pictured is the first permanent structure housing the Black Hills Pioneer. Pioneer file photo 

Laughlin, a shop foreman for The Farmer in Denver, and Merrick, a compositor for the Rocky Mountain News, set out on their mission to start the first newspaper in the Black Hills when they brought their Gordon Press and about $200 in paper, ink and other supplies from Denver to Custer — the site of the first gold rush. But they weren’t in the southern Black Hills long before reports of rich gold deposits in Deadwood started a stampede of prospectors. By that time, the elements of the move had begun to take their toll on Laughlin, who suffered greatly from tuberculosis. The two partners had also exhausted their financial resources to start the paper. Laughlin and Merrick estimated it would cost about $250 (more than $7,000 in modern currency) to move the operation to Deadwood. 

That’s when Capt. C.V. Gardner stepped in. A Civil War veteran who had been a newspaperman in Iowa before following the gold rush to Custer, traveled north ahead of Laughlin and Merrick, where he raised money to bring the paper to Deadwood. 

Shortly after arriving in Deadwood, Laughlin, whose health was rapidly declining, sold his interest in the newspaper to Gardner, who would work alongside Merrick to write articles and report about the events of the time for the first few months, until he sold his interest to Merrick in October 1876. In August 1876, 20-year old gold prospector Dick Hughes joined the Pioneer team as the first reporter in the Black Hills. Annie Tallent, who was reportedly the first white woman in the Black Hills, described Hughes as “the most finished writer that ever wrote a paragraph for a Black Hills paper.” 

From prospecting claims, shootings, stage robberies, and Indian raids, to notable stagecoach arrivals, theater performances, and new businesses, there was plenty to keep the original Pioneer crew busy. The newspaper published every Saturday, until June 17, 1877, when Merrick proudly announced the creation of the Black Hills Daily Pioneer. Shortly after its creation, on June 26, 1877, there is a brief mention about Mark Twain’s visit to the Pioneer offices. Twain was a national newspaper columnist at the time. 

Billed as the new “El Dorado” by many publications of the time, Deadwood was rarely short on news to publish. But occasionally, during slow periods of news, Merrick issued a plea to his readers. 

 press men photo.jpg
Early Black Hills Pioneer pressmen are pictured at their work stations. Pioneer file photo 

“The wheels of justice will get rusty if someone does not raise a fuss of some kind soon,” Merrick wrote in an early edition. “For there has not been an important arrest made in the gulch for some time. Will someone please raise the devil a little and give the officers and reporters a chance.” 

Shortly after the Pioneer’s initial publication, the Cheyenne Leader’s Aug. 17, 1876 edition described the Black Hills paper as, “spicy, prompt in the publication of news, and chuck full of business.” By then, the Pioneer had set up shop in a two-story building, sandwiched between two houses of “vice,” as the Cheyenne Leader reported. 

The original Pioneer staff’s dedication paid off, as Tallent reported that the Pioneer was an immediate financial success. Several accounts tell of Merrick and pressman Joe Kubler, weighing gold dust from paper sales until late into the night. Subscription rates and their modern-day value were $5 ($150) for one year, $3 ($88) for six months, $2 ($60) for three months, and 25 cents ($7) a day. For those who wished to mail the Pioneer to their loved ones at home, the price was 50 cents a day. 

One Pioneer house ad read, “You haven’t time to write? Then send a copy of The Pioneer back each week, and that will do until you get time.”  

News of the Pioneer’s success quickly spread across the country, and it wasn’t long before other newspapers across the country encouraged Americans to purchase the Black Hills Pioneer, to get news about Dakota Territory and the gold rush. Shortly after setting up shop, the Pioneer brokered a deal with a Chicago printing firm, to print between 150,000 to 200,000 copies a week, for distribution in that area and in railway stations throughout the northeastern United States, making the Pioneer then one of the largest circulating weeklies west of the Missouri River. 

But Pioneer readers didn’t just want to see the local news. More than anything, they craved national news from their homeland, and news about how elected officials in Washington D.C. were handling the gold rush and other affairs of the country. On Dec. 2, 1876, Merrick wrote about the arrival of the telegraph. Prior to that time, national news would take months to reach the people of Deadwood, since it was re-printed from other newspapers that were brought into town. But the telegraph was operated at great expense. In an editorial published Feb. 3, 1877, Merrick complains about the high cost of producing the news in Deadwood, with telegraph charges that climbed from an initial $20 a month, to nearly $75 per month (nearly $1,849 in modern currency.) 

On June 17, 1877 Merrick successfully published the first edition of the Black Hills Daily Pioneer. During this same period of booming business, there were a multitude of separate daily and weekly newspapers that started in the northern Black Hills. The Black Hills Daily Pioneer was not to be confused with the Black Hills Daily Times, sometimes referred to as the Deadwood Times, which was published by Porter Warner. The Black Hills Daily Pioneer, under the leadership of Willis H. Bonham, merged with the Black Hills Daily Times in May 1897, to become the Deadwood Pioneer Times. 

Porter Warner wrote, “Thursday, May 13th ends the existence of the Pioneer and Times as individual or separate newspapers and the wedding of the two papers will take place during the early hours of this day, ceremonies to be strictly private. The individuality of the two separate papers ends and what of good (if anything) they contained will be concentrated into the Daily Pioneer-Times.” 

No record of these earliest newspapers would likely exist at all if it was not for the generosity of Pioneer readers. On Sept. 26, 1879, fire ravaged Main Street Deadwood. The fire destroyed 300 buildings, including the offices of the Black Hills Pioneer and the Deadwood times, where printing presses, type, file copies, and early editions from 1876-1879 were lost. Enough issues were salvaged from various sources to produce a record from that time period, and very shortly after the fire, the newspapers resumed printing.  

Lead Daily Call

Before selling to the Pioneer, early newspaper accounts from 1894 reveal an animosity between Deadwood Times publisher Warner and the labor unions. Out of the ashes of that animosity, which resulted in labor unions boycotting the Times, as well as any Deadwood businesses that advertised with the newspaper, arose The Evening Call, which would soon become the Lead Daily Call. With offices located on the south side of Main Street, directly across from the Miners and Merchants bank, the paper was printed on an old press that A.W. Merrick had stored in a shack in Lead. 

J.W. Jones, the first publisher for the long-running Lead newspaper, wrote in his first editorial that the paper was published exclusively for the Lead people, would remain politically neutral, and that “In Call, united labor will have a firm friend, and if at any time we can be of any service to the great army of labor we are theirs to command.” 

At least six publishers would carry on that legacy of the Lead Daily Call, until John A. Stanley purchased the newspaper in 1915. Stanley would remain the owner and publisher of the paper until immediately after World War II, when journalist Fred Seaton, of Hastings, Neb., purchased the newspaper in October 1945, incorporating it under Seaton Publishing Co. of Lead. At that time, the printing plants of the Lead Daily Call and the Deadwood Pioneer Times (Black Hills Pioneer) were combined under one roof in Lead, where they would be published separately until 1974, when the two papers merged. 

In addition to his dedication to journalism, Seaton also had a passion for politics. While operating his newspapers, Seaton also served in the Dwight D. Eisenhower administration in several high-ranking capacities, including as Assistant Secretary of Defense, a distinction from which he was awarded the Medal of Freedom. Seaton also served as the Secretary of the Interior, and was instrumental in bringing Alaska and Hawaii into statehood as the 49th and 50th states as well as the passing of the Alaska Statehood Act. 

The Feb. 25, 1959 Lead Daily Call features a front page article entitled “Seaton Urges Quick Action on 50th State.” 

“Secretary of the Interior Fred A. Seaton today urged quick congressional action to make Hawaii the 50th state to show Asia this country ‘practices what we preach about democracy.’” 

Fred Seaton remained a prominent figure in politics, including campaign finance reform in Nebraska, until his death in January of 1974. At that time his son, Donald Seaton, was the publisher of the Hastings Tribune, and then also assumed the role of president of the Seaton Publishing Company media group.

Queen City Mail 

In nearby Spearfish the newspaper business was largely kept to a small, but notable weekly. The Warren family started the Queen City Mail on Jan. 30, 1889, and they operated it nearly continuously until 1929. 

In 1974 Allen and Alice Hermann purchased the Queen City Mail, and operated it full time, along with advertising manager Bruce Hermann until October 1982, when William C. Sniffin’s corporation, Mountain America Communications, which also included Bill Kunerth and Bruce Hermann, bought the newspaper. Kunerth became co-publisher, and Hermann retained his position as advertising manager. 

In 1983, Seaton Publishing Co. started the Spearfish Daily Star, and in October 1985, Sniffin announced that the Queen City Mail and Spearfish Daily Star would merge. Sniffin said the merger “was no doubt, inevitable.” With the sale, Seaton Publishing Co. also purchased the right to publish the Weekly Prospector shopper’s guide. 

With the sale, the paper became the Daily Queen City Mail. 

Under one roof

In 1993 Donald Seaton merged the Lead Daily Call, the Deadwood-Pioneer Times, and the Queen City Mail into one newspaper, and the Black Hills Pioneer name was resurrected to tie all the publications together. Three years later, in 1996, Seaton moved the Pioneer offices from Lead to the current location in Spearfish as a cost savings measure. 

There, the newspaper’s circulation grew exponentially, and the coverage area grew to include the entire Northern Black Hills area. The newspaper currently serves faithful readers in Spearfish, Lead, Deadwood, Whitewood, Sturgis, Belle Fourche, Nisland, and Newell. The Black Hills Pioneer is also the parent company for the Nation’s Center News, which serves the Buffalo and Harding County area. 

In 2010, after nearly 20 years of management at the Pioneer, Scott and Letitia Lister were given the opportunity to became co-owners of the Pioneer, by Don and Nancy Seaton. Letitia fulfills the role of publisher, and Scott serves as the operations manager. The responsibility of a hometown newspaper is one the Listers take seriously, and they are committed to maintaining the Northern Hills’ primary information source by employing people who live in the very areas they cover. Donald Seaton died in 2018. His wife Nancy Seaton and son Andrew Seaton, along with the Listers have pledged to continue the Seaton publishing journalism legacy to this day and beyond.

Even as Merrick proclaimed his dedication to delivering the news to the prospectors and pioneers of Deadwood, with humble beginnings 150 years ago, the Black Hills Pioneer remains a leader in community journalism, fielding one of the largest newsrooms in South Dakota — proving its continued commitment to this area.

“Don Seaton was known for saying it is paramount to find the right people, put them in charge and get out of their way,” Letitia said. “It sounds simple, but it is true. The communities we serve are not cookie-cutter in their needs. There are basic tenants of our role as the local newspaper that are the same wherever you go, but each community has its own personality and focus. We are the permanent record keepers of our time and place in history. From editorial and opinion columns, to covering government, politics, and social events, and even the advertising all come together to form a snapshot of our society at that particular point in time. 

“The Black Hills Pioneer continues to be a critical part of the community,” she continued. “We have had a long history of stalwart support by our subscribers. It is our goal, on a daily basis, to keep earning that trust and endorsement.”

title: Deadwood duplex damaged in fire
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Firefighters battle a fire on Denver Avenue Thursday afternoon.
_full_text:
Deadwood duplex damaged in fire
Firefighters battle a fire on Denver Avenue Thursday afternoon.  

DEADWOOD — A Thursday afternoon fire caused heavy damage to a Deadwood duplex.

Shortly after 2:30 p.m., Deadwood Fire & Rescue was paged to an address on Denver Avenue for a reported structure fire. 

Deadwood Fire Chief Joel Ellis was the first on scene finding heavy smoke conditions with significant flames on the back side of the home. 

An incident command was established and mutual aid requested from both Lead and Spearfish fire departments. 

An initial searche of both levels of the duplex found no victims. Crews entered both the upper and lower level units of the duplex and attacked the fire from both levels. 

Ellis told the Pioneer Friday that the main floor of the upper level had a “tremendous amount of heat” which ultimately prompted one firefighter to be evaluated for heat exposure on scene. He was released at the scene.

The fire was knocked down in 10-14 minutes, he said.

During the fire fight, firefighters ventilated the structure with positive pressure fans and were able to extinguish the fire. 

Crews had the fire extinguished and began leaving the scene about 2 hours after the call.

There were no injuries to firefighters, occupants, or animals. 

Ellis said the challenge was getting a good firefighter presence.

The initial turnout from Lead and Deadwood was good, and the first firetrucks were able to easily get into position, but with Denver Avenue being extremely narrow additional fire trucks were staged farther away, near the Deadwood library, forcing “firefighters with very heavy gear” to walk to the scene. 

Ellis said the fire appeared to have started on the upper level of the duplex, but declined to comment about the location of ignition or the cause as the incident is under investigation by the state fire marshal’s office. 

He added that the upper level had significant damage and the lower level had smoke and water damage. Both residents were displaced and are being assisted by the American Red Cross and family. 

Agencies assisting were the Lead, Spearfish, and Whitewood fire departments, Whitewood Fire Department Auxiliary, Deadwood Police Department, Monument Health Ambulance, Lawrence County Emergency Management, Black Hills Energy, Montana Dakota Utilities, Deadwood Public Works, and the American Red Cross.
