title: Future construction of US Highway 85 met with mixed emotions
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: A public comment section was held at the Homestake Adams Research and Cultural Center in Deadwood Thursday, where attendees voiced mixed concerns about local impact and applauded efforts to improve safety along the highway. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
Future construction of US Highway 85 met with mixed emotions
A public comment section was held at the Homestake Adams Research and Cultural Center in Deadwood Thursday, where attendees voiced mixed concerns about local impact and applauded efforts to improve safety along the highway. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

DEADWOOD — The winding, scenic drive on US Highway 85 from Spearfish Canyon to the Wyoming border could face reconstruction, including constructing additional shoulders, new grading, and rerouting curves, as early as 2030. 

Administrators from the South Dakota Department of Transportation (DOT) gathered at the Homestake Adams Research and Cultural Center in Deadwood Thursday to discuss current designs and construction plans to a mixed crowd. Opposing crowds voiced concerns about impacts to private land, forest service land, and wildlife, while their counterparts applauded the efforts to improve safety and reduce vehicle crashes on the road. 

Intentions

Todd Seaman, Rapid City region engineer for the DOT, said that the state’s current design has minimal impact on the 9 miles of road from Sunny Hill Trailhead to Cheyenne Crossing. 

“That section of road is going to look just about like it does today,” said Seaman. “There really won’t be much change to that road. We’re going to add a little bit of shoulder, 4 feet on one side and 2 feet of shoulder on the other side.”

Seaman said constructing additional shoulder could be accomplished by moving the road into the existing ditch on the north side of the road. He said that retaining walls will be constructed along the creek adjacent to the road. 

“So, we won’t be blowing up the canyon,” said Seaman. “I’ve got a few emails and I’ve heard we’re blowing up the canyon and ruining Spearfish Creek. That’s not what’s planned, that’s not the intent.”

Mike Behm, director of the division of planning and engineering for the DOT, said that the remaining 7 miles of the road will include grading and reconfiguring of curves with the intention or improving safety and reducing crashes on the road. 

“Crashes have a significant impact, not only on the person involved in the crash but the families that are tied to it,” said Behm. “And when those crashes occur, they not only impact that individual and the family, but they also impact our overall society. We have a goal to drive our crashes, our fatal crashes, towards zero on a downward trend.”

Behm said that the goal of reducing crashes across the state of South Dakota means that the state has to acknowledge what they can and can’t control. 

“We do not have control over the behavior of the person behind the wheel. That’s the individual that has that control,” said Behm. “What we do have control over are safety features that we can consider when building or resurfacing highways. Our number one fatal crash in South Dakota is a single vehicle running off the roadway. So, as we look at what we can do to help get people home safe every day, we want to ensure that we’re given some recovery area. That’s where the shoulder comes into play.”

Behm said that drivers “consistent expectations” contribute to driver safety, meaning a consistent speed limit across great distances without sudden changes. 

“We have a responsibility as an agency to try to do the things we can to get people home safe every day,” said Behm. “That’s our goal.”

Timeline

Michael Carlson, Rapid City area engineer for the DOT, said that the section of highway was selected for redesign in 2018 following a study of roads in the Black Hills that were showing signs of distress and needs for constant maintenance. The study revealed 5 roads in the Northern Hills and 5 in the Southern Hills that qualified for further inspection. Carlson said that the projects chosen from that study went live on the DOT website in 2021, after which the state began receiving public comments. The first public meeting was held in 2023. 

“We actually put the plans together, we had to boards put everything together, just a couple of days before it was presented,” said Carlson. “We looked at those and we go, ‘We don’t want to build this, either.’ And (the public) told us the same thing: don’t build this, you’re doing too much of an impact on the Black Hills. And we agreed.”

Carlson said after the initial design received so much public pushback, the design was reconfigured, and a stakeholder group was created. 

A presented list of stakeholders consulted in further designs of the road included Adjacent landowners, Black Hills Badland Tourism Association, Cheyenne Crossing, Eagle Cliff Ski Association, Flandreau Santee Sioux Tribe, Lawrence County Commission, Lawrence County Highway Department, Lawrence County Sheriff’s Department, Lead Chamber of Commerce, Lead-Deadwood School District, Lead Volunteer Fire Department, local residents, Rochford Volunteer Fire Department, South Dakota Department of Tourism, South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks, South Dakota Highway Patrol, South Dakota Trucking Association, Spearfish Canyon Fire Department, Spearfish Canyon Fly Fisherman, Spearfish Canyon Owner’s Association, Thunderhead Episcopal Church Camp, Trailshead Lodge, United States Forest Service, and the Wickiup Cabins. 

Carlson said that the stakeholders had their first meeting in September 2025. The design of the road was reconfigured and presented to stakeholders in November 2025. The design that was presented to the public on Thursday was presented to stakeholders in April this year. 

“Going forward, later on this year we’ll have a landowner meeting,” said Carlson. “In 2027 we’ll do a final design inspection based on comments tonight and landowner metings. We’ll tweak everything one more time and then we’ll acquire right of ways in tose areas where we need right of way in 2028. Hopefully in 2030, 2031 is when we plan to be constructing this road.”

During construction, Carlson said the goal is to keep the road as open as possible during the short construction window available to them from April to September. Carlson said he hopes to have construction paused during Sturgis Rally.

Safety data

Mark Malone, road design supervisor for the DOT, said the primary goal in reconstructing the section of highway is improving driver experience and safety by reducing fatal crashes on the road. When looking at a road that could potentially be redesigned, Malone said the first thing the DOT looks at is a map of all crashes reported on the road.

“We’re looking for clusters. We do get randoms, maybe a deer hit, but when you find clusters it’s definitely an area where you want to take a closer look at the crash reports,” said Malone. “That’s where you got to take a look at what’s going on, maybe even talk to inviduals. What’s the problem here and why are we coming up with numerous crashes on the same report?”

Malone said crash maps of the section of that highway show cluster of crash reports along the curves of the highway.

A jagged line graph shown during the presentation showed drastic changes in speeds reported at different locations along the highway.

“When you get these jagged lines, that’s possibly locations where crashes are,” said Malone. “This is something that we really look into, and we pay good, strong hard attention to.”

A history of crash reports from 2020 to 2024 along the stretch of highway showed 77 reported crashes. Of those crashes, one was fatal, 46 vehicles left the road, 28 involved motorcycles, 31 resulted in injuries, 21 involved animals being struck, and 4 vehicles came to rest in the creek adjacent to the road. 

“Some people will say, well, it’s wintertime. You’ve got snow causing (the accidents),” said Malone. “Well, guess what? Two-thirds were during the day when roads were dry, and more of the crashes occurred during the summer months than during the winter months, even though we’ve got sharp curves, and we’ve got a lot of snow.”

Malone said that similar data, collected near Cheyenne Crossing befor and after reconstruction, shows 13 crashes, one fatal, 4 with injuries, from 2014 to 2018. After reconstruction, the same stretch of road has had only 2 crashes, one resulting in injury.

“This is what we’re trying to do,” said Malone. “We see a curve that has a crash cluster and we’re seeing if we can soften that curve a little bit and reduce the crash numbers.”

Design 

In public meetings held in 2023, Malone said the public overwhelmingly voiced concerns about impacts to adjacent land and properties when constructing additional shoulder. He said that feedback has resulted in as many as 10 different iterations of the design to the road.

Malone said the DOT has received comments requesting that the road be patched or resurfaced without redesigning the road. 

“If we’re patching the road every year, that means that since the last time it was totally redone, it’s lived it’s useful life,” said Malone. “So, we’ve got to replace that. When we’re doing that, we take a look at the crashes, and then we look into adding shoulders and improving clear zones.”

Malone said that a clear zone is an area that allows a driver to recover after leaving the roadway without flipping their vehicle into a ditch or running into a hillside or tree.

“Less than half the people that had a crash stayed on the road,” said Malone. “So, if you do run off the road, wouldn’t it be nice to have a slope that you might be able to drive and then come back and get back on the road safely without having to flip or turn sideways? We’re not trying to drastically improve and put 200-feet of clear zone. We’re trying to be responsible with the amount of impacts. In the area of the creek, we’re trying to leave it almost the same as what it is, just add a little bit of width.”

Malone said shoulders cannot be built into the hillsides because of sandy, colluvial soils.

“You start getting into that hillside and it keeps coming down,” said Malone. So we’re trying to avoid impacts to that while avoiding impacts to the creek everywhere possible.”

From the Wyoming border to the Sunny Meadows Trailhead, Malone said designs include dropping the speed limit to 55 miles per hour, increasing lane width to 12 feet, and building a 6-foot shoulder with 30 feet of clear zones. He said that certain areas of the road will require the shoulder being reduced to 4 and 2 feet. Guardrails will be installed where shoulders cannot be constructed.

Passing O’Neill Pass, Malone said the highway reaches the steepest grades of the entire highway, reaching 6.5% grade in places.

“This is an area where we said straightening out the road at times is not the anticipated goal,” said Malone. “Here, we’re looking at having a bit more of a goal of straightening it out. When we get those steep grades, if we can make that part of the highway straight, that’s a little bit safer, rather than putting curves in. If it gets icy, or it gets snowy, we can hopefully keep people on the roadways.”

Malone said changes to the road are dependent upon federal environmental requirements, including National Environmental Policy Act studies that will happen before any construction occurs. 

“We’re looking at clean water acts and threatened endangered species,” said Malone. “We take a look at all those things. The environmental process is something that starts right at the beginning of the scoping of the project and the planning all the way through the construction.”

Public comment

Attendees at the meeting voiced concerns about the impact construction of the road through new land on wildlife and scenic value. Other attendees said that safety concerns of the road should be considered part of the “inherent risk” of driving. One comment claimed that human behavior, including driving under the influence of alcohol, is more to blame for fatal crashes than road conditions. 

Malone said that staff at the DOT look at every crash in the state every year. 

“One thing we like to say is even though someone is drunk, we would like to keep them alive, too. Even if they’re making a stupid decision,” said Malone. “Crashes are impactful to a lot of people, and I don’t ever want that to be my family, and I don’t want it to be anybody in this room, either.”

Attendees asked how they can be certain that once the design for the road is approved that change orders won’t drastically change improved design, furthering impact to the land.

Behm said that the South Dakota DOT has the lowest number of change orders in the nation on large projects. 

“There’s a safety component, there’s an efficiency component, and there’s the context of the corridor that we’re in,” said Behm. “So, who watches over us? The Federal Highway Administration watches over us. Whatever the final design is, that’s what’s going to happen. That’s what we’re going to give the contractor to get underway. There could be complications that are a little bit different to plans because all of a sudden, we didn’t know X, Y, or Z was going to be there. That’s going to happen. I wish we were at 0% (of change orders), but last I saw we were at 1.78% statewide, which happens to be the lowest in the upper Midwest and actually one of the lowest in the nation. Our team helps put the designs together to make sure that we’re pretty darn close to being where we need to be with things.”

Behm said a NEPA study will be conducted on the entire scope of the project after a preferred alternative and clearances are completed. He said the NEPA study will include observing endangered species habitats and migration patterns as well as considering impacts to nearby flora, fauna, and water sources.

Proponents of the audience applauded DOT staff for their efforts to improve overall safety for every driver on the road, tourists and landowners alike.

title: Sturgis to re-count special election ballots
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Sturgis to re-count special election ballots
Courtesy photo 

STURGIS — A recount of the Sturgis special election results next week will not change the outcome of the election, but it will ensure that all records are accurate, city officials say. 

On Thursday, the Sturgis City Council met in special session to canvass the special election results and swear in newly elected Mayor Rod Bradley and Ward 1 Councilman Terry Keszler. However, after reviewing the poll books, city council members reported some discrepancies in the numbers for Wards 1, 3, and 4. The numbers for Ward 2 were accurate, Mayor Pro Tempore Tony Dargatz said. 

The ballots for the Sturgis special municipal election June 2 were hand counted.

“We feel the numbers aren’t enough to change the results of the election, but we want to actually have for sure numbers,” Dargatz said.

Election results will remain unofficial until the recount and canvass are completed. 

The council approved a motion to reconvene on Monday, June 8 with a recount and re-canvass.  State law requires the canvass to occur within 7 days after the election. State law also allows each candidate to have 2 representatives present during the recount. 

The special election on June 2 included 3 candidates for mayor and 2 candidates for the Ward 1 city council seat. 

Sturgis was not scheduled to have a municipal election this year. However, the special election became necessary after former Mayor Kevin Forrester submitted his resignation March 23 and passed away shortly afterward from pancreatic cancer. Then Councilman Nick Jones resigned March 25. 

According to state law, the deadline for submitting municipal candidates for the ballot was March 26. And people interested in running for election must have at least a month to circulate petitions, Therefore, the city had to schedule the special election, with separate ballots, to fill the seats, and voters cast 2 separate ballots in 2 separate rooms for the Republican primary and the non-political mayoral and council seats.

title: Cost of Colo. Blvd. sewer upsize increases by $25,331
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: According to Spearfish Public Works, the pictured cracks in road panels and an abandoned manhole need patching on Colorado Boulevard. The city council voted to approve a change order June 1 to pay for the work to move forward. Courtesy graphic
_full_text:
Cost of Colo. Blvd. sewer upsize increases by $25,331
According to Spearfish Public Works, the pictured cracks in road panels and an abandoned manhole need patching on Colorado Boulevard. The city council voted to approve a change order June 1 to pay for the work to move forward. Courtesy graphic 

SPEARFISH — As the city’s sewer main on Colorado Boulevard is upsized from pipe that is 12-inches or fewer in diameter to pipe that is 21-inches in diameter, the project costs have increased by $25,531.60. 

East of 27th Street crews had to remove and lower existing water line, to provide at least 18 inches of separation between the water main and the new sewer main. That increased the project cost by more than $2,000. 

The city also identified a need to remove and replace two concrete panels on Colorado Boulevard. An abandoned manhole on Colorado Boulevard near 27th Street had its casting removed — leaving a hole. 

The project plans already called for a small patch on Colorado Boulevard, but the hole straddles 2 panels that are both cracked. In order to comply with Department of Transportation standards, both panels need to replace. That removal and replacement operation alone is expected to increase the project’s cost by $17,007. 

Both changes bring up the price tag for the entire sanitary sewer upsize project to $2,520,765 and will add 9 additional workdays to the project timeline.

title: Lion Rock promotes a transparent  future for mining in Lawrence County
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Lion Rock Resources, LLC, was recently granted the transfer of a conditional use permit governing a small-scale quarry near the Wyoming border of Lawrence County. The company has been performing exploratory drilling and surface excavations. Pioneer photo by Travis Potter
_full_text:
Lion Rock hits local milestone with transfer of Lawrence County conditional use permit.JPG
Lion Rock Resources, LLC, was recently granted the transfer of a conditional use permit governing a small-scale quarry near the Wyoming border of Lawrence County. The company has been performing exploratory drilling and surface excavations. Pioneer photo by Travis Potter 

Editor’s Note: This is the second of 2 stories about exploratory drilling and excavations happening at a small-scale quarry in Lawrence County.

DEADWOOD — Lion Rock Resources, LLC, a Canadian mining company headquartered in Vancouver, said their main goal in South Dakota is to operate transparently, create jobs, and help America provide essential minerals for the benefit of the American economy.

Lion Rock, a Canadian mining company headquartered in Vancouver, British Colombia, was recently granted the transfer of a small-scale quarry near the Wyoming border of Lawrence County from Duco Mining, LLC at the June 9 county commission meeting. The mining site, located approximately 17 miles southwest of Spearfish, has been largely inactive for more than a decade. At this stage, Lion Rock claims to be in the process of determining if the site is stable enough for further developments as they search for tantalum, tin, lithium, and gold. 

Under the current conditions of the conditional use permit, Lion Rock can only perform surface excavations of 10 acres at a time on the 342-acre property. While crushing, drilling, and blasting are allowed under the permit, processing of material to extract valuable ore would require an amendment to the existing permit and approval of a mining license from South Dakota Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources (DANR). Amending a conditional use permit requires that county commissioners, acting as the board of adjustment, hold a public hearing process and approve the amendment or create a new conditional use permit.

After the ruling of the South Dakota Supreme Court on the Save Centennial Valley vs. Lawrence County case on May 7, a decision made by the board of adjustment is not subject to a referendum by a public vote. Decisions made by the board of adjustment must be appealed to a higher court. 

Search for critical metals

 Nav Headshot.jpg
Nav Dhaliwal, Executive chair, Lion Rock Resources 

Nav Dhaliwal, executive chair of Lion Rock, said that the company has completed phase one of their exploratory drilling and has begun bulk surface extractions to determine the levels of critical metals on the property. 

“How we’re looking at the critical metal side of things and the demand that’s within America right now with these advancements of technology and AI, and everything else that’s going on, if you’re looking at commodity specifics, you can see that there are certain metals that are now appearing on the critical metals list from the government,” said Dhaliwal. “With todays technology, we believe that we can advance this project to become part of a system that is required right now within America.”

The United States Geological Survey published a list of 60 minerals deemed critical for the United States economy on Nov. 6, 2025. Lithium, tantalum, and tin were present on the list. 

“During our drill campaign and after sending it to get analyzed, the assay lab did come back that we have elevated levels of tantalum, which we kind of knew from history (of the area), but we wanted to see it for ourselves,” said Dhaliwal. “It’s giving a strong indication there. But are the grades strong enough, is the system strong enough, to continue to advance this project? We’re at that critical stage where we got to do a lot more exploratory kind of work to ensure this is a viable project, that there is still strength in the system.”

Dhaliwal was present at the county commission meeting when the transfer of the condtional use permit was granted. During the meeting, Dhaliwal and Lion Rock CEO Dale Ginn vocalized that they were searching primarily for the three critical metals on site. However, the Lion Rock website advertises the “Volney Project” in the Black Hills as being primarily a search for gold in the Black Hills. 

“These hills are known for gold,” Dhaliwal told the Pioneer. “When we were doing our field exploration, there’s lots of pegmatite. That’s very apparent. But we found that there’s a fault running through the property. That encouraged us to wait a second. So, we as a company put the efforts in to see if it’s a feasible direction to go. Just with our surface sampling and just with the historical mines just south of us, there was a strong indication that there could be a strong gold system.”

Dhaliwal said exploratory drilling revealed a gold system of 500 meters by 400 meters at a depth of 200 meters. He said Lion Rock does not currently have enough information from exploratory drilling and surface excavations to know if they will apply to DANR for a license to mine gold at this time. 

Plugging violations

According to a violations report attached to Lion Rock Resources’ exploratory drilling permit under DANR, Lion Rock administrators and geologists were repeatedly made aware of South Dakota standards of plugging exploratory drill holes under Administrative Rules of South Dakota (ARSD) 74:11:08 and South Dakota Codified Law (SDCL) 45-6C-30. According to that report, DANR staff Roberta Hudson visited the quarry Oct. 8, 2025, and visited with Dhaliwal, Ginn, geologist Karly Oliver, chief geologist Jeff Hrncir, David Jones of Corexplore Drilling Services, and Jana Morehouse of Vantage Point Solutions. In the violation report, Hudson claims to have made Dhaliwal and other representatives of the project aware of the plugging process and the environmental importance of plugging all exploratory drilling holes correctly. Hudson allegedly made representatives aware of the requirement to allow the opportunity for DANR staff to be present to monitor plugging activites again during this meeting, a requirement of all DANR exploratory drilling permits in South Dakota.

According to ARSD and state law, all exploratory drill holes must be filled from total destination, the bottom depth of the hole, to the top. The state requires that the top 8 feet of all holes be pugged with either cement or bentonite chips and a 5-foot pad of cement grout be placed above the plug. 

According to the violation report, Lion Rock was found in violation for failing to maintain proper correspondence, plugging holes without supervision, and plugging holes incorrectly. 

Lion Rock contested that attempts to maintain the required correspondence were made. In screenshots of correspondence attached to the violations report, 11 of the 16 messages between Hrncir and DANR staff Phil Nesbitt notifying Nesbitt of driledl holes meeting total depth and plugging activities beginning were sent after 5 p.m., on weekends, or over Thanksgiving break between Nov. 23 and 28.

According to the violations report, after DANR officials were made aware of the improperly plugged holes, DANR staff were dispatched to the mine site in February. Jeff Klenner, environmental scientist at DANR, required that all 15 exploratory drill holes be redrilled and properly plugged. Of the 15 holes, Lion Rock claimed to only be able to locate 5. According to the violation report, 10 holes remain missing and improperly plugged. 

Lion Rock did not contest the violation and agreed to pay a $21,000 settlement. By agreeing to settle, the violation was considered closed. Lawrence County Commissioner Eric Jennings said the commission was unaware of the violation when the conditional use permit was granted. 

Dhaliwal said each exploratory hole had a “layer of data” providing the company, geologists, and drilling companies with exact locations of the holes. Dhaliwal said holes were drilled by Corexplore. He said that every hole was searched for but 10 remained improperly filled because of “contractor error.”

“Before you start drilling, within your drill bit you are putting casing down to kind of give it structure in the hole so the drill bit can follow through. The contractor pulled the casings a little too early,” said Dhaliwal. “Knowing where the GPS location was, going back to those locations, you’re working with a 2-inch diameter. We kept trying to dig to get it, but it would fall in on itself. So, as you keep digging, it’s really hard to identify where that hole was. It wasn’t for lack of trying.”

Dhaliwal said that drilling exploratory holes costs Lion Rock an average of $400-600 per meter, depending on factors like availability of crews and equipment. 

“It does get very costly,” said Dhaliwal. “When you drill, it’s a learning process. Well, let’s just slow it down for a second, put boots on the ground. Let’s hire people and educate people.”

 Dhaliwal said that he anticipates that in the event that a campaign for a second exploratory drilling phase is successful, he believes Lion Rock will continue to contract with Corexplore.

Standing on the shoulders of historic giants

Dhaliwal said the history of mining in Lawrence County has allowed Lion Rock to make informed decisions about explorations and future estimations of the property. However, he said, there’s still a lot for the company to learn. 

“We need to walk the road, not run. Let’s walk, get all the information, get legitimate information, and look at reality here,” he said. “Working alongside with the state officials and officials from the county level, let’s make sure that everybody’s looking at a common mindset. Let’s provide information that’s factual.”

Lion Rock is expected to provide an annual report to Lawrence County commissioners in approximately 4 months. Dhaliwal said Lion Rock is working to gather as much information as possible about the potential future of mining activities and the geological makeup of the property.

Dhaliwal said the future of mining in Lawrence County for Lion Rock is still unclear. However, he said Lion Rock strives to maintain operations that are transparent, factual, and beneficial not just for them, but for the communities affected by their work. Those efforts, he said, include pristine reclamation efforts and open communications with government officials, while creating jobs. 

“Lion Rock wants to be a part of the fabric, and we understand that there’s a lot of sensitivity on this, as there should be. We are a very fully transparent company,” he said. “We’re looking at this in the long-term, if we could sew this piece of fabric into the fabric of America and raise that flag for South Dakota to say that it’s a part of a solution that’s required from the critical metal side of things, the advancement of gold at one point in time in the future as well, that it’s all staying within America — that’s a goal for us.”

title: Sturgis to cast wide net for companies to handle Rally sponsorships
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Sturgis city officials want potential Rally sponsorship companies to show what they can do.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

STURGIS — Sturgis city officials want potential Rally sponsorship companies to show what they can do. 

After months of considering the best options for third-party companies that would handle soliciting and managing contracts with sponsors for the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, members of the Sturgis City Council opted Monday to draft a request for proposals for both national and local companies. 

“Would it make sense to have an RFP drafted and take a wide enough path with the RFP where it doesn’t matter where somebody’s from? I believe we can get a lot of information out of the proposals to help us decide what best fits and where we’re headed with this,” said newly-elected Mayor Rod Bradley. “I think it would get clumsy if we try to incorporate a nonprofit into the RFP. But I think drafting an RFP and excluding the nonprofits doesn’t take that option away from us in the future.” 

Sturgis City Attorney Eric Davis previously presented three options for third-party sponsorship companies, including contracting with a national firm with existing relationships with major corporations; a local firm with ties to the community, familiarity with the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally and the city of Sturgis, and a physical presence in the area; and a nonprofit firm that the city would form specifically to handle sponsorship contracts. 

City officials agreed that soliciting proposals from both national and local companies would give the city information about potential services that exist, in order to make an informed decision. The request for proposals will not include nonprofits, since council members agreed that forming a nonprofit to handle sponsorships would require an entirely different process. 

In an effort to maintain transparency with Rally contracts while protecting proprietary information with Rally sponsors, the council voted in March to change the way it handles Rally sponsorships. Instead of soliciting and maintain those contracts in-house, the city will contract with a third-party company that will sell Rally sponsorships on the city’s behalf. Under the arrangement, the city’s contract with the third-party company — including city assets that will be made available and an overall amount of money that is paid in Rally sponsorships, non specific to an individual company — will be transparent, while the specific contracts with Rally sponsors, including how much each company pays to sponsor the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, will remain confidential. 

The move was initiated by former mayor Kevin Forrester, as the result of overall efforts to increase transparency in city government. Originally, Forrester sought to make all sponsorship contracts open to the public. However, some companies claimed information such as how much they pay to the city of Sturgis, could be proprietary, since different amounts are paid to sponsor different rallies around the country. As a result of opening the contracts, several major sponsors pulled out of deals with the city. 

The city of Sturgis gains between $800,000 and $1 million or more every year from sponsorship deals. That funding goes into the city’s general fund, and is used for regular operations throughout the year.

title: Proposed Black Hills uranium mine gets approval to start building infrastructure  on portion of site
byline: By Meghan O’Brien SouthDakotaSearchlight.com
description: The site of the proposed Dewey-Burdock uranium mine in Fall River County, South Dakota. Courtesy of U.S. Bureau of Land Management
_full_text:
Proposed Black Hills uranium mine gets approval to start building infrastructure  on portion of site
The site of the proposed Dewey-Burdock uranium mine in Fall River County, South Dakota. Courtesy of U.S. Bureau of Land Management 

BLACK HILLS — A controversial uranium mining proposal on the edge of the Black Hills received approval from the federal Bureau of Land Management to begin constructing “ancillary infrastructure,” according to a press release from the agency Monday, although the project lacks permission to begin mining.

Uranium is a metallic, radioactive element used as fuel in nuclear weapons and power plants. The Dewey-Burdock project near Edgemont, in southwest South Dakota, has been in the proposal stage for nearly two decades and still requires additional permits. The Trump administration picked the project last year for an expedited permitting process known as FAST-41.

Monday’s approval from the Bureau of Land Management gives Powertech, a subsidiary of Texas-based enCore Energy, the green light to build infrastructure including access roads, four groundwater monitoring wells and overhead power lines on the section of the project site that’s managed by the bureau, according to the press release.

About 240 acres, roughly a third of a square mile, of the project site are on public lands that the bureau oversees. The entire project area is 10,580 acres, or about 16.5 square miles.

“The Dewey-Burdock Project still requires several additional approvals from other federal and state agencies, including a license renewal currently under review by the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission,” said a bureau spokesperson.

EnCore Energy did not immediately provide a response to South Dakota Searchlight questions.

Opposition to project

In April, the bureau published a draft of its environmental assessment and opened it for public comment until May 15. In that monthlong span, the agency received 764 submissions, according to Monday’s press release, “including comments related to groundwater, cultural resources, tribal concerns, environmental justice, and compliance with federal laws.”

The bureau published its final environmental assessment Monday, as well as a finding of no significant impact. If the project receives all other necessary permits, the bureau estimates a start date for the project within the next five years. Infrastructure will remain at the site for 20 years after the implementation of the project, which the environmental assessment describes as the mine’s lifespan.

The environmental assessment is vague about groundwater pollution concerns and impacts on cultural resources in the area such as Native American historic sites, according to Lilias Jarding, a project opponent and executive director of the Black Hills Clean Water Alliance.

“The process was rushed. It’s only been a few weeks between the end of the comment period and this decision coming out in its final form,” Jarding said. “The Bureau of Land Management was being, what I would consider, irresponsible in this situation.”

EnCore Energy plans to use a method known as “in-situ” mining to extract uranium from underground. As opposed to open pits and tunnels, the method involves drilling wells to inject a water-based solution underground, dissolve uranium and pump it to the surface. The water would be pulled from local aquifers and then treated and pumped back underground after being used for mining, causing opponents to fear pollution of local groundwater sources.

“I don’t think the company understands the depth of public opinion against uranium projects in the Black Hills,” Jarding said.

The Black Hills Clean Water Alliance and other project opponents have also been working against another, nearby uranium exploratory drilling project in the southern Black Hills, proposed by Clean Nuclear Energy Corp. and its Canada-based parent company Nexus Uranium.

The decision on Clean Nuclear Energy’s exploration permit is in the hands of the state Board of Minerals and Environment. A hearing on the permit application was paused last month after a project opponent filed a federal lawsuit against the board, the state Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources and Clean Nuclear Energy Corp.

The lawsuit remains pending, and no date has been scheduled to resume the permit hearing.

title: Minor injuries after Lead man backs over steep embankment
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: LEAD — Lead firefighters assisted Monday when a driver backed over a steep embankment and was injured when he tried to exit the vehicle.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

LEAD — Lead firefighters assisted Monday when a driver backed over a steep embankment and was injured when he tried to exit the vehicle. 

Lead Volunteer Fire Chief Nathan Allen said the call came at 4:23 p.m. to respond to the intersection of Gushurst and 11th Street. The area is a vacant lot, where city crews dump snow off the edge of a steep embankment, and in the summer it is sometimes used as a parking lot. Allen said the man backed up too far, and his pickup went over a steep embankment. When the man tried to exit his pickup, reports say he fell about 8 feet down a steep slope and was unable to get out. 

Members of the Lead Volunteer Fire Department and EMS personnel used a stokes basket to bring the man to safety. Allen said he was treated for minor injuries on the scene and released. The vehicle, he said, sustained only minor damage. 

The Lead Police Department and Monument Health Northern Hills Ambulance assisted at the scene.

title: ‘Defining what these devices  are is going to be key’
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Lt. Samantha Lee, left, discusses enforcement options for the small-motorized bikes, or e-dirtbikes, that have become popular with young people in the community while former city attorney Ashley McDonald looks on.  McDonald is helping the city to determine what legal frameworks might be needed to address the issue. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
E-Bikes 2.JPG
Lt. Samantha Lee, left, discusses enforcement options for the small-motorized bikes, or e-dirtbikes, that have become popular with young people in the community while former city attorney Ashley McDonald looks on.  McDonald is helping the city to determine what legal frameworks might be needed to address the issue. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — On her way to the city council meeting Monday, Spearfish resident and local non-profit founder Kelly Harnett said she was nearly hit by a young person on a two-wheeled motorized vehicle.

“I just want to thank you guys for looking into this. On my way here, I had one of those e-motorbikes with no pedal assist, run through a yield sign and almost hit me or I almost hit them,” Harnett said.

It’s incidents like these that drove elected officials to ask for an ordinance to be drafted to curtail the problem with e-dirtbikes and similar vehicles on sidewalks and rec paths in the city.

Just last week, a 5-year-old girl was hit by a two-wheeled motorized vehicle on the rec path.

“About a week ago, my family entered the bike path on Evans Lane and encountered a group of children on electric dirt bikes,” Heath Eggleston told the council Monday. “As customary, we reminded our children to stay to the right. As one of the children rode past my wife, he stated, ‘Watch this.’ Within a split second, he appeared to swerve to the left and struck my 5-year-old daughter with his dirt bike. An argument ensued and culminated with one of the children daring me to call 911. As I dialed, the children fled while yelling obscenities at my wife and children.”

Eggleston said he felt it was important to share his story with the council, because the purpose of the rec path is to provide a safe haven for walkers and cyclists to travel with distance between them and motorized vehicles. He said he felt the issue had been insufficiently addressed.

In 2024, Eggleston pointed out, the parks, recreation, and forestry advisory board heard citizen complaints about e-bikes. With the emergence and increased prominence of even more powerful vehicles, Eggleston said the issue had worsened since then.

 ebikes 1.JPG
They’ve been called many names: e-motorcycles, mini-bikes, e-dirtbikes. Whatever they’re called, the motorized vehicles likely don’t qualify as e-bikes, but they are generating public concern. Citizens have reported conflicts between the vehicle’s young users and pedestrians on roadways, sidewalks, and the rec path. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson  

“Since those discussions, I have been unable to locate any public education campaign, trail user guide, updated signage, or safety outreach addressing concerns, other than 2 Facebook posts by the city police department. One from May 27th with clear signage stating no motorized vehicles and a repost from the Sturgis Police Department 5 days ago,” Eggleston said. “For the past 2 years I’ve watched more and more high-powered electric turbines use our recreation trail system. I hope common sense and courtesy could prevail.”

Mayor John Senden apologized to Eggleston for the incident involving his daughter, and said as a father himself, he understands the impulse to protect children.

“We know that the behaviors that are out there have caused some issues. There is no question about that. We respect that and we’ve had some good emails in with suggestions — whether its producing signage, trying to educate, various things like that,” Mayor John Senden said. “As a council and elected officials, we do recognize that something needs to be done to try and address the situation, but what is the right avenue? How can it be addressed by law enforcement, and how can we try to be as consistent as possible?”

Drafting an ordinance, defining a problem

Former city attorney Ashley McDonald is assisting the city in drafting an ordinance to address concerns from the public.

She noted the issue is made more complicated by a lack of clear definitions. E-bikes are defined in state law. They are bicycles or tricycles with saddles and operable pedals, with 750-watt-or-fewer electric motors.

“The difficulty with this topic in general is that no one really knows what these devices are,” McDonald said. “Some of them meet the legal definition of an e-bike. They have operable pedals, but can operate without the use of the pedals, without human propulsion. Sometimes they meet the definition of a motorized foot scooter, and that is a bit of a misnomer. When I think of a foot scooter, I think of something that you stand on. The way that it is defined includes something that you sit on.”

Many of the bikes encountered by the public don’t have pedals at all. They’ve been called e-dirtbikes, but some public commenters said they don’t believe that is an appropriate label either.

“We need to stop calling them e-dirt bikes altogether. They are vehicles. I have a dirt bike, I love dirt biking. I have a pretty powerful one. I have gone through all the legal junk to make it street legal,” Spearfish resident Aaron Ploog said. “I would never dare take that on a sidewalk or a rec path, because it is a vehicle.”

McDonald said an effective ordinance must define the vehicles and the areas where they would be prohibited.

“There is that specific statute that was discussed a lot during the study session that applies to the sidewalk area. That is not the rec path,” McDonald said, referring to South Dakota Codified Law 32-26-21.1.

That law states, “No person may drive any vehicle other than a bicycle, motorized foot scooter, or an electric personal assistive device upon a sidewalk or sidewalk area.” 

The law does offer a provision allowing city and municipal government to restrict bike, foot scooter, or electric personal assistive devices on sidewalks.

“The sidewalk does tie into our rec path system, so there are sections that are both sidewalk and rec path. If these prohibited devices are on that section, it is enforceable, because it meets the definition of a sidewalk,” McDonald said of the state law.

A need for enforcement

Councilman Scott Hourigan said an ordinance could clear up confusion and give existing rules “teeth.”

Two local educators spoke up to say they believe law enforcement action is needed.

“If we educate them, they’re not going to listen,” said Cassie Myers. “These are the same kids after hitting a kid are back out 4 hours later.”

She said the issues citizens are observing aren’t just a matter of bad etiquette. The kids involved are breaking the law by driving recklessly and failing to follow the rules of the road.

“As a teacher that knows, give them the price tag small before the price tag gets big. They need to learn now,” Myers said.

Spearfish Police Lt. Samantha Lee said that in cases where police aren’t present to see an incident take place, they need parent permission to contact the juveniles involved.

“It seems from what we are gathering it is more behavior. That comes down to parents and handling that behavior at home,” Lee said.

She also told the council, right now police are limited on enforcement options if vehicles are piloted off of city streets.

“Per the state’s attorney’s office, anything on the street we can charge per ordinance. State law does not cover any of these bikes, so they have to be in the street,” Lee said.

Spearfish resident Ryan Wordeman said he’s not convinced the council needs an ordinance before it can take action.

“If the council feels more driven toward an ordinance, which I don’t think is necessary (because) I believed it can be enforced today with what we have and the definition of rec path, versus sidewalk,” Wordeman said. “Rec paths tie into sidewalks. For it to be considered anything other than a sidewalk is not relevant in my opinion. That is a legal question for you guys to answer.”

Wordeman asked that a drafted ordinance be prepared as soon as possible.

“I would ask you to do a first reading in July and a second reading at the second meeting,” Wordeman said.

McDonald said that timeline might be overly restrictive, but she would try to work expeditiously on the effort.

Belle Fourche City Attorney Kellen Willert, who attended part of Monday’s meeting, offered McDonald’s office support in the drafting process.

title: Matthews Opera House to host art walk  at local businesses
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer

The Matthew’s Opera House gallery shut down in May. Pioneer file photo 

 Art Walk 2.JPG
Tia Erins hangs art in the Matthew’s Opera House gallery, before it shut down. Pioneer file photo 

SPEARFISH — The Matthews Opera House will host an art walk, consisting of displays at various local businesses and a reception at the Opera House from 4-6 p.m. Saturday.

Displays will be held at Common Grounds Coffee Shop, Henry’s Bookstore, the Art Nest, Spearfish Clay Works, Grace Balloch Memorial Library, Leones’ Creamery, and Matthew’s Opera House. The displays will be up until the end of next week, and are open to the public. 

“I’m super excited to have the opportunity to continue bringing visual arts to Spearfish,” Tia Erin, visual arts coordinator for the Opera House, said. 

The walk features about 60 artworks by artists including Addie Houser, Allusion Denman, Annalina Scalise, Anthony Kosobud, Bonnie Halsey-Dutton, students from the Canyon Hills Center, Carol Lee Hilgemann, Diane Myers, Donnelle Culver, Dyan Nagel, Kata Thompson, Lilian McCraw, Lynn Birk, Olivia Jacobs, Sandy Newman, Shaelynn Houser, Sharlon Mays, and Erin. 

Erin said that the Opera House hopes to host more art walks in the future. 

“This was a trial run to see how it would go … it’s been super well received and all the locations have been really receptive to the idea and super excited about the opportunity to do it again,” Erin said. 

Amber Wilde, director of Grace Balloch Memorial Library, said that when she heard that the Opera House was shutting down its gallery, and was looking for places to display art, she offered the library as a venue.

“We’re always looking for ways to bring different entities in the community together and bring people into the library, “ Wilde said. “I think it’ll be a great opportunity for people that maybe don’t get to the library that often to come in…and also to experience art as a group.”

The art walk comes a month after the Opera House was forced to shut down their own art gallery, citing an inability to maintain the space.

title: Spearfish ‘Founding Fathers’ slated for celebration at Rose Hill Cemetery Walk
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Rose Hill Cemetery Walk returns to Spearfish Monday and Tuesday. Volunteer reenactors will help tell the stories of some of the city’s founders, and other interesting cemetery residents. Photo courtesy Julie Walkins
_full_text:
IMG_5892.JPEG
The Rose Hill Cemetery Walk returns to Spearfish Monday and Tuesday. Volunteer reenactors will help tell the stories of some of the city’s founders, and other interesting cemetery residents. Photo courtesy Julie Walkins 

Spearfish — America’s 250th anniversary has many a history buff contemplating the lives and legacies of the nation’s founding fathers, but one group of dedicated volunteers has been working hard since January to piece together the life stories of Spearfish’s founders.

Julie Walkins is one of those volunteers.

“There is a team of 4 of us that worked on finding people to present, researching them and crafting their stories,” Walkins said. “We meet at the library, and we look through newspapers and obituaries and try to find people.”

Each person’s story is adapted into a 5-minute script, so that a reenactor in period-costume can help tell their story before a live audience. With 15 reenactors in total, the cemetery walk is roughly an hour and a half long — a chance for citizens to enjoy the serenity of the cemetery while they explore the personal histories of some of its residents.

In order to be featured in the cemetery walk, a “Rose Hill resident,” as Walkins calls them, must have passed on more than 15 years ago.

This year, stories focus on town founders.

“Their lives aren’t what you would expect,” Walkins said. She described a kind of American Odysseus, who became a “founding father of Spearfish.”

“There is one guy who came out to find gold in California, decided he wanted to go back to New York, took a ship because he didn’t want to go back across the land,” Walkins said.”There was no Panama Canal then, so the ship went down around South America. It usually took 4-8 months to get home that way. He took 7 years, because he stopped and looked for gold other places in the world.”

The cemetery walk was created by John Steven Wiley and took place annually in the fall for several years. Walkins got involved first as a volunteer parker (a job that is still critical, as parkers help attendees find a safe, respectful, and convenient place to park before the show.)

During the COVID-19 pandemic, the event “rested” for a while, Walkins said. But it didn’t rest in peace for long.

The Matthews Opera House took the event over after 2020.

“That is how I got involved more, because I am on the board at the opera house and on the theater committee. We are now having fun doing it,” Walkins said. “We pick the middle of June, because those are the longest days of the year. Mother Nature can give us the light.”

It returned in part because of volunteers’ passion for history, and for preserving and sharing the stories of everyday people who called Spearfish home.

“I love how the presenters have said it made them feel so connected to their characters,” Walkins said. “One of the nicest things is, afterwards, when people linger and say, ‘Oh, that was my great-great-grandfather’ or ‘we knew this family,’ and share their story. It helps people remember their own past.”

 IMG_1010.JPEG
The Rose Hill Cemetery Walk returns to Spearfish Monday and Tuesday. Volunteer reenactors will help tell the stories of some of the city’s founders, and other interesting cemetery residents. Photo courtesy Julie Walkins 

The cemetery walk is free for spectators. Walkins encourages attendees to dress appropriately for the weather, and to bring a chair (there aren’t many places for the living to rest among the stones.)

“Each stop has 5 different presentations, so it is about a half hour at each stop,” Walkins said.

Performances are slated for 6:30 p.m. on Monday and Tuesday. Free-will donations in support of the Matthews Opera House will be collected both evenings.

title: Eastside acres plat exception to  “streamline” development process
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Directly west of Sky Ridge on Colorado Boulevard, East Side Acres is under construction. On Monday the city council voted to grant the developers on the project an exception to make submission of a final plat “more streamlined” according to city staff. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Eastside Acres 1.JPG
Directly west of Sky Ridge on Colorado Boulevard, East Side Acres is under construction. On Monday the city council voted to grant the developers on the project an exception to make submission of a final plat “more streamlined” according to city staff. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — Ordinarily, public improvements, including paved streets, waterlines, curb, gutter, sidewalk, and sewer lines must be completed, dedicated to the city, and accepted formally before a subdivision’s final plat can be recorded.

 Eastside Acres 2.JPG
In September, 2025, investors in East Side Acres held an information session on site, west of Sky Ridge on Colorado Boulevard. Pictured is an early map of the development concept where East Side Acres is being built. Pioneer photos by Sierra Ferguson 

 Eastside acres 3.JPG

Per a unanimous Monday vote from the Spearfish City Council, that will not be the case for Eastside Acres.

However, city staff from the community development department said the exception would help streamline the development process.   

“They are not requesting to go vertical (with construction) yet. This is simply a request to go ahead and final plat phase one (of the project),” Assistant Planning Director Jaymia Ecker said. “They are already quite far along in that process.”

Ecker said grading, road grading and seeding, for example, has already begun.

To secure an exception to the ordinance, the developers of the housing development had to submit an itemized invoice for the outstanding improvements. The cost of those improvements was about $714,760.

The developer agreed to provide a letter of credit for 120% of those costs ($857,711.31) before city staff releases a final plat. That financial assurance was part of the reason staff recommended council make an exception for East Side Acres.

“They brought me the letter of credit today, so it is in hand,” Ecker said. “This would enable, if something did go wrong, the city could collect that letter of credit, step in and complete those improvements.”

East Side Acres, upon completion, will be a 40-acre development along Colorado Boulevard, directly west of Sky Ridge. Planners have mapped out space for townhomes, apartments, park, restaurant, and retail space, and a “town square” — envisioning a kind of 5-minute, walkable community between I-90 Exits 14 and 17.

A “5-minute community” as described by East Side Acres investors Nancy Rushford and Lorri Riley, would be a mixed-use development where residents could access dining, retail, and healthcare-related businesses without traveling more than 5 minutes from their home. 

At least some of the development, in Riley and Rushford’s plan, will be dedicated space for businesses that directly address community health, including a med-spa, imaging center, and medical center.

title: Three bats test positive for rabies in Wind Cave
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Three bats recently tested positive for rabies at Wind Cave National Park. Bats are important for healthy ecosystems and provide valuable insect pest control services. Typically, less than 1% of bats in nature have rabies, but it is a serious disease that is fatal in animals and humans without prompt medical care. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Three bats test positive for rabies in Wind Cave
Three bats recently tested positive for rabies at Wind Cave National Park. Bats are important for healthy ecosystems and provide valuable insect pest control services. Typically, less than 1% of bats in nature have rabies, but it is a serious disease that is fatal in animals and humans without prompt medical care. Courtesy photo 

HOT SPRINGS – Since May, Wind Cave National Park has identified 3 bats that tested positive for rabies. The first was found deceased near the park’s elevator building on May 5. The second, discovered near the Visitor Center’s entrance on May 28, was alive but unable to fly. 

The third bat was found deceased at the park’s campground. Fortunately, there have been no reported instances of visitors contacting these bats. Resource management staff with personal protective equipment collected the animals for testing. 

Rabies is a fatal, but preventable viral disease if prompt medical care is received following a potential exposure. Rabies in humans is contracted by exposure to a rabid animal, typically through a bite, scratch, or contact with saliva. Any direct contact with a bat, alive or dead, is considered a potential rabies exposure because bites and scratches from bats can be harder to detect. 

The park is working with South Dakota Department of Health and the National Park Service’s Office of Health and Safety and Wildlife Health Branch on this issue. This coordinated effort underscores the park’s commitment to public health and safety while keeping visitors informed and protected. The last rabies-positive bat discovered in the park was in 2019, which was an isolated case. 

If you believe you or your family members (including pets) had contact with a bat, please contact the South Dakota Department of Health at 1.800.592.1861, along with your medical provider.

title: USFS proposes first national policy for recreational climbing on public lands
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: WASHINGTON D.C. — The U.S. Forest Service announced Wednesday it plans to publish a proposed climbing directive in the federal register and initiate a 30-day public comment period. This proposal establishes the agency’s first national direction for managing recreational climbing opportunities on national forests an  d grasslands that will include guidance for the use and maintenance of fixed anchors and equipment.
_full_text:
US Forest Service Logo

WASHINGTON D.C. — The U.S. Forest Service announced Wednesday it plans to publish a proposed climbing directive in the federal register and initiate a 30-day public comment period. This proposal establishes the agency’s first national direction for managing recreational climbing opportunities on national forests an  d grasslands that will include guidance for the use and maintenance of fixed anchors and equipment. 

The updated proposal replaces a 2023 draft that was overtaken by new requirements in the Expanding Public Lands Outdoor Recreation Experiences (EXPLORE) Act, signed into law last year. 

The EXPLORE Act directs federal land management agencies to recognize recreational climbing — including certain fixed anchors — as an appropriate use in congressionally designated wilderness areas. 

“Recreational climbing continues to grow in popularity, with nearly 30 percent of all outdoor climbing occurring on National Forest System lands,” said U.S. Forest Service Chief Tom Schultz. “This proposed directive provides much-needed national policy for climbing activities and gives local decision makers the ability to work with partners, tribes, climbing organizations, and others to ensure visitors are having safe, responsible, and accessible outdoor experiences.” 

By law, the forest service must develop a climbing directive, consistent with the goals stated in President Donald Trump’s executive order that implements President Donald Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency deregulatory initiative. 

Nationally, it is estimated there are nearly 10.3 million climbers in the United States, of which approximately 2.3 million participated in sport or boulder climbing and approximately 2.4 million participated in traditional ice or mountaineering climbing, according to the Outdoor Industry Association’s 2022 report on outdoor participation trends.

SIOUX FALLS — Jesse Robert Buskol, 45, of Sioux Falls, was sentenced to four years and two months in federal prison, followed by three years of supervised release, and ordered to pay a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund for possession of a firearm by a prohibited person.

The sentencing took place on June 15, 2026. 

Buskol was indicted by a federal grand jury in October 2025. He pleaded guilty on March 16, 2026. 

On July 30, 2025, law enforcement conducted a parole search of Buskol’s home and found a semi- automatic pistol. Buskol was prohibited from possessing a firearm as a result of a prior felony conviction for First Degree Robbery. He was on supervised release for a prior conviction at the time of this offense. 

This case is part of “Operation Take Back America,” a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to repel curtail illegal immigration, achieve the total elimination of cartels and transnational criminal organizations (TCOs), and protect communities from the perpetrators of violent crime. 

Operation Take Back America streamlines efforts and resources from the Department’s Organized Crime Drug Enforcement Task Forces (OCDETFs) and Project Safe Neighborhood (PSN). Through PSN, the District of South Dakota seeks to bring together all levels of law enforcement and the communities they serve to reduce gun violence and make our neighborhoods safer for everyone.

title: South Carolina man sentenced in SD for attempted production of child pornography
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Courtesy photo

Gavel-01
Courtesy photo 

SIOUX FALLS — A 36-year-old Summerville, S.C., man convicted of Attempted Production of Child Pornography was sentenced 17.5 years in federal prison, five years of supervised release, and a special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund in the amount of $100 on June 15. 

Upon release from federal prison, Robert DiOrio must register as a sex offender. 

DiOrio started a conversation on Reddit, a popular communication/posting website, with a person he believed was a 14-year-old girl. The conversation turned sexual, and he asked the 14-year-old girl to meet up for a sexual encounter. DiOrio arrived at the meeting location. Unbeknowst to him, DiOrio had been communicating with an undercover law enforcement officer. He was was arrested by law enforcement. 

DiOrio was indicted by a federal grand jury in August of 2024. He pleaded guilty on March 23, 2026. 

This case was investigated by Homeland Security Investigations, the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force (ICAC), South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation, Sioux Falls Police Department, Watertown Police Department, Tea Police Department, Rapid City Police Department, Minnehaha County Sheriff’s Office, Lincoln County Sheriff’s Office, and South Dakota Highway Patrol. Assistant U.S. Attorney Elizabeth E. Ebert-Webb prosecuted the case. 

This case was brought as part of an undercover operation designed to identify individuals who are seeking to have sex with minors. 

The case was also brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat child sexual exploitation and abuse. Project Safe Child was launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. 

Led by the U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the DOJ’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children, as well as identify and rescue victims.

title: Gunslingers, grooves,  and gold panning
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Wild Bill Days is set to return to Deadwood this weekend, bringing historical reenactments, cultural experiences, and retail therapy to historic Main Street. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Gunslingers, grooves,  and gold panning
Wild Bill Days is set to return to Deadwood this weekend, bringing historical reenactments, cultural experiences, and retail therapy to historic Main Street. Pioneer file photo 

DEADWOOD — Wild Bill Days will make its triumphant return to Deadwood Main Street this weekend, bringing back old favorites and new delights to celebrate the life and times of one of Deadwood’s most famous gunslingers.

Jesse Allen, events coordinator at the Deadwood Chamber of Commerce, said returning events include the vendors market on Main Street featuring more than 50 vendors, free live music, and historical reenactments from the Deadwood Alive! troop of historical reenactors. In place of last year’s children’s activity center, Allen said Wild Bill Camp will be set up in the middle of Main Street featuring historical reenactments and Old West cultural experiences.  

“We’re going to have a teepee with a gentleman talking about Native American culture and we’ll also have an Old West blacksmith on hand that will be doing demonstrations and talking about the history of blacksmithing in the area and how they helped the miners in Deadwood,” said Allen. “We’ll also have a wagon display, so that’s a great photo op with the stagecoach and another wagon from Deadwood History.”

Allen said Deadwood Alive! will be performing all of their usual programming and shootouts along Main Street and is expected to bring out new performances in the spirit of Wild Bill Days. 

Live music is set to begin on Main Street on Friday at 1p.m., with Sarah Carper taking the stage. Tyler Bills is set to follow at 2 p.m. Music at Outlaw Square begins at 6:30p.m. with local darling Jessica Loobey. Headliner Aaron Watson is set to begin at 8 p.m. 

Allen said doors open at 5 p.m. at Outlaw Square on both Friday and Saturday.

Saturday brings another full day of activities, beginning at 10 a.m. with the downtown art festival, gold panning, and continued historical reenactments and cultural experiences.

Ja’net Eastman will kick off the live music on the Main Street stage at 1 p.m., followed by Katie Fee at 2 p.m. and Lonely Rangers at 3 p.m. Johnny Hastings, winner of the 2025 Wild West Songwriter Festival, will get started on the stage at Outlaw Square at 6:30 p.m., with headliner Brandon Jones set to begin at 8 p.m.

Festivities will continue Sunday with lots of opportunities to celebrate dad. Allen said fathers will have free admission at the Adam’s Museum, Days of ’76 Museum, and the Broken Boot Gold Mine. 

A guided hike on the Fuller Brothers Memorial Trail is set to begin at 10 a.m. Allen said crews from the Deadwood Trails Coalition will be at the trailhead at the Broken Boot Gold Mine from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. with maps and information. Hikers are welcome to join the guided hike or set out on their own.

The annual Wild Bill Days car auction will take place Sunday at the Deadwood Mountain Grand. 

Open container will be permitted Friday and Saturday from noon to 10 p.m.

title: New oversight
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: The conditional use permit for a small-scale mining operation southwest of Spearfish was successfully transferred to Lion Rock Resources. The company will be required to submit an annual report of all operations in approximately 4 months. Pioneer photo by Travis Potter
_full_text:
DJI_20260615182230_0041_D.JPG
The conditional use permit for a small-scale mining operation southwest of Spearfish was successfully transferred to Lion Rock Resources. The company will be required to submit an annual report of all operations in approximately 4 months. Pioneer photo by Travis Potter 

Editor’s note: This is the first of 2 stories about exploratory  drilling and excavations happening at a small scale quarry in Lawrence County. To read Lion Rock’s response, read the Thursday edition of the Black Hills Pioneer.

DEADWOOD — Lawrence County Commissioners approved the transfer of a conditional use permit at the June 9 commission meeting for a small-scale quarry operation near the Wyoming border from Duco Mining, LLC., to Lion Rock Resources, LLC., a Canadian mining company headquartered in Vancouver, British Colombia. 

The mine site, previously owned by Duco, Benchmark Enterprises, and Cody Schad, is located approximately 17 miles southwest of Spearfish off of Tinton Road near the Wyoming border. 

The mine site is not at Iron Creek Lake, but further south.

Records from the South Dakota Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources (DANR) show that Lion Rock has been performing exploratory drilling since November 2025 and advertises as a publicly traded company that intends to mine for gold and essential minerals in the Black Hills.

Existing conditions

Commissioner Eric Jennings said that the existing conditions of the conditional use permit limit Lion Rock to activities comparable to small scale gravel quarries, such as drilling, blasting, and crushing. Under the agreed upon conditions, originally issued to Tinton Enterprises, LTD., in 1995, Lion Rock cannot perform processing associated with gold, silver, and lithium mining — processing of ore using selenium, cyanide, or lime.

Since 1995, the conditions were amended once in April 2021, requiring the site comply with an invasive species plan with the county.

The permit has an established haul route, directing traffic of trucks along Boundary Gulch Road, through the northern loop of forest service road 222 (Beaver Creek Road) at the turn off to Iron Creek Lake, and north on Tinton Road to Spearfish. 

Jennings said the conditional use permit limits excavated material to 600 tons per month or a maximum of 25,000 tons per year. 

The permit does not allow for on-site processing of material, such as the process of leeching gold or silver from raw material.

The permit is subject to all noise, dust control, and reclamation mandates required both by the county and DANR.

R. Dale Ginn, president and CEO of Lion Rock, told commissioners that the intent of Lion Rock is to continue exploratory drilling and excavation on the mine site to determine levels of lithium, tantalum, and tin. Ginn said that if further testing of materials prove that profitable amounts of the materials are present at the mine site, an application for a new conditional use permit could be forthcoming. 

Annual report due before snow flies

Jennings said the county commission has agreed that an annual report of all activities at the mine site will be required of Lion Rock, in person, in approximately 4 months.

“Permit wise, they’re not able to go crazy the next 4 months because they’ll need a different permit to move on and do any processing,” he said. “Then we’ll have the plan of operation and then we can adjust the conditions.”

Jennings said he expects a report and annual inspection to be conducted before heavy snowfalls make it difficult for county officials to access the mine site.

According to Lion Rock’s website, the company has discovered gold in what it’s calling “The Volney Project” at the mine site and has applied for another exploratory drilling permit. 

Open exploration permit

Lion Rock Resources, working in collaboration with JT Beatty, current landowner of the private property, was approved for exploratory drilling and an exploratory notice of intent was approved on Aug. 25, 2025, by the DANR. Lion Rock was granted authority to drill as many as 624 holes to a maximum depth of 4,000 feet on an area of approximately 17 acres. 

Lion Rock agreed to fill all exploratory drilling holes according to Administrative Rules of South Dakota (ARSD) 74:11:08 and South Dakota Codified Law 45-6C-30. The laws require that all holes be filled bottom to top with materials approved by DANR. The state requires that the top 8 feet of all holes be plugged with either cement or bentonite chips and a 5-foot column of cement grout be placed above the plug. 

Restrictions were issued to Lion Rock before the company began exploratory drilling operations, wherein it was stated that Lion Rock was required to provide weekly schedules to DANR officials of all drilling activity. Communications were to include where holes would be drilled so that DANR officials could plan inspections and witness plugging activities.

A Van Ruth plug is considered a “bridge plug,” used for filling drill holes with cement. According to a violation report, the plug was not pre-approved by DANR.

 DJI_20260615182353_0046_D.JPG
Pioneer photo by Travis Potter 

Violation of plugging procedures

According to a violation report, filed by DANR March 13, 2026, DANR staff Roberta Hudson and Michael Evans met with Ginn and Lion Rock administrators, including geologist Karly Oliver and executive chair Nav Dhaliwal, to approve proposed drilling sites. While present, Hudson said she held conversations with Dhaliwal and Oliver, reiterating the importance of properly plugging all drill holes. 

Drilling at the mine site began on Nov. 3, 2025. According to the violation report, Jeff Hrncir, chief geologist for Lion Rock, began texting DANR staff Phil Nesbitt on Nov. 7, telling Nesbitt that drilling was underway. That following Sunday, Hrncir texted Nesbitt again with another update. Nesbitt claimed to not have received any correspondence until Monday, Nov. 10, and told Hrncir that DANR staff would be unavailable to witness plugging operations until Nov. 12.  The first of 15 drilling holes was plugged Nov. 9. In the violation reports, it is alleged that Hrncir informed Nesbitt Nov. 12 that the hole had reached total depth and was plugged.

Over the course of the next month, a total of 15 holes were allegedly drilled and plugged without supervision from DANR staff. 

According to the violation report, DANR staff alleged that Lion Rock was not submitting weekly updates about drilling activity as of Dec. 1.  According to information submitted by Lion Rock to DANR, drilling activities were completed Dec. 13. 

On Jan. 15, 2026, Oliver submitted an annual report to DANR, claiming that the 15 drill holes were filled with Van Ruth plugs and cemented. The Van Ruth plugs were not pre-approved by DANR, according to the violation report.

According to the violations report, Nesbitt reported to Hudson that he had only been informed of 5 of the 15 holes that were plugged. Hudson explained to Lion Rock staff that all 15 holes would need to be redrilled and properly plugged.

On Feb. 2, Jeff Klenner, environmental scientist at DANR, arrived at the mining site to supervise the replugging of the first drill hole. During the visit, Phil Hofer, crew lead for Corexplore Drilling Services of Ontario, explained to Hudson over a phone call that he wished to place a Van Ruth plug deeper than the 8-foot mark required by ARSD, requesting instead to place the plug where the bedrock could competently hold the plug. Hudson approved the placement but required that the remainder of the hole be plugged with cement. 

Over the course of the next 15 days, 5 improperly plugged holes were redrilled and filled according to ARSD regulations. However, Lion Rock was unable to locate the remaining 10 drill holes.

Ben Koisti, communications officer for DANR, said it is not typical for mine sites to be unable to locate exploratory drilling holes after plugging them. 

Lion Rock did not contest the violation of failing to properly plug the exploratory holes. Lion Rock asserted that they had attempted to maintain communications during drilling activities and attached screenshots of communications between Hrncir and Nesbitt. Lion Rock agreed to pay $21,000 in fees for the violations.

Open and shut case

Richard Williams, attorney at Gunderson, Palmer, Nelson and Ashmore, LLP., of Rapid City, was present at the commission meeting to represent Lion Rock. Williams told the Pioneer that Lion Rock chose to pay the fee without contesting the violation to stay in “good stead” with DANR. 

“I think there was some dispute as to what the communications were between DANR and Lion Rock, but ultimately Lion Rock did the best they could to find the holes,” said Williams. “They’re very small diameter holes, so once they get sort of covered up, they’re hard to find. They were plugged in a different way than DANR wanted them plugged, so they attempted plugging but didn’t get them plugged the way that DANR wanted. So, (Lion Rock) basically said, ‘Look, we don’t want to contest this, we want to be in good stead with DANR, and if that’s it we’ll pay the fine and close it out.’”

Jennings said that at the time that the conditional use permit was approved, county commissioners were unaware of the violation. 

“At that point, they had a clean bill of health (with DANR). When it comes to (conditional use permits) for the county, DANR doesn’t say anything to us because I guess in their minds it’s all settled and there’s no current violation,” said Jennings. Granted, it does cast suspicion onto the company, but as far as the jurisdiction, it’s not an open violation that we would have been aware of.”

Jennings said that in the scope of mining and gravel conditional use permits, the county can monitor haul road agreements, dust control, noise, and hours of operation. Mining issues like reclamation, disturbed area, and processing, he said, are monitored by DANR to reduce a duplication of services.

Jennings said that violations are monitored on a complaint basis, but he anticipates that the county will be closely watching Lion Rock’s activities in the next 4 months.

“We certainly want to do business with good companies. These issues kind of cast suspicion on them, so we’ll certainly keep an eye on them very closely and make sure that they’re following the conditions of the (conditional use permit) and be ready to pull it if there’s a violation,” Jennings said. “But, until there’s a violation or a complaint, there’s not much we can do.”
