title: Creekside nature area donation dies for lack of action
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: A proposed donation to resurface trails in the Creekside Nature Area, near Evans Park, will not move forward. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Nature area 2.JPG
A proposed donation to resurface trails in the Creekside Nature Area, near Evans Park, will not move forward. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — On Monday, the Spearfish City Council had the opportunity to reconsider a donation from Matt Polich of North Star Construction. Polich had volunteered to complete roughly $50,000-$100,000 worth of trail surfacing in the Creekside Nature Area, at no cost to the city.

His offer, originally brought to the council in May, was met with pushback from the public, who wanted the area to remain untouched.

 Nature Area 1.JPG
Creekside nature area will remain untouched. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

At the Spearfish City Council meeting on June 1, community members like Kelly Harnett voiced concerns about the effects on pollinator habitat. Leslie Kaitfors said she wanted one of the “last remaining nature areas” in the city limits to keep its current character. Bailey Sadowsky said the nature area as it is now offers the city important diversity in green space. Senior wellness advocate Cheryl Jasper asked that the surface remain uneven, specifically to challenge aging hikers.

Given that discussion, newly promoted Spearfish Parks and Recreation Director Rex McDonald and Mayor John Senden suggested that the council refer the topic back to the parks, recreation, and forestry advisory board.

“I know there are some strong sentiments to leave it just as is, but I think those sentiments continue in the majority; there is no one here to force this issue, but there have been some public comments that have been made that are a little more silent in nature, I guess, for us to consider this item,” Senden said. 

McDonald said Polich had offered to surface a sample area so that the public could see what the gravel, originally described as a road-base aggregate, similar to what’s used on the Mickelson Trail, would look like in practice.

“When he described it in more detail to us, he described an alluvial gravel surfacing. Which, alluvial gravel is basically what is over there along the creek right now. It is a more natural surfacing, but just to give everyone a little better idea of what it would look like and give everybody more details on the project, we’ve talked about doing that,” McDonald said. “In the meantime, we would work with Matt to get a demo somewhere on city property that is accessible to the general public.”

McDonald said the demo could be set up in the city campground near the bike skills parking lot, just south of the hydro plant, or in the staging area at Rose Hill Cemetery.

Councilman Scott Hourigan made a motion to refer the donation back to the advisory board for review, where it could make its way back to a study session and find a path back to the council for a vote.

That motion died for lack of a second — effectively ending any further consideration of Polich’s offer.

“Alright, so it’s put to rest. Through the whole process, I think, the Poliches had really good intentions on this. Their hearts were just to kind of see this go a little bit further, but we will communicate with them at this point that it has died,” Senden said.

title: Lead commission rejects latest  Handley funding request
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: A 24-hour access weight room is a popular component of the Handley Recreation Center. The Lead City Commission rejected a request to fund the Handley Center for the remainder of 2026. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Handley weight room.tif
A 24-hour access weight room is a popular component of the Handley Recreation Center. The Lead City Commission rejected a request to fund the Handley Center for the remainder of 2026. Pioneer file photo 

LEAD — The Lead City Commission will not consider restoring funding to the Handley Recreation Center under current circumstances. 

That’s the message commissioners sent on Monday when the Handley Recreation Center asked for $72,000 from the city’s recreation fund. When the commission finalized its 2026 budget, it split the $125,000 the city normally gives the Handley Recreation Center, providing funding for the first six months of the year, and setting aside about $72,000 into a recreation fund. The funding was intended to facilitate the city taking over the facility, but was not expressly earmarked for that purpose. 

Negotiations for the city to take over the Handley Center fell through when the Handley Center asked for deed restrictions that would require the city to operate the Handley Center as a recreation facility. Last month, the commission voted 3-2 to reject a resolution to take over the Handley Center, and deed restrictions were the primary reason. 

But on Monday, Commissioner Dory Hanson asked the city to consider giving the Handley Center $72,917 to fund the operation through the rest of the year. 

Hanson voted against last month’s resolution to take over the facility, but said the reason for her dissenting vote was to allow more time for a plan.

“(Former) Commissioner (Kayla) Klein did set up a very good plan,” Hanson said. “I did follow through with a couple of those things, and some of them were not agreed upon by the organizations that agreed to take on those programs. They were laid out on the plan, but they may not actually be able to work. So that’s why I voted last time not to take on that resolution.” 

Hanson said she is uncertain about the city taking over the Handley Center building. But she does not want to lose the programming that is in place, and she wants time to come up with a plan to preserve programs. 

“I think it is important to what our community has and why people choose to live here,” she said. “That is the gap I’m looking to fill.” 

Darla Auld, president of the Northern Hills Family Recreation Center board, which manages the Handley, said the funding would only be needed until the city can take over. 

“We’re still very much wanting the city to own it,” Auld said. 

Auld reported that the utilities at the building are approximately $50,000 a year, and staff costs about $95,000 a year. Insurance for the city would cost approximately $4,000 a year, compared to the nonprofit board’s price of $19,000, she said. 

Auld also read from the Handley board’s annual meeting minutes, expressing board concerns that they should retain responsibility for protecting confidential membership information, and that the Handley board would assist the city in establishing its own membership and payment processing systems. Additionally, she said the board wants to ensure all independent youth sport and recreation organizations that currently use the facility will still be served.

But Mayor Dustin Heupel said all of those logistical details had already been addressed. He also pointed out that the Handley board has yet to meet and discuss the proposal the city put forth early last month. 

Heupel said he is not interested in entertaining the idea of a city takeover, or funding the Handley Center, unless there is a change in operation or in how the Handley board views the city’s terms to take it over without deed restrictions. 

“We’ve been working on this for over a year,” Heupel said. “I don’t really know what would change in the next 6 months that would get us to a point where you guys are comfortable with the transition and the city taking it on. It’s up to the Handley board. You guys have to make that decision about whether you want that transfer to happen. The resolution can be revisited, expressing our intent to take it over. Until we have that resolution of intent, we are not going to use staff time or more taxpayer dollars to set that up.”  

Heupel questioned whether the Handley Center board has explored other funding sources for their operation. Auld said they have not, because they assumed the city would be taking over. Auld reported that the Handley Center is currently operating with funding it raised from its Mile High Basketball Tournament, but in order to make funding stretch the board has stopped trying to make extra payments on debt it incurred to pay for the all-purpose floor in the gym. 

Thomas said he is not in favor of providing more funding, unless something changes at the Handley. 

“We voted to shut this down,” Thomas said. “They knew the funding was going to end May 31. They had ample opportunity to go out for some funding outside the city taking it over. Until we see another resolution, changing the parameters of what it was prior, this money was not earmarked specifically, but it is still in the budget to be used. I’m not in favor of extending anything.” 

But residents expressed opposition to any more efforts to fund the Handley Center, and weariness about the ongoing discussion. They also repeated requests for a complete financial accounting of the Handley Center. 

“The city did their due diligence on this,” Rose Burns said. “The city has spent a tremendous amount of taxpayer money on salaries for the information that was provided.” 

Residents Pam Millard and Denise Parker both called for the Handley Center to submit their request in writing, and include a full financial accounting of how funds would be used. 

Following some further discussion, Hanson made a motion to table the Handley Center’s request, until the city received a full financial accounting, and for the Handley to submit a new request for funding through the end of the year. However, the motion was defeated on a 2-3 vote. Hanson and Commissioner Rob Carr voted in favor, while Heupel, Thomas, and Commissioner Al Rohrer voted against it.

BHPioneerLogo

ROCHFORD — The Black Hills National Forest will issue a temporary closure at Flag Mountain, including National Forest System Road 416, and the surrounding area for tribal ceremonial purposes. The closure will be in effect June 18-24.

The Rosebud Sioux Tribe requested the closure for traditional and cultural purposes. This closure reflects a government-to-government relationship and supports tribal sovereignty.  

The closure exempts those with a specific authorizing permit, any organized rescue or fire fighting force performing official duty, and any member of the Rosebud Tribe or those invited by the Rosebud Tribe to participate in ceremonial activities.

Closure notices, signs and flagging will be posted at access points to the area as well as a barricade on the closed road and will be removed at the end of the closure period.

description: SPEARFISH — Beginning on Monday, crews will begin work on the intersection improvements and lighting for the Interstate 90, Exit 10 reconstruction project. _full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

SPEARFISH — Beginning on Monday, crews will begin work on the intersection improvements and lighting for the Interstate 90, Exit 10 reconstruction project. During the first stage of construction, North Avenue will be reduced to one lane in each direction as crews remove old pavement and begin constructing the new “Loon” leftturn feature. The I90 on-ramps and off-ramps will remain open throughout the project. Later in the summer, when construction of the median begins, left turns from Old Highway 14 will be prohibited. 

This reconstruction project includes modifying the Exit 10 intersection and adding new traffic signals and luminaires. Drivers should plan for slower speeds and stay alert for changing traffic patterns throughout the work zone.

On Thursday, the SDDOT in collaboration with the project contractor, Tru-Form Construction, Inc., will hold an informational meeting to discuss the upcoming reconstruction project at Exit 10. The informational meeting is scheduled to begin at 5 p.m. in the large conference room at Hudson Hall, located at 222 W. Hudson St. in Spearfish.

The informational meeting is designed to share overall construction project details, traffic flow, and to answer questions for members of the public including impacted residents, local businesses, and emergency service personnel. The meeting will be informal, with opportunities for oneonone conversations with SDDOT engineering staff.

title: Spearfish High School SkillsUSA  members attend national  Leadership & Skills Conference
byline: By Shantayl Pochop Special to the Pioneer
description: SHS SkillsUSA members pictured from left to right, included senior Andrew Willhite, junior Burton Lehtola, and junior Chase Schenk. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
SKILLS USA 3.jpeg
SHS SkillsUSA members pictured from left to right, included senior Andrew Willhite, junior Burton Lehtola, and junior Chase Schenk. Courtesy photo 

SPEARFISH — Three Spearfish High School SkillsUSA members recently attended the 2026 SkillsUSA National Leadership & Skills Conference (NLSC) in Atlanta, Ga., June 1–6. Students Burton Lehtola, Chase Schenk, and Andrew Willhite represented Spearfish High School and South Dakota at the nation’s premier showcase of career and technical education students.

The opportunity to attend NLSC was earned through strong performances at the 2026 South Dakota SkillsUSA State Leadership & Skills Conference (SLSC). Students earning first-place qualified to compete at the national level, including Kiley Harmon in Nurse Assisting, Schenk in Diesel Equipment Technology, and Isabel Wendt in Welding Sculpture.

Students earning second and third place were offered the opportunity to attend NLSC as conference participants. Those students included Landon Redinger, who earned second place in Automotive Maintenance and Light Repair, and the Welding Fabrication team of Willhite, Lehtola, and Wendt, who earned third place.

 SKILLS USA 1.jpeg
Chase Schenk performing at station 6: Transmission Technology. He completed 14 stations total. Courtesy photo 

Throughout the week, students participated in leadership development activities, explored career opportunities, and networked with fellow students, educators, and industry professionals from across the country.

“NLSC is such an amazing opportunity for students,” said SkillsUSA advisor Shantayl Pochop. “It gives them the chance to network with their peers, educators, and industry partners from across the country. They are also exposed to opportunities they may not have known about before, including industry credentials, leadership development, and continuing education options.”

Schenk represented South Dakota in the Diesel Equipment Technology competition, competing against some of the nation’s top students in the field. He earned a 35th-place finish in the high school division.

Despite competing on the national stage, Schenk embraced the challenge.

“It was nerve-racking, but it was also fun knowing that I had a challenge ahead of me,” Schenk said.

 SKILLS USA 2.jpeg
The second group of diesel equipment technology students line up before competition officially starts. Courtesy photo 

Preparing for the competition required significant independent effort.

“One of the biggest challenges was figuring out what and how to study based on the technical standards,” Schenk said.

Pochop highlighted the significance of Schenk’s accomplishment.

“I am extremely proud of Chase. He competed against some of the top diesel technology students in the nation and did so without having received formal diesel technology training. The fact that he was willing to step into that environment, challenge himself, and compete at the national level takes a lot of courage and determination.”

When reflecting on the competition, Schenk said he was most proud of his effort. He also offered advice for future SkillsUSA competitors.

“Don’t get nervous and just have fun,” Schenk said.

Beyond the competition and conference sessions, students said the experience helped them build confidence and develop professional skills.

“The most valuable thing I gained from attending NLSC was the ability to talk to new people with more ease,” said Willhite. “I learned the importance of making connections with people and companies, even if they don’t seem directly related to what you want to do. You never know when those connections might be useful in the future.”

Lehtola said the conference reinforced the importance of networking and preparation.

“The most valuable thing I gained was learning how important it is to make connections and understanding what I need to know for competition next year,” Lehtola said. “One thing I’ll take with me is that the small details matter. Paying attention to detail can make a big difference.”

Students were also impressed by the scale of the event. Willhite said he was surprised by how large the conference facilities were and how much equipment was brought into the competition areas. He also noted how welcoming and friendly everyone was throughout the week. Lehtola said he was surprised by the sheer number of students and industry representatives attending the conference.

In addition to conference activities, students had the opportunity to experience several Atlanta attractions, including the Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta, a Major League Baseball game between the Atlanta Braves and Toronto Blue Jays, the World of Coca-Cola, and the Atlanta Botanical Garden. Willhite cited the Botanical Garden as his favorite experience because of its variety of plants and sculptures, while Lehtola enjoyed learning about the history of Coca-Cola at the World of Coca-Cola.

Pochop also praised the students for the way they represented Spearfish High School throughout the trip.

“This group was such a fun group to take. They were respectful, represented Spearfish High School well, and made the most of every opportunity available to them. I am incredibly proud of all three students.”

Looking ahead, the students are already setting goals for future competitions.

“These students have already expressed interest in competing again at the 2027 SkillsUSA State Leadership & Skills Conference with the goal of returning to NLSC,” said Pochop. “I’m excited to see the growth they achieve over the next year, especially as Andrew begins the Welding Technology program at Western Dakota Technical College.”

This experience was made possible through the support of Spearfish High School, families, and community partners who help provide students with opportunities to participate in SkillsUSA competitions and leadership development activities.

Participation in SkillsUSA competitions and conferences helps students develop technical, leadership, and employability skills while preparing them for future careers and educational opportunities.

title: Multiple chip seal projects scheduled  to begin on Hwy. 212
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Multiple chip seal projects scheduled  to begin on Hwy. 212
Courtesy photo 

BELLE FOURCHE — Today, crews from Asphalt Surface Technologies, a St. Cloud, Minn.-based company, are scheduled to begin chip-sealing sections of Highway 212 from Dupree to Faith, then from Maurine to Newell, before completing the project just east of Belle Fourche. 

Traffic on the highway will be reduced to one lane, with flaggers and pilot cars helping motorists navigate the roadwork area. Drivers should expect delays on the highway through planned work areas during daytime hours. 

Loose rock and fresh oil will be present following chip seal application. Speed limits will be reduced to 40 miles per hour or lower when posted. 

Weather dependent, all sections are expected to be chip sealed by Friday, June 26, with pavement markings to follow.

 The project is expected to cost the state about $2.8 million. Overall completion is scheduled for Oct. 2.

title: DWU launches campus-wide AI initiative  reaching hundreds of students, employees
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: MITCHELL — As AI adoption accelerates across university campuses, Dakota Wesleyan University is investing in and prioritizing responsible AI use by providing more than 1,000 students, faculty members and staff with access to BoodleBox, a collaborative AI platform specifically built-for-higher-education tool and it is designed to be private, safe and secure.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

MITCHELL — As AI adoption accelerates across university campuses, Dakota Wesleyan University is investing in and prioritizing responsible AI use by providing more than 1,000 students, faculty members and staff with access to BoodleBox, a collaborative AI platform specifically built-for-higher-education tool and it is designed to be private, safe and secure. 

This institution-wide implementation strengthens DWU’s position at the forefront of educational innovation and enables the transparent, ethical use of AI in teaching, learning and research.

DWU is the first, and, at this time, the only university in South Dakota launching a campus-wide AI initiative with BoodleBox, offering an AI platform to students, faculty and staff.  For nearly a year, a group of DWU faculty and staff has been testing the platform to fully understand its features and usability.

“Beginning with the upcoming school year, all students will have access to BoodleBox, which will standardize engagement with AI resources, reduce barriers and ensure equitable access,” DWU President Dan Kittle said. “This includes undergraduate and graduate-level students. Now, students won’t have to worry about paying for a premium ChatGPT subscription and competing with their peers who do.”

The university hopes faculty can integrate AI tools into curriculum design to enhance teaching and create more personalized learning pathways — from adapting course materials to developing specialized bots — that meet diverse student needs.

Lori Wehlander, DWU’s teaching and learning specialist, said she is excited. “BoodleBox will allow students to enter the job market knowing the common AI terms and technology. This will set them apart, as businesses and organizations are still learning how to apply AI tools ethically and effectively,” Wehlander said. “DWU students can familiarize themselves with a long list of AI tools, so they are entering the workforce better equipped.”

More than 70,000 professors and students from more than 1,300 colleges and universities have come to rely on BoodleBox.

title: Board approves higher income limit, higher prices for inmate-built affordable housing
byline: By Meghan O’Brien South Dakota Searchlight
description: PIERRE — A governor-appointed board unanimously approved higher prices and a higher income limit Monday for an affordable housing program.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — A governor-appointed board unanimously approved higher prices and a higher income limit Monday for an affordable housing program.

The South Dakota Governor’s House program sells two- and three-bedroom homes built by inmates at Mike Durfee State Prison in Springfield that are shipped across the state to eligible buyers.

The program also offers daycare models, which can be owned by daycare providers or nonprofit organizations. For buyers in rural areas with less than 5,000 people, the authority provides DakotaPlex units intended to be used as duplexes, triplexes or quadriplexes.

Buyers are responsible for buying a building permit, finding a lot, laying the foundation and flooring, and hooking up utilities and appliances.

This year’s change is the “smallest price increase we’ve had in many, many years,” according to Mike Harsma, who heads the Governor’s House program for South Dakota Housing.

On July 1, the start of the new fiscal year, the homes will be priced as follows:

Two bedroom: $89,000, up from $86,000, or a 3.49% increase.

Three bedroom: $99,000, up from $96,000, or a 3.13% increase.

Dakotaplex two bedroom: $99,000, up from $97,000, or a 2.06% increase.

Dakotaplex three bedroom: $109,000, up from $106,000, or a 2.83% increase.

Daycare: $99,000, up from $96,000, or a 3.13% increase.

Last year, units increased at least 6%. The rise in prices this year is due mostly to increased fuel costs, according to Chas Olson, executive director of the South Dakota Housing Development Authority. The cost of delivery for a home is included in the total price of a Governor’s House.

“Whether we’re moving a Governor’s House from Springfield to Sioux Falls or we’re moving it across the state to Buffalo, South Dakota, we get the same amount for that moving fee,” Olson said. “The cost of fuel, where it is now and kind of the uncertainty around that, we had to build in a little bit of a cushion just to be sure that we weren’t taking too big a loss on the fuel.”

Increased income limit

Buyers of Governor’s Houses must meet income requirements. The board approved a higher income limit, now at 100% of the state’s median income, regardless of household size.

Families that make up to $103,400 now qualify for the program. In previous years, buyers in one- to two-person households could qualify if they made $72,380 or less and households of three or more people could qualify if they made $82,720 or less.

“It’s hard to get people qualified at those income levels,” Olson said. It had been about 14 years since that limit was adjusted, he said, “and with the cost of everything now, I mean, it was just time.”

Mortgage assistance program

Board members also approved a program that’s modeled after a piece of legislation that failed earlier this year in the Legislature. It’s a mortgage assistance program for qualifying buyers of manufactured homes.

The authority also provides down payment assistance for traditional homes. Down payments for manufactured homes are often higher than a typical mortgage down payment, according to Amy Eldridge, of the authority.

A manufactured home is a mobile home that’s built on a permanent framework. The homes must have all required utilities, including plumbing and climate control.

Eligible buyers can apply for a low-interest loan of up to 50% of their mortgage down payment from the assistance program, with total assistance not exceeding $10,000. The income limit for the program is $124,080.

Olson hopes to see the program available to interested buyers within the next month.

“We just need more homes at lower price points,” he said, “and we need ways to get that done.”

title: ‘They just won’t listen:’ Rural SD nears postal breaking point
byline: By Molly Wetsch South Dakota News Watch
description: Petersen’s Variety in Philip, S.D., on May 2, 2026. The store advertises that residents can deliver and pick-up mail from UPS at the site. Photo by Molly Wetsch, South Dakota News Watch
_full_text:
Philip-we-ship-via-UPS-1-1.jpg
Petersen’s Variety in Philip, S.D., on May 2, 2026. The store advertises that residents can deliver and pick-up mail from UPS at the site. Photo by Molly Wetsch, South Dakota News Watch 

 Ravellette-Publications-office-1-1.jpg
Ravellette Publications, which publishes the Pioneer Review, in Philip, S.D., on May 2. Photo by Molly Wetsch, South Dakota News Watch 

PHILIP, S.D. – At Petersen’s Variety store, there are no less than three signs in the window advertising that residents of Philip can ship, pick up and drop off packages via UPS. The store is just a block away from the town’s post office. 

Residents in this western South Dakota town may be forgiven for choosing the – often more expensive – private shipping company over the nation’s postal service: Long delivery times and unreliable service have led to growing distrust and dissatisfaction with the United States Postal Service’s operations in rural parts of the state.

In early 2024, USPS downgraded a distribution facility in Huron to a local processing-only facility. The service had also initially planned to downsize its Sioux Falls distribution facility but later said that the plan had been paused.

USPS spokesperson Tara Jarrett offered a few details on the impact of those changes in a statement to News Watch.

“Local mail continues to be processed in our Sioux Falls (570-571 ZIP Codes), Dakota Central (572-575 ZIP Codes), and Rapid City (577 ZIP Codes) plants, and that mail does not leave the state for additional processing if it is staying in that region,” she said. “Mail in the 576 ZIP Codes continues to be served by our Bismarck, ND plant.” 

The organization has also recently begun rolling out its reduced service of rural post offices, stopping delivery vehicles at rural sites once a day, rather than twice. 

The moves, which are part of USPS’s Delivering for America plan, aimed to “modernize the nation’s aged and neglected postal network.” But for thousands of people across the state, including dozens of local newspaper publishers, that effort has significantly hindered day-to-day life and operations.

West River publisher sees dramatic changes in delivery times

Don Ravellette’s family has been publishing papers out of Philip for nearly 50 years through the company Ravellette Publications. The Philip Pioneer Review, the company’s primary imprint, now publishes news from Murdo, Wall, Bison, Kadoka and Faith. 

The Pioneer Review is a true community paper: Recent stories include the details of a new lighted stop sign in Philip, the results of the Harding County regional high school rodeo and a story about how Murdo residents rallied together to clean up a city planter with new soil and flowers. 

Ravellette said that for the past two years, he’s been having a harder time making sure that news is delivered to subscribers in a timely manner. He’s also chosen to regularly direct employees to drive to Wall to deliver papers. Ravellette said the town’s 577 ZIP code – compared to Philip’s 575 – means that subscribers receive papers in a timelier manner.

Pull quote
“There’s no good news here. It’s all bad news when it comes to the future, in terms of what they’ve done to the system, what it’s costing, where they’re at. And Congress is reluctant to do anything about it.”
 — David Bordewyk, executive director of South Dakota NewsMedia Association

“More and more publishers have had to do that, this exceptional dispatch, where they’re literally doing the work of what the post office used to do, in terms of taking these bundles to surrounding post offices. Just to try to get them to expedite the delivery, particularly in the local area,” Dave Bordewyk, president of the South Dakota NewsMedia Association told News Watch.

Ravellette told News Watch he is experiencing more frustration than ever before with the postal service. 

“It’s common talk from the coffee shops to the business owners that the post office is still unreliable. It’s not even funny,” Ravellette said. “And when we send out 1,000 livestock catalogs, it’s sad when the out-of-state ones get delivered before the ones you mail out 25 miles from your house, from your post office.”

In rural areas, the postal service is a lifeline because it is legally mandated to provide delivery and mail services to every ZIP code in the country. That means that routes cannot be discontinued or disrupted if they aren’t used frequently or are not profitable. 

Ravellette said that many of his subscribers do not see the value in having a weekly subscription to the newspaper when they can’t expect it will arrive on time. 

“They were saying, ‘Well, we might just have to quit our subscription, maybe we’ll just stop in and buy a paper whenever we can.’ So there goes 50 bucks. And if you get 100 of those, you do the math,” Ravellette said. 

Ravellette said that he feels like decisions are being made at the national level that aren’t considering the needs of rural America. 

“They just won’t listen. They just won’t,” he said.

Delivery worsened for 65% of papers that responded to survey

Ravellette is not the only publisher frustrated with the postal service. 

Bordewyk recently sent a survey to members of the South Dakota NewsMedia Association, which includes 109 newspaper publishers and digital media outlets from across the state. 

The organization had 64 publishers respond to the survey, of which about 65% said deliveries of their newspapers had worsened in the past year. Just 7% said deliveries had improved. Common complaints issued through the survey were inconsistencies with delivery times, struggles retaining advertisers and subscribers not receiving papers at all.

On June 4, Bordewyk met with the USPS Inspector General’s office to discuss commonly expressed issues with the state’s mailing system. He said that he thought the meeting went well and that the office seemed alarmed at publishers’ complaints. 

But he expressed concern at the organization’s ability to fix what has already been broken. 

“There’s no good news here. It’s all bad news when it comes to the future, in terms of what they’ve done to the system, what it’s costing, where they’re at. And Congress is reluctant to do anything about it,” Bordewyk said.

    

USPS data shows meandering routes, longer delivery times

USPS’ Service Performance Dashboard provides data about on-time delivery rates for four types of mail shipped through the service: First Class Mail, newspapers and periodicals, marketing mail and bound printed matter, media and library mail. 

A News Watch analysis of the data found that at the ZIP3 level, which is the first three numbers of a ZIP code, the percentage of on-time inbound delivery for newspapers and periodicals varies greatly across the state. 

Inbound delivery times illustrate the average time it takes for papers and periodicals to arrive to addresses in a specific ZIP code. Just 57.81% of papers arriving to 575 ZIP codes arrived on time in the second quarter of 2026, compared to 86.37% in 570 ZIP codes. The ZIP3 code 575, where Philip is located, also sees the slowest average delivery time at 4.3 days this year. 

Outbound delivery, though, which measures the timeliness of mail being sent from a specific ZIP code, is a reflection of the on-time rate that local papers can expect when sending their publications to subscribers from their town’s post office. In the 575 ZIP3 code, the average delivery time for outbound newspapers this year is 5.3 days.

“All the newspapers mail us copies of their paper to the (SDNA) office here in Brookings,” Bordewyk said. “One-hundred newspapers are sending them to us. It used to be by the end of the week, by Friday – because most weeklies would be printing and mailing on a Tuesday or Wednesday – we would see more than 90% of the newspapers. Today, by Friday, less than half of them are showing up.” 

Newspapers see much lower on-time delivery rates and more days to deliver than other tracked USPS mail types like First-Class Mail or marketing mail.

Ravellette shared a tracking number with News Watch for a package received by a rancher near Quinn, in western South Dakota. The package, which was shipped on July 28, 2025, from Phoenix, was received on Aug. 12, 2025. 

The archive tracking statement for the package shows that it made its way through 14 cities on its way to Quinn. It notably ended up in Omaha, Nebraska, and Sioux Falls twice – once after making the 600-mile trip out to Billings, Montana. 

The roughly 1,300-mile trip from Phoenix, the package’s original destination, to Quinn turned into a 3,600-mile odyssey under USPS’ care. 

USPS routes for packages sent to rural S.D.

South Dakota News Watch obtained a tracking number and archive tracking information for a package shipped to Quinn, S.D. from Phoneix, A.Z. on July 28, 2025. The package arrived in Quinn on Aug. 12, 2025, and made stops in Olathe, K.S., Omaha, N.E., Sioux Falls, S.D., Billings, M.T. and Rapid City, S.D. before arriving at its destination. Notably, the package was at one point sent from Omaha to Sioux Falls to Billings and then back to Omaha.

USPS maintained in its statement to News Watch that its delivery performance in South Dakota is above average.

“USPS delivery performance in South Dakota is strong. About half of all First-Class Mail is delivered early. In the Sioux Falls area specifically, for the week ending 5/22/26, 92.6% of incoming mail was delivered on time, above our national target of 89%,” Jarrett said. 

The organization did not address questions about whether it is aware of issues in rural South Dakota and if there are any plans to speed up service in those areas.

South Dakota U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds told News Watch that he was unsatisfied with notions that the service in South Dakota was up to par.

“I know there’s information out there suggesting that we have good service in South Dakota. I reject that,” Rounds said. “I think the clear evidence is that the mail service is terrible in South Dakota.”

Members of Congress looking for action

Rounds has previously been vocal about his dissatisfaction with USPS’ performance in the state. 

In a press release in December 2025, he said the service has “deteriorated to critical levels” in South Dakota. He also said that the Postmaster General David Steiner had “downplayed such issue existed in South Dakota.” 

Rounds called for an investigation into the service in the state. The USPS field operations review audit website does not currently display any former or active audits of processing or distribution centers in South Dakota. 

Rounds told News Watch, though, that he is aware of ongoing investigations in South Dakota. On June 11, he sent a letter to chairman Sen. Rand Paul and ranking member Sen. Gary Peters of the Senate Homeland Security Committee. In that letter, he said he would reject any nominations to four open postal service positions until a plan was in place to fix issues in South Dakota.

“I would, at this point, remind South Dakotans that your local postal employees are trying to help us,” Rounds said to News Watch. “This is a systemic problem, and it has to be fixed with a systemic change.”

The impact of slow USPS delivery extends beyond birthday cards and bank statements. 

U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson said in a column in January that he had surveyed 4,000 South Dakotans and held a roundtable in Sioux Falls where constituents shared issues with the postal service. 

Many spoke of financial consequences, concerns with delayed medical prescriptions and other problems that have significantly impacted their day-to-day lives, he said.

“I heard from folks like Susan from Faulkton who incurred a $2,700 late fee because her check took 25 days to get to Sioux Falls. There’s a business in Bath whose customers often don’t receive their checks or get them two months late. And some people like Mary bought Christmas presents early, only to have them travel to nine different states before being delivered to Huron – 10 days late and after Christmas,” Johnson wrote in the column.

Bordewyk said that while conversations with the Inspector General’s office were generally reassuring, newspaper publishers across the state will still have to reckon with the fact that the system may never go back to the way it was – and be willing to make changes.

“The question for all of us is, will the postal service decide to walk back these system changes that they made?” Bordewyk said. “I understand your audience, your subscribers want that printed product, and that still serves a predominant need. But the move to a digital delivery is just going to be more and more necessary for even our smallest newspapers going forward. In order to survive, that’s what’s going to be necessary.”

title: Cattle market congested by  early sales, persistent drought
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer
description: Persistent dryness has created a host of issues for cattle ranchers.
_full_text:
Cattle market congested by  early sales, persistent drought
Persistent dryness has created a host of issues for cattle ranchers.  

SPEARFISH — Drought and dry conditions have led some ranchers in three states to bring their cattle to market months earlier than usual. The early sell-off comes during the latest in a series of dry years, and amid a host of long-term systemic issues that threaten to congest a booming market.

Cows are normally sold in September or October. Five auction house owners who spoke with the Pioneer said that they had seen an uptick in breeding pairs sold in May and June. In some areas, the reported increase was as small as 5%. In others it was as high as 500%. 

For Jay Nordhausen, owner of  Oglala Livestock Auction Market, the roughly 20% increase he saw in sales equated to about 17,000 additional cattle sold. 

The difference in the number of early sales, the ranchers say, was the amount of moisture in the surrounding area. Less rainfall means more cattle sold early, since drier conditions make hay and feed more expensive, and an October sale less profitable. 

The United States Drought Monitor, a service produced in collaboration between the federal government and the University of Nebraska-Lincoln, lists about 83% of South Dakota’s landmass as being in some kind of drought, with about 35% listed as “severe” or “extreme.” About 93% of Nebraska is currently experiencing a drought, with about 55% of the land experiencing a severe or extreme drought. 55% of Montana’s landmass is experiencing a drought, with about 33% being severe or extreme. 

“That’s what ranchers have to sell, their grass,” Craig Deveraux, a rancher and co-owner of Buffalo Livestock Marketing, said. “And when they don’t have any grass to sell — I guess that’s their income for the year.”

Devereaux said that he had sold some cattle early, and that the sale represented about a 17% loss over what he might have made in another year. 

The early sales are motivated both by financial concerns and the increasing difficulty of providing enough hay and feed for animals until they would normally be delivered to buyers.

A booming market under strain

The cattle market remains at an all-time high, buoyed by strong consumer demand for American beef. And whether ranchers sell cattle in the summer or in October, they can expect to be well compensated. 

Simultaneously, however, the ranchers who raise cattle are beset by dwindling herds and a shortage of hay and feed — all of which can be linked, at least in part, to drought and persistent dry conditions. 

Nordhausen said that in Nebraska, hay is about 75% more expensive than it was in previous years, though he said that in the past several years hay prices had been low because of a surplus one year. 

These persistent difficulties have been exacerbated by Nebraska wildfires that destroyed hay.

“The state that is responsible for the majority of the beef in the United States — it burnt,” Patsy Tines, owner of Gordon Livestock, said. “There will be no hay crop.”

Nebraska Governor Jim Pillen has requested that President Trump issue a major disaster declaration as the result of fires in the state. 

The sale of breeding pairs also threatens to drain the area of young profitable cattle. Ranchers with breeding pairs can expect to eventually profit from the resulting offspring. However, once a pair is sold — and possibly moved to an area with more moisture — that potential source of income is lost. 

“We’re selling a lot of pairs,” Deveraux said. “And if we wouldn’t sell the pairs, then we would have had an opportunity to sell those calves year after year.”

Travis Linch, owner of Belle Fourche Livestock Market, said although it was true that sales of breeding pairs made the market tougher, he had seen ranchers try to mitigate that effect.

“People are holding onto their heifers,” he said. “So I’m optimistic that…people are thinking about rebuilding already. They’re culling their olds and they’re holding their heifers.”

Heifers are young female cows that have not yet given birth.

Although the early sales are widespread, at least in some areas, they do not represent a catastrophe. 

“There hasn’t been a mass exodus (of cattle), but there’s definitely been an uptick in pairs that we normally probably wouldn’t see,” Justin Tupper, owner of St. Onge Livestock Auction, said. He said that the number of cattle sold early was relatively small, but that it would increase if conditions stayed dry. 

Joe Waln, owner of Martin Livestock, said that his marketplace had also sold stock earlier than usual, “but nothing severe like you would think yet.” 

Dwindling herds, aging ranchers

While herds remain profitable, over the last several years, they have also gotten smaller.

Linch said that some of his clientele have reduced their herds by up to 25%. 

Jay Nordhausen, owner of Oglala Livestock, also said he knew of ranchers whose herds had declined by 10-20%. 

Ty Thomson, an auctioneer at Public Auction Yards, said his own herd had shrunk every year for the last 8 or 9 years, he said, but did not say by how much. 

As herds are dwindling, the ranchers who take care of them are growing older. 

The Department of Agriculture lists the mean age of non-Hispanic farmers (including ranchers) at 60 years old, and the mean age of Hispanic farmers at 57 years old. 

“It’s hard for a young person to get into this business,” Linch said, citing the high cost of feed, stock, and infrastructure. “Ranchers are getting older.”

Nordhausen said his primary concerns were the increasing age of ranchers and moisture levels. 

An uncertain future 

The cattle owners who spoke to the Pioneer said that even a relatively short period of rainfall can avert catastrophe. 

Waln said that his auction house had been fortunate to have rain in the last two weeks. But before that, he said, conditions were “bleak. Very bleak.” 

Linch said that he hopes rain will come. If not, he said, some ranchers will go out of business. 

“There’s guys that can’t take it,” he said. “You know, it takes so much money right now to operate. … It’s astronomically high the amount of money we go through to make this work.”

title: Deadwood to unveil new interpretive sign
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: DEADWOOD — A new interpretive sign is scheduled to be added to Deadwood’s historic streets Wednesday at 1 p.m.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

DEADWOOD — A new interpretive sign is scheduled to be added to Deadwood’s historic streets Wednesday at 1 p.m.

This panel, titled “Deadwood & Flag City,” will commemorate the long-held tradition of honoring the American flag by the citizens of Deadwood. The sign will be installed outside of 102 – 108 Sherman Street. The public is invited to participate in the unveiling. 

The tradition of honoring the American flag in Deadwood can be traced back to World War I, when the flag was first flown for 24 hours a day from its perch at Mount Moriah Cemetery. Deadwood Mayor Nathan Franklin is credited with having the flag illuminated in its display. 

Since then, the flag has flown periodically from the same location until the bombing of Pearl Harbor Day on Dec. 7, 1941, when the flag was again flown for 24 hours.

Today, the City of Deadwood’s flag is flown in conjunction with the American and South Dakota flags in front of Deadwood City Hall.

If you have any questions about the unveiling of the new outdoor interpretive sign, please contact the Deadwood Historic Preservation office at (605) 578-2082.

title: Jewel Cave hosts wilderness volunteers crew
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: CUSTER — Jewel Cave National Monument hosted a Wilderness Volunteers team of four volunteers and two crew leaders in their Historic Area, May 18-22. The team worked hard with the Jewel Cave Facilities Division to do a multitude of tasks to prepare a portion of the Canyons Trail for a new section of concrete.
_full_text:
CUSTER — Jewel Cave National Monument hosted a Wilderness Volunteers team of four volunteers and two crew leaders in their Historic Area, May 18-22. The team worked hard with the Jewel Cave Facilities Division to do a multitude of tasks to prepare a portion of the Canyons Trail for a new section of concrete.

Wilderness Volunteers is a 501c3 organization founded in 1997 with a mission to engage people in meaningful service that conserves and protects America’s wild lands. Wilderness Volunteers organizes around 40 week-long volunteer projects each year in public lands across the country, assisting land management agencies like the National Park Service with priority maintenance work, including trail maintenance, invasive species removal, campsite rehabilitation, fencing projects, and more.

The team of six Wilderness Volunteers completed an immense amount of work during the four days on site. They sorted and moved 40 cubic yards of concrete rubble, using sledgehammers to break it into smaller pieces and remove 200 pounds of metal re-mesh and 60 pounds of rebar. The scrap metal was recycled, and the crushed concrete was transported to Lithograph Canyon Road, where it was used as fill to repair a low area. The Jewel Cave Facilities Division used motorized buggies to move 105,000 pounds of gravel road base up to the trail, where the Wilderness Volunteers raked and leveled it to ensure a 1% drainage slope and consistent width, and then sprayed and compacted it.

By the end of the week, the team had prepared 600 feet of trail so that contractors could come in the following weeks to pour a finished concrete trail. Team members also dug out the entrances and exits of three separate culverts and placed rocks around the pipes to prevent them from clogging. On the final day, the team built a retaining wall (30 feet long, 3 feet high) to prevent erosion and damage to the newly poured trail. This retaining wall required approximately 22,500 pounds of rocks, and the removal of approximately 1 cubic yard of soil. 

The portion of the Canyons Trail that the team worked on is a very heavily traveled area in the park, as it leads from the Historic Cabin in the Historic Area to the original entrance of Jewel Cave. The path is used by hikers and runners on the Canyons Trail, and by thousands of visitors participating in Historic Lantern Tours in the summer months. The old concrete on the path showed a great deal of wear and tear and needed removal.  New concrete will be poured and cause a brief pause in this summer’s Historic Lantern Tours from June 16-18. The monument is very appreciative of all the work the Wilderness Volunteers team did in preparing the path and helping to keep the Canyons Trail safe and well maintained.

title: History Days draws strong crowd for celebration of Rural Schools and Local Heritage
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Memories of one-room schoolhouses, country teachers, spelling bees and generations of rural families filled the Sturgis Community Center as the 10th Annual Sturgis & Meade County History Days attracted a strong turnout of residents eager to learn, share and preserve local history.
_full_text:
STURGIS — Memories of one-room schoolhouses, country teachers, spelling bees and generations of rural families filled the Sturgis Community Center as the 10th Annual Sturgis & Meade County History Days attracted a strong turnout of residents eager to learn, share and preserve local history.

This year’s event, held June 12-13, focused on “The History of Schools in Sturgis and Meade County.” The theme generated significant interest, with the Sturgis & Meade County Historical Society collecting stories and artifacts spanning more than 150 years of education in both town and country schools.

Exhibits, presentations and personal stories highlighted the important role schools played in shaping communities throughout Meade County.

The history of rural education reflects the changing landscape of the county. As agriculture, transportation and communications evolved, so did the challenges of providing education across a large rural area. Historical records show that by 1931, Meade County had approximately 160 rural school buildings staffed by 163 teachers. By 1939, that number had declined to about 90 schools as consolidation and population shifts began reshaping education.

One of the attendees was former Upper Pleasant Valley School student Mrs. Nancy Remington, whose family history is closely tied to the rural school.

Remington attended the school from 1959 to 1965, completing all eight grades there. Her connection to the school extends back even further.  

“My grandmother, Blair, was a teacher there before she got married in 1912 and 1913,” Remington said. “She boarded with the Blair family, which is how she met my grandpa. My dad and his two sisters went to school there, and all nine of us kids attended there too.”

The former schoolhouse still stands today near Exit 37, about a mile and a half from Interstate 90 at the intersection with Fort Meade Way.

“Darren and Carrie Odle purchased it and have remodeled it,” Remington said. “There are pictures of the restoration on display at the event.”

Remington recalled many fond memories of attending the one-room school.  “I remember the spelling contests when we’d come into town for the county competition and Rally Day,” she said. “We had Christmas programs and practiced for Rally Day events. When I was in second grade, there were only nine kids in the school, five from our family, two cousins and two neighboring girls. It was kind of like a family.”

She also remembered her first teacher, Amy Zink. 

“I had Mrs. Amy Zink for the first three years,” Remington said. “She was excellent with reading and teaching the younger elementary students.”

Saturday’s program featured presentations by Betsey DeLouche on country schools, past and present, while Jim Holland and Mark Rambow presented a timeline of Sturgis schools in the Community Center Theater.

The event also included recognition of individuals who have contributed significantly to preserving local history.

Historical Society President Mark Rambow presented the organization’s annual Friend of History Awards.

Rambow noted that the society honored former country school teacher Edna Haley Smith during Friday evening’s activities.

“We wanted to recognize her again today,” Rambow said. “She received the Friend of History Award for her contributions and dedication to preserving the history of education in this area.”

The society also honored longtime members and volunteers Ross and Jan Lamphere for their years of service and commitment to local history.

“Ross and Jan have been active members of the Historical Society since the very beginning in 2014, and even before that they were deeply involved in preserving history throughout the community,” Rambow said.

He highlighted the couple’s many contributions, including hosting archaeology students from the University of South Dakota during excavations at Soap Suds Row near Fort Meade, assisting with museum acquisitions and supporting numerous historical projects.

“You name it, Ross and Jan have been there for it,” Rambow said. “It was appropriate that we recognize them for everything they’ve done and everything they continue to do.”

A surprised Ross Lamphere accepted the award on behalf of his family. “I had absolutely no idea this was coming,” Lamphere said. “It’s been a real privilege to be involved with the preservation of history in our area. In many respects, our history is still young, and so much of it is still available to be preserved. What a privilege it is to be honored for something like this. Thank you very much.”

The annual History Days event continues to serve as a gathering place where residents can connect with the stories, people and places that helped shape Sturgis and Meade County, ensuring those memories are preserved for future generations.

title: Sturgis Area Arts Council brings classic fairy tale ‘Cinderella’ to the stage June 18-21
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — The Sturgis Area Arts Council will transport audiences into a magical fairytale world when it presents Rodgers and Hammerstein’s Cinderella June 18-21 at the Sturgis Community Center Theater.
_full_text:
STURGIS — The Sturgis Area Arts Council will transport audiences into a magical fairytale world when it presents Rodgers and Hammerstein’s Cinderella June 18-21 at the Sturgis Community Center Theater.

The production marks another milestone for the local theater program, featuring a cast that blends seasoned performers with newcomers making their debut on the Sturgis stage. 

Leading the production is director Thomas Golden, a Sturgis High School graduate and longtime SAAC performer who has returned to guide this year’s musical. 

He is joined by choreographer and co-director Bridgett Farruggia, who, along with her husband Stephen, operates Seraphim Theater in Rapid City.

Taking on the title role is Danilee Pudwill, who returns to the stage after a lengthy hiatus from theater.

Marlene Kotab, a member of the cast, said the production offers a nostalgic experience for audience members while introducing a beloved story to a new generation.

“We can’t wait for our community to enter the fairytale world of Cinderella,” Kotab said. “Many people will remember the songs from the 1960s movie and will be humming along. It is truly a joy to bring back those memories while creating new ones through live theater. We’re also thrilled to welcome little princesses and princes to enjoy this timeless story.”

The classic tale includes all the elements audiences have come to love: a cruel stepfamily, a magical fairy godmother, a charming prince, a glass slipper, and the remarkable transformation of a kind-hearted young woman into a princess.

Performances are scheduled for Thursday through Saturday, June 18-20, at 7 p.m., with a matinee performance Sunday, June 21, at 2 p.m.

Tickets are $20 for adults and $10 for students. In a special promotion, children who attend dressed as Cinderella or Prince Charming will receive free admission.

Organizers invite families and theater lovers of all ages to attend and experience the magic, music, and enduring message of one of the world’s most beloved fairytales.

title: Spearfish Vietnam Veteran Dave Raber enjoys the welcome home he never got in 1968
byline: By Barry Raber Special to the Pioneer
description: A large group of people gathered to welcome veterans home from their day trip to Washington D.C., on Midwest Honor Flight 30. Photo courtesy of Midwest Honor Flight
_full_text:
MWF1-306.jpg
A large group of people gathered to welcome veterans home from their day trip to Washington D.C., on Midwest Honor Flight 30. Photo courtesy of Midwest Honor Flight 

SPEARFISH — When U.S. Navy veteran Dave Raber arrived home from Vietnam in 1968, he didn’t exactly get the hero’s welcome he deserved. But the welcome home he received on May 19 after his Midwest Honor Flight (MHF) tour was off the charts. 

“I just never imagined there could be a welcome home like the one we got in Sioux Falls,” Dave said after returning from a memorable day in Washington, D.C., alongside 82 other veterans from the Upper Midwest.

When Dave arrived home from a turbulent year of war in May 1968, the experience was painfully different.

“There wasn’t anyone to meet me. Not even my wife,” he recalled quietly. “She had confused my arrival time and didn’t make it to the airport to greet me when I got off the plane. There was nobody there at all.”

His beloved wife, Sally, eventually arrived and introduced Dave to his 6-month-old son, who was born while he served in Vietnam. 

That son, Barry Raber, traveled alongside his father on Mission 30, the Midwest Honor Flight’s latest one-day journey to our nation’s capital. Together, father and son visited 7 of America’s most sacred military memorials. 

A Long-Overdue Welcome Home

But it was the journey home that made the biggest impact on Dave.

“For whatever reason, I was the first one off the plane,” Dave said. “I was greeted by a huge group of people lined up the entire length of the Sioux Falls airport. Then the line wrapped back around and went all the way down the other side of the airport.” 

“A bagpipe band was playing. About 1,000 people were waving flags and applauding for us. Kids were holding handmade signs welcoming us home. It seemed like we veterans were shaking hands forever, with people sincerely thanking us for our service,” Dave said. “It was just amazing!”

The emotional reception was part of Operation Welcome Home, a community effort organized by Midwest Honor Flight to ensure that veterans have an opportunity to enjoy the kind of recognition many never experienced when they returned from war— especially Vietnam Veterans like Dave who came home to an America divided by the unpopular war.

“I must’ve shaken hands with 500 people, who each said, ‘Thank you for your service.’ They let us know how much they appreciate what we sacrificed.”

“It was overwhelming,” Dave continued. “The people were so sincere. It kind of wiped out those bad memories that I had from coming home from war all those years ago.”

The Mission of Midwest Honor Flights

Founded in 2017, Midwest Honor Flight transports veterans to Washington, D.C., free of charge, so that veterans who sacrificed for our freedom can visit the national memorials dedicated to their service and sacrifice. Mission 30, the tour Dave and Barry were on, flew 83 veterans — including 74 Vietnam veterans, 5 Korean War veterans, and 4 peacetime veterans — from South Dakota, Northwest Iowa, Northeast Nebraska, and Southwest Minnesota.

Honor Flights are funded entirely through donations. Mission 30 was made possible by the Seed for Success Foundation. Veterans typically wait several years for a seat on an Honor Flight from one of Honor Flight Network’s 130 regional hubs nationwide. Dave’s niece, Tracey Steinbach, applied for his Honor Flight seat nearly 2 years ago.

 IMG_0422.jpeg
Dave Raber poses with his son, Barry, who accompanied him on Midwest Honor Flight 30 to Washington D.C. Photo courtesy of Midwest Honor Flight 

 IMG_0498.jpeg
Several family and friends welcomed Dave Raber home from Washington D.C. The welcome was a stark contrast to Raber’s return home from Vietnam in 1968. Photo courtesy of Midwest Honor Flight 

 IMG_2185.jpg
Dave Raber shakes hands with people who gathered to welcome veterans home after their Midwest Honor Flight. The welcome home was one of the best parts of the flight for Raber, who was not greeted by anyone when he returned home from Vietnam in 1968.  Photo courtesy of Midwest Honor Flight 

“We tried to keep it a surprise, but when he needed a new Real ID driver’s license to fly, we had to tell him,” Barry explained. 

Just like most days in the military, the one-day Midwest Honor Flight tour began long before sunrise. After singing “The Star-Spangled Banner” at 4:20 a.m., veterans boarded a chartered JetBlue aircraft in Sioux Falls at 4:30 a.m. to fly them to the national’s capital.

The night before departure, veterans, their families, volunteers, and supporters attended a banquet at the Sanford Event Barn in Sioux Falls, which was designed to look like the interior of a rustic, Midwest barn. Aaron Van Beek, founder and CEO of Midwest Honor Flights, shared why he started the organization: Because so many veterans lack the means or opportunity to visit the national memorials in Washington, D.C.

“These veterans answered the call to serve our country,” Van Beek explained. “It is now our duty as a grateful nation to ensure they have the opportunity to see the memorials dedicated to their service and their fellow comrades. It is the very least we can do for these brave American heroes.”

Seven memorials in 8 hours

During the whirlwind, 8-hour tour of Washington, D.C., Midwest Honor Flight volunteers guided veterans through memorials, provided mobility assistance, helped them on and off the buses, and distributed water and boxed lunches. The sites they visited included Arlington National Cemetery, the Vietnam Veterans Memorial, the Korean War Memorial, the World War II Memorial, the Navy Memorial, the Air Force Memorial, and the towering Iwo Jima Memorial.

At the U.S. Marine Corps Memorial, the group posed for a photo with the massive 78-foot bronze sculpture of the Iwo Jima Memorial, which depicts 6 brave Marines raising the American flag after a brutal battle for the island.

Dave and Barry got to talk with U.S. Senator John Thune and Congressman Dusty Johnson, who both represent South Dakota. Amid an incredibly busy week in session, Thune and Johnson both made time in their hectic schedules to meet and honor the veterans who had flown in for the day.

One unforgettable part of the tour took place in Arlington National Cemetery, where the group witnessed the ceremonial changing of the guard at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier.

“That was the highlight for me,” Dave said. “The Honor Guard at the Tomb were incredibly well trained and moved with extreme precision. I got a front-row seat to view the whole ceremony, a very moving experience.”

For Barry, seeing Arlington National Cemetery for the first time brought its own perspective.

“I didn’t understand the scale of it,” he said. “There are more than 400,000 people buried there, and they perform 30 military funerals a day.”

One final tour, with honor

The Midwest Honor Flight team made good on its motto, “One final tour, with honor,” in every aspect of the day.

“There had to be nearly 100 volunteers helping us along the way,” Barry said. “There was also a full medical staff prepared for every eventuality.”

Dave summed it up: “It was first-cabin all the way.”

When weather delayed their return flight from Reagan National Airport, Midwest Honor Flight volunteers sang “God Bless the USA” by Lee Greenwood, plus other patriotic songs to entertain the veterans during the wait.

On the flight home, every veteran received a final “Mail Call,” filled with letters from loved ones, elected officials, and school children.

“I got close to 50 letters,” Dave said. “Some were from family and friends. I got one from Thune and Johnson. Some were letters from local kids who included drawings.”

“I’ll enjoy opening and reading them in the days to come.”

Adding another emotional touch, Dave’s daughter, Stacee, and granddaughter, Sally Beth Nault, flew in from Chicago specifically to surprise him during the Operation Welcome Home celebration. 

For Dave, who served as the only commissioned officer assigned to a Patrol Boat Riverine unit during the Vietnam War, survived the Tet Offensive, and later helped spearhead Navy psychological operations, the Honor Flight tour helped to provide final closure on his time in the military.

Dave documented his year at war in a 2025 memoir, From Variety Show to Vietnam. He even handed out signed copies of the book to the delight of fellow veterans, volunteers, and flight attendants on the MHF flight.

Proud to be a U.S. Citizen

Though he felt hesitant about participating on the Midwest Honor Flight tour because of the rigorous schedule, Dave says he would do it again in a heartbeat.

“If you’re a veteran and you have the opportunity, you should go on an Honor Flight,” he said. “You’ll change your mind when you get to D.C. The volunteers are so helpful. They know that you may need help with mobility, and they make it easy to participate.”

Then he added, “This whole experience will make you proud of being a U.S. citizen.”

After decades of carrying the memory of a lonely return home in 1968, Midwest Honor Flights, along with hundreds of patriotic citizens with good hearts who made the effort to honor our selfless veterans, finally gave Dave the welcome home he deserved.

title: What happens when a student is expelled
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — The Spearfish School Board addressed the recent expulsion of two high schoolers at Monday’s meeting.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

SPEARFISH — The Spearfish School Board addressed the recent expulsion of two high schoolers at Monday’s meeting.

Many community members had questions following the incident that occurred on May 5 when a student brought a firearm to the high school campus. Parents were notified of the incident following the school day on May 8.

Board President Ryan Niesent read from a prepared statement.

“The district takes student safety very seriously, and we understand parents or other interested parties may think the school district should notify them immediately when a situation involving student safety arises. While that sounds simple enough, it’s not a simple matter, because it involves the rights of interested parties,” Niesent said. 

With student privacy laws, the information that is allowed to be released is limited. If law enforcement gets involved, another layer of rules apply.

“Whether or not an unauthorized firearm or weapon was or was not involved may not be certain initially, the investigation must be performed carefully and confidentially,” he said. 

“Second, facts collected during the investigation ultimately become part of confidential evidence, presented at a student disciplinary hearing. This hearing is conducted along the lines of a court trial. A public-school student, involved in a disciplinary hearing, is entitled to confidentiality and due process rights under school board policies and South Dakota and federal laws. The school board sits in the place of an unbiased jury, to hear the evidence at the hearing without advance knowledge of the evidence. After the evidence is presented at a hearing, and the school board makes its decision, the only public disclosure is a public motion by the school board to take action concerning an unnamed student. There is no public disclosure of the evidence or identification of the student involved.”

The hearings in this case occurred May 18, during executive sessions by the Spearfish School Board.

The board entered the first of 2 closed sessions to discuss the expulsion, suspension, discipline, assignment of, or the educational program of a student, or the eligibility of a student to participate in interscholastic activities provided by the South Dakota High School Activities Association. The move is allowed as one of only several matters in which a board may exclude the public from proceedings.

An hour and a half later, the board returned to open session where it voted to expel the first student, only identified as Student 1, for 12 months.

A slightly shorter executive session proceeded for Student 2, who received the same expulsion timeframe.

Kirk Easton, superintendent of the Spearfish School District, told the Pioneer following the hearings that, “the findings resulted in a determination that there was a violation related to a firearm being present on our high school campus. Although a weapon was not recovered on school grounds, evidence indicated it was transferred between the 2 students during the school day.”

On May 19, a Sturgis Brown High School student was arrested when he brought an airsoft gun onto the high school campus. Days later, on May 23, a Spearfish student was detained and questioned by law enforcement, officers after the student allegedly brought an airsoft gun to the school.

A meeting is scheduled for June 15 for the Meade School Board to discuss the issue. A meeting for the Spearfish School Board to discuss the airsoft gun incident has not yet been scheduled.

So, what happens to a student when they are expelled from school.

The Pioneer reached out to Easton and Wayne Wormstadt, superintendent of the Meade School District.

Pioneer: If a student brings a “dangerous weapon” onto school grounds, is it an automatic expulsion, or is there a chance for lesser punishment?

Easton: “From our Dangerous Weapons and Firearms policy:

• Consequences – Dangerous Weapons.

Any student that brings a dangerous weapon to school will, except as modified herein, be suspended from school for a period of 3 days. The suspension requirement may be modified by the principal on a case-by-case basis to not less than 1 day, or up to 10 days. The superintendent may consider the violation for long-term suspension or expulsion on a case-by-case basis.

• Consequences - Firearm.

Any student who brings a firearm, as that term is defined in 18 United States Code 921, to school will be expelled from school for one calendar year. The superintendent of schools and the Board of Education shall have the authority to modify the expulsion requirement on a case-by-case basis.”

Wormstadt: “Students are prohibited from bringing dangerous and/or illegal weapons to school or school-sponsored activities. Appropriate disciplinary and/or legal action shall be pursued by the building principal.

A dangerous and/or deadly weapon is defined as any firearm, knife or device, instrument, material, or substance, whether animate or inanimate, which is calculated or designed to inflict death or serious bodily harm, or any object which can reasonably be considered to be a weapon. Look-alike weapons, which are items that resemble or appear to be weapons, also are prohibited.

No firearms are permitted on any school premises, in a school vehicle or any vehicle used for school purposes, or in any school building or other building or premises used for school functions. Exceptions would include weapons under the control of law enforcement personnel, starting guns while in use at athletic events, supervised school training sessions for the use of firearms, weapons used in educational demonstrations, ceremonial presence or unloaded weapons used at color guard ceremonies and look-alike weapons in an approved school performance.”

Wormstadt echoed many of the answers Easton provided thus they are not being included due to space constraints.

Pioneer: What would determine a lesser punishment?

Easton: “According to federal and state law, for possession of a firearm on school grounds the expulsion must be for one calendar year.  For a dangerous weapon such as a knife, type and size of knife, as well as intent, are considered when determining disciplinary action.”

Pioneer: What factors are considered when deciding whether to expel a student?

Easton: “Factors could include:

• Whether it is a mandatory expulsion based upon a student possessing a firearm on campus?

• If not a firearm, what was the incident?

• What is the disciplinary history of the student?

• The outcome of a threat assessment? 

• Is the student on an IEP (individual education program) and was the incident a manifestation of their disability?”

Pioneer: If a student is expelled, are they able to enroll in another school district?

Both: “No.”

Pioneer: Does the home district notify the state or any other agency about the student’s status?

Easton: “No, but the expulsion is entered into our student management database in which the state and other schools can access. Also, when a student looks to transfer from one school to another, principals do a great job of contacting the other school to determine if the student is currently serving a suspension or expulsion.”

Wormstadt: “Same and other districts do a great job of communicating with us.”

Pioneer: Is the home district required to continue to provide education to that student? If so, how is this done?

Easton: “If a student is on an IEP, the district must still provide access to the curriculum during a suspension or expulsion.  This typically would be accomplished through virtual coursework with supports.

For a student that is not on an IEP, we still provide an online curriculum so the student does not fall too far behind his/her peers.”

Pioneer: Are they eligible to attend an alternative school?

Both “No.”

Pioneer: What factors are considered when debating accepting a previously expelled student back or from another district?

Easton: “Did they serve the term of their suspension or expulsion?

Did they complete the requirements that may have been placed upon them for return?

The safety of the school environment.”

Wormstadt: “Meade will not accept a student who is currently expelled or under suspension.

Were there requirements placed on them by the previous school district/board and are they completed and have documentation?

Review whether students would be a safety issue within Meade School District.”

Pioneer: Are expelled students prohibited from attending any school event or activity, on or off school grounds?

Easton: “During expulsion, students are not to be on school grounds for any reason.”

Wormstadt: “Meade, same as Spearfish, and we also note this includes away events outside of the district.”

Pioneer: “How many students have been expelled from your district over the last 5 years?

Easton: “2”

Wormstadt: “4”

title: SDSU Extension encourages  testing forage nitrate levels
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: High nitrate levels in hay and forage can pose serious health risks to livestock, particularly pregnant animals and ruminants such as cattle. Nitrate test strips can give producers a quick, low-cost screening tool to estimate the nitrate levels in their hay and forage. Courtesy image
_full_text:
SDSU Extension encourages  testing forage nitrate levels
High nitrate levels in hay and forage can pose serious health risks to livestock, particularly pregnant animals and ruminants such as cattle. Nitrate test strips can give producers a quick, low-cost screening tool to estimate the nitrate levels in their hay and forage. Courtesy image 

BROOKINGS – South Dakota State University Extension is encouraging producers to test the nitrate levels in their forages.

High nitrate levels in hay and forage can pose serious health risks to livestock, particularly pregnant animals and ruminants such as cattle. Nitrate test strips can give producers a quick, low-cost screening tool to estimate the nitrate levels in their hay and forage. 

Producers who suspect elevated nitrate levels or who receive high strip-test readings should consult a veterinarian, SDSU Extension field specialist, or certified forage-testing laboratory for assistance interpreting results and developing safe feeding strategies.

Environmental conditions including drought stress, frost, cloudy weather, hail damage, or heavy nitrogen fertilization can increase nitrate accumulation in plants. Because nitrate toxicity can lead to reduced performance, illness or death in livestock, testing forage before feeding is an important management practice.

“Don’t let a preventable nitrate issue turn valuable forage into a costly liability,” said Parker Witt, SDSU Extension Crop-Livestock Systems Field Specialist. “Free nitrate testing through SDSU Extension helps forage producers preserve feed value, and livestock owners make informed management decisions before animal health, forage utilization or profitability are affected.”

Nitrate testing is available at the SDSU Extension regional centers in Aberdeen, Lemmon, Mitchell, Pierre, Rapid City, Sioux Falls, Watertown and Winner; Berg Agricultural Hall and Raven Precision Agriculture Center on the SDSU campus in Brookings; and at the Bennett County, Butte County, Clay County, Fall River County and Haakon County offices. To learn more, visit extension.sdstate.edu/nitrate-quiktest-forages.
