title: SD Attorney General joins bipartisan coalition urging Congress to continue legal services for veterans, rural communities
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: PIERRE  — South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley announced he has joined a bipartisan coalition of 40 attorneys general in urging Congressional leaders to continue funding the Legal Services Corporation (LSC), the nation’s largest funder of civil legal aid for low-income Americans.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

PIERRE  — South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley announced he has joined a bipartisan coalition of 40 attorneys general in urging Congressional leaders to continue funding the Legal Services Corporation (LSC), the nation’s largest funder of civil legal aid for low-income Americans.

 “Everyone, regardless of their income level, is entitled to equal justice under the law,” said Attorney General Jackley. “Continued federal funding for LSC helps ensure our justice system works for everyone.”

In a letter to Congressional appropriations leaders, the coalition asked Congress to include continued funding for LSC in the fiscal year 2027 Commerce, Justice, Science, and Related Agencies Appropriations bill. The coalition emphasized that LSC plays a critical role in ensuring access to justice for people who cannot afford legal representation in civil matters and remains a wise investment of federal resources.

Created by Congress in 1974, LSC supports a nationwide network of 129 independent legal aid organizations operating more than 900 offices in every state, the District of Columbia, and U.S. territories. Nearly 95% of LSC’s federal funding is distributed directly to local legal aid providers that help millions of Americans each year address critical civil legal issues involving housing, family safety, consumer protection, veterans’ benefits, and disaster recovery.

The letter was led by the attorneys general of Colorado, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, and Tennessee. Other Attorneys General joining are from: Alaska, American Samoa, Arizona, California, Connecticut, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Georgia, Hawaii, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, the Northern Mariana Islands, Oklahoma, Oregon, Rhode Island, the U.S. Virgin Islands, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, West Virginia, Wisconsin, and Wyoming.

title: Newell state Rep addresses charges
byline: By John Hult South Dakota Searchlight
description: Rep. Travis Ismay, R-Newell, listens to a committee hearing on Jan. 20, at the South Dakota Capitol in Pierre. Photo by Makenzie Huber, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Newell state Rep addresses charges
Rep. Travis Ismay, R-Newell, listens to a committee hearing on Jan. 20, at the South Dakota Capitol in Pierre. Photo by Makenzie Huber, South Dakota Searchlight 

NEWELL — A Republican state lawmaker from Newell was indicted and arrested on a felony charge of intentional damage to a public road this week.

Rep. Travis Ismay, 48, was arrested Wednesday morning and released on a $500 bail bond. The crime he’s accused of committing is a felony that carries up to two years in prison and a $4,000 fine.

Ismay declined to offer details Thursday to South Dakota Searchlight on the alleged incident, citing his search for a lawyer and the ongoing nature of the Butte County criminal case. 

Ismay said he hopes to tell his side of the story eventually, and he wasn’t aware of the existence of the law he’s accused of breaking.

“When it all comes out, I pray that everyone will write about it,” Ismay said.

Ismay’s indictment doesn’t offer details on the incident, aside from saying that the crime allegedly occurred on Friday — three days after he won the Republican nomination to seek reelection to his District 28B state House seat. He’s unopposed in the Nov. 3 general election.

A Butte County grand jury took testimony from a sheriff’s deputy, a highway department employee and a Butte County resident before issuing the indictment.

The law has been on the books since 1877, and was last modified in 1939. It can apply to “every person who intentionally digs up, removes, displaces, breaks, or otherwise injures or destroys any public highway or bridge.”

Including Ismay’s case, there have been seven such charges filed against five individuals in the past 10 years in South Dakota, according to the Unified Judicial System.

Neither the Butte County sheriff nor Butte County state’s attorney immediately returned calls to Searchlight on Thursday.

Ismay has no criminal record in South Dakota beyond a few traffic citations, but he’s sparred with Butte County officials.

In 2023, the year before he was first elected to the Legislature, Ismay was among the leaders of a group of Butte County residents who circulated a petition aimed at removing four commissioners from office over the county’s handling of medical marijuana ordinances. Ismay would go on to unsuccessfully attempt to put a repeal of the state’s voter-backed medical marijuana law on the 2024 ballot, and to introduce a bill in 2025 meant to accomplish the same goal. That medical pot bill failed.

During each of his two years in Pierre, Ismay brought bills to allow citizens to recall county commissioners. During hearings on those bills, Ismay spoke of being ejected from county commission meetings for actions he described as exercising free speech. Both bills failed.

No trial date has been set in Ismay’s case.

title: Are the Black Hills becoming bear country again?
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: This black bear was captured on a home surveillance camera in the Sandstone subdivision in Spearfish last week. Courtesy image
_full_text:
Are the Black Hills becoming bear country again?
This black bear was captured on a home surveillance camera in the Sandstone subdivision in Spearfish last week. Courtesy image 

SPEARFISH — No, the bear captured on a security camera in Spearfish’s Sandstone neighborhood was not AI.

Yes, we do have more and more bear sightings in the Black Hills.

Are they calling the Northern Hills home? Certainly, at times, but always? Maybe.

On Friday, and then again Saturday, numerous security cameras captured images of a black bear ambling through yards in the Sandstone neighborhood.

Once upon a time, bears, including grizzly bears, were widespread throughout the Black Hills. Lt. Col George Armstrong Custer even killed a grizzly bear during his 1874 expedition through the Hills. Grizzlies have long since been exterminated from the area. 

Now when a bear is spotted, it is the smaller black bear.

Bear sightings in the Black Hills are infrequent but growing in number. Most sightings occur in the spring.

South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks officials said the sightings have been state-wide.

“GF&P staff have taken reports of black bears in South Dakota for the last several years. Most of the reports come from western South Dakota, but there have been confirmed sightings of black bears in eastern South Dakota as well,” said Nick Harrington, spokesman for the GF&P. “Over the last 5 years, GF&P staff have confirmed bears sightings in all portions of the Black Hills as well as a few counties in western South Dakota outside of the Black Hills” 

“Based on the presence of identifying characteristics such as ear tags or color phases, staff believe individual bears persist in South Dakota for a short period of time before moving along,” he continued. “There are likely only one or 2 individual transient bears at any given time. Many of the recent reports occur in late May or June, which is the breeding season for black bears. Confirmed bear sightings typically occur very randomly with significant distance between sightings typical of males searching for females across the landscape.”

So, are the bears calling the Northern Hills home year-round?

Wyoming’s Bear Lodge Range, which sits just west of the South Dakota state line, is home to black bears. They are hunted annually. They can easily walk to South Dakota.

While most of the bears seen in South Dakota are young, the one seen this weekend was a bit older. Perhaps 4 years old, bear hunters told the Pioneer.

Bob Speirs, a hunting guide in the Spearfish area, was shown a video 3-4 years ago of a sow, a female bear, with that year’s cubs. The video was taken just north of Spearfish. 

This week, he was shown a photo of a different bear, near his home north of Spearfish.

While most bears have had little interaction with people in the Northern Hills, some bears have found easy access to human impacts.

“There have been instances that bears have gotten into people’s trash or chicken coops, but the bears have moved on very shortly after these incidents,” Harrington said. 

On May 13, 2023, a bear ripped into Annesse Brockley’s chicken coops in the Mountain Plains subdivision on the outskirts of Spearfish. It killed 2 birds and ate all the eggs.

The following day Wyatt and Holly Hansen had a bear at their home on Hill Street.

It killed 5 ducks, a turkey and more than 10 chickens, leaving only 8 of her flock alive.

“All around there were animals and animal parts. It was really gross,” Holly said.

Her chickens were housed in a coop and pen, about a half-acre in size, behind their barn.

She said you could see tracks in the mud and where it tried to climb over an eight-foot-tall fence.

“But then you could see where it just went over the wood pile,” she said.

“We’ve heard that bears will occasionally be seen. But the amount of people who’ve reached out, there are so many bear sightings that go unreported,” she added.

That is something the GF&P would like to fix.

“Individuals are asked to please report any bear sightings to the Rapid City GF&P office at (605) 394-2310,” Harrington said. 

This will help them get a better idea of the bear activity and population.

Harrington encouraged people to visit bearwise.org for tips on securing food attractants and other bear related information.

title: Meade County partners with road district for maintenance
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — With more than 1,100 miles of roads to maintain in Meade County, partnering with area road districts can make sense, commissioners said.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

STURGIS — With more than 1,100 miles of roads to maintain in Meade County, partnering with area road districts can make sense, commissioners said. 

On Tuesday, the Meade County Commission approved that kind of an agreement with Rolling Dice Road District. The agreement has been in the works since April, when Rolling Dice Road District President Gary Mewes asked the commission to consider a joint road project to maintain parts of Dyess Avenue, 223rd Street, and Lucky Lane. 

According to the agreement, the road district will provide road stabilizer material for Dyess Avenue, magnesium chloride water for 223rd Street and Lucky Lane, a water supply and water truck, and some personnel to operate equipment. In return, the county will provide the labor and equipment to do blade preparation for Dyess Avenue, 223rd Street, and Lucky Lane, as well as provide packer equipment for compaction on the roadways. 

Meade County Highway Superintendent Troy Eastman said the agreement makes sense, and solves several problems with Dyess Avenue. 

“They have a large hill there that runs north that has always been a challenge to maintain, and we’d like to add base stabilization to it and put really good gravel down, at their expense,” he said. “They’re basically looking for us to do the work and they’re going to pay for the base stabilization and the materials we’re going to put into it. That way it will be way less work for them and it will last years versus just constant maintenance. It’s a win-win for both of us.” 

Mewes said the road district is very happy with the agreement, because they have funds available to buy the materials. 

“To me, this makes perfect sense,” Commissioner Talbot Wieczorek said. “I applaud it and I think it helps everybody long term.”

title: Shocking snake encounters  offer canines lifetime protection from rattler bites
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Experts say the key to effective rattlesnake avoidance training is the presence of a live rattlesnake that has been defanged for safety. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Rattler.JPG
Experts say the key to effective rattlesnake avoidance training is the presence of a live rattlesnake that has been defanged for safety. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — It doesn’t work if the snake is fake. It doesn’t work if the snake is dead. For rattlesnake avoidance training to really take, and help both dogs and their owners to identify the threat of a live rattler on a trail or in a field, the snake must be alive. It also has to be a rattlesnake — bull snakes and garter snakes neither smell nor behave in quite the same ways.

That’s why Gereth Stillman of Still’s Kennels traps and defangs live rattlesnakes for his avoidance clinics.

The snake he brought to VFW Post 5860 in Spearfish was called “Buzz.” Buzz was willing to rattle his tail, strike at will, and provide the tire-going-flat hissing noise that could really demonstrate the potential menace of a wild rattlesnake.

Despite his ability to reach striking distances up to half the length of his body, Buzz’s efforts alone are not quite enough for a dog to learn to avoid snakes, Stillman said.

Every canine has a distinct personality, different drives, and motivations. Some dogs may be curious and want to sniff every snake they encounter. Some might like to hunt snakes, and be tempted to pick up and shake a rattlesnake in the wild. Both choices could be fatal for a dog.

So, Stillman has an assistant place an e-collar on dogs during avoidance clinics.

Each dog owner or handler is encouraged to approach from the downwind side of the free-roaming, but carefully monitored snake, then walk their pet straight up to, and ideally over the top of Buzz.

In some cases, the fangless serpent would uncoil and strike the unsuspecting dog on approach. All the better, Stillman said.

“It can’t hurt it,” Stillman said. “I want the dog to smell the snake. I want the dog to see the snake.”

As the snake strikes, he uses the e-collar to deliver a single shock to the participating pet.

The dog then learns that rattlesnakes are “high voltage.”

“I want it to hear the snake. Then I want the dog to be curious enough to sniff the snake. At that point when the dog is concentrating on the snake, we shock it, and the dog knows the snake did that to them, and they want nothing to do with the snake anymore,” Stillman said.

Some dogs didn’t notice the snake until they stepped on or over them. Once shocked, many leapt high into the air or bolted back into their owner’s arms. Handlers were instructed to have their dogs on a non-retractable, short lead, and prepared ahead of time to manage their startled canines.

Walking away a little shaken, the dogs would have their collars removed and wait for about 20 minutes for the second half of the training process. “Proofing,” as Stillman calls it, is perhaps the most important part of any clinic.

For proofing, Stillman’s assistant relocated Buzz to a different place on the VFW lawn. Now, each owner in turn would approach the snake with their dog for a second time — no e-collar on this time — and closely monitor their pet’s reaction.

To a one, each dog that attended the VFW clinic reacted very differently — first to the smell, then to the sight, of the poised-to-strike snake in the grass.

Stillman said this has as much value for pets as it does for owners. For one thing, the training generally keeps dogs from putting themselves in a position to suffer a snakebite. Their owners have the added benefit of understanding how their dog’s body language changes when they see a rattler on the trail. That comprehension could have life-saving consequences.

“That (reaction) is important for the owner. Sometimes they’ll hide behind the owners. Sometimes dogs will stop the minute they see it and bark at it. Some will see it, and they want back in the car already,” Stillman said. “We had a German Shorthair 3 years ago that pointed the snake. I had to explain to the owner if he is out pheasant hunting, if a bird doesn’t fly up real quick, don’t go kicking around, because it might be a snake.”

The training takes less than an hour, but Stillman said a single shock, paired with a snake encounter in a controlled, safe environment, has lasting impact.

“This training lasts a lifetime,” Stillman said. He’s had clients come back to clinics just to re-test their dogs. He has offered rattlesnake avoidance training in the Northern Hills for 10 years now.

Prior to that, he had trained dogs for more than 40 years. For three years, he set up trainings with a friend who ran a kennel in Las Cruces, N.M., before leading the trainings himself.  In that time, Stillman said he has never had a re-test failure.

“I moved here 13 years ago from Alaska,” Stillman said. “I’ve hunted South Dakota for the last 25 years, so I understood we were going to have rattlesnakes here. We moved down here, and I was amazed that nobody was putting on rattlesnake avoidance training.”

The need this year might be especially prominent. Nate Keck, the president of the Black Hills Chapter of Pheasants Forever, who hosted the avoidance clinic last week, said he’s already seen more snakes than usual this season.

Keck also encouraged the public to keep an eye out for future clinics — Pheasants Forever is likely to host a repeat event sometime soon.

title: A fast moving problem: City, law enforcement grapple with growing popularity of youth e-dirt bikes
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Heath Eggleston describes an incident earlier this week, when his very young daughter was hit by an electric dirt bike on the rec path in Spearfish. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
A fast moving problem City, law enforcement grapple with growing popularity of youth e-dirt bikes
Heath Eggleston describes an incident earlier this week, when his very young daughter was hit by an electric dirt bike on the rec path in Spearfish. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — After a young girl was allegedly hit by an e-Dirt Bike on the rec path in Spearfish, attorney Eric Nies prepared an opinion that was hand-delivered to the mayor and city council on the legality of the vehicles. In his view, state law prohibits the use of the motorized vehicles on the rec path, and makes their use a misdemeanor.

“The prohibition,” Nies writes, “should be enforced immediately.”

Since weather conditions have improved, children under the age of 16 have been increasingly spotted riding electric-powered two and three-wheeled vehicles on streets, sidewalks, and the rec path in Spearfish.

The mayor and members of the city council acknowledged that public concern has been mounting about the safety of the kids on the vehicles and the community members who also use the city’s transportation network.

“I don’t know if the 10-year-olds in Spearfish had a really good Christmas and got a bunch of these, but it appears that 2 years ago this wasn’t so much of a problem. But it has been a busy spring. I think that if the question is posed, why enforce it now? My home is along the rec path, and I am seeing more conflict, more complaints,” said Dylan Clarkson.

Often referenced as e-bikes in public discussion, the vehicles generating the most concern from residents lack pedals — making them e-dirt bikes, rather than e-bikes.

Nies wrote that the term electric bicycle is defined in state law. E-bikes are “bicycle(s) or tricycle(s) equipped with a seat or saddle, with operable pedals for propulsion, and with an electric motor of 750 watts or less.”

Wednesday, Heath Eggleston approached the city council and told them his 5-year-old daughter had been hit by an e-dirt bike on the rec path earlier this week. She did not suffer serious injuries, but in his view that doesn’t mean the danger shouldn’t be immediately addressed.

The council briefly discussed implementing an ordinance to ban the vehicles on the bike path, but concern emerged that kids on the vehicles might be even more unsafe if they moved from sidewalks to streets.

“I think that if we were to go down the road of meeting or trying to create a city ordinance, in the opinion of the council, which you all have, is not necessary. I think we get better cover relying on state statute that can be enforced now,” Clarkson said.  He witnessed the incident on the bike path this week.

Clarkson and Ryan Wordeman approached Nies to ask for an opinion, in hopes of finding a better definition of and a solution to the problem.

Nies said he does not believe the city needs to pass an ordinance. State law is already clear, in his view, that the e-Dirt Bikes can’t be on sidewalks or the rec path.

“I am not taking any position on whether any other vehicle is allowed on the rec path or if e-dirt bikes are legal on city streets,” Nies writes.

“The question is: how are we going to overcome this? Can we help with signage or public education?  I don’t know if there are enforcement measures that can be taken, but ultimately (this problem) has been growing,” Wordeman said.

Spearfish Police Chief Collin Smith said enforcement is complicated because the issue involves minors. 

“Do you want us to place criminal charges on a 10-year-old? And then you think about it, is that even something we can do? There are other statutes at play here that can keep us from doing that. There are unintended consequences to that,” Smith said.

“There are so many moving parts. What type of bike is it? Do I have the constitutional right to be able to detain this person? I’ve got to physically have this bike in hand to see what it is. There are so many moving parts, where the technology has advanced quicker than the statute.”

Smith asked for patience and grace from the community while the city tries to find the best statutory solution. 

“I understand people keep turning to the police department on this, but please, patience and grace. Understand we have restrictions too. Just like I can’t pull somebody over because I feel like it. Everybody, including children, have constitutional rights.”

Speakers at Wednesday’s study session asked for an immediate solution.

“I am told that I can’t do anything to protect my daughter on the bike path. I’m told the police cannot based on current rules, so either the rules need to change or we need to stand up for the rules we have already,” Eggleston said. “My family lives on the bike path now, and we are afraid to go on the bike path because of the incident we had. I am not sure how we want that to go. Whatever we can do to protect our children on their bikes is what needs to happen.”

In Belle Fourche, police chief Ryan Cherveny said there haven’t been any negative incidents involving either e-bikes or e-dirt bikes yet, but he noted the vehicles are popular in his community too.

Cherveny said he’s been watching a case in California in which a mother was charged with involuntary manslaughter after her son hit and killed an 81-year-old man on a sidewalk on an e-motorcycle she purchased. The threat, Cherveny said, is serious.

So far in Belle Fourche, the police are working to educate parents and children to try and promote safety before an incident.

Smith said the same has been true in Spearfish for roughly the last 6 months.

“When we see these on the road, we will stop them. I was at a gas station and saw one and stopped and talked to the young man and found out that he just honestly didn’t know what the laws were or what the restrictions were. Neither did his parents. I gave him a ride home and educated the father on the rules and regulations on this,” Smith said. “It has honestly advanced so quickly that education and laws are just trying to catch up.”

title: Jack Kucera : Lead native to be  inducted into S.D. Hall of Fame
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Jack Kucera poses with his wife, Vianne. Kucera will be recognized for his philanthropic works when he is inducted into the South Dakota Hall of Fame in September. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
0613 Jack Kucera and wife.tif
Jack Kucera poses with his wife, Vianne. Kucera will be recognized for his philanthropic works when he is inducted into the South Dakota Hall of Fame in September. Courtesy photo 

LEAD — After a lifetime of success in business, almost everything Jack Kucera does is geared toward giving back to the Air Force Academy that changed his life, and working to provide opportunities for youth. 

A Lead native, Kucera will be inducted into the South Dakota Hall of Fame in September. Kucera is being recognized for his philanthropic works across several states, as well as for being an industry visionary for his innovation within large commercial and industrial construction spaces. 

A graduate of Lead-Deadwood High School, Kucera attended the U.S. Air Force Academy in Colorado Springs, with the understanding that upon graduation he would be commissioned as a military officer. However, just months before graduating in 1978, Kucera suffered a severe back injury and his plans for military service were derailed. The Air Force allowed him to graduate with his degree in civil engineering, despite his inability to follow through with a commissioning. 

After graduating, Kucera went on to build a successful career in the world of commercial and industrial air conditioning, building automation and energy services. He helped build Climatec from a mere 7 employees to 850, growing the company to span across Arizona, Nevada, California and Texas. When Bosch purchased part of the company, Kucera retained the HVAC equipment sales portion and re-branded it as Varitec. He also started two major air conditioning businesses — Huntair and BasX. Kucera later sold those businesses. He is currently semi-retired, and he serves as an executive adviser to Japan-based Daikin, the largest air conditioning manufacturer in the world. 

Throughout his success in business, Kucera always kept his obligation to the Air Force Academy at the forefront of his mind, and that shaped his outlook and drive for philanthropy. 

“I wasn’t commissioned to be an Air Force officer, and I carry a sort of Catholic guilt,” he said. “I received this amazing gift of being able to go to the Air Force Academy. When you have an opportunity like that, and you don’t pay it back by serving, I sort of felt compelled to find another way to pay it back. For us, that has been by providing educational opportunities for kids to get ahead in life, by having opportunities that they might not otherwise have had.”

Kucera’s philanthropy is the primary reason for his induction into the South Dakota Hall of Fame. He was involved with creating the Air Force Academy Foundation in Colorado Springs, for which he raised $330 million from 20,000 donors over the course of 6 years, and donated $10 million to renovate the football stadium. He has also piloted more than 400 charity flights, primarily flying football coaches from the Air Force Academy around the country to meet with athletes.

“People ask me why I want to fly the coaches around recruiting,” Kucera said. “They think it’s about football. I’ve taken the Air Force Academy coaches to see kids and we’ll do 20-25 stops in a week, and the coaches have come back at times and said ‘jeez, I went into that neighborhood and I wasn’t too sure. I went into that house and they didn’t have anything but a couch in the living room. So, you take kids like that and you expose them to opportunities like a service academy, or just maybe the opportunity for kids to attend school that never would have.” 

In Arizona, Kucera and his wife, Vianne, were jointly recognized by the Arizona Diamondback Foundation with the Lee T. Hanley Community Leadership award, which is given for making a charitable impact on the community.  

But it’s his work in South Dakota that has Kucera’s heart. Kucera is a member of the Spearfish Canyon Foundation board, and he co-chairs the capital campaign for the Historic Homestake Opera House. Kucera said that as a Homestake electrician, his father once ran the electricity for the opera house, and his wife’s grandmother once played the piano for the “talkies,” or silent movies   held in the theater. He has also actively supported the Children’s Home Society, and he is an active member of the South Dakota Community Foundation. 

“I am absolutely amazed by the organization, the breadth of their success and their reach into communities all over South Dakota,” Kucera said about his work with the South Dakota Community Foundation. “I’ve been kind of blown away by how effective South Dakota Community Foundation is, and how efficient they are. The number of funds they manage for people and the job they do is pretty remarkable.” 

Kucera is one of only 60 Air Force Academy graduates to be named as a distinguished graduate, out of the overall 58,000 graduates from the Academy. That was an amazing honor when it happened, but Kucera said the induction into the South Dakota Hall of Fame is an even greater honor, because it means youth in his home state will be able to see his many accomplishments and learn that they can also achieve great things.  

“I was probably more delighted than I was with the Air Force Academy Distinguished graduate recognition, mostly because it’s my home state,” he said. “I made my business career in Arizona, California, Oregon, Texas, and New Mexico. But Phoenix has never felt like home. Home has always been South Dakota. 

“I’ve been aware of the South Dakota Hall of Fame’s mission, especially their Legends of Learning,” he continued. “Their bottom line is they create profiles of South Dakotans, they database those and make it available to kids. I want South Dakota kids to be able to search that database for whatever they’re interested in — arts, engineering, medicine — or whatever it might be, and see the profiles of people that came before them and know that they can do this too. They say the names don’t matter. It matters a lot to me and my family at the moment. But for some kid who thinks he wants to go to a service academy, so he puts that in the search engine and these profiles pop up … my name won’t matter, but my story will. I think being from a small state like South Dakota, sometimes our kids don’t think they can do big things. That’s just not true.” 

Kucera said his involvement with philanthropy is specifically targeted to try and change the trajectory of children’s lives, and usually tied to some kind of education. 

“Our lives’ trajectory are changed by education,” he said. “So, I think that almost everything I do is geared toward providing opportunities for young people. My wife is as deeply committed as I am. To give young people an opportunity that they might not otherwise have, and see what happens in their life after that.”

The South Dakota Hall of Fame induction ceremony is scheduled for Sept. 11-12, in Chamberlain. The public is invited to attend, and tickets will go on sale in July.

BELLE FOURCHE — At about 10:30 a.m. on Wednesday, a gas leak was reported along Highway 34 in Belle Fourche. Montana-Dakota Utilities Company responded and detected a “flammable volume” of gas above the highway, according to Belle Fourche Police Chief Ryan Cherveny. 

Cherveny said the police department quickly assisted to shut down the highway from the intersection of Highway 85 to Helmer Road, while MDU addressed the leak. Cherveny said the odor of gas was detectable in the area.

title: New digs for The Detail Shop: Decade-old Spearfish business makes  a new home in the industrial park
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — Dane Graham opened The Detail Shop along Colorado Boulevard in Spearfish for a few reasons. There is no better to way, he said, to meet cool people and encounter cool cars. Business ownership also offered a gateway to financial security, which he found especially enticing in October of 2014 — when the shop opened for the first time.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — Dane Graham opened The Detail Shop along Colorado Boulevard in Spearfish for a few reasons. There is no better to way, he said, to meet cool people and encounter cool cars. Business ownership also offered a gateway to financial security, which he found especially enticing in October of 2014 — when the shop opened for the first time.

“I found out that I was going to have a kid, and I was like, I need to man up. I need to provide a lifestyle. Maybe not do the rigmarole of working hourly,” Graham said. “I did that, and I built my business.”

By 2014, Graham already had experience in automotive detailing. It was a skill he picked up straight out of high school.

“I’ve been doing this for 20-plus years. I’ve always been of the mindset that if you’re not learning something new, you’re dying, so I have always looked for more to keep myself busy,” Graham said.

That’s why, over time, he has expanded the offerings of The Detail Shop to include window tinting, ceramic coating, and paint protection film application.

“My whole goal was to be a one-stop shop,” Graham said. “I always just wanted the ability to act on something if a customer said they are really looking into those. I just wanted to be that guy who could say, ‘I can do that too.’“

Now, that one-stop-shop has moved to Spearfish’s industrial park. Graham moved out of his old space at the end of May, and opened in the brand new building at 3165 Venture Court at the very beginning of June.

“It is just a whole new change. Everything is clean. Everything is well put together,” Graham said.

Despite the new building, Graham said his “MO is still the same.”

“Bring me something trashed, and I can make it pretty again,” Graham said. “If you’re not happy with your car, bring it to me, and I can probably make you happy with it again.”

title: Visit Spearfish marks midpoint  of its 18th year of operation
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — On the 130th anniversary of the congressional establishment of the D.C. Booth National Historic Fish Hatchery and Archives, Visit Spearfish awarded both the hatchery and the non-profit Booth Society its Tip of the Spear award for 2025.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — On the 130th anniversary of the congressional establishment of the D.C. Booth National Historic Fish Hatchery and Archives, Visit Spearfish awarded both the hatchery and the non-profit Booth Society its Tip of the Spear award for 2025. 

Visit Spearfish also recognized the lasting impact of outgoing executive director Mistie Caldwell and awarded Black Hills State University Assistant Athletic Director Nicky Winterstein the Friend of Spearfish award Wednesday morning.

Each year, Visit Spearfish hosts a celebratory breakfast to report on and mark milestones in destination marketing for the community.

“As we approach this midway point of the 18th year of operation, we continue to evolve, listen, learn, and adjust,” Caldwell said. “We consider it to be an honor to serve the city of Spearfish as the official destination marketing management organization.”

A fond farewell to Mistie Caldwell

Since 2009, Visit Spearfish has helped attract tourists to the city. Caldwell has been at the helm of the organization since the beginning.

“Visit Spearfish has been privileged to have been led by a tireless, dedicated, compassionate, collaborative, influential leader in Mistie Caldwell,” said Ali Eddy, the president of the board of Visit Spearfish. “Mistie has consistently demonstrated exceptional leadership, determination, and selflessness in advancing tourism while preserving the unique character and values that make Spearfish such a special place.”

Eddy presented Caldwell with a Termesphere in recognition of her time with Visit Spearfish, which Caldwell tearfully accepted.  

“It’s been my honor and my pleasure,” said Caldwell, who recently accepted a job with the Spearfish School District. 

Eddy also noted, under Caldwell’s leadership, Visit Spearfish helped drive enough traffic to the city to bring in $1 million in hospitality tax revenue in 2024 alone.

A slower year for visitation in 2025

In 2025, the city saw a 5.6% decrease in hospitality tax revenue.

“It was a softer economic year for tourism, but we’re optimistic about 2026,” she said. 

Caldwell said snow, or the lack thereof this winter, may have been a factor.

“White gold is necessary not only for tourism, but for the betterment of the Black Hills and the conservation of our natural resources.”

Caldwell said, as tourist season truly kicks off in the city, Visit Spearfish believes 2026 could be a strong year for visitation, and the organization has planned accordingly.

“We want to demonstrate meaningful, measurable marketing outcomes. Through evolving reporting that more accurately determines effective economic growth,” Caldwell said.

Visit Spearfish is funded by the city’s BBB (board, bed, booze) tax and a $2 per room fee that is collected by all nine of the city’s hotels with 36 or more rooms. Spearfish Canyon Lodge, which has a Lead address, also voluntarily contributes to Visit Spearfish’s work — bringing the total number of participating hotels to 10. 

Phoebe Caldwell, the director of marketing at Visit Spearfish, said the organization takes the stewardship of taxpayer dollars very seriously.

Visit Spearfish helped support 63 community events in 2025 — those events had a total estimated attendance of 93,000. Through its website, Visit Spearfish highlights 160 local businesses — including 105 eateries, coffee shops and bars, 33 venues and activities, and 22 lodging businesses. It distributed more than 24,000 visitor guides.

Phoebe said Visit Spearfish tracks where visitors to its website and the city come from. The top three states that generate web traffic are South Dakota, Colorado, and Nebraska. The top 3 states visitors come from are South Dakota, Minnesota, and Wisconsin.

“Destination marketing and management is much more than placing ads in magazines and running a visitor’s center,” Phoebe said. “Success comes from careful planning, thoughtful execution, and thorough review of results to make sure that we make better decisions in the future for ad purchases.”

Honoring the “Tip of the Spear”

Quality of place is perhaps the greatest driver of visitorship to Spearfish, Eddy said. The people in the city are the ones that create and maintain that quality of place.

“Each year Visit Spearfish recognizes outstanding individuals and businesses for their contributions to the city of Spearfish,” Eddy said. This year’s recipient is a village. It is not an individual organization and not just about tourism. Rather, it’s all these things plus education, advocacy and conservation.”

The 2025 recipient of the Tip of the Spear award is the D.C. Booth Historic Fish Hatchery and Archives and the Booth Society.

“It is about something that attracts hundreds of thousands of people each year across the Black Hills region, the country and several other countries outside of the United States, but the influence of this year’s Tip of the Spear award recipient goes beyond the impact to tourism,” Eddy said. “It impacts the entire community, providing quality free family entertainment and community engagement.”

Visit Spearfish honors the 2025 “Friend of Spearfish”

The Friend of Spearfish award honors an individual or business that helps support tourism in ways that may not be very forward facing.

“There are folks who make things special with their own talents and skills, facing accolades in the past,” Caldwell said. “This person at Black Hills State University is rarely seen. They’re working the concession stand, or shoveling snow, or things like that. I will tell you, if you ever encounter this person, they’re wearing a huge smile and they are working at a pace that appears as though he’s either stealing a base; he is never dismissive if you need something from him. Never without a solution; doesn’t see many problems as real problems. We are lucky to be able to work with this person.”

That person is Nicky Winterstein. A former member of the Spearfish Sasquatch baseball team, Winterstein is now the assistant athletic director for events and internal operations at Black Hills State University. Winterstein was not able to attend Wednesday’s breakfast, but BHSU President Steve Elliott accepted the award on Winterstein’s behalf.

title: Sturgis Hospital Auxiliary raises $8,240  for new podiatry chair at Monument Health
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Sturgis Hospital Auxiliary presented a check for $8,240 to Mark Schmidt, President, Monument Health Sturgis to purchase a much-needed podiatry chair for the Sturgis Long Term Care facility and the entire Monument facility Monday during their monthly meeting.  From left are: Ranae Pickar, Renee Armstrong Mark Schmidt, Patty Kennedy,  Sheri Johnson, and Cindy Voyles.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
Sturgis Hospital Auxiliary raises $8,240  for new podiatry chair at Monument Health
The Sturgis Hospital Auxiliary presented a check for $8,240 to Mark Schmidt, President, Monument Health Sturgis to purchase a much-needed podiatry chair for the Sturgis Long Term Care facility and the entire Monument facility Monday during their monthly meeting.  From left are: Ranae Pickar, Renee Armstrong Mark Schmidt, Patty Kennedy,  Sheri Johnson, and Cindy Voyles.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

STURGIS — The Monument Health Sturgis Hospital Auxiliary (MHSHA) presented a check on Monday for $8,240 to Monument Health Sturgis President Mark Schmidt to purchase a new podiatry chair, providing enhanced care for patients throughout the hospital and long-term care facility.

The funds were raised through several community-supported events, including the Spring Fling, bingo nights, bake sales, and a quilt raffle.

Margaret Hunt, president of the MHSHA, said the podiatry chair will be used for both inpatient and outpatient services, as well as for residents in the hospital’s long-term care facility.

Schmidt expressed his appreciation for the auxiliary’s efforts and the impact the new equipment will have on patient care.

“We brought this need to the auxiliary a few months ago as we looked at equipment necessary to expand some of our services,” Schmidt said. “We provide wound care and foot care services, and this chair will help us better serve patients both in the hospital and in our care center.”

He noted that the chair’s mobility and design will make it easier to provide treatment while reducing the need to move patients.

“It’s difficult at times to move patients, especially those in long-term care,” Schmidt said. “Having equipment that can be moved where it’s needed will improve patient comfort and help us deliver care more efficiently.”

Schmidt praised the Auxiliary for quickly embracing the project and successfully raising the needed funds.

“They accepted the challenge, worked hard, and accomplished it in a short period of time,” he said. “A lot of the money was raised through volunteer efforts such as serving meals and hosting bingo events. We’re very grateful for everything they do and excited about the difference this equipment will make.”

Hunt said the auxiliary is already looking ahead to its next fundraising effort. The organization has been asked to consider helping purchase an ultrasound imaging table for the hospital.

“Having this equipment would facilitate faster patient care during procedures,” Hunt said. “We will begin considering ways to work toward that purchase.”

The donation reflects the auxiliary’s ongoing commitment to supporting healthcare services in the Sturgis community through volunteerism and fundraising efforts.

title: Todd Williams, SD poet, talks water, rebirth, and living in Saudi Arabia
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer
description: RAPID CITY — Todd Williams, a Lead native who splits his time between Rapid City and Saudi Arabia, likes to say that he lived in a desert for 15 years, and then wrote a book about water.
_full_text:
RAPID CITY — Todd Williams, a Lead native who splits his time between Rapid City and Saudi Arabia, likes to say that he lived in a desert for 15 years, and then wrote a book about water.

 Todd Williams author.jpg
Todd Williams’ new poetry collection meditates on loss, nostalgia, and memory. Courtesy photo. 

 AWIH_Cover_CR2.pdf
Courtesy photo. 

That book, “All Water is Holy” was released in April. The poems in “All Water” are lean, sometimes bleak, verse. They are, as the title suggests, mostly concerned with water, but in a variety of forms — floods, swimming pools, and even sweat. 

“All Water Is Holy is my most honest and vulnerable poetry to date, and it contains much of my best writing,” Williams said. “Metaphorically, the water theme is reflective of life in general, but it takes on many forms, many meanings. That’s all kind of lofty, but the poems are largely written in my usual, plain-spoken English.”

The poem “Flight 370 Returns” sees the poem’s narrator watching footage of the wreckage of Flight 370 — probably a reference to Malaysia Flight 370, which departed from its flight path and crashed into the ocean in 2014 — and thinking of all the things he’s lost, including “My first marriage and a relentless belief, that one person could save another, from themselves.”

Williams’ began writing creatively when he was in grade-school. But in 2018, he began submitting his poems for publications — and met with quick success. In 2022, his chapbook, “Objects in the Mirror Are Closer Than They Appear,” won the South Dakota State Poetry Society chapbook competition. (A chapbook is a short publication, often of poetry, that is stitched, rather than bound like a book.) 

Outside of creative writing, Williams edited the Black Hills Pioneer on-and-off from 1985-1999. Williams said that although he thought of himself as a newspaper “lifer,” after a downturn in the newspaper industry, he went to work as a PR specialist. 

Williams now splits his time between Saudi Arabia, where he works, and Rapid City, where he plans to retire in October.

title: Quick picks: Waterside reads
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Quick picks: Waterside reads
Courtesy photo 

The sun is shining, and temperatures are high enough to entice the inclined to beaches, creeks, reservoirs, and rivers to bask in the summer heat. If you’re looking for the perfect book to act as companion on your waterside adventures (even if tanning is the most intrepid activity on your list) we’ve got 6 recommendations from librarians at the Grace Balloch Memorial Library in Spearfish that are perfect for you. 

1. “Tom Lake” by Ann Patchett

Genre: Fiction

In the spring of 2020, Lara’s 3 daughters return to the family’s orchard in Northern Michigan. While picking cherries, they beg their mother to tell them the story of Peter Duke, a famous actor with whom she shared both a stage and a romance years before at a theater company called Tom Lake. As Lara recalls the past, her daughters examine their own lives and relationship with their mother, and are forced to reconsider the world and everything they thought they knew.

2. “The Five Star Weekend” by Elin Hilderbrand

Genre: Romance

Hollis Shaw’s life seems picture-perfect. She’s the creator of the popular food blog Hungry with Hollis and is married to Matthew, a dreamy heart surgeon. But after she and Matthew get into a heated argument one snowy morning, he leaves for the airport and is killed in a car accident. The cracks in Hollis’s perfect life — her strained marriage and her complicated relationship with her daughter, Caroline — grow deeper.

3. “People We Meet on Vacation” by Emily Henry

Genre: Romance

Poppy and Alex. Alex and Poppy. They have nothing in common. She’s a wild child; he wears khakis. She has insatiable wanderlust; he prefers to stay home with a book. And somehow, ever since a fateful car share home from college many years ago, they are the very best of friends. For most of the year they live far apart — she’s in New York City, and he’s in their small hometown — but every summer, for a decade, they have taken one glorious week of vacation together.

4. “The Midnight Feast” by Lucy Foley

Genre: Mystery/Thriller

It’s the opening night of The Manor, and no expense, small or large, has been spared. The infinity pool sparkles; crystal pouches for guests’ healing have been placed in the Seaside Cottages and Woodland Hutches; the “Manor Mule” cocktail (grapefruit, ginger, vodka, and a dash of CBD oil) is being poured with a heavy hand. Everyone is wearing linen.

5. “The God of the Woods” by Liz Moore

Genre: Mystery/Fiction 

Early morning, August 1975: a camp counselor discovers an empty bunk. Its occupant, Barbara Van Laar, has gone missing. Barbara isn’t just any 13-year-old: she’s the daughter of the family that owns the summer camp and employs most of the region’s residents. And this isn’t the first time a Van Laar child has disappeared. Barbara’s older brother similarly vanished 14 years ago, never to be found.

6. “Mother-Daughter Murder Night” by Nina Simon

Genre: Mystery

A lighthearted whodunnit about a grandmother-mother-daughter trio of amateur sleuths. Gilmore Girls , but with murder. 

High-powered businesswoman Lana Rubicon has a lot to be proud her keen intelligence, impeccable taste, and the L.A. real estate empire she’s built. But when she finds herself trapped 300 miles north of the city, convalescing in a sleepy   coastal town with her adult daughter Beth and teenage granddaughter Jack, Lana is stuck counting otters instead of square footage — and hoping that boredom won’t kill her before the cancer does.

title: The Mercy Sloane: Chapter 7
byline: By Eliza Blue A work of serialized fiction, special to the Pioneer
description: When Arlo threw open the screen door with a bang, stuttering about the new bride in the store…needed a job…covered in dirt…Marla felt her lips tighten. She was in the middle of scrubbing the kitchen floor, a job she did every morning before 8 am (except on Sundays, of course) because you never knew who would stop by unexpectedly. Marla believed that cleanliness was not only next to Godliness, but might actually be the best worldly expression of Godliness. (Which is why she did sometimes secretly scrub on Sundays, but would go to her grave before she admitted it.) Besides, she was proud of those floors. They were the first and still prettiest linoleum in the county.
_full_text:
The Mercy Sloane Chronicles

When Arlo threw open the screen door with a bang, stuttering about the new bride in the store…needed a job…covered in dirt…Marla felt her lips tighten. She was in the middle of scrubbing the kitchen floor, a job she did every morning before 8 am (except on Sundays, of course) because you never knew who would stop by unexpectedly. Marla believed that cleanliness was not only next to Godliness, but might actually be the best worldly expression of Godliness. (Which is why she did sometimes secretly scrub on Sundays, but would go to her grave before she admitted it.) Besides, she was proud of those floors. They were the first and still prettiest linoleum in the county. 

Marla never used a mop. Leaning over, a tea towel apron covering her blouse, her skirt tucked and tied up in back, she would follow the spiraled pink and green floral pattern of the tiles as she worked from north to south, and she would remember the pink roses in her grandparent’s garden back in Wisconsin, the scent as vivid to her as if they were blooming beneath her bent body right then. When the boys were very young, she’d chase them out to help their father, calling after them, “Don’t come back till the floors are dry!” Now they were grown and gone, and though she missed them with such desperation that it sometimes made it hard to breathe, for the half-hour she spent scrubbing, she had the satisfaction of knowing their absence meant the floors would stay clean all day long, and that was not a cold comfort.

Even after 35 years of marriage, Marla still didn’t enjoy the idea of Arlo seeing her on her knees, dirty rags in both hands, so she always waited until he had gone over to the shop or was out doing chores before she began. Which is why, when Arlo surprised her with his sudden re-entry, she was in no mood to be magnanimous.

“Well, just who does this girl think she is?” Marla said out loud while Arlo shuffled in the doorway. When he didn’t reply, she clicked her tongue loudly against the roof of her mouth, hastily pulled her skirt free of its knot and swept off the apron in one motion (and this is why she always dressed for the day before she scrubbed!) then swept past him into the alley.

 Eliza Blue TMC
Eliza Blue 

“Really, Arlo!” she thought to herself, still clucking, but when she put her hand on the door knob of the shop something stilled her–maybe the scent of prairie roses on the summer wind? She’d been a young bride once, too, full of hope and excitement, in love with a young man who knew nothing of the world. He’d learned fast, and so had she, that their dreams were just that–dreams–and reality was a much more broken and wounded thing. This girl would have to learn that too. Her young husband had left heartbroken, Arlo said, cried all the way to the station. And now she and Arlo were expected to pick up the pieces and take this girl in? Marla didn’t think so. 

No. No, they would not be giving this girl a job, that much Marla was sure of.

But the roses and the wind said something different, and when Marla saw Mercy standing behind the counter, Mercy’s cheap blouse and matching skirt already tattered from a week in the wind and the sun, her face sunburned but studiously scrubbed, the rest of her so caked with dust she looked like she’d emerged from a grave, Marla began nodding her head and couldn’t stop. In Mercy’s eyes, Marla saw fear, determination, and something else. Something Marla couldn’t quite name, but she recognized. And while Marla could be cruel in small ways, she’d known enough sweetness in life to make a different choice just then.

“Yes,” she said to Mercy. “Yes, we do need help. You can start tomorrow morning.”

title: Sturgis honors late Mayor Kevin Forrester
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: Rhea Crane and Sturgis Mayor Rod Bradley, along with elected officials share memories of the late Mayor Kevin Forrester at the ceremony declaring June 10 as Kevin Forrester Day, at Harley-Davidson Rally Point.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
Kevin Forrester day cutline 1.JPG
Rhea Crane and Sturgis Mayor Rod Bradley, along with elected officials share memories of the late Mayor Kevin Forrester at the ceremony declaring June 10 as Kevin Forrester Day, at Harley-Davidson Rally Point.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

 Kevin Forrester day cutline 2.JPG
Hundreds of family members, friends, community leaders, and residents gathered Wednesday evening to celebrate the life and legacy of former Sturgis Mayor Kevin Forrester, at Harley-Davidson Rally Point.  The crowd paused for a quick drone picture before the start of the K4 Bike Race. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

STURGIS — Hundreds of family members, friends, community leaders, and residents gathered Wednesday evening to celebrate the life and legacy of former Sturgis Mayor Kevin Forrester, whose decades of public service, volunteerism, and dedication to the community left a lasting mark on Sturgis, Meade County, and the Black Hills.

The special event, held at Harley Davidson Rally Point in conjunction with the opening of the Music on Main K4 Race Series, included the official proclamation of June 10 as Kevin Forrester Day, recognizing a man remembered as a visionary leader, tireless advocate, devoted family man, and passionate supporter of outdoor recreation and community development.

Rhea Crane, Meade County Executive Director of Equalization, and a longtime friend and coworker of Forrester, welcomed attendees and reflected on the impact he had on countless lives.

“Today is more than a recognition of a life well lived,” Crane said. “Kevin was a true community leader who believed in giving back, lending a hand, and making Sturgis and Meade County a better place for everyone.”

Crane noted that Forrester approached every challenge with determination and optimism, whether tackling major community issues or focusing on the smallest details. She said his generosity, humor, and genuine concern for others created lasting friendships throughout the region.

Sturgis City Council President Tony Dargatz presented a joint proclamation from the city of Sturgis and Meade County, officially designating June 10 as Kevin Forrester Day.

The proclamation highlighted Forrester’s years of public service, his leadership on local and regional issues, and his commitment to protecting the natural resources and quality of life that define the Black Hills. 

“Kevin’s life and service left a lasting impact on the City of Sturgis and Meade County,” Dargatz said. “His leadership helped shape growth, strengthen our sense of community, and inspire others to serve.”

Representing the Greater Sturgis Foundation, Brett Lynass spoke about Forrester’s instrumental role in developing the Sturgis trail system, long before he became mayor.

“Kevin’s vision and leadership in the Sturgis Trails Project created a permanent and positive improvement for the entire area,” Lynass said. “The trails enhance tourism, improve quality of life, and provide a place where families create memories and visitors discover the beauty of our region.”

Lynass said Forrester dedicated countless volunteer hours to the project and was a driving force behind the development of trails that residents and visitors enjoy today.

“His legacy will live on for generations through the trails, the community he strengthened, and the people he inspired,” Lynass said.

Meade County Commission Chairman Gary Deering reflected on the friendship he developed with Forrester during his years on the commission.

“Kevin knew this area, the hills, the plains, as well as anyone,” Deering said. “But what made him special was his unyielding passion to preserve and protect both the beauty of this place and our way of life.”  

Deering said Forrester had a unique ability to make people feel like lifelong friends, even after only a short acquaintance.

“The pain of losing that friend is great,” Deering said. “But tonight we celebrate the legacy he left behind. Whether it’s the trails, community projects, or simply his smile and handshake, Kevin’s impact will be felt for many years to come.”

Newly elected Sturgis Mayor Rod Bradley shared personal memories of his longtime friend and mentor, describing Forrester as someone who lived life at full speed and embraced every opportunity.

“He really used all the day,” Bradley said with a smile, recalling one of Forrester’s favorite sayings. “That was Kevin. Once he set his mind on something, there was no stopping him.”

Bradley said many of his favorite memories involved long days working on trails, exploring the Black Hills, and discussing ideas to improve Sturgis.

As Forrester battled illness, Bradley said his focus remained on family, community, and the projects he cared about most.  

“He was always thinking about how to make Sturgis better,” Bradley said. “That never changed.”  

Bradley also thanked Forrester’s wife, Nikki, and sons Chad, Ty, and Brooks for sharing him with the community.

“We will never be able to fully express our appreciation for the sacrifices your family made while Kevin devoted so much of his time and energy to serving this community,” Bradley said.

Throughout the evening, speakers emphasized that Forrester’s legacy extends far beyond public office. His influence can be seen in the community projects he championed, the trails he helped build, and the relationships he forged with people from all walks of life.

As residents gathered for a commemorative photograph and the evening’s bike race, many reflected on a man whose passion for Sturgis helped shape the community he loved.

Though Kevin Forrester is gone, speakers said his vision, leadership, and spirit will continue to guide Sturgis and Meade County for generations to come.

title: Meade County prepared for runoff election
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Absentee voting in the runoff election for the Republican gubernatorial candidate is scheduled to begin Friday, if county auditors have their ballots in time.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

STURGIS — Absentee voting in the runoff election for the Republican gubernatorial candidate is scheduled to begin Friday, if county auditors have their ballots in time. 

Meade County Auditor Dawn Christenson said she is a little concerned about the short turnaround time to get ballots for the runoff election, but if the county has to push back absentee voting they will put notices out for the public. Ballots for the primary election did not arrive until days after absentee voting was scheduled to start.  

On July 28 South Dakota voters will choose between Gov. Larry Rhoden and businessman Toby Doeden as the state’s Republican candidate for governor. The deadline for voter registration ahead of the runoff election is July 13. 

The runoff election between the front-running candidates is necessary because neither of them received 35% or more of the vote. Doeden received 31% of the vote, while Rhoden received 25%. Challengers Dusty Johnson and Jon Hansen are out of the race, as they received 23% and 21% respectively.

Christenson said Sturgis voters will go to the main gym of Sturgis Brown High School to cast their ballots for the runoff. The usual polling location at the Sturgis Community Center is booked for that day. All other polling locations in Meade County remain the same. 

Christenson’s report to the Meade County Commission followed complaints during the public comment section of the regular commission meeting, when some county residents called for ballots to be hand counted for the runoff election. Resident Dale Buse also questioned methods from the ballot testing, which was used to ensure all equipment and systems were working properly before the June 2 primary. Buse said a minimum of 25 ballots were not used to test each precinct, as outlined in state law. 

However, Deputy State’s Attorney Ken Chleborad said he is satisfied with the way the auditor’s office conducted the testing. There are 2 parts to state law, he said, one that requires at least 25 ballots to be included in each test deck. The second part states that each test deck must be of sufficient size to prove accuracy. 

“You could use the same 25 in each sentence, but it’s not required in my interpretation,” Chleborad said. “Using 17 in some of the precincts is perfectly fine if the auditor feels that is a sufficient size to prove accuracy of the system. There were a couple that were 17 and some that were 40. Everything that the tabulator picks up on gets tested. I was quite satisfied with how Dawn ran it. It was smooth and everything turned out the way it is supposed to.” 

Christenson said there are no plans to do a hand count for the runoff election. However, during the post election audit scheduled for 9 a.m. June 18, the auditor will hand count precincts that were selected at random during the election canvass, for the governor’s race. Those precincts are Rural Blackhawk 15, Southeast Piedmont 13, and Northwest Sturgis 5.

title: Jackley secures settlement regarding overpriced and delayed COVID-19 tests
byline: Pioneer staff report
description: PIERRE — Attorney General Marty Jackley recently announced that South Dakota consumers will receive $50,380 as part of a $4.87 million, 18-state settlement with GS Labs. The settlement resolves claims that the testing company overcharged patients, unlawfully charged administrative fees, and failed to deliver timely COVID-19 test results.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

PIERRE — Attorney General Marty Jackley recently announced that South Dakota consumers will receive $50,380 as part of a $4.87 million, 18-state settlement with GS Labs. The settlement resolves claims that the testing company overcharged patients, unlawfully charged administrative fees, and failed to deliver timely COVID-19 test results.

“South Dakota consumers were misled by GS Lab’s promises that were never kept,” Jackley said. “This settlement negotiated by South Dakota and the other states means our consumers will receive restitution.”

The multistate coalition investigated problems with GS Labs’ nationwide testing practices from 2020 through 2022, that included:

· GS Labs intentionally advertised inflated “cash prices” for COVID-19 tests, sometimes as high as $380 per test or nearly $1,000 for multi-panel tests, that were used to justify overcharging patients with insurance coverage. And while GS Labs offered a “discount” from these “cash prices” to actual cash-paying patients, almost 30,000 patients still paid much more than market rate for their COVID-19 tests.

· For hundreds of thousands of patients, GS Labs guaranteed test results within 3 days and failed to deliver on its promise, sometimes taking a week or longer to get test results to patients.

· Despite advertising that patients with insurance would have no out-of-pocket costs, the company charged administrative fees as high as $49 per test to about 70,000 patients.

Under the terms of the settlement, GS Labs will pay $3,628,718.34 in restitution to patients, including $1,843,375.99 for cash-paying patients that were overcharged for tests, $1,749,568.35 for patients that were charged administrative fees, and $33,692 for cash-paying patients that did not receive test results within three days. South Dakotans that were harmed by GS Labs’ testing practices will receive $50,380 in restitution through the settlement.

GS Labs will also pay $1.25 million to the multi-state group, which includes a payment of $16,669.99 to the State of South Dakota. The state’s share will go to the Attorney General’s Consumer Protection Division.

Attorneys general from Kansas, Nebraska, Minnesota, and Washington negotiated the settlement. Other attorneys general involved in the settlement are from the states of Alabama, Arizona, Colorado, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Massachusetts, Missouri, New Jersey, North Dakota, Ohio, Oregon, and Pennsylvania.

South Dakotans who believe they are eligible for restitution can contact GS Labs at this link: www.gslabstesting.com.

title: Belle Fourche PD’s summer cycling club takes engaged approach to youth bike safety
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Belle Fourche Police Sgt. Jason Huber introduces kids to cycling safety before an afternoon community ride at the rec center, Wednesday. Huber is a founder of “Pigs and Pedals,” a program that aims to encourage safe bike habits and delivers free helmets to kids who need them. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
IMG_6345.JPG
Belle Fourche Police Sgt. Jason Huber introduces kids to cycling safety before an afternoon community ride at the rec center, Wednesday. Huber is a founder of “Pigs and Pedals,” a program that aims to encourage safe bike habits and delivers free helmets to kids who need them. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

BELLE FOURCHE — There will be a small police presence at the Belle Fourche Rec Center every other Wednesday afternoon throughout the summer. That’s because the department’s 2 bicycle patrol officers, Sgt. Jason Huber and Lt. Jucole Jones have started a new summer cycling club for kids, designed to promote best practices for young people traveling on 2 wheels in the community.

They’re calling it Pigs and Pedals.

 IMG_6364.JPG
Police officers in Belle Fourche are encouraging safety and bringing the community along for the ride. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

 IMG_6372.JPG
Police officers in Belle Fourche are encouraging safety and bringing the community along for the ride. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

 IMG_6395.JPG
Police officers in Belle Fourche are encouraging safety and bringing the community along for the ride. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

The program is completely free. Kids come to the rec center with their bicycles, ready to ride. Monument Health has donated helmets, so that anyone who needs a helmet can be fitted for and ride away with one at no cost.

Officers will kick off the ride with a brief education session — going over rules of the road and bicycle etiquette, before embarking on a different ride each week.

Wednesday, for the first week of Pigs and Pedals, the ride was short — a simple loop behind the high school, down a few neighborhood streets, and back to the rec center.

In the future, riders will cruise the river walk and visit what Huber calls “hidden gems of Belle Fourche.” Huber is both a cycling enthusiast and a detective with the Belle Fourche Police Department.

Belle Fourche Police Chief Ryan Cherveny said the summer program is modeled on a community event last fall that brought more than a dozen adults and more than a dozen kids out for a group bike ride through town — which included a stop at Crazee Cow for ice cream.

“We started (the program) primarily to promote community involvement, and to do something fun and positive that included cops,” Cherveny said.

When the department rolled out e-bikes for its patrol officers, Cherveny said neighborhood kids would often grab their bikes and rush out their front doors to ride behind or briefly beside the officers.

This program intentionally invites anyone interested to join police on a group ride.

“We’re going to be respectful of everybody,” Huber said. “Everybody’s riding abilities, everybody’s speed, everybody’s rights.”

Importantly, Pigs and Pedals gives officers a chance to address community safety concerns in a way that is both lighthearted and interactive.

“We’re going to go over bicycle laws,” Huber said. “There are state laws that are applied to all bicycle riders, no matter how old you are.”

He told the assembled kids that the same laws they have to follow when they pedal around town are the same laws he has to follow as an adult cyclist.

“When you ride on the sidewalk, you have the same rights as a pedestrian. All of the laws that apply to pedestrians on a sidewalk apply to cyclists on a sidewalk, except when you’re operating on the sidewalk you have the duty to yield to anybody who is not on a bicycle.”

Huber said cyclists need to slow down and verbally indicate to pedestrians when and where they are going to pass them — whether on the left or right.

“If you hit somebody on the sidewalk with a bicycle, whose fault is it?” Huber asked the room. “It’s the bicyclist’s fault.

He explained that helmets are a requirement, and that cyclists are allowed to ride in the road, as long as they keep to the right curb and are cognizant of cars.

He reminded young cyclists that they have to stop at stop signs and keep speed limits in mind. He also reviewed required hand signals, to give cars and pedestrians a heads-up before cyclists turn.

“Whose responsibility is it to be safe on the road?” Huber asked, to a resounding reply of “Me!”

Cherveny said it’s important to teach kids the rules of the road specifically.

“If they are riding on the road, they must follow the rules of the road,” Cherveny said. “If they aren’t old enough to have a driver’s license, then they don’t know those rules. You don’t need to know those laws usually if you’re 10 or 12 years old.”  

The rise in popularity of e-bikes and electric motorcycle-type vehicles has generated concern across communities in the Northern Hills. Pigs and Pedals hopes to address that concern.

“With all of the e-bikes and crashes that people are seeing — we haven’t had any here yet, knock on wood — we wanted to address it. We have had some close calls,” Cherveny said. He said youth and parental education is key.

This week, Huber used the newly minted bike club to address that burgeoning safety hazard as well.

“How many of you have an e-bike?” Huber asked a room full of kids in attendance. “Who here wants an electric bicycle?” Hands shot up. There were shouts of “Me!” and murmurs of “It sounds fun.”

“They are incredibly fun. I have one,” Huber said. “The term electric bicycle refers to a bicycle or tricycle equipped with a saddle and operable pedals. Electric bicycles have to have operable pedals.”

Then, he explained the difference between classes of e-bikes and the varying rules for each.

“There is a state law that says that all electric bikes have to have a label permanently on the bikes, usually a sticker near the battery, that says what kind of e-bike it is. If that sticker is removed or tampered with, or you put another sticker over it, it is a crime, ” Huber said. “We can tow your bike.”

There are 3 classes of e-bikes. A class one e-bike will only go 20 miles per hour and will only assist a cyclist with pedaling. A class 2 e-bike has a motor in addition to pedal-assist functions. Class 2 e-bikes still only reach a maximum speed of 20 miles per hour.

“Class 3 e-bikes you still have to pedal, but it will go 28 miles per hour,” Huber said. “A class 3, according to state law, in order to operate a class 3 e-bike you have to be 16 years or older. Do you know why? Because you are going faster than a car in a residential zone.”

Huber emphasized that cyclists on e-bikes still have to abide by speed limits. Class 3 e-bikes must be equipped with working speedometers. They are also prohibited on sidewalks.

“I wreck a lot. I can tell you, this is what my bike is; it’s a class one, and I wreck a lot, and it hurts,” Huber said, offering firsthand caution about speed and helmet usage.

Huber is hopeful education and community involvement will help encourage cycling, improve etiquette, and bolster bike safety.

Huber said the Pigs and Pedals program is open to kids from every community in the region, not Belle Fourche alone. He also invited officers from other neighborhood departments to join in on the afternoon rides. 

For Wednesday’s route, Huber rode in the lead, with Jones bringing up the rear. Code enforcement officer Clint Haffner rode alongside kids in the middle of the pack.

Cherveny said the department looks forward to seeing the program grow. The bike patrol program has already made an impact in generating excitement about biking; he hopes this program will maintain that momentum.

The next Pigs and Pedals is June 24 at 12:30 p.m. at the rec center.

title: Lead-Deadwood School District works to rebrand Digger spirit
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: The changed lyrics to the school song in the Lead-Deadwood School District will officially reflect the school’s current identity and colors. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
School song change.JPG
The changed lyrics to the school song in the Lead-Deadwood School District will officially reflect the school’s current identity and colors. Pioneer file photo 

DEADWOOD — The lyrics to the Lead-Deadwood School District’s school song are set to officially change to reflect the current identity, colors, and experience of the students.

More than 50 years ago, the Lead and Deadwood school systems combined in 1971 to create the current Lead-Deadwood School District, but a rebranding of school spirit to reflect current student’s experiences has only been in the works for approximately 5 years. 

Amber Vogt, chairwoman of the Lead-Deadwood School Board, said that the rebranding began when the Classes of 1998, 2026, and 2030 donated funding to hang banners in the high school, middle school, and elementary school buildings, with updated lyrics to the school song.

“If you look at the school song, it referenced Lead High School. Well, we haven’t been Lead High School for a long time,” said Vogt. “So, they changed it to match the name of the school. It also referenced maroon and white, and we haven’t been maroon and white for (55) years. It’s maroon and gold.”

Vogt said the banners were approved by the school board at the time and hung in each gymnasium in the efforts that when the school song played before home games, students would be able to read the words and feel represented in their current experience at the school.

At the same time, Vogt said the district brought back the school mascot, Pickaxe Pete. She said the changes were made to create a cohesive, current environment for the students, bolstering school spirit across the district. 

However, Vogt said those changes have, at times, received pushback from residents. 

“There was a lot of controversy when Deadwood and Lead combined schools, and there was a lot of people that were like, ‘Nope, this is what it’s going to be,’” she said. “I think over time we just have to change and go with what our kids are currently experiencing and what they know. We have to represent the current market. We’ve tried to get away from people always referencing back to Lead High School or Deadwood High School — it’s not anymore and it hasn’t been for a lot of years.”

The next move to rebrand the school spirit and create a cohesive environment for students has come with changing the lyrics of the school song to match the school’s current identity and colors in the student handbooks. Those changes are set to be approved by the school board at the July 14 meeting. 

After that, Vogt said the school board hopes to raise funds to replace the mascot costume. 

“The one we have is probably 15 years old,” she said. “The kids won’t put it on because it’s old and stinky.”

To replace the mascot could cost upwards of $10,000. 

Vogt said that she believes a new mascot, along with the updated wording and other rebranding measures of the Lead-Deadwood School District, could help solidify the new, cohesive environment they’re hoping to foster for the students of the district.
