title: Peak View II aims to expand  Spearfish’s housing inventory with  emphasis on long-range affordability
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Peak View II, the 30-unit affordable housing complex that broke ground last week will be a neighbor and twin to the existing Peak View Apartment Building — with similar amenities, rent caps, renter qualifications, and façade. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Peak View 1.JPG
Peak View II, the 30-unit affordable housing complex that broke ground last week will be a neighbor and twin to the existing Peak View Apartment Building — with similar amenities, rent caps, renter qualifications, and façade. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — There’s a 30-unit apartment complex situated on Paramount Drive near Exit 14 in Spearfish. Peak View Apartments was designed to fill a specific need in the community for low-income housing. To lease apartments there, residents must meet income qualifications between 30% and 60% of area median income (AMI) — a number set by the state.

Peak View Apartments was completed in the fall of 2024 and fully leased by the end of that year.

On Friday, Buxton Enterprises and Lloyd Companies broke ground on roughly 2 acres directly adjacent to the existing Peak View Apartments structure — the new development, Peak View II, will be a twin to the first building.

The second Peak View will also provide 30-units of income-qualified affordable housing. There will be a total of 52 bedrooms and 52 parking spaces available for incoming residents upon completion.

“There are different levels of affordability. This particular unit will have units that are available for tenants that are anywhere from 30% of the area median income to up to 60%. This is meeting a different need in the community,” John Buxton, co-owner of Buxton Enterprises, said. “The other thing that is unique about this project is that the affordability will last for 40 years. These will be affordable long after I’m probably gone.”

 Ground Breaking.JPG
Peak View II broke ground with an official ceremony last week. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

Buxton said the units available to residents who earn 30% of AMI (AMI is currently $102,000) will be able to rent units for about $600 per month with utilities included.

“They have to pay for phone, Internet, cable TV if they want it, and the rents go up to the $1,300 range. They will stay that way for 40 years,” Buxton said.

Spearfish Mayor John Senden said Peak View II slots nicely into the city’s housing inventory.

“This works out really well to give more diversity to our housing needs here,” Senden said. “The new apartment that is going up on Hill Street, I think they are 80% occupied. That will create some opportunities as people fill that. I think it will open the gap.”

The Hollow Gulch Apartments on Hill Street start at about $1,000 per month and go up to $1,908 per month. In its marketing, Hollow Gulch states its aim as providing “contemporary finishes, upscale appliances, and open-concept layouts” alongside other “premium amenities. Hollow Gulch is awaiting the arrival of a water pump system in order to officially open and allow residents to move in.

 Greg Litton.JPG
Greg Litton is the director of strategic housing at the Black Hills Area Community Foundation. He is pictured speaking at the ground breaking ceremony for Peak View II — a 30-unit rent-capped apartment complex on Paramount Drive in Spearfish. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

 John Senden.JPG
Spearfish Mayor John Senden said, “It has taken a lot of diligence to continue to push forward and get these projects underway,” of the second phase of construction at Peak View Apartments. “Any way the city can be participative we will try to do that.” Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

Not far from Peak View II, the city of Spearfish approved the development of a tax increment finance district, TIF 9, to support the development of Stone Ridge Commons, a 94-unit multi-family housing project.

Those 94 rental units will be distributed across 5 buildings — some will be townhome-style with attached garages. Others will be flat-style apartments, according to representatives of Lloyd Companies, who presented to the city council.

Rents at Stone Ridge Commons will be capped at 80% of AMI for 10 years. That figure caps rent for a one-bedroom apartment at $1,635, rent for a 2-bedroom at $1,840, and a 3-bedroom unit at $2,044. That apartment project, like Peak View II, is also being developed by Lloyd Companies.

“Many do not know that Lloyd Companies is a leader in providing affordable housing technical expertise in our state,” explained Greg Litton, the director of strategic housing at the Black Hills Area Community Foundation. “They have a seasoned team of affordable housing financial specialists on their staff, who provide information and guidance to both for-profit and nonprofit organizations alike.”

Peak View II did not leverage tax increment financing to reduce its rent rates. Instead, it utilized tax credits and support from the Black Hills Area Community Foundation (BHACF).

“To compress the rents the way that they do, the impact on cash flow is significant,” Litton said. “To make the numbers work, and make sure that we are providing safe, stable, and dignified housing, we have to find ways to make sure that those rents stay at a price that people can afford.”

Litton said Buxton Enterprises, which is locally owned, was invested in working on an affordable multi-family project and willing to explore funding options.

“In this case, the owner and developer is Buxton Enterprises, they are some individuals who grew up in the community. They really wanted to give back here,” Litton said. “Oftentimes it is a lot easier to get folks who are local and want to give back to their communities to work with them.”

Buxton said that, in order to be awarded tax credits for Peak View Apartments, the company needed to show local support. BHACF made that possible.

“There is a competitive process for awarding tax benefits. We are competing with developers from all around the state, with entities in Sioux Falls, in Watertown, Brookings, everywhere,” Buxton said. “The reason they were key is, when you are competing against other developers in other communities that want these projects, they look at and score local community involvement. It requires local funding and local support from the community to get this project selected.”

title: Candidate condemns  ‘whoever’ approved a runoff law, and it turns out to be a legend from his city
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: SIOUX FALLS — Republican candidate for governor Toby Doeden has some criticism for whichever South Dakota legislator got a law passed requiring runoff elections.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

SIOUX FALLS — Republican candidate for governor Toby Doeden has some criticism for whichever South Dakota legislator got a law passed requiring runoff elections.  

“We should just cancel the 35% rule and just award me the winner, like that’s it,” Doeden said while laughing in a video published Monday on YouTube. He added, without a laugh, “such a silly rule anyway. They put this in back in the ’80s. I don’t know who did it, but whoever did it should be discredited. Like, it’s ridiculous. You ask the people to vote. Whoever gets the most votes wins.”

Doeden doesn’t have to look far to learn who’s responsible. The law is credited to a legendary former lawmaker from Doeden’s own city and party: the late Joe Barnett, an Aberdeen Republican. Northern State University’s Joseph H. Barnett Center, which is Aberdeen’s major indoor athletic venue, was named in Barnett’s honor. 

The former state House speaker and majority leader served 19 years in the House before he died in 1985, the same year his runoff law passed. The law requires a runoff if nobody reaches 35% in a primary with three or more candidates for governor, U.S. Senate or U.S. House. Previously, if nobody reached 35% in such a race, the party’s nomination was decided by delegates at state party conventions.

Doeden, a businessman running his first campaign for elected office, finished first in a four-way Republican primary on June 2. But with 31% support instead of the required 35% to win, he was thrown into a July 28 runoff with Gov. Larry Rhoden, who finished second with 25%.

A Doeden campaign spokesperson sent a written statement Tuesday in response to South Dakota Searchlight questions about Doeden’s comments on the runoff law and its origins.

“Mr. Doeden’s comments were obviously made in jest and did not insinuate anything specifically regarding Former Speaker Barnett or his legislative record,” the statement said. “Joseph Barnett was a great and highly respected leader that Aberdeen was lucky to have.”

Former colleagues of Barnett shared bipartisan praise for the deceased lawmaker in interviews with Searchlight.

Democratic former state lawmaker Lars Herseth represented Brown County alongside Barnett. 

“I don’t know of anyone, in my time, who did more to serve Brown County than Joe Barnett,” Herseth said.

Don Frankenfeld, of Rapid City, served as a Republican in the state Senate while Barnett was in the House. He said Barnett “was a genius, both intellectually and politically.”

“He had tremendous weight in determining legislative decisions,” Frankenfeld said. “He was also a very thoughtful person.”

Kent Frerichs is a Democratic former lawmaker from Wilmot who served with Barnett.

“He went out of his way to try to make sure that everybody would have equal opportunity to be heard,” Frerichs said.

The context for Barnett’s 1985 legislation was the 1986 governor race. Former House Speaker George S. Mickelson was preparing to run in a crowded Republican primary that also included former U.S. Rep. Clint Roberts. 

Frankenfeld said Mickelson was concerned that if no candidate reached 35%, the decision would move to a convention that was “unpredictable, not representative of the party as a whole” and more likely to be driven by “activists.”

“There is a pretty easy chance of it being manipulated,” Frankenfeld said.

Barnett did not live to see the law in action. He died of a heart attack on May 1, 1985. In 1986, Mickelson won the Republican nomination for governor with 35.3% of the votes and went on to beat Herseth in the general election. This year’s July 28 runoff will be the first to be carried out under Barnett’s law.

Frerichs said his concern about Doeden is encapsulated by the candidate’s criticism of the runoff law. 

“He’s confident, but doesn’t seem to know a lot of these things,” Frerichs said of Doeden.

Frankenfeld said that’s attractive to some voters. 

“Part of his appeal, and part of his baggage, is his lack of experience in government,” Frankenfeld said. “He almost wears political ignorance as a badge of honor.” 

The statement from Doeden’s spokesperson said Doeden “knew that the previous nomination process for statewide office was totally bogus and that it should always be the people who choose their leaders, not a powerful few.”

“Mr. Doeden won the June 2nd Primary in tremendous fashion and is beyond grateful for his widespread support,” the statement said. “He looks forward to obtaining the final nomination after the July 28th run off.”

Rhoden campaign spokesman Ian Fury said in a written statement to Searchlight, “Winners win, and losers complain about the rules.”

Rhoden’s running mate, Republican Lt. Gov. Tony Venhuizen, maintains a website called SoDak Governors devoted to South Dakota political history. On that website, Venhuizen wrote in 2017 of Barnett, “it was said he was held in such high regard that legislators of both parties would pass legislation solely on his word.”

title: Meade County to consider sales tax
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Meade County is considering adding a sales tax to its coffers.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

STURGIS — Meade County is considering adding a sales tax to its coffers. 

On Tuesday, Meade County Commissioners scheduled a first reading for Ordinance 60, which will enact a gross receipts tax on sales in the county. The ordinance will be considered, with public comment, at 10 a.m., June 23. 

Senate Bill 96 passed during the 2026 South Dakota legislative session, allows counties to impose a local gross receipts tax, or sales tax, of up to a half percent on tangible personal property, products that are transferred electronically, and services. The new law, which will go into effect July 1, requires counties to put funds from the sales tax into a property tax reduction fund. That fund is to be used to apply a credit against the county’s tax levy on all owner-occupied properties. The county is allowed to retain 2% of the funds in the first year, and up to $20,000 in subsequent years, for administrative costs. 

All additional money in the fund after 100% of the county’s tax levy on owner occupied properties is replaced, is to be applied to a credit against tax levies equally for both agricultural and non-agricultural property. 

While the county has not set a specific amount for the proposed sales tax, Commissioner Talbot Wieczorek suggested that the full half percent be added to the ordinance for discussion purposes, June 23. He also asked for the new tax to take effect Jan. 1, 2027. Wieczorek said the county is required to pass an enabling ordinance for the tax, and send it to the state 90 days before it is imposed. The county’s ordinance cannot be enacted before the legislation goes into effect, July 1, and new taxes can only be applied twice a year, July 1 and Jan. 1.

title: Biden endorses SDDP candidates Democrats name hopefuls for most statewide offices
byline: By Tom Lawrence Special to the Black Hills Pioneer
description: Former President Joe Biden makes a point during his 30-minute speech
_full_text:
Biden endorses SDDP candidates.jpeg
Former President Joe Biden makes a point during his 30-minute speech 

SIOUX FALLS — Three South Dakota Democratic candidates benefited from former President Joe Biden’s appearance in Sioux Falls Friday.

Biden issued endorsements for Dan Ahlers for governor, Julian Beaudion for U.S. Senate and Nikki Gronli for the state’s lone U.S. House of Representatives seat. He said he was “proud” to do so.

“Dan Ahlers has spent his life fighting for small businesses and working families. He knows what it means to roll up your sleeves and do the work,” Biden said in a statement. “Julian Beaudion spent 13 years as a state trooper keeping South Dakotans safe, and now he’s going to fight to make sure families can afford their health care and their kids can get a good education. Nikki Gronli has dedicated her career to making sure rural communities and family farmers get the support they need to not just survive, but thrive.

“These are good, decent people who know where they come from and who they’re fighting for,” the former president said. “The people of South Dakota deserve leaders who will actually show up for them. For South Dakotans this November, that’s Dan, Julian and Nikki.”

Ahlers, Beaudion and Haley, who spoke after Biden at the McGovern Day Dinner, were officially nominated during the party’s state convention on Saturday. Ahlers has yet to select a running mate.

 BHP_photo - 1
Raeann Mettler 

The SDDP also nominated candidates for constitutional offices, including Raeann Mettler of Spearfish, who is running for commissioner of school and public lands. Mettler sought a Spearfish City Council seat in 2025 and ran for a school board position on June 2.

Tom Cool of Sioux Falls, who is running for state auditor. Cool also sought the office in 2018 and ran for secretary of state in 2022. He also has run for the state Senate five times, losing each race.

Frank Kloucek of Scotland, a former longtime state legislator, is running for a seat on the Public Utilities Commission. Margaret Kuipers of Sioux Falls, who ran for a state House seat in 2022, is running for state treasurer. Terrence Davis of Sioux Falls is the party’s candidate for secretary of state. Davis, a former state trooper, has been campaigning for a year.

The party did not nominate a candidate for attorney general. It’s the second straight election without a Democratic candidate for the office.

State Reps. Erik Muckey of Sioux Falls and Eric Emery of Rosebud co-chaired the party gathering, with 192 of 204 eligible delegates from 37 counties present.

“Together, these delegates nominated our constitutional officer candidates for November, built a platform that reflects the best of South Dakota, and passed resolutions on what matters at our kitchen tables: investing in our kids’ education, guaranteeing access to healthcare and housing, protecting the Constitution and our right to vote, restoring competitive markets for our farmers and ranchers, and guarding our communities and our grid from unregulated hyperscale data centers,” Muckey said in a Facebook post. “None of it came together overnight. It took weeks of deliberation, with every delegate sharing their voice and their ideas that now stand as the platform and policies of the South Dakota Democratic Party.

“I’m proud of the work delegates performed and was honored to hold the gavel throughout the deliberations over the platform and resolutions. The ideas proposed by everyday South Dakotans only get better when more people are at the table. I can only imagine how much richer the conversations would have been with even more representation from across the state.”

He said the SDDP has a lot of work to do to have a louder voice in state government. It has not elected a governor since 1974 and has not won a statewide race since 2008. Republicans hold supermajorities in both legislative chambers.

“Plenty of South Dakotans have walked away from this party over the past dysfunction, and plenty are frustrated with Democratic leaders in Congress and with the DNC,” Muckey said. “And right now, I see countless friends who feel so disenfranchised in South Dakota that they’re registering as Republicans to vote in primaries. While I’m sad to see that this is the state of things in South Dakota, I know it’s bigger than me and any one person. And I will do everything in my power to see that fellow South Dakotans have their rights to the democratic process preserved.”

Muckey said the people who came to the convention are willing to work to make a difference and enact change.

“A party platform or a candidate’s journey doesn’t begin in the halls of Congress or the White House,” he said. “It comes from the people, your neighbors in Parker and Timber Lake, Chamberlain and Webster, Vermillion and Mission, who answer you. That’s how this system works.”

title: Sturgis Ambulance  director resigns
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Aden Schillig
_full_text:
Aden Schillig.jpg
Aden Schillig 

 Bryson Kool.jpg
Bryson Kool 

STURGIS – The city of Sturgis announces the resignation of Sturgis Ambulance Director Aden Schillig, effective Friday.

Schillig submitted his resignation to City Administrator Aaron Jordan on June 8 after accepting an opportunity that will allow him to continue advancing his career in emergency medical services.

In his resignation letter, Schillig expressed gratitude for the opportunity to serve the Sturgis community and reflected on the progress made by the ambulance service during his tenure. 

“Serving as the ambulance director for the city of Sturgis has been one of the most rewarding experiences of my professional career,” Schillig wrote. 

In his resignation letter, Schillig highlighted significant improvements in billing processes, policies and procedures, clinical protocols, and education and training programs that have strengthened the department’s ability to provide high-quality emergency medical care. 

In July 2025, Schillig reported that the service had started a trajectory toward self sufficiency and reduced reliance on the city’s general fund budget, utilizing a third-party billing system. 

Jordan thanked Schillig for his leadership and service to the community.

“We appreciate Aden’s dedication to the Sturgis Ambulance Service and the positive impact he has had on the organization,” Jordan said. “His efforts have helped position the service for continued success, and we wish him the very best in his future endeavors.”

To ensure continuity of operations, the city has appointed Bryson Kool to serve as interim ambulance director.

Kool has been a member of the Sturgis Ambulance Service since October 2021 and has played an important role in managing the department’s electronic patient care reporting system, scheduling and payroll functions, and daily operations. 

As a paramedic and shift supervisor, he oversees daily operations, coordinates staffing, and helps ensure the highest level of patient care. Kool is skilled in advanced life support interventions, including airway management, cardiac monitoring, IV therapy, and medication administration. 

In addition to his frontline responsibilities, he plays a key role in training and mentoring new EMTs and paramedics, and serves as an instructor for basic and advanced certification courses. 

In his resignation letter, Schillig described Kool as a respected leader who has demonstrated professionalism, strong leadership, and a commitment to the service. 

“Bryson has earned the respect of his colleagues and has already taken on significant responsibilities within the organization,” Jordan said. “We are confident in his ability to provide steady leadership as we move through this transition.”

The city will begin evaluating long-term leadership options for the ambulance service while working to ensure uninterrupted emergency medical services for the Sturgis community and surrounding area.

Schillig was hired as the new Sturgis Ambulance Service director in May 2025, after former director Shawn Fischer was terminated in March. When he was hired, the city reported Schillig had 29 years of experience in emergency medical care, and had worked in 30 different states and Canada.

title: Lawrence, Butte County to cooperatively  gravel livestock access at fairgrounds
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Lawrence and Butte County have agreed to work cooperatively to re-gravel a section of road used to get livestock to the showgrounds at the Butte/Lawrence County Fairgrounds. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Lawrence, Butte County to cooperatively  gravel livestock access at fairgrounds
Lawrence and Butte County have agreed to work cooperatively to re-gravel a section of road used to get livestock to the showgrounds at the Butte/Lawrence County Fairgrounds. Pioneer file photo 

DEADWOOD — Fairgoers looking to show off their prized livestock at the Butte/Lawrence County Fairgrounds this year will have an easier time getting their animals to the showgrounds thanks to a collaborative effort between Butte and Lawrence County.

Lawrence County Commissioners agreed to pay approximately $4,500 to deliver 150 tons of gravel to the fairgrounds this summer, following a request to work collaboratively with Butte County to re-gravel the road. 

“It’s an old trail, muddy, slimy, it’s got some holes in it, so it’s really a safety concern,” said Lawrence County Commissioner Timm Comer. “If that road’s not available they have to come through the yard and the grounds themselves. And, as we all know, kids are very active out there.”

Comer said Butte County officials have agreed to prepare the road and spread the gravel after it’s delivered. 

John Bey, highway superintendent, said the only hard cost to the county for the project is the estimated $1,950 cost of gravel. He estimated it would take 6 employees approximately 2 hours to load and deliver the gravel.

“We already pay our employees, we already own the trucks,” said Bey. 

Bey said the project would have to fit into the work already scheduled to be completed by his department this summer. 

Commissioner Bob Ewing called the request, “Very reasonable.”

“I’m very familiar with what they want to do, and I think it’s a plus for both Butte and Lawrence (County),” said Ewing. “I certainly support it.”

title: Spearfish saves nearly $350,000 on airport well project
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Spearfish Public Works Director Adam McMahon is pictured, explaining how the city was able to save more than $300,000 on the airport well project. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Spearfish saves nearly $350,000 on airport well project
Spearfish Public Works Director Adam McMahon is pictured, explaining how the city was able to save more than $300,000 on the airport well project. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — This week, the Spearfish City Council voted to close out the first phase of the East Low Zone Water System Improvements Project. By approving the final change order for that phase, the city accepted $346,640.63 in cost savings.

The city received $1,386,000 in federal American Rescue Plan Act funds and $6,882,327 in Clean Water State Revolving Fund loans to help cover the $10,575,533.45 cost. 

The project as a whole was designed by Foth Infrastructure and Environment, LLC. The project was intended to facilitate growth east of the airport, along US Highway 85, by ensuring sufficient access to city water.

“There is a decrease of nearly $350,000 on this project, which is a 30% decrease in the overall cost of the project,” Spearfish Public Works Director Adam McMahon said. “We were fortunate and hit water at a shallower elevation than what was planned, and we had some good fracturing in the limestone, so we didn’t need to use acid in the well to not need to use acid in the well.”

The completion of the airport well marked the conclusion of the first phase of the 4-phase project. The airport well, airport well house, water distribution piping, and water storage tank make up all 4 phases.

Each phase was bid separately, but Water System Drilling, Inc. was awarded the contracts for the well, the well house, piping, and tank.

After unanimously accepting the final change order, the city council unanimously approved the final certificate of completion for the project, setting the start date for the well’s 2-year warranty as Jan. 7.

title: Crescent St. project ahead of schedule
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Renovations to Crescent Street, making the road more pedestrian friendly and improving fire safety at the Days of ’76 Events Center, are ahead of schedule. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
Crescent St. project ahead of schedule
Renovations to Crescent Street, making the road more pedestrian friendly and improving fire safety at the Days of ’76 Events Center, are ahead of schedule. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

DEADWOOD — The work to improve Crescent Street in Deadwood and install a looped system of water lines for the Days of ’76 Events Center is weeks ahead of schedule.

Lornie Stalder, director of public works, said that Hayworth Enterprises, of Belle Fourche, has requested to move forward with completing the installation of a water line going towards the bridge on ’76 Drive, a move that wasn’t scheduled until September. 

“They want to continue and finish the water line so they can move their big equipment to another job site,” said Stalder. “Next, they’ll work on the retaining walls that are behind the parks building.”

Stalder said Crescent Street is set to remain closed until late August, when the new asphalt and sidewalks will be completed, “in one swoop.”

“There will be a walking surface to people to get to the event center, but the road that goes down into the parks department will be open for moving stock trailers and horse trailers in and out during the Days ’76 Rodeo,” said Stalder. “It will be the same accessibility, it just won’t be as pretty.”

The $1.7 million project is set to include a looped system of water lines with additional fire hyrdrants around the events center, new curb, gutter, sidewalk, and asphalt on Crescent Drive behind the grandstands, new retaining walls behind the parks building, and improved pedestrian lighting that will aesthetically match lighting installed behind city hall. The project is being paid for, in part, with a $600,000 community access grant from the South Dakota Department of Transportation and monies made with the sale of The Lodge at Deadwood’s convention center following the dissolution of Tax Increment Financing District 6 in April 2025. The rest of the project will be paid for by the city’s capital improvement budget.

The project has had one change order since the bid was awarded in April. Stalder said a 30-foot-by-80-foot section of existing asphalt was overlooked near the entrance of the park that will be torn up and made consistent with the rest of Crescent Street. A cost of the change order has not been made public yet.

title: Felony arrest warrant issued  for state Rep. Travis Ismay
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer
description: Rep. Travis Ismay, Newell
_full_text:
Felony arrest warrant issued  for state Rep. Travis Ismay
Rep. Travis Ismay, Newell 

BELLE FOURCHE — An arrest warrant was issued Tuesday for recently re-elected Rep. Travis Ismay, R-Newell, on the felony charge of intentional damage to a highway. 

If convicted, he could face up to 2 years in prison or a fine of $4,000.

It was not immediately clear whether Ismay has been arrested.

The indictment alleges that on or about May 5, Ismay deliberately dug up, removed, displaced, or broke the highway, which is a Class 6 felony, the least severe category of felonies.

Around the same time as the indictment alleges Ismay damaged the highway, an individual allegedly used a road grader, without authorization, to grade a portion of Wilson Road, near Belle Fourche, Dwayne Heidrich, who was Butte County highway supervisor at the time of the incident, said.

“They took the crown out of it (the road),” Heidrich said.

The crown of the road is a raised portion of the road that allows water to flow off of the road, similar to the peak of a roof. Without the crown, Heidrich said, the rain or other water will remain on the road, creating potholes and making the road soft. He said that prior to the incident, the road was in good condition, and has since been returned to good condition. 

Heidrich estimated the cost of labor and materials for repairing the road at about $2,000.

Fred Lamphere, Butte County sheriff, did not respond to a request for comment in time for publication.

Tim Barnaud, state’s attorney for Butte County, did not respond to a request for comment Wednesday in time for publication.

Ismay declined comment. 

Under South Dakota law, “a sentence of imprisonment in a state correctional facility for any term suspends the right of the person so sentenced to hold public office” However, if found guilty and fined, state law would not prevent Ismay from serving in office.

Ismay won the District 28B house seat June 2 with 55% of the vote. He beat Larry Schmoltz in the race.

title: How a hospital is helping solve a hometown housing shortage
byline: By Bart Pfankuch South Dakota News Watch
description: The Fall River Health Services of Hot Springs, S.D., shown on May 27, 2026, is investing in a housing project in hopes of attracting new employees. Photo by Bart Pfankuch, South Dakota News Watch
_full_text:
How a hospital is helping solve a hometown housing shortage.jpeg
The Fall River Health Services of Hot Springs, S.D., shown on May 27, 2026, is investing in a housing project in hopes of attracting new employees. Photo by Bart Pfankuch, South Dakota News Watch 

HOT SPRINGS — In what could be a first-of-its-kind project in South Dakota, the small hospital in this Southern Black Hills town is investing in a subdivision project to provide housing for its employees.

Fall River Health Services, an independent nonprofit medical center in Hot Springs, is paying $2.3 million of the overall $3.4 million cost of infrastructure for a subdivision that could create 48 new affordable housing units a few hundred yards from the hospital campus.

Like many South Dakota employers, Fall River Health is enduring a long-range worker shortage that has put pressure on its existing staff and driven up costs due to hiring of expensive traveling, short-term medical employees.

As of May 29, the hospital had 19 job openings, most of them in direct patient care, a shortage of 10% of its needed workforce of 190. The hospital in recent years has lost about 70 prospective workers because they couldn’t find affordable or suitable local housing, said Jesse Naze, chief financial officer at Fall River Health.

“You can’t stop providing care, so we need workforce to care for our local population,” Naze said. “It’s not wages or benefits keeping employees away, it’s simply that housing just isn’t available.”

Naze said he isn’t aware of any South Dakota project in which an employer invested so much money on permanent housing that will benefit the business as well as the community at large for years to come.

The private hospital with 25 beds saved money for years to be able to invest in the proposed housing project in which some homeowners could see a financial benefit if they take jobs at the hospital and stay for at least five years.

“The hospital is fronting the cash to get this infrastructure put in so we can get this project going,” Naze said. “There’s only so much local workforce, so we need to attract employees, and this should be a big help.”

The South Dakota Housing Authority (South Dakota Housing) has high hopes for the Hot Springs project and in October approved a nearly $1.2 million grant to support the project. The money came from the $200 million Housing Infrastructure Financing Program approved by the Legislature in 2023.

Chas Olson, executive director of South Dakota Housing, said the authority had been in discussion with officials from Hot Springs and Fall River Health for several years to generate a plan for an affordable housing project.

“We knew they were having issues recruiting and keeping workers there because the (existing) housing is old and aging,” Olson said.

The current plan for the subdivision, located on the city’s south side east of Highway 71,  is to build a mix of single-family and multi-family buildings that will create 48 total housing units with a wide range of square footages and prices, said Dennis Fischer, a former Hot Springs schools superintendent who now serves on the local hospital and housing boards.

Single-family homes of about 1,300 square feet should cost about $350,000, including the lot. Smaller villas, duplexes and townhomes could come in as low as $285,000, including lot costs, he said.

Project managers are working out details of a special mortgage for hospital employees who buy a home in which lot costs of up to $54,000 could be returned if they remain employed for five years, Fischer said.

So far, the city of Hot Springs and its residents have been big supporters of the Cascade Hills project, said Aerial Allison, city administrator.

With no significant resident opposition and a unanimous city council vote, the city approved a $2.3 million tax increment financing (TIF) district to expedite development, she said.

Quality housing has been increasingly hard to come by as the city’s reputation as a pleasant retirement community has grown. Adding to the demand is a large number of out-of-state people who moved to Hot Springs and bought homes during and since the COVID-19 pandemic.

“Not to blame them for anything, but we’re really excited this project is focused on workforce housing,” Allison said. “We’re trying to get people of working age to come here and bring their family and put their kids in our schools and shop at our local stores.”

title: Spearfish School Board bids farewell to Niesent
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Ryan Niesent, right, was presented with a farewell plaque Monday evening. He served on the Spearfish School Board for the past 8 years. He is pictured with Kirk Easton, who will retire as superintendent at the end of the month. Pioneer photo by Mark Watson
_full_text:
Spearfish School Board bids farewell to Niesent
Ryan Niesent, right, was presented with a farewell plaque Monday evening. He served on the Spearfish School Board for the past 8 years. He is pictured with Kirk Easton, who will retire as superintendent at the end of the month. Pioneer photo by Mark Watson 

SPEARFISH — The Spearfish School Board said goodbye to Ryan Niesent Monday evening.

Niesent, the board president announced his resignation in May after 8 years of service. 

Niesent was promoted to chief operating officer of BankWest and said he believed that he would not have the time necessary to properly serve as a board member. 

“After careful consideration, I believe it is in the best interest of the district for me to step aside so that the position can be filled by someone able to fully dedicate the time and attention this important role demands,” Niesent said in a prepared statement following his resignation announcement.

Since his resignation came outside the timeframe that would have allowed for an election, the board interviewed 4 candidates Monday. Five had applied, but one person withdrew their name from consideration earlier Monday. 

Terssa Markworth was selected as Niesent’s replacement and will likely be sworn in at the July board meeting. 

The district office will see numerous changes. In addition to Niesent’s departure, Superintendent Kirk Easton and Business Manager Craig Crosswait are retiring. 

Nick Gottlob, the principal of West and Mountain View elementary schools, was hired earlier in the year to serve as superintendent. Ashley Anderson, the assistant principal at the schools, was promoted to principal.

Crosswait will be replaced by Mistie Caldwell, who served for the past 17 years as the executive director of Visit Spearfish.

title: SBHS seniors earn more than $1.6 million in scholarships and awards
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: The SBHS Class of 2026 had 65 Regent Scholar Diplomas that were presented recently at the awards ceremony at the high school west gym.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
SBHS seniors earn more than $1.6 million in scholarships and awards
The SBHS Class of 2026 had 65 Regent Scholar Diplomas that were presented recently at the awards ceremony at the high school west gym.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts   

STURGIS – The annual scholarship and awards program at Sturgis Brown High School recently celebrated the achievements of the Class of 2026 as graduating seniors received awards totaling more than $1.63 million for students continuing their education at colleges and technical schools.

Dadra Avery, sophomore and senior class advisor, welcomed students, parents and guests to the ceremony and praised the dedication shown by the graduating class throughout their high school careers.

“Today’s award ceremony celebrates the academic achievements of dedicated students who have attained the high expectations they set for themselves,” Avery said. “This event represents 4 years of hard work. It is a much-awaited day in every student’s life because it reflects the efforts put forth throughout their academic journey. It gives a sense of achievement and responsibility toward fulfilling future commitments.”

SBHS Principal Pete Wilson also addressed the seniors and highlighted several statewide academic honors earned by members of the graduating class.

Wilson noted that on April 27, the Associated School Boards of South Dakota hosted the Academic Excellence Recognition Banquet in Pierre. Schools across the state were invited to recognize one student for every 100 graduates based on academic criteria including GPA, college readiness and exam scores.

Representing Sturgis Brown at the banquet were Kate Bestgen, Hunter Johnson and McKenna LaBeau, who were recognized for their outstanding academic achievements.

Wilson also announced that Quinn Brook was named second-team Daktronics Academic All-State. The honor is based on a formula using SAT or ACT scores along with grade-point average, with students compared against top academic performers from across South Dakota.

The program and awards came from 50 organizations and individuals wanting to help SBHS graduates with the cost of higher education.

title: Belle charities still receiving money  20 years after Banner Health settlement
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer
description: 2026 Banner committee members and recipients of funds from left are: Kathryn Bogner, Louise Reade, Marylin Huston-Engle, Chris Davis, (back), Jody Westburg, Genevive Skoberg, and Mike Reade. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Belle charities still receiving money  20 years after Banner Health settlement
2026 Banner committee members and recipients of funds from left are: Kathryn Bogner, Louise Reade, Marylin Huston-Engle, Chris Davis, (back), Jody Westburg, Genevive Skoberg, and Mike Reade. Courtesy photo 

BELLE FOURCHE — The city of Belle Fourche issued nearly $97,000 to organizations this year thanks to Banner Health settlement funds. 

In 2004, South Dakota Attorney General Larry Long filed a lawsuit against Banner Health after it sold Lookout Memorial Hospital, the David M. Dorsett Nursing Home, Sturgis Community Health Care Center, and Belle Fourche Health Care Center to Rapid City Regional Hospital and West Dakota Health Care.

After Banner Health settled lawsuits brought by the South Dakota Attorney General in 2004 for about $3 million, $1.8 million was split between 5 Northern Hills communities, including Spearfish, Belle Fourche, Sturgis, Eureka, and Gregory. 

Belle Fourche received $100,000. For the last 20 years, the city issued grants with the interest the fund collected. 

During that timeframe, the city has issued $96,689.30 in grants, Kellen Willert, a member of the grant committee, said. He said that the initial $100,000 balance remains intact.

This year, the city received requests for $7,000 in grants and disbursed $4,500. 

Belle Fourche Silver Lining Senior Center, Belle Fourche Compassion Cupboard, Delta Dental Mobile Clinic, Good Shepherd Free Clinic, and the Belle Fourche Rec Center all received grants ranging from $300 to $1,050. Compassion Cupboard, Delta Dental Mobile Clinic, and the Good Shepherd Free Clinic are outlets of the Belle Fourche Global Methodist Church, St. James Episcopal Church, and Our Savior’s Lutheran Church, respectively.  

Recipients of the grants are selected by a 3-person committee composed of Willert, Genevieve Skogberg, and Kathryn Bogner.

Good Shepherd Free Clinic, which provides free medical care to individuals who fall beneath 200% of the federal poverty line regardless of insurance status, received $1,050.

“We are not a business that sells products to earn money,” said Chris Davis, executive director of the clinic. “Any money that we receive through grant applications, individuals, and organizations is money that covers all expenses that Good Shepherd Clinic has each year. We cover prescriptions, dental services, lab testing, but also have accounting fees, medical insurance for our providers, equipment and clinic supplies, payroll, advertising, and more.”

The clinic operates 2 locations, one in Spearfish, at 1020 State St., and another in Lead, at 825 W. Main St.

Delta Dental Mobile Clinic also received money from the fund. The clinic offers free dental care for patients 0 through 21 years old. The program has operated since 2006. 

Louise Reade, secretary of St. James Episcopal, said that the program treats up to 90 patients per year. 

“Since it (the program) has started, we’ve done over a million dollars of free dental work,” Reade said. 

The mobile clinic received $1,050 this year. 

Compassion Cupboard, which donates food to those in need, received $1,050.

“This helps our budget a lot,” Mike Reade, who sits on the board of directors of Compassion Cupboard, said in a city council meeting on May 18. He said that the cupboard feeds 100 to 125 families per month. 

The Belle Fourche Rec Center received $300. 

Jody Westburg, director of the Belle Fourche Rec Center, said that the money would help purchase equipment for aquatics and fitness classes. 

“We really appreciate this, and thank you guys very much for what you do,” Westberg said to the committee. 

Silver Lining Senior Center offers meals at its location at 828 Kingsbury St., and delivers meals to elderly individuals who cannot leave their homes.  

“We do pretty good so far as meeting our goals as far as finances,” Marilyn Huston-Engle, board president of Silver Lining, said. “It’s the delivery meals that are really costing us a lot of money. … So, this is really going to help keep our budget in line.” 

She said that the senior center donates about 60 meals per day. 

Silver Lining received $1,050 this year.

title: Spearfish approves agreements for TIFs 9 and 10
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: This image is a mock-up of the proposed multi-family housing project that is set to be built in TIF District 10 on St. Onge Road. Courtesy image
_full_text:
TIF 9.png
This image is a mock-up of the proposed multi-family housing project that is set to be built in TIF District 10 on St. Onge Road. Courtesy image 

 TIF 10.png
This map shows the location of TIF 9, where a 94-unit apartment complex is set to break ground this week. Courtesy map 

SPEARFISH — The Spearfish City Council approved 2 tax increment financing agreements this week: one for TIF 9, located between Paramount Drive and Platinum Drive near Exit 14, and one for TIF 10, The Pines apartment complex northeast of Peaceful Pines Senior Living Facility. Both TIF districts have already been approved by the city council. Tax increment financing agreements define and establish the developer’s responsibilities and obligations related to the use of funds from a TIF district.

“The purpose of these agreements is to memorialize and enter into a contract with the developer establishing the performance by the developer, their requirement to comply with the approved project plan, and also the requirement for establishing the total maximum amount reimbursable through the TIF,” said Spearfish Community Development Director Peter Wysocki.

Tax increment financing is a public financing system that uses future increases in property taxes to reimburse the costs of public improvements built within a designated TIF boundary. The value of all the properties inside the district is assessed or calculated, and the total amount of property tax generated by all those properties is noted — the base amount of property tax revenues. All property revenue above this base amount, for the life of the TIF, is captured by the TIF to refund the costs of the public improvements or project. This amount — the amount over the base — is called the “tax increment.” Over time, property values are presumed to increase in part due to infrastructure improvements brought about by the TIF project itself. When the TIF is retired, the total taxation values revert to the original taxing entities.

“Importantly, tax increment financing does not involve the city providing upfront funds,

grants, or general tax dollars for a project. Under the pay-as-you-go structure proposed

for this TIF District, the developer advances all costs associated with public

improvements. Reimbursement occurs only if and when tax increment revenues are

generated. If no development occurs, or if tax increment revenues are insufficient, the

City has no obligation to provide payment,” according to the tax increment financing Project plan for TIF 9.

In TIF 9, Spearfish Multifamily, LLC plans to build a 94-unit housing apartment complex. Those 94 rental units will be distributed across 5 buildings — some will be townhome-style with attached garages. Others will be flat-style apartments, according to representatives of Lloyd Companies, who presented to the city council. 

The maximum amount of reimbursement the developer is eligible to receive as they build that apartment complex is $3,233,053.

TIF 10, located on St. Onge Road south of Interstate 90, was created to help support the development of a 98-unit apartment complex called “The Pines.” The developer in TIF 10 is Elkhorn Ridge Apartments, LLC, which is not affiliated with Elk Horn Ridge Resort or RV Park.

The TIF 10 developer is eligible for $2,051,432 in reimbursement from the TIF.

The housing units at both The Pines and the apartment complex on Paramount Drive will have rent restrictions, capped at 80% of Area Median Income — a number determined by the state. Area Median Income, as defined by the state, is more than $100,000.

title: Bradley, Keszler sworn in  after re-canvass of election
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Rod Bradley and Terry Keszler have been officially installed as the newest city leaders in Sturgis.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

STURGIS — Rod Bradley and Terry Keszler have been officially installed as the newest city leaders in Sturgis. 

On Monday, the Sturgis City Council held the second canvass of the election by which Bradley was elected as the new mayor of Sturgis, and Keszler was elected to the Ward 1 city council seat. The second canvass was scheduled after the council found discrepancies in the voter numbers, during the first canvass, June 4. 

Sturgis City Finance Officer Ann Bertolotto said on Monday that after checking with state, county, and local area election officials, as well as with city attorney Eric Davis, she determined that the discrepancies did not fall within the parameters of state law to require a recount. South Dakota Codified Law 12-21-10 states that a candidate can petition for a recount only if there is a vote margin of 2% or less.  

“The research further indicated that the proper action for the canvassing board was to identify and document the discrepancies discovered during the canvassing process, determine whether those discrepancies affected the outcome of the election, and if they did not, certify the election results as submitted by the election workers,” Bertolotto wrote in her report to the council. 

From the beginning, the city council said the discrepancies were not enough to affect the outcome of the election. Bertolotto said after comparing the voter registration numbers with the poll books, and after comparing the poll books with the number of ballots that were taken to the polls and the number that were returned, city staff found 16 vote discrepancies across Wards 1, 3, and 4. There were no discrepancies in Ward 2. 

Bradley received 984 votes, compared to 366 votes for challenger Richelle Bruch and 360 votes for Tammy Bohn. Keszler received 163 votes compared to 121 for challenger Brenda Vasknetz. 

After taking some time to review the poll books, the council voted unanimously to accept the June 2026 election results with the discrepancies. 

Once the official canvass was completed, Bertolotto administered the oath of office for Bradley and Keszler, and Bradley immediately continued with the agenda for the rest of the meeting. Council members elected Tony Dargatz as the city council president, and Alex Usera as the vice president. 

The next regularly scheduled Sturgis City Council meeting will be 6:30 p.m. June 15.

title: Coincidence? You decide
byline: By Tere Froelich Black Hills Pioneer
description: CUSTER STATE PARK — An underlying current running through the entire play, the words “Coincidence? You decide,” anchor the show’s conspiracy-theory premise in Theatre 605: Black Hills Playhouse’s initial stage performance for this year, “The Complete History of America (Abridged).”
_full_text:
CUSTER STATE PARK — An underlying current running through the entire play, the words “Coincidence? You decide,” anchor the show’s conspiracy-theory premise in Theatre 605: Black Hills Playhouse’s initial stage performance for this year, “The Complete History of America (Abridged).” 

In a staged debate between actors Liv Moeller, Jason Reuter and Skyler Weaver, the show takes audience members back to discovery of the new continent, giving focus to the earliest settlers of North America to some of the latest political headlines as conspiracy theories and their impacts are bandied about. The play hits on key points from discovery and colonization, the American Revolution, the world wars, roaring 20s, Cold War and modern scandals, using high energy and comedy to remind audiences the past still resonates. 

Noting his fascination with historical events and the impact they have, director Raimondo (Rai) Genna shares influences for the production within the playbill.

The play, he said, “reminds us that history is not necessarily just what happened in times gone by, but it is also the moment we are living in the now, tomorrow’s history.”

With a wide range of vocals, instrument talents and character portrayals, the actors shed personas quickly, adapting as skits morph into new situations. Actors move fluidly across gender lines, swapping roles as scenes demand.

While the jesting and ribaldry includes satire, lighter humor keeps audience members engaged as centuries of history unfold within the 90-minute show. Breaking the wall between performers and individuals in the seats makes this show personal as questions directed at audience members continually return to the show’s domino conspiracy theory premise: conspiracies lead to each other. Discourse pushes and pulls emotions as people re-discover the America they call home.

A seasoned actor, Reuter moves seamlessly from one era to the next, drawing from his repertoire, most notably as the hard-nosed detective Diamond Spade investigating the conspiracy.

Moeller exhibits strength and ambition in her performances as Amerigo Vespucci and Thomas Jefferson, and later, to her roles as a soldier in the trenches and former President Ronald Reagan.

For his part, Weaver, a comedic showman, fills in pieces with flair and style, sometimes in a wig and dress and other times as a voice in a rapid-fire radio broadcast parody with the rest of the trio.

Providing some of the greatest impact for the performance is the set design by Ahna Packard who researched memorable moments outlined in the play. Taking center stage, the oversized American flag provides space for actors to enter, exit and circle back. A ribbon banner stretching across the flag has decades imprinted upon it to help focus the play’s timeline.

Postage stamp-sized portraits of bygone eras are on display, utilizing comedic elements, such as those viewable in “Schoolhouse Rock” and “Peabody and Sherman” to support the overarching questions posed. Grecian columns underscore the symbolism of deeply held beliefs upon which America was founded. 

Written by Adam Long, Reed Martin and Austin Tichenor, “The Complete History of America (Abridged)” was originally produced and performed by the renowned Reduced Shakespeare Company in 1994. This show was produced by special arrangement with Broadway Play Publishing, Inc., NYC.

Also on the artistic team are scenic designer Packard; costume designer Scott Matthew Anderson; lighting designer Ty Micheel; sound designer Rowan V. Sullivan; and stage manager Izzy Paisley.

Whether history as it is written is coincidence or conspiracy, “The Complete History of America (Abridged)” offers a compelling and uproarious view worth arguing about.

To learn more, visit https://theatre605.org.

title: Last call for Schlitz
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: DEADWOOD — With the announcement that Pabst Brewing Company will no longer brew or distribute Schlitz beer, Madame Peacocks is facing the end of an era with their usual style and panache.
_full_text:
DEADWOOD — With the announcement that Pabst Brewing Company will no longer brew or distribute Schlitz beer, Madame Peacocks is facing the end of an era with their usual style and panache. 

Tom Koth, retired co-owner of Madame Peacock’s in Deadwood, said that when he and his wife, Julie Koth, bought the building in 2012, he announced to his wife that the bar was going to be a Schlitz bar. 

“Schlitz beer was the first beer I ever got a buzz on over 50 years ago,” said Tom. “So, I told my wife we’re going to make it our house beer. We bought one case, just to test it out, 14 years ago. It was kind of a slow to start out with.”

Tom said the beer gained a negative reputation after a recipe change in the 1970s that depleted the beers popularity. Pabst Brewing revived a 1960s formula in 2008, bringing the nostalgic beer’s popularity back for its loyal followers. 

“The common refrain is, ‘I used to steal Schlitz out of my dad’s cooler,’” said Tom. 

“You wouldn’t believe how many people sit down at the bar and say, ‘My dad used to drink Schlitz,’” said Alex Geyerman, Julie’s daughter and owner of Madame Peacocks. “Now they’re having one on their dad’s or their uncle’s behalf. We hear that all the time.”

Michael and Diane Erin, visiting from Chicago, Ill., echoed that sentiment while sitting at the bar. Diane said they saw the sign on the street, advertising Schlitz for sale inside, and made a detour.

“I grew up with it. My dad drank it,” said Diane. “I was probably 10 or 11 (years old when I had my first drink of Schlitz). It was in the fridge, and my dad ate it with crackers and liver sausage while watching wrestling in black and white. Good memories.”

In March, Pabst Brewing Company announced that it was discontinuing Schlitz because of rising shipping and production costs. Tom said he received a tip from a Pabst Brewing insider when the announcement was made.

“As soon as I found that out, I called the distributor in Rapid City and I said, ‘I’ll take every case that you have.’ So, they delivered 170 cases,” said Tom. “We currently have between 80 and 85 (cases left).”

Geyerman said their goal is to sell the last bottle of Schlitz in America, “that isn’t super expired.” In the meantime, the store is taking bets on when the last bottle will be sold in store. 

“We’ve got this countdown, like they do when a baby is due and the due date, but this is when we will run out of Schlitz,” said Geyerman. 

A poster, celebrating the last days of Schlitz in Deadwood is also for sale, along with the “It’s not that bad” T-shirts.

“Whether you’ve never had a Schlitz, or you haven’t had one in 30 years, you take that first sip and say, ‘Hey, it’s not that bad,’” said Tom. “Then we’ll point to the shirt hanging on the wall.”

Tom and Geyerman said that over the decade that they’ve been selling Schlitz in the women’s clothing store, they’ve had customers travel from across the country who come into the store just to drink a Schlitz. In that time, Tom said customers have donated memorabilia and vintage Schlitz merchandise. The donations eventually amounted to the “Mini-Schlitz Museum” behind the bar. Items include a promotional bikini, short sleeved button up, and hat set donated by the daughter of a Schlitz deliveryman, several Schlitz lamps, a cooler, and nametags from a man who worked in the brewery. 

“A guy from North Carolina came in. He had worked at the Winston Salem Brewery for, like, 35 years,” said Tom. “He came in and he says, ‘When I go home, I’m going to send you some souvenirs from my career at the Schlitz brewery. He gave me these personal items that I could keep. He gave me his badge that he wore every day at the brewery. The Schlitz people are so loyal, and if they know you have something in common with that beer, you’re friends.”

Geyerman said she’s unsure what the future house beer will be, once that last bottle of Schlitz is gone, but the museum is here to stay.

title: Cheers to 150 years! Spearfish Brewing Company  crafts limited edition beer to  raise a pint to the Pioneer
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — This year, as the Black Hills Pioneer marks 150 years of reporting on communities in the Northern Hills, the Pioneer would like the community to raise a glass along with us. Spearfish Brewing Company is preparing batches of a special brew in celebration of our ink-slinging anniversary.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — This year, as the Black Hills Pioneer marks 150 years of reporting on communities in the Northern Hills, the Pioneer would like the community to raise a glass along with us. Spearfish Brewing Company is preparing batches of a special brew in celebration of our ink-slinging anniversary.

There, head brewer Carson Wika is making modern magic in sleek stainless steel tanks, using ingredients as old (and older than) our endeavor to bring important, fair, and accurate news coverage to the Black Hills.  

“It’s sort of a pre-prohibition lager. I tried to use ingredients that would have been available 150 years ago,” Wika said. He was a home brewer for a decade before he started at Spearfish Brewing Company. He’s been practicing the science of beer-making there for 5 years since.

The primary pre-prohibition ingredient in our celebratory suds is a 6-row malt grain.

“Most beers I use are 2-row malts. This one we use 6-row, which is something they would have had back on the day. It is not quite as (genetically) modified as our modern 2-row malt that we use now.”

The flavor of the resulting beer is more grain-forward than more modern brews. Lagers were also popular 150 years ago. Many of the earliest beer advertisements in the Pioneer were for establishments that served “Lager Beer.”

“There are only 2 different kinds of beer. There is ale and lager,” Wika said. “Lager is usually fermented colder, more in the 50 degree range. It is just a different type of yeast.”

In explaining the basic process of beer making, Wika has to break down rather complicated chemistry.

“The basic steps are: mill the grain, mash it in, set it at a certain temperature and let the enzymes that work that turn the starch into sugar, then we need the sugar for the yeast to eat. That creates CO2 and alcohol as a by-product. I’m basically just making an environment for the yeast to do the thing,” Wika said.

Wika started brewing the Pioneer’s anniversary beer in March.

On a bright spring day in Spearfish, Dustin Lundstad, one of Wika’s brew assistants, ascended a ladder to the top of a towering stainless steel tank, with a box in tow. That day, the beer was ready for the addition of its primary flavoring agent.

Carefully, as members of our newspaper team looked on, he poured in the special, scarlet red ingredient that aims to capture the very essence of summer flavor.

Vivid red strawberry puree gives our strawberry sesquicentennial lager its unique — and historically significant — flavor.

“We added strawberry to it, since we used to produce all of the strawberries for the area back in the day,” Wika said.

Spearfish Valley has a long history of growing produce, and that produce helped feed the folks who made their way west in search of gold.

The Pioneer has now been the paper of record for a century and a half in the Hills. In that time, we’ve reported on the area’s relationship with the suds. From the period of prospectors to the modern era, we’ve found nothing quite goes together like pints and pioneers.

The Pioneer’s first edition, published this week in 1876, was printed in a tent outdoors.

A later edition ran a story on the construction of its new building, proclaiming that “We feel proud of our new building, rough though it may be, it still is better than the tent which housed our first hand press,” the paper ran another, rather frothy news item. That story proclaimed: “Herrman and Treber received a carload of E. Anheuser’s beer this afternoon.” Anheuser, now Anheuser-Busch, was founded just a few years prior, in 1852, in St. Louis, Mo. Alongside the story announcing the beer delivery, a report that Deadwood had ”one hundred ten too many saloons,” according to “well-known bartender” Jerry Marriatta, also ran under the headline “Too Many Saloons.”

In 1890, one Michael Clause was arrested after allegedly stealing $5,000 in state revenue stamps from the office of the deputy collector the year prior. He used those stamps, according to a story published in the Queen City Mail on February 26, to purchase smuggled beer.

The Strawberry Sesquicentennial Lager now on tap at Spearfish Brewing Company promises to be much more refined than any smuggled beers in the days of yore. We invite you to try it and have a pint in recognition of 150 years of the Pioneer.

title: Sturgis Artwalk unveils 6 new sculptures along historic main street
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Residents and visitors gathered Saturday in downtown Sturgis for the unveiling of 6 new sculptures as part of the Sturgis Artwalk program, adding another collection of public art pieces to Historic Main Street.
_full_text:
STURGIS — Residents and visitors gathered Saturday in downtown Sturgis for the unveiling of 6 new sculptures as part of the Sturgis Artwalk program, adding another collection of public art pieces to Historic Main Street.  

The unveiling ceremony featured an artist reception and remarks from community leaders, who highlighted each sculpture and its significance to the community.

The Sturgis Artwalk is the result of years of collaboration, fundraising, commissions, and volunteer efforts by local organizations and residents. The self-guided tour showcases artwork throughout Sturgis, ranging from detailed bronze sculptures to contemporary installations.

Veronica Grosek of the Sturgis Area Chamber of Commerce said the annual sculpture program plays an important role in enhancing downtown Sturgis.

“We had a sculpture unveiling ceremony that was well attended by people from our community. The Downtown Sturgis Foundation does this project because the arts are so important for a community. In a downtown space especially, art is a big part of beautification,” Grosek said.

The project is made possible through support from several community organizations. Sponsors include the Downtown Sturgis Foundation, the Downtown Business Improvement District, the Sturgis Area Arts Council, the Greater Sturgis Foundation, and the city of Sturgis.

Grosek explained that sculpture selections are made through a partnership with the Sculpture Walk program in Sioux Falls. 

“The program that does the Sculpture Walk in Sioux Falls also works with us,” she said. “A coordinator provides a large list of sculpture options, including photographs, dimensions, materials, and artist information. The Downtown Sturgis Foundation board then reviews those options and selects the pieces that will be displayed in Sturgis.”

The sculptures are not only on display for public enjoyment but some are also available for purchase.

New 2026 Sturgis Artwalk Sculptures:

• Let’s Play by Christine Knapp, of Colorado.  This bronze sculpture captures a playful dog in a pose that invites interaction. According to Knapp, dogs are highly attuned to human body language, and the sculpture encourages viewers to connect with the animal’s playful spirit.

• Ghost of Sage by Tom Ford, of Gillette, Wyo. Inspired by Wyoming’s legendary bucking horse Steamboat, this sculpture celebrates the power, determination, and untamed nature of one of the West’s most iconic animals. Ford said the piece reflects both the horse’s explosive energy and enduring legacy.

• Can You Hear Me Now? by Bobbie Carlyle, of Colorado.  This whimsical bronze depicts a young girl holding a seashell to her ear as though she is speaking on a cellphone. The sculpture blends imagination and nostalgia, suggesting messages carried through the wind and sea.

• Arc of Peace by Lorri Acott, of Colorado.  A graceful figure releases an arc of bronze origami cranes into the air, symbolizing peace, hope, and positive intentions. The sculpture serves as a reminder that peace is something individuals can create and share with the world.

• In a Mystic Forest by Bobbie Carlyle, of Colorado.  Set in an imaginative woodland scene, the sculpture portrays a young boy discovering magical creatures that have stepped from his imagination into reality, creating a sense of wonder and adventure.

• So Proud by Christine Knapp, of Colorado.  This bronze bald eagle commemorates the bird’s official designation as the national bird of the United States in December 2024. The sculpture celebrates the eagle as a symbol of strength, independence, and freedom while recognizing the remarkable recovery of the nation’s bald eagle population.

The 6 sculptures will remain on display throughout the coming year, giving residents and visitors an opportunity to experience public art in the heart of downtown Sturgis while supporting a program that continues to enhance the community’s cultural landscape.

title: Colo. Blvd. chip seal project costs go up by $30,000
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — Once chip seal operations recommence on Colorado Boulevard from Spearfish Canyon to Grant Street, the city is set to spend an additional $30,335 to address further issues identified after the 2025 Chip Seal Project.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — Once chip seal operations recommence on Colorado Boulevard from Spearfish Canyon to Grant Street, the city is set to spend an additional $30,335 to address further issues identified after the 2025 Chip Seal Project.

Just east of Lariat Drive, a leak on a private irrigation line saturated the ground. During the initial chip seal process, the road was patched to provide a level driving surface. Since then, the curb and gutter in the area has settled.

Now that chip sealing operations are going to be re-performed on Colorado Boulevard, Spearfish city staff have indicated that “corrective action should be done to repair the road in this location so that it drains properly because poor drainage can lead to premature failure of the road surface,” in a change order request submitted to city council.

The irrigation system will need to be repaired, and then the ground will need to dry out before the road, curb, and gutter can be repaired. The cost of that is about $30,335.

On Monday, the Spearfish City Council unanimously approved a change order to allow for the additional cost.

In September 2025, the Spearfish City Council approved a $475,385 contract with Dakota Asphalt LLC to chip seal Colorado Boulevard from Spearfish Canyon to Jackson Boulevard. The project came in under the cost estimated by Interstate Engineering (which was $632,352.64), but still required the council to pass a budget supplement of $319,385.56. The total project costs were estimated at $519,385.56 as of Sept. 2, 2025. After the change order passed Monday, the total contract amount is now $529,558.56.

Spearfish Public Works Director Adam McMahon said in September there were several projects that his department had budgeted for 2025 that never moved forward — about $600,000 worth. The supplement came from that amount, which was set aside for incomplete projects.

When it became evident that last fall’s chip seal operation had failed, the city council opted to have Dakota Asphalt re-perform its work from Spearfish Canyon to Grant Street as soon as possible. The original project was never closed out or accepted, so the original contract has been amended through change orders.

title: Downtown Friday Nights, Canyon Acoustics Series return to Spearfish this summer
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — Spearfish will celebrate the summer with weekly Downtown Friday Nights, as well as the Canyon Acoustics Series, which both feature a variety of musical acts.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — Spearfish will celebrate the summer with weekly Downtown Friday Nights, as well as the Canyon Acoustics Series, which both feature a variety of musical acts.

The Canyon Acoustic series will take place weekly on Wednesdays from June 10 to July 29 beginning at 6 p.m. in Spearfish City Park.

Taylor Scott Band will perform on June 10. Humbletown will perform on June 17. Jenny Don’t & the Spurs will perform on June 24. Hot Dawg will perform on July 1. Earl Nelson & The Company will perform on July 7. Deltaphonic will perform on July 15. North Folk Crossing will perform on July 22. Joseph Huber Band will perform on July 29.

Downtown Friday Nights occur weekly from 6-9 p.m. on Main Street beginning June 12. Food and merchandise vendors will be present.

Jacob Westfall will perform on June 12. Randy McAllister will perform on June 19. Sgt. Rock will perform on June 26. Tiffany Johnson will perform on July 3. Arcana Kings will perform on July 10. Clay Aery will perform on July 17. Dustin Evans will perform on July 24. Brandon Jones will perform on July 31. Nate Botsford will perform on Aug. 14. Pop Rocks will perform on Aug. 21.

Britney Hicks, a visitor information specialist for Visit Spearfish, said she also expects Downtown Friday Nights to feature a variety of activities for children, including a bouncy castle and face-painting.

title: Man suspected of shooting at Central States Fairgrounds, shot and killed by tribal police
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: RAPID CITY — A man was shot and injured at the Central States Fairgrounds at 8:45 a.m., Sunday. The shooting suspect was identified as 58-year-old John Troy Lee of Rapid City.
_full_text:
RAPID CITY — A man was shot and injured at the Central States Fairgrounds at 8:45 a.m., Sunday. The shooting suspect was identified as 58-year-old John Troy Lee of Rapid City.

Lee was located by Oglala Sioux Tribal Officials on the Pine Ridge Indian Reservation. There was an officer involved shooting and the suspect is deceased.

The original shooting victim remains hospitalized. His name and condition are not being released at this time.

The Rapid City Police, South Dakota Highway Patrol, Rapid City Fire, US National Park Service, and Oglala Sioux Tribal law enforcement are assisting with this ongoing investigation.
