title: Sturgis Public Works director outlines active, completed capital improvement projects
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — The city of Sturgis has leveraged federal and state funds to maximize the local budget and perform tens of millions of dollars in capital improvement projects, Public Works Director Rick Bush said Monday.
_full_text:
STURGIS — The city of Sturgis has leveraged federal and state funds to maximize the local budget and perform tens of millions of dollars in capital improvement projects, Public Works Director Rick Bush said Monday.

During the regular city council meeting, Bush gave an update about capital improvement projects that are in the planning stages, are underway, or that have been successfully completed.

“Through strong partnerships with state and federal agencies, the city has been able to leverage our outside funding to deliver improvements to our water, our wastewater, our streets, pedestrian, and bicycle network, airport facilities, parks, and public buildings,” Bush said. “These projects help maintain essential services, improve public safety, enhance the quality of life, and position our community for future growth. While the infrastructure needs will continue to evolve, the city remains committed to identifying and delivering projects that provide lasting value to the community through these strong partnerships with state and federal agencies, careful planning and responsible stewardship of public resources. Sturgis is well positioned to continue making meaningful improvements in the years ahead. The progress made during 2025-2027 reflects the dedication of the city staff, our elected officials, and our many funding partners. Together these efforts have resulted in significant investments in our infrastructure and public facilities that support our residents, our businesses, and our visitors every day. So, when people say we’re not doing projects, that simply is not true.”

Some of the most critical projects the city has been working on include water and wastewater improvements, Bush said. The city’s $5 million Well No. 8 project is a Madison aquifer well that is about 1,400 feet deep and produces 460 gallons per minute. Additionally, the city’s $10.3 million north trunk sewer line extends services out to the Avalanche Road area.

The $440,000 Dudley Street sewer replacement and cured in place project was a major addition, that included reconstructing Silver Street, with sidewalk, curb and gutter, and asphalt.

Bike paths have been a major improvement, to increase movement through town, Bush said. The bike path projects will use a transportation alternative grant program from the South Dakota Department of Transportation, which means the state will fund 80% of the projects while the city picks up the remaining 20%.

“The city’s multi-use path system continues to grow through a strategic investment and grant partnerships,” he said. “These projects help improve our recreational opportunities, pedestrian connectivity, and our tourism amenities throughout the community.”

In the last few years, Bush said the city has completed the Vanocker Bike Path — a $750,000 project that utilized the state DOT grant.

The Moose Drive bike path is planned at a total cost of $600,000, with the city contributing $120,000 of that. That project will connect Dolan Creek Road all the way up to Raccoon Road. While the city is building that bike path, Bush said they will also install new storm sewer lines, curb and gutter, and new asphalt for Moose Drive. That, he said, is estimated to be a $1.2 million project that will come out of the city’s capital improvement fund.

In 2027, he said the city also plans to extend the bike path along Highway 14A, to connect Short Track Road west to Mountain View Mobile Home Estates, on the edge of town. That project is expected to cost about $1.5 million, and will also utilize the DOT grant, with a city match of $360,000.

Bush said the planned bike path extension along Highway 14A is a response to citizen safety concerns about crossing Lazelle Street. It goes along with other safety measures that are in the planning stages, for when the DOT reconstructs Lazelle Street.

“The idea with this plan was to help reduce the need to cross Lazelle Street,” he said of the bike path.

City crews have also been busy with street projects,

“A lot of times we get phone calls wanting to know why we’re not doing street projects,” he said. “We are. The street projects to maintain and improve transportation infrastructure always remain a priority.”

Bush said the city is currently in the process of bidding an estimated $885,000 Otter Road improvement project, which will replace and rebuild the base course and asphalt infrastructure on Otter Road, from Vanocker Road all the way down to the creek crossing, and along Raccoon Road to the creek crossing.

Another major road project will be paving Avalanche Road, after the Harvest Meadows Subdivision is finished. The project will widen the road from the bridge to the intersection with three lanes, a curb and gutter and a bike path. Bush said the city will also pave Avalanche Road to the rubble site, solving a multitude of complaints about that road and saving the city money in the long run.

“That will help with dust mitigation and with maintenance,” he said. “Right now, we’re currently about every 2 weeks having to blade that road and we’ve already put the first application of dust control on there. That was about $11,000. So if we do that multiple times through the year, it certainly doesn’t take long to see that making the road asphalt is a pretty good payoff.”

Traffic signals at the intersections of Ballpark Road and Junction Avenue, and Douglas Street and Junction Avenue, are also at the end of their life and are planned for replacement this fall, Bush said. At a cost of about $270,000, Bush said the improvement will include some ADA enhancements, including directional ramps with sound annunciators.

The city’s airport improvement program is an example of Sturgis leveraging federal and state funds, since most improvements are done with a 95% grant from the Federal Aviation Administration, with a 2.5% contribution from the state and 2.5% of the project costs paid by the city.

“The airport serves as an important transportation and economic development asset,” Bush said. “These projects improve safety, operational efficiency and long-term viability, leveraging substantial federal and state funding.”

Currently, Bush said the city is working on two airport projects. The $310,000 terminal reconstruction project is expected to wrap up this week, with a final inspection conducted Tuesday. A $3.5 million parallel taxiway project is also underway, and will allow planes to taxi parallel to the runway. Before that project, planes were forced to taxi down the runway, creating a risk for collision with incoming aircraft.

Improvements at city buildings have included roof repairs at the Sturgis Community Center and at city hall, boiler replacements, HVAC repairs at the library, and miscellaneous repairs at city hall. New, ADA accessible doors at the liquor store were also scheduled to be installed Monday.

In addition to active infrastructure projects, Bush said the city is finishing up its Safe Streets for All program, which identifies safety improvements for the city’s transportation infrastructure, while positioning the city to compete for future federal funding. Last Friday was the deadline for a $1.9 million implementation grant that would help pay for projects identified with that study.

title: Biden fires up Democrats, raises record amount: former president draws 1,200 people for annual dinner
byline: By Tom Lawrence Special to the Black Hills Pioneer
description: SIOUX FALLS — Former President Joe Biden has spoken at countless rallies and Democratic events, so he was right at home in Sioux Falls on Friday night.
_full_text:
SIOUX FALLS — Former President Joe Biden has spoken at countless rallies and Democratic events, so he was right at home in Sioux Falls on Friday night.

Biden was the keynote speaker at the South Dakota Democratic Party’s annual McGovern Day Dinner. It’s the party’s biggest fundraiser of the year, and having a former president as the headliner was great for ticket sales. The crowd was estimated at 1,200 people, and party officials said it raised about $275,000, a record for the party.

Biden started slow, and his voice was rough and ragged. But it grew louder and more confident as he encouraged South Dakota Democrats to stand up for what they believe in.

“I do believe our democracy is at stake,” he said.

Biden said Democrats are doing extremely well in special elections, and he predicted that will continue through the fall. People are fed up with the corruption and the economic maladies facing the nation.

“What do we do about it?” he asked rhetorically. “We’ve got to vote Democratic. Our very democracy is at stake.”

Biden said this is a challenging time, but he remains optimistic.

“We never give up and we can’t give up now,” he said. “There’s no quit in this country. None.”

Biden spoke scornfully of his predecessor and successor in the White House. He expressed outrage at President Trump’s many construction and destruction projects in the nation’s capital.

“My god, tearing down the East Room of the White House to make room for a ballroom more fitting of Versailles?” he said. “Or writing his name on the Kennedy Center. Or building an arch that would dwarf the Lincoln Memorial, or turning the Reflecting Pool into something you might see in a theme park!”

Biden also touched on the billions of dollars the Trump family has secured since Donald Trump returned to power.

“This is the most corrupt president in the history of the United States of America,” he said. “Look, it’s simply stunning to me.”

Biden said while Trump has profited from thousands of stock trades as president, he never bought or sold a stock or a bond during his public career. That’s why he was called “the poorest man in Congress,” he said.

SDDP Chairman Shane Merrill introduced Biden, saying the 46th president had been a friend to the state for many years. Biden carried South Dakota in the 2020 and 2024 Democratic Primaries, but he lost to Trump in 2020 and he and Barack Obama did not win here in 2008 and 2012.

The last time a Democratic presidential candidate won South Dakota was 1964, when President Lyndon Baines Johnson carried it as part of a landslide victory. No South Dakota Democrat has been elected governor since Dick Kneip won his third term in 1974, and the last statewide victory for a Democrat was in 2008, when Sen. Tim Johnson and Rep. Stephanie Herseth Sandlin were re-elected.

It’s been a long dry spell. The Democrats who gathered Friday night, many of them with thinning white hair, cheered loudly and came to their feet repeatedly. They are hungry for the success they once enjoyed, and were eager to hear Biden talk their language.

He spoke fondly of the late George McGovern, whom he served with for eight years in the Senate.

Biden recalled his first run for office in 1972, when McGovern was the Democratic nominee for president. They shared values and were friends, he said.

When McGovern died in the closing days of the 2012 election campaign, Biden came to Sioux Falls to speak at McGovern’s prayer service.

Another former South Dakota senator, Larry Pressler, 84, was the dinner. Pressler served 22 years in Congress as a Republican, but he has adopted an independent point of view in recent years and supported Barack Obama and Biden in the 2008 and 2012 elections. The two old senators shared some time backstage before the speech.

Biden spent 2 hours posing for more than 100 photos and shaking hands with people who paid for the privilege of meeting a president.

Retired state Rep. Linda Dummermuth Duba, a Sioux Falls Democrat who represented District 15, met Biden in the waning days of his presidency at a White House Christmas party in December 2024. They renewed acquaintances on Friday.

“He is so genuine and personable. He likes people,” said Dummermuth Duba, 69. “Barb Johnson (the widow of South Dakota Sen. Tim Johnson) couldn’t make it. Just had knee surgery. I gave her regards to him. He was genuinely touched.

“Decency is lacking these days. He still has it. I thought his speech was good. And just think, he stood for two hours and did photos. He spoke with every person who came for a picture. It’s not about him,” she said. “He truly loves this country and the people.”

Dummermuth Duba said she still regrets Biden’s decision to seek a second term.

 Biden fires up Democrats, raises record amount  2.jpeg
Former President Joe Biden has kept a low profile since leaving office but his appearance in Sioux Falls is one of several scheduled events as he makes a case for Democratic candidates while working to remind people of his work over the last half-century. Photo by Grace Stack 

“Was he perfect? No. He should have kept his word and run only for one term,” she said. “The result is what we have now.”

Owen Reitzel a “lifelong Democrat” from Alexandria, also met with the former president before his speech.

“He was great. Mostly talked to my wife but he was good,” said Reitzel, 68. “I was proud to take my picture with him.”

Merrill said he was honored to spend time with Biden and see the event go over so well.

“It meant the world to me, to see the turnout and so many friends in the audience. I wanted to put on a good show and raise some money and we accomplished that,” he said. “Biden did not charge us a speaking fee, he wanted this to be a good fundraiser for our state since he was such good friends with McGovern, Jim Abourezk, (Tom) Daschle and Johnson.”

Biden’s speech was held under unique circumstances for a politician. The electronic media was forbidden from recording his speech, and the former president did not speak to reporters.

But for more than 1,000 Democrats, it was a complete success. It also was for Biden, who thanked the crowd for “being so nice to me,” as he left the stage with a smile.

title: Northern Hills CASA celebrates 40 years of compassion and advocacy
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — Every year, children moving through the foster care system need champions. That’s the role of a volunteer court-appointed special advocate (CASA). Already in 2026, Northern Hills CASA has supported 69 children.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — Every year, children moving through the foster care system need champions. That’s the role of a volunteer court-appointed special advocate (CASA). Already in 2026, Northern Hills CASA has supported 69 children.

“Sadly, child maltreatment is on the rise,” said Amy Cermak, the executive director of Northern Hills CASA. Despite that, there are 71 local volunteers waiting in the wings to provide consistent support and advocacy for children as they navigate trying and uncertain times.

“We served 80 children in 2025,” Cermak said. “34 volunteers logged over 5,500 hours and traveled nearly 33,000 miles advocating for children and families.”

CASAs receive training to support children as their cases move through the judicial system. They spend time with kids and do extensive research to help judges determine if a child is best served by returning home, having their parent’s rights revoked, or moving to a new foster care placement.

For 40 years, “Northern Hills CASA has stood as a model for safeguarding a child’s right to a stable and permanent home,” Cermak said. The organization marked its banner anniversary with a celebratory event at Spearfish Public House Sunday.

“It is just an incredible outpouring of community efforts that have really got us to this point,” Cermak said.

Right now, Northern Hills CASA has more volunteers than cases, a testament to the organization’s outreach efforts and the community’s willingness to protect the interests of some of its most vulnerable members.

“When children are navigating the chaos and confusion of the foster care system, their world can feel incredibly small and frightening. Adults, such as caregivers, social workers, and therapists, are always rotating in and out of their lives,” Cermak said. “Then a CASA volunteer steps in. They are the one true constant. They listen, they advocate, and they ensure that the court sees the child, not just the case file. They help children grow, heal, and thrive.”

Retired Judge Warren Johnson, who saw the formation of Northern Hills CASA in 1986, explained just how important a CASA’s perspective can be.

“I’ll tell you, as a judge, I spent 32 years on the bench, that it gave you a really good (feeling) to go in there and see a CASA, who was the best informed person in the room,” Johnson said. “They went to the schools. They went to the therapists. They went to the lawyers, they came and made a recommendation, and it was helpful to me. I can remember times when I didn’t know what to do. I had prosecutors telling me one thing, the parents’ lawyers telling me something else, the child’s lawyers telling me something else, so I turned to the CASA, and that’s where I got the best information.”

 CASA 5 alt.JPG
Lara Hawkins, a former Department of Social Services Supervisor, and retired Judge Warren Johnson tell the story of Northern Hills CASA’s foundation at special 40th anniversary celebration Sunday, at the Spearfish Public House. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

Lara Hawkins, a former Department of Social Services Supervisor, remembered the conditions under which the CASA program was founded, and how critical the need was.

“We already felt we had really strong relationships between judges and social workers, but we were all aware of how overwhelmed everyone was,” Hawkins said. “Court-appointed lawyers had limited experience in representing children, and social workers were constantly changing. There was turnover. Even if a child came into care under an investigating social worker who had deep knowledge of the case, when he or she transferred to a foster care worker, things could change.”

Hawkins said she had more than 19 years of experience in child protection.

“It was the most difficult job,” Hawkins said. “I got a salary. I look at all of you who do this out of the goodness of your hearts and maybe occasionally get a little mileage. We are really grateful.”

Johnson said when the program started, he wasn’t sure there would be enough people willing to volunteer so much of their time and energy to help kids through the system. The current number of volunteers, he said, is extremely encouraging.

“I really appreciate what you’re willing to do for kids, because they need you,” Johnson said.

On Sunday, CASA volunteers, donors, and supporters celebrated the organization’s banner anniversary with live music, custom cocktails, and cake.

 CASA 6.JPG
Northern Hills CASA marked 40 years of advocating for children at the Spearfish Public House Sunday, with live music performed by J.J. Kent and the Aces and Eights. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

“This is a day of deep gratitude. To our volunteers, you are the backbone of this organization. You bring compassion, patience, and unwavering dedication to every single child you serve. You have shown up time and time again to lift up our youth and change the trajectory of their future,” Cermak said.

title: GF&P transplanting brown trout from Spearfish to Rapid Creek
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — Most people who tied a fly onto their line and cast it into the waters of Spearfish Creek can tell you what a gem the fishery is.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — Most people who tied a fly onto their line and cast it into the waters of Spearfish Creek can tell you what a gem the fishery is.

Now the South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks, is sharing the love and the trout.

Jeremy Kientz, area fisheries supervisor, told the Pioneer that in fisheries, 1,000 fish per mile is considered to be a high-density fishery. In Spearfish Creek, the population in some sections was around 4,000 fish per mile.

In 2018, Travis Rehm, a graduate student at South Dakota State University, published his master’s degree thesis based on his research of experimental population reduction of brown trout in Spearfish Creek in an attempt to increase size. Kientz said what they found was that fish from up and down stream of the removal sites took the place of the removed trout. Thus, large gains in fish size were not realized.

Then in December 2021 or 2022, Kientz said the Bureau of Reclamation reduced the amount of water being released from the Pactola dam to perform dam maintenance. Delays forced the creek to drop to around 8 cubic feet per second (cfs) – a very low amount.

By the time the creek made its way through the Dark Canyon loss zone – an area where the water drops underground — to Rapid City, the creek was down to about 1 cfs. Coupled with several very cold days, “adult brown trout numbers in Rapid City have been pretty dramatically impacted,” he said. “Some of our sites we were seeing 33% of what our historical norms are.”

“We've been looking at different ways to boost the Rapid Creek population and try to get it back to healthier numbers. One thing that we're conscious of is that stocking hatchery fish on top of wild reproducing populations isn't always a good option, and so knowing that we had the overabundance in Spearfish Creek, we're taking from the overabundance and moving it down into Rapid Creek, so that we're moving wild fish with wild fish.”

Recently, GF&P fisheries staffers electrofished Spearfish Creek.

To do this, a net was placed in a shallow area of the creek to prevent fish from escaping downstream. The team starts 100 yards downstream and walks upstream. Two people have the electrofishing backpacks on.

The backpack has batteries in it. A cord trails behind the person wearing the backpack and they hold a wand that looks similar to a metal detecting want. As they walk upstream, moving the wand side-to-side in the water, fish area attracted to the current. Once close enough, the electrical charge stuns the fish, and they float to the surface.

Other staffers with nets scoop up the trout. If a stunned fish escapes the net, it will float downstream before quickly being revived.

The study is being broken into 3 segments, Kientz said. In the lower and upper 100 yards, the team makes one pass. Every fish is netted and a fin is clipped so that in the future, people know that it had previously been caught and migrated to other areas of the study zone. All fish are returned to the water.

In the middle 100 yards, 3 passes are made.

In the first pass, he said, all fish are removed to be transplanted. Some are also fitted with tags so that “we can see growth metrics if we recapture those fish.”

In the second and third pass, all fish have fins clipped as part of the study.

Survival rates of transplanted fish are fairly high, Kientz said. All the fish in the first 2 transplants he participated in recently swam away on their own.

A sampling of Rapid Creek fish later this summer will help determine how many fish have survived.

title: Bear spotted in Sandstone
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: SPEARFISH — On Friday evening a black bear ambled its way through a backyard in Spearfish’s Sandstone neighborhood.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — On Friday evening a black bear ambled its way through a backyard in Spearfish’s Sandstone neighborhood.

A resident’s home security camera captured about 7 seconds of footage of the black bear sauntering through the frame. It didn’t appear to cause any damage or disturbance, however.

The bear, according to experienced bear hunters, who reviewed the surveillance image, was likely about 4-5 years old.

Bear sightings in the Black Hills are infrequent but growing in number.

Most sightings occur in April and early May as bears leave dens and look for food.

But they have been spotted throughout the spring and summer from Spearfish to Rapid City.

The Pioneer reached out to both the Spearfish Police Department and South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks. Neither agency had received any reports of bear sightings.

title: Melting on Main Street
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — High temperatures over the weekend caused the quality of the road surface on Main Street to further deteriorate. In the summer sun, with temperatures reaching up to 100 degrees, the road surface became soft and tacky in places, and a tar-like substance.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — High temperatures over the weekend caused the quality of the road surface on Main Street to further deteriorate. In the summer sun, with temperatures reaching up to 100 degrees, the road surface became soft and tacky in places, and a tar-like substance.

“The contractor was notified by staff of the issue on Saturday afternoon; they applied sand to the road surface on Sunday. Road conditions will continue to be monitored, and issues addressed until the matter is resolved,” Spearfish Public Works Director Adam McMahon said.

McMahon said the mill and overlay project, which will repair Main Street from Grant Street to Jackson Boulevard, is currently being designed and is scheduled to be bid in August.

“The mill and overlay may be completed this fall or next spring,” McMahon said.

As for the chip seal from Grant Street to Spearfish Canyon, McMahon said the contractor is scheduled to start work the week of June 22, after the Camaro Rally.

“This may be subject to change. A PSA will be published closer to the start of work to notify the community,” McMahon said.

In the meantime, McMahon said the city is working to help citizens address concerns about property damage with the contractor on the project.

“If anyone has any claims of damage, they can contact the city at (605) 642-1333, and we will get them in touch with the contractor to file a claim,” McMahon said.

byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: BLACK HAWK — A manufactured home was fully engulfed in flames when Black Hawk Fire fighters arrived at the scene of a structure fire on JB Road in Black Hawk at about 6:19 p.m., Tuesday. _full_text:
BLACK HAWK — A manufactured home was fully engulfed in flames when Black Hawk Fire fighters arrived at the scene of a structure fire on JB Road in Black Hawk at about 6:19 p.m., Tuesday. The fire was rapidly spreading to neighboring structures, according to first responders. Due to the absence of fire hydrants, fire personnel requested additional support to fight the fire.

Water tenders and personnel were dispatched from Piedmont, North Haines, Rapid City, Box Elder, Whispering Pines, Rapid Valley, Doty, Johnson Siding, and Ellsworth Air Force Base.

Crews focused initially on exposure protection — tactics to prevent the fire from spreading further. In total, 7 nearby structures were either damaged or ignited “as a result of the primary fire,” according to the Black Hawk Fire Department. Three homes sustained “significant or moderate damage.”

The fire is under investigation by the S.D. Fire Marshall’s Office. Details are preliminary, and limited until the investigation concludes.

title: How many Americans can afford high-quality healthcare?
description: WASHINGTON (AP) — Twannetta Weaver felt like she made the responsible choice when she enrolled in a high-deductible health insurance plan through her employer, an option that avoided high premiums and allowed her to save for retirement.
_full_text:
How many Americans can afford high-quality healthcare?

WASHINGTON (AP) — Twannetta Weaver felt like she made the responsible choice when she enrolled in a high-deductible health insurance plan through her employer, an option that avoided high premiums and allowed her to save for retirement.

Then, in 2025, she slipped a disk in her back, requiring medication and physical therapy. Suddenly, the medical bills were so overwhelming that Weaver, an adult learner working toward a leadership degree on the side, had to delay graduation by a year.

“I had to start calculating, am I going to be able to afford to pay my tuition, as well as my books, as well as my living expenses, and continue to care for my family?” the 43-year-old in Sanford, Florida, said in an interview. “It makes you feel powerless as a consumer.”

Weaver’s experience is familiar to a growing number of Americans, according to new data from the West Health-Gallup Affordability Index, which shows only about half of U.S. adults could afford their healthcare and had access to quality care last year. Concerns about affording healthcare in the year ahead were at a record high since tracking began in 2021, signaling that many were feeling anxious about rising healthcare costs as 2025 ended.

The new findings published Thursday draw on a survey conducted from October to December 2025 — before major recent changes to health policy, like Congress’ Medicaid cuts or its decision not to extend Affordable Care Act subsidies, took effect. It demonstrates how the country’s fraught healthcare system is increasingly straining Americans at a time when inflation is driving high costs and affordability concerns are top of mind as midterm elections approach.

 

Americans are worried they won’t be able to pay for care

The index used the responses from multiple questions to place Americans into three categories depending on their access to quality care and ability to pay for care and medicine. In the new data, 49% of U.S. adults were considered “cost secure,” meaning that they had access both to high-quality, affordable care and they had recently been able to afford the care and medicine they needed. In 2021, when the measurement began, 56% of U.S. adults were “cost secure.” That rose to 61% in 2022 but has been falling ever since.

In the survey, about three-quarters of U.S. adults said healthcare costs were a “major” or “minor” financial burden for them and their family. Only about 3 in 10 said they’re not a burden.

Meanwhile, about half of respondents were “extremely concerned” or “concerned” that their household would be unable to pay for needed healthcare services in 2026, up from 42% who said that in 2022.

Inger Perez, 59, from Encino, Texas, is one of those worried Americans. She has a family history of diabetes, high blood pressure and cancer. She said she did blood work recently, and while she wants to know the results, she’s bracing herself for what they could show.

“I literally was crying last night because I’m nervous about what I’m going to find out and how much care that is and how much money that is,” she said in an interview. “I’m terrified that I’ll start a plan of treatment but won’t be able to afford to keep up with it.”

More than half of survey respondents said the cost of healthcare contributes “a lot” or “some” to stress to their daily lives. That’s compared to about 3 in 10 who said these costs contribute “very little stress” and about 2 in 10 who said they contribute “no stress at all.”

Perez said she is also frustrated by the quality of the care she receives, in part because she lives in a rural area about an hour from a doctor’s office. To fit her budget, she had to choose a lower-cost Affordable Care Act marketplace plan with a limited network of covered providers, creating another obstacle to finding good care.

Healthcare affordability is declining across demographics

Younger adults, older adults and women were among several groups of Americans that saw drops in healthcare affordability and access in 2025, according to the findings.

Among Americans under 30, only about one-third were categorized as “cost secure,” down from 46% in 2021. Women were already less likely to be “cost secure” than men, but the gap widened last year. About 57% of men were “cost secure” in the 2025 survey — down from a high of 67% in 2022 — compared to 42% of women.

Older Americans, most of whom are covered by the government’s Medicare health insurance program, are generally more likely to be “cost secure.” However, this group saw meaningful decreases as well, falling from 73% in 2021 to 61% in 2025.

Patients make sacrifices to pay the bills

Several survey respondents who talked to The Associated Press discussed things they have had to give up to pay their health bills.

About 2 in 10 U.S. adults in the 2025 poll said there had been a time in the prior three months when they or a member of their household was unable to pay for medicine or drugs that a doctor had prescribed because of costs. About 3 in 10 said they or someone in their household did not seek treatment for a health problem because of the expense.

One dad in Arizona, 55-year-old Xavier Chapa, said his 50-year-old wife has been fighting her insurance company over a preventive colonoscopy that her doctor had recommended.

He said the company verbally assured her it would be covered, but didn’t honor that after the procedure was completed.

The looming $3,000 bill means they’ve had to cut back their 8-year-old son’s summer camp schedule from full-day to half-day programs, along with trimming their budget elsewhere.

“It’s a lot to deal with,” said Chapa, who moved back to the U.S. from Europe three years ago. “What point does it serve if you’re living in this country and having to pay such a high price and you can’t get some of the basic things?”

The West Health-Gallup Center poll of 5,660 adults was conducted Oct. 27-Dec. 22, 2025 using a sample drawn from Gallup’s probability-based Gallup Panel. The margin of sampling error for adults overall is plus or minus 2.1 percentage points.

title: Expect construction at Exit 10 Monday  DOT to begin installing new  ‘reduced conflict’ intersection
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — South Dakota Department of Transportation (DOT) Rapid City Area Engineer Mike Carlson calls it “dysfunction junction.” On Monday, construction will begin to address long-standing traffic concerns at Exit 10.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — South Dakota Department of Transportation (DOT) Rapid City Area Engineer Mike Carlson calls it “dysfunction junction.” On Monday, construction will begin to address long-standing traffic concerns at Exit 10. 

“We’ve always had issues with (Exit 10)” Carlson said. “We’ve tried to figure out how to fix this so that it works.”

Between now and the end of August, the DOT plans to change the way traffic flows at Exit 10.

“What we’re going to do is called a reduced conflict intersection,” Carlson said.

Drivers will no longer be able to turn left from Old Highway 14 onto Highway 85 toward Belle Fourche.

Instead, they will turn right and be routed to make a U-style turn in a structure called a “loon,” which is designed to accommodate oversized loads and truck traffic.

The loon is the first thing crews will be working to build — starting Monday. North Avenue will be reduced to one lane in each direction as crews remove old pavement and begin constructing the new left turn feature. The I-90 on-ramps and off-ramps will remain open throughout the project.

Motorists should look out for reduced speed limits and changing traffic patterns in the work zone. During the project, speeds will be reduced to no more than 35 miles per hour. After the project concludes, the speed limit will be restored to 45 miles per hour.

Ordinarily, about 62% of the traffic at the Exit 10 intersection is traveling north-south, according to DOT traffic studies. That’s part of why the intersection redesign will look the way it looks.

“North and south always has free movement. Everybody else has to find a gap to get into,” Carlson said.

Carlson said the loon will have a yield sign installed, so that drivers heading back toward Belle Fourche can safely turn back onto the highway.

A raised median will be installed, in the second phase of the project, to help drivers recognize that they can no longer turn left from the old highway.

“During the first beginning phase you can still turn left, but once we start to do that work on the median, that’s when we’ll close it off,” Carlson said.

Carlson noted that turning right before eventually turning left might take a little bit more time. Yet, if traffic patterns remain the same, Carlson said by 2035, drivers on Old Highway 14 may be waiting up to 2 minutes regularly to execute a left-hand turn.

“If you wait that long, you are going to get impatient. Especially the younger drivers,” Carlson said. “They’re going to take a chance. Sometimes that chance will be successful, sometimes they won’t see a vehicle, and we’ll have an accident we don’t want to have.”

Between the eastbound off-ramp on I-90 and the Highway 85 and the on-ramp, the DOT plans to install a traffic signal.

In advance of that signal, DOT plans to install a yellow and black flashing sign to help drivers on the interstate to recognize that traffic is going to halt ahead.

Rather than backing up traffic, Carlson said, designers believe the stoplight could create safer gaps for folks turning from the westbound off-ramp.

“Most of the traffic coming off of that ramp are going to Belle Fourche. Not many are going back into town because they have Exit 14 to get back into town,” Carlson said. “With the signal here, there should be some gaps created (for those drivers) to turn.” 

Carlson said the DOT will monitor signal timing and adjust it if necessary after installation. Once installed, the stoplight isn’t expected to cause delays for drivers. It may, however, delay completion of construction if the poles the light will rest on do not arrive on time.

“There are just a few manufacturers of signal poles, and they are booked year-round, so we get our orders in as soon as we can. We’re just in the queue waiting for the poles to get in,” Carlson said.

The project is expected to wrap up in August, if pole delivery is not delayed. Carlson said the project will not pause for the Rally.

“We won’t take a Rally break. We believe by that time, we won’t really be impacting Rally traffic,” Carlson said.

For additional project information and a video demonstrating how traffic will flow after the intersection is altered, visit: https://dot.sd.gov/i-90exit10.

“We think this design is the ultimate fix for this area right now. We are excited to put it in place and see how it works,” Carlson said.

title: What next for Noem and Dusty?
byline: Tom Lawrence
description: Tom Lawrence
_full_text:
Tom Lawrence
Tom Lawrence 

OPINION — Politics can take sudden turns for prominent people planning their future. Dick Nixon was an expert on the topic.

We’ve had two examples of that in South Dakota this year in Kristi Noem and Dusty Johnson. Both were highly successful politicians who rose steadily — until 2026.

Noem had the biggest fall. She has enjoyed an unblemished run of almost two decades, including two terms in the South Dakota House of Representatives, followed by four terms in the United States House of Representatives, before she was elected governor in 2018 and re-elected in 2022. Noem was riding an impressive streak as well as the horses and motorcycles she often posed on.

She was undefeated in South Dakota politics, a claim that such famous figures as Karl Mundt, George McGovern, James Abourezk, Tom Daschle, Bill Janklow and John Thune could not make.

The late Tim Johnson, a four-term state legislator who won five terms in the U.S. House and three in the Senate, and Mike Rounds, who served five terms in the South Dakota Senate, did two terms as governor and is seeking a third term in the U.S. Senate, also never lost an election. Rounds hopes to keep that impressive streak alive this fall.

Noem was never defeated, at least at the polls. But her career, and personal life, took major hits this year. She was fired as secretary of the Department of Homeland Security in March, after a disastrous performance before the Senate Judiciary Committee and months of missteps in her role.

President Trump, once an ardent admirer, created a new post for her as U.S. Special Envoy for the Shield of the Americas. Let us know if you figure out what the heck that means.

Noem has started to emerge from isolation, appearing on NewsMax with host Greta Van Susteren on Saturday. Van Susteren lobbed a softball question and Noem promptly fouled it off her foot.

She was asked who was our “best friend in South America” right now. Noem praised several nations, including El Salvador and Costa Rica. The problem? Both are located in Central America, not South America.

It’s the kind of thing a special envoy ought to know. Noem, who studied at several South Dakota universities and was handed a diploma by South Dakota State University for her remote studies while in Congress, needs to hit the geography books. 

She also has to ponder her future. There were reports she was considering returning home this spring to make a late entry into the congressional race, but that did not occur. Her life was tipped upside down by continued rumors of an affair with her top aide, political consultant Corey Lewandowski, whose sordid reputation was further blackened by suspicions about his role in approving contracts for DHS.

New chapters of that story will likely unfold.

Then there was the sad saga of Noem’s husband Bryon, and his private sex life as a cross-dresser who paid sex workers for steamy online chats. That was not on many bingo cards. Only Kristi and Bryon know what has, is and will happen within that marriage.

Noem appears to have a very comfortable net worth — $5 million appears in searches — thanks to her government salaries, farm and ranch investments, and other businesses. Does she plan to run for office again? It seems unlikely, at least at this point.

Her reputation, both professionally and personally, is at a low ebb. She can continue along in her obscure but well-paying government job — she made over $250,000 a year at Homeland Security and likely has a similar salary now — and wait for an opportunity.

But what? We are about to elect a governor, so that job is taken for four years. Rounds is facing Democratic candidate Julian Beaudion and independent Brian Bruns. One of those three will be in the Senate until 2033.

A few years ago, Sen. Thune talked to me about not running for a fourth term, saying his wife preferred he call it a career. But he did run and win in 2022.

He is now the Senate majority leader, and it seems to be a post he enjoys, despite having to constantly grit his teeth over another Trump outrage. Thune knows who owns the party.

But he has a solid base of support within the GOP ranks and plans to survive this … odious occupancy of the Oval Office. Will American politics and government recover and return to what Thune has been used to for decades? Can he help lead the way back — and forward?

I’d guess Thune will seek a fifth term. He is just 65, still lean and appears very healthy, if understandably weary and worn a bit. Would Noem consider a primary challenge? That would be a tall order, but she could go Full Trump on him in a bid to seize the seat.

Her old House seat would be available in two years. Is that an option? Maybe it would be if Democrat Nikki Gronli wins. Would Noem take on Republican Marty Jackley in 2028 if he is elected? She defeated him in the 2018 Republican gubernatorial primary.

So, her options are limited. If she survives the rest of Trump’s term as a member of his team, she can hold onto that. What then? Will a conservative media outlet offer her a job? Her own radio show — Riding Herd with Kristi?

Maybe she will return to a quiet life in rural Castlewood. But after the whirlwind she has experienced in the last 16 years, will that satisfy her? Will her marriage survive all this turmoil?

At 54, she has many productive years left. But what will she do with them?

That’s a question she surely didn’t expect to face when she and Lewandowski were trying to turn her into a vice-presidential or even presidential candidate. It went from a pair of jet-set, high-flying positions to a complete train wreck.

Johnson also had an unblemished record as a candidate. Had. Tuesday, June 2, was not the night he anticipated, as he finished out of the running for the GOP nomination.

His biggest issue was ambition, as like Noem, he jumped from job to job as he climbed South Dakota’s political ladder. Johnson was elected to the Public Utilities Commission in 2004 when he was just 28. He was re-elected to another six-year term in 2010 but didn’t serve, resigning to become Gov. Dennis Daugaard’s chief of staff, a post he held until 2014.

Johnson then entered the private sector while eying a run for office. After a tenure at Vantage Point Solutions in Mitchell, he ran for Congress in 2018 as Noem entered the governor’s race.

Johnson was easily elected in 2018 and breezed to three more terms, handily defeating primary and general election opponents, with Democrats passing on the race in 2018 and 2020. Then, came 2026 and the opportunity to move to another post, where he would be one of one, not one of 435.

Noem resigned as governor and Lt. Gov. Larry Rhoden moved up. Johnson liked his chances against Rhoden and announced he would seek the nomination. Rhoden said he would run for a full term, and South Dakota Speaker of the House Jon Hansen also entered the race.

That looked like an interesting contest featuring three well-known public figures. But a fledgling politician with a lot of money to spend, Toby Doeden of Aberdeen, shook up the race with $4 million of his own money and a Trump-like style of tough talk and sneering appearance.

It was a new race. Johnson seemed to adopt two personas. His campaign ran a deluge of TV commercials showing him with his sons and with just plain folks in South Dakota, along with some solo spots of him walking along a rural road, talking about his family’s struggles.

But he also was supported by a series of hard-hitting spots attacking Rhoden and Hansen. They were especially hard on the governor, using harsh terms to describe him.

That caused the normally calm Rhoden to push back, saying Johnson had threatened to be hard on him during the campaign and urging him to stay out. He also said the links between Johnson and the attack ads, paid for by a private political action committee, was clear.

That duality hurt Johnson, I believe. He had spent more than two decades as the folksy, friendly guy in orange who waved from sidewalks, smiled in parades and did pleasant interviews with the media.

Suddenly, he was involved in a bitter campaign and his supporters were playing rough. After early polls showed him the clear favorite, with an opportunity to win the nomination outright, he slipped to third and didn’t even make the runoff.

Rhoden, whom he attacked relentlessly, and Doeden, who took aim at Johnson as well as Rhoden and Hansen, are vying for the nomination. Dusty was left in the, well, dust. Will he endorse either man? Would either want the backing of someone who they so publicly disparaged?

Aw, politics. Friends, enemies and allies, all in just a few months.

Johnson has been mostly silent since this defeat, issuing just this statement: “It has been the honor of my lifetime to represent South Dakota in Congress these past eight years.”

He admitted to being “disappointed in the outcome,” but vowed to help Republican candidates win in November. He didn’t mention any particular candidate. It’s just too soon.

Now what? He faces the same political realities as Noem. All four major offices will be filled in 2027, with only his old House seat and Thune’s seat post up for grabs — maybe — in 2028.

With his name, experience, talents and pleasant nature, Johnson will have many offers and opportunities. Lobbying or serving as a “consultant” while biding his time and weighing his options isn’t a bad life for a man who is so interested in policy and politics. That’s who Dusty always has been, at nature.

Dustin Michael Johnson turns 50 on Sept. 30, and this year marks the end of his run as the boy wonder of South Dakota politics. Now, the man has to wonder why he left the security of a U.S. House seat — and what he is going to do next.

title: New interpretive sign celebrates Old Glory  and a tradition of city pride in Deadwood
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: City residents came together Wednesday to unveil a new interpretive sign at city hall celebrating the city’s history of proudly displaying Old Glory alongside local tradition. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
New interpretive sign celebrates Old Glory  and a tradition of city pride in Deadwood
City residents came together Wednesday to unveil a new interpretive sign at city hall celebrating the city’s history of proudly displaying Old Glory alongside local tradition. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

DEADWOOD — Deadwood residents came together Wednesday to unveil a new interpretive sign celebrating the city’s longstanding history of honoring Old Glory and one fourth grade student’s city flag. 

Tara Silvernail moved to Deadwood in the fourth grade in 1989. That year, her teacher announced there would be a competition to design a flag for the city of Deadwood. Being brand new to the community, the 4 things that came to Silvernail’s mind when she thought of Deadwood were mining, the Black Hills, the Days of ’76, and the emblem of the pickaxe and shovel outside her school. 

After a week of revisions and help from her teacher, Silvernail learned that her design was chosen from 97 entries as the winner. 

“We didn’t know a thing about it,” said Jan Peppmeier, Silvernail’s mother. “She did all of this at school, so we were so surprised when we saw it.”

That summer, Silvernail and the second and third place winners got to ride on top of a firetruck in a parade. Afterwards, the community gathered for a city-wide picnic. 

“It was quite a big thing,” said Peppmeier. “And then the first day of school, (Silvernail) raised the flag at the school and she got to help with that.”

Peppmeier said she still has the finished proof of Silvernail’s design on a foam posterboard at home and the first flag flown with the design printed on it. The items were used to create the design of the new interpretive sign outside of Deadwood’s city hall. 

Silvernail said she didn’t realize it at the time, but the event brought out a creative side of herself. She now uses that energy in a side business designing jewelry.

Silvernail’s creative design was celebrated in conjunction with Peppmeier’s retirement. Peppmeier served as the deputy finance officer for 17 years. Before joining the municipal crew, Peppmeier worked with the Deadwood chamber of commerce during the years when gaming was legalized while attending college at Black Hills State University.

“It was a crazy world. We kept thinking if we can make it to Nov. 1, 1999,” said Peppmeier. “Well, that was silly because then the whole thing exploded and people were calling from all over the country.”

“We’ve really embedded ourselves in this community. It’s fun,” said Silvernail. “There’s been a lot of change in all those years, but it’s been great.”

National pride

Kevin Kuchenbecker, director of historic preservation, said Deadwood has a well-established history of proudly flying the American flag. 

“Since World War One, the American flag has flown over Deadwood from Mount Moriah overlook,” he said. “Deadwood Mayor Nathan Franklin is credited with having the American flag illuminated from (the overlook) in April of 1917. Following the war, the U.S. flag was flown periodically from this location until the bombing of Pearl Harbor in Hawaii on Dec. 7, 1941. After the bombing, Old Glory was once again flown 24 hours a day.”

Kuchenbecker said in 1989, the Deadwood chamber of commerce, Veterans of Foreign Wars post 5969, the American Legion, Daughters of the American Revolution, Elks Lodge 508, and the Boys and Girl Scouts began planning for a flag day celebration on June 14. Those plans culminated in Silvernail’s flag design. The design is still flown at City Hall in conjunction with South Dakota’s flag and the American flag.

title: City invests in tracking software Chamber clears up misinformation at commission meeting
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: LEAD — A Placer.ai subscription could help economic development and city officials track visitor activity in Lead, right down to how many pairs of underwear they buy at Dollar General.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

LEAD — A Placer.ai subscription could help economic development and city officials track visitor activity in Lead, right down to how many pairs of underwear they buy at Dollar General. 

That’s what Emma Garvin, executive director of Deadwood-Lead Economic Development told the Lead City Commission Monday, when she asked them to use money from the third-penny sales tax to purchase a Placer.ai subscription. Garvin said the program, which uses geo-location data based off cell phone service, to track foot traffic within an established boundary, is valuable to economic development officials because it tracks business traffic and spending, and provides valuable data for a housing study. 

“We have such a massive amount of visitors in this area,” Garvin said. “A real life example is Kelly Kirk said there were over 50,000 visitors in May at the visitor’s center. We have no idea whether or not any of them walked up and down Main Street. I think this is information all of our businesses in town should have and all of our surrounding businesses should have, and our businesses that are looking to come here should have this information. We can share it with anybody who wants that information. Sales tax is great. We can see sales tax revenues going up. We can see specifically what categories are going up. This will tell us how many people bought underwear at Dollar General on Saturday. So it’s very specific. It will tell us why people are leaving when they leave Lead and they go to Spearfish, and what are they buying in Spearfish that they couldn’t get in Lead.”

During her presentation to the commission, Garvin reported that the city of Lead had already spent $12,000 last year on the annual software subscription for the Lead Area Chamber of Commerce, but the chamber cancelled the subscription. The price of the subscription is now $15,000, she said, but she asked the city to at least pay $12,000, the same amount that had been given in the past, or to consider paying the full amount. The $12,000 number was not accurate, but more on that in a bit.

Carr questioned whether approving the request would mean the city paid for the subscription twice when it approved the chamber’s 2026 allocation. 

“I agree the Placer.ai is good, useful data,” Carr said at the meeting. “I just really hate paying for something twice. We pay the chamber to renew the subscription and they didn’t. Now we’re going to take $15,000 more out of bed and booze to do it again? I don’t have a problem if you want it. From an accountability standpoint, I want to know from the chamber why they decided not to and what they were going to use that $12,000 for otherwise.” 

Lead Area Chamber of Commerce Director Jami Grangaard said that information was not accurate. Grangaard was not at the city commission meeting, but after Monday’s discussion and commission approval for the funding, she contacted city officials to correct the misinformation, and to clarify the city never paid $12,000 for the subscription. She said in 2025 the city paid $5,000 for a Placer.ai subscription, and the Chamber paid the remaining $7,000 out of membership fees. Grangaard said the chamber did not receive the requested city allocation in 2026, and therefore had to cut expenses.   

The chamber cancelled its Placer.ai subscription in December 2025, after receiving an email from Lead City Administrator Robin Lucero that stated “we are good with not renewing Placer.ai,” Grangaard said.

Grangaard noted that Placer.ai data is more valuable for economic development organizations and municipal governments for sales tax analyses, park usage data, obtaining grants, and broader community planning. 

Following some discussion, the Lead City Commission unanimously voted to use $15,000 in third-penny sales tax money to pay for the Placer.ai subscription. Otherwise known as the “bed and booze” fund, third-penny sales tax dollars have limited uses. It is primarily used to market the city.

title: Lead moves forward with facilities plan
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: City crews respond to a water line break in 2025. The city needs to update its facilities plan to be eligible for the state and federal grants needed to replace water infrastructure. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Lead moves forward with facilities plan
City crews respond to a water line break in 2025. The city needs to update its facilities plan to be eligible for the state and federal grants needed to replace water infrastructure. Pioneer file photo 

LEAD — The city of Lead will pay Brosz Engineering $79,600 to conduct a facility study that is required to become eligible for state and federal infrastructure grants. 

On Monday Lead City Commissioners approved the contract with Brosz that includes $17,000 for a site visit and initial data collection, $52,600 for a report of findings, and $10,000 to present their findings about Lead’s water, sanitary sewer, and storm water system plan. 

“The city has a significant need to update and replace its current underground infrastructure and continue the process of separating its combined sanitary and storm water collection systems,” the Brosz proposal states. “The current combined system requires significant operation and maintenance, overtaxes the treatment plant, and demands extensive financial capital to operate. The water system was inherited (from) Homestake Mine in 1994. The system was, at that time, already old and utilized primarily cast iron mains, which are prone to breaks and water loss.” 

Lead Public Works Director Jason Bauernfeind said in 2025 the city responded to 26 water leaks. The specific causes varied, but they all point to  the city’s need to update and replace water infrastructure. 

“Some of the leaks had probably been leaking underground for years and just hadn’t surfaced until changing frost conditions changed the path of the water and brought it to the surface,” he said. “We also had several ‘frost breaks,’ which happen when freezing conditions reach water lines that aren’t buried deep enough. If those lines had been buried below the frost line, they likely wouldn’t have broken. We’ve seen frost reach depths of up to 5 feet in Lead. Water lines throughout the city range from about 3 feet deep to as much as 16 feet deep. On every new project today, we install water lines at a minimum depth of 6 feet to keep them below the frost line and help prevent future breaks. Not every leak had the same cause, but the age, condition, and depth of our infrastructure all reinforce the need to continue investing in upgrades to the city’s water, storm water, and sewer systems.”

For many years, the city of Lead has used state and federal grants and low interest loans to pay for separating its storm water and sewer water systems, which is mandated by the S.D. Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources. But those grants require a facilities plan that is updated every 5 years, and the Lead plan has not been updated since 2021. The complete facility plan will document existing conditions of city water, sewer, and storm sewer infrastructure, define the need for specific projects, evaluate reasonable alternatives, provide cost comparisons, address environmental considerations, identify permitting and property needs, and establish a practical implementation schedule, for the purposes of planning. The engineer will also verify growth rates expected within the city to determine anticipated future water usage and flow, for the next 30 years, as well as examine historical flow and wastewater loading information from the past 5 years. 

Lead City Administrator Robin Lucero said the city unsuccessfully searched for grants to help pay for the facilities study. In 2025 the city saved $40,000 from its water fund, and $20,000 from the sewer fund to pay for the study. 

“The $79,600 is a little more than what we had budgeted for, but also our budget numbers came from 2024 and the facility plan we have now is quite outdated and will take quite a bit of work,” Lucero said, adding that the city can allocate the remaining $19,600 in its 2027 budget. 

Commissioner Roger Thomas, who had a long career working for the city water department before retiring, said he is very confident Brosz Engineering can fulfill all the requirements of the study. 

“It’s a big project for them and I’m more than comfortable they can take care of the job, and it will set ups up for the net 5 years to get our projects done,” he said.

title: Wild Deadwood Reads connects emerging authors to new audiences in South Dakota
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Cindy J. Vanous believes in vintage, human art over AI. She wrote and brought books like this one to Wild Deadwood Reads. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Wild Deadwood Reads 2.JPG
Cindy J. Vanous believes in vintage, human art over AI. She wrote and brought books like this one to Wild Deadwood Reads. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

DEADWOOD — More than 80 authors descended on Deadwood last weekend for Wild Deadwood Reads — a weekend event that offers authors the chance to connect, build skills, foster community, and interact with readers. The event culminates annually in a book-fair-style event at The Lodge at Deadwood. 

Readers attend for free, navigating booths stocked with books to talk to, and collect autographs and inspiration from authors.

 Wild Deadwood Reads 1.JPG
With more than 80 authors in attendance, Wild Deadwood Reads brought authors and readers together at the Lodge at Deadwood, one week earlier than usual this year. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson  

 Wild Deadwood Reads 3.JPG
Authors and readers interact at Wild Deadwood Reads. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

 Wild Deadwood Reads 4.JPG
North Dakota-based author Calista Rains came to Wild Deadwood Reads for the first time this year. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

Alongside New York Times bestselling author Carolyn Brown, many of the authors in attendance are self-published or contracted with small publishing houses. Deadwood is prospecting country, and there are plenty of hidden and lesser-known gems for readers to discover.

 Wild Deadwood Reads.JPG
Arkansas writer Lora Dail, the creator of a fictional warthog shaman, attended Wild Deadwood Reads last weekend. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

For several of this year’s authors, Wild Deadwood Reads offered a critical chance to expand their readership.

Originally from South Dakota, cozy-mystery author Calista Rains came to Deadwood from North Dakota for the very first time last weekend. Her Knit Wits R Us novels are jam-packed with Midwestern flair.

“When protagonist Harley Donovan moves back to her hometown of Roosevelt, N. D., she takes over her grandmother’s yarn shop,” Rains said, describing the plot of her novel “Knit Fast, Dye Last.” “During the annual Dairy Days celebration when the local milk inspector is trying to buy yarn for his wife, who is busy at her cheese curd booth, he has to go inside the yarn store to buy the right color for her before it runs out.”

That loyal husband is the first victim of a serial killer. 

“All of the knit and crochet group have to get together to figure out who committed the crime and why, before the killer strikes again,” Rains said.

Bringing her books to Wild Deadwood Reads was a way for Rains to introduce Black Hills readers to her work.

“I have met so many great authors and people who have inspired my writing. I have been able to collect their books,” Rains said. “Also talking to different readers to find out what they like to read and why. I am a very deep reader, and I want to know what everyone else is reading.”

Cindy J. Vanous is a children’s book author from Arkansas — who is campaigning for a vintage literature revival in the face of emerging artificial intelligence.

“About 3 years ago, after retiring from a corporate career, I decided to become an author. I never even imagined that would be a part of my life before,” Vanous said. “When I started writing, I wanted to bring the vintage feel from the Little Golden Books of the 50s, 60s, and 70s.”

Her books follow the adventures of cats and dogs, inspired by her real life pets, and the pets in her life— including Brave Belle the yorkie-poo (featured in “Brave Belle Saves the Day” and “Brave Belle’s First Halloween”) and Asher the poodle (who appears in “Asher’s Christmas Wish”.) “Ziva the Great” is about her great-aunt’s rescue cat.

“Bringing a vintage feel — hand drawn, hand painted (illustrations), no AI, we’re going back to artistry — is my main goal,” Vanous said.

In Deadwood, she said she felt welcomed and delighted to see how engaged local readers were.

“A lot of the authors are here from where I am from. It was a 2-day trip, and worth every minute of it,” Vanous said.

Brown, a southern powerhouse and prolific romance and women’s fiction author, invited another Arkansas-based author, Lora Dail, to Wild Deadwood Reads this year.

Dail was once a technical writer for NASA. Now, she’s a life coach and the creator of Mudwhiff — a Namibian warthog shaman.

Dail was inspired by a live footage of a warthog from a feed set up in Namibia that she began watching regularly. Mugwhiff offers readers positive words of support and encouragement. 

“His message is about enough-ness, that you are perfect already. You don’t have to chase it. You don’t have to learn anything. You already are perfect. … I am a life coach, and so the message is mine. I needed somebody to tell people, other than me,” Dail said. “Who better than a warthog with warts and tusks to say that you are beautiful?”

Phoebe Evans, from Minnesota, also made it to Wild Deadwood Reads for the first time. She writes paranormal, fantasy romance, and dark romance.

“I’ve never been here before, but we are trying to build our audience all the way down the Midwest,” Evans said. She added that Wild Deadwood Reads is a great tool for audience building. “It is a fabulous little town; I love it.”

title: S.D. Public Broadcasting remains  committed to SDHSAA state events
byline: By Dana Hess For the S.D. NewsMedia Association
description: PIERRE — Despite national attempts to defund public television, South Dakota Public Broadcasting remains committed to covering state athletic and fine arts events.
_full_text:
SD High School Activities Association sets goals  for new school year

PIERRE — Despite national attempts to defund public television, South Dakota Public Broadcasting remains committed to covering state athletic and fine arts events. 

On Wednesday, June 17, the board of directors of the South Dakota High School Activities Association learned about that commitment during the annual report from representatives of South Dakota Public Broadcasting. 

Brad Van Osdel, assistant general manager and director of content, told the board that broadcasting SDHSAA events was “one of our proudest moments, one of our favorite things to do.”

South Dakota Public Broadcasting purchases the rights to state events. According to Van Osdel, every statewide athletic event and fine arts event receives some sort of coverage. 

State events that are live-streamed and broadcast include soccer, cheer and dance, All-State Chorus and Orchestra, football, volleyball, wrestling, basketball, All-State Band and All-State Jazz Band. Events that are primarily live-streamed include gymnastics, esports, track and girls’ softball. Events with photos and results include golf, tennis, cross-country, journalism, oral interp, debate, student council and the visual arts contest. 

Van Osdel’s report said that in the last school year, using its website and YouTube, S.D. Public Broadcasting reached more than 491,000 users with 2.8 million views and more than 818,000 hours watched.

title: Local election officials reel over ‘logistical nightmare’ of Trump’s vote-by-mail order
byline: By Jonathan Shorman SouthDakotaSearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — As election officials across the country steel themselves for the midterm elections in less than five months, President Donald Trump’s executive order restricting voting by mail threatens to upend their preparations.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — As election officials across the country steel themselves for the midterm elections in less than five months, President Donald Trump’s executive order restricting voting by mail threatens to upend their preparations.

The executive order instructs the U.S. Postal Service to refuse to deliver ballots in states that don’t provide lists of voters or meet other requirements. It has created a sense of deep uncertainty and concern among election officials as they consider how to comply, according to a review of court documents and interviews with election officials and experts on election administration.

The March 31 executive order, and a proposed Postal Service rule published June 2 that would put the order’s requirements into effect, raise serious logistical and procedural challenges for those running elections, they say. Rural areas with limited resources are especially at risk, but jurisdictions of all sizes could be forced to scramble.

The executive order is the latest step taken by Trump to assert control over state-run elections, along with the stalled SAVE America Act, which would require voters to provide documents proving their citizenship. The Justice Department, under Trump’s control, is also trying to obtain state voter rolls.

“This is just another death by a thousand cuts that clerks have been experiencing since the 2020 elections,” said Barb Byrum, the Democratic clerk of Ingham County, Michigan, which includes Lansing.

First-ever national voter list

The order and the rule require states to provide lists of mail-in voters if they want the Postal Service to deliver ballots, marking the first time the federal government has created a national voter list. 

Mail ballot envelopes must meet certain design standards. And federal agencies have to compile lists of voting-age citizens to share with each state in an effort to root out noncitizen voters.

But Democratic states and voting rights groups argue the executive order — and the accompanying proposed rule — represent an illegal overreach by Trump because states administer elections under the U.S. Constitution. Trump and his Republican allies say the restrictions are necessary for election security and to combat noncitizen voting, which occurs extremely rarely.

The Postal Service didn’t respond to questions from States Newsroom. The agency has said the rule “will facilitate the faithful execution of federal law.”

Multiple lawsuits have been brought against the order, but a federal judge in Washington, D.C., in May declined to halt it, partly because the Trump administration hadn’t taken enough action to implement its requirements. Another federal judge in Massachusetts is weighing a separate request to block the order.

With the executive order still in effect, at least for now, election officials and experts who work with them are taking the ramifications of it and the proposed Postal Service rule seriously.

“We don’t have a national voter registration list. We don’t have, currently, a list of sanctioned, authorized voters to vote by mail at the federal level,” said Tammy Patrick, chief programs officer at Election Center, operated by the National Association of Election Officials.  “That’s a big, big change in the way elections have always been conducted.”

Sweeping changes very quickly

In court papers filed in May, local election officials and local governments representing 26 jurisdictions across the country warned the executive order would “severely disrupt” local election administration and force the implementation of sweeping changes within months. Implementation of the order’s requirements will largely fall on local election officials, they argued.

Byrum was among the officials to sign onto the brief, along with others in Boston, and counties in Pennsylvania, Washington, Wisconsin and elsewhere.

Under the executive order, states that want to send ballots through the mail must provide the Postal Service with lists of voters they intend to provide a mail ballot. Local election officials will play a large role in helping states develop these lists, according to the court papers, and will have primary responsibility to help voters address any errors.

And Trump wants it all in place before November. The executive order’s proposed timelines “present a logistical nightmare for local election officials,” the officials warn.

“The general rule is don’t make changes before a big election because there’s always something you didn’t think about,” said Carolina Lopez, executive director of the Partnership for Large Election Jurisdictions, a nonpartisan organization for election officials in jurisdictions of at least 250,000 people.

The proposed Postal Service rule says the agency would launch a portal where states would submit voter lists and make updates. But a number of questions remain, said Lopez, who previously spent a decade administering elections in Miami-Dade County, Florida.

The portal poses the potential for bottlenecks in the election system and it’s unclear what would happen if it was ever offline. The United States has a decentralized election system, with states each running their own elections. By contrast, the Postal Service portal would create a single point of failure, raising concerns about the security of information on tens of millions of voters.

Additionally, while every state maintains a voter registration list, there is no nationwide standard for the formatting of that data. It’s unclear whether the portal will accept data in a variety of formats — the proposed rule only says the Postal Service wouldn’t alter the data provided by states.

“It looks a little different across the country and therefore normalizing the data will be a process,” Lopez said.

Struggle for small, rural counties

The Department of Justice initially said in a court document that the Department of Homeland Security planned to obtain voter data from the Postal Service before backpedaling a few days later. Still, Homeland Security continues to have “preliminary conversations” about data sharing, the Justice Department said in a subsequent court filing.

DHS operates the Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, system that can scan voter data to identify possible noncitizens. The Justice Department has sued 30 states in an effort to force them to turn over their unredacted voter rolls, which include sensitive personal data such as dates of birth, driver’s license and full or partial Social Security numbers, for the purpose of running the information through SAVE.

The proposed Postal Service rule also imposes standards on ballot envelopes that states must meet if they want to send ballots through the mail.

Envelopes must include an election mail logo, be automation compatible and have a bar code that allows for tracking. These are already considered best practices — and many jurisdictions across the country already follow them — but the rule would make them mandatory.

Election offices in small, rural counties may struggle to comply. In many places, a single person is in charge of elections and may not even be on the job full time, Patrick said. 

“There’s rural offices all across the country, some of them don’t have their own computer in their office — they are sharing it with the tax assessor or whatever — they don’t have the ability to generate those serialized tracking codes, intelligent mail bar codes,” Patrick said. “Because they’re physically hand-writing these envelopes out or they’re using a rubber stamp with their address on it.”

Neither the executive order or the proposed Postal Service rule include any federal funding for implementation, something that would likely have to be appropriated by Congress.

Some Republican states have championed the executive order. A dozen GOP state attorneys general filed court documents defending the order and arguing that it “will enhance the security of absentee voting.”

“It is vital to the strength of our republic that we ensure only American citizens vote in our elections and that mail-in and absentee ballots are secure and reliable,” South Carolina Attorney General Alan Wilson said in a statement earlier this spring.

But Matt Crane, a Republican who is the executive director of the Colorado County Clerks Association, said the executive order and the proposed rule mark an overreach by the federal government into duties best left to states and local governments. 

The biggest reaction among Colorado clerks, he said, has been, “why?”

“No offense to our friends at the post office,” Crane said, “but I trust our processes more than I trust theirs.”
