title: Turn your savings into paychecks in retirement
byline: Christa Cantalope
description: Christa Cantalope
_full_text:
Cantalope, Christa.jpg
Christa Cantalope 

OPINION — Margaret had saved diligently for decades. Every paycheck, a portion went toward her retirement account. Then, the day finally came: she retired. Suddenly, the hardest part wasn’t the saving. It was learning to spend.

If that sounds familiar, you’re not alone. Many retirees find the shift from building savings to living off them emotionally difficult, even when they’ve planned carefully. Here are five smart strategies that can help you feel more confident about what’s ahead.

• Give yourself permission to spend conservatively. Your retirement plan likely assumes a certain annual spending amount, with increases each year to account for inflation. All else being equal, the lower those initial withdrawals, the longer your money will last. A financial advisor can help you set up portfolio withdrawals personalized to your goals and situation. Feel free to give yourself permission to spend those amounts, knowing there’s intention behind them. 

For many retirees, the challenge isn’t math — it’s mindset. After years of being rewarded for saving, spending can feel like doing something wrong. It can help to reframe withdrawals as a paycheck you’ve already earned. For example, using your monthly distribution to cover travel, hobbies or time with family isn’t indulgent; it’s the purpose of the plan you built. Connecting spending to your values can make it feel more natural and sustainable.

Do be sure to to review your spending regularly and don’t forget to set aside funds for annual expenses like taxes and insurance.

• Keep some cash on hand. A general rule of thumb for retirees is to keep about 12 months’ worth of withdrawals in a separate account for spending and another three to five years’ worth in short-term, fixed-income investments. This cushion can allow your stock investments time to recover from a market downturn, reducing the need to sell investments when markets are down. That said, holding too much cash carries its own risk, as your portfolio may not grow fast enough to keep pace with inflation. So, while some cash is good, you’ll also want to remain invested in assets with more growth potential to help your portfolio last through retirement.

• Review regularly. Retirement can last 25 years or more, and even the best-laid plans need updating along the way. Review your financial strategy at least once a year or after any major life change.

• Stay flexible. Even small adjustments to your spending can have a big impact on how long your money lasts. Retirees who hold off on spending increases in years when their portfolio declines are often able to stretch their savings further than those who increase withdrawals each year for inflation regardless of market performance.

Making the switch from saving to spending takes both careful planning and a genuine shift in mindset. A financial advisor can help you build out an effective approach to switch from saving to spending, and work with you so you can fully enjoy the retirement you worked so hard to reach.

title: New campground opens in Lead
byline: Black Hills Pioneer By Sam King
description: LEAD — Ripple Creek Campground, a new campground business, opened in Lead last month. The campground is on the same location as the Carson Cottages, another campground, and uses at least some of the same infrastructure, but is under different management.
_full_text:
LEAD — Ripple Creek Campground, a new campground business, opened in Lead last month. The campground is on the same location as the Carson Cottages, another campground, and uses at least some of the same infrastructure, but is under different management.

Laura Krantz, the host of the campground, said that nearly all the visitors to the campground are bicyclists or hikers who come to visit the nearby Mickelson Trail.

“I get a lot of people that just need one night to stay or just a quick place to sleep or pitch a tent,” Krantz said. “And so they’re outdoor enthusiasts … I’ve seen a good little chunk of families taking their kiddos on vacation.”

Krantz said that although the campground is not a nonprofit, it contributes to the nonprofit Ripple Effect, which provides financial assistance to children and families.

The nonprofit’s name is a reference to the aphorism that a ripple can change an entire tide.

“What I’ve been telling people is that ‘your stay is obviously super helpful as far as running the business side of things, but profiting lets us donate right back into Ripple Effect, which then allows us to help people that need help,” Krantz said.

She said that the nonprofit funds a variety of charitable causes, including schools, women’s shelters, and the Ronald McDonald House, which offers temporary housing to children receiving medical care at nearby hospitals and their families.

Krantz said that on the campground she cleans the cabins and RV suites, mows the lawn, stocks the coffee bar, and speaks with guests, which is her favorite part of the job.

“Whatever the day calls for is where I’m at,” she said.

title: Homestake Opera House shows 'Matilda Jr.'
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer
description: LEAD — Director Jacque Bratcher is set to bring a production of “Matilda Jr.” to the Homestake Opera House Wednesday through Friday, starring local children aged 6-17. Shows begin at 7 p.m.
_full_text:
LEAD — Director Jacque Bratcher is set to bring a production of “Matilda Jr.” to the Homestake Opera House Wednesday through Friday, starring local children aged 6-17. Shows begin at 7 p.m.

The play is an adaptation of the 1988 children’s novel by Roald Dahl, who also wrote “Charlie and the Chocolate Factory.” Matilda is a brainy prankster who finds kinship with a teacher, Miss. Honey. The two clash with a draconian teacher, Mrs. Trunchbull, and Matilda’s father, Mr. Wormwood, who is more concerned with selling 150 luxury cars to Russian businessmen than he is caring for his daughter. (Matilda gets her revenge by dyeing his hair green.)

Bratcher said that she wanted to direct this musical for a long time, but was put off by the play’s complexity.

“This one is a lot more hands on, lots more stuff going on,” Bratcher said. “It keeps the kids busy. And I just decided we’ve been building up our kids the last couple of years and they keep coming back. We figured this was the time they could handle a little bit tougher of a show.”

Bratcher was — like Miss Honey — an elementary school teacher, but later moved on to teaching middle school, which is her day job. This is her ninth year as a teacher.

“I’m hoping they (the children) take (from the play) ‘stand up to your bullies … and find who your friends are, and know you can rely on them for support,’’” Bratcher said.

Bratcher said that although many students perform in the play each year, this year there are several new students in lead roles.

The play features Brynlee Nelson as Matilda Alex Carollo as Bruce, Bonnie Bergh as Amanda, Gabby Carollo as Hortensia, Kashlynn Cilvaga as Tammy, Alyssa Nelson as Lavender, Axel Williams as Eric, Talia Thompson as Nancy, Savannah Wiegand as Alice, Dillon Streeter as The Trunchbull, Kenna Pitlick as Miss Honey/Student, Valor Davis as Mr. Wormwood, Lennon Barrett as Mrs. Wormwood, Marshall Bender as Michael, Ava Hanson as Big Kid 1, Ava Tautkus as Big Kid 2, Kimmy Carollo as Acrobat/Big Kid 3, Titus Thompson as Escapologist/Rudolpho, Kaeli Thompson as Mrs. Phelps/Student, Bromley Sanders as Mechanic/Student, Arden Sanders as Cook/Student, Hilde, Hanson as Student/Russian, Nadia Hanson as Student/Russian, Andrew Thompson as Student, Gabriel Rigge as Student, Elijah Wiegand as Sergei/Student, Fritz Daus as Student/Russian, Jocelyn Sanders as Student/Russian, Alora Thompson as Student/Russian, Everett Ward as Student/Russian, Emma Rigge as Student/Russian, Aliyah Wiegand as Student/Russian.

title: Sturgis resident calls for sidewalk fix
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Too many sidewalks in Sturgis have hazardous areas, one resident told the city council recently.
_full_text:
STURGIS — Too many sidewalks in Sturgis have hazardous areas, one resident told the city council recently.

Sturgis resident Linda Chaplin asked members of the city council June 15 to do something to compel homeowners to fix their sidewalks. Chaplin said she takes many walks throughout town, and many times it is safer to walk in the street than it is to walk on sidewalks that are riddled with cracks and tripping hazards.

“They are unsightly,” she said. “They are quite a liability issue for homeowners and probably the town itself. I don’t think a citizen should have to report when they see a sidewalk that needs to be fixed. I think what should happen is there should be a committee who sets up a plan to look at sidewalks in an orderly fashion around town, and send a letter to homeowners whose sidewalks need to be repaired, allow ‘X’ number of days to repair the sidewalk, and if it’s not repaired the city can fix it and a send a bill to the homeowner.”

Mayor Rod Bradley said he has been considering the possibility of coordinating with a local contractor to do work in specific areas of town, and then asking homeowners to sign up for specific dates when the contractor will be in their area.

“It’s hard to get a contractor to work piecemeal,” he said. “That seems like an efficient way to offer it and to cost effectively do it, even though concrete is really expensive right now.”

Following some further discussion about the matter, Sturgis City Administrator Aaron Jordan said the city infrastructure and ordinance committees will discuss the issue and report back to the council about recommended actions.

title: Tri-State Museum’s legal exhibit expands to include noted judge’s desk
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: BELLE FOURCHE — The Tri-State Museum and Visitor Center has long had a legal exhibit, with interesting artifacts from area judges and lawyers. It is now expanded with a significant addition: the desk of Judge Robert Tschetter.
_full_text:
BELLE FOURCHE — The Tri-State Museum and Visitor Center has long had a legal exhibit, with interesting artifacts from area judges and lawyers. It is now expanded with a significant addition: the desk of Judge Robert Tschetter.

Tschetter practiced law in Belle Fourche from 1974 to 1981, when he was appointed to the bench. He served as 8th circuit court judge until his retirement in 1993.

The desk was moved from the Butte County Courthouse in 1995 to a storage facility when the courthouse began renovations. Clerk of Courts Alana Jensen offered it to the museum and Collections Archivist Jada Udager took possession for the Tri-State’s collections.

Judge Tschetter was noted for his wood working skills and the fact that a canoe he had made was suspended from the ceiling of his chambers. He did not, however, make this unique “partner's desk,” which has a deep top and two sets of drawers, one at each end of the pedestal.

The solid oak desk was in good shape but needed to have the laminate top taken off to really set off its attractiveness. Udager used a heat gun provided by Lee Capp to remove the laminate and adhesive below it. The desk was then sanded with a sealer on top and finished with a coat of urethane.

The desk now holds a variety of legal artifacts, including a gavel that belonged to Judge Tschetter. His robe hangs on the wall behind the desk, and there are other artifacts. A photo of Judge Tschetter, smiling as if enjoying a good joke, sits on a back counter.

The Tri-State Museum and Visitor Center is located at 415 Fifth Ave. in Belle Fourche. Its summer hours are 9 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Saturday, and 1-4 p.m. on Sunday. Call (605) 723-1200 for more information.

title: St. Onge hosts 2026 World Livestock Auctioneer Championship
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: ST. ONGE — A sprawling white tent was pitched outside of the St. Onge Livestock Auction Saturday, and packed to the gills with spectators for a very special sale.
_full_text:
ST. ONGE — A sprawling white tent was pitched outside of the St. Onge Livestock Auction Saturday, and packed to the gills with spectators for a very special sale.

Approaching the tent, a low rumbling sound clarified into the melodic, mile-a-minute, cattle rattle of 31 of the world’s finest livestock auctioneers.

 St. Onge hosts 2026 World Livestock Auctioneer Championship

“Today is the culmination of a year-long effort,” said Kristen Parman, the vice president of membership services for the Livestock Marketing Association (LMA) — a nationwide organization that works to actively support and promote livestock marketing and auctions in the US.

10 auctioneers from 3 qualifying events spread across the continental United States, and one international champion from the Calgary Stampede were vying for the LMA’s world champion title. Every year, the championship moves from one LMA member auction to another. This year, it landed in St. Onge — much to members' delight.

 Overflow tent.JPG

“St.Onge requested the opportunity to host. We knew that they would do a tremendous job. We select the sale location first, and then we build our convention and events around it,” Parman said. “Our folks from across the country, really across North America, were excited to come to Deadwood. This has been our biggest convention ever.”

 Auctioneers stand by.JPG

Ross Parks, of New Concord, Ohio, is one of the auctioneers competing for the world title Saturday and has qualified for competition 4 of the last 5 years. He described the 2026 convention as a “good time with good people.”

“It's beautiful country. I would definitely come back again,” Parks said.

Parks grew up going to the sale barn with his grandfather.

 Ross Parks auctioneer.JPG
Ross Parks, of New Concord, Ohio, is one of the auctioneers competing for the world title Saturday and has qualified for competition 4 of the last 5 years. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

“Then, I was working in the ring, selling baby calves and everything. I just grew a knack for it,” Parks said.

In describing the hallmarks of a good auctioneer, Parks said a few elements of performance are paramount.

“To me, it is being clear, being able to communicate with your buyers and sellers, and being able to know the value of the animals when they come into the ring,” Parks said.

His advice to young auctioneers hoping to make their way in the industry — find a strong mentor.

“If you are going to get into the trade, find somebody who has a good reputation within the industry, and somebody who is willing to help you out,” Parks said.

 St. Onge hosts 2026 World Livestock Auctioneer Championship

“The auctioneers themselves, some have come up through family legacy and involvement in the industry, others have been inspired by auctioneers that came before them and just had a passion for this business,” Parman said. “It really is a spark that lights in these individuals. It is everything that drives them.”

Each competitor is scored on two fronts. Friday, they were interviewed by judges on their approach and technique. On Saturday, contestants conducted a sale.

 St. Onge hosts 2026 World Livestock Auctioneer Championship
St. Onge Livestock Auction hosted the Livestock Marketing Association’s 2026 World Livestock Auctioneer Championship Saturday. Pioneer photos by Sierra Ferguson 

“All of our judges are individuals who own or operate livestock auctions across the country,” Parman said Saturday. “Today, they are observing their bid- catching. They (the judges) are observing how they conduct the sale. The most important question our judges are asking as they score them is, ‘Would they hire that auctioneer?’”

Montana’s Jace Thompson walked away from the weekend event with the 2026 World Title. Alongside bragging rights, the auctioneer took home $10,000 cash, one-year use of the world champion truck, a Gist belt buckle, hand-tooled leather briefcase, bronze WLAC sculpture, world champion ring, and a custom engraved Henry Original rifle.

 LMA - WLAC 2026 - SD - R5-2 - William - 02697.jpg
Billings Montana’s Jace Thompson walked away from the weekend event with the 2026 World Title. Photo courtesy Livestock Marketing Association 

Joining him in the winner’s circle were Reserve Champion Troy Robinett and Runner Up Barrett Simon. The LMA also recognized Simon for his high-score interview. Austin Schaben won the Audrey K. Banks Rookie of the Year.

The 2027 World Championship and LMA convention is scheduled to take place in South Lake Tahoe, Nev., and Galt, Calif.

“The Livestock Marketing Association is North America’s largest membership organization, focused solely on that true price discovery,” Parman said. “We provide them all of the services they need to do the best job they can for their buyers and sellers. We try to be the force behind the scenes helping our auctions so that they can have a sale and get the best price possible for their consigners.”

title: Thousands of feet of rope, endless hypotheticals: how emergency response teams stay on top of their game at SURF
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: DEADWOOD — It’s no secret that working a mile underground carries unique risks and opportunities for hazards that can’t be replicated on the surface — that’s why a team of nationally certified rescue experts, emergency medical technicians, and firefighters train throughout the year to ensure they best possible outcome for the worst possible scenarios at Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF).
_full_text:
DEADWOOD — It’s no secret that working a mile underground carries unique risks and opportunities for hazards that can’t be replicated on the surface — that’s why a team of nationally certified rescue experts, emergency medical technicians, and firefighters train throughout the year to ensure they best possible outcome for the worst possible scenarios at Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF).

At SURF, the emergency rescue team (ERT) is made up of a mix of fully trained emergency medical technicians, nurses, firefighters, and volunteers who work full-time at SURF — engineers, mechanics, scientists, communications staff, and beyond. Together, they train at least monthly to develop skills that could prepare them for emergency situations underground.

“A lot of these guys, they work a 7 (days) on, seven (days) off schedule. So (while training), a lot of these guys are all on their days off for the most part,” said Bary Vansickle, ERT supervisor for SURF. “They get paid for their time, but it’s a commitment to put this much time in. Thursdays are a pretty normal training day, so they might be in the middle of a camping trip where they have to drop everything and come in.”

Vansickle said the teams undergo rope training at least 4 times a year and “air training” every other month.

“There’s 3 big things that we do: ropes, medical, and firefighting,” said Vansickle. “We have to have a longer duration breathing apparatus, called a BG4. A normal breathing apparatus that a fire department has lasts up to an hour. Ours lasts up to 4 hours. It’s not like we knock on the front door, we might have to walk a mile to get to the hazard, so we need a longer air supply.”

Vansickle said the nature of SURF, stationed in the underground maze of Homestake Mine, creates unique possibilities for hazards that teams have to train for to best be prepared. That includes specialized firefighting techniques, adapting to breathing apparatuses, and learning how to handle thousands of feet of rope in the event that a victim needs transported through thousands of feet of mine shafts.

William Buckman, technical rescue supervisor for Nolan Independent Management, of Black Hawk, came into the world of wildland search and rescue after spending years rock climbing in national parks across the country. Summiting some rock climbing routes in Yosemite, Zion National Park, and Devil’s Tower, has lent him a wide range of skills that he now utilizes when training ERT at SURF.

“Everybody always tries to be as prepared as they can, and they’ve got all of this equipment. They’ve got trucks, vehicles with things. Well, as you start getting into more remote situations, now all of a sudden, you’re choosing from the amount of gear you brought in and the personnel available,” said Buckman. “Trying to learn how to pick from your large mountain of technical gear, to knowing what individual items you need, and being able to do this in a good, timely manner while knowing that you’re dealing with some pace that’s hard to get to. That mindset is what changes things.”

Buckman said the facilities at SURF, including old crusher plants, simulated mine shafts, and miles of rock, allow him to train ERT members before an emergency happens using techniques and tools they can call upon if the worst happens.

“Last week we were over at the crusher plant with rope systems that spanned the room,” said Buckman. “There was a crane above us, allowing us to go across the room, drop down in the middle, pick somebody up in an isolated spot, bring them up, and trolley the litter back. There’s a lot of oversight to try and create pre-plans, identify areas so they already know what they’re doing ahead of time to help speed up the (rescue) process, but there’s an endless number of hypotheticals in an environment like this. So, what we try to focus on, is concepts that don’t change when we talk about how we’re going to do things. These techniques will remain kind of the threshold. We try to teach them to always make sur ethere’s someone that can still maintain oversight, because once your hands get on ropes, once you start getting muddy and you’re exposed near an edge, you’re not thinking about, ‘How are we going to move this patient in 15 minutes, what do we need to have coming this way?’ It’s like a chess game, actually, just with a physical component.”

Through Nelson Independent Management, Buckman has trained wildland firefighters, wilderness search and rescue teams, members of the Army National Guard, and small companies who want to make sure they can offer assistance if they find themselves in an emergency situation while climbing or caving in an environment like the underground tunnels at SURF. He said that he would recommend that training to anybody who “wants to make a difference.”

“If someone has that desire to change their life and go into this kind of (emergency medical services) technical rescue, being able to segway into firefighting, ambulance services, or park rangers, even the individuals that are outdoor specific personalities or could find themselves in remote environments where a little bit of technical or medical skill could make a difference, they should reach out,” said Buckman. “Most people aren’t going to go around with thousands of dollars of rescue gear, able to help somebody out. But being able to be a part of that team can change things for someone.”

title: Spearfish will pay for gabion structure repair in sanitary sewer upsize project
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — After a special session Monday, the Spearfish City Council voted unanimously to approve a $15,040.28 change order, agreeing to pay for repairs to gabion structures damaged during the ongoing Colorado Boulevard sanitary sewer upsize project.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — After a special session Monday, the Spearfish City Council voted unanimously to approve a $15,040.28 change order, agreeing to pay for repairs to gabion structures damaged during the ongoing Colorado Boulevard sanitary sewer upsize project.

Gabion structures are baskets, typically made of metal, that are filled with stones to provide support for buildings and bridges.

As crews from Woelber Excavating were digging trenches to make way for a new, 21-inch sewer main from 27th Street to False Bottom Creek, they disturbed gabion structures that support the bridge over False Bottom Creek. The contractor did not know the structures extended to the spot where they were trenching.

“The bridge plans that we had on file didn’t exactly show these rocky mediums in that area. They were also buried in a field, so there wasn’t any visual indication from the surface that we needed to investigate further to include this work in the big set of plans,” McMahon said. “They were just following the location as shown, and in doing so they encountered these rock gabions.”

Spearfish Public Works Director Adam McMahon said the structures were likely installed in the late 1970s, before the city was involved.

“This bridge was constructed in 1978. That was when it was part of the state system. Then it was transferred to the county. We received it from the county in the 90s as part of the annexation of Exit 17/Elkhorn Ridge area,” McMahon said.

McMahon said the gabion structures were “buried in a field” so the contractor would not have seen them from the surface before they started digging.

The gabions might have been buried, McMahon said, but that made them no less important to the structural integrity of the bridge.

“It is a critical piece of the bridge infrastructure. We need to do this work to repair the bridge,” McMahon said. “Had we known they were there, it would have been included in the bid items. This is work that we would have paid for, had we known to include it.”

In addition to approving the estimated price for the repairs, the council also unanimously voted to extend the project timeline — updating the substantial completion date for the project to July 13. The total project cost is now estimated at $2,535,805.72.

title: Sturgis approves customized Coke mural for Rally Point
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Sturgis has been chosen as the lone city to host a temporary national mural, commemorating America’s 250th anniversary, but city officials are trying to balance that national exposure with local consideration.
_full_text:
STURGIS — Sturgis has been chosen as the lone city to host a temporary national mural, commemorating America’s 250th anniversary, but city officials are trying to balance that national exposure with local consideration.

Lance Scherer Sturgis Motorcycle Rally sponsorship director told members of the city council recently that the Coca-Cola Company is launching a public art initiative called the “Paint the Nation” mural program. The program is intended to commemorate America’s 250th anniversary, and involves one large mural that will be placed in each state for at least one or 2 years. In Sturgis, the company submitted a request to install the temporary mural at Harley-Davidson Rally Point, a community gathering spot near Main Street, for one year.

“The current concept contemplates a custom-designed mural installed on a temporary wall structure with a wooden substrate, along the rear wall of Rally Point. Participation in the Paint the Nation program would allow Sturgis to be featured as South Dakota’s representative community in a nationally promoted America250 initiative.”

Scherer said under the agreement, the mural would be custom-designed for Sturgis, and the city council would have the authority to approve the final artwork before the installation.

The project does not have a direct financial impact to the city, Scherer said. Project sponsors, including Coca-Cola, will pay for all the design, construction, installation, maintenance, repair, and removal.

Councilwoman Ruth Nichols said she is interested in having the mural for longer than a year, but questioned whether Rally Point is the best location for the mural.

“I think it’s a fantastic initiative,” she said. “I do have concerns. You mentioned emphasis on community. I feel like we’re constantly trying to find this balance between the community year-round and the Rally. That’s why I raised the question about why Rally Point. I wonder if Coke has done research on where people spend the most time when they are here during the Rally.”

Nichols asked Sturgis Communications Manager Deb Holland to check Placer.ai software, which tracks visitor movements within a certain geographic boundary, to see where people spend the most time during the Rally.

But Sturgis City Administrator Aaron Jordan said he believes Coca-Cola does not want the mural to be specific to the Rally. However, the Sturgis Area Chamber of Commerce and the Sturgis Business Improvement District board had concerns about the mural’s location at Rally Point. The chamber, he said, has already sold sponsorships for the city’s weekly Music on Main event, and other activities throughout the year, and those sponsorship banners are hung in the proposed location for the mural.

“I had the comment that the city was selling our soul to the big ones versus the local ones,” Jordan said. “I think we can have both. It’s not selling our soul or having a disruption. Is there a way to incorporate this national program with local events and the sponsorship we have?”

Veronica Grosek, executive director for the chamber, said the mural would be a disruption to the way sponsors for local events are promoted, and existing agreements the chamber has with title sponsors.

“But I feel like there could be workable solutions,” she said. “I think it’s a cool project, but it does have challenges for events this summer that we have already planned out.”

Following some further discussion, the council unanimously approved the outdoor mural agreement, contingent upon negotiating an agreement with existing event sponsors at Rally Point.

title: Colorado Blvd. corrective chip seal begins
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: SPEARFISH — Crews from Black Hawk-based Dakota Asphalt LLC. were scheduled to start work Tuesday that will include: removing existing chip seal on Colorado Boulevard from Jackson Boulevard to Spearfish Canyon Highway 14A, asphalt patching, removing and replacing curb and gutter adjacent to the asphalt patching, reapplication of chip seal (for portions of Colorado Boulevard), and applying pavement markings.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — Crews from Black Hawk-based Dakota Asphalt LLC. were scheduled to start work Tuesday that will include: removing existing chip seal on Colorado Boulevard from Jackson Boulevard to Spearfish Canyon Highway 14A, asphalt patching, removing and replacing curb and gutter adjacent to the asphalt patching, reapplication of chip seal (for portions of Colorado Boulevard), and applying pavement markings.

Dakota Asphalt will not be chip sealing any of the downtown for from Jackson Boulevard to Grant Street. That area will be milled and overlaid as a separate project that has not been awarded to a contractor yet.

The chip seal operation will begin just south of the Grant Street intersection, and continue to Highway 14A. Roads will remain open, and traffic will be reduced to one lane in each direction as the chip seal work is performed. Loose gravel and fresh oil will be present in the project area for the extent of the work period. Traffic is advised to reduce speed or use an alternate route during this time.

Then, the contractor will pivot to pavement markings, working from the intersection of Jonas Boulevard on Jackson Boulevard. Then, they are scheduled to apply pavement marking to Harvard Street from the Jackson Boulevard intersection to the intersection of Harvard Street and Hill Street.

That work is expected to continue until the week of July 6, between the hours of 7 a.m. and 6 p.m. — weather dependent.

title: Construction planned on Highway 85 through Deadwood
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: DEADWOOD — Construction on Highway 85 through Deadwood began Monday and is expected to continue for approximately 3 weeks as staff from South Dakota Department of Transportation work to repair sections of concrete on the box culvert.
_full_text:
DEADWOOD — Construction on Highway 85 through Deadwood began Monday and is expected to continue for approximately 3 weeks as staff from South Dakota Department of Transportation work to repair sections of concrete on the box culvert.

Lornie Stalder, director of public works, said that work will begin on the outside lane of eastbound driving lane from the Silverado to Tin Lizzie Gaming Resort. Eastbound traffic will be reduced to a single lane.

Beginning June 29, Stadler said construction crews will move to the outer westbound lane, during which westbound traffic will be reduced to a single lane.

Stalder said the final leg of construction will take place on the inner sections of the northbound and southbound lanes, beginning July 6.

Stalder said during construction, barriers will be removed during the weekends.

During construction, Stalder said he doesn’t expect traffic to experience major delays, but drivers should be cautious and aware of workers in the road.

title: Annual Sturgis Volksmarch celebrates America’s 250th
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Hikers and outdoor enthusiasts gathered Saturday at Fort Meade for the annual Sturgis Volksmarch, an event that highlighted the area's scenic beauty while celebrating America’s 250th.
_full_text:
STURGIS — Hikers and outdoor enthusiasts gathered Saturday at Fort Meade for the annual Sturgis Volksmarch, an event that highlighted the area's scenic beauty while celebrating America’s 250th.

The Saturday event was part of the association's walking, hiking and biking event in 2026. Hosted in partnership with Sturgis Outdoors and the Black Hills Volkssport Association, participants could choose between a 5-kilometer or 10-kilometer route that featured gravel paths, single-track trails and views of Bear Butte and the Fort Meade National Cemetery. Approximately 60 people participated in this year's event.

Holly Roltgen, one of the event coordinators with the Black Hills Volkssport Association, said the Sturgis Volksmarch has become one of the organization's long running events.

"I think this is the oldest and longest Volksmarch we've had since the Black Hills association started about 40 years ago," Roltgen said. "We're working in conjunction with Sturgis Outdoors to help get people out to see our beautiful area. It's a great place with lots of vegetation, and we want people to understand that exercise is good for you."

Roltgen said the benefits extend beyond physical fitness. "It's good for the body and good for the soul," she said. "It's also a chance to commune with nature and enjoy the outdoors."

The Black Hills Volkssport Association hosts a variety of sanctioned and year-round walking events throughout the region, including walks at Crazy Horse, Keystone, Deadwood and even Devil's Tower.

Richelle Bruch, of Sturgis Outdoors, said the nonprofit organization stepped in to help continue the event after organizational changes left its future uncertain.

"Sturgis Outdoors is a local nonprofit group that promotes outdoor recreation opportunities in Sturgis and the surrounding area," Bruch said. "When the Sturgis Chamber had to make some event cuts, we didn't want to see this event disappear. It fits perfectly with our mission of promoting and providing opportunities for people to get outside and enjoy what this area has to offer."

Among those participating was Diane Johannesen of Sundance, Wyo., who has been involved in Volksmarch events for more than four decades.

"I walk for the health of it, and I get to see things on a walk that I never get to see in a car," Johannesen said.

She began participating in Volksmarch events in 1980 and estimates she has logged thousands of miles while attending walks across the country.

"I've walked in all 50 states and 51 capitals," she said. "I just came back from the Canadian Volksmarch convention this week."

Johannesen said one of the highlights of traveling to events is experiencing different landscapes. "In Canada, the lakes, trees and boulders were beautiful," she said. "It was a completely different experience from what we have around here."

Joining Johannesen was Mary Jayne Jordan of Sundance, who invited walkers to attend Sundance's upcoming Volksmarch event at White Ranch.

"You'll walk at the base of Sundance Mountain," Jordan said. "It's volcanic, similar to Bear Butte, but it's much more wooded."

Organizers hope the Sturgis Volksmarch continues to attract both longtime participants and newcomers for years to come, encouraging people to explore the Black Hills one step at a time while enjoying the physical and mental benefits of spending time outdoors.

title: Les Deux to expand European café –culture-inspired offerings after wine license approval
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — It isn’t every day a coffee shop applies for a wine, cider, or malt beverage license, but Les Deux owner Kami Wrage has a plan.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — It isn’t every day a coffee shop applies for a wine, cider, or malt beverage license, but Les Deux owner Kami Wrage has a plan.

After a public hearing Monday, the Spearfish City Council voted unanimously to grant a retail on-off sale malt beverage, SD farm wine license, and a retail wine and cider license to Les Deux.

Wrage opened the business at 115 Hudson St., with Celine Freszel earlier this year. From the start, Les Deux set out to fill a niche in Spearfish’s coffee scene. Since her career in coffee started in Pittsburgh, Wrage has thought of beverages as opportunities to offer customers unique experiences and a simple, affordable escape from everyday life.

Now, Wrage is planning to expand the daytime café atmosphere into the evening.

“Les Duex has always been, and I personally am, very connected to the European culture of things,” Wrage said. “It is kind of less of a bar scene, more café society.”

The vibes will remain the same, but customers will have the chance to sip wine while they gather, write, read, and work on their laptops.

“We are hoping, especially when college is in session and everything, I’ve heard many people in the community voice their opinion that they want somewhere to go work after 5 that’s not really a bar. I am hoping to fill that space,” Wrage said.

She hopes to expand her hours; right now the café closes at 3 p.m. daily, and her menu to bring customers more chic, niche, European-inspired experiences.

She plans to stock Prosecco to sell by the glass and in mimosas on the weekends. Les Deux is also authorized to sell whole bottles of wine for customers to purchase and sip at home. On the horizon at Les Deux are sparkling bottles of Italian Lambrusco, purple Gamay, and imported Beaujolais.

“I am into red wine. There is a South African wine called Pinotage which I really like and want to offer here,” Wrage said. “I want to offer things that are a little more off the wall than your typical chardonnay or cab.”

title: Fundraising record set at annual Golden Guitars Gala benefitting Children’s Miracle Network
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: RAPID CITY – The Golden Guitars Gala, a Monument Health Foundation fundraiser for Children's Miracle Network, broke fundraising records and welcomed surprise guest Bret Michaels on June 13 at the fifth annual event. The Poison frontman performed a special acoustic set and personally contributed to the evening, helping push the total raised to $781,250, a Foundation record for the largest amount raised at a single event.
_full_text:
RAPID CITY – The Golden Guitars Gala, a Monument Health Foundation fundraiser for Children's Miracle Network, broke fundraising records and welcomed surprise guest Bret Michaels on June 13 at the fifth annual event. The Poison frontman performed a special acoustic set and personally contributed to the evening, helping push the total raised to $781,250, a Foundation record for the largest amount raised at a single event.

Each year, Golden Guitars signed by the musicians who play at The Monument and other select venues are auctioned off during the event. During the live auction, the top-selling guitar signed by Jason Aldean auctioned for $55,000. Funds raised support Children's Miracle Network, with all money staying local to benefit children in the Black Hills, who receive care at Monument Health hospitals.

Following his performance, Michaels added to the excitement with a special package featuring signed guitars and a travel experience to one of his upcoming concerts.

"Raising $781,250 in a single evening is extraordinary, and it is a true reflection of how much this community cares about the children in our region,” said Robin Zebroski Chief Brand Officer, Monument Health. “Every dollar stays here in the Black Hills, supporting the kids and families who need it most, and for that, we are so grateful for every person who made this night possible."

South Dakota artist Kory Van Sickle of Kory and the Fireflies developed the event as part of his company's philanthropic program, Firefly Guitars. Golden Firefly Guitars were autographed by a star-studded lineup, including Dolly Parton, Mötley Crüe, Foreigner, Blake Shelton and Journey.

title: Pronghorn numbers steadily increasing, GF&P still conservative on licenses
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: MADISON — Pronghorn numbers are still below the statewide objective, but biologists with the South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks say the population is heading in the right direction.
_full_text:
MADISON — Pronghorn numbers are still below the statewide objective, but biologists with the South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks say the population is heading in the right direction.

Andy Lindbloom said an aerial survey of pronghorn range shows an educated estimate of about 30,000 adult antelope across the state. That compares to 2024, when the estimate was at about 27,000.

The aerial surveys are conducted in the spring, before most fawns are born, Lindbloom said. Therefore, the estimates are for adult populations only. But using a 3-year average, he said they expect to have about 36,000 pronghorn on the landscape when hunting season starts this year.

That compares to the statewide objective of about 67,000, Lindbloom said.

Lindbloom said the aerial survey showed an estimated 12% increase in adult pronghorn. He attributed that to mild winters and some regulation changes, when in 2022 the GF&P stopped issuing any-antelope licenses, and limited licenses to buck-only.

Pronghorn, he said, are unique in that the GF&P has data for every unit in the state. Some units are well below average, while others are very close to meeting objectives. For example, Wildlife Program Administrator Andrew Norton said on the eastern side of the range, populations are either stable or decreasing. On the western side they are increasing.

“There was definitely some increase in Butte, Lawrence County, Custer, Pennington, and the south side of Perkins,” Norton said. “So things went really good there. One area where we would have liked to increase (licenses) was in Fall River, Custer, and right in the southwest corner, where we saw the biggest (population) increase. But that was also identified as one of the units that we were most aggressive, as far as harvesting percent of bucks. We didn’t increase that even though counts were much higher there. We wanted to be a little conservative to try to maintain a decent age structure for bucks over there.”

Overall, licenses for this year are about 1% higher than the 2024-25 season. Licenses will remain for buck only. Additionally, the GF&P will keep the youth season closed this year.

Based on the data, Lindbloom said the GF&P projects a 5-6% annual growth rate.

“We’ve been extremely conservative for the past 4 to 6 years in regards to harvest,” said Norton. “We’ve been hoping for good weather conditions to have good fawn recuirtment, decent weather survival, and hopefully that leads to some of this population increase that we’re seeing. We’re still really conservative with the license increase, even though this is a male only harvest.”

For the 2026-27 hunting seasons, pronghorn archery licenses will be largely unchanged, except in the Fort Pierre National Grasslands, where they were reduced by 50%, from 10 to 5.

Resident firearm licenses will very by unit. In Butte and Lawrence counties there will be 50 more licenses available, a 25% change. In Custer and central Pennington County licenses will also be up by 25%, from 100 to 125. Northern Meade County will see a 25% reduction in licenses, from 200 to 150, but the southern Meade County unit will remain unchanged. Fall River and southwest Custer counties will not see a change in license allocations. Southern Perkins County will see a 100% increase in licenses, from 100 to 200, while northern Perkins County will remain unchanged.

The largest reductions this year will be in Jones County, where there will be 83% less licenses, from 30 to 5; and the Fort Pierre National Grasslands and Stanley County, where there will be a 50% reduction for both. Ziebach County will see a 33% license reduction.

title: Lead-Deadwood Middle School welcomes new principal
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: DEADWOOD — Zack Clement may be new to his position as the principal of Lead-Deadwood Middle School, but he’s been building relationships and rapport in the district for 3 years.
_full_text:
DEADWOOD — Zack Clement may be new to his position as the principal of Lead-Deadwood Middle School, but he’s been building relationships and rapport in the district for 3 years.

Clement, a graduate of Dakota Wesleyan University, had his first teaching job as a special education and elementary computers educator in Wessington Springs. During that first year he also coached middle school and high school wrestling. From there, Clement took a position in the Mitchell School District, continuing his coaching and educator career while completing a master’s degree in special education at Northwest Missouri State University and gaining a certification in education leadership K through 12.

“I did kind of look around for some administrative jobs, but I didn’t really commit to anything right away. I kind of anticipated teaching and coaching until I retired,” said Clement. “But then the activities director job in the Lead-Deadwood School District came up.”

Since coming to Lead-Deadwood, Clement has worked as a wrestling and football coach and led weight training sessions, allowing him to build rapport in the district with parents, students, and members of faculty. After the announcement of Jay Beagle’s retirement, Clement is ready to bring those relationships and experience with him on the journey ahead of him as he attempts to fill Beagle’s shoes.

“I don’t think there was a single person that’s walked through the doors in the last 16, 17 years that (Beagle) was here that didn’t love him, and that goes for staff members as well as students and parents,” said Clement. “That will be hard to replace, and I don’t think he will ever be replaced, but I’m going to try to do the best I can to continue some of that stuff.”

To prepare for his new role, Clement said that fifth-grade educators gathered with middle school staff to help teachers prepare for the new influx of students, debriefing on classroom dynamics that have worked, some that haven’t, and generally helped teachers get to know students before they arrive on campus in August.

“It doesn’t sound like they’ve really done that before, so now they’ve had an opportunity to know when those kids come into their classrooms, they know them just a little bit more than they did when they saw just a name and a picture on Infinite Campus,” said Clement.

Clement said that he’s prepared to tackle the challenges ahead of him in his first year as principal, including adapting the needs and availabilities of the school to declining enrollment, handling the social learning required of middle school students, and welcoming new career and technical education and science, education, technology, and math programming to the school’s retinue at the conclusion of the middle school renovation, while keeping his eye on more long-term goals as well.

“With the activities director role, I learned that if you have a bunch of new ideas and things that you want to do, it’s going to take a few years to really see that settle in and take off. For now, it’s one of our goals to have as many opportunities in the wood shop, welding, and CAM programs as possible for these kids,” said Clement. “Down the road, one of the hopes is that we can raise some of our smarter balance test scores and continue to give kids opportunities to have as many elective classes as possible. I think it’s really important at this age to expose the kids to as much as possible.”

title: History Days draws strong crowd for celebration of rural schools and local heritage
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Memories of one-room schoolhouses, country teachers, spelling bees and generations of rural families filled the Sturgis Community Center as the 10th Annual Sturgis & Meade County History Days attracted a strong turnout of residents eager to learn, share and preserve local history.
_full_text:
STURGIS — Memories of one-room schoolhouses, country teachers, spelling bees and generations of rural families filled the Sturgis Community Center as the 10th Annual Sturgis & Meade County History Days attracted a strong turnout of residents eager to learn, share and preserve local history.

This year's event, held June 12-13, focused on “The History of Schools in Sturgis and Meade County.” The theme generated significant interest, with the Sturgis & Meade County Historical Society collecting stories and artifacts spanning more than 150 years of education in both town and country schools.

Exhibits, presentations and personal stories highlighted the important role schools played in shaping communities throughout Meade County.

The history of rural education reflects the changing landscape of the county. As agriculture, transportation and communications evolved, so did the challenges of providing education across a large rural area. Historical records show that by 1931, Meade County had approximately 160 rural school buildings staffed by 163 teachers. By 1939, that number had declined to about 90 schools as consolidation and population shifts began reshaping education.

One of the attendees was former Upper Pleasant Valley School student Mrs. Nancy Remington, whose family history is closely tied to the rural school.

Remington attended the school from 1959 to 1965, completing all eight grades there. Her connection to the school extends back even further.

"My grandmother Blair was a teacher there before she got married in 1912 and 1913," Remington said. "She boarded with the Blair family, which is how she met my grandpa. My dad and his two sisters went to school there, and all nine of us kids attended there too."

The former schoolhouse still stands today near Exit 37, about a mile and a half from Interstate 90 at the intersection with Fort Meade Way.

"Darren and Carrie Odle purchased it and have remodeled it," Remington said. "There are pictures of the restoration on display at the event."

Remington recalled many fond memories of attending the one-room school.

"I remember the spelling contests when we'd come into town for the county competition and Rally Day," she said. "We had Christmas programs and practiced for Rally Day events. When I was in second grade, there were only nine kids in the school, five from our family, two cousins and two neighboring girls. It was kind of like a family."

She also remembered her first teacher, Amy Zink.

"I had Mrs. Amy Zink for the first 3 years," Remington said. "She was excellent with reading and teaching the younger elementary students."

The program featured presentations by Betsey DeLouche on country schools, past and present, while Jim Holland and Mark Rambow presented a timeline of Sturgis schools in the Community Center Theater.

The event also included recognition of individuals who have contributed significantly to preserving local history.

Historical Society President Mark Rambow presented the organization's annual Friend of History Awards.

Rambow noted that the society honored former country school teacher Edna Haley Smith.

"We wanted to recognize her again today," Rambow said. "She received the Friend of History Award for her contributions and dedication to preserving the history of education in this area."

The society also honored longtime members and volunteers Ross and Jan Lamphere for their years of service and commitment to local history.

"Ross and Jan have been active members of the Historical Society since the very beginning in 2014, and even before that they were deeply involved in preserving history throughout the community," Rambow said.

He highlighted the couple's many contributions, including hosting archaeology students from the University of South Dakota during excavations at Soap Suds Row near Fort Meade, assisting with museum acquisitions and supporting numerous historical projects.

"You name it, Ross and Jan have been there for it," Rambow said. "It was appropriate that we recognize them for everything they've done and everything they continue to do."

A surprised Ross Lamphere accepted the award on behalf of his family. "I had absolutely no idea this was coming," Lamphere said. "It's been a real privilege to be involved with the preservation of history in our area. In many respects, our history is still young, and so much of it is still available to be preserved. What a privilege it is to be honored for something like this. Thank you very much."

The annual History Days event continues to serve as a gathering place where residents can connect with the stories, people and places that helped shape Sturgis and Meade County, ensuring those memories are preserved for future generations.

title: Make your mark: Spearfish Parks and Rec department wants to know how you use the creek
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — As the Spearfish Parks and Recreation Department begins implementing phase one of its Spearfish Creek Preservation Plan, they’re looking for community input — both in person and online.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — As the Spearfish Parks and Recreation Department begins implementing phase one of its Spearfish Creek Preservation Plan, they’re looking for community input — both in person and online.

On Tuesday, at the W.S. Tretheway Pavilion, parks staff hosted an open house that offered a tactile, in-person approximation of the survey tools it is employing online to gather community feedback.

Spearfish residents were invited to walk around poster board sized maps, and mark — using paper flags — the places they for recreation. Open house attendees were also asked to literally flag areas of concern, including places along the creek where they’ve seen erosion.

“There are 5 different stations, each one with different areas of the creek, aerial views, and you’re going to be placing flags on the maps in areas where you go fishing, where you use the creek for wading or swimming, places where there are areas of erosion or signs of concern, trail usage — since most of the creek follows the rec path,” McDonald said. “Following this, we are going to aggregate all of the data, put it together, and get a better feel for how people are using the creek and recreational access points and where there are concerns.”

On the back of the paper flag markers, open house attendees were able to write comments — explaining why they marked any given part of the creek.

Conversations during the open house also proved enlightening for parks staff. The collaborative event featured plenty of story sharing between citizens and city workers, discussing the past, present, and future of the creek.

McDonald said the leveraging public knowledge will help the city to better plan its stewardship of the creek moving forward.

“The ultimate goal is just to give us a better idea of how people are using the creek and how we can then enhance those recreational access points so that people can still recreate there and we don’t have degradation of the surrounding area,” McDonald said.

If residents missed the open house Tuesday, that’s not a problem.

“What people are doing here in person is the same thing that people can do online with the interactive map,” McDonald said.

title: Piedmont search warrant leads to significant drug seizure
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: PIEDMONT — County, state, and federal law enforcement recovered large amounts of drugs, while executing a search warrant related to suspicions of child exploitation in Piedmont.
_full_text:
PIEDMONT — County, state, and federal law enforcement recovered large amounts of drugs, while executing a search warrant related to suspicions of child exploitation in Piedmont.

On Tuesday, the Meade County Sheriff's Office (MCSO), in partnership with the Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC) Task Force and the South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation (DCI), executed a search warrant at a residence on Deerview Road in rural Piedmont.

The property owner, Kevin Gilmore, 42, had previously been taken into custody in Wisconsin on a warrant related to a child exploitation investigation originating in Minnesota. Based on information developed by investigators in Minnesota, a search warrant was obtained and executed at his Meade County residence.

During the execution of the warrant, ICAC investigators were recovering electronic devices and digital evidence, when they allegedly discovered what they described as a substantial quantity of suspected illegal narcotics. Members of the Unified Narcotics Enforcement Team (UNET) were subsequently called to the scene to assist with the investigation.

UNET investigators recovered about 157 pounds of marijuana, including evidence of a large-scale marijuana cultivation operation; an estimated 10-20 pounds of psilocybin mushrooms; various THC products, including hashish, vape cartridges, and THC infused gummies; and numerous computers, electronic storage devices, and other digital equipment.

Meade County Sheriff Pat West praised the collaborative efforts of the agencies involved.

"The work conducted by these investigators once again demonstrates that significant criminal threats can exist anywhere, including within our own communities," said West. "Strong partnerships and coordinated efforts between local, state, and federal agencies are critical in protecting our children, families, and residents. We remain committed to identifying offenders, making arrests, and ensuring those responsible are held accountable through the criminal justice system.

“This case underscores the reality that criminal activity knows no boundaries. What began as an investigation in Minnesota resulted in an arrest in Wisconsin, and led to the execution of a search warrant here in Meade County. The seamless cooperation between agencies was instrumental in advancing this investigation."

Agencies that are actively pursuing the investigation include South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation (DCI), Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC) Task Force, Unified Narcotics Enforcement Team (UNET), Pennington County Sheriff's Office, Rapid City Police Department, Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security.

This investigation remains ongoing. Additional charges may be pending.

title: Black Hills Renaissance Festival expands with more performers, vendors and immersive entertainment
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — The Black Hills Renaissance Festival is preparing for its biggest and most immersive event yet, featuring more performers, more vendors and more opportunities for visitors to step into a world of fantasy, adventure and medieval fun. The festival will be held Saturday and Sunday at Kickstands Campground, located at 13014 Pleasant Valley Rd., near Sturgis, just off Interstate 90 Exit 34.
_full_text:
STURGIS — The Black Hills Renaissance Festival is preparing for its biggest and most immersive event yet, featuring more performers, more vendors and more opportunities for visitors to step into a world of fantasy, adventure and medieval fun. The festival will be held Saturday and Sunday at Kickstands Campground, located at 13014 Pleasant Valley Rd., near Sturgis, just off Interstate 90 Exit 34.

Festival founder Shareece Tatum said the new venue provides the perfect setting for creating an authentic Renaissance experience.

“Kickstands is perfect for the festival,” said Tatum. “It has tons of space and makes it more immersive, so you really feel like you are stepping into a different time and world. There is so much going on that you will forget that you are in the middle of the Black Hills.”

The Black Hills Renaissance Festival continues to grow in popularity. Last year's event attracted approximately 5,300 attendees, and organizers are expecting another strong turnout this year.

Visitors will find more than 70 vendors and over 20 performers throughout the weekend. New attractions include a mermaid, additional pirates, bards and musicians, creating an even more interactive atmosphere where guests can create their own adventure.

“This year is all about building a more immersive experience,” Tatum said. “Whether you're meeting pirates, listening to musicians, shopping with vendors or watching live performances, there's something happening around every corner.”

Festival-goers are encouraged to wear costumes, although dressing up is not required. Organizers say costumes add to the fun and help create the atmosphere that makes the festival unique. A costume contest and photo contest will also be held, with submissions opening after the event begins.

Entertainment throughout the weekend will include crowd favorites such as jousting demonstrations, sword fighting, fire-breathing performances and a variety of live stage acts. A full schedule of events is expected to be released through the festival's website and social media channels.

“For just a brief weekend, you can step into a different world, forget everything going on around you and just have fun,” Tatum said. “You will find camaraderie and get to feel like a kid again.”

Families will find plenty of activities designed specifically for children. “All of our stage performances are family friendly, and there are activities and experiences for all ages,” said Tatum.

Tickets are currently available online and range from $15 to $35.

title: A new place for Pilates
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — Black Hills Core Collective owner Kassidi Martinez is not afraid to start something new.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — Black Hills Core Collective owner Kassidi Martinez is not afraid to start something new.

In February, she opened her first reformer Pilates studio in Rapid City. She opened a second location at 3025 1st Ave. in Spearfish on May 16.

“I had just found out I was pregnant a week before opening in Rapid too,” Martinez said.

She opened a studio after joking about it with former clients, when she briefly stopped working as an instructor in favor of remote work.

“I missed being around people a lot,” Martinez said. “It was nice to be an instructor and have that fulfilled also. I missed that connection with the clients.”

Her adventurous spirit shines through in the warm, colorful choices she has made to brand the core collective.

Reformer Pilates require the use of a reformer machine — a device that helps provide resistance during exercise. Generally, those reformers are black and white. They populate spare, sleek studios that Martinez noted absolutely fit the minimalist “clean girl” aesthetic.

At the Black Hills Core Collective, Martinez has embraced a different look entirely. The studio is packed with plants, there are disco balls in strategic locations, and the reformers are anything but black and white.

“I’m not like that anyway. My house is decorated kind of like this, with disco balls and a mural in the basement,” Martinez said. “I just like color. I think it brings so much more warmth and welcome.”

Martinez, who has a background in architecture and design, is prioritizing welcome in more ways than one.

Pilates, she said, can offer a strong entry point for people of all fitness levels and abilities to pursue their health goals.

“It is very low impact for your body, so a lot of people will come here with injuries or postpartum. It is pretty easy to get into,” Martinez said.

Unlike mat Pilates, the reformers provide greater tension and intensity, Martinez said.

“All of our classes you hit lower body, upper body, and core within the class. They’re a little bit longer than a classic Pilates class. We are kind of like strength and Pilates combined,” Martinez said. “It’s a little bit higher intensity, higher reps every time, but it is focusing on tension.”

Martinez said she wants people who are motivated to try reformer Pilates to have a low barrier to entry. Her drop-in, trial class rate is $10.

“I just wanted to make it inconsequential for people to come try it,” Martinez said. “If they don’t like it, it is $10. It is not that big of a loss. The regular offering is $20.”

For folks who find reformer Pilates to their liking, Black Hills Core Collective offers memberships and “class packs” with 4, 10, 15, or 20 classes that don’t expire at the end of each month.

“It kind of depends on what people’s fitness goals are and how often they think they can come,” Martinez said. “I like to guide them through their fitness journey.”

title: Belle Fourche chicken ordinance scheduled for second reading Monday
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: BELLE FOURCHE — The Belle Fourche City Council is scheduled to vote on a proposed chicken ordinance at its next regular session meeting.
_full_text:
BELLE FOURCHE — The Belle Fourche City Council is scheduled to vote on a proposed chicken ordinance at its next regular session meeting.

If approved, Title 6 will be amended to formally allow chickens in the city limits.

“Questions regarding whether chickens are permitted within the City of Belle Fourche, along with occasional complaints regarding roosters, come into our offices on a fairly regular basis,” Belle Fourche City Administrator Jason LaFayette said. “Staff felt that, similar to other communities throughout the Northern Hills area, the city would benefit from having an ordinance in place that provides clear direction and guidance.”

Previously, there was no official, written policy to permit or prohibit the keeping of backyard flocks in the city.

The proposed ordinance would not allow roosters.

“Roosters were prohibited for many of the same reasons other communities have chosen to restrict them. The primary concern is neighborhood noise. Additionally, roosters can display aggressive territorial behavior, which can create concerns in residential settings,” LaFayette said.

It also sets a requirement that chickens be kept “within a secure enclosure and provided access to a coop at all times.” Under the proposed rule, hens would have to be kept inside their coop through the night, “from sunset to sunrise.”

“The overnight coop requirement is intended primarily to protect the birds from predators. It also helps reduce the likelihood of attracting predators to residential neighborhoods at night, when they are most active. This benefits both chicken owners and neighboring residents by helping prevent potential nuisance situations,” LaFayette said.

For folks hoping to raise chickens for meat, in addition to eggs, slaughtering will be allowed. However, under the proposed ordinance, slaughtering must take place in “areas not visible from a public right-of-way or adjacent property.”

The new ordinance, if passed, would also prevent the release of chickens into a public area.

The first draft of the ordinance was crafted using other municipal regulations as a starting point.

“The initial draft combined elements from those ordinances into what was, in my opinion, a fairly restrictive starting point. That draft was reviewed several times internally before being presented to the Public Works Committee for public discussion and feedback,” LaFayette said.

After receiving significant feedback from residents, the ordinance was updated to reflect much of that feedback.

“In many cases, we agreed with the concerns raised by residents and made revisions accordingly. The result is an ordinance that we believe addresses community concerns while continuing to keep Belle Fourche a chicken-friendly community. The intent was never to eliminate backyard chickens but rather to establish clear, reasonable guidelines that work for everyone,” LaFayette said.

title: Montana gas explosion destroys family home, injures 3
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer
description: ALZADA — An explosion destroyed a family home in Alzada, Mont., early Sunday morning, seriously injuring 2 children and their mother, who are now all receiving medical treatment in Colorado.
_full_text:
ALZADA — An explosion destroyed a family home in Alzada, Mont., early Sunday morning, seriously injuring 2 children and their mother, who are now all receiving medical treatment in Colorado.

Police, ambulances, and the fire department responded to a report of a house explosion around 3 a.m.

Ambulances took Lenee Richardson and her 2 children, ages 11 and 12, to Monument Health Hospital in Spearfish, where they were then flown to a hospital in Aurora, Colo. to receive further treatment.

Richardson told the Pioneer that her elder child received second-and third-degree burns to about 40% of his body, and her younger child received burns to about 10% of his body and a broken wrist. Both received lacerations.

“I have a concussion and not a lot of memory,” Richardson said. “But from what I’ve gathered … my 12-year-old boy wanted a late-night snack, and he went in to start the oven and cook a frozen pizza, and when he turned on the oven, it blew up the entire house.”

Richardson, who was asleep at the time of the explosion, said that based on conversations with the fire marshal, there was likely natural gas leaking in the house, which contributed to the explosion.

She said that her first memory after the explosion is waking up being tended by her neighbors.

“We love our neighbors for the help they provided us that night,” Richardson said. “Most of the town was there and everybody was amazing.”

Alzada has a population of about 17 residents.

Richardson said that she expects to spend at least the next 3 weeks in the hospital with her children. After that, they hope to return to Montana and buy land.

She said that the cost of a prolonged hospital stay, as well as several ambulance rides and two helicopter rides to the Colorado hospital was “going to be expensive,” but that she didn’t know the exact cost.

An account at First Interstate Bank was established for donations to the Richardsons under the name Lenee Richardson & Family.

Keith Kober, a state fire marshal, said the Alzada incident remains under investigation, but that he did not suspect foul play.

This wasn’t the first time Richardson’s home at Southside Trailer Park was destroyed. Her previous home in Belle Fourche burned down July 17, 2025 while she and her 2 children were inside. Ryan Cherveney, Belle Fourche police chief, said the Belle Fourche Fire Department was not able to determine the cause of the fire, but that there was “nothing of suspicion.”

title: Lead pays more than $100K for 150th celebration concert: expenses offset with sponsorships, anticipated ticket sales
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: LEAD — A rock music festival at Lead’s Mountain Top Field will cost the city about $100,000, but much of those costs will be offset with sponsorships and ticket sales, city officials say.
_full_text:
LEAD — A rock music festival at Lead’s Mountain Top Field will cost the city about $100,000, but much of those costs will be offset with sponsorships and ticket sales, city officials say.

Lead City Administrator Robin Lucero said so far the city has paid more than $60,000 toward the Rock the Hills concert, which will be held as part of the Fourth of July festivities, to mark Lead’s 150th anniversary. Final balances for the event are due either before, or shortly after the July 3 event.

City funds to pay for the event come from the third-penny sales tax, or “bed and booze” tax. That tax is restricted by state law, and can only be used to promote the city and for special events. The funds cannot be used for normal city activities or infrastructure maintenance and repair.

The majority of costs for the event, $56,000, come from Kentucky-based Studio 46, a production company that will bring the 40-foot stage, lights, and sound equipment for the concerts. That bill was paid in full when the city commission approved the bill list at their June 1 meeting, with a line item for Vandemark Productions.

Since the stage setup will be brought in with a semi-truck and trailer, Lucero said the city rented mats to protect the track and field at Mountain Top. Those mats, she said, will cost the city about $7,000.

The city is also paying about $22,000 for the Lexington Lab Band, a classic rock cover band based in Kentucky, that plays hits from the 1970s. So far, Lucero said, the city has paid $6,000 toward that cost, with the balance due when the band arrives for the July 3 performance.

Since the city is paying so much for the production company, Lucero said the event planning committee, which consists of city representatives, Lead business representatives, Lead Area Chamber of Commerce officials, and other volunteers, decided to hire 3 more bands, to create a day-long concert event. Those bands, she said, will cost the city about $4,600.

Security for the event will be contracted out to Badlands Security, for a total cost of about $5,000. Lucero said that company will handle issuing wristbands to distinguish ages for alcohol sales and to allow concert attendees to leave and return to the venue. They will also provide traffic control for the parade and the fireworks on July 4.

Portable restrooms to accommodate the anticipated 2,000 people at the concert will cost the city about $3,000 for 11 toilets — 10 that will be at Mountain Top, and 1 that will be at the Terry Peak parking lot. The restrooms will include basic porta potties, as well as flush toilets with sinks that will be available for VIP ticket holders. The flush toilets will only be available for the July 3 concerts, but the other portable toilets will be available for use throughout the weekend for the All School Reunion, community picnic, and the vintage baseball game.

Ro Sham Bo, of Rapid City, is handling marketing for the event, but Lucero said most of their services are paid with an $8,000 Tourism Advertising Promotion (TAP) grant from the South Dakota Department of Tourism. The city did pay for a website to market merchandise for the event, at a cost of $5,266.

In an effort to provide ample parking for concert attendees, Lucero said the city of Lead will pay Deadwood $391 for use of its trolley to transport concert ticket holders from the Sherman Street lot in Deadwood to Mountain Top Field. The Lead-Deadwood School District will also provide buses to transport attendees from the lower level parking lot at Terry Peak, to Mountain Top and to the Manuel Brothers Park. Lucero said the city will pay the school for the busses after the school calculates their bus driver rate and mileage.

In order to pay for everything, Lucero said the city allocated $50,000 out of its third-penny sales tax, also known as the “bed and booze” fund, in its 2026 budget. The “bed and booze” funds are taxes on lodging, restaurant purchases, event ticket sales, and alcohol sales, that can only be used on special events and marketing for the city. The city has also received $55,735 in cash sponsorships.

Ticket sales, Lucero said, will be $30 for general admission and $50 for VIP ticket holders. The city’s goal, she said, is to sell 1,500 general admission tickets, and 500 VIP tickets — which would generate $70,000 for the city.

In addition to ticket sales, Lucero said the city expects to earn profits from beer and beverage sales at the Mountain Top Field event. For beverage sales, the city paid $800 to rent an ice trailer, with ice that will also be sold to vendors.

Lucero said the city can also generate revenue from merchandise sales of T-shirts, hats, and stickers, which are being sold on the event website.

Following the July 3 event, Lucero said she plans to give a public presentation with the full financial accounting of the Rock the Hills event.

“The production has been paid for. The bands will receive their check on July 3, and the other vendors/companies will send us their invoice after the event,” she said.
