title: Belle Fourche to consider updating ordinance on ADUs
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: BELLE FOURCHE — Accessory dwelling units (ADU)s can help to expand a municipality’s housing inventory, but that's not necessarily why Belle Fourche is updating its ordinances that address them.
_full_text:
BELLE FOURCHE — Accessory dwelling units (ADU)s can help to expand a municipality’s housing inventory, but that's not necessarily why Belle Fourche is updating its ordinances that address them.

“At this time, Belle Fourche does not have a large number of accessory dwelling units, so I would not characterize them as a major housing source within the community. The purpose of these amendments was not to expand or restrict housing opportunities, but rather to better define how ADUs may be used and to distinguish between units intended as rental housing and those intended primarily as guest accommodations,” Belle Fourche City Administrator Jason LaFayette said. “There was nothing particularly unusual or pressing that drove these revisions. They were simply the result of reviewing existing regulations, identifying opportunities for clarification, and making adjustments that will improve administration of the ordinance moving forward.”

Mother-in-law units and their free-standing secondary dwellings on residential property can count as ADUs. So can apartments or rentable units that are attached to an existing home.

Belle Fourche already allows ADUs and has established standards for the housing option.

“The revisions are largely intended to clean up language within the ordinance and make it easier to interpret and administer,” LaFayette said. “We have developments within the city limits where accessory dwelling units are allowed, but in some instances, those units were intended to function as guest houses for family members rather than as rental properties. The revisions help clarify those distinctions and improve consistency within our zoning regulations.”The current law requires property owners to live in either the primary housing unit or an ADU on a residential property for at least 6 months out of the calendar year in order to make use of a secondary dwelling.

On Monday, the city council will consider the second reading of an amendment to its ordinance that will remove that regulation.

The amendment removes the mention of ADUs as an “affordable” housing option and includes guests as well as tenants as clearly allowed occupants for ADUs in the ordinance.

The ordinance the council heard on first reading last week also expands the allowed size of an ADU.

The ordinance currently states, “The finished area of the ADU shall be no larger than 75% of the total ground floor area of the primary unit.”

The proposed amendment would allow ADUs to be no larger than the “allowed lot coverage maximum percentage of the lot’s designated zoning district.”

title: Meade County looks for public comment on sales tax ordinance
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Meade County came one step closer to implementing a sales tax, Tuesday, with nobody from the public appearing to support or oppose the action.
_full_text:
STURGIS — Meade County came one step closer to implementing a sales tax, Tuesday, with nobody from the public appearing to support or oppose the action.

During their regular meeting, Meade County commissioners held the public hearing for the first reading of their ordinance that would institute a half percent sales tax on all goods sold throughout the county. The sales tax receipts will be used to offset property tax levies on owner-occupied structures in the county.

Previously counties in South Dakota did not have the power to institute a sales tax. During the legislative session this year, lawmakers passed Senate Bill 96, which allows counties to enact a sales tax of up to a half penny on all goods and services sold within the county. Revenue generated from those sales taxes must be used to offset property taxes for owner-occupied structures. Once the revenue collected reaches 100% of the county property tax levy for owner occupied structures, any additional revenue is split evenly, to provide property tax relief for nonagricultural and agricultural properties.

According to figures from the South Dakota Department of Revenue, with $423,158,072 in total taxable sales in urban areas, and $360,087,199 in rural taxable sales last year, Meade County’s half-percent sales tax would generate about $3.9 million in revenue, which is 56% of the county’s owner-occupied property tax receipts. Meade County has a total of $2.2 billion in taxable valuation.

The next time the commission is scheduled to discuss the sales tax ordinance is during their regular meeting, July 7. If the ordinance passes and if it is not referred to a vote, the sales tax would go into effect Jan. 1, 2027. That’s because, according to S.D. Department of Revenue regulations, new sales taxes can only be enacted on July 1 or Jan. 1.

Since the tax cannot be implemented until next year, property tax payers will not see an impact on their taxes until the 2027 assessment, for taxes payable in 2028.

Deputy States Attorney Ken Chleborad explained how the tax would be applied. He said the levy for all properties in the county will stay the same. Then, at the end of the year, the county will reduce the levy for owner occupied structures proportionately to how much sales tax is generated.

“You will get a line that says ‘here’s your tax bill at the original levy, less the discount,’” Chleborad said. “It’ll be a savings line and then the amount you pay line. It’s reducing the levy specific.”

Commissioners cautioned taxpayers that if the sales tax passes, they will not see a drastic change in their property tax bills. That’s because there will still be school, municipal, and other miscellaneous tax levies such as road and ambulance districts applied, depending on where the property is located. Deering said county residents will see savings on about 6% of their total tax bill.

Commission Chairman Gary Deering asked for wording to be changed in the first line of the ordinance, which states the purpose of the tax is to provide additional revenue for the county.

“It’s not to provide revenue to the county,” he said. “It’s a tax break. I don’t want people thinking this is additional revenue for the county.”

Commissioners said many rural counties are not implementing the sales tax, because the same residents who get the property tax discounts are paying into the property tax relief fund with goods they purchase locally.

But in Meade County, commissioners said, the hundreds of thousands of visitors who come for the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally can pay into that sales tax fund and help relieve the extra costs of the world-famous event. Commissioner Doreen Creed said recently Meade County Sheriff Pat West reported he budgets about $260,000 for overtime wages costs for the 10 days of the Rally, and that doesn’t include the extra costs for temporary personnel, jail staff, and more.

“If we didn’t have the Rally, this would be a tough decision,” said Commissioner Talbot Wieczorek. “During the Rally we have to add a ton of staff, and there is a lto of cost. Even if it’s only a couple hundred bucks a house, it pays for the extra cost of the Rally. I’m not a pro-tax guy. But this tax for people in Meade County will allow us to at least have some of these costs paid. The Rally is still not going to cover itself, but it is something.”

“If it was not for the Rally, I wouldn’t even be considering this,” Creed said.

But Meade County commissioners expressed concern that there were no public comments offered during the first reading and discussion of the sales tax ordinance, despite offering the opportunity for public comment.

“I haven’t had one person, and I hear from a lot of people, give me their opinion on this tax,” Creed said. “I really would hope that at least for the second reading we would get some input.”

title: Music on Main, K4 Race Series and Sturgis Volunteer Fire Department draw large midweek crowd
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Week 3 of the Sturgis Music on Main and K4 Race Series brought another large crowd to downtown Sturgis on Wednesday evening, combining live music, mountain bike racing, local vendors and family-friendly activities hosted by the Sturgis Volunteer Fire Department.
_full_text:
STURGIS — Week 3 of the Sturgis Music on Main and K4 Race Series brought another large crowd to downtown Sturgis on Wednesday evening, combining live music, mountain bike racing, local vendors and family-friendly activities hosted by the Sturgis Volunteer Fire Department.

The event at Harley-Davidson Rally Point featured Sioux Falls-based rock band Minority Falls, which entertained the crowd with hits spanning several decades while mountain bikers competed on a challenging 9-mile racecourse, up lower and upper Deadman.

Children and families were also drawn to interactive activities hosted by the Sturgis Volunteer Fire Department, where firefighters gave youngsters the opportunity to operate fire hoses and participate in games designed to showcase firefighting skills.

Veronica Grosek, executive director of the Sturgis Area Chamber of Commerce, said the weekly event continues to grow while offering something new for visitors each week.

"Tonight we had a 9-mile racecourse and something special with the Sturgis Fire Department," Grosek said. "The Sturgis Volunteer Firefighters brought their Rosenbauer fire trucks and organized games for the kids. It gave families an opportunity to learn more about what firefighters do, while also helping with recruitment and community outreach."

The Sturgis Volunteer Fire Department used the event as an opportunity to educate the public about volunteer firefighting while giving children a hands-on experience.

"We're here promoting opportunities to join the fire department and giving kids a chance to spray water from a fire hose, which isn't something they get to do every day," firefighter Reed Beldin said.

The department set up two interactive challenges, including the "Junior Firefighter Knockdown Challenge," where younger children used water hoses to knock balls off cones. Older participants tested their aim by spraying a soccer ball into a goal.

"We would have loved for it to be a little warmer so we could have incorporated more water activities," Beldin said. "Maybe that's something we'll be able to do at a future event."

Beldin thanked the Sturgis Area Chamber of Commerce for helping coordinate the activities and highlighted Rosenbauer, whose fire engines are the Official Fire Truck of Sturgis.

The volunteer department currently has approximately 42 members representing a wide range of professions.

"We have ranchers, massage therapists, mechanics, business owners and office workers," Beldin said. "Every one of us is 100 percent volunteer."

While the department is fortunate to receive mutual aid support from neighboring agencies, including Whitewood, Belle Fourche and Vale, Beldin said additional volunteers are always needed.

Grosek said Minority Falls provided the evening's entertainment with a mix of classic and modern rock favorites.

Looking ahead, Grosek said next week's event will feature an expanded Independence Day celebration.

"We'll have Rowan Grace, who became well known as a finalist on The Voice, performing on stage," Grosek said.

"In a volunteer fire department, you're never really fully staffed," he said. "If someone is out of town or unavailable, that's one less firefighter who can respond. We're always looking for people who want to serve their community."

With live music, competitive racing, community organizations and family activities all taking place in the heart of downtown, Music on Main continues to be one of Sturgis' most popular summer attractions.

title: Sturgis voters to vote at HS for runoff election
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Rally activities mean that some voters in Meade County will have to switch polling places for the gubernatorial runoff election, July 28.
_full_text:
STURGIS — Rally activities mean that some voters in Meade County will have to switch polling places for the gubernatorial runoff election, July 28.

Voters who would ordinarily cast their ballots at the Sturgis Community Center will be voting at Sturgis Brown High School for the runoff election that will be held to decide South Dakota’s Republican candidate for governor. On July 28, Gov. Larry Rhoden and Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden, who both received the most votes in a 4-person race, but neither of which received at least 35% of the votes, will face each other in the runoff election.

Meade County Auditor Dawn Christenson said the Sturgis Community Center has prior commitments, and it will be physically impossible to host the election at that location. The city of Sturgis rents vendor spaces up to 2 weeks before the Rally at the community center, and the parking lot is only open to motorcycles and vendor traffic.

Precincts that are affected by the change include East Sturgis 1, Fort Meade 1A, Northeast Sturgis 1-A, Southeast Sturgis 2, South Sturgis 2A, Central Sturgis 3, West Sturgis 4, Southwest Sturgis 4A, Northwest Sturgis 5, Sturgis 5A, Tilford 6, Rural Sturgis 7, Harmony 8, and Bear Butte 9.

Christenson said the voter registration deadline for the runoff election is July 13. At 9 a.m., July 21, the auditor’s office will have a tabulator test that is open to the public, and July 27 is the last day to cast an absentee ballot at the auditor’s office.

title: Greater Sturgis LifeCare Foundation helps refresh entrance at Sturgis  long-term care facility
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: Board members of the Greater Sturgis LifeCare Foundation and the Monument Health employees check out the newly refreshed entrance to the Monument Health Long Term Care facility on Friday in Sturgis. From left:  Cindy Spencer, Jeff DeKraai, Gary Hopkins, Eric Swanson, Paul Bisson, Mallory Strang, Mark Schmidt, and Brenda Sabers. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
Greater Sturgis LifeCare Foundation helps refresh entrance at Sturgis long-term care facility.JPG
Board members of the Greater Sturgis LifeCare Foundation and the Monument Health employees check out the newly refreshed entrance to the Monument Health Long Term Care facility on Friday in Sturgis. From left:  Cindy Spencer, Jeff DeKraai, Gary Hopkins, Eric Swanson, Paul Bisson, Mallory Strang, Mark Schmidt, and Brenda Sabers. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

STURGIS — Residents, visitors and staff at the Monument Health Sturgis Long-Term Care Facility are being welcomed by a refreshed and more inviting entrance thanks to financial support from the Greater Sturgis LifeCare Foundation.  

Representatives of the foundation toured the completed project Friday and viewed the improvements made to the facility’s entryway, which was designed to create a warmer and more welcoming first impression for residents, families and guests.

Eric Swanson, president of the Greater Sturgis LifeCare Foundation, said the organization was pleased to partner with Monument Health on a project that enhances the experience of those who visit and live at the facility.  

“On behalf of the Greater Sturgis LifeCare Foundation, we were pleased to provide financial assistance to help refresh the entrance to the Monument Health Sturgis Long-Term Care Facility,” Swanson said. “The transformation has made a tremendous improvement to the appearance of the facility and creates a more welcoming environment for residents, their families and visitors. Projects like this reflect our mission of supporting quality health care and senior care services in the Sturgis community, and we are proud to help make a positive difference in the lives of those who call the facility home.”

Mark Schmidt, president of the Monument Health Sturgis Market, said the foundation has been an invaluable partner in helping create a more welcoming and healing environment for residents and their families.  

“The GSLCF has long been a caring partner in our mission at Monument Health to make a difference every day,” Schmidt said. “We are so appreciative of their financial support. Their generosity allows us to add additional projects and further our goal to create healing environments for all community members. We also benefit from the Foundation members’ ideas and feedback, which brings valuable perspectives and experiences to consider in our plans.”

The Greater Sturgis LifeCare Foundation is a nonprofit organization dedicated to supporting and promoting health care and senior care throughout the greater Sturgis area. Since its formation in April 2004, the foundation has provided more than $1.2 million in grants and loans to local health care and senior care initiatives.  A

s a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization, the foundation relies on community support and charitable donations to continue funding projects that enhance health care services and improve the quality of life for area residents.

Foundation leaders said projects such as the long-term care facility entrance renovation demonstrate the organization’s ongoing commitment to investing in the health and well-being of the Sturgis community.

title: Fort Meade’s role in establishing the National Anthem
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Today, “The Star Spangled Banner” is the United States’ national anthem. But the song played today at parades and baseball games is the product of a long history, beginning during the War of 1812. What most people don’t know is that the anthem’s long history also winds through Fort Meade, in Sturgis, Jessica Kusser, the director of Fort Meade Museum, said.
_full_text:
STURGIS — Today, “The Star Spangled Banner” is the United States’ national anthem. But the song played today at parades and baseball games is the product of a long history, beginning during the War of 1812. What most people don’t know is that the anthem’s long history also winds through Fort Meade, in Sturgis, Jessica Kusser, the director of Fort Meade Museum, said.

Kusser said the words to what is now the national anthem were written during the War of 1812, the lesser-known conflict between Great Britain, their Native American allies, and the United States. In 1814, Francis Scott Key, a lawyer who later served as the district attorney for Washington, D.C, was being held captive aboard a British ship. Key was there to secure the release of another American prisoner of war, but was detained by the British because they believed he had overheard their plans to assault Baltimore. 

As the British bombarded Fort McHenry, Key struggled to make out who was winning. But he knew that if the British succeeded in their assault they would replace the American flag with the British flag, according to an article in Cooperative Connections. So every time that he saw the American flag illuminated by the “rockets’ red glare,” he also knew that the British were still unsuccessful. 

“The poem was actually titled “Defense of Fort M’Henry,” Kusser said. “But then it became the Star Spangled Banner.” 

According to the Fort Meade website, in the intervening time, Fort Meade was established. The United States had signed a treaty setting aside the Black Hills for the Lakota. However, after gold was discovered, many American prospectors illegally entered the area, and demanded that the U.S. Army establish a presence there. The fort was established to do just that.

In 1892, Col. Caleb Carlton was the officer in command of Fort Meade. He, with the advice of his wife, began the custom of playing the song every night as the American flag was removed from the pole. 

“For 66 years, Fort Meade was a peacekeeping post, and we’re still here as a Veterans Administration complex,”  Kusser said. 

A plaque at Fort Meade Museum claims that the Governor of Pennsylvania, Daniel Hastings, promised to require the anthem’s playing among the state’s militia, and that Secretary of War, Daniel Lamont, ordered the song be played at evening retreats nationally. 

The Department of War, not to be confused with the current, unofficial name for the Department of Defense, was created in 1789 and abolished in 1947.

Some 40 years later, in 1931, the song was established as the national anthem. 

The flagpole where Col Carlton first played the national anthem still stands at Fort Meade museum, and is open to visitors.

title: BH Renaissance Festival draws record crowds with medieval magic, jousting and family fun
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — The sixth annual Black Hills Renaissance Festival drew record crowds to the Kickstand Campground near Sturgis over the weekend, as thousands of visitors stepped into a world of knights, dragons, music, artisan vendors and live entertainment.
_full_text:
STURGIS — The sixth annual Black Hills Renaissance Festival drew record crowds to the Kickstand Campground near Sturgis over the weekend, as thousands of visitors stepped into a world of knights, dragons, music, artisan vendors and live entertainment.  

Festival founder and co-owner Shareece Tatum said the event has grown dramatically since its humble beginnings.

“When we first started, it was a contracted event in Lead and just a one-day festival in the park,” Tatum said. “We had roughly 1,500 people that first year. This year we’re a full 2-day festival, and on Saturday alone we welcomed more than 4,700 people. We were already breaking last year’s attendance records before Sunday even got underway.”

The festival featured more than 80 vendors, 20 performing groups and entertainment throughout the grounds, giving visitors plenty to see and experience.

Among the most popular attractions was the full-contact jousting presented by the Order of Epona, where armored knights charged down the arena before enthusiastic crowds. Sword fighting, medieval games and contests for the festival’s golden trophy kept spectators cheering throughout the day.

Tatum said selecting a favorite attraction is nearly impossible. “I can’t pick favorites,” she said with a laugh. “It’s like asking a parent to choose their favorite child.”

She noted that returning crowd favorites included Aluma the Littlest Dragon, whose fire-breathing performances captivated audiences, and Kazamir the Hungry, known for sword swallowing, fire eating and other sideshow feats. New attractions included Counter Song, performing fantasy and Dungeons & Dragons-inspired tavern music, as well as interactive adventures from Mystic Mercenary. Festival characters, mermaids and roaming performers added to the immersive atmosphere.

Tatum said the wooded setting at Kickstand Campground helped transform the festival into what feels like a medieval village.

“The layout this year is much more immersive because it’s in the trees,” she said. “People really feel like they’ve stepped into another world.”

She expects the festival to return to the same location next year. “We love being at Kickstands, and we’re planning to come back as long as they’ll have us,” Tatum said. “Our goal is to fine-tune the little things, expand where we can and continue growing the festival.”

For Tatum, the Renaissance Festival is about much more than costumes and entertainment.

“I’ve always been a geek and a theater nerd,” she said. “When I was 18, I discovered Renaissance festivals and always dreamed of bringing one to the Black Hills. It finally happened, and now people can forget about the real world for a little while. Whether you’re a child or an adult, everyone needs a little hope and magic.”

Beyond the entertainment, Tatum said the festival provides an important economic boost for local artists, craftsmen and small businesses.

“For many of our vendors, this is one of their biggest events of the year and a significant part of their annual income,” she said. “Supporting this festival also supports local artisans and small businesses throughout the region.”

Visitors spent the weekend browsing handcrafted goods, watching demonstrations such as blacksmithing and foraging, enjoying food vendors and taking in stage performances while soaking up the medieval atmosphere.

One of the festival’s most talked-about performers was Kazamir the Hungry, whose act included lying on a bed of pointed screws while breathing a massive fireball.

Although those stunts drew gasps from the audience, Kazamir said they aren’t the most dangerous part of his performance.

“By far, sword swallowing is the most dangerous thing I do,” he said. “There are only a few dozen performers in the world who do it because it’s so difficult and dangerous.”

Kazamir said he began performing fire acts about 25 years ago while working Renaissance festivals before learning additional skills from fellow performers.

“I kind of fell in with a bunch of carnies,” he joked. “When you’re hanging around a campground full of crazy performers, you end up learning a few things.”

Although he now lives in the Twin Cities, Kazamir said returning to western South Dakota is always special.

“I was actually born in South Dakota, and I have family in the Black Hills,” he said. “This is gorgeous country. I always enjoy coming back.”

With record attendance, expanding entertainment and growing vendor participation, organizers believe the Black Hills Renaissance Festival has become one of the region’s signature summer events, offering visitors of all ages a chance to escape into a magical world of medieval adventure.

title: Belle Fourche Public Library makes  shelf space for your recommendations
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
BF Library shelf expansion 1.JPG
Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

 BF Library shelf expansion.JPG
Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

BELLE FOURCHE — Summer reading is going splendidly in Belle Fourche, according to the librarians at the public library. More than 62,344 minutes of reading time have been logged by participants using the ReaderZone ap; 152 library patrons are using paper logs to track their time.

Harnessing that momentum and engagement, Library Director Joshua Abraham is shining a light on a new-to-Belle-Fourche feature that allows patrons to ask for the titles they want to see in their library.

The library uses a system called “OPEC” to manage its online catalogue.

“People can search through OPEC,” Abraham said. “There is a spot that allows them (readers) to request a book and provide reasoning as to why they were wanting the book and things like that, to give us kind of an idea of what our patrons are looking for or interested in.”

There may also be additional shelf space for patron requests in the near future.

“The children’s section is always really well used in the summer, but we have been running out of room and just using what we have, so we are wanting to expand our shelving in the children’s section. Eventually we will be expanding our adult fiction section as well,” Abraham said. “With a lot of the picture books, they are very thin. They are very easy to overlook. Having an opportunity to have some of those be more easily seen will hopefully increase the number of books that go out.”

Eventually, Abraham has plans to expand shelving in the adult fiction section as well.

title: State’s top election official loses nomination to challenger who supports hand-counting
byline: By Seth Tupper Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: RAPID CITY — Delegates at the South Dakota Republican Convention denied the state’s top election official an opportunity to seek reelection, choosing a nominee Saturday for secretary of state who advocates for hand-counted election results.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

RAPID CITY — Delegates at the South Dakota Republican Convention denied the state’s top election official an opportunity to seek reelection, choosing a nominee Saturday for secretary of state who advocates for hand-counted election results.

Heather Baxter received 59% support in the convention hall at The Monument events center to beat incumbent Monae Johnson. The nomination was one of six decided by about 700 delegates from across the state during the convention’s third and final day.

Baxter’s campaign website says she wants to “ensure every vote is counted accurately via paper ballots that are hand counted.” She received some of the day’s loudest applause when she finished her speech to the convention.

“I know you guys are not looking for someone to impress you. You’re looking for someone you can trust,” Baxter said. “I will not make promises I cannot keep, and I will not flinch when the right answer is the hard one.”

The loss was a turnabout for Johnson, who was a challenger when she beat an incumbent, Steve Barnett, at the 2022 convention.

Johnson won that earlier nomination with the support of activists who denied the legitimacy of President Joe Biden’s victory in the 2020 election and called for changes in election procedures, such as switching from electronic tabulating machines to hand-counting. Since Johnson’s election, some of those activists have grown dissatisfied with her for not delivering changes they sought.

One new procedure Johnson did implement with the support of the Legislature is mandatory post-election audits in all of the state’s counties. She said during her speech that the audits have proven tabulating machines to be accurate.

“I trust the county auditors to do their jobs,” Johnson said, “and I fully support the use of secure, tested ballot tabulators.”

Johnson, of Pierre, will continue serving as secretary of state until her term ends in January.

Baxter, of Rapid City, will advance to face two opponents in the Nov. 3 general election: Democratic nominee Terrence Davis and Libertarian nominee Tamara Lesnar.

Baxter has been serving as a state representative for the past 2 years, but lost a primary race on June 2 and shifted her focus to the secretary of state race. She is a small-business owner from a well-known family in the Black Hills, where her late grandfather Korczak Ziolkowski started the Crazy Horse mountain carving.

Attorney general

Lance Russell, the state’s attorney of Fall River and Oglala Lakota counties, won a 3-way contest for the attorney general nomination that took 2 rounds of voting to decide. Russell will be unopposed in the general election, because Democrats failed to field a candidate and there are no third-party or independent candidates.

None of the three Republican hopefuls topped 50% in the first round of voting. Russell then reached 57% in the second round to beat Austin Hoffman’s 31% and John Fitzgerald’s 12%.

Hoffman is the McPherson County state’s attorney, and Fitzgerald is a former judge and former state’s attorney of Butte and Lawrence counties.

The state’s top law enforcement job is opening up because Republican Attorney General Marty Jackley won the party’s nomination in the June 2 primary election to run for U.S. House. The U.S. House seat is open because Republican Rep. Dusty Johnson unsuccessfully sought the party’s nomination for governor in the June 2 primary.

Commissioner of school and public lands

Incumbent Brock Greenfield, of Pierre, won his nomination with 81% support and will seek reelection as commissioner of school and public lands. He was challenged by James Bialota, a veteran and business owner from Piedmont.

Greenfield will face Democratic nominee Raeann Mettler in the general election.

The Office of School and Public Lands generates revenue for public education by leasing state-owned land for livestock grazing and leasing state-owned mineral rights for mining.

State auditor

Catherine Barranco won the auditor nomination with 53% support in the first round of voting against opponents Tamara Grove and Renae Randall.

Grove is a state senator from Lower Brule who lost her primary race on June 2. Randall is a former employee of the South Dakota Investment Council.

Barranco, of Sioux Falls, formerly worked for the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission investigating financial fraud.

The duties of the Auditor’s Office include auditing state accounts, administering the state payroll, monitoring fund balances and transfers, and filing financial reports. Incumbent Republican Auditor Rich Sattgast is term-limited and has endorsed Barranco.

In the general election, Barranco will face Democratic nominee Tom Cool, of Sioux Falls.

State treasurer

Melissa Hull, an employee of the Treasurer’s Office, won 81% of the votes to win the treasurer nomination over Heath Shields, a businessman from Custer.

The current state treasurer, Republican Josh Haeder, is term-limited and has endorsed Hull.

The Treasurer’s Office is the receiver and custodian of state fund transfers and deposits, and manages banking for the state. It also receives unclaimed private property, such as abandoned bank accounts, and works to return the property to its owners.

Hull will face Democratic nominee Margaret Kuipers of Sioux Falls in the general election.

Public Utilities Commission

Peri Pourier, who’s been a Republican less than a year after leaving the Democratic Party in September, received 45% support but came up short against longtime Republican Don Haggar, who received 55% to win the nomination for a seat on the Public Utilities Commission.

Pourier is a term-limited state representative from Pine Ridge. Haggar, of Sioux Falls, is a former legislator and former state director of Americans for Prosperity. He has a background in real estate, banking and insurance.

Haggar will face Democratic nominee Frank Kloucek in the general election. They are seeking the Public Utilities Commission seat being vacated by Republican Commissioner Gary Hanson, who is not seeking reelection.

The commission’s duties include regulating electric, gas and telephone utilities, and considering permits for power plants, pipelines and related projects.

title: Republican governor candidates spar over  prison policy in dueling speeches
byline: By Seth Tupper Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: RAPID CITY — The 2 remaining Republican candidates for governor of South Dakota clashed over prison policy Friday night in what might have been the closest thing to a debate that voters will see before the party’s nomination is decided in a July 28 runoff election.
_full_text:
RAPID CITY — The 2 remaining Republican candidates for governor of South Dakota clashed over prison policy Friday night in what might have been the closest thing to a debate that voters will see before the party’s nomination is decided in a July 28 runoff election.

The candidates delivered back-to-back speeches to a crowd of hundreds during the Republican state convention at The Monument events center.

Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden said too many people in South Dakota return to prison after being released.

“Our recidivism rate has peaked at 50% — third worst in the country,” Doeden said. “We have a higher recidivism rate than almost every liberal state in the country.”

The 50% figure comes from the state Department of Corrections’ latest annual report, which says half of the people released from prison in South Dakota return within 3 years of their release.

Where South Dakota ranks nationally is difficult to ascertain due to differences in the ways that states define recidivism. Gov. Larry Rhoden has acknowledged the rate is “higher than any of our neighboring states.”

Rhoden responded to Doeden’s criticism, saying “he’s right: our recidivism rate is way too high.”

“And why is that? Because we have no room,” Rhoden said. “We have three prisoners stacked in rooms that are built for one. We have no room for programming.”

Rhoden said he’s solving that problem with a new men’s prison he convinced legislators to build. The $650 million facility, which is under construction in northeast Sioux Falls, will be funded without debt due to money lawmakers set aside for several years before approving the project in September. It will replace the oldest parts of the state’s 145-year-old Sioux Falls penitentiary.

Rhoden said he got the project approved despite dealing with lawmakers whose support was divided among the candidates for governor. There was a “Doeden camp” in the legislative prison debate, Rhoden said, and “the Dusty camp and the Hansen camp” — a reference to U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson and state House Speaker Jon Hansen, who finished third and fourth in the four-way June 2 primary race.

“All 3 of those candidates were lobbing bombs at me, because they didn’t want to see us get a win,” Rhoden said.

Neither Rhoden nor Doeden lobbed many verbal bombs in their speeches Friday, despite an ongoing feud between their campaigns about Rhoden’s refusal to debate. The two men participated in three debates with the other 2 candidates before the primary. Because nobody reached 35% in that election, the top 2 finishers — Doeden at 31% and Rhoden at 25% — advanced to a top-two runoff.

Doeden pledges to be unifying catalyst

The state Republican Party invited Doeden and Rhoden to speak at the convention and limited each of them to 15 minutes. By the flip of a coin, Doeden went first.

He spent the first part of his speech detailing what he described as the 4 principles that would guide him as governor: smaller and more efficient government, lower taxes, strong law and order, and quality educational opportunities for children.

After calling South Dakota “the greatest state in the country,” Doeden offered several critiques, including the recidivism rate. He said state government spending and taxes have increased too much, education in the state has “taken a step backwards,” and “people are living less affordable lives.”

Doeden, in his first run for elected office, pledged to be “the catalyst unifying this party to the strongest place it has been in decades.” He met several people at the convention, he said, who told him they were sorry for saying critical things about him on Facebook before the primary.

“I said it’s OK,” Doeden said. “The slate was wiped clean at midnight on June 2.”

Rhoden: ‘I’m that guy’

After Doeden finished, Rhoden began by saying that the first lady, Sandy Rhoden, is “always suggesting to me that there are things that people don’t know about me that I take for granted.” So, Rhoden used the first part of his speech to talk about serving as an elder in his church, as president of a local cooperative board, as a coach of basketball and softball, as a 6-year member of the National Guard, and as a school board member and legislator.

Rhoden was elevated from lieutenant governor in January 2025 when his predecessor, Gov. Kristi Noem, resigned to accept a job leading the federal Department of Homeland Security in President Donald Trump’s administration.

Rhoden described Noem as “the strongest person I know” and said, “she was the right person for the job at that time,” referring to the COVID-19 pandemic years.

But, Rhoden said, “when I took the reins, the water had gotten pretty choppy in our state.” The unsolved problems he inherited included what he described as the “3 P’s”: a prison, a pipeline and property taxes.

In addition to getting the prison construction project across the finish line, Rhoden brought an end — for now – to a controversial carbon-capture pipeline proposal by signing a bill into law that bans such projects from using a court process known as eminent domain to gain access to private land. He also signed several bills into law that will lower property taxes for homeowners in the coming years, although two of them rely on higher sales taxes to bring property taxes down.

“We absolutely need somebody that can bring our party together and unify people and move an agenda forward,” Rhoden said. “And I’m that guy.”

State Republican party officials allowed media coverage of the speeches after blocking media access to U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune’s convention speech Thursday night. Several apologized to South Dakota Searchlight and said it was a “misunderstanding.”

title: Spearfish embarks on ordinance cleanup effort
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — The city of Spearfish is poised to adopt new engineering and design standards, to provide consistent direction to developers, contractors, and city staff. To go along with those standards, the city’s community development department is proposing several updates to existing ordinances that relate to water, sewer, streets, and community planning. The ordinance revisions are meant to help simplify, clarify, and align city codes with new engineering and design standards, Community Development Director Peter Wysocki said.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — The city of Spearfish is poised to adopt new engineering and design standards, to provide consistent direction to developers, contractors, and city staff. To go along with those standards, the city’s community development department is proposing several updates to existing ordinances that relate to water, sewer, streets, and community planning. The ordinance revisions are meant to help simplify, clarify, and align city codes with new engineering and design standards, Community Development Director Peter Wysocki said.

“The way we have this lined up is, we have the first readings of the ordinances presented tonight, and then second reading of the ordinances and a resolution to adopt the engineering and design standards manual on the same night,” Wysocki said. “That way, we avoid any conflicts of one being adopted before the other.”

Some of the proposed revisions are simple. Department names are updated, and individual fees that may change over time are removed and referred to the city’s master fee schedule — a document that can be easily updated with regularity.

Other revisions remove technical engineering requirements that will appear in the engineering and design standards document instead.

The city council was asked to pass 7 ordinance revisions on first reading, June 15. They were all unanimously approved. On July 6, the council will hold public hearings on each ordinance, and be asked to adopt them.

Ordinance 1419: Utilities

Ordinance 1419 passed on first reading June 15, moving one step closer to amending Chapter 50 of the city’s code. This revision sets city engineering design standards (EDS) as a formal guide for utility service, and clarifies that service can be terminated if a resident refuses to allow public works department staff on their premises for the “repair of a meter or reading of device.”

Under Ordinance 1419, unpaid utility bills will go to a collection agency, rather than being assessed as a lien on property taxes. City staff also updated language to indicate that utility bills we be “sent” not mailed, to allow for updates in technology and the use of email communication.

It removes the “city auditor,” a now defunct position, from ordinance. The Water/Sewer Utilities Superintendent is now replaced with Public Works Department, and a sentence that confused the process of plan review, according to city staff, was removed.

“There was kind of a confusing sentence that said that city council reviews design plans, and that was edited to say the community development department does that, and city council approves them during the correct step in the process,” Larson said.

On the topic of extending utility lines, Chapter 50 reads, “the city shall run water or sewer lines outside the municipal lines solely at the city’s discretion.”

“That was removed and instead a sentence was added toward the end of that section saying that for certain types or utilities, certain agreements may be required,” Larson said. “That is because in the EDS we talk about how service agreements are required for utility use outside of city limits. We also referenced using engineering and design standards for the design of water and sewer systems in this chapter.”

Ordinance 1420: Water

Larson said the biggest changes made to the water section of the city’s codes are organizational.

“There is language here that was taken out of the subdivisions chapter. That is the one thing that I think has been discussed prior, about private and shared well usage. The regulations are not changing. That was, it is the same as it was in subdivisions and moved to the water chapter because it makes more sense to talk about that in the water chapter,” Larson said.

As updates go, this section adds a reference to online licensing portal instead of a “special form furnished to the city.”

Ordinance 1421: Sanitary sewer

“Similar to that water chapter, there was language about when private wastewater collection and treatment systems can be used from the subdivisions chapter,” Larson said.

This chapter makes allowances for septic systems on parcels larger than 8 acres, which reflects the current rules in the subdivision section of city ordinance.

Recently, the city discussed reducing the parcel size requirement for septic systems, especially in an area along Highway 85 north Kerwin Lane.

“We are not discussing the reduction of the 8 acres here,” Wysocki said. “Whatever number we agree upon, we will probably have a much broader ETJ discussion to make those regulations as compatible and consistent between Lawrence County and ETJ designation as possible.”

He also noted the existence of a “no-septic” overlay on the west side of Highway 85 north, which cannot be superseded by city code, even if allowances are made for smaller parcels to install septic systems.

Ordinance 1422: Parks and recreation

The Spearfish Parks and Recreation Department operates as its own, independent department. That is not reflected in the current city ordinance. The amendment would update the city’s code to reflect how the department currently operates.

“The management used to be public works, now it is under the Parks and Recreation Director. This is just clarifying that and correcting it,” Spearfish City Engineer Kyle Mathis said.

The amendment also introduces a reference to the parks and recreation master plan.

“With that inclusion, future facilities and playgrounds would be acquired, equipped, and maintained in accordance with the master plan,” Mathis said. “It is important to note that the master plan is still a policy and recommending document, it is not codified, but it will help guide in the future, when we build recreation facilities, etc.”

Ordinance 1423: Flood prevention and fire protection

On July 6, the council will be asked to repeal and replace the flood prevention section of its ordinance on second reading. That being said, there will be very little difference between the regulations that would be repealed, and the ones that may replace them.

The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) regularly updates its regulations for floodplain areas.

“FEMA has a template ordinance for South Dakota that they issue updates on,” Larson said. “The main issue here is to come into compliance with their updated template ordinance; the actual regulations really have not changed much. There are a lot of updated definitions and really just wording changes that FEMA recommended.”

Larson said the other major change in the replacement language is an allowance the city will be making to help property owners to better improve their property.

“We have a 20-year timeline on our substantial improvement requirement. The substantial improvement is a FEMA regulation where if you are going to improve a structure to greater than 50% of its value the entire structure has to be flood plain compliant,” Larson said. “Let’s say your house is worth $100,000 and you’re going to do more than $50,000 worth of work on it, then not just whatever you’re improving has to be floodplain compliant, now the whole house does. Currently, how our ordinance reads is that when you do those improvements it totals up over 20 years.”

If a property owner hits that 50% limit, they cannot make substantial improvements for the next 20 years.

“It does make it hard for people that own structures in the floodplain to keep them up to date and make improvements to them,” Larson said. “So that’s going to be reduced down from 20 years to 5 years.”

Ordinance 1424: Public ways and property

If Ordinance 1424 passes driveways, curb and gutter, street lighting, and sidewalks will have to be compliant with the new engineering and design standards.

“It also adds allowable uses of the public right of way by owners and leases of abutting properties without an encroachment agreement. This would include things like landscaping, driveways, and sidewalks as permitted by the city. It would remove church signs allowed within the public right of way,” Mathis said. “This conflicted with the city’s current right of way encroachment ordinance and some sign permitting ordinances.”

With regard to public right of ways, Wysocki said amending the city’s current ordinance is an opportunity to come into compliance with federal case law, where sign placement is concerned.

In existing city code, churches are allowed to have signs in the public right of way. This amendment changes that.

“Currently no business or anybody can have a sign in the public right of way without an encroachment agreement,” Mathis said.

“All signs have to be treated equally regardless of what the sign states. There is a limit to First Amendment rights, with obscene language and things of that nature, but we cannot treat one business or one sign differently than another,” Wysocki added. “So if we allowed church signs in the right of way, we would also need to allow regular signs for commercial uses in the right of way.”

Ordinance 1425: Subdivisions

Much like the floodplain regulations, this proposed ordinance will repeal and replace current language.

“This one did include some pretty substantial changes,” Assistant Planning Director Jaymia Ecker said, saying that most of the section needed to be reorganized to move technical details to the EDS.

“We are reorganizing this for clarity. I want to note that the procedure here (for subdividing and plat review) hasn’t changed. The number of public meetings, the number of public hearings that are required for a subdivision, the ability for staff to approve sketch plats administratively and certain final plats, all of that is staying the same here, but it does remove all of those design standards which now will live in EDS,” Ecker said.

Kids get to hose down a house that was set on fire as part of a training exercise.  

 Fire 4.jpeg
A fire was ignited at the residence on Gold Street in Spearfish Saturday for training purposes. 

SPEARFISH — The Spearfish and Whitewood fire departments set fire to a residence at Gold Street in Spearfish for training purposes around 8 a.m. Saturday.

Firefighters used paper and other wood products, along with a propane torch, to ignite fires in individual rooms before extinguishing them.

The fire was held so Spearfish and Whitewood trainee firefighters could get experience fighting a real fire.

“One of the last steps they (trainees) are required to complete is a live fire training, and we were able to get a donated structure to do it in the real world,” Brain Ziegler, Spearfish deputy fire chief, said. 

After containing the fire to individual rooms, the entire house was burned. Ziegler said that about 27 members of the fire department were involved in the training fire. He said that 5 Spearfish and 2 Whitewood trainees will be able to earn their certification as a result of participating in the fire. 

The fire was fully extinguished around 3 p.m. Saturday.

title: Opposition arises to rebuild of  US 85 through the Black Hills
byline: By Bart Pfankuch South Dakota News Watch
description: This photo by renowned landscape photographer Paul Horsted shows the combination of majestic rocky ridge lines and pristine Spearfish Creek that flank U.S., 85 in the northern Black Hills of South Dakota. Photo courtesy of Paul Horsted
_full_text:
Opposition arises to rebuild of  US 85 through the Black Hills
This photo by renowned landscape photographer Paul Horsted shows the combination of majestic rocky ridge lines and pristine Spearfish Creek that flank U.S., 85 in the northern Black Hills of South Dakota. Photo courtesy of Paul Horsted 

CHEYENNE CROSSING — Colorado tourists Kay and Dan Rider made a conscious decision to avoid interstates and busy highways on their way to a family vacation in western South Dakota.

The decision to take the scenic route led them to a stretch of U.S. Highway 85 in the northern Black Hills on Thursday that would eventually take them through the Lead-Deadwood area on their way to Rapid City.

The couple stopped briefly to take a break in one of the many pull-offs that straddle the highway. The small parking areas provide motorists with a spot to soak in the beauty of the majestic pines and rocky ridges that frame the highway or to find calm in the gentle babble of Spearfish Creek that flows a few feet from the travel lanes in some areas.

“We’ve just been talking about how beautiful the drive is and what great shape the road is in,” Kay Rider said of the highway.

The Riders were surprised to learn that the state of South Dakota has plans in 2030 for a major reconstruction of that 16-mile stretch of U.S. 85 from the Wyoming border on the west to its intersection with U.S. 14A at Cheyenne Crossing on the east.

The couple said it didn’t make sense to them that the Department of Transportation would do anything that could alter the aesthetics of the highway.

“If I was paying taxes in South Dakota and that money was going to this project, I would be highly upset,” Dan Rider said.

That sentiment is shared by more than a few residents and business owners in the Black Hills region.

“The scenery and the stream on one side of the road and the cliffs on the other side – there’s nothing that can match that,” said Paul Horsted, a renowned nature and landscape photographer from Custer who is opposed to the current plans to redo U.S. 85.

Horsted said he and others are worried that the DOT could take the same approach to rebuilding U.S. 85 as it has with the ongoing project to reconstruct U.S. 385, another scenic road through the Black Hills.

That 3-year, $72 million project that will conclude in 2027 is bringing wider lanes, extended road shoulders and fewer curves to the north-south highway between Deadwood and Hill City. To improve safety, the DOT has made more room for the highway by clearing trees, blasting rock and scraping away ridges.

DOT data show that U.S. 85 is in poor condition, has 20 curves with reduced speed limits and is marred by eroded roadway edges.

The preliminary $47 million plan is to resurface the roadway and widen traffic lanes from 11 feet to 12 feet in most areas and add 4-foot to 6-foot paved shoulders where ditches, rocky outcrops or the banks of Spearfish Creek mostly exist now.

The 16-mile stretch of 2-lane highway had 140 crashes with three fatalities and 56 injuries reported during the decade from 2013 to 2022.

The crash rate on the road of 8.5 accidents per million vehicle miles traveled was nearly six times the state average of 1.5 accidents for similar highways over that decade, the DOT said.

Stevenson said the agency is considering construction of a short retaining wall to protect the creek.

“Having a safer highway and an aesthetically pleasing highway do not have to be mutually exclusive,” she wrote.

Steve Paula, 74, lives in Brookings but spends a couple months a year at his cabin located on the north side of U.S. 85 a few miles west of Cheyenne Crossing.

Paula said he has witnessed two accidents in recent years that were caused in part by the poor condition and curvy configuration of the highway.

Paula said he has been impressed with the DOT’s willingness to receive public input and is hopeful the agency will find a way to improve safety without harming the aesthetics or damaging Spearfish Creek.

“We don’t want it destroyed,” he said. “But there’s a reasonableness in play in that we want safe roads, and I do believe the DOT is sincere in saying that they don’t want to screw it up either.”

title: Lead responds to retaining wall lawsuit
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: A retaining wall near the Miller Apartments, on Grandview Drive in Lead, and an action to evacuate the apartments is at the center of a lawsuit for which the city of Lead issued a response last week. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Failing retaining wall prompts late night evacuation notice  1.jpg
A retaining wall near the Miller Apartments, on Grandview Drive in Lead, and an action to evacuate the apartments is at the center of a lawsuit for which the city of Lead issued a response last week. Pioneer file photo 

 Failing retaining wall prompts late night evacuation notice 2.jpg
Pioneer file photo 

LEAD — The city of Lead is requesting a trial by jury and refutes claims that its building inspector acted unlawfully when he declared an apartment building unsafe for occupancy after a retaining wall behind the property failed. 

In the summer of 2023, a retaining wall below Washington Street, behind the Miller Apartments on Grandview Drive, began to fail. On June 23, 2023, Lead Building Inspector Dennis Schumacher posted a sign at the Miller Apartments, declaring the building unsafe for human occupancy. The declaration meant 2 building tenants had to move to alternative accommodations for several months, until Schumacher later rescinded it in September. 

At the time, Schumacher said he issued the declaration out of concern that the wall could fall into the building and potentially strike a gas line that provides service to the apartments, causing a major safety concern. Schumacher and then-Lead City Administrator John Wainman, said they had repeatedly asked Miller to fix the wall that is on his property. According to city ordinance, individual property owners are responsible for fixing their own retaining walls. 

But Miller claimed that the wall, which is located below Washington Street in Lead, holds up a city street and therefore its maintenance and replacement is the city’s responsibility. 

In May, Miller filed a 138-paragraph lawsuit against the city of Lead and Schumacher, claiming that the city improperly used condemnation procedures to force repair of the wall that supports public infrastructure, and that the city did not have authority to condemn the building that did not have structural deficiencies. 

Rapid City attorneys Rebecca Mann and Richard Williams, of Gunderson, Palmer, Nelson and Ashmore, LLP law firm, are representing the city of Lead and filed their response to the lawsuit, Wednesday. The response denies multiple points relating to Miller’s allegations about the unlawful evacuation of the building. Additionally, it denies that the wall is located under Washington Street and that Washington Street remained open to traffic after the wall failed. 

The response also claims governmental, statutory, sovereign, and qualified immunity. The immunity types broadly protect governments from being sued without their consent. It also denies that Miller suffered any more damages than those suffered by the general public as a whole. 

It also refutes Miller’s assertion that the city treated a similar retaining wall situation differently, when it responded to a retaining wall failure on Handley Center property in March 2024, just months after the Miller Apartments wall failed. When the Handley Center wall failed, the city of Lead sought federal grants to pay for its replacement. 

“Despite Schumacher publicly acknowledging to local news media serious structural concerns with the Handley Center, Schumacher and the city did not condemn that facility or force immediate evacuation as a response, but rather promptly initiated engineering review, treated the matter as one requiring repair and funding, and facilitated financial assistance to address the problem for the Handley Center,” the lawsuit states. “The contrast between the city’s handling of Miller Apartments and the Handley Center supports the inference that the city used condemnation against Plaintiff not as a neutral safety measure, but as leverage to force Plaintiffs to accept responsibility for a public infrastructure problem.” 

But the city’s response claims equal treatment. 

“Defendants admit the Handley Center was not condemned or evacuated and that federal grants were sought for the Handley Center retainer wall, and as were federal grants sought for the Miller retainer wall,” according to the city’s response in court documents. 

Schumacher confirmed that the city sought federal grants to help pay for the Miller Apartments retaining wall replacement. But the grant from the U.S. Department of Agriculture Rural Development Emergency Community Water Assistance program, was based upon percentage of structures served by water lines located under the road affected by the wall, was denied. Schumacher said the water lines under Washington Street only serve a few houses. That compares to the Handley Center wall, which supports Sunnyhill Road — where a major artery of water lines service more than 100 properties.  

Lead City Administrator Robin Lucero declined to comment about the lawsuit, and referred questions to city attorneys at Gunderson, Palmer, Nelson, and Ashmore, LLP. Mayor Dustin Heupel said the firm is working with city attorney Tim Johns, and is involved as part of the city’s pool insurance. 

Williams declined to comment on the active case. 

No further court appearances for the case have been scheduled. The case is filed in U.S. District Court with the District of South Dakota, Western Division.

title: One patriotic quilt, many talented quilters: Here’s how the Northern Hills Quilt Guild  is raising money to support it annual charitable efforts
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — Once a year, the Northern Hills Quilt Guild leverages their knowledge, experience, and sewing skills to craft one large raffle quilt. It’s the work of many hearts and hands. Quilting, they believe, is best shared.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — Once a year, the Northern Hills Quilt Guild leverages their knowledge, experience, and sewing skills to craft one large raffle quilt. It’s the work of many hearts and hands. Quilting, they believe, is best shared.

“It’s therapy. It’s friendship. It’s a connection, a social connection. I love to quilt,” said Bobbie Edwards, a guild member.

One person might help lead the design. A small committee chooses the theme. Individual quilters receive kits to sew blocks at home, blocks that are then assembled by yet another quilter. The lines of stitching that hold the quilt’s front, batting, and back together — the quilting stitches — are often completed by still another skilled sewer.

The guild quilters come from Belle Fourche, Sturgis, Spearfish, and Wyoming. Usually, they work collaboratively on a “Rally quilt” with a distinctly motorcycle or Black Hills-based theme. This year, the group opted to mark America’s 250th anniversary with a patriotic quilt.

The fabrics involved are red, white, and blue, with scenes from the nation’s founding and images of eagles featured prominently in star blocks.

“The star blocks around the outside were done by 5 or 6 of us … (3 of us) picked the fabric out at Bakery Fabrics in Belle Fourche,” Guild member Bobbie Edwards told the Pioneer.

“I was in there, and I saw this fabric. I was at the meeting, and I said, ‘You guys have got to come see this fabric!’ I didn’t want to be part of it. I wasn’t on the committee, but I thought, ‘This is perfect fabric.’ They agreed. We got the fabric,” said Laura Kramp, the president of the Northern Hills Quilt Guild. “The center block is what is called the carpenter’s block. Luella (Fournell) taught it to all of us as a challenge thing. It worked so well in that middle, so we picked out the blocks that went around it.”

The quilt has been on a journey through the Black Hills since the start of the summer. Guild members have displayed it at Downtown Friday Nights and concerts at the High Plains Western Heritage Center in Spearfish. It’s been hung up at farmer’s markets and a smattering of area community events. For a few days, it’ll be in the window of Bakery Fabrics in Belle Fourche and Heartfelt Quilt Shop in Spearfish.

All the while, the guild has sold raffle tickets to find their masterpiece quilt its forever home, and more importantly, to raise money for the quilts they will make for community causes in the year to come.

The money raised through the sale of raffle tickets will then be used to purchase fabric and batting: the materials the guild needs to make charity quilts.

Fournell, who helped teach the carpenter’s block technique, is also a prolific maker of charity quilts.

“She is our charity quilt queen,” said Edwards.

Fournell said, in total, the guild donated 129 charity quilts in 2025. This year they’re on track to make more.

“They go to the fire and police departments in Spearfish, Belle Fourche; some went to Sturgis. We send them to children in foster care. We send them to Fort Meade. In the past, they’ve gone to hospice and the hospital,” Kramp said.

The guild also makes smaller, shoulder-wrap quilts for seniors in assisted living.

Kramp said sometimes a quilt donated to the fire department might be a source of comfort for a family after they lose possessions in a fire. Charity quilts, literally, wrap people in love.

“(A quilt) is love,” Fournell said. “It’s caring about someone. Handmade gifts, they express more than just the gift (itself).”

Fournell has said, much like the raffle quilt, some of the charity quilts are the result of the efforts of more than one quilter.

“Some of the quilts I brought with me today were quilts that were either started by other quilters (we’ve had a few pass away) or I’ve gotten some fabric from them and finished things for them or in their name if nothing else — that kind of thing too, just sharing,” Fournell said.

She said that tickets have sold well so far. The guild usually sets a goal to earn enough to purchase a year’s worth of materials. They’re not far from achieving that goal.

Kramp said the Rally quilts and this year’s raffle quilt provide more than funding.

“It has been a marvelous way for us to contribute to the communities, because of the charity quilts, but it is interesting, especially when we were out at the stone house, the bikers who would just — the ones that received it were always so excited. They really were,” Kramp said.

title: Gaming in Deadwood sees first dip of the year
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Gaming in Deadwood  sees first dip of the year
Courtesy photo 

DEADWOOD — Gaming activity in Deadwood saw its first dip this year with the gaming handle for the month of May dropping 0.1% compared to the same month last year. 

Despite the slight decrease in handle, the South Dakota Commission on Gaming reported that the overall activity in Deadwood remains 9.11% higher for the first 5 months of 2026 compared to the same period last year. 

“While gaming remained steady compared to May of last year, the performance over the first five months of 2026 is very promising,” said George Milos, director of the Deadwood Gaming Association. “With an increase of more than 9% over 2025, it’s clear that travelers recognize the exceptional value Deadwood offers in food, beverage, hotels, motels, and entertainment. Deadwood remains an outstanding value when compared to other gaming markets.”

Sports wagering saw a 19.7% decrease compared to May 2025 and table games fell by 9.5%. Slot machines saw the only increase, rising only 0.65% over the same period. 

Operators provided $2,054,226.86 in “free play” incentives, bringing the taxable gross revenues to $12,678,933.71. Total taxes collected amounted to $1,141,104.03. Taxes were distributed as follows: $126,789.34 to the state general fund, $405,725.88 to South Dakota Tourism, and $101,431.47 to Lawrence County.

title: Group fails to gather enough petition signatures to put new SD tax law on the ballot
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — Opponents of a new law that uses a higher state sales tax rate to fund property tax reductions for homeowners said Friday they did not collect enough petition signatures to put the measure on the Nov. 3 ballot.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — Opponents of a new law that uses a higher state sales tax rate to fund property tax reductions for homeowners said Friday they did not collect enough petition signatures to put the measure on the Nov. 3 ballot.

South Dakotans for Fair Taxes needed 17,508 signatures from registered South Dakota voters to refer the law. A press release from the group announcing its failure to reach that threshold did not say how many signatures were gathered. The law goes into effect today.

The state sales tax rate is scheduled to return from 4.2% to 4.5% in July 2027, when a temporary rate reduction expires. The new law will capture the revenue from the increase and use it to reduce property taxes imposed by school districts. 

South Dakotans for Fair Taxes said the law unfairly requires renters to pay a higher sales tax while limiting tax relief to homeowners. Ned Horsted chairs the group.

“The cost of living crisis is hitting all South Dakotans,” he said in a statement, adding that the law “disproportionately benefits those with the most expensive homes and is paid for by the rest of us at checkout, including groceries for our families.”

The group’s coalition included Bread for the World South Dakota, the South Dakota AFL-CIO, and Dakota Rural Action.

title: Spearfish, Lawrence Co. look to consolidate dispatch centers
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: DEADWOOD — According to Brian Dean, Lawrence County sheriff, Spearfish and the county are the last 2 entities to operate separate public safety answering points in a single county in the state — that may be about to change.
_full_text:
DEADWOOD — According to Brian Dean, Lawrence County sheriff, Spearfish and the county are the last 2 entities to operate separate public safety answering points in a single county in the state — that may be about to change.

A detailed proposal regarding the consolidation is expected to be presented to the county at the July 30 budget workshop meeting. The consolidation could happen as early as 2027.

Dean told county commissioners at the June 9 commission meeting that discussions to consolidate the centers have been in the works for years. After discussing the issue with Spearfish Mayor John Senden and Collin Smith, chief of Spearfish police, they believe the time has come to consolidate the 2 systems. In order for the consolidation to be successful, Dean said several issues must be resolved, including a wage discrepancy between the city and the county, costs of equipment and operating expenses, and what he called “public surety.”

“We have to make sure the public is comfortable and in support of it, as well as comfort factor and support of our first responders,” said Dean.

In order to hold the additional call load, Dean said the dispatch center would require 14 full-time dispatchers — 6 more than the county currently employs. In a proposed budget submitted to the county, Dean requested the county hire 2 more dispatchers and asked that 4 come from Spearfish in the consolidation process. Spearfish currently employs 5 full-time telecommunicators.

Dean said the bump up in number of full-time employees would allow the county to always keep at least 2-3 dispatchers on-site.

“Much like in the jail, (commissioners) have heard me say that the staff actually tell me by their stress and how they’re handling the numbers in the jail, that’s where I decide where the number (of full-time staff) needs to be,” said Dean. “The same is true with our telecommunicators. These people have a tremendously difficult job with an extreme amount of stress in unpredictable spurts during their shift. So, I think 14 (full-time employees) will work, but at a certain point we’ve got to reassess to see if our inclination has been accurate.”

Historically, Spearfish has used monies from the county’s 911 service line item to pay for its dispatch center. Dean said that if the consolidation should go through, those monies will need to be reassessed if the city agrees to compensate the county for the cost of 4 full-time telecommunicators as well as the total cost of operating equipment to handle the increased call volume.

If the city agreed to transfer ownership of some of its equipment to Lawrence County, the county could save up to $540,000 in costs, bringing the total cost of consolidation to the county to approximately $10,000. The estimated annual cost to the city would be $200,000, an amount Dean called a “tremendous savings to the taxpayers of the city of Spearfish.”

Dean said that dispatch centers require expensive upgrades to equipment every 3-5 years, costing an estimated $700,000. Because of the recent construction of the newly finished Lawrence County Public Safety Center across from The Lodge at Deadwood, Dean said the next round of upgrades are anticipated to happen in 2030.

“That being the case, that’s money that we would have to spend regardless, and money that conversely Spearfish would have to spend regardless,” said Dean. “So, $200,000 in a normal year (for Spearfish to operate), and in a year with a major expense their cost would go up to approximately $393,000.”

Dean pointed out that the majority of savings would go to the city of Spearfish, but the taxpayers of Lawrence County would also see a tax benefit.

“It could end up being a little bit of a cost to the county, but to relieve some duplication of services there it’s good for the whole county, not just the city,” said Commissioner Eric Jennings. “It’s good for the taxpayers in general.”

title: Extreme damage from 131 mph wind brings governor and state response to Highmore
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Matilyn Kerr, left, and sister Brittany Kerr watch as a skid-steer loader pulls a tree from Brittany Kerr’s yard in Highmore Monday, after a severe storm that morning. Photo by Meghan O’Brien, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Extreme damage from 131 mph wind brings governor and state response to Highmore 1.jpg
Matilyn Kerr, left, and sister Brittany Kerr watch as a skid-steer loader pulls a tree from Brittany Kerr’s yard in Highmore Monday, after a severe storm that morning. Photo by Meghan O’Brien, South Dakota Searchlight 

HIGHMORE — Strong storms ripped through portions of central and eastern South Dakota early Monday morning, leaving roofs torn off homes, vehicles tipped over, grain bins caved in and wind turbine towers folded in half.

The National Weather Service received reports of wind gusts as high as 131 miles per hour in and near the small town of Highmore, where electricity was knocked out and much of the worst damage occurred. The service also received reports of tornadoes near Pierpont and Andover.

Matthew Cappucci, a meteorologist, wrote for The Washington Post that the 131 mph gusts “may be the strongest straight-line thunderstorm gusts directly measured since Aug. 1, 1983″ in Maryland, where a gust was measured at 149.5 mph.

Gov. Larry Rhoden visited Highmore later Monday. Officials are surveying the damage, in preparation for a 30-day window to apply for federal assistance. To qualify for federal aid, a storm in South Dakota must cause at least $1.8 million in damage to public property, Rhoden said.

“And so we’ll continue to assess that, whether there’s enough to qualify for an emergency declaration, but in the meantime, it doesn’t matter,” Rhoden told reporters. “We are, as a state, making use of any resources we can to lend to the city to help with their cleanup.”

 Extreme damage from 131 mph wind brings governor and state response to Highmore 2.jpg
Sal Roseland, right, of Seneca, talks with Gov. Larry Rhoden as Rhoden operates Roseland’s skid-steer loader Monday. Roseland drove to Highmore after severe storms to assist cleanup efforts. Photo by Meghan O’Brien, South Dakota Searchlight 

The Governor’s Office said minor injuries to people had been reported.

State officials were posted throughout the town of about 650 residents Monday to direct traffic and help coordinate the response. The South Dakota Highway Patrol, Department of Transportation, Department of Game, Fish and Parks, and 9 inmates were part of that effort.

Brittany Kerr, 38, is a lifelong Highmore resident. She had never seen such severe storm damage.

“By 6 o’clock, it was very loud and just kind of almost sounded like a freight train coming through,” she said. “I heard glass breaking and I could tell that trees or something fell into my house.”

Kerr, who works in health care, helped evacuate dozens of residents from the nursing home in town. Her sister lent a hand in the cleanup on Kerr’s property, which had uprooted trees and visible damage to the house. Throughout town, neighbors and emergency response teams helped residents remove broken tree limbs, downed trees and other debris from yards and roadways.

“In times like this, we’re fortunate to live in an agricultural community where people can provide equipment and people are ready to work and help others,” Kerr said. “And for the damage we sustained, I would say the town is cleaning up rather quickly.”

Highmore was under a no-travel order Monday. Power lines were down and many roadways were blocked by fallen trees and debris.
