title: The work on Exit 10 won’t stop for Rally: Here’s why
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Department of Transportation is working to install “loons” or turning structures on the shoulders of North Avenue near Exit 10. Eventually, drivers will not be able to turn left from Old Highway 14 to Belle Fourche. They will use the loons to travel toward Belle Fourche instead. Pioneer photo by Travis Potter
_full_text:
DJI_20260630091108_0065_D.JPG
The Department of Transportation is working to install “loons” or turning structures on the shoulders of North Avenue near Exit 10. Eventually, drivers will not be able to turn left from Old Highway 14 to Belle Fourche. They will use the loons to travel toward Belle Fourche instead. Pioneer photo by Travis Potter 

SPEARFISH — Beginning in the 1990s, traffic generated by the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally had reached levels that changed the way the Department of Transportation (DOT) planned its projects. 

Often, contractors struggled to reach job sites and bring in material and equipment needed for roadwork to proceed — as a direct result of the influx of bikes. 

Rapid City Area Engineer Mike Carlson said, it just made sense for the DOT to communicate with contractors and plan around the Rally. 

In the decades since, folks may have gotten used to seeing roadwork pause during that fateful week in August, but that is changing slightly — on a project-by-project, case-by-case basis. 

“We’ve gotten better at directing traffic, and have begun to reduce Rally restrictions,” Carlson said. 

Rally pauses can be costly. It takes time to bring projects to a halt, and then energy to get crews back on site, and often luck to ensure projects are complete before the weather changes and winter weather kicks in. 

 Roadwork.JPG
Roadwork at Exit 10 is not scheduled to pause during the Rally. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

“We make decisions on each individual project,” Carlson said. Those decisions are based on weather conditions, the nature of the project, and how traffic can be managed where closures may be warranted. 

Crews have started to build out a system of turn lanes that will eventually transform the way traffic flows through Exit 10, north of Spearfish. That project will not hit the brakes when motorcycles roar into the region. 

In large part, that is because DOT hopes to have the majority of the work on those turning structures, called “loons,” complete by early August. The location of Exit 10, still a high-traffic area, is also not the center of Rally activity. During the project, despite lane closures, drivers and bikers should still be able to travel into and out of Spearfish unimpeded.

title: Independence Day travel  could reach record levels
byline: By Amina Aidarkhanova South Dakota News Watch
description: PIERRE — As Americans prepare to celebrate Independence Day during the nation’s 250th anniversary year, South Dakotans will join millions of travelers on the road despite rising costs for gasoline, hotels and airfare.
_full_text:
SDNewsWatchLogo

PIERRE — As Americans prepare to celebrate Independence Day during the nation’s 250th anniversary year, South Dakotans will join millions of travelers on the road despite rising costs for gasoline, hotels and airfare.

AAA projects that 216,942 South Dakotans will travel during the Independence Day holiday period, which runs from June 27 through July 5. The forecast represents a slight increase from 215,448 travelers in 2025 and 214,201 in 2024, continuing a steady upward trend in holiday travel.

Nationally, AAA expects 72.2 million Americans to travel at least 50 miles from home during the holiday period, setting a new record and surpassing last year’s mark of 71.8 million travelers.

“For many Americans, July Fourth travel is a longstanding tradition, and that tradition remains strong this year even as prices rise for most modes of transportation,” said Shawn Steward, public affairs manager for AAA South Dakota.

Most South Dakotans are expected to travel by car. AAA estimates roughly 181,000 state residents will take road trips, mirroring a national trend in which 85% of holiday travelers are expected to drive.

The continued popularity of road travel comes despite significantly higher fuel costs. According to AAA, the average gasoline price in South Dakota is approximately 80 cents per gallon higher than it was at the same time last year.

Even so, travel experts say many families are adjusting their plans rather than canceling vacations altogether.

“People love to get out and spend time with their families, seeing new places and exploring new things,” Steward said. “People are still making plans to take summer vacations despite the higher costs.”

South Dakota’s ties to 250th anniversary

While inflation and economic uncertainty continue to influence travel decisions, those same factors may create opportunities for South Dakota’s tourism industry.

According to information provided by the South Dakota Department of Tourism, travelers increasingly are seeking affordable destinations, staying closer to home and taking shorter trips. Because South Dakota has traditionally been a regional drive-market destination, tourism officials believe the state is well-positioned to benefit from those changing travel habits.

More than half of South Dakota visitors, approximately 58%, travel from within 150 miles of home, according to tourism research conducted by Future Partners.

The state’s combination of outdoor recreation, scenic drives, historic landmarks and family-friendly attractions aligns with many of the experiences travelers currently prioritize.

“Some people may make changes in where they travel, or maybe stay in a less expensive hotel, or travel closer to home,” Steward said. “But most people are still looking for ways they can get out and enjoy the summer with a vacation.”

Another wave of national attention may come from President Donald Trump’s planned visit to South Dakota.

Freedom 250 announced that Trump plans to attend the July 3 event at Mount Rushmore, which will feature fireworks and other activities tied to the nation’s 250th anniversary. 

In Rapid City, local leaders are preparing for what they expect to be one of the busiest Independence Day weekends in recent memory.

“We thought it was only fitting that Rapid City, being as close as it is to that iconic monument, really embrace America’s 250th birthday,” said Allie Froning, CEO of Visit Rapid City.

The city has organized a five-day “Real America Birthday Bash” from July 1 through July 5 featuring concerts, a parade, food vendors, family activities, fireworks and a drone show.

Froning said she expects between 10,000 and 20,000 people to be participating in downtown festivities at any given time during the celebration.

The festivities coincide with the return of fireworks at Mount Rushmore National Memorial on July 3. Attendance for the event is limited through a public lottery system, but Rapid City plans to host a downtown watch party and livestream for visitors unable to secure tickets.

Tourism officials believe the anniversary is generating additional interest in destinations tied to American history.

“I think there is a lot of energy behind the anniversary and a lot of people traveling to destinations that have a tie to American history,” Froning said. “There is a lot of demand for that right now.”

title: Lead 150th celebration to be this weekend
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: LEAD — Lead will celebrate its 150th anniversary of settlement, along with 100 years of Gold Camp Jubilee days, with 4 days of nonstop activity this weekend.
_full_text:
LEAD — Lead will celebrate its 150th anniversary of settlement, along with 100 years of Gold Camp Jubilee days, with 4 days of nonstop activity this weekend. 

The event will be characterized with historical displays, live music, vendors and food trucks, and fun as the festival that includes the entire town kicks off on Thursday, with a science museum and activity center held at the Sanford Lab Homestake Visitor’s Center, and tours at the Black Hills Mining Museum, both of which will be held from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m. From 10 a.m. to 5 p.m., the History Comes Alive exhibit, featuring notable Women of Lead and information and displays from the city’s original 18 founders, will be held on the second level of the Historic Homestake Opera House. Terry Smith, chairman of Lead Historic Preservation Commission, said this year’s exhibit will also feature a children’s museum. There will be 6 stories about girls’ experiences in the gold mining camps; a workshop to learn how to use and find the North Star for surveying; and a science exhibit. Children are also invited to bring a photograph of their grandparents that can be converted into a coloring page, which they can complete and turn in for inclusion in the city’s time capsule, to be opened in 2076.  

“Then, with their children and grandchildren, they can watch those pictures come out of the time capsule,” Smith said. 

After visitors check out the history exhibit, they are invited downstairs, to the Lead-Deadwood Arts Center, for the Lead-Deadwood Alumni Art Show. Karen Everett, executive director of the Lead-Deadwood Arts Center, said the show will feature about 30 pieces of artwork by 15 Lead-Deadwood High School alumni. Classes that will be represented range from the 1960s to the 2000s. An artist reception will be held from 5-7 p.m. on Thursday and is open to the public. 

Thursday’s activities will culminate with performances for “More Than Gold,” a show that was researched by Lead Historic Preservation Commission Chairman Terry Smith, and written by Historic Homestake Opera House Executive Director Todd Jones. The show chronicles the history of Lead, and highlights popular music that was written by artists who were in Lead at one time. 

On Friday, the second annual Gold Rush Cruisin’ Classics Car Show will be held at the Sanford Lab Homestake Visitor’s Center parking lot. The show will be held from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., with winners announced at 1 p.m. 

At 10 a.m. youth and interested adults are invited to the Lead skatepark for a skate clinic, sponsored by the Northern Hills Recreation Association. The event will feature skating experts on hand to teach kids about skateboarding and more. Additionally, from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m., bounce houses, vendors, and food trucks are scheduled to be set up at Manuel Brothers Park, with live music held in the park shelter from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. 

Starting at noon, the Rock the Hills ticketed concert will be held at Mountain Top Field, behind Lead-Deadwood High School. The rock music festival will feature performances by Bittersweet at noon, and the Brandon Sprague Band at 3 p.m., Stereo Trip at 5 p.m. At 8:30 p.m. the headliner, Lexington Lab Band, will take the stage to play hits from the 60s and 70s. The event will also feature food and beverage vendors. 

“It’s Hairball, but instead of the 80s it’s more classic rock, like the 70s,” Lead City Administrator Robin Lucero said of the Lexington Lab Band. 

A shuttle service will be available throughout the day to transport participants. Shuttles will have stops at the Sherman Street Parking lot, the lower parking lot at Terry Peak, and at the Sanford Lab Homestake Visitor’s Center. 

On Saturday there will be free trolley transportation between Lead and Deadwood. Stops along the way will include the Sherman Street parking lot in Deadwood, the Sanford Lab Homestake Visitor’s Center, the Hampton Inn in Lead, and Lumpy’s Casino Bar in Central City. 

Most activities on Saturday will be centered around the Manuel Brothers Park area, kicking off with a pancake feed from 7-10:30 a.m. at the Rod and Gun Club. At 9 a.m. a horseshoe tournament and a golf chipping contest will start at the horseshoe pit across from the park, with no preregistration required. 

For youth and adults who are more interested in showing off their skills on wheels, the Third Annual Live Like Cash: Skate, Scoot, and Bike Competition will start at 9:30 a.m. at the Lead skatepark. Registration will be held from 9:30-11 a.m., with a $20 donation, and the competition starts at 11 a.m. The event features a variety of hand painted skateboards, bikes, scooters, and accessories for prizes. 

Volleyball will be back again this year, as the annual Mile High Smackdown Volleyball Tournament will start with registration at 10 a.m. Teams of 6 will pay $10 per person to play, and the top 3 teams will receive cash awards at the end of the tournament.  

From 10 a.m. to dusk there will be inflatable games and bounce houses, vendors and food trucks at the Manuel Brothers Park, with a beer garden starting service at 11 a.m. Additionally, at 11 a.m. Erin Woodward will host a book signing at the Sanford Lab Homestake Visitor’s Center, for “The Price of Gold.” At noon, the American Legion Post 31 will raise the flag at the Davis Ring. At 2 p.m. there will be a watermelon eating contest in the park. 

Live music will be held throughout the day. 

At 4:15 p.m., a parade is scheduled for Lead’s Main Street, and at 8 p.m. the Northern Hills Community Band will perform at the Davis Ring. 

The main event of the day will start at approximately 9:30 p.m., when what Lead Area Chamber of Commerce Executive Director Jami Grangaard promises the largest fireworks show the city has ever seen, will be over the Open Cut.  

On Sunday, residents and visitors in Lead and Deadwood area invited to the ballfield at Mountain Top, for the Lead vs. Deadwood vintage baseball game, from 10 a.m. to noon. Then at noon there will be a community potluck lunch from noon to 2 p.m. 

Following events at Mountain Top, pianist Nina McIntire will perform Echoes of Lead: 150 years of Music and Memory at the Lead-Deadwood High School Auditorium. The event will feature a slide show of photographs, submitted by Lead residents, depicting various scenes from long and recent history. Immediately following the event there will be a time capsule reveal, with time capsule items that will be sealed and scheduled to be opened in 2076. 

“This will be quite the show,” said Gary Linn, member of the Lead Historic Preservation Commission. “I think lead’s going to be pretty special with all the events we have going on.”

title: Bear in Hills ‘becoming more habituated’ to people
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: A black bear is seen here near Iron Creek Lake Thursday. Wildlife officials shot it shortly after with rubber buckshot to haze it away from people. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Bear 1.jpg
A black bear is seen here near Iron Creek Lake Thursday. Wildlife officials shot it shortly after with rubber buckshot to haze it away from people. Courtesy photo 

SPEARFISH — A fed bear is a dead bear. And state wildlife officials don’t want that to be the case with a bruin frequently spotted in the Northern Hills.

In early June, the bear was seen in Spearfish. Since then, it has been spotted throughout the Northern Hills, especially in the Spearfish Canyon area, and it is beginning to be too comfortable around people.

“We started receiving reports of that bear June 22, and I think we’ve gotten at least one report every single day, and nearly every report that we’ve gotten involves that bear getting into a garbage can, or a dumpster, or some other artificial food source,” said Trenton Haffley, regional terrestrial resources supervisor for South Dakota Game, Fish and Parks.

On Sunday, it was spotted tearing into garbage bags in Spearfish Canyon, at a home between Elmore and Cheyenne Crossing. It wasn’t the first time the bear visited garbage cans in the area.

“For residential folks, if they could avoid putting their garbage cans out until the last possible minute, the morning of garbage day, or something to that effect,” Haffley said in providing tips to keep the bear, and other animals from getting habituated to people. “That’s all that we can reasonably expect somebody to do at this point in time. Bear-proof garbage containers and stuff like that, is it’s just too much of an ask for right now.”

As far as other food items, he suggested keeping pet food stored inside, barbecues cleaned following their use, bird feeders hung higher and fallen seed picked up, and fruit, from trees, picked up from the ground. 

 Bear 2.jpg
This black bear was seen June 22 near Roughlock Falls. The bear is becoming more used to people and is getting into garbage. Courtesy photo 

“We’ve had a confirmed bear sighting in the Black Hills every single spring for 6 years running,” Haffley said. “So, while (they) may not be widespread everywhere in the Black Hills. We can be reasonably certain at this point that May, June, and July, there’s a pretty good chance we’re going to have a black bear show up.”

While this bear is generating numerous reports, there have been visiting bears that have garnered more calls.

Haffley said that in 2022 or 2023, a bear was getting into human garbage frequently. 

“The difference with that bear was those reports came about 15 or 20 miles apart every single day. He made the loop from the Northern Black Hills to Hot Springs back to the Northern Black Hills. In 9 or 10 days, that bear generated a report, if I remember right, every day or twice a day.”

The bear currently in the Northern Hills, according to experienced bear hunters who have seen photos of the animal estimate the animal to be around 4-5 years old. It is jet black in color.

Wildlife officials have set a trap for the animal so it can be captured, and marked for tracking purposes.

“This is a bear that we likely would consider a category 2 bear, according to our response protocol, which means it’s not necessarily a threat to persons or property yet, but it is becoming more habituated, which kind of just elevates it on our radar,” Haffley said. “It is one that if we get an opportunity, we would like to catch it, mark it, so that we can definitely identify that this bear is the one that’s causing the issues wherever they might show up, and then just keep, kind of, keep better track of, you know, this particular bear and what he does.”

He said the GF&P has 3 categories for their bear response protocol.

Category one would be from a simple bear sighting, or perhaps a bear that got into garbage once.

A bear that is getting into garbage daily, such as the current bear, ‘that’s when it starts becoming a little more cause for concern, elevates it on our radar, that becomes a category 2 bear,” he said. “And then certainly, if a bear were to kill livestock, kill a pet, or it breaks into or enters a house or starts to threaten people, then we elevate it to that highest category. Also, if a bear starts to not be responsive to any sort of adverse conditioning, so if we’re chasing it with pyrotechnics or shooting it with rubber buckshot, and we just can’t get it chased away, that too would elevate it kind of to that highest level.”

So far, the bear is responding appropriately to GF&P staffers’ encouragement to move on.

Wildlife officials shot it at least once with rubber buckshot near Iron Creek Lake. They also chase the animal with hounds.

Haffley said staffers are trying to give the bear negative interactions as often as possible in an effort to persuade the animal from being around humans.

He encouraged people to visit bearwise.org for good tips on how to live in proximity with bears, and for those who see the bear to call a conservation officer or the Rapid City GF&P office at (605) 394-2391.

title: Ag economist encourages careful optimism  amid trade changes and federal assistance
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Andrew Streff drives his combine while harvesting soybeans near Salem. Photo by Joshua Haiar, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Ag economist encourages careful optimism  amid trade changes and federal assistance
Andrew Streff drives his combine while harvesting soybeans near Salem. Photo by Joshua Haiar, South Dakota Searchlight 

PIERRE — Resumption of trade with China and potential year-round availability of E15 biofuel could positively impact the farm economy, according to an agricultural economist who spoke Thursday at the Governor’s Ag Summit in South Dakota.

But David Widmar, who focuses on agricultural trends and decision-making for farmers at Agricultural Economic Insights, said they have to balance their optimism with the tough times they’re still facing.

Federal aid for farmers last year helped some of them survive tariff-related market disruptions, and President Donald Trump is pushing for an additional $11.1 billion. That could provide more relief, Widmar said, but “we can’t continue” on a federal funding “treadmill forever.”

“These are a life raft, not a kayak,” he said. “Kayaks are toys that we can plan on using. Life rafts are things that we use to get to the shore. Make sure we don’t confuse those two things.”

Profits in the livestock sector have been strong, Widmar said, while soybean farmers have been struggling. China temporarily boycotted U.S. soybean purchases last year in response to President Donald Trump’s tariffs on Chinese products.

Trade should be getting “back to normal” after productive diplomacy, Widmar said, but China primarily buys soybeans during the winter months, which is when farmers should expect to see change.

On a longer-term basis, Widmar said the year-round sale of E15 — a gasoline blend containing 15% ethanol — could give farmers more momentum, but it’s “not quite ready for primetime.”

The Trump administration sent a proposal to Congress earlier this week that asks lawmakers to include the year-round sale of E15, among other policy changes, in any supplemental spending bill it approves in the coming weeks and months.

Current federal regulations restrict the sale of E15 from June 1 to Sept. 15 because of its effects on air quality.

title: Guardrail removal underway on I-90 between Spearfish and Whitewood
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Two miles west of Whitewood, crews from Loiseau Construction are removing existing guardrails, which DOT engineers say may be attracting more drivers than they are protecting. Pioneer photo by Mark Watson
_full_text:
Guardrail removal underway on I-90 between Spearfish and Whitewood
Two miles west of Whitewood, crews from Loiseau Construction are removing existing guardrails, which DOT engineers say may be attracting more drivers than they are protecting. Pioneer photo by Mark Watson 

WHITEWOOD — On Interstate 90, between Exit 17 and the Whitewood exit, Exit 23, crews are working to eliminate guardrails and extend box culverts. 

The project began on June 20, and has reduced the speed limit in the area to 45 miles per hour, and traffic to one lane. 

The guardrail crews are removing was installed when the interstate was built, but Rapid City Engineer Mike Carlson said instead of providing a protective barrier between the steep slope at the edge on the road and motorists it seems to attract drivers. 

Between 2016 and 2025, there were 21 crashes involving drivers who struck the guardrail at the project location. Of those, 20 were property damage only and one was fatal, according to SDDOT Highway Safety Engineer Dustin Witt. 

The Department of Transportation has decided to flatten the in-slope, and offer enough grade change for motorists to — ideally — drive back onto the road if they veer off course. The project is expected to cost $3 million, and be completed by Oct. 30.

title: Group wants help for voters affected by proof-of-citizenship law and federal-only designation
byline: By John Hult Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — An organization that advocates for South Dakota voters wants new rules clarifying the administration of what one of its members called a “hastily constructed bill allowed to become a poorly constructed law” on voter registration.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — An organization that advocates for South Dakota voters wants new rules clarifying the administration of what one of its members called a “hastily constructed bill allowed to become a poorly constructed law” on voter registration.

The League of Women Voters petitioned the state Board of Election to create 8 rules in response to Senate Bill 175, which became law when Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden signed it in March.

The bill changed South Dakota’s laws on registration and the kinds of ballots voters get. It requires that first-time registrants show proof of citizenship in the form of a birth certificate, passport, driver’s license, non-driver’s identification card or tribal identification card, or “any other type of acceptable documentation” under federal law. A photocopy of that proof is acceptable for any of those forms except a state- or tribally issued identification card.

The law was also designed to dull the impact of voters who register in South Dakota but don’t live in the state, such as full-time travelers. It defines residency for the purposes of voter registration, and says voters without a physical address in the state get ballots for federal races, but not state or local contests.

At least 1,500 people were designated as federal-only voters ahead of the June 2 primary election, according to a South Dakota Searchlight analysis of voter registration data. 

The proposed rules would make a handful of adjustments to voter registration, designed in some cases to clarify the rules, and in others to offer impacted voters a chance to challenge their designation as ineligible or federal only. 

Among the proposals:

Allowing photocopies or pictures of tribal identification cards or state-issued ID cards to be used as proof of citizenship.

Recognizing tribal IDs from any federally recognized tribe, rather than just the 9 tribes in South Dakota.

Allowing voters given federal-only ballots an opportunity to cast provisional ballots for local elections as they appeal their eligibility to participate.

Adding specific language to the state’s voter registration form to explain that not offering a physical South Dakota address would cause them to be designated as federal-only voters.

Adding language to notifications confirming a voter’s registration clearly saying if the registrant is a federal-only voter, as well as language explaining how to remedy the situation.

Supporters: It should be easier to vote

On Tuesday in Pierre, representatives with the League of Women Voters were joined by supporters from groups for sexual assault and domestic violence survivors, advocates for disability rights and civil rights, and a tribal representatives through about two hours of testimony on rules, which the supporters say would protect legitimate voters from disenfranchisement.

County auditors have applied the law inconsistently around the state, according to Amy Scott-Stoltz, a Sioux Falls-based board member for the League. She said one woman contacted the board after trying to switch her registration to Republican in order to vote in that party’s primary on June 2. The voter was asked to show proof of citizenship, Scott-Stolz said, “even though the law explicitly states that it only applies to people registering to vote for the first time.”

The person had proof of citizenship, Scott-Stoltz said, but “she never should’ve needed it, and many South Dakotans in her position wouldn’t have had it.”

People fleeing domestic violence might be among them, according to Melissa McCauley of the South Dakota Network Against Family Violence and Sexual Assault. Women on the run, jumping from location to location to avoid contact with their abuser, will often leave documents like birth certificates behind, McCauley said.

Getting replacement copies can be a hassle for people dealing with such stressful situations, and McCauley said they shouldn’t have to worry about losing their right to vote in local contests because they don’t have them. 

“Voting is more than casting a ballot for many survivors. It’s a powerful step towards reclaiming their independence and having a voice in decisions that are affecting their lives and their communities,” McCauley said. “We should be making it easier for eligible citizens to participate in democracy, not more difficult.”

Tribal citizens also struggle at times to get replacement documents, according to Cody Russell, vice chairman of the Lower Brule Sioux Tribe. 

Russell was among those testifying who said photocopies of ID cards ought to be accepted, just as photocopies of a birth certificate might be. 

“That clarification matters directly to all of our members,” Russell said. 

Russell also said it’s important for the state to recognize the citizenship of tribal citizens whose ID cards were issued by a federally recognized tribe outside the state’s borders, as some tribal residents of South Dakota maintain membership in out-of-state tribes. 

‘Hastily-written bill’

Erin Rudner, a longtime social studies teacher in Aberdeen, identified herself as a member of that city’s chapter of the League of Women Voters but said she was testifying on her own behalf.

Rudner said she’d spent years guiding students through the registration process after her classes, in which she’d discuss the importance of civic engagements and the right to vote. The students were sometimes a little unsure of what to do when faced with registration forms before the law change. Now, she said, “some kids will be fine” when asked for a birth certificate or ID card to prove their citizenship, but others won’t be prepared for the additional steps.

Rudner thanked the League “for spearheading this push to make right a hastily constructed bill that was allowed to become a poorly constructed law,” and said that the Legislature had left the group to deal with the unintended consequences.

“It shouldn’t be the job of the League of Women Voters to fix this,” Rudner said, adding that “it wouldn’t be the first time some bright and able prairie women” have had to clean up messes created by the Legislature.

Secretary of State Monae Johnson, who heads the Board of Elections, was not in attendance. Tom Deadrick, the deputy secretary of state, ran the meeting in her absence, which he said was due to illness.

The League’s petition for a rule change, submitted on June 2, would typically need a response in 30 days. The group’s lawyer said at the start of the meeting that the League is willing to waive that requirement, but hopes to have an answer from the board by July 7 – one week after Tuesday’s meeting – to make sure the rules can make it through the multi-step administrative process in time for the Nov. 3 general election. 

Supportive votes from the board for the rules would open up a public comment period, after which the rules would get a public hearing. The Legislature’s Rules Review Committee would ultimately vote to adopt or reject the rules.

Possible vote on rules next week

Deadrick promised to try and get the board back together by July 7. He told the board, however, that “you are all busy” and suggested that it might be a heavy lift. He noted that two board members weren’t able to come to Tuesday’s meeting due to other commitments.

No one from Johnson’s office spoke for or against any of the proposed rules on Tuesday, but her office did submit written comments on some of them. 

Adding language on the impact of registering without a South Dakota physical address would make the registration form “unwieldy,” the document says, and voter confirmation notices with a rundown of how to appeal federal-only status would also create an “unwieldy” document. Allowing photocopies of licenses would put the rules in conflict with the text of the law, Johnson’s office said, suggesting that a change to state law would offer a more appropriate fix.

Board member Kent Alberty of Sioux Falls thanked the people who came to the meeting to offer input. He did not throw support behind any particular rule change, but said the law did spark a need for some rule changes, and that “it certainly is worth our time to take this under serious consideration.”

Board member Kristin Matsuda of Spearfish said she didn’t “agree wholeheartedly” with every aspect of the proposed rules but said “I do generally agree that we need uniformity and consistency.”

title: Northern Hills Retired School Personnel  announce another round of winners of the grandparent essay contest
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: SPEARFISH — Students from local schools have been selected as the winners of this year’s Northern Hills Retired School Personnel (NHRSP) grandparent essay contest.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — Students from local schools have been selected as the winners of this year’s Northern Hills Retired School Personnel (NHRSP) grandparent essay contest. 

Earlier this year, fifth-grade teachers were encouraged to ask their students to write an essay titled, “Why my grandparent should be the AARP SD Grandparent of the Year.” Grandparents were defined as any older adult who fulfills a grand parenting or “senior citizen mentor” role for a child. A familial relationship was not necessary to meet the requirement. 

The essays were required to be up to 500 words in length, written in English, and must be original work by the author including components of a formal essay. The writing was judged on creativity and expression, grammar and form, and neatness by NHRSP members.

Local schools that submitted essays included Sturgis, Spearfish, Belle Fourche, Newell, Black Hills Christian Academy, and many homeschool students who were happy to brag about their grandparents. Winners received books by local authors and certificates, while all of their classmates were given treats. Teachers were thanked with gift certificates. Top 3 winners of the contest received medals from NHRSP.

The winners are as follows: First place, Stella Jackson of Creekside Elementary in Spearfish; second place, Kabria Meland of Sturgis Williams Middle School; third place, Dashiell Brooks, homeschooled in Deadwood.

title: Sturgis man sentenced for possessing child pornography
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Gavel01
Courtesy photo 

RAPID CITY — A Sturgis man was convicted of receipt of child pornography and sentenced to federal prison.

Luke Basche, 21, was indicted for the charge by a federal grand jury in February 2025. He plead guilty on March 31, 2026, and sentenced June 29 to 7 years in federal prison, followed by 5 years of supervised release. Basche was ordered to pay $48,750 in restitution and a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund. 

According to court reports, between December 2022, and January 2025, Basche used an internet-based chat application to search for, download, and view sexually explicit images of child pornography using his cellular phone. After receiving and downloading the images, Basche stored the illegal images on Dropbox and Google accounts, which are cloud-based internet storage services. Investigators reportedly found more than 2,500 images and 445 explicit videos on his device, including the abuse of infants and toddlers. 

This case was investigated by the South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation’s Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force, the Rapid City Police Department, and the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office. Former U.S. Attorney Heather Knox and Assistant U.S. Attorney Benjamin Schroeder prosecuted the case.

This case was part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse, launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice (DOJ). Led by the U.S. Attorney’s Offices and the DOJ’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children, as well as identify and rescue victims. 

For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit https://www.justice.gov/psc.

title: USDA’s finalized rule could boost adoption  of regenerative farming practices
byline: By Cami Koons Iowa Capitol Dispatch
description: A farmer plants corn into a cover crop, which is one of several regenerative agriculture practices that a new federal rule holds can reduce the overall greenhouse gas emissions of producing ethanol. Photo by Jacob Tosch, USDA
_full_text:
USDA’s finalized rule could boost adoption  of regenerative farming practices
A farmer plants corn into a cover crop, which is one of several regenerative agriculture practices that a new federal rule holds can reduce the overall greenhouse gas emissions of producing ethanol. Photo by Jacob Tosch, USDA 

Farmers growing corn and soybeans for biofuels can now quantify the carbon intensity of crops grown with certain regenerative agriculture practices, due to a recently finalized federal rule. 

The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Regenerative Feedstock Rule will allow farmers to “capture new value” from agricultural practices like cover crops and reduced tillage, according to a news release from the department.

According to the finalized rule, the production of corn accounts for more than 50% of the direct greenhouse gas emissions associated with producing corn ethanol, and nearly 50% of soybean biodiesel emissions are attributable to the feedstock crop production. 

The greenhouse gas emissions associated with growing corn and soybeans can be reduced with the “low-carbon practices” outlined in the final rule. These tools include reduced tillage, cover crops and nitrification inhibitors. 

Regenerative practices
• Cover crops: seeding a crop between cash crops, can help to keep roots and nutrients in the soil.
 • Reduced tillage or no till: tilling a field in strips, or not at all, helps to keep the carbon dioxide sequestered by growing plants, and other nutrients, in the soil. 
 • Nitrification inhibitor: adding a nitrification inhibitor to fertilizer slows the conversion of ammonia to nitrate in the soil and can reduce nitrous oxide emissions. 

Farmers can also lower the carbon intensity score of a feedstock by following nutrient management guidelines that specify nutrient budgets based on current soil testing and are verified by a third party.

According to the final rule, these practices, which in earlier iterations of proposed rules were called “climate-smart agriculture” practices, generally reduce greenhouse gas emissions or increase soil-carbon sequestration. The adoption of these practices can lower the greenhouse gas emissions of biofuel production and “provide other environmental benefits” like improved water quality and soil health, according to the final rule. 

Along with the finalized rule, USDA released an updated carbon intensity calculator to help farmers “quantify regenerative practices” and market their feedstocks accordingly.

The carbon intensity score of a feedstock is important to low-carbon biofuel producers, as these fuels must be produced within certain total greenhouse gas emissions limits – from the field to distillation. Low-carbon intensity feedstocks can help biofuel producers fit within these limits.

The finalized rule was celebrated by crop and biofuel groups in Iowa, who also called for the adoption of the rule into a U.S. Department of Energy model essential to receiving low-carbon fuel tax credits known as 45Z tax credits. 

The renewable fuels industry has also looked to carbon sequestration pipelines as a way to lower the life cycle greenhouse gas emissions of biofuels, but such projects have faced pushback in Iowa.

Iowa Renewable Fuels Association Executive Director Monte Shaw called the finalization of the USDA rule a “great step forward” and said farmers can benefit from adopting regenerative practices, while biofuels producers will be able to source low-carbon intensity feedstocks and access “massive new markets.” 

“And maybe most importantly, biofuels production will now be the single biggest driver of regenerative ag practices that improve water quality throughout rural America,” Shaw said in a news release. 

Shaw said the DOE needs to “expeditiously” incorporate the USDA tool into the Greenhouse gases, Regulated Emissions, and Energy use in Technologies, or GREET, model that stipulates the life cycle emissions levels a biofuel must be produced within to qualify for the 45Z tax credit. 

“The Treasury Department must immediately recognize that updated model in time for farmers to make decisions this fall,” Shaw said. “It may seem a little early when this year’s harvest isn’t even out of the ground yet, but many farmers will already be making decisions by August that will impact the (carbon intensity) of next year’s crop.”

Mark Mueller, president of the Iowa Corn Growers Association, said the new rule will “jumpstart” opportunities for growers in Iowa who “are committed to doing what’s right for the land and the environment.” 

“For years, Iowa corn farmers have led the nation in adoption and implementation of conservation practices, and today’s USDA rule provides a framework to reward conservation-minded farmers who are stewards of the land,” Mueller said in a news release. 

President Donald Trump also signed an executive order Friday calling for the advancement of regenerative agriculture practices. The order connects the practices to the administration’s Make America Healthy Again initiative. 

“It is the policy of the United States to promote continued advances in precision agriculture technologies; significantly increase Federal investment in regenerative agriculture practices, research, and education; and spur private-sector innovation in farm modernization by reducing red tape and strengthening public-private partnerships,” the order said. 

In addition to regenerative agriculture practices, the order also urged the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to prioritize the registration of substances that can be used as alternatives to “older active ingredients.” It also encouraged EPA to support research into the impacts of chemical exposures on human health. 

A news release from USDA said the executive order and finalized rule represent the “most significant market-driven effort ever undertaken to reward America’s farmers for voluntarily implementing regenerative practices.” 

Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins said the initiatives were examples of Trump’s “America First agenda.”

“(The rule) put farmers, not Washington bureaucrats, in the driver’s seat,” Rollins said in the release. “Instead of mandates, we’re creating market opportunities. Farmers who choose to implement regenerative practices will have new opportunities to earn premium prices, lower their input costs, improve soil health, and strengthen the long-term profitability of their operations.”

title: Here are some fireworks safety tips as you celebrate  America’s 250th birthday
byline: Consumer Product Safety Commission
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Here are some fireworks safety tips as you celebrate  America’s 250th birthday
Courtesy photo 

WASHINGTON — As America celebrates its historic 250th Independence Day, millions of families will gather to enjoy one of the nation’s most enduring traditions — fireworks. The U.S. Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) is encouraging consumers to celebrate responsibly and follow a few simple safety precautions to help prevent injuries.

Every year, fireworks cause thousands of preventable injuries.  Even sparklers, which can burn at temperatures above 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit, can cause serious burns if not used carefully. As we mark this historic national milestone, CPSC wants Americans to celebrate proudly, use common sense, and take a few simple steps to prevent injuries. 

For 2025, CPSC received reports of at least 15 deaths and an estimated 13,000 emergency department-treated injuries linked to fireworks misuse and malfunction. There were an estimated 1,300 injuries involving sparklers alone. The 15-to-24 age group accounted for the largest share of injuries, and burns to the hands, fingers and head were most common. Many of the most severe incidents involved devices that tipped over, malfunctioned or were used too close to people.

“For 250 years, Americans have celebrated our nation’s independence with family, friends, and fireworks,” said Acting CPSC Chairman Peter A. Feldman. “As we mark this historic milestone, enjoy the celebration, use common sense, and treat fireworks with the respect they deserve. On behalf of everyone at CPSC, I wish all Americans a happy, safe and memorable Independence Day.”

Tips to celebrate safely

Buy only legal consumer fireworks from reputable retailers. Never use homemade, altered or illegal fireworks, and always follow the instructions on the label.

Keep children away from fireworks, including sparklers. Sparklers burn at temperatures of about 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit—hot enough to melt some metals—and can cause serious burns in seconds.

Keep water nearby. Have a bucket of water or a garden hose ready in case of fire or to safely soak used fireworks.

Never use fireworks while impaired by alcohol or drugs.

Light one firework at a time, then move away quickly. Never lean over a firework while lighting the fuse.

Never aim, throw or point fireworks at people, animals or buildings. Never hold, wear or attach fireworks to your body or clothing. Use fireworks only as directed by the manufacturer.

Don’t relight a “dud.”  Wait at least 20 minutes, then soak it thoroughly in water before disposing of it.

The safest way to celebrate: Leave fireworks to the professionals and enjoy public fireworks displays in your community.

title: Trump lands in ND for  America 250th celebration
byline: By Jacob Orledge and Michael Achterling North Dakota Monitor
description: BISMARCK, N.D. — President Donald Trump landed in North Dakota on Wednesday morning, taking the first flight on the new Air Force One.
_full_text:
NorthDakotaMonitorLogo

BISMARCK, N.D. — President Donald Trump landed in North Dakota on Wednesday morning, taking the first flight on the new Air Force One. 

After landing in Bismarck, Trump traveled to the western North Dakota tourist town of Medora, where he will help celebrate the opening of the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library.

Trump is taking a private tour of the library before speaking at Burning Hills Amphitheatre, an event that’s part of the Freedom 250 celebration. 

Members of the public began lining up in Medora as early as 6 a.m. to attend the president’s speech. It’s Trump’s fourth visit as president to North Dakota and the first visit during his second term. 

Some attendees arrived early to greet Trump, who is expected to participate in a ceremonial Freedom 250 train arrival. Horseback riders portraying Theodore Roosevelt’s Rough Riders also are set up to escort Trump’s motorcade.

Accompanying Trump on Air Force One are Interior Secretary and former North Dakota Gov. Doug Burgum and his wife, Kathryn, Donald Trump Jr. and his wife, Bettina, Eric Trump, and Rep. Julie Fedorchak, according to a White House pool report. Fedorchak’s office said she’s the first member of Congress to travel on the new plane, donated by the government of Qatar. 

The Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library will open to the public on Saturday, July 4, the 250th anniversary of the United States’ declaration of independence from Great Britain. Roosevelt spent time in the western North Dakota Badlands after the death of his wife and mother and famously said he would not have been president if not for his time in North Dakota.

title: ‘1776’ opens at BH Playhouse
byline: By Mary Garrigan Special to the Pioneer
description: ‘1776’, a Broadway musical about the creation of the Declaration of Independence is being performed at Theatre 605 in Custer State Park through July 12. Photo courtesy of Liam Blue Scates.
_full_text:
‘1776’ opens at BH Playhouse  1.jpg
‘1776’, a Broadway musical about the creation of the Declaration of Independence is being performed at Theatre 605 in Custer State Park through July 12. Photo courtesy of Liam Blue Scates. 

 ‘1776’ opens at BH Playhouse 2.jpg
 ‘1776’, a Broadway musical about the creation of the Declaration of Independence is being performed at Theatre 605 in Custer State Park through July 12. Photo courtesy of Amber Marisa Cook 

 ‘1776’ opens at BH Playhouse 3.JPG
‘1776’, a Broadway musical about the creation of the Declaration of Independence is being performed at Theatre 605 in Custer State Park through July 12. Photo courtesy of Charlie Wood 

CUSTER STATE PARK — It may not be “Hamilton,” but the patriotic musical about the American Revolution running through July 12 at the Theatre 605 Black Hills Playhouse will leave you equally awed by the flawed but phenomenal humans who birthed a new nation 250 years ago.

Director Dan Workman’s version of “1776,” a Broadway musical about the creation of the Declaration of Independence, trades an all-white, mostly male cast of Founding Fathers for one that incorporates a diversity of race and gender through color-blind casting and gender-defying role assignments for many of the 19 actors who bring  27 different characters to life.  There’s not a weak link in the lot. 

You view it all on a stage framed with an oversized parchment of America’s most famous founding document, created by scenic designer Fallon Podrazik. She cuts a stage-sized window into the Declaration of Independence that transports you back to the hot, humid summer of 1776 in Philadelphia where proponents of independence wage a political battle while Gen. George Washington fights a seemingly hopeless military battle against the British.   

Three talented newcomers to the BHP stage lead this large cast. Bryan Curtis plays John Adams as the chief architect of American independence who seems disliked by nearly everyone but his wife.  Dave DeChristopher plays Benjamin Franklin, the wise and witty sage of the Second Continental Congress tasked with keeping Adams’ obnoxious personality in check. Erik K. Larsen, who looks as if he was sent straight out of central casting to portray a young Thomas Jefferson, would rather be wooing his pretty wife than writing America’s Declaration of Independence.  

Curtis is a large, booming presence on stage, and his voice, too, is more than a match for the entire Congress in the musical’s opening number, “Sit Down, John.”  “1776” lacks many signature songs, but this one is the precursor to an iconic line echoed in the hit musical “Hamilton” decades later. 

As Franklin, DeChristopher gets some of the play’s best humorous lines to work with, and his droll delivery is a delight to watch. 

For pure high-energy humor, Skyler Weaver, playing Virginian Founding Father Richard Henry Lee, stole the show with his song and dance number “The Lees of Old Virginia,” choreographed by Katie Gutmann. I found the understated acting Weaver then brought to his portrayal of New Jersey delegate the Rev. John Witherspoon all the more impressive when my 13-year-old theater companion was astounded to later realize they were one and the same actor.   

The power of Workman’s casting choices hits hardest in Act II, though, when slave owner and South Carolina delegate Edward Rutledge, portrayed by Romell Johnson III who is Black, argues with Adams and Jefferson that the 500,000 enslaved Africans already living in America are “not people, they are property.”  The irony of Johnson’s anger performing “Molasses to Rum,” a song that reveals the hypocrisy of New England shipowners over their involvement in the economics of slavery, is an intense piece of theater that is both wondrous and horrible to behold. 

 As Workman says in his director’s note about casting women and people of color into these historical roles, “…we are not just making a stylistic choice; we are honoring the spirit of the revolution rather than the limitations of the era.” 

Costume Designer Amber Marisa Cook updates the colonial-era gentlemens’ clothing by using a lot of denim in the costumes, a material Cook sees as the quintessential fabric of the American worker, her nod to the hard work of independence, or perhaps to all the hardworking men – and women -  who were left out of the political process during America’s early years.   

I once had a job that required me to research the lives of each of the 56 men who signed the Declaration of Independence, so I may have brought more background to the play than the typical audience member. But even someone who has never heard the names of Caesar Rodney, a sickly man who rode 86 miles through the night to vote in favor of independence for Delaware, or Stephen Hopkins, a Rhode Island delegate known for his wit and his love of rum, will find “1776” an entertaining, and largely accurate, history lesson. The play’s humor, dialogue and song lyrics do an admirable job of condensing the years of hard work, political maneuvers and long odds that faced America’s Declaration of Independence.  

The American Revolution really is a miracle that almost didn’t happen.  Seeing “1776” is a great way to celebrate the 250th anniversary of its beginning. 

The play runs through Sunday, July 12, with evening performances at 7:30 p.m. and matinees at 2 p.m.  For tickets, visit theatre605.org

title: ‘More Than Gold’ tells  150 years of Lead history
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: LEAD — The history of Lead is not all about Homestake.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

LEAD — The history of Lead is not all about Homestake. 

It’s about grit. It’s about hope. It’s about joy. It’s about loss. 

And throughout its 150 years of settlement, music has been a major part of life as Lead residents through the ages have frequently expressed themselves with song. 

For one night only, all of those elements will come together to tell the 150-year history of Lead with “More Than Gold,” an original production by Lead Historic Preservation Chairman Terry Smith, and Historic Homestake Opera House Executive Director Todd Jones. 

The show will be held at 7 p.m. tonight. 

As of Tuesday morning, Jones said the opera house sold 170 pre-sale tickets for the show, which he said is more than he’s ever seen. The Historic Homestake Opera House theater capacity for the show is about 400, Jones said, but attendees are still encouraged to purchase tickets ahead of time, even today. 

“I really encourage people to pre-buy, even the day of (the show) because it will backlog our ticketing pretty quickly if that number of people are trying to get in and get settled,” Jones said. 

The show is a unique experience, filled with lesser-known aspects of history. Smith did the research for what Jones said was originally supposed to be a collection of songs written in Lead, with historical narration. But the more Jones dug into the research, the more stories he found that needed to be told. 

“It’s a unique story,” he said. “It’s a story people are somewhat familiar with, but maybe not in this kind of a context where we’re taking these songs that are part of Lead’s history and weaving that story around them.” 

“I think it will surprise everybody,” Smith said. “It’s a twist that people are not accustomed to. If you ask people in Lead, do you know the history of Lead, they’ll start talking about Homestake. Homestake really didn’t start the city. That’s one thing people will learn over this weekend. None of the 18 founders were part of Homestake. Even the early government didn’t include Homestake individuals.” 

While the area of what is now Lead was settled in 1876, the city wasn’t founded until 1890.

The 13 cast members of the show will take the audience through the highest, and lowest points of the last 150 years. From the gold rush to the Black Hills, to the Homestake lockdown of 1910 that Thomas Grier initiated, to the Great Depression and both world wars, and through Homestake closure. The final scene of the show foreshadows Lead’s future. 

“The last act deals with where we might go,” Jones said. “So, it’s where we’ve been, where we are, and there’s a future lying out there.” 

The tagline for the show is “Progress is a Funny Thing,” Jones said. 

“We made a tremendous amount of progress in that amount of time,” he said. “But there’s more. We might not even fully understand what it’s going to look like, but when we get there and look back, we’ll say again, ‘progress is a funny thing. I can’t believe we got here, and this is a good place.’” 

Jones said the show is one that the community of Lead show see, and he hopes it will draw residents together even more as Lead moves into its future. 

“This is a good spot for us to be as a community,” he said. “I think our community needs to hear that right now. We’ve had a lot going on as it deals with the nonprofits and in our community as a whole. I think we need to hear we are in a good place and we are moving forward. There is a future, and it’s good if we decide it’s going to be good. We have to make that decision, and we have to work it out together. It can’t be just one person. We have to do it as a community, and we have to talk it out together.”

title: Preparations for Trump,  Mt. Rushmore fireworks underway
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: President Donald Trump will visit Mount Rushmore National Memorial today.
_full_text:
Preparations for Trump, Mt. Rushmore fireworks underway .jpg
President Donald Trump will visit Mount Rushmore National Memorial today.  

MOUNT RUSHMORE NATIONAL MONUMENT — The National Park Service is designating an area for protesters as the agency prepares to welcome thousands of attendees, including President Donald Trump, to a fireworks display at Mount Rushmore National Memorial today.

The display is the first at the mountain carving in 6 years. In 2020, the Park Service approved a fireworks show after then-Gov. Kristi Noem asked Trump in his first term to reinstate the event — despite concerns about potential wildfires sparking from falling fireworks embers, pollution and litter from exploded fireworks, and the opposition of Lakota people from whom the surrounding Black Hills were taken through broken treaties.

A Native American-led protest along the road leading to Mount Rushmore during the 2020 event resulted in physical clashes with law enforcement, ending in arrests of protesters. Charges were later dropped.

This year, the Park Service has designated a 100-foot-long First Amendment area for protesters along Highway 16A at the edge of the town of Keystone, about 2 miles below the entrance to the memorial.

The Pennington County Sheriff’s Office will have an increased law enforcement presence throughout Keystone and other towns near Mount Rushmore. It’s also increasing patrols throughout the Black Hills, according to Patrol Capt. Casey Kenrick.

“We always increase our staffing in those areas,” Kenrick said. “Obviously, with the fireworks and it being the 250th anniversary of the country, we’re expecting a bigger draw of people to the area.”

Most of the agency’s focus is on the influx of visitors to nearby towns and traffic control. The memorial will be closed to the public starting late Thursday night. Only the 4,800 ticketholders for the fireworks show — who obtained their tickets months ago in an online lottery — can get into the memorial Friday.

“We’re expecting that to cause some traffic delays and traffic headaches, just because we all know about it, but people from outside of the area might not necessarily know that it’s going on or be aware of where the roadblocks are,” Kenrick said.

The department will also monitor protests.

Nick Tilsen, CEO of Rapid City-based Indigenous advocacy group NDN Collective, was a leader of the protests in 2020 and was one of the people arrested. He said his group is “boycotting” the Trump visit this time.

“We’re not participating in any of that,” Tilsen said.

Since 2020, Tilsen said, Native American activists in South Dakota and elsewhere have “chalked up wins” through community organizing. He pointed to a jury trial victory in a lawsuit against owners of the Grand Gateway Hotel in Rapid City who were accused of discriminating against Native American guests, a company’s withdrawal from an exploratory graphite drilling project in a Black Hills meadow used for spiritual ceremonies, and a 20-year ban on mining activity in the Pactola Reservoir and Rapid Creek watershed area of the Black Hills.

“It’s one of the reasons, strategically, that we’re not doing a flashy action when Trump comes to the Black Hills,” Tilsen said. “Quite frankly, we don’t need to feed into his narrative.”

Separately, Tilsen has also helped launch the Day One Movement, described as “the beginning of a new future” on Sunday, the day after the nation’s 250th birthday. The movement includes advocacy for returning lands taken from Native Americans and providing reparations to African American people for slavery, among other goals.

Wildfire risk

Law enforcement authorities are also preparing to help with evacuations in the case of a wildfire.

Wildland firefighting personnel are at full staffing, working seven days a week to support fire suppression, according to Krista Landreneau with the Black Hills National Forest, which surrounds Mount Rushmore.

Landreneau also said there will be “robust aerial support” in the form of two helicopters and an airplane, to help with spotting wildfires and access points for ground crews, fire retardant deployment and coordinating aircraft in the airspace above a wildfire.

Wildfires can start when fireworks embers fall on dry vegetation. Parts of Pennington County — where Mount Rushmore is located — are in severe or extreme drought conditions, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor.

South Dakota’s Department of Tourism entered into a $700,000 contract in April with California-based Pyro Spectaculars to produce the fireworks show, and for “lighting elements that can be utilized if environmental conditions require an alternative to fireworks,” according to the department.

Few details about that alternative have been publicly released.

“If an alternative to fireworks is required, the lighting presentation is designed to illuminate Mount Rushmore National Memorial in a patriotic display, providing visitors with a meaningful visual experience accompanied by an Americana soundtrack,” Department of Tourism Public Relations Director Katlyn Svendsen said in an emailed statement.

A drone light show was considered, but the National Park Service dismissed it from further study as an alternative to the fireworks display, according to the service’s environmental assessment for this year’s event.

Livestreams available

The fireworks event is officially known as South Dakota’s Freedom 250 Mount Rushmore Fireworks Celebration, in honor of the nation’s 250th birthday. The fireworks show is expected to start at 9:30 p.m. Mountain time, preceded by keynote remarks from Trump. A Freedom 250 press release said Interior Department Secretary Doug Burgum — the former governor of North Dakota — and South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden will also speak. U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune and Sen. Mike Rounds, both of South Dakota, have said they will attend.

Livestreams of the event will be available on C-SPAN and on the Travel South Dakota website. Watch parties are planned in Rapid City at Main Street Square and the Hotel Alex Johnson, and at the Custer Beacon in Custer.

Trump also visited the new Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library in Medora, North Dakota, on Wednesday.

South Dakota Searchlight’s John Hult contributed to this report.

title: High winds damage Lead beer tent
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: LEAD — High winds on Monday damaged the city of Lead’s beer tent beyond repair, Public Works Director Jason Bauernfeind said.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

LEAD — High winds on Monday damaged the city of Lead’s beer tent beyond repair, Public Works Director Jason Bauernfeind said. 

In preparation for the city’s 100th annual Gold Camp Jubilee celebration this weekend, city crews set the large tent up by 10:30 a.m., Monday. While Bauernfeind said he was aware of a wind advisory for the area, expected sustained winds of about 15 miles per hour were well within what the tent was designed to withstand. 

But Bauernfeind said he did not expect the wind gusts of about 39 miles per hour, which is what the National Weather Service reported as a high in Lead on Monday. 

Last year a July 5 storm damaged the tent, and several tarps were replaced with insurance claims. Those tarps, Bauernfeind said, were faulty with defective buckles. The defects combined with the strong wind gusts did irreparable damage. 

“It appears those replacement tarps had defective buckles, but that wasn’t apparent until yesterday’s stronger winds,” he said. “Once the wind picked up, nearly every buckle on the replacement tarps failed, causing the tent to come apart.

 “If we’d known the wind gusts were going to reach what they ultimately did, we simply would’ve waited until Tuesday to put the tent up,” Bauernfeind said. 

Bauernfeind praised city crews for their work on Monday, saying they followed all of the proper setup procedures. The wind gusts and the defective equipment, he said, were simply unexpected. 

“Unfortunately, when a piece of equipment or a component fails unexpectedly, there’s only so much anyone can do to prevent the outcome,” he said.

Because of the damage, Bauernfeind said there will not be a beer tent this year. 

“We’ll make the best use of the facilities and equipment we have available,” he said. 

While he said the city is very disappointed in the damage, Bauernfeind said he is thankful nobody was injured, and they discovered the defective tent before the celebration. 

“Our crew put a lot of time and effort into getting everything ready, and nobody wanted to see the tent come down,” he said. “As discouraging as it is, the most important thing is that no one was hurt. In many ways, we’re fortunate this occurred yesterday instead of on the Fourth of July, when the tent could have been full of people. Equipment can be replaced. People’s safety cannot. We’re grateful everyone walked away safely, and that’s what matters most.”

title: Revisiting ‘A Biography of a Mountain’
byline: Special to the Pioneer
description: Published roughly one month after the 100th anniversary of Mount Rushmore, “A Biography of a Mountain” was selected by the South Dakota Humanities Council to be the 2026 “One Book.” Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Biography of a mt. cover.jpeg
Published roughly one month after the 100th anniversary of Mount Rushmore, “A Biography of a Mountain” was selected by the South Dakota Humanities Council to be the 2026 “One Book.” Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

KEYSTONE — Released Nov. 11, 2025, Matthew Davis’ “Biography of a Mountain: The Making and Meaning of Mount Rushmore” offers a comprehensive, contemplative history of Mount Rushmore, in a compelling piece of narrative fiction. Davis looks at the mountain, the monument, and its cultural, social, and political implications. The result is a nuanced piece of reportage that earned its place as the 2026 One Book South Dakota.  Since 2003, the South Dakota Humanities Council selects one book each year, to encourage people across the state to read and discuss a single text. 

Before “A Biography of a Mountain” published last fall, marking the 100th anniversary of Mount Rushmore, the Pioneer talked to Davis about his approach to the complicated, iconic national monument. In honor of the 250th anniversary of the signing of the Declaration of Independence, the Pioneer is revisiting the conversation. 

Editor’s note: Some answers have been edited for brevity.

Q: When and how did your writing journey begin?

 Matthew Davis credit Anne Giebel.jpg
Matthew Davis is the author of “A Biography of a Mountain: The Making and Meaning of Mount Rushmore.” Photo courtesy Anne Giebel 

A: I started writing in earnest in college at the University of Missouri. I was a journalism major and covered high school sports. I was asked to cover the University of Missouri football team for our local paper my senior year, but I chose to study abroad in Spain. It was a sliding doors moment for me in many ways, as instead of building a career in sports journalism, I went down a path of more literary writing and international travel.

When I graduated from college, I joined the Peace Corps in Mongolia and lived in a traditional Mongolian home called a ger, or yurt. This was in Mongolia’s pre-cell phone and pre-Internet days, and so there was very little to do in the Mongolian countryside besides read, write, and meet with friends. I remember many nights reading long, classic novels like “War and Peace” and “Moby Dick,” and spending hours beginning to write my own work.

Q: What inspired you to write this particular story?

A: On July 3, 2020, President Trump gave a speech at Mount Rushmore to honor Independence Day and the resumption of fireworks at the memorial. The speech offered a very specific—and in my view limited—interpretation of American history and the monuments created to tell that story. Though I did not see the speech live, when I read about it, I began to grow curious about why Trump gave that specific speech there, at Mount Rushmore. I started down a rabbit hole about Mount Rushmore that I did not come out of for several years.

Q: How would you describe “A Biography of a Mountain”?

A: Often times, when people think about Mount Rushmore, they only think about the sculpture at its center, the four faces that Gutzon Borglum carved into the mountain. I wanted my book to be a much deeper and broader exploration of the mountain we now call Rushmore and the land in which it resides — the Black Hills.

My hope is that by telling the story of this one mountain, readers are offered a complicated perspective on our history and how we memorialize it. In this way, my book looks at the history of Rushmore before Europeans and Americans came to the Black Hills; how the Hills came to be American territory; why the memorial was built; how it was built; and how its meaning has evolved over the first century of its existence.

In writing and researching this project, I was aware I was telling both an historical story and a contemporary one. There is a lot of history in this book — about South Dakota, about Mount Rushmore, and about the sculptor Gutzon Borglum — but it also explores very contemporary issues. Today, in the United States, there are important debates about how our history should be portrayed and understood. Many believe in a narrow lens of American history, that we should simply champion our past and the Americans who created and grew our country. Others view American history from a darker lens — that our actions as a country have caused the pain and death of millions of people on this continent and that the American story is hard to justify in this context. My book attempts to thread the needle between these two approaches and tell a complicated history that also seeks to understand our desire for national, patriotic stories and memorials and monuments that reflect them.

Q: What makes a good book/story in your genre?

A: Ha — well, this question presupposes I know what genre of book this is! Some of my favorite books break the rules of their specific genres and meld several into one. So, for example, while this could be considered a history book, there are in-scene moments, contemporary characters, and authorial reflections that aren’t usually included in history books.

For me, then, this book falls under a fluid genre called literary nonfiction with a strong emphasis on the relationship between history and place. These are often my favorite books to read — works that include history, reportage, and essay to explore a certain topic or event. What makes these books effective are compelling characters, whether these are historical or contemporary; an understanding of the depth between the past and the present; unexpected intellectual conclusions; and, most importantly, great writing.

 A Biography of a Mountain.JPG
In “Biography of a Mountain” author Matthew Davis revisits Rushmore, it’s making and meaning. Pioneer file photo 

I’m also a sucker for books that are about things we think we know about, and “A Biography of a Mountain” fits this bill. Everyone knows Mount Rushmore, but do we really know Mount Rushmore? In books like these, authors are able to explore and unpack the different elements that make a familiar icon or event so unfamiliar.

Q: What do you hope reader take away from your new book?

A: I hope readers take away an understanding of the complex history of Mount Rushmore National Memorial. Looking at the four faces, there is a feeling of inevitability about them, that, of course, those faces should be in this mountain. But that was not the case, and my book explores exactly why they were placed, how they were built, and the ramifications of the memorial’s construction.

More broadly, I would love readers to interrogate their own ideas about the history and myths of the United States as we enter into our 250th year as a country. This history and these founding myths have always shaped how we view ourselves as Americans, and I want this book to allow readers to consider the complications of American history, how we memorialize that history, and how these ideas reflect our American identities.

Q: What is your writing process like?

A: It depends what I am writing and what stage I am on. For this book, I needed to do a lot of reporting and research before I could write, so I spent months doing that before beginning to write pages. When it comes time for me to write, I wake up early in the morning (around 5 a.m.) and write on my computer. I have two young sons — ages 7 and 4 — so I try to get as much done before they wake up. When I have a workable draft of a chapter or section on my computer, I print it out and edit on the page.

This is my favorite part of the writing process, as it’s where I think best — with the pages around me and a pen in my hand. I will often go through dozens of drafts like this, as for me, this is the best way to fine tune my language and see the big-picture macro structures that I am working with, the themes of the work. When I have a good enough draft done, I usually give it to trusted readers to take a look — my wife, perhaps, or writer friends — and then make more changes.

Q: How have you dealt with rejection in your writing career?

A: If you don’t have any successes as you start out writing, it is easy to get discouraged. Thankfully, though I experienced some rejection early on, I also had a number of successes, regardless of how small in scale. This was both a blessing — as it validated my work in many ways — and also a curse. I came to expect success, and when I hit a lull of several years in terms of achieving that success, I took the rejection more personally than I should have or was warranted. In other words, my identity was more wrapped into a certain kind of success, which caused me to handle the rejection worse than I could and should have.

Handling rejection, though, is a learning process, just like writing itself. And at this point in my career and life, I feel I handle it better, in part because I know that everyone experiences it. Obviously, no one wants to experience rejection, whether for a book or for a magazine article or a fellowship or grant opportunity. But I have the perspective to understand that every writer, regardless of how well-known or well-read, experiences rejection in some form or fashion. What that means, after the sting has gone away, is that usually another opportunity is around the corner.

title: SturCrazy brings indoor family fun,  healthy refreshments and active play to Sturgis
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: McKenzie Williams and her husband Jason, at the large slides in the play area at SturCrazy in Sturgis.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
SturCrazy brings indoor family fun,  healthy refreshments and active play to Sturgis
McKenzie Williams and her husband Jason, at the large slides in the play area at SturCrazy in Sturgis.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

STURGIS — Families in Sturgis now have a new place where children can climb, play and stay active while parents relax and enjoy healthier food options.

SturCrazy, located at 1150 Moose Dr., is now open Sunday through Wednesday. 

Owner McKenzie Williams said the business was created to fill a need for more family-friendly activities in the Sturgis area.  The facility offers an indoor playground, healthier snack choices and space designed to encourage children to stay active while giving parents a comfortable place to spend time together.

“We wanted to create something that would benefit both kids and parents,” Williams said. “Our inspiration came from our own children. Living east of Sturgis, we were constantly driving to Rapid City or Spearfish to find things for our kids to do. We realized many other families were doing the same thing.”

Williams said she and her family recognized that while Sturgis is widely known for the annual motorcycle rally, local families have had limited options for year-round children’s activities. 

“Our goal is to help change that perception by providing something new and exciting for families,” she said.

The response from the community has exceeded expectations.  “It’s been overwhelming and very positive,” Williams said. “People are thankful to have an indoor playground close to home. We’ve also received support from Whitewood, Spearfish, Belle Fourche, Deadwood, Piedmont, Rapid City and even Pierre. That excitement has really motivated us.”

Like many new businesses, getting started came with challenges. Williams said finding the right location proved to be the biggest hurdle. There were also delays with playground equipment deliveries and uncertainty about whether the area could support the business.

Despite those obstacles, she said the encouragement and assistance from friends and family made all the difference.  “We’ve had incredible support from our families and friends throughout this entire process,” Williams said.  When families visit SturCrazy, Williams hopes they leave with more than just tired kids.

“We want families to have a fun, relaxing experience together,” she said. “We want to encourage movement, healthy choices and provide a place where children can burn off energy while parents can enjoy healthier food & drink options.”

SturCrazy is also expanding its programming. The business currently offers a summer program through Aug. 14 with drop-in opportunities available. Williams said plans are underway to develop an after-school program beginning in the fall of 2027.

Although she and her family continue to work full-time jobs, Williams said they hope to continue growing the business over time by adding new programs and features for area families.

Williams also emphasized that SturCrazy was truly a community effort.  “If it hadn’t been for Kristi and Calvin Cammack, we wouldn’t have had a place at all,” she said. “RJ and Megan Royer put in countless hours helping us, and members of Twisted Canyon helped move the entire gym in one day. Our parents watched our kids when we were exhausted. This wasn’t just our investment, it was our village and our community that helped make this dream a reality.”

 For more information about SturCrazy, including summer programming and drop-in opportunities, call (605) 863-5842.
