title: Deadwood’s restoration of  historic property nears completion
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: The restoration of 85 Charles St. in Deadwood by municipal staff, pictured here before and after, is nearing completion. Remaining projects include the construction of a deck, retaining wall, and sidewalk, as well as landscaping.
_full_text:
85CharlesSt2.jpg

 update 85 charles st.jpg
The restoration of 85 Charles St. in Deadwood by municipal staff, pictured here before and after, is nearing completion. Remaining projects include the construction of a deck, retaining wall, and sidewalk, as well as landscaping.  

DEADWOOD — Passersby of 85 Charles St., in Deadwood may have noticed the dramatic transformation the abandoned property has undergone in the last year thanks to the city’s efforts to restore the historic property. 

Kevin Kuchenbecker, director of planning and zoning and historic preservation, said the remaining undertakings on the project include the construction of a porch, a small retaining wall, and landscaping features, and a new sidewalk. 

“After that, we should be very near listing the property for sale,” said Kuchenbecker. “Once we get everything set, we will decide on if we will surplus or sell the property.”

The property, previously abandoned for more than 20 years, was purchased by the city in June 2024, for $75,000 with the intention of stripping the interior to bare bones and completely renovating the exterior. Since then, the city has invested more than $250,000 restoring the property.

The property is expected to have restrictions to buyers, including that the property be purchased as a single-family home and cannot be used as a short-term rental. 

“The project has been a tremendous transformation of a blighted property that was in a state of vacancy and disrepair for several decades,” said Kuchenbecker. “It has gone a little slower than a normal rehabilitation due to the process of municipal government quotes and bids and procurement rules. (The city doesn’t) want to be in the business of property development, but we are in the business of saving historic resources.”

Kuchenbecker said a quote for the retaining wall should come before the city commission in the next month. He anticipates the project will be completed by late summer, early fall.

title: Spearfish Baseball Association pitches indoor facility  to city council
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Dave Donat, pictured, asks the city council for permission to allow the Spearfish Baseball Association to build an indoor practice facility at no cost to the city. The city would be asked to own and ensure the building, at Black Hills Energy Sports Complex, on completion. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Dave Donat.jpeg
Dave Donat, pictured, asks the city council for permission to allow the Spearfish Baseball Association to build an indoor practice facility at no cost to the city. The city would be asked to own and ensure the building, at Black Hills Energy Sports Complex, on completion. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — This year, there are 250 kids between the ages of 5 and 14 signed up for baseball in Spearfish. Roughly 25 kids ages 15-18 participate in Legion and Junior Legion baseball through the Spearfish Baseball Association (SBA).

“This is a fairly major sport in Spearfish,” said Dave Donat. He’s coached SBA baseball for 15 years. Despite major interest, baseball is plagued with retention issues.

“Per age right now we have about 5 kids per age at the uppers, and we might have 30 kids, 40 kids, per age at the bottom,” Donat said. It’s natural for all sports to see some drop-off in engagement as kids age. Some realize they’re not interested in athletics or pivot to a different sport. However, Donat said, Spearfish might be in a tougher spot than other youth sports.

“We honestly just have a hard time competing because Spearfish does not have an indoor facility to practice baseball effectively October through April,” Donat said. “When you don’t have a place to go pitch or hit in the winter, you just lose interest.”

So, he pitched a solution to the city council on Wednesday.

The SBA would like permission to build a 76-foot-wide by 96-foot-long steel indoor baseball practice facility at Black Hills Energy Sports Complex, between the baseball and soccer fields.

 SBA proposed location.png
SBA proposed location: The Spearfish Baseball Association wants to build an indoor baseball training facility at the Black Hills Energy Sports Complex, in the roughly the area pictured here. Aerial map courtesy city of Spearfish 

“It has city water and sewer adjacent to the south side of the building that runs into the existing concession stand and bathrooms that are on site today. Because of that building, it is also right next to existing electrical lines, natural gas lines, and so it has got everything that you need right there,” Donat said. “That is a site that is dead flat, so there is no major dirt work involved with the project.”

Pull quote
“When you don’t have a place to go pitch or hit in the winter, you just lose interest.” — Dave Donat, Spearfish Baseball Association

He added that Kevin Dailey of Dailey Construction, LLC, has offered to lead site-preparation efforts if the council approves the project.

“It is not a bunch of dads out there trying to put up a full building over the weekend. This would have 16-foot sidewalls, a steel building. These come in kits,” Donat said.

The SBA will work with the city to ensure the building meets all wind-load, snow-load, and engineering requirements, Donat said.

The total cost of the structure will likely be $400,000.

“We are trying to do this 100% on our own, without asking the city for a dollar,” Donat said.

Once the structure is built, the association intends to manage its upkeep, pay for the installation and ongoing costs associated with utilities, and insure the activities and kids playing inside the facility.

“Overall, what we are asking for from the city would be permission from the city (to build),” Donat said. “We would also be asking, upon completing the building construction, that the city would own the building, since we are building it on city land. It makes sense that the city would own the building and thus insure the building under the blanket coverage that the city has for structures.”

Donat said in exchange for covering all construction and maintenance costs, the association would like to negotiate a 30-year, renewable lease to use the building.

“If we are going to fundraise something like $400,000 and take that out of Spearfish Baseball and the program specifically to fund this thing, we feel that we should be able to control the operations inside this building,” Donat said.

Finance Officer Michelle DeNeui confirmed for the council that the SBA’s financial commitments could be locked into the terms of their lease. Donat said he would like to see a lease negotiated as soon as possible.

“Urgency has been my thing. We have had 2 building price increases since the beginning of May,” Donat said. “From council, what I am asking is, I would like to get the terms of the lease agreed to.”

With formal approval from the city, the SBA can confidently secure funds and order a building.

“If we had that, then baseball can operate the building itself, then I would feel confident enough to get the building ordered,” Donat said. “We are looking at a minimum of a 3-month turnaround to get the building landed. The contractors we’ve been in talks with can put it up from the end of October to the end of November. It is a one-month kit project. If we wait any longer, for another set of meetings, it can’t get done this year.”

Mayor John Senden said the soonest the topic can be discussed in a regular city council meeting is July 20, so that the city has time to get a formal quote for building insurance costs.

“Your request was to have it on the agenda for July 6. Our request was to have things firmed up more on a contract basis,” Senden said.

DeNeui said she has already requested a quote from the city’s insurance provider.

She noted that the council could opt to hold a special session to begin the process of lease approval.

DeNeui also reminded the council that Spearfish has an indoor baseball facility — that facility is a private business.

“My son grew up in the baseball association t-ball through Legion. We did indoor practice through South Dakota Premiere Workouts,” DeNeui said. “One thing I said to Rex was, ‘Let’s check with those business owners to make sure he is OK with it. This is a direct competition with him.’”

It turns out, the owner of South Dakota Premiere Workouts, Matt Kemp, is on the SBA board. He is aware and in support of the project. The city reached out to him, DeNeui said, and learned that he does not charge the SBA to use his indoor space.

If the SBA had its own space, it would free up time for him to book paying customers.

title: South Dakota Historical Society  publishes new Washington biography
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer
description: Gary Gregg II is the author of a new biography on George Washington. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Gregg headshot.jpg
Gary Gregg II is the author of a new biography on George Washington. Courtesy photo 

SPEARFISH — Gary Gregg II can’t avoid George Washington. For him, a political scientist who wrote his dissertation on the American presidency, Washington looms even larger than he does over the rest of the country. But after a chance conversation with a colleague on what turned out to be the 200th anniversary — give or take — of Washington’s death, Gregg decided to begin studying the first president in earnest. 

That was nearly 30 years ago. In the intervening time, Gregg has been studying and writing about Washington. His new biography, George Washington: “Citizen, Soldier, Statesman,” published this month by the South Dakota Historical Society Press, is the result of that time. 

In his later years, Gregg said, Washington cultivated the image of an aloof statesman. But much of the first half of the biography focuses on Washington’s time as a “raw laddie” gathering intelligence on French movements in Ohio. In that period, Gregg said, Washington didn’t yet have the evenhandedness he would later have as a statesman.

“He was an arrogant snot, frankly,” Gregg said. “But I think part of the story is that he grew out of that. So I think that’s the hopeful story for all of us.” 

 SDGREGG WASHINGTON CVR [17].jpg
Courtesy photo 

It’s hard to say exactly when Washington grew out of his arrogance. For the rest of his life, Washington would deliberately avoid making his personal life public. In particular, during his Revolutionary War service and his time as president — covered in the second half of the biography — Washington is often a blank slate. 

“Washington was already protecting his public image,” Gregg said, “And he’s not introspective, so his diaries don’t include bouts of depression, don’t include things that lots of us go through.” 

From time to time, the private Washington showed through the public persona, either in his frustration with a Congress that was reluctant to fund the Revolution, or his own insecurity about his lack of formal education. 

The most substantial of these personal interruptions was Washington’s mother, who usually disappears from Washington’s story around the time of his birth. Gregg reintroduces Mary Ball Washington into the story. For all of Washington’s achievements — and the biography does linger on his achievements — Mary Ball remained unimpressed.

“He defeated an empire,” Gregg said. “He is now the first president of the United States. He founded a nation. …And there’s nothing, really, in any letter or anything where she’s praising him.”

The end of the biography is devoted to the question of Washington’s relationship with slavery, which began at a shockingly young age.

“When he’s 11, he inherits his first enslaved human beings,” Gregg said. “At 11. … What does that do (to a person) psychologically?”

Washington would be a slaveholder for the rest of his life. But when Washington was dying at Mount Vernon, it seemed as though he had a crisis of conscience regarding his long participation in America’s “peculiar institution,” and arranged for his slaves to be freed — though only after the deaths of himself and his wife. 

“I’ve tried writing a whole postscript on Washington’s relationship to slavery, and I just felt I’m not adequate to do it,” Gregg said. “It’s too heavy. I’m not adequate to do it.”

Gregg is the McConnell Chair in Leadership at the University of Louisville and the director of the McConnell Center. He holds a Ph.D in political science from the University of Miami.

title: Deadwood Public Library showcases 150 years of newspapers
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: DEADWOOD — Deadwood and the Black Hills Pioneer have something in common — both are celebrating their 150th birthday this year.
_full_text:
DEADWOOD — Deadwood and the Black Hills Pioneer have something in common — both are celebrating their 150th birthday this year. 

In celebration of 150 years of shared history, an exhibit at the Deadwood Public Library shows off historic artifacts in the library’s South Dakota Room, a recreation of the first edition of the paper, and a curated selection of editions throughout the 150 years of printing on an interactive touch screen. 

Kennedy Penk, director of Deadwood Public Library, said the exhibit has been open since the end of April. In that time, she said the exhibit has been warmly received by patrons and visitors to Deadwood.  

“We got a lot of positive feedback and a lot of compliments,” said Penk. “Obviously Deadwood is rich in history, but the community loves (the exhibit). They think it’s a great addition to the room.”

Sherri Hall, curator of collections and exhibits at Deadwood History, Inc., said it took 6 months to create the exhibit. In that time, Hall said a team of archivists, representatives of the Black Hills Pioneer, and members of the city of Deadwood’s historic preservation team sifted through years of articles to select a collection that would accurately and succinctly represent Deadwood’s shared history with the newspaper. 

“That’s one thing with exhibits like this, is making sure that the information is as accurate as we can make it and that we have as much information that we can properly give the public,” said Hall. “It takes some time.”

To view the collection, which includes original type sets, a lead ingot, and information about how the Black Hills Pioneer came to Deadwood following the gold rush, visit Deadwood Public Library at 435 Williams St. The exhibit is free to the public and will be on display until the end of the year.

title: Quick picks: America 250th
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Quick Pick: America 250th
Courtesy photo 

To mark 250 years since our nation’s founding, we asked librarians at the Whitewood Public Library to recommend six titles to celebrate the America. 

1. “Unites States of America 250th Anniversary: A Children’s Adventure Through Time” by Cliff Merritt Hilton

Genre: Picture book

When Darcy and Zach discover a mysterious envelope sealed in red wax, they open the door to the adventure of a lifetime — guided by Libby, a witty, kind-hearted bald eagle who loves history almost as much as she loves apple pie.

2. “The American Story: 100 True Tales from American History” by Jennifer Armstrong 

Genre: History

American history comes alive in these 100 true stories that define our country.

 This magnificent treasury tells the story of America through 100 true tales. Some are tales of triumph — the midnight ride of Paul Revere, the Wright brothers taking to the air, Neil Armstrong’s first steps on the moon. Some are tales of tragedy — the fate of the Donner Party, the great fire in Chicago, the eruption of Mount Saint Helens.

3. The “Little House on the Prairie” series by Laura Ingalls Wilder

Genre: Classics/Historical fiction

Meet Laura Ingalls, the little girl who would grow up to write the Little House books.

Pa Ingalls decides to sell the little log house, and the family sets out for Indian country! They travel from Wisconsin to Kansas, and there, finally, Pa builds their little house on the prairie. Sometimes farm life is difficult, even dangerous, but Laura and her family are kept busy and are happy with the promise of their new life on the prairie.

4. “The Journey of Crazy Horse” by Joseph Marshall III

Genre: History/ Nonfiction

As a brilliant leader of a desperate cause and one of the most perennially fascinating figures of the American West, Crazy Horse crushed Custer’s 7th Cavalry and brought the United States Army to its knees. Now, with the help of celebrated historian Joseph Marshall, we finally have the opportunity to know Crazy Horse as his fellow Lakota Indians knew him.

5. “Medal of Honor: Profiles of America’s Military Heroes from the Civil War to the Present” by Allen Mikaelian

Genre: Nonfiction

Medal of Honor portrays 11 recipients of this sacred U.S. military decoration, from the Civil War through the Vietnam War, and examines what drove them to go so far above and beyond the call of duty. Among the stories is an account of the life of the only woman ever to receive the medal; of an officer who staged a daring escape from a German POW camp in WWI; and of a soldier from the legendary WWII Japanese-American 442nd, who went on to earn the medal in the Korean War. The book tells not only of astonishing military actions but also, significantly, of the recipients’ lives before and after their wartime experiences.

6. “A Patriot’s Handbook: Songs, Poems, Stories, and Speeches Celebrating the Land We Love” by Caroline Kennedy 

Genre: History

When John F. Kennedy called America “the land we love” more than 42 years ago, he was reminding us of the lofty ideals on which our country was founded. But what are those ideals, and how have Americans defined them? Is America the land of George Washington and Franklin Delano Roosevelt, who rallied the country’s spirits for unity in wartime, or is it a land of dissent, a land in which Frederick Douglass, Elizabeth Cady Stanton, and Martin Luther King, Jr. remind us of our duty to protect our most fundamental freedoms?

title: The Mercy Sloane Chronicles: Chapter 8
byline: By Eliza Blue A work of serialized fiction, special to the Pioneer
description: Mercy arrived back home with a new pot and pan, a small bag of coal, and a long roll of twine as an advance on her wages. She’d offered to pay with her savings, but Marla waved the offer away. “You keep that money for now,” was all she’d said.
_full_text:
The Mercy Sloane Chronicles

Mercy arrived back home with a new pot and pan, a small bag of coal, and a long roll of twine as an advance on her wages. She’d offered to pay with her savings, but Marla waved the offer away. “You keep that money for now,” was all she’d said.

So now Mercy was facing the potbelly stove that stood in her cabin’s corner. Mercy was a capable, competent girl. She could cook and clean with the ferocity you’d expect from someone who’d been doing both nearly since birth, but somehow, in all that time, she’d never been called upon to light a stove. It had been her mother’s job and later Augustine’s. It couldn’t be hard, could it? She just needed to boil enough water to cook some beans. But how much coal? And did one simply throw in a match? 

When Ardath rode up a short time later, she immediately jumped off her horse and ran toward Mercy’s house faster than she had run toward anything in years. Black smoke was billowing out the open door, and half a second later, a coughing, darkly smeared Mercy emerged as well. 

“Get water, ” Ardath shouted. “As much as you can,” but once inside, she saw that there was no fire, only smoke streaming out of the open door of the potbelly stove. “My goodness, girl!” Ardath laughed heartily with relief as she strode over and flipped a lever at the back of the stove, then slammed the stove’s door shut. “Did you forget to open your flue?”

“I don’t know what a flue is…” Mercy replied shakily, trying to laugh as well, but not finding it as easy as her neighbor. 

‘I figured you might be ready for a little help getting settled, and I guess I timed it right.” Ardath said, grabbing the rumpled blanket Mercy was still using as a bed to start fanning the remaining smoke outside the cabin.

***

When Ardath mounted her pony again hours later, dusk was gathering her bright colored flags above the distant buttes to the west, and the ghost of a full moon was rising in the east. There was a new twine laundry line hung between the sloped porch and the one mostly dead cottonwood tree that stood a few feet from the house. Ardath had cut and gathered the already cured grass to make hay, while Mercy sewed her two blankets together to make a mattress cover. They’d filled the mattress with the hay while beans boiled on the stove. Ardath smiled when she saw Mercy add her last bit of dried beef to the pot of water. “You know how to cook!” Ardath said, and Mercy nodded with shy pleasure. It was a relief to prove she wasn’t entirely useless after the debacle lighting the stove.  

The heat of the day was past, and the breeze sang a soft, companionable melody. The two had eaten in companionable silence on the edge of the porch, one from the new pot, one from the new pan, since there still was no table or chairs or dishes. The puppy’s portion they simply scraped onto the grass. Out beyond the yard, a jack rabbit hopped slowly by, stopping for a moment to stare at them, his tall ears quivering translucent above the golden grass. 

 Eliza Blue TMC
Eliza Blue 

“I don’t know what we were thinking,’ Mercy said against the rising song of the wind through the grass. “Coming out here with nothing but our clothes and two weeks’ worth of food.”

Ardath nodded, “I expect you’re not the first or last ones to make that mistake.” The older woman paused to eat a few more bites before she asked, “Did you name him yet?” 

“Name who?” said Mercy, looking at the jackrabbit who was now leaping away.

“Your dog!” said Ardath, laughing and pointing with her chin.

Mercy turned toward the puppy who had eaten his fill and was now chasing grasshoppers again, tripping over his own chubby belly every few steps.

“Not yet…I guess I’m not that good with names either.” She paused, watching the puppy, feeling a little ashamed because she was thinking again of Granger. 

“Hmmmm,” Ardath replied. She left another long pause before turning to face Mercy. “Here’s the thing about the prairie–it doesn’t matter how many supplies you show up with; you’ll run out eventually.” Ardath grabbed Mercy’s hand suddenly, squeezed it hard, and then smiled. “This prairie is hard to love sometimes, but she’s also hard to quit. You’ll find a way to make it work.”

title: Roosevelt’s Medal of Honor  gifted to his presidential library during its dedication
byline: By Jacob Orledge and Michael Achterling North Dakota Monitor
description: MEDORA, N.D. — President Donald Trump presented a new artifact for the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library during its dedication ceremony Wednesday — the Medal of Honor awarded to Roosevelt.
_full_text:
NorthDakotaMonitorLogo

MEDORA, N.D. — President Donald Trump presented a new artifact for the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library during its dedication ceremony Wednesday — the Medal of Honor awarded to Roosevelt. 

The medal had been displayed in the Roosevelt Room of the White House. 

“I thought this would be a … really appropriate place to have it,” Trump said after being introduced by Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, the former governor of North Dakota. 

Trump and Burgum cut the ribbon in a dedication ceremony for the library honoring Roosevelt, who credited his time in North Dakota for helping him become president. 

“What a magnificent library you built,” Trump said. “It’s a great tribute.”

Trump called the library a “living monument to a legend, statesman, soldier, frontiersman, and a true American hero.” He was effusive in his praise for Roosevelt and what he represents. 

“We come to the heartland of America to pay tribute to a man who embodied the heart and soul and fight and spirit of our country, as much as anyone who ever lived,” Trump said. “He was really quite something.”

The 47th president extolled Roosevelt’s achievements as president, such as constructing the Panama Canal and building the U.S. Navy into a global force, and the impact his tenure in the White House had on American prestige. 

Trump said Roosevelt had “transformed his country by the reach of his vision” and “by the force of his will” by the time the Rough Rider colonel died at the age of 60 in 1919. 

The United States had become “one of the greatest places, one of the greatest empires, one of the most incredible countries, ready to take its rightful place as the strongest and most respected nation anywhere in the world,” Trump said. 

The most enduring legacy of Roosevelt may be the principles behind his drive and determination. 

“He never stopped, never quit, never surrendered,” Trump said. “Again and again, he summoned the will to transcend tragedy and triumph and defeat heartbreak with hard work.”

Trump said some of those principles remain essential for Americans to aspire to for the country to survive and prosper. 

“Theodore Roosevelt reminds us all that to be a great nation, and to be a free nation, we must have courage. Without courage, you have nothing,” Trump said. “As TR once put it, freedom is not a gift that lasts long in the hands of cowards.”

The president also recommitted himself and the United States to that of another legacy, the Declaration of Independence that was signed 250 years ago this Saturday. 

“A government that was honest and accountable was the number one demand of the Declaration of Independence. They want honesty, they want respect, and on this anniversary we recommit ourselves to upholding that righteous legacy,” Trump said. 

Gov. Kelly Armstrong, who led off the slate of speakers in Medora Wednesday afternoon, urged every American to consider what they can do for their country moving forward. 

“As we celebrate these last 250 years of American greatness, we recognize that it is incumbent on each and every one of us to do our part to ensure that the next 250 years are better than the last,” Armstrong said.

The grand opening of the Theodore Roosevelt Presidential Library is being held in conjunction with the 250th anniversary of the United States’ declaration of independence from Great Britain. Roosevelt spent time in the western North Dakota Badlands after the death of his wife and mother, and famously said he would not have been president if not for his time in North Dakota.

title: Lead-Deadwood High School opens its doors to alternative students
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Erik Person, superintendent of the Lead-Deadwood School District, is taking on a new role as director of Gold Prospect Academy, a new alternative high school program scheduled to begin in the fall. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
Gold Prospect Academy.jpg
Erik Person, superintendent of the Lead-Deadwood School District, is taking on a new role as director of Gold Prospect Academy, a new alternative high school program scheduled to begin in the fall. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

LEAD — Students seeking to complete their high school diploma outside of a traditional setting now have a new option with the opening of Gold Prospect Academy in the Lead-Deadwood High School. 

Erik Person, superintendent of Lead-Deadwood School District, will serve as the academy director. He said the academy came from an observed need for a non-traditional option for students in the area as the high school saw increasing numbers of students choosing to homeschool. 

“Our primary responsibility is to serve the kids in our school district. We see more and more people are talking about school choice,” said Person. “We just really see a need in our own district where we need to serve our kids better. Maybe there are some kids with special circumstances that we probably need to work with. Before it was kind of, ‘Here’s our program, take it or leave it.’ That paradigm is really shifting.”

In researching other alternative schools in the area, Person and school board members visited Second Chance High in Mitchell, the alternative program at Sturgis Brown High School, and Boxelder Job Corps. During those visits, Person learned that what made those models successful were shared goals between staff and students, strong relationships, and flexibility. 

“One of the things that we really learned from when we went and visited Job Corps was, we saw that those kids are highly motivated to get their academic work knocked out and they want to get that diploma,” said Person. “They don’t really have discipline problems at Job Corps because it’s all about giving the kids what they need to achieve that goal, and everybody has that shared goal. Sometimes, in the regular public schools, we have a system that works for most kids but not all kids. The system is predicated on having a pretty standard model, and part of that model is, ‘We need to have you here from this time to this time. These are the classes that you take to work towards your diploma.’ I think that for some kids, that just doesn’t work as well.”

Person said that in visiting Second Chance High, the program he called the most flexible, he said that he and board members were impressed by the school’s ability to build programs that could be molded to each student’s needs. 

“We tried to take all of those things that we learned from those different places and put it into what we thought we were identifying as needs with our kids,” said Person. 

Person said that when students apply to Gold Prospect Academy, students will need to include a brief written statement declaring why they believe the academy could be a good fit for them, 2 references (preferably from a previous educator), and a copy of their transcripts. On the application, students are encouraged to select all reasons why a traditional school setting hasn’t worked for them. Reasons include failing 2 or more classes, dropping out of school the year before, returning to public school from a homeschool setting, completing 4 years of high school without earning a diploma, pregnancy or providing care for small children, and social, medical, or attendance issues. 

 Within 10 days of receiving a complete application, Person said an interview will be scheduled between the prospective student, himself acting as academy director, and a school counselor. In that meeting, Person said he’ll talk with students to decide what they need to be successful before creating a student learning contract. 

“That’s going to put into writing what the school is going to do for them and what efforts (the student) is going to make to be successful,” said Person. “We’re looking at it as an investment in our future and the student’s future, and we want to try to make sure we get a return on that investment.”

Person said the academy will employ an online, in-class hybrid model using Edgenuity, an online learning platform that conforms to South Dakota content standards. Four core content educators at Lead-Deadwood High School have been assigned as instructors of record — the teachers will have an assigned hour to offer additional tutoring to students while monitoring grades and progress. The school has hired one full-time paraprofessional, whose job it will be to supervise students while they’re in the classroom and help with troubleshooting and staying on track. 

Person said that using an online hybrid model allows the school to create a flexible schedule to accommodate students who may need to work or care for small children — 2 factors that he guesses have contributed in large ways to students dropping out of a traditional high school setting.  

While meeting their core subject requirements online, students interested in the Gold Prospect Academy are encouraged to also partake in extracurriculars and electives while enrolled in the academy, offering them a unique opportunity to participate in athletics and take an art or career and technical education course. Person said the opportunity allows alternative students to still take advantage of opportunities a traditional high school would offer without segregation into a strictly alternative classroom.

“That would be one of the things I would do as a director when I put together their learning plan. If they want to take art, here’s when an art class is offered Things that they might want that are in the traditional high school setting, some of those classes are going to stiffen up their schedule a little bit and we’ll have to build around it,” said Person. “But these kids that need this alternative setting, a lot of times it’s not an all or nothing deal — it’s not like if they’ve had some struggles with the traditional classroom, they’re not typically unsuccessful in every classroom setting.”

In the short-term, Person said the goal of Gold Prospect Academy is to help provide a previously unmet need in the Lead-Deadwood area. In the long-term, though, Person said he’s hoping to bolster enrollment numbers and welcome back students who have left to pursue homeschool out of frustration with the traditional school setting. 

“This isn’t going to be like every kid that homeschools should be in the alternative school,” said Person. “But I think there’s a fair number that have chosen the homeschool route because traditional school wasn’t working for them. I think we will retain some more of those students and find a better path for them within our walls, and I think this could slow down some of that exodus. I’m really hopeful that even if we could bring back some of the kids in the area who have tone the homeschool route, that if they have the right support and the right flexibility, maybe they would come back to the public school.”

Person warned people interested in the alternative school that summer goes quickly, and the beginning of the next school year is coming fast. 

“I would ask people to not delay,” said Person. “Go to our website, it takes a couple of clicks and get that application. If you are unable to find it, reach out to the school and we’ll help you get signed up.”

To learn more about Gold Prospect Academy and view the application, visit https://www.lead-deadwood.k12.sd.us/page/alt-school. 

For more information please contact the school at (605) 717-3898.

title: Local fire departments respond to fireworks-caused fires
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Local fire departments respond to  fireworks-caused fires
Courtesy photo 

LEAD — In Lead, firefighters were busy putting out spot fires at the launch site for the main fireworks show over the Open Cut. Lead Fire Chief Nathan Allen said the fires spanned about one-10th of an acre, and at one point crews ran out of water and had to call for reinforcements. The fires were extinguished in about 20 minutes, he said. 

“We haven’t had that happen for quite a few years, but it can happen,” Allen said. 

Allen added that the fire department had 2 firefighters and a brush truck stationed at the launch site, who did the initial attack on the fires. A crew of 4 were stationed at the park, and 2 firefighters were on standby at the fire station to provide more water if needed. 

Right before crews ran out of water at the launch site, Allen said fire crews in the park responded to an area near the skate park, where some youth playing with fireworks set a small fire. A Lead police officer was able to control that one with a fire extinguisher, and it was out before the firefighters arrived. 

Overall, Allen said he is happy with the way the weekend went, and he said there were no other incidents over the course of the weekend. 

“I think it went well,” he said. “It was a really good parade and everything went well. You always take a little bit of a risk having the fireworks up there in the summer. That’s why we have the crews. We were a little surprised the spread was a little quicker than we thought it would be. But they got on top of it.” 

In Spearfish, the co-owner of Cycle Farms, Jeremy Smith, was cleaning up after putting in a day’s work on Sunday, when he heard sirens. 

His neighbor’s field, adjacent to where Cycle Farms grows its vegetables was on fire. 

“One of our neighbors started a grass fire with a firework,” Smith said. “It was windy, and blowing towards the vegetable fields.” 

Trish Jenkins, also a co-owner of Cycle Farms, said the circumstances were scary. “We are so grateful for the fire department. It is neat that we have such a dedicated volunteer crew.” 

Neither Jenkins nor Smith saw any structural damage, and said they were relieved the fire didn’t spread. However, they both told the Pioneer they hope their neighbors will be cautious with fireworks in the future. 

Smith noted that the area is under fire restrictions, and that fire risk is a challenge throughout the Hills this year. 

Charles Fetter, fire technician at Deadwood Volunteer Fire Department, said the department responded to 3 incidents over the holiday weekend. Of the 3 incidents, only one was related to fireworks.

On Sunday, Fetter said the department responded to fireworks-related grassfire near the Broadway Parking Ramp. He said the incident was contained within 20 minutes. 

Fetter said the other 2 incidents over the weekend included a truck with hot brakes on Friday and a single vehicle accident involving a motorcycle between the Preacher Smith Monument and The Lodge at Deadwood Saturday afternoon. 

Going into another hot and dry weekend, Fetter asked that residents continue to practice fire safety and refrain from using any fire pits while the fire dangers are very high or extreme. 

“It is so dry right now that it’s not funny,” said Fetter. “It’s important that people practice extreme fire safety and stay hydrated. Drink plenty of fluids if you’re planning on enjoying any recreation this weekend. Hydration is key to making sure you don’t get sick.”

title: Company proposing Black Hills uranium mine eyes state permitting restart after 13-year pause
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Pictured is the site of the proposed Dewey-Burdock uranium mine in Fall River County. Photo courtesy of U.S. Bureau of Land Management
_full_text:
Company proposing Black Hills uranium mine eyes state permitting restart after 13-year pause.jpg
Pictured is the site of the proposed Dewey-Burdock uranium mine in Fall River County. Photo courtesy of U.S. Bureau of Land Management 

HOT SPRINGS — A company spearheading a long-lingering uranium mining proposal in southwestern South Dakota hopes to restart its state permitting process after a 13-year hold.

The Dewey-Burdock project — spanning nearly 20 square miles in Custer and Fall River counties — secured the last of its necessary federal permits for the project last month, according to the federal Permitting Council. The project was included last year in FAST-41, a federal process meant to improve coordination among permitting agencies and hold them accountable to deadlines. 

The project, decades in the making, was added to the process in August of last year. Dewey-Burdock — named for rural locations near Edgemont along the southwestern edge of the Black Hills — requires numerous federal, state and local permits and has been mired in administrative and court appeals for years.

The mining method for the project is “in situ”: drilling wells to inject a water-based solution underground, dissolving uranium and pumping it to the surface. The water would be pulled from local aquifers and then treated and pumped back underground after being used for mining, causing opponents to fear pollution of local water sources. 

Emily Domenech, Permitting Council executive director, said in a news release that the fast-tracking process advanced the project, which is “critical to national security and energy dominance.” Uranium is a metallic, radioactive element used as fuel in nuclear weapons and nuclear power plants.

EnCore Energy Executive Chair William Sheriff said in a news release that the company plans to begin the state permitting process next. 

The South Dakota Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources confirmed that the company submitted new water-rights applications and supporting information. The company has not yet submitted new applications for mine or groundwater discharge permits, said Brian Walsh, department spokesman.

The timeline for processing state permits is “difficult to predict,” Walsh added, depending on the “level of public participation.”

The project’s state applications have been inactive since 2013, while the federal permitting process played out. The South Dakota Water Management Board rejected the company’s request to restart its water permitting process in 2021, due in part to outstanding federal permits and active litigation.

“I just don’t think it’s appropriate for the state of South Dakota and this board to spend millions of dollars once again on an issue and then have the rug pulled out from under our feet after we’ve made a decision,” board member Rodney Freeman said at the time.

Lilias Jarding, executive director of the Black Hills Clean Water Alliance, has been a vocal opponent of the Dewey-Burdock project for years. She is concerned about potential water contamination and the amount of water needed for the project. She expects opponents to push back and attempt to appeal federal permits, which she said could affect the state process and overall project.

“The people don’t want this,” Jarding said. “There will be public pushback.”

The Oglala Sioux Tribe and NDN Collective, a Rapid City-based Indigenous advocacy group, have also opposed the project, citing concerns about potential impacts to historic and cultural sites in the Black Hills — land central to the spiritual beliefs and practices of many tribes.

The same groups also oppose a proposal to conduct exploratory drilling for uranium near Craven Canyon, not far from the Dewey-Burdock project area. A hearing on the permit application for the drilling plan, from Canadian company Nexus Uranium, is on hold as a court considers a lawsuit from a project opponent.

title: GF&P updates depredation  hunt permit numbers
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: The South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks Commission set permit numbers for depredation hunts for the next 3 years at their June meeting. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Doe deer.JPG
The South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks Commission set permit numbers for depredation hunts for the next 3 years at their June meeting. Pioneer file photo 

MADISON — A resolution authorizing depredation hunts in the state will expire this year, but the South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks Commission set new parameters for the hunts at their June meeting. 

The resolution is good for the next 3 years, and authorizes the GF&P to issue no more than 600 permits, plus an additional 200 landowner/operator permits per year for deer, antelope, or turkeys, and no more than 100 elk depredation permits per year.

John Kanta, terrestrial section chief with the GF&P Rapid City office, told the commission that depredation hunts are just one of the ways the agency responds to wildlife damage complaints from landowners. When harsh winters or population issues lead to wildlife congregating on private land and eating stored feed, or causing other damage, GF&P wildlife damage specialists use food plots, fencing, netting, and other resources to try and re-direct the animals. But sometimes, Kanta said, pool hunts are used as a last resort to put pressure on herds to move off the land. 

“These are an opportunity for the department to open a hunt on private property in a very specific area, and so a lot of times we’re dealing with wildlife that are congregating over winter in big groups and hitting one or 2 private properties,” Kanta said. “We have used pool hunts very sparingly, and honestly, in the last several years we have had just one or 2 pool hunts that have popped up for deer. In the last couple of years it’s been very manageable and slow, and we’ve been able to address these requests for service with our other wildlife damage tools.” 

Kanta said each December hunters are invited to sign up for the depredation hunt list online. Then, if a hunt is needed, the department randomizes that list and picks individuals to participate in the controlled hunt. 

“In most all of the cases these are not intended to manage populations,” Kanta said. “It’s intended to put some pressure on those animals and push them off of, typically stored feeds. They’re not meant to significantly impact population numbers, just to provide a precise response to that request for service.” 

GF&P Secretary Kevin Robling said in the 5 years he has been the secretary, he can “count on one hand” the number of depredation hunts that have been held. 

Kanta further explained that elk depredation hunts can be held at any time of the year, outside of the regular elk season. But pool hunts for turkey, pronghorn, deer, and other species can only be held Aug. 15 to March 31 of the following year.

title: Lawrence County could grant $8,500 for mining museum lot repair
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: The parking/display lot at the Black Hills Mining Museum was closed to the public in early May, after some holes in the lot started to get larger, posing a safety risk. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
mining museum 1.jpeg
The parking/display lot at the Black Hills Mining Museum was closed to the public in early May, after some holes in the lot started to get larger, posing a safety risk. Pioneer file photo 

DEADWOOD — Lawrence County Commissioners are expected to consider taking $8,500 out of its contingency fund to pay for engineering plans to fix the Black Hills Mining Museum parking lot, July 14. 

During the June 23 Lawrence County Commission meeting, June 23, Gordon Phillips, executive director of the Black Hills Mining Museum, asked the commission for $8,500. The money, Phillips said, would pay Interstate Engineering to create construction design plans and cost estimates for fixing major structural issues at the museum parking lot, located on Main Street in Lead. 

In May, museum officials closed the area adjacent to the mining museum building, which is currently used as a display lot, after they noticed holes in the parking lot that had gotten larger. At that time, Phillips said the Black Hills Mining Museum board was exploring permanent solutions to fix structural problems with the parking lot that had been ongoing for many years. Phillips told the Pioneer in May that possible plans were to remove the top parking structure, and to open the lower level, which opens up at Julius Street, to be used for museum display space. 

 mining museum 2.jpeg
Pioneer file photo 

The biggest problem, Phillips said, is that a portion of the mining museum building, and the main entrance to the museum, is on the failing parking lot. The building’s emergency egress exits also lead to the upper and lower levels of the parking lot. 

“That structure has a big impact on our ability to get people in and out safely,” he said. “The ultimate goal will be its demolition. The first phase of that overall project will be to shore up the portion of the structure, which leads up to and lies directly beneath our entry.” 

But before they can do anything, the museum board needs engineering design plans for the project. Those plans will cost $8,500, Phillips said during his presentation to the commission. 

Originally, Phillips asked for the money from the mining severance tax fund. However, on June 23 Deputy States Attorney Bruce Outka presented the commission with state statute that outlines eligible projects for those funds. According to South Dakota Codified Law 10-39-54.3, the mining severance tax funds can be used for road and school purposes, for various economic development purposes, or for research activities related to expansion and diversification of the economic base. 

“Ironically this is the mining severance tax fund and this is a request from the mining museum. It’s not immediately clear to me where it fits in the schedule,” Outka said. 

Commissioners agreed with Outka, who suggested that the commission consider granting the money from the county’s contingency fund. While commissioners said they generally support the idea, they will wait to take action on the request when it is on the agenda for the next meeting, July 14.

title: Thousands flood Lead for weekend events
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: A small crowd enjoyed great music at Mountain Top Field for the Rock the Hills concert on Friday. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
LEAD 150th concert crowd.JPG
A small crowd enjoyed great music at Mountain Top Field for the Rock the Hills concert on Friday. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

LEAD — Four days of continuous activity drew thousands of people to Lead to celebrate the 150th anniversary of the town’s settlement, and the 100th anniversary of Gold Camp Jubilee Days. 

Events kicked off on Thursday with the original play, “More than Gold,” written by Lead Historic Preservation Chairman Terry Smith and Historic Homestake Opera House Executive Director Todd Jones. The play, directed by Shirlene Joseph, drew a record crowd of approximately 350 people to the opera house to watch the history of Lead unfold to historical music that was written by Lead natives. 

On Friday, a car show and live music drew a crowd that braved the rain at the Sanford Lab Homestake Visitor’s Center parking lot. At Mountain Top Field, where the Rock the Hills Concert was staged with 4 bands playing throughout the day, crowds were much smaller. Mayor Dustin Heupel said Lead City Administrator Robin Lucero will have information about crowd sizes and costs at the next city commission meeting, July 20. 

On Saturday, sunshine and clear skies drew thousands of people to Lead, with nearly every city street packed with cars from all over the country, as people enjoyed festivities in the park. A trolley provided continuous transportation throughout the day between Lead and Deadwood. A watermelon-eating contest, live music, bounce houses, a nearly hour-long parade, and more kept crowds in Lead until after the popular fireworks show. 

 LEAD 150th concert.JPG
The Lexington Lab Band, of Kentucky, headlined the Rock the Hills concert on Friday with cover selections from the 1970s and 1980s. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

On Sunday, a smaller, more local, and very enthusiastic crowd celebrated Lead’s 27-7 victory over Deadwood in the vintage baseball game at Mountain Top Field. Afterward, participants and spectators enjoyed a community lunch at the field. 

Weekend festivities concluded with a performance and historical slide show by pianist Nina McIntire, and the announcement that the city of Lead is collecting items for a 50-year time capsule. 

 LEAD watermelon girl.JPG
Many kids competed for cash prizes at the third annual watermelon-eating contest, Saturday. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

Jami Grangaard, director of the Lead Area Chamber of Commerce, said the weekend was a huge success. 

“We are absolutely blown away by the incredible turnout we saw over the holiday weekend,” she said. “Even with the rain and cooler temperatures, our car show was a huge success on July 3 and this year’s Fourth of July celebration was truly one for the books. Everywhere you looked, people were out enjoying everything our community had to offer. The park was packed, the food trucks sold out, and I spoke with several of our member businesses who reported record-breaking sales on Saturday. We also received an overwhelming amount of positive feedback about the trolley service. It was a fun and convenient addition that visitors really embraced, and we’re excited to explore making it a permanent part of our Fourth of July celebration in the future.”

title: SD board advances rules allowing $30 million in airport loans from housing fund
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — A South Dakota board advanced rules on Wednesday that allow up to $30 million to be loaned from a state housing infrastructure fund to help finance airport projects in Rapid City and Sioux Falls.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — A South Dakota board advanced rules on Wednesday that allow up to $30 million to be loaned from a state housing infrastructure fund to help finance airport projects in Rapid City and Sioux Falls.

The Housing Development Authority’s members approved the rules without any opposition. The rules implement a bill introduced at Gov. Larry Rhoden’s request and signed into law by him in March. 

The law authorizes loans up to $15 million each to the state’s two largest commercial airports. The loans would carry 2% interest rates with repayment periods of 20 years. Repayments and interest must be returned to the housing fund to support future housing infrastructure projects. 

Rapid City plans a concourse expansion adding five gates and more passenger space. Sioux Falls is building a new concourse that will provide up to five additional aircraft gates and 57,000 square feet of seating and circulation space. The projects are expected to cost more than $100 million apiece. 

The Legislature and former Gov. Kristi Noem created the housing fund and program in 2023 with $200 million: $100 million for grants and $100 million for loans to support streets, sewer, water, and other infrastructure needed for housing developments. The package used $150 million in state money and $50 million in federal American Rescue Plan funds.  

By late 2025, about $65 million remained on the loan side. The program has helped finance 87 projects expected to produce 7,464 single-family lots and 5,882 multifamily units.  

The housing board’s rule change now goes to the Legislature’s Interim Rules Review Committee.

title: 40th annual McBride Military Appreciation BBQ celebrates local heroes
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: RAPID CITY — For 4 decades, the McBride Military BBQ has brought the Black Hills community together to recognize and celebrate the service and sacrifice of our local military and their families.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

RAPID CITY — For 4 decades, the McBride Military BBQ has brought the Black Hills community together to recognize and celebrate the service and sacrifice of our local military and their families.

As the event marks its 40th anniversary, the Black Hills community proudly honors the airmen of Ellsworth Air Force Base and the soldiers of the South Dakota National Guard for their steadfast commitment to protecting our nation and strengthening our local communities.

Hosted by Black Hills Military Advisory Coalition (BHMAC), the 40th Annual McBride Military BBQ will take place from 5-7 p.m., Friday at the Central States Fairgrounds in Rapid City. 

What began as a simple community barbecue and potluck has grown into one of the region’s most cherished events. The event welcomes more than 500 military families and community members each year for an evening full of gratitude, celebration, and connection. 

The event is free and open to the public, though tickets are required for prize purposes. Attendees can enjoy a variety of family-friendly activities, including a kids’ zone, first responder displays, entertainment prior to the program, and the beloved traditional barbecue and pig roast.

title: ‘How do I keep going:?’  Farmer mental health solutions
byline: By Elena Tittel South Dakota News Watch
description: MT. VERNON — About 20 miles from Mitchell sits a 100-year-old barn. Merely driving by, it looks like nothing out of the ordinary: just one of many such farming landmarks off of I-90 surrounded by fields of crops and tall grass.
_full_text:
SDNewsWatchLogo

MT. VERNON — About 20 miles from Mitchell sits a 100-year-old barn. Merely driving by, it looks like nothing out of the ordinary: just one of many such farming landmarks off of I-90 surrounded by fields of crops and tall grass.

That barn belongs to Colleen Stegenga, a licensed clinical social worker and therapist who runs Embracing Change Counseling Services.

Stegenga grew up on a cattle farm about 5 miles from where she currently lives. When one of her family members who ran the family farm had a health crisis three years ago, she and her siblings came together to help out.

“It was a crazy few weeks because it was planting season, the cows still needed to be milked and he still had bills to pay. And so that’s when I started to realize farmers have a lot of stuff they have to deal with,” Stegenga said. “I got a really brief snapshot when I was working with my family. Like how do these people do this?”

Shortly thereafter, she decided to put more focus into helping the agricultural community by transforming an old barn into a safe place offering mental health services. Once the clinic opens in August, she hopes to later incorporate horses, mini highland cows and babydoll sheep.

Work on the farm never ends. 

“(People tell me) how do I keep going? I’m not sleeping, the bank is telling me I have to come up with more collateral and I don’t know what I’m going to do,” Stegenga said.

Karl Oehlke, a physician assistant on the Avera Behavioral Health team, said there is a longstanding history of stigma surrounding mental health among not just agricultural communities but Midwesterners in general.

Because some farmers feel pressure to tough it out, they may fear being recognized while using in-person services such as seeing a live therapist, attending an alcoholics anonymous meeting or even picking up a psychiatric prescription at the local pharmacy.

“I heard a number of folks say that their primary care providers are the same person they see at church or go to a basketball game at the high school with,” Oehlke said. “They’re quite comfortable talking about a plan for cholesterol or diabetes or a broken arm. But divulging that they are having issues psychiatrically is even harder in that situation.”

However, many of those who feel comfortable going in person often can’t.

South Dakota currently has a statewide mental health care provider shortage. Of the state’s 66 counties, only 4 – McCook, Minnehaha, Turner and Lincoln – do not have a geographic shortage of mental health care providers. Those 4 counties instead have a population shortage. A population shortage refers to a shortage of providers within a defined geographic area for a specific group of people, such as those who are low-income or face cultural or social barriers.

For patients of Stegenga’s who cannot easily get to her in-person offices, have fear of being recognized or cannot step away from work, she has found virtual services – whether a phone call or a video chat – to be just as successful.

“I do have people that just step out into their car on their lunch break, and we can do therapy that way,” Stegenga said. “You don’t have to leave work, or for my farmers and ranchers, ‘Hey, if you’re in the field, just get your phone propped up, and we can talk,’ so it is really helpful.”

Dr. David Newman, chief medical officer of virtual care at Sanford Health in Fargo, N.D., said the health center’s virtual care system took off in 2021 after receiving a $350 million virtual care investment.

In 2025, patients who used the virtual services saved an estimated $41 million by reducing the need to take time off from work and pay for travel-related expenses.

For patients of Horizon Health and Monument Health –  two other large health care systems in South Dakota – in-person and virtual services are also available. 

Telehealth appointments are not the only virtual behavioral health resource. Those wanting immediate support from a mental health professional can utilize 24/7 hotlines such as 988 (formally the National Suicide Prevention Line) and the Farm and Rural Stress Hotline (800-691-4436).

title: Police chief to address Spearfish motorized  vehicle concerns, enforcement tonight
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — During this evening’s city council meeting, Police Chief Collin Smith is scheduled to present an enforcement action plan for the motorized electric vehicles, often identified as e-dirt bikes, that have generated community concern about rec path, roadway, and sidewalk safety.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

SPEARFISH — During this evening’s city council meeting, Police Chief Collin Smith is scheduled to present an enforcement action plan for the motorized electric vehicles, often identified as e-dirt bikes, that have generated community concern about rec path, roadway, and sidewalk safety.

Smith previewed his presentation Wednesday. He said officers are already enforcing applicable statutes, but it took time and intention to determine which statutes apply where.

“What you’ll be hearing today we have already put into place. We have already started our enforcement efforts,” Smith said. “That is where, I stress, I appreciate your patience while we learned how we were going to address this. In my world, we have to do it under the very specific language of the law.”

Smith referenced 3 state statutes: South Dakota Codified Law (SDCL) 32-26-21.1, SDCL 32-30-9, and SDCL 32-20-12.

SDCL 32-22-21.1 outlines who can and cannot use sidewalks in the state. “No person may drive any vehicle other than a bicycle, motorized foot scooter, or an electric personal assistive device upon a sidewalk or sidewalk area except upon a permanent or duly authorized temporary driveway.” A violation of that statute is a class 2 misdemeanor, punishable by up to 30 days in a county jail, a $500 fine, or both.

SDCL 32-20-9 applies to motorcycles, prohibiting their use anywhere except normal roadways or designated areas. 

Lastly, SDCL 32-20-12 deals with off-road vehicles and their permitted uses.

“No person may operate on a public street or highway an off-road vehicle except for crossing from one side of the road to the other. A person twelve years of age or older may operate an off-road vehicle in a highway ditch if the vehicle is operated as close as possible to the outer edge of the highway right-of-way,” the chapter reads.

Smith said when residents see a vehicle traveling on the sidewalk or rec path and report reckless driving, it is helpful to officers to have as detailed a description of the vehicle as possible.

“Reckless driving and careless driving is applicable; I want people to be aware, no matter what they’re on. If it is an e-bike, or whatever it might be, if we see reckless or dangerous use, we are going to stop them,” Smith said.

He said officers are stopping vehicles with the goal of educating and warning the often very young drivers.

“What we are doing right now is education. I want to make it very clear my intention is not to be citing juveniles for this type of thing,” Smith said. “I am partnering this with, now we have a legal reason to make contact with them, get them off the road, and let the parents handle it. Do they (officers) have leeway to cite if necessary? Yes, but my walking orders are not to be cutting 12-year-olds citations.”

title: Tough Enough to Wear Pink saddles up to support local patients during Days of ‘76
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Laurie Wince, executive director of Foundation for Health, said the Tough Enough to Wear Pink annual fundraiser typically raises enough money to allow the foundation to do good deeds for an entire year. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
Laurie 2.JPG
Laurie Wince, executive director of Foundation for Health, said the Tough Enough to Wear Pink annual fundraiser typically raises enough money to allow the foundation to do good deeds for an entire year. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

DEADWOOD — Every year, the historic grandstands at the Days of ’76 rodeo grounds fill with a wave of pink shirts as communities unite their voices under one movement: that they are, in fact, tough enough to wear pink.

Laurie Wince, executive director of the Foundation for Health in Lead, Deadwood, and Beyond, said she’s been part of the annual Tough Enough to Wear Pink fundraiser for 14 years. In that time, she said she’s seen the communities come together in a full circle movement to help the foundation raise monies to provide assistance to people in the Northern Hills gain access to critical treatments in their battle against breast cancer and other terminal illnesses. 

“We purchase our shirts locally, we design the logos locally, we sell the shirts locally, and we give the money back locally,” said Wince. “So, it’s all about doing everything we can in the Northern Hills to help as many people as we can in the process.”

Wince said t-shirts with a new Tough Enough to Wear Pink logo is sold for at least $15 every year with the intention of filling Deadwood and the grandstands with a supportive, pink crowd on “pink day” during the Days of ’76 rodeo. This year, the event falls on Friday, July 24, where Wince said people can unite in a common fight — one that she said most people are all too familiar with. 

“Most people have prayed for or have helped people in their own ways, either been on a meal train or gone to visit and try to support people who have illnesses of all different kinds, breast cancer being just one of them,” said Wince. “It brings people together — rodeos do that anyway, but this fundraiser really brings people. It brings people from all over the United States to our community, and it helps people feel like they’re part of a good thing. The goodwill that is felt by so many people is outstanding.”

 Tough Enough to Wear Pink logos.jpg
Every year, Foundation for Health sells a t-shirt with a new Tough Enough to Wear Pink design. The monies are used to help terminally ill patients in the Northern Hills access critical treatments. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

Wince said the money raised is accessible to anyone battling breast cancer or other critical illnesses from St. Onge to Lead, regardless of income threshold. 

“Philosophically, we believe everyone should feel that their community cares about them, even if they have money or if they don’t have money,” said Wince. “Every request we get I bring it to the board, and we decide as a group if it’s something we can do.”

The mission of the Foundation, said Wince, is to help people in rural areas more easily access treatment and support systems to help improve their health and safety. To make that mission possible, the Tough Enough to Wear Pink fundraiser, what Wince called a “pink bubble,” raises funds that can go from anything to repairing headlights so a patient can travel during winter evenings in their own car, airline tickets, or lodging or meals. 

In recent years, Wince said the Foundation for Health has started donating between $15,000-20,000 in prepaid Visa gift cards to the Cancer Care Institute, which distributes the cards to patients who need them. 

“We found out that they know all of those people, and we only know some of them,” said Wince. “So, we hit a greater number of people in our communities by having (the Cancer Care Institute) help us find them.”

This year, Wince said the Foundation for Health will have a table near the entrance to the rodeo, where people can ask questions and access information about prevention and treatment, including where people can go for mammograms locally. Wince said a team will also be there, selling t-shirts.

“The thing that we hear, over and over and over again at that event, is so much gratitude,” said Wince. “It could even be a person who doesn’t receive funds from us. The gratitude that we are shown because of this campaign, whether it’s in the form of a card, donation, or words, it’s very, very neat. It reminds us of why we have to look out beyond ourselves, whether it’s illness or helping someone with something else. People need it. They need that help.”

Last year, Wince said the foundation sold approximately 3,000 shirts between July and October. This year, she’s hoping to sell 2,800 shirts the week of the rodeo. 

“If you think about it, if we have people spending $15 and we sell that many shirts, it’s enough to last us the whole year. It allows us to go beyond and do good things,” said Wince. “Everybody does a little bit, and that’s how it should be.”

Wince said shirts are now available for purchase at Lynn’s Dakotamart in Lead, Bomgaars and 2 Broke Girls Boutique in Spearfish, and through the foundation’s website, foundation4health.com.

title: SURF celebrates 18TH annual Neutrino Day
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Hands-on activities like these are fun for all ages and take place at multiple locations across the town of Lead during Neutrino Day. Photo courtesy of Matthew Kapust
_full_text:
Neutrino-Day-1-by-Matthew Kapust.jpg
Hands-on activities like these are fun for all ages and take place at multiple locations across the town of Lead during Neutrino Day. Photo courtesy of Matthew Kapust 

LEAD — On Saturday, the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) will host the 18th annual Neutrino Day in Lead. This free, citywide science festival features hoistroom tours, science activities and exhibits for all ages, free lectures and performances, and live video chats with engineers and scientists underground.  

 Neutrino Day 2024
The Historic Homestake Opera House is one of the centers of action during Neutrino Day, with free live talks and performances throughout the day. Photo courtesy of Laine Brost 

Neutrino Day takes place at locations across Lead, including the Sanford Lab Homestake Visitor Center; the Sanford Underground Research Facility Yates Hoistroom; Changleska Wakhan, the SURF ethnobotanical garden; the Handley Recreation Center; the Hampton Inn; and the Historic Homestake Opera House. Attendees are encouraged to start the day by registering at the Sanford Lab Homestake Visitor Center, then take a shuttle or stroll along Main Street to other festival locations throughout Lead. 

This year features a performance by Steve Rokusek, who is known as Science Steve, of South Dakota Public Broadcasting. Hands-on science activities include the University of Colorado’s Little Shop of Physics, with experiences that make science accessible to everyone. The South Dakota School of Mines and Technology will also be present with their popular homemade liquid nitrogen ice cream and other STEM activities, including the university’s Museum of Geology. There will be more than 40 interactive booths and spaces with hands-on learning for people of all ages.

The day includes live music by Sequoia Crosswhite at SURF’s ethnobotanical garden. Additional music will be provided at the Homestake Opera House by the One-Armed Bandits, a Spearfish-based trio. Join an underground live stream from the DUNE caverns, learn the story of SURF at a talk titled SURF 101, ask physicists questions during an open-panel discussion, and hear the latest on the deep underground neutrino experiment (DUNE) now being built at SURF.

title: GF&P highlights user facilities
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: The South Dakota Department of Game, Fish, and Parks reported record numbers of campers over Memorial Day weekend. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
camping.jpeg
The South Dakota Department of Game, Fish, and Parks reported record numbers of campers over Memorial Day weekend. Pioneer file photo  

MADISON — Memorial Day saw a record number of campers across the state park system, Jeff VanMeeteren, parks division director told the S.D. Game, Fish, and Parks Commission recently. 

VanMeeteren said the state parks system includes 4,500 campsites at 115 different campgrounds. Over Memorial Day weekend, he said the parks hosted 4,324 sites used for those 3 days of the weekend — running at more than 95% capacity. 

“That’s pretty incredible when you think about it,” he said. “We have sites that, quite honestly, aren’t in maybe the most desirable locations.” 

During the commission’s June meeting, VanMeeteren delivered a synopsis of infrastructure and facilities that support visitors and users across the state. 

“Most of our visitors primarily focus on our campgrounds, our beaches, our trails, our boat ramps, and our lodging,” he said. “But behind the scenes we’ve got all kinds of underground infrastructure, roads, buildings, shops and things like that, that help our visitors and help our staff really keep our parks up.” 

In addition to campsites, VanMeeteren said the GF&P maintains 242 camping cabins that are booked for an average of 100-125 nights a year, with some getting used even more. Modern lodging facilities that include indoor bathrooms and kitchen facilities include about 25 cabins and 7 lodges that can host 12 or more people. One in 3 people, he said, return to use those facilities on a consistent basis. 

Clean and functioning bathrooms in the campgrounds are absolutely essential to the GF&P camping operations, VanMeeteren said. Other important amenities at the campgrounds include playgrounds, disc golf courses, swimming and boating beaches, and shelters. 

In addition to camping and day-use amenities, VanMeeteren said the GF&P maintains 10 visitor centers and museums, and 37 historical structures. 

“Understanding how to maintain those things is really important, so they don’t fall apart,” he said. “We like to think that all of our historical structures are in good shape and have a long life ahead of them.” 

Park utilities, VanMeeteren said, include many miles of underground water, sewer, and electrical systems. Recently, he said the GF&P used about $20 million in funds from the American Rescue Plan Act to maintain some of those lines. 

Roads are also an expensive, but integral part of the GF&P parks system. The GF&P parks road system comprises about 50-60% of the capital development budget for the parks division, and in the last year the department has spent a little more than $8.25 million — about half of its capital development program — to maintain the roads. The GF&P works with the South Dakota Department of Transportation to fund some of that road construction for streets that provide access into the parks system. 

The trails in South Dakota are also an extremely popular and important part of the GF&P parks system. VanMeeteren said the department maintains and manages more than 405 miles of hiking trails, 350 miles of snowmobile trails in the Black Hills, and 925 miles of snowmobile trails in eastern South Dakota. They also manage a 150 mile canoe trail on the Big Sioux River. 

Users who aren’t necessarily looking for trails are often looking for boat ramps and fishing opportunities. The department manages more than 300 boat ramps, and a total of more than 500 public access points for fishing. Additionally, the parks offer 39 grinder units and 10 primitive fish cleaning tables, which users frequently say set South Dakota parks apart from other neighboring states. 

Archery and shooting ranges are also prevalent among the parks system, VanMeeteren said.  The department manages 15 archery ranges, 2 trap shooting ranges, and 2 rifle and handgun ranges, not counting those at the Pete Lien and Sons Shooting Range in Rapid City. 

“We have a very diverse system,” VanMeeteren said of all the offerings. “This diversity is kind of what drives our user opportunities. We have some folks that just use our parks because we have great boat ramps. Then we have some folks that they could care less about boat ramps, they just want any kind of trail or to take their bike to the park. So, it’s really important that we offer this diversity.” 

Maintaining all of these facilities, VanMeeteren said, means that the department has more than 200 projects a year to complete, with projects placed on a 5-year plan. That means that over a 5-year period, they may have up to 1,000 different projects. 

Overall, VanMeeteren said all of the park amenities are integral to providing a quality user experience and encouraging people to get outdoors. 

“Our customers want this,” he said. “If we don’t have a good system of facilities outthere that are well maintained, they’re not going to come to our parks. We feel like we do that. Like any great business, we want to give our visitors a great experience and having great facilities is key to making that happen. Parks are becoming more and more of a gateway as we see a shift in our population from rural to urban. This is, in a lot of wys, a lot of people’s first introduction to the outdoors. So, it’s an important part of our department’s mission.”
