title: Spearfish asks residents to conserve water
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — In the morning hours, when Spearfish residents are often watering their lawns, parts of the city have begun to experience low water pressure. That’s according to Public Works Director Adam McMahon.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

SPEARFISH — In the morning hours, when Spearfish residents are often watering their lawns, parts of the city have begun to experience low water pressure. That’s according to Public Works Director Adam McMahon.

“We did announce voluntary water restrictions starting today, just due to some low pressures that we are experiencing in certain portions of town, mostly due to high-use watering lawns and things like that as things get warmer and drier,” McMahon said Monday.

The city’s water department announced a “code green” water conservation alert.

A green alert asks citizens to “limit outside watering to every other day and to only water during the hours of 6:00 p.m. to 8:00 a.m.”

Typically, water conservation is classed “code blue,” which encourages a general practice of water conservation under “normal conditions.”

Water conservation becomes mandatory under “code yellow.” During “code yellow” periods, city utility customers are placed on an even/odd irrigation schedule. That means they can only water outdoor landscaping on odd or even days of the month — not daily. Code yellow also restricts water hours. Residents are also asked to limit indoor water use.

“Code orange” asks citizens to ration their water, minimizing indoor water use and outdoor water use. Under this alert, outdoor watering is limited to vegetable gardens only between the hours of 6 p.m. and 11 a.m., and only with water cans/buckets or handheld hoses with a nozzle shutoff. The use of water in decorative fountains is prohibited, as well as the washing of vehicles from residential water spigots (unless the cleaning is necessary to preserve the proper function/safe operation of the vehicle). The washing of paved surfaces is also prohibited.

City council must take a vote to elevate the conservation status to code orange or red.

“Code red” is defined as a “critical water conservation alert.”

This alert may be implemented in emergency situations, such as significant damage to infrastructure, severe wildfire/structure fire in the area, prolong power outages, or other catastrophic events.

The intent of this status alert is to be declared for a limited amount of time until the water supply system can be stabilized.

“We are the stewards of this resource, and it is our responsibility to protect and preserve our water supply through conservation efforts,” Miles Burtzlaff, water/wastewater utility superintendent, said.

The sprinklers on city property conform with the water conservation program, and pointed out that the city park and cemetery are irrigated by water from Spearfish Creek. Restrictions do not apply to those using irrigation ditches for landscape watering.

title: Water shortage hampers growth  north of Sioux Falls but solution near
byline: By Bart Pfankuch South Dakota News Watch
description: The aquifer under the Big Sioux River, shown here in Dell Rapids, S.D., on June 9, 2026, is the source of fresh water for much of eastern South Dakota. Photo by Bart Pfankuch, South Dakota News Watch
_full_text:
Water shortage hampers growth  north of Sioux Falls but solution near
The aquifer under the Big Sioux River, shown here in Dell Rapids, S.D., on June 9, 2026, is the source of fresh water for much of eastern South Dakota. Photo by Bart Pfankuch, South Dakota News Watch 

DELL RAPIDS — Scott Buss can only imagine what this town north of Sioux Falls might have looked like – and how many jobs and taxes would have been generated – if there wasn’t a local shortage of available water.

Buss, executive director of the Minnehaha Community Water Corp., sat in the conference room of the rural water system based in Dell Rapids recently and ticked off the industrial and agricultural projects turned away due to a lack of water.

After hitting its limit on how much water it can provide a few years ago, the rural system has had to turn away proposed projects valued at hundreds of millions of dollars that offered an untold number of new jobs, he said.

The rejected projects include the Agropur Cheese plant that eventually opened in Lake Norden. A few proposed hog farms and dairy expansions in northern Minnehaha County were also stalled, Buss said.

 2026-6-9 Dell Rapids water main treatment plant.jpeg
The existing water treatment plant for the Minnehaha Community Water Corp. on June 9, 2026, south of Dell Rapids, S.D. Photo by Bart Pfankuch, South Dakota News Watch 

Other proposals, most of which never came to fruition in South Dakota, included the $1.5 billion Gevo corn-based jet fuel plant, the $5oo million Wholestone Farms hog processing plant, and a data center that at some point all eyed the Dell Rapids area for development.

“All the water rights are spoken for between Dell Rapids and Sioux Falls, so there was no more water to be had in Minnehaha County,” Buss told News Watch in an interview in June. “With all the (residential) development that was coming in, we realized that our well capacity and our treatment capacity was limiting our ability to take on new high water-use customers.”

Buss and the nonprofit corporation’s board of directors aren’t waiting around to potentially miss out on more opportunities.

In a unique arrangement, the corporation is partnering with the neighboring Big Sioux Community Water System to the north on a $170 million expansion project called Shared Resources. The expansion, started three years ago, will use new wells into the Big Sioux Aquifer to generate 8 million gallons of water per day starting this fall.

“It’s going to be a huge and great benefit for Big Sioux and Minnehaha water,” said Jodi Johanson, director of the Big Sioux system based in Egan. “This project is going to make sure that down the road we have enough water for the future.”

As with other rural water systems in South Dakota, the aquifers the systems rely on for their water are either running low or are legally tapped out, or both.

In the case of Minnehaha water corporation, the Big Sioux River Aquifer has gotten drier, but state law is also preventing it from taking more water from the aquifer.

In 1996, the state Water Management Board allocated water rights, or withdrawal limits, to systems that take groundwater from the aquifer, Buss said.

Those limits have now been reached, meaning that Minnehaha water cannot take any more than the 7 million gallons per day it is drawing now.

Directly to the north, the Big Sioux Community Water System produces up to 2 million gallons per day for about 2,400 customers in Moody and Lake counties as well as some in Brookings County and in western Minnesota, Johanson said.

The system still has room within its water rights to draw more water, making it an attractive partner for Minnehaha water.

The system also serves a number of dairies that use significant water and provides water to the Dakota Ethanol plant in Wentworth, which is undergoing an expansion. Farmers in the region are also using greater quantities of water to deliver chemicals onto their land, Johanson said.

The biggest Shared Resources ticket item is a new $80 million water treatment plant that is nearly completed on 240th Street a few miles north of Dell Rapids.

A 20-inch pipeline from the plant to the east will end at a 1.5-million-gallon water tower, and a 24-inch pipeline to the west will terminate at a ground-level storage tank with a 4-million-gallon capacity.

Ratepayers will see a significant increase in their monthly water bills. The average residential consumer in both systems that uses about 7,000 gallons per month will see their bill rise to $135 a month, roughly double the cost in 2020, Buss said.

title: Should teachers have to pass a test?
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: The state Department of Education is researching alternatives, such as temporarily altering certification requirements for school districts with severe teacher shortages or with high poverty rates. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Should teachers have to pass a test.JPG
The state Department of Education is researching alternatives, such as temporarily altering certification requirements for school districts with severe teacher shortages or with high poverty rates. Courtesy photo 

PIERRE — Teacher shortages in rural and tribal schools are driving the South Dakota Department of Education to explore alternatives to licensing exams.

State Education Secretary Joe Graves asked members of the state Indian Education Advisory Council for their input on the possibility last month. He did not offer a timeline for the possible change.

Statewide, the number of teacher openings fell recently to 290, down from a high of 410 at the same time in 2023. But district-specific data show elevated vacancies in rural and tribal districts such as Sisseton, Todd County and Oglala Lakota schools. Those three school districts reported average full-time staff vacancies of 2.64, 3.83 and 7.23, respectively, at the start of the school year from 2019 to 2025. The average school district in South Dakota reported 0.59 vacancies.

Graves said willing, educated teachers with relevant “cultural backgrounds” — particularly Native American teachers — are especially in need but are often failing the licensing exam.

“Meanwhile, we’re replacing them with people not just lacking their cultural background, but people we’re recruiting from across the Pacific Ocean,” Graves said.

In 2025, 446 teachers hired from overseas were leading classrooms statewide. Many of those educators are “high quality people,” but it’s “galling” to some educators observing the situation that they can’t fill that role, Graves told South Dakota Searchlight after the council meeting. Meanwhile, some school districts are relying on untrained, long-term substitutes. 

Offering an alternative certification pathway for some local teachers could help solve the problem, Graves said during the meeting. The state has required teachers to pass a certification exam — the Praxis Series, a standardized test of academic skills and subject knowledge — since 2005.

Sisseton-Wahpeton Oyate Tribal Education Director Sherry Johnson partnered with a national nonprofit to conduct research on alternatives after years of concern about the exam’s impact on Native American teacher candidates. Johnson was awarded a fellow, Diana Martinez, from Leadership for Education Equity to study the issue. Martinez presented her findings to Graves in June.

Johnson said the research stems from a “longtime concern among tribal educator directors” about potential teachers not passing the certification test.

“We can’t always bash and bash the system,” Johnson said. “When you’re going to bash the system, you need to come to officials with some resources and examples and solutions.”

About 61% of all candidates pass the certification exam each year in South Dakota. The certification exam is a “barrier” for aspiring Native American and other minority teachers, contributing to the rural teacher shortage, Martinez said.

According to a 2019 study, the pass rate was 75% for white candidates, 33% for Black candidates, 56% for Latino candidates and 30% for “other races,” which includes Native Americans. Non-white candidates are also less likely to retake the exam, which costs hundreds of dollars.

Research has indicated that the lower success rates for candidates of color may be partly attributable to deficiencies in the educational opportunities they received as children, or to cultural bias in the tests or administration of the tests.

Martinez’s research points to a portfolio approach as the solution: a certification process in which candidates document their teaching, lesson planning, student assessment and professional development skills rather than taking a standardized test.

“We don’t want to produce something to make it easier to be a teacher,” Martinez said. “We want them to go into this having the right skills. This is supposed to be rigorous still. If you make it easier, you won’t get the results you want.”

Martinez said several other states have implemented alternative certification pathways — such as California, Minnesota and New Mexico — resulting in increased certification and retention rates among teachers. Other states have relaxed their professional standards, Graves said.

While Graves said he is “very hesitant” to relinquish the “rigor” of the test, he asked advisory members if there could be a “middle ground.” 

“If we give it up, we’ve lost something in the profession,” Graves said. “And I also think if we keep holding to this standard, we’re driving, say, five teachers out of the profession a year who are particularly well suited to teach at certain schools in the state. That’s a loss as well.”

He said the department is researching alternatives, such as temporarily altering certification requirements for school districts with severe teacher shortages or with high poverty rates.

“How do we address what we hope is a short-term problem of the teacher shortage without creating a long-term liability for the profession?” Graves asked while framing the problem for South Dakota Searchlight.

Members of the advisory committee were split. Some shared stories of difficulties passing the exam. Pierre teacher Megan Deal said the state should keep the exam.

“We want highly qualified teachers in our state,” Deal said. “Are our lawyers not going to have to take the bar anymore? Are doctors not going to have to take anything? Yes, it breaks my heart if they keep failing it, but we’ve all had to pass it to get our teaching certificate.”

In fact, it is now possible to become a lawyer in South Dakota without passing the bar exam. Law school students selected for a pilot program can earn entrance to the state bar by completing two years of full-time public service employment, such as in the office of a state’s attorney or public defender, and passing a review of their work portfolio. 

Brian Wagner, tribal education director with the Lower Brule Sioux Tribe, said children need to see themselves in their teachers. Native American children comprise 10.5% of public school students, yet 1.4% of teachers are Native American, according to Kids Count South Dakota, a nonprofit organization focused on child development.

Schools serving student bodies that are at least 25% Native American — along with rural public schools — have the highest teacher turnover and vacancy rates in the state, according to the same report.

Waiving the certification test could increase Native American teacher representation and improve outcomes for Native American students, Wagner said.

“I’ve worked with people who’ve passed the Praxis that can barely tie their shoes, but they’re good at taking tests,” Wagner said. “I’ve worked with elders who have no degree at all, other than having walked in life, that are the best teachers I’ve ever worked with.”

title: Meade County leader appointed  Sturgis city administrator
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Rhea Crane
_full_text:
Rhea Crane.jpg
Rhea Crane 

STURGIS — Longtime Meade County leader Rhea Crane will take the top job in Sturgis next month. 

On Monday, Sturgis Mayor Rod Bradley appointed Crane as the Sturgis city administrator. Crane has worked for the county for 38 years, and currently serves as the Meade County director of equalization and the county executive director. She also simultaneously served as Meade County auditor for nearly 2 years from October 2023 to November 2025, and she served on the Sturgis City Council from 2016 to 2021. 

Aaron Jordan was appointed as the first Sturgis City Administrator in January 2025, after voters changed the city’s form of government from a city manager lead operation, to an aldermanic form with a strong mayor. Jordan’s appointment came after the city had multiple changes in leadership and staff, and when there were many uncertainties about the city’s financial health. An official statement from the city of Sturgis states that during his tenure he helped strengthen city operations, helped balance the city budget, increased employee retention and morale, and increased public transparency. He announced his resignation in April, and his last day with the city will be July 24. 

Pull quote
I can’t think of a better way to thank him for all he has done, than to appoint somebody who can seamlessly fill his shoes and continue the progress he started. — Rod Bradley, Sturgis mayor

“We want to thank Aaron for all he has accomplished,” Bradley said. “The city administrator is the chief executive officer of the city, responsible for managing day-to-day operations. Aaron has served that role well. I can’t think of a better way to thank him for all he has done, than to appoint somebody who can seamlessly fill his shoes and continue the progress he started. Once Rhea expressed interest in this position, my first thought was that couldn’t be any better. I couldn’t think of a better person to fill this role. She has built a career and reputation committed to serving the citizens of Meade County. She has worked with many elected officials to support their decisions over the years. She has working knowledge of county finance, taxation, and government operations. She is well known in the community and respected by government officials across the state. She has a track record of building productive teams and she is a problem solver. I’ve always known Rhea to be up for a challenge. Our challenge is to keep the progress going in Sturgis, and Rhea has told me she is up for the challenge. I believe she will succeed in that role.” 

Bradley added that his only reservation about appointing Crane is the loss it will mean for Meade County. 

“I’ve talked with the county commissioners, and I know the county staff she has mentored over the years,” Bradley said. “They’ve worked on challenges with her. They’ve learned how to do it and they are well prepared to function without her.” 

Bradley said he has worked closely with Meade County commissioners, especially chairman Gary Deering, and there will be a 30-day transition, which means Crane will be working in city hall by mid-August. 

“Crane leaves big shoes to fill, and while we hate to see her go, we are excited for this next chapter in her career,” Deering said. “The city of Sturgis is gaining a dedicated public servant with an exceptional work ethic and a genuine commitment to serving others.”

Deering said that on behalf of the Meade County Commission, he wanted to thank Crane for her years of outstanding service, congratulate her on this well-deserved opportunity, and wish her nothing but continued success.

“I would also like to congratulate the city of Sturgis as they are gaining a tremendous employee who will no doubt serve its citizens with the same dedication as she has Meade County,” Deering said.

In her letter expressing interest in the position, Crane said her leadership philosophy emphasizes communication, team building, and problem-solving, adding that successful local government depends on strong relationships among elected officials, staff, stakeholders, and residents. She also emphasized her commitment to responsible financial management, regulatory compliance, and continuous improvement. 

“I view this as an exciting new opportunity, allowing me to continue to serve the public locally in another capacity,” Crane said. “Throughout my career, I have learned that successful local government is built on integrity, collaboration, fiscal responsibility, and a commitment to serving people. Those principles have guided me throughout my career, and they will continue to guide me as I begin this new chapter.” 

“It is an honor and a privilege for you to put your trust in me,” she said on Monday. “I really do appreciate the faith you have in me. I look forward to working with you, the elected officials, the staff and the citizens.”

title: Original DUNE collaborator wasn’t always a fan of physics
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Jae Yu poses in front of one of the massive caverns that was excavated to build the deep underground neutrino experiment, 4,850 feet underground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Jae Yu 4850.jpeg
Jae Yu poses in front of one of the massive caverns that was excavated to build the deep underground neutrino experiment, 4,850 feet underground at the Sanford Underground Research Facility. Courtesy photo 

LEAD — Jae Yu, one of the original members of the DUNE collaboration, hated math and physics for most of his childhood and school career. 

But in the 1970s, when the Iranian oil embargo left his home of South Korea with very little oil, Yu knew he wanted to do something related to energy. He had no idea what he could do, since such a feat would require a college degree. In South Korea, students are required to take a national exam to determine whether they can attend college, and core subjects in the test included physics, math, and English. 

Yu was terrible at all 3. 

“But I wanted to be working on something that would mean Korea didn’t have to rely on someone else (for energy),” he said. 

Then, in his senior year of high school, a lesson about radioactive decay — an energy that seemingly materializes out of nothing — completely changed the trajectory of his life. Radioactive decay is a natural process by which unstable atomic nuclei loses energy by emitting radiation. The transformation leads to the formation of different, more stable elements. 

“I thought that was just fascinating, something out of nothing,” Yu said of the first physics lesson that caught his attention. “I didn’t realize physics was that fascinating and I realized I was a bad student in mathematics. So, I started catching up on mathematics, and within a few months I was able to catch up all the way to calculus. In one year I was able to turn into a ‘physics guy.’ All my teachers had given up on me, but later on said ‘I can make it.’” 

At the end of that year, Yu said he passed 2 national exams to attend college as a physics major. After college and his mandatory military service in Korea, he went to Stony Brook University in New York, where he got his doctorate. He then completed 2 consecutive post-doctoral fellowships, one at the University of Rochester, and the other at Fermilab, in Batavia, Ill., where he was eventually hired as a staff scientist. 

“That’s a time in my life that I really worked passionately,” Yu said of his postdoctoral days when he completed 2 fellowships. “I worked passionately before, but it was like 36 hours in a row and then go crash at home for 8 hours, and back for another 36 hours. Stuff like that.” 

 Jae Yu at 4850.jpg
Jae Yu visits the 4,850-foot level of the Sanford Underground Research Facility, to see progress on the long baseline neutrino facility that will host the deep underground neutrino experiment (DUNE). Courtesy photo  

That was before physicists even conceived of the deep underground neutrino experiment (DUNE), and before they knew much of anything about neutrinos. It was during a time when physicists were quite sure that the tiny, subatomic neutrino particles were massless. 

But then Dr. Ray Davis discovered electron neutrinos emanating from the sun, and scientists began to discover neutrinos changing “flavor,” or oscillating, on their journey to earth from the sun. Those discoveries completely changed the standard model of physics, which captured the world’s attention. 

“The standard model says that these neutrinos are very strange particles,” Yu said. “These guys fly as fast as the speed of light, so therefore, their mass should be zero. Well, but then as we were learning and studying more about neutrinos close to the end of the 1990s and early 2000s, we started seeing something strange. Of these neutrinos, one type that we were expecting to see, when they fly a certain distance, those types disappear. At first we thought there was something happening to make these neutrinos disappear. Maybe they turned into something else? There have been all these indications that there really is these neutrinos that are disappearing and appearing as something else, and that’s what we call oscillation. That only happens if neutrinos have mass. The theory is if neutrinos have mass, they will change as they go on.

“What does that mean? That means the standards model says that (neutrino) mass should be zero. But when they oscillate, mass cannot be zero, which means the standard model is wrong. That’s a big deal because the standard model has been able to describe every single thing so far that we’ve been able to see. But there are little cracks here and there, and one of the biggest cracks is neutrinos. So therefore, this is in some sense earth shaking because we have to fix the standard form that seems to be describing everything else but the neutrinos.” 

Yu, who is now in his 25th year of teaching at the University of Texas-Arlington, became involved with DUNE in 2013, when he began building prototypes for the neutrino detectors. That was right before 2 major proposed experiments to study neutrino oscillation — one in Japan (LBNO) and one in the United States (LBNE) — began to merge into the international collaboration for the experiment known as DUNE. After nearly 13 years of perfecting prototypes of the liquid argon detectors that will capture neutrino beams from Fermilab, Yu said progress at the lab to excavate and outfit the long baseline neutrino facility that he saw in May, moves a dream into reality. 

“We were doing a whole lot of prototyping and stuff like that while we were digging the hole,” Yu said. “For 10 years we were digging and digging and I feel like we were staying in the same place. I didn’t feel like we were seeing the light at the end of the tunnel. I went down every year and this year, when I went down, I now see something is real. Now I’m feeling this chill that now we will start building it for real. It’s a feeling that all this time of developing detector technologies and prototyping and working on developing new ideas of using this kind of precise detector is now coming to reality.” 

The project has been an exercise in extreme perseverance, but it’s that same motivation that has shaped the entirety of Yu’s career. 

“It’s not that one does not have ability,” he said of the importance of motivation and perseverance. “It’s just that one has to be motivated. If one gets motivated, that one can do it. You know, I’ve been teaching for 25 years, and some of these students come to me and say that up to last night, everything was in a haze. But then suddenly it turned around. I believe that, because I was like that. At some point we might be like ‘oh, we have lost.’ But then we keep going. That’s a very important thing. You’ve got to be able to make sure we can make these things happen. These are big projects, worth billions of dollars.” 

In addition to his work on DUNE and as a university professor, Yu also actively promotes cooperation between the United State and Korea in science. He has served as the president of the Association of Korean Physicists in America, and the Korean-American Scientists and Engineers Association. While Yu has lived in America for 40 years, he said it’s important to him to honor his heritage by building bridges between countries through science. In fact, he said, science should build bridges and unite people, because scientific discoveries are about advancing humanity. 

“For me this fundamental science is not just for one particular country,” he said. “It’s not just for one particular reason, but for the entire humanity. Even the fact that whatever we learn is not something that’s useful that will give you food on your table tomorrow, but this is something for our next generation, for the entire humanity, or even for thousands of years down the road. Humanity is everybody, not just the United States. Not just Europe. So therefore, to me, it’s important.”

title: Spearfish police chief presents electric motorized bike enforcement plan: Here’s the bottom line
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Spearfish City Councilwoman Pam Jacobs recounts a recent encounter with a motorized bike she said nearly resulted in a crash during Monday’s city council meeting. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Pam.JPG
Spearfish City Councilwoman Pam Jacobs recounts a recent encounter with a motorized bike she said nearly resulted in a crash during Monday’s city council meeting. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — On Monday, Spearfish Police Chief Collin Smith presented an enforcement action plan for electric motorized bikes on city streets, sidewalks, and the rec path.

“I’m very confident with our approach, and our enforcement efforts have already begun,” Smith said.

The bottom line? Motorized bikes are not allowed on rec paths, sidewalks, or city streets.

“You can be on private property. That is it,” Smith said.

Smith established that there is a clear difference between the motorized vehicles that have become a growing problem in the city and e-bikes, which are defined in state law.

E-bikes are defined as vehicles with operable pedals, a seat or saddle, and electric motors operating 750-watts or fewer.

The bikes that police are seeing, typically operated by children, often have much greater speed capabilities than any class of e-bike and lack operable pedals. Officers have observed, in at least one case, modification kits. Drivers have attached pedals to their motorized bikes — a change Smith said does not alter how vehicles are classified or defined under the law.

 Collin.JPG
Spearfish Police Chief Collin Smith presents an enforcement action plan for electric, motorized bikes. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

Smith said these bike-like units are typically sold with a manufacturer’s statement of origin (MSO) or a manufacturer’s certificate of origin (MCO). Those documents, Smith described as a vehicle’s “birth certificate,” outline the unit’s intended purpose. Most of the MCOs and MSOs for the motorized vehicles police are concerned about state that the units are not intended for highway use.

“Manufacturers almost universally market these units as off-road motorcycles, competition motorcycles, not for highway use,” Smith said.

If a vehicle is intended for highway use, it might be eligible for titling.

“Many of these currently do not qualify for titling for highway use,” Smith said. “As written today, there is no statutory authority to license a 2-wheeled electric off-road vehicle for highway use.”

Is it an e-bike? 
Under state law e-bikes have operable pedals and motors with 750-watt motors or less. Each motorized vehicle should have a manufacturer’s description, provided at the time of purchase. That description can help define whether the vehicle is allowed on sidewalks or not. 
 Here are a few examples of vehicle brands that may be out in the community, according to Spearfish police. Are they e-bikes? 
 Aventon Yes
 Rad Power Usually Yes
 Trek Allant Yes
 Sur-Ron Light Bee No
 Talaria Sting No
 E-Ride Pro No
 Yozma No

There are provisions in state law for off-road vehicles to cross roadways between areas where they are allowed to operate. Under SDCL 32-20-12, if a bike is traveling from private property to private property, it can cross a public road to get there. They cannot drive in the road. Off-road motorized vehicles are not allowed on city sidewalks or recreation paths.

It’s possible some of these vehicles might be able to qualify as “motorcycles.”

Smith said that is up to the state to determine during the titling process.

“You can try to make it street legal. That is not our determination to make as law enforcement,” Smith said. “All I can tell you is, if we stop on the street, one of the first things that we are going to look at is, ‘Is it street legal? Does it have everything it needs to have to be on the road?”

If they can be titled, they must be insured, made street legal, and operated by a licensed driver. Because of the nature of the licensing process, most of the drivers of the motorized bikes police are observing would not be old enough to have a driver’s license. Smith added that motorcycles can’t legally be operated on sidewalks or recreation paths.

“At this point, it is not the age (of the operator) that is the issue on the sidewalk and rec path. It is that the unit is prohibited on those areas. If you are on the road, age comes into effect because to be on the road legally you have to be a licensed driver,” Smith said.

SDCL 32-22-21.1 outlines who can and cannot use sidewalks in the state. 

“No person may drive any vehicle other than a bicycle, motorized foot scooter, or an electric personal assistive device upon a sidewalk or sidewalk area except upon a permanent or duly authorized temporary driveway,” according to state law. A violation of that statute is a Class 2 misdemeanor, punishable by up to 30 days in a county jail, a $500 fine, or both. SDCL 32-20-9 applies to motorcycles, prohibiting their use anywhere except normal roadways or designated areas.

“I am not telling our guys to go out and cite 12-year-olds for these definitions and statutes right away. If there is a situation where it is a repeated offense and a repeated offense, then sure, but our goal is more education and letting parents know when this is occurring,” Smith said. “My walking orders to my officers are education and partnering with the parents. If it is a young rider, educate them. Show them the safety precautions and risks that are there operating these in such a way, and contact parents.”

Police officers have stopped at least a half dozen young riders in the last few weeks, Smith said.

“I was coming home from supper last night, and I actually saw a 10-year-old driving a dirt bike on a side street on 8th Street. I about hit him, so I think this due diligence is very important,” Spearfish City Councilwoman Pam Jacobs said. “I was almost going to follow him because I was very upset. It had big tires, and it was going fast.”

Observations like tire size are important for folks to make, Smith said. That’s why Smith stressed the difference between motorized bikes, motorcycles for street use, and e-bikes.

“I want to help you to be able to identify what these things are. When you call us and say, ‘Hey, I just saw this e-dirtbike, we are going to be asking specific questions because we are trying to determine: is it an e-dirtbike? Is it an e-bike? Have patience with us when we ask those questions, because we are trying to determine the type of unit so that we know what we are looking for,” Smith said.

Smith also asked parents of kids with motorized bikes to check the paperwork that came with their purchase. The MCO or MSO should be provided in the box with an ordered bike, or given to a customer by a dealer in store. That document can help parents determine if the vehicle is an off-road vehicle. If so, it is not allowed on sidewalks or rec paths. If the vehicle is eligible for street use, it may be titled, insured, and operated by a licensed driver on city streets.

title: As travel costs rise, many families find summer adventures closer to home
byline: By Amina Aidarkhanova South Dakota News Watch
description: BROOKINGS — Instead of planning long vacations, many South Dakota families are spending summer weekends closer to home, choosing festivals, community events and family attractions that offer affordable ways to make memories.
_full_text:
SDNewsWatchLogo

BROOKINGS — Instead of planning long vacations, many South Dakota families are spending summer weekends closer to home, choosing festivals, community events and family attractions that offer affordable ways to make memories.

Travel officials and local event organizers say the shift reflects a broader trend of travelers taking shorter trips, driving instead of flying and choosing destinations closer to home.

“We did re-coin that term ‘staycation’ again this year,” said Shari Budahl Avery, publicity chair for the Brookings Summer Arts Festival. “If things are a little tight but you want to get away for a day, we can provide that experience.”

Families are redefining summer travel

Travel South Dakota reports that affordability, scenic beauty and family experiences remain among the state’s strongest tourism draws. The department said 58% of visitors travel within 150 miles of their homes, reflecting continued interest in nearby destinations.

Shawn Steward, public affairs manager for AAA South Dakota, said travelers are adjusting their plans rather than abandoning vacations altogether.

“People still want to travel,” Steward said. “They’re just making different choices.”

Steward said those choices often include shorter trips, road travel and destinations that require less time and money.

Local events become summer destinations

Local events across South Dakota are benefiting from that shift. Budahl Avery said the Brookings Summer Arts Festival has long attracted visitors looking for affordable entertainment close to home.

“We’re kind of dead center in a pretty good population center,” she said. “People can come on what one friend from Texas called a ‘tank trip’ - somewhere you can drive on one tank of gas and get home.”

The two-day festival features nearly 180 juried artists, live entertainment, children’s activities, food vendors and historical demonstrations. Budahl Avery said the event gives families an opportunity to spend time together without the expense of a major vacation.

Affordable, convenient entertainment

Other local attractions are seeing similar interest. The Carden International Circus brought families to the Dakota Bank Center in Brookings on June 25, during its summer tour.

Ringmaster and comedian Rulito Videla said families are looking for affordable entertainment options that create lasting memories.

“If they are staying home, support your local events,” Videla said. “The circus is family-oriented entertainment. You create memories.”

Some Brookings-area families said smaller local outings have become part of their summer routines.

Erica Quam said her family often chooses several smaller activities instead of one large vacation.

“We live right near Brookings,” Quam said. “It’s close, there were some coupons that made it more affordable, and it’s just a fun, easy activity.”

Sienna Vanmeveren said staying closer to home helps her family manage costs.

“It’s easier than traveling somewhere,” she said, adding that she would likely travel more if finances allowed.

Not every family is changing its travel habits. Sviatlana Senchanka said her family recently completed a road trip from South Dakota to California and continues to spend time outdoors locally.

For Budahl Avery, the appeal of community events goes beyond saving money.

“What keeps families coming back?” she said. “Tradition. Joy. Making memories.”

Whether families travel across the country or stay close to home, organizers and visitors say meaningful summer experiences do not always require a long-distance trip.

title: Deadwood 3-Wheeler Rally revs up for another week
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Deadwood 3-Wheeler Rally will return to Deadwood this week, bringing trike enthusiasts, live music, and show and shines. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
3-Wheeler Rally pre-story.JPG
The Deadwood 3-Wheeler Rally will return to Deadwood this week, bringing trike enthusiasts, live music, and show and shines. Pioneer file photo 

DEADWOOD — The annual 3-Wheeler Rally will make its return to the Black Hills this week, bringing trike enthusiasts, live music, unique vendor opportunities, and a show and shine. 

According to the event’s website, approximately 510 people are registered to attend this year. Attendees include 6 from Canada, 20 from Florida, and more than 25 from Texas.

The event is scheduled to begin Saturday, with registration and vendors available at the First Gold from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. 

Group rides through Vanocker Canyon, Spearfish Canyon, and along Iron Mountain Road to Mount Rushmore will take place through the weekend. Monday morning, trikes will line historic Main Street from 9–11 a.m. before participants depart on a ride to Buckhorn, Wyo.

Badger Horse will perform live Monday evening at 5 p.m., with line dance instruction and a watermelon feed rounding out the evening until 7: 30 p.m. All proceeds from the evening go to benefit the Deadwood Historic Preservation Committee. 

The event wraps up Wednesday with a ride through Custer State Park and a finale dinner catered by the Horseshoe Restaurant. Trikes will line up at 8:30 p.m. for the annual light parade down Deadwood Main St.

title: Police department construction  passes midpoint in Belle Fourche
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: BELLE FOURCHE — By mid-November, the Belle Fourche Police Department could move into its new, modern facility across from Hermann Park. The building is more than 60% complete.
_full_text:
BELLE FOURCHE — By mid-November, the Belle Fourche Police Department could move into its new, modern facility across from Hermann Park. The building is more than 60% complete.

“We are all excited to have the opportunity to move in there,” said Belle Fourche Police Chief Ryan Cherveny.

In no small part because the old building, a schoolhouse-turned-police-station, had rapidly aged out of usefulness.

“The bullpen, where officers will have their desks and everything set up, one big thing, one big element is we’ll be able to run those computers without tripping the breaker,” said Belle Fourche City Administrator Jason LaFayette.

The old building lacked sufficient storage space for evidence, so officers used a storage container next to the police station in lieu of an evidence room.

Hailstorms in 2022 and 2023, “basically completely demolished our vehicles. We had to spend lots of insurance money to repair those, get the dents out,” LaFayette said.

The new facility will feature a covered sally port and garage, with a mechanic’s bay and space designed for officers to wash and maintain their patrol vehicles.

“We have an officer … who is able to outfit our vehicles with lights, sirens, radios, all the things, and so it is a space for him,” LaFayette said. “Also in there, there is a wash basin so that they can keep their vehicles clean, rather than taking it to car washes, spending taxpayer dollars to keep the vehicles washed.”

Code enforcement will have space to store tools like lawn mowers and 4-wheelers, and investigators will have a right-sized evidence room, LaFayette said.

“(It will have) actual holding cells, where they can’t crawl up the wall, through the roof, and get out,” LaFayette said. “All in all, it is just taking an old school building and replacing it with a police department.”

Contractors are building a training room on the building’s second floor that includes a gym-like space, purpose-built for officers’ tactical training.

“The training room and a proper conference room, I think, are some of the more exciting features. We’ll actually be able to host the trainings and have the space to do physical training also,” Cherveny said. “I think it will have a significant impact on retention.”

LaFayette said that about 5 years ago the police department felt like a revolving door. “It seems like some of our officers that left 5, 7, 10 years ago are coming back because the camaraderie that they have and the leadership that they have is so positive that this is where they want to be.”

Cherveny said the process of building the new department has strengthened ties between the police department and the rest of the city’s operations. That’s in no small part because city staff and police officers have shared space since the old building was demolished.

“City hall has been more than gracious, dealing with the extra people in the building and the other noise that often comes with some of the individuals we deal with. I think it has been eye-opening for us to see what some of the other parts of the city are doing on a daily basis,” Cherveny said. “It is good for them to see what we are doing also. I think we have grown to appreciate each other more than we did before.”

That being said, the police chief is eager to have designated space again.

“This past winter couldn’t have been any better for construction. They didn’t have any real major delays other than the very initial start where we had a bit of rain, which set us back about 2.5 weeks. I think they have made up for that over time. I think they are almost on time or ahead of schedule now,” Cherveny said. “It has been a phenomenal stretch as far as weather and cooperation that way.”

Fiscally speaking, construction has gone smoothly as well, according to LaFayette.

The guaranteed maximum price of the project was $12,173,988.39. To cover the cost, the city took out a bond in the amount of $13,970,000.00. Even with 3 change orders, with a total cost of  $68,715.00, LaFayette said the project is running under budget.

“We have had 3 change orders that contain things like re-routing ductwork … the biggest one so far was regarding the elevator,” LaFayette said, in reference to the $43,239.00 change order. “They actually bid out everything with this project, so there were 2 bids that came into the elevator. One was exactly half the price of the other one. So we went with the cheaper one, but when they did that it changed because this was a hydraulic lift instead of a pulley and cable type lift. There were some changes that were required to make it work.”

The city has $228,211.55 in remaining contingency dollars set aside for the police department’s construction.

The new building might be designed for police, but it city leaders hope it will offer service to the community that extends beyond law enforcement.

“We have been working with the school district, making the parking lot itself a bus stop. The bus isn’t (going to be) stopping in the middle of the road. We are bringing that bus into a safe place,” LaFayette said. “With that, we added a big lobby where they can come in when it’s cold outside. They’ve got somewhere to stay warm and wait for the bus.”

SPEARFISH — South Dakota’s first gubernatorial runoff election will occur July 28. 

Registered Republicans will be able to choose between Gov. Larry Rhoden and businessman Tobey Doeden to be the GOP nominee for governor. 

The last day to register to vote in the runoff is 5 p.m. Monday.

Voters have until that day to change their party registration. Only registered Republicans can vote in the Republican primary. 

The last day for a voter to request an absentee ballot is 5 p.m. July 27. Absentee voting began June 12. 

The winner of the runoff will face Democrat Dan Ahlers in the general election on Nov. 3. The runoff was initiated when neither Rhoden nor Doden received 35% of the vote in the June 2 election primary.

title: SD reports helping with over  800 deportations as feds deliver funding
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Gov. Larry Rhoden speaks to reporters from a podium on July 28, 2025, at the Public Safety Administration Building in Sioux Falls. Also visible are, from left, Dan Satterlee, director of the state Division of Criminal Investigation, and Sam Olson, Minneapolis field office director for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Photo by John Hult, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Rhoden-and-ICE-e1753734439834.jpg
Gov. Larry Rhoden speaks to reporters from a podium on July 28, 2025, at the Public Safety Administration Building in Sioux Falls. Also visible are, from left, Dan Satterlee, director of the state Division of Criminal Investigation, and Sam Olson, Minneapolis field office director for U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Photo by John Hult, South Dakota Searchlight 

PIERRE — South Dakota troopers have assisted in more than 204 immigration-related arrests, and state National Guard soldiers have helped process 807 deportations as the state continues to expand its partnership with federal immigration authorities. 

The update came as Gov. Larry Rhoden announced that President Donald Trump’s administration has provided $150,418 to the state to recoup the costs associated with the South Dakota Highway Patrol’s collaboration with Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Under the terms of an agreement signed in the spring of 2025, state troopers are authorized to carry out some federal immigration enforcement duties. 

The money will go toward payroll, and specialized equipment and technology for the Highway Patrol’s enforcement work. The state expects additional funding as operations continue, according to a news release from Rhoden’s office. 

In May, Rhoden issued a press release saying the federal government had committed to reimbursing the state $165,000. The South Dakota Department of Public Safety did not immediately respond to a question about the total cost of immigration-related enforcement for the state patrol.

Rhoden’s immigration enforcement push, which also loops in the state Department of Corrections and the South Dakota National Guard, is part of a law enforcement undertaking dubbed “Operation Prairie Thunder.” It features periodic saturation patrols by state troopers, 14 of which have taken place in 11 cities across South Dakota since last July. Initial operations focused on Sioux Falls.

“Our partnership with ICE has delivered strong results, and I look forward to continuing to partner with the Trump Administration as we work to keep South Dakota strong, safe, and free,” Rhoden said in the press release.

The governor’s office said 40 Highway Patrol troopers are participating in the program. That’s more than double the number trained in mid-May, when Rhoden announced plans to fold more troopers into the program.

The 204 trooper-assisted apprehensions of people who reportedly lacked legal status is a jump from May, when the state said Highway Patrol reported 150 arrests.

The Corrections Department, meanwhile, has paroled 25 people into ICE custody for deportation. Four more people incarcerated by the state were approved for release into federal custody by the parole board in June, Rhoden’s office said, and the board will consider four more cases in July. 

Each person released from state custody saves the state an average of $34,000 per year, Rhoden’s office said.

Seven South Dakota National Guard soldiers have also remained deployed in Sioux Falls and Rapid City since the fall to help ICE process deportations. National Guard-assisted deportation processing starting in May 2025 rose from 664 through mid-May to 807 as of Tuesday.

The state Department of Public Safety did not immediately respond to a request for the total number of people deported from South Dakota since the state began coordinating with ICE.

Some of the people whose ICE deportations were aided by the state National Guard may not have been living in South Dakota, Rhoden spokesperson Josie Harms told Searchlight, as they could’ve been apprehended while traveling through the state.

ICE did not respond to a request for comment on the total number of people deported from South Dakota since Trump took office.

title: Former city commissioner reaches  plea deal, receives suspended jail time and dismissed charges
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: DEADWOOD — After reaching a plea deal, former Deadwood City Commissioner Blake Joseph pleaded guilty to several charges he received during his tenure as commissioner and had several more dismissed.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

DEADWOOD — After reaching a plea deal, former Deadwood City Commissioner Blake Joseph pleaded guilty to several charges he received during his tenure as commissioner and had several more dismissed.

In court July 1, Joseph pleaded guilty to: speeding; contact by phone to terrorize, threaten, harass, or annoy and a connected violation of no contact order; tampering with a vehicle with the intent to damage and a violation of a protection order; and another violation of a no contact order related to an ongoing domestic violence charge in Butte County.

After pleading guilty, 4 more violations of a no contact order related to the ongoing domestic violence charge were dismissed.

While still a sitting city commissioner, Joseph was accused of sending harassing text messages a male victim through a false phone number. While the case was ongoing, Joseph had a no contact order in place with the victim. Joseph violated the terms of the order when he sent a thumbs up emoji to the victim over Facebook Messenger. Joseph pleaded guilty to both charges July 1 and was sentenced to 30 days jail, all suspended, for each charge.

Contact by phone to terrorize, threaten, harass, or annoy, is a Class 1 misdemeanor, punishable by up to one year imprisonment in a county jail, a $2,000 fine, or both.

While a sitting city commissioner, Joseph allegedly struck his then girlfriend with the open door of his vehicle while driving in reverse outside of Sunny’s 5th Avenue gas station in Belle Fourche. Joseph was charged with 2 counts of simple assault, domestic violence, a Class 1 misdemeanor. A protection order was put in place between her and Joseph while the case is ongoing.

Joseph pleaded guilty to one charge of violating a protection order against the female victim, in which Lead police officer Paige Erickson discovered text messages between Joseph and the woman on her phone. Joseph was saved under “Egypt” in her phone and sent approximately 34 text messages to her the morning of March 5, 2026.

Joseph was sentenced to 30 days in jail, all 30 suspended.

Three more charges of violating a protection order between Joseph and the woman were dismissed July 1.

All suspended jail times are contingent upon Joseph not committing any crimes for 365 days, not contacting his then girlfriend or her ex-husband for 30 days and pay all associated court costs by Oct. 1.

Joseph is scheduled to appear in court in Butte County for the domestic violence case July 22. Simple assault, domestic violence, is a Class 1 misdemeanor, punishable by up to one year in prison, a $2,000 fine, or both.

Joseph also faces felony burglary and identity theft charges in Butte County. According to court documents, Joseph allegedly entered an apartment in Belle Fourche without the consent of the owner Jan. 2, and allegedly used a woman’s debit card to make approximately $110 in purchases at 2 gas stations in Belle Fourche.

Joseph is scheduled to appear in court in Butte County for the burglary and identity theft charges July 22. First-degree burglary is a Class 2 felony, punishable by up to 25 years imprisonment in a state correctional facility, a $50,000 fine, or both. Identity theft is a Class 6 felony, punishable by 2 years imprisonment in a state correctional facility, a fine of $4,000, or both.

In Lawrence County, Joseph still faces 7 charges of identity theft, one charge of petty theft, grand theft, possession of a controlled substance, possession or use of drug paraphernalia, and obstructing a police officer.

According to court documents, Joseph allegedly stole a vehicle belonging to a woman he was staying with at the Travelodge in Deadwood March 14, 2026. While in possession of the vehicle, Joseph allegedly attempted to withdraw cash from an ATM with the woman’s debit card but gave an invalid PIN.

A search warrant for an apartment in Spearfish associated with Joseph revealed multiple glass pipes and methamphetamine residue. Joseph was placed under arrest but allegedly refused a urine sample as ordered by the search warrant.

Obstructing a police officer is a Class 1 misdemeanor, punishable by up to one year imprisonment in a county jail, a $2,000 fine, or both.

Possession of a controlled substance is a Class 5 felony, punishable by up to 5 years imprisonment in a state correctional facility, a $10,000 fine, or both.

Grand theft is a Class 6 felony, punishable by up to 2 years imprisonment, a $4,000 fine, or both.

Petty theft is a Class 2 misdemeanor, punishable by 30 days in a county jail, a $500 fine, or both.

Joseph is scheduled to appear at a July 15 court date for the associated charges.

title: News and Notes
description: Pioneer file graphic
_full_text:
News and Notes
Pioneer file graphic 

City administrator search continues in Spearfish

SPEARFISH — 41 people have applied for the Spearfish city administrator position. The job listing has been taken down from the city’s website, as the first round of applications are considered. Spearfish Mayor John Senden said the first review of applications began June 30. 

—Sierra Ferguson

Communications center consolidation negotiations continue with formal Spearfish approval

SPEARFISH — The city of Spearfish and Lawrence County will continue negotiating the consolidation of their dispatch centers, now with formal support from the city council. Spearfish City Council voted unanimously Monday to continue discussions with the county to merge record systems, staff, and operations. Police Chief Collin Smith said both agencies are working to address pay disparities between transferring staff to reduce the likelihood of pay cuts, and are exploring honoring the tenure of city dispatchers who transfer to the center across from the Lodge at Deadwood. Smith said details of the consolidation will become clearer as talks continue. 

— Sierra Ferguson

Retaining wall, sidewalk contract approved for 85 Charles St., Deadwood

DEADWOOD — Deadwood city commissioners approved a $25,413.30 contract with Competitive Masonry, of Rapid City, to build a retaining wall and sidewalk at 85 Charles St. Monday. 

The property was purchased by the city in 2024 after decades of sitting vacant and neglected. The city has since gutted the interior and renovated the exterior with the intention of selling the property with restrictions. The property will not be used as a short-term rental. 

— Sara Morgan

Deadwood purchases utility box wraps

DEADWOOD — Deadwood city commissioners approved a contract with Quik Signs, of Spearfish, to wrap utility boxes at the Deadwood Recreation and Aquatic Center Monday. 

Kevin Kuchenbecker, director of historic preservation and planning and zoning, said the $7,072.39 contract will be used to wrap utility boxes and the large generator housing at the recreation center with historical photos.

— Sara Morgan

New display screens coming to Deadwood commission room

DEADWOOD — Deadwood city commissioners approved a contract Monday with KT Connections, of Rapid City, to install new display screens in the commission room. 

Kevin Kuchenbecker, director of planning and zoning, said the $12,963.09 contract will be used to move an existing screen and purchase a new screen. Kuchenbecker said the screens will be used to improve connections and interactivity between audiences, commissioners, and department heads during meetings.

— Sara Morgan

375 for More Than Gold

LEAD — Attendance at the More Than Gold production on Thursday was more than the Historic Homestake Opera House has seen since the COVID-19 pandemic, executive director Todd Jones reported Monday. Jones said 375 people attended the play in the theater that has a capacity for about 400. “It was a wonderful event that we hope we can do again,” Jones said. 

— Wendy Pitlick 

Pickleball lessons 

LEAD — The city of Lead will reserve the pickleball courts for lessons that will be held on Sundays, from 3-5 p.m., July 19 through Sept. 27. The classes are meant for beginners to intermediate players, and will be taught by experienced pickleball instructors. Pre-registration for the classes is required. During this time, the pickleball courts will be closed to public use from 2:30-5:30 p.m., to allow for setup and cleanup time after the classes. 

— Wendy Pitlick 

New police officers 

LEAD — Kurt Pickard will step up as a full time patrol officer for the city of Lead, and Tanner Weaver, who is formerly from the Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office will step in as a part-time patrol officer. Lead Police Chief Robert Williams said both candidates have 7 years of law enforcement experience. While the Lead City Commission approved their hiring, they also accepted a resignation from Lead patrol officer Jackson Bong. 

— Wendy Pitlick 

Budget meetings moved 

LEAD — The city of Lead will hold its annual budget hearings a little later this year, to allow the new commissioners time to get acclimated to their new positions before starting the process, Lead Mayor Dustin Heupel said Monday. New commissioners, Valerie Meiners and Dustin Schumacher, were sworn into their positions on Monday. The city of Lead normally starts holding meetings to discuss their budget for the following year at the end of July, with a completed budget that is certified by early September. But on Monday the city commission passed an ordinance that gives them until the first regular meeting in November to certify the budget, which will give the commission an extra month. That meeting is scheduled for Nov. 2. Heupel said the commission will soon announce dates for budget hearings that will likely be held on Mondays, starting at the end of August and continuing through September. 

— Wendy Pitlick 

Mustang and Bronco rallies scheduled 

STURGIS — The annual Mustang Rally will be held in Sturgis Sept. 1-6, with the annual show and shine and Mustang parade scheduled for Sept. 5. The annual Bronco Rally will be held in Sturgis soon afterward, Sept. 23-27, with a show and shine and parade held on Sept. 26. Sturgis will also host a show and shine event during Kool Deadwood Nites, scheduled for Aug. 19. 

— Wendy Pitlick 

Meade County fires 

STURGIS — The Meade County Sheriff’s Office had a busy Fourth of July weekend, Chief Deputy James Johns said. Johns reported that from July 1-5, the department responded to 17 grassland fires, 12 reports of smoke, 2 trash fires, and one vehicle fire. 

— Wendy Pitlick

title: Easton retires from Spearfish School District
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Kirk Easton, retired as superintendent of the Spearfish School District July 1. He is pictured here at the annual Spearfish Foundation for Public Education 3 Cheers Event. Pioneer photo by Mark Watson
_full_text:
Easton retires from Spearfish School District.jpeg
Kirk Easton, retired as superintendent of the Spearfish School District July 1. He is pictured here at the annual Spearfish Foundation for Public Education 3 Cheers Event. Pioneer photo by Mark Watson 

SPEARFISH — Now that it is July, Kirk Easton has officially retired from the Spearfish School District.

After 10 years at the helm, the former superintendent of the district, hit the rule of 85.

“It’s your age plus the number of years you put in, so I guess I just felt that it was probably time for me to step aside and for new blood to step into the leadership,” Easton said. 

His tenure at the district was filled with challenges, perhaps none greater than the COVID-19 pandemic. The district was forced to navigate the challenging time with rapidly changing guidance and politics. Yet, it was also filled with triumphs.

“Certainly, the CTE (career and technical education) Center, I’m proud of that,” Easton said. 

The district broke ground on the CTE center in 2022 and opened it in August 2024. In addition to the courses already offered, medical science, auto shop, and building trades were added. Within those courses, multiple classes were offered.

Recently, approximately 20 students attained their certified nursing assistant certificate.

“That’s something that I think we should be proud of,” he said. “First of all, we’re getting a student some type of certificate before they leave. But what they can do with that certificate? They can certainly go to work for an assisted care center. They go work for a hospital or medical facility sometimes, but it’s also a first step if they want to go into nursing. That’s one of their first steps in a nursing program, is to get their CNA certificate.”

The first building trades class constructed a home that is now owned by a district staff member in the Sky Ridge subdivision east of Exit 17.

In years’ past, students were pushed to earn a 4-year degree. There has been a shift in that.

“What you’re seeing is not just school officials, but also parents, in the community at large, aren’t trying to funnel kids all into one track, which means a four-year degree. I think what you’re seeing now is parents telling their child it’s OK to go to a tech school, it’s OK to just go into work, it’s OK to go into the military rather than just pushing them or funneling them into a 4-year degree, where they may come out without a job or with a pile of debt.”

Easton said that for some students, a 4-year degree is the way to go. For others, it is not.

“I’m extremely proud of my staff, both teaching staff, classified staff, administration. … The staff that we have is tremendous.” 

Additionally, he said the staff have been able to maintain the care of the district’s buildings.

He said that the district’s strategic planning has been a high point and has helped the leadership define their priorities.

While teaching remains a top priority, the district’s strategic plan also focuses on resource management.

“We’re in really good fiscal shape, and that’s with losing over 100 students over the last couple of years,” he added. “Funding is tied to students, and we’re still in fiscally sound shape, that’s a point of pride for us.”

While Easton returned to the classroom in Spearfish the past two school years to teach the building trades course, students always remained a bright spot for him.

“Tt’s hard to remember a lot of specific ones from over the years,” he said when asked what some of his fondest memories of students were over the years. “I could have the worst day I’ve ever had in the office, and I would intentionally go to an elementary school and go see students, walk into a classroom, say ‘hi,’ and then you know them giving you hugs and high 5s and fist bumps and all of that just completely changes the outlook.”

Easton isn’t completely leaving education. 

He has accepted an interim role at Western Dakota Technical College as their executive vice president.

Nick Gottlob was hired earlier this year to take over Easton’s position.

“The nice thing about Nick coming in, he’s very familiar with the current good work we’re doing now, but he has his own ideas,” Easton said. “I’m excited about Nick, not only continuing the good work we’re doing now, but also expanding on that.”

He said he appreciated the support he’s been given.

“The support from the community and the parents and staff that I’ve had over 10 years has meant a lot,” he said. “I’ve worked with a lot of wonderful people, both again in the school district and in the community, and it’s been a great experience.”

title: Lead denies Handley funding — again
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: LEAD — The city of Lead denied providing funding for the Handley Center — again.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

LEAD — The city of Lead denied providing funding for the Handley Center — again. 

On Monday, the Lead City Commission addressed a June 15 request to provide nearly $73,000 in funding, in 6 monthly installments, for the Handley Center. Mayor Dustin Heupel said when the city discussed the request at the June 15 commission meeting, there was some confusion about whether the commission voted on the funding request, or whether they voted to table it. Upon reviewing video from the meeting, Lead City Attorney Tim Johns advised commissioners that they voted to table the issue, which prompted commissioners to re-address the funding request Monday. 

The funding request agenda item sparked questions among residents, who said confusion about the vote was further exacerbated by assurances from the mayor and commissioners that the funding was denied. 

The Pioneer’s second review of the meeting footage from June 15 shows that Commissioner Dory Hanson originally made a motion to approve the funding request. However, just before the commission voted on her motion, she amended it to table the request. When Heupel called the question, he clearly stated the motion to table the request. 

That motion failed with a 2-3 vote, with Commissioners Al Rohrer, Roger Thomas, and Heupel voting against it. 

Following the vote against tabling the issue, the commission moved on to other matters instead of addressing the funding request with a definitive vote. 

At the end of the meeting, resident Denise Parker addressed the city’s inaction with the funding request. 

“Did the can just get kicked down the road,” she said. 

Commissioners appeared to be confused, as both Carr and Heupel said the commission denied the funding request. 

“No. It died. It got denied,” Commissioner Rob Carr said. 

“So then you’re not going to require anything of them,” Parker said. 

“Not unless they come back with a different plan and a new request,” Heupel said. 

During the Monday meeting, Heupel acknowledged the mistake and called for a roll call vote on a motion to approve the request for $72,917. All commissioners except Hanson voted against providing the funding.

title: SD GOP lawmaker may get  plea deal in election fraud case
byline: By John Hult Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Sen. Tom Pischke, R-Dell Rapids, sports a “No on G” shirt at the Life Defense Fund election night watch party in Sioux Falls on Nov. 5, 2024.
_full_text:
Dell Rapids Republican lawmaker may get plea deal in election fraud case.jpg
Sen. Tom Pischke, R-Dell Rapids, sports a “No on G” shirt at the Life Defense Fund election night watch party in Sioux Falls on Nov. 5, 2024.  

SIOUX FALLS – A plea deal is in the works for a Republican state senator from Dell Rapids facing felony charges related to attempted election fraud.

Tom Pischke, 44, was charged with 2 felony counts for allegedly filing documents to get candidates for county party positions on the June 2 primary ballot without those candidates’ knowledge. He pleaded not guilty during an initial appearance Tuesday. Each count carries up to two years in prison. 

The senator was in the courtroom with his lawyer, Ryan Kolbeck, who requested and was granted a preliminary hearing date for Pischke from magistrate Judge Andrew Robertson. 

Defendants charged with felonies in South Dakota are entitled to preliminary hearings upon request, at which prosecutors must present enough evidence to justify the pursuit of charges.

The case may not reach such a hearing, tentatively scheduled for August, if a plea deal is reached. 

“I believe we have a plea deal” for Pischke, said Minnehaha County State’s Attorney Daniel Haggar. He did not elaborate.

After the hearing, Kolbeck confirmed that plea deal discussions are ongoing but said a deal is not yet “imminent.” Pischke declined to comment. 

The charges against Pischke are felonies, but low-level felonies that carry a rebuttable presumption of probation.

Prosecutors say this spring, Pischke filled out and mailed 16 applications for precinct committeeman and committeewoman to the Minnehaha County Auditor’s Office for inclusion on the June 2 primary ballot without the candidates’ knowledge.

Applications to run for precinct committeeman or committeewoman are meant to be filled out and signed only by the candidate, but there’s no law requiring the forms to be notarized, and potential candidates needn’t collect signatures to qualify.

County precinct committeemen and committeewomen are chosen by voters during primary elections or by members of county parties between primary seasons. Those who hold the positions can cast ballots at the state GOP convention to help choose candidates for constitutional offices like secretary of state or auditor. 

Auditor Leah Anderson’s staff spurred the investigation that ultimately led to Pischke when they noticed suspiciously similar handwriting on the applications, according to a detective’s report in Pischke’s case file. The applications were tested for fingerprints and DNA after interviews with the listed candidates, each of whom told sheriff’s deputies they hadn’t signed the forms. 

Pischke serves as a committeeman for the Minnehaha County GOP and is a member of the county organization’s board. 

Pischke did not attend last month’s state GOP convention, however, which began two days after the charges against him were filed. He’s also stepped back from his duties with the state and county party as the charges are pending, party leaders said the week he was indicted.

Pischke is set to run against an independent named Bryan Breitling in November. Breitling had previously served in the state Senate as a Republican.

title: SD confirms 11th measles  case of 2026 in Edmunds Co. child
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: A health care worker handles a dose of the MMR vaccine. Photo by Joshua Haiar, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
SD confirms 11th measles case of 2026 in Edmunds Co. child.jpg
A health care worker handles a dose of the MMR vaccine. Photo by Joshua Haiar, South Dakota Searchlight 

PIERRE — South Dakota Department of Health officials have confirmed the state’s 11th measles case of 2026.

The case involves a child younger than 18 in Edmunds County, department spokeswoman Tia Kafka said. The patient was unvaccinated or their vaccination status is unknown, and the source of exposure is unknown.

The department notified medical providers last week to be alert for measles symptoms in Brown, Campbell, Edmunds, Faulk, McPherson, Potter, Spink and Walworth counties.

The department did not issue a press release about the case because the patient was not known to have visited public locations while infectious, Kafka said. 

The last cases reported before Thursday were in May, according to the department’s measles dashboard. 

So far this year, six measles cases have been confirmed in Grant County, one in Brown and three in Brookings. This is the first case in Edmunds County.

Two of the patients who contracted measles in May were hospitalized. They’ve since recovered, Kafka said.

Ten of the 11 cases involved patients who were unvaccinated or unaware of their vaccination status. Seven of the cases have been among children. Six were exposed through international travel, four have an unknown source, and one was linked to close contact with a known source.

“The measles vaccine (MMR) offers the best protection against measles infection,” Kafka said.

Measles symptoms appear in two stages. Early symptoms can include a runny nose, cough, slight fever and red eyes sensitive to light. Between the third and seventh days, a patient’s temperature can reach 103 to 105 degrees, and a red blotchy rash typically develops on the face before spreading to the entire body.

People who are not immune or vaccinated, or who are unsure of their status, should contact their medical provider, the department said.

According to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, there have been 2,170 confirmed measles cases nationwide in 2026 across 41 states as of July 2. Those states include all of South Dakota’s surrounding states except Iowa.

There were 2,267 confirmed cases across the U.S. in all of 2025, according to the CDC.

Measles was considered fully eradicated in the U.S. in 2000. Falling measles vaccination rates in recent years have contributed to its return. Several areas of the U.S. now have vaccination rates below the 95% threshold needed to prevent outbreaks.

The kindergarten measles vaccination rate in South Dakota has tumbled from 97% to 90% in the past 10 years. Health officials blame disinformation about vaccine safety, which has contributed to a rise in parents claiming religious exemptions to avoid otherwise mandatory school immunizations.
