title: Tick bites are surging in the US this year.  Here’s what to know
byline: By Amelia Twyman States Newsroom
description: A lone star tick, which is a very aggressive tick that bites humans. A circular rash sometimes follows the bite. Photo courtesy Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
_full_text:
Tick bites are surging in the US this year.  Here’s what to know
A lone star tick, which is a very aggressive tick that bites humans. A circular rash sometimes follows the bite. Photo courtesy Centers for Disease Control and Prevention 

WASHINGTON — The prime time for ticks is here in the United States, and after an especially active start to the season, experts are urging the public to stay alert and take preventive measures. 

Monthly emergency department visits for tick bites in April spiked to their highest level since 2017 and continued to remain high throughout May and June, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s tick bite tracker.

Though it’s hard to predict what the rest of the season will look like, given that tick activity depends on a number of different factors, there has definitely been a recent geographic expansion of the area ticks inhabit, said Pilar Fernandez, a disease ecologist and assistant professor at Washington State University. 

The tiny blood-suckers, which tend to thrive in warmer climates, are spreading to places that used to be too cold for their existence, she said during a July 1 SciLine media briefing, as temperatures rise in the United States and around the world.

With more ticks comes a greater risk of individuals developing tick-borne diseases such as Lyme disease, Alpha-gal syndrome and anaplasmosis. That’s why researchers are encouraging people to know their facts and learn how to protect themselves from bites as they venture outdoors. 

What’s going on this year?

According to the CDC, an estimated 31 million people are bitten by ticks each year, with most encounters taking place between April and October. But in 2026, ER visits began rising as early as March. 

Weekly ER trips for tick bites are also up in every U.S. region except for South Central as of June 28, the online tick tracker shows. 

Global warming is certainly one reason behind this recent surge in tick activity, though Fernandez said the whole picture is much more complicated.

Because ticks can live for up to two to three years, it’s difficult to understand the delayed seasonal effects of increased temperatures or precipitation on their population, she said.

Other factors including local environmental conditions and how much time people spend outside can have an impact on annual tick encounters, she added. 

Every spring and summer, she said, people ask her if it’s going to be a “big year” for ticks, which is “a really hard question to answer, because it’s not equal across all locations.” 

Most tick cases are recorded in the Northeast and Midwest, but different species of ticks are found in every region of the country. And as the population expands into areas where people are unaware of how to protect themselves and unaccustomed to checking for bites, the threat of contracting a tick-borne infection grows, Fernandez said. 

Tick-borne diseases

Ticks carry pathogens that they then pass on to humans by biting into their skin and feeding on their blood. An untreated tick bite can lead to the development of one of nearly 20 different human diseases in the U.S., the most common of which is Lyme disease — about 476,000 patients are treated annually, according to the CDC. 

Another tick-borne infection that has been on the rise is Alpha-gal syndrome, which causes people to experience a serious allergic reaction after they eat red meat or other animal products that contain the sugar molecule alpha-gal. It is most commonly associated with the lone star species of tick distributed throughout the Northeastern, Southern and Midwestern United States. 

Initial symptoms of tick-borne illnesses are unspecific and often the same as those that come with regular sickness, such as a fever, headache, muscle aches and joint pain, according to Alvaro Toledo, an associate professor in the Department of Entomology at Rutgers who also spoke at the July 1 media briefing. 

“Physicians need to be vigilant and aware if they receive a patient with symptoms that are compatible with a tick-borne disease,” he said.

What if you find a tick?

If one discovers a tick on the skin, Toledo said the proper response is to first quickly remove the tick with tweezers by pinching and pulling it up in a vertical motion, then disinfecting the area and monitoring for signs of sickness. 

People should not, on the other hand, deal with a tick by burning it off or applying petroleum jelly to the bite, said University of Wisconsin-Madison Assistant Professor Adela Oliva Chavez, a tick researcher, at the briefing. 

“Those are myths,” she warned. 

Ticks typically do not transmit infection until after they have been attached to the skin for 24 hours, which is why the CDC recommends people aim to remove the pests as soon as possible within the first day.   

However, experts say the most effective way to prevent tickborne disease in humans is by limiting exposure to ticks in the first place.  

Toledo said people should use chemical sprays such as permethrin on their clothing and classic bug repellents on their skin to keep ticks away. It’s also a good idea to wear long, light-colored clothing when spending time in forests and other highly vegetated areas where ticks are abundant. 

But, he added as a reminder to the public, there is “no zero-risk zone anywhere when you go out … even in your backyard, risk is not zero.” 

Individuals can further reduce their chance of acquiring a tick bite by checking their pets just as often themselves, according to Oliva Chavez. Dogs and cats can easily bring ticks into the house from outside, and if they aren’t yet attached to the animal’s flesh, they can make their way onto humans, she said.

title: The Mercy Sloane Chronicles: Chapter 9
byline: By Eliza Blue A work of serialized fiction, special to the Pioneer
description: “Kola would be a good name for your dog,” Ardath said later, as she saddled her pony. “My grandma was Hunkpahpa Lakota and she spoke the old language. There aren’t too many who remember those words now, but the prairie still does. She’s new to English.” Ardath laughed as she fit one foot in the stirrup and swung her other foot up and over the pony’s back. “Prairie might be more inclined to help you if she can understand what you’re talking about.”
_full_text:
The Mercy Sloane Chronicles

“Kola would be a good name for your dog,” Ardath said later, as she saddled her pony. “My grandma was Hunkpahpa Lakota and she spoke the old language. There aren’t too many who remember those words now, but the prairie still does. She’s new to English.” Ardath laughed as she fit one foot in the stirrup and swung her other foot up and over the pony’s back. “Prairie might be more inclined to help you if she can understand what you’re talking about.” 

‘Kola,” Mercy repeated out loud. “What does it mean?” The older woman turned in her saddle and glanced down at Mercy’s left side. Mercy followed Ardath’s gaze and saw the little puppy was sitting beside her, head up, back straight as a small soldier’s, staring intently as if coming to her call. 

Ardath laughed again. “Looks like he knows the old words, too,” she said, “So maybe ask him.”

***

That night, Mercy lay down on her new mattress, the smell of dried grass and sage filling her nostrils, and marveled at its softness. Never in her life had it felt so good to lie down in a bed. She let out a long sigh of contentment, then rolled over to face the corner where the puppy was already sleeping. “Kola,” she called softly into the darkness. She saw his dark head lift and the flash of his eyes. “Kola, come!” she said.

The puppy trotted over, the soft click of his nails the only sound other than the wind blowing gently through the open door, and clambered up to tuck himself against the curve of her belly as if they’d done it every night of their lives. “Kola,” she said into the cool darkness as she petted the smooth silk of his ears, and she thought she knew what it meant, too.

***

Neither Marla nor Mercy had considered the fact that Mercy would show up the following morning in the same condition she’d left – which is to say, extraordinarily dirty. In the first light of dawn, Mercy had washed her arms, face, and neck in her new pot filled with cold well water, but there was no hiding the fact that every other part of her was very dusty. The wind coming up during the long walk to town didn’t help either. The few farmers who still attempted to plow up the prairie grass instead of just letting their livestock graze often found their topsoil relocated to the next field over, and today it looked as though much of the soil from the field just north of town had been relocated to Mercy’s body. 

Standing on the wooden boards in front of the store’s plate-glass window, Mercy tried as best she could to brush herself off, while Marla peered at her surreptitiously from behind the counter. Arlo and Marla had decided it would be best for Marla to “train” Mercy on her first day of work. Neither one was at all sure what that meant, as neither one was sure what Mercy was actually going to be doing at the store. 

So Arlo went to the pasture to check the sheep that first morning, and after staring at her through the store window, Marla went to draw a bath for Mercy. After she’d cleaned up, Marla lent her a smart-looking navy blue suit with red piping. “You can keep it here,” Marla said, motioning toward the storage closet in the back of the store, “And change before work, like a uniform,” she added, in case Mercy was embarrassed. 

Mercy just nodded and started dusting. Marla clucked over invoices and greeted the few customers who wandered in, mostly to chat. 

 Eliza Blue TMC
Eliza Blue 

At dinner time, Marla disappeared into the house, then called Mercy to follow her. Marla pulled bread from the bread box, butter from the ice chest, then handed a jar of cucumber pickles to Mercy to set on the table. Next, she pulled a roasting pan from the oven, the earthy brown smell of beef, onions, and potatoes filling the room. 

After two weeks of dried jerky, tack, and beans, Mercy, who was not by nature a dramatic girl, nearly swooned. “Oh, Mrs. Hanson,” she sighed, spontaneously lifting her hand to her heart, “That is the best thing I have ever smelled!”

Marla gave Mercy a sharp look to see if the girl was teasing, then allowed herself a small smile. “Folks say my beef roasts are pretty good,” she murmured, setting the pan down in the table’s center. Noticing that Mercy was nearly swaying on her feet, she added. “You don’t need to wait for Arlo, who knows how long he’ll be.”

Sure enough, they’d nearly finished before Arlo returned, sunburned and nearly as dusty as Mercy had been when she arrived. Marla was instantly up and bustling, fixing her husband a plate. “You’re late, Arlo,” she said, then shooed him away when he leaned to kiss her cheek. (“Oh my, you are too dusty for all that!”) But she piled his plate high, even buttered his bread for him as he washed his hands in the big bowl by the stove. 

Arlo grinned as he sat down to eat, watching as Marla tutted Mercy out the door and across the alley to the shop. “You never know what’s going to happen next, do you?” He thought, “You just never know.”

SPEARFISH – Two Sanford Health dermatology clinicians have started outreach services at the Sanford Health Spearfish Clinic.

Dr. Alexander Reid, and Mindy Row, a certified nurse practitioner, who practice at the Sanford Health Tower Road Clinic in Rapid City, will offer dermatology services to handle the medical and cosmetic needs for patients with both non-surgical and surgical treatments.

Originally from Spearfish and a graduate of Spearfish High School, Reid is excited to return to his hometown and provide care to the community that helped shape him. 

Rowe is a certified nurse practitioner who evaluates and treats a wide range of skin conditions, including acne, eczema, psoriasis, rashes, rosacea, scars, skin lesions and warts. As a Spearfish resident, she is excited for the opportunity to serve patients in her own community and help expand access to dermatology care close to home. Rowe will be providing outreach at Sanford Health Spearfish Clinic every Tuesday and Wednesday.

title: SD board approves $2.4M tax rebate to  assist defense contractor’s Clear Lake expansion
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Gov. Larry Rhoden gives a speech during a groundbreaking for an expansion of Tech Ord in Clear Lake. Photo courtesy of the Governor’s Office
_full_text:
SD board approves $2.4M tax rebate to  assist defense contractor’s Clear Lake expansion
Gov. Larry Rhoden gives a speech during a groundbreaking for an expansion of Tech Ord in Clear Lake. Photo courtesy of the Governor’s Office 

PIERRE — A South Dakota economic development board approved a $2.4 million sales tax rebate Wednesday for a weapons manufacturer’s expansion in Clear Lake.

The approval comes as state leaders are pushing to expand defense contractor presence in the state. 

The South Dakota Board of Economic Development approved AMTEC Corp’s Reinvestment Payment Program application for the $2,434,648 rebate, to be paid as the company spends money in the state to facilitate its expansion. The payment is capped at 75% of the actual state sales and use tax paid on eligible project costs, with eligible costs not to exceed $113.6 million. 

The state program allows companies to earn a rebate for upgrading equipment or constructing a new building in South Dakota. The program is limited to building projects over $20 million or equipment upgrades worth more than $2 million. Companies must meet certain expectations linked to jobs created, wages paid and the size of their physical footprint to qualify for the rebate.

The company recently announced plans to build a new medium-caliber ammunition production and test facility at the existing Tech Ord campus in Clear Lake, which is a division of AMTEC Corp. The project was described by National Presto Industries, of which AMTEC is a subsidiary, as a $90 million investment intended to meet U.S. Department of Defense ammunition needs.

“The investment further strengthens South Dakota’s growing role in supporting national defense and advanced manufacturing while reinforcing the Tech Ord campus as a strategic location for future Defense Industrial Base expansion,” a June 15 press release reads. 

Tech Ord produces detonating and explosive components and materials. The company says its Clear Lake campus spans 640 acres and includes manufacturing, engineering and support operations, storage bunkers and hazardous-waste treatment infrastructure. 

Gov. Larry Rhoden touted the Tech Ord expansion as part of South Dakota’s push to grow its national security industry in a June 19 column.

“They have over six decades of success strengthening our nation’s defense, and they continue to thrive here in South Dakota,” Rhoden wrote. “When their parent company was looking for a place to expand, they chose our state.”

In April, Rhoden announced a $6 million grant to start the South Dakota Defense Institute and a new Rapid City collaboration space intended to connect businesses, schools and government partners with federal defense agencies and contracting opportunities. 

Tech Ord said media inquiries regarding the state funding must go through AMTEC’s Wisconsin office. That office declined to comment or put Searchlight in contact with their media relations staff.

title: Quick picks: Summer skills
description: The longest day has come and gone, but it will be a while before the days shorten noticeably again. Make use of those long summer days to learn something new, and check out one of these titles from your local library.
_full_text:
The longest day has come and gone, but it will be a while before the days shorten noticeably again. Make use of those long summer days to learn something new, and check out one of these titles from your local library. 

This week’s recommendations are courtesy of the librarians at Grace Balloch Memorial Library. 

1. “The Art of People: 11 Simple People Skills That Will Get You Everything You Want” by Dave Kerpen

Genre: Self-help

What does it take to win success and influence?

Some people think that in today’s hyper-competitive world, it’s the tough, take-no-prisoners type who comes out on top. But in reality, argues New York Times bestselling author Dave Kerpen, it’s actually those with the best people skills who win the day. Those who build the right relationships. Those who truly understand and connect with their colleagues, their customers, their partners. Those who can teach, lead, and inspire.

2. “Fluent Forever: How to Learn Any Language Fast and Never Forget It” by Gabriel Wyner

Genre: Language/non-fiction

Gabriel Wyner speaks 7 foreign languages fluently. He didn’t learn them in school — who does? Rather, he mastered each one on his own, drawing on free online resources, short practice sessions, and his knowledge of neuroscience and linguistics.

In “Fluent Forever,” Wyner shares his foolproof method for learning any language. It starts by hacking the way your brain naturally encodes information. 

3. “Flower School: A Practical Guide to the Art of Flower Arranging” by Calvert Crary 

Genre: Crafts/Non-fiction

Create the flower arrangements of your dreams to keep at home, take to the office, or display on any special occasion using the simple tips and tricks and masterful techniques taught by Executive Director and professor Calvert Crary and the master florists at FlowerSchool New York.

4. “DIY Thrift Flip: Sewing Techniques for Transforming Old Clothes into Fun, Wearable Fashions” by April Yang

Join the thrifting revolution! DIY Thrift Flip teaches you how to find, upcycle, and customize secondhand clothing for sustainable style with simple sewing instructions.

Expert thrift-flipper April Yang takes you through every phase of the process, including how to find the best clothes and fabrics and easy ways to alter and tailor shirts, dresses, pants, coats, and more.

5. “Art Before Breakfast: A Zillion Ways to Be More Creative, No Matter How Busy You Are” by Danny Gregory 

Genre: Art/Non-fiction 

Packed with the signature can-do attitude that makes beloved artist Danny Gregory a creativity guru to thousands across the globe, this unique guide serves up a hearty helping of inspiration. For aspiring artists who want to draw and paint but just can’t seem to find time in the day, Gregory offers 5– to 10–minute exercises for every skill level that fit into any schedule — whether on a plane, in a meeting, or at the breakfast table — along with practical instruction on techniques and materials, plus strategies for making work that’s exciting, unintimidating, and fulfilling.

6. “The Total Skywatcher’s Manual: 275+ Skills and Tricks for Exploring Stars, Planets, and Beyond” by Linda Shore, David Prosper, and Vivian White

Genre: Science

With fully illustrated star charts, gorgeous astrophotography, and step-by-step project instruction, this is the only guide you need to navigate the night (and day) sky. Learn about the phases of the moon, how to conduct your own deep-sky observations, how the universe is expanding, our search for life on other planets, meteors vs. meteorites, sunspots and solar flares, best eclipse-viewing techniques--everything you need to know to appreciate the wonder of our universe. “The Total Skywatcher’s Manual” will help stargazers and comet-spotters of all stripes.

title: On partnership, ableism,  acceptance, and love: ‘Catching Sight’ memoirist Deni Elliott to visit Spearfish for seminar event Saturday
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — On the day Deni Elliott was born, both she and her mother received last rites. They were not expected to live. When she arrived home from the hospital, conquering the earliest adversity, Elliott’s big, black, furry family dog, Marty, was there.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — On the day Deni Elliott was born, both she and her mother received last rites. They were not expected to live. When she arrived home from the hospital, conquering the earliest adversity, Elliott’s big, black, furry family dog, Marty, was there.

 CENTER Book Cover.jpg
 “Catching Sight: How a Guide Dog Helped Me See Myself” is a new memoir by Deni Elliott. Courtesy image 

Marty would become Elliott’s first guide.

“Marty had appointed himself my caregiver,” Elliott recalled. “Marty took me around furniture and led me from room to room or around things that other people could see, which I didn’t realize for a really long time.”

In addition to complications during birth, Elliott entered life with low vision.

“My visual field is covered with splotches, basically. I used to, when I was much younger, I talked about looking at the world through a dirty screen door,” Elliott said. “That has gotten grimier over the years. The splotches are bigger. It’s harder to see around them.”

Despite the progressive degradation of her sight, Elliott carved out academic and career-based success. She attended Harvard for graduate studies, became a respected ethics and journalism professor, and a prominent academic — she was the founding director of the Practical Ethics Center at the University of Montana, director of the Dartmouth College’s Ethics Institute, the co-director of the National Ethics Project, and she is included on a list of 33 subject matter experts assembled by the National Center on Disability and Journalism.

“Because my parents and my sister really pushed me to do whatever I could do and be proud of my accomplishments and my success, I have had a pretty nice career,” Elliott said. “Things were going along pretty well until I was told that I was legally blind. I thought, ‘Well, this changes things.”

In 2000, Elliott had to confront the fact that her needs were evolving.

 Deni Elliott
Deni Elliott is the author of “Catching Sight: How a Guide Dog Helped Me See Myself.” She is pictured with her current guide dog, Hildy, looking up at her affectionately. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

“My first thought was, I can’t go through life trailing a cane,” Elliott said. “When you see a white cane, usually the cane is out in front of them. They’re using the cane, sweeping it side to side, looking for obstacles. So that the cane finds it instead of your knee finding it or your foot finding that it’s an elevation change you didn’t expect. I knew I didn’t want to go through life that way.”

Elliott was not used to leading with her disability, and had even become practiced at concealing it.

“I went to the eye doctor, I got new glasses, I did all of the things that my mom and dad taught me to do, so that I could portray as normal as possible,” Elliott said of her youth.

She said her family actively encouraged her to be OK.

“There was pressure to be as normally sighted as I could. One of the things I write about in the book is that my parents would go out on a date night or wherever they were going, and my mom would come in and say, ‘How do I look?’ My job was to find something, anything accurate to say. I mean, ‘Gee mom, you look great.’ That wasn’t going to cut it. ‘I like the red in your dress. You have your hair different.’ Anything that I could see and respond to that was accurate was rewarded,” Elliott said.

She was conflicted about having an aid that could make her low-vision obvious to other people.

“Here I am with a guide dog, how do you make sense of that?” Elliott said. 

Her first guide was Oriole — a puppy she had purchased before she was declared legally blind, with the hope of training her to compete in agility. After an assessment from a seasoned trainer, Oriole was privately trained to guide Elliott.

“A cane finds obstacles, a dog avoids them,” Elliott said. “Until I went to Guiding Eyes for the Blind, which was 13 years later, that is what I thought a guide dog did.” 

It was Elliott’s mother who first suggested she look into acquiring a guide dog through Guiding Eyes for the Blind.

“When I went to Guiding Eyes for the Blind, I met not just my dog, but dogs who people could trust with their lives,” Elliott said. “The dog had the big picture of, ‘Oh, I am the eyes at the end of the harness. I am the eyes that are responsible, not just for me, but also for the person who’s attached to me on the harness.’”

Elliott’s first Guiding Eyes Dog was named Alberta.

“Alberta was the perfect first dog for me. Koala was the perfect second Guiding Eyes dog for me. If they had been switched, I don’t think I would have bonded in the same way that I did with the dogs,” Elliott said. “I needed Alberta’s courage and her ability to say, ‘Come on Deni, we can do this.’ I learned to trust her, and I learned that it was safe to trust her. Koala was an excellent guide dog, but she was more like my analytic side.”

Elliott said each dog who has served as her guiding partner has had a special place in her life, heart, and journey.

“I have described having multiple guide dogs over my life as how it helps to be a serial monogamist. You’ve got to love the one you’re with. When one dog retires, then you have to really have your heart open to accept new love, to accept a new guide dog,” Elliott said. “They are different. I am different at different points in my life as I grow and change.”

But Alberta was such an impactful guide and partner, Elliott felt compelled to tell her story. She started writing in 2020, and this June she published “Catching Sight: How a Guide Dog Helped Me See Myself.”

“The book tells the journey of a Guiding Eyes puppy, a puppy literally from the moment of birth till she gets through advanced training and is ready to be matched with a human partner,” Elliott said.

In order to really explore her partnership with Alberta, Elliott also needed to look into her own past. To think about her beginnings. Her family. How she came to think about navigating life with ever more limited sight. That was a challenge, Elliott said.

She interviewed 22 people to tell Alberta’s story, and her own family to help build a complete picture of who they both would become.

“It ends up being these 2 parallel stories, which for me as a long-time professor of journalism is really kind of interesting,” Elliott said. “In the process of wanting to tell Alberta’s story, so that people really understood the magic of guide dog relationships, I found out that I had to tell my own story of how I got to Guiding Eyes for the Blind.”

The result is a book about 2 stories becoming one.

Elliott’s story involves her grappling with openly presenting as a person with visual impairment, and how having low vision does and doesn’t define her.

“One thing that I hope every single reader that reads Catching Sight takes away is an acceptance that we are all people with limitations. Growth and development is a lifelong process,” Elliott said.

As for Alberta’s story? Elliott thinks it might be helpful to people who have pet dogs at home.

“I hope that they can take some of the techniques that are discussed in “Catching Sight,” that are used to raise guide dog puppies to be confident enough to be guide dogs. It means you can’t do it through force. You can’t do it through punishment. You can’t do it through yelling at them. It has got to be positive, and it has got to be affirmation,” Elliott said. “I hope that people can take some of these ideas to their pet dogs, and say ‘let’s see.’ It is the way you want to treat a human partner. You want to affirm that person and use positive feedback and work together. I think that is what all human canine relationships should be like.”

“Catching Sight” is available in standard, large-print, and audiobook formats, through Beacon Press.

On Saturday, Elliott and her current guide dog Hildy are scheduled for a special ticketed seminar at Henry’s Books at 11 a.m. Directly following that, the general public can meet Elliott, visit with her about her book, and have books signed at the bookshop beginning at 12:30 p.m. for free.

title: Lead citizens demand accounting for  150th anniversary celebration
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: A small crowd gathered at Mountain Top Field to listen to the Lexington Lab Band, a 70s and 80s rock cover band from Kentucky. The band headlined the Rock the Hills 150th Anniversary celebration in Lead on Friday. The Lead citizen watchdog group Checks and Balances by City of Lead Community Friends and Neighbors demanded a full accounting of costs and revenue related to the 150th anniversary celebration. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
Lead citizens demand accounting for  150th anniversary celebration
A small crowd gathered at Mountain Top Field to listen to the Lexington Lab Band, a 70s and 80s rock cover band from Kentucky. The band headlined the Rock the Hills 150th Anniversary celebration in Lead on Friday. The Lead citizen watchdog group Checks and Balances by City of Lead Community Friends and Neighbors demanded a full accounting of costs and revenue related to the 150th anniversary celebration. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

LEAD — Final costs for the Lead Rock the Hills 150th anniversary celebration will be publicly reported after the city receives final invoices for charges, Mayor Dustin Heupel told a standing-room only crows at the Monday city commission meeting. 

Debbie Fisher, a member of a citizen watchdog group Checks and Balances by City of Lead Community Friend and Neighbors, approached the commission with a request the group made in writing for all financial records related to the celebration that featured 4 bands, vendors, food trucks, and more at Mountain Top Field; a Fourth of July parade; a vintage baseball game; and more. The request was mailed to city hall and personally to Heupel and each of the city commissioners, as well as to City Finance Officer Billie Jo Ryan, City Administrator Robin Lucero, and City Attorney Tim Johns. It gave a deadline of June 30 — before the Fourth of July festivities — for city officials to produce total expenses and revenue from third-penny sales tax, sponsorships, and merchandise sales for the event. According to the letter, the information was intended for public inspection at an open meeting of the Checks and Balances group. 

Fisher said when Checks and Balances members Pam Millard and Raquel Rice arrived to pick up the records, they sealed the documents provided by the city in an envelope until that night’s meeting. Fisher presented the commission with copies of the documents the group received from the city, including about $69,000 in bills, with about $2,480 coming out of the third-penny sales tax, or bed and booze fund, so far. 

“Nowhere in here does it have the band, the stage, the bathrooms, the cost of the school buses, Black Hills Security,” Fisher said. “We requested any and all information, so citizens could look it over and also to see if it has been officially approved by the commission and not just unilaterally by a single person. We request again that this information be provided. We would like to have it all broken down so we know where our money is being spent.” 

Heupel reiterated to the public that Lucero plans a detailed public report as soon as the city has received all invoices for the event. Some invoices will be for time and materials, so it is not possible to know exactly how much they were before the bills are issued, he said. Lucero’s anticipated presentation could happen as early as the July 20 or the Aug. 3 city commission meeting. 

The group Checks and Balances by City of Lead Community Friends and Neighbors was originally formed in 2024 by residents who opposed a proposed special assessment tax to pay for street maintenance and improvements. The group successfully referred the tax and voters defeated the tax. Since then, the group meets on Tuesdays after city commission meetings, to discuss community and government related issues.

title: ‘Science Steve’ returns to  Neutrino Day in comeback season
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: LEAD — Steve Rokusek got his start as “Science Steve” in 2008, on stage in Lead, before the Sanford Underground Research Facility started its annual Neutrino Day science festival.
_full_text:
LEAD — Steve Rokusek got his start as “Science Steve” in 2008, on stage in Lead, before the Sanford Underground Research Facility started its annual Neutrino Day science festival. 

Every year after that, Rokusek made it a point to bring engaging demonstrations for all ages to the event that celebrates and encourages science. Neutrino Day helped Rokusek launched his career as a South Dakota Public Broadcasting K-12 education specialist, and he became well known for dynamic performances in physics and chemistry, and for developing educational materials for teachers to bring into their classroom. He travels the state presenting activities, lesson plans, videos and more for teachers. 

But in 2022, illness forced Rokusek off the stage for 30 months. This year marks his return to Neutrino Day — the event that launched “Science Steve.” 

“There’s a little bit something special about this trip,” Rokusek said. “This is my comeback season. I’m very excited to come back to Neutrino Day. I started my career with this and now I’ll be able to come back on this final show of my season and perform.” 

The show will be mostly comprised of physics demonstrations about how air moves, weight and motion with a classic tablecloth demonstration, music, jokes, fog machines, and water. “Science Steve” is known for using all kinds of materials, including watermelons and flying toilet paper, to explain complicated topics. Audiences sitting in the front row or who get invited on the stage are also known to get sprayed a little bit with water. 

“I think you have to experience it and make it fun,” Rokusek said of learning about science. “When kids come to my show, I make it as fun as I can. There’s a lot of music. I have a lot of jokes in there. For every year of age there is a minute of attention span. So, if you’re 10 years old, you have 10 minutes. If you have a child for 50 minutes and they’re 10 years old, you have a 10-minute attention span. You might lecture on 10 minutes, you might do an activity for 5 minutes, you might show a video for 10 minutes, and it’s all on the same topic, but you mix it up, make it more fun. Then you kind of re-start your attention span. With my show, I try incorporating jokes in there and I make people laugh. If you make people laugh, it kind of restarts the clock. Then when you start the demonstration, they’re going to learn science. But in the meantime, we’re also having fun, too.” 

Rokusek said his goal for his presentations is to help people of all ages understand science topics that may otherwise seem complicated and unapproachable. That fits right in with the spirit of Neutrino Day, he said, where science booths, presentations, and lectures dominate the day. 

“What’s nice about a day like this is you can come out and there are a bunch of scientists there and the families can interact with different professionals and realize it’s really approachable,” he said. “It’s nothing to be scared of. We encourage families to go home and try different activities at home with the kids. You want to try this stuff. You want to experience it in order to understand it. There’s really no perfect age. Maybe if you have a third-grader, they might not understand like a senior would or an adult. But they do understand it and they do learn from it. Then you build on that over the years.” 

Providing science education is Rokusek’s favorite part of the SURF mission, as he said the lab’s education specialists also do a great job teaching kids across the state. 

“They have an amazing education department,” he said. “They meet with thousands of kids every year and to me, the amazing part is how you can take that really high level science and bring it down to thousands of kids across the region and make it understandable. That team is awesome. They bring it from the scientists to the kids in an understandable way. To me, that’s the coolest thing is when organizations like that value education from elementary through high school and beyond.” 

Rokusek’s demonstration will be the final event of Neutrino Day festivities, held at the Historic Homestake Opera House from 3-4 p.m., Saturday. The event is free to the public.

title: Belle Fourche bicycle program poised to support Rally enforcement efforts
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Belle Fourche bike patrol officers help manage crowds at the Fourth of July/Roundup Rodeo Parade. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
BF Bike Cop.JPG
Belle Fourche bike patrol officers help manage crowds at the Fourth of July/Roundup Rodeo Parade. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

BELLE FOURCHE — On the Fourth of July, parade attendance was high enough to degenerate bumper-to-bumper traffic heading into and out of the heart of downtown Belle Fourche. That could’ve been a problem, when police were called to a car accident more than a mile away from the downtown core. Enter Belle Fourche’s bike patrol officers. 

“This weekend over the 4th, we had a crash, and the bike patrol actually beat our patrol cars to get through all the traffic,” Belle Fourche Police Chief Ryan Cherveny said. “They literally went a mile and a half across town to get there and were able to beat the patrol cars. That is just how efficient it is.”

Belle Fourche has issued officers e-bikes to use on patrol. The efficiency of the program has prompted its deployment beyond Belle Fourche’s borders, Cherveny said. 

“So last year, our bike patrol went and worked Sturgis. They were actually down in Sturgis with the bikes, operating down there,” Cherveny said. “They are going to be doing that again this year as part of Sturgis’ Rally bike patrol.”

Bikes allow officers to navigate differently through heavy traffic, and provide a different kind of visibility on city streets. 

“I think it is kind of exciting for everybody,” Cherveny said. “Now that’s got the city of Sturgis and other departments looking into e-bikes themselves now and trying to ramp up their program because the 2 officers that kind of run the bike patrol the most, Lt. (Jucole) Jones and Detective (Jason) Huber.”  

The weekly youth bike safety program led by Huber and Jones has also grown in popularity, Cherveny said. On Wednesdays, the 2 have encouraged young people to come to the rec center for safety education and a group bike ride with police officers. Cherveny said, after the first ride, about a dozen kids or more have attended each week.

title: Spearfish man faces felony animal cruelty charges after dead dog found in his house
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Spearfish man faces felony animal cruelty charges after dead dog found in his house
Courtesy photo 

SPEARFISH — A 55-year-old Spearfish man is charged with felony animal cruelty, after a dog died while allegedly locked in a room with no open doors or windows in his house. 

Gary Darland was arrested Monday. 

According to court documents, Spearfish police officers arrived to investigate claims that an animal carcass was decomposing inside a home on 5th Street, and were given permission to enter the house. They discovered an animal that had likely been deceased for “close to 3 months,” according to the statement of probable cause for Darland’s arrest.  

According to court documents, Darland told police he had been ill, and started sleeping in a camper behind his house. He allegedly left the dog in the house while he was sick and told officers he checked on the animal once. Darland reportedly told police he checked on the dog 2 weeks later and found it dead. 

Investigating officers found that there was food available to the animal, but that food appeared molded and untouched.

According to court documents, Darland told police he chose not to move the dog’s body because he was still sick and was dealing with grief over the dog’s death. 

Cruelty to animals is a Class 6 felony, punishable by up to 2 years in prison, a $4,000 fine, or both.

title: Petition to clarify SD proof of citizenship law shot down over technicality
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — Under state law, any “interested person” can petition state boards to change administrative rules.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — Under state law, any “interested person” can petition state boards to change administrative rules.

But South Dakota citizens and organizations don’t qualify as “persons” under that chapter of state law. The existence of that limitation surprised some members of the state Board of Elections on Wednesday during a meeting called for the express purpose of voting to advance or defeat a rules package the body spent 2 hours pondering last week.

The League of Women Voters leaned on what it believed to be its right to petition state board earlier this month when it offered the board a series of rule changes the group argued were necessary to standardize the administration of a new state law that requires first-time voter registrants to provide proof of U.S. citizenship.

The board dismissed the petition in a 5-2 vote on Wednesday after one of the board members told the group that the advocacy nonprofit lacks the legal standing to ask for the changes.

Last minute check of statutes calls petitioners’ status into question

The definition of a “person” able to petition a state board for a rule change only includes political subdivisions or agencies of the state, board member and retired Rapid City attorney Scott McGregor said.

McGregor did not attend the initial board meeting last week when the petition was presented, but he reviewed the matter over the weekend, he told South Dakota Searchlight after the meeting. With a 40-year career “making legal arguments based on statutory interpretations,” McGregor also reviewed relevant laws regarding the petition process.

McGregor said he wanted to see if “interested person” had a broad enough definition to include organizations such as the League of Women Voters.

“‘Person’ in various contexts has an awful lot of definitions,” McGregor said. “It depends on the section of the law you’re dealing with and the level of government you’re dealing with.”

McGregor spoke with the Secretary of State’s Office and its legal counsel earlier this week to confirm his interpretation. Deputy Secretary Tom Deadrick told McGregor that other agencies have accepted rule petitions from individuals.

“Even if other agencies have done it,” McGregor told Searchlight,” that doesn’t change the law.”

McGregor told board members he was “shocked” by the limitations.

“That may be an oversight, but that’s all that’s in there,” McGregor said during the meeting.

Board member Kent Alberty said he was “disappointed” that the law’s restrictions on petitioners wasn’t shared with board members earlier. Alberty, during last week’s meeting, said that he saw a need for at least some standardization in procedures in the administration of the citizenship requirement. 

Alberty voted against the dismissal on Wednesday, as did Dewey County Auditor Jamalia Franzen.

McGregor told South Dakota Searchlight that the law should be reviewed legislatively.

“There is a certain unfairness to it,” McGregor said.

Rule changes, responses

Acceptable documents for proving one’s citizenship under the new law in question on Wednesday include a birth certificate, passport, driver’s license, non-driver’s identification card or tribal identification card, or “any other type of acceptable documentation” under federal law. Photocopies of most of those documents are acceptable, but registrants using state- or tribally issued identification cards must have the physical cards with them.

If a voter does not provide necessary documentation, they are registered as federal-only voters and cannot participate in local or state elections.

The League of Women Voters proposals included:

Allowing photocopies of identification cards, such as tribal IDs and driver’s licenses, to be used as proof of citizenship.

Recognizing tribal identification cards from any federally recognized tribe, rather than just the 9 tribes in South Dakota.

Allowing voters designated as federal-only an opportunity to cast provisional ballots for local elections while appealing their eligibility.

Adding specific language to the state’s voter registration form to explain that not offering a physical South Dakota address would cause them to be designated as federal-only voters.

Adding language to notifications confirming a voter’s registration clearly saying if the registrant is a federal-only voter, as well as language explaining how to remedy the situation.

South Dakota Secretary of State Monae Johnson was ill during last week’s board meeting, at which the group took testimony from supporters of each rule. No one from her office was on hand to rebut the supporters, but her staff did file written responses in opposition.

On Wednesday, Johnson told the board that the new law, as written, does not allow photocopies of driver’s licenses, only the original card. She added that while no formal appeal process exists for voters registered as federal-only, they can remedy their status by resubmitting their registration with proper documentation.

“The League of Women Voters and other concerned organizations could look at amending the current law in the 2027 legislative session, if that is their wish,” Johnson said.

Johnson will not be seeking re-election for secretary of state in November. She lost the Republican nomination at last month’s state party convention to state Rep. Heather Baxter, who supported the bill that created the new law during the legislative session and will oversee its administration if elected. Baxter will face Democratic nominee Terrence Davis in the general election.

Baxter submitted public comment ahead of Wednesday’s meeting and compared the proposed changes to presenting a photocopy of identification to get through security at the airport or purchase alcohol. The state Department of Public Safety does not accept photocopies of identification documents, Baxter said.

“So why allow the League to make such changes to what law already clearly states as well as other state departments?!” Baxter wrote.

Amy Scott-Stoltz, president of the League of Women Voters of South Dakota, said the organization is “disappointed” in the board’s decision and “reviewing our options” regarding advancing its proposals and challenging the board’s dismissal.

The group’s petition was meant to make sure the new law is “uniformly implemented across the state and that voters and county auditors alike would have clear guidance about their obligations under the law in advance of the November election,” Scott-Stoltz said. 

“We intend to continue our work in South Dakota to ensure that every American citizen can access the ballot box,” Scott-Stoltz said.

title: Spearfish man wins national aviation award
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer
description: Lt. Col. Buck DeWeese, of Spearfish earned the Civil Air Patrol’s Aerospace Education Award for promoting aviation education. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Buck DeWeese.JPG
Lt. Col. Buck DeWeese, of Spearfish earned the Civil Air Patrol’s Aerospace Education Award for promoting aviation education. Courtesy photo 

SPEARFISH — Lt. Col. Buck DeWeese, of Spearfish, won the Civil Air Patrol’s (CAP) Frank G. Brewer Memorial Lifetime Aerospace Education Award Sunday.

The CAP is a government nonprofit that flies non-combat missions for the United States Air Force, including search-and-rescue missions. It is the largest operator of single-engine aircraft in the world. 

“His leadership, vision, and personal commitment have directly advanced CAP’s aerospace education mission and established enduring programs that continue to shape aerospace education within the South Dakota Wing of CAP,” Maj. Lori Fussell said in a prepared statement. 

DeWesse said he first dreamed of becoming a pilot when he was in third grade. He took part in Reserve Officer Training Corps (ROTC) while studying at South Dakota State University.

“I was only a B-average (at SDSU), DeWeese said, “But I was top 10% of my ROTC class.”

After graduating, DeWeese joined the Air Force, where he served for 12 years. He then began working as a pilot for Delta Airlines, and worked there for 32 years. 

While as a pilot, DeWeese said he was involved in an aviation disaster in which a technical fault led to his airplane to begin banking just after takeoff. 

“We were passing 60 degrees of bank when bells and whistles started screaming and yelling,” DeWeese said. 

DeWeese and his copilot managed to prevent the engines from stalling and landed the airplane safely. DeWeese flew passengers to San Francisco on a different plane the same night. 

“We (he and the co-pilot) questioned our sanity because post-traumatic stress disorder does not kick in right away,” DeWeese said. “It takes 2 to 3 hours. And when the adrenaline wore off 3 hours later, we were only halfway across the Pacific.”

 He said he and his copilot were later awarded the National Aviation Award for their actions. 

After retiring from Delta, DeWeese joined the CAP, where he still flies search-and-rescue operations and teaches the CAP’s teenage cadets.

“It was very unexpected,” he said of receiving the Aerospace Education Award. “I’m very honored. It’s incredible.”

DeWeese is set to officially receive the award at a CAP conference in August. He recently celebrated his 50th wedding anniversary.

title: Jackley announces state will receive $410K in Cash App settlement
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: PIERRE — South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley recently announced that South Dakota will receive $410,946.38 as the state’s share in a $45 million, 46-state settlement with Block, Inc. The settlement resolves allegations that Block, Inc. misled consumers about the safety of Cash App, a peer-to-peer payment platform, and failed to protect users from fraud.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

PIERRE — South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley recently announced that South Dakota will receive $410,946.38 as the state’s share in a $45 million, 46-state settlement with Block, Inc. The settlement resolves allegations that Block, Inc. misled consumers about the safety of Cash App, a peer-to-peer payment platform, and failed to protect users from fraud.

“Block, Inc. did not provide the fraud protection it promised and that was required by law,” said Jackley. “Consumers were left vulnerable to fraud, and the company failed to help consumers when fraud occurred.”

Jackley said Block, Inc. told Cash App users their money was safe – implying that the app worked like a bank, with the same protections, which wasn’t true. At the same time, Block, Inc. knew fraud on its platform was rising sharply – and instead of warning users or strengthening protections, it doubled down on its marketing.

For years, Block, Inc. actively promoted direct deposits of paychecks and government benefits into Cash App. It made a particular push to reach unbanked and underbanked consumers – people who would often rely on Cash App as their primary financial account, and who were especially vulnerable to fraud. Block, Inc. grew its user base without making sure it could support those users when problems arose.

South Dakota’s share will go to the Attorney General’s Consumer Protection Division to fund future consumer protection efforts.

As part of the multistate settlement, Block, Inc. will distribute between $75 million and $120 million to compensate South Dakotans and consumers nationwide as part of a settlement with the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB). 

Jackley said South Dakota consumers who believe they are entitled to compensation should visit https://www.consumerfinance.gov/enforcement/actions/block-inc/ and https://cashappcfpbsettlement.com/.

Other states that are part of the agreement are: Alabama, Alaska, Arizona, Arkansas California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Georgia, Idaho, Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Michigan, Minnesota, Mississippi, Montana, Nebraska, Nevada, New Hampshire, New Jersey, New Mexico, New York, North Carolina, North Dakota, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Tennessee, Texas, Utah, Vermont, Virginia, Washington, West Virginia, and Wisconsin.

title: Honor Flight gives Sturgis Vietnam veteran  the welcome home he waited  nearly 60 years to receive
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: WASHINGTON, D.C. — For nearly 6 decades, Marine veteran Daniel Jojola carried memories of returning home from Vietnam to a divided nation where many veterans were met with hostility instead of gratitude.
_full_text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — For nearly 6 decades, Marine veteran Daniel Jojola carried memories of returning home from Vietnam to a divided nation where many veterans were met with hostility instead of gratitude.  

 1. vet.jpeg
Daniel Jojola displays his Honorable Discharge from the Midwest Honor Flight upon returning from Washington, DC. Photo courtesy of Noreen Suniga 

 2. vet.jpeg
Daniel Jojola is welcomed home by his daughter Noreen Suniga  and her husband Roger Suniga. Courtesy photo 

A couple weeks ago, the Sturgis resident experienced a very different homecoming.

Jojola was among 84 veterans who traveled to the nation’s capital as part of the Midwest Honor Flight, a nonprofit organization that provides veterans an all-expenses-paid trip to visit the memorials honoring their military service.

For Jojola, the experience was more than sightseeing. It was an emotional journey of remembrance, healing and long-overdue appreciation.

“It feels so gratifying because when I got off the ship, they were spitting on us,” Jojola said. “To be thankful now, better late than never.”

Jojola, who served in the U.S. Marine Corps from 1964 to 1968 with the 2nd Battalion, 7th Marines, said he learned about the Honor Flight from one of his customers while cutting hair.

“He told me I needed to get my name on the Honor Flight list,” Jojola said. “It took about a year before I was selected. I really didn’t know what to expect.”

Although the trip lasted just one day, Jojola said it was packed with unforgettable moments.  

“They treated all of us like royalty,” he said. “You get assigned a guardian, and they don’t want you carrying anything. They want you to enjoy the experience, and we did. It was a great, great time.”

Among the many stops, the Vietnam Veterans Memorial carried the greatest emotional weight.  

Jojola had visited the memorial years earlier, but this trip was different. While searching the wall, he located the name of his Marine Corps drill instructor, who was later killed in Vietnam. 

“He was quite an influence on me,” Jojola said. “I was able to find his name and make a rubbing of it. I’ll keep that forever.”

Jojola enlisted in the Marines at just 17 years old after leaving high school during his junior year.  

“I wish I wouldn’t have done that,” he said. “I never failed a class. I just hated school.”

Originally from Colorado, Jojola moved to Sturgis about 12 years ago after decades of visiting the Black Hills for the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally.  

“When I retired, I said I had to move to the Black Hills. They’re just way too pretty,” he said.

The Honor Flight also gave him the opportunity to connect with fellow veterans, most of whom also served in Vietnam.  

“We exchanged addresses and got to know each other,” he said. “There weren’t a lot of Marines, mostly Army veterans, but it was good being around people who understood.”

While every memorial was meaningful, Jojola said the most powerful moment actually came after returning home.

Hundreds of people gathered late that evening to welcome the veterans back with applause, handshakes, signs and heartfelt thanks.

“That was probably the most profound experience,” he said. “The community came out that late at night, everybody wanted to shake your hand and thank you for your service. We never got that when we came home.”  

Instead, Jojola remembers returning from Vietnam to insults and accusations.

“When I came off the ship, they were calling us baby killers,” he said. “It was a different time.”

The warm reception offered by the Honor Flight helped replace those painful memories with something far more meaningful.  

“You are truly honored by the support from the community and the Honor Flight organization,” he said. “They truly want you to feel welcome home. We did what we were asked to do. We served our country, and to finally feel honored like that was very moving.”

One unexpected highlight came at the World War II Memorial, where 4 young girls thanked him for his service and asked to take a photo with him after sharing a joke. Moments later, a television news crew interviewed him, making the day even more memorable.

Looking back on the experience, Jojola said it is difficult to express his gratitude.  “I can’t thank people enough for what they did,” he said. “How do you say thank you for something like that?”

For one Sturgis veteran, the Honor Flight wasn’t simply a trip to Washington, D.C. It was the welcome home he had been waiting nearly 60 years to receive.

title: Incarcerated women to move into  new RC prison to alleviate overcrowding
byline: By John Hult Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: From left, South Dakota Corrections Secretary Nick Lamb, Warden Eric Aldridge and Gov. Larry Rhoden cut a razor wire at an event to mark the completion of an $87 million women’s prison in Rapid City. Photo courtesy Gov. Larry Rhoden’s office
_full_text:
Incarcerated women to move into new RC prison to alleviate overcrowding.jpg
From left, South Dakota Corrections Secretary Nick Lamb, Warden Eric Aldridge and Gov. Larry Rhoden cut a razor wire at an event to mark the completion of an $87 million women’s prison in Rapid City. Photo courtesy Gov. Larry Rhoden’s office 

RAPID CITY — Incarcerated women will start moving into a new $87 million prison in Rapid City next month, a South Dakota Department of Corrections spokesperson confirmed this week.

The medium-security prison will be the state’s second for women. The South Dakota Women’s Prison in Pierre has operated beyond its capacity for years, with dozens of people serving their sentences at the Hughes County Jail or in halfway house facilities.

The new prison in Rapid City, which was approved by state lawmakers in 2023, will add 288 beds to the state’s capacity. The Department of Corrections will begin transferring women there next month, according to spokesperson Michael Winder, who said the exact date of full operations won’t be released for security reasons

The prison includes a work release area, a mother-infant building that lets new moms stay in a home-like environment with their babies, a vocational training facility to be staffed by instructors from Western Dakota Technical Institute and 96 beds for chemical dependency treatment.

The majority of the women held in South Dakota prisons are incarcerated on nonviolent drug charges, and 97% have a substance use disorder diagnosis.

“Drug addiction is a disease that must be treated,” Corrections Secretary Nick Lamb said at Friday’s ribbon cutting, adding that “Through dedicated treatment space and the therapeutic community, women will receive the counseling support and skills that they need to break the cycle of addiction and successfully return to their families and communities.”

The mother-infant program mirrors one launched a few years ago in Pierre. 

Mothers who qualify under security guidelines stay in a group home separate from the main prison facility with other women and children for the first few years of their child’s life. The program was launched by former Corrections Secretary Kellie Wasko and was championed by Lamb in his first public conversations with lawmakers on the state’s budget committee during the 2026 legislative session.

At Friday’s event, Gov. Larry Rhoden said family connections and parenting skills are key factors in rehabilitation. He framed the program as an extension of a commitment to the well-being of South Dakota families.

“This program gives mothers and their children the opportunity to build that foundation from the very beginning,” Rhoden said.

Rhoden also called out the vocational training, drug treatment and work release programs as vital to rehabilitation — and to public safety by extension. The state recently broke ground on a new $650 million men’s prison in Sioux Falls, which is set to replace the state penitentiary and is also designed to expand programming and rehabilitation.

When combined with pending policy recommendations from the state’s correctional rehabilitation task force, Rhoden said, the new prisons will help improve public safety statewide by reducing the number of people who return to prison within a few years of their release. 

“At the end of the day, every person in our corrections system is a human being,” Rhoden said. “They are sons and daughters. They are mothers and fathers. People who’ve made mistakes but also have the capacity to change.”

Winder, the corrections spokesman, told South Dakota Searchlight that staff will spend the next few weeks training at the new facility in preparation for the arrival of inmates in August.

The state hired Eric Aldridge to serve as warden in March. Aldridge, who came to South Dakota after a stint as warden of a medium-security women’s prison in Troy, Va., said Friday his goal is to “to facilitate an environment, an atmosphere, a culture where people learn, they grow, they heal, and where people develop through dignity and respect.”

title: SD lawmaker asks GF&P  to consider bear hunting season
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Bear sightings in the Black Hills have prompted one lawmaker to ask the Game, Fish, and Parks to consider a bear hunting season. On that same day, residents in Lead began reporting bear sightings in and around town. The bear is shown here near Roughlock Falls in Spearfish Canyon. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
SD lawmaker asks GF&P to consider bear hunting season .jpg
Bear sightings in the Black Hills have prompted one lawmaker to ask the Game, Fish, and Parks to consider a bear hunting season. On that same day, residents in Lead began reporting bear sightings in and around town. The bear is shown here near Roughlock Falls in Spearfish Canyon. Courtesy photo 

WEBSTER — Amidst sightings throughout the Black Hills, one South Dakota lawmaker is inquiring about a possible black bear hunting season. 

Rep. Tim Goodwin, R-Rapid City, appeared before the South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks Commission at their regular meeting, Thursday, to ask them to consider doing a study for possibly instituting a black bear hunting season. 

“We’re having problems with bears in the Black Hills,” Goodwin said. “Keystone has them in their yard and their garbage cans. Hill City does. Custer does. There’s even probably more sightings in the Northern Hills. So, they’re starting to be a nuisance. Other states hunt bears. It isn’t like we’re re-inventing the wheel. We have to go about it cautiously, because there’s crazy lion hunters like me that would crawl into a cave and shoot a sow and she might have cubs, and we’ll have all kinds of controversies if we do that. So, we gotta figure out an ethical way that we could do it, just like we did when we started the lion season in 2005. So, if you would consider maybe doing a study, I’d really appreciate it.” 

Immediately after Goodwin’s request, Black Hawk resident Nancy Hilding asked the commission to research whether the bears are breeding, in order to determine whether they should be placed on the state’s endangered and threatened species list, which the GF&P is currently in the process of updating. 

 Goodwin’s request comes after numerous confirmed bear sightings in the Northern Black Hills. His comments were made during the open forum part of the GF&P meeting, which allows people to comment about any matters, not on the official agenda, that could affect the department. The GF&P Commission did not take action on the request and did not respond to Goodwin’s remarks. 

On that same day, the city of Lead issued a notice for all residents to be aware of black bear activity on the outskirts of Lead near Kirk Road, and at least one Lead resident reported a sighting in his yard. 

“It was coming down the hill towards me by the tramway,” said Fritz Reller. “I was probably like 25 feet away from it. I think it’s awesome. We went for rides, hoping we’d see one on our drive, now that we knew the bears were around. We were hoping we’d see one. But then to be right in my own yard and see it. I trust the black bear a lot better than a mountain lion as far as doing anything wrong, besides maybe tipping your garbage can over.” 

The city of Lead post encouraged residents to be vigilant, and to take precautions to avoid attracting the bears. Officials encouraged residents to keep garbage securely contained and stored, and to not leave pet food, bird seed, or other attractions outside. They also suggested cleaning outdoor grills after use, and to be aware of surroundings while walking or hiking outside. The city statement also encouraged residents to remain calm if they encounter a bear, give it plenty of space and do not approach the bear. Residents who see a black bear in city limits are encouraged to call the Lead Police Department at (605) 584-1616. 

Wildlife officials with the GF&P are trying to trap the bear so that they are able to mark it with an identification mark which will help them track it. Officials ask people to see the bear to notify a conservation officer or call the Rapid City office at (605) 394-2391.

title: Lead busineses report  record sales for July 4 celebration
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: The tent at Manuel Brothers Park was consistently full of people enjoying the Gold Camp Jubilee, Saturday. Thousands of people flooded Lead on the Fourth of July this year. Businesses in Lead reported record sales after the July 4 celebration. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
Gold Camp Jubilee crowd 1.JPG
The tent at Manuel Brothers Park was consistently full of people enjoying the Gold Camp Jubilee, Saturday. Thousands of people flooded Lead on the Fourth of July this year. Businesses in Lead reported record sales after the July 4 celebration. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

LEAD — About 5 businesses in Lead reported record-breaking sales during the Lead Gold Camp Jubilee celebration, July 2-5 

Jamie Grangaard, executive director of the Lead Area Chamber of Commerce, told the city commission on Monday that the 100th annual Gold Camp Jubilee celebration, traditionally held in the park, was a huge success this year. 

“My job is to get people to the park and drive people to the businesses, and I can tell you from hearing from those businesses, we did just that,” Grangaard said. “We will continue to do our days down in the park, if that’s what you want the Chamber to do.” 

Carol Oolman, owner of Miners and Merchants Trading Post on Lead’s Main Street, said she was close to record sales on July 4, and red, white and blue merchandise was golden.

“We had great foot traffic through the store and everyone was in the festive 4th mood,” Oolman said. “We sold out of a lot of my patriotic clothes and jewelry. We heard very positive comments on the great event the Chamber put on.” 

Despite the rainy cold weather on Friday, Grangaard said crowds filled the Sanford Lab Homestake Visitor’s Center parking lot for the second annual Gold Rush Cruisin’ Classics car show, which was resurrected in 2025 after a nearly 7-year hiatus. Awards included best in show for a 1955 Chevy Nomad, owned by Jerry and Jonel Geske; people’s choice for a 1986 AM General M35A2, owned by James Thompson; and judge’s choice, for a 1956 Dodge Lander owned by Morgan Nelson. 

In addition to a car show, the first cornhole tournament brought 9 teams to the park. Morgan Nelson and her family took home the championship, Grangaard said. 

“It was very well attended despite the rain and poor conditions outside,” Grangaard said. 

This year, the Lead Area Chamber of Commerce contracted with the city of Deadwood to provide a trolley that shuttled visitors between Lead and Deadwood for the festivities. Grangaard said that trolley transported 566 visitors, and chamber officials hope to utilize it for future events. 

Grangaard extended special thanks to the Lead Volunteer Fire Department, the Lead Police Department, city crews, and all volunteers, businesses, and bands for working to make the annual event a success. 

“The support was amazing,” she said. “Food trucks sold out. Several member businesses reported record-breaking sales on Saturday, and thousands of residents, alumni, and visitors came together to celebrate.”

title: 25 years of Neutrino Day
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: The front page of the Feb. 23, 2001 Black Hills Pioneer reports the first Neutrino Day celebration in Lead. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
Neutrino Day BHP.jpeg
The front page of the Feb. 23, 2001 Black Hills Pioneer reports the first Neutrino Day celebration in Lead. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick  

LEAD —Lead residents have been celebrating Neutrino Day for nearly 25 years. 

But the celebration has not been held continuously. Since 2001, the only year the Black Hills Pioneer did not report about Neutrino Day was 2003. 

The event that started on Feb. 22, 2001 looked very different from the day-long science festival it is today. Back then, the Feb. 23, 2001 edition of the Black Hills Pioneer reported that the Lead Area Chamber of Commerce strung a banner across Main Street, welcoming scientists to town when 3 members of the National Underground Laboratory committee, chartered by the National Science Foundation, came to town to investigate the possibility of transforming the Homestake Gold Mine into an underground laboratory. The chamber marked the visit with a mixer held at the Golden Hills Inn, where multiple scientists were staying. During the event, University of Pennsylvania scientist Dr. Paul Wildenhain gave an impromptu lecture, after one of the mixer attendees asked the burning question, “What is a neutrino?” 

A year later, in February 2002, the chamber continued the tradition of Neutrino Day with a second mixer. This time, Lead resident Tracy Thacker made a surprise appearance as “Miss Neutrino,” — clad in a red, white, and blue sequined outfit with red tights and sunglasses. 

At that time the prospect of using the recently closed Homestake Gold Mine for science brought renewed hopes and dreams for residents who wondered about Lead’s future, and closely followed federal and state efforts to build an underground laboratory in the United States. Children participated in art contests to draw their version of what a neutrino looks like, and pictures of Dr. Neutrino, and scientists who aspired to do experiments underground in Lead presented updates or lectures about science. 

Karen Everett, then-director of Lead’s chamber, said, “It’s too important for science, for South Dakota, and for tourism, and we will get the job done. We have all the confidence that our delegation and Homestake will get the job done.” 

From 2001 to 2008, Neutrino Day was held on Feb. 23, as a way to mark the day scientists came to Lead to investigate the possibility of locating a deep underground science and engineering laboratory in the mine, according to Pioneer reports from Feb. 22, 2008. 

Since those early days, Neutrino Day has evolved with the development of the Sanford Underground Research Facility. In July 2008, South Dakota Public Broadcasting brought a grant-funded, InNOVAtion science festival to the Sanford Underground Research Facility. The event, which featured presentations from South Dakota Public Broadcasting’s “Science Steve,” and other science booths, changed the face of the annual science festival. Since then, the Sanford Lab has organized Neutrino Day on the second Saturday in July, as a free science festival, marked with hands-on demonstrations, engaging lectures, and other activities. 

Mike Headley, executive director of SURF, said the lab has proudly hosted Neutrino Day for 18 years, and will look forward to celebrating the 20th anniversary of the event in 2028. 

“SURF has proudly hosted Neutrino Day, South Dakota’s largest free science festival for the past 18 years in Lead,” Headley said. “The event has grown tremendously thanks to support from event sponsors, the city of Lead, our community partners and volunteers who come from across the region.” 

This year’s events will kick off at 9 a.m. and will be held throughout Lead. Science demonstrations will be held at the Sanford Lab Homestake Visitor’s Center and at the Handley Recreation Center; traditional Lakota games and presentations will be held at the SURF ethnobotanical garden; science lectures and discussions will be held at the Historic Homestake Opera House; live music will be held at the Historic Homestake Opera House courtyard, and more. The event will culminate with a live physics demonstration by Steve Rokusek, who is known as “Science Steve,” from South Dakota Public Broadcasting.
