title: Temporary party switchers receive encouragement  and criticism ahead of  GOP runoff election
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — The stakes are high enough in the race for the South Dakota Republican Party’s nomination for governor that Nancy Turbak Berry became a Republican, at least temporarily.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — The stakes are high enough in the race for the South Dakota Republican Party’s nomination for governor that Nancy Turbak Berry became a Republican, at least temporarily.

The former Democratic state lawmaker intends to rejoin her preferred party after the July 28 runoff election.

“I wish we would elect Democrats,” said Turbak Berry. “But until the state changes enough so that’s a likely scenario, I think it’s important to have a voice in the primary.”

Turbak Berry voted for Gov. Larry Rhoden in the June 2 primary and intends to vote for him again in the runoff. Rhoden faces businessman Toby Doeden, and the winner will advance to the Nov. 3 general election to face Democratic nominee Dan Ahlers.

Turbak Berry is not alone. 

In South Dakota, only registered Republicans can vote in Republican primary elections, while Democratic primaries are open to registered Democrats, independents and people who register without any affiliation. Democrats did not have any statewide primary races this year.

Voters don’t need to explain their choice to switch parties, and parties gain voters ahead of elections for a host of reasons. But registration statistics suggest that a desire to participate in Republican primaries could drive more voters to the party during election years.

In the 3 months before the June 2 primary election, the total number of Democratic, independent, minor-party or non-politically affiliated voters in the state declined by 1,253. 

The Republican Party added 4,452 voters during the same period.

The number of non-Republican voters has dropped before the primary in 4 of the last decade’s 6 election years – every year without a Democratic presidential primary – with the most significant drop appearing this year. That is a pre-primary phenomenon. The ranks of registered Republicans and non-Republicans both grow in the months leading up to general elections and in non-election years.

In 2026, the pre-primary effect continued through the month of June and early July as voters anticipated casting ballots in the July 28 Republican governor runoff. Between the June 2 primary and July 9, non-Republican voter registrations dropped by 2,919 — more than double the decline in the 3 months leading up to the primary. 

The Republican Party added 5,717 voters in those 37 days. 

The registration changes could be attributable to everyday life events, such as coming of age to vote, deaths or relocations from and to other states. But at least some of the shift involves temporary party switchers like Turbak Berry.

Lincoln County Auditor Sheri Lund said auditors often see voters switch their party affiliation ahead of primaries in South Dakota.

“You’ll see them switch back after the primary,” Lund said. “When they realize they can’t vote for something unless they’re a registered Republican, they might do that.”

GOP leader: ‘Decide who you are’

Former Sioux Falls Mayor Rick Knobe co-authored an opinion piece for The Dakota Scout newspaper shortly after the June 2 primary, encouraging people to temporarily change their voter registration to vote in the runoff. Knobe said he switched from an independent to Republican to vote for Rhoden ahead of the primary.

It was the first time he’s temporarily switched, he said, because he felt compelled to vote for what he described as the “least offensive” candidate in the Republican race. He expects he’ll vote for Democrat Dan Ahlers in the November election. 

Knobe plans to eventually return his registration to independent.

South Dakota Republican Party Chairman Jim Eschenbaum said those who temporarily register as Republicans play “political games” that hurt the Republican Party because it tampers with which candidates will run in November, he said. Eschenbaum himself switched permanently from a Democrat to Republican over a decade ago.

“These people have to decide who they are,” Eschenbaum said. “If you’re a Democrat, vote for the Democrats. Work on your own party. Don’t try to sabotage our party. That’s what they’re doing.”

Eschenbaum said he would support legislation that would restrict South Dakotans’ ability to switch party affiliation, such as only allowing one switch a year.

But Knobe said outrage at South Dakotans switching parties is more partisan than civic.

“On a broader scale, they’re trying to limit people’s participation in the government we all pay for, and I find that un-American,” Knobe said.

Open primary advocate: Shifts are inevitable in closed system

Joe Kirby, a lifelong Republican in Sioux Falls, said non-Republican voters feeling motivated to “game the system on occasion” to participate in elections is a result of South Dakota’s closed primary system. Kirby has led unsuccessful efforts to restructure South Dakota’s primary system into an open primary.

Of South Dakota’s registered voters, about 52% are Republican and 47% are something else: Democratic, independent, a minor party, or not politically affiliated.

“All voters want to have a say in who is going to lead the state or represent them in Congress or in the Legislature. Right now, we have a system that doesn’t give all groups an equal say,” Kirby said. “It’s a warped system that doesn’t make a whole lot of sense, but it’s in place and tough to change.”

Kirby said he believes the increased interest and discussion around temporarily switching party status is partly due to his and others’ efforts to open primaries in 2024 through a citizen-initiated ballot question.

“I think the voters are more aware now of the possibility of open primaries and the negative aspects of our closed primary system,” Kirby said.

title: Precipitation in Northern Hills down significantly from last year, average
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer
description: Almost all of the state is in some form of drought as this year’s precipitation is down significantly from the average. Illustration courtesy US Drought Monitor
_full_text:
Precipitation in Northern Hills down significantly from last year, average.png
Almost all of the state is in some form of drought as this year’s precipitation is down significantly from the average. Illustration courtesy US Drought Monitor 

SPEARFISH — Precipitation levels around the Northern Hills are substantially down from this time last year. 

According to the National Weather Service in Rapid City. Spearfish has received 7.12 inches of moisture, down from 12.94 inches from the same time last year.

Downtown Rapid City has received 5.57 inches of moisture this year, compared to 8.29 inches from the same time last year, and 10.75 inches in the average year. 

Lead has received 11.66 inches this year, down from 17 inches from the same time last year, and 16 inches in the average year. 

The Weather Service does not collect data for Belle Fourche or Deadwood. 

Newell has received less than 5 inches of moisture in 2026, compared to the 10 inches it normally receives.

About 86% of South Dakota is experiencing some kind of drought, according to the United States Drought Monitor, a service produced in collaboration between the federal government and the University of Nebraska-Lincoln. About 18% of the state is experiencing a drought classified as “severe,” “extreme,” or “exceptional” Most of the Black Hills is in “extreme drought” conditions. This is second only to exceptional drought conditions. 

Melissa Smith, a hydrologist for the National Weather Service in Rapid City, said that the dry conditions would lead to greater potential for — and greater danger from — fires.

She said the lack of precipitation is due, in part, to dry conditions in the American Southwest. The period of prolonged rainfall in the Southwest usually carries to South Dakota. However, this year the Southwest is abnormally dry, reducing the chances of rain in South Dakota. 

“It (drought) is going to make the conditions worse across the Black Hills area. It’s going to significantly increase our potential for our fire danger and our fire potential, as well,” Smith said. 

Temperatures are expected to rise through August.

title: UJS proposes merger of Fourth and Seventh Judicial Circuits
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
ScalesJustice
Courtesy photo 

PIERRE — The South Dakota Unified Judicial System (UJS) State Court Administrator’s Office has proposed to the South Dakota Supreme Court consideration of a merger of the administrative structures of the Fourth Judicial Circuit and Seventh Judicial Circuit.

The Fourth Judicial Circuit consists of Butte, Corson, Dewey, Harding, Lawrence, Meade, Perkins and Ziebach counties. The Seventh Judicial Circuit consists of Custer, Fall River, Oglala Lakota and Pennington counties. The proposed merger is intended to increase operational efficiencies for UJS.

A series of public forums will be held on Wednesday, Aug. 26, to present information related to the proposal and gather comments and feedback in advance of any formal rule proposal to the South Dakota Supreme Court. The public forum locations are:

Rapid City: Pennington County Courthouse (Courtroom C2), 315 St. Joseph St., 8:30-9:30 a.m. 

Sturgis: Meade County Courthouse (Courtroom 3), 1425 Sherman St., 11 a.m. to noon.

Lemmon: Lonesome Dove Conference Center, 312 Main Ave., 3:30-4:30 p.m. 

The forums are open to the public. Following a short presentation by the State Court Administrator’s Office, there will be an opportunity for public comments and questions.

Written input or comments may be submitted to the State Court Administrator’s Office by email to comment@ujs.state.sd.us or by mail to State Court Administrator’s Office, Attention: Judicial Circuit Merger Proposal, 500 E. Capitol Ave., Pierre, SD 57501. The deadline to submit written input or comments is Oct. 1.

South Dakota courts are organized into a unified judicial system and currently consist of 7 judicial circuits. The State Court Administrator’s Office provides centralized administrative assistance and support services to South Dakota’s courts to ensure efficient and responsive operation.

title: SD T. rex could bring $30 million  or more at auction Tuesday
byline: Bart Pfankuch South Dakota News Watch
description: A Tyrannosaurus rex fossil discovered on a ranch in western South Dakota will be auctioned off in New York City on Tuesday with a possible sale price of $30 million or more.
_full_text:
A Tyrannosaurus rex fossil discovered on a ranch in western South Dakota will be auctioned off in New York City on Tuesday with a possible sale price of $30 million or more.

The 38-foot-long skeleton, nicknamed Gus, stands more than 12 feet tall and has one of the most complete T. rex skeletons ever found. According to Sotheby’s auction house, which is handling the sale, Gus could bring the highest sale price ever for a dinosaur fossil.

The dinosaur is from the late Cretaceous Period and was believed to have lived on Earth 67 million years ago.

The Harding County ranch where the skeleton was found lies in the famed Hell Creek Formation, a geological region of northwestern South Dakota and parts of Montana, North Dakota and Wyoming where dinosaur finds are fairly common.

Several other major dinosaur finds have been made there, including Sue, the famous T. rex discovered in 1990. After legal wrangling over ownership, Sue was auctioned in 1997 at a sale price of $8.3 million to the Field Museum of Natural History in Chicago, where it remains today.

The first piece of Gus, a metatarsal from the dinosaur’s foot, was found in 2021 sticking out of the ground on a Harding County ranch owned by Gary and Dana Licking. The find was made by paleontologists with Theropoda Expeditions, a Texas company specializing in commercial excavation, preparation and mounting of dinosaur fossils.

The fossil consists of 183 bone elements, making up 61% of the possible bones in the dinosaur’s body and representing 75% to 80% of the original bone mass by weight, Sotheby’s said.

The dinosaur Sue is 40 feet long and 13 feet tall and is considered the largest and most complete T. rex skeleton ever discovered at 90% of possible bone mass.

“This is our longest-term project ever,” Cassandra Hatton, worldwide head of Sotheby’s Science & Natural History division, said in the video. “From the day the first bone was discovered, we’ve been going back and forth to South Dakota to oversee this whole process.”

The lowest opening bid accepted will be $19 million, with an estimated sale price up to $30 million or more depending on buyer interest, Sotheby’s said.

Gus is named after rancher Gary Licking, whose nickname was Gus. Licking died at age 67 in February 2022, before the full extent of the T. rex skeleton was known.

Gary and Dana Licking married in 1983 and lived on their family ranch 11 miles west of Buffalo, according to Gary’s obituary.

Dana Licking said in Sotheby’s video that she was impressed at the level of skill and professionalism displayed by the paleontologists who discovered the skeleton.

“I’m really grateful that they found it because it could have been lost and nobody ever would learn anything about it,” she said.

Walter Stein, owner of PaleoAdventures in Belle Fourche, in western South Dakota, is an independent paleontologist who is also working to uncover fossils in the Hell Creek Formation.

Western South Dakota is likely to remain a hotbed for discovery of dinosaur fossils, said Stein, who last year opened the Dinosaurs of the Hell Creek Museum in Belle Fourche, a 6,500 square-foot museum with a working paleontology lab, interactive exhibits and dinosaur displays.

“Finding a Tyrannosaurus rex skeleton with 183 bones doesn’t happen every day,” he said.

Stein said the auction of Gus could lead to a purchase by either a museum or a private individual or group.

But it is unlikely an American museum would have the funding to acquire Gus because many are struggling or struggling financially, Stein said. Across the world, however, interest remains high in major fossils in countries where funding may be more accessible, such as in Japan, Korea, China, Dubai, Saudi Arabia or in Europe, Stein said.

“On the one hand, I would love for this and every fossil I collect to go to a museum,” he said. “However, there’s so many dinosaur specimens and skeletons on display, it’s not going to affect the science that much if it ends up in private hands.”

title: State water board  approves future use permit for Milbank, citing increased demand
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — The city of Milbank was granted a future use permit from the South Dakota Water Management Board on Wednesday, despite opposition from a neighboring rural water system and concerns about drying the aquifer.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — The city of Milbank was granted a future use permit from the South Dakota Water Management Board on Wednesday, despite opposition from a neighboring rural water system and concerns about drying the aquifer.

The state’s water management board, whose members are appointed by the governor, makes decisions on the appropriation of the state’s water resources, in addition to reviewing streamgage data and data on groundwater levels and water use.

The vote in Milbank’s favor was unanimous.

The future use permit reserves water rights but won’t give the Milbank the ability to use additional water immediately. The city would need to return to the board with a water permit application once it’s identified a specific “beneficial use,” which under state law means a use that is “consistent with the interests of the public.”

Future use permits are also subject to review every seven years to determine if there’s a continuing need for reserved water.

Growth drives Milbank request

Milbank is a city of 3,500 in a section of northeastern South Dakota that’s experienced significant growth in recent years. The city got a $2.5 million grant from the U.S. Economic Development Administration in 2024 to expand its industrial park, and it’s also seen a milk storage operation expand to serves a local cheese factory that’s increased its processing capacity.

A city leader didn’t point to a specific project or development that would need a certain amount of water during Wednesday’s board meeting, but rather pointed to stress on the city’s current infrastructure.

Milbank City Administrator Steve Pendergrass said the city’s experiencing an increased demand for water and issues with treating water and wastewater.

“We’ve got to start looking at alternative routes, so that’s why we’re looking at this future water use,” Pendergrass said.

Milbank uses a yearly average of 1.1 million gallons of water per day, pulled mostly from the Veblen and Revillo aquifers. It’s asking for the right to draw more from the Antelope Valley Aquifer, which rests underneath Grant, Deuel and Codington counties. The permit will allow Milbank to claim an additional 1,120 acre-feet of water per year from that aquifer in the future.

The U.S. Geological Survey describes an acre-foot as “the amount of water that would cover a football field in one foot of water,” or about 325,900 gallons.

Opposition: Aquifer could be strained

The additional 1,120 acre-feet per year withdrawal by Milbank could have a “unique and detrimental effect” on the Grant-Roberts Rural Water System’s existing wells, as well as on the Antelope Valley Aquifer recharge rate, according to the rural water system’s complaint against the permit.

Engineers at the Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources budget available water by subtracting the water already appropriated from an aquifer from the amount added back each year.

The Antelope Valley Aquifer’s recharge rate is an estimated 6,700 acre-feet per year. A little more than 3,500 acre-feet is already reserved for irrigation, drinking water and future use, according to the engineer’s report on Milbank’s application.

There’s enough water in the aquifer to satisfy the permit, according to the department’s report. But an engineer with DGR Engineering told board members there’s a “significant difference” in water availability on either side of Punished Woman Lake, a body of surface water in the aquifer on the northern side.

“Recharge that occurs in the southern half of the aquifer is not available for withdrawal in the northern one-third of that aquifer,” said Matthew Oedekoven of DGR, who questioned the way the state’s hydrologic budget was prepared.

The rural water system uses DGR for engineering expertise. Oedekoven said he has “significant concerns” about whether the aquifer has enough readily accessible water to offer Milbank the 1,120 acre feet annually that the city requested in its permit application.

“There may be some available, but I am concerned that there is the full 1,120,” Oedekovan said.

The Grant-Roberts water system serves about 2,050 customers across Grant, Roberts, Codington and Deuel counties in South Dakota, and LacQui Parle County in Minnesota. It draws water from the Antelope Valley Aquifer. It’s also spending about $600,000 this year to drill two additional wells, General Manager Brent Hoffmann told board members Wednesday.

In the past decade, the system has started supplying water to Big Stone City and Corona. It’s currently building lines into the city of Marvin and is looking to add the city of Summit within coming years.

“We have growth every year,” Hoffmann said. “You have the small communities, we seem to be losing people, but a lot of people want to move up to the Big Stone Lake area and that’s where a lot of growth is.”

Milbank’s future use might impact other areas, Hoffmann said.

“I think Milbank should should have their future water rights,” he said. “I just don’t feel that this permit would be appropriate at this point in time, based on the data as we read it.”

Board member Rodney Freeman acknowledged those concerns before his vote.

“There were some interesting points and issues raised, but I believe those issues will be addressed if and when the city of Milbank comes in and wants to put it into beneficial use,” Freeman said.

The permit put Milbank in line for water, Pendergrass said, but that doesn’t mean they aren’t also looking for water from other sources than the Antelope Valley Aquifer.

“We aren’t putting all our eggs in one basket,” Pendergrass said.

title: Spearfish airport apron project  to commence in phases
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: The new terminal at the Black Hills Airport/Clyde Ice Field needs an apron. The lion’s share of that apron project should be paid for using federal and state grant funds.  Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Airport Apron project.JPG
The new terminal at the Black Hills Airport/Clyde Ice Field needs an apron. The lion’s share of that apron project should be paid for using federal and state grant funds.  Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

 Airport Apron Exp
This diagram shows how the airport apron project is phased. The work outlined in orange and blue will be completed by North Star Construction. The other phases will be bid at a later date. Graphic courtesy Spearfish public works

SPEARFISH — This week, the Spearfish City Council awarded North Star Construction a $4.5 million bid to build the apron for the new airport terminal at Black Hills Airport/Clyde Ice Field, contingent on a grant award from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).

“We are expecting a 95% grant from the FAA and a 2.5% grant from the state. The city portion is about 2.5%,” Spearfish Public Works Director Adam McMahon said. That 2.5% share the city would be responsible for equates to roughly $112,500. 

“We’ve been working with both the FAA and the state on this. They concur with this approach,” McMahon said. 

The apron project has been broken into phases, and the accepted bid applies to the first phase.

In May, 2 bids for the whole project were opened, but they were rejected because they were significantly higher than the engineer’s estimate and exceeded available funding. The project was redesigned with a smaller scope and longer construction window in hopes of awarding a contract fitting within the budget.

“This was done to allow all interested bidders to supply competitive bids. We received 7 bids ranging from $4,505,800.77 to $5,407,240.82, or a 20% difference between the high and low bids,” McMahon told the Pioneer.

This first phase of work includes paving areas connecting the new airport terminal with existing taxiways and runways. The bid from North Star came in under budget.

“The engineer’s estimate was in between the high and low bids at $4,873,305.80,” McMahon told the Pioneer. North Star bid $4,505,800.77.

The bid included both the base project — the paving immediately around the terminal- and additional drainage work.

“The base project was just the bare minimum to make the airport location function,” McMahon said. “Both alternates are recommended in the award of this. One for some additional grading on the drainage channel and detention basin to accommodate the full build-out of the apron expansion for (later) phases as well as another alternate for additional grading and surfacing to complete as much of the airport apron expansion as can be completed without interrupting the current configuration of taxi lanes.”

The work removed from the project will be bid in the future in conjunction with a future grant, McMahon added.

In future phases, the apron will be expanded, and the old terminal building, along with other structures, will be demolished.

title: Vehicle collides with Big D gas station, driver cites mechanical failure
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: A pickup was driven through a front window of the Big D gas station in Deadwood Thursday afternoon, resulting in no injuries to occupants of the vehicle or the staff inside the convenience store. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
Vehicle accident at Big D.jpg
A pickup was driven through a front window of the Big D gas station in Deadwood Thursday afternoon, resulting in no injuries to occupants of the vehicle or the staff inside the convenience store. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

DEADWOOD — At approximately 6 p.m. Thursday evening, a Ford pickup drove through a front window of the Big D gas station in Deadwood. 

Deadwood Police Chief Cory Shafer, said according to the driver’s statement, the 69-year-old man was attempting to park in front of the store when the brakes failed. The driver alleged that the turbo of the vehicle activated, and he drove through the window. Shafer said the collision did not occur at a high rate of speed and “mechanical failure” was listed as the cause of the accident. 

The driver, female passenger, and staff working inside the convenience store were not injured.

Shafer said there was no indication that the driver was impaired, and the driver was issued a citation for not having insurance. 

Deadwood Police Department, Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office, Deadwood Volunteer Fire Department, and the Deadwood Monument Hospital Ambulance responded to the incident. 

Shafer said the incident is still under investigation while officers work to gather information from witnesses and cameras that could verify the driver’s statement.

As of Friday morning, the Big D gas station was open for business.

title: Homeowners near sinkhole lose state Supreme Court case
byline: By Bart Pfankuch South Dakota News Watch
description: Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Homeowners stuck in 6 years of sinkhole limbo.jpg
Pioneer file photo 

BLACK HAWK — A group of homeowners whose properties were impacted by a large sinkhole just west of Rapid City have lost a major legal battle now that the South Dakota Supreme Court has ruled against them in their lawsuit against the state.

The court issued a unanimous decision on Thursday in favor of the state, which argued it was not responsible for damages caused by the opening of the large sinkhole above a former underground gypsum mine in April 2020.

Roughly a dozen homes in the Hideaway Hills subdivision in Black Hawk were condemned and still sit vacant in the neighborhood. Those property owners were joined by about 150 other homeowners in Hideaway Hills in filing a $60 million class-action lawsuit against the state.

In its ruling, the high court affirmed the ruling of a circuit court judge who said the state had sovereign immunity and, therefore, could not be sued by the homeowners.

The plaintiffs had argued the state was responsible for damages because it operated a gypsum mine on the site for more than 60 years before selling it to a private owner in 1994, after which the land was developed into a subdivision. They also said the state was responsible because it retained the underground mineral rights after the sale.

The origins of the sinkhole date back to the early 1900s when a company called Dakota Plaster dug underground mine shafts in search of gypsum, which slows the hardening of concrete.

When the state of South Dakota opened its own concrete plant in Rapid City in 1925, it began mining for gypsum, including on the future subdivision site. Lawyers for the state said mining was done only on the surface and that no underground mining was undertaken, though blasting did occur.

In the 1990s, the state ended mining operations, reclaimed it for grazing and sold it in 1994 to a private owner. That owner lived and ranched on the land before selling it to a developer who obtained permission from Meade County to build a subdivision in the early 2000s.

In July 2024, a class-action lawsuit was filed against the state, arguing that the gypsum mining operation was not properly reclaimed by the state when it sold the land. A circuit judge ruled in favor of the state in September 2024, and the homeowners appealed the case to the Supreme Court, making oral arguments in fall 2025.

With representation by the national law firm of Fox Rothschild, the homeowners argued that the state improperly filled in areas where it had mined with overly soft materials that led to the sinkhole. They argued that the state’s failure to properly close its mining operation is akin to an “inverse condemnation,” or a taking of their land similar to the use of eminent domain.

Other attempts by the homeowners at legal remedies over the past six years have been unsuccessful.

Lawyers for the state had argued that the prior owner’s underground mining on the site led to the sinkhole, and that the state had only mined on the surface. They also said the developer knew of the underground mine before building the homes but did not alert the homeowners.

Retired Supreme Court Justice Janine Kern, who wrote the court’s opinion, said the state’s position was supported by previous case law and the state Constitution.

“Plaintiffs maintain that selling the surface property to private owners while retaining the mineral rights to the property to the present date renders the State strictly liable for any damage to their private property that has occurred or will occur in the future as a result of the prior mining activities on the property,” Kern wrote.

“The Plaintiffs have failed to establish that the State’s retention of the mining rights to the property is a ‘public use’ under the damaging clause of the South Dakota Constitution.”

Near the end of the 23-page ruling, Kern sympathized with the homeowners.

“While we acknowledge the devastating and sympathetic circumstances in which Plaintiffs find themselves, our review is limited to the claims before us, and Plaintiffs have not presented viable claims against the State in the present action,” Kern wrote.

Attorneys with Fox Rothschild did not immediately respond to News Watch contacts seeking comment.

title: City in contact with Corvette Classic organizers as high temperatures impact Main Street
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: On Main Street city officials say they are working with Dakota Asphalt to mitigate the bleed-through of asphalt, caused by high temperatures, by laying down sand. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Main Street.JPG
On Main Street city officials say they are working with Dakota Asphalt to mitigate the bleed-through of asphalt, caused by high temperatures, by laying down sand. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

 Colo Blvd alt.JPG
High temperatures can cause asphalt to bleed up through pavement surfaces. On Colorado Boulevard, its possible to see places where that is happening. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — Over the weekend, Spearfish residents reported temperatures as high as 111 degrees. On Main Street those “high temperatures have had the effect of causing the asphalt to bleed through to the surface,” Public Works Director Adam McMahon said.

The city is working with Dakota Asphalt to blot the road surface by applying sand. That sand can help manage asphalt bled through, McMahon told the Pioneer.

“Our plan is to coordinate with the contractor to ensure any effects of the chip seal are mitigated and have minimal impact on the Corvette Show and Shine on Friday,” McMahon said.

Annually, Main Street Spearfish is the site of the Black Hills Corvette Classics’ Show and Shine — a car show that blends with the live music of Downtown Friday Nights.  

Mayor John Senden said the city has been in contact with Visit Spearfish and the organizers of the Black Hills Corvette Classic— offering road surface updates “since last Tuesday.”

Senden said organizers and city officials have also kept in touch with the Holiday Inn and Convention Center, as an alternative Show and Shine venue, in the event that Main Street’s condition doesn’t meet standards for the anticipated summer event.

Main Street from Jackson Boulevard to Grant is slated for mill and overlay as soon as possible — which, given bid schedules and weather requirements, might be sometime next year.

Meanwhile, the chip seal repair operation on Colorado Boulevard from Grant Street to Spearfish Canyon was met with delays.

Senden said there were curb repairs that had to be completed before the chip seal project began. Those repairs ultimately delayed the chip seal work until after the Corvette Rally this weekend.

That patching is underway and expected to be completed by July 15. “The chip seal work has been postponed until July 20 after the Corvette Rally and Festival in the Park to avoid interference with those events. Pavement markings will be completed shortly thereafter,” according to a prepared statement from Spearfish Public Works.

title: Five historic Deadwood properties set to find new foundations across town
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: DEADWOOD — Five structures in Deadwood are set to be moved from Main Street near Cadillac Jacks to an empty lot on Charles Street near Monument Health Lead-Deadwood Hospital.
_full_text:
DEADWOOD — Five structures in Deadwood are set to be moved from Main Street near Cadillac Jacks to an empty lot on Charles Street near Monument Health Lead-Deadwood Hospital. 

 Deadwood historic homes.jpg
Three residences and 2 garages are set to be moved from Main Street to Charles Street in Deadwood, filling a gap in historic structures in the area and provide single-family housing. Pioneer file photo by Sara Morgan 

The five structures, located at 306, 308, 388, 390, and 390 1/2 Main St., previously known as the “Deadwood Cottages” and the Auer House, functioned as short-term rentals until they were purchased by Optima, LLC. Optima is an affiliate of Liv Hospitality, of Rapid City. The hospitality management company owns Cadillac Jack’s Gaming Resort and Tin Lizzie Gaming Resort.

The structures include 3 residences and 2 garages. According to surveys of the structures, the buildings were built in the early-to-mid 20th century and were owned by different members of the Auer family. The Auer’s, a family of German immigrants, owned and operated the Sinclair Service Station.

Kevin Kuchenbecker, director of planning and zoning and historic preservation, said the buildings have suffered an adverse effect to their historical integrity due to decades of court battles, zoning issues, and the general effect of time. 

“The commission believes the adverse effect has already taken effect from prior projects,” said Kuchenbecker. “And so, in an effort to save the historic resources, the developer and the commission worked together to save the resources and move them to another portion of the historic district where, historically, there was a similar type of residential structures.”

Kuchenbecker said the buildings cannot be moved until the empty parcel of land near the hospital is rezoned to R-1 and re-platted to allow each residence to have its own lot and be sold independently of each other. After successful rezoning and re-platting, Kuchenbecker said the developer will be responsible for building new foundations and infrastructure for the homes. 

In an effort to preserve the historic integrity of the structures, Kuchenbecker said the developer’s agreement includes a mandatory archaeological survey of both sections of land, regular progress meetings, and financial security measures. 

Kuchenbecker said deed restrictions will be put in place on the structures after the move, requiring the residences to be sold as single-family homes and prohibiting them from being used as short-term rentals. He said the project will function not only to fill a gap in historic structures in the area near the hospital but will help the city combat the shortage of family housing.

Kuchenbecker said the tentative schedule of the project outlines zoning meetings and construction through the summer, with the structures set to move this fall.

title: Record heat scorches Northern Hills
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — The weekend brought record-breaking heat to the Northern Hills, according to officials at the National Weather Service in Rapid City.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — The weekend brought record-breaking heat to the Northern Hills, according to officials at the National Weather Service in Rapid City. 

The Sturgis area reached an all-time high temperature of 106 Fahrenheit. 

Gillette, Wyo. reached a new all-time high temperature of 103 F. 

Temperatures in downtown Rapid City reached an all-time high of 101 F. 

The Weather Service does not collect data on Belle Fourche. Some Belle Fourche residents reported temperatures up to 118 F.

Some Spearfish residents reported temperatures of 111 F. The Weather Service had not reported Spearfish weekend temperatures as of Monday morning. 

The Weather Service does not collect data on Deadwood or Belle Fourche.

The Belle Fourche Police Department reported one heat-related medical incident over the weekend. Spearfish Police Department reported zero heat-related medical incidents last weekend. 

Brian Hambek, executive director of Spearfish Ambulance Service, advised residents to stay hydrated and to wear long-sleeved white shirts. 

“Our emergency department has experienced an influx of patients presenting with heat-related illnesses, and our team is prepared to provide timely, compassionate, and expert care for those impacted by extreme heat conditions,” Christine Duerkson, a nurse-practitioner for Monument Health in Lead-Deadwood, said. “As emergency healthcare providers, we are ready to respond, but prevention remains the most effective strategy to keep our community safe.”

title: Great expectations!
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: A recent Sturgis Arts Council production of Cinderella did not use the curtain at the Sturgis Community Center theater because it is in great need of replacement and is nearly falling down, representatives from the arts center say. The Sturgis Arts Council is embarking on a $150,000 capital campaign to renovate the theater and replace the curtains. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
2. arts.jpg
A recent Sturgis Arts Council production of Cinderella did not use the curtain at the Sturgis Community Center theater because it is in great need of replacement and is nearly falling down, representatives from the arts center say. The Sturgis Arts Council is embarking on a $150,000 capital campaign to renovate the theater and replace the curtains. Pioneer file photo 

STURGIS —Sturgis Arts Council members want to do everything they can to preserve a valuable asset to the community. 

On Monday Dedi LaRue and Francie Reubel-Alberts told the Sturgis City Council that the group is embarking on a $150,000 fundraising campaign, for renovations to the Sturgis Community Center theater. The arts center partners with the city to use the theater as its primary performance venue, drawing audiences from throughout the region for a variety of live shows. 

LaRue said the theater is 35 years old this year, and is starting to show its age. In recent years she said the arts council has replaced the sound system, purchased a grand piano, and refurbished the stage floor that had started to become dangerous for performers. The latest fundraising campaign will be to replace the curtains on the stage, replace carpeting and aisles, and to again restore the stage floor. 

“The curtain needs to be replaced, it’s basically falling off,” LaRue said, adding that the arts council did not use the stage curtain during its most recent production of Cinderella. “We are calling this the three R’s — replace, restore, renew — because that is what we have to do in that theater.” 

“The theater is used all the time, extensively,” said Reubel-Alberts. “It has always been our goal to make sure that theater remains usable and well looked at. That’s why we’re very excited about raising all this money.”  

Once the arts council has raised money to renovate the theater, LaRue said they will begin fundraising to continue the city’s public art project, with more historical sculptures to be placed at the south and west entrances to Sturgis. The group is responsible for the Col. Samuel D. Sturgis sculpture, located on the west side of town.

title: Sturgis gives first nod to potential commercial TIF
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — A commercial tax increment finance district could help boost the business economy in Sturgis, city officials said Monday.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

STURGIS — A commercial tax increment finance district could help boost the business economy in Sturgis, city officials said Monday.

Bergman Construction, LLC asked the Sturgis City Council to indicate whether it would consider supporting initial efforts to develop plans for a proposed TIF to develop the land for commercial use. The property is located west of the intersection of 20th and Lazelle streets, within a highway service commercial zoning district. 

On Monday, the city council unanimously approved a resolution that expresses the council’s initial policy support for the continued evaluation of the potential commercial TIF project, developed by Chris Bergman, of Bergman Construction. The resolution states a TIF proposal will require additional statutory review, financial analyses, a project plan, a development agreement, and final action by the city council. 

The city’s vote to support the effort does not mean a TIF has been approved, but is only a formal show of support for efforts to begin the process to develop a plan. 

A tax increment finance district is a public financing system that uses future increases in property tax to reimburse the costs of public improvements built within a designated TIF boundary. The value of all the properties inside the district is assessed or calculated and the total amount of property tax generated by all those properties is noted — the base amount of property tax revenues. All property revenue above this base amount, for the life of the TIF, is captured by the TIF to refund the costs of the public improvements or project. This amount — the amount over the base — is called the “tax increment.” Over time, property values are presumed to increase in part due to infrastructure improvements brought about by the TIF project itself. When the TIF is retired, the total taxation values revert to the original taxing entities. 

For example, if the city receives $1,000 from a property parcel before a TIF is enacted, it will continue to receive those funds for the life of the TIF, which is a maximum of 20 years. The next year, if the taxes go up to $1,100, the county will receive $1,000, while the increased $100 will be used to retire the TIF. 

Mayor Rod Bradley told the council Monday that Bergman purchased the land from the Leveque family, and he plans to elevate it out of the flood plain to make it a usable property for commercial development. But before Bergman embarks on the process to obtain engineering reports and other associated work for the development, he wanted to gauge the council’s interest in the possible TIF to help pay for infrastructure for the project. 

“It’s not a commitment to approve the TIF,” Bradley said. “It’s a commitment to look at it and be open to evaluating it. The resolution is intended to distinguish this potential commercial TIF from the city’s existing residential development TIF experience and to allow staff and the developer to continue evaluating whether a commercial TIF proposal is financially, legally, and economically appropriate.”

Members of the city council expressed support for a possible commercial TIF district. 

Councilman Jim Thompson and Jesse Blakeman said the majority of Sturgis TIF districts are for residential properties, and a commercial TIF could help boost business development in town. 

“I think this is one of the things we lack in Sturgis is investment of businesses,” Thompson said. “This would be an ideal location. Yes, I would like to give him encouragement to continue.”

title: Police investigate  vandalism in Belle Fourche
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Tomato sauce and yogurt caused permanent damage to the sign for Armed Bears Guns and Ammo Supply in Belle Fourche Sunday. The acid from the tomato sauce combined with the hot temperatures likely caused the damage.
_full_text:
Police investigate  vandalism in Belle Fourche
Tomato sauce and yogurt caused permanent damage to the sign for Armed Bears Guns and Ammo Supply in Belle Fourche Sunday. The acid from the tomato sauce combined with the hot temperatures likely caused the damage.  

SPEARFISH — Belle Fourche police are investigating reported vandalism at Armed Bears Firearms and another location at the corner of 8th Avenue and State Street.

In both cases, what appeared to be food product was splattered across signs. The substances looked like sauces, yogurt, or coffee creamer, Belle Fourche Police Chief Ryan Cherveny said.

The incident reports started coming in on Friday, Cherveny said. Only 2 were formally reported, but a third incident, involving a possibly defaced American flag, has also been the topic of discussion on social media.

Cherveny said the incidents are under investigation. Officers are reviewing footage from nearby cars, security cameras, and city cameras. Patrol officers are also on the lookout for the vandal or vandals.

Cherveny said if the same individual or individuals are responsible for the incidents, they could face escalating charges. Damage is added up in vandalism cases, and when the price of repair and cleanup reaches $5,000 under South Dakota Law, the crime becomes a felony.

Intentional damage to property is a Class 1 misdemeanor if property damage is more than $400 dollars and less than $1,000. A Class 1 misdemeanor is punishable by up to one year in a county jail, a $500 fine, or both. Intentional damage to property is a Class 6 felony if the damage to property is $2,500 or less, but more than $1,000. A Class 6 felony is punishable by up to 2 years in prison, a $4,000 fine, or both.

Cherveny encouraged anyone with information about the vandalism to come forward.

“If you see suspicious behavior or you have been a victim of recent vandalism, let us know,” Cherveny said.

The more information police have, the better equipped they are to put a map together and look for possible patterns to catch a suspect.

title: Citizens question historic preservation requirements for demo
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: LEAD — Not all buildings in Lead are part of the historic district, but all property owners who apply for a demolition permit must appear before the Lead Historic Preservation District.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

LEAD — Not all buildings in Lead are part of the historic district, but all property owners who apply for a demolition permit must appear before the Lead Historic Preservation District. 

Terry Smith, chairman of the Historic Preservation Commission, said the board considers all demolition requests, however not all requests are treated the same way. Everything south of Addie Street is outside of the historic district, he said, and is not subject to the same state laws as properties within the historic district. 

“We don’t look at it as a historically correct building unless it’s a targeted structure that we do want to save,” he said. 

Smith added that state law requires the commission to give property owners 180 days before they are allowed to demolish a structure within the historic district. By requiring all properties to come before the commission, Smith said the commission can determine the correct timeline for action. 

“The reason is because if it’s a structure, a house in the district, we have to start thinking about ways we might use that structure,” Smith said. “It could be even requesting that homewoerns sell the property. That is regulation within the state law, under the historic districts. Outside of the historic district, that doesn’t apply.” 

The discussion came right before the city commission approved a demolition permit for a garage at 610 McClellan St. The permit requires property owners to appear before the historic preservation commission, and states that a failure to appear will result in the request being tabled or denied. Residents questioned whether that’s necessary for properties outside of the historic district. 

“Can we make an amendment to state that they must attend if it’s on the historic preservation district, but that they do not have to if it’s deemed it’s not in the historic preservation district,” said resident Debbie Fisher. “If they’re absent it may be tabled or denied, which technically isn’t fair to them if it’s denied and they’re not even in the historic district.” 

However, Smith objected to the idea, stating that everyone who has an interest in demolition should appear before the historic preservation commission. 

Mayor Dustin Heupel said the request is one that the commission may be able to address at a later date, but he urged the city commission to address the singular demolition request on the agenda, for which the historic preservation commission had already recommended approval. City commissioners unanimously approved the request.

title: Spearfish adopts new engineering design standards, with a caveat: The ‘living document’  will be subject to mandatory annual review
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Spearfish City Engineer Kyle Mathis walks the council through the new Engineering Design Standards, which were adopted with an amendment last week. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
EDS.JPG
Spearfish City Engineer Kyle Mathis walks the council through the new Engineering Design Standards, which were adopted with an amendment last week. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — July 6, the Spearfish City Council adopted 7 ordinances revising and, in some cases, repealing and replacing current city codes regulating water, sewer, flood mitigation, and zoning.

The ordinance changes were made to reflect a new, living document: the city’s engineering design standards (EDS) — also adopted last week. The 370-page document takes guidelines that were formally spread out in city code, and consolidates them, outlining things like: the city’s requirements for the construction of streets, wastewater collection systems, water distribution systems, storm drainage infrastructure, grading and environmental considerations, street light and dry utility distribution, and the city’s process for development plan submittal.

“The engineering design standards were developed to clarify and clearly communicate engineering practices by consolidating all the design standards and requirements for land development into one place, into one document,” Spearfish City Engineer Kyle Mathis said. “The EDS formalizes operational procedures and aligns development standards with federal and state regulations as well.”

Some of the details in the new document were previously laid out in ordinance. The changed ordinances now reference the EDS and have been updated to remove defunct fee structures, city staff positions, and departments.

The EDS, according to Mathis, should be easier to update and amend than city ordinances — helping to keep rules, rates, and department references up to date.

“How easy is it to make tweaks?” Councilman Scott Hourigan asked. 

Mathis said updates can be made administratively. He also explained that there is an exception process that might be appropriate for certain projects and developers.

“Where it makes sense, there is an exception process that a consultant or a developer can fill out the form and say, hey, we can’t meet the maximum slope of 8% because the topography is too steep in this one area,” Mathis said. “That can be submitted directly to the city engineer, myself, and I can make those approvals. If they do get denied, then I can have that kicked up to the council for ultimate denial or approval.”

The EDS has been the subject of discussion and internal drafting since 2023.

“As you know, this has taken a long time. The coordination and public input, other city departments, developers, all of you,” Mathis told the city council.

Mathis said it is difficult to reach 100% consensus on all aspects of a document as detailed as the EDS. However, he said nearly all of the stakeholders he has spoken to agree that having a document like this one is a “substantial improvement over what we have currently.”

“We are hoping this is a very good document. We can make tweaks in the future. We are keeping up communication with the public. If they don’t like something in here, we do have forms that they can submit online, and then we can look at those again year-to-year, etc.,” Mathis said.

Because the EDS and ordinance amendments work in tandem, community development staff asked the city council to adopt both policy documents during its July 6 meeting.

City councilman Larry Klarenbeek asked that the council delay its approval of the EDS to formalize an annual review process.

“In the interest of making a motion so that we can have more discussion, I personally would like to see this delayed until the next meeting. One reason is the concerns we have had,” Klarenbeek said. “I would like to introduce that we have a sunset so that we can formalize a one-year review at this time.”

Hourigan and Mayor John Senden asked Klarenbeek to clarify what he meant by a “sunset.”

“So, would we need to revamp the entire thing? What does that mean?” Senden asked.

Spearfish Community Development Director Peter Wysocki asked if, rather than revamping the document annually if the EDS could be made subject to annual review during the July 6 meeting.

“Larry, are you suggesting that the resolution be amended to state that the engineering and design standards shall be brought back to council by a certain date a year from its adoption to evaluate and approve any amendments?” Wysocki said. “The reason that I ask is that I am not quite sure how the timing will lay out, but we just approved those ordinances, and now they will be inconsistent with the engineering design standards. I don’t think I would necessarily reject a report back. That is a concern about bifocating the ordinances from the engineering design standards.”

“You don’t want to get rid of your ordinances until you’re ready to adopt what’s replacing them,” Mathis added. “That’s why they (the agenda items) were back to back, and we waited until the second reading of the ordinances.”

Klarenbeek said he understood the need to have the ordinances refer to an adopted document and amended his motion to add a mandatory annual review to the resolution adopting the EDS during the July 6 meeting.

title: Cheyenne BOPU traces  rare bacteria discharge to  Meta data center contractor
byline: By Alyssa Tolman Wyoming Tribune Eagle
description: CHEYENNE — The Cheyenne Board of Public Utilities (BOPU) has identified Goat Systems LLC, a contractor working on Meta’s in-progress data center campus in the High Plains Business Park, as the source of a discharge that introduced the bacteria Cupriavidus gilardii into the city’s wastewater treatment system.
_full_text:
CHEYENNE — The Cheyenne Board of Public Utilities (BOPU) has identified Goat Systems LLC, a contractor working on Meta’s in-progress data center campus in the High Plains Business Park, as the source of a discharge that introduced the bacteria Cupriavidus gilardii into the city’s wastewater treatment system.

Frank Strong, BOPU’s engineering and water resource division manager, told the Wyoming Tribune Eagle July 2 that the contamination was discovered during routine testing in February.

Cupriavidus gilardii is a rare type of bacteria found naturally in the environment, such as in soil and water, according to the National Institutes of Health. While it typically lives harmlessly in nature, it can occasionally act as an opportunistic pathogen, which means it mostly infects people who are already sick or have weakened immune systems.

As a result, BOPU temporarily suspended Cheyenne’s reclaimed water irrigation program, permanently terminated Meta’s discharge privileges, and adopted a new policy prohibiting wastewater discharges from data centers using closed-loop cooling systems and fill-and-flush systems, which involves circulating purified water to remove construction debris, flux residue and pipe scale, draining it and filling the loop with fresh coolant.

A Meta spokesperson told the Wyoming Tribune Eagle via email that Meta is supporting the efforts of its general contractor, Fortis, to resolve the issue with BOPU.

“When the board shared that it found a substance in the city’s wastewater — not public drinking water — Fortis immediately stopped discharging industrial wastewater and began hauling it offsite,” the spokesperson wrote.

“Fortis also began its own water testing with an independent environmental specialist, which has found no trace of the substance.

“Meta is committed to being a good neighbor in Cheyenne, including through the protection of local water resources, and will continue encouraging collaboration between Fortis and the board until this situation is resolved.”

Construction water identified as source

Strong said Goat Systems discharged fill-and-flush water into the city’s sanitary sewer, and that discharged water already contained Cupriavidus gilardii.

“As soon as we became aware of the bacteria, and then of where it was coming from, we shut them down immediately,” Strong told the Wyoming Tribune Eagle.

However, Strong said he does not know where the bacteria originated. All BOPU officials know is that the water Goat Systems discharged contained it. That water was purchased from BOPU, he said.

Betsey Hale, CEO of Cheyenne LEADS, said she wanted to emphasize that the incident occurred during construction of the Meta facility, rather than during operation of the data center, which is not yet online.

Hale also emphasized that Cupriavidus gilardii is naturally occurring.

“It wasn’t something that they created through the construction process,” Hale said. “It’s already out there. It came into the system at a level that was monitored, caught and needed to be remediated.”

Bacteria discovered during routine testing

Strong said BOPU was not specifically testing for Cupriavidus gilardii. Rather, it was discovered while staff were conducting routine fecal bacteria testing.

“This isn’t something we normally test for,” Strong said. “... We actually had to go through quite a process to figure out what it was.”

He said the incident is highly unusual.

“We haven’t seen this bacteria previously,” Strong said. “We’re not aware of any other discharges of fill-and-flush water to our system.”

Because little information exists about the bacteria and its potential health effects, BOPU took what Strong described as a cautious approach.

He said internet searches suggested there could be health risks for immunocompromised individuals, although information on the bacteria is limited.

Rather than immediately resuming reclaimed water operations, Strong said officials suspended the city’s reuse system while additional testing was conducted.

Why the reuse system was shut down

Strong stressed that the incident never affected Cheyenne’s drinking water.

Instead, it involved the city’s reclaimed water system, which distributes treated wastewater for irrigation of parks, golf courses and other public green spaces.

Strong said the concern was that spraying reclaimed water could infect people in the green spaces.

“The concern we have with our reuse system is we put it into aerosol, where we spray it onto the grass, and that increases the potential for health issues,” Strong said.

Because of that possibility, BOPU chose not to operate the reclaimed water system until testing confirmed the bacteria was no longer present.

Officials have since tested both wastewater treatment plants, and both facilities have tested negative, Strong said.

Reclaimed water irrigation has resumed, and Strong said BOPU will continue monitoring the system.

Some bacteria entered Crow Creek

Although the reclaimed water system was shut down, Strong said the wastewater treatment plant could not remove the bacteria from all wastewater.

As a result, some of the bacteria passed through the treatment process and entered Crow Creek.

Strong said officials believe the public health risk from that release is low because the bacteria is naturally occurring, and people are generally not exposed to Crow Creek the way they could be exposed to irrigation spray.

New policy for data centers

In response to the incident, BOPU announced Thursday it will no longer accept industrial wastewater discharges associated with fill-and-flush operations or closed-loop cooling systems used by data centers.

Erin Lamb, BOPU administrative and public affairs coordinator, said the decision primarily affects future projects.

“I don’t think we have any other data centers that are (using fill-and-flush) right now,” Lamb said. “I think we have some that are coming in wanting to do it, but I think all of the current data centers (use) evaporative cooling. This closed-loop system stuff, I think, is pretty new for reduced water usage.”

Strong said BOPU’s concerns extend beyond the Cupriavidus gilardii bacteria.

Closed-loop systems can contain glycol and other chemicals that municipal wastewater treatment plants are not designed to process, Strong said.

Instead, BOPU now requires industrial companies using closed-loop cooling systems to construct separate collection systems so any water from cooling equipment or associated floor drains is directed into storage tanks, rather than the city’s sanitary sewer.

Existing data centers largely unaffected

Strong said BOPU is not aware of any previous fill-and-flush discharges from existing data centers.

He said Microsoft’s newer facilities use evaporative cooling, rather than closed-loop systems.

Regarding Meta’s campus, Strong said the project includes multiple phases using different cooling technologies.

The first phase under construction uses a closed-loop cooling system, while the second phase will use evaporative cooling.

Continuing investigation

Lamb said she and other BOPU officials understand the public’s interest in learning more about the incident, but said they first needed to verify the source of the contamination before releasing information.

“We understand the frustration and the public wanting to know all this information,” Lamb said, “but we did have to go through a certain process to make sure that everything was done correctly.”

The WTE has requested additional records related to the incident through a public records request. BOPU officials said the request is being processed through the agency’s legal department.

For now, Strong said follow-up testing has found no remaining Cupriavidus gilardii in either of the city’s wastewater treatment plants. The reclaimed water system is back in operation, and Strong said officials will continue routine sampling while implementing the new restrictions on discharges.

title: SD court system eyes third circuit consolidation in 50 years, raising concerns about ‘mega circuit’
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Map shows South Dakota’s seven circuit courts. The Unified Judicial System is proposing merging the Fourth and Seventh circuit courts in western South Dakota. Image courtesy of the Unified Judicial System
_full_text:
SD court system eyes third circuit consolidation in 50 years, raising concerns about ‘mega circuit’
Map shows South Dakota’s seven circuit courts. The Unified Judicial System is proposing merging the Fourth and Seventh circuit courts in western South Dakota. Image courtesy of the Unified Judicial System 

RAPID CITY — South Dakota’s court system intends to merge the Fourth and Seventh judicial circuits, creating one that will cover nearly a third of the state’s land area. 

The Fourth Judicial Circuit encompasses the northwestern quarter of the state, including Butte, Corson, Dewey, Harding, Lawrence, Meade, Perkins and Ziebach counties. The Seventh Judicial Circuit includes the southwestern corner: Custer, Fall River, Oglala Lakota and Pennington counties.

The merged circuit would have the largest population and geographic footprint of any in the state, and the second-largest caseload.

The merger of the Fourth and Seventh circuits would “increase operational efficiencies” within the system, according to a news release from the Unified Judicial System.

The merger would result in one presiding judge, one chief court services officer and one deputy chief court services officer for the combined circuit, said court system spokeswoman Alisa Bousa. Each county would retain its own clerk of court.

If approved by the state Supreme Court, it would be the third circuit consolidation since the system was implemented more than 50 years ago. At least one state’s attorney in northwestern South Dakota worries the consolidation will hurt access to justice for rural residents.

“The way circuits are set up right now makes sure rural counties are always properly served with the right amount of resources so we can do what we need to do,” said Shane Penfield, state’s attorney for Perkins, Dewey, Ziebach and Corson counties. “I think there could be some potential pitfalls with a circuit that large in geographic size.”

The system has not yet presented a formal rule proposal to the state Supreme Court, State Court Administrator Greg Sattizahn said in an email. Sattizahn declined an interview request. He said the system is “focusing on providing information to the public” through in-person forums planned for Aug. 26:

8:30 a.m. at the Pennington County Courthouse in Rapid City.

11 a.m. at the Meade County Courthouse in Sturgis.

3:30 p.m. at the Lonesome Dove Conference Center in Lemmon.

History of consolidation

The Unified Judicial System consists of the Supreme Court and seven circuits, each of which includes more than one county.

The term “unified” stems from the system’s setup, in which the state serves as the administrative overseer while counties manage and fund many day-to-day operations. Prosecutors and public defenders are paid for by counties; judges, court services officers and clerks of court are paid by the state.

The system was established by constitutional amendment in 1972, originally with nine circuit courts and 37 judges. The Supreme Court reduced that number of circuits to eight in 1976 and to seven in 2000, after an internal report recommended equalizing court costs and workloads to balance declining rural populations with growing urban areas, according to Rapid City Journal reporting at the time.

Neil Fulton, dean of the University of South Dakota’s Knudson School of Law, worked in the Sixth Circuit during the 2000 reorganization. 

“In general, these have been responses to the balance of workload,” said Fulton, who characterized the proposed consolidated operations for western South Dakota as a “mega circuit.”

Some circuits, like the Second Circuit serving the Sioux Falls metro area, handle significantly higher caseloads than rural districts, which cover a larger geographic area that involves more travel time. Fulton said the allocation of cases among judges was more balanced after the 2000 consolidation.

“It makes the work of the judiciary more sustainable,” Fulton said. “If we run our judges to the bone then they won’t be able to do things. That consolidation made coverage more reliable and regular so you saw a more predictable schedule in those courthouses.”

Balancing rural population shifts and representation

Currently, South Dakota’s circuit court system has 46 circuit court judges among its seven circuit courts. 

The Seventh Circuit has 8 judges serving 144,356 residents and reported 21,042 criminal filings and 9,213 civil filings during fiscal year 2025, according to the annual report. The Fourth Circuit has 4 judges serving 84,181 residents. It had 11,185 criminal filings and 4,622 civil filings in fiscal year 2025 — the second-fewest in the state.

The proposed merger is a “reflection of reality,” Fulton said.

“We have to consolidate services more in some areas to get judges, clerks and court service officers needed to deliver services,” Fulton said. “You see that with a lot of stuff: healthcare and education, to a degree. I’m not surprised court services is in the same boat.”

Fulton added that the consolidation would expand the pool of potential judges, since there are more lawyers in Rapid City than in the rural northwest.

“I’m 100% confident that UJS’s goal is to provide effective administration of justice for all South Dakotans,” Fulton said. “I think everyone has a shared goal, so let’s be patient working toward that.”

Penfield is open, but more skeptical.

Rapid City may have more lawyers, but Penfield argues it is culturally and economically distinct from the Northern Black Hills and northern plains. A larger Rapid City presence could mean more Rapid City-based judges, who he said have different perspectives than those from less populated counties.

“Combining those 2 would be a disservice not only to folks in the northern plains but to folks in the Northern Hills as well,” Penfield said.

If finding lawyers to serve as judges is the issue, Penfield said, the court system should increase salaries and offer judges additional staffing.

The merger “sends a mixed message,” Penfield said. The court system has invested in incentive programs to draw lawyers to rural areas for over a decade, through the Rural Attorney Recruitment Program and Public Service Pathway pilot program. But the rural-urban divide for South Dakota lawyers has worsened over the past decade.

When Penfield moved back to Lemmon from Rapid City in 2007, he was the fifth lawyer in town. When Lemmon had a circuit judge in the 1980s, there were more. Now there are 2 lawyers in town, he said.

“If there was still a judge seated in Lemmon, I’m guessing there’d be a few more lawyers in town,” Penfield said. “There were other economic changes, but those things have impacts and send messages.”

Penfield said he doesn’t see “where the numbers justify” the consolidation.

The Fourth Circuit has a greater population than the Fifth Circuit, which includes Aberdeen, and a comparable caseload. Its workload and population also exceed those of the Sixth Circuit, which serves Pierre.

Penfield worries that the Seventh Circuit’s existing criminal caseload could create problems for representation in smaller counties and result in reduced services.

“My criminal caseload in my four counties is just a blip — probably not even a week’s worth of cases in Pennington County or a couple of days,” Penfield said. “I see that getting lost.”

Penfield plans to research the impact of the 1976 and 2000 consolidations, and said he plans to keep an open mind about the process.

Written comments on the proposed merger may be submitted by email to comment@ujs.state.sd.us or by mail to the State Court Administrator’s Office. The comment period ends Oct. 1.

title: Alec Baldwin wins  Spearfish Canyon Half Marathon
byline: By Jason Gross Black Hills Pioneer
description: Ty Petrocco, Lane Krautschun, and Alec Baldwin set the pace during the 13.1-mile half marathon race Saturday morning. Baldwin emerged as the champion, followed by Petrocco and Krautschun. Pioneer photo by Jason Gross
_full_text:
Spearfish 1.JPG
Ty Petrocco, Lane Krautschun, and Alec Baldwin set the pace during the 13.1-mile half marathon race Saturday morning. Baldwin emerged as the champion, followed by Petrocco and Krautschun. Pioneer photo by Jason Gross 

SPEARFISH — Alec Baldwin returned to a familiar course Saturday and captured the Spearfish Canyon Half Marathon title in 1 hour, 8 minutes and 50 seconds for the 13.1-mile race.

The Denver, Colo., resident and 2016 Black Hills State University graduate said the course treated him well today.

“Thankfully, it was cool towards the top near the lodge,” Baldwin said of the race that began at 7 a.m. from Savoy. “It warmed up pretty quick.”

Saturday marked the third time Baldwin has run this race, so he generally knows what to expect. He described the course as a generous but gradual downhill.

Many things keep Baldwin returning to this event.

“I love the Black Hills,” he said. “My parents live here in Spearfish; my mom is actually running today.” 

 Spearfish 5.JPG
Numerous runners wear costumes during the race. Pioneer photo by Jason Gross 

 Spearfish 6.JPG
Some spectators at Saturday’s race arrived with the essentials. This Pennington County vehicle bore signs of support for friends and family members. Pioneer photo by Jason Gross 

Baldwin wanted the secure the individual title and did so. His strategy centered on running with some Black Hills-area athletes and trying to run away from them if he felt good.

“It feels really good to conquer the course with the heat we had today,” Baldwin said. He wanted to run a similar time to past races, and his start was more gradual.

He trains with Good Boys Denver, which is a running club featuring many post-collegiate runners.

Baldwin was asked what keeps him running and said it is a lifestyle. 

“Every time I quit, I find myself coming back to it,” Baldwin said. “It keeps me at my normal state.”

Baldwin’s future plans include running the New York City Marathon for the first time this November. He said he would like to better his personal 26.2-mile record of 2 hours, 15 minutes and 36 seconds.

Valerija Curikova emerged as the women’s half-marathon champion in 1 hour, 24 minutes and 27 seconds. She is a resident of Riga, Latvia.

Rapid City’s Lionel Hinosn claimed the Heroes 5-Kilometer Run/Walk crown in 16 minutes 36.5 seconds. Peyton VanDeest of Spearfish was the female winner in 17:58.3.

Top-20 finishers in both races follow. Complete results may be found on the itsyourrace.com website.

title: Sturgis Lions Club fishing derby hooks  record turnout of young anglers
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — More than 110 young anglers gathered at the Lions Club Pond on Saturday for the annual Sturgis Lions Club Fishing Derby, making it one of the largest turnouts in the event’s more than 25-year history.
_full_text:
STURGIS — More than 110 young anglers gathered at the Lions Club Pond on Saturday for the annual Sturgis Lions Club Fishing Derby, making it one of the largest turnouts in the event’s more than 25-year history.

Children lined the shoreline early in the morning, casting their lines in hopes of landing the biggest fish while enjoying a day outdoors with family and friends.

“We’ve had our fishing derby for over 25 years,” said Sturgis Lions Club President Jennifer Ness. “It’s something we take pride in and enjoy because it gives kids a chance to get outside and have fun.”

The derby’s primary goal is simple.  “Just to get the kids out here and have fun,” Ness said.

Participants competed for prizes in several age groups, with awards presented for both the biggest fish caught and the most fish caught.

The event’s popularity continues to grow. Ness said approximately 80 children participated last year, while this year’s derby attracted 110 registered anglers.

A recent beautification project at Lions Club Pond has helped improve the experience for young fishermen. The project was completed through a partnership involving the city of Sturgis and South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks.

“The beautification project is now completed,” Ness said. “We have 3 rock piers extending from the south shore, and the shoreline has been lined with rocks. It helps keep the vegetation down and makes it much easier for our young fishermen to access the water.”

Beyond hosting the annual fishing derby, the Sturgis Lions Club remains active throughout the community.

“We are a service organization that focuses on our local community and helping out where we can,” Ness said.

Among the club’s community projects are providing assistance for eye exams and eyeglasses and awarding scholarships to local high school students pursuing higher education.

The club currently has about 15 members and meets twice each month. During the summer, meetings are held at Lions Park, while winter meetings take place at Pizza Ranch.

Ness encourages community members interested in service and volunteer opportunities to learn more about the organization.

“People can visit our Facebook page and send us a message,” she said. “We can invite them to one of our meetings and show them all the things we do.”

With record participation and improved facilities, the annual fishing derby continues to be one of the Sturgis Lions Club’s signature events, introducing new generations of young anglers to the sport while bringing families together for a day of fun at Lions Club Pond.
