title: Harding County T. rex fetches $50.1 million at NYC auction
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: “Gus” a 67-million-year old Tyrannosaurus Rex discovered in Harding County was the star of Sotheby’s Natural History Auction Tuesday morning. Photo credit Matthew Sherman
_full_text:
Gus Rex 1.png
 “Gus” a 67-million-year old Tyrannosaurus Rex discovered in Harding County was the star of Sotheby’s Natural History Auction Tuesday morning. Photo credit Matthew Sherman 

BUFFALO — One of the most complete, and largest, Tyrannosaurus rex specimens event discovered sold at auction for $50,130,000 at auction. 

Sotheby’s estimated “Gus Rex,” the fossilized Late Cretaceous behemoth, would fetch between $20 million and $30 million, the highest estimate ever placed on a dinosaur. Bids opened Tuesday morning at $17 million.

“We are honored to offer lot 20,” the Sotheby’s auctioneer said Tuesday morning, opening bidding in New York City. She described the fossil specimen as “hailing from Harding County” and “expertly prepared.”  

The specimen was discovered in 2021 by Thomas Heitkamp of Theropoda Expeditions near Buffalo, on a ranch owned by Gary “Gus” Licking and his wife Dana. 

Licking had a deep interest in natural history, and after years of finding teeth and small bone fragments on the ranch, he invited the team from Theropoda to fossil-hunt on his 6,500-acre ranch. Licking suggested that Heitkamp dig in exactly the spot where the T. rex was found.

The dinosaur was dubbed “Gus” in honor of Licking, who passed away before the T. rex could be fully assembled.

 Gus Rex 2.png
Tyrannosaurus Rex has always been an iconic predator. Long before the gavel fell, “Gus,” a T. rex discovered in Harding County was poised to be the most expensive dinosaur specimen ever sold at auction. Photo credit Matthew Sherman 

“It has been an amazing opportunity to follow a discovery as significant as Gus from start to finish,” Dana said. “For me, the added bonus was knowing that Gus was just one of the many pieces of history hidden in the land that Gary and I loved to share.”

It took 5 years to complete, restore, and mount the specimen.

67 million years ago, Gus, the T. rex, would have been a dominant predator in what is now Harding County. The specimen is 38 feet long and 12.5 feet tall with a 54-inch skull. 

A 3-year excavation process uncovered 183 fossilized bone elements belonging to Gus, including 30 gastralia (belly ribs) that are rarely seen on fossil mounts. 

The overall dinosaur is about 63% complete. Gus’ skull is 82% complete.

A 3-year excavation process uncovered 183 fossilized bone elements belonging to Gus, including a rare furcula (wishbone).

The overall dinosaur is 61% complete. Gus’ skull is 82% complete.

“Gus is the culmination of years of rigorous excavation and preparation under some of the most challenging field conditions imaginable,” said Cassandra Hatton, Sotheby’s vice-chairman and world-wide head of science and natural history. “Tyrannosaurus rex is the most iconic prehistoric species in the fossil record, and Gus stands firmly among the greatest examples ever found.”

In addition to the intrinsic value of a fossilized specimen like Gus, this particular find bears scientific significance.

Gus has what scientists describe as “pathologies” — injuries that occurred during the predator’s life that are documented in the fracturing and healing of its bones. There are a number of clear bite marks on several skull bones, and damage to postcranial elements that could have been caused by scavengers after the animal’s death. It also appears several of Gus’ ribs and gastralia were fractured and healed during its life.

Gus is one of a small number of T. rex specimens that are more than 60% complete. He’s also the latest of those to have sold to the highest bidder. Sue, who was also more than 60% complete, was the first T. rex ever sold at auction (now the centerpiece at the Field Museum in Chicago) in 1997. She is now the centerpiece of Chicago’s Field Museum.

Apex, a mounted Stegosaurus, was sold by Sotheby’s for $45 million in July 2024.

title: Lead-Deadwood tunnel rehabilitation project set to begin construction
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer
description: LEAD — The $2 million Spearfish Raw Water Line Tunnel Rehabilitation project is set to begin construction this summer and finish in the fall.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

LEAD — The $2 million Spearfish Raw Water Line Tunnel Rehabilitation project is set to begin construction this summer and finish in the fall.

The goal of the project is to repair pipes that bring water from a source high in Spearfish Canyon down to a water treatment plant in Lead. The pipes, which are several miles long, were previously damaged by rock collapses. 

Once complete, the project will bring as much as 2,000 gallons of water per minute into the city, which would about double current water production. 

Workers will repair damaged pipes, at least in part by placing new smaller pipes inside old existing pipes, a technique called sliplining. The bracing in the tunnels — structures built on the sides of tunnels to reinforce them — will also be repaired. 

After water is brought into the city, it is treated with chlorine and fluoride to make it fit for human consumption, and then sold in bulk to the cities of Lead and Deadwood.

Terry Wolterstorf, manager of Lead-Deadwood Sanitary District, said that the water brought by the project is only intended to be used during periods of peak demand, or in case water from another source was made inaccessible. 

“(The project) won’t necessarily make it (water) cheaper, but hopefully (the canyon will be a) more reliable source,” Wolterstorf said. “Because of the tunnel collapse, we don’t have that water source available.”

Initial planning work for the project began last year. Harrison Western, a construction firm in Colorado, and HDR Engineering will work on the project in conjunction. Harrison Western, a firm which Wolterstorf said has experience with tunnel repair, will serve as the contractor on the project. HDR will provide engineering services. 

“A lot of communities are struggling to have enough water supply,” Wolterstorf said. “We have a tremendous amount of water available to us. We’re very blessed in that case.”

title: SD law change lets young rescuer save more wild game bird eggs
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: WALLACE, S.D. — South Dakota farmers who run into the nests of pheasants, grouse or prairie chickens in their fields can now call someone to rescue the eggs, thanks to a teenager and a new state law.
_full_text:
SD law change lets young rescuer save more wild game bird eggs.jpg

WALLACE, S.D. — South Dakota farmers who run into the nests of pheasants, grouse or prairie chickens in their fields can now call someone to rescue the eggs, thanks to a teenager and a new state law.

Madison Grimm, 19, of Wallace, started Second Chance Flight to rescue viable wild duck eggs from nests destroyed when farmers harvest hay from a field. She hatches and raises the ducklings, and releases them into the wild. 

Grimm already held a U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service permit to rescue the eggs of migratory waterfowl. But state law prevented her from doing the same work with eggs from birds such as pheasants. 

“I decided I really needed to get this law changed because there was a huge problem last year,” Grimm said. 

Grimm’s father Adam, a nationally recognized wildlife artist and 3-time winner of the Federal Duck Stamp Art Contest, traveled with his daughter to Pierre to testify for her bill. 

The new law lets federal permit holders expand their work to other kinds of birds. Gov. Larry Rhoden signed the bill in March, and it took effect July 1.

Grimm had her own private waterfowl aviary prior to Second Chance Flight, with over 100 birds from 21 species. It was originally built as a hobby and a source of reference material for her wildlife paintings. Madison is the only artist to ever win the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service’s Junior Duck Stamp Contest 3 times. 

Farmers visiting the aviary knew she owned incubators. So, when their farm equipment struck nests, they began asking whether she could save the surviving eggs.

At first, Grimm had to decline because she lacked the necessary federal permit.

“It kind of broke my heart,” she said. “I didn’t know this was happening, and there’s apparently nothing anyone can do about it.”

Some farmers told her they could encounter 20 or 30 nests in a single field they are haying, particularly near waterbodies. The machinery may kill the hen and crush some eggs, but other eggs often remain intact and viable.

After researching a similar program in another state, Grimm secured a federal permit and founded Second Chance Flight.

When farmers strike a nest, they contact her, and she or a volunteer retrieves the eggs. She shines a light through to check the embryo’s development, disinfects cracks, and seals the shell with clear nail polish to block bacteria.

Grimm had accepted over 450 eggs as of late June, and nearly 700 since the program launched. She estimates that about 98% of the viable eggs placed in her incubators hatch. She raises the ducklings for 6 to 8 weeks and releases them in groups on wetlands. She releases them shortly before they can fly, so they remain together as they adjust to the wild.

Grimm has also applied for federal permission to place leg bands on released birds. That would help her learn whether the birds survive.

Farmers have welcomed the program, she said. They have to cut hay to feed livestock, but many feel terrible when a hen is caught up in the machinery and disappears in a burst of feathers.

“And they know she’s got a whole nest right there,” Grimm said. 

She hopes to eventually expand Second Chance Flight across the Prairie Pothole Region — an expanse of ponds and wetlands crucial for millions of migratory birds — and train others to conduct rescues.

title: Nisland fire burns 20 acres
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer
description: NISLAND — A fire broke out near Nisland Monday at approximately 4 p.m. and burned about 20 acres before being contained by firefighters from several departments, though it had yet to be fully extinguished as of Tuesday morning.
_full_text:
NISLAND — A fire broke out near Nisland Monday at approximately 4 p.m. and burned about 20 acres before being contained by firefighters from several departments, though it had yet to be fully extinguished as of Tuesday morning. 

The fire began Monday afternoon, likely as the result of a spark from a piece of farm equipment, Fred Lamphere, Butte County sheriff, said. The spark ignited dry material nearby, spread across Highway 212 and traveled north into a hayfield.

Firefighters from Spearfish, Whitewood, Belle Fourche, Newell, Vale, and Nisland responded to the fire. 

The blaze was at least partially extinguished by fire department vehicles dragging long cord-like objects around the fire to smother it in its own ashes. 

As of Tuesday morning, several hay bales were still burning. They were expected to be fully extinguished by Tuesday afternoon. 

“It shouldn’t spread from where it’s at, short of a really hard wind,” Lamphere said. “But those bales just take a long time to get completely extinguished.”

Lamphere estimated the damage caused by the fire to be about $10,000. He said the cost was largely the result of hay bales being destroyed.

Nobody was injured as a result of the fire. The person who initially reported the fire was examined by paramedics, but wasn’t transported to a hospital. 

Lamphere said that residents are generally cautious about fire hazards, but current conditions are so dry that heavy machinery, including farm equipment, can start fires during their normal operation.

He advised that residents keep water in the vehicles, and to ensure vehicles are not hot before they enter tall grass.

title: Sturgis scales back  Rally events
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: The annual mayor’s ride will be one of only 3 city-sponsored activities for the 86th Annual Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
MayorsRide2025.jpg
The annual mayor’s ride will be one of only 3 city-sponsored activities for the 86th Annual Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. Pioneer file photo 

STURGIS — The city of Sturgis will focus more on maintaining city operations and keeping the public safe, than on hosting events during the 86th annual Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, city officials said Monday. 

During their regular meeting, Sturgis City Administrator Aaron Jordan told the city council that they are planning only 3 city-sponsored events for this year’s Rally, which is scheduled for Aug. 7-16.  That is consistent with the number the city hosted during the 2025 Rally, but it compares to 10 events or more in previous years. 

“In 2025, the city re-emphasized its commitment to maintaining safe and clean streets during the Rally by reducing city-sponsored events from 10 to 3,” Jordan said. “This reduction allowed city staff to dedicate additional time and resources to planning, coordinating, and executing core municipal services, with an increased focus on public safety, sanitation, traffic management, and maintaining safe and clean streets throughout the Rally.” 

This year the city will host the opening ceremony at Harley-Davidson Rally Point, scheduled for 3-4 p.m. Aug. 7; the mayor’s ride, scheduled for 9 a.m. Aug. 8; and a military appreciation event, scheduled for 2-3 p.m. Aug. 11. The military appreciation event will be enhanced this year through a partnership with Harley-Davidson. 

On Aug. 11, Jordan said the company will host a complimentary breakfast for active-duty military members and veterans at Harley-Davidson Rally Point. After breakfast, Jordan said the city’s Military Appreciation Day ceremony will begin at 2 p.m. with an anticipated B-1 flyover. The flyover, Jordan said, depends on aircraft availability from Ellsworth Air Force Base. 

Recently, Ellsworth Air Force Base cancelled all of its scheduled B-1 flyovers for Fourth of July celebrations throughout the Black Hills. A statement from Ellsworth Air Force Base said all available aircraft were deployed. 

In a related matter, Mayor Rod Bradley asked the council to reconsider opening up Main Street to non-motorcycle traffic at 2 a.m. Sunday, Aug. 16. He asked the council to instead consider amending the road closure resolution to open the street up at 2 a.m. Monday, Aug. 17, which would allow Main Street to be restricted to motorcycle traffic only for the entire duration of the Rally. 

However, due to some staffing concerns, the proposal died when Sturgis City Council members did not make a motion to vote on the matter.

title: Front footage assessment  fails in Belle Fourche, remains  the same in Spearfish
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — As the Belle Fourche City Council considered adopting a front footage assessment that mirrored Spearfish’s current levy, the Spearfish City Council unanimously passed a resolution to assess $1.25 per square foot of property abutting a city-maintained street at a maximum of $125 per parcel.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

SPEARFISH — As the Belle Fourche City Council considered adopting a front footage assessment that mirrored Spearfish’s current levy, the Spearfish City Council unanimously passed a resolution to assess $1.25 per square foot of property abutting a city-maintained street at a maximum of $125 per parcel.

The discussion of a front foot assessment will not continue in Belle Fourche, at least for now.

A resolution to assess a special maintenance fee, or front foot assessment, failed for lack of action from the city council following community feedback. 

Belle Fourche has not collected a front foot assessment since 2003. At that time, property owners were charged $0.40 per lineal foot of property running along a public road. The tax was capped at $40 per property owner to ensure that properties with more than 100 feet adjacent to city streets were not unfairly burdened.

This time, the proposed tax was $1.25 per “front foot” up to $125 — the same as the adopted 2027 rate in Spearfish. For a property with 10 feet of “front footage,” the annual cost would be $12.50. For a property with 100 or more of front footage, the annual fee would be $125.

Last week, the Spearfish City Council voted unanimously to keep the 2027 rate the same in 2028. In Spearfish, the front foot assessment is a revenue source to the General Fund, bringing in approximately $400,000 for street repairs annually.

If adopted in Belle Fourche, the assessment might have brought in an estimated $250,000 per year — also allocated for street and roadway improvement projects.

Front footage assessments are charged once a year on a per-parcel basis and are collected with property taxes.

title: Limbo assumes command of SD Army National Guard’s 196th Regiment
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: Brig. Gen. David A. Dailey, the assistant adjutant general–Army for the South Dakota National Guard, left, present Col. Scott Linquist a certificate for his work at Regional Training Institute at Fort Meade. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
2. limbo.JPG
Brig. Gen. David A. Dailey, the assistant adjutant general–Army for the South Dakota National Guard, left, present Col. Scott Linquist a certificate for his work at Regional Training Institute at Fort Meade. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

FORT MEADE — A military career that began in Sturgis more than 3 decades ago came full circle Saturday morning as Sturgis native Col. Dana L. Limbo officially assumed command of the South Dakota Army National Guard’s 196th Regiment (Regional Training Institute) during a traditional change of command ceremony at Fort Meade.

Limbo accepted command from Col. Scott A. Linquist in front of fellow soldiers, military leaders, family members and guests gathered on the parade field.

The military’s change of command ceremony is a long-standing tradition symbolizing the formal transfer of authority, responsibility and trust from one commander to another through the passing of the unit’s colors.

For Limbo, the moment carried special meaning because it took place in his hometown, where his military journey first began.

“Today’s the change of command ceremony,” Limbo said following the event. “I’ll be taking over the 196th Regiment. The regiment is responsible for training soldiers and leaders to fight and win our nation’s battles, wars and conflicts. It’s a very important mission, and I’m really looking forward to doing everything we can to make sure we have the right leaders trained and ready so they’re able to take care of soldiers and help bring them back to their families safely.”

Limbo enlisted after graduating from Sturgis Brown High School in 1994. Five years later, he completed officer candidate school at Fort Meade.

“I started the year I graduated in 1994 here in Sturgis,” Limbo said. “In 1999, I graduated OCS here. It was the first Fast Track program they ever had at Fort Meade, and I was one of the candidates. Here I am 27 years later taking over the regiment. It’s really neat to do it here in my hometown.”

During the ceremony, Limbo thanked those who helped him reach the milestone, beginning with his family.

“My mom and dad are here,” he said. “They’ve probably been to most of my middle school and high school athletic events. They were at my basic training graduation, officer candidate school graduation, they’ve been there the whole way.”

He also recognized his wife, Francie, and children Karina, Kyler and Farah, while noting that daughter Kaitlyn was unable to attend because of work.

“This takes sacrifice,” Limbo said. “You’ve supported me the whole way, and I don’t get here on my own. I’ve got a great team, and I appreciate everything you do. I know this position brings more responsibility, and I know you’ll be there for me.”

Limbo also praised Linquist for leaving the regiment in excellent condition.  

“Thank you for handing over an exceptional team,” he said. “Sometimes it’s easier when you go somewhere that needs improvements, but when you take over an exceptional team, it makes the job even harder because you want to continue that level of excellence. Thank you for everything you’ve done and congratulations on a job well done.”

Addressing the soldiers of the regiment, Limbo outlined the leadership philosophy he plans to emphasize, what he calls, “pride, brand and role.”

“I need you to take pride in everything you do,” he said. “If something is worth doing, it’s worth doing well.”

He encouraged every soldier to think about the reputation they build through their daily actions.

“Each and every one of you has your own brand,” Limbo said. “I’m asking you to be the soldier who can be relied upon, the soldier everybody wants to work with. Your brand can always improve.”

He concluded by reminding soldiers that every position within the regiment plays an important part in accomplishing the mission.

“We all have different roles,” he said. “I’m asking you to be a star in your role so others don’t have to carry your load. Pride, brand and role, that’s what you’re going to hear from me, and that’s what I expect.”

The 196th Regiment (Regional Training Institute) is one of the South Dakota Army National Guard’s major commands and is headquartered at historic Fort Meade. The regiment is dedicated to training future military leaders through demanding professional military education.

The organization consists of 2 battalions with separate training missions. The Fort Meade-based 1st Battalion prepares soldiers to become commissioned and warrant officers through officer candidate school and warrant officer candidate school, while the 2nd Battalion, headquartered in Sioux Falls, conducts professional military education for multiple launch rocket system crewmembers and noncommissioned officers.

As Limbo takes command, he said his focus remains clear: preparing capable leaders and well-trained soldiers who are ready to accomplish their mission and return home safely.

byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: SPEARFISH — Spearfish Main Street isn’t the only road that is being plagued by hot temperatures.
_full_text:
SDDOTlogo

SPEARFISH — Spearfish Main Street isn’t the only road that is being plagued by hot temperatures.

The South Dakota Department of Transportation (DOT) issued a warning to motorists Monday stating that due to the extreme heat, the oil blotter on U.S. Highway 385 between Pactola Lake and Sheridan Lake was softening. 

The road will remain open. Sand will be placed on the surface to prevent oil from sticking to tires. 

Motorcyclists should use extreme caution.

The DOT is reconstructing a portion of Highway 385 between the Pennington-Lawrence county line and the south end of Sheridan Lake. Once completed, this section of Highway 385 will feature safety improvements, including wider shoulders on each side of the road where possible, improved road curves to meet current design standards, additional turning lanes to improve traffic flow, and new surfacing.

Find additional project information including maps, timelines, and construction updates on the website at https://www.US-385.com.

title: $10 million settlement over online gaming child exploitation will fund safety, after-school efforts
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley, right, and Lt. Gov. Tony Venhuizen participate in a press conference Monday, in Sioux Falls. Jackley announced a settlement with the Roblox gaming platform. Photo by Makenzie Huber, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
$10 million settlement over online gaming child exploitation will fund safety, after-school efforts
South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley, right, and Lt. Gov. Tony Venhuizen participate in a press conference Monday, in Sioux Falls. Jackley announced a settlement with the Roblox gaming platform. Photo by Makenzie Huber, South Dakota Searchlight 

SIOUX FALLS — Roblox, a gaming platform popular with children, will pay South Dakota nearly $10 million over 4 years and implement new protections for young users under a settlement announced Monday by state Attorney General Marty Jackley.

The settlement also requires Roblox to implement age verification. The company plans to use facial age estimation software and government-issued IDs to confirm users’ ages.

Jackley said the parameters are necessary as child exploitation cases grow in South Dakota and nationwide, particularly on a platform where adults have allegedly posed as children to communicate with children and lure them into dangerous or criminal activity.

“If someone wants to participate in this, then there needs to be protections there,” Jackley said.

The settlement is preventative, he said, since no cases have been filed concerning Roblox and child endangerment in South Dakota.

“I hope with this settlement we never have to,” Jackley said.

South Dakota is the fifth state to settle with Roblox; combined, the agreements have cost the company about $54 million. The other settlements are $12 million with Nevada, $9 million with Mississippi, $12.2 million with Alabama and $11 million with Virginia. Nine other states are suing the company.

Of the settlement funds, $3.6 million will go to the Attorney General’s Office — $1 million for the state’s consumer protection fund and $2.6 million for the Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force.

The task force responds to tips about potential child exploitation cases, including online offenses and human trafficking investigations like those conducted during the annual Sturgis Motorcycle Rally.

Jackley said the program is expensive and one of the office’s busiest divisions.

“That will relieve a burden that’s been building up,” Jackley said.

Another $5 million will go to the state Education Department, with $1 million earmarked for governmental and nonprofit after-school programs. The remaining funds will be spent at the department’s discretion.

Education Secretary Joe Graves spoke at a press conference Monday where state officials announced the settlement.

“The after-school program is exactly where this needs to go because that’s the time of the day when kids who are without frequent parental supervision are going home and then they have kind of free rein,” Graves said. “After-school programs really kind of address that.”

Roblox will spend another $1 million on educational advertisements about children’s online safety for South Dakota families.

In addition to the age verification requirement, the settlement mandates the company make other changes to protect minors, including:

Expanded parental controls allowing caregivers to restrict who users talk to, and restrict the transfer of in-game currency from adults.

Restricted chat features to block adult users from chatting with users under 16 unless they’re identified as “trusted friends” on the platform.

Accessible — rather than encrypted — communications involving minors, allowing law enforcement to better track and disband child exploitation networks.

Jackley said he hopes the provisions, especially the reporting requirements and partnership with law enforcement, will serve as a model for other social media and gaming companies to use. The company will release an annual report regarding its child exploitation prevention efforts in South Dakota.

South Dakota could receive an additional $5.4 million if Roblox fails to meet the settlement’s requirements. The terms allow South Dakota to change to “any improved terms” that Roblox and another state might reach later on.

Ultimately, the burden rests on parents and caregivers to educate children about online safety, said Lt. Gov. Tony Venhuizen.

“This really starts with having conversations at home, with schools teaching kids responsible online habits and with law enforcement protecting kids from these bad actors,” Venhuizen said.

South Dakota is also part of a pending lawsuit against Meta, the parent company of Facebook, over youth mental health and social media addiction.

title: Governor celebrates surplus as Democratic lawmaker says state missed opportunities to help people
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — The deposit of a $69 million budget surplus has grown South Dakota’s state government reserve funds to $325 million, according to an announcement from Gov. Larry Rhoden’s office Monday.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — The deposit of a $69 million budget surplus has grown South Dakota’s state government reserve funds to $325 million, according to an announcement from Gov. Larry Rhoden’s office Monday.

The surplus is from the end of the state’s 2026 fiscal year on June 30.

“South Dakota’s robust economy is driving steady revenue growth, moving our budget in an even stronger direction,” Rhoden said, while additionally crediting “good stewardship of taxpayer dollars.”

The state collected $30 million more than its budgeted revenue for the year, $17 million of which came from higher-than-projected sales tax revenue.

Underspending by state agencies drove the remaining $39 million of the surplus. That’s “a sign of fiscal responsibility,” according to Rhoden’s office, which said the surplus “will be available for one-time investments in future budget years.”

State lawmakers typically distinguish between “one-time” revenue for expenses such as constructing a new building and “ongoing” revenue for expenses such as the day-to-day operations of state government.

Most of the unspent money came from the Department of Social Services, which reverted $32 million from its $1.8 billion departmental budget. The department oversees programs such as Medicaid, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, among others. About $654 million of its budget was from state funding sources, with most of the remainder coming from the federal government.

Jim Terwilliger, commissioner of the Bureau of Finance and Management, declined to explain the details of the department’s reversions Monday and said that information will be presented to the Legislature’s budget panel, the Joint Appropriations Committee, next week.

Democratic lawmaker questions budget decisions

Budget committee member Rep. Erik Muckey, D-Sioux Falls, is “heartened” by the sales tax revenue increase.

“But the message isn’t about the surplus,” Muckey said. “The message is we’ve clearly had opportunities to make a difference, and did we leave money on the table to accomplish that?”

He pointed to the Department of Social Services’ large reversion, “particularly at a time when addiction and behavioral healthcare are seeing significant needs,” and at a time when the state needs funding for programming at a prison under construction in Sioux Falls.

State leaders broke ground on a $650 million men’s prison in the state’s largest city earlier this year. It’s needed, Muckey said, “but not without accompanying programming in terms of rehabilitation, recidivism and so on.”

Muckey has also questioned the Department of Social Services in recent years over its management of Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, a federal-state program. It’s used in South Dakota to assist families with children who need financial support because of the death of a parent, an absent parent, or the unemployment or physical or mental incapacity of a parent. Caregiver participants are required to work, search or train for a job.

Earlier this year, lawmakers partially restored cuts to the program that the department made last year.

“The same question keeps coming up,” Muckey said. “Why are we trimming off the edges of programs that are really having an outstanding impact on people in South Dakota and are known for their impact, while we then turn around and say we don’t really need this money, we can just send it back?”

There will be new ways in the coming years for lawmakers to hold state agencies accountable for their budgets, Muckey said.

That includes Project BISON, a computer system that’s scheduled to come online next summer. Among other updates to state operations, it’ll give lawmakers the ability to see deeper into department budgets and understand the management of specific programming.

Higher-than-usual share of budget in reserves

With the addition of the surplus to the state’s reserve funds, those reserves now make up 12.7% of the current fiscal year’s general fund budget.

Traditionally, about 10% of the budget goes into reserves. In December, Rhoden announced his desire to increase that to 12.5%. Muckey criticized the proposal at the time and renewed the criticism Monday.

He said state officials are “patting ourselves on the back” for the surplus, “when we really could use more of that funding to actually help people and still maintain a very healthy reserve.”

title: Harding County T. rex fetches $50 million at auction
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: BUFFALO — One of the most complete, and largest, Tyrannosaurus rex specimens event discovered sold at auction for $50,130,000 this morning at Sotheby’s New York.
_full_text:
BUFFALO — One of the most complete, and largest, Tyrannosaurus rex specimens event discovered sold at auction for $50,130,000 this morning at Sotheby’s New York.

Sotheby’s estimated “Gus Rex,” the fossilized Late Cretaceous behemoth, would fetch between $20 million and $30 million, the highest estimate ever placed on a dinosaur. Bids opened Tuesday morning at $17 million.

The specimen was discovered by Thomas Heitkamp of Theropoda Expeditions near Buffalo, on a ranch owned by Gary “Gus” Licking and his wife Dana.

Licking had a deep interest in natural history, and after years of finding teeth and small bone fragments on the ranch, he invited the team from Theropoda to fossil-hunt on his 6,500-acre ranch. Licking suggested that Heitkamp dig in exactly the spot where the T. rex was found.

The dinosaur was dubbed “Gus” in honor of Licking, who passed away before the T. rex could be fully assembled.

“It has been an amazing opportunity to follow a discovery as significant as Gus from start to finish,” Dana said. “For me, the added bonus was knowing that Gus was just one of the many pieces of history hidden in the land that Gary and I loved to share.”

67 million years ago, Gus, the T. rex, would have been a dominant predator in what is now Harding County. The specimen is 38 feet long and 12.5 feet tall with a 54-inch skull.

A 3-year excavation process uncovered 183 fossilized bone elements belonging to Gus, including 30 gastralia (belly ribs) that are rarely seen on fossil mounts.

The overall dinosaur is about 63% complete. Gus’ skull is 82% complete.

A 3-year excavation process uncovered 183 fossilized bone elements belonging to Gus, including a rare furcula (wishbone).

The overall dinosaur is 61% complete. Gus’ skull is 82% complete.

“Gus is the culmination of years of rigorous excavation and preparation under some of the most challenging field conditions imaginable,” said Cassandra Hatton, Sotheby’s vice-chairman and world-wide head of science and natural history. “Tyrannosaurus rex is the most iconic prehistoric species in the fossil record, and Gus stands firmly among the greatest examples ever found.”

In addition to the intrinsic value of a fossilized specimen like Gus, this particular find bears scientific significance.

Gus has what scientists describe as “pathologies” — injuries that occurred during the predator's life that are documented in the fracturing and healing of its bones. There are a number of clear bite marks on several skull bones, and damage to postcranial elements that could have been caused by scavengers after the animal’s death. It also appears several of Gus’ ribs and gastralia were fractured and healed during its life.

Gus is one of a small number of T. rex specimens that are more than 60% complete. He’s also the latest of those to have sold to the highest bidder. Sue, who was also more than 60% complete, was the first T. rex ever sold at auction (now the centerpiece at the Field Museum in Chicago) in 1997. She is now the centerpiece of Chicago’s Field Museum.

Apex, a mounted Stegosaurus, was sold by Sotheby’s for $45 million in July 2024.

title: Sturgis Lions Club fishing derby hooks  record turnout of young anglers
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — More than 110 young anglers gathered at the Lions Club Pond on Saturday for the annual Sturgis Lions Club Fishing Derby, making it one of the largest turnouts in the event’s more than 25-year history.
_full_text:
STURGIS — More than 110 young anglers gathered at the Lions Club Pond on Saturday for the annual Sturgis Lions Club Fishing Derby, making it one of the largest turnouts in the event’s more than 25-year history.

Children lined the shoreline early in the morning, casting their lines in hopes of landing the biggest fish while enjoying a day outdoors with family and friends.

“We’ve had our fishing derby for over 25 years,” said Sturgis Lions Club President Jennifer Ness. “It’s something we take pride in and enjoy because it gives kids a chance to get outside and have fun.”

The derby’s primary goal is simple.  “Just to get the kids out here and have fun,” Ness said.

Participants competed for prizes in several age groups, with awards presented for both the biggest fish caught and the most fish caught.

The event’s popularity continues to grow. Ness said approximately 80 children participated last year, while this year’s derby attracted 110 registered anglers.

A recent beautification project at Lions Club Pond has helped improve the experience for young fishermen. The project was completed through a partnership involving the city of Sturgis and South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks.

“The beautification project is now completed,” Ness said. “We have 3 rock piers extending from the south shore, and the shoreline has been lined with rocks. It helps keep the vegetation down and makes it much easier for our young fishermen to access the water.”

Beyond hosting the annual fishing derby, the Sturgis Lions Club remains active throughout the community.

“We are a service organization that focuses on our local community and helping out where we can,” Ness said.

Among the club’s community projects are providing assistance for eye exams and eyeglasses and awarding scholarships to local high school students pursuing higher education.

The club currently has about 15 members and meets twice each month. During the summer, meetings are held at Lions Park, while winter meetings take place at Pizza Ranch.

Ness encourages community members interested in service and volunteer opportunities to learn more about the organization.

“People can visit our Facebook page and send us a message,” she said. “We can invite them to one of our meetings and show them all the things we do.”

With record participation and improved facilities, the annual fishing derby continues to be one of the Sturgis Lions Club’s signature events, introducing new generations of young anglers to the sport while bringing families together for a day of fun at Lions Club Pond.

title: Neutrino Day attracts thousands
description: The 18th annual Neutrino Day science festival attracted thousands of visitors to Lead on Saturday, with science activities, lectures, and presentations held throughout town. The event featured more than 40 booths showcasing various forms of science — including physics, chemistry, geology, and more; cultural demonstrations, lectures about ongoing science experiments at the Sanford Underground Research Facility, hoist room tours, and a special appearance by Steve Rokusek, as “Science Steve,” for South Dakota Public Broadcasting. While organizers are still tallying official registration numbers and attendance, the town of Lead was bustling with activity as people enjoyed the festival at the Handley Recreation Center, the Sanford Lab Homestake Visitor’s Center, and the Historic Homestake Opera House. title: Belle Fourche rallies behind  fire crews in searing heat
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Clint Hafner, left, Nikki Hoyme, and Maxine Rysavy are accepting donated water and sports drinks for area fire department at 2 drop-off locations in Belle Fourche. They are pictured with the donations that came in within the first 2 hours of the drive. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Firefighter donations.JPG
Clint Hafner, left, Nikki Hoyme, and Maxine Rysavy are accepting donated water and sports drinks for area fire department at 2 drop-off locations in Belle Fourche. They are pictured with the donations that came in within the first 2 hours of the drive. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

 Firefighter donation 2.jpg
By mid-morning, Belle Fourche community members had begun dropping off water and sports drinks to support firefighters as temperatures remain high. Photo courtesy Nikki Hoyme 

 Fire fighter donation 3.jpg
A young volunteer helps carry donated drinks for firefighters. Photo courtesy Nikki Hoyme 

BELLE FOURCHE — At city hall and the Monument Health Clinic in Belle Fourche, volunteers began collecting cases of water and sports drinks to support area firefighters Tuesday morning. 

“I was actually speaking with a spouse of a volunteer fireman, and they were out on multiple calls yesterday. So we were discussing how hot and how miserable a lot of them are, and the amount of fluids they are going to need to keep them safe,” said Nikki Hoyme. She works at the clinic and spearheaded the effort to help hydrate first responders.

Hoyme posted on social media Monday evening about the need for water and sports drinks to help firefighters make it through the sweltering, dry week. The clinic started accepting donations at 8 a.m. Just 2 hours later, community members had dropped off 8 cases of water and 2 cases of Gatorade.

“Our community is so generous and giving,” Hoyme said. “Part of why we are a drop-off location is that we are centrally located.”

Belle Fourche Police Code Enforcement Officer Clint Hafner is also helping to collect drink donations at city hall, in his temporary office.

“I can’t imagine what it is like to be a firefighter out in the middle of the prairie with equipment and suit and helmet on and needing all kinds of fluids,” Hafner said. “With my job, yesterday I was outside all day, and it was really hot yesterday, and I was so thankful to have air conditioning in a vehicle. … As the day goes, when dispatch calls, we are in and out of the vehicle and back and forth. These guys are out in the sun, on the prairie, and it’s beating down on them.”

Hoyme and Hafner are working with the Belle Fourche Fire Department Auxiliary and the Butte County Fire Protection District to gather and distribute donations.

“The president of the Butte County Fire Protection District will actually come pick them up and distribute them to all of the departments as their needs are there,” Hoyme said.

The drive will be underway at least through the end of the week, as temperatures remain high.

title: Plocek resigns from Spearfish School Board
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Ellen Plocek
_full_text:
Ellen.jpg
Ellen Plocek 

SPEARFISH — The president of the Spearfish School Board resigned Monday evening.

Ellen Plocek said she resigned for health reasons.

“Thank you to all who supported me while I was on the board,” she said Tuesday. “It was a rewarding experience, and I enjoyed service the school district.”

Plocek was first elected to the board in 2018 – the first election the school district had in 5 years.

Plocek is a retired teacher and moved up to board president following the resignation of Ryan Niesent in May. He resigned after he received a promotion at Bank West and felt he didn’t have the time necessary to dedicate to the board.

Nick Gottlob, superintendent of the Spearfish School District, said the board will need to discuss how to fill the vacancy. He said several options are available to the board

title: Cielo Rojo brings festive spark and fresh food to Deadwood
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: The crew at Cielo Rojo has been working in Deadwood for more than a decade. They’re back in action, bringing fresh new dining options to downtown Main Street. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Cielo Rojo brings festive spark and fresh food to Deadwood
The crew at Cielo Rojo has been working in Deadwood for more than a decade. They’re back in action, bringing fresh new dining options to downtown Main Street. Courtesy photo 

DEADWOOD — Cielo Rojo, located at 610 Main St. in Deadwood, brings fresh new dining options and a unique bar experience to the historic Badlands District. 

Owners Celene Herrere and Jose Vega worked for more than a decade at what used to be Guadalajara’s in Cadillac Jack’s Gaming Resort with their crew of almost 15 people. Herrere said that while the crew is extremely grateful for the opportunities afforded them in the gaming resort, it was time for a change. The only thing they needed was a location. 

Herrere and Vega said they found that location one day on a stroll down Deadwood Main Street. They fell in love with the high ceilings, bar, and open floor plan between the Eagle Bar theater and The Nugget. They inquired towards opening a restaurant in the location with the building’s owners, who Vega said was thrilled with the idea. 

Vega said he and Herrere were pushed to find a new location and get the restaurant running not just for their own interests, but for the family of crew members who they were bringing with them from Cadillac Jack’s. 

“It was about 2 months of no work. Everybody has kids and people they care about,” said Herrere. “But we talked to everyone, and we said, ‘We’re taking the risk together. But if we stay together, we can do it. Please be patient. Everything’s going to be OK.’”

Herrere said the familial crew works together now, in their new location, to make decisions as a group — each member lending their own expertise. 

Vega said some of the challenges of the building, including limited seating and a small kitchen, have contributed to the creation of the new menu. Because the walkway is so small, and capacity is 40-50 people, Vega said the restaurant adopted a seat-yourself concept instead of building a host stand. He said the idea is to maximize efficiency of the small staff and building while giving parties the choice to shop nearby and wait for a table or try their luck for a table later.

Herrere said the small kitchen with limited freezer space means that most items on the menu are made fresh each morning. Vega said the menu is a blend of items that can be made quickly for people who are stopping in to get out of the heat, husbands waiting for their wives to finish shopping, or people interested in their cocktail menu, and full-sized entrees for family outings or date nights. 

Vega said the most popular items on the menu since opening 2 months ago have been the fiesta wedges, potato wedges tossed in lime crema and topped with roasted corn, paprika, and cotija cheese, the dry burritos, and the birria tacos.

“We’ve tried to have a full-service menu, but at the same time we want something for people who are just passing through,” said Herrere. “We’d like to be able to expand eventually, bring in more appetizers and finger food.”

Herrere said until then, she’s overwhelmed with gratitude and love for the opportunities she’s experienced in Deadwood and the loyalty and love of the family she’s built with the crew. 

“We’ve had a great response from the locals, and we’re just so grateful for that,” she said. “The locals, the people of Deadwood, they’re what’s going to sustain us for a long time. We work really hard to provide the best food and the best service that we can. We’re really happy, really excited, and really, really thankful.”

title: Christensen returns home for book signing, shares stories that connect generations
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: Award-winning Sturgis native Tod Christensen returned home for book signing, shares stories that connect generations, July 8 at the Hotel Sturgis Coffee Shop. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
1. book.JPG
Award-winning Sturgis native Tod Christensen returned home for book signing, shares stories that connect generations, July 8 at the Hotel Sturgis Coffee Shop. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

STURGIS — Award-winning author and Sturgis Brown High School graduate Tod Christensen returned to his hometown July 8 to sign copies of his latest book, American Storybook, at the Hotel Sturgis Coffee Shop, reconnecting with readers in the community that first inspired his love of storytelling.

Christensen, a 1982 Sturgis Brown graduate who grew up in Whitewood, has earned national recognition for his work, including an honorable mention at the 2026 Los Angeles Book Festival and the Outstanding Literary Achievement award from the International Impact Book Awards.

Now living in Camp Verde, Ariz., Christensen said the Black Hills will always be home. 

“I grew up in Whitewood, and my brothers always say everybody that grew up in the Hills just says they’re from the Hills,” Christensen said. “I went to Sturgis Brown High School, spent a couple years at Black Hills State, then graduated from Arizona State. I’ve lived in Arizona for years, but this really is home.”

Although many classify his writing as poetry, Christensen prefers to think of it as storytelling. “I’m not a poet,” he said. “What I write is really short stories that rhyme. I’m a storyteller by nature.”

That passion began around the family kitchen table, where both of his parents encouraged him to write.

“My mom and dad were both published in regional publications here in western South Dakota,” he said. “They taught me about rhythm, rhyme and storytelling. At the time, I just thought I was spending time with my parents, but they were teaching me skills that stayed with me.”

Christensen said inspiration often comes unexpectedly. A brief moment, a conversation or a single phrase can spark an entire story in his mind.

“I’ll see something, and in a blink of an eye I’ve got the whole story,” he said. “People ask how long it takes me to write a poem. About 20 minutes if it’s really good, 45 minutes if it’s okay. If it takes longer than that, it usually isn’t going to happen and ends up in the trash.”

His newest book, American Storybook, celebrates ordinary people and everyday moments that often go unnoticed.

“I wanted to shine a light on stories of everyday Americans,” Christensen said. “Not famous people or historical figures, but people whose stories are every bit as important to their families. I think we have far more in common than we do differences, and if we remembered that, we’d probably treat each other a little better.”

Several stories in the book were inspired by members of his own family, including two poems honoring his late brother, Dane Christensen, a longtime Sturgis educator who died of cancer.

While the poems never mention his brother by name, Christensen said readers frequently connect them to their own experiences.

“They’re reading my story, but remembering theirs,” he said. “People will reach out to me and tell me how much a poem meant to them. Sometimes they’ll think I wrote it specifically about them, but it’s really because we all share so many of the same experiences.”

Christensen’s first book, The World According to You, introduced readers to his storytelling style. Since publishing American Storybook, he has already begun writing material for a third collection.

Recently, his work has taken on themes of compassion, respect and social responsibility.

“I’ve started writing more about things I think need to be talked about,” he said. “I want my writing to encourage people to be kinder, more thoughtful and more respectful of each other.”

Although his books have earned literary recognition, Christensen said awards are not what motivates him.

“I don’t do this to make a living,” he said. “What means the most is when someone comes up afterward and tells me a story about how something I wrote touched them. That’s why I write.”

Christensen said he especially enjoys hearing from readers who normally wouldn’t consider themselves fans of poetry.

“The guys will tell me, ‘I never liked poetry, but I like this,’” he said with a laugh. “That’s because it’s really storytelling. There are little life lessons woven into every story, and my experiences really aren’t any different than anyone else’s. I just took the time to write them down.”

title: 25 years after 9/11, beam from South Tower to visit Mt. Rushmore
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer
description: A beam from the South Tower will be displayed at Mt. Rushmore. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
FrankSiller_SteelLoading2.jpg
A beam from the South Tower will be displayed at Mt. Rushmore. Courtesy photo 

RAPID CITY — A beam recovered from the wreckage of the South Tower of the World Trade Center will visit Mount Rushmore on July 28, as part of the Tunnel to Towers Foundation’s Steel Across America Tour.

The tour began on May 2 and is planned to make more than 35 stops in 21 states, including several sports stadiums and West Point Military Academy. It will return to the former site of the World Trade Center on the 25th anniversary of the Sept. 11 attacks. 

The tour will also feature a mobile exhibit with educational materials about 9/11.

“This steel beam represents the best of who we are as a country,” Frank Siller, Tunnel to Towers Foundation chairman and CEO, said in a prepared statement. “As it travels from coast to coast, we hope this symbol brings communities together to remember the heroes we lost, honor the people still suffering from 9/11-related illnesses, support the families forever changed, and pay tribute to those who continue to protect and serve.”

The Tunnel to Towers Foundation is a nonprofit based in New York. The foundation collected more than $500 million in contributions in 2024. 

Other foundation projects include building housing for U.S. veterans and offering graduate and undergraduate scholarships. 

“When we bring the Steel Across America tour to South Dakota, we aren’t just asking people to remember a date on a calendar,” Siller said. “We are asking them to look at the faces of the first responders standing next to them and recognize that the courage we witnessed on Sept. 11 did not die that day. “

title: No immediate threat of New World screwworm affecting SD, state vet says
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Pictured is a close-up of 3 New World screwworm larvae. Photo by Sohath Yuseff-Vanegas, USDA Agricultural Research Service
_full_text:
Screw worm.jpg
Pictured is a close-up of 3 New World screwworm larvae. Photo by Sohath Yuseff-Vanegas, USDA Agricultural Research Service 

PIERRE — Flesh-eating pests spreading north into the United States have so far been kept at bay from South Dakota, but state animal industry leaders are keeping an eye on the threat.

New World screwworm cases surfaced in Texas in early June. The name “screwworm” refers to the larvae, or maggots, that burrow into open wounds, feeding as they go “like a screw being driven into wood,” according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture. They primarily infest livestock, wildlife, pets and birds, leading to sickness or death. In rare cases, they can infect humans.

The larvae grow into flies about the size of a common housefly, with orange eyes, a blue or green body, and three dark stripes along the back.

Across Texas and in southeastern New Mexico, 35 total cases have been reported, primarily in cattle, according to the USDA. No cases have been reported in South Dakota. Texas is working with federal partners to control the population and track animal movements, according to South Dakota State Veterinarian Mendel Miller.

Miller said he has no immediate concerns due to Texas’ containment strategies and South Dakota’s requirements for veterinary inspections and health records on animals coming into the state.

“The system’s in place to prevent it from getting here, provided everybody follows the rules and follows the system,” he said.

New World screwworms reached as far north as South Dakota from 1947 to 1950 via infested livestock shipments, according to the USDA.

A traditional boundary line for screwworm infections runs through central Kansas, Miller said. The imaginary line separates warmer, southern climates that are more welcoming to the insects from cooler, northern climates.

“With global climate change and things like that, milder winters, that line may creep north,” Miller said. “But, we still have winter. That’s probably our best mechanism to prevent it from getting established.”

For now, Miller said South Dakota is “still cold enough.”

“The ground still freezes and we still get snow cover,” he said. “As long as we have winter, we should be fairly safe.”

He recommended keeping a close watch on livestock. Most cattle infections happen during castration, Miller said. Sheep infections happen during dehorning and tail docking, when the tail is removed from the animal.

“The best thing to put on their animal is their eyes,” he said of farmers and ranchers.

Screwworm had been mostly eliminated from the United States in the 1960s, through the use of sterile flies to end the life cycle of other flies, Miller said. Screwworms have been confined mostly to Mexico and Central America since then, although there have been periodic outbreaks in the United States.

The federal government is using sterile flies again in its eradication efforts. Sterilized males mate with females, which lay unfertilized eggs. Because females only mate once in their lifespan, this could reduce and eliminate the population.

The USDA recently broke ground on a $750 million sterile fly facility in Edinburg, Texas, that aims to produce up to 300 million sterile flies per week when it opens next year. The agency has also invested in sterile fly facilities in Mexico and Panama.

The Canadian Food Inspection Agency announced on Monday it would suspend several animal exports from Texas, including cattle, horses, pigs and bison.

BELLE FOURCHE — Due to extreme heat and dry conditions, the Bureau of Reclamation and South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks has implemented fire restrictions at Belle Fourche Reservoir, including Rocky Point State Recreation Area. 

The bureau said that campfires are not allowed, and cooking is allowed only on elevated grills or stoves using propane gas. Vehicle access is allowed only on graveled roads clear of vegetation. 

Restrictions are necessary due to continued dry weather conditions and the fire restrictions enacted by Butte County.

The restrictions are in place until further notice

LEAD — The Historic Homestake Opera House and the Lead Area Chamber of Commerce announced the hiring of Naomi Mac Millan as their new event and community engagement coordinator, a shared position designed to strengthen collaboration, expand community engagement, and support the continued growth of both organizations.

title: Safety not a factor in determining ND pipeline routes, attorney says
byline: By Jeff Beach North Dakota Monitor
description: North Dakota Public Service Commission attorney Zachary Pelham attends a hearing on April 2, 2026, in Fargo. On Tuesday, Pelham argued on behalf of the PSC in a hearing on the Summit Carbon Solutions pipeline. Photo by Jeff Beach, North Dakota Monitor
_full_text:
Safety not a factor in determining North Dakota pipeline routes, attorney says.jpg
North Dakota Public Service Commission attorney Zachary Pelham attends a hearing on April 2, 2026, in Fargo. On Tuesday, Pelham argued on behalf of the PSC in a hearing on the Summit Carbon Solutions pipeline. Photo by Jeff Beach, North Dakota Monitor 

BISMARCK, N.D. — An attorney for North Dakota’s Public Service Commission said Tuesday that the agency can’t consider public safety when issuing a pipeline permit. 

Attorney Zachary Pelham said while the commission must consider public welfare, that doesn’t include safety. 

“Welfare and safety are two distinct things,” Pelham said during a hearing on a dispute over the permit for the Summit Carbon Solutions pipeline. 

Two counties and a group of landowners have sued the Public Service Commission and Summit over what attorneys said were flaws in the permit approval process. The lawsuit seeks to rescind the permit and send the application back to the PSC for further review. 

South Central Judicial District Court Judge Jackson Lofgren did not issue a ruling Tuesday. 

One of the flaws cited Tuesday was that the three-person commission did not seem to consider evidence on what would happen if the pipeline were to rupture. Carbon dioxide is a hazardous material and inhaling it in high concentrations can be fatal. 

Summit Carbon Solutions has developed what is known as a plume dispersion model. The model was not made public or made part of the PSC record in the permit case. 

Attorney Randall Bakke, representing Burleigh County, said the model would help determine the safety risk posed by a carbon pipeline. Bakke noted that Summit provided the model to some people, including a Bismarck developer and an oil industry lobbyist, but did not provide it to attorneys representing stakeholders in the case.

Attorney Steve Leibel said the plume model was relevant for another reason — it would help determine if setbacks passed by Burleigh and Emmons counties could be considered reasonable. Those setbacks — a minimum distance that must be between a pipeline and a residence — are another basis for the permit appeal. 

But Pelham said safety was strictly a federal issue. 

That led Lofgren to ask Pelham, “If the PSC doesn’t have any authority to direct where a pipeline goes or that it’s safe, what role does the PSC have in regulating a pipeline?” 

Pelham answered that PSC can consider things such as the impact to state-owned land and to the environment and wildlife. He said the commissioners can ask questions about things such as pipeline thickness and shut-off valves, but has no authority over those areas. 

Bakke said Pelham’s argument that public welfare doesn’t include safety “simply defies logic.” 

Bakke and Leibel also argued the PSC did not properly address insurance liability concerns from landowners if there was a pipeline rupture and that regulators did not adequately analyze alternate routes. They also challenge the PSC interpretation of state law that state zoning laws preempt local government regulations. 

Safety was one of the main public concerns during commission hearings on the pipeline that was proposed to capture carbon from ethanol plants and bring it western North Dakota for permanent underground storage. 

The Public Service Commission initially denied Iowa-based Summit Carbon Solution a permit in 2023. Summit made changes to its route, including avoiding potential landslide areas. 

The PSC in 2024 approved a revised route. 

The future of the project is unclear, however, as Summit has not been able to secure a state permit in South Dakota.

In addition, two district court judges have determined the underground storage permits and the law they were issued under are unconstitutional. Those cases are being appealed to the North Dakota Supreme Court.

Summit recently announced plans to target a carbon storage area in Wyoming that would bypass the Dakotas and Minnesota. 

A spokesperson said in May that North Dakota, South Dakota and Minnesota “remain important for our company.” The spokesperson did not return a request for comment on Tuesday.

title: Airport expansion loans cleared for takeoff despite turbulence in legislative committee
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — The South Dakota Legislature’s Rules Review Committee approved rules Tuesday allowing up to $30 million in loans from a state housing infrastructure fund to help finance airport expansion projects in Rapid City and Sioux Falls, despite opposition from the state speaker of the House and another lawmaker.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — The South Dakota Legislature’s Rules Review Committee approved rules Tuesday allowing up to $30 million in loans from a state housing infrastructure fund to help finance airport expansion projects in Rapid City and Sioux Falls, despite opposition from the state speaker of the House and another lawmaker.

The rules implement a law that Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden requested last year and signed in March after the Legislature approved it.

The law authorizes loans up to $15 million each to the state’s two largest commercial airports at 2% interest with 20-year repayment periods. Repayments and interest must be returned to the housing fund to support future housing infrastructure projects.

The Legislature and former Gov. Kristi Noem created the housing fund in 2023 with $200 million: $100 million for grants and $100 million for loans to support streets, sewer, water and other infrastructure needed for housing developments. The package used $150 million in state money and $50 million in federal American Rescue Plan funds.  

The rules package passed on Tuesday in a 4-2 vote at the Capitol in Pierre. Sen. Taffy Howard, R-Rapid City, and House Speaker Jon Hansen, R-Dell Rapids, voted against it.

Both said they opposed the rules because the change in how the housing funds can be used should have required a two-thirds majority vote in both legislative chambers — a higher bar than the bill achieved. It passed 22-11 in the Senate, which was two votes short of the two-thirds threshold, and 43-24 in the House, which was 4 votes short of two-thirds support. 

The state constitution requires appropriations bills to receive a two-thirds vote, but legislators sometimes debate what constitutes an appropriation.

Hansen, as the presiding officer in the House, tried to require a two-thirds majority during the legislative session, saying the bill would change the purpose of how the money was being spent. His decision was overruled in a 34-33 House procedural vote, with lawmakers arguing the bill itself didn’t mention “appropriation” and that the funds were being loaned rather than spent. Rep. Tim Walburg, R-Madison, called the bill at the time a “funding transfer.”

Hansen, who is not running for reelection after his failed bid for the Republican nomination for governor last month, said Tuesday the Legislature should revisit how it defines appropriations — specifically whether the definition should cover not just the authorization of new funds but also changes to how previously appropriated funds can be used.

“In this case, the specific purpose was changed to something different. Therefore, it was a new appropriation and should have required a two-thirds vote,” Hansen said. “In the future, I think the Legislature really needs to just sit back, away from any particular bill that’s being driven through the Legislature, and really consider that definition and how to apply it.”

Senate Majority Leader Jim Mehlhaff, R-Pierre, said procedural concerns weren’t a sufficient reason to reject a package that had already cleared the full legislative process. 

“I don’t believe the committee is here to thwart the will of the Legislature,” Mehlhaff said.

The committee approved similar rules following legislative action last year allowing a $15 million, zero-interest loan from the same fund for a new elementary school serving the Douglas School District near Ellsworth Air Force Base. Howard and Hansen both voted for that rule change, after Howard voted for the bill and Hansen voted against it.

Julie Johnson, an Aberdeen lawyer and lobbyist for Homes for South Dakota, told the committee Tuesday the organization supports the change to the rules for airports, but wants to ensure the funds are repaid and directed toward housing infrastructure needs across the state.

“We want to be sure the world knows that this isn’t a slush fund and there are still needs for infrastructure loan monies,” Johnson said.

By late 2025, about $65 million remained in the loan portion of the fund. The program has helped finance 87 projects expected to produce 7,464 single-family lots and 5,882 multifamily units.  

Rapid City plans a concourse expansion at its airport adding five gates and more passenger space. Sioux Falls is building a new concourse with up to five additional aircraft gates and 57,000 square feet of seating and circulation space. The projects are expected to cost more than $100 million apiece.

title: Learn how a paleo artist captures dinosaur death struggle
description: MILES CITY, Mont. — African lions, leopards, and hyenas know this. Apparently, a T. rex knew it too: “Control the head and you can control the body.”
_full_text:
MILES CITY, Mont. — African lions, leopards, and hyenas know this. Apparently, a T. rex knew it too: “Control the head and you can control the body.”

Well, theoretically.

It makes sense to keep one’s surprised and frantic prey at “arm’s length” (a phrase that wouldn’t make much literal sense to a T. rex) — at least far enough away to avoid the kicking, biting, and clawing that follows, and to keep the “menu item” from getting away.

Meet “MOR 1627” — an entire Edmontosaurus head on display at the Museum of the Rockies (MOR). MOR 1627’s crown jewel is a snapped T. rex tooth stuck in the bridge of its snout. The fossilized head is about a yard long. The tooth is a tiny, shiny, root beer-colored bit that peeks out a few inches down the snoot from the gaping eye socket. It glimmers, serrated like a miniature saw blade.

Paleo art is the bridge between dusty bones and living history. When researchers Taia Wyenberg-Henzler and Dr. John Scannella published their groundbreaking study on the MOR 1627 skull, they turned to Jenn Hall of Miles City to illustrate the terrifying encounter.

“We really needed to capture the moment of ‘the bite,’” said Hall. “It’s an unfortunate 60 seconds when you (as the Edmontosaur) are caught up in grazing and let your guard down. All of a sudden, your predator takes advantage of that moment.”

Hall’s style is a fusion of experience gained at the University of Pennsylvania, years of working with paleontologists combined with classical art training at the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts. Sprinkle that with a dose of up-close anatomical observations from a taxidermy sideline, attention to “what-if” details, and a reconstruction of prime prehistoric ambush conditions, and you have a vivid rendition of the final moments of MOR 1627.

Hall described her thought process designing a dynamic action scene—the twisting, wrenching fight between the hunter and the hunted. Big-bodied, heavy flesh-and-bone titans grappling for keeps.

For both modern and prehistoric predators relying on tooth and claw, this isn’t just about dispatching dinner; it’s about avoiding broken bones, dislocations, or a disemboweling kick. Incapacitation means vulnerability and starvation. Don’t forget that a T. rex was — or might have been — on someone else’s menu, too.

Hall’s painting frames the confrontation exactly as the crime-scene evidence indicated: “face-to-face.” In the artwork, you don’t see a T. rex biting a leg or ripping at a flank. Instead, you see the predator locking its massive, bone-crushing jaws directly over the Edmontosaurus’s snout. One can almost sense the bone-cracking force required to drive a massive tooth into that leathery, scaly, duck-bill muzzle — and snap it off clean.

Scientists continue to debate whether T. rex was a majestic top predator or a six-ton flightless vulture roaming what is now the Hell Creek Formation looking for free leftovers. MOR 1627 provides some of the strongest evidence yet for the «predator» column by highlighting a hunting technique used by modern carnivores.

Hall shared a few concept sketches she drew for MOR staff to consider. The T. rex twists in some; it bears down in others. Yet for the Edmontosaurus, the end never changes. Hall described the exchange of ideas with MOR staff regarding possible postures, poses, and body orientations — “the subtle and gestural things,” she called them, like the “grab and the twist.”

“In paleo art, you’re caught between capturing the artistry and communicating the science,” she said, likening the collaboration to “a friendly game of catch where you throw things back and forth.”

When MOR picked their finalist, it was entitled “The Bite.” Judging from the artwork produced throughout the project, it must have been difficult to choose only one. Any piece would have been an excellent choice.

MOR 1627 and its T. rex tooth were excavated from BLM public lands in eastern Montana under the Miles City Field Office. The Hell Creek Formation kept this specimen a secret until paleontologists uncovered it in 2005 — yet another example of how fossils excavated from your lands continue to inform the greater scientific community worldwide.

The actual skull, complete with the tooth, is on display at the MOR “Hall of Horns and Teeth.” You can’t miss it; the case sits low enough to give you a very close look. A complementary resin cast of the skull, supplied by MOR, is also on display at the BLM Montana/Dakotas State Office in Billings.

Under the authority of the Paleontological Resources Preservation Act, the U.S. Department of the Interior oversees a coordinated, science-driven paleontology program across federal lands managed by the BLM, National Park Service, Bureau of Reclamation, and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service.

This program safeguards and curates America’s rich fossil heritage by balancing public education initiatives, like the Junior Paleontologist program, with a strict permitting process for scientific research. Through this federal framework, authorized institutions—including the Museum of the Rockies at Montana State University—can legally excavate these public treasures, transforming raw scientific discoveries into shared global knowledge.

title: BHSU foundation to build 10-plex on St. Joe St., city waives $20K fee
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer
description: 1232 St. Joe street was donated to a private individual. The Black Hills State University Foundation is expected to begin construction of a 10-unit residential apartment building this summer. Pioneer photo by Sam King
_full_text:
BHSU to build apartment 1.JPG
1232 St. Joe street was donated to a private individual. The Black Hills State University Foundation is expected to begin construction of a 10-unit residential apartment building this summer. Pioneer photo by Sam King 

SPEARFISH — Black Hills State University Foundation is about to begin construction on a 10-unit residential apartment building on St. Joe Street.

Each unit will have 2 bedrooms.

Construction on the project, which university officials began planning in January, is set to begin this summer and last about a year. The project is estimated to cost about $2.5 million. The cost will be paid off over about 10 years. 

The Black Hills State University Foundation is a tax-exempt nonprofit that exists to raise money for Black Hills State University.

Conflicting motives

At a city council meeting July 6, Steve Meeker, executive vice president of the BHSU Foundation, and Ryan Wordeman, a local realtor and member of the BHSU Foundation Board of Directors, told the city council that although the apartments would be open to the public, they would be first offered to university faculty. 

“There’s been times where faculty has been in the campus apartments, which are for students, just because it’s been hard to find places (for the faculty) to live,” Wordeman said. 

 BHSU to build apartment 2.png
This artist rendition of an 8-unit apartment building is similar to the planned 10-unit building set to be constructed by the Black Hills State University Foundation. Courtesy photo 

Meeker later told the Pioneer that the apartments were “definitely” for faculty, but that they “could be opened up to the public if we have a need to fill them.” He said that the Spearfish housing market had become expensive enough that faculty sometimes struggled to find housing. 

Meeker’s comments about the housing market were consistent with data from the federal government. 

According to the Census Bureau, in 2015, 62% of Spearfish occupants paid between $0-$999 per month for housing costs. Just 35% paid between $1,000-$3,000. The median housing cost was $733.

By 2024, however, 48.5% of occupants paid between $0-$999. 49.61% paid between $1,000-$3,000, with the median cost per month being $1,010.

However, Meeker said that the apartments would not be rent-subsidized, meaning that the units will likely cost the same as an apartment that was not owned by the university. 

He confirmed that the university expected to make a profit from the building.

Wordeman declined to comment.

Residents removed, houses demolished

The location of the planned apartment building is currently occupied by 3 university-owned houses. 2 are planned to be demolished. 

A third, located at 1232 St Joe St., was donated to a private individual. The house was removed from its foundation by and taken by vehicle to Pierre last week. 

At least one of the other houses was vacant, but at least one other was occupied. Around 9 occupants were told to leave the properties by the end of June. 

“Nobody left unhappy,” Meeker said.

City waives permitting fees 

The city council voted unanimously to waive the mechanical, water, fire suppression, and sewage permitting fees normally associated with building projects, up to $30,000. A report released by the city council estimated the waived fees at about $22,000.

Michelle DeNeui, Spearfish’s finance officer, recommended the council waive the fees. 

“The city has a history of supporting our community organizations when they are performing construction improvements by reducing or waiving the building permit fees,” DeNeui said. 

She said that fees were previously waived for nonprofits such as Spearfish School District, Matthew’s Opera House, and the High Plains Western Heritage Center, among others. 

DeNeui said that she wasn’t aware of any other nonprofit that rented apartments, and that the city did not maintain such information.
