title: Surge in advance voting for July 28 runoff driven  by party switchers, county auditors say
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — Advance voting in the runoff for the South Dakota Republican nomination for governor is ahead of the pace it was on for the primary election, and some county election officials are attributing it to people switching parties.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — Advance voting in the runoff for the South Dakota Republican nomination for governor is ahead of the pace it was on for the primary election, and some county election officials are attributing it to people switching parties.

“I’ve got an election coordinator and that’s basically all she’s been doing since the primary: processing those party changes as they come in,” said Brown County Auditor Lynn Heupel.

Through Monday, 12,617 Republican voters statewide had cast ballots for either Gov. Larry Rhoden or businessman Toby Doeden. The runoff election is July 28.

That’s about 3,300 more than a comparable timeframe ahead of the June 2 primary — a 35% increase. Early voting for the primary, however, started about a week late due to delayed ballot printing. 

Unlike the primary, this election is only for Republican voters (many Democrats, independents and other voters had local races or ballot questions to consider in the primary election). About 19% of advance voters in the primary were non-Republicans, according to data from the Secretary of State’s Office.

In Lawrence County, 295 voters changed their party affiliation to Republicans, said Auditor Brenda McGruder.

In Meade County, there are now 248 more Republicans than there were before the primary, said Auditor Dawn Christianson.

And in Butte County, Auditor Annie Capp said 75 people changed their affiliation to Republican.

Since the primary, the Republican Party in the state has grown by 7,350 voters. In Minnehaha County, the state’s most populous county, the Republican Party has increased by 1,802 voters.

Minnehaha County Auditor Leah Anderson suspects, “based on the activity that’s come to our window,” that much of the growth is from people switching their party affiliation to Republican so they can vote in the runoff.

Voters who filled out the form to switch parties often voted immediately after the change was processed, Anderson said. About 85% of advance voting in Minnehaha County so far has been in-person. Advance voting also includes mailed ballots.

In the last few days before the voter registration deadline, which was Monday, Anderson said requests to switch parties overwhelmed her staff, forcing her office to suspend immediate voting while forms were processed. Those voters can return to cast their ballots anytime until the election on July 28.

“We’ve had a lot of people come and change their party, go vote upstairs and then come down and ask to change it right back,” Anderson added.

Anderson said her office is waiting until after the runoff to implement those reversal requests to ensure voters’ ballots are counted. A stack of requests is sitting in her office.

In Brown County, home of Aberdeen, Heupel said her office processed 65 party affiliation changes on the last day of voter registration. Her office has sent 1,022 voter registration acknowledgments since the primary, which includes party affiliation changes and new voter registrations. The majority, Heupel said, are due to party switchers.

The Republican Party has grown by 785 voters in Brown County since the primary election.

Unlike Minnehaha County, Heupel’s office does not allow voters to cast a ballot immediately after updating their registration — voters must wait to receive a mailed acknowledgment, which can take a few days.

The county has had 980 people vote in-person so far, Heupel said. Another 207 requested mailed ballots.

Lincoln County Auditor Sheri Lund said her office offers advance voting immediately after people change their party affiliation. 

“Probably 90% of those people take us up on that,” Lund said. “A lot of them are shocked they can do that.”

The Republican Party has grown by 1,023 voters in Lincoln County, which includes part of Sioux Falls, since the primary election.

Lund said party affiliation changes are common ahead of primary elections, but are more pronounced this year due to the interest in the runoff.

“I have heard people say this is election fraud. It’s not election fraud at all,” Lund said. “It’s 100% your right to vote however you want to and change your party affiliation if you want to. Is it right or wrong? That’s on their conscience.”

Doeden finished first and Rhoden finished second in the June 2 primary, ahead of U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson and state House Speaker Jon Hansen. Because nobody received 35%, a runoff was triggered between the top two finishers.

The winner of the runoff will face Democratic nominee Dan Ahlers in the Nov. 3 general election.

title: Lawrence Co. grants Black Hills Mining Museum funds for engineering plans
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Black Hills Mining Museum will be able to move forward with engineering plans to repair or remove the building’s parking lot, thanks to money granted from the Lawrence County contingency fund. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Lawrence Co. grants contingency funds to mining museum.jpg
The Black Hills Mining Museum will be able to move forward with engineering plans to repair or remove the building’s parking lot, thanks to money granted from the Lawrence County contingency fund. Pioneer file photo 

DEADWOOD — The Black Hills Mining Museum in Lead will be able to move forward with engineering plans to remove or repair the failing parking lot thanks to funding granted by Lawrence County Commissioners Tuesday. 

Gordon Phillips, executive director of the museum, approached commissioners June 23, requesting $8,500 from the mining severance tax fund for engineering design plans to seek options regarding the museum’s failing parking lot. The lot, which serves as the main entrance to the museum, was closed in May after it was discovered holes in the surface had gotten larger. 

Commissioners continued the request to Tuesday’s meeting, citing South Dakota Codified Law 10.39-54.3. The statute limits mining severance tax funds to road and school purposes, various economic development purposes, and research activities related to expansion and diversification of the economic base of a community. Bruce Outka, deputy state’s attorney, said the statute did not provide a way for the county to pull funds from the mining severance tax balance, but the money could be pulled from the county’s contingency fund. 

During the Tuesday meeting, Commissioner Eric Jennings said he would prefer to see the museum attempt to raise their own funds before involving the county in the project.

“(The museum’s board) needs to be able to prove that they can raise money for engineering inspection, which is only $8,500,” said Jennings. “If they can’t raise that on their own, I don’t know that they should be embarking on that project, and I would rather have the county be more involved when they can prove that they can raise the funds.”

Phillips said because the museum is only open seasonally, all funds raised are “pocketed” to keep the property “solvent through the winter.”

“This has been a problem with the museum in this space for 25 years. I could take you back and show you engineering reports that go back 25 years, saying the museum should do something with the problem,” said Phillips. “Because the museum’s previous boards couldn’t find all the money to do anything, they never got started. We’re at a point where we need to start this first phase, which will allow us to shore up the parking lot area. Without getting this portion done, the museum is at risk of closing.”

Phillips said the museum serves as a vital part of Lead’s historic preservation efforts and given the money, he had no intention of asking the county for additional funding in the future. 

“I will be moving on and asking other entities, including the governor’s office and different other places, to help with different features,” said Phillips. “So, we’re not intending to over burden anybody, and we are definitely trying to raise money on our own to help with this.”

Commissioner Tim Comer asked how much of the museum’s current funding was being used to pay for engineering and design. Phillips said any remaining funding the museum has is considered, “hard money.”

“What that means is it’s restricted by the donor and it cannot be used for any other purpose,” said Phillips. “With the incidents with the last board, they decided that they wanted to go ahead and (use $20,000 for operations in the past). Right off the top of my head, about $125,000 remains of that hard money. We cannot tap into that to touch what were doing now.”

Commissioners voted to approve the $8,500 request from the county’s contingency fund 3-2. Jennings and Comer opposed the motion, and commissioners Bob Ewing, Brandon Flanagan, and Rick Tysdal approved the motion.

title: Hills View Homes hosts  Future Builders’ Camp for local children
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer
description: DEADWOOD — Hills View Homes, in association with Black Hills Home Builders Association, hosted a camp Wednesday at Sky Ridge Housing Development aimed at introducing local children to the construction trades.
_full_text:
DEADWOOD — Hills View Homes, in association with Black Hills Home Builders Association, hosted a camp Wednesday at Sky Ridge Housing Development aimed at introducing local children to the construction trades.

About 30 children performed construction tasks in 6 under-construction houses. Children textured drywall, ran wire, and moved boards. They were taught by adult construction workers working on the same tasks. 

“There’s just a lot of different hands-on things that walk them (the children) through the progression of a house build,” said Rachelle White, executive vice president of the association.

This is the third year that the camp has operated, but the first time that it has been hosted outside of Rapid City. 

“I think there’s going to be a rising demand in skilled trades,” Marty Quinn, an executive at Hills View Homes. “Most of your builders now, their biggest fear is looking 10, 20 years into the future. Who’s gonna be building these homes? … So we’re trying to inspire (the children) that you can be the career paths in different areas within the home building industry.”

Tanner Quinn, CEO of Hills View Homes, added that the company wanted to give back to the community. “We’re a community builder. … Every project we do is a full community. We don’t build one-off homes. We build communities. And we feel a big part of that is giving back to the community. 

Sky Ridge Housing Development is a group of houses located just west of Exit 17.

title: Gillette school children inspire local author to pen chicken-packed children’s book series
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Heidi DeStefano is the author of a series of middle grade novels about a 10-year-old girl who really, really loves chickens. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Heidi-DeStefano-600px.jpg
Heidi DeStefano is the author of a series of middle grade novels about a 10-year-old girl who really, really loves chickens. Courtesy photo 

GILLETTE, Wyo. — Author and illustrator Heidi DeStefano believes that every child deserves books that appeal to their interests and spark a lifelong love of reading.

Some children are fixated on dinosaurs, cars, or ancient Egypt.

For more than a decade, DeStefano taught kindergarten, first grade, and reading intervention teachers. She noticed one topic that was of particular interest to many of her students.

“We always had students that were obsessed with chickens,” DeStefano said. “My belief has always been that there should be a book for every child’s interest, and so I wrote these books for my chicken-obsessed students.”

 Zamboozie Stew Cover.jpeg
“Chickie Jurin’s Tales for the Chicken Obsessed” is a series of middle grade novels that begins with “Chickie Jurin’s Zamboozie Stew.” Courtesy image 

DeStefano already had experience writing to encourage the young readers in her classroom.

“Because you want to get them to love reading, you end up writing books for them. You’ll have them tell you their dreams or stories that they make up in their own head where they are the hero,” DeStefano said. “You write up the stories, and they just love that because it is about them, and it starts encouraging them to read. I wrote a lot of short stories before taking on these novels. That got me into it.”

DeStefano published her first middle grade novel about a plucky 10-year-old misfit Chickie Jurin in 2024.

The novels include sketches in Chickie’s journals, all DeStefano’s original art, and plotlines that revolve around the young protagonist’s desire to become the world’s foremost chicken expert.

“Our whole family really loves to draw, and I thought that would be a fun thing,” DeStefano said. “Also, to be relatable is to draw these myself.”

Since then, she’s written roughly one book per year in the series — all aimed at 9- to 12-year-old readers.

In addition to relying on facts about chickens to maintain reader interest, DeStefano used her own past as a reference point.

“I grew up on the highline of Montana, ranching and farming on the Milk River Valley, Harlem, Chinook, in the Missouri, or north of the Missouri breaks,” DeStefano said.

Her first novel, “Chickie Jurin’s Zamboozie Stew,” is inspired by childhood memories, as much as children with chickens on the brain.

“It is a little bit based on an experience that I had when I was young where my dad had all the whole, all of us kids, and we had 5 in our family, just chopping (ingredients) and making this stew that he said was ‘Zamboozie Stew.’ I don’t know where he got the name, but we had gallons and gallons and gallons of it,” DeStefano said. “When I look it up on the Internet, I’ve gotten all kinds of different hits that were nothing like this stew. I think he heard the word and made up his own soup.”

DeStefano makes use of the chicken dance and other chicken-motifs to engage students during classroom visits — getting them excited about reading.

“It is a vehicle to address stronger themes. It is a comical way of encapsulating some stronger themes that are important for growing. Coming of age type stuff,” DeStefano said. “The family dynamics, it is a sweet family story, but there is sibling rivalry, and then there are also some (tensions) between the parents; the mother is career-minded, and she doesn’t really want to be out on the ranch. …  There are some bigger themes that I think are good for children to look at.”

The Chickie Jurin books are published by Sastrugi Press.

“They liked the idea. Especially with the illustrations. They like that idea and really helped me polish it up. It is a smaller press, so sometimes it’s a little bit more expensive. I didn’t pay to have it published or anything, but it is more expensive to buy because it is a smaller press,” DeStefano said. “I got a lot more hands-on and personal attention to help it come to fruition — which was nice because I had never published a book before.”

Since 2024, DeStefano has met a number of readers.

“It is sort of specific; it is a niche. Kids who love chickens really love it. Kids who love fantasy, not so much. But there should be books for everybody. This is one where the kids that love farming and ranching and more,” DeStefano said.

She plans to publish the final Chickie Jurin book this year.

Then, DeStefano will pivot from chickens to dragonflies — with a story rooted in STEM and wonder.

title: New novel from SD native and Navy vet explores harshest facets of frontier life
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Rocky Dean Matson is a Navy veteran and the author of “The Ordinary Grit: Courage Under an Unforgiving Sky.” Courtesy photo
_full_text:
New novel from SD native and Navy vet explores harshest facets of frontier life
Rocky Dean Matson is a Navy veteran and the author of “The Ordinary Grit: Courage Under an Unforgiving Sky.” Courtesy photo  

PIERRE — South Dakota author and Navy veteran Rocky Dean Matson proudly announces the release of his debut historical action novel, “The Ordinary Grit: Courage Under an Unforgiving Sky,” now available in paperback, Kindle, and audiobook formats.

Set against the rugged backdrop of the South Dakota Badlands in 1889, “The Ordinary Grit” tells the story of ordinary people facing extraordinary challenges during one of the harshest periods of frontier life. As drought grips the actional town of Oak Haven and powerful railroad interests threaten local homesteaders, 4 individuals must decide what they are willing to sacrifce — and what they refuse to surrender.

At the heart of the novel are four unforgettable characters, Elias Thorne, a determined homesteader fighting to save his land; Titus Croft, a blacksmith whose quiet strength is measured in actions rather than words; Eleanor Vance, a educated schoolteacher from Boston; and Samuel Price, a young ranch hand discovering the kind of man the unforgiving plains will shape him to become. 

“’The Ordinary Grit’ is a tribute to the everyday courage that built the American West,” said Matson. “It’s about people who face impossible odds, not because they seek recognition, but because perseverance is the only choice they have.”

Drawing inspiration from his family’s deep roots in the American plains—including ancestors who farmed Nebraska, Kansas, and Colorado, and a great-grandmother who emigrated from Norway to help build a ranch in Wyoming — Matson brings authenticity and heart to this sweeping frontier story.

A resident of South Dakota, Matson served in the United States Navy and has long been fascinated by the resilience, sacrifce, and determination that shaped America’s frontier communities. His wife, Tammy Danielle Matson, contributed illustrations to the project, making the book a true family endeavor.

Early readers have praised the novel’s vivid storytelling, memorable characters, and realistic portrayal of life on the frontier. Fans of “Lonesome Dove,” “Plainsong,” and “True Grit” will and a compelling new addition to the historical Western genre.

title: The Mercy Sloane Chronicles: Chapter 10
byline: By Eliza Blue A work of serialized fiction, special to the Pioneer
description: “This will give you more time to work with the sheep like you’ve been wanting,” Marla told Arlo when she’d informed him the previous day of their new employee. They’d been the sole proprietors of the shop since they’d first opened it after moving to Antelope and had never before had anyone else working with them. (Unless you included the boys during the narrow window of their grade school years.) Arlo nodded solemnly and didn’t mention that he had never before thought he wanted to work more with the sheep.
_full_text:
The Mercy Sloane Chronicles

“This will give you more time to work with the sheep like you’ve been wanting,” Marla told Arlo when she’d informed him the previous day of their new employee. They’d been the sole proprietors of the shop since they’d first opened it after moving to Antelope and had never before had anyone else working with them. (Unless you included the boys during the narrow window of their grade school years.) Arlo nodded solemnly and didn’t mention that he had never before thought he wanted to work more with the sheep. 

That night, however, lying beside Marla in the darkness, he began to consider the idea and realized that there might be some truth to the notion. Maybe he did want to spend more time with the flock. The first summer after they’d bought sheep, he and one of the boys slept out with them to keep coyotes and wolves away, but as they acquired more land and more livestock, they’d been able to hire that job out, usually to an old cowboy or bachelor  shepherd long past his prime. Arlo knew how to run a general store–he’d grown up in one after all–but he didn’t know anything about how to care for the animals and he didn’t need to. There were more than enough of these men didn’t mind the cramped quarters of a sheep wagon; they were happy for a roof and a way to fill their plates a few times a day. It seemed a fair trade.

The first of them was a man whose land Arlo bought cheap because the man was too old and broke down to work much and couldn’t afford to pay his own taxes. When Arlo approached him, offering to buy the land for little more than the man owed in back taxes, the old man said he was glad to sell, but he had no place to go. 

Arlo was confused. Nowhere to go? Surely there was someone, some family member or friend who would take the man in and care for him for however long he had left. 

 Eliza Blue TMC
Eliza Blue 

“Just get me a sheep wagon,” the old man said suddenly. “And I’ll watch your sheep for you.” There was no one, he said again. He had no children, no kin to speak of, and he told Arlo he only had a few years left, but he’d had 100 head of Rambouillet ewes back in the day. “Had to sell them all in the drought of ‘15, and never could afford to buy them back,” he added. “But I’m a good shepherd.” 

The old man’s eyes filled with happy tears the day he’d signed the land over to Arlo for almost nothing, and he kept shaking Arlo’s hand and thanking him. “Don’t know what I would have done…You’re saving me, friend. There’s no way I could pay those taxes and no place else for me to go…” he repeated over and over, his voice cracking with emotion, the rutted skin around his faded blue eyes wet and overflowing like a map of ancient riverbeds.

But it never sat right with Arlo. He’d named the price, even though he knew the land was worth much more, expecting the man would come back with a counteroffer. Arlo’s father had run a thriving mercantile business in Minnesota, so Arlo knew his way around a business negotiation. “Don’t settle for less if they want to pay more,” had been his father’s slogan, and Arlo had taken that advice to heart. Just like his father, Arlo had his own children to think of, and Marla, who liked finer things and for whom prairie life was not easy. But sitting across from the gnarled, broken man he’d just effectively swindled out of several hundred acres of land, he suddenly wasn’t so sure about that advice anymore. 

And yet the man seemed genuinely thankful. As they both stood to part, one man young and strong, the other stooped, Arlo was one hundred percent certain he was carrying a weight the other man wasn’t. The weight of knowing he now owned something he had not earned, and that weight felt heavier than all his other worries combined.

title: Quick picks: Popular children’s books
description: We’re more than half way through the summer, but there is still plenty of time to try and meet summer reading goals. Beat the heat, and spend some time with a popular book. These are the 6 most checked out children’s books at the Deadwood Public Library, and half of them are breezy graphic novel adaptations sure to offer cool variety for young readers.
_full_text:
ReadingBooks.jpg

We’re more than half way through the summer, but there is still plenty of time to try and meet summer reading goals. Beat the heat, and spend some time with a popular book. These are the 6 most checked out children’s books at the Deadwood Public Library, and half of them are breezy graphic novel adaptations sure to offer cool variety for young readers. 

1. “The Crafting Encyclopedia” by Zoey Schrader

Genre: How-to

This title includes step-by-step instructions for projects in drawing, jewelry making, leather and metalworking, painting, woodworking, and more. Features include sections on preparation and safety, the elements of design, composition, and color theory. Informative sidebars provide additional information.

2. “Mr. Wolf’s Class: Mystery Club” by Aron Nels Steinke

Genre: Graphic novels/middle grade fiction

Mr. Wolf has just started teaching at Hazelwood Elementary. He wants the first day of school to go well, but he’s got his hands full with his new class. Some of his students include: Margot, who is new in town and is trying to make friends; Sampson, who brought something special to school for show-and-tell; Aziza, who just wants everyone to be quiet and do their work; and Penny, who is very sleepy because she has a new baby brother at home, goes missing.

3. “Pokemon Big Book of Facts” by Simon Beecroft

Genre: Children’s 

Become a Pokémon expert with the exciting stats and trivia in this fact-packed book. Covering different Pokémon types, regions, habitats, the Pokémon Big Book of Facts will highlight amazing and fascinating information that makes each Pokémon unique.

Discover fun stats and trivia about Pokémon of all sizes and personalities, from smart to sleepy, strong and speedy, Legendary, Mythical, and more.

4. “Artemis Foul” by Eoin Colfer and Michael Moreci, art by Stephen Gilpin

Genre: Graphic novel

In 2001, audiences first met and fell in love with a 12-year-old criminal mastermind named Artemis Fowl. Since then, the series has sold over seven million copies in the United States alone. Now, this phenomenally successful series is being translated into a graphic novel format. Eoin Colfer has teamed up with established comic writer Andrew Donkin to adapt the text.

5. “Warriors: the Prophecies Begin” by Erin Hunter, adapted and illustrated by Natalie Riess and Sara Goetter

Genre: Graphic novel 

With more than 40 million copies sold, Erin Hunter’s Warriors series has taken the world by storm and is now available in a full-color graphic novel adaptation. The first book covers the first two original novels in The Prophecies Begin: Into the Wild and Fire and Ice. A perfect introduction to the world of Warriors for any new readers and the ultimate gift for its legions of fans.

6. “Grumpy Monkey: Freshly Squeezed” by Suzanne Lang, illustrated by Max Lang

Genre: Graphic novels

This early graphic novel chapter book based on the #1 New York Times bestselling “Grumpy Monkey” is perfect for children who love the original picture books and are ready for the next step. Features hilarious dialogue, multiple panels per page, and a longer storyline to keep kids laughing all the way to the end.

title: Asia’s Buttercream Dreams offers sweet treats for Lead
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Asia Ballert, far left, opened Asia’s Buttercream Dreams bakery on Lead Main Street on June 30. Pictured from left to right are Ballert, Taylor Ballert, Ashley Matsamas, and Braylon Percy. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
Asia's Buttercream Dreams1.jpeg
Asia Ballert, far left, opened Asia’s Buttercream Dreams bakery on Lead Main Street on June 30. Pictured from left to right are Ballert, Taylor Ballert, Ashley Matsamas, and Braylon Percy. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

 Asia's Buttercream Dreams2.jpeg
Asia Ballert helps her nephew, Braylon Percy, make cookies at her new bakery, Asia’s Buttercream Dreams. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick  

LEAD — It smells delicious in Lead’s new bakery. 

The soft opening of Asia’s Buttercream Dreams, located at 403 W. Main St., brought the sweet aroma of brownies, cookies, cupcakes, and raspberry turnovers to Lead’s downtown. The bakery fulfills a lifelong dream of Asia Ballert, who has been making custom cakes out of her home kitchen for a few years, and just recently decided to open a store front. 

“I’ve always grown up baking with my grandma when I was little,” Ballert said. “I’d like to say that she’d be proud of us because she did custom cakes and stuff like that too. I’m hoping that it’s a start and we can start bringing more people to a brighter community. We want Lead to have success.” 

Ballert said her bakery offers a variety of sweet treats, including s’mores and turtle brownies, cookies, raspberry turnovers, cupcakes and more. She takes custom orders for every kind of cake, and soon Ballert plans to offer sourdough options. 

Asia’s Buttercream Dreams will not offer donuts or coffee, as Ballert said she does not want to compete with nearby That Place in Lead, a restaurant that offers donut pastries and coffee. Instead, Ballert said she offers “dirty sodas,” which are regular sodas that feature flavored syrups and cream, as well as ice cream. 

“Our idea was we wanted to do a rustic cottage-themed bakery that has seating, so people can come in and just relax and talk and just get away from everything and have a good time,” she said. “We have no intentions of competing with anybody, so we want to do stuff that is specialized to just us. We just want to bring the community together and let them have more of a variety.” 

Ballert said in the near future she wants to expand her seating area, and offer games and activities for kids. 

“So they can just hang outa nd get away from the heat,” she said. “We love having kids here. Our kids are here every day with us. We’re always playing some kind of fun music on the record player.” 

Asia’s Buttercream Dreams is open from 10 a.m. to 3 p.m., Monday through Saturday, and from 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. on Sundays.

title: Doeden calls unfavorable poll ‘fake’ after touting earlier results from same group
byline: By Seth Tupper Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: SIOUX FALLS —South Dakota governor candidate Toby Doeden touted a poll in May that correctly predicted him finishing first in the June 2 primary, but he called results from the same firm “fake” on Wednesday when they showed him trailing by 30 points in a July 28 runoff election.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

SIOUX FALLS —South Dakota governor candidate Toby Doeden touted a poll in May that correctly predicted him finishing first in the June 2 primary, but he called results from the same firm “fake” on Wednesday when they showed him trailing by 30 points in a July 28 runoff election.

KELO-TV commissioned the new poll from Emerson College Polling in Boston, which shows 62% of likely Republican voters supporting Gov. Larry Rhoden, 32% supporting Doeden and the remainder undecided.

The poll was conducted July 12-13 and has a 4.3 percentage-point margin of error.

Doeden, a businessman from Aberdeen, reacted Wednesday in a Facebook post.

“The paid-off media is attempting to influence the outcome of this election with a very fake poll,” he said.

That stands in contrast to his reaction following the May 21 release of a KELO/Emerson poll that showed him leading with 26% support in the four-way primary race.

“KELOLAND News shows us leading in their latest poll,” Doeden posted on Facebook at the time, while sharing a bar chart of the poll results. “Our internal polling looks even better.”

He ended up finishing first on June 2 with 31% of the votes, but his failure to reach the legally required 35% for victory threw him into a runoff with Rhoden, who received 25% of the votes and finished second. The winner of the July 28 runoff will face Democratic nominee Dan Ahlers in the Nov. 3 general election.

Early voting for the runoff is underway, in person and by mail. The runoff is limited to registered Republicans, and the voter registration deadline was Monday.

title: Rescuers return 2 baby raptors to nest after perilous fall, battle against heat and time
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: BELLE FOURCHE — On Monday, Belle Fourche Code Enforcement Officer Clint Hafner looked down at his truck thermometer and noticed that the outside temperature was 112 degrees. That same day, he received a call from the Black Hills Raptor Center about 2 juvenile birds in desperate need of help. At the time, rescuers believed the birds were very young ospreys.
_full_text:
BELLE FOURCHE — On Monday, Belle Fourche Code Enforcement Officer Clint Hafner looked down at his truck thermometer and noticed that the outside temperature was 112 degrees. That same day, he received a call from the Black Hills Raptor Center about 2 juvenile birds in desperate need of help. At the time, rescuers believed the birds were very young ospreys. 

The pair had fallen about 60 feet from their shady treetop nest outside a home near Old Belle Road. After their perilous plunge to the ground, the hatchlings were becoming lethargic and were at risk of serious dehydration in the searing sun.

Hafner and volunteer Nikki Hoyme responded, transporting the young birds to Belle Fourche, where they immediately set to work getting the chicks hydrated — and a race against the clock commenced. The birds needed to return to their nest as soon as possible. Both babies were too young to fly, and too young to survive without the support of a parent. Waiting too long to return them to the wild could lead to the chicks’ abandonment and seriously harm their chances of living to adulthood. 

“I am sure mom is still feeding them,” Hafner told the Pioneer Tuesday morning. “We are on a timeline today, and I am feeling the pressure of it. We need to get them back as quickly as possible so that momma can get back and start to take care of them.”

The fall, Hafner said, was significant given the nest’s height.

“They are lucky just to be alive,” Hafner said. “That is a pretty tall tree. It’s hard to believe that they even survived it.”

On Monday, the focus was hydration. Hafner gave the birds fluids via a syringe and worked to help them cool down.

“I called the raptor center, and we just decided, ‘Hey, you know what, they need more care,’” Hafner said. “Today they’re perky, and we feel like they are safe to pick back up.”

Tuesday morning, Hafner was reaching out to people in all corners of the community to try and find someone with a bucket truck who was willing to help hoist the rescued babies back up to their treetop home.

“We have somebody watching the nest, and mom is hanging around,” Hafner said at about 10:30 a.m. Tuesday. “Mom wants their babies back. That is quite a fall.”

By 2 p.m., the pair, still believed to be ospreys, were traveling back from Rapid City.

Butte Electric volunteered the use of a bucket truck to attempt to restore the birds to their nest. Once the arm of the cherry picker was fully extended, it became immediately clear that the bucket would not reach the nest.

The birds were carefully placed into an orange 5-gallon bucket, with the hope that crews could lift and lower the small bucket, despite the height discrepancy, into their nest in a towering cottonwood tree. That was before the hydraulic pump appeared to start smoking. Concerned about jeopardizing their equipment and endangering volunteers, the crew from Butte Electric was forced to bow out of the rescue effort. The babies returned to Rapid City Tuesday, with one of the nestlings’ condition in question. One chick appeared alert and healthy; the other was largely inert. Both birds needed to continue to hydrate and be kept cool.  

With time against them, rescuers at the nest site began to worry about the fate of the birds. In general, ospreys are not easy to feed and care for properly in captivity, so rescued individuals are not always good candidates to become captive ambassador birds. Rescuers later determined that the two chicks were red-tailed hawks, not ospreys after all. 

Hafner cares deeply about animals, and he said he wants to ensure the young birds have the best chance of surviving and thriving in the wild.

“It is a wonderful experience. To be able to have those birds in your hands and they are just incredibly beautiful,” Hafner said.

He did not stop looking for volunteers and resources that could return the babies home before their mother abandoned them.

By Wednesday morning, he had secured the help of the crew from Tree Wise Men Tree Services. In a matter of minutes, the arborists were able to scale the cottonwood and set up a rope and pulley system to hoist a carrier crate up to the nest. Less than an hour after the chicks returned from Rapid City, they were safely returned to their nest.

“They started squawking right away,” Hafner said. “Then, I took a picture of a bird in the sky that I am fairly sure was their mother. They were squawking for their momma.”

Once the birds parent returned to the nest, it became clear that they had never been ospreys. The mother bird, who rescuers have now seen caring for the chicks, was a red-tailed hawk. Hoyme told the Pioneer that was the final key to identifying the young pair’s species. 

Hafner first connected with the Black Hills Raptor Center after a golden eagle survived being hit by a semi — perking up after she was presumed dead inside the cab of the truck in 2024. Hafner was the law enforcement officer the semi driver called for assistance. He and Hoyme, his partner, helped to coordinate the raptor’s rescue with experts from the raptor center. The eagle not only survived the incident; it was successfully rehabilitated and released.

title: Meade County first to implement sales tax for property tax relief
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Vendors at the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally get ready to wrap up the week. The Meade County Commission passed a sales tax in hopes to capture some of the revenue spent during the Rally, and apply it to property tax relief. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Meade sales tax1.jpg
Vendors at the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally get ready to wrap up the week. The Meade County Commission passed a sales tax in hopes to capture some of the revenue spent during the Rally, and apply it to property tax relief. Pioneer file photo 

STURGIS — Meade County became the first county in the state to implement Gov. Larry Rhoden’s property tax relief effort, Senate Bill 96, when it approved the first county sales tax in the state, Tuesday, according to officials with the South Dakota Department of Revenue. 

Senate Bill 96 allows counties to charge up to a half-cent sales tax on goods and services, with that money going into a fund specifically designated to provide owner occupied property tax relief. 

On Tuesday, the commission approved a half-cent sales tax on all goods and services sold in Meade County. The approval came after a quiet public hearing, where no residents spoke to support or oppose the tax. The additional half cent brings total sales tax in parts of Meade County up to 7 percent, except for restaurant purchases, hotel charges, alcohol sales, and attraction fees, which incur an additional 1 percent. 

The sales tax will go into effect Jan. 1, 2027. 

According to the law, the county assesses its normal levy, and then can issue a credit to owner-occupied homeowners that is based on sales tax collections. The amount of credit is directly proportional to the amount of county sales tax receipts. 

If the sales tax fund reaches 100% of owner occupied tax collections, those dollars are then evenly split to provide property tax relief for agricultural and non-agricultural properties.

The bill is the first time counties have been statutorily allowed to charge a sales tax. 

Meade County Commissioners repeatedly said that the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally is the only reason they considered implementing the sales tax. The county hosts hundreds of thousands of visitors every year for the largest special event in the state, and commissioners said the new sales tax could allow those visitors to pay in to the property tax relief fund, relieving some of the burden on Meade County property owners. 

 Meade sales tax 2.JPG
Meade county commissioners hope to capture some of the revenue spent during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, with a new sales tax that will offer property tax relief. Pioneer file photo 

According to state law, now that the county has approved the sales tax, they could start property tax reductions in tax year 2027. But those reductions would be based upon the S.D. Department of Revenue’s projected sales tax collection in Meade County, and not on actual collections. 

Chief Deputy States Attorney Ken Chleborad said the state Department of Revenue projects owner occupied sales taxes in 2027 to be about $4 million, with a 50% reduction based on those projections. Meade County Commission Chairman Gary Deering clarified that the 50% reduction is just for county property taxes, and does not apply to municipal, school, road district, or any other levies that apply to the tax bill. 

“The focus here is we are generating sales tax,” Chleborad said. “It goes into a fund so that theoretically, when I come in to pay taxes I pay 50% less of the county side and at the same time we will draw from this fund to pay in my reduction.” 

But if the county puts the property tax relief into effect immediately with the 2027 tax year, they could risk a shortfall if sales tax projections are incorrect, commissioners said. 

Because of that, commissioners said they would prefer to collect the sales tax for a year and then issue property tax credits in the next year, after they know how much money is in the relief fund. 

“Do we have to apply it next year? Can we collect it for a year and then apply what we collected? I think that is a much better way to do it,” Commissioner Wieczorek said. 

Deering agreed, adding that he is concerned that some sales tax projections could be faulty, due to the county’s close proximity to Rapid City. Meade County residents who live near Rapid City could buy less online and more in Rapid City, thereby paying Pennington County sales tax, than the more rural residents who may buy more online, with those sales taxes going to Meade County.  

“It’s way more responsible to have a full year of collection and then base your decision on that collection,” Deering said. 

Commissioners did not make a final decision about when to implement the property tax relief on Tuesday. The ordinance establishing the sale tax will become effective 20 days after it is published in the Black Hills Pioneer, if it is not referred to a citizen vote.

title: Leones’ Creamery is in the running for national fan-favorite ice cream competition: Here’s the scoop
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: A new online bracket-style competition platform is on the hunt for the best ice cream shop in America. Leones’ Creamery in Spearfish is in the running. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Leones 1.JPG
A new online bracket-style competition platform is on the hunt for the best ice cream shop in America. Leones’ Creamery in Spearfish is in the running. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — Leones’ Creamery is in the running for the best ice cream shop in America. It was selected and vetted by the team at “The 64,” a relatively new online platform launched by Justin Woo on April 17, 2025. 

Woo wanted to build a different kind of “best of” competition. A competition for everything from barbecue and sushi to waterparks and ice cream offerings, that was truly fan-based. 

“A lot of people run these competitions for “best of” and they are very unfair. They’re often based on advertising and other factors. For this one, none of the contestants can buy any advertising,” Woo said. “The competition is all fan based. These votes are purely fan votes and you can only vote once per round for things. One person can’t cast multiple votes or buy votes or any of those things.”

This competition is not judged by culinary pros, business peers, or ad-revenue Woo said. Whatever the people vote on, reins supreme.

Imagine a kind of March Madness for ice cream. 64 ice cream parlors from all corners of the country are all in a bracket. 

“Each tournament is 18 days,” Woo said. “There are 6 rounds (of voting) of 3 days each round, and then 2 of the competitors will go head to head in each match up and then the one that gets the most votes in that 3 day round will move forward to the next round.”

Round 1 of competition opened on Thursday, with Leones’ up against Stack Creamery, a Jersey City, N.J.-based ice cream sandwich shop specialty shop. 

Businesses are selected based on their websites, social media presence, reviews, and the uniqueness of their products. The team at The 64 also attempts to choose places that are spread out across the US, Woo said. 

“We try to pick people that represent different areas around the country so that it is not all New York places or California places,” Woo said. “A lot of the times the middle of America wins.” 

Woo hopes it will be a way to find hidden gems, and highlight businesses that are doing something special. 

“I am a big foodie and I travel around the world and try things like carrot cakes ad ice creams. Everyone has an opinion about what they like. It’s interesting to see the different people in the different regions compete,” Woo said. 

Woo said past winners are catalogued on The 64 website under “The GOAT” tab. 

“It is great exposure, because then if you are ever in South Dakota, it’s like, I’ve got to go to that place because I heard about it on The 64 and its an amazing ice cream shop,” Woo said. 

Voting and participation is free and open now at the64.com/tournaments/ice-cream-in-America. 

The first round of voting closes at midnight Saturday. Round 2 voting opens at 9 Sunday morning.

title: Spearfish asks residents to adjust watering schedules to conserve water
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: SPEARFISH — A lawn only needs one inch of water per week to stay green and healthy, and in the days to come, the city is hoping residents will water their grass every other day at most.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

SPEARFISH — A lawn only needs one inch of water per week to stay green and healthy, and in the days to come, the city is hoping residents will water their grass every other day at most. 

Residents with odd-numbered addresses are being asked to water only on odd calendar days. Residents with even-numbered addresses are being asked to water only on even numbered calendar days. The schedule, according to a prepared statement from the city, is designed to alleviate the demand a scorching, dry summer has put on the water system. 

Spearfish is asking residents to adjust their watering schedule “in an effort to remain in green (voluntary) water conservation alert status.” The city has continued to observe low water in certain parts of town during peak water usage hours. 

The city water department is asking users to complete their watering before 4 a.m., in addition to staggering water days. This helps provide sufficient water pressure for neighborhoods of town that experience low pressures during normal peak morning usage times.

While conditions remain hot and dry, residents are encouraged to avoid cutting lawns too short. Grass that is 2.5 to 3 inches in height can grow deeper root systems that encourage better moisture absorption and stress tolerance. Grass clippings are best left where they fall to allow for decomposition and return moisture to the soil, while helping to prevent evaporation after watering. 

The city also recommends ensuring sprinkler heads are properly adjusted to avoid watering hard surfaces.

title: 2026 Davis-Bahcall scholars jet-setting lab tour inspires future careers in STEM
byline: By Mike Ray Sanford Underground Research Facility
description: The 2026 cohort of Davis-Bahcall scholars stand for a picture. Photo by Stephen Kenny
_full_text:
Davis Bahcall scholars.jpg
The 2026 cohort of Davis-Bahcall scholars stand for a picture. Photo by Stephen Kenny 

LEAD — The Davis-Bahcall Scholar Program at the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) gives rising university freshmen and sophomores entering science, technology, engineering and math (STEM) fields a chance to explore potential careers in cutting-edge research across a variety of professions. 

For Zachary Conway, a recent graduate from Rapid City Stevens High School, the program hit the mark. 

“Going into this, I was unsure of where I wanted to take myself with a career after my education. Seeing in-person the types of experiments and the unique workplaces in different parts of the world has solidified my aspiration to do this kind of work in the future,” said Conway. 

Sannah Windy Boy, who is attending South Dakota Mines, echoed Conway’s statements. 

“Before this whole program, I didn’t know there was so many different career paths to take,” Windy Boy said. “It’s great to know I don’t have to have a Ph.D. to work in an underground lab or to work with renewable energy, and there’s different avenues I can take with a civil engineering degree.” 

Ethan Oolman, from Sioux Falls, who is attending the University of South Dakota, found additional validation in his conversations with scientists and researchers. 

“Speaking with all these physicists during this program has informed me that I’m surefire in my decision to go in physics,” Oolman said.

Over the past 4 weeks, the scholars traveled across the United States and overseas, visiting various historical sites and science facilities, including the Boulby Underground Laboratory in the United Kingdom. The once in a lifetime experience is offered by The Institute for Underground Science at SURF in partnership with Black Hills State University. The program includes an additional $2,000 learning stipend for each scholar. Logistics, planning, and financial support for the Davis-Bahcall Scholar Program and two chaperones are provided in partnership with the South Dakota Science and Technology Authority and Black Hills State University. 

After starting at SURF, and visiting research facilities and universities across South Dakota, the cohort ventured to the University of Wisconsin-Madison. They toured the physical science lab to see the manufacturing of panels that will be used for the deep undergroundn experiment (DUNE) located at SURF. The group learned about the IceCube Neutrino Observatory — led by the University of Wisconsin-Madison, as part of the global effort to better understand neutrinos. 

Ellie Erbentraut, from Sioux Falls, who is attending the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, found the university lab in Wisconsin particularly inspirational. 

“It’s been really cool seeing the way that engineering and research come together, especially at a place like the physical science lab at the University of Wisconsin-Madison. The engineers work on the instrumentation that goes into these projects, and it was interesting to see all the different modalities required for this research to be successful,” Erbentraut said. 

Their time in the U.S. concluded with a visit to Illinois, where they toured Fermilab’s headquarters and learned more about DUNE, before flying to the United Kingdom. After some London sightseeing, the scholars headed to the  Boulby Underground Lab, for a special tour of the active salt mine, tunnels and laboratory experiments. 

For Lewis Carlyle, a Rapid City Stevens High School graduate, visiting Boulby was a lunar experience. 

“We went up a rock chute, and it was like walking on the moon. There’s polyhalite dust, and it powdered up like you were on the moon, it was the coolest thing,” Carlyle said. 

He was also impressed with the physics experiments at Boulby and the far-reaching nature of the LUX-ZEPLIN dark matter experiment, which is centered at SURF but seemed to be included in just about every stop on the trip. 

“I walked into Davis-Bahcall planning to go into mechanical engineering, but after 2 days and some physics lectures, I decided to change my major to physics and mechanical engineering, and so that is going to impact my future probably more than anything else. I can’t wait,” he said.

Emma Plamp, a Mitchell High School graduate, added that she appreciated the application-based research taking place at the Boulby Underground Lab. 

“They were working on some earth-based energy storage, which was really interesting,” she said. “They were also engaged in underground vertical farming. It was fascinating to see the different ways that we could maybe use underground space to meet our future needs.”

Joshua Wolfe, a graduate of Flandreau High School, was impressed with the globally collaborative nature of scientific research he saw in the multiple stops. 

“One of the biggest things this program has done for me is brought all these high-level researchers down to a level where they can share their passion,” he said. “This program makes me feel like I could also be somebody who does what these people do.” 

Quinn Kellar, a current student at Black Hills State University, also appreciated the passion STEM professionals have for their work. 

“It’s been really encouraging for me to hear how they’re really excited about what they do. These people are super interested and super passionate about their work, and that’s how I want to be,” Kellar said. 

The group of 8 completed the 28-day program in July. They took part in SURF’s annual celebration of Neutrino Day and did the final morning of presentations about their trip to family members and supporters gathered at Black Hills State University. 

More than 150 students have participated in the Davis-Bahcall Scholar Program since 2008, and many of these scholars have gone on to highly successful STEM careers.

The program is hosted by the Institute for Underground Science at SURF in partnership with Black Hills State University and the South Dakota Science and Technology Authority.

title: New project illustrates  SD’s love-hate relationship with solar power
byline: By Bart Pfankuch South Dakota News Watch
description: CANISTOTA — Construction work is proceeding at a rapid pace at the state’s newest solar farm being built on 585 acres of former farmland south of this small eastern South Dakota town.
_full_text:
SDNewsWatchLogo

CANISTOTA — Construction work is proceeding at a rapid pace at the state’s newest solar farm being built on 585 acres of former farmland south of this small eastern South Dakota town.

The story of how the Grant Solar LLC project being developed by Geronimo Power came to fruition provides a good representation of South Dakota’s ongoing love-hate relationship to development of solar energy in the state.

On the one hand, the $165 million, 99-megawatt (MW) solar project just north of state Highway 42 was supported by the Board of Economic Development within the Governor’s Office of Economic Development, which provided the project with $2.8 million in tax relief through the state Reinvestment Payment Program.

The solar farm that will be located on both sides of 446th Avenue is expected to generate $31 million in direct economic impact, $15 million in new tax revenues, $495,000 in local charitable giving and 150 construction jobs and three full-time permanent local positions over its first 20 years of operation, according to a Geronimo spokeswoman.

The project also proves the rising interest of power companies to tap into South Dakota’s abundant resources of both sun and treeless open spaces.

Conversely, the project was opposed by some neighbors who feared negative impacts on the land, nearby property values and their rural lifestyle. It took 2 applications to the McCook County Commission for the project to finally obtain local approval.

“Our approach has been to listen, be transparent and make reasonable adjustments where we can,” Geronimo spokeswoman Emily Morissette wrote to News Watch in an email.

Development of any new solar energy projects in South Dakota will come in spite of opposition from President Donald Trump, who slowed or stopped many wind and solar energy projects and cut funding for sustainable energy programs across the country during his second term.

In 2023, former Gov. Kristi Noem decided against applying for part of a $7 billion program enacted by the Biden administration called “Solar for All” that provided grants to states to get proposed solar projects up and running. 

In late June, the Pennington County Commission voted 3-2 to give final approval to zoning changes that ban new utility-scale wind and solar projects on agricultural land within the county. Pennington County encompasses nearly 2,800 square miles, an area larger than the state of Delaware that includes vast stretches of open prairies.

The measure limits large solar and wind projects to areas zoned industrial and would also prohibit siting of battery storage units that sometimes accompany sustainable energy projects.

South Dakota remains near the bottom of all states in terms of solar power production, ranking 48th with 270 MW of generation.

But some new projects have come online or are under construction, including the 128 MW Wild Springs solar farm operating south of New Underwood and a 5 MW solar field now under construction in Brookings County.

The website for Philadelphia-based energy company Doral LLC lists a project called Six Mile Solar, a 1,000 MW project the company intends to build in Brookings County. No application from Doral has been submitted to the state, however.

Rodger Horr, executive director of the South Dakota Renewable Energy Association, told News Watch that the state should expect to see a “tsunami” of industrial-sized solar projects in the coming years.

“South Dakota has very little solar, but it’s coming,” Horr said.

His predication is based on a few basic facts about solar energy and the current electricity marketplace. First, he said, is the fact that solar arrays – and wind farms for that matter – are fairly quick to install, taking only about 18 months from approval to production.

Chris Nelson, chairman of the state Public Utilities Commission, told News Watch that there are no solar projects currently seeking approval from the commission. By law, the PUC only reviews and approves energy projects that are 100 MW or greater.

Nelson said the rising opposition to solar projects at the local level could create a chilling effect for companies considering building solar farms in South Dakota.

“If we were to step back three or four years, I thought solar was on the edge of taking off, but we haven’t seen that,” he said.

title: Handley Center could  close by November
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Handley Center has hosted children’s activities for Neutrino Day for many years. Board members say without more funding, the Handley Center could close in November. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Handley Center could  close by November
The Handley Center has hosted children’s activities for Neutrino Day for many years. Board members say without more funding, the Handley Center could close in November. Pioneer file photo 

LEAD — The Northern Hills Family Recreation Association board may be able to keep the Handley Center doors open until November without any additional sources of revenue. 

Karen Everett, treasurer of the board reported that unofficial timeline, ahead of an anticipated board meeting this week when the 5 existing board members — Everett, Darla Auld, Dennis Schumacher, Monica Nepper, and Orion Nold, plan to discuss their next steps, after the city commission denied a request for $72,000 that was set aside for recreation in the 2026 general fund budget. 

The vote to stop funding the Handley Center started on June 15, when Commissioner Dory Hanson asked the commission to consider giving the Handley Center the $72,000 it held back for recreation, to sustain the operation for the rest of the year. On July 6, commissioners voted against the proposal, 4-1. 

The $72,000 request would have made up the remainder of the city’s $125,000 allocation it has given for Handley Center operations for many years. When the city built its budget for 2026, commissioners split that allocation, and agreed to give the Handley Center board more than $70,000 to operate for the first 6 months of the year, while city and Handley board officials negotiated an agreement for a city takeover of the facility. The remaining $72,000 was placed in the general fund budget under a recreation line item. City commissioners said at that time they intended to use that money to operate the Handley Center facility if an agreement could be reached. However, the money was not earmarked with a guarantee that it would go back to the Handley Center. 

Those negotiations for a city takeover seemingly fell apart after the Lead City Commission rejected a resolution presented by Mayor Dustin Heupel, which outlined the terms of the takeover — including deed restrictions that required the city to use the building for indoor recreation for 2 years.

Everett said the latest funding request is probably the last time the board will ask for money. 

“I think we are burned out and done,” she said. “It needs to be driven by the community. The board can only do so much.” 

Everett said it’s unfortunate, because historically the city set up the Handley Center as a nonprofit to run recreation for Lead residents. In the 1980s, she said, a group of volunteers formed a YMCA to run recreation at the Handley Center. The idea, she said, was that the city would help provide funding as a partner to the nonprofit entity, for citizen recreation. 

“For more than 25 years that partnership worked,” Everett said. “The city provided annual funding, and the YMCA managed the city’s indoor recreation programs. About 15 years ago, the YMCA affiliation was dropped because the requirements had become too difficult and expensive to maintain and it became known as the Handley Center. The mission never changed, but I think the perception did. Today it feels more like the Handley is asking for a donation than working alongside the city to provide recreation, and I don’t think that’s what was originally intended. That’s why I believe the city should assume ownership of the Handley.” 

Everett called for members of the community to join together, if they want to save the youth recreation opportunities that are offered at the Handley Center. Current youth activities at the Handley Center include archery, spring soccer indoor practices, baseball and softball batting cages, roller skating, birthday parties, pickleball, and more. The facility is also used for youth activities during Neutrino Day, and as a rainy day location for outdoor activities, such as the Schools Out Bike Bash that was held in May.  Supporting the Handley Center, she said, is about much more than the recreation center building, which Schumacher wrote in 2023 was in extremely poor shape, during a campaign to try and raise money to build a new facility. Since then, Handley board members have refuted Schumacher’s claim that the building is dilapidated, and have said they have worked hard to restore it to usable condition. 

But Everett said the conversation should not be about city funding for the building, because that’s not what the Handley Center is about. 

“There’s a perception that $125,000 is going to a building with an uncertain future, and why waste (money) on a building that we don’t know it’s future,” Everett said. “I would agree with that. But that $125,000 is going to keep the doors open. Very little of it goes into the building. That $125,000 is going to utilities, insurance, routine and ongoing maintenance, payroll, cleaning, and loan repayment. That money keeps those doors open so kids can be in the building. If we lose this facility they don’t have a place.” 

“I’m very sad because the money is budgeted for the remainder of the year,” Everett said of the $72,000 request. “It’s not like surprise funding.” 

Currently, Everett said the board has about $64,000 in the bank, with about $100,000 in certified deposits (CDs). Most of the money in CDs is restricted because it was donated for a facility renovation, so board members will have to check with donors to see if the funds can be used for operations. 

The board still owes about $36,000 on a loan it obtained in 2016 to pay for the multipurpose floor in the gym facility. Monthly bills to operate the building average about $16,065, Everett said. The average breakdown of those bills includes electricity at $931; gas for heating at $555; phones and Internet at $301; insurance at $1,740; fire alarms at $60; sewer at $22; water at $55; loan repayment $2,008; payroll at $7,691; miscellaneous administrative costs at $1,750; and miscellaneous maintenance costs at $952. 

When the Handley board was in active negotiations with the city to take over the facility, Everett said the board used about $80,000 of its savings to pay down the floor loan. That was because the Handley wanted to retire the floor debt before the city took over. Now, she said, the board has no savings, and no agreement with the city. 

Other programming through the Handley Center’s nonprofit status has included a pre-school that is run by Judy Mackey, at Lead-Deadwood Middle School. Auld, the board president, said that preschool will continue to run, regardless of what happens to the Handley Center building. Registrations for next year’s classes, she said, begins this week and interested parents should call Mackey directly. 

Everett said she hopes citizens who support indoor recreation will step up to help save the Handley Center. 

“We’ve been here before, and the citizens came and helped us and we saved it,” she said. “I think if the citizens step up and help we can turn the Handley Center into something amazing. There is so much potential and community events we can do to show kids we care about them. Just one person, one enthusiastic person, can make a difference.”

title: T. rex leg sold moments after ‘Gus’ brings $1.7 million to support SD natural history museum
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: A T. rex leg, sold immediately after “Gus,” the Harding County T. rex that broke sale records for dinosaur fossils, was also under the gavel Tuesday. The leg’s sale will benefit the Natural History Museum of the Black Hills. Photo courtesy Black Hills Institute
_full_text:
T. rex leg 1.JPEG
A T. rex leg, sold immediately after “Gus,” the Harding County T. rex that broke sale records for dinosaur fossils, was also under the gavel Tuesday. The leg’s sale will benefit the Natural History Museum of the Black Hills. Photo courtesy Black Hills Institute  

HILL CITY — ‘Gus,’ one of the largest and most complete Tyrannosaurus rex specimens ever found, smashed sale records Tuesday, when it sold at Sotheby’s in New York City for a total of $50.1 million. While the globe set buzzing about the inherent “rex appeal” of the colossal extinct predators, another lot at the same auction was initially missed in the headlines.

Gus was not the only South Dakota T. rex fossil under the hammer this week. Another specimen, also hailing from the Hell Creek formation, was sold during the same auction — and its sale will make an impact in Black Hills.

Gus was named to honor Gary Licking, the late Harding County rancher who owned the land where the 12.5-foot-tall, 38-foot-long, Late Cretaceous predator was unearthed. Sotheby’s sold the fully prepared and mounted titanic theropod for a gavel price of $43 million — and a grand total of $50.1 million after fees. The previous price record was held by “Apex,” a $45 million stegosaurus, also sold by Sotheby’s.

Gus was lot 20 at the “Geek Week” auction Tuesday morning. Lot 21, a T. rex leg discovered in Ziebach County, was sold on behalf of the Black Hills Institute — money from the sale will not only come back to the state, but help ensure that the public can view even more dinosaur specimens in from our Black Hills backyards in our backyard.  

 Pete Larson.JPEG
Black Hills Institute President and Founder Pete Larson, pictured during an interview, was invited by Sotheby’s to give talks on T. rexes and the significance of specimens like Gus an a leg sold by the Black Hills Institute. Photo courtesy Black Hills Institute 

 Adam.JPG
Adam Weaver discusses how a stretch of the new Natural History Museum of the Black Hills will look when its complete. Pioneer file photo  

 T. rex leg.JPEG
This fossil left South Dakota for New York City, and was auctioned by Sotheby’s Tuesday for $1.7 million. The funds from the sale will support Black Hills Institute and the development of the Natural History Museum of the Black Hills. Photo courtesy Black Hills Institute  

“All of the money has gone back to the museum. It allows us to make better, nicer displays for the Black Hills people to enjoy and for people in our area to look at,” said Adam Weaver, the Operations Manager of Black Hills Institute.

The 10-foot-tall leg sold for a total of $1,792,000.

“We have been part of some famous auctions for dinosaurs, but this is the first one ever that actually benefited Black Hills Institute. We are only doing it to help support our museum, so it is kind of a neat thing,” Weaver said.

Pete Larson the president and founder of Black Hills Institute, who literally wrote the book on “Rex Appeal” (the title of his memoir about the search for, and resulting battles over T. rex “Sue”), was flown out by Sotheby’s to give talks prior to the auction.

“He was there and talked about the science of T. rexes on Friday night to kind of prep for the auction. That is kind of a neat thing; Sotheby’s flew him out there for the auction, so that he could talk to people about what is neat about Gus,” Weaver said.

Gus was preceded in sale by Stan, a Black Hills T. rex, sold by Christie’s for nearly $32 million. The institute owned and displayed Stan at its museum prior to the specimen’s sale — which was court-mandated. None of the proceeds supported the museum.

Pull quote
“All of those ranches, all of the vast emptiness that you drive through, the entire way there are fossils.” — Adam Weaver, Black Hills Institute 

“A lot of people think that when Sue was sold we got money, or when Stan was sold, we got money, and we did not,” Weaver said. “Those were both specimens that were lost to us because of those legal actions.”

A genuine T. rex leg fossil, the piece the institute chose to auction with Sotheby’s this week, offered a unique opportunity for an infusion of funds. For the first time, the institution could make a sale that directly benefited its educational endeavors.

“We are a scientific institution. We try to find all of the (parts of) the specimen that there are. In looking for the rest of that T. rex, we dug a tremendously large hole on the ranch that it is from and that is all there was. It is just a leg,” Weaver said.

The very top of the leg showed signs of bite marks, indicating that the rex it belonged to might have been the victim of predation or post-mortem scavenging. 

“If it was a whole dinosaur, we would have kept it together, obviously, but it wasn’t,” Weaver said.  “That allowed us to have a neat piece that a museum or a collector could add to their collection at a relatively affordable cost when you look at it compared to Gus.”

Auctions like the one this week can stir up controversy. Thinking in the words of Indiana Jones, many argue that pieces like these “belong in a museum.” In this case, the sale is meant to support a museum rather than stock it.

“I know most people will think, ‘Why is this leaving our area?’ Well, it’s because we have something more exciting to show. Not that the leg isn’t great, but it is neater when they are attached to a whole dinosaur,” Weaver said. Selling the leg to a private collector or another scientific institution (the identity of the winning bidder remains a mystery at this point) supports the construction and improvement of the institute’s new museum. 

Black Hills Institute is in the middle of transforming the former Prairie Berry Winery, 5 minutes from downtown Hill City, into the Natural History Museum of the Black Hills. The 40,000 square foot museum will provide roughly 10 times the specimen display space currently available at the Museum at Black Hills Institute downtown.

“Obviously we won’t have that (T. rex leg) in our museum, but when our museum opens, we are going to have an original T. rex in there for everyone to see, and we will eventually assemble 2 of our own T. rexes in the museum,” Weaver said. “We will have some South Dakota rexes here in the Black Hills for everybody to see.”

The museum, which is slated to open June 4, 2027, boasts a planned “Hall of Kings” where visitors can view the fossilized remains and casts of up to 7 massive, fearsome “tyrant lizards.”

T. rexes will not be the only imagination-capturing prehistoric megafauna on display. There will be mammoths and ground sloths, and potentially, fossilized whales.

“If we can get it done in time, one of the stars is going to be a Barosaurus,” Weaver said. “Which is a 90-foot-long dinosaur. It will be standing up in the main exhibit hall with its head up in the clouds kind of, so on the third floor, you’ll be eye level with it. On the first floor, you will be at its feet.”

A relative of Diplodocus, Barosaurus has a long neck and lengthy whip-like tail. Scientists believe in their hay-day, Barosaurus weighed about as much as 4 large adult elephants — earning its name, Greek for “heavy lizard.”

“For me, the important thing for people to know is that we are not just selling things to make money. We are selling things to make this museum project better and grander and help us get it done in this super rapid amount of time,” Weaver said.

Weaver noted that, while the museum’s construction is moving quickly, the work of paleontologists is often arduous, expensive and slow.

When you find a T. rex, and you sell it, it can go for a lot of money like we saw today, but it took people years, sometimes decades, to get it from the ground to the auction,” Weaver told the Pioneer just hours after the gavel fell on Gus’ sale. “People see those numbers and it’s like, ‘Oh my gosh,’ but you have to remember this is a long (process) with 10s of 100s of thousands of hours of work to get to New York City.”

Gus was discovered by Thomas Heitkamp in 2021. It took Theropoda Expeditions 5 years to excavate, prepare, mount, and articulate the mammoth adult T. rex.

“One thing about Theropoda, the people who sold Gus, is they do a really good job. At Black Hills Institute, we talk to them all the time,” Weaver said. “When they sell a dinosaur, it is very well documented what it is and exactly what you are getting. They do their best to make it look the way that it is supposed to look ... So, to me, as long as the person making the thing is truthful and they are trying to follow the science to put it together, then whoever is putting it together, that’s great.”

The record-breaking sale of Gus has launched discourse around the advisability of selling specimens that could be scientifically significant at such high prices. Weaver said there is value in encouraging quality, responsible paleontological expeditions and sales.

There are more fossils than there are competing diggers, and paleontology is always working against the clock. With each passing day, there is greater risk of erosion and damage to bones.

“If you drive from Rapid City, South Dakota to Garfield County, Montana, which is many hours away from here, the entire time you are driving there are fossils all along the way. All of those ranches, all of the vast emptiness that you drive through, the entire way there are fossils,” Weaver said. “ There is not really a competition in finding them. It is basically like, how many can be found before the weather destroys them? Anyone who is doing the work at a high grade, good for them if they can find a way to keep doing it because it is hard.”

And in the case of sales like the leg (the first of its kind for BH Institute), the sale of bones to private collectors can fuel science and endeavors that educate and excite the next generation of scientists.

“When you find a T. rex, and you sell it for a bunch of money, it can go for a lot of money like we saw today, but it took people years, sometimes decades, to get it from the ground to the auction,” Weaver said. “That may be all the money a company made for 15 years, and they had to front that and eat ramen noodles to make it happen.”
