title: SD severe weather snapshot
byline: By Elena Tittel South Dakota News Watch
description: Extreme winds caused significant property damage and knocked down power lines in the town of Highmore, S.D., June 29. Photo courtesy of David Swain, Aberdeen Insider.
_full_text:
2026-6-29-Highmore-storm-damage.JPG
Extreme winds caused significant property damage and knocked down power lines in the town of Highmore, S.D., June 29. Photo courtesy of David Swain, Aberdeen Insider. 

 2025-12-23 Custer wind damage.JPG
Significant wind damage at Custer State Park, S.D., as pictured Dec. 23, 2025.  

South Dakota is no stranger to severe weather events. The latest proof: a 131-mph wind gust on June 29 in Highmore that was one of the strongest recorded in U.S. history and the second-highest gust recorded in South Dakota.   

The National Weather Service issued a severe thunderstorm warning at the time of the storm and confirmed the winds did not come from a tornado, according to a fact brief published by News Watch.

Laura Edwards, SDSU Extension state climatologist, said winds exceeding 130 mph are “uncommon,” but with the right conditions, it can occur.

“I think they had just the right perfect conditions with the strengthening storm as it was approaching that area,” she said. 

It was the latest of several recent wind-related events.

In December, a record-breaking winter windstorm swept across Custer, Fall River and Pennington counties, causing widespread damage.

According to a press release from Gov. Larry Rhoden, the storm produced sustained winds and gusts exceeding 90 mph, bringing down power lines, snapping off and topping trees, damaging public infrastructure and leaving thousands of residents without power. It prompted Gov. Larry Rhoden to request a presidential disaster declaration, which was received in April.

16 federal disasters in past decade

Over the past 9 years, there have been 16 federal major disaster declarations, not including the COVID-19 pandemic, in the state of South Dakota, according to the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA). Federal disaster declarations are determined by the president.

The reasons include winter storms, flooding, thunderstorms, tornadoes and straight-line winds.

State disaster declarations, on the other hand, are issued by the governor. Executive orders related to state disasters from the previous decade include severe winter storms, flooding, droughts and straight-line winds.

Drought-like conditions in SD

Aside from the 2 recent major wind-related storms, South Dakota has also seen a lack of precipitation in the southern parts of the state.

Andrew Kalin, senior service hydrologist for the National Weather Service in Sioux Falls, said in the northwest and other parts of the state, precipitation levels are closer to normal.

Data from the U.S. Drought Monitor shows approximately 48% of the state is in moderate to extreme (D1-D4) drought, affecting an estimated 557,792 people. These drier conditions, primarily concentrated within the southern parts of the state, are causing a lack of soil moisture, especially following a drier winter that had less snow, Clabo said.

Edwards said that there has been an ebb and flow of drought in the state over the past five or so years, especially along the southern part of the state. She predicts improvement will be relatively local, meaning it will not be uniform across the state.

“I think the improvement that we’ll see will be relatively local, and I think we’re going to continue to see this ebb and flow of worsening and improvement,” Edwards said.

Staying informed: Weather alert services

In instances of severe weather, South Dakotans have multiple options to stay informed. One of these are weather sirens, which are designed to alert people who are outdoors.

Sometimes, though, not everything goes according to plan.

Back in early June, weather sirens in Aberdeen and Viborg experienced troubles ahead of tornado season ramping up.

Tanner Jondahl, chief of police for the city of Aberdeen, said the backup plan is still working. The sirens are being tested every Wednesday at 6 p.m. and they expect the new primary system to be up and running sometime in August.

In the southeast South Dakota town of Viborg, the sirens on the west side stopped working after a control board burned out. It has been replaced and the sirens are working again, said maintenance superintendent Jody Nelsen. 

Aside from weather sirens, there are multiple ways to stay informed during potentially life-threatening situations. The most widespread weather alert system is NOAA Weather Radio, a nationwide radio station network, providing 24/7 weather alerts. Aside from tuning into the radio, people can also enable wireless emergency alerts on their iPhone or Android’s settings.

However, it’s wise not to rely solely on one weather alert system, due to potential unpredictability.

Looking forward, a forecast from the NOAA Climate Prediction Center, the next one to three months are projected to have warmer than average weather in the west, south and eastern parts of the state, whereas the north-central part of the state may experience near- to below-average temperatures.

title: E-bikes in Deadwood
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: DEADWOOD — With electric bicycles, commonly referred to as e-bikes, on the rise as an economical and sustainable means of in-town transportation and assisted recreation in the Northern Hills, Deadwood Police Chief Cory Shafer weighs in on the restrictions and proper use in his city.
_full_text:
DEADWOOD — With electric bicycles, commonly referred to as e-bikes, on the rise as an economical and sustainable means of in-town transportation and assisted recreation in the Northern Hills, Deadwood Police Chief Cory Shafer weighs in on the restrictions and proper use in his city. 

Shafer said that at this point in time, when e-bikes are rising in popularity, his department is focusing on educating themselves and their community. That education includes knowing what exactly an e-bike is, what the classifications are between them, and where the bikes can be safely and legally ridden while in town. 

Classifications

“Electronic bikes are considered, by South Dakota, as a motor that generates power by the watts generated to propel. Whether it’s a scooter or a bike, that difference is whether it has a saddle, seat, or a platform to stand on,” said Shafer. “E-bikes in South Dakota have a seat and scooters have a platform. So, although they generate the same by watts, they are 2 different classifications.”

Shafer explained that there are 3 different classes of e-bikes, differentiated by whether the bike creates power by pedaling, through a throttle, or both, the speeds the bikes can reach, and when the bike ceases to create power. 

According to South Dakota Codified Law (SDCL) 32-20B-9, a Class 1 electric bicycle, “provides assistance only when the person is pedaling and ceases to provide assistance when a speed of 20 miles per hour is achieved.” A Class 2 electric bicycle is capable of propelling the bicycle without the person pedaling and ceases assistance when a speed of 20 miles per hour is reached. A Class 3 electric bicycle only provides assistance while pedaling and ceases assistance when a speed of 28 miles per hour is achieved. 

Shafer said riders of a Class 3 e-bike must be at least 16 years old, and riders 18 years of age and under must wear a helmet. 

In Deadwood, Shafer said Class 3 e-bike cannot be on the sidewalk and must be on the roadway. Classes 1 and 2 can be ridden on the sidewalk but are prohibited from the business district. 

“The business district is encompassed, pretty much, wherever the main roads are brick,” said Shafer. “So, outside of city hall to Main Street, all the way down.”

Shafer said that Deadwood is choosing to treat e-bikes the same as bicycles so far as restricting the use of them in town. Essentially, anywhere a bicycle can be, a Class 1 or 2 e-bike can be, given the rider yields to pedestrians, has audible signals, and stays on the most outer right lane of the roadway. On recreation paths, like the Mickelson Trail that runs to Deadwood, classes 2 and 3 are prohibited.

Statistics of crashes involving e-bikes

Shafer said his philosophy, as a person dedicated to the public safety of the community, is that higher visibility does not necessarily indicate a problem that needs solved, and too many needless laws can put a burden on law enforcement and a community.

“Statistically, we have very little information to go off of to justify some sort of ordinance, in my opinion, to have repercussions for certain things when we don’t have an issue,” said Shafer. “Now, could we make an ordinance to require individuals who ride on (e-bikes) in city limits to have a helmet on? Sure. As of right now, there’s not a whole lot of laws to enforce, and the ones that are there are difficult to enforce because it’s a perception.”

Shafer said if the police department were to receive complaints about riders on sidewalks or roadways going too fast, it would be difficult for the officer to issue a citation without using a radar to clock the rider’s actual speed. 

“A rider on an e-bike may appear to be going faster to the naked eye of someone walking down the sidewalk in Deadwood. When you have a smaller device with a narrow road and tall buildings, it may appear to the naked eye that it’s going faster than it really is,” said Shafer. “And until police are out patrolling and running radar to get accurate speeds, there’s nothing indicating at this time that an increased number of e-bikes or scooters are driving erratically or speeding.”

Shafer said in 2025, his department responded to 6 accidents with injuries involving vehicles from Jan. 1 to July 13. Of those 6 accidents, only one involved a bicycle. Shafer said according to the accident report, the bicyclist hit a parked car.

Over the same time frame in 2026, Shafer said the department has responded to 5 vehicle accidents with injuries. None of the accidents have involved e-bikes, scooters, or bicyclists.

From Jan. 1 to July 13, 2025, Shafer said the department responded to 70 vehicle accidents with no reported injuries, and 70 similar reports so far this year. Shafer said none of the accidents involve e-bikes or scooters.

Community education

Shafer said the department is engaging in a community education project, releasing information about e-bikes, scooters, and bicycle safety on their Facebook page and including information in the city-wide newsletter. Before summer ends, he said he’s working in collaboration with the city’s department of parking and transportation to create a class designed to teach families and children how to safely ride a bike in city limits. In the future, he said he can’t justify passing ordinances that could restrict the enjoyment of families and visitors in the city and possibly impede small businesses who rely on the income generated by renting e-bikes to provide for their families. 

“With very little to no statistics, it’s a balance of putting too many or the wrong laws out there where a problem doesn’t exist while also trying to prevent (the worst) from happening,” he said. “Unfortunately, the bad part of police work is we can’t control what happens. We can’t control the actions of people and what they do. So, right now, we’re just taking our time and educating ourselves and our community.”

Shafer said he encourages people who want to know the municipal and state laws surrounding e-bikes should consult their state legislation and municipal ordinances. He also encouraged curious families to come to the police station and talk to an officer.

title: Water main break floods part of  Spearfish HS
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — Spearfish school officials got a rude awakening July 1, when they were notified that a water main had broken inside a mechanical room at Spearfish High School.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — Spearfish school officials got a rude awakening July 1, when they were notified that a water main had broken inside a mechanical room at Spearfish High School.

 Water main break 1.jpg
Water, rushing from a 6-inch water main break, flows through a mechanical room at Spearfish High School. Courtesy photo 

 Water main break 2.jpeg
A cavern, 15 feet long, 3-5 feet across, and as deep as 8 feet in one area was created by a 6-hour water main break. Pioneer photo by Mark Watson 

 Water main break 3.jpg
Mud still coats newly-replaced carpet in the high school and middle school in Spearfish. Courtesy photo 

Nick Gottlob, superintendent of the Spearfish School District, said a 6-inch mater main broke. The high-pressure water created a significant cavern underneath hot water heaters. He estimated the cavern is 15 feet long, 3-5 feet across, and as deep as 8 feet in one area. The flooding extended beyond the mechanical room, and flooded parts of the middle school and high school with several inches of reddish brown muddy water.

“Water was pouring out of here and down through the parking lot,” Gottlob said of the exterior mechanical room door.

City staff was notified around 6:20 a.m. and had water to the buildings shut off about 10 minutes later, said Adam McMahon, the city’s public works director. He said it was unknown how much water was lost from the break. However, Gottlob said a review of surveillance cameras showed the leak began before midnight on June 30.

Gottlob said water flooded the hallways, high school locker rooms, and coaches’ offices, from the main corridor to the high school’s main gym.

“Thankfully, this elevation pitch right here was just enough to keep the water back here,” he said of a 2-inch transition from a hallway to the main gym, which was renovated in 2024.

Gottlob said that summer maintenance crews have been busy getting water and mud out of the building. 

“I can’t say enough about Josh Gerhold (director of building and grounds) and his entire maintenance crew. We brought guys from every building over, and it was a long couple days,” he said. 

“The number of hands on deck that day, mopping and squeegeeing, and working incredibly hard. I was proud of all of them,” he added

As of Thursday, water had still not been fully restored. It was back on in the high school, but the middle school remained without water.

“We had over 6 hours of high, high pressure, high volume water intrusion,” he said. “We’re incredibly fortunate it didn’t do more damage than it did. I mean, the proximity we had to our main gym floor that had just been redone, (if it would have flooded) that would have been devastating to not only the repair timeline, but I don’t know that we would have had it restored in time for the (basketball) season.”

Significant cleaning is still needed.

“What remains to be done is get our service line restored, complete the assessment of the damage loss from stored equipment, coach’s office, and locker rooms, and then we obviously need to address the amount of mud that had come in, either by deep cleaning the hall carpets and the rugs,” he said. “The sad part is, all this had just been replaced as part of our locker room renovation.”

“Obviously, insurance is going to help. We’re not that far yet,” he added. “We’re still assessing it. We’ve been in consultation with the insurance, but overall, we’re trying to get a real clear picture of not only damage loss, but also the scope of what the repairs will entail before we make a decision on what direction the district will go.”

title: Lawrence Co. regains cooperative agency status with Forest Service
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Lawrence County has regained cooperative agency status with the U.S. Forest Service, becoming the only county in the state with the status. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Lawrence Co. gains cooperative agency status with Forest Service.JPG
Lawrence County has regained cooperative agency status with the U.S. Forest Service, becoming the only county in the state with the status. Pioneer file photo 

DEADWOOD — After more than 2 years of communication efforts, Lawrence County has entered into a cooperative agency status with the U.S. Forest Service, becoming the only county in the Black Hills National Forest to establish such a relationship. 

Mitch Iverson, chairman of the Lawrence County Natural Resource Committee, helped spearhead the movement to regain the status with the Forest Service after it was lost following the conclusion of the last pine beetle epidemic. Iverson said the relationship is important to allow for better advocacy of sustainable forestry practices while also working to bolster timber harvests in the county and mitigate fuels to wildfire. 

“(Previously) there was a reluctance to share information on or about the projects early. We often found out about projects right before or after the Forest Service had done considerable work, and we could have helped the Forest Service with things in the past, ranging from access to conditions on the ground,” said Iverson. “It was really hard when we didn’t learn about projects until the last minute. Now, with (Patrick Champa), the new district ranger, he’s treated the (memorandum of understanding) and has treated the county very well. He’s allowed for flexibility, and he’s been trying to keep us up to speed on projects that are in the formative stages.”

Iverson said the county has a unique wealth of information and education to offer the Forest Service on projects, including professionals with experience working with the Bureau of Land Management, retired Forest Service employees, private landowners, and people with experience in the timber industry. He said that expertise can help the Forest Service, which has suffered drastic federal cuts in the last year, look at great swaths of acreage with a more precise eye. 

“There are various treatments for different forest conditions, and sometimes you don’t know everything you need to about the conditions throughout larger areas,” said Iverson. “So, when you write a plan and you go to implement it, you may find conditions that are different from what you expected. When conditions are different, you change your prescription based on the actual conditions on the ground. If you find there’s a rare species, you can adjust the treatment instead of rewriting the whole treatment for an entire project or instead of not doing the project in that area. With National Environmental Policy Acts and all the requirements that the Forest Service has, unless you write that into the plan, you can’t modify things very much. So, (with the cooperative agency status), the Forest Service has been trying to write more flexibility into the plan.”

Iverson said that while Lawrence County is unique in South Dakota for having cooperative agency status with the Forest Service, the relationship is not unique on the national scale.

“They have an overall (memorandum of understanding) with the state of Wyoming that includes the counties as well,” said Iverson. “On a lot of other forests, it’s not uncommon at all.”

Promotion of timber harvest

At the June 23 meeting, Lawrence County Commissioners agreed to send a letter to Forest Supervisor Shawn Cochran, asserting that the county takes a proactive stance on increased timber harvest. The letter was in response to a contradicting message about the county that had allegedly reached Washington, D.C.

“On a field trip (with the Forest Service), some representatives of the county were talking about different prescriptions in specific areas based on forest conditions,” said Iverson. “It’s very common to have differences of opinion about forest management treatments, not just about harvest but also thinning. In this case, somehow the message got out that Lawrence County was not supportive of higher levels of timber harvest. The county had heard back from several sources that the message was out there, and it created some confusions with our partners and our local industry was wondering what was going on. The state of Wyoming was confused. So, the county felt it was necessary to set the record straight.”

Iverson said that the Forest Service had prescribed thinning of overstory (mature, tall trees) on large sections of the Black Hills. However, smaller areas within the prescribed area had limited understory (short, underdeveloped trees). 

“Normally, when you do overstory removal, you want to see that there’s medium-sized trees to take the place of the trees you removed,” said Iverson. “The county was advocating that certain areas with limited understory, where the trees were only5-7 feet tall underneath the mature trees, that it wasn’t the best treatment for that area. That’s where things got confused, because they were talking about specific, small areas.”

Iverson said thinning the overstory in specific areas would not only be unaesthetically pleasing, but it would also mean that private industry wouldn’t be able to return to the area for harvest for longer periods of time. 

Iverson said the message has since been resolved and he hopes for continued communication between the district office and the county while hoping for improved communication from Cochran’s office in the future. 

In a request for comment on the status of the cooperative agency status and what it means for the Forest Service and the private timber industry, Cochran’s office said they felt the issue had been resolved and refused further comment.

title: Bobcat harvest management to remain steady this year
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: The GF&P will continue a bobcat harvest management strategy with hunters allowed to take just one cat in the Black Hills and East River zones, and unlimited cats allowed in the West River zone. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Bobcat.JPG
The GF&P will continue a bobcat harvest management strategy with hunters allowed to take just one cat in the Black Hills and East River zones, and unlimited cats allowed in the West River zone. Courtesy photo  

WEBSTER — Bobcat harvest strategies could remain the same for the next couple of years, officials with the South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks said recently. 

During the July 10 GF&P Commission meeting, commissioners considered a proposal to maintain a low harvest strategy for the Black Hills bobcat management zone; a moderate harvest strategy for the western bobcat management zone; and a low harvest strategy for the eastern bobcat management zone. 

A low harvest strategy includes a 52-day bobcat season, when hunters are permitted to only harvest one cat. A moderate strategy is also a 52-day season, but hunters are allowed to harvest unlimited numbers. 

For the 2025-26 season, Senior Wildlife Biologist Chad Lehman said hunters harvested a total of 479 bobcats across the state. Most of that harvest occurred in the West River zone, where 388, or 81% of cats were taken. Nearly 90% of the bobcats harvested were adults, and no kittens were taken, he said. 

Statewide, the bobcat harvest has nearly doubled in the last 10 years, Lehman said. In the 2014-2015 season, hunters harvested 214 cats. That number jumped to 462 in the 2017-2018 season, and then tapered off to 169 in 2022-2023. In the Black Hills, that harvest was at about 42, or 23-24% of the bobcat population in 2022-2023, before the GF&P shifted to a low harvest strategy for the 2024-2025 and 2025-2026 season. In the last season, there were 19 bobcats harvested in the Black Hills.  

In the West River zone, the harvest was up to 388 cats for the 2025-2026 season, up from about 106 in some previous years. 

“Typically what we see year after year is West River is definitely the area where we see the biggest harvest of bobcats in the state,” he said. 

Andrew Norton, wildlife program administrator, said in addition to population and harvests the GF&P also tracks fur prices for bobcats. In the last five years pelt prices have jumped from about $100 to $500. 

“Why is that important? In the Black Hills we did limit it to 1 bobcat per individual a few years ago and you can see the subsequent drop in harvest. It was cut in half. We actually really want to cut it down to about one-third of what it was to have a stable bobcat population. Importantly, if we had not limited that to one, we may be expecting numbers in the 50s, 60s, or even 70s at these current prices. That’s just an example of a good measure we did 2 years ago to ensure we don’t have a continuously decreasing population of bobcats in the Black Hills.”

title: Physical Therapy Center celebrates  Sturgis grand opening
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: The owners of the Physical Therapy Center at 2707 Lazelle St., stand with some of the equipment at the new facility on Friday in Sturgis. From left are: Mariah Heaton, Greg Cagle, and Kelli Olmsted.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
2. therapy.JPG
The owners of the Physical Therapy Center at 2707 Lazelle St., stand with some of the equipment at the new facility on Friday in Sturgis. From left are: Mariah Heaton, Greg Cagle, and Kelli Olmsted.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

STURGIS — The Sturgis Area Chamber of Commerce officially welcomed the Physical Therapy Center to the community Friday with a ribbon-cutting ceremony at the clinic’s new location at 2707 Lazelle St., next to Dairy Queen. 

The clinic, which expanded to Sturgis after establishing a successful practice in Rapid City, offers a wide range of rehabilitation services designed to help patients recover from injuries, surgery and chronic conditions while improving balance, mobility and overall quality of life.

Greg Cagle, one of the clinic’s owners, said the decision to open a Sturgis location came after recognizing a growing need for physical therapy services in the northern Black Hills.  

“We’ve had our office in Rapid City for a number of years, and it was time to expand,” Cagle said. “We realized the Sturgis area definitely needed a little bit of help, so here we are.”

The clinic provides physical therapy and occupational therapy services for patients of all ages as well as breast cancer rehabilitation. Treatments include orthopedic rehabilitation for shoulder, hip, knee and back injuries, post-surgical rehabilitation, cancer rehabilitation, balance training and recovery from everyday injuries. 

“We see everything from post-surgical patients to someone who hurt their back working on the farm over the weekend,” Cagle said. “Our goal is to help people get back to doing the things they enjoy.”

The clinic also offers specialized services that are not widely available in smaller communities. Occupational therapy includes hand therapy and lymphedema treatment, while Cagle specializes in vestibular rehabilitation for patients experiencing vertigo and balance disorders. “Deep inside the inner ear are structures that tell your brain where your body is moving,” Cagle explained. “When those signals aren’t working properly, people can experience dizziness or lose their balance. We work to retrain that system so patients regain confidence and stability.”

Originally from Medford, Ore., Cagle has spent the past 22 years living and working throughout North and South Dakota. Although he currently commutes from Rapid City, he said he has quickly grown fond of Sturgis.  

“I definitely like Sturgis,” he said. “My heart’s here, and I enjoy the drive every day.”

The Physical Therapy Center opened its Sturgis office on April 1, with Cagle beginning full-time service June 1. He said the clinic is actively accepting new patients and plans to expand its staff as demand grows.

“Our access is still very good, and we’re already talking with a couple of people who may eventually join the team,” Cagle said. “We want to continue growing while serving the community.”

title: 4,100 tails submitted for  first coyote bounty program
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: The first coyote bounty program closed this month with 4,100 tails submitted.
_full_text:
usfws-coyote-snow-extra-large.jpg
The first coyote bounty program closed this month with 4,100 tails submitted.  

WEBSTER — A coyote bounty program instituted this year closed before the maximum number of tails were submitted, Jacquie Ermer, regional wildlife supervisor with the South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks said recently. 

During the GF&P Commission meeting, July 10, Ermer told commissioners that in its inaugural year, the coyote bounty program was held from April 1 through July 1. During that time, 573 trappers submitted 4,100 coyote tails, with a payout of $30 per tail for the coyote bounty program. The GF&P planned to spend $300,000 for a maximum of 10,000 tails, Ermer said.

Ermer said adults age 65 and over submitted the most tails, and youth ages 18 and under submitted 12% of the tails. 

The coyote bounty program was first approved in March, when the GF&P rescinded a popular nest predator bounty program that paid $10 per tail, at a maximum of $500,000 for qualifying pheasant predator species. The funding for the program comes from hunting and fishing fees. Wildlife Director Tom Kirschenmann said the coyote bounty program is intended to address increasing reports about the growing coyote population across the state, and its subsequent effects on deer and antelope recruitment, and livestock depredation.

title: Barnaud appointed magistrate judge in Fourth Circuit
description: Timothy Barnaud
_full_text:
barnaud-timothy.jpg
Timothy Barnaud 

PIERRE — The Unified Judicial System announced that the South Dakota Supreme Court has appointed Timothy Barnaud as a magistrate judge for the Fourth Judicial Circuit.

Barnaud fills a magistrate judge vacancy created with Judge Chad Callahan’s recent appointment as a circuit judge for the Fourth Judicial Circuit. Barnaud will take the bench Monday.

Barnaud grew up on a ranch 15 miles northeast of Belle Fourche. He received his undergraduate degree in history from Dakota Wesleyan University, Mitchell, in 2006 and his juris doctor from the University of South Dakota School of Law, Vermillion, in 2009. Barnaud received a master of law degree in environmental and natural resource law from the University of Denver Sturm College of Law in 2011.

After receiving his master’s degree, Barnaud returned to South Dakota and worked as an assistant attorney general for the South Dakota Attorney General’s Office. The majority of his work was in the area of criminal law. 

In 2013, Barnaud opened Barnaud Law Firm in Belle Fourche, where he practiced in the areas of criminal law, estate planning, business law, environmental and natural resource law, appellate advocacy, mineral and petroleum law. Barnaud also served as state’s attorney for Butte County from Jan. 1, 2025, to present. 

The Fourth Judicial Circuit consists of Butte, Corson, Dewey, Harding, Lawrence, Meade, Perkins and Ziebach counties.

title: SURF mourns passing of T. Denny Sanford
byline: By Mike Ray Sanford Underground Research Facility
description: T. Denny Sanford left shakes hands with then Governor Mike Rounds on the 4850 Level of SURF during a dedication ceremony in June of 2009. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Sanford-Rounds-2009-Governors Corner.png
T. Denny Sanford left shakes hands with then Governor Mike Rounds on the 4850 Level of SURF during a dedication ceremony in June of 2009. Courtesy photo 

LEAD — The generosity and vision of T. Denny Sanford helped transform a former gold mine into what is now the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF).

“Our hearts are with Denny Sanford’s family, friends, and all those whose lives he touched. His generosity helped form the foundation that the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) stands on today,” said Mike Headley executive director of the South Dakota Science and Technology Authority and laboratory director at SURF.  “Denny’s legacy continues to inspire world-class research and scientific breakthroughs, alongside the expanded opportunities for tens of thousands of students inspired by SURF’s education and outreach activities each year. We are forever grateful for his incredible generosity.”

In 2004, after the closure of the Homestake Gold Mine, the state legislature created the South Dakota Science and Technology Authority (SDSTA) to secure the site as a viable location for future science. The leadership of then-Gov. Mike Rounds, alongside T. Denny Sanford’s $70-million gift, helped solidify the site selection and proved critical in the creation of America’s underground laboratory in Lead.  

“Denny Sanford loved life. He celebrated it with passion, commitment, and his strong financial support for the causes that he dreamed would improve people’s lives,” said Casey Peterson,  SDSTA charter member and board chair. “He improved rural communities and children’s health, education and outreach for STEM, and world-class research at the Sanford Underground Research Facility, as well as many others. I remember his big smiles and the “thumbs up” when he could see the results of the projects he endorsed. I will miss those celebrations of life with Denny, and his friendship.”

Education was an important component of Denny Sanford’s gift to the facility, and it remains a vital part of SURF’s mission today. The ongoing effort to inspire learning across generations means SURF now reaches more than 20,000 South Dakota students and 400 teachers annually with hands-on science learning and professional development opportunities.  Additionally, the Sanford Lab Homstake Visitor Center sees nearly 60,000 people each year who learn the story of SURF through interactive exhibits and events. 

Ongoing research at SURF will continue well into the 2050s and likely into the next century. Denny believed in what is possible and his legacy will live on through his extraordinary philanthropy and vision to transform healthcare, education, scientific research, and communities across South Dakota and around the world.

STURGIS — The Meade County Sheriff’s Office reported a man took his own life Friday morning while law enforcement officers were make contact with him.

According to the sheriff’s office, at approximately 10:43 a.m., the Spearfish 911 Communications Center received a report of a subject traveling eastbound on Interstate 90 while reportedly holding a firearm. The caller expressed concern for the driver’s welfare.

Shortly thereafter, the South Dakota Highway Patrol located the vehicle traveling eastbound on I-90. An attempt to conduct a traffic stop was unsuccessful as the driver continued into Sturgis. The vehicle exited the interstate and entered the parking lot at 2651 Whitewood Service Rd.

According to a prepared statement, neither agency typically issue press releases regarding suicide-related incidents. However, because this event occurred in a highly public setting and generated significant public concern, they believe it is appropriate to provide accurate information to the community.

This incident is a tragic reminder that mental health struggles can affect anyone. If you or someone you know is struggling with depression, emotional distress, or thoughts of suicide, help is available. Call or text 988 to reach the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline. Trained counselors are available 24 hours a day, 7 days a week. You do not have to face these challenges alone.

title: Judge temporarily blocks SD’s abortion-pill advertising ban as lawsuit continues
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Mayday Health posted signs like this one at gas stations around South Dakota in December 2025 as part of a campaign to spread awareness about the availability of abortion pills. Courtesy of Mayday Health
_full_text:
Judge temporarily blocks SD abortion-pill advertising ban as lawsuit continues.jpg
Mayday Health posted signs like this one at gas stations around South Dakota in December 2025 as part of a campaign to spread awareness about the availability of abortion pills. Courtesy of Mayday Health 

PIERRE — A new South Dakota law that criminalizes the advertising of abortion pills cannot be enforced while a lawsuit against it continues, a federal judge ruled Friday.

Nancy Turbak Berry, who formerly served as a Democratic state legislator from Watertown, and New York-based nonprofit Mayday Health filed the lawsuit in May against Gov. Larry Rhoden and Attorney General Marty Jackley, who are both Republicans. Rhoden signed the legislation in March after legislators approved it, but it wasn’t scheduled to take effect until this month.

South Dakota already had a near-total ban on abortion, except when it’s necessary “to preserve the life of the pregnant female.”

The new law prohibits the dispensing, distribution and advertising of abortion pills and other abortion-related items, and makes violations punishable by felony prosecutions and fines.

Mayday Health and Turbak Berry say the law illegally restricts Turbak Berry’s free speech. As an example, the lawsuit says the prohibition on advertising would prevent her from wearing a sweatshirt sold by Mayday. The sweatshirt says abortion pills can be obtained in all 50 states and encourages people to learn more on Mayday’s website.

“Unless this court grants relief, Turbak will be deterred from wearing the sweatshirt,” and thereby deterred from engaging in First Amendment-protected speech, the lawsuit says.

Mayday also posted advertisements at South Dakota gas stations last year directing people to the organization’s website for information on abortion pills.

Jackley said during a hearing in Rapid City last month that the state is not attempting to criminalize the wearing of a sweatshirt. He said the state is targeting the way Mayday uses its website to connect South Dakotans with abortion-pill providers, which he said is not legal in a state that bans abortion.

“What the First Amendment doesn’t do is protect an illegal drug transaction in South Dakota,” he said.

A Mayday official said during the same hearing that the organization only provides information and does not encourage anyone to obtain abortion pills.

Judge Camela Theeler wrote in her ruling that the state’s lawyers have “not shown that Mayday advertises with the specific intent that another person engage in specific criminal conduct and thus have not shown that Mayday’s advertising is integral to criminal conduct.”

Mayday and Turbak Berry, along with their lawyer, Jim Leach, of Rapid City, will now seek a permanent order blocking the law’s enforcement.

Jackley issued a statement saying the state will continue to defend the new law.

“Protecting and defending innocent life is and remains important to our Legislature, governor, attorney general and citizens,” Jackley said.

title: GF&P denies petition to allow nonresident lion hunting
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: A lack of population estimates and general opposition toward the practice prompted the GF&P to deny a petition to allow non-resident mountain lion hunting. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Mountain lion.JPG
A lack of population estimates and general opposition toward the practice prompted the GF&P to deny a petition to allow non-resident mountain lion hunting. Pioneer file photo 

WEBSTER — General public opposition and the fact that South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks officials are still working through harvest information to determine mountain lion populations prompted the GF&P Commission to deny a recent petition to issue non-resident mountain lion tags. 

Jason Clayton, a former Vermillion resident who moved to Oklahoma, petitioned the GF&P to allow for non-resident mountain lion licenses for boot hunting. He suggested the GF&P issue non-resident hunters 5% of the tags sold. There is no limit on the number of resident licenses sold. There were 3,000 resident tags sold for the 2024-2025 season, so that would equate to about 150 nonresident tags. With a resident boot hunter success rate of 2-4%, he said that would only raise the mountain lion harvest by about 3 to 6 cats per year. 

The state sets a mountain lion harvest limit of 60 total lions, with a maximum of 40 females, and Clayton said the last time that limit was met was in 2008, as the season closes each year April 30. 

“I understand it’s a limit, not a quota,” Clayton said. “But even if all those 6 lions taken were female, it would not have closed any season or impacted the ability of any resident to hunt. Personally, knowing what it’s like to not live in the Black Hills and have the ability to take the time and scout and do the things you need to do in order to be a really effective lion hunter, I feel like the nonresident success rate will be much lower. Using historical data, the risk to impacting the hunting opportunities for residents by my proposal is very low.” 

But during the commission’s open forum section of the meeting, when residents are invited to make public comment, several residents opposed the petition. 

“The individual that put in the petition used to be a resident,” said Dana Rogers, executive director of the South Dakota Wildlife Federation. “When you leave the state, you kind of know the rules and you know the restrictions and what’s going on. So, residency needs to have its privileges.” 

“To allow out of state hunters to boot hunt mountain lions in the Black Hills is an insult to all residents who have spoken up against the mountain lion season and all the amendments that continue to be added to it,” said Julie Anderson, of Rapid City. “Non-residential hunters should not have a say in South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks rules and regulations.” 

Wildlife Director Tom Kirschenmann said public opinion surveys issued in 2024, when the department was working on its mountain lion management plan, indicated that 57% of Black Hills residents and 68% of hunters opposed nonresident lion hunting. Furthermore, he said, it’s premature to make changes to the lion season, since the department is still working to determine population numbers after the 2026 season. 

Following some discussion, the GF&P Commission voted to deny the petition.

title: Restoration artists craft ‘the next phase of history’ in the SD Capitol rotunda
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Restoration artist and foreman Philip Atilano, of Conrad Schmitt Studios, lines up a stencil at the apex of the dome of the State Capitol building during restoration work on July 7. Photo by Meghan O’Brien, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Restoration artists craft ‘the next phase of history’ in the SD Capitol rotunda.jpg
Restoration artist and foreman Philip Atilano, of Conrad Schmitt Studios, lines up a stencil at the apex of the dome of the State Capitol building during restoration work on July 7. Photo by Meghan O’Brien, South Dakota Searchlight 

 Restoration artists craft ‘the next phase of history’ in the SD Capitol rotunda 2.png
Painter Alyssa Johnson applies a coat of gold paint to capitals on columns above the grad staircase in the State Capitol. Photo by Meghan O’Brien, South Dakota Searchlight 

PIERRE — While tour groups, state employees and lawmakers make their way around scaffolding on the second floor of the South Dakota Capitol building, artists including Philip Atilano climb around at nearly 100 feet above — painting, measuring and working to restore the rotunda and dome to its former beauty.

“It’s a humbling experience. It’s almost like we’re the next phase of history,” Atilano said.

But with years of experience under his belt as a professional restorer for Conrad Schmitt Studios in Wisconsin, Atilano said he’s not nervous or stressed about caring for such a historic structure.

“I look at it like we’re here because we should be here,” he said.

Since 2019, South Dakota lawmakers have provided $13 million for Capitol projects including the dredging of Capitol Lake, repairs of cracking plaster, the ongoing paint restoration work, and the creation of a fund to save for a full restoration and renovation that could cost at least $150 million. That rough estimate came from the Bureau of Human Resources and Administration, which is responsible for maintaining the Capitol.

The last full restoration was conducted ahead of the 1989 state centennial, nearly 40 years ago. Construction of the Capitol was completed 116 years ago in 1910.

Recent cracking and damage to ceilings and walls pushed state officials to take a closer look at the building’s needs. That search revealed outdated utilities, like the building’s climate control system, said Leah Haugan, who oversees special projects for the bureau.

“If you go down in the basement, you’ll see that the utilities that run through the ceilings on the basement levels are the utilities that have been here since the beginning,” she said. “We just keep disconnecting those and adding more, so there’s a whole lot of things that need to be updated and repaired.”

That’s why some of the earliest work is in the rotunda, where there aren’t any utilities to repair before painting, Haugan said.

Current restoration work: Like ‘night and day’

Annually from January through March, the Capitol is buzzing with activity as state lawmakers debate policy, lobbyists linger in the halls and stakeholders testify on legislation. After the legislative session wraps, state employees, other elected officials and visitors still use the building on a daily basis.

That’s important to keep in mind for Darin Seeley, the commissioner of the bureau.

“It was designed, in many parts of the Capitol, for how work was done 120 years ago,” he said. “This is both a historic piece and an operating facility.”

Last year, heavy rains and leaks in the ceiling left plaster around galleries and chambers cracked and damaged. That and other aging plaster has since been repaired.

Wall paint, decorative details, and artwork have faded, and lighting has become less visually appealing over time, too. That’s where Atilano’s team comes in.

“It was so dark and dreary in here, initially, for a rotunda. It just didn’t scream ‘state Capitol’ as much as it will now,” Atilano said. “What we’re doing now, it’s going to blow people’s minds. I think people that were used to it before, now they’re going to see it, and I think it’s going to be night and day.”

The first phase of the current restoration work was to repair plaster. The second stage was restoring the painted details along the ceiling of some of the hallways throughout the building.

Now, Atilano’s team is painting the ornamental pieces that cap the columns — called capitals — in the rotunda. It’s a four-step process, said painter Alyssa Johnson: a base coat, followed by a gold coat of paint, staining, then 23-karat gold leaf on the tips of the capitals “for a little extra pizzazz and sparkle,” she said.

“The techniques haven’t really changed. We’re doing the same stuff that was done hundreds of years ago,” Johnson said while working on a platform in the rotunda. “This is like taking that tradition, and feeling like I’m part of this longer flow of art.”

This is Johnson’s first time working on a restoration project that isn’t a church, she said, but there are a lot of similar elements like stained glass, mural work, arches and other decorative elements. Usually, though, the churches are shut down during restorations.

“I’m working right at the level people are walking by, and I almost felt like a zoo animal a little bit, but it was fun,” she joked. “I’ve never had an audience like that before.”

Atilano has been working on the stenciling for painted details near the peak of the rotunda, 96 feet above the floor.

He and his crew have added paint that, from afar, appears to be petrified wood. Greens, browns and reds blend and swirl over columns along the upper rotunda to create the illusion for visitors below. He was also placing stencils that, when painted, will look more like plasterwork than paint.

“I think people are really going to be able to sit in the center of the rotunda, look up and see something that they never saw was here before,” Atilano said. “I think everything will be much more inviting, warm and welcoming.”

The third stage of restoration will bring legislators and members of the judicial and executive branches together to better understand the needs of each group. It’s a large undertaking, Seeley said.

“When you come at it and think about what needs to be done, it’s why the planning has to happen,” Seeley said, “why it’s so critical that we come at this with a full plan in mind, and not piecemealing the building and its renovation.”

The 1989 restoration, including Sharpies

During the restoration ahead of the 1989 statehood centennial, minimum-security inmates had a hand in some aspects of the project, Haugan said. It helped the state save on labor costs.

“They’re very talented artists that were there, and they came and they did beautiful work, and we don’t want to diminish the work that they did by re-restoring it,” she said. “We just would like it to be historically correct.”

Johnson saw signs from that earlier work, including artwork stenciled using permanent markers.

“Nothing wrong with Sharpie,” Johnson said. “I just wouldn’t put it on a state Capitol building. “It seems a little bit irreverent, but it’s obviously held up well, because it’s as old as I am — that work was done about the same time I was born.”

She also found initials carved into a capital — an ornate piece at the top of a column — as she painted it.

“That’s kind of another tradition, is people either leaving little Easter eggs or initials or drawings, but in a spot where only another worker will ever see it,” she said.

Johnson plans to leave her mark with new layers of paint rather than a signature.

“Those things accumulate over time, and they just kind of add character,” she said. “It’s just part of its history now.”

title: Tinton Road complete, Lawrence Co. to continue maintenance
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — Work to improve a 3.9 mile stretch of Tinton Road has been completed, bringing a 5-year-long project to an end.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — Work to improve a 3.9 mile stretch of Tinton Road has been completed, bringing a 5-year-long project to an end. 

John Bey, Lawrence County highway superintendent, said his predecessor, Allan Bonnema, and then-supervisor of the Hills Ranger District Brandon Taglioli, set out to get a section of Tinton Road repaired nearly 5 years ago. The project came to fruition in April, when the Forest Service granted the county a $5,000 grant to resurface 3.9 miles of the road. 

The section of the road, stretching from where county maintenance ends near the intersection of Tinton and McGuigan roads and traveling south to Aspen Hills Road, has had the center of the road re-established, trees removed to create clear zones and improve sight distance, newly established drainage, uncovered and new culverts, 4 inches of gravel, and stabilizing treatments of magnesium chloride. 

Bey said 2 housing developments in the area have increased traffic counts in the area, necessitating safer roads for residents in the area. He said the because the Forest Service contracted with the county, an easement will allow the county to maintain the road into the future. 

Bey said the county received the $500,000 payment from the Forest Service July 14. He said the county was responsible for 20%, or $100,000, of the project costs.

“The grant covered all the expenses that the county incurred, aside from labor and overhead,” said Bey. “A person could make the argument that the county already paid for labor because we’d have to pay our guys whether they were working on this project or somewhere else.”

Bey said the project has received positive feedback from residents and drivers on their way to Iron Creek Lake.

title: State leaders mourn loss  of ‘greatest philanthropist in  SD history’
byline: By South Dakota Searchlight staff
description: Billionaire philanthropist T. Denny Sanford died Saturday at 90. Photo courtesy of First Premier Bank, Premier Bankcard and Sanford Health
_full_text:
State leaders mourn loss  of ‘greatest philanthropist in  SD history’
Billionaire philanthropist T. Denny Sanford died Saturday at 90. Photo courtesy of First Premier Bank, Premier Bankcard and Sanford Health 

SIOUX FALLS —Gov. Larry Rhoden said this weekend that the state “will forever be impacted” by the legacy of businessman and philanthropist T. Denny Sanford.

Rhoden issued his comments after First Premier Bank, Premier Bankcard and Sanford Health announced on Saturday that Sanford, age 90, had died. He owned the two companies and became the namesake of Sanford Health — formerly called Sioux Valley — in 2007 when he donated $400 million to the organization.

Sanford’s total philanthropic contributions to numerous organizations in South Dakota and elsewhere totaled more than $4 billion.

“It is with great sadness that Sandy and I mourn the loss of T. Denny – a man who has so generously and intentionally invested in the great state of South Dakota,” Rhoden said in a news release. “His contributions will not be forgotten, and South Dakota will forever be impacted by his legacy. Put simply, he was the greatest philanthropist in South Dakota history.”

Sanford’s major donations in South Dakota included support for the Sanford Underground Laboratory at the former Homestake Mine in Lead, the Build Dakota and Premier/Freedom scholarships, the Sioux Falls Development Foundation’s future redevelopment of the downtown Smithfield pork plant site, Children’s Home Society of South Dakota, and Crazy Horse Memorial, among others.

“Denny Sanford was a significant donor to practically every charitable campaign in Sioux Falls, and many others throughout the state,” said Lt. Governor Tony Venhuizen. “Beyond his high-profile gifts, Denny was a key reason that Sioux Falls has such a strong culture of philanthropy, and many important community improvements benefited from his support.”

Sanford was born Dec. 23, 1935, in St. Paul, Minnesota. He lost his mother to breast cancer when he was 4, and he began working at his father’s garment shop at the age of 8. After graduating from the University of Minnesota in 1958 with a degree in psychology, he began a career in sales, marketing and materials distribution. His experiences led him to establish Contech Inc., a Minneapolis-based company that manufactured sealants, coatings and adhesives.

After selling the company, he purchased a bank in Sioux Falls in 1986. He renamed it First Premier Bank and expanded into the credit card sector with Premier Bankcard. The success of those businesses made Sanford a billionaire and allowed him to focus on philanthropy.

First Premier Bank, Premier Bankcard and Sanford Health issued joint statements on Sanford’s death. Dana Dykhouse, CEO of First Premier Bank, said Sanford told him “many people live a life of success, but you should try to live a life of significance where you can make an impact on people.” Miles Beacom, CEO of Premier Bankcard, said Sanford “could have done many things with his money, yet he reinvested it in South Dakota.”

“Our universities are stronger today because of Denny,” Beacom said. “Our health care is stronger today because of Denny. He believed in working harder to help someone other than yourself.”

Bill Gassen, president and CEO of Sanford Health, described Sanford as a “driving force in modern medicine, empowering researchers and clinicians to think big and pursue bold, innovative endeavors at a pace not otherwise possible.”

“We are able to provide care for more patients in their time of need because of his generosity,” Gassen said.

Sanford, who was twice divorced, is survived by his sons Scott and Bill, their wives, three grandchildren, and a brother, Charles “Chuck” Sanford and his wife.

Arrangements for a family service followed by a community celebration are pending.

title: Spearfish city council to consider opening bids for liquor licenses amid growing interest
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Liquor License Availability.JPG
Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — It’s been 6 months since the city of Spearfish took bids for its one available on-sale liquor license, but tonight, the council is set to consider launching the process again.

That “bar license” has a minimum bid price of $300,000. The city also has 2 available off-sale (package) liquor licenses, available for a minimum bid price of $100,000. Those are prices current license holders say are too low, and prospective license holders say are too high — according to Spearfish Finance Officer Michelle DeNeui.

“So, I think we found an equitable range to where we are diluting the market too much for those that currently hold the licenses, but also not charging too much. I think we are keeping a good rate with those,” DeNeui said.

She said in the past 6 months there has been growing interest from business owners in bidding — particularly on the off-sale licenses. DeNeui also believes the city may be poised to sell another restaurant liquor license before the calendar year is up.

“Those are set at a rate of $130,000. They do have to comply with having 60% of their revenue coming from the sale of food or non-alcoholic beverages,” DeNeui said. “They have to report annually on that, but they are transferable.”

DeNeui said part of the reason why the city still has the bar license available is that many of the applicants interested in that license are eligible for the less pricey, and much more available restaurant version.

“That restaurant one is not limited by population?” Councilman Scott Hourigan asked.

“No. That is unlimited. It could be limited by your action on the council,” DeNeui said. “We have no limit on them; we just have the fee set at $130,000.”

DeNeui said some Spearfish restaurants already hold a full bar license.

“They can sell that liquor license and buy the restaurant license, and they could actually walk away with $170,000 profit,” DeNeui said.

Neither the off-sale license nor the on-sale license can be purchased outright. Both are subject to a sealed bidding process — which could be initiated by action from the city council in the near future.

title: Fires spark in Northern Hills
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: A structure fire was reported just outside of Deadwood Friday.
_full_text:
Deadwood fire.jpg
A structure fire was reported just outside of Deadwood Friday.  

 Oliver st fire.jpg
Firefighters responded to a grassfire along Oliver Street in Spearfish Sunday afternoon. Photo courtesy of Spearfish Fire Department 

SPEARFISH — Fire departments in the Northern Hills responded to multiple fires this weekend.

According to the Deadwood Fire Department, just after 6:20 a.m. Saturday Deadwood firefighters responded to a report of a house on fire just outside of Deadwood on US Highway 14A. 

First arriving units found a fully involved structure fire with the nearby grass surrounding the structure also ablaze. Officers immediately requested the assistance of Lead and Spearfish fire departments and requested assistance from South Dakota Wildland Fire due to the proximity of a significant hay field, approximately 15 feet away. 

Crews fought the fire for about 2 hours before returning to quarters. 

At approximately 10:16 a.m. Deadwood Fire Rescue was again paged to the same address for a rekindled fire that was again fully involved. 

First arriving units found a fully involved structure fire. Deadwood Hawk 1 initiated an attack with the bumper mounted turret, until Engine 1 arrived on scene. 

Due to water supply issues, Lead Fire Department’s assistance was again requested for a tender and manpower. 

Firefighters again entered the structure and fought the fire for an additional 2 hours pulling walls and ceiling to expose any fire. 

Fire officials said the fire was particularly tough to fight due to sawdust being used in the interior walls as insulation. 

There were no injuries to civilians, animals, or firefighters. 

Responding agencies included Deadwood, Lead, and Spearfish fire departments, South Dakota Wildland Fire, Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office Lead Deadwood Ambulance Lawrence County Emergency Management, and Black Hills Energy 

Grass fire in Spearfish

At 1:30 p.m., Sunday the Spearfish Fire Department was paged out for a report of a grass fire in the area south of Oliver Street. 

According to the department, upon arrival firefighters began to attack the fire, stopping forward progress in short order. South Dakota Wildland Fire, Whitewood Volunteer Fire Department, and Deadwood Volunteer Fire Department, also responded to assist with suppression efforts. 

The fire was contained to approximately 1.1 acres and the cause is being investigated by South Dakota State Wildland Fire. 

Also on scene were Spearfish Police Department, Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office, Spearfish Emergency Ambulance Service, and Lawrence County Office of Emergency Management.

title: Alec Baldwin wins  Spearfish Canyon Half Marathon
byline: By Jason Gross Black Hills Pioneer
description: Ty Petrocco, Lane Krautschun, and Alec Baldwin set the pace during the 13.1-mile half marathon race Saturday morning. Baldwin emerged as the champion, followed by Petrocco and Krautschun. Pioneer photo by Jason Gross
_full_text:
Spearfish 1.JPG
Ty Petrocco, Lane Krautschun, and Alec Baldwin set the pace during the 13.1-mile half marathon race Saturday morning. Baldwin emerged as the champion, followed by Petrocco and Krautschun. Pioneer photo by Jason Gross 

SPEARFISH — Alec Baldwin returned to a familiar course Saturday and captured the Spearfish Canyon Half Marathon title in 1 hour, 8 minutes and 50 seconds for the 13.1-mile race.

The Denver, Colo., resident and 2016 Black Hills State University graduate said the course treated him well today.

“Thankfully, it was cool towards the top near the lodge,” Baldwin said of the race that began at 7 a.m. from Savoy. “It warmed up pretty quick.”

Saturday marked the third time Baldwin has run this race, so he generally knows what to expect. He described the course as a generous but gradual downhill.

Many things keep Baldwin returning to this event.

“I love the Black Hills,” he said. “My parents live here in Spearfish; my mom is actually running today.” 

 Spearfish 5.JPG
Numerous runners wear costumes during the race. Pioneer photo by Jason Gross 

 Spearfish 6.JPG
Some spectators at Saturday’s race arrived with the essentials. This Pennington County vehicle bore signs of support for friends and family members. Pioneer photo by Jason Gross 

Baldwin wanted the secure the individual title and did so. His strategy centered on running with some Black Hills-area athletes and trying to run away from them if he felt good.

“It feels really good to conquer the course with the heat we had today,” Baldwin said. He wanted to run a similar time to past races, and his start was more gradual.

He trains with Good Boys Denver, which is a running club featuring many post-collegiate runners.

Baldwin was asked what keeps him running and said it is a lifestyle. 

“Every time I quit, I find myself coming back to it,” Baldwin said. “It keeps me at my normal state.”

Baldwin’s future plans include running the New York City Marathon for the first time this November. He said he would like to better his personal 26.2-mile record of 2 hours, 15 minutes and 36 seconds.

Valerija Curikova emerged as the women’s half-marathon champion in 1 hour, 24 minutes and 27 seconds. She is a resident of Riga, Latvia.

Rapid City’s Lionel Hinosn claimed the Heroes 5-Kilometer Run/Walk crown in 16 minutes 36.5 seconds. Peyton VanDeest of Spearfish was the female winner in 17:58.3.

title: Explanation of unspent social services money makes some lawmakers celebratory, others concerned
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: The Interim Committee on Appropriations meets at the South Dakota State Capitol in Pierre Monday. Photo by Meghan O’Brien, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Explanation of unspent social services money makes some lawmakers celebratory, others concerned.jpg
The Interim Committee on Appropriations meets at the South Dakota State Capitol in Pierre Monday. Photo by Meghan O’Brien, South Dakota Searchlight 

PIERRE — South Dakota’s top state budget official offered further explanations Monday for the $39 million that state departments left unspent during the recently completed fiscal year, eliciting both praise and concerns from lawmakers.

The fiscal year ended June 30. The Department of Social Services had the biggest budget reversion, returning $32 million.

Jim Terwilliger, commissioner of the state’s Bureau of Finance and Management, told a committee of state lawmakers that the size of the department’s reversion shouldn’t be “a surprise, because it’s the one area in the state budget that is a lot less predictable.”

“There’s only 2 sides of the coin,” he said. “That you have enough funds to get you through, or you’re going to be short.”

Unused funds from state departments made up more than half of the $69 million budget surplus that Gov. Larry Rhoden announced last week. The state also collected $30 million more than its budgeted revenue, $17 million of which came from higher-than-projected sales tax revenue. The surplus went into the state’s reserve funds and “will be available for one-time investments in future budget years,” the governor said.

Department of Social Services reversions

The Department of Social Services’ $32 million of reversions came from a $1.8 billion departmental budget. The department manages programs such as Medicaid, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program and Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, among others. About $654 million of its budget was from state funding sources, with most of the remainder coming from the federal government.

The department’s largest category of unspent funds was in medical services, which includes Medicaid, the joint federal-state program that helps pay for healthcare for low-income people of any age. There were $12.5 million of medical services reversions.

“We’re trying to predict how many people come to the hospital with various acute conditions and so on and so forth,” Terwilliger said. “So, it’s not something that’s easy to predict going forward.”

Medicaid enrollment declined by 968 people, from 143,743 at the start of the fiscal year last July to 142,775 last month.

Lower use of substance use disorder programming and mental health treatment services resulted partially from fewer staff to provide treatment, Terwilliger said. In particular, the Human Services Center, a facility in Yankton dedicated to providing treatment for substance use disorder and mental health, has struggled to hire personnel.

Terwilliger also credited the department’s launch of a program called BEES — the Beneficiary Eligibility and Enrollment System — in 2024, which screens applicants for their eligibility for medical eligibility programs.

Some lawmakers were pleased with the returned funds, including Sen. Taffy Howard, R-Rapid City.

“These are all welfare services, so lower utilization should be cause to celebrate,” she said. “And I hope we aren’t looking for ways to increase utilization just because we happen to have some reversions.”

Sen. Red Dawn Foster, D-Pine Ridge, said she agreed with Howard’s comments, “but I think that the services that we do provide, we want to make sure that there’s a pathway to self-sufficiency and not just attrition.”

Foster also asked if the launch of BEES is causing people to be eliminated from programs. Terwilliger did not provide further information but said “it’s something we can certainly look at.”

Current-year revenue

Legislators received varying predictions Monday about how revenue will fare during the current fiscal year, which began July 1.

Derek Johnson, state economist with the bureau, estimated revenue will be 0.34% higher than originally estimated, resulting in $8.7 million more than lawmakers planned for when they approved the budget in March. Johnson works for the governor in the executive branch.

The state collected $17 million more in sales and use tax during the recently ended fiscal year than predicted, and collections were 6.6% higher than the previous fiscal year. Johnson is projecting continued growth.

Jeff Mehlhaff, who works for lawmakers as interim director of the Legislative Research Council, is also considering last year’s sales tax growth. But he views it as a reason to be conservative.

“I just didn’t expect that much growth, which leads me to pause a little bit,” he said. “Typically when you have a high growth year like that, where you exceed your expectations, the next year usually produces a below average return.”

Mehlhaff predicted this fiscal year’s revenues will be 0.5% lower than estimated, resulting in $13.3 million less than planned.

title: Learning as a lifelong pursuit
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Erica Schumacher, Program manager of education and workforce developement at BHSCC
_full_text:
Erika Schumacher.jpg
Erica Schumacher, Program manager of education and workforce developement at BHSCC 

DEADWOOD — Learning can be a lifelong pursuit, and the Black Hills Special Services Cooperative (BHSCC) is working to make that a reality for people in the Northern Hills.

Twice a year, residents in the Northern Hills receive a newspaper detailing classes adults can take ranging from square dancing to paper making. Because they believe that learning doesn’t end when high school’s over, BHSCC is putting out a call for more instructors to join their division of community education. 

Erika Schumacher, program manager for education and workforce development, said that the goal at BHSCC is to promote lifelong learning by offering classes that encourages continuing education for all walks of life. 

“We offer classes from Medicare (education) to drawing classes,” said Schumacher. “So, a wide variety of classes that can help anybody either learn something new or even something essential that might help them when they’re looking for a job.”

 learning as a lifelong pursuit.jpg
Students practice their skills at a line dancing class offered by the community education department of Black Hills Special Services Cooperative. The class is one of the many diverse learning opportunities offered by the cooperative. Photo courtesy of Black Hills Special Services Cooperative 

Schumacher said that recently, BHSCC has focused on trying to expand their offerings in the communities west of Rapid City. In Belle Fourche, they offer classes in woodworking, welding, and heavy equipment operation. In Sturgis, offerings include cookie decorating, crochet bootcamp, and a cooking class led by a group of sheep farmers that teach students how to cook dishes with lamb. In Lead, one woman teaches paper making, book making, and stained glass. The classes are the beginning of what the cooperative hopes to grow into a robust community service. In order for that to work, though, they need more instructors. 

“To be honest, the possibilities (for instructors) are endless,” said Schumacher. “There are only 2 categories that we really stay away from, and that’s religion and politics. So, we can have anything anybody has a passion for — fly fishing, canoeing, sailing. We can do any outdoor activity and any indoor activity.”

Schumacher said that historically, the classes have been between one and 2 hours long, with classes starting at $20 to attend. Some classes, like the welding and heavy equipment classes offered in Belle Fourche, meet weekly for 10 weeks and cost $425.

“Obviously you’re going to get more out of those classes, though,” said Schumacher. “We’re beginning to offer dual credits. Jim (Hartwell, instructor) is going to do an intro to (computer-aided design), and he’s going to offer credits through the University of Sioux Falls. So, the students can pay a low rate for the credit and actually get something out of it and potentially move up in their job or even have better luck looking for a job.” 

Schumacher said class size also varies depending on instructor’s personal comfort. A silversmithing class in Spearfish only allows for 2 students per session, but a Medicare class can accommodate as many as 30 students. 

“It depends on the instructor and how they see the class going and how comfortable they are teaching. It varies from year to year,” said Schumacher. “This fall an instructor (could) do 2 classes with 10 people, and then the next fall they’ll do 5 classes with 30 people because they gain that confidence as they teach from year to year.”

Facilities for classes can be a bit trickier, said Schumacher. BHSCC partners with the chamber of commerce in some communities, who allow them to use rooms in their buildings to help keep costs lower. Welding and woodworking shops are held in Belle Fourche are held at the Belle Fourche High School, where the equipment already exists in a safely controlled space perfect for education. Schumacher said she’s happy to help potential instructors try to find a space that could work for their class.

People interested in taking a class or becoming an instructor can reach out to Schumacher via email at ESchumacher@bhssc.org.

title: Northern Hills Community Band beats the heat  with summer concert at Harley-Davidson Rally Point
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: The 65-member Northern Hills Community Band performing a concert on Sunday at Harley-Davidson Rally Point. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
Northern Hills Community Band beats the heat  with summer concert at Harley-Davidson Rally Point
The 65-member Northern Hills Community Band performing a concert on Sunday at Harley-Davidson Rally Point. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

STURGIS — Triple-digit temperatures did little to slow the Northern Hills Community Band as the 65-member ensemble entertained a crowd Sunday evening with a lively performance at the Harley-Davidson Rally Point in downtown Sturgis.

With temperatures hovering near 100 degrees, the musicians matched the summer heat with a spirited program featuring marches, movie themes and concert favorites. The audience enjoyed nine selections, including “Strike Up the Band,” “El Abanico,” “Golden Dragon,” and other popular works.

Director Dr. Christopher Hahn said the performance marks the beginning of one of the band’s busiest weeks of the summer as it prepares for the annual Days of ‘76 celebration.

“We’re playing some marches and some movie music, and we’re getting ready for our Days of ‘76 program,” Hahn said. “We played in Lead on Friday, we’re here tonight, then Belle Fourche on Wednesday, Deadwood on Thursday, and then the parades and march concerts on Friday and Saturday. It’s gearing up to be a busy week.”

The Northern Hills Community Band includes musicians from throughout the region, representing a wide range of ages and experience levels.

“We are continuing to get a number of young players, which is great,” Hahn said. “We’ve been trying for a long time to make sure we have a wide range of ages, and we’re getting there. We get a lot of support from the area high school band directors who are sending their best students to play with us, and that’s awesome.”

Before introducing the evening’s second selection, Hahn shared some background on the music with the audience.

Adding to the community atmosphere, members of the Sturgis and Meade County Historical Society sold fresh popcorn and bottled water during the concert to raise funds and increase awareness of the organization.  “This is just a way to get the Historical Society’s name out there,” said volunteer Jim Holland. “History Days was very successful, and we just want to keep the name out there and do something nice for the band. They like having us here doing the popcorn.”

The Northern Hills Community Band continues its summer concert series with a performance on Wednesday, July 22, at Herrmann Park in Belle Fourche, before traveling to Deadwood and participating in several Days of ‘76 events later in the week.

title: ‘Minnesela’ opens Thursday in  Belle Fourche
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Belle Fourche Area Community Theater is in rehearsal for ‘Minnesela’ a western opening July 23. Photo courtesy Hunter Anderson Photography
_full_text:
Minnesela 1.jpg
Belle Fourche Area Community Theater is in rehearsal for ‘Minnesela’ a western opening July 23. Photo courtesy Hunter Anderson Photography 

 Minnesela by Sierra.JPG
Derek Olson promotes Minnesela at the Belle Fourche Fourth of July Parade. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

BELLE FOURCHE — Once upon a time, Belle Fourche and Minnesela were adjacent, contemporary communities, wrestling for prominence on the prairie. Belle Fourche, under the patronage of Seth Bullock emerged as the lasting municipality. Minnesela faded from everything but memory. 

This month, the ghost town will serve as the inspiration for a community theater production. The play, “Minnesela” was pinned by Belle Fourche Area Community Theater Executive Director Derek Olson and his father. It’s a western, and a zany adventure, scheduled for a 4-show-run.

“It is about an orphan named Emma Williams from the big city whose favorite book is a book called “Dry Creek,” which is the adventures of a guy named Tom Bragg out in Minnesela,” Olson said. “She is so inspired by his stories that she runs away from the orphanage to go to Minnesela to meet Tom, the author of the book.”

Minnesela opens at the Belle Fourche Rec Center Auditorium Thursday and will have show times daily through Sunday.
