title: Come From Away recalls kindness of America’s northern neighbors
byline: By Mary Garrigan Special to the Pioneer
description: Come From Away runs through Aug. 2 at Theatre 605 in Custer State Park.
_full_text:
Come From Away recalls kindness of America’s northern neighbors 1.JPG
Come From Away runs through Aug. 2 at Theatre 605 in Custer State Park.  

 Come From Away recalls kindness of America’s northern neighbors 2.JPG
Photo courtesy of Lone Tree Productions 

CUSTER STATE PARK — A play about the kindness of Canadians may seem, at first glance, an outlier among this summer’s Black Hills Playhouse season, as Theatre 605 celebrates the 250th birthday of America with a line-up of patriotic themed productions. 

“Come From Away” is the inspiring hit musical based on the true story of the 38 airplanes and their 7,000 passengers from around the world that were diverted to the small town of Gander, Newfoundland, on Sept. 11, 2001, as America closed its airspace to all incoming air traffic. It takes the audience back to the most devastating day of recent U.S. history, and it doesn’t let go of your emotions for the entire one hour and 45 minutes of the show, which has no intermission. 

There is laughter and light-hearted comedy (and a touch of profanity) in the lyrics and lines delivered by the townspeople of Gander as they rush to respond to the need to feed, lodge and find toilet paper for thousands of unexpected guests. It turns out the “plane people,” forced to sequester for countless hours on the grounded planes without knowledge of where they are or why, are among the last people on the planet to learn of the 9/11 attacks. 

But mostly, there are memories of that tragedy.  I was either in tears, or on the verge of tears, as the cast of “Come From Away”  transported me back to a time that put the worst, and the best, of humanity on full display. Don’t miss this play, but don’t forget to bring a tissue with you. 

Rapid City native Megan Gerlach directs the play, and her experience as a dancer and choreographer is evident in how she moves the large cast of 16 actors (portraying characters too numerous to count) around a small stage. The nearly constant musical numbers require the set to transform from the interior of an airplane cabin to a rollicking party at the local Gander bar to a church, a café and much more. All that movement is made possible by scenic designer Kathy Voecks’ puzzle pieces on wheels — platforms, incline ramps and boxes — that instantly become an air traffic control center, a café, a school, buses, airplane interiors or a path in the woods. 

The set is framed by the trunks of aspen trees which are found in the Newfoundland landscape. Aspen groves share a communal root system, said Gerlach, a metaphor for the deep-seated values of community and connection shared by the people who landed in Gander for 5 days in 2001. 

Thanks to nothing more than the subtle wardrobe changes of costume designer Sara Curran Ice, one minute the actors are portraying the quirky, folksy characters of Gander’s city leaders, the next they are 14 air traffic controllers on emergency duty at the airport. 

Throughout the play, they become an amalgamation of 7,000 people from across the globe, many unable to speak English much less able to understand the unique accent and dialect of the Newfoundlanders, who affectionately refer to themselves as “islanders” in the show’s opening song, “Welcome to the Rock.” 

Speaking of accents, I’m still not sure exactly what a Newfoundland accent is, since it ranged from something sort of British, to Fargo, N.D., to a slight Irish brogue, depending on the actor. Maybe it’s all of those. Or maybe it is the signature voice that can only belong to veteran BHP actor Jeff Kingsbury, who plays Claude, the mayor of Gander.  

Actor Lisa Wepperling brings a soft Texas twang to her role as the real-life American Airlines captain Beverly Bass, the first female to ever pilot a plane for that airline. Beverly is the emotional center of the play and Wepperling finds it. Her personal anthem to the love of flying, “Me and the Sky,” is heart-wrenchingly beautiful, especially when she sings, “the one thing I loved more than anything was used as a bomb.”  

You may need a tissue again when Hannah (Maya Lysinger), a mother stranded in Gander while waiting to learn the fate of her New York City firefighter son, sings the Prayer of St. Francis/Make Me A Channel of Your Peace in the round with others. They are joined by a Jewish rabbi (Skyler Weaver) chanting prayers from the Torah, a Muslim man (Rommell Johnson III) seeking a place to pray amid the rampant racism he faces in the aftermath of 9-11, and a chorus of praying Hindi women.  The scene’s unique musical arrangement has both challenging vocal harmonies and a powerful interfaith message. 

Other notable roles include: newbie radio reporter Janice, played with perfect first-day-on-the-job jitters by Magdalen Eberle; the skeptical American Bob, played to humorous effect by Ty Roberson, who eventually warms to the kindness of total strangers; and Bonnie, Gander’s local Humane Society lady, played by Liv Moeller who captures Bonnie in all her adorable, over-the-top, animal-loving wackiness. Audience favorites are Oz, the bumbling local constable (Erik K. Larsen); the ebullient Beulah (Emily Wirkus) and older travelers Diane (Lynne Rothrock) and Nick (Dave DeChristopher), who are a joy to watch and listen to as their love story develops. 

They all share the stage with the band (Patrick Knowles, Lon Schnittgrund, Mike Palmer, Alan Temple, Balie Albrecht and the always excellent music director Vonnie Houchins.)  

There is so much going on, and so much fast-paced conversation, that some of it is occasionally hard to hear. But the message that the good people of Gander will always welcome the world with a candle in the window and a cup of tea for the stranger comes through loud and clear. 

“Come From Away” runs Aug. 2.  Be aware that the play has no intermission and includes some adult language, topics and discussion of the events surrounding 9/11.

title: Lead With Pride event raises $3K for opera house
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Lead With Pride picnic drew about 71 people to enjoy burgers, brats, potluck side dishes, and vendors at Manuel Brothers Park, Saturday. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
Lead With Pride.jpeg
The Lead With Pride picnic drew about 71 people to enjoy burgers, brats, potluck side dishes, and vendors at Manuel Brothers Park, Saturday. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

LEAD — A Lead With Pride event helped raise more than $3,000 for the Historic Homestake Opera House. 

On Saturday, the Flamy Grant concert, held as part of the Lead With Pride events, raised $3,192 from attendees. The amount, co-organizer Levi Wilson said, will go toward purchasing a new soundboard for the opera house. 

Wilson said the concert drew about 98 people to the Historic Homestake Opera House. It was part of a day of activities that included a picnic in the park, and the show. About 71 people attended the picnic, compared to 65 last year. Rain showers likely affected attendance, Wilson said. 

Wilson said he is very happy about the attendance for the second annual event that was organized by Lead With Pride, a local group of LGBTQ+ residents and their supporters. 

“We are trying to intentionally build a sense of community and to do so in a loving, joyful way,” he said. “Throughout the day I and the other organizers had many people thanking us for hosting such a great event and telling us the personal effect it had on them. For some it was the show of support from the community with all the flags on Main Street. For others, Flamy Grant’s storytelling and music deeply resonated. People appreciated that we were raising money for the opera house, and for everyone it was just a joyful, community-centered day.”  

Both events also drew opposition from some people, which prompted the Historic Homestake Opera House to issue reminders about the venue’s non-discrimination policy. The policy states that as a government-funded, nonprofit organization, the opera house provides space for events based upon availability, and does not discriminate on the basis of race, color, ethnicity, national origin, religion, sex, age, disability, political affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, or any other characteristic.

title: High-speed chase results in crash
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: A high-speed pursuit ended when the driver of a white pickup crashed into a tree and rolled, Friday. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Lead wreck.JPG
A high-speed pursuit ended when the driver of a white pickup crashed into a tree and rolled, Friday. Courtesy photo 

LEAD — A high-speed pursuit from Deadwood to Lead, Friday, resulted in a single-vehicle crash with serious injuries, after the driver lost control and hit a tree. 

At about 10:50 p.m., Lead Police Chief Robert Williams said the Lead and Deadwood police departments were involved in the pursuit of a man who was allegedly driving a white pickup recklessly, at a high rate of speed. The pursuit ended when the driver collided with a tree at 414 S. Main St., and rolled the vehicle. 

The 36-year-old man from Rapid City was ejected from the pickup and suffered serious, life threatening injuries. Firefighters and EMS crews from Monument Health Northern Hills Ambulance worked to stabilize the man, who was transported to the hospital by Black Hills Life Flight. 

Williams said charges are pending against the driver, who is alive and expected to recover from his injuries. 

Emergency responders report there was no damage done to the house, except for a mailbox that was knocked over. Crews closed the road for the duration of the incident, and firefighters remained on the scene until 1:55 a.m. 

Agencies that responded to the scene included the Lead Volunteer Fire Department, Monument Health Northern Hills Ambulance, Black Hills Life Flight, Lead Police Department, Deadwood Police Department, Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office, South Dakota Highway Patrol, and Black Hills Energy.

title: More inmates denied early release as more parolees return through crackdown
byline: By John Hult Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Inmates are pictured in the East Hall of the South Dakota State Penitentiary on July 8, 2025. Courtesy of South Dakota Department of Corrections
_full_text:
More inmates denied early release as more parolees return through crackdown.jpg
Inmates are pictured in the East Hall of the South Dakota State Penitentiary on July 8, 2025. Courtesy of South Dakota Department of Corrections 

PIERRE — The number of people granted discretionary parole by the South Dakota Board of Pardons and Paroles has fallen by 17% over the last 2 years, according to data shared at a board meeting Wednesday.

News of the long-term trend came alongside a more recent spike in returns to prison for those already on parole. It also comes on the heels of efforts by legislators to tighten laws on early release, and by law enforcement to capture more people actively avoiding their parole agents. 

Gov. Larry Rhoden initiated a Department of Corrections-led crackdown on parole violations in response to the late April shooting of a police officer in Sioux Falls. A man on parole supervision is charged in that case. 

Rhoden promised more and faster returns to prison for parolees accused of misbehavior like drug or alcohol use, as well as for arrests on certain new criminal charges — regardless of whether the person on parole has been found guilty.

Rhoden also announced that the state would hire more parole agents to backfill the positions of five experienced agents who’d make up an “enhanced compliance unit” designed to offer intensive supervision to the parolees most in need of it and check in with parolees on nights and weekends. 

Last month, parole board staff screened 176 people for potential parole revocation. That’s a slight drop from May, but still represents a notable increase over the number of revocations in the months before Rhoden’s announcement.

Rhoden initially announced the state’s intention to reform parole in early April. The announcement of the new parole unit and declaration that drug use would result in a certain return to prison came at the end of that month.

There were 111 parolees returned to prison in April and 237 in May. Between July 2025 and March of this year, the monthly tally was never greater than 87.

The appointed board does not supervise parole agents, but rather makes decisions based on their supervisory work, in addition to acting as an advisory panel to the governor on requests for pardons and sentence reductions, known as commutations. 

The recently dictated policy shifts have changed both the workload for the part-time board and the way its members talk about parole with the inmates they deal with.

Myron Rau, the board’s chairman, said Wednesday that he’s begun telling potential parolees that “the world has changed,” and that the days of leniency and second chances are over. 

“You sign a document that says ‘I’m not going to drink,’” Rau said. “If they catch you drinking, you’re coming back to prison. All of this stuff is serious now. There’s no more of this ‘it was just marijuana.’” 

Changes coincide with more repeat offenses

The figures for the month of June were presented as a coda to the fiscal year, which ended on June 30 and is used by the Department of Corrections for statistical compilation purposes. 

Discretionary parole represents around a third of all parole cases. The majority of people on parole get their through presumptive parole. Under that system, sentences are trimmed automatically for good behavior and successful completion of individualized self-improvement plans that include things like earning a GED or finishing chemical dependency treatment.

Inmates get their road map to release during their first few weeks in prison, and needn’t ask the parole board to leave unless they stray from the path. 

Inmates who act up or fail to hit the marks are resigned to make a case for early release to two-person parole board panels. If the two members disagree about whether an inmate deserves release, the full nine-member board weighs in. 

In fiscal year 2024, the board granted discretionary parole to 57% of the inmates who asked for it. During fiscal year 2026, which ended two weeks ago, 40% of inmates in discretionary release hearings earned the blessing of the board. 

“You’ve also seen recidivism tracking upwards” said Shelli Gust, the board’s administrator, using a term for the percentage of released inmates who return to prison within three years. “So that makes sense if you’re trying to look at that. That tells me that people aren’t doing very well on parole.”

The spike in revocation hearings is newer, Gust said, but appears to be durable. The number of revocations for July is on pace to match June, she said, which was slightly down from May, the first month of stricter supervision.

More revocations, more work, jail visits

Gust has noticed another trend emerge, as well, she told board members: revocation hearings involving people who’d been on parole for two years or more. 

“It used to be pretty rare to see somebody who had been out more than two years,” Gust said, referring to the names on her list of revocation requests, “and I’ve seen a lot of people in the last two months that have been out for quite a while.”

Gust said she hasn’t “done a case study” to determine why, but said it’s possible that some of the people who’d been out a long time had been violating the terms of their parole and given multiple chances by their parole agents. 

Board member Kurt Hall said parole agents “are buckling down a little more than they did in the past.” Hall is the sheriff of Faulk County, and said he’s noticed that in the day-to-day, parole agents have been easier to find and work with.

“A few years ago, it seemed like the parole agents were just hiding under a rock,” Hall said. “You couldn’t find one. Now, if you reach out and contact a parole agent, they’re very proactive, very helpful.”

Agents recommend revocations for people on parole, but only the board can actually send someone back to prison. In practice, the agents and other parole staff in Gust’s orbit offer recommendations to board members, who meet in special sessions to consider the arguments of people on parole who believe they should not be sent back.

It’s been difficult to keep up with revocations, but Gust said parole staffers have stepped up to meet the swollen demand for their services. Parole staffers have visited jails in Brookings and Ipswich over the past two months to meet with inmates and process violations.

She warned the board to be prepared to see a jump in the number of discretionary parole requests starting around November. Parolees who return to prison often get a chance to make their case for another shot at freedom eight months after their return on a parole violation. 

November “is about 8 months out from when we had that big bump of people,” Gust said.

Long-term trend toward tough enforcement, sanctions

The focus on parole supervision is wrapped up in efforts to improve Corrections Department cooperation with the wider law enforcement community, as well as a push for restrictions on early release at the legislative level.

The day after the parole board meeting, leaders of local, state and federal agencies held a press conference to trumpet the results of a three-day enforcement action spearheaded by the U.S. Marshals Service. The roundup operation, dubbed “Operation Repeat Offender,” led to the apprehension of 35 people wanted on arrest warrants or for ducking their parole agents.

State troopers lent their assistance to the three-day federal effort, but U.S. Marshal Dan Satterlee said Thursday that the campaign was distinct from another branded series of saturation patrols called “Operation Prairie Thunder.” That operation is led by the South Dakota Highway Patrol, with 14 patrols across 11 cities conducted over the past year to target all manner of criminal activity. Those patrols have collectively led to the apprehension of 21 people wanted for losing touch with their parole officers.  

Sioux Falls Police Chief Jon Thum, who’d called for more parolee accountability following the shooting of one of his officers, said parole agents have grown steadily more involved in local policing efforts over the past few years. 

An absconder apprehension unit was first formed in late 2022 works with sheriff deputies and local police, and the number of parolees listed as absconders — meaning they’ve lost touch with their supervising parole agent on purpose — has since plummeted. 

Even as that happened, however, concerns about second chances for apprehended parolees simmered for leaders like Thum in Sioux Falls and Pennington County Sheriff Brian Mueller, who formed a multi-agency parole task force for the Rapid City area earlier this year.

Since the end of April, Thum said, the level of coordination and communication between correctional staff and policing agencies has been remarkable.

“The conversations, the collaborations we’ve seen since April have been, I’ll put it this way, very, very positive,” Thum said. “I’m very encouraged about the momentum and where we’re headed, and I have no reason to believe that’s not going to continue.”

On the legislative side, lawmakers have passed measures to lengthen prison terms and restrict clemency requests.

A bill known colloquially as “truth in sentencing” became law in 2023, and requires people convicted of certain violent crimes to serve between 85 and 100% of their sentences, cutting off inmates imprisoned for crimes like manslaughter, kidnapping, robbery or burglary eligible for early release through good behavior or program completion. 

Another bill passed by the Legislature and signed into law in 2024 requires people serving life sentences to wait four years between requests for commutations, which can shorten a person’s sentence and make them eligible for parole.

title: Local cave explorer receives national recognition
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Cave exploration is one of the last remaining ways for explorers to chart brand new terrestrial territory. That’s why Adam Weaver, pictured, loves all things speleological. Photo courtesy Adam Weaver
_full_text:
Adam Weaver.jpg
Cave exploration is one of the last remaining ways for explorers to chart brand new terrestrial territory. That’s why Adam Weaver, pictured, loves all things speleological. Photo courtesy Adam Weaver 

SPEARFISH — On this planet, at least, caves are the final frontier. Without plunging deep into the recesses of the ocean, there is no other way to truly tread through never-before-seen tracts of land.

It is the potential for discovery, and the physical challenge, that first drew Adam Weaver to caving.

“Cave exploration is the last thing on our planet that you can do where you can find new places,” Weaver said. “We have found many, many, many miles of new things: giant rooms and lakes and all kinds of things that we are discovering, and there is no other way to discover them without going.”

This month, Weaver received the National Speleological Society (NSS) Lew Bicking Award — one of the highest honors in American speleology. The Lew Bicking Award honors the achievement of cave explorers, surveyors, and expedition leaders.

He led the expedition that mapped the 200th mile of Jewel Cave in 2018. In 2019, Weaver set the record for the most cave discovered in a single day — 2.34 miles. In 2022, in Fort Stanton Cave, Weaver set the record for the most cave traversed in a single trip and the farthest point ever reached from a cave entrance after having traveled more than 13 miles from daylight.

“We go, and we try to go as far as we can and map as much as we can until you basically run out of time because you only have so much time in the cave every trip. Then we leave, and we have our data in our pocket basically. Then we come back, and we process that data and we make the map,” Weaver said. “These maps are, you know, very accurate. We use lasers to map the caves. Then we start again, and we say, ‘okay, that’s what we found, that’s how it looks with the rest of the cave that was already there, and we can decide where we’re going to go next time.’”

In earning the Lew Bicking Award, Weaver joined the ranks of celebrated cavers, speleonking legends like Herb and Jan Conn. The Conns discovered 65 miles of Jewel Cave, including the areas that visitors experience during the Scenic and Discovery Tours offered by the Black Hills national monument. They received the award in 1975. 2020 recipient Renee Ohms is another South Dakota explorer to earn the accolade.

“She’s the person who gives out the award. So, I get to get it from Renee, which is cool because she is the other person now from South Dakota that is active that has it,” Weaver said. He lives in the Hills and works as the business manager for Black Hills Institute in Hill City.

“It’s a pretty crazy thing. I am one of the youngest people that has gotten in it in a long time, and a lot of legends have gotten it,” Weaver said. “In the caving world, there are people that, you know, no caver is famous, but there are people that are really well known in the science and the sport. A lot of them have it. It is kind of exciting to be, you know, one of those people, I suppose.”

The work Weaver has done is featured on the maps of Jewel Cave National Monument available in the gift shop.

“They maintain the map. We make the map, and then we give it to them. If you go to Jewel Cave, it is up on the wall, or they sell copies in the gift shop that people can buy if they just want the map,” Weaver said. “We use it for navigation in the cave, right? We are using it like actively, because the caves in the Black Hills are maze caves.”

It is fitting that Weaver made his mark on the history of Jewel Cave by helping to chart new territory. It was Jewel Cave that first captured his imagination, and sent his imagination careening deeper and deeper underground.

“I was in the Air Force here in the Black Hills, and when you’re in the Air Force you can take any college class you want, so I took some random college classes at Black Hills State. I was driving to Spearfish for them, and I joined the outdoor club,” Weaver said. “Then the very first trip the outdoor club went on was a caving trip, and I went, and I was like, ‘Oh, this is amazing.’”

Many of the caves in the Black Hills are “maze caves.” Weaver described Wind Cave, for example, as a 5-story, 3-dimensional maze.

“What got me excited about that was it was like an obstacle course,” Weaver said.

That first trip, to Jewel Cave, was the last Weaver took with the outdoors club. Instead of trailing along on hiking trips, Weaver joined the Paha Sapa Grotto — a speleological club in the Black Hills. 

“In the Black Hills, our grotto has been here since 1955. We’re the oldest in the country, one of the oldest caving clubs, and there are 250 of them,” Weaver said. “You join a grotto, and you meet all kinds of other crazy cave people that have been doing it for years.”

He’s met cavers who remember when Wind Cave was only known to be 12 miles long. Today, it is mapped to 170 miles.

The knowledge shared in grottos is important for folks who hope to get started in caving, Weaver said.

“Caving is one of those places where there is no weather. So, especially here in the Western United States, everything you touch is there forever. If you put a footprint in the ground, that footprint stays there permanently. If you’re really careful and conscientious about what you are doing and how you are moving your body through the caves, you can get into it in a way that is organized,” Weaver said.

Cavers should be conscious of delicate rock formations and bat populations, Weaver said. It’s important to leave both things untouched. Rousing a bat from hibernation could cost the animal its life.

“When you wake up a bat, they use like a week of stored fat to go back to sleep, to get back into what is called torpor. That is not good for them,” Weaver said. “With cave formations, I would say this is important to know: you never want to take them out. They are very delicate.”

Weaver said it is important for cavers to keep underground environments pristine and clean.

He founded the Cave Preservation Network to create partnerships with show caves and private landowners, raising thousands of dollars for cave protection while educating owners, staff, and visitors. He has also led restoration projects alongside the Bureau of Land Management, U.S. Forest Service, and National Park Service, and serves as Vice President of the Black Hills Cave and Nature Conservancy and sits on the boards of several other cave conservancies.

“My friend Val Werker, who legitimately wrote the book on cave conservation, called ‘Cave Conservation and Restoration.’ She always says everything in caving is conservation. Even exploration,” Weaver said.

Education and conservation are important to Weaver, who is a hydrologist by training.

“Our conservancy owns a cave called Brooks Cave, for instance. Caves like Brooks Cave are a window into the hydrology of that area, because it is open space,” Weaver said. “Brooks Cave in Rapid City is right above where Rapid City gets its water. You can walk up to the Madison Aquifer and touch it. The lakes in that cave are the Madison Aquifer, where the water comes from for Rapid. One of the reasons why we bought that property, to protect forever, is to protect that watershed.”

Weaver is also the managing editor of “NSS News,” a monthly magazine with articles of general interest on all things caving. 

“The National Cave Magazine is produced in the Black Hills, and it gets mailed internationally,” Weaver said.

title: GF&P proposal removes 2 birds from endangered species list
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: A least tern stands near a nest. The species was just taken off of the South Dakota Threatened and Endangered Species list because population number estimates have improved in the state. Photo courtesy of U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service
_full_text:
usfws-least-tern-eggs.jpg
A least tern stands near a nest. The species was just taken off of the South Dakota Threatened and Endangered Species list because population number estimates have improved in the state. Photo courtesy of U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 

 usfws-least-tern-chicks.jpg
Photo courtesy of U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service 

WEBSTER — Two birds could be removed from South Dakota’s threatened and endangered species list — one because its population is considered fully recovered in the state and the other is believed to be extinct. 

On July 9, officials with the South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks recommended permanently revising the state’s threatened and endangered species list to remove the eskimo curlew and the least tern. 

Wildlife biologist Mandy Pearson said the eskimo curlew is believed to be extinct through its range, which includes South Dakota. The last confirmed sighting of the species was in 1963, she said, and the last South Dakota specimen was collected in 1878. Since then, she said there have been no records of the species in the state’s non-game conservation database, and a 2021, 5-year status review survey by the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service indicates a low probability that the population is extant or sustainable. However, Pearson said even if the bird is removed from the state’s threatened list, it will remain on the federally endangered list, and receive full federal protections. 

“Removing it from the state list allows us to focus our limited conservation resources on species where targeted recovery efforts can have the greatest impact,” Pearson said. 

The second bird proposed for removal from the threatened and endangered list is a much better success story. The least tern has been listed as a threatened or endangered species since 1978, but Pearson said survey data collected by the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers indicates the species has met state recovery goals. Additionally, she said the least tern was federally de-listed in 2021. 

“The species has also met recovery goals for productivity and habitat, demonstrating a successful recovery across multiple measures,” she said. “The delisting of least terns is a great example of what can be accomplished through collaboration, long term monitoring, and effective habitat management.” 

De-listing these birds would bring the state’s threatened and endangered list down from 21 to 19 species. 

Wildlife Administrator Andrew Norton called the de-listing a success story, and eluded to the possibility of even more species being removed from the list in the next few years — the osprey and peregrine falcon. 

Pearson said osprey populations are doing extremely well in the Black Hills since the early 2000s. The birds, she said, have met the Black Hills recovery criteria, but osprey have not met that criteria in other parts of the state. The osprey recovery data outside of the Black Hills requires at least 6 active nests per year for at least 3 years within a 7-year period, with at least 4 of those nests being successful. Pearson recommended changing those requirements to 3 active nests per year, with at least 2 of them being successful. 

“The population has never come close to meeting the current delisting criteria for outside the Black Hills,” Pearson said. “With the revised recovery criteria we are hopeful that this species can be delisted in the near future, reflecting its successful recovery in South Dakota.” 

A minor revision in the peregrine falcon recovery criteria will include the definition of a nest as one that “is claimed or built by pair in which eggs are laid during that nesting season.”

“This revision provides clarity when evaluating the recovery criteria,” Pearson said. “The peregrine falcon is doing very well in the Black Hills and was down listed from endangered status in 2022, after meeting its established recovery criteria.” 

Pearson said peregrine falcon surveys show the species has an average of at lest 5 active nests over a 5 year period, within 6 years. The GF&P began a long term monitoring program in 2026, and Pearson said biologists want to monitor the species before moving forward with delisting the bird. 

The proposal for the GF&P to consider also includes new criteria for two snakes on the threatened and endangered species list. To be fully delisted, the proposal requires the eastern hog-nosed snake to have a documented occurrence in at least 3 river basins within a 10-year period, as well as evidence of reproduction in at least 2 river basins within a 5-year period. The lined snakes, she said, must have documented sightings in at least 6 counties and 2 sub basins within a 10-year period, and to be fully delisted there must be evidence of reproduction in at least 4 counties and 2 sub basins within a 5-year period. 

Norton praised Pearson for her efforts to establish the new criteria and for delisting species this year. 

“I definitely want to reiterate the success story here nd the good work that Mandy’s team has been doing,” he said. “The goal is always to remove species from this threatened and endangered list.”  

Revisions to the state’s threatened and endangered species list are available for review, and the GF&P will take public comment until their next meeting, scheduled for Sept. 10-11 in Winner, when the commission is expected to take action on the proposed changes.

title: State-ordered study says  opioid settlement money should target treatment for incarcerated people
byline: By John Hult Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — South Dakota should spend opioid settlement money in the coming years to address the needs of people entering or leaving prisons and jails, according to an assessment prepared for the state Department of Social Services.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — South Dakota should spend opioid settlement money in the coming years to address the needs of people entering or leaving prisons and jails, according to an assessment prepared for the state Department of Social Services.

The department commissioned the $325,000 statewide needs assessment to help guide the state’s investment of settlement dollars. The inadequacy of the programs and services for addicted people in the justice system was a major takeaway, the department secretary told members of the Legislature’s budget committee on Monday at the Capitol in Pierre.

“This is a more intense addiction once you get to that level of opioid use disorder,” Secretary Matt Althoff said. “We still see, as is so often the case, the justice involvement. Laws get broken, they become incarcerated or they become prosecuted, and they are also struggling with addiction.”

The money comes from the makers and sellers of opioid painkillers linked to spikes in addiction and overdose deaths. South Dakota is expected to receive about $99 million in settlement funds through 2038. The state’s collected $32.8 million so far, with 70% of the money tagged for statewide dispersal and 30% going directly to localities.

Thus far, the state has awarded all but $2.7 million of its share through a three-tiered grant system, with awards ranging from $5,000 on the low end to more than $50,000 on the high end. The largest single award went to Avera Health, which is using its grant for an addiction-focused psychiatric residential treatment facility in Sioux Falls.

Medication-assisted addiction treatment

In the future, treatment for those released on supervision could involve the use of medications for opioid use disorder, a class of pharmaceuticals that, at therapeutic levels, deaden the craving for the drugs without producing the high or spurring a higher tolerance and a need for higher doses.

The Department of Corrections already offers the medications inside its institutions, but it has concerns about the availability of the drugs and follow-up care on the outside, said Brenna Koedam, who leads the Department of Social Services’ Behavioral Health Division.

The 2 departments have discussed where they might begin with a collaborative effort, Koedam said, which could be with eight outside prison locations for follow-up care to parolees using the medicines. 

The Department of Social Services and Unified Judicial System have also begun talks on the drugs’ possible use for people on probation, Koedam said. On Tuesday, court system spokeswoman Alisa Bousa said the state courts are interested in “any additional educational and engagement tools that would benefit the probationers.”

At the legislative meeting, Koedam told lawmakers that a stigma and “misconceptions” still surround buprenorphine, methadone and naltrexone, the three medications approved for opioid use disorder by the Food and Drug Administration. 

The department needs to “continue to get the education out there in regards to how effective these medications can be” when administered as part of an addiction treatment program, said Koedam.

Rep. Terri Jorgenson, R-Piedmont, wanted to know how long people take the drugs, on average.

“This isn’t a lifelong thing, is it?” Jorgenson said. 

Koedam told her the answer is complicated and depends on the individual. Some, she said, may use them long-term.

Sen. Taffy Howard, R-Rapid City, said she recognizes that reliance on a non-intoxicating medication is preferable to opioid use, but asked if “we’re trading one addiction for another addiction.”

For some people, Koedam said, such medicines can be “maintenance” medications, not dissimilar to drugs for blood pressure or depression that people commonly take for a lifetime. Some people, she said, will remain on the anti-addiction medicines “for the course of their lifetime.”

Sen. Red Dawn Foster, D-Pine Ridge, urged the department to prioritize “innovative” approaches to addiction for those inside institutions.

“I know a lot of inmates are self-medicating, so this is some type of need,” said Foster, referencing the use of illicit substances in prisons and jails.

Next steps for funding

Questions of ongoing funding bubbled up throughout the meeting. Jorgenson said the settlement money is finite and noted the department’s mention that the award amounts will grow smaller as 2038 draws near.

Howard, meanwhile, said “I’m seeing a lot of new programs,” and said she wasn’t convinced that taxpayers won’t be expected to keep paying for them.

“When somebody comes and asks for this grant, have you considered saying, ‘I need your commitment that you aren’t going to ask for ongoing dollars from this,’” Howard said.

The department denied a sizable stack of funding applications because it prioritized programs that wouldn’t need ongoing money from the state, Althoff said.

“Why did we say ‘no?’ Because a lot of it was not sustainable,” he said.

The next round of funding awards will prioritize applications in the mid-range of the department’s three-tiered grant system, which it calls “organizational” grants of up to $50,000.

The small awards were designed for projects at the idea stage, Althoff said, while the large ones were more about developing infrastructure. Over the next year, the goal will be to get projects into the operational and sustainable stage. 

Near the end of the briefing, Sen. Paul Miskimins, R-Mitchell, praised the department’s willingness to take on opioid addiction. Miskimins, a retired dentist who said he tightened his approach to painkiller prescriptions as their addictive nature became clear, said he hopes lawmakers and the general public remember the human cost of the drugs behind the settlement money.

“One of the finest ladies in my practice was arrested for stealing medications out of a medicine chest at a rummage sale because she was addicted and hiding it from everybody in the world,” said Miskimins. “She was a Sunday school teacher.”

title: MC sheriff asks for  more deputies to  handle call increases
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Calls for service per deputy have more than doubled in Meade County since 2013, Sheriff Pat West said recently.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

STURGIS — Calls for service per deputy have more than doubled in Meade County since 2013, Sheriff Pat West said recently. 

As the Meade County Commission began its budget talks for 2027, July 14, West asked for 2 new deputies as part of his budget request. West told the commission that since 2010, the population of Meade County has increased from 25,453 to nearly 32,000. Additionally, calls for service have increased from 9,159 in 2013, to more than 21,000 in 2025. 

In that same time frame, the sheriff’s office has added 2 positions, increasing the number of sworn deputies from 17 to 19. That means, West said, the calls per deputy have increased from 539 per year to more than 1,100 — a 100% increase. 

The increase has been particularly rapid since 2021, when calls for service jumped from 12,700 to more than 21,000 in 2025, he said. 

Civil calls for service have also seen rapid increases. In 2020, West said the sheriff’s office made 2,622 attempts to serve civil papers, and collected $71,000 in fees. By 2025, that number jumped to 3,528 attempts, with $107,800 collected.

Currently, West said the sheriff’s office is using patrol officers to serve civil papers. If the commission approves adding the 2 additional deputies, he said one would be a full time patrol officer and the other would focus on serving civil papers. 

Commissioner Doreen Creed said commissioners have asked state legislators to introduce a bill that would make statutory changes to how much the sheriff’s office can be reimbursed for serving civil papers, since the practice is costing taxpayers more than the fees. Chief Deputy James Johns said state law allows the Meade County Sheriff’s Office to collect 59 cents per mile, and $50 for each successful civil paper service. Johns explained that each civil paper generally takes more than one attempt to serve, and at $30 per hour for deputies plus vehicle mileage, each civil service can cost $60 or more. There are also costs associated with the extra administrative time it takes to record the civil service, he said. 

“With all costs, we do not even approach breaking even,” he said. 

“Maybe it would be good if the sheriff’s association also put together some data about how much it costs, and how much tax payers are eating,” Creed said.  

Some examples of civil paper service include criminal summons, subpoenas, wage garnishments, summons and complaints for divorce, mental commitments, protection orders, foreclosure notices, and small claims notices. 

While West said 2 new deputies are needed to handle increased calls for service, he also told the commission that a longtime part-time deputy, who provides services in the Union Center area, is considering retiring, which will increase the need for more help. 

“He is an incredible resource in that country because he is a rancher, knows cattle, and knows all the residents out east, to include the Faith country,” West said. “There have been several occasions where people call him directly for help and he drops everything and comes running. He has saved the county countless hours, fuel, and expense. There is so much I want to say about him, as he has been such an incredible asset for us.” 

In addition to personnel, West asked for $125,000 for 3 unmarked vehicles, to be used for investigations and civil service. The existing unmarked vehicles, he said, are very old, with high mileage. The request is not part of the official budget, but is included in the sheriff’s office assignments, which are “wish-list” items for the county to consider if tax collections are higher than anticipated in 2027.

title: 7 things to know ahead of the SD gubernatorial runoff
byline: By Molly Wetsch South Dakota News Watch
description: Gov. Larry Rhoden
_full_text:
Rhoden.png
Gov. Larry Rhoden 

 Doeden.jpg
Toby Doeden 

PIERRE — South Dakota Republican voters once again head back to the polls next week. 

The gubernatorial runoff Tuesday is the result of more than a year of campaigning in a pool of what was once four candidates for the Republican nomination. It comes after the primary election on June 2 declared Gov. Larry Rhoden and Toby Doeden the 2 candidates moving on.

Here’s what to know about the runoff:

It’s the first one

The South Dakota law requiring a runoff if no candidate meets a certain threshold in primary voting has been around for more than 40 years. But this is the first election that it’s been required since the law was passed in 1985 by former lawmaker Joe Barnett.

Doeden received 31% of the vote on June 2 and Rhoden received 25%. Other candidates, Congressman Dusty Johnson and Speaker of the South Dakota House Jon Hansen, received 23% and 21%, respectively. No candidate received 35% of the vote, which is required to advance to the general election.

The runoff brings a new level of uncertainty to the race, which saw one of the most crowded candidate fields in recent memory, as well as once-presumed favorite Johnson fall short in the primary. 

Two very different candidates want the job.

While both candidates are running in the Republican primary, they represent two very different sides of the political spectrum. 

Rhoden is the incumbent candidate. He succeeded Gov. Kristi Noem, as her lieutenant governor, after she left office to join the Department of Homeland Security in January 2025. Rhoden is a rancher from Union Center and has spent 25 years in Pierre as a state representative, state senator and in the executive branch.

Doeden, by contrast, is a businessman from Aberdeen who calls himself an “outsider” and relies on his lack of political experience as an asset. He has largely decried the “establishment” in Pierre and called for new voices in state government. 

The runoff pulls from the largest GOP voter base in state history

Voter registration for South Dakota Republicans is at an all-time high. Nearly 10,000 more voters are able to cast votes for governor on July 28 than were able to at the beginning of this year.

Doeden told News Watch on Friday that he believes some of the growth in Republican voters is part of an effort from non-Republicans to sway the primary.

“It’s pretty natural in a state that has as many independents as we do, that you see them switching regularly,” Doeden said. “Some of those are organic, that would happen in any cycle. But there’s certainly been an uptick, and it would certainly seem to me that the Democrats are trying to steal a Republican election because one of the candidates is far closer to their ideology and political beliefs than I am.”

Rhoden’s campaign did not respond to multiple requests for comment. 

Differing views on property taxes

Property taxes have been a defining feature of both candidates’ campaigns: One with promises to eliminate them and one who hopes that his prior reform efforts will speak for themself. 

Doeden’s well-publicized plan to eliminate property taxes has been the subject of scrutiny from some of his opposition. He has said frequently on the campaign trail that he plans to eliminate property taxes entirely, and hinged much of his campaign on the plan.

On July 17, a spokesperson from Doeden’s campaign told South Dakota Searchlight that plan “has never applied to any classes of property beyond owner-occupied homes.” But Doeden said to News Watch that it was still his goal to eliminate all property taxes, though he said he plans to start with owner-occupied property.

“I think we can get rid of all owner-occupied property taxes within 3 or 4 years. I genuinely do,” Doeden said. “And if we keep and maintain strong conservative leadership in the governor’s office and the Legislature, I think another 4 or 8 years, we can get rid of commercial and ranch and ag land property tax and replace it with taxes that are more fair and equitable, like sales tax. Not raising the sales tax, but growing the economy and generating more sales tax revenue.”

Rhoden has largely touted his previous work in property taxes as a reflection of how he will operate in the future. Most of the bills Rhoden has brought to the table, as a state representative or as governor, have focused on tax reform. Senate bills 96 and 245 are the bills passed in this year’s Legislature that Rhoden said will reduce owner-occupied property taxes by 34%. 

“I think for the time being, we’re going to see how that plays out, see how many counties take advantage of the half-cent side of it,” Rhoden told SDPB’s Jackie Hendry in an interview aired last week. “That coupled with the fact that, like we said before, things are starting to get back on track, I think we’re in pretty good shape.”

It’s gone negative.

South Dakotans have likely gotten used to seeing political ads related to the governor’s race. They also may have noticed that in the past few weeks, those ads have tilted toward attacks of the opposing candidate.

Social media ads paid for by Doeden’s campaign have called Rhoden “Lyin’ Larry” and claim that he has raised taxes 400 times. On his own social media, Doeden has called Rhoden “Larry RhoBiden,” in reference to former President Joe Biden. 

Rhoden’s campaign launched a website last week that casts doubt on Doeden’s property tax strategy and calls Doeden “reckless” and “too risky for South Dakota.” Other ads have called Doeden out for saying he “might have voted for Barack Obama” in prior elections and for not voting in the 2016 and 2020 primaries. 

Doeden told News Watch that the ads his campaign is running are positive and that negative ads against Rhoden are from unaffiliated groups. He maintained that he is running a positive campaign – something he said he believes was the reason for his success in the primary – but that he thinks ads mentioning Rhoden’s record are not attack ads.

“If people want to call it attacking that’s fine, but it’s simply just pointing out the record. Every ad that Toby Doeden has run on this campaign, including since June 3rd, has been 100% positive. I have run the most positive campaign in the history (of the state),” Doeden said. “Now I know there are some people and some organizations that support me that are perhaps attacking Larry. I can’t control that.”

We won’t know much about how it was funded until it’s over

A major point of discussion from the beginning of the race was how candidates were funding their campaigns. 

Doeden notably donated $4 million of his own money to his campaign. Rhoden has reported raising just over $1 million and spending just under $1 million, much of which has come from state and federal political action committees.

But because campaign finance disclosure requirements are not tailored to runoff elections, the public won’t know much about the past eight weeks until Oct. 19 – the next filing deadline. That makes information about who’s funding Rhoden and Doeden’s campaigns, and how they’re spending that money, somewhat obscure. 

Campaign finance disclosures can illuminate which candidates were raising and spending the most money and shed light on what groups may be backing a candidate’s campaign. 

It doesn’t end here

While the victorious candidate will certainly have much to celebrate after the runoff is completed, the campaign will not end on Tuesday. The winning candidate will face Democrat Dan Ahlers in November for the general election. 

A Democratic candidate has not been elected to the office of governor in more than 50 years. Gov. Richard Kneip was elected in 1971 and served until 1978. 

The winning candidate, though they may anticipate election to office in November, will have to find a way to unite Republicans that have been divided over their choice of candidate for nearly the entirety of the campaign. 

Doeden said that he is not concerned about rallying the party behind him if he advances beyond the primary, comparing himself to President Donald Trump, as he has frequently during his campaign.

“Ninety-five percent of the mudslinging has been from the political class towards the outsider. Once the outsider wins, that’ll go away and they’ll unite. The same thing happened to Donald Trump in 2016,” Doeden said.

Rhoden said during the SDPB conversation that politics in South Dakota had undergone “choppy waters.”

“We’ve come a long way just in the last 17 months of getting things back on track, and I think that will continue for the next period of time,” Rhoden said. “I’ve always said we do a lot of things right in South Dakota, and our political process is one of them. Sometimes we’ll get a little off track, but the ship always has a way of righting itself, and we’re in the process right now of the ship righting itself in South Dakota, and I want to continue that.”

A recent Emerson poll from KELO-TV showed Rhoden leading with 62% to Doeden’s 32% of 500 likely voters polled. Rhoden said to KELO that the poll was “encouraging,” while Doeden slammed it as “absurd” and said he was “embarrassed” that he was discussing it.

What else to know 

• Do I have to be a Republican to vote?

Yes. The runoff is part of a closed primary, meaning only Republicans can vote. The deadline to register was June 13.

• Did I have to vote in the primary to vote in the runoff?

No. As long as you are a registered Republican, whether or not you voted in prior elections does not matter.

• Will my polling place be the same?

Not necessarily. Because the primary election on June 2 included municipal and other local elections for several areas, your polling place may have changed. You can check where to vote at sdsos.gov.

title: Deadwood ordinance could allow  city officials to enforce fire code
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: If passed, Ordinance 1447 in Deadwood could help improve life safety in the city by allowing city officials to issue citations to business owners whose property is found to be in non-compliance with the city-adopted International Fire Code.
_full_text:
Deadwood ordinance.jpg
If passed, Ordinance 1447 in Deadwood could help improve life safety in the city by allowing city officials to issue citations to business owners whose property is found to be in non-compliance with the city-adopted International Fire Code.  

DEADWOOD — If passed, Ordinance 1447 in Deadwood could help improve life safety in the city by allowing the Deadwood Volunteer Fire Department to issue citations for buildings that are non-compliant with the adopted International Fire Code. 

Fire Chief Joel Ellis said the goal of the ordinance is not to allow his department to penalize business owners, but to improve life safety for visitors and residents of the city. 

“We’re not looking to go out and write a bunch of tickets,” said Ellis. “We just want people to get buildings into shape early and to be safe not only for the public, but also the employees that are working there.”

Ellis said his department began pushing for the ordinance a year ago, after visits to businesses in town revealed blocked pathways and fire control panels. 

“We’ve done some walkthroughs of commercial buildings within town and we’ve seen some alarming trends with egress patterns,” said Ellis. “Doors were blocked, materials and goods that are being sold and piled up in places they shouldn’t be — piled up on the steps, places where fire controls to sprinkler systems couldn’t be accessed because there were piles of goods that were 4, 5-feet high in spots.”

Ellis said after pulling statistics for calls to service, he discovered that one property in Deadwood accounted for 19% of the total calls from January to the end of March. Most of the calls, he said, were false alarms from improperly placed smoke detector heads. Walkthroughs of hotels have revealed missing detector heads or head that have been tampered with so visitors could smoke in their rooms. 

“It wasn’t that this property was in non-compliance, it was the fact that they had neglected to make the changes needed until we really forced the issue,” said Ellis. “Again, it’s not our goal to cite people. We just want to make sure that people are safe and we’re not needlessly running to the same property over and over again because they decided they didn’t want to make any changes.”

Ellis said the ordinance is meant to inspire a collective effort to prevent fires in the historic city. 

“With the buildings as close as they are, as old as they are, with the type of construction we have, one small thing could be catastrophic,” he said. “It’s best to be proactive and get ahead of it and make sure everybody’s safe.”

According to the proposed ordinance, fire officials must obtain either consent to enter the building or an inspection warrant. Repercussions for being found in non-compliance will be monetary.

The first reading of the ordinance was passed at the Monday meeting. The ordinance is expected to have a second reading at the Aug. 3 meeting. If passed, the ordinance could go into effect 30 days later.

Quentin Riggins, the city attorney, said another ordinance will be forthcoming that will outline who city commissioners will assign to enforce Ordinance 1447.

title: US Senate committee advances bill supporting study of Missouri River pipeline system expansion
byline: By South Dakota Searchlight staff
description: A portion of the Lewis and Clark Regional Water System is installed between Beresford and Sioux Center, Iowa. Photo courtesy of Lewis and Clark Regional Water System
_full_text:
US Senate committee advances bill supporting study of Missouri River pipeline system expansion.jpg
A portion of the Lewis and Clark Regional Water System is installed between Beresford and Sioux Center, Iowa. Photo courtesy of Lewis and Clark Regional Water System 

Another piece of federal legislation seeking funding to study a Missouri River water pipeline project in South Dakota has passed a U.S. Senate committee.

The Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources approved the Lewis & Clark Regional Water System Expansion Feasibility Study Act last week, sending it to the full Senate. Majority Leader John Thune sponsors the bill, and Sen. Mike Rounds is a cosponsor. Both are Republicans from South Dakota.

They announced the bill’s committee approval in a press release.

“Continued access to clean and reliable water is critical to economic development and quality of life in our state,” Rounds said.

The bill would provide $10 million for the Department of the Interior to study the feasibility of expanding the capacity and reach of the Lewis & Clark Rural Water System. The existing system in southeast South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota delivers water to 20 member cities and rural water systems.

Last month, bills from Thune and Rounds cleared a Senate committee that would provide $10 million apiece to support feasibility studies for the Western Dakota Regional Water System and Dakota Mainstem Regional Water System. The Western Dakota Regional Water System aims to build a pipeline from the Missouri River to supply communities across the western portion of the state, whose drinking water needs are currently served by aquifers. The Dakota Mainstem Regional Water System would serve areas in eastern South Dakota, western Minnesota and northern Iowa.

House versions of the three bills from U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, R-South Dakota, are awaiting action by committees in that chamber.

title: Spearfish votes 5-1 to pay off  rec center bond early
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — In a move that could save the city between $6,000 and $7,000, the Spearfish City Council voted 5-1 to pay down a tax revenue refunding bond almost 2 years early.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

SPEARFISH — In a move that could save the city between $6,000 and $7,000, the Spearfish City Council voted 5-1 to pay down a tax revenue refunding bond almost 2 years early.

“This bond was originally issued in 2008 for construction of the rec center, the water park, and the indoor facility there,” Spearfish Finance Officer Michelle DeNeui said. “We did refinance it in 2015; that is why they are called the refunding bonds for lower interest rates.”

The bond would naturally reach maturity in June 2028. During the 2027 preliminary budgeting process, Councilmen Larry Klarenbeek and Dean Myers directed city staff to look into paying off that debt early.

“So I did reach out to US Bank; they hold our bonds. They are the paying agent for our sales tax bonds,” DeNeui said. “We just need to notify our paying agent of when we intend to pay them off, so they can notify the bondholders that we paid off the debt.”

The city pays a $750 payment fee to US Bank each year.

“We’ve only paid that through March 2026, so we still owe a little bit more on that. We just need to notify our paying agent if we wish to pay these off early,” DeNeui said. “My recommendation is to pay them off with our Dec. 1 payment, utilizing our cash balance within the general fund.”

There is $1,245,000 in principal is due, with $62,9000 interest. DeNeui said the city has plenty of cash on hand in the general fund to cover the total remaining balance, but the council will have to pass a budget supplement to have the spending authority to close out the debt.

If the city leaves the cash on hand where it is, DeNeui said, the money isn’t earning enough to justify waiting for the bond’s natural horizon.

“Our current investment return rate that we receive from our funds within our bank account is 3.55%, so doing the comparison, we would actually pay more in interest than what we are earning by a factor of 0.45%,” DeNeui said.

Councilman Scott Hourigan said, in the event that the city spends more than it budgets for in the coming year, and has to dip into cash on hand, it might be wise to leave money in the bank.

“It seems as though earlier comments from the public were for $5.5 million in deficit, right? Which is what we really knew we saved money for. I am concerned that if we throw this out of the contingency, of $1.2 million, we’ve overspent,”Hourigan said. “I wouldn’t be in favor of this. Let it roll out. My opinion.”

It was Klarenbeek who made the motion to pay off the bond now.

“It is always nice to pay off debt, and just reduce the outflow for those other 2 years,” Klarenbeek said.  

Hourigan was the sole member of council who voted to oppose paying off the bond early.

Right now, the city has a total of 6 active bonds.

“We have this bond, which was initially issued for the rec center construction. We have 2 bonds for the Sky Ridge Sports Complex. We have the wastewater treatment plant bond; we have the new East Low Zone water well fund.  Then we are drawing on future debt for the sewer fund for the sewer upsize project on Colorado,” DeNeui said.

Despite those 6 bonds, DeNeui described Spearfish as a “debt-averse” municipality.  

“We are well under our statutory limit, and what we typically see for communities. We’ve been very debt-averse over the course of our existence,” DeNeui said.

title: Water slows Haines Ave. construction, New Underwood Road repairs nearly complete
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Contractors working to rebuild Haines Avenue hit a snag when they encountered a natural spring underneath the road, Meade County Highway Superintendent Troy Eastman said July 14.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

STURGIS — Contractors working to rebuild Haines Avenue hit a snag when they encountered a natural spring underneath the road, Meade County Highway Superintendent Troy Eastman said July 14. 

Eastman told Meade County Commissioners that Western Construction and Contractors, of Rapid City, discovered soft spots related to the spring, that required a change order and different course of action. 

“Basically we put a drain tile underneath the road to help alleviate the water that’s surfacing there because we couldn’t get compaction in those areas,” Eastman said. “Of course, the pipe that we needed is on back order, so it’s on its way,” Eastman said. 

Crews continue to work on Haines Avenue, Eastman said, and they are currently doing asphalt patching in another part of the road. They are also milling patches that are not new. When the project is complete, Eastman said it will be one continuous matte on the top. 

The completion date for the project is Nov. 1, but Eastman said the project needs to be paved before the first frost. Until then, motorists who do not live in the area are asked to find alternate routes, and those who must use the road are asked to follow the 35 miles per hour speed limit. 

“It’s been difficult to keep cars out,” Eastman said. “I know people live there and we expect that. But if everybody else can help us out by letting us get the work done, it makes it a lot easier, especially going slower. Don’t go that way if you don’t have to.” 

In addition to Haines Avenue, Eastman said auto seal and asphalt patching on New Underwood Road has been completed, except for one half-mile stretch of road on the south end, that the commission agreed to pave with a change order they approved July 14. 

Commissioner Gary Deering said he asked for the paving to be done where the Pennington and Meade county lines meet on that road. 

“It’s a terrible spot,” Deering said. “It’s right on a corner, right on a hill, and what’s been happening with this gravel is it’s going to be a change in a level. That change in level right at that curve and right at the top of the hill is a bad safety issue in my opinion. So, what I asked is if we would pave to get basically at the bottom of the hill to more of a straightaway, so we’re not dealing with a bump right on the curve at the top of a hill.” 

The change order will cost the county $365,000 less than the original contract amount of nearly $2.6 million. Eastman said that’s because the county was able to save money by shopping around for oil to use for the otto seal surfacing. The county applied those savings to pay for the asphalt paving on the south end of the road.

title: Proposed Lead-Deadwood School District budget shows lower revenues, increased costs
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: A proposed budget from the Lead-Deadwood School District shows a loss of nearly $1 million in local tax revenue. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
Proposed Lead-Deadwood School District budget shows lower revenues, increased costs .jpg
A proposed budget from the Lead-Deadwood School District shows a loss of nearly $1 million in local tax revenue. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

LEAD — The proposed budget from the Lead-Deadwood School District for the 2026-2027 school year shows a loss in tax revenue of almost $1 million, a loss in enrollment-driven revenue, and a slight rise in expenditures.  

Amanda Trople, business manager of the district, said that general fund is used to pay staff and educator wages and basic supplies. Trople said a mill levy is implemented on local property taxes to put monies into the fund.  

After South Dakota Codified Law (SDCL) 10-12-42 went into effect July 1, school districts across the state are restricted in the amount they can levy against owner occupied properties. For taxes payable in 2027, districts can levy a maximum of $0.669 per $1,000 of assessed value. Lead-Deadwood’s proposed levy is set to decrease from $2.346 to $0.653 per $1,000, resulting in an estimated loss of $1.1 million in revenue from owner-occupied properties.  

For the previous school year, the district was able to request a maximum of $9.3 million from local taxes but requested $642,340 less to make budget. This year, the district is only able to request $8.1 million. Without requesting maximum levies, the district is proposing to save local taxpayers $196,482 towards the district’s general fund for this year’s budget. 

Trople said capital outlay is used to fund, “big, expensive purchases.” 

“Building improvements, or if you’re trying to extend the life of something, that would be capital outlay. Technology can be purchased out of capital outlay,” she said.  

Capital outlay funds are generated through a per-student request from local taxes capped by SDCL 13-16-7. Enrollment numbers from the previous school year are used in the formula. For this year’s capital outlay formula, enrollment has dropped from 637 to 598. The district will be able to request almost $700,000 less than they requested the previous year for the fund. 

Superintendent Erik Person said school’s budgets are split between 2 tax years, requiring the district to average the tax years while creating a budget. The $1 million shortfall in the general fund, he said, will be cut in half when it’s split between last year and the upcoming tax revenues. 

“Because that $1 million shortfall becomes a structural deficit going forward, it’s mitigated in year one by that averaging. Going forward, that disparity is going to be there, so we’ve got to become more efficient with our expenditures,” said Person. 

Expenditures in the district have increased in general fund but have lowered in capital outlay with the conclusion of the renovation of the middle school building. 

“There is a slight increase, but I think that’s to be expected,” said Trople. “Prices are increasing, so we are going to see that. Salaries tend to drive your general fund, that’s the majority of your general fund expenditures. So, now that the state has kind of set limits, we have to watch teacher accountability and limit all unnecessary purchases.” 

Person said next year, utilities are expected to rise 27%. Property and casuality insurance are up 8%, health insurance has risen almost 10%, and staff have received raises. Some of those costs, he said, can be covered by a transfer from capital outlay into general fund. Other deficits, he said, are being looked at with a long-term strategy to become more efficient overall as a district. 

“Because we’ve absorbed some positions and we’ve done some things to become more efficient in our builings, and it’s really cut down our expenditures a lot,” he said. “As we continue that goal, it’s going to take a few years to fully take effect. In the meantime, we’ve got other mitigating factors that are going to bridge this gap.” 

Trople said the district doesn’t have data for expenditures for either budget yet, but she’s working together with Person to create a balanced budget that will compensate for the loss in tax revenue. Person said the district’s history of not requesting the maximum levy from taxpayers may come to an end in coming years as they compensate for the loss in tax revenue. 

“Our taxpayers are still going to see big savings on owner occupied just because statute has the max levy almost zeroed out,” said Person. “Even commercial property owners are probably going to see a slight decrease because we’re levying less in capital outlay. We’re still in pretty good shape, overall. It’s just a lot more imperative that we really hit that target and try to be as efficient as we can. In the past there was smore money available and we just didn’t levy it. We didn’t need it. Going forward, we’re at a point where we’re going to need everything we could potentially levy. We just need to watch how we manage the budget and we’re up to that task.” 

The final budget is expected to be presented to the school board at the Aug. 11 meeting.

title: Consultants to revamp Title 15, Spearfish development code, after 5-1 vote
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — Spearfish is hiring Clarion Group, a land-use consulting firm with bases in Colorado and North Carolina, to complete a thorough update of Title 15 — the city’s land-use code — for $152,675.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

SPEARFISH — Spearfish is hiring Clarion Group, a land-use consulting firm with bases in Colorado and North Carolina, to complete a thorough update of Title 15 — the city’s land-use code — for $152,675.

“We have, I would say, antiquated and incomplete definitions of land uses,” Community Development Director Peter Wysocki said. “Obviously our code, although it has been updated, there have been updates to certain sections, we have not holistically modernized the code — particularly land use definitions.”

The overhaul of Title 15 was recommended in the city’s comprehensive plan.

“The comprehensive plan is obviously a visionary document for the city. It addresses high-level policy issues, but there are a number of tools that cities have to implement their comprehensive plan,” Wysocki said.

Wysocki said one of those tools is an engineering and design standards (EDS) document. The city adopted a new EDS earlier this month. 

“As identified in the comprehensive plan, the top recommendation is also to update the city zoning and subdivision regulations, not only to align the practical implementation and processing of development within the city, but also to ensure our zoning and subdivision regulations are consistent with implementation of the comprehensive plan,” Wysocki said.

Zoning regulations outline what can or cannot be built on property and what development can look like—including requirements for parking, landscaping, signage, setbacks, and building height. 

Wysocki said the code section also addresses the city’s process. It outlines how city staff review and approve development projects.

“It can also provide standards for public hearings and public engagement during that process,” Wysocki said. “It is not the same as building codes. Those deal with vertical construction.”

In addition to modernizing land use definitions and rules that help cultivate and preserve community character, the code update could offer an opportunity to better organize the city’s standards.

“I think that is one of the key components that can make a land development code more ‘user friendly’ is : how the code is organized, how well the code is defined, make sure the process is defined for, like, applications,” Wysocki said. “Under current code we have different public hearing notifications, depending on the application type. For example, conditional use permits require different notifications than zone changes. We would like to make that consistent so that it is easier for staff to administer it, but also more transparent for our customers.”

Wysocki said providing quality customer service is a priority for this department, and one of the reasons why it makes sense to hire an outside consultant, like Clarion, to draft an update for Title 15.

“Given the in-house expertise, would you say … if we did it in-house, how long would it take?” asked City Councilman Larry Klarenbeek.

Wysocki said that building professionals rely on the speed and efficiency of community development staff to review plans in order to do their jobs effectively.

“To pull away staff from our core services at this point, I think will be a disservice to our customers. That is the candid answer,” Wysocki said.

He added that consultants bring extra sets of eyes and fresh perspectives to processes.  

“We will be involved in this. This is not just hiring and consulting and having them do everything. It’s been my experience that staff will be hands-on. We will be editing their work; we will be providing them insight on the local barometer or local appetite for change. I will say though that some of our processes are cumbersome,” Wysocki said. “We can improve our quality.”

Wysocki said Clarion has more than 30 years of experience in land-use code updates in particular. They also represent a neutral party that can help point out what Spearfish does well, and what may be ready for improvement.

That work will not be done without stakeholder involvement, Wysocki said.

“Clarion would also provide project management. What does that mean? They will provide all of the materials. We would work with them to schedule stakeholder meetings,” Wysocki told the city council Monday. “This will not be, you know, the planning department sitting in an office, writing a code. With Clarion, we would invite members of the community, our stakeholders which typically includes design professionals, architects, civil engineers, those companies that submit applications to the city and actually use the code, we would advise home builders, members of the public, typically partner organizations, we would extend an invite to the school district, BH, and also invited 2 of you to sit on the steering committee, and 2 planning commissioners as well, to provide that feedback back to the respective bodies.”

Councilwoman Ana Rath, who made the motion to approve the $152, 675 contract with Clarion, said,  

“I think what you were just saying, on customer service, I think that it is important not to take away from what they (city staff) are trying to do.  I know personally, another day trying to call up there and it’s busy, it is difficult. I think hiring this company to come in, and actually bring an unbiased opinion, as you shared, I think that is awesome. I am all for it.”

Councilwoman Pam Jacobs also voiced her support, saying that she thought bringing in a third party for code updates is a wise approach in this case.

The motion to hire Clarion to update Title 15 passed 5-1, with Klarenbeek opposed.
