title: Sturgis approves Avalanche Road  paving contract
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Avalanche Road, from the Harvest Meadows Subdivision to the city rubble site in Sturgis, will be paved after the Rally this year. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
Avalanche Road.jpeg
Avalanche Road, from the Harvest Meadows Subdivision to the city rubble site in Sturgis, will be paved after the Rally this year. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

STURGIS — The city of Sturgis will start paving Avalanche Road this year.

The gravel road that leads to the city rubble site and a new subdivision is heavily traveled and has been the subject of resident complaints regarding unsafe conditions. In January the city of Sturgis took over maintenance for 1.37 miles of the road that is on the boundary of the city limits, in accordance with South Dakota Codified Law 31-17-16. Before that, Meade County officials provided minimum maintenance on the road.  

On Monday, the Sturgis City Council approved a $326,115 bid from Sacrison Paving, of Whitewood, to pave 3,400 linear feet of the road, from the Harvest Meadows Subdivision to the city rubble site. The finished roadway will be 24-feet wide and will consist of 5 inches of asphalt, Sturgis Public Works Director Rick Bush said. 

The bid is $38,885 less than the original engineer’s estimate of $365,000. Bush said out of the four bids received, Sacrison Paving quoted the lowest responsible price. 

“We felt that it was an excellent response, considering the construction market,” he said about the number of bids received. 

Funding for the project will come out of the city’s capital improvements fund, since the project was not budgeted in 2026. 

“There are several benefits to the community,” Bush said of completing the project this year. “This is an important transportation corridor. It will reduce maintenance costs. We took over that portion of Avalanche Road Jan. 1 of this year. We’ve spent a lot of time and energy and money thus far keeping it bladed, and keeping the dust control down. We moved some of the Exit 32 operations to the rubble site, including the cardboard. We feel this will be improved access to the rubble site. It’ll be a better ride quality and it will be safer.” 

Sturgis Mayor Rod Bradley said the project will be a nice addition to the city. 

“This will be a nice project for all the homes that are going to be out there now and it completes a piece of the whole transition of that area from county to city,” Bradley said.

Due to the upcoming Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, Bush said he expects the project will be done in the Fall, since construction will not be allowed from Aug. 3-20.

title: Homestake AI Act advances SURF’s biology research, aims at disease cures
byline: By Mike Ray Sanford Underground Research Facility
description: Dr. Tanvi Govil, an assistant professor of chemical and biological engineering at South Dakota Mines, examines a sample taken 1,700 feet below the surface at SURF. The Homestake AI Act would enable genome sequencing of the unique and untapped wealth of microbes that thrive in underground environments. Photo by Stephen Kenny
_full_text:
Homestake AI act.jpg
Dr. Tanvi Govil, an assistant professor of chemical and biological engineering at South Dakota Mines, examines a sample taken 1,700 feet below the surface at SURF. The Homestake AI Act would enable genome sequencing of the unique and untapped wealth of microbes that thrive in underground environments. Photo by Stephen Kenny 

LEAD — A new act, being considered in Congress, invests in genome sequencing to tap the wealth of biological life living underground at SURF. This research can lead to breakthroughs in new medicines and potential disease cures.

Sens. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., and Martin Heinrich, D-N.M., introduced legislation Thursday to expedite scientific research on diseases through specimen collection. This is the first piece of legislation introduced using feedback from Rounds and Heinrich’s American Science Acceleration Project (ASAP), a national initiative to support making American science 10 times faster by 2030.

The Homestake AI Act would establish a pilot program in the Department of Energy (DOE), focused on the collection, cataloguing and sequencing of whole genomes and metabolites from samples collected in unique locations. This includes locations exposed to extreme properties such as high heat or pressure, locations at extreme risk of destruction in coming decades, and other locations that hold potential for finding useful organisms to help advance health care treatments.

The Homestake AI Act was inspired by the case of the gila monster. The gila monster, native to the deserts of North America, can survive on just a few meals a year due to a digestion-slowing hormone in its venom. This discovery helped pave the way for Ozempic, a drug for diabetes patients to manage blood sugar.

“The Homestake AI Act would take great strides to accelerate scientific research on diseases here in the United States,” said Rounds. “Evidenced by the gila monster, species who survive in extreme environments usually hold an interesting secret to doing so. Increasing the amount of data we collect from these specimens could unlock cures to diseases such as Alzheimer’s, diabetes and different types of cancers. I’m pleased to be unveiling our first piece of legislation related to our ASAP initiative. Thank you to everyone who provided information to make this legislation possible.”

“We need to leave no stone unturned in the race to discover cures and treatments for cancer, diabetes, and dementia,” said Heinrich. “Our Homestake AI Act will establish a new initiative at the Department of Energy that helps researchers harness the power of AI to identify, catalog, and sequence plants, animals, and microbes that may hold the secret to potential cures and treatments. This is how we keep America at the forefront of scientific innovation, while saving lives.”

Mike Headley, executive director of the South Dakota Science and Technology Authority, which manages the Sanford Underground Research Facility, said SURF supports the legislation. 

“SURF is America’s Underground Lab and has a strong track record of supporting leading biological research deep underground,” Headley said. “We’re excited to potentially play a role in the extremophile whole genome sequencing initiative.”

“Artificial intelligence is only as powerful as the infrastructure that supports it,” said Dr. José-Marie Griffiths, chancellor of Dakota State University. “The Homestake AI Act, the first legislative initiative of the American Science Acceleration Project led by Sen. Mike Rounds and Sen. Martin Heinrich, recognizes that the next generation of breakthroughs will depend not only on advanced computing, but also on access to rich, high-quality biological data. By investing in the collection, preservation, and accessibility of genomic and metabolic data, this act lays the foundation for AI-driven discoveries that could transform how we prevent, diagnose, and treat countless health challenges. Building this research infrastructure today will ensure the United States remains at the forefront of scientific innovation and discovery for decades to come.”

“Biological organisms’ diversity is an incredibly rich resource for America and the world,” said Barry Dunn, president of South Dakota State University. “Their genomes carry the information we need to harness a diversity of organisms’ unique properties for our greater use. The Homestake AI Act is a critically important step toward discoveries that will change the way we live.”

“The Homestake AI Act underscores the tremendous potential of artificial intelligence and scientific discovery to improve lives. By strengthening scientific datasets and accelerating research, this initiative can help unlock new insights into some of our most pressing health challenges,” said Sheila K. Gestring, president of the University of South Dakota. “At the University of South Dakota, we see every day how innovation, data-driven research and strong partnerships can advance knowledge and create meaningful impact. This legislation recognizes the value of investing in discovery today to improve health outcomes for future generations.”

“South Dakota Mines strongly supports the Homestake AI Act,” said Dr. Brian Tande, president of the South Dakota School of Mines. “This bill would accelerate American science by using artificial intelligence and unique datasets to pursue breakthroughs in treating cancer, diabetes, dementia, and other serious diseases. It enhances the kind of bold research we do at Mines every day: driving innovation and improving lives.”

“America’s leadership in AI and biotechnology depends on building the scientific infrastructure that will power the next generation of discovery,” said Ylli Bajraktari, CEO of the Special Competitive Studies Project Action Program. “The Homestake AI Act recognizes that the genomes and molecular diversity of living organisms represent a strategic and largely untapped resource for innovation. By investing in the systematic collection and analysis of these data, the United States can accelerate the development of new therapies, fuel AI-driven scientific breakthroughs, and strengthen our nation’s leadership in innovation, economic competitiveness, and national security for decades to come.”

title: Badlands National Park designated International Dark Sky Park
byline: Pioneer Staff Reports
description: Badlands National Park was designated as the first and only International Dark Sky Park in South Dakota. Photo courtesy of Teresa Hofer
_full_text:
Badlands Aurora 5302 copy (Credit Teresa Hofer).jpg
Badlands National Park was designated as the first and only International Dark Sky Park in South Dakota. Photo courtesy of Teresa Hofer 

BADLANDS NATIONAL PARK — South Dakota is gaining international recognition as one of the world’s premier destinations for experiencing the night sky.

Badlands National Park was designated an International Dark Sky Park by DarkSky International at a special evening ceremony July 17, becoming the first and only International Dark Sky Park in South Dakota and one of only 2 in the National Park Service’s Midwest region.

The internationally recognized designation places the park among an elite group of only 40 National Park Service units nationwide celebrated for protecting some of the world’s darkest and most pristine night skies.

The designation is one of the most prestigious recognitions a place can receive for night sky conservation and visitor experience. Earning the designation requires years of planning, collaboration and investment to meet rigorous standards for sky quality, responsible lighting, public education and long-term stewardship.

“This designation is more than an incredible achievement for Badlands National Park. It’s a milestone for South Dakota,” said James Hagen, secretary of the South Dakota Department of Tourism. “It reinforces what visitors have long known: South Dakota’s wide-open spaces offer experiences that are becoming increasingly rare. Standing beneath an unspoiled sky, watching the Milky Way stretch overhead, spotting the International Space Station, viewing constellations and planets, and experiencing true darkness is something travelers from around the world are actively seeking.”

The recognition comes as interest in astrotourism continues to grow, with travelers planning vacations around destinations known for exceptional stargazing, astrophotography and nighttime outdoor experiences. The designation elevates South Dakota’s profile among both domestic and international travelers while adding another world-class experience to the state’s renowned outdoor recreation opportunities.

“This designation reflects years of collaboration and a shared commitment to protecting one of our most valuable natural and cultural resources,” said Eric Veach, Badlands National Park Superintendent. “It also represents an opportunity to expand how visitors experience the park, through science, storytelling and a deeper connection to the night sky.”

Few places are better suited for the honor than Badlands National Park. Its rugged buttes and pinnacles, remote setting, and exceptionally low levels of artificial light create an unforgettable backdrop for viewing the Milky Way, meteor showers, and thousands of stars with remarkable clarity. Combined with the park’s rich paleontological resources, wildlife, Indigenous cultural significance, and breathtaking scenery and scenic drives, the Badlands offers visitors an experience unlike anywhere else in the region.

“This accomplishment is deeply personal to me. I grew up on a farm in the middle of South Dakota, where seeing the Milky Way each night felt ordinary,” said Marissa Marshall, executive director of the Badlands National Park Conservancy. “It wasn’t until recently that I realized how rare that experience has become. Protecting our night skies ensures future generations can experience that same sense of wonder.”

Badlands National Park now joins more than 250 International Dark Sky Places around the world—an exclusive network of destinations recognized for preserving one of the planet’s increasingly rare natural resources: truly dark skies.

title: Review: “Five” by Ilona Bannister
byline: By Terri Schlichenmeyer Special to the Pioneer
description: “Five” by Ilona Bannister is a thrilled, published earlier this year by Crown Publishing. Courtesy image
_full_text:
Five.jpg
“Five” by Ilona Bannister is a thrilled, published earlier this year by Crown Publishing. Courtesy image 

Blink.

That’s all it takes, a sliver of time between alive and not alive. A blood vessel rupture, an out-of-control vehicle, a trip or slip or twist and blink. Trouble is, you don’t know when that blink will occur, today, tomorrow, next year. But in the new novel “Five” by Ilona Bannister, it will happen in the next few minutes.

It’s 7:01 on a random morning on a train platform beneath an average British city. The 7:06 a.m. train to London will arrive soon, and eight people wait to board.

What they don’t know is that one of them is about to die.

“To Do List,” as she’s nicknamed, didn’t want to get involved when a fight broke out. “Bad Back” didn’t either, so he tried to slink away with his faux-injury. “Medical Student” wanted to help, but overhead sirens sent him into a childhood-memory-induced panic.

Five people. Three witnesses. Five minutes.

And the train is coming...

If you’re sitting down right now, do this: skooch forward about seven or eight inches, settle in, and get used to it. You’ll be perched right there on the edge of your seat, the entire time you’re reading “Five.”

Told by a snarky narrator with a sarcastic sense of macabre humor, set in a subterranean space that’s very poorly staffed, this is one of those novels that you’ll obsessively clutch all night. Author Ilona Bannister leaves no room for air here; her story is tight, the situations are tense, and the characters are all irredeemably awful people. 

Or are they? As you get to know their backstory, as each character becomes a fuller, rounder person and the train nears, the narrator asks a question: who do you want to die? It’s a spot-on, bolt-upright, astute query, one that changes how you regard this book. Wow.

The word “no” was not in Emma’s vocabulary; in fact, she bulldozed past it, and if that ruined someone’s life, well, so what?  Her vengeful desires were why she made a deal with Liam to have a baby he could ignore after conception, but little Gideon turned out to be more than Emma could handle. Still, she adored the willful, incorrigible, shrieking little brat.

On this day, Liam only needed Emma for one thing: to get his brother to sign papers on an expensive business deal. If she wasn’t willing to smooth things along for him, to sweet-talk his brother, Liam was willing to go to court and take Gideon away from his mother. 

He really didn’t want the boy. He wanted the deal.

As a child, Mrs. Worth was forced to dissect dead animals for her obsessive father, which taught her absolutely zero about love. Sonny was told his entire life that he was better than everyone in every way possible, but tens of thousands of pounds in gambling debt indicated otherwise.

This novel is for twisty-tale lovers, and anyone who wants something knife-sharp and rubber-band taut. Pick up “Five” and you’ll be so immersed that you won’t have time to

Blink.

title: The art of literary translation  exposes the limits of AI
byline: Krupa Shandilya Associate Professor of Sexuality, Women’s and Gender Studies, Amherst College
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
AI Books.png
Courtesy photo 

For centuries, people have dreamed of undoing Babel.

Sci-fi novelists envisioned universal translators, and linguists devised international languages, all in pursuit of a world where one person could speak and another could understand, regardless of where either was born.

Artificial intelligence appears to be taking humanity one step closer to that goal.

AI-powered tools are already being widely used by lawyers to translate legal documents from one language to the next. The mass-market romance publisher Harlequin has turned to AI to translate its novels for international audiences. And hospitals are deploying AI translation to communicate directly with patients in multiple languages.

The speed and skill with which these AI-powered translation tools operate are certainly impressive.

But there is an important frontier for translation technology, one that it might never be able to breach: the poem.

That’s because translating poetry, thus far, has been a uniquely human experience. It demands intimate knowledge of two languages, which large language models certainly possess. But it also requires a mastery of different cultures and perspectives, what literary critic Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak calls a “worlding” of language and culture.

Pushing the limits of language

When scholars have studied the creativity of chatbots by prompting them to produce poetry, they’ve noticed that the poems tend to be more homogeneous and standardized than those written by humans.

Chatbots’ poetry translations have similar issues.

AI seems to struggle in three main areas: rendering metaphor, decoding complex sentence structure and creatively conveying mood or emotion.

To demonstrate these flaws, I worked closely with Adeeba Shahid Talukder, an award-winning poet and translator, to write this piece and to translate the 1953 poem “Mulaqat,” or “Meeting,” composed by one of the most famous Urdu poets of the 20th century, Faiz Ahmed Faiz.

Faiz was born in 1911 in Sialkot, in pre-Partition India. In 1947, when that area in the Punjab became part of present-day Pakistan, Faiz became a citizen of the newly founded country, though his relationship with it was marked by both hope and disillusionment. He lived in different parts of the world for long stretches of time, but he returned to Pakistan toward the end of his life. He died there in 1984.

His poetry is celebrated for its marriage of classical tropes like the ache of unfulfilled longing for the beloved, and the lover’s willingness to be consumed or destroyed in his pursuit of her, with the political struggles of his time, like the plight of working people and the dream of a Marxist revolution. His poetry is notoriously difficult to translate because of its highly ornate, extended metaphors, which have few easy equivalents in English. This forces the translator – be it human or machine – to push the limits of language.

From 1951 to 1955, Faiz was imprisoned on allegations of sedition against the Pakistani state. His first three months were spent in solitary confinement.

From Faiz’s letters, scholars learned that despite the isolation of his imprisonment, he felt as if the experience made him more attuned to his senses, as if he were “falling in love again for the first time.” His time in jail was also among his most prolific as a poet, with “Meeting” composed during his sentence.

Here’s our translation of the opening verses of “Meeting”:

 This night is the dark, lush tree of a grief greater than you and I— greater, for caravans of torch-bearing stars have lost themselves in the siege of its branches; in its shadow, a thousand moons have wept away all their light. This night is the dark, lush tree of a grief greater than you and I— but from the tree of this very night the amber leaves of these moments have fallen, grown entangled in your locks and flowered as the fires of pomegranate blossoms; its dew has rained drops of silence upon your brow, bedecked it with a silver string of pearls. 

When prompted to provide a “lyrical translation into English,” ChatGPT produced the following:

 This night is a tree of pain, Vaster than you, vaster than me. Its branches bear Thousands of torches in place of stars, Caravans lost Within a thousand moons’ shadows, And all my light has wept itself away. Yet from this very tree, A few golden leaves of fleeting moments Fall into your hair, Entwined, they bloom like roses. From its dew in quiet, A few drops rest upon your brow, And glitter like tiny diamonds. 

Chatbots fail at translation’s most basic task

When Faiz composed “Meeting,” he had been separated from his wife and two daughters for two years. He was keenly aware of missing parts of their childhoods that would never return.

This biographical information can help translators understand the poem’s exploration of “vasl,” or the meeting of lover and beloved. A common trope in classical Urdu poetry, it usually captures the joy and exultation of the lovers’ union.

But in Faiz’s poem, the union with the beloved also contains an acute awareness of mortality and the transience of beauty – a recognition of what has been lost, and the suffering still to come.

That’s why we rendered the opening lines of “Meeting” as “This night is the dark,/lush tree of a grief greater/than you and I.”

ChatGPT’s translation is more literal: “This night is the tree of pain.”

While there is nothing technically wrong with this translation, the chatbot’s version doesn’t capture the nuances of the tree metaphor and the way its dense, expansive branches can encompass the complexity and beauty of the emotions evoked by the night of the lovers’ union.

AI also fails to grasp the poem’s intricate sentence structure. ChatGPT has translated “in its shadow a thousand moons / have wept away all their light” as a nonsensical construction: “Within a thousand moons’ shadows, / And all my light has wept itself away.”

This error appears to have happened because the chatbot translated “apra” – a reflexive possessive pronoun in Urdu – as “my,” inaccurately parsing it as referring to the speaker instead of the moons.

Finally, and most importantly, AI models lack the ability to express emotion the way a human can. A machine with no bodily experience of being human cannot meaningfully perceive a poem so enmeshed in human experience. Its engagement is merely superficial.

In its attempt to convey the mood of the original piece, ChatGPT offers: “From its dew in quiet, / A few drops rest upon your brow, / And glitter like tiny diamonds.”

It’s clear that ChatGPT is struggling to decode the grammatical structure of the poem and is trying to make the text lyrical enough to convey the awe and wonder of the original. But the model’s contrivances toward the lyrical – for example, describing diamonds as “tiny” or “glittering” – have no relation to the original poem.

“From its dew in quiet” is an incoherent clause. The phrase that seems to have thrown the model off is “isi ki shabnam se khamoshi ke yeh cand qatre,” or “its dew / has rained drops of silence.”

Urdu literary critic Shamsur Rahman Faruqi has explained how Urdu poets “treat metaphor as fact and then go on to create further metaphors from that fact.” In “Meeting,” the metaphor of the night of the reunion as a tree becomes a fact, which allows for the flowering of a new metaphor – that of the dew on its leaves as drops of silence that fall on the lover and their beloved. These silences, heavy with sorrow, then adorn the beloved like precious jewels, conveying the idea that only a profound grief can beget such beauty.

The model has failed at conjuring this sense of wonder because it cannot parse the poem in accordance with the literary conventions of Urdu poetry.

ChatGPT prefaced its translated text by assuring us that it had “crafted a lyrical, poetic English version of Faiz’s ‘Mulaqat,’ keeping the imagery, rhythm, and emotional flow intact so it reads like a poem rather than a literal translation.”

Yet as we have shown, its translation fails to accomplish the most basic task of literary translation: to convey the heart of the original.

Chatbots, in other words, are a poor substitute for the literary translator, and they bolster the assertion of the late Indian poet, scholar and translator A.K. Ramanujan that “only poems can translate poems.”

Adeeba Shahid Talukder helped with the research and writing of this article, in addition to the translation of Faiz’s poem.

title: Lead mayor calls for certified police officers
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: LEAD — Now that the city offers competitive pay, and has loosened its residency policy, Mayor Dustin Heupel wants to try hiring more certified police officers, to fill open positions again.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

LEAD — Now that the city offers competitive pay, and has loosened its residency policy, Mayor Dustin Heupel wants to try hiring more certified police officers, to fill open positions again. 

The discussion came up during the regular Lead City Commission meeting, Monday, when Lead Police Chief Robert Williams asked to hire Katherine Szutz, who is not a certified officer. Williams said new hires who are uncertified spend about 90 days in field training before working any shifts alone, and then they receive about 5 more months of police work before attending the police academy in Pierre for 13 weeks. 

“The 8 months gives the officer a true look at what this job demands, and we are starting to see more often that in that 8 months prior to going to the academy, this is not the right job for them,” Williams said. 

Szutz was part of an original pool of candidates that a city panel interviewed in June, and was one of the top contenders for a position with the police department. Williams said she is a resident of the community and has family ties in the community. 

“She fits a lot of the bill,” Williams said. “If you take out the certification, it would be a no-brainer. Katherine is everything they (commissioners) have wanted for years, which is an officer vested in this community.” 

But Heupel said he wanted to search for more qualified candidates in future hires. In May, the city of Lead adopted a new residency policy that allows employees to live within 13 miles of Lead City Hall, and over the last few years the city has been increasing wages for certified officers, in order to become more competitive. 

“I think it would be wise of us to do better advertising and marketing for the open positions,” Heupel said. “I know you’re short staffed. I know our staff has a lot on their plate already, so getting a person in there is important.” 

But if the city hires a noncertified officer, Heupel said, that officer has to attend the police academy and is not available for at least 13 weeks anyway. Whereas, if the city waited to advertise the position and try to get candidates with existing certification, the new hires would be immediately ready for the job. 

“We haven’t advertised this position since our residency policy has been changed,” Heupel said. “I would like to see how it affects our pool of candidates.” 

Commissioner Valerie Meiners agreed. 

“I just think we should give at least one more try to get a certified person in,” she said. 

But with the Lead Police Department down to 4 officers out of the 7 required to fill all shifts, and with employees who need to have vacations and time off, Williams said he has an immediate need to get officers in uniform. Additionally, he said his officers conduct all of their own investigations — and that workload continues to pile up. 

“I understand it would be nice to have a Hail Mary and get a certified officer,” Williams said. “I understand promoting for that. It’s just how long do we wait for that certified officer?” 

Lead City Administrator Robin Lucero told the commission that during their exit interviews, officers who leave the police department cite burnout and working alone as their primary reasons for leaving. 

“Working alone is not only a fear of what could happen with only one officer responding to critical scenes,” Williams said. “Working alone also affects the case load of the officers, as the case loads can add up quickly, resulting in late and lengthy investigations. That’s not fair to the public or victims in cases. Officers are coming to work sick and sometimes with injuries to fill their shifts, as filling the shifts is a must.

“We do want commitment from the investment we put into officers,” Williams continued. “But overworking the officers and not providing the department with the 7 full time police officers to effectively cover the city is what will (cause us to) continue to have the turnover rate.” 

Following some further discussion, the commission approved hiring Szutz, with a 3-2 vote, with Heupel and Meiners dissenting.

title: Meade Co. Fair and 4-H Achievement Days  offer family fun, competitions and  community spirit this weekend
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: Korie Christinsen won grand champion dairy cow at the 2025 Meade County Fair and 4-H Achievement Days.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
2. fair.JPG
Korie Christinsen won grand champion dairy cow at the 2025 Meade County Fair and 4-H Achievement Days.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

STURGIS — The Meade County Fair and 4-H Achievement Days will bring 3 days of exhibits, livestock shows, contests, family activities and community entertainment to the Meade County Fair Building on the Sturgis Brown High School campus through Saturday.

With activities ranging from animal shows and open class exhibits to watermelon-eating contests, Ag Olympics and mutton busting, organizers are inviting residents of all ages to attend and take part in one of Meade County’s annual summer traditions.

“We invite the entire community to come out to the fair on Friday and Saturday,” said Jenny Voigt, 4-H Youth Program advisor with South Dakota State University Extension. “There really is something for everyone.”

The fair officially began Thursday evening. 

Community members are encouraged to showcase their talents in categories including gardening, baking, quilting, sewing, knitting, crocheting, crafts and more.

“Because this is a county fair, it’s not just a 4-H event,” Voigt said. “We encourage people of all ages to enter exhibits and share their talents.”

Today’s activities center on the small animal shows, featuring poultry, rabbits and companion animals. Throughout the day, visitors can enjoy family-friendly competitions including watermelon-eating contests, turtle races and frog-jumping contests. Children planning to participate in the races should bring their own turtles and frogs.

Food will also be available throughout the day with Mimi’s Prairie Lunchbox food truck and the Meade County 4-H Junior Leaders concession stand.

This evening’s festivities include a free community barbecue, Ag Olympics and the always-popular mutton busting competition.

Voigt said the Northern Hills Ag Fest Committee, a partnership with the Sturgis Area Chamber of Commerce, once again will organize the evening activities.

“We’re thankful they continue to provide these events each year,” Voigt said. “Families should come early to complete the registration forms and waiver. Teams of four kids can compete in the Ag Olympics, and it’s always a lot of fun.”

Saturday begins with the final Brandon Delzer Memorial Run, honoring the longtime Meade County 4-H member. Registration opens at 7 a.m., walkers begin at 7:30 a.m. and runners start at 8 a.m.

Because of the forecast for hot temperatures, livestock show times have been moved earlier in the day. The swine show will begin at 7:30 a.m., followed by a rolling schedule of the remaining large animal shows.

Afternoon activities include a bubble gum blowing contest, dunk tank and an ice cream social before the fair concludes with the annual 4-H Premium Livestock Sale and pie auction.

Voigt said Meade County’s 4-H program continues to grow, with approximately 330 members participating in 13 clubs throughout the county.

“We have everything from shooting sports and rodeo to our traditional clubs that meet throughout the year and complete community service projects,” she said.

In addition to celebrating the accomplishments of local youth, the fair also showcases continued improvements to the Meade County Fair Building.

The volunteer-led fundraising effort has allowed organizers to make significant upgrades over the past several years, including interior improvements and site enhancements.

“We’ve continued finishing the interior of the building and added new gravel,” Voigt said. “Our next big goal is installing permanent restrooms. We’ve been fundraising for that project and we’re getting closer. Hopefully we’ll have those in place by next year’s fair.”

Voigt encourages families, alumni and community members to stop by throughout the weekend to support Meade County’s 4-H members and enjoy the wide variety of activities.

“The fair is a celebration of our youth, agriculture and community,” she said. “We hope everyone comes out and enjoys everything the weekend has to offer.”

title: Black Hills counties among first to adopt new sales tax option for homeowner property tax reduction
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — At least 4 South Dakota counties — including 3 in the Black Hills — have decided to implement sales taxes to lower property taxes for homeowners, while several more plan to consider it later or let voters decide in November.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — At least 4 South Dakota counties — including 3 in the Black Hills — have decided to implement sales taxes to lower property taxes for homeowners, while several more plan to consider it later or let voters decide in November.

The opportunity stems from a new state law that took effect July 1, giving counties in the state their first chance to impose a sales tax (the state and cities already have that authority). Counties can implement up to a half-percent sales tax, deposit the revenue into a property tax reduction fund and apply it as a credit on homeowners’ property tax bills. Counties account for 27% of property taxes in the state. Schools account for 55% and cities 13%.

Revenue beyond what’s needed to offset owner-occupied property taxes must be split evenly between commercial and agricultural property tax reduction. When a county commission decides to impose the sales tax, local residents have the option to petition the decision to a vote of the public.

Black Hills commissioners counting on tourism

A 5-county region of the Black Hills generated $1.83 billion in tourism spending in 2024, according to the state tourism dashboard.

Pennington County Commissioner Ron Weifenbach is counting on tourism spending to pay for a portion of his residents’ property tax bills. The Pennington County Commission unanimously passed an ordinance Tuesday to implement a half-percent sales tax. The tax is scheduled to take effect in January.

County commissioners for Meade and Custer counties also passed sales tax ordinances this month. Both taxes will take effect in January.

While county residents will pay the sales tax whenever they purchase something, Weifenbach said a large share of the sales tax will be paid for by visitors and tourists in the Black Hills area. Pennington County, which includes Rapid City, accounted for over half of the Black Hills region’s tourism spending in 2024.

“We’re doing something instead of nothing” in response to rising property taxes, Weifenbach told South Dakota Searchlight.

According to the Governor’s Office, the owner of a $325,000 home in Pennington County could save 22% on their property taxes.

The Custer County Commission unanimously approved its ordinance on Wednesday. Homeowners there are projected to save 12%.

“It should be a no-brainer for Custer County,” Commission Chairman Jim Lintz told South Dakota Searchlight.

Custer County is in the Black Hills, home to Custer State Park, and is a popular tourist destination.

Meade County passed its ordinance on July 14 with a unanimous vote. Since the tax won’t take effect until January, the county will miss tax collections during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally in August. Homeowners are projected to save 12% on their tax bill.

The details of how the new taxes will lower property tax bills — including when credits will appear — have yet to be determined. Counties can choose to credit homeowners in January, when tax bills come out, or wait until they have a year of collections.

Fall River County commissioners, in the southern Black Hills, chose to put the question to voters in November, Auditor Sue Ganje confirmed. If the measure passes, commissioners would then adopt an ordinance with July 1, 2027, as the earliest possible implementation date.

Lawrence County commissioners, in the Northern Black Hills, plan to discuss the potential tax after they finalize their budget at the end of the month, Commissioner Eric Jennings said.

Discussion takes shape in other counties across state

Codington County, which includes Watertown, passed its ordinance in a 4-1 vote on Tuesday. The sole vote against was from Tyler McElhany, who did not respond to a request for comment from South Dakota Searchlight. The sales tax will take effect in January. 

Doug Allen, a member of the public, spoke against the ordinance, calling it a “regressive tax” because it would apply to necessities like food and clothing, hitting lower-income residents proportionally harder than wealthier ones.

“I’d love some property tax relief. I think we pay quite a bit,” Allen said. “But, that said, I think this is the wrong way to go about it.”

Codington County homeowners are projected to save 23% on their property taxes, according to the Governor’s Office.

Commissioner Lee Gabel spoke in favor.

“This causes us as county commissioners and officials to care more about sales and business in our county in a different way,” Gabel said, “as opposed to just valuations on property.”

Other commissions discussing the idea include Lincoln County (home to part of Sioux Falls), Brown County (home to Aberdeen) and Lyman County, in a rural area of central South Dakota crossed by Interstate 90.

Minnehaha County, which includes Sioux Falls, does not have any “imminent plans” to discuss the sales tax, Commission Administrator Tom Greco said.

Lake County commissioners declined to pursue a county sales tax earlier this month, according to reporting from the Madison Daily Leader.

Day County Auditor Tonya Lehman said the small northeastern county will “sit back and wait.” The largest city in Day County is Webster, with a population of roughly 1,730.

“My opinion is it won’t pay for itself at this point,” Lehman said, adding that the new tax would require new software and additional administrative expenses. “I would almost have to say we’d have to have more businesses in the county to be able to maintain it.”

Beyond the county sales tax option, lawmakers and Gov. Larry Rhoden approved additional legislation in March that will use revenue from a 0.3-percentage-point increase in the state sales tax next year to reduce school property taxes for homeowners statewide.

title: Quickpicks: Inspired by the Odyssey
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
0724 Ocean.png
Courtesy photo 

A summer blockbuster has propelled one roughly 3,000-year-old text to the top 10 most popular audiobooks on Audible this week. Homer’s Odyssey is having an undeniable resurgence. Maybe you’ve seen Christopher Nolan’s new film and are looking for some companion reads. Maybe, you’re caught up in the thrill of Odyssey summer. Either way, we’ve got recommendations for you. 

 1. “The Odyssey” by  Homer, translated by Emily Wilson

Genre: Classics/Poetry

In this fresh, authoritative version — the first English translation of The Odyssey by a woman — this stirring tale of shipwrecks, monsters, and magic comes alive in an entirely new way. Written in iambic pentameter verse and a vivid, contemporary idiom, this engrossing translation matches the number of lines in the Greek original, thus striding at Homer’s sprightly pace and singing with a voice that echoes Homer’s music.

2. “Circe” by Madeline Miller

Genre: Fantasy

In the house of Helios, god of the sun and mightiest of the Titans, a daughter is born. But Circe is a strange child — neither powerful like her father nor viciously alluring like her mother. Turning to the world of mortals for companionship, she discovers that she does possess power: the power of witchcraft, which can transform rivals into monsters and menace the gods themselves.

3. “Mythos” by Stephen Fry 

Genre: Mythology 

In Mythos, the ancient stories of the Greek gods are brought thrillingly to life by one of the great storytellers of our time. Beloved writer, actor, and comedian Stephen Fry retells the legendary myths of ancient Greece with warmth, humor, and extraordinary narrative flair, introducing readers to the dazzling world of gods, titans, and heroes.

4. “Clytemnestra” by Costanza Casati 

Genre: Fantasy

You were born to a king, but you marry a tyrant. You stand by helplessly as he sacrifices your child to placate the gods. You watch him wage war on a foreign shore, and you comfort yourself with violent thoughts of your own. Because this was not the first offence against you. This was not the life you ever deserved. And this will not be your undoing. Slowly, you plot.

5. “The Silence of the Girls” by Pat Barker 

Genre: Historical Fiction

The ancient city of Troy has withstood a decade under siege of the powerful Greek army, which continues to wage bloody war over a stolen woman — Helen. In the Greek camp, another woman — Briseis — watches and waits for the war’s outcome. She was queen of one of Troy’s neighboring kingdoms, until Achilles, Greece’s greatest warrior, sacked her city and murdered her husband and brothers. Briseis becomes Achilles’s concubine, a prize of battle, and must adjust quickly in order to survive a radically different life, as one of the many conquered women who serve the Greek army.

6. “The Penelopiad” by Margaret Atwood

Genre: Fiction

In Homer’s account in The Odyssey, Penelope—wife of Odysseus and cousin of the beautiful Helen of Troy—is portrayed as the quintessential faithful wife, her story a salutary lesson through the ages. Left alone for 20 years when Odysseus goes off to fight in the Trojan War after the abduction of Helen, Penelope manages, in the face of scandalous rumors, to maintain the kingdom of Ithaca, bring up her wayward son, and keep over a hundred suitors at bay, simultaneously. When Odysseus finally comes home after enduring hardships, overcoming monsters, and sleeping with goddesses, he kills her suitors and — curiously — 12 of her maids. In a splendid contemporary twist to the ancient story, Margaret Atwood has chosen to give the telling of it to Penelope and to her 12 hanged maids, asking: “What led to the hanging of the maids, and what was Penelope really up to?”

title: Sturgis approves  school resource officer contract
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — An agreement between the city of Sturgis and the Meade School District will put one police officer in the high school, and have one officer who splits time between the middle and elementary schools.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

STURGIS — An agreement between the city of Sturgis and the Meade School District will put one police officer in the high school, and have one officer who splits time between the middle and elementary schools. 

On Monday, the Sturgis City Council approved the school resource officer contract that has been in place for many years. Sturgis Police Chief Geody VanDewater said the school district and city have had one school resource officer for about 20 years, but a few years ago the city received federal grants to pay for 2 officers. The contract states the school district will reimburse the city $125,709, or 75% of the salary and fringe benefits for the officers who will work in the schools during the 9 month school year. The city of Sturgis will absorb the remaining 25% of the personnel costs, provide vehicles, equipment, uniforms, and other operational support, and utilize the officers during the summer months. 

According to the contract, the school resource officers will emphasize student safety, educate and provide support for crime prevention, mentor students, provide educational outreach, and foster positive relationships between law enforcement, students, staff and the community. 

The school resource officers in Sturgis are Officers Matthew Jacobs and Josh Buntain, who have worked in that capacity for about 4 years, VanDewater said. 

The contract will be effective Sept. 1 through Aug. 31, 2027.

title: The Mercy Sloane Chronicles: Chapter 11
byline: By Eliza Blue A work of serialized fiction, special to the Pioneer
description: Arlo had bought the old man’s land in late winter. Once they’d gotten the flock moved to the new pasture, Arlo went out every few days to check on the man, bring him supplies, and see how lambing was progressing. The older man was always happy to see him, always offered him a cup of weak coffee brewed on the sheepwagon’s tiny wood stove. The man would talk about this ewe and that, gesturing toward the flock. _full_text:
The Mercy Sloane Chronicles

Arlo had bought the old man’s land in late winter. Once they’d gotten the flock moved to the new pasture, Arlo went out every few days to check on the man, bring him supplies, and see how lambing was progressing. The older man was always happy to see him, always offered him a cup of weak coffee brewed on the sheepwagon’s tiny wood stove. The man would talk about this ewe and that, gesturing toward the flock. That one had had an easy birth in the night; that one had needed help. Arlo would nod along, though the truth was he didn’t have a clue what the man was talking about. All the ewes looked the same to him.

One morning, Arlo arrived to find the man cradling a newborn lamb in his arms. Only its wooly white head was visible; the rest of its body was wrapped inside the man’s coat. 

“Just got a bit chilled,” the old man said in a soft, twinkling voice, the voice you’d use to talk to a small child or your beloved. “He’ll be right as rain once he warms.”

It was a gray morning, and a gentle mist lingered in the air. The sun had risen an hour before, but was covered by clouds. Arlo stood watching the man and the lamb and the swirling mist. The spring wind was pushing the fog north, and suddenly, a few thin rays of light broke through, touching the man and the lamb, bathing them in a circle of soft gold. The air began to spark, and Arlo heard humming, rich and deep, like the vibrating wings of a thousand hummingbirds or the angular bowing of an ancient, hidden violin. He looked to his right and to his left, but saw only the wind brushing the tips of the grass as gently as a lover might. 

Arlo backed away from the man and the lamb, muttering something about a forgotten chore, and when he looked at them again from the rearview of his pickup, the light had changed, the humming was gone. The old man was just a man, and the lamb was just a lamb again.

Arlo stayed away for almost a week. After the day of mist, there had been two days of rain, and now everything was glowing with new life. As he drove across the pasture, he could smell the wet soil and hear a meadowlark calling bright and high, stringing together a melody of dizzying trills. Funny how much you missed, he thought, living in town.

On the seat next to him was a clean rag wrapped around half a dozen of Marla’s fresh buns, still warm from her oven. He’d also brought a thermos of coffee with cream and a heaping spoon of sugar, too. Didn’t the old man deserve something sweet for once? 

Arlo had spent the week trying to decide what he was going to tell the man, because he knew he had to tell him something. He could still hear the humming, still see the golden light, and he knew he was being offered a chance to make things right. Should he deed the land back? Offer to move the man to town somehow? Buy him a better wagon? All his ideas seemed silly or unrealistic–Arlo was rich by Antelope standards, but not by many others. That’s why he’d stayed away. Something had to change, but he didn’t know what.

When he pulled up to the sheep wagon, he was greeted by a strange sight. The flock was gathered in a bunch, slowly milling in a circle. Some had their heads bowed, grazing, but most were looking at the sheep wagon while their babies nursed and slept beneath them. 

As Arlo climbed out of the pickup and walked toward the sheep and the wagon, the old man’s dog bolted wildly from a nearby thicket of brush, barking an alarm. The dog was obviously the cause of the flock’s unusual behavior, and Arlo started to yell and shoo her off, but as soon as she saw him, the dog began to pant and whine, her whole body trembling. 

 Arlo had never heard that dog bark before; usually, she stayed hidden, waiting for him to leave so she and the old man could resume the lives that had been interrupted by his intrusion. Now, she came up beside him and then lay down at his feet, still trembling, her brown eyes staring up into his. Arlo let out a long, ragged sigh. He knew in that moment exactly what he was going to find in the wagon.

 Eliza Blue TMC
Eliza Blue 

The old man was lying peacefully on his bed. His arms were folded over his chest. His eyes were closed. He’d been dead for a while, the skin of his face slack and stiff around his skull, and the first flies of the year already gathered and buzzing. Arlo set the coffee and buns down on the two parallel planks of wood that served as the wagon’s table, then sat down on the wagon’s only chair, holding his knees with his hands.

Arlo shook his head and crossed his arms as tears poured down his face. He thought about his childhood–his mother’s kisses, his father’s gruff and hard-earned compliments. He thought about the morning light on Marla’s face when he peeked through the kitchen window to watch her scrub the floors. He thought about his boys, already so grown up, when only moments ago they’d been babies. 

“Lord have mercy,” Arlo had whispered. “Lord, have mercy,” and then he bowed his head to pray.

That had been fifteen years ago. He was the old man now. Lying next to Marla in the darkness, he crossed his arms over his chest and closed his eyes. “I think I would like to spend more time with the sheep.” he said aloud, and then fell immediately to sleep.

title: Sturgis adopts Safe Streets and Roads for All plan
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Lazelle Street was identified as a major priority for safety improvements in the city’s latest Safe Streets and Roads for All plan. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
Sturgis safe route1.JPG
Lazelle Street was identified as a major priority for safety improvements in the city’s latest Safe Streets and Roads for All plan. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

STURGIS — A transportation plan that establishes Sturgis priorities for providing safer roadways and reducing fatal and serious crashes has been completed, Public Works Director Rick Bush said. 

On Monday, the Sturgis City Council approved the Safe Streets and Roads For All plan, which was developed through a federal grant the city received in 2024 from the United States Department of Transportation. The plan is the result of a year of technical analyses, public engagement, and coordination with federal and state transportation partners. Over the course of 2025, representatives from J.O. Consultants examined crash data from the past 10 years, and evaluated the safety of the city’s transportation system for pedestrians, motorists, bicyclists, motorcyclists, and more. 

“The plan establishes a data driven process for identifying safety priorities and reducing fatal and serious injury crashes,” Bush said. “It also provides the policy framework needed to pursue future federal and state transportation funding. The plan will guide future prioritization, planning, engineering, maintenance, and operational decisions. Throughout the project, crash history was analyzed, public input was gathered, and roadway conditions were evaluated across the community. The result is a prioritized list of recommendations focused on reducing fatal and serious injuries for everyone who uses our transportation system.

“In short, adopting the plan prepares us for future opportunities, without committing the city to every recommendation today,” he continued. “Adoption establishes the city’s long-term transportation safety network, while preserving the council’s authority over every future project, budget agreement, and funding commitment.” 

Bush stressed to the council that adopting the plan does not commit the city to any specific project, but it establishes a framework of priorities for future projects. 

According to the plan, top priority safety corridors include Lazelle Street and Junction Avenue. Additional priority locations include Sherman Street, Ballpark Road, Douglas Street, and Third Street. 

“These locations are not only areas that may receive improvements, but they represent where the data indicates the greatest opportunity to reduce severe crashes,” Bush said. 

He added that recommendations are not limited to major construction projects, but can also include engineering improvements, operational changes, and policy updates. For example, some changes included in the plan were improved pedestrian crossings and ADA accessibility, enhanced pedestrian and bicycle connectivity, school zone speed management, and more. 

Bush also said work the South Dakota Department of Transportation has planned to improve Lazelle Street, could address some of the priorities in the plan. The first phase of the plan could include adding a center island to Lazelle Street, so pedestrians have a landing place, and can cross Lazelle in 2 sections. 

“What that does is it eliminates that big time gap to be able to get from one side of the street to the other,” he said. “Some of the things we looked at as part of this plan and that we’ve heard from community members coming to council is the lack of the ability to safely cross Lazelle Street.” 

Bush said the plan was developed with significant public input from all sectors of the community. 

“We had kids from out at the high school that were a part of one of our committees,” he said. “We had a big group of people. This wasn’t just a city initiative. Actually, the city had the least part in it. Most of what is in here actually came form the citizens and where they felt unsafe, and where they wanted to see improvements made.”

title: BH National Forest  increases fire restrictions
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Courtesy graphic
_full_text:
Have your say Black Hills National Forest treatment project opens for public feedback
Courtesy graphic 

CUSTER — The Black Hills National Forest will implement Stage 2 Fire Restrictions starting at 12:01 a.m. on Monday due to critical fire weather conditions.

Fire danger is increasing, and these restrictions are being implemented to protect public and firefighter safety amid current and anticipated elevated wildfire risk. The restrictions apply to all Black Hills National Forest lands within the states of South Dakota and Wyoming, including all developed recreation sites such as campgrounds and day use areas. Restrictions will remain in place until Dec.27, unless rescinded earlier.

Under Stage 2 Fire Restrictions, the following are prohibited:

·       Igniting, building, maintaining, attending, or using a fire, campfire, charcoal barbecue, or grill, except if using a device solely fueled by liquid or gas that can be turned on and off in an area barren or cleared of all flammable materials within three feet of the device. 

·       Smoking, except in an enclosed vehicle or building. 

·       Welding or operating an acetylene or other torch with open flame. 

·       Using an explosive. 

·       Possessing or using a motor vehicle off established roads, motorized trails or established parking areas, except when parking in an area devoid of vegetation within 10 feet of the vehicle.

title: Lead pushes  budget to November  Property tax levies still  due by October
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: LEAD — The city of Lead has pushed its budget timeline back a few months.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

LEAD — The city of Lead has pushed its budget timeline back a few months. 

On Monday, the Lead City Commission approved an ordinance that states the city will introduce its 2027 budget during the first meeting in November. In previous years, the city has finalized its budget at its second meeting in September. 

According to South Dakota Codified Law 9-21-34, a municipality may move the deadline for introducing its budget to the first meeting in November, if it passes an ordinance that authorizes the move. 

Mayor Dustin Heupel said he wanted to push the budget timeline back to late September, so the city will have a better idea of how much revenue could be available from sales taxes. In previous years, when the city started budget talks in July, commissioners only had sales tax revenue data for the first 6 months of the year. Heupel said he wants to have as much data as possible, moving into the budget discussions. 

Lawrence County Auditor Brenda McGruder said while state law allows the city to push its budget approval back to November, the city’s property tax levy must be certified to the county by Oct. 1, so property tax notices can be prepared and sent out. Lead City Administrator Robin Lucero said before Oct. 1 commissioners will review Lead property assessment values from the county to determine their tax request for 2027, and that request will determine the city’s levy amount for taxes payable in 2027. The city commission has not yet determined when that discussion will take place, she said. 

In the past, other neighboring municipalities, including Sturgis and Deadwood, have also moved their budget approval deadlines to November. 

According to the city’s timetable that was introduced on Monday, budget discussions will begin Sept. 21, when commissioners will introduce the budget process and goals and review the city’s strategic plan. On Sept. 28, the commission will discuss employee wages and its revenue forecast for the coming year. The Oct. 4 and Oct. 11 meetings will be when the commission discusses department head budgets, and prioritize upcoming projects. On Oct. 18 the city will discuss nonprofit organization requests. A draft budget is scheduled for completion by Oct. 25, and on Nov. 2 the city commission will consider the first reading of its 2027 budget ordinance, with final adoption scheduled for Nov. 15. 

All meetings are subject to change, including adding or removing meetings according to the commission’s need for discussion, according to the budget timetable.

title: Nisland to host  Butte-Lawrence County Fair
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Lawrence-Butte County Fair will host a variety of attractions starting Monday. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Fair 1.JPG
The Lawrence-Butte County Fair will host a variety of attractions starting Monday. Pioneer file photo 

NISLAND — The annual Butte-Lawrence County Fair kicks off Monday in Nisland.  

The fair office will be open from around 7:30 a.m. to 6 p.m. each day. 

Attractions at the fair include a horse show, pig wrestling, turtle racing, an auction, a free barbecue, and a chicken bingo event, in which participants take bets predicting where a chicken will defecate. 

“That’s a lot of fun,” said Cindy Riley, administrative assistant for Butte-Lawrence County Extension Office.

Ribbons are awarded to participants in certain events. According to the 2026 South Dakota 4-H State Fair Book, purple ribbons designate “superior” performance. Blue ribbons designate “excellent” performance. Red ribbons designate “average” performance. White ribbons designate a performance that has “room for improvement.”

Riley said that new events include a Bred and Fed event and a Farm Olympics event. 

4-H is a youth organization funded by the federal government with a focus on agriculture. Some event divisions are open only to 4-H members. Others are open to the public.

title: Contractor hired for $464K to complete  Spearfish airport water main extension
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: The new terminal at Black Hills Airport/Clyde Ice Field will be served by a larger water main and hydrants Wilson Contracting will now install. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Airport waterline.JPG
The new terminal at Black Hills Airport/Clyde Ice Field will be served by a larger water main and hydrants Wilson Contracting will now install. Pioneer file photo 

SPEARFISH — Improvements at the Black Hills Airport/Clyde Ice Field will continue through at least the spring of 2027, after the Spearfish City Council, Monday, awarded a water main extension project — which will service the new terminal at the fixed base operation — to Piedmont-based Wilson Contracting for $464,706.97.

The work includes installation of an 8-inch water main, connecting the newly built airport terminal and extending the line to hydrants within the airport.

“We had 11 bids that we received in this project. The engineer’s estimate was $765,000 and change, so well below the engineer’s estimate,” Spearfish Public Works Director Adam McMahon said. “The budget for this project is $1.6 million. That’s combined for this project as well as the access road and parking lot for the terminal.”

The city agreed to cover the cost of the utilities, parking lot, and road improvements, as a condition for the award of a Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) grant that covered the cost of the new terminal construction.

Wilson Contracting’s bid was reviewed by FMG Engineering and recommended for approval.

“On Wilson Contracting, have we worked with these folks before?” Mayor John Senden asked McMahon.

“We haven’t, but we checked references on them, and we received positive feedback from them. They’re a smaller company, but it sounds like they do quality work,” McMahon said.

title: Billionaire-funded national group seeks to influence voters in SD runoff election
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — Some of the political postcards mailed to South Dakota voters in the week ahead of Tuesday’s runoff election for the Republican nomination for governor are financed by a national group that received all of its recent contributions from a Pennsylvania billionaire.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — Some of the political postcards mailed to South Dakota voters in the week ahead of Tuesday’s runoff election for the Republican nomination for governor are financed by a national group that received all of its recent contributions from a Pennsylvania billionaire. 

Federal Election Commission records show that the School Freedom Fund political action committee has raised $15 million since last year from billionaire and Republican mega-donor Jeffrey Yass, whose net worth is an estimated $67.4 billion. Yass is an investment trading firm owner, TikTok investor and advocate of school-choice options, including public funding to help children attend private schools. 

School Freedom Fund is a type of political action committee known as a super PAC, which can raise and spend unlimited amounts of money as long as it doesn’t coordinate with candidates. 

School Freedom Fund’s treasurer, Adam Rozanzky, did not immediately respond to a Searchlight message asking about the group’s motivation for getting involved in a South Dakota campaign.

Despite School Freedom Fund’s name, two postcards it sent to South Dakota voters do not mention schools or education. Instead, they characterize Gov. Larry Rhoden as a “big taxin’” politician for several actions throughout his career as governor and previously as a legislator, without providing context. 

The postcards say, for example, that Rhoden “raised our sales taxes 3 times.” 

Rhoden did sign 3 sales tax bills into law earlier this year. One uses revenue from a previously scheduled increase in the state sales tax rate to lower the school-imposed portion of homeowner property taxes, another creates an optional county sales tax to be applied toward homeowner property tax reduction, and the third creates an optional sales tax that cities can use temporarily to fund special projects such as building an arena. 

Rhoden faces Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden in Tuesday’s runoff election. The winner will advance to the Nov. 3 general election to face Democratic nominee Dan Ahlers.

title: Own a piece of Deadwood history
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Jason Mook, owner of Deadwood Custom Cycles, pictured left, stands with his wife, Deadwood Mayor Charlie Struble-Mook, in front of a motorcycle that is being custom built and raffled to celebrate 150 years of history in Deadwood. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
Deadwood 150 years motorcycle raffle.jpg
Jason Mook, owner of Deadwood Custom Cycles, pictured left, stands with his wife, Deadwood Mayor Charlie Struble-Mook, in front of a motorcycle that is being custom built and raffled to celebrate 150 years of history in Deadwood. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

DEADWOOD — In celebration of Deadwood’s 150 years of wild west, gunslinging history, Deadwood Custom Cycle is giving back to the community with a raffle for a Deadwood-themed custom motorcycle. 

“I’m a firm believer that you have to give back, and you have to give back and you have to give back,” said Jason Mook, owner of Deadwood Custom Cycles. “Deadwood has been so great to me. When I decided to relocate my shop here, everybody just accepted me and accepted the idea of a full service, full custom motorcycle shop right smack dab in the middle of town.”

With the sesquicentennial bringing events to town throughout the year, Mook said that he saw an opportunity to honor not just the history but the community that has accepted him and continues to support his business.

“I just felt like, how many times is this going to happen? How many times are we going to be able to say that we were a part of this,” said Mook. “Between the festivities and the baseball games, and the patriotism everywhere, I just thought a motorcycle would be my way of helping to commemorate it.” 

Jim Williams, executive director of Deadwood History, Inc., said Mook approached him in May with the idea of selling 500 tickets for $100 each for a chance to win a motorcycle, with the intention of raising $50,000 for Deadwood History, Inc.

“It was something that was just absolutely very moving, that he had been thinking about developing a bike that represents Deadwood in its 150-year history,” said Williams. “He said that he has a passion for history and for the community and asked if we would be interested in accepting that as a donation.”

Williams said the money raised will be earmarked for preservation and educational programming. 

“We consider educational programming as a part of our efforts towards preservation, because we’re educating on the story and the information,” said Williams. “It’s going to enhance what we’re able to do, particularly those preservation aspects. There’s a couple things that are at a point where we need professional assistance with them, and this is going to be a great opportunity to assist those efforts.”

Designing a piece of history

Mook said that one of his mentors, Donnie Smith, a renowned builder of custom motorcycles from Minnesota, gave him one of the best pieces of advice when it came to building and designing custom motorcycles. 

“He said to me at one time, ‘People like custom bikes, but they don’t know why they like them. It’s because of the lines,’” said Mook. “To me, motorcycles are built around the motor. So, the motor has to be something very unique and very custom. A bike is a wheel on each end and a motor in the middle, and that’s where you kind of start.”

Mook said that he starts his builds by drafting the build on a piece of paper. From there, him and his team work together to build a piece of art. 

“I have a couple hard and fast rules when it comes to building bikes that I like to follow. Certain front ends don’t belong with certain frames, everything has to make sense as far as how it all flows together,” Mook said. “The idea for the 150th bike, we couldn’t put a big, gigantic gas tank on it that comes stock. It would have been easier and it would have been a lot cheaper, but it wouldn’t have fit with the rest of the lines. It would have been out of place.”

Mook said he’s worked to design a bike that looks vintage but has all the modern necessities and reliability a person would expect from a new build.

“It wouldn’t really fit with the theme if we did some newfangled, space age, George Jetson motorcycle,” he said. “So, we’re doing a bike with hidden suspension, modern electronics, modern starting, but from 100 feet away it’s going to look like it’s 120 years old. It’s going to be very retro looking.”

Mook said he took inspiration from motorcycles built between 1920-1940 when designing the frame and silhouette of the bike. Fine details, like paint and finish, will commemorate Deadwood with blacks, gold, and brass details. 

“We’re putting the 150th commemorative coin that Deadwood History has done, we’re going to integrate that into the bike, so it’ll be right there for everybody to see,” he said. “We’re going to start teasing it a lot on Facebook and Instagram, start teasing it a lot more.”

America’s V-twin community

Mook said a big reason the bike is possible is because of donated parts from industry giants around the country. Those donors include S&S cycles, BDL Belt Drives, Paul Yaffe Originals, Klock Werks, LePera Seats, Open Throttle Custom Paintwork, MSI of Belle Fourche, Hawg Halters, and Legend Suspension. 

“Whenever I call these guys for something like this, no sooner do I get the words out of my mouth then they’re like, ‘Yep, we’re going to box it up and it’s on its way,’” he said. “The American V-twin industry is full of absolutely amazing people. I’m very, very blessed.”

To keep costs down on building the motorcycle, Mook said he will be using parts he already owned and custom-building parts in house.

“I have a very good team here, I’m not just a one man show,” he said. “Everybody has a say. Everybody gets some input, and everybody helps.”

Party at the 10

Mook said the drawing won’t take place until all 500 tickets are sold. 

“Once we’ve got maybe 20, 25 tickets left, then we’ll schedule the part at the Saloon No 10,” he said. “Then I’m going to ride that motorcycle right through the front door and into the sawdust. As long as Louie (LaLonde, owner of the Saloon No 10) is ok with it.”

To purchase a ticket, visit deadwoodhistory.com, call (605) 722-4800, or visit Rose Speirs, communications director, and Williams on Gold Street and Main Street on Friday and Saturday or every day during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally.

title: Monument Health Sturgis Hospital unveils healing outdoor space for patients, families and caregivers
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: A tree was planted in honor of the hospital staff that had the idea for a secure outdoor area at the Monument Health Sturgis Hospital, and the major contributors to the project. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
2. care..JPG
A tree was planted in honor of the hospital staff that had the idea for a secure outdoor area at the Monument Health Sturgis Hospital, and the major contributors to the project. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

STURGIS — Monument Health Sturgis Hospital celebrated the completion of a new outdoor healing space with a ribbon-cutting ceremony Wednesday, providing patients, families, caregivers and staff with a peaceful place to rest, recover and reconnect with nature.

The project was made possible through a partnership between Monument Health Sturgis Hospital, the Greater Sturgis LifeCare Foundation and the Monument Health Foundation.

The hospital’s Outdoor Space Committee submitted a proposal to the Greater Sturgis LifeCare Foundation in August 2025 after identifying the need for a dedicated outdoor area designed to promote healing and wellness. Committee members cited research showing that spending time in nature can reduce stress, lower anxiety and support physical recovery.

The newly completed space offers patients and their loved ones a safe, comfortable setting to enjoy fresh air and spend time together during the healing process. Hospital staff also will benefit from a quiet retreat where they can recharge during the workday, supporting morale and overall well-being. 

Committee Member Angie Dahlke, Sturgis director of nursing said, “Fresh air and sunshine can make all the difference to a person who is hospitalized for an extended period of time. Our team wanted to create an environment where patients could enjoy these benefits while still being able to provide an appropriate level of monitoring. This updated courtyard will give more patients access to an outdoor space. It’s inspiring to see what can happen when our community invests in local health care, and we’re thankful to the donors who gave through the Monument Health Foundation’s Sturgis Greatest Needs Fund, as well as the Greater Sturgis LifeCare Foundation, for helping make this space possible.”

The outdoor area features a welcoming pergola, comfortable seating, a decorative retaining wall and thoughtfully designed landscaping, creating a peaceful environment for relaxation and reflection.

Janine Short, vice president of the Greater Sturgis LifeCare Foundation, said the project reflects the foundation’s mission of improving the health and well-being of the community.

“Healing extends beyond medicine. We know that having access to a peaceful outdoor environment can make a meaningful difference for patients, provide comfort for families during difficult times, and give caregivers and hospital staff a place to recharge. The Greater Sturgis LifeCare Foundation is proud to partner with Monument Health on projects like this that invest in the health and quality of life of our community.”

The Greater Sturgis LifeCare Foundation is a nonprofit organization dedicated to supporting and promoting health care and senior care throughout the greater Sturgis area. Since its formation in April 2004, the foundation has provided more than $1.2 million in grants and loans to local health care and senior care initiatives.

As a 501(c)(3) nonprofit organization, the foundation relies on community support and charitable donations to continue funding projects that enhance health care services and improve the quality of life for area residents.

SPEARFISH — Black Hills Community Bank is celebrating a record-breaking milestone after collecting 110,985 diapers during its 15th Annual Diaper Drive, making 2026 the most successful year in the drive’s history. 

Throughout the month of June, Black Hills Community Bank invited the Black Hills community to help support local families by donating diapers, making monetary contributions, and participating in an online auction. The annual drive benefits the Cornerstone Mission Women’s and Children’s Home in Rapid City, and Bella Pregnancy Center in Spearfish. 

This year’s goal was to collect a combined 60,000 diapers, with a goal of 50,000 diapers in Rapid City and 10,000 in Spearfish. Both communities surpassed expectations. 

Rapid City collected 62,722 diapers, while Spearfish collected 48,263 diapers, bringing the grand total to 110,985 diapers. The total breaks Black Hills Community Bank’s previous Diaper Drive record of 99,273 diapers, set in 2022.

title: USDA reversal on crop insurance change welcomed by farm groups
byline: By Jeff Beach North Dakota Monitor
description: WASHINGTON, D.C. — The U.S. Department of Agriculture is reversing course on a change to a federal crop insurance policy to allow farmers to buy more protection if weather or field conditions prevent them from planting a crop.
_full_text:
NorthDakotaMonitorLogo

WASHINGTON, D.C. — The U.S. Department of Agriculture is reversing course on a change to a federal crop insurance policy to allow farmers to buy more protection if weather or field conditions prevent them from planting a crop. 

USDA had eliminated the option to buy additional prevented planting insurance going into the 2026 growing season. This raised concerns from growers in North Dakota, where the buy-up option has been a popular risk-management tool.  

In a Tuesday hearing of the Senate Agriculture Appropriations Committee, U.S. Sen. John Hoeven, R-N.D., asked Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins where the department stood on the policy. 

“We are 100% supportive of that and are moving forward to execute that buy-up option,” Rollins said. 

The change will restore the 5% buy-up option, which provided additional coverage for more than 67 million acres across the country in 2025. North Dakota accounted for 10 million of those acres, Hoeven said. 

Justin Sherlock, past president of the North Dakota Soybean Growers Association and a director with the American Soybean Association, said restoring the buy-up option is welcome news, but that farm groups felt that USDA was required by law to offer it.  

He said defending crop insurance in general was the bigger issue. 

“It was the concern that this could be a bigger infringement upon the crop insurance program as Congress intended it.” 

While he was encouraged by Rollins’ comments, Sherlock said he would like to see the change noted in the Federal Register or in a formal statement from USDA.

Prevented planting was not a major issue in North Dakota this year, but Sherlock did benefit from hail insurance on some land in Griggs County. 

“I wouldn’t be farming without it,” Sherlock said of federal crop insurance.  

Hoeven credited working with Chair Sen. John Boozman, R-Ark.,and Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., of the Senate Agriculture Committee on emphasizing the need to return to the previous policy.   

“Given the challenges facing farm country, we worked very hard to restore this prevented plant buy-up option to provide our producers with an additional layer of protection when disaster prevents them from planting their fields,” Hoeven said in a news release.
