title: State fairgrounds undergoes extensive cleanup after tornado strikes Huron
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: HURON — South Dakota State Fair staff, state prison inmates and volunteers spent two weeks clearing debris and repairing damage after a tornado swept through Huron.
_full_text:
State fairgrounds undergoes extensive cleanup after tornado strikes Huron.jpeg

HURON — South Dakota State Fair staff, state prison inmates and volunteers spent two weeks clearing debris and repairing damage after a tornado swept through Huron.

Despite widespread damage across the fairgrounds, no one was injured, the grounds are now in good shape, and no events will be canceled for the fair Sept. 2-7. 

“We’re really blessed,” State Fair Manager Peggy Besch told the State Fair Commission on Tuesday, adding that the damage could have been much worse.

A tornado with peak winds of 90 mph struck Huron on July 2, followed by extreme wind, including a 106 mph gust. Besch said 23 families were camping at the fairgrounds at the time, and they waited it out in designated shelters. The grounds were set to host the national Family Campers and RVers Campvention, with opening ceremonies set for July 4. People involved with the event had arrived early.

The storm toppled numerous large trees and damaged multiple buildings on the fairgrounds. Damage included a tree crashing through a skylight, an announcer’s stand being overturned, one building being shifted off its foundation and toppled power poles.

Besch said the state rented a crane to remove large hanging tree limbs, while inmates from the South Dakota Department of Corrections spent two weeks helping to clear debris.

According to a department press release, a July 3 deployment included 15 minimum-security inmates and four department staff members from Sioux Falls. Another department crew of 25 inmates and three staff returned to the fairgrounds on July 5 to continue with cleanup. From there, efforts expanded beyond the fairgrounds throughout Huron. The department also dispatched help after an earlier storm in Highmore.

“This DOC initiative is a perfect win-win example,” Gov. Larry Rhoden said in the release. “Our communities receive much-needed help, and our inmates have the opportunity to get outside and contribute to something greater than themselves.” 

Besch said students from South Dakota State University also assisted with the cleanup at the fairgrounds.

The fairgrounds’ newly completed Dakota Events Complex escaped without damage, Besch told South Dakota Searchlight. She said no cost estimate for the cleanup and repairs is available yet.

title: Universities ask for $24.5 million to launch and maintain artificial intelligence system
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — The board that oversees South Dakota’s public universities plans to ask state lawmakers for nearly $60.5 million for building projects and maintenance, the launch of a national defense center in Rapid City, and technology upgrades related to artificial intelligence.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — The board that oversees South Dakota’s public universities plans to ask state lawmakers for nearly $60.5 million for building projects and maintenance, the launch of a national defense center in Rapid City, and technology upgrades related to artificial intelligence.

The Board of Regents also endorsed construction funding requests Thursday during a meeting in Spearfish, including funding to begin the previously announced move of the University of South Dakota Sanford School of Medicine to Sioux Falls.

Board member Pam Roberts said the requests are an “investment in South Dakota’s future.”

“It helps keep us affordable, it helps with workforce development and makes sure that we’re responsive to all the needs of South Dakota,” Roberts said.

Gov. Larry Rhoden will take up the requests later this year and decide whether to include them in his fiscal year 2028 budget proposal ahead of the legislative session, which begins in January.

Funding for artificial intelligence

As the board plans to use artificial intelligence in its business and educational operations, it’s requesting $20 million in one-time funding to build out its AI technology system and $4.5 million in ongoing funding to maintain it.

The board approved a new AI policy at its Thursday meeting, and the board will launch a system-wide software this fall that supports several AI uses and future emerging technologies, said David Overby, interim system chief information officer.

“This policy provides a way to enable AI innovation across the regental system while maintaining clear boundaries around data protection, security, oversight and accountability,” Overby said. “It supports responsible adoption without treating AI as unmanaged or standalone technology.”

The board also approved four AI academic programs on Thursday: a doctorate in AI at Dakota State University and bachelor’s, master’s and doctoral degrees in artificial intelligence engineering at South Dakota State University.

The $4.5 million additional ongoing request would be used to maintain the AI infrastructure by replacing aging equipment, building out technology infrastructure and funding cybersecurity needs. South Dakota State University President Barry Dunn said AI is increasingly used at universities across the nation. 

“This opportunity is not simply to make AI tools available, but to use AI responsibly to improve service efficiency, accessibility and decision-making across the regental system,” Dunn said. 

The ongoing funding request is essential, said Northern State University President Alan LaFave.

“Core technology is now core infrastructure,” LaFave said. “It has to be maintained, replaced and funded on a predictable cycle just like buildings, utilities and other essential campus systems.”

The regents plan to use another $1.6 million annually from student tuition fees to support the technology updates.

Launching a national defense center

Several university presidents spoke in support of a $1 million request to launch a Center for National Defense in Rapid City, which aligns with Gov. Rhoden’s creation of the South Dakota Defense Institute in April. The center will require seven full-time workers.

The defense industry is one of the “fastest growing sectors in our state’s economy,” Black Hills State University President Steve Elliott said.

The center will develop the workforce needed for defense acquisition, systems engineering and emerging defense technologies, among other needs, Elliott added.

Elliott said the collaboration would offer students work-based learning projects, internships and fellowships with nearby Ellsworth Air Force Base, the South Dakota National Guard, defense contractors and government agencies in the area.

Dakota State University President John Ballard said he’s spent “most of my life in this area.” He attended the United States Naval Academy, served in faculty and administrative roles at several military and defense colleges, and served as president of the National Intelligence University in Washington, D.C., where he led technology integration across the intelligence community.

“I can tell you with a great deal of certainty that programs like this are not only highly productive but also highly beneficial to the people that they’re designed to serve,” Ballard said. 

Return to building maintenance goals

The board sets an annual goal to fund campus maintenance needs at 2% of the total replacement cost for campus buildings. For fiscal year 2028, that would be $18.78 million.

Last year, lawmakers underfunded the maintenance request, which board member Roberts called “shortsighted and disappointing” at the time.

Sheila Gestring, University of South Dakota president, said university buildings are among the state’s “most valuable public assets” because they support economic and workforce development.

“When maintenance is deferred, costs don’t disappear, they grow,” Gestring said. 

The fiscal year 2028 request is about $1.65 million more than fiscal year 2027’s request.

Capital project requests

Gestring requested $6.2 million to begin relocating the Sanford School of Medicine from Vermillion to Sioux Falls. The relocation includes moving instructional, office and faculty space, and an anatomy lab temporarily to existing buildings on the Sanford Health campus in central Sioux Falls.

The university plans to build a new Sioux Falls facility within the next decade, costing about $150 million. Gestring told South Dakota Searchlight in an interview last year that she hopes most of the funding will come from donors.

Dunn requested $10 million to construct a new building to house SDSU’s business and economics programs. The programs’ enrollment grew from 730 students in 2018 to 1,300 in 2025, and is expected to reach 1,500 in 2030.

title: As national death rate dips, some states did better than others
byline: By Tim Henderson Stateline
description: WASHINGTON — The nation’s death rate may have fallen to a historic low last year as many of the killers of young people such as drug overdoses, gun homicides and traffic accidents continued receding in 2025, according to new federal statistics.
_full_text:
StatelineLogo

WASHINGTON — The nation’s death rate may have fallen to a historic low last year as many of the killers of young people such as drug overdoses, gun homicides and traffic accidents continued receding in 2025, according to new federal statistics.  

States have not shared equally in the success, though, according to a Stateline analysis of provisional data by state. And the low ebb may reflect the effects of past health care expansion efforts that are threatened by today’s Trump administration moves to curtail Medicaid expansion and cut funding for rural hospitals. 

In South Dakota, according to the data provided saw a 3.5% increase in age-adjusted death rate. The death rate in 2015 was 714.4 per 100,000 people. In 2025, it increased to 740.7 per 100,000 people. The most distinctive cause of death in 2025 was alcoholic liver disease which is 3.1 times higher than the national average. 

Some states in the Northeast have seen death rates drop by the most between 2015 and 2025 — led by New Jersey (down 8.3%), Rhode Island (down 8%), New York (down 7.9%), Massachusetts (down 7.4%) and the District of Columbia (down 7.0%). Some experts credit states’ attention to health care, traffic issues and gun violence. 

New Jersey has taken the lead in decreases because of a long-term commitment to expanding health care to people with low incomes, said Stephen Crystal, director of Rutgers University’s Center for Health Services Research.

Even before Medicaid expansion under the federal Affordable Care Act, New Jersey and Massachusetts, among other states, were pooling funds with hospitals to cover more low-income residents, Crystal said. 

“New Jersey has been doing this for a long time, and you’re seeing the effects in the lower mortality rates for the big killers,” he said. 

The state stands out for having less than half the national rate of firearm deaths, both suicide and homicide, as well as deaths from heart and kidney diseases caused by high blood pressure. The rate of traffic accident deaths is also well below the national rate. 

There’s also a more confrontational attitude toward speeding and less tolerance for guns in the Northeast, he said. 

“Here’s something that annoys a lot of New Jerseyans. The state troopers have the cojones to pull you over if you’re doing 90 on the turnpike. This is not the case in Wyoming,” Crystal said. “Also if you go out West where gun possession is very high, then the firearm suicide deaths become enormous.” 

Nationally most of the decrease between 2024 and 2025 came from young age groups. The things most likely to kill them dropped after spiking during the early pandemic, including drug overdoses, traffic accidents, gun violence and suicide, according to an analysis of death counts by Mary Pat Campbell, an actuary and life insurance analyst in New York state.

Northeastern states have an advantage in tackling those problems based on wealth, she said. 

“There has been an increasing separation of mortality outcomes by socioeconomic status,” Campbell said, noting that traffic accidents are rarer in places like New Jersey partly because so many people commute on public transportation. 

“For New Jersey, a lot of it really is that there are a bunch of high-income people who have lower-than-average mortality, just like people on Long Island and the rich parts of Westchester (in New York state),” she added.

Some states have not improved since 2015 in the provisional statistics analyzed by Stateline, which may change as the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention makes new age adjustments at the state level. 

New Mexico had an age-adjusted death rate 9% higher last year than 10 years ago, as drug overdose deaths continue to plague the state at more than twice the national rate.  

In June, New Mexico Democratic Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham called for restitution from the federal government over allegations that U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration officials knowingly let fentanyl shipments into the state during multiple presidential administrations. In one case, a whistleblower alleged, agents stood by while 1.8 million fentanyl pills were trafficked in hopes of catching higher-ranking dealers and suppliers down the line.

New Mexico also struggles with higher death rates from alcoholic liver disease and gun homicide. Neighboring Arizona, where the death rate is 5% higher than 10 years ago, also stands out for a high overdose death rate and a high gun suicide rate.  

Iowa and Oklahoma death rates are also up 5% from 2015. Iowa stands out for a higher-than-national rate of fall-related deaths, typical of an aging rural population with little day-to-day supervision. Oklahoma has a similarly high rate of fall-related deaths, as well as almost four times the national rate of deaths from high blood pressure and hardening of the arteries — both problems that can be controlled with medication. 

Iowa “recognizes fall-related deaths as a significant public health concern,”  wrote a spokesperson for the state Department of Health and Human Services, Danielle Sample, in an e-mail statement. Those falls are associated with older age groups and possibly rural access to health care and preventive services, she said. 

The state has a falls prevention program that stresses exercise to maintain mobility and monitoring excessive medication that could cause dizziness, poor vision and unsafe home conditions. 

Almost two-thirds of the national death rate improvement for 2024 to 2025 came from people between the ages of 15 to 44, Campbell told Stateline. 

Improvements were especially large for young people 25 to 34, a group including younger Millennials and older Gen Z, a demographic hard hit by homicides and drug overdose deaths early in the pandemic, Campbell told Stateline. The rate for accidents, a category that includes drug overdoses, gun accidents and traffic accidents, dropped 6% in one year, and the homicide rate dropped 14%, she said. 

It’s hard to be sure how much death rates really changed between 2024 and 2025 because the methodology changed, Crystal noted, accusing the CDC of “grabbing for a good news headline” by reporting the apparently historic decrease prominently in a blog item.    

For 2025, the CDC used different methods to calculate rates, including more adjustments to 2020 census data used as a basis for age adjustment, noting in the report that the results could change and “should be interpreted with caution.” 

Asked about the issue, the CDC said in a statement to Stateline that “as this is a provisional report, we did not go in depth about the change in population denominators” and that it is “planning a brief report that will show the impact” of the changes on death rates and birth rate in new statistics. 

In any case, the Trump administration likely can’t claim credit for current decreases in death rates, which would reflect policy changes from years ago that slowly take effect, Crystal said. 

“This is not the time to see the effect of what Trump is doing now. It’s going to take five years,” Crystal said. 

One killer of young people has not dropped: The rate of gun suicide has increased 14% since 2015, according to the Stateline analysis. Suicide has affected Gen Z young people more than previous generations.  

Over the past 10 years, rates for Black and Hispanic people have increased while rates for other groups have gone down, according to the Stateline analysis. 

“As a country we are improving. We should celebrate that. But many segments of the population are left behind,” said Ali Mokdad, a professor of health metrics sciences at the University of Washington. 

Mokdad credited some medical advances for decreases in heart disease that came in spite of increased obesity. 

“That decline in cardiovascular disease was due to better controlled blood pressure,” Mokdad said. “Blood pressure medication, when it came out, was very expensive. Now blood pressure medication is so cheap you can get a three-month supply for less than the price of a cup of coffee.”

title: High speed pursuit from Box Elder ends in Wyo.
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: SPEARFISH — A Rapid City man was arrested Friday afternoon following a multi-county pursuit that started in Box Elder and ended in Wyoming.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — A Rapid City man was arrested Friday afternoon following a multi-county pursuit that started in Box Elder and ended in Wyoming.

According to the South Dakota Highway Patrol, just before 10:40 a.m. Friday, a 50-year-old Rapid City man was left the Love’s Truck Stop in Box Elder after Pennington County dispatch received a call of an alleged theft on the store.

The Box Elder Police Department located the 2019 Toyota Tundra traveling east on Interstate 90 and attempted a traffic stop. The driver allegedly failed to stop and a pursuit was initiated. The South Dakota Highway Patrol joined the pursuit which extended to Highway 14/16 and rural roads before turning west on I-90.

According to police radio scanner traffic, speeds reached as high as 120 mph and the driver turned around twice on the interstate in Lawrence County, at times, driving the wrong way on the interstate. Several attempts to stop the vehicle with spike strips were apparently unsuccessful.

Shortly after crossing into Wyoming, the vehicle entered a spin and ran off the road. The driver attempted to regain control when a South Dakota Highway Patrol unit pinned the Toyota against a tree. The driver was taken into custody without further incident.

Other agencies involved were the Box Elder Police Department, the Meade County Police Department, the Pennington County Sherriff’s Office, the Cook County Sherriff’s Office, and the Wyoming Highway Patrol.

title: SD universities’ Native American enrollment  rises to pre-pandemic level
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Native American enrollment increased 28% at Black Hills State University. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
SD universities’ Native American enrollment rises to pre-pandemic level.JPG
Native American enrollment increased 28% at Black Hills State University. Pioneer file photo 

Native American student enrollment at South Dakota public universities has returned to its pre-pandemic level, according to a new report.

Black Hills State University in Spearfish had 227 Native American students during the 2025-26 school year, up 49 from 178 the year before. That 28% increase was a major factor in the 6% systemwide growth in Native American students compared to the prior year. 

The university’s student body typically has the highest percentage of Native American students of the 6 institutions in the system. Urla Marcus, director of the Center for American Indian Studies at the university and a member of the Northern Cheyenne Tribe, said the recent numbers are a sign that new programs are working to recruit and retain more students.

Higher enrollment leads to a “ripple effect,” Marcus added.

“They can go back to their communities and make an impact, set that example that more people are attaining these degrees,” Marcus said.

In 2019, the Legislature required the South Dakota Board of Regents, which oversees the public universities, to develop programs aimed at increasing Native American student enrollment and retention. The board submits a report by July 1 each year detailing activities and progress made.

Systemwide, Native American enrollment decreased during the COVID-19 pandemic and stayed lower for several years afterward despite increases at some universities. 

The Native American percentage of the systemwide student body also dipped below 3% for several years but now stands at 3.2%. South Dakota’s overall population is 9% Native American.

Black Hills State’s latest increase pushed systemwide Native American enrollment to 1,155 — nearly reaching the 1,157 recorded in 2017. Native American enrollment increased this past school year by 16 students at South Dakota Mines and 15 at the University of South Dakota, but decreased by 5 at South Dakota State University, 4 at Northern State University and 2 at Dakota State University.

This is the first year since the pandemic that Native American enrollment decreased at South Dakota State. The university has played a significant role in increasing Native American enrollment within the South Dakota public university system in the last decade. President Barry Dunn, a member of the Rosebud Sioux Tribe, launched the Wokini Initiative in 2017 to recruit, retain and support Native American students. Enrollment of Native Americans at the university grew from 259 in 2017 to a peak of 329 in 2024.

Scholarships and financial aid awarded to Native American students across the state have nearly doubled since the 2022 school year, driven largely by a near doubling in Pell Grants and scholarships from institutions and private foundations.

Black Hills State has not yet recovered its own pre-pandemic Native American enrollment numbers, despite the recent gains. Students at the time of the pandemic, Marcus said, were “very cautious,” and many chose not to enroll outside tribal land, with some opting for tribal colleges instead. Those schools offered incentives that the university did not, such as tuition discounts and supplies.

Between 2015 and 2022, the latest data available from the National Center for Education Statistics, enrollment at Oglala Lakota College on the Pine Ridge Reservation fell by 189 students and at Sinte Gleska University in Rosebud by 103. Sisseton Wahpeton College on the Lake Traverse Reservation gained 55 students over the same period.

As the pandemic receded and tribal college incentive programs ended, Marcus said more students have shown interest in enrolling at Black Hills State. Marcus said the university’s location in the Black Hills, an area of historical and spiritual significance for several tribes, is a draw for students. The school has Native faculty and staff working with the center.

“Students see a lot of opportunities for them to grow and be successful,” Marcus said.

In addition to more targeted recruiting efforts, Marcus said the center has strengthened or created new programs to support students, including mentorship and scholarship programs.

The Native Scholars program is in its third year. Students in the program regularly engage with advisers and the center’s administration, participate in cultural activities and mentor their peers. Graduates receive a stole and star quilt. The program graduated 6 students last spring and expects to graduate another 13 next spring.

The peer mentor program grew organically before being formalized in recent years, Marcus said. The center pairs upperclassmen with freshmen and sophomores who share similar fields of study and home regions.

“We have a lot of silent leaders in our center,” Marcus said. “These students have taken some years getting closer and closer to graduation. Younger students look up to them, ask them questions and allow upperclassmen to share what they’ve learned and what they’ve stumbled on.”

Proposed ND pig iron plant to turn Minnesota mine waste into steel, a first for US .jpg
Structures from a defunct mining operation stand on the Hill Annex Mine State Park in Calumet, Minnesota. Calumet Reclamation proposes to reclaim the iron waste and transport it to Minot, N.D., for processing. Photo by Peyton Haug, For the North Dakota Monitor 

CALUMET, Minn. – Enormous piles of iron-rich waste sitting dormant in Minnesota are about to see movement for the first time in decades, soon heading hundreds of miles west to North Dakota.  

North American Iron plans to develop a 2,400-acre site near Minot to produce pig iron, an essential ingredient in steel-making. The operation, which could produce 2 million metric tons annually, would be the first of its kind in the country and aims to boost domestic production.

Jim Bougalis, CEO and founder of North American Iron and sister company Calumet Reclamation Co., said high tariffs and global conflict, coupled with North Dakota’s interest in the project, added to its momentum. 

The facility is slated to bring 650 permanent jobs to the Minot area.

“This is one of those projects that adds an economic pillar to our city and region,” said Mark Lyman, economic development specialist for the Minot Area Chamber. “It being so brand new adds diversification to our economy.”

Iron to feed the country for ‘centuries’

The Mesabi Iron Range, famous for its mining activity, encompasses over 100 miles of northeastern Minnesota, where industry and population has ebbed and flowed drastically for nearly 150 years, ramping up when the price of ore does and downturning when it falls. 

Because America’s steel-ready pig iron is imported from other countries, the Trump administration’s aggressive tariff policies have made it expensive to import from major producing countries — namely Brazil, Ukraine and Russia. The military depends heavily on the material to build things like warheads, submarines and aircrafts.  

Bougalis grew up on the range in Hibbing, just down the road from Calumet where his company holds mineral leases for millions of tons of iron-rich waste sitting on 20 square miles. 

Minnesota has enough iron to feed the country for centuries, according to Bougalis, who claims there are approximately 3 billion tons sitting on the surface of the range. 

Stockpiles dating back to the second World War stretch city blocks and stand like small mountains, some over 300 feet tall. Soon, the waste will be railed nearly 500 miles to Minot.

The project is being touted as a low-impact way to domestically produce iron, not only because it will put to use idle waste, but because it will be processed using newer technology that emits far less carbon than traditional processing. 

In essence, the rock or “feed stock” is crushed and made into preconcentrate, material that resembles a pile of wet sand. That process takes place in Minnesota before hitting the rail to North Dakota. 

When it reaches the pig iron plant, the material is then concentrated into a finer sand or dirt-like substance before transforming into small iron pellets to be later used for steel.

Pig iron factories have historically involved workers shoveling coal into huge blast furnaces to burn oxygen off the iron, turning ore into liquid and emitting carbon dioxide in the process. It’s among the most intensive parts of production. 

The facility going up in Minot, however, will use a lower-temperature chemical process to remove the oxygen from the iron ore without turning it into liquid. The highly mechanized system has both less risky working conditions and fewer emissions, reflecting how technological advancements have changed the industry. 

Instead of using coal to refine the ore, the facility will use the hydrogen found in natural gas, which emits water vapor, not carbon dioxide. 

The company is working with the Energy and Environmental Research Center at the University of North Dakota to explore the potential for underground carbon dioxide storage at the site, Bougalis said. No applications have been filed so far for carbon sequestration wells, and planning materials submitted to state environmental regulators don’t include that process.

Minot’s new neighbor

The project was initially proposed for Underwood, North Dakota, but is now planned for industrial land northeast of Minot. Renderings show the tallest structure standing more than 250 feet, a height that rivals the North Dakota Capitol. 

It will recycle city waste water, not drinking water, using a closed-looped system, Lyman said. A heavy film will be sprayed over the ore in Minnesota to minimize dust as it travels. 

A major component of the planned site is using natural gas produced in western North Dakota. WBI Energy is proposing the Minot Industrial Pipeline, an 87-mile project to bring up to 250 million cubic feet per day of natural gas from Tioga, according to the North Dakota Pipeline Authority. A WBI spokesperson said the project is still under development and the final scope is subject to customer commitments, regulatory review and final project approvals. The pipeline would require approval from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.

The pig iron plant also will involve construction of a 300-megawatt natural gas-fired power generation facility at the Minot site, according to Bougalis.

“The opportunity to keep natural gas in the state and use it to the benefit of a new industry is a win all around,” Lyman said.

The 650 jobs added to Minot will include high-paying jobs, company leaders say. 

When it comes to finding workers, Calumet Reclamation plans to start recruiting locally with North Dakota universities and the Minot Air Force Base. It will then turn its efforts national before handing off recruitment to a third party for building an immigrant workforce, if necessary, according to Bougalis. 

Lyman of Minot said the city has plenty of housing to accommodate the incoming workforce. Peak construction will entail up to 4,000 jobs. 

“I don’t think we’re in some housing crunch that’s unsolvable, even with a couple thousand employees. But still, we’re thinking about that. We’re already talking with property developers,” he said. 

Why North Dakota? 

Access to surplus power, quicker permitting and existing infrastructure makes it cheaper to build a factory in North Dakota than in Minnesota, Bougalis said. 

He said North Dakota has also become one of the project’s biggest investors, putting in $7 million from the Clean Sustainable Energy Authority and just over $2.6 million from the Department of Commerce. 

Northwest Landowners Association Chairman Troy Coons said the group doesn’t have an official stance on the project, but he hopes the development adequately addresses environmental and landowner impacts on the front end.

He noted that industries often come to North Dakota for processing because Minnesota regulations are more strict. 

The Minnesota Department of Natural Resources is conducting an environmental review known as an environmental assessment worksheet. Once that becomes public, which is anticipated this fall, that will prompt a 30-day public comment period, according to a spokesperson. After that, the department will evaluate whether a more rigorous environmental impact statement is required, the department said.

In North Dakota, regulators are evaluating an application for an air quality permit, said Karl Rockeman, deputy director of the Department of Environmental Quality.

Together, various aspects of the operation — from the gas-powered energy generation to the iron roasting machines — will be considered a “major source” of potential air pollution under the Clean Air Act, meaning the company will have to demonstrate its emissions are below a certain threshold and monitored regularly, Rockeman said.

The department’s Division of Solid Waste also will evaluate the project, Rockeman said.

Both reviews require a 30-day public comment period, neither of which have happened yet. Rockeman said the company could also need a permit for wastewater disposal, but that plan is still being developed. 

The company’s application for an air quality permit can be found on the department’s public portal. 

Calumet Reclamation and North American Iron expect permitting to be completed this fall, with construction expected to begin around 2027 and production commencing in 2029.

title: Spearfish motorcyclist  dies from injuries
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: SPEARFISH — A 56-year-old Spearfish man died from injuries sustained in a motorcycle crash Saturday.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

SPEARFISH — A 56-year-old Spearfish man died from injuries sustained in a motorcycle crash Saturday.

According to the accident report from South Dakota Highway Patrol, the man was driving a 1995 Harley-Davidson FLHTCU westbound on I-90 at approximately 5:45 p.m., when he started to lose control of the motorcycle and laid it down. In the process, he became separated from the motorcycle. 

The driver was taken to the Spearfish hospital before being transferred to a Rapid City hospital. He died Sunday. 

He was not wearing a helmet. 

The name of the man has not been released pending notification of family members.

The accident remains under investigation.

title: Meade Co. Fair and 4-H Achievement Days thrive despite triple-digit heat
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Triple-digit temperatures couldn’t keep families, exhibitors and volunteers away from the Meade County Fair and 4-H Achievement Days, as hundreds gathered at the Meade County Fairgrounds on the Sturgis Brown High School campus for 2 full days of livestock shows, exhibits, contests and community celebrations.
_full_text:
STURGIS — Triple-digit temperatures couldn’t keep families, exhibitors and volunteers away from the Meade County Fair and 4-H Achievement Days, as hundreds gathered at the Meade County Fairgrounds on the Sturgis Brown High School campus for 2 full days of livestock shows, exhibits, contests and community celebrations.

Despite temperatures climbing above 100 degrees on Friday and Saturday, fair organizers, volunteers and exhibitors adapted to the extreme conditions, adding extra fans, misting stations and water to protect both animals and people. The swine show even began an hour early Saturday morning to beat the worst of the heat.

For Jenny Voigt, SDSU Extension 4-H educator, the fair’s success was measured by more than attendance.

“We’ve had so much fun this fair, and the exhibits we’ve seen this year are absolutely phenomenal,” Voigt said. “The number of exhibits may have been down a little, but the quality has improved tremendously. I’d rather see young people perfect a skill than try to do 10 different things.”

Voigt praised the creativity and dedication shown by local 4-H members, especially in the companion animal division.

“We had some fun new animals this year, including an alpaca, a hedgehog and even a goose,” she said. “People may think that’s unusual, but those are projects these kids are proud of. They learn responsibility, and they get the opportunity to explain to the judge why their animal is important to them.”

Throughout Friday evening, the fairgrounds buzzed with activity as families gathered for a free community barbecue before enjoying the annual Ag Olympics, mutton bustin’, calf scramble, turtle races, frog jumping contest and other family activities.

Safety remained a top priority throughout the weekend. 

“The fair board has done a phenomenal job with more fans, misters and lots of water to keep both our animals and our people safe,” Voigt said. “We did have to cancel the rocket launch because conditions were simply too dry.”

Meade County Fair Board Secretary Shelley Sedivy said the fair continues to fulfill its mission of bringing together the agricultural community and the public while highlighting the work of local youth.

“The fair really started Thursday evening with the exhibits,” Sedivy said. “Friday is our community night, bringing together both our agricultural and non-agricultural families for a fun evening. Saturday is all about our livestock exhibitors and the projects they’ve worked on throughout the year.”

Sedivy said the Meade County Fair Association works year-round to maintain the fairgrounds and provide opportunities for area youth.

“We lease the property from the school district and maintain the barn throughout the year,” she said. “It’s used by 4-H, FFA, the Northern Hills Rabbit Association, Art in the Barn and many other community organizations. We’re proud to support agriculture and the kids of Meade County.”

Among the exhibitors celebrating success was Brooklyn Baird, who earned senior poultry showmanship honors with her English Buff Orpington hen, Buffy.

“I really enjoy poultry showmanship,” Baird said. “It’s my favorite thing I do at the fair, so it means a lot to do well. I’ve been showing chickens since I was seven years old.”

Buffy, just 5 months old, will eventually lay about 250 brown eggs each year. Although this marks Baird’s final year as a 4-H exhibitor, she doesn’t plan to stay away from the fairgrounds.

“I may be done showing, but I’ll always be back,” she said. “There are always projects to judge and opportunities to help. They’ll find a way to bring me back.”

The family-friendly competitions once again proved to be crowd favorites.

Ben Sobotka captured first place in the First Interstate Bank Turtle Races, while Kandley Donald and her turtle, White River, finished second. Trey Cotton won the frog jumping contest after his frog, Billy, leaped 17½ inches, edging runner-up Colby Smith.

Even under blazing sunshine and soaring temperatures, the spirit of the Meade County Fair remained strong, showcasing the accomplishments of local youth while bringing the community together for another successful year of agriculture, education and family fun.

title: Gaming numbers soar in June
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
SlotMachines.png
Courtesy photo 

DEADWOOD — The most recent report from the South Dakota Commission on Gaming shows Deadwood’s gaming handle increased by 12% in June compared to the same month in 2025. 

The commission reported a 9.63% rise overall for the first half of 2026. Slot machines drove most of the growth, showing a 12.3% increase, while table games also rose by 7.74%.

Sports wagering declined by 16.5% compared the same month in 2025.

“We are very enthusiastic about the increase in numbers for the first six months of 2026,” said George Milos, director of the Deadwood Gaming Association. “Compared to other gaming markets, Deadwood consistently distinguishes itself as an exceptional value. With a full slate of special events, historic experiences, and a wide selection of food, beverages, and accommodations, guests are always assured of a truly outstanding experience.”

Operators distributed $1,974,676.40 in ‘free play’ incentives in June, resulting in taxable gross revenues of $14,471,876.47 for the month. The total gaming taxes collected came to $1,302,468.88, of which $144,718.77 was allocated to the state’s general fund; $463,100.05 to South Dakota Tourism; and $115,775.01 to Lawrence County.

title: State fund helps 911 centers consolidate, with more mergers on the way
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — South Dakota has awarded more than $630,000 in the last year to facilitate three emergency dispatch consolidations, using funds from a statewide fee increase on phone lines that lawmakers approved to support efficiency and equipment upgrades.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — South Dakota has awarded more than $630,000 in the last year to facilitate three emergency dispatch consolidations, using funds from a statewide fee increase on phone lines that lawmakers approved to support efficiency and equipment upgrades.

The consolidations were recommended in a 2025 efficiency report commissioned by the South Dakota 911 Coordination Board. The report recommended the board financially assist consolidation efforts and target consolidations of centers with low call volumes, staffing shortages and high costs per 911 call.

The board created a grant program last year for consolidation costs and equipment upgrades using a portion of funds from a statewide $2 monthly fee on phone lines and 2% tax on prepaid wireless services. State lawmakers raised the fee from $1.25 to $2 in 2024 and made the increase permanent last year.

The board puts $80,000 a month into the 911 efficiency grant fund, which currently has $640,000 in it.

Seven of the state’s 32 dispatch centers were identified as consolidation candidates in the 2025 report. The board has awarded funding for 3 consolidations so far:

$65,370 for Sanborn County and the Mitchell Police Department in October 2025.

$237,744 for Miner County and Lake County in October 2025.

$327,121 for Lawrence County and Spearfish this month.

The other centers identified as consolidation candidates are in Spink, Moody, Fall River and Butte counties.

Spearfish and the Lawrence County dispatch center in Deadwood are 15 miles apart in the Black Hills. The 2 plan to merge by January, with Lawrence County’s dispatch center absorbing Spearfish’s center and one of its dispatchers. The move will cut 2 dispatch positions.

Jamie Pesicka Olson, with the Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office, told board members the consolidation would ensure Lawrence County residents receive dependable emergency communications.

“It improves coordination and operability and efficiency,” Pesicka Olson said.

Michelle DeNeui, a state 911 board member who recused herself from the award decision because she works for Spearfish, said the county is an “oddball” because it had 2 dispatch centers. Most dispatch centers serve multiple counties.

The grants can help county commissions get past the initial hurdle of short-term consolidation costs, said Jason Husby, the state’s 911 coordinator.

“This is where previous consolidations fell: Two agencies wanted to join, they see this initial cost and then they back out of it,” Husby said.

Perkins County Sheriff Kelly Serr, who chairs the 911 board and the subcommittee that reviews applications before they come to the board, said the Spearfish-Lawrence County merger would pay for itself within 9 years.

The Miner-Lake consolidation should be wrapped up by the end of the year, said April Denholm, director of Lake County 911 Communications. Radio equipment and software still need to be installed and tested. The grant primarily covered those costs.

Consolidation makes sense for smaller, rural counties, Denholm said. While the average Miner County resident likely won’t notice much change, it can mean faster response times and cost savings for the county.

“With Miner being a much less populated county, running a full-time dispatch center is a drain. Running a dispatch center is a drain for any county, but making sure you have someone there 24/7 is more difficult with a smaller county,” Denholm said.

Before the Miner-Lake consolidation, Miner County Dispatch had also covered Sanborn County’s emergency calls. Denholm said her center couldn’t absorb Sanborn’s needs, which is why Sanborn merged with the Mitchell Police Department dispatch.

Crow Creek Sioux Tribe and Buffalo County dispatch centers, in central South Dakota, are working to merge with the Winner Police Department dispatch, according to the Department of Public Safety. The board has not yet received a funding request for that consolidation.

title: Sturgis approves  first step to lease land to  cell tower company
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — The city of Sturgis approved initial steps toward a possible cell tower construction, Monday.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

STURGIS — The city of Sturgis approved initial steps toward a possible cell tower construction, Monday. 

On Monday, the Sturgis City Council approved the first of 3 steps to approve an option and lease agreement for land near the Exit 32 recycling containers. The agreement with Vertical Bridge, LLC, would have the company pay the city $1,050 for an option payment, and then $1,050 per month in rent, with annual rent increases of 1.99%, for an initial 4-year term, with 7 additional 5-year renewal options.  The option and lease agreement would be in place while Vertical Bridge, LLC researched the feasibility of building a cell tower in that location. 

Sturgis Public Works Director Rick Bush stressed that approving the resolution to lease the land did not approve the construction of a cell tower. Rather, it was the first of 3 statutorily required steps toward leasing the land to the company. State law requires the city to pass a resolution to lease the land, then to publish a notice for a public hearing, and then to hold the public hearing.  

Bush told the council that Vertical Bridge, LLC is the largest privately owned wireless infrastructure company in the United States, operating more than 18,000 communication towers across the country. Bush said city officials have been working with the company to determine the best location for the lease. They final settled on a site that is west of the Exit 32 recycling fence.

“This location met the company engineering requirements,” he said. “It is one of the best city controlled sites available. The property is located within the Interstate 90 corridor, where there is already significant vertical infrastructure, including highway lighting, parking lot lighting, billboards, pole signs, and flagpoles. As a result, the proposed location is consistent with the surrounding character of that corridor.” 

Earlier this year, Bush said the city council approved amendments to its telecommunications ordinance, which changed the required setbacks for towers. Now, communication towers must be 750-feet from residential zoning district boundaries, instead of from any existing structure. 

“That amendment simply created a clearer, more practical standard and made this location eligible for construction,” he said. 

While the company is leasing the land, Bush said, it will work on engineering, environmental reviews, and other assessments to determine if the location is suitable for a new cell tower. If the company decides not to move forward with construction, Bush said the agreement would expire. If the lease terminates, he said, the company is required to remove all improvements and restore the land to its original condition, he said. 

A new cell tower in Sturgis could have significant public benefit, Bush said. 

“While this is ultimately a private investment, there are important public benefits that can result from improved wireless infrastructure, including better cellular coverage, increased network capacity, improved communication reliability, greater network resiliency during emergencies, and improved services for residents, visitors, businesses, emergency responders, and travelers along the Interstate 90 corridor.”

title: Landfill fires are becoming more common, and your discarded vapes and toothbrushes are part of the problem
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: This fire at the landfill burned for roughly 6 weeks. When a fire starts at the landfill, Superintendent Sean Gallagher said, you never know what kind of trash is burning and what might off-gas as a result. Photo courtesy Shawn Gallagher
_full_text:
March.JPG
This fire at the landfill burned for roughly 6 weeks. When a fire starts at the landfill, Superintendent Sean Gallagher said, you never know what kind of trash is burning and what might off-gas as a result. Photo courtesy Shawn Gallagher 

 May.JPG
Before you throw away your vape pens, cellphones, or rechargeable power tool batteries, landfill staff hope you think twice. Those devices can spark fires — like one this spring that burned roughly 20 acres of landfill. Photo courtesy Shawn Gallagher 

BELLE FOURCHE — Since Belle Fourche Landfill Superintendent Shawn Gallagher took over operations in 2024, there have been 5 fires that required fire department response. 

About once a month, landfill personnel put out what they call “smokers” —which can usually be extinguished with shovels without help from the fire department.

“It’s definitely not par for the course. We are definitely over par,” Belle Fourche Fire Chief Aaron Thramer said. “We have had a lot, a lot more calls out there.”

Landfill fires are becoming more and more frequent, not only in Belle Fourche, but across the state and country. Gallagher, a member of the South Dakota Solid Waste Board, said that’s because people are throwing away more of their rechargeable items.

“Think about all of the rechargeable devices we have these days. Every one of those has a lithium-ion battery in it, and there’s more and more and more every time we turn around,” Gallagher said.

Rechargeable wireless power tool batteries, vape pens, laptops, cellphones, and even rechargeable toothbrushes contain lithium-ion batteries. Those batteries, when they’re disturbed by heavy equipment at the landfill, release a pulse of heat and energy — often igniting fires.

“As soon as you hit these with one of our machines, they burst,” Gallagher said. “The bigger the battery, the bigger the problem is.”

Batteries used in Milwaukee or DeWalt tools, for example, are likely to cause large fires. What Gallagher calls “smokers” generally start when tools strike discarded vape pens or cellphones.

Even small fires could have negative long-term consequences for landfill workers.

The problem with landfill fires is that they can be especially dangerous for the people in the surrounding area. During the last fire at the landfill, Gallagher told the Pioneer crews smelled chlorine, implying that chlorine gas might’ve been emitted by something that caught flame in the acres of landfill that burned. 

“You have no idea what is in the trash when it’s burning,” Gallagher said.

Gallagher said the best way to prevent dangerous fires is to dispose of rechargeable batteries and devices responsibly.

The Belle Fourche landfill accepts batteries and rechargeable items for free.

“We do have a free place to dispose of any battery like that, and then we can properly handle it,” Gallagher said. “You can bring a 5-gallon bucket full. We had a bunch the other day. Dump them into the battery bin and be done. It doesn’t cost you a thing.”

The Tri-City Rubble Site, on Yellow Creek Road in Lead, does not accept lithium-ion batteries or items that contain them.

“Rapid City has Batteries Plus. Most cellphone places will take old phones and properly dispose of their batteries,” Gallagher said. “There are other places around that take used batteries too that could be properly disposed of, beyond just us. Most of them have no charge to it.”

title: ‘Butterfly wishes and chocolate kisses’ raises funds to support survivors of domestic violence
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: BELLE FOURCHE — Butterflies are symbols of hope and transformation — and they’re a key part of an important annual fundraiser for Shirley Speaks, a non-profit that supports survivors of domestic violence.
_full_text:
BELLE FOURCHE — Butterflies are symbols of hope and transformation — and they’re a key part of an important annual fundraiser for Shirley Speaks, a non-profit that supports survivors of domestic violence.

Danielle “Dani Jo” Butler founded Shirley Speaks to honor her mother after she suffered a debilitating attack at the hands of her long-time abuser. She died of her injuries after the attack.

“Before my mom actually passed, she had a handful of butterflies on a stick. She told us that she would come visit us as a butterfly when she was gone,” Butler said.

On Saturday, guests at Butterfly Wishes and Chocolate Kisses, a fundraiser for Shirley Speaks, released live butterflies in the afternoon.

Before that, there were chocolate tastings, a free lunch, activities for kids, flash tattoos, and a silent auction.

“This event will raise anywhere from $2,500 to $10,000 for us today,” Butler said.

Those funds will be used to offer free mental health and healing services to survivors of domestic violence throughout the northern and southern hills.

In addition to raising funds, the event raises awareness — which Butler said can be equally important.

“There are so many people in our own communities that we don’t know are really suffering and so many stories that have come forward. Even when I went to the gas station this morning, one lady saw that I had my (Shirley Speaks) shirt on and said, ‘I would like to tell you my story someday,’” Butler said. “By bringing more awareness to domestic violence, we are helping more people to feel safe to come forward and ask for help.”

Butler said, if you or someone you love is experiencing domestic abuse, or think you might be a victim, visit shirleyspeaksfoundation.org for resources. Survivors can also find support by calling (605)801-0528.

title: Larry Rhoden: Rancher, welder and 3-decade politician makes his case to earn SD’s trust
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Gov. Larry Rhoden drinks a cup of coffee on June 26, in the living room at his ranch near Union Center. Photo by Makenzie Huber, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Rhoden 1.jpg
Gov. Larry Rhoden drinks a cup of coffee on June 26, in the living room at his ranch near Union Center. Photo by Makenzie Huber, South Dakota Searchlight 

South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden leaned forward in a leather recliner in his living room, considering the criticism from a former colleague about their disagreements.

“I think there’s probably some fair statements in there,” Rhoden finally said.

In his late 30s and early 40s while on the Meade School District Board, Rhoden couldn’t back up his opinions effectively during debates, Terry Koontz said. She served with him on the board more than 25 years ago.

“Of all the board members I worked with, he’s the worst,” Koontz said.

The 2 clashed over policies ranging from rural education and homeschooling to the proposed location of a rodeo arena near Sturgis Brown High School. Rhoden became frustrated and angry when the board didn’t vote his way — which Koontz said was often.

Koontz’s characterization of Rhoden stands at odds with the reputation he’s built in state politics over the last 2 decades as a convener and collaborator. Rhoden, 67, said he’s changed.

“At that age, I wasn’t patient with people, especially when I thought they were stuck on stupid. It got me angry.” 

That frustration, he said, pushed him to be more considerate of others’ opinions as he continued in politics. He believes those and other life lessons have prepared him to seek his own 4-year term as South Dakota’s lead executive, after being elevated from lieutenant governor ago when Gov. Kristi Noem resigned to join President Donald Trump’s administration.

“Every step of the way you learn, you mature,” Rhoden said.

Ranch provides roots and a refuge

Walking along the gravel road winding through his ranch, Rhoden points out a small white house hidden behind trees and overgrown shrubs. He grew up there with his father, mother, 3 brothers and twin sister.

Rhoden learned how to drive at 8 years old on a tractor pulling a mower in a nearby field, and he attended a 2-room country school down the road in Union Center. One of his first memories of chores on the ranch was gathering and washing chicken eggs with his sister to sell at a Sturgis grocery store about 45 miles away.

He knew his future was on the family ranch spanning a couple thousand acres. Both sets of grandparents homesteaded within 20 miles of his home, and he can point toward the location of the log cabin his mother grew up in nearby.

He surrounds himself with reminders of his family history, including furniture he crafted from his mother’s childhood cabin, and a gavel and knife handles he made from a black walnut tree that shaded his childhood summers. 

His ancestors came to South Dakota with “big ideas and big hopes, and then they got slapped in the face with reality the first winter they spent out here,” Rhoden said. 

His family stuck it out, and he sees that same determination in his neighbors today.

“It was the ones who were the toughest and the most industrious, that gutted it out, the smartest that were able to find a way to eke out a living, and that became the foundation for our state,” Rhoden said. “I think about that a lot.”

But as Rhoden’s career in politics has advanced, his time on the ranch has dwindled.

During his 16 years in the Legislature, he struggled to keep up with chores at home. A neighbor drove several miles to his ranch daily to feed his cattle during the 3-month legislative sessions. When Noem asked Rhoden to temporarily add interim secretary of agriculture to his duties as lieutenant governor, he sold the cattle to that neighbor’s son and leased some of his land out to him.

Rhoden’s father taught him to weld, and Rhoden started a business years ago on the ranch making custom branding irons. Since he became governor, the youngest of his 4 sons has largely taken that over. 

Now, welding serves as therapy. 

“Anytime we come home, if there’s still daylight, I’ll change clothes and come out to the shop and light up the forge,” Rhoden said.

National Guard, political experience

Rhoden graduated from high school at the private Sunshine Bible Academy in 1977. He attended a vocational ranch management program in Rapid City but dropped out, saying he didn’t think the vocational classes were practical enough for ranch life. Rhoden is one of 12 governors in South Dakota history to lack a college degree.

He joined the South Dakota National Guard in 1978, went to welding school for his occupational specialty and served for six years, mostly in a maintenance battalion in Sturgis as part of the 842nd Engineer Company. 

His time at basic training tested his mental and physical limits, he said. Being “yelled at in the face” taught him to keep his cool in stressful situations, something he said served him well while leading lawmakers in the “pressure cooker” of the Legislature as assistant House majority leader and then House majority leader. He served as a legislator from 2001 to 2014 and again from 2017 to 2018.

Rhoden’s wife, first lady Sandy Rhoden, learned alongside him in his political career. The two met and married each other in their early 20s, raised their 4 sons and now have 9 grandchildren. Though Sandy, a former teacher, said she didn’t expect her husband to become governor, she saw he was “cut out for leadership” positions early on.

“There’ve been times I’ve had to encourage him to do things because I feel like I have a really good perspective of his abilities. If it’s not something I think he’d be good at, I’m not going to encourage him to do it,” Sandy said. “But if I think he should, then I do. And with the governor’s race, I don’t know of anybody else who I think is more capable of governing right now.”

Rhoden suffered some setbacks while attempting to win higher offices. He lost a bid for majority leader in the state Senate in 2011 and said he learned how to “be effective because of who you are and not what your position is” as a rank-and-file member. He described learning how to “lose well” in his failed bid for the U.S. Senate in 2014, when he finished second in a 5-way primary that included former governor and eventual U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds.

Rhoden introduced and endorsed Rounds at that year’s Republican convention, and called for party unity.

“That paid dividends for me for years after that,” Rhoden said, “because they had all of the leaders of the party there, and my stock went up in value because of that. And I think it ultimately had an impact on Kristi’s decision to ask me to be a running mate.”

It took Rhoden “probably a total of 3 seconds,” he said, to accept Noem’s invitation to be her running mate in 2018. The 2 had previously served together as legislators.

“It’s that sense that God put you on the planet to do more than serve yourself,” said Rhoden, a lifelong Baptist.

“I remember an old-timer who told me, ‘You should run for office for what you can do, not what you can be,’” Rhoden added. “I think there’s a lot of wisdom in that. Too many people want a title rather than want to make a difference in serving the state.”

After he took over for Noem when she departed in January 2025, she sparked national controversy as secretary of the Department of Homeland Security. Federal agents under her authority fatally shot 2 people during immigration enforcement operations in Minneapolis.

“There are people that think it’s a detriment to be tied to Kristi, and people that think it’s an advantage,” Rhoden said. “For me, it doesn’t really matter, because other people’s opinions aren’t going to change the way I view my relationship with her, my past working experience with her, and how much I valued the job she did.”

Trust and relationships

Rhoden said his faith is what makes him effective as governor.

“Having the moral compass of speaking the truth all the time and putting that ahead of any political agenda is central for me when I talk about my ability to build relationships and bring people together,” Rhoden said. “That’s all predicated upon trust and people’s trust in your integrity.”

But he acknowledged he can still get frustrated and angry like he did when he served on the school board. Some of his modern colleagues have observed that.

Republican former Senate President Pro Tempore Lee Schoenbeck, of Watertown, said he’s gone “toe to toe” with Rhoden behind closed doors.

“But the thing with Larry is I always knew even if we disagreed about one thing he’d have my back as far as the institution went on another thing,” Schoenbeck said.

Schoenbeck added that Rhoden was accessible to make deals and talk through issues during Noem’s administration when she was not. Schoenbeck expects an inclusive decision-making process if Rhoden is elected.

“Larry understands that when you live in Union Center, you can see a lot of land but not many people,” Schoenbeck said. “He gets that he needs a lot of those other folks that come from a lot of different places and perspectives to make sure he’s making good decisions.”

Nancy Turbak Berry, a Democratic former legislator who served with Rhoden, said she has appreciated Rhoden’s commitment to civility in difficult situations. She is a plaintiff in a lawsuit attempting to invalidate anti-abortion-pill legislation that Rhoden signed into law in March. 

Despite their political differences, Turbak Berry said Rhoden has been “open and respectful” to her input through the years — including her unsolicited text messages to him during his governorship and on the campaign trail.

“A lot of people in Republican politics in South Dakota have become so arrogant about the power that comes with a one-party state that they think they don’t have to deal with anybody outside of the party,” Turbak Berry said. “A lot of people would ignore me or respond with hostility. Rhoden has never done that.”

That dynamic has earned her vote — she temporarily switched her party affiliation ahead of the primary to vote for him, she said. She plans to vote for him again in the runoff before switching her registration back.

“I trust him,” Turbak Berry said.

Rhoden was registered as a Democrat early in his life. Both of his parents were children of the Great Depression and “beholden,” he said, to President Franklin D. Roosevelt and his Depression-era federal work programs. 

“I always say I was Democrat by birth and Republican by choice,” Rhoden said, adding that Ronald Reagan (who was also a former Democrat) had the largest political influence on him as a young man.

It wasn’t until the 1990s, a few years before he made a run for the Legislature, that he switched his party affiliation to Republican.

Legislative record

During his legislative career, Rhoden worked to support what he called “conservative values.”

He sponsored a successful bill in 2004 that exempted trucking services from sales taxes, saving trucking companies and costing the state about $4 million annually.

He worked for years to restrict the Department of Game, Fish and Parks’ use of the open fields doctrine, which allowed the department’s law enforcement officers to enter private land without a landowner’s permission while enforcing hunting and fishing laws. In 2021, while Rhoden was lieutenant governor, lawmakers passed legislation he supported that specified when the department’s officers can enter private land and when they must obtain permission or a warrant.

Rhoden was the main sponsor of a bill to change the taxable valuation of agricultural land from a market-based system to a productivity-based system, which helped to limit the growth of property taxes on farm and ranch land.

Rhoden supported pro-gun bills and anti-abortion legislation. That included the 2005 abortion trigger ban that went into effect after the U.S. Supreme Court’s Dobbs decision in 2022. The law prohibits all abortions except those deemed medically necessary to save the life of the mother.

“It’s kind of laughable when I see stuff on Facebook of people trying to brand me as moderate or whatever,” Rhoden said. “I think people get confused. They think you can’t be conservative if you get along with people, or that if you’re not picking fights then you’re not a conservative.”

Rhoden also introduced the successful legislation in 2003 that designated rodeo as the official sport of South Dakota.

‘Steady hand at the helm’

After taking over for Noem, Rhoden said, he didn’t decide to seek his own term as governor until he proved to himself that he could do the job.

His potential candidacy ultimately hinged, he said, on his ability to win approval for the construction of a $650 million men’s prison in Sioux Falls — the largest capital project in state history, which had already failed in the Legislature once — during a special legislative session in September of last year. Rhoden argued a new prison is needed to replace dangerously out-of-date facilities at the state’s 145-year-old penitentiary, and to provide more programming space to help people avoid returning to prison after their release.

By the time of the special session, there were already three other Republican candidates for governor, all with lawmakers supporting them who didn’t particularly want Rhoden getting a policy win and joining the race, he recalled. Lawmakers approved the prison plan, using money set aside during the prior several years to avoid taking on debt. 

That was the last of what Rhoden has called the “three P’s” that he inherited as unresolved issues when he became governor: the prison, a pipeline and property taxes.

In addition to getting the prison approved, he brought an end — for now – to a controversial carbon-capture pipeline proposal by signing a bill into law that bans such projects from using a process known as eminent domain for gaining access to private land. He also signed several bills into law that will lower property taxes for homeowners in the coming years, including two that rely on higher sales taxes to bring property taxes down. 

Dave Knudson served as Senate majority leader in the Legislature while Rhoden was House majority leader. 

“I think the important thing is we have a steady hand at the helm of state government that won’t run us off the road at all and just continue to make life better on an incremental basis for the average citizen,” Knudson said. “I think Rhoden has the ability to do that.”

If he makes it past the runoff and is elected in November against Democratic nominee Dan Ahlers, Rhoden said the next four years will look similar to the last year and a half: task forces and roundtables to seek understanding and collaboration on divisive issues, conservative fiscal policy, and investment in South Dakota’s industries and workforce.

“It’s hanging meat on the bones of the visions we’ve laid out,” Rhoden said.

“I’m not just talking big talk. We’ve delivered results,” he added. “I’ve been doing the job, and we’ve been doing a pretty good job of delivering results for South Dakota, and that’s what we’ll continue to do if they give me another 4 years.”
