title: Toby Doeden: A bitcoin evangelist and anti-property-tax crusader who wants to be governor
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Republican candidate for governor Toby Doeden speaks with members of the South Dakota NewsMedia Association June 11, in Sioux Falls. Photo by Joshua Haiar, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Doeden1 .jpg
Republican candidate for governor Toby Doeden speaks with members of the South Dakota NewsMedia Association June 11, in Sioux Falls. Photo by Joshua Haiar, South Dakota Searchlight 

Toby Doeden says he was born into poverty but climbed out of it through salesmanship, risk-taking and the force of his personality. He thinks those same traits could rescue South Dakota, a state he says needs saving. 

The 51-year-old Republican businessman, landlord, developer, entrepreneur and bitcoin investor has put at least $4 million of his own money into his campaign for governor, according to campaign finance reports. It’s his first run for elected office.

“I’m risking literally everything I have to fight for the future of South Dakota,” Doeden told South Dakota Public Broadcasting last year. 

His critics, meanwhile, describe him as a pitchman whose confidence veers into overpromising about his campaign pledge to eliminate property taxes, and whose outspokenness has veered into offensive remarks on social media. A fellow Aberdeen resident and Republican, state Sen. Michael Rohl, is one of those critics. 

“He enjoys the comfort of opinion without the discomfort of thought,” Rohl said of Doeden.

Doeden stunned the political establishment by finishing first in the June 2 Republican primary ahead of the governor, a U.S. representative and the state speaker of the House. But Doeden failed to reach 35%, setting up a July 28 runoff with Gov. Larry Rhoden, the second-place finisher.

Neither Doeden nor his campaign team followed through on pledges to schedule an interview for this story, despite exchanging multiple messages with South Dakota Searchlight. Doeden sent written comments in some of those messages, including one accusing Rhoden of being unwilling to face the media. Rhoden, for his part, allowed a Searchlight reporter to interview him at his ranch in rural Union Center.

Rhoden has declined to debate Doeden ahead of the runoff, after they and the 2 other candidates in the June 2 primary all participated in 3 debates before that election. Doeden wants another debate.

“Someone unwilling to make themselves available to the press and to the people in advance of an election has no business holding an office as important as governor,” Doeden wrote to Searchlight.

Although Doeden did not grant an interview for this story, he has revealed much about himself in past interviews and media appearances, including a podcast he started in 2024 called “Toby Doeden — Unfiltered.” 

Growing up in a ‘loose environment’

Doeden grew up in Groton, a town of fewer than 1,500 people about 25 miles from Aberdeen in northeast South Dakota. He told SDPB he had a disabled father, a constantly working mother, and three much older siblings. 

He said his parents left him “behind a little bit,” explaining in his podcast that “by the time they get to their fourth child, especially when it’s a ‘oops,’ so to speak,” his parents were “kind of done with it.”

That shaped him, he said. 

“As a young kid, I remember always having to look for ways to entertain myself,” Doeden said on the podcast. “From a very, very young age, I always had many entrepreneurial ideas. I was a daydreamer.”  

Doeden was interviewed in June for a YouTube show called “After the Call.” He has been criticized for his outspokenness since childhood, he said in that interview. Teachers, bosses, coaches — and now political opponents — have all wanted him to act differently. Doeden’s answer is that he can’t turn it off.

“This is what you get,” Doeden said. “I’m Toby 24 hours a day, 365 days a year, and I’ll never change. I don’t care who likes it. I don’t care who doesn’t.” 

That brashness has manifested in controversial ways. Doeden has commented on Facebook that LGBTQ+ pride celebrations are a “smokescreen to distract the lost” from acknowledging “emptiness” and “loneliness,” stemming from “hyper-sexualized narcissistic lifestyles.” A string of Doeden’s social media posts in 2023 encouraged the shooting of immigrants in gangs, used a profane insult to describe President Joe Biden, and labeled statistics about hatred of Jewish Americans as “fake.” 

During the 2024 campaign season, Doeden’s political action committee hosted a rally featuring a video message from Mark Robinson, a Republican who was running for governor of North Carolina. CNN had just reported that Robinson made racist and sexually explicit remarks more than a decade earlier on a pornographic website’s message board. 

Doeden stood by Robinson. In response to Republican officials who condemned the event, Doeden told Searchlight at the time that the critics “aren’t conservatives.” 

“These people are hacks. They’re clowns. They’re disgusting,” Doeden said. 

Doeden traces his outspokenness to his upbringing, saying in the YouTube interview that his parents allowed him and his siblings to grow up in a “loose environment.” That upbringing became “the number one driving factor to my success today,” Doeden said, “and nobody will ever convince me any different.” The environment gave him the freedom to try and fail, he said, and to express his creativity. 

Struggling to ‘make a buck’

Doeden said on his podcast that he tried college, but it wasn’t for him. He does not have a college degree.

From there, he tried almost everything. Owning vending machines. Selling and installing satellite dishes. Factory work. Starting a paint business with his parents.

“If there was a way to try to make a buck, I tried it,” he said on his podcast. 

While newly married to Liz — his wife of 30 years — and expecting the first of their 4 children, Doeden was working at a gas station in Groton.

Then, in 1997, he landed a job as a car salesman at Aberdeen Chrysler Center. In his first month, he said on his podcast, he sold 20 vehicles.

“I had made more money than I had ever dreamed of,” Doeden said.

He ultimately rose to become general manager, then a partner, and then bought out the mentor who hired him. Doeden said on his podcast that he eventually became uneasy with having all his wealth tied up in his vehicle dealership, and he wanted to diversify.

Charitable giving

Now that he has the means, Doeden said in the YouTube interview, he often opens the GoFundMe charitable giving website, searches “South Dakota,” and looks for people in need.

Some GoFundMe donations are publicly viewable, though donors can give anonymously. Searchlight found $3,000 from Doeden to an Aberdeen woman allegedly assaulted in her home and hospitalized, $2,000 to a Sioux Falls child fighting leukemia, $300 to help a couple care for their premature baby, and $500 for a similar situation. 

Kelsea Schwab said her family encountered Doeden when he made an unexpected $2,000 donation for her seriously ill daughter who was dealing with liver failure in 2022, after the family had already lost a younger daughter to sudden infant death syndrome. Doeden kept checking in afterward, used his businesses to help raise money for the deceased child’s headstone, and donated “thousands and thousands of dollars” during a Ronald McDonald House gala at her invitation, Schwab said.

“Yes, he has a lot of money, but he also uses it for a lot of good,” Schwab told Searchlight.

Doeden founded a charity, the 4J Foundation, in 2020, primarily focused on Aberdeen-area children and pets in need. In 2021, the foundation gave $250,000 to the Aberdeen Area Humane Society, which used the money to build the Doeden Family Animal Shelter.

“I’ve donated literally millions of dollars to charities, families, humane centers, humane societies,” Doeden told the Aberdeen Insider newspaper in June, adding “nobody has been more generous, not just in giving money, but just giving my time to people.”

Thares said he could not recall Doeden “contributing in a significant way to any of the projects” of which Thares has knowledge from his years of involvement in the community. 

Harvey Jewett of Aberdeen is a philanthropist, attorney, entrepreneur, former president of Super 8 Motels, and former longtime member of the state Board of Regents, which oversees South Dakota’s public universities. He disputes Doeden’s characterization about the extent of Doeden’s charitable giving.

“If someone had donated millions of dollars in the Aberdeen area, I would have known about it,” Jewett said. 

Fighting his own property taxes while pledging to eliminate them

Doeden has also invested extensively in real estate, including buying and renovating dilapidated apartments.

Searchlight located a total of $39.8 million worth of property owned by Doeden or his companies in Brown, Spink and Edmunds counties, with the majority in Brown County, which includes Aberdeen as the county seat. Taxes on those properties total more than $680,000, according to public records.  

Property tax rates are applied to a property’s value, which is assessed by county officials. Property owners who think their assessed value is too high can appeal to a local board.

One of Doeden’s companies appealed the valuations of 47 Brown County properties this year, according to county Equalization Office records, but later withdrew all but nine of the appeals. The other nine were adjusted downward.

Doeden announced his bid for governor in May 2025 in Aberdeen with a pledge about property taxes. 

“As governor, I will fight to eliminate property taxes so that each and every resident — regardless of class, color, creed or profession — can truly own their home and their land once and for all,” Doeden said. 

He has continued to make similar pledges, sometimes saying he will “phase out” property taxes. More recently, Doeden’s campaign spokesman told Searchlight the plan only applies to owner-occupied properties — in other words, homeowners, not agricultural or commercial properties.

South Dakotans paid $1.86 billion in property taxes last year, including $815 million from homeowners, but none of that money goes to state government. It all goes to schools, counties, cities and smaller units of government. Searchlight asked Doeden in a May podcast interview how he would make up that lost revenue for those jurisdictions.

“Once the economy starts growing, and it will; once I start collecting external revenue, which we will; and once I cut all the fat and pork out of our state budget, you are going to see, very quickly, within a matter of a couple years, a significant amount of annual budget surpluses,” Doeden said. “And yes, I will use that money to target the phase-out of things like property tax.” 

One of the opponents Doeden beat in the June 2 primary, U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, criticized Doeden’s tax plan in an April debate.

“The math just doesn’t work,” Johnson said. “Hopes and dreams didn’t work for Obama and they’re not going to work for eliminating property taxes either.”

Bitcoin evangelism

Beyond his businesses and rental properties, Doeden is an evangelist for bitcoin. It’s a cryptocurrency, which is a type of digital money secured by encryption technology. Cryptocurrencies enable the transfer of value online without a bank or payment processor, and some cryptocurrencies, including bitcoin, are used as investment vehicles.

Investing in bitcoin means buying and later selling it when its value increases. New bitcoin is “mined” using large amounts of electricity to make trillions of calculations. The goal is to solve a puzzle that awards the “miner” a newly created bitcoin. 

Doeden devoted an entire episode of his podcast to discussing and promoting bitcoin. 

“As I learned more and more about it, I just kept essentially taking almost all of my cash reserves from all of my companies that I knew I wasn’t going to need anytime soon, and we just converted it from cash to bitcoin,” he said.

In 2022, Doeden’s Plaza Rentals company and his son, Jackson, received permission from a local zoning board to operate a bitcoin mining facility in Aberdeen. When Searchlight sent Doeden messages asking for more information about that operation, Doeden responded by text message: “I don’t think there’s a single reader in the state that’s gonna find this interesting.” 

He did not respond to a message asking how much of his current wealth is from or is invested in cryptocurrencies. 

State Rep. Logan Manhart, R-Aberdeen — who lost in the June 2 primary election — has been working with Doeden’s campaign. Manhart sponsored bills each of the last two legislative sessions to allow the South Dakota Investment Council to invest in bitcoin.

The council manages investments that fund the pensions of public employees in the state, ranging from teachers to state office workers to police, as well as other investment funds that produce revenue for the state budget.

Doeden supported Manhart’s bitcoin legislation and took it a step further, posting on social media in January 2025 that “South Dakota needs a Bitcoin Reserve,” while sharing Manhart’s post about his legislation.

The Investment Council and the governor’s budget office were among the opponents who testified against Manhart’s legislation, saying bitcoin is too volatile and would damage the state’s standing with bond-rating agencies. The value of one bitcoin has swung dramatically, from less than $20,000 in 2023 to more than $100,000 last year. 

State law requires the council to prioritize the safety of its funds, “not speculation,” explained Matt Clark, who leads the council.

“Bitcoin does not have any underlying physical use,” Clark said in his testimony. 

Politically activated by a pandemic and a pipeline

Doeden said on his podcast that he was not politically engaged until around the time of the COVID-19 pandemic, which is also when he and his wife became empty nesters, and when both of Doeden’s parents died — one of cancer and the other of heart disease. 

In his June YouTube interview, Doeden said he started thinking about running for office after attending a pandemic-era rally supporting landowners fighting a carbon sequestration pipeline. Doeden recalled standing up at the rally and declaring that U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, R-South Dakota, would become governor “over my dead body.” The crowd’s response, Doeden said, was an “aha moment.” 

Johnson, who led in several early polls, finished third behind Doeden and Rhoden in the June 2 Republican governor primary, ahead of state House Speaker Jon Hansen.

Doeden said he decided to run for governor after the assassination attempt against President Donald Trump in July 2024 at Butler, Pennsylvania. Doeden told the NewsMedia Association that he looked at his wife and said he had “never felt more like a coward.”

title: Costs and benefits
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Spearfish City Finance Officer Michelle DeNeui presents an early version of the city’s budget. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Budget.JPG
Spearfish City Finance Officer Michelle DeNeui presents an early version of the city’s budget. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — Employees are often an organization’s greatest resource. They are generally also the greatest expense. As Spearfish city leadership prepares preliminary budgets for 2027, they’re finding that wages are a fast-increasing expense.

In August 2025, the Spearfish City Council adopted a new job classification and compensation plan, prepared by consultants from Clarion and Associates. That plan evaluated each job in the city based on the required knowledge, supervisory controls, complexity, scope and effect, personal contacts, purpose of contacts, physical demands, and work environment for each employee. Based on that, it proposed a wage scale. The scale takes an employee’s job description and level of responsibility into account, assigning each job a grade. Individuals also receive a “step” classification based on their qualifications and tenure.

On an annual basis, it increased employee wages by 3.94% or $375,374 a year.  

But part of the plan was not implemented immediately. Consultants from Condrey and Associates recommended “equity steps” for the years of service put in by tenured employees who were on staff before the wage scale was implemented.  Beginning in January 2027, employees with 5 years of service are scheduled to move up 2 pay scale steps; employees with 10 years of service will move up 3 steps, and employees with 20 years or more tenure will move up 5 steps on the city’s wage scale.

The goal was to limit wage compression — creating scenarios where newly hired employees were paid more than their long-serving colleagues.

The cost of implementing the Condrey study is particularly clear in the library budget — in part because as much as 90% of that budget is made up of staff wages.

The amount budgeted for personnel in 2026 was $560,779; in 2027, it is $ 623,153.

“We have a lot of longevity in the library,” said Grace Balloch Memorial Library Director Amber Wilde. “I think at least 5 of us are affected by that.”

The remainder of the library budget, which factors in collection and digital content costs and technology expenses, is on track to increase by $208 in 2027.

“We are not looking at much of an increase at all,” Wilde said. “What really happens in the library is that certain things just kind of adjust. We find that certain things are getting used less and certain things are getting used more, and we keep adjusting as we need to. Really the bulk of our operation and the heart of our operation is our staff, so that is where most of our funds go.”

In the finance office, 2 staff members will qualify for longevity adjustments under the second implementation phase of the Condrey study. 

Reducing travel, training budgets for employees

“That is where you’re seeing the increase in personnel costs and then seeing an increase in our audit costs,” DeNeui said. In 2027, DeNeui said the city must pay an actuary to assess the city’s finances.

“I think there is a $7,000 or $8,000 a year cost in one year, and you’re scored for 3 years,” DeNeui said. 

DeNeui said the funds for the actuary could be covered by reducing the employee travel budget. DeNeui said in 2027, cuts are planned in the city administrator department budget.

“There is $32,000 in reductions in other line items within the city administrator budget. The largest came from travel in the city administrator budget,” DeNeui said. “We did have some extra funds put in there for all employee trainings, where we could bring in trainers to train all the city staff or provide additional training to staff.”

Mapping potential wages for incoming department leadership 

The city administrator position is vacant. 

“Under the city administrator it took a midpoint for that. The position is a grade 28. We have a budgeted amount for step 9. It would be a total of $220,000 a year salary, plus family health insurance coverage for that position. That is just setting the budget authority,” DeNeui said. “That does not mean that its what has to be paid or anything, it just gives you the budget authority when negotiating with any potential staff members to fill that position.”

The city attorney position, also vacant, is a grade 26, budgeted for a step 11 — a total salary of $189,633 for 2027. That could change before the budget reaches final adoption, or be adjusted during the hiring process if a qualified candidate is brought onboard. 

An $83,000 HR budget, sans wages

The human resources budget is poised to increase by $5,500 in 2027, to a total of $83,000 — staff wages not included.

“That money, from the operating fund, basically supports our department’s main responsibilities, which are employment law compliance, drug and alcohol testing, background investigations, employee training, recruitment and hiring activities, and also professional memberships and resources that we use to be able to do our positions,” said Human Resources Director Jodi Mathis.

Mathis said her department budgeted for a 15% increase in insurance costs.

“Health insurance is the largest employee benefit that Spearfish offers to staff,” Mathis said.

Investing in AI

In the IT budget, human resources has included $5,591, plus a $1,000 one-time implementation fee for “Workable” — new software Mathis said will help her department adjust to AI’s rapidly growing role in job application and candidate search-processes.

“This investment is an additional $5,591. We currently pay $5,000 for an application tracking system that we have right now,” Mathis said.

Workable harnesses artificial intelligence to help recruit candidates for positions.

“The AI Recruiting Agent feature of Workable will help staff complete administrative tasks more efficiently, such as organizing applications, drafting job descriptions, scheduling interviews, and improving communication with candidates,” Mathis told the Pioneer.

Workable is also designed to help sift through noise — which is often generated by AI.

“AI-generated resumes are becoming more common. To prevent misuse of AI to enhance a resume, we verify employment history, conduct interviews, check references, and, when appropriate, perform background checks and skills assessments,” Mathis said. ”Workable’s AI helps with tasks such as drafting job descriptions, summarizing applications, identifying candidates whose experience appears to match the qualifications of a position, and improving communication throughout the hiring process. These tools improve efficiency, but they do not replace the City’s evaluation process. Every hiring decision is ultimately made by our hiring managers and interview panels.”

Potential parental benefits

In the coming year, Mathis would like to offer city employees paid parental leave. Council will have a chance to approve or deny that request this fall during a planned update of the personnel policy manual.

“There was an individual who wanted to know what our paid parental leave policy was with the city,” Mathis said. “She was looking at a state agency where they receive 12 weeks. Little by little, it keeps coming up. So, I visited with John about possibly adding this in 2027 … basically this will assist individuals who are starting families, whether it be for a birth or an adoption.”

Mathis would like to offer 160 hours of paid time off for parents either adopting or having a baby. Birthing mothers would be eligible to receive an additional 80 hours of paid time off, under the proposed policy.

title: Deadwood moves towards regaining certified local government status
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: The city of Deadwood is moving towards regaining certified local government status, which will qualify the historic preservation commission for funding and training offered by the state historic preservation office. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
Deadwood moves towards regaining certified local government status
The city of Deadwood is moving towards regaining certified local government status, which will qualify the historic preservation commission for funding and training offered by the state historic preservation office. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

DEADWOOD — Deadwood is moving towards regaining its status as a certified local government with the South Dakota Historical Preservation Office after almost 20 years of lapsed rating.

“A certified local government is a term used through the historic preservation act of 1966, as amended,” said Kevin Kuchenbecker, director of historic preservation. “Those communities that are certified through the state historic preservation office and eventually the National Park service through the Department of Interior, for having a preservation commission ordinance and administration of protecting their historic resources.”

Kuchenbecker told historic preservation commissioners July 21 that the city has been performing as a certified local government for the last 2 decades by participating in conferences and workshops, but reclaiming the status would qualify the city for state and federal grant monies.

“Ten percent of all federal funds through the historic preservation fund, which is offshore oil reserves, are sent out to the different states,” said Kuchenbecker. “Each state gets so much, but some of it is on their own preservation programs and how many communities are involved. Ten percent of those federal funds coming from the historic preservation foundation to the state is required to be granted back to the certified local governments. We will pretty get allocated $2,000 and then compete for the rest in grants.”

Kuchenbecker said nearly all preservation projects in the city would qualify for the funds.

“Additional work to staff would be just combining our minutes into a report at the end of the year and highlighting some of our projects that we do,” said Kuchenbecker. “I think it’s going to be worthwhile and get us on the same field as other communities.” 

Kuchenbecker said other communities in the Northern Hills that qualify as certified local governments include Spearfish, Belle Fourche, Hot Springs, and Rapid City.

Qualifying as a certified local government has 5 requirements, 4 of which Deadwood already meets. Kuchenbecker said those requirements are to enforce state and local legislation for the protection of the historic properties (done through municipal ordinances); establish an historic preservation commission (established in Deadwood in 1973); maintain a system for survey and inventory of historic properties; provide public participation in local preservation programs (performed both by the city and Deadwood History, Inc.); and perform other responsibilities dedicated to the city by the state historic preservation by mutually written agreements.

Kuchenbecker said the written agreements will be made after city commissioners agree to regaining status as a certified local government. The issue is expected to be presented to commissioners at the Aug. 3 meeting.

After regaining status, Kuchenbecker said maintaining it will require an annual summary of the historic preservation commission’s minutes.   

“No new ordinances, no new rules or regulations (will be) associated with the status, it’s really a recognition since we’re doing all of the above anyway,” said Kuchenbecker. 

Kuchenbecker said if the state historic preservation office approves their application to regain certified local government status, the city could begin applying for funding as early as Jan. 1.

title: Lead building inspector plans to retire Aug. 7
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Lead Building Inspector Dennis Schumacher stands behind his desk at city hall. Schumacher will retire from the position he’s held for 20 years Aug. 7. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
Dennis Schumacher.jpeg
Lead Building Inspector Dennis Schumacher stands behind his desk at city hall. Schumacher will retire from the position he’s held for 20 years Aug. 7. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

LEAD — When Dennis Schumacher took the job as the Lead building inspector in August 2005, Lead was pretty depressed, as the city that had been supported by Homestake for 125 years struggled to survive when the mining company closed. 

Businesses were gone. 

Longtime residents had moved away. 

Properties were falling apart. 

“When I first started here it was dead,” Schumacher said. “The city of Lead had nothing. We had no money. A classic example was the city was so broke that one of their pickups was so old that they were driving down Main Street and the door fell off.” 

Amidst all of that turmoil were property ISO (Insurance Service Offices) ratings, which is a rating property insurance companies set to determine premium costs. Rated on a scale of 1 as the best, to 10 as the worst, the city of Lead ranked as a 9 for the system that assessed how well an area can handle fire and other property damage prevention and response. 

In his capacity as the building inspector, Schumacher said he has worked hard to lower that rating to a 4, through obtaining certifications, training, improving record keeping practices, and implementing policies and procedures. 

“I feel really good about that because of what we accomplished,” Schumacher said. 

Schumacher recently announced his retirement from the city of Lead, which will be effective Aug. 7. During his 20 years at the helm of building in Lead, the job has changed significantly. He started as the fire and building inspector, EMS coordinator, and the Lead wildland fire protection coordinator. But since 2008, when the fire department became a separate entity from the city, Schumacher has been able to focus on building inspection, building codes, zoning, and other planning related tasks. 

Pull quote
“The city was so broke that one of their pickups was so old that they were driving down Main Street and the door fell off.” — Dennis Schumacher

When he first started, he said Lead had about 30 properties that were abandoned or in various stages of dilapidation. While he had to approve demolition permits for half of them, he has also successfully overseen the rehabilitation of the rest. 

“A building inspector’s job is real easy if it’s nothing but brand-new homes,” he said. “They’re just going to follow the code. But when you go to rehab old homes, sometimes it’s a challenge to get that rehab or get that remodel and meet the code. Sometimes it’s almost impossible. You’re not going to take a house up here on Alert Street, where the lot’s really small and you can barely get a lawnmower between 2 houses, and you’re not going to get a backhoe in there to re-do the foundation to 4 feet deep. You just gotta make adjustments. I figure out how to make that happen and still make it safe.” 

In his 20 years with the city, he’s watched Lead slowly grow back to a bustling community. 

“Lead has prospered,” he said. “People can say it hasn’t, but it has. In my days when I was here as a kid, we had 9,000 people and 2,400 guys working at the mine. My class had 175 kids. That’s not reality today, but we’re still growing. Our tax base is still going. Our houses are being built. We have businesses on Main Street. So I’ve seen the very bad and I think it’s good now.” 

During his time with the city, Schumacher said he has had the privilege of working in a supportive environment, with quality co-workers who are dedicated to making the city better. 

“They’re dedicated and they care,” he said. “The citizens of Lead, not everybody’s happy, but you can’t keep everybody happy. There’s going to be the ones that aint happy and the ones that just think everything’s great. The employees, they do a great job. They sometimes do jobs that don’t get too much thanks for it. But the city of Lead has treated me very well. When I had cancer and stuff, they stood behind me to make sure I got through. I can’t ask for better.”

title: Estimated cost of proposed eastern SD water pipeline at $8.4 billion+
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: A map of water providers that would be served by the proposed Dakota Mainstem Regional Water System pipeline project. Image courtesy of Dakota Mainstem
_full_text:
Estimated cost of proposed eastern SD water pipeline at $8.4 billion+.jpg
A map of water providers that would be served by the proposed Dakota Mainstem Regional Water System pipeline project. Image courtesy of Dakota Mainstem 

SIOUX FALLS — One of several proposed pipeline systems to deliver Missouri River water in South Dakota could cost $8.4 billion to $10 billion, according to estimates shared Monday.

Dakota Mainstem Regional Water System Executive Director Kurt Pfeifle was on a panel speaking to the Rotary Club of Downtown Sioux Falls. 

“That includes about a 30% contingency, but right now, there’s just so many unknowns,” Pfeifle said, referring to a cost estimate buffer. 

The system’s proposed pipeline would serve nearly 60 water providers across much of eastern South Dakota and portions of three neighboring states, with a capacity of 195 million gallons per day.

Pfeifle said the organization recently completed an initial study to arrive at those numbers and is beginning a $4.2 million feasibility study expected to take about two and a half years. 

Pending federal legislation sponsored by South Dakota’s congressional delegation would provide funding to help with that study and two other studies for the proposed Western Dakota Regional Water System pipeline, which has an estimated projected cost of $4 billion, and a planned expansion of the Lewis & Clark Regional Water System in southeast South Dakota, which has an estimated project cost of $2.5 billion. 

Lewis & Clark Regional Water System Executive Director Troy Larson and Minnehaha Community Water Corporation Executive Director Scott Buss were also on the panel.

Construction began on the Lewis & Clark system in 2003 and is ongoing, although the constructed portion already serves 20 member cities and rural water systems. Completion of the 3-state, 44-million-gallon-per-day “base system” is estimated to cost $825 million, with completion sometime in 2028. Federal funding covers 80% of the cost.

Larson said the planned expansion will increase capacity to 60 million gallons per day by 2030. But he said the system’s members already project they will need an additional 95 million gallons per day over the next 40 years.

“That’s 60 plus 95, not 60 and then get to 95,” Larson said.  

The projects are driven by industry and population growth.

Minnehaha Community Water is a member-owned utility that receives water from the Lewis & Clark pipeline and the Big Sioux River aquifer, and delivers it to 5,300 rural customers and seven cities. Buss said the system has approached its limits during recent summers — particularly during droughts — and has rejected some economic development opportunities because it could not guarantee it would be able to deliver enough water.

title: Belle Fourche asphalt recycler fills  500+ potholes in first 6 months
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Belle Fourche has had its asphalt recycler for almost 6 months now. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Asphalt recycler 1.JPG
Belle Fourche has had its asphalt recycler for almost 6 months now. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

 Asphalt recycler 2.JPG
An asphalt oil brick, designed to be fed into an asphalt recycler is pictured here with Belle Fourche City Councilman Clark Sowers in the background. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

BELLE FOURCHE — In a presentation to the Belle Fourche City Council, Public Works Director Ryan Stedillie said the new asphalt recycler — purchased at the beginning of the year — has been used to fill more than 500 potholes. After 500, the public works director told the council he stopped counting.

The machine is designed specifically to recycle asphalt and fill potholes. It’s not intended to mill and overlay streets, for example.

“It was never intended to provide a curb-to-curb overlay or resurfacing. Our crews have been working throughout the city and have done an excellent job learning the new equipment. Like anything new, there has been a learning curve, but they’ve adapted well and continue to improve the process,” Stedillie said.

The piece of equipment operates like a spinning kiln, reaching temperatures of about 400 degrees Fahrenheit in order to heat crushed asphalt and bricks of asphalt oil.  It takes 2 men to operate, about 20 minutes to heat, and has a 4-ton capacity.

The Belle Fourche landfill collects and crushes asphalt pulled up during street replacement and repairs. That material can be loaded into the recycler. Crews also feed asphalt oil bricks, which cost about $12 each, into the machine. After heating and spinning, the recycler spits out asphalt that can be scooped out and applied to roadways.

“The crew is learning the “recipe,” and some of the issue is the recycled product and learning the best process as we operate it,” Councilman Clark Sowers told the Pioneer.

Sowers visited the public works shop in January to inspect the machine and learn about how it worked, before approving the $90,000. The city was able to negotiate that price — a new asphalt recycler would have cost about $106,000.

He said the public reaction to the recycler has been mixed. 

“Some people are happy with it, some don’t realize we have it and are using it. Some expect an overlay of the street with this machine, which is not what it is designed for,” Sowers said. “It’s designed to fill in a hole so one doesn’t drive in it. The pothole when filled may have a “hump” in it, but it’s not a hole,” Sowers said.

Sowers said there are a few places in town he’d like to see patched next, but noted that crews have been handling other city projects — especially surrounding the week of the Black Hills Roundup.

As summer event season winds down, budget season winds up. The city is working on its draft 2027 budget, and Stedillie said his department will be looking for ways to optimize the asphalt recycler and reduce the cost of street maintenance efforts across the board.

“As the City Council continues reviewing the proposed 2027 budget, we are evaluating additional ways to improve the efficiency of our pavement maintenance operations,” Stedillie said.

title: Plans for ND nickel processing  unclear as company also  evaluates Michigan site
byline: By Peyton Haug North Dakota Monitor
description: A ceremony last year celebrated a key step in converting a former North Dakota coal mine into a processing site for nickel mined in Minnesota.
_full_text:
NorthDakotaMonitorLogo

A ceremony last year celebrated a key step in converting a former North Dakota coal mine into a processing site for nickel mined in Minnesota.

But now the future of the project looks less clear, with a feasibility study also examining whether to send the nickel by rail to Michigan.

At an event last May, Westmoreland Mining signed an agreement to let Talon Metals use parts of an old coal mine in Beulah to transform ore into concentrate. 

Joined by multinational mining company Rio Tinto, Talon Metals proposes to target a high-grade nickel reserve 2,000 feet underground at a site near Tamarack, Minnesota. Nickel is mostly used for batteries and stainless steel, often coming from foreign markets. 

Support for the project is rooted in a national push to keep critical minerals on U.S. soil and out of “adversarial” countries. In 2023, the Department of Defense awarded Talon Metals $20.6 million for nickel exploration. 

North Dakota’s governor and congressional delegation joined for the signing ceremony for the project that would be the first of its kind in the country.   

One year after the Beulah signing, however, major details about the project remain out of public view — like who will use the material, where it will be processed and how much the entire operation will cost. 

It was signaled in the May 2025 agreement the processing site would be in North Dakota. 

However, according to the company’s external affairs manager, Jess Johnson, Talon Metals might instead use its existing Eagle Mine and Humboldt Mill site in Michigan’s Upper Peninsula for processing. 

“We are evaluating both options for ore to either go to North Dakota or go to the already operating mill in Michigan,” she said. “It could be both.” 

North Dakota regulators have not received applications for the project.

A Talon Metals press release from July 9 refers to both a Beulah processing facility and Michigan ore processing facility.  

If the company opts for North Dakota, it would need to employ approximately 150 people for operations. Whereas in Michigan, it would use the existing 450-person workforce, Johnson said. But railing the ore through northern Wisconsin to Michigan will likely cost more than railing it directly to North Dakota. 

After recent talks with Talon Metals, Beulah Economic Development Director Granville “Beaver” Brinkman is under the impression the company still plans on coming to North Dakota.

“The state has a lot to offer a company like Talon Metals. I hope they don’t go somewhere else,” he said, citing jobs and tax revenue as some major pluses of bringing the industry to small-town Beulah. 

According to Westmoreland Mining External Affairs Director and Counsel Jon Heroux, Talon Metals isn’t bound to the land; it merely has an option to use it for the processing facility. 

The decision is expected to come this fall as part of an overall feasibility study. 

Other information will be folded into that study, according to Johnson. 

The company held onto a $115 million Department of Energy grant amid a flurry of cuts made at the federal level, and entered an informal deal with Tesla. 

According to public filings from 2024, the project would involve supplying the electric vehicle maker with 75,000 metric tons, or 165 million pounds, of processed nickel once operations begin. 

Talon Metals vowed to use “commercially reasonable efforts” to begin production on or before Jan. 1, 2026. That hasn’t happened, but the agreement allows for both Talon Metals and Tesla to decide whether to move forward with the deal by the end of the year. 

Talon Metals has also been in early talks with Fargo-based defense technology company Packet Digital. 

As it stands, the 18-month construction of the mine in Minnesota would begin in late 2028 or early 2029; earliest production from a processing facility could begin in 2030, according to Johnson.

That timeline largely hinges on the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources environmental impact study, which includes a public comment period that runs through Sept. 12. Additional permitting will follow depending on the results of the report.

Neither the North Dakota Department of Environmental Quality nor the Department of Water Resources has received any applications for the Beulah site. Deputy Director Karl Rockeman said earlier this month the department has had preliminary discussions with the company, but hasn’t heard from it in around a year. 

Minnesota opposition

Paula Maccabee, executive director and attorney for Water Legacy, said she has never seen a project of such magnitude have so many details that are unavailable. Water Legacy is an environmental advocacy group based in Minnesota. 

Maccabee has been holding onto documentation released to the public since plans for the nickel mine in Minnesota were announced, and has noticed that the initial environmental-forward plans outlined in the outset of the project are absent in recent communications.

Johnson confirmed those plans — from using electric vehicles on site to experimenting with carbon sequestration — are being evaluated in the feasibility study. 

For some, the stagnance allows for more time to stop the project altogether.  

On the Minnesota side, communities surrounding the site are scared of its potential impact on local ecosystems, said Kelly Applegate, natural resources commissioner for the Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe.  

Documents submitted to Minnesota regulators show the mine could use up to 50 million gallons of water yearly and occupy around 380 acres. 

Applegate said locals first learned about the project when it hit news headlines.

“Sadly, it’s a problem and a theme that happens within Indian Country,” he said of that timeline. “We become just a box on a checklist; they reach out and have a little conversation with us, and we bark back a little bit back and forth, and then they say ‘OK we’re done with the consultation.’ We want to be at the table at the beginning.”

The closest Band members live approximately 1.3 miles from the proposed mine site, which is tucked into wetlands, rivers, lakes and streams that surrounding people rely heavily on for sources of food and medicine.

Taking into account those concerns, Johnson said the company altered the mine design to be completely underground. 

“Trust is something that is built and earned over time. And I think we’re very aware of that and want to continue open communication and work to engage as best as we can,” Johnson said. 

Applegate said the community is concerned about the risks of transporting raw materials. 

“When you’re railing it across all of these wetlands, train derailments happen, there’s the risk. Those sealed rail cars aren’t impervious to water and if they spill over and go into wetlands and whatnot, there could be some significant damage done,” Applegate said. 

The biggest concerns are tied to tailings, the toxic byproducts leftover after processing ore, which have historically destroyed ecosystems and polluted drinking water.

Though, because the project hasn’t seen movement in North Dakota since last May, it hasn’t been as much of a hotbed topic in comparison to Minnesota, according to Scott Skokos, executive director of the Dakota Resource Council. 

He said the council is generally against waste coming from out of state to North Dakota for processing or permanent disposal. 

“A lot of the locals we’re getting calls from keep asking ‘Why does Minnesota keep sending its waste to North Dakota?’” Skokos said. 

Water Over Nickel, the Mille Lacs Band of Ojibwe, the Minnesota Center for Environmental Advocacy, Dakota Resource Council, Friends of the Mississippi River and Water Legacy are groups leading the multi-state campaign against the proposed operation. 

Anyone is able to participate in the Minnesota Department of Natural Resources’ public comment period. More information can be found on its website.

SPEARFISH — Spearfish School Board members approved a slight increase in school meal prices at their annual board meeting July 13.

Lunch for students in kindergarten through fifth grade was set at $3.65 while students in sixth through 12th grade will pay $3.90. Both are a $.20 increase.

Breakfast for students in kindergarten through fifth grade was set at $1.70 while students in sixth through 12th grade will pay $1.95. Both are a $.10 increase.

The U.S. Department of Agriculture oversees school meal programs and has a formula called the “Lunch Price Equity Tool” that the Spearfish School District uses to set meal prices.

title: Gov. seeks federal help for  damages from summer storms
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasserachlight.com
description: Inmates assist with the cleanup effort at the South Dakota State Fairgrounds in Huron in early July 2026 after a tornado and windstorm hit the area. Photo courtesy of the South Dakota Department of Corrections
_full_text:
Gov. seeks federal help for damages from summer storms.jpeg
Inmates assist with the cleanup effort at the South Dakota State Fairgrounds in Huron in early July 2026 after a tornado and windstorm hit the area. Photo courtesy of the South Dakota Department of Corrections 

PIERRE — Gov. Larry Rhoden has asked the federal government to help pay for nearly $4.6 million in damage to public property in South Dakota caused by storms late last month and early this month.

Wind gusts of 100 miles an hour or more tore through central and eastern South Dakota between June 28 and July 3, hitting Hyde and Beadle counties the hardest.

Hyde County estimates $2.8 million in damages to public property due to a June 29 “mini-derecho,” as classified by the National Weather Service’s Storm Prediction Center. Wind gusts of up to 131 miles per hour downed trees and powerlines, snapped wind turbine towers in half and left Highmore residents without power for days.

A July 3 storm in east-central South Dakota left “devastation” in Huron as well, Rhoden said in a press release, where a tornado with peak winds of 90 mph followed by wind gusts of up to 106 families toppled trees and damaged multiple buildings in areas including the South Dakota State Fairgrounds. Beadle County suffered almost $897,000 in public property damage.

Bennett, Buffalo, Day, Hand, Hughes and Stanley counties, along with the Crow Creek and Lower Brule reservations, were also included in the request. 

Rhoden’s disaster declaration, signed on Wednesday, opens the door to possible assistance from the Federal Emergency Management Agency. If FEMA approves the declaration, it would pick up 75% of the price of repairs to public property. Counties would pay 15%, and the state would pay 10%.

title: Stolen vehicle, multi-agency pursuit results in  Meade Co. arrest
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Stolen vehicle, multi-agency pursuit results in  Meade Co. arrest
Courtesy photo 

FAITH — A driver who allegedly stole a pickup and then led police on a chase across 2 counties, was apprehended with the help of a rancher, who deployed his plane to assist in the search. 

On Sunday, at approximately 4:15 p.m., the Faith Police Department identified a vehicle that had been reported stolen out of Dupree, S.D. When officers attempted to conduct a traffic stop, the driver allegedly refused to stop, and officers initiated a vehicle pursuit.

The pursuit traveled through the city of Faith. Due to the suspect’s alleged excessive speeds and reckless driving, law enforcement reduced their involvement to protect the safety of the public. The suspect was temporarily able to evade pursuing officers.

Multiple law enforcement agencies, including the South Dakota Highway Patrol, Meade County Sheriff’s Office, and Ziebach County Sheriff’s Office, responded to assist in locating the stolen vehicle.

A short time later, the stolen pickup was located near Highway 212 and Avance Road. As officers attempted to intercept the vehicle, the suspect again fled at a high rate of speed while driving recklessly, eventually disappearing from the sight of law enforcement.

While assisting with the incident, Ziebach County Sheriff Don Cudmore contacted a local Meade County rancher who volunteered the use of his private aircraft to assist in the search. During the aerial search, Cudmore located the stolen pickup west of Highway 212, near Udager Place, and directed responding officers to the location.

Law enforcement officers converged on the area and located both the stolen vehicle and the suspect. During the encounter, the suspect claimed to be armed with a firearm and refused repeated lawful commands from officers. Due to the suspect’s aggressive behavior and failure to comply, officers deployed multiple less-lethal beanbag rounds, allowing the suspect to be safely taken into custody without serious injury to officers or the suspect.

The suspect was identified as Justin Garter, 23, of Sioux Falls. After being evaluated by medical personnel at the scene, Garter was transported to the Meade County Jail.

Garter has been charged with aggravated eluding, a Class 6 felony, and possession of a stolen motor vehicle, a Class 5  felony.

Additional charges are pending as the investigation continues.

The sheriff’s office thanked the Faith Police Department, South Dakota Highway Patrol, Ziebach County Sheriff’s Office, and the Opal Volunteer Fire Deparmtent for their assistance during this incident:

The sheriff’s office also thanked rancher who volunteered his aircraft to assist in locating the suspect, stating “his willingness to assist law enforcement was instrumental in bringing this incident to a safe conclusion.”

title: Box Elder man charged with attempted murder

RAPID CITY — A 23-year old Box Elder man was arrested and charged with attempted murder after an alleged shooting, Monday. 

At 3:10 a.m. police were dispatched to the area of Van Buren Street and Dilger Avenue for a report of an individual who had just been shot. On arrival, police located the male gunshot victim walking in the roadway. Police administered emergency first aid, and a medical unit arrived to transport the male to the hospital for treatment of his injury. 

Police received information that residences at 736 N. 7th St. had been involved in the incident. Officers went to the address and detained several individuals. One of the individuals was identified as 23-year-old Mario Moran of Box Elder, and he was placed under arrest for possession of a controlled substance, after police allegedly found that he was carrying methamphetamine. During the course of subsequent witness interviews, police determined that Moran was the alleged shooter from the original incident. Officers arrested Moran for attempted murder. The investigation into the incident remains active and ongoing.

Sanford Lab welcomes NEMESIS 1.jpg
The NEMESIS installation team from left are: Frederick Shuckman, Brianna Mount, Katie Pedneau, Harkirat Riyat, Doug Tiedt, Alex Barzilov, and Wladyslaw Trzaska. Photo by Stephen Kenny 

 Sanford Lab welcomes NEMESIS 2.jpg
The NEMESIS collaboration arrives at SURF. Pictured are: Alexander Barzilov, Thomas Ward and Wladyslaw Trzaska. Photo by Stephen Kenny 

LEAD — It seems appropriate that a deep underground laboratory should have an experiment called NEMESIS. The name conjures a science fiction trope, complete with a bespeckled villain in a lab coat surrounded by minions on a quest for world domination.  

It may disappoint some that nothing happening at the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) will lend itself to a sci-fi blockbuster. 

In reality, the actual scientists who work at SURF find the NEMESIS experiment more compelling than any Hollywood science fiction.  

NEutron MEasurementS In SURF (NEMESIS) is working to better characterize causes for bursts of neutrons—called high neutron multiplicity events. You can think of these events as a cue scattering pool balls across a table—neutron showers result when high-energy cosmic-ray muons passing through matter break one or more atomic nuclei. 

These high neutron multiplicity events constitute a background that is not fully understood. They can cause a headache for physicists who work on ultra-sensitive experiments in underground labs like SURF, as they create false signals in the data.  Knowing the neutron background can help scientists be more confident when conducting searches for extremely rare processes. 

“We will certainly contribute to the whole underground research community by improving the knowledge on the neutron background,” said Thomas Ward, the chief scientist for TechSource Inc. and a lead researcher on NEMESIS.  

At 82, Ward has been at this work for much of his life. He started as a postdoc at Brookhaven National Laboratory in the 1970’s with an office a few doors down from Ray Davis, who went on to win a Nobel Prize for his pioneering work at the site that is now SURF. For Ward, NEMESIS is a culmination of his own life’s work—it follows up on previous studies at the Pyhäsalmi mine in Finland, which showed some interesting results as published in the journal Nuclear Physics. Ward says the research was stopped only when the host mine shut down and the underground lab space was to be flooded.    

“We had an experimental station in Finland until December 2024, but it is now underwater, so we are very happy to be at SURF,” Ward said. 

Previous experiments in Finland and elsewhere have shown some anomalies in these high neutron multiplicity events. Physicists often find anomalies interesting, because they can yield new science. 

NEMESIS collaborators say that while the neutron background anomalies could come from high-energy cosmic rays streaming in from outer space or from radiation emitted naturally inside the Earth’s crust or even from some previously uncharacterized source, the anomalies could also come from another cause: dark matter.

“This experiment is probably the most definitive effort to examine these high neutron multiplicity events. It remains to be seen whether they’re some sort of background that has been previously undefined or whether they are caused by dark matter, so I’m excited to be at SURF. Excited to be with my partners doing this experiment,” said Ward.  

Wladyslaw Trzaska, a physicist at the University of Jyväskylä, Finland, is working alongside Ward on NEMESIS. He says the Black Hills State Underground Campus (BHUC) at SURF is the best place to probe this question. 

“We are trying to make significant measurements of these events at various depths. The BHUC on the 4850 Level is a beautiful laboratory space with a nice clean room. We hope to put another station on the 1700 Level, closer to the surface,” Trzaska said.  

Alexander Barzilov, a physicist at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, is the principal investigator on NEMISIS. He is enthusiastic that future expansion with two NEMESIS detectors at different underground elevations, with different rates of cosmic ray muons, will provide the most robust data set on neutron anomalies. 

“Our plans include running twin systems on both levels at the same time with multiple neutron detectors. This will allow us to see and confirm how the results change with depth,” said Barzilov.

An experiment like NEMESIS also benefits SURF’s ongoing mission to advance world class science and inspire learning across generations.  This timelapse video shows the team installing the experiment on the 4,850 Level BHUC. Brianna Mount, an associate professor of physics at Black Hills State University, is the director of the Black Hills State University Underground Campus.   

“NEMESIS brings an exciting new detection capability to the BHUC user facility,” Mount said. “It aligns well with one of the BHUC’s goals of understanding rare event search backgrounds and might lead to surprising physics discoveries as well!”

Jaret Heise, the director of science at SURF, echoes Mount. 

“We’re very happy to welcome the NEMESIS experiment to SURF. NEMESIS expands the breadth of the SURF science program and is a great example of research that aims to take advantage of the unique attributes of our facility such as access to multiple depths,” Heise said.

NEMESIS researchers add that hunting for indirect evidence of dark matter with this experiment complements the ongoing world-leading dark matter search underway at SURF in LUX-ZEPLIN.  

“Before anything is confirmed and accepted by a scientific community, you need multiple proofs. What we are doing is not a contradiction of what SURF’s LUX-ZEPLIN dark matter experiment is doing – quite the opposite. We are exploring a small range of what the dark matter particle mass might be as a very complementary effort to direct interaction searches,” said Trzaska. 

Ward, Trzaska, and Barzilov describe the effort to indirectly detect dark matter with NEMESIS as a long shot. While this may be true, it’s also true that the history of science is punctuated by long shots that hit their target, and this makes NEMESIS worth all the effort.  

And who knows, maybe a project like NEMESIS will inspire some future Hollywood writer to produce a big-screen blockbuster on the ongoing hunt for dark matter below the Black Hills of South Dakota.

title: American Legion Auxiliary Unit 33 celebrates statewide honors and youth achievements
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: American Legion Auxiliary Meade Sturgis Unit 33 recognizes award winners at the Sturgis Chamber of Commerce board room.  From left are: Isla Rohde (Girls State), Jessica Kusser (American Legion Auxiliary member of the unit for SD), Breann Cichosz (Poetry) and Carol Edwards, president of the American Legion Auxiliary Unit 33.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
1. aux..JPG
American Legion Auxiliary Meade Sturgis Unit 33 recognizes award winners at the Sturgis Chamber of Commerce board room.  From left are: Isla Rohde (Girls State), Jessica Kusser (American Legion Auxiliary member of the unit for SD), Breann Cichosz (Poetry) and Carol Edwards, president of the American Legion Auxiliary Unit 33.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

STURGIS — The American Legion Auxiliary Unit 33 in Sturgis recognized an outstanding member and students during its monthly meeting recently, celebrating volunteer service, leadership and academic achievement.

Among those honored was Jessica Kusser, who was named the American Legion Auxiliary State of South Dakota Unit Member of the Year, the organization’s highest annual recognition for outstanding service to veterans.  Also recognized were Isla Rohde, a Sturgis Brown High School junior who attended the 2026 American Legion Auxiliary Girls State program, and Breann Cichosz, a sixth-grade student at Sturgis Williams Middle School who earned second place in the state Americanism Poetry Contest.

American Legion Auxiliary Unit 33 President Carol Edwards said Kusser’s selection reflects her exceptional dedication to serving veterans throughout the community.

“Each year our 8 districts select one outstanding member based on what they have done for veterans, how they have served veterans and how they have stepped up to help their local unit,” Edwards said. “Jessica won at the district level in April and then competed against the other district winners at the state convention in Aberdeen, where she was selected as the State Unit Member of the Year.”

Kusser said the recognition was unexpected and credited the many volunteer opportunities that allowed her to serve local veterans.

“I’ve just been volunteering and taking care of our veterans,” Kusser said.

Among her projects was coordinating the Hero Tree program with staff at the Fort Meade VA Medical Center’s long-term care unit, helping provide Christmas gifts for veterans. She also volunteered during the annual Got Your Six veterans resource event at the Sturgis Community Center, assisting veterans and their families with information and services.

In addition to her volunteer work, Kusser serves as director of the Fort Meade Museum. Receiving the award from fellow auxiliary members made the honor especially meaningful.

“I was raised by two veterans,” Kusser said. “I’ve always been around veterans. My uncles and cousins are veterans too, so being able to give back to those who have served means a great deal to me.”

Rohde shared her experience attending Girls State, held this summer on the campus of the University of South Dakota in Vermillion.

She said participants spent the week learning about government, leadership and civic engagement while taking part in mock elections and community-building activities.

“They kept us busy every day,” Rohde said. “Everything focused on politics, community and working together. We built leadership skills by communicating with others and running for different offices.”

Rohde campaigned for the position of keynote speaker, finishing as runner-up. “It was so much fun,” she said. “I got to encourage people and help get everyone excited.”

She encouraged other students to apply for Girls State in the future. 

“You learn about politics, leadership and how you can make a difference in your community,” Rohde said. “It helps you understand your rights as a citizen and gives you confidence to become involved.”

Edwards also recognized Breann Cichosz for her success in the American Legion Auxiliary’s annual Americanism Poetry Contest. This year’s theme was “Happy 250th Birthday, America.”

After winning at the local and district levels, Cichosz’s poem advanced to the state competition, where she earned second place in the sixth-grade division.

“It is the first time that I know of that we’ve had a state placer in the poetry contest,” Edwards said.

Cichosz said writing the poem began as a classroom assignment but soon became more personal. “I was just kind of inspired,” she said.

She also drew inspiration from her grandfather, a Vietnam War veteran. “My grandpa served in Vietnam,” Cichosz said. “That gave me some inspiration.”

The meeting highlighted the American Legion Auxiliary’s ongoing commitment to honoring veterans while encouraging leadership, patriotism and community service among the next generation.

title: Sturgis issues 41 Rally camping permits for 860 campers under new ordinance
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Residential camping has been a common practice during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally for many years, but up until this year the city code did not allow the practice. In May, the city council updated its ordinance to allow property owners to obtain a free permit for more than 10 guests. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Rally camping.jpg
Residential camping has been a common practice during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally for many years, but up until this year the city code did not allow the practice. In May, the city council updated its ordinance to allow property owners to obtain a free permit for more than 10 guests. Pioneer file photo 

STURGIS — In the weeks leading up to the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, the city of Sturgis has issued 41 residential camping permits. 

Sturgis Planning Director Casey Baldwin said that represents 860 campers who will be pitching tents or parking RVs on residential properties in the city limits. 

Based on what he’s seen in previous years, Sturgis Public Works Director Rick Bush said those permits don’t cover the total number of properties that will host residential campers within Sturgis city limits. But the goal was never to have 100% compliance, he said. The goal was to have an ordinance in place to try to track and regulate the popular practice of residential camping. That way, if neighbors issued a complaint to the city, officials could have an enforcement tool. 

“I think we feel pretty good, being that this is the first year,” Bush said. “We’ve accomplished what we’re trying to do. I think it provided a reasonable balance between the property owners’ rights and what the city needed to accomplish, without being too restrictive. Prior to the adoption of this ordinance, there simply was no camping allowed. So everything we’ve done is try to enable property owners to better utilize their property and provide some kind of public health, safety, and neighborhood quality of life.” 

In May, the Sturgis City Council passed a residential camping ordinance that defines Rally camping as any residential camping that occurs 7 days before the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, and 3 days after. It allows property owners to have up to 3 camping units, with up to 10 guests, by right. More camping units and guests require property owners to obtain a free permit, which is available after the property owner submits a plan to the city building inspector or planner. 

The ordinance was highly controversial, as many landowners in Sturgis protested what they perceived as an invasion of property owners’ rights. The city council took public comment about the matter for months, and brought several different drafts of the ordinance to the table before the final vote to approve. 

Bush said the idea of the ordinance was to regulate residential camping for health and safety standards, and to have those regulations in place to handle complaints. The ordinance also protects property owners, because it gives them recourse against complaints if they obtain a legal permit. Before the latest residential camping ordinance was passed, Bush said existing code just didn’t allow the practice. 

“There was never an intention of (enforcement),” Bush said. “You’re not going to go out there and find people and arrest them. That was never the intention of the ordinance. The whole idea is to try and get as much compliancy as we can.”

Bush and Baldwin said the city is learning a lot with the permit process. Next year, Bush said, the city will start issuing residential camping permits after Jan. 1, and they will set a deadline date for approval before the Rally. 

For right now, Baldwin said she wants people to know just how easy it is to get a permit. 

“There were definitely a lot of misconceptions and just wrong information that people had been given,” Baldwin said. “I had a large amount of people physically stopped out at the office and we walked through the permit and at the end of the day, everyone was happy. They were amazed at how easy it was. They completely understood it, once it was explained. It’s been positive feedback from everybody that I have dealt with throughout this process.”

title: Newell is managing an irrigation water crisis: Here’s how residents can help
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: NEWELL — The town of Newell has already used its 18-inch water allotment from the Belle Fourche Irrigation District this summer.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

NEWELL — The town of Newell has already used its 18-inch water allotment from the Belle Fourche Irrigation District this summer.

“If you drive past the Orman Dam (Belle Fourche Reservoir), you will see that water levels are getting low.  To keep our community green through the Labor Day season and ensure our local farmers have enough water, we must all work together to manage this shared resource,” said Newell Mayor Tara Tennis. “The town of Newell is asking for your immediate help to conserve our unique and valuable irrigation water.”

Citizens are asked to begin restrictions immediately, watering their lawns only on odd or even days — odd addresses on odd dates, even addresses on even dates. Lawns should be watered only in the early morning or late evening, and sprinklers should be adjusted to prevent water from running down streets.

“The town is taking proactive steps to manage this crisis.  We are purchasing an additional 50 acre-feet of irrigation water to help bridge the gap.  Once that extra supply is exhausted, the town will be forced to switch to expensive city water for irrigation, which we want to delay as long as possible through your conservation efforts,” Tennis said.

Tennis said Newell’s drinking water supply is secure.

“We have reliable local wells, and we are working closely with Butte Meade Water District on a mutual-aid partnership to ensure a steady supply of clean, potable drinking water for both communities,” Tennis said. “Newell is one of the few towns in the United States blessed with access to dam-fed irrigation water.  Let’s show our community’s resilience and cooperation by protecting it.  Thank you for your mindful watering and dedication to keeping Newell green.”

title: State Rep. Travis Ismay pleads not guilty  to highway destruction charge
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer
description: Rep. Travis Ismay
_full_text:
Travis Ismay(MUG).jpg
Rep. Travis Ismay 

BELLE FOURCHE — State Rep. Travis Ismay, R-Newell, pleaded not guilty Wednesday morning to a felony charge of intentionally damaging a highway.

Ismay was arraigned at Butte County Courthouse, appearing alongside his lawyer, Timothy Rensch of Rapid City.

The judge in the case set a non-evidentiary motions hearing for Aug. 27.

Ismay is accused of damaging Wilson Cemetery Road, near his Newell residence in early May. Dwayne Heidrich, who was highway supervisor at the time of the incident, inspected the road after the crime allegedly occurred. He said the road was damaged, and estimated the cost of repairs at $2,000. 

Ismay was arrested July 10 and released the same day after paying a $500 bond. 

The nearly month-long gap between the alleged crime and Ismay’s arrest is likely because grand juries in Butte County only convene once per month. Grand juries are a special kind of jury convened to determine whether there is enough evidence to charge somebody with a crime. All felony charges in South Dakota must be heard before a grand jury before an indictment can be brought. 

In South Dakota, class 6 felonies are punishable by 2 years in prison or a $4,000 fine.

Under state law, if Ismay is sentenced to prison, he will be barred from serving in any public office, including in his current role as a state representative. However, if Ismay is sentenced to a fine, he will still be eligible to hold office. 

Ismay won the District 28B house seat June 2 with 55% of the vote, beating Larry Schmoltz. 

Ismay declined to comment.

title: SD runoff voters talk decision-making, party switching, ‘the lesser of two evils’
byline: By Seth Tupper Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
IMG_9564.JPG
Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

PIERRE — Lucy Burdick didn’t really vote in favor of anybody in Tuesday’s runoff election for the South Dakota Republican Party’s nomination for governor.

She voted against somebody.

“Today we have two choices,” said the 71-year-old Burdick, of Fort Pierre. “Not Toby is who I picked.”

She was talking about her opposition to Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden, who qualified for Tuesday’s runoff by finishing first in a four-way June 2 primary. Doeden failed to reach 35% in that election, which threw him into Tuesday’s top-two contest with the primary’s second-place finisher, Gov. Larry Rhoden.

Burdick said she dislikes Doeden’s pledges to eliminate or phase out property taxes, which she said would “hurt the counties.” All property tax revenue in the state goes to counties, schools, cities and other local governments.

Burdick said in the primary, she voted for U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, who finished third.

Ronald Millar, 71, of Sioux Falls, also voted for Johnson in the primary and said his runoff vote was, “more of a vote against Toby Doeden rather than a vote for Larry Rhoden.”

He described Doeden as “more of a sound bite guy than someone who has an understanding of policy.”

“It also came down to trust and the ability to collaborate with others,” Millar said. “I don’t always agree with Rhoden, but he has shown he is willing to listen to and work with others in making decisions about what is best for South Dakota.”

Alfred Slaathaug, 75, of rural Brandon, said he switched his registration from Democrat to Republican so he could vote for “the lesser of 2 evils” in the runoff, which was only open to Republican voters.

He was one of potentially thousands of party switchers voting Tuesday, judging by the 7,382-person rise in registered South Dakota Republicans during the six weeks between the primary and the runoff registration deadline.

“I changed my party just to vote for Rhoden,” Slaathaug said. “I don’t trust Doeden at all.”

The winner of the runoff will advance to the Nov. 3 general election to face Democratic nominee Dan Ahlers, a former legislator. The last time South Dakota elected a Democratic governor was 52 years ago in 1974.

South Dakota Searchlight reporters also encountered Doeden supporters Tuesday at the polls.

Kris Kluver, 47, of rural Sioux Falls, described Doeden as an, “outsider who can bring a different perspective.” Kluver said he previously voted for state House Speaker Jon Hansen, who finished fourth in the primary.

Dawn Geerdes, 58, of Brandon, voted for Doeden in the primary and the runoff and said Doeden “really wants to make South Dakota a good place.”

“There wasn’t anything that didn’t appeal to me about Rhoden,” Geerdes said. “Doeden just had more of what I was looking for. It was a tough race in my head and heart. I was going back and forth.”

At a polling place in Pierre, 55-year-old Scott Isburg said he voted for Rhoden in the primary and the runoff. Isburg said he trusts that Rhoden will “run government in a way that’ll actually work.”

“I was a little bit concerned with some of the potential policies from Toby, whether they would work or not,” Isburg said.

South Dakota Searchlight’s Meghan O’Brien, Joshua Haiar and Makenzie Huber contributed to this report.

title: Ownership of Wild Bill Bar sign moves from city to building owners, conservatorship maintains protection of city landmark
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Wild Bill Bar sign shines bright above the historic location of Wild Bill’s demise in 1876. Ownership of the bar has transferred from the city to the owners of the bar along with a conservatorship of the city landmark.
_full_text:
Ownership of Wild Bill Bar sign moves to building owners.jpg
The Wild Bill Bar sign shines bright above the historic location of Wild Bill’s demise in 1876. Ownership of the bar has transferred from the city to the owners of the bar along with a conservatorship of the city landmark.  

DEADWOOD — Ownership of the Wild Bill Bar sign, one of the city’s historic landmark signs, has been transferred from the city to the owners of the bar, signifying the conclusion of a successful restoration and repair effort from the city. 

Kevin Kuchenbecker, director of historic preservation, said the sign marks the location of Wild Bill’s demise 150 years ago, when he was shot in the back by Jack McCall at the then Nuttal and Man’s Saloon. More than a decade ago, the sign was moved from its historic location at 624 Main St., before the city took ownership of the neon sign.

“In order to get it back to its original location, we did acquire it, restore it, and work out an agreement with the ownership group of the Wild Bill Bar to reinstall it with the idea that they would pay for the restoration and acquisition over a period of 10 years.”

Kuchenbecker said the city restored the sign with paint and work to the metal and neon tubing. 

Kuchenbecker said Marquerite and Richard Oleson, current owners of the bar, have agreed to a conservatorship of the sign. The agreement pairs the sign to the building, requires regular maintenance and upkeep, and prohibits selling the sign or causing damage that could compromise the historic character.

Kuchenbecker said the sign qualifies under the city’s municipal codes as a landmark sign, having been built before 1940, and is protected by the city’s sign ordinances and historic preservation.

Kuchenbecker said the restoration of the sign’s appearance and relocation has been the result of a, “great partnership with all involved.”
