title: Rise in US preteen suicide rate  alarms mental health experts
byline: By Nada Hassanein Stateline
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
TeenMentalHealth1.jpeg
Courtesy photo 

Suicide deaths among US children ages 8 to 12
Suicide among children ages 8 to 12 has risen sharply in the past two decades. Provisional CDC data shows that last year, preteen deaths by suicide were more than four times higher than in 2008, when deaths were at their lowest in the past two decades.
 This chart shows the number of suicide deaths among children ages 8 to 12 across the U.S., according to the CDC.

 0730 TeenSuicideTableOne.jpg

Editor’s note: If you or someone you know needs help, call or text 988, the U.S. suicide and crisis lifeline, or access online chat at 988lifeline.org.

For months, Marie’s 11-year-old daughter wasn’t acting like herself. The fifth grader was often fatigued, sleeping more. She wasn’t eating enough and spent more time alone.

“She wasn’t really motivated to do things with her friends,” Marie said.

The Chicago girl had been overwhelmed with worry for her father, who was recovering from diabetes complications after a serious infection. She also felt intense pressure at school, aiming for straight As.

“Ever since Dad went to the hospital, it just made it more intense,” she told her mom in a written note. “I don’t know how to feel. I’m having thoughts about hurting myself. I’m tired, and afraid of death.”

Earlier this year, she told her mom she’d tried to cut herself in the bathroom, and said she was hurting herself at school. Stateline is withholding Marie’s full name to protect her daughter’s privacy.

Marie took her to the emergency room. The ER staff tried to transfer the girl to a psychiatric facility, but several refused to take her. Most only served teenagers, while others didn’t accept her insurance plan. The emergency department team finally found a place for her at a child psychiatric facility nearly an hour away.

Marie’s daughter recently finished an intensive outpatient therapy program, and is seeing a therapist regularly. 

“We were able to get her the help that she needed,” Marie said. “But a lot of the times, there’s kids that struggle and unfortunately, do end up taking their life.” 

In the past several years, numerous studies have pointed to a mental health crisis among America’s youth. Much of the attention has focused on teenagers, who have higher suicide rates. 

But preteens are struggling, too.

The number of preteens — ages 8 to 12 — who die by suicide in the United States each year is relatively small. But the total in 2025 was 194 — the most since at least 2001, according to preliminary data from the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Since 2008, the rate of preteen suicide has increased by an average of 8.2% annually, according to researchers at the National Institutes of Health. Their analysis, published in 2024, found that Black preteens had the highest overall suicide rate, while girls and Hispanic preteens had the greatest percentage increase. Native American preteens also saw some of the most pronounced increases.

Suicide is complex and is often the result of a combination of factors. Talking with trusted adults and connecting kids with help can aid in prevention, and research shows most who have suicidal thoughts do not carry through with them. Mental health experts and advocates are calling for more mental health check-ins with preteens, earlier screenings and tailored interventions for Native, Black and LGBTQ+ preteens.

Jenny Britton, chief clinical officer at the Washburn Center for Children in Minneapolis, a nonprofit mental health practice, has noticed the long-term trend during her 25-year career.

“I’ve watched the age of kids who struggle with suicidal ideation and suicidality get younger and younger over that time,” she said. “Now, we’re seeing even as young as our 7- and 8-year-olds.”

Last year, the overall suicide rate in Minnesota increased by 4% compared with the year before, according to preliminary state data. But the suicide rate among children ages 10 to 14, the youngest age group included in the state’s report, more than doubled compared with the five years prior, from 2.2 per 100,000 people to 5.8.

Four years ago, when the inpatient mental health unit opened at Children’s Minnesota, a Minneapolis-based health system, providers mostly saw teenagers, said Dr. Prachi “PJ” Striker, a child and adolescent psychiatrist. That’s still true, but over the past year-and-half, the unit has seen more 10- to 12-year-olds who have harmed themselves, attempted suicide or said they’ve considered it.

“(We’re) seeing more of the younger age group coming in,” Striker said. “Depression, anxiety, hopelessness, feeling overwhelmed, suicidal thoughts.”

The American Academy of Pediatrics now recommends that pediatricians start screening all patients starting at age 12 for suicidal thoughts. But for preteens ages 8 to 11, the academy only recommends a suicide screening if the child is coming to the doctor for behavioral health concerns or has a history of suicidal thoughts.

But Striker said screening as early as age 8 can prevent kids from slipping under the radar.

“How do we start identifying kids who are in trouble faster?” Striker said. “Kids are feeling unsupported. They have more alone time. They’re more isolated. People aren’t really picking up on some of the clues of depression as early.”

Stressors

Pull quote
There’s this myth that if you talk to kids about suicide, you’re going to put the idea in their head. — Lisa Horowitz, U. of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine

Many mental health experts point to COVID-19 as a major factor that harmed the mental health of kids who are now preteens. 

“You have to remember these kids who are like 10 to 12, their early elementary years were COVID years, and so kindergarten, first grade, second grade were often at home. They didn’t have those normal experiences of going to school, starting to socialize,” Striker said. “They’re going into third, fourth, fifth grade, having been home and quarantined for the first few years of their school lives.”

Thousands of kids lost loved ones to COVID-19, including their parents. Children of color make up a disproportionate number of those whose caregivers were killed by the virus. 

“I was hopeful that as people were able to get back to their friends and school and normalize, that that would get better, but it really hasn’t,” said Dr. Maria Hughes Rahmandar, chair of the American Academy of Pediatrics’ Council on Adolescents and Young Adults and an associate professor of pediatrics at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine. “Preteens and teens are really continuing to struggle with more and more mental health concerns.” 

Experts also point to other stressors for preteens, including social media use, lack of sleep, bullying both online and in person, and policies restricting gender-affirming care for trans kids that have created fear for some LGBTQ+ youth.

Jeremy Pettit, a professor of psychology at Florida International University who specializes in depression, anxiety and suicidal behaviors in children and adolescents, is studying how sleep – and screen time right before bed – relates to kids’ mental health.

“When (sleep is) disrupted, it’s bad for everything – physical health and mental health. The data are pretty clear that our kids are not getting enough sleep at night,” said Pettit, who directs FIU’s Center for Children and Families. 

“We’ve got early school times in most of the country, even though the data, the research is pretty clear, it would be healthier for our kids not to have them go to school at 7 every morning,” he said.

Peter Gray, a researcher and emeritus professor of psychology at Boston College, contends that changes in schooling in recent decades, such as the standardization of curriculum, created “a new source of anxiety and depression on top of everything else.” He also pointed to a trend of less unstructured playtime outside.

“That’s normal childhood,” Gray said of unstructured play. “This is how children learn to take charge of their own lives. It’s how children learn to negotiate differences with other people. It’s how children learn that they can solve their own problems. 

“We have been gradually, over time, taking that away from children,” he said.

Unlike many other child development experts, Gray argues that computers and smartphones have actually helped children by re-creating some of the social networking that used to happen outside. 

But a 2024 analysis by the CDC found that frequent social media use was associated with bullying at school, persistent feelings of sadness or hopelessness, and some suicide risk among students. More than 40 states have sued social media companies over mental health concerns among kids.

Other experts say too much exposure to media of all kinds may also be causing kids stress. 

“I think about my childhood in the ’70s and ’80s. I didn’t know all the details of shootings or a bomb going off, or you had to read about it in the newspaper or watch the news,” said Britton, of the Washburn Center for Children. 

“Kids are wrestling with things differently than I wrestled with things. They know more, so they’re thinking about more.”

Talking with kids

Experts say parents, teachers, coaches, clergy — anyone who interacts with kids — shouldn’t fear talking to them about suicide and mental health, especially if they notice withdrawal, sadness or stress.

Jamie Freeny, who was the director of the Center for School Behavioral Health at Mental Health America of Greater Houston until earlier this year, said that more elementary schools have started to ask for suicide prevention training.

“If the elementary schools are asking for it, that lets me know that there’s a reason,” said Freeny, who now works as a mental health consultant. “It’s very, very sad.”

Lisa Horowitz, a visiting professor of child psychiatry at the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine and who conducts research for the National Institutes of Health, said many parents tell her they’re afraid to bring the topic up with their kids.

“There’s this myth that if you talk to kids about suicide, you’re going to put the idea in their head,” Horowitz said, adding that research shows talking about it can actually help. 

“If you can detect suicide risk early, like in preteens or even even younger, then you can intervene early, and and then you can prevent a lot of psychiatric disorders that occur in adulthood.” 

Kids may tell their friends and may not necessarily come to their trusted adult first, making proactive conversations important, added Horowitz, who co-authored the study on the annual increase in preteen suicide and has developed screening tools.

“Most parents are surprised by a suicide attempt, and it’s not because they’re a bad parent, and it’s not because they’re not paying attention. It’s because kids keep these thoughts to themselves,” she said. 

“It’s an awkward but critical conversation to start. … So even if you say to a kid, ‘OK, this is really awkward, and I’m not even sure how to ask about this, but I care about your life. So, do you ever think about killing yourself?’”

Britton said even just asking about a change in a child’s mood can help.

“Work hard to figure out how to engage with your kids around really hard topics,” said Britton. “It does something so innate within the human experience if another person can say, ‘Today you looked really sad. Is there anything you want to share with me about that?’”

In Chicago, Marie and her husband have started fundraising for the American Foundation for Suicide Prevention. As they’ve shared their story, other parents have opened up to them about the struggles of their own preteen kids.

“My husband and I want to be our daughter’s voice,” Marie said. “To help somebody else — even if it’s one person.”

The American Foundation for Suicide Prevention has resources for parents or others who frequently interact with children, including a toolkit called “Talk Saves Lives” that offers guidelines and tips for steering conversations. Find information at https://afsp.org/talk-saves-lives/

title: East River senator facing election-related  criminal charges ends his reelection campaign
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: State Sen. Tom Pischke, R-Dell Rapids, speaks in the South Dakota Senate on March 3, 2025, at the Capitol in Pierre. Photo by Makenzie Huber, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
East River senator facing election-related criminal charges ends his reelection campaign.png
State Sen. Tom Pischke, R-Dell Rapids, speaks in the South Dakota Senate on March 3, 2025, at the Capitol in Pierre. Photo by Makenzie Huber, South Dakota Searchlight 

DELL RAPIDS —Sen. Tom Pischke, R-Dell Rapids, ended his reelection campaign Tuesday as he continues to face felony charges for allegedly filing false or forged election-related documents.

“I have always prided myself on conducting campaigns with complete transparency on every issue,” said a portion of a statement Pischke sent in response to South Dakota Searchlight questions. “Unfortunately,” he added while citing the pending criminal charges, “I would not have been able to maintain that standard during the upcoming November election.”

Pischke’s withdrawal comes more than a month after prosecutors charged him with 2 felony counts alleging he submitted 16 candidate petitions for Minnehaha County Republican precinct committee positions without the candidates’ knowledge. 

The prosecution is playing out amid a long-running struggle over leadership of the county party. Obtaining a meeting quorum requires the presence of 20% of voting members, and filling more positions could make it more difficult for the county party’s leaders to obtain a quorum and conduct official business.

Pischke has pleaded not guilty, and lawyers involved in the case have said a plea deal is possible.

Pischke’s withdrawal leaves Republicans searching for a replacement candidate ahead of the Nov. 3 general election. Republican county party central committee members who reside in his district have until Aug. 11 to make a selection.

Bryan Breitling, an independent from Dell Rapids, is the only other candidate on the ballot for the District 25 Senate seat. The district includes Moody County and part of Minnehaha County. 

“It has been an incredible honor to represent the wonderful people of District 25 over the past 10 years, and I look forward to whatever God has planned for me next,” Pischke said in his statement.

title: SD Mines receives $3.1 million grant to  accelerate critical minerals exploration
byline: Pioneer Staff Reports
description: South Dakota Mines has been awarded a $3.1 million grant from the U.S. Department of Energy’s Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E) to lead a new research effort aimed at developing advanced technologies that could locate and map rare earth elements (REE) and critical minerals with greater speed and at a reduced cost. The university’s multidisciplinary research team includes William Roggenthen, professor emeritus of geology and geological engineering, Zhi Ye, assistant professor of geology and geological engineering at Mines and the principal investigator, Kai Ren, assistant professor of electrical engineering, Mingyuan Cheng, assistant professor of nanoscience and biomedical engineering. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
SD Mines receives $3.1 million grant to accelerate critical minerals exploration.jpg
South Dakota Mines has been awarded a $3.1 million grant from the U.S. Department of Energy’s Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E) to lead a new research effort aimed at developing advanced technologies that could locate and map rare earth elements (REE) and critical minerals with greater speed and at a reduced cost. The university’s multidisciplinary research team includes William Roggenthen, professor emeritus of geology and geological engineering, Zhi Ye, assistant professor of geology and geological engineering at Mines and the principal investigator, Kai Ren, assistant professor of electrical engineering, Mingyuan Cheng, assistant professor of nanoscience and biomedical engineering. Courtesy photo 

RAPID CITY — South Dakota Mines has been awarded a $3.1 million grant from the U.S. Department of Energy’s Advanced Research Projects Agency-Energy (ARPA-E) to lead a new research effort aimed at developing advanced technologies that could locate and map rare earth elements (REE) and critical minerals with greater speed and at a reduced cost. 

The grant is part of $72 million in ARPA-E funding for early-stage research and development projects to boost domestic magnet manufacturing and help secure America’s supply chains for critical minerals essential to energy security, economic competitiveness and the industrial base. The Mines project, RAPID-REE, is one of 13 projects selected under the ARPA-E’s ROCKS program, joining leading research universities, national laboratories and technology companies in advancing critical minerals innovation.

The RAPID-REE project will develop next-generation exploration and sensing technologies that integrate advanced surface and subsurface sensing with AI- and machine-learning-assisted inversion techniques to more directly detect, map and characterize underground mineral deposits.

“South Dakota has a long history as a mining state, providing essential minerals and resources to the nation, including documented rare earth elements (REE) occurrences,” said Zhi Ye, Ph.D., assistant professor of geology and geological engineering at Mines and the principal investigator for the ARPA-E project. “Advancing critical minerals and REE research and development is an important area of strategic focus for South Dakota Mines, and this initiative will be instrumental in improving critical minerals assessment and enabling responsible development.

The project aims to create accurate 3D maps of ore deposits and reduce uncertainties to improve access to critical minerals. Currently, exploration of critical minerals and rare earth elements can take many years and, in some cases, more than a decade. ARPA-E’s ROCKS program aims to dramatically reduce that timeline. 

“We will develop and integrate novel surface sensing technologies combined with advanced subsurface and downhole sensing technologies to more quickly and accurately map ore bodies and determine their grade, size and depth,” Ye said. 

Research will include both laboratory and field work, along with techno-economic analysis to support prototype development, testing and eventual commercialization. 

Mines is the lead institution and will oversee the project, as well as design, develop and test both the surface and subsurface sensing prototypes. The university’s multidisciplinary research team also includes Kai Ren, Ph.D., assistant professor of electrical engineering, Mingyuan Cheng, Ph.D., assistant professor of nanoscience and biomedical engineering, and William Roggenthen, Ph.D., professor emeritus of geology and geological engineering. 

Other key project partners include the University of Oklahoma and New Mexico Tech. The University of Oklahoma team, led by Ahmad Ghassemi, Ph.D., professor of petroleum engineering, will support laboratory testing and numerical simulations to evaluate prototype performance. New Mexico Tech, led by Alex Gysi, Ph.D., associate professor in the Department of Earth and Environmental Science, will provide expertise in REE mineralogy and economic geology and assist with 3D geological modeling for mapping and interpretation.

“South Dakota Mines has a long-standing mission in energy and mineral resources,” said Ghassemi, who earned his master’s degree in geological engineering from Mines in 1986. “I am glad to reconnect with Mines through this exciting project and help strengthen its mission in critical minerals R&D.”

Dakota Gold Corp. will serve as the project’s key industry partner, providing REE samples, industry expertise and access to its Richmond Hill site for prototype testing and validation. 

“The Richmond Hill site hosts high-concentration, underexplored REE deposits, making it an excellent site for the project’s field-testing efforts,” said Jack Henris, president and chief operating officer of Dakota Gold and a Mines geological engineering alumnus. 

Dakota Gold’s project team will be led by Mark Rantapaa, vice president of operations, and Bill Gehlen, senior manager of geology. Together, they bring more than 50 years of combined mining industry experience to support successful field-scale validation and help establish a practical pathway for future large-scale deployment.

title: Number of unauthorized immigrants hit new high of nearly 16 million in 2024, report says
byline: By Ariana Figueroa States Newsroom
description: A section of the U.S.-Mexico border wall near El Paso, Texas, on June 6, 2024. Photo by Ariana Figueroa, States Newsroom
_full_text:
Number of unauthorized immigrants hit new high of nearly 16 million in 2024, report says.jpg
A section of the U.S.-Mexico border wall near El Paso, Texas, on June 6, 2024. Photo by Ariana Figueroa, States Newsroom 

WASHINGTON — The unauthorized U.S. immigrant population grew to its highest level ever by mid-2024, increasing to 15.8 million after hovering at about 11 million since 2010, according to data released Wednesday by a nonpartisan think tank that tracks migration. 

The increase primarily stemmed from the historic levels of migration at the southern border that started in 2021 and the Biden administration’s wide use of humanitarian parole and other temporary legal status for millions of people, according to a Migration Policy Institute report based on the most recent data from the U.S. Census Bureau’s American Community Survey in 2024. 

“Between 2019 and 2024, MPI estimates the unauthorized immigrant population experienced a net growth of approximately 5 million people, or an average of 8 percent per year,” according to the report. 

“The increases were driven by the uncommonly strong U.S. economic recovery after the COVID-19 pandemic as well as the large-scale displacement from countries throughout the Americas fueled by gang violence, political repression, and economic challenges.” 

But under the second Trump administration’s aggressive deportation campaign and continued practice of revoking previously granted legal status for immigrants, a decrease in the unauthorized population is likely.

“Should the administration succeed in its efforts to sizably ramp up deportations and if border entries remain at their remarkably low levels, the unauthorized immigrant population may begin to decrease into 2026 and beyond,” according to the report. 

Some of that 2024 growth was also due to several Biden administration policies. The administration created new humanitarian parole programs that allowed migrants from Afghanistan, Cuba, Haiti, Nicaragua, Ukraine and Venezuela to legally enter the United States and obtain work permits, according to the report. 

Another tool rolled out by the Biden administration, the CBP One app, which allowed migrants to schedule appointments to apply for asylum, also contributed to the growth of migration to the U.S. 

The biggest growth spurt occurred between 2022 and 2023, with an increase of 1.6 million newly arrived migrants.

The report also found that while Mexico typically stands as the top country of origin for migrants arriving, “the Mexican share of the unauthorized population has dropped dramatically — from being the overwhelming share in the 1980s and 1990s, to 62 percent in 2010 and 35 percent as of 2024.”

Migrants from Central and South America have driven the change in nationality makeup, according to the report. 

“This trend reflects sharp increases in recent arrivals of Ecuadorians, Colombians, and especially Venezuelans, as well as steady growth in unauthorized arrivals from Guatemala and Honduras,” according to the report.

In 2023, the Biden administration created two new humanitarian parole processes. One was for Cubans, Haitians, Nicaraguans and Venezuelans. The second was for migrants using the CBP One app. 

Those humanitarian programs were similar to one created in 2021 for Afghans, after the chaotic U.S. withdrawal from the country, and for Ukrainians, after Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022. In total, those humanitarian parole programs included roughly 1.4 million immigrants. 

The second Trump administration ended those humanitarian parole protections, turned the CBP One app into a self-deportation tool, and has moved to end Temporary Protected Status for hundreds of thousands of immigrants.

title: Reenactment of Wild Bill Hickock’s funeral honors Deadwood’s 150th anniversary
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: DEADWOOD — Deadwood History, Inc., and the city of Deadwood’s historic preservation commission invite the public to commemorate the 150th anniversary of Wild Bill Hickock’s death with a reenactment of his assassination and funeral at noon on Monday, Aug. 3 at Outlaw Square.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

DEADWOOD — Deadwood History, Inc., and the city of Deadwood’s historic preservation commission invite the public to commemorate the 150th anniversary of Wild Bill Hickock’s death with a reenactment of his assassination and funeral at noon on Monday, Aug. 3 at Outlaw Square. 

The free event will begin with a reenactment of Hickock’s assassination, immediately followed by a historic funeral ceremony led by his loyal friend, Colorado Charlie Utter. Based on real events, the reenactment will offer visitors a powerful glimpse into the day that forever secured Hickock’s place in American history. 

This one-of-a-kind event will combine authentic storytelling, living history, and community-wide celebration. Enthusiasts of history, families, and visitors to Deadwood during the pre-Sturgis Motorcycle Rally festivities are encouraged to attend. 

For more information, visit dadwoodhistory.com, deadwood.com, or cityofdeadwood.com.

title: Rhoden wins Republican nomination to seek his own term
byline: By Seth Tupper Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden won the Republican Party’s nomination for governor Tuesday in a runoff election, earning the chance to seek his own four years in office after filling out the remainder of former Gov. Kristi Noem’s last term.
_full_text:
South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden won the Republican Party’s nomination for governor Tuesday in a runoff election, earning the chance to seek his own four years in office after filling out the remainder of former Gov. Kristi Noem’s last term.

The Associated Press called the race at 8:08 p.m. Central. Complete returns several hours later showed Rhoden with 71% of the votes and a 42-point win over Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden, with 29%. Rhoden won in 64 of the state’s 66 counties, with only Fall River and Todd counties going for Doeden.

Rhoden spoke to his supporters at a results watch party in Sioux Falls at about 9 p.m. He reflected on the early days of the campaign when he trailed in multiple public polls.

“There were times when I really felt like the good Lord was trying to teach me something,” Rhoden said. “And there were times when all I had to rely on was the Scripture: You walk by faith, not by sight. And that’s what we do. You keep moving forward.”

Doeden spoke to his supporters in Aberdeen at about the same time and said he had called Rhoden to congratulate him and to pledge support for him in the general election.

“I have said since day one on this long, crazy journey that my singular goal was to unite our amazing Republican Party and move this state forward, and that journey has not ended here, my friends,” Doeden said.

Doeden and Rhoden made it into the runoff by finishing first and second in a four-way June 2 primary election. Nobody in that race reached 35%, which triggered the first use of a 1985 state law requiring a runoff when no candidate meets that threshold in a statewide primary.

Republican turnout for the runoff was 36%, after 43% of Republican voters turned out for the primary. Only registered Republicans were allowed to vote in the runoff.

Rhoden will face Democratic nominee Dan Ahlers, a former state legislator, in the Nov. 3 general election. The last time South Dakota elected a Democratic governor was 52 years ago in 1974.

Gov. Kristi Noem kickstarted the Republican primary race when she resigned in January 2025 to accept a job in President Donald Trump’s administration. Rhoden was Noem’s lieutenant governor and was automatically promoted to serve the last two years of her second term.

U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, R-South Dakota, entered the race as the presumptive frontrunner and led in several early polls. He had the most campaign money at his disposal and the highest statewide profile due to his four terms in the U.S. House, his previous service on the state Public Utilities Commission, and his 20-plus years of involvement in politics.

On primary election night, Doeden — who had never previously sought elected office — stunned the political establishment by finishing first at 31%, followed by Rhoden at 25%, Johnson at 23% and state House Speaker Jon Hansen at 21%. Johnson and Hansen not only failed to make the runoff but will leave office when their respective terms in the U.S. and state House end in January.

From the June 2 primary through the July 13 registration deadline for Tuesday’s runoff, the number of registered Republicans in the state grew by more than 7,300. One of those new Republicans was Alfred Slaathaug, of rural Brandon, who said in a polling-place interview that he had switched his registration from the Democratic Party.

“I changed my party just to vote for Rhoden,” Slaathaug said. “I don’t trust Doeden at all.”

Doeden ran on shifting anti-property tax pledges

Doeden spent at least $4 million of his own money in the race, according to campaign finance reports. The 51-year-old built his fortune by owning vehicle dealerships and diversifying into other businesses and real estate. He has also described himself as an investor in bitcoin, a type of digital money secured with encryption technology.

Doeden tried to position himself early in the campaign as the most pro-Trump candidate, often mentioning Trump in advertisements and appearances — although not as much in recent months as Trump’s national approval rating fell below 40%.

Doeden also ran on an anti-property tax platform, pledging at times to eliminate property taxes, at other times to phase them out, and saying earlier this month that his pledge applied only to homeowners.

Homeowner property taxes rose sharply in parts of South Dakota as homebuyers flocked to the state and drove up prices during and immediately after the COVID-19 pandemic, when Noem invited people to relocate for the state’s freedom from mask mandates, business restrictions and other pandemic precautions.

South Dakotans paid more than $1.8 billion in property taxes last year, including $815 million by homeowners, but none of that money goes to state government, which is primarily funded by sales tax revenue. Property taxes go to schools, counties, cities and other local governments.

Searchlight asked Doeden in a May podcast interview how he would replace lost property tax revenue for local governments.

“Once the economy starts growing, and it will; once I start collecting external revenue, which we will; and once I cut all the fat and pork out of our state budget, you are going to see, very quickly, within a matter of a couple years, a significant amount of annual budget surpluses,” Doeden said. “And yes, I will use that money to target the phase-out of things like property tax.”

A Sioux Falls voter, Mandy Berkhof, said Tuesday at her polling place that she voted for Doeden in the primary and the runoff.

“I just feel like he is going to bring a lot to South Dakota communities, things that we need and want, a little bit more than the other person,” Berkhof said.

Rhoden criticized Doeden, touted own record

Rhoden said eliminating local property tax revenue would require the state to replace it, and he said that would blow a $1.8 billion hole in the state budget. The Rhoden campaign launched a “Reckless Toby Doeden” website featuring those assertions during the runoff campaign.

Those criticisms resonated with 55-year-old Scott Isburg, who said Tuesday at his polling place in Pierre that he voted for Rhoden in the primary and the runoff. Isburg said he trusted Rhoden to “run government in a way that’ll actually work.”

“I was a little bit concerned with some of the potential policies from Toby, if they would work or not,” Isburg said.

Rhoden also aired advertisements during the runoff campaign about Doeden’s lack of past involvement in Republican politics, including an audio recording of Doeden saying “I think I may have even voted for Barack Obama.” Doeden has since denied voting for Obama.

Aside from those criticisms of his opponent, Rhoden ran on his record from nearly 18 months as governor, which has included working with legislators to sign several major bills into law.

Those include laws capturing revenue from sales tax increases to reduce homeowner property taxes, a law banning the use of a legal procedure known as eminent domain to gain land access for carbon capture pipelines, and a law funding construction of a $650 million replacement for the oldest parts of the state’s 145-year-old penitentiary.

“Good policy makes good politics,” Rhoden said while launching his campaign in November.

Sioux Falls voter Susan DeSautel said Tuesday at her polling place that Rhoden’s experience was an important factor in her support for him.

“I know there are a lot of people who like Doeden. I think they want somebody totally from left field, who’s not a politician,” DeSautel said. “And I understand that, but you’ve got to have some experience as a politician. We need that in a governor.”

Before Rhoden served as lieutenant governor and governor, he was a rancher, custom welder and legislator. He lives on a ranch near Union Center in the western part of the state.

If he wins in November, the 67-year-old Rhoden could potentially choose to run again four years later for what would amount to a third term. The state constitution includes term limits, saying “no person shall be elected to more than two consecutive terms as governor,” but Rhoden is serving his current stint as governor through the line of succession rather than direct election to the job.

South Dakota Searchlight’s John Hult, Joshua Haiar, Makenzie Huber and Meghan O’Brien contributed to this report.

title: USFS seeks public comment on proposed Bull Hill Mine development
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: SUNDANCE — The Black Hills National Forest is welcoming comment for an environmental impact statement for Rare Element Resources, Ltd.’s proposed development of the Bull Hill Mine in northeast Wyoming. Publication of this notice begins a 30-day public comment period.
_full_text:
SUNDANCE — The Black Hills National Forest is welcoming comment for an environmental impact statement for Rare Element Resources, Ltd.’s proposed development of the Bull Hill Mine in northeast Wyoming. Publication of this notice begins a 30-day public comment period. 

Rare Element Resources, Ltd., proposes to develop an open-pit mine on approximately 260 acres of National Forest System lands. The Bear Lodge Rare Earth Project is designated as a Fast-41 project, which ensures streamlined federal coordination while maintaining environmental standards. The project also advances an executive order to take immediate measures to increase American mineral production. 

“The Forest Service is required by regulation to consider mining plans of operations on forest lands, ensure compliance with environmental regulations, and minimize adverse impacts where feasible,” said Black Hills National Forest Supervisor Shawn Cochran. “Rare Element Resources, Ltd., has submitted a plan of operation proposing to re-start mining, and we are seeking public input on their proposal.” 

Public comments will help shape the scope of the environmental analysis and identify issues and alternatives for consideration. Additional details, including meeting information and project documents, will be available on the project website. 

Submit comments online, by email, or in person, Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m., to Shawn Cochran, forest supervisor, in care of Wendy Schuyler, project manager, Black Hills National Forest, 1019 N. 5th St., Custer, S.D. 57730.

title: Runoff turnout affected by  motivation, polling, lack of ‘second choice’ enthusiasm, professor says
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — Turnout among Republicans in Tuesday’s runoff election fell by about 20,000 voters compared to the June primary — a drop that a University of South Dakota political science professor said was predictable.
_full_text:
PIERRE — Turnout among Republicans in Tuesday’s runoff election fell by about 20,000 voters compared to the June primary — a drop that a University of South Dakota political science professor said was predictable.

Participation fell from 43% in June to 36% Tuesday, driven by low motivation, polling that made the race look like a foregone conclusion and other factors, according to Julia Hellwege.

“It’s about what I’d expect,” she said.

Toby Doeden and Gov. Larry Rhoden made it into the runoff for the Republican nomination for governor by finishing first and second in a four-way June 2 primary election. Nobody in that race reached 35%, which triggered the first use of a 1985 state law requiring a runoff when no candidate meets that threshold in a statewide primary. Rhoden won in the runoff.

Runoff elections typically draw fewer voters than the elections preceding them. Unlike South Dakota primaries, held the first Tuesday in June, or the general election, the first Tuesday in November, runoffs have no well-known date for voters to plan around.

Voters less engaged with politics are more likely to miss runoffs, Hellwege said, both because of limited awareness and because voting itself demands time and effort: researching candidates, finding polling locations and making time to show up.

Turnout among registered Republican voters in the runoff ranged from a low of 9.31% in Oglala Lakota County, which is part of the Pine Ridge Reservation, to a high of 54.58% in Sully County in central South Dakota.

Doeden received 7,282 fewer votes in the runoff than in the June primary. Some of those voters may have backed Rhoden instead, but the majority likely stayed home, Hellwege said.

Motivation also played a role. With Doeden finishing the June primary at 31% and Rhoden at 25%, most voters heading into the runoff were choosing between candidates who weren’t their first pick.

“It’s not quite as motivating to go out and vote for your second choice,” Hellwege said.

Competitive races drive the most engagement, Hellwege said — and June’s four-way primary was the second-highest Republican primary turnout in the past decade. The runoff turned out to be far less competitive.

Pre-runoff polling from Emerson College, commissioned by KELO-TV, showed Rhoden with a wide lead, which may have further dampened turnout.

“When things are unpredictable, it can draw people out,” Hellwege said. “If they see a poll that says it’s skewed they might think, ‘It doesn’t look that competitive so I don’t need to put as much effort into this and vote.’”

Alfred Slaathaug, of rural Brandon, said he voted for Rhoden on Election Day but debated whether he needed to participate because of the poll results.

“But on principle, I decided not to skip it,” Slaathaug said.

Slaathaug was one of thousands of South Dakotans who registered or switched party affiliations ahead of the runoff specifically to participate in it. Slaathaug switched from the Democratic Party and plans to switch back.

Slaathaug’s and other new Republican votes had little effect on the final margin given Rhoden’s wide win — garnering 71% of the vote — but they may have nudged turnout upward, Hellwege noted.

Advance voting — mail-in and in-person ballots cast before Election Day — made up 22% of total runoff turnout, up slightly from the 18% to 19% typical of recent Republican primaries.

Auditors attributed the uptick to party switchers voting immediately after changing their registration. Hellwege said the shift wasn’t dramatic but made sense: Voters registering specifically to support a candidate are more likely to vote early, as are committed partisans who had already made up their minds in June.

“More than likely, early voters were folks who had a clear idea of who they were going to vote for, which makes it easier to submit their ballot ahead of time,” Hellwege said.

The next election will be Nov. 3, when voters will choose between Rhoden and Democratic challenger Dan Ahlers in the race for governor. The general election ballot will also include other statewide and local races and ballot questions.

title: Belle Fourche budgets for a  lean year in 2027
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: BELLE FOURCHE — In 2027, the Belle Fourche Library director plans to cut the number of new books he orders in half. The Tri-State Museum and Visitor’s Center is looking at eliminating more than $15,000 from its advertising budget and $1,000 from its exhibit supplies budget. Public works is only budgeting enough money to purchase one mower this year. The department used to purchase 2.
_full_text:
BELLE FOURCHE — In 2027, the Belle Fourche Library director plans to cut the number of new books he orders in half. The Tri-State Museum and Visitor’s Center is looking at eliminating more than $15,000 from its advertising budget and $1,000 from its exhibit supplies budget. Public works is only budgeting enough money to purchase one mower this year. The department used to purchase 2.

Several city department heads described 2027 as an upcoming “lean year.”

“A major factor in the 2027 budget discussion is that the city has been relying on reserves to complete a number of projects in recent years,” said Belle Fourche Finance Officer Wayne Tonsager. “For 2027, the focus is on scaling back spending and living within the revenues the city earns rather than drawing down reserves. As a result, expenditures are currently projected to be lower than prior years, while revenues are projected to be higher.”

Where possible, in places where expenses are going up, Tonsager said the city is taking steps to mitigate rising costs.

Spending on postage is one example.

“The city spent approximately $18,000 on postage in 2025. That expense has increased due to the transition to the new utility billing system, which returned all utility accounts to paper billing,” Tonsager said. “We are actively working to move customers who prefer email-only billing back to paperless statements, which should help reduce postage costs over time.”

In other cases, rising expenses might be unavoidable.

During a recent budget work session, City Councilman John Fyffe pointed out that the police department’s utility budget had increased significantly.

“In the past, there have been what $11,000, $9,000 in utilities. Now we’re budgeting $30,000 for utilities,” Fyffe said.

In 2027, the Belle Fourche Police Department plans to move into its new 33,000-square-foot building across from Hermann Park.

The sheer size of the building is one of the reasons why utilities will cost more. City officials also pointed out that in 2025, the police department spent virtually nothing on utilities because they were based out of city hall.

“But it was only $11,000 something or $14,000 two years ago,” Fyffe said.

“I have no idea what the actual utility budget (for the new building) is going to be, so I sat down with Wayne (Tonsager) and came up with an estimate,” Police Chief Ryan Cherveny said. “They based it off of what we were using before, but the problem was that we didn’t have enough power, so stuff was shutting down on us.”

The old police department building, a former schoolhouse, had electrical issues.

“Our server had crashed a couple times. The computers crashed. We replaced a bunch of them because they got fried because of it. Part of that is to prevent that stuff from ever happening again. I don’t know if they can give us a solid number or not,” Cherveny said.

title: Deadwood announces recipients  of the second round of  Outside of Deadwood Grants
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: DEADWOOD — Deadwood announced the recipients of the second round of funding of the Outside of Deadwood Grants July 20, continuing a decades-long preservation effort across the state.
_full_text:
DEADWOOD — Deadwood announced the recipients of the second round of funding of the Outside of Deadwood Grants July 20, continuing a decades-long preservation effort across the state.

The city received 8 grant requests this round, bringing the total project amount to $193,083 and $80,235 in total requested funds. Seven projects were approved to split the $50,000 budget.

“The Deadwood historic preservation commission and office are pleased to participate in outstanding historic preservation projects across the state,” said Kevin Kuchenbecker, director of historic preservation. “We’ve been committed for over 20 years, providing funding from gaming revenues to communities across the state for their historic preservation projects that have a connection with the city of Deadwood.”

In the 20-plus years the grant has been active, Kuchenbecker said the city has given nearly $5 million in funding to different entities in South Dakota.

According to South Dakota Codified Laws 42-7B-48, and 42-7B-48.1, a portion of gaming revenue must be allocated to state and municipal historic preservation funds. Previously, the city set aside $250,000 for the Outside of Deadwood Grant to be disbursed twice a year but reduced the amount to $100,000 for the last 5 years. With the passage of Senate Bill 102 in 2026, which changed the complex gaming revenue formula to gradually reduce the amount of revenue given to the state and increase the amount of revenue given to the city over a period of 4 years, Kuchenbecker said he’s hopeful the amount given annually through the Outside of Deadwood Grant will increase. 

Summer 2026 recipients

Projects awarded funding in the summer grant cycle are as follows: Friends of Whitewood Cemetery, of Whitewood; Czech Heritage Preservation, of Tabor; Little Spearfish Conservation and Historic Preservation Society, of Rapid City; Sully County Courthouse, of Onida; the city of Central City; Historic Rapid City McGillicuddy House, of Rapid City; and Roberts County Courthouse, of Sisseton.

The Friends of Whitewood Cemetery were awarded $5,000 to build a sign for the entrance of the Whitewood Cemetery.

The Czech Heritage Preservation in Tabor was awarded $10,000 to restore the wooden cedar shingles of the log school roof. 

According to the packet attached to the grant cycle, shingles installed in 1976 will be removed, potential damage to the structure of the roof will be repaired, and new shingles will be installed. The report claims the school, built in approximately 1872, is the oldest public building in South Dakota.

Little Spearfish Conservation and Historic Preservation Society was awarded $5,000 to restore a hunter’s cabin on homesteading land near the headwaters Little Spearfish Creek. 

According to the packet, the scope of work includes replacing siding and trim to the exterior of the building, removing existing concrete steps and replacing them with a wooden deck, replacing 6 windows and 2 doors, and replacing sheetrock on the ceiling of the cabin.

The hunter’s cabin is located near a log cabin built in 1910 by Charles Anderson, a Swedish immigrant who came to the Hills searching for gold. 

The Sully County Courthouse was awarded $7,500 to repair the front steps and landing of the building. 

According to the packet, the scope of work includes pressure washing the steps, repairing mortar joints, and cleaning and resealing all perimeter window frames. The handrailing on the front steps will be removed, repaired, and replaced. Damaged and fractured stone on the exterior of the building will be removed and patched with matching stone and mortar. Landing stones will also be removed and replaced with matching materials.

The courthouse was designed by W.M. Rick of the Black Hills Company of Deadwood and built between 1911 and 1913. 

The city of Central City was awarded $10,000 to repair the foundation of the city’s catholic church. 

According to the packet, the hillside is causing the church to shift sideways, and the walls are bowing out towards neighboring homes. The scope of work will include bracing the building for safety, lifting and supporting the roof, rebuilding or resetting the load-bearing walls of the church, and constructing new footing and supports on one side of the building. The project is considered an emergency.

According to the packet, the church was the first Catholic church in the Lead-Deadwood area.

Historic Rapid City McGillycuddy House was awarded $5,000 to reconstruct the chimney. According to the packet, the chimneys were removed from the structure when the house was transformed into a bungalow. The scope of work includes rebuilding the larger, functional block and brick chimney. 

The Roberts County Courthouse was awarded $7,500 to replace windows in the dome of the structure. 

According to the packet, the dome is undergoing structural stabilization work. Installing new windows to the structure will help protect the dome from damage from weather and animals entering the structure.

title: RC man sentenced for sex crimes against a child
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: RAPID CITY — A Rapid City man was sentenced July 24 following his conviction of several charges related to sex crimes against a minor
_full_text:
RAPID CITY — A Rapid City man was sentenced July 24 following his conviction of several charges related to sex crimes against a minor

According to court reports, Kyle Beck, 23, was convicted of attempted sexual exploitation of a minor, attempted enticement of a minor using the internet, and attempted receipt of child pornography.

Beck was sentenced to 15 years in federal prison, followed by 5 years of supervised release, and ordered to pay a $300 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund.

Beck was indicted by a federal grand jury in March 2024. He was convicted following a court trial on May 12, 2026.

At his trial, the evidence established that on May 28, 2023, Beck messaged a 15-year-old girl via Instagram and requested sexually explicit photographs of her. Beck was subsequently interviewed and admitted to his conduct.

This case was investigated by the South Dakota Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC) Task Force, the South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation, the Rapid City Police Department, and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security-Homeland Security Investigations. 

Beck was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service.

title: RC man sentenced on child porn charges
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: RAPID CITY — A Rapid City man was sentenced July 24 to federal prison on charges of receipt of child pornography.
_full_text:
RAPID CITY — A Rapid City man was sentenced July 24 to federal prison on charges of receipt of child pornography.

According to court reports, Parker Behrns, 27, was sentenced to 8 years and one month in federal prison, followed by 5 years of supervised release, and ordered to pay $6,095 in restitution and a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund. 

Forfeiture was also ordered.

Behrns was indicted for the charge by a federal grand jury in September 2025. He pleaded guilty on Feb. 9.

Between September 2022 and July 2024, Behrns used his cellular phone and the internet-based application Discord, to search for and receive images and video files containing sexually explicit visual depictions of minors. In some instances, Behrns posed as a minor female to request child pornography from other Discord users.

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse, launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by the U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the DOJ’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children, as well as identify and rescue victims. 

Behrns was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service.

title: Spirit of Dakota Award marks 40 years of recognizing women
byline: By Amina Aidarkhanova South Dakota News Watch
description: The winner’s name had not been announced yet.
_full_text:
The winner’s name had not been announced yet.

One by one, descriptions echoed through the banquet hall as organizers introduced the woman selected for the 2025 Spirit of Dakota Award. She had spent decades teaching. She had devoted countless hours to volunteering. Then came one final detail.

“She wore high heels until the day she retired.”

“When she said that,” Deanell Backlund recalled, “I knew I had won.”

The retired middle school English teacher from Mitchell became the 2025 recipient of one of South Dakota’s longest-running honors recognizing women for leadership and community service.

“What meant the most was knowing someone took the time to nominate me,” Backlund said. “It’s a very involved process.”

As the Spirit of Dakota Award celebrates its 40th anniversary this year, organizers say that commitment to recognizing others has helped sustain the award for 4 decades.

Inspired by a statue

The award traces its roots to the nine-foot bronze Spirit of Dakota statue in Huron, created by South Dakota artist laureate Dale Lamphere in 1987. The sculpture depicts a prairie woman standing strongly against the wind, symbolizing resilience, courage and determination.“The Spirit of Dakota statue illustrates the toughness, courage and strength of character of South Dakota women,” said Marilyn Hohm Hoyt, chairwoman of the Spirit of Dakota Award Society.

Inspired by the sculpture, community leaders created an annual award honoring women whose lives reflect those same qualities.

“This is not Mother of the Year or Teacher of the Year,” Hoyt said. “It recognizes women who demonstrate leadership, help others and contribute to their communities.”

40 years of recognizing quiet leadership

Since 1987, recipients have come from communities across South Dakota, representing education, health care, agriculture, business, tribal leadership, nonprofit organizations and public service. Hoyt said one noticeable change has been the age of nominees.

“When the award first started, many nominees were older,” she said. “Now we’re seeing younger women making extraordinary contributions while raising families and building careers.”

Despite those changes, Hoyt said, the award’s mission has remained the same.

“It speaks volumes that people continue to nominate women from their communities,” she said. “If they didn’t believe it mattered, they wouldn’t take the time to tell those stories.”

The work behind the recognition

Backlund spent 33 years teaching middle school English before retiring while also serving as a grant writer, fundraiser and volunteer for her church, the Mitchell Concert Series and other community organizations.

“I would turn around and do it all over again,” she said.

One memory still stands out from her nomination. A former student teacher wrote that years later, former students continued stopping Backlund to thank her for being their teacher.

“Middle school kids can be notoriously difficult,” Backlund said. “To know that I was appreciated by children that age meant a great deal to me.”

Her friend Joan Anderson spent more than a year preparing Backlund’s nomination.

“Joan is a very gifted writer. She knows what to say and how to say it,” Backlund said. “She believed that people deserve recognition while they’re still living rather than posthumously.”

Looking ahead

Nominations for this year’s Spirit of Dakota Award remain open through Aug. 1.

Hoyt hopes the anniversary encourages South Dakotans to recognize women whose work often happens quietly in schools, churches, civic organizations and neighborhoods.

Backlund believes recognition inspires others to serve.

“I think recognition motivates other people to become involved,” she said. “It lets people know what’s happening in their communities.”

After 40 years, Hoyt said the award continues to fulfill its original purpose.

“The Spirit of Dakota Award recognizes your friend, your neighbor or your mother,” she said. “Someone who has lived a life of helping others, demonstrating leadership and making their community a better place.”

title: Lightning strike causes house fire
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: SPEARFISH — A lightning strike caused a house fire in downtown Spearfish, Wednesday.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — A lightning strike caused a house fire in downtown Spearfish, Wednesday. 

Spearfish Fire Department Fire Chief Scott Deaver said at about 4:30 p.m. the department responded to 321 N. 7th St., for a report of smoke rising out of the roof. 

About a dozen firefighters from Spearfish, 5 from Deadwood, and 2 from Whitewood worked together to extinguish active flames that were visible coming from that space. 

No further information was available by press time.

title: Experts: Cyberattack on Pennington Co. likely by foreign adversary
byline: Bart Pfankuch South Dakota News Watch
description: A line of about three dozen people waited to obtain in-person services from the Treasurer’s Office at the Pennington County Administration Building in Rapid City, S.D., on July 28, 2026. Photo by Bart Pfankuch, South Dakota News Watch
_full_text:
Cyberattack on Pennington Co. likely by foreign adversary.jpg
A line of about three dozen people waited to obtain in-person services from the Treasurer’s Office at the Pennington County Administration Building in Rapid City, S.D., on July 28, 2026. Photo by Bart Pfankuch, South Dakota News Watch 

RAPID CITY — Based on information released by authorities so far, 2 cybersecurity experts said it is likely that a malicious foreign entity is behind the recent cyberattack that crippled communications and other computer-based systems in Pennington County government.

Two federal agencies, meanwhile, have recently warned state and local governments across the U.S. that cyberattacks are increasingly likely, and that such attacks are likely to originate in Iran, China or Russia.

On July 5, Pennington County announced that a “cybersecurity incident” had occurred and affected parts of the county’s computer network. The county shut down public access to government services for a day and has since embarked on a major multi-agency investigation. The county continues efforts to bring back communication and other computer-based systems.

County officials said critical county services such as the sheriff’s office, courts, 911 dispatch and jails have remained operational since the incident. Several county functions such as computer-based communications, internet access and providing record keeping and registration services to the public were slowed or otherwise affected by the incident and response.

Pennington County State’s Attorney’s Office spokeswoman Katy Urban, who is handling all media contacts during the investigation, told News Watch that the county is not discussing the incident or the subsequent investigation and is limiting public statements to those related to how residents can access government services.

“Unfortunately, there’s not a lot I can say because it’s an ongoing investigation,” Urban told News Watch. “If anyone’s personal information has been compromised, we will contact them directly as required by state law.”

Likelihood a foreign government is behind it

Elements of the cyberattack point to an adversarial foreign government as the responsible party, said John Strand, owner of Black Hills Information Security, a Sturgis-based company that is an industry leader in cybersecurity.

Strand told News Watch in an interview that cyberattacks on American government entities typically originate from one of two sources: international organized crime groups that seek money from victims or international adversaries that either seek intelligence on U.S. networks and systems or intend to disrupt daily life in America.

Since county officials have not discussed any demands for ransom from the cyberattacker, it is more likely that a foreign adversary of the U.S. is behind the attack, Strand said.

“So then you’re looking at Iran, you’re looking at Russia, you’re looking at China,” Strand said. “Most of the time, they want to dwell (within the system) and to gain access to critical infrastructure, and they want to maintain access for as long as they possibly can.”

The New York Times on July 30 quoted anonymous state and federal sources in an article indicating that Iran is the likely culprit of a major cybersecurity attack that sought to disrupt water systems in more than 30 communities across Minnesota in late July. The Times said federal officials were concerned the cyberattacks could be a new salvo by Iran in its ongoing war with the United States.

The goal of a dwell is to gain access to a system, stay there as long as possible and gain intelligence about how American systems work or where vulnerabilities may lie, Strand said. 

“If you’re looking at Iran, though, right now because we are in a hot conflict, their motivations would be very different,” he said. “They may want to gain access and cause immediate damage to get the press around what they were able to do in the United States.”

A more aggressive cyberattack could not only disrupt critical services in the U.S. but could interfere with systems that keep people safe, Strand said. 

For example, a cyberattacker could contaminate or limit access to drinking water, send sewage to places it shouldn’t go, disrupt medical or prescription drug information or even affect safe operation of traffic lights, he said.

“The biggest concern that I have is a cyberattack that leads directly to a loss of life or multiple people losing their lives,” Strand said. “There needs to be a prioritization of security across all government entities and health entities.”

Minnesota water systems suffer cyberattack

On July 28, Minnesota officials announced that a “coordinated cyberattack” had targeted computerized operational systems at more than 30 municipal water systems in the state, disrupting processes in at least five communities.

The city of Braham, about 70 miles north of Minneapolis, told residents that the city water system was offline for about two hours on July 27 due to a “malicious cyberattack of computerized operating systems by unknown actors.”

The city reported that the attack did not affect water quality and that the city was able to maintain uninterrupted service.

“This attack did not alter or cause any issue to the physical water plant or water quality or safety,” the city said in a press release. “Rather, the attackers shut down the operating controls which shut down the well and water treatment plant, causing the city to provide water to residents with only water held in the water tower.”

No water quality issues or use restrictions arose as a result of the attack, the state said. The Minnesota IT Services (MNIT) department said it is working with a wide range of state and federal partners to investigate the attack and bolster security against future incidents. 

“Cyberattacks against critical infrastructure require a coordinated, whole-of-government response,” John Israel, MNIT assistant commissioner and state chief information security officer, said in a July 28 news release.

“This incident demonstrates why Minnesota has invested in strong cybersecurity capabilities and partnerships. Our response worked as intended, enabling agencies at every level of government to rapidly coordinate, contain the incident, and help prevent more serious impacts to critical services.”

Federal agencies raise increasing concerns

The South Dakota and Minnesota cyberattacks came amid warnings by a pair of federal agencies about the increased risk of cyberattacks on critical infrastructure systems, including local drinking water and wastewater systems.

In May, the U.S. Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA)

warned that infrastructure systems that use programmable logic controller systems and which rely on the internet for communication or control were under increasing threat of cyberattack.

An updated CISA bulletin in July expanded the scope of the concern to “urgently warn U.S. organizations of ongoing Iranian-affiliated cyber targeting of internet-connected operational technology.”

The advisory said attacks could occur “through malicious project file interactions and manipulation of data.”

As far back as May 2024, the federal government issued warnings about potential cyberattacks on U.S. water systems and lax security systems in place at community water systems. An Environmental Protection Agency alert noted that attacks were likely to come from the Iran government’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard and state-sponsored bad actors in Russia or China.

“Cyberattacks against (community water systems) are increasing in frequency and severity across the country,” the EPA said at the time. “Based on actual incidents we know that a cyberattack on a vulnerable water system may allow an adversary to manipulate operational technology, which could cause significant adverse consequences for both the utility and drinking water consumers. Possible impacts include disrupting the treatment, distribution, and storage of water for the community, damaging pumps and valves, and altering the levels of chemicals to hazardous amounts.”

The EPA said previous inspections found “alarming cybersecurity vulnerabilities at drinking water systems across the country” that included poor password usage, single login access to the system and failure to properly lock out former employees.

Vulnerabilities found in county governments

County governments in particular may be highly vulnerable to attack for a number of reasons, including a high amount of information held within systems that are often understaffed and may not have sufficient system protections in place.

A January 2025 article in the Journal of Cybersecurity drew upon a University of Maryland study that examined security risks at nearly 3,100 county governments in the U.S. – including those in South Dakota – and found worrisome gaps on cybersecurity.

County governments need greater cyber protection systems and improved employee processes because counties are often responsible for providing water, policing, education and elections, and possess significant personal and financial information about residents.

“The consequences of poor cybersecurity at the local level can be disastrous,” the authors concluded. “Given their impact on society, documented gaps in county government cybersecurity are alarming,” the authors wrote.

‘Cannon fodder’ in the ongoing war?

Both governments and private industry should expect more cyberattacks in the future as more public services and commerce are conducted online and through computer networks, said Bryce Austin, a cybersecurity expert and the CEO of TCE Strategy, a Minnesota-based firm that provides cybersecurity protection and compliance services.

The “one-two punch” of cyberattacks in South Dakota and Minnesota within the same month is concerning but not overly surprising, he said.

Several signs point to cyberattacks by Iran, which may be trying to make a statement as it continues to battle the U.S. in war, Austin said.

“I think we’re cannon fodder in the Iran war,” he said. “It’s like they’re trying to send a message that they can attack us from halfway around the world.”

Russia tends to seek disruptions of American systems for political or military purposes while China often seeks intelligence that can help its economy or competitiveness in the global marketplace, Austin said.

Federal, state and local government agencies need to invest in stronger systems protections, employee training and larger IT workforces to potentially prevent future attacks, he said.

“You don’t need your county infrastructure to have perfect cybersecurity,” Austin said. “It just needs to be significantly more difficult to hack than many other counties.”

Strand, who launched his family-run company in his basement near Deadwood in 2008, has grown the firm to 160 employees who conduct 950 security assessments annually across the world. 

He complimented Pennington County on how it has handled the security breach so far but said it would be a “tragic mistake” if the county doesn’t release a full accounting of the attack and its response at some point.

“Just trying to hide it and bury it is almost always the wrong answer, and I’m hoping with these other breaches that we’re seeing they will release information so that this can get fed back into the broader ecosystem, so everyone can learn,” Strand said. “We better get used to it because this is the new normal.”

title: Dolan Creek Senior Living opens new Respite Care Suite to support families and caregivers
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: The new Respite Care Suite at Dolan Creek Senior Living is now open.
_full_text:
3. respit.jpeg
The new Respite Care Suite at Dolan Creek Senior Living is now open.   

STURGIS — Families caring for aging loved ones now have a new option when they need temporary support.  The new Respite Care Suite at Dolan Creek Senior Living, located at 2171 Moose Dr. is now open. 

The new suite is designed to provide short-term care for seniors while family caregivers travel, recover from illness, or simply take a well-earned break from the demands of caregiving.

Teresa Henderson, administrator of Dolan Creek Senior Living and Aspen Grove Assisted Living, said the respite suite fills an important need in the community.

“This gives families peace of mind,” Henderson said. “If someone has to be out of town for a few days or needs a temporary break from caregiving, we can step in and provide complete care for their loved one until they’re able to return.”

Residents staying in the respite suite become part of the Dolan Creek community during their visit, receiving the same services and amenities as full-time residents.

“We provide 3 hot meals a day, medication management, assistance with activities of daily living, housekeeping, laundry, and opportunities to participate in all of our daily activities,” Henderson said. “They’re part of our community from the moment they arrive.”

The respite program is designed around a planned stay of 14 days or more, although guests may stay for fewer days while reserving the suite for the full 2-week period.

Beyond offering relief for family caregivers, Henderson said the suite can also serve as a transitional apartment for seniors preparing to move into permanent assisted living.

“Sometimes families know a move is coming but need a little extra time to get furniture moved or make other arrangements,” she said. “This gives them a comfortable place to stay while everything comes together.”

Dolan Creek Senior Living opened June 5, 2023, and is the sister community to Aspen Grove Assisted Living, which has served the Sturgis area for 13 years. Both facilities are owned and operated by Kind Care Management.

While Aspen Grove specializes in higher levels of assisted living, hospice services and more advanced care, Dolan Creek offers a blend of independent and assisted living designed to allow residents to age in place as long as possible.

“Our first floor is entirely assisted living, our second floor is a blend of assisted and independent living, and our third floor is independent living,” Henderson explained. “Many residents start with independent living and transition to additional levels of care as their needs change.”

Residents enjoy a full calendar of activities that encourages social interaction and healthy living. Henderson said morning exercise classes are held daily, along with bingo, card games, movies, crafts, birthday celebrations, church services, and one of the community’s favorite activities, blackjack.

“They absolutely love their blackjack,” she said with a smile. “Every day is a little different, but we always have something going on.”

Henderson said Dolan Creek currently has apartments available on its second and third floors and encourages anyone interested in learning more about independent living, assisted living or the new respite care program to contact the facility.

“We’re excited to offer another service that helps seniors remain safe while also supporting the families who care for them,” Henderson said. “Sometimes caregivers simply need time to recharge, and knowing their loved one is receiving compassionate care can make all the difference.”

title: Rural radiology technician shortage motivates new tech college program
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Rural radiology technician shortage motivates new tech college program .jpeg
Courtesy photo 

A shortage of rural radiology technicians prompted the South Dakota Board of Technical Education to approve a new program Thursday for a technical college in the northeastern part of the state.

Radiology technicians conduct imaging exams such as X-rays, CT scans and MRIs.

Two South Dakota technical schools already have radiology technician programs: Mitchell Technical College and Western Dakota Technical College in Rapid City. The new 2-year program will be at Lake Area Technical College in Watertown.

The presidents from Mitchell Tech and Western Dakota Tech collaborated with Lake Area Tech on its application and how it could fit into the technical education system.

The Lake Area program fills a gap left when Presentation College in Aberdeen closed its radiology technician program in 2023. Northern State University in Aberdeen is also developing an associate degree program, though it remains in the planning stages.

Health care representatives urged the board to approve the program, citing shortages expected to grow as health care demand rises and experienced technicians retire.

Without qualified imaging staff, timely diagnosis and treatment become difficult — “and at times impossible,” said Natalie Gauer, administrator and CEO of Milbank Area Hospital Avera. 

Radiology technician positions at the hospital have remained vacant for years, Gauer added, which stresses workers. The hospital contracts with a traveling radiology technician, which costs three times what a local staff member would. 

Josh Mages, imaging account manager at GE Healthcare in Watertown, said he regularly speaks with radiology managers across the state who are experiencing growing demand.

“When I come and talk to a customer about exam growth, we’re seeing 50% to 100%. So if you’re doing 100 CTs a month right now, in 5 years we’re going to expect you to do 200,” Mages said. “We’re going to need to add headcounts.”

Some rural healthcare systems have begun training lab technicians to perform X-rays because they can’t find licensed radiology technicians, Mages said. While legal in South Dakota, he prefers professionally trained staff.

Prospective students increasingly want local options rather than relocating hours away, Gauer said — and even when they’re willing to move, programs at other colleges are sometimes full.

“I had a high school student approach us last year. She wanted to come back to our campus after training for rad tech, but she did not get into a program because they were full,” Gauer said. “She simply changed her major. So we will now have lost that opportunity of a greatly needed professional in our community.”

All board members present at the Thursday meeting voted in support of the new program.

Lake Area President Tiffany Sanderson plans to begin fundraising with businesses in the area to remodel a space on the campus for a simulation lab and classroom. The program will likely start in 2028.

“Even though the programs in the state and the tech college system have ramped up to help meet the demand,” Sanderson said, “there remains strong demand, especially in the northeast portion of the state in our rural communities.”

SPEARFISH — Very high fire danger in the Northern Black Hills helped spart 2 wildland fires Thursday.

At 12:43 p.m. Spearfish firefighters responded to a report of smoke west of McGuigan Road.

Upon their arrival, they found a wildfire burning. Federal firefighters soon joined the local crews. 

The Game Farm Fire burned about .25 acres, according to online fire reports. Fire crews had it contained in about 30 minutes with heavy rain falling in the area.

Then around 2:20 p.m., they responded to the Canyon View Fire, located on the rim of Spearfish Canyon. 

Radio scanner traffic indicated they had difficulty finding access to the fire. It was contained to about .1 acre.

It was unclear how the fires started.

Calls to the Spearfish Fire Department for more information were not returned Friday.
