title: Deadwood narrows in on closing FEMA account
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Deadwood is getting closer to closing out an account with FEMA after receiving more than $7 million from the federal agency. The project restored city infrastructure after a high water event destroyed retaining walls and sidewalks along Whitewood Creek. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Deadwood narrows in on closing FEMA account.JPG
Deadwood is getting closer to closing out an account with FEMA after receiving more than $7 million from the federal agency. The project restored city infrastructure after a high water event destroyed retaining walls and sidewalks along Whitewood Creek. Pioneer file photo 

DEADWOOD — The city of Deadwood has received more than $8 million in federal monies from Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), allowing them to close out a loan from the state and move closer to closing out the FEMA account altogether. 

City commissioners acknowledged the receipt of $7.45 million from FEMA July 20. Of that total, $6.6 is owed to pay off the city’s remaining balance of the Infrastructure Disaster Recovery Program with the state. 

“When we originally got approved through FEMA, they allowed us to do a loan through South Dakota Office of Emergency Management to help us cover the costs at 0 – 2% interest during that time,” said Jessicca McKeown, city finance officer. “We did that very early on. Now we’ve gotten our FEMA money so we can pay back our loan to the state for that amount.”

A severe storm July 3, 2019, caused extensive damage to city infrastructure when Whitewood Creek flooded. Repairs to the city were broken into 2 contracts — a $1.8 million contract to Complete Concrete to restore the creek along the Deadwood Mountain Grand and Water Street and another $7.5 million to RCS Construction to build new sidewalks, retaining walls, relocating overhead power, and parking lot and landscape improvements.   

McKeown said the City has finished up the “CAT Z,” administrative expenses incurred by the City in an amount of almost $400,000.  She said the request was submitted last week and should be closed out by the end of August.  

“The additional amount allowed under the program assists the city with the portion of the project which the city was required to pitch in by collecting reimbursement for staff time and additional costs associated with the project,” said McKeown. “Those documents were tracked, monitored and reconciled by the finance and historic preservation offices.”

McKeown said the project is an example of a successful collaboration between local, county, state, and federal offices.

title: GF&P reports  decreased federal funds  for 2027 budget
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
0801 PittmanRobinsonFund.jpeg
Courtesy photo 

PIERRE — A slow in gun and ammunition sales are contributing factors to a sizeable reduction in federal dollars that make up a quarter of the South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks’ Wildlife Division budget, officials say. 

Before presenting their 2027 budget to the Game, Fish, and Parks Commission for approval in June, GF&P management noted that the budget includes a decline in Pittman-Robertson funds. The federal funds, available through the Pittman-Robertson Act, are derived from an 11% federal excise tax on sporting firearms, ammunition, and archery equipment, and a 10% tax on handguns. The funds are distributed across the stateS based on a formula that considers the ratio of the individual states’ total land area compared to the total area of all 50 states, and the ratio of paid hunting license holders in the state compared to the total number of paid license holders nationwide. 

The Pittman-Robertson funds are used as a 75% match for projects and expenses, while the remaining 25% of costs are paid with license fees. The funds are issued to the state on a reimbursement basis, but each state is allotted a certain amount based on available dollars and qualifying factors.  

GF&P Wildlife Director Tom Kirschenmann, said the Pittman-Robertson funds comprise about 25% of the state wildlife division’s budget, and is a critical revenue source. The funds are primarily used for habitat and access programs, including maintaining the state’s 280,000 in game production areas. The GF&P also uses Pittman-Robertson funds to support access programs for public and private lands; to pay $1.6 million in property taxes for game production areas to the counties where the lands are located; to fund wildlife surveys that are used to set policy and determine harvest limits; and to support shooting ranges across the state. 

“It’s a very significant and important part of our operation and what we do with the programs and services we have available to landowners, sportsmen, and working with all of our partners across the state,” he said. 

For the last 10 years, Kirschenmann said Pittman-Robertson funds to the state of South Dakota have fluctuated between $10 million and $19.8 million. In 2023, those funds were at $19.8 million. But in 2026, they dipped to $14.3 million. 

While distribution of Pittman-Robertson funds is partially tied to license sales in the state, South Dakota license numbers have remained steady. In 2022, resident habitat stamps were at 152,104; in 2023 they were at 153,684; in 2024 they were at 155,198; and in 2025 they totaled 154,455. Nonresident habitat stamps were at 151,449 in 2022; 153,248 in 2023; 158,786 in 2024; and 162,900 in 2025. Habitat stamps are required for anyone who is 18 and over, who purchases a hunting or fishing license in the state. 

“The primary precipitator on the ups or downs is really going to be the sales of those guns and ammunition, and the production of it,” Kirschenmann said. “So what we have seen is just a steady decline over the last couple of years in those overall production and sales. There’s fewer dollars available at the national level to allocate to the states through that apportionment process, and then that’s adjusted accordingly on an annual basis.” 

Due to the national decline in gun and ammunition sales, manufacturing, and other factors, Kirschenmann said other states have also likely felt the pinch from smaller apportionments of Pittman-Robertson funds. 

Kirschenmann said despite the decreased funds, he remains hopeful that the GF&P will be able to rely more on license sales to maintain the same levels of quality service and programs. By providing quality habitat and access, and increasing the quality of opportunities, he said they will build a base that can be used to grow the number of paid license holders in the state. License fees are not likely to increase, he said, since just over a year ago the S.D. Game, Fish, and Parks Commission set fees for the next 5 years. 

“You build that opportunity for folks and so you have more people participating,” he said. “So, we’re hopeful we’re continuing to go in a strong direction that we have been going. License sales have remained strong, and we’ll continue to do that.” 

Additionally, Kirschenmann said the state has been researching other grant opportunities from federal agencies such as the U.S. Department of Agriculture and the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. 

“We’re confident we are going to retain our programs and services moving forward,” he said. “We’re just having to be a little more diligent in some areas, and we’re looking at additional alternatives, maybe some new funding sources.” 

The GF&P Wildlife Division is funded entirely with license fees and federal resources, and it does not take money from the state general fund budget.

title: Options to revamp or replace West Elementary discussed
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Spearfish school officials will have to make a decision to renovate or rebuild West Elementary School. Pioneer photo by Travis Potter
_full_text:
DJI_20260728153941_0003_D.JPG
Spearfish school officials will have to make a decision to renovate or rebuild West Elementary School. Pioneer photo by Travis Potter 

SPEARFISH — In the not so far off future, Spearfish School Board members will need to decide what to do with the aging West Elementary School building – renovate or replace.

Jason Roberdeau, president and principal architect of 3Peak Architecture, presented options to school board members recently. The firm, along with JLG Architecture, for the past several months have looked at options to present to the board members.

These are very high-level sort of options,” Roberdeau told board members to kick off the discussion. “Nothing’s been fully vetted, or fully investigated, but we’re trying to get it to a point where we can get a little bit of a direction. Are we doing nothing, or are we building a new building? Or more than likely, probably somewhere in between.”

Editor's Note
To discuss the options the district has for renovating or replacing West Elementary School, a special Spearfish School Board meeting was set for 5:30 p.m. Tuesday at the district’s administration building.

The options presented ranged from doing nothing to replacing the facility.

He said the facility, which has a capacity of approximately 400 students in first and second grades, has a lot of deficiencies ranging from structural issues, an aged HVAC system, lack of fire protection system, old, single-paned windows that are not energy efficient, drainage problems, and more.

Left alone, they can be maintained minimally. 

“But you’re living with a building that has several things that are on the verge of needing addressed,” Roberdeau said.

And when certain items need to be addressed, an entire system must be brought up to current building codes. An example of this was when the board debated what to do with East Elementary School. Built in 1924, the HVAC system, for one, needed upgraded. Because that system was built based on a previous building code, if a part of it needed to be replaced, the entire HVAC system needed to be upgraded to comply with today’s codes. That failing system, as well as other issues, led the district to make the decision to build Creekside Elementary School, which opened in 2011.

Adding a new gym

The board listened to a proposal to add a gym to the school. The current gym hosts PE classes, school lunch, and afterschool programs. Space and time are issues the school has to juggle. However, at the July school board meeting, the board was notified that the subcommittee tasked with studying the school, removed the gym-only proposal as an option as it would have not provided a, “suitable return investment,” said Nick Gottlob, superintendent of the district. 

A new gym and classrooms

A second option would be a 2-phase approach in which a new gym and classrooms would be added, Roberdeau said.

This, he said, would allow the kindergarten to return to West Elementary. In 2013, following years of overcrowding at West, the kindergarten was moved to Mountain View Elementary School. That facility is in the 1961 addition of the former high school located on Hudson Street.

The new gym, new classroom wing, and new parking on the north end of the site, would allow for the separation of the bus traffic and teacher parking from parent drop off parking, he said. The construction would also address site issues, such as storm water. 

The second phase of the build would be renovating the existing building — bringing it up to current standards. 

Roberdeau estimated this option would cost approximately $34.5 million for both phases spread out over 4 years.

New school while still using West Elementary

An option would be to construct a new facility while maintaining West Elementary temporarily. After the new building was open, the old school would be razed. This way the district does not, “deal with the structural deficiencies, not deal with the old HVAC systems, not deal with trying to insulate the outside walls better as fast as all that sort of stuff,” Roberdeau said. “Instead of trying to spend money to fix those things, what if we just limped it along in its existing conditions while we build new?”

In this option, phase one would be to build a 2-grade-level building and parking lot, west of the building and east of the softball field. 

“That building, although it’s really, really tight, could be done while West Elementary continues to operate its existing conditions,” he said. 

After the new facility is open, school officials could demolish West Elementary school and then pause the project if desired, depending on budget and other factors, or they could move into phase 2. 

This phase would be to construct an addition onto the school allowing the kindergarten to be moved into the same facility.

Roberdeau said a very rough estimate for the construction of both phases and the renovation would be around $50 million and take 4 years.

Other options

Roberdeau also presented other options including renovating the school, which may cost around $20 million. Additionally, a new school could be constructed at a completely different location. The new school in a new location may be cheaper than a new school at the current site; however, there are many unknowns and this would rely on site preparation work that would not be extensive.

History 

West Elementary School was first constricted in 1965. An 8-classroom addition was built in 1987, and the office was added in 2004.

This is not the first time the district has been faced with a decision on what to do with an aging facility. When school officials were trying to decide whether to renovate or replace East Elementary School cost definitely came into play. The older part of the school, built in 1924, was not appropriate for young students with the number of steps in the building. It’s HVAC system needed replaced, among other issues. A newer section of the old high school, built in 1961, became Mountain View Elementary School.

The school board approved building Creekside Elementary School to replace the aging East facility. It opened in August 2011 at a price of $12.5 million. At the time, the building was constructed to allow for 20 years of projected growth. However, amid a skyrocketing student population, it quickly became full and 2 additions were added for $1.3 million. The new classrooms opened in August 2015.

Before the addition was added though, the district renovated the 1961 portion of the former high school opening it in August 2013 at a cost of about $2.7 million.

Construction costs have risen drastically since 2011 when Creekside Elementary School was first opened. The U.S. Inflation Calculator indicates that the equivalent of the $16.6 million, for the new school, the additions, and the renovation of Mountain View Elementary School, in 2015, when the construction on the projects were fully completed, that would equate to about $23.4 million today.

To discuss the options the district has for the school project, a special board meeting was set for 5:30 p.m. Tuesday at the district’s administration building. At that time, more in-depth proposals, costs, and financial options are expected to be discussed.

title: Local author releases new book, ‘Harris & Lottie: The Great Pacifier Hunt’
byline: By Sam King Black Hills Pioneer
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
HovdenessBook.jpg
Courtesy photo 

 HovdenessMug.jpg
Victoria Hovdeness released her second book this month. Courtesy photo 

SPEARFISH — Spearfish author Victoria Hovdeness released a new book in her “Harris and Lottie” series, titled “Harris and Lottie and the Great Pacifier Hunt” this month.

The plot sees Harris and his little sister, Lottie, searching their home for Lottie’s pacifiers. After searching the living room and the pantry, they find the missing pacifiers stashed in Lottie’s pajama drawer. 

Hovdeness, herself the mother of 2 children, said that the story was inspired by searching for pacifiers for her youngest child. 

“Writing children’s books is my outlet,” Hovdeness said. “I’m a stay-at-home mom, so this (writing) is something that, although it’s based on my kids, it’s also something of mine.”

Hovdeness’ previous book, “Harris and Lottie: Harris Meets Lottie” was published in 2024. 

Hovdeness said that before she took up writing, her life was completely focused on her children, and she felt as though she had lost some part of herself. She said that writing helped her see the person that she was before becoming a mother. 

Hovdeness said that she plans to write more Harris and Lottie books, and that she has several ideas for potential plots. 

“I have had one (idea) for a while about having to share our toys,” she said. “Or we had a medical instance a few years ago and I thought about trying to turn that into something.” But, she said, “it’s not easy to just sit down and write all the time.” 

Both Harris and Lottie books are published by Farmhouse Publishings with art by HaMeo Art.

title: Scammers pose as  Penguin Random House Employees
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Penguin Random House (PRH) has issued an alert warning authors: fraudsters are impersonating PRH employees and literary agents.
_full_text:
ScamAlert.jpg

Penguin Random House (PRH) has issued an alert warning authors: fraudsters are impersonating PRH employees and literary agents. 

“Here at Penguin Random House we understand the value of a good story,” the prepared statement said. “Unfortunately, bad actors do too.”

According to PRH scammers have asked writers to pay “required fees” to facilitate the publishing process or to cover the cost of “third-party services or certifications.”

“These tactics are fraudulent. PRH will never seek a fee from an author or require outside services to consider a manuscript. Reputable literary agents will not seek an up-front payment to represent a client,” the statement from PRH reads. 

The publisher recommends watching out for fraudulent email domains. 

“If you are contacted by someone claiming to be PRH on social media or over the phone, ask them to send you an email from their PRH email address. Be skeptical if the person gives an excuse for not doing so,” the statement said. “Pay close attention to the email domain, as scammers often spoof a legitimate email address. PRH’s official company email domain in the United States is: @penguinrandomhouse.com or @prh.com.”

PRH is not affiliated with, nor does it do business as: Penguin Literary House, Penguin Publishing Agency, Penguin Publishing Experts, Penguin Publishing House, Penguin Publishers Hug, PenguinPublishers.com, Penguin Self Publishing, Penguin Writer House, Penguins Classic Writers. According to PRH scammers have also impersonated specific people — Robbie Guillory and Rose Taylor, with Underline Literary Agency, and a real editor, Alexis Stratton. 

“These scammers are willing to play the long game to garner trust and often seek payment from writers,” PRH’s bulletin reads.  

PRH does not ask authors for any form of payment or bank account information during the  manuscript submission process. 

Scammers aren’t only targeting prospective authors. They’re also engaged in fake hiring schemes. 

“Individuals using the email handle @applicantsinformation.com to offer fraudulent job opportunities as part of a ploy to steal personal information and money. These individuals have been known to impersonate PRH employees and contact their targets via email, LinkedIn, FreshTeam, and/or CareerBuilder,” the statement said. 

Often scammers will ask for social security numbers for employment verification or bank account information to cover the cost of a company laptop. 

There are also active scams targeting translators. In all cases, PRH recommends vigilance and trusting your instincts.  

Authors, freelancers, translators, and prospective employees who believe they may have been the victim of a scam should contact law enforcement. If you receive an unsolicited email from Penguin Random House, verify its authenticity by contacting fraud@penguinrandomhouse.com

title: Quick picks: children’s books
description: It’s the last day of July — time for a new month, and a perfect time to discover a new story. This week’s picks are new and noteworthy, and recommended by the friendly crew at the Whitewood Public Library.
_full_text:
ReadingOpenBook.jpg

It’s the last day of July — time for a new month, and a perfect time to discover a new story. This week’s picks are new and noteworthy, and recommended by the friendly crew at the Whitewood Public Library. 

1. “My Little Book of Bald Eagles” by Hope Irving Marston

Genre: Children’s nonfiction 

This is a delightful story about a new family of bald eagles. From newborn’s first lessons in life to the first solo flight, this beautifully illustrated book is ideal for introducing young children to the wonders of nature.

2. “Dinos Love Donuts” by Ben Okon, illustrated by Komal Sharma

Genre: Picture book

If you laughed your tricera-tops off at the New York Times’ best selling Dragons Love Tacos, you’ll be jelly-rolling on the floor laughing with “Dinos Love Donuts!”

3. “The Sun Thief” by Alice Hemming, illustrated by Nicola Slater

Genre: Picture book

Squirrel is back, and he’s enjoying the long, sunny summer days.

But wait: why is Bird going to bed when the sun is still up? What a silly idea. Squirrel could never fall asleep while it’s still light.

When the sun starts to disappear earlier and earlier each night,

Squirrel is convinced there must be a sun thief about!

 4. “How to Catch a Bookworm” by Alice Walstead, illustrated by Andy Elkerton

Genre: Picture book

Read alongside the “How to Catch” kids as they scour their books for the squiggly-giggly Bookworm that has escaped their local bookstore. It’s up to the Catch Club kids to find this wiggly critter before class begins. Filled with STEAM concepts and an adorably bookish creature, this hilarious picture book is parents, educators, and readers ages 4-10.

5. “Nibbles the Book Monster” by Emma Yarlett

Genre: Picture book 

Nibbles is a very naughty book monster. He’s chomping, munching, and nibbling his way through fairytales that don’t belong to him. Can you help catch him and put him back in his own story? Lift the flaps, peek through the peepholes, and chase Nibbles through a fantastical world of fairy tales including Little Red Riding Hood, Jack and the Beanstalk and Goldilocks and the Three Bears.

6. “The Wise Turtle” by Sami Murtezai

Genre: Children’s fiction

This is a warm and meaningful story for children about the importance of learning. On a beautiful spring morning, the little animals set off into the forest to pick flowers. But as the weather suddenly turns gloomy, they lose their way and begin to feel afraid. While the others panic, one small turtle stays calm. Using what she learned in school, she finds a way to guide her friends safely back home — showing that knowledge can make all the difference.

_full_text:
The Mercy Sloane Chronicles

Back at the shop, Mercy’s first day was passing quickly. Word had obviously gotten out that the jilted, or rather jilt-ing wife, was working at the store with Marla, and foot traffic increased significantly. There were even a few country wives who stopped in because “They thought they better have a visit. They’d needed to come to town anyway, you know. And how was Marla’s health? And Arlo? Heard from the boys lately?” And of course, they all had their own news:  the baby was teething, or they’d finally gotten a letter from the cousin who’d gone back east, or their milk cow was poorly. All the while, their eyes scanned the aisles, hoping to catch a glimpse of Mercy.

Marla was prepared for all this. “Oh Pearl, how wonderful to see you. Yes, it has been a spell since you came to town… Say, have you met our new girl, Mercy? Oh my, she is just saving us. Mercy, come meet Pearl!” She’d call, and then, “Yes, here she is! Worked in a fancy shop in Iowa City before she came here!  We are so lucky to have her helping us out,” Marla would then extend her arm to cup Mercy’s shoulder, turning toward Mercy with a warm, magnanimous expression, lest there be any confusion about who was helping whom. Marla had done the right thing for the right reasons, and there was no sense not making sure everyone knew it.

The women would smile and nod too, “Oh, how nice! How lovely! How lucky!” They would say, and then inevitably they’d offer an invitation to Mercy, “We ranch by Mud Butte, not too far from your place, dear.” (Their eyes would rove a little awkwardly then, having accidentally revealed they knew more about Mercy than they’d let on…) “Come over for supper soon.” Some of the women were loud and nosy, looking Mercy up and down, not even trying to hide their curiosity. Others were prim or shy, round as fresh-dug potatoes, or tall and lean, but their invitations were all earnest, and their smiles genuine. This girl’s arrival might be a little odd, but a neighbor was a neighbor. 

One lady stood out, mainly because she was young, maybe even younger than Mercy herself. She said almost nothing, didn’t even smile, and of all the customers who paraded through the store that afternoon, she seemed like she might have been the only one who was actually there just to buy something. She counted out her pennies on the counter with slow precision, while Mercy stood next to Marla behind the counter, unsure what to do with herself. 

Mercy still didn’t know how to use the cash register, and she rather doubted she’d ever be taught. Marla seemed perfectly content to have Mercy clean and not much else. Considering the amount of swirling dust that blew in every time the shop door opened, Mercy might have some job security after all. Turned out the dirt on the canned goods was not from neglect but from the wind whipping down Main Street’s gravel. So she just stood awkwardly, while the girl counted her pennies as if each one were a rare and precious jewel.

Finally, the girl finished, grabbed her packages, and scurried through the door without another word.

“Well!” exclaimed Marla, her eyebrows shooting up as she turned to Mercy, the bell above the just-closed door still ringing. “What do you think of that?”

In that moment, Mercy got her first inkling of what her job at the store (other than dusting and being a point of interest for customers) was actually going to be: The corroborator of any and all gossip that Marla gathered and disseminated from her station behind the counter. This was a role Mercy knew she would be marvelously ill-suited to fill. She also guessed she would be better at it than Arlo had been. 

 Eliza Blue TMC
Eliza Blue 

Mercy was immediately proved right on both counts. The next customer, another country wife with a babe-in-arms, arrived mere seconds later, and this time Marla raced through her introductions. In Marla’s approximation, Mercy was no longer the most interesting thing she had to share with customers.

“You’ll never guess who just was here!” she whispered, leaning over the counter as soon as they’d rushed through the pleasantries. 

“It was Leslie Shaw, wasn’t it?” The woman murmured, setting her baby on the counter and leaning forward, too. “I passed her on my way in!”

“She came in, did her shopping, and never said a word, did she, Mercy? Not a word!” Marla replied, turning again to Mercy, eyes wide. Mercy nodded.  “Just counted her bill out in pennies and left!” Marla continued 

“Oh my,” the other woman sighed, shaking her head. 

Just then, Arlo poked his head through the door leading to the alley. “Heading back to the pasture. I’m going to fix fence!” He said.

“Arlo, you will never believe what just happened, Leslie Shaw came into the shop…” Marla began.

“You don’t say…” Arlo replied, stepping backwards into the alley without missing a beat. “Have a good afternoon, ladies!” he called, his voice already an echo.

title: Hydro plant opens for Spearfish Creek Watershed Festival tours
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — Before Spearfish Creek flows through town, it travels through 5 miles of underground pipe to the hydroelectric plant originally built by Homestake Mining Company to power gold mining operations in Lead.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — Before Spearfish Creek flows through town, it travels through 5 miles of underground pipe to the hydroelectric plant originally built by Homestake Mining Company to power gold mining operations in Lead.

“That is bypassing a large loss zone that is in the natural streambed of Spearfish Creek,” said Ben Tieszen, the hydroelectric plant superintendent. “So, if the water were not being diverted and bypassing the loss zone, a lot of the water would disappear into the underground aquifer. This time of year and a hot and dry year like this, our flows in Spearfish Creek would be significantly less than what we are used to having because we are skipping the loss zone. That is why the city purchased this. That’s why the city continues to operate this. The main reason behind that is to ensure a consistent flow to Spearfish Creek.”

Homestake used power from the plant until at least 1994. The city took ownership of the hydro plant in 2004, and operates the facility as an enterprise fund — essentially as an independent business with its own revenue streams and expenditures. 

The plant still generates power and works on the Black Hills Energy grid.

On Saturday morning, Tieszen led tours through the plant, explaining, among other things, that the plant shuts down during power outages so that repairs can be made to the power system without the plant feeding energy into lines that need to be shut off for repairs.

Tieszen invited members of the public to learn about how the plant operates — how it monitors water levels in the creek today, and how the monitoring differed in the past.

At 10:30 a.m. Saturday, a monitor in the neither air-conditioned nor heated main entry to the hydro plant showed that water levels at the 4-bay pond in ever-updating graphics that read “7.12.”

“24/7 we are monitoring that water level. Before technology, that is where the guy with the telescope comes in,” Tieszen said. “There’s a telescope on the main floor down there. They actually have a float inside the standpipe, with a cable that came up over the top with a board that’s ona gage on the side of the standpipe. They can look through the telescope up to the standpipe and look at what the water level was. That was how they would operate the plan. They would manually open and close the valves. So somebody’s job, every 30 minutes, every hour, was to look up there and see what the water levels were.”

Tourists had the chance to see that telescope themselves. The morning tours were part of the annual Spearfish Creek Watershed Festival — an event that invites the community to learn about, clean up, and engage with Spearfish Creek. The 10:30 a.m. tour was attended by young children and folks in their golden years — all interested in the antique plant and its modern use and application.

“We have had a great turnout, a lot of questions, a lot of locals who had no idea what this was and what it did. I think that is super cool that people have taken an interest,” Tieszen said.

title: ‘I have no reason to quit’
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Gerald Frame, 83, stands outside of his auto repair shop in Whitewood, South Dakota. He’s owned the shop since 1980 and has volunteered on the town’s ambulance crew since 1997. Photo by Meghan O’Brien/South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
SD EMTs still lending a hand in their 80s 1.jpg
Gerald Frame, 83, stands outside of his auto repair shop in Whitewood, South Dakota. He’s owned the shop since 1980 and has volunteered on the town’s ambulance crew since 1997. Photo by Meghan O’Brien/South Dakota Searchlight 

 SD EMTs still lending a hand in their 80s 2.jpg
Jim Wallace, 83, is pictured in his Rapid City dive shop. He’s volunteered with the Spearfish Ambulance Service for over a decade. Photo by Meghan O’Brien/South Dakota Searchlight 

When he first earned his emergency medical technician certification almost three decades ago, Gerald Frame didn’t expect to still be a volunteer EMT at age 83.

He’s also still running an auto mechanic shop.

“Who knew?” he said. “That’s my life. My world is pretty small — it’s the ambulance and it’s the customers that I do repairs for.”

South Dakota’s emergency medical services workforce is aging, according to data gathered by the state Department of Health. The average age of an EMS provider in the state is 51 years old. More than 30 providers are in their 70s, and two of the oldest are 83: Frame and Jim Wallace, who both volunteer in western South Dakota.

Frame volunteers in the small town of Whitewood, where his mechanic shop is located and where the ambulance service is affiliated with the one in Spearfish.

Frame’s journey in emergency medical services started in the 1990s when he heard about an EMT class in Whitewood.

“And I thought, ‘what the heck?’” he said. 

More than a decade ago, Frame had a heart attack. It was the executive director of the Spearfish Ambulance Service, Brian Hambek, who recognized the symptoms.

“So, for this last 11 years or so, I’m paying it back,” Frame said. “I got some help when I needed it, I like to help people, so in a way, it’s kind of paying back for my heart, him catching my heart attack.”

Hambek is glad to have him.

“Gerald is 83, but he’s spry as a billy goat, and I love him to death,” Hambek said. “He’ll do anything for his community in Whitewood. He just will.”

These days, Frame mostly drives the ambulance, stocks it with supplies and does what he can to make patients feel safe and heard in an emergency, said Andy Binder, operations director for the Spearfish Ambulance Service.

“He’s found ways to continue doing what he can do,” Binder said. “Maybe he doesn’t get to go carry the patient out of the ditch, but that doesn’t mean that he can’t drive the truck perfectly safe. It doesn’t mean he can’t do a good assessment and do vitals.”

Frame has no plans to stop.

“I have no reason to quit,” he said. “If I can continue to do it, I’ll continue to do this.”

Staying involved as a trainer

An hour southeast of Spearfish, 83-year-old Jim Wallace teaches scuba diving classes at his shop in Rapid City. He also teaches EMT courses in Spearfish and volunteers for the Spearfish Ambulance Service when he can.

“I’m in it just to keep my certifications up and better my knowledge, because everything changes constantly,” Wallace said. “I’m constantly learning, and that’s what I love.”

Wallace first earned an EMT certification in the 1970s as a member of the U.S. Coast Guard. He served as a volunteer EMT in Clark, near Watertown in northeast South Dakota, after he retired. He and his wife moved to Rapid City 12 years ago.

After taking a refresher course with Hambek, Wallace started volunteering with Spearfish while he and his wife worked on moving west. He’d travel across the state — nearly 350 miles — to Spearfish on a Monday and stay all week before returning home to Clark, with a few weeks off in between.

“That’s how much I like being a paramedic,” Wallace said. “I’ll keep on doing it until I’m pushing daisies up.”

While running a dive shop, Wallace sometimes struggles to find time for volunteering in the field. But he makes sure his presence is there in the classroom, teaching new EMTs and seasoned veterans.

“He does all of my EMT education through here. That’s a way of him being a paramedic,” Hambek said. “He can help out and help train new people in this profession.”

Navigating challenges in rural areas

Black Hills State University is in Spearfish, and some college students take Wallace’s classes, whether it’s because they’re merely interested in getting their certification or because they need it for ski patrol or Forest Service jobs in the Black Hills, Hambek said.

“They’ll stick around for two, three years, until they graduate college, and then they’re gone,” Hambek said. “But at least I have them for a couple years.”

The flight of younger residents from rural areas is part of the reason for South Dakota’s aging emergency medical services workforce. The remaining people in rural areas might not have enough time to commit to coursework.

Some services pay their staff, but for some people, the pay is not worth the demanding aspects of the job.

If rural services don’t recruit more young providers, Hambek said, they’re at risk of closing their doors once providers retire or physically cannot provide care any longer. That means longer wait times for people to get help in an emergency situation.

“So, it’s a never-ending circle downward, which is sad,” Hambek said.

Hambek’s Spearfish ambulance crew listens in to Whitewood’s radio, and sends backup if the crew needs it. The Spearfish service responds to calls in a 600-square-mile area, sometimes lending a hand to neighboring communities like St. Onge and Belle Fouche, along with Whitewood.

“If you’re a small town with only a handful of patients, you can’t pay a bunch of staff, but if you have enough calls that people can’t volunteer, then how do you cover that?” Binder said. “You end up with the guys that have been around forever, that stay around and keep going because they want to help their neighbors out.”

Paramedics usually leave that position after less than a decade, Hambek said, usually to move on to different healthcare professions.

Less than 25% of the state’s ambulance services rely solely on volunteers, according to the state Department of Health. Others pay for part-time help. In Whitewood, for example, part-time EMTs get paid about $20 per hour, just for the time that it takes to respond to a call. In Spearfish, where call volumes are much higher, EMTs get paid for the entire time they’re on call, at about $15 per hour.

Wages vary across the state, Hambek said, depending on call volumes and staffing levels.

To get the money for wages and salaries, services say they need higher reimbursement rates from insurance companies and Medicaid. In smaller communities, providers might only respond to about 100 calls a year — less than half of what Spearfish does in a month, Hambek said.

“That means there’s income coming into the service, that I can afford to pay people to do the job,” he said of the Spearfish service. “But these smaller communities, they just don’t have the resources, both manpower and financial. And they’re tied. They’re linked together.”

Lawmakers seeking solutions

An 11-member legislative task force is spending time this summer learning more about how to support and fund local emergency medical services.

At its first meeting in June, healthcare leaders in the state told lawmakers they’re looking at regionalization as a possible solution to the shrinking EMS workforce, creating “workforce pools” so EMS leaders can rely on other services from neighboring areas when needed.

Bridget Hathaway, of the Jones County Ambulance, compared the approach to travel nursing. It could help services like Jones County “who are on the smaller side and might just need somebody for a couple days once in a while,” like during the summertime, she said, when communities often have more outdoor activities and celebrations.

In smaller communities with older providers, state EMS Director Marty Link said, a solution might require “having the tough conversation to say, is it sustainable?”

“That might mean that ambulance service does dissolve,” Link said. “And that might mean they can still provide service to their community, but maybe more as a first response unit.”

That would involve coordination with bigger communities to step in if a patient needs transportation to a hospital.

Lawmakers on the task force have until November to provide proposals that could be introduced as bills in next year’s legislative session, which begins in January. The task force’s second meeting is scheduled for Aug. 24.

title: Cultivating a finer than  fair future for area agriculture
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: NISLAND — For kids in the region, the Butte-Lawrence County Fair represents the culmination of a year’s worth of work and preparation.
_full_text:
NISLAND — For kids in the region, the Butte-Lawrence County Fair represents the culmination of a year’s worth of work and preparation.

That was certainly true for Colt Blair, this year’s champion beginner showman, whose breeder heifer won the title of grand champion.

“We raise black Angus heifers, so we go out into our pasture and look around at the cattle and see which ones are fit. Then we pick them out, halter break ‘em and work ‘em all summer till the fair,” Blair said. “Once you get to the show, you recognize all of your hard work and effort. When you do good, it just really feels good.”

This year’s judge for beef cattle was Colbey Steeke, the Newell High School ag teacher. He said that feeling of accomplishment kids get at the fair is important for the future of agriculture.

“Production ag is dying. We know that. The grandpa, the grandma, that doesn’t have anybody to turn it over to, to turn the place that they have worked for 60/70 years to turn it over to,” Steeke said. “This is where it starts. Getting students, getting young adults involved in shows and getting them involved.”

Steeke grew up on a commercial Simmental/Angus cattle operation.

Pull quote
“This is where it starts. Getting students, getting young adults involved in shows and getting them involved.” — Colbey Steeke, livestock judge

“For parents and grandparents, one of the most beneficial things my parents have ever done is make sure that I had a seat at the table,” Steeke said. “My 2 sisters had a seat at the table deciding what kind of things were going to happen on our operation.”

In Steeke’s view, raising an animal for the fair teaches responsibility. It also offers kids a seat at the table.

“There are kids that will work at home their whole lives, but they don’t take any ownership. Allowing kids to bring an animal to the county fair allows them to take ownership,” Steeke said. Then, gesturing at a Now, when this red Angus heifer goes to calve, 9 months from now, this young man is going to say, ‘Hey, dad, I want to go check my heifer. Hey dad, what does that heifer’s calf look like? Hey grandpa, what are we going to do with this offspring.’ All of a sudden now, these kids have a seat at the table.”

Teegan Frederickson took home the title of grand champion in senior class showmanship. He’s been showing cattle for 10 years and said Steeke asked probably the toughest questions he’s received from a judge in the ring.

“These kids are outstanding. These animals, these kids are bar none,” Steeke said. “I think it is pertinent to ask these kids about the kind of animal that they bring in. I want to make sure that they are up to date in the production agriculture and beef production industry.”

Steeke acknowledged that he has some tough questions at the ready. He asked about bloodlines, finish market rate, and the difference between quality grade and yield grade.

“Quality grade has to deal with marbling. It has to do with intramuscular fat. I had a few young kids out here explain that to me,” Steeke said. “Then yield grade, it’s simple; it’s restricting that carcass between the 12th and 13th rib, we’re taking an eye size: how big that ribeye is, and comparing it to fat. … I do feel it is important for young adults in the beef industry to know things like carcass weight or carcass traits.”

Tiernan Frederickson, Teegan’s brother, was named reserve grand champion in showmanship. He competed, and often placed, in 3 different classes.

“He did give some tough questions,” Tiernan said. “I think it’s good to always kind of be prepared for that stuff. Going over that stuff the night before, possible questions like that and having some knowledge behind your animal helps with that.”

Tiernan noted that this year’s high temperatures presented some challenges, but conditions through a mild winter help support the growth of some hearty competition steers.

“I think we’ve had some worse weather here than last year, but it has still been good. I think, just the steers this year have been a little bit bigger, so that helps. They’ve been eating better, which is a difference from last year to this year,” Tiernan said. “I am most proud of just how we brought our steers from the beginning year to here. How much they came along, how much they developed, weight, how they look, how tame they are, just how they come along through the year — I think that is one of the most fun things.”

The other most fun thing about the fair according to the decorated young competitor? Watching younger kids enter the show ring for the first time.

“I think that is one of the most amazing things. I think that is why a lot of older kids show — to see younger kids getting involved, to see the future of agriculture in the hands that are right here at the county fair,” Tiernan said.

For Blair, that certainly seems to be the case. His sights are set firmly on a future in livestock production, but he told the Pioneer he might also consider being on the volunteer fire department.  

“I want to do the same thing as my dad, and be a rancher and run my ranch,” Blair said.

title: Thune praises tourism, public safety efforts ahead of 86th Sturgis Motorcycle Rally
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Meade County Sheriff Pat West, left, and Sturgis Police Chief Geody VanDewater, speak with Sen. John Thune, R-S.D., about preparations for the 86th Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Thune in Sturgis.jpg
Meade County Sheriff Pat West, left, and Sturgis Police Chief Geody VanDewater, speak with Sen. John Thune, R-S.D., about preparations for the 86th Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. Courtesy photo 

STURGIS – With the 86th Sturgis Motorcycle Rally just one week away, U.S. Sen. John Thune praised the event’s economic impact while recognizing the extensive planning and collaboration required to safely welcome hundreds of thousands of visitors to the Black Hills each year.

Speaking to local officials and community leaders Friday in downtown Sturgis, Thune reflected on his upbringing in Murdo, where his family, like many others, depended on tourism during the summer months. 

“I know firsthand how important that business is to our economy out here in western South Dakota,” Thune said, recalling that his family depended on summer tourism through jobs in hospitality, restaurants, and local attractions. “We want to make sure we’re doing everything that makes it easier — not harder — and, less expensive — not more expensive — to be in business out here.”

Thune congratulated Mayor Rod Bradley and city leaders on their preparations in anticipation of another successful Rally and thanked the many city employees, first responders, volunteers, and businesses whose work helps make the event a safe and welcoming experience for visitors from around the world.

Before speaking to community members, Thune visited with Sturgis Volunteer Fire Department Chief Scott Lensegrav about the unique challenges firefighters face during Rally week. 

Their discussion focused on increased traffic, staffing needs, wildfire prevention, and public education efforts, including reminders for motorists not to discard cigarettes along roadways. They also discussed the importance of cooperation among local agencies to quickly respond to emergencies during one of the busiest weeks of the year.

Thune also spoke with Sheriff Pat West and Sturgis Police Chief Geody VanDewater to learn more about the extensive law enforcement planning that supports the Rally. 

West explained that Meade County brings in additional personnel for patrol, dispatch, and jail operations and even reopens the county’s former jail to accommodate the increased number of detainees during Rally week. Both law enforcement leaders emphasized that while months of planning go into the event, once the Rally begins, agencies must be prepared to respond to whatever challenges arise.

VanDewater and West also highlighted the close partnerships among local, state, and federal agencies, which share intelligence, coordinate resources, and work together throughout the Rally to ensure the safety of residents and visitors. Thune thanked the officers for their dedication, calling the Rally a monumental undertaking and praising the collaboration that has become a hallmark of the event.

When asked about the economy, Thune acknowledged that higher grocery and fuel prices continue to affect South Dakota families and businesses. At the same time, he said he is encouraged that people continue to travel and that tourism in the Black Hills remains strong.

title: Fires near Devils Tower  still active, but not growing
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Grass is cured and fire danger is extreme in the Northern Hills. Two fires are actively burning near Devils Tower. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Fires near Devils Tower  still active, but not growing
Grass is cured and fire danger is extreme in the Northern Hills. Two fires are actively burning near Devils Tower. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

HULLETT, Wyo. — Fire crews have stopped much of the forward progress on 2 fires burning near Devils Tower National Monument.

Ed Robinson, the emergency management coordinator and interim fire coordinator for Crook County, said the fires are basically static.

“Progress has been stunted. I don’t know right now on the containment,” Robinson said. 

Sunday evening the Left Creek Fire, first reported shortly after 10:30 a.m. Saturday, was 25% contained. The Newton Fire, which was reported around 1 p.m. Sunday, was 0% contained. However, the once billowing smoke from both fires has subsided and mostly smoky haze took its place Monday morning. 

“Things could change dynamically. Especially with the wind we are supposed to get today,” Robinson told the Pioneer Monday morning. “The Newton Fire caused us some trepidation when it was running to the west. We thought it was going to jump the highway. They got the fire turned and trapped it down in a canyon”

Fire officials closed parts of Highway 24 and Devils Tower National Monument due to the proximity of the blazes. Both have since reopened. 

“The guys really got on them. And not just the county guys, but the Forest Service, BLM (Bureau of Land Management), air attack. They all got after it,” he said.  

At one time, about 150 firefighters were on the Left Creek Fire. While firefighters remain working both incidents, Robinson said the number has been reduced.

Air assets, including 4 large air tankers, 2 single-engine air tankers (SEATS), and 4 helicopters, also worked the fires.

Robinson said he was thankful for the support network of people helping to bring food and water to fire crews.

He said he believed that both fires started from a Friday evening thunderstorm. It caused 17 fires, most of which were kept very small, he said. 

He added that he would be recommending to county commissioners Tuesday that fire restrictions increase from Stage 2, which prohibits open flame fires, unless they are fueled by liquid or gas, smoking outside of vehicles, welding or using a torch with open flames, to a more restrictive State 3 burn ban that essentially prohibits all fire.

“I would expect the commissioners to approve it,” he said. “That will likely go into effect Wednesday morning.

title: Extreme fire danger prompts burn bans
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: NORTHERN HILLS — Fire danger across the Black Hills is listed as very high to extreme, and all open fires and burning are prohibited.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

NORTHERN HILLS — Fire danger across the Black Hills is listed as very high to extreme, and all open fires and burning are prohibited.

The Black Hills National Forest issued extreme fire danger warnings for the Black Hills Fire Protection District, including Lawrence, Meade, Butte, and Pennington counties. Very high fire danger is listed for Crook County, Wyo. Extreme fire danger means all fires are considered potentially serious, as even small fires have great potential for developing into high intensity burning. Very high danger means fires can start quickly and spread rapidly. Both designations signal serious fire danger conditions. 

On July 24, the Forest Service issued an advisory about Stage 2 fire restrictions in effect, due to persistent fire weather and drought. The Stage 2 listing bans all open burning, including campfires in established fire rings, charcoal barbecue grills, smoking outside, open flame torches for welding, explosives, and all motorized off road travel. It is the highest fire restriction before the USFS completely closes the forest with a Stage 3 restriction. 

In Crook County, Emergency Management Director Ed Robinson is expected to ask commissioners to implement Stage 3 restrictions, after crews spent the weekend battling the Left Creek fires, near Devil’s Tower National Monument.  

The Bureau of Reclamation has also declared a complete burn ban in all areas surrounding the Belle Fourche Reservoir. The ban includes all campfires and open burning. Propane and electric cookstoves are allowed. 

Lawrence, Meade, and Butte counties have active burn bans in place that also prevent open burning of any kind, including charcoal grills, internal combustion engines without a spark arresting device, smoking, welding, explosives and all motorized off road travel. Butte County Commissioner Tom Brunner said the Butte County ban encourages residents to call the local fire chief to inquire about controlled burning. 

Deadwood Fire Chief Joel Ellis said even a chain dragging from a trailer can cause a spark that can turn into a dangerous fire. 

Northern Hills cities are following the respective county burn bans, with open fires of any kind prohibited. On July 27 the city of Spearfish issued an announcement that all campfires are prohibited in the Spearfish City Campground. 

Sturgis Fire Chief Scott Lensegrav said his department has been very busy with fires. So far the department has responded to at least 36 fires across Meade County. 

“Every time a cloud comes through it seems like it has dry lightning with it and it’s parking all these fires out east,” he said.

During their regular meeting today the Meade County Commission is scheduled to consider pyrotechnic requests related to the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, but Lensegrav sent the commission a letter advising against approval. 

“The only way I see to let them have their pyrotechnics is to only have the ones that stay close to the ground and no aerial fireworks,” he wrote. “If they are allowed to use these, they must be set off in a noncombustible area and have their fire crews on standby.  They must also agree to pay all fire suppression bills if they would happen to cause a fire from their pyrotechnics.”

title: Governor grants Mitchell  $1 million for industrial park
byline: By John Hult Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Gov. Larry Rhoen cuts a ribbon with other state and local officials during the Mitchell High Plains Processing facility’s grand opening on Sept. 9, 2025. On Friday, Rhoden awarded $1 million from a state fund for a Mitchell industrial and business park. Photo by Joshua Haiar, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Governor grants Mitchell $1 million for industrial park.jpg
 Gov. Larry Rhoen cuts a ribbon with other state and local officials during the Mitchell High Plains Processing facility’s grand opening on Sept. 9, 2025. On Friday, Rhoden awarded $1 million from a state fund for a Mitchell industrial and business park. Photo by Joshua Haiar, South Dakota Searchlight 

MITCHELL — Gov. Larry Rhoen cuts a ribbon with other state and local officials during the Mitchell High Plains Processing facility’s grand opening on Sept. 9, 2025. On Friday, Rhoden awarded $1 million from a state fund for a Mitchell industrial and business park. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)

South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden issued $1 million Friday from an economic development fund under his control to support an industrial and business park in Mitchell.

The money comes from the Future Fund, which is built up through fees submitted by employers when they pay taxes to support unemployment benefits. 

The governor awards the dollars at his discretion, although a state law that took effect July 1 places new restrictions on the fund, including a more detailed description of acceptable uses and a requirement that awards must be recommended by the Governor’s Office of Economic Development.

The grant for Mitchell comes atop a $1 million loan from the U.S. Department of Agriculture and $1 million in local funding.

The Mitchell Area Development Corporation will use the money to prepare just over 18 acres of land on the south side of Interstate 90 on the western edge of town, installing utilities and roads.

That infrastructure is meant as an incentive for businesses considering expanding or locating in Mitchell, according to Development Corporation Director Mike Lauritsen.

“Once you put in the water, sewer and streets, it obviously becomes more attractive for businesses,” Lauritsen said of the land, which the corporation purchased three years ago. “We want to make it shovel-ready.”

Lauritsen said his office signed a detailed agreement with the state on the expectations for the project, which includes a payback provision if the park isn’t filled within 10 years of the infrastructure’s completion. Between the loan, local investment and the new dollars from Rhoden, Lauritsen said, the project is fully funded.

In a press release on the Future Fund award, Rhoden said the money would help Mitchell “attract new businesses, create quality jobs, and support long-term economic growth.”

Rhoden has awarded Future Fund dollars to several projects in 2026, including putting money recently toward funding for a program that creates a pathway for teaching certifications for paraprofessionals in K-12 schools.

title: Gov. Armstrong announces special session, emergency actions to ban kratom in ND
byline: By Jack Dura and Michael Achterling North Dakota Monitor
description: BISMARCK, N.D. — North Dakota Gov. Kelly Armstrong on Monday declared a public health emergency banning all kratom products and called a special session of the Legislature for September to further address enforcement.
_full_text:
Gov. Armstrong announces special session, emergency actions to ban kratom in ND.jpg

BISMARCK, N.D. — North Dakota Gov. Kelly Armstrong on Monday declared a public health emergency banning all kratom products and called a special session of the Legislature for September to further address enforcement.

Kratom is a substance derived from a tropical tree in Southeast Asia that officials say can be synthesized into highly potent forms and put into products readily available at gas stations and smoke shops. They have linked those products to overdoses and deaths. 

“Doing nothing is not an option,” said Armstrong, flanked by Attorney General Drew Wrigley, top lawmakers and others at a Capitol press conference. 

Kratom has been used as an energy booster, for pain management and to cope with withdrawals from drugs such as fentanyl and heroin. Two psychoactive ingredients known as mitragynine and 7-OH are found in kratom leaves. State officials point to rising calls to Poison Control and a “health crisis” of deaths resulting from the substances.

The special session is set to begin Sept. 2, with a goal of lasting 3 days. Armstrong said the issues can’t wait for the regular legislative session, which begins in January, because new laws take effect Aug. 1, roughly a year from now.

“This is, quite frankly, too important to wait that long,” the Republican governor said.

Sen. Michelle Axtman, R-Bismarck, who has been drafting legislation to ban kratom, will take a lead in bringing proposals for the special session.

Lawmakers might address other topics in the special session, such as a fundraising shortfall that paused construction of the Military Gallery on the state Capitol grounds.

From 2019 through June 2026, kratom and related substances were part of the primary cause of death for 23 people, according to the State Epidemiology Office.

That means “the medical examiner or certifying physician determined that (kratom’s) effects contributed to, whether alone or in combination, the fatal toxicity,” an office spokesperson said.

The substances were part of the contributing cause of death for one other person, and were present in the toxicology results of 26 other cases during the same time period, according to the office.

Kratom-related calls to Poison Control in North Dakota have risen in recent years, from seven in 2024 to 22 last year, according to a state epidemiologist report. That threefold spike suggests “a true increase in kratom-related exposures,” the report said. At least three-fourths of those calls from 2021-2025 were for males. Nearly half of the calls were for people ages 20-39.

Last month, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration moved to temporarily classify 7-OH and three related compounds as controlled substances. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has endorsed restricting certain 7-OH products.

Armstrong said the DEA’s actions are what led to the emergency orders in North Dakota. His public health emergency order is effective Aug. 5 for 30 days.

The governor also said he has authorized an emergency rule by the North Dakota Board of Pharmacy to classify 7-OH as a Schedule I controlled substance, effective Wednesday and consistent with the DEA’s action.

title: SDSU Extension increases drop boxes  for free nitrate testing
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: BROOKINGS — In an effort to ensure a safe feed supply for livestock as dry conditions linger across the state, South Dakota State University (SDSU) Extension is increasing its number of drop-off locations for free nitrate testing.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

BROOKINGS — In an effort to ensure a safe feed supply for livestock as dry conditions linger across the state, South Dakota State University (SDSU) Extension is increasing its number of drop-off locations for free nitrate testing. 

Nitrates accumulate in common forages such as oats, sorghum, sudan grass, and corn during dry conditions. High nitrate levels in hay and forage can pose serious health risks to livestock, particularly pregnant animals and ruminants such as cattle.

SDSU will be picking up samples weekly and communicating results as soon as testing is done. The Extension welcomes livestock owners and forage growers to bring in their forage samples at the following livestock auction locations: Worthing, Yankton, Mitchell, Kimball, Platte, Burke, Winner, Presho, Mobridge, Phillip, Faith, Martin, St. Onge, Belle Fourche, and Newell. 

Forage samples should be collected in gallon-size plastic or paper bags. Before bringing a sample to a drop-off location, please complete a submission form and staple it to the sample bag. Proper sampling will increase the accuracy of results. 

To learn more about how to take proper forage samples, visit https://extension.sdstate.edu/forage-sampling-procedures.

For a free, how-to guide on using nitrate test strips at home, visit https://extension.sdstate.edu/how-test-hay-and-forage-nitrate-levels-using-test-strips.

title: Left Creek Fire prompts evacuation of  Devils Tower, Newton Fire starts nearby
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: The Left Creek Fire, burning near Devils Tower National Monument, prompted the evacuation of the monument Saturday. Photo courtesy of Jenny Pierson Photography
_full_text:
Devils Tower Fire Jennifer Pierson.jpg
The Left Creek Fire, burning near Devils Tower National Monument, prompted the evacuation of the monument Saturday. Photo courtesy of Jenny Pierson Photography 

HULLETT, Wyo. — Two fires started over the weekend near Devils Tower, one of which prompted the evacuation of the monument.

The Left Creek Fire, first reported shortly after 10:30 a.m. Saturday, forced park law enforcement officers to order the evacuation of Devils Tower National Monument. 

According to fire reports, when it was about 20 acres in size, park law enforcement officers forced the evacuation of visitors and staff around 12:30 p.m. Saturday. It grew quickly and by 8 p.m. it had grown to about 250 acres in size. 

There were 150 firefighters assigned to fire, along with 4 large air tankers, 2 single-engine air tankers (SEATS), and 4 helicopters.  

By late Sunday morning, the fire, located just southwest of the park boundaries, had grown to 282 acres and was 0% contained. 

Fire crews were able to make progress on the fire throughout Sunday and had the blaze 25% contained.

Then, shortly after 1 p.m., a new fire sparked east of the monument.

According to fire reports, the Newton Fire prompted the closure of parts of Highway 24. It was reported Sunday evening as 300 acres in size and 0% contained.

Monday morning updates were not available as of press time.

Devils Tower officials planned on reopening the monument this morning; however, all trails and backcountry resources will remain closed for visitor safety until further notice.

title: CHAMPIONS: Sasquatch defend crown in nail-biting series
byline: By Brandon Woltkamp Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Spearfish Sasquatch players, staff, and interns pose behind home plate, excited after the Sasquatch’s second championship win in a row. The Sasquatch collected 617 runs in the season and 51 home runs. Pioneer photo by Brandon Woltkamp
_full_text:
Their reign goes on.jpg
The Spearfish Sasquatch players, staff, and interns pose behind home plate, excited after the Sasquatch’s second championship win in a row. The Sasquatch collected 617 runs in the season and 51 home runs. Pioneer photo by Brandon Woltkamp 

SPEARFISH — “There isn’t a group of kids that I’d rather have won this with,” said Spearfish Sasquatch head coach Phil Dimas. 

The Spearfish Sasquatch reigned as Independence League Baseball champions for a second time in a row after defeating the Casper Spuds 8-5 on Friday and 12-9 on Saturday. Spearfish won the best-of-3 series 2 games to 0.

“I knew the Spuds were going to be challenging, but we never let that momentum go,” Samson the Sasquatch said.

Featured in Game 2 of the Independence League Baseball championship was a home run rally that gave Spearfish the decisive edge. 

“It changed the dynamic of everything,” said Dimas. “The dynamic of the game, of the team. It felt like once it happened, you could see the end of the tunnel.”

Recaps of both games follow.

Friday: Spearfish 8, Casper 5

 SPS v CAS champ 5.jpg
Sasquatch head coach Phil Dimas gets a sports drink jug dunked on him by Garrett Houston and Carter Baete as fans look onwards. Pioneer photo by Brandon Woltkamp 

Spearfish scored 3 runs in the eighth inning to break a 5-5 tie and win game 1 of the series. 

Zach Pearrow reached on error to score Bo Iandoli and gave Spearfish 1-0 lead in the first inning.

Cole Barta singled in the second to bring in Stone Vacek and pull the Spuds in a 1-1 tie.

Braden Smith homered in the third to put the Sasquatch ahead 2-1.

A double by Ethan Schlotterback brought in Kaeden Wilcox and kept Casper in a 2-2 tie in the fourth.

Sam Kwapnioski doubled to bring in Grant Sommers in the fifth as the Sasquatch led 3-2.

Malakai Lopez homered in the seventh to make the score 4-2 for the Sasquatch. Crew Moeller grounded into a fielder’s choice to score Sommers and keep Spearfish ahead 5-2 in the seventh.

Hunter Stonecipher hit a 2-run homer to also bring in Cal Cosen and bring the Spuds within 5-4 in the eighth. A wild pitch scored Elijah Reeves as Casper tied the game 5-5 in the eighth. 

A single by Braden Smith brought home Iandoli and Wilson Kieffer as Spearfish led 7-5 in the eighth. Kwapnioski flew out to bring in Sommers later in the eighth and gave the Sasquatch its first win in the championship series.

Sommers scored 3 runs for the Spearfish offense, and Smith collected 4 hits.Mac Hibben earned the pitching win. 

Stonecipher, Reeves, Vacek, Wilcox, and Cosen scored one run apiece for Casper. Hunter Billingsley collected a team-high 2 hits. Dylan Zajicek took the pitching loss.

Spearfish runs: Grant Sommers 3, Bo Iandoli 2, Malakai Lopez 1, Braden Smith 1, Wilson Kieffer 1. 

Spearfish singles: Smith 3, Iandoli 2, Sam Kwapnioski 2, Kieffer 2, Lopez 1, Kendrick Aragon 1. 

Spearfish doubles: Kwapnioski 1. 

Spearfish home runs: Smith 1, Lopez 1. 

Spearfish pitching: Giovanni Casas 7 innings, 4 runs, 6 hits, 2 walks, 3 strikeouts; Mac Hibben 2 innings, 1 run, 0 hits 1 walk, 4 strikeouts. 

Aug. 1; Spearfish 12, Casper 9

The Sasquatch took the lead for good during a 4-run fifth inning that featured home runs from Malakai Lopez, Kendrick Aragon, and Grant Sommers. 

Hunter Billingsley singled to score Elijah Reeves to give the Spuds a 1-0 lead in the first.

Sam Kwapnioski drew a bases-loaded walk in the first and put the Sasquatch into a 1-1 tie.

Andrew Witt flew out in the second to bring in Trey Brooks as Casper led 2-1. 

A single by Lopez scored Garrett Houston and Aragon to put Spearfish up 3-2 in the second. Sommers doubled to bring in Bo Iandoli and Lopez as the as the Sasquatch led 5-2 later in the second.

Sommers scored on a passed ball in the second and extended the Sasquatch’s edge to 6-2. 

Hunter Stonecipher doubled in the fourth to bring in Witt and Reeves as the Spuds trailed 6-4. Billingsley’s double scored Stonecipher and pulled Casper within 6-5.

A bases-loaded double by Stone Vacek later in the fourth scored Kaeden Wilcox, Billingsley, and Cole Barta as the Spuds forged an 8-6 lead.

Aragon homered in the fifth inning to bring Spearfish within 8-7. A 2-run homer by Lopez that also scored Iandoli, and a solo homer by Sommers later in the fifth, put the Sasquatch ahead 10-8.

A single by Braden Smith scored Lopez and Iandoli as the Sasquatch led 12-8 in the sixth.

Billingsley singled in the eighth to score Reeves and bring the Spuds within 12-9, but they got no closer. 

Iandoli’s 4 runs and Sommers’ 5 hits paced the Spearfish offense in those categories.  Colter Wilson earned the pitching win.

Elijah Reeves led the Spuds’ offense with 3 runs and 3 hits. Luis Lepe took the pitching loss.

Spearfish runs: Bo Iandoli 4, Malakai Lopez 3, Grant Sommers 2, Kendrick Aragon 2, Garrett Houston 1. 

Spearfish singles: Braden Smith 4, Sommers 3, 

Spearfish doubles: Crew Moeller 1, Sommers 1. 

Spearfish home runs: Sommers 1, Aragon 1, Lopez 1.

Spearfish pitching: Carte Baete 3 1/3 innings, 7 runs, 8 hits, 3 walks, 4 strikeouts; Colter Wilson 5 2/3 innings, 2 runs, 3 hits, 1 walk, 8 strikeouts. 

 “You can do all these cool things, but if you don’t win at the end of the day, none of that matters,” said Dimas. 

Dimas reflected on his progression as head coach. “I definitely learned a lot as far as learining your team, learning how to distribute,” said Dimas.

Dimas said he taught more than baseball. “They are better young men and better baseball players at the end of the day,” said Dimas.

The Spearfish Sasquatch owner Eric Schmidt said thanks to those who have attended the games this year.

title: ND mammoth dig unearths ‘rare’ array of bones from beneath garage
byline: By Michael Achterling North Dakota Monitor
description: Team members excavate mammoth bones under the supervision of the North Dakota Geological Survey beneath a garage in Burke County in June. Photo courtesy of North Dakota Geological Survey
_full_text:
North Dakota mammoth dig unearths ‘rare’ array of bones from beneath garage.jpg
Team members excavate mammoth bones under the supervision of the North Dakota Geological Survey beneath a garage in Burke County in June. Photo courtesy of North Dakota Geological Survey 

A mammoth excavation under a northwest North Dakota garage is unearthing a more complete prehistoric beast than paleontologists had hoped for when the discovery was made in the 1980s.

The excavation in Burke County is being spearheaded by the North Dakota Geological Survey, which has used its team, summer interns and some geology students from the University of North Dakota since June to carefully dig out the iconic animal.

“When you dig something up, you never know if it’s going to be one bone and the whole thing is going to be over,” North Dakota State Geologist Clint Boyd said. “Very quickly it became clear, no, there is a reason we are digging here.”  

Boyd said this mammoth skeleton is a rare find and the most complete mammoth from North Dakota, though not as encompassing as the mammoth site in Hot Springs, S.D.

He said the team is still working to determine the type of mammoth, either woolly or Columbian. The team is also trying to determine the sex of the mammoth. 

Boyd said the excavation underneath the garage could wrap up in September so the garage can be reconstructed for the home owner this fall. He added the excavation team plans to return in spring 2027 to excavate areas outside of the garage.

So far, he said the team has recovered bits of the skull, lower jaw and some ribs. They are beginning to find the limbs of the animal and are hopeful to find the mammoth’s tusks waiting to be uncovered outside of the garage. The timeline to complete the mammoth excavation remains fluid.

The bones were discovered on a northwestern North Dakota property in 1988 while the owner was digging a foundation for a garage. The family sent a couple of teeth to North Dakota State University, which verified that the teeth had come from a mammoth that lived during the Pleistocene Epoch, commonly called the Ice Age. 

However, by the time the North Dakota Geological Survey was notified of the verified discovery, the garage foundation had already been poured, and the garage, attached to the home, had been constructed. The Geological Survey was not able to fund the demolition of the garage, excavation and construction of a new garage in an agreed timeline with the owner.

For about 35 years, the mammoth stayed under that garage until former North Dakota State Geologist Ed Murphy reexamined his old notes from the 1988 discovery and learned the property had changed hands over the years. He reached out, spoke to the new owner and agreed to conduct site testing around the garage.

“They’ve been wonderful to work with,” Boyd said.

In 2025, state lawmakers allocated $150,000 for the excavation as part of Senate Bill 2014.

Andrew Clark, deputy state historic preservation officer, told members of the State Historical Society Board at their July meeting that a team from the Historical Society convinced the landowner to rip up the garage floor and used ground penetrating radar to evaluate the mammoth site.

Clark said radar results showed the mammoth skeleton may have been damaged by the construction of the garage due to some “pushing around” of the bones. 

The excavation team discovered when the property’s former owner dug the 3-foot foundational footings for the garage, some of the bones were severed, removed as part of the construction process and then returned to the site as part of soil backfill, Boyd said.

He added the situation is unique because if the construction crew hadn’t struck the bones, they would have never known they were there.

“But, you’d prefer less of it had gotten hit than actually did,” Boyd said

The skeleton may be at the Burke County property because water carried it from the location it died, he said. Though Boyd said they don’t think the water carried the mammoth far, most likely yards instead of miles.

The property owner has indicated the mammoth will become part of the North Dakota state fossil collection though a formal agreement has not yet been finalized, he said.

“Ideally, it will eventually go on display upstairs in the Heritage Center,” Boyd said.

If a display at the museum is not possible, he said they would look to display the mammoth near the place it was discovered. Any display is still years away.

Boyd said the excavation should not need any additional state funding until they are ready to prepare an exhibit, which might not be until the 2029-31 biennium.

He said his team’s first mammoth excavation was in the Freedom Mine near Beulah in 2023, which yielded a large tusk, part of a hip and some ribs from what was likely a Columbian mammoth. 

If a fossil discovery is made on private land, there are no mandatory reporting requirements in the state for encountering fossils. Residents will not lose their rights to fossil finds on private land if they alert the Geological Survey, Boyd said.

“We’re mostly coming there to give the landowner information, and if they decide that they want to keep it, that’s their right,” Boyd said. “But, if we get to see it, where it was found, that adds to our information about the state.”

The team is working with the property owner to finalize a name for the skeleton.

Meanwhile, about 160 people have participated in public fossil digs this year supervised by the Geological Survey. The digs this year are being held in the Pembina Gorge, Dickinson and Bismarck areas. 

In July, one dig participant found a 3.5-inch T. rex tooth.

The 2026 events are sold out, but a wait list is available through the department’s website. Fossil events in 2027 are expected to be posted this fall with sign-ups occurring in January or February.
