title: South Dakotans condemn endangered species rule change as state government takes no position
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service designated the northern long-eared bat, found in the Black Hills, as an endangered species. Photo courtesy US Fish and Wildlife Service
_full_text:
South Dakotans condemn endangered species rule change as state government takes no position.jpg
The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service designated the northern long-eared bat, found in the Black Hills, as an endangered species. Photo courtesy US Fish and Wildlife Service 

PIERRE — The state of South Dakota did not submit official comments on a major change to the federal Endangered Species Act that will roll back protections for forests, wetlands, deserts and other habitats where endangered species live.

The new rule will open some landscapes to development, logging, mining, and oil and gas drilling, due to a more limited definition of “harm” as actions that directly injure or kill endangered species. A previous definition included harm to habitats where endangered species live.

Some South Dakotans blasted the rule change, which was finalized July 10. Their comments were among more than 350,000 submitted during the public comment period. 

The South Dakota Ornithologists’ Union submitted comments saying the rule change will “wantonly put us on a path to massive loss of species.” 

Lester Flake, a distinguished professor emeritus of wildlife at South Dakota State University, described the new rule as “a crazy move by President Trump that must be stopped.” 

Caitilin Kane described herself as “a voter from South Dakota, where a large part of our livelihood depends on maintaining healthy ecosystems and protecting endangered species of all kinds, both plant and animal.”

“I beg you, please do the right thing, and strengthen and maintain regulations protecting our native species here in South Dakota and across the country!” Kane wrote. 

John Weidler, a biologist for the South Dakota Department of Game, Fish and Parks, submitted personal comments calling the move “incredibly harmful to wildlife.” He criticized the new rule’s more limited definition of “harm” as actions that directly injure or kill endangered species. The previous definition included harm to habitats where those species live.

“To define ‘harm’ as only directly harming a plant or animal is pretty stupid from a biological point of view, because no organism can survive without habitat,” Weidler wrote. “Destroy the habitat and the organism will eventually die.” 

The South Dakota Department of Game, Fish and Parks did not submit an official departmental comment on the rule; nor did the South Dakota Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources.

Game, Fish and Parks spokesperson Nick Harrington replied to South Dakota Searchlight with a written statement, but he did not address Searchlight’s questions about the department’s position or whether the department has the staffing and funding to adequately protect endangered species under the new rule.  

“Our department maintains a list of state threatened and endangered species, but also tracks those on the federal list as some can overlap,” Harrington wrote. “Conservation efforts for all wildlife is the responsibility of GFP and biologists and managers of multiple disciplines engage in these conservation activities.” 

Some other states expressed concerns about the proposal, saying it would threaten their plans to safeguard endangered species. 

At least one state contradicted itself.

North Dakota’s Game and Fish Department submitted comments against the change, saying “there is clear consensus that habitat loss, destruction, and fragmentation are significant contributors to species declines” and “there can be no doubt that the loss of habitat-focused programs and strategies for species recovery would ultimately lead to further declines.” 

But North Dakota’s Department of Agriculture submitted comments in favor of the change, especially the narrower “harm” definition. Doug Goehring, North Dakota’s agriculture commissioner, wrote that the new definition “will restore and protect private property rights and further positive land development.” 

Federal officials described the rule as a move to give state leaders freedom to manage wildlife without burdensome federal regulations. States that wish to continue protecting habitats can do so under state law, the Interior Department and other federal agencies wrote in their new regulations. 

But some legal experts and many wildlife veterans say that almost no states have endangered species laws on the books that allow state officials to prevent habitat destruction in the name of saving wildlife. Many states have laws to stop poaching, but the protection of nesting trees, spawning streams and other resources has long fallen to the federal Endangered Species Act. 

Portions of this story were written by Alex Brown and originally published by Stateline.

title: Online prediction markets rile up state lawmakers
byline: By Kevin Hardy Stateline
description: CHICAGO — The escalating feud between states and online prediction markets was on full display at a summit of state lawmakers this week as legislators publicly scolded Kalshi and Polymarket, the two most prominent platforms.
_full_text:
StatelineLogo

CHICAGO — The escalating feud between states and online prediction markets was on full display at a summit of state lawmakers this week as legislators publicly scolded Kalshi and Polymarket, the two most prominent platforms.

Prediction market platforms say they are like commodity markets that offer contracts to speculate on the future price of corn or oil — not sportsbooks that allow gamblers to place bets. But many states reject those justifications, arguing the platforms are a backdoor to skirt state gambling regulations, particularly on sports.

The issue has sparked action from state regulators, new legislation, and a flurry of lawsuits from states, prediction markets, and the Trump administration, which has sought to sideline state oversight.

During a sometimes-heated panel discussion at the annual gathering of the National Conference of State Legislatures in Chicago, Iowa Republican state Sen. Dan Dawson told the audience that a group of students at his son’s high school recently enrolled in Kalshi to bet on World Cup matches. In Iowa, people must be at least 21 to participate in legal online sports betting.

“States are the ones that pick up the pieces,” Dawson said as a Kalshi executive looked on.

Dawson has previously raised concerns about the public health consequences of prediction markets. While an industry representative pledged to work with states, Dawson said a legislative subcommittee that recently studied the issue could not get even basic information from the prediction markets about their reach in Iowa.

“We couldn’t get one answer,” he said.

In March, Kalshi preemptively sued to block Iowa Attorney General Brenna Bird, a Republican, from taking civil or criminal enforcement action against it. In its suit, Kalshi claimed there was “a substantial risk that the attorney general of Iowa will bring an enforcement action.”

Regulation of prediction markets

Sara Slane, Head of Corporate Development at Kalshi, told lawmakers in Chicago that the company was committed to building relationships with the states. But she said the prediction markets are not subject to state oversight, as they are regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, which regulates derivatives such as futures contracts on stocks.

She said prediction markets require a national standard rather than a “state-by-state regulatory patchwork.”

“This was exactly what the commodity exchange was set up for,” she said.

The five-member, presidentially appointed CFTC currently has four vacancies. But it has aggressively sought to exclude states from overseeing prediction markets, suing red and blue states alike to maintain its jurisdiction over the markets.

Earlier this week, a coalition of 44 state attorneys general wrote to the agency, arguing it does not have the power to regulate sports-related event contracts, which they say are subject to state gambling regulations.

In addition to encroaching on state-regulated and state-taxed sports gambling, states argue that prediction markets are subject to potential insider trading, lack consumer oversight and can fuel problem gambling.

Slane said her firm works to prevent money laundering and allows people who have problems with gaming to block themselves from the site. She said Kalshi also works with major sports leagues to prevent athletes and referees from trading on sports events.

“We take this very seriously,” she said. “We want to promote integrity around our exchange.”

But prediction markets continue to gain national attention for allowing people to unfairly bet on the outcome of events by leveraging nonpublic information.

This week, the White House announced the president’s teleprompter operator was no longer on staff after he was accused of using inside knowledge to make bets about presidential speeches on Kalshi.

Minnesota Democratic Gov. Tim Walz on Tuesday signed an executive order prohibiting state employees from using inside information to bet on prediction markets. At least eight states, including Arizona, California, Maryland and Wisconsin, have implemented similar restrictions.

Mick Mulvaney, executive director of the Gambling is Not Investing Coalition, said he was sympathetic to the argument that prediction markets want to avoid a regulatory patchwork across the states.

“That being said, there’ve been two areas where the states have almost always been entirely sovereign: That’s on booze and gambling,” he said.

Mulvaney, a Republican, represented South Carolina in the U.S. House and served as acting White House chief of staff during President Donald Trump’s first term. His organization argues that prediction markets should be subject to the same state and tribal regulations as other forms of gambling.

With litigation flying, he said there’s no question the debate is heading toward the U.S. Supreme Court. Mulvaney said it’s unclear how the conservative court will rule, given its recent decisions. Some of those rulings have allowed the expansion of federal executive power, while others have tilted toward the states.

“So that will be fascinating to see how it shakes out at the Supreme Court,” he told Stateline. “But I have every expectation that this is going all the way up.”

Threat to tribal casinos 

Casino gambling has been the sole economic engine for many Native American tribes for years, said Michael Hoenig, vice president and associate general counsel for gaming at the Yuhaaviatam of San Manuel Nation in Southern California.

He said tribes have built up the gambling industry over the last 40 years — sometimes in cooperation with states, other times “in friction with the states.”

“This is just a profound affront to tribal sovereignty, tribal self-government,” he said. “Tribes are supposed to have the sovereign right to decide who gets to operate gaming on their lands and who doesn’t.”

Aside from regulatory concerns, state leaders worry about how the rise of prediction markets may impact the financial and mental health of their residents. Since a 2018 U.S. Supreme Court ruling opened the door for states to legalize sports gambling, 39 states and the District of Columbia have done so.

Advocates, researchers and lawmakers are already raising alarms about how the burgeoning market could fuel gambling addiction and hurt household finances. 

Aside from regulation, there is little difference between the potential impacts of prediction markets and online sports betting, said Rachel Volberg, a professor emerita of epidemiology at the University of Massachusetts Amherst.

Volberg, who has studied gambling addiction for 40 years, told lawmakers in a separate presentation that the research is clear about how over involvement in gambling can hurt individuals and families. However, she told Stateline that legal sports gambling is too new for researchers to fully measure how much the high-speed and accessible world of online gaming has changed the dynamics.

In North Carolina, a new poll found that most people generally approve of sports betting, but a majority wants the state to ban prediction markets.

In the Meredith College poll released Tuesday, 51% of registered voters said they were satisfied with state regulation of sports gambling. Only 11% said they were dissatisfied, while 38% said they didn’t know.

In that poll, two-thirds of registered voters said they would support state legislation banning prediction markets, while 24% said they should be legal.

Though sports fans, policymakers and the researchers continue to grapple with the quickly evolving landscape, experts gathered in Chicago were clear that this industry is here to stay.

“It’s not going anywhere,” said Anthony D’Angelo, who leads responsible gaming efforts at Fanatics Betting & Gaming.

D’Angelo said his company’s sportsbook invests heavily in providing assistance for problem gamblers, flags potentially problematic transactions and incentivizes customers to set and stick to betting limits.

He said lawmakers can help keep people away from illegal and offshore betting platforms that have no oversight or consumer protections.

“We all want the same things to happen,” he said. “I think we want a sustainable, long-term industry where customers are protected.”

title: BH Christian Academy  gains state accreditation
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Students in Brenda Karp’s preschool class work on writing to begin their day at Black Hills Christian Academy. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
DSC_0172.JPG
Students in Brenda Karp’s preschool class work on writing to begin their day at Black Hills Christian Academy. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

 DSC_0175.JPG
Students in Brenda Karp’s preschool class work on writing to begin their day at Black Hills Christian Academy. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

 DSC_0178.JPG
Ashley Schorzmann teaches her third grade students at Black Hills Christian Academy. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

 DSC_0179.JPG
Gregg Dennison delivers a religion lesson for high school students at Black Hills Christian Academy. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

SPEARFISH — Black Hills Christian Academy celebrated a milestone in 2025 when it received accreditation from the state of South Dakota. 

The private school in Spearfish serves a small population of about 115 students in preschool through 12th grade, and was established in 1992. For the last 2 years school officials have been working toward gaining their accreditation status, and administrator Lauren Jones said she is very excited about the achievement. 

“We just kind of reached a stage where we’re no longer a mom and pop shop, where we might just hire Billy’s mom to teach science and Johnny’s mom to teach reading,” Jones said. “Now it’s a requirement for them to have their teaching certification. That’s huge with just the accountability piece.” 

Jones said the accreditation also qualifies the school to receive some equitable services, such as utilizing reading specialists from the Spearfish School District. 

“It’s just a way for us to partner with the public schools as far as sharing resources and things like that,” Jones said. 

Kirk Easton, superintendent of the Spearfish School District, said the accreditation means the district will collaborate with Black Hills Christian Academy to share some services. He applauded the school for obtaining the accreditation. 

“I think it brings credibility to what they offer students and families and so I applaud them for their efforts to become state accredited,” he said. 

Additionally, Jones said the accreditation will make it easier for high school credits to transfer from school to school. Previously, she said when students started their freshman year at Black Hills Christian Academy, they would have to commit to the school for 4 years to receive their degree, or take a risk that all of their credits would not transfer to another school. With the accreditation, all credits should be transferrable. 

“Let’s say they’re here their freshman and sophomore year and dad gets a job in Michigan, we want to make sure those credits transfer with the kiddo and that they don’t have to re-take any courses,” Jones said. 

Black Hills Christian Academy serves students in the Northern Hills area, Sundance and Beulah, Wyo., by providing a Christ-centered education with small class sizes. The non-denominational school population represents about 20 different religious denominations. 

“It’s not uncommon to see teachers praying with kiddos who are struggling personally,” Jones said. “I think that kind of drives home the relationship aspect of the school. That’s probably the biggest thing that we hear is small class sizes. The teachers actually know the kiddos and they actually have a relationship with the kids. I think that’s what sets us apart. Kids are known for who they are and they’re celebrated, loved, and prayed for. We get the privilege of not just educating kids, but also pointing them to Jesus, and I think that’s a pretty cool thing.”

title: Sixth annual Drama Camp draws 40 young performers for ‘Into the Woods Jr.’
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: “Into the Woods, Jr.” was held recently at the Sturgis Community Center theater.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
1. drama.JPG
“Into the Woods, Jr.” was held recently at the Sturgis Community Center theater.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

STURGIS – Forty aspiring actors from across the Sturgis area spent a recent week singing, acting and building friendships as they prepare to present “Into the Woods Jr.” during the sixth annual Drama Camp sponsored by the Sturgis Area Arts Council.

The weeklong camp brings together students in grades 6-12 from Whitewood Elementary, Sturgis Williams Middle School, Stagebarn Middle School and Sturgis Brown High School for 5 days of intensive rehearsals before taking the stage for final performance.

Drama Camp Director Hillary Hill said one of the most rewarding parts of the camp is seeing experienced performers mentor younger students.

“This is our sixth annual drama camp, and it’s a really cool experience because we have students from several different schools all together in one camp,” Hill said. “Our older, more seasoned actors are able to help and teach some of our younger actors, and it’s wonderful to watch those relationships develop throughout the week.”

This year’s production is “Into the Woods Jr.,” a condensed version of Stephen Sondheim’s acclaimed Broadway musical that weaves together several classic fairy tales into one story filled with humor, adventure and life lessons.

“We’re doing Into the Woods Jr., which is a shortened version of the original Broadway musical that has been around for a long time,” Hill said.

Students rehearsed throughout the week.

“We have 40 kids here, and in just 5 days of rehearsal, we put together this entire production,” Hill said. “The dedication and hard work the students put in each day is amazing.”

Hill credited several individuals and organizations for helping make the camp possible.

Assistant directors Cyrus Lyons and Angel Orenstein helped lead rehearsals alongside Hill. 

The production also featured new microphones recently purchased through funding from the Wharf Resources Grant Program, enhancing the quality of this year’s performance.

title: Lawrence Co. Commissioners discuss potential property tax bill, ask for public vote
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: DEADWOOD — As Meade and Pennington counties pass ordinances to implement a new sales tax to relieve owner-occupied property taxes, Lawrence County commissioners discussed potential paths forward Thursday, noting the bill is a tax shift and asking for a public vote.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

DEADWOOD — As Meade and Pennington counties pass ordinances to implement a new sales tax to relieve owner-occupied property taxes, Lawrence County commissioners discussed potential paths forward Thursday, noting the bill is a tax shift and asking for a public vote. 

Commissioner Eric Jennings opened discussions Thursday refreshing the public and commissioners how property taxes are used on the municipal, county, and state level. Jennings said property taxes are used, primarily, to fund schools, cities, and counties, while sales tax is used to fund state programing. 

“The state doesn’t have any income tax; they don’t take any property tax. It’s mostly sales tax that funds them,” said Jennings. “So, the state employees, Medicaid, the roads, National Guard, all of that funding comes from sales tax. The state does collect some property tax to fund schools from their state fund formula.”

Jennings said Senate Bill (SB) 96, passed during this year’s legislative session, would allow county governments to enact an additional sales tax of up to a half percent, and all revenue generated would go towards relieving owner-occupied property taxes. 

“If the county were to adopt or implement the county sales tax, the process would be the retailers would collect the tax, they would send that tax to the Department of Revenue, the Department of Revenue would then send the county’s share back to the county,” said Jennings. “I think they were issuing payment twice a month. Our auditor would set up a separate property tax relief fund, so she would track that money, put that money into the fund, and then when the homeowners then got their tax bill, the county would apply the money in that fund as a credit to their tax bill.”

As an example, Jennings said property owners with a $3,000 tax bill with a $500 credit from the new sales tax would have a new bill of $2,500. 

Jennings said he, as chairman, has been cautious to bring the bill forward while he waited for more accurate sales tax revenue numbers to be published by the Department of Revenue.

The bill became law in January but was effective July 1. Jennings said the Department of Revenue requires 90 days’ notice from the counties before they’re able to collect taxes and can only collect county sales tax January and July 1.

“If you do that math, (to collect Jan. 1) if it’s implemented, that comes back to the first part of October. So, the county would need to adopt an ordinance to get this ordinance passed by the end of September. There’s still time to get that done,” said Jennings. “There’s nearly no advantage to getting it done before that. The counties that have adopted it in July, they’re not going to be able to collect tax before the counties that would adopt this in September.”

Jennings said SB 96 allows the county 2 options for providing relief to property owners. First, he said, the county is permitted to wait until a year’s worth of sales tax is collected, after which the amount is split between owner-occupied property taxpayers based on individual valuations. The first option requires money to be collected in 2027 and applied in 2028. 

Secondly, Jennings said counties are permitted to estimate how much sales tax is going to be collected and then offer credits in 2027.

“There’s certainly some risk in doing that,” he said. “Sales tax has been fairly stable in Lawrence County. I think the figures that the state was using when they were working on this in January was a little under $6 million and when I checked it a couple weeks ago, they thought it was going to be a little over $6 million. It’s a pretty stable $6 million.”

Jennings said that if the county were to implement the tax, additional software would be required. Bruce Outka, deputy state’s attorney, said the county currently uses a software built in-house instead of boxed, bringing the potential for missteps and additional work lower than other counties.

Jennings said that he would like to see county residents move to take a public vote on the issue, whether as an initiative or to refer an action made by the commissioners. The sentiment was echoed by commissioners Brandon Flanagan and Bob Ewing.

Ewing said he believes property owners are in favor of the bill. 

“Sales tax is probably the fairest tax that we have,” Ewing said. “The people coming and going through our community, like the influx of people we’re going to have in this next month, they help pay for it. So, it’s a win-win for us to take advantage of this half percent. I know that just going to the grocery store, that half percent’s not going to jump out and bite you.” 

Flanagan said he wanted to remind the public and commissioners that the bill is a tax shift, not a tax cut. 

“It’s getting paid one way or the other,” Flanagan said. “The other thing is, a lot of people, and I understand, they want some relief, and they want it now. The ones that own property, the ones that don’t have a different idea. We’re getting emails and phone calls daily that some people want to stomp on the gas and get it done right now, realizing it just became law 30 days ago.”

Flanagan asked the public to, “take a breath” and allow the commission to make informed decisions. 

“I’m cautiously optimistic right now, and things look like they’re heading in the right direction, but some of the emails and some of the stuff you see on social media, people know better than we do, people know better than the state and everybody else. Well, if you want that kind of decision making, then get that kind of decision making,” Flanagan said. “I like to see what I’m doing before I make a decision. I think we’re proceeding down a responsible path. We’ll let somebody else jump out in front of us and take a point until we’re comfortable, and then we’ll get out and do it ourselves.”

The possible ordinance is expected to be placed on the August 11 agenda.

In order for the ordinance to pass, it has to go through a first and second reading and be published in the Black Hills Pioneer. If passed at both readings, the ordinance could go into effect 20 days after the second reading. 

Because the ordinance is not a planning and zoning matter, a public hearing is not required.

title: When you think of gas price impacts, you probably don’t think about pools
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: In preparing the rec center’s budget, Director Jody Westberg is thinking about efficiency and consolidation while maintaining a focus on quality service.
_full_text:
Exterior.JPG
In preparing the rec center’s budget, Director Jody Westberg is thinking about efficiency and consolidation while maintaining a focus on quality service.  

 Pool 1.JPG
Rising fuel prices are bringing up costs at the Belle Fourche Rec Center pool. Pioneer photos by Sierra Ferguson 

BELLE FOURCHE — We all know that when prices go up at the pump, we’ll feel it in more than one corner of our budget. The same is true for the Belle Fourche Rec Center — where fuel prices that might intuitively seem to have little effect on a community pool are a real concern for city staff as they work on a budget for 2027.

Utility costs, for the rec center overall, are projected to increase from approximately $134,000 in 2026 to $155,000 in 2027, according to Belle Fourche Finance Officer Wayne Tonsager.

The pool is heated using a boiler system, so it uses gas. As gas prices soar, so does the cost of running the pool.

“One of the things we get complimented on is the temperature of the pool. It is run at 84 degrees. People love that, especially in the winter, because we are year-round,” Belle Fourche Rec Center Director Jody Westberg said. Tonsager said the city will likely adjust the temperature of both the pool and the building to mitigate the rising cost of heating both the water and the building.

Those cuts may be necessary to keep rec center resources available to the community that uses them.

Just after 9 a.m., the Belle Fourche Rec Center is a bustling place. Folks are gathered at round tables in the lobby, enjoying their morning coffee. A handful of adults are headed to the swimming pool or the gym to get a workout in before the heat of the day sets in.

Throughout the year, and the day, the makeup of patrons and their goals will change. In the fall, the afternoons bring busloads of children to the rec center. The evenings see folks getting off work, attending fitness classes, or heading to the theater to rehearse for a community play.

“I love this comment from Councilman Clark Sowers; he told me the rec center was a gift to the community. We try to be very respectful and responsible about that,” said Westberg. She thinks about the rec center as a resource for the entire community to share.

“I, as a city employee, understand that it is tax dollars that pay for this rec center, that pay our salaries. We are mindful of that, and we are taking care of that,” she said.

Westberg said the rec center has been well cared for in the building’s more-than-30-year lifespan. That’s part of why she brought in experts to help ensure the city is stewarding the center into the next 30 years with just as much care — and an eye on efficiency.

“The rec center came about in 1992; you can tell it’s been cared for. It has been well cared for, because it is an older building. We’re going on 34 years, but even companies we bring in from the outside — for example, we brought in a certified pool operator to teach a course, and he couldn’t believe how well kept this building had been,” Westberg said.

That pool operator trained 11 city staff members to operate and evaluate the pool and improve its functionality.

“That is to make sure that that pump room, our pool, our hot tub are running as efficiently as they can. If not, we can look at what changes we can make to make that happen,” Westberg said.

Right now, the pool’s chlorine tank is located in the rec center pump room.

“When you walk into this building, you know there is a pool. You can smell it,” Westberg said. “We want to move the chlorine tank, which currently sits in the pump room, outside. That is going to help with lots of things. It is going to help with that chlorine smell, but also it is caustic, so that adds wear and tear to the mechanical equipment that is in the pump room, and the mechanical equipment throughout the building. So, getting that outdoors, which we are doing this year as part of our city improvement plan, is going to help keep things, keep the longevity of mechanical items here.”

In 2024, the liner was replaced. In 2027, the waterslide stairs are slated for sandblasting and powder coating to extend their life.

“It is time. There is humidity; it is caustic from some of the chemicals in the environment, and there’s some rust on those steps, and they need to be redone to keep them safe and keep them looking nice,” Westberg said. “We just redid that pool deck; we don’t need rust from the stairs dripping on that deck. The council has already approved that improvement project, so this fall they will be down for about 2 weeks. We won’t have that slide going, but it is going to look gorgeous when we come back.”

Decisions to invest in the pool’s infrastructure are not made lightly. They’re also made with an experienced eye on expenses.  

Westberg took over the rec center in April 2024 — after a 27-year career at Sea World in San Diego. Originally from Whitewood, Westberg moved back to the area to spend quality time with family.

“Time passes very quickly. I still have a grandmother who is alive, and my nieces and nephews were growing up. There were just moments that I didn’t want to miss, so I moved back, and I needed a job,” Westberg said. “Happily, the rec center director position was open, so I have been here the last 2 years.”

Westberg has a lot of experience maintaining aquatic environments. She said frankly, pools are expensive to operate and maintain for everyone.

“It is also one of the most expensive things to run — not just for the city of Belle Fourche. For any building that has a pool, they are expensive. They are costly,” Westberg said. “What I have been committed to doing, because I have a background of 27 years at Sea World in San Diego, I want to make sure that we are being thoughtful and running that pool as efficiently as we can.”

The city has to bring in chemicals to keep the pool clean. Those chemical companies are also passing along price increases to consumers — in this case, the consumer is the city. 

The aquatics department’s utility expenses alone were $32,000 in 2025. They are projected to reach about $42,000 in 2026, with $55,000 budgeted for 2027. Tonsager said the aquatics department represents approximately 42% of the recreation center’s total budget.

For all their costs, pools are also wildly popular. The rec center pool brings in swimmers from around the region that don’t have heated indoor pools — like Spearfish and Whitewood.

“I think there are a lot of different things that bring big appeal,” Westberg said. 

The pool offers swim times exclusively for adults. It hosts water walking classes. It hosts open swim for families and recreators of all ages, along with teen nights for young people to come out and play in the water.

“We do have a lot of lakes and rivers around here: Belle Fourche, beautiful fork. Offering swimming lessons for all ages, from infant to adult, is also important to us,” Westberg said.

title: Trails non-profit tracks major progress, develops new Spearfish trails for users of all stripes
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — The Spearfish Trails Coalition (STC) has a simple aim: to make more epic, accessible trails available to all Spearfish users. That may mean developing new infrastructure or maintaining and improving existing trail systems. In 2025, the non-profit tracked toward that goal, installing 3 trails on Lookout Mountain — 1 half-mile trail, and 2 quarter-mile trails — that connect existing trails to the Sandstone neighborhood. STC also took major steps toward solidifying community partnerships and laid the foundation for a new series of biking and hiking trails in the city campground.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — The Spearfish Trails Coalition (STC) has a simple aim: to make more epic, accessible trails available to all Spearfish users. That may mean developing new infrastructure or maintaining and improving existing trail systems. In 2025, the non-profit tracked toward that goal, installing 3 trails on Lookout Mountain — 1 half-mile trail, and 2 quarter-mile trails — that connect existing trails to the Sandstone neighborhood. STC also took major steps toward solidifying community partnerships and laid the foundation for a new series of biking and hiking trails in the city campground.

STC is a chapter of the International Mountain Bike Association (IMBA).

At its founding, STC developed a detailed master plan, with input from the city, that identified 4 unused or underutilized areas or “zones” where trail development could be beneficial. Those zones are: near the ice rink in city campground, around the city’s existing bike skills part, close to the disc golf course, and on Lookout Mountain.

STC raises the money, hires the designers, pays for construction, and works in partnership with the city to make sure they have the proper permissions and public interest in mind.

Board President Emily Brown and Vice President Kevin Jasper both work at SRAM, a bike components manufacturer with operations in Spearfish, and they care deeply about getting people excited and engaged in outdoor activities — whether that’s hiking, mountain biking, or trail running.

The group decided, early on, they would utilize professional trail design professionals to help execute the project, and leverage connections in the biking and outdoor recreation communities to develop lasting, state-of-the-art trails for the community to enjoy.

“With professionally designed, professionally built trails, you gain things like maintenance,” Jasper said. “They think about water flow. They think about drainage. They think about how the trail is compacted so that it will last longer, which will require less maintenance in the future. For our volunteer group, that’s helpful. While the upfront cost is more than if you tried to do some kind of grassroots build, it ends up being so much better. For us, it saves time, it saves money in the future as well.”

Volunteers with STC wielded rakes, shovels, and mini-excavators — grading red dirt, and lending elbow grease to the development of its Lookout Mountain trails. Those are now open to the public and are receiving quite a bit of use. 

“The trail opening party was our opportunity to have a really public-facing example of the work that has been done behind the scenes,” Brown said. “That was really fun and exciting because it is fun to see your work translate into a trail happening, people using things, translating into something that the community can see. That is our first big unveiling, but so much stuff has been happening behind the scenes.”

A similar grand-opening party is pending for a gravity skills bike area in the city campground between the ice skating rink and the hydro-electric plant. The trails are mostly complete, and crews spent Saturday installing signage to direct cyclists and improve safety on the system. 

“It is what we’re calling a gravity skills area,” Brown said. “You have one trail that you ride up, and then you can ride several trails down.”

Designed to be lappable, or usable over and over again, the gravity skills area will allow cyclists to level up their downhill riding abilities at their own pace.

“One of the surprising things that has been happening over the last year is that, for sure, community members and recreational users are excited, but one way that we can kind of notice the impact that we are making is by other organizations and foundations and things actually reaching out to us to say, ‘Hey, how do we support you? How do we get involved?’” Brown said.

Despite the non-profit’s accomplishments in developing trails for all users, she said the greatest success was reaching the community and making meaningful connections.

“We’re at a point where people are coming to us and asking … how can we support that? That has transpired over the year and kind of snowballed. To me, that is one way to measure the impact that we are having, even outside the cycling community or just the outdoor rec community,” Brown said.

title: Inside the Belle Fourche warehouse  moving 20% of America’s Wool
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Center of the Nation Wool CEO Larry Prager holds a core sample of wool. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Core sample.JPG
Center of the Nation Wool CEO Larry Prager holds a core sample of wool. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

BELLE FOURCHE — Center of the Nation Wool sold 4.2 million pounds of wool last year. On an annual basis, about 20% of the wool in the country moves through the big silver warehouse next to the railroad tracks in downtown Belle Fourche.

However, CEO Larry Prager said that same steel building can be a bit of a mystery to the surrounding community. Yes, Center of the Nation Wool is a warehouse. Between Valentine’s Day and Memorial Day, shearing season, it’s packed to the gills with bales of unprocessed wool.  

But, Center of the Nation Wool is not in the business of storage. The company’s primary purpose is marketing.

“Whether you’ve got 10 sheep or 10,000, the system works the same. We are going to find the spot where your wool can be the most valuable, and we are going to try and sell it into that market,” Prager said.

Producers from all over the region bring their wool, baled, to Center of the Nation Wool. The small but mighty warehouse crew assigns lot numbers, marks the bales, weighs them, and performs a core test.

“I think a lot of people have the idea that they bring wool in and we are going to open it and re-bale and do something magical with it. Nope. The only re-baling we do is when we have to,” Prager said.

Using a tool that resembles an extra-large, hollow-tipped corkscrew, a warehouse worker will stab the fabric-wrapped bales and spit out a perfectly cylindrical sample of the wool inside. That core test can then be sent to a lab — either in Texas or New Zealand — for evaluation.

“Core tells you 3 basic things: average fiber diameter, percentage of clean wool, and percentage of vegetable matter,” Prager said. “A core test does not tell you how uniform the wool is, how well it is prepared, what the length is.”

Those things can be determined in-house.

 Core sampling 1.JPG
Center of the Nation Wool CEO Larry Prager demonstrates core sampling. Pioneer photos by Sierra Ferguson 

 Core sampling.JPG
Center of the Nation Wool CEO Larry Prager demonstrates core sampling. Pioneer photos by Sierra Ferguson 

“When shearing happens, you (the producer) are going to shear the belly first. The belly is short and not so nice, you are going to bring us maybe a bale of bellies,” Prager said. “Then you’re going to have a bale of tags and pieces, whatever you’ve got. We are going to look at every component and put our description on it. How clean it is, how long it is, any of the deciding factors that are going to affect the affordability of it.”

Based on each lot’s marketability, Center of the Nation Wool matches agricultural commodity— wool— with prospective buyers and processors — think woolen mills and spinners.

Things like vegetable matter — think hay, straw, weeds, and burrs — can reduce the value of wool. Color and cleanliness are markers of quality.

Different types of wool — say, fibers that are sheared from a sheep’s belly — have different potential uses.

“The bellies are actually fine, good quality wool, but you have to root out the vegetable matter,” Prager explained. Because wool sheared from bellies can be soft, it can help soften textiles as they’re produced.

The finest wools that come through Center of the Nation wool are generally bound for peacoats and U.S. Military dress uniforms. Prager described the business’s military contract as its “backbone.”

“From the first day I walked in the door, that was a fact. It is still a fact today,” Prager said. He started working at the warehouse in 1978, before it was renamed and incorporated as Center of the Nation Wool in 1984.  “(For the military) it’s got to be quality, fine wool production. Good color, good length.”

The majority of the wool that isn’t eventually made into dress uniforms is processed, spun, and woven or knit into textiles.

Wool is naturally moisture-wicking and antimicrobial, making it ideal for athletic and active wear. In contrast to alternative materials — like polyester and spandex, which are plastic or petroleum-based — wool is also biodegradable and sustainable.

“In today’s world, we have concerns about microplastics. We have a return to the natural fiber industry base, and we have throughout the wool industry today, top to bottom, supply chain driven by performance fabrics,” Prager said.

Long prized for durability and inherent fire-resistance, wool has also taken reputational hits over time. People are concerned that it will be scratchy or unpleasant to wear. In some cases, it can be — a military surplus blanket, for example, doesn’t have a great hand-feel, but not all wool products are that coarse. 

Wool garments and blankets also require different care. The very properties that make it great for crafting textiles also cause wool to shrink in the wash. Wool fibers bind together, felting, when they are agitated. That means most wool is not machine washable.

“We have seen, though, in the last 20 years, technology has developed processes for shrink-resistant wool,” Prager said. “At the end of the day, consumer-friendly items, machine-washable wools, have changed the entire industry.”

Now, very soft “smart wools” are beginning to rehabilitate wool’s appeal.

“Duckworth is a crew out of Montana, a family that runs 5,000 or more (head of sheep), they’ve got a lot, and they basically take their clip and will make it into all the Duckworth products,” Belle Fourche Area Manager Dallin Brady described one of Center of the Nation Wool’s clients. “We are kind of on a cusp. I think a lot more people in the last little bit are thinking about what they are wearing or thinking about what they are eating. Thinking about what goes into what they consume.”

Brady said thoughtful consumption is good for the wool industry.

“This is natural,” Brady said.  “The sheep grow it every year. The people who raise sheep do it in a way that is multi-generational. They love what they do. They are stewards of the land.”

The culture, climate, and even geology of the territory that sends its shearing to the Center of the Nation make the product that comes out of Belle Fourche some of the highest quality in the world, Prager said.

“This territory, the inter-mountain region — western South Dakota, North Dakota, Montana, Wyoming, those are where the good ones are,” Prager said. “We have solid, fine wool genetics. … We’ve got these native grassland places where sheep can run without contamination. They have great color. These hard clay soils just don’t blow, so we have clear wool, better color wool, and lower contamination. We are living pretty well.”

Prager traveled to China with a party of half a dozen American wool warehouse operators on a business trip. The warehousemen met with some of the “big dogs” in global textile production.

“We sit down in a room full of Chinese textile groups,” Prager recalled. “When they found out I was from Belle Fourche, you could see them just turn around and focus on me.”

Prager later learned Belle Fourche had been quietly earning global recognition.

“What had happened over time, is that there had been enough wool going in to China, they found out those (fibers) were the ones that worked. The high-quality wools, the cleaner wools,” Prager said. “Over the last 20 years, Belle Fourche has become a wool type internationally.”

On that world stage, Center of the Nation advocates for the smallest family producers and the large regional sheep operations with equal fervor — it’s a role he and his team take very seriously.

“Growing up, we didn’t have a big ranch, but our rule was, you had to go feed the livestock before you got breakfast. People take care of livestock before they take care of themselves,” Brady said. “Those are our clients, generations of people that do that.”

Since its inception, even before it was incorporated under its current name, the business that became Center of the Nation Wool has focused on and been run by wool producers. What started out as a “wool pool” of producers in the late 1950s and early 1960s to sell and market quality fibers remains a thriving business today, because of that focus, Prager said. Many of Center of the Nation’s stockholders today belong to the families that formed that early cooperative. 

“Our focus as far as marketing has always been what these wools are going to return back at the breakfast table for folks out here on the ranch,” Prager said.

title: Final hand revisited
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Deadwood Alive presented a reenactment of the funeral of Deadwood legend Wild Bill Hickock Monday. The reenactment included a reading of the eulogy by Charlie Utter. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
20260803_121024.jpg
Deadwood Alive presented a reenactment of the funeral of Deadwood legend Wild Bill Hickock Monday. The reenactment included a reading of the eulogy by Charlie Utter. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

DEADWOOD — Deadwood celebrated the life and death of one of the town’s legendary figures Monday with a reenactment of Wild Bill Hickock’s funeral at Outlaw Square. 

A reenactment of the funeral was portrayed by the Deadwood Alive crew, which set the scene with Hickock’s last moments in the Nuttal & Mann’s Saloon. Hickock famously died after being shot in the back by Jack McCall while playing cards.

Ty Sanford, assistant director of the troupe, posed as Hickock’s good friend Charlie Utter and read Hickock’s eulogy at the mock funeral.

“Bill’s death came after a long and harrowing life filled with danger and adventure,” said Sanford. “He never spoke much about his early life, saying only that he was born in Illinois in 1837. He would leave home as a young man looking for adventure and finding it in Nebraska when he had to deal with the McCanleses. Not long after that, the country would be wrenched asunder by a war started in the slaveholding states of the South.”

Sanford detailed Hickock’s service in the Civil War, leading eventually to his time in Missourri and Wyoming before heading to Deadwood in search of gold and fortune with Charlie Utter and Calamity Jane. 

 IMG_0711.JPG
People gathered in Deadwood’s Outlaw Square Monday to celebrate the 150th anniversary of Wild Bill Hickock’s funeral. A reenactment was presented by the Deadwood Alive acting troupe. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

“(Hickock) and I would leave Cheyenne on the wagon train to make a brief stop at Fort Laramie to pick up some people from the post: some miners, a couple of working girls, and a curious and foul specimen of a woman named Martha Jane — though she did insist on being called Calamity Jane,” said Sanford. “She knew how to crack a whip, and she had the mouth of a bullwhacker, that’ for sure. That woman knew how to swear.”

Sanford detailed Hickock’s brief stay in Deadwood, a nearly 2-week-long visit peppered with drinking, gambling, and very little work. 

“I tried setting (Hickock) up with working freight, but he seemed to only want to spend his time in the saloon playing cards,” said Sanford. “Each morning, just before breakfast, he would crawl out of the wagon and clad his shirt, trousers, and boots. He would tie his hair in a knot at the back of his head, shove his big revolver down inside the waistband of his trousers, and run like a sprinter down the gulch to the nearest saloon.”

Sanford closed the ceremony by touching Hickock’s shoulder, saying, “I’ll take care of everything for you, Wild Bill. You don’t have anything to worry about.”

After being exhumed from his first grave in 1878, Hickock was buried at Mount Moriah Cemetery, where he still rests today.

title: Grant program supports tribal food truck operation
byline: By Elena Tittel South Dakota News Watch
description: SIOUX FALLS — A grant program providing funding for community oriented projects is supporting a food truck operation to deliver meals to tribal communities.
_full_text:
SIOUX FALLS — A grant program providing funding for community oriented projects is supporting a food truck operation to deliver meals to tribal communities.

Team Buche Cares - Underdog Foundation, the nonprofit arm of GF Buche Co., aims to serve families in need and offer meaningful change on behalf of the communities they serve. One way they do this is through the Mobile Hunger Hero, a food truck able to deliver a large number of meals to remote locations.

Carrie Sanderson, executive director of Team Buche Cares, said the idea came from an experience CEO and president RF Buche of the GF Buche Co. had 2 years ago. He was feeding about 5,000 children a day at the Pine Ridge Reservation by the end of the summer, which opened his eyes to the need for more accessible food.

“He knew he was going to make his life mission to continue to fight food insecurity across rural and tribal areas,” Sanderson said. “He said, ‘We need a food truck. We need to be able to get a mobile pantry out to the people.’”

Team Buche Cares purchased the Mobile Hunger Hero in 2025 that currently serves about 121 rural and tribal communities across the state. In 2026 alone, there have been 38 food distributions.

Sanderson said as their operation was growing, they recognized a grant was a needed area for them to tell their story and show proof of concept with the Mobile Huger Hero.

Partnering with the Bush Foundation based in St. Paul, Minnesota, South Dakota Community Foundation will award $1.2 million each year for 6 years to eligible nonprofits in South Dakota. This marks the fifth year of the initiative.

The Underdog Foundation was selected as one of 13 nonprofits chosen as a 2025 recipient from a pool of 143 applicants. (South Dakota News Watch received $100,000 for its housing solution stories.)

Ginger Niemann, senior program officer at South Dakota Community Foundation, said the Beyond Idea Grant Program was designed to fund established or early stage projects that are in the process of developing, testing or spreading ideas that can make the region better for everyone.

“Being able to get the food in the hands of those who really need it through a food truck was really an important initiative that the reviewers saw that met all the criteria that the Beyond Idea Grant Program wishes to see,” Niemann said.

Since receiving the grant six months ago, they have been able to improve their tracking systems as well as coordinate outreach and communication regarding when the distributions are occurring.

As of now, Team Buche Cares has been able to complete monthly distributions in addition to holiday meal giveaways. The goal is to continue completing at least one distribution a month.

Food insecurity in South Dakota

According to 2023 Feeding America data, approximately 113,750 people are food insecure in South Dakota, meaning they have limited or unstable access to adequate food, detailed in the graphic below.

People who are food insecure are also more likely to be malnourished, which can lead to early death and numerous adverse health outcomes. 

Native Americans in South Dakota have the highest rate of deaths from avoidable causes in the nation. The 2026 State Health Disparities Report from the Commonwealth Fund found deaths from avoidable causes among Native Americans was 1,089 deaths per 100,000 people. That’s 5 times the rate of white South Dakotans.

Sanderson said that for people living in some of these communities, accessing a grocery store can be difficult. Some people may have to travel long distances to the nearest grocery store, and if there is a lack of transportation, this becomes even harder.

However, even for those who can access a grocery store, they may not have proper ways to store their food or be able to afford healthy options, Sanderson said.

Looking forward, she said they hope to buy an additional truck to further expand distributions within the 9 tribal reservations.

“It’s a fun project to be a part of, and I think the best thing is seeing change every time you’re able to do a food distribution. How grateful people are, and just knowing that access to food will create stronger students, stronger community workers and relieve some burdens on health care and even law enforcement by having access to good food,” Sanderson said.

title: Review: “Whistler” by Ann Patchett
byline: By Terri Schlichenmeyer Special to the Pioneer
description: Courtesy image
_full_text:
Whistler.jpg
Courtesy image 

You were there the whole time.

From the moment you were born, until you were an adult, you were around for every minute of your childhood. It’s not like you could escape it, or erase it, or undo it, it’s not like you made it all up. You were there. But, as in the new novel, “Whistler” by Ann Patchett, what did you miss?

For sure, they were being followed.

Daphne Fuller thought it was creepy that a random old man was following her and her husband around in the Metropolitan Museum of Art. Everywhere they turned, there he stood– as it turned out, for good reason: the elderly man was Daphne’s first stepfather, who recognized her and whom she hadn’t seen in decades. She hadn’t, in fact, thought about Eddie since she was a kid, and there he was, in an accidental, fortuitous meeting. 

Daphne was eager to reconnect.

Back when her mother was married to him, Daphne loved Eddie to bits. She practiced using his last name as her own, telling herself that he was her dad, wishing that he really was her birth father. He was fun, loving, thoughtful, wise, and kind, a publishing-slash-editorial professional who made her love books. And then one day, her mother threw him out and they were divorced – no explanation, no take-backs. 

Daphne and her sister never heard from Eddie again, as if he didn’t exist.

She wondered what happened, but she couldn’t ask and then life interfered. Forty-some years passed, and she couldn’t get enough of him. He was the same Eddie, just older and wiser and, as always, he had things to tell her.

Before the divorce, there’d been a car accident and Daphne’s sister had been sick. Daphne only remembered some of that, and it was nice to know the details. It was even nicer to reconnect with Eddie, and to be his daughter again.

She’d missed him all those years. She “had missed him every day of my life.” 

Bring your tissues?  Eh, not really. “Whistler” – titled after a haunting, misunderstood photograph – is more heartwarming than heartbreaking, but there absolutely will be a few cardio-twinges, never fear.

Mostly, this is a book about love, relationships, skewed childhood memories, and the things we thought we knew but that we couldn’t possibly be more wrong about. It’s a gentle story, simple and tight, with characters you’ll wish were real, though the story may feel slow now and again, especially if you’re used to faster-moving novels. That’s not detrimental, certainly not so much that you’ll want to quit it. It’ll help to know that there’s a bit of timeline play that is confusing, if you’re not aware – but now you are.

If you carry old memories that don’t quite make sense, this novel will ring true and you’ll love it. If you need something gentle with the sweetest of drama for a summer read you’ll likewise devour this book. The hype is true. Find “Whistler,” settle in your best, most comfortable chair, and there you are.

title: The Mercy Sloane Chronicles: Chapter 13
byline: By Eliza Blue A work of serialized fiction, special to the Pioneer
description: “I don’t know what to think of it all,” Mercy told Ardath that night as they sat together on Ardath’s front porch. Mercy had ridden over on the old pony when she’d gotten home from work, Kola on her lap, and she’d not fallen off or even started to fall once. _full_text:
The Mercy Sloane Chronicles

“I don’t know what to think of it all,” Mercy told Ardath that night as they sat together on Ardath’s front porch. Mercy had ridden over on the old pony when she’d gotten home from work, Kola on her lap, and she’d not fallen off or even started to fall once. It helped that riding the pony was like piloting a schooner – the old girl was just as slow to turn and almost as wide–but Mercy was proud of herself nonetheless. She could still get places more easily walking than riding, but that wasn’t going to change unless she practiced.

She’d come because she needed to talk about the day, even though she wasn’t entirely sure what she wanted to say. Ardath was cooking outside, a large pot bubbling over an open fire.

“I hoped you’d stop over,” said Ardath, lifting her spoon with a jolly wave. “I made too much on purpose. I’m not one for gossip, but I’ll admit I’m itching to hear about your first day.”

“Really and truly, I don’t know where to start,” Mercy said, handing Ardath the puppy and then sliding off the pony and landing with only a slightly awkward thud. “Not much happened, and so much happened. I think I must have met every woman that lives in a 50-mile radius, and I can’t remember the name of a single one…well, except Leslie Shaw.”

“Leslie Shaw came in?” said Ardath, so startled she nearly dropped the spoon she’d just picked up again after setting the puppy down. “Well, well, well … that is memorable.”

“But why?” asked Mercy, kneeling by the fire. “That’s the same reaction everyone has had, but no one is saying why. 

Ardath let out a long sigh. “People are too much in each other’s business here, but also sometimes not enough. It’s easy to talk about your neighbors behind closed doors, not so easy to talk to them face-to-face. I think Leslie Shaw reminds everyone of that fact and why it’s a shortcoming.” Ardath eased back heavily on her heels, staring toward the west, where the sun was beginning to set.

Mercy wasn’t one to pry, and when Ardath didn’t say more, she didn’t press her. She knew the story would come out eventually. All those years working in a boarding house had taught her that most secrets don’t keep.

“The strangest thing about today,” Mercy said later while they were eating. “Is how it didn’t feel that strange. I mean, I’m the same me I was in Iowa City, you know, before all this. I’ve been working in shops for years, cleaning up, helping customers. And Marla, and those ladies coming to have a look at me, they’ve all got an idea of who I am, or who I’ll be, but they don’t know anything about me.” She paused, struggling to put her thoughts into words. “They don’t know anything about me except how I got here–and, well, it changes how they see me, but it doesn’t change me. I’m still the same foolish girl who stepped on that train two weeks ago without a care in the world.” Then she stopped again, letting the silence linger like the tall shadows of the grass on the horizon, the breeze whispering softly against her face, wondering if anything she’d just said was true. 

 Eliza Blue TMC
Eliza Blue 

Ardath didn’t interrupt the silence, or rather didn’t interrupt the conversation the prairie was having all around them. The birds singing the last songs of the light and the first songs of the dark, the horses nickering companionably back. The grasses with their own lullabies and stories of the day, the soil warm with the memory of the afternoon heat.

“Maybe I’m not the same!’ Mercy said finally, “Maybe that’s what feels strange. Maybe I don’t know myself either.”

“Ah, Mercy,” said Ardath, resting her chin on her hand, and turning to face the younger woman. “I don’t know, but I’m glad you came, and purely for selfish reasons. You say the quiet things out loud, and keep the loud things to yourself, and that is rare. I’m lucky to have you as a neighbor, and Antelope is lucky to have you.” 

Mercy looked down and blushed. “I feel lucky too,” she said, feeling like she might cry and wondering why. “I AM lucky,” she said again. Then the wind picked up suddenly, rushing through the ash trees, and Mercy had the distinct impression it was offering its agreement.

**

The rest of the week passed uneventfully and might have spilled into another, except that on Friday Mercy received a registered letter, and with it, a chance to see if she was indeed the same girl or not.

title: Costs for Lead’s 150th celebration mostly covered with private funds
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Fourth of July fireworks were the largest display the city has ever had, in honor of the city’s 150th anniversary and the 100th anniversary of the Gold Camp Jubilee Days. On Monday, city officials said the majority of funds from Lead’s 150th anniversary celebration came from private donors and sponsors, city officials said Monday. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
Lead's 150th.jpeg
The Fourth of July fireworks were the largest display the city has ever had, in honor of the city’s 150th anniversary and the 100th anniversary of the Gold Camp Jubilee Days. On Monday, city officials said the majority of funds from Lead’s 150th anniversary celebration came from private donors and sponsors, city officials said Monday. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

LEAD — More than half of the revenue to host Lead’s 150th anniversary celebration came from private donations, grants, and sponsorships, and the city did not spend its entire budget for the event. 

That’s what Lead City Administrator Robin Lucero said Monday when she gave a report about the event during the regular Lead City Commission meeting. The event that was held July 2-5 featured an original play at the Historic Homestake Opera House, a 4-band, day-long concert at Mountain Top Field, a car show, a cornhole tournament, traditional activities in Manuel Brothers Park, a large fireworks display, a vintage baseball game, and more. 

The event has been the subject of scrutiny over the last month, as concerned citizens from a government watchdog group, Checks and Balances by City of Lead Community Friends and Neighbors, have repeatedly asked the city for a complete financial accounting, with all receipts and invoices to be turned over for inspection. 

Lucero said as of Monday, all bills for the event have been received and paid, and she invited citizens from the watchdog group to collect any missing records from city hall. 

Lucero reported that more than half of the budget for the event was derived from private grants, sponsorships, and merchandise and ticket sales. The budget for the event was $184,889 over the course of about 18 months, with planning starting in 2024. Because planning started early, the city started funding the event with $90,000 in bed and booze funds, split across 2 years. 

Lucero said members of the public, business owners, community leaders, and any interested persons were invited to participate in planning meetings that were held on the second Wednesday of the month for 2 years. 

Cash sponsorships, grants, donations, tickets and merchandise sales generated about $94,889, including $56,233 from event sponsors and donations, giving organizers a $184,889 budget, Lucero said. 

However, Lucero said when the final bills for the event came in the city spent a total of $165,524, which was $19,365 less than the budget. 

Additionally, she said the city granted $14,199 more than normal to the Lead Area Chamber of Commerce for extra fireworks, bounce houses, marketing and other items for the festivities. After those expenses, Lucero said the city came out ahead by $5,116. 

The largest expense from the celebration came from the concert at Mountain Top Field, where 4 bands played throughout the day on July 3 with a total cost of $102,722. The concert sold 328 tickets. 

Marketing costs were at $29,544, and merchandise cost about $10,485. Extra picnic tables in the park were covered with a $7,835 grant from Fermilab, Lucero said. An Echoes of Lead concert by Nina McIntire at Lead-Deadwood High School cost the city $7,293; $4,994 went into the vintage baseball game; $2,090 was spent on the patriotic buntings, which were later sold; and $560 went into traffic control expenses. 

Lucero said according to placer.ai reports from Deadwood-Lead Economic Develoment Corporation, the 4-day event drew 33,700 visitors to Lead.

The event contributed to the largest July sales and tourism tax collections Lead has ever seen, Lucero said. 

In July 2026, the city collected $331,454, compared to $207,225 in July 2025, $104,965 in July 2024, $223,841 in 2023, $219,113 in 2022, $163,342 in 2021, and $161,320 in 2020, according to reports from the South Dakota Department of Revenue.  

The event also raised $20,450 in July third penny sales taxes that are charged on restaurant purchases, hotel fees, alcohol sales, and ticket sales for attractions. 

While Lucero said the jump in July sales tax dollars was not solely attributed to the 150th anniversary and Fourth of July celebration, the 4-day event contributed significantly to the business environment in Lead, with many businesses reporting record sales and food vendors running out of product in the park. 

“The bottom line is that we celebrated big, managed costs carefully, and finished with money left over,” Lucero said. “The city invested in a once-in-150 years celebration while keeping a disciplined financial posture. The final story is not ‘we spent money.’ The final story is ‘our 150th celebration was a grand success.’”

title: Sturgis Motorcycle Museum announces  key events for 2026 Rally
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: STURGIS — The Sturgis Motorcycle Museum & Hall of Fame is revving up for an action-packed schedule during the 2026 Rally.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

STURGIS — The Sturgis Motorcycle Museum & Hall of Fame is revving up for an action-packed schedule during the 2026 Rally. 

While the annual Hall of Fame Induction Breakfast remains a cornerstone of the rally, the museum has an expanded lineup of public events, alongside a historic digital broadcast milestone.

Celebrating Women in Motorcycling at the second annual Pearl’s Jam

On Monday, from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., the museum will host Pearl’s Jam. Named in honor of Pearl Hoel, wife of Pappy Hoel and co-founder of the Sturgis Rally, the event celebrates the vital contributions of women in motorcycling.

This year’s Pearl’s Jam recognizes the posthumous induction to the Hall of Fame for 2 legendary female motorcyclists: Bessie Stringfield, the “Motorcycle Queen of Miami” who famously broke racial and gender barriers by riding solo across the U.S. in the 1930s and 40s, and Mary McGee, a pioneering racer who became the first American woman to compete in motorcycle road racing and motocross. The event will also spotlight Florence Emde, the trailblazing matriarch of a multi-generational racing dynasty who features prominently in a new book about her racing champion husband, Floyd Emde.

In addition to historic tributes, attendees will witness the reveal of a custom, specialized piece of art by Dana KT of Metalwood Garage, designed to celebrate the modern experiences of women in the sport. 

Noted motorcycling women will be in attendance throughout the day, including past Pearl Hoel Legacy Award recipients and the 2026 Pearl Hoel Award winner, Heather Callen. 

Named for Pearl Hoel, the Pearl Hoel Legacy Award celebrates people who leave the motorcycle world better than they found it. Heather Callen, the “heart” of the longest running independent motorcycle media outlet, Cycle Source, was recently named the winner of the award for 2026. She has handled almost every task imaginable in the business: editor, photographer, event organizer, production manager, accountant, travel coordinator, television producer and problem solver. She’s the friendly face that’s part of every Cycle Source event.

History in the Making: Free Live Stream of the Hall of Fame Induction Breakfast

For the first time in history, the perennially sold-out Hall of Fame Induction Breakfast will be accessible to fans worldwide. The entire induction ceremony, which takes place in Deadwood on Wednesday will be live streamed at no charge. For those unable to watch live, the video broadcast will remain available for free, on-demand viewing throughout the year. A link to the live stream is on the museum’s website.

Hall of Famers on Main Street for the Inductee Meet & Greet

The celebration continues the day after the HOF breakfast. On Thursday, starting at 11 a.m., the museum will host the popular Inductee Meet & Greet event. This public gathering offers a rare opportunity for rally attendees to meet, chat with, and get autographs from the newly inducted 2026 HOF members alongside returning Hall of Fame legends.

Celebrating the 250th with S&S Cycle Custom Bikes

The S&S Cycle Independence Tour is a showcase of six custom motorcycles built specifically to celebrate 250 years of American independence. The tour makes its Sturgis Rally stop at the Museum from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m. on Aug.14. S&S will spotlight six bikes from the top custom bike builders in the country and is showcasing them on this nationwide tour. 

“The team here at the museum continues to seek more opportunities to connect the Museum with riders around the country,” said Executive Director Heidi Haro. “Pearl’s Jam, the Meet & Greet with inductees and the Hall of Fame live stream are celebrations of the special things that the museum offers to the riding community.”
