title: Changing the conversation about substance use disorder
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Angela Kennecke, founder of Emily’s Hope, distributed more than 500 Naloxone kits during Sturgis Motorcycle Rally last year in remembrance of her daughter. This year, she said she hopes to distribute at least that many. Photo courtesy of Emily’s Hope
_full_text:
Emily_s Hope Naloxone Kits.jpeg
Angela Kennecke, founder of Emily’s Hope, distributed more than 500 Naloxone kits during Sturgis Motorcycle Rally last year in remembrance of her daughter. This year, she said she hopes to distribute at least that many. Photo courtesy of Emily’s Hope 

SIOUX FALLS — After the tragic death of Angela Kennecke’s daughter, Emily, to accidental fentanyl poisoning, Kennecke made it her mission to save lives through research-based prevention and education about substance abuse disorders, the dangers of opiates, and removing financial barriers and stigma for treatment and recovery. In 2026, that mission means expanding the number of Naloxone kits across the state and debuting a high school prevention and education curriculum.

Kennecke, who worked for KELO-TV for 33 years as an anchor and investigative reporter, said her journey began on May 16, 2018, when her daughter accidentally overdosed on heroin laced with fentanyl. Kennecke took a few months off from work for bereavement leave before announcing her daughter’s death on television and launching Emily’s Hope.

“I named my daughter after Emily Dickinson, after her poem, ‘Hope is the Thing with Feathers,’” said Kennecke. “I never gave up hope on my daughter. Even after you lose somebody, you can still find hope.”

Kennecke started raising funds for a fund at the Avera Care Center almost immediately after her daughter died. Since then, the organization has raised more than $500,000 in treatment scholarships that have been given to more than 300 people to the center. 

Kennecke said one thing that has always stood out to her is the impact a special she did for KELO on methamphetamine had on Emily when she was in third grade.

“We showed her the before and after photos of people who used meth, we talked to people whose lives had been ruined or even ended because of meth, and (Emily) was always anti-meth,” Kennecke said. “That really sunk in. That really left an impression on her. She didn’t get the whole story, though. Even though she was a poster child for D.A.R.E., she started with marijuana and Xanax and eventually she moved onto harder drugs.”

Knowing that prevention with youth starts with education at a young age, Kennecke gathered a panel of experts (teachers, addiction counselors, professors, medical doctors, and school counselors) to create a K-12 curriculum that can be taught in schools by professionals the children are already familiar with — a school counselor, nurse, or instructor.

“We start in kindergarten with 4 lessons, and we work our way up,” she said. “We have 7 lessons in second grade and 8 lessons in third grade. It’s a very engaging curriculum. It’s got characters, we have books, animations, and each lesson has activities. They learn about their bodies and their brains, how to protect their bodies and their brains and what substances do to their brains. And there’s no scare tactics, it’s all very age appropriate. It’s science-based learning using multimedia tools.”

In elementary classrooms, the curriculum focuses on brain health, emotions, and being able to identify the difference between candy and prescription drugs. By middle school, students are learning about peer pressure, the risks of substance abuse, and the permanent effects on the body and brain early addiction can have on young people’s lives.

Kennecke said the curriculum has been taught to more than 30,000 students from Kindergarten to middle school in 6 states and Uganda and includes children’s books for elementary students and graphic novels for middle school students. Her surviving daughter, Abby Groth, attended Minneapolis College of Art and Design and has partnered with Kennecke as the illustrator. 

“She has done the character development and all of the illustrations,” Kennecke said. “It’s been really kind of cool to use that family connection and provide her with something that she could do in the wake of her sister’s death.”

This year, Emily’s Hope is launching its high school curriculum, which Kennecke described as more “project based.” The curriculum invites students to get involved in research and advocacy with their peers and communities. Kennecke said Emily’s Hope has received $500,000 grant from the South Dakota Department of Social Services opioid prevention funds to help make the curriculum free for schools across South Dakota. 

“We will be identifying schools that want the curriculum with the help of the prevention resource centers,” she said, “We’ll help launch it and get schools connected, then the state will reimburse us those costs. We do a lot of research and outreach with the Department of Social Services, and this will help us do more for those schools.”

Naloxone kits

Alongside education and treatment, part of saving lives is slowing down an overdose while waiting for emergency services arrive. Kennecke said those prevention measures happen by getting a naloxone kit into the hands of everyone who wants one and making them readily available in public spaces. 

Naloxone, the generic form of Narcan, is an opioid antagonist. If a person comes across an individual they believe might be suffering from an opioid overdose, the drug can be administered as an inhalant, one puff in the victim’s nostril. The drug binds with opioid receptors in the brain, blocking the effects of opioids. 

The naloxone kits assembled by Emily’s Hope are enclosed in a pencil box and contain 2 doses of the drug, a glove, instructions detailing how to administer the drug, and a card with resources for getting help with treatment and recovery.

Since May 2025, Kennecke said Emily’s Hope has distributed 17,000 naloxone kits across the state. During Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, Emily’s Hope partnered with Action for the Betterment of our Community, a treatment center in Sturgis, distributing 500 kits to tattoo shops, bars, and restaurants, and the armory. Kennecke said she hopes to distribute at least that many this year. 

“We also provide naloxone kits for people to put by their defibrillators,” she said. “We’d like to see naloxone kits at every defibrillator out there, make them just as common as a fire extinguisher.” 

Kennecke said Emily’s Hope is working with the Department of Social Services to continue distribution efforts with the hopes of expanding the number of kits they can distribute while also keeping known distribution sites, such as the armory in Strugis, stocked with effective kits.

“There’s an expiration date on these kits and we want to be able to replenish people’s supply,” she said. “Most overdoses, close to 90% of them, happen in residences. We want to be able to keep people supplied so they can have them in their homes, and we want them to have one that’s up to date and not outdated.”

Kennecke said the kits her team has distributed don’t expire for a “few more years,” but efforts to restock those supplies have to start now.

Kennecke said current opioid analogs, such as Nitazenes, are up to 40 times more powerful than fentanyl and can require up to 6 doses of naloxone to completely stop an overdose. Knowing that, she still encourages people to take only one kit. 

“That’s why it’s important to get emergency medical personnel there right away,” Kennecke said. “You may not have enough naloxone, if it’s truly a nitazine. It wears off and that person can start overdosing again. You don’t necessarily know if they’re ok. You want to get them medical attention right away. This is just something that can keep somebody alive until medical personnel can get there. That’s clear on all of the instructions for the kits.”

Turning a personal tragedy into a message of hope

Kennecke said she’s grateful for all of the help that she’s received from people who have gathered around her to help save lives, spread awareness, and improve education about substance use disorders. 

“It’s not easy taking a personal tragedy and trying to create purpose out of it, but I’m really glad that I’ve done that,” she said. “I know that Emily’s Hope has saved lives in Emily’s name, and I know that her death wasn’t in vain.”

Kennecke said the support she’s received from the people around her have been life changing — not just for her, but for thousands of people who have received help from Emily’s Hope. 

“I think we’ve changed the conversation surrounding substance use disorder in South Dakota, and I think we’ve made parents and students aware of the hidden dangers of fake pills and about fentanyl and overdoses,” she said. “I think it’s made a really big difference, and nothing has helped me more than helping other people.”

title: Breaking ground in TIF 9: Stone Ridge Commons to offer 94 rental units at 80% AMI
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Below-market rate housing, like the 94-units planned at Stone Ridge Commons in Spearfish, is intended to supply the “missing middle” — Spearfish’s workforce and Black Hills University students — with a place to live. Representatives from the city, Black Hills Community Foundation, and Lloyd Companies were present for a groundbreaking ceremony off of Paramount Drive, Tuesday. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Ground Breaking 1.JPG
Below-market rate housing, like the 94-units planned at Stone Ridge Commons in Spearfish, is intended to supply the “missing middle” — Spearfish’s workforce and Black Hills University students — with a place to live. Representatives from the city, Black Hills Community Foundation, and Lloyd Companies were present for a groundbreaking ceremony off of Paramount Drive, Tuesday. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

 Ground Breaking 2.JPG
Greg Litton, the director of strategic housing for the Black Hills Community foundation speaks to the need for housing in Spearfish on the site where Stone Ridge Commons will be built. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — On Tuesday, Lloyd Companies broke ground on a 94-unit multi-family housing development, Stone Ridge Commons, in Tax Increment Finance District 9 — along Paramount Drive, west of the Holiday Inn and Convention Center in Spearfish.

The 94 rental units will be distributed across 5 buildings — some will be townhome-style with attached garages. Others will be flat-style apartments.

“Barring the fact that we are standing next to condos, most of our Black Hills communities either have single-family housing units or traditional multi-family apartment buildings with a hallway down the middle and units on each side,” said Greg Litton, the director of strategic housing at Black Hills Area Community Foundation, at the ground-breaking ceremony Tuesday. “What we often don’t see, and we don’t get, is what is known as missing middle housing. We don’t get structures like townhomes and condos. This specific development will be a mixture of townhomes and flat-style condo units. Those things are demanded and requested in basically every community that we work in.”

The units will be offered for rent at 80% of area median income, and prospective tenants will not need to meet income qualifications.

“The ability for us to come together and do the things that we are doing today matters. If we think about the folks in our community, whether that is nurses, teachers, educators, first responders, those folks are being priced out of our communities,” Litton said.

Kory Menken, the executive director of the Spearfish Economic Development Corporation, said attainable housing keeps the community running.

“It has been a real challenge in our community, and it is not just our existing businesses. We hear it from young professionals, our Black Hills State University graduates, but we also hear from new companies looking to come in that it has been a deterrent,” Menken said. “It concerns us, and it is really frustrating and disappointing when some of our largest employers told us they’ve lost candidates that have been great and would have been great for our community, because they couldn’t find acceptable housing in our community.”

Housing at Stone Ridge Commons will also be available to college students.

“A lot of affordable housing programs in our state are restricted, and they are not available to college students,” Litton said. “This type of facility, specifically in a community like Spearfish and Black Hills State University being here, is going to matter a lot for those people that come here to gain higher education. … If we can’t support our students and they can’t afford to live here, they’re not going to come to college here.”

Lloyd Companies used a number of funding mechanisms to offer below-market rate housing at Stone Ridge Commons.

“This specific project is made possible with support from a TIF from Spearfish, housing infrastructure financing dollars from the state of South Dakota, and our strategic housing initiative with support from the South Dakota Ellsworth Housing Authority and the local Spearfish Advisory Board that we collaborate with in town,” Litton said.

In April, the Spearfish City Council approved the establishment of TIF 9.

Tax increment financing is a public financing system that uses future increases in property taxes to reimburse the costs of public improvements built within a designated TIF boundary. The value of all the properties inside the district is assessed or calculated, and the total amount of property tax generated by all those properties is noted — the base amount of property tax revenues. All property revenue above this base amount, for the life of the TIF, is captured by the TIF to refund the costs of the public improvements or project. This amount — the amount over the base — is called the “tax increment.” Over time, property values are presumed to increase in part due to infrastructure improvements brought about by the TIF project itself. When the TIF is retired, the total taxation values revert to the original taxing entities.

The maximum amount of reimbursement the developer is eligible to receive as they build that apartment complex is $3,233,053.

“What I like to point out is not simply a social issue: housing is infrastructure. When built responsibly, it will strengthen and update the infrastructure in all of our communities. Housing is also quality of life. It builds families, communities, and shared experience. Housing is workforce development both currently and in the future,” Litton said.

title: Quick picks: Revved up for Rally
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
MotocycleRoad.jpg
Courtesy photo 

The bikes are back in town for the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. That’s why, this week, we’ve got a round-up of Rally-ready reads for both motorcycle enthusiasts and curious readers who’ve never ventured onto the saddle of a bike. 

1. “Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance” by Robert M. Pirsig

Genre: Philosophy

Robert M. Pirsig’s “Zen & the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance” is an examination of how we live, a meditation on how to live better set around the narration of a summer motorcycle trip across America’s Northwest, undertaken by a father and his young son.

2. “The Bikeriders” by Danny Lyon 

Genre: Photography

In 1965, Danny Lyon, a 23-year-old veteran of the Southern civil rights movement, joined the Chicago Outlaw Motorcycle Club. Riding a 650-cc Triumph and shooting with a Nikon Reflex and a Rolleiflex, he produced one of the seminal books of the 1960s: “The Bikeriders.” This work of realism read like fiction and presented a world as dangerous and romantic as the one depicted in films such as Easy Rider - released a year after the publication of “The Bikeriders.” Recognized as a powerful work of photodocumentary, “The Bikeriders” helped sear the counterculture into the American mind.

3. “Let’s Ride: Sonny Barger’s Guide to Motorcycling”

Genre: Nonfiction

One of the founders and the most famous member of the infamous Hell’s Angels Motorcycle Club, Ralph “Sonny” Barger says, “Let’s Ride” with this ultimate guide to motorcycling. With expert co-author Darwin Holmstrom — former writer for Motorcyclist magazine and author of The Complete Idiot’s Guide to Motorcycles — Barger, “The archangel of all Hells Angels” (New York Post) is ready to take you on the ride of your life with this exhilarating and practical nuts-and-bolts master class in the fine art of freedom.

4. “Hell’s Angels” by Hunter S. Thompson 

Genre: Nonfiction

“California, Labor Day weekend . . . early, with ocean fog still in the streets, outlaw motorcyclists wearing chains, shades and greasy Levis roll out from damp garages, all-night for the Monterey peninsula, north of Big Sur. … The Menace is loose again.”

Thus begins Hunter S. Thompson’s vivid account of his experiences with California’s most notorious motorcycle gang, the Hell’s Angels. In the mid-1960s, Thompson spent almost two years living with the controversial Angels, cycling up and down the coast, reveling in the anarchic spirit of their clan, and, as befits their name, raising hell.

5. “Race to Dakar” by Chalrey Boorman with forward by Ewan McGreggor

Genre: Travel/Nonfiction

 In January 2006, 230 people raced in trucks, cars, and motorbikes from Lisbon to Dakar in the 28th annual Dakar rally — the most challenging race in existence. Taking part was a team of three bikers — Matt Hall, Simon Pavey, and actor and bike nut Charley Boorman. After his celebrated trip round the world with Ewan McGregor, documented in Long Way Round , Charley was keen for another challenge. Racing in the Dakar had always been a dream of his, and so it was the obvious choice for a new adventure.

6. “Lone Rider: The First British Woman to Motorcycle Around the World” by Elspeth Beard

Genre: Nonfiction/Travel 

In 1982, at the age of just 23 and halfway through her architecture studies, Elspeth Beard left her family and friends in London and set off on a 35,000-mile solo adventure around the world on her 1974 BMW R60/6.

title: Deadwood approves platting and zoning requests in preparation to relocate 5 historic structures
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: A section of land near Deadwood Hospital has been rezoned from commercial to R-1 in preparation for 5 historic structures to move from Lower Main Street to Charles Street. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
Deadwood approves platting and zoning requests in preparation to relocate 5 historic structures.jpg
A section of land near Deadwood Hospital has been rezoned from commercial to R-1 in preparation for 5 historic structures to move from Lower Main Street to Charles Street. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

DEADWOOD — In preparation for the move of 3 historic homes from Lower Main Street to Charles Street, Deadwood city commissioners approved a platting and zoning request for a section of land near Deadwood Hospital.

Kevin Kuchenbecker, director of planning and zoning, said the boundaries of the land were redefined to allow for 3 single-family residential lots. Since approved, the lots will accommodate the 3 homes, one with an attached garage and 2 with detached garages, currently located at 306, 308, 388, and 390 1/2 Main St.

The properties, previously known as the “Deadwood Cottages” and the Auer House, have served as short-term rentals until they were purchased by Optima, LLC., an affiliate of Liv Hospitality in Rapid City. The hospitality management company owns Cadillac Jack’s Gaming Resort and Tin Lizzie Gaming Resort. 

After approving the platting request, commissioners approved a request to rezone the section of land on Charles Street from commercial to R-1 residential. According to city ordinances, R-1 can be used for multi-family dwellings, bed and breakfasts, and house museums by conditional use only, requiring a permit approved by planning and zoning and city commissioners. Approved uses by right in the area are limited to small day cares serving 5 or less children, single-family homes, gas distribution lines, parks and recreation lands, and wildlife preserves. 

The zoning is contiguous to the R-1 zone to the south of the property.

Commissioner Sharon Martinisko thanked Austin Burnham, vice president of operations for the Northern Hills for Liv Hospitality, for agreeing to change the zoning to R-1. 

“We are looking at expanding R-1 to keep our housing stock secure and our vacation rentals at a minimum,” said Martinisko. “And so, this is huge. This is important, for us to continue to expand that R-1 zone.”

Kuchenbecker said deed restrictions will be put in place on the historic homes after the move, requiring the residences to be sold as single-family and prohibiting them from being used as short-term rentals. 

The structures are expected to move to their new foundations this fall.

title: ‘A race against time  through the Black Hills’
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: “Black Road” is the third Mackay’s Justice novel by Spearfish native M.J. Witt. Courtesy image
_full_text:
Black Road Cover.jpg
“Black Road” is the third Mackay’s Justice novel by Spearfish native M.J. Witt. Courtesy image 

SPEARFISH — U.S. Deputy Marshall William Mackay returns home to celebrate 150 years of his family’s Montana ranch, when duty calls, and he’s asked to track down an escaped federal witness who authorities believe may be in Sturgis for the Rally.

“As often happens during the bike Rally, in real life, there is a call put out for any law enforcement officers that want to help with enforcement at the Rally; there are special task forces set up to focus on particular areas and that sort of thing,” said author M.J. Witt. “It is sort of uncovered that there is an escaped witness that has a federal witness that was under witness protection, and he sort of slips his halter and takes off and does a runner. They think he may be at the Rally. They try to find this witness, because this witness has a contract out on his life, so they want to catch him before the killers do.”

Witt used his personal experience with the Rally, growing up in the Northern Hills, as inspiration for his rancher/Marshall main character’s August adventure.

“It was a really fun book to write, because it allowed me to, being from Spearfish and growing up in the Black Hills, it gave me a chance to circle back and mention a lot of businesses and locations, favorite haunts of mine and all across Sturgis and Deadwood and Spearfish all the way south to Edgemont,” Witt said. 

In high school, Witt worked for vendors during the Rally — selling hot dogs and burgers one year and t-shirts and other apparel the next.

“It is such a colorful carnival of anything and everything that you can think of,” Witt said. “Whether it is related to bikes or not, it comes through with the half a million visitors or more that come in for those 2-3 weeks. I’ve always enjoyed it.”

Mackay said he relished throwing Mackay into the Rally mix in this novel.

“He’s spent 25 years as a deputy in the US Marshal Service,” Witt said of his main character. “Day to day they (US Marshals) do anything they can cover everything from protecting witnesses, protecting federal judges and fugitives, to prison security and escapes. It provides a wide line of options and possibilities. That provides for more of the episodic nature of it, because it gives the backdrop. While the backdrop is Montana and this rural life, you have this explorative avenue with the chasing bad guys and the daily actions the Marshal’s service takes.”

Witt said he’s been thinking about Witt as a complete character for a long time, and he’s hoping to add texture and development in the law enforcement officer’s life and personality as the books progress.

“Before I started writing, I sat down and wrote the whole backstory for the family and the ranch and the character himself to give me a sense of where he was starting, but I didn’t have a clear vision of where I wanted him to go,” Witt said. “I think character growth is important, and one of the challenges in writing an action thriller novel like this is, as a writer, you want your main character to be a heroic figure in some ways. It is very easy to build them as the perfect hero with no flaws. How do you introduce flaws that make him real, rather than a cookie-cutter comic book hero?”

In “Black Road,” Witt must grapple with the challenge of assembling and managing a team — along with ever-complicated personal relationships.

On the ranch, Witt’s family is working to protect the mineral rights they’ve held for generations.

Witt’s ranch background is also informed by Witt’s personal experience on family ranches. The ranching aspect of the novel also places “Black Road” into the broader context of popular modern westerns.

“It is a hard life, but I think it provides a sort of rural western tableau that a lot of modern westerns that we’ve seen are why they’ve drawn interest,” Witt said. “You’re looking at Yellowstone and Longmire and the Joe Pickett series. There are a lot of modern westerns coming out that people are connecting with.”

“Black Road” was released on May 26.

title: BHSU to host 14th annual Ride for Veterans
description: Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Jacket Ride.JPG
Pioneer file photo 

SPEARFISH — Black Hills State University invites motorcyclists and supporters to take part in the 14th annual BHSU Jacket Ride for Veterans, benefiting scholarships for student veterans during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally.

The 2026 Jacket Ride for Veterans will be held Tuesday, Aug. 11. Registration begins at 8:30 a.m. at the Joy Center on the BHSU campus, with kickstands up at 10 a.m.

“This is a great way to give back to our student veterans,” said Kanda Guthmiller, scholarship director for the BHSU Foundation. “We are a very military-friendly school, and this is one of many ways we support our veterans here on campus.”

Escorted by the American Legion Riders of the Black Hills and the Iron Horse Clan of Hot Springs, riders will travel through Spearfish Canyon to Lead and Nemo before heading down Vanocker Canyon and finishing at Wareing Motors in Sturgis.

This year’s ride marshals are Jared “Cappie” Capp and Alex “Sprout” Headley from Magnolia Network’s hit TV series Building Outside the Lines. In celebration of America’s 250th anniversary, special guest participants will include Purple Heart recipients and a World War II vehicle. A catered lunch by Catering by Dave will be served at the dealership.

Registration is $50 for a single rider and $75 for a rider and passenger. Registration includes lunch, a T-shirt, and door prize entry. All proceeds support scholarships for veteran students at BHSU.

Guthmiller said that thanks to sponsors Lowe Roofing, the Black Hills Pioneer, and Wareing Motors, all event costs — including the ride, meal, and t-shirts — are fully covered, meaning 100% of rider registration funds go directly toward veteran scholarships.

“Group rides are so much fun,” Guthmiller said. “You’re with friends, enjoying the camaraderie. We have many returning riders and make new friends every year.”

In 2025, 46 book scholarships totaling $7,425 were awarded to BHSU student veterans through support from Jacket Ride participants. Since its inception, the event has raised more than $56,000 in scholarships.

For more information or to register, visit www.BHSU.edu/JacketRide or contact Guthmiller at (605) 642-6335 or Kanda.Guthmiller@BHSU.edu.

title: Cops on campus: BHSU strikes deal with Spearfish PD for security support
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Last year, the state legislature passed a bill to allow concealed carry on college campuses. In response, BHSU would like to fortify security with the help of a police officer. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Campus alt.JPG
Last year, the state legislature passed a bill to allow concealed carry on college campuses. In response, BHSU would like to fortify security with the help of a police officer. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — The state legislature took steps to allow guns on campus. Monday, the Spearfish City Council unanimously approved an agreement with Black Hills State University to retain an officer on campus in response.

Senate Bill 100 allows anyone on a college campus to lawfully carry a concealed weapon and appropriate ammunition as long as they hold an enhanced permit, a restricted enhanced permit, or a reciprocal permit. The new law also allows the carrying of stun guns and pepper spray, mace, or other chemical irritants. 

Corey Compton the director of public safety at BHSU and Spearfish Police Chief Collin Smith have worked together on an agreement that will furnish the university with a campus officer (CO) to help manage and fortify security for the next 3 years.

“What we are trying to build here is an atmosphere where teachers feel safe to teach, and students feel safe to learn,” said Spearfish Police Chief Collin Smith.

Smith presented the agreement between BHSU and the city to the Spearfish City Council on Monday.

BHSU agreed to pay for the wages, health benefits, and equipment for one police officer — who will remain an employee of the Spearfish Police Department. The total estimated cost of the CO’s equipment is $14,658.

“Anything above that is paid for by the city, so overtime or if there is a family plan that’s needed for a health plan,” Smith said. “The idea there would be hopefully that CO can flex that time. You know, if they know they need to be in for a football game, they can flex that time, but in law enforcement you have to pick up some OT.”

The officer will respond to and handle criminal offenses and matters of public safety. Violations of BHSU policy will not be handled by the CO.

“They will also be held to the same standard of FERPA (the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act),” Smith said. “All of the same language that’s in our contract and agreement with K through 12 is applied here.”

Like a school resource officer (SRO), the CO will maintain a presence on campus beyond their response to crime. 

“Not only will they be there on campus, but we want them involved on campus: putting on classes and presentations, programs, things of that nature that are towards students and building those relationships with students and staff alike,” Smith said.

The agreement will sunset after 3 years.

“They (BHSU security) are entertaining the idea of trying to become law enforcement. That being said, that is a long road, and there are a lot of things that come along with that. So, these 3 years will help determine if that is feasible for Black Hills State,” Smith said. 

That officer will not be a new hire, Smith added.

“It will be a more seasoned officer, if you will, so that we have some things in place on our end. It won’t be just a 6-month officer fresh out of the academy,” Smith said. “We want somebody there that knows the city, knows that campus, and has all of the right training in place to be able to react.”

Unlike a school resource officer, who is posted at a K-12 school during the school year and on patrol in the summer, the CO will be on campus at BHSU year-round.

“Do you have somebody in mind for this position?” Councilman Scott Hourigan asked Smith. “We’re taking a police officer from our patrolling officers to use for this position, correct?”

“Correct. In a sense (it creates another vacancy). What we are really banking on, too, is we are having a really good push now for recruitment,” Smith said.

In the meantime, Spearfish Police are planning on a schedule that reflects the addition of a CO for BHSU.  

“We have our schedule built in preparation for the absence of that officer from the patrol level,” Smith said.

title: How SD hospitals fared in the latest quality ratings
byline: Bart Pfankuch South Dakota News Watch
description: Two hospitals in South Dakota were rated “below average” in 2026 based on a regular review of patient care and medical outcome benchmarks set by the federal government.
_full_text:
Two hospitals in South Dakota were rated “below average” in 2026 based on a regular review of patient care and medical outcome benchmarks set by the federal government.

 2024-4-17 Monument Health signage.JPG

 2026-02-03 Avera St. Luke_s Aberdeen.jpeg
Avera St. Luke’s Hospital, shown Feb. 3, 2026, in Aberdeen, S.D., received a 4-star rating in 2026 from the U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services. Courtesy photo 

 Avera-St.-Mary-s-in-Pierre-from-FB-1.jpg
Avera St. Mary’s Hospital is the primary health care provider in Pierre, S.D. Photo courtesy of  Avera St. Mary’s Facebook page 

But those poor results were far from the norm, as most hospitals statewide received average or better grades in the annual Overall Hospital Quality Star Ratings determined by the U.S. Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS).

The ratings range from 1 star on the low end to 5 stars at the top and are based on categories including mortality, safety of care, readmission, patient experiences and timely and effective care.

The 2 South Dakota hospitals rated 2 stars in 2026 were Avera St. Mary’s in Pierre and Huron Regional Medical Center. Both had some positive and negative findings in their overall reviews, but they had lower-than-average recommendation rates by patients.

Five hospitals received top 5-star marks in 2026, up from three last year.

Tim Rave, CEO of the South Dakota Association of Healthcare Organizations, called the ratings “an important benchmark” and added they are far from the only metric hospitals and the public should use to evaluate the quality of patient care.

“While the overall star rating provides helpful information for consumers, hospital leaders rely on much more detailed data to identify opportunities for improvement and ensure they are providing safe, high-quality care,” Rave said in an email to News Watch.

Here is a look at how each South Dakota hospital that was rated fared in 2026, with the 2025 Star Rating included in parentheses where applicable.

5 stars (much above average):

Avera Heart Hospital, Sioux Falls (5 stars in 2025)
Avera St. Benedict Health Center, Parkston (no rating in 2025)
Sanford USD Medical Center, Sioux Falls (4 stars in 2025)
VA Medical Center, Sioux Falls (5 stars in 2025)
VA Healthcare System, Sturgis (4 stars in 2025)

4 stars (above average):

Avera McKenna H/UMC, Sioux Falls (3 stars in 2025)
Avera Queen of Peace, Mitchell (no rating in 2025)
Avera St. Luke’s, Aberdeen (5 stars in 2025)
Brookings Health System, Brookings (4 stars in 2025)
Monument Health, Spearfish (no rating in 2025)
Sanford Medical Center, Aberdeen (4 stars in 2025)

3 stars (average):

Avera Sacred Heart, Yankton (4 stars in 2025)
Monument Health, Rapid City (4 stars in 2025)
Prairie Lakes Healthcare, Watertown (4 stars in 2025)

2 stars (below average):

Avera St. Mary’s, Pierre (3 stars in 2025)
Huron Regional MC, Huron (no rating in 2025)

1 star (much below average):

No South Dakota hospital at this rating

Cale Feller, director of corporate communications for Avera Health said the CMS ratings use data from as far back as 2021 and there is a slim margin between star rating levels.

“Avera’s commitment to deliver safe, effective and compassionate care remains steadfast,” Feller wrote to News Watch in an email.

Monument Health representatives said they have taken numerous steps toward improving patient care and outcomes at Rapid City Hospital, which raised its star rating from a 1 in 2023 to a 4 in 2025. The Rapid City hospital fell to a 3-star rating this year.

“Many of our quality outcomes remain strong and continue to improve,” Melissa Haught, director of communications at Monument Health, wrote to News Watch in an email.

Both Feller and Haught said their health systems have used the CMS ratings as motivation to improve, and that both systems took specific actions to improve patient care and potentially boost future ratings.

Destiny Price, chief operating officer at Huron Regional, said the independent hospital voluntarily entered into the CMS evaluation system last year.

“We recognized the value of being transparent to identify where we’re not hitting all the targets so we can start working on those things,” Price said.

For example, before the 2-star rating was announced, leaders of the 25-bed hospital recognized issues in sepsis care and took steps to minimize infections and improve outcomes, Price said.

Huron Regional has also created a multi-disciplinary team that meets daily with each hospitalized patient, added a chronic care nurse and community health worker, and has a renovated birthing center and a new robot to aid in orthopedic surgeries.

“The quality of care we deliver now is not reflected in the rating,” she said.

title: Wildfire veterans fear federal tactics, extreme fires could put crews at risk
byline: By Alex Brown Stateline
description: Longtime firefighters are questioning the “full suppression” directive ordered before the beginning of this year’s fire season. Pictured here, a slurry bomber drops a load on the 2016 Crow Peak Fire. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Wildfire veterans fear federal tactics, extreme fires could put crews at risk.JPG
Longtime firefighters are questioning the “full suppression” directive ordered before the beginning of this year’s fire season. Pictured here, a slurry bomber drops a load on the 2016 Crow Peak Fire. Pioneer file photo 

 Wildfire veterans fear federal tactics, extreme fires could put crews at risk 2.jpg
Fire crews clean up hot spots from the 2016 Crow Peak Fire. Veteran firefighters are questioning this year’s “full suppression” directive. Pioneer file photo 

As millions of acres burn across the western United States, some wildland fire veterans are fearful that aggressive fire suppression tactics ordered by the Trump administration — coupled with extreme, fast-moving blazes — could put firefighters in danger as conditions escalate this month. 

Those extreme weather conditions fueled disaster in Eastern Washington Saturday when a fast-moving wildfire jumped the Spokane River and swept through neighborhoods of Spokane, destroying more than 600 structures and forcing 60,000 residents to evacuate. Incident Commander Tom Clemo called the blaze “probably the largest, most destructive fire in Washington’s history.” 

No deaths have yet been reported in Spokane, but Mayor Lisa Brown told local journalists the city is “still assessing the potential for lives to be lost.”

“There is not a fire department in the U.S. that can handle a wind-driven event this size,” said Spokane Assistant Fire Chief Lance Dahl to the Spokane Spokesman-Review. 

Leading up to this year’s fire season, federal officials with the U.S. Forest Service and the Interior Department directed their wildfire crews to use a “full suppression” strategy and attack wildfires urgently. Following a hot, dry winter that left much of the West parched, federal land managers said it was imperative to contain fires quickly before they get out of control.

But following several dangerous incidents, including the deaths of four federal firefighters in Colorado in June, some longtime wildland fire leaders are questioning that strategy. Many see it as a return to the Forest Service’s decades-old “10 a.m.” policy, which sought to suppress all fires by the morning after they were reported. 

While many states also adhere to “full suppression” policies that aim to keep blazes contained, federal officials have previously had more discretion to let fires burn under supervision if they’re not threatening communities. More concerning, wildfire veterans say, is the possibility that rhetoric from Trump administration officials is putting pressure on fire crews to use aggressive tactics to meet those suppression goals.   

Federal policies that sought to extinguish all fires quickly over much of the past century are now understood by foresters to be a major contributor to the current wildfire crisis. In many places, forests that used to experience fire at regular intervals have grown denser than historical norms, with trees competing for water and thick underbrush covering the forest floor. That gives fuel to the fires and contributes to fast-moving blazes.

“No one in the agencies have said it, but it sure looks like (a return to the 10 a.m. policy) when you read the directions,” said Jane Darnell, a wildfire veteran who spent more than 30 years with the Forest Service before retiring in 2020. “We lived with the 10 a.m. policy for 100 years, and we got here. This full suppression promise to the public is a promise that can’t be kept.”

Many wildfire leaders say they’ve seen extreme, unprecedented fire behavior this season that only adds to the risk of deploying crews aggressively. 

‘Full suppression’

In April, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins and Interior Secretary Doug Burgum sent directions to agency leaders in preparation for the summer wildfire season. Both called for a “full suppression” strategy.

“Accelerate initial attack and use a full suppression strategy, in coordination with our interagency partners, across all land jurisdictions to suppress fires early and limit growth,” Rollins wrote. 

Burgum called for “prompt, decisive” suppression of fires, adding that decisions should be “balanced with firefighter safety and a clear assessment of probability of success.”

While both letters mention safety, some wildland fire veterans say agency leaders have put a clear emphasis on attacking fires aggressively. Some fear that crew leaders are being pressured to deploy close to the fire line, rather than choosing the safest place to make a stand. 

“I found it disturbing,” said Riva Duncan, a former wildland fire chief who served more than 30 years with the U.S. Forest Service. “You’ve got somebody in a suit in an office who’s never fought fires saying you’ve got to go direct attack.” 

Duncan serves as president of Grassroots Wildland Firefighters, a nonprofit that advocates on behalf of wildfire professionals.

In addition to the agency directives, wildfire veterans noted the rhetoric from President Donald Trump, who has threatened to impose tariffs on Canada as retaliation for wildfire smoke. 

“If managers and leaders are hearing from the politicos, ‘put them all out, put them all out,’ are we putting people in where we shouldn’t be?” said Bobbie Scopa, who had a 45-year career as a firefighter and now serves as vice president with Grassroots Wildland Firefighters. “I’m hearing from some young firefighters who feel like they are getting pressure to take actions. It’s stupid and you’re scratching your head and people are getting hurt.”

The Department of Interior did not respond to a Stateline interview request. The Forest Service declined to comment, saying its resources are focused on fire response.

Dangerous incidents

Already this year, fire crews across the country have been involved in a number of dangerous incidents, including the tragedy in Colorado that left four firefighters dead after a fast-moving blaze overran their position. 

“We’ve already had nine entrapments (firefighters having their position surrounded by fire) this year. That’s crazy,” Duncan said. “That suggests to me that fires are moving quickly and growing so fast.”

Federal officials have said an investigation team is reviewing the Colorado incident. 

“I do trace the tragedy in Colorado to that policy that compelled them to go out and aggressively attack the fires even when conditions did not favor safety or success,” said Timothy Ingalsbee, a former wildland firefighter who now serves as executive director for Firefighters United for Safety, Ethics & Ecology, a group that advocates for ecological fire management. 

I’m hearing from some young firefighters who feel like they are getting pressure to take actions.

– Bobbie Scopa, vice president, Grassroots Wildland Firefighters

“This policy that compels crews to blindly rush out and attack all fires is just not smart and it’s very unsafe,” Ingalsbee said. “They’re throwing back to the policy of the 1930s, ignoring everything we’ve learned about fire ecology and fire behavior”

Other wildland fire veterans say they need to see more details before blaming the deaths in Colorado on federal strategy.

“It’s just really hard to connect that at this time,” Duncan said. “I have faith that the investigation team is looking at that.”

But many former firefighters decried the feds’ abandonment of “managed fire” as a tool. Under that approach, federal land managers in previous years have been given the discretion to let some fires burn under supervision, so long as they didn’t threaten homes or infrastructure. In those cases, advocates say, agency leaders recognized the ecological benefits of fire, along with the potential to reduce the risk of catastrophic blazes in the future. 

“The problem is not fire itself, it’s our relationship with it,” said Darnell, the retired Forest Service firefighter. “We can work with these fires that are highly unlikely to have catastrophic effects on infrastructure, keep them on there until the weather puts them out.”

Ingalsbee, with the firefighter safety group, shared a similar sentiment. 

“Excluding fire from the landscape and attacking all fires, that policy ended in the ’70s because it was failing,” he said. “It’s performative firefighting, it’s failing to accomplish tangible goals and it’s putting lives in danger. Fire is nature’s recycling.”

At the state level, foresters in the Pacific Northwest — the region hardest hit by fires this year — say they have not yet seen evidence that federal agency directives are causing firefighters to take more risks. 

Most state agencies are required by state law to suppress, rather than manage, fires. Oregon state forester Kacey KC said the state’s landscape is too parched this year to safely manage fires for ecological benefits. 

“Every fire we can keep small is good,” she said. “Especially in conditions like this, there is not good fire right now on this landscape.”

In Washington, state forester George Geissler said he had not heard of federal crews taking extra risks. But he cautioned that federal leaders should be careful of their rhetoric.

“If you set goals, but you don’t set a good leadership tone related to safety, you can have those type of decisions being made,” he said.

Geissler said the bigger concern this year has been chaos within the leadership of the federal agencies. Under Trump, the Forest Service and Department of the Interior have been hit with severe staff reductions. The Forest Service is in the midst of a major reorganization. And firefighting operations from multiple agencies within the Interior Department have been consolidated into the U.S. Wildland Fire Service, established by Trump this year without congressional approval. 

“In the past, you knew who to go to, you knew which position had what,” Geissler said. “Now with the rapid changes, the loss of personnel, it’s a little bit scattered.”

Federal crews aren’t the only ones that have been involved in dangerous wildfire situations this year. Two separate incidents in Washington state left firefighters injured as a fire overran their position. One of those incidents, the Lyons Ferry Fire, involved a Washington Department of Natural Resources helicopter crew. Geissler said that was a wakeup call for the agency that fire conditions are extreme this year. 

“When the weather is this bad, all of those (safety protocols) become more and more critical,” he said. “We did a full safety standdown over it, because that was an extremely close call for those firefighters.” 

Darnell, the retired Forest Service firefighter, said she would not be surprised to hear of more incidents in which firefighters deploy their individual emergency shelters — last-resort devices that can save lives but do not offer full protection in extreme scenarios. 

“We’ve got conditions on the ground that are so explosive, it really begs us to be really careful about where we put people,” Darnell said. “I hope we don’t see any significant loss of life for firefighters.”

title: Governor and attorney general appeal to defend SD’s ban on abortion-pill advertising
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — Gov. Larry Rhoden and Attorney General Marty Jackley, both Republicans, filed an appeal Monday in defense of a new law that criminalizes abortion-pill advertising in the state.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — Gov. Larry Rhoden and Attorney General Marty Jackley, both Republicans, filed an appeal Monday in defense of a new law that criminalizes abortion-pill advertising in the state.

They’re seeking to set aside a lower court’s order blocking enforcement of the law while the litigation plays out.

Nancy Turbak Berry, who formerly served as a Democratic state legislator from Watertown, and New York-based nonprofit Mayday Health filed a lawsuit in May against Rhoden and Jackley. Rhoden signed the legislation into law in March after lawmakers approved it, but it wasn’t scheduled to take effect until July 1.

In mid-July, a federal judge in Rapid City ruled the state could not enforce the new law while the lawsuit played out. On Monday, Jackley and Rhoden appealed that decision to the U.S. Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals.

South Dakota already had a near-total ban on abortion, except when it’s necessary “to preserve the life of the pregnant female.”

The new law prohibits the dispensing, distribution and advertising of abortion pills and other abortion-related items, and makes violations punishable by felony prosecutions and fines.

Mayday Health and Turbak Berry say the law illegally restricts Turbak Berry’s free speech. As an example, the lawsuit says the prohibition on advertising would prevent her from wearing a sweatshirt sold by Mayday. The sweatshirt says abortion pills can be obtained in all 50 states and encourages people to learn more on Mayday’s website.

“Unless this court grants relief, Turbak will be deterred from wearing the sweatshirt,” and thereby deterred from engaging in First Amendment-protected speech, the lawsuit says.

U.S. District Judge Camela Theeler wrote in her July ruling that the state’s lawyers have “not shown that Mayday advertises with the specific intent that another person engage in specific criminal conduct and thus have not shown that Mayday’s advertising is integral to criminal conduct.”

In court documents filed Monday, Jackley and Rhoden criticized Theeler’s ruling and Mayday’s advertising, which formerly included placards at gas station pumps in the state.

“The Court has legalized the solicitation and aiding and abetting of an illegal drug and erroneously broadened the scope of the term advertising,” the state said in its court filing, adding that the ruling “could just as easily protect the solicitation and aiding and abetting of online methamphetamine sales by groups who claim to simply ‘provide information’ about methamphetamine and offer consumers the ‘choice’ to commit an illegal act.”

title: Wildfire smoke is now the primary pollutant affecting pregnancy, study shows
byline: By Kelcie Moseley-Morris Stateline
description: A new study examining pollution levels across a 16-year span found that while general pollution levels from sources such as cars and industry have significantly declined, recent increases in wildfire smoke air pollution have offset those gains and could be contributing to negative outcomes for pregnant women and babies such as low birth weight and preterm births.
_full_text:
StatelineLogo

A new study examining pollution levels across a 16-year span found that while general pollution levels from sources such as cars and industry have significantly declined, recent increases in wildfire smoke air pollution have offset those gains and could be contributing to negative outcomes for pregnant women and babies such as low birth weight and preterm births.  

Published by Frontiers in Environmental Health, the study included data from about 64.5 million pregnancies between 2003 and 2019, covering more than 2,800 counties in 48 states. Even in regions that are not strongly associated with wildfire, such as the southeast region of the U.S., wildfire pollution rates grew substantially during that time period. The study did not account for any movement between counties or regions during pregnancy, or whether pregnant people used any protection against smoke such as masks, air filters or temporary relocation.

Wildfire pollution is included in the same type of pollution as exhaust from cars or industrial outputs, but the study authors looked at two models of pollutants, one of which removed all fire-related pollution to determine how much of it was correlated with wildfire. Over the study period, about 65% of the days that recorded pollution levels above the National Ambient Air Quality Standard could be attributed to wildfire smoke.

Menglu Liang, leading author of the study and assistant clinical professor of biostatistics at the University of Maryland, said in a news release that efforts to reduce other forms of pollution have not been in vain.

“Those gains have genuinely protected pregnant people and unborn babies, and without them, exposures today would be considerably worse,” Liang said. “What our findings show is that wildfire smoke is offsetting a growing share of these hard-won improvements.”

The study time period does not include some of the most recent, most explosive wildfire seasons in the United States and Canada, such as 2020, 2024 and this year. By mid-July this year, there were more than 800 wildfires burning across Canada, leading to hazardous levels of wildfire smoke across parts of the Midwest and northeast, and in late July, a rash of wildfires across Oregon created hazardous air over much of the northwest. 

Recent reports show Oregon is on track to have its worst fire season on record, with nearly 1.8 million acres already burned and at least two months left of the peak season. The previous record was set in 2024, with 1.9 million acres burned.

The study found that some regions were disproportionately affected by the smoke, including in the Northwest, where rates of pollution from wildfire more than doubled over that period. The study noted that the burdens were highest in low-income, rural areas with significant populations of American Indian and Alaska Native communities, and areas with maternity care shortages.

 Recent studies have correlated wildfire smoke exposure with an increased risk of preterm birth, low birth weight and other negative outcomes such as stillbirth and some congenital anomalies. Scientists believe the body’s inflammatory responses to wildfire smoke can be harmful to the placenta, which is central to fetal survival, and some of the pollutants could cross the placental barrier and affect fetal growth and development.

“These outcomes matter well beyond the delivery room and harms experienced before birth can echo for decades,” Liang said in the release. “That makes prenatal exposure a particular public health concern.”

title: Local women help set record for longest women’s motorcycle ride
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Corinne Hoard celebrates the record-breaking ride. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
IMG_9902.jpeg
Corinne Hoard celebrates the record-breaking ride. Courtesy photo 

 IMG_0890.jpeg
Corinne Hoard, of Beulah, Wyo., prepares to make the 31-mile-long trek that would become the world’s largest women’s motorcycle ride. Courtesy photo 

 IMG_0898.jpeg
More than 1,400 women met, June 13, at the Hardrock Casino in Rockford, Ill., to complete the world’s largest women’s motorcycle ride. Courtesy photo 

STURGIS — The largest all-female motorcycle ride in the world included 1,433 bikers, stretched out for 8 miles on a deserted stretch of Interstate 90, for a ride that spanned about 31 miles, according to the Atlas World Records. 

Three Northern Black Hills women were there for the ride that was held June 13. They soaked up every bit of the record-breaker that never took them out of second gear on their bikes. Corinne Hoard, of Beulah, Wyo., Nancy Veres, of Sturgis, and Eva Veres, of Sundance, Wyo., were among the group of 1,433 women who came from every U.S. state and Canada, to set the record for largest women’s motorcycle ride, with Atlas World Records. The event was organized by Ellie Rains, of Midwest Women Riders, and was held in Rockford, Ill. 

“It was exhilarating,” Eva said. “It was powerful. It was unifying. It was hopeful. In today’s time, when our hopes get beaten down and we get bombarded with all of this negativity all around us, all this doom and gloom, this was such a nice oasis of hope renewed, of being alive and bonding with other humans.” 

 “It was a phenomenal experience,” said Nancy of the ride. “It’s one that I’ll probably never experience again in this lifetime.” 

Nancy, who fulfilled a lifelong dream to own a motorcycle when she bought her bike in 2003, said she learned about the plans to break the world record with the Midwest Women’s Riders, in January. She immediately wanted to be part of that effort, and began looking for like-minded women from this area, who wanted to blaze a trail and set the world record. She met Hoard and Eva. The 3, who share a passion for motorcycles, became fast friends as they embarked on the adventure of a lifetime to ride a total of 1,941 miles to Rockford, Ill. and back, just to be able to ride 31 miles to set the record. 

“For me, it wasn’t about how long the ride was,” Eva said. “It was just the energy that you feel with people who are like-minded, who may be different on many different levels. But just to unite on that one aspect together, it was exhilarating.” 

Staging for the ride was held at the Hard Rock Casino in Rockford, Ill., where it took about 51 minutes to get all of the riders on the road at the same time. Local authorities shut down 15 miles of Interstate 90 in both directions to accommodate the ride. For safety reasons, Hoard said even the riders did not know the route until the morning of the event. 

“They had the snowplow trucks out and they blocked traffic (on the interstate),” Hoard said. “Nobody could get on or off. It was incredible. We were the only motorcycles on the highway. We all needed to be moving to set the record. So that was just amazing to see these motorcycles. I was crying the whole time. It was just the feeling that all of us could come together for one purpose, and it happened.”

The interstate was closed for at least 2 hours. 

“The only people that were on the road were photographers,” Hoard said. “People were standing on the overpasses, waving like we were some kind of celebrities, and all we were doing was riding motorcycles. We were women on motorcycles, trying to break the record.” 

Before this year, the longest women’s motorcycle ride was listed as a 2016 event in Australia. 

Women who participated in the ride paid an entrance fee that helped raise $11,400 for the Susan G. Komen Foundation for breast cancer awareness. The entrance fee included the ride, a dinner and a party, with a wide variety of speakers who are considered trailblazers in the world of women motorcycling. Karen Davidson, who is the great granddaughter of Willie G. Davidson, founder of Harley-Davidson, and fashion designer for the motor company, was the keynote speaker. She was also joined by American Motorcycle Association Hall of Famer Cris Sommers; Wendy Crockett, who holds the Guinness World Record for completing the longest motorcycle ride in a single country, and more.

Hoard said she viewed the speakers as the women who paved the way for her to ride, in an industry that has been historically male dominated.

“When they started riding, women couldn’t ride motorcycles,” Hoard said. “It wasn’t a thing to do. These women tell these stories about how they had to struggle back then, and that was just 25-30 years ago. Now, here we are, setting world records because we all came together for a sense of purpose.” 

Other inspiring women, Hoard said, included a 73-year-old rider from Pennsylvania, who completed a Hoka Hey Motorcycle challenge — a 10,000-mile endurance ride across North America, for which riders must use paper maps, and camp next to their bikes for the duration of the ride.  

“She told me how she hit 2 deer on her way to Alaska on a motorcycle,” Hoard said. “She lived through it. The stuff she had to do, according to her challenge, like when she hit an animal she had to fix her bike on the side of the road to make it rideable. So she found a local and they beat her front fender out with a 2-by-4 (board.) Just hearing that, I’m like ‘wow! You’re 70-something years old, beating your fender on the side of the road because you hit a deer!’ Can I do that? I don’t know if I can, but I’m sure gonna try. Not hitting the deer, but to be 70 years old and riding my motorcycle to Alaska. It gives me hope for my future.” 

For Hoard, the record-setting ride was particularly meaningful because of how important her bike became to her after she returned from Operation Iraqi Freedom in 2004. A Marine combat veteran, Hoard said she needed something to calm her post-traumatic stress disorder, and “wind therapy” definitely did the trick. She rides about 8,000 miles a year on her Harley Davidson Road Glide Limited. 

“It puts you in a different mindset,” Hoard said of how riding helped her PTSD. “You’re able to think about things a lot slower, because you’re concentrating on other things, so you get to slow your mind down. ‘Wind therapy,’ that’s a real thing. It’s been one of the best passions that I have had.”

Hoard said the experience of setting the record is one she will never forget. 

“I don’t know if I’ve had a better moment in my life when it comes to me and my self-worth, my self healing, and the growth that I’ve done for myself,” she said. “Being surrounded with those women … the lady I actually rode on I-90 with, I didn’t even know her name. But by the end of that ride, I knew her name. We didn’t get out of second gear on the highway. It was a very slow ride. So we got to talk the whole ride. For all of us to come together for one purpose, it was just miraculous.” 

Women who participated in the record-breaking ride will be included in the parade of bikers that will begin opening ceremonies for the annual Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. The event is scheduled for 3 p.m. Friday, Aug. 7.

title: Veteran motorcyclist group with a drive to serve
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Militiamen Veteran Motorcycle Club of the Northern Hills has donated more than $70,000 over the last 15 years to the Spearfish Veteran’s Monument with funds raised from their annual poker run. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Veteran motorcyclist group with a drive to serve.JPG
The Militiamen Veteran Motorcycle Club of the Northern Hills has donated more than $70,000 over the last 15 years to the Spearfish Veteran’s Monument with funds raised from their annual poker run. Courtesy photo 

SPEARFISH — Chad Hartley, president of the Northern Hills chapter of the Militiamen Veterans Motorcycle Club, said that when most people think about motorcyclists they don’t tend to think about generous men and women who come together to do charity work for their communities — but that’s exactly what his chapter does. 

Hartley said the club is an 80-20 split of veterans and other first responders, including firefighters, lawyers, and doctors, who strive to develop a bond between military members and public servants while striving to provide assistance to people serving and their families in their time of need. His chapter was founded in 2012, and since then the chapter has created a $1,000 scholarship at Black Hills State University, become involved at the Black Hills National Cemetery, the South Dakota Veterans Cemetery Support Council, and the Cornerstone Mission for Homeless Veterans, among various other outreach programs in the Northern Hills schools and communities. 

“We don’t just help veterans, other people reach out that might need assistance, and we help those people that are in need if we are able to,” Hartley said. “It’s been a rewarding thing to be a part of over the last 14 years.”

Hartley, who now works in the finance department at South Dakota National Guard’s Camp Rapid in Rapid City, served for 26 years in the Army before retiring as a Sergeant 1st class. During his service, he was deployed to Iraq to serve in Operation Iraqi Freedom in 2003 and 2004 and again in 2010 and 2011 to serve in Afghanistan during Operation Enduring Freedom. He said those experiences are a big part of why he continues to strive to bring servicemen together with a common goal. 

“Our primary goal (when we founded the chapter) was to just keep serving,” Harley said. “You kind of have a sense of loss when you’re not serving overseas and you’re no longer serving your country. So, we wanted to do something so we could continue to serve and do something to give back to the community and just kind of carry on that military heritage and tradition within our community and help our veterans. A lot of us, when we come back (from deployment), we struggled with PTSD and other things like that. Anxiety. This was a way for us to bond and get together, as well as deal with those types of issues.”

In 2011, Hartley was approached by a group of his classmates who wanted to build a veteran’s monument in Spearfish. The project quickly became his chapter’s main charity. 

“I thought it was really important to make sure that all the veterans within the Spearfish area got recognized on a monument,” he said. “A few of my classmates, who were also veterans, were on the Spearfish Veterans Monument Committee and they had asked me when they were starting up the project, ‘What do you think about doing a poker run to maybe help raise the funds to help us get this think kicked off and started?’ I just absolutely jumped at the chance to do it. It’s helping support their cause and it’s helping get veterans names up there and get them to be honored for their service to their community and their country.”

Hartley said in the first year, they were able to raise between $700 and $800 for the monument by hosting a poker run. 

“We were just getting started, and it was a really quick turn around,” he said. “We didn’t have much time to plan, and I don’t even think we held it during Rally. It wasn’t a great turnout, but we were able to raise some money for them in the beginning. But it’s just gotten bigger and bigger every year, and everybody knows about it and people look forward to the ride every year.”

Hartley said the poker run is held every year during the first weekend of Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. Participants can register for $20 per person or $30 per couple, and anybody is welcome to join. 

“All vehicles are welcome,” Hartley said. “Cars, side by sides, as long as the vehicle you’re in can do the speed limit, anybody is welcome.”

Hartley said the poker run begins with registration at the Spearfish Veterans of Foreign Wars Post 5860. From there, the ride heads to Beulah, Wyo., where they stop at the Saloon 333, before heading to Hulett, Aladdin, then the Stone House Saloon in Belle Fourche, the St. Onge Bar, and then wrapping up the ride back at the beginning at the Spearfish VFW. 

“People really like the route, because they can go by Devil’s Tower, they love each stop,” Hartley said. “The way we have it organized, everybody just knows how the route’s going to go and how everything is planned out.”

Hartley said depending on weather, he can expect anywhere from 200 to 230 motorcyclists to participate in the ride every year. Last year, the ride raised $12,000 for the monument, bringing the total amount of donations his chapter has made to $70,300 in 14 years. 

“I think we’ve been very successful with our mission statement,” Hartley said. “A lot of people have come up to us and thanked us for what we do for the community and for the veterans. That makes me feel really good. I also think it helps with how people think about bikers. They associate a biker with people that aren’t always good. But I can tell you the biker community probably has the biggest hears and they’re the first people to step up to help out anybody that needs help.”

To learn more about the Northern Hills chapter of the Militiamen Veterans Motorcycle Club, including updates on their next poker run and other charitable events, visit their Facebook page.

title: Northern Hills Training Center  celebrates 50 years of service this month
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: As Northern Hills Training Center gears up for their 50th anniversary, they’ve dug in the archives for photos of past clients who they’ve helped find stable housing, employment, and connection. Photo courtesy Northern Hills Training Center
_full_text:
NHTCH anniversary.JPG
As Northern Hills Training Center gears up for their 50th anniversary, they’ve dug in the archives for photos of past clients who they’ve helped find stable housing, employment, and connection. Photo courtesy Northern Hills Training Center    

SPEARFISH — For 50 years, Northern Hills Training Center has served adults with developmental disabilities by providing residential care, day services, job training, and medical care.

The then-Northern Hills Community Living Facility began offering residential services in a 4-bedroom house at 1005 Canyon St. Four of the original 6 clients to receive support still live in Spearfish and are still served by the training center.

In 1976, the first person receiving support from Northern Hills Training Center received their first job placement gardening in Lower Valley, where they learned to irrigate, weed, and tend to produce.

By 1992, NHTC opened its “Job Shop,” which further focuses on preparing people with disabilities to enter and participate in the workforce. Just 6 months after welcoming residents to Canyon Street, the first workshop was established at the Snappers Club.

The current CEO of NHTC, Laura Wendland, said the training center has had great success with job placement and career longevity for its clients.

“We’ve had somebody with the city of Spearfish for 25-30 years, so the longevity with good community partners, neighbors, I mean, we are embedded in Spearfish and Spearfish has been so kind to everybody from Northern Hills for so long,” Wendland said.

Wendland said, in the next 50 years, she hopes to continue that tradition of connection between the city, the community, and the training center.

“I think Spearfish is growing, and I want to reach people who didn’t know we were here,” Wendland said. “It is not anywhere close to an institutional setting. People can pick and choose their services.”

She started working at NHTC when it relocated from the current Black Hills Christian Academy location on 32nd Street, to its current building on Harvard Street. That was 2003.

“It took a little time to get out of it completely, but back then there weren’t so many computer cords that you had to worry about. It was so fun to move in here,” Wendland said of the purpose-built location. Not only did the new building offer a significant increase in office space, but it also came equipped with a woodshop.

Wendland said the training center hasn’t necessarily grown in terms of the number of people it serves. Rather, the training center has expanded its approach and its offerings.

“I think it is important to acknowledge the last 50 years, but it is also important to recognize how the scope of services has changed. The next 50 years might be unrecognizable,” Wendland said. “Some things resemble group homes and residential settings and the day programs that we started 50 years ago, but that might have a completely different look in the future.”

Wendland left the training center for about 10 years. She returned as CEO on March 9.

“It was just like stepping back into the place I felt the most ease at. Even I grew up here,” Wendland said. “Of course, none of us are in human services for the paycheck. When we find the people who genuinely enjoy coming to work every day is the key.”

She said a strong, caring staff has helped the center to succeed for 50 years.

From 4-7 p.m. Aug. 25, NHTC will celebrate its anniversary with a block party in the Fred Romkema Center and Parking Lot on Harvard Street — many former employees and leaders are expected to attend.

title: Rhoden awards  $1 million for new  Rapid City industrial park
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: RAPID CITY — Gov. Larry Rhoden announced Tuesday the awarding of $1 million from the Future Fund for Elevate Rapid City’s development of a new business and industrial park in Rapid City.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

RAPID CITY — Gov. Larry Rhoden announced Tuesday the awarding of $1 million from the Future Fund for Elevate Rapid City’s development of a new business and industrial park in Rapid City.

“Strong communities don’t wait for opportunity. They prepare for it and take action,” said Rhoden. “By investing in development-ready sites today, we’re helping ensure Rapid City can compete for tomorrow’s jobs, businesses, and investments.”

Once complete, the business park will provide additional industrial and commercial sites for companies considering expansion or relocation to South Dakota. The Future Fund award will help finance the purchase of land and installation of public infrastructure needed to prepare the property. The project builds on a significant local commitment, including $1 million from Elevate Rapid City and donor funding.

“This investment in Northline Business Park will give local businesses room to grow and help Rapid City compete for new employers,” said Jack Valentine, president and CEO of Elevate Rapid City. “By preparing land businesses can build on, we are laying the groundwork for private investment, quality jobs and lasting opportunity for generations of people who call western South Dakota home.”

As part of the agreement, Elevate Rapid City will prepare the property for full development, continue marketing the sites to prospective businesses, and provide ongoing progress reports to the Governor’s Office of Economic Development.

title: Hall of fame honors local kids who  believe no veteran should be forgotten
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — On Memorial Day, Zayne Bartol’s grandmother took him to Black Hills National Cemetery in Sturgis to place flowers on the grave of his great-grandfather, Chuck. Zayne noticed that there were no flowers at many of the surrounding graves, belonging to veterans. He insisted on a trip to Walmart to purchase more flowers for the men and women surrounding Chuck. His grandmother obliged.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — On Memorial Day, Zayne Bartol’s grandmother took him to Black Hills National Cemetery in Sturgis to place flowers on the grave of his great-grandfather, Chuck. Zayne noticed that there were no flowers at many of the surrounding graves, belonging to veterans. He insisted on a trip to Walmart to purchase more flowers for the men and women surrounding Chuck. His grandmother obliged.

That was 15 years ago.

Since then, the Bartol family has refined their “Memorial Day Mission.” Today, Zayne has enlisted the support of his parents and the help of his brothers — Zander and Zaiden to place about 3,000 flowers annually. The family founded a non-profit in 2019 to manage donations for the purchase of flowers, and they’ve extended their cemetery visits beyond Memorial Day — placing wreaths on graves during the winter holidays. Their current goal is to place 1 flower on each of the 29,000 graves at Black Hills National Cemetery.

The South Dakota Hall of Fame awarded Zayne, Zander, and Zaiden Bartol a 2026 Act of Excellence Award with a ceremony at Studio 621 in Spearfish last week. Every year, the Hall of Fame inducts about 10 new members. Its second program, recognizing everyday South Dakotans for their extraordinary community contributions, is the Acts of Excellence Award Program.

Sponsored by Sanford Health, Acts of Excellence Awards recognize individuals and organizations whose efforts have made a lasting impact in their communities.

“What started with the pure empathy of a 3-year-old boy has grown into one of South Dakota’s most heartfelt tributes to veterans,” said Laurie Becvar, the CEO of the South Dakota Hall of Fame. “Zayne, soon to be 18, has set a powerful example for his brothers.”

Rena Bartol, the boy’s mother, said they’ve seen firsthand how much the small act of placing a flower can mean to families.

“When we were out and putting flowers out. We saw this older couple with their iPad out, and they were probably in their 80s. We always come out with our phones and apps and grave locators, because it is hard to find what’s up there. We’ll go help them, and then they found it, and we just had one flower left,” Rena said. “Zayne just happened to go, ‘Oh, can I leave this flower for them?’ and they were like, ‘Oh, that would be so kind. Zane puts the one flower down, and they were crying, and I was crying.’ That meant so much to them.”

Rena said since all 3 of her boys learned to talk, they have never hesitated to walk up to thank veterans they see in public for their service.

“We often honor those who have passed on, but we also want to honor those who are still here,” Rena said. “They bee-line straight to them and say, ‘Thank you for your service.’ They are never shy. Sometimes I’m like, ‘Where are you going?’”

Rena said, in her experience, those small exchanges can mean a lot.

“Sometimes we forget, with all of the things that happen in the world, how much that means,” Rena said.

The boys are now looking to expand the Memorial Day Mission still further. They’re hoping to volunteer to offer services for veterans who may need landscaping support. Zayne’s already mowed a few lawns, she said.

Inspired by ‘Angel Tree’ programs, the Bartols are also working on a program that could bring gifts to veterans in need throughout the year.
