title: Charges dismissed in murder case
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: - UPDATED -
_full_text:
- UPDATED -
BELLE FOURCHE — The state dropped charges against 2 men accused in the murder and disappearance of Beverly Ozuna-Ulrich.
In November 2025, Steven Lee Ulrich was arrested and charged with murder. 
Max Piekkola, of Rapid City, was also charged in connection with Ozuna-Ulrich’s disappearance; he was charged with accessory to a felony. 
On Wednesday, the Butte County State’s Attorney released a prepared statement.
“Following a review of the evidence currently available, the Butte County State’s Attorney’s Office has determined that the state does not presently have sufficient evidence to prove the charged offenses beyond a reasonable doubt,” according to the statement.
Additionally, it noted that charges were dismissed without prejudice, meaning that charges could be filed in the future if additional evidence is developed.
Ozuna-Ulrich was last seen in Belle Fourche on Oct. 17, 2003. 
Ozuna-Ulrich, a mother of 8 and member of the Lakota tribe, was living in Belle Fourche at the time of her disappearance.
Her family was “devastated by the state’s decision to dismiss the charges in both cases.”
“Over the course of this case, we have endured obstacle after obstacle. From our perspective, the previous state’s attorney’s departure in the middle of the case and what we believe has been a failure by our county commissioners to fulfill their responsibilities have only added to our frustration and heartbreak. Our family deserves answers, accountability, and a justice system that sees this through,” Bobbie Ljunggren, Ozuna-Ulrich’s niece, told the Pioneer in a prepared statement.
Known for her devotion to her children and her large, close-knit family, Ozuna-Ulrich was the youngest of 16 siblings. According to the Belle Fourche Police Department, Ozuna-Ulrich would occasionally travel without notice, but she had a reputation for maintaining close contact with her siblings and children.
Ten days after she was last seen, reportedly at Ulrich’s home, her family reported her missing.
“We remain committed to seeking justice for Beverly, and we will never stop fighting on her behalf. We urge anyone with information — no matter how small or seemingly insignificant — to come forward. Even the smallest detail could help hold those responsible accountable,” Ljunggren said. “Thank you to everyone who has continued to stand with our family. We will not give up. We will continue to fight for Beverly until justice is served.”
Belle Fourche Police Chief Ryan Cherveny told the Black Hills Pioneer in December his department had been working diligently on the cold case for the last 6 years — collaborating with the South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigations (DCI).
“It is such a big case,” Cherveny said. “We had 23 (22) years of interviews and evidence to work through.”
According to November 2025 court documents, Ulrich had been charged with first-degree murder, a Class A felony; or second-degree murder in the alternative, a Class B felony. 
According to November 2025 court documents, Piekkola was accused of having rendered “assistance by concealing, destroying, or altering any physical evidence that might aid in the discovery, detection, apprehension, prosecution, conviction or punishment of the other person.”

title: Spearfish expects Colorado Blvd. chip seal completion Thursday
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: SPEARFISH — Dakota Asphalt is expected to finish chip seal operations on Colorado Boulevard from Grant Street to Spearfish Canyon Highway 14A by Thursday.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — Dakota Asphalt is expected to finish chip seal operations on Colorado Boulevard from Grant Street to Spearfish Canyon Highway 14A by Thursday.

Fog seal operations started this week — the final step in the chip seal process. A fog seal is a thin layer of emulsified asphalt, intended to lock any loose chips in place and extend the life of the chip seal underneath.

Pavement markings, including bike lanes, will be applied one week following the application of the fog seal. The week in between the fog seal and pavement marking allows for traffic to run on the fog seal uninterrupted, strengthening the bond between the fog seal and the chips.

title: SD’s Democratic nominee for US Senate drops out
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Julian Beaudion, a Sioux Falls businessman and former state trooper, announced Tuesday that he’s withdrawing from the race for U.S. Senate. Photo by Joshua Haiar, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
SD’s Democratic nominee for US Senate drops out.jpg
Julian Beaudion, a Sioux Falls businessman and former state trooper, announced Tuesday that he’s withdrawing from the race for U.S. Senate. Photo by Joshua Haiar, South Dakota Searchlight 

South Dakota’s Democratic U.S. Senate nominee ended his campaign Tuesday.

“In recent weeks, my family has faced extraordinary personal challenges,” Julian Beaudion said in a written statement. “As many of you know, we experienced a devastating house fire while continuing to navigate significant personal financial hardship.”

The deadline for the state Democratic Party Central Committee to nominate a replacement candidate is next Tuesday. The party issued a news release Tuesday evening that did not say whether party leaders will pick a new nominee. Instead, the news release said the party “respects Julian Beaudion’s decision to suspend his campaign for U.S. Senate” and added that he “would have made an outstanding U.S. senator for South Dakota.”

Party officials did not immediately provide a response to South Dakota Searchlight questions on Tuesday evening.

Beaudion is a businessman and former state trooper. He had been receiving support from party officials, but some other Democrats had been calling for Beaudion to drop out, saying they believe the independent candidate in the race, Brian Bengs, has a better chance to beat incumbent Republican Sen. Mike Rounds. Bengs ran as the Democratic nominee against Republican U.S. Sen. John Thune in 2022 and received 26% of the vote.

Beaudion alleged in his statement that “an opponent and those associated with the opponent, hit my family and I with intimidating threats to drop out of this race.”

“Those attacks were personal and never about politics,” Beaudion’s statement said. “The mental and physical safety of my family is my priority and for this reason alone, I step aside.”

The Bengs campaign replied to Searchlight questions by sending a written statement from Bengs.

“I have never spoken ill of Julian, and I won’t start now,” Bengs’ statement said, in part. “He is a patriot and I applaud his action. We were both under a great deal of stress, but I entirely reject the notion that there was some behind-the-scenes conspiracy. Nobody has been attacked or threatened.”

The effort to force Beaudion out of the race included American Muckrakers, a website operated by a North Carolina man.

American Muckrakers published articles in recent weeks praising Bengs and sent an email to South Dakota media outlets in June containing allegations about Beaudion, with references to some of the personal struggles Beaudion ultimately alluded to in his statement Tuesday.

The Bengs campaign, in response to earlier Searchlight questions, said it has no formal relationship with American Muckrakers or its author.

Several people who spent decades working in Democratic politics had also been calling for Beaudion to leave the race. They included Steve Jarding, a former executive director of the South Dakota Democratic Party; Steve Hildebrand, who was the deputy national campaign manager for then-Sen. Barack Obama’s successful 2008 presidential campaign and worked on earlier campaigns for former South Dakota U.S. Sens. Tom Daschle and Tim Johnson; and Drey Samuelson, who was Johnson’s chief of staff for 28 years.

Hildebrand had said there’s a stigma associated with the Democratic brand in South Dakota that would prevent Beaudion from winning, and Jarding said “the Democratic brand in South Dakota is dead.” They said Beaudion should drop out to consolidate votes and resources behind Bengs. Beaudion said in his statement Tuesday that he will not endorse Bengs or Rounds.

Democrats have not held a statewide office in South Dakota since January 2015, when Sen. Johnson — who was slowed by health problems — left office after opting against a reelection campaign. Rounds, a former governor, won the race for Johnson’s Senate seat and has held it ever since. 

The gap between registered Republican and Democratic voters in South Dakota has widened in recent years, and Republicans now outnumber Democrats 2.5 to 1. The Democratic Party has been further subjugated by the rise of independents and voters who list no label or affiliation on their registration, who now collectively outnumber Democrats in the state.

South Dakota Democratic Party Chairman Shane Merrill told Searchlight prior to Tuesday that he disagreed with the assertions by Jarding, Hildebrand and Samuelson that the party’s brand is too damaged to win statewide elections in South Dakota.

“I find it rich that the folks that made their living off the South Dakota Democratic Party are now running away from the brand instead of trying to help build and strengthen the brand,” Merrill said. “If we would all work together, we could probably accomplish more.”

Rounds has used the Democratic feud over Beaudion to raise campaign donations, sending emails to potential donors saying “the Democrats are running a fake independent to flip my seat.”

title: Black Hills highway project pits safety against scenery as public comments pour in
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: A vehicle drives down U.S. Highway 85 with the Spearfish Canyon cliffs on its right and Spearfish Creek on its left. Photo courtesy of Paul Horsted
_full_text:
Black Hills highway project pits safety against scenery as public comments pour in 1.jpg
A vehicle drives down U.S. Highway 85 with the Spearfish Canyon cliffs on its right and Spearfish Creek on its left. Photo courtesy of Paul Horsted 

Public comments
Submit public comments for the U.S. Highway 85 reconstruction project by Sept. 4 by emailing Project Manager Mark Malone at mark.malone@state.sd.us.

LEAD — Paul Horsted calls himself a “re-photographer.” He takes new photos at historic places to show what has and hasn’t changed.

His projects have included photography books retracing the 1874 Custer expedition into the Black Hills, and pairing historic photos of Yellowstone National Park with modern ones. 

“There’s a joy to that for me,” he said.

Horsted, of Custer, and dozens of other people who appreciate the beauty of the Black Hills are worried about changes that could be wrought by a state highway project. The South Dakota Department of Transportation plans to reconstruct a 16-mile stretch of U.S. Highway 85 from the Wyoming border to the intersection with U.S. Highway 14A at Cheyenne Crossing, which includes picturesque stretches through a canyon cut by Spearfish Creek. 

The department says the $47 million project will make the road safer for locals, commuters and visitors. But a surge in public concern about the project’s potential impact on the scenic character of the area led the department to extend the public comment deadline from June 19 to Sept. 4. The department has received more than 200 comments so far regarding the latest version of the proposal.

Horsted walked near the highway earlier this summer. He saw snails and butterflies, and trout swimming in the creek.

“We can’t stand in the way of all development and progress, but something is always lost along the way,” Horsted said. “That’s what some of us are longing for and aiming to preserve as much as we can when it comes to this project and the incremental development that comes with it.”

The organizer of opposition to the project is David Miller, who grew up in Deadwood and lives in Rapid City. He chooses not to live within the Black Hills, he said, hoping to leave as little impact on the forest as possible. 

“We would sacrifice a lot of what makes this place what it is for speed and convenience,” Miller said of the highway project.

State says balance needed between beauty and safety

U.S. 85 has been regraded, resurfaced or repaired 10 times since 1950, but hasn’t been touched since 2010. The department says the roadway is in poor condition, and the project would also widen lanes, add paved shoulders and extend “clear zones” — buffer areas just beyond the road’s edge — to increase safety in case of run-off-the-road crashes. 

The goal is to find a balance between traffic safety and preserving the Black Hills, said Mark Malone, department project manager.

“Having a safer highway and an aesthetically pleasing highway do not have to be mutually exclusive,” Malone said in an email.

Engineers have been refining the proposal since a June open house. In an email to Miller, Malone said the team plans to “take a closer look” at a segment of the project to “identify areas where centerline shifts may not be necessary.” As of June, the proposal had eight locations where the road would be realigned.

In Spearfish Canyon, there’s little room to maneuver. Any shift toward the canyon walls risks disturbing rock faces and vegetation, project critics say, and any shift toward the creek risks encroaching on the waterway and its banks.

Malone said that as the department “develops alternatives or refines current options” it will seek to minimize work near the creek and “strive to reduce impacts” to landowners along the road.

About 600 vehicles traverse the highway each weekday, and 850 per day on weekends. The speed limit is 55 mph in most stretches, though curves have slower advisory speed limits.

The June proposal calls for roadway adjustments to provide a “consistent design speed,” Malone said.

“This inconsistency on the existing roadway creates issues for driver expectations for unfamiliar drivers as well as leads drivers either speeding up or slowing down,” Malone said. “The variations in their speed, especially the large differential between vehicles, create safety concerns and lead to crashes.” 

Between 2020 and 2024, 77 crashes resulted in one fatality and 31 injuries, a crash rate more than six times higher than the statewide average for “similar facilities” — roads of comparable type and traffic volume — over that time period. The roadway’s crash rate is 9.07 crashes per million vehicle miles traveled. A comparable roadway is U.S. Highway 14A, which has a crash rate of 1.27.

About a third of the crashes involved motorcycles and more than one-fourth involved wild animals. Vehicles left the roadway in about 60% of crashes.

Most of the crashes happened in optimal driving conditions, during daylight hours when the road was dry. More than half occurred between June and September — a period that includes the annual Sturgis Motorcycle Rally — and about one-third involved turning or lane changing.

Concerns about ‘incremental development’

Horsted, Miller and others opposed to the project are sensitive to the potential impacts on the environment after witnessing other recent road construction in the Black Hills — particularly on U.S. 385, a $72 million project from Deadwood to Hill City that widened lanes, extended shoulders, straightened curves and required clearing trees and blasting rock.

Such reconstruction favors convenience over land stewardship, Horsted said, potentially turning U.S. 85 into “just another strip of pavement through the Black Hills.”

Horsted wonders if widening the road and shoulders is the only way to make the highway safe, or if reduced speed limits or other traffic-calming measures could work.

Not everyone opposes the project. Robin Nichols Miller, a local who drives on U.S. 85 daily, said the road is a hazard.

“There are no shoulders on this road, so if someone slides or runs off it, they will more than likely incur a rollover crash,” Nichols Miller wrote in response to a social media post by Horsted.

She added that some crashes have blocked traffic for hours and that existing pullouts are often too short for large trucks or campers to pull over and let other traffic pass.

“Progress and growth, whether in population or visitors, requires making things safe for everyone,” Nichols Miller said. “Many of us who drive or ride this road on an almost daily basis recognize the road needs to be made safer and can’t wait for them to get started.”

Horsted hopes the department will host another public meeting given the public interest and the potential changes being considered. The department has said it does not plan to do so.

“We’re on guard,” Horsted said. “I hope the Department of Transportation will listen carefully.”

title: Spearfish School Board declares emergency to replace flood damaged middle school gym floor
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Spearfish School Board declared an emergency Tuesday allowing school officials to make an emergency procurement for a new middle school gym floor, and other necessary items, following a June 30 water main leak that flooded parts of the school and high school. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Water main break 1.jpg
The Spearfish School Board declared an emergency Tuesday allowing school officials to make an emergency procurement for a new middle school gym floor, and other necessary items, following a June 30 water main leak that flooded parts of the school and high school. Courtesy photo 

SPEARFISH — Damaged caused by a June 30 water main break at Spearfish High School and Middle School was greater than initially thought prompting the Spearfish School Board to declare an emergency Tuesday to make an emergency procurement of a replacement gym floor and cleaning of all impacted spaces to ensure a safe and sanitary environment.

“We have discovered that the scope of the water intrusion and the damage was beyond what we could initially assess, and that the subfloor water had migrated underneath the middle school floor beyond what we could dry,” said Nick Gottlob, superintendent of the Spearfish School District. “Josh Gerhold’s team did an exceptional job of drying what we could on the perimeters, running floors, running dehumidifiers, but at the end of the day, their efforts were not able to save the floor.”

Gerhold is the district’s director of building and grounds.

Shortly before midnight on June 30, a 6-inch mater main broke underneath the mechanical room at the school. The high-pressure water created a significant cavern underneath hot water heaters. He estimated the cavern is 15 feet long, 3-5 feet across, and as deep as 8 feet in one area. The flooding extended beyond the mechanical room, and flooded parts of the middle school and high school with several inches of reddish brown muddy water.

The city staff was notified around 6:20 a.m. and shut off water about 10 minutes later, Adam McMahon, the city’s public works director, told the Pioneer. 

In the meantime, the damage had already been done.

“Water was pouring out of here and down through the parking lot,” Gottlob said of the exterior mechanical room door.

Water was several inches deep in the mechanical room, nearby hallways, newly-renovated locker rooms and coaches’ offices. 

Gottlob said during a tour of the damaged area days after the leak, that he was hopeful the water had not damaged the middle school gym floor. In the days following the water leak, staff realized they were not so lucky.

The water, fortunately, he said, did not flood the high school gym.

This elevation pitch right here was just enough to keep the water back here,” he said during a tour of the damage. That elevation change was a 2-inch transition from a hallway to the main gym, which was renovated in 2024.

On Aug. 7, the district’s insurance company deemed the middle school gym floor a total loss.

School begins Aug. 27 and a new floor will not be in place at that time, Gottlob said. 

While the district waits for approval from the insurance company, some invoices have already arrived.

“We expect estimated cost for the recovery to be somewhere between $250,000 and $350,000. This is why we have insurance,” he said. 

South Dakota Codified Law 5-18A-9 permits the emergency declaration and purchases.

“A purchasing agency may make or authorize others to make an emergency procurement without advertising the procurement if rentals are not practicable and there exists a threat to public health, welfare, or safety or for other urgent and compelling reasons. … An emergency procurement shall be made with such competition as is practicable under the circumstances. A written determination of the basis for the emergency and for the selection of the particular contractor shall be included in the contract file,” according to the law.

“It would be our intent to seek multiple proposals for the removal and for the replacement and for the sanitary efforts,” Gottlob said. “To this point, any of the contractors and any of the assessments have all been at the discretion of the insurance adjustment company. So, we have not solicited any direct proposals. They’ve all been directed through the insurance company. … (I won’t) sign any authorizations of work until we have an authorization of coverage and a scope of coverage to make sure that the district doesn’t authorize work that may not be subject to reimbursement.”

Immediately following the water leak, cleaning crews from all school buildings, worked on cleaning and sanitizing the flooded areas, in addition to the standard summer cleaning. With some high school practices already underway, and football and volleyball practices beginning next week, the activities department cannot provide various services and programming until repairs are made. Affected areas include, but are not limited to, varsity and middle school locker rooms, the training room, cheer and dance room, educational storage spaces, hallways, and coach’s offices.

Dalton Wademan, activities director for the high school, said for the most part they will be unaffected, but they will need to be somewhat flexible.

“For the most part, we’ll be running like normal,” Wademan said.

title: Pennington Co. Commissioners address cybersecurity incident
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: RAPID CITY — The Pennington County Board of Commissioners recognizes the frustration many residents have experienced following the recent cybersecurity incident that affected county operations. Commissioners want the public to know that restoring all county services remains a top priority.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

RAPID CITY — The Pennington County Board of Commissioners recognizes the frustration many residents have experienced following the recent cybersecurity incident that affected county operations. Commissioners want the public to know that restoring all county services remains a top priority.

“We know this has been frustrating, and we want our residents to know that we hear them,” said Commission Chair Ron Weifenbach. “Even with limited access to some of our technology, most county services are now available again because our department heads and employees have found creative ways to adapt and continue serving the public.”

While some services continue to experience temporary interruptions, county departments continue adapting their operations to meet the needs of residents whenever possible. Many county services remain available in one capacity or another. Residents can find the latest information on available county services by visiting the Pennington County website.

County staff continues working to safely restore all county systems while maintaining as many services as possible. The Board of Commissioners remains optimistic that additional services will continue coming back online as recovery efforts progress.

“Our information technology team has been working around the clock to restore our systems safely and securely, and we appreciate the expertise and support of our local, state, and federal partners assisting in this effort,” Weifenbach said. “We appreciate the patience and understanding our community has shown throughout this process, and we look forward to restoring full services as soon as it is safe to do so.”

title: Sturgis Motorcycle Rally Grand Marshal fulfilling bucket list
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Tim Duffy rides his motorcycle into lower Manhattan to help during the terrorist attacks on Sept. 11. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Firefighter Tim Duffy arrives downtown after 1st tower collapse
Tim Duffy rides his motorcycle into lower Manhattan to help during the terrorist attacks on Sept. 11. Courtesy photo  

 Grand Marshal Tim Duffy 2.png
Tim Duffy will serve as grand marshall of the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally for 2026. Courtesy photo 

STURGIS — For Tim Duffy, motorcycles have never just been about the ride.

They’ve been about freedom, about clearing your head, about connection.

“Riding has meant freedom, independence, and stress relief,” Duffy says. “That’s what wind therapy is.”

This August, that lifelong connection to the road brings him to the Black Hills for the first time, as grand marshal of the 2026 Sturgis Motorcycle Rally.

Why Tim Duffy you may ask.

This year marks the 25th anniversary of 9/11, and on that Tuesday, Sept. 11, 2001, though off duty, Duffy put on his firefighter gear and rode his 2000 Harley-Davidson Super Glide Sport into lower Manhattan to help. He arrived at the World Trade Center just as the South Tower collapsed, burying him in debris.

He survived and went on to help rescue others throughout the day.

Photographer Allan Tannenbaum captured what would become a historic image of Duffy astride his motorcycle amid the debris-strewn streets of Manhattan. Duffy says that moment in history changed the course of his life.

Looking back on 9/11, Duffy describes the devastation as overwhelming. But even in that moment, his focus never shifted far from others.

“When everything went quiet it was time to go to work,” he said. 

That mindset, service before self, has stayed with him ever since.

More than two decades later, Duffy continues to live with purpose. He remains proud of his time as a New York City firefighter, calling it “the best job in the world,” and stays deeply connected to the people he served alongside.

What began in a moment of crisis has become a life defined by service, healing, and the freedom found on two wheels.

For Duffy, being named Grand Marshal of the 2026 Sturgis Motorcycle Rally is more than a personal honor, it is a chance to recognize the motorcycle brotherhood that has supported him throughout his journey. 

“I’m honored and humbled,” he says. “I feel like I represent a lot of people standing out in front of me. And it’ll be special for my family to see the motorcycle community and brotherhood that’s supported me over the years.”

Though he’s ridden across the country and attended rallies of all kinds, Sturgis has always held a special place in Duffy’s mind.

“This will be my first trip to Sturgis,” he says. “It’s been on my bucket list for a long time. I’ve been to all sorts of other rallies, but this is the mother of them all, and the one I’ve really wanted to get to.”

Like so many riders making their annual pilgrimage, Duffy is drawn not just by the roads but by the people.

“The best part of this (motorcycle) community is the generosity,” he says. “It’s one of the most giving groups of people I’ve ever come across.”

That sense of connection, of instant camaraderie between strangers, is something he knows well.

“The brotherhood is everything,” Duffy says. “I’ve seen it in different parts of my life, but the motorcycle community has its own kind of bond.”

Those ideas of freedom, brotherhood, and resilience, often used to describe the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, also happen to describe Duffy’s life.

“I feel like those three words are part of what defines me,” he said. “From my time in the Navy, to the New York City Fire Department, to the biker community, that brotherhood has always been there.”

And resilience, as he puts it simply, is something he carries with him every day.

“I’m still here,” he says.

When asked what his perfect ride during Rally week might look like, Duffy doesn’t hesitate.

“A long ride on a road less traveled,” he says, “with an old saloon somewhere along the way.”

It’s a vision that fits perfectly with the Black Hills, where winding highways, quiet byways, and unexpected stops define the experience as much as the destination.

And like many riders arriving in Sturgis for the first time, he’s ready to take it all in.

As Grand Marshal, Duffy will lead not just with presence, but with perspective, and his message to the hundreds of thousands who will roll into Sturgis this summer is simple and rooted in the culture that binds them.

“Enjoy the moment,” he says. “Respect the road. And enjoy being part of something bigger than yourself.”

Because to Duffy, that’s what the Rally is really about, not just the bikes, not just the miles, but the shared experience.

That perspective is shaped by a life of service, first in the United States Navy, and later as a firefighter with the FDNY, where standing shoulder to shoulder with others was part of everyday life.

“You take care of your own,” he says. “That’s just how it works.”

That philosophy continues today through his nonprofit, 1 Soldier 1 Dog 1 Team, which pairs veterans and first responders with shelter dogs to help address PTSD and mental health challenges.

“We’re saving two lives, the dog and the veteran,” Duffy says. “And showing people they’re not alone.”

Today Duffy finds hope in the next generation.

“What gives me hope is seeing young people who still believe in this country,” he says. “What it is, and what it should be.”

And now, that journey brings him to Sturgis, to the roar of engines, to the open road, to a community that understands, perhaps better than most, what freedom really feels like.

For Tim Duffy, it’s not just another ride.

It’s one he’s been looking forward to for a long time.

title: Masonry work approved for Deadwood Public Library and Broadway Parking Ramp
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Contracts were approved with Competitive Masonry to repair the exteriors of the Deadwood Public Library and Broadway Parking Ramp. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
Competitive Masonry.jpg
Contracts were approved with Competitive Masonry to repair the exteriors of the Deadwood Public Library and Broadway Parking Ramp. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

DEADWOOD — Deadwood City Commissioners approved 2 contracts Monday with Competitive Masonry, of Rapid City, to complete work on the public library and Broadway Parking Ramp. 

Lornie Stalder, director of public works, told city commissioners Monday that work to complete the garden outside the public library disturbed the historic sandstone exterior of the building. 

“Over the last 5 years, we built a beautiful garden in the back of the library. They buried the utilities underground and during that underground utility burial we sustained some damage to the sandstone walls and sandstone entry,” said Stalder. “It’s a 120-year-old building, gorgeous, gorgeous landmark that we have in the city of Deadwood. Of course, funded by Andrew Carnegie in 1903, he gave $15,000 this library and the sandstone is beautiful, and it just needs updated and improved. It’s been a 3-1/2-year journey to find a mason that would do it, so we’re very excited to finally be able to present a quote to get the repairs to the masonry.”

The $37,056.60 contract will repair the sandstone steps, foundation, fence and capstones of the building. The work will be paid partly by historic preservation capital assets and partly by historic preservation general maintenance line items. 

Jessicca McKeown, finance officer, said the work will be split between the 2 line items as work is completed, depending on what work will be considered general maintenance and what work will increase the life expectancy of the building. 

A separate contract with Competitive Masonry was approved for $44,064 to repair damage at the Broadway Parking Ramp. 

The scope of work is expected to include capstone, brick, and concrete repairs, replacements, caulking, and tuckpointing. 

“There are some large cracks on the façade of the structure that need tuckpointing and repair, along with some broken bricks and the capstones have been deteriorating in spots,” said Justin Lux, director of parking and transportation. “We plan on patching some and replacing entirely and rebooting some spots. There’s a couple spots in the ramp where the concrete barriers have been damaged, either hit by cars or during snow removal, so those either need a patch or repair to those areas.”

The work to the parking ramp will be paid for by the Broadway repair line item.

title: Lead hires open government expert to train new commissioners, give public presentation
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Rapid City attorney Sarah Frankenstein gave an open government presentation at the Aug. 3 Lead City Commission meeting. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
Lead open government.jpeg
Rapid City attorney Sarah Frankenstein gave an open government presentation at the Aug. 3 Lead City Commission meeting. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

LEAD — Government actions taken in executive session are invalid, one expert in open meeting law said Monday. 

Sarah Frankenstein, a Rapid City attorney with Gunderson, Palmer, Nelson, and Ashmore, LLP, who has 26 years of experience in South Dakota’s open government laws, made a presentation at the Lead City Commission meeting, and discussed the state’s laws in detail. The Lead City Commission authorized paying $2,000 for Frankenstein’s public presentation. 

Lead City Administrator Robin Lucero said the presentation replaces a regular training by the South Dakota Municipal League (SDML), for newly elected officials. The SDML is not doing that training this year, and Lucero said with 3 of the 4 commissioners in their first year, the training in open government is necessary. Additionally, to justify the $2,000 expenditure, she said the city budgets money for elected official training. 

“The benefit to this is that it is a public presentation,” Lucero said. “It goes through all the regulations that all the municipalities have to follow.” 

Frankenstein, who served as a city attorney for more than 20 years, and who is paid by the South Dakota Public Insurance Alliance to take hotline calls to answer questions from government officials, as well as defends government officials in criminal cases regarding open meetings violations, is considered an expert in the field of South Dakota open government law. During her presentation, she explained in detail a pamphlet that the S.D. Attorney General distributes, and which state law requires local governments to review annually. 

“All that you will learn if you read this is what will keep you out of criminal trouble, and what’s required of you to make sure you don’t run afoul of criminal laws and get yourself prosecuted for either wrongfully closing a meeting, or discussing and working on things that weren’t properly (on the agenda). What it does not do, or help you with thinking through at all, is how (the city can be) liable for acting in ways that are contrary to these statutes. So, I’m going to cover the bases that you must cover to meet the statutes, not only to keep yourself out of the court system criminally, but to keep the city from being sued.” 

Frankenstein began by explaining that the state’s open meetings laws exist to ensure governmental entities conduct all public business in front of the public. Any time a quorum communicates via phone, email, text message, social media messaging, or in person, those communications need to be in front of the public, she said. Additionally, she advised against commission members texting during meetings, as that could be publicly construed as secret communication during a public meeting. 

“I wouldn’t do that,” she said. “It’s along the same lines of discussing with each other outside of the public’s ears.” 

Every time there will be a quorum, or majority of members of the commission, present at any event where issues are discussed, there must be an agenda posted at city hall and on the city’s website 24 hours before the meeting. Additionally, she said the commission must include a public comment period on the agenda, which she recommended be held at the beginning of the meeting. 

Frankenstein also discouraged the commission from adding agenda items at the meeting, except in emergency cases. On Monday, the city commission added an emergency burn ban to its agenda, and Frankenstein said she would consider that an emergency add-on. 

“You can subtract stuff,” she said. “But you should not add content. You cannot act on stuff that is added to the agenda.” 

In addition to the agenda, Frankenstein said all documents that are included in the commission’s packet, except for privileged attorney-client information, must be made available to the public. 

Executive sessions are one of the chief ways local governments can get into trouble, Frankenstein said, and she described state law extensively for the commission. When executive sessions are listed on the agenda, she said the commission must be specific about what they are discussing, and include the subsection of the state law that addresses the executive session purpose. 

“So you shouldn’t just say public works and then put executive session, because that tells the public nothing about what is being discussed,” she said. “You can say we’re going to take up public works personnel. Executive session doesn’t have to be on the agenda, but the topic does.” 

Local governments can go into executive session to discuss personnel matters and to consult with legal counsel. However, Frankenstein said governmental bodies may not discuss contracts in executive session, unless the discussion involves legal counsel, negotiations, or some marketing or pricing strategies. 

“You can talk about preparing for contract negotiations and employees without an attorney and still do it in private,” she said. 

Above all, Frankenstein said governmental bodies are never permitted to make decisions in executive session. In fact, she said any negotiations, contractual approvals, or other actions taken in executive session are not valid. 

“One thing I see with executive sessions that can really get you sued is when decisions are made in exec, and how that makes you liable,” she said. “If you went into executive session and said, ‘We’ve got this problematic employee, let’s give him a severance package in exchange for him saying nothing disparaging about the city. Let’s make that decision and handle that in secret in executive session, that agreement has no legal validity … you can be sued in any number of ways.” 

Frankenstein also stressed the importance of elected officials’ maintaining the confidentiality of executive session discussions. 

“When you’re legitimately in executive sessions and talking about employees issues, and they’re scandalous or concerning, it is really important to keep that in-house, to retain attorney-client privilege,” she said. “You’re entrusted with public funds. What can sabotage that is if you go home and talk to your spouse. That takes off like wildfire. It’s not a crime to let that out, but you are doing a disservice to the city as an entity by putting its liability at risk. I see this most often with employees and there are defamation lawsuits that can come of that.” 

Frankenstein said when governmental bodies come out of executive session, they do not have to continue discussing matters, and they are permitted to take action on what was previously discussed. 

While official governmental bodies must always meet in public, the same laws don’t always apply to task forces, committees and working groups. However, Frankenstein said in the spirit of transparency, and to ensure there are no meeting violations, she always recommends that those meetings are open. However, if the committee does not exercise sovereign power, which means they do not make decisions on behalf of the city, those meetings are not required to be public. But if the committee performs other traditional government functions, the meetings must be open to the public. Traditional government functions are in the “eye of the beholder,” she said, and are not clearly defined. 

“Just to be safe, have all of the committees and groups meet openly,” she said.

title: Whitewood imposes temporary moratorium against data centers
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: WHITEWOOD — Whitewood city commissioners passed a resolution Monday imposing a temporary moratorium against data centers, allowing the city 12 months to study the potential economic and environmental impacts.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

WHITEWOOD — Whitewood city commissioners passed a resolution Monday imposing a temporary moratorium against data centers, allowing the city 12 months to study the potential economic and environmental impacts.

The resolution places a year-long pause on the approval or issuance of building, planning, or use permits for data collection, storage, or processing centers and bitcoin mining facilities that exceed a power capacity of 250 kilowatts. The pause begins Sept. 7.

According to the resolution, the city claims that data centers, “Have the potential to create an excessive burden on energy and water resources and potential to create noise pollution, effecting nearby property owners, as well as residents, who rely on the local power distribution grid for electricity or subterranean aquifers for portable water.” 

Mayor Sara Fitzgerald said the moratorium, which mirrors recent action taken by Yankton, is done in accordance with South Dakota Codified Law 11-4-3.1. The law requires municipalities to create zoning ordinances “on a rational basis.” 

“Our city attorney researched it and that’s the approach we’re taking,” said Fitzgerald. “It allows us to find information and study the environmental impact and get feedback from the community. If we were going to do a ban on (data centers), then we could include specific language with planning and zoning afterwards. This is just a good faith effort because then people can’t say, ‘Well, the city is acting in bad faith, and they don’t want (data centers).’ No, the city took the steps to investigate it and see what the impact could be and what could happen. This is the city trying to make educated decisions backed by research and sound thinking rather than a bias.”

Fitzgerald said the city has not been approached by contractors looking to build data centers at this time.

title: S.D. pilot accounted for from Vietnam War
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Nearly 60 years after South Dakota pilot Col. Walter A Renelt went missing in the Vietnam War, his remains have been positively identified. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Renelt Photo 1.jpg
Nearly 60 years after South Dakota pilot Col. Walter A Renelt went missing in the Vietnam War, his remains have been positively identified. Courtesy photo 

WASHINGTON — The U.S. Department of Defense POW/MIA Accounting Agency (DPAA) announced Wednesday that U.S. Air Force Col. Walter A. Renelt, 40, of Roberts County, S.D., who was killed in action, was accounted for June 23, 2025.

Renelt’s family recently received their full briefing on his identification, therefore, additional details on his identification can now be shared.

In 1969, Renelt served with the 20th Tactical Air Support Squadron. On Nov. 20, he was an instructor pilot aboard an O-2A Skymaster aircraft with another crew member, on a visual reconnaissance mission over the Lao People’s Democratic Republic. During the mission, the plane was hit by enemy fire and crashed. Bad weather and enemy activity around the crash site prevented ground rescue attempts, and subsequent searches for both crew members were unsuccessful. The United States Air Force made a presumptive finding of death on July 12, 1973.

Beginning in 1994, the Department of Defense initiated a comprehensive review of each case involving unaccounted-for American service members or civilians from the war in Southeast Asia. Between 1995 and 2022, the DoD and Laotian government conducted a number of joint field activities, in an attempt to find Renelt and his crew member. The team found a rank insignia individualized to Renelt.

In May 2025, the team discovered possible human remains, possible material evidence, and possible bone material. All items recovered from the site were accessioned into the DPAA Laboratory for scientific analysis.

To identify Renelt’s remains, scientists from DPAA used dental analysis, as well as material evidence.

Today, Renelt is memorialized on the Courts of the Missing at the National Cemetery of the Pacific in Honolulu, and on the Vietnam Veterans Memorial Wall in Washington, D.C. A rosette will be placed next to his name to indicate he has been accounted for.

Renelt will be buried at Arlington National Cemetery in Arlington, Va., on Aug. 17.

title: SD State Penitentiary loses fourth warden in 5 years amid senior staff shake-up
byline: By John Hult Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: SIOUX FALLS — The South Dakota Department of Corrections has lost its fourth penitentiary warden since 2021 amid staffing changes that also include the departure of 2 other high-ranking officials.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

SIOUX FALLS — The South Dakota Department of Corrections has lost its fourth penitentiary warden since 2021 amid staffing changes that also include the departure of 2 other high-ranking officials.

Joseph Roemmich, who came to South Dakota from New Mexico just over a year ago to oversee the employees and inmates at the oldest parts of the penitentiary in Sioux Falls, is no longer employed by the state, according to department spokesman Michael Winder. He also confirmed the departures of Director of Prison Operations Amber Pirraglia and Maj. Cody Hanson.

Pirraglia was Roemmich’s superior. In addition to Sioux Falls, Pirraglia oversaw prisons in Springfield, Yankton, Pierre and Rapid City. She had previously worked in corrections in Colorado, and came to South Dakota shortly after the hiring of another Colorado transplant, former Corrections Secretary Kellie Wasko.

Wasko hired Roemmich last year, a few months before she resigned. Gov. Larry Rhoden hired Secretary Nick Lamb, who’d worked most recently in Iowa, to succeed Wasko. 

Hanson, who worked for the prison system prior to Wasko’s arrival, was an administrative major at the prison who’d testified to lawmakers as an advocate for a new men’s prison. He’d also helped lead media tours of the penitentiary.

Tabatha Benting, warden of the maximum security Jameson Annex, located on the state penitentiary campus, is now serving as penitentiary warden.

Winder did not offer departure dates or other details on the circumstances surrounding the exit of the three employees. 

A statement from Lamb on Wednesday said staffing changes are part of a broader effort to improve operations across the prison system, though he did not mention any staff members by name. The statement noted the expansion of community service work by inmates, the adoption of a prison seminary program and additional training programs, the expansion of educational partnerships with Southeast Technical College and Western Dakota Technical College, and a tightening of parole supervision.

“I have been evaluating the agency operations, and we are making some personnel changes consistent with the agency’s mission and the steps we’re taking,” Lamb wrote.

Rhoden, in a separate statement, said he’s “proud of the work” Lamb’s done in his first 9 months on the job and called him “a strong leader” who “clearly shares my mission to keep South Dakota strong, safe, and free.”

History of shake-ups amid debate over new construction

The state split warden duties in Sioux Falls into two positions last year. Prior to Roemmich’s arrival, the entire state penitentiary campus — which includes the 1881 penitentiary complex, the Jameson Annex and a separate work release center — was supervised by a single warden.

Roemmich’s predecessor, Teresa Bittinger, served less than two years and oversaw a period of controversy and unrest, which included lockdowns and a temporary shutdown of tablet-based inmate communications. She was appointed in 2023 to replace Dan Sullivan, who also served fewer than two years. He replaced Darin Young, ousted in a staff shake-up initiated by then-Gov. Kristi Noem in 2021.

State lawmakers voted last fall to replace the oldest parts of the penitentiary, which was built prior to South Dakota statehood, with a $650 million facility now under construction on the eastern side of Sioux Falls. The other two prison buildings on the penitentiary campus, located on a hill overlooking Falls Park less than a mile from downtown Sioux Falls, will continue to house inmates when the new prison complex opens in 2029.

Commission member: Loss of institutional knowledge is concerning

Rep. Kadyn Wittman, D-Sioux Falls, is chair of the state’s Corrections Commission. The group is meant to offer guidance on corrections policy, and to approve any spending decisions on prison industries.

The loss of so many leaders is a concern for Wittman. Beyond the wardens, other long-term employees — including Doug Clark, the former deputy corrections secretary who served as interim warden after Young’s departure — have left the prison system over the past five years.

“There’s no real institutional knowledge left,” Wittman said. 

Wittman would like to see the commission move toward monthly meetings and address questions about leadership and institutional knowledge, as well as employee retention more broadly, but said it had been difficult to get traction during Wasko’s term.

The former secretary had sought to limit the commission’s scope of discussion and access to information, and some of the commission’s work has been taken on by the Correctional Rehabilitation Task Force. 

The latter group was formed following the Legislature’s prison funding vote, with a promise from Gov. Rhoden to address the state’s high reoffense rate. 

Lamb has appeared at both of the Corrections Commission meetings held since Wasko’s departure, introducing himself in the first and offering rundowns of the task force’s discussion points during the second.

Wittman said she expects the next Corrections Commission meeting to take place within the next few months. The next meeting of the Correctional Rehabilitation Task Force is scheduled for Aug. 19.

title: SD’s Democratic nominee for US Senate drops out
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Julian Beaudion, a Sioux Falls businessman and former state trooper, announced Tuesday that he’s withdrawing from the race for U.S. Senate. Photo by Joshua Haiar, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
SD’s Democratic nominee for US Senate drops out.jpg
Julian Beaudion, a Sioux Falls businessman and former state trooper, announced Tuesday that he’s withdrawing from the race for U.S. Senate. Photo by Joshua Haiar, South Dakota Searchlight 

South Dakota’s Democratic U.S. Senate nominee ended his campaign Tuesday.

“In recent weeks, my family has faced extraordinary personal challenges,” Julian Beaudion said in a written statement. “As many of you know, we experienced a devastating house fire while continuing to navigate significant personal financial hardship.”

The South Dakota Democratic Party will not select a replacement candidate for the U.S. Senate nominee who ended his campaign Tuesday, a party official said.

That statement came Wednesday from state Democratic Party Deputy Director Joe Zweifel in response to South Dakota Searchlight questions. The deadline to select a new nominee is next week.

Beaudion is a businessman and former state trooper. He had been receiving support from party officials, but some other Democrats had been calling for Beaudion to drop out, saying they believe the independent candidate in the race, Brian Bengs, has a better chance to beat incumbent Republican Sen. Mike Rounds. Bengs ran as the Democratic nominee against Republican U.S. Sen. John Thune in 2022 and received 26% of the vote.

Beaudion alleged in his statement that “an opponent and those associated with the opponent, hit my family and I with intimidating threats to drop out of this race.”

“Those attacks were personal and never about politics,” Beaudion’s statement said. “The mental and physical safety of my family is my priority and for this reason alone, I step aside.”

The Bengs campaign replied to Searchlight questions by sending a written statement from Bengs.

“I have never spoken ill of Julian, and I won’t start now,” Bengs’ statement said, in part. “He is a patriot and I applaud his action. We were both under a great deal of stress, but I entirely reject the notion that there was some behind-the-scenes conspiracy. Nobody has been attacked or threatened.”

The effort to force Beaudion out of the race included American Muckrakers, a website operated by a North Carolina man.

American Muckrakers published articles in recent weeks praising Bengs and sent an email to South Dakota media outlets in June containing allegations about Beaudion, with references to some of the personal struggles Beaudion ultimately alluded to in his statement Tuesday.

The Bengs campaign, in response to earlier Searchlight questions, said it has no formal relationship with American Muckrakers or its author.

Several people who spent decades working in Democratic politics had also been calling for Beaudion to leave the race. They included Steve Jarding, a former executive director of the South Dakota Democratic Party; Steve Hildebrand, who was the deputy national campaign manager for then-Sen. Barack Obama’s successful 2008 presidential campaign and worked on earlier campaigns for former South Dakota U.S. Sens. Tom Daschle and Tim Johnson; and Drey Samuelson, who was Johnson’s chief of staff for 28 years.

Hildebrand had said there’s a stigma associated with the Democratic brand in South Dakota that would prevent Beaudion from winning, and Jarding said “the Democratic brand in South Dakota is dead.” They said Beaudion should drop out to consolidate votes and resources behind Bengs. Beaudion said in his statement Tuesday that he will not endorse Bengs or Rounds.

Democrats have not held a statewide office in South Dakota since January 2015, when Sen. Johnson — who was slowed by health problems — left office after opting against a reelection campaign. Rounds, a former governor, won the race for Johnson’s Senate seat and has held it ever since. 

The gap between registered Republican and Democratic voters in South Dakota has widened in recent years, and Republicans now outnumber Democrats 2.5 to 1. The Democratic Party has been further subjugated by the rise of independents and voters who list no label or affiliation on their registration, who now collectively outnumber Democrats in the state.

South Dakota Democratic Party Chairman Shane Merrill told Searchlight prior to Tuesday that he disagreed with the assertions by Jarding, Hildebrand and Samuelson that the party’s brand is too damaged to win statewide elections in South Dakota.

“I find it rich that the folks that made their living off the South Dakota Democratic Party are now running away from the brand instead of trying to help build and strengthen the brand,” Merrill said. “If we would all work together, we could probably accomplish more.”

Rounds has used the Democratic feud over Beaudion to raise campaign donations, sending emails to potential donors saying “the Democrats are running a fake independent to flip my seat.”

Seth Tupper contributed to this report.

title: Two killed in second Boulder Canyon crash Thursday
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: DEADWOOD — Two people died in a vehicle crash involving a motorcycle near Deadwood Thursday.
_full_text:
DEADWOOD — Two people died in a vehicle crash involving a motorcycle near Deadwood Thursday.

According to the South Dakota Highway Patrol, at approximately 6:27 p.m. a 15-year-old girl from Sturgis was driving a 2009 Jeep Grand Cherokee westbound on U.S. Highway 14A near mile marker 47 in Boulder Canyon. At the same time, a 59-year-old man from Frederick, Colo., was traveling east on a 2020 Harley-Davidson Street Glide with a 54-year-old female passenger and failed to negotiate a turn. The motorcyclist allegedly crossed into the westbound lane and collided with the Jeep.

The motorcyclist and passenger both sustained fatal injuries. Neither were wearing helmets. The driver of the Jeep was not injured, but one passenger sustained minor injuries.

The highway was closed for approximately 3 hours.

The incident remains under investigation.

This was the second crash of the day in Boulder Canyon. Just after 1 p.m., a 2-motorcycle crash occurred just 3 miles away claiming the life of a Sioux Falls woman.

title: 2 killed in Hwy. 385 crash
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: HILL CITY — Two people from Illinois died in a crash Thursday near Hill City involving one vehicle and 2 motorcycles.
_full_text:
HILL CITY — Two people from Illinois died in a crash Thursday near Hill City involving one vehicle and 2 motorcycles.

Names of the those involved have not been released pending notification of family members.

According to the South Dakota Highway Patrol, just before 2 p.m., a 1953 Harley-Davidson, ridden by a 69-year-old man from Emden, Ill., and a passenger, a woman, also 69 years old from Emden, and a 1956 Harley-Davidson FLE 74CI, ridden by a 72-year-old man from Glendale, Ariz., were traveling northbound on U.S. Highway 385 at mile marker 89. At the same time the driver of a 2011 Toyota 4Runner, driven by a 67-year-old woman was in the northbound lanes, waiting for oncoming traffic to pass so she could turn left onto Wrinkle Valley Road. 

Another vehicle was between the Toyota and the Harley-Davidsons. That vehicle passed the Toyota on the right shoulder.

The Harley-Davidson riders attempted to stop and their brakes locked. The driver of the 1956 Harley-Davidson laid his motorcycle onto the road. The 1953 Harley-Davidson collided with the Toyota and caught fire, which spread to the Toyota.

The driver and the passenger of the 1953 Harley-Davidson sustained fatal injuries. Both were wearing helmets. The driver of the 1956 Harley-Davidson was transported to a Rapid City hospital with serious non-life-threatening injuries.

The driver and passenger, a 62-year-old woman of the Toyota were not injured.

U.S. Highway 385 was closed for approximately 4 hours.

The investigation is ongoing.

title: Lawrence Co. commissioners to discuss  consolidation of Spearfish dispatch
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: DEADWOOD — Lawrence County commissioners are expected to discuss the consolidation of the county’s dispatch center with Spearfish, taking possible action on budgetary items to include wage discrepancies, software agreements, and how the state 911 monies will be distributed in coming years.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

DEADWOOD — Lawrence County commissioners are expected to discuss the consolidation of the county’s dispatch center with Spearfish, taking possible action on budgetary items to include wage discrepancies, software agreements, and how the state 911 monies will be distributed in coming years. 

The consolidation is expected to begin Jan. 1, 2027.

Sheriff Brian Dean told commissioners July 30 that 2 positions in Spearfish will require the creation of new positions in the county’s pay scale. Dean said of the 5 dispatchers currently employed by Spearfish, one holds a senior supervisor position, and one has 15 years tenure with the city. The supervisor is set to lose $3.75 per hour, approximately $7,800 per year, in wages if they are hired by the county. The tenured telecommunicator will require longevity benefits and a higher wage than other positions. Dean said he has asked the city of Spearfish to consider a severance package for the supervisor to help smooth the first year of transition and lost wages and pay the approximately $14,000 difference in wage discrepancy for the 2 positions.

Dean said the pay scale and benefits will only apply so long as the supervisor and tenured telecommunicator work for the county. The increased benefits, wages, and titles will not be transferrable to new hires or promoted positions. 

“If those 2 decide to quit and go somewhere else, or otherwise retire, we no longer have a pay discrepancy to accommodate for,” said Dean. “After that, we can make that shift if we need to.”

Dean asked the county to ask Spearfish to pay for 4 telecommunicators, which he said will equate to the Spearfish specific call volume the county’s dispatch center is expected to take on with the consolidation. He said Spearfish will also be asked to compensate the county for the usage of data management software and equipment. 

To off-set the cost the county is requesting from Spearfish, Dean offered to continue to pay the city 50% of the preceding year’s 911 monies. 

“It isn’t fair, given the need to have a close relationship with our counterpart, to take that money from them and then hit them with another $200,000 for employees,” said Dean. “So, what I have presented is that every year we would calculate 50% of the preceding year’s 911 surcharge to count that in Spearfish as a discount. Everybody benefits. We keep the surcharge that helps us pay for the cost of the employees, they get the benefit from money that historically they have been given.”

Regardless of whether or not the city and county consolidate, Dean said the county will need a new server. Dean said he has requested that the city pay the $327,000 cost to upgrade the server, a cost that he said will be reimbursed by a state grant. 

“We can’t operate a (Public Safety Answering Point) PSAP with 2 different systems. They have to be the same system if everybody’s talking,” said Dean. “Spearfish is doing everything they can to reduce the data they want to transfer … which gives us more gap room to try to get them to pay for the server and the maintenance cost of the server.”

Dean said the server will require $15,119 to annually maintain.

To properly maintain the dispatch center, with increased call volume and increased equipment, Dean said the county will need to hire 2 additional telecommunicators on top of the 4 transferring from Spearfish. 

“You need 8 telecommunicators, at minimum, to run your PSAP. Spearfish has 5,” said Dean. “Spearfish has a telecommunicator that hasn’t had a day off in over 60 days. They’re hurting. They’re working 12-hour shifts, they’ve got months to go before we would hit Jan. 1 and consolidate. We are already working on a plan. They’d still be Spearfish employees, but if we can bring them up the hill to get them working in our environment, maybe we can get them a day off by using our staff. That’s some of the exigency that’s going on. We don’t need these people being wore out and burnt out by the time they get up here. The need is real.”

Spearfish Police Chief Collin Smith told Spearfish council members that he’s confident the overall cost to consolidate will not exceed $300,000. If the city does not consolidate, the projected cost to operate a separate PSAP is approximately $980,000. 

“Obviously this is a cost savings and having had the opportunity to tour the Lawrence County facility, they definitely have the capacity room-wise to merge together with us,” said Spearfish Mayor John Senden. “For those who haven’t had the opportunity to see it, that Lawrence County facility is pretty impressive.”

title: Meade Co. Commissioner questions  Rally sales tax collections
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — The state of South Dakota may not be collecting all the sales tax that is due during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, some officials say.
_full_text:
STURGIS — The state of South Dakota may not be collecting all the sales tax that is due during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, some officials say.  

In the wake of approving a new county sales tax to effect property tax relief, a Meade County Commissioner is calling for the S.D. Department of Revenue to examine its bond structure and sales tax collection practices for temporary vendors at the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. 

On July 14, Meade County became the first county in the state to pass an ordinance establishing a one-half percent sales tax, with that money earmarked for property tax relief on owner occupied structures. The commissioners stated the annual Sturgis Motorcycle Rally as one of their primary reasons for passing the tax, since the event draws hundreds of thousands of visitors to Meade County every year. The sales tax revenue generated from people visiting the area, commissioners said, could go a long way toward property tax relief for local citizens. 

But in order to take full advantage of sales taxes during the Rally, Commissioner Doreen Creed said the South Dakota Department of Revenue may need to revise some of its collection practices. 

“I’m completely convinced that 90% of the outside vendors that come to Sturgis would not be coming if indeed their sales only matched the bond that the Department of Revenue asks from its vendors, more or less in a self-reporting situation,” Creed told Michael Houdyshell, secretary for the S.D. Department of Revenue (DOR), during the commission meeting. Houdyshell called in to the meeting to answer questions the commissioners had about a possible county sales tax. 

“You’re telling me that a vendor, who charges $20 for a hot dog, is only paying a $500 bond for sales tax collection,” Creed said. “You cannot convince me that anyone would come to Sturgis if they were only going to sell 500 hot dogs, no drinks or anything else, and only produce $500 in sales taxes.” 

Houdyshell said bond amounts are based on the vendors’ anticipated gross receipts during the Rally. 

Kendra Baucom, marketing and communications specialist with the DOR, said temporary vendors who are new to the Rally, or who have a history of tax delinquency, are required to post a $500 bond before receiving their temporary sales tax license. The bond, she said, is a safeguard to ensure all sales taxes are paid, and once all obligations are met the bond is released and returned to the vendor. 

Baucom said the state regularly reviews the $500 bond amounts, and makes adjustments for individual vendors based on their previous compliance with sales tax reporting. The goal, she said, is to return bonds to vendors within 90 days after all taxes are paid. In some cases that could take longer, she said, but the DOR usually only has to seize about 5 bonds annually due to nonpayment. 

Baucom said vendors who are delinquent on their sales taxes are placed on a list, and they are not permitted to obtain a sales tax license until they have paid amounts due. Each year, she said less than 1% of vendors previously licensed for the Rally have a history of delinquency in filing their sales tax returns or paying sales tax. This year, she said there are 9 vendors on the list of delinquent returns. 

DOR employees conduct manual, in-person inspections during the Rally and temporary vendors are required to file mid-event and end-of-event tax returns. Baucom said the two-step filing process reduces the likelihood that a vendor could leave Sturgis with an outstanding tax obligation.  

“The mid-event return provides an early check-in on sales activity, and the final return ensures accurate reporting before the vendor departs,” Baucom said. “We have a team that performs collection activities on temporary vendors and all businesses operating in South Dakota that do not file and pay returns promptly. Together, these measures make it very difficult for a vendor to pay only the bond, fail to report sales, and leave with unpaid taxes.” 

Despite assurances about the effectiveness of the state’s processes, Creed said she suspects that a large amount of the state’s increased sales taxes during the Rally come from established businesses that have a permanent sales tax license, and can be easily audited, rather than from temporary vendors who leave the state immediately after the Rally.  

“The amount of sales tax we collect, I do not believe reflects the (actual) sales,” Creed told Houdyshell at the meeting. “I believe you would reap great benefits if the bond structure was altered significantly when you see the prices charged.” 

According to the DOR, Rally vendors are subject to the same review and audit statutes as any other business operating in South Dakota. Baucom said the last time the DOR audited a temporary vendor was 2025, but did not report the outcome of the audit. 

“The department cannot disclose information regarding individual vendors or any lists related to licensing restrictions or past tax delinquencies,” she said. “While we do maintain internal records to support compliance and licensing decisions, the number of vendors with a history of delinquency is confidential.” 

In 2025, the state of South Dakota collected almost $1.6 million in sales tax from temporary Rally vendors, a 13% increase from 2024 collections of $1.4 million. The amounts included $901,512 in state sales tax, $299,619 in tourism taxes, and $380,603 in municipal sales tax.

In 2025, for the 85th Annual Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, there were 1,181 temporary vendors set up throughout the Black Hills — a 32% increase over 2024. Of those, 1,069 were in the Northern Black Hills and generated about $1.2 million in sales tax revenue. Internal calculations prepared for this report show that at the general sales tax rate of 7.7% inside city limits, that represents approximately $14,578 in taxable sales from each vendor. 

These numbers are not exact, but are meant to provide an illustration of vendor revenue. They are not exact because there are different tax rates based upon the nature of the vendor businesses and where they are located. In Sturgis, Deadwood, Lead, Spearfish, Custer, Hill City, Whitewood, Keystone, Rapid City, Hot Springs, and Belle Fourche, the general sales tax rate is 7.7%; food and alcohol vendors are charged 8.7%; and motorcycle rental vendors are charged 11.9%. In Newell and Piedmont, vendors charge 7.7% for food and other merchandise. Outside of city limits, vendors charge a 5.7% general sales tax, food and alcohol, and a 9.9% tax for motorcycle rentals. 

Baucom said when it comes to temporary vendors during the Rally, the DOR does not track sales tax receipts from separate categories, therefore it is not possible pinpoint estimated taxable sales in each category. While the DOR lists monthly statistical information for general, food, and motorcycle rental vendors, those figures also include permanent businesses, and are tracked across the state. 

The costs to do business during the Rally can vary. In Sturgis, all vendors are required to obtain a vendor license from the city, with costs ranging from $560 to $1,500, based on square footage of the vendor booth. 

The cost of vendor spaces varies greatly. City-owned vendor booth costs start at about $2,000 for a 10-foot by 10-foot space, and can go up to $20,000 or more. Other privately-owned properties may charge different rates for vendor space, and various other fees apply for specialty vendors such as food service, tattoo, body piercing, and others. 

In order to handle the increased volume of temporary vendor sales, Houdyshell said the DOR brings in extra staff from across the state during the Rally, and agents are regularly interacting with vendors to ensure proper collection amounts. Baucom said about 25-35 DOR employees support operations during the Rally, which represents about 10% of the department’s workforce. Not all of those employees work onsite all the time, but the DOR usually opens a temporary office at Sturgis City Hall on the Tuesday before the Rally begins, and closes it the Monday after the event. Agents typically spend more than 1,000 hours on the ground in Sturgis and the surrounding areas, and put in a total of about 100 hours of overtime, checking temporary vendor compliance. Baucom said the staff review vendor sales records, inventory, and purchase invoices, to ensure the correct amount of tax is paid. 

Recently, Houdyshell said the DOR started an electronic filing system that allows vendors to pay their taxes immediately, which streamlines the process. 

 “They’re definitely putting in overtime during the Rally when they’re out there working, and you know we’ve got a pretty good presence that’s out there, doing the best we can to keep tabs on all these temporary vendors,” Houdyshell said. “It’s a challenge. It’s certainly something we’re more than willing to discuss with the county, and we’re always open to ideas on how we can manage the rallies more effectively. It is by far our biggest special event that we work, and clearly it’s something that we believe we put a lot of time and effort into. But that doesn’t mean we can’t learn and improve going forward.”

Fatal Crashes:

• At approximately 4:41 p.m. Saturday, on U.S. 85, near mile marker 35: A 2003 Harley-Davidson Electra Glide motorcycle, operated by a 72-year-old man, was traveling north on U.S. 85 near mile marker 35. The driver braked when approaching a turning motorcycle in front of him. The driver lost control of the vehicle and became separated from the motorcycle. The driver was transported to Monument Health in Spearfish. The driver sustained fatal injuries.

Injury Crashes:

• At 9:19 a.m. Saturday, on US Highway 16A, near mile marker 33: A 2017 Harley-Davidson motorcycle operated by a 68-year-old man (Unit 1) was driving westbound on US 16A near MM 33. A 2026 Harley-Davidson motorcycle operated by a 60-year-old male (Unit 2) was driving westbound in front of Unit 1 with a 61-year-old female passenger. Unit 2 slowed for traffic and Unit 1 was unable to slow and collided with the rear of Unit 2. All riders were wearing helmets and received non-life-threatening injuries.

• At 11:20 a.m. Saturday, at North Rochford Road and US 14A: A 2007 Harley-Davidson motorcycle, operated by a 67-year-old male, was traveling in a group, northbound on North Rochford Road, near its intersection with US 14A. The driver entered a left curve and lost control. The driver became separated from the motorcycle and came to final rest on the northbound shoulder. He was not wearing a helmet. He was life-flighted to Rapid City Monument Health with serious injuries.

• At 11:46 a.m. on Saturday, on US Highway 14A, near mile marker 32: A 2018 Harley-Davidson motorcycle, operated by a 59-year-old man, was driving eastbound on Highway 14A near mile marker 32. The driver failed to negotiate a curve in the roadway and enter the ditch. The driver was separated from his motorcycle. The driver was transported to Lead-Deadwood Monument Health for treatment of his injuries.

• At 4:50 p.m. on Saturday, US Highway 14A, mile marker 47: A 2026 Harley-Davidson motorcycle, operated by a 54-year-old man, was traveling east on US 14A. An unidentified vehicle was westbound and crossed the center of the roadway, making contact with the male driver of the Harley. The driver of Harley was transported to Monument Health for treatment of his injuries.

• At 6:32 p.m. on Saturday, South Dakota Highway 44, near mile marker 34: A 2016 Harley-Davidson motorcycle, operated by a 39-year-old man, was traveling westbound near mile marker 34 on South Dakota 44 with a 28-year-old female passenger. A 2019 Subaru Forester, operated by a 66-year-old woman, was in front of the motorcycle attempting to make a left turn. The motorcycle switched lanes and collided with Subaru as it turned. The driver of the Subaru was transported to Monument Health for treatment of minor injuries.

• At 6:48 p.m. on Saturday, US Highway 16, near mile maker 59: A 2019 Harley-Davidson motorcycle, operated by a 69-year-old man, was westbound on US 16 near mile marker 59. The motorcycle’s rear tire failed, and the driver was unable to maintain control and became separated from the motorcycle. He was wearing a helmet and was transported to Monument Health for treatment of his injuries.
