title: Grace Lutheran Church serves up breakfast, fellowship during Sturgis Motorcycle Rally
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: Connie Hurlburt and Marlene Kotab serve up the breakfast on Sunday in the basement of the Grace Lutheran Church in Sturgis.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
1. grace.jpeg
Connie Hurlburt and Marlene Kotab serve up the breakfast on Sunday in the basement of the Grace Lutheran Church in Sturgis.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

STURGIS — The smell of pancakes, sausage, biscuits and gravy filled Grace Lutheran Church Saturday morning as the church welcomed motorcycle riders and visitors for its annual Rally Motorcycle Breakfast.

The breakfast began Saturday and will continue each morning through Friday, giving Rally-goers another opportunity to enjoy a hot meal while visiting with friends, meeting new people and experiencing some Sturgis hospitality.

David Lyons, chairman of the Grace Lutheran Church Rally Motorcycle Breakfast, said this year’s menu includes several traditional breakfast favorites.

“We are serving our biscuits and gravy, and then our pancakes, sausage and eggs,” Lyons said. “It takes a lot just to get it all together, but it’s all worth it in the end because you meet a lot of good people.”

The breakfast is served from 6:30-11 a.m. each day.

The popular event requires about 20 volunteers to keep the kitchen, serving area and dining room running smoothly. With large numbers of visitors coming through the doors during the rally, volunteers often find themselves working at a fast pace.

“We’re really swamped,” Lyons said Saturday morning, taking a brief break from the busy breakfast service. “But we welcome anybody to come down and have breakfast with us.”

For Grace Lutheran’s pastors, the annual breakfast is about more than simply serving a meal. It is an opportunity for the congregation to put its faith into action by welcoming visitors and serving others.

Grace Lutheran Pastor Kevin Jensen said the breakfast’s mission connects closely with the biblical story of Jesus feeding the 5,000.

“Since the gospel text recently was about Jesus feeding the 5,000, we have our Lord behind us as we feed the nearly 1,500 people who come to our Rally breakfasts every year,” Jensen said. “Our feeding ministry reminds us of the importance of giving for the sake of others. Remembering that helps our volunteers delight in sharing a meal and fellowship with all who come, especially the many bikers who return every year.”

Pastor Carla Nelson said the church is happy to open its doors to anyone looking for a meal and a welcoming place during the rally.

“We are always so happy to extend hospitality, provide a place where all are welcome and feed hungry people just as Jesus did,” Nelson said.

For many visitors, the Grace Lutheran breakfast has become an annual tradition, with returning customers making a point of stopping at the church each year during the rally.

The event also provides an opportunity for fellowship beyond the breakfast table. The Christian Motorcycle Riders gather upstairs at the church, providing riders with a place to visit, connect with others and share their faith.

In addition to breakfast and fellowship, Grace Lutheran also offers a selection of quilts for sale, with the church’s women showcasing their handiwork during the rally.

The combination of food, fellowship and hospitality has made the annual breakfast a popular stop for both longtime rally visitors and those experiencing it for the first time.

title: Microbes discovered at SURF engineered to convert corn into cancer-fighting drug
byline: By Sarah Rusell and Audrey Arndt Dakota BioWorx
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
microbes fight cancer.jpg
Courtesy photo 

LEAD — A set of microbes, discovered by South Dakota School of Mines and Technology researchers deep underground at SURF, are being used to convert corn into an enhanced cancer therapy. The emerging technology is a boon for both South Dakota’s agriculture and biotech economies.

More than a mile beneath the surface of Lead, in conditions of intense pressure, complete darkness, and near-total isolation from the outside world, microorganisms have survived for millennia by developing biochemical capabilities found nowhere else on Earth.

Now, a South Dakota research team is turning those survival strategies into a platform for precision cancer therapy.

Dr. Rajesh Sani, distinguished professor in the Karen M. Swindler Department of Chemical and Biological Engineering and Chemistry, Biology & Health Sciences at South Dakota Mines and director of the MASON Laboratory, has received a biomedical research award to develop biodegradable drug delivery systems for cancer treatment. The grant is administered through the Haarberg 3D Center at South Dakota State University, a Governor’s Research Center funded by the South Dakota Board of Regents.

The source material for the research: extremophilic microbes collected from the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) in Lead, the largest and one of the deepest, most scientifically significant research environments in the world.

“These organisms have spent millions of years solving problems that we’re only beginning to understand,” said Sani. “What they’ve developed to survive extreme conditions, the polymers, the enzymes, the bioactive compounds, turns out to have remarkable potential in therapeutic applications.”

Delivering drugs where they’re needed most

At the center of the project is the development of so-called “smart” drug carriers: tiny, biodegradable particles engineered to carry chemotherapy or other cancer medications directly to a tumor site, releasing their payload in response to the specific chemical conditions found within tumors. The goal is to dramatically reduce the systemic side effects that make many cancer treatments debilitating.

“If we can deliver drugs more precisely, we can improve outcomes and quality of life at the same time,” Sani said. “Our goal is to help cancer treatments work where they’re needed most while reducing the burden on patients.”

The research draws on biopolymers and compounds originally developed by Sani’s group for entirely different applications, clean energy systems and space exploration environments, that are now being adapted for biomedical use for the first time.

“This award represents a significant milestone in my research program, marking the first time my group’s extremophile-based biopolymer platforms are being translated into biomedical and cancer-focused applications,” Sani said.

SURF: A scientific resource below the surface

As America’s Underground Lab, and one of 16 similar labs around the world, SURF is home to world-class physics experiments, including groundbreaking dark matter detection and neutrino research. The facility’s deep subsurface environment, including 370 miles of tunnels and shafts, also serves as a reservoir of biological diversity that remains largely unexplored. Sani was among the first biologists to conduct sampling at SURF and has been carrying out research underground there for nearly 2 decades. Under those extreme conditions (high pressure, scarce nutrients, and near-zero oxygen levels) only the most biochemically resourceful organisms survive. The result is microbial life with molecular capabilities that simply do not exist in surface environments.

“As a dedicated scientific facility, SURF is proud to serve the entire underground science community, with incredible potential to impact a range of research disciplines. The tremendous breadth and environmental diversity at SURF is especially relevant for those in the life sciences community, and we are thrilled to have played a role in these impressive advances made by Dr. Sani and his state-wide collaborators,” said Dr. Jaret Heise, science director at SURF. 

Sani’s team at South Dakota Mines has isolated and characterized more than 500 extremophilic microorganisms using advanced multi-omics approaches, including next-generation sequencing genomics, epigenomics, transcriptomics, metabolomics, and proteomics. This work is helping develop a fundamental understanding of how these organisms function in extreme environments and how their unique biomolecules can be harnessed for bioprocessing, biomaterials, and biomedical applications. 

This entire effort can be further enhanced with research funding legislation now being considered in the U.S. Congress. The bipartisan Homestake AI Act invests in genome sequencing to tap the wealth of biological life living underground at SURF. This research can lead to breakthroughs in new medicines and potential disease cures.

Scaling the science at Dakota BioWorx

Translating laboratory discoveries into materials that can be tested, refined, and eventually manufactured at scale requires infrastructure that most academic labs cannot provide alone. That’s where Dakota BioWorx comes in.

Based at the SDSU Research Park in Brookings, Dakota Bioworx is a bioprocess contract development and manufacturing organization built specifically to bridge the gap between early-stage research and real-world production. Sani’s team, including Co-PI and research scientist Dipayan Samanta, Ph.D., graduate student Anjali Thapliyal, and undergraduate researchers Nathaniel Strickland, Samantha Harris, Kaleb Borges, and Kara Fletcher, is conducting pilot-scale fermentation and biomass harvesting at the Dakota BioWorx facility.

“South Dakota Mines is doing important work at the leading edge of biomedical research,” said Craig Arnold, CEO of Dakota BioWorx. “Dakota BioWorx exists to provide the infrastructure that helps that kind of innovation scale, giving researchers the ability to test, refine, and advance their work in a real-world bioprocessing environment.”

The work is being developed from the outset with future clinical use in mind, following production and documentation standards designed to support eventual regulatory review and industry partnership.

A South Dakota Story

The collaboration connecting SURF’s subsurface environment, South Dakota Mines’ research capabilities, and Dakota BioWorx’s bioprocessing infrastructure represents something unusual in the life sciences: a fully in-state pipeline from discovery to development, anchored by a diverse set of stakeholders across state government and universities, committed to keeping that work here.

Support for the broader research program also includes applications associated with corn grind supplied by South Dakota State University, which serves as the primary feedstock for cultivating the extremophilic microbes at the heart of Sani’s platform.

“Dakota BioWorx was built to be the infrastructure layer that South Dakota’s biotech ecosystem needed,” Arnold said. “We’re not just supporting local research — we’re working with biotech innovators from across the United States and internationally who are choosing South Dakota as their development and manufacturing partner. That’s how you build a bioeconomy. You build the infrastructure first, and the ecosystem grows around it.”

The combined ecosystem is tied closely to South Dakota’s agriculture industry, one of the top economic drivers in the state. The research represents a new use case for corn, connecting South Dakota’s largest commodity crop to one of the most active areas of biomedical innovation and potentially opening a South Dakota-grown pathway for next-generation cancer therapy technologies.

The research is ongoing. Results will inform future development pathways and potential industry partnerships as the team advances the platform toward translational and clinical application.

title: Candidates for SD governor  will debate twice in September
byline: By John Hult Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Democratic nominee Dan Ahlers, left, will face Republican nominee Gov. Larry Rhoden in the Nov. 3 general election. South Dakota Searchlight photos by Joshua Haiar and Makenzie Huber
_full_text:
Candidates for SD governor  will debate twice in September
Democratic nominee Dan Ahlers, left, will face Republican nominee Gov. Larry Rhoden in the Nov. 3 general election. South Dakota Searchlight photos by Joshua Haiar and Makenzie Huber 

HURON — Two debates between South Dakota’s candidates for governor will take place in September.

The first will be at the South Dakota State Fair in Huron during the fair Sept. 2-7, with the time and date of the debate yet to be confirmed. 

The second is scheduled for 7 p.m. on Sept. 28, and will take place at the South Dakota Public Broadcasting studio in Sioux Falls, in partnership with South Dakota News Watch.

Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden won the nomination to be his party’s candidate after finishing second in a four-way primary on June 2, and then defeating Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden in a July 28 runoff.

The general election will take place on Nov. 3. 

Rhoden is seeking to be elected governor for the first time. The former lieutenant governor assumed the governorship in January of 2025, when then-Gov. Kristi Noem took a job with President Donald Trump’s administration. 

Rhoden is running with his lieutenant governor, Tony Venhuizen. 

Democrat Dan Ahlers, a former lawmaker from Dell Rapids, has yet to announce a running mate, but told South Dakota Searchlight on Friday he expects to reveal his pick “very shortly.”

In a press release announcing Rhoden’s intention to participate in the two debates, Venhuizen preemptively challenged Ahlers’ running mate to a debate.

Ahlers, who said he’d accepted the invitations for the two debates, said his running mate is prepared to debate Venhuizen.

title: Meade Co. Commission enacts emergency burn ban due to extreme fire danger
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: MEADE COUNTY – Due to extremely dangerous fire conditions throughout Meade County, the Meade County Commission has enacted a new resolution, effective immediately.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

MEADE COUNTY – Due to extremely dangerous fire conditions throughout Meade County, the Meade County Commission has enacted a new resolution, effective immediately.

Recent weather conditions have created an exceptionally high fire risk across the county. Prolonged heat, dry vegetation, and persistent winds have combined to produce conditions where a single spark could quickly develop into a large and destructive wildfire.

Residents and visitors are urged to exercise extreme caution and comply with all provisions of the burn ban. The burn ban prohibits open fires; burn barrels; any activities that produce embers or sparks capable of igniting surround dry material; smoking outdoors; and outdoor grills. 

With the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally bringing thousands of visitors to the Black Hills, Meade County welcomes everyone to enjoy the area responsibly. However, current fire conditions require heightened awareness from everyone who lives in or visits the county.

A single careless act could threaten lives, homes, livestock, businesses, and thousands of acres of public and private land.

In addition to the burn ban, Meade County Commissioners also directed the county equalization office to not issue any licenses for temporary vendors who sell fireworks. That ban on selling fireworks will be in effect through Dec. 31.

title: 24th annual Mayor’s Ride celebrates Sturgis tradition, honors late Mayor Kevin Forrester
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: A large group of riders joined the 24th annual Sturgis Mayors Ride on Saturday for a ride throughout the hills, raising money for a local charity. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
2. ride.JPG
A large group of riders joined the 24th annual Sturgis Mayors Ride on Saturday for a ride throughout the hills, raising money for a local charity. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

 3. ride.JPG
Sturgis Mayor Rod Bradley and his mother lead the 24th annual Sturgis Mayors Ride on Saturday from the community center parking lot. Pioneer photo Tim Potts 

STURGIS — The 24th annual Sturgis Mayor’s Ride rolled through the Black Hills Saturday, bringing motorcycle enthusiasts together for a day of riding, camaraderie and support for local charities.  

This year’s ride was especially meaningful for Sturgis Mayor Rod Bradley, who participated in his first Mayor’s Ride after years of working the night shift during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally.

Bradley said former Mayor Kevin Forrester, who died in April, talked with him about the event after participating in last year’s ride.

“He told me how much fun he had and what a great group of people it was,” Bradley said. “So, for me at least, I’ll be riding with or for him today, and I’m looking forward to that.”

Riders wore a special K4 patch during this year’s event in memory of Forrester, a Sturgis mayor and community leader.

Bradley said the ride route was changed this year, with riders returning to Sturgis City Park for lunch rather than traveling to Custer State Park.

“They’ve switched the route up a bit,” Bradley said. “We end up back in Sturgis at the city park for lunch. Before, they ended up in Custer State Park, and logistically this is a little better. It will also give this group of people a chance to enjoy the city park.”

The Mayor’s Ride is more than a motorcycle tour through the Black Hills. Proceeds from the event are donated to a local charity selected by the mayor.

Bradley said he had not yet received a final rider count, but he expected a strong turnout.

Bradley said the community support surrounding the Mayor’s Ride is one of the reasons the event has remained an important part of the rally.

“We really appreciate that,” Bradley said of the ride’s support of local charities. “That’s always something that the town looks forward to, you guys coming together to ride today and support the local charities.”

The Sturgis Police Department provided an escort for the ride, helping guide the group through the Black Hills.

Sturgis Police Officer Jameson Tebben led the ride on one of the department’s newer motorcycles, a Harley-Davidson Pan America 1200.

Tebben said the department added the motorcycle to its fleet in 2024. Sturgis Responder Supply helped outfit the bike with emergency lights.

“It’s a little more agile. It’s off-road, so it lends itself to being able to do a little bit tighter turns and patrol function,” Tebben said. “But it’s a good bike and runs fast and adds a little bit of a new character to the fleet.”

The Pan America joins the department’s traditional Harley-Davidson Electra Glide motorcycles. “It’s not to replace the Electra Glide,” Tebben said. “We can’t replace the classic one.”

Bradley encouraged riders to enjoy the day while keeping safety a priority.

“We’ve got a great route today,” Bradley said. “The Sturgis Police will escort us through it, and we want everybody to ride safe.”

A Harley-Davidson representative noted the connection between the motorcycle company and the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally.

“I’m thrilled to be here this morning,” the representative said. “It’s Harley-Davidson’s 123rd year, Sturgis’ 86th year, and glad to say we’ve been riding with you ever since. Beautiful morning, great day for a ride. Let’s get after it.”

The 24th annual event continued a tradition of bringing riders together to experience the Black Hills while giving back to the Sturgis community.

title: Second chip seal complete on Colorado Boulevard
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Colorado Boulevard is pictured on Thursday, before all lanes of traffic were reopened. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Thursday chip seal.jpeg
Colorado Boulevard is pictured on Thursday, before all lanes of traffic were reopened. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

 Friday alt.JPG
Colorado Boulevard, where chip sealing has wrapped up, is pictured on Friday. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — Colorado Boulevard from US Highway 14A at Spearfish Canyon to Grant Street has reopened both lanes of traffic, and a second application of chip seal is complete.

“Our staff has inspected the product. Additionally, a representative from the South Dakota Local Transportation Assistance Program (SD LTAP) has inspected the product and is confident that the product will perform as intended,” said Spearfish Public Works Director Adam McMahon. “The SD LTAP representative is a person with over 30 years of experience with roadways and chip seals.”

On Thursday, there were places where chips seemed sparse, and oil appeared to bleed through the road surface. The Pioneer asked about these areas, and if they could be the result of vehicles frequently turning off of the arterial road and into the parking lots and side streets that flank Colorado Boulevard.

“It is not uncommon for there to be some bleed-through in some locations on a chip seal project. The reapplication made this especially challenging to account for an inconsistent amount of residual oil from the previous chip seal. Blotting sand will be used again in the future if the oil bleeds through and starts to track onto tires,” McMahon said.

As far as high traffic volumes and frequent turning are concerned, McMahon said there are examples of roads that have been chip sealed successfully and are subject to similar conditions.

“We inquired about this with the representative from SD LTAP about this concern, and they assured us that the chip seal should still perform at the traffic volume levels we see on Colorado Boulevard. Chip seals are commonly used on municipal roadways with similar amounts of turning traffic in many other areas of the state and the country,” McMahon said.

Old Highway 14 has an estimated average daily traffic (ADT) count of 4,300 vehicles. Colorado Boulevard east of Ext 14 sees about 7,200 vehicles each day. Both stretches of road have been chip sealed.

“Colorado Boulevard from Grant Street to US Hwy 14A has an ADT of approximately 9,700 vehicles per day with 2 lanes of traffic in each direction,” McMahon said. “ The average number of vehicles per day per lane on Colorado Boulevard from Grant Street to US Hwy 14A is within the range of other successful chip seals in our area.”

The project will be warrantied after the city council accepts the completed result, McMahon added.

The city plans to mill and overlay the remainder of Colorado Boulevard from Grant Street to Jackson Boulevard. A contract for that work still needs to be awarded.

title: 3-wheeled cycles a hot ride in Sturgis even as hidden safety issue arises
byline: By Bart Pfankuch South Dakota News Watch
description: Bikers say three-wheeled cycles are more stable and provide greater space for carrying things, including dogs that wear goggles, as seen in downtown Sturgis. Photo by Bart Pfankuch, South Dakota News Watch
_full_text:
3-wheeled cycles a hot ride in Sturgis even as hidden safety issue arises 1.jpg
Bikers say three-wheeled cycles are more stable and provide greater space for carrying things, including dogs that wear goggles, as seen in downtown Sturgis. Photo by Bart Pfankuch, South Dakota News Watch 

 3-wheeled cycles a hot ride in Sturgis even as hidden safety issue arises 2.jpg
Bob Walker, 83, of New York, rode his three-wheeled Harley-Davidson to the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally this year and stopped briefly at a discount store in Summerset. Photo by Bart Pfankuch, South Dakota News Watch 

 3-wheeled cycles a hot ride in Sturgis even as hidden safety issue arises 3.jpg
Sue and Craig Hillman stand by their Can-A Spyder three-wheeled motorcycle in downtown Sturgis. Photo by Bart Pfankuch, South Dakota News Watch 

STURGIS — It takes only a brief drive through the streets of Sturgis during the 2026 Rally to realize that 3-wheeled cycles have become a hot trend in the biker world.

Motorcycles with 3 wheels instead of 2 can readily be seen driving in traffic, parked amid the rows of bikes on Main Street or displayed at temporary sales and rental lots that pop up during the Sturgis rally that attracts more than 500,000 bikers each August.

The key innovations of 3-wheelers are greater stability while driving or stopped, increased visibility for users and among other motorists, more spacious rider and passenger seating and expanded cargo space. The three-wheelers are also more adaptive for riders with physical limitations or disabilities.

But while they are by design more stable than 2-wheelers, they also carry navigation challenges that can increase loss of control or rollover risk in some travel situations, namely while turning, navigating curves or steering at high speeds.

“The people who are moving to a 3-wheeled machine do need to realize that it takes a lot more strength to steer,” said Gina Suelflow, a certified cycle trainer with the South Dakota Safety Council. “We’ve seen a lot of people get themselves into trouble there because they don’t have the upper body strength required.”

Suelflow said people who shift from two-wheeled to three-wheeled motorcycles need to know that trikes do not allow for leaning of the bike, the main method for turning a 2-wheeled cycle. Three-wheelers are often heavier than traditional motorcycles and do not always handle well at high speeds, she said.

“It is harder to steer at a higher speed, especially given that you have more weight and you have to press much harder to steer,” said Suelflow, a Rapid City-based trainer with the statewide nonprofit safety group. “They’re fun, but they just need to be navigated correctly.”

Sioux Falls woman killed in 3-wheeler wreck

The risks associated with driving a trike – or any cycle for that matter – were made tragically clear in an Aug. 1 accident that killed a Sioux Falls woman who was riding on a 2025 Can-Am Spyder RT three-wheeled cycle.

Dawn Hillman, 67, was killed in the single-vehicle accident that happened just after 11 a.m. on South Rochford Road about 5 miles west of Rochford in the Northern Black Hills, according to the South Dakota Highway Patrol. 

The wreck occurred when the driver of the 3-wheeled cycle, Randall Lee Hillman, 72, of Sioux Falls, failed to negotiate a curve and left the road, causing the vehicle to roll, the state said.

He was taken to a Rapid City hospital with serious, non-life-threatening injuries. Both occupants were wearing helmets, and the investigation into the accident is ongoing. News Watch reached Hillman by phone on Aug. 5 but he declined to discuss the accident.

Sales higher and expected to rise more

Three-wheeled cycles fall largely into 2 main categories – those with 2 wheels in the rear and one in front, and those with 2 wheels in front and one in back. In both cases, navigation and turning is done via the front wheel or wheels.

The cycles with 2 wheels at the rear are often called trikes, and Harley-Davidson is a major manufacturer.

Those with two wheels in front are mainly referred to by their trade names, including the Can-Am Spyder and Ryker, the Polaris Slingshot and the Yamaha Niken or Tricity.

Three-wheeled cycle sales are on the rise across the U.S. and are expected to continue to climb over the next decade, according to Future Market Insights, a financial research firm. Overall sales were $1.9 billion in 2020, rose to $2.7 billion in 2025 and could reach $5.5 billion by 2035, an industry analysis showed.

Accident data not provided for 3-wheelers

Safety data is hard to come by because the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration lumps crash and fatality data on 3-wheelers into the same category as 2-wheeled cycles, which still dominate the market.

But some statistics can still be helpful in understanding the risks of 3-wheelers and for motorcycles overall.

For example, motorcycles remain much less safe than passenger cars and trucks, with a fatality rate that’s 28 times greater for cycles on a per-mile basis. Motorcycle deaths have risen by 23% since 2019, with the highest fatality rate on cycles coming among drivers aged 50 years or older.

Alcohol was a factor in 26% of fatal cycle wrecks in 2023, and during August of each year, South Dakota has by far the highest per-capita cycle death rate among all U.S. states.

The NHTSA does compile accident data on all-terrain vehicles, which the agency says are increasingly being driven on public roadways. 

ATV deaths in the U.S. rose by 66% in a recent 10-year period, from 325 in 2014 to 540 in 2024. About 70% of fatalities came in single-vehicle wrecks and more than two-thirds of deaths occurred in rollover accidents.

He likes his trike, but goes easy on turns

Bob Walker of upstate New York rode his 2010 Harley-Davidson Tri Glide three-wheeler 1,900 miles through Canada and back into the United States on his way to attend the 2026 Sturgis Rally.

Walker, 83, said he rode 3-wheeled cycles for decades but transitioned to the trike when his knees got weak and it became more difficult to keep a traditional motorcycle upright.

“I love this bike, and you can’t beat it,” Walker said. “You don’t have to worry about stabilizing yourself or holding yourself upright.”

Walker said he has noticed the increasing popularity of 3-wheelers at cycle rallies in Sturgis and at other biker events he attends across the U.S.

But he doesn’t care for the look or handling of cycles with 2 wheels up front. He has taken test rides of cycles with two wheels in front and said they remind him of the difficult maneuverability of a forklift, which he drove at work prior to retirement.

He said his trike handles well and takes curves with ease, even in the Black Hills where bikers often ride scenic 2-lane highways with limited shoulders and numerous hills, curves and switchbacks.

But Walker said slower speeds for 3-wheelers are mandatory to be safe in turns. On rough, bumpy surfaces, greater care is also required on his trike because the low weight of the front wheel can cause it to jump around or sometimes lift off the ground, resulting in a brief loss of navigability.

“You’ve got to watch every corner around here,” he said. “And you have to be careful no matter what you ride.”

Medical conditions drive shift to a Spyder

Craig Hillman and his wife, Sue, trailered a 3-wheeler for him and a 2-wheeler for her from their home in Plymouth, Mass., to attend the 2026 Sturgis Rally as a celebration of Craig’s 65th birthday. The couple was shopping on Main Street in Sturgis on Aug. 5 with their cycles parked on the street.

Craig shifted to his 2024 Can-Am Spyder with 2 wheels in front for greater stability after it became difficult to maneuver his two-wheeled cycle and keep it upright while stopped.

“I’m full of medical hardware,” he said, citing past surgeries in his hips, foot and wrist. “It’s just the ease of riding it and you don’t have to put your feet down to hold it up.”

The Hillmans said they see more 3-wheeled cycles on the roads and have attended state rallies specific to Spyder models. Craig said that while he feels safer on his Spyder, caution is required to maintain control in some situations.

“It’s very user-friendly and easy to drive,” he said. “But you cannot take corners fast, you just can’t.”

title: Lead saves on Dwight Street  retaining wall repair
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Lead city crews work to repair the Dwight Street retaining wall. Work was completed in late July, Public Works Director Jason Bauernfeind said. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
Dwight street wall 1.jpeg
Lead city crews work to repair the Dwight Street retaining wall. Work was completed in late July, Public Works Director Jason Bauernfeind said. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

LEAD — Repairs to the Dwight Street retaining wall cost the city of Lead less than expected, officials say. 

During the Aug. 3 Lead City Commission meeting, Public Works Director Jason Bauernfeind said crews were able to fix the wall for about $6,700, plus $4,300 for replacing a section of asphalt crews took out in order to fix the wall. Bauernfeind said the total cost includes the purchase of a few blocks, base coarse, clean rock, drain tile and geogrid. 

In June the city of Lead closed Dwight Street to the public, in order to replace the retaining wall under a section of the street. Many of the blocks from the wall could be re-used, Bauernfeind said, which contributed to cost savings for the repair.  

In a related matter, the commission also approved a quote from Johner Paving to repair an asphalt section at the end of Julius Street, where the concrete ends.

“It’s kind of a bomb zone down there,” Bauernfeind said. “It’s been on the books that we wanted to get that done and we have the money in the budget.” 

The quote for the Julius Street project was for $22,600, but Bauernfeind said Johner Paving also agreed to lay asphalt down on a section of Dwight Street that was torn up due to the wall repair, at the extra cost of $4,300. If the city added Dwight Street to the awarded bid, Bauernfeind said it would save on mobilization costs for the contractor, resulting in a less expensive bid. Overall, the commission approved $26,900 to fix sections of both Julius and Dwight streets.

title: Motorists be warned – road construction underway as Rally begins
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — Several construction projects are underway as the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally gets into full swing.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

SPEARFISH — Several construction projects are underway as the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally gets into full swing. 

Highway 14 near Exit 10

Work is underway on Highway 14 to create a “loon.”

To help alleviate congestion at the intersection of Highway 85 and Old Highway 14 as well as the off ramps for Interstate 90, a stoplight will be installed at the intersection. Turning left from Old Highway 14 and onto Highway 85 will be prohibited. Instead, traffic will be directed to turn right on North Avenue. A turnaround area, called a “loon” will allow traffic to return to their desired northbound traffic. 

Mike Carlson, Rapid City area engineer for the South Dakota Department of Transportation, said, paving is underway but the project will not reach full completion until the fall.

“We have to get that signal (light) up at the eastbound on and off ramps, and it takes a while to get those signal poles manufactured and sent to us,” he said. “The bulk of the work will be done this summer, maybe just after Rally, but we’ll be doing the signals on the lights later on this fall.”

Cheyenne Crossing

Two projects are underway near Cheyenne Crossing.

One, on Highway 14A, saw a rock buttress holding up the hillside removed.

“We had to take out some dirt, put a bunch of big rocks in to anchor that hillside. So that job is just about done. It should wrap up pretty soon,” he said. 

Traffic remains one lane only controlled by traffic lights. 

Just east of Cheyenne Crossing a large box culvert was installed to replace an old one.

“We call that Ice Box,” Carlson said. “There’s a little creek running underneath there, and so we’re replacing the old box with a new box. The box reached the end of its life, so we put a new box in there.

Colorado Boulevard

A chip seal project was just completed on Colorado Boulevard. 

A fog seal was applied late last week, and pavement markings have yet to be installed. This should occur in about a week — allowing for traffic to run on the fog seal uninterrupted, strengthening the bond between the fog seal and the asphalt chips.

“Just like always, when (motorists) go through construction projects, take your time, go slow,” Carlson said. “We absolutely know we impact traffic, and you know, we don’t like doing that. But in order to get these jobs accomplished, what choice do we have other than reducing lanes and making things a little bit messy until we get things built back.”

title: Speed Demon: Manning holds 3 records for fastest motorcycle,  going for 4th all-time high this year
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Denis Maning poses next to one of his streamliners. Manning has built 8 streamliners in his life, and he holds 3 world records for fastest motorcycle on earth. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Denis Manning.jpg
Denis Maning poses next to one of his streamliners. Manning has built 8 streamliners in his life, and he holds 3 world records for fastest motorcycle on earth. Courtesy photo 

STURGIS — Denis Manning has a need for speed. 

The motorcycle streamline fabricator and designer has set 11 world records, including 3 for having the fastest motorcycle on earth “and any nearby planets,” as he puts it. 

His latest record for the fastest motorcycle was in 2009, when driver Chris Carr set a then-land speed record of 367.382 miles per hour on Manning’s BUB Seven Streamliner. 

BUB is the name of Manning’s fabrication company, and it stands for “Big Ugly Bastard,” a nickname that world renowned motorcycle racer Conrad (Dutch) Mueller, also known as “The Flying Dutchman,” gave Manning that refers to his height. At 6 feet, 4 inches, Manning towers over many shorter racers who sport smaller frames that don’t weigh as much, and are able to travel at faster speeds. 

As a boy, Manning said many of his friends fantasized about major league baseball heroes. But Manning said he wanted to be just like Mickey Thompson, who set speed records with race cars. It was a lofty goal, that even his high school counselors said “portrayed illusions of grandeur.”

He wishes he could see those counselors now, because while Manning didn’t make it as a streamliner racer, he quickly discovered a unique ability to build speed machines that make history. He has smashed records all over the world, and is featured in the American Motorcyclist Association Hall of Fame. on Wednesday, he will be inducted into the Sturgis Motorcycle Museum Hall of Fame. 

Immediately after he is inducted, Manning, 80, plans to blaze a trail to the Bonneville Salt Flats for the Bonneville Motorcycle Speed Trials. There, he plans to reclaim his title for fastest motorcycle on earth, which he lost in 2010. In order to get the record, Manning’s streamliner has to beat Rocky Robinson’s fastest time of 376 miles per hour. This year, Manning said Valerie Thompson, who is the world’s fastest female motorcycle racer and 10-time speed record holder, as well as a fellow inductee into the Sturgis Motorcycle Museum Hall of Fame, will ride his streamliner to get the fastest time. 

“One of the toughest parts about getting the land speed record at this level is losing it, and then wanting it back again,” Manning said. “It’s resulted in me building 8 streamliners. One streamliner is enough for a person. Two, they start figuring out you’re a little crazy. Three, they pat you on the back and say you’re a nice guy. It’s been a helluva ride. This is at a world class level. If you were raised on a dirt bike, and you enter a slow-turn on the motorcycle and win, it’s because the rest of the guys didn’t finish. The land speed record deal, you’re competing against the best time there ever was. So, unless you do better than what’s ever been done in history, you’re just there for the hell of it.” 

Manning started breaking records in 1970, when he built a Harley-Davidson streamliner in his garage, and rider Cal Rayborn averaged 265 miles per hour on it. 

After setting that record, Manning decided to pursue his dream to build his own motor for racing. Starting with a pen and paper, Manning crafted the engine and transmission that he took to test land speed in Australia. That’s where the motor blew up due to an oil tank issue that was the result of a faulty design. 

“The aerodynamics were all wrong,” he said. “The nose was pushing down at about 2,000 pounds, and the rear of the machine was trying to fly.” 

It’s a problem that perplexed Manning, because when he took the bike to the wind tunnel for testing, the results showed a completely different outcome than what was actually occurring. It wasn’t until he was watching a 60 Minutes episode about salmon migration, when a lightbulb went off in Manning’s head, and he called a ichthylogist friend, who specializes in the study of fish, from the University of Missouri.

“I asked him how fast a salmon can swim,” Manning said. “He said, for a short time, 50 miles an hour. 50 miles an hour is 400 miles an hour in air. So, I had a shape. I had something to start with. I went on to duplicate what I thought was a salmon for a streamliner, only to find out that wind tunnel tests done by NASA, when they were trying to go 400 miles per hour with airplanes, there’s was in the same shape. So, I built the mold for it and then built carbon composite chassis for it. I put the thing together and in (2006) I put together a deal with Chris Carr. He’s in the Hall of Fame as a 7-time grand national champion. He climbed in the thing and we set a record at 350 miles per hour. It was unreal. It was a brand new machine, brand new shape, brand new everything, and it worked.” 

Two years later, Manning lost that record when rider Rocky Robinson took his streamliner to 360 miles per hour. In 2009, Manning continued to push the needle and got his top spot back, at 367 miles per hour. 

“Now you’re going places nobody has ever been aerodynamically,” Manning said of the records he continues to chase, after Robinson beat him again at 376 miles per hour. “Every little bit is a milestone. You don’t know what’s going to happen. It’s very unpredictable. 

After a long career of speed, Manning said he is extremely happy to be included in the Sturgis Motorcycle Museum’s Hall of Fame. The list of innovators, entrepreneurs, and motorcycle legends he will join with that distinction is a great honor that he takes very seriously, since Sturgis is where he finds his “people.” 

“Close your eyes and think about how many people who have ever ridden a motorcycle. Many,” Manning said. “Put them all in one place. You’d have to do a coliseum, or who knows how big of a place to take everybody who has ever ridden one. Now, compare them to how many people are in the Hall of Fame. Now you know. It’s important.

“As a kid there were a couple times I was told that I was just a biker,” Manning continued. “One time a gal told me she couldn’t go out with me because I was a motorcyclist. In Sturgis, I feel normal. They’re just like me. It’s just something I can relate to and I like it.” 

While he can relate to other bikers easier than anyone else, Manning said there are still several important distinctions that make life interesting. 

“The majority of the people ride the motorcycles,” he said. “Some people work on them. Some people, like Arlen (Ness) and there are a number of people in the hall of fame, that’s not good enough for them. They want to personalize them or customize them. That’s not good enough for me. It’s got to go fast.”

title: Law enforcement appreciation BBQ honors officers, raises funds for Meade County Cares
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: A number of dignitaries attended the Law Enforcement Appreciation BBQ on Sunday at the Woodland Shelter in the Sturgis park. From left are: Sturgis Mayor Rod Bradley, U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds, Meade County Sheriff Pat West, and Gov. Larry Rhoden.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
Law enforcement appreciation BBQ honors officers, raises funds for Meade County Cares.JPG
A number of dignitaries attended the Law Enforcement Appreciation BBQ on Sunday at the Woodland Shelter in the Sturgis park. From left are: Sturgis Mayor Rod Bradley, U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds, Meade County Sheriff Pat West, and Gov. Larry Rhoden.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

STURGIS — Law enforcement officers working the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally were honored Sunday evening during the annual Law Enforcement Appreciation Barbecue at Sturgis City Park, an event that also raised money to support families and children through Meade County Cares.

Meade County Sheriff Pat West hosted the event, which brought tog ether law enforcement officers, community members and several state officials, including South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden, U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds and Attorney General Marty Jackley.

West said the barbecue was revived to recognize the men and women who come to the Black Hills to help provide law enforcement during the rally.

The event traces its roots to former U.S. Marshal Gene Abdallah, who also served as South Dakota Highway Patrol superintendent and a Meade County chief deputy. Abdallah started the appreciation barbecue years ago as a way to provide law enforcement officers with a good meal before the rally began.

After Abdallah died in 2019, the event began to fade away. West said he wanted to bring it back when he became sheriff.

“Part of that was to bring it back to show appreciation for law enforcement,” West said.

The barbecue has also become a fundraiser for Meade County Cares, a nonprofit created by the sheriff’s office to assist local families and children in need.

West said the organization was established after law enforcement encountered families who needed financial assistance but had few resources available.

“We wanted to help,” West said. “It was tough to pass the hat every week, so we created this nonprofit called Meade County Cares.”

The organization supports programs such as the sheriff’s annual Shop with the Sheriff event, which allows children from area families to shop for Christmas presents. Meade County Cares has also provided financial assistance to local families facing difficult circumstances.

During Sunday’s event, Glen and Gary Smith donated $10,000 to Meade County Cares.

Glen Smith said the brothers have been attending the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally for more than two decades and wanted to support the organization’s efforts to help children and law enforcement.

“When we found out about Meade County Cares, we like to take care of the kids and law enforcement,” Smith said. “It’s a great, great project.”

Another donation was presented by Olive Branch Lodge 47 in Sturgis. Bob Tesch, secretary of the Masonic lodge, presented West with a $1,000 check for the National Child Safety Council.

West said the organization works with local law enforcement to provide safety materials and other items that officers can use when interacting with children in the community.

“This money is extremely important for us, just because it allows us to be able to spend that money and give back to the public,” West said.

Jackley, the South Dakota Attorney General, a Sturgis native, thanked the sponsors and community members who support law enforcement and local charitable efforts.

“Sturgis is my hometown,” Jackley said. “Rally’s pretty special to me and my family because it does a lot for our community, and this community is so wonderful to law enforcement.”

Senator Rounds also praised the work of law enforcement officers, noting that protecting the public is one of government’s fundamental responsibilities.

“Thank you for what you do to protect society from those who would do us harm,” Rounds told the officers attending the barbecue.

Governor Rhoden said South Dakota continues to have a strong respect for law enforcement and thanked officers for putting themselves in harm’s way to protect others.

“As long as I’m governor, we always will (have that respect) for our law enforcement,” Rhoden said. “They still provide that fundamental respect for what our law enforcement provides of putting themselves in harm’s way so we can sleep sound at night.”

Sturgis Mayor Rod Bradley also thanked the officers who travel to the area during the rally.

Bradley said the rally’s success depends on more than motorcycles, scenic Black Hills roads and visitors. A safe environment created by law enforcement is an important part of allowing visitors to enjoy their time in Sturgis.

“A big piece of it that you can’t overstate is how all you people, or law enforcement, provides a safe environment for people to come here and rally,” Bradley said. “That’s really important.”

Bradley also praised West and his wife, Cassie, for creating Meade County Cares and said the nonprofit is another example of how the rally can benefit the local community.

The evening also included a prayer for law enforcement officers, Rally visitors and the community before attendees shared a meal and fellowship.

title: Legends Ride numbers down, organizers optimistic about fundraising totals
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — The number of participants for the 19th annual Buffalo Chip Legends Ride were down this year, but organizers are confident this year’s event will mark $3 million raised for local charities.
_full_text:
STURGIS — The number of participants for the 19th annual Buffalo Chip Legends Ride were down this year, but organizers are confident this year’s event will mark $3 million raised for local charities. 

Cody Ertman, spokesman for the Buffalo Chip Campground said there were about 90 riders registered for the Legends Ride this year. That compares to about 120 riders last year. 

The event is known for attracting celebrity riders from the motorcycle, film, art, and music industries, and it is a fundraiser for the Sturgis Motorcycle Museum and the Rapid City Flame, South Dakota Special Olympics. This year’s celebrities included members of the rock band P.O.D., Sonny Sandoval, Traa Daniels, and Marcos Curiel; actor and producer Frankie Loyal; former UFC heavyweight champion Tim Sylvia; professional off-road racer Paul Wolff; custom motorcycle builders Cory and Zach Ness; Jim York, who holds world records for jumping various vehicles over long distances; and Buffalo Chip Campground owner Rod Woodruff. 

While Ertman said the totals from this year’s event have not been tallied, the Legends Ride has raised a total of $2.8 million, over the last 19 years. Ertman said he is confident this year’s event will push that cumulative total up over $3 million. 

Woodruff told the crowd on Monday that 100% of the proceeds from the event support the Sturgis Motorcycle Museum and the Rapid City Flame, of the South Dakota Special Olympics. In the past, representatives from the South Dakota Special Olympics said proceeds from the Legends Ride event have helped the Rapid City Flame build 16 new bocce ball courts that host local and state competitions; purchase a van to transport athletes to special events; and build a new gym that is used for a variety of activities. Heidi Haro, director of the Sturgis Motorcycle Museum and Hall of Fame, said their portion of the funds is used to keep the doors of the museum open, and to help preserve the history of motorcycling. 

Final fundraising totals for the event that featured a live auction, a poker tournament, and a special biker reception, were not available by press time. However, the auction raised about $4,800. A limited edition, autographed painting by Scott Jacobs sold for about $1,000. An exclusive painting by renowned Harley-Davidson artist Ray Drea, of YungBlud, a Grammy-winning rock artist known for his high energy performances and close relationship with late rock legend Ozzy Osbourne, sold for $1,700. An original, autographed David Uhl painting that was numbered 1 of 2, sold for $2,000, and a drum skin signed by members of the band P.O.D. sold for $100. 

In addition to live auction items, the Buffalo Chip announced an online motorcycle auction that will launch Aug. 30. The auction will feature a Buffalo Chip B4 004 Edition, which is a performance bagger that was custom built from a 2025 Indian Chieftain PowerPlus Limited. The online auction can be accessed at buffalochip.com, or sturgisauctions.com.

title: State’s expenses  for Rushmore fireworks were greater than economic impact, Tourism Department says
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Fireworks explode above Mount Rushmore National Memorial on July 3, after a speech by President Donald Trump to mark the 250th anniversary of the founding of the United States. Photo by Meghan O’Brien, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
State’s expenses for Rushmore fireworks were greater than economic impact, Tourism Department says.jpg
Fireworks explode above Mount Rushmore National Memorial on July 3, after a speech by President Donald Trump to mark the 250th anniversary of the founding of the United States. Photo by Meghan O’Brien, South Dakota Searchlight 

MOUNT RUSHMORE — The fireworks display last month at Mount Rushmore cost the state of South Dakota $450,000 more than the event generated in economic impact, according to the state Department of Tourism.

The state spent $2.8 million to plan and produce the July 3 celebration, which generated $2.35 million of economic impact, the department said in a Monday press release. The department attributed the economic analysis to the research firm Tourism Economics.

Broadcast and digital media coverage generated nearly $51 million in additional “publicity value” from 53.7 billion “audience impressions,” according to the department, although the publicity value was not included as part of the economic impact. The department said the publicity included 107,000 views of the event’s video livestream.

South Dakota Tourism Secretary James Hagen celebrated the numbers.

“It’s an investment that strengthened our tourism economy while reinforcing South Dakota’s place as one of America’s most iconic destinations,” Hagen said in the press release.

The costs included $700,000 for pyrotechnics and lighting effects, according to a public contract between the department and California-based Pyro Spectaculars. The department said other costs included media production, shuttle bus contracts and cost recovery payments to the National Park Service. The Park Service manages Mount Rushmore as a national memorial.

South Dakota Searchlight sent questions to the department about whether the costs reported in the press release included expenses incurred by other public entities such as the city of Keystone, Pennington County and the U.S. Forest Service. The department said it would it work on responses and supply them later.

The $2.35 million economic impact estimate includes visitor spending, hotel room rentals and sales tax revenue, the department said in the press release. There were 4,800 tickets for the event, and the department said attendees came from 40 states.

The event, officially known as South Dakota’s Freedom 250 Mount Rushmore Fireworks Celebration, featured a keynote speech from President Donald Trump — which he used to allege a “mortal threat” to the nation from communism — and a fireworks display above the carved faces of Mount Rushmore in South Dakota’s Black Hills.

This year’s event and past fireworks displays at the national memorial have drawn criticism for the wildfire threat to the surrounding national forest posed by stray sparks from fireworks, and for litter and pollutants from fireworks packaging and chemicals. There was no organized protest against the fireworks this year, but a group of Native Americans advocating for the return of the Black Hills to Lakota tribes protested the prior event in 2020.

Fatal Crashes:

• At 3:22 p.m. Monday, on U.S. Highway 16A, near mile marker 27: A 2002 Yamaha motorcycle, operated by a 63-year-old male, was traveling westbound on U.S. 16A near mile marker 27. The motorcycle left the roadway to the right, entered the westbound ditch, and overturned. The driver became separated from the motorcycle. The driver sustained fatal injuries.

• At 3:34 p.m. Monday, on Deerfield Road and Marshall Gulch Road: A 2008 Harley-Davidson motorcycle, operated by a 46-year-old male, was driving northbound on Deerfield Road near Marshal Gulch Road. The motorcycle passed a vehicle in a no-passing zone. The driver lost control when returning to its lane. The motorcycle entered the northbound ditch and rolled. The driver was not wearing a helmet and sustained fatal injuries.

Injury Crashes:

• At 9:45 a.m. Monday, on U.S. Highway 14A, near mile marker 25: A 2006 Kawasaki motorcycle, operated by a 44-year-old female, was driving westbound on U.S. 14A near mile marker 25. The driver lost control of the motorcycle and became separated from the vehicle. The driver was wearing a helmet and was transported to Lead-Deadwood Monument Health with non-life-threatening injuries.

• At 1:20 p.m. Monday, on Wildlife Loop, near mile marker 15, in Custer State Park: a 2003 Harley-Davidson motorcycle, operated by a 64-year-old male, was traveling southbound on Wildlife Loop near mile marker 15 with a group of motorcycles. The motorcycles in front of the motorcycle slowed. The rider attempted to avoid collision and overturned the motorcycle. The driver was separated from the motorcycle. He sustained minor injuries and refused transport.

• At 1:26 p.m. Monday, on South Dakota Highway 244, near mile marker 30: A 2007 Harley-Davidson motorcycle, operated by a 40-year-old male, was westbound on SD Highway 244 at mile marker 30. He was negotiating a right-hand curve on a grade when he lost control and crossed the center line. A 2025 Harley-Davidson motorcycle, operated by a 72-year-old male, was eastbound at this location with a 69-year-old female passenger. The bikes collided. All occupants sustained injuries and were transported Monument Health in Rapid City.

• At 3:05 p.m. Monday, on Nemo Road and Old Ridge Road: A 2016 Harley-Davidson motorcycle, operated by a 69-year-old male, was traveling east on Nemo Road. The driver failed to negotiate a curve in the roadway. He became separated from the motorcycle and left the roadway. He was transported to Monument Health in Rapid City with serious injuries.

• At 3:30 p.m. Monday, on U.S. Highway 16, near mile marker 15: A 2008 Harley-Davidson motorcycle, operated by a 52-year-old male, was traveling eastbound on U.S. Highway 16 near mile marker 15. The driver lost control and slid into the north side ditch. The driver was separated from the unit and was transported to Monument Health in Custer for his injuries.

title: Bear Butte fire  at 457 acres
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Watching just how fast the Bear Butte Fire spread was scary, one local farmer says.
_full_text:
STURGIS — Watching just how fast the Bear Butte Fire spread was scary, one local farmer says. 

Rick Grosek, owner of Bear Butte Gardens, said one of his employees discovered the fire in a ditch along Highway 79, about 100 feet from his property. By the time Grosek’s employee got to the house, and his wife called 911, it had already grown significantly. 

“I noticed the fire was moving faster than you could walk,” Grosek said. 

On Tuesday morning, the South Dakota Department of Public Safety, Wildland Fire Division reported about 10 firefighters remained on scene to mop up the Bear Butte Fire, which started about 1 mile south of Bear Butte. The fire was 50% contained Tuesday morning, and had burned about 457 acres. 

The fire was just across the highway from the Iron Horse Campground, and Grosek said campground owners immediately attempted to fight it, using a water tank and pump. But the blaze rapidly increased in intensity, and moved too fast for the initial attack. 

“It overwhelmed them,” he said. “It was just too much. It was just going so fast and so strong.” 

Air and ground fire crews from local, state, and national agencies responded the fire Monday afternoon, after the initial call came in at about 12:50 p.m. 

There were no evacuations issued. 

Grosek, who lost a small part of his fence when the fire burned through a couple of acres on his property, said he is thankful the wind was blowing in a northwest direction, and not toward the campgrounds. 

“It’s just crazy that we even hold the Rally with the risk to property damage and life,” he said. “If the wind would have been blowing in a different direction, it could have gone over to Glencoe Camp Resort and those campers would never get out. They’d be trapped. Or, if it went the other direction to the Iron Horse Campground, there’s hundreds of RVs packed in there as tight as they can. If it went that direction in a matter of 5 minutes, there would have been a pile of people dying. So we’re so lucky in the route that it actually took.”

The fire danger is serious, and Grosek said it has never been more important for people to follow the restrictions on the burn ban Meade County instituted last week. The ban includes a restriction on smoking outside, which includes smoking on a motorcycle, he said. 

“The official burn ban is that you cannot smoke a cigarette outside,” he said. “You have to be inside a vehicle or a structure. People just don’t understand that. All these people coming in from faraway places, and they want to have fun, but it’s just so dangerous.”

title: Minnesota couple plans  40th ride to Sturgis
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Ralph Waldo Emerson said, “It’s not the destination, it’s the journey.”
_full_text:
STURGIS — Ralph Waldo Emerson said, “It’s not the destination, it’s the journey.” 

For Sherry Olson, that’s only half true. When taking the ride to Sturgis, the journey and the destination are equally important.  

Sherry and her husband, Al Olson, are preparing to make their 40th ride to the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally from their home base of Saint Cloud, Minn. The 600 miles of mostly interstate riding helps to cleanse the mind, Sherry said, and the beauty of the Black Hills boosts the soul. 

“We’re alone in our helmets to kind of have time for therapeutic levels of introspection, and kind of a deep cleansing of sorts from the head,” Sherry said. “It seems like these days there is so little privacy anywhere, so the solitude of bike week kind of feels like a hallowed gift that’s rare.” 

“Sherry sings to herself all the way out,” Al said. “She’ll make up songs.” 

Sherry and Al have been taking the ride to Sturgis every year since 1985, except for 1986. That was the year Sherry made the switch from a music teacher to a probation officer, and they weren’t able to make the trip. 

“From working with little children who want to be good and cooperate, to working with predominantly male felony offenders, was a change,” Sherry said. 

The trip to Sturgis never gets old — even while fighting the wind on the interstate. 

Pull quote
“We’re alone in our helmets to kind of have time for therapeutic levels of introspection, and kind of a deep cleansing of sorts from the head.” — Sherry Olson

“We like to do our Steve McQueen best and try to cross South Dakota with the winds blowing — the kind that forces you to find a balance between gusts of wind and gravity, and then the semi trucks that kind of suck you into their self-created mini tornadoes,” Sherry said. 

“We like to ride across Interstate 90, through South Dakota,” Al said. “Sherry likes to watch all of the other motorcycles joining the crowd. It’s really special when we hit the Missouri River, there by Chamberlain, and it feels like once we get west of that river we’re getting into the real heart of the west, with all the smells. Then, as we’re coming into Rapid City, you start seeing the Black Hills in the distance and you know the smells of the trees. It’s an excitement that never goes away.” 

“You’d think that at the 40-year point it would be kind of boring, but it’s not,” Sherry said. “It’s never boring out there. Riding around the Black Hills is just gorgeous and that’s kind of where that ‘it’s not the destination, it’s the journey,’ comes in. It’s a combination.” 

Over the years, Al and Sherry said they’ve taken a variety of different rides through the Hills. While they enjoy the usual rides through Spearfish Canyon, Iron Mountain Road, and Vanocker Canyon, it’s the back roads that brought them some of the most lasting memories. 

“One of the scariest experiences we had was a road that got smaller, and went from gravel to dirt,” Sherry said. “It’s almost a path and it’s a wooded area, and there’s open range. We came to an area that’s a little bit of a clearing, and there’s a buffalo standing there. We can’t turn around, because there’s no room. So, Al just slowly went by, and the buffalo just stood there. I slowly went by after I said a prayer. It turned out OK, but that was quite scary.” 

Another memorable moment, Al said, could have been the result of Sherry being a woman rider in the 1980s. 

“One time we were riding across South Dakota, and we may have been breaking the speed limit a little bit,” Al said. “The highway patrol rode alongside Sherry for probably a mile, looking at her. It was pretty unusual to see a gal on a motorcycle. So, he never stopped her. He let her go.” 

That was one of the only times Sherry said she may have been treated differently as a woman rider in the 1980s and 1990s. While the industry was predominantly comprised of male riders, Sherry, whose mother also rode motorcycles, said she never thought anything about it, except when people asked to take her picture on her bike. 

For the last 40 years, the Rally has changed significantly, the couple said. One of the most exciting rallies they’ve been to, Al said, was the 50th Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, in 1990. 

“It seemed like everybody really let loose that year and there were a lot of sights to see,” he said. “That one was pretty fun.” 

But the evolution of the Rally has brought some improvements. Whereas in the early days the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally was not a place to bring small children, today it has become a very family-oriented event that boosts tourism. 

Both Al and Sherry said one of their favorite activities during the Rally, is sitting on Main Street, watching people for hours. 

“A couple of years ago when we were there sitting on the bench, watching people and bikes go down Main Street, on one side of us were some Christian Motorcyclist Association members. On the opposite side of our bench was another group of people talking and they had Hells Angels patches on them. There’s so much diversity,” Sherry said. 

Sometimes, Sherry said, she can’t help but notice the lack of bugs on some of the bikes the ladies ride down Main Street. The lack of riding experience is one of the less desirable changes to the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, she said. 

“We sit on Main Street, and there will be gals riding their bikes and they’re all dolled up, and we say, ‘you know, there’s no bugs on that bike. They definitely didn’t ride it here.’ That’s concerning, because they don’t have that experience. They haven’t ridden from wherever their home is and spent that time on the bike,” Al said. “If you just jump on a bike, you’re not used to the machine. You’re just not.” 

“It’s become more trendy for women to ride motorcycles now and you learn it later in life,” Sherry said. “Al and I both grew up riding motorcycles, and things are easier to learn when you’re young. So, we’ve had a lot of experience. But a lot of the riders at Sturgis have not had experience.” 

Alcohol along with that lack of experience on the road can also make riding unsafe, they said. As longtime Rally attendees, Al and Sherry said their biggest piece of advice is to not drink and ride. They’ve noticed that the later in the day it gets, the more it seems people have had to drink, and the more chances they take on the road. As a result, the couple try to plan to be safe in their hotel room by about 6 p.m. 

“Beer and motorcycles don’t mix,” Sherry said. “I mean, it’s bad.” 

“We’ve seen so many accidents in the Hills,” Al said. “You gotta remember, you’re coming out there to enjoy the scenery, not to die.” 

Helmets and proper riding clothes, including rain gear, is also essential for riding in general, but especially during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, Sherry said. 

“Another piece of advice is if a person doesn’t like crowds, they probably don’t want to go to Sturgis,” Sherry said. 

As a couple who only takes what they can strap to their bike to the Rally, Sherry said packing light for the week contributes to a much more enjoyable experience. Sherry recommends wearing a pair of jeans and packing an extra pair, packing a couple of T-shirts and washing them through the week. 

“Keep it light,” she said. “For me, it’s refreshing. No hair curler needed. No makeup. I don’t have to dress like I’m going to be in court when I was working.” 

“Yeah, we go pretty light,” Al said. “Just a couple of waterproof bags on our bikes. We tie them on and that’s it.” 

Overall, Al and Sherry said they are looking forward to attending this year, and many future years, of the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. They’ve been to other rallies around the country in Daytona, Laconia, N.H., and others — but none of them compare to Sturgis. 

“Sturgis truly is the granddaddy of them all, because of the size and personality,” Sherry said.

title: ‘What the Constitution Means to Me’ rounds out Theatre 605 season
byline: Mary Garrigan Special to the Pioneer
description: Photo courtesy of Lone Tree Productions
_full_text:
‘What the Constitution Means to Me’ rounds out Theatre 605 season 1.JPG
Photo courtesy of Lone Tree Productions 

CUSTER STATE PARK — The last play of the year at the Black Hills Playhouse is also a rapid-fire lecture on the best, and the worst, of the U.S. Constitution. But don’t take that as a bad thing. 

“What the Constitution Means to Me,” with just 6 more shows through Saturday, is a highly-personalized monologue that re-enacts playwright Heidi Schreck’s own high-school history of earning money to pay for college by competing in constitutional debate competitions. The debates are hosted by American Legion Posts all around the country, and scenic designer John Paul Devlin’s set is a spot-on version of every American Legion Hall anywhere in the country, complete with framed veteran portraits from every war adorning the walls and a shutter-framed window that you just know leads to the kitchen where the fish-frys and the pancake breakfasts are made. 

If that all sounds like a boring premise for a play, trust me when I say that actor Emily Wirkus will change your mind once Schreck’s 15-year-old self is resurrected as a vivacious, people-pleasing teen with an encyclopedic knowledge of the U.S. Constitution.   

Wirkus showcases a phenomenal ability for memorization with an astounding amount of dialogue. This autobiographical play switches rapidly between Schreck’s teen-age enthusiasm for the beauty of the U.S. Constitution, and her 40-something self’s much more disparaging view of the racial and gender biases that were baked into it by the white, male Founding Fathers who wrote it. Wirkus holds the tension expertly between Schreck’s early passion for, and her later disillusionment with, this foundational document of American life. 

Early on, a brief reference is made to Schreck’s great, great grandmother. That woman eventually serves as the entry point for the playwright’s critique of the constitution and its failures to offer many Americans the same legal protections it affords to others.  If you are a white man with a thin skin regarding your privileged status in American history, be forewarned that this may not be your favorite way to spend two hours. 

Wirkus is joined on stage for the bulk of the play only by Erk K. Larsen in small roles portraying the American Legion debate moderator and one of Schreck’s real life friends. 

The play delves into difficult topics from Schreck’s own life as a lens through which to view the U.S. Constitution, including a shocking amount of domestic violence against the women in her family and her abortion at the age of 21. Sometimes, the play is a history lesson on topics of slavery, immigration, birthright citizenship, voter suppression, the oppression of indigenous peoples and abortion rights. Sometimes, it seems like you are in someone else’s therapy session.  And, at times, it seems longer than its run time of 90 minutes. There is no intermission. 

It ends with yet another boundary-breaking tactic, when Wirkus steps out of the role of Schreck and invites 12-year-old Finley Nelson, a student at Southwest Middle School in Rapid City, on to the stage for a “debate” about the future of the U.S. Constitution.  Audience participation ensues, and Finley does a great job holding her own in defense of the position that the U.S. Constitution should not be abolished and replaced with a more modern, progressive update. 

The play may have its limitations as pure “entertainment,” but I know that it succeeds as an important, timely piece of theater because my two theater companions and I discussed it all the way home.

title: Fulton Street Bash celebrates 21 years of  hot rods, music and community
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: The 21st annual Fulton Street Bash drew a number of hot rods, classic cars, live music and food on Saturday in Sturgis. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
2. Fulton.JPG
The 21st annual Fulton Street Bash drew a number of hot rods, classic cars, live music and food on Saturday in Sturgis. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

 3. fulton ...JPG
A wide variety of cars were at the car show at the Fulton Street Bash on Saturday in Sturgis. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

 5. fulton.JPG
Rob Selting brought his 1958 Chevy pickup to the Fulton Street Bash on Saturday in Sturgis. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

STURGIS — The roar of hot rods, the sound of live music and the smell of barbecue filled Fulton Street Saturday during the 21st annual Fulton Street Bash, bringing friends, families, car enthusiasts and rally visitors together for an afternoon of food, fun and fellowship.  What began more than 2 decades ago as a small gathering of friends has grown into a popular annual event during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, featuring classic cars, hot rods, race cars, live music and plenty of barbecue.

Bruce Bradley, one of the organizers, said the event has come a long way from its humble beginnings.

“This is something that has been going on for 21 years, and it started out not even on Fulton Street, to be honest with you,” Bradley said.

The original gathering took place on Sunset Street and grew out of friendships Bradley made with people from Iowa while attending the Knoxville National Sprint Car Races.

“A couple years went by, and a couple hot rods showed up just stopping by to visit,” Bradley said. “We moved down here, and it just evolved from there.”

When the event first moved to Fulton Street, only about 50 people attended, with a handful of cars parked along the residential street. Over the years, the gathering continued to grow into the car show and block party it is today.

While the cars may be what initially attracts many visitors, Bradley said the event has always been about something more important, bringing people together.

“The whole purpose of this, and it wasn’t from the beginning, was to meet with good family and friends,” Bradley said. “It’s evolved into something that has created a very large group of people, including family members, friends and local businesses that are supporting this event for the community.”

The Fulton Street Bash combines 3 of Bradley’s favorite ingredients for a successful gathering: hot rods, barbecue and live music.

“We’ve got bands, we’ve got barbecue, and we’ve got hot rods,” he said. “Those all three go together.”

The event has also retained the feel of a neighborhood gathering despite its growth. Bradley said the property where the bash is held has been in his family for more than 50 years and has long served as a gathering place for family and friends.

What began as a private gathering eventually grew large enough to require a city street closure permit, but Bradley said the original spirit of the event remains.

“Initially, it was a private party,” Bradley said. “It’s evolved into people passing by, and you can’t ignore the fact that there’s a lot of cool things going on with the cars, the live music, the smell of barbecue and people having a great time.”

The event is also designed to be a family-friendly gathering during a week when thousands of visitors descend on the Black Hills for the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally.

The annual bash has become a place where local residents, Rally visitors and car enthusiasts can slow down, visit with one another and enjoy a more relaxed community atmosphere.

After 21 years, Bradley said that simple idea remains at the heart of the Fulton Street Bash. “That’s what it’s about,” he said.

STURGIS — Justin Jutting, Meade School Board president, is now a member of the Associated School Boards of South Dakota (ASBSD) Board of Directors. 

Jutting was elected to represent Western Region Schools with enrollment between 1,400 and 9,999 students. 

A post-secondary instructor at Western Dakota Technical College, Jutting served on the Meade County School Board for 5 years — 3 as president, 1 as vice president. At various times throughout his tenure, he also chaired the school board’s finance and policy committees. 

Now, with ASBSD Jutting is Meade’s representative at delegate assembly, attending various events and trainings and presenting multiple times at ASBSD-SASD Annual Convention. 

“We’re thrilled to have Justin join the board of directors and share his thoughts and perspective,” ASBSD Executive Director Heath Larson said. “He is an informed and experienced leader in public education and we’re excited to work with him in our support of public education in South Dakota.”

ASBSD is a private, non-profit association representing around 850 South Dakota school board members, the 147 school districts they govern. The 18-member ASBSD Board of Directors is made up of local school board members elected from four geographic regions and 5 enrollment size categories. The regions are: Central, Northeast, Southeast and Western. The 5 enrollment size categories are 265 and fewer, 266-699, 700-1,399, 1,400-9,999 and 10,000 and more.
