title: Federal judge dismisses legal challenges  to SD drug discount law
byline: By John Hult Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — A judge has ruled in favor of a South Dakota law that helps rural healthcare providers buy discounted drugs and mark up their sale price to fill budget holes created by low Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement rates.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — A judge has ruled in favor of a South Dakota law that helps rural healthcare providers buy discounted drugs and mark up their sale price to fill budget holes created by low Medicare and Medicaid reimbursement rates.

AbbVie, maker of the arthritis drug Humira, among other medications, sued the state in April 2025. The Chicago-based company argued that South Dakota lawmakers unconstitutionally regulated interstate commerce with Senate Bill 154, which they passed and Gov. Larry Rhoden signed into law earlier that year.

The drug company AstraZeneca filed a similar lawsuit last August, and the trade group Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America filed one in September.

The law, which took effect last year, blocks drug companies from restricting which pharmacies health care providers can use to access discounts through the federal 340B program. It requires drugmakers who want to participate in Medicare and Medicaid to offer steep discounts to hospitals and clinics that deliver care to underserved or vulnerable populations. Providers who qualify for 340B can then upcharge patients for the drugs, which helps them pay their bills when federal reimbursement rates are too low to cover the cost of providing service.

SD among states to restrict drug company contracting

The 340B program initially required discounts for providers that serve mostly Medicaid clients. It was expanded to “sole providers” under the Affordable Care Act in 2010, which opened it up to rural healthcare providers in places like South Dakota. Federal guidance issued that same year also allowed participating providers to contract with an unlimited number of pharmacies. Until then, providers had to use one.

In response to the expanding 340B usage that followed, drug companies have moved to restrict the pharmacies through which providers can purchase discounted drugs.

Supporters of Senate Bill 154 argued that such restrictions can put 340B discounts out of reach for rural hospitals that need the financial boost of participation to stay open and serve their rural clientele.

Other states have passed similar laws, and faced similar lawsuits. 

The laws amount to an unconstitutional “taking” of drug company property through forced discounts, the lawsuits have argued, as well as to state-level regulations on interstate commerce. They also argue that because 340B is a federal program, states can’t regulate it.

Judge: SD law is constitutional, protects ‘legitimate interest’ 

The ruling from U.S. District Judge Roberto Lange dismissed all 3 lawsuits against South Dakota. Lange relied in part on appeals court rulings supporting similar laws in states including Arkansas and Missouri. 

Lange noted that 340B participation is optional. Other courts, and now Lange, have ruled that drug companies cannot opt into a voluntary program and then argue that their products have been taken without just compensation. 

The judge also ruled that South Dakota’s law does not unfairly burden interstate commerce, in part because the state has a “legitimate interest in regulating the delivery of 340B drugs ultimately dispensed to its citizens.”

To the argument that the state cannot change the setup of a federal program, Lange ruled that South Dakota’s law deals with the delivery of drugs. It doesn’t make any changes to the federal law, he wrote, because the federal law deals with drug pricing.

South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley praised Lange’s decision in a press release.

“This ruling guarantees that our healthcare providers will continue to access these discounted medications and use them in ways that best serve their communities,” Jackley wrote.

AbbVie appealed Lange’s decision to the Eighth Circuit on Monday morning. AstraZeneca and Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America had not appealed as of Monday afternoon. Lawyers for the latter two did not immediately respond to emails requesting comment.

title: Mitchell baseball libel lawsuit against  American Legion, media dismissed
byline: By Molly Wetsch South Dakota News Watch
description: MITCHELL — A South Dakota judge has ruled in favor of the American Legion and 2 media companies in a defamation lawsuit filed by a former Mitchell baseball player.
_full_text:
SDNewsWatchLogo

MITCHELL — A South Dakota judge has ruled in favor of the American Legion and 2 media companies in a defamation lawsuit filed by a former Mitchell baseball player. 

Nexstar Media Group, which owns KELO-TV, and Forum Communications, which owns the Mitchell Republic, were defendants in the case revolving around a sentence in a letter by a representative from the American Legion sent to members of the Mitchell Baseball Association. 

In November 2024, American Legion adjutant C.P. Van Delist sent the letter to members of the Mitchell Baseball Association saying that Mitchell Baseball would be immediately barred from participating in the American Legion after a rape case involving 6 players made its way through court. 

In July 2025, Peyton Mandel, one of the 6 players involved in the case, filed a civil lawsuit saying that Van Delist made “false, malicious, and defamatory” statements about him. Besides the American Legion, Nexstar and Forum were also named in the lawsuit. 

Both news organizations published stories containing Van Delist’s letter, which named all 6 players involved in the case and said, “All of these individuals are guilty of accessory to a felony, acknowledging by affirmation of their guilty pleas, that the felonies they were charged with, rape and aiding and abetting, did take place.”

Mandel was a player for the Mitchell Baseball team and one of 6 involved in a hazing incident that took place in 2023 at a Rapid City hotel room. The event, in which another player said the boys held him down and performed forcible digital anal penetration on him, was later characterized as a rape case. He pled guilty in 2024 to one count of accessory to a felony as part of a plea deal.

Quote
It’s always a good feeling when journalism and investigative reporting wins. This shows our community that our newspaper cares about the truth and isn’t afraid of telling it, no matter who is involved or what the story is about. — Luke Hagen Mitchell Republic editor

Circuit Judge David Knoff heard the defamation case in May and took it under advisement. The court published its decision Friday, which granted summary judgment to the defendants, which ends the case instead of taking it to trial.

“The statement made by Van Delist and published by the Media Defendants were

substantially true. Mandel (sic) pled guilty to being an accessory to a felony. He never used the word ‘rape’, but the actual act is undisputed and was acquiesced to by his silence at sentencing,” the judge wrote in Friday’s ruling. 

Mitchell Republic editor Luke Hagen said the ruling was a relief. 

“It’s always a good feeling when journalism and investigative reporting wins,” he said. “This shows our community that our newspaper cares about the truth and isn’t afraid of telling it, no matter who is involved or what the story is about.”

Case defines defamation, truth defense

Mandel’s lawyer, Tucker Volesky, said during the hearing in May that the contested sentence in the letter indicated Mandel was a rapist when that was not the charge that Mandel pled guilty to. Volesky said that because Mandel pleaded guilty to accessory to a felony, it was wrong to name him in the letter next to the statement of rape taking place. 

The lawsuit stated that Van Delist’s statements and the subsequent news articles “falsely (represented) and (characterized) Plaintiff as an admitted rapist.” The lawsuit also says that Mandel was “denied reapplication for an employment or experiential opportunity in the medical field” as a result of the articles published by KELO and the Mitchell Republic.

Truth is considered an “absolute defense” in defamation cases, which means that if a statement is undeniably true, then it cannot legally be considered defamation. The court’s ruling said that prior court cases involving Mandel and the other players established the “factual basis” for this case, and the statement made in Van Delist’s letter was true.

“Mandel (sic) relies on a vague admission and the argument that he technically did not admit in court to an accessory to rape or aiding and abetting rape. The Letter is at a minimum substantially true,” the ruling said. “While our Constitution doesn’t explicitly address minor inaccuracies in publications, South Dakota courts have recognized that minor errors don’t necessarily defeat a truth defense when the real substance of the publication remains accurate.”

title: Spearfish School Board considers options for  West Elementary
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: The placement of West Elementary School on its lot, skewed instead of parallel to King and Mason streets, are another hurdle school officials face when planning whether to renovate or replace the school. Pioneer photo by Travis Potter
_full_text:
DJI_20260728154127_0007_D.JPG
The placement of West Elementary School on its lot, skewed instead of parallel to King and Mason streets, are another hurdle school officials face when planning whether to renovate or replace the school. Pioneer photo by Travis Potter 

SPEARFISH — During a 2-hour long work session recently, Spearfish School Board members visited with architects, and building and financial planners about options for renovating or replacing West Elementary School.

In July, school board members got the 100,000-foot-view of options the district has to deal with the school that was constructed in 1965. Last week came the 50,000-foot-view.

The deficiencies the school has range from structural issues, an aged HVAC system, lack of fire protection system, old, single-paned windows that are not energy efficient, drainage problems, and more.

Additionally, the school has space for about 400 students. That is the general makeup of first and second grade, which is housed in the building. Kindergarten was moved to Mountain View Elementary School in 2013, as West Elementary was full. Ideally, the district would like to return kindergarten to the building.

“However, if we wanted to put a third grade level, there’s not adequate space for the grade level, much less ancillary services of OT, PT, special education, specials, lunch, gym, all those things,” said Nick Gottlob, superintendent of the Spearfish School District.

Discussions on what to do with West Elementary date back to the early 2000s. In 2022, a group of around a dozen staff members toured schools throughout the state to evaluate the different facilities and educational programs.

 Options to revamp or replace West Elementary discussed.jpeg
West Elementary School, first opened in 1965, has “good bones” but many decencies that are leading school officials to decide whether a major overhaul is needed, or a new facility. Pioneer photo by Mark Watson 

Fast forward to earlier this year, and the district got serious about evaluating the issues, what repairs would need to be done to the existing facility if the district were to maintain it, or what a new school might look like.

It hired 3Peak Architecture and JLG Architects, both Spearfish firms. Together, they came up with 6 plans. Two have since been rejected and 4 remain.

One of the main factors, for whether the board decides to build a new school or renovate the existing facility is simply the cost. 

Costs over 4 years, from 2011-2015, when the district opened Creekside Elementary School, and later added onto it, as well as when it renovated the old high school turning it into the kindergarten campus, totaled $16.6 million. The U.S. Inflation Calculator indicates that the equivalent of that amount today would equate to about $23.4 million. However, construction costs have skyrocketed since then.

“Post COVID, we also then saw costs per square foot go from what previously was estimated at $285 to $550-$600,” Gottlob said. 

That means a new school could cost around $50 million.

“When we entered any dialog with a $50 million price tag, those conversations simply weren’t palatable,” he added. “None of that changes the fact that at some point we will need a plan for the West Elementary footprint. We will need a plan for the future educational programs and services for kids.”

Jason Roberdeau, president and principal architect of 3Peak Architecture, and Ron Olsen, principal architect for JLG Architects, discussed options the board faces.

Do nothing but maintenance

Option one is to do nothing, Roberdeau said.

“It’s kind of a misnomer because you can’t do nothing,” Roberdeau said. “Doing nothing is making a decision in a more specific way down the road, but it’s basically deferred maintenance.”

That down the road decision is to build a new school.

Roberdeau said the school has numerous deficiencies, but isn’t going to fall in on itself. Inefficient windows, drainage issues, asbestos tile, and a HVAC system so old that parts are no longer available from the manufacturer, are among the issues. Additionally, because of an elevation change from the gym to the rest of the school roof, snow will accumulate and, given enough drifting, will need to be shoveled off.

There is no estimated dollar amount, but rather an ongoing list of issues that will need to be addressed.

“We can kick the can down the road a little bit longer in order to make these sorts of decisions,” Roberdeau said. “But something eventually has to be done.”

Add a gym and classroom addition, and remodel the rest of the school

The next 3 options are significant construction projects and will take multiple years, with significant costs.

Option 2 calls for adding a gym and a classroom wing. Additionally, the remainder of the school would be remodeled. 

Roberdeau said the phased approach would allow for kindergarten to eventually be returned to West Elementary, as the addition would allow for about 600 students.

The plans call for the 10-classroom addition to be created to the west of the current footprint along King Street. Once done, one grade level could move into it, allowing a portion of the remainder of the school to be renovated. Once that step is completed, the final grade level would move into the newly-renovated portion of the school allowing the final overhaul to be competed.

“We have to upgrade mechanical, electrical, structural finishes, exterior envelope, all those things I mentioned with the existing facility have to be addressed,” Roberdeau said. “It would be phased over time. It’s probably a four-year sort of ordeal over time. When it’s done in concept, it’s a new building. It’ll look like a look like a new building, function like a new building.”

Rough estimates show that the addition would cost around $18.9 million, with another $18.2 million for the renovation. The total cost would be in the ballpark of $37.1 million, and take around 4 years to complete.

New building in 2 phases

Part of the problem with considering how to use the current West Elementary lot space is how the current building is placed. Rather than placing the building square to Mason and King streets, it sits at an angle.

“This building was skewed on there, so it consumes a lot of real estate,” Olsen said. “If you’re a geometry teacher in the crowd, you kind of start to understand how that takes away so much space.”

Option 3 calls for adding a new school directly to the west of the current facility, and very close to one corner of it. The second phase of construction would actually be built over part of the current footprint.

Phase one would consist of constructing a new building with one wing, close to King Street, 2 stories tall. Once that portion is complete, Phase 2 would see West Elementary razed and a 10-classroom wing added parallel to Mason Street and directly over a portion of the current building site. This would allow kindergarteners to return to the school. New parking lots, a bus lane as well, and a parent dropoff lane would be added as well.

The total project would take about 4 years to complete and cost around $39.7 million for the replacement facility, and another $10.5 million for the kindergarten wing.

The kindergarten wing would not need to be added right away, and if the construction costs for the entire project are greater than the school board is comfortable funding, the second phase could be delayed until the debt load could be reduced. If this is the desired route, costs for the total project may go up, but the current estimate, for both phases, is around $50.2 million.

New building, new site

The fourth option is to build a new 600-capacitiy school at a completely different location. 

The cost estimate is around $50 million, but would depend on the site preparations needed. Options 2, 3, and 4 will all take an estimated 4 years to complete, which includes time to design the project.

Location, location, location

Olsen said a school should be built on no less than 10 acres, and 20 acres would be more ideal to allow ample space for the facility, parking lots, playground, and fields.

While the district owns open space near existing schools, they are not conducive to adding an elementary school.

“The field to the east of the high school CTE Center would not be conducive to add an elementary school; the building footprint alone would consume the space. Not to mention the challenge of adding an additional 600 students to the site, and the logistics of busing, parent access, parking, etc.,” Gottlob said. “Much like the high school space, the field space adjacent to Creekside (Elementary School) towards the creek would not be conducive to add an additional school. There is not enough available land out of the floodplain. In addition, the district previously committed to not creating a through-street to the backside of the existing school. Therefore, there is one access point. You’ve likely experienced the issues that accompany pickup and drop-off at Creekside; the addition of another school and potentially having 1,200 students at that location with the existing school is not a viable plan.”

Even the space adjacent to West Elementary has issues.

“The entire site … presents challenges whether considering an addition, or a new build at that location,” he added. “The primary issues presented by topography and slope, as well as the storm drain infrastructure running through the property, limit the ability to simply build to the West or add on with much flexibility. The designs presented by 3Peak and JLG aim to fit an addition of classrooms and a gymnasium, allowing in a manner that works around these factors. A new build, while still educating students in the existing West, has incredibly tight tolerances to fit into the buildable space, while leaving West in Phase 1 and not interfering with the aforementioned issues.” 

The district does own a parcel in the Green Acres subdivision.

Mistie Caldwell, the district business manager, discussed this land and its potential use, as it was a site option for Creekside Elementary School, and why it was rejected.

“The limitations that you’re seeing are, look at the access. There’s one way in, one way out,” Caldwell said.  “Once you get off at Exit 14 to get to that point, is almost a 7-minute drive. … The bus service was challenging. The access to it, that was the issue to that.”

A secondary point as to the rejection of this site previously was the rocky terrain; however, Caldwell said, the logistics of getting students to and from there, and the distance from other schools, are significant.

“If you have a third grader and a kindergartner, you’re almost 18-20 minutes apart,” she said. 

Gottlob said the district will continue to narrow its vision.

“Moving ahead after tonight, what we hope to do is keep narrowing the funnel to what’s viable fiscally and responsibly with taxpayer resources, but also what meets the needs of our current students and sets up future boards and future leadership and the community to be able to offer cutting-edge, world-class, quality education to our students,” he said. 

He added that it is the district’s desire to present the plans to the community this fall or early winter. If the board wants work to begin in 2028, “a decision by next spring is going to be prudent.”

title: Job Corps program in Black Hills open and fully funded
byline: By Bart Pfankuch South Dakota News Watch
description: Students from the Boxelder Job Corps facility in Nemo, participated in wildfire training held by the U.S. Forest Service in 2025. Photo courtesy of USDA
_full_text:
Job Corps 1.jpg
Students from the Boxelder Job Corps facility in Nemo, participated in wildfire training held by the U.S. Forest Service in 2025. Photo courtesy of USDA 

 Job Corps 2.jpg
Students from the Boxelder Job Corps center in Nemo, helped clear trails and replace damaged footbridges after a bad storm in the Black Hills National Forest in 2017. Photo courtesy of USDA 

NEMO — The future once again looks stable for the federal Job Corps workforce training center in the Black Hills of South Dakota now that Congress has fully funded the federal program and a recent lawsuit settlement provided a symbolic boost to the program’s status.

“We’re doing great and we’re thriving,” said Bonnie Fuller, director of the Boxelder Job Corps Civilian Conservation Center near Nemo, South Dakota. 

That optimistic outlook is a major shift over early 2025, when the future of the 125 Job Corps programs across the country looked bleak.

Launched in 1964, Job Corps is designed to provide education and job training to income-qualified youths and young adults who struggled in traditional schools. 

The taxpayer-funded program offers tuition-free housing, classroom education, job training, meals and health care for low-income qualified youths and young adults. The program enrolls about 60,000 students a year and has an annual total cost around $1.8 billion, according to federal budget documents.

The federal government issued a memorandum in May 2025 calling for pausing of operations at 99 contractor-operated Job Corps centers across the country. The memo required the pending closure of centers operated by contractors hired by the U.S. Department of Labor.

That same memo, obtained recently by News Watch, also called for the closure of another 25 centers operated by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, which included campuses in South Dakota and northwestern Nebraska.

At the same time, the Trump administration also called for defunding of the entire program.

Memo laid out closure plans

In a May 2025 news release, then-Labor Secretary Lori Chavez-DeRemer said a government report showed that the contractor-run programs operated at a $140 million deficit in 2024, did not meet participant graduation or job goals and had seen nearly 15,000 reports of sexual, violent or drug-related incidents on its campuses.

The department said its decision aligned with President Trump’s Fiscal Year 2026 budget guidelines to ensure wise use of taxpayer dollars.

Those actions put the future of the Nemo facility and a similar Pine Ridge Job Corps facility near Chadron, Neb., in jeopardy.

According to the USDA, the Boxelder Job Corps facility in 2024 had about 80 enrollees aged 16-24, about half of whom were Native American. USDA documents showed the facility had an average annual budget ranging from $4.5 million to $6 million in recent years. Staffing consists of roughly 40 employees.

The proposed elimination of the federal program drew significant opposition across the country, including within the public and among a bipartisan group of congressional lawmakers. Most closures, including in South Dakota and Nebraska, were delayed by a lawsuit that led a federal judge to stay the closures until the case could be settled.

The uncertainty lingered for months, but Job Corps programs received new life in February 2026 when Congress passed the Consolidated Appropriations Act, which included $1.76 billion in funding for Job Corps centers. President Trump had called for zero funding, but Congress overrode that recommendation.

Lawsuit settlement bolsters program status

This week, the Trump administration decided to settle the lawsuit that held up the pending closure of Job Corps centers run by the Labor Department, according to Adam Pulver, a lawyer for the Public Citizen Litigation Group, which represented the plaintiffs in the case.

The legal case centered around the claim that the Department of Labor violated written procedures required prior to closure of any Job Corps centers, and that the proposed elimination of the program was arbitrary and capricious.

“The wholesale slashing of the Job Corps program wasn’t going to be accepted by the courts, and we’ve seen also that it’s not going to be accepted by Congress,” Pulver told News Watch in an interview. “The Job Corps program is very popular in rural areas and places where people are really struggling to get the skills needed to find high-paying work.”

In addition to offering a path toward a high school diploma or General Educational Development (GED), the Nemo facility offers training in multiple disciplines, including certified nursing assistant, culinary arts, carpentry, painting, welding, office administration and maintenance. 

The center also works closely with the U.S. Forest Service to provide firefighting and other skill sets to Job Corps enrollees.

Fuller told News Watch that several contingents of Boxelder Job Corps enrollees had been dispatched to fight wildfires in South Dakota earlier this year. Other groups of students were also sent to battle wildfires or provide firefighting support at fires in Colorado and in the Boundary Waters area of northern Minnesota.

The congressional funding for Jobs Corps will cover spending only through June 2027, but lawmakers appear to be supportive of the program moving forward, Pulver said. 

The recent court settlement will also protect the centers, and even though it did not directly relate to the USDA-run centers, the administration’s capitulation should provide further stability to those Job Corps programs, he said.

“The fact that support has been so bipartisan in Congress made it clear that you can’t just get rid of the program,” Pulver said. “I wouldn’t expect to see any more of these radical plans to get rid of the program.”

title: It’s opening night for ‘Stage Black’ the area’s new, innovative community theater company
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Joanna and Mitchell Mechaley were married on stage at the Matthews Opera House. Now, they’re the founders of “Stage Black,” the region’s newest community theater company. Photo by Smith & Jones, Rapid City, courtesy of Joanna Mechaley
_full_text:
IMG_2206.jpg
Joanna and Mitchell Mechaley were married on stage at the Matthews Opera House. Now, they’re the founders of “Stage Black,” the region’s newest community theater company. Photo by Smith & Jones, Rapid City, courtesy of Joanna Mechaley 

SPEARFISH — Husband and wife duo Joanna and Mitchell Mechaley share a love that was born and cemented on the stage, but their latest theatrical endeavor may not need a stage at all.

 Clowns Hannay.jpg
 A new area theater company plans to premiere “The 39 Steps” tonight at the Black Hills State University Black Box Theater. Cast members pictured during rehearsal are pictured from left: Mitchell Mechaley, Colt Scott, Casey S. Hibbert. Photo courtesy of Stage Black 

They met acting in a production of the comedy “Noises Off” at the Matthews Opera House. Joanna hadn’t planned to act in the show, but was convinced by director Shirlene Joseph to take on a role. On a lark, and with encouragement from his mother and a fateful newspaper clipping, Mitchell joined the cast for his first-ever foray into community theater. The pair hit it off, and it was curtains up on a lifelong adventure.

 Hannay Crofter Margaret.jpg
Rehearsing for “The 39 Steps,” which opens tonight at the Black Hills State University Black Box Theater are, from left, left Colt Scott, Mitchell Mechaley, and Stephanie Bussiere. Photo courtesy of Stage Black 

The Mechaleys were married on stage at the Matthews.

“Fast forward 20 years and our daughter got married on stage at the opera house. Two of our daughters have been involved in many shows that we have done, sometimes all of us together, sometimes piecemeal. It is a love of theater, it is a love of each other and our family and our visions that we can create together, building our lives,” Mitchell said. “We took about 13 years off to raise our girls because we understood that was a much bigger role to play in life — being parents, than running off and doing theater.”

With their youngest daughter old enough to explore her own creative ambitions, the couple returned to community theater and started to dream outside the box — or the stage, as the case may be.

 Hannay Pamela.jpg
Spy thriller “The 39 Steps” opens tonight — the first show from Stage Black. Actors pictured from left are: Stephanie Bussiere and Colt Scott. Photo courtesy of Stage Black 

“We just set out with the idea of performing really quality theater in small spaces — pushing the boundaries of what we can do, what other people can do, and just celebrating all of the aspects that go into making a really magical show, which is not just the performers,” Joanna said. “The dream is to produce shows in some really strange locations — all of those to be determined.”

Enter Stage Black.

“We named it that because that is the color of a blank canvas for the stage. You paint it black at the end, the curtains are black, the crew wears black. It just accents all the action on stage,” Joanna said.

Unlike other community theater programs in the region, which are anchored to historic venues like the Matthews or the Homestake Opera House, or cities like Belle Fourche and Sturgis, Stage Black is rootless by design.

Without the strictures of a physical stage, the company could perform outside, in restaurants, or wherever the imagination of its creators can dream of taking it. Joanna said the company plans to pair shows and locations that complement each other, and nurture partnerships in the community to expand the landscape of community theater in an area blessed with what she calls “a deep well of talent.”

For its first production, Stage Black has chosen “The 39 Steps,” a spy thriller adapted for the big screen by none other than Alfred Hitchcock. It will be performed at Black Hills State University’s Black Box Theater.

“We have a chase scene outside of a train. We have plane crashes. We have every character portrayed in the movie, portrayed by 4 actors. The action is non-stop. It is super quick.

Super quick scene changes, lightning fast costume changes, accents, well over 100 sound cues, a cinematic score underneath. It is just crazy,” Joanna said. “It is very physical. It has a lot of work with accents and all of these special skills.”

To tackle this ambitious first show, the pair hand-picked their cast and crew.

“The 39 Steps” will star Mitchell, Colt Scott, Stephanie Bussiere, and Casey Hibbert. Joanna is directing, and Sandy Tarrant is on board as assistant director.

“This show has been so much fun because I am directing. Mitchell is on stage. Our daughter Rose has stepped in as our digital marketer. She has designed the website, the social media, all of those things, and then our youngest daughter Killian is part of the crew. She is going to run our box office. She designed the soundtrack, and she is backstage running like mad with scene changes and costume changes,” Joanna said. “We are all on deck here.”

By virtue of their own story, the Mechaleys have an almost implicit understanding of the capacity of theater to build connection. That’s part of why shows will be subject to open casting calls in the future.

“We don’t want to see the same people on the stage every time for every single show. We always- that is what community theater is when we started to do this, to start our own theater company; we want to include everybody,” Mitchell said. “Both Joanna and I are big proponents of welcoming new actors. You have no idea who that next person is. It doesn’t always matter the quality of acting. It is the passion behind it. You just need somebody who jumps in to go, ‘I love this! I can’t wait to do it again.’ We go, ‘Yes! We can’t wait for you to do it again.’”

Love and passion for theatrical storytelling is worth nurturing, Joanna said, because theater is “one of the most powerful tools when it comes to building empathy to the world around you.”

“We talk a lot about empathy in theater because you are really in a scenario, both as a performer and as an audience, to accept that your reality, your perception, is not the only one out there,” Joanna said. “As a performer, you have to actively step into those shoes and portray a character that you don’t understand the way this type of person thinks, but you’re forced to dive into it and accept that this is a reality. As an audience member, you find that you hurt for or root for somebody different than yourself.”

For the magic of theater work, the Mechaleys say the most important ingredient is an audience. “The 39 Steps” opens tonight at 7 p.m., followed by a 2 p.m. matinee Sunday, and evening performances on Monday, Wednesday, Thursday, and on Saturday, Aug. 22. The final performance is slated for Sunday, Aug. 23 at 2 p.m.

Tickets to “The 39 Steps” are available for presale online at stageblack.productions and at the door.

title: I-90 closures planned for reconstruction project near Piedmont
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Road Closed
Courtesy photo 

PIEDMONT — Lane closures are planned between Exits 44 and 48 on I-90 near Piedmont, beginning Monday.

During lane closures, traffic will be limited to a single lane in each direction as workers build new exit ramps, bridge foundations, and drainage structures.

The speed limit will be reduced to 45 MPH when workers are present, 65 MPH through the work zone. 

Lane closures on both the westbound and eastbound lanes are anticipated to remain in place through November.

Upcoming construction is part of a project that will reconstruct exit 46 and portions of Elk Creek Road and Sturgis Road in Piedmont. The multi-year project includes new exit ramps, a new bridge over I-90, elimination of an at-grade railroad crossing on Elk Creek Road by constructing a bridge over the railroad, replacement of drainage structures, and new concrete pavement on I-90 between Exit 44 and mile marker 47.

Heavy Constructors, of Rapid City, was awarded the $77.7 million contract for the project. Projected completion date is December 2028.

To find additional information about the project, visit https://dot.sd.gov/i90exit46.

title: Kool Deadwood Nites returns to the Hills
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Hot on the heels of the Sturgis Motorcycles Rally, Kool Deadwood Nites will return Tuesday, bringing classic cars, live music, and parades to the Black Hills. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Kool Deadwood Nites returns to the Hills.JPG
Hot on the heels of the Sturgis Motorcycles Rally, Kool Deadwood Nites will return Tuesday, bringing classic cars, live music, and parades to the Black Hills. Courtesy photo 

DEADWOOD — Hot on the heels of Sturgis Rally, Kool Deadwood Nites swings into town Tuesday, bringing show and shines, parades, and plenty of live music to Deadwood. 

“Kool Deadwood Nites is one of the biggest events of the year in Deadwood,” said Jesse Allen, events coordinator for the chamber of commerce. “If you’re into classic cars, live music, and that classic ‘50s and ‘60s vibe, this is definitely the event for you.”

The event kicks off Tuesday with a show and shine on Main Street from 6-9 p.m.

Mr. Wu’s will be offering free entertainment, giveaways, and deals on bottomless draft beers all week. Free concerts at the lower Main Street casino will begin at 3 p.m., featuring Kuhl & The Gangstas, with shows continuing daily featuring local favorites.

Registration will take place daily at the Deadwood Welcome Center from noon to 6 p.m.

Wednesday, another show and shine is scheduled in Sturgis for registered cars only. Participants will receive a free lunch catered by the Knuckle Saloon. Winner of the Sturgis Choice Award will be announced Wednesday on Main Street stage and awarded Thursday.

Surfin’ Safari will play Wednesday at 6 p.m. at Outlaw Square, followed by El Loco Fandango, a ZZ Top tribute band, at Mr. Wu’s at 7 p.m.

The annual sock hop and People’s Choice Awards is scheduled for Thursday at the History and Information Center parking lot. 

The fun continues Friday with the annual Rod Run, featuring 2 runs from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. Participants will depart from the Days of ’76 Rodeo Grounds following a free breakfast offered to registered participants at The Lodge at Deadwood from 7–10 a.m. 

Concerts continue Friday at the Main Street Stage, featuring Stereo Trip at 5 p.m., followed by Play Some Petty at 6 p.m. and Hotel California at 8 p.m.

“(Aug. 22) morning is when the big Kool Deadwood Nites car show takes place at the Deadwood Event Complex beginning at 8 a.m.,” said Allen. “It’s a great chance to see an incredible lineup of classic cars all in one place.”

Aug. 23 parade participants are encouraged to line up at the Rodeo Grounds beginning at 7 a.m., with the parade scheduled to begin at 9 a.m. A show and shine along Deadwood Main Street will follow directly afterwards, with awards announced at 11 a.m. at the History and Information parking lot.

“Kool Deadwood Nites is truly such a fun weekend and we are so excited to welcome everyone back to Deadwood for classic cars, great music, and an unforgettable trip back in time,” said Allen.

title: Church group brings food and fellowship to Judy’s Assisted Living Center
byline: Pioneer staff report
description: BELLE FOURCHE — Residents at Judy’s Assisted Living Center enjoyed a morning of food, fellowship, and heartfelt conversation on Aug. 6 as volunteers from St. James Lutheran Church, Belle Fourche, continued their monthly outreach tradition. The gathering, known as “Cookies and Chatter,” has been a cherished ministry for the past 3 years.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

BELLE FOURCHE — Residents at Judy’s Assisted Living Center enjoyed a morning of food, fellowship, and heartfelt conversation on Aug. 6 as volunteers from St. James Lutheran Church, Belle Fourche, continued their monthly outreach tradition. The gathering, known as “Cookies and Chatter,” has been a cherished ministry for the past 3 years.

Each first Thursday of the month, the ladies of St. James Lutheran Church arrive with homemade treats and smiles, spending time visiting with residents who often have limited social interaction. 

The recent visit featured cherry cheesecake, watermelon, cantaloupe, and homemade fudge served in the dining area. Conversations centered on gratitude and the importance of kindness, encouraging residents to reflect on small joys and the value of connection.

“We come here to remind them they’re not forgotten,” said ministry coordinator Genevieve Skogberg, who has helped organize the monthly visits since the program began. “A simple conversation or sharing a meal can brighten someone’s entire week. Our ladies are dedicated to these special visits, and we are honored to spend time with each other.”

Center manager Judy Riedel, said residents eagerly anticipate each visit, often asking, “Are they coming?” She described the gatherings as a time of togetherness — sharing stories, enjoying food, and building a sense of family within the center. Staff members assist residents throughout the event, helping create a warm and welcoming atmosphere.

title: Meade Co. sheriff announces  $67K in equipment grants
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Three grants totaling nearly $67,000 will allow the Meade County Sheriff’s Department to purchase much-needed equipment, Sheriff Pat West announced recently.
_full_text:
STURGIS — Three grants totaling nearly $67,000 will allow the Meade County Sheriff’s Department to purchase much-needed equipment, Sheriff Pat West announced recently. 

During the Meade County Commission meeting, Aug. 4, West said his office received a $17,000 highway safety grant that will pay for overtime for increased speed and seatbelt enforcement. The grant will also buy new radar devices. 

“So how far away does that thing read? I just want to know how much time I have to hit the brakes,” Commissioner Doreen Creed jokingly asked. 

“If you see them, they’ve got you,” West said. 

West said his office also received a $13,000 grant from the Department of Homeland Security. The grant will help purchase binoculars, so deputies can watch incidents or suspects from a long range. 

The largest grant of $36,290 also came from the Department of Homeland Security, and West said that money will be used to purchase a new off-road UTV with tracks. West told the commission that Meade County Emergency Management Director Sean Henderson was instrumental in securing the grant for the sheriff’s office. 

“If we get in a position where we get a lot of snow, we can actually get somewhere and get people picked up and back to safety,” West said. “I’ve been arm wrestling to try to get some money for that, and it finally came through.” 

In addition to the grants for the sheriff’s office, West said Henderson was also responsible for securing a $72,000 grant for the Blackhawk Fire Department, to be used for equipment.

title: SD board approves $500K in loans, grants for business projects
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — A South Dakota board approved a total of $481,199 in state loans and grants Wednesday for businesses in Rapid City and De Smet.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — A South Dakota board approved a total of $481,199 in state loans and grants Wednesday for businesses in Rapid City and De Smet.

The Board of Economic Development approved a $300,000 loan for Chemistry Distilling, a Rapid City company founded in 2024. The money will help the company purchase and renovate an industrial facility to manufacture and store high-purity ethanol. 

The company’s Sam Papendick said in a statement to South Dakota Searchlight that Chemistry Distilling is taking existing ethanol and putting it through an additional purification process to “remove trace impurities and water to produce very high-purity, 200-proof ethanol that can meet specifications for higher-value markets.”

Papendick said those markets include pharmaceutical and laboratory applications, food and flavor processing, personal care products, extraction and other specialty chemical uses. 

“We also have a beverage side of the business, where high-purity neutral spirits can become the base for products like vodka and other distilled beverages,” he said in the statement. 

The loan comes from the SD Works Program, which provides low-interest financing for eligible business projects. The Governor’s Office of Economic Development said the project is expected to create seven full-time jobs over five years.

Dakota Evergreen received a $90,000 loan from the same program to purchase a chiropractic clinic in De Smet. The loan is expected to help retain four full-time jobs and keep the clinic operating. A press release from the Governor’s Office of Economic Development said it is the only chiropractic provider in a 35-mile radius.

“These projects strengthen local communities, support good-paying jobs, and build a strong, diverse economy that is ‘Open for Opportunity,’” said Gov. Larry Rhoden in the release. 

The board also approved a grant of up to $91,199 through the South Dakota Jobs Program for Innovative Materials & Processes to expand its Rapid City operation with a new building and manufacturing and warehouse equipment. The jobs program provides grants tied to qualifying business investments and job creation.

The defense contractor and research firm was founded in 1999, and researches and manufactures explosives, pyrotechnics and more for the U.S. Army and Navy. The state release said the expansion is expected to create 18 to 24 jobs.

title: State commission accepts $290 million  bid for Platte-Winner Bridge
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: The South Dakota Highway 44 Platte-Winner Bridge, which crosses the Missouri River in the southeast part of the state. Photo courtesy of the South Dakota Department of Transportation
_full_text:
State commission accepts $290 million bid for Platte-Winner Bridge.png
The South Dakota Highway 44 Platte-Winner Bridge, which crosses the Missouri River in the southeast part of the state. Photo courtesy of the South Dakota Department of Transportation 

PIERRE — The South Dakota Transportation Commission on Thursday approved a nearly $290 million bid — about $40 million above the state’s estimate — to replace the Platte-Winner Bridge.

The vote means the state is moving forward with what Department of Transportation Secretary Joel Jundt called  “the largest project that the DOT has ever led.” 

The commission accepted Ames Construction’s $289.99 million bid to replace the state Highway 44 bridge over the Missouri River in the southeast part of the state. The bid is about $39.25 million, or 15.7%, above the state’s estimate of $250.74 million.

Ames Construction is headquartered in Burnsville, Minnesota. Three other companies submitted higher bids ranging from $306 million to $450 million.

Ames also submitted a $652,125 bid for a smaller bridge project in Douglas County that was bundled with the Platte-Winner project. That bid was about $64,500 below the state’s estimate.

Jundt told commissioners the state has enough money to proceed despite the Platte-Winner bid coming in substantially higher than anticipated.

“Do we have the money to afford the project?” Jundt said. “We would answer the question as a positive yes.”

Jundt said the department has spent years planning how to pay for it without overstressing the federal funding the state relies on for major highway projects. 

Beyond that, the Platte-Winner project has received a $65 million Federal Highway Administration Competitive Highway Bridge Program grant and $25 million secured by the state’s congressional delegation.

Jundt said the department is also awaiting a decision on another federal grant application and will continue pursuing other federal funding.

Jundt told commissioners the higher cost can be covered with the department’s regular federal funding. Because construction will take several years, the department will not pay the entire contract at once. Contractors are reimbursed as work is completed and accepted by the state.

Department staff attributed the higher bids to complexities with building in deep water, specialized equipment, the bridge’s size, market conditions and the remote location, which creates logistical costs.

The new bridge will be about 5,770 feet long and built just north of the existing bridge, allowing traffic to continue using the old structure during construction. Work could begin this fall. 

The department hopes the bridge will be open to traffic by June 2030, with final completion, including removal of the existing bridge, scheduled for November 2031.

The existing bridge opened in 1966 and, at 5,655 feet, is South Dakota’s longest. The department has said deterioration and long-term structural concerns require a replacement.

While Jundt said the state can afford the Platte-Winner Bridge project, he cautioned commissioners the same cannot yet be said about the state’s next major bridge replacement. 

“I do not feel comfortable moving forward,” Jundt said. 

The next bridge is the U.S. Highway 212 Forest City Bridge over the Missouri River, west of Gettysburg in the north-central part of the state. The existing bridge opened in 1958, and the department has said landslides along its southern approach have resulted in millions of dollars in repairs and mitigation work.

Jundt told commissioners the project is expected to be even more expensive.

“The funding is not there for that project, nor the other projects in the future,” he said.

Jundt said the state will have to determine how to finance those projects in coming years, depending in part on future federal funding.

“We’ll cross that bridge, pun intended, here in the next few years,” he said.

title: A view from the dash cam
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Sgt. Chris Williams watches traffic closely during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
IMG_1043.jpeg
Sgt. Chris Williams watches traffic closely during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

STURGIS — Riding with Sgt. Chris Williams during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally can give a person hope for the future of law enforcement and the overall respect the general public has for the profession.

On Aug. 7-8, I rode with Williams for a cumulative total of 4 hours, patrolling Lazelle Street and Highway 34 out to the Buffalo Chip Campground, in a Meade County Sheriff’s Office pickup. As I rode in the passenger seat, I watched Williams smile at passers by. I watched many bikers make eye contact with the police officer and mouth the words “thank you,” as he drove slowly by. There were handshakes, and good vibes all around for the sergeant with the Meade County Sheriff’s Office.

“It’s 95% of the people who have our back,” Williams said, as he explained the gestures of gratitude we saw on the street. “It’s that 5% out of all the contacts we have that are not. We’ve had deputies get a handshake at the end of arresting somebody. It’s an ‘I appreciate you’ kind of thing. I feel like the majority supports us.”

Pull quote
“We don’t use the ‘Q’ word, but a quiet day is a good day,” Williams said. “A quiet day is a safe day.” — Sgt. Chris Williams, Meade County Sheriff’s Office

Working to keep his friends and neighbors safe in his hometown is what Williams likes most about the job.

“This is where I live, and it makes me proud to be part of what keeps us safe and a destination,” Williams said as he waived to a group of bikers at a house on Main Street. “My son used to mow their lawn when he was younger. He doesn’t mow lawns anymore, so now I do it.”

Williams, who grew up in Sturgis, graduated from Sturgis Brown High School in 1997 and then joined the U.S. Marine Corps. as an infantryman. He served from 1997-2001, and when he got out of the military, he worked for his uncle’s medical supply business for a short time. He soon found himself applying at the Meade County Sheriff’s Office, where they were looking for a few good men.

 DSC_0850.JPG
Sgt. Chris Williams helps conduct a traffic stop on Saturday, Aug. 8, during the first part of the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick  

Ready or not for Rally

“I love to see these guys,” Williams said of the extra conservation officers and other law enforcement officers who come from outlying areas to help work the Rally. Every year, he said the Meade County Sheriff’s Office doubles their personnel during Rally time by putting partners with the 12 deputies on staff. Williams has made friends with many of them who come to the Rally every year, and always makes sure to get his annual picture with them.

“I look forward to it every year,” he said. “Everybody always asks, ‘are you ready?’ Well, sheriff’s office, it’s coming whether we’re ready or not. So, we just go to work. There’s really no getting ready, other than planning and getting a couple partners and making sure your ticket book or that kind of thing is taken care of.”

Our ride together on the official day of the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally was pretty quiet, as thousands of bikers seemed to behave themselves and enjoy the massive party that descends upon Sturgis every year.

“We don’t use the ‘Q’ word, but a quiet day is a good day,” Williams said. “A quiet day is a safe day.

 IMG_1042.jpeg
Sgt. Chris Williams poses with his longtime friend, Corey Jonas, who joins the Meade County Sheriff’s Office to help provide law enforcement every year during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick  

“Everybody around us gets a bunch of traffic,” he added, as he referred to the Rally sprawl that occurs across the entire Black Hills area. “Well, Meade County and Sturgis, we get 250,000 guests that are staying here for the Rally, and we treat them as such. I want them to be able to come back. These guys are here to have a good time. I’d love to meet everybody, but we really don’t want to meet. Because if we meet, something’s wrong.”

Williams explained that in addition to the Rally traffic in and around Sturgis, the Meade County Sheriff’s Office is responsible for their regular calls throughout the county. Deputies frequently get called to Piedmont or Blackhawk, which is about 25 miles away, and sometimes they have to go from there to Faith, which is an additional 75 miles.

A quiet shift is not typical, Williams said. Most years, the Meade County Sheriff’s Office responds to about 1,400 calls over the 10-day period, a number that hasn’t changed much from when Williams started in 2004, when they responded to 1,200 calls. The exception, he said, was the 75th anniversary of the Rally, which drew an official count of about 750,000 bikers — the largest Rally on record. In that year, he said, deputies only logged about 800 calls for service.

“We associate that with the amount of traffic,” he said. “It’s harder for us to get around. It’s harder to turn on that vehicle, so we’re short traffic stops, and those are our really big numbers.”

Williams was recently promoted to the rank of sergeant, a supervisory role in the sheriff’s office. But for many years he worked as an investigator. He assisted with the outlaw motorcycle gang task force, and partnered with DCI agents on patrol during the Rally. This year’s Rally is only the second year he has worked the day shift, and he said it’s an adjustment. The difference is the larger number of drug and DUI arrests on the night shift, versus the number of medical calls and crashes during the day.

 DSC_0841.JPG
Sgt. Chris Williams helps divert traffic from a routine traffic stop along Highway 34. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

As Williams discussed the many different kinds of calls for different shifts, he pulled onto 132nd Road, at the Buffalo Chip Campground, where a gate attendant immediately jumped out of his chair and opened the gate.

“That’s where we go for all of our medical and criminal calls,” Williams said. “That’s why that gentleman just opened the gate. He’s so used to when he sees us or EMS, he automatically opens the gate.”

But instead of turning into the campground, Williams waived and smiled. He stopped to throw a football back to a group of parking attendants, and continued on his route back up Highway 34 to Lazelle Street.

During a slow shift, Williams said he could sometimes log 50-60 miles driving the same route, watching for activity. He figures it’s the calm before the storm, before activity starts to ramp up for the Rally.

Traffic stops

While we drove together on the second day, one of the first calls Williams received was from an investigator with the sheriff’s office. The investigator conducted a traffic stop in her unmarked car, and she needed more traffic tickets. While she finished the traffic stop, Williams assisted with traffic control.

Traffic stops are how many arrests are made during the Rally, Williams said. Some of the best interdictionists, or police who take illegal goods that are being transported, are the ones who make the most traffic stops, he said. In fact, he said police refer to the stretch of Highway 34 between Sturgis and the Buffalo Chip Campground as “the gauntlet,” due to the number of traffic stops and arrests made after concerts.

“If you see 6 sets of headlights, 5 of them are cops,” he said.

But while we rode together, Williams did not conduct any traffic stops. Since it was the middle of the day, we were always immersed in high traffic situations. Sometimes, he said, when a vehicle is only slightly over the limit, it’s not worth the safety risk to turn around in traffic.

“Sometimes you just gotta not do that,” he said. “It’s just not worth making a U-turn. Even though you are an emergency vehicle with your red and blues on, it’s not worth pulling that car over when it’s going 10 miles over the speed limit.”

But in one instance, Williams observed a few semi-trucks and a camper, attempting to turn from Highway 79 into the Full Throttle Saloon. The endeavor caused a significant traffic jam on a blind hill crest, and Williams decided to help provide traffic control.

“Traffic is backed up over that blind hill. I’ll just keep my lights on until that semi gets off the road. If there’s somebody coming over that hill at 65, and there’s a bunch of motorcycles stopped, that’s not good,” he said. “It’s getting to the point here where they’re going to need to figure out something, because they’re backing traffic up northbound, beyond the property line.”

Rally stories

“I’ve never seen the good side of any of these establishments,” Williams said about major campgrounds and bars east of Sturgis along Highways 34 and 79. “I would never say no to my son if there was a band out here that he really wanted to see. But, just be aware. That’s the thing with these places. We see the bad side of these establishments. So, it may be an absolute riot and just a good vibe inside, which I would imagine it is. But we don’t get to see that. We only see the outskirts and the runoff that comes out of there.”

Just that morning, Williams explained that one of his deputies arrested a man at Glencoe Campground, for pushing over another man’s motorcycle and smashing the mirror. Williams frequently responds to calls at Glencoe Campground, where deputies often find themselves in uncomfortable situations. One Glencoe road in particular, which dispatchers refer to as “Tata Alley,” is particularly bad, he said.

“The majority of our calls are at that alley, and it’s from golf cart crashes, side by side crashes, motorcycle crashes, and you have 1,000 people,” Williams said. “Then you throw in a set of police lights, well now you have 5,000 people standing around you. It’s a very crummy situation and a crummy place to have to conduct a criminal investigation,” he added. “The crashes are the worst, because there’s 1,000 people and nobody saw anything. Each year we end up with somebody that has fallen off a golf cart and the driver of the golf cart can never be found, and we get somebody that’s got severe injuries.

“There have been times where we’ve had to get in with the crowd and try to bring somebody out,” Williams continued about his experiences at Glencoe Campground. “There have been times when we’re going ‘OK, this is scary.’ Because now the crowd is that 5%, and they’re starting to get owly with us, and protest their friend being arrested. Then it just agitates everybody around them.”

When it comes to helping law enforcement respond to calls east of town, Williams said the Buffalo Chip Campground and the Full Throttle Saloon are the most helpful. Those establishments have their own security teams that usually bring the perpetrators, or witnesses, out to the deputies. By doing that, the investigation is conducted outside of the main event area and away from onlookers.

One of those times, Williams said, was at 4 a.m. one year when a man decided to drive a large pickup through the Buffalo Chip Campground — running over tents. One woman was sleeping in a tent that got run over, he said. She survived, but suffered lifelong injuries.

One of Williams’ most memorable moments at the Buffalo Chip Campground, was when he was assisting with an undercover investigation to arrest a sex offender. It was Williams’ first year as an investigator, and he was partnered with a DCI agent. The two were assisting the Internet Crimes Team with the takedown of a suspect. The code word to mobilize the deputies was “Disneyland,” he said. But, unfortunately, the undercover agent spoke the code word at the exact moment the concert ended for the night. When officers began to jump out of vehicles, screaming “get on the ground,” most people around the area didn’t realize the undercover officers were actually conducting a real operation.

“All these people around us, these concert goers, were mimicking us. ‘Oh, it’s the cops! Get on the ground!’ It was like a joke to them. They didn’t know it was legit. We get the bad guy on the ground and we’re cuffing him when (the DCI agent) comes around and he is gassed. He is out of breath. We literally threw this guy in our car and we took off. I asked (the DCI agent) ‘why were you so out of breath and late? I was sitting right behind you and I beat you.’ He said while he was sitting there in our gear, he readjusted his vest and his seatbelt was still on. He velcroed his seatbelt to his vest. So, when we took off to run at the bad guy, it was like a dog on the end of a leash. So, he’s on the ground trying to undo his vest. It was pretty good. I wish it would have been on camera.”

Coping with the job

From dealing with sex crimes and crimes against children, to handling the medical calls or the drug arrests, or investigating fatalities, the job comes with a variety that can showcase the very worst of humanity. After awhile, he said all the Rallies start to run together, as getting the “bad guys” off the street becomes a routine mission. For Williams, a great Rally would include zero fatalities, and record-breaking drug arrests that mean the poison and “bad guys” are off the streets.

But when the heat gets turned way up at work, Williams said that’s when he relies on his faith, family, friends and teammates at the Meade County Sheriff’s Office. The longtime deputy sheriff, who has built a career investigating heinous criminal activity, got emotional when asked about how he decompresses after work.

“That one gets me, because the last thing I want to do is take this stuff home,” he said, stressing that he makes a conscious decision to not bring work home with him. He places high value on his relationships, especially those he has with his wife of 22 years, and his 18 and 16-year-old children. Those relationships, and his strong faith, are what get him through the hardest times.

“I have investigated the death of over a dozen children. I rely heavily on my faith,” he said.

Weekends on the water are also important for relieving the stress of the job, as Williams loves to take his boat out to the lake or to the Missouri River in Pierre.

“This will be the first weekend we have missed the lake since May,” he said.

But when it’s time for bed, and he still can’t get his mind to shut off from his day at work, Williams said there’s only one tried-and-true remedy.

“I will fall asleep watching Disney movies,” he said. “I’m a big Ratatouille fan.”

title: Law enforcement continues  to grapple with parking  near Boar’s Nest
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Sheriff Brian Dean told Lawrence County commissioners his office moved more than 200 bikes that were illegally parked outside the Boar’s Nest in one day at the Tuesday commission meeting. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
20260812_155532.jpg
Sheriff Brian Dean told Lawrence County commissioners his office moved more than 200 bikes that were illegally parked outside the Boar’s Nest in one day at the Tuesday commission meeting. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

DEADWOOD — Lawrence County commissioners heard from Sheriff Brian Dean Tuesday, who reported his office moved approximately 200 bikes the previous day that were parked illegally outside the Boar’s Nest, a restaurant outside of Lead operating under a conditional use permit marked for annual review. 

“That’s just in the first attempt, it doesn’t count what we had to do when we went back,” said Dean. “I’m happy to report that the owners of the Boar’s Nest seem to be working with us, but I think it kind of puts to scale what we’re trying to get our hands around, so to speak. I don’t find it too dissimilar from the situation that we dealt with a few years ago at Devil’s Bathtub. It takes a while to figure out what’s going to work. Perhaps one of the differences here, though, is the strong influx over a short period of time. I would consider this to be of some exigency.”

The malt liquor license for the restaurant located on US Highway 14A south of Lead came under scrutiny in May, when neighbors and citizens voiced concerns about safety surrounding motorcyclists and vehicles parking along the highway. Law enforcement voiced concerns at that time about pedestrians being struck by vehicles rounding corners at high speeds near the restaurant.

Dean said vehicles are considered illegally parked only if their vehicle is parked on the road side of the white line. 

Dean said other concerns this time of year include the extreme fire danger, with hot engines on bikes and vehicles being parked in the dry grass along the roadway.

Dean said it’s possible that a deputy will be posted outside of the restaurant in 2-hour shifts to monitor the situation. 

“I might add that this is a deputy we don’t necessarily have to spare,” he said. 

Pull quote
“This is a deputy we don’t necessarily have to spare.” — Brian Dean, Lawrence County sheriff

Dean said deputies have worked with towing companies to remove bikes from the roadway.

“I don’t want to make light of it, but basically when a couple uniformed deputies in marked vehicles show up with a wrecker, and they start loading bikes up on the wrecker, there is a sprint to try to prevent your bike from getting towed,” he said. “So, I don’t mean to imply that the deputy physically touched 200 bikes, but that just gives you the scale of what they’re dealing with up there. It’s a mad dash.”

Dean said his office has worked in collaboration with the highway department and emergency management, who have agreed to move 2 digital signs from projects on Nemo Road to US Highway 14A. He said the signs will be used to caution drivers to slow down and be aware of pedestrians in the road. 

With Kool Deadwood Nites approaching Aug. 18 - 23, and the restaurant being a known stop and location of occasional burn outs during the event, Dean asked commissioners to consider the purchase of a third digital sign.

John Bey, highway superintendent, said digital signs range in price from $18,000-20,000. He said the highway department could make use of the sign year-round. 

Bruce Outka, deputy state’s attorney, said commissioners have approximately $42,000 in contingency funds that could be used to pay for the sign. 

Commissioners are expected to discuss the possible purchase of a third digital sign in the coming commission meetings.

title: SD attorney general plans to introduce ‘safeguards’ for license plate readers
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — South Dakota’s top law enforcement official announced Wednesday that he plans to propose state legislation limiting the use of automatic license plate readers, such as Flock cameras, to “legitimate law enforcement purposes.”
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — South Dakota’s top law enforcement official announced Wednesday that he plans to propose state legislation limiting the use of automatic license plate readers, such as Flock cameras, to “legitimate law enforcement purposes.”

Republican Attorney General Marty Jackley said it’s important to have “reasonable safeguards” statewide, while allowing uses that help solve criminal investigations.

He said the technology was “instrumental” in finding a 9-year-old girl who was abducted in Clark County in 2023 and in the investigation into the disappearance and death of 14-year-old McKenna Wendel, of Sioux Falls, which is the subject of an ongoing prosecution.

“I think this is, because of really what’s happened nationally, something that I think deserves legislative attention and proper legislation that allows law enforcement to use vital tools and has safeguards for private, individual privacy,” Jackley said.

National groups including the American Civil Liberties Union have raised concerns about how the data collected by Flock cameras is used. In other states, police officers have been accused of abuses such as using the technology to track romantic partners or exes.

Jackley said he believes there’s bipartisan support for using the technology to solve serious crimes.

“But if you’re doing that, you need to safeguard our privacy, we take that very seriously in South Dakota,” he said, adding “let’s put in the safeguards, put it in the law so that everybody knows what those safeguards are.”

Sioux Falls and Madison are among the South Dakota cities already using the technology. Earlier this year, law enforcement in those cities said the technology helps find criminal suspects. The cameras capture images of license plates on passing vehicles, which can be checked against databases of reported crimes.

Decisions on how the technology is used, how records are kept and where the cameras are placed are all up to local authorities, Jackley said. He said the goal of his legislation would be to ensure data from license plate readers may only be collected, accessed or used for law enforcement investigations into criminal activity, and to require that any information gathered must be protected and deleted within an established period of time unless it is directly relevant to an ongoing criminal investigation.

Jackley said he’s engaging groups like the state’s attorneys association, the sheriff’s association and the police chief’s association, as well as other states’ attorneys general to learn about how other states regulate the cameras.

The attorney general in South Dakota can ask lawmakers to sponsor bills on his behalf. Jackley’s term as attorney general ends in January, the same month that the annual legislative session begins. Jackley is running for the U.S. House rather than for reelection as attorney general.

Jackley told South Dakota Searchlight he plans to involve Lance Russell, the unopposed Republican nominee for attorney general, in conversations about the legislation. Russell did not immediately respond to a message from Searchlight.

title: Middle school gym floor  removed following flooding
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — The gym floor at Spearfish Middle School has been removed.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

SPEARFISH — The gym floor at Spearfish Middle School has been removed.

Nick Gottlob, superintendent of the Spearfish School District, said the removal began Tuesday morning following the June 30 water main leak that flooded parts of the high school and middle school.

The floor was removed so samples of the subfloor and HVAC system could be taken to determine if additional repairs or cleaning is required. 

He said the varsity boys’ locker room should have been sanitized as of Tuesday and the girls’ locker room and coaches’ office is anticipated to be fully cleaned by Sunday.

He said the hallway carpet likely can be salvaged, which is good, as it is 2 years old.

The water line, Gottlob said, has been fully repaired, but there are fans still blowing in the cavern the high-pressure water carved out in the middle of the night. 

“At some point, we’ll need to get some engineered material in there to backfill that cavity that was left by the washout from the water pressure,” he said. 

He said the district has a proposal from a company to replace the gym floor. If approved by the insurance company, materials may arrive by Aug. 20-22.

Typically, he said, the floor once fully installed, has to wait about 30 days before it can be sealed and then used. 

“The boards need to acclimate,” he said. “It needs to adjust the humidity. The subfloor is no different than your home. Things need to stretch, and at some point, we’ll be looking to Mr. (Don) Lyon (middle school principal) and his team to help with the floor designs.”

Shortly before midnight on June 30, a water main broke, and for about 6 hours, it spewed dirt and water throughout the gym, locker rooms, coaches’ office and hallways. 

It did not damage the high school floor thanks to a small elevation gain.

“I’m going to again thank Josh Gerhold and his team. We had a full plate this summer without that,” Gottlob said.

title: Spearfish fire requests more personnel in 2027
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Spearfish Fire Chief Scott Deaver presents his department’s draft budget to the city council. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Deaver.JPG
Spearfish Fire Chief Scott Deaver presents his department’s draft budget to the city council. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — In 2027, the Spearfish Fire Department would like to hire a new paid firefighter, and plans to cover half the salary of an administrative coordinator in the coming year. The preliminary budget for wages in 2027 is more than $100,000 more than in 2026 — an increase from $361,296 to $487,933.

The department services a 186-square-mile protection district, and Fire Chief Scott Deaver said the city’s call volume has “jumped.”

“If we could get some full-time positions in there to right-size with our call volume at the growth of the city, and the coverage district, that would help very much,” Deaver said.

On its year-round payroll, the department has one fire inspector, one firefighter who was added in 2026, one wildland engine boss, Deaver, and Deputy Chief Brian Ziegler. Three other seasonal firefighters are employed by the city and used around the country as needed. This, wildland fire program, provides a revenue stream for the city. 

 Tower.png
Progress has begun on the new fire training tower, as shared by Spearfish Fire Chief Scott Deaver. Photo courtesy Spearfish Fire Department 

“With the demand for service stuff, we were averaging for them 90 hours during a pay period,” Deaver said. Wildland firefighters 

Deaver described volunteers as the “heartbeat of the department,” but said that even volunteer stipends can become a large expense when resources are stretched thin.

“One of the questions that Councilman (Dean) Myers had was how much are the volunteers paid, and they’re given a $15 stipend per call and for other things such as training attended, apparatus inspection nights, and special events,” Deaver said. “Believe it or not, with the call volume and stuff like that, it turns out to be an enormous amount of money when we start putting that together.”

Deaver said that often quality volunteers will train with the Spearfish Fire Department, only to leave for a job as a paid firefighter in another jurisdiction.

“If we hire full-time positions, that eliminates the pain of having very good people leave,” Deaver said.

He said additional paid staff could help generate revenue.

“There are things that we have adopted through the fire code for revenue builders, if you will — like annual fire inspections and stuff,” Deaver said. “We simply do not have the personnel during our day to follow through with that.”

Pull quote
“We are looking at safety. We are looking at job burnout as something that is real.” — Scott Deaver, Spearfish Fire Chief 

The other revenue generated by the fire department generally comes from the wildland crew. However, the department’s budget doesn’t necessarily reflect that.

“Typically, wildland fire is a revenue generator for the city. As we send the firefighters out, we are able to bill through our cooperative agreement with the state,” said Spearfish Finance Officer Michelle DeNeui. “The budget you have before you in wildland is as if there are zero wildland calls. That is how we develop the expenditure side of the budget. Then I do plug in the revenue to make the fund have a net zero.”

To achieve net zero in the wildland fund, the program will need to earn $355,844 in intergovernmental revenue from deployments. That would require expected revenue from contract fires to increase from $281,586 in 2026.

Deaver said staff is the biggest change in the budget for 2027 is the request for new employees. The total fire budget for the coming year is $1,088,440 compared to 951,082 in 2026.

As budget season rolls on at city hall, the Spearfish Fire Department is seeing significant progress in the construction of its fire training facility.

“This is the project that has really hit a stride. We began this in 2019 — the planning of the site and stuff like that,” said Deaver. “And now we’ve got something in there; the excitement is we actually see its real and it is coming.”

The tower is the centerpiece for what may turn into a larger training center — with classroom space and facilities that can be used by other city departments.

For the coming year, the training center construction accounts for $400,000 in the budget.

“A request is being made for a training center to be added to the fire training tower location, and that is proposed to be fully funded with a donation from the Volunteer Fire Association,” said DeNeui. “They have participated in the cost of the fire training center; about $355,000 is what they are contributing to the cost of the training tower construction.”

Deaver said the department is also looking for grant funding to make up the difference.

“What we will do is look for grants with something that is real and presentable. It will help us with our cost engineering and make sure that we curb costs where we can,” Deaver said.

The other big-ticket item Deaver is requesting in 2027 is a $500,000 replacement chassis for engine one.

Engine one is a 2006 model.

“It’s 20 years old,” Deaver said. “The body and such is in very good condition. … If we simply do, through a vendor, a chassis replacement, it takes the potential of a $1.4 million total replacement closer, and again it is escalating, to $500- $800,000.”

Deaver said it would likely take 2 years, 2 budget cycles to replace the chassis for engine one.

“Like we did with engine 3, there is a certain deposit required for them to start the build. The rest is payable upon delivery,” Deaver said. “It resets the age of the equipment back to like-brand-new.”
