title: Governor awards $500,000 to task force working on cybersecurity and infrastructure resilience
byline: By Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden announced Tuesday that he awarded $500,000 from a fund under his control to support the continued work of his Governor’s Resilience and Infrastructure Task Force.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden announced Tuesday that he awarded $500,000 from a fund under his control to support the continued work of his Governor’s Resilience and Infrastructure Task Force.

The money comes from the Future Fund, which employers support with fees they submit while paying taxes to support unemployment benefits.

The governor awards money from the fund at his discretion, although a state law that took effect July 1 places new restrictions on the fund, including a more detailed description of acceptable uses and a requirement that awards must be recommended by the Governor’s Office of Economic Development. One of the fund’s allowed uses is “development of infrastructure required to support economic development in this state.”

Rhoden established the Governor’s Resilience and Infrastructure Task Force last year, saying it would “serve as a strategic advisory body to develop policy recommendations, assess risks and vulnerabilities, and support long-term planning and investment in critical infrastructure systems across our state.”

The Future Fund money is going to the state Department of the Military, which supports the task force administratively in collaboration with the Governor’s Office and the state Department of Public Safety. A news release from Rhoden’s office said the money will “equip the task force to build effective communication tools for citizens, gather resources to collect and integrate geographic information system (GIS) data that will enhance statewide infrastructure planning, and work with industry and academic partners to strengthen South Dakota’s resilience efforts.”

The task force’s work includes cybersecurity. Several recent cybersecurity incidents have generated news coverage in South Dakota, including a cyberattack in Pennington County that disrupted some services for weeks, an attempted cyberattack on Rapid City’s wastewater system, and a reported email hacking incident affecting the city of Mitchell.

Rhoden’s other recent Future Fund awards have benefited industrial and business parks in Rapid City and Mitchell, a program helping paraprofessionals become teachers, the addition of a gunsmithing program to to a technical college in Rapid City, and the establishment of a South Dakota Defense Institute seeking to bring more defense industry contracts to the state.

title: SD Mines included in Trump announcement of $180M for mining education
byline: By Sam Gauntt States Newsroom
description: A fall 2022 view of Rapid City from the hills above the South Dakota Mines campus. Photo by Seth Tupper, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
SD Mines included in Trump announcement of $180M for mining education.jpg
A fall 2022 view of Rapid City from the hills above the South Dakota Mines campus. Photo by Seth Tupper, South Dakota Searchlight 

WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump said the federal government will fund $180 million in grants for mining schools across the country, including South Dakota Mines, as part of his administration’s goal of rebuilding the U.S. coal industry.

The grants, announced Friday, will include $100 million from the Department of Energy spread across the 14 accredited mining schools in the U.S., while the Department of Defense will dedicate just over $80 million for three major schools of mining and metallurgy: the Colorado School of Mines, South Dakota Mines and Johns Hopkins University.

The Johns Hopkins University grant will help to create a new “multi-material recycling innovation hub,” while South Dakota Mines’ funding will go toward establishing a consortium of workforce development programs alongside the University of Kentucky and Missouri S&T University.

South Dakota Mines, in Rapid City, said Tuesday it’s slated to receive $25 million to establish the Critical Minerals Merit Scholars Consortium.

“This funding accelerates our longstanding mission of producing highly skilled graduates ready to strengthen domestic critical minerals supply chains,” said Mines President Brian Tande in a news release.

Trump framed the announcement as part of his ongoing effort to rebuild the U.S. coal industry and reopen mines, a central pillar of his energy policy. He has previously sought to shorten the regulation process for new mines and limit the impact of environmental regulations.

Trump stressed the national importance of funding mining programs, given that other countries, such as China, graduate students at a far higher rate. Accredited mining programs at U.S. educational institutions graduate less than 170 mining engineers each year, he said, while China graduates more than 3,000 annually.

“We’re not doing you favors,” Trump told a crowd, including miners and many of the schools’ representatives, at a ceremony at the State Department building in Washington. “We’re doing ourselves favors. We need your industry.”

Half of the U.S. mining workforce is set to retire within the next three years, he added.

“That’s why my administration is making an unprecedented financial commitment to our nation’s mining schools,” Trump said. “It’s going to keep us nice and young and vibrant.”

In addition to increasing support for mining education, Trump announced more than $2 billion worth of new mining contracts and projects.

Those investments include $150 million for Minnesota-based Niron Magnetics to develop rare-earth-free magnets that are domestically produced to support the defense industrial base and $1.4 billion for Sila Nanotechnologies, a California-based firm, to “expand production of silicon-carbon battery anodes and build out a lithium-ion battery cell manufacturing facility to strengthen the supply chains of satellite operations, unmanned aerial systems, and munitions,” according to a White House fact sheet.

Several of the speakers during the ceremony Friday, including Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick, highlighted the national security benefits of increasing U.S. mine production.

“At the core of this is our industrial strength,” Rubio said. “But also our national sovereignty — that we never depend on other countries for things we need to prosper and to defend ourselves as a people.”

The staff of South Dakota Searchlight contributed to this report.

title: Rally traffic counts down from 5-year average
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Traffic counts for the 86th Sturgis Motorcycle Rally continue to go down as the week progresses, according to reports from the South Dakota Department of Transportation (DOT).
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

STURGIS — Traffic counts for the 86th Sturgis Motorcycle Rally continue to go down as the week progresses, according to reports from the South Dakota Department of Transportation (DOT). 

The DOT maintains nine traffic counters at various locations that operate from Aug. 7-16. According to information released on Thursday, about 54,515 vehicles entered Sturgis on Aug. 7, and 58,519 vehicles arrived in Sturgis Aug. 8. That’s nearly 3% more than the 5-year average, for the same timeframe. 

But starting Sunday, Aug. 9, the numbers started to taper off. On Sunday, 55,448 vehicles entered Sturgis, a number that is down 7.5% from the 5-year average. On Monday, 55,226 vehicles arrived in Sturgis, or 8.4% less than the 5-year average, and on Tuesday 51,742 entered the city, which was 11.8% lower than the 5-year average for the same timeframe. Wednesday, Aug. 12 saw the biggest drop in traffic numbers, with 42,964 vehicles entering Sturgis, a 23.6% drop from the 5-year average in the same timeframe. 

So far, DOT reports there have been 318,414 vehicles in Sturgis, which is down 7.8% from the 5-year average of 345,226 vehicles.

title: Democratic nominee for lt. gov. brings legislative and agricultural experience to race
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.co
description: m
_full_text:
Democratic nominee for lieutenant governor brings legislative and agricultural experience to race.jpg

m

SIOUX FALLS — A farmer who formerly served in the Legislature emerged Wednesday as the Democratic nominee for lieutenant governor of South Dakota.

Steven McCleerey, 73, of rural Sisseton, served 6 years in the state House of Representatives from 2015 to 2020. He said his approach as lieutenant governor would be focused on cooperation rather than partisan conflict.

“We’re here to help solve problems, not cause problems,” McCleerey said.

He will be the running mate of another former legislator, Dan Ahlers, of Dell Rapids, who is the Democratic nominee for governor. 

Ahlers said McCleerey’s legislative experience, including serving as assistant House minority leader, taught McCleerey how to earn support from Republicans, given that Democrats do not have the numbers in Pierre to pass a bill on their own. 

McCleerey raises crops and cattle and said he has served about 20 years on his local hospital board, along with serving on a nursing home board. Ahlers said those experiences make McCleerey a useful adviser on agricultural, rural health and long-term care issues.

Ahlers is challenging Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden, who is seeking his own full term after being elevated from lieutenant governor when Gov. Kristi Noem resigned last year to accept a job in President Donald Trump’s administration. Rhoden’s running mate is Lt. Gov. Tony Venhuizen.

Ahlers and Rhoden have accepted invitations to participate in two September debates. Venhuizen preemptively challenged Ahlers’ running mate to a debate, before Ahlers announced his pick.

McCleerey said he is open to facing Venhuizen, but would prefer a “roundtable discussion” or an open forum where the audience asks the questions. 

The general election is Nov. 3.

title: The power of purpose: Local author shares life experience, wisdom in  new book “Wake Up and Live”
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Alesha Limbo is the author of “Wake up and Live.” Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Alesha Limbo.jpeg
Alesha Limbo is the author of “Wake up and Live.” Courtesy photo 

SPEARFISH — Alesha Limbo believes in the power of purpose. As a life coach and public speaker in her signature yellow-framed glasses, she’s been sharing the harrowing story that launched her journey into building an intentional life. Now, she’s taking a new tack and broadening the audience for her message.

Limbo is a trained counselor and, as of this summer, a published author.

Her book, “Wake Up and Live,” was published by Proverbs Woman Publishing in late June.

“I realized about 3 years ago that I was floating through life. I had a very life-changing experience. It woke me up to going, ‘Oh my goodness! While I have been intentional in some areas, I wasn’t living with real purpose,’” Limbo said. “I’ve pretty much put that into a book and have put it out there.”

Limbo’s book is deeply rooted in her Christian faith, and it’s intended to help people reframe their approach to life.

“I see that most people are where I was at — just floating through life and wondering, ‘Why am I here?’ Then, we just begin to go about our life and forget we are a masterpiece. That’s one of my biggest things,” Limbo said.  

Her book is structured into 3 sections: living with awareness, living with intention, and living with purpose.

“First off, just be aware of what you think, what you do, and what you say. Most of us aren’t. We just say things, and we don’t even know the impact,” Limbo said. She hopes her book will help readers move from a reactive mindset to a proactive mindset.  Proactivity is shaped by intention. 

“Intention shifts how we live life,” Limbo said. “Honestly, there are adults that don’t know why we respond the way we do, why we think what we think because we don’t take the time to actually evaluate it.”

Limbo said she believes it is important to “walk through things” rather than ignoring difficult topics or experiences.

“Let’s identify what we are going through and acknowledge our emotions, our pain, our experiences. We don’t avoid them, but we don’t stay in them,” Limbo said.

In the first few pages of “Wake Up and Live,” Limbo discusses instances of both suicide and self-harm.

“I am really honest about that. I had a suicide attempt when I was in my 20s,” Limbo said. “I share about that, and there are so many people walking through that.”

She believes suffering thrives in isolation. 

“You keep these thoughts to yourself. Do not share with others. Keep it here, and then those thoughts just take control,” Limbo said. “The more we share our story, the more we begin to realize that other people are going through the same thing. … We are more similar than we realize. We have way more in common than we realize. It is a powerful thing to understand that.”

Writing a book has been a long-time dream for Limbo. Finally, with encouragement from friends and a shot of courage from her participation in another book project, she set aside 5 days to make her dream happen. She stayed for a week at a friend’s cabin, placing her nose to the proverbial grindstone.

“I had written a little bit beforehand, but I just hunkered down, and I knew if I didn’t do that, if I didn’t finish it while I was there, I would come back home and it just wouldn’t have happened. So I just dialed in and got it done,” Limbo said.

Writing her book was an important way for Limbo to live out her own purpose. She believes purpose is not something you reach for; it’s something you come by naturally.

“Live through purpose, instead of striving for purpose,” Limbo said. “So many people are striving for purpose or striving for an identity. They have life circumstances happen around them and think, ‘Well, that’s my identity now. We live in that identity, and we think, ‘Maybe my purpose is this, or maybe it’s this.’ We are constantly striving at it, instead of looking at the fact that we were given an identity.”

So far, Limbo said she’s had booksellers reach out from as far away as New Jersey asking to stock “Wake Up and Live.” Her book has also become a centerpiece at Christian book studies.

“It’s just crazy the impact,” Limbo said.

title: Quick picks: Beat the heat
description: Rain might’ve offered some relief from high temperatures in the region this week, but there is no denying — it’s been one hot summer. One great way to beat the heat, is to spend time with a good book, ideally in an air conditioned space or a shady spot near a creek or river. This week’s recommendations are from Sam Kingston at the Belle Fourche Public Library.
_full_text:
HammockReading.jpg

Rain might’ve offered some relief from high temperatures in the region this week, but there is no denying — it’s been one hot summer. One great way to beat the heat, is to spend time with a good book, ideally in an air conditioned space or a shady spot near a creek or river. This week’s recommendations are from Sam Kingston at the Belle Fourche Public Library.

1. “The Bear and the Nightingale” by Katherine Arden

Genre: Fantasy

At the edge of the Russian wilderness, winter lasts most of the year and the snowdrifts grow taller than houses. But Vasilisa doesn’t mind — she spends the winter nights huddled around the embers of a fire with her beloved siblings, listening to her nurse’s fairy tales. Above all, she loves the chilling story of Frost, the blue-eyed winter demon, who appears in the frigid night to claim unwary souls. Wise Russians fear him, her nurse says, and honor the spirits of house and yard and forest that protect their homes from evil.

2. “City of the Lost” by Kelley Armstrong 

Genre: Mystery/Thriller

Casey Duncan once killed a man and got away with it. Since then she’s become a talented police detective, tethered only to her job, her best friend, Diana, and the occasional evening with her sexy, no-strings-attached ex-con lover, Kurt. But then Diana’s abusive ex finds her again, despite all Casey has done to help her disappear. And Casey’s own dark past begins to catch up with her. The two women need to run — and Diana’s heard of a place where they won’t be found, a town especially for people like them.

3. “The Unselected Journals of Emma M. Lion” By Beth Brower

Genre: Historical fiction

The Year is 1883 and Emma M. Lion has returned to her London neighborhood of St. Crispian’s. Emma’s plans for a charmed and studious life are sabotaged by her eccentric Cousin Archibald, her formidable Aunt Eugenia, and the slightly odd denizens of St. Crispian’s. Emma M. Lion offers up her “Unselected Journals,” however self-incriminating they may be. Armed with wit and a sideways amusement, There, she documents the curious realities of her life at Lapis Lazuli House.

4. “One Dark Window” by Rachel Gillig 

Genre: Fantasy/romance

Elspeth needs a monster. The monster might be her. Elspeth Spindle needs more than luck to stay safe in the eerie, mist-locked kingdom she calls home — she needs a monster. She calls him the Nightmare, an ancient, mercurial spirit trapped in her head. He protects her. He keeps her secrets. But nothing comes for free — especially magic.

5. “Every Heart a Doorway” by Seanan McGuire

Genre: Fantasy/Young Adult

Children have always disappeared under the right conditions; slipping through the shadows under a bed or at the back of a wardrobe, tumbling down rabbit holes and into old wells, and emerging somewhere ... else. But magical lands have little need for used-up miracle children. Nancy tumbled once, but now she’s back. The things she’s experienced. They change a person. The children under Miss West’s care understand all too well. And each of them is seeking a way back to their own fantasy world.

6. “The Bookshop on the Corner” by Jenny Colgan 

Genre: Fiction/romance

Nina Redmond is a librarian with a gift for finding the perfect book for her readers. But can she write her own happy-ever-after? In this valentine to readers, librarians, and book-lovers the world over, the New York Times-bestselling author of “Little Beach Street Bakery” returns with a funny, moving new novel for fans of Nina George’s “The Little Paris Bookshop.”

title: The Mercy Sloane Chronicles: Chapter 14
byline: By Eliza Blue A work of serialized fiction, special to the Pioneer
description: The rest of the week passed uneventfully, and might have spilled uneventfully into another, except on Friday, Mercy received a registered letter.
_full_text:
The Mercy Sloane Chronicles

The rest of the week passed uneventfully, and might have spilled uneventfully into another, except on Friday, Mercy received a registered letter. 

She was standing in the back of the store when Melissa from the post office came bursting through the door. Melissa was strong and red-cheeked, with almond brown hair she wore in a simple braid down her back. She saw something in Mercy she liked right away, and that’s why she’d been coming by so often, at first with an excuse of some kind or another, but, for the last few days, just to chat when they were both done with their work days 

Melissa was the postmistress and sole employee at the Antelope post office because the only qualification was having the time and energy to take on a somewhat thankless job that required a fair amount of both. A surprisingly lot of mail passed through Antelope. Almost everyone in the county came from somewhere else, and mail was still the main form of connection with far-flung family and friends. 

Sorting it was actually the easiest part of the job, however. Managing the anxiety of a mother waiting on news of her first grandchild or passing on a notice about unpaid taxes to a farmer who was about to lose everything was the harder task. 

It also meant Melissa was in possession of a lot of sensitive information about other people’s lives, and being a kind and tender-hearted woman, that often felt like a burden she was not wholly prepared to bear–especially since she tended to say the exact right thing at the completely wrong time. She’d complained to her mother about it once, and her mother had given Melissa’s shoulder a little squeeze then kissed the top of her head but said nothing, knowing–like so many of life’s problems–no amount of advice would replace the wisdom of experience.

 Eliza Blue TMC
Eliza Blue 

Anyway, it wasn’t like Melissa had other options for employment. When she’d graduated from Antelope High School, it was take the postmistress job, find a husband, or look for work in some faraway city. Melissa didn’t think she’d like big city life and was even more confident she’d rather sort mail than marry one of the boys from school she’d known since birth. She was mostly content with her choice, but she was also a little lonely. 

Standing together on the dusty boards of Main Street Thursday afternoon, Melissa had offered to help Mercy plant a small garden that weekend. “It’s not too late for beets and carrots and lettuce,” Melissa said with a kind smile. “And I’ve got a few seeds leftover from my garden.”

“That would be wonderful!” Mercy replied, “My mother and I had a little kitchen garden in Iowa, but it’s so different here; I guess I’m scared I won’t know how to make anything grow.”

“You’ll need to water more,” Melissa said. “And the wind does dry things out something awful, but we will find a good spot to start, and you can plant more next year.”

Melissa said the last part and then left a pause, realizing she had no idea if Mercy intended to stay. “I mean, if you are still here…” Melissa began again, awkwardly stumbling over her words, her cheeks even redder than usual. “Or…I mean…” 

Being a kind and tenderhearted girl herself, Mercy grabbed Melissa’s hand and squeezed it hard. “I would love that. Thank you.” And in that moment, Melissa felt a tiny bit of her burden lift.

Which is why, the next morning, when Melissa found a registered letter addressed to a Mrs. Mercy Carr nee Sloane postmarked from Iowa City in that day’s mail bag, her hands began to shake. She was worried Mercy was about to receive some very hard news and that she was about to lose her new friend before their friendship had even begun.

As she passed the letter to Mercy and watched Mercy’s wide smile fade as suddenly as it had appeared, she knew Mercy was feeling the exact same way.

title: Women have a place to claim in western history, and C.K. Van Dam is exploring those stories
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: “Proving Her Claim” is the first novel published by author C.K. Van Dam. Courtesy image
_full_text:
Proving_Her_Claim_frontcover.jpg
“Proving Her Claim” is the first novel published by author C.K. Van Dam. Courtesy image 

SPEARFISH — The Homestead Act of 1862 granted adult heads of families 160 acres of surveyed public land to accelerate settlement in the West. Women who were single, divorced, or widowed could be considered heads of household under the law — and able to pursue property and own land.

Those real women inspire author C.K. Van Dam. She joyfully crafts characters with gumption and grit.

“I like writing and reading about strong women,” Van Dam said. “I learned that 12% of homesteaders were women. 42% proved their claims. Only 37% of men proved their claims. I thought, there is a story there.”

She started writing her first novel, “Proving Her Claim,” 25 years ago. It follows Anna Olson, a woman who pins her future on the prairie after the prospects of marriage and family begin to look bleak in her life.

 Untitled design - 1
C.K. Van Dam is a historical fiction author, who writes specifically about women homesteaders in the American West. Courtesy photo 

In 2022, the novel was published and set Van Dam on a path to publishing at least one novel about a woman claiming land in the West per year.

Her stories follow civil war widows and a pair of plucky sisters determined to find new fates on the prairie.

In writing her “On the Dakota Frontier” series, which includes “Proving Her Claim,” “Lone Tree Claim,” “Medicine Creek Claim,” and “Iron Horse Claim,” Van Dam prioritized research.

She spent time looking into everything from the details of the Homestead Act itself to the intricacies of assembling a windmill. That research has now sparked a non-fiction project for a Montana-based publishing house. As she builds a body of research, she said she would like help from ordinary South Dakotans — whether they are history buffs or long-time locals with homesteading women in the roots of their family trees.

“I would love leads on women homesteaders,” Van Dam said.

To contact Van Dam, visit ckvandam.com/contact.

title: Lawrence Co. commissioners move on property tax relief
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Lawrence County commissioners heard the first reading of Ordinance 2026-01, allowing the county to implement an additional half cent sales tax to provide property tax relief on owner occupied properties. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
Lawrence Co. commissioners move on property tax relief.jpg
Lawrence County commissioners heard the first reading of Ordinance 2026-01, allowing the county to implement an additional half cent sales tax to provide property tax relief on owner occupied properties. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

DEADWOOD — Lawrence County commissioners heard the first reading of Ordinance 2026-01, allowing the county to implement an additional half cent sales tax beginning Jan. 1, 2027, that will generate revenue to relieve owner occupied property taxes. 

Commissioners drafted an ordinance in the shadow of Meade and Pennington counties, striking lines from the draft ordinance provided by the state that claim the tax provides additional needed revenue and instead writing simply that the county chooses to impose a county tax on gross receipts. 

The passage of Senate Bill 96 allowed counties to implement a half-cent sales tax on goods and services sold in Lawrence County. Revenue generated will go into a fund designated to provide property tax relief based on the assessed value of owner-occupied homes. Commissioners have the option to distribute relief based on revenues estimated by the Department of Revenue or wait until the tax is collected to distribute relief.

The county chose to include a section in the ordinance allowing the county to collect 2% of all revenue generated the first year to supplement the costs of additional software and staff time needed to implement the tax and $20,000 every year thereafter. 

Sen. Randy Deibert, R-Spearfish, was amongst the people who spoke during the public hearing. He clarified that the tax will provide relief only to county levies.

“It’s important to note that Lawrence County does have one of the lowest mill levies in the state for a county tax. It’s 2.81, roughly, and that’s where the relief is coming from this sales tax shift,” said Deibert. “There will not be relief at the city mill levies or the special levies. So, those people that live in the city limits, Spearfish has roughly a 1.93 mill levy, Deadwood and Lead are both 4-plus. There’s not going to be a property tax relief there and there’s not going to be property tax relief through this effort at the school district level. Senate Bill 245 will give relief there. So those that live in the city limits will not see as big a percentage decrease in their taxes as those that live solely in the county.”

Brenda McGruder, county auditor, clarified that Senate Bill 245 provides relief only to mill levies imposed by school districts. According to the bill, the state treasurer transferred $55 million from the general revenue replacement fund to the homeowner property tax reduction fund. In conjunction with the fund transfer, schools are only allowed to impose a $0.669 per $1,000 mill levy on owner occupied properties. 

McGruder said the transfer will occur only once, as a sunset on sales tax across the state ends July 1, 2027, renewing state funds to schools.

According to Gov. Larry Rhoden’s website, taxpayers are estimated to save 21%, or approximately $732 on a $325,000 property with the implementation of Senate Bill 96. With the implementation of Senate Bill 245, which created a homeowner property tax reduction fund with the state treasury, transferring money from the state to school districts general funds to relieve owner occupied mill levies, homeowners are projected to save an additional 15%, or $547, in property taxes on a $325,000 home. Combined, the website projects a potential savings of 36%.

Commissioner Tim Comer said Senate Bill 96 is not a tax relief bill, but a tax shift. 

Rep. Mary Fitzgerald, R-St. Onge, argued that the tax shift has already happened. 

“In the state legislature, we have said that the tax shift has already occurred, and that it has occurred to the homeowners of our state,” Fitzgerald said. “We pay more tax than any other group. That is why we say that shift has already happened.”

Fitzgerald urged the county to implement the new county sales tax, saying she’s heard from taxpayers across the county in her capacity as representative for years, begging for tax relief. 

“Senate Bill 96 is Gov. Rhoden’s bill that was passed by the legislature in an effort to try to help those people that are in need of a reduction in their property taxes,” she said. “We heard from a lot of elderly people that are really struggling to stay in their homes, and we think that this is a good solution, and I would urge you to please vote for this.”

Commissioners did not discuss whether they would implement relief in 2028 based on estimated sales tax revenue from the Department of Revenue or if they would wait until the funds were collected and placed into a property tax relief fund. Deibert encouraged commissioners to choose to wait to distribute relief until taxes had been collected.

“I think it’s important to be cautious with that, because you can’t predict that very well. And the estimates that we have are just that, they are estimates,” Deibert said. “My thought would be, if you invoke this, to collect the money before you distribute it — not to speculate.”

The ordinance is scheduled for a second reading at 9:45 a.m., Aug. 25. Commissioners are expected to vote on the ordinance at that time. 

A public hearing is not required for the county to enact the ordinance.

If passed, the ordinance will go into effect 20 days after publication in the Black Hills Pioneer.

title: Cattle producers cope with ‘gut-wrenching’ losses from July heat wave
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: South Dakota suffered at least 2,000 cattle deaths attributed to a recent heat wave. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Cattle producers cope with ‘gut-wrenching’ losses from July heat wave.JPG
South Dakota suffered at least 2,000 cattle deaths attributed to a recent heat wave. Pioneer file photo 

SIOUX FALLS — George Kenzy said he did all he could to prepare his family’s feedlot for extreme heat and humidity. That included extra water tanks, covering the ground with light-colored bedding to reduce heat absorption, and keeping the ground as wet as possible.

“And it seemed like Mother Nature just had the upper hand on this one,” Kenzy said.

Thousands of cattle in South Dakota died of heat stress last month. Though locations across the state experienced unusually high temperatures, data from the Rapid City office of the National Weather Service help illustrate the historic nature of the heat wave: It was the city’s second hottest July on record, according to several indicators, and the city experienced its highest-ever recorded temperatures on July 25 downtown (110 degrees) and at the airport (112 degrees).

July was also the warmest month on record for the contiguous United States, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, with an average temperature of nearly 77 degrees.

Days of heat, high humidity, a lack of wind and cooler nighttime temperatures created a dangerous mix, according to Warren Rusche, a South Dakota State University Extension feedlot management specialist.

“Heat stress is one of those issues we have to be ready for all the time in South Dakota,” Rusche said. “What’s different is we haven’t seen widespread death losses like we saw in quite a few years. Normally the approaches we’ve taken have been successful enough that we’ve avoided some of these larger scale death-loss events.”

Rusche estimates at least 2,000 cattle deaths across the state, though he said that’s “likely too low.” No official count is available and likely won’t be for weeks as producers document their losses, he said.

Individual and overall financial impacts

South Dakota ranks seventh in the nation with 3.6 million cattle, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture.

Brule County, which includes Chamberlain and Kimball, lost between 1,500 and 2,000 cattle from heat stress, Rusche said, which equates to about $6 million of financial losses.

“As devastating as this is for individual ranchers, it’s going to have minimal effect on our beef industry as a whole, just because a lot of producers didn’t get hit with significant death loss,” Rusche said. “The drought, probably, is going to play more of a role in cow numbers than the actual death loss events that we experienced.”

Cattle producers should report their losses to their local Farm Service Agency office, Gov. Larry Rhoden said in a statement on social media. The U.S. Department of Agriculture offers livestock indemnity payments to producers who face “livestock deaths in excess of normal mortality caused by adverse weather.” Those payments are equal to 75% of market value of the livestock lost. 

Financial impacts are not the only thing on the minds of producers like Kenzy.

“Initially, it’s shock and awe,” he said. “It’s the absolute gut-wrenching loss of life of the cattle that you’ve cared for so much, put so much work into and then, yeah, you have to clean up the carnage and move on.”

Much of the impact spread through central and southeast parts of the state, including Kenzy’s operation near Gregory. He did not specify how many cattle he lost.

Feeding operations were more heavily impacted by the heat than cow-calf operations, according to Warren Symens, past president of the South Dakota Cattlemen’s Association.

“When you get a 1,500-pound animal that’s been fed to gain fast and grow fast and be ready for consumers, they suffer a lot more because they’re much bigger and they’re in a different environment,” he said. “They can’t go stand in a water pond like a cow on a pasture can.”

The nation’s cattle herd is at a 75-year low, Symens said, “so, anything that’s removing pounds of cattle from the system has an effect,” including on the already high price of beef.

Rising temperatures across the state

South Dakota’s average temperatures are climbing, according to State Climatologist Laura Edwards.

“Most of those increases are driven by warmer nights,” she said. “So, really, that’s not unusual to see warmer nights, but that stretch in July was really unusual, even for the trend that we’re on.”

The state’s also seeing increased humidity levels due in part to a difference in row crops in recent decades, Edwards said. Some farmers have transitioned from spring wheat, which is usually harvested by this time of year, to corn and soybeans, which are continuing to pump water into the air, creating humid conditions, Edwards said.

“We see that it may be affecting humidity on a local scale, which could be a contributing factor to the cattle,” she said. “But it’s not enough on its own to really make that much of a difference, when we’re talking about livestock issues that we’ve seen all across the region.”

Larger-scale weather patterns, like hot air being pushed north from the Gulf of Mexico, creates more humidity than regional crop changes, Edwards said.

A Sioux Falls-based nonprofit, South Dakota Green Project, reported earlier this year that the state’s average temperatures have increased by two degrees since 1900. Days with extreme heat are becoming more frequent, according to the report. Compared to the 1970s, Sioux Falls now experiences 10 more heat warning days per year and Mitchell experiences 16 more.

“As our climate continues to warm, bouts of extreme heat become longer, more frequent, and more intense, increasing the risk of heat-related illness and mortality,” the report reads.

Encouraging producers to ‘check on each other’

Symens, of the Cattlemen’s Association, noted producers might have disagreements about issues affecting the industry, “but we’re all in this together.”

“With these losses, give your friends and neighbors a call and see how they’re doing and just check on each other,” he said. “We’re pretty notorious for not asking for help when we need it. There’s nothing wrong with reaching out to each other.”

Andrea Bjornestad, a professor and mental health Extension specialist at SDSU, said cattle deaths and financial losses could cause chronic stress and anxiety for ranchers that manifest as physical symptoms — chest tightness, shakiness, rapid heart rate — and emotional symptoms such as feelings of hopelessness, guilt and shame.

Chronic stress can also push people to isolate themselves to avoid talking about their struggles with friends and family, and to avoid social activities.

“All of these things can contribute to stress on the body, the mind, as well as stress within relationships, whether it’s family members or friends,” Bjornestad said, “and contribute to a decline in mental health.”

Bjornestad’s been researching the mental health of farmers and ranchers for more than a decade. She’s worked with producers during past major losses such as the ongoing avian flu outbreak that’s killed millions of birds and during the COVID-19 pandemic when large pork packing plants closed, forcing farmers to reckon with euthanizing their pigs.

“The ranchers talk so much about their connection with their animals and how their animals actually help them have positive mental health,” Bjornestad said. “So, I think to significantly lose animals in itself is such a huge loss, not just financially, but emotionally, because that connection is lost.”

Counselors can be a “neutral party” for producers who want to talk about their struggles, Bjornestad said. SDSU offers a grant-funded agricultural behavioral health voucher program for five free counseling sessions for producers and their immediate family members.

title: Military Appreciation Day honors  2 longtime servants to country  and community
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: Cindy Gray, on behalf of her late husband Charlie Gray, and Craig Sanderson, hold their awards following the Honorees Presentation on Tuesday at Military Appreciation Day. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
5. military.JPG
Cindy Gray, on behalf of her late husband Charlie Gray, and Craig Sanderson, hold their awards following the Honorees Presentation on Tuesday at Military Appreciation Day. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

STURGIS — A lifetime of military and community service was honored Tuesday as Craig Sanderson and the late Charles R. “Charlie” Gray were recognized during Military Appreciation Day at the 86th Sturgis Motorcycle Rally.  

Sanderson and Gray were named this year’s Military Appreciation Day honorees during a ceremony that brought together veterans, active-duty military members, community leaders and Rally visitors to recognize the men and women who have served the nation.

The annual event included a presentation of colors by the Legion Riders Color Guard, the national anthem performed by Jesse James Dupree, prayers, remarks from military and state leaders, and presentations recognizing the two honorees. A scheduled B-1 bomber flyover was canceled because of weather.

Sturgis Mayor Rod Bradley welcomed those attending and called Military Appreciation Day one of the most meaningful traditions of Rally Week. 

“Today gives us time to pause and really reflect on what it means to be America and have its 250th birthday this year,” Bradley said. “This is the most meaningful tradition we have during Rally Week.”

Bradley also thanked veterans, first responders and Harley-Davidson for helping make the event possible.  

“This gives us the chance to say thank you for all that’s been done serving in the military or first responders,” he said.

Sanderson honored for lifetime of service.  For Sanderson, the recognition represents a lifetime spent serving his country and supporting fellow veterans.

“I was born military,” Sanderson said. “I’ve been military all my life in some way, shape, or form.”

Born in Canton, S.D., Sanderson grew up as the son of a career Army serviceman and World War II veteran. His father’s assignments took the family to several locations around the country and overseas before they eventually returned to South Dakota.

After graduating from Canton High School in 1964, Sanderson participated briefly in Army ROTC before joining the South Dakota Army National Guard. He later enlisted in the U.S. Air Force and served as a security police.

His military service eventually led to a more than 4-decade career with the Department of Veterans Affairs. During his 43½ years with the VA, Sanderson worked in several locations before retiring in 2010 as chief of logistics in Sturgis.

Sanderson continued serving veterans after retirement. He became active with the Sturgis Honor Guard and American Legion and currently serves as commander of American Legion Post 33 and co-commander of the Sturgis Honor Guard.

Over the past 15 years, Sanderson has participated in more than 1,900 military funeral honors ceremonies throughout western South Dakota.

Whether ceremonies are held at Black Hills National Cemetery or in smaller communities, Sanderson said honoring veterans is something he considers a privilege.

“It isn’t a pleasure. It’s an honor,” he said. “That’s why we do it.”

Despite his decades of service, Sanderson said he was humbled by being selected for the Military Appreciation Day honor.

“Well, it’s a very humbling experience. It’s an exciting experience, and it’s one that I don’t know if I deserve,” Sanderson said. “I’d like to accept this for all of the veterans at the rally and in the Sturgis area.”

Sanderson said his hope for the country during its 250th anniversary year is simple. “Unity,” he said. “Be proud of this country. Let’s get together and accomplish something that’s good for everybody.”

Gray remembered for service, family and community.

Gray, who died March 10, was honored posthumously for a lifetime of military service, community involvement and dedication to his family.

Gray was born Feb. 22, 1948, in Rapid City and spent his early childhood on his family’s ranch near Hereford. His family later moved to Sturgis, where he attended St. Martin’s Catholic School before graduating from Sturgis Brown High School in 1966.

After graduation, Gray joined the South Dakota National Guard. He later served 4 years as a Meade County sheriff’s deputy before returning to the Guard full time.

His military career included numerous leadership positions, including commander of the 109th Engineer Battalion, Recruiting and Retention commander and chief of staff of the South Dakota Army National Guard. He retired in 2008 as the property and fiscal officer for South Dakota.

While Gray’s military accomplishments were significant, his family and community were equally important parts of his life.

He married Cynthia Bonin in 1974, and together they raised three children. Gray later became a proud grandfather and great-grandfather and was known for supporting his family and the Sturgis community.

A former wrestler himself, Gray remained a passionate Sturgis Scooper supporter and could frequently be found in the stands cheering for his children, grandchildren and friends.

Cindy Gray said the posthumous recognition was something the family never expected but believes Charlie deserved.

“I think it’s something that we never ever imagined,” she said. “I think Charlie did deserve it. He always supported the Sturgis community.”

She recalled his support of the National Guard, wrestling and his church, as well as the many young people he helped along the way.

Gray also had a lifelong connection to the western lifestyle and was known for his love of family gatherings, friends, card games and the Cowboy Channel.

Those who knew him remembered his sense of humor, distinctive laugh and willingness to show up for the people and causes he cared about.

Gray’s legacy, his family said, extends well beyond his military career. His influence can be seen in the family he helped build, the people he mentored, the veterans he supported and the Sturgis community he called home.

South Dakota Gov. Larry Rhoden also addressed the crowd, drawing on his own family’s history of military service and his 6 years in the South Dakota National Guard.

Rhoden said serving as commander in chief of the South Dakota National Guard is one of the honors of his life.

“Our men and women in uniform are a crucial part of keeping our nation free,” Rhoden said.

Rhoden connected the military celebration with the spirit of the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, saying both ranchers and bikers share an appreciation for freedom.

“The rally is a great opportunity for us to come and celebrate freedom,” Rhoden said. “Men and women from across our country and around the globe come to the Black Hills ... and just to be free.”

But Rhoden emphasized that freedom comes with responsibility. 

“Freedom is not promised to us,” he said. “We have to do what it takes to defend it.”

For those gathered at Military Appreciation Day, the stories of Sanderson and Gray offered two examples of that commitment — one continuing to serve veterans and another remembered for a lifetime of service to his country, family and community.

The ceremony served as a reminder that while the Sturgis Rally celebrates motorcycles, freedom and fellowship, it also provides an opportunity to recognize the men and women whose service helps protect those freedoms.

title: ABC offering free Narcan kits during Sturgis Motorcycle Rally
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: Kara Graveman, Executive Director of ABC along with staff and volunteers hit the streets on Friday morning distributing NARCAN kits to businesses, vendors, and anyone that would like one.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
ABC offering free Narcan kits during Sturgis Motorcycle Rally.JPG
Kara Graveman, Executive Director of ABC along with staff and volunteers hit the streets on Friday morning distributing NARCAN kits to businesses, vendors, and anyone that would like one.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

STURGIS — Action for the Betterment of our Community (ABC) will once again make free naloxone, commonly known by the brand name Narcan, available to local businesses and community members during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally.

Following a successful partnership last year with the State of South Dakota and Emily’s Hope, ABC is continuing its effort to increase access to the medication during one of the busiest weeks of the year in the Black Hills.

The Sturgis Motorcycle Rally brings hundreds of thousands of visitors to the region each year. ABC officials say the large influx of people also creates additional challenges related to alcohol and drug use, making access to naloxone an important part of community safety.

“Naloxone is one way we can put our mission into action and help create a safer community for everyone,” said Kara Graveman, executive director of ABC and the New Dawn Center. “Our mission is to improve the quality of life for our citizens by collaborating to reduce drug and alcohol use among youth and adults while addressing other social issues that threaten the health and safety of our community and families.”

Naloxone is a medication that can temporarily reverse an opioid overdose, giving a person additional time to receive emergency medical care.

“Our goal is simple: to ensure that if an overdose occurs, someone nearby has the tools to respond before emergency medical services arrive,” Graveman said.

ABC officials say carrying naloxone does not encourage drug use, but instead provides another tool to respond to a medical emergency. They also point out that a person may unknowingly consume fentanyl through a counterfeit pill or another substance.

South Dakota’s State Unintentional Drug Overdose Reporting System reported 73 unintentional and undetermined overdose deaths in 2024. From 2020 through 2024, 62% of overdose deaths had at least one potential opportunity for intervention, including the presence of a bystander.

“Having naloxone available is simply being prepared for a medical emergency, just like having a first aid kit or an AED,” Graveman said. “It allows you or your staff to respond to a suspected opioid overdose while emergency responders are on the way.”

South Dakota law provides certain protections for people who administer naloxone and for businesses that stock the medication. State law provides civil-liability protection for people who administer opioid antagonists in good faith, as well as immunity provisions for employers that dispense or administer naloxone. The state also provides limited protections related to reporting a drug-related overdose to emergency medical services.

ABC is encouraging businesses that serve the public during the Rally, as well as other community members, to consider keeping naloxone available.

“If you or your business would like to keep naloxone on hand during the Rally, or year-round, please contact Courtney at ABC,” Graveman said. “We are happy to provide kits at no cost.”

For information about recognizing the signs of an opioid overdose, how naloxone works and how to administer it, ABC recommends visiting the Let’s Be Clear SD website and selecting “Reverse an Overdose” under the Prevention tab.

ABC officials say the goal is straightforward: increase preparedness, give bystanders another tool to respond to an emergency and potentially save lives during the Rally

title: Lead leases sign kiosk to local business
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: A 3-sided sign kiosk will be leased to Aspire Boutique owner Sarah Larson, with the cost of the lease to be negotiated between city staff and Larson, the Lead City Commission decided Aug. 3. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
Lead sign kiosk.jpeg
A 3-sided sign kiosk will be leased to Aspire Boutique owner Sarah Larson, with the cost of the lease to be negotiated between city staff and Larson, the Lead City Commission decided Aug. 3. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

LEAD — A publicly-owned sign kiosk on Main Street will be leased to a local business owner, city officials decided Aug. 3. 

During their regular meeting the Lead City Commission approved a request from Sarah Larson, owner of Aspire Boutique in Lead, to lease a 3-sided advertising kiosk located near her shop on Main Street. The lease will be for one year, with a cost negotiated between city staff and Larson. 

Larson said she wants to spruce up the structure that Lead Parks and Recreation Director Jerry Mertesdorf said has sat empty for more than 20 years. 

“I’ve asked the chamber to use it. I’ve asked the opera house to use it. Nobody has ever used it,” Mertesdorf said. 

“It’s right behind my building, and I want to make it beautiful and use it for advertising,” Larson said. “I want to paint the background to go with my color scheme.” 

Larson explained that she will use corrugated plastic poster board to change signs out behind the plexiglass of the kiosk, and she will paint the plywood of the structure. But before she proceeds, Larson said she wanted to have approval from the city with some kind of written agreement. 

The lease was originally listed on the city’s agenda as $120 for a 12-month period. Lead City Administrator Robin Lucero said any fee below $500 does not require a public hearing before approval. 

Resident Debbie Fisher questioned why the city would charge Larson to use the kiosk that has always been available for free use. Mayor Dustin Heupel responded that if Larson wants full control of the kiosk, there should be a fee associated with that. However, if it is opened to the public then Larson could be allowed to paint the kiosk and manage it with no fee. 

Larson expressed that she originally wanted to use the kiosk for her business advertising, but that she is potentially open to allowing local nonprofit organizations to use it. 

Pam Berreth, a member of the Lead Historic Preservation Commission, pointed out that the kiosk is in the city’s historical district, and therefore the historic preservation commission should approve Larson’s paint design before it is done. 

“That historical stretch is a state designation and there’s guidelines,” Berreth said. “Once somebody pays for something, and it turns out obnoxious or whatever, and they paid $1,000 to do it, then it’s kind of too late because people are saying they already spent the money. So, it’s a matter of there is a procedure and it’s often not followed, to just make sure everything is copacetic with the whole reason for having a historic preservation area. There’s nothing where anybody wants to do details. We just want to make sure that it aesthetically fits with the historic area.” 

Commissioner Valerie Meiners said she agrees that there should not be a charge for Larson to improve and use the kiosk. 

“If she’s going to take care of it and put all the things in it at her own cost, why is she buying that opportunity? And if she’s willing to share the space occasionally with other people, that just makes it better. So then we have a cooperative, instead of this thing just sitting there empty all the time.”

title: GF&P tag fish from D.C. Booth fish hatchery
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: SPEARFISH — South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks, fisheries biologists recently tagged trout from D.C. Booth Historic National Fish Hatchery and Archives in an effort to better understand growth and survival of fish stocked into Pactola Reservoir.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — South Dakota Game, Fish, and Parks, fisheries biologists recently tagged trout from D.C. Booth Historic National Fish Hatchery and Archives in an effort to better understand growth and survival of fish stocked into Pactola Reservoir. 

Brown trout were tagged using passive integrated transponder (PIT) tags, which are very small tags inserted into the body cavity to help staff identify individual fish during future capture efforts in the Pactola Reservoir system. The information provided by these tags upon recapture will help biologists understand the contribution of specific stockings to the reservoir population and assess growth rates of individual fish since their stocking date. “This is a great partnership between GF&P and U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service and we greatly appreciate D.C. Booth staff for providing adult brown trout for stocking into Pactola Reservoir,” said Jeremy Kientz, area fisheries supervisor for the GF&P in Rapid City. “This partnership will help support South Dakota’s recreational trout fishery and Game, Fish and Parks’ stocking programs.”  T

he fish utilized are Crawford strain of brown trout that were hatched at the Saratoga National Fish Hatchery in Saratoga, Wyo., and raised to approximately 11 inches at D.C. Booth fish hatchery in Spearfish.

title: Federal appeals court protects longer  petitioning time for SD ballot questions
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — A South Dakota group won another victory Tuesday in its effort to preserve adequate time for petitioning questions onto statewide ballots, but a state official immediately pledged to continue the fight in court.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — A South Dakota group won another victory Tuesday in its effort to preserve adequate time for petitioning questions onto statewide ballots, but a state official immediately pledged to continue the fight in court.

A federal appeals panel upheld a lower court’s ruling that state lawmakers violated the First Amendment when they moved up the deadline for submitting petition signatures by three months. After the 3-judge appeals panel issued its ruling, South Dakota’s attorney general said he will request a review by the entire 11-member 8th Circuit Court of Appeals.

Petitioners need 17,508 signatures from registered voters to put a proposed law on the ballot in South Dakota, and 35,017 signatures for a proposed state constitutional amendment. South Dakota lawmakers approved legislation last year that moved the deadline for filing signed petitions in a general election year from the first Tuesday in May to the first Tuesday in February.

A group that’s been involved in numerous ballot questions, Dakotans for Health, challenged the law in federal court. Last August, a district court judge ruled the law violates the First Amendment, writing that moving the deadline three months earlier “arguably goes beyond merely inconvenient and enters the realm of severe.” The state appealed that ruling.

During arguments heard by the 3-judge appeals panel in June, the state’s lawyer, Paul Swedlund of the state Attorney General’s Office, said a shorter deadline gives more time for potential litigation over ballot questions to play out.

“The more time that you have to litigate a case, the better chance it is that you’re going to get it finished,” Swedlund said then.

Judge Raymond Gruender disagreed with that assertion, writing in Tuesday’s opinion that “even if that were the case, however, nothing in the record indicates that the new deadline advances that interest in any meaningful way.”

Gruender added that the state didn’t provide “sufficient factual or legal support” for its argument that pre-election litigation on petitions would bolster the confidence of voters in the initiative and referendum process. Judge Jane Kelly joined Gruender in the decision.

In a dissenting opinion, Judge James Loken wrote, “the Constitution does not authorize this federal court micromanagement of state elections.” The now-unenforceable law would have furthered South Dakota’s “interest in election integrity by extending the time for pre-election petition litigation,” Loken added.

Republican South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley highlighted Loken’s comments Tuesday in a news release.

“While we respect the panel’s decision, we still believe the South Dakota Legislature reached a fair solution to our petition process, without infringing on the First Amendment,” Jackley said.

Law and litigation affect petitioning efforts

Rick Weiland of Dakotans for Health told South Dakota Searchlight in June that his group was still collecting signatures for two potential ballot questions. He believed there was no enforceable deadline, because state lawmakers had not passed any further legislation regarding the petition deadline as the lawsuit played out.

Though the group is still collecting signatures, the effort may be winding down soon, Weiland said. Counties face a Sept. 16 deadline to have ballots printed for the Nov. 3 general election.

“We’re really far away from being able to close this loop in a quick, fast way,” he said. “I think it’s very unlikely we’re going to be able to submit.”

The law “did have a chilling effect on our ability to raise the funds we needed, and to basically get volunteers engaged,” Weiland said. “It takes a well-funded, well-coordinated effort to be successful, and with that bill hanging over our heads and tied up in the courts, it’s very difficult to get that kind of support.”

His group is circulating two potential constitutional amendments that Weiland said would be a check on the power legislators have in Pierre.

The first of those amendments would protect voter-approved ballot measures from being changed by state lawmakers for seven years. Then, lawmakers would need a supermajority vote in both chambers and would still need voter approval.

The second would require that changes to the initiated ballot measure process that are approved by the Legislature — like regulations on how organizations or individuals collect signatures — would automatically be referred to voters at the next general election.

Legislators have placed four of their own proposed constitutional amendments on the ballot this year. Those amendments would allow the state to withdraw from expanded Medicaid if federal funding for it declines, clarify that a voter must be a U.S. citizen, establish a trust fund for unclaimed property proceeds, and require that future state constitutional amendments receive 60% support from voters rather than a simple majority.

title: Patients wary of government, companies pushing AI as a rural healthcare solution
byline: By Arielle Zoints and Darius Tahir KFF Health News
description: Doug Nikkila of Sturgis, South Dakota, says technology like AI can be used for good and bad. But he thinks nursing homes should use artificial intelligence to help prevent neglect by monitoring residents and sending reminders to staff when residents are due for diaper changes or other care. Photo by Arielle Zionts, KFF Health News
_full_text:
Patients wary of government, companies pushing AI as a rural healthcare solution 1.jpg
Doug Nikkila of Sturgis, South Dakota, says technology like AI can be used for good and bad. But he thinks nursing homes should use artificial intelligence to help prevent neglect by monitoring residents and sending reminders to staff when residents are due for diaper changes or other care. Photo by Arielle Zionts, KFF Health News 

 Patients wary of government, companies pushing AI as a rural healthcare solution 2.jpg
Robert Parker and Stephanie Keller of Hot Springs, South Dakota, are skeptical of the healthcare industry’s embrace of artificial intelligence technology. “AI will never replace a person” because it can’t possibly grasp the complexity of patients, Keller says. Photo by Arielle Zionts, KFF Health News 

HOT SPRINGS — Two of the nation’s most powerful health officials predict artificial intelligence will play a key role in solving rural America’s health challenges.

Health secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. told a panel of U.S. senators that AI nurses can provide “concierge care” to rural patients. Mehmet Oz, who leads the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services, has said “the best way to help some of these communities is going to be AI-based avatars” that connect rural patients to mental health services.

And many state health leaders agree. They are using some of their funding from the $50 billion federal Rural Health Transformation Program to expand AI among rural health organizations.

AI is computer technology that performs tasks that typically rely on human intelligence by finding patterns or generating words. It has the potential to improve the healthcare system by automating back-office work or identifying patients at risk, but several reports contend there’s little evidence AI can improve access to care and patient health in rural areas. It’s unclear how well states will track and share outcomes of the tech they invest in.

Meanwhile, some rural Americans are skeptical, according to interviews with people in Hot SpringsS.D., a city of about 3,400 residents at the southern end of the Black Hills.

“I get artificial intelligence for certain things, but for personal healthcare — no,” Tara Haffner said while standing outside the American Legion.

Haffner said she’s worried about AI making mistakes and wants healthcare to stay between her and her doctor.

But Phillip Mues, who oversees technology at Cherry County Hospital and Clinic in rural Valentine, Nebraska, said AI is already helping clinicians save time, reduce burnout, and focus more on patient care.

“I think it will help reduce burden on actual staffing,” he said. “It won’t replace people, but I think it will help in rural communities.”

Still, Mues said, AI can’t fix every challenge. Rural hospitals at risk of closing or ending certain services probably can’t use AI to save enough money to prevent those consequences, he said.

Congressional Republicans created the five-year Rural Health Transformation Program last summer as a last-minute sweetener to President Donald Trump’s signature One Big Beautiful Bill Act. The funding was intended to offset concerns about the outsize fallout anticipated in rural communities from the law, which is expected to reduce overall Medicaid spending by more than $900 billion over a decade.

The word on the street

Hot Springs, which has a 25-bed independent hospital and a Department of Veterans Affairs hospital, is known for its sandstone buildings, veterans’ services, and, yes, hot springs. Residents must drive at least an hour for more advanced care.

Six people interviewed there by KFF Health News said the biggest problem in rural healthcare is the cost or long wait times caused by staffing shortages.

Doug Nikkila, a heavy equipment operator, said AI and other technology come with benefits and risks.

“If it’s not utilized correctly, it becomes a burden,” he said.

Nikkila, who’s concerned about nursing home residents being neglected amid staffing shortages, said he thinks AI should send reminders to staff when their residents are due for diaper changes or other care. He also wondered whether AI-powered video monitors could send alerts when they detect falls or illness symptoms. 

The healthcare industry is rapidly adopting AI despite the tools being “poorly evaluated,” according to a recent report from ARISE, a Stanford- and Harvard-led group that evaluates health-related AI. The report says that while some AI has been successful in controlled settings, there’s less evidence it can perform in the real world. It also said few studies track patient outcomes.

Evidence is especially lacking in rural areas. A recent academic paper found that only 26 peer-reviewed studies about AI in rural healthcare were published from 2010 through April 29, 2025. Few analyzed implementation or outcomes.

Despite the dearth of results, some states appear interested in bold experiments — such as using AI to suggest diagnoses or recommend treatments. Utah officials said in their application to the rural health program that they are interested in funding a controversial experiment in AI-powered prescription refill requests.

Even tools proven to work in urban settings may not work in rural ones, said Qian Huang, an assistant professor at the Center for Rural Health and Research at East Tennessee State University.

She said the technology is usually tested at large, academic hospitals and trained on data from urban patients, who may not have the same health issues and obstacles — such as a lack of transportation — as rural patients.

A KFF Health News review of states’ plans for the Rural Health Transformation Program shows they’re interested in using AI to automate time-consuming, behind-the-scenes tasks, such as medical charting, coding, referrals, and prior authorization requests. Some states also mentioned ways AI can save money, such as Washington, which discussed tools that “identify and recover” money it’s owed.

Mues said the Valentine clinic has been using AI scribes that record appointments and generate notes describing the visit. He said surveys of clinicians before and after they started using the technology show the scribes have helped reduce burnout by letting providers focus on patient care with “eye contact on the patient, not the computer.”

States also mentioned funding AI that directly affects patient care, such as tools that recommend possible diagnoses and treatment options to clinicians. Mississippi wants to use predictive AI algorithms to “guide” emergency medics with “triage, routing, and treatment decisions.”

Several states want to use AI to analyze patients’ medical charts and remote monitoring devices to identify immediate or future health risks. North Dakota’s plans mention AI to “detect early signs of chronic disease and behavioral health conditions,” while New Hampshire’s discusses AI that identifies patients “at high risk of adverse drug events.”

Some states plan to give patients access to chatbots or wearable devices that transmit data to their clinicians. Utah is interested in funding AI-powered fetal-monitoring devices, while Kentucky will explore using AI chatbots to “deliver personalized nudges and education” through “health coaching, gamified incentives, and rewards.”

Whether the technology appeals to consumers is another matter. Hot Springs resident Stephanie Keller wears a smartwatch to track her fitness but has no interest in an AI chatbot using her data to encourage her to reach her health goals.

“I don’t have the time to chat with AI every day. I mean, are you kidding me? I don’t want to spend my time on a cellphone,” she said.

Rural health facilities also face challenges in implementing AI.

Huang, who has written about AI in rural healthcare, said rural hospitals and clinics may not have the hardware or IT staff needed to support the technology. She said clinicians and staff may already be doing three jobs at once and not have time to go through AI training.

Rural health facilities may not have fast-enough internet to use AI, while patients may have slow connections at home — if they have internet at all — or may not feel comfortable using AI, Huang said.

“In rural communities, trust and a personal relationship is essential,” she said.

Roy Ehlers, a Hot Springs resident, said he doesn’t trust AI in healthcare, or anywhere else.

“I’m old-fashioned. I don’t believe in it. Technology is not my forte,” Ehlers said.

Mues said that while some rural patients are “scared of AI,” most have let their clinicians at the Valentine facility use the scribing technology to record patients’ visits.

Will states share AI results?

Despite questions about implementation, the boom is on. Jordan Everson, an assistant professor at the Georgetown University Department of Family Medicine, said both urban and rural health facilities are rushing to use AI.

“The risk of signing contracts that rural healthcare organizations come to regret is pretty high,” said Everson, who previously worked in the information technology office at the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.

Several states are addressing that risk by using their rural health funding to create groups that will help rural health facilities vet, select, or monitor AI tools while offering training, ongoing assistance, or funding for upfront costs.

CMS spokesperson Timothy Foster said the agency doesn’t have any AI-specific reporting requirements but is working on a form for states to report their overall progress and outcomes.

Abraham Pritzker, who works at Julota, a company that helps health organizations track data, said states should measure more than how often AI programs are used.

For example, states can measure whether the tech reduces falls, 911 calls, or hospital admissions, said Pritzker, a former paramedic. Huang said it’s also important to ask clinicians and patients about their experiences using AI.

Yet many states’ applications to the rural health program mention tracking only AI adoption metrics, not what happens after facilities deploy the tech. Some of these states may add further reporting requirements down the road.

Vermont spokespeople did not respond when asked why their state’s funding opportunity for AI scribes requires organizations to report only how many clinicians and patients are served by the tech, not how much time they save.

States requiring recipients to report outcomes include Connecticut, which will track how often AI-powered patient monitoring devices trigger accurate alerts. Texas will require organizations to track cost savings, while Wisconsin lists “patient outcomes” and “productivity and efficiencies” as possible metrics.

Huang said that after collecting results, states need to share them so other states and healthcare organizations can learn from their experiences.

“We do not have a lot of resources to waste on tools that don’t work in rural areas,” she said.
