title: Spearfish expects higher rec center revenues, lower campground receipts in 2027
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Aside from a waterslide coating project, the city isn’t planning to spend more at the rec center in 2027. If anything, officials expect the rec center to earn more money in the coming year. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Rec center .JPG
Aside from a waterslide coating project, the city isn’t planning to spend more at the rec center in 2027. If anything, officials expect the rec center to earn more money in the coming year. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

 cemetery.JPG
The budget for Rose Hill Cemetery in 2027 is expected to be lower than it was in 2026. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — Newly minted Spearfish Parks and Recreation Director Rex McDonald oversees a department with 4 individual budgets: parks and spectator recreation, campground, rec and aquatics center, and cemetery.

“The operating budgets were created for 2027 using historic budgets, adjusting for inflation, as well as identifying specialized equipment and procedures for maintaining our current infrastructure,” McDonald said.

Parks and spectator recreation

The parks and spectator recreation budget includes each of the city’s park districts and its sports fields.

In 2027, the parks and spectator rec budget is projected to be the smallest it’s been in 4 years — a total of $1,968,301.

In 2026, that same slice of the budget was approved at $2,024,739.

“We didn’t plan for any significant operational changes in 2027,” McDonald said.

McDonald said he hopes to purchase an ABI infield maintenance machine, for $50,000, and infield material for the Legion baseball field, for $15,000.

“This is different than if you go to a baseball game or a softball game and see somebody out there pulling a mat drag between games. That just smooths out the surface. What this machine will actually do is we can laser grade the fields to ensure that we have the proper crowns on the field, which increases the drainage,” McDonald said. “It gets water off the field more quickly.”

The machine uses laser grading, which McDonald said would be more accurate than the equipment his staff uses currently.

The manufacturer, ABI, held an equipment demonstration at the Keating Resources SportsPlex in 2025.  

“There were several other municipalities and sports-use groups that were there at that demo. Rapid City was one of them. After that demo, they ended up purchasing one of the units this year and got it in earlier this spring,” McDonald said. “I met with them, I talked with them, just to get their feedback. They said that it is a great machine. They use it almost every day during the spring and summer as they get their ball fields ready for play.”

Using a private donation, the parks and rec department plans to purchase a mini-excavator for use maintaining trails on Lookout Mountain.

McDonald said there is $30,000 allocated to transfer a roughly 700-acre city-held conservation easement on Lookout Mountain from one non-profit to another in the coming year. 

“When Tyler (Ehnes) was still here, he was looking at transferring the conservation easement to a separate, different entity than currently has it. The South Dakota Wildlife Foundation currently holds a conservation easement. They have since its inception. They told us about a year ago that they were no longer interested in holding the conservation easement,” McDonald said. “They’ve kind of changed their operations, and objectives are primarily that of a fundraising organization at this point. We were tasked with looking outside for a different entity to maintain that conservation easement.

McDonald said the city has been in talks with the South Dakota Ag Land Trust to take over stewardship of the easement.

“Nothing is set in stone, but part of an agreement with South Dakota Ag Land Trust, there would be a one-time transfer of $30,000 that we would have to pay them in order for them to take over the conservation easement. That is why that is listed there,” McDonald said.

Rec and Aquatics Center

The budget for the rec and aquatics center is expected to increase by $186,091. There are no major operational changes planned, but McDonald said he hopes to recoat the waterslides at the waterpark for about $200,000 in the coming year.

“The 3 current waterslides that we have have been there since the rec center opened up. They’ve been in operation for about 18 years now. They are probably about 20 years old now. The manufacturer recommends at 15 years to do a recoating. This will help with the longevity of the slides,” McDonald said.

The paint is chipping on some of the waterslides as a result of ordinary, expected wear and tear, McDonald said.

“Doing this recoating project will help seal them and protect them from ultraviolet radiation and things like that and will increase the lifespan another 15 years,” McDonald said. “Since we don’t really have a lot of other projects planned this year, we thought this year would be a good year to go after that.”

The city is also looking at its options to reduce the impact of credit card fees on the rec center revenues. The city has a new credit card processing vendor.

“We’re looking at saving on average about $10,000 a month with this new credit card provider,” said Spearfish Finance Officer Michelle DeNeui.

Overall rec center revenues are projected to increase by  $51,500.

“Primarily this is based on membership revenue trends. We think we will be able to generate revenue,” McDonald said.

City campground

In contrast, McDonald expects the campground to make less money in 2027 — to the tune of $45,000

The decrease is expected — the most likely result of an early-season closure in 2026.

“We are thinking that we are going to see a dip in revenue this year, in 2026, because of the closure for the waterline project. We are planning on closing the campground after Labor Day weekend,” McDonald said. “We will be spending a large portion of the cash balance that we have for the waterline project.”

McDonald said, in addition to the closure’s impacts this year and the need for a more conservative estimate to make up for planned spending, the campground expects to have fewer bookings in the coming year, as campers have already reported soaring gas prices as a driver of cancellations.

“Every time we get a cancellation, our staff are trained to ask the reason for that, to see if there is anything that we need to do on our end,” McDonald said. “The primary driver of cancellation is just that it costs too much for people to travel from far distances.”

Rose Hill Cemetery

The cemetery budget also falls under the parks and rec umbrella. The proposed budget for that department is  $157,266 compared to $170,906.

McDonald said the change reflects the completion of the ground penetrating radar (GPR) project, and the expansion of master planning for the next 2 to 5 years.

“Doing the GPR this year, we were able to get a better idea of how many spaces are still available for purchase,” McDonald said. “There were several areas that were questionable, either from historical areas that were incomplete or based on the topography up there. There is a lot of underlying bedrock that can pose some challenges when it comes to digging full burials versus cremating. So, with that, we are waiting on a report. We will have that shortly, but it is going to tie in with our expansion master plan, which is expansion of the cemetery and what that looks like.”

title: Hamsters USA raises  $385,600 for kids at  LifeScape in Rapid City
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: SPEARFISH — The international motorcycle group Hamsters USA has been helping kids thrive in the Black Hills for more than 20 years.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — The international motorcycle group Hamsters USA has been helping kids thrive in the Black Hills for more than 20 years. 

Their annual fundraiser for LifeScape’s Rapid City clinic was Monday in Spearfish, raising an amazing $385,600.

All the funds stay local, helping more than 1,600 children in western South Dakota get the physical, occupational, speech, and behavior therapies they need to grow strong and thrive.

“The 1,600 children, their families, and the staff of LifeScape are incredibly grateful to the Hamsters USA and their friends for their generous support. Children across the Black Hills region have access to the best therapies and education services for diagnosis such as Autism, spina bifida, cerebral palsy, rare genetic disorders, developmental delays, and recovery from accidents and major surgeries because the Hamsters USA care,” said LifeScape Foundation President Jessica Wells. “Without their support, children would not have the consistent physical, occupational, speech, and behavior care services they need to learn and grow.”

The fundraiser was part of the Hamsters USA annual meeting during Rally Week. Gov. Larry Rhoden helped welcome the group to South Dakota again this year. Four-year-old Kaiya also greeted Hamsters with a big smile and stickers for their shirts. Born with a hole in her heart and only one pulmonary artery, Kaiya was airlifted from Rapid City during an April blizzard to have her first open heart surgery at just 6 days old. She had a second surgery when she was 5 months old to open her arteries and replace the tiny valve as her heart grew. She was later also diagnosed with DiGeorge syndrome which is marked by developmental delays. Kaiya loves her therapists and coming to LifeScape for physical and occupational therapy. She is working hard on increasing her balance, navigating stairs, jumping, and even rode a bike with pedals for the first time this week!

While Kaiya is known for being the first person to greet everyone in the waiting room and hallways of LifeScape’s Rapid City clinic, she also used her charm at the event when she got on stage and sang “This Little Light of Mine” to the crowd, nearly bringing everyone to tears.

LifeScape’s Rapid City clinic served 1,600 children last year. Clinicians also drove more than 10,000 miles every month to deliver needed outreach therapies to kids in their own communities, whether that be in their home, school, and daycare. This allows children living in rural areas of western South Dakota the opportunities to still receive developmental help without their parents having to take time off work to drive them.

LifeScape’s mission is to empower children with disabilities to live their best lives. With the help of Hamsters USA, West River kids are growing strong and thriving.

title: Ashley McDonald to return as Spearfish city attorney
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — On Monday, the Spearfish City Council unanimously approved an employment contract with Ashley McDonald to return to her former role as the city’s legal council.
_full_text:
Ashley McDonald rehired.jpeg

SPEARFISH — On Monday, the Spearfish City Council unanimously approved an employment contract with Ashley McDonald to return to her former role as the city’s legal council. 

McDonald stepped down as city attorney in July 2024 to go into private practice. She initially took on the role in 2018, Spearfish Human Resources Director Jodi Mathis said. 

“I have enjoyed my time representing the city and I will always be grateful to the 2 mayors I served under, the council, my coworkers, and the public for allowing me to serve the people of Spearfish,” McDonald told the Black Hills Pioneer back in 2024. “The residents of Spearfish have the best team of dedicated professionals representing their interests and that makes this work enjoyable.”

Since her departure, McDonald has served in an interim capacity on and of, including the period before former City Attorney David Knox was hired in the fall of 2024 and after his departure this spring.  

She rejoins the city with a salary of $166,150.40 — a grade 26, step 7 on the city’s adopted wage scale. 

“Then there are 80 hours credited to her PTO bank upon hire and then the last item was negotiated was PTO accrual of 7.7 hours per pay period,” Mathis said. 

McDonald will also receive 3 months pay as severance if she resigns or is dismissed without cause. The same provision was included in her original employment contract with the city.

title: Haines Avenue base not thick enough, county asks for contractor pay cut, extended warranty
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: RAPID CITY — Meade County will deduct some pay, and require an extended warranty for road work on Haines Avenue, after testing showed the bottom lift of asphalt was less than the engineering specifications.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

RAPID CITY — Meade County will deduct some pay, and require an extended warranty for road work on Haines Avenue, after testing showed the bottom lift of asphalt was less than the engineering specifications. 

Troy Eastman, Meade County highway superintendent, told the Meade County Commission at their Aug. 4 meeting that engineering specifications for the Haines Avenue reconstruction required a 2-inch asphalt lift and a density of 92% after compaction, but Western Construction laid a bottom lift that averaged one and seven-eighths inches, according to the core samples taken. The thickness is important, he said, so the road lasts for a long time. 

“We are working with the contractor to try to remedy the situation,” Eastman said. “We don’t want to have to rip out a brand new road, but we don’t want it to fail in the near future. A second set of test results show that it is better, but still below the required minimum of 92%. The core samples taken are a little thin and not exactly what we’re looking for. We need to work out the details, but we want to keep the project moving as well.” 

Eastman said asphalt testing shows the product is good. Replacing the thin parts of asphalt would mean patching the road, which could deteriorate faster, he said. Instead, he suggested a pay deduct for those bid items that do not meet the specifications, and he said the county will ask for an extended warranty and a thicker top lift, instead of removal or patching the bottom lift of asphalt. 

“The patching in my opinion is the very last way I would do anything, especially the bottom lift,” Commissioner Earl Severn said. “At this point in time, it’s either the pay deduct and extended warranty or removing the entire first lift. Patching that together on a brand new road with the treated sub base and everything we got under there … would be my least favorite option.” 

Eastman said heavy trucks have already been traveling on the road with a single lift of asphalt, with no problems. 

“They’ve been working and hauling loaded trucks across this on that single lift for 3 weeks now, and it looks great,” Eastman said. “But 3 weeks is not 3 years. But if it was a terrible mix design, or if it was bad asphalt, you’d see it right away, especially with the heat that we’ve had. So, I’m not saying it’s great and it won’t fall apart, but I do feel better just having the time on it that we have to see what it’s going to do. Either way, it’s not ideal by any means, when we’ve designed it a certain way and it doesn’t meet what we’re asking for. It’s kind of frustrating.” 

The news comes as Western Construction and subcontractors prepare to finish the reconstruction of that section of Haines Avenue. Eastman said if the weather cooperates, the company expects construction to be finished by the end of the month, with a slight delay on striping. 

“The paving and everything should be taken care of here within the next couple of weeks,” he said. 

The nearly $3.1 million project to reconstruct a section of Haines Avenue from a half mile south of Peterson Raod to about a quarter mile north of Husker Place, started in May. The deadline for the entire project to be completed is Nov. 1.

title: Crescent St. project in Deadwood  receives first change order
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Work to improve pedestrian access and improve safety at the Days of ’76 rodeo grounds and improve infrastructure along Crescent Street in Deadwood is ahead of schedule and has received only one change order. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
20601.jpg
Work to improve pedestrian access and improve safety at the Days of ’76 rodeo grounds and improve infrastructure along Crescent Street in Deadwood is ahead of schedule and has received only one change order. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

DEADWOOD — A project to improve pedestrian access and safety on Crescent Street and the Days of ’76 rodeo grounds in Deadwood has received its first change order but remains ahead of schedule for the projected completion date. 

The $20,838.11 change order included the replacement of a fire hydrant, installation of bollards around the fire hydrant, removal of a concrete wall, upsizing of 2 inlet boxes, modifications to a downspout on the grandstand, additional PVC fittings, work associated with a thickened-edge sidewalk, and repairs to the foundations of one corner of the grandstand. 

“That stretch of ground actually has the oldest fire hydrant in Deadwood, so we thought we might as well replace it if we’re already down there and can bring all the infrastructure to that fire hydrant,” said Lornie Stalder, director of public works. “We put some bollards around the fire hydrant. We ran into a couple things at the grandstands that we had to deal with. It was just a bad foundation around the south corner of the grandstands.”

Stalder said Hayworth deemed a concrete slab supporting one of the pillars at the south end of the grandstands to be inadequate and proposed building a larger slab to properly support the corner post.

The retaining wall behind the city shop on Crescent Street is complete. Stalder said the larger retaining wall improved the city’s storage capacity in the area. Backfill on the disturbed area is expected to be complete this week.

The full scope of work of the project includes new curb, gutter, sidewalk, and pedestrian lighting, new asphalt, a retaining wall between the city’s park building and grandstands, and a 6-inch water line that will create a looped system with additional fire hydrants and improved safety at the grandstands. The road connecting the Days of ’76 Campground to the rodeo grounds is also set to receive improvements.

The change order brings the total cost of the project to $1,792,874.88. The contract was awarded to Hayworth Enterprises, of Belle Fourche, in April 2026, and is being paid for in part by a $600,000 community access grant from the South Dakota Department of Transportation. The rest of the project is funded by the city’s capital improvement budget and monies gained from the sale of the convention center at The Lodge in Deadwood after the dissolution of Tax Increment Financing District 6 in April 2025.

Stalder said the change order equates to approximately 1% of the total value of the project, remaining well within the 10% or $75,000 required by South Dakota Codified Law 5-18B-19 before the proposed additional work must undergo a bidding process.

Stalder said the completion date of the project is under negotiation now that the project includes paving a section of road from the check-in station at the campgrounds with a trolley turn around all the way to the creek at the Department of Transportation (DOT) shop. He said the additional work will take approximately a month to complete, but he believes the work will be completed by Oct. 15. 

“It’s all still a little bit ahead of schedule, but with the additional work we’re going to try to negotiate the timeframe that (Hayworth) can enter into the campground area,” Stalder said. “The date we had previously agreed upon (with the Days of ’76 Committee, Lead-Deadwood Sanitary District, and DOT) was around Sept. 15 and we might have to see if we can get an earlier access date so that we can get in there and take on the additional work.”

Rehabilitation of disturbed vegetation is projected to be completed by May 1, 2027.

title: Spearfish Art in Public Places board  meets for the first time
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Spearfish Community Planner Jaymia Ecker addresses the first meeting of the Art in Public Places Advisory Board. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Art Committee 1.JPG
Spearfish Community Planner Jaymia Ecker addresses the first meeting of the Art in Public Places Advisory Board. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

 Art Committee 2.JPG
Bonnie Halsey, right, and Terry Flamboe sit on the dais for the first Art in Public Places Advisory Board meeting in Spearfish. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

 Art Committee 3.JPG
Desy Schoenweiss, Anton Peterson, and Anna Robinson attend their first meeting as Art in Public Places Advisory board members. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — Bonnie Halsey, Terry Flamboe, Anna Robinson, Anton Peterson, Desy Schoeneweis, Amy Davidson, and Diana Reth are the inaugural members of Spearfish’s new Art in Public Places Advisory Board. 

The board met for the first time on August 13. 

Established under city ordinance 1426, the art in public places advisory board is meant to promote and encourage public programs that further “public awareness of and interest in the arts” and to “provide for the maintenance of existing art in public spaces.”

“We hope that we can make art in Spearfish a little more visible, a little more important, and grow the program to the fullest extent possible and really see it as a city asset,” said Spearfish Community Development Director Peter Wysocki, as he addressed the new board for the first time. “You’re sitting in the same chair where the city council and the mayor sit, and you’re going to be making some big decisions.”

Every time a building permit is issued in the city, 5% of the permitting fee is set aside for the art in public places fund — to be used for the establishment and maintenance of public art.

The fund was originally established in 2005.

“But this board, as far as I understand, was never stood up. The good thing is that there are actually funds for this board to help make decisions around how those are spent, which is lucky and somewhat unique that you are starting here with some money,” Spearfish Community Planner Jaymia Ecker said. “The current fund balance is $158,000. We don’t have the authority to spend all of that at this point, but the annual spending is determined through the annual budgeting process and then anything beyond that annual allocation we have had to go to council for an amendment if a large project came up and you wanted to spend more than what’s allocated in an annual budget.”

The new public art advisory board will direct the use of public art funds, acting as advisors to both the city council and community development department staff — including Ecker and Wysocki.

Wysocki told the board that they will have options when it comes to using the funds for the public good. They could purchase statues, host art competitions, or even establish grants. He encouraged them to use the time between meetings to think about how the board should be shaped moving forward.

“As a board now, what would be your goals, your strategy to meet those goals, and how we will measure success? Not just, ‘Oh, we want a statue.’ Let’s think about community outreach, community education about public art? How do we market Spearfish as an art community?” Wysocki said.

By design, the board is made up of citizens with diverse interests in the arts. One member is a working artist. Another is an art professor. Another isn’t an artist at all, just an engaged community member who hopes to support art in the community.

“What I hope to accomplish on the board is to be a strong advocate for expanding our community’s art projects,” said Peterson. “I have zero artistic capabilities myself … but my daughter is an artist, and I would like to see that continue to grow. I think it definitely adds to the overall vibe of the community.”

Peterson was elected chair at the first meeting; Robinson was elected vice chair — both votes were unchallenged and unanimous.

“I wanted to join because, as a working artist, I wanted to have a little say in what I know of artists’ needs in the area, but also I have moved around a lot throughout my life,” Robinson said. “Having come across cities with a strong art presence, it tends to be a thriving community for family, locals; it attracts a lot of people and a lot of business. I want to be a part of that.”

Schoenweiss said public art contributes to a community’s character. She is an art professor at Black Hills State University.

“I think that having a visual identity and public art is so important to creating a unique space,” Schoenweiss said.

She was part of the “Layers of Spearfish” mural project in 2018 — the result of which can be seen on Main Street and Jackson Boulevard.  

“That was a one-year endeavor. That was awesome. Some of my favorite moments are walking my dog and seeing people take selfies and photos in front of it to this day,” Schoenweiss said. “It is something that is cyclical and changes consistently. As much as I love that mural, I know someday somebody is going to create another more beautiful mural in that space. I just want to encourage the community to keep producing and keep creating that identity.”

Each member of the board was appointed by the mayor, with support from city council.

Reth and Davidson sit on the board as representatives from the Parks and Recreation Department and the Planning Commission, respectively.  

Each present board member drew a term length from a bucket, so that all board members don’t have simultaneously expiring terms.

Schoenweiss will serve a 2-year term, Peterson a 1-year term, Robinson a 1-year term, Flamboe a 2-year term, and Halsey a 3-year term.

After a review of open meetings law, the board adjourned. During its next meeting, the board is expected to discuss and potentially adopt its bylaws.

title: Medical marijuana home cultivation licenses surge in SD
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: A marijuana plant at the Dakota Herb grow operation near Tea. Photo by John Hult, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Medical marijuana home cultivation licenses surge in SD.jpg
A marijuana plant at the Dakota Herb grow operation near Tea. Photo by John Hult, South Dakota Searchlight 

PIERRE — A South Dakota Health Department official told lawmakers Monday that the number of medical marijuana patients in the state who are licensed to grow medical cannabis at home has grown by more than 1,000% over the past four years.

Whitney Brunner, administrator of the state’s medical cannabis program, told the legislative Medical Marijuana Oversight Committee during a meeting at the Capitol in Pierre that the number of home cultivators grew from 61 in fiscal year 2022 to 715 in fiscal year 2026 — an increase of 1,072%. Medical marijuana has been legal in South Dakota since 2021, but recreational marijuana use remains prohibited.

Home cultivators may not grow more than two flowering cannabis plants and two non-flowering cannabis plants, according to state law.

Patients can add a home cultivation license to their medical marijuana card for $20. Applicants must submit a photo of the grow room, a photo of the lock on the door and a diagram of the grow location. Brunner said those diagrams are often hand-drawn and lack detail.

“The lack of regulation in this area is a bit concerning for us,” Brunner told lawmakers.

Brunner said she doesn’t want to assume home cultivators are abusing the licenses, but said the department is considering tighter regulation.

“We have looked into if there is anything more that can be done, but I think that’s a greater conversation to be had,” Brunner said. “It does present some legal and safety considerations if we were to attempt to regulate this further.”

Brunner did not say if new regulation would require legislation. Committee member Sen. John Carley, R-Rapid City, told South Dakota Searchlight after the meeting that lawmakers hope to learn more.

“We were glad the department had more information,” Carley said. “Many of us will be looking at that exact item and will come back to that concern next meeting.”

The rise in home cultivation comes amid growth in the overall program. At the end of June, there were 19,375 medical marijuana cardholders in South Dakota — a 30.5% increase from 14,843 last fiscal year.

“We did experience a true spike in early fiscal year 2026 but, by fall, that number had started to level off,” Brunner said, adding that the number of cardholders in the state “remained fairly stable” most of the year.

Most cardholders are in their 30s and 40s, according to department data, and more than 70% report severe debilitating pain as a reason for their cannabis use.

title: City council proclaims Aug. 26 Women’s Equality Day
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Representatives from the Lawrence County Democrats led the effort to have Women’s Equality Day proclaimed in Spearfish. Representatives from the group received the proclamation from Spearfish Mayor John Senden, Monday. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Women's Equality Day proclaimation.JPG
Representatives from the Lawrence County Democrats led the effort to have Women’s Equality Day proclaimed in Spearfish. Representatives from the group received the proclamation from Spearfish Mayor John Senden, Monday. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — On Aug. 26, 1920, then-Secretary of State Bainbridge Colby certified the 19th Amendment, which granted women the right to vote.

South Dakota afforded women the right to vote on Nov. 6, 1918, after the passage of the Citizenship Amendment. That amendment passed with 64% of the vote.

On Monday, in celebration of the suffragettes who fought for women’s rights, and to mark the contributions women have made to the nation’s government and history, Spearfish Mayor John Senden proclaimed Aug. 26, 2026, Women’s Equality Day.

“Women in South Dakota contribute to voter turnout and female candidates running for local governance and … enhance local decision making,” the proclamation reads. The proclamation was authored on behalf of the Lawrence County Democrats.

To mark Women’s Equality Day, a nonpartisan celebration of women’s equality will be held at Spearfish Brewing Company from 5:30–8 p.m., featuring live music, a raffle, and games. Funds raised during the event will be donated to the Good Shepherd Clinic.

title: Rawlings brings Gas Monkey flair to Sturgis Rally with Harley giveaway
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: Josh Paris, is the head of the team that works on the Gas Monkey Garage YouTube shop’s highprofile automotive builds announces the name of the winner of the motorcycle give away on Thursday in Sturgis. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
Rawlings brings Gas Monkey flair to Sturgis Rally with Harley giveaway.JPG
Josh Paris, is the head of the team that works on the Gas Monkey Garage YouTube shop’s highprofile automotive builds announces the name of the winner of the motorcycle give away on Thursday in Sturgis. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

STURGIS — Richard Rawlings has spent years building cars, motorcycles and the Gas Monkey Garage brand into a nationally recognized name. During the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, he is bringing that passion to Sturgis with a custom Harley-Davidson giveaway and a celebration of the motorcycle lifestyle.  Rawlings, founder of Gas Monkey Garage and owner of Gas Monkey Sturgis, and Josh Paris announced the winner of a custom 2026 Harley-Davidson Low Rider S on Thursday at Gas Monkey Sturgis.  The name drawn was Brooklynn Borgeson of Albert Lea, Minnesotan and she was not present.  Paris called Borgeson and her first comment was “oh my gosh, I have never won anything.”  Paris is a fabricator at Gas Monkey Garage YouTube and is part of the team that works on the shop’s highprofile automotive builds

The motorcycle features a red, white and blue 250th anniversary-themed paint scheme and an exclusive Gas Monkey Garage design.  For Rawlings, returning to Sturgis during Rally week is about more than business. “I love it here, especially during the Rally because there’s nothing else like it in the world,” Rawlings said. “Seeing hundreds of thousands of bikes rolling into the Black Hills and getting to ride, hang out and drink beers with everyone is the ultimate good time.”

With the United States celebrating its 250th birthday this year, Rawlings said Gas Monkey wanted to do something special.  “We wanted to do something extra this year by giving away this custom 2026 Harley-Davidson Low Rider S all decked out in our nation’s colors,” he said. “And to do it here at Gas Monkey Sturgis during Rally week – doesn’t get better than that!”

Rawlings has been visiting Sturgis for about two decades, drawn in part by the riding opportunities throughout the Black Hills. “I’ve been coming to Sturgis for 20 years because I love riding through the Black Hills,” he said. “It’s truly one of the most beautiful places to ride.”

That connection eventually led Rawlings and business partner Mike Sisk to open Gas Monkey Sturgis.  

“So what could be better than to have a place of my own here to hang with like-minded folk who have a passion for bikes and the lifestyle?” Rawlings said.

The Sturgis location has continued to grow, adding a Gas Monkey merchandise store and an outdoor bar alongside the restaurant and full bar.

“It’s the ultimate playground and Gas Monkey is right in the middle of it all,” Rawlings said.

The giveaway motorcycle also reflects Rawlings’ approach to the Gas Monkey brand, combining American pride with the company’s distinctive style. “We wanted to pay tribute to America and had to do it with our signature Gas Monkey twist,” Rawlings said. “With the sleek, custom red, white and blue paint job and, of course, an exclusive Uncle Sam Gas Monkey, it shows our pride in our nation and there’s nothing like the freedom of riding a Harley.”

As someone who has spent years building and customizing vehicles, Rawlings said the first thing that catches his eye on the Low Rider S is its appearance.

“The overall look of the bike with that sexy paint job and all that chrome,” he said.

The 2026 Harley-Davidson Low Rider S is powered by a Milwaukee-Eight 117 High Output V-Twin engine producing 114 horsepower and 128 pound-feet of torque. It also features selectable Road, Rain and Sport ride modes, advanced rider safety systems, upgraded suspension and full LED lighting. For Rawlings, however, the motorcycle and the business ultimately come back to the people who visit Gas Monkey Sturgis.  

“The Rally is important for all businesses in Sturgis, but most importantly, we want everyone from local regulars to Rally die-hards or people just passing through, to come to Gas Monkey Sturgis and have a good time,” he said.  “Enjoy the food, full bar, and each other – that’s what we’re all about.”

The Harley-Davidson giveaway is open to the public, with the winner scheduled to be announced at 4 p.m. Thursday at Gas Monkey Sturgis during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally.

title: Second Chance Comedy brings laughter,  recovery stories to Rapid City
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: Joe Huisman, founder of Second Chance Comedy along with other comedians will be performing at the Dahl Arts Center in Rapid City on August 29th at 7:00 pm. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
1. Second Chance comedy.jpg
Joe Huisman, founder of Second Chance Comedy along with other comedians will be performing at the Dahl Arts Center in Rapid City on August 29th at 7:00 pm. Courtesy photo 

RAPID CITY — A stand-up comedy show coming to Rapid City this month will tackle some serious subjects — addiction, recovery, mental health, grief and the struggles of everyday life, but its founder hopes audiences leave remembering one thing: they are not alone.

Second Chance Comedy will present “We’re All Doing Great...And Other Lies” at the Dahl Arts Center at 7 p.m., Aug. 29. The show will feature nationally touring comedian Von Sprecken, Jeremy Cash, and Second Chance Comedy founder Joe Huisman also part of the lineup.

Huisman created Second Chance Comedy after 2 very different parts of his life came together, his years of addiction and recovery and his discovery of stand-up comedy.

Huisman said he spent nearly a decade using drugs before getting sober. Recovery changed the direction of his life and taught him the importance of connection, honesty and moving beyond shame. In 2023, he began performing stand-up comedy.  As he spent more time on stage, he began to see comedy as more than entertainment. It became a way to create connection and open conversations about some of life’s most difficult experiences, including anxiety, depression, addiction, relationships and grief.

That realization led to Second Chance Comedy.  

“I think comedians were already talking about many of the same things people discuss in recovery meetings and therapy,” Huisman said. “It made me wonder: What would happen if we created a comedy show where those conversations weren’t hidden in the background but became part of the show itself?”

Huisman said the goal was never to create a comedy show exclusively for people in recovery. Instead, Second Chance Comedy is designed for a broader audience, recognizing that addiction and mental health issues affect families and communities in many different ways.

The organization’s mission is to use humor and personal stories to challenge the stigma surrounding addiction while providing a platform for comedians with personal connections to recovery and other difficult life experiences. The organization also works to support recovery organizations through its shows.

For Huisman, humor can provide a way into conversations that otherwise might be difficult to have.  

“Humor creates connection,” he said.

He believes laughter can lower people’s defenses and help audiences recognize shared experiences. 

“A comedian can say something on stage that might be uncomfortable in an ordinary conversation, and suddenly an entire room is laughing because they recognize themselves in it,” Huisman said.

That doesn’t mean the show makes light of addiction or mental health. 

“Authenticity has to come first,” Huisman said. “The goal of the show isn’t to make light of addiction or mental health. The goal is to tell honest stories and find the humor that already exists within those experiences.”

He said the comedians featured in Second Chance Comedy generally draw from their own lives, sharing struggles, failures, victories and observations rather than making jokes at someone else’s expense. 

“Sometimes that honesty is heartbreaking, and sometimes it’s hilarious,” Huisman said. “More often than not, it’s both.”

The Rapid City performance will be headlined by Von Sprecken, a nationally touring comedian whose experiences include recovery, health care and supporting family members dealing with addiction and mental health challenges.

Huisman said Sprecken brings a perspective that allows him to find humor in difficult experiences while keeping the material relatable and approachable.

“He’s able to tackle serious subjects without ever making them feel heavy,” Huisman said. “He’s also just a tremendously funny comedian.”

Sprecken has been involved with the recovery community for more than a decade and has experience with addiction and mental health issues as a patient, family member and health care worker. He began performing comedy in Denver in 2017 and has performed at venues around the country.

Huisman hopes audiences who attend the Rapid City show won’t feel they need to have a personal connection to addiction or recovery to enjoy the evening.

“First and foremost, this is a comedy show,” he said. People may see subjects such as addiction and mental health and assume the evening will be heavy, Huisman said, but he hopes audiences will instead discover a night of laughter and shared experiences.

“You don’t have to be in recovery to enjoy the show,” he said. “You don’t have to be struggling with your mental health. You don’t even need a personal connection to either topic. What you do need is a sense of humor.” The show’s title, “We’re All Doing Great...And Other Lies,” reflects Huisman’s belief that people often feel pressure to make it appear as though everything in their lives is going well, even when they are struggling.

He hopes the Rapid City audience will leave with a little more compassion for themselves and others, and perhaps a little lighter than when they arrived.

“I hope people leave feeling a little less alone,” Huisman said.

The Rapid City Arts Council describes the performance as a stand-up comedy show dealing with the realities of mental health, addiction and everyday life. More information about the show and Second Chance Comedy is available through https://SecondChanceComedy.com

title: Middle school track and field  work nearing completion
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Crews from Mammoth Construction are busy redoing the Spearfish Middle School track and field. Pioneer photo by Travis Potter
_full_text:
DJI_20260804173228_0019_D.JPG
Crews from Mammoth Construction are busy redoing the Spearfish Middle School track and field. Pioneer photo by Travis Potter 

SPEARFISH — Construction crews are anticipating laying asphalt on the new Spearfish Middle School track this week. Shortly after, the artificial turf will be installed.

Nick Gottlob, superintendent of the Spearfish School District, provided an update of the construction project to Spearfish School Board members Monday.

“We’re estimated that to begin prior to Aug. 24,” Gottlob said. “So, less than 2 weeks from today, that that brown space should be green, and it’s going to get exciting from that point forth.”

The previous track and field, built more than 30 years ago, was constructed on substandard soil, which has led to cracking asphalt, a few potholes in the track, and other drainage issues on the field. 

Initially, the construction costs came in around $3.25 million. Several changes were made to reduce the cost, and the final price for the district came in around $2.7 million. However, on Monday, the board approved a change order in the amount of $59,685, to add 2 jumping pits and a runway.

Gottlob said that school and track and field officials met in June and determined the additional runway and pits were necessary.

“If we intend to use that facility to host middle school meets or high school duels or quads, we either have to start jumping at 5 a.m. to be done at 8 p.m. or we need to reconsider that design,” he told board members. 

Activities Director Dalton Wademan added between both boys’ and girls’ events of long and triple jump, the extra pits were necessary.

The board unanimously approved the change order.

Gottlob said the substantial completion of the track and field should be done around Sept. 10.

title: Judge affirms Piedmont voluntary annexation, dismisses lawsuit
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Fourth Circuit Court Judge Michelle Comer dismissed a lawsuit alleging that a voluntary annexation in Piedmont was unlawful, and affirmed the city’s decision to approve the annexation petition.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

STURGIS — Fourth Circuit Court Judge Michelle Comer dismissed a lawsuit alleging that a voluntary annexation in Piedmont was unlawful, and affirmed the city’s decision to approve the annexation petition. 

The ruling was for a case filed by P5, LLC, owned by members of the Policky family, represented by Zachary Policky and attorney Michael Nadolski. The case was against the city of Piedmont, and stems from the voluntary annexation of 130 acres, which the city approved in February. Seven of 8 landowners signed the voluntary  annexation petition, which was submitted in January. 

P5, LLC was the lone property owner that did not sign the petition that included 59 acres of their land. Policky filed the motion for a writ of certiorari on March 2 as part of a lawsuit intended to prevent the voluntary annexation from taking effect, and to protect business interests for the Policky family. 

South Dakota Codified Law 9-4-1 requires annexation petitions to include signatures from at least 75% of the landowners who represent at least 75% of the total valuation of land included in the annexation. It used Meade County valuation data from 2024, which placed the total assessed value of the annexed property at $3.76 million, with signatures from property owners who represented $3.18 million of that valuation. The petition states the valuation of the P5, LLC property is $310,000. 

In the lawsuit, P5, LLC argues that their land was greatly undervalued in the petition, which means the statutory requirements of 75% of the land valuation were not met without P5, LLC representatives’ signature on the petition. The lawsuit states that the 59 acres of P5, LLC property was part of a 92-acre purchase made in 2022 for $3 million, and if that amount is proportionally allocated, the 59-acre tract has a material value of about $1.9 million. 

Additionally, the P5, LLC lawsuit alleges that projected royalty values the company expects to receive contribute to the increased land value. In court documents, P5, LLC acknowledges a deal with Simon Contractors to allow the company to operate a limestone quarry on the P5 property, and states that the limestone mining company has already paid P5, LLC $40,000 to option the use of the property. The 59 acres included in the annexation petition includes approximately 3 to 4 million tons of limestone, and the lawsuit acknowledges a pending deal for Simon Contractors to pay P5, LLC about $1.25 per ton, with customary royalty values ranging from $1 to $2 per ton. 

The lawsuit alleged that the city of Piedmont did not independently verify land values before approving the annexation. 

But in its response to the writ of certiorari, the city of Piedmont, represented by Zachary Peterson, stated that using the assessed value of property is the legal and accepted way of determining value for annexation. 

Comer’s ruling was issued on Aug. 11 to affirm the voluntary petition annexation and dismiss the writ of certiorari.

title: False Bottom Creek Fire now fully contained
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Fire crews from multiple agencies as well as local residents helped fight the False Bottom Creek Fire that started west of St. Onge Sunday afternoon. Pioneer photos by Mark Watson
_full_text:
False Bottom Creek Fire now fully contained 1.JPG
Fire crews from multiple agencies as well as local residents helped fight the False Bottom Creek Fire that started west of St. Onge Sunday afternoon. Pioneer photos by Mark Watson 

 False Bottom Creek Fire now fully contained 2.JPG
A fenceline along 196th Street was charred by the False Bottom Creek Fire Sunday, but the fire did not jump the road. Pioneer photo by Mark Watson 

ST. ONGE — Fire crews now have the False Bottom Creek Fire fully contained.

On Monday morning, several fire crews were seen crisscrossing the burn area looking for hot spots to extinguish. 

A strong thunderstorm with lightning rolled through the area shortly before the fire was reported, around 3:42 p.m., Sunday several miles west of St. Onge and just south of 196th Street.

Fanned by winds, the fire spread north where it was stopped at 196th Street. It was burning in a cut hayfield and burned some timber and round bales of hay. Nearby residents worked on corralling the fire by creating lines around the fire with tractors and by hand. 

The St. Onge Fire Department initially was in command of the fire but turned the lead role over to South Dakota Wildland Fire, which has more resources. 

Firefighters from St. Onge, Belle Fourche, Whitewood, Spearfish, and Deadwood fire departments as well as South Dakota Wildland Fire, U.S. Forest Service, Lawrence County Emergency Management, Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office, Lawrence County Dispatch responded to the fire. Crews from Alabama and North Carolina were also on the scene.

title: SD taxpayers spend millions on cyberattacks after federal grant rejected
byline: By Bart Pfankuch South Dakota News Watch
description: Mike Waldner spoke to congressional staff members at a cybersecurity meeting held at Dakota State University in Madison, S.D., on Aug. 11. Photo of Courtesy of DSU
_full_text:
DSU Mike Waldner.jpg
Mike Waldner spoke to congressional staff members at a cybersecurity meeting held at Dakota State University in Madison, S.D., on Aug. 11. Photo of Courtesy of DSU 

PIERRE — South Dakota turned down millions of dollars in federal cybersecurity grants and instead is spending more than $7 million in state taxpayer funds to battle what has become a constant threat of attacks on computer systems used by government, industry and individuals.

In addition to recent high-profile cyberattacks on government operations in Pennington County, Rapid City and Mitchell, the South Dakota Attorney General’s Office receives frequent reports of digital information breaches.

Over the past 5 years, the agency has had 1,062 online security breaches reported to its Consumer Affairs Division, including 127 so far in 2026, according to agency data.

Those breaches include data hacks perpetuated on individuals, businesses and government entities, according to AG spokesman Tony Mangan, who responded to a News Watch request. State law prevents the public release of where or upon whom those breaches took place, Mangan said.

But the frequency at which data and systems are being infiltrated illustrates the increasing risk of storing important personal and government information online at a time when experts say nefarious actors are constantly trying to hack into computer systems across the U.S., including in South Dakota.

 2026-07-31 Rapid City IT director.jpeg
Rapid City’s information technology director, Jim Gilbert, discusses cybersecurity from a bench outside City Hall in Rapid City, S.D. on July 31, 2026.  

“We are always under a constant threat, and we are always mitigating something somewhere,” said Mike Waldner, director of SecureSD and Project Boundary Fence, the state’s 2 main cyber security prevention programs. “We always have an active case that we’re working on.”

Recent cyberattacks on local governments have only heightened concerns that systems are being targeted by either organized crime groups seeking ransom or by foreign adversaries such as Russia, China or Iran, which is currently engaged in a war with the United States.

 2026-07-28 Penn County waiting in line.jpeg
 A line of people waited to obtain in-person services from the treasurer’s office at the Pennington County Administration Building in Rapid City, S.D., on July 28, 2026. Photo by Bart Pfankuch, South Dakota News Watch 

Experts theorize that Iran-backed hackers are responsible for large-scale cyberattacks on communication systems in Pennington County and the city of Mitchell as well as breaches into water systems in Minnesota and possibly up to a dozen more states.

South Dakota lost out on at least $5 million and likely much more in federal funding for cybersecurity efforts by cities and counties when former Gov. Kristi Noem declined to apply for part of a $1 billion federal grant program in fiscal year 2023.

Ian Fury, a spokesman for Noem at the time, said the funding from the Biden administration was wasteful and required the state to use one-time funding to create a long-term program.

Instead, state lawmakers allocated $7 million to cybersecurity prevention efforts that include SecureSD and the Project Boundary Fence, both programs aimed at preventing and mitigating hacks on state, county and local governments as well as utilities.

 2026-07-28 Pennington TV screen.jpeg
A television screen was offline at the Pennington County Administration Building in Rapid City, S.D., on July 28, 2026. Photo by Bart Pfankuch, South Dakota News Watch 

Gov. Larry Rhoden on Aug. 11 appropriated $500,000 in Future Fund money to the South Dakota Department of the Military to boost efforts of the Governor’s Resilience and Infrastructure Task Force, of which cybersecurity is one objective.

The first high-profile cyberattack on a municipal government in South Dakota took place in Brown County in August 2021. More recently, in October, someone working in Tripp County government was caught up in an email “phishing” scam and mistakenly sent more than $826,000 in taxpayer money to a fake account.

The South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation is working with federal agencies on an investigation into the incident, the release said. To date, the funds have not been recovered.

Rapid City technology staffers quickly contained an attempted hack on a sewage lift station monitoring system in late July, IT director Jim Gilbert said. Gilbert said the city computer system has redundancies built in to notify system regulators and stave off implications of attacks if they occur.

For the past few years, the state has funded 2 separate but aligned efforts to prevent cybersecurity attacks under the auspices of Dakota State University in Madison.

SecureSD and Project Boundary Fence are voluntary programs to combat cyber attacks and data breaches at municipalities, counties, and nonprofit entities providing drinking water and sewer utilities across the state. 

“We’re trying to build that cybersecurity culture and secure what we call the ‘human firewall,’” Waldner said. “Like it or not, as a government employee, you are under constant threat, and the expectation from citizens is that you are protecting their data and information like they expect it to be protected.”

title: Harrington honored as honorary Meade Co. deputy
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: Meade County Sheriff Pat West honors Sturgis resident Greg Harrington, as an honorary Meade County Deputy on Sunday at the law enforcement appreciation barbeque in the Sturgis Park.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
1. harrington.JPG
Meade County Sheriff Pat West honors Sturgis resident Greg Harrington, as an honorary Meade County Deputy on Sunday at the law enforcement appreciation barbeque in the Sturgis Park.  Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

STURGIS — Meade County Sheriff Pat West honored Greg Harrington for his longtime support of law enforcement and the community, appointing him an honorary Meade County deputy during the annual law enforcement appreciation barbeque on Sunday at the City Park.

West said Harrington’s commitment to public safety and veterans made him a natural choice for the honor.

“Greg is a friend of mine, and we met a long time ago,” West said. “He is a retired trooper with the Maryland State Police. He’s also a retired Army veteran, 4 tours.”

Harrington also is active with the American Legion Riders and regularly participates in events honoring fallen service members. West said Harrington helps escort fallen soldiers to the National Cemetery, calling his dedication to veterans and the community “pretty special.”

“Based on that, I’m going to announce that Greg Harrington has been recognized for the strong support of the Sheriff’s Office, public safety and law enforcement, and has been appointed honorary deputy sheriff for Meade County,” West said.

As part of the recognition, Harrington received a shadow box containing a former Meade County Sheriff’s Office patch, the current sheriff’s office patch, a Sturgis Rally patch and an official deputy sheriff badge.

Harrington said he was humbled by the honor and joked that his years as a Maryland state trooper would not be forgotten.  “I just want to say, for the troopers, I will wear my trooper hat when I’m a deputy,” Harrington said. “Thank you so much, Pat. I’m real humbled by this, and God bless all you police out there, and stay safe.”

West also spoke about Harrington’s willingness to stand beside law enforcement when needed.

“Greg’s one of those guys where I had a couple situations, and I was dealing with some people, and I turned around and he was right on my hip, ready to go like a rabid dog,” West said. “So, I love that guy.”

The honorary deputy recognition highlighted the strong relationships between local law enforcement, military veterans and community members who regularly support public safety efforts throughout the Sturgis and Meade County area.

title: Six men arrested in sex crimes operation at Sturgis Rally
byline: Pioneer Staff Reports
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Arrested
Courtesy photo 

STURGIS — South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley announced Monday that 6 men have been arrested on charges of attempted sex crimes with minors. 

The arrests were the result of an undercover operation conducted during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally by the state Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC) Task Force.

“This week’s operation is a strong reminder of the importance of our local, state and federal partnerships, including agreements such as our 287(g) immigration authority, in locating and removing dangerous individuals from our communities,” Jackley said. “This operation is about protecting our children and was a success thanks to the hard work and dedication of our ICAC Task Force.”

The ICAC Rally Operation was conducted from Aug. 7, through Wednesday. Agents and detectives posed as children and/or as traffickers offering children for prostitution. During the operation, the law enforcement officers posted ads and/or profiles on various Internet sites and social media platforms providing offenders the opportunity to communicate with whom they believed to be minors or traffickers offering children for prostitution.

Arrested, all on state charges, were:

• Johan Vazquez-Garza, 33, of Rapid City for solicitation of a minor. Vazquez-Garza, who has been deported 5 times since 2009, may face additional federal immigration related charges.

• Bo Bo Aung, 38, of Box Elder for first-degree human trafficking, attempted first-degree human trafficking, and attempted fourth-degree rape. Aung, a Myanmar national, who illegally absconded from a work visa program in Texas 7 years ago may face federal deportation proceedings following the conclusion of state proceedings.

• Adrian Tomas Randles, 39, of Rapid City, solicitation of a minor. Randles is a registered Sex Offender resulting from a 2013 conviction for solicitation of a minor.

• Steven Clay Brown, 62, of Sturgis for solicitation of a minor.

• Kevin Orlanda Tassion Brown, 30, of Dillon, S.C., for first-degree human trafficking, attempted first-degree human trafficking, and attempted fourth-degree rape.

• Jay Anderson, 39, Hot Springs. Solicitation of a Minor.

This was the 14th consecutive year of the ICAC operation during the Sturgis Rally. Since its inception, the operation has resulted in the arrest of approximately 104 offenders who were willing to sexually abuse children.

Agencies assisting ICAC in this year’s operation were the South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation, the Attorney General’s Office, Rapid City Police Department, Pennington County Sheriff’s Office, Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), US Marshals Service, and Pennington County State’s Attorney’s Office.

“The Sturgis Motorcycle Rally brings thousands of people together, and with that comes a shared responsibility to keep the community safe. HSI is grateful for the hard work and vigilance of our federal, state, and local partners, who stood with us to find and stop those who would exploit the vulnerable or harm children,” said HSI St. Paul Acting Special Agent in Charge Tonya Price. “This effort shows what strong law enforcement partnerships can do: protect victims, remove predators from our communities, and make clear that child exploitation will not be tolerated.”

All 6 are being prosecuted by the South Dakota Attorney General’s office in partnership with the Pennington County State’s Attorney’s Office.

title: Temporary Rally officer arrested for DUI
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — A Georgia law enforcement officer who traveled to Sturgis to work the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally was arrested early Sunday morning for driving under the influence.
_full_text:
STURGIS — A Georgia law enforcement officer who traveled to Sturgis to work the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally was arrested early Sunday morning for driving under the influence. 

Sturgis Police Chief Geody VanDewater confirmed on Monday that Roy Linkous, of Columbus, Ga., was one of the many officers the city of Sturgis hires to help provide law enforcement during the annual Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. VanDewater said Linkous had ended his shift at 6 p.m. on Saturday, and decided to consume alcohol on his personal time. He was arrested at about 4:30 a.m., Sunday, for DUI. 

“This was a guy who was off duty and arrested for drinking and driving,” VanDewater said. “It’s just like anybody else who went down to the bar on his personal time. At the end of the day he made a bad decision. Those decisions don’t reflect on the values and goals of the Sturgis Police Department.” 

VanDewater said Linkous was a part time officer at an agency in Georgia, but he did not specify his regular place of employment. Officers from across the country submit applications to the city of Sturgis to work the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, and the city of Sturgis verifies each applicant’s certification as a law enforcement officer. Linkous was a verified law enforcement officer. 

Following his arrest, Linkous was transported to the Meade County Jail, where he was booked on the DUI charges.

title: Q&A: Thune says Republicans can hold their majority — if they stop fighting each other
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: SIOUX FALLS — U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune’s Republican Party faces midterm elections amid economic anxiety, high gas prices and a war with Iran.
_full_text:
Thune says Republicans can hold their majority — if they stop fighting each other.jpg

SIOUX FALLS — U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune’s Republican Party faces midterm elections amid economic anxiety, high gas prices and a war with Iran. 

But Thune, of South Dakota, said the biggest threat to the party’s Senate majority might be Republicans themselves.

Thune told South Dakota Searchlight and other journalists Friday during an event at Southeast Technical College that Republicans need to “turn our fire on Democrats, not on each other.”

Thune has been under fire from Republican President Donald Trump for not eliminating the filibuster, the Senate rule that requires the votes of at least 60 senators to end debate. Trump has repeatedly demanded the termination of the filibuster to help pass his SAVE America Act, which would require proof of U.S. citizenship when registering to vote and a photo ID when casting a ballot.

Republicans hold 53 of the seats in the Senate, and there are 33 seats up for election on Nov. 3. Thune doesn’t face reelection until 2028.

The following question-and-answer session between Thune and several reporters has been edited for length and clarity.

Q: How much is the war with Iran making your job harder?

It’s complicated on a lot of levels and certainly going into an election year with the politics around that. If you look at the things that have been achieved, there have been some great accomplishments there, but ultimately the way people are going to judge this is: How is it affecting the economy, how is it affecting gas prices, is the Strait of Hormuz open?

I think that’s got to be the singular, clear-eyed focus of the White House administration right now — ensuring that we get the shipping lanes open and get the fuel moving again and ensure that our economy here in the U.S. is not suffering as a result of this.

Q: Do you get the sense there’ll be an improvement before the midterms?

I hope so. I think they continue to, or they are trending toward a deal on that to get the strait open. But these are really complicated issues and you’re dealing with a regime that’s dishonest and is not going to play by the rules that the rest of the world community plays by, so you’ve got to be tough. I think the president has leaned into this in ways that puts a lot of pressure on the regime, but the regime is not going to go quietly. I think there are challenges ahead, but I also feel like they’re on a path toward landing something that will at least get things moving again and hopefully lessen some of the pressure on fuel prices here. 

Q: Can the Republican Party maintain its majority in the midterm elections?

I think the headwinds that are there, can it improve? It can. Can it get worse? Maybe. We’re facing typical midterm election political headwinds and some economic headwinds, because people are concerned about the economy and costs and everything else, which they should be since those are pocketbook issues. That’s what most elections are really about. 

I still think in spite of those headwinds, we’ve got really good candidates in the right places at the right time. You look at a state like Michigan, things really broke our way. Minnesota broke our way. The Democrats in both places nominated far-left candidates. We have candidates who are really, really accomplished people with a message I think is really going to resonate with voters in those states. Those are hard states, but we need to be on offense in a few places and we are in Michigan, as we’ll be in Minnesota, New Hampshire, Georgia.

We’re defending some ground too and the places where we’re defending there’s a firewall that if we don’t keep certain states, we’ll lose control of the Senate: Maine, Ohio, Iowa, Alaska — that’s the firewall of the Senate.

If we could win one of those races around the country, that obviously would be a huge success too, but it’s a tough year. These midterms always are. This one’s obviously complicated by some factors that we simply don’t control, but we’re doing everything we can within our control: recruiting a good crop of candidates, raising the resources that are necessary for them to get their messages out, and hopefully succeeding in the ground game, which is the “get out the vote” thing that you have to do come Election Day if you’re going to win elections. That’s harder, especially for low propensity voters who typically don’t vote in a non-presidential year. We’ve got to get a lot of those Trump voters out, so there’s a real effort being made. 

Q: Can you speak to your evolving relationship with President Trump and about him declining to say whether he supports you continuing as Senate majority leader because of your decisions in that role, including retaining the filibuster?

I take all of that with a grain of salt. There is a natural dynamic between any White House and the Senate. Most presidents, in my experience, don’t like the Senate and view it as an obstacle to getting the things they want to get done. But we obviously have a different way of doing things by design, which makes it harder sometimes. The House in a lot of ways is an extension of the White House. It’s a majoritarian body, while the Senate is a non-majoritarian body. It’s designed to give a voice to the minority in this country, so it’s harder to get things done because most things require a supermajority.

Those are the facts I have to live with, and I have very honest conversations with the president. He is entitled to his views about the things that we’re doing in the Senate. I would certainly expect that he has a way of doing things. He’s got a business model that’s full speed ahead, and I know that sometimes in the Senate, just by virtue of the reality on the ground that we have to deal with, we have to pump the brakes occasionally on that. And that’s not something that obviously he probably is good with, but nevertheless we get a lot done and if you look at the record of accomplishment, I think it’s second to none.

We can’t get everything done because it’s a function of votes. I tell people that the math is the math, and the math on the issue that he cares the most about right now isn’t going to change, at least not until after the election. Then we’ll see from there. We get along fine and work together, but if he wants somebody else in the job he’s welcome to that view.

Q: Do you worry that President Trump’s critical view of the body and fellow Republicans right now will be a hindrance ahead of the midterms?

What I’ve said, and I make this point quite regularly, is that we are less than 90 days away from an election. The election ought to be painting a contrast between us and the Democrats and not creating conflicts with fellow Republicans. 

I’ve tried to deliver that message in the work that we’re doing right now, the work we’re focused on keeping, protecting and preserving our majority in the Senate — maybe even expanding it if we could get a win in a state or two. But I am a clear-eyed realist about what we have to do, what’s in front of us and the best way for us to be successful, which is to have everybody pull in the same direction and turn our fire on Democrats, not on each other.

That’s a message I deliver regularly and it seems to be getting across at least on some level, but I think it’s in everybody’s best interest — if you want to have a Republican Senate majority after the election — is not to have us turning fire on each other, but drawing contrasts with Democrats, and there are plenty to draw.

If you want to have a debate about the future of this country, you can really do it because there is a clear division in my view between the two visions of where the parties are headed and where the candidates are headed. I mean, look at Michigan and Minnesota, look at some of these states where you’ve got these far-left, radical Democrats winning elections or winning primaries at least. I think that represents a great opportunity to contrast with them in the fall, and that’s where we ought to be focused.

title: Thune says year-round higher ethanol blend will require compromising with small oil refiners
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: From left, moderator Kimberly Reed, former president and chair of the Export-Import Bank of the United States, asks questions of U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, R-South Dakota, and U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-South Dakota, at the Midwest Agricultural Export Summit in Sioux Falls on Wednesday.
_full_text:
Thune says year-round higher ethanol blend will require compromising with small oil refiners.jpg
From left, moderator Kimberly Reed, former president and chair of the Export-Import Bank of the United States, asks questions of U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, R-South Dakota, and U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-South Dakota, at the Midwest Agricultural Export Summit in Sioux Falls on Wednesday.  

SIOUX FALLS — The year-round sale of higher ethanol-blended gasoline, called E15, does not have enough votes in the U.S. Senate unless it comes with compromises for small oil refineries, said Majority Leader John Thune, R-South Dakota.

Ethanol is a gasoline additive made primarily from corn, and a lower E10 blend is already available year-round. Supporters of year-round E15 availability say it would strengthen the farm economy and make the country more energy independent. Without a law authorizing year-round E15, summertime sales require a federal waiver.

Opponents point to research showing emissions from higher ethanol blends could worsen summer smog — although the biofuels industry disputes that — while encouraging the conversion of grasslands for corn farming. Some lawmakers from oil-producing and refining states also oppose the expansion. 

The U.S. House approved a bill in May authorizing year-round E15 sales, and year-round E15 language is in the Senate version of the farm bill under consideration by that chamber’s Ag Committee.

Walter Wendland, president of the South Dakota Ethanol Producers Association, asked Thune during Wednesday’s Midwest Agricultural Export Summit in Sioux Falls whether Congress could approve year-round E15 without making concessions to small oil refiners regarding the exemptions they receive from the Renewable Fuel Standard.

“Probably not,” Thune said.

Thune said E15 supporters need senators on board from states with small oil refiners. He listed Montana, Wyoming, Oklahoma, Arkansas and Tennessee lawmakers as those who might be inclined to support E15, but won’t without addressing small refineries’ concerns.

“At some point, we’ve got to get this done,” Thune said. “And I think at some point it becomes a decision of what can you get the votes to do.” 

The dispute centers on the Renewable Fuel Standard, overseen by the Environmental Protection Agency. It requires oil refiners to blend a minimum amount of renewable fuels, such as ethanol, into their fuel supply, or pay for compliance credits. 

Refineries processing 75,000 or fewer barrels per day can obtain a small refinery exemption if they can show that complying with the standard would cause them “disproportionate economic hardship.” 

Whether the Renewable Fuel Standard is actually met depends partly on whether larger refiners make up for the exemptions granted to small refiners.

Current law allows no automatic exemptions. Small refiners must prove a hardship and can receive full or half exemptions. 

The House bill would allow small refiners to receive automatic 75% exemptions, but the bill would require companies to aggregate their facilities rather than applying exemptions to individual plants. Seventeen of the 33 facilities that applied last year would be ineligible under that scenario. The House bill would not require exempted amounts to be reallocated to other refiners.

The Senate version would grant automatic full exemptions to small refiners without changing rules regarding aggregate versus individual facilities. The Senate version would require some reallocation of exempted amounts to other refiners.

Thune told the Sioux Falls audience that, “try as we did on the House-passed version of it, we weren’t going to get there, and it was the small refineries issue.” The Senate bill is a work in progress. 

Sioux Falls-based POET ethanol’s Senior Vice President of Corporate Affairs Joshua Shields said year-round E15 would be a positive development for biofuels, regardless of the changes to small refinery exemptions. 

“This is about expanding market access for homegrown biofuels,” he said in a statement. “When motorists are given the freedom to fuel with E15, a cleaner, more affordable option, that relies less on volatile petroleum spikes, we are confident that’s what they will choose.”
