title: Special education federal shift:  commitment remains, but future is unclear
byline: By Elena Tittel South Dakota News Watch
description: SIOUX FALLS – Parents in South Dakota who believe their child is being discriminated against at school who have not reached a resolution at the local level may turn to the Office of Civil Rights. But a recent federal shift raises questions about the future of special education discrimination in civil lawsuits.
_full_text:
SDNewsWatchLogo

SIOUX FALLS – Parents in South Dakota who believe their child is being discriminated against at school who have not reached a resolution at the local level may turn to the Office of Civil Rights. But a recent federal shift raises questions about the future of special education discrimination in civil lawsuits.

There are currently 7 elementary and post-secondary schools under pending investigation filed to the Office for Civil Rights related to disability discrimination as of January 2025.

Between 2013 and 2026, there have been 27 resolutions related to disability discrimination in the Office for Civil Rights. Of these 27 resolutions, 25 involved specific school districts or post-secondary learning institutions. 

According to publicly available letters published by the Office for Civil Rights, the agency has taken as few as three months and 10 days to as long as five years and three days to return letters of resolution between the years of 2015 and 2022.

Among the allegations against school districts, according to published letters of resolution: free appropriate public education (FAPE) violations, not creating and enforcing appropriate accommodations and not properly following 504 plans, which provide a student with a mental or physical impairment with equal access to learning through special accommodations and support.

A freedom of information request (FOIA) was filed in June 2026 requesting records from the Chamberlain School District and Tea Area School District cases that has not yet been fulfilled.

Cases can be handled at state level

Not all special-education disputes go directly to the Office for Civil Rights. Under the Individuals With Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), parents can pursue an administrative due process complaint. 

For example, in Marson v. Estelline, a federal lawsuit filed June 3, plaintiff Heather Marson alleged that the Estelline School District denied their son a FAPE. Her initial complaint filed to the state Oct. 6, 2025, followed an Oct 1. incident in which her son was unsupervised for almost 30 minutes and soiled himself. 

The superintendent told the parents in an email two days after the incident that, going forward, having someone with him is the “best way” for him to know where he needs to be. In an email reply to the superintendent, his mother asked, “Why after 5 years of us constantly advocating for a full time aide is one now being provided?”

According to the due process hearing decision, while his Individualized Education Program (IEP) stated he needed staff support for exercise completion, walking and toileting, the IEP did not include accommodations for supervision while traveling between classes.

The district testified during the April 2026 hearing that the supervision had “no educational purpose,” and was not needed for FAPE. 

The Marsons declined an interview request, due to the pending federal appeal. According to PacerMonitor, the case now sits in the U.S. District Court for the District of South Dakota.

What does this federal shift mean?

Regardless if handled at the federal or local level, the future of education oversight, including special education, in light of ongoing changes raises questions.

The Trump Administration announced in June a new shift within the Department of Education that reflects ongoing efforts to rearrange and dismantle the Education Department, an effort President Trump said will return power back to the states.

The Department of Justice will hold responsibilities of civil rights in education, and The Department of Health and Human Services will oversee special education. The two offices involved are the Office of Special Education (Department of Health and Human Services) and the Office for Civil Rights (Department of Justice). Both help defend the rights of children with disabilities experiencing discrimination, The Associated Press reported.

Savannah Newhouse, press secretary for the U.S. Department of Education, said to News Watch in a written statement that the new partnership will not stop the department’s staff from executing federal responsibilities.

“The federal government will ensure dollars continue to flow, students with disabilities still receive the services they deserve and civil rights protections remain firmly enforced,” Newhouse said.

Children with disabilities are entitled to a free and appropriate education

Under IDEA, originally passed in 1975, children with disabilities are entitled to a free and appropriate education (FAPE). The law ensures they receive special education and related services.

Cole Uecker, executive director of Disability Rights South Dakota, said a free and appropriate public education is a concept that all kids should be able to attend public schools and receive an appropriate and beneficial education.

For example, a child can receive a modified curriculum to help them further develop their knowledge, skills and adaptive behavior just like any other kid. 

One way children with special needs are ensured a free and appropriate education can be through an individualized education program (IEP).

An IEP is defined by the Center for Parent and Information Resources as a written statement of an educational program designed to meet a child’s individual needs. 

At the state level, Laura Scheibe, deputy secretary of the South Dakota Department of Education, said the interagency agreement and shift in the division of special education oversight will not change IDEA’s requirements that the state must follow.

However, some disability advocates raise concerns.

Future outcomes are currently unclear

Uecker, with Disability Rights South Dakota, said a concern with the federal shift is how the change will work. He said there are still more questions than there are answers, and he’s unsure if the Department of Justice has the bandwith.

“I think there’s still a lot of ambiguity around the topic, which makes it very difficult to say one way or another whether it’s going to result in better services for kids in special education, or if it’s going to be more complicated, more chaotic, in the current situation,” Uecker said.

Another potential concern, specifically with the Department of Health and Human Services, is whether children’s disabilities will be viewed using a medical model. The American Psychological Association defines the medical model as when a disability is viewed as an impairment, and the goal is to return the body or system back to normal as possible.

“When that mindset drives education decisions, students are more likely to be segregated, underestimated or treated as separate from the school community,” Robyn Linscott, director of education and family policy at The Arc of the United States, said in a press release. 

Jennifer Lowery, superintendent of the Harrisburg School District, said within her school district, they will be watching this federal shift closely.

“Keeping an eye out for any changes and how that collaboration will continue and needs to continue for our kids is a priority,” she said.

Increasing support and staying informed

What comes next regarding special education discrimination cases remains unclear. But parents can continue to stay informed of their rights and how to utilize local resources to support their children.

Jackie Waldie, a special education coach, advocate and owner of Inspire Education, said ultimately parents just want to support their kids and do what is best for them.

In South Dakota, there are multiple groups that help support and advocate for children with special needs. Among them: 

• Center for Disabilities at University of South Dakota

• Disability Rights South Dakota

Inspire Education

• South Dakota Department of Health Services - Division of Developmental Disabilities 

• South Dakota Parent Connection

• South Dakota Services for the Deaf

Waldie said another way parents can stay informed is by thoroughly reading their procedural safeguards book, which should be provided to parents who have a child with a disability at least once every school year. 

If parents are confused, they should not hesitate to reach out to local experts, whether it’s their district’s director of special education or an advocacy group, Waldie said.

“That’s one of the uphill battles that people don’t understand of having a child with a disability because now you have to become an expert in the medical side of things, the academic side of things, educational jargon and the social, emotional and mental toll,” Waldie said. “You have to become an expert in the law, and that’s a huge burden.”

title: False Bottom Creek Fire  chars 242 acres
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: ST. ONGE — Firefighters from multiple agencies contained the fast-moving False Bottom Creek Fire Sunday afternoon.
_full_text:
ST. ONGE — Firefighters from multiple agencies contained the fast-moving False Bottom Creek Fire Sunday afternoon.

A strong thunderstorm with lightning rolled through the area shortly before the fire was reported, around 3:42 p.m. several miles west of St. Onge and just south of 196th Street.

Winds pushed the fire north as it burned in a cut hayfield. It appeared as if the fire stopped at 196th Street. In addition to fire crews, local residents worked to the flanks of the fire with tractors and 4-wheelers.

“This was a very fast-growing fire which had the potential to turn uglier than it did,” according to a statement on the St. Onge Fire Department’s Facebook page.

Firefighters from St. Onge, Belle Fourche, Whitewood, Spearfish, and Deadwood fire departments as well as South Dakota Wildland Fire, U.S. Forest Service, Lawrence County Emergency Management, Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office, Lawrence County Dispatch responded to the fire. Crews from Alabama and North Carolina were also on the scene.

Crews remained on the scene overnight.

title: Spartan boys soccer strikes first win against Tea, draws against Aberdeen Central
byline: By Brandon Woltkamp Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — The Spearfish Spartan boys’ soccer team defeated the Tea Titans 2-1 in its season opener home game Friday at the Black Hills Energy Sports Complex.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — The Spearfish Spartan boys’ soccer team defeated the Tea Titans 2-1 in its season opener home game Friday at the Black Hills Energy Sports Complex. 

Spartans’ head coach Anthony Bradley showed excitement at the team’s victory. 

“They boys hanged in there; they did not get discouraged,” said Bradley. “They answered the call, they played as a team, and they have carried that message that we have been working on all preseason.”

The Spartans started the match with an aggressive offense on the pitch with Evan Duncan leading the charge with a goal attempt in the first 10 minutes of the match.

Jaxon Skvicalo took 2 attempts within 5 minutes at shooting the goal but was blocked by Tea’s goalkeeper Brax Johnson both times. The first half ended 0-0.

A penalty shot taken by John McGuckin at the start of the second half brought Tea to a 1-0 lead.

“You have to play with a different mentality when you’re behind,” Bradley said. 

Brooks Meyer, despite sustaining a blow to the head earlier in the match, secured 2 goals for Spearfish within a 10-minute frame near the end of the second half.

“Brooks put in the work, and for him to come in and do that, he had one hell of a game,” said Bradley. 

Bradley jokingly mentioned that Meyer was not feeling the greatest after the head blow.

“I forget that he gets tired,” said Bradley.

One unsung hero of the match, Spartan goalkeeper Tristan Limbo, earned several saves during the match. 

“He made some amazing saves at crucial times and made great plays,” Bradley said. “That is what he brings to the keeper position, and it is so important to have a trusty keeper that you can rely on.” 

Bradley emphasized the importance of Friday’s win.

“It was a team effort and a team win,” said Bradley. “ We want to represent Spearfish. We want to represent Spartan soccer, keep it, and bring it back up to that standard.” 

The Spartans drew a 1-1 tie against Aberdeen Central on Saturday, leaving the Spartans with a 1-1-0 record.

Spearfish will face Mitchell on Friday Aug 21 in Mitchell and Huron on Saturday Aug 22 in Huron. The Spartans will host Sioux Falls Washington on Aug 28 at 6 p.m.

title: Ahead of grand opening, AARP tours Spearfish Bike Skills Park
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Community Challenge Grants from AARP have helped fund trails projects in Spearfish in the past. This year, they helped make the new Spearfish Bike Skills Park possible. Representatives from AARP toured the beginner loop near the Winterville parking lot with Spearfish Trails Coalition Board Member and City Planner Jaymia Ecker. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
AARP 1.JPG
Community Challenge Grants from AARP have helped fund trails projects in Spearfish in the past. This year, they helped make the new Spearfish Bike Skills Park possible. Representatives from AARP toured the beginner loop near the Winterville parking lot with Spearfish Trails Coalition Board Member and City Planner Jaymia Ecker. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — With support from an AARP Community Challenge Grant, the Spearfish Trails Coalition built the Spearfish Bike Skills Park — a series of trails near the hydroelectric plant and campground ice rink that are designed to help cyclists get comfortable with their bikes, build fitness, experience new terrain and obstacles to gain confidence and skills, and facilitate family rides.

 AARP 2.JPG
AARP Business Operations Analyst Jill Biltoft, Spearfish Trails Coalition Board Member Jaymia Ecker, AARP Director of Community Outreach Lindsey Holmquest, and AARP State Director Erik Gaikowski tour the Beginner Loop in the Spearfish Bike Skills Park. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

 AARP 4.JPG
Cyclists make use of a new trail built by Spearfish Trails Coalition, near the hydroelectric plant and Winterville Drive. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

Last week, representatives from AARP met with STC Board Member and Spearfish City Planner Jaymia Ecker to tour one of the skills park trails — the “Beginner Loop” that branches off from the rec path near the Winterville Drive Parking Lot. 

Ecker led AARP State Director Erik Gaikowski, AARP Director of Community Outreach Lindsey Holmquest, and AARP Business Operations Analyst Jill Biltoft on the trail, where they passed several cyclists already using the winding trails.

“What I have noticed today, just being out here, is that it is so intergenerational. We’ve seen some older adults, some 40-year-olds, and now obviously, some kids I’m sure are using this too. That is a huge aspect for us,” Gaikowski said.

“Projects like these are exactly what the community challenge grant program is meant to fund,” Holmquest added. “AARP wants people to have opportunities to get out, be social, be active, and engage with people of all ages in the community. This project just exemplifies all of that.”

During the AARP’s last grant cycle, a challenge grant helped to fund some of the Spearfish Trails Coalition project on Lookout Mountain. Before that, a community challenge grant helped to fund wayfinding signs on the recreation path throughout the city system.

“This was one of 9 statewide grants, part of the AARP community challenge grant application process. Over the last decade, we’ve given out a little over half a million dollars to community organizations across the state of South Dakota,” Gaikowski said.

“Spearfish has been really fortunate to have some really amazing projects here in the city, and we are just happy to be here and actually get to see some of the cool stuff that Spearfish is putting together,” Gaikowski said.

Now that the bike skills park is complete, remaining grant funds will help the trails coalition and the city to host a grand opening and ribbon cutting for the new system on August 29.

The community will be invited to park at city park and walk or bike to the campground ice rink to explore the new trails, enjoy a skills clinic, patronize food trucks, and listen to live music. At 7 p.m., the evening culminates in a “light up the woods” ride on illuminated trails.

“AARP is helping with a skills clinic and also some of the expenses,” Ecker said.

Eventually, more wayfinding signs will be added to the bike trails, and a trails hub will be constructed by Pangea Designs.

“We’re really excited for the support,” Ecker said.

title: Deadwood library wins statewide recognition for continued dedication  to excellence and engagement
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Deadwood Public Library was chosen as one of the top 5 libraries across the state for their decorations over the youth summer reading program. Pictured from left are: Monica Nepper, education program coordinator, George Seamon, South Dakota state librarian, and Kennedy Penk, director. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
1 Deadwood Public Library wins statewide recognition for continued dedication to excellence and engagement.jpg
Deadwood Public Library was chosen as one of the top 5 libraries across the state for their decorations over the youth summer reading program. Pictured from left are: Monica Nepper, education program coordinator, George Seamon, South Dakota state librarian, and Kennedy Penk, director. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

DEADWOOD — It’s been an exciting week at the Deadwood Public Library, with the South Dakota State Library acknowledging Deadwood’s decorations for the summer reading program as one of the top 5 in the state and recognizing the staff for voluntarily continuing their education and credentials through a state-accredited program. 

“It’s an exciting time,” said Kennedy Penk, director. “It’s been a lot of fun and it’s fun when hard work gets recognized, too. Makes it all worth it. It’s worth it every other day of the week, but little things like this are fun.”

Unearth a story

Penk said the decorations for the youth summer reading program were awarded as one of the top 5 participating libraries across the state. 

The statewide theme this summer, unearth a story, centered around dinosaurs, fossils, and digging deep to reach goals and discover exciting stories throughout the summer. In the basement of the Deadwood library, Monica Nepper, education program coordinator, worked with staff hoarding boxes and packing materials that were transformed into a jungle in the children’s section. Pillars were transformed into tree trunks, vines stretch across the room, and leaves and snakes add to the atmosphere. 

 2 Deadwood Public Library wins statewide recognition for continued dedication to excellence and engagement.jpg
Librarians hoarded recyclable materials for months to create a jungle in the basement of the Deadwood Public Library. The decorations were acknowledged as one of the top 5 in the state by the South Dakota State Library. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

“It’s kind of a Jurassic Park vibe,” said Penk. 

Nepper said students also took advantage of the library’s outdoor space, where they planted seeds in raised garden beds, helped care for the plants, and harvested fruits and vegetables. 

Nepper said one child, a young boy from Thailand, was delighted to plant and harvest strawberries.

“He said they couldn’t grow strawberries in Thailand, so it was so fun to watch him realize that they were growing in the garden and he could pick them and eat them,” she said. “He was so amazed. I think he’s turned into a lifelong lover of gardening.”

Penk and Nepper said they plan to keep the tree and vines up year-round, intending to change the leaves and other decorations seasonally to keep children engaged during their after school programming. 

South Dakota State Library certification

All staff members of the Deadwood Public Library were acknowledged for voluntarily engaging in continuing education through the state library’s accreditation program. 

“Staff members choosing to continue their education from the South Dakota State Library highlights the library staff’s commitment to delivering high quality library service, continually strengthening their professional skills, and having a certified director is considered one of the essential standards for South Dakota public libraries under the South Dakota State Library accreditation program,” said Charlie Struble-Mook, Deadwood mayor at the Monday commission meeting. 

Requirements for accreditation are separated into 3 grades for directors and staff members, ranging from master’s degrees in library sciences or a related field approved by the accreditation committee, plus a set number of hours of continuing education through the state library program. 

Penk said that acknowledgement from the state of the staff’s completion of the program acknowledges their work ethic and dedication to providing high quality services to their community.

_full_text:
BHSU logo

SPEARFISH — Black Hills State University students in the University Honors Program will soon have a new pathway to law school through an agreement with the University of South Dakota Knudson School of Law. 

The memorandum of understanding, approved by the South Dakota Board of Regents, creates the Honors Law Opportunity Program, allowing up to 5 qualifying BHSU Honors Scholars each year to earn pre-admission to USD Law while completing their undergraduate studies at BHSU.

Students may apply for the program during their sophomore or junior year. Those accepted will have the opportunity to secure early admission to law school and compete for a scholarship for their first year at the University of South Dakota Knudson School of Law.

“This agreement provides an excellent opportunity for our honors students who are interested in a career in law,” said Dr. Katrina Jensen, director of the University Honors Program. “Securing a spot in law school as early as their sophomore year at BHSU will help our students plan their career pathways.”

To remain eligible, students must complete all requirements to graduate as a University Honors Scholar, successfully complete and defend their Honors Capstone Project, and maintain a cumulative GPA of 3.5 or higher.

The partnership provides motivated students with a clear and accelerated route to legal education while also helping address workforce needs across the state. By encouraging graduates to build their careers in South Dakota, the program supports both student success and the long-term strength of local communities.

title: Rapid City man convicted of child pornography charges, sentenced to 5 years in federal prison
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Conviction - Justice
Courtesy photo 

RAPID CITY — A Rapid City man has been sentenced to 5 years in federal prison on child pornography charges.

Jesse Luiz Jaso, 22, was sentenced to 5 years in federal prison for each count, followed by 5 years of supervised release. Each sentence was ordered to run concurrently. Further, Jaso was ordered to pay a $300 special assessment to the federal crime victims fund, a $1,000 fine, and will be required to register as a sex offender under the Sex Offender Registration and Notification Act. 

Jaso was convicted of distribution of child pornography, receipt of child pornography, and possession of child pornography. The sentencing took place Aug. 14. A federal grant jury indicted Jaso in February 2024. He was found guilty of all counts on May 21, following a 2-day jury trial in federal district court in Rapid City. 

In February 2023, a Rapid City Police Department Internet Crimes Against Children detective received a cybertip from Snapchat, that Jesse Jaso was distributing child pornography. Through the investigation and subsequent search and seizure of Jaso’s phone, law enforcement learned he had been communicating with individuals online, purchasing child pornography, and soliciting others to exchange child pornography. 

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse, launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by the U.S. Attorney’s offices and the DOJ’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children, as well as identify and rescue victims. 

Agencies involved in this investigation included the South Dakota Internet Crimes Against Children task force, the South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation, the Rapid City Police Department, and the U.S. Department of Homeland Security-Homeland Security Investigations. Assistant U.S. Attorney Megan Poppen prosecuted the case. 

Jaso was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service.

title: DOT reports 10% decrease in Rally numbers
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: The number of vehicles that entered Sturgis Aug. 7-16 was down 10% below the 5-year average. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
Rally crowds.JPG
The number of vehicles that entered Sturgis Aug. 7-16 was down 10% below the 5-year average. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

STURGIS — Traffic numbers at the 86th annual Sturgis Motorcycle Rally steadily decreased as the week progressed, according to reports from the South Dakota Department of Transportation. 

During the official Rally that was held Aug. 7-16, the DOT maintained 9 traffic counters at various locations around Sturgis. According to information released Monday, traffic numbers were up by nearly 3% over the 5-year average Aug. 7-8, with 54,515 vehicles counted on Aug. 7 and 58,519 vehicles counted Aug. 8. But after that, numbers started to drop. On Aug. 9, traffic counters reported 55,448 vehicles entering Sturgis, down 7.5% from the 5-year average. On Aug. 10 there were 55,226 in Sturgis, down 8.4% from the 5-year average. 

By Aug. 11, decreases were in the double digits with 11.8% less vehicles in Sturgis, at 51,742. On Aug. 12 was down by nearly 9,000, with 42,964 vehicles and a 23.6% decrease. On Aug. 13, 41,702 vehicles entered Sturgis, an 18% decrease. On Aug. 14, 39,716 vehicles entered Sturgis, and on Saturday there were 28,679 vehicles in Sturgis, numbers which reflect a 14% and 17% decrease. On Sunday, there were 19,655 vehicles in Sturgis. 

Overall the traffic counters reported 448,166 vehicles that entered Sturgis between Aug. 7-16, which is 10% less than the 5-year average.

title: How much should retirees  worry about inflation?
byline: By Christine Benz Morningstar
description: Inflation can be scary for retirees. True, Social Security provides inflation increases in line with the consumer price index, or CPI. But any portfolio income, save allocations to inflation-protected bonds, isn’t inherently inflation-protected. And if inflation occurs early in your retirement, those higher prices will do more damage throughout retirement, potentially jeopardizing your portfolio’s ability to last.
_full_text:
The 4 rules for cash: How to manage  your money the smart way

Inflation can be scary for retirees. True, Social Security provides inflation increases in line with the consumer price index, or CPI. But any portfolio income, save allocations to inflation-protected bonds, isn’t inherently inflation-protected. And if inflation occurs early in your retirement, those higher prices will do more damage throughout retirement, potentially jeopardizing your portfolio’s ability to last.

To gauge your inflation risk and how strenuously you need to defend against it, ask yourself three questions.

1. Where are you spending?

You may not have stopped to consider it before, but CPI is meant to capture the spending experiences of all consumers. Categories like housing receive the biggest weighting in the CPI calculation, while recreation and apparel get smaller weightings.

But a retired older adult who no longer has a mortgage will likely have smaller housing-related outlays, as a percentage of household spending, than the general population, but healthcare expenditures may well be a bigger share of the budget.

Given those variations, it can be helpful to use the CPI’s weightings as a starting point for understanding inflation’s impact on your household. But you can get closer to a personal inflation rate by looking at your actual spending in each of the major categories alongside the inflation we’re seeing in those areas.

2. How much of your income is inflation-adjusted?

Next look at how much of your cash flow needs are coming from income sources that have some inflation insulation.

Social Security is an ideal income source because individuals receive income adjustments that track CPI. Some public-sector pensions also track CPI or offer inflation adjustments that are even more generous. If you have a fixed annuity with an inflation rider, you’ll also see your income adjusted by a fixed percentage per year, though it won’t perfectly track CPI. (You can’t buy an annuity whose payouts are linked to CPI today, unfortunately.)

On the portfolio side, I bonds and Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities are the only investments that are specifically structured to protect against inflation. That’s why building a laddered portfolio of TIPS bonds, with one to mature in each year of retirement, can be a straightforward way to address inflation risk with your portfolio withdrawals. You could invest enough in the TIPS ladder to deliver inflation-adjusted income to cover any fixed living expenses, above and beyond what you can address with Social Security and/or a pension.

Other portfolio constituents don’t offer as precise a structural defense against inflation, but some asset types do have a good track record of gaining during inflationary periods. Commodities-tracking investments, quite intuitively, top the list: As Amy Arnott notes in this article, they gained ground in all six of the inflationary periods she examined. Stock returns, meanwhile, have been inconsistent or poor in inflationary periods. However, they’ve done a phenomenal job of beating inflation over time. Inflation has run at about a 3% rate since the late 1920s, while equities have gained about 10% on a nominal basis. Thus, a way to think about stocks is that they’re a long-run defense against inflation but won’t necessarily protect your purchasing power year in and year out.

At the other extreme, fixed-income sources that deliver income in nominal/noninflation-adjusted terms, whether cash or bonds, will tend to be vulnerable in inflationary periods; rising prices have the potential to gobble up all of your income. There are still good reasons to hold cash and bonds in your portfolio— ballast in recessionary environments, for one thing—but their vulnerability in inflationary environments is a major reason not to overdo them.

3. Where are you in your retirement?

Finally, consider where you are in your retirement. As Jamie Hopkins and others have pointed out, high inflation early in retirement is just another form of sequence risk, like bad market returns early in retirement. The reason is that if inflation flares up early in someone’s retirement period, those higher costs will elevate costs through the whole retirement period; deflation is very rare.

In our retirement spending research, we found that those who started retirement at the beginning of a period with unusually high inflation would have a more difficult time sustaining spending for a full 30-year period. To be clear, not every person who retires into a high-inflation environment will run out of money: There have been historical periods where market returns have been strong enough to offset the drag of higher costs. However, because you can’t know how the market will behave as retirement unfolds, it’s wise to curtail spending (to the extent that you can) if inflation happens to flare up early in your retirement. Amy has written extensively about various dynamic withdrawal strategies that can help improve retirees’ odds of success in varying market conditions and boost their lifetime portfolio income.

title: Reclassification eases taxes and banking for medical cannabis, but leaves state with questions
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — A federal change in medical marijuana’s legal classification should help South Dakota’s medical cannabis industry claim business tax deductions and gain access to banking, officials told state lawmakers Monday, but questions remain about the broader impact.
_full_text:
Reclassification eases taxes and banking for medical cannabis, but leaves state with questions.jpg

PIERRE — A federal change in medical marijuana’s legal classification should help South Dakota’s medical cannabis industry claim business tax deductions and gain access to banking, officials told state lawmakers Monday, but questions remain about the broader impact.

Whitney Brunner, administrator of the state’s medical cannabis program, told the legislative Medical Marijuana Oversight Committee during a meeting at the Capitol in Pierre that the federal government has shared little information about the change with the state — other than to request data.

“At the state level, we probably have more questions than answers,” Brunner said.

In April, the federal government moved medical marijuana from Schedule I to Schedule III under federal drug law. Schedule I drugs are considered to have no accepted medical use and a high potential for abuse. Schedule III drugs are recognized as having accepted medical uses and a lower potential for abuse.

Recreational marijuana remains a Schedule I drug under federal policy, even though 24 states and the District of Columbia allow recreational cannabis in various forms. South Dakota does not allow recreational marijuana use.

Medical marijuana has been legal in South Dakota since 2021, after voters approved it through a citizen-led ballot measure in 2020. Since then, South Dakota has built a regulatory framework — including licensing systems, testing requirements and oversight.

Brunner did not say whether South Dakota businesses will be required to register with the Drug Enforcement Administration to participate in the state program or what new compliance requirements they might face. Kittrick Jeffries, chairman of the Cannabis Industry Association of South Dakota and owner of Puffy’s Dispensary in Rapid City, said some businesses are taking the initiative.

“A lot of our establishments within our association are currently going through the DEA inspection process to become licensed under the DEA,” Jeffries said.

Cannabis businesses have long been blocked from taking certain federal tax deductions because marijuana was classified as a Schedule I substance — meaning they couldn’t deduct ordinary business expenses the way other businesses can. Banks have also largely avoided working with cannabis businesses because marijuana remains broadly illegal under federal law, exposing financial institutions to regulatory penalties even in states where it’s legal.

The reclassification will allow medical cannabis businesses to claim deductions, said Nicole Ezeh, a presenter with the National Conference of State Legislatures. It should also ease banking access for the industry.

The federal changes come as South Dakota’s program is in transition. Brunner told lawmakers the department overhauled its medical cannabis inspection program over the last year, after inspectors were missing violations and citing establishments inconsistently.

“We realized last year, and it wasn’t a difficult realization to make, that we had a lot of work to do on inspections and our processes,” Brunner said.

The department created new procedures and training, reorganized its supervisor structure and added a formal process for businesses to challenge citations, Brunner said.

Rob Krogstad, who operates Bad River Cannabis in Fort Pierre, told lawmakers his business was fined $3,000 for two “clerical errors” that were corrected before inspectors left the building.

“There will be human error,” Krogstad said, adding that the fine forced the business to delay other operational expenses. He suggested a three-strikes approach for minor clerical errors, with immediate fines reserved for more serious violations.

A rules package moving through administrative review would “make this a little easier on establishments,” Brunner said. The package would simplify language around inventory tracking training and reduce how long businesses must store security camera footage — changes Brunner said would be less expensive and less “cumbersome.”

The rules package would also restructure the fines system, making first-offense minor violations result in a corrective action plan rather than an immediate fine.

title: Mice may drive Lyme disease more than deer
byline: By Amanda Watford Stateline
description: Several ticks rest on top of a plant. New research suggests that mice, not deer, are closely linked to increases in young ticks, while large acorn crops can help predict higher tick numbers 2 years later. Photo courtesy of Robin Moore, Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies
_full_text:
Mice may drive Lyme disease more than deer.jpg
Several ticks rest on top of a plant. New research suggests that mice, not deer, are closely linked to increases in young ticks, while large acorn crops can help predict higher tick numbers 2 years later. Photo courtesy of Robin Moore, Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies 

For more than 3 decades, researchers have been tracking ticks, mice, oak trees and other wildlife in a New York forest to better understand what makes Lyme disease more likely to spread.

Their latest findings challenge some long-held assumptions — including the idea that deer are a major driver of Lyme disease risk.

Researchers at the Cary Institute of Ecosystem Studies, a nonprofit environmental research group, found that white-footed mice, not white-tailed deer, are closely linked to the number of young blacklegged ticks, the life stage most likely to infect people with Lyme disease.

A year with a large mouse population was followed by about a 40% increase in nymphal ticks the following year. But more mice don’t necessarily mean a higher percentage of ticks carrying Lyme bacteria. Researchers initially expected the two to rise together because white-footed mice are especially good at transmitting the bacteria to ticks.

The researchers found that other animals, including skunks, squirrels and opossums, also feed larval ticks. Because those animals are less efficient at transmitting the bacteria, the mix of hosts can affect how many ticks become infected.

In other words, mouse populations can help predict how many ticks there will be, but not necessarily how many will carry Lyme bacteria.

The researchers also found that large crops of acorns can set off a chain reaction: More acorns mean more food for mice, which can mean more ticks 2 years later.

The findings come as tick-borne diseases are an increasing public health concern. Lyme disease is the most commonly reported tick-borne disease in the United States, with nearly half a million people diagnosed each year, according to the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

The study, published in the peer-reviewed Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences journal, draws on data collected since 1991 at a 2,000-acre research site in Dutchess County, New York.

The researchers also found that extreme heat and cold don’t necessarily kill blacklegged ticks in the wild. The ticks appear able to shelter in soil and leaf litter during extreme temperatures. The team plans to continue monitoring how ticks, wildlife, trees and climate interact — and what those changes could mean for human health, according to a news release.

This new research comes as scientists and public health officials are also watching ticks expand into new parts of the country.

Lone star ticks, once primarily associated with the Southeast, are now established across much of the South, Midwest and Northeast. An adult female is distinguished by a white dot or “lone star” on her back. The ticks can transmit several diseases and are associated with alpha-gal syndrome, an allergy to a molecule found in red meat and other products from mammals.

As lone star tick populations have spread, more states are paying attention to alpha-gal syndrome, which experts believe is significantly underdiagnosed.

Massachusetts, Missouri and Oklahoma have expanded surveillance or public education efforts in recent years, and all three have joined the growing list of states that require alpha-gal syndrome to be reported to public health officials.

At least 14 states have added or will soon add alpha-gal syndrome to their lists of reportable diseases, according to the Alpha-gal Alliance Action Fund, a nonprofit advocacy group. In those states, health care providers and laboratories must report cases to state health departments.

Lawmakers in Ohio also are considering a similar measure that would make alpha-gal syndrome a reportable disease. The bill has passed the House and remains under consideration in the Senate. The legislature will adjourn in December.

Unlike Lyme disease, alpha-gal syndrome is not required to be reported nationwide, making it difficult to determine how common the condition is or how its prevalence is changing. The CDC estimates that as many as 450,000 people in the United States may have the disease.

title: Staffing costs drive fee increase for  program meant to deter livestock theft
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: The state brand board approved a fee change Tuesday for brand inspections. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
0820 Staffing costs drive fee increase for program meant to deter livestock theft.tif
The state brand board approved a fee change Tuesday for brand inspections. Pioneer file photo 

PIERRE — South Dakota’s Brand Board will raise its livestock ownership inspection fee for the first time since 2013, after a legislative committee approved the rule change Tuesday.

The committee, made up of 3 state senators and 3 state representatives, voted 5-1 in favor of the change. Sen. Taffy Howard, R-Rapid City, voted no.

The Brand Board is responsible for tracking livestock ownership in South Dakota counties west of the Missouri River, where cattle are more likely to roam across wide open spaces. Inspectors check to make sure that horses, cattle and mules sold or moved from those counties belong to the people who sell or move them.

Livestock sold at markets in western South Dakota are inspected for ownership when they arrive. Livestock sold privately also need inspections. At markets, the per-animal fees are withheld from the sale price and remitted to the Brand Board.

The new fee will be $1.45 per head starting Oct. 1. Brand Board Executive Director Debbie Trapp told lawmakers they need the additional funding to pay for the ownership inspection program.

“This change is needed due to increasing personnel and operating expenses, and the brand board operates entirely on funds generated by the programs it administers,” Trapp told lawmakers.

Over the past two years, the board had to rely on $900,000 from its other programs to maintain the ownership inspection program, according to Brand Board Vice President Cory Bierle, “and we’re still behind.”

With a projected number of livestock inspected at 1.5 million, the fee is expected to generate an additional $601,000 through the remainder of the current fiscal year and $675,000 per fiscal year going forward. The state fiscal year runs from July 1 through June 30.

Though the number of animals is decreasing, “the numbers that we still have are there, and they all still need to be inspected,” Bierle said. “And we have to have the staff on hand inspect the ones that are present.”

Livestock inspection fees largely pay for staffing and staff-related expenses. The state Bureau of Finance and Management increased its per-mile reimbursement for state employees from 67 cents to 70 cents a mile last year.

There are 12 full-time inspectors, four of whom are regional supervisors, as well as office staff and livestock investigators. All are considered state employees, who typically receive annual lawmaker-approved salary increases. The most recent increased state employee pay by 1.3%. The board also employs 129 part-time local brand inspectors.

The board gets most of its funding through brand renewal registrations, which are $90 fees that livestock owners pay every five years to maintain the brands they use to identify animals as theirs. In recent years, the board’s needed to dip into those funds to pay for the inspection program.

Opponent says ranchers can’t afford fee hike

Rick Fox, a rancher from Hermosa, spoke in opposition to the change. He said it could be delayed a year to provide some financial relief for producers affected by the drought. The change would cost him about $400, he said.

“Most ranchers don’t have any kind of reserves. If their hay fund is low, then you’ve got to get it from a different fund or borrow the money,” Fox said. “The Brand Board has a pool of money sitting there that they can borrow from.”

Sen. Howard said that “now is not the time for a 45% increase,” citing financial struggles of West River ranchers.

Brand Board leaders said the increase represents an amount the Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources, South Dakota Stockgrowers Association and South Dakota Cattlemen’s Association could agree on.

The Brand Board still hasn’t reached the legal cap on how much it can charge per head for the inspection fee. Earlier this year, lawmakers and the governor set the cap at $1.65 per head.

“And based on projections,” for ongoing costs to the program, Trapp said, “chances are, we will be back in a few years, probably to increase it again towards the cap.”

Fox, the rancher who opposed the fee increase, told lawmakers that the ownership inspection program is “the best theft deterrent we have.”

“If I was not to brand my cattle, I’d be a little nervous about if one gets gone somewhere,” Fox said. “That’s our return address.”

title: SD governor expands rural fire response amid drought
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: The False Bottom Creek Fire burned 242 acres Sunday near St. Onge. Pioneer photo by Mark Watson
_full_text:
SD governor expands rural fire response amid drought.JPG
The False Bottom Creek Fire burned 242 acres Sunday near St. Onge. Pioneer photo by Mark Watson 

PIERRE — Gov. Larry Rhoden authorized state firefighting resources to support local governments in fire suppression.

Volunteer fire departments, often supported in part by local governments and fundraising, supply the first responders for blazes across most of South Dakota’s land area.

“As a volunteer firefighter, I understand that every second counts when attacking a fire. And as a lifelong rancher, I recognize the difficulty feeding livestock during this ongoing drought,” Rhoden said in a news release Tuesday. “Supplementing local resources with approved state assistance will improve response time, saving lives and property.”

Rhoden’s executive order, signed Tuesday, expands South Dakota Wildland Fire’s resources to areas outside the Black Hills Forest Fire Protection District. That region starts at the Wyoming-South Dakota border and runs east through parts of the Black Hills region, but does not include any area within any nearby city limits.

A majority of the state is in abnormally dry to severe drought conditions, according to the U.S. Drought Monitor. Parts of southwestern South Dakota are under extreme drought conditions.

Wildfires in western parts of the state burned through thousands of acres this year — including the Qury Fire in Custer County which burned more than 9,000 acres. The False Bottom Fire Creek near St. Onge burned 242 acres over the weekend. The Bear Butte Fire burned 400 acres the week before in Meade County, where the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally was taking place.

Rhoden also extended a July order that eases restrictions on hay haulers, allowing producers to move hay two hours before sunrise and two hours after sunset. That measure is meant to make sure livestock have enough food in spite of parched grasses and depleted feed supplies.

In May, Rhoden activated the Drought Task Force, a group of state agencies that evaluates potential drought impacts on agriculture, fire management and water supply.

title: Anderson takes over as elementary principal
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Ashley Anderson spends time with students who were honored with pride lunches based on their showcasing Spartan PRIDE expectations. Anderson will take over principal duties at West and Mountain View elementary schools. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Anderson takes over as principal.jpg
Ashley Anderson spends time with students who were honored with pride lunches based on their showcasing Spartan PRIDE expectations. Anderson will take over principal duties at West and Mountain View elementary schools. Courtesy photo 

SPEARFISH — When students head back to West and Mountain View elementary schools in Spearfish next week they will see a familiar face with a new job.

Ashley Anderson, who was previously the assistant principal at the schools takes over as principal.

“I am excited for the opportunity to continue to serve in the Spearfish School district and community. We have amazing staff, students, parents, and community partnerships. I enjoy supporting the development of teachers as instructional leaders and helping students enjoy the learning process,” she said. “One of my favorite pieces of education is collaborating and problem solving with a team to best support students’ educational experience, and I look forward to continuing to do so.  I am also grateful to work with a great administrative team who I have learned a lot from.” 

Anderson takes over for Nick Gottlob who was hired as the district’s superintendent.

Anderson earned her bachelor’s degree in elementary education from Black Hills State University in 2011. 

She found that teaching the young students how to read is her passion.

“Reading has always been my baby,” she said. “That’s actually what I’m most excited about with K-2 is the reading progression that takes place. It’s astonishing what kids learn in just that short amount of time. If you can read, you can do anything. And so just watching them grow as readers, I think that’s just so magical.”

She started off teaching first grade in Wyoming until 2013 when she began teaching third grade at Creekside Elementary School. She stayed there until 2021 when she accepted the position of assistant principal.

Along the way, she’s earned a master’s degree in curriculum and instruction in reading through Chadron State College, English as a new language endorsement, math specialist endorsement, and another master’s degree in educational leadership from the University of South Dakota in 2021.

“It just so happened that the elementary assistant principal came open, and I applied and was fortunate enough to get it,” she said. 

She said leaving the classroom for the front office was hard that first year.

“The relationships you build with teachers, you’re all on the same page, and then you have to become kind of the boss,” she said. 

However, that didn’t mean she was kept out of the classroom. 

“What my favorite part is, is being able to go in the classrooms and help coach (the teachers),” she said.

She said being able to help guide the staff further is what she is looking forward to most in her new position.

“The part that excites me is working with more teachers and more kids and more parents,” Anderson added. “Spearfish is amazing: supporting families, and supporting kids in education. I really want to continue my work with PLCs (professional learning communities) in the classroom, supporting teachers and collaborating with teachers, and I love when they share ideas with one another and to grow as educators, because that’s truly what helps them grow.”

While she is looking forward to taking over as principal, she encourages people to consider teaching for a career.

“You really can make a meaningful impact on so many lives,” Anderson said. “Getting to see students grow and learn through the year and become successful citizens in our community and know you were a part of that journey is really fulfilling.”

title: City council approves $29,434.35 change to Colorado Blvd. roadway improvement project
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: This map shows the closure area, and the stretch of Colorado Boulevard included in the Colorado Boulevard roadway improvement project. Courtesy map
_full_text:
Colorado Blvd.jpg
This map shows the closure area, and the stretch of Colorado Boulevard included in the Colorado Boulevard roadway improvement project. Courtesy map 

SPEARFISH — The total cost of the Colorado Boulevard roadway improvement project, originally intended to widen and modernize the roadway from Highway 85 to Colorado Loop, has increased to nearly $4.5 million from $3.4 million after a fourth change order was approved by the Spearfish City Council this week.

On April 1, 2025, work began to widen the then 2-lane stretch of Colorado Boulevard near Sky Ridge.  Almost immediately, the project was met with delays — the result of “poor subgrade conditions and an unusually wet 2025 construction season,” according to a change order description from public works.

Crews from Dakota Redi-Mix (DRM) also encountered a water main that hadn’t appeared in plans for the project prior to excavation. That water main needed to be lowered to make way for new storm sewer infrastructure.

That was done, and the section of the work from Colorado Loop to Aurora Avenue was finished before winter weather shut down the project in late October.  Colorado Boulevard opened to traffic for the winter before work resumed this spring.

Over the winter, public works collaborated with HDR Engineering to redesign the project and “leave some of the thick, existing asphalt in place to help keep the underlying soil dry and save money.”

Meanwhile, the developers of East Side Acres, on 40 acres directly west of Sky Ridge, asked that the road be widened and extended to about 700 feet west of Aurora Avenue — the approach into their development.

East Side Acres planners have mapped out space for townhomes, apartments, park, restaurant, and retail space, and a “town square” — envisioning a kind of 5-minute, walkable community between I-90 Exits 14 and 17. Anticipating that the road might have had to be widened in the future to accommodate resident traffic, the city council decided to extend the road improvements.

“It became apparent that it would be more cost-effective for both the developer and the city to have the city’s contractor, DRM, make the developer’s required improvements to Colorado Boulevard as part of the City’s project, and to reimburse the City for their share of the cost to extend the improvements of Colorado Boulevard to the west extent of their development,” said Public Works Director Adam McMahon.

That change order, the third for the project, included a Rally shutdown.

Earlier this summer, the developers of East Side Acres moved directly from the first phase of construction to the second phase of construction — and noticed a few minor changes needed to be made to the west end of the development where it tied in to Colorado Boulevard to complete the second entrance to the new neighborhood.

“Consequently, they’ve completed their design for phase 2. Consequently, they’ve completed their design for phase 2, and we found that some minor adjustments to the way we did our tie-in would make things a lot better, to where we wouldn’t have to close that intersection again to extend the tie-in through that intersection,” McMahon said.  

The city issued a field directive to the contractor on July 15, 2026, to “proceed with this change before council approval to keep the project moving forward,” an explanation of the change order approved by the city council Monday reads.

That work was not described in the city’s contract with DRM, so the city needed to reimburse the contractor for time and materials spent under the “field directive.”

That cost amounted to $14,542.66. The remainder of the $29,434.35 cost increase approved by the city council came from adjustments to the subgrade conditions crews struggled with last spring.

“We encountered some subgrade issues when they showed up to pave, so we authorized some additional subgrade stabilization before they came back and completed the paving,” McMahon said. “That was another about $15,000 change.”

Paving on the project is done. Sealant has been applied to Colorado Boulevard on the section from Colorado Loop to just past Aurora Avenue. McMahon said the road closure for the project should be lifted later this week.

title: Thune calls energy development permitting reform a rare opportunity for bipartisan action
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., left, speaks with Northwestern Energy President and CEO Brian Bird Tuesday in Sioux Falls. Photo by Joshua Haiar, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Thune calls energy development permitting reform a rare opportunity for bipartisan action.jpg
U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., left, speaks with Northwestern Energy President and CEO Brian Bird Tuesday in Sioux Falls. Photo by Joshua Haiar, South Dakota Searchlight 

SIOUX FALLS — U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., said this week that permitting reform could offer a rare opportunity for bipartisan action in Congress. 

Thune discussed the issue on Tuesday during a summit hosted by Northwestern Energy, which has about 65,000 customers in the state and plans to merge with Black Hills Energy to become Bright Horizon Energy Corporation. 

Thune told attendees lawmakers are considering shorter federal reviews for energy projects and time limits on legal challenges from project opponents. 

“As soon as they’re ready to go, we’ll put it on the floor” of the Senate for a vote, Thune said. 

The politics around the issue, Thune said, have shifted because developers of coal, natural gas, wind, solar and nuclear projects have run into similar obstacles, and have brought those concerns to their elected officials. Democrats have watched renewable energy projects encounter those hurdles, which he said has created momentum for reform.

Support from Democrats matters in the Senate, he said, where major legislation requires 60 votes to overcome a filibuster. Republican senators need some Democratic support. 

The Senate Environment and Public Works Committee and Energy and Natural Resources Committee are hashing out potential permitting reform, he said. 

Ranking Democratic members of the two committees said in March they want a bipartisan bill to speed up development, lower energy costs, and create jobs. The Democrats warned, however, that progress depended in part on the Trump administration backing off its opposition to  renewable energy projects. 

Among other policy shifts, the administration has argued that offshore wind is a national security threat, tightened eligibility requirements for wind and solar tax credits and moved to pull back Biden-era “Solar for All” grants. Last October, the Bureau of Land Management cancelled what would have been the nation’s largest solar energy project.

Thune said the negotiations come at a time when Congress is more partisan and polarized than he has ever seen. That makes bipartisan policymaking difficult, but energy permitting reform may be an exception. 

“I’m a realist,” Thune said. “But I feel good about where things stand.” 

Permitting reform

Northwestern and other utilities anticipate rapidly growing demand, including that associated with data centers. Thune said faster and more predictable permitting could unlock more private investment at a time when the nation needs additional electricity generation and transmission.

Congress should put permitting reform into federal law rather than rely on regulations that can change from one presidential administration to another, Thune said. He said different administrations will continue to treat fossil fuels and renewables differently. Thune, for his part, said he favors an “all of the above” energy strategy. 

A permitting “shot clock” to establish deadlines for the review process is one possibility, he said. He also wants Congress to address litigation after permits are issued, including how quickly courts deal with litigation and who can file legal challenges.

Nuclear power

Nuclear power could also draw bipartisan support, he said, particularly small modular reactors. The reactors are designed to be smaller than traditional nuclear plants, looking more like a warehouse than a large power plant. They produce up to 550 megawatts of electricity, according to information shared by Northwestern Energy. 

“Nuclear is, you know, it’s kind of back in vogue, especially the smaller modular reactors,” Thune told Searchlight. “We want to, as much as we can, create conditions that are favorable for investment there.” 

Northwestern Energy has spent more than $800,000 studying small modular nuclear reactors in South Dakota. The company is evaluating potential sites and is helping establish a nonprofit to educate the public about nuclear power, dubbed the “South Dakota Nuclear Collective” in documents filed by the company with  the state Public Utilities Commission.

title: “Leading from Within”: Writing about process has helped this retired professional process life’s changes, whether her book publishes or not
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Writing has offered an outlet for former Northern Hills District Ranger Rhonda O’Byrne as she transitioned into retirement. She’s working on a book that could help other professionals, regardless of their career path. Photo courtesy Rhonda O’Byrne
_full_text:
Rhonda O'Byrne.jpeg
Writing has offered an outlet for former Northern Hills District Ranger Rhonda O’Byrne as she transitioned into retirement. She’s working on a book that could help other professionals, regardless of their career path. Photo courtesy Rhonda O’Byrne   

BELLE FOURCHE — After 34 years working for the United States Forest Service, including a stint as the Northern Hills District Ranger, Rhonda O’Byrne was suddenly looking at early retirement.

It was March 2025, the same month the Trump Administration announced its plans to restructure the Forest Service. The agency’s headquarters relocated to Salt Lake City, and the consolidation of leadership positions got underway.

“The last almost 10 years of my career I was actually with a group that was based out of our Washington, D.C., office,” said O’Byrne. “We were over 300 employees that worked on projects all across the nation.”

She said she believes that change can be positive, and there is always room for improvement, but she started to wonder if her job might be at risk.

“Once Congress started talking about changing retirement benefits for employees, I was like, ‘I didn’t work over 34 years to lose my benefits in retirement,’ and I was eligible. It was a risk, a weighted risk one way or the other, and I chose to retire.”

That decision wasn’t easy for O’Byrne. Neither was her transition out of public service.

“I think I was a bit traumatized by the experience of retiring unexpectedly, and kind of a little lost in the world,” O’Byrne said. “I wasn’t quite ready to retire, but I have all of this experience.”

To process the change, she started writing. She wrote about her experience leading people. She wrote about how she grew, and how she failed over the years en route to jobs in management. She wrote about her career and why it mattered to her.

Eventually, she realized her diary might have value beyond the catharsis it was offering her personally.

“I started to think, ‘Hey, others could learn from these experiences,’” O’Byrne said. In her mind, she started to reframe her reflections as a book project. A book she’s titled “Leading from Within: Reflections on Failure, Courage, and Growth.”

“Is it really going to be a book that I am going to publish? I am not there yet,” O’Byrne said. “At the very least, it has helped me immensely move through this process.”

On the other hand, O’Byrne has her eyes on publication in one form or another. She said she has enough interest in the project from friends that she might offer her diary-style advice in the form of a newsletter or a downloadable PDF.

“If it gets published, my hope is that there are those that could find themselves in my stories,” O’Byrne said. “

O’Byrne spent decades attending leadership training and coaching leaders. In retirement, she has started substitute teaching in Belle Fourche. Sharing knowledge came naturally, and a book seemed like a new an interesting avenue for instruction.

“One of the key values I have always had is service,” O’Byrne said. If her manuscript can be of service, she said she will find a way to share it.

The book discusses failure and endeavors that don’t work out. O’Byrne started writing about leadership, warts and all, before she even considered an audience.

“I am going to talk openly about the good, the bad, the ugly. Leadership was hard. It wasn’t easy. It was messy. It hurt at times, but oh my gosh, the rewards were amazing, so let’s acknowledge all of that and celebrate that stuff,” O’Byrne said.

She believes some of the keys to leadership are integrity, honesty, and authenticity, but she hopes “Leading from Within” will offer more than a picture of what a leader is.

“It is very much a diary-style leadership reflection about aligning your actions and your values. One of the things in this reflection, I went to a lot of leadership training classes, and I’ve read a lot of leadership books. Not all of them, but a lot of what my experience was, it was telling you, ‘This is what a really good leader looks like. This is what a really good leader does.’ But you know what, getting there is really, really messy,” O’Byrne said. “It is the process of becoming a leader and getting into leadership. There are successes, but there are a lot of failures, and there is so much growth and so many missteps and so many times where you were just darn lucky.”

She writes about the leaders who inspired her and shaped both her management style and her personality.

“One of the reflection pieces is the good, the bad, and the ugly, because we have all had those really great leaders and sometimes you don’t know what made them so great, but they were so wonderful to work with, all of the way to, ‘Geez, this person, nobody wants to show up to work because they are so awful,’” O’Byrne said. “You probably learn more from them than you do from the good ones.”

She described the project as “ripping the veil off” to reveal how leadership works.

“I’m talking about the process,” O’Byrne said.

She’s still writing her manuscript, drafting as inspiration comes: a deviation from her process as a structure-driven government employee.

“My whole entire career, I am very much a planner, an organized person. I was the one you came to. I had the checklist. I knew the process and all of the right steps that I was going to follow and all of the right orders and everything. That was me. That was my personality and how I did things,” O’Byrne said. “I am letting that go in writing this book.”

She’ll remember an anecdote that fits around chapter 4, and write it, then pivot to sussing out ideas for chapter 2. She is not beholden to deadlines nor allowing herself to be limited by organizational constraints.

“34 years being a professional in my career, I worked very, very differently than I’m working with this, and that is fascinating to me, and that it is working! It seems to be working anyway,” O’Byrne said.

She said she’d attempted 2 other book projects. Both she approached with a plan. Both ultimately amounted to nothing. “Leading from Within” has made it much further.

title: Deadwood Police Department reports Sturgis Rally numbers
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Deadwood Police Department reported higher visibility and lower arrests during the Sturgis Rally. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
Deadwood rally numbers 1.JPG
The Deadwood Police Department reported higher visibility and lower arrests during the Sturgis Rally. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

DEADWOOD — The Deadwood Police Department has released their numbers of calls to service during the Sturgis Rally, reporting higher visibility and lower accidents. 

“This year’s Rally was another seamless yet eventful occasion,” said Cory Shafer, chief of police. “Although calls for service experienced a slight increase, this uptick coincides with decreases in other categories. The rise in calls and traffic stops, along with the presence of our officers on foot patrol downtown, suggest that increased law enforcement visibility positively influences individual’s behavior and decision making.”

Deadwood’s reported numbers are as follows: calls for service, 466 (up 24 from last year); traffic stops, 166 (up 78 from last year); injury crashes, 3 (down 2 from last year); non-injury crashes, 4 (down 5 from last year); driving under the influence investigations, 3 (up one from last year); zero fatal crashes; simple assault, 1 (unchanged); simple assault, domestic violence, 1 (down 3 from last year), disturbances, 9 (unchanged); and arrests, 9 (down 15 from last year).

“In addition to (numbers reported), the department also facilitated numerous motorcycle escort rides entering and exiting town,” said Shafer. “The Deadwood Police Department takes great pride in serving our community and managing events throughout the year. I would especially like to commend our dedicated staff for their continued motivation and exceptional performance through one of the 3 largest annual events.”

title: The Mercy Sloane Chronicles: Chapter 15
byline: By Eliza Blue Special to the Pioneer
description: As Melissa passed the registered letter to Mercy and watched Mercy’s wide smile fade as suddenly as it had appeared, she knew Mercy was feeling the exact same way — that no good was going to come of the contents.
_full_text:
The Mercy Sloane Chronicles

As Melissa passed the registered letter to Mercy and watched Mercy’s wide smile fade as suddenly as it had appeared, she knew Mercy was feeling the exact same way — that no good was going to come of the contents.

“What does it say?” Melissa blurted before Mercy even had a chance to open the envelope, then immediately clapped her hand over her mouth. “Oh Mercy, I’m so sorry! Of course it’s none of my business. I’ll leave you in peace. Come find me later if you need to talk,” she said, her eyes welling up with tears of embarrassment and worry.

“No,” Mercy replied in a voice barely louder than a whisper, “Stay, please.” But she made no move to open the letter, just stood there holding it in front of herself with both hands, letting the pristine white rectangle quiver like a leaf in the wind.

“Mercy?!” Marla called from behind the counter. Though the store was small, the back corner where Mercy had been cleaning was not visible from Marla’s perch by the cash register. Marla had slightly more patience than Melissa as to the contents of the letter … but only slightly more. She’d seen Melissa’s stricken face, noticed the envelope clutched in Melissa’s hand as she’d burst through the door without so much as a ‘hello,’ and had rightly surmised that Mercy was about to get some life-altering news.

When neither Melissa nor Mercy answered her, Marla stepped out from behind the counter, her skirt swishing, tutting in frustration that was actually deep sadness. How could it be that Mercy had only been there two weeks and she already couldn’t imagine Antelope without her? In the few steps it took her to cross from the front of the shop to the back, Marla was picturing Mercy helping clear the dishes after the midday meal…Mercy happily smoothing the bodice of the summer dress Marla had lent her to wear at the shop…Mercy nodding patiently at all Marla’s elaborate tales of Antelope’s short history. Just like Melissa, Marla realized that since Mercy had come into her life she’d felt something she hadn’t felt in a very long time: HAPPY.

And now Mercy, Melissa, and Marla all stood in the last, cramped aisle of dusty canned goods, staring at the letter, contemplating all they might be about to lose — Melissa, a friend; Marla, the daughter she’d always longed for; and most of all Mercy, who was getting a chance to experience life for the first time on her own terms. 

 Eliza Blue TMC
Eliza Blue 

Which is exactly why Mercy didn’t want to open the letter. She’d been right when she’d told Ardath that she might not know herself at all. For 22 years she’d been a good daughter, a good student, a good worker, and very, very briefly a good wife, but that very first day, standing on her front porch, looking out on the horizon, she’d had a feeling she’d never had before. A feeling so new and strange she hadn’t been able to name it then. It was the same feeling she got waking at dawn to the nickering of her pony just outside the window, and at the close of day when the wind sang to her through the open door. It was the feeling that welled up inside her when she’d told Granger that she couldn’t go back with him. And even when he’d shouted himself hoarse, and then cried, and then stopped crying and told her he’d make sure she’d regret making a fool of him, the feeling, emanating from somewhere beneath her rib cage, had stayed steady and strong. 

Staring at the letter, the feeling was still there, and Mercy realized she finally knew what to call it. It was the feeling of freedom. 

“It doesn’t matter what this letter says,” she said suddenly, startling Melissa and Marla. “I’m staying in Antelope. He can’t make me leave.”

So when she did rip open the envelope and found the deed to the homestead along with a formal letter annulling her marriage on account of abandonment, as well as a note from Granger’s parents saying they never wanted to hear from her again, everyone let out a sigh of relief. But Mercy knew even as she said a silent prayer of gratitude that she’d gained far more than a piece of property. She’d gained what it takes most folks a lifetime to figure out: that her life was her own and no one could change that.

title: Lead January sales tax windfall result of audit, back taxes paid
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: The city of Lead says $331,454 in sales tax collected in July was a direct result of the 150th anniversary celebration, and was the largest amount the city has ever raised in a single month. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
LEAD 150th concert crowd.JPG
The city of Lead says $331,454 in sales tax collected in July was a direct result of the 150th anniversary celebration, and was the largest amount the city has ever raised in a single month. Pioneer file photo 

LEAD — A nearly $200,000 sales tax mistake by a business looks like the city of Lead had a financial windfall in January, but actually skews the real picture of 2026 commerce in the city, according to reports from the South Dakota Department of Revenue (DOR).   

Municipal sales tax reports listed on the DOR website show that in January the city collected $367,012.65 in sales tax. That compares to $173,815.03 in 2025, and is the largest sales tax reported for the city in a single month. 

However, according to email correspondence dated Feb. 6 between Lead City Finance Officer Billie Jo Ryan and DOR Business Tax Division Business Manager Katrina Christopherson, as well as official correspondence between the DOR and the city of Lead, the January amount reported includes $196,616 in unpaid taxes that were discovered after a routine DOR audit. 

“A taxpayer was audited and found they were not reporting to Lead when they should have been,” Christopherson wrote in a Feb. 6 email response to Ryan, when she questioned the large amount. “The audit was completed and paid out.” 

Ryan said the DOR declined to tell the city which taxpayer was audited, but the money was included in the February sales tax payment from the DOR to Lead. 

The amount of January sales taxes reported became an issue at Monday’s Lead City Commission meeting, when resident Pam Millard questioned the city’s report about the outcome of the Rock the Hills 150th anniversary celebration that the city hosted over the Fourth of July weekend. In her report, Lead City Administrator Robin Lucero said July sales tax numbers were the largest the city has ever seen in a single month, at an approximate total of $331,454. But Millard pointed to the January sales tax collections as evidence that Lucero’s report was inaccurate. 

“This was not from any type of influx in visitors or an event or anything like that,” Ryan said of the January sales tax numbers. “That is not a true picture of a sales tax collection in January 2026.” 

In July the city received $331,454 in sales tax payments. That’s $104,677 more than the city’s July 2025 sales tax collection, and $150,000 more than the 5-year average for July payments. 

Ryan said the DOR sends the city 2 payments a month for its 2% sales tax revenue. The first payment in July was for the last half of June. But the second payment was from sales generated in the first half of July, and shows direct impact from the Lead 150th anniversary celebration. 

According to DOR regulations, businesses have until Aug. 20 to report July sales tax, and the deadline for payment is Aug. 25. The July payments, Ryan said, are the result of early payments, and the city expects to receive even more money in August as more businesses report July revenues.    

“This (event) actually did generate income for the city, and not only did it generate income, but it generated the biggest tax payment that we’ve ever received,” Ryan said.
