title: Spearfish grants paid parental leave to employees
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Mayor John Senden asks Spearfish Human Resources Director Jodi Mathis questions about the city’s new parental leave policy. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Parental Leave.JPG
Mayor John Senden asks Spearfish Human Resources Director Jodi Mathis questions about the city’s new parental leave policy. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — Spearfish City Council members voted unanimously on Monday to offer paid parental leave to its employees.

“This will be a new policy. It will give individuals 4 weeks of paid time off for either an adoption or a non-birthing parent. A birthing parent would receive 6 weeks of paid leave off to care for their child and for bonding,” said Spearfish Human Resources Director Jodi Mathis.

Rapid City offers the same benefit to its employees. Mathis said the City of Yankton does as well.

Mathis said Spearfish found that paid parental leave may help attract employees for “hard-to-fill positions.”

“We did have one of our hard-to-fill positions which we still do not have filled; one of the questions the individual asked was, ‘Do you have paid parental leave?’ So, it is a deciding factor for individuals who are at the stage in their life where they are looking at starting a family,” Mathis said.

Councilman Larry Klarenbeek asked if that was why the policy was brought to the council for consideration.

“Is this just a productivity issue, where no one fills the position? What do you anticipate the cost to be to offer this benefit?” Klarenbeek asked.

Mathis said that, regardless of the benefit, employees who start families will leave their position for a period of time. Federal law, under the Family and Medical Leave Act (FMLA), guarantees parents the right to take time off while preserving their employment and insurance. It does not guarantee pay. 

“We do have individuals who pick up additional duties. We don’t really hire temporaries to come in and fill; it is just additional duties being handed off to other people,” Mathis said.

The paid time off for family leave will only be available to employees who have worked for the city for at least 12 months before they take their leave.

Spearfish Councilwoman Jamie Hafner asked if employees could potentially stack parental paid leave on top of other benefits.

“Is this then on top of the personal emergency leave? How many hours would someone qualify for this after working a year? They get how many weeks you said?” Hafner asked

“The issue that we have is, we switched to PTO. There are not as many employees who have the vacation and the sick leave. Under the sick leave policies, individuals have the ability to take 2 weeks off, 80 hours, to care for individuals who were part of their immediate family.

The problem we run into now is that everybody we hire is on PTO,” Mathis said. “There are very few employees left who have sick leave and vacation. If somebody was under that, they could take their 2 weeks and use it to care for a child.”

title: Rounds announces bill to encourage converting cropland back to pasture
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Cattle are pictured in a pasture near St. Onge. On Wednesday, Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., along with Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., introduced a bill that would pay farmers to convert less-productive cropland back to grass and allow the acres to be grazed by livestock. Photo by Seth Tupper, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Rounds announces bill to encourage converting cropland back to pasture.jpg
Cattle are pictured in a pasture near St. Onge. On Wednesday, Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., along with Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., introduced a bill that would pay farmers to convert less-productive cropland back to grass and allow the acres to be grazed by livestock. Photo by Seth Tupper, South Dakota Searchlight 

MITCHELL – Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds unveiled a bipartisan bill Wednesday at Dakotafest that would pay farmers to convert less-productive cropland back to grass and allow the acres to be grazed by livestock all season.

The Rebuilding America’s National Cow Herd Act, or RANCH Act, would create a voluntary federal program with an enrollment cap of 20 million acres. Democratic Sen. Amy Klobuchar of Minnesota co-sponsors the legislation. 

Under the proposal, eligible land would need to have had crops planted on it in at least four of the previous six years or have history of being cropped, according to a bill summary from Rounds’ Office. Farmers would sign 10- to 15-year contracts and establish and maintain perennial grasses or non-woody vegetation like wildflowers, buckwheat or radishes.

The program has additional incentives for beginning farmers and ranchers, and would prioritize contracts for poorly performing and highly erodible cropland.

A South Dakota State University study estimated the state lost about 1.8 million acres of grassland between 2006 and 2012, predominantly to cropland conversion. Across the Great Plains, 32 million acres of grassland were converted from 2012 through 2021, with row-crop expansion identified as the leading cause, according to a World Wildlife Fund analysis.

Under Rounds’ new bill, participants would receive annual payments equal to 75% of their county’s average cropland cash rental rate. The program would also pay 50% of the cost of establishing grass, increasing to 75% for beginning farmers and ranchers. Producers are still eligible for other federal cost-share programs that help establish things like fencing. 

The federal government has a program that permits livestock grazing while paying landowners to maintain it as grassland, called the Grassland Conservation Reserve Program. In April 2024, nearly 1.5 million South Dakota acres were enrolled in that program, totaling $23.67 million in payments; the average annual payment per acre was about $16.

The existing program, however, pays to preserve existing grass. Rounds’ bill would pay to convert cropland back to grass, and it does not include seasonal grazing restrictions like the current program. It would also pay landowners at a rate based on the land’s cropland value, rather than its pastureland value, which would amount to larger payments. 

Rounds said the legislation’s cost has not yet been calculated. Its supporters await a congressional budget estimate that accounts not only for the new payments, but also the savings that would come with removing up to 20 million marginal crop acres from federal subsidized crop insurance programs. 

“You might very well save money on the insurance side of it,” Rounds told reporters. 

Rounds said he hopes to add the proposal to this year’s farm bill, which has not yet advanced out of the Senate Agriculture Committee. 

Rounds shared the news of the proposal during a panel discussion held by South Dakota Farm Bureau that also included U.S. Congressman Dusty Johnson, R-S.D., and Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D.

All three agreed that getting the 60 votes in the Senate needed to pass the farm bill — which would require some Democrats to support it in an election year where they’re assumed to gain more control — was unlikely.

title: Agora now open, pouring new sips from day to night
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Agora, a coffee and cocktail bar at the Deadwood Gulch, is now open and ready to serve fresh, modern drinks and foods. Photo courtesy of Agora
_full_text:
Agora now open.jpeg
Agora, a coffee and cocktail bar at the Deadwood Gulch, is now open and ready to serve fresh, modern drinks and foods. Photo courtesy of Agora 

DEADWOOD — After an extensive, 9-month long remodel, Agora at the Deadwood Gulch is now open and ready for business, slinging coffees and cocktails alongside never-frozen foods in a modern setting. 

Tijana Harper, co-owner of the Deadwood Gulch at 300 Cliff St., said her and her husband, Russ Harper, and a team of partners are in the business of slowly remodeling hotels. The team works to create locally focused, luxury hospitality experiences. 

After finishing a project in Taos, New Mexico, she said her and her husband decided it was time to start a new adventure. 

“It was my husband’s responsibility to choose a place,” Tijana said. “He found this hotel and he really liked Deadwood, the gulch, and the creek. The place was ready for purchase, so we decided, ‘OK, let’s give it a go.’ Now our goal is to remodel it and bring it back to life.”

Tijana said after arriving, they discovered more work waiting for them than they had anticipated. Because they are a small company, working with a team of their own employees rather than contracting projects out, work to remodel the Deadwood Gulch will be slow. However, Tijana said, that slow process allows them to intentionally choose every detail.

“We are going for an upscale vibe, but also a very comforting and inviting one,” said Tijana. “We are very big on hospitality and taking care of our guests. Just people feeling comfortable, being there for them, welcoming them in and saying, ‘Thank you,’ on the way out, making sure they have a great experience. That’s what we’re focusing on when it comes to food, as well.”

Tijana said the kitchen in Agora has been deep cleaned and new equipment has been purchased. The full menu of breakfast items, including burritos, tacos, sandwiches, and pastries, are all made in-house. In the evening, the menu transitions to serve pizza with freshly made dough and premium ingredients. 

“We had a pizza chef come out from Florida, and he taught us how to make pizza,” said Tijana. “What I wouldn’t eat, I definitely wouldn’t serve. We have a very high standard when it comes to that. Me, my mom, and my cousin work the kitchen, so we make sure everything is good and clean and the food tastes really good.”

Tijana said she is constantly researching trends online, working to serve up a coffee menu that feels fresh and modern. The most popular items on the coffee menu are the blueberry latte and the coffee flight — 4, 4-ounce cups of the most popular items on the coffee menu. 

Agora serves cocktails in the evenings, featuring a rhubarb cocktail with syrup made in-house. 

“I didn’t even know about rhubarb (before moving here),” said Tijana. “We heard about it and how popular it is here, so we make the syrup in-house and it’s become our most popular cocktail. 

Tony Costanzo, another owner, said that type of constant curation and drive to channel local energy is what makes the Harper team unique. 

“I live in Southern California, and this is not how these guys would build and design something in Southern California,” Costanzo said. “But if you told them to design one there, it would feel modern and local to Southern California. It always feels updated, elevated, and very much in line with where we are doing business and how we are going to meet our customers in the moment. Then we build accordingly, and that goes back even to the food and drinks. You have to pay attention, and listen, and build, or else you’ll build the wrong thing, and you have to do it all again.”

With Agora open and very nearly complete, Tijana, Russ, and Costanzo said their next goal is to remodel the casino and all 90 rooms of the hotel. 

“It’s going to be a lot of work, we’re constantly moving through new ideas and iterations, but it’s going to be beautiful,” said Russ. “This is a great spot with a great community, and we’re so happy to be here and be a part of it.”

title: Lead considers creating ordinance officer position
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: A proposed new position would enforce Lead city ordinances for lawn maintenance, and assist the building inspector with various tasks. Several properties in Lead do not have proper lawn maintenance. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
IMG_1154.jpeg
A proposed new position would enforce Lead city ordinances for lawn maintenance, and assist the building inspector with various tasks. Several properties in Lead do not have proper lawn maintenance. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

 IMG_1158.jpeg
Broken sidewalks such as this are among some of the issues an ordinance officer could address in Lead. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

LEAD — Creating an ordinance officer position could relieve some of the duties of the Lead Police Department, and improve compliance with city laws, officials said Monday. 

Lead City Commissioner Valerie Meiners brought the proposal to the city commission meeting for discussion. She said the idea came from a needs and retention committee, which Mayor Dustin Heupel formed to address the challenges of recruiting city employees, specifically for the police department.  

“When we looked at officer retention, one of the things that burdens the police department is ordinance enforcement,” Meiners said. “One or the other takes a back seat. Time to be a policeman or time to enforce an ordinance. It’s a lot. I, along with the committee, decided it would be a good thing to move it over to building inspection, because that’s more where it belongs. It does not take a certified officer to be an ordinance officer. So that hopefully will relieve some of the burden on the police department.” 

This year the Lead Police Department has struggled to maintain a full staff of 7 officers. Mayor Dustin Heupel said during several of the exit interviews, former officers cited the burden of ordinance enforcement as a problem with the department. 

On Monday, Officer Marshall Rood’s resignation made him the fourth officer to resign this year. Meiners said Rood decided not to attend the police academy. 

“Marshall gives us an opportunity, because what he told me was that he just doesn’t want to be a cop,” Meiners said. “It’s just not him. It’s not what he thought. But he’s going to be here a little while longer, and he already knows what he needs to do to be an ordinance officer. It’s easy to just slide him over into that position.” 

While creating the position could leave the Lead Police Department with a full staff of only 6 officers, Meiners said it would also reduce the workload of the department as a whole. 

During discussion about the idea, Commissioner Dustin Schumacher questioned whether ordinance enforcement requires a full time position.

“The grass grows every summer, and the snow falls every winter,” Heupel answered. “That’s a lot of what this job is. I don’t know that they’d ever be caught up on it because it’s a matter of the change of seasons, and you’re gonna have people violate those ordinances.” 

Following some further discussion, commissioners agreed to re-visit the idea during a future meeting, and no action was taken on the matter.

title: Violent crime in US fell at record pace in 2025
byline: By Amanda Watford Stateline
description: Violent crime in the United States fell by an estimated 9.3% in 2025, marking the largest year-to-year decline in the national violent crime rate since the FBI began estimating crime in 1936, according to new national data.
_full_text:
StatelineLogo

Violent crime in the United States fell by an estimated 9.3% in 2025, marking the largest year-to-year decline in the national violent crime rate since the FBI began estimating crime in 1936, according to new national data.

The estimated murder and nonnegligent manslaughter rate also fell 18.1%, to 4.1 killings per 100,000 people — tying the lowest rate recorded since national estimates began. The rate matches those recorded in 1955 and 1956, according to the FBI.

The decline across major crime categories was broad. The estimated robbery rate fell 18.5%, aggravated assault fell 7.2% and rape fell 7.6%. Property crime also dropped sharply, declining 12.4% from 2024. Motor vehicle theft fell 22.7%, while burglary declined 15.8%.

The FBI’s figures are based on reports of crimes submitted by law enforcement agencies, meaning they do not capture offenses that aren’t reported to police. Participation in the FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting program is voluntary, and agencies submit their data either through state programs or directly to the FBI. 

In 2025, 17,075 law enforcement agencies submitted data, covering 96.2% of the U.S. population. Every city agency with populations over a million submitted a full year of data. 

Crime statistics can be affected by changes in reporting practices and public willingness to report crimes, particularly as trust in law enforcement and government institutions varies.

An estimated 1.12 million violent crimes occurred nationwide in 2025, with the violent crime rate falling from 362.9 offenses per 100,000 people in 2024, to 327.6 per 100,000 in 2025.

The findings largely align with other recent estimates. The nonpartisan Council on Criminal Justice, which analyzed crime trends in 40 large U.S. cities, found that 11 of 13 offenses it tracked, including homicide, declined in 2025. 

The sharp drop in homicides has persisted in 2026. Data analyzed by the council shows killings continued to decline through June across the cities it tracks, putting the nation on pace for another historic low.

“The homicide drop is historic and crystal clear. But right now, what’s driving it is about as clear as a glass of milk,” Adam Gelb, the council’s president and CEO, said in a statement. 

“Rates are falling in cities with very different public safety strategies, economic conditions, and political leadership,” Gelb said. “The consistency across the map should make us cautious about handing credit to any one leader, party, policy, or program before the evidence catches up.”  

Experts say it is difficult to pinpoint exactly what is driving the declines. Researchers have pointed to a range of possible factors, including the normalization of social activity after the pandemic, changes in policing and violence-prevention strategies, demographic shifts and the unwinding of the factors that contributed to the pandemic-era crime surge.

The declines also began before President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025, making it difficult to attribute the national trend to policies implemented by his administration.

Cities with populations between 500,000 and 999,999 recorded the largest drop in violent crime, at 15.3%, according to the FBI. Smaller cities also saw double digit declines in overall violent crime. 

Nonmetropolitan counties saw violent crime decline 6%, the smallest decrease among the population groups analyzed. No population group recorded an overall increase in violent crime. 

Cities with populations over 1 million saw a 1.2% increase in rape between 2024 and 2025, the only increase in a specific violent crime among the population groups.

The data shows continued declines in several crimes that had surged in recent years. The estimated motor vehicle theft rate fell to 197 per 100,000 people in 2025, a 23% decrease from 2024 and a 38.8% decline from its 2023 peak. The robbery rate, at 49.4 per 100,000, was the lowest estimated rate in 20 years. Burglary and larceny-theft rates also reached 20-year lows.

The FBI reported declines in arrests of juveniles as well. The number of people under 18 arrested for violent crimes fell 5% in 2025, from 39,117 to 37,156, while juvenile arrests for property crimes fell 12.2%, from 77,779 to 68,281. 

By comparison, adult violent-crime arrests fell 1.7%, and adult property-crime arrests fell 3.8%.

Despite the decline in reported crime, law enforcement cleared less than half of reported violent crimes in 2025. Agencies cleared 47.4% of reported violent crimes through an arrest or exceptional means, while just 17.4% of reported property crimes were cleared.

Some crime rates also remain higher than before the pandemic. The 2025 aggravated assault rate of 238 offenses per 100,000 people, for example, was lower than recent years but remained higher than every year from 2013 through 2015.

The FBI said preliminary data indicate crime continued to decline during the first half of 2026. Compared with the same period in 2025, violent crime was down 10.6%, while murder and nonnegligent manslaughter fell 23%, rape fell 18.6%, robbery fell 19.6% and aggravated assault fell 7.2%.

The latest national figures provide the most comprehensive accounting yet of the sharp decline in crime that followed the pandemic-era surge. The FBI’s 2025 murder rate of 4.1 per 100,000 compares with a recent high of 6.6 in both 2020 and 2022.

title: Quick picks: Chapter Books
description: It’s time to break out the backpacks, and pick out those “first day of school” outfits — summer is over and its back to the classroom for kids across the region. That’s why this week, we are bringing you 6 book recommendations to gear up for back to school season.
_full_text:
ReadingOpenBook.jpg

It’s time to break out the backpacks, and pick out those “first day of school” outfits — summer is over and its back to the classroom for kids across the region. That’s why this week, we are bringing you 6 book recommendations to gear up for back to school season. 

1. “Junie B. Jones and the Stupid Smelly Bus” by Barbara Park 

Genre: Children’s chapter book

Meet the world’s funniest kindergartner — Junie B. Jones! Remember when it was scary to go to school? In the first Junie B. Jones book, it’s Junie B.’s first day and she doesn’t know anything. She’s so scared of the school bus and the meanies on it that when it’s time to go home, she doesn’t.

2. “Vampires Don’t Wear Polka Dots” by Debbie Dadey and Marcia Thornton Jones

Genre: Children’s chapter book

The kids in the third grade at Bailey Elementary are so hard to handle that all of their teachers have quit. But their new teacher, Mrs. Jeepers, is different to say the least. She’s just moved from the Transylvanian Alps and she seems to have some strange powers that help her deal with these mischief-makers. Her methods may be a little unconventional, but, then again, Mrs. Jeepers may be just what the Bailey School kids need.

3. “Sideways Stories from Wayside School” by Louis Sachar

Genre: Middle grade short story

There was a terrible mistake. Wayside School was built with one classroom on top of another, 30 stories high (the builder said he was sorry.) Maybe that’s why all kinds of funny things happened at Wayside-especially on the 13th floor.

4. “Tales of a Fourth Grade Nothing” by Judy Blume

Genre: Young adult fiction

Life with his little brother, Fudge, makes Peter Hatcher feel like a fourth grade nothing. Whether Fudge is throwing a temper tantrum in a shoe store, smearing mashed potatoes on the walls at Hamburger Heaven, or trying to fly, he’s never far from trouble. He’s an almost 3-year-old terror who gets away with everything, and Peter’s had it up to here! When Fudge walks off with Dribble, Peter’s pet turtle, it’s the last straw. Peter has put up with Fudge for too long. Way too long! How can he get his parents to pay attention to him for a change?

5. “Everything Sad is Untrue” by Daniel Nayeri

Genre: Young adult 

At the front of a middle school classroom in Oklahoma, a boy named Khosrou, whom everyone calls “Daniel,” stands, trying to tell a story. His story. But no one believes a word he says. To them he is a dark-skinned, hairy-armed boy with a big butt whose lunch smells funny; who makes things up and talks about poop too much.

6. “High Score” by Destiny Howell

Genre: Middle grade

My name’s Darius James — but everyone calls me DJ. At my old school, I was the go-to guy for all kinds of tricky problems that needed creative solutions. But at my new school, Ella Fitzgerald Middle, I’m just trying to blend in.

Well, I was, anyway, until my best friend, Conor, got himself transferred to the Fitz too. Now Conor owes 100,000 arcade tickets to the biggest bully around — and he only has 2 weeks to make it happen. Impossible? Not with my head in the game. Oceans 11 goes to the arcade in this wildly entertaining heist adventure that is perfect for fans of Gordon Korman, Varian Johnson, and Celia Perez.

title: Deadwood approves change order to Crescent St. project in special meeting
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Deadwood city commissioners called a special meeting Friday, where they approved additional work to the Crescent Street reconstruction project. The reconstruction now includes new asphalt between the Days of ’76 Campground entrance and the entrance to the South Dakota Department of Transportation shop. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
Crescent Street change order 2.jpg
Deadwood city commissioners called a special meeting Friday, where they approved additional work to the Crescent Street reconstruction project. The reconstruction now includes new asphalt between the Days of ’76 Campground entrance and the entrance to the South Dakota Department of Transportation shop. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

DEADWOOD — Deadwood city commissioners called a special meeting Friday morning, where they approved additional work, financial agreements, and maintenance agreements to extend repairs on Crescent Street from the entrance of the Days of ’76 Campground to the entrance of the South Dakota Department of Transportation (DOT) shop.

Jessicca McKeown, finance officer, said the city had not yet received enough documentation to approve the work and agreements by the Monday meeting. She said the meeting was called Friday, in part, to ensure work could continue towards the Oct. 15 completion date. 

Lornie Stalder, public works director, said the $218,697.50 change order came after years of communications and negotiations between the city, Lead-Deadwood Sanitary District, DOT, and the Days of ’76 Rodeo Committee, which owns and manages the campground. He said the stretch of asphalt road running from the entrance of the Days of ’76 Campground to the DOT shop is heavily used, with city snowplows, DOT gravel trucks, and campground use, and has been in need of repair for years, and all 4 entities agreed to repair the road while the reconstruction of Crescent Street between the entrance to the event complex and the city parks building was taking place. 

Stalder said a deduction in the total cost will eventually come before the commissioners. 

“We are, as of even yesterday, meeting with Hayworth Construction (of Belle Fourche) and the engineering staff,” said Stalder. “We’re going to remove some trees for them and remove all the asphalt to help (Hayworth) meet their deadlines, and they’ll actually lower our cost share portion, too.”

Commissioners passed a financial agreement between the 4 entities, splitting the cost of the change order. Cost splitting is as follows: DOT, $75,004; Lead-Deadwood Sanitary District, $35,580.30; city of Deadwood; $57,939.10; Days of ’76 Rodeo Committee, $50,174.10. 

Commissioners passed an updated maintenance and use agreement on the stretch of road.

“(The city) is actually the highest user, and if you want to call it abuser, of that area, just with our dump trucks, our chains, and our equipment that’s traveling over that new surfaced area,” said Stalder. “We’ve agreed to do the lion’s share of that maintenance.”

Hayworth was awarded the contract to reconstruct Crescent Street in April. The scope of work of the project included constructing new curb, gutter, sidewalk, and pedestrian lighting, new asphalt, a retaining wall between the city’s park buildings and the rodeo’s grandstands, and a 6-inch water line. The water line will create a looped system with additional fire hydrants. 

The project was paid in part by a $600,000 community access grant from the DOT. 

The second change order brings the running total of the project to $2,011,572.38.

title: One uranium project takes a step toward state permit, while another stays stalled by legal questions
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Opponents of a proposed project to drill for uranium in the southern Black Hills listen to a meeting of the Board of Minerals and Environment at the Joe Foss Building in Pierre, South Dakota, on Aug. 20, 2026. Photo by Meghan O’Brien,South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
One uranium project takes a step toward state permit, while another stays stalled by legal questions.jpg
Opponents of a proposed project to drill for uranium in the southern Black Hills listen to a meeting of the Board of Minerals and Environment at the Joe Foss Building in Pierre, South Dakota, on Aug. 20, 2026. Photo by Meghan O’Brien,South Dakota Searchlight 

PIERRE — A long-lingering South Dakota uranium mining proposal restarted its state permitting process Thursday with approval from a state board to commission a study, and the board continued discussing a different proposal to conduct exploratory drilling for uranium in the same area of the state.

Uranium is a metallic, radioactive element used as fuel in nuclear weapons and nuclear power plants. Interest in uranium exploration and mining has risen recently. That’s in response to nuclear energy’s potential to supply electricity for data centers.

The proposed Dewey-Burdock uranium mine would cover nearly 20 square miles of land in Custer and Fall River counties along the southern edge of the Black Hills, near the city of Edgemont. It requires federal, state and local permits. Legal challenges kept it in a 13-year stalemate since its initial application for a state permit, but the project secured the last of its federal permits earlier this year, according to the federal Permitting Council.

On Thursday, South Dakota’s Minerals and Environment Board granted Powertech, a subsidiary of Texas-based enCore Energy, approval to hire a Wyoming-based company to conduct a socioeconomic assessment, which is an initial step in mine permitting.

The study will help evaluate the project’s effects, including its economic impact, changes in air or water quality, local employment opportunities and use of resources like grazing land. The board can deny a mining permit application if the negative impacts of a project outweigh benefits.

The mining method for the project is “in situ” — drilling wells to inject a water-based solution underground, dissolving uranium and pumping it to the surface. The water would be pulled from local aquifers and then treated and pumped back underground after being used for mining, causing opponents to fear pollution of local water sources.

Drilling proposal stalled by language interpretation law

Another proposed uranium project in the same general area of the Southern Black Hills will stay stalled after board members announced they’re seeking a state judge’s opinion on a relevant law.

The board indicated it wants clarity on a new state law that took effect in July. The law requires language translation services for some government proceedings.

Clean Nuclear Energy Corp., a subsidiary of Canada-based Nexus Uranium, is seeking a permit to drill dozens of exploratory holes as much as 700 feet deep on state land, while seeking federal permission for additional drilling on federal land. The proposed sites are near the rim of Craven Canyon in the southern Black Hills.

Dozens of people and some organizations have raised formal complaints about the project to the state Board of Minerals and Environment, which will decide on the permit. Opponents have said the drilling could disturb ancient Native American petroglyphs on the canyon’s walls, disrupt Lakota ceremonies and potentially contaminate groundwater, among other concerns.

A hearing on the permit began earlier this year in Hot Springs. It was cut short after a project opponent filed a federal lawsuit against the company, the board and the state Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources. That lawsuit is still pending, and the board has not resumed the hearing.

Project opponent Elizabeth Lone Eagle filed the lawsuit on the third day of what was planned to be a 5-day hearing. She alleged “systematic, ongoing, and deliberate denial of meaningful participation to Lakota first-language speaking” project opponents.

The board was not legally obligated to provide interpretation services to Lakota first-language speakers at the May hearing, but agreed to do so anyway, noting that the law requiring translation services would come into effect just a couple of months later.

But on the first day of the hearing, Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources staff said they had not reached agreement with a Lakota translator and did not provide one. The staff later contracted with 2 Lakota speakers for the following days of the hearing, but project opponents including Lone Eagle accused the board of improperly conducting some parts of the hearing without interpretation.

The board discussed the matter Thursday in a closed meeting known as an executive session, citing the discussion of legal matters. Afterward, the board emerged back into a public session and voted to seek a state judge’s declaratory ruling on a portion of state law that includes the new interpretation provision. Board members did not publicly explain their reasoning for seeking the ruling, but the board’s lawyer told South Dakota Searchlight that board members are hoping for clarity about their obligations under the new language interpretation law.

title: Bike week proclaimed in Spearfish
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Spearfish councilman Larry Klarenbeek delivers the Spearfish Bike Week Proclamation to organizers and advocates of cycling and the Dakota Five-O. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Bike Week.JPG
Spearfish councilman Larry Klarenbeek delivers the Spearfish Bike Week Proclamation to organizers and advocates of cycling and the Dakota Five-O. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — It all started with a mountain bike race. Spearfish Bike Week revolves around the Dakota Five-O, but it has grown to promote cycling for trail users and road bikers of all ages. 

The Dakota Five-O is in its 26th year. 

“We’ve been working hard on the 50-mile course,” said Dakota Five-O organizer Perry Jewett. “We have 450 volunteer hours into perfecting that course for locals to enjoy and the many visitors that come throughout the year to celebrate cycling in Spearfish and participate in the Dakota Five-O and Spearfish Bike Week. “As the Dakota Five-O has grown, so have the activities surrounding it.”

On Aug. 29, the week’s events will kick off with a grand opening of the new bike skills park near the city campground. That will be followed by a community ride on Aug. 30, a family-friendly bicycle scavenger hunt race on Sept. 1, a bicycle poker run for adults on Sept. 2, an all ages “High Five-O” pre-party with music and strider races at the city park on Sept. 4, and various activities including bike shop led group rids throughout the week. 

“These events bring together families, riders, visitors, volunteers, community members, for a full week of opportunities to connect, have fun, and experience what our community has to offer,” Jewett said. “What began as a mountain bike race has grown into so much more. A celebration of our trails, our community, and the people who make this area such a special place to visit and call home.”

title: Spearfish spends more than $1.6 million ordering equipment for public works
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — The Spearfish City Council authorized public works staff members to purchase a new plow/dump truck, a dump truck, a front-end loader, a camera van and camera, and a sewer jet/vac truck for the motor pool and sewer fleet. The purchases appear in the 2027 budget, but Public Works Director Adam McMahon asked the council to consider ordering the equipment this calendar year.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

SPEARFISH — The Spearfish City Council authorized public works staff members to purchase a new plow/dump truck, a dump truck, a front-end loader, a camera van and camera, and a sewer jet/vac truck for the motor pool and sewer fleet. The purchases appear in the 2027 budget, but Public Works Director Adam McMahon asked the council to consider ordering the equipment this calendar year.

“What that means is that some of that equipment will likely show up in 2027 when it is budgeted here. Other items may show up in 2026, so then we will be asking to supplement back into 2026 for those purchase if some of those equipment, some of that equipment shows up,” McMahon said.

He said the move to buy the vehicles now could both expedite vehicle delivery and avoid potential price increases.

“The bigger pieces of equipment — primarily the plow/dump truck, the dump truck, the front end loader, the sewer camera van, and the jet truck — all of those take a lot of lead time to get purchased,” McMahon said. “If the council is open to the idea of authorizing staff to start those purchase processes now so that we can get those pieces of equipment coming early.”

The council authorized the early purchases to replace aging equipment in the city fleet.

“Our motor pool fleet includes 17 trucks that are one ton and larger. The oldest one is 35 years of age, and the highest mileage truck is 258,000 miles,” McMahon said. “We have 8 trucks, currently that are overdue for replacement.”

The $272,980 plow/dump truck will replace a 2002 International model which failed its most recent DOT inspection due to “excessive frame rust.” The vehicle will be used for snow removal and “hauling materials,” according to the agenda item report presented to the city council before the purchase was authorized.

The new dump truck, expected to cost $207,188, is set to replace a 1999 Volvo model.

A 1994 Komatsu front-end loader will be replaced by a new Caterpillar with a V-plow $293,205 machine. Each of those purchases will be paid for using funds for the motor pool.

The council also approved the purchase of more than $800,000 in sewer equipment — a $311,674 camera van and camera and a $569,957 sewer jet and vac truck.

The city owns a camera van and camera already, and it’s at least used once a week. It’s used for routine storm sewer and sanitary sewer inspections and warranty inspections. That van has broken down at least 4 times in the last year, and requires regular maintenance. Some parts are no longer available for replacement, according to public works.

The sewer jet/vac truck is used to clean underground pipes, remove obstructions, and bore holes for locating ground utilities. The city’s current unit was built in 2002, and has “insufficient power which limits where it can be used,” and it “requires frequent maintenance due to its age.” The older unit is set to be declared surplus and sold to help offset the cost of the new truck.

“Part of the reason for the 2 sewer equipment purchases this year is to extend the life of the capital projects that need to happen,” McMahon said. “We’re kind of light on capital improvement projects (in 2027). So, we’re kind of making up that difference with purchasing some of the equipment that we need to maintain our infrastructure and try to help ensure that we are extending the life of our infrastructure, so that was the reason for making both of those requests.”

A garbage truck requested in the 2027 preliminary public works budget may also be purchased before next year, once the public works department secures a final quote from the manufacturer.

“Out of our solid waste, we’re due to replace a garbage truck for $400,000 and a sewer camera van for $320,000 and a sewer jet for $600,000. Part of the reason for the 2 sewer equipment purchases this year is to extend the life of the capital projects that need to happen,” McMahon said.

In 2027, public works has also requested funds to purchase 2 police department vehicles.

“Those are replacements for a total of $160,000. As a note, the police department’s vehicle pool is 21 vehicles total. The oldest vehicle is 13.5 years, and the highest mileage vehicle is 156,000 miles. There are a few vehicles overdue for replacement,” McMahon said. “We are also asking for an additional $20,000 to add grill guards to put on existing patrol vehicles.”

Those vehicle and grill guard purchases did not need to be made this year, Police Chief Collin Smith said.

“With the system we have in place with our current vendor, we have already reached out to who we get our cars from, and we’re going to be just fine. The price actually ended up going down as we are seeing a decrease in some of the pricing for equipment,” Smith said.

Next calendar year, the public works department would like to replace a few lighter vehicles — 3 pickups and 1 SUV in its motor pool fleet.

“That excludes the police vehicles I referenced earlier, and the oldest vehicle was 28 years old and 167,000 miles was the highest mileage vehicle,” McMahon said. “There are currently 14 vehicles over 20 years of age and an additional 17 vehicles between 15 and 20 years of age. We do have a number of vehicles that are overdue or due for replacement.”

Councilwoman Jamie Hafner asked if those vehicles could be purchased used.

“We don’t have to buy brand new. There are provisions allowing the purchase of new vehicles,” McMahon said. “I would say in our experience with the pricing that we can get with a fleet vehicle that we are able to purchase, those are much better priced than a vehicle off of the dealership lot. A lot of the features that you see are kind of stripped down to the bare minimum.”

Hafner also asked if there was a specific reason why the city needs a new SUV.

“What is the SUV earmarked for?” Hafner asked.

“That might just be a check-out vehicle, so it could be used for out-of-town trips by any staff as well as various different meetings and other things throughout town where somebody can check out those vehicles for use,” McMahon said.

McMahon said, in the next couple of months, he hopes to assess the motor pool to determine where replacements are most needed and where vehicles might be unnecessary.

“There is a lot of coordination with other department heads to figure out whether there are efficiencies we can gain with vehicle and equipment assignments and whether we reduce the size of the fleet to help address some of our older pieces of equipment and vehicles that are overdue for replacement,” McMahon said. “Then, figure out how are we going to catch up on some of our replacements.”

title: State Rep. Ismay fined $1,750 after ‘no contest’ plea to misdemeanor road damage
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Travis Ismay, pictured, appeared in court Friday, where he pleaded “no contest” to a misdemeanor road damage charge. File photo
_full_text:
Travis Ismay.jpg
Travis Ismay, pictured, appeared in court Friday, where he pleaded “no contest” to a misdemeanor road damage charge. File photo 

BELLE FOURCHE — State Rep. Travis Ismay, R-Newell, was sentenced to pay Butte County $1,750 in restitution for damaging Wilson Cemetery Road, near his home in Newell, in May, after he pleaded no contest to a Class 2 misdemeanor Friday. 

He was not sentenced to any jail time, and he was allowed by the court to apply the $500 bond he paid after his July 10 arrest to the court ordered restitution. By press time, Ismay had already paid the court ordered fine in its entirety. 

On July 29, Ismay entered a plea of “not guilty” to the charge of intentionally damaging a highway, a Class 6 felony. On Friday, under the terms of a plea agreement, Ismay pleaded no contest to “damage of a highway grade or ditch.” The felony charge was dropped as a “benefit of the bargain” according to Timothy Rensch, Ismay’s attorney.

According to the complaint filed with the Butte County magistrate court, Ismay “injure(d) a highway by removing, destroying or otherwise altering the grade of a highway” in May. By entering a plea of “no contest” Ismay formally acknowledged that he did not dispute the facts of the case. Dwayne Heidrich, who was highway supervisor at the time of the incident, inspected Wilson Cemetery Road after Ismay attempted to work on it. He said the road was damaged, and estimated the cost of repairs at $2,000. 

Because Ismay was not sentenced to serve any time behind bars, he is not disqualified to serve in public office. He may return to Pierre as a legislator. 

Ismay was arrested just one month after he was elected to represent District 28B in the South Dakota House of Representatives. Ismay earned 55% of the vote in that race, beating Larry Schmoltz.

title: Meade Co. approves new  PT state’s attorney
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — A steadily increasing case load and several months of being short staffed mean that the Meade County State’s Attorney’s office needs some extra help.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

STURGIS — A steadily increasing case load and several months of being short staffed mean that the Meade County State’s Attorney’s office needs some extra help. 

During the regular Meade County Commission meeting Tuesday, State’s Attorney Michele Bordewyk asked for approval to hire a part-time state’s attorney, who can help with the burgeoning case load. Bordewyk said in March a full time state’s attorney resigned, and her office was not able to fill the position until this month. While Bordewyk said her team of 3 attorneys has done a good job keeping up with the caseload, the office needs the extra help. 

“Due to the 5 months that passed while the position was open, and the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally leaving hundreds of new misdemeanor cases, a part-time deputy states attorney could assist the office with resolving back logs, preventing future backlogs, reduce reliance on plea negotiations, and assist in meeting statutory discovery deadlines involving digital forensic and body worn cameras that are very time consuming to review,” Bordewyk wrote to the county commission. 

A report Bordewyk submitted of prosecution numbers from 2010-2024, shows that in 2010, her office prosecuted 869 cases. By 2020 that number nearly doubled to 1,636. In 2024, they handled 1,704 cases. There was no data available for 2025. 

Following some discussion, the commission approved the part time position through the end of 2026.

title: Lead citizen says city erred when it included  budgeted funds in event revenue report
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: LEAD — Taxpayer dollars that were budgeted to pay for the 150th anniversary celebration in Lead should not be counted as revenue from the event, a resident said Monday.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

LEAD — Taxpayer dollars that were budgeted to pay for the 150th anniversary celebration in Lead should not be counted as revenue from the event, a resident said Monday. 

Resident and business owner Pam Millard told the Lead City Commission on Monday that Lead City Administrator Robin Lucero’s report about the 150th anniversary celebration, “Rock the Hills,” was misleading because it referred to $90,000 that the city budgeted for the event as revenue. 

Lucero delivered her report at the Aug. 3 city commission meeting, which detailed revenue and expenses for the event, as well as sales tax receipts generated to date in July. In her report, she included the city’s budgeted $90,000 in her revenue total of $184,000. She also stated that more than half of the revenue, or $94,000 was derived from event sponsors, private donations, grants, and merchandise and ticket sales. 

Expenses from the event totaled $165,000, according to Lucero’s report that claimed the city came out ahead by $19,000. 

But Millard said that math is not honest, because it includes money that was budgeted for the event from the city’s third-penny sales tax, which is an extra penny assessed for restaurant, lodging, and alcohol purchases and can only be used for restricted purposes. 

“You can’t say there was $184,000 in revenue against $165,000 in expenses, to come up with positive revenue,” Millard said. “Yes, you budgeted it. But it can’t be considered revenue. The event is $70,000 in the hole.” 

Millard is a member of a government watchdog group Checks and Balances by City of Lead Friends and Neighbors, which has demanded a full financial accounting related to the 150th anniversary celebration, from the city of Lead. On Aug. 3, Lucero said the city had received and paid most of its bills related to the event, and invited members of the group to request any bills or receipts that had not already been provided. Millard said a request for the city’s bank statements was not honored. Lucero said that’s because the city awaits a legal opinion from City Attorney Tim Johns, about whether certain expenses need to be redacted. 

“We have to have a handle on how to spend the taxpayers’ dollars,” Millard said. “These kinds of things are misrepresenting what’s really happening.” 

The Rock the Hills 150th anniversary celebration event was held July 2-5, and included a variety of activities, including a day-long concert at Mountain Top Field.

title: Dozens of cities and counties sue fire truck  makers over soaring costs, delivery delays
byline: By Anna Claire Vollers Stateline
description: In the summer of 2023, a third of the fire engines owned by the fire department in Kansas City, Kansas, were unusable. Five of 15 pumper trucks were out of commission, and the department was waiting on parts from the manufacturer.
_full_text:
StatelineLogo

In the summer of 2023, a third of the fire engines owned by the fire department in Kansas City, Kansas, were unusable. Five of 15 pumper trucks were out of commission, and the department was waiting on parts from the manufacturer.

So, Kansas City fire officials went on a nationwide hunt for trucks. But their frantic search turned up just 4 they could buy immediately, and the vehicles were designed for smaller, more rural departments.

Their experience was not unusual: Municipalities and fire departments in every state are struggling with soaring prices and years-long delivery times for trucks. It’s a crisis many cities and departments lay squarely at the feet of the country’s biggest fire apparatus manufacturers.

“There must come a day of reckoning when the manufacturers of our most important tools are held accountable for runaway pricing and extended delivery times,” Dennis Rubin, the chief of the Kansas City Fire Department, told U.S. senators last fall at hearing convened to investigate price increases and delivery delays on fire trucks.

Kansas City is one of more than 60 cities, counties and fire departments across the nation — from Milwaukee to San Diego, Pittsburgh to Tampa — that say the country’s three biggest fire truck manufacturers have conspired to suppress competition, resulting in skyrocketing prices for fire trucks and repair parts, and yearslong manufacturing delays.

In April, a federal court rolled up their claims into a trio of antitrust class action lawsuits in a Wisconsin district court.

The defendants are fire apparatus manufacturers REV Group Inc., Oshkosh Corporation and Rosenbauer Group, along with some of their subsidiaries and related companies, as well as their trade group, the Fire Apparatus Manufacturers’ Association.

By some estimates, the three manufacturers together control 70-80% of the U.S. fire truck market. Fire engine prices have nearly doubled since 2020, from about $589,000 to over $1 million, according to the International Association of Fire Fighters.

Fire departments also are reporting extended wait times for new fire trucks. In 2024, officials with the Seattle Fire Department noted it took more than 4 years to replace a ladder truck — a process that had previously taken just a year.

And some departments are accusing manufacturers of charging them “floating prices” that increase soon before a truck is ready to be delivered. The president of a volunteer fire department in Delaware County, Pennsylvania, said his department paid a 50% deposit on a fire truck and the supplier later said it could no longer deliver at that price, leading to the department paying an additional $110,000, reported the Pennsylvania Capital-Star.

“By hiking prices for trucks and replacement parts without competition, the defendants have made it harder for the city of Pittsburgh and other municipalities across the country to make the required investments in lifesaving services and put the burden back on our communities,” Pittsburgh Mayor Corey O’Connor said in a July statement announcing its antitrust lawsuit. A city representative declined to comment further.

The plaintiffs in the suit assert that manufacturers worked together to throttle the production of fire trucks nationwide and minimize competition to increase prices. Many cities and fire departments also allege the Fire Apparatus Manufacturers’ Association — the industry’s primary trade group — helped the manufacturers coordinate price increases and limit production by passing secret or proprietary data between them.

Dan Meyer, vice president of sales at Pierce Manufacturing, a subsidiary of Oshkosh, has said his company has worked to expand its manufacturing capabilities and hired more workers. REV Group did not respond to Stateline’s request for comment.

On Tuesday, the defendants moved to dismiss 2 of the suits.

“The pandemic prompted skyrocketing demand and disrupted supply chains causing price increases and longer wait times,” they said in a joint court filing. “None of that has anything to do with an antitrust violation.”

The defendants also assert that the trade association shared “anonymized and aggregated industry statistics” that weren’t anticompetitive, and that the rollups and acquisitions of fire truck manufacturers occurred “many years ago” and didn’t result in anticompetitive harm to the plaintiffs.

Some states, too, have recently jumped into the fray.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican, launched an investigation in February into potential anticompetitive conduct of the same three manufacturers, after hearing complaints from Texas cities and their fire departments. His office said it had already uncovered “multiple potentially unlawful price hikes” involving Texas fire departments.

California has also filed an antitrust suit, asserting that REV Group and its former private equity owner, American Industrial Partners, created monopolies in fire truck markets. In Pennsylvania, state Rep. Jennifer O’Mara, a Democrat, held a hearing in her district in March, proposing future legislation to address the issue.

And Congress is getting involved. In July, U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Massachusetts Democrat, and U.S. Sen. Jim Banks, an Indiana Republican, along with Democratic Rep. Becca Balint of Vermont and Republican Rep. Ben Cline of Virginia, filed a resolution directing the Federal Trade Commission to investigate the consolidation in the fire truck manufacturing industry.

The resolution comes on the heels of a 2025 Senate investigation, launched by Warren and Banks, into the effects of private equity rollups in the fire truck manufacturing industry.

At local, state and even federal levels, there’s a bipartisan appetite for antitrust enforcement, said Basel Musharbash, an attorney who represents some of the cities involved in the class action suit, including Little Rock, Kansas City and Las Vegas.

“You can look at any number of industries that supply things to municipalities and you’ll see the same dynamic,” he said, pointing to consolidation in the ambulance industry, public works and public transit buses.

“Across the economy, there’s no shortage of industries where we’re seeing decision-making and control being concentrated in the hands of a few executives at a few companies, and that’s just inconsistent with American’s views about freedom and markets and democracy.”

Attracting investors

Last fall, the Garden City Fire Department in rural Garden City, Kansas, had been waiting nearly two years for the two new fire trucks it had ordered for one of its fire stations. The department serves all of Finney County, an agricultural area in the southwest part of the state.

Without the new trucks, the department was moving trucks around from its other stations to try to fill the void, and using three aging backup vehicles — the oldest was built in 1989; the newest in 2006 — that had a host of repair issues and few or no safety features.

Fire truck manufacturers rely on cities, counties and other local and state governments to purchase their products — and that steady flow of public funding has proven attractive to investors.

A decade ago, private equity firm American Industrial Partners began buying fire truck manufacturers around the country, eventually rolling them up into one conglomerate called the REV Group. As it consolidated smaller companies, it also shut down some of its manufacturing plants even as fire truck orders climbed after federal pandemic assistance dollars flowed to state and local governments, said Musharbash.

REV Group may control as much as 40% of the market now, he said, with Oshkosh subsidiary Pierce Manufacturing controlling around 25-30% and Rosenbauer a smaller piece.

In 2024, REV Group’s private equity fund owner, American Industrial Partners, divested from its fire truck conglomerate, and the other companies are publicly traded. But they’ve boosted profits through private equity-like tactics, he said.

For example, Los Angeles County and other municipalities say that Oshkosh, a publicly traded company, boosts its profits partly by requiring customers of Pierce Manufacturing to purchase only Pierce proprietary parts, despite cheaper prices available from competitors.

Draining public dollars

In Providence, Rhode Island, city officials purchased 3 pumper trucks in 2021 from Oshkosh subsidiary Pierce Manufacturing for $449,159 per truck. In 2024, when the city bought 5 more, the cost had jumped more than 63% to $734,320, officials said in court filings. Those trucks won’t be delivered until next year.

Fire chiefs, industry watchers and local officials hope the FTC will commission a study to dig into the industry to better understand why smaller manufacturers are having a hard time entering the industry.

“In an industry like fire trucks, where you’ve seen skyrocketing prices, backlogs, deteriorating quality over a period of more than half a decade, we should be seeing a large number of new manufacturers cropping up,” Musharbash said. “We should see smaller manufacturers expanding, and yet that’s not happening.”

Musharbash said cities and local lawmakers should reexamine how they purchase fire trucks, ambulances, city transit buses and other equipment manufactured by big corporations.

“There are these rackets in these industries that local governments depend on, and they’re draining dollars out of municipal budgets and state budgets. It’s a huge waste of public funds.”

title: Poor coordination, missing documents, mismatched training Report analyzes prison releases in SD
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Pictured is a housing unit at the new women’s prison in Rapid City. Photo courtesy of South Dakota Department of Corrections
_full_text:
Poor coordination, missing documents, mismatched training Report analyzes prison releases in SD.jpg
Pictured is a housing unit at the new women’s prison in Rapid City. Photo courtesy of South Dakota Department of Corrections 

RAPID CITY — South Dakota prisons struggle to prepare inmates for release, and the support systems meant to help them on the outside often fall short, according to a report from a national nonprofit.

The assessment found consistent gaps in support, employment, housing and mental health and addiction treatment for people leaving prison. It also found the state lacks the data and oversight structure needed to track and improve outcomes.

The state paid the Council of State Governments Justice Center $160,000 to study reentry on behalf of the Correctional Rehabilitation Task Force, which met Wednesday in Rapid City.

Gov. Larry Rhoden created the task force to study ways of reducing repeat offense rates and improving rehabilitation programming. The task force came on the heels of a legislative vote to replace the oldest parts of the state penitentiary with a $650 million men’s prison in Sioux Falls, which is under construction. The state opened a new $87 million prison for women in Rapid City this summer, the state’s second for female inmates.

South Dakota’s recidivism rate is 50%, meaning half of all inmates released from state prison return within three years.

Ryan Brunner, senior policy adviser for Rhoden, told lawmakers at the meeting that the report will help guide the expansion and operation of treatment and programming at the new prisons.

The Department of Corrections, Brunner said, “is certainly taking this data and focusing on it, and it’s good for us to have that conversation.”

System inconsistencies

When someone leaves prison, the assessment says, coordination breaks down. Access to support depends more on personal relationships between inmates, staff members and outside organizations than on formal systems, said Megan Pfeiffer, deputy policy director with the Council of State Governments Justice Center.

“There are some deep challenges here,” Pfeiffer said. 

The Department of Corrections has a reentry initiative in place to help people released from prison reenter society, but the assessment found people frequently leave prison without the transition support they need. Community handoffs are inconsistent and rushed, and inmates often leave without vital documents — identification cards, Social Security cards, birth certificates — that they need to find work or access services.

More than 80% of men and 95% of women serve two years or less in prison — a “narrow window” to address rehabilitative needs, Pfeiffer said. Many inmates leave without programming — 35% of people released in 2025 hadn’t had programming, the report found. Most of those people were incarcerated for less than a year.

The assessment recommends starting reentry planning the day someone enters prison, not weeks before they leave, and says the state should create a permanent reentry council and formalize how agencies share data and coordinate services.

Employment barriers

Participation in vocational programming inside prison is low. Structured referrals to such programs and job placement services are largely absent, and the state has no data on whether people find and keep jobs after release.

Even motivated inmates who get vocational programming in prison frequently lose connection with workforce services the moment they’re released, Pfeiffer said.

“We heard that there’s often competing appointments and needs, and people get lost in the shuffle where employment isn’t prioritized as one of their primary needs,” Pfeiffer said. “Transition can take a long time to walk through the assessment and appointment process, which leaves people unemployed for a longer period of time.”

State laws also restrict where people with felony convictions can work after release.

More than 250 legal and regulatory employment barriers can be triggered by any felony conviction in South Dakota, Pfeiffer said. South Dakota is one of fewer than 15 states without “fair chance” hiring laws, which limit when employers can ask about criminal history.

Sioux Falls Republican Rep. Bobbi Andera said her “biggest concern” is putting state resources toward programming without considering how hireable people are when they’re released.

“Programming is great, but programming is only great if they get a job,” Andera said.

A 2025 Department of Labor and Regulation survey found that 84% of South Dakota employers cite finding skilled workers as their top challenge, but only 40% said they’d hire someone with a criminal record.

The Department of Corrections trains inmates in areas such as welding, electrical work, auto service, plumbing, machining and carpentry — but those skills don’t align with the state’s most in-demand jobs, which include heavy truck drivers, sales representatives, nurses and dental assistants. The gap is especially stark in healthcare, where workforce demand is highest. State laws and regulations for healthcare, however, create more employment barriers for people with felony convictions than in any other industry.

“There’s a real gap here that we talk about as an opportunity,” Pfeiffer said. “There’s the workforce need and there’s a population that wants and needs employment.”

Brunner told lawmakers the state is exploring more employment programming options, including a 5-week commercial driver’s license program and a medical technician training partnership with Western Dakota Technical College and Sanford Health. Felons can be medical technicians in South Dakota.

Behavioral health, housing needs unaddressed

About 91% of men and 97% of women in prison were diagnosed with substance use disorder upon admission, according to the 2025 Department of Corrections statistical report.

Staff can coordinate treatment referrals before release, but provider shortages, lack of transportation and fewer options in rural areas often stymie access to care for inmates upon release. The state also doesn’t have enough residential mental health space.

The assessment says the state should improve Medicaid enrollment for departing inmates and work to expand treatment access in rural and tribal areas.

Sen. Jamie Smith, D-Sioux Falls, said the assessment confirmed his belief that South Dakota shouldn’t be “punishing someone with illness,” and that the state needs to improve its mental health infrastructure as a whole. 

The behavioral health aspect of rehabilitation should not be the Department of Correction’s job, he said.

“We can look at all the programs we want in recidivism and all the things within our correction system that we want — and we need to do a better job, and I think there’s a lot of things we’re going to learn — but unless we look at it holistically and from all the different departments, we’re not going to do anything,” Smith said.

Insufficient affordable housing is also one of the “greatest barriers” to successful reentry, the assessment said, and the state should prioritize housing stability for people leaving prison.

The state has some housing programs in place, but they don’t meet demand. Given employment challenges, a person earning a minimum wage would need to work 1.4 full-time jobs to afford a one-bed rental home, the report says. The gap in affordable housing options is worst in rural and tribal areas.

Lt. Gov. Tony Venhuizen chairs the task force and said the group focuses on programming within the prison system, even as the assessment revealed issues in the community that factor into recidivism.

“We’re obviously not going to solve the housing issue,” Venhuizen said. “But we can identify that as an issue and talk about some ideas for continuing work on that.” 

Venhuizen said he plans to have a “good idea” of recommendations for the governor and lawmakers by their October meeting.

title: Scooptown appreciation event raises $4,500 for theater campaign
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Scooptown Car Wash’s fifth annual Customer Appreciation Event raised $4,500 for the Sturgis Area Arts Council and helped launch a $150,000 capital campaign to renovate the community theater.  Families gathered for an evening featuring live music, food, inflatable attractions, vendors and refreshments. Three bands performed during the event, with each donating money back to the theater campaign.
_full_text:
STURGIS — Scooptown Car Wash’s fifth annual Customer Appreciation Event raised $4,500 for the Sturgis Area Arts Council and helped launch a $150,000 capital campaign to renovate the community theater.  Families gathered for an evening featuring live music, food, inflatable attractions, vendors and refreshments. Three bands performed during the event, with each donating money back to the theater campaign.

Scooptown owner Chris Bergman said the event was an opportunity to thank customers while supporting an important community resource.

“We’ve got jump castles, Dippin’ Dots, doughnuts, the farmers market and live music,” Bergman said. “The arts council is helping cook food, make plates and hand out drinks. Everything is available for a donation, and it is all going back to the Arts Council.”

Bergman said Scooptown partnered with the Sturgis Scooper Booster Club during the previous 3 appreciation events, donating approximately $7,000 to the organization.

“The community has always supported us,” he said. “We couldn’t do what we do without the community. I think it is important to give back and be part of the community, and this is one way we can do that.”

Bergman opened Scooptown Car Wash in Sturgis in May 2020. Later that year, he purchased the Flying Pig Car Wash in Rapid City. The business expanded with Crazy Clean Car Wash in Spearfish in 2023 and buck n’ broncs car wash in Belle Fourche in 2025.

Admission for the event was free, although donations were accepted for the Kiwanis Food Pantry.  

“The event would not be possible without the city of Sturgis, Grocery Mart, SEDC, Twice the Ice of the Black Hills and Sturgis Brewery,” said Tylea Bergman.  She also thanked, Travis Bartels, Sturgis BrewBerry Bistro, for donating food and did all of the grilling, and Pioneer Bank also sponsored a portion of the food.

The appreciation event served as the public kickoff for the Sturgis Area Arts Council’s Community Theater Capital Campaign.

Arts Council representative Francie Ruebel-Alberts said the organization hopes to raise $150,000 for repairs and improvements to the theater inside the Sturgis Community Center.

“We are very happy they are holding this event for us and helping us get the campaign started,” Albers said. “We need new curtains because the current ones have been there for about 35 years. The lighting is questionable, we want to install carpeting in the aisles and on the steps, and the stage floor needs some repairs.”

Albers said the theater is used by numerous organizations in addition to the Arts Council.  “It is a real asset to our community, and we want to keep everything working and make it as usable as possible,” she said.

Arts Council President Dede LaRue first announced the campaign during the organization’s production of “Cinderella,” but Albers said the Scooptown event marked its official fundraising kickoff.

The Sturgis Community Center was completed in June 1992 and included a 440-seat theater. The Arts Council raised the money for the original seats, while Wells Fargo Bank donated the stage curtains.

More than three decades later, the curtains have been repaired numerous times and can no longer reliably hold stitching. The campaign will also help pay for new stage lighting, carpeting in the aisles and repairs to the stage floor.

Campaign giving levels include Ensemble, $25 to $99; Actor, $100 to $249; Stage Star, $250 to $499; Playwright, $500 to $999; Curtain Call, $1,000 to $4,999; Director’s Circle, $5,000 to $9,999; and Executive Producer’s Circle, $10,000 or more.

Donations may be sent to the Sturgis Area Arts Council, P.O. Box 901, Sturgis, SD 57785. For more information, call (605) 490-1113.

title: Indie tattoo artist approaches one-year milestone
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — There’s a moment when a tattoo, particularly a color tattoo, comes to life — and that moment is why independent tattoo artist and Bright Light Tattoo shop owner Becca Braschko likes working with color most of all.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — There’s a moment when a tattoo, particularly a color tattoo, comes to life — and that moment is why independent tattoo artist and Bright Light Tattoo shop owner Becca Braschko likes working with color most of all.

She has a large, blue, tropical flower blooming on her thigh, which she gestured to by way of an explanation.

Blues are the most magical, Braschko explained, because once the darker and medium shades in a piece have been added, the highlights breathe sudden life into a piece.

“Once you get the lights in there, it just pops,” Braschko said.

As much as she loves color, she’s also capable when it comes to working in shades of gray.

“I really like doing color, full color and flowers, but I am pretty versatile in what I can do. Like I do a lot of fine line and lettering, black and gray too,” Braschko said.

Most of all, the artist said, she likes the act of creation — and generally that creativity involves needles. When she’s not wielding ink, she’s cross-stitching or quilting.

She also loves to draw, which has extended into her career as an artist. She started working as an apprentice at Dark Arts Studio in Belle Fourche, where she honed her skills for 5 years.

“The first tattoo that I did for a client was a little tiny heart on her ankle. I was so nervous,” Braschko said. Now she’s done much more comprehensive pieces, and has a total of 7 years of experience behind her.

She’s practiced different tattoo styles on herself — beginning with a lizard on her leg, and expanding to a stretch of snakeskin over her left arm.

“I love tattooing, and it is so nice being out on my own,” Braschko said.

Her shop at 3207 W. Fairgrounds Loop is approaching a milestone this November. It will have been open for one full year. Braschko is the shop’s sole artist, and books appointments over the phone or via social media.

title: SD Dept. of Health expands 'All Women Count!'
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: PIERRE — The South Dakota Department of Health (DOH) is expanding eligibility for the All Women Count! (AWC!) Program by lowering the minimum age from 30 to 21, allowing more South Dakota women to access breast and cervical cancer screening and diagnostic services. The expanded eligibility will take effect Sept. 1.
_full_text:
PIERRE — The South Dakota Department of Health (DOH) is expanding eligibility for the All Women Count! (AWC!) Program by lowering the minimum age from 30 to 21, allowing more South Dakota women to access breast and cervical cancer screening and diagnostic services. The expanded eligibility will take effect Sept. 1.

“Early detection plays an important role in improving outcomes for women diagnosed with breast or cervical cancer,” said DOH Secretary Melissa Magstadt. “By expanding eligibility for All Women Count!, we are helping more South Dakota women access recommended screenings and diagnostic services, regardless of whether they have adequate health insurance coverage.”

Beginning Sept. 1, cervical cancer screening through AWC! will be available to income-eligible women ages 21 to 64. The change aligns the program’s cervical cancer screening eligibility with U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendations, which recommend cervical cancer screening beginning at age 21.

Breast cancer eligibility is also expanding. Women ages 21 to 29, who have a sign or symptom suspicious for breast cancer, such as a breast lump, will now be eligible for AWC! breast cancer diagnostic services if they meet the program’s income requirements.

AWC! breast cancer services will be available to women ages 40 to 64; women ages 30 to 39 who are at high risk for breast cancer; and women ages 21 to 39 who have a sign or symptom suspicious for breast cancer.

Women under age 40 who need a breast cancer screening or diagnostic service must receive pre-authorization from the AWC! program before the service is provided.

The AWC! program provides breast and cervical cancer screening and diagnostic services at no cost to eligible women through participating healthcare providers across South Dakota. The program serves women who are uninsured or underinsured, and have a household income at or below 250 percent of the Federal Poverty Level.
