title: SD’s cybersecurity program is running out of time, money as local governments face attacks
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: RAPID CITY — Pennington County residents haven’t been able to access some services since a cyberattack knocked out county computer systems in July.
_full_text:
RAPID CITY — Pennington County residents haven’t been able to access some services since a cyberattack knocked out county computer systems in July.

The water system in Rapid City, which is part of Pennington County, was among the first of dozens of utilities targeted in a nationwide wave of cyberattacks this summer. The attackers did not access its network in Rapid City, city officials said.

Mitchell, meanwhile, is recovering from its own breach, which left city staff without computer access.

The three incidents — all hitting South Dakota local governments within weeks of each other — underscore a vulnerability that state officials have spent years and millions of dollars trying to address.

Local governments hold sensitive taxpayer data, but often lack the staff, budget or expertise to protect it from cyberattacks. A 2025 report by the Multi-State Information Sharing and Analysis Center found that 68% of state, local, tribal and territorial governments lack the budget to address major cybersecurity priorities, and that small and rural communities are especially vulnerable.

A state-funded program in South Dakota is working to close that gap — but time and money are running short.

State funding in place of declined federal funding

SecureSD is a $7 million program run by the South Dakota Attorney General’s Office and Dakota State University that delivers cybersecurity tools, training and technical support to local governments.

Lawmakers launched the program with funds in 2024 in response to Gov. Kristi Noem rejecting a piece of $1 billion in cybersecurity grants to states. Noem spokesman Ian Fury told South Dakota Searchlight at the time that the grants were “wasteful spending,” adding the administrative burden of the grant “would have far exceeded the allowable administrative cost.”

That 2022 4-year federal grant program, part of the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, faces an uncertain future. Congress extended the program through next month, but did not provide new funding. Efforts to reauthorize the program haven’t cleared both chambers.

South Dakota’s SecureSD program is led by Mike Waldner, who previously directed South Dakota’s centralized education email system.

The program reviews regular vulnerability reports from the Department of Homeland Security for local governments that sign up for the program, which flag issues like outdated software or misconfigured firewalls. It also helps transition local governments to more secure data and email, purchases equipment or contracts with information technology companies to monitor cybersecurity needs, and trains local employees. SecureSD also runs Project Boundary Fence, in which cybersecurity experts test local governments’ defenses and report back on weaknesses.

Most counties have participated in at least one aspect of the program, including Project Boundary Fence, and participation has “ramped up” in recent years, Waldner said.

“It’s like walking through a parking lot and checking doors. We’re not there to steal anything, but we’ll tell people when their doors are unlocked so they can fix it,” Waldner said.

The “hands down number one priority” of SecureSD, Waldner said, is moving local governments onto professionally managed email systems that meet federal security standards — a step up from the patchwork of local setups many counties currently rely on. 

More than half of county-level email addresses, based on a South Dakota Searchlight analysis of county auditor email addresses, are not on government domains, making them more vulnerable to attacks and impersonation. Only verified U.S.-based public sector organizations, including state and local governments, can get a .gov email address, and agencies must have advanced security protocols that make it harder for scammers to copy or fake official government messages.

“We’re working our tails off to remedy that and fix that, for a number of reasons,” Waldner said.

Rapid City is transitioning to a government, cloud-based email system using SecureSD funding, said Jim Gilbert, the city’s director of information technology. Katy Urban, public information officer with the Pennington County State’s Attorney Office, said the county is in the process of the same transition.

The $7 million in state funding for SecureSD expires June 30, 2028. Waldner said all of it will be spent — but once it runs out, local governments will have to absorb the cost of maintaining any improvements themselves. That uncertainty is “one of the biggest reasons an entity pauses” when considering cybersecurity upgrades, he said.

Waldner has had to prioritize the secure data and email transition as the expiration date nears. He said additional funding could eventually allow the program to expand into other areas, including cybersecurity management and data backup.

“My hope is we can secure funding and not only pay for the data and email solution, but pay for additional cybersecurity functions I know are needed,” Waldner said.

Future of state help for local governments

Sen. Randy Deibert, R-Spearfish, was among the lawmakers who championed the $7 million appropriation in 2024. A former Lawrence County commissioner, he said the program’s upcoming funding deadline was a built-in inflection point for the Legislature.

“It’s probably time to take a good look at that local government cybersecurity program and get an update on it for lawmakers: what’s working, what’s not, what should work,” Deibert said. “We should have some recommendations after a couple of years.”

Deibert said the original vision wasn’t just funding — it was to offer state-level IT support to counties that couldn’t afford their own, similar to how the state helped school districts move onto secure email systems. He noted that Lawrence County has been fortunate to have a strong IT person on staff, but acknowledged not every county is in that position.

“I’m not certain that throwing dollars at it is the key,” Deibert said.

Lt. Gov. Tony Venhuizen leads the Governor’s Resilience and Infrastructure Task Force. That group is evaluating South Dakota’s critical infrastructure — energy, water, data networks and more — and identifying vulnerabilities to natural disasters and cyberattacks. The task force discussed SecureSD at its August meeting and plans to recommend legislative proposals next session, including how to expand and continue the program.

“We haven’t made a final decision on what to propose, but it’s clear the need is still there and is going to still be there to continue to serve local governments in this way,” Venhuizen said.

The task force is also considering how much the state should require local governments to participate in cybersecurity programs, rather than leaving it voluntary.

Gov. Larry Rhoden recently awarded $500,000 to the task force to primarily fund research by Dakota State University and South Dakota Mines. The money is meant to build a map of the state’s critical infrastructure systems to identify vulnerabilities and redundancies. The funding will also support public education on cybersecurity and how residents can prepare for disruptions.

title: SD airport directors seek additional funding for construction projects
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: RAPID CITY —The directors of the Rapid City and Sioux Falls airports urged the state Thursday to provide additional financial support for their construction projects.
_full_text:
RAPID CITY —The directors of the Rapid City and Sioux Falls airports urged the state Thursday to provide additional financial support for their construction projects.

The two projects are already each set to benefit from $15 million in low-interest state loans, which the Legislature and Gov. Larry Rhoden authorized from a state housing infrastructure fund earlier this year. The loans carry 2% interest over 20-year terms, with repayments returning to the housing fund for future development projects. 

Rapid City Regional Airport Executive Director Patrick Dame and Sioux Falls Regional Airport Executive Director Dan Letellier briefed the South Dakota Aeronautics Commission about the expansion projects. They asked the commission to form a subcommittee to tour their facilities and discuss funding in more depth. 

Rapid City Regional Airport

Dame reported a record 452,195 passengers boarded commercial flights in Rapid City last year, up 5.8% and the airport’s third consecutive year of growth. 

He said gate congestion is a problem, including passengers standing in hallways due to a lack of seating. A shortage of overnight parking is also discouraging airlines from adding routes, he said.

“We actually do get notifications of upwards of 45-minute wait times to get through TSA,” Dame said, in addition to baggage being moved largely by hand and gate areas designed for 76-seat jets handling aircraft carrying up to 115 passengers.

A $70.6 million project to rebuild the Transportation Security Administration checkpoint, baggage screening, and ticketing areas is funded roughly 70% by federal sources, 25% local and 5% state. Dame said the new TSA checkpoint is scheduled to open in October.

The larger project is a $121 million addition of five gates. Forty million dollars is expected in federal funding. The rest of the funding is state and local, including the $15 million state loan.

“So there is a considerable amount of local funding going into this project, because our community views us to be a very important project and very instrumental to the future development of western South Dakota,” Dame said. 

However, Dame said inflation is taking a toll on project costs. He declined to name a specific amount of extra money he’d like to receive from the state, saying he’d rather work through a subcommittee, but when pressed he estimated “$5 million between the two airports.“

Sioux Falls Regional Airport

Letellier’s Sioux Falls Regional Airport presentation centered on its $135 million project to expand the terminal, runways and taxiways, and to relieve capacity and gate constraints. 

“We’ve seen consistent passenger growth, really for the last 25 years, averaging 3.5% per year,” Letellier said. 

He said gate areas built for 50 to 60 people are now serving flights carrying 180 passengers, and that the existing concourse is “grandfathered” against current fire code standards and would fail them if rebuilt as-is.

The airport has secured $83.9 million in federal funding, with another $5 million requested. State funding stands at $3.5 million, plus the anticipated $15 million loan. Local funding is projected between $47 million and $50 million. Although Lettelier’s presentation described a $135 million project, the various requested and obtained funding sources add up to almost $160 million.

Separately, Letellier said talks earlier this year with Southwest and American Airlines about new routes cooled after fuel prices spiked amid the Iran war, causing airlines broadly to reassess their schedules.

Beyond that, Letellier asked the commission to support additional state funding — either as a match for federal grants already received, or toward an $8.5 million terminal reconstruction project that is $5 million unfunded.

title: Meade Co. approves TIF 2 refinancing
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — An approval to refinance Meade County’s first tax increment finance (TIF) district will come with restrictions that the refinancing package cannot add additional debt.
_full_text:
STURGIS — An approval to refinance Meade County’s first tax increment finance (TIF) district will come with restrictions that the refinancing package cannot add additional debt.

On Tuesday, Kent Hagg, of Elk Creek Properties, asked the Meade County Commission to approve refinancing what is officially known as TIF 2, which was approved in 2015. The original amount of the TIF was about $10 million, scheduled to be paid off in 2035. It primarily included widening and paving a portion of 141st Street and repairing a bridge. The TIF total is at about $1.88 million, and is on track to be paid off about 3 or 4 years early.

A tax increment finance district is a public financing system that uses future increases in property tax to reimburse the costs of public improvements built within a designated TIF boundary. The value of all the properties inside the district is assessed or calculated and the total amount of property tax generated by all those properties is noted — the base amount of property tax revenues. All property revenue above this base amount, for the life of the TIF, is captured by the TIF to refund the costs of the public improvements or project. This amount — the amount over the base — is called the “tax increment.” Over time, property values are presumed to increase in part due to infrastructure improvements brought about by the TIF project itself. When the TIF is retired, the total taxation values revert to the original taxing entities. 

For example, if the city receives $1,000 from a property parcel before a TIF is enacted, it will continue to receive those funds for the life of the TIF, which is a maximum of 20 years. The next year, if the taxes go up to $1,100, the county will receive $1,000, while the increased $100 will be used to retire the TIF. 

The Elk Creek Properties development included with TIF 2 is located about 5 miles north of Rapid City, near Elk Creek Road and Haines Avenue.

Commissioner Talbot Wieczorek explained that while TIF districts can take up to 20 years to pay off, most commercial loans only have a term for 5 or 10 years. The loan for TIF 2 is scheduled to be due, which made refinancing necessary. But according to the project plan, refinancing the loan required the Meade County Commission’s approval.

Hagg said the improvements made with the TIF 2 resulted in rapid growth in the new subdivision, and because of that they expect the TIF to be paid off 3-4 years early.

“It’s a very healthy TIF,” Hagg said. “It’s a great example of a public/private partnership. It worked exactly how TIFs are supposed to work, and we’re proud of it and we appreciate Meade County being part of this.”

“It was remarkable what the improvements of paving streets did to sales,” said John Way, who oversaw the original TIF financing and now works as a consultant for Elk Creek Properties. “There are actually no lots left from the original development, so it did exactly what it was supposed to do.”

During discussion, Commissioner Doreen Creed pointed out that none of the current commissioners were sitting on the board when the original TIF was created in 2015. But Wieczorek, who was on the planning commission when the TIF was approved, said he has been continually frustrated about the lack of updates developers have shared about the project.

“A couple of times I have been frustrated that you put the county through thousands of hours of work to try and make the numbers work to justify the expense, and then after we spent thousands of dollars worth of time, you dropped more receipts on us that would have cleared it up much earlier,” he said. “Your record keeping and working with the county has been very frustrating for me and cost us a lot of extra work.”

Wieczorek also said since the county was not involved in refinancing negotiations with Legends West Bank of Spearfish, it was unclear whether a financing package at 7.5% interest includes further improvements to the development, such as a new water system. Wieczorek also expressed frustration that developers waited for interest rates to rise before bringing the refinancing package proposal to the county.

“A loan that is essentially guaranteed to pay off 3 years early should get better rates,” he said. “I appreciate your bank lending against the water system. But a note backed by government tax revenue that shows payoff likely to be 3 years early, I would think would be better terms than a much more high risk note on a development water system. For months we’ve know that this note’s coming due, and the fact that it takes a back burner while rates are creeping up bothers me more.

Wieczorek questioned whether Hagg shopped for better rates from other banks on just refinancing the TIF, without any other projects included. Hagg responded that he did approach other banks, but there are very few that finance TIF districts.

“There’s only a handful of banks that do TIF loans,” Way said. “Some people aren’t comfortable, regardless of the backing from the taxing authority of the county.”

Brian Hagg, who is also a partner in the development, said changes in county personnel have slowed communication, but overall the TIF has been successful.

“We have a momentum that I think has no changed the playing field,” he said. “We paid off millions of dollars. We’ve used our own resources. I apologize for any inconvenience in getting this thing to the finish line. The point of the matter, this is your first TIF. There was change over in county personnel. It’s taken a lot of focus and a lot of commitment. I respectfully request the approval of this assignment, because with that we can move forward with the program in a timely and efficient manner.”

Creed, who has been critical of TIF districts in the past, disagreed.

“I do not believe anything with this TIF has been timely and efficient, and it has tainted my view of ever going forward with more TIFs,” she said.

Following an executive session, during which commissioners discussed legalities of the refinanced TIF, the commission voted unanimously to approve the refinancing.

title: History comes alive at 58th BH Threshing Bee
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — The rumble of antique tractors, the whistle of steam engines and the rhythmic sound of a working sawmill brought agricultural history to life during the 58th annual Black Hills Steam and Gas Threshing Bee.  The Western Dakota Antique Club’s annual gathering featured vintage machinery, demonstrations, tractor pulls, a children’s pedal tractor pull, parades and other activities celebrating the equipment and traditions that helped build rural America.
_full_text:
STURGIS — The rumble of antique tractors, the whistle of steam engines and the rhythmic sound of a working sawmill brought agricultural history to life during the 58th annual Black Hills Steam and Gas Threshing Bee.  The Western Dakota Antique Club’s annual gathering featured vintage machinery, demonstrations, tractor pulls, a children’s pedal tractor pull, parades and other activities celebrating the equipment and traditions that helped build rural America.

John Deere equipment was the featured attraction this year, according to William Huston, vice president of the Western Dakota Antique Club.

“We had a variety of John Deere equipment from 1930 all the way up to 2022,” Huston said. “People got to see how things have evolved over nearly 100 years in farm equipment.”

The weekend began with a tractor drive Friday. Saturday’s activities included the children’s pedal tractor pull, antique tractor pull and the event’s largest parade. A church service opened Sunday’s schedule, followed by another parade and demonstrations throughout the grounds.

Huston estimated that more than 100 pieces of equipment participated in Saturday’s parade. “Saturday is always our biggest day, and it was a phenomenal show,” he said. “The weather was perfect.”

Among the popular demonstrations was a working sawmill powered by a belt connected to a tractor or steam engine. It takes four to six people to operate the mill, from rolling logs onto the skid and guiding them through the saw to removing the finished boards.  “You can walk in and see the sawmill in action,” Huston said. “We have bleachers there, so people can sit and watch it operate.”

Another centerpiece of the grounds is a massive Corliss steam engine housed in the club’s Corliss Building. Huston said the engine has a flywheel measuring approximately 18 to 20 feet in diameter.

The engine originally operated in Winchester, Idaho, where it ran a sawmill during the day and generated electricity for the town at night. It was brought to the Threshing Bee grounds in the late 1970s.

“The South Dakota National Guard set it up for us as a project, and then we built the building around it,” Huston said. “We operate it every year.”

The Threshing Bee began in 1969 when a group of antique-equipment enthusiasts gathered at the Alkali Community Hall. The first 3 shows were held there, and the Western Dakota Antique Club was formed to organize and continue the event. Huston said the Kenoyer family donated the club’s present grounds in 1973, and the show has been held there ever since.

The event continues to attract families and antique-machinery enthusiasts from across the region and throughout the country. Huston estimated that at least 1,000 people passed through the gates Saturday.

“You walk through the parking lot and see so many states represented,” he said.

One family traveled from Pennsylvania and Maryland and included an 11-year-old who was given the opportunity to drive a tractor in the parade.

“People come out just to see a certain person drive through the parade,” Huston said. “That’s pretty cool.”

The children’s pedal tractor pull has also become one of the event’s biggest attractions. Open to children ages 4 through 12, the competition features miniature pedal tractors pulling a small weighted sled.

A company from Reliance conducts the competition, and American Ag Equipment of Belle Fourche served as this year’s sponsor.

“It has really become a big hit for the show,” Huston said. “It’s awesome to watch all the kids participate. It also brings a completely new crowd to the Threshing Bee that may never have been here before.”

While children powered miniature tractors with their feet, Devin Soucy was preparing a full-size 1917 Waterloo steam traction engine for the parade.

Soucy, who attended the event with the Jacobs family, said the engine was manufactured in Waterloo, Ontario, and was brought to the Black Hills in the 1980s. It was completely restored and continues to be carefully maintained.

“It’s a whole year’s worth of work,” Soucy said. “We try to keep it looking nice and polish it up.”

Before the parade, Soucy used the engine’s water injectors and loaded logs into its firebox. He said the wood must be spread evenly to maintain consistent heat and prevent excessive wear in one area of the firebox.

The engine is operated at approximately 80 pounds of steam pressure, allowing it to run for 20 to 30 minutes before the fire must be replenished. 

Soucy said additional maintenance could eventually allow the engine to operate safely at 100 pounds, providing approximately an hour of work.

Steam traction engines once provided power for a variety of farm and industrial equipment. A large flywheel on the side of the boiler transferred power through belts to threshing machines, sawmills, rock crushers and other machinery.  “This was pretty much your everything power,” Soucy said.

Another unusual piece of machinery on display was a 1949 No. 3 Co-op tractor. The tractors were produced from the late 1930s into the early 1950s and assembled in St. Paul, Minnesota, for Farmers Union cooperatives.

Together, the restored tractors, steam engines and working exhibits offered visitors more than a static look at history. They showed how earlier generations farmed, built communities and powered the equipment needed for everyday life.

For Huston and other Western Dakota Antique Club members, keeping those machines operating and introducing them to younger generations remains at the heart of the Black Hills Steam and Gas Threshing Bee.

title: Lead to raise mill levy this year
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Limited developable space is one of the reasons city officials cited for a slight increase in the Lead property tax increase this year. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
IMG_1217.jpeg
Limited developable space is one of the reasons city officials cited for a slight increase in the Lead property tax increase this year. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

 IMG_1215.jpeg
Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

LEAD — Property owners in Lead will pay higher property taxes in 2027. 

As the city of Lead prepares to send its 2027 property tax request to the county by Sept. 1, Lead City Administrator Robin Lucero said the city plans to take the maximum allowable amount of property taxes. That means the mill levy will increase from 5.40 assessed in 2025 for taxes payable in 2026, to 5.48 assessed in 2026 for taxes payable in 2027.  

“We are taking the max request because we have unique circumstances with limited ability to generate growth due to our topography and relatively limited developable area,” Lucero said. “The growth that does occur creates additional demands on city infrastructure and services.” 

The 2027 mill levy is the first time there has been an increase since 2018, when the rate increased from 8.557 in 2017 to 8.610 in 2018. Since then, mill levies have been steadily decreasing in Lead. In 2024 the mill levy was at 5.734; in 2023 it was 6.341; in 2022 it was 6.449; and in 2021 it was at 8.256. 

According to the 2027 tax budget for the city of Lead, with a tax base of more than $284 million, the mill levy means the city will have about $1.56 million in property taxes to plan for when it starts budget discussions next month. In past years, the Lead City Commission has built a budget in July and August, certifying its property tax request to the county in September, based on budgeted amounts. Property taxes must be certified to the county by Sept. 1, so assessments can be distributed in October. 

But when it comes to budgeting, Lucero said state law allows cities to certify budgets to the state by November, giving officials more decision time for the upcoming year. This is the first year the city of Lead has moved its budget timeline. 

“This will give the city staff and elected officials a more complete financial picture before finalizing the following year’s budget,” Lucero said. “Under the previous timeline, we were essentially projecting revenues and expenditures for the remaining almost half of a year, while calculating next year’s budget off of those projections. The later budget timeline allows us to have more actual financial information available and make more informed projects, and thus more informed decisions.” 

Public meetings to discuss the 2027 budget will begin after the regular commission meeting, Sept. 21, with an introduction of the budget calendar, process, regulations and goals; a review of the city’s strategic plan; and a review of prior year’s performance and audit outcomes. On at 5:30 p.m. Sept. 28, commissioners will discuss the revenue outlook and economic forecast, employee wages, and review employee healthcare and benefit updates. After the city commission meeting, Oct. 5, city officials will discuss department head budgets and prioritize upcoming projects. 

At 5:30 p.m. Oct. 12, city officials will continue discussions of department head budgets. On Oct. 19 they will discuss nonprofit organization requests, and on Oct. 26 the city plans to have a draft budget to present for review and finalization. The first reading of the 2027 budget is scheduled for the Nov. 2 city commission meeting, and finalization is scheduled for Nov. 16.

title: SD faces lawsuit over proof-of-citizenship voter registration law
byline: By John Hult Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — A nonprofit organization and a Sioux Falls voter filed a lawsuit Monday in federal court over the implementation of South Dakota’s new proof-of-citizenship requirement for voter registration.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — A nonprofit organization and a Sioux Falls voter filed a lawsuit Monday in federal court over the implementation of South Dakota’s new proof-of-citizenship requirement for voter registration.

Senate Bill 175, passed by lawmakers and signed into law by Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden in March, requires documentary proof of citizenship from people registering to vote.

That proof can take forms including a birth certificate, passport, driver’s license, non-driver’s identification card or tribal identification card, or “any other type of acceptable documentary evidence of citizenship” under federal law. Photocopies are acceptable for any of the documents except driver’s licenses or state or tribal ID cards. 

People who don’t provide those documents are registered but receive a “federal-only” ballot, meaning one that lists only candidates for federal offices such as the president and Congress, but not state or local offices.

In addition to proof of citizenship, the new law requires a person to provide a physical address in South Dakota, other than a mail-forwarding service or post office box, to be registered for voting in state and local elections. That provision — enforceable at the time of registration or upon a request for an absentee ballot — targets people such as full-time recreational vehicle drivers who may receive forwarded mail and register their vehicles in the state but otherwise don’t live there.

An analysis of voter data by South Dakota Searchlight in May showed that about 1,500 people in South Dakota had been registered as “federal only.”

The lawsuit alleges that South Dakota’s rollout of the proof-of-citizenship requirement has disqualified eligible voters over erroneous minutiae and failed to offer them a realistic shot at fixing problems with their registration application.

The lawsuit asks a judge to force the state to: 

Accept photocopies of driver’s licenses, tribal IDs and nondriver IDs for voter registration.

Rescind guidance requiring in-person registration for people who use such IDs as proof of citizenship. 

Make sure registrants designated as federal-only are offered accurate explanations as to why they’ve been denied access to state and local ballots. 

Offer voters registered as federal-only an opportunity to challenge the designation. 

The lawsuit also seeks a ruling that the non-acceptance of photocopies for state and tribal IDs violates the U.S. Civil Rights Act, and asks the state to pay the plaintiffs’ attorney fees.

Group’s proposed rule changes previously rejected

The League of Women Voters is a nonpartisan, nonprofit group that holds registration drives, provides voter education and lobbies on voting rights issues.

Members of its South Dakota chapter argued before the state’s Board of Elections for rule changes earlier this summer that would have addressed the issues raised in their lawsuit. The board voted the changes down 5-2, ruling that the League lacked the legal standing to propose them.

The League’s lawsuit, which also includes a Sioux Falls man named Jaysen Hill as a plaintiff, names South Dakota Secretary of State Monae Johnson, the state Board of Elections and each board member as defendants.

The lawsuit says the League’s representatives have tried to work with Johnson’s office to fix what they see as issues with the law’s administration, but that her office has been unwilling to do so.

The complaint says Minnehaha County registered Hill as federal-only after he applied to register by mail, sending a photocopy of his state identification card in May. 

The card showed his address, the lawsuit says, but the letter he received telling him he’d be registered federal-only said he’d failed to provide a physical address. Hill was “confused” about the letter, which the lawsuit says is a form letter sent to those registered as federal-only.

Hill “now believes he was registered as a federal-only voter because he submitted a photocopy of a state identification card,” the lawsuit says, running afoul of the requirement to present the actual ID card.

“It was never made clear to Plaintiff Hill by any state or local officials that he was registered as a federal-only voter because he failed to provide documentary proof of citizenship, nor is it clear to Plaintiff Hill how he should go about fixing his application.”

Hill “was unable to participate” in the June 2 primary election, the lawsuit says. 

State says it’s yet to see lawsuit

Hill and the League are represented by lawyers from the American Civil Liberties Union of South Dakota and the ACLU Foundation, a lawyer from the Sioux Falls law firm Heidepriem Purtell Siegel Hinrichs, and attorneys for the Campaign Legal Center, a nonpartisan legal aid organization in Washington, D.C., founded more than two decades ago by a former member of the Federal Election Commission. 

Kathryn Johnson, president of the League of Women Voters’ South Dakota chapter, said in a press release that the state’s approach to the proof-of-citizenship issue “has not only effectively shut down our League’s ability to register new voters, but it has pointlessly caused voter confusion and made voting harder.”

Andrew Malone, a lawyer with the ACLU of South Dakota, said in the release that the case is about making sure the state’s new law is administered “in compliance with federal mandates.”

“There is no proof of widespread voter fraud or evidence of non-citizens voting that justifies a law that imposes burdensome show-your-papers requirements for eligible voters to cast their ballots,” Malone said.

Tony Mangan, spokesman for South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley, told South Dakota Searchlight on Monday evening that the office had yet to be served with the lawsuit.

Secretary of State Monae Johnson and a spokesman for her office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: Unlicensed vacation and short-term rentals to receive $200 per day fine in Pennington Co.
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: RAPID CITY —The Pennington County Planning and Zoning Department plans to begin mailing notices to vacation home rental (VHR) and short-term rental (STR) owners who are operating without a required county license.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

RAPID CITY —The Pennington County Planning and Zoning Department plans to begin mailing notices to vacation home rental (VHR) and short-term rental (STR) owners who are operating without a required county license.

Property owners who receive a notice of noncompliance with Pennington County will have until Dec. 3 to obtain the required license. After the deadline, rentals that continue to operate without a license may be subject to a $200-per-day fine.

The Pennington County Board of Commissioners previously gave VHR and STR operators a 6-month period, beginning June 3, to obtain the required license before enforcement actions begin.

“This notice is an important reminder to property owners who are operating without the required license that the compliance deadline is approaching,” said Brittney Hand, director of planning and zoning. “We want operators to take action now rather than wait until penalties begin accruing. A license costs $150 and is valid for three years, while operating without one after the deadline could result in a $200 fine for each day the property remains out of compliance.”

To help identify potentially unlicensed properties, Pennington County uses data provided by Deckard Technologies, a company specializing in short-term rental analytics and compliance services. 

Deckard uses publicly available information to identify active short-term rental listings and provides the county with information on property ownership and license status, booking trends, average rental rates, and rental platform usage. 

The data can also identify properties advertising occupancy levels that may exceed county regulations.

The county encourages property owners who receive a notice to contact the planning and zoning department with any questions and to complete the licensing process before the Dec. 3 deadline.

title: Hardrocker football captain’s  heroic action saves Texas teen
description: This summer, while back home in Houston, Jameson Mallon-Echols helped pull a teen from his former high school out of a burning vehicle. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Hardrocker football captain’s heroic action saves Texas teen.jpg
This summer, while back home in Houston, Jameson Mallon-Echols helped pull a teen from his former high school out of a burning vehicle. Courtesy photo  

RAPID CITY — For South Dakota Mines student-athlete Jameson Mallon-Echols, being a Hardrocker is more than what happens on the football field. 

Mallon-Echols, a junior from Houston, Texas, and mechanical engineering major, found himself in a situation where he had the opportunity to help someone in need – and he didn’t hesitate. 

On June 11, Mallon-Echols was driving to a friend’s house in Houston when he saw a car traveling in the opposite direction lose control, cross the median and crash. 

He pulled his car over, called 911 and ran straight towards the wreck. 

“It was just instinct,” Mallon-Echols said. “I saw it happen and just immediately ran in there.”

Three teenagers were inside the vehicle. The driver, a 16-year-old, was seriously injured and trapped inside. After getting the 2 other teenagers out of the vehicle, Mallon-Echols turned his attention to the driver. 

Then the vehicle caught fire underneath the driver’s seat.  

As more people arrived at the scene, he continued looking for a way to get the driver out. He used his shirt to try and put out the flames while the driver remained trapped inside. Eventually, another man was able to get the driver’s seat belt off. The 2 worked together to pull the teenager from the vehicle, but his legs were still trapped in the wreckage.

After removing pieces of metal that were holding him in place, they were finally able to get him out. 

The two men carried the teenager across the road and away from the vehicle. Shortly afterward, the car was completely engulfed in flames.

“The car was engulfed in flames seconds after we got him out,” Mallon-Echols said. 

Paramedics arrived shortly afterward and transported the teenager to the hospital. Mallon-Echols stayed at the scene into the early morning hours, answering questions from police before eventually heading home. 

“It was scary,” he said. “I was focused, didn’t freak out or lose my cool. That’s just who I am. That’s how I was raised.” 

It wasn’t until later that Mallon-Echols learned the driver was someone he had more in common with than he initially realized. 

Both attended Bridgeland High School in Houston. With nearly 4,000 students at the school, their paths never crossed, but both were athletes. The teenager was a soccer player entering his senior year.  

Mallon-Echols eventually learned that the teenager had survived and was recovering in the hospital. 

The driver’s younger brother found Mallon-Echols on Instagram and reached out to him. The family wanted to meet the person who had helped their son. 

“I was so grateful,” Mallon-Echols said. “His mom hugged me and was crying. She called me their guardian angel. It was an amazing moment.” 

The teenager suffered a broken spine and severe injuries to his arm and lost his leg as a result of the crash. 

For Mallon-Echols, meeting the teenager and his family provided a sense of relief. 

“They’re going to be part of my life forever,” he said. “I’m just so grateful I was able to help.” 

Mallon-Echols doesn’t consider himself a hero. He believes he simply did what he felt necessary in the moment. “Everyone thinks someone else is going to help,” he said. “Someone else is going to call 911. Someone else is going to pull them out of the car. Someone has to be that person that stops.” 

That instinct to help others is something Mallon-Echols credits to his upbringing. 

He said his mother taught him to recognize how fortunate he was growing up and to understand that he had the ability to help others.

The experience has also given Mallon-Echols a different perspective heading into his junior season with the Hardrockers. 

As a captain of the South Dakota Mines football team, Mallon-Echols understands that his role extends beyond what he does on the field.

“Everything I do represents Hardrocker football,” Mallon-Echols exclaimed. “This experience makes me appreciate my teammates and the time we have together.” 

That appreciation has carried into the way he approaches the upcoming season.

The workouts, the physical demands and the daily grind of college football have taken on a different meaning for Mallon-Echols after seeing how quickly life can change.

“Enduring the grind of the season is so easy now that I’ve seen how precious life is and how easy it is to be removed,” he said. 

For Mallon-Echols, the experience in Houston reinforced the importance of appreciating the opportunities he has — including the opportunity to play football and represent South Dakota Mines.

He doesn’t know why he happened to be driving down that road at that exact moment. 

He just knows that when he saw someone who needed help, he stopped.

title: BHSU student organizations recognized  with SD Board of Regents awards
description: SPEARFISH — Three Black Hills State University student organizations were recognized for their outstanding academic, community, and organizational achievements during the South Dakota Board of Regents meeting held on the BHSU campus in July.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — Three Black Hills State University student organizations were recognized for their outstanding academic, community, and organizational achievements during the South Dakota Board of Regents meeting held on the BHSU campus in July.

 buzz-marketing.jpg
Courtesy photo 

Buzz Marketing receives Academic Excellence Award

Buzz Marketing received the Board of Regents Award for Academic Excellence for its applied marketing and market research projects supporting BHSU enrollment initiatives.

Over the past several years, students in Buzz Marketing have worked closely with Dr. John Allred, vice president for Enrollment Management, applying concepts learned in the classroom to support the university’s strategic enrollment goals. The organization has completed program improvement projects for BHSU-Rapid City, the MBA program, and the College of Business, providing recommendations designed to strengthen program marketing and increase enrollment.

In addition to their research efforts, Buzz Marketing students have developed Instagram content for the College of Business based on their project findings and market analyses. The organization has received letters of recognition for all three major projects and continues to provide members with valuable hands-on learning experiences that prepare them for successful careers after graduation.

The award was accepted by Buzz Marketing members Phoebe Allbright, Rachel Manderscheid, as well as faculty member Adam Bailey.

 RHA.jpg
Courtesy photo 

Residence Hall Association earns Community Service Award

The Residence Hall Association (RHA) received the Board of Regents Community Service Award for its commitment to service and community engagement through its annual RA Auction fundraiser.

Now in its 12th year, the RA Auction raises funds for the Spearfish Volunteer Fire Department through the auction of donated prizes provided by Residence Life staff, resident assistants, and RHA executive team members. This year’s event was record-breaking, generating more than $900 to support the department and its efforts to keep both the campus and local community safe.

Beyond the auction, RHA members regularly volunteer throughout the Spearfish community through residence hall programs and small-group service projects. Their efforts include supporting nonprofit organizations, assisting local shelters, working with senior citizens, and participating in community cleanup activities.

The award was accepted by RHA member Liz Parsons and advisor Megan Kenney.

 psychology-club-award.jpg
Courtesy photo 

Psychology Club recognized for Organizational Leadership

The Psychology Club received the Board of Regents Organizational Leadership Award for its efforts to promote advocacy, awareness, student development, and campus engagement.

One of the organization’s signature initiatives is “Take Back the Night,” an event dedicated to raising awareness about sexual violence, supporting survivors, and connecting participants with resources.

In addition to its advocacy work, the Psychology Club creates opportunities for students to build connections with peers and faculty while developing leadership skills and confidence. Through events such as graduate school panels, students gain insight into academic and professional opportunities, including graduate programs, research experiences, and scholarships. The organization strives to foster an inclusive environment where students feel welcomed, supported, and empowered to succeed both academically and personally.

The award was accepted by Psychology Club member Kara Daum and faculty advisor Dr. Cheryl Anagnopoulos, chair of the School of Behavioral Sciences.

title: Rapid City man sentenced to 10 years in prison for receiving child pornography
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Conviction - Justice
Courtesy photo 

RAPID CITY — Hayden Sengua, 26, of Rapid City, was sentenced to 10 years and one month in federal prison, followed by 5 years of supervised release, and ordered to pay $15,685 in restitution and a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund, for receipt of child pornography. The court also ordered Sengua to forfeit his external hard drive and two cellular phones. 

Sengua was indicted by a federal grand jury in June 2025. He pleaded guilty on Jan. 21 and was sentenced by U.S. District Judge Camela C. Theeler Monday.  

Beginning in 2018 and continuing into January 2025, Sengua knowingly downloaded image and video files containing sexually explicit visual depictions of young children. 

Sengua saved the files on his cell phone, in his Google account, and on an external hard drive. 

Altogether, Sengua was found to be in possession of approximately 15,000 total media files depicting child sexual abuse. Some of the imagery Sengua collected depicts the sexual abuse of infants and toddlers, as well as the bondage and torture of minors. Sengua also used a virtual machine to attempt to hide his collection of child pornography. 

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse, launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. 

Led by the U.S. Attorneys’ Offices and the DOJ’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children, as well as identify and rescue victims. 

This case was investigated by the South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation’s Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC) Task Force, and the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office. Former Assistant U.S. Attorney Heather Knox and Assistant U.S. Attorney Kathryn N. Rich prosecuted the case. Sengua was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service, following sentencing. 

For more information about Project Safe Childhood, please visit https://www.justice.gov/psc.

title: Mexican national sentenced in federal court for illegal reentry after deportation
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
2 sentenced to life in prison for RC double homicide
Courtesy photo 

RAPID CITY — Angel Takashi Cano-Meza, 36, will be deported to Mexico after he pleaded guilty to illegal reentry after deportation on Aug. 17. 

That same day, he was sentenced to time served and imminent deportation by Chief Judge Roberto A. Lange in U.S. District Court. 

Cano-Meza, who was in the country illegally, has been deported twice before — once in 2022 and once in 2024.  

Cano-Meza was indicted for illegal reentry after deportation by a federal grand jury in July, after he was arrested in Pennington County for possession of a fictitious driver’s license, impersonation to deceive law enforcement, and open container in a motor vehicle. 

Local authorities notified Immigration and Customs Enforcement, who discovered Cano-Meza’s true identity and history of deportations. 

It is a federal felony for an alien to be in the United States after having been deported from the United States without obtaining the consent of the Secretary of the United States Department of Homeland Security and the Attorney General of the United States to apply for lawful admission into the United States. 

This case is part of Operation Take Back America, a nationwide initiative that marshals the full resources of the Department of Justice to stop illegal immigration and eliminate cartels. 

This case was investigated by the U.S. Department of Homeland Security Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office. Assistant U.S. Attorney Benjamin Schroeder prosecuted the case.

title: Despite record low in veteran homelessness, half the states saw increases
byline: By Robbie Sequeira Stateline
description: A veteran waves from a housing unit built exclusively for veterans by a Utah-based nonprofit. Despite national veteran homelessness reaching a record-low in 2025, half the states recorded increases during the January 2025 point-in-time count. Photo courtesy of USA Project Valor
_full_text:
Homeless veterans.jpg
A veteran waves from a housing unit built exclusively for veterans by a Utah-based nonprofit. Despite national veteran homelessness reaching a record-low in 2025, half the states recorded increases during the January 2025 point-in-time count. Photo courtesy of USA Project Valor 

Veteran homelessness dipped slightly from 2024 to 2025, according to the latest results from the January 2025 point-in-time count.

The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development counted 32,495 veterans experiencing homelessness, 387, or 1.2%, fewer than the previous year. HUD counted 18,877 veterans in shelters, and 13,518 living unsheltered in places not meant for habitation.

Twenty-five states recorded increases in veteran homelessness from 2024 to 2025, and 23 recorded decreases. Just 2 states — Alaska and Massachusetts — saw no change.

The state with the largest increase, by raw numbers, was Oregon, which saw 228 added veterans, a 16% increase. Pennsylvania saw an increase of 98 veterans, a 14% increase, while New York, with an additional 93 homeless veterans, had a nearly 8% increase.

The U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development counted 43 homeless veterans in South Dakota in 2025, up one from the previous year.

Mississippi had the largest percentage increase, rising 88%, going from 40 homeless veterans in 2024 to 75 a year later. Utah and Wyoming saw increases of 36% and 30%, respectively.

California recorded the largest numerical decline, with 624 fewer veterans experiencing homelessness, a 7% dip to 8,686. Florida declined by 192, while Indiana and Illinois each recorded 79 fewer homeless veterans. North Dakota’s numbers dropped 36% to 28 homeless veterans.

Since 2010, veteran homelessness has fallen by more than 56%, reaching an all-time low in 2025, and it’s been one of the few sustained decreases in any subset of homelessness during that time span. Details from this past January’s point-in-time count have not been released.

Adam Ruege, principal of policy and evaluation at Community Solutions, a national nonprofit that works with cities, counties and states to reduce homelessness, said the long-term decline resulted from sustained federal investments in housing and mental health services dating back to 2009. 

States have taken a bigger role in addressing veteran homelessness, with programs ranging from incentives for landlords, to coordinated services.

“Twenty years ago, being a veteran increased your likelihood of being homeless,” said Ruege, who previously worked for the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs. “What we’re seeing states do now, is that they are filling the gap between what the federal response isn’t doing and what localities can’t do because of funding constraints. 

In July, New Jersey announced that its Bringing Veterans Home initiative saw more veterans finding housing than entering homelessness. According to state officials, since the initiative launched in November 2024, it has permanently housed more than 2,500 veterans, backed by more than $30 million in state and federal money. There’s pending legislation to codify the program.

In March, the Minnesota Department of Veterans Affairs had a statewide by-name registry that allows agencies and service providers to coordinate individual cases instead of making veterans navigate programs independently. The registry, at last update, showed 150 veterans experiencing homelessness, dropping 25% in a year and 41% in two years.

States making efforts to incent or spur landlord participation in voucher and other housing programs, Ruege said, is one of the biggest steps toward getting veterans into permanent housing.

Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis approved a statewide measure in June that created a pilot program getting landlords to participate in a federal voucher program that compensates landlords for holding a vacant unit for up to 45 days while a veteran prepares to move in and reimburse up to $2,000 in qualifying property losses beyond the security deposit.

Maine Democratic Gov. Janet Mills signed a law in April that establishes an incentive program that can give grants to nonprofits for landlord and housing provider incentives, risk-mitigation payments and veterans’ past due rent.

“I think a big factor in their success has been recruitment of landlords,” said Ruege. “It’s just a matter of political and private will, and in some ways, the will of a landlord, to make strides in cutting down homelessness on the local level.” 

California announced $109.6 million in July for 278 permanent supportive homes across four communities, including 103 units reserved for veterans.

In March, Pennsylvania awarded about $805,000 from its Veterans’ Trust Fund to county agencies and nonprofits, including programs providing emergency housing assistance, residences, for veterans leaving homelessness and services for veterans exiting homelessness.

Erin Healy, a principal for large-scale change at Community Solutions, said veterans have often been treated differently from other groups experiencing homelessness.

“So, there is a sense of urgency around veteran homelessness, which doesn’t necessarily exist, even though it should, for all homelessness,” Healy said. “But we know these solutions and more empathy can still work for these other groups that are experiencing homelessness.”

Since the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2024 Grants Pass v. Johnson ruling gave governments greater latitude to enforce public camping restrictions, at least 14 states and more than 350 cities have adopted tougher laws targeting camping, sleeping or other activities associated with unsheltered homelessness. 

Indiana, for example, enacted a statewide public camping ban that took effect in July, while Georgia and Oklahoma have adopted laws that can hold local governments accountable for failing to enforce restrictions on public camping and related conduct.

South Dakota Searchlight staff contributed to this report.

title: Avian flu affects 77,700 SD birds, raising state’s 4-year outbreak total to 8.1 million
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Avian flu has returned to South Dakota hitting 2 flocks. One commercial turkey flock of 74,900 and one backyard flock of 2,800 birds. The standard practice is to euthanize the entire flock when the disease is discovered. Photo courtesy USDA
_full_text:
Avian flu had returned to South Daktoa.jpg
Avian flu has returned to South Dakota hitting 2 flocks. One commercial turkey flock of 74,900 and one backyard flock of 2,800 birds. The standard practice is to euthanize the entire flock when the disease is discovered. Photo courtesy USDA 

PIERRE – Bird flu has returned to South Dakota, with federal officials confirming detections in 2 flocks this month after nearly a month without U.S. cases.

The highly pathogenic avian influenza virus — H5N1, a strain that spreads quickly and kills birds rapidly — struck a flock of 74,900 commercial meat turkeys in Beadle County on Aug. 12 and a backyard flock of 2,800 birds in Brule County on Thursday. Euthanizing the entire affected flock is the standard practice when a detection is confirmed. 

The Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service of the U.S. Department of Agriculture tracks detections nationwide. Federal officials also confirmed the virus in 2 Idaho backyard flocks of 10 and 50 birds on Thursday.

The South Dakota Department of Health issued an alert Friday for potential human infections among patients who may have been exposed to infected animals. Providers should ask patients with flu-like symptoms — fever, chills, cough or sore throat — about recent contact with sick or dead animals, the alert said.

Since the national bird flu outbreak began in 2022, the virus has affected 8.1 million birds in South Dakota from 144 commercial flocks and 31 backyard flocks.

Federal policy requires officials to kill all birds at affected sites to prevent the virus from spreading to nearby farms. Former South Dakota State Veterinarian Beth Thompson told South Dakota Searchlight previously that “foaming” is the most common method in turkey barns, where foam is sprayed atop turkeys inside the barn to suffocate them.

Federal and state officials oversee the process, and the federal government reimburses farmers for their losses through indemnity payments.  

Avian influenza detections rise as wild birds spread the virus during seasonal migrations, which are underway.

title: City working to restore Wi-Fi for L-D football season
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: DEADWOOD — Deadwood city officials said they are working on restoring Wi-Fi capabilities at Ferguson Field to continue to allow Lead-Deadwood School District to live stream football games.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

DEADWOOD — Deadwood city officials said they are working on restoring Wi-Fi capabilities at Ferguson Field to continue to allow Lead-Deadwood School District to live stream football games. 

Lornie Stalder, director of public works and events, said the school district historically connected to Wi-Fi provided by the Days of ’76 Museum. After the museum changed internet providers, he said they chose to downgrade their internet capabilities to better suit their needs. That change in capability temporarily hindered the school’s ability to stream football games, but Stalder said the city is working on moving around existing equipment to continue to provide free internet to the school.

“I’m confident we will give them internet and a solution. I’m confident we will,” said Stalder. “It’s just a short window.”

Stalder said museums operated by Deadwood History, Inc., are leased from the city and are under no obligation to provide internet to the school. The school district currently leases Ferguson Field from the school, but the contract does not explicitly state the city is obligated to provide internet. However, Stalder said the city is excited about the school’s athletic season and is happy to work towards maintaining previous arrangements.

RAPID CITY — A Sturgis man convicted for receipt of child pornography and possession of child pornography, was sentenced to 6 years and 3 months in federal prison, followed by 5 years of supervised release, Aug. 17. 

United States Attorney Ron Parsons announced Wednesday that Carl Wahl, 55, received the sentence from Chief Judge Roberto A. Lange, of U.S. District Court. Wahl is also ordered to pay a $100 special assessment to the Federal Crime Victims Fund for each charge, as well as $30,285 in restitution. 

A federal grand jury indicted Wahl for the charge in February 2025. He pleaded guilty on April 1, 2026. 

Between May and August 2023, the South Dakota Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force received CyberTips for investigation. A search warrant for Wahl’s residence and electronic devices was obtained. Several of Wahl’s electronic devices, including his HP laptop and his 2 cell phones, were examined and all 3 devices contained visual depictions of child sexual abuse material that Wahl knowingly and intentionally viewed, possessed, and received using the Internet. 

This case was brought as part of Project Safe Childhood, a nationwide initiative to combat the growing epidemic of child sexual exploitation and abuse, launched in May 2006 by the Department of Justice. Led by the U.S. Attorney’s Offices and the DOJ’s Child Exploitation and Obscenity Section, Project Safe Childhood marshals federal, state, and local resources to locate, apprehend, and prosecute individuals who exploit children, as well as identify and rescue victims. 

This case was investigated by the South Dakota Division of Criminal Investigation’s Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC) Task Force, the Rapid City Police Department, and the Pennington County Sheriff’s Office. Former Assistant U.S. Attorney Heather Knox and Assistant U.S. Attorney Connie Larson prosecuted the case. 

Wahl was immediately remanded to the custody of the U.S. Marshals Service.

title: 3 injured in 2-vehicle crash at  North Ave. and Rd. intersection
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — Three people were injured, and one person had to be extricated from his vehicle after a crash at the intersection of North Avenue and Ryan Road, just after 3 p.m. Tuesday. Spearfish police and fire departments responded to the 2-vehicle collision and found one vehicle emitting smoke.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — Three people were injured, and one person had to be extricated from his vehicle after a crash at the intersection of North Avenue and Ryan Road, just after 3 p.m. Tuesday. Spearfish police and fire departments responded to the 2-vehicle collision and found one vehicle emitting smoke. 

According to the results of an initial investigation, a 2022 Chrysler Pacifica that had been traveling southbound on North Avenue was waiting to turn east onto Ryan Road. The SUV appears to have turned, colliding with a 1994 Chevrolet S10 pickup that was traveling north on North Avenue. 

Both vehicles sustained front-end damage, and the Chrysler Pacifica came to rest in the ditch adjacent to North Avenue, in front of Dana Dental.

Both drivers and a passenger were injured in the crash, and transported by ambulance to Spearfish Monument Health Hospital. The driver of the Chevrolet had to be extricated from his vehicle and was later transferred from the Spearfish hospital to Rapid City Monument Health Hospital. 

The driver of the Chrysler Pacifica, a 78 year-old female from Michigan, was cited for failure to yield.

“Be patient and aware of oncoming traffic when waiting to turn,” said Spearfish Police Chief Collin Smith, in a joint statement with the Spearfish Fire Department. “This collision is still under investigation. We would like to thank the Spearfish Emergency Ambulance Service, the Spearfish Fire Department, and Sunshine Towing for their response.”

title: Tupper honored for service to agriculture,  rural communities
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: Justin Tupper was awarded the Rural Neighbor Award at the Central States Fair on Monday in Rapid City.  Pictured are Tif Robertson, left, emcee, of the event, Tupper, and Quinten Regan. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
1... ag.JPG
Justin Tupper was awarded the Rural Neighbor Award at the Central States Fair on Monday in Rapid City.  Pictured are Tif Robertson, left, emcee, of the event, Tupper, and Quinten Regan. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

RAPID CITY — For Justin Tupper, supporting rural communities means more than talking about what needs to be done. It means being willing to get involved.

Tupper, owner and manager of the St. Onge Livestock Auction, received the Rural Neighbor Award during the fourth annual Ag Appreciation Night at the Central States Fair.

The award recognizes an individual who has made outstanding contributions to the Central States Fair and Black Hills Stock Show while making a lasting impact on agriculture and rural communities.

Tupper has dedicated his career to serving cattle producers and the livestock marketing industry.

Since taking over management of St. Onge Livestock in 2007 alongside his wife Brooke, Tupper has helped develop the business into one of the region’s trusted livestock markets, building relationships with cattle producers throughout the area.

He also serves as president of the United States Cattlemen’s Association, representing independent cattle producers and advocating on issues affecting the U.S. beef industry.

During the award presentation, Tupper was recognized for his willingness to work with livestock producers, agricultural organizations and industry partners at the local, state and national levels.

After receiving the award, Tupper said community service has always been important to him.

“What a privilege and an honor to be awarded that,” Tupper said. “Community service is something I believe in very deeply, and it’s really the fabric of rural America.”

Tupper recalled an experience from his younger years that helped shape his philosophy toward community involvement.

“I remember when I was young, one time I was bitching about the local school board, and somebody said, ‘Put up or shut up,’” Tupper said. “I’ve remembered that all my life.”

That lesson, he said, taught him that people who want their communities and organizations to improve also need to be willing to contribute.

“I really believe that if you can contribute, you need to really get in there and dig in,” Tupper said. “It’s a great thing, and sure a privilege and an honor to receive this award.”

Ag Appreciation Night celebrates agriculture and rural life while recognizing people and businesses that have made significant contributions to the region.

A complimentary meal was served during the event with help from several public officials, including U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds, U.S. Rep. Dusty Johnson, Gov. Larry Rhoden, Attorney General Marty Jackley, Rapid City Mayor Jason Salamun and Pennington County Sheriff Brian Mueller.

title: Otter, Racoon Road projects bid at nearly $300K less than engineer estimate
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Work to improve Otter and Racoon roads is expected to be completed by Nov. 14, after the Sturgis City Council awarded the bid for the project on Monday. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
OTTER ROAD.jpeg
Work to improve Otter and Racoon roads is expected to be completed by Nov. 14, after the Sturgis City Council awarded the bid for the project on Monday. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

STURGIS — Bids for the Otter Rod and Raccoon Road street improvement project came in well under the engineering estimate, Sturgis Public Works Director Rick Bush said. 

On Monday, Bush reported that 5 bids on the project came in substantially less than the total project estimate of $746,073 from Brosz Engineering. That amount included a 10% contingency. Without the contingency, the Brosz estimated construction cost was $678,248. 

The city provided options for contractors to bid on a schedule 1, which required the project to be completed by Nov. 14, or a schedule 2 that would allow contractors to push the work into their future plans with a completion date of June 30, 2027. 

The Sturgis City Council approved a bid from Woelber Excavating, LLC to complete the project this year for $452,529, which was about 39% less than the engineering estimate. The Belle Fourche company submitted the only bid to complete the project this year. 

Other bids were to schedule the project for a June 2027 completion, and ranged from $496,596 to $558,738 in cost. 

While some council members expressed concern about the difference between the engineering estimates and actual bids, Councilman Jesse Blakeman said the 5 contractor bids made him feel better, since they were all close in price. 

“If they (Woelber Excavating) were the only ones low, and the rest were high, that would be concerning to me,” Blakeman said. 

Bush explained that many companies could have locked in their oil prices for the asphalt before prices went up, resulting in the lower bids. 

The Otter and Raccoon roads street improvement project will include substantial rehabilitation for the roadway, including roadway excavation and shaping, full depth reclamation, salvaging and re-using existing asphalt and granular materials, placement of geogrid reinforcement, putting down an aggregate base and new asphalt pavement, concrete improvements, pavement markings, erosion control, and traffic control. 

Bush said the project will start at Vanocker Road, near the Sturgis Animal Shelter, and continue to the west. The road work was identified as a priority project for 2026. 

“The project represents a significant reconstruction of 2 aging city streets and will improve pavement condition, roadway structural integrity, drainage, and long-term serviceability,” Bush said.

title: With an eye on enrollment: Here’s an introduction to the 2 new members of the Belle Fourche School Board
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Wendy Bowers
_full_text:
Wendy Bowers.jpg
Wendy Bowers 

 Nathan Juelfs.JPEG
Nathan Juelfs 

BELLE FOURCHE — This school year is going to be a little different for Wendy Bowers. Her son graduated from Belle Fourche High School in the spring, and this fall she’s taking her seat on the school board.

“It’s a different perspective, being on the board versus being a parent. I’m excited to learn more about how things operate,” Bowers said.

A Belle Fourche High School grad herself, Bowers has been active in community organizations for years. She’s sat on the board for the Belle Fourche Chamber of Commerce _ she currently serves on the Belle Fourche Development Corporation; she’s treasurer of the Bronc Bird Busters and the South Dakota Chapter of the American Foundation for Suicide Prevention.

“We’ve got a solid board,” Bowers said of her newest role. She said she did not join because of any particular complaints or concerns — rather, she hoped to help effect positive change.

Retired Army National Guardsman Nathan Juelfs, who also joins the board this year, ran for similar reasons.

“It is about planning for the future,” Bowers said. 

“I’d been approached on a couple of different occasions, whether it be for school board or city council, county commission,” Juelfs said. “It is my time to step up and meet those opportunities as a good citizen.”

A father of 4 daughters, all of whom attended school in Belle Fourche, Juelfs stepped up and joined the school board because he felt it was an important part of fulfilling his civic duty.

“It is about planning for the future,” Juelfs said.

A healthy school district is an important element of community development, Bowers said.

“If the school goes south, the community will follow,” Bowers said.

A community that offers quality education is more likely to attract and retain young families, and by extension a more robust workforce and economy, she noted.

Both Juelfs and Bowers say one of the biggest issues facing the school district is declining enrollment.

“A lot of that is connected to those individuals that are choosing to homeschool. Our homeschool numbers continue to rise, lowering the numbers of students in the school district,” Juelfs said. “I don’t think homeschooling is a bad thing; it just takes students out of our classrooms, and then that affects funding as well.”

“Enrollment and funding are a huge concern,” Bowers added. “Funding affects programming and staff retention.”

Now that the school year is kicking off, work on addressing those issues can begin. Both new members told the Pioneer that the first step is getting settled and getting their footing on the board.

title: Lawrence County Commissioners  approve county sales tax
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Lawrence County commissioners voted to approve a new county sales tax Tuesday, implementing property tax relief to owner-occupied properties. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
Lawrence County implements property tax relief.jpg
Lawrence County commissioners voted to approve a new county sales tax Tuesday, implementing property tax relief to owner-occupied properties. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

DEADWOOD — Lawrence County commissioners Tuesday approved Ordinance 2026-01, implementing a half-cent county sales tax that will generate revenue for property tax relief for owner-occupied houses.

Counties were given the opportunity to implement the additional tax with the passing of Senate Bill 96 in March. The new tax will apply to all taxable purchases, excluding some agricultural purchases and health-associated costs like doctors’ visits, hospital stays, prescription medications, and surgeries.

Commissioner Eric Jennings said the South Dakota Department of Revenue estimates that the county could make approximately $6 million in revenue. However, he said that estimate tracks only taxes generated in municipalities. 

“Lawrence County has a lot of sales tax collections outside of the municipalities,” said Jennings. “Think about winter sports recreation, activities that go on, and industries that we have that have to pay a sales tax. It certainly could be more than $6 million, but it could be less.”

Jennings said according to 2024 valuations of owner-occupied properties and the estimated $6 million in revenue, the tax could provide up to 70% relief of the county portions of property tax. 

“Remember that of the total property tax bill, there’s only about 23 – 25% of that total bill that is the county’s share,” said Jennings. “So, 70% of that would be reduced through the property tax reduction sum of the sales tax.”

Jennings said the amount of relief taxpayers receive will be based on their valuation. 

“We’ll take the total amount of the sales tax generated and divide that by the total amount of valuation and come up with a tax credit based on that number,” he said.

Jennings said commissioners have 2 options when deciding how to implement relief to property owners. Commissioners can choose to implement relief on property taxes payable in 2027 using an estimated revenue number or may choose to wait until a full year of taxes are collected and implement relief on taxes payable in 2028.

“If we project the amount of tax that we request for that property tax relief fund, we could offer a credit in 2027,” he said. “The risk to the county is if we don’t achieve those revenue estimates, that would put the county in a negative revenue situation and run us out of money,” he said. “If we wait for a year and apply the property tax relief to taxes payable in 2028, we will know exactly what that amount is going to be and offer all of that amount to the property tax relief. In that scenario, people are going to be paying the sales tax for a full year before they see any property tax relief.”

The new sales tax will be implemented Jan. 1, 2027.

Jennings said how the county will implement the relief is expected to be voted on by commissioners before December.

Implementing the new property tax will require the county to change their software to track and bill the property taxes. According to Senate Bill 96, counties are allowed to withhold 2% of all revenue in the first year to cover those costs. 

“The county actually built their own software package that they use to administer property tax,” said Jennings. “We’ll have to keep track of that time. Our staff is going to have to work a little harder. They have full-time jobs now, and then you throw an extra task onto them, it takes more time after hours. We have an excellent (internet technology) department, and I’m fully confident they can handle the situation. We’re very lucky to have the staff we do in that regard.”

Ordinance passed 3-2

Commissioners passed the ordinance 3-2, Jennings and Commissioner Tim Comer voting opposed. Commissioners Bob Ewing, Rick Tysdal, and Brandon Flanagan voted to pass the ordinance.

Before voting, Jennings said he’d been struggling to make a decision on the ordinance.

“I’ve given this ordinance a lot of thought in the past 10 or more months. Given that much time to consider the issue, I had not reached a decision until a few days ago,” he said. “On one had, we do have homeowners in Lawrence County who, due to increased demand for housing in our county, has driven up the valuation of their home which in turn has driven up the property tax. In many cases, this is affecting homeowners who are living on a fixed income and do not have the ability to generate additional income. There’s no doubt they need some relief. On the other hand, we have residents who are living near or below the poverty line. These residents are typically renting their living arrangements and will not experience the property tax relief they are being asked to help pay for through an increased sales tax.”

Jennings said he has received countless emails, letters, and phone calls in the last few months, all with different concerns.

“Some will argue the population in the lower income brackets have assistance programs to help them along. That is true, but an additional sales tax represents another hurdle for them to climb over,” he said. “Even more challenged are the ones that are just over the income level limits for assistance programs, but they’re struggling to make ends meet. These are our residents who are filling important jobs in our community, and we need to create an environment for them to succeed, not make it more challenging.”

Jennings argued that an additional sales tax would create an additional challenge to private contractors and industries within the county.

“While a county sales tax would provide some property tax relief, I don’t feel it would provide enough of a difference to homeowners to justify the effects on the lives on non-homeowners, businesses, and industries.”

Comer said that he takes his position as a county official seriously, and makes his decisions based on analyzing information, data, and reading every email and letter presented to him. 

“My vote will be coming down to this: I will be supporting what I have concluded is best for the entire population of the people that make up Lawrence County,” Comer said. 

Commissioner Brandon Flanagan said he’s struggled with the decision, believing the ordinance will cause pain whether it’s passed or denied.

“I’d like to think smarter people than me help put this together, but I’m not sure that’s the case,” said Flanagan. “It may be the only feasible way to do some property tax relief. It’s unfortunate that it hurts the way it does. I’ve seen other states that are trying to do what they think will help by cutting services. That’s hard, from this board’s perspective, to do.”
