title: Average BH Energy customer faces potential $45 increase in monthly bill
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: A sign identifies the location of the Lange II natural gas-powered electrical generation plant under construction in northwestern Rapid City. Photo by Seth Tupper, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Average Black Hills Energy customer faces potential $45 increase in monthly bill.jpg
A sign identifies the location of the Lange II natural gas-powered electrical generation plant under construction in northwestern Rapid City. Photo by Seth Tupper, South Dakota Searchlight 

RAPID CITY — The average Black Hills Energy residential electric customer in South Dakota faces a monthly bill that will be $45 higher if state regulators approve a pending rate increase and surcharge.

The company’s latest application this month seeks to add a monthly surcharge of $19.70 for the average residential customer, to recoup costs for the $320 million construction of the Lange II natural gas-powered electrical generation plant in northwestern Rapid City. The company has said the plant will meet growing power demands from current customers following the planned retirement of the 1960s-era Ben French plant, and is not in response to any proposals for data center construction. 

“Our most important responsibility is providing safe, reliable energy to our customers and communities,” said Wes Ashton, vice president of South Dakota and Wyoming utilities for Black Hills Energy, in an Aug. 5 news release. “Lange II will replace the Ben French units as a critical system resource to serve customers while enhancing the reliability of our Black Hills Energy electric system.”

The company plans to start collecting the surcharge in December, when the new plant is expected to start delivering power. If the state Public Utilities Commission has not made a decision by then, the company could collect the surcharge on an interim basis, subject to refunds for customers later if the commission rejects or reduces the surcharge. The commission would then review the surcharge annually.

The surcharge would come on top of a general rate increase that Black Hills Energy is requesting of about $25 per month for the average residential customer. That proposal would generate $50.6 million in additional annual revenue for the company, which serves roughly 75,000 customers in western South Dakota and also serves customers in seven other states. The company has said the rate increase is justified by infrastructure investments, inflation and the lack of a rate increase since 2014. 

“Our electric base rates have been unchanged for more than a decade, allowing our customers to experience rate stability, which is a priority for us,” said Lynn Kendall, regional public affairs manager for Black Hills Energy. “We are requesting this rate review because it’s necessary for us to update rates to account for the critical investments and improvements we’ve made to our system over the past 12 years, while also accounting for the increased operating costs to serve our customers.”

The company began collecting the higher rate on an interim basis Aug. 18, because the Public Utilities Commission did not make a decision within a 180-day review period. Customers would receive refunds if state regulators ultimately reject the increase or approve a smaller increase. 

Rapid City resident John McKee submitted comments to the commission about the proposed rate increase in March, writing that the increase would “directly and materially affect my household’s financial obligations, energy access, and long-term cost stability.” He warned that higher rates could impose “significant financial burdens” on residential customers.

Commission documents show that if both requests are approved at the proposed amounts, the average residential customer’s monthly bill would rise from $98.96 to $143.70 — a 45% increase. 

A group representing some of Black Hills Energy’s largest South Dakota customers, including Monument Health, manufacturers, and mining and materials companies, has filed comments in both commission proceedings. The group wrote that the proposed surcharge would “greatly increase” its members’ cost of doing business.

In addition to its surcharge and rate request to the Public Utilities Commission, Black Hills Energy’s parent company, Black Hills Corp., is pursuing a merger with Sioux Falls-based NorthWestern Energy. Among the states affected by the merger, Montana is the only one in which regulators have not yet approved it.

title: 90 years of Iron Creek Lake campground
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Sleep family, some members pictured here, have owned and operated the land around Iron Creek Lake and the campground for 90 years. Photo courtesy of Jodi Sleep
_full_text:
1 90 years of Iron Creek Lake.jpeg
The Sleep family, some members pictured here, have owned and operated the land around Iron Creek Lake and the campground for 90 years. Photo courtesy of Jodi Sleep 

 2 90 Years of Iron Creek lake.jpeg
Richard Sleep, pictured with his children Jeff, Matthew, and Melissa, operated the Iron Creek Lake Campground for 50 years with his wife, Karen Sleep. Photo courtesy of Jodi Sleep 

SPEARFISH — For nearly a century, families and outdoor enthusiasts have been traveling up Tinton Road, venturing into the woods, and spending quality recreation time at the Iron Creek Lake Campground. 

Jeff and Jodi Sleep, owners of the campground and store, are inviting the neighboring communities to come celebrate 90 years of slowing down and making memories at the lake at 5 p.m. Saturday. 

Jodi said the celebration will include free roast beef sandwiches and birthday cake while supplies last, with live music from local artists. Guitarist and vocalist Alvin McAmis and pianist Emily Beiler are scheduled to entertain.

“We’re going to have a campfire. If there’s a fire ban, we’ll have a propane campfire,” said Jodi. “We’ll do an old-fashioned singing with the guitar around the campfire.”

Jodi said lovers of the area are invited to bring their photos and memories to share and compare their stories to old newspaper clippings.

Building a family legacy

Jeff said it’s a little bit of a family mystery how his great-grandfather, Alfred Sleep, managed to create a family legacy around the lake. He said in 1936, a group of sportsmen, Lawrence County, and the chambers of commerce for Spearfish, Lead, and Deadwood, were looking to build a dam in the area of Iron Creek Lake in an effort to mitigate flooding in Spearfish. 

“We don’t know exactly what happened, but somewhere along the line he bought the mineral claim from a guy in Nebraska at the same time that Lawrence County bought the land that the lake went on,” said Jeff. “He was also buying other mineral claims in the Black Hills, around Tinton, so the best I know is he had some vision of doing some recreational things with the land.”

Jodi said according to old newspaper clippings, the intention of the sportsman’s groups and surrounding chambers of commerce was to create a major recreation destination.

Between 1968 and 1969, Jodi said Lawrence County purchased the lake for $1 from the sportsman’s groups and chambers of commerce.

“They were better equipped to manage it and handle all the issues that go along with owning a lake,” she said. “So, the campground is the private property from 120-feet back from the shoreline. 

The land around the lake, running from 120-feet from the shoreline, is owned by an LLC, shared by the Sleep siblings and extended family, and the campsite has been run by the Sleep family for 6 generations. She said operation of the campground passed from Alfred to his son, Eugene, who passed it on to Richard and Karen Sleep. The couple operated the campground and store for 50 years before passing operation duties on to Jeff and Jodi. Their daughter and son-in-law, Sydney and Ben Meyers, live at the lake full-time and manage the campsite and store while raising a family today.

Over the decades, the Sleep family would expand the campground and store. The area grew from a few private cabins and campsites to more long-term, full-service sites, trailer sites, and a toboggan run. 

“There wasn’t quite enough snow, consistently, to have a toboggan run,” said Jeff. “But there was a new store built in the 1960s and more campsites were developed over the last 90 years.”

Keeping memories and traditions alive

Jeff said he has fond memories of his childhood at the lake. Fishing, exploring with friends, and spending Sunday afternoons floating the lake on tubes. 

“We have a lot of good memories up there, and we continued those memories with our kids,” he said. 

Jeff said one man from North Dakota recently approached him, who told him he’s been camping at Iron Creek Lake over the summers for more than 60 years. 

“There are numerous people like that, that have spent most of their life coming down and enjoying the lake in some fashion,” said Jeff. “It’s a nice, quiet place. It’s not overdeveloped, it’s still rustic and peaceful.”

Jeff and Jodi said their intentions for the future of Iron Creek Lake Campground are to keep the lake rustic, underdeveloped, and accessible to everyone who can make the drive.

“We want something that everybody can enjoy,” said Jeff. “It’s affordable to anyone that wants to come. It’s not a situation that’s only for exclusive people. It’s for everybody.”

Jodi said her family is extremely grateful for the opportunity to provide lasting memories for families and lovers of the outdoors. 

“It’s a cool opportunity to be involved with the lake, just because there’s so many families and people, not just in the area but from quite a ways away, that have such fun memories and it’s a favorite destination for a lot of people,” said Jodi. “It’s such a privilege to be able to continue those traditions for people and keep it family friendly and accessible to anybody.”

title: Police caution drivers  and students as school gets underway
byline: By Neil Whitney Black Hills Pioneer
description: School is back in session, and area law enforcement officers are cautioning kids and drivers alike to look twice. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
Back to school safety.JPG
School is back in session, and area law enforcement officers are cautioning kids and drivers alike to look twice. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

SPEARFISH — As school comes back into session, it can feel like people move in haste. Parents are hurrying to drop kids off so they can get to work, other kids are hurrying to get to the bus stop, and bikes move faster than ever when kids race to school. 

With an increase in traffic in the morning and in the afternoon, the heightened chance of an accident between a kid and a driver can worry parents. The Spearfish Police Department wants the public to know that there are still things that citizens can do to help keep students and children out of harm’s way. 

The department reminds drivers and pedestrians to be more alert when in school zones, and that kids may not be attentive at times.

“Expect the unexpected, as children can be unpredictable and are not always aware of their surroundings,” department officials said in a prepared statement. 

They also want parents to be aware of the impression that they leave on their kids. If a kid sees that their parents are being safe, they might start acting safer themselves. 

“Be a good role model, especially when you are with your kids. Always buckle up in the car, always wear a helmet when biking, and always follow pedestrian safety rules,” according to the department. 

In fact, the entire Black Hills region is making sure that everyone is being safe around this time of year. In Deadwood, Cory Shafer, chief of police, is instilling good principles into the public.

“In light of kids returning to school, the department encourages and reminds all parents, drivers and students to make safety their top priority … to be patient, attentive, and considerate of everybody around them,” he said.

To the point of attentiveness, Shafer wants to make it clear that cell phone distractions are among the more important things to be aware of and is a habit that people should break when walking and driving. 

“Students walking with a cell phone or drivers with cell phones in hand, paying attention to those distractions.” 

Classes started in the Lead-Deadwood School District Wednesday and start in Spearfish and the Meade School District today. In Belle Fourche, school started Aug. 20.

title: Lawmakers discuss regionalization as a possible solution for local ambulance problems
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: A state summer study panel has looked at possible legislation to support ambulance services across the state. Pioneer file photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
IMG_9459.JPG
A state summer study panel has looked at possible legislation to support ambulance services across the state. Pioneer file photo by Sierra Ferguson 

PIERRE — State healthcare officials told South Dakota lawmakers this week that coordination among neighboring communities could strengthen local emergency medical services that are struggling with staffing and funding.

“This is truly critical to the transformation of EMS in South Dakota,” said Emily Kiel, director of the state Department of Health’s Division of Healthcare Access.

An 11-member task force of state lawmakers that met Monday is using the summer to consider ideas for legislation to support ambulance services across the state. Some services struggle with managing human resources or billing services, said Marty Link, deputy director of the Division of Healthcare Access, and regionalization could lighten the load of administrative tasks.

Regionalization involves sharing resources and functions among ambulance services across a specific geographical area, Link said. It also involves sharing recruitment and retention efforts such as training, continuing education and leadership development.

Kiel told lawmakers that regionalization could eventually lead to a stronger workforce.

“A strong workforce doesn’t simply mean obtaining a magic number of people on a roster,” she said. “A strong workforce understands a patient’s needs and anticipates downstream care priorities.”

Department officials plan to use a portion of South Dakota’s funding over the next five years from the federal government’s Rural Health Transformation Program to support regional emergency medical services hubs. South Dakota has received $189.5 million from the program so far.

Congress included the program in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, in response to concerns that the bill’s Medicaid cuts would hurt rural health providers. Medicaid is a federal-state program that provides health insurance for people with disabilities or low incomes.

The Department of Health consulted with the South Dakota Foundation for Medical Care to design a regional hub system, which could be supported over the coming years with federal funding. But the question lawmakers must answer is how to fund that system long-term, after the rural health program funding is spent.

“We will have to come up with funding,” said Sen. Ernie Otten, R-Tea. “I think the citizens of South Dakota deserve something better than a conversation going on here in the Legislature for over 20 years, and the best that we’ve got is to come up with a model that is self-destructing in front of us.”

Coordinated efforts could lead to faster response times

Link told lawmakers he hopes to achieve a goal of “15 minutes to life” through regionalization.

“It challenges every community and region to consider how they can help ensure that, regardless of where an emergency occurs, a person can receive meaningful care within that 15 minute timeframe or less,” Link said.

An ambulance may not be able to immediately arrive at a rural emergency scene, Link said, and that isn’t the goal.

“The goal here is to really design a system where the closest, appropriately trained resource can begin life-saving action early, connect with that patient, and then enter into that broader healthcare system through EMS,” Link said. “Fifteen minutes to life is really an outcome. Regional infrastructure is what makes it possible.”

In an example of regionalization, Spink County Ambulance Director Eric Schueth told lawmakers about a secondary crew spread across the northern part of the county, called Wildcat Rescue. It’s a mix of EMTs, nurses and one paramedic.

Schueth’s service responds to 911 calls across a 1,800-square-mile area in northeastern South Dakota. Last year, it responded to 565 calls.

Wildcat Rescue can often respond to emergencies in rural areas before the Spink County ambulance crew can arrive on scene. While Wildcat Rescue team members provide primary care, the Spink County ambulance is on its way to provide transport to a hospital if needed.

Spink County also collaborates with Clark, Hand and Faulk counties and with nearby towns such as Huron and Wolsey. After learning about the Department of Health’s vision for regional collaboration, Schueth and leaders of neighboring ambulance crews began meeting in March to learn how each agency could support one another.

“What does everybody need?” Schueth said the service’s leaders are asking. “How can we make each one of our services successful?”

For the coalition in northeastern South Dakota, the answer to that question is sharing resources such as staff, equipment and continuing education instructors. It also means operating under the same policies for patient care, Schueth said, so that “everybody functions as one.”

Some lawmakers on the task force said the success in Spink County could be a sign that regionalization works.

Chief Don Rowland of Watertown Fire Rescue told lawmakers that collaboration is difficult in areas with few volunteer services.

“We do not have another volunteer service in our county, so I provide protection to more than 17 townships in our county,” Rowland said.

Rowland said his department responds to more than 3,000 calls annually and provides service across about 730 square miles.

The task force plans to meet at least two more times over the next two months. Members hope to provide legislative proposals in November, to be considered during the 2027 legislative session that starts in January.

title: Father-daughter physicians honored for commitment to rural health
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: Dr. Charles Lewis and Dr. Sarah Lewis were presented the Rural Healthcare Neighbor Award on Monday at the Monument Stage at the Central States Fair in Rapid City.  From left are: Tif Robertson, Jimmy Seward, Monument Health, Dr. Sarah Lewis, Dr. Charles Lewis, and Mark Schmidt, Monument Health. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
1. ag.JPG
Dr. Charles Lewis and Dr. Sarah Lewis were presented the Rural Healthcare Neighbor Award on Monday at the Monument Stage at the Central States Fair in Rapid City.  From left are: Tif Robertson, Jimmy Seward, Monument Health, Dr. Sarah Lewis, Dr. Charles Lewis, and Mark Schmidt, Monument Health. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

RAPID CITY — A father-daughter team of Sturgis physicians was recognized for decades of service to rural patients during the fourth annual Ag Appreciation Night on Monday at the Central States Fair.

Dr. Charles Lewis and his daughter, Dr. Sarah Lewis, received the 2026 Rural Healthcare Neighbor Award, sponsored by Monument Health. The award recognizes individuals who have made significant contributions to improving health care in rural communities.

Tif Robertson, rancher, entrepreneur and former Central States Fair board president, introduced the Lewis’s during the ceremony at the Monument Health Stage.

Robertson said the award recognizes individuals who work to improve access, quality and equity in rural health care.

“This year’s recipients exemplify the spirit not as one individual, but as two generations of the same family answering that call,” Robertson said.

Dr. Charles Lewis began practicing family medicine in Sturgis in 1984 and has spent more than four decades caring for patients in western South Dakota.

His daughter followed him into medicine and returned to her hometown to practice family medicine, continuing a family legacy of providing community-based health care.

Dr. Charles Lewis credited his wife, family and the many health care professionals he has worked alongside throughout his career.

“It’s been a long journey, an enjoyable journey,” he said. “I couldn’t have done it all these 40 years without my wife taking care of all of the rest of my life.”

Lewis also recognized the laboratory employees, X-ray technicians, nurses and others who helped him care for patients over the years.

“It has truly been a privilege to help take care of western South Dakota people’s health,” he said. “There’s nobody tougher, and I do mean tough.”

He then turned his attention to the next generation.  “I’m happy to hand over the reins to my daughter Sarah,” he said.

Dr. Sara Lewis brought some humor to the ceremony as she talked about what she has learned while caring for western South Dakota farmers and ranchers.

She said there are certain times of the year when a doctor knows something must really be wrong if a rancher takes the time to come to the clinic.

“If it is calving season and they’re coming in to see you, something is wrong,” she said.

The same applies during lambing, branding and haying seasons, she said. Another warning sign is when a rancher shows up at the doctor’s office without being encouraged to go by his wife.

In a more serious tone, Lewis said caring for the region’s agricultural community has been rewarding.

“Taking care of the farmers and ranchers in West River has got to be the easiest doctoring gig in the country because they don’t complain about silly stuff,” she said. “They come in when something’s really wrong, and you’ve never met a more humble and hardworking group of people.”

Lewis said she hopes to continue serving those patients for decades to come.  “I’m looking forward to hopefully 30 years,” she said.

Ag Appreciation Night is held during the Central States Fair to recognize individuals and businesses that have made significant contributions to agriculture, rural communities and the people who call the region home.

title: Lawmaker salaries could top $16,000  during next year’s SD legislative session
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Interim Legislative Research Council Director Jeff Mehlhaff speaks to South Dakota lawmakers during a meeting of the Legislature’s Executive Board Wednesday, at the Capitol in Pierre. Photo by Meghan O’Brien, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Lawmaker salaries could top $16,000 during next year’s South Dakota legislative session.jpg
Interim Legislative Research Council Director Jeff Mehlhaff speaks to South Dakota lawmakers during a meeting of the Legislature’s Executive Board Wednesday, at the Capitol in Pierre. Photo by Meghan O’Brien, South Dakota Searchlight 

PIERRE — A committee of South Dakota lawmakers endorsed budget increases Wednesday for the Legislative Research Council to cover the anticipated rise in legislator pay.

The council manages the Legislature’s day-to-day operations, helps lawmakers draft bills and is responsible for updating the state’s code of laws. Interim Director Jeff Mehlhaff asked for a $29,479 addition to the council’s fiscal year 2027 budget to cover rising lawmaker salaries, and a $96,872 increase in the council’s fiscal year 2028 budget to cover rising lawmaker salaries and “per diem” payments — Latin for “per day” — which help cover lawmakers’ daily living expenses during the annual legislative sessions.

The salary for legislators is 20% of the South Dakota median household income as reported by the U.S. Census Bureau, according to state law. The number is reported in September, Mehlhaff said. He told lawmakers their salary could increase from $15,970 to $16,608 for the legislative session that begins in January — a 4% increase.

The per diem, which lawmakers earn on top of their salary during the session and for committee meetings outside of the session, is tied to rates set by the federal government. The council’s existing budget is based on a per diem of $161.95, but the current per diem is $178. During this year’s 38-day legislative session, the total per diem paid to each lawmaker was $6,764.

Legislators also receive mileage at a rate set by the Bureau of Finance and Management, which is currently 70 cents per mile.

The council’s total anticipated budget for legislator pay during the 2028 fiscal year is about $2.8 million.

title: Data centers in ND  have received millions in  sales tax breaks
byline: By Jack Dura North Dakota Monitor
description: Data center owners in North Dakota have reaped tens of millions of dollars in state sales tax breaks in the last two years, figures that have ballooned as public scrutiny has intensified on data center projects.
_full_text:
NorthDakotaMonitorLogo

Data center owners in North Dakota have reaped tens of millions of dollars in state sales tax breaks in the last two years, figures that have ballooned as public scrutiny has intensified on data center projects.

The Legislature’s interim Tax Reform and Relief Advisory Committee on Wednesday heard a series of reports about data center tax exemptions and incentives, including what North Dakota and other states offer. State Tax Commissioner Brian Kroshus outlined exponential growth in sales and use tax exemptions for data center owners on information technology equipment, such as computer hardware, servers, routers, cooling systems and other infrastructure. 

Those sales tax breaks, which are not for construction, ranged from $5.4 million in 2021 to $7.8 million in 2023, then leapt to $15.3 million in 2024 and more than $65 million last year. 

“It’s a number that I think will grow without question,” Kroshus told the panel.

Data centers are huge facilities housing computers that handle everything from financial transactions to email to artificial intelligence.

The 2015 Legislature approved the original tax exemption, with the current version set by the 2021 Legislature, Kroshus said. 

“I don’t think anyone at the time, the Legislative Assembly, could have envisioned what this would become just 11 years later,” Kroshus said. 

In a 2015 House floor debate, bill sponsor Rep. Mark Owens, R-Grand Forks, who died in 2024, said he brought the bill to make North Dakota more attractive for data centers looking to relocate. He said he had precision agriculture, drones, banking, finance and jobs for North Dakota college and university graduates in mind with the bill. 

North Dakota’s cold climate and a reliable source of electricity in the state are draws for data center companies, Sen. Mark Weber, R-Casselton, said Wednesday. North Dakota is “on the radar” across the U.S. for data centers, he said. 

“I’m wondering if the time at the next legislative session is to have some of this discussion,” Weber said. “Are we – I don’t want to say giving away the store, but I think it warrants some discussion amongst all of us.” 

Data center developers have emphasized the significant property taxes they pay to local communities as a benefit to the state.

In addition, data centers also created or retained 332 permanent jobs from 2021 to 2025, Kroshus said.

Data center companies evaluate states for years prior to locating their projects, said Matt Marshall, an economic development manager with Minnkota Power Cooperative.

“They’re looking at lots of different metrics, and by the time we get the call, you’d be amazed at how educated they are about our area,” Marshall told the panel. 

North Dakota has a number of data centers, including ones built near Ellendale and Williston, under construction near Harwood or in planning stages near Mandan and Center.

Data centers have drawn scrutiny and criticism from citizens for their size, water usage, noise and other factors.

In its upcoming special session, North Dakota’s Republican-led Legislature will consider a bill to temporarily ban nondisclosure agreements between industrial projects and government officials. Critics say those agreements keep the public in the dark about data center projects.

At least 38 states offer a dedicated tax exemption or incentive for data centers, some dating back to the early 2000s, said Nicholas Miller, a policy associate with the National Conference of State Legislatures’ Fiscal Affairs Program, who presented to the panel.

States see jobs, economic benefits and property tax revenue as reasons to create the incentives, though some states have considered walking back or adding requirements to their incentives, Miller said. Concerns related to data centers’ energy use and water use and the loss of tax revenue might be why some states are pumping the brakes on their incentives, he said.

“And I think increasingly data centers are a hot topic just in general,” Miller told the panel.

The data center presentations will be helpful for lawmakers in their upcoming special session and in the 2027 Legislature, said committee chair Sen. Brad Bekkedahl, R-Williston. He pointed to community benefit agreements with developers as one potential topic.

“They need to engage the communities. They need to provide a direct benefit to the communities,” Bekkedahl told the North Dakota Monitor. “They’ve talked about property tax benefits, but there’s other things involved with that as well.”

title: ‘The In-Between Library’ invites young readers to travel into chapter books
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: “The In-Between Library” is a series of fantasy fiction chapter books for young readers. Courtesy image
_full_text:
Nora and Jack Get into Hot Water - 1
“The In-Between Library” is a series of fantasy fiction chapter books for young readers. Courtesy image 

SPEARFISH — Wyoming author Kathy Bjornstad is a high-school teacher turned full-time indie author — with an imaginative take on time travel for middle grade readers.  

Middle grade books often include chapters, and are designed to appeal to children between the ages of 8 and 12 (third and sixth graders). 

Her book series, “The In Between Library,” follows farm-kids Nora and Max Rigby on adventures through time. The children don’t use anything as mundane as a time machine in order to visit historical figures like Teddy Roosevelt and Clara Barton. Their ride to the past is an enchanted out house — an enchanted outhouse that pops up in their yard one day, with a pint-sized dragon named “Finli the Fixer” inside.

“It’s kind of like “Magic Tree House” or “I Survived,” Bjornstad said. “He (Finli) sends them to a historical era where a person needs a little persuading to be on the path they’re about to go on to make the world a better place.”

Their first mission takes Finli, Nora, and Max to Yellowstone National Park in 1903 to meet and inspire Teddy Roosevelt. 

“This is a way to get kids into reading whether they like history, or magic, or action adventure,” Bjornstad said. “I think any kids who like any of those things would like (the series). I made the kids’ ages kind of nebulous so that it didn’t get walked into it is only for third graders or second graders. It could go a little bit older.” 

Bjornstad said she always hopes her books inspire children to be excited about reading. 

When she was young, she loved books packed with fantasy-style adventure like “The Tale of Desperaux” by Katie DiCamillo by “The Hobbit” by J.R.R. Tolkien. 

Bjornstad wrote her first novel when she was in the fifth grade. 

“It was terrible,” Bjornstad said. “It was a take off on the Hobbit.”

That book might’ve been a non-starter, but she was undettered. She won an essay contest in school, and emboldened, submitted poetry that was later published in “Young Miss” magazine. 

After college and a 19-year career teaching English and language arts put her authorial aspirations on hold, but she kept writing in her spare time. After retirement, she published her first book as an independent author — effectively starting a second career. 

“It’s a lot of work,” said Bjorstad. “It is true, because you are doing. Unless you pay people to help with certain aspects of it, you’re doing all of the marketing , all of the printing, the formatting.”

But the work is worth it, to interact with readers, Bjornstad noted. 

“I’ve done author visits, and it is really fun to meet those kids in person. They still treat you like you’re famous,” Bjornstad said. 

She loves seeing kids who are excited to read, and she savors the challenge of making readers laugh. 

“It is exciting to create something with a simple vocabulary, but they can still learn new words, a plot that is simple enough, but fast-paced enough — I love a challenge, so all of that stuff is fun,” Bjornstad said. “Always with kids I hope that it will be the thing that gets them excited about reading. I find that if kids can just find the one book that gets them excited about reading, then they’ll become readers.” 

There are 3 “In Between Library Books” out now — including the most recent title “Nora and Max Dodge a Bullet,” which features a runaway hamster, and a heroic civil war-era nurse.

title: Review: “Ain’t Nobody’s Fool”  by Martha Ackmann
byline: By Terri Schlichenmeyer Special to the Pioneer
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Ain't Nobody's Fool.jpg
Courtesy photo 

Editor’s Note: This review of Dolly Parton’s biography previously ran in the January. We’ve chosen to share in again this week, in honor of the late musician, actress, and pop culture icon. 

Not too bright.

That’s what people once thought about you. Your language didn’t conform, you had your own sense of style, and you were ignorant about modern things and places and foods. But you were no dummy. You were different, and you had a secret: as in the new biography, “Ain’t Nobody’s Fool: The Life and Times of Dolly Parton” by Martha Ackmann, you knew exactly where you were going.

When Avie Lee Owens and Lee Parton first married, they had the very basics: “two knives, two forks, two spoons, a skillet, a butcher knife, and an old iron kettle.” He was seventeen; she was fifteen. Babies came quick. The fourth one was named Dolly, after two great-aunts.

Almost from the time she could walk, Dolly sang. Before she was old enough to attend school, she wrote poetry, and she’d begun to notice rhythms and beats she could make with her fingers. As a schoolchild, she created her own musical instruments out of scraps, and she was eager to perform whenever anyone asked her – and they asked often, because Dolly Parton was a nice girl, and her sense of humor conveyed a warmth that drew people in.

Growing up in  the Tennessee mountains, Parton was independent, shunning marriage and child-raising, instead focusing on a dream of being a star. By the time she was in high school, she’d had a regular gig on local television but she recognized that there were few opportunities for fame in the mountains, so she left for Nashville the day after high school graduation, with the snickers of naysayers ringing in her ears.

She stayed with an aunt and uncle there, and she beat the streets, dined on grocery store samples to get by, and missed her family and friends. And they worried about her, but they knew nothing would derail her plans. They knew Dolly would be fine.

As a friend said, “’She had her head on pretty good.’”

Chances are that if you’ve listened to music any time in the last sixty years, you’ve heard Dolly Parton through her words or her music or both. Now you need to learn more about her, and “Ain’t Nobody’s Fool” is where to do it.

Here’s a biography that grabs you on the first page with the tiniest bit of family tree, but not so much that you get bored with it. Author Martha Ackmann writes about Dolly Parton’s early life, putting hardships and experiences in context, both personally and historically. There are name-drops, but not overly so, as Ackmann takes you through Parton’s career, her heartbreaks, her marriage, and her years with Porter Wagoner, in detail but not dramatically embellished or outrageously told. It’s a biography that’s just right, sourced well and written with a fresh take that, like its subject, tells a good story. 

Fans, of course, will want this highly-researched book but music lovers of any age or type will eat it up. That means you, so use up that Christmas gift certificate. “Ain’t Nobody’s Fool” just shines.

title: The Mercy Sloane Chronicles: Chapter 16
byline: By Eliza Blue A work of serialized fiction, special to the Pioneer
description: Life took on a gentle rhythm after the arrival of the letter deeding Mercy the homestead. As promised, Melissa came and helped Mercy plant a small garden of beets and carrots and lettuce. Neither had said much about Mercy’s windfall. Instead they talked of the things two young women just getting to know each other might discuss: Childhood memories, favorite books, all the little stories describing how they’d gotten where they were.
_full_text:
The Mercy Sloane Chronicles

Life took on a gentle rhythm after the arrival of the letter deeding Mercy the homestead. As promised, Melissa came and helped Mercy plant a small garden of beets and carrots and lettuce. Neither had said much about Mercy’s windfall. Instead they talked of the things two young women just getting to know each other might discuss: Childhood memories, favorite books, all the little stories describing how they’d gotten where they were. 

They’d also gone to visit Ardath and she’d revealed that she had a tiny, spring-fed pond hidden behind the stand of trees a half mile west of her house. The days were growing hotter and drier, and Ardath told them if they wanted to use it as a swimming hole they’d better get to it–the pond was sure to be mostly mud before too much longer.

In truth, the pond was already mostly mud, but the two girls went out wading in their underwear anyway, laughing and pushing each other down till they were both thoroughly soaked and much dirtier than they’d started. They washed off with a bucket of water from Ardath’s well, and didn’t bother to dry themselves, just put on their clothes and rode Mercy’s pony back to her house still dripping wet. It was the coolest they’d been in days.

Her house. Mercy still couldn’t believe it. She had a house. She had land! And she also had a diamond wedding ring that she belatedly (and correctly) realized was probably worth more than the house and the land put together.

She’d brought up the idea of returning the ring, but both Ardath and Melissa shook their heads adamantly at the suggestion. “Mercy,” Ardath said to her the afternoon she and Melissa went swimming. “It’s to your credit you’ve not spoken ill of a man you jilted, but it’s also pretty clear that he comes from people who have had far more given to them than is good for a body.” Ardath, who was cutting strips of leather to repair an old saddle, stopped her work, and looked out past the girls at the rolling hills of grass, thinking hard about what she wanted to say next. 

The wind picked up suddenly, and a song sparrow landed on the fence post right next to Ardath, cocked his head, and sang two short notes before flying away. This broke Ardath out of her reverie for a moment, and she chuckled, but didn’t say why.

 Eliza Blue TMC
Eliza Blue 

Mercy had noticed this before–the silent conversations Ardath sometimes seemed to be having that didn’t include the other humans. It was too awkward to address directly, but in that moment Mercy had the distinct impression the bird was speaking in a language Ardath understood.

Now it was Ardath’s turn to break the silence. “Before the homesteaders came here,” Ardath said suddenly, “The land didn’t belong to anyone. The people belonged to the land, not the other way around.” Ardath stopped again, and all three let this idea spool around them. Even the wind quieted for a few long moments to let everyone ponder the implication of Ardath’s statement.

“When I die,” Ardath continued in a huskier voice, still staring off into the distance. “I want to be buried right here beside the barn. This land has given me everything I’ve ever needed and most of the things I’ve wanted too.” Ardath shifted her gaze and looked at Mercy. “Those folk don’t need that ring, Mercy. I’m guessing they won’t find what they need in this lifetime.” Ardath sighed and then pick up the knife and went back to cutting leather. “I’m guessing you won’t need that diamond either, but I’d trust you to figure out what to do with it a lot a lot quicker than they ever would.” 

Ardath winked at the girls then. “You’ve got something special, Mercy. Some might call it luck. I don’t reckon it’s as simple as that. But I know one thing–you can’t be afraid to accept the gifts life offers. That ring is yours for now. I think you’ll know what to do with it when the time is right.”

title: Building the  quantum workforce
byline: By Mike Ray Sanford Underground Research Facility
description: The third annual Quantum Partnership Workshop was held at the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) this summer. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Workshop at SURF explores the future of next generation technology.jpg
The third annual Quantum Partnership Workshop was held at the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) this summer. Courtesy photo 

History is full of examples of disruptive technology. The Luddites of the 19th century rebelled against the Industrial Revolution and the use of machines to lower wages, bypass labor standards, and destroy their livelihoods.

They broke into factories at night and smashed looms with sledgehammers, spurring a major government crackdown. It took more than a century to see the creation of new labor laws, such as minimum wage, child labor standards, and a 40-hour workweek.

This history seems important to reflect on today.

“Quantum technologies, including computing, networking, basic quantum science, are going to be the drivers for the next phase of technological change,” said Mickey Slimp, executive director of the Great Plains Network.

Making way for a quantum future and building regional networks to leverage its potential were key topics at the third annual Quantum Partnership Workshop, held at the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) this summer. The annual workshop is hosted by the Great Plains Network (GPN) and the Institute for Underground Science at SURF, in partnership with the South Dakota Quantum Center. The collaborative gathering sought to advance quantum science, technology, and networking while expanding education and workforce development efforts.

The emergence of quantum technology, alongside ongoing advancements in AI, has the potential to revolutionize a broad range of industries, including medicine, energy and cybersecurity.

Eden Figueroa from Stony Brook University and the Brookhaven National Lab led a virtual discussion during the workshop on the latest in quantum networking technologies. The challenges in building quantum infrastructure and a quantum internet poses both unique challenges and opportunities for the future.

It’s true that the quantum future relies on technological advancements in networking and computing. It’s also true that the quantum workforce of tomorrow is not just people with Ph.D.’s. doing cutting edge research. There is room for all.

“I think one of the biggest myths about quantum is that people aren’t already empowered with the right skill sets,” said Emily Easton, the director of education and workforce development at the Chicago Quantum Exchange and keynote speaker at the workshop. “Welders, pipe fitters, mechanical engineers—all of these are examples of roles that include valuable skill sets that easily transition into quantum. So even if someone doesn’t have a quantum-focused degree or background, they’re still incredibly useful in a range of roles.”

One of Easton’s core messages to those working to develop and push the boundaries of quantum is that preparing the workforce of tomorrow is just as important as advancing technological breakthroughs.

“We know that this technology is coming which means now is the time for ecosystems to start thinking about all of the different assets they have—including those that are perhaps less obvious,” Easton said. “This is also a good time to explore how those assets integrate with each other and with the assets of other ecosystems. Quantum is inherently interdisciplinary and the way that we approach the research, commercialization, and workforce preparation needs to be similarly multifaceted.”

The future quantum economy does not have to be centered only on the coasts and in places like Silicon Valley. The focus of the Great Plains Network (GPN) is to see the Midwest both benefit from and prepare for the future of this technology. Slimp points out that this effort is already underway with multiple organizations, universities and institutions.

“We have a lot of activities dealing with quantum throughout the Midwest,” Slimp said. “It’s just never been pulled together, and so when I looked at National Science Foundation funding, we had over 200 projects in the past 15 years in the Midwest that included some aspect of quantum physics, quantum computing or other quantum sensing. GPN is pulling together the states in this region to give us a core of resources and people to really have an impact on all of this.”

For Easton, this kind of organization and networking is essential ahead of the coming changes.

“No one organization or discipline is prepared to do all the things we need to do to scale up in quantum. That’s why it’s so important we’re building those networks and connections now, so we can draw on those resources as they come,” Easton said.

She points out that South Dakota has a history of recognizing the massive returns investment in future technology can bring.

“South Dakota, I think, is already a great example of a technology center that is using what it has to deliver results in new ways. For example, repurposing a gold mine into an underground research facility is genius. How can we find other synergies that leverage existing assets to ensure that South Dakota is included in the economic and workforce benefits we know are coming with quantum?” Easton said.

Institutions in South Dakota are already leading the way for the rest of the state. The Quantum Partnership Workshop spent the last day at South Dakota Mines in the Department of Nanoscience & Biomedical Engineering. Department head and professor Steve Smith explained his team’s investigation of the optical and electronic properties of quantum nanomaterials. Both South Dakota Mines and Dakota State University in Madison have been key players in the South Dakota Quantum Center and in ongoing cutting-edge research around the country.

For her part, Easton applauds the ongoing efforts across the state and at SURF.

“These types of national laboratory settings are ideal sites for these collaborations because they bring together that interdisciplinary research, but also provide the outreach piece, the workforce piece, the public engagement piece, to help universities, schools, community colleges, individual efforts come together. I think there’s a real role for SURF specifically to play in the quantum economy in South Dakota,” she said.

Quantum technology in both computing and sensing has huge benefits and opportunities for SURF as well. Physics has always been on the cutting edge of new computing technology and applications. Simultaneous preparation for the quantum economy, through robust outreach, education, and workforce development efforts, can expand opportunities to broad swaths of the public and help avoid any repeat of the 19th-century Luddite uprising.

The Institute for Underground Science at SURF is already in planning for next year’s Quantum Partnership Workshop set for July 27–30, 2027.

title: Quick picks: Imagination Library Books
description: Dolly Parton reads her book "Coat of Many Colors," at the Library of Congress in Washington on Feb. 27, 2018. AP Photo
_full_text:
Obit Dolly Parton
Dolly Parton reads her book "Coat of Many Colors," at the Library of Congress in Washington on Feb. 27, 2018. AP Photo 

Dolly Parton, pop culture icon, reigning country music queen, and larger-than-life actress and entertainer, died this week at age 80. She may be remembered for her prolific song writing, dazzling wit, and over-the-top style, but one of her most celebrated projects had more to do with reading the rhinestones. She founded Dolly Parton’s Imagination Library — a non-profit that gifts free books to children from birth to age 5 — 31 years ago. 

Parton founded the non-profit to honor her father, who was unable to read. Today there are 

more than 3,197,250 kids registered for the program, receiving books at no charge. 

This week’s list includes one book distributed by Dolly’s Imagination Library from each eligible age-group/reading level category. We hope it offers some inspiration! 

1. “Sleep Tight, Polar Bear” by Sabina Gibson 

Genre: Picture book

Join a polar bear cub and her fuzzy arctic friends as they curl up for a cozy, snowy night in this board book. In “Sleep Tight, Polar Bear,” readers will see seal pups dozing while narwhals count fish instead of sheep as they drift off to sleep. Imagination library gift this title to children younger than 1 year of age. 

2. “Llama Llama Red Pajama by Anna Dewdney

Genre: Picture book

In this infectious rhyming read-aloud, Baby Llama turns bedtime into an all-out llama drama! Tucked into bed by his mama, Baby Llama immediately starts worrying when she goes downstairs, and his soft whimpers turn to hollers when she doesn’t come right back. But just in time, Mama returns to set things right. Children will relate to Baby Llama’s need for comfort, as much as parents will appreciate Mama Llama’s reassuring message. Imagination Library gifts this book to children aged 1 (born in 2025). 

3. “The Big Slide” by Daniel Kirk

Genre: Picture book

Little Pup isn’t as little as he used to be, and he’d love to try out the playground’s big slide. Day after day he eyes it, but he just can’t seem to work up the courage. Fortunately he meets someone in the same boat — Little Duck — and the two provide each other with just the bravery boost needed to climb that ladder and enjoy the slide! Kids will relate to Little Pup’s struggle to gain enough confidence to move out of his comfort zone and try something new.

Imagination Library gift this book to children aged 2 (born in 2024). 

4. “Corduroy” by Don Freeman

Genre: Picture book 

Corduroy has been on the department store shelf for a long time...

Yet as soon as Lisa sees him, she knows that he’s the bear she’s always wanted. Her mother, though, thinks he’s a little shopworn — he’s even missing a button! Still, Corduroy knows that with a bit of work he can tidy himself up and be just the bear for Lisa. And where better to start than with a quick search through the department store for a new button!

Imagination Library gift this book to children aged 3 (born in 2023). 

5. “Coat of Many Colors” by Dolly Parton

Genre: Picture book

Winter is coming to Tennessee and there’s no money to buy a new coat, so a little girl’s mama sews one for her out of rags. The little girl wears it to school proudly, and when the other children laugh, she gives them a quick lesson about what it means to be rich. Judith Sutton’s beautiful paintings bring one of Dolly Parton’s best-loved songs to life.

Imagination Library gift this book to children aged 4 (born in 2022) 

6. “You are a Honey Bee!”  

Genre: Picture books/non-fiction

The first in an adorable, STEM nonfiction picture book series that encourages very young readers to learn — through gentle interactivity and play — about the animals who share their world

Swish, swoosh, fly! You might have heard the words “busy as a bee,” but what do bees actually do each day? Did you know bees clean their rooms, help feed baby bees, and build the hive they live in? From birth to first flight and beyond, discover all that goes into being a bee in this charming picture book, the first in the “Meet Your World” series.

Imagination Library gift this book to children aged 5 (born in 2021)

byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Main Street may be fully repaved by the end of the year, according to city officials. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Main Street Contract.JPG
Main Street may be fully repaved by the end of the year, according to city officials. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

 Main Street Contract 1.JPG
Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — It’s going to cost the city of Spearfish at least $348,662 to mill and overlay Main Street from Jackson Boulevard to Grant Street. During a special city council meeting Wednesday, scheduled to help expedite the process of paving the roadway after a failed chip seal project last fall, the city council awarded the contract for the project to Johner and Sons Inc., of Spearfish.  

Three bids were opened on Aug. 19. DGR Engineering recommended that the bid be awarded to Johner and Sons Inc. — the low bidder. The next lowest bid was from Sacrison Paving, at $394,099. Western Construction also submitted a bid for $434,441. 

The engineer’s estimate put the project cost at $418,968 for work that includes a mill-and-overlay of existing asphalt on Main Street. 

The council directed city staff to mill and overlay Main Street — in the face of community demand for a fix after oil started bled through the failed chip seal this summer. Because the action wasn’t planned during budget season, the council will need to pass a budget supplement to pay for the work.  

“The mill and overlay of Main Street, we just awarded that tonight, it is budgeted in streets general fund for $400,000 for next year, so we will eliminate that. The contractor is shooting to be done before the end of this year,” said Spearfish Finance Officer Michelle DeNeui. 

According to public works, mill-and-overlay projects “trigger compliance with the Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA).” That means that curb ramps and pedestrian push-button crossing upgrades will also need to be completed. 

“I don’t remember the exact number, but quite a few of the corners needed some work or rework. Whether it is adjusting curb ramp or the landing or adjusting where some of the buttons are located for the rapid flashing beacons, as well as the crosswalk at Hudson,” McMahon told the city council during the special meeting. 

McMahon added that, weather permitting, the work should be completed this fall.

title: Fourth, Seventh judicial circuit merger proposal draws opposition
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: State Court Administrator Greg Sattizahn presents the Proposed Merger of 4th and 7th Judicial Circuits on Wednesday in the Meade County Courthouse. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts
_full_text:
0828 Fourth, Seventh judicial circuit merger proposal draws opposition(RGB).tif
State Court Administrator Greg Sattizahn presents the Proposed Merger of 4th and 7th Judicial Circuits on Wednesday in the Meade County Courthouse. Pioneer photo by Tim Potts 

STURGIS — A proposal to merge the administrative structures of South Dakota’s Fourth and Seventh judicial circuits drew opposition Wednesday during a public forum at the Meade County Courthouse.  

Approximately 80 people filled Courtroom 3 to hear a presentation from State Court Administrator Greg Sattizahn and provide feedback on the proposal. When one attorney asked opponents of the merger to raise their hands, nearly everyone in the room did so.

The South Dakota Unified Judicial System’s State Court Administrator’s Office is asking the state Supreme Court to consider combining the 2 circuits for administrative purposes.

The Fourth Judicial Circuit consists of Butte, Corson, Dewey, Harding, Lawrence, Meade, Perkins and Ziebach counties. The Seventh Judicial Circuit includes Custer, Fall River, Oglala Lakota and Pennington counties.

Under the proposal, the combined circuit would operate with one presiding judge, one circuit administrator, one chief court services officer and one deputy chief court services officer. The 2 circuits currently have separate administrative structures.

Sattizahn said the proposal is intended to give the Unified Judicial System greater flexibility to share judges, court services personnel and clerk resources while responding to changing workloads.

“We don’t have a workload problem, but we do have a work-distribution problem as far as where our offices are, where our employees are and how we match those up in perhaps a better way,” he said.

Sattizahn emphasized that the proposal remains in its early stages and that no formal rule has been submitted to the Supreme Court. He said the purpose of the public forums is to explain the proposal and gather comments before officials decide how to proceed.

“This is really just the start of a process,” he said.  The merger would not change judges’ duty stations, courthouse locations or office hours, Sattizahn said. Officials also do not intend to consolidate the circuits’ treatment courts.

He said the Fourth and Seventh circuits already have a history of cooperation, including sharing judges when recusals or conflicts arise. The proposed merger would make it easier for the system to respond to short-term demands without requiring approval from two separate administrative authorities.

Sattizahn said South Dakota established 9 judicial circuits when the Unified Judicial System was created in 1972. The number was reduced to 8 in 1976 and to the current 7 circuits in 1999.

Circuit boundaries have not been examined extensively in more than 25 years, he said. Factors considered in determining those boundaries include population changes, caseloads, employee locations, trade areas and workload demands.

Despite those assurances, court employees and attorneys questioned what problem the merger would solve and warned that it could weaken local control and access to court services.

Amber Richey, director of the Lawrence County Public Defender’s Office, said she supports improving efficiency but is concerned about restructuring the circuits without a clear explanation of how the change would improve their operation.

“I’m not opposed to efficiency or opposed to making changes, and I agree every county does things differently,” Richey said. “I worked in Meade County for 6 years and Lawrence County since then, and it’s clear we are not unified.”

She said each county has its own needs, practices, personnel and methods of delivering court services.

“I keep coming back to this question: What particular problem is this merger trying to solve?” she asked.

Belle Fourche attorney Ken Barker said the proposal could become a step toward the gradual erosion of local services. He compared the merger to regional firms taking over small-town businesses and promising that nothing would change.

“You see this as a small adjustment,” Barker said. “I see it as a step away from local identity, local access and local confidence in the courts.”

Lead attorney Joe Kosel said opposition was intensified by how the proposal was introduced. He said many people view it as an attempt to fix a system that is working well within the Fourth Circuit.

“The opposition to this merger is extreme because of the way it’s been rolled out,” Kosel said. “Nobody cared about how it was rolled out, or they completely misjudged how it would land here.”

Cosell also questioned whether the one-hour meeting provided enough time to gather meaningful public input. He said the Fourth and Seventh circuits operate differently and expressed concern.

Members of the public may submit written comments by emailing comment@ujs.state.sd.us or mailing them to the State Court Administrator’s Office, Attention: Judicial Circuit Merger Proposal, 500 E. Capitol Ave., Pierre, SD 57501.

The deadline for comments is Oct. 1.

byline: Pioneers staff reports

_full_text:
SDDOTlogo

DEADWOOD — The South Dakota Department of Transportation (DOT) has proposed a project to reconstruct a horizontal curve on U.S. Highway 385 located 4 miles south of U.S. Highway 85 in Lawrence County. 

Section 4(f) of the Department of Transportation Act of 1966 requires a special effort be made to preserve the natural beauty of the countryside and public and recreation lands, wildlife and waterfowl refuges, and historic sites. In accordance with the Federal Highway Administration comments are being solicited regarding the effects this project would have on the Strawberry Hill picnic area and fishing pond, managed by the United States Forest Service. 

The Strawberry Hill picnic area is considered a section 4(f) property because it is a public recreation area with attributes and features including a picnic area, fishing pond, and campground. The project will include the acquisition of a minor amount permanent easement and temporary easement on the Strawberry Hill picnic area by DOT for the intended purpose of straightening the horizonal curve on Highway 385. This requires additional permanent right-of-way to maintain appropriate right-of-way clearance throughout the corridor. The temporary easement is necessary to realign the entrance to Strawberry Hill picnic area. The proposed project will result in approximately one-third acre of permanent incorporation of the Strawberry Hill picnic area into a transportation facility (Highway 385). The proposed project will also result in approximately 3.25 acres of temporary easement which will last for the duration of the project. The minor amount of permanent incorporation will not adversely affect the recreational use or attributes and features of the picnic area.

The following measures to minimize harm will be incorporated into the plans as plan notes and as environmental commitments in the environmental document:

• Appropriate signage shall be installed to alert users of Strawberry Hill picnic area of construction activities, access restrictions or closures, and to direct users to secondary access points;

• The staging and/or storage of construction equipment or construction materials shall not take place outside proposed construction limits that are within the defined boundaries of the 4(f) property, and waste materials will not be disposed of on Forest Service land; 

• The contractor shall be required to closely coordinate the construction schedule with DOT and the Forest Service prior to the start of construction activities; and

• Access to Strawberry Hill picnic area shall always be maintained during construction activities via flagging operations.

After a steady month of events in July, gaming numbers saw an overall rise of 6.74 percent. Pioneer file photo. 

DEADWOOD — The gaming handle in Deadwood rose 4.05% in July compared to 2025 data according to numbers reported by the South Dakota Commission on Gaming, contributing to an overall gain in activity by 8.63% for the first 7 months of 2026. 

“We’re encouraged to see 2026 figures continuing to outperform 2025,” said George Milos, director of the Deadwood Gaming Association. “A strong lineup of special events throughout Deadwood and the value we offer guests continue to help drive growth. We hope that momentum carries through the rest of 2026.”

Compared to the same time last year, gaming handles increased as follows: slot machines, 4.2%; table games, 2.34%; and sports wagering, down 13.44%.

Operators distributed $2,303,773.59 in ‘free play’ in July, resulting in a taxable gross revenue of $15,817,946.53. Total taxes collected from gaming amounted to $1,423,615.19.

Taxes were distributed as follows: South Dakota general fund, $158,179.47; South Dakota Tourism, $506,174.29; Lawrence County, $126,543.57.

title: BHSU president delivers  state of the university address
description: SPEARFISH — Black Hills State University President Steve Elliott presented the annual State of the University address to faculty and staff Wednesday in the newly renovated Woodburn Theatre. The address highlighted the university’s momentum, evolving strategic priorities, and commitment to preparing students to meet the workforce needs of South Dakota and the region.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — Black Hills State University President Steve Elliott presented the annual State of the University address to faculty and staff Wednesday in the newly renovated Woodburn Theatre. The address highlighted the university’s momentum, evolving strategic priorities, and commitment to preparing students to meet the workforce needs of South Dakota and the region.

The event began with the recognition of 23 BHSU staff and faculty members for their longevity, with service ranging from 10 to 35 years. Collectively, the honorees represented more than 400 years of service to BHSU and the South Dakota Board of Regents. 

 Vice President for University Advancement Steve Meeker announced this year’s recipients of the annual employee awards: 

Presidential Outstanding Employee: Gus Karinen, buzz card specialist

Presidential Rising Star Staff: Alyssa Blake, lead financial aid advisor

Presidential Rising Star Faculty: Katelynn Kelly, assistant professor of political science

Presidential Outstanding Student Employee: Anthony Corbine

Presidential Team Excellence Award: Administrative Information Management Services, including Anthony Conklin, Haden Goodwin, David Pruitt, Anne Stevens, and Ven Thompson. 

 President Elliott’s address provided a comprehensive campus update highlighting positive trends in student enrollment, efforts to align academic programs with workforce needs, and initiatives designed to support student success and strengthen BHSU’s position in an evolving higher education landscape.

 “This really has been a year of momentum,” Elliott said. “We have an opportunity as a university to build on this progress, to lead through the change that we’re experiencing, and to strengthen the university that we’re going to hand to the next generation of Yellow Jackets.” 

Within Academic Affairs, Elliott highlighted several recently approved programs, including a bachelor of science in criminal justice, associate degrees in education and early childhood education, a master of science in STEM education, a business analytics specialization, and a certificate in American Indian studies.

He also discussed the role of BHSU in a proposal with South Dakota Mines and Dakota State University to establish a Center for National Defense Studies that would support South Dakota’s expanding national defense workforce needs. If approved, BHSU would lead work in areas including national defense policy, public administration, federal systems, defense acquisition, contracting, and program management. 

Beyond academics, Elliott shared updates on strategic initiatives across the university, including enrollment and marketing efforts and the continued expansion of opportunities for adult, place-bound, and military-connected learners through BHSU-Rapid City.

Campus improvement projects were another focus of the address, including the recently completed renovation of Woodburn Theatre, which will officially reopen to the public with a production of “Fiddler on the Roof” in October and additional grand opening activities scheduled for Sept. 8.

Elliott also highlighted ongoing campus infrastructure improvements, the implementation of a comprehensive campus wayfinding project, and a new partnership with the Spearfish Police Department that will provide a full-time police officer on campus.

Elliott closed his address by announcing that BHSU will begin developing its next strategic plan this fall through a series of listening sessions with faculty, staff, students, alumni, and community partners.

“I do believe deeply in the future of Black Hills State, and together we’re really doing more than just educating students,” Elliott said. “We are preparing the people who will shape the future of South Dakota.”

title: Motorcyclist on life-saving journey across the country to stop in Sturgis, Saturday
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Richard Williams, 75, spent his life keeping his hemophiliac son alive, and now he is embarking on a cross-country motorcycle trip to raise awareness and funds to help families around the world who have been impacted by hemophilia. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Richard Williams.jpg
Richard Williams, 75, spent his life keeping his hemophiliac son alive, and now he is embarking on a cross-country motorcycle trip to raise awareness and funds to help families around the world who have been impacted by hemophilia. Courtesy photo 

STURGIS — Richard Williams has worked his entire life to keep his son alive. 

Now, he’s riding across the country, so other parents across the world can give their children life-saving treatments. 

Many years ago, one of Williams’ twin sons died before birth due to uncontrollable bleeding. His remaining son, Trevor, was diagnosed at birth with severe hemophilia A, a congenital condition that means he is missing a blood protein. Without the protein, his body is unable to create blood clots and platelets, causing extreme external and internal bleeding. Treatments include introducing blood factors to replace the missing protein, and at the time they cost about $250,000 a year. 

“(The cost) was baffling to us as new parents,” Williams said. “We couldn’t get our head around how much it cost to be able to keep him alive. Then we had to take him to the emergency room sometimes every 5-6 days. He’d sometimes just bleed spontaneously into an elbow or into a wrist, into a knee or an ankle. If we touched his little body and we could feel one joint warmer than the other that meant he was bleeding inside and so we’d have to get him to the emergency room. They’d have to introduce factor through one of his veins and at the time, it was human blood factor, which (could have been) tainted with hepatitis C, HIV, or other blood borne diseases. It was frightening. A couple of years later the synthetic factor came out, so we switched to that and that was a relief.” 

With a constant need for the expensive treatments, Williams, a mechanical engineer, said he regularly changed jobs to maintain insurance coverage. Most companies’ insurance policies capped out at $1 million, but Williams’ family quickly met that limit. 

“We burned through that policy, sometimes in 3 years, and I ran out of insurance,” he said. “I couldn’t buy a factor for my son. That would probably mean that he could bleed to death and die. So, I would update my resume, circulate my resume, and get another job. I would interview the HR person and say ‘tell me about your medical plan.’ If she told me there was a lucrative plan that had $1 million cap and they offered me the job, I would take it because mainly I was after the insurance. We did that for 20 years.” 

While Williams and his wife, Rita, were fighting to save Trevor’s life, Rita suddenly became ill. She died after a brief battle with colon cancer. 

“She was in one hospital, dying of cancer, while I was taking my little boy to these other clinics to try and keep him from bleeding out,” he said. 

After Rita’s death, Williams said he met another woman and re-married. She became a phlebotomist, and the 2 worked together to care for their blended family of children. 

For many years, Williams lived in fear that he wouldn’t be able to maintain the life-saving treatments for his son. Today, Williams said his son is 40 years old and living independently in California, where he continues with regular treatments. 

 Richard Wiliams motorcycle.jpeg
Richard Williams is making his cross-country trek on a 1980 Honda Goldwing. Courtesy photo 

As a result of his journey to help his hemophiliac son, Williams said he met many people who have had similar experiences. He became connected with Save One Life, an international nonprofit organization that serves families affected by bleeding disorders in resource-limited countries. Through those connections, he learned about people who make bicycle trips across the United States to raise money and awareness for hemophilia treatments. 

At 75 years old, the longtime motorcyclist decided he wanted to join the effort, entitled “Wheels for the World, which is a major fundraiser for Save One Life. Recently, Williams embarked on a self-funded, solo motorcycle ride across the United States, to raise money for the organization. He left his home in Fort Shaw, Mont., on Aug. 20, and rode to Portland, Ore., where he did several media interviews to raise awareness about Save One Life. He then traveled back to Montana, and on Saturday he will be in South Dakota, with plans to stop at the Sturgis Motorcycle Museum and Hall of Fame, Mount Rushmore, and other Black Hills attractions, before heading for the East Coast, stopping at various locations along the way. Eventually, his cross-country journey will culminate in Portland, Maine, at the Cape Elizabeth Lighthouse. 

“My story has gained some traction, and there’s some interested people,” he said. “But that’s why I’m doing this, because I’m in a position now to bring some recognition to other families. Other new parents with hemophilia were probably in a panic the way I was years ago. They may even lose a loved one or more the way I did.”  

Throughout his journey, Williams said he is posting photographs and updates on social media, with each post mentioning the SaveOneLife.net website. On the website, Williams said people can choose to sponsor a hemophiliac child, to help with their treatments, or they can make a donation to the cause. With personal contacts and friendships in the organization, Williams said he can guarantee all contributions go to help kids in 14 different countries, and money is distributed through the Hemophilia Society or Hemophilia Foundation in each country. Save One Life is primarily funded by pharmaceutical companies, who cover administrative costs for the organization, so donations can go directly to help hemophiliac children and young adults. 

Some donations, he said, are used to provide scholarships for hemophiliacs, or to purchase necessary equipment for them to support themselves. 

“After 25 years we have not had one issue,” he said. “Save One Life also offers scholarships to older hemophiliacs, if they’re fortunate to live to their 20s and want to go to school. I also serve on the scholarship committee and I review those scholarships of those young people once a month who are asking for money. The difference between tuition in their country and tuition here is significant. I mean, if we can spend over $800 to pay for somebody’s college education, so they can get a job, that’s pretty cool.” 

Williams said the education is important, because in many cultures the signs and symptoms of hemophilia can be viewed as curses or bad omens. 

“If they have a swollen arm from a constant bleed, or they’re limping, they may not have an easy chance of getting a job because in those countries, they don’t understand what hemophilia is,” he said. “Hemophilia has the stigma of not being the same as everyone else. Save One Life does the best it can to help those people who are looking to start a business. If they want to do upholstery, we can buy them a sewing machine and they can go into business for themselves. If all they need is a laptop to do accounting or finance, which is a great job for a hemophiliac because they sit in a chair all day without impacting their joints.”

title: Sturgis Ambulance Service bills  out over $500K so far this year
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: As the Sturgis Ambulance Service goes into its annual budgeting system, Director Bryson Kool reported it has billed out more than $500,000 in services. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Sturgis ambulance 2.JPG
As the Sturgis Ambulance Service goes into its annual budgeting system, Director Bryson Kool reported it has billed out more than $500,000 in services. Pioneer file photo 

 Sturgis ambulance 1.JPG
Pioneer file photo 

STURGIS — In the first 6 months of this year, the Sturgis Ambulance Service billed out $582,277, and collected $583,464, Bryson Kool, director of the service said. 

On Monday Kool gave a financial report to the Sturgis City Council that included a monthly breakdown of billing for the ambulance service. The report showed a steady flow of income, averaging from $91,000 to $104,000 per month. The report is through June, because that is when the most recent complete billing information is available. 

Kool said he does not yet have exact numbers for the Sturgis Ambulance Service costs for a comparison, as medical bills vary quite a bit and billings are sometimes not paid until many months down the road. As he works on the 2027 budget, he is compiling those numbers. The 2026 budget for the Sturgis Ambulance Service is $1.5 million. 

“This is our first look at some financial information from the Sturgis Ambulance Service,” Kool said. “It’s very important to be as transparent as possible.” 

In April 2025, the Sturgis Ambulance Service contracted with Physicians Claims Company (PCC), a Rapid City-based company that works with emergency services agencies to provide billing services. Prior to that, the Sturgis Ambulance Service handled billing internally, and bills were not always submitted within 30 days of services rendered, which affected reimbursement from the VA, Medicare, and other insurance providers. Because of that, many bills were unpaid. However, when the city contracted with PCC that changed, and by July 2025, former director Aden Schillig reported that the service was on the road to self-sufficiency and a reduced reliance on city funding from the general fund budget. 

In a related matter, Kool reported that calls for service during the 2026 Sturgis Motorcycle Rally were down, with 156 calls this year compared to 190 in 2025. Kool said the service averaged about 15.6 calls per day, with 120 9-11 calls compared to 164 last year. Overall, he said there was an 18% decrease in calls for service. 

This is the first year the Sturgis Ambulance Service brought in extra help during the Rally, with 6 contracted EMS personnel hired to help with the increased work load. But as the number of calls for service decreased throughout the week, Kool reduced his work force proportionately, Mayor Rod Bradley said. 

“They came and worked their butts off for us,” Kool said.
