title: Community supports Sturgis students  through Sabers Agency school supply drive
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: A community member stops and drops off a box of school supplies to Brenda Sabers and Alan Roth during the 5th annual school supply drive on Tuesday in Sturgis.  Photo courtesy of Scott Sabers
_full_text:
1. supply.jpg
A community member stops and drops off a box of school supplies to Brenda Sabers and Alan Roth during the 5th annual school supply drive on Tuesday in Sturgis.  Photo courtesy of Scott Sabers 

STURGIS — The fifth annual Sabers Insurance Agency School Supply Drive collected a large amount of supplies Tuesday for students in the Meade School District.

The donations will benefit students at Sturgis Elementary School, Williams Middle School and Sturgis Brown High School. All supplies collected through the drive go directly to the local schools.

Brenda Sabers said donations were down slightly compared with previous years, but the event still brought in boxes of crayons, markers, notebooks, scissors and glue.

“Sabers Agency has looked forward to this day for the past 5 years,” Sabers said. “It is great to see our community come together and support our Sturgis schools through donations of school supplies.”

She said the drive helps ensure students begin the year with the materials they need to succeed.

School staff members have expressed their appreciation for the donations, Sabers said, noting that the supplies help make certain all students are equipped for the school year. The donations also allow the schools to use their resources to purchase items that may not appear on traditional supply lists.

Those additional needs can include snacks for after-school programs and sweatpants and undergarments for elementary school students.

During the collection event, Sabers Insurance staff members served coffee and doughnuts to community members who stopped by with donations.

“Scott and I have made it a priority to give back to our Scooper community since moving back to the area in 2005,” Sabers said. “We are SBHS alumni and take pride in helping current and future Scooper students succeed.”

Sabers thanked community members for supporting the drive throughout its five-year history.

“We want to thank the Sturgis community for supporting our School Supply Drive for the past 5 years and look forward to hosting the event again next year,” she said.

title: Sales tax growth, drought and labor shortages shape SD’s budget outlook
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: PIERRE — The South Dakota Governor’s Office is entering the state’s next budget-writing season with a rosier revenue picture than feared earlier this year, but advisers warned Thursday of uncertainty around federal policy, drought and workforce shortages.
_full_text:
SearchlightLogo

PIERRE — The South Dakota Governor’s Office is entering the state’s next budget-writing season with a rosier revenue picture than feared earlier this year, but advisers warned Thursday of uncertainty around federal policy, drought and workforce shortages.

The Governor’s Council of Economic Advisors met by video conference to give state financial officials ground-level economic insight as they work to prepare the annual budget that Gov. Larry Rhoden will propose to lawmakers in December. The budget is influenced by economic factors that affect various tax revenues.

Revenue reports and sales tax growth

The state finished last fiscal year with revenue that was $29.7 million, or 1.08%, above predictions.

State sales tax revenue in July, the first month of fiscal year 2027, was up 12.8% compared to the same period last year.

Marnie Herrmann, of Rapid City and chief banking officer at Security First Bank, said average debit card transactions exceeded $50 for the first time this summer. Those payments generally reflect gas and grocery purchases, she said.

“That’s a little bit of a harbinger, if you will, of price pressures,” Herrmann said. 

Agriculture and manufacturing

Farm income has rebounded from a difficult stretch based on first-quarter 2026 reports, said Derek Johnson, state economist with the Bureau of Finance and Management.

Beef prices have risen, and grain prices have increased recently, creating some optimism among farmers, Herrmann said.

Other advisers warned that outside factors, especially shifts in federal policy and climate, are creating uncertainty.

Drought is affecting roughly 75% of the state, and extreme heat during corn’s pollination stage will impact yields, South Dakota economics professor Evert Van der Sluis warned. Federal farm program payments make up between 25% and 30% of net farm income, he added, and federal budget pressures could put those payments at risk.

“We’ve seen these federal payments fluctuate quite a bit in response to trade policies, especially,” Van der Sluis said.

Tariffs have cut into the agriculture and manufacturing industries. An ongoing dispute with Canada is increasing costs for some manufacturers and limiting sales for others, said Carla Gatzke, a former executive at Daktronics, a Brookings-based manufacturer of scoreboards and other electronic displays. Gatzke said the “swings in tariffs” over the last year discouraged development and capital investment in the Brookings area.

Labor force, housing and childcare

South Dakota’s unemployment rate was 2% in July, with roughly three job openings per unemployed person, Johnson said. But labor force participation is declining, and advisers tied that trend to childcare and housing challenges in the state.

People can’t work if they can’t find someone to care for their children or find a place to live, said Doug Sharp, owner of Sharp Automotive in Watertown.

Several advisers shared stories of young family members staying home after having children. Sharp said a lack of data on childcare across the state makes it difficult to quantify the shortage or propose solutions.

Efforts to address the childcare shortage in recent years have stalled in the state Capitol, including a bill offering financial assistance to childcare workers that Gov. Larry Rhoden vetoed.

Housing, advisers said, is an easier challenge to address, though the costs remain a significant barrier to new single-family development. The cost of construction, said Karl Adam of the South Dakota Bankers Association, has “gone through the roof.”

“We still need single-family homes that are affordable in central South Dakota,” Adam said, “but we just don’t seem to be able to get that process started. The cost of construction is an impediment.”

Multifamily construction is making a “huge comeback” in Sioux Falls after a lag in recent years, city Finance Director Shawn Pritchett said.

Sharp said communities are working to incentivize builders.

“Every city will pull out all the stops to figure out how to build out the market,” Sharp said.

title: Spearfish finished traffic safety marking painting, and saved money on the project
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — How many gallons of paint does it take to paint all of the crosswalks, stop bars, and turn arrows in Spearfish? Fewer than the contractor estimated — and that means cost savings for the city.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

SPEARFISH — How many gallons of paint does it take to paint all of the crosswalks, stop bars, and turn arrows in Spearfish? Fewer than the contractor estimated — and that means cost savings for the city. 

On Wednesday, the Spearfish City Council voted unanimously to approve a final change order on the painting project for a new decrease of $4,233.30.

The contractor, BH Striping, had estimated the project would take 326.1 gallons of paint to complete. It took 285 gallons instead.  

Some of the areas in town are thermoplastic and did not require painting, according to public works. Other spots included in the project were painted during other unrelated paving operations. 

“Recently (they) finished this project and included the final inspections, so we wanted the final acceptance of the project and the final change order to match field measured quantities. It is always nice when there is a decrease. The reason was that we had a few locations where there was overlap with other projects, as well as a few locations that have been converted to thermoplastics.”

title: More workers than retirees drove SD’s growth
byline: By Amina Aidarkhanova South Dakota News Watch
description: For years, retirees have been closely associated with South Dakota’s population growth, especially in communities known for recreation and features of lifestyle.
_full_text:
SDNewsWatchLogo

For years, retirees have been closely associated with South Dakota’s population growth, especially in communities known for recreation and features of lifestyle.

But Census migration estimates tell a different story.

Working-age adults ages 18 to 64 represented the largest share of people moving into South Dakota from other states each year from 2021 through 2024, according to an analysis of U.S. Census Bureau data.

During that period, an average of about 21,000 working-age adults moved into South Dakota annually, compared with roughly 5,000 children and 2,000 retirees. In 2022 alone, more than 22,500 working-age adults moved into the state, while about 1,800 retirees arrived.

The findings suggest retirees remain an important part of South Dakota’s migration story but are not the state’s largest group of newcomers.

David Sorenson, professor of economics at Augustana University in Sioux Falls, said statewide migration patterns challenge a common assumption.

“If the common conception is that it’s elderly driving our migration, that’s absolutely false,” Sorenson said.

He said some counties continue attracting retirees, but statewide data show working-age adults dominate migration. The findings also raise questions about who those workers are, including younger professionals, families and people approaching retirement.

Some newcomers are returning for connection, community and quality of life

Danielle Schulz returned to White, after spending about 40 years in California.

She moved west at age 19 hoping to experience different cultures.

“I wanted to meet people from other countries,” Schulz said. “I wanted to see a part of the world that I wasn’t exposed to.”

She returned after her father’s death gave her the opportunity to buy the family farm.

Although returning meant taking a substantial pay cut, she said the move offered something she valued more.

“I wanted solitude,” Schulz said.

She also wanted to reconnect with family and her community.

“The people you meet in your life are what keep you somewhere,” she said.

Sorenson said migration decisions often involve jobs, family ties and lifestyle preferences rather than a single factor.

The post-pandemic migration surge also coincided with expanded remote work and South Dakota’s “Freedom Works Here” campaign, although previous South Dakota News Watch reporting found local officials lacked evidence directly linking migration gains to the advertising effort.

Migration data shows arrivals but not whether people stay

Migration estimates measure people moving into South Dakota, but not whether they remain.

Jared McEntaffer, CEO of the Dakota Institute, said net migration – the difference between arrivals and departures – provides a better measure of long-term population growth.

“The net number is really important,” he said.

While more than 20,000 working-age adults moved into South Dakota annually during the study period, net domestic migration has slowed since its pandemic-era peak. South Dakota gained more than 8,100 net domestic residents during 2021-22, but annual gains later dropped to about 2,000 as more residents left the state.

Sorenson also cautioned against drawing conclusions from a single year’s estimates.

Retirees remain visible but may not drive statewide migration

Retirees continue to play an important role in parts of South Dakota, particularly in western counties that attract RV travelers and outdoor recreation enthusiasts, Sorenson said.

Migration patterns vary by county, meaning some communities attract more retirees while others draw younger workers and families.

A shift in 2024 raises new questions

In 2024, working-age migration declined while retiree migration reached its highest level during the study period. Both Sorenson and McEntaffer said more years of data are needed to determine whether the change represents a lasting trend.

“It raises your antenna,” Sorenson said. “But you’d want to see this repeat or continue.”

Attracting newcomers is only part of the migration challenge

For South Dakota, the larger question is not only who moves to the state, but whether those newcomers remain.

Working-age residents play a key role in the state’s workforce and economy. Whether recent migration translates into sustained population growth will depend not only on attracting new residents but also on convincing them to stay.

title: Broken chiller leads to hot buildings at BHSU
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Students walk back to their dorms at Black Hills State University Thursday. A mechanical failure of one of 2 chillers on campus has left the campus buildings hot.  Pioneer photo by Mark Watson
_full_text:
BHSU 1.jpeg
Students walk back to their dorms at Black Hills State University Thursday. A mechanical failure of one of 2 chillers on campus has left the campus buildings hot.  Pioneer photo by Mark Watson 

SPEARFISH — Students at Black Hills State University face an unexpected challenge this first week of school — very hot living and learning conditions.

One of 2 chillers on campus suffered a mechanical failure Aug. 21 — move-in day for students — taking it offline. Facilities services is making use of the second cooling system while planning to replace the broken system this winter or this coming spring, said Maegan Detlefs, assistant director of marketing and communication at the university.

Since its failure, facilities services staff and external contractors have been evaluating the equipment and working to maximize the cooling capacity available from the campus’s remaining chiller, said Kyle Nelson, associate vice president of facilities services.

“It’s been horrible. It’s been like 86 (degrees) in our dorms,” Clara Delbridge, a freshman living in Bordeaux Hall said Thursday. “I think it might have been working this morning. It was 72. But before, it wasn’t working at all.”

Cooper Daigla, a sophomore living in Wenona Cook Hall, said his dorm has air conditioning, but added that the classes have been hot.

“There’s a class I have in Jonas Science. It’s been dreadful in there,” he said. “I have it for 2 hours, and I’m just dying of heat. But it wasn’t as bad yesterday. I think they got one of the coolers up and running.”

He said one class was held outside which was nice.

Ashtyn Hight, a freshman living in Heidi Hall, said air conditioning has also been out in her dorm. 

She said, with outside temperatures hovering around 90 degrees, the room temperatures have been comparable.

“It’s hot,” she said. “It’s about like it is out here right now.”

Numerous students said they are trying to beat the heat by opening windows in their rooms at night and have fans blowing on them constantly. Most also agreed that Meier Hall seemed to be the hottest.

“Meier Hall has been pretty bad,” Hight said. “They let us out early. Jonas (Hall) hasn’t been too terrible. My Spanish class that’s in Meier Hall, got canceled and put online tomorrow because of the heat.”

 BHSU 2.JPG
A mechanical failure in one of 2 chillers at Black Hills State University has left the campus buildings hot this first week of school. Pioneer file photo 

Delbridge said one of her classes in Meier Hall was moved from its scheduled location to a choir room on the first floor which helps.

Several facilities on campus are on their own cooling systems. Those include the Joy Center, the Young Center, and the Life Sciences Laboratory.

“The failed unit serves a substantial portion of the campus cooling network,” Detlefs said. “While BHSU continues to operate its secondary cooling system, that system does not provide the same level of cooling capacity as normal operations, which can result in warmer temperatures in some campus facilities.”

She added that instructors have been authorized to make temporary adjustments if excessive heat affects the learning environment. Depending on classroom conditions, instructors may relocate classes to cooler campus spaces, temporarily move instruction online, or implement other reasonable accommodations to support student learning.

Nelson said that the primary cause of the failure was its age and condition. 

“The chiller has exceeded its expected service life, and BHSU has been closely monitoring its performance in recent years,” Nelson said. “Recognizing that replacement would eventually be necessary, BHSU began planning and identifying funding last year for a replacement scheduled for this coming winter.”

The job of replacing the chiller is no small task.

“Replacing a chiller of this size is a significant project. Large commercial chillers often have long manufacturing and delivery lead times, and the replacement also requires engineering, coordination, removal of the existing equipment, installation of the new chiller, and commissioning before it can be placed into service,” Nelson said. “Our goal is to have the replacement completed as quickly as possible, with the current anticipated timeline extending into the winter or spring.”

BHSU uses a central chilled water system to provide cooling to multiple buildings across campus, he said. This type of system is typical for college campuses because it allows one central system to efficiently serve several buildings. The chiller produces chilled water that is circulated through underground pipes to the buildings it serves, where it is used to provide air conditioning.

title: Iowa regulators investigate BH Energy’s high number of pipeline safety violations
byline: By Cami Koons Iowa Capital Dispatch
description: The Iowa Utilities Commission is investigating a high volume of safety violations from Black Hills Energy. Photo by Cami Koons, Iowa Capital Dispatch
_full_text:
Iowa regulators investigate BH Energy’s high number of pipeline safety violations.jpg
The Iowa Utilities Commission is investigating a high volume of safety violations from Black Hills Energy. Photo by Cami Koons, Iowa Capital Dispatch 

The Iowa Utilities Commission is evaluating potential penalties and corrective action for Black Hills Energy following a hearing Thursday on an investigation into the gas company’s safety and management practices in Iowa.

Routine inspections from IUC revealed Black Hills Energy had disproportionally more instances of probable violations than the other top gas providers in Iowa over the past several years. The IUC also flagged that Black Hills has significantly longer correction times for probable violations than the other major gas providers. 

Black Hills representatives acknowledged that the number of probable violation instances was high in a recent audit and said the company has a “structured continuous improvement approach” to address the commission’s concerns and improve compliance.

Pete Hamell, the general manager for Black Hills Energy Iowa Gas, said that while the number of probable violations is notable, the “nature of the observations really isn’t alarming.”

Hamell said many of the probable violations observed by IUC were related to environmental, homeowner or business factors. That means things like oxidation of pipes over time, damage from homeowners doing landscaping projects or regulatory changes. 

“We have alignment with the commission that the safe, reliable, and affordable delivery of gas service to our customers in all of our communities is a shared responsibility and priority for us,” Hamell said, speaking as a witness during the hearing. “We take the commission’s, not only their observations, but the commission’s partnership to heart.”

Volume of violations 

In June 2025, IUC submitted a routine inspection report on Black Hills’ Spencer Unit in northwest Iowa that had more than 100 safety issues in 16 violation categories. IUC said that while the violations didn’t pose and immediate threat to the public, the high volume was cause for an investigation.

As IUC reviewed additional data with other Black Hills operations in the state, it “became increasingly concerned” about potential “company-wide safety issues” across Black Hills’ operations in the state, according to a news release from IUC. 

While IUC can levy civil penalties to utilities that commit violations, the commission decided to defer its final decision on civil penalties for Black Hills until it could evaluate compliance standards through the rest of the utility’s systems in Iowa. 

According to IUC, Black Hills is the smallest of the three major natural gas utilities in Iowa, behind Interstate Power and Light Company and MidAmerican Energy Company. According to data presented by IUC Thursday, Black Hills has just under 3,000 miles of main pipe in Iowa, compared to more than 4,500 miles operated by IPL and more than 11,000 miles operated by MidAmerican. 

While smaller than the 2 other major operators, an IUC chart showed Black Hills’ instances of probable violations between 2023 and 2025 were nearly the same as MidAmerican’s. When scaled to the number of violations in the time frame per 1,000 service lines, Black Hills’ violations were nearly three times that of MidAmerican or IPL. 

Adam Buhrman, corporate counsel for Black Hills Energy, said the utility was not given this data prior to the hearing to verify its accuracy. 

In Black Hills’ July 29 filed response, it said certain inspection reports contained “a significant number of findings” but that “none of those findings involved active leaks or other immediate threats to public safety.” 

The findings from the recent reports pertained to issues like compliance, documentation, maintenance, corrosion prevention or facility maintenance, according to Black Hills’ filing. In its response to IUC’s notice, Black Hills contended that civil penalties were “not warranted” as part of the commission’s review.

“The Company believes that continued implementation of its corrective action plan, together with ongoing reporting, collaboration, and evaluation of compliance performance, will provide a more effective means of addressing the Commission’s concerns and promoting continued improvement than the assessment of civil penalties,” Black Hills’ filing said.

Hamell said many of the instances flagged in the Spencer report that initiated the IUC’s investigation were related to what Black Hills would call “oxidation” which he said “is not necessarily bad for pipelines.” 

Further discussion around oxidation and corrosion in the hearing led commissioner Joshua Byrnes to say that it seems IUC inspectors are seeing instances of corrosion while Black Hills technicians see oxidation. 

“How do we get to a point where we’re all seeing the same thing?” Byrnes asked. 

Matt Mangin, a senior specialist with Black Hills overseeing corrosion control, among other things, said the training would need to be equal between the agencies to properly identify the difference between oxidation and corrosion. Corrosion, he said, is an electrochemical reaction and has to present all 4 elements of corrosion. 

Speediness

IUC also presented information comparing Black Hills’ correction times compared to other utilities from 2023 through 2025. While MidAmerican and IPL had an average time to correct issues of about 30 days, Black Hills’ average was 132 days. 

Hamell said certain projects take longer to complete than others, due to things like engineering and permitting. But generally, Hamell said to his knowledge, Black Hills’ response times have not “exceeded” the standards set by the U.S. Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration, or PHMSA. 

Many of the questions from commissioners centered on staffing concerns at Black Hills, but Hamell assured commissioners that staffing was not currently a concern for the company. 

In its June 29 order giving notice of possible civil penalties, IUC noted that Black Hills closed violations from the 2025 Spencer audit “faster than those found throughout the remainder of Black Hills’ gas system.” IUC said faster response time must be examined to understand why it has not been replicated in the utility’s other Iowa systems.  

Black Hills, in its filed response, said past closure times “needed improvement” and that its “current trend demonstrates meaningful progress in that regard.” 

Kevin Jarosz, the vice president of Black Hills’ Iowa & Nebraska gas operations, said safety is the “highest priority” at the company. 

“We firmly commit safety to our employees, our customers, and communities that we serve, and we also commit to a strong compliance program, investment in our infrastructure, and continuously improving where we need to,” Jarosz said during the hearing. “We also commit to continue to work collaboratively with the commission to ensure that safe operations continue, and we will continue to provide safe, reliable service to our customers, like we have for decades and into the future.”

The Iowa Utilities Commission will review the testimony and the written responses to determine applicable civil penalties and corrective actions in the matter.

title: Lawrence Co. moves forward with bridge replacements
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Four structures on Hanna Road had decks replaced with panel-lam systems purchased from Wheeler Lumber of Whitewood. Photo courtesy of Lawrence County Highway Department
_full_text:
Lawrence Co. moves forward with bridge replacements.jpg
Four structures on Hanna Road had decks replaced with panel-lam systems purchased from Wheeler Lumber of Whitewood. Photo courtesy of Lawrence County Highway Department 

DEADWOOD — Lawrence County highway department Aug. 25 reported progress made on structures, including replacing the decks of structures on Hanna Road and approving Brosz Engineering for construction management of projects on Nemo Road. 

Hanna Road structures receive deck replacement

John Bey, highway superintendent, told county commissioners Tuesday his department continues to work to replace the deck of structures on Hanna Road. The decks on 4 structures on the road are being replaced with panel-lam systems purchased from Wheeler Lumber of Whitewood. 

“The abutments the decks are sitting on are sound. We’re able to do the work in-house,” said Bey. “If we don’t have to replace the abutments, and we don’t have to do anything in the creek channel, we don’t really have to go through any of the process of getting permits, any kind of 404 permits, any kind of NEPA (National Environmental Policy Act) studies. We get a nice, new structure that is rated for legal loads, and we can do it a lot quicker.”

Bey said the decks can be removed and replaced, including guard rails, within an 8-hour workday. 

Bey said the last of the 4 structures were exected to be replaced Monday, requiring a temporary road closure. Upon completion, he said all 4 structures will have pavement repaired in the near future.  

“The road will not be closed for pavement,” he said. “There will be some delays, but the road will not be closed. The pavement will go pretty fast.”

After receiving new pavement, Bey said the load limit of the structures will increase.

Bey said the structures were purchased 2 at a time over the last 2 fiscal years for $44,000 each. The structures were paid for by the department’s road and bridge repair budget. 

Nemo Road projects move forward

A project to repair a 3.63-mile section of road and replace 2 structures on Nemo Road has made headway after commissioners agreed to allow Brosz Engineering to perform construction management for a portion of the project. 

Bey said it’s possible that one of the structures will be removed in November. At that time, a diversion crossing private access roads will be opened for the duration of the project. 

“We are not going to open that diversion until the last moment it has to be used,” he said. “The diversion is in place, and we do have to put a layer of gravel on it, but we’re not going to do that until the last minute because we don’t want to encourage people to start driving there.”

The 2 structures will be replaced by cast-in-place box culverts. Bey said it will be possible to replace the structures through the winter. He said the substantial completion date for the project is Nov. 26, 2027.

The contract to replace the structures was awarded to Halme, Inc., in May 2026 for $1.8 million. The project is being paid for, in large part, by a bridge improvement grant. The county will be responsible for 20% of the total cost.

title: ‘Building Outside the Lines’ did not film a fourth season
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Alex “Sprout” Headley and Jared “Cappie” Capp did not film a fourth season of their show ‘Building Outside the Lines.’ Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Cappie and Alex.jpg
Alex “Sprout” Headley and Jared “Cappie” Capp did not film a fourth season of their show ‘Building Outside the Lines.’ Pioneer file photo 

SPEARFISH — Jared “Cappie” Capp and Alex “Sprout” Headley made an announcement on their official social media channels late last week — they did not film a fourth season of their Emmy-nominated Magnolia Network show ‘Building Outside the Lines’ this summer. 

“Our contract with Magnolia network is up and (we) have not been picked up for another season. We appreciate everyone’s love and support, and will be continuing to build weird,” Capp wrote in a Facebook post. 

The television show: set and filmed primarily in Spearfish followed the Capp and his step-daughter as they designed and built unusual and occasionally awe-inspiring structures commissioned by local clients. 

 “We’ve gotten a lot of questions on the socials, and we are so grateful for the fan support, but we’ve gotten a lot of questions about when season 4 will be out, we are here to tell you a season 4 will not be coming this year,” Headley said in a video. It is not clear if the show might be renewed, or film again next year. An official reason for the halt in filming has not been offered at this time. 

Headley is starting college, and encouraged fans to continue to follow her journey on Instagram at @thisisalexheadley. 

“Please continue to support us,” Capp said in the post. “We’re going to film some of it on our own. Now that Sprout’s 18, maybe we can do some traveling.”  

The Pioneer has reached out to Magnolia Network for comment, but have not heard back before press time.

title: Strong winds wallop NW SD
byline: By Mark Wartson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — The combination of a cold front moving through the area along with thunderstorms that passed through the northwest part of the state caused some very strong outflow winds Sunday afternoon.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

SPEARFISH — The combination of a cold front moving through the area along with thunderstorms that passed through the northwest part of the state caused some very strong outflow winds Sunday afternoon.

Ben Schweigert, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service in Rapid City, said outflow winds are created when a cloud begins to release rain. That rain cools the air which pushes out from the storm.

He added Sunday’s wind event was a bit unique as the storm “tag teamed” with the cold front created very strong winds.

A weather station near Buffalo recorded a wind gust of 100 mph.

Near Ludlow, winds topped out at 87 mph and 78 near Mud Butte.

Winds reached 73 mph just south of Camp Crook and 67 near Newell. Just east of Sturgis, winds hit 61 mph. On the west side of Sturgis, dust from a construction site drifted heavily across the interstate reducing visibility, and north of town, dust from the burn scar created during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, had some people thinking a fire started once again due to the black dust.

Just out of Belle Fourche, a 62 mph gust was recorded.

Winds topped out at 60 in Union Center and the Rapid City Airport. They hit 56 at Ellsworth Air Force Base and near Nisland. And just outside of Spearfish, winds hit 52 mph.

title: SD seeks to ban use of food assistance for soda purchases as court ruling clouds issue
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Pioneer photo by Brandon Woltkamp
_full_text:
SODA CAN BY BRANDON.jpg
Pioneer photo by Brandon Woltkamp 

PIERRE — The South Dakota Department of Social Services said Monday that it submitted a request to the U.S. Department of Agriculture to bar the purchase of soft drinks with government food assistance, after a June court decision vacated similar bans in five states and caused some other states to delay implementing their bans.

A Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program waiver from the federal government is necessary for states to limit the kinds of food or beverages that can be purchased using the benefits, which in South Dakota are loaded onto cards that function like debit cards. South Dakota’s Legislature and governor approved a law earlier this year requiring the state Department of Social Services to seek a waiver to ban soft drink purchases, and to submit the waiver application by this Tuesday. 

The new law defines a “soft drink” as “a nonalcoholic beverage that contains natural or artificial sweeteners,” with exemptions for milk or milk products; rice, soy or similar milk substitutes; and some juices.

Benefits are available to income-eligible families, and in South Dakota they can be used to purchase nearly any kind of food or beverage. Roughly 72,000 people, or 36,500 households, receive benefits in South Dakota, according to the department.

The department said in a news release that the ban on soft drinks will begin six months after federal approval, though it did not address the federal court decision or delays in other states.

North Dakota was set to ban candy, soda and other sweetened drinks this week, but delayed its rollout. The North Dakota Health and Human Services Department received a letter from the USDA citing the recent federal court decision that struck down similar bans in five states. The decision criticized the USDA for not following requirements to publish notice of the restrictions and accept public comment.

North Dakota and South Carolina are among the states postponing their restrictions to Nov. 1 to allow the USDA to consider the impact of the court decision, publish a public notice in the Federal Register and assess public comment before each state’s ban goes into effect.

The USDA has approved 23 SNAP food restriction waivers, according to its website, including the five states where the waivers were vacated by the court ruling.

Sioux Falls Republican Rep. Taylor Rehfeldt introduced the bill requiring South Dakota to seek a waiver. Rehfeldt, a nurse anesthetist, said the submitted waiver is “progress,” despite the potential delay.

“I think it’s important that we move forward with what’s best for South Dakota,” Rehfeldt said. “And what’s best for South Dakota is getting unhealthy, sugary drinks out of the SNAP program — both from a patient and holistic health standpoint and as responsible stewards of taxpayer dollars.”

Opponents said during the legislative session that the bill would create administrative burdens for the state and retailers without producing the desired effects.

“If our goal is better nutrition, we should reward nutritious choices instead of punishing food choices,” said Rep. Liz May, R-Kyle, during debate on the bill in February. May is a grocery store owner.

An estimate prepared by the Legislative Research Council said hiring the staff and paying for the software necessary to implement a ban would cost the state $310,000 in the first two years, and about a quarter-million dollars annually thereafter.

title: Spearfish celebrates new bike trails in the  heart of town
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — A trail can be a lot more than an outdoor space for exploration and recreation. Emily Brown, president of the non-profit Spearfish Trails Coalition (STC), said a trail system can prove the power of collective action.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — A trail can be a lot more than an outdoor space for exploration and recreation. Emily Brown, president of the non-profit Spearfish Trails Coalition (STC), said a trail system can prove the power of collective action.

“At first glance it just looks like we built a few trails, and we have, and that’s awesome and that’s reason enough to come together and celebrate today, but I do want us to take a little bit of a closer look,” Brown said during a ribbon cutting event Saturday at the new gravity skills bike trail system, directly adjacent to the city campground ice rink parking lot. “I want us as a community to train our eyes to see something a little bit deeper. These aren’t just trails. This is what happens when a community decides to do something a little different. They’re the result of people showing up, having conversations, and deciding that they want to be a part of making things better, instead of wishing for somebody else to do something. They’re the result of sharing ideas, disagreeing, compromising, solving problems, and ultimately deciding that they want to build something together.”

Spearfish Parks and Recreation Director Rex McDonald noted that STC worked for years to plan, design, and ultimately make real a professionally built public trail system — at no cost to taxpayers.

“I’ve had the privilege of working with STC since its inception, and their collective passion and desire to enhance and develop our community trail system is truly a tremendous asset for our community,” McDonald said. “It will serve as an incredible outdoor recreation destination in Spearfish for generations to use and enjoy.”

McDonald said the trails reflect recent innovation in trail building, and are expertly designed to create, “opportunities for fun trail experiences for all users of all skill levels.”

“These new trails offer an experience that we have never had in the community: progressive and technical features including drops, jumps, berms, and gravity flow trails,” McDonald said. “The intentional and thoughtful locations and designs maximize the use of our public spaces while taking into consideration connectivity with our entire trail system across the community.”

Brown thanked McDonald and his predecessor Tyler Ehnes for their work with the trails coalition to bring more diverse trails to the area. She also thanked the city for their willingness to work with STC’s dedicated board — and the small army of volunteers and community members who helped make it possible for people to don helmets, hop on their bikes, and build skills on their bikes.

“It took a whole community of people to make this happen,” Brown said. “We are so proud of the trust and collaboration that we have been able to build with the city of Spearfish, and we look forward to many, many years of building trails in the community.”

Brown noted that trails are an important space that can facilitate community building.

“When I look at a new trail system, or I see the preservation or maintenance of a new trail system, I see social infrastructure. I see a place where people who might not otherwise cross paths sharing a space,” Brown said. “People of different ages, different backgrounds, different backgrounds, different perspectives, different experiences, they are all sharing the same space together.”

Spaces like the new trails in and near the campground don’t just happen, Brown said.

“They happen when people decide to participate in them, when we volunteer. When we know our neighbors. When we take care of the places that we share, when we believe that the things we build together are worth protecting,” Brown said. “I have been told once or twice that maybe trails won’t solve every problem in the world, but the process of building one teaches us something very important. We are not powerless. We can identify something our community needs, bring people together, work through the hard parts, and create something that didn’t exist before. We can do that, because we just did that.”

title: State readjusts childcare assistance after complaints about rate change, but concerns remain
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasdearchlight.com
description: Students in the Sioux Falls School District play on a playground. Photo courtesy of Sioux Falls School District
_full_text:
State readjusts childcare assistance after complaints about rate change, but concerns remain.jpg
Students in the Sioux Falls School District play on a playground. Photo courtesy of Sioux Falls School District 

SIOUX FALLS — A Sioux Falls after-school coordinator said she fielded calls from panicked parents this month after the state altered childcare assistance payments — in some cases slashing assistance by more than 80%, she said.

Rebecca Wimmer is the coordinator for the Sioux Falls School District’s after-school program. She reported hearing from families who said it would be more cost-effective for a parent to quit working and stay home with their kids than to pay for the lost assistance. She relayed those stories to state lawmakers, the Governor’s Office and the state Department of Social Services.

Child Care Assistance is a federal-state program that helps low-income working parents, students and job trainees afford childcare. South Dakota’s program costs the state about $6.7 million and the federal government $28.4 million. It covered 3,346 children in June.

At the start of this month, the Department of Social Services made a change to its payment model that Wimmer said would have cut payments to some individual families by hundreds of dollars.

The switch was part of a planned overhaul of the department’s payment model, meant to make payments more predictable for childcare providers. Complaints from affected families and providers resulted in the department readjusting payments a little over a week later for urban after-school programs, where the effects were especially severe. Urban counties include Minnehaha, Lincoln, Meade and Pennington.

Change to tiered, flat rates

State Rep. Brian Mulder, R-Sioux Falls, advocated on behalf of families for the readjustment. Mulder works with Volunteers of America, which provides after-school care. He is grateful for the department’s decision.

“For this school year, we’re in a spot where school can start and families can feel confident they have proper funding for out-of-school care to support their needs and child’s needs,” Mulder said.

Under the old system, program payments were based on a child’s actual hours of attendance, which meant payments could fluctuate and make it hard for providers to predict their income.

The department switched to three tiers of flat weekly rates earlier this month: a full-time rate for more than 28 hours of care per week, part-time for 16-27 hours and limited for 1-15 hours. 

The rates were informed by a 2024 market survey of Child Care Assistance-enrolled providers. For after-school programs in Sioux Falls and Rapid City, the new rates set full-time reimbursement at $185 a week, with part-time dropping to $92.50 and limited to $46.50. 

The change cut some families’ state payments by hundreds of dollars a month, Wimmer said, including one family that would have had state payments cut from $950 a month to $185 — a monthly cost of $765.

After the readjustment, part-time and limited rates were both raised to $101.25 — which “gets us very close” to the cost of after-school care, Wimmer said.

Department spokeswoman Tracy Mercer did not say if such a drastic change for families’ payments was intentional or an oversight by the department. The tiered approach, she said, is a “responsible use of program dollars.” Some providers have called for the state to cover full-time enrollment no matter how many hours children attend.

“Program dollars should not cover significant periods when a child is not receiving care,” Mercer said. “CCA funds are limited, and the department has a responsibility to use those dollars as effectively as possible so they can stretch to serve as many eligible families as possible.”

The state estimated the weekly, tiered payment plan would cost the state $3 million more overall before rolling it out — money that would benefit providers and families across the state. The expected increase was within the department’s budget, Mercer said. The department did not immediately share an updated estimate with the readjusted rates.

Overall ‘revamp’ still needed, provider says

Wimmer said there are staffing and overhead costs outside of a child’s physical attendance. Her program runs at school sites, requiring staff to arrive before the school day ends to transform cafeterias into program spaces. Other off-site providers need staff to drive to a school, wait and then transport children to the off-site care location.

“The market for childcare is just not set up where a part-time rate payment works very well,” Wimmer said.

Wimmer said she expects the department will ultimately have to “revamp the whole model,” because part-time and limited rates for younger children still don’t reflect what it actually costs providers to operate and leave too many costs for providers and families to absorb.

Mulder, the lawmaker, said he heard criticism of the change from after-school providers and families. He did not hear from childcare providers for younger children or their families in the Sioux Falls area. Nor did he hear from suburban or rural after-school programs.

The department will begin its next market rate survey this fall. The department plans to update rates in fiscal year 2028.

Mercer said the department “remains open to receiving additional feedback” on the new payment model from other childcare providers.

Governor candidates react

South Dakota Democratic nominee for governor Dan Ahlers said in a news release that the fallout from the rate change “should never have happened in the first place.” The readjustment is not enough, he said.

Ahlers serves as president of the Dell Rapids before- and after-school program, where he said state funding decisions can “put enormous pressure on providers and families.”

Childcare providers already struggle to balance worker wages, affordability for families and quality care for a service that is “essential to our economy, our workforce and the future of our communities,” he added.

“As governor, I will work with parents, providers, employers and communities to make quality childcare more affordable for families and help providers remain viable,” Ahlers said.

Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden, Ahlers’ opponent in the Nov. 3 election, told South Dakota Searchlight that the Department of Social Services addressed “some of the immediate concerns” of families and providers.

“We’ll continue to peel these issues off as they come and work for solutions for whatever it might be,” Rhoden said, “but I’m pretty happy with the way that our team has responded so far, and we’ll continue to try and respond appropriately on issues as they come forward.”

Billy Mawhiney, with the South Dakota Afterschool Network, said any changes should increase access and affordability, not reduce it.

“If kids are going to an after-school program, their grades will be higher, their self esteem will be higher, their reading scores and math scores — everything we want for a child is going to improve,” Mawhiney said. “The better opportunity, more affordability and more access we can get for after-school care, the more South Dakota kids will have access to a better life.”

title: Lead-Deadwood falls  in football opener
byline: By Jason Gross Black Hills Pioneer
description: DEADWOOD — Lead-Deadwood’s football team endured a rough first quarter Friday night and dropped a 36-7 decision to Wall in the Golddiggers’ season opener, played at Ferguson Field.
_full_text:
DEADWOOD — Lead-Deadwood’s football team endured a rough first quarter Friday night and dropped a 36-7 decision to Wall in the Golddiggers’ season opener, played at Ferguson Field.

The contest marked Lead-Deadwood’s 9-man debut after many years of competing in the 11-man ranks.

“We’re not going to make excuses. Wall’s a great team,” said Golddiggers’ head coach Michael Barnaud, whose team trailed 20-0 after the first 12 minutes.

Tanner Volmer scored on a 2-yard run to end Wall’s opening drive spanning 6 plays and 52 yards. Shooter Frederick kicked the extra point as the Eagles led 7-0.

Wall ended its next possession when Volmer threw a 37-yard touchdown pass to Frederick. The conversion by Frederick put the Eagles up 14-0 following a 3-play, 55-yard drive.

Volmer’s 8-yard touchdown pass to Carter Sundall ended the next Eagles’ possession that lasted 2 plays and covered 15 yards. An unsuccessful conversion kept Wall’s advantage at 20-0 as the first period ended.

The first Wall drive of the second quarter stalled at the Golddiggers’ 12-yard line when the Lead-Deadwood defense forced an incomplete pass on fourth down.

Blake Janssen caught a 12-yard pass on the next possession to give the Golddiggers their initial first down of the game. The drive stalled, and Lead-Deadwood had to punt.

Wall faced a fourth down and 1 from Lead-Deadwood’s 5-yard line in the first half’s final minute. The Golddiggers’ defense stopped a run for no gain to keep the halftime score at 20-0.

Lead-Deadwood started the third quarter at its 32-yard line. Three first downs (Janssen’s 10-yard reception, Garrett Rantapaa’s 8-yard reception, and Zade Seaman’s 18-yard run) helped move the Golddiggers to the Wall 24. A fourth and 1 play lost 7 yards to give the ball back to the Eagles.

Volmer’s 10-yard touchdown run put the Eagles on the scoreboard in the third quarter. Frederick caught the 2-point pass to give Wall a 28-0 lead at quarter’s end.

An 86-yard touchdown run by Volmer further extended Wall’s advantage. Frederick caught a 2-point pass as the Eagles went up 36-0.

Rantapaa recovered a fumble for Lead-Deadwood at the Wall 23-yard line. Blaze Artz fired a 23-yard scoring strike to Braydon Munier with one minute left. Janssen’s extra point accounted for the 36-7 final.

Barnaud agreed that the Golddiggers got more used to the more open style of 9-man football as the game progressed. He said that Volmer, who is Wall’s quarterback, is a special player.

“Football comes down to blocking, tackling, catching; it comes down to fundamentals,” Barnaud said. “We didn’t do enough of it well tonight.”

Barnaud said the Golddigger defense improved its tackling and got a better feel for the opponent about 75 percent of the way through the first quarter.

Lead-Deadwood (0-1) will visit Philip next Friday.

“We look at the things that went well, and we have to continue to try doing those things better,” Barnaud said. He cited the importance of having the right attitude of getting better at the game and scheme.

title: Every arrest protects children
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Marty Jackley says the Internet Crimes Against Children task force has made 104 arrests in the last 14 years. South Dakota Searchlight photo
_full_text:
Marty Jackley.jpg
Marty Jackley says the Internet Crimes Against Children task force has made 104 arrests in the last 14 years. South Dakota Searchlight photo 

SPEARFISH — Every arrest the Internet Crimes Against Children (ICAC) task force makes during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally represents a child who was protected from sexual predators. 

That’s how South Dakota Attorney General Marty Jackley views the work of the task force, which involves a collaboration of federal, state, and local law enforcement and state’s attorneys. In the last 14 years, Jackley said the Internet Crimes Against Children task force has made 104 arrests during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, for child exploitation, pornography, and human trafficking charges. 

“Really, for me this is what it’s all about. What can we do to be proactive, to protect our kids, to make sure that we’re doing everything we can to stop the trafficking, to stop the exploitation of kids,” Jackley said. “These operations are very proactive. In other words, there is not a child put in jeopardy. There’s not a child involved. It is an ICAC member, the DCI agent, where they’re posing as a child. So, when the bad actor shows up, they’re meeting law enforcement. So we’re preventing them from human trafficking, kidnapping, or the sexual assault of a child.” 

During the operation, Department of Criminal Investigation (DCI) agents and detectives post ads and/or profiles on various Internet sites and social media platforms, inviting offenders to communicate with people the offenders believe to be children, to arrange a meeting for the purpose of sexual activity. 

 Rally main street vertical.JPG
The Internet Crimes Against Children task force typically conducts operations during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally because of the large volume of people who attend ever year. Pioneer file photo 

This year’s ICAC operation during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally was the first year Jackley said he took advantage of Section 287(g) of the Immigration and Nationality Act, which allows the U.S. Department of Homeland Security to deputize state and local law enforcement to enforce federal immigration laws. This year 2 of the 6 men arrested for sex crimes were immigrants. Johan Vazquez-Garza, 33, of Rapid City had been deported 5 times since 2009. In addition to solicitation of a minor, Vazquez-Garza faces additional federal immigration charges. Bo Bo Aung, 38, of Box Elder, who was arrested for first degree human trafficking, attempted first degree trafficking, and attempted fourth degree rape, is a Myanmar National, whom Jackley said allegedly illegally absconded from a work visa program in Texas 7 years ago, and who faces federal deportation proceedings after he answers to his sex crime charges in South Dakota. 

Pull quote
"The fact that over 14 years we have had 104 arrests tells me this is a significant problem that we need to stay ahead of with proactive activity." — Marty Jackley

“This would have been the first year where immigration played this significant of a role,” Jackley said. “There have been illegal immigrants in the past, but 2 of those arrests were issues where the immigration system has failed us. It hasn’t done what it needs to do to protect us, protect kids. I think it signifies why that open border was such a concern, and the importance of closing that southern border, not just for the drug trade, not just for the illegal gun trade, but the human trafficking trade.” 

Other arrests included registered sex offender Adrian Tomas Randles, 39, of Rapid City, who was charged with solicitation of a minor; Steven Clay Brown, 62, of Sturgis, who was charged with solicitation of a minor; Kevin Orlanda Tassion Brown, 30, of Dillon, S.C., who was charged with first degree human trafficking, attempted first degree human trafficking, and attempted fourth degree rape; and Jay Anderson, 39, of Hot Springs, who was charged with solicitation of a minor.

Jackley said his ICAC task force specifically conducts operations during the Sturgis Motorcycle Rally, because of the large concentration of people. Unfortunately, he said, many local predators and others feel like they can use the cover of hundreds of thousands of visitors, to get away with exploiting children. 

“You’ve got a handful of local individuals that weren’t here because of the Rally, but looked to be taking advantage of and perhaps covered with a lot of traffic, a lot of people around,” he said. 

A major boost for the ICAC task force, Jackley said, was a $15 million settlement with Internet gaming platform Roblox, which was accused of failing to protect children from online predators. At least $2.6 million from that settlement went to the ICAC task force to purchase new technology to help officers with the task force identify offenders and run more operations to arrest sexual predators. The settlement also came with stipulations for Roblox to change key parts of its gaming platform, including requiring age verification, facial age estimation technology, and government-issued ID age confirmation for users. 

Jackley said that settlement was key to working with Internet platforms to improve safety for children, which is a priority for him. He is also encouraging other attorney generals to prioritize child Internet safety. 

“For me, it’s always been the injunctive relief, the proactive relief, where these companies become better partners in preventing this and working with law enforcement,” he said. “We did that with Roblox, and that has been our position with Google. It’s our position with Meta. We are making every effort we can to have these tech companies use that technology to work with us to protect kids.” 

Overall, Jackley said whether he is helping to plan an operation, assisting with the technology aspect, or donning a bulletproof vest to accompany officers on an arrest, fighting sex crimes is a mission he takes very seriously, and will continue to pursue. He considers every arrest by ICAC to be a success and one more step toward protecting children. 

“I consider it to be successful in that there are now 6 individuals that are not out there doing this to real children,” he said. “The fact that over 14 years we have had 104 arrests tells me this is a significant problem that we need to stay ahead of with proactive activity. That’s why I put such an effort into supporting ICAC. Every time I speak to appropriators, I talk about their good work and the need to make sure they’ve got the tools, the technology, the protections out there for successful operations.”

title: Indictment filed, arrest warrant issued in Spearfish Rams embezzlement case
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Justice03.TIF
Courtesy photo 

SPEARFISH — An indictment was filed Aug. 26 and an arrest warrant was issued Monday morning in the case of the Spearfish Rams embezzlement case.

Ashley M. Spilman, 39, is accused of embezzling money from the Spearfish Rams organization in the Black Hills Youth Football League. 

According to court reports, Spilman, around the month of March, allegedly stole the funds. She was charged with grand theft by embezzlement of more than $2,500, but less than $5,000 — a Class 5 felony.  

The Rams’ board of directors shared the news on its Facebook page June 2. It asked anyone who has donated or sponsored funds to the Rams between Dec. 1, 2025, and now to contact the program right away, as those funds were never received. 

The commissioner of the organization was terminated.

“This discovery has been devastating to everyone involved, especially because this organization exists for one reason, our kids,” a post on social media by the Rams’ board of directors reads. 

“We understand the anger, disappointment, and frustration many of you might feel. As leaders and volunteers within this organization, we take this situation very seriously, and we sincerely apologize to every family, sponsor, supporter, and community member who placed their trust in us. 

The post indicates that the situation was allegedly caused by the actions of one individual, and that the board recognizes that the organization should have had stronger financial oversight. 

“We are actively working to address those failures immediately by implementing additional accountability measures, reviewing all financial records, and cooperating fully with the local police department,” according to the post from the board. 

Following the announcement, the Pioneer contacted the Spearfish Police Department for information. Police Chief Collin Smith confirmed officers had a suspect and were investigating to get a true account of missing funds, but declined to provide more information at this time. 

An email to the Spearfish Rams seeking comment was not immediately returned.

This marked the second time that the Spearfish Rams has had money taken from the organization. 

In 2018, Nicholas Edward Hoffman pleaded guilty to one count of grand theft by embezzlement from Spearfish Youth Wrestling Club. As part of a plea agreement, 2 other identical charges were dropped. Those charges were for embezzlement from the Queen City Futbol Club and Spearfish Rams Football. In addition of jail time, Hoffman was ordered to pay restitution of $14,549.33 total to the 3 clubs. Hoffman was commissioner of the Rams during that timeframe.

title: Butte County Commission calls  for public input on Senate Bill 96
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: BELLE FOURCHE — During its 9:30 a.m. meeting tomorrow, the Butte County Commission plans to discuss Senate Bill 96, which allows counties to implement a new sales tax to reduce owner-occupied property taxes.
_full_text:
BELLE FOURCHE — During its 9:30 a.m. meeting tomorrow, the Butte County Commission plans to discuss Senate Bill 96, which allows counties to implement a new sales tax to reduce owner-occupied property taxes.

The bill allows the county to impose a 0.5% sales tax. The funds from that tax would go into a “property tax reduction fund.”

Under the new law, if the sales tax is implemented, “the governing body of a county shall allocate all moneys in the county’s property tax reduction fund as a credit against the county property tax levy on all property classified as owner-occupied.”

At its last meeting, the commission encouraged community participation and public comment to guide its decision on whether or not to implement the higher localized sales tax to reduce property taxes for homeowners.

Commission Vice-Chair Tom Brunner told the Pioneer, “We’d like a lot of people to weigh in before we make a decision.”

“It is very important that the public comes out and gives their input,” said Commissioner James Ager. “I know as government entities, as we work through these processes, the public input is the most valuable input we can get.”

Brunner expressed concern that the property tax reduction measures in SB 96 may not provide relief to the majority of people in the county.

“When you look at the numbers, there are people that rent, people with young families that will see no benefit,” Brunner said.

Brunner added that Butte County is an “ag community.” The property tax relief does not apply to agricultural land.

During the last commission meeting, the board discussed concerns that, Belle Fourche excepted, the county didn’t have major spending hubs — especially compared to Lawrence County. Still, Brunner told the Pioneer property tax revenues might be more robust than some might think because Belle Fourche draws in shoppers from Wyoming as well as Butte and Lawrence Counties.

In the end, Ager said there is an appetite on the commission to send the matter to a public vote.

“As I understand that bill, there were 2 options for implementation. One of them was that through public input the commissioners could make a decision,” Ager said. “Our plan is definitely to put that to a public vote.”

Brunner agreed. He told the Pioneer the “majority on our commission” want the people of  Butte County to express their opinion at the ballot box.

title: Social media companies are trying harder  to know which users are kids
byline: By Barbara Ortutay AP Technology Writer
description: Of the child safety measures agreed to in Meta’s landmark legal settlement, no category contains more detailed requirements than its commitments on age assurance — and for good reason. No matter how well the protections work, they are of little use if Meta can’t tell which users are kids.
_full_text:
APLogo

Of the child safety measures agreed to in Meta’s landmark legal settlement, no category contains more detailed requirements than its commitments on age assurance — and for good reason. No matter how well the protections work, they are of little use if Meta can’t tell which users are kids.

Determining which accounts belong to children is also the linchpin of child safety measures that other companies, including Google, TikTok, and Roblox, are ramping up as public and regulatory sentiment turns against them in the U.S. and other countries.

The Meta settlement — with protections the company says could become industry standards — will give the social media giant a year to refine its approach. But the options are limited, and improving age verification technology presents steep challenges, including navigating privacy implications not just for children but for adults who could have to prove they are over 18.

The $18 billion settlement resolves claims from state attorneys general that it hurt children’s mental health by deliberately designing its Instagram and Facebook platforms in ways that hooked young people’s attention. The agreement announced last week with the Menlo Park, California, company involves 48 states plus the District of Columbia and U.S. territories.

Tech companies lean on AI for estimating ages

In the offline world, people use government-issued IDs to prove they are over 18 or 21, whether they want to get into a club or buy cigarettes. While this technically works online too, many people are not comfortable giving a Big Tech company like Meta or Google access to their driver’s license or passport.

Meta accepts IDs to check ages, and promises to delete them within 30 days. Beyond IDs, though, a growing number of tech companies are using artificial intelligence to try to determine users’ ages. This is not true age verification. While AI can estimate a person’s age, often accurately, it can’t verify a person’s birth date.

Last year, Google began using an age-assurance system for YouTube that relies on AI to differentiate between adults and minors based on their watch histories. Meta does the same.

AI age checks use clues to determine how old someone is. On Instagram, this includes “contextual clues” such as posts about birthday celebrations or school, and things like which posts people like, comment or linger on, who their friends are, as well as the times of day they log in. For instance, someone who is offline during school hours would likely be school-aged.

In a blog post last year, Meta said its AI also looks at photos people post for visual cues, including “height or bone structure, to estimate someone’s general age; it does not identify the specific person in the image.”

“By combining these visual insights with our analysis of text and interactions, we can significantly increase the number of underage accounts we identify and remove,” the company added.

Under the settlement, Meta agreed to strengthen its age-checking technology using its own tools, as well as third-party ones, with regular outside audits on how well it is working. The agreement also includes specific goals around false positive rates — that is, minors who are identified as over 18. And if a user is identified as under 13 and kicked off one of its platforms, Meta will check the ages of their friends, too.

Face scans count as age assurance on some sites

Identity verification companies like Yoti and Persona, which work with tech companies like Meta and Roblox, use video selfies people upload to estimate their ages.

The gaming site Roblox, which, unlike social media platforms, allows kids under 13 to sign up, requires players to take a video selfie to estimate their age. Roblox says the videos are deleted after the age check is processed. Users are not required to submit a face scan to use the platform, only if they want to chat with other users.

Some users have reported inaccuracies, and some experts have expressed caution about the reliability of facial age estimation tools, especially for women or certain racial or ethnic groups. But Matt Kaufman, chief safety officer at Roblox, said last year that for people between about 5 and 25, the system can accurately estimate their age within one or two years.

Some websites and social media companies such as Meta have argued that age verification should be done by app store owners, such as Apple and Google, and not individual platforms. This would mean that app stores would have to verify their users’ ages before they allow them to download apps. Unsurprisingly, Apple and Google disagree.

“Billed as ‘simple’ by its backers, including Meta, this proposal fails to cover desktop computers or other devices that are commonly shared within families. It also could be ineffective against pre-installed apps,” Google said in a blog post last year.

Privacy concerns remain an obstacle

Age checks are meant to keep kids out of online spaces that are not safe or appropriate for them, whether that’s social media or adult websites. But critics of online age verification see a worrisome trend toward a less secure, less private and less free internet, where people can be denied access not just to pornography but news, health information and the ability to speak openly and anonymously.

What’s considered harmful to minors can be subjective, and this is where experts believe laws requiring age verification can run afoul of the First Amendment. The question could lead to people being required to verify their ages to access anything, from Netflix to a neighborhood blog.

The digital rights group Electronic Frontier Foundation has been warning for years about “age-gating the internet.”

“(No) matter the method, every system demands users hand over sensitive and immutable personal information that links their offline identity to their online activity,” EFF writes in a blog post. “Once that valuable data is collected, it can easily be leaked, hacked, or misused.”

title: Stain-soaked rags spontaneously combust, starting Deadwood dumpster fire Monday
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: DEADWOOD — Deadwood Fire and Rescue was paged to a reported structure fire on Pillar Peak Place at 6:30 p.m. Monday in rural Deadwood.
_full_text:
DEADWOOD — Deadwood Fire and Rescue was paged to a reported structure fire on Pillar Peak Place at 6:30 p.m. Monday in rural Deadwood. 

When they arrived, firefighters found a roll-off dumpster outside of a newly constructed home “fully involved” in flames, according to a post of the Deadwood Volunteer Fire Department’s social media. 

The fire was quickly brought under control, with no one injured and no structures lost or damaged. 

The likely cause of the fire was soiled oil- or stain-soaked rags left in the dumpster by a staining crew who had been working on the house just 3 hours before the fire started. 

Stain or oil soaked rags can spontaneously combust.

 “Proper disposal of stain and oil soaked rags is extremely important! This is the second dumpster fire from oil/stain soaked rags in the area in the past month,” the post from the Deadwood Fire Department reads. 

Charles Fetter, Fire Technician with the Deadwood Fire Department, recommended that rags soaked in any kind of solvent be stored in a metal garbage can, away from anything that might be able to catch fire. 

The fire department also noted that they were able to respond very quickly, because they were on their way to a monthly training exercise nearby. 

In addition to resources from Deadwood, the Lead Fire Department and Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office also responded to the fire.

title: L-D School District approves budget, closing mill levy gaps between request and maximum
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Lead-Deadwood School District has finalized the 2026-2027 budget, showing a smaller gap between requests and maximum when setting mill levies. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
SchoolBudget-Horz.jpg
The Lead-Deadwood School District has finalized the 2026-2027 budget, showing a smaller gap between requests and maximum when setting mill levies. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

DEADWOOD – Lead-Deadwood School District has adopted a budget for the 2026-2027 school year, showing higher mill levies to compensate for state-capped maximums.

In general fund, South Dakota Codified Law (SDCL) 10-12-42 went into effect July 1, restricting the maximum mill levy schools can request against owner occupied properties to $0.669 per $1,000 of assessed value. Last year, the school levied $2.346 per $1,000 on owner-occupied and owner-occupied mobile home properties. This year, the school has chosen to levy $0.653 per $1,000 on the same properties. The law has resulted in an estimated loss of $1.1 million in revenue to the school’s general fund.

Comparatively, the school has set the agricultural mill levy at 1.026 (a 1.051 maximum), the mobile home levy at 4.750 (4.867 maximum), and other non-agricultural and utilities as 4.750 (4.867 maximum). 

The mill levies leave a potential revenue of $193,439.94 the district will not acquire by requesting less than the maximum allowed.

The gap between request and maximum mill levy allowed is smaller than previous years. Amanda Trople, business manager, said the legislature’s restriction on possible requests has required the schools to close the gap between possibility and request when setting the levies.

“The reason that we’re closer to the max than we have been in the past is because the maximum (allowed) did decrease so much,” said Trople. “We’re still trying to request under and be good stewards of our taxpayers’ dollars, but it does look like there’s a closer gap.”

In capital outlay, the district is restricted in requesting a capped dollar amount per student, unless that dollar amount is less than 3% of the assed value of properties in the district. Because of the assessed value in the district, the schools request the capped dollar amount per student. 

The per-student number used is the district’s enrollment number on the last Friday of the preceding school year. For taxes payable in 2027, the district may request $3,966 per student. Using enrollment numbers from the previous school year, the district is projecting 593 students. 

The district will request approximately $1.9 million, $287,152.80 less than the maximum amount. The formula funds the district capital outlay fund, used for brick-and-mortar repairs, maintenance, and purchases. Trople said the number is subject to change after final enrollments come in.

Trople said declining enrollment contributes to savings to taxpayers, with less money being requested per student.  The request is less than what we could have requested even with declining enrollment.

Due to unexpected maintenance on gas lines in the middle school and high school, Trople said the budget for capital outlay has increased between the proposed budget to the final budget. Expenditures to capital outlay increased by $219,509 after a gas leak in the elementary school required significant concrete work to fix. 

After the completion of the renovation to the middle school, the capital outlay budget has decreased from $3.7 million to $1.8 million. 

General fund increased $628,000 from last year, growing to $10,053,000. However, from proposed to final budget, the fund decreased by $64,016. 

“We were able to go through some line items and determined that there was maybe too much budgeted,” said Trople. “There have been some changes in staffing, too.”

Trople said the district requested $486,874 less than the maximum in special education. She said the mill levy increased in the fund, but the district only requests what is deemed necessary to meet the specific needs of special needs students attending their schools. 

“Those funds are geared towards that program specifically, we can’t use them for anything else,” said Trople. 

She said the district has a “healthy fund balance” in special education and will not need to request extraordinary costs from the state.

title: Spearfish council moves to address snag  in sanitary sewer upsizing project
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Crews work on the Colorado Boulevard Sanitary Sewer Upsizing project along the city’s main thoroughfare in July. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson
_full_text:
Sewer upsize.JPG
Crews work on the Colorado Boulevard Sanitary Sewer Upsizing project along the city’s main thoroughfare in July. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

SPEARFISH — On Wednesday, Woelber Excavating encountered a problem while installing an upsized sewer main along Colorado Boulevard. 

“Today, we encountered something unexpected on that project. Shown on the plans is a reinforced concrete culvert. It turned out to be a box culvert, and a triple-barrel box culvert at that,” said Spearfish Public Works Director Adam McMahon. 

A box culvert is a much larger obstacle for crews to work around than a concrete culvert, McMahon said. 

“It is going to require the contractor to jack and bore a steel casing pipe underneath that box culvert to install the upsized sewer in that location,” McMahon said. 

He asked the city council to authorize the contractor to move forward with the work-around during the special meeting. McMahon said public works plans to bring a formal change order to the next regular city council meeting on Sept. 8.

“The estimated dollar amount of those changes are in that $125,000 range,” McMahon said. “The budget for the project was $2 million, and we awarded it at $1.7 million. We did carry that budget amount forward into 2026, so there was some additional budget authority above the base contract amount for some change orders.”

The Colorado Boulevard Sanitary Sewer Upsize Project is funded in part with grants and state revolving fund (SRF) loans, so the change order will also need approval from the state. Authorizing city staff to work with the contractor to address the problem now will keep the project moving forward, McMahon said.

byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Courtesy photo
