PIERRE — South Dakota Unified Judicial System (UJS) wants to hear from members of the public about their experiences with the state court system — part of a bid to build public trust and confidence in the courts through transparency, communication, education and community engagement. 

UJS is conducting the 2026 Court User Survey to collect anonymous feedback from court users to improve court services. Participation is voluntary, anonymous, and will not affect any court case. Two surveys are available during the month of September. 

The first survey is available in English and Spanish through QR codes displayed on flyers at court locations across the state where court users are likely to see them. The survey website links are also included on the flyer for those who do not have a cell phone or prefer not to scan a QR code.

A second online survey is available to people who use the UJS website.

“The Unified Judicial System wants to hear from the public about how we are doing as a court system so we can best serve our communities,” said State Court Administrator Greg Sattizahn. “Anyone who has had any experiences in our courts can participate in this survey. We have made it very easy and safe to let us know your thoughts. All survey responses are anonymous, and it takes just a minute or two to complete.”

The surveys are open to all court users including defendants, witnesses, attorneys, law enforcement, service providers, individuals attending court with someone else, and those present for meetings or other court business. Areas of inquiry include purpose of courthouse or website visit, ability to complete business or find what you needed, experience satisfaction, and any challenges encountered.

title: Bush Foundation grant to expand investment  in rural and native communities
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: SISSETON — GROW South Dakota has been awarded a $2,315,000 grant from the Bush Foundation to develop an innovative model of addressing the need for housing and economic development through a partnership with NeighborWorks Dakota Coalition. The grant could increase investment in rural and Native communities across South Dakota and North Dakota.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

SISSETON — GROW South Dakota has been awarded a $2,315,000 grant from the Bush Foundation to develop an innovative model of addressing the need for housing and economic development through a partnership with NeighborWorks Dakota Coalition. The grant could increase investment in rural and Native communities across South Dakota and North Dakota.

“Through our Community Innovation program, we look for ideas to develop, test and spread, and the work of GROW South Dakota is a great example,” said Rebecca Cruse, grant-making officer at the Bush Foundation. “They are working with partners to build a model that can provide more flexible financing options to grow housing and small business development in rural and Native communities across South Dakota and North Dakota.”

The NeighborWorks Dakota Coalition is a partnership formed in 2022 to amplify the needs and opportunities of rural and Native communities. Coalition members include: GROW South Dakota (in Sisseton); Neighborhood Lending Services (in Deadwood); CommunityWorks North Dakota (in Mandan, N.D.); and Lakota Funds (in Kyle).

“This investment represents an exciting opportunity to rethink how we collaborate to better serve rural and Native communities,” said Marcia Erickson, CEO of GROW South Dakota. “By bringing together various internal and external partners, we’re creating new pathways for investment that can strengthen local economies, increase housing opportunities, and support entrepreneurs across our region. We are incredibly grateful to the Bush Foundation for this opportunity.”

title: Wells drying up at homes and ranches due to heat and drought
byline: Bart Pfankuch South Dakota News Watch
description: CAPUTA — Each morning this summer, Gordon and Connie Howie have awoken on their cattle ranch in central Pennington County and turned on the kitchen faucet, unsure if any water will come out.
_full_text:
CAPUTA — Each morning this summer, Gordon and Connie Howie have awoken on their cattle ranch in central Pennington County and turned on the kitchen faucet, unsure if any water will come out.

“We can’t do laundry or dishes or take showers other than with a little trickle,” said Connie Howie, 76. “Other times we have a little water because it seems to come and go.”

Like many ranchers and residents in rural areas of western South Dakota, the Howie family relies on a well to provide them with water for their lives and livelihood.

Pull quote
“I’ve lived here my whole life and I’ve never seen it this dry, this hot, this long. We’ve seen some drought, but this is the worst one I can remember, and I’m 77 years old.” — Gordon Howie, Caputa rancher who served in the Legislature from 2009-2011 and ran for governor in 2010

But this year, perhaps the worst in recent memory, many shallow wells are running slow or have gone completely dry, forcing people to go to great lengths and expense to provide clean water for themselves or their livestock.

Experts say several consecutive years of limited winter snowpack and a shortage of rainfall have combined with increased consumption of water to cause a decrease in the levels of some underground aquifers that are a main source of water for a large swath of the Black Hills region. The problem is most acute in areas outside the reach of pipes from municipal and rural water systems.

High heat this summer exacerbated the problem as people, crops and animals all require more water than usual to survive.

“We have a well at the house, but it’s just not keeping up because the aquifer is dry,” said Gordon Howie. “For 20 years you could trust that well 24/7, and it never quit on us, but now it’s not providing enough water for everything we need.”

The Howies are buying bottled water for drinking and positioning jugs of fresh water throughout the house for daily uses.

“I’ve lived here my whole life, and I’ve never seen it this dry, this hot, this long,” said Gordon Howie, who served in the Legislature from 2009-2011 and ran for governor in 2010.

All across the plains of western South Dakota, residents who rely on shallow wells — generally 1,000 feet deep or less — are being forced to find alternative water sources. 

Some are utilizing a somewhat obscure system of obtaining water in which users insert quarters or bills into a vending machine that triggers a hanging water spout to provide fresh water that is collected in tanks in pickups or on trailers. Such water stations are available in Black Hawk, Deadwood, Piedmont, Rapid City, Spearfish and Sturgis.

Those self-serve water stations are much busier than usual this summer, particularly in Rapid City, where the spout at J&J Asphalt is the only bulk water available in town and is often accessible only after a long wait.

“Everybody is hauling water these days,” said Nick Randall, shop foreman at J&J Asphalt, whose shop and water station are located in an industrial area off Dyess Avenue.

Many rural residents have clean water delivered by truck, which requires planning and expense.

Businesses such as Frontier Water in Rapid City are extremely busy this summer. 

“With all these shallow wells going dry, it’s really boosted my business,” said Darin Klapperich, the owner of Frontier who also ranches northwest of Rapid City.

Klapperich gathers purified fresh water from municipal systems across the Black Hills and delivers it to customers.

On arrival, the water is dumped into a cattle tank or a holding tank for household use. At some locations, he fills underground concrete cisterns people use to store water on their properties and occasionally drains the water into a well to fill it part way, Klapperich said.

To avoid future dry spells, the Howies plan to drill a new, deeper well to replace the 30-foot well that has run dry. The couple will continue to use a reverse osmosis system in the house to purify the well water for drinking and other uses.

Until then, he’ll continue his twice-weekly water-gathering ritual, positioning his trailer below the J&J spigot, climbing a ladder to connect an extension pipe to the spout, unfurling bills into the payment slot and filling the tank on his trailer.

“I let every last dribble go in, because those cattle have got to have water,” he said.

title: Marcia Hultman to move from Dept. of Labor to senior advisor role in Rhoden administration
description: Kendra Ringstmeyer will serve as interim secretary of the department of labor. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
KendraRingstmeyer.jpg
Kendra Ringstmeyer will serve as interim secretary of the department of labor. Courtesy photo 

 Marcia-Hultman.jpg
Marcia Hultman will serve as senior advisor to Gov. Rhoden. Courtesy photo 

 PIERRE —Tuesday, Governor Larry Rhoden announced the current Department of Labor and Regulations (DLR) Secretary Marcia Hultman will continue to serve in the Rhoden Administration as a Senior Advisor in his office, effective September 14. Kendra Ringstmeyer will serve as interim secretary of DLR.

 “South Dakota is an incredible state, and I have an incredible team serving alongside me,” said Governor Larry Rhoden. “Marcia brings a new set of skills and expertise that will round out my exceptional policy team and elevate our efforts to keep South Dakota strong, safe, and free.”

 Hultman is a native of Belle Fourche, South Dakota. Just like her grandmother and mother before her, Marcia was trained to be a teacher. She taught school in Hot Springs, Custer, and Rapid City before joining state government in 1997. Hultman had served in a variety of leadership roles with DLR for seventeen years before taking the role of DLR Secretary in 2014. Marcia received a bachelor’s degree in education from Black Hills State University.

 “I am honored by the trust Governor Rhoden has placed in me. I have great respect for his leadership and look forward to contributing to his mission,” Hultman said. “As a Senior Advisor, I will bring my years of experience, belief in relationship building, foundation in education, and capacity to learn to the position.”

 Hultman and her husband, Brian, live in Pierre. Hultman enjoys reading, gardening, and all things baking-related. 

 “I have the utmost respect for Secretary Hultman, as do her colleagues, state legislators, key stakeholders, and the team at DLR. She leads with civility and approaches solving problems with an open mind,” said Mackenzie Decker, chief of staff for Governor Larry Rhoden. “She brings needed strengths to our office and leaves behind a capable team at DLR who will continue meeting the workforce needs of our state.”

 Kendra Ringstmeyer, who currently serves as the director of workforce development for DLR, will serve as the interim Secretary. 

 Kendra has made a career in workforce development, with 15 years at DLR. She currently serves as the workforce development director at DLR where she focuses on building partnerships that bridge gaps and create opportunities for individuals to engage in the workforce and contribute to their community. She holds a bachelor’s degree from Southwest Minnesota State University and a master’s in public administration from University of South Dakota.

 Kendra and her husband, Phil, are both natives of Winner, SD. They have raised three daughters in the Pierre area.

title: Shedding light
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: LZ scientists work to analyze data from the most sensitive dark matter experiment in the world. Photo by Mattew Kapust/Sanford Underground Research Facility
_full_text:
20240926-LZ Crew_Stephen Kenny_LR-16.jpg
LZ scientists work to analyze data from the most sensitive dark matter experiment in the world. Photo by Mattew Kapust/Sanford Underground Research Facility  

LEAD — Scientists with the LUX-ZEPLIN experiment at SURF may have discovered dark matter, but for right now they are just calling it, “an interesting event.” 

Scientists with the LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) experiment at the Sanford Underground Research Facility (SURF) are being very careful about how they refer to their most recent observation of a single particle interaction. The interaction is unlike anything the experiment has seen since beginning its underground operations in 2021. The experiment, which has been hailed as the most sensitive in the world, said the particle interaction could be dark matter, but more study and data analysis are needed to confirm that. 

“The collaboration is not claiming they’ve seen dark matter,” said Director of Science Jaret Heise. “But they are seeing an interesting event in an area that could be dark matter. To say more will require more data – from the LZ collaboration itself, as well as the rest of the scientific community. It’s an unexpected event in a region that is essentially background free without competing signals. That’s why we are managing our enthusiasm to a certain degree. It’s interesting, but more careful science is needed before LZ will claim to have seen dark matter.” 

 31667821088_f762d2c200_o.jpg
When a WIMP collides with a xenon atom, the xenon atom emits a flash of light and electrons. The light is detected at the top and bottom of the liquid xenon chamber. An electric field drifts the electrons to the top of the chamber, where they generate a second flash of light. Graphic illustration by Greg Stewart/SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory  

LZ searches for dark matter by looking for signature flashes of light from energy deposited in the detector. The collaboration leverages multiple methods to prevent or account for particle interactions caused by normal matter. This includes the mile of rock that shields the detector from cosmic rays from space, a water tank and outer detectors that protect the central detector from background neutrons, and a suite of computational tools that disentangle particle interactions and reject dark matter mimics. 

 20201120-LZVisit-13-Matt Kapust - SURF.jpg
The LUX-ZEPLIN main detector in a surface lab before installation underground.  

LZ is an international collaboration of 250 scientists and engineers from 39 institutions, including Black Hills State University. The detector is managed by the U.S. Department of Energy’s Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory (Berkeley Lab) and operates nearly one mile below ground at SURF. The experiment uses 10 tonnes of ultrapure liquid xenon to search for dark matter and is optimized to look for WIMPs, or weakly interacting massive particles.

Markus Horn, senior research scientist at SURF, who is also a member of the LZ collaboration, is quick to point out that scientists have only seen one event of interest, and he stressed that more significant study is required. While he said the “interesting event” is in an area where scientists would expect a dark matter particle to be, all of their background models are predicting very few events in that high-energy region. That’s what has physicists perplexed and their interest piqued. 

Before this one event, physicists with LZ, or any other dark matter experiment around the world, have not seen anything unexpected like this, Heise said. 

The results were announced Tuesday morning in Japan, at the TeV Particle Astrophysics conference. 

The LZ collaboration studies experimental data in batches. In the new result, researchers analyzed 220 live days of data collected between March 2023 and April 2024. The collaboration had previously searched this dataset for faint signals from the simplest kinds of WIMP interactions. The new analysis searched for a broader range of possible WIMP interactions that could deposit more energy in the detector. LZ is particularly sensitive to such signals while also minimizing false positives. 

“This was a detailed study in a region we hadn’t explored within this dataset, and we spent months of additional effort to understand all the possible causes of background events,” said Sam Eriksen, a senior research associate at the University of Bristol in the U.K. and lead author of the study. “We understand our detector and the backgrounds so well that even a single outstanding event, like the one we found, is important. We expect dark matter events to be extremely rare, so only a handful could mark the first detection of WIMP dark matter.”

 mod-190124-LZ-lower-PMT-array-0104-Pano-HDR-Edit-5953 x 5953px.jpg
 Photo by Matthew Kapust/Sanford Underground Research Facility  

If the anomalous event was caused by dark matter, the WIMP that generated it would likely have a mass of at least 200 gigaelectronvolts, or more than 200 times the mass of a proton. It would also suggest a specific type of interaction between WIMPs and ordinary matter beyond the simplest model. The LZ results have not reached “5-sigma” significance, the statistical threshold considered a discovery in physics. The new analysis is 2.6 sigma, meaning there is approximately a 0.5% chance that the event could be explained by known backgrounds. 

 LZ-inner-photomultiplier - Matthew Kapust - SURF.jpg
Photomultiplier tubes inside the LZ detector are designed to capture faint flashes of light that could signal a dark matter interaction. Photo by Matthew Kapust/Sanford Underground Research Facility  

The search for dark matter has been ongoing since the 1930s and has improved with each new discovery. The first dark matter experiment was conducted underground in Lead in the 1980s using germanium detectors, located in a small nook near what is now known as the Davis Campus. With each new generation of detectors, the search becomes even more sensitive. 

Observing this new particle interaction is just one piece of the building blocks of science, Heise said. 

“We’re building on the science that has been conducted over decades,” Heise said. “LZ didn’t suddenly appear out of nowhere and have this result. They’re building on technology and expertise developed over many years culminating in the results we’re seeing today.” 

Horn said it’s possible that the one particle interaction scientists have seen is simply a different background and not an actual event. That’s why more study is necessary, and scientists are being very cautious regarding the announcement. 

“We can be cautiously excited,” Heise said. 

The LZ experiment plans to take data at SURF until 2028. Another significantly larger experiment called XLZD, is proposed to continue the dark matter search. However, the Department of Energy has paused all funding for new experiments for the next 5 years, and that includes XLZD. Meanwhile, the next generation of the Chinese Panda X dark matter experiment is in its development phases. That experiment is larger than LZ, with 20 tonnes of xenon that has already been purchased, and could begin taking data in early 2028.

“They might catch up to LZ because they’ll have a larger instrument, a larger target, by the end of the decade,” Heise said. 

In the meantime, Heise said, a proposal has been submitted to the DOE to continue funding LZ operations for several more years. The DOE has not yet made a determination about extending LZ, but today’s announcement could change that. With additional data, researchers can test whether the finding continues to grow in significance or fades away. 

“With this new result, continuing the LZ program at SURF, at least until the competition catches up, would be a good return on investment, especially with the pause on funding for new experiments into the 2030s. Keeping what is today the world’s leading dark matter experiment to shed additional light on this interesting event.” 

BHSU researchers contribute to the experiment through the Black Hills Underground Campus (BHUC), located on the 4,850-foot level of SURF. Faculty and students use ultra-sensitive screening equipment to measure trace levels of radioactivity in materials used throughout the detector. Currently, they are aiding in the ongoing effort to understand and model the background radiation present within the experiment, a critical step in this latest analysis.

“We are so thrilled to have been involved from the early days of LZ. From helping to choose materials by determining their levels of radioactivity and suitability for use in the detector, to screening chosen materials to enable background simulations, to now aiding in the backgrounds analyses to which these BHUC measurements have contributed, BHSU students and researchers have played a role throughout the experiment’s development.” said Dr. Brianna Mount, professor of physics and director of the BHUC. “I’ve always thought about the hunt for dark matter as a wonderful adventure. We are exploring the very nature of most of the matter in our universe. We’re at an interesting part of this quest, having this possible hint that exciting things might be just around the corner.”

“Outlier events in the data are not unexpected, but they usually stand out as a background of some kind when you look at them deeper,” said Aaron Manalaysay, a physicist at Berkeley Lab and the chair of LZ’s Institutional Board. “This is the first example in any experiment I’ve worked on of an outlier that appears valid in every way. Of course, we’re still twisting our brains trying to think if there’s a rare background mechanism we could’ve missed, but it’s thrilling to wonder if this could be the first hint of a dark-matter observation.”

title: Meade Co. to receive $1.6M for road repairs
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: STURGIS — Meade County will receive a small portion of money paid for infrastructure improvements related to the Ellsworth Air Force Base expansion.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

STURGIS — Meade County will receive a small portion of money paid for infrastructure improvements related to the Ellsworth Air Force Base expansion. 

Senate Bill 130 allocates $8 million to be split between Meade County, the city of Box Elder, the city of Rapid City, and Pennington County. 

On Tuesday, the Meade County Commission approved a letter of intent to state appropriations to spend $1.6 million of that. The amount is the result of several meetings with the city of Box Elder, to break down allocations between the four communities, based upon infrastructure need related to the base expansion. 

Eastman said the $1.6 million will help repair Elk Vale Road, which is seeing increased traffic levels. By accepting the funding, the county is committing to paying costs that exceed the $1.6 million allocation, as well as committing to maintaining the roads once repairs are made. 

Meade County Commissioners acknowledged that the $1.6 million in funds is small, compared to what is actually needed. Eastman said he identified about $10 million in necessary road work. 

“I’m sure we could easily use that money along with a couple more zeros,” Commissioner Doreen Creed said. “It’s about the only money we’ve gotten out of the billions that have been sent there for that project.” 

“We knew going into this that $8 million was going to be a drop in the pan, but it’s something,” Commission Chairman Gary Deering said. 

Sen. Helene Duhammel, R-Rapid City, secured the $8 million from the general fund to restore roads in the Meade and Pennington County area that withstand greater stress related to construction work to prepare Ellsworth Air Force Base for the B-21 Raider stealth bomber. Sen. Taffy Howard, R-Rapid City, supported the bill, pointing out that up to 250 double semi trucks drive the roadways each day, rapidly accelerating the road deterioration.

title: S.D. Department of Revenue reports decrease in Rally sales tax
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Decreased Rally crowds and a decrease in vendors contributed to an 11% dip in sales tax collections from the 2026 Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick
_full_text:
Rally sales tax 1.JPG
Decreased Rally crowds and a decrease in vendors contributed to an 11% dip in sales tax collections from the 2026 Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. Pioneer photo by Wendy Pitlick 

PIERRE — The South Dakota Department of Revenue estimates tax collections from the 2026 Sturgis Motorcycle Rally at $1,404,408, an 11% decrease from the 2025 total of $1,581,736. 

The lower collections reflect a slowdown in overall Rally traffic, which contributed to reduced vendor activity and lower taxable sales. The total includes state sales tax, state tourism tax, municipal sales tax, and municipal gross receipts tax.

State sales tax remained the largest share of collections at $796,998, down from $901,513 in 2025. The 2026 rally also generated $275,598 in state tourism tax and $331,812 in municipal taxes. A drop in vendor participation mirrored the decline in traffic at this year’s Rally, with 822 temporary vendors operating during the rally — 30% less than in 2025. This was expected, as Rally traffic typically decreases slightly after an anniversary year, and 2025 marked the 85th annual Sturgis Motorcycle Rally. 

In the Northern Black Hills, including Sturgis and surrounding communities in Meade and Lawrence counties, 661 vendors generated $930,740 in tax revenue, representing a 20% decrease from last year. In contrast, the Southern Black Hills, Rapid City, Custer, Hill City, and Keystone saw 161 vendors generate $473,668 in tax collections, a 15% increase from 2025.

title: ‘I made a promise to myself’: How higher education is transforming lives in Wyoming prisons
byline: By Maya Shimizu Harris WyoFile
description: One spring afternoon when the sun beamed down on the Wyoming Women’s Center, a prison in Lusk, six students sat in a fluorescent-lit room with laptops open before them. A brown and gold University of Wyoming banner with a cowboy on a bucking bronc hung on the far wall.
_full_text:
WyoFileLogo

One spring afternoon when the sun beamed down on the Wyoming Women’s Center, a prison in Lusk, six students sat in a fluorescent-lit room with laptops open before them. A brown and gold University of Wyoming banner with a cowboy on a bucking bronc hung on the far wall.

“So, who’s going first?” asked Rob Colter, a gray-bearded UW philosophy professor. “Final presentation. Create your own festival.”

One of the students, Taylor Nicks, snapped her fingers in approval.

“First victim,” Colter said, waiting for a volunteer.

It was their last day of class on heavy metal philosophy, and a few months before graduation. The course was one of many the students, who wore their orange prison uniforms to class, took to earn their four-year bachelor’s degrees in general studies from the University of Wyoming. Earlier this month, the six women finally reached that finish line, making them the first cohort in Wyoming to earn bachelor’s degrees through a university program called Pathways from Prison.

Kelly Turner, who wore a small cross on a chain around her neck, volunteered to go first. She handed out flyers with the name of her festival — Metal for the Ages — handwritten in a red, white and blue steampunk font. A skull in a black top hat, one eye socket framing the American flag, grinned below the title. The flyers featured a long list of metal artists — Beyond the Black, Slipknot, Jinjer, Spiritbox, Unleash the Archers, Face Yourself, Nervosa.

“Our country was built on freedom, and as we have learned through this class and other philosophy classes, freedom is mostly a figment of your mind. The only way you can really be free is how you see yourself,” Turner told her peers, gesturing with her hands. “The freedom that they have to express themselves through the arts is beautiful, even if they’re kind of scary looking.”

The students laughed.

“So, your theme is freedom, is that right?” Colter asked. “Are there specific ways in which some of these bands talk about freedom?”

“A lot of them talk about politics,” Turner said. “We just listened to the Lamb of God song that was about being so tied up into technology that we are not free.”

“Metallica talks about politics quite a little bit in their music,” a student added.

“Jinjer too,” another said.

In 2022, the U.S. Department of Education chose Wyoming Pathways from Prison — UW’s prison education initiative, which Colter heads — to be one among about 200 programs in the country participating in the Second Chance Pell Experiment, an Obama administration initiative that opened Pell Grant eligibility for some prison inmates.

Before the federal initiative, the Pathways from Prison program offered free UW courses to people in Wyoming prisons, but the courses didn’t culminate in any degree. Extra funding from the Second Chance Pell Experiment has helped the program offer a four-year UW degree in general studies for people incarcerated here.

Research suggests that participation in any form of educational program in prisons decreases the likelihood of recidivism — by about 7 to 15%, according to one paper — and increases the likelihood of being employed after release. But for the six students at the Wyoming Women’s Center, most of whom have long or life sentences, the program provided more than an avenue for employment in the world outside the prison’s walls. It gave them a way to “be an example” for their children and peers, as well as a sense of purpose that was like “giving a lifeline to someone who is drowning,” as Nicks later described in her graduation speech.

The next student up, Nicks, discovered something in her research about mosh pits that “outraged” her: “I read an article that quoted a new slogan that misogynistic men have been passing around. It was ‘No Clit in the Pit.’” Nicks, who has long, black hair and music notes tattooed on her arm, decided to parody the slogan, calling her festival “Mo’ Clit in the Pit.”

“This festival is all about empowering women within the metal community not only to jump into the mosh pits with the boys, but in life also,” Nicks said. “This is going to be a two-day festival that includes some of the baddest female artists.”

The festival would take place at the Women’s Rights National Historical Park on July 19 and 20 — the same dates as the 1848 Seneca Falls Convention, the first formal women’s rights convention held in the U.S. “We have come a long way since this time,” Nicks continued. “In 2026, women have the right to vote, work, run for office. And we damn sure have the right to mosh.”

Lorrie Hood, reading her notes from index cards, created a festival called Hood Fest. She was raised thinking that metal and those who listened to it “were evil, demonic.” But the philosophy class showed her that this music expresses the stories of real people and the struggles they endure. Amy Doerr’s festival, Synthetica, represented the synthesis of different cultures from bands across 13 countries. The festival featured a square with vendors and guest speakers, including Colter, who would give a talk on metal as a philosophy of life.

“Hope you’re available,” she joked with her professor.

Paulette Iliff’s festival would take place on a cruise ship traveling through ports in the Caribbean — a route she had taken herself years before. “We’re going to have meet and mingle with your favorite performers, growling seminars,” — the class cheered — “head banging lessons, picks and sticks with guitar and drum lessons, and that will be done, yes, with Scott Ian and Tommy Lee.”

Sharay Burnett’s festival, Odd Fellows, would “celebrate all of what society deems as odd.” “It’s an affirmation of myself and of the struggle that some of these band members and bands have gone through, and that we have come out on the other side,” Burnett said. The festival would be “metal tie only,” instead of black tie. The students burst into laughter. “That seems dangerous for mosh pits,” Colter commented.

Throughout the presentations, the students played clips of music from various artists. A woman mopping the floor outside the classroom hummed along to one song.

More than four years ago, the students sat in a room across the hall making their case for being a part of this program to a panel of UW faculty. As a cohort, they decided what they wanted their general studies degree to focus on, landing on anthropology and psychology. Their coursework included classes in math, the philosophy of Socrates, psychopathy, Spanish, theater, the psychology of death and dying. They often studied together in the classroom or the room next door. “For math, we’ve been down here every night,” one student said. Several of them hope to one day pursue graduate degrees.

“So, I really appreciate how much thought you all put into those presentations,” Colter said at the end of class. “It was clear that you were thinking about how stuff fits together, and there were some pretty creative options. I think the boat would destroy me.” The students laughed.

Colter then posed a question: “What do you think this class was about?”

The students threw out a list of words: Politics, activism, culture, thinking, subversion, imagery, community. Writing, researching, questioning.

“I don’t think we’ve hit it,” one student laughed.

“What it is for me is learning on a deeper level what the music meant, what it’s about,” another said.

“So you really think it’s about metal?” Colter asked.

They wrestled with the question for a while longer. “This is why you’re not allowed to ask questions,” Nicks told Colter.

He laughed. “What if I were to say what it’s really about is being human?,” Colter said. “I mean, we’re using a particular lens, right? The lens of a particular kind of music, particular kind of art, particular kind of community. But one of the things that I keep coming back to with all this stuff is how this is just a way of being human, and a way of exploring what it means to each of us to be human.”

Pathways from Prison is set to graduate more students — a group of men from Torrington’s Medium Correctional Institution — next summer. The program received funds to expand to other facilities and support previous graduates in serving as mentors for new students.

At the Wyoming Women’s Center, students for the new class have already been chosen. They sat in the audience at their peers’ Aug. 20 graduation ceremony. The graduating students’ friends and family members filled the room, which had been decorated with brown and gold flowers, balloons and streamers. A poster behind the podium read: “Congratulations! Class of 2026.”

The students, wearing graduation caps and gowns, stood to receive their diplomas from Colter. “I couldn’t be prouder than I am at this moment,” Colter told the gathered people. The students moved their tassels from the right to the left and flung their caps into the air. After the ceremony, Iliff took photos with her best friend. Hood greeted her parents. Nicks embraced her son.

“When I got arrested, my son was 2, and I’ve been locked up seven years now,” Nicks had said earlier.

“I made a promise to myself and to God when I got arrested that I wasn’t gonna let this time be wasted. I’m away from my family, and my son’s having to grow up without me, and I didn’t want to not grow from this experience. I wanted to take every opportunity that this place offered me and grow.”

title: Four paws and a badge: LD schools welcome new friendly faces
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Deadwood Police Department has welcomed 2 new friendly faces to the walls of the Lead-Deadwood School District. Pictured from left, Diggs, therapy dog, handler Officer Brandon Webb, Officer Keegan Holzapfel, and Chief Cory Shafer. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
LDSD welcomes 2 more friendly faces.jpg
The Deadwood Police Department has welcomed 2 new friendly faces to the walls of the Lead-Deadwood School District. Pictured from left, Diggs, therapy dog, handler Officer Brandon Webb, Officer Keegan Holzapfel, and Chief Cory Shafer. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

DEADWOOD — The Lead-Deadwood School District has welcomed 2 new friendly faces into their halls from the Deadwood police department — Keegan Holzapfel, a new school resource officer working with the elementary school, and Diggs, a six-month-old golden retriever. 

Holzapfel joined the department 3 years ago after completing a 2-year degree in law enforcement technology from Lake Area Technical College. In that time, he worked as a Taser instructor, field training officer, and served on the community events response team. Most recently, he was chosen as the new school resource officer. 

“I worked with Officer Holzapfel at the football game Friday, and I’m already seeing the impact he’s making,” said Officer Brandon Webb, resource officer serving the middle and high schools. “We had multiple elementary-age kids come up to us, just wanting to talk to him.”

Holzapfel said he thinks he’s had a smooth transition from a leadership position in the department to providing an approachable, safe law enforcement presence in Deadwood Elementary. 

“The week prior to school starting, I was just in doing a walkthrough, getting used to my computer, and one of the first graders asked me if my Taser was a net gun,” said Holzapfel. “They watched Batman, and Batman has a net gun.”

Police Chief Cory Shafer confirmed the department does not use any net guns. 

Shafer said that he, along with elementary Principal Dan Van Bibber and Superintendent Erik Person, agreed Holzapfel was the right fit for the job, whose mission is to break the stigma of law enforcement in the public image while providing safety and support to staff, educators, and families. 

“I’m a big believer in 2 things, and that’s presence and communication,” said Shafer. “If you’re apt to see a law enforcement officer, most individuals in society could be influenced to make better decisions at that time. It’s no different than if you’re driving a car and you see a cop, you’re going to slow down. (A school resource officer) provides a sense of security for parents, students, and teachers, seeing and having law enforcement there present and visible. Communication is very important, because when school resource officers, or anybody for that matter, say or mention the words, ‘bridge the gap,’ that’s where effective communication comes in.”

Holzapfel said he hopes to help bridge that gap between a learned fear of law enforcement and seeing officers as a helpful entity by being a force for good within the school. 

“We have the safety impact, in case something arises in the school, we can be the safety net to fall back on for the students and staff,” said Holzapfel. “With that, just having that positive interaction with the students, there might be times where students see law enforcement in a negative aspect. Having that personality in the elementary school, making those connections with students, and having that positive feedback within the learning setting is important for me.”

Diggs has also joined the team of officers serving the Lead-Deadwood schools with the intentions of improving officer rapport and approachability while serving as a valuable tool to de-escalate situations within the schools. 

“He’s only 6 months old, so he still has some room to grow out of his puppy stage,” said Webb, Digg’s handler. “But so far, I’m pretty impressed.”

Webb said he’s working to train Diggs with Jerrid Geving, owner of Sacred Mountain Retreat, who works to train service dogs for veterans. Shafer said the department is currently in the works of negotiating a cost sharing program for training and expenses for Diggs between the city and the schools.

Webb said Diggs joined his family in early June and has been spending half-days at the school to get used to his new job. He said so far, Diggs has been very well received by staff and students. 

“He’s very friendly with the kids and staff, so he’s doing his job so far,” said Webb. “His job is to be a therapy dog. If a kid needs a break, they can come pet Diggs, hang out with him, de-escalate situations as they arise. We haven’t had to do it yet, fortunately, but should they arise dogs can be a great tool. He’s not a traditional K-9 dog, so we don’t have to worry about him as a bite dog. He’s there to help support and bridge the gap between law enforcement and students.” 

Webb said the idea of law enforcement using a therapy dog in schools was presented to him at a national association of school resource officers training when police officer from Billings, Mont., brought in a dog he used in his schools. After returning home, he proposed the idea to the police department and the school board. Webb said both entities were very supportive of Diggs joining the team. 

“We’re always in a spotlight, especially a national spotlight, of law enforcement and fighting misperceptions out there,” said Shafer. “We can’t change what we can’t control, but on a local, smaller level, this has worked for us as a department and (for Webb’s) family to welcome Diggs. Diggs can be a great asset to the team and to the department. He’s a distraction. A good one.”

Shafer said Diggs will work to soften student’s hardest days at school, making it easier for officers and support staff to get to the root of student’s problems.

“Diggs is a great aspect for the police department and the community coming together,” said Webb. “I feel like students and staff will feel like they have a stake in Diggs when they see him around every day. I’ve already seen it with the kids. They’ll come running across the hallway to come see Diggs. It’s pretty cool already, the effect he’s having.”

title: SD utility regulator candidates clash over  AI data center pause
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: The candidates for a South Dakota Public Utilities Commission seat are Democratic nominee Frank Kloucek, left, and Republican nominee Don Haggar. Photos by South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Art & Illustration
The candidates for a South Dakota Public Utilities Commission seat are Democratic nominee Frank Kloucek, left, and Republican nominee Don Haggar. Photos by South Dakota Searchlight 

PIERRE — A South Dakota Democratic Public Utilities Commission candidate is calling for a one-year ban on new artificial intelligence data centers in the state, while his Republican opponent calls the proposal “reckless and pandering” and says new state laws regulating the industry are sufficient.

Frank Kloucek, a farmer from rural Scotland, S.D., and a Democratic former 22-year state lawmaker, proposed the moratorium. He said large data centers require large investments in electrical infrastructure — from generation to transmission — and South Dakotans should not subsidize their development through higher energy bills.

“Slow down, get the facts, protect the ratepayers and make sure South Dakota is in control of its own future,” Kloucek said.

State lawmakers passed, and Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden signed, 2 data center bills into law earlier this year.

One allows the Public Utilities Commission to assess data center companies the cost of regulatory reviews related to their projects. The other requires local water providers to determine whether the water use of large data centers — for cooling of spaces filled with heat-emitting servers — is compatible with the local water supply. It also requires electrical providers to establish separate terms and conditions for large data centers and to require reimbursement for all costs fairly attributed to data centers. Additionally, the law prohibits the state from overriding local ordinances limiting, prohibiting or otherwise regulating data centers.

Lawmakers rejected other proposals that would have incentivized data centers, such as a proposed sales tax exemption for data center equipment and software purchases. Lawmakers also rejected moratoriums on data center development.

Don Haggar, of Sioux Falls, who previously served 5 years in the Legislature, is the Republican nominee for the Public Utilities Commission. He said in a statement sent to South Dakota Searchlight that the new state laws are “the right foundation for how these decisions should be made going forward, case by case, on their unique merits.”

Haggar said the regulatory role of commissioners means “every case that comes before us deserves a fair, unbiased hearing, not a verdict decided in advance, and not a rubber stamp either.”

“It’s reckless and pandering to propose what my opponent has just done,” Haggar said in the statement.

Kloucek said the new state laws “lack any teeth.” The law regulating water and electricity use does not add any penalties for violations. Kloucek said a one-year moratorium would give the state more time to study the issue before any new projects move ahead.

South Dakota has small data centers but none of the large centers, known as hyper-scale, that have proliferated elsewhere. Proponents of data center development said during the legislative session that the state is missing out on high-paying jobs and millions in additional property tax revenue, while putting America at risk of falling behind foreign competitors. On Monday, President Donald Trump said on social media, “The only reason that communities throughout the U.S.A. should not want Data Centers is if they want to end up being backward and poor.”

Meanwhile, 23 Democratic candidates for the South Dakota Legislature have signed a pledge to implement public protections, greater transparency and local control in data center development, while opposing tax incentives. The laws approved earlier this year received bipartisan support.

Haggar and Kloucek are seeking the Public Utilities Commission seat being vacated by Republican Commissioner Gary Hanson, who is not seeking reelection. The commission has three positions, one of which is up for election this year. The election is Nov. 3, and advance voting starts Sept. 18.

The last Democrat on the commission was Steve Kolbeck, who served from 2006 to 2011. He’s now a Republican state senator but is not running for reelection to the Legislature this year.

title: Food landscape assessment reveals SDs gaps in access, affordability and assistance
byline: By Makenzie Huber Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Canned foods stand on grocery store shelves. A recent study in South Dakota identified gaps in food affordability, access, assistance, availability and quality statewide. Photo by Cami Koons, Iowa Capital Dispatch
_full_text:
Food landscape assessment reveals SDs gaps in access, affordability and assistance.jpg
Canned foods stand on grocery store shelves. A recent study in South Dakota identified gaps in food affordability, access, assistance, availability and quality statewide. Photo by Cami Koons, Iowa Capital Dispatch 

PIERRE — In a survey weighted toward South Dakotans most likely to experience food insecurity, 30% indicated they were skipping meals to stay within their budget, according to the recently released South Dakota Food Landscape Assessment.

The assessment is the first of its kind in the state, identifying gaps in food affordability, access, assistance, availability and quality statewide. The information will give policymakers, lawmakers, researchers and community organizers a shared foundation to improve programs and drive policy changes, said Jennifer Folliard, principal consultant at Health and Nutrition First and coordinator for the South Dakota Healthy Nutrition Collaborative.

With the skipped meals and affordability information in hand, for example, the report recommends introducing produce prescriptions in South Dakota — a program that lets healthcare providers “prescribe” fruits and vegetables, redeemable at grocery stores or farmers markets. Other states have funded similar programs through Medicaid waivers, which allow states to use federal health insurance dollars in new ways, or through nonprofit funding.

Community conversations

The South Dakota Healthy Nutrition Collaborative will host 5 community conversations about the South Dakota Food Landscape assessment findings including at 5:30 p.m. Sept. 18 at the Journey Museum in Rapid City.

The idea was discussed during the latest legislative session, Folliard said, when lawmakers approved a law that requires the state Department of Social Services to seek a waiver to ban soft drinks from the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. The state submitted its waiver request on Monday.

“When we were talking about SNAP restrictions, we also tried to raise the idea that if you restrict, it’s also good to incentivize healthy food,” Folliard said. “I think we can have those conversations next session a little bit more based on the data that came from this report.”

The state Department of Health has already designated child food sufficiency as a priority through its maternal and child health programs, providing momentum for the collaborative’s work, Folliard said.

The longer-term goal is a full food systems plan — a coordinated, statewide strategy for how food is grown, distributed and accessed, especially during times of economic stress. The collaborative is seeking funding to create the plan. 

The assessment was produced through a partnership with the state Department of Health, Avera Research Institute, University of South Dakota’s Center for Prevention of Child Maltreatment, and the South Dakota Healthy Nutrition Collaborative. The collaborative brings together 40 organizations, including the state departments of Health, Human Services and Social Services.

More than 500 people participated in the assessment survey — including 217 community members (weighted toward South Dakotans most at risk of food insecurity based on age, geography and tribal affiliation) and 295 people involved in the food system, in fields such as healthcare, education, policy, etc. The assessment also included one-on-one interviews and focus groups.

Food security information is often scattered across agencies and organizations, Folliard said, making it hard for anyone to see the full picture.

“Food is at the base of all health,” said Folliard, who co-authored the assessment. “It’s everywhere, so no one’s taking ownership of it. The organizations that came together for this assessment recognized that we all have to play a part in figuring this out together.”

In South Dakota, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, 1 in 8 people and 1 in 5 children have limited or uncertain access to enough food, and 1 in 8 residents eat enough fruits and vegetables each day. 

Those gaps don’t just affect individual health — they can drive up healthcare costs, strain schools and social services, and limit economic opportunity across the state, the assessment said.

In addition to affordability, the assessment included findings in key areas of food security and the state’s food system, including:

Assistance: About 70,000 South Dakotans rely on the federal-state Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, and income cutoffs create a “benefits cliff” where earning slightly more can cost a family nearly $1,000 in monthly food assistance.

Access: 13 counties have food insecurity rates above the national average and 43 counties are considered food swamps, which are areas where dollar stores and convenience stores outnumber grocery stores.

Availability: 359 of South Dakota’s 28,299 farms are specialty operations growing the fruits, vegetables and whole foods that improve nutrition security.

The assessment’s data extends beyond the published report. The state Department of Health recently launched an interactive dashboard because of the assessment, drawing on several datasets — dollar-store counts, diabetes rates, farm-to-school participation and SNAP vendor locations — that the department will update periodically.

That information gives local governments, community organizations and researchers the ability to examine their specific county and identify where targeted action is most needed, said Christine Hockett, director of community research at Avera Research Institute and a University of South Dakota associate professor who co-authored the assessment.

“When reports like these are published, a lot of times it happens once and then it’s like, ‘OK, what happens now?’ There’s no sustainability plan,” Hockett said. “As we were harmonizing and bringing the data together, we were doing it with the idea that we would ultimately share this with the Department of Health to make it accessible to everybody.”

title: Banking with a caffeine boost
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — A bank established in Nebraska more than 128 years ago has opened a brand new branch in Spearfish — and their vision for the future is anything but antiquated.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — A bank established in Nebraska more than 128 years ago has opened a brand new branch in Spearfish — and their vision for the future is anything but antiquated. 

Security First Bank opened Aug. 4 in the new building on Colorado Boulevard in front of the Monument Health Rehabilitation Clinic and Bomgaars. The sleek black building will also house a Starbucks — complete with a drive thru, in a matter of weeks. 

“We try to do concepts with a tenant. We signed a long-term lease with Starbucks. We designed the building based on that lease,” said Brent Russ, Spearfish branch president.

“We wanted to invite a high-traffic business model to bring people to this area,” said Callie Wagner, director of marketing for Security First. “It is a very good location.”

But pairing coffee with banking isn’t as forward thinking as the method that powers the building. Securities First Bank prioritizes sustainability, Wagner said. As a result, the Spearfish location runs on geothermal energy, tapped from 24 wells on site. 

“We are very committed to Spearfish. We are here to stay. The organization has given us the tools that we need to be successful here,” Russ said. 

Before opening the full-service banking branch, Security First was already looking at ways to invest in the community Wagner said. 

“Community involvement is very important to us,” Wagner said. “A couple of years ago we were one of the first sponsors to sign on for the sports complex. That is a 10-year commitment. We were very excited to sign on to that and show our support for the sports community at large.”

Russ said the new branch has gone above and beyond when it comes to landscaping — they’re planning to bring in a sculpture from a local artist, and are hoping the effect will beautify the area. 

“It helps reinforce community development here at Exit 14 and out at Exit 17 too,” Wagner said. “We are looking forward and like to be involved in any community impacts that we can.”

Security First originated in Nebraska. In South Dakota, it established a corporate headquarters and branches in Rapid City. Before expanding its banking services to Spearfish, it opened a loan production office (LPO) in 2022. 

“Our goal there was to gather some clientele on the loan side before we opened a full service branch,” Russ said. “Here in Spearfish at this branch, we are a full service bank: we can take deposits, give out loans, give out mortgages, CDs, cash checks, exchange coin, you name it, we can do it.”

The bank hired tellers, so that customers can come inside and bank in person. 

“The only thing that can differentiate ourselves from the other banks is how we treat our customers. When they come in the door, call them by their name,” Russ said. “Customer service is key.”

The branch also has an outdoor, drive thru ATM for customers to use both during and after business hours. 

Security First and Starbucks are planning a joint grand opening on Sept. 28. 

“We encourage community members and customers to come check out both spaces and find out what we’re all about,” Wagner said.

title: The Mercy Sloane Chronicles: Chapter 17
byline: By Eliza Blue A work of serialized fiction special to the Pioneer
description: It was nearly the middle of August before Mercy stopped to think about anything other than the present moment. _full_text:
The Mercy Sloane Chronicles

It was nearly the middle of August before Mercy stopped to think about anything other than the present moment. She still wore a dress for work at the shop, but had taken to wearing trousers and a battered cowboy hat she’d found in Ardath’s barn much of the rest of the time. Her sunburn had long since faded to tan, and her hair was bleached lighter than it had been since she was a child. Her arms and legs were strong from riding her pony, walking miles a day to and from town, and working on her little house. Ardath had lent her tools and she was slowly replacing rotten boards and shingles and fixing the sagging porch. She wondered if anyone from her old life would even recognize her now.

Her friendship with Melissa had also blossomed. Melissa technically lived in the little apartment above the post office, but went home to her family’s homestead for supper most nights. She was the oldest of twelve, and there was still one in diapers, so her mother welcomed as much help as Melissa had time to give. Mercy often came with and helped, too. Melissa taught her to milk a cow and churn butter from the cream and make farm cheese from the skim. Sometimes Melissa and Mercy slept over, laying blankets down on the hay in the hayloft, the hay door flung open so they could stargaze. Before bed, the whole family would sit on the porch to watch the sunset, and Melissa’s younger sister Lila would braid purple wildflowers into Mercy’s hair while a roly-poly toddler slept on Mercy’s lap. It felt a little like heaven to Mercy, although Melissa assured her if she ever had to pass a prairie blizzard with everyone crowded around the woodstove for warmth, she’d know that it definitely was not.

July and August had not been all cozy, twilight chats on porches, however. For Mercy, at least, the dominant feeling was actually that she was being baked in an oven. The late garden Mercy and Melissa planted was struggling, the seedlings stunted and straggly even with daily watering. The muddy pond by Ardath wasn’t even mud now, just a circle of slightly darker dirt where the water had been. And during the day, the store was stuffy and full of flies despite the screen door Marla was constantly fussing about keeping closed.

“I don’t know, Melissa,” Mercy said when Melissa made her comment about prairie blizzards. They were lying in the hayloft, both still sweating despite the cooling breeze. “I think a blizzard sounds like heaven right now.”

Melissa laughed, and patted Mercy’s cheek patronizingly. “Oh, just you wait, child,” she said. “Just you wait.”

Meanwhile, the shop had turned into a kind of farmer’s market. Marla bought vegetables from whoever had extra to sell to those who didn’t have enough. Most families kept kitchen gardens to supplement their supply of canned goods, and the distribution of this produce was an important part of the local economy every year. For the last few days, however, produce coming into the shop had dwindled to next to nothing, giving Marla another thing to fret about as her own garden was offering little more than a few bitter cucumbers and even fewer mealy tomatoes. 

 Eliza Blue TMC
Eliza Blue 

Because the summer had been so dry and hot, some local families were planning to travel down to the Black Hills to a town called Spearfish. Spearfish was tucked into a valley blessed with rich soil, and away from the hard winds of the open plains, was a much kinder climate to grow vegetables. Families from Antelope and other nearby ranching communities often travelled to Spearfish in August, set up camp for the week, and after buying a year’s worth of produce, canned it all so they could travel home with their winter stores all ready to be stacked in root cellars and pantries.

Melissa’s family decided to make the journey, and Melissa invited Mercy along. 

“It’s like the olden days,” she said. “ My folks have that car now, but they still hitch up the old wagon so we can fit all the kids and the jars and the camp stove and the old tent. It’s slow going, but it will be fun, too, I promise.”

Mercy wasn’t sure how Marla would feel about her asking for the time away, but Marla was overjoyed. “Mercy, you bring back as much as you can. I need winter stores and so do you. Whatever we have left, I know we can sell.”

And so it was decided. Mercy borrowed saddlebags from Ardath for her pony, a blanket, and a canteen from the shop, and was ready to take her first trip to the mountains.

title: Larson quarry delivers annual report, claims zero silica and minimal noise disturbance
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Larson quarry, located on Homestake Road and operated by Croell, delivered its first annual report Tuesday. Croell reported no silica and minimal noise disturbances. Pioneer photo by Travis Potter
_full_text:
dji_fly_20260811_075216_0151_1786456552068_photo.JPG
The Larson quarry, located on Homestake Road and operated by Croell, delivered its first annual report Tuesday. Croell reported no silica and minimal noise disturbances. Pioneer photo by Travis Potter 

DEADWOOD — The Larson gravel pit on Homestake Road, operated by Croell, marked its first year of operation under a conditional use permit with an annual report Tuesday to Lawrence County commissioners. 

Brian Marchant, general manager for Croell, told commissioners the quarry ceased blasting and crushing operations Aug. 27. He said the quarry produced 140,599 tons of material — 9,401 tons less than the limit posed by the sites conditional use permit within the first year. Of those tons produced, 7,423 tons have been sold.

Marchant said going forward, one man will be on site operating a loader and material will be sold from the pit using an automatic scale system. 

“When trucks come in, they’ll tear in, they’ll get their weight, and we remotely do that with a secretary in Sundance,” he said. “She has a camera, and she’ll get the truck number, tear them in, they’ll go back there with the loader operator, get loaded, come back around the camera, and the girl in Sundance will print out their ticket. They don’t even have to get out of their truck.”

Marchant said the site has hauled in approximately 400,000 gallons of water to the site for dust control.

County commissioners allowed Croell to crush 250,000 tons of material in the second year of operation, having deemed that the pit performed “with no significant issues” in the first year. Marchant said the site will not excavate and crush more material until current material on site has been sold.

Silica, noise, and seismic activity

Marchant told commissioners Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) requires the site to undergo respirable dust and crystalline silica exposure tests to monitor silica in workers. An air sampling report was prepared by Forged Sentinel Group, Inc., of Hiawatha, Iowa. To test the exposure levels of breathable dust, silica quartz, cristobalite, and tridymite, 5 employees wore an SKC AirChec Connect Pump for approximately 11.5 hours on site. Employees ranged from loader operators, dozer operators, and ground men, who cleaned out and around the plant and conveyors.

According to the report, crystalline silica was not detected in any personal breathing zone sample, and all results were below MSHA’s required action level and permissible exposure limit.

According to the report, “Although neighboring properties have expressed concerns regarding visible dust, the industrial hygiene monitoring data collected during normal production activities demonstrates that respirable dust exposures remained low, and that respirable crystalline silica was not detected in any employee sample. These findings indicate that the quarry’s existing dust suppression measures, work practices, and operational controls are effectively minimizing airborne respirable dust generation and protecting employee health.”

“I know that was a big (concern) at previous hearings, so hopefully all the neighbors can breathe a little easier,” said Marchant. “It’s not going to harm them.”

Noise levels were tested at 4 locations at the quarry: at the entrance before and after crushing operations began, the property boundary closest to the crusher, and approximately 6 feet and 200 feet from the crusher. 

According to the annual report, noise decibels were tested using an MSHA approved decibel meter Model 3M Edge 4 and a cell phone utilizing a National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health app. The cellphone was used to detect noise levels below 63.1 decibels.

According to MSHA regulations, noise levels for mining operations must remain below 85 decibels. 

Reported noise levels are as follows: 63.9 decibels at the entrance to the quarry during operations; 46.7 decibels at the boundary nearest the crusher; 85.2 decibels 6 feet from the crusher; 80.9 decibels 200 feet from the crusher.

According to a decibel level comparison chart published by Yale University, 60-70 decibels are comparable to normal conversation, 75 decibels are comparable to a vacuum cleaner, 75-85 decibels are comparable to chamber music in a small auditorium, and 80 decibels are comparable to a telephone dial tone.

Marchant said Instantel was hired to test blast vibrations. 

“The only readings you get are within 3,000 feet of blasts,” said Marchant. “You get out to around 3,000 feet and it doesn’t even trigger the seismographs.”

According to the blasting report presented to commissioners, “The blast events at the Larson quarry have been below the levels that could produce cosmetic damage and far below any potential for structural damage.”

According to the report, a seismograph placed 3,078 feet away, near a neighbor to the southwest that reported structural shaking, did not trigger during blasting events. 

Formal complaints

In the first year of operation, the quarry received 4 formal complaints. 

Bruce Outka, deputy state’s attorney, said 3 complaints were concerning dust during high wind events and one voiced concerns of scale usage on site. 

Outka said the concerns about the scale were addressed immediately and have been resolved. 

Marchant said during all 3 dust complaints, the foreman had already stopped crushing operations. However, he said crushers must move remaining material off of the belts before they can fully stop movement. 

“When you’re running a crusher, you can’t just turn the thing off,” Marchant said. “There’s a cycle, and it has to run, or our crushers get plugged up with rock. It takes a long time to clean them, and if you have to clean them by hand that’s dangerous. So, it takes a while to get those crushers clean when they shut off. I was notified by one of the commissioners that it was getting dusty, so I called the foreman, and he said it was shut off, it just had to cycle. Then they went and got water and watered the pile and did what they could.”

Outka said 2 complaints were received Sunday during a high winds event. The National Weather Service reported gusts of 52 mph near Spearfish. 

Marchant said the site operates on 4, 10-hour shifts. He said men will water the piles of material before leaving for the weekend to attempt to minimize dust. With weather conditions reaching record-breaking highs and minimal rain fall, he said it’s difficult to keep top levels of soil from being disturbed. 

“We have followed up on every complaint, and (Croell) has been very responsive each and every time,” said Outka. 

Marchant said future plans for the site include moving pits from the top of the hill, where it is more easily disturbed by winds, into the pit itself to minimize dust.

title: Dakota Gold  prepares to grow
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Dakota Gold contractors drill at the company’s site along Maitland Road. If all goes according to the scheduled plan, the company hopes to start mining gold by 2029. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Dakota Gold.JPG
Dakota Gold contractors drill at the company’s site along Maitland Road. If all goes according to the scheduled plan, the company hopes to start mining gold by 2029. Pioneer file photo 

LEAD — If all goes according to plan, Dakota Gold in Lead hopes to be mining gold by 2029. 

Jack Henris, chief executive officer and president of the gold exploration and development company in Lead said the company is working on its pre-feasibility study right now, with a goal to publish a notice of intent to mine, and a determination of scenic and unique lands for the S.D. Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources to examine late this year. After that, the company will move into working on a feasibility study, with a goal to acquire a full-scale mining permit by 2029 pending regulatory review. 

Dakota Gold has been drilling for gold on private land at Richmond Hill and the Maitland area since about 2022, following plans Homestake once had for expanding its mining operation before low gold prices forced the company to close in 2002. 

There’s a lot of work to do before Dakota Gold confidently moves forward with mining, Henris said. 

“We drilled 70 holes and I think 47 of them we had intercepts of the Homestake formation, which was the ore bearing formation for the Homestake Mine,” Henris said of drilling in the Maitland area, which has a deep underground ore deposit. “(It was) similar grades and similar thicknesses that were mined at Homestake. So we’re very excited about that.” 

Henris said the company’s strategy is to start with an open pit mine at Richmond Hill, in order to generate income. He acknowledged public concern about open pit mining, and said the operation will be conducted with as minimal environmental impact as possible. 

“What is unique about our proposed approach at Richmond Hill is that we envision 6 different phases of mining,” Henris said. “We’ll mine a pit, then we’ll start mining a second one, but we’ll take material that we don’t process and we’ll backfill the first. When we mine the third one, we’ll backfill the second one. When we’re done at Richmond Hill, all the pits will be backfilled and they’ll be topsoiled, re-vegetated, and we’ll plant trees and grasses.” 

Minimal environmental impact has been a company goal since it began gold exploration, as Dakota Gold has historically conducted activities on land that Homestake had previously disturbed, Henris said. 

“One of our fundamentals is to reduce our footprint as much as possible, and to kind of follow in Homestake’s footsteps,” he said. 

Once the company is able to generate income at Richmond Hill, Henris said plans for the next step are to develop an underground mine at Maitland at some point in the future. 

Henris said the mining will benefit all of South Dakota, but especially Lawrence County, where 20% of mining severance tax will go to the county to be granted for education and community projects. With a budget of about $15 to $25 million a year, Henris said the local company has spent about $145 million in the Lead-Deadwood community since 2019, and expect to invest another $450 million to bring Richmond Hill into production. 

“What’s really great about our company is our headquarters are right here,” Henris said. “We know what we’re going to do and what’s really great is we’re going to generate cash here. This is the head office. We’re not going to send checks to some place else in the country or to a different country.” 

Contributing to the community is part of the core fundamental values of Dakota Gold, Henris said. The company is small right now, with about 40 employees — 90% of whom are from Lead and the surrounding area. In the future the company plans for about 250-300 employees. But slow growth is key to maintaining the company’s vision and values for community support, he said. 

“It’s easier for us to establish the culture of the company we want to be when there’s 35-40, than when there’s 250-300 of us,” he said. “So we’re setting the tone.” 

With so many of its employees from the Lead-Deadwood area, supporting the community is part of the core value system at Dakota Gold, Henris said. Whether they are helping set up and maintain local parks, helping to serve community meals, coaching sports teams, getting involved with various boards and committees, and just generally helping out around town, volunteerism is very important at the company. 

“You want the community to want you here,” Henris said. “For them to want us here, we’ve got to be active and we’ve got to be doing these kinds of things. That’s the beauty of having local folks, because our folks love the community. Homestake not only had the benefits for all the employees, like healthcare and those kinds of things, but all the volunteer hours that Homestake employees did as well. They were very active. That’s really kind of our blueprint. If we can be that generational company, that’s what we’re hoping to be. We don’t generate any money currently. We do donate to different organizations, but we can’t do what Homestake did and we can’t currently do what Wharf does. But for now, we can volunteer. That should be a fundamental premise of what we build the company on.” 

A connection to Lead is the reason Dakota Gold purchased the former Lotus Up building, at 95 E. Main St, which it will renovate to add more office space. As the company prepares to grow, Henris said it has outgrown its current space at the Roundhouse, and the goal is to move employees into the new building by next year. When that happens, Henris said the company is still unsure about what it will do with the Roundhouse building. 

“The Roundhouse is beautiful,” Henris said. “We love the building. But for an office, it’s not very functional. So we’re looking for a home that is a little bit more functional for office space and those kinds of things.”  

Other Dakota Gold properties in Lead include the former cement plant at the bottom of Washington Street, where the company processes its core samples, and a former Homestake electrical plant on Washington Street, where Dakota Gold core samples are stored.

title: ‘Mourning Bands On’ explores cultural attitude shift toward police
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Author Troy Bobbitt. Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Author Headshot-Bobbitt.jpg
Author Troy Bobbitt. Courtesy photo 

 Mourning Bands On Cover-WDR.jpeg
“Mourning Bands On” is a cultural examination of how public perception of law enforcement has changed in America. Courtesy photo 

LEAD — When Troy Bobbitt became a law enforcement officer after 9/11, the police were respected and honored across the country. 

By the time he retired in 2024, all of that had changed and Bobbitt said random strangers were giving him obscene gestures in traffic, just because he was in his squad car. 

What caused the shift, and how did American perception of law enforcement change so drastically, so quickly? 

Those are the questions Bobbitt seeks to answer in his book, “Mourning Bands On.” The book is a cultural examination of law enforcement in America, starting with history from colonial times to the Civil War and the institution of the 14th Amendment, which established federal police powers for the first time; the evolution of the development of Constitutional law for the Fourth Amendment; development of technology to supplement law enforcement personnel and training in the wake of budget constraints during the 2008 recession; to the most recent tragic deaths of Michael Brown, Trayvon Martin, Breonna Taylor, and George Floyd, that sparked riots, protest movements, and calls for defunding the police. 

Using official reports from the U.S. Department of Justice that were released years after each of those deaths occurred, along with newspaper accounts from the time and historical information from Wikipedia, Bobbitt explores the evolution of American cultural perspective of law enforcement. 

“There was a perception that we militarized the police,” Bobbitt said. “Well, how did that perception develop? I look at those things from a cultural point, not a political point. I try to leave the political out of it. When I look at the Trayvon Martin, or George Floyd, or Breonna Taylor (cases), I look at it from what does Wikipedia say? Wikipedia is the common perception of the people. But what really came out of it when the FBI did their investigations? So, I try to show both sides.” 

Technology, and how it has helped and hindered law enforcement, is also a major part of Bobbitt’s book. The recession of 2008 created the environment for government to use more technology for enforcement, he said, as seen with the development of traffic cameras that have since morphed into technology used by flock cameras. Additionally, he said a grant from President Barack Obama to equip all police officers with body cameras, led to a need for more data storage. 

“Lead has 5 police officers,” he said. “They all wear body cameras. But the city of Lead has to store the data. When you’re recording video and audio on 5 police officers, that’s a lot of data. You have to store that. Just purchasing the cameras is one thing, but now the city has to pay, for the rest of eternity, a computer system that’s capable of storing the data, maintaining the data, recovering the data for court usage. So, President Obama’s grant program was great. Get the information out there so incidents like Breonna Taylor don’t happen again. But what about the after effect? The federal government has 150,000 law enforcement officers and they have to store all that data. So, one of the big issues right now is why don’t federal agents have body cameras? Where’s the government going to store it? Data centers are another big issue right now. Well, if you don’t have a data center, how do you store the data?”

The title of the book, “Mourning Bands On,” is a play on words and a statement. When a law enforcement officer, border patrol agent, or first responder dies, Bobbitt said officers wear a blue and black band around their badge as a sign of mourning. 

“It’s a play on words that we’re losing our police,” he said. “The more pressure that was put on our police by the public, you create a generation of children that don’t want to go into policing. So, how do you backfill people like me? I retired. Well, somebody has to backfill me.” 

Bobbitt said part of his career with the border patrol was recruiting, interviewing and hiring law enforcement agents. Over time, he said the hiring pool began to steadily decrease. 

“We were filling an agency that had 20,000 personnel,” he said. “We were losing 900 to 1,000 every year, but we were only backfilling 250-300. When I came into the border patrol after 9/11, we were hiring 4,000 to 5,000. Now, we can only hire 200-300, because people just weren’t going into the job because there was a negative connotation. Well, the policing is the same thing. Mourning Bands comes from the fact that we’re losing our police.” 

Bobbitt said he will be setting up vendor booths to sell his books, “Mourning Bands On,” and “Cartel Bands On,” at the Deadwood Farmer’s Market today. He also will set up at the Spearfish Farmer’s Market on Saturday, and he plans to have a booth during the Deadwood Prospector Bowl, 

Bobbitt moved to Lead after he retired in 2025. He is active in the Trinity United Methodist Church and the Lead-Deadwood Kiwanis Club.
