title: Piedmont passes first reading of tiered mining protective ordinance
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: This map shows the land that was voluntarily annexed into Piedmont and is subject to current ordinances that prohibit mineral extraction within city limits. On Tuesday, the Piedmont City Commission gave its first approval to an ordinance that extends controls beyond city borders. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Piedmont mine map 1.png
This map shows the land that was voluntarily annexed into Piedmont and is subject to current ordinances that prohibit mineral extraction within city limits. On Tuesday, the Piedmont City Commission gave its first approval to an ordinance that extends controls beyond city borders. Pioneer file photo 

PIEDMONT — The city of Piedmont is one step closer to regulating mining outside of its boundaries. 

On Tuesday, the Piedmont City Commission passed the first reading of it’s “Tiered Industrial and Mining Protective Ordinance,” which designates land areas on the outskirts of the city, and establishes specific mining requirements based upon those area locations.   

According to the ordinance, it is intended to protect the citizens of Piedmont from adverse effects of mining, including dust, particulate emissions, noise, vibration, and surface and groundwater contamination associated with mining, quarrying, aggregate crushing/processing, and similar operations near the city. 

The ordinance seeks to exercise the city’s full power of jurisdiction over lands that extend one mile beyond the city’s boundary; exercises the city’s full plat authority; attaches protective conditions to any city permit, utility connection, or road use agreement that an operator voluntarily seeks from the city for any distance; and preserves the city’s authority to submit formal comment during county or state permitting proceedings, and to pursue remedies for any nuisances or harm the city experiences.  

Piedmont City Commissioner Shannon Blotske said the city’s boundaries are very jagged, and in some areas the city shares a boundary with nearby Summerset. That’s why the ordinance establishes 2 specific areas, with different regulations for each area set forth by the ordinance. 

Area 1 includes lands within a mile from the city limits, and institutes strict requirements for air quality, dust control, and water quality, enforceable by police power. Mining operations within Area 1 must include an extensive dust control plan and install ambient air meters. Under the ordinance, dust may not cause a visible plume of more than 20% opacity, crossing the operation’s property boundary, and blasting requires 24 hours prior notice, and must be done according to U.S. Bureau of mines/OSMRE standards. Mining operations in Area 1 are required to complete a hydrogeologic study that shows the operation does not pose a threat to the municipal water supply. Water monitors are also required within Area 1. 

Violations of requirements within Area 1 constitutes a Class 2 misdemeanor, punishable by a fine of $500, 30 days in prison, or both, with each day of continuing violation considered a separate offense. 

Area 2 includes lands that extend beyond the one-mile jurisdiction line, within the city’s subdivision plat approval authority, and does not include police power enforcement authority. This section of the ordinance requires mines within Area 2 lands to post a public bond or other financial commitment, and to maintain a public complaint response plan. It also allows the city to deny utility service, road use agreements, or permits to any industrial operation that does not agree to provide protections. 

Violating requirements for Area 2 constitute a breach of contract, and can result in the immediate revocation of city permissions that enable the operation. 

The ordinance comes less than a month after Fourth Circuit Court Judge Michelle Comer affirmed the legality of the city’s voluntary annexation of 130 acres, which are within the boundaries of a state-approved limestone mine permit for Simon Contractors. P5, LLC, owned by members of the Policky family that owns Big D convenience stores across the region, challenged the voluntary annexation because it included 59 acres of their property, which was under contract to allow Simon to set up its mining operation. Since the land has been annexed into the city, Blodgett said the city of Piedmont already has ordinances in place that prohibit mining within city limits. 

Tuesday’s first reading is the first of 2 approvals the city commission must agree upon. City Commissioners are scheduled to do second and final reading of the ordinance at their Sept. 15 meeting. After that, the ordinance will be published in the city’s legal newspaper, and residents will have 20 days after that to refer the action to a vote. If it is not referred, the ordinance will become effective later this fall.

title: Crow Creek tribal member to be SDs next Missing  and Murdered Indigenous People liaison
byline: By John Hult Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Marlys Big Eagle is the new Missing and Murdered Indigenous People liason for South Dakota. Photo courtesy of South Dakota Attorney General’s Office
_full_text:
Crow Creek tribal member to be SDs next Missing and Murdered Indigenous People liaison.jpg
Marlys Big Eagle is the new Missing and Murdered Indigenous People liason for South Dakota. Photo courtesy of South Dakota Attorney General’s Office 

PIERRE — A Fort Thompson resident and member of the Crow Creek Sioux Tribe who has more than two decades of experience working with crime victims will serve as South Dakota’s Missing and Murdered Indigenous People specialist. 

Marlys Big Eagle will fill the role vacated earlier this summer by Allison Morrisette, who in 2022 became the first to serve in the position. 

Attorney General Marty Jackley, under whose office the liaison serves, announced Big Eagle’s hiring in a press release Wednesday. 

“Marlys has spent her career helping victims of violence and families looking for missing loved ones,” Jackley said in the release. “Her credibility with tribal communities, law enforcement, and prosecutors makes her an outstanding choice.”

Big Eagle worked with crime victims for the U.S. Department of Justice for 27 years. For 23 of those years, she worked as the supervisory victim witness coordinator for the U.S. Attorney’s Office in South Dakota. For the past four years, she’s worked for the department’s Washington, D.C., executive office as the agency’s first Native American outreach services liaison for Missing and Murdered Indigenous People cases occurring in tribal areas.

The job of state-level liaison was created by the Legislature in 2021 but not funded. Initially, Morrisette’s salary was paid by a nonprofit organization. Jackley successfully lobbied to make the position permanent and state-funded shortly after she was hired.

The liaison works to connect family members to resources and the law enforcement agencies investigating their loved ones’ cases. In June, Morrisette told South Dakota Searchlight that serving as the first MMIP liaison for the state was an honor, but that the new position she accepted, working with juveniles for the Unified Judicial System, was a better fit for her growing family. 

In the press release on her hiring, Big Eagle said she’s “deeply honored” to have been selected to work with families “as they seek answers and confirmation about what may have happened to their loved ones.”

“I look forward to working alongside other MMIP stakeholders and partners to help bring answers, support, and justice to these important cases,” Big Eagle said.

Nationwide, Native Americans are more likely than non-Natives to die by homicide. In 2023, homicide rates for Native Americans were nearly five times higher than for non-Hispanic whites, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Native Americans are also disproportionately represented in missing people cases. South Dakota maintains an online clearinghouse for all people reported missing to a law enforcement agency within the state’s borders. Consistently, 60% of the cases involve Native Americans, while around 8.5% of the state’s population is Native. 

As of Wednesday afternoon, 58 of the state’s 93 missing people were Native American. Thirty of the 48 missing women were Native American.

The South Dakota liaison position was created the year after state lawmakers voted to create that public-facing missing people site in 2020. A few months later, Congress passed the Not Invisible Act, which created a commission to investigate the underlying causes and identify improvements to help address the overrepresentation of Native Americans in missing people cases and violent crimes.

Nine tribal nations share borders with the state of South Dakota, which has one of the highest per-capita populations of Native Americans in the U.S.

title: Monument Health awarded grants to expand access to care across western SD
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: RAPID CITY — Monument Health has been awarded 2 grants through South Dakota’s Rural Health Transformation Project, state funding aimed at strengthening access, quality, and long-term sustainability of rural health care.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

RAPID CITY — Monument Health has been awarded 2 grants through South Dakota’s Rural Health Transformation Project, state funding aimed at strengthening access, quality, and long-term sustainability of rural health care. 

The grants will support Care Connect and the Telemed Transfer Center, two initiatives designed to bring more timely, specialized care to patients across Monument Health’s rural and frontier service area.

“We’re honored to receive this support from the state of South Dakota and CMS,” said Alan Solano, vice president of governmental affairs for Monument Health. “Both of these projects are about the same thing, getting patients the right care, closer to home, faster. That matters everywhere we serve, but it matters most in our rural and frontier communities, where a delay in specialty access can mean the difference between a manageable health issue and a preventable emergency.”

Care Connect will expand access to Monument Health’s existing specialty and primary care capacity through centralized scheduling, referral management, digital self-scheduling and expanded use of Epic Cheers. The program is expected to create capacity for more outpatient visits, with an estimated 18,000 Medicaid recipients benefiting annually, a population disproportionately affected by transportation barriers and limited local care options. Phase 1 will prioritize primary care and obstetrics & gynecology, addressing significant gaps in maternal health access across the region.

The Telemed Transfer Center will expand telemedicine infrastructure across Monument Health’s Critical Access Hospital network, including telestroke and teletrauma consultation, along with expanded specialty support in behavioral health, cardiology, pulmonology, endocrinology, and infectious disease. The project is expected to directly benefit more than 85,000 rural residents, reducing unnecessary transfers, improving stroke response times, and strengthening the ability of rural providers to care for patients locally.

Monument Health is working with the South Dakota Department of Health and Department of Social Services to finalize grant contracts and will share additional updates as the projects move forward.

title: FEMA to reimburse 8 SD counties,  3 tribes for storm-related infrastructure fixes
byline: By John Hult Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Matilyn Kerr, left, and sister Brittany Kerr watch as a skid-steer loader pulls a tree from Brittany Kerr’s yard in Highmore, on June 29, after a severe storm that morning. Photo by Meghan O’Brien, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
FEMA to reimburse eight South Dakota counties, three tribes for storm-related infrastructure fixes.jpg
Matilyn Kerr, left, and sister Brittany Kerr watch as a skid-steer loader pulls a tree from Brittany Kerr’s yard in Highmore, on June 29, after a severe storm that morning. Photo by Meghan O’Brien, South Dakota Searchlight 

PIERRE — The federal government will reimburse up to 75% of public infrastructure repair costs from storms that hit eight South Dakota counties and two Native American reservations in late June and early July, the Federal Emergency Management Agency announced Wednesday.

The Oglala Sioux Tribe, meanwhile, is in line for the same level of reimbursements for repairs to public infrastructure caused by storms in early June, and individual tribal members will be eligible for financial aid to cover some property losses from that incident.

Gov. Larry Rhoden requested a presidential disaster declaration from the Trump administration in late July, in a letter laying out $4.5 million in public property damage from a storm system that moved through the state between June 28 and July 3. 

Rhoden said, first in a Tuesday evening social media post and again in a press release on Wednesday, that President Donald Trump called him directly to tell him about approving the state’s request for a disaster declaration. 

On X, Rhoden shared a post from Trump in which the president wrote “South Dakota is a special place, which I won by Historic margins, three times, and I will always deliver BIG for them.”

The disaster declaration for the state as a whole will reimburse public property repair costs in Beadle, Bennett, Buffalo, Day, Hand, Hughes, Hyde and Stanley Counties, along with the Crow Creek and Lower Brule reservations. Roads, power systems, parks, recreation areas and public facilities were damaged in the storm, with the heaviest impacts in Hyde and Beadle counties.

Lower Brule Sioux Tribe President Boyd Gorneau told South Dakota Searchlight on Wednesday that the tribe lost some center-pivot irrigation systems on its agricultural land in the storm. 

FEMA sent a press release on disaster declarations for South Dakota on Wednesday, but the release did not include dollar figures. 

A FEMA spokesperson told Searchlight the reimbursement isn’t limited to the $4.5 million in damage cited in Rhoden’s request to President Trump, whose post said he’d “approved” $3.4 million — a figure that would cover 75% of the cost to repair that damage.

The actual amount paid in reimbursement will be based on the cost to repair infrastructure, the spokesman said, provided local governments and state officials adhere to FEMA guidelines and protocols.

The same will be true for the Oglala Sioux Tribe’s public infrastructure. The tribe, which requested a disaster declaration separately, was hit with flash flooding June 2-4 after a heavy rain and hail storm.

During the first round of storms, according to the National Weather Service, “6 to 7 inches of rain fell in a short period, causing streets and ditches to fill extremely quickly,” in addition to strong winds and hail. A tornado touched down near Ideal in Tripp County the following day, damaging mostly agricultural land.

The individual assistance program, part of the FEMA announcement for the tribe, will allow residents to work with FEMA to obtain “grants for temporary housing and home repairs, low-cost loans to cover uninsured property losses and other programs to help individuals and families recover from the effects of the disaster,” the spokesperson wrote in an email.

A separate press release from FEMA on the tribal disaster declaration said that tribal members who experienced losses in the storms “should document their damage, keep any receipts for repairs, and file a claim with their insurance provider.”

“Information on how individuals may apply for federal disaster assistance will be announced when it is available,” the press release said.

The FEMA spokesperson said the tribe has not requested a disaster declaration for a more recent hailstorm, which dropped baseball-sized hail on some areas of tribal land, damaging school buses and homes and forcing a delayed start to the school year.

The tribe’s public information officer did not immediately return calls and emails seeking comment on Wednesday.

title: Spearfish Middle School field in place
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: The new artificial turf at the Spearfish Middle School track and field is in place, complete with markings for football and soccer. Pioneer photo by Travis Potter
_full_text:
Spearfish Middle School field in place.JPG
The new artificial turf at the Spearfish Middle School track and field is in place, complete with markings for football and soccer. Pioneer photo by Travis Potter 

SPEARFISH — Crews from Mammoth Sports Construction are nearing the finish line for construction on the new track and field at Spearfish Middle School.

The new artificial turf has been rolled out and is in place, complete with markings for both football and soccer fields. The track has fresh asphalt and a rubberized covering coating it.

The previous track and field, built more than 30 years ago, was constructed on substandard soil, which has led to cracking asphalt, a few potholes in the track, and other drainage issues on the field. 

Initially, the construction costs came in around $3.25 million. Several changes were made to reduce the cost, and the final price for the district came in around $2.7 million. In August, the school board approved a change order in the amount of $59,685, to add 2 jumping pits and a runway.

In June, school officials determined that the additional runway and pits were necessary if the facility was going to host track and field meets.

The substantial completion of the track and field should be done around Sept. 10.

title: Driver’s license and identification cards debut new look
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: Driver’s licenses and identification cards in South Dakota will debut a new look in September. Photo courtesy of South Dakota Department of Public Safety
_full_text:
New driver's license look.jpg
Driver’s licenses and identification cards in South Dakota will debut a new look in September. Photo courtesy of South Dakota Department of Public Safety 

PIERRE — Driver’s licenses and identification cards in South Dakota are debuting a new look this month. 

The South Dakota Driver’s Licensing Program said the new cards feature advanced security technology to help prevent fraud and identity theft, including updated printing methods and embedded design elements that make the credentials more secure and harder to replicate. Along with improved safety features, the new design will increase readability and usability for both customers and law enforcement. 

“This redesign ensures that South Dakota continues to provide secure, reliable credentials that keep pace with evolving technology,” said Jeannelle Yitagesu, program manager. “We’re proud that the new cards also highlight the beauty and character of the state.”

Existing licenses will remain valid until their expiration date. No immediate action is required from current cardholders. 

Exam stations across the state will begin issuing the new design in September, with rollout dates varying by site as each office transitions to the updated system. Residents will receive the new style of card during renewal or when applying for new credentials. 

For more information, visit the driver licensing website at dps.sd.gov or contact your local driver exam station.

title: Quick picks: Dive into a book
description: Courtesy photos
_full_text:
0904 StingRayHC1608_source(RGB).jpg
Courtesy photos 

A library provides an ocean of information, and leagues of support for community members. As the Whitewood Public Library dives into its brand new aquatic themed fall reading program, its head librarian Deb Terhune recommended these 6 titles to inspire your child’s curiosity. 

1. “Commotion in the Ocean” by Giles Andreae

Genre: Picture book

This delightful board book by the author of “Giraffes Can’t Dance” features a collection of rhyming poems with colorful illustrations and is a wonderful way to introduce little ones to the animals and fish who live in the and around the ocean. 

2. “How Deep in the Ocean? Ocean animal habitats” by Monika Davies 

Genre: Science/picture book

Journey to the depths of the ocean and meet the animals that live at different levels of the sea. Comparisons to familiar objects give perspective and illustrated rulers show numeric distances of each depth range. Includes a map, glossary, and further resources.

3. “Ocean: A Photicular Book” by Dan Kainen

Genre: Nonfiction

A “New York Times” bestseller, Ocean is like being on a dive. Using Photicular technology, each image is like a 3-D movie on the page, delivering a rich, fluid visual experience. Open the book, and the reader is swept into the magic of an underwater world, face-to-face with a floating Yellow-Banded Sweetlips; with a glow-in-the-dark Deep-Sea Anglerfish; with a Sea Horse swaying in balletic motion; with a Sand Tiger Shark gliding along the ocean floor, its gaze haunting, its hook-toothed mouth gulping open and closed.

4. “Babies in the Ocean” by Ginger Swift

Genre: Children’s

 0904 ClownfishHC1709_source.jpg
Courtesy photos 

Come play in the ocean with our sea turtle friends, Tillie and Tyde. Introduce your baby or toddler to sea animals including turtles, whale sharks, octopuses, hermit crabs, dolphins, and more in this adorable lift-a-flap board book. Simple sentences reinforce future language structure while grasping and lifting the sturdy flaps helps develop fine motor skills.

5. “The Ocean: Exploring Our Blue Planet” by Miranda Krestovinkoff 

Genre: Picture book/nonfiction

Oceans cover more than 70% of the world — and so much science is lurking underneath that water’s surface. This survey-style book explores an incredible collection of narratives, featuring fascinating facts and stories about the world’s deepest seas and oceans. This is an eye-catching, comprehensive look at the creatures and plants that populate these waters and the people who have explored it, as well as a critical look at what is at stake now in protecting it.

6. “We Both Read: About the Ocean” by Sindy McKay

Genre: Nonfiction/science

Explores many aspects of the ocean environment, from coral reefs to deep seas to sandy shores and presents facts about life in the ocean, including dolphins, sharks, whales, starfish, and other creatures.

title: Anthrax found in Meade Co. cattle herd
byline: By Mark Watson Black Hills Pioneer
description: SPEARFISH — A cow/calf cattle herd in Meade County has tested positive for anthrax.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — A cow/calf cattle herd in Meade County has tested positive for anthrax.

It is the first confirmed case of anthrax in South Dakota this year.

Dakota’s State Veterinarian Dr. Mendel Miller said the herd initially began experiencing deaths while pastured in Butte County, where exposure is believed to have occurred. The cattle were later moved to Meade County where they continued to experience symptoms.

Samples from the herd were taken and sent to the Animal Disease Research and Diagnostic Laboratory at South Dakota State University which confirmed the disease.

The herd, according to the South Dakota Animal Industry Board, has been quarantined and neighboring herd owners have been notified. If additional herds are impacted, they will be quarantined as well.

“Veterinary oversight is important when faced with disease concerns, and the Animal Industry Board will continue to work with ranchers and private veterinarians to quickly respond to anthrax,” Miller said. “Anthrax vaccine has proven effective and allows ranchers to take steps to protect their herd.”

A naturally occurring bacteria, anthrax spores survive indefinitely in soil. Significant weather events, such as drought, floods, and high winds, can cause exposure leading to infection, according to the board.

“The anthrax bacteria form spores and those are in the soil, so it is nearly impossible to determine if a particular piece of ground has anthrax,” Miller told the Pioneer. “If there is any history of anthrax in the area, it is likely that it can become a problem, depending on circumstances. Almost anywhere in SD can have an anthrax issue, but history is a good indication of the risk.”

If anthrax is suspected, contact your local veterinarian or the Animal Industry Board at (605) 773-3321. If sudden death occurs in your herd, do not move the suspect carcasses until a diagnosis is made. The proper handling of affected carcasses by burning and burying them is important to help prevent additional impacts of healthy animals coming into contact with infected animals.

Miller said that anthrax is transmittable from animals to humans, generally, “via an open wound and contact with infected tissue. Animal to animal isn't as common or easy as some other diseases, but can occur with exposure to bodily fluids or carcasses of animals which have died of anthrax.”

According to the Merck Veterinary Manual, in animals, the clinical course ranges from peracute to chronic.

“The peracute form, common in cattle and sheep, is characterized by sudden onset and a rapidly fatal course. In cattle, sheep, and goats, staggering, dyspnea, trembling, collapse, a few convulsive movements, and death after only a brief period of illness may occur,” according to the manual.

“In acute anthrax of cattle and sheep, there is an abrupt onset of fever and a period of excitement followed by lethargy, stupor, respiratory or cardiac distress, staggering, seizures, and death. Often, the course of disease is so rapid that illness is not observed, and animals are found dead.”

Body temperatures may reach as high as107F, rumination ceases, milk production is materially reduced, and pregnant animals may abort. Bloody discharges from the natural body openings may be noted, according to the manual.

In horses, symptoms may be acute, according to the manual.

“Clinical signs may include fever, chills, severe colic, anorexia, depression, weakness, bloody diarrhea, and swellings of the neck, sternum, lower abdomen, and external genitalia. Death usually occurs within 2–3 days following onset of signs of disease,” it indicates.

title: US Senate challenger says Wounded Knee medals ‘should not stand’; incumbent says more info needed
byline: By Meghan O’Brien Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: An arch topped with a cross marks the entrance to the Wounded Knee Memorial and cemetery on the Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota. Photo by Makenzie Huber, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Wounded Knee.jpg
An arch topped with a cross marks the entrance to the Wounded Knee Memorial and cemetery on the Pine Ridge Reservation in South Dakota. Photo by Makenzie Huber, South Dakota Searchlight 

PIERRE — South Dakota Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds said he wants to “get the facts” before deciding whether any medals awarded to soldiers who were at the 1890 Wounded Knee Massacre should be rescinded, while his opponent said the medals “should not stand.”

Independent candidate Brian Bengs is Rounds’ only challenger in the Nov. 3 election after the Democratic nominee withdrew. Bengs served 26 years in the U.S. military and taught at the NATO School in Germany and the U.S. Air Force Academy, including courses on the law of war.

“And I will say categorically: Those medals are not earned. They are not deserved. They should not stand,” Bengs said. “Their continuing standing is a dishonor to the individuals who currently hold the Medal of Honor.”

Bengs spoke to South Dakota Searchlight for a recent episode of its Searchlight Report podcast, after Searchlight interviewed Rounds for an earlier episode.

Rounds is a member of the Senate Armed Services Committee. In a recent report about the pending National Defense Authorization Act, the committee included language directing the secretary of defense to “provide the full report and unredacted materials” from a recent review of the Wounded Knee medals.

In September, Secretary Pete Hegseth announced that a review ordered during President Joe Biden’s administration had been completed and the medals would not be rescinded. The department has said about 20 soldiers were awarded the Medal of Honor for actions at Wounded Knee, though the exact number is unclear due to incomplete or unclear records.

Rounds said he and other committee members are responding to survivors’ descendants who want more information.

“There’s a lot of people in South Dakota that live on the reservations that have relatives that were wounded or killed during that massacre that occurred in December of 1890,” Rounds said. “Those people still feel strongly about the loss to their families.”

Rounds said he ultimately wants the military to decide about the medals, “rather than having Congress get in the middle of it.” Multiple attempts to pass congressional legislation rescinding the medals have failed, with neither Rounds nor any other member of the state’s congressional delegation signing on as sponsors or cosponsors.

“Under the conditions at that time, there may very well have been the delivery or the awarding of those Medals of Honor appropriately, but there may also have been other areas where they may not have been,” Rounds said. “But rather than arbitrarily saying we support it or we don’t support it, let’s get the facts.”

The massacre occurred on Dec. 29, 1890, near Wounded Knee Creek in southwestern South Dakota, where a large group of Lakota people camped while traveling to the Pine Ridge Agency. They were surrounded by hundreds of Army soldiers. A shot rang out while the soldiers attempted to disarm the camp, and the soldiers opened fire.

Fewer than 40 soldiers were killed (some by friendly fire, according to historians), while estimates of Lakota deaths are 200 or more, including men, women and children. After some of the bodies froze on the ground for several days, a military-led burial party placed them in a mass grave.

The Department of Defense created a 5-member panel to review the medals in 2024.

In a redacted report obtained by South Dakota Searchlight, the panel’s Defense-appointed chairman wrote, “While the actions of leadership were suspect, circumstances chaotic, and non-combatants tragically killed, three of the five panel members believe that individual soldiers distinguished themselves in action and found no disqualifying information.”

title: Northern Hills Diversion marks another year of community repair, teen volunteer opportunities
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Northern Hills Diversion, also known as Teen Court, marked another successful year of diverting local youths from the criminal justice system. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
Northern Hills Diversion.jpg
Northern Hills Diversion, also known as Teen Court, marked another successful year of diverting local youths from the criminal justice system. Pioneer file photo 

DEADWOOD — Northern Hills Diversion marked another successful year of diverting local youths from the criminal justice system after Lawrence County agreed to grant the program another round of the Juvenile Justice Reinvestment Initiative (JJRI) grant. 

The purpose of the JJRI grant is to incentivize counties to divert youth out of the court system,” said Lexi Lux, executive director of Northern Hills Diversion. “So, for every successful completion that the county has in a diversion program, the county is reimbursed $750 per successful completion.”

Lux said at its core, “Northern Hills Diversion is a justice program designed to help at-risk and justice-involved youth repair the harm caused by their behaviors to their communities.”

“The ultimate goal of our program is for youth that have been accused of a criminal offense to take responsibility for their choices and to give back to their communities,” she said. 

Lux said youth accused of crimes, typically misdemeanors, are put through a court system that is run by their peers along with case management and informal probation managed by Lux’s team. 

“They meet with their case manager on a weekly basis and their consequences are decided by the youth, their guardian, the state’s attorney’s office if they so choose, and the case manager,” said Lux. “It’s just a little bit different as far as how the sentence comes about, the consequences come about.”

Lux said the program also serves youths on conditional release from the juvenile detention system in Rapid City who could be facing more serious charges. 

“The youth that are placed on conditional release are still given the opportunity to participate in teen court as jury members, they just don’t have their consequences determined by teen court,” she said. “Typically, it’s because they’re more serious offenses, like felonies, or it is something that is inappropriate for teen court purposes. The example I like to use is sexting (texting sexually explicit photos) — I will never put a kid through teen court to talk about how they were sexting.”

Lux said in order to successfully complete the program, all youths must complete a “choices class.” The classes are designed to help the children understand how their brains are developing, and how that development can sometimes encourage them to make decisions without thinking about long-term consequences.

“Then they learn about what they can do to help them kind of override that gap,” she said. “We have 2 other in-person classes, one is called ‘Law and You,’ and the other one is called ‘Growth Mindset.’”

Lux said children facing traffic offenses complete ‘Alive at 25,’ a class taught in collaboration with the South Dakota Safety Council.

“It is designed to help teach young drivers about safety when driving a motor vehicle, and we teach that one Saturday a month up here in Deadwood,” she said. “It is the only Alive at 25 class that is offered outside of Sioux Falls in South Dakota.”

Lux said the class is available to any driver under the age of 25. 

Program success

In 2025, Lux said the program had 144 referrals of youth to the program. In 2026, she said the program has handled 85 referrals so far. 

“Fall is our busiest time of year,” she said. “When kids go back to school and start connecting with people they haven’t seen in a while, or frankly just getting caught because they’re at school. We’ll usually see a pretty big influx of cases by about October.”

Lux said in 2025, the program maintained a 93% successful completion rate. Of those successful children, she the program has a 19% recidivism rate in the first 12 months, and 15% in the first 6 months.

“So, what the numbers are really showing us is that if you can make it to take 6-month mark without committing another offense, then you are less likely to commit future offenses,” she said. “That is a higher recidivism rate than we’re used to. However, I think a lot of that can be put down to the type of cases that we’re seeing nowadays.”

Lux said the majority of the cases referred to the program are substance abuse related — alcohol and drug offenses, primarily related to marijuana. In 2025, however, she said her program saw a spike in assault charges. 

“Most of our assault charges were placed on the conditional release program, which is designed to keep kids who are not at risk to their community outside of the juvenile services center in Rapid City,” she said. “So, using the assaults as an example, yes, they committed an assault, but they’re separated from whoever their victim was and they’re not likely to commit another crime within the community.”

Lux said her program was able to increase the number of higher-need cases they took on this year with the upgrade from 2 full-time staff and one part-time staff members to 3 full-time staff members. 

“The staff I have working for me, they do such a wonderful job working directly with the kids, and they have the time and the ability to get to know the kids, get to know the families, their unique situations, and really help give them the framework for success,” she said. 

Lux said the program saw an increase in teen volunteers this year, primarily from Sturgis Brown High School and Lead-Deadwood High School.

Teens are sentenced to community service by their peers as a part of their consequence. Lux said in 2025, the kids served approximately 8,900 hours collectively of community service.

Fundraising efforts

Historically, the program has received $120,000 annually from the Juvenile Detention Alternative Initiative. In 2025, the grant amount was reduced to $52,500. 

“That was expected. However, it’s still concerning when those things happen,” said Lux. “But we also understand that that’s part of the process and part of making sure that there is funding available for other programs that need it for other newer diversion programs.”

To close the gap of funding, Lux said her team and teen volunteers have been busy with grassroots fundraising efforts. Over the summer the team did walking taco fundraisers, and the city of Sturgis allowed the program to host a photo booth during Sturgis Motorcycle Rally.

Lux said the program’s annual golf tournament is scheduled for Sept. 18 and is still selling tickets and taking donations. 

“As far as fundraising efforts beyond that, I’m always looking for grants and applying for different grants,” she said. “I try to stick to more state and local grants, just because the money is staying locally. For me, the big thing is staying away from mission creep. I want to make sure we’re continuing to provide excellent services to the youth that we serve and the communities that we serve. I don’t want to broaden beyond that and get to where we can’t meet the needs of the people that our organization was formed to help.”

For more information about Northern Hills Diversion, including inquiring towards volunteer opportunities, to purchase a ticket for the golf tournament, or to make a donation, please call (605) 722-8889.

title: Yellowstone’s ‘thumping’ hot springs
byline: By Michael Poland USGS
description: Black Sand Pool, in Yellowstone National Park’s Upper Geyser Basin. The hot spring is known for it’s thumping behavior, which occurs every few minutes due to collapse of bubbles within the spring. The thumping is strong enough to be heard and felt by anyone nearby. USGS photo by Mike Poland
_full_text:
Yellowstone.jpg
Black Sand Pool, in Yellowstone National Park’s Upper Geyser Basin. The hot spring is known for it’s thumping behavior, which occurs every few minutes due to collapse of bubbles within the spring. The thumping is strong enough to be heard and felt by anyone nearby. USGS photo by Mike Poland 

Yellowstone National Park is rightly famous for spectacular geysers. It also has hot springs that create thumps you can hear and feel.

Black Sand Pool, in Yellowstone National Park’s Upper Geyser Basin (near Old Faithful), is a hidden gem.  Although it is not far from a road and is very accessible via an easy trail, few people visit the hot spring.  Those that make the short walk and stay a few minutes are rewarded with a special treat—every several minutes the pool starts to thump, and it is strong enough to feel and hear. It’s as if a giant in an underground cavern is striking the cavern’s ceiling with a hammer.

Another famous “thumper” is Doublet Pool on Geyser Hill, also in Upper Geyser Basin.  The thumping at Doublet Pool varies over time, lasting up to a few minutes with intervening quiet times that have varied between 13 and 35 minutes in recent years.  The thumping is so strong that you can see the water in the spring “jump.”

One of best places in Yellowstone National Park to see this process in action is Firehole Spring, which is along Firehole Lake Drive in Lower Geyser Basin.  This small one-way side road off the main highway is often closed due to bear management and also poor road conditions (the road lies on very hot ground and so the asphalt tends to melt), but when it is open, Firehole Spring is along the north side of the road just before Great Fountain Geyser.  The spring’s water is very clear, providing a view of bubbles that rise from the vent at the bottom of the pool.  The bubbles often collapse as they rise, creating an audible “thump” as they implode.

Many other hot springs in Yellowstone also thump — for example, pools in Norris Geyser Basin.  But what causes this activity?

The collapse of the bubbles is due to the variable temperature and pressure conditions within the hot springs. As bubbles rise within a thermal pool, their volumes increase and internal pressures decrease.  At the same time, the cooler temperatures near the tops of the pools cause the steam in the bubbles to condense back into liquid water, and this, combined with the decreasing internal pressure, causes the bubbles to implode. If the bubbles are large enough, the thump can be felt.  The components for thumping are not that common, which explains why only a few hot springs in Yellowstone demonstrate that behavior.

Scientists investigated the thumping at Doublet Pool by deploying seismometers around the area to record how the thumping changes with time. They found a number of interesting correlations.  For example, when strong winds blew, the time between thumping was longer than on calm days. This is because the wind cooled the pool by removing heat from the surface.  There were also changes that corresponded to activity at nearby features.  In September 2018, Ear Spring, a short distance from Double Pool, erupted for the first time in decades. At that time, the interval between thumping periods at Doublet Pool was only about 13 minutes—a very short time period that may have been due to an overall increase in thermal input to Geyser Hill.

That the rate of thumping seems to change due to heat input indicates that monitoring the thumping interval could be a useful way to track hydrothermal activity in a region. For instance, if interval between thumping at Doublet Pool suddenly starts to decrease, it might be a sign of deeper variations in heat input that could impact other thermal features in the region, perhaps even leading to the formation of new thermal features as occurred in 2023.

If you have a chance to visit Yellowstone National Park, be sure to check out one of the thumping springs—Doublet Pool, Black Sand Pool, and Firehole Spring are easily accessible. You can literally hear and feel the changes that are happening in one of the most spectacular hydrothermal systems on Earth.

Michael Poland, geophysicist with the U.S. Geological Survey and scientist-in-charge of the Yellowstone Volcano Observatory.

title: Plan to import cheap beef ‘devastating’ to local ranchers
byline: By Mark Watson and Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Sale days at the St. Onge Livestock Auction are on Fridays, but following 2 actions by the Trump Administration, local ranchers are seeing less in their sale checks. Pioneer photo by Mark Watson
_full_text:
Plan to import cheap beef ‘devastating’ to local ranchers COVER.JPG
Sale days at the St. Onge Livestock Auction are on Fridays, but following 2 actions by the Trump Administration, local ranchers are seeing less in their sale checks. Pioneer photo by Mark Watson 

ST. ONGE — Along with the sing-song chant of the auctioneer at the St. Onge Livestock Auction Aug. 21, was the talk among cattle producers of how presidential action will affect their bottom line. And the news was not rosy.

One week earlier, President Donald Trump announced that he would roll back tariffs and import 300,000 metric tons of ground beef to be sold at below-market prices for the next 90 days. The clock started this Tuesday. Days after Trump announced the tariff rollback, the U.S. reopened the Southern Border to Mexican cattle. The border had been closed to cattle imports in response to the new world screwworm, a parasite with flesh-eating larvae that can infest and even kill cattle or other animals.

“It was pretty devastating,” said Whitewood rancher Ted Thompson who was at the auction buying yearlings. “It took quite a little money off the cattle. It took money off the fat cattle. It took money off the feeder cattle. A lot of these guys that have yearlings they are selling right now, they probably ain’t worth it. The same on the fat cattle deal, they’re losing money big time on these.”

 Plan to import cheap beef ‘devastating’ to local ranchers 2.JPG
In 2 weeks, the price of feeder cattle dropped around $20 per 100 pounds while the price of live cattle dropped at least $10 per 100 pounds. When you consider an animal that weighs 1,500 pounds, that’s $150 or $200 per animal less that ranchers are making. Pioneer photo by Mark Watson 

Mark Robin, a rancher and feedlot operator from Lemmon, can attest.

“We’re already selling at a $300 or $400 a head loss,” Robin said. 

He acknowledged that prices are better than they were 2 years ago and are comparable to 2025 numbers; however, the expenses of growing those cattle have vastly outpaced the profits.

“Everything has gone way up,” Thompson said. “You know all our expenses, diesel fuel’s higher, gas is higher, repairs are higher. You know everything we do now. This year we’re so short on feed in this country in a pretty big area. Feed is double what it should cost.”

Cattle terms
Bull: A male bovine with testicles intact. 
 Calves: Young cattle of either sex, less than one year of age.
 Cow: Female cattle that have produced one or more calves.
 Heifers: Female cattle under 2 years of age, that have not calved.
 Steers: Male cattle that are castrated before reaching sexual maturity.
 Yearling: Heifer steer or bull between one and two years old.
 Finished: A term indicating the animal is sufficiently fattened and grown out for slaughter.
 Finishing: The phase of cattle production where cattle are fed high-concentrate diets to fatten them before slaughter.
 Feeder cattle: Younger, lighter weight (approximately 500-850 pounds) animals, steers or heifers, that are ready to be sold to other operations for fattening or finishing, typically at a feedlot.
 Fat cattle: Cattle that are being fed a higher concentration of feed to achieve the desired weight gain (approximately 850-1,400 pounds) to consider them as “finished.” Finished cattle are ready for sale to a packer that will then process and package them for consumption.
 CWT (hundredweight) – is a unit of weight used to price and sell livestock. Pricing for cattle is calculated by dividing the total weight of the animal(s) in pounds by 100, to get the hundredweight. Then that number is multiplied by the price per CWT.
 Example: 800-pound steer sells for $330 CWT. (800 ÷ 100) x $330 = $2,640.00

According to AAA, the price of diesel fuel has increased 54% from a year ago. According to the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, on July 1, regular gasoline was 25.3% more than July 1, 2025. Vehicle maintenance and servicing increased 6.6% in the year. Vehicle repair costs grew by 6.2%. Veterinarian costs increased 4.7%. 

Thompson said that because of the extreme drought conditions in the area, hay prices have doubled from 2025. He said he is paying about $250 a ton compared to $110-$120 a ton last year. And water has to be trucked in rather than herds drinking from stock ponds.

“I’ve got neighbors that are hauling 2 or 3 semi loads a day, putting in their water source. Some have storage tanks that they’re putting it in to supplement their pipelines. Even some of them are out of water.

“We have a ranch out in Wyoming, and the Belle Fourche River runs through it,” he continued. “If it wasn’t for the river, we would have zero water. All the dams are dry. We’re seeing wells north of Newell, big, deep wells, that just ain’t producing. Some of them guys … they’re going to town and getting semi loads of water.”

Trump said he signed the orders in an effort to bring down the cost of beef at the grocery store. 

“I’ve already, in this business, almost lost my retirement,” Robin said. “What I kind of see right now, is that people my age and older, we are going to jump out and quit. It is going to stop the cow (herd) rebuilding. I don’t know where Trump gets his info, but it ain’t good. I don’t know where he is getting his info, but he shouldn’t be hurting the very people that helped him.”

The U.S. Cattlemen’s Association denounced Trump’s announcement. When he signed the order they responded again, saying that his “quick fix” will likely not provide relief at the grocery store, and instead will hurt the ranchers.

“We very much disagree with the president in this case. Bringing in 300,000 metric tons of hamburger at a supposed discounted price does not mean that it will be cheaper to the consumer,” said Justin Tupper, owner of the St. Onge Livestock Auction and president of the U.S. Cattlemen’s Association. “That has to go through the importer, from the importer to the retailer and from the retailer to the consumer. There is no guarantee that those prices will be cheaper.”

The negative impact of Trump’s announcement came swiftly for ranchers. 

Thompson said prices dropped around $20 per 100 pounds on feeder cattle and at least $10 per 100 pounds on live cattle compared to just 2 weeks ago.

And that loss in revenue adds up quickly.

“Take that times 1,500 pounds. That’s $150 or $200 a head,” he said. 

 Plan to import cheap beef ‘devastating’ to local ranchers 3.JPG
The St. Onge Livestock Auction, and other sale barns around the country are a hub of cattle sales. Pioneer photo by Mark Watson 

Trump, taking negative feedback from members of Congress of both parties as well as the livestock industry, then announced on Aug. 28 that soon farmers and ranchers would have a right to “process their own food.”

The South Dakota Cattlemen’s Association spoke against his announcement stating, “President Trump’s latest announcement is not a serious plan to strengthen America’s beef supply chain. It is a distraction from an import policy the cattle industry overwhelmingly rejected.”

“Farmers and ranchers may already process livestock for their own use. What producers cannot do is sell uninspected meat into commercial markets. That distinction protects consumers and preserves confidence in American beef,” according to the statement. “SDCA supports more inspected small and regional processors, more competition, and more opportunities for producers. We do not support weakening food safety standards.

“Food safety is NOT red tape. Consumer confidence is NOT optional,” the statement continued. “America established federal meat inspection more than a century ago because unsafe and unsanitary processing conditions threatened public health and trust. Following serious E. coli outbreaks in the 1990s, government and industry strengthened pathogen prevention and food safety controls. Those safeguards have been essential to rebuilding consumer confidence and protecting demand for American beef. Weakening them risks both public health and the market every cattle producer depends on.”

Thompson noted his concerns.

“How are they inspecting it,” he questioned of the cheap imported beef. “How can they bring that many pounds of ground product in and get it through the channels and get it inspected?”

 Plan to import cheap beef ‘devastating’ to local ranchers 4.jpeg
The board at sale barns are closely watched as it shows the number of animals for sale in a lot, the total and average weight, and price per hundred weight or CWT. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

He said he was not too concerned with the new world screwworm since there are medicines to treat any animal that may become infected. 

“The best thing we could have is a freeze (in temperature), but they’re releasing all those sterile flies, and they’ll get a handle on it,” he said. “But with the wormers and stuff that we use and the treatments we use, it ain’t like the old days.”

Efforts have been underway to introduce sterile male screwworm flies into the existing population in Mexico and Central America. The sterile males breed with the females, who are only able to mate once during their life span, and effectively eliminate the ability for the fly to lay eggs in an animal host. 

“That effectively stops things in their tracks,” said Russ Daly, an SDSU Extension veterinarian. “When this was geographically confined to a really narrow part of the continent, in Panama, it was easy to do that, to flood the area with these sterile flies. Now the geographic area has gotten so big, we just need so many more of these flies. That is the worry, that we wouldn’t have enough of these sterile flies to saturate the area if they get established closer to the United States.”

 Plan to import cheap beef ‘devastating’ to local ranchers 5.jpeg
Livestock producers say the announcement by President Donald Trump that 300,000 metric tons of ground beef would be imported without tariffs and sold below market value will do little at the grocery store but is devastating to their livelihood. Pioneer photo by Sierra Ferguson 

Thompson has a bigger concern than screwworms.

“I’m more concerned about bringing in this beef, and who knows what it is, and not identifying the product,” Thompson said. “They mix it with U.S. beef, and they want to sell cheap. That’s fine. Label it.”

Country of origin labeling is critical, he said. 

“That’s the no-brainer to me,” he said. “Then people have a choice. We have to label a bottle of ketchup, what’s in it, and where it comes from. The packers have fought it, you know, because it supposedly costs them money.”

There are 4 major packers, 3 of them are foreign owned, explained Tupper, who also wants country of origin labeling. 

“We’ve worked hard on trying to get country of origin labeling. It did get put into the farm bill, but the farm bill ultimately has not passed yet,” Tupper said. “It still has a chance here in September, but we would love to see that and I think the same notions apply there. 

“That doesn’t necessarily make U.S. beef higher, but the consumer can differentiate what he wants to buy — whether it would be beef from Argentina or if it’s a mix of beef from all of the places,” he added. “However it is labeled, the consumer would be able to choose.” 

He said it is primarily a food-safety matter.

“All of those countries that we are going to import that beef from, they do not have the same safety practices that we have. They don’t use the same standards we do with regard to animal wellbeing or any of the things,” Tupper said. “Many have been known forced labor users, they’ve been known (to contribute to) deforestation, so for lots of reasons not just because the market is lower.

 Plan to import cheap beef ‘devastating’ to local ranchers 6.JPG
Pioneer photo by Mark Watson 

“We understand the markets. We want free and fair markets. We just don’t want them to have intervention in them,” he added. “By the president dumping 300,000 metric ton into our market, devaluing our safest, best protein on the planet that we raise here — U.S. beef — we just think that is a real problematic thing.”

Thompson also said the dumping is detrimental to the system and ranchers. 

“It’s a big deal. If we keep putting people out of business, they’ll find out how cheap food really is,” he said. “We have the safest, cheapest food percentage of income that there is in the world. There are some countries in the world where they spend 80%- 90% of their income just to eat, and we don’t. We have a very safe product, and it’s cheap compared to everywhere else in the world.”

title: Road improvements to shooting  complex cost GF&P $492K
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: The South Dakota Department of Game, Fish, and Parks paid nearly $500,000 to improve a 3-mile section of Elk Vale Road and Bill Janklow Road, to access the Pete Lien & Sons Shooting Complex. Pioneer file photo
_full_text:
0614 shooting complexRGB).tif
The South Dakota Department of Game, Fish, and Parks paid nearly $500,000 to improve a 3-mile section of Elk Vale Road and Bill Janklow Road, to access the Pete Lien & Sons Shooting Complex. Pioneer file photo 

STURGIS — Road improvements to access the Pete Lien & Sons Shooting Sports Complex cost the state nearly $500,000. 

On Tuesday the Meade County Commission approved a final cost agreement with the South Dakota Department of Game, Fish, and Parks, for improvements made to Elk Vale and Bill Janklow roads. Meade County Highway Superintendent Troy Eastman said the state paid 100% of the material costs to add gravel and base stabilization to 3 miles of Elk Vale Road, and some otta seal paving to a short section of Bill Janklow Road that accesses the new state shooting range. 

Otta seal is a type of bituminous surface treatment that is named for the location where it was developed, in Otta Valley, Norway. Originally developed as a temporary surface for roadways, it has been used for more permanent roads due to its strength. 

The total cost for work in 2025 and 2026 was $492,060. The costs include $140,746 for gravel and base stabilization in 2025, and $351,314 in gravel and otta seal paving in 2026. 

Meade County Auditor Dawn Christenson noted that the GF&P has paid $140,000 toward the bill already. 

In June 2025, the GF&P agreed to pay for the materials for improvements to Elk Vale Road, from Elk Creek Road to the Pete Lien and Sons Shooting Complex, as part of the deal for the shooting range construction. At the time, the value of the base coarse stabilization and gravel was $400,000, but over the last year those costs have increased. 

“This was slated to be done in 2024,” Meade County Commissioner Rich Liggett said. “2025 rolled through and we didn’t get it completed. GF&P has been working with us on this. They had money approved a year and a half ago on this project. The numbers worked at that time and they’ve been pushing it through.” 

According to the 5-year agreement, Meade County will perform routine maintenance on the new roadway. Non routine maintenance costs related to weather events, heavy use, or unforeseen conditions will be borne by GF&P as funding allows.

title: Harvest Fest returns to Spearfish Sept. 12
byline: By Neil Whitney Black Hills Pioneer
description: Harvest Fest returns to Spearfish Sept. 12. Pioneer file photos
_full_text:
Harvest Fest 1.JPG
Harvest Fest returns to Spearfish Sept. 12. Pioneer file photos 

 Harvest Fest 2.JPG
Harvest Fest returns to Spearfish Sept. 12. Pioneer file photos 

SPEARFISH — Every year around mid-September, an annual gathering of fall festivities takes place on Main Street between Hudson and Jackson Street.

This year it’s being put on by Visit Spearfish from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., on Sept. 12.

In the past, it had been called Harvest Fest, but after some time, they changed it to Autumn Fest. The festival itself stayed the same, and this stylistic choice continued for about 7 years. 

Now, they are going back to the name Harvest Fest with a new mindset and different events. This year, Harvest Fest is bringing a more “fair-like” atmosphere to Spearfish and the community. To Phoebe Caldwell, director of marketing for Visit Spearfish, it’s just what a place like Spearfish needs. 

“Our hope is just bringing back that more family-oriented event and bringing the harvest part of it to amplify the produce vendors,” Caldwell said, referring to the Neighbors 2 Neighbors Farmers Market at Lions Park that coincides with the festival.

The fair-like activities that are taking place this year are made to be more interactive than ones in the past. This year, The Western Hills Humane Society will be doing a “collar-toss” similar to a ring toss that you might see at carnivals and other fairs. There will also be a highland cow for kids to pet and take pictures with. Other photo opportunities that people and kids will have include a horse and carriage that will be brought by the Spearfish Museum.

Throughout the life of Harvest Fest, while it’s gone by different names, it used to be run by the Downtown Business Association (DBA). DBA and Visit Spearfish are frequent collaborators, and now that Visit Spearfish is involved, the event has become bigger while still hoping to keep people driven to go to the downtown businesses.

“Downtown Business Association used to run it all. Now both the DBA and Visit Spearfish are responsible for the Harvest Fest … we hope that as they’re participating in our fair stuff, they still bop down to the downtown businesses and go shopping,” Caldwell said. 

Visit Spearfish wants to make a good family friendly time for the community, but they also want spearfish to be appealing to tourists and visitors. The non-profit organization prides itself on marketing Spearfish as a destination for outsiders.

“We hope that you can make a day trip out of different things to do. And it just seems like it’s a good kickstart, you start seeing the leaves change and everything like that,” Caldwell said.

title: Spearfish PD wants to invest in a drone program
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Butte County Sheriff’s Office drone, pictured, has been a “great asset” said Sheriff Fred Lamphere. Photo courtesy Butte County Chief Deputy Jason March
_full_text:
Butte County Drone alt.JPEG
The Butte County Sheriff’s Office drone, pictured, has been a “great asset” said Sheriff Fred Lamphere. Photo courtesy Butte County Chief Deputy Jason March 

SPEARFISH — The Butte County Sheriff’s Office launched its drone program last year, and Sheriff Fred Lamphere said it’s been “a great asset.” Now, Spearfish would like to buy a drone as well — calling it a “strategic investment” in public safety.

During a budget presentation to the city council, Spearfish Police Chief Collin Smith said the drone the department would like to purchase would cost between $16,910 and $19,326.92 before warranties.

“What we are asking for is an addition of $15,000 (to the police department budget) to help with the drone purchase,” Smith said. “The reason you’re seeing such a high number is that it is not like you can go on to Amazon and just buy whatever drone you want. We are heavily regulated by the American Security Drone Act that states we can only purchase American-made drones, and we can only purchase drones on what is called the ‘blue list.’ That significantly limits what drones are available to law enforcement, both federal and state, and the costs of those, of the machine equipment went up significantly as of December 2025.”

The $16,910 package includes the Parrot ANAFI UKR drone the police would like to purchase, a controller, battery, battery charger, a hard case and landing pad.

Lamphere said the drone in Butte County has already needed to have a propeller replaced because of field damage.

Replacement propellers for the Parrot ANAFI UKR drone the Spearfish Police Department would like to purchase could cost $200, based on prices provided to the city council. If Spearfish purchases the most expensive package, at $19,326.94, extra propellers will be included — along with online training for $299, a 128-gigabyte SD card for $59.99, an additional XLR Battery for $1,160, and the Parrot ANAFI UKR kit.

The city council has not formally approved the police department budget yet.

“A drone program has been considered for many years,” Smith said. “Now that the federal regulations, such as the drone “blue list”, have come into focus, we are now comfortable that the regulations have become stable and the program can be successful. To add, costs will continue to rise; therefore, purchasing in 2027 will prevent drone prices from becoming unattainable for our department.”

Spearfish has a sworn police officer, Adam Scanlan, who is a licensed drone pilot, on staff.

“He was a drone pilot in Nebraska at his previous agency,” Smith said. “It’s actually been very beneficial having an officer who was a drone pilot for a different agency. He knows what the Fourth Amendment restrictions are. We are aware of the FAA requirements for this drone.

Pull quote
 “We’ve used it for officer safety when we have had to implement search warrants. We can activate it and keep an eye overhead on human activity when we’re doing a high-risk search warrant.” — Butte County Sheriff Fred Lamphere

The purpose of it for us is things like missing persons, search and rescue, crime scene mapping, officer safety, dangerous suspects.”

That’s not dissimilar to the Butte County Sheriff’s office either.

“We have been talking about a drone. My chief deputy, Jason March, had had some prior experience with them. We talked about the benefits and what they would be, because overall we are a pretty small agency,” Lamphere said.

When the department secured grant funding to buy its drone, the sheriff said he had just 5 full-time deputies.

“We are a pretty big area and probably have only one or 2 (deputies) on sometimes,” Lamphere said.

Eyes in the sky could help fill in the gaps — and improve officer safety.

“We’ve used it for officer safety when we have had to implement search warrants. We can activate it and keep an eye overhead on human activity when we’re doing a high-risk search warrant,” Lamphere said.

Lamphere said he takes privacy very seriously — that’s why they’re used when a warrant has already been issued.

“I think the biggest role, and I really take it to heart, is protecting people’s rights as the sheriff. We are very cognizant of that. There are some pretty hard-set rules, and you have to follow them. I really commend my chief deputy and another deputy who are our drone operators. They are very aware of that when things go,” Lamphere said. “We have to have a reason, and we have to have probable cause to implement the drone. We can’t just go searching.”

Law enforcement drones are subject to regulation and restrictions to protect citizen privacy.

The device Spearfish would like to purchase, for example, will offer “full data sovereignty,” according to specs presented to the city council. No data will be shared with third parties or outside agencies by default.

“The department will ensure that drone operations do not circumvent Fourth Amendment protections. If the drone is being used in a manner that itself constitutes a search, officers must have the appropriate legal authority, such as a warrant or a recognized exception to the warrant requirement,” Smith said. “A drone does not give officers greater search authority simply because it can observe an area from the air.”

The drones Spearfish is looking at are equipped with infrared technology — like the one in Butte County. Lamphere said search and rescue was a big reason why the department wanted a drone in the first place.

“The drone program has been useful with our reservoir and for emergency calls out there: stranded boats in distress, and we’ve got some remote big walk-in areas for hunting,” Lamphere said. Infrared technology can help search-and-rescue crews find people in remote areas.

“We’ve used it even at nighttime, looking for people also following fires; if you got some heat detection capabilities, you can utilize that,” Lamphere said. “Getting eyes out there when you’re doing a lot of searching, especially up in rough canyons and things. If you’re either looking for people, or wildfire, or whatever, it is a great tool to cover a lot of country very efficiently.”

The drone the police department would like to purchase can operate in extreme cold and heat — between -32.8 degrees and 122 degrees Fahrenheit. It is equipped with a 21-megapixel wide-angle camera and zoom capabilities that can detect objects up to 1,100 meters away.

Spearfish may not have a large reservoir, where it makes sense to fly over the water and find a boat in distress. It does, however, have car accidents that might benefit from the information overhead photographs can provide, Smith said.

“If there is a major accident, this can go up in the air and give us a mapping of this accident. Major crime scenes that can maybe travel multiple blocks. This drone can help us map it,” Smith said. “One thing that we really thought of was the flood — how beneficial it would have been to go and put a drone in the sky to get a lay of the land instead of having officers and other first responders up to their shoulders in water. That is the purpose of this drone: for extreme measures in the sense of danger to the public, missing persons, search and rescue, disaster response, things of that nature.”

Mayor John Senden said that perhaps Spearfish was behind the curve in adopting the technology.

“It makes sense moving technology to that next step that we are probably a little behind on,” Senden said.

title: Communities split on automatic license plate readers (Flock cameras)
byline: By Molly Wetsch South Dakota News Watch
description: Some local law enforcement agencies in South Dakota are pulling back on the use of Flock cameras, and the state attorney general is drafting legislation that would put limits on their use in the state.
_full_text:
SDNewsWatchLogo

Some local law enforcement agencies in South Dakota are pulling back on the use of Flock cameras, and the state attorney general is drafting legislation that would put limits on their use in the state.

The cameras, formally known as automatic license plate readers (ALPR), have drawn the ire of people concerned about privacy, largely because the Flock company shares data about vehicles nationally. 

The legislation would be the first of its kind in the state. And it would add South Dakota to a small group of states with laws dictating how the ALPR technology can be used by police departments and other organizations. 

In a conversation with News Watch, Attorney General Marty Jackley, the Republican candidate for U.S. House, compared the potential legislation to the state’s prescription drug monitoring program. That program is a state-operated database that tracks the prescription and distribution of controlled substances in the state.

“We haven’t had any abuses of that (prescription drug program), and I think it’s because we have strong safeguards in place,” Jackley said.

But what are automatic license plate readers, and how do they actually affect South Dakotans? News Watch answered a few common questions about the technology:

What are automatic license plate readers?

Automatic license plate readers are forms of technology used most often by law enforcement to identify vehicle makes, models and license plate information. New technology can also identify specific features like toolboxes, bike racks or bumper stickers.

The Department of Homeland Security says the cameras have been used by law enforcement for “well over 2 decades.” 

While the ability for cameras to read license plates has been around for some time, the advancement of both artificial intelligence and camera quality has allowed for the widespread, affordable dissemination of the technology, according to DHS. 

Flock Safety, a Georgia-based company that was founded in 2017, is one of the largest providers of the technology. It’s also receiving the most criticism because Flock’s national database allows for sharing of information among jurisdictions and across state lines. That’s different from other companies like Axon, which typically keep data on local servers. 

Flock says its national database means vehicles that may have been reported stolen in other states or are on national hotlists can be identified across jurisdictional borders.

But such data-sharing has raised concerns about federal overreach or security issues, though the company said last month it does not collaborate with federal agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

“Flock does not share customer data on behalf of customers with any entity, federal or otherwise, without their permission and does not grant access to customer data without a customer’s explicit choice and control,” the company said in a statement. 

Are ALPR cameras used in South Dakota?

Yes. Madison became the first city to use the technology when the city’s police department deployed Flock cameras in 2022. Now, there are 29 cameras in the city. 

The Sioux Falls Police Department uses 34 Flock cameras around the city, which it began installing in June 2025. The department formalized a $168,000 contract with the security company in January 2025.

ALPRs are also present in other areas around the state, including in Rapid City, where the city’s police department currently operates four Axon cameras. DeFlock uses crowdsourced data to identify ALPRs across the country, and its South Dakota map displays dozens across the state.

Recently, Aberdeen residents overwhelmingly decried the city’s hopes to discuss the use of license plate reader cameras in a city council meeting. A Facebook post from Mayor Travis Schaunaman garnered over a thousand comments as of Aug. 24. In that post, he asked residents their thoughts on the technology.

Schaunaman later clarified that due to the feedback, the Aberdeen City Council would not be going forward with the discussion and that Flock cameras would not be placed in the city. 

“For Aberdeen, this issue is settled,” he said.

Aberdeen is not the only city to pull back its consideration of the technology. 

All of the Flock cameras in Codington County have been temporarily removed due to vandalism, Codington County Sheriff Brad Howell said during an Aug. 25 commission meeting. Those cameras were placed throughout the county, and mostly assisted in stolen vehicle cases, he said.

How are Flock cameras used?

In some cities across the state, including Sioux Falls and Madison, data from ALPR cameras can only be stored for 30 days under city policy. 

According to the Sioux Falls Police Department’s Flock Transparency Portal, the only data that is detected from Flock cameras in the city are license plates and vehicle models. Facial recognition data is not detected and it is prohibited to use data for immigration enforcement, harassment, or intimidation or personal use.

The portal also shows that in the past 30 days, SFPD made 464 searches of the Flock camera system and detected 550,146 unique license plates. 

In Madison, there have been 17 searches of the system in the past 30 days and 59,401 unique license plates were detected. 

Sioux Falls Chief of Police Jon Thum told News Watch that the city has also made its policy surrounding the technology public, which includes that data cannot be stored for more than 30 days and cannot be used to enforce speeding, red light or parking violations. 

The technology has assisted in recent cases involving violent crimes in Sioux Falls, including in the arrest of a suspect in a recent shooting case, he said.

“In the series of basically 5 minutes of searching and refining and working through this process, we were able to identify the shooter’s vehicle. And then within 10 minutes, passing that information onto our patrol officers, we found the vehicle and conducted the necessary follow-up,” Thum said. “I mean, this is the efficiency of this piece at work on a case where we likely never would have been able to find that vehicle.”

On Sept. 1, Jackley also credited ALPRs in the arrest of a suspect near Plankinton who abducted a 15-year-old girl, after the state’s Internet Crimes Against Children Task Force was notified that Wyoming law enforcement was searching for a vehicle involved in the abduction. 

“This incident demonstrates how valuable technology can be in protecting the public and assisting officers to locate a vulnerable juvenile and bring her to safety within an hour,” Jackley said in a press release.  

Thum said that the city intentionally made its policy on the technology public and maintains the Flock Transparency Portal – which is optional for cities to participate in – because of the potential for resident concern.

“We wanted to be so palms-up on what we were doing. We want the transparency portal because we already told you we’re doing this, and this is one more layer,” Thum said. “Our policy regarding the usage of this, we immediately made forward-facing and public. Because that’s just part of good implementation of technology, in this regard, is to be transparent about it.”

But he also said that he would welcome statewide legislation on the technology and understands that not all law enforcement technology is right for every community.

“The catalyst for using technology should not be because you’re behind or not be because you’ve had a tragedy, a kidnapping or something like that. It should be because you’ve found the right way to optimize it for your community, with best practices, and do it in a way to serve the public,” Thum said.

What would a law look like?

Jackley told News Watch that while the details of the potential legislation around license plate reading technology hasn’t been finalized, he has been in touch with police departments and lawmakers about how it could shape up.

Jackley said that there were several components to consider, including data retention policies, questions of access and how to ensure transparency with the public.

“I spoke to several chiefs, several sheriffs, states’ attorneys and will be addressing it with the state’s attorney board,” Jackley said. 

“We’ve had good conversations about it. I think we both have arrived at the (thought) that safeguards are a good idea to make sure what’s happened elsewhere doesn’t happen in our state. So when I look at safeguards, my perspective as the state’s attorney general, I would only want to see it where the local authorities desire to have that technology as part of public safety.”

Howell said during the Codington County Commission meeting that his office will wait until legislation is discussed during the 2027 legislative session to decide the fate of Flock cameras in the county.

“I don’t think it’s responsible to be spending more resources on this. The deputies have been spending a lot of time babysitting the cameras,” Howell said. “We’ve got cameras on cameras. At what point do you pull back and reevaluate the process here a little bit?”

Jackley said no specific abuse of ALPRs has yet occurred in South Dakota, but the legislation would be in place to prevent it. 

In other states, there have been crimes linked to the use of the technology – like in Florida, where a police officer was recently accused of using Flock camera data more than 700 times to stalk his ex-wife. That’s one of several similar cases across the country, which has raised concerns nationwide about citizen safety and the potential for unwanted surveillance.

Legislation in 16 other states includes policies as strict as Arkansas, which entirely bans the use of ALPRs for any non-law enforcement entities, and others states that regulate who has access to the data, like Maryland.

Jackley said that because of resident concerns about privacy, transparency measures that would allow the public to understand how the system is being used may also be a part of the legislation.

“It would be like, what is generally being searched for and how many times? When was it utilized? There is a challenge with that in a sense, though, that there are several companies out there. And because this has really been left to the local jurisdictions, they utilize different companies, and so they have different levels of ability to provide that transparency,” Jackley said.
