title: Are there Flock cameras in your community?
byline: By Sierra Ferguson Black Hills Pioneer
description: Flock Security is a leading producer of advanced license plate reader (ALPR) technology and camera systems. A Flock camera is pictured here. Photo courtesy Flock Security
_full_text:
Flock Camera 1.jpg
Flock Security is a leading producer of advanced license plate reader (ALPR) technology and camera systems. A Flock camera is pictured here. Photo courtesy Flock Security 

 Communities split on automatic license plate readers (Flock cameras)
Some local law enforcement agencies in South Dakota are pulling back on the use of Flock cameras, and the state attorney general is drafting legislation that would put limits on their use in the state. 

SPEARFISH — After a 15-year-old Sundance girl was abducted on Monday, authorities used automated license plate reader (ALPR) technology to quickly locate her and apprehend the suspect, according to Attorney General Marty Jackley. 

Cutting edge ALPR technology uses both artificial intelligence, a nation-wide network of cameras, and surveillance capable of recording vehicle sightings in specific places and times, reading license plates and noting the make, model, and distinguishing features of a vehicle to help law enforcement apprehend suspects and gather evidence — sometimes across state lines. Flock Safety, a company founded in 2017, has harnessed that technology to great effect. According to Flock, more than 5,000 cities use their products to solve approximately 2,000 crimes a day. The systems do not use facial recognition, but they deliver alerts to law enforcement agencies in their network based on “vehicle specific data.” 

On Monday, the youth sexual abduction suspect was stopped on I-90 near the Aurora County Line, east of Plankinton — one hour after state authorities were first notified of the crime, according to the South Dakota Attorney General’s Office. Authorities had suspected that 36-year-old suspect, Dalton Renollet of Maricopa, Ariz., was headed back to Arizona with the victim, until ALPR cameras located him in South Dakota. 

Renollet has been charged with one count of sexual contact with a minor in Aurora County. 

“A 15-year-old abducted and traumatized girl has been brought to safety by the excellent work of law enforcement. This incident demonstrates how valuable technology can be in protecting the public and assisting officers to locate a vulnerable juvenile and bring her to safety within an hour,” said Jackley.  “I remain committed to strict safeguards and oversight to ensure this technology protects the public from serious crimes with strong protections in place to safeguard personal privacy.”

Jackley has announced plans to propose legislation to ensure that ALPR technology is used appropriately. 

Four years ago, the state Department of Criminal Investigation (DCI) installed a Flock camera in Belle Fourche along Highway 85. Belle Fourche Police Chief Ryan Cherveny said DCI tested both a Flock camera and a Motorola camera to see which technology would work best. The camera has since been moved. 

 Flock Camera 2.jpg
Photo courtesy Flock Security 

Locally, the Sturgis, Spearfish, Deadwood, and Belle Fourche Police departments do not use Flock cameras; however they do use surveillance cameras in certain locations.

 In August, the Belle Fourche Police Department issued a statement to address public questions about the city’s surveillance cameras. 

“The cameras operated by the city of Belle Fourche and the Belle Fourche Police Department are not part of the Flock camera system or any national network,” according to the Aug. 8 statement. 

Pull quote
“It is a very valuable tool. It is just one that has to have the right structures in place.” — Ryan Cherveny, Belle Fourche Police Chief

The cameras the city uses come from Verkada Security Systems. They do use ALPR technology. 

“We looked into Flock a few years ago. At the time DCI was also looking at Flock,” Cherveny told the Pioneer. “We had already started with Verkata in city hall, and there is a local IT guy who is trained on maintenance and repairs.” Verkata had a more cost efficient system. 

The city’s surveillance cameras are set up in parks, buildings, and “a small number of roadway locations where most traffic crashes and complaints occur.” They are not linked to any outside system and are not able to share data on any national or state networks. 

Police officers can pull up the footage from those cameras to investigate specific incidents or determine a subject’s direction of travel. 

Those cameras are not monitored 24/7, and unlike Flock cameras, do not allow other agencies inherent access to location information. 

“We aren’t tied in with any other programs,” Cherveny said. “Ours is in-house.” 

Cherveny said law enforcement partners can ask for information, and provide a reason. Officers are able to review footage, but they can’t perform license plate searches to track a subject’s movement without the presence of a supervisor and a call for service number that links the documented search to a case. Those checks and balances are important, Cherveny said, especially given the proven uses the cameras have. He said those measures protect privacy and keep officers safe. 

Cherveny said the cameras in city parks have reduced vandalism by “almost 100%.”

The police chief said, “They have saved a ton of money for public works.” The small number of vandalism cases that have occurred recently have been solved using surveillance footage, Cherveny said. 

He said last year, after the Exit 8 gas station in Spearfish and the St. Onge bar were both victims of break-ins, a suspect was apprehended in Belle Fourche after they drove by one of the city’s parks. 

According to court documents, surveillance cameras provided critical evidence that helped identify the suspects involved in an assault in Jones Park in April 2025. The victim was beaten, robbed, and kicked in the head “soccer style” by a group of young men. Much of the attack was captured on surveillance footage. 

“That is the purpose of this technology. To catch criminal activity,” Cherveny said. “We have solved assaults, including 2 sexual assaults this year alone using this technology.” 

Just one week after the Verkada cameras were installed, Cherveney said they were used to help identify a vehicle that was being used in a kidnapping. Preliminary reports from other law enforcement agencies had officers looking for a pickup truck. Using a combination of telephone tracking technology and the cameras in Belle Fourche, officers were able to determine that the vehicle was an SUV not a pickup, to stop that SUV, and safely return the child to their family. 

“We never would have known which vehicle it was without capturing the plate.” 

The cameras are regularly used to locate missing children who may have gotten off their school bus at the wrong stop, or adults with dementia who have gotten lost in the community. 

 “This technology is one of the greatest assets to law enforcement for finding missing people,” Cherveny said. 

Deadwood does use license plate reading cameras on its parking ramp to determine who has, and has not, paid for parking. The cameras can also be used to determine if vehicles are damaged before or after they enter the parking lot — to help address any incidents that might happen in the parking structure. 

Deadwood Police Chief Cory Shafer said there is a distinct difference between Flock cameras and the basic license plate readers that are used on the parking ramp. 

“It’s intent and capabilities are not that of a Flock camera,” Shafer said. The camera does not collect identifying details, and does not connect to any larger network for data sharing. 

At this time, Shafer said, the department is not looking at acquiring more advanced ALPR cameras. 

“ALPRs are not new, but Flock is new and there are a lot of unknowns that come with that technology,” Shafer said. “It is OK to sit back and not make decisions about technology like this until we know more.” 

Deadwood is a high-traffic area — tourists visit from all corners of the country. Using technology like Flock cameras could help catch criminals from other jurisdictions Shafer said. But, with the positive possibilities are growing privacy concerns and fears about over-surveillance and misuse. 

Sturgis Police Chief Geody VanDewater noted that there have already been examples of officers abusing the technology — cases he said, “unfortunately give both the technology and law enforcement a bad name.”

 A Kentucky police officer was arrested after allegedly tracking his ex-girlfriend using Flock cameras. A Georgia police chief was arrested for allegedly using the technology to stalk and harass multiple people. 

“They have their place in our society,” VanDewater said of advanced ALPR technology. “And there are more positives than negatives,” while noting safeguards must be put in place to prevent misuse. 

He said the attorney general’s office helped shed light on the positive use of the cameras by issuing a statement on the abduction this week and it’s outcome. 

“I bet the victim (of that crime) is happy about this technology,” Shafer noted, while maintaining a balanced tone and clarifying that there are no plans to implement Flock or Flock-style cameras in the near future in Deadwood. 

Sturgis does not use ALPR technology. 

“The department has contemplated using them,” VanDewater said, “But the cost is a barrier. That money is needed to keep up on our current equipment.”  

Spearfish does not use ALPR technology, but Police Chief Collin Smith did not rule out acquiring them in the future.  

“The Spearfish Police Department will continually evaluate all new technologies that may assist in protecting and serving the public,” Smith said. 

The city council recently approved the purchase of new security cameras for the rec center and the police department that will allow remote access — a measure Smith said will help with the public safety answer point (PSAP) consolidation the city and Lawrence County are working toward. The 2 public safety agencies are hoping to merge resources and run dispatch and 911 answering services out of the county’s new public safety and services center on Tatanka Drive in Deadwood. 

“With the consolidation of the PSAP this new system will allow the telecommunicators to monitor the activity at city hall and within the police department 24/7,”Smith said. “This is currently being done by Spearfish PD communications officers so allowing them to continue to perform this while being stationed at the Lawrence County Sheriff Office is essential for the safety and security of our facilities, staff, and citizens.”

That system has little in common with Flock or ALPR cameras — those cameras are used strictly for routine surveillance. 

“It is a very valuable tool. It is just one that has to have the right structures in place,” Cherveny said. He also said that cellphones offer much more surveillance than Verkada or even Flock cameras can. He said officers can see learn more about a person in 5 minutes based on the contents of their phone than they can from surveillance footage.

title: Lawrence Co. treasurer:  Wells Fargo tax letters sent in error
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Deb Tridle, Lawrence County treasurer, said Wells Fargo sent letters in error telling customers with home loans the county was no longer sending the bank individual tax bills for special assessments. Tridle said business should continue as normal. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
20260904_094010.jpg
Deb Tridle, Lawrence County treasurer, said Wells Fargo sent letters in error telling customers with home loans the county was no longer sending the bank individual tax bills for special assessments. Tridle said business should continue as normal. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

DEADWOOD —Lawrence County Treasurer Deb Tridle estimates that between 200-300 residents received letters from Wells Fargo, falsely claiming her office was withholding real estate tax bills for special assessments, informing property owners they would be responsible for making their own payments to the county. 

Residents of Lawrence County with home loans from Wells Fargo received letters claiming the county was refusing to send the bank their special assessment bill. 

“Since your taxing authority won’t give us a bill any longer, we’ve removed these taxes from your escrow account. This means you will pay this bill yourself going forward,” claimed the letter reviewed by the Black Hills Pioneer. “It’s important that you contact your taxing authority to let them know to send you all future bills. This will help ensure you won’t miss a due date or be charged any penalties.” 

Tridle said when her office started receiving calls asking about the letters, she thought it was a routine scam. 

“Once we started getting more calls and we started digging into it, we realized it was all Wells Fargo customers that got those letters,” she said. “So, I reached out to the third party, CoreLogic, to see if they’d heard anything because they collect the money for Wells Fargo. I did try to get ahold of somebody at Wells Fargo, but ultimately it was CoreLogic that got to the bottom of it with me.”

Tridle said 2 years ago, Wells Fargo partnered with CoreLogic, of Irvine, Calif., to collect escrow payments for home loans. The company recently rebranded as Cotality, but still operates with the county as CoreLogic.

Before now, Tridle said her office has worked with CoreLogic and Wells Fargo without any problems.

“When I send my files to Wells Fargo or CoreLogic, I send one file that’s all special assessments with the parcel numbers and the real property taxes,” said Tridle. “Then, they pick their customers by parcel numbers that are corresponding to each other, and they give me the total of those 2 and they mail them to me. They’ll send me 2 files back via email, and I process them to make sure there’s no errors. I run the special assessment file first and then I run the real property second.”

Tridle said special assessments can consist of road district fees, properties with front footage, or delinquent fees imposed by cities. The fees for special assessments vary drastically, running from $30-2,800, and must be paid before her office can collect real property taxes. 

“Special assessments aren’t split in half like real property taxes are. The special assessment is all one full payment,” she said. “They’re on a separate file and my system is only set up to allow me to move on to real property taxes after specials are paid.”

Historically, Tridle said she’s received payments of approximately $6.5 million per tax payment cycle from CoreLogic. 

“That includes the property taxes as a whole, the county, the city, the schools, everything,” she said. “It all comes in in one payment, and then on the 15th of each month the auditor’s office distributes the portions that go to the cities and the schools and different entities.”

Tridle said that process has been uninterrupted.

Tridle said some customers had also received refunds from their escrow accounts.

“After checking with some people and with CoreLogic, I found that Wells Fargo was auditing their escrow accounts and they were holding too much money and they were sending some back,” she said. “I’ve told the people that had refund checks, they do need to check with Wells Fargo to make sure that they are supposed to have it and it didn’t short their escrow.”

After communicating with CoreLogic, Tridle and the representative were able to determine that the letters were sent out in error. She was informed that Wells Fargo would not be reaching out to its customers to send out a letter clarifying the mistake. In the meantime, she has personally called 47 concerned taxpayers to assure them that their special assessments are being paid as normal and encouraged them to check with their bank to ensure the status of their escrow account.

A message on the Lawrence County Treasurer’ website further clarifies that the letters were sent out in error, that taxes are being paid as normal, and concerned customers and taxpayers should check with Wells Fargo or call Tridle’s office. Callers reaching out to the treasurer’s office hear a similar message.

“I just want to clear up the message, so our customers aren’t concerned,” Tridle said. “I believe CoreLogic was also going to reach out to some customers to let them know, also, that everything has been taken care of and it has been updated. It’s just good customer service.”

In the spirit of ease and transparency, Tridle said her office is working with the director of equalization, who uses a software named Beacon that allows realtors and banks to log in and see a parcel’s assessment information.

“I’m trying to tag in with them. Brett (Runge, director of equalization) is helping me and trying to get me set up with Beacon,” said Tridle. “That way, my taxes will show up as an option on that program so people will be able to go in and look and see what their property taxes are and if they’ve been paid. It can help alleviate calls from banks and the lending agencies and lend peace of mind to people who want to check in on their property. Maybe they’re sitting down, trying to make a budget after hours, or they’re out of town and want to make sure their taxes got paid.”

Tridle said the software will require county commissioners to sign a contract and make a one-time payment of $4,400.

“I think it’s going to be an investment that’s going to be well used by the public,” she said.

The proposal to include the treasurer’s office in the software has not yet gone before the commission.

title: Grounded Car Show bringing ‘lower and louder’  vehicles to Sturgis Main Street Saturday
byline: By Tim Potts Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Grounded Car Show rolls into Sturgis on September 12th, Fresh Detailing owns this 2023 Nissan 400z and will be on display at the show on Main Street Sturgis. Photo by Aiden Shattuck visuals and Jakd media
_full_text:
Grounded Car Show bringing ‘lower and louder’ vehicles to Sturgis Main Street Saturday.jpg
The Grounded Car Show rolls into Sturgis on September 12th, Fresh Detailing owns this 2023 Nissan 400z and will be on display at the show on Main Street Sturgis. Photo by Aiden Shattuck visuals and Jakd media 

STURGIS — Downtown Sturgis will welcome a new kind of automotive gathering when the inaugural Grounded Car Show rolls onto Main Street Saturday.

The family-friendly event will run from 11 a.m. to 10 p.m., featuring lowered and customized vehicles, classics, trucks, motorcycles and other unique rides. Spectators can attend free of charge. 

Main Street will be closed giving participants room to display vehicles throughout the heart of downtown. Vendors, games and other activities will be centered around Rally Point.

“We want the car community as a whole,” organizer Ranni Boyd said. “There are all kinds of age groups and diverse people who want to be part of it.”

Boyd and her business partner Ian Zook, both Sturgis natives, created the event as a way to celebrate their hometown while bringing together automotive enthusiasts from across the Black Hills and beyond.

“We chose Sturgis because my business partner and I were both born and raised here,” Boyd said. “Downtown is iconic, and it seemed perfect for our style and what we are trying to do with the lowered vehicles and classics.”

The organizers hope the show will help expand the region’s car-show scene beyond Rapid City, where many smaller automotive gatherings are held.

“There is a large car community in Rapid City, and we wanted to spread that out,” Boyd said. “Since ours is a show with a lot more to it, we wanted to pick a unique location.”

The name “Grounded” reflects the organizers’ “lower and louder” theme and their interest in lowered vehicles. Boyd said the show will provide a positive setting where people can learn more about the style and meet those who are passionate about customizing their vehicles.

“If it’s scraping, then it’s low enough,” Boyd said with a laugh.

The idea developed from the organizers’ appreciation for lowered cars and a desire to introduce the style to a broader audience. Several members of their friend group own lowered vehicles and wanted to create an event where those cars could be displayed alongside many other types of vehicles.

In addition to the vehicle displays, the Grounded Car Show will include awards in several classifications. Spectators and participants will be able to vote online for their favorite vehicle, which will determine the top three people’s choice awards. The organizers will judge the categories that include pickups, mini trucks, motorcycles, classics, and cars, with a score sheet at the end. Category winners as well as the top three vehicles will receive awards.

A Grounded merchandise and information tent at Rally Point will offer apparel, stickers, website links and information from event sponsors. Games and other activities are also planned in the Rally Point area.

The show is designed as an all-ages event, and no open containers will be permitted within the event area. Downtown restaurants, bars and businesses will remain conveniently located near the festivities.

“Spectators are free, everyone is welcome and it is appropriate for kids,” Boyd said. “We want people to come downtown, see the vehicles and enjoy the show.”

Vehicle registration costs $20 in advance or $30 on the day of the event. A small processing fee may apply to credit-card payments.

Organizers hope the inaugural show will bring new visitors downtown, support Sturgis businesses and create a welcoming gathering for anyone who appreciates cars, trucks, motorcycles and automotive creativity.

title: Scams, Scams, and More Scams free public presentation in Lead to protect consumers
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: LEAD — A young adult who was preparing to purchase their first home is now out $95,000, after falling victim to a convincing email scam.
_full_text:
BHPioneerLogo

LEAD — A young adult who was preparing to purchase their first home is now out $95,000, after falling victim to a convincing email scam. 

Jody Gillaspie, from the South Dakota Attorney General’s Office of Consumer Protection, said she is currently working with the victim, who sent what he thought was a down payment on a home to an email address that appeared to be from the mortgage company. 

“There were several ‘red flags’ that were identified with this one,” Gillaspie said. “Unfortunately, the scammers know how to disguise the email address, because they’ve gained access to one of the parties’ systems. Because of this, the scammer knew where the consumer was at with his real estate transaction. Scammers know how to push the buttons of urgency in order to get the consumer to send the funds in the manner that the scammer is requesting.” 

Gillaspie said unfortunately the case is one of many that her office investigates. At 6 p.m., Sept. 10, Gillaspie will present Scams, Scams, and More Scams at the Historic Homestake Opera House, to try and help raise awareness about scams and what can be done to prevent them. The event is sponsored by the Lead-Deadwood Kiwanis Club and the Lead Police Department, and will be free to the public.

“From phishing emails to financial fraud, scams are becoming more sophisticated and more targeted, especially in rural and aging communities like our own,” the promotional flier states. “In this presentation, Jody will highlight the most prevalent scams impacting South Dakotans today. She’ll share real-world examples, red flags to watch for, and actionable tips. Learn how to stay informed, stay alert, and safeguard your community from financial exploitation.” 

Gillaspie said during her presentation she will discuss the latest scams her office has been seeing, and ways to combat them. She will also discuss identity theft, the importance of checking credit reports, and the pros and cons of placing freezes on credit information. 

The presentation is scheduled for an hour, but Gillaspie, who has 14 years of experience in the field, said she will stay as long as necessary to answer everyone’s questions. 

“Providing knowledge to consumers is empowering for them,” she said. “It gives them a sense of preparedness and confidence, confidence that they will not fall victim to the scams.”

title: Meade Co. study shows cost savings for new road material
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Meade County roads crews are saving substantial amount of money by using new products. Courtesy photos
_full_text:
Meade Co road improvements 1.JPG
Meade County roads crews are saving substantial amount of money by using new products. Courtesy photos 

STURGIS — A recent cost analysis of road improvements for the last few years shows that Meade County has saved substantial amounts of money using new products, Commissioner Rich Liggett reported Tuesday. 

 Meade Co road improvements best.JPG
Courtesy photo 

During the regular Meade County Commission meeting, Highway Commissioner Liggett reported results from a cost study he has been conducting on about 20 miles of road improvements for the last few years, when each road project has included a test section of base stabilization product to track gravel usage and maintenance needs. 

Using the base stabilization, Liggett said, is saving the county about $5,000 a year per mile of road, and about $112,000 a year, per mile, over a 7-year timeframe.  

“It seems like it doesn’t help, but in the long term we’re not losing gravel and we’re not spending blade hours,” Liggett said. 

Meade County Highway Superintendent Troy Eastman said the new base stabilization material is polymer based and it preserves the gravel so it does not blow away or leave the roadway. It is similar to paving, and reduces the need for blading maintenance or magnesium chloride water treatments. 

Moving forward, Eastman said future repairs on roads that have high traffic counts will include the new baseline stabilization treatments. 

“Gravel is what we were doing before, and we would do mag water on certain roads. The base stabilization lasts for years, whereas mag water can last a few months, depending on the weather,” Eastman said. “The base stabilization has a glue, a polymer to it, that doesn’t allow it to get diluted and leave the roadway. It just stays right where you put it.” 

Additional savings for the product are in labor costs, and safety improvements, as Eastman said his crews don’t have to spend as much time blading the roads that have the base stabilization. 

“I’m a big fan of it,” Eastman said. “It has reduced the amount of maintenance on the roads that have such high traffic, to allow us to work on other roads. Overall it’s gonna help the county, and it definitely saves money.”

title: Lookout Mountain fire spreads to 300+ acres
description: SPEARFISH - A wildfire has burned a significant portion of Lookout Mountain.

SPEARFISH - A wildfire has burned a significant portion of Lookout Mountain. 

The fire resource app Watch Duty indicates that  the fire has burned an approximate 300 acres. 

On Sunday evening, a semi truck carrying a load of hay caught fire. Fire crews worked to extinguish that fire. 

Earlier today, fire crews were called back to the scene as the hay caught fire again. It appears as if the fire spread from the interstate to the northwestern parts of Lookout Mountain. 

The fire spread through the norther slopes but was stopped before it reached Kerwin Lane. 

Fire crews could be seen high on the mountain presumably for structure protection. 

Shifting winds took the fire back down to the interstate where a Type 1 helicopter dropped loads of water, at one point hitting firefighters on the shoulder of the road with water. 

Numerous large air tankers dropped loads of slurry on the fire. 

Later this evening, fire crews could be seen starting back fires along the interstate.

title: Lookout Fire mapped at 443 acres
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: SPEARFISH — The Lookout Fire has burned approximately 443 acres, and is 0% contained as of Tuesday morning.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — The Lookout Fire has burned approximately 443 acres, and is 0% contained as of Tuesday morning. 

Forward progress on the north end of the fire has been stopped as of Tuesday morning, as firefighters continue working to hold the south fire line.

Steve Long, information officer for the state Department of Public Safety, said a drone mapped the fire this morning. 

“We don’t have any containment on the fire yet. We are continuing to reinforce lines. And establish control lines around the fire,” said Cody Griffee, incident commander and South Dakota wildland firefighter. “Right now there are areas of concern, there are no mandatory evacuations in place, but crews are in those areas reinforcing the line, make sure that is not going to progress any further.”

The main summit and its ridge appeared to be untouched by the flames; firefighters contained the fire to the northwest summit ridge. The fire stopped in a saddle between the 2 summits. A heavy line of slurry was visible in that saddle. 

As of 10:30 a.m. Tuesday, there were about 150 people fighting the fire, and more wildland crews dispatched to provide ground support.

According to a statement from incident command, crews remained on site overnight. 

“The objective today is to keep the fire in its current footprint thereby lessening threat to the line. Specific objectives include keeping the fire south of Kerwin Lane, north of Lookout Peak, east of Interstate 90, and west of Lookout Mountain Lane,” the incident command statement said. 

“One of Spearfish’s wonderful assets is Lookout Mountain. The fire incident on Lookout is certainly our current highest priority amongst city staff, local fire officials, volunteer firefighters, and elected officials,” said Spearfish Mayor John Senden. “The state of South Dakota Wildland Fire is currently in charge as the incident command for firefighting efforts. There will be close monitoring of hot spots around the clock for the next 48 hours and beyond as determined by the people involved with incident command.”

Griffee said South Dakota Wildland Fire established incident command Monday, and upgraded the incident to Type 3 Tuesday morning. 

On Sunday, shortly before 7 p.m., according to the South Dakota Highway Patrol, a 2005 freightliner semi-truck was hauling hay in the westbound lanes on Interstate 90, near mile marker 11, when smoke was observed coming from the hay. After the truck was pulled over by the Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office, the hay became fully engulfed in flames. The driver safely exited the vehicle. No one was injured.

The westbound driving lanes were closed for approximately 2 and a half hours while the Spearfish Fire Department put out the fire.

Fire crews returned to the fire Monday morning after the hay ignited again.

It was not immediately known what time that was. 

“The investigation and reporting on timing of events will come from fire officials when they can focus on releasing accurate information but as for now the main focus is control of hot spots and preventing any further spreading of the fire and damaged area. The mild wind conditions from Monday evening into the morning hours Tuesday have helped keep the fire in check,” Senden said.  

Around 2:45 p.m., the fire spread from the hay pile and traveled north over the edge of Lookout Mountain toward Kerwin Lane.

With the region in extreme fire danger conditions, the blaze moved quickly in the grass, spreading north and east.

Fire crews worked the flanks of the fire stopping the northern progress well short of Kerwin Lane. 

Crews could be seen high on the northeastern slopes of the mountain, presumably for structure protection. They also worked the western face to ensure the fire did not jump Interstate 90. 

Six large air tankers, one very large air tanker, and at least one Type 1 helicopter dropped loads of fire retardant and water on the fire.  

At one point Monday evening, the helicopter providing fireline protection along the interstate, doused firefighters and vehicles with water.

“We used a lot of aircraft to stop the forward progress and protect homes,” Griffee told the Pioneer Tuesday. “Then … last night we did some burnout operations, put in a lot of dozer and road grader lines, and we are continuing to reinforce certain areas we built yesterday.”

Late Monday, crews could be seen lighting backfires with drip torches and then shooting, what appeared to be flares.

On Tuesday morning, the red slurry could be seen on the interstate from drops close to the road. 

“The helicopter was from nearby stock ponds and the creek. He would drop his tank, he would head over and get more. He was just on a continuous cycle,” Griffee said. “2 of them came in from Rapid City. Others came in from surrounding areas — Colorado and Montana. They were reloading fire retardant from Rapid City airport.”

There is a temporary flight restriction over the perimeter of the Lookout Fire. No planes or drones that are not connected to fire fighting operations are allowed in the airspace around the fire area. 

On Tuesday, firefighters faced warm and dry conditions, with a high temperature near 80 degrees and humidity dropping to 20% or below the forecast for the fire area. Wind gust of 25 miles per hour were expected throughout the day. Still, Griffee said, there are reasons to remain optimistic. 

“Today is a bit more favorable. We had stronger, gustier winds yesterday. Winds are still a big threat, unfortunately. We’ve been so hot and dry that things will continue to be an effort,” Griffee said. “Everything’s looking really good today. Yesterday we had some extreme fire behavior, and luckily things kind of went in our favor.”

Traffic is closed in one lane on I-90 westbound between mile markers 10 and 12. 

By noon, hay spread on the shoulder between those mile markers was smoking, and several spots along the ridge to the north saw the renewed rise of columns of smoke in the afternoon. 

Kerwin Lane and Highway 85, Kerwin Lane and Lookout Road, and Lookout Mountain Road and Airport Road are also closed to through traffic. The public is asked to avoid the area due to ongoing active fire suppression activity including personnel and equipment.

The Spearfish Police Department is asking residents to avoid calling 9-1-1 unless they are experiencing an emergency. They ask the community not to call the emergency number to ask for fire information. 

The Pioneer will update this story as more information comes available.

title: Lithium ion batteries possible cause  of fire at BF landfill
byline: By Wendy Pitlick Black Hills Pioneer
description: Fire crews quickly extinguished a small fire at the Belle Fourche landfill, Monday.
_full_text:
Belle Fourche landfill .jpg
Fire crews quickly extinguished a small fire at the Belle Fourche landfill, Monday.  

BELLE FOURCHE — Lithium ion batteries may have been the cause for a fire at the Belle Fourche landfill, Monday. 

Belle Fourche City Administrator Jason LaFayette said Tuesday that the fire started at about 5:30 p.m. in a hole that crews have been working to fill. He said the cause could have either been a lithium ion battery, or a reflective item that heated up with the sun. 

Shawn Gallagher, manager of the Belle Fourche landfill, said the fire burned about an acre. Burning tires in the area caused heavy black smoke, as crews from the Butte County Fire Department, Belle Fourche Volunteer Fire Department, and the Nisland-Arpan Fire Department worked to extinguish the flames. Fire crews providing material aid to the Lookout Fire were released to respond to the landfill fire. 

“It wasn’t very big,” LaFayette said. “There was just a lot of smoke. Within a half hour of the fire starting they had water on it and the black smoke cleared up.” 

On Monday evening the Belle Fourche Police Department posted a public notice about safely disposing lithium ion batteries. 

“Lithium ion batteries discarded in household trash or at the landfill can ignite when crushed or damaged,” according to the statement. “Please do not place lithium batteries, vape devices, power tool packs, laptops, or similar items I nteh garbage.” 

The statement instructs consumers to tape the terminals of the batteries with electrical tape, and to place each battery in a separate plastic bag. Lithium ion batteries can only be disposed of at a battery recycling location, a participating retailer, or a household hazardous waste collection site. The Belle Fourche landfill accepts the batteries, but they have to be declared with a load so the batteries can be disposed of in the proper place. The batteries should never be placed in household garbage. 

Gallagher said Monday’s fire marked the seventh time the fire department has been called to the landfill since he started in January 2024, but there have been about 30-40 other fires that landfill crews have extinguished on their own. Monday’s fire started after landfill hours, when crews were not on site to immediately respond.

title: Rhoden, Ahlers both slam Trump on beef imports but clash on other debate topics
byline: By Joshua Haiar Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: South Dakota’s candidates for governor, Democratic nominee Dan Ahlers, left, and Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden chat with attendees at the South Dakota State Fair in Huron on Saturday. Photos by Joshua Haiar, South Dakota Searchlight
_full_text:
Untitled-1
South Dakota’s candidates for governor, Democratic nominee Dan Ahlers, left, and Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden chat with attendees at the South Dakota State Fair in Huron on Saturday. Photos by Joshua Haiar, South Dakota Searchlight 

HURON — Republican Gov. Larry Rhoden and Democratic challenger Dan Ahlers both criticized President Donald Trump Saturday during a debate at the South Dakota State Fair, with Rhoden saying he agrees with Trump on other issues but could not support the president’s decision to import more foreign beef.

“I thought he was wrongheaded in his logic, and the things that came out of that administration trying to defend it, I think, were weak,” Rhoden said.

Trump endorsed Rhoden last month. Rhoden said he plans to press U.S. Secretary of Agriculture Brooke Rollins to create an advisory committee so Trump has better information “before he makes decisions like that and then gets in front of a microphone.”

“He’s kind of an impulsive guy,” Rhoden said.

Trump announced last month that he would pause tariffs on imported beef, which he said would bring prices down for consumers and allow U.S. ranchers to build up their herds from historically low levels. The backlash from U.S. cattle ranchers was swift.

Ahlers said the announcement was not the first time the Trump administration suggested importing more foreign beef, and Ahlers said the state has to be “a stronger advocate for our farmers and ranchers.” He said that means working with South Dakota’s congressional delegation to apply more pressure on Trump.

The 2 candidates disagreed on several other issues during the debate, which was their first since each of them won their respective party’s nomination. The debate was hosted on the fair’s Freedom Stage by the South Dakota Farmers Union.

Economic development spending

Ahlers said the governor’s economic development office has favored recruiting out-of-state companies over funding homegrown ventures. He said a Wakonda hemp producer built a hemp-based concrete plant in another state after failing to secure incentives to build it in South Dakota.

“Those are companies that are in our hometowns, that make our hometowns better, that pay better, and have people that invest right back here in South Dakota,” Ahlers said.

Rhoden said roughly 85% of the office’s economic development dollars stay in South Dakota. He said the department supported the 3 largest economic development projects in state history during the past several years: the Smithfield pork plant being relocated from downtown to northern Sioux Falls, CJ Schwan’s breaking ground in that city on a food production plant, and a new soybean crushing plant in Mitchell.

“We do a lot to promote ag,” Rhoden said.

On Medicaid expansion

A state constitutional amendment placed on the Nov. 3 ballot by the Legislature would repeal the requirement to offer expanded Medicaid eligibility if federal funding for it drops below 90%.

Medicaid is a federal-state health insurance program for people with low incomes. In 2022, South Dakota voters expanded Medicaid eligibility from traditional coverage groups such as children, disabled people and the elderly to adults with incomes up to 138% of the poverty level. About 31,000 South Dakotans are enrolled through the expansion, out of a total of about 143,000 South Dakotans enrolled in Medicaid, according to data from the state Department of Social Services.

Ahlers said that after voters approved Medicaid expansion, Republican lawmakers are trying to undo the people’s will. He warned that rolling back Medicaid eligibility would threaten the financial viability of rural hospitals, maternity units and emergency rooms. He noted a majority of Medicaid recipients are children.

“We know that when we have healthcare, and everyone has access to it, we all do better,” Ahlers said.

Rhoden said the ballot measure would only remove the requirement to continue with expanded eligibility if federal funding drops below 90%. He opposed expansion, he said, over concerns about the federal government one day pulling funding.

“When we have $40 trillion in debt in our nation, you can bet the feds are going to be kicking that down to the states,” Rhoden said.

Separating ag and environment departments

Former Gov. Kristi Noem merged the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Environment and Natural Resources by executive order, creating the Department of Agriculture and Natural Resources.

Ahlers said he would restore a standalone Department of Agriculture with its own secretary.

“These 2 departments have different missions, although they do work together on projects,” Ahlers said. “It is important that each has their own voice and a seat at the table.”

Rhoden defended the merger, saying criticisms that it supported agriculture at the expense of environmental protection were unfair.

“Nobody on the planet has a more vested interest in protecting our environment and our natural resources, and the sustainability of our ag land, than the people that are producing on that ag land,” Rhoden said.

Rhoden, of rural Union Center, has been governor since early 2025, when he was elevated from lieutenant governor after then-Gov. Noem resigned to take a job in the Trump administration. Ahlers is a businessman and former legislator from Dell Rapids.

The 2 candidates will face each other in the general election Nov. 3. Advance voting begins Sept. 18, and the voter registration deadline is Oct. 19.

title: Lawrence Co. approves 5-year  highway plan, outlining projects,  structures, and equipment purchases
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: The Lawrence County Highway Department presented a 5-year highway plan, outlining gravel and pavement projects, structure replacement and repairs, and equipment purchases. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan
_full_text:
LawrenceCountyHighway.jpg
The Lawrence County Highway Department presented a 5-year highway plan, outlining gravel and pavement projects, structure replacement and repairs, and equipment purchases. Pioneer photo by Sara Morgan 

DEADWOOD — To improve chances of receiving state and federal grants, establish budgets, and plan for bridge and highway projects, Lawrence County Commissioners approved a 5-year road, bridge, and equipment purchasing plan. 

John Bey, highway superintendent, said the plan does not cement a 5-year itinerary for the department. Instead, the plan is created with the intention of improving chances of receiving state and federal grants, particularly for projects set more than 2 years in the future. 

“The state requires that we submit a 5-year road and bridge plan, and this is to be eligible for any grants, namely the BIG grant (Bridge Improvement Grant),” said Bey. “A couple of the requirements for the 5-year plan is that we have the county implement a wheel tax, which we have, and adopt the 5-year road and bridge improvement plan. That plan is exactly what it says — it’s merely a plan. It’s not written in stone, it’s not a requirement. It’s a budgeting tool to put in order what structures or what projects we’re going to do in what time frame.”

Bey warned that budgets listed on the plan are estimations of inflation and material costs.

Every year, Bey said the department plans to re-gravel 205 miles of roads, treat 121.5 miles of road with magnesium chloride, and restripe 85 miles of pavement. Additionally, he said the county will attempt to chipseal and fogseal approximately 10 miles of road every year, but those goals are limited by budget. 

Upcoming gravel, paving, and structure projects

In 2027 and 2028, a project to repave and resurface Nemo Road continues with a 3.63-mile section from Hay Creek Lane to the junction of US Highway 385, amounting to approximately $1.7 million, and similar work and channel stabilization to an approximately 0.3-mile section north of Waterwheel Lane, estimated to cost approximately $1.25 million.  

Work over the next 2 years on Nemo Road will include the replacement of 2 structures. The project is being paid for in large part by a BIG grant, with the county responsible for 20% of the overall cost. 

In 2027, the department plans to chipseal and fogseal sections of Nemo Road, Brookview Road, Hillsview Road, East Oliver Street, Westview Drive, West Oliver, Mineral Place, Winterville, and Maitland Road. 

Bey said there is a slightly larger section of roads slated for chipseal and fogseal in 2027 as the department catches up with budget cuts made in 2026 to purchase new equipment.

In 2027, rout and crackseal projects include sections of Nemo Road and Crook City Road. 

The same year, Bey said the department hopes to be able to replace a structure on the Whitewood Service Road that has been delayed because of archaeological and environmental findings. He said the department is hopeful that the structure will go to bid in November. 

In 2028, the department plans to chipseal and fogseal sections of Nemo Road, Crook City Road, Whitewood Service Road, and Whitewood Valley Road. 

Rout and crackseal projects for 2028 include sections of Nemo Road and St. Onge Road.

If the department receives a BIG grant to replace a structure on West Highway 14, which Bey said he will apply for in 2027, work could begin in 2028.

In 2029, Bey said the Rural Access and Infrastructure Fund will sunset, giving him 2 years to use monies to replace qualifying structures or return the funds to the state. 

“We are eligible to use that fund on county secondary roads and for small structures only,” he said. “We don’t have very many that qualify, but we have a couple, and we have identified these 2 projects, and that would be a culver on the Lewie’s end of Kirk Road.”

Paving projects delayed

Plans to possibly pave 1.5 miles of Maitland Road from Christensen Drive to Forest Park, 1.44 miles of Hill Street and North Tinton Road, and 1.6 miles of McGuigan Road, have been pushed to 2031. 

“Just for clarification and transparency, I moved those 2 projects to the end of the list. They’ve been up further, and we just move them back,” Bey said. “It all depends on funding. Just because it’s on this list does not mean it happens. It’s on the list, and it’s on the list for the reason if funding becomes available through the state, if we try to get a grant for any of these projects, it has to be on these pages.”

Equipment purchases

Over the next 5 years, the highway department has a budget of approximately $415,000 to purchase new equipment. 

In 2027, Bey said the department hopes to purchase a new truck and snow equipment. 

In 2028, the department plans to purchase a mini excavator, equipment trailer, and another truck.

“We moved a truck up because we recently lost a truck in an accident,” he said. “We also switched around a mini excavator with a motor. We don’t own a mini excavator at this time, but we see the value in owning one. We’ve been renting excavators a lot lately, and a mini would be a little bit smaller than we’ve been renting, but I believe it would be very beneficial for us to own one.”

Bey said purchases through the next five years are intended to stay on top of warranties, equipment usage, and replacement plans.

title: Minnesota man arrested in Deadwood stabbing incident, victim hospitalized in stable condition
byline: By Sara Morgan Black Hills Pioneer
description: Courtesy photo
_full_text:
Arrested
Courtesy photo 

DEADWOOD — A Minnesota man has been arrested and charged with attempted first degree murder and aggravated assault following a stabbing incident at 2:02 a.m. Sunday in Deadwood. 

Police Chief Cory Shafer said dispatch received a call reporting an altercation in the parking lot of Cadillac Jacks early Sunday morning. At 2:06 it was noted the suspect tried to flee the scene, but was located by police in the area of Whitewood Creek at 2:12 a.m.

Shafer said 20-year-old Preston Wolowicz has been charged for allegedly stabbing a 44-year-old Minnesota man approximately 4 times with a black handled knife. Shafer said the blade was sharp edged with a press-release function that expends the blade from the handle. Wolowicz was charged with aggravated assault, attempt to cause seriously bodily injury, a Class 3 felony, punishable by up to 15 years imprisonment and/or affine of $30,000, and attempted first-degree murder, a Class 2 felony punishable by up to 25 years imprisonment and/or a fine of $50,000.

The victim was immediately hospitalized and placed into critical care. Shafer said as of Tuesday morning, the victim is in stable condition but still hospitalized.

Shafer said it is believed that Wolowicz was intoxicated but has not received further charges as of Tuesday morning. 

“This report will still be reviewed by the state’s attorney’s office for any possible further charges,” said Shafer. “Officers believe that there was an odor of alcohol. How intoxicated he truly was, or if he truly was, is yet to be determined.”

Shafer said 9 first responders and officers responded to the scene, including Deadwood Monument Ambulance, Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office, and Deadwood Police Department’s detective and lieutenant. 

“At this point, the incident still remains under investigation,” said Shafer. “There are many more details to try to uncover, to verify, to get a better understanding of, but at this point I would like to share my gratitude towards the officers and first responders who responded to the incident and how they handled it so quickly and professionally. Everything from the situation at hand all the way to the evidence that was found and collected.”

The Pioneer will continue to report on the incident as more information becomes available.

title: Q&A: SD’s next attorney general aims to undo criminal justice reforms, just not right away
byline: By John Hult Southdakotasearchlight.com
description: Lance Russell will be South Dakota’s next attorney general whether you vote for him or not.
_full_text:
South Dakota’s next attorney general aims to undo criminal justice reforms, just not right away.jpg

Lance Russell will be South Dakota’s next attorney general whether you vote for him or not. 

At the Republican state convention in June, Russell earned the party’s nomination to seek the job of the state’s top law enforcement official, and its defense attorney when the state is sued.

Attorney general is among the statewide offices in South Dakota whose nominees are chosen by delegates at party conventions, not by voters in primary elections. The current attorney general, Republican Marty Jackley, is running for the U.S. House.

Russell is running unopposed to succeed Jackley in Nov. 3 general election. The South Dakota Democratic Party hasn’t nominated anyone to run for attorney general since 2018.

Russell, a Hot Springs native and 1999 graduate of the University of South Dakota School of Law, has spent more than half his career as the Fall River County state’s attorney, beginning soon after he passed the bar exam. He’s also the state’s attorney for neighboring Oglala Lakota County, which is part of the Oglala Sioux Tribe’s Pine Ridge Reservation. Russell prosecutes the cases in that county that fall under state jurisdiction.

From 2009-2020, he stepped away from the prosecutor job to serve four terms in the state House of Representatives and two in the state Senate. He was elected state’s attorney for Fall River County again in 2020 and 2024, and will leave two years early to assume the role of attorney general. 

Russell bested Austin Hoffman and John Fitzgerald at the state convention with a campaign focused on undoing some of the reforms to criminal justice he opposed during his time in Pierre. 

Those reforms, to the adult system in 2013 and the juvenile one in 2015, ushered in drug courts, a presumption of probation for low-level felonies and a host of other policies meant to hold down the state’s prison population without hurting public safety. 

Russell argues the reforms haven’t worked for the adult system — South Dakota is building two new prisons in spite of them — and says institutions like the now-defunct boot camp for teens in Custer did a better job helping juveniles change their ways than the alternatives now used for kids who break the law.

The following conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

You’ll be the first attorney general since Gordon Mydland, who led the office from 1969 to 1973, to have served in the Legislature. How do you think your years in Pierre will color your approach to the job?

The nice thing is that I have the perspective of the legislator. I understand how they’re perceiving their job, so I can articulate to them in a manner that they hopefully will understand. 

The other thing is that I got a front row seat to watch the attorney general’s work in the Legislature. Legislators have a number of ideas. Marty did a really nice job of getting together with the legislators, having a relationship with them. He could talk to them and help them with their legislation and make sure that it wasn’t unconstitutional or illegal in some fashion.

That’s one of the big issues for the attorney general’s staff, to make sure that they have good communication with lawmakers so that we’re not passing legislation that gets us into federal court and gets us enjoined for doing something stupid.

As attorney general, you will have a Missing and Murdered Indigenous People liaison position. What do you see your office doing on the MMIP issue?

They have someone that has quite a bit of experience (in Marlys Big Eagle), so I’m excited about that. It’s my understanding that we do, in fact, have a robust office that is working with the tribes to a large degree and trying to implement something very close to the Amber Alert (for missing Native Americans). I’m thankful for that, and yes, I will be an advocate for it.

How would you approach tribal relations, and what have you learned by serving as a prosecutor adjacent to the Pine Ridge Reservation?

I feel like I have worked cooperatively over the last 25 years with the Oglala Lakota County commissioners and the tribe, and that we’ve had a pretty good working relationship. So I’m hoping to put that into effect statewide so we don’t get ourselves into trouble and get banned from the tribe.

I think that, unfortunately, a lot of what happened with (former Gov.) Kristi Noem getting banned from the Indian reservations just had to do with a lot of not understanding the different jurisdictions and what the state’s jurisdiction actually is. Because if you realize that you have limited jurisdiction on the Indian reservation and understand the contours of it, I think it helps you talk to people in a manner that is constructive, respectful and non-threatening. If you just understand your role as the state, I think that helps dramatically.

You opposed criminal justice reform as a lawmaker back in 2013 and 2015, arguing that leaning on community supervision would backfire. You campaigned on the premise that it has. What problems do you see?

The effectiveness of our juvenile justice system between when I started and now is like night and day. It’s just not working. If you talk to people at the schools, you will get a real good education in how destructive it’s been for the school systems to have these delinquents, who are adjudicated as such, essentially being sent right back to school. The schools have had a very difficult time dealing with it. 

The system no longer works. We just don’t have the resources we used to have. I remember when I would have kids come into the system that were absolutely defiant to the judges. Then they would spend 60 or 90 days at the boot camp up there in Custer. They would come back, they would stand in front of the judge, and they would stand up straight. They’d look the judge in the eye. They would respond appropriately. Then they’d go back to the high school here in Hot Springs or in Edgemont, and they would graduate. It would be a success story. 

But these days, it just seems like we eventually have these kids just dropping out of school. They’re not being given the resources they need. We no longer have the boot camp now. We have to send a lot of the children that need help out of state because we don’t have adequate resources here.

What would you want to see changed during your term as attorney general? Would you want to bring back a boot camp?

Over the next four years, it’s my intention to try and reform the system, but it is going to be an enormous job. It’s not going to happen overnight. I know that the attorney general’s office has been working on legislation, and my intention this first year is to try and implement a lot of the things that Marty’s been working on, not have an ambitious reform package for myself. Give me a year to work to explain the problems to the legislators and to the governor’s office, and to try and build some consensus to bring some legislation in subsequent sessions to try and fix some of the problems. 

Quite frankly, that’s the reason I ran for attorney general. My job has become so much more difficult to do since I came back from the Legislature than it was before, and I knew that I couldn’t fix it from Hot Springs. 

I’m going to do my best over the next four years to get some reforms that I think make some sense for the people, for the taxpayers and the victims, and quite frankly, for the people that are coming through the system, so they have the tools they need when they’re released to go back into the community and be successful.

Drug courts and other specialty courts are often cited as successful outgrowths of criminal justice reform. Do you see the value in those?

Here in Fall River and Oglala Lakota County, we don’t have any of those courts. My understanding of how they work is all third-hand. I tend to think I just need to be more educated on what they do, because I haven’t had a lot of experience with them.

Do I think that they’re as effective as they were envisioned to be? Probably not. But I need to not be too critical because I haven’t interfaced with it myself personally.

In a smaller jurisdiction that hasn’t gotten a lot of those resources, almost all of my experience has been that (the reforms) have made the work much more difficult for everybody involved in the process.

Is there anything else in particular you’d like people to know as we approach your first term?

Marty Jackley has done a great job as attorney general, as far as I can see. I want to continue a lot of his programs. I do want to tweak the system and make it work better for the locals, but what I will tell you is that at the state level, I think that the Division of Criminal Investigation, the State Crime Lab, the entities that are under the attorney general, have been working very well. Frankly, I don’t feel like I could have a better situation going in.

title: Fire on Lookout Mountain mapped at 443 acres
byline: Pioneer staff reports
description: SPEARFISH — The Lookout Fire has burned approximately 443 acres as of Tuesday morning. There is no recorded containment.
_full_text:
SPEARFISH — The Lookout Fire has burned approximately 443 acres as of Tuesday morning. There is no recorded containment.

Steve Long, information officer for the state Department of Public Safety, said a drone was mapping the fire this morning. 

On Sunday, shortly before 7 p.m., according to the South Dakota Highway Patrol, a 2005 freightliner semi-truck was hauling hay in the westbound lanes on Interstate 90, near mile marker 11, when smoke was observed coming from the hay. After the truck was pulled over by the Lawrence County Sheriff’s Office, the hay became fully engulfed in flames. The driver safely exited the vehicle. No one was injured.

The westbound driving lanes were closed for approximately two and a half hours while the Spearfish Fire Department put out the fire.

Fire crews returned to the fire Monday morning after the hay ignited again.

It was not immediately known what time that was. 

Around 2:45 p.m., the fire spread from the hay pile and traveled north over the edge of Lookout Mountain toward Kerwin Lane.

With the region in extreme fire danger conditions, the blaze moved quickly in the grass, spreading north and east.

Fire crews worked the flanks of the fire stopping the northern progress well short of Kerwin Lane. 

Crews could be seen high on the northeastern slopes of the mountain, presumably for structure protection. They also worked the western face to ensure the fire did not jump Interstate 90.

Six large air tankers, one very large air tanker, and at least one Type 1 helicopter dropped loads of fire retardant and water on the fire.  At one point Monday evening, the helicopter providing fireline protection along the interstate, doused firefighters and vehicles with water.

On Tuesday morning, the red slurry could be seen on the interstate from drops close to the road. 

Late Monday, crews could be seen lighting backfires with drip torches and then shooting, what appeared to be flares.
